title: Social Bayesian Learning in the Wisdom of the Crowd
Abstract: Aggregating the beliefs of many individuals into a single belief is a fundamental problem in social, economic, and political processes like policy making, market pricing, and voting. While various models and mechanisms for aggregation exist, methods and literature for handling influence and learning between individuals are lacking. This gap is partly due to the limited models of belief updating when exposed to others' beliefs, making it challenging to quantify dependencies between mental models, crucial for minimizing aggregation redundancies. This paper explores models of user influence and learning, benchmarking them against the well-known DeGroot model. The contributions include: 1) a new dataset of unprecedented size and detail to be made publicly available, 2) a new Social Bayesian model for user mental model updating, and 3) a comparison of the Social Bayesian model with other social learning models. The Social Bayesian model is shown to outperform other models tested.
label: AI

title: Minimizing Polarization and Disagreement in Social Networks
Abstract: The rise of social media and online social networks has had a significant impact on society. Opinions are increasingly shaped by interactions on these platforms, leading to social phenomena like disagreement and polarization becoming prevalent in everyday life. This paper investigates the structure of social networks that minimize both polarization and disagreement simultaneously, given a set of agents with initial opinions reflecting their core values on a topic and an opinion dynamics model. This question is central to recommender systems, where a trade-off exists between promoting links between users with similar opinions to minimize disagreement and connecting users with different opinions to expose them to diverse viewpoints and reduce polarization. The paper formalizes this question as an optimization problem and presents an exact, time-efficient algorithm. It proves the existence of a network with O(n/ε²) edges that approximates the optimum within a factor of (1+ε). For a fixed graph, the paper shows how to optimize the objective function over the agents' innate opinions in polynomial time. An empirical study using synthetic and real-world data verifies the value of the proposed methods for understanding the trade-off between disagreement and polarization. Results show significant potential for reducing both in real-world networks. For instance, on a Reddit network discussing politics, the methods achieve a ~60,000-fold reduction in polarization and disagreement.
label: AI

title: Toward Continual Learning for Conversational Agents
Abstract: While end-to-end neural conversation models have made significant progress in reducing hand-crafted features and errors from traditional complex system architecture, they typically require vast amounts of data due to their lack of modularity. Previous studies have adopted a hybrid approach with knowledge-based components for extracting domain-specific information or augmenting data to cover diverse patterns. Conversely, this paper proposes a direct solution using recent advancements in continual learning for neural models. It employs a domain-independent neural conversational model and introduces a novel neural continual learning algorithm enabling a conversational agent to accumulate skills across different tasks efficiently. This is the first work to apply continual learning to conversation systems. The method's effectiveness is verified through conversational skill transfer from synthetic or human-human dialogs to human-computer conversations in a customer support domain.
label: AI

title: Gradient Regularization Improves Accuracy of Discriminative Models
Abstract: Regularizing the gradient norm of a neural network's output with respect to its inputs is a powerful technique that has been rediscovered multiple times. This paper provides evidence that gradient regularization consistently improves classification accuracy on vision tasks using modern deep neural networks, particularly when training data is limited. The paper introduces regularizers as part of a broader class of Jacobian-based regularizers. Empirical results on real and synthetic data demonstrate that the learning process leads to controlled gradients beyond training points, resulting in solutions that generalize well.
label: AI

title: On the Challenges of Detecting Rude Conversational Behaviour
Abstract: This study aims to identify moments of rudeness between two individuals in conversations. It categorizes occurrences of rudeness into three distinct categories and attempts to identify each category using machine learning algorithms. The study extracts acoustic and semantic signals from conversations for rudeness detection. It acknowledges the challenges and shortcomings in this task and highlights the inherent difficulty of the problem. The paper concludes by outlining future steps necessary for continued success in identifying rudeness in conversations.
label: AI

title: Rapid Adaptation with Conditionally Shifted Neurons
Abstract: This paper describes a mechanism called "conditionally shifted neurons" that enables artificial neural networks to learn rapid adaptation – the ability to adapt to new tasks on the fly with minimal data. This mechanism is implemented within the framework of metalearning, aiming to replicate human learning flexibility in machines. Conditionally shifted neurons adjust their activation values using task-specific shifts retrieved from a memory module populated quickly based on limited task experience. On metalearning benchmarks from vision and language domains, models augmented with conditionally shifted neurons achieve state-of-the-art results. |||

title: What do we need to build explainable AI systems for the medical domain?
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML), has achieved significant practical success in diverse domains, such as autonomous driving, speech recognition, and recommender systems. Deep learning approaches, trained on massive datasets or employing reinforcement learning methods, have even surpassed human performance in visual tasks, notably in games like Atari and Go. Remarkable results have also emerged in the medical field. However, these models are often regarded as black boxes, lacking an explicit knowledge representation despite understanding their underlying mathematical principles. This limitation hinders their ability to generate explanatory structures, creating a need for systems that make decisions transparent, understandable, and explainable. The increasing legal and privacy concerns, highlighted by the European General Data Protection Regulation, further necessitate transparency. While not requiring a complete explanation, the regulation demands the ability to retrace results upon request. This paper outlines research topics within the emerging field of explainable-AI, focusing on medical applications. The medical domain poses unique challenges due to the use of distributed, heterogeneous, and complex data sources. This paper concentrates on three sources: images, omics data, and text. We argue that research in explainable-AI would significantly facilitate the implementation of AI/ML in medicine, promoting transparency and building trust.
label: AI

title: Visualizing the Loss Landscape of Neural Nets
Abstract: Neural network training hinges on finding effective minimizers for highly non-convex loss functions. It is well-established that certain network architecture designs, such as skip connections, simplify training, and well-chosen training parameters (batch size, learning rate, optimizer) contribute to better generalization. However, the reasons behind these differences, and their impact on the underlying loss landscape, remain unclear. This paper investigates the structure of neural loss functions and their effect on generalization using a range of visualization methods. We introduce a simple "filter normalization" method that visualizes loss function curvature, enabling meaningful comparisons between loss functions. We then utilize various visualizations to explore how network architecture influences the loss landscape and how training parameters affect the shape of minimizers.
label: AI

title: Improved Inception-Residual Convolutional Neural Network for Object Recognition
Abstract: Machine learning and computer vision have driven significant advancements in the modeling of Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs). While research has primarily focused on enhancing recognition accuracy through improved DCNN models and learning approaches, the recurrent convolutional approach has seen limited adoption beyond a few DCNN architectures. Meanwhile, Inception-v4 and Residual networks have gained immense popularity within the computer vision community. This paper introduces a novel DCNN model, the Inception Recurrent Residual Convolutional Neural Network (IRRCNN), leveraging the strengths of Recurrent Convolutional Neural Networks (RCNN), Inception networks, and Residual networks. This approach improves the recognition accuracy of the Inception-residual network while maintaining the same number of network parameters. Furthermore, the proposed architecture generalizes Inception networks, RCNN, and Residual networks with significantly enhanced training accuracy. The IRRCNN model's performance was empirically evaluated on various benchmarks including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet-200, and CU3D-100. The experimental results demonstrate superior recognition accuracy compared to most popular DCNN models, including RCNN. We also examined the IRRCNN approach against its counterparts, the Equivalent Inception Network (EIN) and the Equivalent Inception Residual Network (EIRN), on the CIFAR-100 dataset. The IRRCNN achieved around 4.53%, 4.49%, and 3.56% improvement in classification accuracy compared to RCNN, EIN, and EIRN on the CIFAR-100 dataset, respectively. Moreover, experiments on TinyImageNet-200 and CU3D-100 datasets revealed that IRRCNN outperforms Inception Recurrent CNN (IRCNN), EIN, and EIRN in terms of testing accuracy.

title: Handwritten Bangla Character Recognition Using The State-of-Art Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: Despite advancements in object recognition technology, Handwritten Bangla Character Recognition (HBCR) remains largely unsolved due to the presence of many ambiguous handwritten characters and highly cursive Bangla scripts. Existing recognizers, even the most advanced ones, fail to achieve satisfactory performance for practical Bangla character recognition applications and significantly lag behind systems developed for English alpha-numeric characters. To improve HBCR performance, this paper presents the application of state-of-the-art Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), including VGG Network, All Convolution Network (All-Conv Net), Network in Network (NiN), Residual Network, FractalNet, and DenseNet, for HBCR. Deep learning approaches excel at extracting and utilizing feature information, improving the recognition of 2D shapes with high invariance to translation, scaling, and other distortions. We systematically evaluated the performance of DCNN models on a publicly available Bangla handwritten character dataset called CMATERdb, achieving superior recognition accuracy when using DCNN models. This improvement would contribute to the development of an automatic HBCR system for practical applications.

title: Connecting Software Metrics across Versions to Predict Defects
Abstract: Accurate software defect prediction can assist software practitioners in efficiently allocating test resources to defect-prone modules. In recent decades, significant effort has been devoted to building precise defect prediction models, including developing quality defect predictors and modeling techniques. However, commonly used defect predictors like code metrics and process metrics fail to adequately describe how software modules evolve throughout the project lifecycle, which we believe is crucial for defect prediction. To address this issue, this paper proposes utilizing the Historical Version Sequence of Metrics (HVSM) in continuous software versions as defect predictors. Furthermore, we leverage Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), a popular modeling technique, to utilize HVSM as input for building software prediction models. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed HVSM-based RNN model significantly surpasses the performance of commonly used baseline models in terms of effort-aware ranking effectiveness in most cases.

title: Accurate Bayesian Data Classification without Hyperparameter Cross-validation
Abstract: This paper extends the standard Bayesian multivariate Gaussian generative data classifier by considering a generalization of the conjugate, normal-Wishart prior distribution and deriving the hyperparameters analytically via evidence maximization. The behavior of the optimal hyperparameters is investigated in the high-dimensional data regime. The classification accuracy of the resulting generalized model is competitive with state-of-the-art Bayesian discriminant analysis methods but without the usual computational burden of cross-validation.

title: A Multi-Scale and Multi-Depth Convolutional Neural Network for Remote Sensing Imagery Pan-Sharpening
Abstract: Pan-sharpening, a fundamental task in remote sensing imagery processing, involves utilizing high-resolution spatial details from panchromatic images to enhance the spatial resolution of multi-spectral (MS) images. Inspired by the powerful representation of non-linear relationships by deep neural networks, this paper introduces multi-scale feature extraction and residual learning into the basic convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture and proposes the multi-scale and multi-depth convolutional neural network (MSDCNN) for pan-sharpening remote sensing imagery. Both quantitative and visual assessments confirm that the proposed network produces high-resolution MS images that surpass those generated by existing state-of-the-art methods.

title: Learning to Customize Network Security Rules
Abstract: Security is a major concern for organizations adopting cloud computing. To mitigate security vulnerabilities, public cloud providers offer firewall functionalities. Properly configured firewalls protect cloud networks from cyber-attacks. However, effective firewall configuration demands in-depth knowledge of the protected system, high expertise, and ongoing maintenance. As a result, many organizations fail to utilize firewalls effectively, leaving their cloud resources vulnerable. This paper presents a novel supervised learning method, along with a prototype, that generates recommendations for firewall rules. Recommendations are based on sampled network traffic meta-data (NetFlow) collected from a public cloud provider. Labels are extracted from firewall configurations deemed to be authored by experts. NetFlow is collected from network routers, avoiding expensive collection from cloud VMs and addressing privacy concerns. The proposed method captures network routines and dependencies between resources and firewall configuration. It predicts IPs to be allowed by the firewall. A subsequent grouping algorithm generates a manageable number of IP ranges, each representing a parameter for a firewall rule. Experiments on real data show a ROC AUC of 0.92, compared to 0.58 for an unsupervised baseline. These results validate the hypothesis that firewall rules can be automatically generated based on router data and demonstrate the effectiveness of an automated method in blocking a high percentage of malicious traffic.

title: Siamese LSTM based Fiber Structural Similarity Network (FS2Net) for Rotation Invariant Brain Tractography Segmentation
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel deep learning architecture combining stacked Bi-directional LSTM and LSTMs with the Siamese network architecture for segmenting brain fibers obtained from tractography data into anatomically meaningful clusters. The proposed network learns the structural differences between fibers of different classes, enabling highly accurate fiber classification. Importantly, capturing such deep inter and intra-class structural relationships ensures robust segmentation against relative rotations among test and training data, allowing its application to unregistered data. Extensive experimentation on hundreds of thousands of fibers demonstrates that the proposed model achieves state-of-the-art results, even in cases of significant relative rotations between test and training data.

title: Topic Compositional Neural Language Model
Abstract: This paper presents a Topic Compositional Neural Language Model (TCNLM), a novel method designed to simultaneously capture both the global semantic meaning and the local word ordering structure within a document. TCNLM learns the global semantic coherence of a document through a neural topic model. The probability of each learned latent topic is then used to build a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model, where each expert (corresponding to one topic) is a recurrent neural network (RNN) responsible for learning the local structure of a word sequence. To efficiently train the MoE model, a matrix factorization method is applied, extending each weight matrix of the RNN to be an ensemble of topic-dependent weight matrices. The degree to which each member of the ensemble is used is tied to the document-dependent probability of the corresponding topics. Experimental results across various corpora demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms both pure RNN-based models and other topic-guided language models. Furthermore, our model yields sensible topics and possesses the capability to generate meaningful sentences conditioned on given topics.

title: Mass and Age of Red Giant Branch Stars Observed with LAMOST and \emph{Kepler}
Abstract: Obtaining accurate and precise masses and ages for large numbers of giant stars is crucial for unraveling the assembly history of the Galaxy. This paper estimates masses and ages of 6940 red giant branch (RGB) stars using asteroseismic parameters derived from Kepler photometry and stellar atmospheric parameters obtained from LAMOST spectra. The typical uncertainties in mass are a few percent, while the uncertainty in age is approximately 20%. The sample stars reveal two distinct sequences in the age-[α/Fe] relation—a high-α sequence with stars older than approximately 8 Gyr and a low-α sequence comprising stars with ages ranging from younger than 1 Gyr to older than 11 Gyr. We further investigate the feasibility of directly deducing ages and masses from LAMOST spectra using a machine learning method based on kernel-based principal component analysis, utilizing a subset of these RGB stars as a training dataset. The results demonstrate that ages derived through this method achieve an accuracy of approximately 24%. We also explored the feasibility of estimating ages and masses based on spectroscopically measured carbon and nitrogen abundances. The results are quite satisfactory and significantly improved compared to previous studies.

title: Deep Architectures for Automated Seizure Detection in Scalp EEGs
Abstract: Automated seizure detection using clinical electroencephalograms (EEGs) is a challenging machine learning problem due to the multichannel signal's extremely low signal-to-noise ratio. Events of interest, such as seizures, are easily confused with signal artifacts (e.g., eye movements) or benign variants (e.g., slowing). Commercially available systems suffer from unacceptably high false alarm rates. Deep learning algorithms employing high-dimensional models have not been effective due to the lack of large-scale data resources. This paper utilizes the TUH EEG Seizure Corpus to evaluate various hybrid deep structures, including Convolutional Neural Networks and Long Short-Term Memory Networks. We introduce a novel recurrent convolutional architecture that achieves 30% sensitivity at 7 false alarms per 24 hours. We further evaluated our system on a held-out evaluation set based on the Duke University Seizure Corpus, demonstrating similar performance trends to the TUH EEG Seizure Corpus. This is a significant finding because the Duke corpus was collected using different instrumentation and at different hospitals. Our work demonstrates that deep learning architectures integrating spatial and temporal contexts are critical for achieving state-of-the-art performance and will enable a new generation of clinically acceptable technology.

title: Automatic Analysis of EEGs Using Big Data and Hybrid Deep Learning Architectures
Abstract: Objective: A clinical decision support tool that automatically interprets EEGs can reduce time to diagnosis and enhance real-time applications such as ICU monitoring. Clinicians have indicated that a sensitivity of 95% with a specificity below 5% is the minimum requirement for clinical acceptance. We propose a high-performance classification system based on principles of big data and machine learning. Methods: A hybrid machine learning system combining hidden Markov models (HMM) for sequential decoding and deep learning networks for postprocessing is proposed. These algorithms were trained and evaluated using the TUH EEG Corpus, the world's largest publicly available database of clinical EEG data. Results: Our approach achieves a sensitivity above 90% while maintaining a specificity below 5%. This system detects three events of clinical interest: (1) spike and/or sharp waves, (2) periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges, (3) generalized periodic epileptiform discharges. It also detects three events used to model background noise: (1) artifacts, (2) eye movement, (3) background. Conclusions: A hybrid HMM/deep learning system can deliver a low false alarm rate on EEG event detection, making automated analysis a viable option for clinicians. Significance: The TUH EEG Corpus enables the application of highly data-intensive machine learning algorithms to EEG analysis. Performance is approaching clinical acceptance for real-time applications.

title: Differentially Private Matrix Completion Revisited
Abstract: This paper presents the first provably joint differentially private algorithm with formal utility guarantees for the problem of user-level privacy-preserving collaborative filtering. Our algorithm is based on the Frank-Wolfe method and consistently estimates the underlying preference matrix as long as the number of users m is ω(n5/4), where n is the number of items, and each user provides her preference for at least √n randomly selected items. We also provide an optimal differentially private algorithm for singular vector computation, based on the celebrated Oja's method, which significantly reduces space and time complexity while operating on sparse matrices. We empirically evaluate our algorithm on a suite of datasets and demonstrate its consistent outperformance compared to state-of-the-art private algorithms.

title: PixelSNAIL: An Improved Autoregressive Generative Model
Abstract: Autoregressive generative models consistently achieve the best results in density estimation tasks involving high-dimensional data, such as images or audio. They frame density estimation as a sequence modeling task, where a recurrent neural network (RNN) models the conditional distribution over the next element given all preceding elements. In this paradigm, the bottleneck lies in the RNN's ability to model long-range dependencies. The most successful approaches rely on causal convolutions, which provide better access to earlier parts of the sequence compared to conventional RNNs. Drawing inspiration from recent work in meta reinforcement learning, where addressing long-range dependencies is also crucial, we introduce a novel generative model architecture that combines causal convolutions with self-attention. This note describes the resulting model and presents state-of-the-art log-likelihood results on CIFAR-10 (2.85 bits per dimension) and 32×32 ImageNet (3.80 bits per dimension). Our implementation is available at https://github.com/neocxi/pixelsnail-public.

title: Directional Statistics and Filtering Using libDirectional
Abstract: This paper introduces libDirectional, a MATLAB library for directional statistics and directional estimation. It supports a wide range of commonly used distributions on the unit circle, including the von Mises, wrapped normal, and wrapped Cauchy distributions. Moreover, various distributions on higher-dimensional manifolds, such as the unit hypersphere and the hypertorus, are available. Based on these distributions, several recursive filtering algorithms implemented in libDirectional enable estimation on these manifolds. The functionality is implemented in a clear, well-documented, and object-oriented structure that is both user-friendly and easily extensible.
label: AI

title: Extrapolating Expected Accuracies for Large Multi-Class Problems
Abstract: The difficulty of multi-class classification generally increases with the number of classes. Can we predict how well a classifier will scale with an increased number of classes using data from a subset of the classes? Assuming that the classes are sampled identically and independently from a population and that the classifier is based on independently learned scoring functions, we demonstrate that the expected accuracy when the classifier is trained on k classes is the (k-1)st moment of a specific distribution that can be estimated from data. We present an unbiased estimation method based on this theory and illustrate its application in a facial recognition example.
label: AI

title: Learning More Universal Representations for Transfer-Learning
Abstract: A representation is considered universal if it encodes any element of the visual world (e.g., objects, scenes) in any configuration (e.g., scale, context). While not expecting purely universal representations, the goal in the literature is to improve the universality level, starting from a representation with a certain level. To achieve this, the state-of-the-art involves learning CNN-based representations on a diversified training problem (e.g., ImageNet modified with annotated data). While this effectively increases universality, it still necessitates significant effort to satisfy the need for annotated data. This work proposes two methods to improve universality while limiting the requirement for annotated data. We also propose a unified framework for these methods based on diversifying the training problem. Finally, to better align with Atkinson's cognitive study on universal human representations, we propose relying on the transfer-learning scheme and a new metric for evaluating universality. This metric aims to demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods on 10 target problems related to classification tasks and various visual domains.
label: AI

title: Deep learning for universal linear embeddings of nonlinear dynamics
Abstract: Identifying coordinate transformations that approximate strongly nonlinear dynamics as linear is a fundamental challenge in modern dynamical systems. These transformations have the potential to enable prediction, estimation, and control of nonlinear systems using standard linear theory. The Koopman operator has emerged as a leading data-driven embedding, as its eigenfunctions provide intrinsic coordinates that globally linearize the dynamics. However, identifying and representing these eigenfunctions has proven mathematically and computationally challenging. This work leverages the power of deep learning to discover representations of Koopman eigenfunctions from trajectory data of dynamical systems. Our network is parsimonious and interpretable by construction, embedding the dynamics on a low-dimensional manifold that reflects the intrinsic rank of the dynamics and is parameterized by the Koopman eigenfunctions. Specifically, we identify nonlinear coordinates on which the dynamics are globally linear using a modified auto-encoder. We also generalize Koopman representations to include a ubiquitous class of systems exhibiting continuous spectra, ranging from the simple pendulum to nonlinear optics and broadband turbulence. Our framework parametrizes the continuous frequency using an auxiliary network, enabling a compact and efficient embedding at the intrinsic rank while connecting our models to half a century of asymptotics. Through this approach, we benefit from the power and generality of deep learning while maintaining the physical interpretability of Koopman embeddings.

title: On the estimation of correlation in a binary sequence model
Abstract: We consider a binary sequence generated by thresholding a hidden continuous sequence. The hidden variables are assumed to have a compound symmetry covariance structure with a single parameter characterizing the common correlation. We study the parameter estimation problem under such one-parameter models. We demonstrate that maximizing the likelihood function does not yield consistent estimates for the correlation. We then formally prove the non-estimability of the parameter by deriving a non-vanishing minimax lower bound. This counter-intuitive phenomenon reveals an interesting insight: one-bit information from each latent variable is insufficient for consistently recovering their common correlation. On the other hand, we further show that ternary data generated from the hidden variables can consistently estimate the correlation with a parametric convergence rate. Thus, we uncover a phase transition phenomenon regarding the discretization of latent continuous variables while preserving the estimability of the correlation. Numerical experiments validate these conclusions. |||

title: Combining Representation Learning with Logic for Language Processing
Abstract: Representation learning methods, which learn distributed vector representations of symbols via gradient-based optimization, have become the state-of-the-art in many natural language processing and automated knowledge base completion tasks. These methods require minimal hand-crafted features, eliminating the need for most preprocessing steps and task-specific assumptions. However, representation learning often necessitates a significant amount of annotated training data to generalize well to unseen data. Human annotators typically use formal logic to specify these annotations. This research explores different combinations of representation learning methods with logic to reduce the need for annotated training data and improve generalization.

title: Neural network augmented inverse problems for PDEs
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to enhance classical methods for inverse problems by incorporating artificial neural networks. The neural network acts as a prior for the coefficient to be estimated from noisy data. Neural networks are global, smooth function approximators, eliminating the need for explicit regularization of the error functional to recover smooth solutions and coefficients. The authors provide detailed examples using the Poisson equation in 1, 2, and 3 space dimensions, demonstrating the robustness of this approach with respect to noisy and incomplete data, mesh, and geometry.

title: A Light-Weight Multimodal Framework for Improved Environmental Audio Tagging
Abstract: The lack of strong labels has significantly hindered the scalability of state-of-the-art fully supervised audio tagging systems to larger datasets. While audio-visual learning models based on unlabeled videos have been successfully applied to audio tagging, they are resource-intensive and require extensive training time. This paper proposes a lightweight, multimodal framework for environmental audio tagging. The audio branch of the framework is a convolutional and recurrent neural network (CRNN) based on multiple instance learning (MIL), trained using audio tracks from a large collection of weakly labeled YouTube video excerpts. The video branch leverages pretrained state-of-the-art image recognition networks and word embeddings to extract information from the video track and map visual objects to sound events. Experiments on the audio tagging task of the DCASE 2017 challenge demonstrate that incorporating video information improves a strong baseline audio tagging system by 5.3% absolute in terms of F1 score. The entire system can be trained within 6 hours on a single GPU and readily adapted to other audio tasks, such as speech sentimental analysis.

title: Momentum and Stochastic Momentum for Stochastic Gradient, Newton, Proximal Point and Subspace Descent Methods
Abstract: This paper investigates various classes of stochastic optimization algorithms augmented with heavy ball momentum. Among the methods studied are: stochastic gradient descent, stochastic Newton, stochastic proximal point, and stochastic dual subspace ascent. This work marks the first time momentum variants of several of these methods have been analyzed. The analysis is conducted in a setting where all these methods are equivalent. The paper proves global nonasymptotic linear convergence rates for all methods and various measures of success, including primal function values, primal iterates (in L2 sense), and dual function values. Additionally, the paper demonstrates that primal iterates converge at an accelerated linear rate in the L1 sense. This is the first instance of proving a linear rate for the stochastic heavy ball method (i.e., stochastic gradient descent method with momentum). Under slightly weaker conditions, a sublinear convergence rate is established for Cesaro averages of primal iterates. Furthermore, the paper introduces a novel concept called stochastic momentum, designed to reduce the cost of performing the momentum step. The paper proves linear convergence of several stochastic methods with stochastic momentum and demonstrates that in certain sparse data regimes and for sufficiently small momentum parameters, these methods exhibit better overall complexity compared to methods with deterministic momentum. The findings are corroborated by extensive numerical testing on both artificial and real datasets, including data from average consensus problems.
label: AI

title: Multiple Instance Deep Learning for Weakly Supervised Small-Footprint Audio Event Detection
Abstract: State-of-the-art audio event detection (AED) systems rely on supervised learning using strongly labeled data, which severely limits their scalability to large datasets where high-resolution annotations are prohibitively expensive to obtain. This paper presents a small-footprint multiple instance learning (MIL) framework for multi-class AED using weakly annotated labels. The proposed MIL framework employs audio embeddings extracted from a pre-trained convolutional neural network as input features. The paper demonstrates that using audio embeddings, the MIL framework can be implemented using a simple DNN, achieving comparable performance to recurrent neural networks.  The approach is evaluated by training an audio tagging system using a subset of AudioSet, a large collection of weakly labeled YouTube video excerpts. Combining the MIL framework with a late-fusion approach improves the F1 score of a baseline audio tagging system by 17%. The paper shows that audio embeddings extracted by convolutional neural networks significantly boost the performance of all MIL models. This framework reduces the model complexity of the AED system, making it suitable for applications where computational resources are limited.

title: CNN Is All You Need
Abstract: The Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) has demonstrated its unique advantages in audio, image, and text learning, and has recently challenged Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) with long short-term memory cells (LSTM) in sequence-to-sequence learning. CNNs are easily parallelizable, while RNN computations are primarily sequential, leading to a performance bottleneck. However, unlike RNNs, CNNs inherently lack the history sensitivity required for sequence transformation. Therefore, enhancing the sequential order awareness, or position-sensitivity, becomes crucial for making CNNs a general deep learning model. This paper introduces an extended CNN model with enhanced position-sensitivity, called PoseNet. A notable feature of PoseNet is the asymmetric treatment of position information in the encoder and the decoder. Experiments show that PoseNet significantly improves the accuracy of CNN-based sequence-to-sequence learning, achieving around 33-36 BLEU scores on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task and around 44-46 BLEU scores on the English-to-French translation task.

title: The information bottleneck and geometric clustering
Abstract: The information bottleneck (IB) approach to clustering takes a joint distribution $P\\!\\left(X,Y\\right)$ and maps the data $X$ to cluster labels $T$ that retain maximal information about $Y$ (Tishby et al., 1999). This objective leads to an algorithm that clusters data points based on the similarity of their conditional distributions $P\\!\\left(Y\\mid X\\right)$. This contrasts with classic "geometric clustering" algorithms like $k$-means and Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs), which cluster data points based on their geometric (typically Euclidean) distance from one another. This paper demonstrates how to use the deterministic information bottleneck (DIB) (Strouse and Schwab, 2017), a variant of IB, for geometric clustering by choosing cluster labels that preserve information about data point location on a smoothed dataset. The paper also introduces a novel method for selecting the number of clusters, based on identifying solutions where the tradeoff between the number of clusters used and spatial information preserved is strongest. The authors apply this approach to various simple clustering problems, showing that DIB with their model selection procedure recovers the generative cluster labels. The paper further shows that in specific limits of their model parameters, clustering with DIB and IB is equivalent to $k$-means and EM fitting of a GMM with hard and soft assignments, respectively. Thus, clustering with (D)IB generalizes and provides an information-theoretic perspective on these classic algorithms.

title: On Convergence of some Gradient-based Temporal-Differences Algorithms for Off-Policy Learning
Abstract: This paper examines off-policy temporal-difference (TD) learning methods for policy evaluation in Markov decision processes with finite spaces and discounted reward criteria. The authors present a collection of convergence results for several gradient-based TD algorithms with linear function approximation. The algorithms analyzed include: (i) two basic forms of two-time-scale gradient-based TD algorithms, referred to as GTD, which minimize the mean squared projected Bellman error using stochastic gradient descent; (ii) their "robustified" biased variants; (iii) their mirror-descent versions, combining the mirror-descent idea with TD learning; and (iv) a single-time-scale version of GTD that solves minimax problems formulated for approximate policy evaluation. The authors derive convergence results for three types of stepsizes: constant stepsize, slowly diminishing stepsize, and the standard type of diminishing stepsize with a square-summable condition. For the first two types of stepsizes, the weak convergence method from stochastic approximation theory is applied to characterize the asymptotic behavior of the algorithms. For the standard type of stepsize, the algorithmic behavior is analyzed with respect to a stronger mode of convergence, almost sure convergence. The convergence results are presented for the aforementioned TD algorithms with three general ways of setting their $\\lambda$-parameters: (i) state-dependent $\\lambda$; (ii) a recently proposed scheme of using history-dependent $\\lambda$ to keep the eligibility traces of the algorithms bounded while allowing for relatively large values of $\\lambda$; and (iii) a composite scheme combining the preceding two schemes and enabling a broader class of generalized Bellman operators for approximate policy evaluation with TD methods.

title: A Composite Quantile Fourier Neural Network for Multi-Step Probabilistic Forecasting of Nonstationary Univariate Time Series
Abstract: Point forecasting of univariate time series is a challenging problem with extensive research. However, nonparametric probabilistic forecasting of time series, such as in the form of quantiles or prediction intervals, presents an even greater challenge. This paper aims to expand the possible forecasting paradigms by devising and exploring an extrapolation-based approach that has not been previously applied for probabilistic forecasting. The authors introduce a novel quantile Fourier neural network for nonparametric probabilistic forecasting of univariate time series. Multi-step predictions are provided as composite quantiles, using time as the only input to the model. This effectively constitutes a form of extrapolation-based nonlinear quantile regression applied for forecasting. Experiments are conducted on eight real-world datasets exhibiting a variety of periodic and aperiodic patterns. Nine naive and advanced methods, including quantile regression neural network, support vector quantile regression, SARIMA, and exponential smoothing, are used as benchmarks. The empirical results validate the effectiveness of the proposed method in providing high-quality and accurate probabilistic predictions.

title: An empirical evaluation for the intrusion detection features based on machine learning and feature selection methods
Abstract: Despite significant advancements in information technology, particularly the Internet, computer networks, global information exchange, and its positive impact on all aspects of daily life, it has also contributed to the development of penetration and intrusion. These pose a significant risk to the security of information organizations, government agencies, and result in substantial economic losses. Various techniques have been designed for protection, such as firewalls and intrusion detection systems (IDS). IDS comprises software and/or hardware techniques used to detect hacker activities within computer systems. Two types of anomalies are employed in IDS to detect intrusive activities that deviate from normal user behavior. Misuse relies on a knowledge base containing all known attack techniques, and intrusion is discovered through research within this knowledge base. Artificial intelligence techniques have been introduced to improve the performance of these systems. The primary function of IDS is to identify unauthorized access attempts to compromise confidentiality, integrity, or availability of the computer network. This paper investigates the Intrusion Detection (ID) problem using three machine learning algorithms: BayesNet algorithm, Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), and Support Vector Machine (SVM). The algorithms are applied to a real, Management Information Based (MIB) dataset collected from a real-life environment. To enhance the detection process accuracy, a set of feature selection approaches is employed: Infogain (IG), ReleifF (RF), and Genetic Search (GS). The experimental results demonstrate that the three feature selection methods enhance classification performance. GS with BayesNet, MLP, and SVM yield high accuracy rates, with BayesNet with GS achieving a 99.9% accuracy rate.

title: An Artificial Neural Network-based Stock Trading System Using Technical Analysis and Big Data Framework
Abstract: This paper presents a neural network-based stock price prediction and trading system utilizing technical analysis indicators. The developed model first converts financial time series data into a series of buy-sell-hold trigger signals using commonly preferred technical analysis indicators. Subsequently, a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) artificial neural network (ANN) model is trained in the learning stage on daily stock prices between 1997 and 2007 for all Dow30 stocks. The Apache Spark big data framework is employed during the training stage. The trained model is then evaluated using data from 2007 to 2017. The results indicate that by selecting appropriate technical indicators, the neural network model achieves comparable performance to the Buy and Hold strategy in most cases. Furthermore, fine-tuning the technical indicators and/or optimization strategy can enhance the overall trading performance.

title: Memory-Efficient Deep Salient Object Segmentation Networks on Gridized Superpixels
Abstract: Computer vision algorithms for pixel-wise labeling tasks, such as semantic segmentation and salient object detection, have witnessed a significant accuracy increase with the integration of deep learning. Deep segmentation methods slightly modify and fine-tune pre-trained networks containing hundreds of millions of parameters. This paper questions the necessity of such memory-intensive networks for the specific task of salient object segmentation. To this end, the authors propose a method to learn a memory-efficient network from scratch by training it exclusively on salient object detection datasets. Their method encodes images into gridized superpixels that preserve both object boundaries and connectivity rules of regular pixels. This representation enables the use of convolutional neural networks that operate on regular grids. By utilizing these encoded images, the authors train a memory-efficient network using only 0.048% of the parameters found in other deep salient object detection networks. The method demonstrates comparable accuracy to state-of-the-art deep salient object detection methods, providing a faster and significantly more memory-efficient alternative. Due to its ease of deployment, such a network is preferable for applications in memory-limited devices like mobile phones and IoT devices.
label: AI

title: DeepIEP: a Peptide Sequence Model of Isoelectric Point (IEP/pI) using Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs)
Abstract: The isoelectric point (IEP or pI) is the pH at which the net charge on the molecular ensemble of peptides and proteins is zero. This physical-chemical property depends on protonable/deprotonable sidechains and their pKa values. This paper presents a pI prediction model trained from a database of peptide sequences and pIs using a recurrent neural network (RNN) with long short-term memory (LSTM) cells. The trained model achieves an RMSE and R$^2$ of 0.28 and 0.95 for the external test set. Notably, the model does not rely on pKa values, but predictions for constructed test sequences show similar rankings to known pKa values. The prediction primarily depends on the presence of known acidic and basic amino acids, with fine adjustments based on the neighboring sequence and position of the charged amino acids in the peptide chain.
label: AI

title: Consensus-based Sequence Training for Video Captioning
Abstract: Captioning models are typically trained using the cross-entropy loss, although their performance is evaluated on other metrics designed to better correlate with human assessments. Recent studies have shown that reinforcement learning (RL) can directly optimize these metrics in tasks like captioning. However, this approach is computationally expensive and requires specifying a baseline reward at each step to ensure training convergence. This paper proposes a fast approach to optimize a specific objective of interest through the REINFORCE algorithm. The authors demonstrate that by replacing model samples with ground-truth sentences, RL training can be viewed as a form of weighted cross-entropy loss, leading to a fast, RL-based pre-training algorithm. They further propose using the consensus among ground-truth captions of the same video as the baseline reward, which can be computed efficiently. The complete proposal is termed Consensus-based Sequence Training (CST). Applied to the MSRVTT video captioning benchmark, the proposed approach trains significantly faster than comparable methods and establishes a new state-of-the-art on the task, improving the CIDEr score from 47.3 to 54.2.
label: AI

title: Co-Morbidity Exploration on Wearables Activity Data Using Unsupervised Pre-training and Multi-Task Learning
Abstract: Physical activity and sleep play a crucial role in the prevention and management of numerous chronic conditions. Understanding their impact on these conditions is a complex task. Currently, data from electronic health records (EHRs), sleep lab studies, and activity/sleep logs are utilized. The increasing popularity of wearable health devices provides a substantial new data source, enabling real-time tracking of user lifestyles through web interfaces, potentially benefiting both consumers and their healthcare providers. However, a gap currently exists between lifestyle data (e.g., sleep, physical activity) and clinical outcomes typically captured in EHRs. This gap hinders the use of this new signal source for healthcare decision-making. Applying deep learning to wearables data offers a promising opportunity to bridge this gap. To address the problem of limited availability of clinical data for a significant portion of subjects and unrepresentative subject populations, this paper proposes a novel unsupervised (task-agnostic) time-series representation learning technique called act2vec. act2vec learns useful features by considering the co-occurrence of activity levels along with the periodicity of human activity patterns. The learned representations are then leveraged to enhance the performance of disorder-specific supervised learning models. Furthermore, recognizing that many disorders are often interconnected (co-morbidity), the authors utilize a multi-task learning framework to exploit the shared structure of disorder-inducing lifestyle choices partially captured in the wearables data. Empirical evaluation using actigraphy data from 4,124 subjects demonstrates that the proposed method outperforms conventional time-series symbolic representational methods and task-specific deep learning models in terms of performance and generalization.

title: Tensor Regression Networks with various Low-Rank Tensor Approximations
Abstract: Tensor regression networks achieve high compression rates of neural networks with minimal performance impact. They accomplish this by imposing low tensor rank structure on the weight matrices of fully connected layers. While tensor regression networks have been investigated from the perspective of their compressive power, the regularization effect of enforcing low-rank tensor structure has not been sufficiently explored. This paper examines tensor regression networks using various low-rank tensor approximations, aiming to compare the compressive and regularization power of different low-rank constraints. The authors evaluate the compressive and regularization performances of the proposed model using both deep and shallow convolutional neural networks. The experimental results suggest that the Global Average Pooling Layer outperforms the Tensor Regression Layer when applied to deep convolutional neural networks with the CIFAR-10 dataset. Conversely, shallow convolutional neural networks with a tensor regression layer and dropout achieved lower test error than both Global Average Pooling and fully-connected layers with dropout function when trained with a limited number of samples.
label: AI

title: Exploring the Space of Black-box Attacks on Deep Neural Networks
Abstract: Existing black-box attacks on deep neural networks (DNNs) have primarily focused on transferability, where an adversarial instance generated for a locally trained model can be "transferred" to attack other learning models. This paper introduces novel Gradient Estimation black-box attacks for adversaries with query access to the target model's class probabilities, eliminating the reliance on transferability. The paper also proposes strategies to decouple the number of queries required to generate each adversarial sample from the dimensionality of the input. An iterative variant of the proposed attack achieves near 100% adversarial success rates for both targeted and untargeted attacks on DNNs. The authors conduct extensive experiments for a comprehensive comparative evaluation of black-box attacks, showing that the proposed Gradient Estimation attacks outperform all transferability-based black-box attacks tested on both MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, achieving adversarial success rates comparable to well-known, state-of-the-art white-box attacks. The Gradient Estimation attacks are also successfully applied against a real-world Content Moderation classifier hosted by Clarifai. Additionally, the paper evaluates black-box attacks against state-of-the-art defenses. The results demonstrate that the Gradient Estimation attacks are highly effective even against these defenses.
label: AI

title: Robust Loss Functions under Label Noise for Deep Neural Networks
Abstract: In many classifier learning applications, training data is affected by label noise. Deep networks are learned using massive training datasets where the problem of noisy labels is particularly relevant. Current techniques proposed for learning deep networks under label noise focus on modifying network architecture and algorithms for estimating true labels from noisy labels. An alternative approach would be to explore loss functions inherently tolerant to noise. Theoretical results exist for binary classification concerning loss functions robust to label noise. This paper provides sufficient conditions on a loss function such that risk minimization under that loss function would be inherently tolerant to label noise for multiclass classification problems. These results generalize existing findings on noise-tolerant loss functions for binary classification. The authors study some widely used loss functions in deep networks and demonstrate that the loss function based on the mean absolute value of error is inherently robust to label noise. Thus, standard back propagation is sufficient to learn the true classifier even under label noise. Through experiments, the authors illustrate the robustness of risk minimization with such loss functions for learning neural networks.
label: AI

title: Sketching for Kronecker Product Regression and P-splines
Abstract: TensorSketch is an oblivious linear sketch introduced in Pagh'13 and later utilized in Pham, Pagh'13 in the context of SVMs for polynomial kernels. Avron, Nguyen, Woodruff'14 showed that TensorSketch provides a subspace embedding, enabling its application for canonical correlation analysis, low-rank approximation, and principal component regression for the polynomial kernel. This paper extends TensorSketch beyond the context of polynomial kernels, demonstrating its utility in applications where the underlying design matrix is a Kronecker product of smaller matrices. This allows the authors to solve Kronecker product regression and non-negative Kronecker product regression, as well as regularized spline regression. The main technical result lies in extending TensorSketch to other norms. While TensorSketch provides input sparsity time for Kronecker product regression with respect to the 2-norm, the authors show how to solve Kronecker product regression with respect to the 1-norm in time sublinear in the time required for computing the Kronecker product, and for more general p-norms.
label: AI

title: Multi-modal Geolocation Estimation Using Deep Neural Networks
Abstract: Estimating the location where an image was taken based solely on its contents is a challenging task, even for humans. Accurately labeling an image in this manner relies heavily on contextual information and is not as simple as identifying a single object. Therefore, any methods attempting this task must account for these complexities, and no single model currently addresses all challenges. This work contributes to the research in image geolocation inferencing by introducing a novel global meshing strategy, outlining various training procedures to overcome the significant data limitations when training these models, and demonstrating how incorporating additional information can enhance the overall performance of a geolocation inference model. The authors show that Delaunay triangles are an effective type of mesh for geolocation in relatively low-volume scenarios compared to results from state-of-the-art models using quad trees and an order of magnitude more training data. Additionally, the time of posting, learned user albuming, and other metadata are easily incorporated to improve geolocation by up to 11% for country-level (750 km) locality accuracy to 3% for city-level (25 km) localities. |||
