title: Timely Feedback in Unstructured Cybersecurity Exercises
Abstract: Cybersecurity exercises are valuable for training professionals to defend against cyberattacks. However, traditional methods provide delayed feedback, hindering learning. This paper proposes a new feedback tool that offers an interactive, personalized timeline of exercise events, providing immediate insights for learners. The tool was successfully deployed during an international exercise and received positive feedback from participants. This approach can be readily applied to any exercise utilizing a scoring system based on individual objectives, enabling immediate reflection and enhanced learning.
label: AI

title: Horn-ICE Learning for Synthesizing Invariants and Contracts
Abstract: We propose a novel algorithm for learning invariants using Horn implication counterexamples (Horn-ICE). This algorithm is based on decision-tree learning and operates in polynomial time. It utilizes statistical heuristics to construct compact trees that satisfy the Horn-ICE samples. As most verification proofs can be represented using Horn clauses, Horn-ICE learning offers a robust method for learning inductive annotations to prove program correctness. Our experiments demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness in efficiently learning suitable inductive invariants and contracts for various sequential and concurrent programs.
label: AI

title: Mapping to Declarative Knowledge for Word Problem Solving
Abstract: Math word problems provide a natural framework for tackling various quantitative reasoning tasks, such as understanding financial news, sports results, and war casualties. Solving these problems demands comprehension of several mathematical concepts, including dimensional analysis and subset relationships. This paper presents a framework for incorporating declarative knowledge into word problem solving by translating natural language descriptions of these concepts into mathematical expressions. Our approach learns to map word problem text to mathematical expressions by selecting relevant declarative knowledge for each operation in the solution expression. This allows for handling multiple concepts within a single problem while maintaining interpretability of the answer expression. We model the mapping to declarative knowledge as a latent variable, eliminating the need for expensive annotations. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates that our domain knowledge-based solver outperforms existing systems and exhibits better generalization capabilities in scenarios where training data differs from test data.
label: AI

title: Scaling GRPC Tensorflow on 512 nodes of Cori Supercomputer
Abstract: This study investigates the scalability of distributed TensorFlow with GRPC primitives on the Cori supercomputer, utilizing up to 512 Intel Xeon Phi (KNL) nodes with synchronous stochastic gradient descent (SGD). We examine the scaling efficiency of two convolutional neural networks: ResNet-50, a state-of-the-art deep network for classification with approximately 25.5 million parameters, and HEP-CNN, a shallow network with less than 1 million parameters commonly used in scientific applications. Our results show that ResNet-50 achieves greater than 80% scaling efficiency on up to 128 workers using 32 parameter servers (PS tasks). However, the efficiency declines sharply to 23% for 512 workers with 64 PS tasks. Analysis indicates that this efficiency drop is attributed to low network bandwidth utilization, resulting from a combination of factors: the heterogeneous distributed parallelization algorithm, load imbalance among PS tasks, and inefficiencies in the GRPC communication primitive on Cori's high-speed interconnect. HEP-CNN, requiring less interconnect bandwidth, demonstrates greater than 80% weak scaling efficiency for up to 256 nodes with only 1 PS task. Our findings are applicable to other deep learning networks, highlighting challenges faced by large networks with millions of parameters and demonstrating that shallower networks like HEP-CNN can efficiently scale even with a single parameter server.
label: AI

title: RLlib: Abstractions for Distributed Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms typically involve deeply nested and highly irregular computational patterns, presenting opportunities for distributed computation. This paper advocates for distributing RL components in a composable manner by adapting algorithms for top-down hierarchical control. This approach encapsulates parallelism and resource requirements within short-running compute tasks, enabling efficient scalability. The benefits of this principle are demonstrated through RLlib, a library that provides scalable software primitives for RL. These primitives enable a broad range of algorithms to be implemented with high performance, scalability, and significant code reuse. RLlib is publicly available at https://rllib.io/.
label: AI

title: IHT dies hard: Provable accelerated Iterative Hard Thresholding
Abstract: This paper investigates the use of momentum motions within classic iterative hard thresholding (IHT) methods for convex optimization problems with non-convex constraints. By modifying standard IHT, we analyze its convergence behavior under standard assumptions and observe significant improvements in diverse scenarios compared to state-of-the-art projected gradient descent and Frank-Wolfe variants. Our analysis further examines the impact of selecting the momentum parameter, revealing two distinct modes of behavior – "rippling" and linear – depending on the level of momentum, similar to convex settings.
label: AI

title: Entropy-SGD optimizes the prior of a PAC-Bayes bound: Generalization properties of Entropy-SGD and data-dependent priors
Abstract: We analyze Entropy-SGD, a learning algorithm that optimizes a PAC-Bayes bound on the risk of a Gibbs (posterior) classifier. This classifier is a randomized classifier obtained by perturbing the weights of a learned classifier using a risk-sensitive approach. While Entropy-SGD optimizes the bound's prior, it violates the PAC-Bayes theorem's assumption that the prior is chosen independently of the data. We observe that Entropy-SGD achieves zero training error on random labels, raising concerns about its generalization ability. To address this, we leverage a result showing that data-dependent priors derived from stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD) yield valid PAC-Bayes bounds if the target distribution of SGLD is ε-differentially private. Our findings suggest that test error on MNIST and CIFAR10 falls within the empirically non-vacuous risk bounds computed under the assumption of SGLD reaching stationarity. This suggests that Entropy-SGLD can achieve relatively tight generalization bounds while still fitting real labels, although it may not attain state-of-the-art performance.
label: AI

title: HACS: Human Action Clips and Segments Dataset for Recognition and Temporal Localization
Abstract: This paper introduces a new large-scale dataset for recognizing and temporally localizing human actions in Web videos, called HACS (Human Action Clips and Segments). We leverage both consensus and disagreement among visual classifiers to automatically identify candidate short clips from unlabeled videos, which are subsequently validated by human annotators, resulting in the HACS Clips dataset. We also collect annotations defining action segment boundaries, forming the HACS Segments dataset. HACS Clips contains over 1.5 million annotated clips sampled from 504,000 untrimmed videos, while HACS Segments comprises 139,000 action segments densely annotated in 50,000 untrimmed videos spanning 200 action categories. HACS Clips offers more labeled examples than any existing video benchmark, establishing it as a large-scale action recognition benchmark and an excellent resource for spatiotemporal feature learning. Our transfer learning experiments on three target datasets demonstrate that HACS Clips outperforms Kinetics-600, Moments-In-Time, and Sports1M as a pre-training source. On HACS Segments, we evaluate state-of-the-art methods for action proposal generation and action localization, highlighting the novel challenges posed by our dense temporal annotations.
label: AI

title: Building Robust Deep Neural Networks for Road Sign Detection
Abstract: Deep neural networks are designed to generalize beyond their training data using techniques like regularization, early stopping, and dropout. However, they are often vulnerable to adversarial examples, intentionally crafted inputs designed to mislead the network. This paper investigates the vulnerability of deep neural networks to adversarial attacks and proposes methods to enhance their robustness. We use the GTSRB dataset to create adversarial samples using the Fast Gradient Sign Method and Jacobian Saliency Method. These adversarial samples are then used to attack a deep convolutional neural network. We further enhance the network's resilience against adversarial attacks through defensive distillation and adversarial training, making it more robust and capable of handling such manipulations.
label: AI

title: Who is Smarter? Intelligence Measure of Learning-based Cognitive Radios
Abstract: Cognitive radio (CR) is considered a key technology for dynamic spectrum access, improving spectrum efficiency. While CR was initially conceived with the core idea of cognition, measuring CR cognitive capabilities and intelligence remains largely unexplored. Quantifying CR intelligence could lead to the development of novel CR technologies and enable better network configuration by integrating CRs with diverse cognitive abilities. This paper proposes a data-driven methodology for quantitatively measuring the intelligence factors of CRs with learning capabilities. Our methodology involves testing CRs in various spectrum environments under different settings, collecting performance data across multiple metrics. Factor analysis is then applied to the performance data to identify and quantify intelligence factors and cognitive capabilities. A case study involving 144 different CRs with varying learning-based dynamic spectrum access strategies, sensor counts, sensing accuracy, processing speed, and algorithmic complexity is presented. Five intelligence factors are identified through data analysis, demonstrating their alignment with the characteristics of the tested CRs and validating the proposed intelligence measure methodology.
label: AI

title: Zero-Shot Learning via Latent Space Encoding
Abstract: Zero-Shot Learning (ZSL) typically relies on a class semantic embedding space to transfer knowledge from seen classes to unseen ones. Capturing the common semantic characteristics between the visual modality and the class semantic modality (e.g., attributes or word vectors) is crucial for ZSL's success. This paper proposes a novel encoder-decoder approach, Latent Space Encoding (LSE), to connect semantic relations across different modalities. Unlike previous methods that require projection functions to transfer information between modalities, LSE facilitates interactions through a feature-aware latent space, learned implicitly. Different modalities are modeled separately but optimized jointly. For each modality, an encoder-decoder framework is employed to learn a feature-aware latent space by maximizing both the recoverability of the original space from the latent space and the predictability of the latent space from the original space. To relate different modalities, their features associated with the same concept are forced to share the same latent codings, generalizing the common semantic characteristics across modalities through latent representations. LSE readily extends to incorporate more modalities. Extensive experimental results on four benchmark datasets (AwA, CUB, aPY, and ImageNet) demonstrate the superiority of the proposed approach on various ZSL tasks, including traditional ZSL, generalized ZSL, and zero-shot retrieval (ZSR).
label: AI

title: Quantum Learning Algorithms and Post-Quantum Cryptography
Abstract: Quantum algorithms have shown promising speed-ups over classical algorithms in the context of computational learning theory, even in the presence of noise. This paper provides an overview of recent quantum speed-ups, revisits the Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm in a novel learning problem extension over an arbitrary cyclic group, and discusses its applications in cryptography, such as the Learning with Errors problem. The paper then delves into post-quantum cryptography, investigating attacks where an adversary has quantum access to a classical encryption scheme. New notions of security under non-adaptive quantum chosen-ciphertext attacks are explored, and symmetric-key encryption schemes based on quantum-secure pseudorandom functions are proposed, meeting these definitions. To prove security, novel relabeling techniques are introduced, demonstrating that no quantum algorithm making superposition queries can reliably distinguish between functions that are randomly relabeled at a small subset of the domain, even with arbitrary advice states in an oracle model. Finally, the paper discusses current progress in quantum computing technology, focusing on implementations of quantum algorithms on the ion-trap architecture, and highlights the relevance and effectiveness of common noise models adopted in computational learning theory.
label: AI

title: Scalable Prototype Selection by Genetic Algorithms and Hashing
Abstract: Classification in the dissimilarity space has emerged as a vibrant research area, offering a solution to learn from data represented as pairwise non-metric dissimilarities, which are otherwise challenging to handle. Prototype selection is a crucial step in constructing the dissimilarity space. However, despite previous efforts to find good prototypes, selecting the optimal representation set remains an open issue. This paper presents scalable methods for selecting a set of prototypes from large datasets. The methods are based on genetic algorithms, dissimilarity-based hashing, and two distinct unsupervised and supervised scalable criteria. The unsupervised criterion is based on the Minimum Spanning Tree of the graph formed by prototypes as nodes and dissimilarities as edges. The supervised criterion counts matching labels between objects and their closest prototypes. The suitability of these algorithms is analyzed specifically for dissimilarity representations. Experimental results demonstrate that the methods effectively select good prototypes from large datasets while maintaining low runtimes.
label: AI

title: A Real-Time Autonomous Highway Accident Detection Model Based on Big Data Processing and Computational Intelligence
Abstract: Traffic congestion is becoming a major problem in the 21st century due to increasing urban populations and the growing number of motor vehicles. Accidents are a primary cause of congestion, leading to casualties, financial losses, and wasted time. Early accident detection can potentially save lives, expedite road openings, reduce wasted time and resources, and improve efficiency. This study proposes a preliminary real-time autonomous accident-detection system based on computational intelligence techniques. Istanbul City traffic-flow data from various sensor locations for the year 2015 is analyzed using big data processing methodologies. Extracted features are then fed into a nearest neighbor model, a regression tree, and a feed-forward neural network model to predict the likelihood of an accident. The results indicate that while the system generates a significant number of false alarms, it can still provide valuable information for status verification and early reaction to potential accidents.
label: AI

title: Machine Learning Cosmic Expansion History
Abstract: This paper utilizes machine learning techniques to study the background evolution of the universe using 30 cosmic chronometers. From seven machine learning algorithms, Bayesian ridge regression is identified as the optimal method for extracting information from these chronometers, based on minimizing mean squared error on the testing set. Using a power-law polynomial expansion, the study obtains the first Hubble constant estimation of $H_0=65.95^{+6.98}_{-6.36}$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ through machine learning. The machine learning perspective allows for ruling out numerous cosmological models with more than three physical parameters, including $H_0$. Notably, the parameter spaces of three specific cosmological models can be effectively compressed by considering both their explanatory and generalization abilities.
label: AI

title: Chaos-guided Input Structuring for Improved Learning in Recurrent Neural Networks
Abstract: Anatomical studies demonstrate that the brain reformats input information to generate reliable responses for performing computations. However, the mechanisms by which neural circuits encode complex spatiotemporal patterns remain unclear. This paper shows that neural dynamics are significantly influenced by the phase alignment between input and spontaneous chaotic activity. Structuring input along the dominant chaotic projections stabilizes chaotic trajectories into stable channels (or attractors), enhancing the computational capacity of recurrent networks. Mean field analysis is used to derive the impact of input structuring on the overall stability of the formed attractors. The results indicate that input alignment determines the extent of intrinsic noise suppression, influencing attractor state stability and ultimately controlling the network's inference ability.
label: AI

title: Algorithmic Regularization in Over-parameterized Matrix Sensing and Neural Networks with Quadratic Activations
Abstract: We demonstrate that the gradient descent algorithm implicitly regularizes the learning of over-parameterized matrix factorization models and one-hidden-layer neural networks with quadratic activations. Specifically, we show that given $\tilde{O}(dr^2)$ random linear measurements of a rank $r$ positive semidefinite matrix $X^{\star}$, we can recover $X^{\star}$ by parameterizing it as $UU^T$ with $U \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ and minimizing the squared loss, even when $r \ll d$. Our proof demonstrates that starting from a small initialization, gradient descent recovers $X^{\star}$ in $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{r})$ iterations with a high degree of accuracy. These results address the conjecture proposed by Gunasekar et al. (2017) under the restricted isometry property. The presented technique can be applied to analyze neural networks with one-hidden-layer quadratic activations with some technical modifications.
label: AI

title: The Robust Manifold Defense: Adversarial Training using Generative Models
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel attack method for finding adversarial examples for image classifiers by leveraging spanners, deep neural networks with low-dimensional input spaces that approximate the set of images of interest. Spanners can be generators from Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) or decoders from Variational Autoencoders (VAEs). Our attack searches over latent code pairs to identify those that generate nearby images with different classifier outputs. We argue that this approach is more effective than searching over perturbations of real images. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this stronger attack can reduce the accuracy of Defense-GAN to 3%, addressing an open problem from the work of Athalye et al. We combine our attack with standard adversarial training to achieve the most robust MNIST classifier known, significantly improving the state of the art against Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) attacks. Our formulation involves solving a min-max problem, where the minimizer sets the classifier parameters and the maximizer executes our attack, searching for adversarial examples in the low-dimensional input space of the spanner. All code and models are available at https://github.com/ajiljalal/manifold-defense.git.
label: AI

title: Actionable Email Intent Modeling with Reparametrized RNNs
Abstract: Workplace emails often represent intentional calls to action for recipients. This paper proposes a novel approach to annotate these emails based on the recipient's intended action. We argue that this action-based annotation scheme is more scalable and theory-agnostic than traditional speech-act-based email intent annotation, while preserving important semantic and pragmatic information. Our action-based annotation demonstrates good inter-annotator agreement. We further demonstrate that threaded messages from other domains exhibiting comparable intents can be leveraged using domain-adaptive RAINBOW (Recurrently AttentIve Neural Bag-Of-Words). On a collection of datasets encompassing IRC, Reddit, and email, our reparametrized RNNs outperform common multitask/multidomain approaches in various speech act-related tasks. Experiments with a minimally supervised scenario of email recipient action classification also show that reparametrized RNNs learn a useful representation.
label: AI

title: Deep Meta Learning for Real-Time Target-Aware Visual Tracking
Abstract: This paper presents a novel real-time visual tracking framework based on Siamese matching networks and meta-learner networks. Conventional deep convolutional feature-based discriminative visual tracking algorithms require continuous retraining of classifiers or correlation filters, involving complex optimization tasks to adapt to the changing appearance of a target object. To address this complexity, our proposed algorithm incorporates a meta-learner network to provide the matching network with new appearance information of the target objects by adding target-aware feature space. The meta-learner network instantly provides parameters for the target-specific feature space through a single forward pass. By eliminating the need for continuous optimization tasks during tracking, our algorithm achieves real-time speeds while maintaining competitive performance against other state-of-the-art tracking algorithms.
label: AI

title: Variational Bayes Estimation of Discrete-Margined Copula Models with Application to Time Series
Abstract: We introduce a novel variational Bayes estimator designed for high-dimensional copulas with discrete, or a combination of discrete and continuous, margins. This approach utilizes a variational approximation to a tractable augmented posterior, offering significant speed advantages over previous likelihood-based methods. We employ this estimator to estimate drawable vine copulas for univariate and multivariate Markov ordinal and mixed time series, which pose significant challenges for traditional methods due to their high dimensionality ($rT$, where $T$ represents the number of observations and $r$ the number of series).  The vine pair-copulas are carefully selected to accommodate heteroskedasticity, a common feature of ordinal time series data. Coupled with flexible margins, the resulting time series models capture other typical characteristics of ordinal data, including zero inflation, multiple modes, and under- or over-dispersion.  We demonstrate the model's flexibility and the estimator's efficacy through six example series, analyzing copulas with up to 792 dimensions and 60 parameters, surpassing the scale and complexity of previously estimable copula models for discrete data.
label: AI

title: Towards Measuring Membership Privacy
Abstract: Machine learning models, increasingly accessible through public query interfaces, are vulnerable to malicious users who can infer sensitive information about training data. While differential privacy offers protection against such attacks, not all models can readily achieve this guarantee without compromising utility.  We delve into the mechanisms of membership attacks to understand their success, leading to the development of Differential Training Privacy (DTP). This empirical metric quantifies the privacy risk of releasing a classifier when differential privacy methods are inapplicable. DTP is a classifier-specific measure with respect to its training dataset, and we demonstrate its efficient calculation in various practical scenarios. We validate DTP using state-of-the-art machine learning models like neural networks on real-world datasets. Our findings show that DTP strongly predicts the success of membership attacks, implying that reducing DTP also reduces privacy risk.  We advocate for DTP as a decision-making tool when considering classifier publication, proposing the DTP-1 hypothesis: classifiers with a DTP value exceeding 1 should not be released.
label: AI

title: Strongly Hierarchical Factorization Machines and ANOVA Kernel Regression
Abstract: High-order parametric models incorporating feature interaction terms are crucial for data mining tasks where ground truth depends on feature interactions. However, with sparse data, the high-dimensional parameters associated with these interactions present significant challenges: expensive computation, difficulty in parameter estimation, and lack of structure.  Prior work has addressed these issues partially, with factorized parameters (e.g., Factorization Machines) and sparse learning algorithms (e.g., FTRL-Proximal) tackling the first two issues but failing to address the lack of structure.  Unstructured parameters often require constraints or complex regularization terms to impose hierarchical structures, complicating the optimization problem.  We introduce Strongly Hierarchical Factorization Machines and ANOVA kernel regression, addressing all three issues without increasing optimization difficulty. Experimental results demonstrate that these models significantly outperform existing approaches in cold-start user response time prediction and stock volatility prediction.
label: AI

title: General-Purpose Visual Language and Information System with Case-Studies in Developing Business Applications
Abstract: Learning computer programming has historically been a challenging endeavor. Since the 1960s, researchers have developed Visual Programming Languages (VPLs) to aid in this process. This thesis examines ten specifically selected VPLs through detailed study, experimentation, and evaluation using fifteen metrics.  Comparisons, classification, and gap analysis are presented, leading to the development of a comprehensive list of requirements for a general-purpose VPL and a guide for novice programmers to select appropriate tools.  The thesis culminates in the creation and presentation of PWCT (Programming Without Coding Technology), a novel general-purpose visual programming language. PWCT has been launched as a Sourceforge project, amassing over 230,000 downloads for the language and more than 19,500,000 downloads for samples, tutorials, and movies. Numerous business applications and projects have been developed using PWCT, further exemplified by the development of the Supernova and Ring programming languages. Developer feedback and research results indicate that PWCT is an appealing, competitive, and powerful language.
label: AI

title: Generative Adversarial Nets for Multiple Text Corpora
Abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have proven successful in generating artificial image data.  While much work has been dedicated to generating natural language from single corpora, we explore the use of GANs with multiple text corpora as input data.  This approach presents two key applications: (1) creating consistent cross-corpus word embeddings given different word embeddings per corpus; and (2) generating robust bag-of-words document embeddings for each corpus. We demonstrate our GAN models on real-world text datasets from various corpora, showing that embeddings from both models enhance performance in supervised learning problems.
label: AI

title: SAGA: A Submodular Greedy Algorithm For Group Recommendation
Abstract: This paper presents a unified framework and algorithm for the group recommendation problem, where a fixed number of items or alternatives must be recommended to a group of users. This problem arises frequently in real-world contexts and shares similarities with the budgeted social choice problem studied in economics.  We frame the group recommendation problem as selecting the subgraph with the highest group consensus score in a fully connected graph defined by the item affinity matrix. A fast greedy algorithm with strong theoretical guarantees is proposed, showing that it outperforms existing group recommendation algorithms in terms of relevance and coverage performance measures on a benchmark dataset.
label: AI

title: Overcomplete Frame Thresholding for Acoustic Scene Analysis
Abstract: This work derives a generic overcomplete frame thresholding scheme based on risk minimization. Overcomplete frames, favored for analysis tasks like classification, regression, and anomaly detection, are leveraged for real-world applications through thresholding.  We validate the method on a large-scale bird activity detection task using the scattering network architecture, employing continuous wavelets known for their effectiveness as dictionaries in audio environments.
label: AI

title: NNDrone: a toolkit for the mass application of machine learning in High Energy Physics
Abstract: Machine learning has emerged as an indispensable tool for selecting interesting events in high-energy physics, a role that will become even more critical as detector upgrades and data rates increase dramatically.  We propose a toolkit enabling the creation of a "drone classifier" from any machine learning classifier, allowing different classifiers to be standardized into a single form and executed in parallel.  We demonstrate the drone neural network's ability to learn the required properties of the input neural network without relying on labels from the training data, instead utilizing appropriate questioning of the input neural network.
label: AI

title: On Connecting Stochastic Gradient MCMC and Differential Privacy
Abstract: Machine learning's application to real-world scenarios has yielded significant success, but concerns regarding the privacy of training data have arisen.  Differential privacy offers a principled and rigorous privacy guarantee for machine learning models.  While injecting noise is a common method for designing differentially private models, balancing privacy and utility remains a challenge. We demonstrate that stochastic gradient Markov chain Monte Carlo (SG-MCMC), a class of scalable Bayesian posterior sampling algorithms, satisfies strong differential privacy with carefully chosen step sizes.  We develop theory on the performance of this differentially-private SG-MCMC method and conduct experiments supporting our analysis. These experiments show that a standard SG-MCMC sampler, without modifications, can achieve state-of-the-art performance in both privacy and utility for Bayesian learning.
label: AI

title: Deep Blind Image Inpainting
Abstract: Image inpainting, a challenging problem requiring the restoration of information in corrupted regions, often assumes knowledge of the corrupted regions' positions.  Unlike existing methods making assumptions about these regions, we introduce an efficient blind image inpainting algorithm for directly restoring a clear image from a corrupted input.  Inspired by residual learning algorithms, which aim to learn missing information, our algorithm employs an encoder and decoder architecture to capture more useful information and develops a robust loss function to handle outliers. This allows the algorithm to predict missing information in corrupted regions, facilitating clear image restoration.  Both qualitative and quantitative experiments demonstrate the algorithm's ability to handle corrupted regions of arbitrary shapes and outperform state-of-the-art methods.
label: AI

title: Leveraging Long and Short-term Information in Content-aware Movie Recommendation
Abstract: Movie recommendation systems provide users with ranked lists of movies based on individual preferences and constraints.  Two common types of models are used for ranking: long-term models and session-based models. While long-term models represent user-movie interactions that change slowly over time, session-based models encode short-term information about user interests and movie attribute dynamics.  This paper presents LSIC, a model leveraging long and short-term information in content-aware movie recommendation using adversarial training.  In the adversarial process, a generator, acting as a reinforcement learning agent, sequentially recommends the next movie to a user.  A discriminator simultaneously attempts to distinguish between generated and real movie lists.  Movie poster information is integrated to further enhance performance, particularly crucial when ratings are limited. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed model significantly surpasses competitors and sets a new state-of-the-art. The source code will be released upon publication.
label: AI

title: Automatic Image Cropping for Visual Aesthetic Enhancement Using Deep Neural Networks and Cascaded Regression
Abstract: Despite recent progress, computational visual aesthetic remains a challenging area. Image cropping, involving the removal of unwanted scene areas, is a crucial step for improving image aesthetic quality. However, evaluating the aesthetic appeal of cropping outcomes is subjective, making the task challenging.  We propose a novel cascaded cropping regression (CCR) method for image cropping, learning from professional photographers.  CCR improves the convergence speed of the cascaded method, which directly uses random-ferns regressors.  We also introduce a two-step learning strategy within CCR to address the lack of labeled cropping data.  A deep convolutional neural network (CNN) classifier is first trained on large-scale visual aesthetic datasets. This CNN model is then designed to extract features from several image cropping datasets, enabling the prediction of cropping bounding boxes by CCR.  Experimental results on public image cropping datasets demonstrate the proposed method's significant outperformance compared to existing image cropping techniques.

title: Neural Collaborative Autoencoder
Abstract: Deep neural networks have achieved state-of-the-art performance on numerous tasks. While some recent works have explored combining deep learning with recommendation, existing models face three key limitations: (1) inability to work with both explicit and implicit feedback due to network structures tailored to specific cases; (2) limited exploitation of deep learning's expressive potential in explicit models due to training challenges; and (3) susceptibility to overfitting in the implicit setting compared to shallow models.  To address these issues, we introduce Neural Collaborative Autoencoder (NCAE), a generic recommender framework for collaborative filtering that effectively handles both explicit and implicit feedback.  NCAE captures subtle hidden relationships between interactions through a non-linear matrix factorization process.  We develop a three-stage pre-training mechanism combining supervised and unsupervised feature learning to optimize NCAE's deep architecture.  Furthermore, an error reweighting module and a sparsity-aware data-augmentation strategy are proposed to prevent overfitting in the implicit setting.  Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that NCAE significantly surpasses the state-of-the-art.

title: Domain Adaptation Meets Disentangled Representation Learning and Style Transfer
Abstract: Numerous methods have been proposed for solving the domain adaptation problem, often relying on the assumption of fully transferable domain information. This assumption can lead to negative transfer, degrading domain adaptation when it is not met.  This paper introduces a novel learning network addressing three tasks simultaneously: domain adaptation, disentangled representation, and style transfer.  The learned features are disentangled into common and specific parts. Common parts represent transferable features suitable for domain adaptation with reduced negative transfer, while specific parts capture the unique style of each individual domain.  This allows for feature exchange across domains, enhancing both the transferability of common features and their applicability to image style transfer.  We incorporate five training objectives to realize these challenging tasks.  Experimental results demonstrate the architecture's adaptability to both full and partial transfer learning, facilitated by a well-learned disentangled representation.  Furthermore, the trained network demonstrates high potential for generating style-transferred images.
label: AI

title: Geochemical discrimination and characteristics of magmatic tectonic settings; a machine learning-based approach
Abstract: Geochemically discriminating between magmatism in different tectonic settings is fundamental to understanding magma generation processes within Earth's mantle.  We present a machine-learning (ML) approach for quantitative tectonic discrimination and feature selection using global geochemical datasets for volcanic rocks generated in eight distinct tectonic settings.  This study utilizes support vector machine, random forest, and sparse multinomial regression (SMR) methods.  All ML methods, employing data for 20 elements and 5 isotopic ratios, successfully discriminated between igneous rocks formed in the eight settings, achieving a discriminant ratio exceeding 83% for all settings except oceanic plateaus and back-arc basins.  SMR, particularly powerful and interpretable, quantitatively identifies geochemical signatures characterizing the tectonic settings of interest and provides membership probabilities for each sample in each setting.  We also present the most representative basalt composition for each tectonic setting, offering reference points for future geochemical discussions.  Our results highlight the need for at least 17 elements and isotopic ratios to characterize each tectonic setting, suggesting that geochemical tectonic discrimination cannot be achieved using only a limited number of elements or isotopes.  The findings indicate unique geochemical signatures for volcanic rocks formed in different tectonic settings, reflecting the close connection between volcanic rock geochemistry, magma generation processes, and tectonic setting.

title: Stratified Transfer Learning for Cross-domain Activity Recognition
Abstract: Activity recognition often requires expensive and time-consuming acquisition of sufficient activity labels.  Transfer learning addresses this challenge by leveraging labeled samples from a source domain to annotate the target domain with limited or no labels. Existing approaches typically focus on global domain shift, neglecting the intra-affinity between classes, which hinders performance.  We propose a novel and general cross-domain learning framework, Stratified Transfer Learning (STL), exploiting the intra-affinity of classes to perform intra-class knowledge transfer.  STL significantly enhances classification accuracy in cross-domain activity recognition.  Specifically, STL first obtains pseudo labels for the target domain using majority voting.  It then iteratively performs intra-class knowledge transfer, transforming both domains into the same subspaces. Finally, target domain labels are acquired through a second annotation.  Extensive experiments on three large public activity recognition datasets (OPPORTUNITY, PAMAP2, and UCI DSADS) demonstrate that STL outperforms other state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 7.68% improvement in classification accuracy.  We further investigate STL's performance across different degrees of similarity and activity levels between domains, exploring its potential in other pervasive computing applications for future research.

title: Null Dynamical State Models of Human Cognitive Dysfunction
Abstract: The hard problem in artificial intelligence explores how the shuffling of syntactical symbols in a program can lead to systems experiencing semantics and qualia. We address this question in three stages. First, we introduce a new class of human semantic symbols that emerges when unexpected and drastic environmental changes cause humans to experience surprise, confusion, uncertainty, and in extreme cases, unresponsiveness, passivity, and dysfunction. For this class of symbols, pre-learned programs become inoperative, indicating that they cannot be the source of experienced qualia. Second, we model the dysfunctional human response to radically changed environments as the natural response of any learning machine encountering novel inputs far outside its previous training set.  In this situation, learning machines are unable to extract information from their input and typically enter a dynamical state characterized by null outputs and a lack of response. This state directly predicts and explains the characteristics of human semantic experiences in similar circumstances. Third, we consider learning machines trained to implement multiple functions in simple sequential programs, using environmental data to specify subroutine names, control flow instructions, memory calls, etc.  Drastic changes in any of these environmental inputs can again lead to inoperative programs. By examining changes specific to people or locations, we can model human cognitive symbols featuring these dependencies, such as attachment and grief. Our approach links known dynamical machine states with human qualia, offering new insights into the hard problem of artificial intelligence.

title: Stochastic Multi-armed Bandits in Constant Space
Abstract: We address the stochastic bandit problem within the sublinear space setting, where recording the win-loss record for all $K$ arms is infeasible.  We present an algorithm requiring $O(1)$ words of space with regret \[\sum_{i=1}^{K}\frac{1}{\Delta_i}\log \frac{\Delta_i}{\Delta}\log T \], where $\Delta_i$ represents the gap between the best arm and arm $i$, and $\Delta$ is the gap between the best and second-best arms. If the rewards are bounded away from 0 and 1, this regret is within an $O(\log 1/\Delta)$ factor of the optimal regret achievable without space constraints.

title: Efficient Algorithms for t-distributed Stochastic Neighborhood Embedding
Abstract: t-Distributed Stochastic Neighborhood Embedding (t-SNE) is a widely popular dimensionality reduction and visualization method. While efficient implementations exist, they scale poorly to datasets with hundreds of thousands to millions of high-dimensional data points. We introduce Fast Fourier Transform-accelerated Interpolation-based t-SNE (FIt-SNE), significantly accelerating t-SNE computation.  The most time-consuming step of t-SNE, a convolution, is accelerated by interpolating onto an equispaced grid and employing the fast Fourier transform.  We also optimize the computation of input similarities in high dimensions using multi-threaded approximate nearest neighbors.  We further present "late exaggeration," a modification to t-SNE that facilitates cluster identification in t-SNE embeddings. For datasets exceeding memory capacity, we introduce out-of-core randomized principal component analysis (oocPCA), allowing computation of the top principal components without fully loading the matrix, enabling t-SNE of large datasets on resource-limited machines.

title: RIDI: Robust IMU Double Integration
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel data-driven approach for inertial navigation, learning to estimate trajectories of natural human motions using only an inertial measurement unit (IMU) in every smartphone.  The core observation is that human motions are repetitive and consist of a few major modes (e.g., standing, walking, or turning). Our algorithm regresses a velocity vector from the history of linear accelerations and angular velocities, then corrects low-frequency bias in linear accelerations, which are integrated twice to estimate positions.  We acquired training data with ground-truth motions across multiple human subjects and phone placements.  Qualitative and quantitative evaluations demonstrate that our algorithm surprisingly achieves results comparable to full visual inertial navigation.  To our knowledge, this is the first study integrating sophisticated machine learning techniques with inertial navigation, potentially opening a new line of research in data-driven inertial navigation.  We will publicly share our code and data to facilitate further research. |||

title: Kernel Regression with Sparse Metric Learning
Abstract: Kernel regression is a prevalent non-parametric technique used for function estimation. It estimates target values for new inputs by calculating a weighted average of nearby training examples. The weights are determined by a kernel function, which depends on the distances between examples. This paper introduces a novel kernel regression method, termed kernel regression with sparse metric learning (KR_SML), which leverages advancements in sparse metric learning. KR_SML employs a mixed (2,1)-norm regularization on the metric matrix to learn a Mahalanobis distance metric. This gradient descent procedure effectively reduces dimensionality and improves prediction accuracy. Our work represents the first integration of sparse metric learning into kernel regression. Its effectiveness is validated on 19 regression datasets and demonstrated in practical short-term traffic flow forecasting scenarios. Comparisons with three related kernel regression methods on various datasets indicate the superiority of KR_SML.

title: Android Malware Detection using Deep Learning on API Method Sequences
Abstract: The widespread adoption of Android has made it vulnerable to malicious applications. MalDozer is a novel framework for automatic Android malware detection and family attribution using deep learning. Analyzing sequences of app API calls, MalDozer identifies malicious patterns to detect malware. Its portability allows for deployment on servers, mobile devices, and even IoT devices. Evaluation on datasets containing thousands of malware and benign apps showcases MalDozer's effectiveness, achieving F1-Scores of 96%-99% and a low false positive rate of 0.06%-2%.

title: Network-Scale Traffic Modeling and Forecasting with Graphical Lasso and Neural Networks
Abstract: Accurately forecasting short-term traffic flow is crucial for intelligent transportation systems. This paper investigates network-scale traffic flow forecasting models, proposing single-link and multi-link models combined with single-task and multi-task learning. Integrating multi-link models with multi-task learning enhances both efficiency and accuracy. Furthermore, a novel multi-link single-task approach combining graphical lasso (GL) with neural networks (NN) is presented. GL utilizes L1 regularization to construct sparse graphical models based on the sparse inverse covariance matrix. Gaussian process regression (GPR), a classic Bayesian machine learning technique, is also applied to traffic flow forecasting, demonstrating its potential. Comprehensive experiments compare the proposed methods, providing a comprehensive assessment of their performance.

title: Leveraging Native Language Speech for Accent Identification using Deep Siamese Networks
Abstract: Automatic accent identification is essential for applications like speaker profiling, recognition, and speech recognition system improvement. Accent variation stems from the influence of a speaker's native language on their speech. This paper presents a novel accent identification system that leverages both native and accented speech during training. A deep Siamese network model learns associations between accented speech recordings and their corresponding native language recordings. The Siamese networks are trained using i-vector features extracted from speech recordings, employing either unsupervised Gaussian mixture models (GMM) or supervised deep neural networks (DNN). Experiments conducted on the CSLU Foreign Accented English (FAE) corpus demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving significant performance improvements compared to baseline DNN-based systems.  A detailed error analysis of the proposed system further strengthens its robustness.

title: Smart Fog: Fog Computing Framework for Unsupervised Clustering Analytics in Wearable Internet of Things
Abstract: The rise of wearable technology in smart telehealth generates vast amounts of heterogeneous medical data. Cloud and fog computing services process this data to support clinical procedures. This paper explores the use of low-resource machine learning on fog devices, positioned closer to wearables, to enhance smart healthcare. Instead of relying solely on cloud-based processing, a fog-based unsupervised machine learning architecture is proposed for analyzing physiological data. Intel Edison and Raspberry Pi serve as fog computers in this architecture. Validation studies on real-world pathological speech data from Parkinson's disease (PD) patients demonstrate the architecture's potential. This architecture utilizes machine learning to analyze speech data acquired from smartwatches worn by PD patients, highlighting its applicability for low-resource clinical machine learning. The proposed architecture holds promise for other wearable IoT applications in smart telehealth scenarios, transitioning machine learning from cloud-based to edge computing devices.

title: Learning to Run with Actor-Critic Ensemble
Abstract: This paper introduces an Actor-Critic Ensemble (ACE) method for enhancing the performance of the Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) algorithm. During inference, ACE utilizes a critic ensemble to select the best action from proposals generated by multiple actors operating in parallel. This approach expands the set of candidate actions, preventing potentially detrimental actions while maintaining determinism. ACE contributed to a second-place finish in the NIPS'17 Learning to Run competition under the team name "Megvii-hzwer".

title: On Statistical Optimality of Variational Bayes
Abstract: This paper addresses the long-standing problem of justifying the use of variational Bayes methods for parameter estimation. It establishes general conditions for obtaining optimal risk bounds for point estimates derived from mean-field variational Bayesian inference. These conditions relate to the existence of specific test functions for the distance metric on the parameter space and minimal assumptions on the prior. A general recipe for verifying these conditions is outlined, applicable to existing Bayesian models with or without latent variables. The paper illustrates these principles through applications to Latent Dirichlet Allocation and Gaussian mixture models.

title: Mean Field Residual Networks: On the Edge of Chaos
Abstract: This paper analyzes randomly initialized residual networks using mean field theory and difference equations. Classical feedforward neural networks exhibit exponential behavior when propagating inputs forward or gradients backward. This leads to rapid collapsing of the input space geometry and vanishing/exploding gradients. The paper demonstrates that residual networks, through the addition of skip connections, exhibit subexponential or even polynomial forward and backward dynamics, depending on the nonlinearity. Analytical methods are used to determine the exponents of these polynomials, which are verified empirically. These subexponential and polynomial laws allow residual networks to "hover over the boundary between stability and chaos," preserving input space geometry and gradient information flow. Experiments on MNIST with different hyperparameters and activation functions show that the initialization time theory accurately predicts test time performance. The paper also shows that commonly used initializations like Xavier or He schemes are not optimal for residual networks. Finally, new identities for the kernels of powers of ReLU functions are derived, relating them to the zeroth Bessel function of the second kind.

title: Spurious Local Minima are Common in Two-Layer ReLU Neural Networks
Abstract: This paper examines the optimization problem associated with training simple ReLU neural networks. It provides a computer-assisted proof that spurious local minima can exist even with a standard Gaussian input distribution, arbitrarily large dimensions, and target values generated by a network with orthonormal parameter vectors. This result holds for networks with 6 ≤ k ≤ 20 neurons. A concentration of measure argument suggests that nearly all target networks of these sizes exhibit spurious local minima in high input dimensions. Experiments confirm the high probability of encountering these local minima, which increases with network size. However, the paper also finds that mild over-parameterization significantly reduces the occurrence of spurious local minima, highlighting its necessity for positive results in this setting.

title: Machine learning technique for morphological classification of galaxies from the SDSS. I. Photometry-based approach
Abstract: This paper explores the application of machine learning techniques to galaxy morphological classification. It compares the performance of human labeling, multi-photometry diagrams, and various supervised machine learning methods, including Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine, Random Forest, and k-Nearest Neighbors. The study focuses on a sample of galaxies from the SDSS DR9 with specific redshift and absolute magnitude ranges. Using features like absolute magnitudes, color indices, and inverse concentration index, the Support Vector Machine classifier achieved the highest accuracy, correctly classifying 96.4% of galaxies. Random Forest demonstrated comparable performance with 95.5% accuracy. These findings highlight the effectiveness of machine learning algorithms for automated galaxy classification.

title: Player-Compatible Learning and Player-Compatible Equilibrium
Abstract: Player-Compatible Equilibrium (PCE) introduces restrictions on the magnitudes of players' "trembles" onto different strategies, capturing the idea that trembles represent deliberate experiments by agents uncertain about the prevailing distribution of play. Unlike trembling-hand perfect equilibrium and proper equilibrium, PCE selects intuitive equilibria in various scenarios. The paper demonstrates that rational learning and weighted fictitious play imply PCE's compatibility restrictions in a steady-state setting.

title: Judicious Judgment Meets Unsettling Updating: Dilation, Sure Loss, and Simpson's Paradox
Abstract: This paper delves into statistical learning with imprecise probabilities, which offers an alternative approach to reducing irreplicable findings by minimizing unwarranted assumptions. However, model updating, a mathematical operation, remains inherently exact. Updating imprecise models requires user judgment in choosing among competing updating rules. These rules often lead to incompatible inferences and exhibit phenomena like dilation, contraction, and sure loss, absent in the Bayes rule with precise probabilities. The paper re-examines famous "paradoxes," revealing that a logical fallacy arises from seemingly plausible yet jointly incompatible assumptions when updating imprecise models. It establishes an equivalence between Simpson's paradox and the implicit use of aggregation rules that induce sure loss. The paper also explores discrepancies between the generalized Bayes rule, Dempster's rule, and the Geometric rule as alternative posterior updating rules for Choquet capacities. It reveals that the generalized Bayes rule and Geometric rule are unable to update without prior information, while Dempster's rule and the Geometric rule can contradict each other regarding dilation and contraction. The findings emphasize the importance of careful judgment when handling low-resolution information and applying learning rules to update imprecise probabilities.

title: A Survey of FPGA-Based Neural Network Accelerator
Abstract: Neural networks have demonstrated significant advantages over traditional machine learning algorithms based on handcrafted features and models. Their widespread adoption in image, speech, and video recognition is challenged by high computational and storage complexities during inference. CPUs lack the required processing power, while GPUs offer a viable solution due to their high computation capacity and user-friendly development frameworks. This paper explores FPGA-based neural network inference accelerators as a potential alternative to GPUs. FPGAs, with their specifically designed hardware, offer potential for exceeding GPU speed and energy efficiency. The paper reviews previous work on FPGA-based accelerators and summarizes the main optimization techniques employed. A comprehensive analysis from software to hardware, covering circuit and system levels, provides insights into FPGA-based accelerator design and serves as a guide for future work.

title: Deep Learning for Massive MIMO CSI Feedback
Abstract: In frequency division duplex (FDD) systems, downlink channel state information (CSI) must be sent to the base station through feedback links to realize the full potential of massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO). However, excessive feedback overhead hinders this transmission. This paper introduces CsiNet, a novel CSI sensing and recovery mechanism that leverages deep learning to learn channel structure from training samples. CsiNet learns transformations between CSI and a near-optimal number of representations (codewords) and vice versa. Experiments demonstrate that CsiNet significantly improves CSI reconstruction quality compared to existing compressive sensing (CS)-based methods. Even at very low compression levels where CS-based methods fail, CsiNet maintains effective beamforming gain.

title: Building a Sentiment Corpus of Tweets in Brazilian Portuguese
Abstract: The abundance of data on social media, forums, and websites fuels research in Natural Language Processing (NLP), particularly in sentiment analysis. This paper introduces TweetSentBR, a sentiment corpora for Brazilian Portuguese, manually annotated with 15,000 sentences from the TV show domain. Seven annotators labeled these sentences into three classes (positive, neutral, negative) following established guidelines for ensuring annotation reliability. Baseline experiments on polarity classification using three machine learning methods demonstrate promising results, achieving 80.99% F-Measure and 82.06% accuracy in binary classification, and 59.85% F-Measure and 64.62% accuracy in three-point classification.

title: Bayesian Nonparametric Causal Inference: Information Rates and Learning Algorithms
Abstract: This paper investigates the estimation of causal effects of treatments on individual subjects from observational data. It utilizes the Neyman-Rubin potential outcomes model and measures estimation accuracy using the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the estimated and true distributions. The information rate of the Bayesian causal inference procedure is defined as the expected value of the KL divergence. Using the Fano method, the paper establishes a fundamental limit on the information rate achievable by any Bayesian estimator, independent of selection bias in the observational data. It characterizes Bayesian priors that achieve the optimal information rate, showing that a widely used class of priors falls short of optimality. A broader class of priors, however, can achieve the optimal information rate. The paper proposes a prior adaptation procedure, named the information based empirical Bayes procedure, which optimizes the Bayesian prior by maximizing an information-theoretic criterion on the recovered causal effects rather than maximizing the marginal likelihood of the observed data. Based on this analysis, the paper constructs an information-optimal Bayesian causal inference algorithm.

title: Weighted Data Normalization Based on Eigenvalues for Artificial Neural Network Classification
Abstract: This paper presents a novel method for improving the performance of Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) by preprocessing the raw data. Recognizing that different features play varying roles, the method leverages Principle Component Analysis (PCA) to preprocess the data and then weights the principal components by their corresponding eigenvalues. Theoretical and practical aspects are analyzed, and the method's effectiveness is validated on three classification problems using an active learning algorithm. Empirical results demonstrate significant performance improvements in ANNs.

title: Optimal Weighting for Exam Composition
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework that uses machine learning algorithms to optimize exam question weights based on overall class grade as a proxy for student ability. By adjusting weights, the framework aims to improve the accuracy of exam scores. Experiments demonstrate significant error reduction compared to standard weighting schemes, identifying "good" and "bad" exam questions that can inform future evaluation methods.

title: Maximizing the Collective Learning Effects in Regional Economic Development
Abstract: Recent studies have revealed the presence of collective learning effects in economic development, but research on maximizing these effects remains limited. This paper explores the maximization of collective learning effects using a propagation model to study the diversification of industries on real networks built on Brazilian labor data. For inter-regional learning, the optimal strategy involves balancing core and periphery industries during initial activation, considering the core-periphery structure of the industry space. For inter-regional learning, the optimal strategy focuses on balancing connections between nearby and distant regions, taking into account the spatial structure of the integrated adjacent network. Findings suggest that near-to-random strategies are likely to maximize collective learning effects, promoting regional economic development. |||

title: Predicting Rich Drug-Drug Interactions via Biomedical Knowledge Graphs and Text Jointly Embedding
Abstract: Minimizing adverse reactions caused by drug-drug interactions is a significant research area in clinical pharmacology. While clinical trials can detect some interactions before drug release, the sheer number of potential combinations makes this process challenging. Big data offers new opportunities for uncovering drug-drug interactions, but the resulting data is often noisy and incomplete. Existing research primarily focuses on predicting binary interactions between drug pairs, neglecting other types of interactions. This paper proposes a novel framework, called PRD, for predicting drug-drug interactions. The framework utilizes graph embedding to address issues of data incompleteness and sparsity, enabling the prediction of multiple DDI labels. It generates a large-scale drug knowledge graph from various sources and embeds it into a low-dimensional space using comprehensive biomedical text. The learned embeddings are then employed to efficiently compute rich DDI information through a link prediction process. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of PRD, demonstrating superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baseline methods in terms of capability and accuracy.

title: Neural Network Multitask Learning for Traffic Flow Forecasting
Abstract: Traditional neural network approaches for traffic flow forecasting typically employ single-task learning (STL) models, which fail to leverage information from related tasks. In contrast, multi-task learning (MTL) has the potential to improve generalization by transferring information across training signals. This paper explores the use of MTL-based neural networks for traffic flow forecasting. A backpropagation (BP) network incorporating traffic flows at multiple contiguous time instants into an output layer is constructed. Nodes in the output layer represent outputs of different but closely related STL tasks. Comprehensive experiments on urban vehicular traffic flow data, compared to STL, show that MTL in BP neural networks is a promising and effective approach for traffic flow forecasting.
label: AI

title: Whatever Does Not Kill Deep Reinforcement Learning, Makes It Stronger
Abstract: Recent advancements have highlighted the vulnerability of deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) to policy manipulation attacks through adversarial perturbations. This paper investigates the robustness and resilience of deep RL to training-time and test-time attacks. Experimental results demonstrate that under noncontiguous training-time attacks, Deep Q-Network (DQN) agents can recover and adapt to adversarial conditions by adjusting their policy. Findings also suggest that policies learned under adversarial perturbations exhibit greater robustness to test-time attacks. Furthermore, the study compares the performance of ε-greedy and parameter-space noise exploration methods in terms of robustness and resilience against adversarial perturbations.

title: Let's Make Block Coordinate Descent Converge Faster: Faster Greedy Rules, Message-Passing, Active-Set Complexity, and Superlinear Convergence
Abstract: Block coordinate descent (BCD) methods are widely employed for large-scale numerical optimization due to their low computational cost, modest memory requirements, parallelization capabilities, and ability to exploit problem structure. Three primary algorithmic choices influence BCD performance: block partitioning strategy, block selection rule, and block update rule. This paper explores variations for each of these building blocks to significantly improve the progress made by each BCD iteration. The study (i) proposes novel greedy block-selection strategies guaranteeing more progress per iteration than the Gauss-Southwell rule, (ii) examines practical considerations for implementing these rules with "variable" blocks, (iii) investigates the use of message-passing for efficient matrix or Newton updates on large blocks for problems with sparse dependencies between variables, and (iv) explores optimal active manifold identification, leading to bounds on the "active-set complexity" of BCD methods and achieving superlinear convergence for specific problems with sparse solutions. Numerical results for classic machine learning problems like least squares, logistic regression, multi-class logistic regression, label propagation, and L1-regularization support the findings.

title: Towards Collaborative Conceptual Exploration
Abstract: In domains characterized by extensive knowledge distribution, a natural objective is to establish foundational principles for collaborative interactive learning environments. This paper presents the first mathematical characterization of a collaborative learning group, a consortium, based on closure systems of attribute sets and the well-known attribute exploration algorithm from formal concept analysis. The study introduces (weak) local experts for subdomains of a given knowledge domain. These entities can refute or accept a given (implicational) query for a closure system that is a restriction of the whole domain. Building on this, the paper defines a consortial expert and provides initial insights into its ability to answer queries. Furthermore, the study outlines techniques for addressing falsely accepted implications and combining counterexamples. Leveraging concepts from combinatorial design theory, the paper expands these insights to provide preliminary results on the decidability problem of whether a given consortium can explore a target domain. Applications in conceptual knowledge acquisition and collaborative interactive ontology learning are discussed.

title: Transfer Regression via Pairwise Similarity Regularization
Abstract: Transfer learning methods address the scenario where limited labeled training data exists for the "target" problem but abundant training data is available from a related "source" domain. However, most transfer learning methods are designed for simple settings where source and target predictive functions are nearly identical, limiting their applicability to real-world data. This paper proposes a novel, weaker property of the source domain that can be transferred even when source and target predictive functions diverge. The method assumes that source and target functions share a Pairwise Similarity property, meaning that if the source function makes similar predictions on a pair of instances, then the target function will also make similar predictions. The study introduces Pairwise Similarity Regularization Transfer, a flexible graph-based regularization framework that incorporates this modeling assumption into standard supervised learning algorithms. The paper demonstrates how users can encode domain knowledge into the regularizer in the form of spatial continuity and pairwise "similarity constraints," and how the method can be scaled to large datasets using the Nystrom approximation. Finally, the paper presents positive and negative results on real and synthetic datasets, discussing when the Pairwise Similarity transfer assumption holds in practice.

title: Dual Long Short-Term Memory Networks for Sub-Character Representation Learning
Abstract: Characters have traditionally been considered the minimal processing unit in Natural Language Processing (NLP). However, many non-Latin languages have hieroglyphic writing systems with extensive alphabets containing thousands or millions of characters. Each character is composed of smaller parts, often overlooked in previous work. This paper proposes a novel architecture employing two stacked Long Short-Term Memory Networks (LSTMs) to learn sub-character level representation and capture deeper levels of semantic meaning. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this neural architecture, the paper uses Chinese Word Segmentation as a research case. Chinese is a typical example, where each character contains several components called radicals. The networks utilize a shared radical level embedding to address both Simplified and Traditional Chinese Word Segmentation without additional conversion. This end-to-end approach simplifies word segmentation compared to previous methods. Radical level embeddings capture deeper semantic meaning below character level and improve system performance. By tying radical and character embeddings together, the parameter count is reduced, and semantic knowledge is shared and transferred between levels, significantly boosting performance. The proposed method surpasses state-of-the-art results on 3 out of 4 Bakeoff 2005 datasets by up to 0.4%. The results are reproducible, and source codes and corpora are available on GitHub.

title: Optimization and Testing in Linear Non-Gaussian Component Analysis
Abstract: Independent component analysis (ICA) decomposes multivariate data into mutually independent components (ICs). The ICA model is subject to the constraint that at most one component is Gaussian, which is required for model identifiability. Linear non-Gaussian component analysis (LNGCA) generalizes the ICA model to a linear latent factor model with any number of non-Gaussian components (signals) and Gaussian components (noise), where observations are linear combinations of independent components. While individual Gaussian components are not identifiable, the Gaussian subspace is identifiable. This paper introduces an estimator along with its optimization approach that estimates non-Gaussian and Gaussian components simultaneously, maximizing the discrepancy of each non-Gaussian component from Gaussianity while minimizing the discrepancy of each Gaussian component from Gaussianity. When the number of non-Gaussian components is unknown, a statistical test based on resampling and the discrepancy of estimated components is developed to determine it. Through various simulation studies, the paper demonstrates the improvements of the proposed estimator over competing estimators and the effectiveness of the test for determining the number of non-Gaussian components. The method's practical value is illustrated by applying it to real data examples.
label: AI

title: Large-Scale Object Discovery and Detector Adaptation from Unlabeled Video
Abstract: This paper explores object discovery and detector adaptation based on unlabeled video sequences captured from a mobile platform. A fully automatic approach for object mining from video, building upon a generic object tracking approach, is proposed. The study demonstrates the robustness and generality of this method by applying it to three large video datasets from autonomous driving and mobile robotics scenarios. Based on object mining results, a novel approach for unsupervised object discovery through appearance-based clustering is proposed. The paper shows that this approach successfully discovers interesting objects relevant to driving scenarios. Additionally, the study performs self-supervised detector adaptation to improve detection performance on the KITTI dataset for existing categories. The proposed approach has direct relevance for enabling large-scale object learning for autonomous driving.
label: AI

title: A Framework for Enriching Lexical Semantic Resources with Distributional Semantics
Abstract: This paper presents an approach for combining distributional semantic representations induced from text corpora with manually constructed lexical-semantic networks. While both semantic resources offer high lexical coverage, the aligned resource combines domain specificity and contextual information from distributional models with the conciseness and high quality of manually crafted lexical networks. Starting with a distributional representation of induced senses of vocabulary terms, accompanied by rich context information from related lexical items, the study automatically disambiguates these representations to obtain a full-fledged proto-conceptualization, a typed graph of induced word senses. In a final step, this proto-conceptualization is aligned to a lexical ontology, resulting in a hybrid aligned resource. Unmapped induced senses are associated with a semantic type to connect them to the core resource. Manual evaluations against ground-truth judgments for different stages of the method, along with an extrinsic evaluation on a knowledge-based Word Sense Disambiguation benchmark, indicate the high quality of the new hybrid resource. The paper also highlights the benefits of enriching top-down lexical knowledge resources with bottom-up distributional information from text for addressing high-end knowledge acquisition tasks such as cleaning hypernym graphs and learning taxonomies from scratch.

title: Distributed Coupled Multi-Agent Stochastic Optimization
Abstract: This work develops effective distributed strategies for solving constrained multi-agent stochastic optimization problems with coupled parameters across the agents. In this formulation, each agent is influenced by only a subset of the entries of a global parameter vector or model and is subject to convex constraints that are known only locally. Problems of this type arise in various applications, including disease propagation models, minimum-cost flow problems, distributed control formulations, and distributed power system monitoring. The focus is on stochastic settings, where a stochastic risk function is associated with each agent, and the objective is to find the minimizer of the aggregate sum of all risks subject to a set of constraints. Agents are unaware of the statistical distribution of the data and can only rely on stochastic approximations in their learning strategies. The paper derives an effective distributed learning strategy capable of tracking drifts in the underlying parameter model. A detailed performance and stability analysis shows that the resulting coupled diffusion strategy converges at a linear rate to an O(μ)-neighborhood of the true penalized optimizer.
