title: Are words easier to learn from infant- than adult-directed speech? A quantitative corpus-based investigation
Abstract: This study investigates whether infant-directed speech (IDS) facilitates word form learning compared to adult-directed speech (ADS). The analysis examines the distribution of word forms at two levels: acoustic and phonological, using a large database of spontaneous speech in Japanese. At the acoustic level, the study confirms previous findings for phonemes, showing that word realizations are more variable and less discriminable in IDS than in ADS. At the phonological level, an opposite effect is observed: the IDS lexicon contains more distinctive words (such as onomatopoeias) than the ADS counterpart. Combining acoustic and phonological metrics into a global discriminability score reveals that the greater separation of lexical categories in the phonological space does not compensate for the opposite effect observed at the acoustic level. As a result, IDS word forms remain globally less discriminable than ADS word forms, although the effect is numerically small. The study discusses the implications of these findings for the view that the functional role of IDS is to enhance language learnability.
label: AI

title: Merging $K$-means with hierarchical clustering for identifying general-shaped groups
Abstract: Clustering partitions a dataset into groups where observations within a group are similar but different from those in other groups. Hierarchical and K-means clustering are two approaches with distinct strengths and weaknesses. Hierarchical clustering identifies groups in a tree-like structure but suffers from computational complexity in large datasets, while K-means clustering is efficient but designed to identify homogeneous spherically-shaped clusters. This paper presents a hybrid non-parametric clustering approach that combines these two methods to identify general-shaped clusters applicable to larger datasets. The proposed method first partitions the dataset into spherical groups using K-means. These groups are then merged using hierarchical methods with a data-driven distance measure as a stopping criterion. The proposal has the potential to reveal groups with general shapes and structure in a dataset. The study demonstrates good performance on several simulated and real datasets.
label: AI

title: An Approximate Bayesian Long Short-Term Memory Algorithm for Outlier Detection
Abstract: Long Short-Term Memory networks trained with gradient descent and backpropagation have achieved significant success in various applications. However, point estimation of network weights is prone to overfitting problems and lacks important uncertainty information associated with the estimation. While exact Bayesian neural network methods are intractable and unsuitable for real-world applications, this study proposes an approximate estimation of weight uncertainty using Ensemble Kalman Filter, which is easily scalable to a large number of weights. The study further optimizes the covariance of the noise distribution in the ensemble update step using maximum likelihood estimation. The proposed algorithm's effectiveness is assessed by applying it to outlier detection in five real-world events retrieved from the Twitter platform.
label: AI

title: Learning-Based Computation Offloading for IoT Devices with Energy Harvesting
Abstract: Internet of Things (IoT) devices can leverage mobile-edge computing (MEC) and energy harvesting (EH) to provide satisfactory quality of experience for computation-intensive applications and extend battery life. This paper investigates computation offloading for IoT devices with energy harvesting in wireless networks with multiple MEC devices, such as base stations and access points, each with varying computation resources and radio communication capabilities. The study proposes a reinforcement learning-based computation offloading framework for an IoT device to select the MEC device and determine the offloading rate based on the current battery level, previous radio bandwidth to each MEC device, and the predicted amount of harvested energy. A "hotbooting" Q-learning-based computation offloading scheme is proposed for an IoT device to achieve optimal offloading performance without knowing the MEC model, energy consumption, and computation latency model. The paper also presents a fast deep Q-network (DQN)-based offloading scheme, combining deep learning and hotbooting techniques to accelerate the learning speed of Q-learning. The study shows that the proposed schemes achieve optimal offloading policy after sufficient learning time and provide performance bounds under two typical MEC scenarios. Simulations are performed for IoT devices using wireless power transfer to capture ambient radio-frequency signals for battery charging. Simulation results demonstrate that the fast DQN-based offloading scheme reduces energy consumption, decreases computation delay and task drop ratio, and increases the utility of the IoT device in dynamic MEC compared to benchmark Q-learning-based offloading.
label: AI

title: On Estimation of Conditional Modes Using Multiple Quantile Regressions
Abstract: This paper proposes an estimation method for the conditional mode when the conditioning variable is high-dimensional. The proposed method first estimates the conditional density by solving quantile regressions multiple times. The conditional mode is then estimated by finding the maximum of the estimated conditional density. The proposed method offers two advantages: computational stability due to the absence of initial parameter dependencies and statistical efficiency with a fast convergence rate. Synthetic and real-world data experiments demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed method compared to existing approaches.
label: AI

title: Multidisciplinary learning at the University scientific museums: the Bunsen burner
Abstract: This paper reports on a laboratory activity conducted with secondary school (high-school) students aimed at increasing their interest in historical scientific instruments and stimulating their scientific approach. The study proposes a hands-on activity that can be effectively performed at university scientific museums. A one-week summer stage was organized at the Historical Collection of Physics Instruments and the Museum of Chemistry of the University of Palermo. A group of selected students attended the stage, guided by university researchers. The students were shown Bunsen burners from the collections, how they are restored, how they work, and how they were used in chemical laboratories. At the end of the stage, students introduced museum visitors to these instruments, describing them and discussing their activities.
label: AI

title: Online Forecasting Matrix Factorization
Abstract: This paper addresses the problem of forecasting high-dimensional time series, modeled as matrices where each column represents a measurement. When missing values are present, low-rank matrix factorization approaches are suitable for predicting future values. The paper formally defines and analyzes the forecasting problem in the online setting, where data arrives as a stream, and only a single pass is allowed. Novel matrix factorization techniques are presented and analyzed, enabling effective learning of low-dimensional embeddings in an online manner. Based on these embeddings, a recursive minimum mean square error estimator is derived, learning an autoregressive model on them. Experiments with two real datasets containing tens of millions of measurements demonstrate the benefits of the proposed approach.
label: AI

title: Combining Weakly and Webly Supervised Learning for Classifying Food Images
Abstract: Food classification from images is a fine-grained classification problem. Manual curation of food images is expensive, time-consuming, and difficult to scale. While web data is readily available, it often contains noise. This paper addresses the problem of classifying food images with minimal data curation. The study also tackles a key challenge with web-sourced food images, where multiple food types often co-occur but are weakly labeled with a single label. The paper demonstrates that sequentially adding a few manually curated samples to a larger uncurated dataset from two web sources increases the top-1 classification accuracy from 50.3% to 72.8%. To address the issue of weak labels, the deep model is augmented with Weakly Supervised Learning (WSL), resulting in a performance improvement to 76.2%. Qualitative results are presented to provide insights into the performance enhancements using the proposed ideas.
label: AI

title: Denoising of 3D magnetic resonance images with multi-channel residual learning of convolutional neural network
Abstract: Denoising magnetic resonance (MR) images is crucial for improving acquired image quality. Numerous methods have been proposed to retrieve noise-free images with good performance. However, state-of-the-art denoising methods require time-consuming optimization processes, and their performance heavily depends on the estimated noise level parameter. This manuscript proposes denoising MRI Rician noise using a convolutional neural network. The proposed methodology's advantage is that the learning-based model can be directly used in the denoising process without optimization or the noise level parameter. Specifically, a ten-convolutional layer neural network combined with residual learning and a multi-channel strategy is proposed. Two training approaches, training on a specific noise level and training on a general level, are conducted to demonstrate the capabilities of the methods. Experimental results on synthetic and real 3D MR data show that the proposed network achieves superior performance compared to other methods in terms of both peak signal-to-noise ratio and the global structural similarity index. Without the noise level parameter, the general noise-applicable model also outperforms other compared methods in two datasets. Furthermore, the training model demonstrates good general applicability. |||
label: AI

title: Query-limited Black-box Attacks to Classifiers
Abstract: Minimizing query cost in black-box attacks on machine learning classifiers is a critical challenge. This work focuses on minimizing the number of queries needed to attack a classifier while adhering to a budget for feature modification cost. The proposed approach uses Bayesian optimization to efficiently identify optimal attacks, significantly reducing the required queries (up to 90%) compared to random strategies, especially for low budget scenarios.
label: AI

title: Variational Autoencoders for Learning Latent Representations of Speech Emotion: A Preliminary Study
Abstract: Unsupervised learning of latent data representations provides valuable features for improving classifier performance. This study proposes using Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) to learn latent representations of speech signals for emotion recognition. This novel application of VAEs, which have proven successful in image processing,  achieves state-of-the-art results on the IEMOCAP dataset for speech emotion classification.
label: AI

title: On the Universality of Memcomputing Machines
Abstract: Universal Memcomputing Machines (UMMs) offer a unique computational model where memory serves both storage and processing functions. This paper establishes the computational equivalence of UMMs to both Liquid-State Machines (reservoir computing) and Quantum Machines (quantum computing) using set theory and cardinality arguments. While UMMs can simulate these models, this analysis addresses their computational capabilities, not resource efficiency, providing a framework for understanding UMMs within various computational paradigms.
label: AI

title: Interpretable Counting for Visual Question Answering
Abstract: Visual Question Answering (VQA) systems struggle with questions requiring object counting in images. This paper presents a novel approach that treats counting as a sequential decision process, forcing the model to make discrete choices about what to count. The model sequentially selects objects and learns their interactions, enabling intuitive and interpretable outputs with automatic grounding in the image. This approach outperforms state-of-the-art VQA architectures on multiple counting-related metrics.
label: AI

title: Aerial Spectral Super-Resolution using Conditional Adversarial Networks
Abstract: Inferring spectral signatures from ground-based images has become a popular application of deep learning. However, aerial spectral images suffer from low spatial resolution and high noise. This paper proposes a conditional adversarial network that learns an inverse mapping from a trichromatic space to 31 spectral bands within the 400-700 nm range. The network is trained on AeroCampus, a novel aerial hyperspectral dataset, and achieves a baseline root mean square error of 2.48 on synthesized RGB test data, demonstrating the feasibility of generating spectral signatures in aerial imagery.
label: AI

title: Sampling for Approximate Bipartite Network Projection
Abstract: Bipartite networks often exhibit a stream of edges representing transactions (e.g., retail purchases), where similarity among nodes is commonly measured using neighborhood-based metrics. This paper introduces a weighted sampling algorithm that efficiently estimates the similarity matrix from a bipartite graph stream projection. The algorithm maintains a reservoir of sampled edges, prioritizing high-similarity nodes, and generates similarity updates from arriving edges. These updates are aggregated in a second reservoir, resulting in an unbiased estimate. Experiments on real-world graphs show that a 10% sample at each stage yields accurate estimates of high-similarity edges.
label: AI

title: RelSifter: Scoring Triples from Type-like Relations - The Samphire Triple Scorer at WSDM Cup 2017
Abstract: This work presents RelSifter, a supervised learning approach for assigning relevance scores to triples expressing type-like relations (e.g., profession, nationality). By integrating information from Wikidata and DBpedia, two large-scale knowledge graphs, RelSifter analyzes typical "activities" associated with specific types (e.g., actors starring in movies, scientists with academic affiliations) to predict relevance scores. The approach achieves accuracies of 73% and 78% for profession and nationality triples respectively, demonstrating its effectiveness in evaluating facts despite data skewness.
label: AI

title: Relevance Scoring of Triples Using Ordinal Logistic Classification - The Celosia Triple Scorer at WSDM Cup 2017
Abstract: This paper describes the authors' participation in the WSDM Cup 2017 Task 2: Triple Scoring. The task involved predicting relevance scores (0-7) for triples with type-like relations (profession, nationality). The authors developed a supervised machine learning model using well-designed features and Logistic Ordinal Regression for classification. The system achieved an overall accuracy of 0.73 and a Kendall's tau score of 0.36.
label: AI

title: A Mixture of Matrix Variate Bilinear Factor Analyzers
Abstract: High-dimensional data necessitates dimension reduction techniques, especially in clustering and classification tasks. While dimension reduction for multivariate data has been well-studied, three-way (matrix variate) data remains relatively unexplored. This paper proposes a mixture of matrix variate bilinear factor analyzers (MMVBFA) model for clustering high-dimensional matrix variate data. This work introduces both the first matrix variate bilinear factor analysis model and the first MMVBFA model, discussing parameter estimation and illustrating its application with simulated and real data.
label: AI

title: A short variational proof of equivalence between policy gradients and soft Q learning
Abstract: Recent research has demonstrated the equivalence of Q-learning and policy gradients under specific conditions. This paper connects this equivalence to the convex duality of Shannon entropy and the softmax function, known as the Donsker-Varadhan formula, providing a concise proof. Furthermore, the paper leverages convex analysis to derive a new policy inequality relative to soft Q-learning.
label: AI

title: Dropout Feature Ranking for Deep Learning Models
Abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), while achieving state-of-the-art performance, lack interpretability, limiting their use in hypothesis-driven domains. This paper introduces a novel feature ranking method for DNNs, aiming to enhance interpretability and facilitate resource-efficient feature selection. The method, simple yet effective, performs competitively with existing feature ranking methods across various datasets and tasks. Its application on a drug response dataset demonstrates the identification of genes relevant to drug response.
label: AI

title: Least-Squares Temporal Difference Learning for the Linear Quadratic Regulator
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has proven successful in continuous control tasks, but its sample complexity for these problems remains largely unexplored. This paper analyzes the performance of RL on the classic Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) problem using the Least-Squares Temporal Difference (LSTD) estimator. The first finite-time analysis of LSTD for estimating the value function of a fixed state-feedback policy is provided, establishing the number of samples needed to achieve a specific error bound. The paper also generalizes a result on the minimum eigenvalue of the empirical covariance matrix for fast-mixing stochastic processes, supporting the experimental findings.
label: AI

title: Find the Conversation Killers: a Predictive Study of Thread-ending Posts
Abstract: Improving the quality of online conversations has become a critical area of research, with engaged and responsive discussions impacting the social life of internet users. This study focuses on identifying posts unlikely to receive further replies, effectively terminating a conversation thread. The authors propose ConverNet, a deep learning model that effectively captures the internal structure of long conversations and encodes contextual information through attention mechanisms. Empirical experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate ConverNet's effectiveness in predicting conversation termination.
label: AI

title: Predicting protein-protein interactions based on rotation of proteins in 3D-space
Abstract: Protein-protein interactions (PPIs) play crucial roles in biological functions, but experimental techniques for detecting them suffer from high false positive and false negative rates. This work proposes a sequence-based method for predicting PPIs using N-Gram encoding to represent amino acids and a Relaxed Variable Kernel Density Estimator (RVKDE) as a machine learning tool. Considering the undirected nature of amino acid compositions due to protein rotation reduces the dimensionality of the vector space. Results show improved F-measure (2.5%) on the Human Protein Reference Dataset (HPRD), demonstrating the method's predictive superiority.
label: AI

title: Learning Based on CC1 and CC4 Neural Networks
Abstract: This paper argues that a general learning system should incorporate three types of agents representing sensory, short-term, and long-term memory to facilitate both context-free and context-sensitive learning. These agents perform complementary functions, mirroring aspects of human cognition. The paper investigates the use of CC1 and CC4 networks as models for short-term and sensory memory, respectively.
label: AI

title: Obtaining Accurate Probabilistic Causal Inference by Post-Processing Calibration
Abstract: Discovering accurate causal Bayesian network structures from observational data is valuable across various scientific fields. This paper introduces a novel framework for deriving calibrated probabilities of causal relationships from observational data. The framework employs three components: an approximate method for initial probability estimates, a calibration training set with known causal relationships, and a calibration method for generating calibrated probabilities for remaining relationships. A new calibration method based on a shallow neural network is also presented. Experiments on simulated data support the framework's ability to improve calibration, precision, and recall of causal edge predictions.
label: AI

title: Learning in the Machine: the Symmetries of the Deep Learning Channel
Abstract: Biological neural systems require local learning rules in space and time. Non-local information must be communicated to deep synapses through a learning channel. This paper identifies various architectures for this learning channel (Bidirectional, Conjoined, Twin, Distinct) and six symmetry challenges related to architecture, weights, neurons, derivatives, processing, and learning rules. The work addresses the last two symmetries through simulations, demonstrating that random backpropagation (RBP) and its variations can achieve them. These approaches utilize the same non-linear neurons and adaptation algorithms in both forward and backward channels, simplifying implementation. Mathematical results in simple cases support the convergence of learning equations and the symmetry of weights.
label: AI

title: Learning the Kernel for Classification and Regression
Abstract: This paper explores learning kernel problems involving polynomial combinations of base kernels for solving regression and classification tasks. Numerical experiments on various datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of polynomial kernels in both regression and classification scenarios.
label: AI

title: Letter-Based Speech Recognition with Gated ConvNets
Abstract: Traditional phone-based speech recognition systems often require word pronunciation modeling and forced alignment during training. This paper proposes a letter-based speech recognition system leveraging a ConvNet acoustic model with Gated Linear Units and high dropout. The ConvNet maps audio sequences to their letter transcriptions using either CTC or ASG. Coupled with a simple decoder at inference time, the system matches the performance of existing letter-based systems on WSJ and achieves near state-of-the-art performance on LibriSpeech.
label: AI

title: Adaptive Stochastic Dual Coordinate Ascent for Conditional Random Fields
Abstract: This paper investigates the use of the stochastic dual coordinate ascent (SDCA) algorithm for training conditional random fields (CRFs). While SDCA exhibits strong performance and linear convergence in binary classification, its application to CRF training remains unexplored. The authors adapt SDCA to train CRFs and enhance it with an adaptive non-uniform sampling strategy. Experiments on standard sequence prediction tasks demonstrate that SDCA achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods and even outperforms them in cases involving sparse features. |||
label: AI

title: An Incremental Self-Organizing Architecture for Sensorimotor Learning and Prediction
Abstract: Robots executing visuomotor tasks require a mechanism to compensate for inherent delays in their sensorimotor systems.  This is particularly crucial in dynamic environments where visual input constantly changes, such as when interacting with a human demonstrator. To address this challenge, we propose a novel neural network architecture capable of learning prototypical visuomotor representations and generating accurate predictions based on visual input.  These predictions are used in real-time to compensate for motor delays.  We evaluate the performance of our method through experiments involving a humanoid robot tasked with learning and replicating visually observed arm motions. Our results demonstrate the accuracy of the network's predictions, including its ability to adapt to novel movements and handle incomplete data sequences. This indicates the robustness of our architecture even in noisy and imperfect visual sensor conditions.
label: AI

title: The Heisenberg Defense: Proactively Defending SGX Enclaves against Page-Table-Based Side-Channel Attacks
Abstract: Protected-module architectures (PMAs) aim to provide robust isolation guarantees, even on compromised systems. However, the limitations of Intel SGX, the only publicly available high-end PMA, have been exposed, demonstrating only partial isolation.  Attackers exploiting control over untrusted page tables can extract enclave secrets by analyzing page access patterns.  Fortifying existing PMAs against side-channel attacks in real-world settings is an extremely difficult task as system software (hypervisors, operating systems, etc.) must maintain full control over the underlying hardware. Existing solutions often employ a reactive defense mechanism that monitors for attack signatures.  Unfortunately, these approaches struggle to detect novel attacks, suffer from false positives, and burden enclave developers with heavy remediation efforts when attacks are detected.  We introduce Heisenberg, a proactive defense mechanism that guarantees complete protection against page table-based side channels.  We ensure that any attack is either prevented or detected automatically before any sensitive information is leaked.  Heisenberg consistently enables secure resumption of enclave execution, even when the attacker persists in the system. We present two implementations. Heisenberg-HW leverages limited hardware features to defend against page table-based attacks.  This approach, demonstrated on the x86/SGX platform, can be adapted to different platforms supporting protected-module architectures.  Heisenberg-SW avoids hardware modifications and offers immediate applicability. However, its reliance on Intel Transactional Synchronization Extensions (TSX) may introduce significant performance overhead under real-world conditions.
label: AI

title: Diversifying Support Vector Machines for Boosting using Kernel Perturbation: Applications to Class Imbalance and Small Disjuncts
Abstract: Diversifying support vector machines (SVMs) for boosting presents a challenge due to their strong learning nature. We propose two kernel perturbation-based boosting schemes that address this challenge. By modifying the SVM kernel in each round, these schemes aim to enhance the resolution of the kernel-induced Riemannian metric in the vicinity of misclassified data points from the previous round. We introduce a method for identifying disjuncts in a dataset, eliminating the reliance on rule-based methods for this task. We also propose a new performance measure called Geometric Small Disjunct Index (GSDI) to quantify performance on small disjuncts for balanced and imbalanced datasets.  Through an experimental comparison with a wide range of state-of-the-art algorithms, selected using a novel multi-criteria decision-making approach, our proposed method demonstrates superior performance on diverse datasets (ranging from mildly to highly imbalanced and characterized by varying disjunct counts) across three different performance indices, including the GSDI.
label: AI

title: Training and Testing Object Detectors with Virtual Images
Abstract: Deep learning has revolutionized computer vision, yielding state-of-the-art models often reliant on massive labeled datasets.  However, collecting and annotating real-world images is labor-intensive and costly.  Furthermore, building datasets with specific characteristics, such as small objects and high occlusion levels, proves challenging using passive data collection methods.  This paper presents a purposeful approach within the Parallel Vision framework to design artificial scenes and automatically generate virtual images with precise annotations.  We introduce ParallelEye, a virtual dataset designed for various computer vision tasks.  By training both Deformable Parts Models (DPM) and Faster R-CNN detectors, we demonstrate the potential for significantly improving model performance by combining ParallelEye with real-world datasets during the training phase.  Moreover, we explore the utility of intentionally designed virtual datasets for testing trained models from specific perspectives, aiming to uncover model weaknesses.  Our experimental results validate the viability of using virtual datasets to train and test object detectors.
label: AI

title: True Asymptotic Natural Gradient Optimization
Abstract: We present True Asymptotic Natural Gradient Optimization (TANGO), a simple algorithm that converges to a true natural gradient descent in the limit of small learning rates, without requiring explicit Fisher matrix estimation.  For quadratic models, TANGO coincides with averaged stochastic gradient descent, where the parameter is a moving average of a fast, constant-rate gradient descent.  TANGO can be viewed as a particular de-linearization of averaged SGD and often exhibits significant differences for non-quadratic models. This connection further strengthens the link between averaged SGD and natural gradient descent, both arguably optimal asymptotically.  In high-dimensional scenarios, small learning rates are required to accurately approximate the natural gradient. Nevertheless, our findings demonstrate the possibility of achieving arbitrarily close approximation of exact natural gradient descent using a lightweight algorithm.
label: AI

title: Inverse Classification for Comparison-based Interpretability in Machine Learning
Abstract: In the realm of post-hoc interpretability, this paper tackles the task of explaining classifier predictions when no information is available about the classifier itself or the processed data (training or test data). We propose an instance-based approach that identifies minimal changes needed to alter a prediction. Given a data point whose classification requires explanation, our method identifies a closely related but differently classified neighbor.  The definition of closeness incorporates a sparsity constraint.  We implement this principle using observation generation within the Growing Spheres algorithm. Experimental results on two datasets highlight the effectiveness of our approach, which provides valuable insights into the classifier's decision-making process.
label: AI

title: Taking Visual Motion Prediction To New Heightfields
Abstract: While Newtonian mechanics provide fundamental laws, explaining a physical scenario still necessitates manual modeling with appropriate equations and parameter estimation. To leverage the approximation capabilities of artificial intelligence techniques in such physics-related contexts, researchers have resorted to handcrafting relevant states and employing neural networks to learn state transitions using simulation runs as training data.  However, these approaches are unsuitable for complex real-world scenarios where manually defining state spaces becomes tedious and challenging.  This paper investigates whether neural networks can implicitly learn physical states of real-world mechanical processes solely from visual data, internally modeling non-homogeneous environments and enabling long-term physical extrapolation.  We develop a recurrent neural network architecture for this task and characterize resultant uncertainties using evolving variance estimates. We evaluate our system by extrapolating the motion of rolling balls on bowls of varying shapes and orientations, as well as on arbitrary heightfields, using only images as input. Our results demonstrate significant improvements over existing image-based methods in terms of prediction accuracy and scenario complexity, achieving performance comparable to approaches that rely on access to internal physical states, which we do not assume.
label: AI

title: Alchemical and structural distribution based representation for improved QML
Abstract: We introduce a representation for any atom in any chemical environment, enabling the construction of efficient quantum machine learning (QML) models for predicting common electronic ground-state properties.  Our representation utilizes scaled distribution functions that explicitly account for elemental and structural degrees of freedom.  The resulting QML models exhibit favorable learning curves for properties of out-of-sample systems, including organic molecules, non-covalently bonded protein side chains, (H$_2$O)$_{40}$-clusters, and diverse crystals. The inclusion of elemental components contributes to lower learning curves and, through interpolation across the periodic table, even enables "alchemical extrapolation" to predict covalent bonding between elements not included in the training data.  This is evident for single, double, and triple bonds among main-group elements.
label: AI

title: On the Integration of Optical Flow and Action Recognition
Abstract: Many top-performing action recognition methods treat optical flow as a "black box" input. This paper delves deeper into the interplay between optical flow and action recognition, investigating the underlying reasons for its effectiveness, the qualities of a suitable flow method for action recognition, and potential avenues for improvement.  We examine the impact of different flow algorithms and input transformations on a state-of-the-art action recognition method, providing insights into their influence. Furthermore, we fine-tune two neural-network flow methods end-to-end on the widely used UCF101 action recognition dataset.  Based on these experiments, we present five key observations: (1) optical flow is beneficial for action recognition due to its appearance invariance, (2) optical flow methods are optimized to minimize end-point-error (EPE), but current methods exhibit a weak correlation between EPE and action recognition performance, (3) for the tested flow methods, accuracy at boundaries and small displacements is most closely linked to action recognition performance, (4) training optical flow to minimize classification error instead of EPE improves recognition performance, and (5) optical flow learned for action recognition differs significantly from traditional optical flow, particularly within the human body and at its boundaries.  These findings encourage optical flow researchers to explore alternative goals beyond EPE and guide action recognition researchers towards seeking better motion cues, paving the way for a tighter integration between the optical flow and action recognition communities.
label: AI

title: A Compositional Coalgebraic Semantics of Strategic Games
Abstract: We provide a compositional coalgebraic semantics for strategic games.  Our framework, inspired by the semantics of functional programming languages, uses coalgebras to represent the observable behavior of systems derived from the behavior of their constituent parts over an unobservable state space. We utilize coalgebras to describe and program stage games, including finitely and potentially infinitely repeated hierarchical or parallel games with imperfect and incomplete information, based on deterministic, non-deterministic, or probabilistic decisions made by learning agents within potentially endogenous networks.  Our framework is compositional, allowing for the construction of arbitrarily complex networks of games.  The coalgebraic approach enables the representation of self-referential or reflexive structures like institutional dynamics, strategic network formation within the network, belief formation, learning agents, and other self-referential phenomena that characterize complex social systems of cognitive agents.  Finally, our games directly correspond to runnable code in functional programming languages, amenable to analysis by sophisticated verification and logical tools employed in software engineering.
label: AI

title: Music Genre Classification with Paralleling Recurrent Convolutional Neural Network
Abstract: Deep learning has demonstrated effectiveness and efficiency in music genre classification.  However, existing approaches suffer from shortcomings that hinder performance. This paper proposes a hybrid architecture that combines parallel convolutional neural network (CNN) and bidirectional recurrent neural network (Bi-RNN) blocks.  The CNN blocks focus on extracting spatial features, while Bi-RNN blocks capture temporal frame order information.  The outputs from these two blocks are then fused into a powerful representation of musical signals, which is subsequently fed into a softmax function for classification. The parallel network design ensures the robustness of extracted features in representing music.  Our experiments demonstrate that this architecture improves music genre classification performance, with the additional Bi-RNN block serving as a valuable complement to the CNNs.
label: AI

title: Differential geometry and stochastic dynamics with deep learning numerics
Abstract: This paper explores the implementation of deterministic and stochastic dynamics on manifolds, as well as differential geometric constructions, using modern computational frameworks that blend symbolic expressions with efficient numerical computations.  Specifically, we leverage the symbolic expression and automatic differentiation capabilities of the Python library Theano, originally developed for high-performance deep learning computations.  We illustrate how various aspects of differential geometry and Lie group theory, including connections, metrics, curvature, left/right invariance, geodesics, and parallel transport, can be formulated with Theano using automatic computation of derivatives to any order.  We further demonstrate the formulation and optimization of symbolic stochastic integrators and concepts from non-linear statistics using concise code.  We present explicit examples on low-dimensional classical manifolds for visualization and highlight how this approach enables both concise implementation and efficient scaling to high-dimensional problems.
label: AI

title: On Using Backpropagation for Speech Texture Generation and Voice Conversion
Abstract: Inspired by recent work on neural network image generation that relies on backpropagation towards network inputs, we present a proof-of-concept system for speech texture synthesis and voice conversion based on two mechanisms: approximate inversion of the representation learned by a speech recognition neural network and matching statistics of neuron activations between different source and target utterances. Similar to image texture synthesis and neural style transfer, our system optimizes a cost function with respect to input waveform samples.  To achieve this, we employ a differentiable mel-filterbank feature extraction pipeline and train a convolutional CTC speech recognition network. Our system can extract speaker characteristics from limited target speaker data, as little as a few seconds, and can be used to generate realistic speech babble or reconstruct an utterance in a different voice.
label: AI

title: Integrating Knowledge from Latent and Explicit Features for Triple Scoring - Team Radicchio's Triple Scorer at WSDM Cup 2017
Abstract: The objective of the triple scoring task in WSDM Cup 2017 is to compute relevance scores for knowledge-base triples of type-like relations.  For example, consider Julius Caesar, who held various professions including Politician and Author.  Given the triples (Julius Caesar, profession, Politician) and (Julius Caesar, profession, Author), the former triple is likely to have a higher relevance score (also known as "triple score") because Julius Caesar was widely recognized as a politician but not as an author.  Accurate prediction of such triple scores significantly benefits real-world applications, such as information retrieval and knowledge base querying.  In these scenarios, the ability to rank all relations (Profession/Nationality) can enhance the user experience.  We propose a triple scoring model that integrates knowledge from both latent and explicit features via an ensemble approach. Latent features consist of representations for a person learned using a word2vec model and representations for profession/nationality values extracted from a pre-trained GloVe embedding model.  Additionally, we extract explicit features for person entities from the Freebase knowledge base. Experimental results demonstrate the competitive performance of our proposed method at WSDM Cup 2017, achieving third place with an accuracy of 79.72% for predicting within two places of the ground truth score.

title: Event-based Failure Prediction in Distributed Business Processes
Abstract: Traditionally, Business Process Management research has focused heavily on centralized and intra-organizational processes.  However, today's business processes are increasingly distributed and decentralized, requiring novel methodologies for detecting and responding to unforeseen events, such as errors during process runtime.  This article demonstrates how to employ event-based failure prediction in business processes.  This approach leverages the strengths of both traditional Business Process Management Systems and event-based systems. Our approach utilizes machine learning techniques and considers various types of events.  We evaluate our solution using two business process datasets, including one from a real-world event log, demonstrating our ability to detect errors and predict failures with high accuracy.

title: Towards dense object tracking in a 2D honeybee hive
Abstract: From human crowds to cells in tissue, the detection and efficient tracking of multiple objects in dense configurations pose a significant and unresolved challenge. Past limitations in image analysis have restricted studies of dense groups to tracking a single or subset of marked individuals or to coarse-grained group-level dynamics, resulting in incomplete information.  We combine convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with the model environment of a honeybee hive to automatically recognize all individuals in a dense group from raw image data.  We introduce novel, adapted individual labeling and employ the U-Net segmentation architecture with a loss function dependent on both object identity and orientation.  Leveraging the temporal regularities of the video recording in a recurrent manner, we achieve near human-level performance while reducing the network size by 94% compared to the original U-Net architecture.  To address our novel application of CNNs, we generate extensive problem-specific image data, where labeled examples are produced through a custom interface with Amazon Mechanical Turk.  This dataset encompasses over 375,000 labeled bee instances across 720 video frames at 2 FPS, providing a substantial resource for the development and testing of tracking methods.  We correctly detect 96% of individuals with a location error of approximately 7% of a typical body dimension and an orientation error of 12 degrees, closely mirroring the variability of human raters.  Our findings represent a crucial step towards efficient image-based dense object tracking by enabling the accurate determination of object location and orientation across time-series image data within a single network architecture.

title: Deep Hashing with Category Mask for Fast Video Retrieval
Abstract: This paper introduces an end-to-end deep hashing framework with category mask for fast video retrieval.  Our network is trained in a supervised manner, fully exploiting inter-class diversity and intra-class identity.  Classification loss is optimized to maximize inter-class diversity, while intra-pair loss is introduced to learn representative intra-class identity.  We analyze the distribution of binary bits related to categories, revealing a strong correlation between bit effectiveness and data categories.  Some bits may degrade classification performance for specific categories.  We then design a hash code generation scheme with a category mask to filter out bits with negative contributions.  Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms several state-of-the-art techniques across various evaluation metrics on public datasets.
label: AI

title: Benchmarking Decoupled Neural Interfaces with Synthetic Gradients
Abstract: Artificial neural networks, a class of learning systems modeled after biological neural functions, exhibit a notable affinity for Hebbian learning ("neurons that wire together, fire together"). However, unlike their biological counterparts, artificial neural networks exhibit a tight and inflexible coupling between neuronal modules. This coupling or locking imposes a rigid and inflexible structure on the network, preventing layers from updating their weights until a complete feed-forward and backward pass has occurred.  While this constraint may have sufficed in the past, it is no longer feasible in the era of very large-scale machine learning, coupled with the growing demand for parallelization of the learning process across multiple computing infrastructures. To address this challenge, synthetic gradients (SG) with decoupled neural interfaces (DNI) are introduced as a viable alternative to the backpropagation algorithm.  This paper conducts a speed benchmark comparing the speed and accuracy capabilities of SG-DNI against a standard neural interface using a multilayer perceptron (MLP).  SG-DNI shows promising results, not only effectively addressing the learning problem but also demonstrating a 3-fold speed advantage due to its asynchronous learning capabilities.
label: AI

title: Source-side Prediction for Neural Headline Generation
Abstract: The encoder-decoder model is widely employed in natural language generation tasks. However, the model sometimes generates repetitive and redundant text, misses important phrases, and includes irrelevant entities.  To address these shortcomings, we propose a novel source-side token prediction module.  Our method jointly estimates the probability distributions over source and target vocabularies to capture a correspondence between source and target tokens. Experimental results show that our proposed model outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in the headline generation task.  Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method can learn a reasonable token-wise correspondence without requiring any true alignments.
label: AI

title: Learning and Transferring IDs Representation in E-commerce
Abstract: Numerous machine intelligence techniques are developed in E-commerce, with one of the most essential components being the representation of IDs, including user ID, item ID, product ID, store ID, brand ID, category ID, etc.  Traditional encoding methods, such as one-hot encoding, are inefficient due to sparsity problems arising from their high dimensionality. Moreover, they fail to capture the relationships, both homogeneous and heterogeneous, between IDs. This paper proposes an embedding-based framework for learning and transferring ID representations.  Leveraging the implicit user feedback, a vast amount of item ID sequences can be readily collected from interactive sessions.  By jointly utilizing these informative sequences and the structural connections between IDs, all types of IDs can be embedded into a single low-dimensional semantic space.  The learned representations are subsequently utilized and transferred in four scenarios: (i) measuring item similarity, (ii) transferring from seen items to unseen items, (iii) transferring across different domains, and (iv) transferring across different tasks.  We deploy and evaluate our proposed approach in the Hema App, and the results validate its effectiveness. |||

title: Recurrent Pixel Embedding for Instance Grouping
Abstract: We propose a novel, differentiable, end-to-end trainable framework for solving pixel-level grouping problems, like instance segmentation. Our framework consists of two key components. First, we embed pixels into a hyper-spherical space where pixels from the same group exhibit high cosine similarity, while those from different groups have similarity below a predefined margin. We analyze the relationship between embedding dimension, margin, and theoretical results on uniform point distribution on the sphere. Second, we employ a modified mean-shift clustering, implemented as a recurrent neural network parameterized by kernel bandwidth, for instance grouping. This recurrent module is differentiable, exhibits convergent dynamics, and offers probabilistic interpretability.  The group-weighted loss backpropagated through this module allows for targeted correction of embedding errors that won't be rectified during subsequent clustering. Our framework, while conceptually simple and theoretically well-founded, demonstrates practical efficacy and computational efficiency. We showcase substantial improvements over state-of-the-art instance segmentation for object proposal generation and highlight the benefits of grouping loss for classification tasks, such as boundary detection and semantic segmentation.
label: AI

title: Beyond saliency: understanding convolutional neural networks from saliency prediction on layer-wise relevance propagation
Abstract: Despite significant progress in computer vision tasks using deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs), understanding their internal workings remains a challenge. We present a novel two-step understanding method, the Salient Relevance (SR) map, to shed light on how deep CNNs recognize images and learn features from specific areas, referred to as attention areas. Our method begins with layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP), which estimates a pixel-wise relevance map over the input image. Subsequently, we construct a context-aware saliency map, the SR map, from the LRP-generated map, predicting areas close to the foci of attention rather than isolated pixels as revealed by LRP.  Human visual systems prioritize regional information over individual pixels for recognition. Consequently, our approach closely emulates human recognition.  Experimental results on the ILSVRC2012 validation dataset using two widely adopted deep CNN models, AlexNet and VGG-16, demonstrate that our approach effectively identifies not only key pixels but also attention areas contributing to the network's understanding of the given images. The SR map provides a convenient visual interface unveiling the network's visual attention and revealing which object types the model has learned to recognize after training. The source code is available at https://github.com/Hey1Li/Salient-Relevance-Propagation.
label: AI

title: Federated Control with Hierarchical Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: We present a framework that combines hierarchical and multi-agent deep reinforcement learning approaches to solve coordination problems among numerous agents using a semi-decentralized model. This framework extends the multi-agent learning setup by introducing a meta-controller that guides communication between agent pairs, enabling agents to focus on communicating with only one other agent at a time. This hierarchical task decomposition facilitates efficient exploration and learning of policies that identify globally optimal solutions, even as the number of collaborating agents increases. We demonstrate promising initial experimental results on a simulated distributed scheduling problem.
label: AI

title: Linear centralization classifier
Abstract: We introduce a novel classification algorithm, the Linear Centralization Classifier (LCC), which seeks to find a transformation that effectively maps instances from the feature space to a space where they cluster towards the center of their respective classes, while maximizing the distance between class centers. We formulate the classifier as a quadratic program with quadratic constraints. We then simplify this formulation into a linear program that can be efficiently solved using a linear programming solver (e.g., simplex-dual).  We extend the LCC formulation to enable the use of kernel functions for non-linear classification applications. We compare our method with two standard classification methods (support vector machine and linear discriminant analysis) and four state-of-the-art classification methods on eight standard classification datasets. Our experimental results indicate that LCC classifies instances more accurately (based on the area under the receiver operating characteristic) than other tested methods on the chosen datasets. We also report results for LCC with a specific kernel for solving synthetic non-linear classification problems.
label: AI

title: ReabsNet: Detecting and Revising Adversarial Examples
Abstract: Despite the remarkable success of deep neural networks in recent studies and applications, they remain vulnerable to adversarial perturbations that are imperceptible to humans. To address this vulnerability, we propose a novel network called ReabsNet to achieve high classification accuracy in the face of various attacks. Our approach augments an existing classification network with a guardian network to detect whether a sample is natural or has been adversarially perturbed.  Instead of simply rejecting adversarial examples, we revise them to obtain their true labels. We leverage the observation that a sample containing adversarial perturbations may revert to its true class after revision. We demonstrate that ReabsNet outperforms state-of-the-art defense methods under various adversarial attacks.
label: AI

title: Graph Clustering with Dynamic Embedding
Abstract: Graph clustering, also known as community detection, has been a subject of considerable research in web mining and information networks. Recent literature on this topic has established a consensus that node contents and link structures should be integrated for reliable graph clustering, particularly in unsupervised settings. However, existing methods based on shallow models often struggle with content noise and sparsity. In this work, we propose leveraging deep embedding for graph clustering, motivated by the well-recognized power of neural networks in learning intrinsic content representations.  We capture the dynamic nature of networks through the principle of influence propagation and calculate the dynamic network embedding. Network clusters are then identified based on the stable state of this embedding. Unlike most existing task-agnostic embedding methods, we simultaneously solve for the underlying node representations and the optimal clustering assignments in an end-to-end manner. To provide further insight, we theoretically analyze our interpretation of network clusters and uncover its underlying connections with two widely applied approaches for network modeling.  Extensive experimental results on six real-world datasets, including both social networks and citation networks, demonstrate the superiority of our proposed model over state-of-the-art methods.

title: How Well Can Generative Adversarial Networks Learn Densities: A Nonparametric View
Abstract: In this paper, we investigate the rate of convergence for learning densities within the Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) framework, drawing insights from nonparametric statistics. We introduce an improved GAN estimator that achieves a faster rate by simultaneously leveraging the level of smoothness in the target density and the evaluation metric. This theoretically mitigates the mode collapse problem reported in the literature. We construct a minimax lower bound to show that when the dimension is large, the exponent in the rate for the new GAN estimator is near optimal.  Our results can be interpreted as a quantitative assessment of how well GAN learns a wide range of densities with varying smoothness properties, under a hierarchy of evaluation metrics.  As a byproduct, we also obtain improved generalization bounds for GAN with deeper ReLU discriminator networks.

title: ConvSCCS: convolutional self-controlled case series model for lagged adverse event detection
Abstract: The increased availability of large electronic health records (EHR) databases presents an opportunity to enhance health risk screening. Most post-marketing detections of adverse drug reactions (ADRs) rely on spontaneous reports from physicians, leading to underreporting. To address this challenge, we develop a scalable model to estimate the effect of multiple longitudinal features (drug exposures) on a rare longitudinal outcome.  Our procedure is based on a conditional Poisson model, also known as self-controlled case series (SCCS). We model the intensity of outcomes using a convolution between exposures and step functions, penalized using a combination of group-Lasso and total-variation. This approach avoids the need for specifying precise risk periods and allows for the simultaneous study of multiple exposures within the same model. We demonstrate that this approach improves the state-of-the-art for estimating relative risks, both through simulations and using a cohort of diabetic patients extracted from the large French national health insurance database (SNIIRAM). This database is a SQL database built around medical reimbursements for over 65 million individuals. This work was conducted in collaboration between Ecole Polytechnique and CNAMTS (responsible for SNIIRAM).

title: Estimating activity cycles with probabilistic methods II. The Mount Wilson Ca H&K data
Abstract: The debate over the existence of branches in the stellar activity-rotation diagrams continues. The application of modern time series analysis tools to study mean cycle periods in chromospheric activity indices is lacking. We develop such models, based on Gaussian processes, for one-dimensional time series and apply them to the extended Mount Wilson Ca H&K sample. Our primary aim is to study the impact of the commonly used assumption of strict harmonicity of stellar cycles, as well as the handling of linear trends, on the results. We introduce three methods of varying complexity, starting with the simple Bayesian harmonic model followed by Gaussian Process models with periodic and quasi-periodic covariance functions. We confirm the existence of two populations in the activity-period diagram.  We find only one significant trend in the inactive population, namely that cycle periods shorten with increasing rotation. This contrasts with earlier studies that posited the existence of trends in both populations.  In terms of the rotation to cycle period ratio, our data aligns with only two activity branches, suggesting that the active branch merges with the transitional one. The retrieved stellar cycles are uniformly distributed over the R'HK activity index, indicating that the operation of stellar large-scale dynamos proceeds smoothly over the Vaughan-Preston gap. However, around the solar activity index, evidence suggests a disruption in the cyclic dynamo action. Our study shows that stellar cycle estimates depend significantly on the model applied.  Such model-dependent aspects include the improper treatment of linear trends, while the assumption of strict harmonicity can lead to the appearance of double cyclicities that are more likely explained by the quasi-periodicity of the cycles.
label: AI

title: CaloGAN: Simulating 3D High Energy Particle Showers in Multi-Layer Electromagnetic Calorimeters with Generative Adversarial Networks
Abstract: Precise modeling of subatomic particle interactions and propagation through matter is crucial for advancing nuclear and particle physics searches and precision measurements. The most computationally demanding step in the simulation pipeline of a typical experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is the detailed modeling of the full complexity of physics processes governing the motion and evolution of particle showers inside calorimeters. We introduce \textsc{CaloGAN}, a novel fast simulation technique based on generative adversarial networks (GANs). We apply these neural networks to the modeling of electromagnetic showers in a longitudinally segmented calorimeter and achieve speedup factors comparable to or exceeding existing full simulation techniques on CPU (100x-1000x) and even faster on GPU (up to ~10^5x). While challenges remain in achieving precision across the entire phase space, our solution can reproduce a variety of geometric shower shape properties of photons, positrons, and charged pions. This represents a significant step towards a full neural network-based detector simulation that could significantly reduce computing time and enable numerous analyses, both present and future.
label: AI

title: Interventions over Predictions: Reframing the Ethical Debate for Actuarial Risk Assessment
Abstract: Actuarial risk assessments are often perceived as a neutral way to counteract implicit bias and increase fairness in decisions made throughout the criminal justice system, from pretrial release to sentencing, parole, and probation.  However, these assessments have come under increasing scrutiny, as critics argue that the underlying statistical techniques may perpetuate existing patterns of discrimination and historical biases reflected in the data. Much of this debate centers on competing notions of fairness and predictive accuracy, relying on the contentious use of variables that act as "proxies" for characteristics legally protected against discrimination, such as race and gender. We argue that the core ethical debate surrounding the use of regression in risk assessments is not simply one of bias or accuracy but rather one of purpose.  If machine learning is solely operationalized to predict individual future crime, then it becomes difficult to break cycles of criminalization driven by the iatrogenic effects of the criminal justice system itself. We posit that machine learning should not be used for prediction but rather to surface covariates that are fed into a causal model for understanding the social, structural, and psychological drivers of crime.  We propose an alternative application of machine learning and causal inference, shifting away from predicting risk scores to risk mitigation.

title: Estimating activity cycles with probabilistic methods I. Bayesian Generalised Lomb-Scargle Periodogram with Trend
Abstract: Period estimation is a central topic in astronomical time series analysis, where data is often unevenly sampled.  Studies of stellar magnetic cycles pose a particular challenge, as the periods of interest are comparable to the length of the datasets themselves. Datasets often contain trends, originating from either a real long-term cycle or instrumental effects, which cannot be reliably separated. These effects can lead to erroneous period determinations if not properly handled.  In this study, we aim to develop a method capable of appropriately handling trends, and through extensive testing, we demonstrate that this is the optimal procedure compared to methods that do not directly include the trend in the model. We also investigate the impact of the noise form (constant or heteroscedastic) on the results. We introduce a Bayesian Generalized Lomb-Scargle Periodogram with Trend (BGLST), which is a probabilistic linear regression model using Gaussian priors for the coefficients and a uniform prior for the frequency parameter. Using synthetic data, we show that when there is no prior information on whether and to what extent the true model of the data contains a linear trend, the introduced BGLST method is preferable to methods that either detrend the data or leave the data untrended before fitting the periodic model. Whether to employ noise with a variance other than constant in the model depends on the density of the data sampling and the true noise type of the process.

title: Block-Diagonal and LT Codes for Distributed Computing With Straggling Servers
Abstract: We propose two coded schemes for the distributed computing problem of multiplying a matrix by a set of vectors. The first scheme involves partitioning the matrix into submatrices and applying maximum distance separable (MDS) codes to each submatrix. For this scheme, we prove that up to a given number of partitions, the communication load and computational delay (excluding encoding and decoding delay) are identical to those of the scheme recently proposed by Li et al., based on a single, long MDS code. However, due to the use of shorter MDS codes, our scheme yields a significantly lower overall computational delay when the delay incurred by encoding and decoding is also considered.  We further propose a second coded scheme based on Luby Transform (LT) codes under inactivation decoding. Interestingly, LT codes may reduce the delay compared to the partitioned scheme at the expense of an increased communication load. We also consider distributed computing under a deadline and show numerically that the proposed schemes outperform other schemes in the literature, with the LT code-based scheme yielding the best performance for the scenarios considered.

title: Analysis-synthesis model learning with shared features: a new framework for histopathological image classification
Abstract: Automated histopathological image analysis offers promising opportunities for the early diagnosis of several medical conditions, including cancer. However, there are significant practical challenges: 1) discriminative features from such images for separating diseased vs. healthy classes are not readily apparent, and 2) distinct classes, e.g., healthy vs. stages of disease, continue to share several geometric features.  We propose a novel Analysis-synthesis model Learning with Shared Features algorithm (ALSF) for more effectively classifying such images. In ALSF, a joint analysis and synthesis learning model is introduced to simultaneously learn the classifier and the feature extractor. This approach significantly reduces the computational load in patch-level based image classification.  Crucially, we integrate into this framework the learning of a low-rank shared dictionary and a shared analysis operator, which more accurately represents both similarities and differences in histopathological images from distinct classes. ALSF is evaluated on two challenging databases: (1) kidney tissue images provided by the Animal Diagnosis Lab (ADL) at the Pennsylvania State University and (2) brain tumor images from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database. Experimental results confirm that ALSF offers advantages over state-of-the-art alternatives.
label: AI

title: Robust Detection of Covariate-Treatment Interactions in Clinical Trials
Abstract: Detecting interactions between treatment effects and patient descriptors in clinical trials is critical for optimizing the drug development process. The increasing volume of data accumulated in clinical trials presents a unique opportunity to discover new biomarkers and advance the goal of personalized medicine, but it also requires innovative robust biomarker detection methods capable of detecting non-linear, and sometimes weak, signals.  We propose a set of novel univariate statistical tests, based on the theory of random walks, which are able to capture non-linear and non-monotonic covariate-treatment interactions. We also propose a novel combined test that leverages the power of all our proposed univariate tests into a single general-case tool. We present results for both synthetic trials and real-world clinical trials, comparing our method with state-of-the-art techniques and demonstrating the utility and robustness of our approach.

title: The Census and the Second Law: An Entropic Approach to Optimal Apportionment for the U.S. House of Representatives
Abstract: The Constitutionally mandated task of assigning Congressional seats to the various U.S. States proportionally to their represented populations ("according to their numbers") has generated considerable contention but relatively less consensus. Using the same principles of entropic inference that underlie the foundations of information theory and statistical thermodynamics, and that have found fruitful application in image processing, spectral analysis, machine learning, econometrics, bioinformatics, and a growing number of other fields, we motivate and explore a method for Congressional apportionment based on minimizing relative entropy (also known as Kullback-Leibler divergence) or, equivalently, maximizing Shannon entropy. In terms of communication theory, we might say that the entropic apportionment gives each constituent as equal a voice as possible. If we view representational weight as a finite resource to be distributed amongst the represented population, the entropic measure is identical to the Theil index, long employed in economics to measure inequality in the distribution of wealth or income, or in ecology to measure the distribution of biomass or reproductive fitness. Besides Congressional apportionment, the method is also directly applicable to other multi-regional or multi-constituency legislatures, to party-list proportional voting systems used in various parliamentary elections, and similar settings where the task is to allocate a discrete number of seats or other resources, and the primary goal is one of maximal proportionality or equity.  In addition, the same entropic figure-of-merit can be used in parallel to compare different choices for the total number of representatives and then subsequently to assess different Congressional district sizes after seats are assigned and proposed district boundaries drawn.

title: Fair Forests: Regularized Tree Induction to Minimize Model Bias
Abstract: The potential lack of fairness in the outputs of machine learning algorithms has recently gained attention both within the research community and in society more broadly. Surprisingly, there is no prior work developing tree-induction algorithms for building fair decision trees or fair random forests. These methods are widely popular because they are among the few to be simultaneously interpretable, non-linear, and easy-to-use. In this paper, we develop, to our knowledge, the first technique for the induction of fair decision trees. We show that our "Fair Forest" retains the benefits of the tree-based approach while providing both greater accuracy and fairness than other alternatives, for both "group fairness" and "individual fairness." We also introduce new measures for fairness that can handle multinomial and continuous attributes as well as regression problems, as opposed to binary attributes and labels only. Finally, we demonstrate a new, more robust evaluation procedure for algorithms that considers the dataset in its entirety rather than only a specific protected attribute.

title: A Deep Reinforcement Learning-Based Framework for Content Caching
Abstract: Content caching at edge nodes is a promising technique for reducing data traffic in next-generation wireless networks. Inspired by the success of Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) in solving complex control problems, this work presents a DRL-based framework with a Wolpertinger architecture for content caching at the base station. The proposed framework aims to maximize the long-term cache hit rate and requires no knowledge of the content popularity distribution. To evaluate the proposed framework, we compare its performance with other caching algorithms, including Least Recently Used (LRU), Least Frequently Used (LFU), and First-In First-Out (FIFO) caching strategies.  Meanwhile, since the Wolpertinger architecture can effectively limit the action space size, we also compare the performance with Deep Q-Network to identify the impact of dropping a portion of the actions. Our results show that the proposed framework achieves improved short-term cache hit rate and improved and stable long-term cache hit rate compared to LRU, LFU, and FIFO schemes. Additionally, the performance is shown to be competitive compared to Deep Q-learning, while the proposed framework provides significant savings in runtime.

title: A Fast Algorithm for Separated Sparsity via Perturbed Lagrangians
Abstract: Sparsity-based methods are widely used in machine learning, statistics, and signal processing. There is now a rich class of structured sparsity approaches that expand the modeling power of the sparsity paradigm and incorporate constraints such as group sparsity, graph sparsity, or hierarchical sparsity. While these sparsity models offer improved sample complexity and better interpretability, the improvements come at a computational cost: it is often challenging to optimize over the (non-convex) constraint sets that capture various sparsity structures. In this paper, we make progress in this direction in the context of separated sparsity - a fundamental sparsity notion that captures exclusion constraints in linearly ordered data such as time series.  While prior algorithms for computing a projection onto this constraint set required quadratic time, we provide a perturbed Lagrangian relaxation approach that computes provably exact projection in only nearly-linear time. Although the sparsity constraint is non-convex, our perturbed Lagrangian approach is still guaranteed to find a globally optimal solution. In experiments, our new algorithms offer a 10x speed-up already on moderately-sized inputs.

title: Unifying Map and Landmark Based Representations for Visual Navigation
Abstract: This work presents a formulation for visual navigation that unifies map-based spatial reasoning and path planning with landmark-based robust plan execution in noisy environments. Our proposed formulation is learned from data and is thus able to leverage statistical regularities of the world. This allows it to efficiently navigate in novel environments given only a sparse set of registered images as input for building representations for space. Our formulation is based on three key ideas: a learned path planner that outputs path plans to reach the goal, a feature synthesis engine that predicts features for locations along the planned path, and a learned goal-driven closed-loop controller that can follow plans given these synthesized features. We test our approach for goal-driven navigation in simulated real-world environments and report performance gains over competitive baseline approaches.|||
