title: Improving science yield for NASA Swift with automated planning technologies
Abstract: The Swift Gamma-Ray Burst Explorer is a highly capable mission, equipped with three onboard instruments and the ability to rapidly reposition itself. It serves as a versatile satellite observatory, addressing a wide range of astronomical phenomena, from gravitational wave counterparts to cometary research. Swift conducts an average of 125 observations daily, consistently exceeding its capacity by responding to approximately one hundred Target of Opportunity (ToO) requests monthly from the astrophysics community, as well as collaborating and following up with other observatories. Since its launch in 2004, the demands placed on Swift have steadily increased in terms of the number and types of targets, as well as scheduling complexity. To accommodate this growth, the Swift team has developed various scheduling tools and technologies to enhance the mission's scientific output. However, these tools have primarily been used to aid human operators in exploring the optimal schedule and resolving constraint violations. The computational complexity of the scheduling task has hindered the development of an automated tool capable of producing schedules of equal or superior quality to those generated by skilled human schedulers within the given time constraints. This paper formalizes the Swift Scheduling Problem as a dynamic fuzzy Constraint Satisfaction Problem (DF-CSP) and explores the global solution space. It outlines several approaches to achieving the goal of surpassing human-quality schedules using conventional optimization and algorithmic techniques, along with machine learning and recurrent neural network (RNN) methods. The paper concludes by discussing the potential scientific benefits and broader impact on the astrophysics community that would result from further development and adoption of these technologies.
label: AI

title: A Deep Learning Interpretable Classifier for Diabetic Retinopathy Disease Grading
Abstract: Deep neural networks have proven highly successful in image classification tasks, including medical diagnosis, but their lack of interpretability is a significant concern. They function as intuition machines with high statistical confidence but fail to provide interpretable explanations for their results. The vast number of parameters in these models makes it difficult to infer a rational interpretation. This paper introduces an interpretable diabetic retinopathy classifier capable of classifying retinal images into different disease severity levels and explaining its results by assigning a score to each point in the hidden and input spaces, quantifying their contributions to the final classification in a linear manner. The generated visual maps can be interpreted by an expert to compare their own knowledge with the model's interpretation.
label: AI

title: Truncated Variational Sampling for "Black Box" Optimization of Generative Models
Abstract: This research explores the optimization of two probabilistic generative models with binary latent variables using a novel variational EM approach. This approach distinguishes itself from prior variational methods by utilizing latent states as variational parameters. Efficient and general-purpose sampling procedures are employed to vary the latent states, investigating the "black box" applicability of the resulting optimization procedure. For general applicability, samples are drawn from approximate marginal distributions of the considered generative model and the model's prior distribution. Consequently, variational sampling is defined in a generic form, directly executable for a given model. As a proof of concept, the novel procedure is applied to Binary Sparse Coding (a model with continuous observables) and basic Sigmoid Belief Networks (models with binary observables). Numerical experiments demonstrate that the investigated approach effectively and efficiently increases a variational free energy objective without requiring additional analytical steps.
label: AI

title: Profit Driven Decision Trees for Churn Prediction
Abstract: Customer retention campaigns increasingly rely on predictive models to identify potential churners within large customer bases. From a machine learning perspective, predicting customer churn can be framed as a binary classification problem. Using historical behavioral data, classification algorithms are built to accurately predict the probability of a customer defecting. Predictive churn models are typically selected based on accuracy-related performance measures, such as the area under the ROC curve (AUC). However, these models often fail to align with the core business objective of profit maximization because they do not consider misclassification costs and the benefits associated with correct classification. Therefore, the goal is to develop churn prediction models that are both profitable and interpretable. The recently developed expected maximum profit measure for customer churn (EMPC) has been proposed to select the most profitable churn model. This paper presents a new classifier that integrates the EMPC metric directly into the model construction. The technique, called ProfTree, uses an evolutionary algorithm to learn profit-driven decision trees. In a benchmark study using real-life datasets from various telecommunication service providers, ProfTree demonstrates significant profit improvements compared to traditional accuracy-driven tree-based methods.
label: AI

title: Multiview Deep Learning for Predicting Twitter Users' Location
Abstract: Predicting the location of users on large social networks like Twitter has become increasingly relevant for real-world applications, such as social unrest detection and online marketing. Twitter user geolocation presents a challenging and actively researched topic with extensive literature. Most proposed methods follow either a content-based or a network-based approach. The former leverages user-generated content, while the latter utilizes the connection or interaction between Twitter users. This paper introduces a novel method that combines the strengths of both approaches. Specifically, it proposes a multi-entry neural network architecture named MENET, leveraging advancements in deep learning and multiview learning. MENET's generalizability enables the integration of multiple data representations. In the context of Twitter user geolocation, MENET is implemented with textual, network, and metadata features. Given the natural distribution of Twitter users across the geographical area of interest, the Earth's surface is subdivided into multi-scale cells, and MENET is trained using the labels of these cells. The paper demonstrates that MENET significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on three benchmark datasets.
label: AI

title: Learning Intelligent Dialogs for Bounding Box Annotation
Abstract: This paper introduces Intelligent Annotation Dialogs for bounding box annotation, training an agent to automatically select a sequence of actions for a human annotator to produce a bounding box in the shortest possible time. The agent considers two actions: box verification, where the annotator verifies a box generated by an object detector, and manual box drawing. Two types of agents are explored, one based on predicting the probability of a box being positively verified and the other based on reinforcement learning. The findings demonstrate that: (1) the agents can learn efficient annotation strategies in various scenarios, automatically adapting to image difficulty, desired box quality, and detector strength; (2) in all scenarios, the resulting annotation dialogues accelerate annotation compared to manual box drawing alone and box verification alone, outperforming any fixed combination of verification and drawing in most scenarios; (3) in a realistic scenario where the detector is iteratively retrained, the agents evolve a series of strategies reflecting the shifting trade-off between verification and drawing as the detector improves.

title: Long-Term Mobile Traffic Forecasting Using Deep Spatio-Temporal Neural Networks
Abstract: Accurately forecasting mobile user data traffic volume is becoming increasingly crucial for precision traffic engineering, demand-aware network resource allocation, and public transportation. However, data collection in dense urban deployments is complex and expensive, and post-processing for predictions is highly non-trivial due to the intricate spatio-temporal variability of mobile traffic caused by user mobility. To address these challenges, this paper leverages the exceptional feature extraction capabilities of deep learning and proposes a Spatio-Temporal neural Network (STN) architecture specifically designed for precise network-wide mobile traffic forecasting. A mechanism is presented for fine-tuning the STN, enabling its operation with limited ground truth observations. The paper then introduces a Double STN technique (D-STN), uniquely combining STN predictions with historical statistics, facilitating faithful long-term mobile traffic projections. Experiments conducted with real-world mobile traffic datasets collected over 60 days in both urban and rural areas demonstrate that the proposed (D-)STN schemes perform up to 10-hour long predictions with remarkable accuracy, irrespective of the time of day they are triggered. Specifically, these solutions achieve up to 61% smaller prediction errors compared to widely used forecasting approaches, while operating with up to 600 times shorter measurement intervals.

title: Note on Attacking Object Detectors with Adversarial Stickers
Abstract: Deep learning has proven to be a powerful tool for computer vision and has gained widespread adoption for numerous tasks. However, deep learning algorithms are known to be vulnerable to adversarial examples. These adversarial inputs are designed to be mislabeled when provided to a deep learning algorithm. This vulnerability is problematic when deep learning is used to support safety-critical decisions. Recent research has shown that classifiers can be attacked by physical adversarial examples under various physical conditions. Given that state-of-the-art object detection algorithms are more resistant to the same set of adversarial examples, this paper demonstrates that these detectors can also be attacked by physical adversarial examples. The paper presents both static and dynamic test results. An algorithm is designed to generate physical adversarial inputs that can fool the YOLO object detector and also attack Faster-RCNN with relatively high success rates based on transferability. Furthermore, the algorithm can compress the size of adversarial inputs into stickers that, when attached to the targeted object, cause the detector to either mislabel or fail to detect the object a high percentage of the time. This paper provides a preliminary set of results, with a comprehensive evaluation on other object detectors and a detailed presentation of the algorithm planned for a future paper.

title: A brain signature highly predictive of future progression to Alzheimer's dementia
Abstract: Early prognosis of Alzheimer's dementia is challenging. Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) typically precedes Alzheimer's dementia, but only a fraction of MCI individuals progress to dementia, even when screened using biomarkers. This paper proposes to identify a subset of individuals who share a common brain signature highly predictive of oncoming dementia. This signature, composed of brain atrophy and functional dysconnectivity, was discovered using a machine learning model in patients suffering from dementia. The model recognized the same brain signature in MCI individuals, 90% of whom progressed to dementia within three years. This result significantly improves prognostic precision compared to existing methods, while the brain signature still identifies 47% of all MCI progressors. Thus, a sizable MCI subpopulation has been identified, representing an excellent recruitment target for clinical trials at the prodromal stage of Alzheimer's disease.

title: Variable selection for Gaussian processes via sensitivity analysis of the posterior predictive distribution
Abstract: Variable selection for Gaussian process models is often performed using automatic relevance determination, which uses the inverse length-scale parameter of each input variable as a proxy for variable relevance. This implicitly determined relevance has several drawbacks that prevent the selection of optimal input variables in terms of predictive performance. To address this, this paper proposes two novel variable selection methods for Gaussian process models that utilize the predictions of a full model in the vicinity of the training points, thereby ranking the variables based on their predictive relevance. Empirical results on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate improved variable selection compared to automatic relevance determination in terms of variability and predictive performance.

title: Autism Classification Using Brain Functional Connectivity Dynamics and Machine Learning
Abstract: This study aims to identify autism using machine learning techniques and resting-state brain imaging data, leveraging the temporal variability of functional connections (FC) as the sole source of information. FC variability across brain regions was estimated and compared between typical, healthy subjects and autistic individuals by analyzing brain imaging data from a global multi-site database known as ABIDE (Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange). The analysis revealed that patients diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) exhibit increased FC variability in several brain regions associated with low FC variability in typical brains. The enhanced FC variability of these brain regions was then used as features for training machine learning models for ASD classification, achieving 65% accuracy in identifying ASD versus control subjects within the dataset. Node strength, estimated from the number of functional connections per node averaged over the entire scan, was also used as a feature for ASD classification. The results indicate that dynamic FC measures outperform or are comparable to static FC measures in predicting ASD.

title: Siamese Neural Networks for One-shot detection of Railway Track Switches
Abstract: Deep Learning methods have been widely employed to analyze video data, extracting valuable information by classifying image frames and detecting objects. This paper describes a unique approach for using video feed from a moving locomotive to continuously monitor the railway track and detect significant assets like switches. The technique used is called Siamese Networks, which utilize two identical networks to learn the similarity between two images. In this case, a Siamese network is used to continuously compare track images and detect any significant differences. Switches are one of the images that will be different, and the network will find a mapping that clearly distinguishes the switch from other potential track anomalies. The same method can be extended to detect abnormalities on the railway track. Railway transportation is unique in that it involves wheeled vehicles, trains pulled by locomotives, running on guided rails at very high speeds nearing 200 mph. Multiple tracks on the rail network are connected to each other using equipment called switches or turnouts. Switches are either manually operated or controlled automatically from a control center, governing the movement of trains on different tracks of the network. Accurate location of these switches is critical for railroads, and understanding their real-time state in the field is essential. Modern trains utilize high-definition video cameras facing the track, continuously recording video footage. Using a Siamese network and comparing against benchmark images, this paper describes a method to monitor the track and highlight anomalies.

title: A Comparative Study of Different Source Code Metrics and Machine Learning Algorithms for Predicting Change Proneness of Object Oriented Systems
Abstract: Change-prone classes or modules are defined as software components in the source code that are likely to change in the future. Predicting change-proneness is beneficial for maintenance teams as they can optimize and focus their testing resources on modules with a higher likelihood of change. Change-proneness prediction models can be built using source code metrics as predictors or features within a machine learning classification framework. This paper computes twenty-one source code metrics to develop a statistical model for predicting change-prone modules. Since the performance of the change-proneness model depends on the source code metrics, they are used as independent variables or predictors for the model. Eleven different feature selection techniques, including the use of all twenty-one proposed source code metrics, are employed to remove irrelevant features and select the optimal set of features. The effectiveness of the set of source code metrics is evaluated using eighteen different classification techniques and three ensemble techniques. Experimental results demonstrate that the model based on the selected set of source code metrics after applying feature selection techniques achieves better results compared to the model using all source code metrics as predictors. The experimental results reveal that the predictive model developed using LSSVM-RBF yields better results compared to other classification techniques.

title: Matching Code and Law: Achieving Algorithmic Fairness with Optimal Transport
Abstract: Algorithmic discrimination is increasingly recognized as a societal and legal problem. In response, a number of criteria for implementing algorithmic fairness in machine learning have been developed in the literature. This paper proposes the Continuous Fairness Algorithm (CFA$\\theta$), which enables a continuous interpolation between different fairness definitions. More specifically, the paper makes three main contributions to the existing literature. First, the approach allows decision-makers to continuously vary between specific concepts of individual and group fairness. As a result, the algorithm enables decision-makers to adopt intermediate "worldviews" on the degree of discrimination encoded in algorithmic processes, adding nuance to the extreme cases of "we're all equal" (WAE) and "what you see is what you get" (WYSIWYG) proposed in the literature. Second, optimal transport theory, specifically the concept of the barycenter, is used to maximize decision-maker utility under the chosen fairness constraints. Third, the algorithm can handle cases of intersectionality, i.e., multi-dimensional discrimination of certain groups based on several criteria. The paper discusses three main examples (credit applications, college admissions, insurance contracts) and outlines the legal and policy implications of the approach. The explicit formalization of the trade-off between individual and group fairness allows this post-processing approach to be tailored to different situational contexts where one or the other fairness criterion may take precedence. Finally, the model is evaluated experimentally.

title: Improvements to Inference Compilation for Probabilistic Programming in Large-Scale Scientific Simulators
Abstract: This paper addresses the problem of Bayesian inference in the family of probabilistic models implicitly defined by stochastic generative models of data. In scientific fields ranging from population biology to cosmology, low-level mechanistic components are combined to create complex generative models. These models result in intractable likelihoods and are typically non-differentiable, posing challenges for traditional inference approaches. The paper extends previous work in "inference compilation," which combines universal probabilistic programming and deep learning methods, to large-scale scientific simulators and introduces a C++ based probabilistic programming library called CPProb. CPProb is successfully used to interface with SHERPA, a large codebase used in particle physics. The paper describes the technical innovations realized and planned for this library.

title: Non-convex Optimization for Machine Learning
Abstract: A vast majority of machine learning algorithms train their models and perform inference by solving optimization problems. To accurately capture learning and prediction problems, structural constraints such as sparsity or low rank are frequently imposed, or the objective itself is designed to be a non-convex function. This is particularly true for algorithms operating in high-dimensional spaces or training non-linear models, such as tensor models and deep networks. While the freedom to express the learning problem as a non-convex optimization problem provides immense modeling power to algorithm designers, these problems are often NP-hard to solve. A common workaround is to relax non-convex problems into convex ones and use traditional methods to solve the relaxed optimization problems. However, this approach can be lossy and presents significant challenges for large-scale optimization. On the other hand, direct approaches to non-convex optimization have achieved remarkable success in several domains and remain the methods of choice for practitioners, as they frequently outperform relaxation-based techniques. Popular heuristics include projected gradient descent and alternating minimization, although these are often poorly understood in terms of their convergence and other properties. This monograph presents a selection of recent advances that bridge a long-standing gap in our understanding of these heuristics. It guides the reader through several widely used non-convex optimization techniques and their applications. The goal of this monograph is to introduce the rich literature in this area and equip readers with the tools and techniques needed to analyze these simple procedures for non-convex problems.

title: A Deep Policy Inference Q-Network for Multi-Agent Systems
Abstract: This paper presents DPIQN, a deep policy inference Q-network that targets multi-agent systems composed of controllable agents, collaborators, and opponents that interact with each other. The paper focuses on a challenging issue in such systems: modeling agents with varying strategies. It proposes employing "policy features" learned from raw observations (e.g., raw images) of collaborators and opponents by inferring their policies. DPIQN incorporates the learned policy features as a hidden vector into its own deep Q-network (DQN), enabling it to predict better Q values for the controllable agents than state-of-the-art deep reinforcement learning models. An enhanced version of DPIQN, called deep recurrent policy inference Q-network (DRPIQN), is proposed for handling partial observability. Both DPIQN and DRPIQN are trained by an adaptive training procedure that adjusts the network's attention to learn the policy features and its own Q-values at different training phases. The paper presents a comprehensive analysis of DPIQN and DRPIQN, highlighting their effectiveness and generalizability in various multi-agent settings. The models are evaluated in a classic soccer game involving both competitive and collaborative scenarios. Experimental results performed on 1 vs. 1 and 2 vs. 2 games show that DPIQN and DRPIQN demonstrate superior performance to the baseline DQN and deep recurrent Q-network (DRQN) models. The paper also explores scenarios where collaborators or opponents dynamically change their policies, demonstrating that DPIQN and DRPIQN lead to better overall performance in terms of stability and mean scores.

title: Multiagent-based Participatory Urban Simulation through Inverse Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: Multiagent-based participatory simulations are prominent in urban planning, as the acquired model is considered a hybrid system of domain knowledge and local knowledge. However, the key problem of generating realistic agents for specific social phenomena remains unresolved. Existing models have attempted to dictate the factors involved in human behavior, which has proved intractable. This paper introduces Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) to address this problem. IRL is developed for computational modeling of human behavior and has achieved significant success in robotics, psychology, and machine learning. The paper draws conclusions about the possibilities presented by this new modeling style and highlights the associated challenges.

title: Estimating the Success of Unsupervised Image to Image Translation
Abstract: While validation error is an unbiased estimator of generalization (test) error in supervised learning, and complexity-based generalization bounds are abundant, no such bounds exist for learning a mapping in an unsupervised way. Consequently, when training GANs, particularly when using them for learning to map between domains in a completely unsupervised manner, selecting hyperparameters and stopping epochs relies on subjectively examining multiple options. This paper proposes a novel bound for predicting the success of unsupervised cross-domain mapping methods, motivated by the recently proposed Simplicity Principle. The bound can be applied both in expectation, for comparing hyperparameters and selecting a stopping criterion, or per sample, to predict the success of a specific cross-domain translation. The utility of the bound is demonstrated in an extensive set of experiments using multiple recent algorithms. The code is available at https://github.com/sagiebenaim/gan_bound.

title: Simulating Patho-realistic Ultrasound Images using Deep Generative Networks with Adversarial Learning
Abstract: Ultrasound imaging relies on the backscattering of waves during their interaction with scatterers present in biological tissues. Simulating synthetic ultrasound images is a challenging task due to the inability to accurately model various factors, including intra-/inter scanline interference, transducer to surface coupling, artifacts on transducer elements, inhomogeneous shadowing, and nonlinear attenuation. Current approaches typically solve wave space equations, making them computationally expensive and slow. This paper proposes a generative adversarial network (GAN)-inspired approach for fast simulation of patho-realistic ultrasound images. The framework is applied to intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) simulation. A stage 0 simulation using a pseudo B-mode ultrasound image simulator generates speckle mapping of a digitally defined phantom. The stage I GAN subsequently refines these mappings to preserve tissue-specific speckle intensities. The stage II GAN further refines them to generate high-resolution images with patho-realistic speckle profiles. The patho-realism of simulated images is evaluated using a visual Turing test, indicating an equivocal confusion in discriminating simulated from real images. The paper also quantifies the shift in tissue-specific intensity distributions of the real and simulated images to demonstrate their similarity. |||

title: A probabilistic interpretation of replicator-mutator dynamics
Abstract: In this paper, we explore the connection between probabilistic updating mechanisms and discrete-time replicator-mutator dynamics. Building on the established relationship between Bayesian updating and replicator dynamics, we extend the analysis to replicator-mutator dynamics by considering prediction and filtering recursions in hidden Markov models (HMMs). Our findings demonstrate that the evolution of a population's frequency vector under the replicator-mutator equation can be interpreted as a posterior predictive inference procedure within an HMM. This perspective enables us to derive a dual version of the replicator-mutator equation, corresponding to the updating of the filtering distribution. Finally, we discuss the implications of this interpretation and its relevance to recent debates surrounding evolution and learning.

title: Multi-task learning of time series and its application to the travel demand
Abstract: We investigate the problem of modeling and predicting a set of temporal events in the context of intelligent transportation systems. To leverage the shared information among events, we propose a multi-task learning framework. We develop a support vector regression model for joint learning of mutually dependent time series, extending the previously developed regularization-based multi-task learning for classification to time series data. Recognizing the relatedness of observed time series, we first employ the dynamic time warping distance measure to identify groups of similar series. We then consider both time and scale warping and propose aligning multiple time series by inferring their common latent representation. We evaluate our proposed models on the problem of travel demand prediction within Nancy (France) public transport system, analyzing the benefits of multi-task learning.

title: Prediction of laminar vortex shedding over a cylinder using deep learning
Abstract: We employ a deep learning technique, a generative adversarial network (GAN), to predict unsteady laminar vortex shedding over a circular cylinder, focusing on the potential of learning solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations. Numerical simulations at two distinct Reynolds numbers, with varying time-step sizes, generate training datasets of flow field variables. We use a GAN to predict unsteady flow fields in the future at a Reynolds number not included in the training datasets. Our predicted flow fields demonstrate qualitative and quantitative agreement with flow fields obtained through numerical simulations. Our study suggests that deep learning techniques can be used to predict laminar wake flow, offering an alternative to solving the Navier-Stokes equations.

title: Blended Mastery Learning in Mathematics
Abstract: This paper presents a study on the development of a teaching cycle closely aligned with Bloom's Learning for Mastery (LFM). This teaching cycle addresses practical challenges associated with LFM by integrating the STACK online assessment system to provide automated assessment and feedback to students. We report a clinical trial of this teaching cycle involving groups of university-level engineering students. While our results are modest, they are positive: performance on exercises shows a limited degree of correlation with mastery levels indicated by formative tests. Students also expressed support for the use of this new teaching cycle.

title: Reachable Set Computation and Safety Verification for Neural Networks with ReLU Activations
Abstract: Neural networks are widely used to solve complex real-world problems. The complex, nonlinear, and non-convex nature of neural networks necessitates formal safety guarantees for their output behavior, especially in safety-critical systems. This paper addresses the output reachable set computation and safety verification problems for a class of neural networks employing Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) activation functions. We develop a layer-by-layer approach to compute the output reachable set. This computation is formulated as a set of manipulations for a union of polyhedra, facilitating efficient application with polyhedron computation tools. Using the results from output reachable set computation, safety verification for a ReLU neural network can be achieved by examining the intersections between unsafe regions and the output reachable set represented by a union of polyhedra. A numerical example of a randomly generated ReLU neural network demonstrates the effectiveness of the approach presented in this paper.

title: DropMax: Adaptive Variational Softmax
Abstract: We introduce DropMax, a stochastic version of the softmax classifier. At each iteration, DropMax drops non-target classes based on dropout probabilities adaptively determined for each instance. Specifically, we apply binary masking variables over class output probabilities, learned input-adaptively through variational inference. This stochastic regularization effectively constructs an ensemble classifier from exponentially many classifiers with diverse decision boundaries. Moreover, learning dropout rates for non-target classes on each instance allows the classifier to focus on classification against the most confusing classes. We evaluate our model on multiple public datasets for classification, achieving significantly improved accuracy compared to the regular softmax classifier and other baselines. Further analysis of the learned dropout probabilities reveals that our model indeed selects confusing classes more frequently during classification.

title: Geometrical Insights for Implicit Generative Modeling
Abstract: Learning algorithms for implicit generative models can optimize various criteria that measure the difference between the data distribution and the implicit model distribution, including the Wasserstein distance, the Energy distance, and the Maximum Mean Discrepancy criterion. A careful examination of the geometries induced by these distances on the space of probability measures reveals interesting differences. Notably, we establish surprising approximate global convergence guarantees for the $1$-Wasserstein distance, even with a nonconvex parametrization of the parametric generator.

title: Indoor Sound Source Localization with Probabilistic Neural Network
Abstract: Indoor sound source localization faces significant challenges posed by adverse environments such as high reverberation and low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). To address this challenge, we propose a sound source localization algorithm based on probabilistic neural networks, named Generalized cross correlation Classification Algorithm (GCA). Experimental results in adverse environments with high reverberation time T60 up to 600ms and low SNR down to -10dB demonstrate that GCA achieves an average azimuth angle error of 4.6 degrees and an elevation angle error of 3.1 degrees. Compared to three recently published algorithms, GCA significantly improves the success rate of direction of arrival estimation while exhibiting robust performance under environmental changes. These findings suggest that the proposed GCA can accurately and robustly localize sound sources in diverse indoor applications where site acoustic features can be studied prior to the localization stage.

title: Multi-dimensional Graph Fourier Transform
Abstract: Many real-world signals, such as digital images, sensor observation time series, and movie ratings on Netflix, appear on Cartesian product graphs. These signals are "multi-dimensional" and exhibit directional characteristics along each factor graph. However, the existing graph Fourier transform fails to distinguish these directions and assigns 1-D spectra to signals on product graphs. Furthermore, these spectra often exhibit multi-valuedness at certain frequencies. Our primary result is a multi-dimensional graph Fourier transform that addresses these shortcomings of the conventional GFT. Leveraging the algebraic properties of Cartesian products, our proposed transform rearranges the 1-D spectra obtained through the conventional GFT into the multi-dimensional frequency domain. Each dimension in this domain represents a directional frequency along each factor graph. Consequently, the multi-dimensional graph Fourier transform enables directional frequency analysis, supplementing the frequency analysis provided by the conventional GFT. Moreover, this rearrangement resolves the multi-valuedness of spectra in some cases. The multi-dimensional graph Fourier transform serves as a foundation for novel filterings and stationarities that utilize the dimensional information of graph signals, which we discuss in this study. Our proposed methods are applicable to a wide variety of data that can be viewed as signals on Cartesian product graphs. This study also notes that multivariate graph signals can be regarded as 2-D univariate graph signals. This correspondence provides natural definitions for the multivariate graph Fourier transform and the multivariate stationarity based on their 2-D univariate versions.

title: Wolf in Sheep's Clothing - The Downscaling Attack Against Deep Learning Applications
Abstract: This paper examines security risks embedded within the data processing pipeline of common deep learning applications. Deep learning models typically assume a fixed scale for their training and input data. To enable deep learning applications to handle a wide range of input data, popular frameworks like Caffe, TensorFlow, and Torch provide data scaling functions to resize input to the dimensions used by deep learning models. Image scaling algorithms aim to preserve visual features after scaling. However, common image scaling algorithms are not designed to handle human-crafted images. Attackers can manipulate scaling outputs to appear dramatically different from the corresponding input images. This paper presents a downscaling attack targeting the data scaling process in deep learning applications. By carefully crafting input data that mismatches the dimension used by deep learning models, attackers can create deceptive effects. A deep learning application effectively consumes data that is not the same as those presented to users. The visual inconsistency enables practical evasion and data poisoning attacks against deep learning applications. We demonstrate proof-of-concept attack samples against popular deep-learning-based image classification applications. To address downscaling attacks, we suggest multiple potential mitigation strategies.

title: Model-Based Clustering of Nonparametric Weighted Networks with Application to Water Pollution Analysis
Abstract: Water pollution is a significant global environmental problem posing a major threat to public health and biodiversity. This work investigates the potential environmental risks of coal mining, specifically focusing on increased sulfate concentrations in river networks, which do not follow simple parametric distributions. Existing network models primarily focus on binary or discrete networks and weighted networks with known parametric weight distributions. We propose a principled nonparametric weighted network model based on exponential-family random graph models and local likelihood estimation. We analyze its model-based clustering capabilities and apply it to large-scale water pollution network analysis. Our approach does not require any parametric distribution assumptions on network weights. The proposed method significantly expands the methodology and applicability of statistical network models. Furthermore, it scales effectively to large and complex networks in large-scale environmental studies. We demonstrate the power of our proposed methods through simulation studies and a real-world application to sulfate pollution network analysis in the Ohio watershed located in Pennsylvania, United States.

title: Towards a Deep Improviser: a prototype deep learning post-tonal free music generator
Abstract: We have constructed two modest-sized symbolic corpora of post-tonal and post-metric keyboard music, one algorithmic and the other improvised. Deep learning models for each corpus have been trained and largely optimized. Our goal is to develop a model with sufficient generalization capacity to generate distinctive outputs in response to a small amount of fresh input seed material, rather than simply recreating the learned corpora or the seed material. We assessed this objective statistically using k-sample Anderson-Darling and Cramer tests, demonstrating its achievement. Music generated using this approach has been informally judged to be on par with algorithmic and composed music in related forms. Future research will focus on enhancing the model to evaluate its performance in terms of expression, meaning, and utility in real-time performance.

title: Deep learning for predicting refractive error from retinal fundus images
Abstract: Refractive error, a leading cause of visual impairment, can be corrected through simple interventions like eyeglasses. We trained a deep learning algorithm to predict refractive error from fundus photographs obtained from participants in the UK Biobank cohort, which comprised 45-degree field of view images, and the AREDS clinical trial, containing 30-degree field of view images. Our model utilizes the "attention" method to identify features correlated with refractive error. We evaluated the algorithm's mean absolute error (MAE) in predicting refractive error compared to the values obtained in the AREDS and UK Biobank datasets. The resulting algorithm achieved an MAE of 0.56 diopters (95% CI: 0.55-0.56) for estimating spherical equivalent on the UK Biobank dataset and 0.91 diopters (95% CI: 0.89-0.92) for the AREDS dataset. The baseline expected MAE (obtained by predicting the mean of the population) was 1.81 diopters (95% CI: 1.79-1.84) for UK Biobank and 1.63 (95% CI: 1.60-1.67) for AREDS. Attention maps suggested that the foveal region was one of the most crucial areas used by the algorithm for prediction, although other regions also contribute. The ability to accurately estimate refractive error from retinal fundus photos is novel and demonstrates the potential of deep learning for making novel predictions from medical images. Given the recent feasibility of acquiring retinal fundus photos using mobile phones and inexpensive attachments, this research may be particularly relevant in regions lacking readily available autorefractors.

title: The Character Thinks Ahead: creative writing with deep learning nets and its stylistic assessment
Abstract: We explore techniques for controlling outputs from deep learning models of text corpora to create contemporary poetic works. We assess the success of these controls in generating stylometric distinctiveness. Our specific case study is the piece "The Character Thinks Ahead" (2016/17), highlighting the broad potential applications of this approach.

title: Deep Unsupervised Clustering Using Mixture of Autoencoders
Abstract: Unsupervised clustering is a fundamental challenge in machine learning. A prevalent hypothesis posits that data originates from a union of low-dimensional nonlinear manifolds. Therefore, a clustering approach involves identifying and separating these manifolds. This paper proposes a novel approach to solve this problem using a mixture of autoencoders. Our model consists of two parts: 1) a collection of autoencoders, each learning the underlying manifold of a group of similar objects, and 2) a mixture assignment neural network, which takes the concatenated latent vectors from the autoencoders as input and infers the distribution over clusters. By jointly optimizing these two parts, we simultaneously assign data to clusters and learn the underlying manifolds of each cluster.

title: Setting the Foundation for Scientific Inquiry and Computational Thinking in Early Childhood using Lego Machines and Mechanism Education Kit
Abstract: This paper presents a case study and experience report on teaching engineering skills to young learners aged 7 to 10. Through a constructivist approach involving hands-on activities, such as designing and building machines and mechanisms using concrete objects, we aim to enhance problem-solving abilities in children. These activities also lay the foundation for computer programming courses and scientific inquiry at the elementary level. We utilize a learning environment and curriculum based on Lego simple machines and mechanisms kits. Our objective is not only to teach concepts of basic machines but also to develop essential skills like teamwork and collaboration, communication, and time management in students within the early childhood age group. We conducted experiments on a group of five students during a summer camp, employing a mixed-method approach to collect both qualitative and quantitative data regarding their learning and behavior. Our research and findings provide empirical evidence supporting the possibility of developing engineering skills at the early childhood level, alongside the development of language literacy and mathematical thinking.

title: Carbon stars identified from LAMOST DR4 using Machine Learning
Abstract: This work presents a catalog of 2651 carbon stars identified from the fourth Data Release (DR4) of the Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopy Telescope (LAMOST). We used an efficient machine-learning algorithm to identify these stars from a dataset of over seven million spectra. As a by-product, we report 17 carbon-enhanced metal-poor (CEMP) turnoff star candidates in this paper, preliminarily identified based on their atmospheric parameters. Excluding 176 stars without spectral types, we classify the remaining 2475 carbon stars into five subtypes: 864 C-H, 226 C-R, 400 C-J, 266 C-N, and 719 barium stars, based on a series of spectral features. Furthermore, we divide the C-J stars into three subtypes: CJ(H), C-J(R), and C-J(N). Consistent with previous literature, approximately 90% of these stars are cool N-type stars. In addition to spectroscopic classification, we also match these carbon stars to multiple broadband photometries. Using ultraviolet photometry data, we find that 25 carbon stars have FUV detections, suggesting they are likely in binary systems with compact white dwarf companions.

title: Controlled Information Fusion with Risk-Averse CVaR Social Sensors
Abstract: Consider a multi-agent network composed of risk-averse social sensors and a controller jointly seeking to estimate an unknown state of nature, given noisy measurements. The network of social sensors performs Bayesian social learning, where each sensor fuses the information revealed by previous social sensors with its private valuation using Bayes' rule to optimize a local cost function. The controller sequentially modifies the cost function of the sensors through discriminatory pricing (control inputs) to achieve long-term global objectives. We formulate the stochastic control problem faced by the controller as a Partially Observed Markov Decision Process (POMDP) and derive structural results for the optimal control policy as a function of the risk-aversion factor in the Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) cost function of the sensors. We demonstrate that the optimal price sequence when the sensors are risk-averse is a super-martingale; that is, it decreases on average over time.

title: Combining Static and Dynamic Features for Multivariate Sequence Classification
Abstract: Model precision in a classification task is highly dependent on the feature space used for training. Moreover, the nature of features, whether sequential or static, dictates the applicable classification method, as most machine learning algorithms are designed for one type of data or the other. However, real-life scenarios often involve both static and dynamic features, or these features can be extracted from the data. This work demonstrates how generative models such as Hidden Markov Models (HMM) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) artificial neural networks can extract temporal information from dynamic data. We explore how this extracted information can be combined with static features to enhance classification performance. We evaluate existing techniques and propose a hybrid approach that outperforms other methods on several public datasets.
label: AI

title: Contemporary machine learning: a guide for practitioners in the physical sciences
Abstract: Machine learning is finding increasingly broad application in the physical sciences. This often involves building models that represent the relationship between a measurable output and a set of controllable but complicated input variables. We present a tutorial on current machine learning techniques, serving as a jumping-off point for interested researchers to advance their work. We focus on deep neural networks, emphasizing the demystification of deep learning. We begin with fundamental concepts in machine learning and provide example applications from current research in plasma physics. We discuss supervised learning techniques for modeling complex functions, starting with familiar regression schemes and progressing to more sophisticated deep learning methods. We also address unsupervised learning and techniques for reducing the dimensionality of input spaces. Throughout the tutorial, we describe methods that practitioners can use to ensure their models generalize from training data to unseen test data. We cover various classes of tasks, including predicting scalars, handling images, and fitting time-series, preparing the reader to select appropriate techniques. Finally, we highlight some limitations of modern machine learning and speculate on how practitioners from the physical sciences can contribute to overcoming these challenges.
