title: Development and evaluation of a deep learning model for protein-ligand binding affinity prediction
Abstract: Structure-based ligand discovery is one of the most successful approaches for augmenting the drug discovery process. Currently, there is a notable shift towards machine learning (ML) methodologies to aid such procedures. Deep learning has recently gained considerable attention as it allows the model to "learn" to extract features relevant to the task at hand. We have developed a novel deep neural network that estimates the binding affinity of ligand-receptor complexes. The complex is represented with a 3D grid, and the model utilizes a 3D convolution to produce a feature map of this representation, treating the atoms of both proteins and ligands in the same manner. Our network was tested on the CASF "scoring power" benchmark and Astex Diverse Set and outperformed classical scoring functions. The model, together with usage instructions and examples, is available as a git repository at http://gitlab.com/cheminfIBB/pafnucy.
label: AI

title: The NarrativeQA Reading Comprehension Challenge
Abstract: Reading comprehension (RC), unlike information retrieval, requires integrating information and reasoning about events, entities, and their relations across a full document. Question answering is conventionally used to assess RC ability in both artificial agents and children learning to read. However, existing RC datasets and tasks are dominated by questions that can be solved by selecting answers using superficial information (e.g., local context similarity or global term frequency). These datasets fail to test the essential integrative aspect of RC. To encourage progress on deeper comprehension of language, we present a new dataset and set of tasks where the reader must answer questions about stories by reading entire books or movie scripts. These tasks are designed so that successfully answering their questions requires understanding the underlying narrative rather than relying on shallow pattern matching or salience. We show that while humans solve these tasks easily, standard RC models struggle. We provide an analysis of the dataset and the challenges it presents.
label: AI

title: Snake: a Stochastic Proximal Gradient Algorithm for Regularized Problems over Large Graphs
Abstract: We study a regularized optimization problem over a large unstructured graph, where the regularization term is tied to the graph geometry. Typical regularization examples include total variation and Laplacian regularization over the graph. When applying the proximal gradient algorithm to solve this problem, there exist affordable methods to implement the proximity operator (backward step) in the special case where the graph is a simple path without loops. This paper proposes an algorithm called "Snake" to solve such regularized problems over general graphs by leveraging these fast methods. The algorithm involves carefully selecting random simple paths in the graph and performing the proximal gradient algorithm over these simple paths. This algorithm is an instance of a new general stochastic proximal gradient algorithm, whose convergence is proven. Applications to trend filtering and graph inpainting are provided among others. Numerical experiments are conducted over large graphs.
label: AI

title: Automatic Renal Segmentation in DCE-MRI using Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: Kidney function evaluation using dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI (DCE-MRI) images could aid in diagnosing and treating kidney diseases in children. Automatic segmentation of renal parenchyma is a crucial step in this process. This paper proposes a time and memory-efficient fully automated segmentation method that achieves high segmentation accuracy with running times in the order of seconds for both normal kidneys and kidneys with hydronephrosis. The proposed method is based on a cascaded application of two 3D convolutional neural networks that simultaneously utilize spatial and temporal information to learn the tasks of kidney localization and segmentation, respectively. Segmentation performance is evaluated on both normal and abnormal kidneys with varying levels of hydronephrosis. We achieved a mean Dice coefficient of 91.4 and 83.6 for normal and abnormal kidneys of pediatric patients, respectively.
label: AI

title: Privacy-Preserving Adversarial Networks
Abstract: We propose a data-driven framework for optimizing privacy-preserving data release mechanisms to achieve the information-theoretically optimal tradeoff between minimizing distortion of useful data and concealing specific sensitive information. Our approach employs adversarially-trained neural networks to implement randomized mechanisms and perform a variational approximation of mutual information privacy. We validate our Privacy-Preserving Adversarial Networks (PPAN) framework through proof-of-concept experiments on discrete and continuous synthetic data, as well as the MNIST handwritten digits dataset. For synthetic data, our model-agnostic PPAN approach achieves tradeoff points very close to the optimal tradeoffs analytically derived from model knowledge. In experiments with the MNIST data, we visually demonstrate a learned tradeoff between minimizing pixel-level distortion and concealing the written digit.
label: AI

title: Any-gram Kernels for Sentence Classification: A Sentiment Analysis Case Study
Abstract: Any-gram kernels provide a flexible and efficient way to employ bag-of-n-gram features when learning from textual data. They are also compatible with the use of word embeddings, allowing for the consideration of word similarities. While the original any-gram kernels are implemented on top of tree kernels, we propose a new approach that is independent of tree kernels and more efficient. We also propose a more effective way to utilize word embeddings than the original any-gram formulation. When applied to the task of sentiment classification, our new formulation achieves significantly better performance.
label: AI

title: Bilinear residual Neural Network for the identification and forecasting of dynamical systems
Abstract: Due to the increasing availability of large-scale observation and simulation datasets, data-driven representations are emerging as efficient and relevant computational representations of dynamical systems for a wide range of applications. Model-driven models based on ordinary differential equations remain state-of-the-art approaches. In this work, we investigate neural networks (NN) as physically-sound data-driven representations of such systems. Reinterpreting Runge-Kutta methods as graphical models, we consider a residual NN architecture and introduce bilinear layers to embed non-linearities that are intrinsic features of dynamical systems. From numerical experiments for classic dynamical systems, we demonstrate the relevance of the proposed NN-based architecture in terms of forecasting performance and model identification.
label: AI

title: An Automorphic Distance Metric and its Application to Node Embedding for Role Mining
Abstract: Role is a fundamental concept in analyzing the behavior and function of interacting entities represented by network data. Role discovery is the task of uncovering hidden roles. Node roles are commonly defined in terms of equivalence classes, where two nodes have the same role if they fall within the same equivalence class. Automorphic equivalence, where two nodes are equivalent when they can swap their labels to form an isomorphic graph, captures this common notion of role. The binary concept of equivalence is too restrictive, and nodes in real-world networks rarely belong to the same equivalence class. Instead, a relaxed definition in terms of similarity or distance is commonly used to compute the degree to which two nodes are equivalent. In this paper, we propose a novel distance metric called automorphic distance, which measures how far two nodes are from being automorphically equivalent. We also study its application to node embedding, showing how our metric can be used to generate vector representations of nodes that preserve their roles for data visualization and machine learning. Our experiments confirm that the proposed metric outperforms the RoleSim automorphic equivalence-based metric in generating node embeddings for different networks. |||
label: AI

title: Unsupervised Word Mapping Using Structural Similarities in Monolingual Embeddings
Abstract: Existing methods for automatic bilingual dictionary induction rely on prior alignments between languages, which are often unavailable. This paper proposes an unsupervised method for learning a bilingual dictionary using independently-learned monolingual word embeddings. The method exploits local and global structures in vector spaces to align similar words, achieving performance comparable to supervised methods using seed dictionaries.
label: AI

title: Mining Smart Card Data for Travelers' Mini Activities
Abstract: Public transport modeling often generates over-optimistic trip simulations that don't reflect real passenger choices. This paper introduces "mini activities" as a way to explain this mismatch, and proposes extracting these activities from smart card data.  A Markov chain model is used to integrate mini activities into trip simulations, ensuring that selected characteristics converge to desired distributions. Experiments on Nancy, France passenger trip data demonstrate significant reduction in mismatch.
label: AI

title: Safe Policy Improvement with Baseline Bootstrapping
Abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of Safe Policy Improvement (SPI) in Batch Reinforcement Learning (Batch RL), where a policy is trained from a fixed dataset without direct access to the environment. The proposed approach, SPI with Baseline Bootstrapping (SPIBB), utilizes a "knows-what-it-knows" paradigm, bootstrapping the trained policy with the baseline when uncertainty is high.  Two algorithms are presented: $\\Pi_b$-SPIBB with theoretical SPI guarantees, and $\\Pi_{\\leq b}$-SPIBB for practical efficiency.  Experiments demonstrate SPIBB's superiority in safety and performance over existing algorithms, with a model-free version showing benefits in a navigation task using deep RL.
label: AI

title: Ensemble Models for Detecting Wikidata Vandalism with Stacking - Team Honeyberry Vandalism Detector at WSDM Cup 2017
Abstract: The WSDM Cup 2017 challenged participants to classify Wikidata revisions as vandalism or non-vandalism. This paper describes a method utilizing machine learning techniques such as undersampling, feature selection, stacking, and ensembles of models. The paper confirms the validity of each technique by comparing model performance with and without their use. An analysis of the results provides insights into improving models for vandalism detection. The final submission achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.94412.
label: AI

title: ComboGAN: Unrestrained Scalability for Image Domain Translation
Abstract: Recent advancements in image translation, such as CycleGAN, have been limited to two domains at a time, requiring a quadratic increase in model training for more domains.  This paper proposes a multi-component image translation model that scales linearly with the number of domains, both in terms of resources and time. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated on datasets of paintings by 14 artists and images of the four seasons in the Alps, requiring significantly fewer models than traditional approaches.
label: AI

title: Cross-language Framework for Word Recognition and Spotting of Indic Scripts
Abstract: Handwritten word recognition and spotting for low-resource scripts are difficult due to limited training data. This paper introduces a novel cross-language platform for these tasks, where training is performed on a large dataset of a readily available script and testing is done on low-resource scripts. The platform exploits the similarities of Indic scripts, utilizing zone-wise character mapping for efficient learning. An entropy-based script similarity score is devised to assess the feasibility of cross-language transcription. The approach is evaluated on Bangla, Devanagari, and Gurumukhi scripts, demonstrating promising results.
label: AI

title: Learning Fixation Point Strategy for Object Detection and Classification
Abstract: This paper presents a novel recurrent attentional structure for joint object localization and recognition. The network learns to extract a sequence of local observations with detailed appearance and context, bypassing sliding windows or convolutions. These observations are then fused for detection and classification. A hybrid loss function is used to learn the network's parameters end-to-end, employing a stochastic and object-awareness strategy to select rich context and ensure fixation near the object.  The method achieves high speed and accurate bounding box prediction, and its performance can be easily tuned by adjusting the number of recurrent steps.  The source code is publicly available.
label: AI

title: Using Machine-Learning to Optimize phase contrast in a Low-Cost Cellphone Microscope
Abstract: Cellphones with high-quality cameras and powerful processors offer a cost-effective solution for medical diagnosis in developing countries. This paper presents a smartphone microscope designed using 3D printing and off-the-shelf components, enabling real-time applications. A convolutional neural network (CNN) is used to learn the relationship between samples and optimal light source shapes, improving phase contrast and the impression of resolution without additional optics. The approach is validated through experimental measurements.
label: AI

title: Pattern recognition techniques for Boson Sampling validation
Abstract: Validating large-scale quantum devices, such as Boson Samplers, is challenging. This paper proposes a data-driven approach using unsupervised machine learning to identify common pathologies. A classifier trained with K-means clustering distinguishes between Boson Samplers using indistinguishable photons and those that do not. The model is trained on simulations of small-scale devices and validated on larger simulations and photonic chips. The effectiveness of the approach relies on particle-type-dependent correlations present in the output distributions, outperforming previous methods and demonstrating generalization beyond training data.
label: AI

title: End-to-end weakly-supervised semantic alignment
Abstract: Semantic alignment aims to compute dense correspondences between images depicting objects of the same category.  This paper presents a convolutional neural network architecture for semantic alignment trained end-to-end using weak image-level supervision. The architecture incorporates a differentiable soft inlier scoring module inspired by RANSAC, which computes alignment quality based on geometrically consistent correspondences, reducing the effect of background clutter. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks for semantic alignment.
label: AI

title: Subword and Crossword Units for CTC Acoustic Models
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach for creating a unit set for CTC-based speech recognition systems.  By leveraging Byte Pair Encoding, an unit set of arbitrary size can be learned from training text, providing a trade-off between unit set size and available data. Both Crossword and Subword units are evaluated, and the approach is combined with decoding methods using a separate language model to achieve state-of-the-art results for grapheme-based CTC systems.
label: AI

title: Estimation of Individual Micro Data from Aggregated Open Data
Abstract: This paper proposes a method for estimating individual micro data from aggregated open data based on semi-supervised learning and conditional probability.  The method uses locality sensitive hashing (LSH) to find a subset of support data similar to aggregated open data and classifies them using an ensemble model learned via semi-supervised learning.  Conditional probability is then applied to estimate individual micro data by identifying the most suitable record based on the probability distribution. Experiments on estimating individual building data from aggregated fire open data achieve an average accuracy of 59.41%.
label: AI

title: Two-dimensional Anti-jamming Mobile Communication Based on Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: Jammers can dynamically adapt their jamming policies based on opposing security mechanisms, even inducing mobile devices into specific communication modes. This paper proposes a two-dimensional anti-jamming mobile communication scheme where a mobile device leaves a heavily jammed frequency or area.  The scheme utilizes reinforcement learning techniques to achieve an optimal communication policy without requiring knowledge of the jamming, interference, or channel models. A hotbooting deep Q-network-based scheme is proposed that leverages experiences from similar scenarios to accelerate learning. Simulations demonstrate improved signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio and utility against cooperative jamming compared to benchmark schemes.
label: AI

title: A remark on "Robust machine learning by median-of-means"
Abstract: This paper examines the results presented in "Robust machine learning by median-of-means: theory and practice" by G. Lecué and M. Lerasle.  It argues that these results are essentially obvious outcomes of the machinery developed in [4] for the study of tournament procedures.
label: AI

title: Learning Representations from Road Network for End-to-End Urban Growth Simulation
Abstract: Urban growth is heavily influenced by transportation networks. This paper proposes a method to integrate road network data into an existing rule-based end-to-end urban growth prediction framework, eliminating the need for manual feature engineering. Recurrent neural networks are used to represent road networks in a structured way, enabling their integration into the framework. The proposed approach improves the performance of the framework in terms of various metrics.
label: AI

title: Mining Point Cloud Local Structures by Kernel Correlation and Graph Pooling
Abstract: Semantic learning on 3D point clouds using deep networks is challenging due to the unordered data structure. While PointNet has achieved promising results, it doesn't fully exploit local neighborhoods.  This paper presents two new operations to improve PointNet: a point-set kernel for capturing local 3D geometric structures and recursive feature aggregation for exploiting local high-dimensional feature structures. Experiments demonstrate the network's ability to capture local information and achieve improved performance on major datasets.
label: AI

title: HotFlip: White-Box Adversarial Examples for Text Classification
Abstract: This paper presents an efficient method for generating white-box adversarial examples to deceive character-level neural classifiers.  The method relies on an atomic flip operation that swaps tokens based on gradients of the one-hot input vectors. This approach enables adversarial training, making the model more robust to attacks.  Furthermore, with semantics-preserving constraints, the method can be adapted to attack word-level classifiers.
label: AI

title: Efficient Algorithms for Searching the Minimum Information Partition in Integrated Information Theory
Abstract: Integrated Information Theory (IIT) proposes that consciousness is related to the amount of integrated information ($\\Phi$) in the brain.  Computing $\\Phi$ requires finding the Minimum Information Partition (MIP), which is computationally expensive for large systems.  This paper investigates whether an optimization algorithm can be applied to non-submodular measures of $\\Phi$, empirically evaluating its accuracy on simulated and real neural data. The results show that the algorithm effectively identifies the MIP even for non-submodular measures, enabling practical computation of $\\Phi$ in large systems.
label: AI

title: PixelBNN: Augmenting the PixelCNN with batch normalization and the presentation of a fast architecture for retinal vessel segmentation
Abstract: Analyzing retinal fundus images is crucial for eye care. Accurate fundus and retinal vessel maps support various applications, including disease assessment, surgery preparation, and biometrics. This paper presents PixelBNN, a highly efficient deep method for automating fundus morphology segmentation. The model is trained and evaluated on DRIVE, STARE, and CHASE\\_DB1 datasets, achieving comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods while being significantly faster.
label: AI

title: Deformable Classifiers
Abstract: Object recognition is challenged by geometric variations that do not alter the object class. This paper introduces a framework for training deformable classifiers, where latent transformation variables are introduced to compute a transformation of the object image to a reference instantiation. The classifier outputs for each class, after transformation, are compared to make the final decision.  The approach utilizes a two-step training mechanism that alternates between optimizing transformation variables and classifier parameters. Experiments on rotated MNIST, Google Earth, MNIST, and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art or competitive results. |||
label: AI

title: Multilingual Topic Models
Abstract: Scientific publications have developed various techniques to address vocabulary mismatch when indexing, retrieving, and assessing article similarity. These techniques range from focusing on essential article sections like titles and abstracts to assigning keywords, often drawn from controlled vocabularies, either manually or through automated annotation. Different document representation schemes come with their own trade-offs. This paper proposes a novel approach that models diverse representations of the same article as translations of one another, all generated from a shared latent representation in a multilingual topic model. The paper presents a methodological overview of latent variable models for parallel document representations, highlighting their potential across various information science tasks. It demonstrates how solving the inference problem of mapping diverse representations into a shared topic space enables the evaluation of representations based on their topical similarity to the original article. Furthermore, this approach offers a means to identify areas where different concept vocabularies require improvement.
label: AI

title: Accurate Inference for Adaptive Linear Models
Abstract: Estimators derived from adaptively collected data exhibit distinct behavior compared to their non-adaptive counterparts. The sequential dependence of the collection policy can introduce significant distributional biases, which persist even with an infinite amount of data. This paper proposes a general method, known as **W**-decorrelation, to transform the bias of adaptive linear regression estimators into variance. This method leverages only coarse-grained information about the data collection policy and does not necessitate access to propensity scores or exact knowledge of the policy. The paper provides bounds for the finite-sample bias and variance of the **W**-estimator, and develops asymptotically correct confidence intervals based on a novel martingale central limit theorem. The empirical benefits of the generic **W**-decorrelation procedure are demonstrated in two distinct adaptive data settings: the multi-armed bandit and the autoregressive time series.
label: AI

title: Synthesizing Novel Pairs of Image and Text
Abstract: Generating novel image-text pairs is a problem that blends computer vision and natural language processing. This paper presents strategies for generating novel image-caption pairs based on existing captioning datasets. The model leverages recent advancements in generative adversarial networks and sequence-to-sequence modeling. It generalizes to generate paired samples from multiple domains. The paper further investigates cycles – generating from image to text and back to image, as well as its connection to autoencoders.
label: AI

title: word representation or word embedding in Persian text
Abstract: Text processing constitutes a sub-branch of natural language processing. Recently, machine learning and neural network methods have gained significant attention in this field. Consequently, word representation, or converting words into vectors, has become crucial. This article focuses on word representation in Persian text. The research updates GloVe, CBOW, and skip-gram methods to generate embedded vectors for Persian words. For training the neural networks, the Bijankhan corpus, Hamshahri corpus, and UPEC corpus were combined and used. Ultimately, 342,362 words obtained vectors in all three models. These vectors have wide applications in Persian natural language processing.
label: AI

title: MEBoost: Mixing Estimators with Boosting for Imbalanced Data Classification
Abstract: The class imbalance problem has been a persistent challenge in machine learning and data mining, as most real-world datasets exhibit an imbalance. Several existing machine learning algorithms prioritize maximizing accuracy by correctly identifying majority class samples, neglecting the minority class. However, the concept of minority class instances often holds greater interest than the majority class. In recent years, various cost-sensitive methods, ensemble models, and sampling techniques have been employed to address imbalanced datasets. This paper introduces MEBoost, a novel boosting algorithm specifically designed for imbalanced datasets. MEBoost combines two different weak learners with boosting to enhance performance on imbalanced datasets. MEBoost serves as an alternative to existing techniques like SMOTEBoost, RUSBoost, Adaboost, etc. The performance of MEBoost was evaluated on 12 benchmark imbalanced datasets using state-of-the-art ensemble methods like SMOTEBoost, RUSBoost, Easy Ensemble, EUSBoost, and DataBoost. Experimental results demonstrate significant improvements over other methods, suggesting that MEBoost is an effective and promising algorithm for handling imbalanced datasets. The Python version of the code is available at: https://github.com/farshidrayhanuiu/
label: AI

title: Towards the Augmented Pathologist: Challenges of Explainable-AI in Digital Pathology
Abstract: Digital pathology is not only a promising field in diagnostic medicine but also a hot topic for fundamental research. It goes beyond simply converting histopathological slides into digital representations. The integration of diverse data sources (images, patient records, and *omics data) combined with advancements in artificial intelligence/machine learning allows for the generation of novel information accessible and quantifiable to human experts, information that remains unavailable and unexploited in current medical settings. The ultimate goal is to achieve usable intelligence to understand data within the context of application tasks, making machine decisions transparent, interpretable, and explainable. Building an "augmented pathologist" requires an integrated approach. While machine learning algorithms necessitate thousands of training examples, a human expert often works with limited data points. Notably, humans excel at learning from limited examples and can instantly interpret complex patterns. Therefore, the ultimate goal is to combine the capabilities of artificial intelligence with human intelligence, finding a well-suited balance to achieve what neither can accomplish alone. This can elevate the quality of education, diagnosis, prognosis, and prediction of cancer and other diseases. This paper identifies (incomplete) research issues that require integrated and concerted efforts to pave the way for the augmented pathologist.
label: AI

title: Objects that Sound
Abstract: This paper aims to develop networks that can embed audio and visual inputs into a common space suitable for cross-modal retrieval, and a network capable of localizing the object that sounds in an image given the audio signal. Both objectives are achieved by training from unlabeled video using only audio-visual correspondence (AVC) as the objective function. This constitutes a form of cross-modal self-supervision from video. To this end, new network architectures are designed that can be trained for cross-modal retrieval and sound source localization in images using the AVC task. The contributions include: (i) demonstrating the learning of audio and visual embeddings that enable both within-mode (e.g., audio-to-audio) and between-mode retrieval; (ii) exploring various architectures for the AVC task, including those for the visual stream that process a single image, multiple images, or a single image and multi-frame optical flow; (iii) showcasing the ability to localize the semantic object that sounds within an image using only sound, without motion or flow information; and (iv) providing a cautionary tale on avoiding undesirable shortcuts in data preparation.
label: AI

title: When Not to Classify: Anomaly Detection of Attacks (ADA) on DNN Classifiers at Test Time
Abstract: A significant threat to the widespread deployment of machine learning-based systems, including deep neural networks (DNNs), is adversarial learning attacks. This paper analyzes possible test-time evasion-attack mechanisms and demonstrates that, in certain scenarios, correctly classifying an attacked image holds no utility: (i) when the attacked image is selected from the attacker's cache, even arbitrarily; (ii) when the attacker is the sole recipient of the classifier's decision. Moreover, in specific application domains and scenarios, detecting the attack, regardless of correct classification, is highly actionable (with classification still performed if no attack is detected). The paper hypothesizes that, even if imperceptible to humans, adversarial perturbations are machine-detectable. It proposes a purely unsupervised anomaly detector (AD) that, unlike previous works: (i) models the joint density of a deep layer using highly suitable null hypothesis density models (matched to the non-negative support for RELU layers); (ii) exploits multiple DNN layers; (iii) leverages a "source" and "destination" class concept, source class uncertainty, the class confusion matrix, and DNN weight information to construct a novel decision statistic grounded in the Kullback-Leibler divergence. Tested on MNIST and CIFAR-10 image databases under three prominent attack strategies, the approach outperforms previous detection methods, achieving strong ROC AUC detection accuracy on two attacks and better accuracy than recently reported for a variety of methods on the strongest (CW) attack. The paper also evaluates a fully white-box attack on the system. Finally, it assesses other important performance measures, such as classification accuracy versus detection rate and attack strength.
label: AI

title: Third-order Smoothness Helps: Even Faster Stochastic Optimization Algorithms for Finding Local Minima
Abstract: This paper proposes stochastic optimization algorithms that can locate local minima faster than existing algorithms for nonconvex optimization problems by exploiting third-order smoothness to escape non-degenerate saddle points more efficiently. Specifically, the proposed algorithm requires only $\\tilde{O}(\\epsilon^{-10/3})$ stochastic gradient evaluations to converge to an approximate local minimum $\\mathbf{x}$, satisfying $\\|\\nabla\nf(\\mathbf{x})\\|_2\\leq\\epsilon$ and $\\lambda_{\\min}(\\nabla^2 f(\\mathbf{x}))\\geq\n-\\sqrt{\\epsilon}$ in the general stochastic optimization setting, where $\\tilde{O}(\\cdot)$ hides logarithm polynomial terms and constants. This improves upon the $\\tilde{O}(\\epsilon^{-7/2})$ gradient complexity achieved by state-of-the-art stochastic local minima finding algorithms by a factor of $\\tilde{O}(\\epsilon^{-1/6})$. For nonconvex finite-sum optimization, the algorithm also outperforms the best known algorithms in a specific regime.
label: AI

title: Parallel Complexity of Forward and Backward Propagation
Abstract: This paper demonstrates that forward and backward propagation can be formulated as solutions to lower and upper triangular systems of equations. For standard feedforward (FNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs), the triangular systems are always block bi-diagonal, while for a general computation graph (directed acyclic graph), they can exhibit a more complex triangular sparsity pattern. The paper discusses direct and iterative parallel algorithms that can be used for solving these systems and interpreted as different ways of performing model parallelism. It shows that for FNNs and RNNs with k layers and $\\tau$ time steps, backward propagation can be performed in parallel in O($\\log k$) and O($\\log k\n\\log \\tau$) steps, respectively. Finally, the paper outlines the generalization of this technique using Jacobians, potentially allowing for handling arbitrary layers.
label: AI

title: ES Is More Than Just a Traditional Finite-Difference Approximator
Abstract: A variant of evolution strategy (ES) based on a simplified natural evolution strategy has recently garnered attention due to its surprisingly strong performance in challenging deep reinforcement learning domains. It searches for neural network parameters by generating perturbations to the current parameter set, evaluating their performance, and moving in the aggregate direction of higher reward. Its resemblance to a traditional finite-difference approximation of the reward gradient can lead to confusion. However, this ES optimizes for a different gradient than just reward: it optimizes for the average reward of the entire population, thereby seeking parameters that are robust to perturbation. This difference can channel ES into distinct areas of the search space compared to gradient descent, resulting in networks with distinct properties. This unique robustness-seeking property, and its implications for optimization, are demonstrated in several domains. These domains include humanoid locomotion, where networks from policy gradient-based reinforcement learning are significantly less robust to parameter perturbation than ES-based policies solving the same task. While the implications of such robustness and robustness-seeking remain open to further study, the paper's main contribution is to highlight these differences and their potential importance.
label: AI

title: Deep Neuroevolution: Genetic Algorithms Are a Competitive Alternative for Training Deep Neural Networks for Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: Deep artificial neural networks (DNNs) are typically trained using gradient-based learning algorithms, namely backpropagation. Evolution strategies (ES) can rival backprop-based algorithms like Q-learning and policy gradients on challenging deep reinforcement learning (RL) problems. However, ES can also be considered a gradient-based algorithm because it performs stochastic gradient descent via an operation similar to a finite-difference approximation of the gradient. This raises the question of whether non-gradient-based evolutionary algorithms can function at DNN scales. This paper demonstrates that they can: the weights of a DNN are evolved using a simple, gradient-free, population-based genetic algorithm (GA), and it performs well on challenging deep RL problems, including Atari and humanoid locomotion. The Deep GA successfully evolves networks with over four million free parameters, the largest neural networks ever evolved with a traditional evolutionary algorithm. These results (1) expand our understanding of the scale at which GAs can operate, (2) suggest that following the gradient might not always be the best choice for optimizing performance, and (3) make available the multitude of neuroevolution techniques for performance improvement. The paper demonstrates the latter by showing that combining DNNs with novelty search, which encourages exploration on tasks with deceptive or sparse reward functions, can solve a high-dimensional problem where reward-maximizing algorithms (e.g., DQN, A3C, ES, and the GA) fail. Additionally, the Deep GA is faster than ES, A3C, and DQN (it can train Atari in ${\\raise.17ex\\hbox{$\\scriptstyle\\sim$}}$4 hours on a single desktop or ${\\raise.17ex\\hbox{$\\scriptstyle\\sim$}}$1 hour distributed across 720 cores), and enables a state-of-the-art, up to 10,000-fold compact encoding technique.
label: AI

title: On the Relationship Between the OpenAI Evolution Strategy and Stochastic Gradient Descent
Abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) has proven effective in optimizing neural networks with millions of parameters, and few viable alternatives exist. This has made it a central element in leading approaches to reinforcement learning (RL). The recent result from OpenAI showing that a specific type of evolution strategy (ES) can rival the performance of SGD-based deep RL methods with large neural networks caused surprise. This result is challenging to interpret due to the lingering ambiguity surrounding the relationship between ES and SGD. This paper aims to significantly reduce this ambiguity through a series of MNIST-based experiments designed to uncover their relationship. As a simple supervised problem without domain noise (unlike in most RL), MNIST allows for (1) measuring the correlation between gradients computed by ES and SGD, and (2) developing an SGD-based proxy that accurately predicts the performance of different ES population sizes. These innovations provide a new level of insight into the capabilities of ES, leading to unconventional means of applying ES to supervised problems, shedding further light on its differences from SGD. Incorporating these lessons, the paper concludes by demonstrating that ES can achieve 99% accuracy on MNIST, exceeding any previously published result for an evolutionary method. While not suggesting that ES should replace SGD in supervised learning, the suite of experiments enables more informed decisions on the application of ES within RL and other paradigms.
label: AI

title: Safe Mutations for Deep and Recurrent Neural Networks through Output Gradients
Abstract: While neuroevolution (evolving neural networks) boasts a successful track record across various domains, from reinforcement learning to artificial life, its application to large, deep neural networks is rare. A key reason is that while random mutation generally works in low dimensions, a random perturbation of thousands or millions of weights is likely to disrupt existing functionality, providing no learning signal even if some individual weight changes were beneficial. This paper proposes a solution by introducing a family of safe mutation (SM) operators that aim to find, within the mutation operator itself, a degree of change that minimally alters network behavior while facilitating exploration. Importantly, these SM operators do not require any additional interactions with the environment. The most effective SM variant leverages the intriguing opportunity to scale the degree of mutation of each individual weight according to the network's output sensitivity to that weight. This requires computing the gradient of outputs with respect to the weights (instead of the gradient of error, as in conventional deep learning). This safe mutation through gradients (SM-G) operator significantly increases the ability of a simple genetic algorithm-based neuroevolution method to find solutions in high-dimensional domains requiring deep and/or recurrent neural networks (which tend to be particularly brittle to mutation), including domains requiring processing raw pixels. By enhancing our capacity to evolve deep neural networks, this new safer approach to mutation expands the scope of domains amenable to neuroevolution.
label: AI

title: The Power of Interpolation: Understanding the Effectiveness of SGD in Modern Over-parametrized Learning
Abstract: This paper aims to provide a formal explanation for the observed fast convergence of SGD in modern machine learning. The key observation is that most modern learning architectures are over-parametrized and trained to interpolate the data by driving the empirical loss (classification and regression) close to zero. While the reason for the effectiveness of these interpolated solutions on test data remains unclear, the paper demonstrates that these regimes allow for fast convergence of SGD, comparable in iteration count to full gradient descent. For convex loss functions, the paper obtains an exponential convergence bound for {\\it mini-batch} SGD, parallel to that for full gradient descent. It shows the existence of a critical batch size $m^*$ such that: (a) SGD iteration with mini-batch size $m\\leq m^*$ is nearly equivalent to $m$ iterations of mini-batch size $1$ (\\emph{linear scaling regime}). (b) SGD iteration with mini-batch $m> m^*$ is nearly equivalent to a full gradient descent iteration (\\emph{saturation regime}). Moreover, for the quadratic loss, the paper derives explicit expressions for the optimal mini-batch and step size, explicitly characterizing the two regimes. The critical mini-batch size can be considered the limit for effective mini-batch parallelization. It is also nearly independent of the data size, implying an O(n) acceleration over GD per unit of computation. The paper provides experimental evidence on real data that closely aligns with the theoretical analyses. Finally, it discusses how these results fit within recent developments in training deep neural networks and connections to adaptive rates for SGD and variance reduction.
label: AI

title: Improving Exploration in Evolution Strategies for Deep Reinforcement Learning via a Population of Novelty-Seeking Agents
Abstract: Evolution strategies (ES) are a family of black-box optimization algorithms capable of training deep neural networks nearly as well as Q-learning and policy gradient methods on challenging deep reinforcement learning (RL) problems, but they are significantly faster (e.g., hours vs. days) due to better parallelization. However, many RL problems necessitate directed exploration because their reward functions are sparse or deceptive (containing local optima), and it is unknown how to promote such exploration with ES. This paper shows that algorithms designed to encourage directed exploration in small-scale evolved neural networks using populations of exploring agents, specifically novelty search (NS) and quality diversity (QD) algorithms, can be hybridized with ES to improve its performance on sparse or deceptive deep RL tasks while retaining scalability. The experiments confirm that the resulting new algorithms, NS-ES and two QD algorithms, NSR-ES and NSRA-ES, avoid local optima encountered by ES to achieve higher performance on Atari and simulated robots learning to walk around a deceptive trap. This paper introduces a family of fast, scalable algorithms for reinforcement learning that are capable of directed exploration. It also adds this new family of exploration algorithms to the RL toolbox, raising the intriguing possibility that analogous algorithms with multiple simultaneous paths of exploration might also integrate well with existing RL algorithms beyond ES.
label: AI

title: Size-Independent Sample Complexity of Neural Networks
Abstract: This paper investigates the sample complexity of learning neural networks by providing new bounds on their Rademacher complexity, assuming norm constraints on the parameter matrix of each layer. Compared to previous work, these complexity bounds exhibit improved dependence on the network depth, and under some additional assumptions, are entirely independent of the network size (both depth and width). These results are derived using novel techniques that may be of independent interest.
label: AI

title: Nonparametric Inference for Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes
Abstract: The goal is to learn latent representations that are low-dimensional and highly interpretable. The Gaussian Process Latent Variable Model (GP-LVM) possesses these characteristics. The benefits and drawbacks of the GP-LVM complement those of the Variational Autoencoder (VAE), with the former providing interpretable low-dimensional latent representations, while the latter handles large amounts of data and can use non-Gaussian likelihoods. This paper draws inspiration from these two approaches to reap their combined benefits. It introduces a novel approximate inference scheme inspired by the GP-LVM and the VAE. Experimentally, the approximation allows for an arbitrarily large capacity of the generative bottleneck (Z) of the VAE without sacrificing highly interpretable representation. This enables unlimited reconstruction quality by Z, while simultaneously using a low-dimensional space for ancestral sampling and reasoning about the embedded data.
label: AI

title: Dynamic Weight Alignment for Temporal Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: This paper proposes a method for improving temporal Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) by determining the optimal alignment of weights and inputs using dynamic programming. Conventional CNN convolutions linearly match shared weights to a window of the input. However, a more optimal alignment of weights might exist. Therefore, the paper proposes the use of Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) to dynamically align weights to the input of the convolutional layer. Specifically, the dynamic alignment overcomes issues like temporal distortion by finding the minimal distance matching of the weights and inputs under constraints. The effectiveness of the proposed architecture is demonstrated on the Unipen online handwritten digit and character datasets, the UCI Spoken Arabic Digit dataset, and the UCI Activities of Daily Life dataset.
label: AI

title: Deep generative models of genetic variation capture mutation effects
Abstract: The functions of proteins and RNAs are determined by a myriad of interactions between their constituent residues, but most quantitative models of how molecular phenotype depends on genotype must approximate this by simple additive effects. While recent models have relaxed this constraint to also account for pairwise interactions, these approaches do not provide a tractable path towards modeling higher-order dependencies. This paper demonstrates how latent variable models with nonlinear dependencies can be applied to capture beyond-pairwise constraints in biomolecules. It presents a new probabilistic model for sequence families, DeepSequence, that can predict the effects of mutations across a variety of deep mutational scanning experiments significantly better than site-independent or pairwise models based on the same evolutionary data. The model, learned in an unsupervised manner solely from sequence information, is grounded with biologically motivated priors, reveals latent organization of sequence families, and can be used to extrapolate to new parts of sequence space.
label: AI

title: Semi-groups of stochastic gradient descent and online principal component analysis: properties and diffusion approximations
Abstract: This research investigates the properties of Markov semigroups for two machine learning algorithms: stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and online principal component analysis (PCA). The study focuses on the impact of small jumps on the semigroups' regularity-preserving and $L^{\infty}$ contraction properties. These semigroups are dual to the semigroups for probability evolution, which are $L^{1}$ contracting and positivity preserving. The research demonstrates that stochastic differential equations (SDEs) in $\\mathbb{R}^d$ (or on the sphere $\\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$) can be used to weakly approximate SGD (or online PCA). These SDEs provide insights into the behavior of these algorithms.

title: Discovery of 36 eclipsing EL CVn binaries found by the Palomar Transient Factory
Abstract: This research reports the discovery and analysis of 36 new eclipsing EL CVn-type binaries, more than doubling the known population of these systems. These binaries consist of a core helium-composition pre-white dwarf and an early-type main-sequence companion. Supervised machine learning methods were used to search 0.8 million lightcurves from the Palomar Transient Factory, combined with data from SDSS, Pan-STARRS, and 2MASS. The new systems have orbital periods ranging from 0.46 to 3.8 days and apparent brightness ranging from 14 to 16 magnitudes in the PTF $R$ or $g^{\\prime}$ filters. Radial velocity curves for twelve of the systems were obtained using the Intermediate Dispersion Spectrograph at the Isaac Newton Telescope. The lightcurves, radial velocity curves, and spectral energy distributions were modeled to determine the system parameters. The radii (0.3-0.7 $\\mathrm{R_{\\odot}}$) and effective temperatures (8000-17000 K) of the pre-He-WDs are consistent with stellar evolution models, while the masses (0.12-0.28 $\\mathrm{M_{\\odot}}$) show more variance than predicted by models. This study highlights the effectiveness of using machine learning techniques on large synoptic survey data to discover significant samples of binary systems in short-lived evolutionary stages.

title: Multi-Fidelity Reinforcement Learning with Gaussian Processes
Abstract: This research tackles the problem of Reinforcement Learning (RL) with a focus on minimizing the number of real-world samples required. The study proposes two versions of Multi-Fidelity Reinforcement Learning (MFRL), model-based and model-free, which leverage Gaussian Processes (GPs) to learn the optimal policy in a real-world environment. In the MFRL framework, an agent uses multiple simulators of the real environment to perform actions. As the fidelity of the simulators increases, the number of samples used in subsequent simulators can be reduced. The incorporation of GPs in the MFRL framework empirically demonstrates a reduction of up to 40% in samples for model-based RL and 60% for the model-free version. The algorithms' performance is evaluated through simulations and real-world experiments using a ground robot for navigation.

title: Multi-modal Face Pose Estimation with Multi-task Manifold Deep Learning
Abstract: Human face pose estimation aims to determine the gazing direction or head postures from 2D images. This information is crucial for understanding communicative gestures, saliency detection, and other applications, making it an active research area. The challenge lies in the complexities of background, varied orientations, and face appearance visibility.  This paper proposes a novel face pose estimation method utilizing multi-modal data and a deep learning framework called Multi-task Manifold Deep Learning ($M^2DL$). This framework employs feature extraction with improved deep neural networks and multi-modal mapping relationships using multi-task learning. Manifold Regularized Convolutional Layers (MRCL) enhance traditional convolutional layers by learning relationships among neuron outputs. The proposed mapping relationship learning method effectively combines different modalities of face representations to learn the mapping function from face images to poses. This approach improves the computed mapping model through multiple tasks. Experimental results on three challenging benchmark datasets, DPOSE, HPID, and BKHPD, demonstrate the superior performance of $M^2DL$.

title: Super-Resolution with Deep Adaptive Image Resampling
Abstract: Recent advances in deep learning have significantly improved the performance of Single Image Super-Resolution (SISR) methods. This work revisits traditional interpolation-based methods, previously popular, and introduces a deep learning approach. Specifically, the paper proposes using a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to estimate spatially variant interpolation kernels and apply them adaptively to each position in the image. This end-to-end trained model explores strategies for enhancing results for large upscaling factors, introducing a recursive extension of the basic model. This approach achieves results comparable to state-of-the-art methods. Visualizing the estimated adaptive interpolation kernels provides insights into the effectiveness of the method. The paper further extends the method to joint image filtering, again achieving state-of-the-art performance.

title: A Shapelet Transform for Multivariate Time Series Classification
Abstract: Shapelets are phase-independent subsequences designed for time series classification. This research proposes three adaptations to the Shapelet Transform (ST) to capture multivariate features in multivariate time series classification. A unified dataset is created for benchmarking the work and comparing it with three other algorithms. The results demonstrate that multivariate shapelets perform comparably to other state-of-the-art algorithms.
label: AI

title: Critical neural networks with short and long term plasticity
Abstract: Self-organized critical neuronal models have recently provided insights into the avalanching behavior observed in neuronal systems. These models show that dynamical synapses, a form of short-term plasticity, can induce critical neuronal dynamics. Long-term plasticity, such as Hebbian or activity-dependent plasticity, plays a crucial role in shaping network structure and enabling learning abilities in neural systems. This work presents a model that combines both plasticity mechanisms acting on different time scales. The measured avalanche statistics align with experimental results for both avalanche size and duration distributions, incorporating biologically observed percentages of inhibitory neurons. The neuronal activity time series exhibits temporal bursts, leading to 1/f decay in the power spectrum. The presence of long-term plasticity allows the system to learn binary rules like XOR, setting the foundation for future research on more complex tasks such as pattern recognition.

title: On the Effectiveness of Least Squares Generative Adversarial Networks
Abstract: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) have achieved considerable success in unsupervised learning. Traditional GANs employ a discriminator as a classifier using the sigmoid cross entropy loss function. However, this loss function can lead to vanishing gradients during training. To address this issue, this paper proposes Least Squares Generative Adversarial Networks (LSGANs) that utilize the least squares loss for both the discriminator and generator. Minimizing the objective function of LSGAN is shown to be equivalent to minimizing the Pearson $\\chi^2$ divergence. The derived objective function for minimizing the Pearson $\\chi^2$ divergence outperforms the traditional least squares classification approach. LSGANs offer two key advantages over regular GANs: they generate higher quality images and demonstrate greater stability during training. Qualitative and quantitative experiments demonstrate the ability of LSGANs to generate higher quality images compared to regular GANs. The stability of LSGANs is evaluated in two groups: comparing LSGANs with regular GANs without gradient penalty and comparing LSGANs with gradient penalty (LSGANs-GP) with WGANs with gradient penalty (WGANs-GP).  Experimental results highlight the success of LSGANs-GP in training for various difficult architectures, including the 101-layer ResNet, commonly used in WGANs-GP.

title: Squeezed Convolutional Variational AutoEncoder for Unsupervised Anomaly Detection in Edge Device Industrial Internet of Things
Abstract: This paper introduces the Squeezed Convolutional Variational AutoEncoder (SCVAE) for anomaly detection in time series data for Edge Computing in Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT). The proposed model is evaluated using labeled time series data from UCI datasets for precise performance assessment and applied to real-world data for indirect model performance comparison. By comparing models before and after applying Fire Modules from SqueezeNet, the study demonstrates a reduction in model size and inference times while maintaining similar levels of performance.
label: AI

title: Language and Noise Transfer in Speech Enhancement Generative Adversarial Network
Abstract: Deep learning systems for speech enhancement typically require extensive training data to function effectively in various conditions or real-world applications. This makes adapting these systems to new, low-resource environments a significant challenge. This work investigates the adaptability of a speech enhancement generative adversarial network by fine-tuning the generator with limited amounts of data. The study examines the minimum data requirements for achieving stable performance in terms of various objective metrics in two distinct languages: Catalan and Korean. The research also analyzes the variability of test performance on unseen noise based on the availability of different noise types during training. Results indicate that adapting a pre-trained English model with only 10 minutes of data achieves performance comparable to models trained with two orders of magnitude more data. The results further highlight the relative stability of test performance with respect to the number of training noise types.

title: Gender response to Einsteinian physics interventions in School
Abstract: The growing interest in introducing Einsteinian concepts of space, time, light, and gravity across the entire school curriculum has led to the development of intervention programs. This research evaluates the effectiveness of these programs in terms of student attitudes towards physics and their ability to understand these concepts, using classes from Years 6 to 10.  Significant levels of conceptual understanding and improved student attitudes were observed in all cases, although the magnitude of improvement varied depending on age group and program duration. This paper reports an unexpected outcome regarding gender effects. The study compared male and female outcomes, finding that females consistently entered the programs with significantly lower attitude scores than males, but upon completion, their attitudes were comparable to those of the boys. This finding strongly supports the widespread implementation of Einsteinian conceptual learning across the school curriculum. Possible reasons for this effect are discussed.

title: Visual Explanation by Interpretation: Improving Visual Feedback Capabilities of Deep Neural Networks
Abstract: Interpretation and explanation of deep models are crucial for the widespread adoption of systems that rely on them. This paper proposes a novel scheme for both interpretation and explanation. Given a pre-trained model, the method automatically identifies internal features relevant to the set of classes considered by the model without requiring additional annotations. Model interpretation is achieved through average visualizations of this reduced set of features. At test time, the network prediction is explained by accompanying the predicted class label with supporting visualizations derived from the identified features. The paper also addresses artifacts introduced by stridded operations in deconvNet-based visualizations and introduces an8Flower, a dataset specifically designed for objective quantitative evaluation of visual explanation methods. Experiments on MNIST, ILSVRC12, Fashion144k, and an8Flower datasets show that the proposed method produces detailed explanations with good coverage of relevant features for the classes of interest.

title: A Bridge Between Hyperparameter Optimization and Learning-to-learn
Abstract: This research focuses on a class of nested optimization problems involving inner and outer objectives. The study shows that explicitly accounting for the optimization dynamics of the inner objective leads to a general framework that unifies gradient-based hyperparameter optimization and meta-learning (or learning-to-learn). The variables of the outer objective take on the meaning of hyperparameters in a supervised learning problem or parameters of a meta-learner, depending on the specific setting. The framework demonstrates that some recently proposed methods in the meta-learning setting can be instantiated within this framework and addressed using the same gradient-based algorithms. The research concludes by discussing design patterns for learning-to-learn and presenting encouraging preliminary experiments for few-shot learning.
label: AI

title: A New Data-Driven Sparse-Learning Approach to Study Chemical Reaction Networks
Abstract: Chemical kinetic mechanisms can be represented by sets of elementary reactions that are easily translated into mathematical terms using physicochemical relationships. The schematic representation of reactions captures the interactions between reacting species and products. Determining the minimal chemical interactions underlying the dynamic behavior of systems is a crucial task. This paper introduces a novel approach for identifying influential reactions in chemical reaction networks for combustion applications, using a data-driven sparse-learning technique. The proposed approach identifies a set of influential reactions based on species concentrations and reaction rates, with minimal computational cost and without requiring additional data or simulations. The new approach is applied to analyze the combustion chemistry of H2 and C3H8 in a constant-volume homogeneous reactor. The influential reactions identified by the sparse-learning method are consistent with current knowledge of chemical mechanisms. Additionally, the study demonstrates that a reduced version of the parent mechanism can be generated as a combination of influential reactions identified at different times and conditions. For both H2 and C3H8, this reduced mechanism closely approximates the parent mechanism in terms of ignition delay across a wide range of conditions. The results demonstrate the potential of the sparse-learning approach as an effective and efficient tool for mechanism analysis and reduction.

title: Deep Neural Generative Model of Functional MRI Images for Psychiatric Disorder Diagnosis
Abstract: Accurate diagnosis of psychiatric disorders is crucial for improving patient quality of life and potentially supporting the development of new treatments. Many studies have investigated machine learning techniques using brain imaging data to identify specific biomarkers for disorders. These studies face the dilemma of overfitting to a small number of high-dimensional samples when using direct classification, while unsupervised feature extraction risks extracting irrelevant signals. Furthermore, such studies often provide diagnoses without explaining the reasoning behind them. This study proposes a deep neural generative model of resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data. The model is conditioned on the assumption of the subject's state and estimates the posterior probability of the subject's state given the imaging data using Bayes' rule. This study applied the proposed model to diagnose schizophrenia and bipolar disorders. The diagnostic accuracy achieved a significant improvement over competitive approaches, including classifications of functional connectivity, discriminative/generative models of region-wise signals, and those with unsupervised feature extractors. The proposed model visualizes brain regions largely related to the disorders, motivating further biological investigation.

title: A Survey on Multi-View Clustering
Abstract: With advances in information acquisition technologies, multi-view data has become ubiquitous. Multi-view learning has gained significant popularity in machine learning and data mining fields. Multi-view unsupervised or semi-supervised learning approaches, such as co-training and co-regularization, have received considerable attention. While multi-view clustering (MVC) methods have seen rapid development recently, a comprehensive survey summarizing and analyzing current progress is lacking. This paper reviews common strategies for combining multiple views of data and proposes a novel taxonomy of MVC approaches based on this summary. The relationships between MVC and multi-view representation, ensemble clustering, multi-task clustering, and multi-view supervised and semi-supervised learning are discussed. Several representative real-world applications are elaborated upon. To promote future development of MVC, the paper identifies several open problems that warrant further investigation and thorough examination.
label: AI

title: Misspecified Nonconvex Statistical Optimization for Phase Retrieval
Abstract: Existing nonconvex statistical optimization theory and methods heavily rely on the correct specification of the underlying "true" statistical models. To address this issue, this research takes a step towards mitigating model misspecification by studying the high-dimensional sparse phase retrieval problem with misspecified link functions.  The study proposes a simple variant of the thresholded Wirtinger flow algorithm that, given a proper initialization, linearly converges to an estimator with optimal statistical accuracy for a broad family of unknown link functions. Extensive numerical experiments support the theoretical findings.
label: AI

title: Panoramic Robust PCA for Foreground-Background Separation on Noisy, Free-Motion Camera Video
Abstract: This work presents a novel robust PCA method for foreground-background separation in freely moving camera video, handling potential dense and sparse corruptions. The proposed method registers frames of the corrupted video and encodes the varying perspective due to camera motion as missing data in a global model. This formulation enables the algorithm to generate a panoramic background component that automatically stitches together corrupted data from partially overlapping frames to reconstruct the full field of view. The registered video is modeled as the sum of a low-rank component capturing the background, a smooth component capturing the dynamic foreground, and a sparse component isolating outliers and other sparse corruptions. The low-rank portion of the model is based on a recent low-rank matrix estimator (OptShrink), known for its superior low-rank subspace estimates in practice. A weighted total variation framework is used to estimate the smooth foreground component, enabling the method to reliably decouple the true foreground from sparse corruptions. Extensive numerical experiments on static and moving camera videos subject to various dense and sparse corruptions demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of the proposed method compared to existing methods, both in terms of foreground and background estimation accuracy.

title: Visual Explanations from Hadamard Product in Multimodal Deep Networks
Abstract: Visual explanation of learned representation in models helps to understand the fundamentals of learning. Attentional models in previous works visualized attended regions in images or text using learned weights to confirm their intended mechanisms. Kim et al. (2016) showed that the Hadamard product in multimodal deep networks, known for its joint function in visual question answering tasks, implicitly performs an attentional mechanism for visual inputs. This work extends their work to demonstrate that the Hadamard product in multimodal deep networks performs attentional mechanisms for both visual and textual inputs simultaneously, utilizing the proposed gradient-based visualization technique. The attentional effect of the Hadamard product is visualized for both visual and textual inputs by analyzing the two inputs and the output of the Hadamard product with the proposed method, and compared with learned attentional weights of a visual question answering model.

title: Predicting Individual Physiologically Acceptable States for Discharge from a Pediatric Intensive Care Unit
Abstract: This study aims to predict patient-specific vital signs considered medically acceptable for discharge from a pediatric intensive care unit (ICU).  The mean values of each patient's heart rate (hr), systolic blood pressure (sbp), and diastolic blood pressure (dbp) measurements between their medical and physical discharge from the ICU were computed as a proxy for their physiologically acceptable state space (PASS) for successful ICU discharge. These individual PASS values were compared using root mean squared error (rMSE) to population age-normal vitals, a polynomial regression through the PASS values of a Pediatric ICU (PICU) population, and predictions from two recurrent neural network (RNN) models designed to predict personalized PASS within the first twelve hours following ICU admission. Data from 6,899 PICU episodes (5,464 patients) collected between 2009 and 2016 was used, including 375 variables representing vitals, labs, interventions, and drugs, as well as time indicators for medical and physical discharge. The rMSEs between individual PASS values and population age-normals (hr: 25.9 bpm, sbp: 13.4 mmHg, dbp: 13.0 mmHg) were larger than the rMSEs corresponding to the polynomial regression (hr: 19.1 bpm, sbp: 12.3 mmHg, dbp: 10.8 mmHg). The rMSEs from the best performing RNN model were the lowest (hr: 16.4 bpm; sbp: 9.9 mmHg, dbp: 9.0 mmHg). The findings suggest that PICU patients are a unique subset of the general population, and general age-normal vitals may not be suitable as target values for indicating physiological stability at discharge. Age-normal vitals derived specifically from the medical-to-physical discharge window of ICU patients may be more appropriate targets for "acceptable" physiological state in critical care patients. An RNN model, beyond simple age bins, can provide more personalized target values. |||

title: Dark Energy Survey Year 1 Results: Measurement of the Baryon Acoustic Oscillation scale in the distribution of galaxies to redshift 1
Abstract: We present a novel method for measuring angular diameter distances using the baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) scale in the distribution of galaxies observed by the Dark Energy Survey (DES). Our analysis utilizes over 1.3 million galaxies within a 1318 square degree footprint, spanning redshifts between 0.6 and 1, with typical redshift uncertainties of 0.03(1+z). The galaxy sample was meticulously selected to balance number density and redshift uncertainty, as detailed in a companion paper. We examine the BAO signal in projected clustering using three different conventions: angular separation, comoving transverse separation, and spherical harmonics. Additionally, we compare results obtained from template-based and machine learning photometric redshift determinations. Employing 1800 simulations that closely resemble our sample, we generate covariance matrices and validate our distance scale measurement methodology. Our analysis yields a precise measurement of the angular diameter distance, D_A, at the effective redshift of our sample divided by the true physical scale of the BAO feature, r_d, resulting in D_A(z_eff=0.81)/r_d = 10.75 ± 0.43. These findings are consistent with the flat ΛCDM concordance cosmological model, which is supported by numerous other recent experimental results. All data products are publicly accessible at https://des.ncsa.illinois.edu/releases/y1a1/bao.

title: Path-Based Spectral Clustering: Guarantees, Robustness to Outliers, and Fast Algorithms
Abstract: We investigate the clustering problem using the longest-leg path distance (LLPD) metric, which is particularly effective for elongated and irregularly shaped clusters. We present finite-sample guarantees on the performance of clustering with respect to LLPD when data is drawn from multiple intrinsically low-dimensional clusters embedded in high-dimensional space, in the presence of numerous high-dimensional outliers. Combining these results with spectral clustering based on LLPD, we provide conditions under which the Laplacian eigengap statistic accurately determines the number of clusters for a wide range of datasets. Furthermore, we prove guarantees on the labeling accuracy of the proposed algorithm. Our methods are generalizable and provide performance guarantees for spectral clustering using any ultrametric. Additionally, we introduce an efficient and easily implementable approximation algorithm for LLPD based on a multiscale analysis of adjacency graphs, allowing the runtime of LLPD spectral clustering to be quasilinear in the number of data points.

title: Probabilistic Semantic Retrieval for Surveillance Videos with Activity Graphs
Abstract: We introduce a novel framework for identifying complex activities from cluttered surveillance videos based on user-defined queries. The wide range of potential queries, coupled with the scarcity of annotated activity data, hinders the training of activity models. To bridge this semantic gap, we propose a method where users describe an activity as a semantic graph, associating object attributes and inter-object relationships with nodes and edges, respectively. During training, we learn node/edge-level visual predictors. At test time, we retrieve activities by identifying potential locations in the video that match the semantic graph. We formulate a novel CRF-based probabilistic activity localization objective that accounts for misdetections, misclassifications, and track losses, outputting a likelihood score for a candidate grounding location of the query within the video. Our aim is to find groundings that maximize overall precision and recall. To address the combinatorial search across all high-probability groundings, we propose a highest precision subgraph matching algorithm. Our method outperforms existing retrieval methods on benchmark datasets.

title: Attenuation correction for brain PET imaging using deep neural network based on dixon and ZTE MR images
Abstract: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is a functional imaging modality commonly employed in neuroscience studies. Obtaining meaningful quantitative results from PET images requires attenuation correction during image reconstruction. In PET/MR hybrid systems, PET attenuation presents a challenge due to the fact that Magnetic Resonance (MR) images do not directly reflect attenuation coefficients. To address this issue, we propose deep neural network methods for deriving continuous attenuation coefficients for brain PET imaging directly from MR images. Leveraging only Dixon MR images as input, we adopt the existing U-net architecture. An analysis using forty patient datasets demonstrates its superiority over other Dixon-based methods. When both Dixon and zero echo time (ZTE) images are available, we introduce a modified U-net architecture, called GroupU-net, which efficiently utilizes both Dixon and ZTE information through group convolution modules at deeper network layers. Quantitative analysis based on fourteen real patient datasets demonstrates that both network approaches outperform standard methods, with the GroupU-net architecture further reducing PET quantification error compared to the U-net structure.

title: Structured Optimal Transport
Abstract: Optimal Transport (OT) has recently gained significant attention in machine learning for applications spanning domain adaptation, sentence similarities, and deep learning. However, its ability to capture frequently occurring structures beyond the "ground metric" is limited. In this work, we present a nonlinear generalization of (discrete) optimal transport capable of reflecting substantially more structure. We demonstrate how to leverage the geometry of this new model for fast algorithms and explore its connections and properties. Illustrative experiments highlight the benefits of the induced structured couplings for tasks in domain adaptation and natural language processing.
label: AI

title: Learning Sequential Channel Selection for Interference Alignment using Reconfigurable Antennas
Abstract: Machine learning techniques have recently been explored to support, enhance, or augment wireless systems, particularly at the physical layer of the protocol stack. Traditional ML-based approaches or optimization are often unsuitable due to their algorithmic complexity, reliance on existing training data, and/or distributed settings. This paper formulates a reconfigurable antenna-based channel selection problem for interference alignment in a multi-user wireless network as a learning problem. Specifically, we propose a sequential learning approach to effectively select channels or channel combinations to enhance interference alignment using reconfigurable antennas. We first formulate channel selection as a multi-armed bandit problem aiming to optimize the network's sum rate. We demonstrate that by employing an adaptive sequential learning policy, each node in the network can learn to select optimal channels without requiring full and instantaneous Channel State Information (CSI) for all available antenna states. We perform performance analysis of our technique for a MIMO interference channel using a conventional IA scheme and quantify the benefits of pattern diversity and learning channel selection.

title: Towards a Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach for Tower Line Wars
Abstract: Recent years have witnessed numerous breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, particularly in Deep Reinforcement Learning's success in playing and winning complex computer games. There is a growing expectation that Deep Reinforcement Learning will play a crucial role in the development of AI that can master the intricate gameplay required to defeat professional Real-Time Strategy (RTS) game players. To achieve this, a game environment that targets and promotes AI research, specifically Deep Reinforcement Learning, is needed. While some game environments exist, they are either overly simplistic, such as Atari 2600, or excessively complex, such as Starcraft II from Blizzard Entertainment. We propose a game environment that bridges the gap between Atari 2600 and Starcraft II, specifically targeting Deep Reinforcement Learning algorithm research. The environment is a variant of Tower Line Wars from Warcraft III, Blizzard Entertainment. To demonstrate the environment's suitability for Deep Reinforcement Learning algorithms, we propose and implement a Deep Q-Reinforcement architecture. The architecture simplifies the state space, making it applicable to Q-learning and improving performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods. Our experiments show that the proposed architecture learns to effectively play the environment, achieving a 33% improvement over standard Deep Q-learning, proving the environment's usefulness for AI research.
