title: Coupled Self-Organized Hydrodynamics and Navier-Stokes models: local well-posedness and the limit from the Self-Organized Kinetic-fluid models
Abstract: A coupled system of self-organized hydrodynamics and Navier-Stokes equations (SOH-NS), which models self-propelled particles in a viscous fluid, was recently derived by Degond et al. We first transform SOH-NS into a non-singular system using stereographic projection and then prove the local-in-time well-posedness of classical solutions using the energy method.  Furthermore, employing the Hilbert expansion approach, we justify the hydrodynamic limit from the self-organized kinetic-fluid model to macroscopic dynamics. This provides the first analytically rigorous justification for the modeling and asymptotic analysis presented in the original work.

title: Recovery from Maunder-like Grand Minima in a Babcock--Leighton Solar Dynamo Model
Abstract: The Sun occasionally experiences Maunder-like extended grand minima, periods where its magnetic activity significantly drops for several decades. While various theories attempt to explain the origin of these minima, how the Sun recovers from such inactive phases remains enigmatic. Babcock-Leighton type dynamos, successful in explaining many solar cycle features, are not expected to operate during grand minima due to the lack of sufficient sunspots.  This work explores the question of how the Sun recovers from grand minima through the Babcock-Leighton dynamo.  Using a three-dimensional dynamo model, we demonstrate that grand minima arise spontaneously as a result of random variations in the tilt angle of emerging active regions. We find that the Babcock-Leighton process can still operate during grand minima with minimal sunspots, allowing the model to emerge from these phases without requiring an additional mechanism for generating the poloidal field. The key element in our model is a downward magnetic pumping that inhibits the diffusion of magnetic flux across the solar surface.

title: Negative flare in the He I 10830 Å line in facula
Abstract: A small-scale solar flare (B2) occurred in a spotless active region observed at a ground-based telescope equipped with a spectrograph. During the flare, we observed a 25% increase in absorption in the He I 10830 Angstrom line, while other chromospheric and coronal spectral lines showed increased brightness at the same location. This phenomenon, termed a negative flare, has been rarely observed on the Sun before.  This paper analyzes the morphology and dynamics of this flare using spectral observations and space imaging data. We found that the H-alpha and He I 10830 Angstrom lines reached their peak intensities 5 and 6 minutes after the 171 Angstrom line, respectively. The brightening initially appeared in the 171 Angstrom and 193 Angstrom Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) channels, followed by the 94 Angstrom, 304 Angstrom, and 1600 Angstrom signals approximately 2 minutes later. Notably, abrupt changes in line-of-sight (LOS) velocities in the chromospheric lines occurred simultaneously with intensity changes in the 304 Angstrom and 1600 Angstrom lines, exhibiting a downward motion followed by two upward motions.  The measured horizontal speed of perturbation propagation was close to 70 km/s in both chromospheric and coronal lines.  We hypothesize that we observed the photoionization-recombination process caused by UV radiation from the transition region during the coronal flare.  This explanation raises challenges in interpreting the time lag between the emission maximum in the SDO UV channels and the second absorption maximum in the He I 10830 Angstrom line.

title: Critical role of quantum dynamical effects in the Raman spectroscopy of liquid water
Abstract: Understanding Raman spectroscopy at the atomistic level is crucial for elucidating dynamical processes in liquid water.  Since polarizability (or its time derivative) often exhibits highly nonlinear behavior with respect to coordinates and momenta, we employ the linearized semiclassical initial value representation for quantum dynamical simulations of liquid water (and heavy water) under ambient conditions. Our simulations are based on an ab initio flexible, polarizable model (the POLI2VS force field). Results demonstrate that quantum dynamical effects play a critical role in reproducing the peaks in the intermediate region between the librational and bending bands, those between the bending and stretching bands, and the double-peak in the stretching band observed in the experimental isotropic Raman spectrum.  In contrast, while quantum dynamical effects are important, they are less decisive in the anisotropic Raman spectrum.  By selectively freezing either the intramolecular O-H stretching or H-O-H bending mode, we demonstrate that the peak in the intermediate region (2000-2400 cm-1) of the isotropic Raman spectrum originates from the interplay of stretching and bending motions, while a significant portion of the peak in the same region of the anisotropic Raman spectrum can be attributed to the combined motion of bending and librational modes.

title: Directed flow in Au+Au collisions from the RHIC Beam Energy Scan at the STAR experiment
Abstract: We present results of the first Fourier coefficient ($v_1(y)$) and its rapidity derivative ($dv_1/dy$) near mid-rapidity for pions, kaons, K_s^0, protons, antiprotons, Lambda, anti-Lambda, and phi mesons from Beam Energy Scan Au+Au collisions at center-of-mass energies ranging from 7.7 to 200 GeV, measured using the STAR detector at RHIC. The $dv_1/dy$ of pions, kaons, and K_s^0 mesons remains negative across all beam energies.  The $dv_1/dy$ of protons and Lambda baryons exhibits a sign change around 10-15 GeV, while net baryons (net protons and net Lambda) indicate a double sign change.  The $dv_1/dy$ of antiprotons, anti-Lambda, and phi mesons show a similar trend for center-of-mass energies greater than 14.5 GeV.  For the first time, $v_1$ measurements are used to test a quark coalescence hypothesis.  Many measurements are found to be consistent with particles being formed via coalescence of constituent quarks. The observed deviations from this consistency offer a new approach for probing the collision process at the quark level.

This process provides a distinct signature that helps discriminate the signal from standard model backgrounds.

title: Objective evaluation metrics for automatic classification of EEG events
Abstract: Evaluating machine learning algorithms in biomedical applications involving sequential data often lacks standardization.  Common quantitative scalar evaluation metrics like sensitivity and specificity can be misleading, depending on the specific requirements of the application. Ideally, evaluation metrics should reflect user needs while being sufficiently sensitive to guide algorithm development.  Feedback from critical care clinicians using automated event detection software in clinical settings consistently emphasizes that a low false alarm rate, typically measured in units of errors per 24 hours, is the most important criterion for user acceptance.  Although examining performance across a range of operating conditions is generally more insightful, there is a need for a single scalar figure of merit. This paper addresses the shortcomings of existing metrics for a seizure detection task and proposes several new metrics that offer a more balanced view of performance. We demonstrate these metrics on a seizure detection task using the TUH EEG Corpus.  Two promising metrics are a measure based on the concept of Actual Term-Weighted Value (ATWV) borrowed from the spoken term detection literature, and a new metric, Time-Aligned Event Scoring (TAES), which accounts for the temporal alignment of the hypothesis to the reference annotation.  We show that while state-of-the-art deep learning technology exhibits impressive performance, it still requires significant improvement to meet stringent user acceptance criteria.

title: Variance swaps under Lévy process with stochastic volatility and stochastic interest rate in incomplete markets
Abstract: This paper focuses on the pricing of variance swaps in an incomplete market where the stochastic interest rate and the price of the stock are driven by the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model and the Heston model with simultaneous Lévy jumps, respectively.  Using an equilibrium framework, we obtain the pricing kernel and the equivalent martingale measure.  Furthermore, under the forward measure (instead of the risk-neutral measure), we derive a closed-form solution for the fair delivery price of the discretely sampled variance swap by employing the joint moment generating function of the underlying processes.  Finally, we provide numerical examples demonstrating that variance swap values not only depend on stochastic interest rates but also increase in the presence of jump risks.

title: Enhanced Radar Imaging Using a Complex-valued Convolutional Neural Network

We propose a processing framework that employs a complex-valued CNN (CV-CNN) to enhance radar imaging.  We introduce two modifications to the CV-CNN to adapt it to radar imaging tasks.  The method for generating training data is shown, along with implementation details. Simulations and experiments demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method in terms of imaging quality and computational efficiency.

title: A novel array response control algorithm via oblique projection
Abstract: This paper presents a novel array response control algorithm and its application to array pattern synthesis.  The proposed algorithm addresses how to flexibly and precisely adjust the array responses at multiple points based on a single given weight vector.  Employing the principle of adaptive beamforming, we show that the optimal weight vector for array response control can be equivalently obtained through a linear transformation applied to the quiescent weight. This new strategy is used to achieve multi-point precise array response control from a single weight vector, resulting in a closed-form solution.  A careful analysis reveals that response levels at given points can be independently, flexibly, and accurately adjusted by simply varying the parameter vector, while the uncontrolled region remains largely unchanged.  An effective pattern synthesis approach is devised by applying the proposed algorithm.  Simulation results demonstrate the performance of the proposed algorithm.

The applications of the multi-point OPARC algorithm to array signal processing are investigated, including array pattern synthesis (general and large array cases), multi-constraint adaptive beamforming, and quiescent pattern control. An innovative concept of normalized covariance matrix loading (NCL) is proposed. Simulation results validate the superiority and effectiveness of the multi-point OPARC algorithm.

title: OPARC: Optimal and Precise Array Response Control Algorithm -- Part I: Fundamentals

The interference-to-noise ratio (INR) is determined based on the desired level.  Parameter optimization is performed to achieve maximal array gain. This resulting scheme is referred to as optimal and precise array response control (OPARC).  To enhance understanding, its properties are discussed, and a comparison with the existing Accurate Array Response Control (A^2RC) algorithm is provided. title: Application of Convolutional Neural Network to Predict Airfoil Lift Coefficient

A multi-layered perceptron (MLP) is also used for training sets, allowing for comparison with the CNN results. title: Low-Level Augmented Bayesian Optimization for Finding the Best Cloud VM
Abstract: The emergence of big data applications, often characterized by longer execution times, makes choosing the right cloud virtual machine (VM) for these applications crucial for performance and economic reasons. Our large-scale empirical study of 107 different workloads on three popular big data systems revealed that an incorrect choice can lead to a 20-fold slowdown or a 10-fold increase in cost. Bayesian optimization is a technique for optimizing expensive (black-box) functions.  Previous attempts have only considered instance-level information (like number of cores and memory size), which is insufficient to represent the search space. This work identifies a fragility problem with this approach, leading to either high search costs or sub-optimal solutions.  We introduce a novel low-level augmented Bayesian optimization method that leverages low-level performance information to improve the optimization process. Our method rarely performs worse than current practices and often performs significantly better (in 46 of 107 cases).  Furthermore, it significantly reduces the search cost in nearly half of our case studies.  We conclude that using general-purpose off-the-shelf methods for configuring cloud instances without augmenting them with essential systems knowledge, such as CPU utilization, working memory size, and I/O wait time, is often insufficient.

title: Homogenization and Shape Differentiation of Quasilinear Elliptic Equations
Abstract: This thesis consists of five chapters and focuses on the effectiveness of a chemical, as defined by R. Aris, for semilinear elliptic equations. The first chapter explores homogenization in quasilinear diffusion-reaction problems within domains containing small particles. Classical results are extended to less smooth nonlinearities and more general shapes, particularly for the critical case.  The second chapter deals with Steiner symmetrization of semilinear elliptic and parabolic equations. The third chapter focuses on shape differentiation with both smooth and non-smooth nonlinearities.  The fourth chapter examines linear elliptic equations with a potential, -Delta u + nabla u dot b + V u, where the potential, V, "blows up" near the boundary.  These equations arise from the shape differentiation process in the non-smooth case. The fifth chapter develops the second part of the thesis, incorporating results obtained during a 2017 visit to Professor Brezis. We show that the basis of eigenvalues of -Delta with Dirichlet boundary conditions is the unique basis for approximating functions in H_0^1 in L^2 in an optimal way.

title: Corpus specificity in LSA and Word2vec: the role of out-of-domain documents
Abstract: Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) and Word2vec are among the most widely used word embedding techniques. Despite their popularity, the precise mechanisms by which they acquire new semantic relations between words remain unclear. This article investigates whether the ability of LSA and Word2vec to identify relevant semantic dimensions increases with the size of the corpus.  One intuitive hypothesis suggests that the capacity to identify relevant dimensions should increase as the amount of data grows. However, if the corpus size increases in topics unrelated to the domain of interest, the signal-to-noise ratio may weaken.  We aim to examine and differentiate these alternative hypotheses.  To investigate the effects of corpus specificity and size on word embeddings, we study two methods for progressive elimination of documents: removing random documents versus removing documents unrelated to a specific task. Our results demonstrate that Word2vec benefits from all documents, achieving its best performance when trained on the entire corpus. In contrast, specializing the training corpus by removing out-of-domain documents, combined with dimensionality reduction, can enhance LSA word-representation quality while accelerating processing time.  Furthermore, specialization without dimensionality reduction in LSA can lead to a significant performance reduction in specific tasks.  From a cognitive modeling perspective, we suggest that LSA's word-knowledge acquisition may not effectively exploit higher-order co-occurrences and global relations, while Word2vec does. |||

title: Triggered Star Formation Inside the Shell of a Wolf-Rayet Bubble as the origin of the Solar System
Abstract: The high $^{26}$Al/$^{27}$Al abundance ratio observed in the early solar system, significantly exceeding the Galactic average, poses a challenge to the supernova injection hypothesis. However, a triggered star formation scenario within a Wolf-Rayet (W-R) bubble provides a plausible explanation. During the evolution of the massive star, $^{26}$Al is produced and released in the stellar wind during the W-R phase. These aluminum isotopes condense into dust grains, which survive passage through the reverse shock and low-density shocked wind. The dust grains then reach the dense shell swept up by the bubble, detach from the decelerated wind, and are injected into the shell. Portions of this shell subsequently collapse, forming the dense cores that give rise to solar-type systems. The subsequent aspherical supernova does not inject significant amounts of $^{60}$Fe into the proto-solar-system, thus accounting for the observed low abundance of $^{60}$Fe. This model is a viable explanation for the initial abundances of $^{26}$Al and $^{60}$Fe, and estimates that 1-16% of Sun-like stars could have formed in such a triggered star formation environment within a W-R bubble.

title: Caching under Content Freshness Constraints
Abstract: Many real-time delay-sensitive applications require varying levels of data freshness. Standard cache replacement policies, agnostic to these demands, are likely suboptimal. This paper investigates caching policies under a request arrival process incorporating user freshness demands, using the steady-state cache hit probability as the performance metric. A universal upper bound on the performance of any caching policy is established. The content-wise hit-rates for the Least Popular (LP) policy are analytically derived, and sufficient conditions for its asymptotic optimality are identified. An accurate approximation for LRU hit-rates is obtained in the regime of large content population by mapping the characteristic time of a content in the LRU policy to the Coupon Collector's Problem, demonstrating its sharp concentration around its mean. Modified versions of these policies are developed to eject cache redundancies in the form of stale contents. Finally, a new policy outperforming the aforementioned ones is proposed, which explicitly leverages freshness specifications of user requests to prioritize cached content. Extensive simulations corroborate the analytical insights.

However, it should be observable in clusters with sufficiently large Hilbert spaces. title: Revisiting non-Gaussianity from non-attractor inflation models
Abstract: Non-attractor inflation, a single-field inflationary scenario, is the only one that can violate the non-Gaussianity consistency relation with the Bunch-Davies vacuum state and generate large local non-Gaussianity. However, non-attractor inflation is incomplete and requires a subsequent phase of slow-roll attractor, separated by a transition process. This paper investigates the detailed evolution of non-Gaussianity through the transition phase into the slow-roll attractor phase, considering different transition types. The findings indicate that the transition process significantly affects the size of local non-Gaussianity. The net contribution of non-Gaussianities at the end of inflation in canonical non-attractor models is calculated. The $\mathcal{O}(1)$ local non-Gaussianity generated in the non-attractor phase can be completely erased by subsequent evolution, although the consistency relation remains violated, in cases of smooth transition or sharp transition scenarios where curvature perturbations keep evolving. In extremal sharp transition scenarios where super-horizon modes freeze immediately after the non-attractor phase ends, the original non-attractor result is recovered. title: Why Long-Term Debt Instruments Cannot Be Deposit Substitutes

First, they fail to simultaneously replicate the twin features of capital preservation and liquidity, essential to deposit substitutes. Second, deposit substitutes are integral to the maturity transformation process in financial intermediaries, requiring short-term maturity to ensure low borrowing costs. The paper situates the function of deposit substitutes within the context of shadow banking, highlighting their origin and typical use. The incompatibility between deposit substitutes and long-term debt instruments is demonstrated through the application of bond value theory to 10-year zero-coupon treasury notes called "PEACe Bonds" in Banco De Oro, et al. vs. Republic (2015 and 2016). title: Chiral liquid crystal colloids

This study investigates the effects of distortions caused by chiral springs and helices on colloidal self-organization in a nematic liquid crystal using laser tweezers, particle tracking, and optical imaging. The results reveal that chirality of colloidal particles interacts with nematic elasticity to predetermine chiral or racemic colloidal superstructures in nematic colloids. These findings are consistent with numerical modeling based on the minimization of Landau-de Gennes free energy. This study highlights the role of chirality in defining the mesoscopic order of liquid crystal colloids, suggesting its potential as a tool to modulate the global orientated self-organization of these systems.

title: Low-Energy Effective Field Theory of Lepton-Proton Bremsstrahlung

The commonly used peaking approximation, employed to evaluate the radiative tail for the elastic cross section, is shown to be inapplicable for muon proton scattering at the low-energy MUSE kinematics. title: Estimation and prediction of Gaussian processes using generalized Cauchy covariance model under fixed domain asymptotics

The results are presented in three parts. The first part characterizes the equivalence of two Gaussian measures with GC covariance functions and provides sufficient conditions for equivalence between Gaussian measures with Matérn (MT) and GC covariance functions, and between Gaussian measures with Generalized Wendland (GW) and GC covariance functions. The second part establishes strong consistency and asymptotic distribution of the maximum likelihood estimator for the microergodic parameter associated with the GC covariance model under fixed domain asymptotics. The final part focuses on optimal prediction with the GC model, providing conditions for asymptotic efficiency prediction and asymptotically correct estimation of mean square error using a misspecified GC, MT, or GW model under fixed domain asymptotics. Simulation studies illustrate the finite sample behavior of the maximum likelihood estimation of the microergodic parameter and compare the finite-sample behavior of prediction and its associated mean square error when the true model is GC and prediction is performed using both the true model and a misspecified GW model.

title: Probing the CP properties of top Yukawa coupling at an $e^+e^-$ collider

title: Spectral Methods in the Presence of Discontinuities

This paper explores and improves upon a post-processing technique, optimally convergent mollifiers, to recover exponential convergence from a poorly-converging spectral reconstruction of non-smooth data. title: Gradient Regularization Improves Accuracy of Discriminative Models

title: Quantification of coarse-graining error in Langevin and overdamped Langevin dynamics

The approach allows for vectorial coarse-graining maps, with the quality of the chosen coarse-graining measured by certain functional inequalities reflecting the scale separation of the Gibbs measure. title: Phi-entropies for Fokker-Planck and kinetic Fokker-Planck equations

The paper reviews their properties for diffusion equations of Fokker-Planck type, presents new and simplified proofs, and adapts these methods to a kinetic Fokker-Planck equation acting on a phase space with positions and velocities. At the kinetic level, where diffusion only acts on the velocity variable, the transport operator plays a crucial role in the relaxation process. The paper adopts the $H_1$ point of view and establishes a sharp decay rate. Rather than providing general but quantitatively vague estimates, the paper focuses on simple cases, benchmarks available methods, and obtains sharp estimates on a key example. Certain $\phi$-entropies lead to improved entropy-entropy production inequalities, resulting in faster decay rates for entropy estimates of solutions to non-degenerate diffusion equations. The main result proves that faster entropy decay also holds at the kinetic level and that optimal decay rates are achieved only in asymptotic regimes.

title: Models for a multimode bosonic tunneling junction

title: On the rate of convergence for the length of the longest common subsequences in hidden Markov models

title: Higgs Portals for Thermal Dark Matter - EFT Perspectives and the NMSSM -
Abstract: We analyze a low-energy effective model of dark matter where the thermal relic density is determined by a singlet Majorana fermion interacting with Higgs fields through higher-dimensional operators. The direct detection signature of this fermion may be suppressed if blind spot solutions exist, which naturally arise in models with extended Higgs sectors. Explicit mass terms for the Majorana fermion can be forbidden by a $Z_3$ symmetry, which also reduces the number of higher-dimensional operators. Furthermore, a weak-scale mass for the Majorana fermion is naturally obtained from the vacuum expectation value of a scalar singlet field. The correct relic density can be achieved through the s-channel exchange of Higgs and gauge bosons, with the longitudinal mode of the Z boson (the neutral Goldstone mode) playing a significant role in the annihilation process. This model shares many properties with the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (NMSSM) with light singlinos and heavy scalar and gauge superpartners. To assess the validity of the low-energy effective field theory, we compare its predictions with those of the ultraviolet complete NMSSM. Expanding our framework to include $Z_3$ neutral Majorana fermions, analogous to the bino in the NMSSM, we find the emergence of a new bino-singlino well-tempered dark matter region.

title: Coherence orders, decoherence and quantum metrology

In this work, we address this issue using the language of coherence orders, developed by the NMR community. This allows us to investigate the role of different subspaces of the Hilbert-Schmidt space in physical processes and quantum protocols. We establish connections between decoherence and each coherence order. Moreover, we propose a sufficient and straightforward criterion for assessing the usefulness of a given state for quantum-enhanced phase estimation, based on a minimal set of elements from the density matrix.

title: Indirect Inference for Lévy-driven continuous-time GARCH models

The asymptotic theory of the Indirect Inference estimator relies on a uniform SLLN and asymptotic normality of the parameter estimates of the auxiliary model, which necessitate continuity and differentiability of the COGARCH process with respect to its parameter. We prove these properties using Kolmogorov's continuity criterion. This leads to consistent and asymptotically normal Indirect Inference estimates under moment conditions on the driving Lévy process. A simulation study demonstrates that the method yields a substantial reduction in finite sample bias compared to previous estimators.

title: A non-biased trust model for wireless mesh networks

Existing trust models address these attacks by employing different trust aggregation techniques to process recommendation trusts and combine them with direct trust values to form a combined trust value. However, these models are biased as recommendation trusts deviating significantly from one's own opinion are discarded. In this paper, we propose a non-biased trust model that considers all available recommendation trusts, regardless of their quality. Our trust model is based on a combination of two techniques: the dissimilarity test and the Dempster-Shafer Theory. The dissimilarity test determines the amount of conflict between two trust records, while the Dempster-Shafer Theory assigns belief functions based on the results of the dissimilarity test. Numerical results demonstrate that our trust model is robust against reputation-based attacks compared to trust aggregation techniques such as linear opinion pooling, subjective logic model, entropy-based probability model, and regression analysis. Additionally, our model has been extensively tested using the network simulator NS-3 in Infrastructure-based and Hybrid-based wireless mesh networks, demonstrating its ability to mitigate blackhole and grayhole attacks.

title: On Pareto Joint Inversion of guided waves

For both waves, we utilize the dispersion relations derived by Dalton et al. (2017). Numerical results are presented for three angular frequencies (15 Hz, 60 Hz, and 100 Hz) and for two, five, and seven modes, respectively. Comparisons of the model parameters with the values inverted using error-free input indicate an accurate process. However, introducing a 5% error to the input significantly reduces the accuracy of the results, highlighting the error sensitivity of the inverse operation, even though it is stable. Correlations between the inverted elasticity parameters suggest that the layer parameters are more sensitive to input errors than the halfspace parameters. In agreement with Dalton et al. (2017), the fundamental mode is primarily sensitive to the layer parameters, while higher modes are sensitive to both layer and halfspace properties; for the second mode, the results are more accurate for lower frequencies.

title: Development of high vorticity structures and geometrical properties of the vortex line representation
Abstract: The incompressible three-dimensional Euler equations exhibit the development of very thin pancake-like regions of increasing vorticity. These regions evolve with a scaling of $\\omega_{max}\\sim\\ell^{-2/3}$ between the vorticity maximum and the pancake thickness, as observed in recent numerical experiments [D.S. Agafontsev et al, Phys. Fluids 27, 085102 (2015)]. We investigate the process of pancake formation using the vortex line representation (VLR), which represents a partial integration of the Euler equations with respect to conservation of the Cauchy invariants and describes the compressible dynamics of continuously distributed vortex lines. We present, for the first time, high-accuracy numerical simulations of the VLR equations, performed on adaptive anisotropic grids of up to $1536^3$ nodes. Through these simulations, we demonstrate that vorticity growth is connected to the compressibility of the vortex lines and identify geometric properties responsible for the observed scaling of $\\omega_{max}\\sim\\ell^{-2/3}$.

title: Connecting Software Metrics across Versions to Predict Defects

To address this issue, we propose using the Historical Version Sequence of Metrics (HVSM) in continuous software versions as defect predictors. Furthermore, we leverage Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), a popular modeling technique, to utilize HVSM as input for building software prediction models. title: Rigorous results in space-periodic two-dimensional turbulence

We then examine various consequences of these properties: strong law of large numbers, central limit theorem, and random attractors associated with a unique stationary measure. We also discuss Donsker-Varadhan and Freidlin-Wentzell-type large deviations, as well as the inviscid limit and asymptotic results in 3d thin domains. We conclude with some open problems.

title: On the statistical properties of turbulent energy transfer rate in the inner Heliosphere
Abstract: The transfer of energy from large to small scales in solar wind turbulence is a crucial aspect of the long-standing question regarding the mechanism of interplanetary plasma heating. Previous studies have shown that magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence is statistically consistent with the observed solar wind heating as it expands in the heliosphere. However, to understand which processes contribute to plasma heating, a local description of the energy flux across scales is necessary. To this end, it is customary to employ indicators like the magnetic field partial variance of increments (PVI), which is associated with the local, relative, scale-dependent magnetic energy. A more complete evaluation of the energy transfer should also include other terms related to velocity and cross-helicity. This is achieved here by introducing a proxy for the local, scale-dependent turbulent energy transfer rate epsilon_Dt(t), based on the third-order moment scaling law for MHD turbulence. Data from Helios 2 are utilized to determine the statistical properties of this proxy in comparison with the magnetic and velocity fields PVI, and the correlation with local solar wind heating is computed. PVI and epsilon_Dt(t) are generally well correlated, however, epsilon_Dt(t) is a very sensitive proxy that can exhibit large amplitude values, both positive and negative, even for low amplitude peaks in the PVI. Furthermore, epsilon_Dt(t) is very well correlated with local increases of temperature when large amplitude bursts of energy transfer are localized, suggesting an important role played by this proxy in the study of plasma energy dissipation.

title: Extremal Behavior of Aggregated Data with an Application to Downscaling

For a large class of aggregating functionals $\\ell$, we introduce the $\\ell$-extremal coefficient, which quantifies this difference as a function of the extremal spatial dependence in $X$. We also obtain the joint extremal dependence for multiple aggregation functionals applied to the same process. Explicit formulas for the $\\ell$-extremal coefficients and multivariate dependence structures are derived in important special cases. The results provide a theoretical link between the extremal distribution of the aggregated data and the corresponding underlying process, which we exploit to develop a method for statistical downscaling. We apply our framework to downscale daily temperature maxima in the south of France from a gridded data set and use our model to generate high-resolution maps of the warmest day during the 2003 heatwave.

title: Observational Properties of SNe Ia Progenitors Close to the Explosion

The photometric properties remain constant for a few decades before the explosion. During the last few months, the luminosity decreases very rapidly. The corresponding decline in the optical bands varies from a few hundredths up to one magnitude, the exact value depending on both the WD total mass and the braking efficiency at the end of the mass transfer. This feature is related to the exponentially increasing energy production that drives the formation of a convective core rapidly extending over a large part of the exploding object. Additionally, a drop in the angular velocity occurs. title: Performance of a large aperture GEM-like gating device for the International Linear Collider

Consequently, non-negligible degradation of azimuthal spatial resolution occurs due to this IBF. Meanwhile, collecting primary ionized electrons is necessary to maintain the intrinsic performance of the MPGDs. The MPGD-based TPC is currently planned as the central tracking detector of the International Large Detector (ILD), which is one of the detector concepts for the future International Linear Collider (ILC) project. The ILD requires fine azimuthal spatial resolution of less than 100 ${\\rm \\mu m}$ over the drift length of the TPC to achieve high momentum resolution. Due to the unique beam structure of the ILC, the IBF is a critical issue for the realization of the ILD-TPC. To suppress ion back-flow to the drift volume while allowing primary electrons to pass through, a large aperture GEM-like gating device has been developed. Several bench tests have been conducted to confirm the performance of the gating device, and beam tests with the full detector module equipped with the gating device were carried out to verify the resolution that the full module can provide. title: Deep Architectures for Automated Seizure Detection in Scalp EEGs
Abstract: Automated seizure detection using clinical electroencephalograms is a challenging machine learning problem due to the multichannel signal's extremely low signal-to-noise ratio. Events of interest, such as seizures, are easily confused with signal artifacts (e.g., eye movements) or benign variants (e.g., slowing). Commercially available systems suffer from unacceptably high false alarm rates. Deep learning algorithms employing high-dimensional models have not previously been effective due to the lack of big data resources. In this paper, we utilize the TUH EEG Seizure Corpus to evaluate a variety of hybrid deep structures, including Convolutional Neural Networks and Long Short-Term Memory Networks. We introduce a novel recurrent convolutional architecture that delivers 30% sensitivity at 7 false alarms per 24 hours. We have also evaluated our system on a held-out evaluation set based on the Duke University Seizure Corpus and demonstrate that performance trends are similar to the TUH EEG Seizure Corpus. This is a significant finding because the Duke corpus was collected with different instrumentation and at different hospitals. Our work shows that deep learning architectures integrating spatial and temporal contexts are crucial for achieving state-of-the-art performance and will enable a new generation of clinically-acceptable technology.

title: Automatic Analysis of EEGs Using Big Data and Hybrid Deep Learning Architectures
Abstract: **Objective:** A clinical decision support tool that automatically interprets EEGs can reduce time to diagnosis and enhance real-time applications such as ICU monitoring. It also detects three events used to model background noise: (1) artifacts, (2) eye movement, (3) background. **Conclusions:** A hybrid HMM/deep learning system can deliver a low false alarm rate on EEG event detection, making automated analysis a viable option for clinicians. **Significance:** The TUH EEG Corpus enables the application of highly data-intensive machine learning algorithms to EEG analysis. title: A Divide-and-Conquer Bayesian Approach to Large-Scale Kriging
Abstract: We propose a three-step divide-and-conquer strategy within the Bayesian paradigm that delivers massive scalability for any spatial process model. We partition the data into numerous subsets, apply a readily available Bayesian spatial process model to each subset in parallel, and optimally combine the posterior distributions estimated across all subsets into a pseudo-posterior distribution that conditions on the entire data. The combined pseudo-posterior distribution replaces the full data posterior distribution for predicting responses at arbitrary locations and for inference on the model parameters and spatial surface. Based on distributed Bayesian inference, our approach, called "Distributed Kriging" (DISK), offers significant advantages in massive data applications where the full data are stored across multiple machines. We demonstrate theoretically that the Bayes $L_2$-risk of the DISK posterior distribution achieves the near-optimal convergence rate in estimating the true spatial surface with various types of covariance functions and provide upper bounds for the number of subsets as a function of the full sample size. The model-free feature of DISK is demonstrated by scaling posterior computations in spatial process models with a stationary full-rank and a nonstationary low-rank Gaussian process (GP) prior. Moreover, we extend this formalism to systems lacking a bipartite structure. Specifically, we demonstrate that, given suitable non-bipartite processes, heat flow in a subsystem can still be identified, requiring the present formalism to recover generalizations of the second law. title: Impact of Spatial Filtering on Distortion from Low-Noise Amplifiers in Massive MIMO Base Stations

title: Rewriting in Free Hypergraph Categories

title: Distributed Laser Charging: A Wireless Power Transfer Approach

title: ALICE HLT TPC Tracking of Pb-Pb Events on GPUs

Pipelined processing allows the tracking to be performed on the GPU, with data transfer and preprocessing occurring concurrently on the CPU. To keep CPU pre- and post-processing in sync with the GPU, the pipeline utilizes multiple threads. Splitting the tracking into multiple phases, first searching for short local track segments, improves data locality and makes the algorithm suitable for GPU execution. Due to special optimizations, this approach is not inferior to a global approach. Non-associative floating-point arithmetic makes a direct binary comparison between the GPU and CPU trackers infeasible. However, a track-by-track and cluster-by-cluster comparison reveals a concordance of 99.999%. title: On the Semantics of Intensionality and Intensional Recursion

The main contribution is a framework where mathematical and computational constructions can be considered either extensionally (as abstract values) or intensionally (as fine-grained descriptions of their construction). title: Exploring Zeptosecond Quantum Equilibration Dynamics: From Deep-Inelastic to Fusion-Fission Outcomes in $^{58}$Ni+$^{60}$Ni Reactions

Experimental outcomes were compared to theoretical predictions using Time Dependent Hartree Fock and Time Dependent Random Phase Approximation approaches, which incorporate one-body energy dissipation and fluctuations, respectively. Excellent quantitative agreement was found between experimental results and calculations, indicating that microscopic models incorporating one-body dissipation and fluctuations provide a potential tool for exploring dissipation in low-energy heavy ion collisions.

The paper determines potential distribution along the magnetopause based on the balance condition of substance entering the transition layer from the solar wind on one side and exiting through the gap between the magnetosphere and the bow shock front and through the magnetopause on the other. To a first approximation, this distribution differs from the potential distribution at the BS front only by a constant multiplier. title: REDBEE: A Visual-Inertial Drone System for Real-Time Moving Object Detection

title: Method of Higher-Order Operators for Quantum Optomechanics

title: Towards Measuring Membership Privacy

The study advocates for DTP as part of the decision-making process when publishing a classifier. The DTP-1 hypothesis is proposed: classifiers with a DTP value above 1 should not be published.

title: Intermolecular mechanism for multiple maxima in molecular dynamic susceptibility

title: The Age of Information in Multihop Networks

However, numerical results indicate that the preemptive LGFS policy can be significantly far from optimal for certain NBU transmission time distributions. Finally, when preemption is prohibited and packet transmission times are arbitrarily distributed, the non-preemptive LGFS policy minimizes age processes across all network nodes among all work-conserving policies (again in a stochastic ordering sense). title: Analytic signal in many dimensions

title: Optimal detection and error exponents for hidden multi-state processes via random duration model approach
Abstract: The paper investigates the detection of random signals contaminated by noise that undergoes state transitions from a finite set of possible values at unknown points in time.  Such signals are modeled using a random duration model, where each state is associated with a probability mass function controlling the statistics of its duration occurrences. Assuming two possible signal states and Gaussian noise, the optimal likelihood ratio test is derived and shown to have a computationally tractable matrix product form. The number of matrices involved in the product corresponds to the number of process observations. Each matrix in the product has a dimension equal to the sum of the duration spreads of the two states and can be decomposed as a product of a diagonal random matrix governed by the process observations and a sparse constant matrix controlling state transitions.  This result demonstrates that the Neyman-Pearson error exponent is equivalent to the top Lyapunov exponent for the corresponding random matrices.  Utilizing large deviation theory, a lower bound on the error exponent is derived.  Finally, numerical simulations confirm the tightness of this bound.

As diffusion relaxes the concentration gradient, a non-monotonic density profile emerges.  The study reveals the crucial role of density gradients in the stability of miscible Rayleigh-Taylor fingering.  The combination of Rayleigh number (Ra) and density gradients is proposed to provide a better understanding of RT fingering instabilities, leading to the definition of a new dimensionless group, gradient Rayleigh number (Ra$_g$). title: Neural Collaborative Autoencoder
Abstract: Deep neural networks have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance on numerous tasks in recent years. While some studies have explored the integration of deep learning with recommendation systems, several limitations remain. Finally, neural network models are more susceptible to overfitting in implicit settings compared to shallow models.  To address these issues, this paper presents a generic recommender framework called Neural Collaborative Autoencoder (NCAE) for collaborative filtering.  NCAE effectively captures subtle hidden relationships between interactions through a non-linear matrix factorization process. Moreover, an error reweighting module and a sparsity-aware data-augmentation strategy are proposed to prevent overfitting in implicit settings. While the method for eliminating the second type of mechanical movement is not verified here, it is considered straightforward and commercially available.  The combination of both solutions is estimated to achieve spectral measurement on a millisecond timescale. title: Physical Properties and Evolutionary States of EA-type Eclipsing Binaries Observed by LAMOST
Abstract: By June 16, 2017, the LAMOST telescope had observed approximately 3196 EA-type binaries (EAs), and their spectral types were determined. The period distribution of EAs suggests that the period limit for tidal locking in close binaries is around 6 days.  The study finds that EAs exhibit higher metallicity compared to EWs, indicating that EAs are generally younger and serve as progenitors for EWs.  Long-period EWs (0.4 < P < 1 days) have similar metallicities to EAs with comparable periods, but their Log (g) values are typically lower.  These observations support the evolutionary process where EAs transform into long-period EWs through a combination of angular momentum loss (AML) via magnetic braking and case A mass transfer.  Short-period EWs have lower metallicities than EAs but higher gravitational accelerations.  This suggests that they may form from cool, short-period EAs through AML via magnetic braking with limited mass transfer.  Some EWs with high metallicities may be contaminated by material from the evolution of unseen neutron stars and black holes, or they may have third bodies that facilitate rapid formation through a short pre-contact evolution timescale. title: Change points, memory and epidemic spreading in temporal networks

The paper evaluates the multiscale model's ability to reproduce the spreading of epidemics on the temporal network, demonstrating a synergistic effect where statistically significant features are uncovered that would remain hidden when treating each time scale independently.

title: Comparative Opinion Mining: A Review
Abstract: Opinion mining leverages natural language processing, text analysis, and computational linguistics to identify and extract subjective information from textual material.  Also known as sentiment analysis, opinion mining has gained significant attention in recent times due to its ability to analyze public opinion on various topics.  Comparative opinion mining is a subfield that focuses on identifying and extracting information expressed in a comparative form, such as "paper X is better than paper Y."  Comparative opinion mining plays a crucial role in evaluating entities by providing a reference point for comparison.  This paper presents a review of the field of comparative opinion mining.  As the first review specifically dedicated to this topic (previous reviews primarily covered general opinion mining), this survey examines comparative opinion mining from two perspectives: techniques and comparative opinion elements.  It also incorporates preprocessing tools and datasets used by past researchers, which can be beneficial for future researchers in this field. |||

title: A Survey of FPGA-Based Neural Network Accelerator
Abstract:
Recent research on neural networks has demonstrated significant advantages in machine learning compared to traditional algorithms based on handcrafted features and models. Neural networks are now widely adopted in areas such as image, speech, and video recognition. However, the high computational and storage complexity of neural network inference presents significant challenges for its application. CPU platforms struggle to provide sufficient computational power, while GPU platforms, with their high computational capacity and user-friendly development frameworks, are the preferred choice for neural network processing.

On the other hand, FPGA-based neural network inference accelerators are emerging as a research area. Utilizing specifically designed hardware, FPGAs hold the potential to surpass GPUs in terms of speed and energy efficiency. Numerous FPGA-based accelerator designs have been proposed incorporating software and hardware optimization techniques to achieve high speed and energy efficiency. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of previous work on FPGA-based neural network inference accelerators and summarizes the main techniques employed. An investigation spanning from software to hardware, from the circuit level to the system level, is conducted to complete the analysis of FPGA-based neural network inference accelerator design, serving as a guide for future research.

title: Deterministic Sampling of Expensive Posteriors Using Minimum Energy Designs
Abstract: Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods rely on a large number of samples to approximate a posterior distribution, which can be computationally expensive when the likelihood or prior is costly to evaluate. The number of samples can be reduced by avoiding repeated samples and those that are close to each other. This is the principle behind deterministic sampling methods such as Quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC). However, existing QMC methods aim to sample from a uniform hypercube, which can miss high-probability regions of the posterior distribution, leading to poor approximation. Minimum energy design (MED) is a recently proposed deterministic sampling method that utilizes posterior evaluations to obtain a weighted space-filling design in the region of interest. However, existing MED implementations are inefficient due to their reliance on several global optimizations, requiring numerous posterior evaluations. This article develops an efficient algorithm capable of generating MED with a limited number of posterior evaluations. Additionally, several improvements are introduced to the MED criterion to enhance its performance in high dimensions. The advantages of MED over MCMC and QMC are illustrated using an example of calibrating a friction drilling process.

title: Probing the $P$-wave charmonium decays of $B_c$ meson
Abstract:
Driven by the recent observation of a large number of $B_c$ meson decay modes by several detectors at the LHC, we present a detailed analysis of the $B_c$ meson decay to $P$-wave charmonium states and a light pseudoscalar ($P$) or vector ($V$) meson within the framework of perturbative QCD factorization. The $P$-wave charmonium distribution amplitudes are extracted from the $n=2,l=1$ Schr$\\ddot{o}$dinger states for a Coulomb potential, which can be considered universal nonperturbative objects for analyzing hard exclusive processes involving $P$-wave charmonium production. Our analysis reveals that these decays have large branching ratios of the order of $10^{-5}\\sim 10^{-2}$, which seem to be within the reach of future experiments.

We also provide predictions for the polarization fractions and relative phases of $B_c\\rightarrow (\\chi_{c1},\\chi_{c2},h_c)V$ decays. Based on quark helicity analysis, it is expected that longitudinal polarization amplitudes dominate the branching ratios, and the magnitudes and phases of parallel polarization amplitudes are approximately equal to those of perpendicular ones. The obtained results are compared with available experimental data, our previous studies, and numbers from other approaches.

title: Search for $R$-parity violating supersymmetry in pp collisions at $\sqrt{s} = $ 13 TeV using b jets in a final state with a single lepton, many jets, and high sum of large-radius jet masses
Abstract: This paper reports results from a search for physics beyond the standard model in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\\sqrt{s} = $ 13 TeV. The search utilizes a signature characterized by a single lepton, high jet and bottom quark jet multiplicities, and a high sum of large-radius jet masses, without any requirement on the missing transverse momentum in an event. The data sample corresponds to an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ recorded by the CMS experiment at the LHC. No significant excess beyond the prediction from standard model processes is observed. The results are interpreted in terms of upper limits on the production cross section for $R$-parity violating supersymmetric extensions of the standard model using a benchmark model of gluino pair production, where each gluino decays promptly via $\n{\\mathrm{\\widetilde{g}}} \\rightarrow \\mathrm{t} \\mathrm{b} \\mathrm{s} $. Gluinos with a mass below 1610 GeV are excluded at 95% confidence level.

title: Building a Sentiment Corpus of Tweets in Brazilian Portuguese
Abstract: The abundance of data available in social media, forums, and websites motivates research in various areas of Natural Language Processing, including sentiment analysis. The popularity of this field due to its subjective and semantic characteristics encourages research on novel methods and approaches for classification. Therefore, there is a high demand for datasets across different domains and languages. This paper introduces TweetSentBR, a sentiment corpus for Brazilian Portuguese manually annotated with 15,000 sentences on the TV show domain. The sentences were labeled into three classes (positive, neutral, and negative) by seven annotators, following literature guidelines to ensure annotation reliability. We also conducted baseline experiments on polarity classification using three machine learning methods, achieving 80.99% F-Measure and 82.06% accuracy in binary classification, and 59.85% F-Measure and 64.62% accuracy in three-point classification.

title: Asymptotic Behaviors for Critical Branching Processes with Immigration
Abstract: This paper investigates the asymptotic behaviors of the critical branching process with immigration $\\{Z_n, n\\ge 0\\}$. We first derive an estimation for the probability generating function of $Z_n$. Based on this estimation, we obtain a large deviation for $Z_{n+1}/Z_n$. Lower and upper deviations for $Z_n$ are also studied. As a byproduct, an upper deviation for $\\max_{1\\le i\\le n}\nZ_i$ is obtained.

title: Evidence for the associated production of the Higgs boson and a top quark pair with the ATLAS detector
Abstract:
This paper reports a search for the associated production of the Higgs boson with a top quark pair ($t\bar t H$). The search is performed in multilepton final states using a dataset corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ of proton--proton collision data recorded by the ATLAS experiment at a center-of-mass energy $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV at the Large Hadron Collider. Higgs boson decays to $WW^*$, $\tau\tau$, and $ZZ^*$ are targeted. Seven final states, categorized by the number and flavor of charged-lepton candidates, are examined for the presence of the Standard Model Higgs boson with a mass of 125 GeV and a pair of top quarks. An excess of events over the expected background from Standard Model processes is found with an observed significance of 4.1 standard deviations, compared to an expectation of 2.8 standard deviations. The best fit for the $t\bar t H$ production cross section is $\sigma(t\bar t H) =
790^{+230}_{-210}$ fb, in agreement with the Standard Model prediction of
$507^{+35}_{-50}$ fb. Combining this result with other $t\bar t H$
searches from the ATLAS experiment using the Higgs boson decay modes to $b\bar
b$, $\gamma\gamma$ and $ZZ^* \to 4\ell$, yields an observed significance of 4.2 standard deviations, compared to an expectation of 3.8 standard deviations. This provides evidence for the $t\bar t H$ production mode.

title: Weighted Data Normalization Based on Eigenvalues for Artificial Neural Network Classification
Abstract: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are highly valuable tools for solving learning problems. Enhancing the performance of ANNs can be achieved through two main approaches: optimizing the ANN architecture and normalizing the raw data for ANN input. This paper proposes a novel method that improves ANN performance by preprocessing the raw data, leveraging the fact that different features should play distinct roles. The raw dataset is first preprocessed using principal component analysis (PCA), and then the principal components are weighted by their corresponding eigenvalues. Several aspects of analysis are conducted to examine the theoretical foundation and applicable scenarios. Three classification problems are implemented using an active learning algorithm to validate the proposed method. Empirical results indicate that the proposed method can significantly improve the performance of ANNs.

title: Concepts of quantum non-Markovianity: a hierarchy
Abstract: Markovian approximation is a widely used concept in describing the dynamics of open quantum systems (OQSs). Although it is often claimed to be inspired by classical Markovianity, the term "quantum Markovianity" is inconsistently and often unrigorously used in the literature. This report compares the descriptions of classical stochastic processes and quantum stochastic processes (as arising in OQSs), revealing inherent differences that lead to the non-trivial problem of characterizing quantum non-Markovianity. Rather than proposing a single definition of quantum Markovianity, we explore a range of Markov-related concepts in the quantum regime. Some of these concepts have long been used in quantum theory, such as quantum white noise, factorization approximation, divisibility, Lindblad master equation, etc. Others are introduced for the first time in this report, including past-future independence, no (quantum) information backflow, and composability. All of these concepts are defined within a unified framework, enabling us to rigorously build hierarchical relationships among them. Through various examples, we argue that the current most commonly used definitions of quantum Markovianity in the literature do not fully capture the memoryless property of OQSs. In fact, quantum non-Markovianity is highly context-dependent. The results of this report, summarized as a hierarchy figure, provide clarity regarding the nature of quantum non-Markovianity.

title: Blind Image Deblurring via Reweighted Graph Total Variation
Abstract: Blind image deblurring, i.e., deblurring without knowledge of the blur kernel, presents a highly ill-posed problem. The problem can be addressed in two parts: i) estimating a blur kernel from the blurry image, and ii) given the estimated blur kernel, deconvolving the blurry input to restore the target image. This paper proposes a novel approach by interpreting an image patch as a signal on a weighted graph. We argue that a skeleton image, a proxy that retains the strong gradients of the target but smooths out details, can be used to accurately estimate the blur kernel and possesses a unique bimodal edge weight distribution. We then design a reweighted graph total variation (RGTV) prior that effectively promotes a bimodal edge weight distribution given a blurry patch. However, minimizing a blind image deblurring objective with RGTV results in a non-convex non-differentiable optimization problem. We propose a fast algorithm that solves for the skeleton image and the blur kernel alternately. Finally, with the computed blur kernel, recent non-blind image deblurring algorithms can be applied to restore the target image. Experimental results demonstrate that our algorithm can robustly estimate the blur kernel with large kernel sizes, and the reconstructed sharp image is competitive with state-of-the-art methods.

title: Predicting Rich Drug-Drug Interactions via Biomedical Knowledge Graphs and Text Jointly Embedding
Abstract: Minimizing adverse reactions caused by drug-drug interactions (DDIs) has always been a critical research topic in clinical pharmacology. Detecting all possible interactions through clinical studies before a drug is released to the market is a demanding task. The power of big data is opening up new approaches to discovering various DDIs. However, these discoveries contain a significant amount of noise and provide knowledge bases that are far from complete and trustworthy for practical use. Most existing studies focus on predicting binary DDIs between drug pairs, neglecting other interactions. This paper proposes a novel framework, called PRD, for predicting DDIs. The framework utilizes graph embedding, which can overcome data incompleteness and sparsity issues to achieve multiple DDI label prediction. First, a large-scale drug knowledge graph is generated from various sources. Then, the knowledge graph is embedded with comprehensive biomedical text into a common low-dimensional space. Finally, the learned embeddings are used to efficiently compute rich DDI information through a link prediction process. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, extensive experiments were conducted on real-world datasets. The results demonstrate that our model outperforms several state-of-the-art baseline methods in terms of capability and accuracy.

title: The NANOGrav 11-year Data Set: High-precision timing of 45 Millisecond Pulsars
Abstract: This paper presents high-precision timing data over time spans of up to 11 years for 45 millisecond pulsars observed as part of the North American Nanohertz Observatory for Gravitational Waves (NANOGrav) project, which aims to detect and characterize low-frequency gravitational waves. The pulsars were observed with the Arecibo Observatory and/or the Green Bank Telescope at frequencies ranging from 327 MHz to 2.3 GHz. Most pulsars were observed with approximately monthly cadence, with six high-timing-precision pulsars observed weekly. All pulsars were observed at widely separated frequencies at each observing epoch to fit for time-variable dispersion delays. The paper describes methods for data processing, time-of-arrival (TOA) calculation, and the implementation of a new, automated method for removing outlier TOAs. A timing model is fitted for each pulsar, including spin, astrometric, and, if necessary, binary parameters, in addition to time-variable dispersion delays and parameters quantifying pulse-profile evolution with frequency. The new timing solutions provide three new parallax measurements, two new Shapiro delay measurements, and two new measurements of large orbital-period variations. Models characterizing sources of noise for each pulsar are fitted. The analysis reveals that 11 pulsars exhibit significant red noise, with generally smaller spectral indices than typically measured for non-recycled pulsars, suggesting a different origin. Future papers will utilize these data to constrain or detect the signatures of gravitational-wave signals.

title: QCD Constituent Counting Rules for Neutral Vector Mesons
Abstract: QCD constituent counting rules define the scaling behavior of exclusive hadronic scattering and electromagnetic scattering amplitudes at high momentum transfer in terms of the total number of fundamental constituents in the initial and final states participating in the hard subprocess. The scaling laws reflect the twist of the leading Fock state for each hadron and hence the leading operator that creates the composite state from the vacuum. Therefore, constituent counting scaling laws can be used to identify the twist of exotic hadronic candidates, such as tetraquarks and pentaquarks. Effective field theories must consistently implement these scaling rules to be consistent with the fundamental theory. This paper examines the application of constituent counting rules for the exclusive production of one or two neutral vector mesons $V^0$ in $e^+ e^-$ annihilation, processes in which the $V^0$ can couple via intermediate photons. In the case of a (narrow) real $V^0$, the photon virtuality is fixed to a precise value $s_1 = m_{V^0}^2$, effectively treating the $V^0$ as a single fundamental particle. Each real $V^0$ thus contributes to the constituent counting rules with $N_{V_0} = 1$. Effectively, the leading operator underlying the $V^0$ has twist 1. Therefore, in the specific physical case of single or double on-shell $V^0$ production via intermediate photons, the predicted scaling from counting rules coincides with Vector Meson Dominance (VMD), an effective theory that treats $V^0$ as an elementary field. However, the VMD prediction fails in the general case where the $V^0$ is not coupled through an elementary photon field, and then the leading-twist interpolating operator has twist $N_{V_0} = 2$. Analogous effects appear in $pp$ scattering processes.

title: A Low-Cost Robust Distributed Linearly Constrained Beamformer for Wireless Acoustic Sensor Networks with Arbitrary Topology
Abstract: This paper proposes a new robust distributed linearly constrained beamformer that utilizes a set of linear equality constraints to reduce the cross power spectral density matrix to a block-diagonal form. The proposed beamformer has a convenient objective function suitable for arbitrary distributed network topologies while achieving performance identical to a centralized implementation. Furthermore, the new optimization problem is robust to relative acoustic transfer function (RATF) estimation errors and target activity detection (TAD) errors. Two variants of the proposed beamformer are presented and evaluated in the context of multi-microphone speech enhancement in a wireless acoustic sensor network, and are compared with other state-of-the-art distributed beamformers in terms of communication costs and robustness to RATF estimation errors and TAD errors.

title: Framework of Channel Estimation for Hybrid Analog-and-Digital Processing Enabled Massive MIMO Communications
Abstract: This paper investigates a general channel estimation problem in the massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) system employing a hybrid analog/digital precoding structure with limited radio-frequency (RF) chains. By properly designing RF combiners and performing multiple trainings, the proposed channel estimation can approach the performance of fully-digital estimations, depending on the degree of channel spatial correlation and the number of RF chains. Addressing hybrid channel estimation, the optimal combiner is theoretically derived by relaxing the constant-magnitude constraint in a specific single-training scenario, which is then extended to the design of combiners for multiple trainings using Sequential and Alternating methods. Additionally, a technique is developed to generate phase-only RF combiners based on the corresponding unconstrained ones to satisfy the constant-magnitude constraints. The performance of the proposed hybrid channel estimation scheme is examined through simulations under both nonparametric and spatial channel models. The simulation results demonstrate that the estimated CSI can approach the performance of fully-digital estimations in terms of both mean square error and spectral efficiency. Moreover, a practical spatial channel covariance estimation method is proposed, and its effectiveness in hybrid channel estimation is verified through simulations.

title: Dual Long Short-Term Memory Networks for Sub-Character Representation Learning
Abstract: Characters have traditionally been considered the minimal processing unit in Natural Language Processing (NLP). However, many non-Latin languages employ hieroglyphic writing systems with large alphabets containing thousands or millions of characters. Each character is composed of smaller parts, which are often overlooked by previous work. This paper proposes a novel architecture employing two stacked Long Short-Term Memory Networks (LSTMs) to learn sub-character level representation and capture deeper levels of semantic meaning. To conduct a concrete study and substantiate the efficiency of our neural architecture, we use Chinese Word Segmentation as a research case example. Chinese is a typical example, where every character contains several components called radicals. Our networks utilize a shared radical level embedding to address both Simplified and Traditional Chinese Word Segmentation, eliminating the need for extra Traditional to Simplified Chinese conversion. This highly end-to-end approach significantly simplifies word segmentation compared to previous work. Radical level embeddings can also capture deeper semantic meaning below the character level, improving the system's learning performance. By tying radical and character embeddings together, the parameter count is reduced while semantic knowledge is shared and transferred between the two levels, significantly boosting performance. On 3 out of 4 Bakeoff 2005 datasets, our method surpassed state-of-the-art results by up to 0.4%. Our results are reproducible, and source codes and corpora are available on GitHub.

title: Gene expression for simulation of biological tissue
Abstract: BioDynaMo is a biological processes simulator developed by an international community of researchers and software engineers working closely with neuroscientists. The authors have been working on gene expression, which is the process by which the heritable information in a gene, the sequence of DNA base pairs, is transformed into a functional gene product, such as protein or RNA. Typically, gene regulatory models employ either statistical or analytical approaches, with the former being well understood and widely used. This paper utilizes analytical approaches to represent regulatory networks by means of differential equations, such as Euler and Runge-Kutta methods. The two solutions are implemented and have been submitted for inclusion in the BioDynaMo project. They are compared for accuracy and performance.

title: Spatial Motifs for Device-to-Device Network Analysis in Cellular Networks
Abstract: Device-to-device (D2D) communication is a promising approach to efficiently disseminate critical or viral information. Realizing the benefits of D2D-enabled networks depends on choosing the optimal content dissemination policy subject to resource and user distribution constraints. This paper proposes a novel D2D network analysis framework to study the impacts of frequently occurring subgraphs, known as motifs, on D2D network performance and to determine an effective content dissemination strategy. In the proposed framework, the distribution of devices in the D2D network is modeled as a Thomas cluster process (TCP), and two graph structures, the star and chain motifs, are studied in the communication graph. Based on the properties of the TCP, closed-form analytical expressions for the statistical significance, the outage probability, as well as the average throughput per device, are derived. Simulation results corroborate the analytical derivations and show the influence of different system topologies on the occurrence of motifs and the D2D system throughput. More importantly, the results highlight that as the statistical significance of motifs increases, the system throughput will initially increase and then decrease. Therefore, network operators can obtain statistical significance regions for chain and star motifs that map to the optimal content dissemination performance. Furthermore, using the obtained regions and the analytical expressions for statistical significance, network operators can effectively identify which clusters of devices can be leveraged for D2D communications while determining the number of serving devices in each identified cluster.

title: Hierarchy of Information Scrambling, Thermalization, and Hydrodynamic Flow in Graphene
Abstract: This paper determines the information scrambling rate $\\lambda_{L}$ due to electron-electron Coulomb interaction in graphene. $\\lambda_{L}$ characterizes the growth of chaos and has been argued to provide information about the thermalization and hydrodynamic transport coefficients of a many-body system. The analysis demonstrates that $\\lambda_{L}$ behaves for strong coupling similar to transport and energy relaxation rates. However, a weak coupling analysis reveals that scrambling is related to dephasing or single-particle relaxation. Furthermore, $\\lambda_{L}$ is found to be parametrically larger than the collision rate relevant for hydrodynamic processes, such as electrical conduction or viscous flow, and the rate of energy relaxation, relevant for thermalization. Thus, while scrambling is obviously necessary for thermalization and quantum transport, it generally does not set the time scale for these processes. Additionally, a quantum kinetic theory for information scrambling is derived, resembling the celebrated Boltzmann equation and offering physically transparent insights into quantum chaos in many-body systems.

title: Thermalization and prethermalization in isolated quantum systems: a theoretical overview
Abstract: The approach to thermal equilibrium, or thermalization, in isolated quantum systems is among the most fundamental problems in statistical physics. Recent theoretical studies have revealed that thermalization in isolated quantum systems exhibits several remarkable features that emerge from quantum entanglement and are quite distinct from those in classical systems. Experimentally, well-isolated and highly controllable ultracold quantum gases offer an ideal system for studying the nonequilibrium dynamics in isolated quantum systems, triggering intensive recent theoretical endeavors on this fundamental subject. Besides thermalization, many isolated quantum systems display intriguing behavior in relaxation processes, particularly prethermalization. Prethermalization occurs when there is a clear separation in relevant time scales and has several different physical origins depending on individual systems. This review provides an overview of theoretical approaches to the problems of thermalization and prethermalization. |||

title: Stochastic Geometry Modeling and Analysis of Single- and Multi-Cluster Wireless Networks
Abstract: This paper presents a stochastic geometry-based approach for modeling and analyzing wireless networks, encompassing both single- and multi-cluster configurations. By utilizing finite homogeneous Poisson point processes, we model the distribution of transmitters in a confined region, representing a single-cluster network. We analyze the coverage probability for a reference receiver under two selection strategies: closest-selection, where the receiver is served by the closest transmitter, and uniform-selection, where the serving transmitter is chosen randomly. We extend the model and analysis to multi-cluster networks by employing Matern cluster processes. In this multi-cluster setting, receivers are categorized into two types: closed-access and open-access. Closed-access receivers are located around the cluster centers according to a normal distribution and can only be served by transmitters within their respective clusters. Open-access receivers, in contrast, are distributed independently of the transmitters and can be served by any transmitter. For all scenarios, we derive the link distance distribution and Laplace transform (LT) of the interference. Additionally, we derive closed-form lower bounds on the LT of interference for single-cluster networks. We further examine the impact of various parameters on network performance.

title: Texture Object Segmentation Based on Affine Invariant Texture Detection
Abstract: To address the challenge of segmenting images with rich textures, we introduce a novel detection method based on the affine invariance principle. Recognizing the similarity between texture regions, we apply affine transformations to generate numerous shapes and employ the Karhunen-Loève Transform (KLT) algorithm to verify their similarity. These transformations encompass rotation, proportional scaling, and perspective deformation to accommodate diverse scenarios. To handle boundary issues during segmentation, we propose an enhanced Local Binary Pattern (LBP) method combined with Canny edge detection. The method also incorporates a user-friendly human-computer interaction feature, allowing users to easily separate matched texture areas from the original images.

title: A reference model for interaction semantics
Abstract: This article introduces a reference model for interaction semantics among communicating discrete systems, aiming to provide a framework for discourse on interoperability. The model is built upon a simple yet comprehensive classification of system interactions based on information transport and processing. Information transport is categorized as uni- or bidirectional, while information processing is further classified along the binary dimensions of state, determinism, and synchronicity. For interactions with bidirectional information flow, we define a criterion for a layered system structure. We designate a bidirectional interaction as "horizontal" if all interacting systems exhibit the same behavior with respect to state, determinism, and synchronicity. In contrast, we classify it as "vertical" --- providing a semantic direction --- if there is a behavioral asymmetry among the interacting systems regarding these properties. We demonstrate that horizontal interactions are inherently stateful, asynchronous, and nondeterministic, and are typically described by protocols. Vertical interactions, on the other hand, are characterized by top-down usage, described by object models or operations, and bottom-up observation, described by anonymous events. This reference model facilitates understanding the significant relationships established between interacting discrete systems through their interactions and guides discussions on discrete system interoperability. To illustrate its conceptual power, we apply the model to assess several other architectural models, communication technologies, and software design or architectural styles, including Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) and RESTful APIs.
