title: The Effects of Running Gravitational Coupling On Rotating Black Holes
Abstract: This research investigates the implications of modifying gravitational coupling on the properties of rotating black holes. Beyond the changes induced in the spacetime structure of such black holes, we also study the effects on the Penrose process and geodetic precession. Our motivation stems from the functional form of gravitational coupling previously explored in the context of the infrared limit of asymptotic safe gravity theory. The inclusion of a new parameter, $\\tilde{\\xi}$, in this solution distinguishes it from the Schwarzschild black hole. We analyze the Killing horizon, event horizon, and singularity of the computed metric, noting that the ergosphere expands as $\\tilde{\\xi}$ increases. Focusing on the black hole solution in the equatorial plane, we explore the geodesics of particles, both null and timelike. The effective potential is calculated and graphically analyzed for various values of the parameter $\\tilde{\\xi}$. We investigate energy extraction from the black hole through the Penrose process. For the same spin parameter values, numerical results suggest that the efficiency of the Penrose process is higher in quantum-corrected gravity compared to the Kerr Black Hole. Finally, we briefly discuss the Lense-Thirring frequency.

title: Cointegration and Representation of Cointegrated Autoregressive Processes in Banach Spaces
Abstract: We extend the concept of cointegration to encompass time series taking values in a potentially infinite-dimensional Banach space. Examples of such time series include stochastic processes in the space of continuous functions on the unit interval, equipped with the supremum distance, and those in a finite-dimensional vector space equipped with a non-Euclidean distance. We then develop versions of the Granger-Johansen representation theorems for integrated processes of orders 1 and 2 (I(1) and I(2)) for autoregressive (AR) processes in such a space. To achieve this, we first observe that an AR(p) law of motion can be characterized by a linear operator pencil through the companion form representation. We then delve into the spectral properties of a linear operator pencil to establish a necessary and sufficient condition for a given AR(p) law of motion to admit I(1) or I(2) solutions. These operator-theoretic results serve as the fundamental basis for our representation theorems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our operator-theoretic approach constitutes a closely related extension of the conventional approach employed in a Euclidean space setting. Our theoretical findings could be particularly relevant in the growing field of functional time series analysis in Banach spaces.

title: Block row recursive least squares migration
Abstract: Recursive estimation of large systems of equations within the framework of least-squares fitting is a prevalent practice in diverse fields of study. Notably, recursive adaptive filtering finds extensive application in signal processing and control applications. The need for recursive algorithms in solving least-squares problems arises from the demand for fast real-time signal processing strategies. The computational cost associated with using least-squares algorithms can also limit their applicability in geophysical problems. This paper investigates the recursive least-squares solution for wave equation least-squares migration with sliding windows, involving multiple rank-K downdating and updating computations. This technique is applicable to both dynamic and stationary processes. It can be shown that for stationary processes, the spectrum of the preconditioned system clusters around unity, leading to superlinear convergence with probability one when sufficient data is used in each windowed setup. Numerical experiments are presented to illustrate the effectiveness of this technique for least-squares migration.

title: Electromagnetically induced transparency control in terahertz metasurfaces based on bright-bright mode coupling
Abstract: We demonstrate a classical analogue of electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) in a highly flexible planar terahertz metamaterial (MM) composed of three-gap split ring resonators. The key to achieving EIT in this system lies in the frequency detuning and hybridization processes between two bright modes coexisting within the same unit cell, as opposed to the conventional bright-dark mode coupling. We present experimental validation of two-bright mode coupling for a terahertz EIT-MM, supported by numerical results and theoretical analysis based on a coupled Lorentz oscillator model. Additionally, a hybrid variation of the EIT-MM is proposed and implemented numerically to enable dynamic tuning of the EIT window. This tuning is achieved by incorporating photosensitive silicon pads in the split gap region of the resonators. As a consequence, this hybrid MM offers the potential for active optical control of the transition between the on-state (EIT mode) and the off-state (dipole mode).

title: Collective behavior of bulk nanobubbles produced by the alternating polarity electrolysis
Abstract: Nanobubbles in liquids are enigmatic gaseous objects exhibiting exceptional stability. While holding promise for a wide range of applications, their production remains poorly controlled and localized. Alternating polarity electrolysis of water offers a method for spatially and temporally controlling the production of bulk nanobubbles without generating larger bubbles. Utilizing the schlieren technique, we visualize in detail the three-dimensional structure of a dense cloud of nanobubbles above the electrodes. The thermal effects are shown to produce distinct schlieren patterns and exhibit different dynamics. A localized volume enriched with nanobubbles can be separated from the parent cloud and exists independently. This volume demonstrates buoyancy, from which we estimate the concentration of nanobubbles to be 2x10^18 m^-3. This concentration is lower than that found in the parent cloud. Dynamic light scattering reveals that the average size of nanobubbles during the process is 60-80 nm. The bubbles are observed 15 minutes after switching off the electrical pulses, but their size shifts to larger values of approximately 250 nm. Thus, we propose an efficient method for generating and controlling nanobubbles.

title: Denoising of 3D magnetic resonance images with multi-channel residual learning of convolutional neural network
Abstract: Denoising magnetic resonance (MR) images is a crucial task for enhancing image quality. Numerous methods have been proposed in the literature to retrieve noise-free images with good performance. However, state-of-the-art denoising methods often require time-consuming optimization processes and their performance heavily depends on the accuracy of the estimated noise level parameter. This manuscript proposes a novel approach for denoising MRI Rician noise using a convolutional neural network. The proposed methodology offers the advantage of a learning-based model that can be directly applied for denoising without optimization or even knowledge of the noise level parameter. Specifically, we propose a ten-layer convolutional neural network incorporating residual learning and a multi-channel strategy. Existing methods typically adapt each transmitter's transmission strategy only to the fading process of its direct channel to the receiver, essentially adopting a single-user strategy designed for single-user channels. However, the contribution of each user to a network-wide measure (e.g., sum-rate capacity) depends not only on the user's direct channel but also on the quality of other channels. Based on this premise, this paper proposes an alternative broadcast strategy where transmitters adapt their transmissions to the combined states resulting from all users' channels. This leads to a larger number of information streams generated by each transmitter and a different decoding strategy employed by the receiver. title: Modeling Spatial Overdispersion with the Generalized Waring Process

Indeed, Diggle and Milne conjectured that no negative binomial model could fulfill all three properties. In response to this limitation, we present a novel process based on the Generalized Waring Distribution, an alternative overdisperse count model. This Generalized Waring process, while comparable in tractability and flexibility to negative binomial processes, satisfies all the required properties and encompasses both negative binomial and Poisson processes as limiting cases. Consequently, the Generalized Waring process offers an approximate resolution to the dilemma raised by Diggle and Milne.

To enable deep learning applications to handle a wide range of input data, popular frameworks like Caffe, TensorFlow, and Torch provide data scaling functions to resize input to the dimensions used by deep learning models. Image scaling algorithms are intended to preserve image visual features after scaling. However, common image scaling algorithms are not designed to handle human-crafted images. Attackers can manipulate scaling outputs to appear dramatically different from their corresponding input images. This paper presents a downscaling attack targeting the data scaling process in deep learning applications. By carefully crafting input data that mismatches the dimension used by deep learning models, attackers can create deceptive effects. Deep learning applications effectively consume data that differs from what is presented to users. This visual inconsistency enables practical evasion and data poisoning attacks on deep learning applications. This paper provides proof-of-concept attack samples against popular deep-learning-based image classification applications. To address downscaling attacks, the paper also suggests multiple potential mitigation strategies.

title: Modification of $Δ(1232)$ in the neutrino nucleus reaction
Abstract: Significant observations in pion-induced and charge exchange reactions on a nucleus include the substantial shift and broadening of the Δ(1232)-peak compared to free pion-nucleon scattering. According to Adler's partially conserved axial current theorem, the weak process (νl,l) on a nucleon, for forward-going massless leptons, is linked to pion-nucleon scattering. This mechanism is also applicable to nuclei. Therefore, the modification of the Δ-peak in a nucleus can be observed in the (νl,l) reaction as it is connected to pion-nucleus scattering. To investigate this quantitatively, double differential cross sections of the forward-going ejectile l energy distribution in the (νl,l) reaction are calculated in the Δ-excitation region for both protons and nuclei. Measured pion-nucleon and pion-nucleus scattering cross sections in the quoted energy region are used as input in these reactions. As the (νl,l) reaction is connected to pion-induced scattering, its features exhibit similarities to those of the latter.

title: Towards a Deep Improviser: a prototype deep learning post-tonal free music generator
Abstract: Two modest-sized symbolic corpora of post-tonal and post-metric keyboard music have been constructed, one algorithmic, the other improvised. Deep learning models for each corpus have been trained and extensively optimized. Our goal is to create a model with sufficient generalization capacity that, given a small amount of fresh input seed material, can generate outputs that are distinctive rather than recreative of the learned corpora or the seed material. This objective has been statistically assessed, and as judged by k-sample Anderson-Darling and Cramer tests, has been achieved. Music generated using this approach has been evaluated informally, and these judgments place it roughly on par with algorithmic and composed music in related forms. Future work will aim to enhance the model for evaluation in terms of expression, meaning, and utility in real-time performance.

title: Gibbs sampler with jump diffusion model: application in European call option and annuity
Abstract: This paper presents a method for estimating market parameters modeled by a jump diffusion process using a Gibbs sampler. The estimated parameters include drift, volatility, jump intensity, and occurrence rate. The paper demonstrates how to use these parameters to estimate the fair price of European call options and annuities when the market is modeled by a jump diffusion process with varying intensity and occurrence. The results are compared to conventional options to observe the impact of jump effects.

title: From Dissipativity Theory to Compositional Construction of Finite Markov Decision Processes
Abstract: This paper proposes a compositional approach for constructing finite Markov decision processes (MDPs) of interconnected discrete-time stochastic control systems. The proposed approach leverages the interconnection topology and the concept of stochastic storage functions, which describe joint dissipativity-type properties of subsystems and their abstractions. The first part of the paper derives compositional conditions for quantifying the error between the interconnection of stochastic control subsystems and their abstractions. The second part proposes an approach to construct finite MDPs along with their corresponding stochastic storage functions for classes of discrete-time control systems satisfying an incremental passivability property. Under this property, finite MDPs can be constructed by appropriately discretizing the input and state sets. Additionally, we show that this property can be easily verified using a matrix inequality for linear stochastic control systems. We apply our proposed results to temperature regulation in a circular building by compositionally constructing a finite MDP for a network of 200 rooms. The compositionality condition does not require any constraint on the number or gains of the subsystems. We use the constructed finite MDP as a substitute to synthesize policies regulating the temperature in each room over a bounded time horizon.

title: Electrically Pumped Orbital Angular Momentum (OAM) Laser at Telecom Wavelengths
Abstract: Semiconductor lasers capable of generating vortex beams with specific orbital angular momentum (OAM) orders are highly attractive for applications ranging from nanoparticle manipulation, imaging, and microscopy to fiber and quantum communications. This work demonstrates the fabrication of an electrically pumped OAM laser operating at telecom wavelengths by monolithically integrating an optical vortex emitter with a distributed feedback (DFB) laser on the same InGaAsP/InP epitaxial wafer. A single-step dry etching process is adopted to complete the OAM emitter, equipped with specially designed top gratings. The vortex beam emitted by the integrated laser is captured, and its OAM mode purity is characterized. The electrically pumped OAM laser eliminates the external laser requirement for silicon- or silicon-on-insulator (SOI)-based OAM emitters, showcasing its potential for applications in communication systems and the quantum domain.

title: Controlled Information Fusion with Risk-Averse CVaR Social Sensors
Abstract: Consider a multi-agent network composed of risk-averse social sensors and a controller that collaboratively estimate an unknown state of nature based on noisy measurements. The network of social sensors performs Bayesian social learning, where each sensor fuses information from previous social sensors and its private valuation using Bayes' rule to optimize a local cost function. The controller sequentially modifies the sensor cost functions using discriminatory pricing (control inputs) to achieve long-term global objectives. We formulate the controller's stochastic control problem as a Partially Observed Markov Decision Process (POMDP) and derive structural results for the optimal control policy as a function of the risk-aversion factor in the Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) cost function of the sensors. We demonstrate that the optimal price sequence when sensors are risk-averse is a super-martingale, implying a decrease on average over time.

title: A self-consistent model of the coronal heating and solar wind acceleration including compressible and incompressible heating processes
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel one-dimensional model encompassing both shock and turbulence heating, quantifying their contributions to coronal heating and solar wind driving. Compressible MHD simulations automatically account for shock formation and dissipation, while turbulent dissipation is modeled using a one-point closure based on Alfvén wave turbulence. Numerical simulations were conducted with varying photospheric perpendicular correlation lengths λ0, a critical parameter of Alfvén wave turbulence, and different root-mean-square photospheric transverse-wave amplitudes δv0. For various λ0, we obtain a low-temperature chromosphere, high-temperature corona, and supersonic solar wind. Our analysis reveals that turbulence heating consistently dominates when λ0≲1 Mm. This does not imply ignoring compressibility, as the analysis indicates that compressible waves and associated density fluctuations enhance Alfvén wave reflection and, consequently, turbulence heating. Density fluctuation and cross-helicity are strongly influenced by λ0, while coronal temperature and mass loss rate exhibit weak dependence on λ0.

title: Cavity enhanced Raman heterodyne spectroscopy in Er:YSO for microwave to optical signal conversion
Abstract: The efficiency of the frequency conversion process at the heart of Raman heterodyne spectroscopy was enhanced by nearly four orders of magnitude through resonant enhancement of both the pump and signal optical fields. Our results using an erbium-doped Y2SiO5 crystal at temperatures near 4K suggest that this approach holds promise for the quantum conversion of microwave to optical photons.

title: A Unified Asymptotic Analysis of Area Spectral Efficiency in Ultradense Cellular Networks
Abstract: This paper analyzes the asymptotic properties of average area spectral efficiency (ASE) in a downlink cellular network in the limit of very dense base station (BS) and user densities. This asymptotic analysis relies on three assumptions: (1) interference is treated as noise; (2) BS locations follow a Poisson point process; (3) the path loss function is bounded above and satisfies mild regularity conditions. We consider three possible definitions of average ASE, all of which yield units of bits per second per unit bandwidth per unit area. In the absence of constraints on the minimum operational signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) and with instantaneous full channel state information (CSI) available at the transmitter, the average ASE is proven to saturate to a constant, which we derive in a closed form. For the other two ASE definitions, where either a minimum SINR is enforced or CSI is unavailable, the average ASE is shown to collapse to zero at high BS density. We provide several familiar case studies for the class of considered path loss models, demonstrating that our results encompass most previous models and results on ultradense networks as special cases.

title: Enhance Visual Recognition under Adverse Conditions via Deep Networks
Abstract: Visual recognition under adverse conditions is a significant and challenging problem with high practical value due to the ubiquitous presence of quality distortions during image acquisition, transmission, or storage. While deep neural networks have been extensively used in techniques for low-quality image restoration and high-quality image recognition tasks, respectively, few studies have addressed the critical problem of recognition from very low-quality images. This paper proposes a deep learning-based framework for improving the performance of image and video recognition models under adverse conditions using robust adverse pre-training or its aggressive variant. Robust adverse pre-training algorithms leverage the power of pre-training and generalize conventional unsupervised pre-training and data augmentation methods. We further develop a transfer learning approach to handle real-world datasets with unknown adverse conditions. The proposed framework is comprehensively evaluated on various image and video recognition benchmarks, achieving significant performance improvements under diverse single or mixed adverse conditions. Our visualization and analysis further enhance the explainability of the results.

title: Linking Administrative Data: An Evolutionary Schema
Abstract: Statistics New Zealand (Stats NZ) has fully committed to an administrative data first policy. Consequently, all new methods implemented at Stats NZ are evaluated within this context, and discussions about strategies for using administrative data are an integral part of daily operations. As statistical methodologists, the authors were drawn into these discussions. Like most methodologists, we view surveys and the publication of their results as a process where estimation is the key tool to achieve accurate statistical outputs. Randomness and sampling support this goal, and it became clear that incoming administrative data sources were not randomly selected. These sources were clearly biased and would produce biased estimates. Therefore, we sought to design a strategy to address this issue. This led us to the concept of representativeness, which is closely related to statistical bias but has a wider context encompassing both randomness and judgment. The representativeness issue was the primary question we set out to answer. The necessary components for our solution are summarized in this paper.

title: Optimal control of a probabilistic dynamic for epidemic spreading in arbitrary complex networks
Abstract: This paper presents a discrete-time probabilistic dynamic for simulating a contact-based epidemic spreading using a discrete-time Markov chain process, focusing on the susceptible-infectious-removed (SIR) model. The phase diagram of this model is presented. The paper then derives equations representing optimal control strategies, using Pontryagin's maximum principle, in two different cases: a vaccination policy and a combined vaccination-hospitalization policy. Finally, numerical simulations for these equations are performed using the standard forward-backward sweep procedure.

title: Beyond News Contents: The Role of Social Context for Fake News Detection
Abstract: Social media has become a popular source of news due to its rapid dissemination, easy access, and low cost. However, it also facilitates the spread of fake news, which is intentionally false information. Detecting fake news is crucial, not only to ensure users receive authentic information but also to maintain a trustworthy news ecosystem. The majority of existing detection algorithms focus on analyzing news content, which often proves ineffective as fake news is intentionally designed to mislead users by imitating true news. Therefore, exploring auxiliary information is essential to improve detection. The social context surrounding news dissemination on social media forms an inherent tri-relationship among publishers, news pieces, and users, which holds potential for enhancing fake news detection. For instance, partisan-biased publishers are more likely to publish fake news, while low-credibility users are more likely to share it. This paper investigates the novel problem of leveraging social context for fake news detection. We propose a tri-relationship embedding framework, TriFN, which simultaneously models publisher-news relations and user-news interactions for fake news classification. Experiments conducted on two real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms other baseline methods for fake news detection.

title: Multiphase imaging of freezing particle suspensions by confocal microscopy
Abstract: Ice-templating is a widely established technique for producing porous ceramics. Understanding and controlling the solidification microstructures is crucial due to the structure-property relationships. Ice-templating relies on the segregation and concentration of particles by growing ice crystals. Current knowledge of the process is based on observations from optical or X-ray imaging techniques or characterization of ice-templated materials. However, in situ observations at the particle scale are still lacking. This study demonstrates that confocal microscopy can provide multiphase imaging of ice growth, particle segregation, and organization. The benefits of this approach are illustrated by observing particles and pore ice in the frozen structure, the dynamic evolution of the freeze front morphology, and the impact of PVA addition on solidification microstructures. These results highlight the importance of controlling both the temperature gradient and growth rate during ice-templating.

title: GSM-CommSense-based through-the-wall sensing
Abstract: A novel communication-sensing (CommSense) scheme that utilizes the channel equalization blocks of telecommunication systems to sense environmental changes has been proposed. Following initial positive results, a GSM-based CommSense system was tested for through-the-wall sensing. Due to the inherent under-determined nature of the system, statistical machine learning techniques were employed to sense environmental changes in behind-the-wall experiments. With limited data per GSM frame (577 µs), a person could be detected across a wall with an accuracy of 77.458%, and a person carrying a weapon could be detected with an accuracy of 95.208%. This paper details the experiments and the encouraging results obtained.

title: Limits for Rumor Spreading in stochastic populations
Abstract: Biological systems can share and collectively process information to produce emergent effects despite inherent communication noise. While man-made systems often rely on intricate structural solutions to overcome noise, biological systems often have a more amorphous structure. How communication noise affects the computational repertoire of such groups remains unclear. To address this question, the basic collective task of rumor spreading is considered, where information from a few knowledgeable sources needs to flow reliably to the rest of the population. To study the effect of communication noise on the ability of groups lacking stable structures to efficiently solve this task, a noisy version of the uniform PULL model is analyzed. A lower bound is proven, implying that even moderate levels of noise affecting all aspects of communication prevent any scheme from significantly outperforming the trivial one where agents must wait for direct interaction with the sources. These results demonstrate an exponential separation between the uniform PUSH and PULL communication models in the presence of noise. This separation suggests that achieving efficient rumor spreading requires either some degree of structural stability or a noise-immune facet of communication. The theoretical findings are corroborated by a new analysis of experimental data on recruitment in Cataglyphis niger desert ants.

title: The galaxy environment in GAMA G3C groups using the Kilo Degree Survey Data Release 3
Abstract: This study aims to investigate the galaxy environment in the GAMA Galaxy Groups Catalogue (G3C) using a volume-limited galaxy sample from the Kilo Degree Survey Data Release 3. The k-Nearest Neighbour technique is adapted to account for the probability density functions (PDFs) of photometric redshifts in the calculations. This algorithm was tested on simulated KiDS tiles, demonstrating its ability to recover the relationship between galaxy color, luminosity, and local environment. Characterization of the galaxy environment in G3C groups reveals systematically steeper density contrasts for more massive groups. Red galaxy fraction gradients in these groups are evident for most group mass bins. The density contrast of red galaxies is systematically higher at group centers compared to blue galaxies. Additionally, distinct group center definitions are employed to show that the results are insensitive to center definitions. These findings confirm the galaxy evolution scenario where environmental mechanisms drive a slow quenching process as galaxies fall into groups and clusters, resulting in smooth observed color gradients in galaxy systems.

title: Floquet Scalar Dynamics in Global AdS
Abstract: This study examines periodically driven scalar fields and the resulting geometries with global AdS asymptotics. These solutions describe the strongly coupled dynamics of dual finite-size quantum systems under a periodic driving, interpreted as Floquet condensates. The solutions span a continuous two-parameter space extending the linearized solutions on AdS. The regions of stability in the solution space are mapped. A significant portion of the unstable subspace leads to two very different endpoints depending on the sign of the perturbation. Collapse into a black hole occurs for one sign, while the opposite sign yields a regular solution with periodic modulation. Quenches with continuously varying driving frequency and amplitude are constructed. Quasistatic quenches can interpolate between pure AdS and sourced solutions with time-periodic vev. By appropriately choosing the quasistatic path, one can obtain boson stars dual to Floquet condensates at zero driving field. The adiabaticity of the quenching processes is characterized. The study speculates on possible connections of this framework with time crystals.

title: Deep Learning with Lung Segmentation and Bone Shadow Exclusion Techniques for Chest X-Ray Analysis of Lung Cancer
Abstract: Recent advancements in computing, machine learning, and particularly deep learning for image recognition have significantly impacted the automatic detection of various diseases from chest X-ray images (CXRs). This study demonstrates the effectiveness of lung segmentation and bone shadow exclusion techniques for analyzing 2D CXRs using a deep learning approach. This approach assists radiologists in identifying suspicious lesions and nodules in lung cancer patients. Training and validation were performed on the original JSRT dataset (dataset #01), the BSE-JSRT dataset (same JSRT dataset but without clavicle and rib shadows, dataset #02), the original JSRT dataset after segmentation (dataset #03), and the BSE-JSRT dataset after segmentation (dataset #04). The results demonstrate the high efficiency and usefulness of the considered pre-processing techniques, even in simplified configurations. The pre-processed dataset without bones (dataset #02) exhibits significantly better accuracy and loss results compared to the other pre-processed datasets after lung segmentation (datasets #02 and #03).

title: Beyond Powers of Two: Hexagonal Modulation and Non-Binary Coding for Wireless Communication Systems
Abstract: Adaptive modulation and coding (AMC) is widely implemented in modern wireless communication systems to enhance transmission efficiency by adjusting the transmission rate according to channel conditions. AMC provides highly efficient use of channel resources, especially over fading channels. Quadrature Amplitude Modulation (QAM) is an efficient and widely employed digital modulation technique. It typically uses a rectangular signal constellation, leading to square partitions of the two-dimensional signal space as decision regions. However, hexagons, rather than squares, provide the most compact regular tiling in two dimensions. This compact tiling allows for a denser packing of constellation points, resulting in more energy-efficient data transmission. Hexagonal modulation can be challenging to implement due to its incompatibility with the usual power-of-two symbol sizes used with binary data. To address this issue, non-binary coding is combined with hexagonal modulation in this paper, creating a system compatible with binary data. The feasibility and efficiency of this approach are evaluated using a software-defined radio (SDR) based prototype. Extensive simulation results show that this approach can enhance energy efficiency and spectrum utilization in wireless communication systems.

title: Improving Generalization Performance by Switching from Adam to SGD
Abstract: Adaptive optimization methods like Adam, Adagrad, and RMSprop, despite achieving superior training outcomes, have been observed to generalize poorly compared to Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). These methods perform well initially but are outperformed by SGD in later training stages. This study investigates a hybrid strategy that starts training with an adaptive method and switches to SGD when appropriate. Specifically, SWATS, a simple strategy that switches from Adam to SGD when a triggering condition is met, is proposed. The proposed condition relates to the projection of Adam steps on the gradient subspace. The monitoring process for this condition adds minimal overhead and does not increase the number of hyperparameters in the optimizer. Experiments on several standard benchmarks, including ResNet, SENet, DenseNet, and PyramidNet for CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets, ResNet for the tiny-ImageNet dataset, and language modeling with recurrent networks on PTB and WT2 datasets, are reported. The results demonstrate that this strategy effectively closes the generalization gap between SGD and Adam for most tasks.

title: Temporal logic control of general Markov decision processes by approximate policy refinement
Abstract: Formal verification and controller synthesis for Markov decision processes evolving over uncountable state spaces are computationally challenging and typically rely on approximations. This study focuses on the correct-by-design control of general Markov decision processes (gMDPs) with respect to temporal logic properties by leveraging approximate probabilistic relations between the original model and its abstraction. A novel robust satisfaction approach is introduced for constructing and verifying control strategies, which allows for deviations in both the outputs of the gMDPs and the probabilistic transitions. Computations are performed on the reduced or abstracted models, ensuring that a property robustly satisfied on the abstract model is also satisfied on the original model with respect to a refined control strategy.

title: $W^+ W^- H$ Production at Lepton Colliders: A New Hope for Heavy Neutral Leptons
Abstract: This paper presents the first study of Standard Model Higgs boson production at a lepton collider in association with a pair of W bosons, e+e− → W+W−H, within the inverse seesaw model. Considering all relevant experimental and theoretical constraints, sizable effects due to additional heavy neutrinos are observed, leading to up to -38% reduction in the total cross-section at a center-of-mass energy of 3 TeV, and even up to -66% with suitable cuts. This finding motivates a detailed sensitivity analysis of the e+e− → W+W−H process as it could provide a new, highly competitive experimental probe of low-scale neutrino mass models.

title: A non-local mixing-length theory able to compute core overshooting
Abstract: Turbulent convection is a fundamental and complex issue in stellar physics. Limited understanding of this process introduces significant uncertainty regarding the internal structure and evolution of stars. A striking example is overshoot at the edge of convective cores. Most stellar evolutionary codes treat overshooting zones in a very approximative way, considering both extent and the profile of the temperature gradient as free parameters. Although sophisticated theories of stellar convection exist, such as Reynolds stress approaches, they also require adjusting a considerable number of free parameters. This study presents a new theory, based on plume theory and mean-field equations, but without relying on the usual Taylor's closure hypothesis. This theory leads to a set of eight differential equations plus a few algebraic ones and constitutes a non-mixing length theory. It enables the calculation of the temperature gradient in a shrinking convective core and its overshooting zone. The case of an expanding convective core is also discussed, albeit more briefly. Rapid improvements in numerical simulations in recent years suggest that they will soon provide a convection model suitable for computing 1D stellar models.

title: Supermarket Model on Graphs
Abstract: This study analyzes a variation of the supermarket model where servers can communicate with their neighbors and where neighborhood relationships are described by a suitable graph. Tasks with unit-exponential service time distributions arrive at each vertex as independent Poisson processes with rate λ, and each task is irrevocably assigned to the shortest queue among the one it first appears and its d-1 randomly selected neighbors. This model has been extensively studied when the underlying graph is a clique, reducing to the well-known power-of-d scheme. Results from Mitzenmacher (1996) and Vvedenskaya et al. (1996) show that as the size of the clique grows, the occupancy process associated with queue-lengths at various servers converges to a deterministic limit described by an infinite system of ordinary differential equations (ODE). This study considers settings where the underlying graph need not be a clique and can be suitably sparse. It is shown that if the minimum degree approaches infinity (however slowly) as the number of servers N approaches infinity, and the ratio between the maximum and minimum degree in each connected component approaches 1 uniformly, the occupancy process converges to the same system of ODE as the classical supermarket model. This indicates that the asymptotic behavior of the occupancy process is insensitive to the precise network topology. The study also investigates the case where the graph sequence is random, with the N-th graph being an Erdős-Rényi random graph on N vertices with average degree c(N). Annealed convergence of the occupancy process to the same deterministic limit is established under the condition c(N)→∞, and under a stronger condition c(N)/ln N→∞, convergence (in probability) is shown for almost every realization of the random graph.

title: A ROOT Based Event Display Software for JUNO

title: An Analytical Perspective to Traffic Engineering in Anonymous Communication Systems
Abstract: Anonymous communication systems (ACS) offer privacy and anonymity through the internet. As free tools, they are popular among users worldwide. While they ensure privacy under certain conditions, their anonymity is compromised by high-performance processing units. To address these issues, this study investigates traffic engineering methods in ACS, proposing an analytical view of current challenges in ACS privacy and anonymity. title: Effect of Ag and Zr solutes on dislocation emission from the Σ11(332)[110] symmetric tilt grain boundary in fcc Cu
Abstract: Adding solutes is a common practice to stabilize nanocrystalline materials against grain growth. However, segregating at grain boundaries, these solutes also affect the process of dislocation nucleation from grain boundaries under applied stress. This study uses atomistic simulations to demonstrate that the effect of solutes on dislocation nucleation strongly depends on the distribution of solutes at the grain boundary, which can vary significantly depending on the solute type. Specifically, the study reveals that solutes with a smaller size mismatch can be more effective in suppressing dislocation emission from grain boundaries. Since dislocation slip originating from grain boundaries or their triple junctions is the dominant mechanism of plastic deformation at the nanoscale, this emphasizes the importance of searching for optimal solute additions that stabilize the nanocrystalline material against grain growth while effectively suppressing dislocation nucleation from the grain boundaries.

title: Optimal Discrete Spatial Compression for Beamspace Massive MIMO Signals
Abstract: Deploying a massive number of antennas at the base station side can significantly enhance cellular system performance. However, this approach introduces substantial radio-frequency (RF) front-end complexity, hardware costs, and power consumption. To address this challenge, a beamspace-multiple-input-multiple-output (beamspace-MIMO) based approach is proposed as a promising solution. This paper demonstrates that traditional beamspace-MIMO suffers from spatial power leakage and imperfect channel statistics estimation. A beam combination module, consisting of a small number of low-resolution (possibly one-bit) digital (discrete) phase shifters after the beamspace transformation, is proposed to further compress the beamspace signal dimensionality, reducing the number of RF chains beyond beamspace transformation and beam selection. The optimal discrete beam combination weights for the uplink are obtained based on the branch-and-bound (BB) approach. Solving the embodied sub-problem, whose solution is derived in a closed-form, is crucial for the BB-based solution. Based on this solution, a sequential greedy beam combination scheme with linear-complexity (with respect to the number of beams in the beamspace) is proposed. Link-level simulation results based on realistic channel models and long-term-evolution (LTE) parameters demonstrate that the proposed schemes can reduce the number of RF chains by up to 25% with a one-bit digital phase-shifter-network.

title: Anchored Network Users: Stochastic Evolutionary Dynamics of Cognitive Radio Network Selection

However, this approach is less practical, requiring each user to have access to global information on the network state to reach a Nash equilibrium. title: i-Process Contribution of Rapidly Accreting White Dwarfs to the Solar Composition of First-Peak Neutron-Capture Elements
Abstract:
Rapidly accreting white dwarfs (RAWDs) have been proposed as sources of heavy elements in the Milky Way. This study investigates the potential contribution of RAWDs to the solar abundance of first-peak neutron-capture elements. By incorporating the metallicity-dependent contribution of RAWDs into the one-zone galactic chemical evolution code OMEGA, we find that RAWDs could significantly contribute to the solar composition of elements like Kr, Rb, Sr, Y, Zr, Nb, and Mo, ranging from 2% to 45%. This contribution could potentially explain the missing solar Lighter Element Primary Process for certain elements, such as Sr, Y, and Zr. While we do not overproduce any isotope relative to solar abundances, we observe a similar production level of ⁹⁶Zr. The i-process efficiently produces the stable Mo isotopes ⁹⁵Mo and ⁹⁷Mo. Combining nuclear reaction rate uncertainties with GCE uncertainties, the upper limits of the predicted RAWD contribution increase by factors of 1.5-2 for Rb, Sr, Y, and Zr, and by 3.8 and 2.4 for Nb and Mo, respectively. We discuss the implications of these findings for the single degenerate Type Ia supernova scenario. ||| 
Water content is a key factor in the internal evolution of terrestrial planets and icy bodies. The distribution of water in planetary systems is influenced by the temperature structure of protoplanetary disks and the dynamics and migration of planetesimals and planetary embryos. This leads to the formation of these objects with varying compositions, water contents, and oxidation levels. The internal evolution and formation time of planetesimals relative to the timescale of radiogenic heating from the decay of short-lived ²⁶Al can influence the abundance of hydrous silicates and rock-ice mixtures in their late stages. Water content can also affect early internal evolution, particularly metal-silicate separation processes. Moreover, it can contribute to increased oxygen fugacity, influencing the concentrations of siderophile elements in the silicate reservoirs of Solar System objects. Finally, water content plays a crucial role in the differentiation rate of icy moons, controlling their internal evolution and governing alteration processes in their deep interiors. ||| 
The rapid growth of digital information online has led to the widespread use of search engines and recommendation systems. Recent advancements in deep learning have gained significant attention in speech recognition, image processing, and natural language processing, and have also shown promise in the field of recommendation systems and information retrieval. This review focuses on recent developments in recommendation systems using various deep learning techniques, categorized into collaborative, content-based, and hybrid systems. It also examines the integration of deep learning-based recommendation systems into various application domains. The review concludes by discussing the impact of deep learning on recommendation systems and whether it has significantly improved upon conventional systems. Future research directions based on current trends in deep learning applications for recommendation systems are also outlined. ||| 
This paper introduces the class of 𝐻-valued autoregressive (AR) processes with a unit root of finite type, where 𝐻 represents an infinite-dimensional separable Hilbert space. It derives a generalization of the Granger-Johansen Representation Theorem applicable to any integration order 𝑑 = 1, 2, …. An existence theorem establishes that the solution to an AR with a unit root of finite type is necessarily integrated of a finite integer 𝑑 and exhibits a common trends representation with a finite number of common stochastic trends resembling (cumulated) bilateral random walks and an infinite-dimensional cointegrating space. A characterization theorem clarifies the relationships between the structure of the AR operators and (i) the order of integration, (ii) the structure of the attractor space and the cointegrating space, (iii) the expression of the cointegrating relations, and (iv) the Triangular representation of the process. The representation of 𝐻-valued ARs with a unit root of finite type closely resembles that of typical finite-dimensional VARs, which correspond to the special case 𝐻 = ℝ𝑝, with the exception that the number of cointegrating relations integrated of order 0 is infinite. ||| 
Concepts from forensic linguistics are increasingly employed in Natural Language Processing (NLP) using machine learning techniques. While forensic linguistics previously played a more benign role, it is now being used for potentially questionable purposes. Certain methods are applied without considering their scientific limitations and ethical concerns. This paper uses the specific case of forensic linguistics as an example of these trends in NLP and machine learning, highlighting a broader issue present in various scientific and data-driven domains. It suggests that some applied sciences are exceeding their legal and scientific boundaries. The paper emphasizes how careless implementations can undermine due process in legal systems and violate ethical codes. ||| 
This study investigates the potential for detecting a five-plet singly charged Higgs H5± in the Georgi-Machacek model at ep colliders. The charged Higgs bosons are produced through the ZW± fusion process p e⁻ → j e⁻ H5±, decaying as H5± → Z W± → (l⁺ l⁻) (jj). Detector-level simulations for FCC-eh and LHeC are used to perform a multivariate analysis, setting limits on the production cross section times branching ratio σ (p e⁻ → j e⁻ H5±) × BR(H5± → Z W±) and the model parameter sinθH for charged Higgs masses ranging from 200 to 1000 GeV. The impact of electron beam polarization is also explored. ||| 
This work explores the use of rational approximation to enhance the accuracy of spectral solutions of differential equations. Spectral methods can face challenges in the vicinity of solutions with singularities, exhibiting reduced convergence rates or even complete convergence failure. This paper describes a Padé approximation-based method to improve the approximation within the Tau method solution of ordinary differential equations. This process is well-suited for constructing rational approximations to solutions of differential problems when their exact solutions exhibit singularities near their domain. ||| 
Accelerating deep neural networks (DNNs) has become increasingly important for applications requiring powerful visual recognition on devices with limited computing resources. A typical approach involves a two-stage process: operating on trained DNNs (e.g., using tensor decomposition for convolutional filters) and fine-tuning the modified network. However, balancing acceleration with performance preservation presents a challenge. This paper proposes a Wavelet-like Auto-Encoder (WAE) for a general and comprehensive approach to neural network acceleration. The WAE decomposes the original input image into two low-resolution channels (sub-images), incorporating the WAE into classification neural networks for joint training. These channels carry low-frequency information (e.g., image profiles) and high-frequency information (e.g., image details or noise), respectively, enabling the reconstruction of the original input image through the decoding process. The low-frequency channel is then fed into a standard classification network (e.g., VGG or ResNet), while a lightweight network fuses with the high-frequency channel to obtain the classification result. Compared to existing DNN acceleration solutions, this framework offers advantages: i) tolerance to existing convolutional neural networks for classification without structural modifications, and ii) an interpretable way to preserve essential input image components for classification. ||| 
Hyperpolarized ¹³C-MRI allows real-time observation of metabolism in vivo. Imaging sequences have been developed to track the metabolism of [1-¹³C]pyruvate and extract reaction kinetics, providing insights into tumor treatment response. This study applies a fitting model and algorithm to imaging data from mice tumor models, determining error estimates for relevant parameters. Data was fitted to a two-site exchange model in MATLAB using least-squares fitting, followed by statistical analysis to assess model performance. Inference using MCMC was also conducted. The modeling and inference process effectively and reproducibly extracted quantitative information, demonstrating metabolic activity and intratumor heterogeneity. Novel fitting methods were evaluated, and further recommendations were made. ||| 
A theoretical study on the process χc0(1P)→ ̅ΛΣπ, considering final state interactions of πΣ and π̅Λ based on the chiral unitary approach, is presented. This process, filtered by isospin I = 0 for the πΣ channel and I = 1 for the π̅Λ channel, provides a means to explore the molecular structure of the Λ(1405) resonance and test the existence of predicted states Σ(1380) and Σ(1430) with spin-parity JP = 1/2⁻. Results indicate a peak around 1350-1400 MeV and a cusp near the ̅KN threshold in the πΣ invariant mass distribution, characteristic features of the molecular state Λ(1405). Additionally, a peak around 1380 MeV and a cusp near the ̅KN threshold in the π̅Λ invariant mass distribution are found, associated with the Σ(1380) and Σ(1430) resonances. ||| 
This paper applies Minkowski Tensor statistics to two-dimensional slices of the three-dimensional density field. Minkowski Tensors are functions sensitive to directionally dependent signals in data and can quantify the mean shape of density peaks. The paper introduces an algorithm for constructing bounding perimeters around subsets of a two-dimensional field and reviews the definition of Minkowski Tensors. Focusing on the translational invariant statistic W1,12 – a 2×2 matrix – the eigenvalues are calculated for both the entire excursion set (Λ1, Λ2) and for individual connected regions and holes within the set (λ1, λ2). The eigenvalue ratio Λ2/Λ1 indicates the presence of global anisotropies in the data, while ⟨λ2/λ1⟩ quantifies the mean shape of peaks and troughs in the density field. These quantities are studied for a Gaussian field and then investigated for their modifications due to gravitational collapse using the latest Horizon Run 4 cosmological simulation. Λ1,2 are found to be essentially independent of gravitational collapse, as the process maintains statistical isotropy. However, the mean shape of peaks is significantly modified, with overdensities becoming more circular compared to underdensities of the same area. Applying the statistic to a redshift space distorted density field reveals a significant signal in the eigenvalues Λ1,2, suggesting their potential for probing the large-scale velocity field. ||| 
Stochastic geometry models are commonly used to study wireless networks, particularly cellular phone networks, but research often focuses on the typical user, neglecting atypical events that can be highly disruptive and of interest to network operators. This paper examines atypical events, such as unexpected large proportions of disconnected or connected users, using a hybrid approach combining ray launching simulation and point process theory. This work is motivated by recent advancements in large deviations theory applied to the signal-to-interference ratio, providing a tool for analyzing disruptive events, especially in high-density transmitter scenarios. A new stochastic model of a single network cell is introduced, utilizing ray launching data generated with the open-source RaLaNS package for a section of a European city, providing deterministic path loss values. Statistics on the fraction of (dis)connected users in the uplink are collected, revealing that the probability of a large proportion of disconnected users decreases exponentially as the transmitter density increases. This suggests that denser networks become more stable in terms of reduced probability of deviation in the fraction of (dis)connected users from the mean. Empirically obtained and illustrated densities of users for network configurations during disruptive events highlight that such bottleneck behavior arises not only from excessive users at the cell boundary but also from the near-far effect of numerous users near the base station. Implications of these findings and potential future research directions are discussed. ||| 
If dark matter production occurred in the early universe prior to Big Bang nucleosynthesis, the modified cosmological history can significantly impact the abundance of relic dark matter particles. This study considers a scenario where an additional species dominates radiation in the early universe, resulting in a faster expansion rate at a given temperature compared to the standard radiation-dominated case. It demonstrates that this scenario leads to a dramatic suppression of dark matter production via freeze-in, where dark matter interacts weakly and is dumped out of equilibrium in the early universe through decay or scattering processes involving particles in the thermal bath. This phenomenon is illustrated and analyzed quantitatively and analytically for three paradigmatic freeze-in scenarios. To achieve dark matter abundance consistent with observations, couplings between dark matter and visible-sector particles need to be enhanced by several orders of magnitude. This sheds light on the potential detectability of dark matter produced by freeze-in, which otherwise faces significant experimental and observational challenges. ||| 
SQUID and FMR magnetometry experiments were conducted to clarify the relationship between two reported magnetic exchange effects arising from interfacial spin-polarized charge transfer within ferromagnetic metal (FM)/molecule bilayers: the magnetic hardening effect and spin-interface-stabilized molecular spin chains. To separate these effects, both of which can influence FM magnetization reversal, the magnetic moment of the metal phthalocyanine molecule central site was tuned to selectively enhance or suppress the formation of spin chains within the molecular film. Findings demonstrate that both effects are distinct and additive. In the process, this study: 1) expanded the list of FM/molecule candidate pairs known to exhibit magnetic exchange effects, 2) experimentally confirmed the predicted increase in anisotropy upon molecular adsorption, and 3) showed that spin chains within the molecular film can enhance magnetic exchange. This magnetic ordering within the organic layer suggests structural ordering. Therefore, by separating the magnetic hardening and exchange bias contributions, this study confirms that the milestone of spintronic tunneling across structurally ordered organic barriers has been achieved through previous magnetotransport experiments, mirroring progress in inorganic spintronics. This paves the way for solid-state device studies that utilize the quantum physical properties of spin chains, particularly through external stimuli. ||| 
Exploring novel chemical spaces is crucial in cheminformatics for supporting the drug discovery process. Properly designed and trained deep neural networks provide a viable alternative to brute-force de novo approaches or other machine learning techniques for generating novel drug-like molecules. This article presents a method for generating molecules using a long short-term memory (LSTM) neural network and analyzes the results, including a virtual screening test. Using this network, one million drug-like molecules were generated in two hours. These molecules are novel, diverse (containing numerous new chemotypes), possess favorable physicochemical properties, and demonstrate good synthetic accessibility, despite these qualities not being specific constraints. While novel, their structural features and functional groups remain within the drug-like space defined by bioactive molecules from ChEMBL. Virtual screening using the profile QSAR approach confirms that the potential of these novel molecules to exhibit bioactivity is comparable to the ChEMBL set from which they were derived. The molecule generator written in Python used in this study is available upon request. ||| 
Consistently changing physiological properties in developing children's brains pose challenges for data-intensive technologies like brain-computer interfaces (BCI). Enhancing signal processing methods in these technologies to be more sensitive to developmental changes could improve their functionality and usability in pediatric populations. Utilizing the multi-dimensional structure of EEG data through tensor analysis offers a framework for extracting relevant developmental features from pediatric resting-state EEG datasets. This study analyzes three pediatric datasets from different developmental states and populations using a developed two-step constrained Parallel Factor (PARAFAC) tensor decomposition. These datasets include the Muir Maxwell Epilepsy Centre, Children's Hospital Boston-MIT, and the Child Mind Institute, representing two impaired and one healthy population, respectively. Within-dataset cross-validation using support vector machines (SVM) for classification of out-of-fold data predicted subject age as a proxy measure of development. t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) maps complemented classification analysis through visualization of high-dimensional feature structures.  Results demonstrate successful identification of development-sensitive features for the developmental conditions of each dataset. SVM classification accuracy and misclassification costs improved significantly for both healthy and impaired pediatric populations. t-SNE maps revealed that appropriate tensor factorization was crucial for extracting developmental features. This approach presents a promising tool for incorporating unique developmental features present throughout childhood EEG into emerging technologies like BCI and its applications. ||| 
Detecting feature interactions is crucial for accurate performance prediction of highly configurable systems. State-of-the-art performance prediction techniques rely on supervised machine learning for detecting feature interactions, which, in turn, requires time-consuming performance measurements to obtain training data. Providing information about potentially interacting features can reduce the number of required performance measurements, making the overall performance prediction process more efficient. The paper proposes that this information can be obtained through static analysis of the source code of a highly configurable system, which is computationally less expensive than performing multiple performance measurements. A qualitative case study was conducted to explore the relationship between control-flow feature interactions (detected through static program analysis) and performance feature interactions (detected by performance prediction techniques using performance measurements). Results indicate the existence of a relationship that can potentially be exploited for predicting performance interactions. ||| 
This paper utilizes the Laplace method to derive approximate inference for Gaussian process (GP) regression in the location and scale parameters of the Student-t probabilistic model. This approach allows for the variation of both the mean and variance of the data as a function of covariates. The Student-t model, widely used for robustifying data analysis, presents challenges in approximate inference for GP regression due to the analytical intractability of the posterior distribution and the lack of concavity of the log-likelihood function. The paper introduces a natural gradient adaptation for the estimation process, leveraging the orthogonal parameterization of the Student-t model with respect to location and scale parameters. This property enables the introduction of an alternative Laplace approximation using the Fisher information matrix instead of the Hessian matrix of the negative log-likelihood function. Experimental results show that this alternative approximation provides very similar posterior approximations and predictive performance compared to the traditional Laplace approximation. Both Laplace approximations are then compared to the Monte Carlo Markov Chain (MCMC) method. Additionally, the heteroscedastic Student-t model and GP regression are compared to the heteroscedastic Gaussian model. The paper discusses how this approach can improve inference algorithms even when the probabilistic model assumed for the data is not log-concave. ||| 
Molecular communication has been proposed as an energy-efficient solution for nanoscale communication. However, the histogram of molecule hitting times, which constitute the molecular signal at the receiver, exhibits a heavy tail. Reducing the effects of this heavy tail, known as inter-symbol interference (ISI), has been a major focus of previous research. This paper proposes a novel approach for decreasing ISI by defining a counting region on the spherical receiver's surface facing towards the transmitter node. The rationale lies in the fact that molecules received from the back lobe of the receiver are more likely to have traveled longer paths, contributing to ISI. To justify this concept, the joint distribution of arriving molecules with respect to angle and time is derived. Using this distribution, the channel model function is approximated for the proposed system, i.e., the partially counting absorbing spherical receiver. After validating the channel model function, the characteristics of the molecular signal are investigated, revealing improved performance. Furthermore, the optimal counting region in terms of bit error rate is analytically determined. ||| 
Age of information is an emerging network performance metric that quantifies the freshness of information at end-users. This paper investigates age of information from a scheduling perspective. It considers a wireless broadcast network where a base station (BS) updates multiple users on random information arrivals under a transmission capacity constraint. For the offline case where the arrival statistics are known to the BS, a structural MDP scheduling algorithm and an index scheduling algorithm are developed using Markov decision process (MDP) techniques and Whittle's methodology for restless bandits. Exploring optimal structural results simplifies deriving a closed form for the Whittle index and reduces the computational complexity of the MDP-based algorithm. Moreover, for the online case, an MDP-based online scheduling algorithm and an index-based online scheduling algorithm are developed. Both the structural MDP scheduling algorithm and the MDP-based online scheduling algorithm asymptotically minimize the average age, while the index scheduling algorithm minimizes the average age when the information arrival rates for all users are the same. Extensive numerical studies validate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms. |||

title: Shorter unentangled proofs for Ground State Connectivity
Abstract: Can a proof for a quantum problem be significantly shortened using a protocol with a constant number of unentangled provers? This work examines a frustration-free variant of the QCMA-complete Ground State Connectivity (GSCON) problem for a system of size n with a proof of superlinear-size. It is demonstrated that this proof can be shortened in QMA(2), meaning there exists a two-copy, unentangled proof with length of order n, up to logarithmic factors, while the completeness-soundness gap of the new protocol becomes a small inverse polynomial in n.

title: Multi-stage generation of extreme ultraviolet dispersive waves by tapering gas-filled hollow-core anti-resonant fibers
Abstract: This study numerically investigates a practically feasible design for a tapered Ne-filled hollow-core anti-resonant fiber, reporting the generation of multiple dispersive waves (DWs) in the 90-120 nm range, extending into the extreme ultraviolet (UV) region. Simulations assume an 800 nm pump pulse with 30 fs 10 μJ pulse energy, launched into a 9 bar Ne-filled fiber with 34 μm initial core diameter, which is then tapered to a 10 μm core diameter. The simulations utilize a new model providing a realistic description of both loss and dispersion of the resonant and anti-resonant spectral bands of the fiber, importantly including the material loss of silica in the UV. By initially generating solitons that emit DWs in the far-UV region in the pre-taper section, optimization of the subsequent taper structure enables re-collision with the solitons and further up-conversion of the far-UV DWs to the extreme-UV with energies up to 190 nJ in the 90-120 nm range. This process introduces a novel method for generating light in the extreme-UV spectral range using relatively low gas pressure.

title: Space-Time-Parallel Poroelasticity Simulation
Abstract: Accurately, reliably, and efficiently approximating multi-physics processes in heterogeneous porous media with varying media coefficients that include fluid flow and structure interactions is crucial for diverse applications in energy, environmental, petroleum, and biomedical engineering fields. Key applications include subsurface compaction drive, carbon sequestration, hydraulic and thermal fracturing, and oil recovery. Biomedical applications encompass simulations of vibration therapy for osteoporosis processes in trabeculae bones, estimating stress levels induced by tumor growth within the brain, and next-generation spinal disc prostheses. Variational space-time methods offer significant advantages such as the flexibility of triangulation for complex geometries in space, natural local time stepping, straightforward construction of higher-order approximations, and application of efficient goal-oriented (duality-based) adaptivity concepts. Moreover, uniform space-time variational methods demonstrate advantages for stability and a priori error analyses of discrete schemes. Particularly, (high-order) discontinuous in time approaches exhibit favorable properties due to the weak application of initial conditions. The development of monolithic multi-physics schemes, rather than iterative coupling methods between physical problems, is a key research component to reduce modeling errors. This research emphasizes the development of efficient multi-physics and multigrid preconditioning technologies and their implementation. The simulation software DTM++ is a modularized framework written in C++11 and builds upon deal.II toolchains. The implementation allows parallel simulations from notebooks to cluster scale.

title: Particles Systems for Mean Reflected BSDEs
Abstract: This paper addresses Reflected Backward Stochastic Differential Equations (BSDEs) where the constraint is not on the paths of the solution, but on its law, as introduced by Briand, Elie, and Hu in [3]. It extends the recent work [2] of Briand, Chaudru de Raynal, Guillin, and Labart on chaos propagation for mean reflected SDEs to the backward framework. When the driver does not depend on z, general reflections can be treated for the particle system. For cases where the driver depends on z, linear reflection is considered. In both scenarios, the rate of convergence of the particle system towards the square integrable deterministic flat solution to the mean reflected BSDE is determined.

title: Monte-Carlo methods for the pricing of American options: a semilinear BSDE point of view
Abstract: This paper extends the viscosity solution characterization proved in [5] for call/put American option prices to the case of a general payoff function in a multi-dimensional setting, where the price satisfies a semilinear reaction/diffusion type equation. Based on this, two new numerical schemes inspired by the branching processes based algorithm of [8] are proposed. Numerical experiments demonstrate that approximating the discontinuous driver of the associated reaction/diffusion PDE by local polynomials is inefficient, while a simple randomization procedure yields very good results.

title: Intermittent dynamics in complex systems driven to depletion
Abstract: Complex systems driven to extinction by external factors can exhibit intermittent dynamics between relative tranquility and bursts of activity, often leading to catastrophic consequences. To understand and predict such dynamics, this paper proposes an underlying mechanism based on sharp thresholds of a local generalized energy density that naturally leads to negative feedback. A transition from a continuous regime to an intermittent one is observed, where avalanches can be predicted despite the stochastic nature of the process. This model has potential applications in various natural and social complex systems where rapid resource depletion or generalized energy drives the dynamics. Specifically, the model accurately describes the time evolution and avalanches present in a real social system.

title: Extreme Value Analysis Without the Largest Values: What Can Be Done?
Abstract: This paper analyzes heavy-tailed data when a portion of the extreme values is unavailable, motivated by an analysis of degree distributions in a large social network. The degree distributions of such networks typically exhibit power law behavior in the tails. The study focuses on the Hill estimator, crucial in heavy-tailed modeling. The Hill estimator for this data displayed a smooth and increasing "sample path" as a function of the number of upper order statistics used in constructing the estimator. This behavior became more apparent with the artificial removal of more upper order statistics. Building on this observation, a new version of the Hill estimator is introduced. It depends not only on the number of upper order statistics used in the estimation but also on the number of unavailable extreme values. Functional convergence of the normalized Hill estimator to a Gaussian process is established. An estimation procedure based on limit theory is developed to estimate the number of missing extremes and extreme value parameters, including the tail index and the bias of Hill's estimator. This approach is illustrated through simulations and real data examples.

title: Thermal responses in a coronal loop maintained by wave heating mechanisms
Abstract: This work investigates the thermal responses of a coronal loop to dynamic dissipation processes of MHD waves using a full 3-dimensional compressible magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulation. When the foot points of the loop are randomly and continuously forced, MHD waves are excited and propagate upward. This leads to the natural production of a 1-MK temperature corona as the wave energy dissipates. The excited wave packets become nonlinear just above the magnetic canopy, and the wave energy cascades into smaller spatial scales. Furthermore, collisions between counter-propagating Alfvén wave packets increase the heating rate, resulting in impulsive temperature increases. The model demonstrates that the heating events in the wave-heated loops can be nanoflare-like, being spatially localized and temporally intermittent.

title: Studying Pulsed Laser Deposition conditions for Ni/C-based multi-layers
Abstract: Nickel carbon-based multilayers offer a promising path towards future hard X-ray and soft γ-ray focusing telescopes. This study investigates the Pulsed Laser Deposition growth conditions of such bilayers using Reflective High Energy Electron Diffraction, X-ray Reflectivity and Diffraction, Atomic Force Microscopy, X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy, and cross-sectional Transmission Electron Microscopy analysis, focusing on optimizing process pressure and substrate temperature during growth. The thin multilayers are grown on a treated SiO substrate, resulting in Ni and C layers with surface roughnesses (RMS) of ≤ 0.2 nm. Small droplets formed during target surface melting increase roughness and cannot be avoided. Sequential processing at temperatures exceeding 300°C leads to intermixing between the two layers, which negatively impacts the reflectivity of the multilayer.

title: EstimatedWold Representation and Spectral Density-Driven Bootstrap for Time Series
Abstract: The second-order dependence structure of purely nondeterministic stationary processes is characterized by the coefficients of the well-known Wold representation. These coefficients can be obtained by factoring the spectral density of the process. This relationship, along with a spectral density estimator, is used to derive consistent estimators of these coefficients. A spectral density-driven bootstrap for time series is then developed, utilizing the entire sequence of estimated MA coefficients together with appropriately generated pseudo innovations to obtain a bootstrap pseudo time series. It is shown that if the underlying process is linear and the pseudo innovations are generated using an i.i.d. wild bootstrap mimicking the moment structure of the true innovations to the necessary extent, this bootstrap proposal asymptotically works for a wide range of statistics. The relationships of the proposed bootstrap procedure to other bootstrap procedures, including the autoregressive-sieve bootstrap, are discussed. It is shown that the latter is a special case of the spectral density-driven bootstrap when a parametric autoregressive spectral density estimator is used. Simulations investigate the performance of the new bootstrap procedure in finite sample situations. Furthermore, a real-life data example is presented.

title: Improvement of Resting-state EEG Analysis Process with Spectrum Weight-Voting based on LES
Abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a non-invasive technique for recording brain bioelectric activity, holding potential applications in fields like human-computer interaction and neuroscience. However, analyzing EEG data presents numerous challenges, including its complex composition, low amplitude, and low signal-to-noise ratio. Existing analysis methods often rely on feature extraction and machine learning to differentiate schizophrenia phases. However, medical research demands machine learning methods not only to provide accurate classification results but also to generate results applicable to pathological studies. This study aims to obtain weight values representing the influence of each frequency band on schizophrenia phase classification using the LES feature extraction method, a more effective classification technique. These weight values are then processed and applied to improve the accuracy of machine learning classification. A method called weight-voting is proposed to obtain the weights of sub-band features by using classification results for voting to match the actual categories of EEG data and using these weights for reclassification. This method enables the determination of each band's influence in distinguishing three schizophrenia phases and analysis of the effect of band features on schizophrenia risk, contributing to psychopathology research. Results demonstrate a high correlation between the change in weight of the low gamma band and the difference between HC, CHR, and FES. Reclassifying using features adjusted according to these weights improves the accuracy compared to the original classifier, confirming the role of the band weight distribution.

title: Photocurrent Generation in a Metallic Transition Metal Dichalcogenide
Abstract: Light-induced current in two-dimensional (2D) layered materials arises from mechanisms such as the photothermoelectric effect, photovoltaic effect, or nonlocal hot carrier transport. Semiconducting layered transition metal dichalcogenides have been extensively studied due to the crucial role of light-induced current generation in optoelectronic and photovoltaic devices. However, photocurrent generation is unexpected in metallic 2D layered materials unless a photothermal mechanism is dominant. Typically, high thermal conductivity and low absorption of the visible spectrum hinder photothermal current generation in metals. This study reports photoresponse from two-terminal devices of mechanically exfoliated metallic 3R-NbS2 thin crystals using scanning photocurrent microscopy (SPCM) at both zero and finite bias. SPCM measurements reveal that the photocurrent primarily emerges from metal/NbS2 junctions of the two-terminal device at zero bias. At finite biases, along with the photocurrent generated at metal/NbS2 junctions, a negative photoresponse from the entire NbS2 crystal is observed. The results indicate that the observed photocurrent can be attributed to local heating caused by laser excitation. These findings highlight NbS2 as one of the few metallic materials where photocurrent generation is possible.
