title: Android Malware Characterization using Metadata and Machine Learning Techniques
Abstract: The increasing popularity of smartphones and tablets has led to the rise of Android malware. While previous work focused on inherent characteristics of Android apps for malware detection, this study analyzes indirect features and meta-data to identify patterns in malicious applications. Experiments show that: (1) app permissions offer moderate performance results, (2) publicly available features from Android Markets, such as developer and certificate issuer, are more relevant for malware detection, and (3) compact and efficient classifiers can be constructed for early malware detection before code inspection or sandboxing.
label: AI

title: Hawkes Processes for Invasive Species Modeling and Management
Abstract: The spread of invasive species to new areas threatens ecosystem stability and causes significant economic losses in agriculture and forestry. This research proposes a novel approach to minimizing the spread of invasive species with limited intervention budgets. The study models invasive species propagation using Hawkes processes, deriving closed-form expressions for quantifying the impact of intervention actions on the invasion process. This enables the development of an optimal intervention plan based on integer programming, which is compared against several ecologically-motivated heuristics. Empirical studies on two variants of the invasive control problem, minimizing the final invasion rate and minimizing the number of invasions within a given time horizon, demonstrate that the optimized intervention achieves nearly the same level of control as complete eradication, with a 20% cost saving. Additionally, a heuristic intervention strategy based on invasive individual density and life stage is proposed, surprisingly closely resembling the optimized strategy and potentially serving as a practical rule of thumb in invasive species management.
label: AI

title: Simulated Autonomous Driving on Realistic Road Networks using Deep Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) offers a promising approach for various tasks in (simulated) autonomous driving. However, current research primarily focuses on learning in unusual driving environments. This paper presents Driving School for Autonomous Agents (DSA^2), a software for validating DRL algorithms in more usual driving environments based on artificial and realistic road networks. The paper also presents results of using DSA^2 to handle the task of driving on a straight road while regulating vehicle velocity according to different speed limits.
label: AI

title: Automated Cinematography with Unmanned Aerial Vehicles
Abstract: The growing use of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) in the film industry necessitates dedicated tools. While various techniques exist for automated drone control, none have addressed the real-time production of cinematographic camera motion for shooting purposes. This paper presents an approach to UAV navigation for autonomous cinematography, with two main contributions: (i) adapting virtual camera control techniques to UAV navigation, and (ii) introducing a drone-independent platform for high-level user interactions integrating cinematographic knowledge. Results demonstrate the tool's capabilities in capturing live movie scenes with one or two moving actors.
label: AI

title: Deep Echo State Network (DeepESN): A Brief Survey
Abstract: Research on deep recurrent neural networks (RNNs), particularly deep Reservoir Computing (RC), is gaining significant attention within the neural networks community. The recently introduced Deep Echo State Network (DeepESN) model has enabled a highly efficient approach for designing deep neural networks for temporal data. Studying DeepESNs has shed light on the intrinsic properties of state dynamics developed by hierarchical compositions of recurrent layers, providing insights into the role of depth in RNN architecture design. This paper summarizes advancements in the development, analysis, and applications of DeepESNs.
label: AI

title: Generating and Estimating Nonverbal Alphabets for Situated and Multimodal Communications
Abstract: This paper discusses a formalized approach for generating and estimating symbols (and alphabets) that can be communicated through various non-verbal means, tailored to specific user requirements (medium, priorities, type of information). It provides a concise characterization of basic terms and parameters of such symbols, outlining approaches for their generation. The paper then presents a framework, experimental setup, and machine learning methods for estimating the usefulness and effectiveness of non-verbal alphabets and systems. Previous results show that multimodal data sources (wearable accelerometers, heart monitors, muscle movement sensors, brain-computer interface) combined with machine learning approaches offer a deeper understanding of the usefulness and effectiveness of such alphabets for nonverbal and situated communication. The generated and estimated symbols may prove useful in various applications, ranging from synthetic languages and constructed scripts to multimodal nonverbal and situated interactions between humans and artificial intelligence systems via Human-Computer Interfaces (mouse gestures, touchpads, body gestures, eye tracking cameras, wearables, brain-computing interfaces), especially in areas like elderly care and assistive technologies for individuals with disabilities.
label: AI

title: A Generic Model for Swarm Intelligence and Its Validations
Abstract: Modeling emergent swarm intelligence poses a significant challenge, with existing approaches failing to accurately capture its nature. Existing models are either too abstract for practical application or lack the generality to describe diverse emergence phenomena. This paper introduces a contradiction-centric model for swarm intelligence, where individuals determine their behaviors based on internal contradictions, associating and interacting to update these contradictions. The model hypothesizes that: (1) the emergence of swarm intelligence is rooted in the development of individuals' internal contradictions and their interactions with the environment, and (2) swarm intelligence is a combined reflection of individual contradiction configurations and their distributions across individuals. The model is formally described and applied to five swarm intelligence systems, demonstrating its broad applicability and effectiveness in describing the emergence of various kinds of swarm intelligence. The studies highlight the model's simplicity in application, requiring no complex computations.
label: AI

title: A Low-Cost Ethics Shaping Approach for Designing Reinforcement Learning Agents
Abstract: This paper proposes a low-cost, easily implementable strategy for equipping reinforcement learning (RL) agents with ethical behavior. The model allows RL agent designers to focus solely on achieving the desired task without needing to implement multiple trivial ethical patterns. Assuming that human behavior, regardless of the goals pursued, is predominantly ethical, the design integrates human policy with the RL policy to achieve the target objective with reduced chances of violating ethical codes typically followed by humans.
label: AI

title: Interpretable Policies for Reinforcement Learning by Genetic Programming
Abstract: The search for interpretable reinforcement learning policies is of significant academic and industrial interest. Industrial systems, in particular, are more likely to adopt autonomously learned controllers if they are understandable and easy to evaluate. Basic algebraic equations meet these requirements as long as their complexity is adequately constrained. This paper introduces Genetic Programming for Reinforcement Learning (GPRL), an approach based on model-based batch reinforcement learning and genetic programming, which autonomously learns policy equations from existing state-action trajectory samples. GPRL is compared to a straightforward symbolic regression method that generates policies mimicking an existing high-performing but non-interpretable policy. Experiments on three reinforcement learning benchmarks (mountain car, cart-pole balancing, and an industrial benchmark) demonstrate the superiority of GPRL over the symbolic regression method. GPRL successfully produces high-performing interpretable reinforcement learning policies from existing default trajectory data.
label: AI

title: Mining Non-Redundant Local Process Models From Sequence Databases
Abstract: Sequential pattern mining techniques extract patterns corresponding to frequent subsequences from a sequence database. A practical limitation of these techniques is the overwhelming number of patterns generated. Local Process Model (LPM) mining, an alternative approach from process mining, addresses this issue. Unlike traditional sequential pattern mining, where a pattern describes a single subsequence, an LPM captures a set of subsequences. Additionally, while traditional sequential patterns match subsequences observed in the database, LPMs can capture unobserved subsequences related to observed ones, generalizing the behavior observed in the database. This property allows a set of LPMs to cover a much larger set of sequential patterns. However, existing LPM mining techniques still suffer from pattern explosion due to redundant LPMs. This paper proposes heuristics to mine a set of non-redundant LPMs from either a set of redundant LPMs or a set of sequential patterns. Empirical comparisons between the proposed heuristics and existing (local) process mining techniques evaluate coverage, redundancy, and complexity of the resulting LPM sets.
label: AI

title: Toward `verifying' a Water Treatment System
Abstract: Modeling and verifying real-world cyber-physical systems is challenging, especially for complex systems where manual modeling is infeasible. This work combines model learning and abstraction refinement to analyze a complex Secure Water Treatment system (SWaT). Given safety requirements, the objective is to determine whether the system is safe with high probability (minimizing system shutdowns due to safety violations). Due to the system's complexity, the research applies automatic model learning techniques to construct a set of Markov chains through abstraction and refinement, utilizing two long system execution logs (one for training, one for testing). For each probabilistic safety property, the study either reports that it does not hold with a certain probabilistic confidence or demonstrates its validity by presenting evidence in the form of an abstract Markov chain. These Markov chains can subsequently be implemented as runtime monitors in SWaT.
label: AI

title: Benchmarking Single Image Dehazing and Beyond
Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive study and evaluation of single image dehazing algorithms using a new large-scale benchmark called REalistic Single Image DEhazing (RESIDE), comprising both synthetic and real-world hazy images. RESIDE encompasses diverse data sources and image contents, divided into five subsets serving different training or evaluation purposes. The paper proposes a rich variety of criteria for evaluating dehazing algorithms, including full-reference metrics, no-reference metrics, subjective evaluation, and a novel task-driven evaluation. Experiments on RESIDE provide insights into the comparisons and limitations of state-of-the-art dehazing algorithms, suggesting promising future directions.
label: AI

title: Time Matters: Multi-scale Temporalization of Social Media Popularity
Abstract: Social media popularity evolution exhibits rich temporality, with popularity changes occurring over time at various levels of temporal granularity. This is influenced by temporal variations in public attention or user activities. For example, Flickr's street snap popularity patterns reflect distinct fashion styles at specific time scales, such as season-based periodic fluctuations for Trench Coats or one-off peaks for Evening Dresses. However, existing popularity modeling research often overlooks this fact. This paper presents the first study incorporating multiple time-scale dynamics into online popularity prediction. The authors propose a novel computational framework called Multi-scale Temporalization, which estimates popularity based on multi-scale decomposition and structural reconstruction in a tensor space of user, post, and time using joint low-rank constraints. Addressing context inconsistency noise, the paper designs a data rearrangement step based on context aggregation as preprocessing to enhance contextual relevance in the tensor space. This approach leverages multiple levels of temporal characteristics while reducing noise in data decomposition for improved modeling effectiveness. Evaluation on two large-scale Flickr image datasets (over 1.8 million photos) for popularity prediction demonstrates significant outperformance compared to existing techniques, achieving a relative improvement of 10.9%-47.5% in prediction accuracy.
label: AI

title: Sequential Prediction of Social Media Popularity with Deep Temporal Context Networks
Abstract: Predicting popularity has profound implications for social media, offering opportunities to uncover individual preferences and public attention from evolving social systems. While existing research yields promising results, it overlooks a distinctive characteristic of social data: sequentiality. The popularity of online content is generated over time through sequential post streams on social media. To investigate the sequential prediction of popularity, this paper proposes a novel framework called Deep Temporal Context Networks (DTCN) that incorporates both temporal context and temporal attention. DTCN comprises three main components: embedding, learning, and predicting. A joint embedding network generates a unified deep representation of multimodal user-post data in a common embedding space. Based on the embedded data sequence over time, temporal context learning recurrently learns two adaptive temporal contexts for sequential popularity. Finally, a novel temporal attention mechanism predicts new popularity (for new user-post pairs) with temporal coherence across multiple time scales. Experiments on a released image dataset (approximately 600K Flickr photos) demonstrate that DTCN outperforms state-of-the-art deep prediction algorithms, achieving an average of 21.51% relative performance improvement in popularity prediction (Spearman Ranking Correlation).
label: AI

title: Deep Learning for Reliable Mobile Edge Analytics in Intelligent Transportation Systems
Abstract: Intelligent transportation systems (ITSs) will play a crucial role in tomorrow's smart cities. However, realizing ITS's full potential necessitates ultra-low latency and reliable data analytics solutions capable of combining heterogeneous data streams in real-time from the ITS network and its environment. Conventional cloud-centric data processing techniques cannot provide these capabilities due to high communication and computing latency. Instead, edge-centric solutions tailored to the unique ITS environment must be developed. This paper introduces an edge analytics architecture for ITSs where data is processed at the vehicle or roadside smart sensor level, addressing ITS latency and reliability challenges. Leveraging the enhanced capabilities of passenger mobile devices and intra-vehicle processors, this distributed edge computing architecture utilizes deep learning techniques for reliable mobile sensing in ITSs. The research investigates ITS mobile edge analytics challenges related to heterogeneous data, autonomous control, vehicular platoon control, and cyber-physical security, proposing deep learning solutions for these challenges. These solutions empower ITS edge analytics by equipping ITS devices with powerful computer vision and signal processing functions. Preliminary results indicate that the proposed edge analytics architecture, coupled with deep learning algorithms, can provide a reliable, secure, and truly smart transportation environment.
label: AI

title: In a Nutshell -- The Sequential Parameter Optimization Toolbox
Abstract: The performance of optimization algorithms heavily depends on their parameterization. Finding optimal parameter settings is known as algorithm tuning. The sequential parameter optimization (SPOT) package for R is a toolbox for tuning and understanding simulation and optimization algorithms. Model-based investigations are common approaches in simulation and optimization. Sequential parameter optimization has been developed to address the need for sound statistical analysis of simulation and optimization algorithms. SPOT incorporates methods for tuning based on classical regression and analysis of variance techniques; tree-based models like CART and random forest; Gaussian process models (Kriging); and combinations of different meta-modeling approaches. The paper demonstrates how optimization algorithms can be tuned using SPOT with a simple simulated annealing algorithm. It explains key concepts of the SPOT approach, including exploratory fitness landscape analysis and sensitivity analysis. Numerous examples showcase SPOT's application in understanding algorithm performance and gaining insight into their behavior. The paper further demonstrates how SPOT can function as an optimizer, highlighting the effectiveness of a sophisticated ensemble approach combining several meta-models via stacking. This article exemplifies how SPOT can be used for both automatic and interactive tuning. |||
label: AI

title: The Eigenoption-Critic Framework
Abstract: Eigenoptions (EOs), a promising method for generating diverse options through the graph Laplacian, have shown potential for efficient exploration in reinforcement learning. However, current algorithms face limitations, including the need for separate eigenoption discovery and reward maximization steps, restricted application to discrete state-spaces, and difficulty in integrating the environment's reward function during EO discovery. To address these issues, we introduce the eigenoption-critic (EOC) algorithm, based on the Option-critic (OC) framework. EOC enables simultaneous learning of intra-option policies and the policy over options, reducing computational and storage demands. We extend EOC to continuous state-spaces using the Nyström approximation, making it applicable to a broader range of problems. EOC can also be viewed as an extension of OC to nonstationary settings, where discovered options are not task-specific.
label: AI

title: Learning Robust Dialog Policies in Noisy Environments
Abstract: Modern virtual assistants offer a convenient interface for completing daily tasks through voice commands. However, these assistants face challenges in recovering from errors in automatic speech recognition (ASR) and natural language understanding (NLU). This paper focuses on learning robust dialog policies to mitigate these errors. We develop a user simulator that interacts with the assistant using voice commands in realistic scenarios, including noisy audio. This simulator is used to learn dialog policies through deep reinforcement learning. Human evaluators confirm that dialogs generated by our simulator are indistinguishable from human-generated ones. Preliminary results demonstrate that learned policies in noisy environments achieve the same execution success rate with fewer dialog turns compared to traditional rule-based policies.
label: AI

title: Detecting Qualia in Natural and Artificial Agents
Abstract: The Hard Problem of consciousness has been dismissed as an illusion. This paper challenges this notion by demonstrating that computers are capable of experiencing, suggesting rudimentary consciousness with potential for superconsciousness. The paper introduces a test for confirming subjective experiences in an agent. It then analyzes the benefits and challenges of conscious machines and discusses the implications of such capabilities on the future of computing, machine rights, and artificial intelligence safety.
label: AI

title: Investigating the Impact of Data Volume and Domain Similarity on Transfer Learning Applications
Abstract: Transfer learning enables the application of knowledge acquired from previous tasks (source task) to new tasks or domains (target task) that share commonalities. The performance of transfer learning models is significantly influenced by two key factors: the size of the target dataset and the similarity in distribution between source and target domains. This paper investigates the impact of these factors through a series of experiments. The findings indicate that more data is always advantageous, with model performance improving linearly with the log of data size until data saturation. As source/target domain differences increase, larger datasets are required, and fine-tuning outperforms feature extraction. When source/target domains are similar and data size is small, fine-tuning and feature extraction yield equivalent performance. This quantitative investigation aims to inspire further exploration of the significance of data in developing more accurate statistical models.
label: AI

title: MINOS: Multimodal Indoor Simulator for Navigation in Complex Environments
Abstract: This paper presents MINOS, a simulator designed to support the development of multisensory models for goal-directed navigation in complex indoor environments. Leveraging large datasets of intricate 3D environments, MINOS facilitates flexible configuration of multimodal sensor suites. We utilize MINOS to benchmark deep-learning-based navigation methods, analyze the influence of environmental complexity on navigation performance, and conduct a controlled study of multimodality in sensorimotor learning. The experiments reveal that current deep reinforcement learning approaches struggle in large, realistic environments. Additionally, the experiments highlight the benefits of multimodality in learning to navigate cluttered scenes. MINOS is open-sourced to the research community at http://minosworld.org. A video showcasing MINOS can be accessed at https://youtu.be/c0mL9K64q84.
label: AI

title: MURA: Large Dataset for Abnormality Detection in Musculoskeletal Radiographs
Abstract: MURA is a large dataset of musculoskeletal radiographs, comprising 40,561 images from 14,863 studies, where each study is manually labeled by radiologists as either normal or abnormal. To rigorously evaluate models and estimate radiologist performance, we gathered additional labels from six board-certified Stanford radiologists on a test set of 207 musculoskeletal studies. The majority vote of three radiologists serves as the gold standard for this test set. We trained a 169-layer DenseNet baseline model for abnormality detection and localization. Our model achieves an AUROC of 0.929, with an operating point of 0.815 sensitivity and 0.887 specificity. Comparing our model and radiologists using Cohen's kappa statistic, which measures agreement with the gold standard, reveals comparable performance to the best radiologist on finger and wrist studies. However, the model's performance falls short of the best radiologist in detecting abnormalities on elbow, forearm, hand, humerus, and shoulder studies. We believe this task presents a significant challenge for future research. To encourage advancements, we have made our dataset freely available at https://stanfordmlgroup.github.io/competitions/mura.
label: AI

title: DeepConfig: Automating Data Center Network Topologies Management with Machine Learning
Abstract: Significant advancements have been made in data center networks in recent years, resulting in improved performance and efficiency. However, these techniques often rely on heuristics that exploit domain-specific properties of workloads or hardware. This paper argues that many data center networking techniques, including routing, topology augmentation, and energy savings, despite diverse goals, share design and architectural similarities. We propose a deep learning-based approach for developing general intermediate representations of network topologies, enabling the solution of various data center problems. We introduce DeepConfig, a framework that simplifies the processing of configuring and training deep learning agents using the intermediate representation to learn different tasks. To illustrate the strength of our approach, we configure, implement, and evaluate a DeepConfig-Agent for the data center topology augmentation problem. Initial results are promising, demonstrating comparable performance to the optimal solution.
label: AI

title: NestedNet: Learning Nested Sparse Structures in Deep Neural Networks
Abstract: The need for compact deep architectures to eliminate unnecessary redundancy and enhance inference speed has gained momentum. While many recent works focus on reducing redundancy by eliminating unnecessary weight parameters, a single deep architecture cannot be applied to multiple devices with varying resources. When new devices or conditions necessitate a new deep architecture, it is necessary to construct and train a new network from scratch. This work introduces a novel deep learning framework called a nested sparse network, which utilizes an n-in-1-type nested structure in a neural network. A nested sparse network comprises multiple levels of networks with different sparsity ratios associated with each level. Higher level networks share parameters with lower level networks, enabling stable nested learning. This framework realizes a resource-aware versatile architecture, enabling the same network to meet diverse resource requirements. Furthermore, the nested network can learn different forms of knowledge at different levels, enabling multiple tasks using a single network, such as coarse-to-fine hierarchical classification. We propose efficient weight connection learning, channel and layer scheduling strategies for training the nested sparse network. Evaluation on various tasks, including adaptive deep compression, knowledge distillation, and learning class hierarchy, demonstrates that nested sparse networks perform competitively but more efficiently compared to existing methods.
label: AI

title: Cogniculture: Towards a Better Human-Machine Co-evolution
Abstract: Artificial Intelligence research is constantly pushing technological boundaries, with new algorithms and high-performance computing enabling previously unimaginable possibilities. While AI advancements are making life easier for humans, concerns remain about the potential threat AI-based systems pose to humanity. The AI community holds diverse opinions regarding the pros and cons of AI mimicking human behavior. Instead of dwelling on these concerns, we propose a novel concept of cognitive agents, encompassing both humans and machines, coexisting in a complex adaptive ecosystem. This ecosystem fosters collaboration on human computation, producing essential social goods and promoting the sustenance, survival, and evolution of the agents' life cycle. We highlight research challenges and technological barriers to achieving this goal and propose a governance mechanism to ensure ethical behavior among all cognitive agents. Alongside novel use-cases of Cogniculture, we discuss the roadmap for this journey.
label: AI

title: A novel model-based heuristic for energy optimal motion planning for automated driving
Abstract: Predictive motion planning is crucial for achieving energy-efficient driving, a key benefit of automated driving. Researchers have been studying velocity trajectory planning, a simplified form of motion planning, for over a decade, resulting in numerous methods. Dynamic programming has emerged as the most popular choice due to its numerical foundation and ability to incorporate nonlinear constraints and models. However, while it systematically plans an optimal trajectory, dynamic programming does not leverage problem-specific knowledge to guide exploration, leading to the exploration of all possible trajectories. A* is a search algorithm that enables using knowledge about the problem to prioritize exploration towards the most promising solutions. This knowledge must be represented as a heuristic function, which provides an optimistic cost estimate for transitioning to the final state, a non-trivial task. This paper presents a novel heuristic function incorporating air drag, auxiliary power, and operational costs of the vehicle, in addition to kinetic and potential energy and rolling resistance known in the literature. We also derive the optimal cruising velocity, dependent on vehicle aerodynamic properties and auxiliary power. Results are compared for different heuristic function variants and dynamic programming.
label: AI

title: Robust Deep Reinforcement Learning with Adversarial Attacks
Abstract: This paper investigates adversarial attacks against Reinforcement Learning (RL) and explores methods to enhance the robustness of Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) algorithms to parameter uncertainties. We demonstrate that even a naively engineered attack successfully degrades the performance of DRL algorithms. We further improve the attack using gradient information from an engineered loss function, resulting in further performance degradation. These attacks are then utilized during training to improve the robustness of RL within a robust control framework. We show that adversarial training of DRL algorithms like Deep Double Q learning and Deep Deterministic Policy Gradients leads to significant increases in robustness to parameter variations for RL benchmarks such as Cart-pole, Mountain Car, Hopper, and Half Cheetah environments.
label: AI

title: Tuning the Molecular Weight Distribution from Atom Transfer Radical Polymerization Using Deep Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel technique for controlling the shape of polymer molecular weight distributions (MWDs) in atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP). This technique leverages recent advancements in simulation-based, model-free reinforcement learning (RL) and the numerical simulation of ATRP. We build an ATRP simulation that allows an RL controller to add chemical reagents throughout the reaction. The RL controller incorporates fully-connected and convolutional neural network architectures and bases its decisions on the current state of the ATRP reaction. The initial, untrained controller results in ending MWDs with significant variability, allowing the RL algorithm to explore a vast search space. When trained using an actor-critic algorithm, the RL controller successfully discovers and optimizes control policies that achieve various target MWDs, including Gaussians of different widths and more diverse shapes like bimodal distributions. The learned control policies are robust and transferable to similar but not identical ATRP reaction settings, even in the presence of simulated noise. This work provides a proof-of-concept for employing modern artificial intelligence techniques in the synthesis of new functional polymer materials.
label: AI

title: Towards Fully Environment-Aware UAVs: Real-Time Path Planning with Online 3D Wind Field Prediction in Complex Terrain
Abstract: Currently, low-altitude fixed-wing Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are primarily limited to primitively following user-defined waypoints. To enable fully autonomous remote missions in complex environments, real-time environment-aware navigation is required, considering both terrain and strong wind drafts. This paper presents two initial contributions towards this goal. First, we introduce the first-ever 3D wind field prediction method capable of running in real-time onboard a UAV. The approach retrieves low-resolution global weather data and utilizes potential flow theory to adjust the wind field, accounting for terrain boundaries, mass conservation, and atmospheric stratification. Comparison with 1D LIDAR data demonstrates an overall wind error reduction of 23% compared to the commonly used zero-wind assumption in UAV path planning. However, further research is needed to improve the accuracy of vertical wind resolution. Second, we present a sampling-based path planner that iteratively considers aircraft dynamics in non-uniform wind using Dubins airplane paths. Performance optimizations, including obstacle-aware sampling and fast 2.5D-map collision checks, make the planner 50% faster than the Open Motion Planning Library (OMPL) implementation. Test cases in Alpine terrain reveal that wind-aware planning performs up to 50x fewer iterations than shortest-path planning, making it slower in low winds. However, it consistently delivers lower-cost paths in stronger winds. More importantly, unlike the shortest-path planner, it always produces collision-free paths. Our initial research demonstrates the feasibility of 3D wind field prediction from a UAV and the advantages of wind-aware planning. This lays the foundation for future research on fully autonomous environment-aware navigation of UAVs in real-life missions and complex terrain.
label: AI

title: Study of Peer-to-Peer Network Based Cybercrime Investigation: Application on Botnet Technologies
Abstract: The scalable, low overhead attributes of Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Internet protocols and networks make them susceptible to exploitation by criminals for a wide range of cybercrimes, including copyright infringement, sharing of illicit images of children, fraud, hacking/cracking, denial of service attacks, and virus/malware propagation through worms, botnets, malware, viruses, and P2P file sharing. This project focuses on studying active P2P nodes and analyzing the undocumented communication methods employed in these large unstructured networks. We achieve this through the design and implementation of an efficient P2P monitoring and crawling toolset. Investigating P2P-based systems extends beyond obvious cybercrimes, as legitimate P2P applications, such as voice over IP and instant messaging, may also be relevant to digital forensic investigations. The increasing diversity of network topologies and the evolving range of P2P applications have made investigating these networks challenging. This work introduces the Universal P2P Network Investigation Framework (UP2PNIF), which significantly accelerates and simplifies investigations of newly discovered P2P networks by leveraging commonalities in P2P network functionality. In conjunction with a reference database of known network characteristics, UP2PNIF aims to enable instant investigation of any known P2P network by intelligently determining the optimal investigation methodology and expediting the evidence gathering process. A proof-of-concept tool was developed for conducting investigations on the BitTorrent network.
label: AI

title: NAG: Network for Adversary Generation
Abstract: Adversarial perturbations pose a significant threat to the deployment of machine learning systems. Recent works have demonstrated the existence of image-agnostic perturbations that can deceive classifiers across most natural images. Existing methods employ optimization approaches to craft perturbations by solving a fooling objective with an imperceptibility constraint. However, these methods generate one perturbation at a time, representing a single instance from the manifold of adversarial perturbations. To build robust models, exploring the manifold of adversarial perturbations is crucial. This paper proposes, for the first time, a generative approach to model the distribution of adversarial perturbations. The proposed model's architecture is inspired by Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and is trained using fooling and diversity objectives. The trained generator network aims to capture the distribution of adversarial perturbations for a given classifier and readily generate a wide range of such perturbations. Experimental evaluation shows that perturbations crafted by our model achieve state-of-the-art fooling rates, exhibit wide variety, and deliver excellent cross-model generalizability. This work represents a significant step towards inferring the complex manifolds of adversarial perturbations.
label: AI

title: Deep Learning for IoT Big Data and Streaming Analytics: A Survey
Abstract: In the era of the Internet of Things (IoT), a vast number of sensing devices collect or generate diverse sensory data over time for various fields and applications. Depending on the application's nature, these devices generate big data or fast/real-time data streams. Applying analytics over such data streams to discover new information, predict future insights, and make control decisions is a crucial process that makes IoT a valuable paradigm for businesses and a quality-of-life enhancing technology. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of using Deep Learning (DL), a class of advanced machine learning techniques, to facilitate analytics and learning in the IoT domain. We begin by outlining IoT data characteristics and identifying two primary treatments for IoT data from a machine learning perspective: IoT big data analytics and IoT streaming data analytics. We discuss why DL is a promising approach for achieving the desired analytics in these data types and applications. The potential of emerging DL techniques for IoT data analytics is explored, highlighting its promises and challenges. A comprehensive background on different DL architectures and algorithms is presented. We analyze and summarize major reported research attempts that leveraged DL in the IoT domain. Smart IoT devices that have incorporated DL into their intelligence background are discussed. DL implementation approaches on fog and cloud centers supporting IoT applications are surveyed. Finally, we shed light on challenges and potential directions for future research. Lessons learned based on our experiments and review of recent literature are highlighted at the end of each section.
label: AI

title: Assumed Density Filtering Q-learning
Abstract: While off-policy temporal difference (TD) methods have gained widespread use in reinforcement learning due to their efficiency and simple implementation, their Bayesian counterparts have seen less frequent utilization. One reason for this is the non-linear max operation in the Bellman optimality equation, which makes it difficult to define conjugate distributions over value functions. This paper introduces a novel Bayesian approach to off-policy TD methods, called ADFQ, which updates beliefs on state-action values, Q, through an online Bayesian inference method known as Assumed Density Filtering. We formulate an efficient closed-form solution for the value update by approximately estimating the analytic parameters of the posterior of the Q-beliefs. Uncertainty measures in the beliefs not only are used in exploration but also provide a natural regularization for the value update, considering all available actions. ADFQ converges to Q-learning as the uncertainty measures of the Q-beliefs decrease and addresses common drawbacks of other Bayesian RL algorithms, such as computational complexity. We extend ADFQ with a neural network. Our empirical results demonstrate that ADFQ outperforms comparable algorithms on various Atari 2600 games, achieving significant improvements in highly stochastic domains or domains with a large action space.
label: AI

title: Nintendo Super Smash Bros. Melee: An "Untouchable" Agent
Abstract: Nintendo's Super Smash Bros. Melee fighting game can be emulated on modern hardware, allowing us to inspect internal memory states, such as character positions. We developed an AI that avoids being hit by training using these internal memory states and outputting controller button presses. After training on a month's worth of Melee matches, our best agent learned to avoid the toughest AI built into the game for a full minute 74.6% of the time.
label: AI

title: AI Safety and Reproducibility: Establishing Robust Foundations for the Neuropsychology of Human Values
Abstract: This paper proposes a systematic effort to identify and replicate key findings in neuropsychology and related fields that contribute to understanding human values. Our aim is to ensure that research underpinning the value alignment problem in artificial intelligence is sufficiently validated to inform the design of AI systems.
label: AI

title: Social Emotion Mining Techniques for Facebook Posts Reaction Prediction
Abstract: As of February 2016, Facebook allows users to express their experienced emotions about a post using five reactions. This research paper proposes and evaluates alternative methods for predicting these reactions to user posts on public pages of firms/companies (like supermarket chains). We collected posts (and their reactions) from Facebook pages of large supermarket chains, constructing a dataset available for other research. To predict the distribution of reactions for a new post, neural network architectures (convolutional and recurrent neural networks) were tested using pretrained word embeddings. The performance of these neural networks was further improved by introducing a bootstrapping approach for sentiment and emotion mining on the comments associated with each post. The final model, combining the neural network and a baseline emotion miner, effectively predicts the reaction distribution on Facebook posts, achieving a mean squared error (or misclassification rate) of 0.135. |||

title: Building competitive direct acoustics-to-word models for English conversational speech recognition
Abstract: Direct acoustics-to-word (A2W) models in the end-to-end paradigm have gained significant traction compared to conventional sub-word based automatic speech recognition models that rely on phones, characters, or context-dependent hidden Markov model states. This shift in focus is attributed to the simplicity of A2W models, which directly recognize words from speech without requiring decoders, pronunciation lexicons, or externally-trained language models. Prior research has indicated that A2W models necessitate considerably more training data to achieve performance comparable to traditional models. Our previous work corroborated this accuracy gap when utilizing the English Switchboard-Fisher dataset. This paper presents a recipe for training an A2W model that bridges this gap and reaches parity with state-of-the-art sub-word based models. We achieve a word error rate of 8.8%/13.9% on the Hub5-2000 Switchboard/CallHome test sets, without employing any decoder or language model. Our investigation reveals that model initialization, training data order, and regularization have the most significant impact on the A2W model's performance. Subsequently, we introduce a joint word-character A2W model that initially spells the word and then recognizes it. This model provides a richer output to the user, instead of merely presenting simple word hypotheses, making it particularly valuable when encountering words unseen or rarely encountered during training.

title: A Class of Logistic Functions for Approximating State-Inclusive Koopman Operators
Abstract: A fundamental challenge in nonlinear systems theory is the identification or learning of a given nonlinear system's Koopman operator directly from data or models. Advances in extended dynamic mode decomposition approaches and machine learning techniques have enabled data-driven discovery of Koopman operators, for both continuous and discrete-time systems. Given that Koopman operators are often infinite-dimensional, they are approximated in practice using finite-dimensional systems. The fidelity and convergence of a given finite-dimensional Koopman approximation is a subject of ongoing research. This paper introduces a class of Koopman observable functions that confer an approximate closure property on their corresponding finite-dimensional approximations of the Koopman operator. We derive error bounds for the fidelity of this class of observable functions, as well as identify two key learning parameters that can be used to tune performance. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated on two classical nonlinear system models: the Van Der Pol oscillator and the bistable toggle switch.

title: A Heuristic Search Algorithm Using the Stability of Learning Algorithms in Certain Scenarios as the Fitness Function: An Artificial General Intelligence Engineering Approach
Abstract: This paper introduces a non-manual design engineering method based on heuristic search algorithms to identify candidate agents in the solution space, which is formed by artificial intelligence agents modeled on the principles of bionics. Compared to the artificial design method represented by meta-learning and the bionics method represented by neural architecture chips, this method is more feasible for realizing artificial general intelligence and exhibits a more robust interaction with cognitive neuroscience. Simultaneously, the engineering method is underpinned by the theoretical hypothesis that the final learning algorithm is stable in certain scenarios and possesses generalization ability in various scenarios. The paper preliminarily discusses this theory and proposes a potential correlation between the theory and the fixed-point theorem in mathematics. Given the author's current knowledge limitations, this correlation is presented as a conjecture.

title: Coordinate Descent with Bandit Sampling
Abstract: Coordinate descent methods typically minimize a cost function by updating a randomly selected decision variable (corresponding to one coordinate) at a time. Ideally, we would update the decision variable that yields the largest decrease in the cost function. However, finding this coordinate would necessitate checking all of them, effectively negating the improvement in computational tractability that coordinate descent aims to achieve. To address this issue, we propose a new adaptive method for coordinate selection. First, we determine a lower bound on the amount the cost function decreases when a coordinate is updated. We then employ a multi-armed bandit algorithm to learn which coordinates result in the largest lower bound by interleaving this learning with conventional coordinate descent updates, except that the coordinate is selected proportionally to the expected decrease. We demonstrate both theoretically and experimentally that our approach enhances the convergence of coordinate descent methods.

title: Collaborative Company Profiling: Insights from an Employee's Perspective
Abstract: Company profiling is an analytical process that aims to develop a comprehensive understanding of a company's fundamental characteristics. It serves as an effective tool for acquiring vital information about a target company and gaining business intelligence. Traditional approaches to company profiling heavily rely on the availability of rich financial information about the company, such as financial reports and SEC filings, which may not be readily available for many private companies. However, the widespread adoption of online employment services has enabled a new paradigm: obtaining a diverse range of company information from their employees' online ratings and comments. This shift in approach raises the challenge of developing company profiles from an employee's perspective. To this end, this paper proposes a method named Company Profiling based Collaborative Topic Regression (CPCTR) for learning the underlying structural patterns of companies. By formulating a joint optimization framework, CPCTR can effectively model both textual (e.g., reviews) and numerical information (e.g., salaries and ratings). Notably, with the identified patterns, including positive/negative opinions and the latent variable influencing salary, we can effectively perform opinion analysis and salary prediction. Extensive experiments conducted on a real-world dataset validate the effectiveness of CPCTR. The results demonstrate that our method provides a comprehensive understanding of company characteristics and delivers more effective salary predictions than other baseline approaches.

title: Nonconvex Sparse Spectral Clustering by Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers and Its Convergence Analysis
Abstract: Spectral Clustering (SC) is a widely used data clustering method that first learns a low-dimensional embedding of data by computing the eigenvectors of the normalized Laplacian matrix, then performs k-means on the transposed embedding to obtain the final clustering result. Sparse Spectral Clustering (SSC) extends SC by incorporating sparse regularization on the product of the embedding and its transpose, leveraging the block diagonal structure prior of this product in the ideal case. However, encouraging sparsity in this product leads to a heavily nonconvex problem, which is challenging to solve. The work by Lu, Yan, and Lin (2016) proposes a convex relaxation to indirectly pursue this aim. Nevertheless, convex relaxation generally results in a loose approximation, and the quality of the solution remains unclear. This work instead focuses on directly solving the nonconvex formulation of SSC, which explicitly encourages sparsity in the product of the embedding and its transpose. We propose an efficient Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to address the nonconvex SSC and provide convergence guarantees. Specifically, we prove that the sequences generated by ADMM always have a limit point and that any limit point is a stationary point. Our analysis does not rely on any assumptions on the iterates, making it practically applicable. Our proposed ADMM for nonconvex problems allows the stepsize to be increasing but upper-bounded, leading to significant efficiency in practice. Experimental analysis on several real datasets validates the effectiveness of our method.

title: Recruitment Market Trend Analysis with Sequential Latent Variable Models
Abstract: Recruitment market analysis provides invaluable insights into industry-specific economic growth and plays a crucial role for both employers and job seekers. With the rapid advancement of online recruitment services, a massive volume of recruitment data has been accumulated, enabling a new paradigm for recruitment market analysis. However, traditional methods for recruitment market analysis rely heavily on the expertise of domain experts and classic statistical models, which often lack the specificity to model large-scale dynamic recruitment data and struggle to capture fine-grained market trends. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a novel research paradigm for recruitment market analysis by leveraging unsupervised learning techniques to automatically discover recruitment market trends based on extensive recruitment data. Specifically, we develop a novel sequential latent variable model, named MTLVM, designed to capture the sequential dependencies of corporate recruitment states and automatically learn latent recruitment topics within a Bayesian generative framework. Notably, to capture the variability of recruitment topics over time, we introduce hierarchical Dirichlet processes for MTLVM. These processes dynamically generate evolving recruitment topics. Finally, we implement a prototype system to empirically evaluate our approach using real-world recruitment data from China. Through visualization of the results from MTLVM, we successfully reveal numerous interesting findings, such as the peak popularity of LBS-related jobs in the second half of 2014 followed by a decline in 2015.

title: OneDataShare: A Vision for Cloud-hosted Data Transfer Scheduling and Optimization as a Service
Abstract: Fast, reliable, and efficient data transmission across wide-area networks constitutes a primary bottleneck for data-intensive cloud applications. This paper introduces OneDataShare, designed to address the issues hindering effective cloud-based data transfers of varying file sizes and across incompatible transfer endpoints. OneDataShare aims to achieve high-speed data communication, interoperability between multiple transfer protocols, and accurate estimation of delivery time for advance planning, ultimately maximizing user-profit through improved and faster data analysis for business intelligence. The paper elaborates on the desirable features of OneDataShare as a cloud-hosted data transfer scheduling and optimization service and how it aligns with the vision of harnessing the power of the cloud and distributed computing. Experimental evaluation and comparison with existing real-life file transfer services demonstrate that the transfer throughput achieved by OneDataShare is 6.5 times greater.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Statistics
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is inherently data-driven. It demands the application of statistical concepts through human-machine collaboration during data generation, algorithm development, and result evaluation. This paper explores how such human-machine collaboration can be achieved through the statistical concepts of population, question of interest, representativeness of training data, and scrutiny of results (PQRS). The PQRS workflow provides a conceptual framework for integrating statistical ideas with human input into AI products and research. These ideas encompass experimental design principles of randomization and local control, as well as the principle of stability to enhance reproducibility and interpretability of algorithms and data results. We discuss the application of these principles in the contexts of self-driving cars, automated medical diagnoses, and examples from the authors' collaborative research.

title: Physarum-inspired Network Optimization: A Review
Abstract: Physarum-inspired Algorithms (PAs) hold great potential for solving challenging network optimization problems. However, existing research on PAs remains immature and far from being fully recognized. A major contributing factor is the lack of comprehensive organization of this research. This paper aims to address this issue. We begin by introducing Physarum and its intelligence from a biological perspective. Subsequently, we summarize and categorize four types of Physarum-inspired networking models. Following this, we analyze the network optimization problems and applications that have been tackled by PAs based on these models. Finally, we discuss existing research on PAs and identify two fundamental questions: 1) What are the characteristics of Physarum networks? 2) Why can Physarum solve certain network optimization problems? Answering these questions is crucial for the future development of Physarum-inspired network optimization.

title: Network Analysis for Explanation
Abstract: Safety critical systems strongly necessitate the quality aspects of artificial intelligence, including explainability. In this paper, we analyze a trained network to extract features that significantly contribute to inference. Based on this analysis, we developed a simple solution to generate explanations of the inference processes.

title: Columnar Database Techniques for Creating AI Features
Abstract: Recent advancements in in-memory columnar database techniques have significantly enhanced the performance of analytical queries on very large databases and data warehouses. Concurrently, advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms have increased the ability to analyze data. We use the term AI to encompass both Deep Learning (DL or neural network) and Machine Learning (ML aka Big Data analytics). Our exploration of the AI full stack has led to a cross-stack columnar database innovation that efficiently creates features for AI analytics. This innovation introduces Augmented Dictionary Values (ADVs) to existing columnar database dictionaries to enhance featurization efficiency by minimizing data movement and data duplication. We demonstrate how various forms of featurization (feature selection, feature extraction, and feature creation) can be efficiently calculated in a columnar database. The full-stack AI investigation has also led us to propose an integrated columnar database and AI architecture. This architecture incorporates information flows and feedback loops to improve the overall analytics cycle during multiple iterations of extracting data from data sources, featurization, and analysis.

title: A Pilot Study on Using an Intelligent Life-like Robot as a Companion for Elderly Individuals with Dementia and Depression
Abstract: This paper presents the design, development, methodology, and results of a pilot study investigating the use of an intelligent, emotive, and perceptive social robot (aka Companionbot) to improve the quality of life of elderly individuals with dementia and/or depression. Ryan Companionbot, prototyped for this project, is a rear-projected life-like conversational robot. Ryan is equipped with features that enable it to (1) interpret and respond to users' emotions through facial expressions and spoken language, (2) proactively engage in conversations with users, and (3) remind them about their daily life schedules (e.g., taking their medicine on time). Ryan also engages users in cognitive games and reminiscence activities. We conducted a pilot study with six elderly individuals with moderate dementia and/or depression residing in a senior living facility in Denver. Each individual had 24/7 access to a Ryan in their room for a period of 4-6 weeks. Our observations of these individuals, interviews with them and their caregivers, and analysis of their interactions during this period revealed that they established rapport with the robot and greatly valued and enjoyed having a Companionbot in their room.

title: Perspectival Knowledge in PSOA RuleML: Representation, Model Theory, and Translation
Abstract: In Positional-Slotted Object-Applicative (PSOA) RuleML, a predicate application (atom) can have an Object IDentifier (OID) and descriptors that can be positional arguments (tuples) or attribute-value pairs (slots). PSOA RuleML explicitly specifies for each descriptor whether it should be interpreted under the perspective of the predicate in whose scope it occurs. This predicate-dependency dimension refines the space between oidless, positional atoms (relationships) and oidful, slotted atoms (framepoints): While relationships utilize only a predicate-scope-sensitive (predicate-dependent) tuple, and framepoints utilize only predicate-scope-insensitive (predicate-independent) slots, PSOA employs a systematics of orthogonal constructs also permitting atoms with (predicate-)independent tuples and atoms with (predicate-)dependent slots. This supports data and knowledge representation where a slot attribute can have different values depending on the predicate. PSOA thus extends object-oriented multi-membership and multiple inheritance. Based on objectification, PSOA laws are given: Besides unscoping and centralization, the semantic restriction and transformation of describution permits rescoping of one atom's independent descriptors to another atom with the same OID but a different predicate. For inheritance, default descriptors are realized by rules. On top of a metamodel and a Grailog visualization, PSOA's atom systematics for facts, queries, and rules is explained. The presentation and (XML-)serialization syntaxes of PSOA RuleML are introduced. Its model-theoretic semantics is formalized by extending the interpretation functions for dependent descriptors. The open-source PSOATransRun system implements PSOA RuleML through a translator to runtime predicates, including for dependent tuples (prdtupterm) and slots (prdsloterm). Our tests demonstrate efficiency advantages of dependent and tupled modeling.

title: End-to-End Offline Goal-Oriented Dialog Policy Learning via Policy Gradient
Abstract: Learning a goal-oriented dialog policy is typically performed offline using supervised learning algorithms or online using reinforcement learning (RL). Furthermore, as companies accumulate massive quantities of dialog transcripts between customers and trained human agents, encoder-decoder methods have gained popularity because agent utterances can be directly treated as supervision without the need for utterance-level annotations. However, a potential drawback of such approaches is their myopic generation of the next agent utterance without considering dialog-level considerations. To address this concern, this paper describes an offline RL method for learning from unannotated corpora that can optimize a goal-oriented policy at both the utterance and dialog level. We introduce a novel reward function and utilize both on-policy and off-policy policy gradient to learn a policy offline without requiring online user interaction or an explicit state space definition.

title: A Deep Network Model for Paraphrase Detection in Short Text Messages
Abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of paraphrase detection. The ability to detect similar sentences written in natural language is crucial for numerous applications, including text mining, text summarization, plagiarism detection, authorship authentication, and question answering. Given two sentences, the objective is to determine whether they are semantically equivalent. A significant insight from this work is that existing paraphrase systems demonstrate good performance when applied to clean texts, but they do not necessarily deliver comparable performance against noisy texts. Paraphrase detection on user-generated short texts, such as Twitter, presents challenges due to language irregularity and noise. To overcome these obstacles, we propose a novel deep neural network-based approach that relies on coarse-grained sentence modeling using a convolutional neural network and a long short-term memory model, combined with a specific fine-grained word-level similarity matching model. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches on user-generated noisy social media data, such as Twitter texts, and achieves highly competitive performance on a cleaner corpus.

title: Using Rule-Based Labels for Weak Supervised Learning: A ChemNet for Transferable Chemical Property Prediction
Abstract: With access to vast datasets, deep neural networks (DNN) have achieved human-level accuracy in image and speech recognition tasks. However, in chemistry, data is inherently limited and fragmented. This work develops an approach that leverages rule-based knowledge to train ChemNet, a transferable and generalizable deep neural network for chemical property prediction that learns in a weakly supervised manner from large unlabeled chemical databases. When combined with transfer learning approaches to predict other smaller datasets for chemical properties that it was not originally trained on, we show that ChemNet's accuracy surpasses contemporary DNN models trained using conventional supervised learning. Moreover, we demonstrate that the ChemNet pre-training approach is equally effective on both CNN (Chemception) and RNN (SMILES2vec) models, indicating that this approach is network architecture agnostic and effective across multiple data modalities. Our findings suggest that a pre-trained ChemNet that incorporates chemistry domain knowledge facilitates the development of generalizable neural networks for more accurate prediction of novel chemical properties.

title: Group Activity Selection on Social Networks
Abstract: We introduce a novel variant of the group activity selection problem (GASP), where agents are situated on a social network, and activities can only be assigned to connected subgroups (gGASP). We demonstrate that finding a stable outcome is straightforward if multiple groups can simultaneously engage in the same activity, as long as the network is acyclic. Conversely, if each activity can be assigned to only a single group, finding stable outcomes becomes computationally intractable, even for very simple underlying networks. Determining whether a given instance of a gGASP admits a Nash stable outcome proves to be NP-hard when the social network is a path or a star, or if the size of each connected component is bounded by a constant. We then examine the parameterized complexity of finding outcomes of gGASP that are Nash stable, individually stable, or core stable. For the parameter 'number of activities', we propose an FPT algorithm for Nash stability in the case of acyclic social networks and obtain a W[1]-hardness result for cliques (i.e., for standard GASP); similar results hold for individual stability. In contrast, finding a core stable outcome is difficult even if the number of activities is bounded by a small constant, both for standard GASP and when the social network is a star. For the parameter 'number of players', all problems we consider are in XP for arbitrary social networks; on the other hand, we prove W[1]-hardness results with respect to the parameter 'number of players' for the case where the social network is a clique.

title: Adversarial Examples that Fool Detectors
Abstract: An adversarial example is an input that has been subtly modified to cause a system to produce an incorrect output during testing. To date, adversarial example constructions have been demonstrated for classifiers, but not for detectors. If adversarial examples capable of fooling a detector exist, they could be maliciously used to create security hazards in environments populated with autonomous vehicles, for instance. This paper demonstrates a construction that successfully fools two standard detectors, Faster RCNN and YOLO. The existence of such examples is surprising, given the significant difference between attacking a classifier and attacking a detector, and the inherent structure of detectors, which must search for their own bounding box and cannot estimate it with high accuracy, makes it quite likely that adversarial patterns are heavily disrupted. We show that our construction produces adversarial examples that generalize well across digital sequences, even though large perturbations are required. We also demonstrate that our construction yields physical objects that are adversarial.

title: CURE-TSR: Challenging Unreal and Real Environments for Traffic Sign Recognition
Abstract: This paper examines the robustness of traffic sign recognition algorithms under challenging conditions. Existing datasets are limited in terms of their size and coverage of challenging conditions, motivating us to generate the Challenging Unreal and Real Environments for Traffic Sign Recognition (CURE-TSR) dataset. It includes over two million traffic sign images based on real-world and simulator data. We benchmark the performance of existing solutions in real-world scenarios and analyze performance variations with respect to challenging conditions. Our findings show that challenging conditions can significantly degrade the performance of baseline methods, particularly when they result in loss or misplacement of spatial information. We also investigate the impact of data augmentation and demonstrate that utilizing simulator data alongside real-world data enhances average recognition performance in real-world scenarios. The dataset is publicly available at https://ghassanalregib.com/cure-tsr/. |||

title: Conflict-driven Hybrid Observer-based Anomaly Detection
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel anomaly detection method that combines discrete and continuous state observers. The method focuses on detecting anomalies caused by intelligent attacks that can bypass traditional methods. By analyzing the relationships between continuous and discrete variables, three conflict types are defined, providing conditions for guaranteed anomaly detection. The effectiveness of this "conflict-driven" approach is demonstrated mathematically and illustrated on a Train-Gate (TG) system.

title: Named Entity Sequence Classification
Abstract: Named Entity Recognition (NER) aims to identify and classify named entities in text. For certain applications, such as content recommendation systems, reliable confidence levels for detected entities are crucial. This paper addresses the problem of finding confidence levels for NER, framing it as a binary classification problem. Using NER and recurrent neural networks, the probability of a candidate entity being a real named entity is calculated. The approach is applied to Twitter data, demonstrating the identification of high-confidence named entities from Tweets.

title: Pose-Normalized Image Generation for Person Re-identification
Abstract: Person Re-identification (re-id) faces challenges due to the lack of paired training data across different views and the difficulty of learning discriminative identity-sensitive features while being invariant to pose variations. This work proposes a deep person image generation model called Pose-Normalization GAN (PN-GAN) to address these issues. The model synthesizes realistic person images based on pose information, enabling the learning of pose-invariant features. This approach leads to more robust re-id features and generalizes well to new datasets without requiring retraining. This scalability makes the model potentially impactful for re-id applications.

title: Distribution-Based Categorization of Classifier Transfer Learning
Abstract: Transfer Learning (TL) aims to transfer knowledge from a source problem to a target problem, eliminating the need to build the target model from scratch. Due to its significance, TL has gained attention in the Machine Learning community for its potential to create adaptable learning models. This paper presents a comprehensive review of TL methods, focusing on classification tasks. A distribution-based categorization of TL is proposed, with a standardized nomenclature to clarify the field. This framework identifies three main TL categories, discussing their characteristics and illustrating them with examples.

title: Distance-based Self-Attention Network for Natural Language Inference
Abstract: Attention mechanisms have been used to enhance RNNs and CNNs, but the Transformer architecture has achieved state-of-the-art performance in machine translation while significantly reducing training time. Inspired by the Transformer, this paper introduces the Distance-based Self-Attention Network, a fully attention-based sentence encoder that incorporates word distance information. By using a distance mask, the model captures local dependencies without sacrificing global dependency, leading to improved performance on Natural Language Inference (NLI) tasks. The model achieves new state-of-the-art results with SNLI data and shows particular strength with long sentences or documents.

title: Learning General Latent-Variable Graphical Models with Predictive Belief Propagation
Abstract: Learning general latent-variable probabilistic graphical models is a fundamental challenge in machine learning and artificial intelligence. Existing methods, including EM and spectral algorithms, suffer from limitations that restrict their applicability and affect performance. This paper introduces a novel message-passing inference method called Predictive Belief Propagation and proposes a new learning and inference algorithm for latent-variable graphical models based on this formulation. The algorithm transforms the parameter learning problem into a series of supervised learning problems, unifying the learning of different latent graphical models into a single framework. The algorithm is local-optima-free, statistically consistent, and outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and speed.

title: S-Shaped vs. V-Shaped Transfer Functions for Antlion Optimization Algorithm in Feature Selection Problems
Abstract: Feature selection is a crucial preprocessing step for classification problems, aiming to select near-optimal features from the original dataset. This paper proposes a wrapper feature selection method based on the Ant Lion Optimizer (ALO), a recent metaheuristic algorithm. Six ALO variants are introduced, each employing a transfer function to map a continuous search space to a discrete space. The performance of these approaches is evaluated on 18 UCI datasets and compared to existing methods, demonstrating their effectiveness in exploring the feature space and selecting informative features, leading to improved classification accuracy.

title: SMILES2Vec: An Interpretable General-Purpose Deep Neural Network for Predicting Chemical Properties
Abstract: Chemical databases store information in text representations, with SMILES being a widely used standard in cheminformatics software. This work introduces SMILES2vec, a deep RNN that learns features from SMILES strings to predict chemical properties without explicit feature engineering. Using Bayesian optimization to tune the network architecture, SMILES2vec is shown to be a general-purpose neural network for predicting diverse chemical properties, outperforming MLP networks that rely on engineered features. Additionally, an explanation mask is developed to provide interpretability by highlighting important characters in making predictions. The model's accuracy and interpretability make it a valuable tool for the chemical industry.

title: Deep Anticipation: Light Weight Intelligent Mobile Sensing in IoT by Recurrent Architecture
Abstract: The rapid growth of the Internet of Things (IoT) is shaping the future of mobile services, enabling heterogeneous connectivity and mobile sensing perception systems. This paper addresses the challenges of analyzing and interpreting the vast amounts of IoT data in mission-critical applications, specifically focusing on latency, packet loss, and measurement noise. To overcome these challenges, a novel architecture that leverages recurrent neural networks (RNN) and Kalman filtering is proposed. The RNN learns environmental dynamics, while Kalman filtering provides prediction and correction steps to enhance the robustness of IoT communication. This approach balances prediction and measurement, achieving a new level of IoT intelligence and being particularly suitable for resource-constrained mobile applications.

title: An analysis of incorporating an external language model into a sequence-to-sequence model
Abstract: Attention-based sequence-to-sequence models for automatic speech recognition jointly train an acoustic model, a language model, and an alignment mechanism. This results in the language model being trained only on transcribed audio-text pairs, leading to shallow fusion with an external language model during inference. This paper examines the behavior of shallow fusion under various conditions, including different language models, decoding units, and tasks. Using Google Voice Search, it is shown that shallow fusion with a neural language model with wordpieces significantly improves word error rate (WERR) compared to the competitive attention-based sequence-to-sequence model, eliminating the need for second-pass rescoring.

title: Short-Term Prediction of Signal Cycle in Actuated-Controlled Corridor Using Sparse Time Series Models
Abstract: Traffic signals, as part of intelligent transportation systems, play a crucial role in making cities smarter. Traditional fixed-time control systems often result in unused green time. Actuated traffic lights offer real-time control and responsiveness to traffic demand. This paper explores the use of multivariate time series models for analyzing signal cycle lengths of multiple intersections along a corridor. Five signalized intersections with different spacing and traffic demand levels are modeled. To address the high-dimensional nature of the problem, penalized least squares are used to generate sparse models. The proposed sparse time series methods capture signal data effectively and outperform conventional models, demonstrating their potential for real-time traffic signal optimization.

title: Recognizing Plans by Learning Embeddings from Observed Action Distributions
Abstract: Recent advances in visual activity recognition have opened up possibilities for applications like automated video surveillance. However, recognizing agent plans from video data remains a challenge. While traditional plan recognition algorithms rely on sophisticated domain models, learning approximated domain models directly from activity sequences has shown promise. This paper addresses the limitation of such approaches that expect observed action sequences as inputs. The work proposes a data-interface that allows a plan recognition module to directly handle probabilistic action distributions as input. Two approaches are presented: resampling distribution sequences to single action sequences and learning action distribution embeddings through a proposed Distr2vec model. Both approaches facilitate the construction of an affinity model for plan recognition, enabling more robust and flexible plan recognition systems.

title: A Slow Read attack Using Cloud
Abstract: Cloud computing relies on shared computing resources, offering an alternative to local servers. Its growing popularity has introduced new security challenges, particularly in relation to distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks. This paper examines how DDoS attacks can exploit cloud resources and how traditional techniques may fail to detect them. A novel solution leveraging cloud resources is proposed, offering a potential approach to counter these attacks.

title: Predicting Demographics, Moral Foundations, and Human Values from Digital Behaviors
Abstract: Personal electronic devices, such as smartphones, provide access to behavioral signals that can reveal insights into individual characteristics and preferences. This study explores the connection between demographic and psychological attributes and digital behavioral data collected from a large cohort of 7,633 individuals representative of the US population. The study combines demographic data, self-reported assessments on psychometric questionnaires, and passively collected multimodal digital data from web browsing and smartphone usage. Machine learning models are developed to predict both demographic and psychological attributes from behavioral data. The results show promising accuracy for predicting demographic attributes, while performance for moral traits and human values is less robust. These findings highlight the potential of digital behavioral data for personalized services and interventions while acknowledging the need for further research to fully understand the relationship between behavior and psychology.

title: FlagIt: A System for Minimally Supervised Human Trafficking Indicator Mining
Abstract: This paper focuses on the indicator mining problem in the online sex advertising domain. The FlagIt system, currently under development, combines expert system benefits with semi-supervision and unsupervised text embeddings to identify indicators of human trafficking within large amounts of text data. The system's open-source technology stack shows promising performance compared to alternative approaches. FlagIt is actively being refined and integrated into a domain-specific search system used by law enforcement agencies to combat human trafficking, highlighting its potential for real-world impact.
