title: Modular Continual Learning in a Unified Visual Environment
Abstract: A core aspect of human intelligence is the ability to rapidly learn new tasks and flexibly switch between them. This paper presents a modular continual reinforcement learning paradigm inspired by these human abilities. We introduce a visual interaction environment that unifies various types of tasks within a single framework. A reward map prediction scheme is described that robustly learns new tasks in the extensive state and action spaces required by such an environment. We investigate the influence of module architecture properties on task learning efficiency, demonstrating that a module motif incorporating specific design principles (early bottlenecks, low-order polynomial nonlinearities, and symmetry) significantly outperforms more standard neural network motifs, requiring fewer training examples and neurons to achieve high performance. Finally, we present a meta-controller architecture for task switching based on a dynamic neural voting scheme, allowing new modules to leverage information from previously learned tasks to substantially improve their own learning efficiency.
label: AI

title: The Promise and Peril of Human Evaluation for Model Interpretability
Abstract: Transparency, user trust, and human comprehension are prominent ethical motivations for interpretable machine learning. Researchers evaluate model explanation performance using humans and real-world applications, which presents a challenge in many areas of artificial intelligence. This position paper proposes a distinction between descriptive and persuasive explanations. We discuss reasoning suggesting that functional interpretability may be correlated with cognitive function and user preferences. If this is the case, evaluating and optimizing explanations using functional metrics could perpetuate implicit cognitive bias, threatening transparency. Finally, we propose two potential research directions to disambiguate cognitive function and explanation models, maintaining control over the trade-off between accuracy and interpretability.
label: AI

title: Teaching a Machine to Read Maps with Deep Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: The ability to use a 2D map to navigate a complex 3D environment is remarkable, even challenging for many humans. Localization and navigation are critical problems in domains like robotics, and have recently become a focus of the deep reinforcement learning community. In this paper, we teach a reinforcement learning agent to read a map in order to find the shortest path out of a random maze it has never encountered before. Our system combines several state-of-the-art methods like A3C and incorporates novel elements, such as a recurrent localization cell. Our agent learns to localize itself based on 3D first-person images and an approximate orientation angle. The agent generalizes well to larger mazes, demonstrating its acquired localization and navigation capabilities.

title: Implementing the Deep Q-Network
Abstract: The Deep Q-Network proposed by Mnih et al. [2015] has become a benchmark and starting point for much deep reinforcement learning research. However, replicating results for complex systems is often challenging as original scientific publications may not provide detailed descriptions of all important parameter settings and software engineering solutions. This paper presents results from our work reproducing the results of the DQN paper. We highlight key areas in the implementation that were not thoroughly covered in the original paper to facilitate replication, including termination conditions and gradient descent algorithms. Finally, we discuss methods for improving computational performance and provide our own implementation designed to work with a range of domains, not just the original Arcade Learning Environment [Bellemare et al., 2013].

title: How morphological development can guide evolution
Abstract: Organisms are shaped by adaptive processes acting across different time scales, one such interaction being that between development and evolution. Models have shown that development influences multiple traits in a single agent, sometimes revealing promising static traits. Subsequent evolution can then canalize these rare traits, suggesting that development can, under appropriate conditions, increase evolvability. This paper reports a previously unknown phenomenon occurring when embodied agents are allowed to develop and evolve: evolution discovers body plans robust to control changes, these body plans become genetically assimilated, but controllers for these agents are not assimilated. This allows evolution to continue climbing fitness gradients by modifying the developmental programs for controllers within these permissive body plans. This highlights a previously unknown aspect of the Baldwin effect: instead of all useful traits becoming genetically assimilated, only traits conferring robustness to changes in other traits become assimilated. We refer to this as differential canalization. This finding has implications for the evolutionary design of artificial and embodied agents like robots: robots robust to internal controller changes may also be robust to external environmental changes, such as transitioning from simulation to reality or deploying in novel environments.
label: AI

title: Classification with Costly Features using Deep Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: We study a classification problem where each feature can be acquired at a cost, and the goal is to optimize a trade-off between the expected classification error and the feature cost. We revisit a former approach that frames the problem as a sequential decision-making problem and solves it using Q-learning with a linear approximation, where individual actions are either requests for feature values or terminate the episode with a classification decision. On a set of eight problems, we demonstrate that replacing the linear approximation with neural networks makes the approach comparable to state-of-the-art algorithms designed specifically for this problem. This approach is flexible, as it can be improved with any new reinforcement learning enhancement, allowing the inclusion of pre-trained high-performance classifiers. Unlike prior work, its performance is robust across all evaluated datasets.
label: AI

title: Bayesian Active Edge Evaluation on Expensive Graphs
Abstract: Robots operate in environments with varying implicit structure. For instance, a helicopter flying over terrain encounters a drastically different obstacle arrangement than a robotic arm manipulating objects on a cluttered table. State-of-the-art motion planning systems do not exploit this structure, expending valuable planning effort searching for implausible solutions. We are interested in planning algorithms that actively infer the underlying structure of the valid configuration space during planning to find solutions with minimal effort. Consider the problem of evaluating edges on a graph to quickly discover collision-free paths. Edge evaluation is costly, both for robots with complex geometries like robot arms and for robots with limited onboard computation like UAVs. Until now, this challenge has been addressed through laziness, deferring edge evaluation until absolutely necessary, hoping that edges turn out to be valid. However, all edges are not equally valuable. Some have many potentially good paths flowing through them, while others indicate the likelihood of neighboring edges being valid. This leads to our key insight: instead of passive laziness, we can actively choose edges that reduce uncertainty about the validity of paths. We show that this is equivalent to the Bayesian active learning paradigm of decision region determination (DRD). However, the DRD problem is not only combinatorially hard but also requires explicit enumeration of all possible worlds. We propose a novel framework combining two DRD algorithms, DIRECT and BISECT, to overcome both issues. We demonstrate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art algorithms on a spectrum of planning problems for mobile robots, manipulators, and autonomous helicopters. |||

title: Vision-and-Language Navigation: Interpreting visually-grounded navigation instructions in real environments
Abstract: Since the days of the Jetsons, the dream of a robot that can follow natural language instructions has persisted. While this dream remains elusive, recent advances in vision and language methods have made remarkable progress in related fields. Notably, a robot interpreting a natural-language navigation instruction based on its visual input is similar to the Visual Question Answering task. Both involve visually grounded sequence-to-sequence translation, making many methods applicable to both. To encourage the use of vision and language methods for interpreting visually-grounded navigation instructions, we introduce the Matterport3D Simulator – a large-scale reinforcement learning environment using real imagery. This simulator, capable of supporting various embodied vision and language tasks in the future, provides the first benchmark dataset for visually-grounded natural language navigation in real buildings – the Room-to-Room (R2R) dataset.

title: Facets, Tiers and Gems: Ontology Patterns for Hypernormalisation
Abstract: Many methodologies and techniques exist to simplify ontology construction. This paper explores the intersection of two of these: ontology normalization and fully programmatic ontology development. Normalization involves standardizing ontology organization with singly inherited self-standing entities and smaller taxonomies for refining entities. The former are described and defined in terms of the latter, managing the polyhierarchy of self-standing entities. Fully programmatic development involves using a domain-specific language within a programming language to develop an ontology. This enables not only defining ontological entities but also adding arbitrary patterns or new syntax within the same environment. This paper explains how new patterns can be used to enable a new style of ontology development called hypernormalization.
label: AI

title: MaMaDroid: Detecting Android Malware by Building Markov Chains of Behavioral Models (Extended Version)
Abstract: As Android's popularity has grown, so has the prevalence of malware targeting it. This has led the research community to propose various detection techniques. However, the ever-evolving nature of the Android ecosystem and malware makes it challenging to design robust tools that can operate for extended periods without needing modifications or costly retraining. To address this issue, this work focuses on malware detection from a behavioral perspective, modeled as sequences of abstracted API calls. The paper introduces MaMaDroid, a static-analysis-based system that abstracts API calls performed by an app to their class, package, or family. It builds a model from these sequences obtained from an app's call graph as Markov chains. This ensures model resilience to API changes and keeps the feature set manageable. Evaluation using a dataset of 8.5K benign and 35.5K malicious apps collected over six years shows that MaMaDroid effectively detects malware (with up to 0.99 F-measure) and maintains detection capabilities for long periods (up to 0.87 F-measure two years after training). MaMaDroid significantly outperforms DroidAPIMiner, a state-of-the-art detection system relying on raw API call frequency. To assess the contribution of API abstraction and sequencing modeling to MaMaDroid's effectiveness, a variant using frequency instead of sequences of abstracted API calls was evaluated. This variant was found to be less accurate, failing to capture maliciousness when trained on malware samples including API calls with frequencies similar to or higher than those used by benign apps.
label: AI

title: Model Extraction Warning in MLaaS Paradigm
Abstract: Cloud vendors are increasingly offering machine learning services as part of their platform and service portfolios. These services allow the deployment of machine learning models on the cloud, offered on a pay-per-query basis to application developers and end users. However, recent research has shown that hosted models are susceptible to extraction attacks. Adversaries can launch queries to steal the model, compromising future query payments or the privacy of the training data. This paper presents a cloud-based extraction monitor that can quantify the extraction status of models by observing the query and response streams of both individual and colluding adversarial users. A novel technique using information gain is introduced to measure the model learning rate by users with increasing query counts. Additionally, another technique maintains intelligent query summaries to measure the learning rate relative to the coverage of the input feature space in the presence of collusion. Both approaches have low computational overhead and can easily be offered as services to model owners to warn them of potential extraction attacks. Performance results for these approaches are presented for decision tree models deployed on the BigML MLaaS platform, using open-source datasets and different adversarial attack strategies.
label: AI

title: Maximizing Submodular or Monotone Approximately Submodular Functions by Multi-objective Evolutionary Algorithms
Abstract: Evolutionary algorithms (EAs) are a nature-inspired general-purpose optimization algorithm that has shown empirically good performance in solving various real-world optimization problems. Over the past two decades, promising results on the running time analysis (a key theoretical aspect) of EAs have been obtained, but most have focused on isolated combinatorial optimization problems. This does not reflect the general-purpose nature of EAs. To provide a general theoretical explanation of EAs' behavior, studying their performance on general classes of combinatorial optimization problems is desirable. Currently, the only result in this direction is the provably good approximation guarantees of EAs for the problem class of maximizing monotone submodular functions with matroid constraints. This work aims to contribute to this line of research. Considering that many combinatorial optimization problems involve non-monotone or non-submodular objective functions, the paper studies general problem classes, including maximizing submodular functions with/without a size constraint and maximizing monotone approximately submodular functions with a size constraint. The paper proves that a simple multi-objective EA called GSEMO-C can generally achieve good approximation guarantees in polynomial expected running time.
label: AI

title: Situationally Aware Options
Abstract: Hierarchical abstractions, also known as options, are a type of temporally extended action that enables a reinforcement learning agent to plan at a higher level, abstracting away from lower-level details. This work explores learning reusable options whose parameters can vary, encouraging different behaviors based on the current situation. These behaviors can include vigor, defense, or even risk-averseness, encompassing situational awareness (SA). This paper incorporates SA, in the form of vigor, into hierarchical RL by defining and learning situationally aware options in a Probabilistic Goal Semi-Markov Decision Process (PG-SMDP). This is achieved using the Situationally Aware Options (SAP) policy gradient algorithm, which comes with a theoretical convergence guarantee. Reusable options are learned in different scenarios in a RoboCup soccer domain (i.e., winning/losing). These options learn to execute with varying levels of vigor, resulting in human-like behaviors such as "time-wasting" in the winning scenario. The potential of the agent to escape bad local optima using reusable options in RoboCup is demonstrated. Finally, using SAP, the agent mitigates feature-based model misspecification in a Bottomless Pit of Death domain.
label: AI

title: Is prioritized sweeping the better episodic control?
Abstract: Episodic control has been proposed as a third approach to reinforcement learning, alongside model-free and model-based control, drawing an analogy to the three types of human memory: episodic, procedural, and semantic memory. However, the theoretical properties of episodic control are not well understood. This paper demonstrates that in deterministic tree Markov decision processes, episodic control is equivalent to a form of prioritized sweeping in terms of sample efficiency, memory, and computation demands. For general deterministic and stochastic environments, prioritized sweeping performs better even when memory and computation demands are restricted to be equal to those of episodic control. These findings suggest generalizations of prioritized sweeping to partially observable environments, its combined use with function approximation, and the exploration of possible implementations of prioritized sweeping in brains.
label: AI

title: Parameter Reference Loss for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation
Abstract: The success of deep learning in computer vision is largely attributed to the abundance of data available. However, collecting large-scale data, especially with supervised labels, is not always feasible. Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to leverage labeled data from a source domain to learn a model that generalizes to a target domain of unlabeled data. Many existing approaches employ Siamese network-based models, where two streams of neural networks process the source and target domain data, respectively. However, most of these approaches focus on minimizing domain discrepancy, neglecting the importance of preserving the discriminative ability for target domain features. A critical issue in UDA research is how to evaluate methods properly. Common evaluation procedures require target domain labels for hyperparameter tuning and model selection, contradicting the definition of the UDA task. To address this contradiction, this paper proposes a more reasonable evaluation principle that avoids this issue by simply using the latest model snapshot for evaluation. This adds an additional requirement for UDA methods: stability during training. This paper introduces a novel method that connects the target domain stream to the source domain stream with a Parameter Reference Loss (PRL) to simultaneously address these issues. Experiments on various datasets demonstrate that PRL not only improves performance on the target domain but also stabilizes the training procedure. Consequently, PRL-based models do not require the contradictory model selection process, making them more suitable for practical applications.

title: Dynamic Neural Program Embedding for Program Repair
Abstract: Neural program embeddings have shown great promise recently for various program analysis tasks, including program synthesis, program repair, fault localization, etc. However, most existing program embeddings are based on syntactic features of programs, such as raw token sequences or abstract syntax trees. Unlike images and text, a program has an unambiguous semantic meaning that can be difficult to capture by considering only its syntax. Syntactically similar programs can exhibit vastly different run-time behavior, limiting the effectiveness of syntax-based program embeddings. This paper proposes a novel semantic program embedding learned from program execution traces. The key insight is that program states expressed as sequential tuples of live variable values not only capture program semantics more precisely but also offer a more natural fit for Recurrent Neural Networks to model. Different syntactic and semantic program embeddings are evaluated on predicting the types of errors students make in their submissions to an introductory programming class and two exercises on the CodeHunt education platform. Evaluation results show that the new semantic program embedding significantly outperforms syntactic program embeddings based on token sequences and abstract syntax trees. Additionally, augmenting a search-based program repair system with predictions obtained from the semantic embedding significantly improves search efficiency.

title: Interactive, Intelligent Tutoring for Auxiliary Constructions in Geometry Proofs
Abstract: Geometry theorem proving is a major and challenging component in K-12 mathematics curricula. A particularly difficult task is adding auxiliary constructions (additional lines or points) to aid proof discovery. While many intelligent tutoring systems have been proposed for geometry proofs, few teach students how to find auxiliary constructions. The few exceptions are limited by their underlying reasoning processes for supporting auxiliary constructions. This paper addresses these limitations of prior systems by introducing an interactive geometry tutor, the Advanced Geometry Proof Tutor (AGPT). It leverages a recent automated geometry prover to provide combined benefits that no geometry theorem prover or intelligent tutoring system can achieve alone. AGPT can automatically process images of geometry problems directly and interactively train and guide students towards discovering auxiliary constructions independently. AGPT was evaluated in a pilot study with 78 high school students. The study results show that there is no significant perceived difference between AGPT and human tutors in training students how to find auxiliary constructions, and AGPT is significantly more effective than the state-of-the-art geometry solver that produces human-readable proofs.

title: CleanNet: Transfer Learning for Scalable Image Classifier Training with Label Noise
Abstract: This paper explores the problem of learning image classification models with label noise. Existing approaches relying on human supervision are generally not scalable, as manually identifying correct or incorrect labels is time-consuming. Approaches not relying on human supervision are scalable but less effective. To reduce human supervision for label noise cleaning, the paper introduces CleanNet, a joint neural embedding network. CleanNet only requires a fraction of the classes to be manually verified, providing knowledge of label noise that can be transferred to other classes. CleanNet and a conventional convolutional neural network classifier are integrated into a single framework for image classification learning. The effectiveness of the proposed algorithm is demonstrated for both label noise detection and image classification on noisy data on several large-scale datasets. Experimental results show that CleanNet can reduce label noise detection error rate on held-out classes with no human supervision available by 41.5% compared to current weakly supervised methods. It also achieves 47% of the performance gain of verifying all images with only 3.2% of images verified on an image classification task. Source code and dataset are available at kuanghuei.github.io/CleanNetProject.

title: Modeling Epistemological Principles for Bias Mitigation in AI Systems: An Illustration in Hiring Decisions
Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been extensively used in automatic decision-making across various scenarios, from credit ratings for loans to movie recommendations. Traditional design guidelines for AI models focus primarily on accuracy maximization. However, recent work has shown that economically irrational and socially unacceptable scenarios of discrimination and unfairness are likely to arise unless these issues are explicitly addressed. This undesirable behavior can stem from biased datasets used for training that may not be detected in black-box models. After outlining the connection between such bias in AI and the problem of induction, this paper focuses on Popper's contributions after Hume, offering a logical theory of preferences. An AI model can be preferred over others on purely rational grounds after one or more attempts at refutation based on accuracy and fairness. Inspired by such epistemological principles, this paper proposes a structured approach to mitigate discrimination and unfairness caused by bias in AI systems. In the proposed computational framework, models are selected and enhanced after attempts at refutation. This discussion focuses on hiring decision scenarios where an AI system filters job applicants for the interview phase.

title: The destiny of constant structure discrete time closed semantic systems
Abstract: Constant structure closed semantic systems are systems where each element receives its definition through a fixed set of other elements within the system. Discrete time implies that element definitions change iteratively and simultaneously based on "neighbor portraits" from the previous iteration. This paper proves that the iterative redefinition process in this class of systems quickly degenerates into a series of pairwise isomorphic states and discusses future research directions.
label: AI

title: Decentralized High-Dimensional Bayesian Optimization with Factor Graphs
Abstract: This paper presents a novel decentralized high-dimensional Bayesian optimization (DEC-HBO) algorithm. Unlike existing HBO algorithms, DEC-HBO can exploit the interdependent effects of various input components on the unknown objective function's output, boosting BO performance while preserving scalability in the number of input dimensions without requiring prior knowledge or a low (effective) dimension of the input space. To achieve this, a sparse yet rich factor graph representation of f is proposed. This representation is exploited to design an acquisition function that can similarly be represented by a sparse factor graph and hence be efficiently optimized in a decentralized manner using distributed message passing. Despite richly characterizing the interdependent effects of input components on the output of f with a factor graph, DEC-HBO can still guarantee no-regret performance asymptotically. Empirical evaluation on synthetic and real-world experiments (e.g., sparse Gaussian process model with 1811 hyperparameters) shows that DEC-HBO outperforms state-of-the-art HBO algorithms.

title: Discriminant Projection Representation-based Classification for Vision Recognition
Abstract: Representation-based classification methods such as sparse representation-based classification (SRC) and linear regression classification (LRC) have gained significant attention. This paper proposes a novel method called projection representation-based classification (PRC) for image recognition, aiming to improve representation quality. PRC is based on a new mathematical model where the "ideal projection" of a sample point x on the hyper-space H is iteratively computed by projecting x on a line of the hyper-space H using a specific strategy. Therefore, PRC can iteratively approximate the "ideal representation" of each subject for classification. Furthermore, the paper introduces discriminant PRC (DPRC), which obtains discriminant information by maximizing the ratio of the between-class reconstruction error over the within-class reconstruction error. Experimental results on five typical databases demonstrate that PRC and DPRC are effective and outperform other state-of-the-art methods on various vision recognition tasks.
label: AI

title: Intelligent Word Embeddings of Free-Text Radiology Reports
Abstract: Radiology reports are a valuable resource for advancing deep learning applications in medicine by leveraging the large volume of data continuously being updated, integrated, and shared. However, significant challenges exist due to the ambiguity and subtlety of natural language. This paper proposes a hybrid strategy combining semantic-dictionary mapping and word2vec modeling to create dense vector embeddings of free-text radiology reports. The method leverages the benefits of both semantic-dictionary mapping and unsupervised learning. Using the vector representation, radiology reports are automatically classified into three classes indicating the confidence in the diagnosis of intracranial hemorrhage by the interpreting radiologist. Experiments were conducted with varying hyperparameter settings for word embeddings and a range of classifiers. The best performance achieved was a weighted precision of 88% and a weighted recall of 90%. This work offers the potential to leverage unstructured electronic health record data by allowing direct analysis of narrative clinical notes.
label: AI

title: How the Experts Do It: Assessing and Explaining Agent Behaviors in Real-Time Strategy Games
Abstract: How should an AI-based explanation system explain an agent's complex behavior to ordinary end users who lack AI background? Addressing this question is an active research area. If an AI-based explanation system could effectively explain intelligent agents' behavior, it could enable end users to understand, assess, and appropriately trust (or distrust) the agents attempting to help them. To gain insights into this question, the paper turns to human expert explainers in the real-time strategy domain, "shoutcaster," to understand: (1) how they foraged in an evolving strategy game in real time, (2) how they assessed the players' behaviors, and (3) how they constructed pertinent and timely explanations from their insights and delivered them to their audience. The results provided insights into shoutcasters' foraging strategies for gleaning information necessary to assess and explain the players; a characterization of the types of implicit questions shoutcasters answered; and implications for creating explanations using these patterns.
label: AI

title: Computational Results for Extensive-Form Adversarial Team Games
Abstract: This paper provides, to the best of the authors' knowledge, the first computational study of extensive-form adversarial team games. These games are sequential, zero-sum games in which a team of players, sharing the same utility function, faces an adversary. Three different scenarios are defined based on the communication capabilities of the team. In the first scenario, teammates can communicate and correlate their actions both before and during the play. In the second scenario, they can only communicate before the play. In the third scenario, no communication is possible. The most suitable solution concepts are defined, and the inefficiency caused by partial or null communication is studied, showing that the inefficiency can be arbitrarily large depending on the size of the game tree. Furthermore, the computational complexity of the equilibrium-finding problem in the three scenarios is investigated. For each scenario, an exact algorithm is provided. Finally, the scalability of the algorithms is empirically evaluated in random games, and the inefficiency caused by partial or null communication is assessed.
label: AI

title: Run, skeleton, run: skeletal model in a physics-based simulation
Abstract: This paper presents an approach to solve a physics-based reinforcement learning challenge, "Learning to Run," with the objective of training a physiologically-based human model to navigate a complex obstacle course as quickly as possible. The environment is computationally expensive, has a high-dimensional continuous action space, and is stochastic. State-of-the-art policy-gradient methods are benchmarked, and various improvements, such as layer normalization, parameter noise, action and state reflecting, are tested to stabilize training and improve sample efficiency. The Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient method is found to be the most efficient method for this environment, and the introduced improvements help stabilize training. The learned models are able to generalize to new physical scenarios, such as different obstacle courses.
label: AI

title: Learning to select computations
Abstract: Efficient use of limited computational resources is crucial for intelligence. Optimally selecting computations according to rational metareasoning would achieve this, but it is computationally intractable. Drawing inspiration from psychology and neuroscience, this paper proposes the first concrete and domain-general learning algorithm for approximating the optimal selection of computations: Bayesian metalevel policy search (BMPS). The paper derives this general, sample-efficient search algorithm for a computation-selecting metalevel policy based on the insight that the value of information lies between the myopic value of information and the value of perfect information. BMPS is evaluated on three increasingly difficult metareasoning problems: when to terminate computation, how to allocate computation between competing options, and planning. Across all three domains, BMPS achieved near-optimal performance and compared favorably to previously proposed metareasoning heuristics. Finally, the practical utility of BMPS is demonstrated in an emergency management scenario, even accounting for the overhead of metareasoning.

title: Anonymous Hedonic Game for Task Allocation in a Large-Scale Multiple Agent System
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel game-theoretical framework for autonomous decision-making in multi-agent task allocation. Focusing on cooperation among self-interested agents, the proposed decentralized algorithm ensures convergence to a Nash stable partition (social agreement) within polynomial time, even in asynchronous environments. The algorithm relies on local interactions among neighboring agents under a strongly-connected communication network.  A mathematical formulation is presented to compute the lower bound of suboptimality for the solution. Moreover, the paper proves that at least 50% suboptimality can be guaranteed if social utilities are non-decreasing functions with respect to the number of collaborating agents. Numerical experiments confirm the scalability, adaptability, and robustness of the proposed framework.
label: AI

title: Bio-Inspired Local Information-Based Control for Probabilistic Swarm Distribution Guidance
Abstract: This paper proposes a new framework for solving the swarm distribution guidance problem in large-scale robotic swarms. Unlike existing methods relying on global information, this framework utilizes local information available to each agent to generate time-varying stochastic policies. This approach offers advantages such as shorter timescales for information utilization and potential for asynchronous decision-making. Theoretical analysis proves that the framework guarantees convergence to the desired density distribution using only local information, while maintaining the benefits of global-information-based approaches. The paper explicitly outlines the design requirements for these advantages and provides specific examples of framework implementation. Numerical experiments validate the effectiveness and comparability of the proposed framework compared to global-information-based alternatives.
label: AI

title: Acquiring Common Sense Spatial Knowledge through Implicit Spatial Templates
Abstract: Spatial understanding is a fundamental task with numerous real-world applications. Spatial knowledge is often represented using spatial templates, which define regions of acceptability for two objects under an explicit spatial relationship (e.g., "on", "below"). While previous work focused on explicit spatial prepositions, this paper extends the concept to implicit spatial language, where the spatial arrangement is only implied (e.g., "man riding horse").  The paper introduces a task of predicting spatial templates for two objects under a relationship, which can be seen as a spatial question-answering task with a continuous output. Two neural-based models are presented that leverage annotated images and structured text to learn this task. The models achieve good performance, demonstrating the predictability of spatial locations from implicit spatial language. Notably, the models maintain similar performance in a generalized setting where the object-relation-object combinations are novel. The paper further explores the models' ability to handle unseen objects, proving that they acquire common sense spatial knowledge allowing for generalization.
label: AI

title: Scalable Relaxations of Sparse Packing Constraints: Optimal Biocontrol in Predator-Prey Network
Abstract: Cascades represent rapid changes in networks, and the spread of invasive species in geographical landscapes presents an example with ecological and economic impact. Biocontrol, introducing a predator to control the invasive population, is a promising management strategy. This paper formulates and studies the problem of optimal biocontrol, aiming to minimize the harmful prey population by optimally seeding the predator cascade over time.  The paper addresses recurring budget constraints, common to conservation organizations, by proposing a novel and scalable randomized algorithm based on a width relaxation. This algorithm, applicable to a broad class of combinatorial optimization problems, outperforms existing methods in terms of scalability and solution quality. The paper evaluates the algorithm in the context of biocontrol for the Hemlock Wolly Adelgid (HWA) insect pest, finding near-optimal strategies for HWA control in fine-grained networks.
label: AI

title: Co-attending Free-form Regions and Detections with Multi-modal Multiplicative Feature Embedding for Visual Question Answering
Abstract: The Visual Question Answering (VQA) task has garnered significant attention in artificial intelligence. Existing VQA methods primarily employ visual attention mechanisms to associate input questions with corresponding image regions.  This paper argues that free-form region-based and detection-based visual attention mechanisms offer complementary information that can be effectively integrated.  A novel deep neural network for VQA is proposed, integrating both attention mechanisms. The framework fuses features from free-form image regions, detection boxes, and question representations through a multi-modal multiplicative feature embedding scheme. This allows the model to jointly attend question-related free-form image regions and detection boxes, enhancing question answering accuracy. The proposed method is extensively evaluated on COCO-QA and VQA datasets, surpassing state-of-the-art approaches. Source code is available at https://github.com/lupantech/dual-mfa-vqa.
label: AI

title: A Generalized Genetic Algorithm-Based Solver for Very Large Jigsaw Puzzles of Complex Types
Abstract: This paper introduces new types of square-piece jigsaw puzzles, where pieces require not only determining their location and orientation, but also whether they need to be flipped. These puzzles, relevant to numerous real-world problems, are computationally challenging.  The paper presents a novel generalized genetic algorithm (GA)-based solver capable of handling both Type 2 puzzles (unknown location and orientation) and Type 4 puzzles (two-sided pieces with unknown location, orientation, and face). The solver achieves a new state-of-the-art, solving previously attempted puzzles faster and more accurately, handling larger puzzle sizes than ever before, and assembling the newly introduced two-sided puzzles effectively.  The paper includes the most extensive set of experimental results on Type 2 puzzles to date.
label: AI

title: Scalable Recollections for Continual Lifelong Learning
Abstract: Given the recent success of deep learning in various single tasks, the paper explores human-realistic settings, particularly continual lifelong learning. This setting demands that models learn online from a continuous stream of non-stationary data.  Successful continual lifelong learning systems must possess three key capabilities: the ability to learn and adapt over time, retention of learned knowledge, and efficiency in training time and memory. This paper focuses on the efficiency of experience storage over long timeframes, considering the case where experiences are O(n) bits and memory is limited to O(k) bits (k << n). A novel scalable architecture and training algorithm are proposed, demonstrating considerable performance gains over state-of-the-art methods like GEM.
label: AI

title: Learning to Organize Knowledge and Answer Questions with N-Gram Machines
Abstract: Despite their success in natural language processing, deep neural networks struggle with knowledge-intensive AI tasks like open-domain Question Answering (QA). Existing end-to-end deep QA models process the entire text after observing the question, leading to linear complexity with text size.  This paper proposes to address this scalability issue using symbolic meaning representations, which can be efficiently indexed and retrieved with complexity independent of text size. The proposed approach, called the N-Gram Machine (NGM), is applied to three tasks. First, NGM successfully solves bAbI tasks of synthetic text, demonstrating proof-of-concept. Second, NGM scales to large corpora through experiments on "life-long bAbI", a version of bAbI with millions of sentences. Finally, on the WikiMovies dataset, NGM is used to induce latent structure and answer questions from Wikipedia text with only QA pairs as weak supervision.
label: AI

title: ATRank: An Attention-Based User Behavior Modeling Framework for Recommendation
Abstract: This paper proposes an attention-based user behavior modeling framework called ATRank, designed primarily for recommendation tasks. The framework accounts for heterogeneous user behaviors by projecting different behavior types into multiple latent semantic spaces, where self-attention facilitates influence among behaviors. Downstream applications can utilize the user behavior vectors through vanilla attention. Experiments demonstrate improved performance and faster training compared to existing methods. The paper explores using ATRank to predict various user behaviors with a single unified model, achieving comparable performance to highly optimized individual models.
label: AI

title: Driven to Distraction: Self-Supervised Distractor Learning for Robust Monocular Visual Odometry in Urban Environments
Abstract: This paper introduces a self-supervised approach to ignoring "distractors" in camera images for robust vehicle motion estimation in cluttered urban environments. By leveraging offline multi-session mapping approaches, the paper automatically generates per-pixel ephemerality masks and depth maps for each input image. These maps are used to train a deep convolutional network. At runtime, the predicted ephemerality and depth are incorporated into a monocular visual odometry (VO) pipeline, using either sparse features or dense photometric matching. This approach achieves metric-scale VO using a single camera, enabling accurate egomotion recovery even with 90% of the image obscured by dynamic objects. The paper evaluates the robust VO methods on over 400km of driving data from the Oxford RobotCar Dataset, demonstrating reduced odometry drift and significantly improved egomotion estimation in the presence of moving vehicles.
label: AI

title: Superpixels Based Segmentation and SVM Based Classification Method to Distinguish Five Diseases from Normal Regions in Wireless Capsule Endoscopy
Abstract: Wireless Capsule Endoscopy (WCE) is a novel technology for examining the entire gastrointestinal tract, capturing over 55,000 frames during a single examination.  The time-consuming manual review of these images is prone to human error, highlighting the need for intelligent methods to assist physicians. This paper proposes superpixel-based methods for segmenting five diseases: bleeding, Crohn's disease, Lymphangiectasia, Xanthoma, and Lymphoid hyperplasia. Two superpixel methods, simple linear iterative clustering (SLIC) and quick shift (QS), are compared for semantic segmentation. Segmented superpixels are then classified into normal and abnormal classes using support vector machines (SVM) with texture and color features. Both SLIC and QS achieve accuracy, specificity, sensitivity, and precision around 92%, 93%, 93%, and 88%, respectively. However, SLIC demonstrates significantly faster performance compared to QS.

title: Evolving soft locomotion in aquatic and terrestrial environments: effects of material properties and environmental transitions
Abstract: Designing soft robots presents numerous challenges, making automated design approaches particularly appealing. Evolutionary soft robotics utilizes optimization algorithms inspired by natural evolution to enable soft robots (morphology and controllers) to evolve spontaneously in physically-realistic simulated environments. This paper introduces a powerful evolutionary system for investigating the free-form evolution of walking and swimming soft robots in different environments. Three sets of experiments are reported, exploring different aspects of soft locomotion evolution. The first two sets investigate the effects of material properties on terrestrial and aquatic soft locomotion, demonstrating how different materials lead to variations in morphology, behavior, and energy-performance tradeoffs. The third set investigates the effects and benefits of major environmental transitions (land-water) during evolution, revealing morphological exaptation phenomena and potential asymmetry between land-water and water-land transitions.

title: Metric Map Merging using RFID Tags & Topological Information
Abstract: A map merging component is crucial for the proper functionality of multi-robot systems performing exploration, as it enables integration and distribution of crucial information: explored-covered space and its morphology. This paper proposes a metric map merging approach based on environmental information in conjunction with spatially scattered RFID tags localization. The approach consists of three parts: approximate rotation calculation using obstacle poses and localized RFID tags, translation based on the best localized common RFID tag, and final transformation refinement using an ICP algorithm.
label: AI

title: Dependent landmark drift: robust point set registration with a Gaussian mixture model and a statistical shape model
Abstract: Point set registration aims to find point-by-point correspondences between point sets, each representing the shape of an object. This paper introduces a novel point set registration method utilizing the Gaussian mixture model with prior shape information encoded as a statistical shape model. The transformation model combines similar transformation, motion coherence, and the statistical shape model. This approach proves effective for point sets with outliers, missing regions, or rotations.  The computational cost is reduced to linear, making the method scalable for large point sets.  The paper demonstrates the method's effectiveness through comparisons with existing algorithms using datasets of human body shapes, hands, and faces.
label: AI

title: Learning to Play Othello with Deep Neural Networks
Abstract: AlphaGo's superhuman playing level highlighted the capabilities of convolutional neural architectures (CNNs) in capturing complex spatial patterns. This success was partially attributed to analogies between Go board states and 2D images, particularly translational invariance and a relatively large board. This paper investigates whether CNN-based move predictors are effective for Othello, a game with distinct characteristics, including a smaller board size and complete lack of translational invariance. The paper compares several CNN architectures and board encodings, augments them with state-of-the-art extensions, trains them on an extensive database of expert moves, and examines their move prediction accuracy and playing strength. The empirical evaluation confirms the high capabilities of neural move predictors and reveals a strong correlation between prediction accuracy and playing strength. The best CNNs surpass all other 1-ply Othello players and defeat Edax, the best open-source Othello player.
label: AI

title: Wikipedia for Smart Machines and Double Deep Machine Learning
Abstract: While data-centric deep learning algorithms have achieved impressive performance in transactional point applications of Artificial Intelligence (AI) like face recognition or EKG classification, they have limitations for non-transactional AI applications like medical diagnosis beyond EKG results. These applications require deeper and broader knowledge integration, combining anatomy and physiology with EKG results and other patient findings. This paper examines these limitations for several real-life AI applications and proposes solutions. The "Wikipedia for Smart Machines" initiative aims to build repositories of software structures representing humanity's science and technology knowledge, accessible to smart machines. AI software developers will have access to these "Reusable Knowledge" structures, hence the name ReKopedia.  The paper argues that Big Knowledge, obtained from data and humanity's knowledge repository, is as crucial as Big Data.  The paper proposes a paradigm for integrating data-centric deep learning algorithms with algorithms leveraging deep knowledge, such as evidential reasoning and causality reasoning. A project is described to produce ReKopedia knowledge modules for medical diagnosis of approximately 1,000 disorders.  The paper emphasizes the equal importance of data and deep, basic, commonsense knowledge.
label: AI

title: Neuromorphic computing with multi-memristive synapses
Abstract: Neuromorphic computing presents a promising path towards building intelligent computing systems of the future. Memristive devices, exhibiting history-dependent conductivity modulation, have been proposed as efficient representations for synaptic weights in artificial neural networks. Achieving precise modulation of device conductance over a wide dynamic range, necessary for high network accuracy, remains a challenge. This paper introduces a multi-memristive synaptic architecture with an efficient global counter-based arbitration scheme. Focusing on phase change memory devices, the paper develops a comprehensive model and demonstrates its effectiveness for both spiking and non-spiking neural networks through simulations. Experimental results involving over a million phase change memory devices for unsupervised learning of temporal correlations using a spiking neural network are presented. This work represents a significant step towards realizing large-scale, energy-efficient neuromorphic computing systems.
label: AI

title: Win Prediction in Esports: Mixed-Rank Match Prediction in Multi-player Online Battle Arena Games
Abstract: Esports has gained popularity as both a player and spectator genre, supporting a global entertainment industry. Esports analytics addresses the need for data-driven feedback, focusing on cyber-athlete evaluation, strategy, and prediction. Previous work has utilized match data from various player ranks, from hobbyists to professionals. However, professional players exhibit different behavior than lower-ranked players. This paper investigates whether mixed-rank match datasets can be used to create models that predict winners in professional matches and provide simple in-game statistics for viewers and broadcasters. The paper demonstrates that, despite a slight reduction in accuracy, mixed-rank datasets can be used to predict professional match outcomes with suitably optimized configurations.
label: AI

title: Approximately Stable Matchings with Budget Constraints
Abstract: This paper examines two-sided matching with budget constraints, where one side (firm or hospital) can make monetary transfers (offer wages) to the other (worker or doctor). In a standard model, a hospital has a maximum quota for doctors.  This paper introduces a model where hospitals have fixed budgets, constraining the total amount of wages allocated to doctors.  With budget constraints, stable matchings may not exist, and checking for their existence is challenging. To address this issue, the paper extends the "matching with contracts" model of Hatfield and Milgrom to handle approximately stable matchings.  Two novel mechanisms are proposed that efficiently return such a stable matching while exactly satisfying budget constraints. The first mechanism achieves the best possible bound by sacrificing strategy-proofness. Additionally, a special case is identified where a simple mechanism is strategy-proof for doctors while maintaining the best possible bound of the general case.
label: AI

title: Using KL-divergence to focus Deep Visual Explanation
Abstract: This paper presents a method for explaining image classification predictions of deep convolution neural networks by highlighting the pixels that influence the final class prediction. The paper identifies Kullback-Leibler divergence as a heuristic method for selecting parameters deemed most relevant in prediction. This approach aims to improve understanding and interpretation of deep network predictions. The paper evaluates the performance of two popular networks in this context of interpretability. |||

title: Timely Feedback in Unstructured Cybersecurity Exercises
Abstract:
Cybersecurity exercises provide valuable hands-on training for professionals, allowing them to develop skills in preventing and responding to cyberattacks. However, the lack of timely and detailed feedback limits the effectiveness of these exercises. To address this, we developed a new feedback tool that provides an interactive timeline of exercise events, enabling learners to reflect on their experience immediately after the exercise. We deployed this tool during an international exercise, and the results show that participants found it useful and appreciated its personalized nature. This tool can be applied to any exercise using a scoring system based on individual objectives, making it a valuable resource for improving cybersecurity training.  ||| 
Cyberattacks on databases and critical infrastructure have become a major threat to both public and private sectors, while ubiquitous tracking and wearable computing raise serious privacy concerns. As a response, researchers have proposed using defensive deception to leverage the information asymmetry typically enjoyed by attackers to protect systems. However, the concept of deception has been used broadly and with different meanings. This paper provides a systematic analysis of 24 articles published from 2008 to 2018 that use game theory to model defensive deception in cybersecurity and privacy. We propose a taxonomy that defines six types of deception: perturbation, moving target defense, obfuscation, mixing, honey-x, and attacker engagement. These types are differentiated by their information structures, agents, actions, and duration, all of which are captured by game theory. Our aim is to rigorously define these types, provide a snapshot of current research, offer a menu of models for applied research, and identify promising areas for future work.  ||| 
Accelerating inexact string matching procedures is crucial for applications requiring real-time processing of large datasets, such as bioinformatics and cybersecurity. These procedures often produce numerous "shadow hits" that require filtering to extract meaningful results. Traditional filtering methods are computationally demanding and performed offline, hindering real-time analysis. This paper introduces a novel algorithm for Online Approximate String Matching (OASM) that filters shadow hits on-the-fly using priority rules to prioritize overlapping hits. An FPGA hardware implementation of OASM is proposed and compared to a serial software version. The FPGA implementation achieves high parallelism and superior performance compared to the software version, even on entry-level FPGAs. This makes the developed architecture highly competitive in terms of both performance and cost for the overall computing system.  ||| 
Cybersecurity games are an effective method for active learning, but most existing games are designed for experienced players, which can lead to frustration for less experienced learners. To address this, we focus on diagnostic assessment of participants entering the games. We hypothesize that information about players' knowledge, skills, and experience can be used to provide personalized assistance and maximize learning during the game. This paper presents an experiment examining the predictive value of a short quiz and self-assessment for identifying learners' readiness before playing a cybersecurity game. Our results show that a well-designed pre-test can accurately predict player performance, while self-assessment is not a reliable predictor. We also discuss challenges in designing pre-tests for cybersecurity games, including calibrating questions with game-relevant skills, minimizing length while maximizing informative value, and integrating the pre-test into the game.  ||| 
Learning-based pattern classifiers, including deep networks, have achieved remarkable performance in various domains, from computer vision to cybersecurity. However, they are vulnerable to adversarial input perturbations crafted at training or test time, which can easily subvert their predictions. This vulnerability, known as adversarial examples, has been extensively investigated in the field of adversarial machine learning. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of this research area, tracing its evolution over the past decade. Starting from early work on non-deep learning algorithms, we cover recent advances in understanding the security properties of deep learning algorithms in the context of computer vision and cybersecurity tasks. We reveal interesting connections between these seemingly disparate research lines, highlighting common misconceptions about the security evaluation of machine learning algorithms. We review the main threat models and attacks, discuss the limitations of current work, and outline future challenges in designing more secure learning algorithms.  ||| 
Traditional perimeter-based security measures are the cornerstone of cybersecurity, but their effectiveness against sophisticated and coordinated attacks is increasingly questioned. In contrast to perimeter-based security, mission-centric cybersecurity focuses on protecting critical assets by understanding how attacks can impact mission success. This strategic approach prioritizes resources to mitigate vulnerabilities and protect critical assets, unlike the tactical approach of perimeter-based security. We propose MISSION AWARE, a framework that assists in identifying system components that, if compromised, would destabilize the overall mission. MISSION AWARE utilizes a structured elicitation process, hierarchical modeling methods, and evidence generation to analyze mission requirements, functional behaviors, and system architectures. The framework then traces evidence back to mission requirements to determine the most impactful threats. This approach provides a more comprehensive understanding of cyber risks and enables more effective resource allocation for mission-critical systems.  ||| 
Connected vehicle (CV) environments, with their diverse data collection, communication, and computing infrastructure, are vulnerable to cyberattacks, jeopardizing the expected safety, mobility, and environmental benefits of these technologies. Cyberattacks can lead to severe traffic incidents, making cybersecurity a critical concern in CV applications. This paper investigates the impact of cyberattacks on the vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I) network from a V2I application perspective and develops a novel V2I cybersecurity architecture called CVGuard. CVGuard is designed to detect and prevent cyberattacks in the V2I environment, considering challenges such as scalability, resiliency, and future usability. A case study involving a distributed denial of service (DDoS) attack on a V2I application, Stop Sign Gap Assist (SSGA), demonstrates CVGuard's effectiveness in mitigating the adverse effects of the attack. The results show that CVGuard successfully reduced inter-vehicle conflicts by 60% at an unsignalized intersection where a DDoS attack compromised the SSGA application. This study highlights the importance of robust cybersecurity solutions for ensuring the safety and reliability of connected vehicle applications.  ||| 
Electric vehicles (EVs), like all modern vehicles, rely on electronic control systems embedded within networks that are susceptible to cyberattacks. These vulnerabilities are amplified in EVs due to the unique risks associated with EV battery packs, which are known for their specific energy, cost, and fire-related safety concerns. This study develops a systematic framework to assess the impact of cyberattacks on EVs. While current research focuses on the short-term physical safety implications of cyberattacks, it is crucial to consider long-term attacks that aim to cause financial losses through accrued impact, especially in the context of EVs. Faulty battery management system components, such as a compromised voltage regulator, could lead to cyberattacks that overdischarge or overcharge the battery, resulting in significant damage and safety risks. This study highlights the need for a comprehensive approach to EV cybersecurity that considers both immediate and long-term consequences of cyberattacks.  ||| 
Efficient monitoring and management of solar energy generation are crucial for achieving net-zero energy buildings. This paper presents a dependable control system based on the Internet of Things (IoT) to control and manage the energy flow from solar panels within a microgrid. The system utilizes data from local sensors and real-time meteorological information to optimize solar panel performance. To enhance system fault tolerance, dependable controllers are developed to ensure reliable operation even in the event of failures in communication, hardware, or cybersecurity. These controllers optimize photovoltaic array tracking performance to maximize solar energy capture and maintain system resilience. Experimental results demonstrate the validity of the proposed approach, showcasing its ability to maintain system performance and reliability despite potential failures.  ||| 
Data science and machine learning algorithms running on big data infrastructure are increasingly used in various applications, from business intelligence and cybersecurity to smart city management. As these algorithms become integral to daily operations, understanding their execution time on big data infrastructure is crucial for controlling costs and delivery times. This paper discusses the challenges involved in understanding the runtime of iterative machine learning algorithms and provides a case study of the K-Means algorithm. We present a statistical characterization and model of the runtime of a K-Means implementation for the Spark big data engine using the Edward probabilistic programming language. This research helps improve our understanding of algorithm performance on big data platforms and enables more efficient resource allocation and optimization.  ||| 
Analyzing an organization's computer network activity is essential for early detection and mitigation of insider threats, a growing concern for many organizations. Raw system logs are a prime example of streaming data that can quickly overwhelm human analysts. To address this challenge, we present an online unsupervised deep learning approach to detect anomalous network activity from system logs in real time. Our models decompose anomaly scores into individual user behavior features, enhancing interpretability and assisting analysts in reviewing potential insider threat cases. Using the CERT Insider Threat Dataset v6.2 and threat detection recall as our performance metric, our deep and recurrent neural network models outperform traditional anomaly detection methods like Principal Component Analysis, Support Vector Machine, and Isolation Forest. Our best model demonstrates the potential to significantly reduce analyst workloads by identifying insider threat activity with high accuracy.  ||| 
Online social platforms are plagued by hateful speech, content that expresses hatred towards individuals or groups. Such content can intimidate, silence, and even inspire violence among users. Despite the recognized dangers, reliable solutions for detecting hateful speech remain elusive. This paper explains why keyword-based methods are inadequate for detection and proposes a novel approach using content produced by self-identifying hateful communities as training data. This approach bypasses the costly annotation process required for keyword systems and performs well across various platforms, significantly outperforming current state-of-the-art methods.  ||| 
Word embedding is a Natural Language Processing (NLP) technique that automatically maps words to numerical vectors in an embedding space. This technique has been widely used to enhance performance in various NLP tasks, such as Named Entity Recognition, Syntactic Parsing, and Sentiment Analysis. Traditional word embedding methods like Word2Vec and GloVe work well with large text corpora, but often struggle with sparse texts found in specialized domains, such as cybersecurity. This paper describes a novel method for training domain-specific word embeddings from sparse texts. In addition to domain texts, our method leverages diverse domain knowledge, such as domain vocabulary and semantic relations. We propose a general framework for encoding this knowledge as text annotations and develop a new Word Annotation Embedding (WAE) algorithm to incorporate these annotations into word embedding. Our method is evaluated on two cybersecurity text corpora: a malware description corpus and a Common Vulnerability and Exposure (CVE) corpus. The evaluation results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in learning high-quality domain-specific word embeddings.  ||| 
Biometric-based cybersecurity systems for active authentication are gaining attention as a more secure alternative to traditional methods. We propose a new concept that utilizes continuous tracking of biochemical processes in skin secretions for user authentication. Skin secretions contain a rich composition of metabolites and small molecules that can be analyzed for identification purposes. This paper argues that amino acids found in sweat can be exploited to create an amino acid profile unique to each individual user of a mobile or wearable device. Individual and combinations of amino acids processed by biocatalytic cascades produce measurable physical signals, creating a time-series of outputs that collectively authenticate a specific user based on statistical criteria. Initial results indicate that single amino acid levels can provide analog signals that vary by individual, but with limited resolution due to noise. However, some assays offer digital separation into distinct ranges of values based on characteristics such as age, sex, race, and physiological state. By combining multiple amino acid signals and continuous-tracking time-series data, active authentication at the individual level becomes feasible.  ||| 
Capture the Flag (CTF) competitions are growing in importance for the Brazilian cybersecurity community as educational and professional tools. However, CTF platforms are susceptible to security vulnerabilities, which can give unfair advantages to certain competitors. To address this issue, we propose NIZKCTF, the first open-audit CTF platform based on non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs. This platform aims to ensure fair competition by guaranteeing the integrity and security of the challenges, enabling participants to verify the correctness of solutions and detect any potential security flaws.  ||| 
Knowledge graphs and vector space models are powerful knowledge representation techniques with distinct strengths and weaknesses. Vector space models excel at determining similarities between concepts but struggle with complex dependency relations and logic-based operations, which are strengths of knowledge graphs. This paper introduces the VKG structure, which unifies knowledge graphs and vector representations of entities. VKG enables powerful inference methods and search capabilities by combining the complementary strengths of both approaches. We conceptualize this as thinking "fast" in vector space while simultaneously thinking "slow" and "deeply" through reasoning over the knowledge graph. We have developed a query processing engine that decomposes complex queries into subqueries optimized for execution on either the knowledge graph or vector view of a VKG. We demonstrate that VKG can efficiently handle queries that are challenging for either vector spaces or knowledge graphs alone. The VKG structure and query processing engine are evaluated in a system called Cyber-All-Intel, which is designed for knowledge extraction, representation, and querying in the cybersecurity informatics domain.  ||| 
There have been significant efforts in government, academia, and industry to anticipate, forecast, and mitigate cyberattacks. A common approach involves time-series forecasting of cyberattacks based on data from network telescopes, honeypots, and intrusion detection/prevention systems. This research has revealed important insights into the systematicity of cyberattacks. This paper proposes an alternative perspective by forecasting attacks that are analyst-detected and verified instances of malware. We refer to these occurrences as cyber event data. Specifically, our dataset comprises analyst-detected incidents from a large operational Computer Security Service Provider (CSSP) for the U.S. Department of Defense, which rarely relies solely on automated systems. We use a Bayesian State Space Model for forecasting and find that events one week ahead can be predicted. To quantify bursts, we employ a Markov model. Our findings of systematicity in analyst-detected cyberattacks align with previous work using other sources. The advanced information provided by our forecast can enhance threat awareness by providing a probable value and range for future cyber events one week in advance. This information can be valuable for proactive resource allocation, security resource estimation, and effective risk management strategies.  ||| 
There is no standardized approach to measuring and controlling the costs associated with implementing cybersecurity programs. To advance research and practice in this area, we develop a mapping using the well-known concept of quality costs and the Framework Core within the Cybersecurity Framework produced by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). This mapping can be easily adopted by organizations using the NIST CSF for cybersecurity risk management to plan, manage, and continuously improve their cybersecurity operations. Even organizations not using the NIST CSF can benefit from this mapping by linking elements in their accounting systems associated with cybersecurity operations and risk management to a quality cost model. This framework provides a valuable tool for quantifying and managing the cost of cybersecurity programs, leading to more effective decision-making and resource allocation.  ||| 
We developed a simulation game to study the effectiveness of decision-makers in addressing two complexities inherent in building cybersecurity capabilities: potential delays in capability development and uncertainties in predicting cyber incidents. Analyzing 1,479 simulation runs, we compared the performances of experienced professionals with those of an inexperienced control group. While experienced subjects did not demonstrate a better understanding of delay mechanisms than inexperienced subjects, they were better able to learn the need for proactive decision-making through an iterative process. Both groups exhibited similar errors when dealing with the uncertainty of cyber incidents. Our findings underscore the importance of training for decision-makers with a focus on systems thinking skills and lay the groundwork for future research on uncovering mental biases related to cybersecurity complexities.  ||| 
In a world of interconnected systems, effective cybersecurity policy design is a critically understudied element of national security strategy. Enterprise cyber technologies are often implemented without considering the complex interactions between humans and the new technology. Furthermore, interactions between individuals can significantly impact the newly implemented technology. The absence of a rigorous, evidence-based approach to ground an employment strategy and elucidate the emergent organizational needs that arise with new cyber capabilities leaves us speculating about the impact of novel technologies on the overall functioning of the enterprise. This paper explores a scenario in which a hypothetical government agency applies a complexity science perspective, supported by agent-based modeling, to gain a deeper understanding of the impacts of strategic policy decisions. We present a model to explore the socio-technical dynamics of these systems, discuss lessons learned using this platform, and suggest further research and development.  |||

title: Creating a Cybersecurity Concept Inventory: A Status Report on the CATS Project
Abstract: This project aims to develop and validate a Cybersecurity Concept Inventory (CCI) to assess the quality of cybersecurity education. The CCI is designed to identify core cybersecurity concepts and assess students' understanding of those concepts. The project involves a Delphi process to identify key concepts, student interviews to uncover misconceptions, and the development of a draft CCI. The draft CCI is being validated through cognitive interviews, expert reviews, and psychometric testing. The CCI provides a framework for rigorous evidence-based improvement of cybersecurity education. It can be used to compare different instructional methods by measuring how well students learn core cybersecurity concepts, particularly adversarial thinking.

title: MTDeep: Boosting the Security of Deep Neural Nets Against Adversarial Attacks with Moving Target Defense
Abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are susceptible to adversarial attacks, where an attacker can manipulate input data to cause misclassification. To address this challenge, we propose a meta-defense technique called MTDeep, inspired by Moving Target Defense (MTD) principles from cybersecurity and multi-agent systems. MTDeep employs an ensemble of DNNs, randomly selecting one network for classification. This random selection is modeled as a Bayesian Stackelberg Game (BSG) between a defender and legitimate/malicious users. We demonstrate that MTDeep significantly reduces misclassification on perturbed images while maintaining high accuracy on legitimate images. This meta-defense approach can be combined with existing defense mechanisms to enhance resilience against adversarial attacks. To quantify the robustness of MTDeep, we introduce the concept of differential immunity, which formalizes the notion of attack transferability.
label: AI

title: On the Reliable Detection of Concept Drift from Streaming Unlabeled Data
Abstract: Machine learning classifiers deployed in real-world environments face the challenge of concept drift, where the data distribution changes over time, leading to declining predictive performance. Traditional drift detection techniques rely on labeled data for model validation, which is impractical due to the cost and time involved in labeling. Unsupervised techniques, while label-free, are unreliable due to high false alarm rates. To address these issues, we propose the Margin Density Drift Detection (MD3) algorithm. MD3 tracks the number of samples in a classifier's uncertainty region as a drift metric. It is distribution-independent, application-independent, model-independent, unsupervised, and incremental, enabling reliable drift detection from data streams. Evaluations on drift-induced and cybersecurity datasets demonstrate that MD3 effectively detects drifts with significantly fewer false alarms than unsupervised feature-based detectors. This leads to a more credible, label-efficient, and generally applicable drift detection scheme.

title: The INSuRE Project: CAE-Rs Collaborate to Engage Students in Cybersecurity Research
Abstract: Since 2012, several National Centers of Academic Excellence in Cyber Defense Research (CAE-Rs) have collaborated on a course aimed at engaging students in applied cybersecurity research. This paper describes the experiences and outcomes of this collaborative Information Security Research and Education (INSuRE) course. It outlines the project-based research course methodology, provides examples of student projects, and discusses the lessons learned.

title: Data Driven Exploratory Attacks on Black Box Classifiers in Adversarial Domains
Abstract: Modern web applications, while aiming to create societal impact, are increasingly vulnerable to sophisticated adversarial attacks. To address this threat, a data-driven approach using machine learning is crucial. However, machine learning's assumption of data stationarity is violated in adversarial settings. This paper presents an adversary's perspective on classification-based systems and introduces the Seed-Explore-Exploit framework. This framework simulates the generation of data-driven and reverse engineering attacks on classifiers. Experimental evaluation on real-world datasets demonstrates the vulnerability of classifiers and the ease with which evasion attacks can be conducted. The proposed framework aims to foster the development of secure machine learning systems by providing a white-hat analysis of vulnerabilities.

title: Crowdsourcing Cybersecurity: Cyber Attack Detection using Social Media
Abstract: Social media platforms can act as crowdsourced sensors for various societal events, including cyberattacks. This paper describes an approach for detecting a broad range of cyberattacks (e.g., DDoS attacks, data breaches, account hijacking) in an unsupervised manner using a limited set of seed event triggers. A novel query expansion strategy leverages convolutional kernels and dependency parsing to model reporting structure and identify key event characteristics. Through a large-scale Twitter analysis, this approach consistently identifies and encodes cyberattack events, outperforming existing methods.

title: Towards Secure and Safe Appified Automated Vehicles
Abstract: The rise of autonomous vehicles (AVs) has opened up new opportunities for third-party developers to contribute functionalities through crowdsourcing. However, this openness raises concerns about security and safety, as untrusted code may compromise the vehicle. This paper introduces the concept of an Appified AV platform that allows third-party development while addressing these challenges. It proposes AVGuard, an enhanced appified AV design schema that focuses on mitigating threats from untrusted code. AVGuard leverages vehicle evaluation theory and cybersecurity program analysis techniques to ensure safety. The study provides guidelines and practices for the future design of open AV platforms.
