title: Internet of Cloud: Security and Privacy issues
Abstract:
The convergence of cloud computing and the Internet of Things (IoT) has led to significant benefits for IoT growth, but it has also introduced new security challenges. This chapter examines the components of cloud computing and IoT, highlighting the security and privacy issues they face. It delves into existing solutions for safeguarding security and privacy, specifically focusing on the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT). The chapter identifies open issues and proposes future research directions. ||| 
Six years after the adoption of the 4.0 standard, the Bluetooth Special Interest Group (SIG) has released Bluetooth 5.0, a significant advancement in short-range wireless communication technology. The SIG claims this new standard will revolutionize the IoT, making it more ubiquitous and seamless. This article explores future IoT scenarios and use cases that warrant the adoption of Bluetooth 5. It presents the new technical features of Bluetooth 5, highlighting their advantages and drawbacks. ||| 
This research proposes a new paradigm for telecommunications, drawing on concepts from information theory and computational theory, adapted from complex system science. It presents a systematic framework for understanding and analyzing network complexity, divided into layers. The modelling layer, forming the foundation, captures the significant attributes and interactions within networks using tools such as agent-based modelling and graph theory. The analysis layer links these newly derived metrics to overall network performance. The tuning layer incorporates algorithms to automatically guide networks towards desired conditions. To maximize impact, the proposed approach is rooted in relevant, near-future architectures and use cases in 5G networks, such as IoT and self-organizing cellular networks. ||| 
Denial of Service (DoS) attacks pose a serious security threat to the modern Internet, especially for IoT devices with limited computing power, memory, and security mechanisms. This paper presents a model simulating the unique characteristics of an IoT device network, including components that implement "Crypto Puzzles" - a DoS mitigation technique. The paper simulates a DoS attack on the system and conducts a quantitative analysis to evaluate the potential impact, assessing the trade-off between security and throughput in the IoT system. The model uses stochastic model checking in PRISM and provides evidence supporting this approach for comparing the efficiency of different IoT system implementations. ||| 
This article presents both analytical and numerical performance analysis of Multi-Service Oriented Multiple Access (MOMA), a non-orthogonal multiple-access scheme for scenarios with numerous concurrent connections from different service classes with varying Quality-of-Service (QoS) profiles. MOMA operates on both handheld terminals and IoT devices. The scheme utilizes a class-dependent hierarchical-spreading transmission approach and a per-class reception structure. The performance analysis in this article is based on realistic channel and signal models, considering a base station equipped with multiple antennas. It provides asymptotically exact approximations of the ergodic rates achievable by MOMA. ||| 
Blockchain, an emerging decentralized security system, has been applied in various applications, including Bitcoin, smart grids, and the Internet of Things. However, the energy consumption and computing resource demands of the mining process restrict the use of blockchain in mobile environments. This paper proposes deploying edge computing services to support mobile blockchain. An auction-based edge computing resource market model is proposed, where the provider allocates resources to miners. The model considers allocative externalities (positive and negative) due to competition among miners. The proposed auction mechanism maximizes social welfare while ensuring truthfulness, individual rationality, and computational efficiency. Using blockchain mining experiments, a hash power function is defined, characterizing the probability of successfully mining a block. Extensive simulations evaluate the performance of the auction mechanism, demonstrating its efficiency in solving the social welfare maximization problem for the edge computing service provider. ||| 
Vehicles play a crucial role in modern transportation systems, and number plates serve as standard identification. Automatic license plate recognition systems were developed for this purpose, consisting of four main steps: image pre-processing, license plate region extraction, segmentation, and character recognition. Existing research often relies on Sobel edge detection or thresholding for license plate region extraction, which proves ineffective in high-intensity lighting conditions. Morphological operations can also distort characters during segmentation. This paper proposes a novel algorithm addressing these issues with a unique edge detection approach. Additionally, the need for frequent database updates of required vehicles is addressed through the use of the Internet of Things (IoT), enabling an online database that can be updated instantly from any module. Furthermore, connecting all cameras in a geographical area to one server through IoT creates a universal eye, significantly increasing the probability of tracing a vehicle compared to manual databases associated with individual cameras. ||| 
Delimited continuations, as shown by Filinski's 1994 paper, are considered the "mother of all monads" because they can implement any monadic effect, simplifying effect management for programmers. However, their availability in programming languages is limited. This article explores an alternative approach: implementing delimited continuations using exceptions and state, called "thermometer continuations." While traditional implementations require capturing intermediate states, thermometer continuations achieve this by replaying the entire computation from the start, guided by a recording. The article explains delimited continuations and monadic reflection, demonstrating how thermometer continuations can express any monadic effect through the Filinski construction. It also presents an elegant special case for nondeterminism and discusses why theoretical limitations on exceptions and state do not preclude this construction. ||| 
This paper presents a new proof of the equivalence between the Taut String Algorithm and the one-dimensional Rudin-Osher-Fatemi model. The proof relies on duality and the projection theorem in Hilbert space, providing a strictly elementary approach. It also demonstrates the existence and uniqueness of solutions for both denoising models as byproducts. The standard convergence properties of the denoised signal are revisited, and efficient proofs are provided. Additionally, a new and fundamental bound on the denoised signal is derived, implying, among other things, the strong convergence (in the space of functions of bounded variation) of the denoised signal to the original signal as the regularization parameter approaches zero. The methods presented in this paper can be adapted to address other applications, such as isotonic regression. ||| 
Matching streaming time series patterns with low latency under limited computing resources poses a critical challenge, particularly in the context of Industry 4.0 and the Industrial Internet of Things. Unlike traditional single pattern matching problems, patterns can contain multiple segments representing different statistical properties or physical meanings for more precise and expressive matching in real-world scenarios. This paper introduces a new problem, "fine-grained pattern matching," allowing users to specify varying granularities of matching deviations for different segments of a pattern and fuzzy regions for adaptive breakpoint determination between consecutive segments. A novel two-phase approach is proposed. The pruning phase utilizes Equal-Length Block (ELB) representation along with a Block-Skipping Pruning (BSP) policy, guaranteeing low-cost feature calculation, effective pruning, and no false dismissals. In the post-processing phase, a delta-function is introduced for linear-complexity exact matching. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms the brute-force method and MSM, a multi-step filter mechanism over the multi-scaled representation. ||| 
In requirements specification, software engineers create textual descriptions of envisioned systems and develop conceptual models using tools such as Universal Modeling Language (UML) and System Modeling Language (SysML). This paper explores a tool called FM, an extension of the INPUT-PROCESS-OUTPUT (IPO) model, which has been widely used in various disciplines. The paper focuses on understanding the "PROCESS" aspect of the IPO model, arguing that verbs are the fundamental way to describe processes. The use of language has significant implications for systems modeling as verbs express actions and movements. This paper investigates English verbs as a bridge to understand processes, focusing on the five verbs forming the basis of FM states: create, process, receive, release, and transfer. The paper focuses on verb classification and how to model verb actions diagrammatically. This study, while not a linguistic analysis, potentially benefits linguistics by providing insights into verb classes, relevant for tasks like machine translation, language generation, and document classification. ||| 
This research demonstrates that the quadratic entropic bound for the rate functions of nonequilibrium currents in Markov diffusion processes can be interpreted as an effective process that suboptimally generates current fluctuations. This effective process modifies only the non-reversible part of the drift or force while maintaining the reversible part constant. This interpretation clarifies the bound's relation to the fluctuation relation, linear response, and reversible limits. The paper also explores the existence of more general quadratic bounds and related uncertainty relations for physical quantities beyond currents. ||| 
As the computing landscape shifts towards distributed architectures like the Internet of Things (IoT), enterprises are transitioning from traditional perimeter-based security models to zero trust networking (ZTN) models. These models treat both the intranet and the Internet as inherently untrustworthy, incorporating dynamic and situational factors (such as device location and security risk level) into access control decisions. Researchers have developed risk models like RAdAC (Risk Adaptable Access Control) to handle dynamic contexts, which have been applied to medical and other scenarios. This position paper describes ongoing work to apply RAdAC to ZTN. A policy management framework, FURZE, is developed to facilitate fuzzy risk evaluation and adapt to dynamically changing contexts. The paper also explores how enterprise security situational awareness (SSA), describing the potential impact on an organization's mission based on current threats and the relative importance of the information asset under threat, can be incorporated into a RAdAC scheme. ||| 
The Internet of Things (IoT) paradigm presents opportunities to solve real-world problems, particularly in energy management, where collecting energy usage data, analyzing it, and optimizing consumption through control strategies are crucial. In industrial environments, however, achieving such optimization is complex due to changing business rules, process controls, and customer requirements. This paper introduces a Semantic Rules Engine (SRE) for industrial gateways that enables dynamic and flexible rule-based control strategies. This engine is simple, expressive, and allows on-the-fly rule management without service interruption. Additionally, it handles semantic queries and provides results by inferring knowledge from ontologies. The SRE has been validated on different hardware platforms and in commercial products, with performance evaluations demonstrating its conformance to customer requirements. ||| 
Industrie 4.0 is a future vision outlined in the German government's high-tech strategy, relying on information and communication technologies such as Cyber-Physical Systems, Internet of Things, Physical Internet, and Internet of Services to achieve high production flexibility, increased productivity through real-time monitoring and diagnosis, and reduced material waste. Adapting higher education, especially engineering education, to the requirements of Industrie 4.0 is crucial. This paper presents a roadmap consisting of three pillars: curriculum development, lab concept, and student club activities, outlining the necessary changes and enhancements. The paper also reports on the current application of this roadmap at the Turkish-German University in Istanbul. ||| 
The Internet of Things (IoT) will involve a massive number of machine-type devices that need to wirelessly transmit, in near real-time, diverse sets of messages sensed from their environment. Designing resource allocation schemes to support such coexistent, heterogeneous communication is a key IoT challenge, requiring self-organizing solutions that can handle IoT's unique features, such as large scale and strict resource constraints. This paper proposes a novel finite memory multi-state sequential learning framework enabling diverse IoT devices to share limited communication resources while transmitting both delay-tolerant, periodic messages and urgent, critical messages. The framework allows IoT devices to learn the number of critical messages and reallocate resources accordingly. It explicitly considers IoT device limitations in memory and computational capabilities. The paper proves the convergence of the learning framework and derives the lowest expected delay achievable by IoT devices using this framework. The effectiveness of the learning algorithm in IoT networks with various delay targets, network densities, probabilities of detection, and memory sizes is analyzed in terms of successful random access request probability and the percentage of devices that learned correctly. Results show that the proposed learning algorithm effectively reduces the delay of urgent, critical messages by intelligently reallocating resources. ||| 
The future of the Internet is predicted to be cloud-based, leading to more complex and intensive computing but potentially a less secure digital world. The concentration of resources in the cloud makes it a target for DDoS attacks, which are particularly dangerous in private, resource-constrained clouds. This paper examines several prominent approaches introduced to counter DDoS attacks in private clouds and discusses the challenges and issues in mitigating such attacks in this context. ||| 
Flexibility is essential for channel coding in modern wireless communication systems, requiring channel decoders to support various code lengths and rates. This need for flexibility applies to polar codes, considered for control channels in the future 5G standard. This paper presents a generic and flexible implementation of a software Successive Cancellation List (SCL) decoder. A wide range of parameters can be dynamically fine-tuned without recompiling the software source code: code length, code rate, frozen bits set, puncturing patterns, cyclic redundancy check, list size, decoding algorithm type, tree-pruning strategy, and data quantization. This generic and flexible SCL decoder enables exploration of trade-offs between throughput, latency, and decoding performance. Several optimizations are proposed to achieve competitive decoding speed despite the constraints of genericity and flexibility. The resulting polar list decoder is approximately 4 times faster than a generic software decoder and only 2 times slower than a non-flexible unrolled decoder. The decoder's flexibility facilitates the implementation of the fully adaptive SCL algorithm, achieving higher throughput than any other comparable decoder in the literature (up to 425 Mb/s on a single processor core for N = 2048 and K = 1723 at 4.5 dB). ||| 
Cloud computing is significantly transforming the computing industry, built around core concepts like virtualization, processing power, connectivity, and elasticity. This allows IT resources to be stored and shared via a broad network. While cloud computing enables the advancement of Big Data, IoT, mobile and web applications, and other technologies, it also faces challenges like governance, security, and privacy. This paper focuses on the security and privacy challenges of cloud computing, specifically regarding user authentication and access management for cloud SaaS applications. The proposed model leverages the stateless and secure nature of JWT for client authentication and session management. It efficiently manages authorized access to protected cloud SaaS resources. The model introduces a Policy Match Gate (PMG) component and a Policy Activity Monitor (PAM) component. Additionally, other subcomponents, such as a Policy Validation Unit (PVU) and a Policy Proxy DB (PPDB), are implemented for optimized service delivery. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the model offers a secure, lightweight, and highly scalable system for improved cloud resource security and management. ||| 
This paper proposes a novel formal criterion for secure compilation, providing strong security guarantees for components written in unsafe, low-level languages with C-style undefined behavior. Unlike recent proposals focused on protecting the trace properties of a single component against an adversarial context, this criterion models dynamic compromise in a system of mutually distrustful components. Each component is protected from others until it receives an input triggering undefined behavior, causing compromise and enabling attacks on uncompromised components. The paper demonstrates a secure compilation chain for an unsafe language with buffers, procedures, and components, compiled to a simple RISC abstract machine with built-in compartmentalization. The protection guarantees offered by this abstract machine can be achieved at the machine-code level using either software fault isolation or tag-based reference monitoring. The paper is working on machine-checked proofs demonstrating that the compiler satisfies the proposed secure compilation criterion. |||

title: Sensory Metrics of Neuromechanical Trust
Abstract: Digital media consumption, while unprecedented in its ability to deliver sensorimotor data, has been linked to poorly understood conditions like Internet Addiction Disorder and Internet Gaming Disorder. This paper proposes a mathematical framework for understanding human sensorimotor processing as a multiscale, continuous-time vibratory interaction. We quantify human informational needs using signal processing metrics such as entropy, noise, dimensionality, continuity, latency, and bandwidth. Based on these metrics, we define trust as a primitive statistical algorithm processing finely grained sensorimotor data from neuromechanical interaction. This definition implies that artificial sensorimotor inputs and interactions attracting low-level attention through frequent discontinuities and enhanced coherence will recalibrate a brain's representation of the world over the long term, violating the implicit statistical contract for which self-calibration evolved. This approach allows us to model addiction as a consequence of homeostatic regulation gone awry in novel environments, with digital dependency being a specific case where the recalibration caused by digital sensorimotor data drives further consumption. We predict that institutions can utilize these sensorimotor metrics to quantify media richness and improve employee well-being; that dyads and family-size groups will bond and heal best through low-latency, high-resolution multisensory interaction such as shared meals and reciprocated touch; and that individuals can improve sensory and sociosensory resolution through deliberate sensory reintegration practices. We conclude that humans are the victims of their own success, their skilled hands filling the world with captivating things and their innocent eyes eagerly following.

title: On spectral radii of unraveled balls
Abstract: Given a graph $G$, the unraveled ball of radius $r$ centered at a vertex $v$ is the ball of radius $r$ centered at $v$ in the universal cover of $G$. We prove a lower bound on the maximum spectral radius of unraveled balls of fixed radius. We show that if the average degree of $G$ after deleting any ball of radius $r$ is at least $d$, then its second largest eigenvalue is at least $2\sqrt{d-1}\cos(\frac{\pi}{r+1})$.

title: Replacement AutoEncoder: A Privacy-Preserving Algorithm for Sensory Data Analysis
Abstract: The proliferation of sensors in mobile devices, Internet of Things (IoT), and wearable devices generates time-series measurements of physical activities. While access to this data is crucial for applications like health monitoring and activity recognition, it can also reveal potentially sensitive information about individuals, which is difficult to protect using traditional privacy methods. This paper proposes a privacy-preserving sensing framework for managing access to time-series data, balancing utility and privacy. We introduce Replacement AutoEncoder, a novel algorithm that learns to transform discriminative features corresponding to sensitive inferences into features observed in non-sensitive inferences, safeguarding user privacy. This efficiency is achieved through a user-customized objective function for deep autoencoders. Our replacement method not only eliminates the possibility of recognizing sensitive inferences but also eliminates the possibility of detecting their occurrence, addressing a major weakness of other approaches like filtering and randomization. We evaluate the algorithm's efficacy in an activity recognition task within a multi-sensing environment using extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets. Our results demonstrate the ability to retain the recognition accuracy of state-of-the-art techniques while preserving the privacy of sensitive information. Finally, we utilize GANs to detect the occurrence of replacement after data release, showing that this is possible only if the adversarial network is trained on the users' original data.

title: Social Learning Against Data Falsification in Sensor Networks
Abstract: Surveillance and sensor networks play a crucial role in the Internet of Things, but sensor nodes are often vulnerable to tampering due to their widespread deployment. This letter focuses on data falsification attacks where an intelligent attacker takes control of critical network nodes, including fusion centers. To address this security challenge, we propose a data aggregation scheme based on social learning, mimicking the way agents make decisions in social networks. Our findings suggest that social learning enhances network resilience even when a significant portion of nodes are compromised. Finally, we demonstrate the suitability of our scheme for sensor networks by developing a low-complexity algorithm facilitating the social learning data fusion rule in devices with limited computational power.

title: Planck-scale distribution of nodal length of arithmetic random waves
Abstract: We investigate the nodal length of random toral Laplace eigenfunctions ("arithmetic random waves") restricted to decreasing domains ("shrinking balls"), down to the Planck scale. We find that, up to a natural scaling, for "generic" energies, the variance of the restricted nodal length follows the same asymptotic law as the total nodal length, and these are asymptotically fully correlated. This allows, among other things, for a statistical reconstruction of the full toral length based on partial information. A key novel ingredient of our work, borrowed from number theory, is the use of bounds for the so-called spectral Quasi-Correlations, i.e., unusually small sums of lattice points lying on the same circle.

title: Hierarchical Fog-Cloud Computing for IoT Systems: A Computation Offloading Game
Abstract: Fog computing, providing low-latency computing services at the network edge, enables the emerging Internet of Things (IoT) systems. This paper examines the allocation of fog computing resources to IoT users in a hierarchical computing paradigm encompassing fog and remote cloud computing services. We formulate a computation offloading game to model the competition between IoT users and allocate limited fog node processing power efficiently. Each user aims to maximize its own quality of experience (QoE), reflecting its satisfaction with computing services in terms of reduced computation energy and delay. Employing a potential game approach, we prove the existence of a pure Nash equilibrium and provide an upper bound for the price of anarchy. Given that the time complexity to reach equilibrium increases exponentially with the number of users, we propose a near-optimal resource allocation mechanism and prove that in a system with $N$ IoT users, it achieves an $\epsilon$-Nash equilibrium in $O(N/\epsilon)$ time. Through numerical studies, we evaluate the users' QoE and equilibrium efficiency. Our findings reveal that the proposed mechanism benefits more users compared to existing offloading mechanisms. Additionally, our proposed mechanism significantly reduces computation delay and enables low-latency fog computing services for delay-sensitive IoT applications.

title: The Removal Lemma for Tournaments
Abstract: Suppose one needs to modify the direction of at least $\epsilon n^2$ edges of an $n$-vertex tournament $T$ to make it $H$-free. A standard application of the regularity method shows that in this case, $T$ contains at least $f^*_H(\epsilon)n^h$ copies of $H$, where $f^*_H$ is some tower-type function. It has been observed that many graph/digraph problems become simpler when assuming the host graph is a tournament. It is natural to ask if the removal lemma becomes easier when assuming the digraph $G$ is a tournament. Our main result is a precise characterization of the tournaments $H$ for which $f^*_H(\epsilon)$ is polynomial in $\epsilon$, stating that such a bound is achievable if and only if $H$'s vertex set can be partitioned into two sets, each spanning an acyclic directed graph. The proof of this characterization relies on a novel application of a regularity lemma for matrices due to Alon, Fischer, and Newman, and on probabilistic variants of Ruzsa-Szemerédi graphs. Finally, we show that even when restricted to tournaments, deciding if $H$ satisfies the condition of our characterization is an NP-hard problem.

title: Joint Radio Resource Allocation, 3D Placement and User Association of Aerial Base Stations in IoT Networks
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel method for joint radio resource allocation (RRA), three-dimensional placement (3DP), and user association of aerial base stations (ABSs) as a key problem in Internet of Things (IoT) networks. Our proposed model considers two schemes: a) line of sight (LoS) and b) generalized. In the LoS scheme, all ABSs must have line-of-sight to IoT users. In the generalized scheme, ABSs can have line-of-sight to some IoT users and non-line-of-sight to others. The primary goal is to minimize the overall transmit power of IoT users while satisfying quality of service (QoS) constraints in the uplink scenario. To solve the complex optimization problems, we decompose them into two subproblems: the 3DP subproblem and the joint RRA and user association (JRU) subproblem. We utilize Semi Definite Relaxation (SDR) and Geometric Programming (GP) to address the optimization problems. Finally, through simulations, we evaluate the performance of the proposed schemes for various network parameters.

title: On the Philosophy of Bitcoin/Blockchain Technology: Is it a Chaotic, Complex System?
Abstract: The philosophy of blockchain technology encompasses blockchain ontology, its characterization, creation, implementation, adoption, operation in the world, and evolution over time. This paper investigates whether Bitcoin/blockchain can be considered a complex system and, if so, whether it exhibits chaotic behavior. Beyond academic curiosity, a positive response would raise concerns about the likelihood of Bitcoin/blockchain entering a 2010-Flash-Crash-type chaotic regime, with potentially catastrophic consequences for financial systems based on it. The paper begins by highlighting relevant details of the Bitcoin/blockchain ecosystem, including the blockchain itself, bitcoin end users (payers and payees), capital gains seekers, miners, full node maintainers, and developers, along with their interactions. We then briefly discuss the Information Theory of Complex Systems for later use. Finally, we analyze the blockchain using Crutchfield's Statistical Complexity measure. The obtained low non-null statistical complexity value suggests that the blockchain may be considered algorithmically complicated but unlikely to be a complex system and unlikely to enter a chaotic regime.

title: Robots as-a-Service in Cloud Computing: Search and Rescue in Large-scale Disasters Case Study
Abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) is poised to enable a vast array of applications by connecting objects like sensors and robots over the internet. IoT applications range from healthcare to autonomous vehicles and include disaster management. Enabling these applications in cloud environments necessitates the design of appropriate IoT Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IoT IaaS) to simplify the provisioning of IoT objects as cloud services. This paper presents a case study on search and rescue IoT applications in large-scale disaster scenarios. It proposes an IoT IaaS architecture that virtualizes robots (IaaS for robots) and provides them to upstream applications as-a-Service. Node- and Network-level robot virtualization are supported. The proposed architecture satisfies identified requirements such as the need for a unified description model for heterogeneous robots, a publication/discovery mechanism, and federation with other IaaS for robots when needed. A validating proof of concept is developed, and experiments are conducted to evaluate its performance. Lessons learned and prospective research directions are discussed.

title: Knowledge is at the Edge! How to Search in Distributed Machine Learning Models
Abstract: With the rise of the Internet of Things and Industry 4.0, a massive amount of data is generated at the network edge. Due to limited computing power, this data is currently sent to the cloud where centralized machine learning models are trained to extract higher-level knowledge. Recent developments in specialized machine learning hardware for mobile devices usher in a new era of distributed learning, raising a new research question: how can we search in distributed machine learning models? Machine learning at the network edge offers benefits such as low-latency inference and enhanced privacy. These distributed machine learning models can also be personalized for human users, specific contexts, or application scenarios. Since training data remains on the devices, control over potentially sensitive data is preserved as it is not shared with a third party. This new form of distributed learning results in the partitioning of knowledge across multiple devices, making access challenging. This paper tackles the problem of finding specific knowledge by forwarding a search request (query) to the device best equipped to answer it. To this end, we employ an entropy-based quality metric that considers the context of a query and the learning quality of a device. We demonstrate that our forwarding strategy achieves over 95% accuracy in an urban mobility scenario using data from 30,000 people commuting in Trento, Italy.

title: A Robust Dynamic Edge Network Architecture for the Internet-of-Things
Abstract: A massive number of devices are expected to perform sensing, processing, and control tasks in cyber-physical Internet-of-Things (IoT) systems, demanding new applications and connectivity requirements. In this context, limited spectrum resources must accommodate high traffic volumes with stringent requirements for low latency, high reliability, and energy efficiency. Traditional centralized network architectures may not be able to meet these requirements due to backhaul link congestion. This article presents a novel design for a robust dynamic edge network architecture (RDNA) for IoT that leverages recent advances in mobile devices (e.g., their ability to act as access points, storage and computing capabilities) to dynamically harness unused resources and alleviate network congestion. However, traffic dynamics can compromise the availability of terminal access points and channels, impacting network connectivity. The proposed design incorporates solutions at the physical, access, networking, application, and business layers to improve network robustness. The high density of mobile devices provides alternatives for close connectivity, reducing interference and latency, thus increasing reliability and energy efficiency. Moreover, the computing capabilities of mobile devices bring intelligence to the edge, which is desirable for autonomous and intelligent decision-making. A case study illustrates the performance of RDNA. Potential applications of this architecture in the context of IoT are outlined. Finally, some challenges for future research are presented.

title: Short-Packet Downlink Transmission with Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access
Abstract: This work introduces downlink non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) into short-packet communications. NOMA has the potential to enhance fairness and spectral efficiency compared to orthogonal multiple access (OMA) for low-latency downlink transmission, making it attractive for the emerging Internet of Things. We consider a two-user downlink NOMA system with finite blocklength constraints, optimizing transmission rates and power allocation. We investigate the trade-off between transmission rate, decoding error probability, and transmission latency measured in blocklength. A one-dimensional search algorithm is proposed to address the challenges arising from the achievable rate affected by finite blocklength and the unguaranteed successive interference cancellation. We also analyze the performance of OMA as a benchmark to fully demonstrate the benefits of NOMA. Our simulation results show that NOMA significantly outperforms OMA in terms of achieving higher effective throughput under the same finite blocklength constraint or incurring lower latency to achieve the same effective throughput target. Interestingly, we find that with finite blocklength, the advantage of NOMA over OMA is more pronounced when the effective throughput targets at the two users become more comparable.

title: True self energy function and reducibility in effective scalar theories. (Revised)
Abstract:
This is the revised version of Sections I-IV of the paper https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevD.89.125022, originally published in 2014. The original text was insufficiently clear and contained typos (due to my error). This revised version addresses these issues. 

Original abstract: This is the eighth paper in the series dedicated to the systematic study of effective theories. We discuss the renormalization of the one-loop two-leg functions in multicomponent effective scalar theory. It is shown that only a part of the numerous contributions that appear in the general expression for a two-leg graph can be considered as the true self-energy function. This part is completely determined by the values of minimal coupling constants; it is the only part that should be considered in the conventional process of summing Dyson's chain, leading to an explicit expression for the full propagator. The other parts provide well-defined finite corrections for graphs with more than two legs (n > 2). It is also shown that there is no need to introduce renormalization prescriptions for the higher derivatives of the two-leg function on the mass shell; the requirements of finiteness and diagonability are sufficient.

title: Lagrange's Theorem for Binary Squares
Abstract: We demonstrate how to prove theorems in additive number theory using a decision procedure based on finite automata. Among other results, we obtain the following analogue of Lagrange's theorem: every natural number greater than 686 is the sum of at most four natural numbers whose canonical base-2 representation is a binary square, that is, a string of the form xx for some block of bits x. The number four is optimal in this context. While we cannot embed this theorem itself in a decidable theory, we show that stronger lemmas that imply the theorem can be embedded in decidable theories, and we demonstrate how automated methods can be used to search for these stronger lemmas.

title: Working Group 5: Physics with Heavy Flavours
Abstract: This paper summarizes selected topics discussed during Working Group 5 of the Deep Inelastic Scattering 2017 conference, "Physics with Heavy Flavours," related to the study of charm, bottom, and top quark physics. While the programme of this Working Group was structured by thematic areas, this conference fostered intense cross-pollination between traditionally distinct research lines. All four LHC experiments contribute to heavy-flavor physics, with some degree of overlap in most areas, while experiments at other accelerators provide vital input in complementary kinematic regions. Theorists can now incorporate input from a wider range of sources, and experimentalists focus on measurements that maximize utility. The interplay of LHC heavy quark cross-section measurements with DIS expertise is significantly improving PDF precision, leading to much improved models that, among other things, better inform the prospects for future colliders.

title: 3D Printing of 2D Atomically Thin Materials
Abstract: The emerging paradigm of Internet of Things technologies necessitates device miniaturization to combine several functional components, such as sensors, actuators, and powering elements, on a single on-chip platform. A crucial requirement is for these devices to have a small footprint, necessitating three-dimensional extension to ensure adequate performance. Three-dimensional printing is a suitable technique for realizing devices with complex architectures and virtually any size. While its use has primarily been at the macroscale, this paper reports the first 3D printed architectures via robocasting of two-dimensional atomically thin transition metal dichalcogenides, demonstrating their use as miniaturizable supercapacitors. The structures are fabricated via direct printing of a liquid ink composed of chemically exfoliated 2D nanosheets. These 3D printed architectures exhibit footprints on the mm2 scale with micron-sized features, demonstrating mechanical robustness and chemical stability. They exhibit areal capacitance of 1450 mF/cm2, rivalling and surpassing comparable devices. Microsupercapacitors comprising two-dimensional atomically thin sheets enable miniaturization and upscaleable production technologies for widespread adoption.

title: Link Quality Aware Channel Allocation for Multichannel Body Sensor Networks
Abstract: Body Sensor Networks (BSNs) are a typical Internet-of-Things (IoT) application for personalized healthcare. They consist of economically powered, wireless, and implanted medical monitoring sensor nodes designed to continuously collect medical information from target patients. Multichannel communication is often used in BSNs to reduce spectrum competition among the numerous sensor nodes, and the problem of channel assignment has attracted significant research attention. Health sensing data in BSNs often needs to be delivered to a sink node (or server) before a certain deadline for real-time monitoring or health emergency alarms. Therefore, deadlines are crucial for multichannel allocation and scheduling. While existing works aim to meet deadlines, they often overlook the impact of unreliable wireless links. Consequently, health sensing data can still be overdue due to scheduled lossy links. Additionally, potential collisions in the schedules can cause considerable delays in delivering sensing data. This paper proposes a novel deadline-driven Link quality Aware Channel Assignment scheme (LACA) that considers link quality, deadlines, and collisions jointly. LACA prioritizes links with urgent deadlines and heavy collisions. Moreover, LACA allows for the exploitation of spare slots for retransmissions on lossy links, further reducing retransmission delay. Extensive simulation experiments show that, compared to existing approaches, LACA can better utilize the wireless spectrum and achieve higher packet delivery ratio before the deadline.

title: Recent Advances in Information-Centric Networking based Internet of Things (ICN-IoT)
Abstract: Information-Centric Networking (ICN) is emerging as a promising approach to address the shortcomings of current IP-address-based networking. ICN models are based on naming the content to overcome address-space scarcity, accessing the content via name-based routing, caching the content at intermediate nodes for reliable and efficient data delivery, and self-certifying contents for enhanced security. The evident benefits of ICN in terms of fast and efficient data delivery and improved reliability make it a highly promising networking model for Internet of Things (IoTs) environments. IoT aims to connect anyone and/or anything at any time, by any path, in any place. Over the past decade, IoTs have attracted both industry and research communities. However, IoTs are an emerging research field still in its infancy. This paper explores the potential of ICN for IoTs by providing a state-of-the-art literature survey. We briefly discuss the feasibility of ICN features and their models (and architectures) in the context of IoT. Subsequently, we present a comprehensive survey of ICN-based caching, naming, security, and mobility approaches for IoTs with appropriate classification. Furthermore, we present operating systems (OS) and simulation tools for ICNIoT. Finally, we identify important research challenges and issues faced by ICN for IoTs.

title: Management of solar energy in microgrids using IoT-based dependable control
Abstract: Solar energy generation requires efficient monitoring and management as we transition towards technologies for net-zero energy buildings. This paper presents a dependable control system based on the Internet of Things (IoT) to control and manage the energy flow of renewable energy collected by solar panels within a microgrid. Data for optimal control includes not only measurements from local sensors but also real-time meteorological information retrieved from online sources. To achieve system fault tolerance across the distributed control system featuring multiple controllers, dependable controllers are developed to control and optimize the tracking performance of photovoltaic arrays to maximize solar radiation capture and maintain system resilience and reliability in real time. These controllers can operate despite failures of one or more redundant controllers due to communication, hardware, or cybersecurity issues. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. |||

title: XYZ Privacy
Abstract:
Future autonomous vehicles will play a crucial role in the emerging Internet of Things (IoT), generating, collecting, aggregating, and consuming massive amounts of data. While data communications in vehicles are notoriously challenging, the privacy of this data has received less attention. Ensuring data privacy is essential for developing secure and efficient transportation solutions.

This paper introduces the XYZ Privacy mechanism, a novel method that allows data creators to submit multiple contradictory responses to a query while preserving data utility, measured as the absolute error from the original data. The mechanism is scalable and secure, enabling the obfuscation of sensitive data, such as location data, while maintaining its usefulness.  The approach integrates seamlessly with existing systems, like Waze, using a new cryptographic primitive called Function Secret Sharing for non-attributable data writes, achieving an order of magnitude improvement over default implementations.

title: Optimization of Privacy-Utility Trade-offs under Informational Self-determination
Abstract:
The proliferation of the Internet of Things (IoT) generates vast quantities of personal data from smart devices, including smartphones, wearables, and embedded sensors. Analyzing this data requires transferring it to centralized computational systems, raising concerns about user privacy. Data consumers managing these systems may not prioritize user privacy, focusing instead on improving utility, often measured by performance, cost, and quality of service.

This paper investigates the trade-off between data utility and privacy in data analysis.  It explores parameterizations of privacy settings, which balance maximum utility with minimum privacy and vice versa, using various data masking techniques, including differential privacy. The paper analyzes both homogeneous data sharing, where privacy settings are applied uniformly, and heterogeneous data sharing, where users control their data sharing. A novel computational framework is introduced for measuring and optimizing privacy-utility trade-offs under both scenarios, providing theoretical and empirical insights into the impact of data sharing diversity on privacy-utility trajectories.

title: Artificial Neural Networks-Based Machine Learning for Wireless Networks: A Tutorial
Abstract:
Next-generation wireless networks must support ultra-reliable, low-latency communication and manage a massive number of Internet of Things (IoT) devices in real-time, within a highly dynamic environment. Meeting these stringent quality-of-service (QoS) requirements demands integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning into the wireless infrastructure and end-user devices.

This paper provides a comprehensive tutorial on machine learning, specifically focusing on artificial neural networks (ANNs) and their applications in wireless communications. It presents a thorough overview of different neural network types, including feed-forward, recurrent, spiking, and deep neural networks, covering their architectures, training procedures, challenges, and opportunities. The paper examines a wide range of wireless communication problems amenable to ANN solutions, from unmanned aerial vehicle communication to virtual reality and edge caching, providing detailed examples of use cases and future research directions. This tutorial offers a comprehensive overview of machine learning techniques tailored to the needs of future wireless networks.

title: Concurrent Kleene Algebra: Free Model and Completeness
Abstract: Concurrent Kleene Algebra (CKA) was introduced as a framework for reasoning about concurrent programs. This paper proves the completeness of the CKA axioms with bounded parallelism for the semantics proposed in the original paper. This result settles a conjecture by Hoare and collaborators, establishing that these semantics form the free model for this fragment.  Furthermore, the techniques developed in this paper are reusable, enabling the use of pomset automata as an operational model for CKA.

title: Five-Nines Reliable Downward Routing in RPL
Abstract:
Despite a decade of research in low-power data collection, reaching arbitrary nodes in a network remains a significant challenge. The leading low-power IPv6 routing protocol, RPL, is often studied in multipoint-to-point scenarios, making downward routing (from root to node) particularly challenging. This hinders the development of Internet of Things applications that involve actuation.

This paper focuses on achieving industrial-grade reliability levels (1e-5 failure rate) in RPL downward routing.  It classifies the different causes of packet loss and introduces mechanisms to mitigate each source.  The paper proposes a gradient metric that favors reliable links, enhances neighborhood awareness for accurate link selection, and ensures robust routing state maintenance and packet forwarding.  Through extensive experiments on four testbeds with up to 352 nodes, the paper demonstrates RPL downward routing with loss rates in the order of 1e-5.  The solution is further validated on a low-power TSCH scheduler, achieving sub-percent low duty cycles and a channel utilization of 0.07% at every node, spread over 16 channels.

title: Distributed Hybrid Simulation of the Internet of Things and Smart Territories
Abstract:
This paper explores the use of hybrid simulation to model and represent the Internet of Things (IoT).  Hybrid simulation combines multiple modeling and simulation modalities to represent complex scenarios.  The approach decomposes complex scenarios into simpler ones, each simulated using a specific strategy.  These simulation building blocks are synchronized and coordinated.  This methodology is particularly well-suited for IoT setups, which often involve heterogeneous scenarios due to the massive deployment of sensors and devices.

The paper presents a use case for simulating smart territories, a novel view of decentralized geographical spaces that leverages IoT to manage resources sustainably.  Three different simulation models are combined: an adaptive agent-based parallel and distributed simulator, an OMNeT++ based discrete event simulator, and a script-language simulator based on MATLAB.  Performance analysis confirms the viability of using hybrid simulation to model complex IoT scenarios.

title: The Quest for Scalability and Accuracy in the Simulation of the Internet of Things: an Approach based on Multi-Level Simulation
Abstract: This paper presents a methodology for simulating the Internet of Things (IoT) using multi-level simulation models.  This approach allows for tuning the level of detail in different parts of the model without compromising scalability.  As a use case, a two-level simulator is developed to study the deployment of smart services in rural territories.  The higher level uses a coarse-grained, agent-based adaptive parallel and distributed simulator.  This simulator spawns OMNeT++ model instances to evaluate wireless communication issues in more detail in specific areas of the simulated world.  The performance evaluation confirms the viability of multi-level simulations for IoT environments.

title: McDiarmid Drift Detection Methods for Evolving Data Streams
Abstract:
Internet of Things (IoT) domains, such as sensor networks, smart cities, and social networks, generate vast amounts of data that are unbounded, rapidly evolving, and dynamically changing over time.  These changes, known as concept drifts, are caused by variations in the underlying data generation mechanisms.  In classification settings, concept drift can render previously learned models inaccurate, unsafe, and unusable.

This paper introduces the McDiarmid Drift Detection Method (MDDM) for detecting and handling concept drift.  MDDM utilizes McDiarmid's inequality to detect drift by sliding a window over prediction results and associating window entries with weights.  Higher weights are assigned to recent entries to emphasize their importance.  The algorithm compares a weighted mean of elements inside the window with the maximum weighted mean observed so far.  A significant difference between these means, bounded by McDiarmid's inequality, indicates a concept drift.  Extensive experimentation on synthetic and real-world data streams demonstrates that MDDM outperforms existing methods in detecting concept drift, with shorter detection delays, lower false negative rates, and high classification accuracy.

title: Sandwich semigroups in locally small categories I: Foundations
Abstract:
This article explores the theory of sandwich semigroups in locally small categories.  For fixed objects $i$ and $j$ in a locally small category $S$, the set of morphisms $i \to j$ forms a semigroup under an operation defined using a fixed morphism $a \in S_{ji}$.  This semigroup, called a sandwich semigroup, is denoted by $S_{ij}^a$.

The paper delves into the structural properties of sandwich semigroups, examining regularity, Green's relations, and stability.  It explores the relationships between these properties on $S_{ij}^a$ and the whole category $S$.  The paper then identifies a condition called sandwich regularity, which ensures that the set of regular elements of $S_{ij}^a$ forms a subsemigroup.  Under this condition, the structure of the semigroup of regular elements is analyzed, relating it to certain regular subsemigroups of $S_{ii}$ and $S_{jj}$ and a regular sandwich monoid defined on a subset of $S_{ji}$.  The paper also investigates combinatorial invariants like the rank of various semigroups, providing lower bounds and showing their sharpness under a specific condition.  Applications to concrete categories of transformations and partial transformations are discussed in a separate part.

title: FOCAN: A Fog-supported Smart City Network Architecture for Management of Applications in the Internet of Everything Environments
Abstract:
The smart city vision leverages emerging communication technologies, including Fog Computing (FC), to significantly reduce latency and energy consumption in Internet of Everything (IoE) devices running various applications. FC distinguishes itself by distributing communication and computing resources over the wired/wireless access network, providing resource augmentation and cyberforaging capabilities for resource-limited devices.  Smart city applications aim to improve urban flow management and enable real-time responses to challenges arising in user transactions.

This article presents Fog Computing Architecture Network (FOCAN), a multi-tier architecture for fog-supported smart cities.  In FOCAN, applications running on IoE devices collaboratively compute, route, and communicate through the smart city environment, reducing latency, improving energy provisioning, and enhancing service efficiency for diverse devices.  FOCAN emphasizes minimizing data transfer to distant devices, focusing on covering the nearest region for each IoT application.  The paper defines three types of communication between FOCAN devices to manage applications effectively. FOCAN's main advantage is its ability to provide services with low energy usage and efficiency.  Simulation results for a case study demonstrate the significant impact of FOCAN's energy-efficient solution on the communication performance of various devices in smart cities.

title: Cloud/fog computing resource management and pricing for blockchain networks
Abstract:
Blockchain mining requires solving resource-intensive proof-of-work puzzles, making it challenging to implement on mobile devices. This paper explores edge computing as a solution for mobile blockchain, focusing on resource management and pricing strategies for supporting mobile blockchain applications.

The paper proposes a two-stage Stackelberg game to maximize the profit of the edge computing service provider and the individual utilities of miners. The service provider sets the price of edge computing nodes in the first stage, while miners decide on their service demand based on the observed prices in the second stage.  The paper analyzes the sub-game perfect equilibrium in each stage for both uniform and discriminatory pricing schemes using backward induction.  For uniform pricing, the existence and uniqueness of the Stackelberg equilibrium are validated by identifying the best response strategies of miners.  For discriminatory pricing, the existence and uniqueness of the equilibrium are proven using Variational Inequality theory.  The paper concludes with real experimental results to justify the proposed model.

title: Time Series Management Systems: A Survey
Abstract:
The collection of time series data is growing rapidly due to the increased deployment of monitoring and automation systems, ranging from household IoT devices to large-scale distributed Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs).  Managing and analyzing these vast amounts of data requires specialized Time Series Management Systems (TSMSs) to overcome the limitations of general-purpose Database Management Systems (DBMSs).

This paper presents a comprehensive analysis and classification of TSMSs developed through academic and industrial research.  The classification is organized into categories based on the observed system architectures.  The paper provides an overview of each system, highlighting its motivational use case, functionality for storage and querying of time series, components, and capabilities regarding stream processing and approximate query processing (AQP).  The paper concludes by summarizing research directions proposed by other researchers and presenting a vision for a next-generation TSMS.

title: Decentralized User-Centric Access Control using PubSub over Blockchain
Abstract:
This paper presents a mechanism that empowers users to control access to their data collections.  Building upon fundamental security mechanisms, the solution utilizes capabilities, access lists, and access rights based on well-established formal notions for access control.

The proposed mechanism is practical, correct, auditable, transparent, distributed, and decentralized, making it suitable for emerging environments like the Internet of Things, smart cities, precision medicine, and autonomous cars.  It leverages proven principles and practices used in distributed authorization, cryptocurrencies, and scalable computing.

title: Real-Time Wind Noise Detection and Suppression with Neural-Based Signal Reconstruction for Mult-Channel, Low-Power Devices
Abstract:
Active wind noise detection and suppression techniques are essential for enhancing speech recognition (ASR) functionality in smart glasses and other wearable and smart devices within the broader Internet of Things (IoT). This paper introduces two algorithms for wind noise detection and suppression, designed for challenging, low-energy environments.

The first algorithm, Real-Time Wind Detection (RTWD), uses low-dimensional signal features to accurately discriminate the presence of wind noise.  For suppression, the Attentive Neural Wind Suppression (ANWS) algorithm utilizes a neural network to reconstruct the wearer's speech signal from wind-corrupted audio.  The paper presents real-time experiments conducted with low-power, multi-microphone devices and a wind simulator, testing the algorithms under various wind intensities and challenging detection criteria.
label: AI

title: Checking and Enforcing Security through Opacity in Healthcare Applications
Abstract:
The Internet of Things (IoT) has the potential to revolutionize healthcare, benefiting hospitals, doctors, and patients. However, protecting IoT healthcare systems from interference, including service attacks and malware, poses a significant challenge. Opacity, a confidentiality property, describes a system's ability to hide certain behaviors from passive observers.

This paper introduces an IoT-based heart attack detection system designed to safeguard patient privacy while providing life-saving capabilities.  The paper focuses on verifying and enforcing opacity in three forms to detect potential privacy leaks in the system.  Furthermore, it develops an efficient Symbolic Observation Graph (SOG)-based algorithm for enforcing opacity.

title: Neutrino Mass, Leptogenesis, and Dark Matter from The Dark Sector with $U(1)_{D}$
Abstract:
This paper proposes a new extension to the Standard Model (SM) by introducing a dark sector with additional particles and a local $U(1)_{D}$ symmetry.  This dark sector introduces new physics beyond the SM, leading to several interesting implications.

The model generates the tiny neutrino mass through a hybrid see-saw mechanism, achieves leptogenesis at the TeV scale, and accounts for cold dark matter, all stemming from the dark sector.  The paper highlights the feasibility of testing the model predictions and probing the dark sector in upcoming experiments.
label: AI

title: Privacy Preserving Identification Using Sparse Approximation with Ambiguization
Abstract:
This paper proposes a privacy-preserving encoding framework for identification applications in biometrics, physical object security, and the Internet of Things (IoT).  The framework is based on a sparsifying transform, consisting of a trained linear map, an element-wise nonlinearity, and privacy amplification. The transform and amplification are not symmetric for data owners and users.

The paper demonstrates a close relationship between the proposed approach and Sparse Ternary Codes (STC), a recent information-theoretic concept for fast approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search in high-dimensional feature spaces.  STC offers significant benefits over sparse approximation and binary embedding approaches.  The paper shows that the proposed approach preserves the privacy of both the database outsourced to a server and the data user, while maintaining low computational cost, storage, and communication burdens.
label: AI

title: Reservoir Computing using Stochastic p-Bits
Abstract:
This paper presents a general hardware framework for building networks that directly implement Reservoir Computing, a software method for implementing and training Recurrent Neural Networks, particularly suited for temporal inferencing and pattern recognition.  A specific example of a candidate hardware unit based on a combination of soft-magnets, spin-orbit materials, and CMOS transistors is provided.

Efficient non-von-Neumann hardware implementation of reservoir computers can open up new possibilities for integrating temporal neural networks into a wide range of emerging systems, such as Internet of Things (IoT), industrial controls, bio- and photo-sensors, and self-driving automobiles.

title: Efficient Convolutional Neural Network For Audio Event Detection
Abstract:
Wireless distributed systems used in sensor networks, the Internet of Things, and cyber-physical systems demand high resource efficiency. Advanced preprocessing and classification of data at the network edge can reduce communication demand and the amount of data processed centrally.  In the area of distributed acoustic sensing, combining algorithms with high classification rates and resource-constrained embedded systems is crucial.

This paper addresses the challenges of implementing acoustic event detection algorithms, which typically have high memory and computational demands, on resource-constrained edge devices. It applies structural optimizations to a convolutional neural network for audio event detection, achieving a reduction in memory requirement by a factor of more than 500, a reduction in computational effort by a factor of 2.1, and an improvement in performance by 9.2%.
label: AI

title: Ambient Backscatter Networking: A Novel Paradigm to Assist Wireless Powered Communications
Abstract:
Ambient backscatter communication technology, which leverages existing radio frequency (RF) signal resources for communication without requiring an external power supply or dedicated carrier emitter, is emerging as a promising choice for self-sustainable communication systems. This technology enables sustainable and independent communications, opening up new applications for the Internet of Things (IoT).

This paper investigates the integration of ambient backscatter with wireless powered communication networks (WPCNs).  It provides an overview of backscatter communication systems, focusing on ambient backscatter technology.  The paper proposes a novel hybrid transmitter design that combines the advantages of both ambient backscatter and wireless powered communications.  In a cognitive radio environment, a multiple access scheme is introduced to coordinate hybrid data transmissions.  The performance evaluation shows that the hybrid transmitter outperforms traditional designs.  The paper concludes by discussing open issues related to ambient backscatter networking. |||
