title: Proactive Defense Against Physical Denial of Service Attacks using Poisson Signaling Games
Abstract:
The Internet of Things (IoT) holds immense potential to enhance energy efficiency, healthcare, and transportation systems. However, its susceptibility to cyberattacks, particularly distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, poses a significant threat. DDoS attacks overwhelm servers with excessive traffic, but in the context of IoT devices integrated into cyber-physical systems (CPS), they can be exploited to launch "physical" denial-of-service (PDoS) attacks, overloading the physical bandwidth of a CPS. This paper delves into the population-based risk of IoT devices targeted by malware for PDoS attacks. To model bot recruitment, we introduce a "Poisson signaling game," a signaling game with an unknown number of receivers possessing varying detection capabilities for deception. This framework is then used to analyze two mechanisms (legal and economic) for deterring botnet recruitment. Equilibrium analysis reveals that 1) defenders can effectively limit botnet activity, and 2) legislating minimum security standards has a limited impact, while incentivizing active defense can significantly reduce botnet activity. This research provides a quantitative foundation for proactive PDoS defense strategies. ||| 
Wireless powered backscatter communications offers a compelling solution for next-generation low-power sensor networks, such as the Internet of Things (IoT). However, backscattering faces challenges related to collisions from multiple simultaneous transmissions and the dyadic backscatter channel, which significantly attenuates the received signal at the reader. This paper addresses backscatter communications in sensor networks from a large-scale perspective, considering various collision resolution techniques: directional antennas, ultra-narrow band transmissions, and successive interference cancellation. Analytical expressions are derived for the decoding probability, demonstrating the significant gains achievable through these techniques. ||| 
The proliferation of mobile devices and the Internet of Things (IoT) has heightened the importance of developing robust privacy solutions for time series applications. While differential privacy is the gold standard for database privacy, many time series applications require a different type of guarantee. Recent research has explored the use of inferential privacy to address these situations. However, a significant barrier to practical implementation of inferential privacy lies in its lack of graceful composition. Even if the same or related sensitive data is used in multiple releases that are individually secure, the combined release may exhibit poor privacy properties. This paper investigates the composition properties of a form of inferential privacy called Pufferfish when applied to time-series data. While general Pufferfish mechanisms may not compose gracefully, we demonstrate that a specific Pufferfish mechanism, known as the Markov Quilt Mechanism, recently introduced, possesses strong composition properties comparable to those of pure differential privacy when applied to time series data. ||| 
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable performance in various machine learning tasks. As sensor-equipped Internet of Things (IoT) devices become ubiquitous in modern life, the ability to execute computationally intensive CNN inference on resource-constrained devices has become increasingly critical. To address this challenge, this paper presents Cappuccino, a framework for synthesizing efficient inference software targeting mobile System-on-Chips (SoCs). Cappuccino proposes techniques for efficient parallelization of CNN inference targeting mobile SoCs, exploring the underlying tradeoffs. Experiments with different CNNs on three mobile devices demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. ||| 
This paper is a comprehensive survey of the Internet of Things (IoT), covering fundamental concepts, known but unpublished findings, and published but less-known information. ||| 
Designing quality into products is a fundamental principle of modern quality management philosophies. Design for X (DfX) techniques provide guidelines, heuristics, and metrics to ensure specific quality attributes are incorporated into a design. While hundreds of papers have explored DfX approaches, few researchers have systematically investigated the application of multiple DfX within a specific problem context. As the Internet of Things (IoT) evolves, the boundaries between people, computers, and objects will become increasingly blurred, highlighting the need for more holistic design. This paper utilizes mixed methods to examine the utility of DfX in the emerging IoT ecosystem. We identify DfX applicable to IoT-related design and uncover gaps requiring further research and development. The findings of this study can assist designers and quality managers in selecting or developing appropriate DfX for designing components for the Internet of Things (IoT), supporting actionable strategies for quality and customer satisfaction. ||| 
Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) offer significant accuracy in image detection. To enable image detection using CNNs on Internet of Things (IoT) devices, this paper proposes a streaming hardware accelerator that optimizes energy efficiency by minimizing unnecessary data movement. The accelerator utilizes a unique filter decomposition technique to support arbitrary convolution window sizes. Additionally, max pooling functionality can be computed in parallel with convolution using a separate pooling unit, enhancing throughput. A prototype accelerator was implemented using TSMC 65nm technology with a core size of 5mm2. The accelerator supports major CNNs and achieves a peak throughput of 152GOPS and an energy efficiency of 434GOPS/W at 350mW, making it a promising hardware accelerator for intelligent IoT devices. ||| 
Given a property of representations satisfying a basic stability condition, Ramakrishna developed a variant of Mazur's Galois deformation theory for representations with that property. This paper introduces an axiomatic definition of pseudorepresentations with such a property. Notably, we show that pseudorepresentations with this property enjoy a well-defined deformation theory, generalizing Ramakrishna's theory to pseudorepresentations. ||| 
This paper complements the work by Villone and Rampf (2017) titled "Hermann Hankel's On the general theory of motion of fluids, an essay including an English translation of the complete Preisschrift from 1861" and associated documents. We provide a critical assessment of Hankel's work, which covers many important aspects of fluid dynamics from a Lagrangian-coordinates perspective: variational formulation in the spirit of Hamilton for elastic (barotropic) fluids, transport (what we would now call Lie transport) of vorticity, the Lagrangian significance of Clebsch variables, etc. Hankel's work is also placed within the context of previous and future research, spanning nearly two centuries: from Lagrange's 1760-1761 Turin paper on variational approaches to mechanics and fluid mechanics problems to Arnold's 1966 founding paper on the geometrical/variational formulation of incompressible flow. The 22-year-old Hankel, who tragically died 12 years later, emerges as a highly innovative master of mathematical fluid dynamics, fully deserving Riemann's assessment that his Preisschrift contains "all manner of good things." ||| 
The Internet of Things (IoT) aims to provide ubiquitous connectivity among diverse entities or "things." While its goal is to deliver effective and efficient solutions, the security of devices and the network remains a significant challenge. The large number of connected devices and the ad-hoc nature of the system further exacerbate the situation. Therefore, security and privacy have become paramount concerns for the IoT. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of privacy and security challenges in the IoT. We examine these challenges from the perspective of technologies and architecture used. The paper focuses on inherent IoT vulnerabilities and security challenges across various layers, based on the security principles of data confidentiality, integrity, and availability. This survey analyzes articles published for the IoT and relates them to the current security landscape and future projections. ||| 
Despite the flourishing research on Information-Centric Networking (ICN), its adoption remains elusive. This paper proposes Edge-ICN, a novel approach for deploying ICN in a single large network, such as an Internet Service Provider's network. Edge-ICN requires only an SDN-based network supporting the OpenFlow protocol with ICN-aware nodes at the network edges, offering the same benefits as a clean-slate ICN architecture without the deployment complexities. Moreover, by proxying legacy traffic and transparently forwarding it through Edge-ICN nodes, all existing applications can operate seamlessly while benefiting from advantages such as native support for scalable anycast, multicast, and multi-source forwarding. This paper demonstrates how the proposed functionality at the network edge can specifically benefit CoAP-based IoT applications. Our measurements reveal that Edge-ICN incurs the same average control plane overhead for name resolution as a centralized approach, while enabling IoT applications to utilize anycast, multicast, and multi-source forwarding primitives. ||| 
The buildup and release of musical tension is a crucial aspect of the listening experience. A veridical computational model of perceived musical tension would be a valuable tool for various music informatics applications. This paper presents a novel approach to modeling harmonic tension based on a distributed representation of chords. The underlying hypothesis is that harmonic tension as perceived by human listeners is related, among other factors, to the expectedness of harmonic units (chords) within their local harmonic context. We train a word2vec-type neural network to learn a vector space that captures contextual similarity and expectedness, and define a quantitative measure of harmonic tension based on this representation. To assess the model's accuracy, we compare its outputs on well-defined chord classes and cadential contexts to results from relevant empirical studies in music psychology. Statistical analysis demonstrates that the model's predictions align closely with empirical evidence obtained from human listeners. ||| 
The Internet of Things (IoT) is providing unprecedented observational data used for managing Smart City utilities. Edge and Fog gateway devices play a vital role in IoT deployments, acquiring real-time data and enacting controls. Edge-computing is emerging as a first-class paradigm to complement Cloud-centric analytics. However, a key limitation is the lack of a platform-as-a-service for applications spanning Edge and Cloud. This paper proposes ECHO, an orchestration platform for dataflows across distributed resources. ECHO's hybrid dataflow composition can operate on diverse data models – streams, micro-batches, and files – and interface with native runtime engines like TensorFlow and Storm to execute them. ECHO manages the application's lifecycle, including container-based deployment and a registry for state management. It can schedule dataflows on different Edge, Fog, and Cloud resources and dynamically migrate tasks between resources. We validate the ECHO platform for executing video analytics and sensor streams for Smart Traffic and Smart Utility applications on Raspberry Pi, NVidia TX1, ARM64, and Azure Cloud VM resources, presenting our results. ||| 
This paper addresses the challenge of accurately simulating the Internet of Things (IoT). IoT simulation allows for evaluating strategies for deploying smart services across diverse territories. However, the heterogeneity of scenarios significantly complicates this task, necessitating sophisticated modeling and simulation techniques. This paper explores novel approaches for providing scalable simulation scenarios that enable real-time execution of massively populated IoT environments. We focus on novel hybrid and multi-level simulation techniques, which, when combined with agent-based, adaptive Parallel and Distributed Simulation (PADS) approaches, can provide highly detailed simulations on demand. To support this claim, we present a use case involving the simulation of vehicular transportation systems. ||| 
Multidimensional data is becoming increasingly prevalent, driven by the rise of the Internet of Things (IoT), leading to the need to ingest and analyze data streams at faster rates than ever before. Certain industrial IoT applications require ingesting millions of records per second while processing queries on recently ingested and historical data. Unfortunately, existing database systems suitable for multidimensional data exhibit low per-node ingestion performance. Even if they can scale horizontally in distributed settings, they require a large number of nodes to meet these ingest demands. This paper evaluates a single-node multidimensional data store designed for high-velocity sensor data. Its design centers around a two-level indexing structure, with an in-memory R*-tree as the global index and serialized kd-trees as local indices. This study focuses on records with numerical indexing fields and range queries, evaluating ingest throughput, query response time, and storage footprint. Our findings show that the adopted design streamlines data ingestion, offering ingress rates two orders of magnitude higher than those of Percona Server, SQLite, and Druid. Our prototype also reports query response times comparable to or better than those of Percona Server and Druid, and compares favorably in terms of storage footprint. Additionally, we evaluate a kd-tree partitioning scheme for grouping incoming streamed data records. Compared to a random scheme, this scheme produces less overlap between groups of streamed records, but contrary to our expectations, this reduced overlap does not translate into improved query performance. In contrast, local indices prove much more beneficial to query performance. We believe this research is valuable for practitioners and researchers alike interested in developing database systems for high-velocity multidimensional data. ||| 
In the pursuit of a smart future information society, the Internet of Things (IoT) and Content Centric Networking (CCN) break down two key barriers for both front-end sensing and back-end networking. However, a missing piece in current research is the lack of knowledge that penetrates both sensing and networking, holistically integrating them. This paper envisions leveraging emerging machine learning and deep learning techniques to create knowledge-driven aspects for facilitating design. Specifically, we can extract knowledge from collected data to achieve reduced data volume, enhanced system intelligence and interactivity, improved service quality, and communication with better controllability and lower cost. We refer to this knowledge-oriented traffic control and networking management paradigm as Knowledge Centric Networking (KCN). This paper presents the rationale, benefits, related works, and research opportunities of KCN. ||| 
Trigger-Action platforms are an emerging class of web-based systems that enable users to create automation rules (or recipes) in the form of "If there is a smoke alarm, then turn off my oven." These platforms connect various online services, including Internet of Things devices, social networks, and productivity tools, by obtaining OAuth tokens on behalf of users. Unfortunately, these platforms also introduce a long-term security risk. If compromised, an attacker can misuse the OAuth tokens belonging to millions of users, arbitrarily manipulating their devices and data. This work first quantifies the risk users face in the context of If-This-Then-That (IFTTT). We conduct the first empirical analysis of IFTTT's OAuth-based authorization model using semi-automated tools we built to overcome the challenges of IFTTT's closed-source nature and online service API inconsistencies. Our findings reveal that 75% of IFTTT's channels, an abstraction of online services, utilize overprivileged OAuth tokens, increasing risks in the event of a compromise. Even if OAuth tokens were to be privileged correctly, a compromise of IFTTT would not prevent their misuse. Motivated by this empirical analysis, we design and evaluate Decoupled-IFTTT (dIFTTT), the first trigger-action platform where users do not have to grant highly privileged access to their online services. Our design pushes the notion of fine-grained OAuth tokens to its extreme, ensuring that even if the cloud service is controlled by an attacker, it cannot misuse OAuth tokens to invoke unauthorized actions. Our evaluation establishes that dIFTTT imposes modest overhead: it adds less than 15ms of latency to recipe execution time and reduces throughput by 2.5%. ||| 
Given a logic presented in a sequent calculus, a natural question arises regarding the equivalence of proofs: to determine whether two given proofs are equated by any denotational semantics, i.e., any categorical interpretation of the logic compatible with its cut-elimination procedure. This notion can usually be captured syntactically by a set of rule permutations. Generally, proof nets can be defined as combinatorial objects that provide canonical representatives of equivalence classes of proofs. The existence of proof nets for a logic provides a solution to the equivalence problem of that logic. In certain fragments of linear logic, it is possible to define proof nets with desirable computational properties, making them a suitable representation of proofs for studying the cut-elimination procedure, among other things. Recent research has shown that such a notion of proof nets cannot exist for the multiplicative (with units) fragment of linear logic due to the equivalence problem for this logic being Pspace-complete. This paper investigates the multiplicative-additive (without unit) fragment of linear logic and demonstrates its close relationship to binary decision trees. We construct a representation of proofs based on binary decision trees, reducing proof equivalence to decision tree equivalence, and provide a converse encoding of binary decision trees as proofs. Our main result establishes that the complexity of the proof equivalence problem for the studied fragment is Logspace-complete. ||| 
Several domains have adopted the increasing use of IoT-based devices to collect sensor data for generating abstractions and perceptions of the real world. This sensor data is multi-modal and heterogeneous in nature. This heterogeneity induces interoperability issues during the development of cross-domain applications, limiting the reusability of sensor data for creating new applications. As a solution, semantic approaches have been proposed in the literature to address interoperability problems related to sensor data. Various ontologies have been developed to handle different aspects of IoT-based sensor data collection, ranging from discovering IoT sensors for data collection to applying reasoning on collected sensor data for drawing inferences. This paper surveys these existing semantic ontologies to provide an overview of recent developments in this field. We highlight the fundamental ontological concepts (e.g., sensor capabilities and context-awareness) required for IoT-based applications and survey the existing ontologies that incorporate these concepts. Based on our study, we identify the shortcomings of currently available ontologies, paving the way for the need for a common unified ontology for the IoT domain. ||| 
Energy harvesting is a promising technology for the Internet of Things (IoT), enabling self-sustainability for involved devices. However, the intermittent and unreliable nature of harvested energy demands intelligent management of device operation to ensure sustained performance of the IoT application. This work addresses the problem of maximizing the quality of reported data under the constraints of energy harvesting, energy consumption, and communication channel impairments. Specifically, we propose an energy-aware joint source-channel coding scheme that minimizes the expected data distortion, considering realistic models of energy generation and energy spent by the device to process data when communication occurs over a Rayleigh fading channel. The performance of the scheme is optimized using a Markov Decision Process framework. |||

title: Application Protocols enabling Internet of Remote Things via Random Access Satellite Channels
Abstract: The rapid increase in Machine-to-Machine (M2M) and Internet of Things (IoT) traffic necessitates the use of satellites for efficient data delivery. This study explores the performance of two prevalent M2M/IoT protocol stacks on a satellite Random Access (RA) channel, based on the DVB-RCS2 standard. The key performance metric is the completion time, aiming to identify the protocol stack that delivers the most efficient performance.

title: Simultaneous Lightwave Information and Power Transfer (SLIPT) for Indoor IoT Applications
Abstract: Simultaneous Lightwave Information and Power Transfer (SLIPT) offers a promising solution for indoor Internet-of-Things (IoT) applications. This paper proposes novel SLIPT strategies that can be implemented through Visible Light or Infrared communication systems, using a simple solar panel-based receiver. These strategies, namely Adjusting transmission, Adjusting reception, and Coordinated adjustment of transmission and reception, are performed at the transmitter, receiver, or both. The study addresses the trade-off between harvested energy and quality-of-service (QoS) by maximizing energy while ensuring the required QoS. Two optimization problems are formulated and solved to achieve this objective. Computer simulations confirm the optimality of the proposed solutions, demonstrating a significant increase in harvested energy compared to SLIPT with fixed policies.

title: Asynchronous Massive Access and Neighbor Discovery Using OFDMA
Abstract: A fundamental challenge in wireless Internet of Things (IoT) is enabling reliable access to shared channels for a massive number of devices, particularly those transmitting short, random, and sporadic messages. This paper proposes a novel signaling scheme for grant-free massive access, where each device encodes its identity and/or information within a sparse set of tones, implemented in the form of orthogonal frequency-division multiple access (OFDMA). Under certain conditions and assuming bounded unknown device delays, sparse OFDMA is proven to allow arbitrarily reliable asynchronous device identification and message decoding with a codelength of O(K(log K + log S + log N)). Here, N represents the total device population, K is the number of active devices, and log S corresponds to the number of bits a device can transmit (including its identity). By leveraging the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), computational complexity for discovery and decoding can be made sub-linear in the total device population. To demonstrate the concept, a specific design is presented that can identify up to 100 active devices out of 2^38 possible devices with up to 20 symbols of delay and moderate signal-to-noise ratios and fading. This codelength significantly outperforms standard slotted ALOHA and carrier-sensing multiple access (CSMA) schemes.

title: Machine-to-Machine (M2M) Communications in Virtualized Cellular Networks with MEC
Abstract: Machine-to-machine (M2M) communications, a vital aspect of the Internet-of-Things (IoT), are explored in this paper in the context of virtualized cellular networks. The integration of mobile edge computing (MEC) aims to reduce energy consumption, optimize computing resource allocation, and enhance computing capabilities. Based on different functions and quality of service (QoS) requirements, the physical network is virtualized into multiple virtual networks, allowing each Mobile Terminal Communicating Device (MTCD) to choose the appropriate virtual network for access. The random access process of MTCDs is modeled as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) to minimize system cost, comprising both energy consumption and computing task execution time. To facilitate network integration, software-defined networking (SDN) is introduced to handle diverse protocols and standards. Extensive simulation results show that the proposed scheme significantly improves system performance compared to existing solutions.

title: ROS Navigation Tuning Guide
Abstract: The ROS navigation stack, a powerful tool for mobile robot navigation, provides a reliable mechanism for moving robots from one location to another. The navigation stack processes data from odometry, sensors, and environmental maps to generate safe paths for robot execution. Optimizing the performance of this stack requires fine-tuning its parameters, a complex task that can be time-consuming and challenging. This article aims to guide users through the process of fine-tuning navigation parameters, providing a reference for understanding the "how" and "why" behind parameter settings. The guide assumes familiarity with the ROS navigation stack and focuses on optimization techniques. It summarizes the author's experience with the ROS navigation stack.

title: Rate-Distortion Classification for Self-Tuning IoT Networks
Abstract: Future wireless sensor networks and the Internet of Things are expected to embrace a software-defined paradigm, where protocol parameters and behaviors are dynamically adjusted based on signal statistics. New protocols can be injected as software in response to specific events. For example, data compressors can be reprogrammed on-the-fly as the monitored signal type or its statistical properties change. This paper focuses on a lossy compression scenario where the application tolerates some signal distortion in exchange for improved energy efficiency. To fully realize the benefits of this paradigm, an automatic sensor profiling approach is discussed, utilizing machine learning techniques (support vector machines and neural networks) to automatically assess the signal class and its corresponding rate-distortion curve. This curve can be reliably estimated on-the-fly by computing a small number of statistical features from time windows containing a few hundred samples.

title: The IoT energy challenge: A software perspective
Abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) ushers in a new era of embedded applications, many of which rely on deeply embedded systems powered by limited or unreliable energy sources like batteries or energy harvesters. Meeting the energy demands of these applications presents a significant challenge, potentially hindering the future growth of the IoT. Software holds the key to optimizing energy consumption in these systems. Currently, programmers lack feedback on how their software affects energy consumption. Energy transparency, a concept that makes a program's energy consumption visible from hardware to software, can provide this crucial feedback. This paper discusses the need for energy transparency in software development and highlights how it can be implemented to address the IoT energy challenge.

title: Interpolation and extrapolation of strictly singular operators between $L_p$ spaces
Abstract: This study investigates the interpolation and extrapolation properties of strictly singular operators between different L_p spaces. The analysis focuses on the structure of strictly singular non-compact operators between L_p-L_q spaces, clarifying the relationship between strict singularity and the L-characteristic set of an operator. In particular, the paper extends Krasnoselskii's interpolation theorem for compact operators to the class of strictly singular operators.

title: StreamLearner: Distributed Incremental Machine Learning on Event Streams: Grand Challenge
Abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) generates massive amounts of streaming data from smart devices, demanding automatic analysis for realization. The Complex Event Processing (CEP) paradigm promises low-latency pattern detection on event streams. However, extending CEP systems with Machine Learning (ML) capabilities, such as online training and inference, is essential for detecting fuzzy patterns (e.g., outliers) and improving pattern recognition accuracy during runtime through incremental model training. This paper presents a distributed CEP system called StreamLearner for ML-enabled complex event detection. The proposed programming model and data-parallel system architecture enable a wide range of real-world applications and allow for dynamic scaling of system resources for low-latency, high-throughput event processing. The DEBS Grand Challenge 2017 case study (anomaly detection in smart factories) seamlessly integrates into the StreamLearner API. Experiments validate StreamLearner's scalability and high event throughput.

title: Variety of $(d + 1)$ dimensional Cosmological Evolutions with and without bounce in a class of LQC -- inspired Models
Abstract: The bouncing evolution of a universe within Loop Quantum Cosmology is effectively described by a set of effective equations involving a function sin(x). This paper generalizes these equations to (d + 1) dimensions and to any function f(x). The cosmological evolutions in these Loop Quantum Cosmology-inspired models vary depending on the function f(x), ranging from singular to non-singular. The paper delves into a detailed study of these evolutions. Notably, the scale factor a(t) is found to be proportional to t^(2q/((2q - 1)(1 + w)d)) for f(x) = x^q, and explicit Kasner-type solutions are obtained when w = 2q - 1. A particularly intriguing result is that for f(x) = √x, the evolution is non-singular and the scale factor a(t) grows exponentially at a rate determined not by a constant density but by a quantum parameter related to the area quantum.

title: A conceptual approach to the problem of action-angle variables
Abstract: This paper presents a general conceptual approach to the problem of action-angle variable existence for dynamical systems, leveraging the fundamental conservation property of associated torus actions: anything preserved by the system is also preserved by the associated torus actions. This approach leads to: a) a concise and conceptual proof of the classical Arnold-Liouville-Mineur theorem, b) a unifying framework for recovering known results on action-angle variables in various contexts with simplified proofs, and c) new findings on action-angle variables in various contexts, including systems on contact manifolds, presymplectic and Dirac manifolds, action-angle variables near singularities, stochastic systems, and more. Even in the absence of natural action variables, this approach yields useful normal forms for dynamical systems, not necessarily integrable.

title: Fog Computing in Medical Internet-of-Things: Architecture, Implementation, and Applications
Abstract: In the rapidly growing market of the Internet of Things (IoT), the healthcare sector is expected to significantly benefit from the proliferation of wearables and internet-connected sensors. These devices collect and transmit unprecedented data on symptoms, medication, food intake, and daily activities, impacting health and wellness. However, IoT-driven healthcare faces several challenges: 1) the increasing demand for data storage on cloud servers, leading to complex medical big data analysis, 2) security and privacy concerns regarding data communication, 3) the cost and energy consumption associated with continuous data transmission, and 4) the difficulty of managing and maintaining sensors directly from cloud servers. This book chapter introduces Fog Computing as a solution for medical IoT. Conceptually, Fog Computing acts as a service-oriented intermediary layer, bridging sensors and cloud servers to facilitate connectivity, data transfer, and local database querying. The chapter describes the implementation and testing of a Fog Computing system using Intel Edison and Raspberry Pi, enabling the acquisition, computation, storage, and communication of various medical data, including pathological speech data of individuals with speech disorders, Phonocardiogram (PCG) signal for heart rate estimation, and Electrocardiogram (ECG)-based Q, R, S detection.

title: Reducing biases on $H_0$ measurements using strong lensing and galaxy dynamics: results from the EAGLE simulation
Abstract: Cosmological parameter constraints derived from time-delay lens observations are becoming increasingly precise. However, these measurements can be significantly biased and scattered due to factors such as the mass-sheet degeneracy. To estimate these uncertainties, the paper analyzes strong lenses from the largest EAGLE hydrodynamical simulation. By applying a mass-sheet transformation to the radial density profiles of lenses and selecting lenses near isothermality, the study finds that the bias on H0 can be reduced to 5% with an intrinsic scatter of 10%, confirming previous results from a different simulation dataset. The paper further investigates whether combining lensing observables with kinematic constraints helps mitigate this bias. No significant dependence of the bias on lens model parameters or observational properties of the galaxy is detected, but a bias may persist depending on the source-lens configuration. Cross lenses provide an accurate estimate of the Hubble constant, while fold (double) lenses tend to be biased low (high). With kinematic constraints, double lenses show bias and intrinsic scatter of 6% and 10%, respectively, while quad lenses show bias and intrinsic scatter of 0.5% and 10%, respectively. For lenses with a reduced χ^2 > 1, a power-law dependence of the χ^2 on the lens environment (number of nearby galaxies) is observed. Finally, the paper models in greater detail two significantly biased double lenses, demonstrating the potential to remove the bias and suggesting that remaining biases could be reduced by carefully considering additional systematic uncertainties.

title: IoT-enabled Distributed Cyber-attacks on Transmission and Distribution Grids
Abstract: The Internet of things (IoT) will enable the interconnection and simultaneous control of distributed electrical loads. However, the deployment of IoT-operated loads without adequately addressing potential cyber-security challenges raises significant technical and regulatory concerns. A hypothetical scenario where an ensemble of IoT-controlled loads can be hacked with malicious intent to compromise electrical grid operations is envisioned. Under this scenario, an attacker could utilize geographically distributed IoT-controlled loads to manipulate their net power injections into the electrical grid, potentially disrupting normal grid operations. This paper presents a modeling framework for analyzing grid impacts of distributed cyber-attacks on IoT-controlled loads. The framework demonstrates how such attacks propagate from the distribution electrical grid, where IoT-controlled loads are expected to be installed, to the transmission electrical grid. Techno-economic interactions between the distribution and transmission electrical grids are accounted for using bilevel optimization. The case study is conducted on modified versions of the 3-area IEEE Reliability Test System (RTS) and the IEEE 13-bus distribution feeder. Numerical results show that the severity of such attacks depends on the penetration level of IoT-controlled loads and the attacker's strategy.

title: Smart Wireless Communication is the Cornerstone of Smart Infrastructures
Abstract: Emerging smart infrastructures, such as Smart City, Smart Grid, Smart Health, and Smart Transportation, require intelligent wireless connectivity. However, current wireless networks cannot meet the demands of these smart infrastructures. A new wireless infrastructure is needed to address unprecedented requirements for agility, reliability, security, scalability, and partnerships. This paper discusses the convergence of machine learning (ML), the Internet-of-Things (IoT), and robotics, leading to a revolution in how we interact with technology. Smart infrastructures monitor and process vast amounts of data collected from a dense and wide distribution of heterogeneous sensors (e.g., the IoT) and web applications like social media. Machine learning allows real-time detection of patterns and relationships in the data over space, time, and applications, enabling predictions, resource management, decision-making, and device actuation to optimize metrics such as cost, health, safety, and convenience.

title: The Augmentation Property of Binary Matrices for the Binary and Boolean Rank
Abstract: This paper introduces the Augmentation property for binary matrices with respect to different rank functions. A matrix A has the Augmentation property for a given rank function if, for any subset of column vectors x_1,...,x_t where the rank of A does not increase when augmented separately with each vector x_i (1 ≤ i ≤ t), the rank also does not increase when augmenting A with all vectors x_1,...,x_t simultaneously. While this property holds trivially for the usual linear rank over the reals, it becomes more complex when considering the binary and boolean rank of a matrix. The paper proves a necessary and sufficient condition for this property to hold under the binary and boolean rank of binary matrices: a matrix has the Augmentation property for these rank functions if and only if it has a unique base that spans all other bases of the matrix with respect to the given rank function. For the binary rank, a concrete characterization of a family of matrices exhibiting the Augmentation property is presented, based on the possible types of linear dependencies between rows of V in optimal binary decompositions of the matrix as A=U⋅V. The Augmentation property is then utilized to construct simple families of matrices where a gap exists between their real and binary rank and between their real and boolean rank.

title: Passive Classification of Source Printer using Text-line-level Geometric Distortion Signatures from Scanned Images of Printed Documents
Abstract: In the digital age, printed archives remain a crucial component in many critical domains, including contract papers, legal tenders, and proof of identity documents. With advancements in printing, scanning, and image editing techniques, forgeries on these legal documents pose a serious threat. The ability to easily and reliably identify the source printer of a printed document can significantly reduce this menace. Printer hardware introduces unique geometric distortions in printed character locations and shapes, invisible to the naked eye. These distortions, referred to as geometric distortions, can serve as a unique signature for each printer and can be used for printer classification. This paper proposes a set of features for characterizing text-line-level geometric distortions, termed geometric distortion signatures, and presents a novel system for utilizing them to identify the origin of a printed document. Extensive experiments conducted on thirteen printers demonstrate that the proposed system achieves state-of-the-art performance, achieving high accuracy even with limited training data. For four training and six test pages of three different fonts, the proposed method achieves a 99% classification accuracy.

title: Combining edge and cloud computing for mobility analytics
Abstract: Mobility analytics, leveraging data generated from the Internet of Mobile Things (IoMT), faces numerous challenges, ranging from ingesting data streams from a vast number of fog nodes and IoMT devices to preventing cloud overflow with useless massive data streams that can trigger bottlenecks. Data flow management is becoming a critical aspect of the IoMT, dictating where analytical tasks should run in the future. Data flows typically consist of out-of-order tuples with high input rates, and mobility analytics requires real-time data flow in both directions: from the edge to the cloud and vice-versa. Before transferring data streams to the cloud, edge data stream processing is necessary for detecting missing, broken, and duplicated tuples, as well as recognizing tuples with out-of-order arrival times. Analytical tasks like data filtering, data cleaning, and low-level data contextualization can be executed at the network edge. Conversely, more complex analytical tasks such as graph processing can be deployed in the cloud, and the results of ad-hoc queries and streaming graph analytics can be pushed to the edge as needed by user applications. Graphs provide efficient representations in mobility analytics, unifying knowledge about connectivity, proximity, and interaction among moving things. This poster describes preliminary results from an experimental prototype developed for supporting transit systems, combining edge and cloud computing to process transit data streams forwarded from fog nodes into a cloud. The research aims to understand how to perform meaningful mobility analytics on transit feeds by integrating cloud and fog computing architectures to enhance fleet management, mass transit, and remote asset monitoring.

title: Compactification of certain Kähler manifolds with nonnegative Ricci curvature
Abstract: This paper presents compactification theorems for certain complete Kähler manifolds with nonnegative Ricci curvature. Among other findings, it proves that a complete noncompact Kähler Ricci flat manifold with maximal volume growth and quadratic curvature decay is a crepant resolution of a normal affine algebraic variety. Furthermore, this affine variety degenerates in two steps to the unique metric tangent cone at infinity.

title: Hey, you, keep away from my device: remotely implanting a virus expeller to defeat Mirai on IoT devices
Abstract: Mirai is a botnet that targets outdated Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices. The disruptive Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack last year significantly impacted major Internet companies, causing intermittent service disruptions for millions of users. Since affected devices typically lack firmware update capabilities, removing these vulnerable devices from the wild poses a significant challenge. Both industry and academia have made substantial efforts to address this situation, but none of these efforts are easily deployable and simultaneously effective in resolving the problem. This paper proposes a collaborative defense strategy to combat Mirai. The key idea is to leverage human involvement in a minimally intrusive manner. During a negotiated time slot, a customer is required to reboot the compromised device, allowing a "white" Mirai operated by the manufacturer to immediately break into the clean-state IoT devices. The "white" Mirai then expels other malicious Mirai variants, blocks vulnerable ports, and maintains a heartbeat connection with the server operated by the manufacturer. If the heartbeat connection is lost, the server promptly re-implants the "white" Mirai. A full prototype of the proposed system has been implemented, and results demonstrate its effectiveness in evading Mirai attacks. |||

title: On the arithmetic of graphs
Abstract: The Zykov ring of signed finite simple graphs, defined with topological join as addition and compatible multiplication, is an integral domain but not a unique factorization domain. This is shown by its isomorphism to the strong Sabidussi ring, obtained through graph complements, which has disjoint union as addition. The Euler characteristic is a ring homomorphism from the strong ring to the integers, as proven by demonstrating the strong ring's homotopy to a Stanley-Reisner Cartesian ring. The Kuenneth formula holds for the strong ring, making the Poincaré polynomial compatible with its structure. The Zykov ring has the clique number as a ring homomorphism. Additionally, the Cartesian ring exhibits a multiplicative functor that associates a graph's connection Laplacian spectrum to it. This is due to the connection Laplacians behaving like adjacency matrices for the weak ring under multiplication. The strong ring product of two graphs contains both the weak and direct product graphs as subgraphs. The Zykov, Sabidussi, and Stanley-Reisner rings are manifestations of a network arithmetic with remarkable cohomological properties, dimensionality, and spectral compatibility, but the complexity of prime detection and factorization remain understudied. The Zykov arithmetic is illustrated with examples from the subring generated by point graphs, encompassing spheres, stars, and complete bipartite graphs. While formulated in graph theory, these constructions generalize to the larger category of finite abstract simplicial complexes.

title: CFI CaRE: Hardware-supported Call and Return Enforcement for Commercial Microcontrollers
Abstract: The increasing scale of Internet of Things (IoT) deployments has heightened concerns about IoT security, particularly memory corruption attacks that allow remote compromise of devices. Control-flow integrity (CFI) offers a promising and generic defense against these attacks. However, existing protection mechanisms for traditional computing environments, including CFI, require adaptation for the unique characteristics of IoT deployments. This paper addresses the challenges of enabling CFI on microcontroller (MCU) based IoT devices and introduces CaRE, the first interrupt-aware CFI scheme for low-end MCUs. CaRE leverages TrustZone-M security extensions in the ARMv8-M architecture to protect CFI metadata in a novel way. Its binary instrumentation approach preserves the memory layout of the target MCU software, enabling pre-built bare-metal binary code to be protected. The implementation on a Cortex-M Prototyping System demonstrates CaRE's security and acceptable performance and memory impact.

title: Smart Asset Management for Electric Utilities: Big Data and Future

Condition monitoring of assets generates large datasets during daily operations. The question arises: How can information be extracted from these vast quantities of data? Big data analytics, powered by machine learning techniques, challenges the notion of "rich data, poor information." In conjunction with technological advancements like the Internet of Things (IoT), big data analytics will play a pivotal role for electric utilities. This paper proposes pathways and guidelines to transform current asset management practices into smarter ones for the future.

title: A Review of Internet of Things Architecture, Technologies and Analysis Smartphone-based Attacks Against 3D printers
Abstract: Humans, seeking to alleviate the burden of laborious tasks, have turned to machines to work on their behalf. The Internet, with its latest technological advancements, provides platforms for human relaxation and unburdened feelings. The Internet of Things (IoT) field empowers human beings with intelligent decisions through Machine-to-Machine (M2M) communication globally. The significance of the IoT field is undeniable, especially considering the widespread adoption of applications like smartphones. IoT field sensors play a crucial role in sensing intelligent objects/things and making intelligent decisions after sensing them. The rapid development of smartphone-based applications globally poses a significant challenge for the IoT community: security against side channel attacks targeting highly intensive 3D printing systems. Smartphone-formulated Intellectual Property (IP) of side channel attacks investigates 3D printers in the physical domain by reconstructing G-code files through primitive operations. The smartphone (Nexus 5) effectively addresses key problems, including orientation fixing, model accuracy of frame size, and validating feasibility and effectiveness in real-world case studies against the 3D printer. The 3D printing market reached an estimated value of $20.2 billion in 2021. Thermal cameras are used to explore side channel attacks by reconstructing objects against 3D printers. The researcher analyzed IoT security issues and proposed strategies for future mitigation, including enhanced security mechanisms, encryption, and machine learning-based algorithms, utilizing latest technologies, schemes, and protocols efficiently.

title: Stochastic Modeling and Simulation of Viral Evolution
Abstract: RNA viruses exist as vast populations of closely related but genetically diverse entities known as quasispecies. Understanding the mechanisms governing the generation and maintenance of this extreme diversity is crucial for comprehending viral persistence and pathobiology in infected hosts. This paper explores quasispecies theory through a mathematical model based on multitype branching processes, aiming to elucidate the role of mechanisms contributing to viral diversity, persistence, and extinction. This understanding is achieved through a combination of computational simulations and theoretical analysis of the model. The mathematical model has been implemented into a computational platform capable of running simulations and presenting results in a graphical format in real time. Among other findings, the paper demonstrates that the establishment of virus populations can exhibit four distinct regimes from introduction into new hosts until reaching equilibrium or undergoing extinction. Simulations of various fitness distributions representing distinct environments within a host, both favorable and hostile to viral success, were conducted. The paper also addresses lethal mutagenesis and mutational meltdown, two mechanisms commonly used to explain the extinction of RNA virus populations. It establishes a correspondence between these two mechanisms, suggesting the existence of a unifying principle leading to the extinction of RNA viruses.

title: Memory Efficient Forwarding Information Base for Content-Centric Networking
Abstract: Content-Centric Networking (CCN) is a new paradigm for the future Internet, replacing TCP/IP networks by addressing content using hierarchically organized names. Unlike IP addresses, these names have arbitrary length and are larger than the four bytes of IPv4 addresses. The Forwarding Information Base (FIB) in CCN stores prefixes of names with corresponding forwarding faces, but long prefixes pose challenges for memory-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) devices. This work derives FIB requirements for IoT and surveys potential solutions. Memory-efficient FIB solutions based on hashes and Bloom-Filters are investigated, designed, and compared. For a large number of prefixes with equal distribution to faces, a FIB implementation based on Bloom-Filters is recommended. In all other cases, an implementation with hashes is suggested.

title: Topological finiteness properties of monoids. Part 1: Foundations
Abstract: This paper initiates the study of higher dimensional topological finiteness properties for monoids by developing the theory of monoids acting on CW complexes. The foundation for $M$-equivariant homotopy theory, where $M$ is a discrete monoid, is established. For projective $M$-CW complexes, fundamental results like the homotopy extension and lifting properties are proven, serving as the basis for the $M$-equivariant Whitehead theorems. A left equivariant classifying space is defined as a contractible projective $M$-CW complex. Its uniqueness (up to $M$-homotopy equivalence) is demonstrated, along with a canonical model via the nerve of the right Cayley graph category of the monoid. Topological finiteness conditions left-$\\mathrm{F}_n$ and left geometric dimension are then defined for monoids in terms of the existence of a left equivariant classifying space with appropriate finiteness properties. The bilateral notion of $M$-equivariant classifying space is introduced, proving uniqueness and providing a canonical model via the nerve of the two-sided Cayley graph category, leading to the definition of the associated finiteness properties bi-$\\mathrm{F}_n$ and geometric dimension. Connections between these topological finiteness properties and well-studied homological finiteness properties of monoids (important in string rewriting systems, including $\\mathrm{FP}_n$, cohomological dimension, and Hochschild cohomological dimension) are explored. The paper also develops the theory of $M$-equivariant collapsing schemes (i.e., $M$-equivariant discrete Morse theory) and applies it to provide topological proofs of Anick, Squier, and Kobayashi's results regarding the left-, right-, and bi-$\\mathrm{FP}_\\infty$ properties of monoids admitting presentations by complete rewriting systems.

title: Sequential Channel Estimation in the Presence of Random Phase Noise in NB-IoT Systems
Abstract: Channel estimation (CE) in narrowband Internet-of-Things (NB-IoT) systems is investigated, considering the impact of random phase noises arising from fluctuations in receiver and transmitter oscillators and residual frequency offset (FO). These noises occur due to discontinuous reception of repetition coded transmit data-blocks. While the coherent-time of fading channel can be assumed long due to the low mobility of NB-IoT user-equipments (UEs), these phase noises necessitate consideration before combining channel estimates over repetition copies to enhance accuracy. This paper derives a sequential minimum-mean-square-error (MMSE) channel estimator in the presence of random phase noise, sequentially refining CE with each received repetition copy. This estimator offers low complexity and minimal data storage. Simulations show that the proposed sequential MMSE estimator improves the mean-square-error (MSE) of CE by 1 dB in the low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) regime compared to a traditional sequential MMSE estimator that does not fully account for the effects of random phase noises.

title: Service Allocation in a Mobile Fog Infrastructure under Availability and QoS Constraints
Abstract: The next generation of mobile networks, namely 5G, and the Internet of Things (IoT) have introduced a large number of delay-sensitive services. To reduce latency, cloud services are migrating to the edge of networks, leading to the concept of Fog computing, where the edge actively participates in service execution. This emphasizes the importance of efficiently formulating and optimizing the problem of mapping service demand to supply. This work addresses this problem, taking into account two key aspects of service allocation in Fog: modeling the cost of executing a given set of services and the randomness of resource availability, which can stem from pre-existing load or server mobility. An integer optimization formulation is introduced to minimize the total cost while ensuring service execution despite uncertainty in resource availability.

title: COPSS-lite: Lightweight ICN Based Pub/Sub for IoT Environments
Abstract: Information Centric Networking (ICN) is a new networking paradigm that prioritizes content as a first-class entity, providing content to users regardless of its location. Publish/subscribe systems have gained popularity on the Internet, eliminating the need for users to request every content of interest. Content is delivered to interested users (subscribers) as and when it is published. CCN/NDN, popular ICN proposals widely accepted in the ICN community, lack an efficient pub/sub mechanism. COPSS enhances CCN/NDN with an efficient pub/sub capability. The Internet of Things (IoT) is a rapidly growing topic of interest in both academia and industry. Current IoT designs rely on IP, but IoT devices are resource-constrained, and IP is too heavy for their operation. IoT's information-centric nature makes ICN a more suitable candidate for supporting IoT environments. Although NDN and COPSS are effective for the Internet, their current full-fledged implementations are not suitable for resource-constrained IoT devices. CCN-lite, a lightweight, interoperable version of the CCNx protocol, supports IoT devices but lacks an efficient pub/sub mechanism. This paper presents COPSS-lite, an efficient and lightweight implementation of pub/sub for IoT. COPSS-lite enhances CCN-lite and supports multi-hop connection by incorporating the RPL protocol for low-power and lossy networks. A preliminary evaluation demonstrates operability with real-world sensor devices in an IoT lab. Results show that COPSS-lite is compact, operates on all platforms supporting CCN-lite, and offers significant performance benefits in IoT environments.

title: Swapping of Gaussian Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen steering
Abstract: Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen (EPR) steering, a quantum mechanical phenomenon, enables one party to steer the state of a distant party by exploiting shared entanglement, offering potential applications in secure quantum communication. This paper presents two swapping schemes of Gaussian EPR steering – single-channel and dual-channel schemes – through entanglement swapping. Two space-separated independent EPR steering states, without direct interaction, exhibit EPR steering after deterministic swapping. Comparison between the single-channel and dual-channel schemes reveals that the transmission distance of the single-channel scheme is significantly longer than the symmetric dual-channel scheme. Unlike entanglement swapping, one-way EPR steering occurs after swapping over lossy channels. Interestingly, the EPR steering direction changes in the dual-channel scheme. The paper also shows that excess noise in a quantum channel shortens the transmission distance of the swapping, potentially leading to the sudden death of EPR steering. The presented schemes provide a technical reference for remote quantum communications using EPR steering.

title: Multistatic Scatter Radio Sensor Networks for Extended Coverage
Abstract: Scatter radio, communication through reflection, has recently emerged as a viable ultra-low power solution for wireless sensor networks (WSNs). This work provides a detailed comparison between monostatic and multistatic scatter radio architectures. In the monostatic architecture, the reader acts as both the illuminating transmitter and receiver of signals scattered back from the sensors. The multistatic architecture employs multiple ultra-low cost illuminating carrier emitters and a single reader. Maximum-likelihood coherent and noncoherent bit error rate (BER), diversity order, average information, and energy outage probability comparisons are performed under dyadic Nakagami fading, addressing a gap in existing literature. The study reveals that: (i) the multistatic architecture surpasses the monostatic in diversity order, BER, and tag location-independent performance bounds; (ii) energy outage due to radio frequency (RF) harvesting for passive tags is less frequent in multistatic than monostatic architectures; and (iii) multistatic coverage exceeds that of monostatic. Furthermore, a proof-of-concept digital multistatic scatter radio WSN, featuring a single receiver, four low-cost emitters, and multiple ambiently-powered, low-bitrate tags, is experimentally demonstrated (at 13 dBm transmission power), covering an area of 3500 m$^2$. The research findings are applicable to the industries of WSNs, radio frequency identification (RFID), and emerging Internet-of-Things.

title: LoRaWAN in the Wild: Measurements from The Things Network

The measurement data covers the early stages up to the production-level deployment of LoRaWAN. The paper analyzes packet payloads, radio-signal quality, and spatio-temporal aspects to model and estimate the performance of LoRaWAN. Empirical findings are used in simulations to estimate packet loss.

title: Renewal-Theoretic Packet Collision Modeling under Long-Tailed Heterogeneous Traffic
Abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT), with its vision of billions of connected devices, introduces massive heterogeneity to wireless connectivity in unlicensed bands. Variations in medium access parameters, transmit power, and activity levels among coexisting networks result in detrimental cross-technology interference. The stochastic traffic distributions shaped under CSMA/CA rules, interfering network behavior, and channel fading pose challenges in modeling and analyzing the performance of interfered networks. To study the temporal interaction between traffic distributions of two coexisting networks, this paper develops a renewal-theoretic packet collision model and derives a generic collision-time distribution (CTD) function for an interfered system. The CTD function is applicable to any busy- and idle-time distributions of the coexisting traffic. As previous studies suggest long-tailed idle-time statistics in real environments, the model only requires the Laplace transform of long-tailed distributions to determine the CTD. Furthermore, a packet error rate (PER) model is presented under the proposed CTD and multipath fading of interfering signals. This model enables computationally efficient PER approximation for interference-limited cases, facilitating the analysis of interfered link performance.

title: A Mean-Field Stackelberg Game Approach for Obfuscation Adoption in Empirical Risk Minimization
Abstract: Data ecosystems are expanding in size and complexity due to online tracking, wearable computing, and the Internet of Things. However, privacy concerns threaten to erode the potential benefits of these systems. Users have developed obfuscation techniques to issue fake search engine queries, undermine location tracking algorithms, or evade government surveillance. These techniques create two conflicts: one between each user and the machine learning algorithms tracking them, and another between the users themselves. This paper uses game theory to capture the first conflict with a Stackelberg game and the second conflict with a mean field game. Both are combined into a dynamic and strategic bi-level framework that quantifies accuracy using empirical risk minimization and privacy using differential privacy. The equilibrium analysis identifies necessary and sufficient conditions for: 1) incentivizing each user to obfuscate if others are doing so; 2) enabling the tracking algorithm to avoid obfuscation by promising a level of privacy protection; and 3) ensuring that this promise is incentive-compatible for the tracking algorithm.

title: Blockchain based trust & authentication for decentralized sensor networks

title: Stranger Things about Forcing without AC

title: Facial Emotion Detection Using Convolutional Neural Networks and Representational Autoencoder Units
Abstract: Emotions, being subjective, have posed a long-standing challenge for industry, where leveraging knowledge and science behind labeled data and extracting constituent components is difficult. The results indicate that with fine-tuning and increased depth, the CNN model outperforms state-of-the-art methods for emotion recognition. title: The Samuel realcompactification of a metric space
Abstract: This paper introduces a realcompactification for any metric space (X, d), defined using the family of all real-valued uniformly continuous functions. It is referred to as the Samuel realcompactification, analogous to the well-known Samuel compactification associated with the family of all bounded real-valued uniformly continuous functions. The corresponding problem of Samuel realcompactness for metric spaces is studied, revealing a Kat\\v{e}tov-Shirota type result in this context. Completeness is replaced by Bourbaki-completeness (a notion recently introduced by the authors), and closed discrete subspaces are replaced by uniformly discrete ones. Specifically, it is proven that a metric space (X, d) is Samuel realcompact if and only if it is Bourbaki-complete and every uniformly discrete subspace of X has non-measurable cardinal. Consequently, it is derived that a normed space is Samuel realcompact if and only if it has finite dimension. This highlights the significant difference between realcompactness and Samuel realcompactness. The paper also presents results connecting this realcompactification with the Lipschitz realcompactification, the classical Hewitt-Nachbin realcompactification, and the completion of the initial metric space. |||

title: Lighting Two Candles With One Flame: An Unaided Human Identification Protocol With Security Beyond Conventional Limit
Abstract: For over two decades, designing a robust protocol to prevent recording-based attacks in the presence of a powerful eavesdropper remains a significant challenge. This challenge is further amplified during authentication, where the lack of a secure connection between the prover and verifier makes the system vulnerable to information leakage. Existing solutions focus on improving aspects of previous methods while overlooking areas where their proposed schemes are deficient, often leading to impractical or insecure solutions. To address these limitations, we introduce the concept of "leakage control," which restricts the inherent information leakage rate, enhancing both usability and security standards. Additionally, our scheme incorporates a threat detection strategy (based on the "honeyword" concept), proactively identifying and mitigating attacks. This two-pronged approach not only resolves the long-standing conflict between security and usability in practical scenarios but also safeguards the secret at both the client and server sides within a distributed framework, exceeding conventional security boundaries.

title: On the Fundamental Limits of Random Non-orthogonal Multiple Access in Cellular Massive IoT
Abstract: Machine-to-machine (M2M) communication forms the foundation of the Internet of Things (IoT) vision, enabling billions of multi-role devices to interact with each other or the underlying data transport infrastructure with minimal human intervention. Focusing on non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA), we investigate how devices can share the same radio resources for data transmission, maximizing channel efficiency. This approach has been shown to achieve optimal throughput from an information theoretic perspective. We analyze a realistic system model and assess performance in terms of throughput and energy efficiency in a NOMA scenario with a random packet arrival model. The analysis also derives the stability condition necessary to guarantee system performance.

title: Indoor UAV Navigation to a Rayleigh Fading Source Using Q-Learning
Abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are valuable tools for localizing victims, delivering first-aid, and maintaining wireless connectivity during search/rescue and public safety operations. Assuming the source transmits RF signals, we utilize a Q-learning algorithm to guide the UAV to the source's vicinity. Our findings demonstrate that optimizing the time averaging window and exploration rate for the Q-learning algorithm results in faster UAV navigation to the IoT device. As a result, Q-learning achieves optimal performance with significantly reduced convergence time.

title: Learning Belief Network Structure From Data under Causal Insufficiency
Abstract: Although belief networks (representing joint probability distributions) and causal networks (representing causal relationships) differ conceptually, they are closely intertwined. Both assume an underlying directed acyclic graph (DAG) structure representing relationships between variables. When the Markov and faithfulness conditions are met, a causal network effectively becomes a belief network. However, distinctions arise when recovering belief and causal network structures from data. Causal network structures may be incompletely recoverable from data as causal link directions might not be uniquely determined. However, a similar result is lacking for causally insufficient sets of variables. To address this, Spirtes, Glymour, and Scheines developed a CI algorithm, leaving some critical questions unanswered. This paper aims to resolve a key question: whether bidirectional edges (indicating a common cause) are sufficient to construct a belief network from the product of CI or if additional hidden variables need to be introduced.

title: User Selection and Widely Linear Multiuser Precoding for One-dimensional Signalling

The results reveal that WL processing can potentially double the number of simultaneous users compared to linear processing of one-dimensionally modulated signals. Additionally, a user selection algorithm compatible with WL processing of one-dimensionally modulated signals is proposed to address the growing number of communication devices. title: Defending against Phishing Attacks: Taxonomy of Methods, Current Issues and Future Directions

Then, we will provide a comprehensive taxonomy of various phishing attack types. Second, we will categorize existing solutions proposed in the literature to protect users from phishing, aligning them with the attack types identified in our taxonomy. Furthermore, we will analyze the impact of phishing attacks in the Internet of Things (IoT). title: Uniform generators, symbolic extensions with an embedding, and structure of periodic orbits
Abstract: For a topological dynamical system $(X, T)$, we define a uniform generator as a finite measurable partition such that the symmetric cylinder sets in the generated process uniformly shrink in diameter to zero. The problem of existence and optimal cardinality of uniform generators has led to new challenges in the theory of symbolic extensions. We first demonstrate that uniform generators can be identified with symbolic extensions with an embedding, meaning extensions with an equivariant measurable selector from preimages. We then focus on such extensions and aim to characterize the collection of corresponding extension entropy functions on invariant measures. For aperiodic zero-dimensional systems, we show that this collection coincides with that of extension entropy functions in arbitrary symbolic extensions. This collection is known to coincide with the set of all affine superenvelopes of the entropy structure of the system. In particular, we recover, after [Bu16], that an aperiodic zero-dimensional system is asymptotically h-expansive if and only if it admits an isomorphic symbolic extension.  Next, we examine systems with periodic points and introduce the concept of a period tail structure, which captures the local growth rate of periodic orbits.  Finally, we precisely identify the desired collection of extension entropy functions in symbolic extensions with an embedding: these are all the affine superenvelopes of the usual entropy structure that lie above a specific threshold function determined by the period tail structure. This characterization allows us to estimate (and in examples, compute precisely) the optimal cardinality of a uniform generator.

title: Learning Optimal Routing for the Uplink in LPWANs Using Similarity-enhanced epsilon-greedy

title: BRPL: Backpressure RPL for High-throughput and Mobile IoTs

title: Joint Uplink and Downlink Coverage Analysis of Cellular-based RF-powered IoT Network
Abstract: Ambient radio frequency (RF) energy harvesting has emerged as a promising solution for powering small devices and sensors in the massive Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystem due to its ubiquity and cost efficiency. This paper investigates joint uplink and downlink coverage in cellular-based ambient RF energy harvesting IoT, assuming the cellular network as the sole source of RF energy.  We adopt a time division-based approach for power and information transmission, dividing each time slot into three sub-slots: (i) a charging sub-slot where cellular base stations (BSs) act as RF chargers for IoT devices, with devices using harvested energy for information transmission and/or reception during the remaining two sub-slots, (ii) a downlink sub-slot for receiving information from the associated BS, and (iii) an uplink sub-slot for transmitting information to the associated BS. For this setup, we characterize the joint coverage probability, which represents the joint probability of a typical device successfully harvesting sufficient energy within the given time slot and achieving both uplink and downlink signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) coverage with respect to its associated BS. This metric significantly generalizes prior work on energy harvesting communications, which typically focused on downlink or uplink coverage separately. The key technical challenge lies in handling the correlation between the amount of energy harvested during the charging sub-slot and the information signal quality (SINR) in the downlink and uplink sub-slots. A dominant BS-based approach is developed to derive a tight approximation for this joint coverage probability. The THINGS (The HI Nearby Galactic Survey), recently extended to include a sample of 25 dwarf galaxies known as the LITTLE THINGS Survey, offers a valuable dataset for this purpose. This paper presents a comprehensive application of alternative gravitational models to the LITTLE THINGS survey, specifically focusing on conformal gravity and Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND). The analysis explores the results of fitting these models to the data, including the resulting rotation curve predictions. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates how both conformal gravity and MOND can account for the recently observed universal trends in centripetal accelerations in spiral galaxies. The authors posit that these two alternative gravitational models provide accurate descriptions of galactic dynamics without requiring the presence of dark matter.

title: Theory of optically controlled anisotropic polariton transport in semiconductor double microcavities
Abstract: Exciton polaritons in semiconductor microcavities exhibit a range of fundamental physical phenomena, some of which can be controlled by external fields. The transport of polaritons is influenced by the polaritonic spin-orbit interaction, arising from the splitting of transverse-electric and transverse-magnetic (TE-TM) modes. This interaction forms the basis for a polaritonic Hall effect, known as the optical spin Hall effect (OSHE). OSHE is associated with the formation of spin/polarization textures in momentum space, leading to anisotropic ballistic transport and corresponding textures in real space. Coulombic interactions between the excitonic components of polaritons can further impact OSHE. This paper presents a theoretical analysis of OSHE and its optical control in semiconductor double microcavities, which are particularly suitable for creating polaritonic reservoirs that influence the spin-texture-forming polaritons. The theory is formulated using a set of double-cavity spinor-polariton Gross-Pitaevskii equations. Numerical solutions highlight features such as controlled rotation of the spin texture in momentum space. The theory also allows for the identification of the effective magnetic field component that determines the optical control in phenomenological pseudo-spin models, expressed in terms of exciton interactions and the polariton density in the second lower polariton branch.

title: Decentralized demand response for temperature-constrained appliances
Abstract: The evolution of the power grid towards the so-called Smart Grid, where information technologies enhance the efficiency of electricity production, distribution, and consumption, allows for the utilization of fine-grained control enabled by Internet of Things (IoT) capabilities. This paper examines the demand-response potential of coordinating large numbers of appliances that must maintain a specific temperature within a fixed range through the ON/OFF functioning of a temperature modifier. A mathematical model and methods are introduced to coordinate appliances with given requirements, aiming to achieve a global energy demand reduction for a desired duration while satisfying temperature constraints and minimizing communication overhead. The paper quantifies the maximum power reduction achievable as a function of the reduction duration requested by the grid.

title: Fluorescent Troffer-powered Internet of Things: An Experimental Study of Electric-field Energy Harvesting
Abstract: This paper presents a novel energy harvesting architecture that utilizes ambient electric-field (E-field) emitted from fluorescent light fixtures. A copper plate, measuring 50 x 50 cm, is positioned within the ambient field to extract energy through capacitive coupling. A low voltage prototype is designed, structured, and tested on a conventional ceiling-type 4-light fluorescent troffer operating on a 50 Hz 220 V AC power grid. The harvester is shown to collect approximately 1.25 J of energy in 25 minutes when a 0.1 F super-capacitor is used. The paper provides both the equivalent circuit and the physical model of the proposed harvesting paradigm, and the attainable power is evaluated theoretically and experimentally. The harvested energy is intended for powering battery-less Internet of Things (IoT) networks responsible for sensing environmental parameters, analyzing the collected data, and remotely informing a higher authority within predefined periods.

title: An Authentication Protocol for Future Sensor Networks
Abstract: Authentication is a fundamental security service in Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) for ensuring secure data sessions. Sensor node authentication guarantees the confidentiality and validity of data collected by the sensor node, while user authentication ensures that only legitimate users can access the sensor data. In mobile WSNs, sensor and user nodes move across the network and exchange data with multiple nodes, leading to frequent authentication processes. The integration of WSNs with Internet of Things (IoT) introduces new WSN architecture with stricter security requirements, including the need for multiple concurrent secure data sessions. Concurrent data sessions increase the frequency of re-authentication proportionally to the number of concurrent connections, making security more challenging. Existing authentication protocols, designed for autonomous WSNs, do not address these new requirements. This paper presents a novel, lightweight, and efficient key exchange and authentication protocol suite called the Secure Mobile Sensor Network (SMSN) Authentication Protocol. In SMSN, a mobile node undergoes an initial authentication procedure and receives a re-authentication ticket from the base station. This ticket can then be used for establishing multiple data exchange sessions and/or moving across the network, reducing the communication and computational complexity of the authentication process. The paper rigorously analyzes the security of the protocol and simulates SMSN and previously proposed schemes in an automated protocol verifier tool. Finally, it compares the computational complexity and communication cost of SMSN with well-known authentication protocols.
