The collected data on parsec and kiloparsec scales indicate that the current typically flows inward along the jet axis and outward in a more extended region surrounding the jet, resembling a coaxial cable structure. This current structure is accompanied by a self-consistent system of nested helical B fields, whose toroidal components give rise to the observed transverse RM gradients. These findings provide conclusive evidence for a preferred direction of toroidal B-field components and currents in AGN jets. Determining the origin of this current-field system is crucial for understanding the physical mechanisms leading to the formation of the intrinsic jet B field, likely playing a role in jet propagation and collimation. Our new techniques demonstrably improve both system performance and energy efficiency. We also delve into the crucial relationship between supply voltage and latency in modern DRAM chips and develop novel mechanisms that exploit this voltage-latency trade-off for enhanced energy efficiency. title: Smart, Sparse Contours to Represent and Edit Images

title: Choreographic and Somatic Approaches for the Development of Expressive Robotic Systems

This interpretation by the human counterpart is critical to the system's successful integration: the system's controls must make sense to a human counterpart; an artificial agent should have a means of notifying a human counterpart of changes in system state, potentially through motion profiles; and the motion of a human counterpart may hold important contextual clues for task completion. Therefore, professional choreographers, dance practitioners, and movement analysts are crucial to robotics research. They possess design methods for movement aligned with human audience perception, can identify simplified movement features for human-robot interaction goals, and have detailed knowledge of human movement capabilities. Based on this context, methods including embodied exercises, writing prompts, and community-building activities have been developed to facilitate interdisciplinary research. title: Inflation from High-Scale Supersymmetry Breaking
Abstract: Supersymmetry breaking close to the scale of grand unification can explain cosmic inflation. title: Resilience and efficiency in transportation networks

These findings demonstrate that many urban road systems operating inefficiently under normal conditions are nevertheless resilient to disruptions, while some more efficient cities are more fragile. title: Interpolation Macdonald polynomials and Cauchy-type identities
Abstract:
Let Sym denote the algebra of symmetric functions, and $P_\mu(\,\cdot\,;q,t)$ and $Q_\mu(\,\cdot\,;q,t)$ be the Macdonald symmetric functions (recall that they differ by scalar factors only). The $(q,t)$-Cauchy identity 
$$\sum_\mu P_\mu(x_1,x_2,\dots;q,t)Q_\mu(y_1,y_2,\dots;q,t) = \prod_{i,j=1}^\infty \frac{(x_iy_jt;q)_\infty}{(x_iy_j;q)_\infty}$$
expresses the fact that the $P_\mu(\,\cdot\,;q,t)$'s form an orthogonal basis in Sym with respect to a special scalar product $\langle\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,\rangle_{q,t}$. This paper deals with the inhomogeneous \emph{interpolation} Macdonald symmetric functions
$$I_\mu(x_1,x_2,\dots;q,t) = P_\mu(x_1,x_2,\dots;q,t) + \text{lower degree terms}.$$
These functions arise from the $N$-variate interpolation Macdonald polynomials, extensively studied in the 90s by Knop, Okounkov, and Sahi. The aim of this paper is to construct symmetric functions $J_\mu(\,\cdot\,;q,t)$ with the biorthogonality property 
$$\langle I_\mu(\,\cdot\,;q,t), J_\nu(\,\cdot\,;q,t)\rangle_{q,t} = \delta_{\mu\nu}.$$
These new functions reside in a natural completion of the algebra Sym. As a corollary, we obtain a new Cauchy-type identity in which the interpolation Macdonald polynomials are paired with certain multivariate rational symmetric functions. The degeneration of this identity in the Jack limit is also described.

title: A unified picture of strong coupling stochastic thermodynamics and time reversals
Abstract: Strong-coupling statistical thermodynamics is formulated as Hamiltonian dynamics of an observed system interacting with another unobserved system (a bath). We show that the entropy production functional of stochastic thermodynamics, defined as the log-ratio of forward and backward system path probabilities, is in one-to-one relation with the log-ratios of joint initial conditions of the system and the bath. A version of strong-coupling statistical thermodynamics where the system-bath interaction vanishes at the beginning and the end of a process is, as is also weak-coupling stochastic thermodynamics, related to the bath initially in equilibrium by itself. The heat is then the change of bath energy over the process. It is discussed when this heat is a functional of system history alone. The version of strong-coupling statistical thermodynamics introduced by Seifert and Jarzynski is related to the bath initially in conditional equilibrium with respect to the system. This leads to heat as another functional of system history, which needs to be determined by thermodynamic integration. The log-ratio of forward and backward system path probabilities in a stochastic process is finally related to log-ratios of initial conditions of a combined system and bath. We show that the entropy production formulas of stochastic processes under a general class of time reversals are given by the change of a bath energy in a larger underlying Hamiltonian system. The paper highlights the centrality of time reversal in stochastic thermodynamics, even in the case of strong coupling.

We also present mathematical arguments supporting its universality. This note is a preliminary version of a more extended work, where we also discuss the equality between the effective conductance of the resistor network and the critical conductance.

title: Horizon Feedback Inflation
Abstract: We investigate the effect of Gibbons-Hawking radiation on the inflaton in the situation where it is coupled to a large number of spectator fields. We show that it is possible to obtain enough e-folds of expansion as well as the correct spectrum of perturbations without hugely fine-tuned parameters in the potential (albeit with many spectator fields). title: A Comparative Study of Different Source Code Metrics and Machine Learning Algorithms for Predicting Change Proneness of Object Oriented Systems

title: A Note on Flips in Diagonal Rectangulations
Abstract: Rectangulations are partitions of a square into axis-aligned rectangles. Numerous results provide bijections between combinatorial equivalence classes of rectangulations and families of pattern-avoiding permutations. Other results deal with local changes involving a single edge of a rectangulation, referred to as flips, edge rotations, or edge pivoting. Such operations induce a graph on equivalence classes of rectangulations, related to so-called flip graphs on triangulations and other families of geometric partitions. In this note, we consider a family of flip operations on the equivalence classes of diagonal rectangulations and their interpretation as transpositions in the associated Baxter permutations, avoiding the vincular patterns $\{3\{14\}2, 2\{41\}3\}$. This complements results from Law and Reading (JCTA, 2012) and provides a complete characterization of flip operations on diagonal rectangulations, in both geometric and combinatorial terms.

title: Doping-induced redistribution of magnetic spectral weight in substituted hexaborides Ce$_{1-x}$La$_x$B$_6$ and Ce$_{1-x}$Nd$_x$B$_6$
Abstract: We investigate the doping-induced changes in the electronic structure of CeB$_6$ on a series of substituted Ce$_{1-x}R_x$B$_6$ samples ($R$ = La, Nd) using diffuse neutron scattering. We observe a redistribution of magnetic spectral weight across the Brillouin zone, which we associate with the changes in the Fermi-surface nesting properties related to the modified charge carrier concentration. In particular, a strong diffuse peak at the corner of the Brillouin zone ($R$ point), which coincides with the propagation vector of the elusive antiferroquadrupolar (AFQ) order in CeB$_6$, is rapidly suppressed by both La and Nd doping, like the AFQ order itself. The corresponding spectral weight is transferred to the $X(00\frac{1}{2})$ point, ultimately stabilizing a long-range AFM order at this wave vector at the Nd-rich side of the phase diagram. At an intermediate Nd concentration, a broad diffuse peak with multiple local maxima of intensity is observed around the $X$ point, evidencing itinerant frustration that gives rise to multiple ordered phases for which Ce$_{1-x}$Nd$_x$B$_6$ is known. On the La-rich side of the phase diagram, however, dilution of the magnetic moments prevents the formation of a similar $(00\frac{1}{2})$-type order despite the presence of nesting. Our results demonstrate how diffuse neutron scattering can be used to probe the nesting vectors in complex f-electron systems directly, without reference to the single-particle band structure, and emphasize the role of Fermi surface geometry in stabilizing magnetic order in rare-earth hexaborides.

title: The Graph Structure of the Generalized Discrete Arnold's Cat Map
Abstract: Chaotic dynamics is an important source for generating pseudorandom binary sequences (PRNS). Then, its real graph (cycle) structure in any binary arithmetic domain is disclosed. The regular and beautiful patterns of the Cat map demonstrated in a computer adopting fixed-point arithmetics are rigorously proved and experimentally verified. The results will facilitate research on the dynamics of variants of the Cap map in any domain and its effective application in cryptography. In addition, the methodology used can be used to evaluate the randomness of PRNS generated by iterating any other maps.

title: Fragility of the Dirac Cone Splitting in Topological Crystalline Insulator Heterostructures
Abstract: The 'double Dirac cone' 2D topological interface states found on the (001) faces of topological crystalline insulators such as Pb$_{1-x}$Sn$_{x}$Se feature degeneracies located away from time-reversal invariant momenta and are a manifestation of both mirror symmetry protection and valley interactions. In addition, the operation of this or similar devices outside of ultra-high vacuum will require encapsulation, and the consequences of this for the topological interface state must be understood. Here, we address both topics for the case of 2D surface states using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. We examine bulk Pb$_{1-x}$Sn$_{x}$Se(001) crystals overgrown with PbSe, realizing trivial/topological heterostructures. We demonstrate that the valley interaction that splits the two Dirac cones at each $\bar{X}$ is extremely sensitive to atomic-scale details of the surface, exhibiting non-monotonic changes as PbSe deposition proceeds. This includes an apparent total collapse of the splitting for sub-monolayer coverage, eliminating the Lifshitz transition. For a large overlayer thickness, we observe quantized PbSe states, possibly reflecting a symmetry confinement mechanism at the buried topological interface. |||

Furthermore, our model suggests a transient accelerating phase, with the universe decelerating in the past, accelerating currently, and returning to a decelerating phase in the near future. title: Improving DRAM Performance by Parallelizing Refreshes with Accesses
Abstract: Commodity DDR DRAM refreshes cells at the rank level, negatively impacting performance due to the inability to serve memory requests during refresh. LPDDR DRAM, used in mobile platforms, supports per-bank refresh, alleviating some performance degradation by enabling bank-level refresh. However, per-bank refresh has limitations: sequential round-robin refreshing of banks and access delays for banks undergoing refresh. To mitigate these limitations, we propose DARP (Dynamic Access Refresh Parallelization) and SARP (Subarray Access Refresh Parallelization). DARP schedules per-bank refreshes to idle banks in an out-of-order manner, utilizing write drain intervals. SARP leverages mostly-independent subarrays within a bank, enabling access to idle subarrays while another subarray is refreshed. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our mechanisms significantly enhance system performance and energy efficiency compared to existing refresh policies, especially with increasing DRAM density.

title: Tracking Cyber Adversaries with Adaptive Indicators of Compromise

title: Joint spreading models and uniform approximation of bounded operators

Abstract: This paper presents the first cosmological constraint on dark matter scattering with protons in the early universe for the entire mass range between 1 keV and 1 TeV. The constraint is derived from Planck measurements of cosmic microwave background (CMB) temperature and polarization anisotropy, as well as CMB lensing anisotropy. These results significantly improve upon previous CMB constraints, covering a broader range of low-mass dark matter candidates. The study focuses on two canonical interaction scenarios: spin-independent and spin-dependent scattering with no velocity dependence. With 95% confidence, the findings exclude spin-independent interactions with cross sections exceeding 5.3 × 10−27 cm2 for 1 keV, 3.0 × 10−26 cm2 for 1 MeV, 1.7 × 10−25 cm2 for 1 GeV, and 1.6 × 10−23 cm2 for 1 TeV dark matter mass. The paper discusses the implications of these results for dark matter physics and future observations.

title: Quantum state engineering of a Hubbard system with ultracold fermions

The approach utilizes an ultralow entropy doublon band insulator, achieved through entropy redistribution. By isolating the band insulator and modifying the underlying potential, the authors expand it into a half-filled system. The resulting many-body state exhibits strong antiferromagnetic correlations and a temperature below the exchange energy. While an increase in entropy is observed, the paper attributes this to the many-body physics involved in the final step of the process. This technique holds promise for low-temperature studies of cold-atom-based lattice models.

title: The impact of baryons on the sensitivity of dark energy measurements
Abstract: The impact of baryonic effects on large-scale structure can introduce significant biases in dark energy constraints unless properly accounted for. The complex and not fully understood physics of baryons necessitates the introduction of additional parameters that must be marginalized over, increasing the uncertainty in inferred cosmological parameters. With forthcoming weak lensing surveys aiming for percent-level precision on the dark energy equation of state, a thorough examination of this issue is crucial. The authors utilize a halo model with modifications to capture the impact of adiabatic contraction of baryons and feedback on the matter power spectrum. They also generalize the Navarro-Frenk-White profile to account for a possible inner core. A Fisher analysis predicts a 40% degradation in the w0-wa Figure of Merit for a Euclid-like survey and up to 80% for other cosmological parameters. The study forecasts potential inner core constraints of a few kpc, while for a fixed inner core, adiabatic concentration and feedback parameters are constrained to a few percent. Examining the scales where baryons and dark energy contribute most to the Fisher information reveals that probing increasingly nonlinear scales does little to reduce degradation. Including external baryon information improves the forecasts, but achieving a 1% reduction in degradation requires strong priors. Adding Planck cosmic microwave background priors enhances the Figure of Merit by a factor of 2.7 and almost completely recovers the individual marginalized errors on w0 and wa. The paper quantifies the calibration of baryon modeling needed to reduce biases in dark energy forecasts to acceptable levels for upcoming lensing surveys.

title: Solar-driven variation in the atmosphere of Uranus

Spectral analysis reveals that this non-seasonal variability tracks the 11-year solar cycle. The paper investigates two potential mechanisms for this solar modulation: (a) nucleation onto ions or electrons created by galactic cosmic rays (GCR) and (b) UV-induced aerosol color changes. Ion-aerosol theory is employed to identify expected relationships between reflectivity fluctuations and GCR flux, which are then tested using multiple regression and compared to the linear response predicted between reflectivity and solar UV flux. The statistical analysis indicates that 24% of the variance in reflectivity fluctuations at 472 nm can be attributed to GCR ion-induced nucleation, compared to 22% for a UV-only mechanism. Similar GCR-related variability exists in Neptune's atmosphere, making the findings at Uranus the first example of common variability in two planetary atmospheres driven by energetic particle modulation from their host star.

title: Convective blueshifts in the solar atmosphere, I. Absolute measurements with LARS of the spectral lines at 6302 Å
Abstract: Solar convection manifests as granulation and intergranulation at the solar surface, inducing Doppler shifts in spectral lines due to convective motions in the photosphere. The observed convective blueshift varies across the solar disk. This paper investigates the impact of solar convection on the atmosphere, aiming to resolve its velocity stratification in the photosphere. Using the Laser Absolute Reference Spectrograph (LARS) at the Vacuum Tower Telescope, the authors performed high-resolution spectroscopic observations of the solar spectrum in the 6302 Å range. A laser frequency comb enabled the calibration of spectra to an absolute wavelength scale with an accuracy of 1 m s−1. Systematic scans of the Quiet Sun from disk center to the limb were conducted at ten selected heliocentric positions, analyzing 99 time sequences up to 20 min in length. Through ephemeris and reference corrections, wavelength shifts were translated into absolute line-of-sight velocities. A bisector analysis of line profiles revealed the shapes and convective shifts of seven photospheric lines. At disk center, the bisector profiles of iron lines exhibit a pronounced C-shape with maximum convective blueshifts reaching -450 m s−1 in the spectral line wings. Towards the solar limb, the bisectors transform into a \ shape with saturation in the line core at a redshift of +100 m s−1. The center-to-limb variation of line core velocities shows a slight increase in blueshift as heliocentric angles increase from the disk center. This blueshift increase is more pronounced for the less magnetically active meridian than for the equator. Near the solar limb, the blueshift decreases and can even turn into a redshift. The accurate spectroscopic measurements enabled the precise determination of absolute convective shifts in the solar photosphere.

title: Homomorphism thresholds for odd cycles
Abstract: The interplay between minimum degree conditions and structural properties of large graphs with forbidden subgraphs is a central theme in extremal graph theory. For a given graph F, the homomorphism threshold is defined as the infimum over all α ∈ [0, 1] such that every n-vertex F-free graph G with minimum degree at least αn has a homomorphic image H of bounded order (independent of n), which is also F-free. Removing the F-free restriction on H leads to the definition of the chromatic threshold, which was determined for all graphs F by Allen et al. [Adv. Math. 235 (2013), 261-295]. This paper focuses on the less understood homomorphism threshold, addressing the problem for odd cycles.

title: Thermal Rectification in CVD Diamond Membranes Driven by Gradient Grain Structure
Abstract: Thermal diodes, essential components in phononics, exhibit asymmetric heat current transmission similar to electronic rectifiers and diodes in microelectronics. They efficiently conduct heat in one direction while blocking it in the other. This work reports on an easily-fabricated mesoscale chemical vapor deposited (CVD) diamond thermal diode without sharp temperature change, driven by the gradient grain structure of CVD diamond membranes. The authors develop a spectral model of diamond thermal conductivity incorporating complete phonon dispersion relations to demonstrate significant thermal rectification in CVD diamond membranes. To explain the observed thermal rectification, the temperature and thermal conductivity distribution within the CVD diamond membrane are studied. The paper also explores the effects of temperature bias and diamond membrane thickness, providing insights into tuning thermal rectification in CVD diamond membranes. The conical grain structure makes CVD diamond membranes, and potentially other CVD film structures with gradient grain structures, promising candidates for easily-fabricated mesoscale thermal diodes without sharp temperature changes.

title: Fast neutrino flavor conversion: roles of dense matter and spectrum crossing

This fast neutrino flavor conversion has been suggested to require a crossing in the electron lepton number (ELN) angular distribution or spectrum. This paper examines a few simple analytical models to elucidate the roles of dense matter and ELN spectrum crossing in fast neutrino flavor conversions. The authors demonstrate that a large matter density can induce fast neutrino flavor conversions in specific astrophysical scenarios, such as the early epoch of a core-collapse supernova.

title: Fractional Elliptic Quasi-Variational Inequalities: Theory and Numerics
Abstract: This paper introduces a class of elliptic quasi-variational inequality (QVI) problems with fractional diffusion of order s ∈ (0, 1), investigating the existence and uniqueness of solutions and developing a solution algorithm. The paper first examines the existence and uniqueness of solutions for this extended QVI and then transfers the results to the fractional QVI, introducing a novel paradigm in the field of fractional QVIs. By truncating the semi-infinite cylinder, the authors demonstrate that the solution to the truncated problem converges to the solution of the extended problem, under relatively mild assumptions, as the truncation parameter τ tends to infinity. As the constraint set changes with the solution, the authors develop an argument using Mosco convergence. (2015) empirically analyzed and modeled long-term solar modulation. title: Nonparametric MANOVA in Mann-Whitney effects
Abstract: Multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) is a powerful and versatile method for inferring and quantifying main and interaction effects in metric multivariate multi-factor data. Unlike existing rank-based procedures, this approach infers hypotheses formulated in terms of meaningful Mann-Whitney-type effects instead of distribution functions. The tests are based on a quadratic form in multivariate rank effect estimators, with critical values obtained through bootstrapping. This newly developed procedure provides asymptotically exact and consistent inference for general models, including the nonparametric Behrens-Fisher problem and multivariate one-, two-, and higher-way crossed layouts. Computer simulations in small samples confirm the reliability of this method for both ordinal and metric data with covariance heterogeneity. The paper concludes with an analysis of a real data example, illustrating the applicability and correct interpretation of the results.

title: Scattering fans
Abstract: Scattering diagrams emerged in the context of mirror symmetry, Donaldson-Thomas theory, and integrable systems. title: Effect of magnetic twist on nonlinear transverse kink oscillations
Abstract: Magnetic twist is believed to play a crucial role in many structures within the solar atmosphere. One of the effects of twist is to modify the properties of eigenmodes in magnetic tubes. In the linear regime, standing kink solutions are characterized by a change in polarization of the transverse displacement along the twisted tube. In the nonlinear regime, magnetic twist affects the development of shear instabilities that emerge at the tube boundary during lateral oscillations. These Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities (KHI) arise either from the jump in the azimuthal component of velocity at the edge of the sharp boundary between the tube's internal and external parts or from the continuous small length-scales produced by phase-mixing when there is a smooth inhomogeneous layer. This work consistently investigates the impact of twist by solving the time-dependent problem, including the energy transfer process to the inhomogeneous layer. The findings reveal that twist consistently delays the appearance of shear instability, but for tubes with thin inhomogeneous layers, the effect is relatively small for moderate twist values. Conversely, for tubes with thick layers, the effect of twist is significantly stronger. These results could have significant implications for observations of transverse kink modes and KHI itself. |||

title: Learning Fixation Point Strategy for Object Detection and Classification

More broadly, these results establish the utility of O-$K$ edge RIXS for investigating collective excitations in a range of $5d$ materials, which are gaining interest due to their novel magnetic and electronic properties. title: End-to-end weakly-supervised semantic alignment

title: Minimax joint spectral radius and stabilizability of discrete-time linear switching control systems
Abstract: Traditionally, numeric quantities like the joint spectral radius $\\rho(\\mathcal{A})$ and the lower spectral radius $\\check{\\rho}(\\mathcal{A})$ are used to estimate the growth rate of matrix products $A_{n}\\cdots A_{1}$ with factors from a set of matrices $\\mathcal{A}$. The joint spectral radius characterizes the maximum growth rate of the norms of these products, while the lower spectral radius characterizes the minimal growth rate. In the theory of discrete-time linear switching systems, $\\rho(\\mathcal{A})<1$ serves as a stability criterion, and $\\check{\\rho}(\\mathcal{A})<1$ as a stabilizability criterion. For matrix products $A_{n}B_{n}\\cdots A_{1}B_{1}$ with factors $A_{i}\\in\\mathcal{A}$ and $B_{i}\\in\\mathcal{B}$, where $\\mathcal{A}$ and $\\mathcal{B}$ are sets of matrices, this paper introduces $\\mu(\\mathcal{A},\\mathcal{B})$ and $\\eta(\\mathcal{A},\\mathcal{B})$, termed the lower and upper minimax joint spectral radii of the pair $\\{\\mathcal{A},\\mathcal{B}\\}$, respectively. These quantities characterize the maximum growth rate of the matrix products $A_{n}B_{n}\\cdots A_{1}B_{1}$ over all sets of matrices $A_{i}\\in\\mathcal{A}$ and the minimal growth rate over all sets of matrices $B_{i}\\in\\mathcal{B}$. In this sense, the minimax joint spectral radii can be viewed as generalizations of both the joint and lower spectral radii. As an application, the paper demonstrates how these quantities can be used to analyze the stabilizability of discrete-time linear switching control systems in the presence of uncontrolled external disturbances of the plant.

Abstract: $\\gamma$-ray flares from the Crab nebula observed by {\\it AGILE} and {\\it Fermi}-LAT between 2007-2013 reached GeV photon energies and lasted several days. The strongest emission, observed during the 2011 April "super-flare," exceeded the quiescent level by more than an order of magnitude. These observations challenge standard models for particle acceleration in pulsar wind nebulae, as the radiating electrons possess energies exceeding the classical radiation-reaction limit for synchrotron. Particle-in-cell simulations have suggested that the classical synchrotron limit can be surpassed if electrons experience electrostatic acceleration due to shock-driven magnetic reconnection. This paper revisits the problem using an analytical approach based on solving a fully time-dependent electron transport equation describing electrostatic acceleration, synchrotron losses, and escape experienced by electrons in a magnetically confined plasma "blob" as it encounters and passes through the pulsar-wind termination shock. The model successfully reproduces the $\\gamma$-ray spectra observed during the rising and decaying phases of each sub-flare component of the 2011 April super-flare. Integrating the spectrum for photon energies $\\ge 100\\,$MeV yields the light curve for the event, which agrees with the observations. Strong electrostatic acceleration is found to occur on both sides of the termination shock, driven by magnetic reconnection. The dominant mode of particle escape transitions from diffusive escape to advective escape as the blob passes through the shock.

title: Evolution of magnetic Dirac bosons in a honeycomb lattice
Abstract: The presence and evolution of magnetic Dirac nodes in the Heisenberg honeycomb lattice are examined. Using linear spin theory, the collinear phase diagram and the change in spin dynamics with various exchange interactions are evaluated. The findings reveal that the ferromagnetic structure produces bosonic Dirac and Weyl points due to the competition between superexchange interactions. Furthermore, the criteria for magnetic Dirac nodes are shown to be coupled to the magnetic structure, not the overall crystal symmetry, with broken inversion symmetry significantly affecting antiferromagnetic configurations. The tunability of the nodal points through variation of exchange parameters presents the possibility of controlling Dirac symmetries through external manipulation of orbital interactions.

title: Solar Radius at Subterahertz Frequencies and its Relation to Solar Activity
Abstract: The Sun emits radiation at various wavelengths across the electromagnetic spectrum. In the optical band, the solar radius is 695,700 km, defining the photosphere, the visible surface of the Sun. These measurements provide insights into the solar atmosphere, and the radius dependence on the solar cycle serves as a good indicator of changes in atmospheric structure. This paper measures the solar radius at the subterahertz frequencies of 0.212 and 0.405 THz – corresponding to the altitudes where these emissions primarily originate – and analyzes the radius variation over the 11-year solar activity cycle. Radio maps of the solar disk between 1999 and 2017, reconstructed from daily scans by the Solar Submillimeter-wave Telescope (SST) at El Leoncito Astronomical Complex (CASLEO) in the Argentinean Andes, are used for this analysis. The measurements yield radii of 966.5" $\\pm$ 2.8" for 0.2 THz and 966.5" $\\pm$ 2.7" for 0.4 THz, implying a height of $(5.0 \\pm 2.0 \\times 10^6)$ m above the photosphere. title: Variable Order Fractional Fokker-Planck Equations derived from Continuous Time Random Walks
Abstract: Continuous Time Random Walk models (CTRW) of anomalous diffusion are investigated, where the anomalous exponent $\\beta(x) \\in (0,1)$ varies spatially. This scenario arises, for example, in biophysics where the density of the intracellular matrix varies throughout a cell. CTRW scaling limits are known to have probability distributions that solve fractional Fokker-Planck type equations (FFPE). While this correspondence between stochastic processes and FFPE solutions has useful extensions to nonlinear particle interactions and reactions, it has not yet been sufficiently developed for FFPEs of the "variable order" type with non-constant $\\beta(x)$. This article derives variable order FFPEs (VOFFPE) from scaling limits of CTRWs. The key mathematical tool is the 1-1 correspondence of a CTRW scaling limit to a bivariate Langevin process, tracking the cumulative sum of jumps in one component and the cumulative sum of waiting times in the other. The spatially varying anomalous exponent is modeled by spatially varying $\\beta(x)$-stable L\\\'evy noise in the waiting time component. The VOFFPE displays spatially heterogeneous temporal scaling behavior, with generalized diffusivity and drift coefficients whose units are length$^2$/time$^{\\beta(x)}$ and length/time$^{\\beta(x)}$, respectively. A global change in the time scale results in a spatially varying change in diffusivity and drift. A consequence of the mathematical derivation of a VOFFPE from CTRW limits is that a VOFFPE solution can be approximated via Monte Carlo simulations. Based on these simulations, the VOFFPE is confirmed to be consistent under a change in the global time scale.

title: Similar ultrafast dynamics of several dissimilar Dirac and Weyl semimetals
Abstract: Recent years have witnessed the rapid discovery of solids with massless, linear dispersion low-energy electrons, such as Weyl, line-node, and Dirac semimetals. This paper measures the ultrafast dynamics of four materials that share non-trivial band structure topology but differ chemically, structurally, and in their low-energy band structures: ZrSiS, which exhibits a Dirac line node and Dirac points; TaAs and NbP, which are Weyl semimetals; and Sr$_{1-y}$Mn$_{1-z}$Sb$_2$, where Dirac fermions coexist with broken time-reversal symmetry. Their rapid relaxation suggests that these and related materials may be suitable for optical switches and fast infrared detectors. title: Effect of Zn doping on the antiferromagnetism in kagome Cu$_{4-x}$Zn$_x$(OH)$_6$FBr

Neutron-diffraction measurements reveal a hexagonal-to-orthorhombic structural transformation with decreasing temperature in the $x$ = 0 sample. While confirming the 3D antiferromagnetic nature of low-temperature magnetism, the study finds vanishingly small magnetic moments on some Cu$^{2+}$ sites on the kagome planes, indicating the presence of strong frustration in barlowite. High-temperature magnetic susceptibility and specific heat measurements suggest the emergence of intrinsic magnetic properties of kagome spin liquid planes from $x>0.3$ samples. These results indicate that the Cu$_{4-x}$Zn$_x$(OH)$_6$FBr system provides an experimental platform for systematically exploring the quantum phase transition from a long-range antiferromagnet to a topologically ordered quantum spin liquid.

Consequently, the three-dimensionality of particle motion, specifically particle momentum, arises as a result. This paper proposes two assumptions regarding the spin properties of photons and subsequently deduces a relationship between the direction of photon momentum and the spin plane associated with the photon spin state. This relationship establishes the three-dimensionality of photon momentum as an inherent property of the photon. Moreover, it provides a deeper understanding of well-established theoretical results, including the transformation rules for the spin states of spin-1 particles under space rotation and the connection between the momentum direction of classical electromagnetic waves and the directions of the electric and magnetic fields.

The study examines the new degeneracies that arise in the presence of a sterile neutrino, which are absent in the standard three-flavor framework. title: Temperature-Driven Topological Transition in 1T'-MoTe2
Abstract: The topological nature of Weyl semimetals necessitates the presence of unique surface states. While spectroscopy measurements have visualized these surface states, their connection to the topological character of the material remains largely unexplored. 1T'-MoTe2 offers a unique opportunity to investigate this connection. The material undergoes a phase transition at 240K, altering its structure from orthorhombic (putative Weyl semimetal) to monoclinic (trivial metal), while largely preserving its bulk electronic structure. This study utilizes temperature-dependent quasiparticle interference measurements to demonstrate that this structural transition also acts as a topological switch for surface states in 1T'-MoTe2. At low temperatures, strong quasiparticle scattering is observed, consistent with theoretical predictions and photoemission measurements for the surface states in this material. Conversely, measurements at room temperature show the complete absence of the scattering wavevectors associated with the trivial surface states. These distinct quasiparticle scattering behaviors highlight 1T'-MoTe2 as an ideal system for separating topological and trivial electronic phenomena via temperature-dependent measurements.

title: Pragmatic Primitives for Non-blocking Data Structures
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel set of primitive operations that significantly simplify the implementation of non-blocking data structures in asynchronous shared-memory systems. These operations act on a collection of Data-records, each containing multiple fields. The operations are generalizations of the well-known load-link (LL) and store-conditional (SC) operations, termed LLX and SCX. The LLX operation captures a snapshot of a specific Data-record. An SCX operation performed by a process $p$ succeeds only if no Data-record in a specified set has been modified since $p$ last executed an LLX on it. Upon successful execution, the SCX atomically updates a particular field of a Data-record within the set and prevents any future changes to a specified subset of those Data-records. The paper presents a provably correct implementation of these new primitives based on single-word compare-and-swap. As a simple demonstration, the paper illustrates how to implement a non-blocking multiset data structure using LLX and SCX.

title: Interpolating wave packets and composite wave functions in QFT and neutrino oscillation problem
Abstract: This paper presents a consistent, constructive, and covariant description of the neutrino flavor transition amplitude in vacuum. To achieve this, a special generalized relativistic wave packet is constructed with a proper extension to higher spins. This packet is uniquely defined as an "interpolating" wave packet, which, through a relativistically invariant "width," accurately interpolates between states localized in momentum space and in coordinate space. The wave packet is unambiguously determined by the analytical properties of Wightman functions in complex coordinate space, naturally connected with its minimization properties. The packet provides a natural relativistic generalization of the non-relativistic Gaussian wave packet but only includes covariant states of particles (antiparticles) with positive (negative) energy signs. It propagates without mixing or changing its relativistically invariant width. For the diagrammatic treatment of oscillation using these wave packets for external particles, the concept of a covariant composite wave function for the intermediate neutrino is introduced. This function naturally connects both oscillation pictures, providing an effective language for detailed description of this process and resolving issues related to causality and covariant equal-time prescription for the intermediate neutrino picture. It is closely related to the overlap function of neutrino creation/detection vertices, illuminating a covariant meaning of the "pole integration" procedure. Their space-time asymptotic behavior in the narrow-packets approximation naturally aligns with the one-packet state approximation and the asymptotic behavior of the oscillation amplitude. The respective overlap function is explicitly calculated for a two-packet example of the pion decay vertex. Its correspondence and differences with previous approximate calculations are analyzed.

title: Inverting a normal harmonic oscillator: Physical interpretation and applications
Abstract: The harmonic oscillator with time-dependent mass $m(t)$ and a time-dependent (squared) frequency $\\omega^2(t)$ is a fundamental model for numerous physical systems. It is commonly believed that systems with $m(t)>0$ and $\\omega^2(t)>0$ (normal oscillator) are stable, while systems with $m(t)>0$ and $\\omega^2(t)<0$ (inverted oscillator) are unstable. This study demonstrates that it is possible to represent the same physical system as both a normal oscillator and an inverted oscillator by redefining dynamical variables. While one would expect physics to remain invariant under such redefinitions, the mechanism for this invariance is not immediately apparent. The paper investigates the relationship between these two representations of an oscillator in detail, using both the Heisenberg and Schr\\"{o}dinger pictures, to clarify various conceptual and technical aspects. The situation becomes more complex when the oscillator is coupled to another (semi)classical degree of freedom $C(t)$, and the back-reaction of the quantum system $q(t)$ on $C(t)$ needs to be studied in the semi-classical approximation. The paper presents a simple prescription for the back-reaction based on energy conservation and investigates the dynamics of the full system in both the normal and inverted oscillator representations. Again, physics remains invariant, but some additional subtleties are addressed and clarified. The implications of these results for quantum field theory in cosmological backgrounds are briefly discussed in an appendix.

title: Major Merging History in CANDELS. I. Evolution of the Incidence of Massive Galaxy-Galaxy Pairs from z=3 to z~0
Abstract: Theoretically, the rate of major galaxy-galaxy merging is predicted to increase steadily with redshift during the peak epoch of massive galaxy development ($1{\\leq}z{\\leq}3$). This study uses close-pair statistics to objectively investigate the incidence of massive galaxies (stellar $M_{1}{\\geq}2{\\times}10^{10}M_{\\odot}$) hosting major companions ($1{\\leq}M_{1}/M_{2}{\\leq}4$; i.e., $<$4:1) at six epochs spanning $0{<}z{<}3$. The companions are selected from a nearly complete, mass-limited ($\\geq5{\\times}10^{9}M_{\\odot}$) sample of 23,696 galaxies in the five CANDELS fields and the SDSS. Using $5-50$ kpc projected separation and close redshift proximity criteria, the study finds that the major companion fraction $f_{\\mathrm{mc}}(z)$ based on stellar mass-ratio (MR) selection increases from 6% ($z{\\sim}0$) to 16% ($z{\\sim}0.8$), then turns over at $z{\\sim}1$ and decreases to 7% ($z{\\sim}3$). However, if a major F160W flux ratio (FR) selection is used, $f_{\\mathrm{mc}}(z)$ increases steadily until $z=3$ due to increasing contamination from minor (MR$>$4:1) companions at $z>1$. The study shows that these evolutionary trends are statistically robust to changes in companion proximity. Discrepancies between published results are resolved when selection criteria are closely matched. However, using an evolving $T_{\\mathrm{obs,pair}}(z){\\propto}(1+z)^{-2}$ from Snyder et al., the MR-based rates align with theoretical predictions at $0{<}z{<}3$. This analysis highlights the need for detailed calibration of $C_{\\mathrm{merg,pair}}$ and $T_{\\mathrm{obs,pair}}$ as a function of redshift, mass, and companion selection criteria to more accurately constrain the empirical major merger history.

title: Is there a UV/X-ray connection in IRAS 13224-3809?
Abstract: This paper presents results from the optical, ultraviolet, and X-ray monitoring of the NLS1 galaxy IRAS 13224-3809 using Swift and XMM-Newton during 2016. title: Safe Mutations for Deep and Recurrent Neural Networks through Output Gradients
Abstract: Neuroevolution, the process of evolving neural networks, has proven successful across diverse domains, ranging from reinforcement learning to artificial life. However, its application to large, deep neural networks is infrequent. A primary reason is that while random mutation generally works in low dimensions, a random perturbation of thousands or millions of weights is likely to disrupt existing functionality, providing no learning signal even if some individual weight changes were beneficial. This paper proposes a solution by introducing a family of safe mutation (SM) operators that aim to find a degree of change within the mutation operator itself that does not significantly alter network behavior but still facilitates exploration. Importantly, these SM operators do not require any additional interactions with the environment. The most effective SM variant leverages the opportunity to scale the degree of mutation of each individual weight according to the network's output sensitivity to that weight. This requires computing the gradient of outputs with respect to the weights (instead of the gradient of error, as in conventional deep learning). This safe mutation through gradients (SM-G) operator significantly enhances the ability of a simple genetic algorithm-based neuroevolution method to find solutions in high-dimensional domains that require deep and/or recurrent neural networks (which tend to be particularly sensitive to mutation), including domains that require processing raw pixels. By improving the ability to evolve deep neural networks, this new safer approach to mutation expands the scope of domains amenable to neuroevolution.

Recently, the concept of phase transitions has been extended to non-equilibrium dynamics of time-independent systems induced by a quantum quench, i.e., a sudden change in a Hamiltonian parameter. In such systems, the return probability of the system to its ground state exhibits singularities in time, which are dubbed dynamical quantum phase transitions. We demonstrate that a quantum quench in a discrete time crystal leads to dynamical quantum phase transitions. The return probability of a periodically driven system to a Floquet eigenstate before the quench reveals singularities in time. This indicates that dynamical quantum phase transitions are not limited to time-independent systems and can also be observed in periodically driven systems. We discuss how this phenomenon can be observed in ultra-cold atomic gases.

We show the transformation of the functional dependence between measured values (RHEED reflexes intensity picture) and the degree of surface coverage by reconstruction domains, as the domains' average size and distribution density change. We tested two cases: using grain shape parameters only and using both grain shape parameters and transparency values. Our findings indicate that sample classification is more consistent with their eruption style when using both parameters. Additionally, one of the families of non-universal equilibria also bifurcates from another universal equilibrium (the antipodal arrangement) at s = −2. While the bifurcation at s = −4 is analytical, the one at s = −2 is not. This bifurcation analysis serves as a template for similar N-point equilibrium problems on the d-dimensional sphere for small N.

title: Random non-Abelian G-circulant matrices. Spectrum of random convolution operators on large finite groups

For regular sequences of groups, we demonstrate that the limiting distribution of eigenvalues (singular values) is a mixture of eigenvalue (singular value) distributions of Ginibre matrices, with the mixing measure determined by the limiting behavior of the Plancherel measure of the group sequence. Notably, for the sequence of symmetric groups, the limiting distributions coincide with the circular and quarter-circular laws, while for dihedral groups, the limiting distributions have unbounded supports and differ from the Abelian case. We also show that under additional assumptions on the group sequence (specifically for symmetric groups of increasing order), families of stochastically independent random projection operators converge in moments to free circular elements. Finally, we establish Central Limit Theorems for linear eigenvalue statistics in the Gaussian case.

title: Penalty Dual Decomposition Method For Nonsmooth Nonconvex Optimization
Abstract: Many signal processing, machine learning, and wireless communication applications involve nonconvex nonsmooth optimization problems.  Efficient algorithms for these problems are often lacking, particularly when optimization variables are nonlinearly coupled within nonconvex constraints. We propose an algorithm, named Penalty Dual Decomposition (PDD), for addressing these challenges and explore its various applications.  PDD is a double-loop iterative algorithm. Its inner iterations solve a nonconvex nonsmooth augmented Lagrangian problem inexactly using block-coordinate-descent-type methods, while its outer iteration updates dual variables and/or a penalty parameter.  In Part I, we describe the PDD algorithm and rigorously prove its convergence to Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) solutions. In Part II, we evaluate PDD's performance by customizing it to three applications arising from signal processing and wireless communications.

title: Predicting physiological developments from human gait using smartphone sensor data
Abstract: Coronary artery disease, heart failure, angina pectoris, and diabetes are among the leading causes of morbidity and mortality globally.  Susceptibility to these disorders is compounded by factors such as changing lifestyles, poor dietary habits, aging, and obesity.  Traditional diagnostics have limitations in detecting these pathologies at an early stage. This necessitates the development of automated recommender systems that can effectively monitor and predict pathogenic behaviors within the body. We propose using human gait analysis to predict two important physiological parameters associated with various diseases: body mass index (BMI) and age. Predicting BMI and age by profiling gait samples could provide personalized healthcare recommendations. However, existing strategies for predicting BMI and age often require stringent experimental settings to achieve satisfactory performance.  For instance, precisely recorded speech signals have been used to predict BMI in different subjects, and age groups have been predicted using gait samples from on-body and wearable sensors. These specialized methods restrict active and convenient profiling of human BMI and age.  We address these limitations by utilizing smartphone sensors for recording gait signals.  Using onboard accelerometers and gyroscopes facilitates the development of accessible and user-friendly systems for predicting BMI and age. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we collected gait samples from sixty-three subjects, classified them into BMI and age groups using six well-known machine learning classifiers, and evaluated our system using two different windowing operations for feature extraction: Gaussian and Square.

title: Micromagnetics of anti-skyrmions in ultrathin films
Abstract: This study examines the equilibrium energy, size, and shape of anti-skyrmionic magnetic configurations using a combination of analytical and numerical micromagnetic methods. Anti-skyrmions can be stabilized when the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction has opposite signs along two orthogonal in-plane directions, breaking the magnetic circular symmetry.  We compare the equilibrium properties of anti-skyrmions and skyrmions stabilized in environments with anisotropic and isotropic Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, respectively, while maintaining the same strength of magnetic interactions. When dipolar interactions are neglected, the skyrmion and anti-skyrmion have identical energy, shape, and size within their respective environments. However, when dipolar interactions are considered, the anti-skyrmion's energy is significantly reduced, and its equilibrium size is increased compared to the skyrmion. While the skyrmion configuration exhibits homochiral Néel magnetization rotations, anti-skyrmions display a combination of Néel and Bloch rotations. The latter do not produce magnetic charges, resulting in lower dipolar energy costs. Both magnetic configurations are stable when the magnetic energies nearly cancel each other, indicating that small variations in parameters can drastically alter their configuration, size, and energy.

title: Brout-Englert-Higgs physics: From foundations to phenomenology
Abstract: This review explores the field-theoretical foundations of Brout-Englert-Higgs (BEH) physics and explains how the conventional phenomenology arises from it. This requires defining the underlying physics precisely and gauge-invariantly, which is complicated by the fact that concepts like the Higgs vacuum expectation value or the distinction between confinement and the BEH effect lose their meaning beyond perturbation theory. To address this, we carefully construct the corresponding theory space and the quantum phase diagram. The physical spectrum is then expressed in terms of gauge-invariant, composite states. Using gauge-invariant perturbation theory, as developed by Froehlich, Morchio, and Strocchi, we rederive conventional perturbation theory. This derivation explicitly clarifies why the description of the Standard Model in terms of unphysical, gauge-dependent, elementary states of the Higgs, W-bosons, Z-boson, and elementary fermions is both adequate and successful. These are unavoidable consequences of the field theory underlying the Standard Model, from which the familiar picture emerges. The validity of this emergence can only be tested non-perturbatively. Such tests, particularly using lattice gauge theory, will be reviewed and fully confirm the underlying mechanisms. The review will demonstrate that the structure of the Standard Model is very special, and qualitative changes occur beyond it. We will also discuss the extension beyond the Standard Model, paying particular attention to structural differences in phenomenology. Again, non-perturbative tests of these results will be reviewed. Finally, to make this review self-contained, we will briefly discuss issues like the triviality and hierarchy problems and how they fit into a fundamental field-theoretical formulation.

title: Quasar outflow energetics from broad absorption line variability
Abstract: Quasar outflows have been recognized as potential contributors to the co-evolution between supermassive black holes (SMBHs) and their host galaxies. Understanding the role of outflows in AGN feedback processes requires observational constraints on wind locations and kinetic energies. We utilize broad absorption line (BAL) variability to investigate the properties of a sample of 71 BAL quasars with P-V broad absorption. The presence of P-V BALs indicates that other BALs like C-IV are saturated, suggesting that variability in those lines is driven by clouds crossing the line of sight. Using these constraints with measurements of BAL variability, we estimate outflow locations and energetics. Our data set consists of multiple-epoch spectra from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and MDM Observatory. We detect significant (4σ) BAL variations from 10 quasars in our sample over rest-frame time scales between < 0.2-3.8 years. Our derived distances for the 10 variable outflows are nominally < 1-10 pc from the SMBH using the transverse-motion scenario and < 100-1000 pc from the central source using ionization-change considerations. These distances, combined with the estimated high outflow column densities (i.e., N_H > 10^22 cm^-2), yield outflow kinetic luminosities between ~ 0.001-1 times the bolometric luminosity of the quasar, indicating that many absorber energies within our sample are viable for AGN feedback.

title: Complex crystalline structures in a two-dimensional core-softened system
Abstract: A cascade of phase transitions from a square to a hexagonal lattice is investigated in a 2D system of particles interacting via a core-softened potential. The presence of two length scales of repulsion enables different local configurations with four, five, and six neighbors, leading to the formation of complex crystals. We generalize the previously proposed interpolation method for calculating pair correlations in crystals with elemental cells containing more than one particle. The method's high efficiency is demonstrated using a snub square lattice as an illustrative example.  Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that the snub square lattice breaks under heating, generating a high-density quasicrystalline phase with 12-fold symmetry. A simple theoretical model is proposed to explain the physical mechanism governing this phenomenon: with increasing density (from square to hexagonal phases), the concentrations of different local configurations, randomly realized through plane tiling, change to minimize the system's energy. The calculated phase diagram in the intermediate density region justifies the existence of the HD12 phase and demonstrates a cascade of first-order transitions ("square - HD12 - hexagonal") solid phases with density growth. Our results enhance our understanding of the physical mechanisms responsible for quasicrystal formation, making them relevant to a broad community in material science and soft matter.

title: Energy-Efficient Non-Orthogonal Transmission under Reliability and Finite Blocklength Constraints
Abstract: This paper investigates an energy-efficient non-orthogonal transmission design problem for two downlink receivers with stringent reliability and finite blocklength (latency) constraints. The Shannon capacity formula, widely used in traditional designs, requires the assumption of infinite blocklength and is therefore no longer appropriate. We adopt the newly developed finite blocklength coding capacity formula to explicitly specify the trade-off between reliability and code blocklength. However, conventional successive interference cancellation (SIC) may become infeasible due to heterogeneous blocklengths. We consider several scenarios with different channel conditions, both with and without SIC. By carefully examining the problem structure, we present closed-form expressions for the optimal power and code blocklength for energy-efficient transmissions. Simulation results provide insightful information about the conditions under which non-orthogonal transmission is more energy-efficient than orthogonal transmission, such as Time Division Multiple Access (TDMA).

title: The Astrobiology of the Anthropocene
Abstract: Human influence on the biosphere has been evident since the development of widespread agriculture, and some stratigraphers have suggested that the activities of modern civilization indicate a transition to a new geological epoch. The study of the Anthropocene as a geological epoch, and its implications for the future of energy-intensive civilizations, is an emerging transdisciplinary field in which astrobiology can play a significant role. Habitability research of Earth, Mars, and exoplanets examines extreme cases relevant for understanding climate change as a planetary process. Energy-intensive civilizations will also face thermodynamic limits to growth, which provides an important constraint for estimating the longevity of human civilization and guiding the search for extraterrestrial intelligence. We recommend that mission concepts such as LUVOIR, HabEx, and OST be pursued to make significant progress towards understanding the future evolution of life on our planet and the possible evolution of technological, energy-intensive life elsewhere in the universe.

title: Nonlinear quantile mixed models
Abstract: In regression applications, the presence of nonlinearity and correlation among observations poses computational challenges not only in traditional settings such as least squares regression but also (and especially) when the objective function is non-smooth, as in the case of quantile regression. In this paper, we develop methods for modeling and estimating nonlinear conditional quantile functions when data are clustered within two-level nested designs. This work extends the linear quantile mixed models of Geraci and Bottai (2014, Statistics and Computing). We develop a novel algorithm that combines a smoothing algorithm for quantile regression and a second-order Laplacian approximation for nonlinear mixed models. To assess the proposed methods, we present a simulation study and two applications, one in pharmacokinetics and one related to growth curve modeling in agriculture.

title: Controlling invasive ant species: a theoretical strategy for efficient monitoring in the early stage of invasion
Abstract: Invasion by the red imported fire ant, Solenopsis invicta Buren, has destructive effects on native biodiversity, agriculture, and public health. This ant's aggressive foraging behavior and high reproductive capability have enabled its establishment of wild populations in most regions into which it has been imported. Eradication requires thorough nest monitoring and destruction during early invasion to prevent range expansion. We investigate the intensity of monitoring required to eradicate the fire ant, assuming that the ant was introduced into a region and that monitoring was conducted immediately after nest detection in an effort to detect all other potentially established nests.  We developed a mathematical model to investigate detection rates. Setting the monitoring limit to three years, the detection rate was maximized when monitoring was conducted by shifting bait trap locations and setting them at intervals of 30 meters for each monitoring. Monitoring should be conducted within a radius of at least 4 kilometers around the source nest, or wider depending on how late a nest is found.  For ease of application, we also derived equations for finding the minimum bait interval required in an arbitrary ant species for thorough monitoring.

title: Sampling alien species inside and outside protected areas: does it matter?
Abstract: Data on alien species presences are generally more readily available in protected areas than non-protected areas due to higher sampling efforts within protected areas. We investigate whether the results and conclusions based on analyses of data collected in protected areas are representative of wider non-protected regions.  We address this question by analyzing recently published data on alien plants in Greece.  Mixed effects models were used with alien species presences in 8.25 x 8.25 km cells as the dependent variable and the percentage of protected area, as well as the agricultural and artificial land cover types richness (as indicators of human presence) as independent variables. Additionally, the spatial cross-correlation between the percentage of protected area and alien species richness was examined across scales. Results indicated that the percentage of protected area per cell is a poor predictor of alien species richness.  Spatial analysis indicated that cells with a higher percentage of protected areas have slightly fewer alien species than cells with a lower percentage of protected areas. This result is likely driven by the overall negative correlation between habitat protection and anthropogenic activities.  Thus, the conclusions drawn from data deriving from protected areas are likely to hold true for patterns of alien species in non-protected areas when human pressures are accounted for.

title: Automated Image Analysis Framework for the High-Throughput Determination of Grapevine Berry Sizes Using Conditional Random Fields
Abstract: Berry size is a crucial fruit trait in grapevine breeding. Non-invasive, image-based phenotyping offers a fast and precise method for monitoring grapevine berry size. This study develops an automated image analysis framework to estimate grapevine berry size from images in a high-throughput manner. The framework includes (i) the detection of circular structures that are potentially berries and (ii) the classification of these structures into the 'berry' or 'non-berry' class using a conditional random field. The approach utilizes the concept of one-class classification, as only the target class 'berry' is of interest and needs to be modeled.  The classification is performed using an automated active learning approach, requiring no user interaction during the classification process.  Additionally, the process adapts automatically to changing image conditions, such as illumination or berry color. The framework was tested on three datasets consisting of a total of 139 images. The images were captured in an experimental vineyard at different stages of grapevine growth according to the BBCH scale. The mean berry size of a plant estimated by the framework correlates with the manually measured berry size by 0.88.

title: Single gene dynamics under controlled mating
Abstract: We aim to develop models for the genotype evolution of agricultural animals involved in primary production processes. Classical genotype evolution models have tended to be very simple to allow for analytic methods. Unfortunately, these models fail to describe processes in artificially controlled populations, including agricultural livestock.  We describe an approach to stochastically modeling the dynamics of a biallelic polymorphism herd under conditions of controlled mating and restricted herd size from above. The system of stochastic differential equations we propose is based on jump diffusion processes to provide an effective platform for Monte Carlo simulation.  A key feature of the model is the division of the population into a main herd comprising animals involved in the production process and a replacement herd of animals not currently in the production process (typically juvenile animals). This feature allows for exploring different strategies for adding replacement animals to the main herd without altering the part of the model concerned with the dynamics of the main herd. A discrete-time version of the model has been developed that reflects the typical practice of New Zealand dairy herd management. Our Monte Carlo simulation has demonstrated that an isolated deme whose size is bounded above exhibits size stabilization at a level less than the control limit, resembling partial extinction, an effect well-known in classic models.

title: Hawkes Processes for Invasive Species Modeling and Management
Abstract: The spread of invasive species to new areas threatens the stability of ecosystems and causes major economic losses in agriculture and forestry. We propose a novel approach to minimizing the spread of an invasive species given a limited intervention budget.  We first model invasive species propagation using Hawkes processes and then derive closed-form expressions for characterizing the effect of an intervention action on the invasion process. We use this to obtain an optimal intervention plan based on an integer programming formulation and compare the optimal plan against several ecologically-motivated heuristic strategies used in practice. We present an empirical study of two variants of the invasive control problem: minimizing the final rate of invasions and minimizing the number of invasions at the end of a given time horizon. Our results show that the optimized intervention achieves nearly the same level of control that would be attained by completely eradicating the species, with a 20% cost saving. Additionally, we design a heuristic intervention strategy based on a combination of the density and life stage of the invasive individuals, and find that it comes surprisingly close to the optimized strategy, suggesting that this could serve as a good rule of thumb in invasive species management.

title: On Metropolis Growth
Abstract: We consider the scaling laws, second-order statistics, and entropy of the consumed energy of metropolis cities, which are hybrid complex systems comprising social networks, engineering systems, agricultural output, economic activity, and energy components.  We abstract a city in terms of two fundamental variables: s resource cells (of unit area) that represent energy-consuming geographic or spatial zones (e.g., land, housing, or infrastructure) and a population comprising n mobile units that can migrate between these cells. We show that with a constant metropolis area (fixed s), the variance and entropy of consumed energy initially increase with n, reach a maximum, and then eventually diminish to zero as saturation is reached. These metrics are indicators of the spatial mobility of the population. Under certain situations, the variance is bounded as a quadratic function of the mean consumed energy of the metropolis. However, when population and metropolis area are endogenous, growth in the latter is arrested when n ≤ s/2 log(s) due to diminished population density. Conversely, population growth reaches equilibrium when n ≥ s log(n) or equivalently when the aggregate of both overpopulated and underpopulated areas is large. Moreover, we also draw the relationship between our approach and multi-scalar information when economic dependency between a metropolis's sub-regions is based on the entropy of consumed energy. Finally, if the city's economic size (domestic product, etc.) is proportional to the consumed energy, then for a constant population density, we show that the economy scales linearly with the surface area (or s).

title: Assessing the capacity and flow of ecosystem services in multifunctional landscapes: evidence of a rural-urban gradient in a Mediterranean small island state
Abstract: Distinguishing between the capacity of ecosystems to generate ecosystem services (ES) and the actual use of these services (ES flow) in ES assessment and mapping is crucial for understanding the sustainability of ES use.  This study assesses the spatial variation in ES capacity and flow in the Mediterranean small island state of Malta. The services included in this study were crop provisioning, beekeeping and honey production, fodder and livestock production, crop pollination, air quality regulation, and aesthetic ES. This assessment develops different spatial models, which utilize available datasets, causal relationships between datasets, including a generated land use land cover (LULC) map, and statistical models and indicators based on direct measurements. Individual ES indicators were mapped to visualize and compare their spatial patterns across the case study area. Subsequently, an analysis of ES associations and bundles was carried out using Pearson parametric correlation tests for both ES capacity and flow indicators generated from this study, and through Principal Component Analysis. Results demonstrate several significant synergistic interactions between ES capacity and flow in rural landscapes characterized with agricultural and semi-natural LULC categories, indicating high landscape multifunctionality. In contrast, predominantly urban areas tend to be characterized by low ecosystem capacity and ES flow, suggesting that ES delivery in the landscapes of the study area is determined by land use intensity. These findings support the notion that multifunctional rural landscapes provide multiple ES, making an important contribution to human well-being, and that land use planning that develops green infrastructure in urban areas can significantly contribute to supporting biodiversity and ES delivery.

title: Bayesian Measurement Error Correction in Structured Additive Distributional Regression with an Application to the Analysis of Sensor Data on Soil-Plant Variability
Abstract: The flexibility of the Bayesian approach to account for covariates with measurement error is combined with semiparametric regression models for a class of continuous, discrete, and mixed univariate response distributions, with potentially all parameters depending on a structured additive predictor. Markov chain Monte Carlo enables a modular and numerically efficient implementation of Bayesian measurement error correction based on the imputation of unobserved error-free covariate values. We allow for very general measurement errors, including correlated replicates with heterogeneous variances. The proposal is first assessed by a simulation trial, then it is applied to the assessment of a soil-plant relationship crucial for implementing efficient agricultural management practices. Observations on multi-depth soil information forage ground cover for a seven hectares Alfalfa stand in South Italy were obtained using sensors with very refined spatial resolution. Estimating a functional relation between ground cover and soil with these data involves addressing issues linked to the spatial and temporal misalignment and the large data size. We propose a preliminary spatial interpolation on a lattice covering the field and subsequent analysis by a structured additive distributional regression model accounting for measurement error in the soil covariate. Results are interpreted and commented on in connection to possible Alfalfa management strategies.

title: Julian Ernst Besag, 26 March 1945 -- 6 August 2010, a biographical memoir

title: Real-Time Robust Finger Gaits Planning under Object Shape and Dynamics Uncertainties
Abstract: Dexterous manipulation, vital for tasks in assembly lines, warehouses, and agriculture, often necessitates sequential adjustments of grasping gestures, known as finger gaits, to manage workspace limitations and ensure object stability. The second stage employs a robust manipulation controller, leveraging robust control and force optimization, to mitigate object dynamics uncertainties and external disturbances. title: (Un)predictability of strong El Niño events
Abstract: The El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is a prominent mode of interannual variability in the coupled equatorial Pacific atmosphere-ocean system. However, its strength exhibits irregular fluctuations on decadal time scales. Notably, exceptionally strong El Niño events occurred in 1982-83, 1997-98, and 2015-16, impacting weather patterns globally. Predictions in 2014 anticipated the 2015-16 event a year earlier. Accurately forecasting El Niño's strength is crucial due to its profound effects on hydroclimate and agriculture worldwide. This paper investigates the frequency and regularity of strong El Niño events within the framework of chaotic dynamical systems. The research identifies a mechanism that limits predictability in a conceptual "recharge oscillator" model of ENSO. Weak seasonal forcing or noise in this model can induce irregular transitions between an oscillatory state with strong El Niño events and a chaotic state lacking strong events. In this regime, the timing of strong El Niño events on decadal time scales remains unpredictable.

Abstract: Agriculture serves as a driver of economic opportunity through innovation, fosters rural prosperity, promotes agricultural production that nourishes Americans, and aims to conserve natural resources through healthy private working lands, conservation efforts, improved watersheds, and restored forests. Agriculture, from production to food supply, supports both rural and urban economies across the US, accounting for 10% of US jobs and creating new opportunities in the burgeoning field of data-driven farming. However, US global competitiveness in food and nutrition security is at risk due to accelerated investments in agriculture, food, energy, and resource management by other countries. To ensure US global competitiveness and long-term food security, it is crucial to develop sustainable physical and cyber infrastructures that enable self-managing and sustainable farming. These infrastructures should support next-generation precision farms by harnessing modern and emerging technologies such as small satellites, broadband Internet, tele-operation, augmented reality, advanced data analytics, sensors, and robotics.

title: Development and properties of composite cement reinforced coconut fiber with the addition of fly ash

The composite cement comprises 20% fly ash and 80% sand by weight. Different weight percentages of coconut fiber (3%, 6%, 9%, 12%, and 15%) are incorporated as reinforcement for the cement composites. The water-to-cement ratio ranges from 0.55 to 0.70, adjusted to maintain workability. The cement composites are cured in water for 7, 14, and 28 days, respectively. The study presents results for physical properties (density, moisture content, water absorption) and mechanical properties (compressive strength, modulus of rupture).

title: Machine Vision System for 3D Plant Phenotyping
Abstract: Machine vision for plant phenotyping is an emerging research area with significant potential for high-throughput applications in agriculture and crop science. While 2D-based approaches have limitations, 3D plant analysis is becoming the standard for current phenotyping technologies. This paper presents an automated system for analyzing plant growth in indoor conditions. A gantry robot system is used to perform scanning tasks in an automated manner throughout the plant's lifetime. A 3D laser scanner, mounted as the robot's payload, captures surface point cloud data of the plant from multiple views. The plant is monitored from vegetative to reproductive stages in light/dark cycles within a controlled growth chamber. An efficient 3D reconstruction algorithm aligns multiple scans to generate a 3D mesh of the plant, followed by surface area and volume computations. The entire system, including the programmable growth chamber, robot, scanner, data transfer, and analysis, is fully automated, allowing a naive user to initiate the system with a mouse click and receive growth analysis results at the end of the plant's lifetime without any intermediate intervention. As evidence of its functionality, the study shows and analyzes quantitative results of the rhythmic growth patterns of the dicot Arabidopsis thaliana (L.) and the monocot barley (Hordeum vulgare L.) plants under their diurnal light/dark cycles.

title: Aggregation and visualization of spatial data with application to classification of land use and land cover

PlaniSphere incorporates an algorithm to aggregate remote sensing images with census data for the classification and visualization of land use and land cover (LULC). The results demonstrate that PlaniSphere effectively classifies LULC geospatial datasets from multiple formats. National census datasets can be used for calibrating remote sensing LULC classifications, providing a novel approach for classifying remote sensing data. The approach proposed in this paper is valuable for LULC classification in environmental spatial analysis.

title: Coupling of Crop Assignment and Vehicle Routing for Harvest Planning in Agriculture
Abstract: This paper presents a method for harvest planning based on the coupling of crop assignment with vehicle routing. The setting involves multiple fields, a path network connecting them, and multiple depots where harvesters are initially located. The primary question addressed is: Which crop, from a set of different crops, should be assigned to each field considering the given setting? This question is fundamental for farm managers at the beginning of each work-cycle, starting with planting and ending with harvesting. Instead of solely solving an assignment problem, the method considers the connectivity between fields. In practice, fields are often geographically dispersed, and traveling costs of machinery and limited harvesting windows necessitate optimized operations and route planning. Therefore, the proposed method outputs crop assignments to fields and simultaneously determines crop-tours, which are optimized sequences for servicing fields of the same crop during harvest. This approach is particularly relevant for large farms and groups of farms collaborating and sharing machinery. The paper derives exact algorithms based on integer programming. For large numbers of fields, where these algorithms may become computationally intractable, elements of clustering and the solution of local Traveling Salesman Problems are incorporated, rendering the method heuristic and generally suboptimal but maintaining large-scale applicability.
