title: Quantification of avoidable yield losses in oilseed Brassica caused by insect pests
Abstract: A six-year field study was conducted from 2001-2002 to 2006-2007 at Punjab Agricultural University, Ludhiana, India, to investigate seed yield losses in different Brassica species (B. juncea, B. napus, B. carinata, B. rapa, and Eruca sativa) due to insect pest infestation. The experiment employed a randomized block design with three replications, divided into two sets: protected/sprayed and unprotected. Data on insect pest infestation and seed yield were recorded weekly and at harvest, respectively. The study revealed that seed yield losses, attributed to mustard aphid and cabbage caterpillar, ranged from 6.5% to 26.4%. E. sativa suffered the least seed yield loss and harbored the lowest population of mustard aphid (2.1 aphids/plant) and cabbage caterpillar (2.4 larvae/plant). Conversely, B. carinata exhibited high susceptibility to cabbage caterpillar (26.2 larvae/plant) and experienced the maximum yield loss (26.4%).

title: Multiresolution Mapping and Informative Path Planning for UAV-based Terrain Monitoring
Abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) offer timely and cost-effective delivery of high-quality sensing data. However, determining when and where to take measurements in complex environments remains a challenge. To address this issue, this study introduces a novel multiresolution mapping approach for informative path planning in terrain monitoring using UAVs. The strategy leverages the spatial correlation encoded in a Gaussian Process model as a prior for Bayesian data fusion with probabilistic sensors. This allows incorporating altitude-dependent sensor models for aerial imaging and performing constant-time measurement updates. The resulting maps are used to plan information-rich trajectories in continuous 3-D space through a combination of grid search and evolutionary optimization. The framework is evaluated on the application of agricultural biomass monitoring. Extensive simulations demonstrate that the proposed planner outperforms existing methods, with mean error reductions of up to 45% compared to traditional "lawnmower" coverage. Proof of concept is demonstrated using a multirotor to map color in different environments.

title: A mixture model approach to infer land-use influence on point referenced water quality
Abstract: Assessing water quality across space and time is of significant interest for both agricultural and public health reasons. The standard method for evaluating water quality in a catchment or group of catchments typically involves collecting point measurements of water quality and additional information, such as the date and time of measurements, rainfall amounts, land-use and soil-type of the catchment, and elevation. Some of this auxiliary information is point data, measured at the exact location, while others, such as land-use, are areal data often in a compositional format. Two challenges arise when incorporating this information into a statistical model to predict (e.g., the influence of land-use on water quality). First is the spatial change of support problem that occurs when using areal data to predict outcomes at point locations. Second, the physical process driving water quality is not compositional; rather, it is the observation process that yields compositional data. This paper presents an approach that addresses these two issues by using a latent variable to identify the land-use most likely influencing water quality. This latent variable is employed in a spatial mixture model to estimate the influence of land-use on water quality. The potential of this approach is demonstrated using data from a water quality research study in the Mount Lofty range in South Australia.

title: Fast and robust curve skeletonization for real-world elongated objects
Abstract: This paper addresses the problem of extracting curve skeletons of three-dimensional, elongated objects from a noisy surface, finding applications in agricultural contexts such as extracting the branching structure of plants. The method's runtime ranges from hundreds of milliseconds to less than four seconds on large, challenging datasets, making it suitable for situations requiring real-time decision-making. Experiments on synthetic models and data from real-world objects, some collected in challenging field conditions, demonstrate the approach's favorable performance compared to classical thinning algorithms and recent contributions to the field.

title: The Diffusion of Humans and Cultures in the Course of the Spread of Farming
Abstract: The most profound change in the relationship between humans and their environment was the introduction of agriculture and pastoralism. For a comprehensive understanding of the expansion process, it appears appropriate to apply a diffusive model. Broadly, these numerical modeling approaches can be categorized as correlative, continuous, and discrete. Common to all approaches is the comparison with collections of radiocarbon data, which reveal the apparent wave of advance of the transition to farming. However, these datasets vary in entry density and data quality, often disregarding local and regional specifics, research gaps, or dating uncertainties. Consequently, most of these databases may only be used on a very general, broad scale. One of the pitfalls of utilizing irregularly spaced or documented radiocarbon data becomes evident from the map generated by Fort (this volume, Chapter 16). While the general east-west and south-north trends are apparent, some areas appear to have undergone anomalously early transitions to farming. This could be attributed to faulty entries in the database, regional problems with radiocarbon dating, or unnoticed or undocumented laboratory mistakes.

title: Sequestration of atmospheric carbon dioxide as inorganic carbon in the unsaturated zone under semi-arid forests
Abstract: Inorganic carbon, in the form of allogenic (transported) and pedogenic (soil) carbonates in semi-arid soils, may constitute a significant carbon sink. Carbon dioxide (CO2), originating from the atmosphere and exhaled by tree roots into the soil, can be hydrated by soil water within the unsaturated zone (USZ) of semi-arid soils, producing the carbonic acid (H2CO3) solutes HCO3- bicarbonate and H+ Hydrogen ion. This H+ can then dissolve relict soil CaCO3 carbonate (calcite), releasing Ca+2 calcium cations and more HCO3- bicarbonate. When conditions allow, one mole of Ca+2 and two moles of HCO3- combine to precipitate one mole of calcite, releasing one mole of CO2: Ca+2 + 2HCO3- --> CaCO3 + CO2 + H2O. However, it has been claimed that such carbonates do not sequester significant amounts of present-day atmospheric CO2. The reasons cited are that they originate partly from pre-existing limestone and that for every mole of calcite precipitated, one mole of CO2 may be liberated to the atmosphere. It was argued that only if the Ca+2 cation is derived from a non-carbonate source can sequestration be assumed. This study tests these assumptions under field conditions at two semi-arid sites in Israel. The findings reveal that bicarbonate, originating from root exhalation, is depleted and incorporated within the USZ as carbonates precipitate. Therefore, a net sequestration of atmospheric CO2 occurs under semi-arid forests. Moreover, most of the CO2 liberated in the precipitation reaction may remain in the soil. Additionally, Ca+2 in the sediment may also be supplied from sources other than pre-existing calcite. Forestation can therefore enhance pedogenic carbonate formation. By extrapolating the data globally, the study suggests that worldwide semi-arid forests (existing and to be planted) may sequester 5-20% of the current annual anthropogenic increase of atmospheric carbon dioxide as pedogenic carbonate.

title: An association between information and communication technology and agriculture knowledge management process in Indian milk co-operatives and non-profit organizations: an empirical analysis

The proposed set of metrics can serve as common tools to measure ICT performance in KM processes within agricultural organizations and for future research.

title: Towards Unsupervised Weed Scouting for Agricultural Robotics
Abstract:
Weed scouting is a critical aspect of modern integrated weed management but can be time-consuming and sparse when performed manually. Automated weed scouting and destruction typically rely on classification systems that can classify a predefined set of species. This significantly limits deployability as classification systems need retraining for any field with a different set of weed species present. To overcome this limitation, this paper explores a clustering approach to weed scouting that can be utilized in any field without requiring prior species knowledge. The system is demonstrated using challenging data collected in the field from an agricultural robotics platform. The study shows that significant improvements can be achieved by (i) learning low-dimensional (bottleneck) features using a deep convolutional neural network to represent plants in general and (ii) tying views of the same area (plant) together. By deploying this algorithm on in-field data collected by AgBotII, the researchers successfully clustered cotton plants from grasses without prior knowledge or training for the specific plants in the field.

title: Differential imprints of distinct ENSO flavors in global patterns of very low and high seasonal precipitation
Abstract: Recent research has extensively examined the impact of El Niño's two distinct flavors, East Pacific (EP) and Central Pacific (CP)/Modoki El Niño, on global climate variability. While most studies rely on linear multivariate statistics or composite analysis, these methods assume a uniform linear statistical dependency across different phases of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), which may not be entirely accurate. This study statistically analyzes the co-occurrence of very high or very low seasonal precipitation sums over vast global land areas with the presence of EP and CP types of both El Niño and La Niña. Using event coincidence analysis, the study reveals differential imprints of both flavors on extreme seasonal precipitation patterns in distinct regions worldwide. These findings highlight the potential significant impacts on agriculture, biomass production, and public health. Notably, the analysis reveals statistically significant event coincidence rates with hydrometeorological anomalies at larger spatial scales during EP periods, compared to sparser patterns observed during CP periods. This statistical analysis confirms previously reported interrelations for EP periods and identifies additional distinct regional patterns of very high/low seasonal precipitation, including increased rainfall over Central Asia alongside CP periods, previously unreported. The results underscore the critical need to differentiate between El Niño and La Niña flavors to comprehend the emergence of strong regional hydrometeorological anomalies and predict their associated ecological and socioeconomic consequences.

title: Understanding food inflation in India: A Machine Learning approach
Abstract: Persistent high inflation, especially in food prices, has posed a challenge to India's economic growth over the past decade. The BRT results indicate the importance of all predictor variables in explaining food price fluctuations, with MSP and farm wages being relatively more influential than others. International food prices were found to have limited relevance in explaining variations in domestic food prices. title: Changing U.S. Extreme Temperature Statistics
Abstract: Global mean temperature rise only partially captures the warming phenomenon. For various purposes, including agriculture and human life, temperature extremes might be more significant than temperature means, and changes in local extremes might hold more weight than mean global changes. This study defines a nonparametric statistic to describe extreme temperature behavior by quantifying the frequency of local daily all-time highs and lows, normalized by their frequency in the null hypothesis of no climate change. Averaging this metric over 1218 weather stations in the contiguous United States, the study reveals significantly fewer all-time lows than predicted by the null hypothesis of unchanging climate. In contrast, record highs exhibit no significant trend. The metric is evaluated by Monte Carlo simulation for stationary and warming temperature distributions, allowing comparison of historical temperature records with modeled behavior.

title: Asymptotic generalized bivariate extreme with random index
Abstract: In numerous biological, agricultural, military, and quality control problems, achieving a fixed sample size is often impossible due to the inevitable loss of observations. Assuming the random sample size is independent of the basic variables and its df converges weakly to a non-degenerate limit, the study identifies the necessary and sufficient conditions for the weak convergence of the random bivariate extreme GOS. Moreover, when the interrelation of the random size and the basic rv's is not restricted, sufficient conditions for convergence and the forms of the limit df's are deduced. title: A model-based approach to assist variety evaluation in sunflower crop

The study also identifies prominent efforts involving IoT and patient-generated health data (PGHD) in converting multimodal data into actionable information (big data to smart data). To address the challenge of limited clinical data availability from a significant portion of subjects and unrepresentative subject populations, this study proposes a novel unsupervised (task-agnostic) time-series representation learning technique called act2vec. act2vec learns valuable features by considering the co-occurrence of activity levels alongside the periodicity of human activity patterns. Abstract: The increased availability of large databases of electronic health records (EHRs) presents an opportunity to enhance health risk screening. title: Assessing public health interventions using Web content

title: Migrations, vaccinations and epidemic control

When migration is included in the model, the second region is assumed to have a disease risk that encourages its inhabitants to accept vaccination, while the population in the first region tends to reject vaccination, perceiving it as riskier than the disease. Therefore, the second region acts as a "buffer zone" between the two extreme regions. The study investigates the basic reproductive ratio as a function of vaccination in all regions and migration among them. Numerical analysis reveals explicit situations where migration has an overall positive effect on disease dynamics, both with and without vaccinations. The study also identifies explicit formulas for the limits of small ("closed borders") and high migration ("open borders").

title: Model-Based Clustering of Nonparametric Weighted Networks with Application to Water Pollution Analysis

title: A new microscopy for imaging retinal cells

title: GW170817: $\textit{Swift}$ UV detection of a blue kilonova, and improving the search in O3

title: Activity and Circadian Rhythm of Sepsis Patients in the Intensive Care Unit

title: Automatic Classification of Functional Gait Disorders

title: Towards a science of human stories: using sentiment analysis and emotional arcs to understand the building blocks of complex social systems

title: Modeling Individual Cyclic Variation in Human Behavior
Abstract: Cycles are fundamental to human health and behavior. Modeling these cycles in time series data poses a challenge, as they are often not labeled or directly observed and need to be inferred from multidimensional measurements over time. This study introduces CyHMMs, a cyclic hidden Markov model method for detecting and modeling cycles in a collection of multidimensional heterogeneous time series data. In contrast to previous methods, CyHMMs address several challenges encountered in real-world cycle modeling: they can model multivariate data with discrete and continuous dimensions, explicitly model and are robust to missing data, and share information across individuals to model variation within and between individual time series. Experiments on synthetic and real-world health-tracking data demonstrate that CyHMMs infer cycle lengths more accurately than existing methods, achieving 58% lower error on simulated data and 63% lower error on real-world data compared to the best-performing baseline.  CyHMMs can also perform functions that baselines cannot, including modeling the progression of individual features/symptoms over the cycle, identifying the most variable features, and clustering individual time series into groups with distinct characteristics.  Applying CyHMMs to two real-world health-tracking datasets—menstrual cycle symptoms and physical activity tracking data—yielded important insights, including which symptoms to expect at each point during the cycle.  The study also found that individuals fall into several groups with distinct cycle patterns, and these groups differ along dimensions not provided to the model.  For instance, by modeling missing data in the menstrual cycles dataset, the study discovered a medically relevant group of birth control users, even though information on birth control was not given to the model.

title: On the Sample Complexity of Multichannel Frequency Estimation via Convex Optimization

This paper analyzes atomic norm minimization for multichannel frequency estimation from noiseless compressive data, demonstrating that the sample size per channel required for exact estimation decreases with an increasing number of channels under mild conditions. Specifically, given L channels, order K(log K)(1 + 1/L log N) samples per channel, selected randomly from N equispaced samples, are sufficient to ensure with high probability the exact estimation of K frequencies that are normalized and mutually separated by at least 4/N.  Numerical results corroborate the analysis.

title: Health Data in an Open World

title: Prevalence of DNSSEC for hospital websites in Illinois

The study highlights the need for increased awareness and adoption of security measures to protect critical healthcare websites.

title: Exploring atmospheric radon with airborne gamma-ray spectroscopy
Abstract: Radon-222 (222Rn) is a noble radioactive gas produced along the uranium-238 (238U) decay chain, commonly present in soils and rocks. Simultaneously, 222Rn is a widespread atmospheric tracer, with its spatial distribution often used as a proxy for climate and pollution studies.  Airborne gamma-ray spectroscopy (AGRS) typically treats 222Rn as a source of background, affecting the indirect estimation of equivalent 238U concentration.  This study presents the first application of the AGRS method for quantifying the presence of 222Rn in the atmosphere and assessing its vertical profile.  High-statistics radiometric data acquired during an offshore survey was fitted as a superposition of a constant component due to the experimental setup background radioactivity plus a height-dependent contribution due to cosmic radiation and atmospheric 222Rn.  The refined statistical analysis provides conclusive evidence of AGRS 222Rn detection, yielding a 222Rn concentration of 0.96 ± 0.07 Bq/m3 and an atmospheric layer depth of 1318 ± 22 m, fully compatible with existing literature data.

title: Quantifying a qualitative framework of patients perceptions, attitudes and behavior relevant to oral health related quality of life

title: Increased adaptive immune responses and proper feedback regulation protect against clinical dengue
Abstract: Dengue is the most prevalent arthropod-borne viral disease, with clinical symptoms ranging from mild dengue fever to severe, life-threatening dengue shock syndrome. However, most DENV infections are asymptomatic. Asymptomatic DENV-infected patients offer a unique opportunity to understand host immune responses that lead to virus elimination without negative health impacts. title: Interactions between Health Searchers and Search Engines

title: Quantitative toxicity prediction using topology based multi-task deep neural networks

Extensive numerical studies indicated that the proposed topological learning methods outperformed state-of-the-art methods in the literature for quantitative toxicity analysis. title: Iterated filtering methods for Markov process epidemic models

Both infections were associated with reduced survival, and neither infection was associated with reduced fecundity. The model successfully reproduced co-infection patterns in the data and predicted contrasting impacts of co-infection at individual and population scales. While BTB facilitated brucellosis infection at the individual level, the model predicts a strong negative impact of brucellosis on BTB at the population level. Modeled populations with brucellosis exhibited lower endemic prevalence and basic reproduction number (Ro) of BTB compared to populations without brucellosis. However, mammogram segmentation is challenging due to its dependence on the types of mammary tissues. This study introduces a new semi-supervised segmentation algorithm based on a modified version of the GrowCut algorithm for automatic mammographic image segmentation. The modification involves using fuzzy Gaussian membership functions to improve the evolution rule of the original GrowCut algorithm, enabling the estimation of the uncertainty of a pixel being an object or background. This approach significantly reduces the expert effort required for seed point initialization in GrowCut, eliminating the need for selecting background seeds. The study also developed an automatic point selection process using the simulated annealing optimization method, eliminating the need for human intervention. The proposed approach was qualitatively compared to other state-of-the-art segmentation techniques based on the shape of segmented regions. To validate the proposal, an image classifier using a classical multilayer perceptron was constructed. Zernike moments were employed to extract segmented image features. This analysis utilized 685 mammograms from the IRMA breast cancer database, focusing on fat and fibroid tissues. The method was evaluated using numerical phantoms consisting of electrical conductivity images with subjects positioned at the center, between the center and the edge, and on the edge of a circular section, utilizing meshes of 415 finite elements. title: Causal inference taking into account unobserved confounding

The intervals are derived by analyzing the bias introduced by unobserved confounders, enabling comparison of bias due to unconfoundedness violation with bias due to model misspecification. Numerical experiments demonstrate that bias from moderate unobserved confounding often dominates misspecification bias in typical situations. The empirical coverage of these uncertainty intervals is also investigated, and the results are applied to a study on the effect of regular food intake on health. title: Spectral Methods for Immunization of Large Networks

Theoretical guarantees on the algorithm's running time demonstrate its efficiency compared to existing solutions. The algorithm's performance is evaluated on several real-world graphs. title: Scalable Approximation Algorithm for Network Immunization

title: Kirigami-based Elastic Metamaterials with Anisotropic Mass Density for Subwavelength Flexural Wave Control

title: MEDOC: a Python wrapper to load MEDLINE into a local MySQL database

title: Replacement AutoEncoder: A Privacy-Preserving Algorithm for Sensory Data Analysis

This paper proposes a privacy-preserving sensing framework for managing access to time-series data, balancing utility with individual privacy protection. The study introduces Replacement AutoEncoder, a novel algorithm that learns to transform discriminative features corresponding to sensitive inferences into features commonly observed in non-sensitive inferences. This efficiency is achieved by defining a user-customized objective function for deep autoencoders. The replacement method not only eliminates the possibility of recognizing sensitive inferences but also prevents detection of their occurrence, addressing a key weakness of filtering or randomization approaches. The algorithm's efficacy is evaluated with an activity recognition task in a multi-sensing environment using extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets. The study shows that Replacement AutoEncoder retains the recognition accuracy of state-of-the-art techniques while preserving privacy. Finally, the study utilizes Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to detect the occurrence of replacement after data release, demonstrating that this is only possible if the adversarial network is trained on the users' original data.

title: Design Considerations of a Sub-50 μW Receiver Front-end for Implantable Devices in MedRadio Band
Abstract: Emerging health-monitor applications, such as information transmission through multi-channel neural implants and image and video communication from inside the body, demand ultra-low active power (<50 μW) high data-rate, energy-scalable, highly energy-efficient (pJ/bit) radios. This paper investigates the power performance trade-offs of each front-end component in a conventional radio, including active matching, down-conversion, and RF/IF amplification, prioritizing them based on the highest performance/energy metric. The analysis reveals that 50 Ω active matching and RF gain are prohibitive for a 50 μW power budget. A mixer-first architecture with an N-path mixer and a self-biased inverter based baseband LNA, designed in TSMC 65nm technology, demonstrates that sub-50 μW performance can be achieved up to 10 Mbps (<5 pJ/b) with OOK modulation.

title: Categorization of an emerging discipline in the world publication system (SCOPUS): E-learning

The analysis reveals that a set of 219 publications exhibits high bibliometric interrelation and spans social sciences, computer science, and health. title: A generalization of moderated statistics to data adaptive semiparametric estimation in high-dimensional biology

While the size of these datasets continues to grow, so does the complexity of identifying biomarkers from exposure patterns in health studies that measure baseline confounders. Moreover, avoiding model misspecification remains a persistent issue. Efficient estimators capable of incorporating flexible, data-adaptive regression techniques in estimating relevant components of the data-generating distribution offer a potential solution for mitigating model misspecification. However, in the context of high-dimensional problems demanding the simultaneous estimation of numerous parameters, standard variance estimators have proven unstable, leading to unreliable Type-I error control even after standard multiple testing corrections. We introduce a general approach for applying empirical Bayes shrinkage to variance estimators of a family of efficient, asymptotically linear estimators of population intervention causal effects. Our generalized shrinkage-based variance estimators enhance inferential stability in high-dimensional settings, facilitating the use of these estimators for deriving nonparametric variable importance measures in high-dimensional biological datasets with limited sample sizes. The outcome is a data-adaptive approach for robustly uncovering stable causal associations in high-dimensional data within studies with limited samples. The performance of our generalized variance estimator is evaluated against alternative variance estimators through numerical experiments. title: Semi-Supervised Approach to Monitoring Clinical Depressive Symptoms in Social Media

title: Ensemble Kalman Filters (EnKF) for State Estimation and Prediction of Two-time Scale Nonlinear Systems with Application to Gas Turbine Engines

This augmentation results in a two-time scale nonlinear system that is used for developing health estimation and prediction modules within a health monitoring framework. To this end, a two-time scale filtering approach is developed based on the ensemble Kalman filtering (EnKF) approach, leveraging the concept of model reduction. The performance of our proposed two-time scale ensemble Kalman filters is shown to be superior and computationally less intensive in terms of the equivalent flop (EF) complexity metric compared to well-known particle filtering (PF) approaches. Our proposed methodology is then applied to a gas turbine engine affected by turbine erosion as the degradation phenomenon and damage mechanism. Comprehensive comparative studies are conducted to validate and demonstrate the advantages and capabilities of our proposed framework and methodology.

title: Explaining Aviation Safety Incidents Using Deep Temporal Multiple Instance Learning

This work proposes a precursor mining algorithm that identifies events in the multidimensional time series that are correlated with the safety incident. Precursors are valuable for systems health and safety monitoring and in explaining and forecasting safety incidents. Existing methods struggle with scalability to high-dimensional time series data and are inefficient in capturing temporal behavior. We propose an approach combining multiple-instance learning (MIL) and deep recurrent neural networks (DRNN) to leverage MIL's ability to learn using weakly supervised data and DRNN's capacity to model temporal behavior. The algorithm, data, the rationale behind taking a MIL approach, and a comparative analysis of the proposed algorithm with baseline models are described. The application to a real-world aviation safety problem using data from a commercial airline company is discussed, along with the model's capabilities and shortcomings. title: Batch-based Activity Recognition from Egocentric Photo-Streams Revisited

The proposed batch-based approach achieved an overall accuracy of 89.85%, surpassing state-of-the-art end-to-end methodologies. title: Vector-borne disease risk indexes in spatially structured populations
Abstract: Applying prevention and control strategies for urban vector-borne diseases faces economic and physical limitations. Consequently, there is growing concern and interest in designing efficient strategies and regulations that health agencies can follow to mitigate the imminent impact of viruses like Dengue, Zika, and Chikungunya. These measures include fumigation, abatization, reducing breeding grounds, trash collection, and information campaigns. A fundamental question arises when designing control strategies regarding which areas and which strategies should be prioritized. In other words, one seeks to understand whether preventing contagion or reducing vector populations, and in which areas of the city, is more efficient. This work proposes risk indexes based on the concept of secondary cases from patch to patch. Thus, they account for human mobility and indicate which patch has a higher chance of being a corridor for disease spread and which is more vulnerable. They can also identify the neighborhood where controlling breeding grounds will reduce the number of potential cases more effectively. To illustrate the usefulness of these indexes, a set of numerical simulations is run in a mathematical model that considers urban mobility and differences in population density across the city's areas. If "i" represents a particular neighborhood, the transmission risk index TR_i measures the potential secondary cases caused by a host in that neighborhood. The vector transmission risk index VTR_i measures the potential secondary cases caused by a vector. Finally, the vulnerability risk index VR_i measures the potential secondary cases in the neighborhood. Transmission indexes can be used to prioritize geographically certain neighborhoods when implementing prevention and control measures. On the other hand, the vulnerability index can be helpful for implementing monitoring campaigns or public health investments.

title: One-step Estimation of Networked Population Size: Respondent-Driven Capture-Recapture with Anonymity
Abstract: Population size estimates for hidden and hard-to-reach populations are particularly crucial when members are known to suffer from disproportionate health issues or pose health risks to the larger ambient population in which they are embedded. Efforts to derive size estimates are often hindered by various factors that preclude conventional survey strategies, including social stigma associated with group membership or members' involvement in illegal activities. This paper expands upon prior research on network population size estimation, building on established survey/sampling methodologies commonly used with hard-to-reach groups. Three novel one-step, network-based population size estimators are presented, intended for use in the context of uniform random sampling, respondent-driven sampling, and situations where networks exhibit significant clustering effects. Provably sufficient conditions for the consistency of these estimators (in large configuration networks) are provided. Simulation experiments across a wide range of synthetic network topologies validate the performance of the estimators, demonstrating their effectiveness on a real-world location-based social networking data set with significant clustering. Finally, the proposed schemes are extended to allow for use in settings where participant anonymity is required. Systematic experiments reveal favorable tradeoffs between anonymity guarantees and estimator performance. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that reasonable population estimates can be derived from anonymous respondent-driven samples of 250-750 individuals, within ambient populations of 5,000-40,000. This method represents a novel and cost-effective means for health planners and agencies concerned with health and disease surveillance to estimate the size of hidden populations. Limitations and future work are discussed in the concluding section.

title: Is repulsion good for the health of Chimeras?

The study reports an enhancement in the appearance of chimera states in one layer of the multiplex network in the presence of repulsive coupling in the other layer. Furthermore, it demonstrates that a small amount of inhibition or repulsive coupling in one layer is sufficient to induce chimera states in another layer by disrupting its synchronized behavior. These findings offer insights into the dynamical behaviors of systems where both attractive and repulsive coupling exist among their constituents.

title: Link Quality Aware Channel Allocation for Multichannel Body Sensor Networks
Abstract: Body Sensor Network (BSN) is a typical Internet-of-Things (IoT) application for personalized health care. It comprises economically powered, wireless, and implanted medical monitoring sensor nodes designed to continuously collect medical information from target patients. Multichannel communication is often employed in BSNs to reduce spectrum competition among the numerous sensor nodes, and the channel assignment problem has attracted significant research attention. Health sensing data in BSNs often needs to be delivered to a sink node (or server) before a specific deadline for real-time monitoring or health emergency alarms. Consequently, deadlines are crucial for multichannel allocation and scheduling. Existing solutions, while designed to meet deadlines, often neglect the impact of unreliable wireless links. As a result, health sensing data can still be overdue due to scheduled lossy links. Moreover, potential collisions in the schedules can also introduce significant delays in delivering the sensing data. This paper proposes a novel deadline-driven Link quality Aware Channel Assignment scheme (LACA), where link quality, deadlines, and collisions are jointly considered. LACA prioritizes links with urgent deadlines and heavy collisions. Furthermore, LACA allows the exploitation of spare slots for retransmissions on lossy links, which further reduces retransmission delay. Extensive simulation experiments demonstrate that compared to existing approaches, LACA can better utilize the wireless spectrum and achieve higher packet delivery ratios before the deadline.

title: Analyzing gender inequality through large-scale Facebook advertising data

Understanding gender inequality in social media is challenging due to the need for data sources that can provide large-scale measurements across multiple countries. This paper demonstrates how the Facebook Gender Divide (FGD), a metric based on aggregated statistics of over 1.4 billion users in 217 countries, explains various aspects of worldwide gender inequality. Our analysis shows that the FGD encodes gender equality indices in education, health, and economic opportunity. We find gender differences in network externalities that suggest that using social media has an added value for women. Furthermore, we find that low values of the FGD are associated with increases in economic gender equality. Our results suggest that online social networks, while suffering from evident gender imbalance, may lower the barriers that women face in accessing informational resources and help to narrow the economic gender gap.

title: Statistical Methods and Workflow for Analyzing Human Metabolomics Data

The range of options and potential approaches that may be employed at each stage of data management, analysis, and interpretation is discussed, offering guidance on analytical considerations that are crucial for implementing an analysis workflow. Certain pervasive analytical challenges facing human metabolomics warrant ongoing research. Addressing these challenges will allow for more standardization in the field and lead to analytical advances in metabolomics investigations, potentially elucidating novel mechanisms underlying human health and disease.

title: Development of computational models for emotional diary text analysis to support maternal care
Abstract: This paper proposes new computational models for analyzing self-reported emotional diary texts of pregnant women to support maternal care. Thirty-five individuals with Finnish as their native language provided affective ratings for 195 emotional adjectives and 16 pregnancy-related nouns in Finnish across the dimensions of pleasure, arousal, and dominance. New models were developed to represent dependencies and differences in affective ratings between various population subgroup categorizations, including "women without children," "women with children," and "men without children," which are considered crucial population segments to be addressed in maternal care. The affective ratings showed significant correlations between pleasure and dominance (similar to Warriner et al., 2013) and with previous data collections (Söderholm et al., 2013; Eilola & Havelka, 2010; Warriner et al., 2013). The affective ratings had significant effects on categorizations based on gender, gender-parental role, and the time of day and duration of giving ratings. The results indicate concordance with significant affectivity differences in gender and age (Warriner et al., 2013) and motherhood (Rosebrock et al., 2015). The proposed models aim to support health-related communication. These findings suggest gathering affective ratings from patients receiving maternal care in a real clinical setting next.

title: Combination interventions for Hepatitis C and Cirrhosis reduction among people who inject drugs: An agent-based, networked population simulation experiment
Abstract: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is endemic among people who inject drugs (PWID), with prevalence estimates exceeding 60% for PWID in the United States. Previous modeling studies indicate that direct-acting antiviral (DAA) treatment can lower overall prevalence in this population. However, treatment is often delayed until the onset of advanced liver disease (fibrosis stage 3 or later) due to cost. Lower-cost interventions featuring syringe access (SA) and medically assisted treatment (MAT) for addiction are known to be less expensive but have shown mixed results in lowering HCV rates below current levels. Limited knowledge exists about the potential synergistic effects of combining DAA and MAT treatment, and large-scale tests of combined interventions are rare. While simulation experiments can reveal potential long-term effects, most prior simulations have been conducted on closed populations of model agents, a scenario quite different from the open, mobile populations known to most health agencies. This paper uses data from the Centers for Disease Control's National HIV Behavioral Surveillance project, IDU round 3, collected in New York City in 2012 by the New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene to parameterize simulations of open populations. The results show that, in an open population, SA/MAT alone has only minor effects on HCV prevalence, while DAA treatment alone can significantly reduce both HCV and HCV-related advanced liver disease prevalence. More importantly, the simulation experiments suggest that cost-effective synergistic combinations of the two strategies can dramatically reduce HCV incidence. The conclusion is that adopting SA/MAT implementations alongside DAA interventions can play a critical role in reducing the long-term consequences of ongoing infection.

title: Protecting sensitive research data and meeting researchers needs: Duke University's Protected Network

The environment extensively utilizes virtualization and authorization groups to isolate data, provide elasticity of resources, and flexibly meet a range of computational requirements within tightly controlled network boundaries. Since its inception in 2011, the environment has supported approximately 200 research projects and groups and has served as a foundation for specialized and protected IT infrastructures in the social sciences, population studies, and medical research. This article outlines key features of the development of the Protected Network and details the IT infrastructure design and organizational features that Duke has employed in establishing this resource for researchers. title: Checkpoint Ensembles: Ensemble Methods from a Single Training Process
Abstract: This paper presents the checkpoint ensembles method, which can learn ensemble models during a single training process. While checkpoint ensembles can be applied to any parametric iterative learning technique, this study focuses on neural networks. Neural networks' composable and simple neurons allow them to capture numerous individual and interaction effects among features. However, small sample sizes and sampling noise may lead to patterns in the training data that do not accurately reflect the true relationship between the features and the outcome. As a solution, regularization during training is often used (e.g., dropout). However, regularization is not a panacea—it does not perfectly address overfitting. Even with methods like dropout, two methodologies are commonly used in practice. The first is to utilize a validation set independent of the training set as a way to decide when to stop training. The second is to use ensemble methods to further reduce overfitting and take advantage of local optima (i.e., averaging over the predictions of several models). This paper explores checkpoint ensembles—a simple technique that combines these two ideas within a single training process. Checkpoint ensembles enhance performance by averaging the predictions from "checkpoints" of the best models within a single training process. Three real-world datasets—text, image, and electronic health record data—are used, employing three prediction models: a vanilla neural network, a convolutional neural network, and a long short-term memory network, to demonstrate that checkpoint ensembles outperform existing methods: a method that selects a model based on the minimum validation score, and two methods that average models by weights. The results also show that checkpoint ensembles capture a portion of the performance gains that traditional ensembles provide.

title: Bayesian Propensity Scores for High-Dimensional Causal Inference: A Comparison of Drug-Eluting to Bare-Metal Coronary Stents
Abstract: High-dimensional data can be valuable for causal inference by providing numerous confounders that may strengthen the plausibility of the ignorability assumption. Simulations demonstrate the utility of horseshoe priors and Bayesian additive regression trees paired with the new estimator, highlighting the importance of including variance from the treatment and outcome models. title: Characterizing in-text citations in scientific articles: A large-scale analysis

Perhaps most significantly, the study finds substantial field-level differences reflected in position within the text, citation interval (or reference age), and citation counts of references. Generally, the fields of Biomedical and Health Sciences, Life and Earth Sciences, and Physical Sciences and Engineering have similar reference distributions, though they vary in their specifics. The remaining two fields, Mathematics and Computer Science, and Social Science and Humanities, exhibit distinct reference distributions from the other three fields and from each other. The study also shows that across all fields, the numbers of sentences, references, and in-text mentions per article have increased over time, and there are field-level and temporal differences in the numbers of in-text mentions per reference. title: CTD: Fast, Accurate, and Interpretable Method for Static and Dynamic Tensor Decompositions
Abstract: How can patterns and anomalies in a tensor, or multi-dimensional array, be identified efficiently and in a directly interpretable manner? How can this be achieved in an online environment where a new tensor arrives at each time step? Finding patterns and anomalies in a tensor is a critical problem with numerous applications, including building safety monitoring, patient health monitoring, cybersecurity, terrorist detection, and fake user detection in social networks. Standard PARAFAC and Tucker decomposition results are not directly interpretable. While a few sampling-based methods have previously been proposed for better interpretability, they need to be made faster, more memory efficient, and more accurate. This paper proposes CTD, a fast, accurate, and directly interpretable tensor decomposition method based on sampling. CTD-S, the static version of CTD, provably guarantees high accuracy that is 17-83x more accurate than that of the state-of-the-art method. Additionally, CTD-S is made 5-86x faster and 7-12x more memory-efficient than the state-of-the-art method by removing redundancy. CTD-D, the dynamic version of CTD, is the first interpretable dynamic tensor decomposition method ever proposed. It is also made 2-3x faster than the already fast CTD-S by exploiting factors at previous time steps and by reordering operations. Using CTD, the study demonstrates how the results can be effectively interpreted in the context of online distributed denial of service (DDoS) attack detection.

Reinforcement learning aims to optimize interactions with real-world systems by balancing exploration and exploitation. Multi-armed bandit algorithms are a common approach for such learning, and randomized probability matching, based on Thompson sampling, has recently shown promising results. Thompson sampling permits generative and interpretable Bayesian modeling, incorporating prior knowledge and capturing the complete state of knowledge through computed posteriors. This work leverages the information within the Bayesian posterior and estimates its sufficient statistics through sampling. This is particularly beneficial in domains like health and medicine, where interactions can be expensive and invasive, while model sampling is relatively inexpensive. Exploiting this, a double sampling technique is proposed, driven by the uncertainty in the learning process. The technique prioritizes exploitation when confident about the properties of each arm, while exploring otherwise. The algorithm is distribution-agnostic and applicable to complex reward distributions as long as Bayesian posterior updates are computable. Utilizing the estimated posterior sufficient statistics, double sampling autonomously balances exploration and exploitation, leading to more informed decisions. Empirical evidence demonstrates its reduced cumulative regret compared to state-of-the-art alternatives in representative bandit settings.

However, most of these methods rely on massive labeled data. This paper proposes a general deep learning framework that can enhance risk prediction performance with limited EHR data. The model utilizes a modified generative adversarial network, ehrGAN, which can generate plausible labeled EHR data by mimicking real patient records, augmenting the training dataset in a semi-supervised learning manner. This generative model is combined with a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based prediction model to improve onset prediction performance. Experiments conducted on two real healthcare datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework generates realistic data samples and achieves significant improvements in classification tasks with the generated data, outperforming several state-of-the-art baselines.

title: Semi-Supervised Recurrent Neural Network for Adverse Drug Reaction Mention Extraction
Abstract:
This work presents a novel semi-supervised learning approach for data-driven modeling of asset failures when health status is only partially known in historical data. The approach combines a generative model parameterized by deep neural networks with a non-linear embedding technique. This allows for the creation of prognostic models with limited health status information for the precise prediction of future asset reliability. The proposed method is evaluated on a publicly available dataset for remaining useful life (RUL) estimation, showing significant improvement even with a sparse amount of data with known health status (as low as 1% of the total). The study suggests that the non-linear embedding based on a deep generative model can effectively regularize complex models with deep architectures while achieving high prediction accuracy with minimal dependence on the availability of health status information. ||| 
Many studies in biomedical and health sciences involve small sample sizes due to logistical or financial constraints. Identifying weak but scientifically interesting associations between a set of predictors and a response often requires pooling datasets from multiple diverse labs or groups. While there is a substantial body of literature in statistical machine learning addressing distributional shifts and inference in multi-site datasets, it remains unclear when such pooling is beneficial and when it is not, independent of the inference algorithms used. This paper presents a hypothesis test to answer this question, both for classical and high-dimensional linear regression. The study precisely identifies regimes where pooling datasets across multiple sites is sensible and how such policy decisions can be made through simple checks executable on each site before any data transfer occurs. Focusing on Alzheimer's disease studies, empirical results show that in regimes suggested by the analysis, pooling a local dataset with data from an international study improves power.

title: Boosting Deep Learning Risk Prediction with Generative Adversarial Networks for Electronic Health Records
Abstract: The utility of fetal heart rate (FHR) monitoring can only be realized with an acquisition sampling rate that preserves the underlying physiological information on the millisecond time scale (1000 Hz rather than 4 Hz). This necessitates fetal ECG (fECG) acquisition instead of relying on ultrasound for FHR derivation. This study evaluated one recently developed algorithm, SAVER, and two widely applied algorithms to extract fECG from a single channel maternal ECG signal recorded over the xyphoid process rather than the routine abdominal signal. ECG was attached to near-term ewes and fetuses at 126 days of gestation (n=12) at the shoulders, manubrium, and xyphoid processes. fECG served as the ground truth for comparison with the fetal ECG signal extracted from the simultaneously acquired maternal ECG. All fetuses were in good health during surgery. Results showed that none of the single-lead fECG extraction algorithms could extract fECG from the maternal ECG signal over the xyphoid process with an F1 score exceeding 50%. These findings suggest that the applied fECG extraction algorithms may be unsuitable for maternal ECG signals over the xyphoid process, or that the signal may not contain sufficient fECG information, despite the lead's proximity to the mother's abdomen. While the fetal sheep model is widely used to mimic various fetal conditions, ECG recordings in a publicly available dataset format are not available to test the predictive ability of fECG and FHR. This dataset is being made openly available to other researchers to foster non-invasive fECG acquisition in this animal model.

title: Semi-supervised Learning with Deep Generative Models for Asset Failure Prediction
Abstract: Timely and accurate forecasts of seasonal influenza are essential for public health decision-makers to plan intervention strategies, allocate resources efficiently, and potentially save lives. Producing these forecasts, however, has proven challenging due to noisy and limited data, incomplete understanding of disease transmission, and the mismatch between the disease transmission process and the data-generating process. This paper introduces a dynamic Bayesian (DB) flu forecasting model that addresses model discrepancy through a hierarchical model. The DB model enables forecasts of partially observed flu seasons by borrowing discrepancy information from previously observed flu seasons. The DB model was compared to all models that competed in the CDC's 2015-2016 flu forecasting challenge. The DB model outperformed all competing models, highlighting its potential as a leading influenza forecasting model.

title: When can Multi-Site Datasets be Pooled for Regression? Hypothesis Tests, $\ell_2$-consistency and Neuroscience Applications
Abstract: Large-scale national-level Personal Health Records (PHRs) have been implemented in Australia. However, usability, data quality issues, and limited functionalities have resulted in low utility, affecting enrollment and participation rates by both patients and clinicians. Developing new applications that leverage the secondary utility of data can enhance the use of PHRs. However, there is limited understanding of the processes involved in developing third-party applications with nationally run PHRs. This paper presents an analysis of the processes and regulatory requirements for developing applications using data from My Health Record, the Australian national PHR. It subsequently discusses the implementation of a patient-oriented software application using data sourced from My Health Record.

title: Non-invasive acquisition of fetal ECG from the maternal xyphoid process: a feasibility study in pregnant sheep and a call for open data sets
Abstract: This paper addresses the problem of estimating an unknown high-dimensional signal from noisy linear measurements, assuming the signal exhibits a group-sparse structure in a known fixed dictionary. Signals are generated according to a natural probabilistic model, and new conditions are established under which the set of indices of the non-zero groups of the signal (the group-level support) can be accurately estimated using the group Lasso. The results strengthen existing coherence-based analyses that exhibit the "square root" bottleneck, allowing for the recovery of a number of non-zero groups nearly as large as the total number of groups. A sufficient recovery condition is established, relating the number of non-zero groups and the signal-to-noise ratio (quantified by the ratio of the squared Euclidean norms of non-zero groups and the variance of the random additive measurement noise). This trend is validated empirically. Finally, the implications of these results are explored in the context of a structural health monitoring application. The group Lasso approach facilitates the demixing of a propagating acoustic wavefield, acquired on the material surface by a scanning laser Doppler vibrometer, into antithetical components. One of these components indicates the locations of internal material defects. |||

title: Randomized Predictive P-values: A Versatile Model Diagnostic Tool with Unified Reference Distribution
Abstract: Examining residuals, such as Pearson and deviance residuals, is a standard tool for assessing normal regression models. However, for discrete responses, these residuals cluster on lines corresponding to distinct response values. Their distributions are far from normal, making graphical and quantitative inspection of these residuals unhelpful for model diagnosis. Marshall and Spiegelhalter (2003) defined a cross-validatory predictive p-value for identifying outliers. Predictive p-values are uniformly distributed for continuous responses but not for discrete responses. This paper proposes the use of randomized predictive p-values (RPP) for diagnosing models with discrete responses. RPPs can be transformed into "residuals" with a normal distribution, which we call NRPPs. NRPPs can be used to diagnose all regression models with scalar responses in the same way that normal regression models are diagnosed. NRPPs are nearly identical to the randomized quantile residuals (RQR), previously proposed by Dunn and Smyth (1996), but remain relatively unknown. This paper provides an exposition of RQR using the RPP perspective. This exposition contributes by: (1) rigorously proving the uniformity of RPP and providing illustrative examples to explain the uniformity under the true model; (2) conducting extensive simulation studies to demonstrate the normality of NRPPs under the true model; (3) showing through simulation studies that the NRPP method is a versatile diagnostic tool for detecting various model inadequacies due to a lack of complexity. The effectiveness of NRPP is further demonstrated with a health utilization dataset.

title: How to disentangle psychobiological stress reactivity and recovery: A comparison of model-based and non-compartmental analyses of cortisol concentrations
Abstract: This article addresses the challenge of measuring specific process components of psychobiological stress responses. The change in cortisol secretion due to stress exposure has been discussed as an endophenotype of many psychosomatic health outcomes. To assess its process components, a variety of non-compartmental parameters (composite measures of substance concentrations at different points in time) like the area under the concentration-time curve (AUC) are used. However, a systematic evaluation and validation of these parameters based on a physiologically plausible model of cortisol secretion has not been performed. This study develops a population pharmacokinetic (mixed-effects SDE) model that was fitted to densely sampled salivary cortisol data from 10 males in Montreal, Canada, and sparsely sampled data from 200 mixed-sex participants in Dresden, Germany, who completed the Trier Social Stress Test (TSST). The model incorporates two major process components representing (1) stress-related cortisol secretion (reactivity) and (2) cortisol elimination (recovery), along with two additional often disregarded components: (3) the secretory delay after stress onset, and (4) deviations from the projected steady-state concentration. The fitted model (R2 = 99%) was used to investigate the correlation structure of the four individually varying, readily interpretable model parameters and eleven popular non-compartmental parameters. Based on these analyses, the minimum-maximum cortisol difference and the minimum concentration are recommended as proxy measures of reactivity and recovery, respectively. Finally, statistical power analyses of the reactivity-related sex effect illustrate the consequences of using impure non-compartmental measures of the different process components that underlie the cortisol stress response.

title: Deep Belief Networks used on High Resolution Multichannel Electroencephalography Data for Seizure Detection
Abstract: Ubiquitous bio-sensing for personalized health monitoring is becoming increasingly possible with the growing availability of small, diverse, robust, high-fidelity sensors. This flood of data raises the question of how to extract useful information from it. This paper explores the use of various representations and machine learning algorithms applied to seizure detection in high-resolution, multichannel EEG data. The study examines classification accuracy, computational complexity, and memory requirements to understand which approaches are most suitable as the number of people involved and the amount of data they produce grows. In particular, the paper shows that layered learning approaches, such as Deep Belief Networks, excel in these dimensions.

title: Robust Viability Analysis of a Controlled Epidemiological Model
Abstract: Managing infectious diseases is a global public health issue with significant uncertainties. This paper analyzes the problem of viable control of a dengue outbreak under uncertainty. To this end, a controlled Ross-Macdonald model in discrete time, with mosquito vector control by fumigation and uncertainties affecting the dynamics, is developed. The robust viability kernel is the set of all initial states for which there exists at least one insecticide spraying strategy that guarantees the number of infected people remains below a threshold, for all times, and regardless of the sequences of uncertainties (scenarios). By selecting three nested subsets of uncertainties – a deterministic one (without uncertainty), a medium one, and a large one – the incidence of uncertainties on the size of the kernel, particularly its reduction relative to the deterministic case, can be measured. The numerical results demonstrate that the viability kernel without uncertainties is highly sensitive to the variability of parameters, specifically the biting rate, the probability of infection to mosquitoes and humans, and the proportion of female mosquitoes per person. Therefore, the robust viability kernel is a potential tool for revealing the importance of uncertainties regarding epidemics control.

title: Determining Positive Cancer Rescue Mutations in p53 Based Cancers by using Artificial Intelligence
Abstract: A mutation in a protein-coding gene in DNA can alter the protein structure coded by the same gene. Structurally altered proteins often lose their functions and may gain undesirable functions instead. These types of mutations and their effects can lead to genetic diseases, antibiotic-resistant bacteria, and other health issues. Significant curing methods have been developed for detecting mutations against AIDS and genetic diseases. Another example is the influenza virus. The reasons why a vaccination developed to fight influenza may not work the following year are (a) mutation of its DNA and (b) the outbreak of the virus after it has mutated, especially if it is a virus that escaped the vaccination target. Due to these reasons, it is crucial to know in advance the location of potential mutations in a protein, as well as the problems they might cause for medical science. This study utilizes artificial neural networks, a recent artificial intelligence technology, to determine the effects of cancer mutations. The developed model has yielded more successful results compared to other methods. The authors anticipate that their model will bring a new dimension to medical research and the medical industry.

title: Surface temperatures in New York City: Geospatial data enables the accurate prediction of radiative heat transfer
Abstract: Despite three decades of research seeking to derive the urban energy budget, the dynamics of the thermal exchange between densely built infrastructure and the environment are still poorly understood. This study presents a novel hybrid experimental-numerical approach for analyzing radiative heat transfer in New York City. The aim is to contribute to the calculation of the urban energy budget, particularly the stored energy. Improved understanding of urban thermodynamics, incorporating the interaction of various bodies, will have implications for energy conservation at the building scale, as well as human health and comfort at the urban scale. The platform presented is based on longwave hyperspectral imaging of nearly 100 blocks of Manhattan and a geospatial radiosity model that describes the collective radiative heat exchange between multiple buildings. The close comparison of temperature values derived from measurements and the computed surface temperatures (including streets and roads) suggests that this geospatial, thermodynamic numerical model applied to urban structures holds promise for accurate and high-resolution analysis of urban surface temperatures.

title: Batch-Based Activity Recognition from Egocentric Photo-Streams
Abstract: Activity recognition from long unstructured egocentric photo-streams has various applications in assistive technology, including health monitoring and frailty detection. However, one of the main technical challenges is dealing with the low frame rate of wearable photo-cameras, which causes abrupt appearance changes between consecutive frames. As a result, important discriminatory low-level features from motion, such as optical flow, cannot be estimated. This paper presents a batch-driven approach for training a deep learning architecture that relies heavily on Long Short-Term Memory units to address this problem. The study proposes two different implementations of the same approach that process a photo-stream sequence using batches of fixed size to capture the temporal evolution of high-level features. The main difference between these implementations is that one explicitly models consecutive batches by overlapping them. Experimental results on a public dataset acquired by three users demonstrate the validity of the proposed architectures to exploit the temporal evolution of convolutional features over time without relying on event boundaries.

title: An Ensemble Classifier for Predicting the Onset of Type II Diabetes
Abstract: Predicting disease onset from patient survey and lifestyle data is becoming an increasingly important tool for diagnosing a disease before it progresses. This study uses data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) questionnaire to predict the onset of type II diabetes. An ensemble model using the output of five classification algorithms was developed to predict the onset of diabetes based on 16 features. The ensemble model achieved an AUC of 0.834, indicating high performance.

title: Modeling water supply networks and gastrointestinal disorder symptoms with CAR models
Abstract: Direct modeling of water networks is not common practice in modern epidemiology. While space often serves as a proxy, this can be problematic. There are multiple ways to directly model water networks, but these methods are not straightforward and can be difficult to implement. This study suggests a simple approach for modeling water networks and diseases and applies this method to a dataset of self-reported gastrointestinal conditions from a questionnaire-based population health survey in central Norway. The approach is based on a standard conditional autoregressive (CAR) model. An inverse matrix is constructed, with nodes weighted based on the distance to neighboring nodes within the networks. This matrix is then fitted as a generic model. To illustrate its possible use, data from a questionnaire-based population health survey, the HUNT Study, is utilized to measure self-reported gastrointestinal complaints. For hypothesis testing, the deviance information criterion (DIC) is used, and variables are included in a stepwise manner. The full model converged after six hours. The study found no relation between the water networks and the health conditions of people whose residences connected to different parts of the network in the geographical area studied. All water network models are simplifications of real networks. Nevertheless, this study suggests a valid approach for distinguishing between the general spatial effect and the water network using a generic model.

title: Persuasive Technology For Human Development: Review and Case Study
Abstract: Technology is a powerful tool that can be leveraged for human development and social good. Due to the importance of the environment and human psychology in driving human behavior and the ubiquity of technology in modern life, there is a need to combine insights and capabilities from both fields to nudge people towards optimal behavior (personally or socially). In this regard, the field of persuasive technology, which proposes infusing technology with appropriate design and incentives using insights from psychology, behavioral economics, and human-computer interaction holds great promise. While persuasive technology is already being developed and used in many commercial applications, it can have a significant social impact in the field of Information and Communication Technology for Development (ICTD), which uses Information and Communication Technology (ICT) for human developmental ends, such as education and health. This paper explores what persuasive technology is and how it can be used for human development. To develop these ideas in a concrete setting, a case study is presented outlining how persuasive technology can be used for human development in Pakistan, a developing South Asian country, which faces many problems common to developing countries.

title: Big Data Meets HPC Log Analytics: Scalable Approach to Understanding Systems at Extreme Scale
Abstract: Modern high-performance computing (HPC) systems are heavily instrumented, generating logs containing information about abnormal events, such as critical conditions, faults, errors, failures, system resource utilization, and resource usage of user applications. These logs, when fully analyzed and correlated, can provide detailed information about system health, root causes of failures, and analyze an application's interactions with the system, providing valuable insights for domain scientists and system administrators. However, processing HPC logs requires a deep understanding of hardware and software components at multiple layers of the system stack. Additionally, most log data is unstructured and voluminous, making it difficult for system users and administrators to manually inspect the data. With rapid increases in the scale and complexity of HPC systems, log data processing is becoming a big data challenge. This paper introduces an HPC log data analytics framework based on distributed NoSQL database technology, which provides scalability and high availability, and the Apache Spark framework for rapid in-memory processing of the log data. The analytics framework enables the extraction of a range of information about the system, allowing system administrators and end users alike to obtain necessary insights for their specific needs. The paper describes the experience of using this framework to glean insights from log data about system behavior from the Titan supercomputer at the Oak Ridge National Laboratory.

title: Classification of Radiology Reports Using Neural Attention Models
Abstract: The electronic health record (EHR) contains a large amount of multi-dimensional and unstructured clinical data of significant operational and research value. Unlike previous studies, this approach embraces a double-annotated dataset and avoids obscure "black-box" models in favor of comprehensive deep learning models. This paper presents a novel neural attention mechanism that not only classifies clinically important findings but also provides insights into the classifier's decision-making process. Specifically, convolutional neural networks (CNN) with attention analysis are used to classify radiology head computed tomography reports based on five categories that radiologists consider when assessing acute and communicable findings in daily practice. The experiments show that the CNN attention models outperform non-neural models, especially when trained on a larger dataset. The attention analysis demonstrates the intuition behind the classifier's decision by generating a heatmap that highlights attended terms used by the CNN model. This is valuable when potential downstream medical decisions are to be made by human experts or when classifier information is used in cohort construction for epidemiological studies.

title: Smart City Analytics: Ensemble-Learned Prediction of Citizen Home Care
Abstract: This paper presents an ensemble learning method that predicts large increases in the hours of home care received by citizens. The method is supervised and uses different ensembles of either linear (logistic regression) or non-linear (random forests) classifiers. Experiments with data available from 2013 to 2017 for every citizen in Copenhagen receiving home care (27,775 citizens) show that prediction can achieve state-of-the-art performance as reported in similar health-related domains (AUC=0.715). The study also finds that competitive results can be obtained by using limited information for training, which is very useful when full records are not accessible or available. Smart city analytics does not necessarily require full city records. To the authors' knowledge, this preliminary study is the first to predict large increases in home care for smart city analytics.

title: Segmentation of retinal cysts from Optical Coherence Tomography volumes via selective enhancement
Abstract: Automated and accurate segmentation of cystoid structures in Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) is of interest in the early detection of retinal diseases. However, it is a challenging task. This paper proposes a novel method for localizing cysts in 3D OCT volumes. The proposed work is biologically inspired and based on selective enhancement of cysts by inducing motion to a given OCT slice. A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) is designed to learn a mapping function that combines the result of multiple such motions to produce a probability map for cyst locations in a given slice. The final segmentation of cysts is obtained via simple clustering of the detected cyst locations. The proposed method is evaluated on two public datasets and one private dataset. The public datasets include the one released for the OPTIMA Cyst segmentation challenge (OCSC) in MICCAI 2015 and the DME dataset. After training on the OCSC train set, the method achieves a mean Dice Coefficient (DC) of 0.71 on the OCSC test set. The robustness of the algorithm was examined by cross-validation on the DME and AEI (private) datasets, with mean DC values of 0.69 and 0.79, respectively. Overall, the proposed system outperforms all benchmarks. These results underscore the strengths of the proposed method in handling variations in both data acquisition protocols and scanners.

title: On the topology effects in wireless sensor networks based prognostics and health management
Abstract: This work considers the usage of wireless sensor networks (WSN) to monitor an area of interest and diagnose its state in real time. Each sensor node forwards information about relevant features to the sink, where the data is processed. However, energy conservation is a key issue in the design of such networks, and once a sensor exhausts its resources, it is dropped from the network. This leads to broken links and data loss. Therefore, it is important to keep the network running for as long as possible by preserving the energy held by the nodes. Saving the quality of service (QoS) of a wireless sensor network for a long period is crucial to ensure accurate data. This leads to more accurate area diagnosis. Additionally, packet transmission consumes the highest amount of energy compared to other network activities. Consequently, the network topology significantly impacts energy efficiency, and therefore data and diagnosis accuracies. This paper studies and compares four network topologies: distributed, hierarchical, centralized, and decentralized topology, and shows their impact on the resulting estimation of diagnostics. Six diagnostic algorithms are used to evaluate both prognostic and health management with variations in the type of topology in WSN.

title: An Improved Multi-Output Gaussian Process RNN with Real-Time Validation for Early Sepsis Detection
Abstract: Sepsis is a poorly understood and potentially life-threatening complication that can occur as a result of infection. Early detection and treatment improve patient outcomes, posing a significant challenge in medicine. This study develops a flexible classifier that leverages streaming lab results, vitals, and medications to predict sepsis before it occurs. Patient clinical time series are modeled with multi-output Gaussian processes, maintaining uncertainty about the patient's physiological state while also imputing missing values. The mean function accounts for the effects of administered medications on the trajectories of the physiological variables. Latent function values from the Gaussian process are then fed into a deep recurrent neural network to classify patient encounters as septic or not. The overall model is trained end-to-end using back-propagation. The model is trained and validated on a large dataset of 18 months of heterogeneous inpatient stays from the Duke University Health System, and a new "real-time" validation scheme is developed to simulate the model's performance as it will actually be used. The proposed method substantially outperforms clinical baselines and improves on a previous related model for detecting sepsis. The model's predictions will be displayed in a real-time analytics dashboard for use by a sepsis rapid response team to help detect and improve the treatment of sepsis.
