title: Is Female Health Cyclical? Evolutionary Perspectives on Menstruation
Abstract: The question of why some females menstruate has implications for understanding the close relationship between reproductive function and organismal immunity. This paper examines the growing evidence suggesting that menstruation is a by-product of a "choosy" uterus. It presents a theoretical argument for the idea that female immunity is cyclical in menstruating species, evaluates the evidence for the menstrual modulation of immunity and health in humans, and speculates on the implications of cyclical female health for female behavior, male immunity, and host-pathogen interactions. The paper argues that understanding the evolution of the female reproductive system is essential for tackling future challenges in global women's health and predicting eco-evolutionary dynamics in species with cyclical reproduction.

title: Prediction and Inference with Missing Data in Patient Alert Systems
Abstract: This paper describes the Bedside Patient Rescue (BPR) project, which aims to predict the risk of adverse events for non-ICU patients using approximately 200 variables (vitals, lab results, assessments, etc.). Missing predictor values are common in healthcare data, and the BPR project utilizes a Bayesian approach to address the challenges associated with missing predictors. The Bayesian approach offers several advantages over standard methods: (1) it readily handles uncertainty arising from imputation; (2) it flexibly models the predictor distribution as an infinite normal mixture with latent variables, explicitly accounting for discrete predictors; and (3) it effectively addresses certain missing not at random (MNAR) situations by incorporating the indicator of missingness into the predictor distribution.  This approach provides a distribution for the prediction, including the inherent uncertainty associated with imputation. This enables answering questions such as: is it possible this individual is at high risk, but there is insufficient information to know for sure? How much would the uncertainty in the risk prediction be reduced by obtaining a particular missing value? The paper applies this approach to the BPR problem, demonstrating its excellent predictive capability in identifying deteriorating patients.

title: Identifying spatiotemporal dynamics of Ebola in Sierra Leone using virus genomes
Abstract: Containing the recent West African outbreak of Ebola virus (EBOV) required significant global resources.  Operational efforts involved healthcare workers and surveillance teams treating cases, collecting genetic samples, and tracking case contacts. While significant progress has been made in analyzing and modeling EBOV epidemiological data, a comprehensive characterization of the spatiotemporal spread of Ebola cases remains a challenge. This paper offers a novel perspective on the EBOV epidemic that utilizes virus genome sequences to inform population-level, spatial models. These dynamic spatial models, calibrated to phylogenetic linkages, provide unique insights into the disease mobility of EBOV in Sierra Leone.  Furthermore, the study developed a model selection framework that identifies important epidemiological variables influencing the spatiotemporal propagation of EBOV.  Consistent with previous findings, the results show that the spread of EBOV during the early and middle stages of the epidemic strongly depended on the size and distance between populations.  The analysis also revealed a substantial decline in the dependence on population size towards the end of the epidemic, coinciding with the large-scale intervention campaign Operation Western Area Surge.  More broadly, the framework presented in this paper, combining molecular diagnostics with dynamic models, holds potential as a powerful forecasting tool and can offer operationally relevant guidance for surveillance and sampling strategies during epidemics.

title: Spatial disease mapping using Directed Acyclic Graph Auto-Regressive (DAGAR) models
Abstract: Hierarchical models for regionally aggregated disease incidence data typically involve region-specific latent random effects modeled jointly as having a multivariate Gaussian distribution. The covariance or precision matrix captures the spatial dependence between regions. Common choices for the precision matrix include the widely used ICAR model, which is singular, and its nonsingular extension, which lacks interpretability. This paper proposes a new parametric model for the precision matrix based on a directed acyclic graph (DAG) representation of the spatial dependence. This model guarantees positive definiteness, ensuring its validity as a prior for regionally spatially correlated random effects and enabling it to directly model outcomes from dependent data such as images and networks. Theoretical results establish a link between the model parameters and the variances and covariances of the random effects.  Extensive simulations demonstrate that the improved interpretability of this model leads to accurate recovery of the latent spatial random effects and improved inference on the spatial covariance parameters. Under moderate spatial correlation, this model outperforms CAR models, while performance is similar when spatial correlation is strong. The study also assesses sensitivity to the choice of ordering in DAG construction using theoretical and empirical results, confirming the model's robustness.  A large-scale public health application showcases the model's competitive performance.

title: FWDA: a Fast Wishart Discriminant Analysis with its Application to Electronic Health Records Data Classification
Abstract: Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) applied to Electronic Health Records (EHR) data is widely used for early disease detection. However, traditional LDA for EHR data classification faces two significant challenges: ill-posed estimation of LDA parameters (e.g., covariance matrix) and the "linear inseparability" of EHR data. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel classifier, Fast Wishart Discriminant Analysis (FWDA), which makes predictions in an ensemble manner. FWDA first approximates the distribution of inverse covariance matrices using a Wishart distribution estimated from the training data.  It then averages the classification results of multiple LDA classifiers parameterized by the sampled inverse covariance matrices using a Bayesian voting scheme. The weights for voting are dynamically updated to adapt to each new input data point, enabling nonlinear classification.  Theoretical analysis indicates that FWDA exhibits fast convergence and robust performance on high-dimensional data. Extensive experiments on a large-scale EHR dataset demonstrate that FWDA significantly outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms.

title: Fluid-structure interaction modelling and stabilisation of a patient-specific arteriovenous access fistula
Abstract: This paper presents a patient-specific fluid-structure interaction (FSI) model of a phase-contrast magnetic resonance angiography (PC-MRA) imaged arteriovenous fistula. The numerical model is developed and simulated using a commercial multiphysics simulation package, employing a semi-implicit FSI coupling scheme that combines a finite volume method blood flow model and a finite element method vessel wall model.  A pulsatile mass-flow boundary condition is applied at the artery inlet of the model, with a three-element Windkessel model at the artery and vein outlets. The FSI model is freely available for analysis and extension. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of combining several stabilization techniques to simultaneously overcome the added-mass effect and optimize the efficiency of the overall model.  The PC-MRA data, fluid model, and FSI model results show nearly identical flow features in the fistula, particularly in a flow recirculation region in the vein that could potentially lead to fistula failure.  |||

title: Surrogate-based artifact removal from single-channel EEG
Abstract: The emergence of low-cost, portable electroencephalography (EEG) devices has paved the way for a new generation of applications in health monitoring and brain-computer interfacing. However, these recordings are often contaminated by noise from various sources, hindering accurate interpretation of the underlying brain state. This study introduces a novel data-driven algorithm, Surrogate-based Artifact Removal (SuBAR), designed to effectively eliminate ocular and muscular artifacts from single-channel EEG signals. SuBAR utilizes time-frequency analysis of surrogate data to automatically identify and filter these artifacts. Comparative evaluations using artificially contaminated EEG signals demonstrate SuBAR's superiority in noise removal and signal preservation compared to established single-channel EEG denoising techniques, such as wavelet thresholding and canonical correlation analysis combined with empirical mode decomposition. Notably, SuBAR achieves significantly lower relative error (4-5 times lower) even in the presence of severe artifacts. This study highlights SuBAR as a promising solution for mobile environments, such as ambulatory healthcare systems, sleep stage scoring, and anesthesia monitoring, where limited EEG channels or even a single channel are available.

title: High-dimensional confounding adjustment using continuous spike and slab priors
Abstract: In observational studies, estimating the causal effect of a treatment on an outcome requires careful adjustment for confounding variables. When the number of potential confounders ($p$) exceeds the number of observations ($n$), direct control becomes impractical. Existing approaches for dimension reduction and penalization often prioritize outcome prediction and are less suitable for causal effect estimation. Under standard penalization methods like Lasso, variables strongly associated with the treatment ($T$) but weakly associated with the outcome ($Y$) can be shrunk towards zero, leading to confounding bias.  This study proposes continuous spike and slab priors on the regression coefficients ($\\beta_j$) corresponding to potential confounders ($X_j$) under the assumption of a linear model for the outcome and sparsity. The proposed prior effectively avoids shrinking to zero the coefficients of $X_j$ that are strongly associated with $T$ but weakly associated with $Y$. Comparisons with existing methods reveal that the proposed approach effectively reduces confounding bias in high-dimensional settings, shrinks towards zero coefficients of instrumental variables, and achieves good coverage even with small sample sizes. The method is demonstrated using the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) data to estimate the causal effects of persistent pesticide exposure on triglyceride levels.

title: Large-Scale Sleep Condition Analysis Using Selfies from Social Media
Abstract: Sleep quality is closely linked to overall health. The proposed method predicts a sleep-deprived fatigue rate based on a selfie provided by the subject, serving as a proxy for their sleep condition. To gain deeper insights into human sleep patterns, the study analyzed approximately 100,000 faces from selfies collected on Twitter and Instagram, automatically identifying age, gender, and race. The study revealed interesting findings regarding sleep condition distributions across these demographics. Notably, the highest fatigue percentage was observed in the 0-20 youth and adolescent group, suggesting higher prevalence of poor sleep conditions in this age group. Additionally, females exhibited a higher fatigue percentage compared to males, indicating a higher proportion of females experiencing sleep issues. Among ethnic groups, Caucasians showed the highest fatigue percentage, followed by Asians and African Americans.

title: Medical Text Classification using Convolutional Neural Networks

title: Deep Learning for Medical Image Processing: Overview, Challenges and Future
Abstract: The healthcare sector, unlike other industries, carries a high priority and faces immense societal expectations for exceptional care and services regardless of cost. title: Identifying the stored energy of a hyperelastic structure by using an attenuated Landweber method
Abstract: This paper tackles the nonlinear, inverse problem of identifying the stored energy function of a hyperelastic material using both full knowledge of the displacement field and surface sensor measurements. The displacement field is represented as a solution to Cauchy's equation of motion, a nonlinear elastic wave equation. Hyperelasticity implies that the first Piola-Kirchhoff stress tensor is derived as the gradient of the stored energy function. Assuming a dictionary of suitable functions is available, the goal is to recover the stored energy with respect to this dictionary. This inverse problem is crucial for developing structural health monitoring systems, as the stored energy encodes the mechanical properties of the underlying structure, enabling detection of defects from boundary displacement measurements. This article presents a numerical solver for both settings using the attenuated Landweber method. The paper demonstrates that the parameter-to-solution map satisfies the local tangential cone condition, supporting the local convergence of the attenuated Landweber method when the full displacement field is measured. title: Computationally efficient methods for fitting mixed models to electronic health records data
Abstract: Motivated by two case studies using primary care records from the Clinical Practice Research Datalink, this paper outlines statistical methods for analyzing "tall data," characterized by very large numbers of observations. The focus is on investigating the association between patient characteristics and an outcome of interest while accounting for variation among general practices. The study explores the use of mixed effects models for tall data, incorporating predictors of interest, confounding factors as covariates, and random intercepts to capture heterogeneity in outcome across practices. The paper introduces two methods for reducing dataset size and analysis time: (1) weighted regression and (2) meta-analysis of estimated regression coefficients from each practice. Both methods are compared to an existing subsampling approach. The study finds that all methods yield similar point estimates, while weighted regression and meta-analysis provide standard errors comparable to those obtained from analyzing the entire dataset. Subsampling, however, produces larger standard errors. The study concludes that weighted regression is equivalent to fitting the mixed model to the entire dataset when all data are discrete. In the presence of a continuous covariate, meta-analysis proves useful. Both methods are readily implementable in standard statistical software.

title: NEURAL: quantitative features for newborn EEG using Matlab

title: Francesco Fontana and his "astronomical" Telescope
Abstract: In the late 1620s, Neapolitan telescope maker Francesco Fontana became the first to observe the sky using a telescope with two convex lenses, which he had crafted himself. Fontana's meticulous observations resulted in the most accurate lunar surface maps of his time, gaining widespread popularity through publications across Europe, albeit without attribution to their creator. By the end of 1645, facing declining health and the need to defend his authorship, Fontana undertook an intense observational campaign, hastily documenting his findings in his *Novae Coelestium Terrestriumque rerum Observationis* (1646), his only published work. His observations encompassed the Moon's primary craters, including the crater Tycho, which he named Fons Major, along with their radial patterns and shifting positions due to lunar motions. He observed the gibbosity of Mars at quadrature and, in collaboration with Jesuit G.B. Zupus, described the phases of Mercury. Fontana meticulously observed the two, and sometimes three, major bands of Jupiter, and deduced the rotational movement of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, challenging the Aristotelian view of their attachment to a celestial sphere. He came close to revealing Saturn's ring structure and suggested the existence of additional moons around Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn, sparking a debate that persisted for over a century. Throughout his book, Fontana repeatedly asserted his invention of the first positive eyepiece in 1608, presenting a declaration from Zupus attesting to the use of his telescope since 1614. This declaration remains the earliest known record of such a device. Finally, the paper suggests that the telescopes depicted in the two *Allegory of Sight* paintings by J. Brueghel the Elder, belonging to Albert VII, may have been made by Fontana, and that he may have inspired the *Sight* by Jusepe Ribera (c. 1616).

title: Effective Warm Start for the Online Actor-Critic Reinforcement Learning based mHealth Intervention
Abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) is gaining popularity for personalized mobile health (mHealth) interventions. This delay can be particularly detrimental in mHealth, where users tend to quickly disengage with apps. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a novel online RL methodology focusing on an effective warm start. The core idea is to leverage the data accumulated and decision rule achieved in a previous study to enrich the data size at the beginning of online learning. This approach accelerates the online learning process for new users, leading to improved performance not only initially but throughout the entire learning process. Additionally, the study utilizes decision rules from a previous study to initialize the parameters in the online RL model for new users, providing a beneficial starting point for the algorithm. title: Recognizing Activities of Daily Living from Egocentric Images

title: User-driven Intelligent Interface on the Basis of Multimodal Augmented Reality and Brain-Computer Interaction for People with Functional Disabilities

title: Abnormal Working Hours: Effect of Rapid Releases and Implications to Work Content

The impact of transitioning from a traditional release cycle to a rapid release cycle on work patterns is investigated. Additionally, the study compares Mozilla Firefox's work pattern with another Mozilla product, Firefox OS, which has a different release cycle. The findings reveal healthy working patterns in both projects, characterized by reduced activity during weekends and outside of office hours. Firefox demonstrates proportionally higher weekend activity compared to Firefox OS (Cohen's d = 0.94). The transition to rapid releases has led to a decrease in weekend work (Cohen's d = 1.43) and night work (Cohen's d = 0.45). This result holds even when the analysis is limited to hired resources, specifically individuals with Mozilla foundation email addresses, although the effect sizes are smaller for weekends (Cohen's d = 0.64) and nights (Cohen's d = 0.23). Further analysis using dissimilarity word clouds reveals that weekend work tends to be more technical, while weekday work exhibits a more positive sentiment with words like "good" and "nice". title: A nearly perfect omnidirectional shear-horizontal (SH) wave transducer based on a thickness poled, thickness-shear (d15) piezoelectric ring

For practical applications, phased array systems based on omnidirectional SH0 wave transducers are highly advantageous as they can cover a wide range of a plate. However, the development of omnidirectional SH wave transducers has been limited. This paper proposes an omnidirectional SH piezoelectric transducer (OSH-PT) based on a thickness-poled piezoelectric ring. The ring is divided into twelve sectors, and an electric field is applied circumferentially, resulting in a new thickness-shear (d15) mode. Finite element analysis demonstrates that the proposed OSH-PT can effectively excite single-mode SH0 waves and receive only SH0 waves. Experimental validation confirms the performance of the proposed OSH-PT, showing its ability to generate and receive single-mode SH0 waves over a wide frequency range with nearly uniform sensitivities in all directions. The simplicity, compact size, and low cost of the proposed OSH-PT are expected to significantly promote the applications of SH waves in NDT and SHM.

title: Federated Tensor Factorization for Computational Phenotyping

The proposed solution utilizes secure data harmonization and federated computation procedures based on the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). Multiple hospitals iteratively update tensors and securely transfer summarized information to a central server, where this information is aggregated to generate phenotypes. title: Bayesian Inference of Individualized Treatment Effects using Multi-task Gaussian Processes
Abstract: Motivated by the increasing availability of electronic health records, this paper investigates the problem of inferring individualized treatment effects using observational data. Building upon the potential outcomes model, the study proposes a novel multi-task learning framework where factual and counterfactual outcomes are modeled as outputs of a function within a vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert space (vvRKHS). The paper develops a nonparametric Bayesian method for learning treatment effects using a multi-task Gaussian process (GP) with a linear coregionalization kernel as a prior over the vvRKHS. The Bayesian approach enables the computation of individualized measures of confidence in the estimates through pointwise credible intervals, crucial for realizing the full potential of precision medicine. The impact of selection bias is mitigated through a risk-based empirical Bayes method for adapting the multi-task GP prior, jointly minimizing the empirical error in factual outcomes and uncertainty in unobserved counterfactual outcomes. Experiments conducted on observational datasets for an interventional social program applied to premature infants and a left ventricular assist device applied to cardiac patients awaiting heart transplants demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches.

title: A Comparative Study for Predicting Heart Diseases Using Data Mining Classification Methods

To demonstrate the practical viability of the approach, these classifiers were implemented using MATLAB with two datasets. The experimental results reveal that all classification algorithms exhibit predictive capability and provide relatively accurate answers. title: Chronic Kidney Disease of Unknown aetiology (CKDu) and multiple-ion interactions in drinking water

Specifically, the analysis suggests that cadmium (Cd²⁺) in the presence of fluoride (F⁻) and magnesium (Mg²⁺) ions, but not calcium (Ca²⁺), is expected to be more nephrotoxic. The findings are applied to a case study of chronic kidney disease in Sri Lanka, revealing that F⁻, Cd²⁺, and Mg²⁺ ions in stagnant household well water may act together, enhancing toxicity and likely contributing to the disease. title: Reach and speed of judgment propagation in the laboratory
Abstract: Social contagion, the spread of judgments and behaviors from person to person, is a well-documented phenomenon observed across various domains. This paper introduces a novel experimental design that allows for the rigorous study of judgment propagation. Participants in experimental chains revise their initial judgments in a visual perception task after observing a predecessor's judgment. The presence of a highly skilled performer at the top of the chain creates a performance gap, triggering waves of judgment propagation down the chain. The study revealed that while strong social influence exists within pairs of individuals, the reach of judgment propagation rarely extends beyond three to four degrees of separation. Computer simulations further indicated an exponential decay in the speed of judgment propagation as social distance from the source increases. The research identifies information distortion and the overweighting of errors as individual-level mechanisms that hinder judgment propagation at the scale of the chain. These findings contribute to our understanding of social contagion processes, and the experimental method developed offers promising opportunities for future research on judgment propagation in laboratory settings.

title: Probabilistic Search for Structured Data via Probabilistic Programming and Nonparametric Bayes

title: Perfect Prediction in Normal Form: Superrational Thinking Extended to Non-Symmetric Games
Abstract: This paper introduces a new solution concept for non-cooperative games in normal form with no ties and pure strategies: the Perfectly Transparent Equilibrium. Players are assumed to be rational in all possible worlds and possess knowledge of each other's strategies in all possible worlds, collectively referred to as Perfect Prediction. The anticipation of a player's decision by their opponents is counterfactually dependent on the decision, unlike in Nash Equilibra where decisions are made independently. When it exists, the equilibrium is unique and Pareto optimal. This equilibrium serves as the normal-form counterpart of the Perfect Prediction Equilibrium, where prediction occurs "in another room" rather than in the past. The equilibrium can also be viewed as a natural extension of Hofstadter's superrationality to non-symmetric games. Algorithmically, an iterated elimination of non-individually-rational strategy profiles is performed until at most one remains. An equilibrium is a strategy profile immune against knowledge of strategies in all possible worlds and rationality in all possible worlds, representing a stronger concept than common knowledge of rationality but also stronger than common counterfactual belief of rationality. We formalize and contrast the Non-Nashian Decision Theory paradigm, common to this and several other papers, with Causal Decision Theory and Evidential Decision Theory. We define the Perfectly Transparent Equilibrium algorithmically and, when it exists, prove its uniqueness, Pareto-optimality, and its coincidence with Hofstadter's Superrationality on symmetric games. We also relate to concepts found in literature such as Individual Rationality, Minimax-Rationalizability, and the Correlated Equilibrium. title: Predicting Demographics, Moral Foundations, and Human Values from Digital Behaviors
Abstract: Personal electronic devices, including smartphones, provide access to behavioral signals that can be used to learn about individual characteristics and preferences. This study explores the connection between demographic and psychological attributes and digital behavioral records for a cohort of 7,633 individuals, closely representative of the US population in terms of gender, age, geographical distribution, education, and income. Along with demographic data, we collected self-reported assessments on validated psychometric questionnaires for moral traits and basic human values and combined this information with passively collected multi-modal digital data from web browsing behavior and smartphone usage. A machine learning framework was then designed to infer both demographic and psychological attributes from the behavioral data. In a cross-validated setting, our models predicted demographic attributes with good accuracy, as measured by the weighted AUROC score (Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic), but performed less effectively for moral traits and human values. These results call for further investigation as they are still far from uncovering individuals' psychological fabric. This connection, along with the most predictive features we provide for each attribute, could prove useful for designing personalized services, communication strategies, and interventions and can be used to sketch a portrait of individuals with similar worldviews.

title: Autonomous development and learning in artificial intelligence and robotics: Scaling up deep learning to human--like learning
Abstract: Autonomous lifelong development and learning are fundamental human capabilities that differentiate us from current deep learning systems. However, other branches of artificial intelligence have designed crucial ingredients towards autonomous learning: curiosity and intrinsic motivation, social learning and natural interaction with peers, and embodiment. These mechanisms guide exploration and autonomous goal selection, and integrating them with deep learning opens up stimulating perspectives. Deep learning (DL) approaches have made significant advances in artificial intelligence but are still far from human learning. As convincingly argued by Lake et al., differences include human capabilities to learn causal models of the world from limited data, leveraging compositional representations and priors like intuitive physics and psychology. However, there are other fundamental differences between current DL systems and human learning, as well as technical ingredients to fill this gap, that are either superficially or inadequately discussed by Lake et al. These fundamental mechanisms relate to autonomous development and learning and are bound to play a central role in future artificial intelligence. Current DL systems require engineers to manually specify a task-specific objective function for every new task and learn through offline processing of large training databases. In contrast, humans learn autonomously open-ended repertoires of skills, deciding for themselves which goals to pursue or value and which skills to explore, driven by intrinsic motivation/curiosity and social learning through natural interaction with peers. Such learning processes are incremental, online, and progressive. Human child development involves a progressive increase in complexity in a learning curriculum where skills are explored, acquired, and built upon each other through particular ordering and timing. Finally, human learning occurs in the physical world, through bodily and physical experimentation, under severe constraints on energy, time, and computational resources. title: Explainable AI: Beware of Inmates Running the Asylum Or: How I Learnt to Stop Worrying and Love the Social and Behavioural Sciences
Abstract: In his seminal book "The Inmates are Running the Asylum: Why High-Tech Products Drive Us Crazy And How To Restore The Sanity" (2004, Sams Indianapolis, IN, USA), Alan Cooper argues that a primary reason why software is often poorly designed (from a user perspective) is that programmers are responsible for design decisions rather than interaction designers. As a result, programmers design software for themselves rather than for their target audience, a phenomenon he refers to as "the inmates running the asylum." This paper argues that explainable AI risks a similar fate. While the re-emergence of explainable AI is positive, this paper argues that most of us as AI researchers are building explanatory agents for ourselves rather than for the intended users. However, explainable AI is more likely to succeed if researchers and practitioners understand, adopt, implement, and improve models from the vast and valuable bodies of research in philosophy, psychology, and cognitive science, and if the evaluation of these models is focused more on people than on technology. From a light scan of literature, we demonstrate that there is considerable scope to infuse more results from the social and behavioral sciences into explainable AI and present some key results from these fields that are relevant to explainable AI. |||

title: Facial Dynamics Interpreter Network: What are the Important Relations between Local Dynamics for Facial Trait Estimation?
Abstract: Human face analysis is a crucial aspect of computer vision. Research in cognitive psychology suggests that facial dynamics play a significant role in facial analysis. The movement of specific facial regions during an expression is interconnected with the movement of other regions. This paper introduces a novel deep learning approach called the "facial dynamics interpreter network" to analyze these interrelationships and estimate facial traits from sequences of expressions. The network encodes a relational importance, interpreting the connection between local facial dynamics and facial traits. Comparative experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, particularly in gender classification and age estimation. The facial dynamics interpreter network helps identify important relationships between local facial dynamics in these tasks, exceeding the performance of existing state-of-the-art methods.

title: Identification of and correction for publication bias
Abstract: Selective publication bias, where studies with certain results are more likely to be published than others, distorts scientific understanding. This paper proposes two methods for determining the conditional probability of publication based on study results. The first method relies on systematic replication studies, while the second utilizes meta-studies. For known publication probabilities, median-unbiased estimators and confidence sets are introduced to correct for bias. The methods are applied to recent large-scale replication studies in experimental economics and psychology, and to meta-studies of the effects of minimum wages and de-worming programs.

title: Simulating outcomes of interventions using a multipurpose simulation program based on the Evolutionary Causal Matrices and Markov Chain
Abstract: Predicting the long-term impact of interventions is crucial for educational and social policies that affect society significantly. However, conducting such predictions using large-scale experimental data can be challenging due to time and resource constraints. This paper presents a computer simulation model based on Evolutionary Causal Matrices and Markov Chains, utilizing relatively small-scale lab data to predict long-term outcomes. Python classes implementing this model are introduced, demonstrating its application in predicting outcomes of diverse interventions. The model is tested with both real experimental data and hypothetical data informed by social psychological theories. The class-structured simulation module provides researchers and practitioners with a practical and feasible method for prospectively simulating intervention outcomes.

title: STAR-RT: Visual attention for real-time video game playing
Abstract: This paper introduces STAR-RT, the first functional prototype of the Selective Tuning Attention Reference (STAR) model and Cognitive Programs (CPs). The Selective Tuning (ST) model, extensively supported by psychological and neurophysiological experiments, is expanded in the STAR framework and applied to practical visual tasks. Similar to other cognitive architectures, STAR integrates the visual hierarchy (based on ST) with components like executive controller, working and short-term memory, and fixation controller. CPs facilitate communication between these components for visual task execution. To evaluate STAR-RT in a realistic context, its components are implemented and CPs are designed for playing two closed-source video games: Canabalt and Robot Unicorn Attack.  Since both games run in a browser window, STAR-RT receives the same information and has the same reaction time as a human player. STAR-RT plays both games in real time using only visual input, achieving scores comparable to human expert players. This demonstrates the effectiveness of the CP structure and primitives used, suggesting further experimentation and verification in broader scenarios.

title: Riemannian tangent space mapping and elastic net regularization for cost-effective EEG markers of brain atrophy in Alzheimer's disease
Abstract: The diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease (AD) in routine clinical practice primarily relies on subjective clinical interpretations. Quantitative electroencephalography (QEEG) measures have been shown to reflect neurodegenerative processes associated with AD, potentially providing affordable and readily available markers for objective AD assessment. This paper presents a novel framework that combines Riemannian tangent space mapping and elastic net regression for developing brain atrophy markers. Unlike most AD QEEG studies, which are limited by small sample sizes and psychological test scores as outcomes, this study uses data from one of the largest prospective EEG AD trials ever conducted, incorporating MRI biomarkers of brain atrophy.

title: Asymmetric return rates and wealth distribution influenced by the introduction of technical analysis into a behavioral agent based model
Abstract: Behavioral Finance challenges traditional financial models by incorporating the psychological aspects of investors to explain stock market dynamics. This paper presents an agent-based model to quantify the relationship between investor behavior and stock market features. To simulate the complexity of real markets, the model connects investors through a small-world network, each with unique psychological profiles (Imitation, Anti-Imitation, Random) and two decision-making strategies: one based on trust within their network and the other based on technical analysis of market momentum. The model analyzes market index fluctuations, wealth distribution among investors based on their psychological profiles, and return rate distribution. It also examines the influence of changing the psychological profile of the network's hub, revealing that anti-imitation becomes the most profitable investment strategy under specific conditions. An intriguing asymmetry in return rate distribution, explained by the behavioral aspects of investors, is consistently observed even with different decision-making algorithms, a result not previously reported.

title: Soft Sides of Software
Abstract: Software development is a field of rapid change, with technologies quickly becoming obsolete. Lifelong learning is a key attribute for software engineers, emphasizing the social and psychological aspects of professional development. Organizations that encourage learning and reward it foster an environment where change is readily embraced. However, the software industry often focuses on short-term project success, neglecting individual and team capacity building. This paper argues for increased research into software psychology to fully understand how to enhance effectiveness and personal fulfillment for software engineers working individually and in teams.

title: Learning to select computations
Abstract: Efficient utilization of limited computational resources is essential for intelligence. Optimally selecting computations through rational metareasoning is ideal but computationally intractable. This paper proposes Bayesian metalevel policy search (BMPS), inspired by psychology and neuroscience, as the first concrete and domain-general learning algorithm for approximating optimal computation selection. The algorithm, derived based on the value of information, is evaluated on three increasingly complex metareasoning problems: computation termination, allocation of computation between options, and planning. BMPS achieves near-optimal performance across all domains and outperforms existing metareasoning heuristics. Its practical utility is demonstrated in an emergency management scenario, accounting for metareasoning overhead.

title: Towards Deep Learning Models for Psychological State Prediction using Smartphone Data: Challenges and Opportunities
Abstract: Mobile sensing technologies and machine learning are increasingly used for mental health monitoring and intervention. Researchers have effectively leveraged contextual information, like mobility, communication, and mobile phone usage patterns, to quantify mood and wellbeing. This paper investigates the use of neural network models for predicting stress levels using location information collected by smartphones. The approach characterizes individual mobility patterns through GPS metrics and uses these metrics as input to the network. The model is evaluated using the open-source StudentLife dataset. The paper discusses the challenges and trade-offs associated with building machine learning models for digital mental health and highlights potential future work.

title: A novel low-rank matrix completion approach to estimate missing entries in Euclidean distance matrices
Abstract: A Euclidean Distance Matrix (EDM) is a table of squared distances between points in a k-dimensional Euclidean space, used in various fields. One common problem involves missing or uncertain EDM elements. This paper addresses the issue of missing data in EDM through low-rank matrix completion techniques. It leverages the fact that an EDM's rank is limited to k+2, independent of the number of points, which is typically much larger than k. The paper proposes a Singular Value Decomposition approach that incorporates matrix rank and iteratively adjusts a parameter to control convergence. Computational experiments demonstrate the method's ability to accurately recover random EDMs with over a thousand points and up to 98 percent missing data in a few minutes. This method also requires fewer iterations compared to other state-of-the-art techniques.

title: PQSER: A Matlab package for spectral seriation
Abstract: Seriation, the problem of finding the optimal ordering of a set of units interconnected by a bipartite graph, is relevant in fields such as archaeology, anthropology, psychology, and biology. This paper presents a Matlab implementation of an algorithm for spectral seriation by Atkins et al., using the Fiedler vector of the Laplacian matrix associated with the problem, which encodes potential solutions into a PQ-tree. The paper introduces numerical improvements to the original algorithm, highlighting the significant impact of multiple Fiedler values on approximating solutions with inconsistent data sets. Practical examples and numerical experiments demonstrate the toolbox's use in processing real-world data.

title: A Tutorial on Estimating Time-Varying Vector Autoregressive Models
Abstract: Time series data from individual subjects have become prevalent in psychological research. Such data allow for the estimation of within-subject dynamic models, addressing the issue of making within-subject inferences from between-subjects data and accounting for individual heterogeneity. Vector Autoregressive (VAR) models, where each variable is predicted as a linear function of past values, are popular for this type of data. However, a key assumption of VAR models is stationary parameters, which may not be valid in many psychological research areas. This tutorial introduces methods for estimating time-varying VAR models using splines and kernel-smoothing, with and without regularization. Simulations evaluate the performance of these methods in typical research scenarios, highlighting their strengths and weaknesses. A step-by-step tutorial demonstrates how to apply these methods to an openly available time series of mood-related measurements.

title: Research on two-dimensional traffic flow model based on psychological field theory
Abstract: This paper explores the influence of fan-shaped buffer zones on the performance of toll plazas. A two-dimensional traffic flow model and a comprehensive evaluation model based on mechanical and psychological principles are established. The traffic flow model is simulated using a coordinate system. The paper first analyzes vehicle behavior entering the toll plaza using queue theory. Then, a two-dimensional steady car-following model is established based on psychological field theory to analyze vehicle behavior leaving the toll plaza. By analyzing force conditions influenced by vehicles within the observation area and obstacles, the paper determines the impact on acceleration of following vehicles. This analysis provides information about changes in vehicle speed and position. Simulations are conducted based on vehicle states and state-changing rules to determine toll plaza throughput. The paper evaluates the system's performance using bearing pressure, cost, and safety factor, ultimately concluding that the presence of a fan-shaped buffer zone improves toll plaza performance.

title: Neural-Symbolic Learning and Reasoning: A Survey and Interpretation
Abstract: Understanding human behavior is relevant across disciplines, including computer science, artificial intelligence, cognitive science, philosophy, and psychology. Computational-logic systems, connectionist cognitive models, and models of uncertainty are prominent tools in behavior modeling. Recent studies in cognitive science, AI, and psychology have produced cognitive models of reasoning, learning, and language grounded in computation. Additionally, computer science research has yielded cognitive computational systems integrating machine learning and automated reasoning, showing promise in various applications. This joint survey examines the perspectives of researchers on neural-symbolic learning and reasoning, covering the scope and goals of neural-symbolic computation, its realizations, systems, applications, challenges, and future research directions.

title: Depression Severity Estimation from Multiple Modalities
Abstract: Depression, a major debilitating disorder affecting people of all ages, is increasingly prevalent. The need for automatic detection of depression presence and severity has led to the development of techniques using various modalities, including speech, language, and facial visual features. This AVEC challenge explores these modalities to design and develop methods for automatic depression detection. The PHQ-8 questionnaire, a well-established tool for measuring depression severity, is used as a benchmark. This paper investigates the automatic prediction of PHQ-8 scores from features extracted from different modalities. Results show that visual features derived from facial landmarks perform best in estimating PHQ-8 scores, with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 4.66 on the development set. Speech-based behavioral characteristics achieve an MAE of 4.73, while language features yield a slightly higher MAE of 5.17. On the test set, turn features derived from audio transcriptions achieve the best performance, scoring an MAE of 4.11 (corresponding to an RMSE of 4.94), making this system the winner of the AVEC 2017 depression sub-challenge.

title: Mean Field Limit of a Behavioral Financial Market Model
Abstract: Over the past decade, agent-based econophysical financial market models have gained increasing interest, aiming to understand stylized facts of financial data. This paper derives the mean field limit of the econophysical model by Cross, Grinfeld, Lamba, and Seaman (Physica A, 354) and demonstrates that the kinetic limit is a good approximation of the original model. The kinetic model replicates some of the most prominent stylized facts, including fat-tails of asset returns, uncorrelated stock price returns, and volatility clustering. Notably, psychological misperceptions of investors are identified as the source of these stylized facts. The mesoscopic model allows for analytical study, enabling the derivation of steady-state solutions and entropy bounds of the deterministic skeleton. These results provide insights into the complex dynamics of the model.

title: Kurt Lewin, psychological constructs and sources of brain cognitive activity
Abstract: Understanding mind-brain-environment relationships is a key topic in psychology. Inspired by theoretical physics, Kurt Lewin aimed to establish topological and vector psychology by analyzing patterns of interaction between individuals and their environments. This paper argues that the time is ripe to reformulate Lewin's ambitious goals, seeking to interpret objectively measured brain processes using appropriate psychological constructs. Connecting cognitive and social psychology constructs to neurophenomics, as practiced in psychiatry, should ground these constructs in physical reality.

title: Snow Queen is Evil and Beautiful: Experimental Evidence for Probabilistic Contextuality in Human Choices
Abstract: This paper provides unambiguous experimental evidence for (quantum-like) probabilistic contextuality in psychology. Previous attempts to find contextuality in psychological experiments were unsuccessful due to significant violations of marginal selectivity in behavioral data, rendering traditional quantum mechanics tests inapplicable. In a crowdsourcing experiment, participants made two simple choices: selecting one of two characters in a story (The Snow Queen by Hans Christian Andersen) and choosing one of two characteristics, such as Kind and Evil, to match the storyline. The experiment's structure mimicked the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen paradigm in the Bohm-Bell version. While marginal selectivity was violated, indicating a direct influence between choices, a mathematical test developed in the Contextuality-by-Default theory, extending traditional quantum-mechanical tests, revealed strong evidence of contextuality, not reducible to direct influences.

title: From Attention to Participation: Reviewing and Modelling Engagement with Computers
Abstract: Over recent decades, the internet and mobile technology have established the digital realm as a public sphere of life. Designers are tasked with creating engaging digital experiences, where engagement is often viewed as a psychological state or a participatory concept. This paper reviews and discusses both perspectives, proposing a new definition to clarify the concept of engagement with computers. Engagement is defined as the quality of an active connection between a user and a computing product, encompassing websites or mobile apps. Studying engagement requires understanding user affect, motivation, and attention, as well as product design, content, and composition. The paper suggests aligning these concepts with engagement and integrating them into a preliminary model to measure its manifestations.

title: Learning Neural Representations of Human Cognition across Many fMRI Studies
Abstract: Cognitive neuroscience is experiencing a rapid increase in extensive public brain-imaging datasets, paving the way for large-scale statistical models. Finding a unified perspective for all available data requires scalable and automated solutions to the challenge of aggregating heterogeneous information on brain function into a universal cognitive system. This system should relate mental operations, cognitive processes, and psychological tasks to brain networks. This paper addresses this challenge using a machine-learning approach to predict conditions from statistical brain maps across different studies. Leveraging multi-task learning and multi-scale dimension reduction, the paper learns low-dimensional representations of brain images that carry cognitive information and can be robustly associated with psychological stimuli. The multi-dataset classification model achieves the best prediction performance on several large reference datasets compared to models without cognitive-aware low-dimension representations, significantly improving the analysis of small datasets and identifying universal template cognitive concepts. |||

title: Crossing Behaviour of Social Groups: Insights from Observations at Non-signalized Intersection
Abstract: Environmental, demographic, and psychological factors significantly influence risky crossing behaviors. This study investigates the impact of social factors, specifically group crossing decisions, on pedestrian behavior. The research analyzes video recordings of single pedestrians and pairs crossing at non-signalized intersections.  The findings reveal three distinct phases of crossing behavior: approaching, appraising (decision-making), and crossing. Notably, pairs walk slower than single pedestrians in all phases. Within pairs, a leader emerges, making the decision to cross first, followed by their companion. However, the study found no difference in the accepted safety gap between singles and pairs. Understanding the factors influencing crossing decisions within social groups is crucial for developing more realistic agent-based simulations of pedestrian-vehicle interactions.

title: Respiratory and cardiac monitoring at night using a wrist wearable optical system
Abstract: Sleep monitoring offers valuable insights into an individual's overall health and assists in diagnosing sleep-related disorders. Polysomnography, considered the gold standard for sleep monitoring, is cumbersome and unsuitable for long-term analysis. This paper introduces a non-intrusive wearable system that utilizes photoplethysmography to reliably estimate beat-to-beat intervals, pulse rate, and breathing rate during sleep. The system's performance was evaluated empirically at the University of Fribourg, with participants wearing two Ava smart bracelets and a complete polysomnographic setup for reference. The results demonstrate mean absolute errors of 17.4 ms (MAPE 1.8%) for beat-to-beat intervals, 0.13 beats-per-minute (MAPE 0.20%) for pulse rate, and 0.9 breaths-per-minute (MAPE 6.7%) for breath rate.

title: Frame-Induced Group Polarization in Small Discussion Networks
Abstract: This research proposes a novel explanation for the group polarization effect, which suggests that discussions among like-minded individuals lead to shifts toward extreme viewpoints. The theory differentiates between the quantitative policy under debate and the discussion's rhetorical frame, such as the likelihood of an outcome. If the policy and frame position are mathematically related, with frame position increasing more slowly as the policy becomes more extreme, the formation of a majority at the extreme is favored, shifting consensus toward extremism. Additionally, the use of a heuristic frame can shift the frame reference point away from the policy reference, resulting in differential polarization on opposing policy sides. The paper presents a mathematical model that predicts consensus policy based on group member initial preferences and network structure. An online group discussion experiment manipulated policy side, disagreement level, and network structure. The results, challenging existing polarization theory, align qualitatively and quantitatively with the proposed theory and model.

title: An Online Consent Maturity Model: Moving from Acceptable Use towards Ethical Practice
Abstract: The distinctive characteristics of qualitative longitudinal research in psychology and social science have led to the development of informed consent practices. These characteristics share similarities with data collection and analysis in online settings. By examining the theoretical and practical development of informed consent in qualitative longitudinal research, we can gain valuable insights into its application in online environments. Based on this analogy, the paper proposes criteria for ethically evaluating consent practices in online data handling activities and outlines a consent maturity model. The authors argue that drawing from the history of informed consent in qualitative longitudinal research, we should strive for an Ethics of Virtue approach to informed consent online, representing the highest level of maturity.

title: Text Mining Descriptions Of Dreams: aesthetic and clinical efforts
Abstract: Dreams are highly valued in both Freudian psychoanalysis and less conservative clinical traditions. Text mining, a powerful tool for extracting meaning from texts, offers unique possibilities for analyzing dream descriptions. This paper presents the methods, uses, and results obtained from mining dream descriptions collected from participants in a Schizoanalysis course (Clinical Psychology). Using various techniques, the researchers generated poems and summaries from the dream descriptions, which were then incorporated into clinical sessions through music and declamation. The results were found to be aesthetically appealing and effective in engaging the audience. Future work will focus on expanding the corpus, refining mining methods, and exploring strategies for utilizing the derivatives for art and therapy.

title: Understanding Early Word Learning in Situated Artificial Agents
Abstract: Neural network-based systems have advanced to the point where they can locate word and phrase referents in images, answer questions about visual scenes, and execute symbolic instructions as first-person actors in partially-observable worlds. This ability, known as grounded language learning, requires overcoming challenges faced by infants when acquiring their first words. While it is remarkable that models with no meaningful prior knowledge can overcome these obstacles, understanding the underlying mechanisms remains unclear. This paper investigates this issue by focusing on a simple neural network-based language learning agent trained via policy-gradient methods to interpret single-word instructions in a simulated 3D world.  Inspired by experimental paradigms in developmental psychology, the research explores conditions under which established human biases and learning effects emerge in the artificial agent. Additionally, the paper proposes a novel method for visualizing semantic representations within the agent.

title: Dynamic Social Balance and Convergent Appraisals via Homophily and Influence Mechanisms
Abstract: Social balance theory explains allowable and forbidden configurations in signed directed social appraisal networks. This paper proposes two discrete-time dynamical systems that model how an appraisal network converges to social balance from an initially unbalanced state. These models are based on distinct socio-psychological mechanisms: the homophily mechanism and the influence mechanism. The paper provides a comprehensive analysis of both models, encompassing three steps. First, the well-posedness and bounded evolution of interpersonal appraisals are established. Second, the equilibrium points are fully characterized, showing that each equilibrium network consists of an arbitrary number of complete subgraphs satisfying structural balance. Third, the equivalence among three distinct properties is established: non-vanishing appraisals, convergence to all-to-all appraisal networks, and finite-time achievement of social balance.  Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that the non-vanishing appraisal condition holds for generic initial conditions in both models. Numerical comparisons between the two models suggest that the homophily-based model might be a more universal explanation for the formation of social balance. Using the homophily-based model, the research presents numerical results on the mediation and globalization of local conflicts, competition for allies, and the asymptotic formation of a single versus two factions.

title: On Universality of Classical Probability with Contextually Labeled Random Variables
Abstract: Claims often arise that classical (Kolmogorovian) probability theory cannot handle or even contradicts certain empirical findings or substantive theories. This paper joins previous attempts to refute these claims, illustrating the misinterpretations through examples related to the (non)existence of joint distributions, probabilities of ordered events, and additivity of probabilities. The paper emphasizes that contextual labeling of all involved random variables can prevent these misinterpretations. Furthermore, contextual labeling offers a valuable approach to analyzing probabilistic aspects of empirical situations by determining whether the random variables constitute a contextual system, extending the concept from quantum mechanics.  The Wang-Busemeyer QQ equality for the question order effect demonstrates that the system describing this phenomenon is noncontextual. Similarly, the double-slit experiment and its behavioral analogues form a noncontextual system, sharing the same probabilistic format (cyclic system of rank 4) as the one describing the spins of two entangled electrons.

title: Asymptotically Optimal Sequential Design for Rank Aggregation
Abstract: Rank aggregation, a sequential design problem encountered in psychology, politics, marketing, sports, and other fields, involves a decision maker ranking K items by sequentially collecting pairwise noisy comparisons from judges.  The decision maker must choose a pair of items for comparison in each step, determine when to stop data collection, and make a final decision based on the sequential flow of information. Due to the complex ranking structure, existing sequential analysis methods are inadequate. This paper formulates the problem under a Bayesian decision framework and proposes asymptotically optimal sequential procedures. These procedures achieve optimality by balancing exploration (finding the most indistinguishable pair of items) and exploitation (comparing the most indistinguishable pair based on current information). The paper develops novel analytical tools to prove the asymptotic results, combining advanced change of measure techniques for handling likelihood ratio level crossing with classic large deviation results for martingales.  A mirror-descent algorithm is presented for computing the proposed sequential procedures.

title: Large Scale Replication Projects in Contemporary Psychological Research
Abstract: Replication in psychological research presents challenges due to the impossibility of direct or exact replications of studies investigating a given phenomenon, leading to varying effect sizes across studies. While large-scale replication projects are a significant step toward assessing replicability, they provide limited information as they often fail to assess or aim to eliminate heterogeneity. Consequently, the observed heterogeneity in these projects represents a lower bound. This paper advocates for embracing heterogeneity in future large-scale replication projects, arguing that it is essential for assessing replicability. If effect sizes are sufficiently heterogeneous, even with consistent effect sign, the phenomenon in question may not be considered particularly replicable, suggesting a poorly constructed underlying theory that requires refinement. Uncovering the reasons behind heterogeneity and revising theory in light of it will lead to improved theories that explain heterogeneity and enhance replicability.  Large-scale replication projects can thus play a crucial role in assessing replicability and advancing theory.

title: Quantum field inspired model of decision making: Asymptotic stabilization of belief state via interaction with surrounding mental environment
Abstract: This paper justifies the use of quantum-like models for decision-making based on the theory of open quantum systems, treating decision-making as a decoherence process. The process is modeled as the interaction between a decision maker, Alice, and a mental (information) environment surrounding her. This interaction results in the "dissipation of uncertainty" from Alice's belief-state into the environment and the asymptotic stabilization of her belief-state to a steady state, which represents the decision state. Mathematically, the challenge lies in finding constraints on the mental environment that ensure this stabilization. The paper presents a partial solution to this problem in the form of sufficient conditions and analyzes decision-making for a specific class of mental environments, "almost homogeneous environments." Illustrative examples include a) the behavior of an electorate interacting with the mass-media "reservoir" and b) consumer persuasion. The paper also discusses other classes of mental environments.

title: ThermSense: Smartphone-based Breathing Sensing Platform using Noncontact Low-Cost Thermal Camera
Abstract: The ability to sense breathing is becoming increasingly important for technology designed to support both psychological and physical well-being. This paper introduces ThermSense, a novel breathing sensing platform based on smartphone technology and a low-cost thermal camera, enabling contact-free measurement of breathing patterns. With key functions such as Thermal Voxel Integration-based breathing estimation and respiration variability spectrogram (RVS, a bi-dimensional representation of breathing dynamics), the platform provides scalability and flexibility for collecting respiratory physiological measurements ubiquitously. The functionality has applications ranging from stress monitoring to respiration training.

title: O Teorema de Poincare-Hopf
Abstract: The Poincaré-Hopf Theorem, one of the most widely used theorems in various scientific fields, has applications in physics, chemistry, biology, economics, psychology, and more. The theorem connects an invariant of combinatorial topology, the Euler-Poincaré characteristic, to an invariant of differential geometry, the index of vector fields. The theorem's ability to bridge two vastly different areas of mathematics makes it remarkably beautiful, useful, and fruitful.

title: Personalized Saliency and its Prediction
Abstract: Existing visual saliency models primarily focus on predicting a universal saliency map applicable to all observers. However, psychological studies suggest that visual attention among different observers can vary significantly, especially in scenes containing multiple salient objects. To study this heterogenous visual attention pattern across observers, the paper proposes a personalized saliency dataset and investigates correlations between visual attention, personal preferences, and image content. The research proposes decomposing a personalized saliency map (PSM) into a universal saliency map (USM) predictable by existing models and a discrepancy map across users characterizing personalized saliency.  Two solutions for predicting these discrepancy maps are presented: a multi-task convolutional neural network (CNN) framework and an extended CNN with Person-specific Information Encoded Filters (CNN-PIEF). Extensive experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of these models for PSM prediction and their generalization capability for unseen observers.

title: The Nuts and Bolts of Micropayments: A Survey
Abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive survey of key trends and innovations in the development of research-based and commercial micropayment systems. The authors argue that past solutions have largely failed due to a heavy focus on cryptographic and engineering innovation while neglecting fundamental issues related to usability, psychology, and economics. The paper contextualizes the range of existing challenges for micropayment systems, discusses potential deployment strategies, and identifies critical stumbling blocks that researchers and developers have yet to fully recognize. The goal is to motivate and guide future development of micropayment systems.

title: Extended Formulations for Order Polytopes through Network Flows
Abstract: Mathematical psychology has a long tradition of modeling probabilistic choice using distribution-free random utility models and associated random preference models. For these models, the predicted choice probabilities often form a bounded and convex polyhedral set, or polytope. Polyhedral combinatorics have played a key role in studying the mathematical structure of these models. However, standard methods for characterizing these polytopes face a combinatorial explosion in complexity as the number of choice alternatives increases, particularly for random preference models based on linear, weak, semi-, and interval orders.  The paper utilizes the method of extended formulations to overcome these limitations. For each type of preference, an appropriate network is constructed, and it is shown that the associated network flow polytope provides an extended formulation of the choice model's polytope.  This extended formulation offers a simple linear description that is more parsimonious than descriptions obtained by standard methods for large numbers of choice alternatives. The result is a computationally less demanding approach for testing the probabilistic choice model on data. The paper outlines how this approach interfaces with recent developments in contemporary statistics.

title: Power analysis for a linear regression model when regressors are matrix sampled
Abstract: Multiple matrix sampling is a survey methodology technique that randomly selects a small subset of items for presentation to survey respondents, reducing respondent burden. The resulting data are missing completely at random (MCAR), requiring special missing data techniques for linear regression and other multivariate statistical analyses. This paper derives asymptotic variances of regression parameter estimates, enabling power analysis for linear regression models fitted to data obtained using a multiple matrix sampling design. The ideas are illustrated with a variation of the Big Five Inventory of psychological traits. An exploration of the regression parameter space reveals instability in sample size requirements and substantial precision losses with matrix-sampled regressors. A simulation with non-normal data demonstrates the advantages of a semi-parametric multiple imputation scheme.

title: A discrete choice model for solving conflict situations between pedestrians and vehicles in shared space
Abstract: When streets are designed according to the shared space principle, road users are encouraged to interact spontaneously for space negotiation. These interactions are governed by psychological and social principles related to safety, comfort, and time pressure, rather than clearly defined traffic rules. However, these principles are difficult to capture and quantify, hindering the simulation of road user behavior. This paper investigates traffic conflict situations between pedestrians and motorized vehicles, focusing on developing a discrete choice model for identifying conflict resolution strategies. A shared space street in Hamburg, Germany, with high pedestrian volumes, serves as a case study for model formulation and calibration. Conflict situations are automatically detected through trajectory prediction and comparison. Standard evasive actions for both pedestrians and vehicles are identified by observing behavioral patterns.  The paper formulates and tests the significance of potential parameters influencing evasive action choices, including geometrical aspects (distance and speed) and conflict-specific ones (time to collision). A multinomial logit model is calibrated and validated on real situations. The developed approach is realistic and ready for implementation in motion models for shared space or other less organized traffic environments.

title: A Serious Game Design: Nudging Users' Memorability of Security Questions
Abstract: Security questions are a technique used for password recovery. A major limitation is that users find strong answers difficult to remember, leading them to prioritize convenience over security. Previous research suggests that increased fun and enjoyment can enhance memorability and improve the learning experience. This paper investigates whether a serious game can improve the memorability of strong answers to security questions. The research adapted the popular "4 Pics 1 word" mobile game, known for its use of pictures and cues, which psychology research has shown to be important for memorability.  The findings suggest that the proposed serious game could potentially improve the memorability of security question answers, potentially reducing the trade-off between usability and security in fallback authentication.
label: AI

title: Changing users' security behaviour towards security questions: A game based learning approach
Abstract: Fallback authentication is used to retrieve forgotten passwords, with security questions being a key technique. This paper proposes a serious game design that utilizes system-generated security questions to enhance the usability of fallback authentication.  The design is based on the popular picture-based "4 Pics 1 word" mobile game, selected for its use of pictures and cues, which prior research has shown to be crucial for aiding memorability.  The game asks users to identify the word related to given pictures.  The research customized this game by incorporating features that maximize memory retrieval skills, including: (a) verbal cues (hints with verbal descriptions), (b) spatial cues (maintaining the same picture order), (c) graphical cues (showing 4 images for each challenge), and (d) interactivity and engaging nature of the game. |||

title: Disabling External Influence in Social Networks via Edge Recommendation
Abstract:
Existing socio-psychological studies suggest that social network users rely on their neighbors' opinions to form their own. The DeGroot opinion formation model highlights the importance of the asymptotic consensus value, a weighted sum of user opinions based on their eigenvector centrality. This value acts as an attractor for opinions within the network, making it a prime target for external influence. However, any malicious manipulation of opinion distribution within a social network is undesirable. Therefore, it's crucial to develop methods that prevent external attempts to strategically alter the asymptotic consensus value.

This research assumes that an adversary aims to maximize the asymptotic consensus value by manipulating the opinions of select users in a network. Consequently, the DIVER problem is defined, an NP-hard problem that aims to neutralize such external influence attempts by strategically adding a limited number of edges to the network. Leveraging Markov chain theory, perturbation analysis reveals how eigenvector centrality, and thus DIVER's objective function, changes in response to edge additions. This analysis facilitates the development of a pseudo-linear-time heuristic for DIVER, relying on efficient estimation of mean first passage times within a Markov chain. The theoretical findings are validated through experimental verification. ||| 
The connection between two seemingly distinct problems—understanding consciousness and the emergence of time and space in the quantum mechanical world—is explored. A toy-model is proposed for the emergence of time from a timeless, quantum-like "unus mundus" space, using Aharonov's two-state formalism of quantum mechanics. The discussion then delves into these issues from a quantum cognitive perspective, focusing on two recent papers in this field. One paper, by Aerts et al., advocates a panpsychist top-down approach to consciousness, while the other, by Blutner et al., proposes a quantum cognitive model for Jung's psychological type structure. The relationship between these concepts and the central thesis of time as a measure of individuality is explored. The primary motivation is to provide arguments that encourage mainstream physicists to seriously consider a panpsychist worldview, a position widely embraced by many modern philosophers.

title: Time and Consciousness in a Quantum World
Abstract: Traditional theory-driven research in psychology relies heavily on laboratory experiments, but rarely tests or refutes its findings using big data. This paper uses a dataset of 418,000 travel photos with traveler ratings to test the influential "broaden-and-build" theory, which posits that positive emotions broaden one's visual attention. The core hypothesis tested is that positive emotions are associated with wider attention, leading to wide-angle photographs of highly-rated tourist sites. Analysis of travel photos reveals a strong correlation between a preference for wide-angle photos and high ratings of tourist sites on TripAdvisor. This analysis was made possible by deep learning algorithms that classified photos into wide and narrow angles, demonstrating the potential of big data and deep learning to test laboratory findings in real-world settings.

title: Happy Travelers Take Big Pictures: A Psychological Study with Machine Learning and Big Data
Abstract:
Depression is a significant mental health disorder with a rapidly increasing impact worldwide. It affects not only emotional well-being but also physical and psychological states, manifesting in symptoms like loss of interest in daily activities, low mood, anxiety, frustration, weight loss, and even self-hatred. This report details a project conducted during a BTech summer internship for the Audio Visual Emotion Challenge (AVEC) 2017, focusing on automatic depression detection using machine learning algorithms. 

The project involved a multimodal feature extraction and decision-level fusion approach. Features were extracted from the Distress Analysis Interview Corpus-Wizard of Oz (DAIC-WOZ) database, utilizing techniques like Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) clustering and Fisher vector analysis on visual data, statistical descriptors on gaze and pose, low-level audio features, head pose, and text features. Classification was performed on both fused and independent features using Support Vector Machine (SVM) and neural networks. The results achieved surpassed the provided baseline on validation data, demonstrating a 17% improvement on audio features and a 24.5% improvement on video features.
label: AI

title: Depression Scale Recognition from Audio, Visual and Text Analysis
Abstract: This paper tackles the challenge of detecting expressions of moral values in tweets through content analysis. This problem is particularly complex because moral values are often implicitly signaled in language, and tweets, due to their length limitations, lack contextual information. To address these obstacles, a novel approach is introduced that automatically acquires background knowledge from an external knowledge base to enrich input texts and improve moral value prediction. Combining basic text features with this background knowledge, the context-aware framework achieves performance comparable to a single human annotator. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt to incorporate background knowledge for predicting implicit psychological variables in the field of computational social science.
