title: Acquiring Background Knowledge to Improve Moral Value Prediction
Abstract:
As computational power continues to increase and sensors become more accurate, cognitive and immersive systems (CAISs) are emerging at the intersection of AI and HCI/HRI. These systems interact with and assist human agents, leveraging AI to understand and reason about their knowledge, beliefs, goals, communications, plans, etc. This paper presents an approach to engineering CAISs, emphasizing the development and reasoning capabilities of a "theory of mind" for human partners. This entails a sophisticated AI model of human beliefs, knowledge, goals, desires, emotions, etc. To achieve this, a highly expressive formal framework is required, in this case, a cognitive event calculus, a type of quantified multi-operator modal logic, alongside a matching automated reasoner and planner. The paper demonstrates that this calculus satisfies a set of formal requirements, enabling a CAIS to comprehend psychologically complex scenarios within the cognitive polysolid framework (CPF). It also formally proves that a room meeting these requirements possesses a useful property termed "expectation of usefulness". CPF, a subclass of cognitive microworlds, provides mechanisms to represent and plan not just over blocks and actions, but also over agents and their mental attitudes towards other agents and inanimate objects. ||| 
Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance in a wide range of complex tasks. Recent research has focused on analyzing their black box characteristics to understand their learning behaviors, tendencies, and limitations. This paper investigates the limitations of DNNs in image classification tasks, drawing inspiration from cognitive psychology. By examining failure cases in ImageNet classification, the hypothesis is proposed that DNNs do not adequately learn to associate related classes of objects. To verify this, experiments were conducted on an image database used in cognitive psychology. ImageNet-trained DNNs were applied to this database containing pairs of related and unrelated object images to compare feature similarities and determine matching pairs. Results indicate that DNNs exhibit limited performance in determining relatedness between object classes. While DNNs show somewhat improved performance in discovering relatedness based on similarity, they perform less effectively in discovering relatedness based on association. These experiments provide a novel analysis of DNN learning behaviors and highlight limitations that need to be addressed.

title: Toward Cognitive and Immersive Systems: Experiments in a Cognitive Microworld
Abstract: Traditionally, psychometric tests have been used to profile incoming workers. These methods utilize the DISC profiling technique to categorize individuals into distinct personality types, which are then used to predict their fit within the organizational culture. This paper proposes a novel approach that further extends this concept by predicting the psychological compatibility between a newly hired worker and their assigned manager. This is achieved using a multilayer perceptron neural network, capable of adaptive training to showcase the true nature of the compatibility index. The proposed prototype model quantifies relevant attributes, trains the prediction engine using these attributes, and defines the necessary data pipeline.

title: Can Deep Neural Networks Match the Related Objects?: A Survey on ImageNet-trained Classification Models
Abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive overview of research conducted in the Virtual Reality (VR) environment, encompassing definitions, its presence across various fields, market players, and their VR technology projects. It also aims to gain insights into the psychological mechanisms underlying the experience of using VR devices. The literature survey is based on research articles, analysis of company projects, and their findings in diverse areas of interest. The survey reveals that recent advancements in VR enabling technologies have led to a wide variety of virtual devices that facilitate human interaction with the digital world. Researchers have strived to integrate reality and VR in the form of intuitive computer interfaces over the past two decades. These efforts have resulted in numerous potential benefits of VR across various applications, including news, healthcare, entertainment, tourism, military, and defense. However, despite extensive research in creating virtual system environments, widespread adoption in everyday life remains elusive.

title: An Automated Compatibility Prediction Engine using DISC Theory Based Classification and Neural Networks
Abstract: This paper presents a Bayesian procedure for simultaneous variable and covariance selection using continuous spike-and-slab priors in multivariate linear regression models. The model regresses q potentially correlated responses onto p predictors. Instead of relying on stochastic search through the high-dimensional model space, an ECM algorithm, similar to the EMVS procedure by Rockova & George (2014), is developed to target modal estimates of the regression coefficient matrix and residual precision matrix. By varying the scale of the continuous spike densities, dynamic posterior exploration is facilitated, enabling the gradual filtering out of negligible regression coefficients and partial covariances. The proposed method demonstrates significant performance improvements compared to regularization competitors on simulated data. Its effectiveness is illustrated by re-examining data from a recent observational study on the impact of high school football participation on various later-life cognitive, psychological, and socioeconomic outcomes.

title: Virtual Reality: Blessings and Risk Assessment
Abstract: The issue of optional stopping in Bayesian hypothesis testing has been a subject of debate within the Bayesian psychology community. Rouder (2014) argues that optional stopping is not a concern for Bayesians, even recommending its use in practice, as do Wagenmakers et al. (2012). This paper addresses the question of whether optional stopping is problematic for Bayesian methods, specifying the circumstances and the extent to which it is or is not problematic. By slightly modifying and expanding Rouder's (2014) experiments, the paper illustrates that when parameters of interest are equipped with default or pragmatic priors, which is common in most practical applications of Bayes factor hypothesis testing, resilience to optional stopping can break down. The paper distinguishes between three types of default priors, each with its own specific issues with optional stopping, ranging from no problem at all (Type 0 priors) to quite severe (Type II priors).

title: Simultaneous Variable and Covariance Selection with the Multivariate Spike-and-Slab Lasso
Abstract:
Pedestrians typically stop and wait for a signal from a driver when encountering vehicles, indicating whether to cross or wait. However, the advent of autonomous vehicles raises the question of how to communicate intent to pedestrians in the absence of a human driver. This paper addresses this issue by introducing an intent communication system (ICS) that serves as a substitute for a human driver. 

The ICS is designed to account for pedestrian psychology, incorporating their expectations and familiarity with human drivers. The system integrates these expectations into both physical system design and mathematical algorithms. The goal is to ensure simple, yet effective communication without fostering distrust in autonomous vehicles. To validate the ICS, two types of experiments were conducted: field tests with an autonomous vehicle to observe real-world human-ICS interactions and simulations to model multiple potential behaviors. Results from both experiments indicate that humans react more positively and predictably when the vehicle's intent is communicated compared to when it is unknown. The simulation results specifically showed a 142% difference in pedestrian trust in the vehicle's actions when the ICS is enabled and the pedestrian has prior knowledge of the vehicle compared to when the ICS is not enabled and the pedestrian lacks prior knowledge.

title: Why optional stopping can be a problem for Bayesians
Abstract: Technology holds immense potential for human development and social good. Given the crucial roles of environment and human psychology in driving human behavior, and the ubiquitous presence of technology in modern life, leveraging insights and capabilities from both fields is essential for nudging individuals towards optimal behavior, whether for personal or societal benefit. Persuasive technology, which aims to infuse technology with appropriate design and incentives using insights from psychology, behavioral economics, and human-computer interaction, offers significant promise in this regard. While persuasive technology is already being developed and utilized in many commercial applications, it has the potential for substantial social impact in the field of Information and Communication Technology for Development (ICTD), which employs Information and Communication Technology (ICT) for human development goals such as education and health. This paper explores the concept of persuasive technology and its application for human development. To provide a concrete example, a case study is presented outlining how persuasive technology can be used to promote human development in Pakistan, a developing South Asian country facing challenges typical of developing nations.

title: Intent Communication between Autonomous Vehicles and Pedestrians
Abstract:
DeepBreath, a deep learning model for automatically recognizing people's psychological stress levels (mental overload) from their breathing patterns, is proposed. This model utilizes a low-cost thermal camera to track breathing patterns as temperature changes around the nostril. 

The technical contributions of this paper are threefold: 

1. **Data Transformation:** Instead of hand-crafted features, the unidimensional breathing signals are transformed into two-dimensional respiration variability spectrogram (RVS) sequences, capturing the complexity of breathing dynamics.
2. **Spatial Pattern Analysis:** A spatial pattern analysis based on a deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) is directly applied to the spectrogram sequences without the need for hand-crafted features.
3. **Data Augmentation:** A data augmentation technique, inspired by solutions for overfitting in deep learning, is applied to allow the CNN to learn from a small-scale dataset of short-term measurements.

The model is trained and tested using data collected from individuals exposed to two types of cognitive tasks (Stroop Color Word Test, Mental Computation test) with varying difficulty levels. Using normalized self-reported stress levels as ground truth, the CNN achieves 84.59% accuracy in discriminating between two stress levels and 56.52% accuracy in discriminating between three levels. Additionally, the CNN outperforms powerful shallow learning methods based on a single-layer neural network. The dataset of labeled thermal images will be made publicly available for further research.

title: Persuasive Technology For Human Development: Review and Case Study
Abstract:
Transfer learning leverages knowledge from a source domain to facilitate learning in a target domain. The key challenges in transfer learning lie in determining what knowledge to transfer and how to transfer it. Different transfer learning algorithms result in the transfer of different knowledge between domains. To identify the optimal transfer learning algorithm that maximizes learning performance in the target domain, researchers would need to exhaustively explore all existing algorithms, a computationally intractable task. As a compromise, a sub-optimal algorithm is often selected, requiring significant expertise and an ad-hoc approach. 

Inspired by educational psychology, which recognizes the development of human transfer learning skills through meta-cognitive reflection on inductive transfer learning practices, a novel transfer learning framework called Learning to Transfer (L2T) is proposed. This framework automates the determination of what and how to transfer by leveraging past transfer learning experiences. L2T operates in two stages: 1) it learns a reflection function that encapsulates transfer learning skills from past experiences, and 2) it infers what and how to transfer for newly encountered domains by optimizing the reflection function. Extensive experiments demonstrate L2T's superiority over state-of-the-art transfer learning algorithms and its effectiveness in discovering more transferable knowledge. ||| 
Analyzing and recognizing driving styles is crucial for intelligent transportation systems and vehicle calibration. This paper presents a novel driving style analysis framework utilizing primitive driving patterns learned from naturalistic driving data. 

To achieve this, a Bayesian nonparametric learning method based on a hidden semi-Markov model (HSMM) is introduced to extract primitive driving patterns from time series driving data without prior knowledge of the number of patterns. The Bayesian nonparametric approach utilizes a hierarchical Dirichlet process (HDP) instead of learning the unknown number of smooth dynamical modes of HSMM, generating the primitive driving patterns. Each pattern is clustered and labeled using behavioral semantics based on drivers' physical and psychological perception thresholds. 

For each driver, 75 primitive driving patterns in car-following scenarios are learned and semantically labeled. To demonstrate the utility of HDP-HSMM in learning primitive driving patterns, two other Bayesian nonparametric approaches, HDP-HMM and sticky HDP-HMM, are compared. Naturalistic driving data from 18 drivers was collected from the University of Michigan Safety Pilot Model Deployment (SPDM) database. 

Individual driving styles are discussed based on the distribution characteristics of the learned primitive driving patterns, and differences in driving styles among drivers are evaluated using the Kullback-Leibler divergence. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed primitive pattern-based method effectively captures and semantically understands driver behaviors and driving styles.

title: DeepBreath: Deep Learning of Breathing Patterns for Automatic Stress Recognition using Low-Cost Thermal Imaging in Unconstrained Settings
Abstract:
Rank data is commonly encountered in marketing, finance, organizational behavior, and psychology. Most rank data analyses in the literature assume the presence of one or more variables (sometimes latent) based on whose values the items are ranked. This paper analyzes rank data using a purely probabilistic model where observed ranks are considered perturbed versions of the true rank, with each perturbation having a specific probability of occurrence. The general case with covariate information and its impact on rankings is addressed. An empirical Bayes approach is employed to estimate model parameters. 

The Gibbs sampler, known for its slow convergence to the target posterior distribution, is shown to be inadequate in this context. Additionally, commonly used empirical convergence diagnostic tools may fail to detect this lack of convergence. A novel, fast-mixing sandwich algorithm is proposed for exploring the posterior distribution. An EM algorithm based on Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling is developed for estimating prior hyperparameters. A real-world rank data set is analyzed using the developed methods, showcasing their effectiveness in analyzing rank data with covariate information.

title: Learning to Transfer
Abstract:
Face detection is a fundamental task and a necessary pre-processing step for numerous applications, including facial landmark detection, pose estimation, sentiment analysis, and face recognition. Beyond its importance in computer vision applications, face detection plays a crucial role in computational psychology, behavioral imaging, and other fields where researchers might not be familiar with computer vision frameworks and state-of-the-art detection applications. 

A significant portion of existing research relying on face detection as a pre-processing step utilizes readily available out-of-the-box detectors like the HoG-based dlib and the OpenCV Haar face detector. However, these detectors are no longer considered state-of-the-art, primarily used due to their ease of use and accessibility. 

This paper introduces Dockerface, a highly accurate Faster R-CNN face detector packaged in a Docker container, eliminating the need for training and simplifying installation and use.

title: Driving Style Analysis Using Primitive Driving Patterns With Bayesian Nonparametric Approaches
Abstract:
Human-human joint-action in short-cycle repetitive handover tasks was investigated for a bottle handover task using a three-fold approach: work-methods field studies in multiple supermarkets, simulation analysis using an ergonomics software package, and an in-house lab experiment on human-human collaboration recreating the supermarket environment and conditions. 

Evaluation encompassed both objective and subjective measures. Subjective evaluation, conducted from a psychological perspective, highlighted, among other things, the differences in how a common joint-action is perceived by individual team partners depending on their role (giver or receiver). 

This proposed approach offers a systematic method for analyzing similar tasks. Combining results from all three analyses, this research sheds light on the science of joint-action for short-cycle repetitive tasks and its implications for human-robot collaborative system design.

title: A novel sandwich algorithm for empirical Bayes analysis of rank data
Abstract:
Research from diverse fields, including psychology and linguistics, has identified correlations and patterns between personal attributes and behavior. However, efforts to understand the broader heterogeneity in human behavior have yet to integrate these approaches and perspectives with a cohesive methodology. This paper presents a novel approach that extracts patterns in behavior and relates them together in a high-dimensional picture. 

Dimension reduction techniques are used to analyze word usage in text data from the online discussion platform Reddit. The analysis reveals that pronouns can be used to characterize the space of the two most prominent dimensions that capture the greatest differences in word usage, even though pronouns were not included in the determination of these dimensions. These patterns overlap with patterns of discussion topics, revealing relationships between pronouns and topics that describe the user population. This analysis corroborates findings from previous research identifying word use differences across populations and synthesizes them relative to each other. The authors believe this is a significant step towards understanding how differences between individuals are related to one another. |||

title: Fake News Detection on Social Media: A Data Mining Perspective
Abstract: Social media has become a popular source of news, offering easy access and rapid information dissemination. However, its potential for spreading "fake news," or intentionally misleading information, poses a significant threat to individuals and society. Consequently, fake news detection on social media has emerged as a crucial research area.  Detecting fake news on social media presents unique challenges that traditional news media detection algorithms cannot effectively address.  Fake news is intentionally designed to deceive readers, making content-based detection difficult.  Therefore, incorporating auxiliary information, such as user engagement patterns, becomes essential.  Analyzing this auxiliary information presents its own challenges due to the massive, incomplete, unstructured, and noisy nature of social media data.  This survey provides a comprehensive review of fake news detection on social media, covering psychological and social theories, data mining algorithms, evaluation metrics, representative datasets, related research areas, open problems, and future research directions.

title: Empathy in Bimatrix Games
Abstract: The concept of empathetic preferences, though still evolving, is increasingly recognized as a significant factor influencing player behavior in interactive decision-making.  This paper examines one-shot bimatrix games from a psychological game theory perspective, introducing a new empathetic payoff model that aligns with empirical observations.  Both pure and mixed equilibria are investigated, and the bimatrix game is categorized into four generic classes based on the realized empathy structure.  The study reveals a notable level of engagement in empathetic one-shot games compared to non-empathetic ones, even in cases with dominated strategies.  Partial altruism is shown to promote symmetry breaking, reduce payoff inequality, and facilitate the selection of socially beneficial and efficient outcomes.  Conversely, partial spite and self-abnegation can exacerbate payoff inequity.  Empathetic evolutionary game dynamics are introduced to capture empathetically stable strategies under various revision protocols, including Brown-von Neumann-Nash, Smith, imitation, replicator, and hybrid dynamics.  The paper further explores mutual support and Berge solutions, demonstrating their connections to empathetic preferences.  Importantly, pure altruism is shown to be logically inconsistent, requiring a balance with some partial selfishness to create a consistent psychological framework.

title: Identification of Probabilities
Abstract: There is growing interest across psychology, neuroscience, and artificial intelligence in the idea that the brain constructs probabilistic models of sensory and linguistic input, essentially inferring a probabilistic model from a sample.  This raises fundamental questions about the feasibility of such inference, given the brain's limited data and computational resources.  This paper explores these questions and presents surprisingly positive and general findings.  First, for a broad class of probability distributions characterized by computability restrictions, a learning algorithm is specified that almost surely identifies a probability distribution in the limit, given a sufficiently large (but unknown) finite i.i.d. sample.  This finding is similarly shown to hold for sequences generated by a broad class of Markov chains, subject to computability assumptions.  The strong law of large numbers serves as the technical tool in this analysis.  Second, an algorithm is specified for a large class of dependent sequences that identifies in the limit a computable measure for which the sequence is typical, in the sense of Martin-Lof.  The theory of Kolmogorov complexity forms the basis for this result.  The associated predictions in both cases are analyzed, and the implications for language learning and wider theoretical implications for psychology are briefly discussed.

title: Modeling and Forecasting the Evolution of Preferences over Time: A Hidden Markov Model of Travel Behavior
Abstract: Preferences, as defined by taste parameters and consideration sets, are known to evolve over time in response to various factors such as demographics, situations, psychological and sociological constructs, and available alternatives.  However, existing representations often overlook the influence of past experiences on current preferences.  This study develops, applies, and tests a hidden Markov model with a discrete choice kernel to model and forecast the evolution of individual preferences and behaviors over long-range horizons.  The hidden states represent different preferences, specifically the modes considered in the choice set and sensitivity to level-of-service attributes.  The evolution of these hidden states is hypothesized as a first-order Markov process.  The framework is applied to examine the evolution of travel mode preferences (modality styles) over time, specifically in response to a major change in the public transportation system.  Longitudinal travel diary data from Santiago, Chile, consisting of four one-week pseudo travel diaries collected before and after the introduction of Transantiago, a comprehensive public transportation system redesign, is used.  The model identifies four modality styles in the population: drivers, bus users, bus-metro users, and auto-metro users.  These styles differ in terms of their considered travel modes and sensitivity to level-of-service attributes.  Significant shifts in the distribution of individuals across modality styles are observed before and after the system change, but the distribution stabilizes in the post-change periods.  Comparing the proposed dynamic framework to comparable static frameworks reveals discrepancies in aggregate forecasts for different policy scenarios.

title: Toward an Epistemic-Logical Theory of Categorization
Abstract: Categorization systems, widely studied in psychology, sociology, and organization theory, play a critical role in decision-making by structuring information.  This paper introduces a sound and complete epistemic logic of categories and agents' categorical perception, using Kripke-style semantics.  The semantics are defined in terms of data structures based on two domains: one representing objects (e.g., market products) and the other representing the features relevant to agents' decision-making.  This framework facilitates logic-based formalizations of core concepts from psychological, sociological, and organizational research in categorization theory.

title: Proceedings Sixteenth Conference on Theoretical Aspects of Rationality and Knowledge
Abstract: This volume presents papers from the Sixteenth Conference on Theoretical Aspects of Rationality and Knowledge (TARK), held at the University of Liverpool, UK, from July 24 to 26, 2017.  TARK conferences bring together researchers from diverse fields, including computer science, economics, linguistics, philosophy, and cognitive psychology, to advance understanding of issues related to reasoning about rationality and knowledge.

title: A Gamified Approach to Improve Users' Memorability of Fall-back Authentication
Abstract: Security questions are commonly used for password recovery in fallback authentication systems.  This paper proposes a game design aimed at improving the usability of system-generated security questions.  The design adapts the popular "4 Pics 1 word" mobile game, asking users to identify the word connecting a set of given pictures.  This game was chosen due to its use of pictures and cues, known to enhance memorability according to psychological research.  The proposed game design focuses on encoding information into users' long-term memory and promoting memorability through memory retrieval skills:  (a) graphical cues (images in each challenge), (b) verbal cues (verbal descriptions as hints), (c) spatial cues (consistent picture order), and (d) interactivity (engaging gameplay through persuasive technology principles).

title: Three-way symbolic tree-maps and ultrametrics
Abstract: Three-way dissimilarities, a generalization of (two-way) dissimilarities, can indicate the lack of homogeneity or resemblance between any three objects.  These maps have applications in cluster analysis and have been used in fields such as psychology and phylogenetics, where three-way data tables arise.  Special cases of such dissimilarities include three-way tree-metrics and ultrametrics, derived from leaf-labelled trees with edges labelled by positive real numbers.  This paper examines three-way maps arising from leaf-labelled trees where the interior vertices are labelled by an arbitrary set of values.  For unrooted trees, these maps are called three-way symbolic tree-maps; for rooted trees, they are called three-way symbolic ultrametrics, representing a generalization of the (two-way) symbolic ultrametrics of B\"ocker and Dress.  The paper demonstrates that, similar to two- and three-way tree-metrics and ultrametrics, three-way symbolic tree-maps and ultrametrics can be characterized via specific k-point conditions.  In the unrooted case, this characterization is mathematically equivalent to one presented by Gurvich for a particular class of edge-labelled hypergraphs.  The paper also shows that determining whether an arbitrary three-way symbolic map is a tree-map or a symbolic ultrametric can be achieved using a triplet-based approach relying on the BUILD algorithm.  This algorithm determines when a set of 3-leaved trees or triplets can be displayed by a single tree.  The results of this study have the potential to contribute to the development of new approaches and algorithms for understanding 3-way data, particularly in the field of phylogenetics.

title: Predicting Personality from Book Preferences with User-Generated Content Labels
Abstract: Psychological research has established a link between personality traits and book preferences.  However, past findings are based on questionnaires focusing on conventional genres and may not adequately represent niche content.  This study leverages a massive archive of content labels (tags) created by users of Goodreads.com, an online book catalogue, to provide a more comprehensive measure of book content.  By combining this tag data with preference and personality scores collected from Facebook users, the study achieves high accuracy in personality prediction by psychological standards.  The study also groups tags into broader genres to validate findings against previous research.  The results demonstrate robustness across both tag and genre levels of analysis, aligning with existing literature.  Moreover, user-generated tag labels reveal unexpected insights, including cultural differences, reading behaviors, and non-content factors influencing preferences.  This study represents the largest exploration of the relationship between personality and book content preferences to date.
label: AI

title: Application of Bayesian Networks for Estimation of Individual Psychological Characteristics
Abstract: Accurately assessing human potential is crucial for organizations and collectives.  This paper proposes using Bayesian networks to develop more precise overall estimations of individual psychological characteristics, based on psychological test results.  These networks identify the degree to which an individual possesses specific traits, such as stress resistance, risk-taking propensity, or the ability to concentrate on complex tasks.  While psychological testing is the most common method for studying individual characteristics, overall estimations often rely on personal experiences and the subjective perceptions of psychologists.  The proposed Bayesian network approach offers a more objective and data-driven method for assessing psychological traits.

title: ExGUtils: A python package for statistical analysis with the ex-gaussian probability density
Abstract: Reaction times and their underlying cognitive processes are a key area of study in psychology.  The ex-Gaussian distribution provides a good fit for multiple empirical reaction time datasets, but its complexity necessitates computational tools for analysis.  This manuscript discusses mathematical details of the ex-Gaussian distribution and introduces ExGUtils, a Python-based package containing functions and numerical tools for data analysis involving the ex-Gaussian probability density.  The package's validity is demonstrated through an extensive analysis of fits obtained using ExGUtils, comparing least squares and maximum likelihood methods and quantitatively evaluating the goodness of fit.  This analysis allows for the identification of outliers in empirical datasets and the determination of whether and where data trimming is necessary.

title: Automatic Recognition of Facial Displays of Unfelt Emotions
Abstract: Humans modify their facial expressions to communicate internal states and sometimes to mislead observers about their true emotions.  Experimental psychology research has shown that discriminative facial responses are short and subtle, suggesting that such behavior would be easier to distinguish with high-resolution capture at increased frame rates.  This paper introduces SASE-FE, the first dataset of facial expressions that are either congruent or incongruent with underlying emotional states.  The study demonstrates that recognizing authentic or feigned emotional expressions can be effectively addressed by learning spatio-temporal representations of the data.  A method that aggregates features along fiducial trajectories in a deeply learned space is proposed.  Performance analysis reveals that distinguishing genuine facial expressions of emotion is generally easier than distinguishing unfelt expressions, and certain emotion pairs, such as contempt and disgust, are more challenging to differentiate than others.  Furthermore, the proposed methodology improves state-of-the-art results on CK+ and OULU-CASIA datasets for video emotion recognition and achieves competitive results when classifying facial action units on the BP4D dataset.

title: Cognitive Biases in Software Engineering: A Systematic Mapping Study
Abstract: Cognitive biases, while extensively studied in cognitive psychology, have only recently gained attention in software engineering (SE) research.  This paper provides a systematic mapping, aggregation, and synthesis of the literature on cognitive biases in SE, aiming to create a comprehensive body of knowledge, assess current research, and provide guidelines for future research and practice.  Focusing on bias antecedents, effects, and mitigation techniques, the study identifies 65 articles published between 1990 and 2016 that investigate 37 cognitive biases.  Despite growing interest, the results highlight a scarcity of research on mitigation techniques and a lack of strong theoretical foundations for understanding and interpreting cognitive biases.  While bias-related research has yielded new insights within the SE community, specific bias mitigation techniques are still needed to help software professionals overcome the negative effects of cognitive biases on their work.

title: Parameter uncertainty in structural equation models: Confidence sets and fungible estimates
Abstract: Current concerns about the reliability of psychological findings necessitate methodological developments to provide stronger evidence for scientific conclusions.  This paper emphasizes the value and importance of two types of parameter uncertainty quantified by confidence sets (CSs) and fungible parameter estimates (FPEs).  Both provide crucial information regarding the defensibility of scientific findings.  The paper introduces a general perturbation framework based on the likelihood function within the structural equation model, unifying CSs and FPEs and shedding light on their conceptual distinctions.  A targeted illustration demonstrates factors influencing CSs and FPEs, highlighting their theoretical differences.  Three empirical examples, including initiating conversations with strangers, posttraumatic growth in caregivers of children with palliative care needs, and the direct and indirect effects of spirituality on youth thriving, illustrate how CSs and FPEs provide unique information that leads to more informed scientific conclusions.  The paper discusses the importance of considering information from CSs and FPEs in strengthening the interpretation of statistical results in substantive research, concludes with future research directions, and provides OpenMx code for computing CSs and FPEs.

title: Common Counterfactual Belief of Rationality Subsumes Superrationality On Symmetric Games
Abstract: This paper demonstrates that, for symmetric games in normal form, strategy profiles satisfying Hofstadter's Superrationality criterion also satisfy both Halpern and Pass's criteria under Common Counterfactual Belief of Rationality: minimax-rationalizability and individual rationality.

title: Automatic estimation of harmonic tension by distributed representation of chords
Abstract: The buildup and release of tension is a fundamental aspect of the music listening experience.  Developing a veridical computational model of perceived musical tension would be valuable for various music informatics applications.  This paper proposes a novel approach to modelling harmonic tension based on a distributed representation of chords.  The hypothesis is that perceived harmonic tension is influenced by the expectedness of harmonic units (chords) within their local harmonic context.  A word2vec-type neural network is trained to learn a vector space capturing contextual similarity and expectedness, and a quantitative measure of harmonic tension is defined within this space.  The model's veridicality is assessed by comparing its outputs on well-defined chord classes and cadential contexts to results from relevant empirical studies in music psychology.  Statistical analysis reveals a strong correlation between the model's predictions and empirical evidence obtained from human listeners.

title: What happens when software developers are (un)happy
Abstract: The growing literature on affect among software developers primarily focuses on the link between happiness, software quality, and developer productivity.  Understanding happiness and unhappiness in their entirety, encompassing positive and negative emotions and moods, is an important and attractive area of research.  Scholars in industrial and organizational psychology suggest that understanding happiness and unhappiness could lead to cost-effective ways of enhancing working conditions, job performance, and reducing the occurrence of psychological disorders.  However, our comprehension of the consequences of (un)happiness among developers remains limited, primarily expressed in terms of development productivity and software quality.  This paper investigates the impact of happiness and unhappiness during software development.  Qualitative data analysis of responses from 317 questionnaire participants identified 42 consequences of unhappiness and 32 of happiness.  The study found both beneficial and detrimental consequences of happiness and unhappiness for developers' mental well-being, the software development process, and the produced artifacts.  The classification scheme, available as open data, opens new research opportunities on cause-and-effect relationships related to happiness and can serve as a guideline for practitioners to identify detrimental effects of unhappiness and promote happiness in the workplace.

title: An Investigation into Laboucheres Betting System to Improve Odds of Favorable Outcomes to Generate a Positive Externality Empirically
Abstract: The Labouchere gambling system is hypothesized to increase the probability of winning a predetermined profit in 1:1 payout systems like coin flips or roulette.  However, the system also increases the downside monetary risk in case of multiple losses.  The player starts by creating a series of consecutive integers with a sum equal to their desired profit.  Using the system, the player either wins the sum of the initial series or loses all their capital.  This sequence was simulated multiple times to determine the statistical characteristics of returns and losses per betting round.  Simulating millions of Labouchere rounds allowed for analyzing the probable outcomes and mapping the average return on initial capital investment.  The Labouchere system is psychologically appealing due to its consistent linear returns over time, but there is a critical point where available betting capital is exceeded, leading to total loss.  The study found that as the number of bets increases, the outcome of applying the sequence approaches zero.

title: On Dynamical Systems Theory in Quantitative Psychology and Cognition Science: A Fair Discrimination Between Deterministic and Statistical Counterparts Is Required
Abstract: This paper presents a set of observations that meet both deterministic and statistical formal requirements within the framework of dynamical systems theory, with a focus on initial data.  It argues that statistical approaches can be ambiguous, leading to virtual discrepancies in psychological and cognitive data analyses, sometimes referred to as questionable research practices.  The paper emphasizes the need for understanding data origins to determine whether an exponential (Malthus type) or algebraic (Pareto type) statistical distribution should be considered in practical interpretations.  This also relates to the frequency of specific patient behaviors and their significance in determining progression or regression, involving memory effects.  The paper discusses how a sensitively applied hazardous or triggering factor can be beneficial for controlled psychological strategic treatments, including those addressing obsessive/compulsive disorders or self-injurious behaviors.  It highlights the criticality and complexity of these treatments, emphasizing the relationship between therapist and patient.

title: Cognitive Psychology for Deep Neural Networks: A Shape Bias Case Study
Abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved exceptional performance on complex tasks, surpassing our understanding of the nature of their solutions.  This has led to increasing interest in methods for enhancing interpretability in modern neural systems.  This work proposes addressing the interpretability problem in DNNs by drawing upon the rich history of problem descriptions, theories, and experimental methods developed by cognitive psychologists to study the human mind.  To explore the potential value of these tools, the study applies a well-established analysis from developmental psychology that explains how children learn word labels for objects to DNNs.  Using datasets of stimuli inspired by the original cognitive psychology experiments, the study finds that state-of-the-art one-shot learning models trained on ImageNet exhibit a similar bias to that observed in humans: they prefer to categorize objects based on shape rather than color.  The magnitude of this shape bias varies significantly among architecturally identical but differently seeded models, even fluctuating within seeds throughout training despite nearly equivalent classification performance.  These results demonstrate the applicability of cognitive psychology tools for uncovering hidden computational properties of DNNs, while simultaneously providing a computational model for human word learning.

title: A preference elicitation interface for collecting dense recommender datasets with rich user information
Abstract: We introduce a user interface designed to efficiently gather user preferences for visual stimuli, such as photographs, artwork, and screensavers, alongside detailed user information. Our goal is to create dense recommender datasets that complement existing sparse industry-scale datasets. This interface and the collected data aim to bridge the gap between recommender systems research and social and behavioral science. We plan to utilize these datasets to analyze the diversity of human preferences in various visual domains, measure psychological effects like preference consistency and anchoring biases, and facilitate evaluation in counterfactual learning experiments.

title: The Impact of Social Curiosity on Information Spreading on Networks
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel information propagation model that considers the individual curiosity level of each user. Unlike traditional models that assume homogeneous users, our model acknowledges that individuals' curiosity can dynamically influence their information-seeking behavior. We evaluate the model's effectiveness compared to existing models like SIR and IC across various artificial and real-world networks, including Google+, Facebook, and the United States road map. We show that curiosity significantly increases information spreading in all networks, particularly in spatial networks. Our results highlight the importance of accounting for curiosity in information propagation models, as curious individuals are more receptive to new products, concepts, and ideas.

title: Explanation in Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Social Sciences
Abstract: The field of explainable artificial intelligence is rapidly gaining attention as researchers and practitioners seek to make their algorithms more transparent. While much research focuses on explaining decisions to human observers, this paper argues that we can learn from how humans explain to each other. We highlight the rich body of research in philosophy, psychology, and cognitive science on how people define, generate, and evaluate explanations, demonstrating that humans utilize cognitive biases and social expectations in this process. This paper advocates for integrating this existing research into explainable AI, providing a framework for developing more effective and human-centered explanations.

title: Scalable Co-Optimization of Morphology and Control in Embodied Machines
Abstract: Evolutionary processes shape both the physical structure and nervous systems of organisms over time. However, in artificial intelligence and robotics, robot designs are typically created manually, with control policies optimized for the fixed design. This paper addresses the challenge of co-optimizing morphology and control for embodied robots. Building upon the theory of embodied cognition, which posits a close link between body plan and sensorimotor control, we introduce a technique called "morphological innovation protection." This technique temporarily reduces selection pressure on recently morphologically-changed individuals, allowing evolution to adapt to the new morphology. We demonstrate the potential of this method to avoid local optima and achieve similar highly fit morphologies across varying initial conditions. This approach offers a first step towards scalable optimization of embodied machines and provides a platform to investigate the theory of embodied cognition.

title: Personalized advice for enhancing well-being using automated impulse response analysis --- AIRA
Abstract: Personalized mental health care is gaining significant attention. Analyzing individual-specific research data, such as time series sensor data or longitudinal study data, provides valuable insights into participant heterogeneity, leading to more precise and individualized results than group-based methods. However, utilizing this data for self-management and individual well-being improvement remains challenging. This paper introduces Automated Impulse Response Analysis (AIRA), a novel approach that automatically generates personalized advice using time series data from longitudinal studies. AIRA analyzes vector autoregression models of well-being by generating impulse response functions, revealing variables with the most significant influence on well-being. This information can be used to support self-management. We demonstrate AIRA's practical utility by applying it to longitudinal self-reported data on psychological variables. The results, evaluated on two datasets, demonstrate the efficacy and comparability of AIRA to previously published studies. AIRA offers a cost-effective solution for accurate individualized health models with the potential for scalability.

title: A Theoretical Solution of the Mind-Body Problem: An Operationalized Proof that no Purely Physical System Can Exhibit all the Properties of Human Consciousness
Abstract: This article presents a solution to the mind-body problem grounded in rigorous theoretical reasoning. It identifies the operation of self-certainty – the capacity of healthy conscious humans to "know" with certainty that they are conscious – as a necessary property of all healthy human conscious individuals. This operation is demonstrated to be incompatible with any meaningful definition of a physical system. This inconsistency is proven through a "no-go" theorem, applicable to any physical system capable of human logical reasoning, demonstrating that such reasoning cannot be both sound and consistent. The proof is both general and recursive, implying that any physical process subserving this function inevitably leads to another such function. This conclusive resolution of the mind-body problem, at least for one aspect of human consciousness, provides a foundation for future research.

title: Evaluating (and improving) the correspondence between deep neural networks and human representations
Abstract: Decades of research in psychology have been dedicated to understanding how people learn features and categories. Empirical validation of these theories often relies on artificial stimuli with simple representations. The emergence of deep neural networks, achieving human-level accuracy in tasks like object recognition, provides a powerful tool for capturing psychological representations of real-world stimuli. This paper investigates the ability of state-of-the-art object classification networks to predict human similarity judgments for natural images. While these networks achieve surprisingly accurate predictions, they fail to capture certain aspects of human representation. We demonstrate a simple transformation, obtained through convex optimization, that corrects these discrepancies. Using these improved representations, we predict the difficulty of learning novel categories of natural images. Our findings expand the scope of psychological experiments and computational modeling by enabling the use of large natural stimulus sets.

title: Spin and Wind Directions II: A Bell State Quantum Model
Abstract: This two-part article continues the analysis of a cognitive psychology experiment where participants selected pairs of directions representing "Two Different Wind Directions." Part one demonstrated that the data violate the CHSH version of Bell's inequality, exhibiting a similar magnitude to typical Bell-test experiments in physics. This second part presents a symmetrized version of the experiment, still violating the CHSH inequality but now adhering to the marginal law. We provide a full quantum modeling in Hilbert space, utilizing a singlet state and chosen product measurements. We address criticisms regarding the lack of genuine entanglement in such experiments, explaining that these criticisms stem from a restrictive view of entanglement that fails to encompass all possible connections between physical and conceptual entities. We further illustrate the connection between violations of the marginal law and Bell inequalities with different mechanisms using a mechanical model.

title: SocioSense: Robot Navigation Amongst Pedestrians with Social and Psychological Constraints
Abstract: This paper introduces SocioSense, a real-time algorithm for socially-aware navigation of robots in pedestrian environments. By leveraging Bayesian learning and Personality Trait theory, SocioSense computes time-varying pedestrian behaviors and psychological characteristics. These insights enable long-term path prediction and the generation of proximic characteristics for each pedestrian. By combining these psychological constraints with social constraints, SocioSense facilitates human-aware robot navigation in low- to medium-density crowds. The algorithm's ability to estimate time-varying behaviors and pedestrian personalities improves long-term path prediction accuracy by 21% compared to previous interactive path prediction algorithms. Simulations with tens of pedestrians demonstrate the benefits of socially-aware navigation.

title: Using Cognitive Dimensions Questionnaire to Evaluate the Usability of Security APIs
Abstract: Usability issues in security APIs often lead programmers to embed them incorrectly in their applications, introducing security vulnerabilities. This paper investigates the effectiveness of a cognitive dimensions questionnaire-based usability evaluation methodology for identifying usability issues in security APIs. A generic questionnaire based on cognitive dimensions was used to collect feedback from programmers participating in the study. The results revealed significant usability issues in four commonly used security APIs and confirmed the methodology's ability to identify these issues. This research provides valuable insights for improving the usability of security APIs and enhancing application security.

title: Human-Robot Collaboration: From Psychology to Social Robotics
Abstract: Human-robot collaboration (HRC) is rapidly gaining importance with the advancements in robotic technology. For robots to autonomously interact with humans, they need active decision-making capabilities that consider human partners. However, current HRC research often relies on a leader-follower framework, hindering autonomous decision-making. We argue that this limitation stems from the lack of reliable representation of the human and environment. This paper proposes an embodied approach to HRC inspired by psychological studies of human-human interaction (HHI). We review neuroscientific and psychological findings on sensorimotor patterns governing HHI and analyze their implications for robotics. We further examine the robotic community's advancements towards embodied HRC, focusing on mechanisms enabling active, physical collaboration. Finally, we discuss similarities and differences between the two fields of study, identifying future research directions.

title: Quantum probability updating from zero prior (by-passing Cromwell's rule)
Abstract: Cromwell's rule, also known as the zero priors paradox, highlights a constraint in classical probability theory. If a prior probability of 0 or 1 is assigned to a hypothesis, the posterior probability must also be 0 or 1. This rule, which is a direct consequence of Bayes's rule, appears to contradict our intuitive understanding of how humans update probabilities. This paper presents two simple decision-making experiments that seem inconsistent with Cromwell's rule. Quantum probability theory, an alternative framework for probabilistic inference, provides a solution to this inconsistency. Quantum probability theory is not subject to Cromwell's rule and can accommodate changes from zero or small priors to significant posteriors. We propose a quantum theory-based model of decision-making that can explain the observed changes in our experiments.

title: A pedestrian hopping model and traffic light scheduling for pedestrian-vehicle mixed-flow networks
Abstract: This paper presents a pedestrian hopping model and a traffic signal scheduling strategy that consider both pedestrians and vehicles in urban traffic systems. A novel mathematical model with logic constraints describes pedestrian flow in the urban traffic network, with dynamics captured by the hopping rule, which represents the changing capacity between waiting zones. Based on this model, pedestrian traffic light scheduling problems are formulated using two performance standards: pedestrian delay and pedestrian unhappiness. The scheduling problem is solved using mixed integer linear programming (MILP) for the pedestrian delay model and discrete harmony search algorithm (DHS) for both models. Additionally, a mathematical model for the vehicle traffic network is introduced, accounting for drivers' psychological responses to traffic light signals. A traffic light scheduling strategy that minimizes the trade-off between pedestrian and vehicle delays is proposed. This strategy is formulated as a MILP problem that can be solved using existing tools like GUROBI. Numerical simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of the real-time traffic light scheduling for pedestrian movement and its impact on vehicle traffic flows.

title: Modeling observers as physical systems representing the world from within: Quantum theory as a physical and self-referential theory of inference
Abstract: Szilard, in 1929, recognized the role of the observer in analyzing experiments. The same year, Bohr highlighted the concept of complementarity in psychology, where both the objects of perception and the perceiving subject are part of our mental content. This paper argues that the formalism of quantum theory can be derived from two intuitive principles: (i) inference is a physical process performed by physical systems (observers), which are part of the experimental setup, implying non-commutativity and imaginary-time quantum mechanics; (ii) experiments must be described from a first-person perspective, leading to self-reference, complementarity, and real-time quantum dynamics. This approach sheds light on the foundations of quantum theory and suggests that fundamental equations in physics are typically second-order due to the physical nature of the observer. It also offers experimental conjectures: (i) the quantum of action may be related to the energy required for consciousness; (ii) humans can observe a single photon of visible light; (iii) self-aware systems may have a double-hemisphere architecture like the brain. This approach may bridge the gap between science and human experience, with potential implications for consciousness and contemplative science research. It also shows that message-passing algorithms and stochastic processes can be written in a quantum-like manner and provides evidence for the connection between non-stoquasticity and non-equilibrium phenomena.

title: Predicting Rising Follower Counts on Twitter Using Profile Information
Abstract: When evaluating the cause of popularity on Twitter, the number of tweets is often considered the primary driver. While there is debate about the type of tweets to publish, the information provided in user profiles is often overlooked. This paper investigates the influence of profile information, specifically given names, on follower count. Studies in psychology and economics have established correlations between first names and factors like school marks and job interview chances. We analyzed profiles of 6 million Twitter users, grouping them based on their name field (first name, English word, or neither). Assuming that names and words impact discoverability and subsequently follower count, we developed a classifier to predict users who will increase their follower count within a month using different models based on user group. The classifiers, evaluated using the area under the receiver operator curve score, achieved a score above 0.800.

title: Manifold Relevance Determination: Learning the Latent Space of Robotics
Abstract: This paper presents the basics of manifold relevance determination (MRD) and explores its potential applications. Section 1 serves as a tutorial on the ideas developed in previous work, while Section 2 discusses possible applications in sensor fusion, multi-agent SLAM, and "human-appropriate" robot movement (e.g., legibility and predictability). We demonstrate how MRD can be used to construct underlying models in a data-driven manner, rather than relying solely on first-principles theories. This approach offers an alternative to traditional methods in fields like sensor fusion, SLAM, and human-robot interaction. Notably, MRD has been leveraged for correcting unstable robot grasps to stable grasps.

title: Metacognitive Learning Approach for Online Tool Condition Monitoring
Abstract: As manufacturing processes become increasingly automated, the need for intelligent tool condition monitoring (TCM) becomes critical. Worn tools affect product quality, leading to higher rejection rates. While various TCM approaches have been proposed, most suffer from the limitations of traditional machine learning algorithms. They focus on the "how" of learning without addressing the crucial aspects of "what" to learn and "when" to learn. These aspects are essential for self-regulation, enabling the selection of training samples and determining the optimal time instants for model training. This paper introduces a novel TCM approach based on the metacognitive scaffolding theory, utilizing a recently published algorithm called recurrent classifier (rClass). The learning process encompasses three phases: what to learn, how to learn, and when to learn, utilizing a generalized recurrent network structure as a cognitive component. Experimental studies with real-world manufacturing data streams demonstrate rClass's superior accuracy and low complexity compared to its counterparts.

title: Interface and Data Biopolitics in the Age of Hyperconnectivity
Abstract: This article explores the biopolitical implications of Hyperconnectivity – the shift towards networked and digital communication – for design. Interfaces, algorithms, artificial intelligences, quantified self practices, and information bubbles are examined in terms of interface and data biopolitics, highlighting their implications for freedom, transparency, justice, and accessibility to human rights. The article presents a working hypothesis for technologically relevant design practices and educational processes to confront these issues critically, ethically, and inclusively.

title: A Deep Learning Perspective on the Origin of Facial Expressions
Abstract: Facial expressions play a crucial role in human communication and behavior. Psychologists have extensively studied the relationship between facial expressions and emotions, leading to the development of the Facial Action Coding System (FACS) to classify and model facial expressions. Automatic facial expression recognition opens up new possibilities in fields like human-computer interaction, social gaming, and psychological research. This paper investigates the relationship between the features extracted by convolutional neural networks (CNN) and the FACS and Action Units (AU). Using CNN understanding methods, we verify our findings on the CK+, NovaEmotions, and FER2013 datasets. We apply these models to various tasks and tests using transfer learning, including cross-dataset validation and cross-task performance. Finally, we leverage the nature of FER-based CNN models for the detection of micro-expressions, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy using a simple long-short-term-memory (LSTM) recurrent neural network (RNN).

title: Robust Inference under the Beta Regression Model with Application to Health Care Studies
Abstract: Data on rates, percentages, or proportions are common in various applied disciplines like medical biology, health care, and psychology. This paper develops a robust inference procedure for the beta regression model, used to describe such response variables taking values between 0 and 1. While the existing maximum likelihood-based inference suffers from a lack of robustness against outliers, generating erroneous results in the presence of data contamination, this paper proposes the robust minimum density power divergence estimator and a class of robust Wald-type tests for the beta regression model. We derive their asymptotic properties and theoretically demonstrate their robustness through influence function analyses. Simulation studies and real data applications in health care and psychology validate the proposed estimators and tests' finite sample performance. Although the focus is on beta regression models with a fixed dispersion parameter, indications for extension to variable dispersion beta regression models are also provided.

title: Teaching computer code at school
Abstract: The educational landscape is witnessing a renewed focus on teaching coding and computer programming in schools. Educators are discussing not only the feasibility of coding instruction, but also its potential intellectual and cognitive benefits for students. This debate involves multifaceted considerations, drawing upon arguments and interpretations from various domains, including technology, education, culture, cognition, and psychology. Ultimately, this phenomenon hints at a profound transformation in the future of learning and teaching, paving the way for a new digital humanism.

title: A Rule-Based Computational Model of Cognitive Arithmetic
Abstract: Cognitive arithmetic delves into the mental processes involved in solving mathematical problems. This research area explores the retrieval mechanisms and strategies employed by individuals during a common cognitive task. Past research has established a correlation between human performance in arithmetic operations and the numerical size of the problem. This study examines this trend in the context of retrieval strength, error checking, and strategy-based approaches. The paper introduces a rule-based computational model capable of performing the four basic arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division) on two operands. The model's validity is assessed by comparing its performance to observed psychological experiments. These experiments focus on the problem size effect, an activation-based model for fact retrieval, backup strategies for retrieval failures, and optimization strategies for large operands. The model's response times were found to be comparable to those observed in human participants during similar tasks. The paper discusses the model's ability to replicate these results and incorporate accuracy into its framework.

title: A Network Perspective on Attitude Strength: Testing the Connectivity Hypothesis
Abstract: Attitude strength, a key characteristic of attitudes, differentiates between strong attitudes, which are enduring and impactful, and weak attitudes, which fluctuate and have minimal influence. The Causal Attitude Network (CAN) model, a comprehensive measurement model of attitudes, conceptualizes attitudes as networks of causally connected evaluative reactions (beliefs, feelings, and behavior towards an attitude object). This study investigates the central postulate of the CAN model: highly connected attitude networks correspond to strong attitudes. Using data from the American National Election Studies (1980-2012) on attitudes towards presidential candidates (n = 18,795), the study demonstrates that political interest predicts connectivity of attitude networks. It further reveals that connectivity is strongly associated with two defining features of strong attitudes: stability and impact on behavior. These findings suggest that network theory offers a promising framework for deepening our understanding of attitude strength.

title: The Social Benefits of Balancing Creativity and Imitation: Evidence from an Agent-based Model
Abstract: While creativity is often celebrated in the abstract, it is frequently discouraged in educational and workplace settings. This study explores the idea that tempering the novelty-generating effects of creativity with the novelty-preserving effects of imitation is beneficial for society. Using an agent-based model of cultural evolution, the study investigates the relationship between the ratio of creators to imitators and the level of creativity exhibited by creators. The results reveal a trade-off between the two, highlighting that excessive creativity can be detrimental as creators invest in unproven ideas at the expense of propagating established ones. The study then examines whether society benefits when individuals adjust their creativity levels based on their creative success. The findings show that social regulation, where effective creators create more and ineffective creators create less, leads to a temporary increase in output fitness. However, this effect is limited by a ceiling on output fitness. By allowing for the chaining of simple outputs into arbitrarily complex ones, the study demonstrates that the benefits of social regulation can be sustained indefinitely. These findings offer insights into the optimal balance between creativity and imitation in cultural evolution.

title: Deep Cross-Modal Audio-Visual Generation
Abstract: Cross-modal audio-visual perception, a longstanding area of study in psychology and neurology, has revealed strong correlations between human perception of auditory and visual stimuli. This paper presents a novel approach to solving this problem by leveraging the power of deep generative adversarial training. Specifically, conditional generative adversarial networks are employed to achieve cross-modal audio-visual generation of musical performances. The study explores different encoding methods for audio and visual signals, investigating two scenarios: instrument-oriented generation and pose-oriented generation. The paper introduces two new datasets comprising pairs of images and sounds of musical performances by various instruments. Experiments involving classification and human evaluations demonstrate the model's ability to generate one modality (audio or visual) from the other. title: Smoothness-constrained model for nonparametric item response theory
Abstract: This paper focuses on the nonparametric item response theory (NIRT) for estimating item characteristic curves (ICCs) and latent abilities of examinees on educational and psychological tests. Unlike parametric models, NIRT models can estimate various forms of ICCs under mild shape restrictions, such as monotone homogeneity and double monotonicity. However, NIRT models often suffer from estimation instability due to the flexibility of nonparametric ICCs, particularly with limited item-response data. To address this, the paper proposes a novel NIRT model incorporating constraints based on monotone homogeneity and smoothness, using ordered latent classes. These smoothness constraints prevent overfitting of nonparametric ICCs by ensuring they remain close to logistic curves. The paper also introduces a tailored expectation-maximization algorithm for efficient calibration of the smoothness-constrained NIRT model. Computational experiments comparing the model to the common two-parameter logistic model and the monotone-homogeneity model demonstrate its superior performance in terms of estimation accuracy, particularly when examinee abilities follow bimodal distributions.

title: A New Theoretical Framework for Curiosity for Learning in Social Contexts
Abstract: Curiosity, a vital metacognitive skill in educational contexts, is often evoked through individual activities but its interplay with social factors in group work remains underexplored. The framework distinguishes between individual and interpersonal functions contributing to curiosity, and identifies multimodal behaviors that fulfill these functions. Validation through a longitudinal latent variable modeling approach confirms the positive predictive relationship between individual and interpersonal functions on curiosity, with interpersonal functions exerting a stronger influence. The framework serves as a stepping stone towards designing learning technologies that can recognize and evoke curiosity during social learning.

title: A Domain Based Approach to Social Relation Recognition
Abstract: Social relations are fundamental to human daily life. Developing techniques to analyze these relations from visual data holds significant potential for building machines that better understand and interact with humans at a social level. This paper advocates for the domain-based theory from social psychology as a systematic approach to this problem. The theory provides a comprehensive framework encompassing all aspects of social relations, offering concrete and predictive insights into the visual attributes and behaviors defining relations within each domain. The paper introduces the first dataset based on this holistic conceptualization of social life, comprising a hierarchical label space of social domains and relations. It also presents the first models for recognizing these domains and relations, demonstrating superior performance for attribute-based features. The study identifies interpretable features aligning with predictions from social psychology literature. These contributions bridge visual recognition and social psychology theory, offering data-driven models of social life.

title: Introduction: Toward an interdisciplinary science of spontaneous thought
Abstract: The nascent field of spontaneous thought faces numerous questions: what constitutes spontaneous thought, why does our brain engage in such thinking, and under what conditions is it most likely to occur? This volume seeks to synthesize perspectives from neuroscience, psychology, philosophy, phenomenology, history, education, contemplative traditions, and clinical practice to address the ubiquitous yet poorly understood phenomenon of spontaneous thought. Despite its familiarity in daily life, spontaneous thought remains a complex and challenging subject to understand and explain scientifically. This volume represents the first attempt to integrate diverse perspectives in order to address the what, when, why, and how of spontaneous thought.

title: The case of 'Less is more': Modelling risk-preference with Expected Downside Risk
Abstract: This paper challenges the commonly held view of a positive relationship between risk (variance) and reward (expected return). The study argues that contradicting empirical findings might stem from an inaccurate definition of risk perception, which is corrected by introducing the concept of Expected Downside Risk (EDR). EDR, similar to Expected Shortfall or Conditional Value-at-Risk, measures tail risk and provides a more accurate representation of investors' utility perception. The paper demonstrates that when using EDR as a risk measure, both positive and negative relationships between expected return and risk can be derived under standard conditions (expected utility theory and positive risk aversion). title: A Layperson Introduction to the Quantum Approach to Humor
Abstract: Despite our familiarity and appreciation for humor, the underlying psychology of this complex and nuanced phenomenon has been poorly understood until recently. Cognitive psychologists have begun to investigate how people understand humor and why certain things are funny. This chapter introduces a new cognitive approach to modeling humor, referred to as the "quantum approach," which will be explained in intuitive, non-mathematical terms. The quantum approach is particularly promising because it can represent states of ambiguity and define states and variables within a specific context. Contextuality and ambiguity play crucial roles in humor, often hinging on ambiguous words, phrases, or situations that may be nonsensical or socially unacceptable outside the specific context of the joke. While not attempting to explain all aspects of humor, the quantum approach aims to mathematically model the underlying cognitive process of "getting" a joke. The chapter provides a brief overview of relevant historical antecedents and related approaches in cognitive psychology, presents the theoretical basis of the quantum approach, and outlines a recent study providing empirical support for it.

title: Abnormal Working Hours: Effect of Rapid Releases and Implications to Work Content

The study examines the working patterns of developers within the Mozilla Firefox project, a large and long-lived open-source project. Specifically, it investigates the impact of transitioning from a traditional to a rapid release cycle on work patterns. The study also compares the work patterns of Mozilla Firefox with another Mozilla product, Firefox OS, which has a different release cycle. The findings suggest that both projects exhibit healthy working patterns, with lower activity during weekends and outside of office hours. Firefox experiences proportionally more weekend activity than Firefox OS. The study also reveals that switching to rapid releases has reduced weekend work and working during the night. This result holds even when considering only hired resources, although the effect sizes are smaller for weekends and nights. Additionally, dissimilarity word clouds indicate that weekend work is more technical, while weekday work expresses more positive sentiment. The findings suggest that transitioning to rapid releases has a positive impact on work health and work-life balance for software engineers. However, further research is needed due to the limited dataset and focus on a single organization.

title: What we really want to find by Sentiment Analysis: The Relationship between Computational Models and Psychological State

While CNN performed best among other deep neural network algorithms (LSTM, GRU), its results were unrelated to psychological state. GRU, however, demonstrated more explainable results based on the psychological state. title: Multiscale Bayesian State Space Model for Granger Causality Analysis of Brain Signal
Abstract: Modelling time-varying and frequency-specific relationships between two brain signals is becoming an essential methodological tool in experimental neuroscience for answering theoretical questions. This article proposes a frequency Granger causality statistic that varies in time to evaluate functional connections between two brain regions during a task. The study utilizes an adaptive Kalman filter-type estimator for a linear Gaussian vector autoregressive model with time-evolving coefficients. Estimation is achieved through variational Bayesian approximation and is extended to multiple trials. This Bayesian State Space (BSS) model provides a natural dynamic Granger-causality statistic. The paper proposes extending the BSS model to include the à trous Haar decomposition, a wavelet-based forecasting method that allows for capturing short- and long-range dependencies between signals at multiple scales. This approach enables the derivation of the desired dynamic and frequency-specific Granger-causality statistic. Application of these models to intracranial local field potential data recorded during a psychological experimental task reveals complex frequency-based cross-talk between the amygdala and medial orbito-frontal cortex.

title: The Neuroscience of Spontaneous Thought: An Evolving, Interdisciplinary Field

title: Need for a Soft Dimension

Dealing with human errors is more complex and frequently overlooked during evaluation, as developers prioritize issues that are more familiar and comfortable to solve. title: Psychological and Personality Profiles of Political Extremists
Abstract: The global recruitment of individuals into radical Islamic movements has reignited interest in the appeal of political extremism. The debate centers on whether this appeal is a rational response to material conditions or an expression of psychological and personality disorders associated with aggressive behavior, intolerance, conspiratorial thinking, and paranoia.
