title: Object categorization in finer levels requires higher spatial frequencies, and therefore takes longer
Abstract: The human visual system is characterized by a hierarchical sequence of modules that contribute to visual perception at different levels of abstraction: superordinate, basic, and subordinate levels. A key question is to identify the "entry" level at which visual representation commences in the process of object recognition. Traditionally, the basic level was believed to have an advantage over the other two levels, a claim that has recently been challenged. This study employed a series of psychophysics experiments using a rapid presentation paradigm, as well as two computational models with bandpass filtered images, to investigate the processing order of categorization levels. The experiments manipulated the spatial frequency bands of the input image to determine the type of visual information required for categorizing objects at each level. The results from both psychophysics experiments and computational models consistently indicate that different spatial frequency information has distinct effects on object categorization at each level. The absence of high-frequency information negatively impacted subordinate and basic level categorization but not superordinate level categorization. This suggests that low-frequency information is sufficient for superordinate level categorization but not for basic and subordinate levels, which require high-frequency information. The processing of high-frequency information takes longer, resulting in longer reaction times. To mitigate ceiling effects, the study evaluated the robustness of the results by adding varying levels of noise to the input images and repeating the experiments. While categorization accuracy decreased and reaction times increased significantly, the trends remained consistent. This confirms that the findings are not a result of ceiling effects.

title: How brains are built: Principles of computational neuroscience
Abstract: Nobel laureate Richard Feynman famously stated, "If I cannot build it, I do not understand it." Applying this metric, our understanding of physics is relatively robust, our grasp of chemistry is less complete, and our understanding of biology is quite limited. True understanding of a phenomenon involves specifying its entire sequence of events, causes, and effects in such detail that it becomes possible to fully simulate it, preserving all its internal mechanisms. Achieving this level of understanding is rare and is comparable to constructing a comprehensive design for a machine that could serve as a substitute for the thing being studied. Understanding a phenomenon sufficiently to fully simulate it signifies computational understanding. "Computation" does not refer to computers per se, but rather to the underlying principles and methods that make them work. As Turing Award recipient Edsger Dijkstra stated, computational science "is no more about computers than astronomy is about telescopes." It is the study of the hidden rules governing complex phenomena across diverse domains, from physics to psychology. Computational neuroscience, therefore, aims to understand the brain well enough to simulate its functions, achieving the twin goals of science and engineering: comprehending the intricate workings of our brains and constructing simulacra of them. Just as simple robots today substitute for human physical abilities in factories and hospitals, brain engineering will create stand-ins for our mental abilities, potentially even enabling us to repair our brains when they malfunction.

title: Inverse Risk-Sensitive Reinforcement Learning

title: Is This a Joke? Detecting Humor in Spanish Tweets

title: Cheetah Experimental Platform Web 1.0: Cleaning Pupillary Data

title: Gestalt Principles re-investigated within Heisenberg uncertainty relation

title: Interactive Natural Language Acquisition in a Multi-modal Recurrent Neural Architecture

The model utilizes a continuous-time recurrent neural network with varying leakage characteristics, operating on multiple timescales for each modality and associating higher-level nodes from all modalities into cell assemblies. title: Learning to Partition using Score Based Compatibilities
Abstract: This research investigates the problem of learning to partition users into groups, where the goal is to optimize groupings by learning user compatibilities. Four natural objectives are defined, optimizing for average and worst-case compatibilities, and new algorithms are proposed for adaptive learning of optimal groupings. In the absence of structure on compatibilities, the group formation objectives are shown to be NP-hard to solve, leading to either approximation guarantees or inapproximability results. The introduction of an elegant structure, known as intrinsic scores, makes many of these problems polynomial time solvable. The optimal groupings under this structure are explicitly characterized, revealing their relationship to homophilous and heterophilous partitions, concepts well-established in the psychology literature. For one of the four objectives, NP-hardness is demonstrated even under the score structure, and a 1/2 approximation algorithm is provided, improving upon the lack of constant approximation guarantees previously available. Finally, an online, low-sample complexity PAC algorithm is proposed for learning the optimal partition under the score structure. The algorithm's efficacy is demonstrated on synthetic and real-world datasets.

title: \$1 Today or \$2 Tomorrow? The Answer is in Your Facebook Likes
Abstract: Delay discounting, a concept used in economics and psychology, describes individuals' choices between immediate smaller rewards and delayed larger rewards. Individuals with a higher delay discounting rate (DDR) tend to prioritize immediate gratification, while those with a lower discounting rate prefer delayed but larger rewards. The ability to delay gratification plays a crucial role in decision-making, with a lower discounting rate often predicting better social, academic, and health outcomes. Conversely, a higher discounting rate is associated with problematic behaviors such as alcohol/drug abuse, gambling, and credit card debt. Research on understanding and moderating delay discounting holds the potential for significant societal benefits.

title: Gestalt Phenomenon in Music? A Neurocognitive Physics Study with EEG

This research analyzes the effects of various frequency bands of music on human brain rhythms using EEG data from five participants. Four popular Rabindrasangeet clips were subjected to wavelet transformation to extract five resonant frequency bands. These bands were presented to the subjects as auditory stimuli, and EEG signals were recorded simultaneously at 19 brain locations. Noise-cleaned EEG signals were processed using Multifractal Detrended Fluctuation Analysis (MFDFA) in the alpha, theta, and gamma frequency ranges. The resulting complexity values (multifractal spectral width) in these EEG rhythms were analyzed in relation to the different frequency bands of music. The study identified frequency-specific arousal-based responses in different brain lobes and specific EEG bands corresponding to musical stimuli. These findings hold significant implications for cognitive music therapy.

title: Measuring Cognitive Conflict in Virtual Reality with Feedback-Related Negativity
Abstract: As virtual reality (VR) gains mainstream adoption, designers are exploring novel interaction techniques to enhance user experience. To address this, an EEG-based experiment framework is proposed for evaluating interaction techniques in VR by measuring intentionally elicited cognitive conflict. This framework analyzes the feedback-related negativity (FRN) and other quantitative measures to assess the effects of variables of interest. The framework is applied to the fundamental task of 3D object selection using direct 3D input (tracked hands in VR). Cognitive conflict is elicited by manipulating the selection radius of the target object. The initial behavioral experiment validates the framework, aligning with findings of conflict-induced behavior adjustments reported in classical psychology experiments. A subsequent EEG-based experiment examines the effect of virtual hand appearance, revealing a correlation between FRN amplitude and the realism of virtual hands, consistent with the Uncanny Valley theory.

title: On the Unhappiness of Software Developers
Abstract: The "happy-productive worker" thesis suggests that happy workers are more productive. However, the literature suggests that mitigating unhappiness could be a cost-effective way to foster happiness and productivity among workers. Psychological disorders like job burnout and anxiety could also be reduced by limiting negative experiences for software developers. Nonetheless, a baseline assessment of happiness and unhappiness, along with insights into developer experiences, are lacking. This paper investigates unhappiness among software developers, examining (1) the population distribution of happiness and unhappiness, and (2) the causes of unhappiness during software development. A large-scale quantitative and qualitative survey was conducted, incorporating a psychometrically validated instrument for measuring happiness and unhappiness, with 2220 developers, yielding 1318 complete responses. Results indicate that software developers are a slightly happy population, but the need to minimize unhappiness remains. The study identified 219 factors contributing to unhappiness during software development. These results, available as open data, can serve as guidelines for managers and developers to foster workplace happiness. The authors recommend considering happiness in future studies of both human and technical aspects of software engineering.

title: On Quitting: Performance and Practice in Online Game Play
Abstract: This study examines the relationship between performance and practice by analyzing the activity of numerous players in a casual online game. Significant heterogeneity is observed in player performance improvement, measured by score. To address this, players are grouped into similar skill levels, and each player's activity is segmented into sessions (sequences of game rounds without extended breaks). After data disaggregation, a positive correlation between performance and practice is observed across all skill levels. Notably, players are more likely to end their session after a substantial performance improvement, leading to a peak score in their final game of a session. Success is strongly associated with a lower quitting rate when scores drop, and only weakly correlated with skill, aligning with psychological findings about the importance of persistence and "grit." Successful players demonstrate resilience in their practice despite experiencing lower scores. Finally, an epsilon-machine, a type of hidden Markov model, is trained to identify a plausible mechanism of game play that can predict player performance and quitting behavior. This research suggests the possibility of real-time assessment and behavior prediction for optimizing human performance.

title: Reviewing Literature on Time Pressure in Software Engineering and Related Professions - Computer Assisted Interdisciplinary Literature Review

title: Counterfactuals, indicative conditionals, and negation under uncertainty: Are there cross-cultural differences?

In a 2x2 between-participants design, 63 Japanese university students were divided into four groups, crossing indicative conditionals and counterfactuals, with random task order presentation. The data show strong agreement between the responses of Easterners and Westerners. The modal responses provide substantial support for the hypothesis that conditional probability is the best predictor for both counterfactuals and indicative conditionals. The overwhelming majority of responses are probabilistically coherent, supporting the psychological plausibility of coherence-based probability logic as a framework for psychological reasoning research.

Interestingly, a minority of participants disregarded some relevant imprecision in the premises when inferring lower or upper probability bounds on the target conditional/counterfactual ("halfway responses"). The results are discussed within the framework of coherence-based probability logic and the emerging paradigm of psychology of reasoning.

title: Modeling the Ellsberg Paradox by Argument Strength
Abstract: This paper presents a formal measure of argument strength that combines the ideas that conclusions of strong arguments are (i) highly probable and (ii) their uncertainty is relatively precise. An experiment (N = 60) further supports the psychological plausibility of this approach. The data show that the proposed measure predicts human inferences in the original Ellsberg task and in corresponding argument strength tasks. title: Sustained sensorimotor control as intermittent decisions about prediction errors: Computational framework and application to ground vehicle steering
Abstract: This paper proposes a conceptual and computational framework for modeling human sensorimotor control, exemplified by the task of steering a car. The framework emphasizes control intermittency and expands upon existing models by suggesting that the nervous system implements intermittent control using a combination of (1) motor primitives, (2) prediction of sensory outcomes of motor actions, and (3) evidence accumulation of prediction errors. It demonstrates that approximate but useful sensory predictions in the intermittent control context can be constructed without detailed forward models, as a superposition of simple prediction primitives, resembling neurobiologically observed corollary discharges. This mathematical framework allows for straightforward extension of intermittent behavior from existing one-dimensional continuous models in the linear control and ecological psychology traditions. Empirical observations from a driving simulator provide support for some framework assumptions: human steering control in routine lane-keeping and demanding near-limit tasks is better described as a sequence of discrete stepwise steering adjustments rather than continuous control. Moreover, the amplitudes of individual steering adjustments are well predicted by a compound visual cue signaling steering error, further enhanced by adjusting for predictions of how the cue is affected by previous control. Finally, evidence accumulation explains observed covariability between inter-adjustment durations and adjustment amplitudes, seemingly outperforming the threshold mechanisms typically assumed in existing models of intermittent control.

title: Black Holes and Vacuum Cleaners: Using Metaphor, Relevance, and Inquiry in Labels for Space Images

title: Opinion dynamics model based on cognitive biases

title: Collective phenomena in crowds - where pedestrian dynamics need social psychology

title: Empathy in One-Shot Prisoner Dilemma

title: How Much Does Users' Psychology Matter in Engineering Mean-Field-Type Games

title: Modeling Social Organizations as Communication Networks

title: Powerful statistical inference for nested data using sufficient summary statistics

title: An Operational Semantics for the Cognitive Architecture ACT-R and its Translation to Constraint Handling Rules

A focusing effect is observed in the region towards the critical endpoints related to the strange quark phase transitions. Environmental fluctuations can significantly influence or even destroy universality properties.  This research explores the effects of compressible velocity fluctuations, representing a random environment, on the directed bond percolation process.  Using field-theoretic models and renormalization group methods, eleven universality classes are identified, with four being stable in the infrared limit and therefore macroscopically accessible.  In contrast to models without velocity fluctuations, a regime with relevant short-range noise is identified as a potential candidate for a realistic three-dimensional case.  Critical exponents of the directed percolation process are calculated, depending on the dimensionality of space and the structure of the turbulent flow.  In the limit of a purely transversal velocity field random force, the critical exponents align with the incompressible results obtained by previous researchers.  The study reveals intriguing non-universal behavior arising from the combined effects of compressibility and advection.

The findings have important implications for researchers studying influence and language, and for community analysts seeking to understand entity-level influence dynamics.

title: Water and the interior structure of terrestrial planets and icy bodies

Additionally, water content may contribute to increased oxygen fugacity, influencing the concentration of siderophile elements within the silicate reservoirs of Solar System objects. Finally, water content significantly influences the differentiation rate of icy moons, controlling their internal evolution and altering processes within their deep interiors.

title: Influence of galactic arm scale dynamics on the molecular composition of the cold and dense ISM I. Observed abundance gradients in dense clouds
Abstract: This study investigates the impact of large-scale dynamics on the molecular composition of the dense interstellar medium during the transition from diffuse to dense clouds.  We simulated the formation of dense clouds (on sub-parsec scales) by incorporating the dynamics of the interstellar medium at galactic scales. We utilized results from smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) simulations, extracting physical parameters as inputs for our comprehensive gas-grain chemical model. These simulations follow the evolution of interstellar matter for approximately 50 Myr.  The warm, low-density interstellar medium gas flows into spiral arms, where orbit crowding leads to shock formation and the creation of dense clouds, temporarily held together by external pressure. Our results demonstrate that the molecular composition of the modeled dense clouds exhibits a high dispersion in computed abundances, even for similar local physical properties, depending on the individual SPH particle's physical history. Carbon chains are particularly affected, with these variations directly linked to differences in (1) the electronic fraction, (2) the C/O ratio, and (3) local physical conditions.  We propose that variations in the dynamical evolution of the gas forming dense clouds could account for the observed molecular diversity both between and within these clouds.  This study highlights the crucial role of past physical conditions in shaping the chemical composition of the dense interstellar medium.

title: Grover search under localized dephasing
Abstract: Decoherence in quantum searches, particularly Grover's search, has been extensively studied, revealing a rapid loss of the quadratic speedup over classical methods when searching for a target (marked) element within a set of size N.  Previous research has predominantly focused on global noise models. This paper investigates Grover's search under the influence of localized partially dephasing noise with a rate of p. Our analysis reveals that when the size k of the affected subspace is significantly smaller than N (kp << √N) and the target is unaffected by the noise, the quadratic speedup is retained. However, once these conditions are not met, the quadratic speedup is lost. Specifically, if the target is affected by the noise, the noise rate needs to scale as 1/√N to maintain the speedup. We also observe an intermediate region where, if k ~ N^μ and the target is unaffected, the speedup appears to follow N^μ, which for μ > 0.5 is worse than the quantum case but better than the classical case. We contextualize these results for quantum searches in relation to quantum walks and searches on graphs.

title: On Profiles of Boson Stars with Self-Interactions
Abstract: Under the influence of gravity, light scalar fields can form bound compact objects called boson stars.  This study employs the technique of matching asymptotic expansions to obtain the profile for boson stars where the constituent particles exhibit self-interactions.  We derive parametric representations of these profiles as a function of self-interactions, including cases with very strong interactions.  Our methods are shown to agree with solutions obtained through purely numerical methods.  We observe significant distortions compared to the noninteracting case, highlighting the impact of self-interactions on boson star profiles.

title: Pr$_2$Ir$_2$O$_7$: when Luttinger semimetal meets Melko-Hertog-Gingras spin ice state
Abstract: We investigate the interplay between local moments and itinerant electrons in the context of pyrochlore iridates, focusing on the topological band structure and its engineering possibilities.  In the metallic iridate Pr$_2$Ir$_2$O$_7$, the Ir 5d conduction electrons interact with the Pr 4f local moments via the f-d exchange. While the Ir electrons form a Luttinger semimetal, the Pr moments can be tuned into an ordered spin ice with a finite ordering wavevector, known as the "Melko-Hertog-Gingras" state, by varying Ir and O contents.  We highlight that the ordered spin ice of the Pr local moments generates an internal magnetic field that reconstructs the band structure of the Luttinger semimetal.  Besides the widespread existence of Weyl nodes, we predict that the magnetic translation of the "Melko-Hertog-Gingras" state for the Pr moments protects the Dirac band touching at specific time reversal invariant momenta for the Ir conduction electrons.  We propose using magnetic fields to control the Pr magnetic structure, indirectly influencing the topological and other properties of the Ir electrons. This prediction can be directly tested in ordered Pr$_2$Ir$_2$O$_7$ samples.  Our work is expected to stimulate further investigation of the band structure, magneto-transport, and other properties of Pr$_2$Ir$_2$O$_7$.

title: Global research collaboration: Networks and partners in South East Asia

The paper also highlights the role of co-authoring collaborations in knowledge production within the leading specializations of the ASEAN6. title: Online human aggregation under pressure moves beyond preferential attachment
Abstract: Online human activity often involves clandestine or illicit behavior, leading to individuals operating under the threat of exposure or capture. This research investigates the evolutionary dynamics of pro-ISIS online communities, analyzing the growth of 95 such communities on a global social media platform. Contrary to conventional preferential attachment models, the study finds that these communities' evolution is best described by a new model called the active attraction (AA) model. The AA model incorporates locality and group heterogeneity, factors crucial for online behavior under pressure, which are absent in traditional models. By capturing both group-specific and macroscopic observations across all size ranges, the AA model highlights the significant role of heterogeneity and locality in the dynamics of online extremist support. The study derives approximate expressions for group size distributions in two simple systems involving group joining, leaving, and account banning, demonstrating how these processes influence group size distribution. This research offers valuable insights into understanding a wide range of online human activities characterized by clandestine or illicit behavior.

title: Control energy scaling in temporal networks
Abstract: Controlling a network involves manipulating a large number of nodes with a limited number of external inputs, facilitated by paths that propagate the influence of controlled driver nodes. While temporal networks offer control advantages over static counterparts due to the frequent availability of such paths, the underlying reasons remain unclear. This study investigates the scaling behavior of a key control cost – control energy – in temporal networks. It reveals that the energy cost is determined solely by the spectral properties of an "effective" Gramian matrix, similar to static networks. Surprisingly, this scaling is primarily influenced by the first and last network snapshots, regardless of the number of intervening snapshots, initial and final states, or the number of driver nodes. These findings uncover the fundamental principles governing the energy savings of temporal networks compared to their static counterparts.

title: Magnetic and universal magnetocaloric behavior of rare-earth substituted DyFe0.5Cr0.5O3
Abstract: This study investigates the magnetic and magnetocaloric behavior of a mixed metal oxide DyFe0.5Cr0.5O3 after partial substitution of the Dy-site by rare-earths (Gd, Er, and La). Structural analysis reveals minimal influence of rare-earth substitution on the crystal structure. Magnetic and heat capacity measurements indicate that the magnetic transition around 121 K remains unaffected by rare-earth substitution, while the lower magnetic transition temperature is suppressed or enhanced by magnetic or non-magnetic substitution respectively. Arrott plots confirm the second-order nature of the magnetic transition in all compounds. Compared to DyFe0.5Cr0.5O3, magnetic rare-earth substitution increases the magnetic entropy change and relative cooling power, whereas non-magnetic substitution decreases these values. Magnetic entropy change follows a power law dependence on magnetic field, and the exponent 'n' indicates ferromagnetic correlations within an antiferromagnetic state. A phenomenological universal master curve is constructed for all compounds by normalizing the entropy change with a rescaled temperature, further confirming the second-order nature of the magnetic phase transition in these mixed metal oxides.

title: seasonal influence on age-structured invasive species with yearly generation
Abstract: This study investigates the influence of seasonal successions on the propagation dynamics of an age-structured invasive species. The model assumes offspring reproduction in spring and maturation in fall within the same year, represented by a reaction-diffusion system with yearly periodic time delay and spatially nonlocal response. Using recently developed dynamical system theories, the invasion speed c* is determined, coinciding with the minimal speed of time periodic traveling waves. Analysis of c* suggests that time delay decreases the speed, and its periodicity may further reduce it. The optimal time to slow down the invasion is during the season without juveniles, and the speed increases to infinity with the square root of the diffusion rate.

title: Thermonuclear X-ray bursts
Abstract: Type-I X-ray bursts originate from unstable thermonuclear burning of accreted fuel on neutron star surfaces. This chapter reviews the fundamental physics of these burning processes, summarizing recent observational, numerical, and nuclear experimental advancements over the past decade. It discusses the current understanding of burst ignition conditions and the influence of burst fuel on observational characteristics. The chapter provides an overview of processes shaping the burst X-ray spectrum, including elusive discrete spectral features. It explores timing behavior related to nuclear burning, including burst oscillations and mHz quasi-periodic oscillations. The increasing role of nuclear experimental physics in interpreting astrophysical data and models is highlighted. The chapter surveys simulation projects and the growing collaboration between modelers, observers, and nuclear experimentalists. Finally, it identifies open problems with potential resolutions in the near future.

title: Influence of Waviness on the Elastic Properties of Aligned Carbon Nanotube Polymer Matrix Nanocomposites
Abstract: Aligned carbon nanotubes (A-CNTs) hold promise for enhancing the performance of polymeric materials, but their actual mechanical properties in polymer matrix nanocomposites (A-PNCs) fall short of theoretical predictions. This discrepancy stems from the waviness of A-CNTs, often overlooked in theoretical models that rely on simplified straight geometries. This study uses a simulation framework analyzing 10^5 wavy CNTs with realistic stochastic morphologies to investigate the influence of waviness on the compliance contribution of A-CNTs to A-PNC effective elastic modulus. It shows that waviness causes significant over-prediction of the A-PNC effective modulus by existing theoretical frameworks that neglect shear deformation and do not properly account for CNT morphology. Future work will focus on quantifying A-PNC morphology in three dimensions and simulating their full elastic constitutive relations.

title: Using Machine Learning to Enhance Vehicles Traffic in ATN (PRT) Systems
Abstract: This paper explores new techniques for enhancing Automated Transit Networks (ATN, previously known as Personal Rapid Transit – PRT) using Artificial Intelligence tools. The primary focus is on improving cooperation between autonomous modules through negotiation protocols, adhering to the IoT paradigm. The aim is to increase ATN system throughput by optimizing autonomous vehicle cooperation. Machine learning (ML) is employed to refine algorithms designed by human programmers. Existing near-optimal solutions are used as "existing controls" to build refinement models that accurately link system dynamics to performance. Empty Vehicle Management (EVM) is identified as a crucial factor influencing ATN performance. ML is used to tailor individual behavioral policies, improving algorithms and tuning them to current conditions. The use of ML techniques is facilitated by the algorithmic reliance on a set of parameters, allowing for tuning of weights and thresholds for better decisions regarding empty vehicle movement across the track.

title: Priority Rules on ATN (PRT) Intersections

title: Assessing virtualization effects in simulations of distributed robotics

The two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test is used to assess the significance of performance variations under different experimental settings. Results reveal that the selection of virtualization technology significantly impacts simulation, and this effect can be amplified by certain operating systems. These findings highlight the importance of careful virtualization strategy selection in robotics research, while also offering optimism for repeatable robotics research using virtualization.

title: Ultrametricity increases the predictability of cultural dynamics
Abstract: A comprehensive understanding of societies requires integrating empirical data and mathematical models. Models of cultural dynamics aim to explain the emergence of culturally homogeneous groups through social influence. Traditionally, initial cultural traits are chosen randomly, focusing on characterizing model outcomes independent of initial conditions. This study takes a different approach, focusing on the effect of specific initial conditions, including those derived from real data, on the final cultural state. It investigates the predictability of the social content of final cultural groups, based on the knowledge of initial cultural traits, using an information-theoretic framework. The study finds that, compared to random and shuffled initial conditions, the hierarchical ultrametric-like organization of empirical cultural states significantly enhances the predictability of final social content by largely confining cultural convergence within the lower levels of the hierarchy. Moreover, predictability correlates with the compatibility of short-term social coordination and long-term cultural diversity, a property consistently observed in empirical data. The study introduces a null model generating initial conditions that retain the ultrametric representation of real data, demonstrating significantly enhanced predictability compared to random and shuffled cases, confirming the usefulness of the empirical hierarchical organization of culture for forecasting the outcome of social influence models.

title: New magnetic field instability and magnetar bursts
Abstract: This research considers a system of massive electrons with non-zero anomalous magnetic moments, interacting electroweakly with background neutrons in the presence of an external magnetic field. The Dirac equation for these electrons is solved exactly, revealing that a non-zero electric current can flow along the magnetic field. Accounting for this new current in the Maxwell equations, the study demonstrates the instability of the magnetic field in this system. Focusing on the case of a degenerate electron gas, which is prevalent in neutron stars, the study shows that a seed magnetic field can be amplified by more than an order of magnitude. The results are discussed in the context of explaining the electromagnetic radiation emitted by magnetars.

title: Nonlinear Instability Modelling of a Nonlocal Strain Gradient Functionally Graded Capacitive Nano-Bridge Under van der Waals force in Thermal Environment
Abstract: This paper develops a theoretical model to investigate the static pull-in instability of functionally graded (FG) electrostatic nano-bridges under the influence of electrostatic and van der Waals (vdW) forces in a thermal environment. The model utilizes nonlocal strain gradient theory (NLSGT) of elasticity, Euler-Bernoulli beam theory, and incorporates the non-linear geometric effect of mid-plane stretching. The material properties of the FG nano-beam are assumed to vary gradually along the thickness direction according to a simple power-law form. A new surface reference is introduced to eliminate the coupling between stretching and bending due to asymmetrical material variation along the thickness. The nonlinear integro-differential governing equation is derived using the minimum total potential energy principle, linearized using the step-by-step linearization method (SSLM), and solved by the Galerkin based weighted residual method. Numerical investigations focus on the effects of nonlocal parameter, material characteristic length scale, material gradient index, thermal effect, and intermolecular force on the static pull-in instability of the FG nano-beam. The validity of the model is established by comparing results with experimental and numerical data from previous studies.

title: Short-wavelength secondary instabilities in homogeneous and stably stratified shear flows
Abstract: This study presents a numerical investigation of three-dimensional, short-wavelength linear instabilities in Kelvin-Helmholtz (KH) vortices in homogeneous and stratified environments. The base flow, generated using two-dimensional numerical simulations, is characterized by the Reynolds number and the Richardson number, based on the initial one-dimensional velocity and buoyancy profiles. The local stability equations are solved on closed streamlines within the vortical base flow, assuming quasi-steady conditions. For the unstratified case, the elliptic instability at the vortex core dominates initially, followed by the hyperbolic instability at the vortex edge. In the stratified case, early time instabilities include a dominant elliptic instability at the core and a hyperbolic instability significantly influenced by stratification at the edge. At intermediate times, the local approach reveals a new branch of instability (convective branch) emerging at the vortex core and moving towards the edge. Additional convective instability branches appear at the core and move away, eventually coalescing into the most unstable region inside the vortex periphery at later times. The dominant instability characteristics from the local approach show good qualitative agreement with results from global instability studies for both homogeneous and stratified cases. Compartmentalized analyses elucidate the roles of shear and stratification on the identified instabilities, highlighting the critical role of buoyancy after the primary KH instability saturates, with the dominant convective instability occurring in regions with the strongest statically unstable layering. The study concludes by emphasizing the potential of the local approach for understanding secondary instabilities in other flows.

title: On the Degree of Ill-Posedness of Multi-Dimensional Magnetic Particle Imaging
Abstract: Magnetic particle imaging (MPI) is a relatively new imaging modality that exploits the non-linear magnetization response to reconstruct the concentration of nanoparticles. The degree of ill-posedness of the associated linear integral operator is analyzed using singular value decay estimates for Sobolev smooth bivariate functions, discussing the influence of various experimental parameters. title: The Borexino Thermal Monitoring & Management System and simulations of the fluid-dynamics of the Borexino detector under asymmetrical, changing boundary conditions
Abstract: A comprehensive monitoring system for the thermal environment inside the Borexino neutrino detector was developed and installed to reduce uncertainties in determining temperatures throughout the detector. A complementary thermal management system limits undesirable thermal couplings between the environment and Borexino's active sections. This strategy improves radioactive background conditions in the region of interest for the physics signal due to reduced fluid mixing in the liquid scintillator. Although fluid-dynamical equilibrium has not been fully achieved, and thermal fine-tuning is possible, the system has proven highly effective in stabilizing the detector's thermal conditions while providing precise insights into its internal thermal transport mechanisms. Furthermore, a Computational Fluid-Dynamics analysis was performed based on empirical measurements from the thermal monitoring system, providing information on current and future thermal trends. A two-dimensional modeling approach was implemented to understand thermal and fluid dynamics in Borexino, optimized for different regions and periods of interest, focusing on critical effects influencing background concentrations. Literature experimental case studies were reproduced to benchmark the method and settings, and a Borexino-specific benchmark was implemented to validate the modeling approach for thermal transport. Finally, fully-convective models were applied to understand general and specific fluid motions impacting the detector's Active Volume.

title: Effect of NBTI/PBTI Aging and Process Variations on Write Failures in MOSFET and FinFET Flip-Flops
Abstract: The assessment of noise margins and the associated probability of failure in digital cells is increasingly crucial as nano-scale CMOS and FinFET technologies face reliability issues caused by aging mechanisms like NBTI and variability in process parameters. These phenomena significantly impact Write Noise Margins (WNM) in memory elements, as a wrong stored logic value can disrupt the system state. This study calculates and compares the effect of process variations and NBTI aging on the actual WNM of various CMOS and FinFET-based flip-flop cells over time. Massive transistor-level Monte Carlo simulations produce both nominal (mean) values and associated standard deviations of the WNM for the chosen flip-flops. This allows for calculating the subsequent write failure probability as a function of input voltage shift on the flip-flop cells and comparing the robustness of different circuit topologies and technologies.

title: graphTPP: A multivariate based method for interactive graph layout and analysis
Abstract: Graph layout involves creating a visual representation of a graph using a node-link diagram. Node-attribute graphs store additional data on nodes, describing their properties. TPP enables user control over the projection and is optimized for clustering. Three case studies in influence graphs, network security, and citation networks demonstrate that graphTPP outperforms standard force-directed techniques and other dimension reduction methods in terms of clarity of clustered structure in the layout, association between structure and attributes, and elicited insights in each domain. |||

title: Effects of Disorder on the Pressure-Induced Mott Transition in $κ$-BEDT-TTF)$_2$Cu[N(CN)$_2$]Cl
Abstract: We investigated the influence of disorder on the Mott metal-insulator transition in the organic charge-transfer salt κ-(BEDT-TTF)₂Cu[N(CN)₂]Cl. Disorder was introduced by controlled x-ray irradiation of single crystals, followed by tuning across the Mott transition using He-gas pressure at low temperatures. Thermal expansion and resistance measurements revealed that the first-order character of the Mott transition persisted for low irradiation doses (up to 100 hours). In these crystals with moderate disorder, we observed a first-order transition line terminating in a second-order critical endpoint, similar to the pristine crystals. However, both the critical pressure (p_c) and critical temperature (T_c) were significantly reduced, consistent with the theoretical prediction of a soft Coulomb gap in the presence of strong correlations and small disorder. Moreover, similar to the pristine sample, the Mott transition after 50 hours of irradiation showed sizable lattice effects, whose critical behavior could be described by mean-field theory. Our results demonstrate that the Mott transition remains essentially unchanged at low disorder levels. However, after 150 hours of irradiation, no clear signatures of a discontinuous metal-insulator transition were observed, suggesting that above a certain disorder level, the transition becomes a smeared first-order transition with some residual hysteresis.

title: Hauser-Feshbach fission fragment de-excitation with calculated macroscopic-microscopic mass yields
Abstract: The Hauser-Feshbach statistical model was applied to the de-excitation of primary fission fragments, using input mass yields calculated with macroscopic-microscopic models of the potential energy surface. The sensitivity of prompt fission observables to the input mass yields was tested for two important reactions, 235U(n_th,f) and 239Pu(n_th,f), for which experimental data are available. General traits of the mass yields, such as peak locations and widths, influenced prompt neutron and γ-ray multiplicities and their spectra. Using several mass yields, a linear correlation was found between the calculated prompt neutron multiplicity (ν̄) and the average heavy-fragment mass (⟨A_h⟩) of the input mass yields (∂ν̄/∂⟨A_h⟩ = ± 0.1 n/f/u). The mass peak width influenced the correlation between the total kinetic energy of the fission fragments and the total number of prompt neutrons emitted (ν̄_T(TKE)). Typical biases on prompt particle observables from using calculated mass yields instead of experimental ones were: δν̄ = 4% for the average prompt neutron multiplicity, δM̄_γ = 1% for the average prompt γ-ray multiplicity, δε̄_n^LAB = 1% for the average outgoing neutron energy, δε̄_γ = 1% for the average γ-ray energy, and δ⟨TKE⟩ = 0.4% for the average total kinetic energy of the fission fragments.

title: A Data-Driven Analysis of Workers' Earnings on Amazon Mechanical Turk
Abstract: Crowd work on online platforms, characterized by low wages, has become increasingly prevalent. However, our understanding of wage distribution and the factors driving low/high earnings is limited. We analyzed data from 2,676 workers performing 3.8 million tasks on Amazon Mechanical Turk. Our task-level analysis revealed a median hourly wage of only ~$2/h, with only 4% of workers earning more than $7.25/h. The average requester paid more than $11/h, although lower-paying requesters posted significantly more work. Our wage calculations are influenced by the inclusion of unpaid work, such as task searching, rejected tasks, and unsubmitted tasks. We further investigated the characteristics of tasks and working patterns associated with higher hourly wages. Our analysis provides insights for future platform design and worker tools to create a more positive future for crowd work.

title: Growth and evolution of satellites in a Jovian massive disc
Abstract: Satellite system formation in circum-planetary discs is analogous to rocky planet formation in proto-planetary discs, particularly Super-Earths. Therefore, studying systems with large satellites can provide insights into formation theories applicable to extrasolar planets. Additionally, understanding the origin of satellites can shed light on the environment near the growing planet during the final stages of planet formation. This work investigates the formation and migration of the Jovian satellites through N-body simulations. We simulated a massive, static, low-viscosity, circum-planetary disc adhering to the minimum mass sub-nebula model prescriptions for its total mass. Hydrodynamic simulations revealed no signs of gaps, implying no type II migration. Therefore, we employed analytic prescriptions for type I migration, eccentricity and inclination damping, and performed N-body simulations incorporating damping forces. Detailed parameter studies showed that the number of final satellites is significantly influenced by the initial distribution of embryos, the disc temperature, and the initial gas density profile. Steeper initial density profiles facilitate the formation of systems with multiple satellites in resonance, while a flatter profile favors the formation of satellites close to the region of the Galilean satellites. We demonstrate that the formation of massive satellites like Ganymede and Callisto can be achieved for hotter discs with an aspect ratio of H/r ~ 0.15, where the ice line was located around 30 R_J.

title: Quantitative Implementation Strategies for Safety Controllers
Abstract: The symbolic controller synthesis approach enforces safety specifications on perturbed, nonlinear control systems. In each system state, multiple control values may be applicable to enforce safety, requiring a selection of a specific value from potentially many. We introduce a class of implementation strategies to obtain a controller with performance guarantees. This class encompasses two existing strategies from the literature, based on discounted payoff and mean-payoff games. We unify both approaches through games characterized by a single discount factor that determines the implementation. We experimentally evaluated different implementations from our class on two case studies. The choice of the discount factor significantly impacts average long-term costs, and the best performance guarantee for the symbolic model does not necessarily result in the best implementation. Comparing the optimal discount factor with previously proposed values revealed cost differences of up to 50%. Our approach systematically selects a good implementation for safety controllers with quantitative objectives.

title: Large-scale photospheric motions determined from granule tracking and helioseismology from SDO/HMI data
Abstract: Large-scale flows in the Sun play a crucial role in the dynamo process linked to the solar cycle. Important large-scale flows include differential rotation and meridional circulation, with amplitudes of km/s and a few m/s, respectively. These flows also exhibit cycle-related components, namely torsional oscillations. Our aim is to determine large-scale plasma flows on the solar surface by deriving horizontal flow velocities using techniques such as solar granule tracking, dopplergrams, and time-distance helioseismology. Coherent structure tracking (CST) and time-distance helioseismology were employed to investigate solar differential rotation and meridional circulation at the solar surface using a 30-day HMI SDO sequence. The influence of a large sunspot on these flows was also studied using a specific 7-day HMI SDO sequence. The large-scale flows measured by CST on the solar surface and those determined from the same data using helioseismology in the first 1 Mm below the surface showed good agreement in amplitude and direction. Torsional waves were also located at the same latitudes with similar amplitudes. We were able to accurately measure the meridional circulation using the CST method with just three days of data and averaging between + and -15 degrees in longitude. We conclude that the combination of CST and Doppler velocities allows us to properly detect differential solar rotation and smaller amplitude flows, such as meridional circulation and torsional waves. The results of our methods are consistent with helioseismic measurements.

title: Proximity effect in normal-metal quasiparticle traps
Abstract: Quasiparticle excitations are detrimental in many superconducting devices, including qubits. A normal metal (N) in contact with a superconductor (S) can trap these excitations, potentially improving device performance. The mutual influence of these materials, known as the proximity effect, has been studied since the 1960s. This work investigates whether the proximity effect limits potential performance improvements in superconducting qubits. We revisited the proximity effect in uniform NS bilayers and presented novel findings for the density of states, despite the long history of this problem. We then extended our results to describe a non-uniform system near a trap edge. Combining these results with a phenomenological model for quasiparticle density suppression due to the trap, we found an optimal trap-junction distance in a transmon qubit that minimizes the qubit relaxation rate. This optimal distance, ranging from 4 to 20 coherence lengths, arises from the competition between the proximity effect and quasiparticle density suppression. We conclude that the harmful influence of the proximity effect can be avoided as long as the trap is located farther away from the junction than this optimal distance.

title: Adaptive kNN using Expected Accuracy for Classification of Geo-Spatial Data
Abstract: The k-Nearest Neighbor (kNN) classification approach is conceptually simple but widely applied due to its practical effectiveness. However, using a global constant k value does not always provide an optimal solution, especially for datasets with irregular data point density distributions. The efficient Egalitarian rule protects individual agents but not coalitions. A comprehensive analysis of equilibria and convergence properties is conducted for both irreducible and reducible influence networks. In irreducible influence networks, the single-timescale DF model exhibits similar behavior to the original DF model, predicting, among other things, that social power ranking asymptotically aligns with centrality ranking, social power accumulates at the top of the centrality hierarchy, and autocratic (or democratic) power structures arise when centrality scores are maximally non-uniform (or uniform). Second, when the associated network has multiple sinks, the two models exhibit stark differences: the original DF model has a single globally attractive equilibrium, while any partition of social power among the sinks is possible at equilibrium in the single-timescale DF model.

title: Astrophysical gyrokinetics: Turbulence in pressure-anisotropic plasmas at ion scales and beyond

Thirdly, a simple model is used to show that pressure anisotropy can cause large variations in the ion-to-electron heating ratio due to the dissipation of Alfvenic turbulence. title: Unsupervised Learning for Color Constancy

This calibration process is time-consuming, ideally performed individually for each sensor, making it a bottleneck in achieving high color constancy accuracy. Statistics-based methods do not require calibrated training images but are less accurate. This paper proposes an unsupervised learning-based method that learns its parameter values by approximating the unknown ground-truth illumination of the training images, avoiding the need for calibration. The proposed method outperforms all statistics-based methods and many learning-based methods in terms of accuracy. The paper also presents an extension of the method that learns the necessary parameters from non-calibrated images captured with one sensor and can be applied to images captured with another sensor, enabling inter-camera unsupervised learning for color constancy. Additionally, a new high-quality color constancy benchmark dataset with 1707 calibrated images is created, used for testing, and made publicly available. title: On the accuracy of Monte Carlo based beam dynamics models for the degrader in proton therapy facilities

title: Learning to Segment Moving Objects

The framework employs a two-stream neural network with an explicit memory module. The two streams encode appearance and motion cues, respectively, while the memory module captures object evolution over time, leveraging temporal consistency. The motion stream is a convolutional neural network trained on synthetic videos to segment independently moving objects in the optical flow field. The memory module, which builds a "visual memory" of all video frames, is implemented using a convolutional recurrent unit learned from a limited number of training video sequences. For each pixel in a test video frame, the approach assigns an object or background label based on learned spatio-temporal features and the video-specific "visual memory." title: ALMA Observations of the Physical and Chemical Conditions in Centaurus A

These observations resolve physical sizes down to 40 pc. By observing multiple chemical probes, the study determines the physical and chemical conditions of the nuclear interstellar medium of NGC 5128. This region contains molecular arms associated with the dust lanes and a circumnuclear disk (CND) interior to the molecular arms. The CND is approximately 400 pc by 200 pc and exhibits distinct chemical properties compared to the molecular arms. It is dominated by dense gas tracers, while the molecular arms are dominated by $^{12}$CO and its rare isotopologues. The CND has a higher temperature, elevated CN/HCN and HCN/HNC intensity ratios, and much weaker $^{13}$CO and C$^{18}$O emission than the molecular arms, suggesting an influence from the AGN on the CND molecular gas. Absorption against the AGN is also observed, with a low velocity complex near the systemic velocity and a high velocity complex shifted by about 60 km s$^{-1}$. The chemical properties of the CND in emission are similar to both the low and high velocity absorption complexes, implying that both likely originate from the CND. If the high velocity complex indeed originates in the CND, then the gas would correspond to gas falling toward the supermassive black hole.

These methods are extensively compared on eight real-world datasets across three application areas, providing both inter- and intra-group comparisons. The paper measures convergence runtime speed, cross-validation performance, sparse and noisy prediction performance, and model selection robustness. The analysis offers insights into the trade-offs between prior and likelihood choices for Bayesian matrix factorization on small datasets, revealing that Poisson models provide poor predictions and that nonnegative models are more constrained than real-valued models.

title: Calculation of the ratios and absolute rates of the $Ξ_b^- \to π^- (D_s^- ) \ Ξ_c^0 (2790) \left(Ξ_c^0 (2815) \right)$ and $Ξ_b^- \to \barν_l l \ Ξ_c^0 (2790) \left(Ξ_c^0 (2815) \right)$ decays

title: $R$-band host galaxy contamination of TeV $γ$-ray blazar Mrk 501: effects of the aperture size and seeing

These correlations introduce illusive large amplitude variations at short timescales, masking intrinsic micro variability and hindering its detection. Both aperture size and seeing condition affect flux measurements, with aperture size having a more significant impact. Utilizing elliptical galaxy parameters from Nilsson et al. The simulated host galaxy data effectively weaken the significant seeing-brightness correlations for the host-subtracted brightness of Mrk 501, aiding in the discovery of intrinsic short timescale micro variability. title: Spin-resolved electron waiting times in a quantum dot spin valve

The paper analyzes the behaviors of WTDs in short times, correlating them with current behaviors for different spin polarizations and noncollinear angles. The cross-channel WTD reflects the correlation between the two spin channels and can be used to characterize the spin transfer torque process. The influence of earlier detection on subsequent detection is studied from the perspective of cross-channel WTD, defining the influence degree quantity as the cumulative absolute difference between cross-channel WTDs and first passage time distributions to quantitatively characterize the spin flip process. title: Fundamental Principles in Bacterial Physiology - History, Recent progress, and the Future with Focus on Cell Size Control: A Review
Abstract: Bacterial physiology is a branch of biology that seeks to understand the fundamental principles governing cellular reproduction. Many crucial issues in bacterial physiology are inherently quantitative, and leading contributors to the field have often combined tools and perspectives from various disciplines. This article provides a comprehensive overview of major ideas and approaches developed since the early 20th century for those interested in fundamental problems in bacterial physiology. The article is divided into two parts. The first part (Sections 1 to 3) reviews the "golden era" of bacterial physiology from the 1940s to the early 1970s, providing a complete list of key references from that period. The second part (Sections 4 to 7) explains how pioneering work from the first golden era has influenced the rediscovery of general quantitative principles and significant further development in modern bacterial physiology. Specifically, Section 4 presents the history and current progress of the "adder" principle of cell size homeostasis. Section 5 discusses the implications of coarse-graining cellular protein composition and how the coarse-grained proteome "sectors" re-balance under different growth conditions. Section 6 focuses on physiological invariants, explaining how they are key to understanding the coordination between growth and the cell cycle that underlies cell size control in steady-state growth. Section 7 overviews how the temporal organization of all internal processes enables balanced growth. Finally, Section 8 concludes by discussing remaining challenges for the future in the field. |||

title: Speaker identification from the sound of the human breath
Abstract: This paper investigates the potential of breath sounds for speaker identification in continuous speech. While speech primarily occurs during exhalation, speakers must inhale periodically. Intra-speech inhalation, often through the mouth, has been extensively studied for patterns, cadence, and energy variations. However, the *sound* produced during inhalation has largely been disregarded.  Intra-speech inhalation is rapid and energetic, utilizing an open mouth and glottis, exposing the entire vocal tract for maximum air intake. This results in vocal tract resonances generated by turbulence, which are unique to the speaker's speech-producing apparatus.  Therefore, inhalation sounds are expected to carry information about the speaker's identity.  Unlike other spoken sounds that are subject to active control, inhalation sounds are more natural and less influenced by voluntary control. This research aims to demonstrate that breath sounds are bio-signatures that can be used for speaker identification. The paper presents findings that show remarkably accurate speaker recognition using appropriate feature representations and classification frameworks, indicating that these sounds alone can be effective for identification.

title: The Influences of Edge Asymmetry on Network Robustness

Simulation studies revealed that the effectiveness of the EA-based attack strategy increased with greater network asymmetry.  The computational complexity of EA is significantly lower than that of EB, making EA-based attack strategies more efficient. title: Two-component Marangoni-contracted droplets: friction and shape
Abstract: When a mixture of propylene glycol and water is deposited on a clean glass slide, it forms a droplet with a specific apparent contact angle instead of spreading as expected on a high-energy surface.  This droplet is stabilized by a Marangoni flow, driven by non-uniform component concentrations between the droplet's border and center due to evaporation. These self-contracting droplets exhibit unique properties, including the absence of pinning and the ability to move under an external humidity gradient.  The droplet's apparent contact angle is influenced by its concentration and the external humidity. This study investigates the motion of such droplets sliding down slopes, their deformation at high speeds, and compares these results to typical non-volatile droplets. By precisely controlling external humidity and examining the impact of volume, viscosity, surface tension, and contact angle, we observed negligible pinning force for small velocities. In this case, the capillary number (Ca) is directly proportional to the Bond number (Bo): Ca = Bo sinα, with α representing the slope angle.  As the droplets move at higher velocities, deformation occurs when Ca exceeds a threshold, and smaller droplets are deposited when Ca reaches twice this threshold.

The focus is on low-latency cyber-physical systems where real-time control actions are required in response to changes in the state of an IoT node. In such scenarios, deploying controller software on a cloud server is often impractical due to the delay between the network edge and the cloud.  Therefore, moving controller logic closer to the network edge becomes desirable, trading reliability for latency. Modeling the IoT node as a dynamical system evolving linearly with quadratic penalties for state deviations, recursive expressions for the optimal control policy and the resulting minimum cost value are derived considering virtual fog controller reliability and response time latency.  Our findings indicate that latency is more critical than reliability in provisioning virtualized control services over fog endpoints, as it dictates the responsiveness of the fog control system and the timeliness of state measurements. An extensive simulation study, based on a realistic drone trajectory tracking model, demonstrates the influence of reliability and latency on autonomous vehicle control over fog.

title: Multiscale modeling of a rectifying bipolar nanopore: explicit-water versus implicit-water simulations
Abstract: This paper presents computer simulation results for a rectifying bipolar nanopore using a multiscale modeling approach at two distinct levels. An all-atom model employs explicit water to simulate ion transport directly through the molecular dynamics technique.  In a reduced model, implicit water is used alongside the Local Equilibrium Monte Carlo method and the Nernst-Planck transport equation. This hybrid method enables rapid calculation of ion transport at the cost of reduced detail. The implicit-water model effectively represents the explicit-water model when considering the system at the device level (input vs. output). Both models exhibit qualitatively similar electrical current behavior across different voltages and model parameters. However, detailed analysis of concentration and potential profiles reveals significant differences between the two models. Despite these differences, they do not affect the model's fundamental behavior as a device, as they do not influence the z-dependence of concentration profiles, the primary determinants of current. These findings address a long-standing paradox: how do reduced models, whose assumptions should break down at the nanoscale, predict experimental data?  Our simulations demonstrate that reduced models can still accurately capture overall device physics, even if they deviate in certain aspects of molecular-scale physics. This is because they incorporate the essential physics for device function. Therefore, reduced models are sufficient for general device understanding and design, while more detailed models may be needed for molecular-level comprehension.

title: Probabilities of causation of climate changes
Abstract: Over the past decades, multiple changes in Earth's climate system have been observed. We argue that these concepts are relevant and readily extendable to the detection and attribution of long-term climate change trends (D&A). In accordance with the "fingerprinting" principle used in the conventional D&A framework, a change trajectory is converted into an event occurrence by maximizing the causal evidence associated with the forcing under investigation.  Key assumptions from the conventional D&A framework, particularly those related to numerical model error, can be readily adapted to this approach.  This proposal bridges the conventional framework with standard causal theory, aiming to enhance the quantification of causal probabilities. title: Using the CIFIST grid of CO5BOLD 3D model atmospheres to study the effects of stellar granulation on photometric colours. I. Grids of 3D corrections in the UBVRI, 2MASS, Hipparcos, Gaia, and SDSS systems

Each CO5BOLD model has a corresponding one-dimensional (1D) plane-parallel LHD model computed for the same atmospheric parameters. This allows us to define a "3D correction" that can be applied to colors calculated from fluxes obtained using any 1D model atmosphere code. While 3D corrections on colors are generally small, on the order of a few hundredths of a magnitude, they are far from negligible.  Our findings indicate that neglecting granulation effects can lead to underestimation of Teff by up to 200K and overestimation of gravity by up to 0.5dex when using colors as diagnostics. This study demonstrates that the typically considered dissipative gravitational tidal evolution of rocky planet rotation could, in principle, be stalled by thermal tide resonances for Earth-analog worlds in the liquid water orbital zone of stars more massive than approximately 0.3 solar masses. The study examines the possibility of feedback effects between a planetary biosphere and the planetary rotational evolution. Building upon previous research, it suggests that atmospheric oxygenation and ozone production could play a key role in planetary rotation evolution, representing a surprising but potent form of biological imprint on astronomically accessible planetary characteristics.

title: Dissipative instabilities in a partially ionised prominence plasma slab: II. The effect of compressibility
Abstract: This study investigates the dissipative instability that arises in a compressible, partially ionized plasma slab embedded in a uniform magnetic field, modeling the plasma state in solar prominences. In the partially ionized plasma, the dominant dissipative effect is Cowling resistivity. The regions outside the slab, representing the solar corona, are fully ionized, and the dominant dissipation mechanism is viscosity. Analytical solutions to the extended magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) equations are derived for both the interior and exterior of the slab, and these solutions are matched at the slab boundaries. The dispersion relation is obtained and solutions are found analytically in the slender slab limit. The conditions necessary for the appearance of the instability are numerically investigated for the entire parameter space. The study focuses on the effect of compressibility on the generation and evolution of instabilities. The results indicate that compressibility reduces the threshold of the equilibrium flow, where waves can become unstable, to a level comparable to the internal cusp speed, which is of the same order as flow speeds currently observed in solar prominences. The study addresses only slow waves, as they are the most likely perturbations to become unstable, but the time scales of the instability are found to be quite large, ranging from 10^5 to 10^7 seconds. The instability threshold is further influenced by the concentration of neutrals and the strength of the coronal viscosity, with these two aspects having opposing effects. Numerical analysis shows that the interplay between the equilibrium flow, neutrals, and dispersion can significantly alter the nature of waves.

title: Compensation temperature in spin-$1/2$ Ising trilayers: A Monte Carlo study
Abstract: This study examines the magnetic and thermodynamic properties of a spin-1/2 Ising system comprising three layers, each composed exclusively of one of two possible types of atoms, A or B. The A-A and B-B bonds are ferromagnetic, while the A-B bonds are antiferromagnetic. Monte Carlo simulations utilizing the Wolff algorithm are employed, and the data is analyzed using the multiple-histogram reweighting technique and finite-size scaling tools. The study confirms the occurrence of a compensation phenomenon and determines the compensation and critical temperatures of the model as functions of the Hamiltonian parameters. The influence of each parameter on the overall system behavior is discussed in detail, and the results are presented as phase diagrams dividing the parameter space into regions where the compensation phenomenon is present or absent. The results may provide valuable information for experimentalists seeking to build materials with specific desired characteristics.

title: Magnetic properties, spin waves and interaction between spin excitations and 2D electrons in interface layer in Y3Fe5O12 / AlOx / GaAs-heterostructures
Abstract: This study describes the synthesis of submicron Y3Fe5O12 (YIG) films sputtered on GaAs-based substrates and presents results from an investigation of ferromagnetic resonance (FMR), spin wave propagation, and the interaction between spin excitations and 2D electrons in the interface layer of YIG/AlOx/GaAs heterostructures. The results show that the relaxation process contributes about 2% to the FMR linewidth. However, FMR linewidths are generally high in all samples. Sputtered YIG films exhibit magnetic inhomogeneity, which is the primary contributor to the FMR linewidth. Transistor structures with two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) channels in the AlOx/GaAs interface governed by YIG-film spin excitations are designed. An effective influence of spin excitations on the current flowing through the GaAs 2DEG channel is observed. Light illumination results in significant changes in the FMR spectrum. The study also finds that an increase in the 2DEG current leads to an inverse effect, causing notable changes in the FMR spectrum.

title: Opinion influence and evolution in social networks: a Markovian agents model
Abstract: This paper models and investigates the effect of filtering algorithms managed by social network platforms on collective opinions. A stochastic multi-agent model for opinion dynamics is proposed, accounting for centralized tuning of the interaction strength between individuals. The evolution of each individual opinion is described by a Markov chain, whose transition rates are influenced by the opinions of neighbors through influence parameters. The model's properties are studied in a general setting as well as in specific interesting cases. A general result is that the overall model of the social network behaves like a high-dimensional Markov chain, suitable for Monte Carlo simulation. Assuming identical agents and unbiased influence, the study shows that influence intensity affects the variance, but not the expectation, of the number of individuals sharing a specific opinion. Additionally, a detailed analysis is conducted for the Peer Assembly, which describes the evolution of binary opinions in a fully connected graph of identical agents. It is demonstrated that the Peer Assembly can be lumped into a birth-death chain amenable to complete analytical characterization. Both analytical results and simulation experiments are used to highlight the emergence of specific collective behaviors, such as consensus and herding, depending on the centralized tuning of influence parameters.

title: Effect of fixation target on the contrast sensitivity in the foveal and parafoveal area
Abstract: This study investigates the influence of a fixation target on contrast sensitivity when the stimulus is presented in two retinal locations, foveal and parafoveal. Four young adults with 0.0 logMar acuity participated in the study. The stimulus consisted of vertical sinusoidal gratings masked by a circle (for foveal area) or a ring (for parafoveal area). To increase the luminance resolution of the display, a bit-stealing technique was used. Four different sets of stimuli were generated, two for exploring foveal sensitivity and two for parafoveal sensitivity. The sets designed for the same area differed in the presence or absence of a fixation target (a white cross) at the center of the stimulus. A modified staircase method was implemented. The results show a decrease in contrast sensitivity when the fixation target is present on the stimulus for frequencies smaller than 4 cycles per degree. The presence of fixation targets reduces contrast sensitivity for low to mid frequencies across different concentric areas of the retina. This could be attributed to fixational eye movements, as different patterns of eye movements were observed using an eye tracker. The relationship between sensitivity in the foveal area and the parafoveal area agrees with previously reported findings using different designs, confirming that the new stimulus design is suitable for measuring contrast sensitivity outside the foveal area.

title: Surface effects on ionic Coulomb blockade in nanometer-size pores
Abstract: Ionic Coulomb blockade in nanopores is a phenomenon sharing some similarities but also differences with its electronic counterpart. This study investigates this phenomenon using all-atom molecular dynamics simulations of ionic transport through nanopores approximately one nanometer in diameter and up to several nanometers in length. The goal is to understand the role of atomic roughness and structure of the pore walls in the ionic Coulomb blockade. The simulations reveal the following general trends: first, nanopore selectivity changes with its diameter, and the nanopore position in the membrane influences current strength; second, ionic transport through the nanopore occurs in a hopping-like fashion over a set of discrete states caused by local electric fields due to membrane atoms, sometimes creating a slow-varying "crystal-like" structure of ions inside the nanopore; third, while at a given voltage, the resistance of the nanopore depends on its length, the slope of this dependence appears independent of the molarity of ions. An effective kinetic model that captures the ionic Coulomb blockade behavior observed in MD simulations is formulated.

title: Butterfly Effect: Bidirectional Control of Classification Performance by Small Additive Perturbation
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel algorithm for controlling classification results by generating a small additive perturbation without modifying the classifier network. Inspired by existing works generating adversarial perturbations that degrade classification performance, this work aims to generate perturbations that enhance overall classification performance. To address this performance enhancement problem, a perturbation generation network (PGN) influenced by the adversarial learning strategy is proposed. In this approach, information from a large external dataset is summarized by a small additive perturbation, which helps improve the performance of the classifier trained with the target dataset. In addition to performance enhancement, the proposed PGN can be adapted to solve the classical adversarial problem without requiring information about the target classifier. These characteristics of the method are verified through extensive experiments on publicly available visual datasets.

title: Inferring type and scale of noncommutativity from the PTOLEMY experiment
Abstract: If neutrinos are Dirac particles and their right-handed component can be abundantly produced in the early universe, they could influence the direct observation of the cosmic neutrino background, most likely achieved by the recently proposed PTOLEMY experiment. For the production mechanism of right-handed neutrinos, this study uses a state-of-the-art version of gauge field theory deformed by spacetime noncommutativity, to reveal not only the decoupling temperature for this neutrino component but also the otherwise hidden coupling temperature. Considering two relevant processes, plasmon decay and neutrino elastic scattering, the study investigates the interplay between the structure of the noncommutativity parameter (type of noncommutativity) and the reheating temperature after inflation to obtain an elusive upper bound on the scale of noncommutativity. If the PTOLEMY enhanced capture rate is due to spacetime noncommutativity, the study verifies that a non-trivial maximum upper bound on the scale of noncommutativity emerges for a space-like noncommutativity parameter and sufficiently high reheating temperature.

title: An adaptive multiphysics model coupling vertical equilibrium and full multidimensions for multiphase flow in porous media
Abstract: Efficient multiphysics models that adapt to varying physical process complexity in space and time are desirable for modeling fluid migration in the subsurface. Vertical equilibrium (VE) models are simplified mathematical models that are computationally efficient but rely on the assumption of instant gravity segregation of the two phases, which may not be valid at all times or locations in the domain. This study presents a multiphysics model that couples a VE model to a full multidimensional model without any dimensionality reduction. A criterion is developed to determine subdomains where the VE assumption is valid during simulation. The VE model is then adaptively applied in these subdomains, reducing the number of computational cells due to the dimensionality reduction, while the rest of the domain is solved by the full multidimensional model. The study analyzes how the threshold parameter of the criterion influences the accuracy and computational cost of the new multiphysics model, providing recommendations for optimal threshold parameter selection. Finally, a test case of gas injection demonstrates that the adaptive multiphysics model is significantly more computationally efficient than using the full multidimensional model in the entire domain, while maintaining much of the accuracy.
