title: Control of surface plasmon-polaritons in magnetoelectric heterostructures
Abstract: This work focuses on investigating surface plasmon polaritons in metal-dielectric heterostructures containing materials with magnetoelectric properties. Analyzing various possible configurations reveals that the magnetoelectric effect influences the plasmonic surface wave polarization, localization, and dispersion. The specific case of chromium (III) oxide as a magnetoelectric dielectric is described in detail, highlighting the switching between different regimes of magnetoelectric impact on plasmon-polaritons. Plasmonic heterostructures with magnetoelectric constituents can be used as polarization- and dispersion-sensitive instruments to detect magnetoelectric coupling, potentially acting as optical tools for controlling surface plasmon-polariton dispersion and dynamics via external electric and magnetic fields. Additionally, the described effects can be applied to manipulate the far-field optical response of plasmonic structures. Composite magnetoelectric materials, such as BaTiO3/BiFeO3, exhibiting a giant magnetoelectric effect are promising for these applications.

title: Life and work of Egbert Brieskorn (1936 - 2013)
Abstract: Egbert Brieskorn passed away on July 11, 2013, a few days after his 77th birthday. He was a remarkable individual who left a lasting impact on everyone who knew him, both within and outside of mathematics. While Brieskorn was a brilliant mathematician, his interests, knowledge, and activities extended far beyond the field. This tribute, deeply influenced by the authors' long-standing personal connection with Brieskorn, aims to provide a deeper understanding of his life and work. It highlights his personal commitment to peace and the environment, as well as his long-term study of the life and work of Felix Hausdorff and the publication of Hausdorff's collected works. However, the main focus of this article is on presenting his remarkable and influential mathematical contributions.

title: Interpretable Convolutional Neural Networks for Effective Translation Initiation Site Prediction
Abstract: The rapid evolution of sequencing techniques has led to an ever-increasing abundance of genomic data. Determining gene structure is crucial for effectively interpreting gene function and regulation. An important step in this process is the identification of translation initiation sites. This paper proposes a novel approach for automatic prediction of translation initiation sites, utilizing convolutional neural networks that enable automatic feature extraction. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 75.2% decrease in the false positive rate and a 24.5% decrease in the error rate on chosen datasets. A detailed analysis of the decision-making process used by the predictive model reveals that the neural network implicitly learns biologically relevant features from scratch, without requiring prior knowledge, such as the Kozak consensus sequence, the influence of stop and start codons in the sequence, and the presence of donor splice site patterns. In summary, the findings provide a better understanding of the internal reasoning of a convolutional neural network when applied to genomic data.

title: Structure propagation for zero-shot learning
Abstract: The core of zero-shot learning (ZSL) lies in finding an information transfer model that bridges the gap between images and semantic information (texts or attributes). Existing ZSL methods typically construct a compatibility function between images and class labels, considering the relevance of semantic classes (the manifold structure of semantic classes). However, the relationship between image classes (the manifold structure of image classes) is equally important for constructing the compatibility model. Due to unseen classes, capturing the relationship among image classes is challenging, often leading to the neglect of the manifold structure of image classes in ZSL. To complement the information from both the manifold structure of image classes and that of semantic classes, this study proposes structure propagation (SP) for improving ZSL classification performance. SP jointly considers the manifold structure of image classes and that of semantic classes to approximate the intrinsic structure of object classes. Additionally, SP describes the constraint condition between the compatibility function and these manifold structures to balance the influence of the structure propagation iteration. The SP solution provides not only unseen class labels but also the relationship between the two manifold structures, encoding the positive transfer in structure propagation. Experimental results demonstrate that SP achieves promising results on the AwA, CUB, Dogs, and SUN databases.

title: Simulating outcomes of interventions using a multipurpose simulation program based on the Evolutionary Causal Matrices and Markov Chain
Abstract: Predicting long-term outcomes of interventions is essential for educational and social policy-making processes that can significantly influence our society in the long term. This paper introduces Python classes implementing a computer simulation model and presents some pilot implementations demonstrating how the model can be utilized for predicting outcomes of various interventions. The study also introduces the class-structured simulation module using both real experimental data and hypothetical data formulated based on social psychological theories. The classes developed and tested in this study provide researchers and practitioners with a feasible and practical method to prospectively simulate intervention outcomes.

title: Point of Interest Recommendation Methods in Location Based Social Networks: Traveling to a new geographical region

However, this approach may be inadequate when a user moves to a new region with little or no activity history. This study proposes a location-aware POI recommendation system that models user preferences primarily based on user reviews and categories of POIs. The algorithm is evaluated using the Yelp dataset, and experimental results demonstrate that it achieves better accuracy. |||

title: Effects of wall-normal and angular momentum injections in airfoil separation control
Abstract: This computational study examines the effectiveness of wall-normal and angular momentum injections in suppressing laminar flow separation over a NACA 0012 airfoil at an angle of attack of 9 degrees and a Reynolds number of 23,000. Using large-eddy simulations, swirling jets are introduced into the separated flow through model boundary conditions, independently injecting wall-normal momentum and angular momentum. The study analyzes the flow field and surface vorticity fluxes in response to various actuation input combinations. The results reveal that combining wall-normal momentum injection with angular momentum input enhances the suppression of flow separation.  Lift enhancement and separation suppression are characterized by modifying the standard definition of the coefficient of momentum, incorporating the effect of angular momentum through a characteristic swirling jet velocity based on the non-dimensional swirl number. This modified coefficient of momentum successfully categorizes controlled flows into separated, transitional, and attached states.

title: Noise Resistant Quantum Control Using Dynamical Invariants
Abstract: A systematic approach to design robust control protocols against various noise sources is presented. The protocols aim to protect the decay of populations, avoiding dissipation in both adiabatic and non-adiabatic regimes and minimizing dephasing effects. The effectiveness of these protocols is demonstrated in two distinct systems. The first case examines population inversion of a two-level system in the presence of one or two simultaneous noise sources. The second case explores the expansion of coherent and thermal states in harmonic traps subject to noise arising from monitoring and modulation of the control, respectively.

title: Hyperons in hot dense matter: what do the constraints tell us for equation of state?
Abstract: Accurate equations of state (EoS) are crucial for simulating core-collapse and neutron star mergers, providing a realistic description of the underlying dense and hot matter. This study presents two newly constructed EoS, encompassing the entire baryon octet and compatible with experimental and theoretical constraints from nuclear physics. One of the EoS accurately predicts the maximum mass for cold, beta-equilibrated neutron stars at 2 solar masses, consistent with recent observations. The study compares the predictions of these new EoS with the results obtained from DD2Y, the only currently existing EoS containing the baryon octet that meets the same constraints. The main difference between the new EoS models and DD2Y lies in the harder symmetry energy of the latter. The study shows that the density dependence of the symmetry energy directly influences the amount of strangeness within hot and dense matter, subsequently impacting thermodynamic quantities like the temperature for a given entropy per baryon. These differences are expected to affect the evolution of a protoneutron star or binary neutron star mergers. Additionally, several parametrizations calibrated to lambda hypernuclei, based on the DD2 and SFHo models, are proposed, satisfying the two solar mass constraint.

title: Magnetization reversal in bent nanofibers of different cross-sections
Abstract: Artificial ferromagnetic nanofiber networks with unique electronic, magnetic, mechanical, and other physical properties can be prepared using electrospinning, offering potential as bio-inspired cognitive computing units. This study investigates the physical parameters of these nanofiber networks using micromagnetic simulations. The study focuses on elementary single nanofibers with varying bending radii, from straight fibers to half-circles, examining their magnetization reversal processes under different angles with respect to the external magnetic field. As expected from the high aspect ratios and strong shape anisotropy, all magnetization reversal processes occur through domain wall processes. The study finds that changing the cross-section from circular to a circle-segment or rectangle significantly alters the coercive fields and their dependence on the bending radius, especially for magnetic fields oriented perpendicular to the fiber axes. For all three cross-sections, an angle of 45 degrees between the fiber orientation and the external magnetic field resulted in the least influence of the bending radius. The shapes of the longitudinal and transverse hysteresis curves exhibit strong differences, depending on cross-section, bending radius, and orientation to the magnetic field, often showing distinct transverse magnetization peaks perpendicular to the fibers for fibers not completely oriented parallel to the magnetic field. Varying these parameters provides a broad spectrum of magnetization reversal processes in magnetic nanofibers, enabling diverse scenarios for fiber-based information processing.

title: Personalized and Occupational-aware Age Progression by Generative Adversarial Networks
Abstract: Face age progression, predicting future appearances, is crucial for various applications and has garnered significant attention. The paper proposes a new occupational-aware adversarial face aging network that learns human aging processes under different occupations, considering both personality preservation and visually plausible texture changes for different occupations. Personalized networks with personalized losses in deep autoencoder networks are proposed to maintain personalized facial characteristics, while occupational-aware adversarial networks with occupational-aware adversarial losses are used to achieve more realistic texture changes. Experimental results demonstrate the advantages of the proposed method by comparing it with other state-of-the-art age progression methods.

title: Solar flares and their associated processes
Abstract: The evolution of the solar neutrino flux, described by the wave function, is examined in this study. The analysis holds for any standard model extensions with non-zero dipole magnetic and anapole moments. When the solar neutrino flux traverses the solar flare region during the preflare period, additional resonance conversions occur compared to the standard model. This leads to a weakening of the electron neutrino flux. Additionally, the existence of these resonances results in the appearance of electron antineutrinos that could be detected by terrestrial detectors. The hypothesis of electron neutrino-induced beta decays is also discussed, suggesting a potential decrease in the beta-decay rate for certain elements before a large solar flare. The possible influence of the electron antineutrino flux produced in superflares on the regime of a hypothetical georeactor is considered.

title: New closed analytical solutions for geometrically thick fluid tori around black holes: Numerical evolution and the onset of the magneto-rotational instability
Abstract: When a black hole accretes well below the Eddington rate, a geometrically thick, radiatively inefficient state of the accretion disk is established. There is a limited number of closed-form physical solutions for geometrically thick (non-selfgravitating) toroidal equilibria of perfect fluids orbiting a spinning black hole. These solutions are predominantly used as initial conditions for simulations of accretion in the aforementioned mode. However, different initial configurations might lead to different results and thus observational predictions drawn from such simulations. This study expands the known equilibria by introducing a number of closed multiparametric solutions with varying possibilities of rotation curves and geometric shapes. The study then investigates whether choosing these solutions as initial conditions influences the onset of accretion and the asymptotic state of the disk. A set of examples from the derived solutions is investigated in detail, analytically estimating the growth of the magneto-rotational instability (MRI) from their rotation curves. These analytically obtained tori are then evolved using the 2D magneto-hydrodynamical code HARM. The properties of these evolutions are studied through the mass, energy, and angular-momentum accretion rates. The study finds that the rotation curve plays a decisive role in the numerical onset of accretion, consistent with analytical MRI estimates. In the initial orbital periods, the average accretion rate is linearly proportional to the initial MRI rate in the toroids. The final state obtained from any initial condition within the studied class after an evolution of greater than or equal to 10 orbital periods is largely qualitatively identical, with quantitative properties varying within a single order of magnitude. The average values of the energy of the accreted fluid have an irregular dependency on initial data, and in some cases, fluid with energies many times its rest mass is systematically accreted.

title: The influence of the Coulomb interaction in electron bunch on the structural parameters determined by time-resolved electron diffraction
Abstract: Transitioning to temporal resolutions on the order of 1 picosecond or less raises questions about the accuracy of estimating dynamic parameters based on the analysis of time-dependent scattering intensity. The use of ultrashort pulses necessitates increasing the total exposure time and lengthening the data acquisition time. This can be partially mitigated by increasing the charge per pulse. However, increasing the number of electrons is limited by Coulomb repulsion between them, leading to distortion of the diffraction pattern and increased pulse duration. This study develops an analytical technique for estimating the deformation of the diffraction pattern caused by Coulomb repulsion of electrons in an electron bunch with a duration of less than 10 picoseconds, investigating the impact of this effect on the accuracy of determining interatomic distances.

title: The Impact of an AirBnb Host's Listing Description 'Sentiment' and Length On Occupancy Rates

However, the results show that while longer summary lengths may positively influence occupancy rates, more positive summary descriptions have no effect. The study concludes that other factors, such as the number of reviews and amenities, in addition to summary length, are better indicators of occupancy rate.

Abstract: CRISPR-Cas, a genetic adaptive immune system unique to prokaryotes, protects cells from phage and plasmid threats. Host cells adapt by incorporating DNA sequences from invading phages or plasmids into their CRISPR locus as spacers. These spacers are expressed as mobile surveillance RNAs that guide CRISPR-associated (Cas) proteins to protect against subsequent attacks. The study highlights recent research on phage mechanisms of CRISPR-Cas evasion and the conditions for population coexistence of phages with CRISPR-protected prokaryotes.

title: Critically excited states with enhanced memory and pattern recognition capacities in quantum brain networks: Lesson from black holes
Abstract: This study implements a mechanism, originally proposed as a model for the large memory storage capacity of black holes, in quantum neural networks. The study demonstrates that an exponentially increased capacity of pattern storage and recognition is achieved in certain critically excited states, without relying on synaptic plasticity. The study considers a simple network of interconnected quantum neurons with weak excitatory synaptic connections. The study reveals that for frozen synaptic weights, there exist critical states with enhanced memory storage capacity. These states are achieved through high excitation levels of some neurons, dramatically lowering the response threshold of other less-excited neurons despite weak synaptic connections. Consequently, these weaker-excited neurons acquire the capacity to store an exponentially large number of patterns within a narrow energy gap. The study demonstrates that these stored patterns can be recognized and retrieved with perfect response under arbitrarily soft input stimuli, contrasting with the absence of recall in the ground state of the system under the same stimuli. The study concludes that the state with the highest micro-state entropy and memory storage capacity is not necessarily a local minimum of energy, but rather an excited critical state. This phenomenon has a smooth classical limit and can serve to enhance memory storage capacity in classical brain networks.

title: Influence of surfactants on the electrohydrodynamic stretching of water drops in oil
Abstract: This paper presents experimental and numerical studies of the electrohydrodynamic stretching of a sub-millimeter-sized salt water drop immersed in oil with added non-ionic surfactant, subjected to a suddenly applied electric field approaching 1 kV/mm. By varying drop size, electric field strength, and surfactant concentration, the study covers the entire range of electric capillary numbers from 0 to the limit of drop disintegration. The results are compared with the analytical result by Taylor (1964) which predicts the asymptotic deformation as a function of electric capillary number. The study finds that the addition of surfactant damps transient oscillations and allows drops to stretch slightly beyond the stability limit established by Taylor. Further analysis of the damping of oscillations reveals that increasing surfactant concentration has a dual effect: initially increasing damping at low concentrations, followed by increasing the asymptotic deformation at higher concentrations. This behavior is explained by comparing the Marangoni forces and interfacial tension as the drops deform. Finally, the study observes a significant hysteresis effect when drops in oil with high surfactant concentration are subjected to repeated deformations with increasing electric field strengths. This effect is not attributed to flow or interfacial surfactant transport.

title: Survival behavior in the cyclic Lotka-Volterra model with a randomly switching reaction rate
Abstract: This study examines the survival behavior of the non-spatial cyclic Lotka-Volterra model, also known as the zero-sum rock-paper-scissors game, used to metaphorically describe the cyclic competition between three species. In large and finite populations, demographic fluctuations drive two species to extinction in a finite time, with the species with the smallest reproduction-predation rate being most likely to survive ("law of the weakest"). This study models environmental (external) noise by assuming that the reproduction-predation rate of the "strongest species" randomly switches between two values, representing more and less favorable external conditions. The study investigates the combined effects of environmental and demographic noise on species survival probabilities and mean extinction time, examining whether survival probabilities follow the law of the weakest and their dependence on external noise intensity and switching rate. Remarkably, when there is a finite number of switches before extinction, the survival probability of the predator of the species with a switching reaction rate typically varies non-monotonically with the external noise intensity, exhibiting optimal survival around a critical noise strength. The study also outlines the relationship with the case where all reaction rates switch on markedly different time scales.

title: The relationship between Mg II broad emission and quasar inclination angle

While the significance is not very strong (86%), a possible negative relationship between inclination angle and Fe II strength is observed, which, if true, could explain the Fe II anti-correlation with [O III] strength associated with Eigenvector 1. title: Region-based Quality Estimation Network for Large-scale Person Re-identification
Abstract: One of the primary limitations of video-based person re-identification is partial noise caused by occlusion, blur, and illumination. Since different spatial regions of a single frame have varying quality, and the quality of the same region changes across frames in a tracklet, effectively aggregating complementary information from all frames in a sequence is crucial. title: Cross Temporal Recurrent Networks for Ranking Question Answer Pairs

This paper explores the idea of learning temporal gates for sequence pairs (question and answer), jointly impacting the learned representations in a pairwise manner. The approach involves learning temporal gates through 1D convolutional layers and subsequently cross-applying them across question and answer for joint learning. Empirically, the study demonstrates that this conceptually simple sharing of temporal gates leads to competitive performance across multiple benchmarks. Intuitively, the network learns representations of question and answer pairs that are aware of each other's memory and forgetfulness, resulting in pairwise temporal gating. title: Delay Aware Intelligent Transient Stability Assessment System

However, most existing research assumes negligible measurement data transmission delay. To address this issue, a delay-aware intelligent system is developed, utilizing an ensemble of multiple long short-term memory networks. The proposed system enables early assessments with a significantly shorter response time by leveraging incomplete system variable measurements. Compared to existing work, this system achieves accurate assessments with improved efficiency. Numerous case studies demonstrate the superiority of the proposed intelligent system, enabling accurate assessments with a response time one-third less than state-of-the-art methodologies. Simulations indicate that noise in the measurements has a minimal impact on assessment performance, demonstrating the robustness of the proposed system.

title: Ionic Modulation of Interfacial Magnetism through Electrostatic Doping in Pt/YIG bilayer heterostructure

title: Relaxed Oracles for Semi-Supervised Clustering

Two realistic weak oracle models are considered, where ambiguity in answering depends on the distance between two points. The study shows that a small query complexity is sufficient for effective clustering with high probability by providing better pairs to the weak oracle. Experimental results on synthetic and real data demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in overcoming supervision uncertainties and achieving high-quality clusters.

title: Modular Continual Learning in a Unified Visual Environment

The research investigates how module architecture properties influence task learning efficiency, showing that a module motif incorporating specific design principles (e.g., early bottlenecks, low-order polynomial nonlinearities, and symmetry) significantly outperforms standard neural network motifs, requiring fewer training examples and fewer neurons to achieve high performance. Finally, a meta-controller architecture for task switching is presented, based on a dynamic neural voting scheme, allowing new modules to utilize information learned from previously seen tasks to substantially improve their own learning efficiency.

title: Non-Contextual Modeling of Sarcasm using a Neural Network Benchmark

title: Design of Sampling Set for Bandlimited Graph Signal Estimation

By relaxing this problem to a convex optimization problem, the study obtains the proportion of samples for each node given a budget for the total sample size. A probabilistic quantization is then used to determine the number of samples for each node. title: Positive semi-definite embedding for dimensionality reduction and out-of-sample extensions

title: Influence of jump-at-default in IR and FX on Quanto CDS prices

title: Role of Helium-Hydrogen ratio on energetic interchange mode behaviour and its effect on ion temperature and micro-turbulence in LHD

Notably, the occurrence rate of these EICs is significantly lower in He-rich discharges. We discuss the mechanisms responsible for the changes in drive and damping of these modes with He concentration. These EIC bursts are characterized by marked changes in the radial electric field, which is derived from the phase velocity of turbulence measured using the 2D phase contrast imaging (PCI) system. Similar bursts are detected in edge fast ion diagnostics. We identify gyro-Bohm scaling as a contributing factor to the change in ion temperature, although fast ion losses due to these EIC modes may also play a role in the dependence of ion temperature on He concentration, particularly in controlling the height of an "edge-pedestal" in the Ti profile. The steady-state level of fast ions is found to be larger in Helium-rich discharges based on measurements from a compact neutral particle analyser (CNPA) and the fast-ion component of the diamagnetic stored energy. These events also influence turbulence and transport. The large velocity shear induced during these events transiently enhances confinement and suppresses turbulence, with a larger net effect when bursts are more frequent in Hydrogen discharges. title: SU($N$) spin-wave theory: Application to spin-orbital Mott insulators
Abstract: We present the application of the SU(N) (N>2) spin-wave theory to spin-orbital Mott insulators exhibiting magnetic orders. This leads to the lowest spin-orbital locking energy levels due to inevitable spin-orbital multipole exchange interactions, making the SU(N) spin-wave theory a more suitable choice over the SU(2) theory. To implement this application, we introduce an efficient general local mean field approach that incorporates all local fluctuations into the SU(N) linear spin-wave theory. Our approach is first tested by calculating the multipolar spin-wave spectra of the SU(4) antiferromagnetic model. Subsequently, we apply it to spin-orbital Mott insulators. Our results indicate that Hund's coupling significantly influences the effectiveness of the isospin-1/2 representation when the spin-orbital coupling is not sufficiently large. Furthermore, we calculate the spin-wave spectra based on first principle calculations for two specific materials, α-RuCl3 and Sr2IrO4. title: Wetting properties of structured interfaces composed of surface-attached spherical nanoparticles

As pressure on the liquid film increases, the interface becomes more curved, and the three-phase contact line shifts along the spherical surface. However, due to re-entrant geometry, the contact line remains stable. Our molecular dynamics simulations demonstrate that the critical pressure for the Cassie-Baxter wetting state agrees well with the critical pressure estimated by numerically minimizing interfacial energy.

title: Spin-orbit coupling and magnetic field dependence of carriers states in a self-assembled quantum dot

Our findings demonstrate that the complex magnetic field dependence of the hole p-shell, observed in numerical simulations, can be accurately fit using a phenomenological model. title: Nucleosynthesis of transuranium nuclides under conditions of Mike, Par and Barbell thermonuclear explosions

Our model considers the time dependence of external parameters and processes accompanying the beta decay of neutron-rich nuclei. Beta-delayed process probabilities are calculated based on the microscopic theory of finite Fermi systems. We perform calculations of transuranium nuclides yields Y(A) for three experimental USA thermonuclear explosions: "Mike" (YM), "Par" (YP), and "Barbel" (YB). The root-mean-square deviations between our calculations and experimental data (r.m.s.) are 91% for YM, 33% for YP, and 29% for YB, significantly lower than other known calculations. We perform an exponential approximation of the experimental Y(A) dependences, obtaining r.m.s. values of 56%, 86.8%, and 60.2% for YM, YP, and YB, respectively, which is better or comparable to other calculations. title: The Cultural Evolution of National Constitutions

Using these topics, we construct a diffusion network for borrowing from ancestral constitutions back to the US Constitution of 1789. Our analysis reveals that constitutions are complex cultural recombinants. This process results in a small number of highly innovative (influential) constitutions, some of which remain unidentified in the current literature. Our findings provide novel insights into the critical nodes within the constitution-making network. The structure of the constitutional network reflects periods of intense constitution creation and systematic patterns of variation in constitutional lifespan and temporal influence.

title: Sustenance of phytoplankton in the subpolar North Atlantic during the winter through patchiness
Abstract: This study investigates the influence of two factors that affect mixed layer depth and potentially contribute to phytoplankton sustenance over winter: 1) variability of air-sea fluxes and 2) three-dimensional processes arising from strong fronts. Our results indicate that during winter, when the average mixed layer is significantly deeper than the euphotic layer and daylight hours are short, phytoplankton production is relatively insensitive to high-frequency variability in air-sea fluxes. The duration of upper ocean stratification due to high-frequency variability in air-sea fluxes is brief and has a minimal impact on phytoplankton production. Conversely, slumping of fronts creates patchy, stratified, shallow regions that persist considerably longer than stratification caused by changes in air-sea fluxes. Our simulations show that before spring warming, the average MLD with fronts is about 700 m shallower than the average MLD without fronts. Therefore, fronts increase the residence time of phytoplankton in the euphotic layer and contribute to phytoplankton growth. Our results indicate that before spring warming, the depth-integrated phytoplankton concentration is approximately twice as large in the presence of fronts compared to scenarios without fronts. Hence, fronts play a crucial role in setting the MLD and sustaining phytoplankton during winter. title: Small world yields optimal public goods in presence of both altruistic and selfish cooperators
Abstract: Empirical studies have demonstrated that individual behaviors are significantly influenced by social conformity, including punishment. However, a coevolutionary theoretical framework that considers the effects of conformity on individuals' punishment behaviors has yet to be established. This study proposes a coevolutionary game model to extend the theory of cooperation with conformity in the spatial public goods game by incorporating pool punishment and two converse feedback modes of conformity that significantly affect cooperators' punishment behaviors. We investigate how different parameters and spatial structures govern evolutionary dynamics on three types of networks using mean-field analysis based on replicator dynamics and Monte Carlo simulations. On regular lattices, defectors are generally eliminated as cooperators, particularly selfish cooperators, have significant evolutionary advantages due to strong network reciprocity. Simultaneously, the number of altruistic cooperators declines. Conversely, abundant shortcuts in regular random networks lead to the prevalence of altruistic cooperators; however, cooperators suffer from free-riding behaviors by defectors. Notably, we find that small-world topology can simultaneously enhance cooperators' ability to outperform defectors through strong network reciprocity and facilitate the expansion of altruistic cooperators by providing rich contacting opportunities with defectors. Therefore, we conclude that small-world topology is the optimal network structure for the dominance of altruistic cooperators.

title: Local Clustering Coefficient of Spatial Preferential Attachment Model
Abstract: This paper examines the clustering properties of the Spatial Preferential Attachment (SPA) model. This model combines geometry and preferential attachment using the concept of spheres of influence. Previous research has shown that graphs generated by the SPA model resemble real-world networks in many aspects. Moreover, the SPA model has been successfully applied to various practical applications. However, the clustering properties of the SPA model have not been fully analyzed. The clustering coefficient is a crucial characteristic of complex networks, closely related to its community structure. In this paper, we investigate the behavior of C(d), which represents the average local clustering coefficient for vertices of degree d. Empirical evidence suggests that in real-world networks, C(d) typically decreases as 1/d^a for some a>0, often with a=1. We prove that in the SPA model, C(d) decreases as 1/d. Furthermore, we demonstrate that not only the average but also the individual local clustering coefficient of a vertex v with degree d behaves as 1/d if d is sufficiently large. These findings further confirm the suitability of the SPA model for fitting various real-world complex networks.

title: Whole planet coupling between climate, mantle, and core: Implications for the evolution of rocky planets
Abstract: Earth's climate, mantle, and core interact over geologic timescales. Climate influences the occurrence of plate tectonics on a planet, with cool climates being favorable because they enhance stresses in the lithosphere, suppress plate boundary annealing, and promote hydration and weakening of the lithosphere. Plate tectonics plays a vital role in the long-term carbon cycle, which helps maintain a temperate climate. Plate tectonics provides long-term cooling of the core, essential for generating a magnetic field. The magnetic field, in turn, shields atmospheric volatiles from the solar wind. Coupling between climate, mantle, and core may explain the divergent evolution of Earth and Venus. As Venus lies too close to the sun for liquid water to exist, there is no long-term carbon cycle, resulting in an extremely hot climate. Consequently, plate tectonics cannot operate, and a long-lived core dynamo cannot be sustained due to insufficient core cooling. On planets within the habitable zone where liquid water is possible, a wide range of evolutionary scenarios can occur, depending on initial atmospheric composition, bulk volatile content, or the timing of plate tectonics initiation, among other factors. Many of these evolutionary trajectories would render the planet uninhabitable. However, there is still significant uncertainty regarding the nature of the coupling between climate, mantle, and core. Future research is needed to constrain potential evolutionary scenarios and the likelihood of an Earth-like evolution.

title: Designing Coalition-Proof Reverse Auctions over Continuous Goods
Abstract: This paper examines reverse auctions involving continuous values of different types of goods, general nonconvex constraints, and second stage costs. We aim to design payment rules and conditions that prevent coalitions of participants from influencing the auction outcome to obtain higher collective utility. Under the incentive-compatible Vickrey-Clarke-Groves mechanism, we demonstrate that coalition-proof outcomes are achieved if submitted bids are convex, and constraint sets are of a polymatroid-type. However, these conditions fail to capture the complexity of the general class of reverse auctions under consideration. By relaxing the property of incentive-compatibility, we investigate further payment rules that are coalition-proof without any additional conditions on submitted bids and constraint sets. Since calculating payments directly for these mechanisms is computationally challenging for auctions involving numerous participants, we present two computationally efficient methods. Our results are validated using several case studies based on electricity market data.

title: Shot noise of charge and spin transport in a junction with a precessing molecular spin
Abstract: Magnetic molecules and nanomagnets can be used to influence electronic transport in mesoscopic junctions. In a magnetic field, the precessional motion of the molecular spin leads to resonances in the dc- and ac-transport properties of a nanocontact, where electrons are coupled to the precession. Quantities like dc-conductance or ac-response provide valuable information about the level structure and coupling parameters. This study focuses on the current noise properties of such contacts, specifically examining charge current and spin-torque shot noise. Both types of noise exhibit step-like behavior as functions of bias voltage and magnetic field. The charge current noise shows pronounced dips around the steps, which we attribute to interference effects of electrons in quasienergy levels coupled by molecular spin precession. We demonstrate that certain components of the spin-torque current noise are directly related to Gilbert damping and, therefore, experimentally accessible. Our findings show that noise characteristics provide a more detailed investigation of the coherence of spin transport in contacts containing magnetic molecules.

We propose a novel hard negative-constant loss function for learning affine regions. The affine shape estimator, AffNet, trained with the hard negative-constant loss, outperforms state-of-the-art methods in bag-of-words image retrieval and wide baseline stereo. We find that, out to ${\\sim} 20$ pc from Sgr A$^*$, the XUV flux emitted during its quasar phase can remove several percent of a planet's H/He envelope by mass. In many cases, this removal results in bare rocky cores, many of which are situated in the habitable zones (HZs) of G-type stars. The erosion of sub-Neptune sized planets may be one of the most prevalent channels by which terrestrial super-Earths are created near the Galactic Center. Consequently, the planet population demographics may be significantly different near Sgr A$^*$ compared to the Galaxy's outskirts. The high stellar densities in this region (about seven orders of magnitude greater than the solar neighborhood) imply that the distance between neighboring rocky worlds is short ($500-5000$~AU). This proximity between potentially habitable terrestrial planets may enable widespread interstellar panspermia near the nuclei of galaxies. More generally, we predict these phenomena to be ubiquitous for planets in nuclear star clusters and ultra-compact dwarfs. Conversely, globular clusters are less affected by the black holes.

title: ATRank: An Attention-Based User Behavior Modeling Framework for Recommendation
Abstract: A user can be represented by their historical actions. A common approach to user modeling involves manually extracting aggregated features from heterogeneous behaviors. Recent works utilize RNN-based methods to provide an overall embedding of a behavior sequence, which can then be exploited by downstream applications. However, this approach can only preserve limited information or aggregated memories of a person. When downstream applications require modeled user features, they may lose the integrity of the specific, highly correlated behavior of the user, introducing noise from unrelated behaviors. This paper proposes an attention-based user behavior modeling framework called ATRank, primarily used for recommendation tasks. Our model considers heterogeneous user behaviors by projecting all behavior types into multiple latent semantic spaces, where influences can be exchanged among behaviors via self-attention. Downstream applications can then utilize the user behavior vectors using vanilla attention. Experiments demonstrate that ATRank achieves better performance and a faster training process. We further explore ATRank's ability to utilize a single unified model to predict different types of user behaviors simultaneously, showing comparable performance to highly optimized individual models.

title: The solutions to uncertainty problem of urban fractal dimension calculation

title: Poverty Mapping Using Convolutional Neural Networks Trained on High and Medium Resolution Satellite Images, With an Application in Mexico
Abstract: Mapping poverty distribution in developing countries remains a challenging and costly endeavor. These "poverty maps" are crucial for poverty targeting, public goods provision, political accountability, and impact evaluation, especially given the geographic dispersion of the poorest individuals. This paper explores the use of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to directly estimate poverty from high and medium-resolution satellite imagery. The study utilizes Planet and Digital Globe imagery covering 2 million square kilometers of Mexico, with spatial resolutions of 3-5 square meters and 50 square centimeters, respectively. Benchmark poverty estimates come from the 2014 MCS-ENIGH combined with the 2015 Intercensus, used to estimate poverty rates for 2,456 Mexican municipalities. CNNs are trained using data from 896 municipalities in the 2014 MCS-ENIGH. The study experimented with various architectures, including GoogleNet and VGG, ultimately using GoogleNet with weights fine-tuned from ImageNet. The findings indicate that: 1) the best models, incorporating satellite-estimated land use as a predictor, explain approximately 57% of poverty variation in a validation sample; 2) across all MCS-ENIGH municipalities, explanatory power reduces to 44% for the CNN prediction and landcover model; 3) CNN predictions alone explain 47% of poverty variation in the validation sample and 37% across all MCS-ENIGH municipalities; 4) in urban areas, Digital Globe imagery slightly outperforms Planet imagery, explaining 61% and 54% of poverty variation, respectively. The study concludes that CNNs can be trained to estimate poverty from satellite imagery but further research is needed to understand the influence of the training process on out-of-sample validation.

The precession frequency affects filament aggregation and conformation by changing the net torques on the filament ends. Using a time-dependent precession angle provides flexibility in choosing properties for filament aggregates. As an example, the study designs a field that twists chains together to dynamically assemble a self-healing gel.

title: Spin-orbit torques and tunable Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction in Co/Cu/Co trilayers

The bottom Co layer is assumed to have a fixed in-plane magnetization, while the top Co layer can be switched. The results reveal that the SOT on the top ferromagnet can be controlled by the bottom ferromagnet due to the nonlocal nature of the SOT in this system. Consequently, the SOT is anisotropic, with its magnitude varying with the direction of the applied electric field. The study also demonstrates that the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI) in the top layer is anisotropic, meaning the spin-spiral wavelength of spin-spirals depends on their in-plane propagation direction. This suggests that DMI can be readily tuned in magnetic trilayers by adjusting the magnetization direction of the bottom layer. For comparison, the study examines SOTs and DMI in Co/Cu magnetic bilayers. Interestingly, the SOTs and DMI are surprisingly large despite the small spin-orbit interaction of Cu.

title: A Modification of Particle Swarm Optimization using Random Walk
Abstract: Particle swarm optimization (PSO) has undergone significant modifications since its inception in 1995, primarily focused on adjusting inertia parameters in the velocity updating equation to enhance convergence rate. This paper proposes a novel approach where particle movement is not determined by velocity but instead by a constrained biased random walk. This random walk involves two parameters: a random process (e.g., coin toss) and the displacement magnitude of a particle. The proposed approach uses a biased random operation to determine the direction of particle movement, resulting in non-uniform movement across the solution space. This constrained, non-uniform movement helps the randomly walking particles converge faster than classical PSO. This approach eliminates the velocity term (Vi) and introduces a new parameter (K), a probabilistic function. Global best particle (PGbest), local best particle (PLbest), and constriction parameter (W) are replaced with Ptarg, which is loosely influenced by PGbest. The algorithm is tested on five benchmark functions and compared with classical PSO and Quantum Particle Swarm Optimization (QPSO). The results demonstrate significantly better performance than basic PSO and sometimes outperform QPSO in terms of convergence, search space, and number of iterations.

title: A generalized Levi condition for weakly hyperbolic Cauchy problems with coefficients low regular in time and smooth in space
Abstract: This paper examines the Cauchy problem for weakly hyperbolic m-th order partial differential equations with coefficients that are low-regular in time and smooth in space. It is well-known that Levi conditions are generally required for C^∞ or Gevrey well-posedness, even with smooth coefficients. The study uses moduli of continuity to describe the time regularity of the coefficients, weight sequences for characterizing their space regularity, and weight functions to define solution spaces. A generalized Levi condition is proposed to model the influence of multiple characteristics more freely. The paper establishes sufficient conditions for well-posedness of the Cauchy problem, linking the Levi condition, modulus of continuity, and weight sequence of the coefficients to the weight function of the solution space. Furthermore, the study shows that the influences of the Levi condition and low regularity of coefficients on the weight function of the solution space are independent of each other.

title: Cholesteric and screw-like nematic phases in systems of helical particles
Abstract: Recent numerical simulations of hard helical particle systems revealed a novel chiral nematic phase termed screw-like, characterized by the helical organization of particle C$_2$ symmetry axes around the nematic director with a periodicity equal to the particle pitch. This phase forms at high density and can follow a less dense uniform nematic phase, with their relative occurrence depending on helix morphology. As the simulations were conducted under three-dimensional periodic boundary conditions, two questions remained unanswered: 1) the real nature of the lower density nematic phase, expected to be cholesteric, and 2) the influence of the cholesteric phase on the existence and stability of the screw-like nematic phase. To address these questions, Monte Carlo and molecular dynamics simulations were performed on helical particle systems confined between two parallel repulsive walls. The study found that removing the periodicity constraint along one direction allows a relatively long-pitch cholesteric phase to form, replacing the uniform nematic phase, with a helical axis perpendicular to the walls. Importantly, the existence and stability of the screw-like nematic phase were not significantly affected by this change in boundary conditions.

title: Cosmological magnetic fields in turbulent matter

The study demonstrates that the amplification of the magnetic field results solely from the presence of the chiral magnetic effect. The influence of matter turbulence on magnetic field evolution is examined for different seed magnetic fields.

title: A Design-Time/Run-Time Application Mapping Methodology for Predictable Execution Time in MPSoCs

This paper presents a methodology that involves design space exploration coupled with formal performance analysis. This process yields multiple resource reservation configurations optimized for various objectives, with verified real-time guarantees for each individual application. Pareto-optimal configurations are then passed to run-time management, which selects a suitable mapping based on this information. To ensure real-time guarantees, the performance analysis must be composable and the influence of applications on each other must be bounded. The proposed approach achieves this through either spatial or temporal isolation of tasks, and by exploiting composable NoCs. Temporal isolation allows tasks from different applications to be mapped to the same resource, while spatial isolation assigns a computing resource exclusively to a single application. Experiments show that the proposed temporal isolation can increase the success rate in finding feasible application mappings by up to 30% and reduce energy consumption compared to spatial isolation.

Any quantum state with a second-order correlation function below 1/2 has a non-zero projection on the single-photon Fock state. The amplitude p of this projection is arbitrary and independent of g^{(2)}(0). However, the study extracts a lower bound on the single-to-multi-photon-projection ratio. A vacuum contribution in the quantum state of light artificially increases the value of g^{(2)}(0), concealing the actual single-photon projection. The paper proposes an effective second-order correlation function ˜g^{(2)}(0) that considers the influence of vacuum and provides lower and upper bounds on p. The study reinterprets single-photon purity, a common figure-of-merit in experiments, within these results and provides an effective version of this quantity. The paper compares various experimental and theoretical results and suggests a possible measurement scheme for determining ˜g^{(2)}(0).

Several of these jumps had identical heights within measurement error, suggesting entry of a limited number of vortices at a defect. The observed behavior aligns with recent theoretical predictions regarding vortex entry at grain boundaries in the material.

title: An Optimal and Progressive Approach to Online Search of Top-k Influential Communities
Abstract: Community search over large graphs is a fundamental problem in graph analysis. Recent studies propose computing top-k influential communities, where each reported community is a cohesive subgraph and has a high influence value. Existing approaches to top-k influential community search fall into two categories: index-based algorithms and online search algorithms without indexes. Index-based algorithms, while efficient for community searches, require pre-computation of a specialized index and only work for one built-in vertex weight vector. This paper investigates online search approaches and proposes an instance-optimal algorithm, LocalSearch, with time complexity linearly proportional to the size of the smallest subgraph accessed by a correct algorithm without indexes. The paper also proposes techniques to allow LocalSearch to progressively compute and report communities in decreasing influence value order, eliminating the need to specify k. Furthermore, the framework is extended to the general case of top-k influential community search for other cohesiveness measures. Extensive empirical studies on real graphs demonstrate that the proposed algorithms outperform existing online search algorithms by several orders of magnitude.

title: Analyzing Before Solving: Which Parameters Influence Low-Level Surgical Activity Recognition
Abstract:
Automatic low-level surgical activity recognition is a significant technical bottleneck for developing smart and situation-aware assistance in operating rooms. This study investigates sensors and signals that could facilitate this recognition. Low-level surgical activity represents semantic information about a surgical procedure, typically expressed by an action verb, surgical instrument, and operated anatomical structure. The study hypothesized that activity recognition does not require sensors for all three elements. A large-scale deep learning study was conducted on semantic data from 154 operations across four surgeries. The results showed that instrument and verb encode similar information, implying that only one needs to be tracked, preferably the instrument. However, the anatomical structure provides unique cues and is crucial for recognition. For all surgeries studied, a combination of two elements, always including the structure, proved sufficient for confidently recognizing activities. In the presence of noise, combining information about the instrument, structure, and historical context produced better results than a simple combination of all three elements. The study also made several observations regarding surgical practices, providing insights for designing a new generation of operating rooms.

Our results demonstrate improved detection performance and provide insights into the process of contextual inference for object detection. Abstract:
We investigate a stochastic transport equation with a multiplicative noise term. Assuming an $L^q(0,T;W^{1,p}({\mathbb R}^d;{\mathbb R}^d))$ drift coefficient and $W^{1,r}({\mathbb R}^d)$ initial data, we prove the existence and uniqueness of stochastic strong solutions (in $W^{1,r}_{loc}({\mathbb
R}^d)$). Specifically, when $r=\infty$, we establish a Lipschitz estimate for solutions, a question left open by Fedrizzi and Flandoli in the case of an $L^q(0,T;L^p({\mathbb R}^d;{\mathbb R}^d))$ drift coefficient. Notably, in contrast to the deterministic case, where an $L^q(0,T;W^{1,p}({\mathbb
R}^d;{\mathbb R}^d))$ drift coefficient and $W^{1,p}({\mathbb R}^d)$ initial data might lead to non-existence of strong solutions (in $W^{1,p}_{loc}({\mathbb
R}^d)$), we demonstrate that a multiplicative stochastic perturbation of Brownian type is sufficient to ensure well-posedness of the equation. This provides an intriguing example of a deterministic PDE that becomes well-posed under the influence of multiplicative Brownian noise. Our findings extend the existing results in  \cite{FF2,FGP1}.

title: Height of a faceted macrostep for sticky steps in a step-faceting zone
Abstract: This study explores the influence of driving force on the surface velocity, average height of merged steps, terrace-surface-slope, and elementary step velocity in a non-equilibrium steady-state using the Monte Carlo method. The study is based on a lattice model, the restricted solid-on-solid model with point-contact type step--step attraction (p-RSOS model). The temperature is chosen to be in the step-faceting zone, where the surface is surrounded by the (001) terrace and the (111) faceted step at equilibrium. Long-time simulations are conducted at this temperature to obtain steady-states for various driving forces affecting surface growth/recession. A Wulff figure of the p-RSOS model is produced using the anomalous surface tension calculated via the density-matrix renormalization group method. Although the p-RSOS model is simplified, it exhibits a wide range of dynamics in the step-faceting zone. There are four characteristic driving forces, $\\Delta \\mu_y$, $\\Delta \\mu_f$, $\\Delta\n\\mu_{co}$, and $\\Delta \\mu_R$. For $\\Delta \\mu_{co}<|\\Delta \\mu|<\\Delta \\mu_R$, the surface grows/recedes through successive step attachment-detachment to/from a macrostep. When $|\\Delta \\mu|$ exceeds $\\Delta \\mu_R $, the macrostep vanishes, and the surface undergoes kinetic roughening. Classical 2D heterogeneous multi-nucleation is determined to be valid with slight modifications based on Monte Carlo results of step velocity and surface slope changes. Finite size effects are also found to be distinct near equilibrium.

title: Feature importance scores and lossless feature pruning using Banzhaf power indices

title: Modelling stochastic resonance in humans: the influence of lapse rate
Abstract: Adding noise to a sensory signal typically degrades human performance. However, noise can also enhance performance through a phenomenon known as stochastic resonance (SR). This paradoxical effect can be exploited in psychophysical experiments to gain insights into the sensory system's noise processing capabilities. This work develops a model for stochastic resonance to investigate the influence of noise on human perception, incorporating the biological parameter of 'lapse rate'. We demonstrate that including lapse rate allows for the occurrence of stochastic resonance in terms of the performance metric d'. Conversely, high levels of lapse rate eliminate stochastic resonance. We also show that noise generated in the brain (i.e., internal noise) can obscure any stochastic resonance effects in experimental settings. Further, we relate the model to a standard equivalent noise model, the linear amplifier model, and show that lapse rate can function to scale the threshold versus noise (TvN) curve, similar to the efficiency parameter in equivalent noise (EN) models. Consequently, lapse rate provides a psychophysical explanation for reduced efficiency in EN paradigms. Moreover, ignoring lapse rate may lead to overestimation of internal noise in equivalent noise paradigms. Overall, describing stochastic resonance using signal detection theory, incorporating lapse rate, could offer valuable new insights into how human performance is influenced by internal and external noise.

title: Finite volume effects on the chiral phase transition from Dyson-Schwinger equations of QCD
Abstract: Within the framework of Dyson-Schwinger equations of QCD, we investigate finite volume effects on the chiral phase transition, specifically focusing on the influence on the position of the possible pseudo-critical end point (pCEP). Our results show that in the chiral limit case (current quark mass $m=0$), the absolute value of quark condensate decreases for smaller volumes. More interestingly, the pseudo-critical temperature $T_c(\\mu=0)$ also decreases, aligning with Polyakov Nambu--Jona-Lasinio model results and contradicting the Polyakov linear sigma model prediction. These conclusions hold for the $m>0$ case in our calculations. Additionally, the results for pCEP as a function of different volumes indicate that $T$ of pCEP decreases for smaller volumes, while $\\mu$ of pCEP increases, which are qualitatively closer to Polyakov linear sigma model results. For our model setup, results for systems larger than (5 fm)$^3$ closely approximate those from infinite volume, but for smaller volumes, the corrections become non-negligible, even significantly affecting signatures of the results from an infinite system. There is also a possibility that if the system size is too small, the entire phase transition would become a crossover, meaning no pCEP exists. It is evident that finite volume effects require further research.

title: Characterizing Dust Attenuation in Local Star Forming Galaxies: Inclination Effects and the 2175Å Feature

The highest inclination subpopulation (b/a<0.42) exhibits a NUV excess in its average selective attenuation, which, if interpreted as a 2175\\AA\\ feature, is best fit with a bump strength of 17-26% of the MW value. No excess is observed in the average attenuation curve of lower inclination galaxies. The differential reddening between the stellar continuum and ionized gas decreases with increasing inclination. We find that higher inclination galaxies have slightly higher values of $R_V$, although this is poorly constrained due to uncertainties. We outline possible explanations for these trends within a two-component dust model (dense cloud+diffuse dust) and find that they can be naturally explained if carriers of the 2175\\AA\\ feature are preferentially destroyed in star-forming regions (UV-bright regions).

title: Quantum information in the Posner model of quantum cognition
Abstract: Matthew Fisher recently proposed a mechanism for quantum phenomena influencing cognition: phosphorus nuclear spins may resist decoherence for extended periods, particularly when present in Posner molecules, serving as biological qubits. Assuming Fisher's hypothesis is correct, we explore the potential for biological systems to process quantum information (QI) effectively. We establish a framework for answering this question and construct applications of biological qubits for quantum error correction, communication, and computation. First, we propose a model for how QI encoded by spins transforms as Posner molecules form, pointing to a natural computational basis for qubits within these molecules. From this basis, we construct a quantum code that detects arbitrary single-qubit errors, with each molecule encoding one qutrit. Shifting from information storage to computation, we define the model of Posner quantum computation. To illustrate its quantum communication capabilities, we show how it can teleport information incoherently, transferring a state's weights. Dephasing results from simulating a coarse-grained Bell measurement during the entangling operation. While the universality of Posner quantum computation remains an open question, the model's operations can efficiently prepare a Posner state usable as a resource in universal measurement-based quantum computation. This state emerges from deforming the Affleck-Kennedy-Lieb-Tasaki (AKLT) state and is a projected entangled-pair state (PEPS). Finally, we demonstrate that entanglement can affect molecular binding rates, boosting binding probability from 33.6% to 100% in an example. title: The origin of ultra diffuse galaxies: stellar feedback and quenching

They represent a mostly uniform population of dark matter-dominated galaxies with M_star ~1e8 Msun, low metallicity, and a broad range of ages. The most massive simulated UDGs require earliest quenching and are therefore the oldest. Our simulations provide a good match to the central enclosed masses and velocity dispersions of observed UDGs (20-50 km/s). The enclosed masses of simulated UDGs remain largely fixed across a broad range of quenching times because the central regions of their dark matter halos complete their growth early. A typical UDG forms in a dwarf halo mass range of Mh~4e10-1e11 Msun. The most massive red UDG in our sample requires quenching at z~3 when its halo reached Mh ~ 1e11 Msun. If it instead continues growing in the field, by z=0 its halo mass reaches > 5e11 Msun, comparable to the halo of an L* galaxy. If our simulated dwarfs are not quenched, they evolve into bluer low-surface brightness galaxies with mass-to-light ratios similar to observed field dwarfs. While our simulation sample covers a limited range of formation histories and halo masses, we predict that UDG is a common, and perhaps even dominant, galaxy type around Ms~1e8 Msun, both in the field and in clusters.

title: Exocomets in the Proxima Centauri system and their importance for water transport
Abstract: The scenario and efficiency of water transport by icy asteroids and comets remain among the most important unresolved questions in planetary system formation. Observations suggest the presence of a second planet with a period longer than 60 days. Notably, we find that the ratio of learning rate to batch size is a key determinant of SGD dynamics and the width of the final minima, with higher values of this ratio leading to wider minima and often better generalization. title: Kerr-Newman-AdS Black Hole Surrounded by Perfect Fluid Matter in Rastall Gravity
Abstract: Rastall gravity is a modified Einstein general relativity where the energy-momentum conservation law is generalized to $T^{\\mu\\nu}_{~~;\\mu}=\\lambda\nR^{,\\nu}$. In this work, we derive the Kerr-Newman-AdS (KN-AdS) black hole solutions surrounded by perfect fluid matter in Rastall gravity using the Newman-Janis method and Mathematica package. We then analyze the black hole properties surrounded by two specific perfect fluid matter types: dark energy ($\\omega=-2/3$) and perfect fluid dark matter ($\\omega=-1/3$). Firstly, the Rastall parameter $\\kappa\\lambda$ can be constrained by the weak energy condition and strong energy condition. Secondly, analyzing the number of roots in the horizon equation, we determine the range of the perfect fluid matter intensity $\\alpha$, which depends on the black hole mass $M$ and the Rastall parameter $\\kappa\\lambda$. Thirdly, we study the influence of perfect fluid dark matter and dark energy on the ergosphere. We find that perfect fluid dark matter significantly affects ergosphere size, while dark energy has a smaller impact. Lastly, we observe that perfect fluid matter does not alter the singularity of the black hole. Furthermore, we investigate the rotation velocity in the equatorial plane for the KN-AdS black hole with dark energy and perfect fluid dark matter. We propose that the rotation curve diversity in Low Surface Brightness galaxies could be explained within the framework of Rastall gravity when both the perfect fluid dark matter halo and the baryon disk are considered.

The openness of the resonator is accounted for exactly by employing a spectral representation for the Green's function based on a set of non-Hermitian modes. Any discrete-level quantum system interacting with the electromagnetic continuum is subject to radiative decay and renormalization of its energy levels. Inside a cavity, these quantities can be significantly modified compared to vacuum. Typically, this modification can be captured by considering only the closest resonant cavity mode. However, in circuit-QED architecture with substantial coupling strengths, these rates are significantly influenced by far off-resonant modes. A multimode calculation over the infinite set of cavity modes leads to divergences unless an artificial cutoff is imposed. Previous studies have not identified the source of this divergence. The paper demonstrates that any multimode calculations of circuit-QED quantities are bound to diverge unless the effect of $A^2$ is accounted for to all orders exactly. The distribution function of particle displacement is found to be described by a Gumbel law with a shape parameter independent of time and strain amplitude $\\gamma$. Despite this universality, the mean squared displacement of a tagged particle exhibits power laws as a function of time, with an exponent dependent on $\\gamma$ and the time interval considered. These results are attributed to microscopic relaxation mechanisms involving friction and memory effects, suggesting that granular systems exhibit qualitatively different dynamical behavior compared to thermal glass-formers, instead resembling complex fluids. The paper concludes that granular materials can relax even under weak driving forces, impacting our understanding of granular solids.

title: Lazily Adapted Constant Kinky Inference for Nonparametric Regression and Model-Reference Adaptive Control
Abstract: Nonlinear Set Membership prediction, Lipschitz Interpolation, and Kinky Inference are machine learning approaches that utilize presupposed Lipschitz properties to compute inferences over unobserved function values. These methods offer convergence guarantees and bounds around predictions if a priori knowledge of the true best Lipschitz constant of the target function is available. Considering a more general setting based on Hölder continuity relative to pseudo-metrics, this paper proposes an online method for estimating the Hölder constant from function value observations potentially corrupted by bounded observational errors. Using this estimated constant to compute adaptive parameters within a kinky inference rule results in a nonparametric machine learning method for which strong universal approximation guarantees are established. This method can learn any continuous function within a worst-case error bound dependent on the level of observational uncertainty as data density increases. The paper demonstrates the application of this method to nonparametric model-reference adaptive control (MRAC), outperforming recently proposed alternatives based on Gaussian processes and RBF-neural networks in simulated aircraft roll-dynamics and performance metrics. Guarantees on the tracking success of learning-based controllers are provided for both batch and online learning settings in discrete-time systems.
label: AI

title: Very Fast Kernel SVM under Budget Constraints
Abstract: This paper introduces a fast online Kernel SVM algorithm under tight budget constraints. The algorithm splits the input space using LVQ and trains a Kernel SVM within each cluster. To enable online training, the size of the support vector set for each cluster is limited using different strategies. Experiments demonstrate that the algorithm achieves high accuracy while processing a large number of samples per second during both training and evaluation phases.
label: AI

title: Data-Driven Forecast of Dengue Outbreaks in Brazil: A Critical Assessment of Climate Conditions for Different Capitals
Abstract: Local climate conditions play a crucial role in the development of the mosquito population responsible for transmitting Dengue Fever. As the *Aedes Aegypti* mosquito is also a primary vector for the recent Zika and Chikungunya epidemics across the Americas, detailed monitoring of periods with favorable climate conditions for mosquito proliferation can improve the timing of vector-control efforts and other public health strategies. This study applies dimensionality reduction techniques and machine-learning algorithms to climate time series data to analyze their connection to Dengue outbreaks in seven major Brazilian cities. The analysis identifies two key variables and a specific period during the annual cycle that are highly predictive of epidemic outbreaks: the frequency of precipitation and temperature during an approximately two-month window of the winter season preceding the outbreak. These simple climate signatures may influence Dengue outbreaks months before their occurrence. Compressive-sensing procedures are employed to estimate missing entries in temperature and precipitation records for some of the more challenging datasets. Results indicate that each Brazilian capital considered has a unique signature of precipitation and temperature frequency in the winter preceding a Dengue outbreak. These climate contributions to vector populations are key factors in dengue dynamics and can potentially lead to more accurate prediction models and early warning systems. The paper highlights that critical temperature and precipitation signatures can vary significantly across cities, suggesting a more complex interplay between climate variables and dengue outbreaks than previously understood.
label: AI

title: Improved Stereo Matching with Constant Highway Networks and Reflective Confidence Learning
Abstract: This paper presents an improved three-step pipeline for stereo matching, introducing novelties at each stage. A new highway network architecture is proposed for computing the matching cost at each possible disparity, based on multilevel weighted residual shortcuts, trained with a hybrid loss that supports multilevel comparison of image patches. A novel post-processing step employs a second deep convolutional neural network for pooling global information from multiple disparities. This network outputs both the image disparity map, replacing the conventional "winner takes all" strategy, and a confidence score for the prediction. The confidence score is achieved by training the network with a new technique called reflective loss. Finally, the learned confidence is utilized for improved outlier detection in the refinement step. The proposed pipeline achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on the largest and most competitive stereo benchmarks, and the learned confidence outperforms existing alternatives.
label: AI

title: Abstracting Event-Driven Systems with Lifestate Rules
Abstract: This paper introduces lifestate rules, an approach for abstracting event-driven object protocols. Developing applications against event-driven software frameworks poses significant challenges, often stemming from the complex protocols that abstract the internal framework behavior. These protocols intertwine the proper registration of callbacks for receiving control from the framework with appropriate application programming interface (API) calls for delegating back to the framework. Lifestate rules unify lifecycle and typestate constraints in a single specification language. The paper's main contribution is a model of event-driven systems from which lifestate rules can be derived. These rules are then learned for Android framework types using specification mining techniques. The implementation identifies several rules characterizing the actual behavior of the Android framework.
label: AI

title: NIPS 2016 Tutorial: Generative Adversarial Networks
Abstract: This report summarizes a tutorial on generative adversarial networks (GANs) presented at NIPS 2016. The tutorial covers the following topics: (1) the importance of generative modeling, (2) the workings of generative models and comparison of GANs to other generative models, (3) the detailed operation of GANs, (4) research frontiers in GANs, and (5) state-of-the-art image models combining GANs with other methods. The tutorial concludes with three exercises for readers, along with their solutions.
label: AI

title: Expanding Subjective Lexicons for Social Media Mining with Embedding Subspaces
Abstract: Recent sentiment lexicon induction approaches have leveraged pre-trained word embeddings that capture latent semantic properties. However, embeddings optimized for a specific task, such as predicting contextual words, may not be optimal for other applications. This paper addresses this problem by exploiting task-specific representations induced through embedding sub-space projection, expanding lexicons describing multiple semantic properties. For each property, the model jointly learns suitable representations and the corresponding predictor. Experiments conducted on multiple subjective lexicons show that the model outperforms previous work and baselines, even in low training data regimes. Furthermore, lexicon-based sentiment classifiers built on top of these lexicons outperform similar resources and achieve performance comparable to supervised models.
label: AI

title: Cutting-off Redundant Repeating Generations for Neural Abstractive Summarization
Abstract: This paper addresses the issue of redundant repeating generation often observed in RNN-based encoder-decoder models. The proposed solution involves jointly estimating the upper-bound frequency of each target vocabulary in the encoder and controlling the output words based on this estimation in the decoder. The method demonstrates significant improvement over a strong RNN-based encoder-decoder baseline and achieves its best results on an abstractive summarization benchmark. |||
label: AI

title: On The Security Evaluation of Partial Password Implementations
Abstract: Partial passwords, widely used in the financial sector, offer a cheap way to prevent malware or key-loggers from capturing a user's full password. However, despite their prevalence, the security of this mechanism remains largely unexplored. This paper analyzes the security of partial password schemes under various challenge generation methods, specifically focusing on how the security varies with the number of challenge-response pairs available to an attacker. Additionally, the paper discusses server-side implementations based on information security experts' online discussions. This research aims to encourage further academic study on this topic.
label: AI

title: iMapD: intrinsic Map Dynamics exploration for uncharted effective free energy landscapes
Abstract: iMapD is a computer-assisted method for accelerating the exploration of uncharted Free Energy Surfaces (FES) and extracting coarse-grained information from atomistic simulations. It integrates Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations with nonlinear manifold learning techniques. iMapD biases the MD simulator towards unexplored regions of phase space by exploiting the smooth, low-dimensional geometry of the FES, which gradually becomes apparent during exploration.
label: AI

title: Learning Weighted Association Rules in Human Phenotype Ontology
Abstract: The Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) is a structured repository of disease-associated concepts, called HPO Terms.  Annotation is the process of associating HPO Terms with diseases. The Information Content (IC) of both HPO terms and annotations plays a crucial role in evaluating their relevance and specificity. HPO-Miner, a novel methodology presented in this paper, extracts Weighted Association Rules (AR) from annotated HPO data. By taking into account the source of annotation and its importance, HPO-Miner effectively identifies relevant rules from a biological perspective. A case study using publicly available HPO annotation datasets demonstrates the effectiveness of this methodology.
label: AI

title: p-DLA: A Predictive System Model for Onshore Oil and Gas Pipeline Dataset Classification and Monitoring - Part 1
Abstract: The increasing frequency of militant activity and rogue behavior in oil and gas regions has led to a surge in oil pipeline disruptions, resulting in substantial financial losses for multinational operators. To prevent such incidents, this paper proposes an artificial intelligence predictive monitoring system capable of classifying and recognizing patterns in pipeline datasets. This system employs a highly sparse Deviant Learning Algorithm (p-DLA) to synthesize a sequence of memory predictive clusters for monitoring, control, and decision-making.
