title: Visualizing the Effects of Predictor Variables in Black Box Supervised Learning Models
Abstract: When fitting black-box supervised learning models, visualizing the main effects of individual predictor variables and their low-order interaction effects is often essential. Partial dependence (PD) plots are the most popular approach for achieving this. However, PD plots suffer from a significant drawback when predictor variables are highly correlated, a common occurrence with large observational datasets. Specifically, PD plots require extrapolation of the response at predictor values far outside the multivariate envelope of the training data, potentially leading to unreliable results. While marginal plots (M plots) avoid such extrapolation, they produce biased and misleading results when predictors are dependent, analogous to the omitted variable bias in regression. This paper presents a novel visualization approach termed accumulated local effects (ALE) plots, which inherits the desirable characteristics of PD and M plots without their shortcomings. Like M plots, ALE plots do not require extrapolation; and like PD plots, they are not biased by the omitted variable phenomenon. Moreover, ALE plots are significantly less computationally expensive than PD plots.

title: Randomized Block Frank-Wolfe for Convergent Large-Scale Learning
Abstract: Frank-Wolfe (FW) solvers, known for their low-complexity iterations, are well-suited for various large-scale learning tasks. In the presence of block-separable constraints, randomized block FW (RB-FW) further reduces complexity by updating only a fraction of coordinate blocks per iteration. This work develops step sizes for RB-FW that enable flexible selection of the number of blocks to update per iteration while ensuring convergence and feasibility of the iterates. Convergence rates of RB-FW are established through computational bounds on a primal sub-optimality measure and on the duality gap. The novel bounds extend existing convergence analysis, which only applies to a step-size sequence that does not generally lead to feasible iterates. Furthermore, two classes of step-size sequences guaranteeing feasibility of the iterates are proposed to enhance flexibility in choosing decay rates. The novel convergence results are significantly broadened to encompass nonconvex objectives, and further assert that RB-FW with exact line-search reaches a stationary point at rate $\\mathcal{O}(1/\\sqrt{t})$. The performance of RB-FW with different step sizes and number of blocks is demonstrated in two applications, namely charging of electrical vehicles and structural support vector machines. Extensive simulated tests demonstrate the performance improvement of RB-FW compared to existing randomized single-block FW methods.

title: Unsupervised Learning for Computational Phenotyping
Abstract: The vast amounts of healthcare data available have led to the emergence of computational phenotyping, utilizing machine learning techniques to describe illnesses and other clinical concepts directly from the data. The traditional approach of using supervised learning relies on domain experts and faces two main limitations: requiring skilled humans to provide correct labels limits scalability and accuracy, and relying on existing clinical descriptions restricts the types of patterns that can be discovered. For example, it may fail to recognize that a disease treated as a single condition might actually have several subtypes with different phenotypes, as observed in asthma and heart disease. Recent research has shown successes using unsupervised learning methods, highlighting the potential for discovering hidden patterns in Electronic Health Records (EHRs) that can lead to a deeper understanding of conditions and treatments. This work implements a method derived from Lasko et al., but implements it in Apache Spark and Python, generalizing it to laboratory time-series data in MIMIC-III. It is released as an open-source tool for exploration, analysis, and visualization, available at https://github.com/Hodapp87/mimic3_phenotyping.

title: Correlated signal inference by free energy exploration
Abstract: Inferring correlated signal fields with unknown correlation structures is highly relevant in scientific and technological contexts but poses significant conceptual and numerical challenges. To address these challenges, the correlated signal inference (CSI) algorithm is developed within information field theory (IFT), and its numerical implementation is discussed. The free energy exploration (FrEE) strategy is introduced for numerical information field theory (NIFTy) applications. The FrEE strategy allows the mathematical structure of the inference problem to determine the dynamics of the numerical solver. FrEE utilizes the Gibbs free energy formalism for all involved unknown fields and correlation structures without marginalizing nuisance quantities. This approach avoids the complexity often imposed by marginalization in IFT equations. FrEE simultaneously solves for the mean and uncertainties of signal, nuisance, and auxiliary fields, while exploiting any analytically calculable quantities. Finally, FrEE employs a problem-specific and self-tuning exploration strategy to quickly identify the optimal field estimates and their uncertainty maps. For all estimated fields, properly weighted posterior samples can be generated from their exact, fully non-Gaussian distributions. The FrEE strategies are developed for the CSI of a normal, a log-normal, and a Poisson log-normal IFT signal inference problem, and their performances are demonstrated through their NIFTy implementations.

title: Multi-Region Neural Representation: A novel model for decoding visual stimuli in human brains
Abstract: Multivariate Pattern (MVP) classification offers significant potential for decoding visual stimuli in the human brain using task-based fMRI data sets. MVP techniques face several challenges, including noise and sparsity reduction, defining effective regions of interest (ROIs), visualizing results, and the cost of brain studies. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a novel neural representation model that automatically detects active regions for each visual stimulus and utilizes these anatomical regions for visualizing and analyzing functional activities. This model allows neuroscientists to investigate the effect of a stimulus on each detected region rather than simply studying voxel fluctuations in manually selected ROIs. The method analyzes snapshots of brain images to reduce sparsity instead of using the entire fMRI time series. Additionally, a new Gaussian smoothing method is introduced for removing noise from voxels at the ROI level. The proposed method enables the combination of different fMRI data sets to reduce the cost of brain studies. Experimental studies on 4 visual categories (words, consonants, objects, and nonsense photos) confirm that the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

title: Clustering Algorithms: A Comparative Approach
Abstract: Many real-world systems can be analyzed in terms of pattern recognition tasks, making the application of machine learning methods in practical applications essential. While numerous classification methods have been proposed, there is no consensus on which methods are most suitable for a given dataset. Consequently, it is crucial to comprehensively compare methods across various scenarios. This paper systematically compares 7 well-known clustering methods available in the R language. To account for the many possible variations in data, artificial datasets with tunable properties (number of classes, separation between classes, etc.) are considered. Additionally, the sensitivity of the clustering methods to their parameter configuration is evaluated. The results indicate that the spectral approach generally outperforms other clustering algorithms when considering the default configurations of the adopted methods. The default configuration of the adopted implementations is found to be inaccurate in many cases. In these instances, a simple approach based on random selection of parameter values proves to be a good alternative for improving performance. Overall, the reported approach provides guidance for selecting clustering algorithms.

title: Abstractive Headline Generation for Spoken Content by Attentive Recurrent Neural Networks with ASR Error Modeling
Abstract: Headline generation for spoken content is essential because spoken content is difficult to display on screen and browse by users. It is a special type of abstractive summarization where summaries are generated word by word from scratch without utilizing any part of the original content. Many deep learning approaches for headline generation from text documents have been proposed recently, all requiring large amounts of training data, which is difficult to obtain for spoken document summarization. This paper proposes an ASR error modeling approach to learn the underlying structure of ASR error patterns and incorporate this model into an Attentive Recurrent Neural Network (ARNN) architecture. This enables the model for abstractive headline generation for spoken content to be learned from abundant text data and ASR data for specific recognizers. Experiments show promising results, verifying the effectiveness of the proposed ASR error model even when the input spoken content is recognized by a recognizer significantly different from the one the model was trained on.

title: Image-Text Multi-Modal Representation Learning by Adversarial Backpropagation
Abstract: This paper presents a novel method for image-text multi-modal representation learning. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first approach to apply adversarial learning concepts to multi-modal learning without exploiting image-text pair information to learn multi-modal features. Unlike most previous methods that utilize image-text pair information for multi-modal embedding, this approach only uses category information. The paper demonstrates that multi-modal features can be achieved without image-text pair information, and the proposed method results in a more similar distribution between image and text in multi-modal feature space compared to other methods using image-text pair information. The multi-modal feature is shown to possess universal semantic information, even though it was trained for category prediction. The model is end-to-end backpropagation, intuitive, and easily extended to other multi-modal learning tasks.

title: Text Summarization using Deep Learning and Ridge Regression
Abstract: Models are developed and relevant features are extracted for automatic text summarization, investigating the performance of different models on the DUC 2001 dataset. Two different models are developed: a ridge regressor and a multi-layer perceptron. Hyperparameters are varied, and their performance is evaluated. The summarization task is segregated into two main steps: sentence ranking and sentence selection. In the first step, given a document, sentences are sorted based on their importance. In the second step, to obtain non-redundant sentences, sentences with high similarity to previously selected sentences are eliminated.

title: Generalized Optimal Matching Methods for Causal Inference
Abstract: An encompassing framework for matching, covariate balancing, and doubly robust methods for causal inference from observational data, called generalized optimal matching (GOM), is developed. The framework is obtained by generalizing a new functional-analytical formulation of optimal matching, leading to the class of GOM methods. A single unified theory is provided to analyze tractability, consistency, and efficiency for these methods. Many commonly used existing methods are included in GOM and, using their GOM interpretation, can be extended to optimally and automatically trade off balance for variance and outperform their standard counterparts. As a subclass, GOM gives rise to kernel optimal matching (KOM), which is notable for combining many of the positive properties of other methods in one. KOM, solved as a linearly constrained convex-quadratic optimization problem, inherits both the interpretability and model-free consistency of matching but can also achieve the $\\sqrt{n}$-consistency of well-specified regression and the efficiency and robustness of doubly robust methods. In settings of limited overlap, KOM enables a very transparent method for interval estimation for partial identification and robust coverage. These benefits are demonstrated in examples with both synthetic and real data.

title: Denoising Poisson Phaseless Measurements via Orthogonal Dictionary Learning
Abstract: Phaseless diffraction measurements recorded by a CCD detector are often affected by Poisson noise. This paper proposes a dictionary learning model employing patches based sparsity to denoise Poisson phaseless measurement. The model consists of three terms: (i) a representation term by an orthogonal dictionary, (ii) an $L^0$ pseudo norm of the coefficient matrix, and (iii) a Kullback-Leibler divergence to fit phaseless Poisson data. Fast Alternating Minimization Method (AMM) and Proximal Alternating Linearized Minimization (PALM) are adopted to solve the established model with convergence guarantee, and global convergence for PALM is derived. The subproblems for both algorithms have fast solvers, and the solutions for sparse coding and dictionary updating both have closed forms due to the orthogonality of learned dictionaries. Numerical experiments for phase retrieval using coded diffraction and ptychographic patterns are performed to show the efficiency and robustness of the proposed methods, which, by preserving texture features, produce visually and quantitatively improved denoised images compared to other phase retrieval algorithms without regularization and local sparsity promoting algorithms.

title: Proactive QoE Provisioning in Heterogeneous Access Networks using Hidden Markov Models and Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: Provisioning Quality of Experience (QoE) in heterogeneous access networks (HANs) can be achieved through handoffs. Existing approaches for QoE-aware handoffs either lack a network path probing method or lack efficient methods for QoE prediction. Additionally, current approaches do not explore the benefits of proactive QoE-aware handoffs, where user QoE is maximized by learning from past network conditions and by actions taken by the mobile device regarding handoffs. This paper makes two main contributions. First, a novel method for QoE prediction based on passive probing is proposed, developed, and validated. This method, based on hidden Markov models and the Multi-homed Mobility Management Protocol, eliminates the need for additional probe packets for QoE prediction, achieving an average QoE prediction accuracy of 97%. Second, a novel reinforcement learning-based method for proactive QoE-aware handoffs is proposed, developed, and validated. This method outperforms existing approaches by reducing the number of vertical handoffs by 60.65% while maintaining high QoE levels and extending crucial functionality such as passive probing mechanisms.

title: Understanding Neural Networks through Representation Erasure
Abstract: While neural networks have been successfully applied to numerous natural language processing (NLP) tasks, they come at the cost of interpretability. This paper proposes a general methodology to analyze and interpret decisions from a neural model by observing the effects of erasing various parts of the representation, such as input word-vector dimensions, intermediate hidden units, or input words. Several approaches are presented for analyzing the effects of such erasure, ranging from computing the relative difference in evaluation metrics to using reinforcement learning to erase the minimum set of input words in order to flip a neural model's decision. In a comprehensive analysis of multiple NLP tasks, including linguistic feature classification, sentence-level sentiment analysis, and document-level sentiment aspect prediction, it is shown that the proposed methodology not only offers clear explanations about neural model decisions but also provides a way to conduct error analysis on neural models.

title: Ideology Detection for Twitter Users with Heterogeneous Types of Links
Abstract: Ideology detection involves studying the latent (political) placement of individuals. Traditionally, this has been investigated for politicians based on their voting behaviors. Recently, an increasing number of studies have started to address the ideology detection problem for ordinary users based on their online behaviors captured through social media, such as Twitter. However, most existing methods for ideology detection on social media oversimplify the problem as a binary classification problem (e.g., liberal vs. conservative). Additionally, although social links can play a crucial role in determining an individual's ideology, most existing work ignores the heterogeneous types of links present in social media. This paper proposes a method for detecting *numerical* ideology positions for Twitter users based on their *follow*, *mention*, and *retweet* links to a selected set of politicians. A unified probabilistic model is proposed that can (1) explain the reasons for link formation between individuals in terms of their ideology, (2) integrate heterogeneous types of links together in determining people's ideology, and (3) automatically learn the quality of each type of link in deciding one's ideology. Experiments have demonstrated the advantages of the proposed model in terms of both ranking and political leaning classification accuracy. It is shown that (1) using multiple types of links is more effective than using any single type of link alone to determine an individual's ideology, and (2) the model is even superior to baselines when dealing with individuals who are sparsely linked in one type of link. The detected ideology for Twitter users is shown to align well with intuition.

title: Predicting the Industry of Users on Social Media
Abstract: Automatic profiling of social media users is an important task for supporting a multitude of downstream applications. While several studies have used social media content to extract and study collective social attributes, there is a lack of substantial research addressing the detection of a user's industry. This task is framed as classification using both feature engineering and ensemble learning. The proposed industry-detection system utilizes both posted content and profile information to detect a user's industry with 64.3% accuracy, significantly outperforming the majority baseline in a taxonomy of fourteen industry classes. Qualitative analysis suggests that a person's industry not only affects the words used and their perceived meanings but also the number and type of emotions being expressed. |||

title: Unsupervised Video Segmentation via Spatio-Temporally Nonlocal Appearance Learning
Abstract: Video object segmentation is challenging due to factors such as rapid motion, cluttered backgrounds, and variations in object appearance and shape. Existing methods primarily utilize appearance information between consecutive frames, neglecting valuable long-term nonlocal information, leading to difficulties in handling significant viewpoint changes and non-rigid deformations. This paper proposes a simple yet effective approach to leverage long-term spatio-temporally nonlocal appearance information for unsupervised video segmentation. The approach leverages the reoccurrence of region appearance within a video. It first generates superpixels representing the foreground and background, then updates each superpixel's appearance based on its long-term spatio-temporally nonlocal counterparts identified using approximate nearest neighbor search with the efficient KD-tree algorithm. These updated appearances are then used to construct a spatio-temporal graphical model incorporating superpixel label consistency potentials. Finally, segmentation is achieved by optimizing the graphical model iteratively through appearance model updates and label estimations. Extensive evaluations on the SegTrack and YouTube-Objects datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, outperforming several state-of-the-art approaches.

title: Families of DFAs as Acceptors of $ω$-Regular Languages
Abstract: Families of deterministic finite automata (FDFAs) provide an alternative formalism for recognizing ω-regular languages. FDFAs were introduced to align automaton states with right congruence relations, similar to the Myhill-Nerode theorem for regular languages. This correlation proves beneficial for learning algorithms. Recently, it was shown that ω-regular languages can be learned from membership and equivalence queries using FDFAs as acceptors. This paper investigates the suitability of FDFAs for defining ω-regular languages, examining the complexity of Boolean operations (complementation and intersection) on FDFAs, decision problems (emptiness and language containment), and the succinctness of FDFAs compared to standard deterministic and nondeterministic ω-automata. It demonstrates that FDFAs share the advantages of deterministic automata regarding Boolean operations and decision problems, as these can be performed in nondeterministic logarithmic space. Polynomial translations are provided from deterministic Büchi and co-Büchi automata to FDFAs and vice versa. However, translating an NBA to an FDFA can involve an exponential blowup. Additionally, FDFAs are more succinct than deterministic parity automata (DPAs) as translating a DPA to an FDFA can be done with only a polynomial increase, while the opposite direction inevitably involves an exponential blowup in the worst case.

title: Improving Human-Machine Cooperative Visual Search With Soft Highlighting
Abstract: Advances in machine learning have led to systems that achieve human-level performance in certain visual tasks, such as object identification. However, other tasks requiring visual expertise, such as satellite and medical imagery analysis, are unlikely to be entrusted to machines for the foreseeable future. This paper presents a human-machine cooperative approach to visual search, aiming to surpass the performance of either humans or machines alone. Traditionally, augmenting human performance with automatic classifiers involves highlighting regions of an image likely containing a target. However, human experts typically find this "hard highlighting" approach unsatisfactory. Instead, the paper proposes a "soft highlighting" technique that modulates the saliency of regions of the visual field based on the confidence level of the classifier. Experiments conducted on both synthetic and natural images demonstrate that soft highlighting achieves a performance synergy that surpasses that of hard highlighting.

title: Tensor clustering with algebraic constraints gives interpretable groups of crosstalk mechanisms in breast cancer
Abstract: This paper introduces a tensor-based clustering method for extracting sparse, low-dimensional structure from high-dimensional, multi-indexed datasets. This framework enables the detection of data clusters while incorporating structural requirements encoded as algebraic constraints in a linear program. The proposed clustering method is general and adaptable to various applications in science and industry. The method is illustrated through experiments measuring the response of genetically diverse breast cancer cell lines to an array of ligands. Each experiment involves a cell line-ligand combination and includes time-course measurements of the early-signaling kinases MAPK and AKT at two different ligand dose levels. By imposing appropriate structural constraints and respecting the multi-indexed structure of the data, cluster analysis can be optimized for biological interpretation and therapeutic understanding. The paper then performs a systematic, large-scale exploration of mechanistic models of MAPK-AKT crosstalk for each cluster. This analysis quantifies the heterogeneity of breast cancer cell subtypes and generates hypotheses about the signaling mechanisms mediating the cell lines' responses to ligands.

title: The prevalence of chaotic dynamics in games with many players
Abstract: This paper investigates adaptive learning in a typical p-player game where payoffs are randomly generated and remain fixed. Player strategies evolve over time as they learn, resulting in trajectories in the strategy space exhibiting diverse qualitative behaviors, including attractors such as unique fixed points, multiple fixed points, limit cycles, and chaos. In the limit of complicated games with numerous possible player actions, a generating-functional approach is used to determine the parameter range where learning dynamics converge to a stable fixed point. The size of this region diminishes as the number of players increases, suggesting that complex non-equilibrium behavior, exemplified by chaos, might be the norm for intricate games with many players.

title: On Spectral Analysis of Directed Signed Graphs
Abstract: The adjacency eigenspace of a network has been shown to hold crucial information about its underlying structure. However, spectral analysis of adjacency matrices for directed signed graphs remains unexplored. This paper derives theoretical approximations of spectral projections from such directed signed networks using matrix perturbation theory. The derived theoretical results are used to analyze the influences of negative intra-cluster and inter-cluster directed edges on node spectral projections. A spectral clustering-based graph partition algorithm, SC-DSG, is developed and evaluated on both synthetic and real datasets. Both theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.

title: Constructing Effective Personalized Policies Using Counterfactual Inference from Biased Data Sets with Many Features
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach for constructing effective personalized policies in scenarios where observed data lacks counter-factual information, is biased, and possesses many features. This approach is applicable in various settings ranging from healthcare and advertising to education and finance. These settings share the common characteristic that the decision maker can observe an array of features, the action taken, and the realized reward for each instance, but not the rewards for actions that were not taken (counterfactual information). Learning in such settings is further complicated by the typical bias in the observed data due to the existing policy and the vast array of features potentially affecting the reward. The presented approach estimates propensity scores for the observed data, infers counterfactuals, identifies a small set of features most relevant for each possible action and instance, and prescribes a policy to be followed. Comparisons with the state-of-the-art algorithm on actual datasets demonstrate that the proposed algorithm achieves significant performance improvements.

title: Correlation Preserving Sparse Coding Over Multi-level Dictionaries for Image Denoising
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel image denoising method based on correlation-preserving sparse coding. The performance of dictionary-driven denoising methods can be limited by the instability and unreliability of correlations among basis sets. To address this, two effective regularized strategies are employed in the coding process. A graph-based regularizer is constructed to preserve global similarity correlations, adaptively capturing both the geometrical structures and discriminative features of textured patches. Edge weights in the graph are obtained by seeking a nonnegative low-rank construction. Additionally, a robust locality-constrained coding automatically preserves both spatial neighborhood information and internal consistency present in noisy patches while learning an overcomplete dictionary. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art denoising performance in terms of both PSNR and subjective visual quality.

title: Active Learning and Proofreading for Delineation of Curvilinear Structures
Abstract: Many state-of-the-art delineation methods rely on supervised machine learning algorithms, requiring manually annotated training data, which is time-consuming to obtain. Moreover, even minor classification errors can significantly impact the final result's topology. This paper presents a generic approach to addressing both of these problems by considering the influence of potential misclassification on the resulting delineation. In an Active Learning context, parts of linear structures are identified for annotation first to effectively train a classifier. Similarly, in a proofreading context, regions of the resulting reconstruction are identified for prioritized verification to achieve near-perfect results. By focusing the human expert's attention on potential classification mistakes, which are the most critical parts of the delineation, the required supervision is reduced. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated on microscopy images depicting blood vessels and neurons.

title: RSSL: Semi-supervised Learning in R
Abstract: This paper introduces an R package called RSSL for semi-supervised learning research in the R programming language. The purpose, methods included, their usage, and implementation are discussed. The paper then provides code examples to demonstrate how the package can be used to replicate well-known results from the semi-supervised learning literature.

title: DeMIAN: Deep Modality Invariant Adversarial Network
Abstract: Obtaining common representations from different modalities is crucial for their interchangeability in classification problems. For example, a classifier trained on image features in the common representations can be applied to text features in the representations. Existing multi-modal representation learning methods primarily focus on extracting rich information from paired samples and training a classifier based on corresponding labels. However, collecting paired samples and their labels simultaneously is labor-intensive. Addressing paired modal samples without their labels and single modal data with their labels independently is much easier than addressing labeled multi-modal data. To obtain common representations in such a situation, this paper proposes to make the distributions over different modalities similar in the learned representations, resulting in modality-invariant representations. A novel algorithm for modality-invariant representation learning, named Deep Modality Invariant Adversarial Network (DeMIAN), is proposed, utilizing the concept of Domain Adaptation (DA). DeMIAN's learned modality-invariant representations achieve better classification accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods, particularly for zero-shot learning benchmark datasets.

title: Supervised Opinion Aspect Extraction by Exploiting Past Extraction Results
Abstract: A key task in sentiment analysis of product reviews involves extracting product aspects or features that users have expressed opinions on. This paper focuses on supervised sequence labeling as the base approach for performing this task. While several extraction methods using sequence labeling methods like Conditional Random Fields (CRF) and Hidden Markov Models (HMM) have been proposed, this paper demonstrates that this supervised approach can be significantly improved by leveraging concept sharing across multiple domains. For instance, "screen" is an aspect in iPhone reviews but also appears in reviews of other electronic devices. When "screen" appears in a review of a new domain or product, it is likely to be an aspect too. This knowledge enables more accurate extraction in the new domain. The paper proposes a novel extraction method that leverages this idea in the context of supervised sequence labeling. Experimental results demonstrate significantly better performance compared to methods that do not use past information.

title: EnhanceNet: Single Image Super-Resolution Through Automated Texture Synthesis
Abstract: Single image super-resolution involves inferring a high-resolution image from a single low-resolution input. Traditionally, algorithm performance is measured using pixel-wise reconstruction measures like peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), which have been shown to correlate poorly with human perception of image quality. Algorithms minimizing these metrics often produce over-smoothed images lacking high-frequency textures, appearing unnatural despite high PSNR values. This paper proposes a novel application of automated texture synthesis combined with a perceptual loss that focuses on creating realistic textures rather than optimizing for pixel-accurate reproduction of ground truth images during training. By using feed-forward fully convolutional neural networks in an adversarial training setting, the approach achieves a significant boost in image quality at high magnification ratios. Extensive experiments on various datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, yielding state-of-the-art results in both quantitative and qualitative benchmarks.

title: DARN: a Deep Adversial Residual Network for Intrinsic Image Decomposition
Abstract: This paper presents a new deep supervised learning method for intrinsic decomposition of a single image into its albedo and shading components. The method utilizes a new fully convolutional neural network that jointly estimates absolute albedo and shading. The solution relies on a single end-to-end deep sequence of residual blocks and a perceptually-motivated metric formed by two adversarially trained discriminators. Unlike classical intrinsic image decomposition methods, this approach is fully data-driven, eliminating the need for physical priors like shading smoothness or albedo sparsity and geometric information like depth. Compared to recent deep learning techniques, the architecture is simplified, making it easier to build and train, and constrained to generate a valid and reversible decomposition. The set of quantitative metrics is rediscussed and augmented to account for the more challenging recovery of non-scale-invariant quantities. The architecture is trained and demonstrated on the publicly available MPI Sintel dataset and its intrinsic image decomposition, showcasing attenuated overfitting issues and discussing generalizability to other data. Results show that the proposed work outperforms state-of-the-art deep algorithms both qualitatively and quantitatively.

title: A Base Camp for Scaling AI
Abstract: Modern statistical machine learning (SML) methods share a significant limitation with early AI approaches: the lack of a scalable method for adapting to new domains. Human learning partially solves this by leveraging a rich, shared, updateable world model. This scalability requires modularity, where updating part of the world model should not impact unrelated parts. This modularity requires both "correctability" (to correct errors without introducing new ones) and "interpretability" (to understand which components need correcting). Achieving this could involve adapting state-of-the-art SML systems to be interpretable and correctable or exploring the potential of simple, interpretable, and correctable learning methods. This paper focuses on the latter approach, investigating two main ideas: "Teacher Assisted Learning" (leveraging crowdsourcing to learn language) and "Factored Dialog Learning" (factoring application development into roles with isolated language competencies to enable non-experts to quickly create new applications). These ideas are tested in an "Automated Personal Assistant" (APA) setting with two scenarios: detecting user intent from a user-APA dialog and creating event reminder applications where a non-expert "teacher" can create specific apps. For intent detection, a dataset of a thousand labeled utterances from user dialogs with Cortana is used, demonstrating that the approach matches state-of-the-art SML methods while providing full transparency, allowing the entire model to be summarized on one human-readable page. For the reminder app task, user studies verify the approach's efficacy.
label: AI

title: Spectral algorithms for tensor completion
Abstract: In the tensor completion problem, the goal is to estimate a low-rank tensor based on a random sample of revealed entries. Earlier work revealed a significant gap between estimation with unbounded computational resources (using tensor nuclear norm minimization) and polynomial-time algorithms. For third-order tensors, the best statistical guarantees have been proven using the sixth level of the sum-of-squares (SOS) semidefinite programming hierarchy, but the SOS approach does not scale well to large problems. Spectral methods, based on unfolding or matricizing the tensor, are attractive for their low complexity but are believed to require a much larger sample size. This paper presents two main contributions. First, a new unfolding-based method is proposed that outperforms naive methods for symmetric k-th order tensors of rank r. This result involves studying singular space estimation for partially revealed matrices with a large aspect ratio, which may be of independent interest. For third-order tensors, the proposed algorithm matches the SOS method in terms of sample size (requiring approximately rd^(3/2) revealed entries) but under a stricter rank condition (r << d^(3/4) instead of r << d^(3/2)). This is complemented by a different spectral algorithm for third-order tensors in the overcomplete (r ≥ d) regime. Under a random model, this second approach successfully estimates tensors of rank d ≤ r << d^(3/2) from approximately rd^(3/2) revealed entries.
label: AI

title: Human Action Attribute Learning From Video Data Using Low-Rank Representations
Abstract: Representing human actions as a sequence of human body movements or action attributes facilitates the development of models for human activity recognition and summarization. This paper presents an extension of the low-rank representation (LRR) model, termed the clustering-aware structure-constrained low-rank representation (CS-LRR) model, for unsupervised learning of human action attributes from video data. The model is based on the union-of-subspaces (UoS) framework and integrates spectral clustering into the LRR optimization problem to improve subspace clustering results. An efficient linear alternating direction method is developed to solve the CS-LRR optimization problem. A hierarchical subspace clustering approach, termed hierarchical CS-LRR, is introduced to learn attributes without requiring prior specification of their number. By visualizing and labeling these action attributes, the hierarchical model can semantically summarize long video sequences of human actions at multiple resolutions. Human actions or activities can also be uniquely represented as a sequence of transitions between action attributes, enabling human action recognition. The effectiveness of the proposed model for semantic summarization and action recognition is demonstrated through comprehensive experiments on five real-world human action datasets.
label: AI

title: A State Space Approach for Piecewise-Linear Recurrent Neural Networks for Reconstructing Nonlinear Dynamics from Neural Measurements
Abstract: The computational properties of neural systems are often attributed to their network dynamics. Therefore, recovering system dynamics from experimentally observed neuronal time series, such as multiple single-unit (MSU) recordings or neuroimaging data, is crucial for understanding its computations. Ideally, one would seek not only a state space representation of the dynamics but also access to its governing equations for in-depth analysis. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs), a computationally powerful and dynamically universal formal framework, have been extensively studied from both computational and dynamical systems perspectives. This paper develops a semi-analytical maximum-likelihood estimation scheme for piecewise-linear RNNs (PLRNNs) within the statistical framework of state space models, accounting for noise in both the underlying latent dynamics and the observation process. The Expectation-Maximization algorithm is used to infer the latent state distribution through a global Laplace approximation, iteratively estimating PLRNN parameters. After validation on toy examples, the approach is applied to MSU recordings from the rodent anterior cingulate cortex during a classical working memory task, delayed alternation. A model with 5 states proved sufficient to capture the essential computational dynamics underlying task performance, including stimulus-selective delay activity. The estimated models rarely exhibited multistability but were tuned to exhibit slow dynamics near a bifurcation point. This work advances a semi-analytical (reasonably fast) maximum-likelihood estimation framework for PLRNNs that can recover relevant dynamics from observed neuronal time series, directly linking them to computational properties.
label: AI

title: "What is Relevant in a Text Document?": An Interpretable Machine Learning Approach
Abstract: Text documents can be described using abstract concepts like semantic category, writing style, or sentiment. Machine learning (ML) models have been trained to automatically map documents to these concepts, enabling annotation of vast text collections beyond human capacity. Beyond accurate category prediction, understanding the categorization process is highly desirable. This paper demonstrates that such understanding can be achieved by tracing the classification decision back to individual words using layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP), a technique for explaining predictions of complex non-linear classifiers. Two word-based ML models, a convolutional neural network (CNN) and a bag-of-words SVM classifier, are trained on a topic categorization task, adapting the LRP method to decompose the predictions onto words. The resulting scores indicate each word's contribution to the overall classification decision. This enables extracting relevant information from text documents without explicit semantic information extraction. The word-wise relevance scores are further used to generate novel vector-based document representations capturing semantic information. A measure of model explanatory power is introduced based on these document vectors, showing that while SVM and CNN models perform similarly in terms of classification accuracy, CNN exhibits higher explainability, making it more comprehensible for humans and potentially more useful for other applications.
label: AI

title: Understanding Image and Text Simultaneously: a Dual Vision-Language Machine Comprehension Task
Abstract: This paper introduces a new multi-modal task for computer systems, posed as a combined vision-language comprehension challenge: identifying the most suitable text describing a scene from several similar options. Accomplishing this task requires comprehension beyond recognizing "keywords" or key-phrases and their corresponding visual concepts. It demands aligning representations of the two modalities to achieve a visually-grounded "understanding" of various linguistic elements and their dependencies. This new task offers an easily computable and well-studied metric: the accuracy in detecting the true target among decoys. This paper presents several contributions: an effective and extensible mechanism for generating decoys from human-created image captions, a large-scale machine comprehension dataset (based on COCO images and captions) made publicly available, human evaluation results on this dataset establishing a performance upper-bound, and several baseline and competitive learning approaches illustrating the task's utility in advancing image and language comprehension. The paper also demonstrates that, in a multi-task learning setting, performance on the proposed task is positively correlated with the end-to-end task of image captioning.
label: AI

title: Learning from Simulated and Unsupervised Images through Adversarial Training
Abstract: Recent advances in graphics have made it feasible to train models on synthetic images, potentially eliminating the need for expensive annotation. However, the disparity between synthetic and real image distributions may hinder performance. To address this gap, we introduce Simulated+Unsupervised (S+U) learning, which aims to improve the realism of a simulator's output using unlabeled real data while preserving annotation information.  Our S+U method utilizes an adversarial network similar to GANs but with synthetic images as input. We incorporate key modifications to the standard GAN algorithm, including self-regularization, local adversarial loss, and a discriminator updated with a history of refined images. These modifications enable the generation of highly realistic images, demonstrated through qualitative analysis and a user study.  Quantitative evaluation on gaze and hand pose estimation tasks shows significant improvement over using synthetic images alone, achieving state-of-the-art results on the MPIIGaze dataset without labeled real data.
label: AI

title: Logic-based Clustering and Learning for Time-Series Data
Abstract: Analyzing and designing cyberphysical systems (CPS) presents a data deluge challenge, with complex models and experiments generating massive amounts of data. This paper proposes using monotonic Parametric Signal Temporal Logic (PSTL) to design features for unsupervised classification of time series data. This enables the use of off-the-shelf machine learning tools for automatic clustering of similar traces based on a given PSTL formula.  Illustrative examples showcase how this technique produces interpretable formulas that facilitate analysis and understanding. Case studies related to automotive engine testing, highway traffic analysis, and auto-grading massively open online courses demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach.
label: AI

title: First-Person Activity Forecasting with Online Inverse Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: Predicting long-term goals of a first-person camera wearer, including their future actions, locations, and intended objectives, is a challenging task. Unlike prior trajectory forecasting work, our proposed algorithm, DARKO, focuses on reasoning about semantic states (e.g., "will I pick up an object?") and future goal states that are distant in both space and time.  DARKO learns and forecasts from first-person visual observations of user behavior using an Online Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) approach. Unlike traditional batch IRL, which only discovers rewards, DARKO extracts states, transitions, rewards, and goals from streaming data. We demonstrate that DARKO outperforms competing methods in predicting goals, both in noisy and ideal settings. The approach is theoretically and empirically no-regret.
label: AI

title: Asynchronous Operations on Qubits in Distributed Simulation Environments using QooSim
Abstract: Operations on entangled qubits are traditionally represented using the tensor product, which acts synchronously across the entire entangled system. While this approach is practical for simulations within a single physical system, it becomes challenging when simulating entangled systems distributed across a network. This paper presents a method for simulating operations on entangled states in a distributed environment, which is equivalent to the conventional approach but allows for distributed quantum systems on physically separate hardware. This advances the possibilities for demonstrating distributed quantum algorithms in research, teaching, and learning.  The paper also examines the impact of amplitude damping errors on quantum key distribution protocols, characterizing allowable tolerances and observing the dependency of these errors on the eavesdropper's location.  Furthermore, the paper introduces QooSim, a new quantum simulation library.
label: AI

title: Highway and Residual Networks learn Unrolled Iterative Estimation
Abstract: Recent breakthroughs in deep learning, such as Highway and Residual networks, have enabled the training of feedforward networks with hundreds of layers using simple gradient descent. While deep representations have been attributed to their success, there are indications that these architectures challenge the prevailing view of deep learning as a hierarchical computation of increasingly abstract features.  This report argues that this view is incomplete and proposes an alternative viewpoint based on unrolled iterative estimation. This perspective suggests that successive layers refine estimates of the same features rather than computing entirely new representations. We demonstrate how this viewpoint directly leads to the construction of Highway and Residual networks. Preliminary experiments highlight similarities and differences between the two architectures.
label: AI

title: Adversarial Examples Detection in Deep Networks with Convolutional Filter Statistics
Abstract: Despite significant advancements in visual recognition, deep learning architectures remain vulnerable to adversarial examples that can degrade performance. This paper focuses on detecting adversarial examples by analyzing their distributional similarity to normal examples. Instead of training a deep neural network for adversarial detection, a simpler approach based on statistics from convolutional layer outputs is proposed.  A cascade classifier is designed to efficiently detect adversarial examples. Notably, the classifier, trained on a specific adversarial generating mechanism, can effectively detect adversarials from different mechanisms. The resulting classifier is non-subdifferentiable, hindering adversarial attacks that exploit classifier gradients.  The paper further demonstrates that many adversarial examples can be recovered by applying a simple averaging filter to the image. These findings provide insights into the classification mechanisms of deep convolutional neural networks.
label: AI

title: Collaborative Alerts Ranking for Anomaly Detection
Abstract: The challenge of characterizing complex relationships between heterogeneous categorical alerts from an anomaly detection system, filtering out false positives, and delivering trustworthy rankings and suggestions to end users is addressed in this paper. This problem is motivated by and generalizes applications in enterprise security and attack scenario reconstruction.  The proposed framework, CAR, exploits both temporal and content correlations from heterogeneous categorical alerts. CAR first constructs a tree-based model to capture both short-term correlations and long-term dependencies in each alert sequence, identifying abnormal action sequences.  An embedding-based model then learns content correlations between alerts through their categorical attributes. By integrating temporal and content dependencies into a single optimization framework, CAR ranks both alerts and their corresponding alert patterns.  Experiments using real-world enterprise monitoring data and real attacks demonstrate CAR's ability to accurately identify true positive alerts and effectively reconstruct attack scenarios.
label: AI

title: Statistical limits of spiked tensor models
Abstract: This paper examines the statistical limits of both detecting and estimating a rank-one deformation of a symmetric random Gaussian tensor. Upper and lower bounds on the critical signal-to-noise ratio are established under various priors for the planted vector: uniformly sampled unit vector, i.i.d. ±1 entries, and sparse vector with a constant fraction of i.i.d. ±1 entries. For each case, the upper and lower bounds match up to a 1+o(1) factor as the tensor order increases.  Furthermore, the bounds are asymptotically tight in the sparse limit for any fixed order. The upper bounds demonstrate a phenomenon akin to the work of Baik, Ben Arous, and Péché, where an eigenvalue emerges from the bulk at a lower signal-to-noise ratio than the perturbation itself exceeding the bulk. General results for broader classes of priors are also provided, highlighting the difference in threshold location asymptotics between discrete and continuous priors.  Finally, replica prediction from statistical physics is carried out for the uniformly sampled unit vector and i.i.d. ±1 entry priors, conjectured to provide the exact information-theoretic threshold for any fixed order.  The paper also introduces a new improvement to the second moment method for contiguity, enabling tighter bounds by conditioning away from rare "bad" events. This addresses gaps present in previous works.
label: AI

title: Understanding Tree: a tool to estimate one's understanding of knowledge
Abstract: Human learning is a continuous and diverse process, encompassing a wide range of subjects and contexts. With the explosion of knowledge, evaluating one's understanding becomes increasingly complex. This paper proposes an Understanding Tree method to estimate individual understanding of knowledge by tracking learning activities.  The method addresses limitations of traditional assessments like tests and interviews, offering complementary insights.
label: AI

title: Set2Model Networks: Learning Discriminatively To Learn Generative Models
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel "learning-to-learn" approach for rapid concept learning from small-to-medium training sets, particularly designed for web-initialized image retrieval.  At its core is a Set2Model network, which maps sets of examples to generative probabilistic models (e.g., Gaussians, mixtures of Gaussians) in the descriptor space. The embedding parameters are trained end-to-end in the meta-learning stage using a set of training learning problems.  A key technical contribution is the derivation of backpropagation through mixture model fitting, making the likelihood of the resulting models differentiable with respect to input descriptor positions.  While the meta-learning process is discriminative, the trained Set2Model network performs generative learning, facilitating learning in scenarios with no negative examples, polysemous concepts, or noisy training sets. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of Set2Model networks in picking visual concepts from raw internet image search outputs, outperforming existing methods.
label: AI

title: Secure Network in Business-to-Business application by using Access Control List (ACL) and Service Level Agreement (SLA)
Abstract: This paper investigates secure network design for Business-to-Business (B2B) applications by implementing Access Control Lists (ACL) and Service Level Agreements (SLA). The data analyzed includes reports of external and internal attacks, providing insights into attack types, ratios, and temporal distribution.  The paper presents advanced techniques and methodologies for reducing attacks and vulnerabilities, minimizing attack ratios, and ensuring network security and application stability.  It further identifies attack locations, motivations, and techniques.  The paper emphasizes the ongoing evolution of system security, highlighting the importance of understanding web attacks and security measures for effective exploration. Statistical analytics on various attack types and their characteristics are provided, backed by simulations to validate the findings.
label: AI

title: Structured Sequence Modeling with Graph Convolutional Recurrent Networks
Abstract: This paper introduces the Graph Convolutional Recurrent Network (GCRN), a deep learning model for predicting structured sequences of data. GCRN generalizes classical recurrent neural networks (RNN) to data structured by an arbitrary graph, encompassing scenarios like video frames, spatio-temporal sensor measurements, or random walks on vocabulary graphs for language modeling.  The model combines graph convolutional neural networks (CNN) for identifying spatial structures and RNN for detecting dynamic patterns. Two possible GCRN architectures are studied and applied to practical problems: predicting moving MNIST data and modeling natural language with the Penn Treebank dataset. Experiments demonstrate that exploiting both graph spatial and dynamic information enhances prediction accuracy and learning speed.
label: AI

title: Hardware for Machine Learning: Challenges and Opportunities
Abstract: Machine learning plays a crucial role in extracting valuable information from vast sensor data. While some applications focus on data analysis and trend identification, others require immediate action based on the data.  Local embedded processing near the sensor is often preferred over cloud-based approaches due to privacy, latency, and bandwidth concerns.  However, sensors often face constraints on energy consumption, cost, and computational resources.  This paper discusses how these challenges can be addressed at various levels of hardware design, ranging from architecture and hardware-friendly algorithms to mixed-signal circuits and advanced technologies.  The emphasis is on reducing data movement and energy consumption, particularly in machine learning tasks involving high-dimensional data transformations.
label: AI

title: Jointly Extracting Relations with Class Ties via Effective Deep Ranking
Abstract: Class ties, the connections between relations in relation extraction, are prevalent in distantly supervised scenarios where entity tuples may have multiple relation facts. Exploiting these ties can significantly improve relation extraction.  However, previous models are ineffective or ignore this property. This paper proposes a unified model that integrates convolutional neural networks (CNN) with a general pairwise ranking framework to leverage class ties.  Three novel ranking loss functions are introduced, and an effective method addresses class imbalance issues.  Experiments on a widely used dataset demonstrate the enhanced extraction performance achieved by exploiting class ties, highlighting the model's ability to learn these connections. The proposed model outperforms baselines and achieves state-of-the-art results.
label: AI

title: Finding Statistically Significant Attribute Interactions
Abstract: Identifying groups of attribute interactions specific to a variable of interest is crucial in many data exploration tasks. This paper presents a novel method based on statistical significance testing to verify if a dataset has been generated by a factorized class-conditional joint distribution with attribute partitioning.  The proposed ASTRID method automatically finds an attribute partition describing the generating distribution. State-of-the-art classifiers are utilized to capture interactions by systematically breaking them and observing the impact on classifier performance.  Empirical evaluations demonstrate the utility of this approach using real and synthetic data.
label: AI

title: Quantum Learning with Noise and Decoherence: A Robust Quantum Neural Network
Abstract: Noise and decoherence pose significant challenges for large-scale quantum computing. The no-cloning theorem prohibits simple redundancy, and unwanted environmental interactions can destroy coherence, hindering computation. This paper explores the robustness of quantum neural networks (QNNs) to noise and decoherence.  Inspired by the parallel and distributed nature of classical neural networks, QNNs are shown to be robust to both noise and decoherence, with improved robustness as the system size increases.  Furthermore, noise and decoherence can even be beneficial during training by mitigating overfitting.  The robustness is demonstrated using entanglement for pattern storage in a qubit array. The findings suggest that machine learning approaches can overcome challenging problems in quantum computing.
label: AI

title: DroidGen: Constraint-based and Data-Driven Policy Generation for Android
Abstract: DroidGen, a tool for automatic anti-malware policy inference, is presented in this paper. DroidGen employs a data-driven approach, utilizing a training set of malware and benign applications, and leverages a constraint solver to generate a policy that maximizes malware exclusion while allowing benign applications.  Preliminary results show promising performance, with DroidGen generating a policy that filters out 91% of tested Android malware.  Compared to black-box machine learning classifiers, DroidGen generates policies in a declarative, readable format.  The approach, implementation, and preliminary results are discussed.
label: AI

title: On the function approximation error for risk-sensitive reinforcement learning
Abstract: This paper derives informative error bounds for the policy evaluation algorithm proposed by Basu et al. when evaluating risk-sensitive costs using exponential utility.  The approach utilizes Bapat's inequality and Perron-Frobenius eigenvectors (assuming irreducible Markov chain) to obtain new bounds.  The novelty lies in exploiting the irreducibility of the Markov chain, unlike the previous work by Basu et al. which employed a spectral variation bound.  Examples are provided where the new bounds match the "actual error," outperforming the previous bound.  The paper also discusses the relationship between the bounds and presents a bound between the largest eigenvalues of two irreducible matrices in terms of their entries.
label: AI

title: The SP Theory of Intelligence as a Foundation for the Development of a General, Human-Level Thinking Machine
Abstract: This paper summarizes the "SP theory of intelligence" and its realization in the "SP computer model," showcasing how it simplifies and integrates concepts across artificial intelligence and related fields. This framework provides a promising foundation for developing a general, human-level thinking machine, aligning with the goal of artificial general intelligence research.  The key to this simplification and integration is the powerful concept of "multiple alignment," adapted from bioinformatics. This concept holds the potential to be the "double helix" of intelligence, similar to DNA's significance in biological sciences.  The SP system boasts strengths in representing diverse knowledge, versatility in intelligence aspects (including unsupervised learning, natural language processing, robust pattern recognition at multiple levels of abstraction, diverse reasoning types, planning, problem solving, and seamless integration of knowledge and intelligence). It offers potential applications in addressing big data challenges, developing human-level intelligence in robots, serving as an intelligent database, and aiding medical knowledge and diagnosis.
label: AI

title: Non-Deterministic Policy Improvement Stabilizes Approximated Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: This paper examines a type of instability linked to greedy policy improvement in approximated reinforcement learning.  Empirical evidence shows that non-deterministic policy improvement can stabilize methods like LSPI by controlling the stochasticity of improvements.  Additionally, a suitable representation of the value function can contribute to solution stabilization.  The proposed approach is simple and readily adaptable to more advanced algorithms like deep reinforcement learning. |||
label: AI

title: A Revisit of Hashing Algorithms for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
Abstract: Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (ANNS) is a crucial problem in machine learning and data mining. Numerous hashing algorithms have been proposed for solving this problem, each claiming to outperform existing methods. However, evaluations in these papers have often been insufficient, and the claims require reevaluation. The primary objective of an ANNS method is to provide accurate answers (nearest neighbors) in the shortest time possible. When implemented correctly, most hashing methods see improved performance as the code length increases. Nevertheless, many existing studies only report performance with code lengths shorter than 128. This paper comprehensively revisits the problem of search with a hash index, analyzing the advantages and disadvantages of two popular hash index search procedures. We propose a simple but effective two-level index structure and conduct a thorough comparison of eleven popular hashing algorithms. Surprisingly, random-projection-based Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH) emerges as the top performer, contradicting claims made in the other ten hashing papers. Despite its simplicity, our results show that the capabilities of random-projection-based LSH have been significantly underestimated. For the sake of reproducibility, all codes used in this paper are released on GitHub, providing a testing platform for fair comparisons between various hashing algorithms.
label: AI

title: Identification of Interesting Objects in Large Spectral Surveys Using Highly Parallelized Machine Learning
Abstract: The LAMOST multi-object spectrograph archives contain millions of fully reduced spectra. Automatic pipelines have generated catalogs of numerous parameters for individual objects, including their approximate spectral classification. However, this classification primarily relies on the global shape of the entire spectrum and integral spectral properties within specific bandpasses, such as the presence and equivalent width of prominent spectral lines. For identifying certain object types (e.g., Be stars or quasars), the detailed shape of only a few lines is critical. Machine learning offers a new methodology for improving the reliability of classifying such objects, even in boundary cases. This paper presents results from a Spark-based semi-supervised machine learning approach applied to LAMOST spectra to automatically identify single and double-peak emission of the H alpha line, characteristic of Be and B[e] stars. The labeled sample was obtained from the archives of the 2m Perek telescope at Ondřejov observatory. A simple physical model of spectrograph resolution was used for domain adaptation to the LAMOST training domain. The resulting list of candidates includes dozens of Be stars (some likely unknown), as well as intriguing objects resembling quasar and even blazar spectra, along with numerous instrumental artifacts. The verification of the nature of interesting candidates benefited considerably from cross-matching and visualization within the Virtual Observatory environment.
label: AI

title: Handwriting recognition using Cohort of LSTM and lexicon verification with extremely large lexicon
Abstract: State-of-the-art handwriting recognition methods rely on Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) recurrent neural networks (RNNs), currently achieving impressive character recognition performance. Character recognition is typically coupled with a lexicon-driven decoding process that integrates dictionaries. Unfortunately, these dictionaries are limited to hundreds of thousands of words in the best systems, hindering language coverage and limiting overall recognition performance. This article proposes an alternative to lexicon-driven decoding based on a lexicon verification process, coupled with a novel cascade architecture. The cascade comprises a large number of complementary networks extracted from a single training (termed "cohort"), simplifying the learning process. This proposed method achieves new state-of-the-art word recognition performance on the Rimes and IAM databases. Handling a gigantic lexicon of 3 million words, the method also demonstrates promising performance with a fast decision stage.
label: AI

title: Robustness of Voice Conversion Techniques Under Mismatched Conditions
Abstract: Most existing voice conversion (VC) research is conducted under acoustically matched conditions between source and target signals. However, the robustness of VC methods in the presence of mismatches remains uncertain. This paper presents a comparative analysis of different VC techniques under mismatched conditions. Extensive experiments using five VC techniques on the CMU ARCTIC corpus indicate that VC method performance significantly degrades in noisy conditions. The study found that bilinear frequency warping with amplitude scaling (BLFWAS) outperforms other methods in most noisy scenarios. The paper further explores the suitability of various speech enhancement techniques for robust conversion. Objective evaluation results suggest that spectral subtraction and log minimum mean square error (logMMSE) based speech enhancement techniques can improve performance in specific noisy conditions.
label: AI

title: On Coreset Constructions for the Fuzzy $K$-Means Problem
Abstract: The fuzzy $K$-means problem is a widely adopted generalization of the well-known $K$-means problem to soft clusterings. This paper presents the first coresets for fuzzy $K$-means with size linear in the dimension, polynomial in the number of clusters, and poly-logarithmic in the number of points. We demonstrate that these coresets can be used to compute a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximation for fuzzy $K$-means, improving upon previously presented results. Furthermore, we show that our coresets can be maintained in an insertion-only streaming setting, where data points arrive sequentially.
label: AI

title: Causal Effect Identification in Acyclic Directed Mixed Graphs and Gated Models
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel family of graphical models consisting of graphs with potentially directed, undirected, and bidirected edges but without directed cycles. We demonstrate that these models are suitable for representing causal models with additive error terms. We provide a set of sufficient graphical criteria for identifying arbitrary causal effects when the new models contain directed and undirected edges but no bidirected edges. We also present a necessary and sufficient graphical criterion for identifying the causal effect of a single variable on the rest of the variables. Additionally, we develop an exact algorithm for learning the new models from observational and interventional data using answer set programming. Finally, we introduce gated models for causal effect identification, a new family of graphical models that leverage context-specific independences to identify additional causal effects.
label: AI

title: Noise Mitigation for Neural Entity Typing and Relation Extraction
Abstract: This paper addresses two distinct types of noise encountered in information extraction models: noise arising from distant supervision and noise originating from pipeline input features. Our target tasks are entity typing and relation extraction. For the first noise type, we introduce multi-instance multi-label learning algorithms using neural network models and apply them to fine-grained entity typing for the first time. This approach yields comparable performance to the state-of-the-art supervised approach, which utilizes global embeddings of entities. For the second noise type, we propose methods to improve the integration of noisy entity type predictions into relation extraction. Our experiments demonstrate that probabilistic predictions are more robust than discrete predictions and that joint training of the two tasks performs best.
label: AI

title: Continuous multilinguality with language vectors
Abstract: Existing multilingual natural language processing (NLP) models typically treat language as a discrete category, making predictions for one language or the other. In contrast, we propose using continuous vector representations of language. We demonstrate that these representations can be learned efficiently with a character-based neural language model and used to improve inference about language varieties not seen during training. Experiments involving 1303 Bible translations into 990 different languages empirically explore the capabilities of multilingual language models and show that the language vectors capture genetic relationships between languages.
label: AI

title: How to Train Your Deep Neural Network with Dictionary Learning
Abstract: Currently, two primary methods exist for training deep neural networks: using restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) and using autoencoders. RBMs are stacked in layers to form a deep belief network (DBN), where the final representation layer is connected to the target to complete the deep neural network. Autoencoders are nested within each other to form stacked autoencoders; once the stacked autoencoder is learned, the decoder portion is detached, and the target is attached to the deepest layer of the encoder to create the deep neural network. This work proposes a novel approach for training deep neural networks using dictionary learning as the basic building block. The idea is to utilize features from shallower layers as inputs for training the next deeper layer. Any type of dictionary learning (unsupervised, supervised, discriminative, etc.) can be used as basic units until the pre-final layer. In the final layer, one needs to employ the label-consistent dictionary learning formulation for classification. We compare our proposed framework to existing state-of-the-art deep learning techniques on benchmark problems, consistently achieving results within the top 10. In actual problems of age and gender classification, our approach outperforms the best-known techniques.
label: AI

title: Deep Blind Compressed Sensing
Abstract: This work addresses the problem of extracting deeply learned features directly from compressive measurements. No prior work has been conducted in this area. Existing deep learning tools only achieve good results when applied to the full signal, often after preprocessing. These techniques require the signal to be reconstructed first. This work demonstrates that by learning directly from the compressed domain, significantly better results can be obtained. This work extends the recently proposed framework of deep matrix factorization combined with blind compressed sensing, hence the term "deep blind compressed sensing". Simulation experiments have been conducted on imaging via single-pixel camera, undersampled biomedical signals arising in wireless body area networks, and compressive hyperspectral imaging. In all cases, the superiority of our proposed deep blind compressed sensing is evident.
label: AI

title: Towards Linear Algebra over Normalized Data
Abstract: Providing machine learning (ML) over relational data is a fundamental requirement for data analytics systems. While most ML tools demand input data to be presented as a single table, many datasets are multi-table, forcing data scientists to join those tables first, leading to data redundancy and runtime waste. Recent research on "factorized" ML mitigates this issue for a few specific ML algorithms by pushing ML through joins. However, their approaches require manual rewriting of ML implementations. These piecemeal methods introduce significant development overhead when extending these ideas to other ML algorithms. This paper demonstrates that this overhead can be mitigated by leveraging a popular formal algebra for representing the computations of numerous ML algorithms: linear algebra. We introduce a new logical data type to represent normalized data and devise a framework of algebraic rewrite rules to convert a large set of linear algebra operations over denormalized data into operations over normalized data. We show how this enables automatic "factorization" of several popular ML algorithms, unifying and generalizing prior works. We prototype our framework in the popular ML environment R and an industrial R-over-RDBMS tool. Experiments using both synthetic and real normalized data reveal that our framework achieves significant speedups, up to 36x on real data.
