title: Improving Tweet Representations using Temporal and User Context
Abstract: This paper presents a novel representation learning model that accurately computes semantic representations for tweets. The model utilizes chronologically adjacent tweets ("context") from user timelines to capture the semantic meaning of a tweet. Furthermore, the model incorporates user-specific knowledge, such as writing style and topic preferences, to enhance representation accuracy. title: Mixing Times and Structural Inference for Bernoulli Autoregressive Processes
Abstract: This paper introduces a Bernoulli Autoregressive Process (BAR), a novel multivariate random process that models binary interactions in various graphical structures. BAR models a discrete-time vector random sequence of Bernoulli processes with autoregressive dynamics. The process efficiently describes a transition matrix with a reduced number of parameters and exhibits rapid mixing properties. The paper presents a greedy algorithm for learning the structure of the underlying directed graph with a sample complexity nearly optimal. Simulation results illustrate the algorithm's performance in various setups, including a model for a biological signaling network.

title: Quantization and Training of Low Bit-Width Convolutional Neural Networks for Object Detection
Abstract: This paper introduces LBW-Net, an efficient optimization-based method for quantization and training of low bit-width convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The method quantizes weights to zero or powers of two during backpropagation, minimizing the distance between full-precision and quantized weights. The paper characterizes the quantization problem and proposes a semi-analytical thresholding scheme for efficient quantization. Experimental results on PASCAL VOC dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of LBW-Net, achieving near-lossless performance in object detection tasks compared to its 32-bit counterpart while significantly improving deployment speed.

title: Nonnegative Matrix Factorization (NMF) with Heteroscedastic Uncertainties and Missing data
Abstract: This paper presents vectorized update rules and a convergence proof for Nonnegative Matrix Factorization (NMF) with heteroscedastic measurements and missing data. The rules are implemented in Python and demonstrated using an optical spectroscopic dataset. The technique has potential applications in image processing of planetary disks.
label: AI

title: Self-Correcting Models for Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: This paper examines the issue of model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) failing in environments with inaccurate dynamic models. Hallucinated Replay, a method that trains the model to correct its own errors, is theoretically analyzed. The paper presents a novel error bound highlighting the relationship between a model's self-correction ability and MBRL performance. These findings inspire an MBRL algorithm for deterministic MDPs with robust performance guarantees despite model class limitations.
label: AI

title: A Hidden Absorbing Semi-Markov Model for Informatively Censored Temporal Data: Learning and Inference
Abstract: This paper introduces the Hidden Absorbing Semi-Markov Model (HASMM), a probabilistic model for modeling continuous-time physiological processes. HASMM is capable of capturing modern electronic health record (EHR) data, including irregularly sampled, temporally correlated, and informatively censored physiological data. The model learns from EHR data using a novel forward-filtering backward-sampling Monte-Carlo EM algorithm, exploiting knowledge of endpoint clinical outcomes. Real-time inferences are drawn via a forward-filtering algorithm operating on a discrete-time embedded Markov chain. The paper demonstrates HASMM's diagnostic and prognostic utility in a critical care prognosis setting using a real-world dataset.
label: AI

title: Inexact Proximal Gradient Methods for Non-convex and Non-smooth Optimization
Abstract: This paper addresses the limitations of existing inexact proximal gradient methods in non-convex optimization problems. The paper proposes three inexact proximal gradient algorithms, including a basic version and Nesterov's accelerated version. The algorithms' convergence rates are theoretically analyzed, demonstrating their performance in the non-convex setting. The algorithms are applied to three representative non-convex learning problems, confirming their effectiveness.  |||

title: Sample-efficient Deep Reinforcement Learning for Dialog Control
Abstract: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) offer an appealing approach to representing dialog policies due to their ability to handle partial observability, infer latent state representations, and be optimized using supervised learning (SL) or reinforcement learning (RL). While policy gradient methods are a natural choice for RL, they suffer from sample inefficiency. This paper introduces three methods to reduce the number of dialogs required to optimize an RNN-based dialog policy using RL. The core principle is to maintain a second RNN that predicts the value of the current policy and apply experience replay to both networks. Empirical results on two tasks demonstrate that these methods reduce the number of dialogs/episodes required by about a third compared to standard policy gradient methods.
label: AI

title: Target and (Astro-)WISE technologies - Data federations and its applications
Abstract: The Astro-WISE technology, first implemented in 2003, has been deployed in numerous European countries and is used for producing the KiDS survey data. This technology, nicknamed WISE, has been further applied to a wide range of projects within the multi-disciplinary Target initiative. This paper highlights the data handling of various astronomical applications, including VLT-MUSE and LOFAR, along with non-astronomical applications such as the medical projects Lifelines and GLIMPS, the MONK handwritten text recognition system, and business applications by Target Holding. It discusses key lessons learned and outlines the application of the WISE data-centric approach to the Science Ground Segment of the Euclid satellite.

title: On the existence of fractional Brownian fields indexed by manifolds with closed geodesics
Abstract: This paper establishes a necessary geometric condition for the existence of the $H$-fractional Brownian field indexed by a Riemannian manifold. The condition is particularly strong for the L\\'evy Brownian field ($H=1/2$) indexed by manifolds with minimal closed geodesics. Notably, it is shown that compact manifolds admitting a L\\'evy Brownian field must be simply connected. Furthermore, the nondegenerescence of the L\\'evy Brownian field indexed by hyperbolic spaces is derived from this result. These findings emphasize the need for alternative kernels on nonsimply connected manifolds to enable Gaussian modeling or kernel machine learning of functional data with manifold-valued entries.

title: Nonexistence of fractional Brownian fields indexed by cylinders
Abstract: This paper demonstrates the non-existence of an $H$-fractional Brownian field indexed by the cylinder $\\mathbb{S}^1 \\times ]0,\\varepsilon[$ equipped with its product distance $d$ for any $\\varepsilon>0$ and $H>0$. This implies that $d^{2H}$ is not a negative definite kernel, which also poses a challenge in proving the positive definiteness – or covariance – of many classical stationary kernels, such as the Gaussian and exponential kernels, on the cylinder. The paper generalizes this result from the cylinder to any Riemannian Cartesian product with a minimal closed geodesic. It also explores the case of the cylinder endowed with a distance asymptotically close to the product distance in the neighborhood of a circle. Another consequence is the discontinuity of the set of $H$ values for which $d^{2H}$ is negative definite with respect to the Gromov-Hausdorff convergence on compact metric spaces. These findings expand our understanding of kernel construction on metric spaces and emphasize the need for alternative approaches to classical kernels for Gaussian modeling and kernel method learning on cylinders.

title: An IoT Endpoint System-on-Chip for Secure and Energy-Efficient Near-Sensor Analytics
Abstract: Near-sensor data analytics holds promise for IoT endpoints by minimizing communication energy and reducing network load. However, it raises security concerns due to the storage or transmission of valuable data at various stages of the analytics pipeline. Encryption offers a solution to protect sensitive data at the boundary of the on-chip analytics engine. To address the combined workload of analytics and encryption within a tight power envelope, this paper proposes Fulmine, a System-on-Chip based on a tightly-coupled multi-core cluster augmented with specialized blocks for compute-intensive data processing and encryption functions. The Fulmine SoC, fabricated in 65nm technology, consumes less than 20mW on average at 0.8V and achieves an efficiency of up to 70pJ/B in encryption, 50pJ/px in convolution, or up to 25MIPS/mW in software. Experimental results for three secure analytics use cases – secure autonomous aerial surveillance, local CNN-based face detection with secured remote recognition, and seizure detection with encrypted data collection from EEG – provide a strong argument for the platform's real-life flexible application.

title: An Integrated Optimization + Learning Approach to Optimal Dynamic Pricing for the Retailer with Multi-type Customers in Smart Grids
Abstract: This paper examines a realistic smart grid scenario where an electricity retailer serves three distinct customer types: those with an optimal home energy management system embedded in their smart meters (C-HEMS), those with only smart meters (C-SM), and those without smart meters (C-NONE). The paper focuses on supporting the retailer in making optimal day-ahead dynamic pricing decisions for this mixed customer pool. A two-level decision-making framework is proposed, where the retailer, acting as the upper-level agent, announces electricity prices for the next 24 hours, and customers, acting as lower-level agents, subsequently schedule their energy usages accordingly. The lower-level problem models the price responsiveness of different customers based on their unique characteristics. The upper-level problem optimizes the dynamic prices for the retailer to maximize its profit while adhering to realistic market constraints. This two-level model is addressed using genetic algorithms (GA) based distributed optimization methods, and its feasibility and effectiveness are validated through simulation results.

title: Adversarial Deep Structural Networks for Mammographic Mass Segmentation
Abstract: Mass segmentation plays a crucial role in mammogram analysis by providing effective morphological features and regions of interest (ROI) for mass detection and classification. Inspired by the success of deep convolutional features in natural image analysis and conditional random fields (CRF) for structural learning, this paper proposes an end-to-end network for mammographic mass segmentation. The network employs a fully convolutional network (FCN) to model the potential function, followed by a CRF for structural learning. Since mass distribution varies significantly with pixel position, the FCN is combined with position priori for the task. Due to the limited size of mammogram datasets, adversarial training is employed to control overfitting. Furthermore, four models with different convolutional kernels are fused to enhance segmentation results. Experimental results on two public datasets, INbreast and DDSM-BCRP, demonstrate that the proposed end-to-end network, combined with adversarial training, achieves state-of-the-art results.

title: Deep Multi-instance Networks with Sparse Label Assignment for Whole Mammogram Classification
Abstract: Mammogram classification is directly linked to computer-aided diagnosis of breast cancer. Traditional methods require significant effort to annotate training data through costly manual labeling and specialized computational models to detect these annotations during testing. This paper leverages the success of deep convolutional features in natural image analysis and multi-instance learning for labeling sets of instances/patches to propose end-to-end trained deep multi-instance networks for mass classification based on whole mammograms. The proposed approach eliminates the costly need to annotate training data. Three different schemes are explored to construct deep multi-instance networks for whole mammogram classification. Experimental results on the INbreast dataset demonstrate the robustness of the proposed deep networks compared to previous approaches that rely on segmentation and detection annotations during training.
label: AI

title: Resolving the paradox of evolvability with learning theory: How evolution learns to improve evolvability on rugged fitness landscapes
Abstract: Evolution's ability to produce remarkable adaptations has been attributed to its enhancement of its own evolutionary capacity – "the evolution of evolvability." Rupert Riedl, a pioneer in evolutionary developmental biology, proposed that the evolution of complex adaptations is facilitated by a developmental organization that is itself shaped by past selection to promote evolutionary innovation. However, selecting for traits that enable future innovation appears paradoxical: natural selection cannot favor structures for benefits they have not yet produced, and favoring traits for benefits already produced does not constitute future innovation. This paper resolves this paradox by exploiting a formal equivalence between the evolution of evolvability and learning systems. It uses the conditions that enable simple learning systems to generalize, i.e., to use past experience to improve performance on previously unseen, future test cases, to demonstrate conditions where natural selection can systematically favor developmental organizations that benefit future evolvability. Numerical simulations of evolution on highly epistatic fitness landscapes illustrate how the structure of evolved gene regulation networks can lead to increased evolvability, capable of avoiding local fitness peaks and discovering higher fitness phenotypes. These findings support Riedl's intuition that developmental organizations "mimicking" the organization of constraints on phenotypes can be favored by short-term selection and also facilitate future innovation. Significantly, the conditions that enable the evolution of such surprising evolvability stem from the same non-mysterious conditions that permit generalization in learning systems.

title: A Probabilistic Representation for Dynamic Movement Primitives
Abstract: Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMPs) have proven successful in applications such as imitation learning, trial-and-error learning, reinforcement learning, movement recognition and segmentation, and control. This has made them a popular representation for motor primitives. This paper showcases how DMPs can be reformulated as a probabilistic linear dynamical system with control inputs. This probabilistic representation of DMPs makes algorithms like Kalman filtering and smoothing directly applicable for performing inference on proprioceptive sensor measurements during execution. The paper demonstrates that inference in this probabilistic model automatically introduces a feedback term to online modulate the execution of a DMP. Furthermore, it shows how inference can be used to measure the likelihood of successful execution of a given motion primitive. Initial results of using the probabilistic model to detect execution failures on a simulated movement primitive dataset are presented.
label: AI

title: Distributed Generalized Cross-Validation for Divide-and-Conquer Kernel Ridge Regression and its Asymptotic Optimality
Abstract: Tuning parameter selection is crucial for kernel ridge regression. While data-driven tuning methods for divide-and-conquer kernel ridge regression (d-KRR) are lacking in the literature, this paper proposes a distributed Generalized Cross-Validation (dGCV) as a data-driven tool for selecting tuning parameters in d-KRR. The proposed dGCV is computationally scalable for massive datasets and, under mild conditions, is shown to be asymptotically optimal in the sense that minimizing the dGCV score is equivalent to minimizing the true global conditional empirical loss of the averaged function estimator. This extends the existing optimality results of GCV to the divide-and-conquer framework.
label: AI

title: Learning a No-Reference Quality Metric for Single-Image Super-Resolution
Abstract: Numerous single-image super-resolution algorithms have been proposed, but few studies address the problem of performance evaluation based on visual perception. While most super-resolution images are evaluated using full-reference metrics, their effectiveness is unclear, and ground-truth images are not always available in practice. To address these issues, this paper conducts human subject studies using a large set of super-resolution images and proposes a no-reference metric learned from visual perceptual scores. Specifically, three types of low-level statistical features in both spatial and frequency domains are designed to quantify super-resolved artifacts, and a two-stage regression model is learned to predict the quality scores of super-resolution images without relying on ground-truth images. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed metric in assessing the quality of super-resolution images based on human perception.
label: AI

title: Building Diversified Multiple Trees for Classification in High Dimensional Noisy Biomedical Data
Abstract: It is common for a trained classification model to be applied to operating data that deviates from the training data due to noise. This paper demonstrates that an ensemble classifier, Diversified Multiple Tree (DMT), is more robust in classifying noisy data than other widely used ensemble methods. DMT is tested on three real-world biomedical datasets from different laboratories in comparison with four benchmark ensemble classifiers. Experimental results show that DMT significantly outperforms other benchmark ensemble classifiers on noisy test data. The paper also discusses a limitation of DMT and its potential variations.

title: Deep Learning on Lie Groups for Skeleton-based Action Recognition
Abstract: Skeleton-based action recognition has emerged as a popular 3D classification problem in recent years. State-of-the-art methods typically represent each motion sequence as a high-dimensional trajectory on a Lie group with an additional dynamic time warping, followed by shallow learning of favorable Lie group features. This paper integrates the Lie group structure into a deep network architecture to learn more appropriate Lie group features for 3D action recognition. Within the network structure, rotation mapping layers are designed to transform input Lie group features into desirable ones, aligning them better in the temporal domain. To reduce high feature dimensionality, the architecture is equipped with rotation pooling layers for elements on the Lie group. Furthermore, a logarithm mapping layer is proposed to map the resulting manifold data into a tangent space, facilitating the application of regular output layers for final classification. Evaluations of the proposed network on standard 3D human action recognition datasets clearly demonstrate its superiority over existing shallow Lie group feature learning methods and most conventional deep learning methods.
label: AI

title: 3D Shape Induction from 2D Views of Multiple Objects
Abstract: This paper investigates the problem of inducing a distribution over three-dimensional structures given two-dimensional views of multiple objects taken from unknown viewpoints. The proposed approach, "projective generative adversarial networks" (PrGANs), trains a deep generative model of 3D shapes whose projections match the distributions of the input 2D views. The addition of a projection module allows for inferring the underlying 3D shape distribution without relying on any 3D, viewpoint information, or annotation during the learning phase. The paper demonstrates that the approach produces 3D shapes of comparable quality to GANs trained on 3D data for various shape categories, including chairs, airplanes, and cars. Experiments also show that the disentangled representation of 2D shapes into geometry and viewpoint leads to a good generative model of 2D shapes. The key advantage of this approach is that it enables predicting 3D and viewpoint, and generating novel views from an input image in a completely unsupervised manner.

title: New Architecture for Dynamic Spectrum Allocation in Cognitive Heterogeneous Network using Self Organizing Map
Abstract: This paper presents a hybrid architecture for dynamic spectrum allocation in hierarchical networks, combining centralized and distributed architectures to achieve optimal allocation of radio resources. The architecture dynamically interacts to limit interference and enhance spectrum efficiency while maintaining desired Quality of Service (QoS) in the network. The paper introduces a dynamic framework for this interaction. The proposed architecture utilizes a simple learning rule based on Hebbian learning for sensing the primary network and allocating the spectrum.

title: Dynamic Adaptive Streaming using Index-Based Learning Algorithms
Abstract: This paper presents a unified framework for designing scalable dynamic adaptive video streaming algorithms based on index-based policies (dubbed DAS-IP) to maximize the Quality of Experience (QoE) provided to clients using video streaming services. The distributed nature of the algorithm makes it easily implementable. The paper begins by considering the simplest setup of a one-hop wireless network where an Access Point (AP) transmits video packets to multiple clients over a shared unreliable channel. The video file for each client is fragmented into multiple packets, and the server maintains multiple copies (each of different quality) of the same video file. Clients maintain individual packet buffers to mitigate the impact of uncertainty on video interruption. Streaming experience, or the QoE of a client, depends on factors such as starvation/outage probability, average video quality, average number of starvation periods, and temporal variations in video quality. The paper poses the problem of making dynamic streaming decisions to maximize total QoE as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP). Considering the associated dual MDP suggests that the problem is significantly simplified if the AP is allowed to charge a price per unit bandwidth usage from the clients. More specifically, a "client-by-client" QoE optimization leads to network-wide QoE maximization, resulting in a decentralized streaming algorithm. This enables clients to independently determine optimal streaming choices in each time slot, yielding a highly desirable client-level adaptation algorithm. The optimal policy exhibits an appealing simple threshold structure.

title: Roundtable: What can we learn about confinement and anomalous effects in QCD using analog systems?
Abstract: This paper explores recent connections between emergent phenomena in many-body systems in atomic and condensed matter physics and confinement and other non-perturbative effects in quantum chromodynamics.

title: Joint Spatial-Angular Sparse Coding for dMRI with Separable Dictionaries
Abstract: Diffusion MRI (dMRI) enables the reconstruction of neuronal fibers in the brain, *in vivo*, by measuring water diffusion along angular gradient directions in q-space. High angular resolution diffusion imaging (HARDI) provides better estimates of fiber orientation than the widely used diffusion tensor imaging, but the high number of samples required to estimate diffusivity necessitates longer patient scan times. To accelerate dMRI, compressed sensing (CS) has been employed by exploiting a sparse dictionary representation of the data, discovered through sparse coding. The sparser the representation, the fewer samples are needed to reconstruct a high-resolution signal with limited information loss. Thus, finding the sparsest possible representation of dMRI is an important area of research. However, current reconstruction methods rely on an angular representation *per voxel* with added spatial regularization, requiring at least one non-zero coefficient per voxel for non-zero signals. This means the global level of sparsity must be greater than the number of voxels. In contrast, this paper proposes a joint spatial-angular representation of dMRI that allows for achieving levels of global sparsity below the number of voxels. A major challenge is the computational complexity of solving a global sparse coding problem over large-scale dMRI. This work presents novel adaptations of popular sparse coding algorithms that become better suited for solving large-scale problems by exploiting spatial-angular separability. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves significantly sparser representations of HARDI than is possible with state-of-the-art techniques.
label: AI

title: What can we Learn from Predictive Modeling?
Abstract: The majority of inferences drawn in empirical political research are based on model-based associations, such as regression. This paper articulates the benefits of predictive modeling as a complementary approach. Predictive models aim to specify a probabilistic model that provides a good fit to testing data not used to estimate the model's parameters. The paper has three objectives: first, to review the central benefits of this under-utilized approach from a perspective uncommon in the existing literature, focusing on how predictive modeling can complement and augment standard associational analyses. Second, to advance the state of the literature by laying out a simple set of benchmark predictive criteria. Third, to illustrate the approach through a detailed application to the prediction of interstate conflict. |||

title: EgoTransfer: Transferring Motion Across Egocentric and Exocentric Domains using Deep Neural Networks
Abstract: Mirror neurons, found in the primary motor cortex of primates like humans and monkeys, activate both when performing an action and when observing the same action performed by another. To develop fully autonomous intelligent systems with human-like learning capabilities, modeling mirror neurons is crucial. Recent advancements in egocentric cameras offer new opportunities for studying vision from a first-person perspective. However, traditional cameras capture actions from an exocentric third-person perspective. This research bridges the gap between these perspectives by training models to predict motion in one view by observing it from the other. This allows models to predict how an egocentric motion would appear from an external viewpoint. Linear and nonlinear models were trained and evaluated for their ability to transfer motion information across views. Experimental results demonstrate the successful transfer of motion information between egocentric and exocentric perspectives.

title: In-situ Adaptive Encoding for Asymmetric Quantum Error Correcting Codes
Abstract: We introduce techniques to enhance the performance of asymmetric stabilizer codes in the presence of unital channels with unknown parameters. Our method estimates channel parameters using information retrieved from syndrome measurements during standard stabilizer quantum error correction, adaptively aligning the codespace to minimize uncorrectable errors. For dephasing channels with a single angle parameter, our scheme achieves lifetimes dominated by the bit-flip error rate, benefiting from the asymmetric code's improved distance. For general unital channels, we learn and exploit channel orientations that consistently improve code lifetime. Our adaptive and online method effectively models the impact of drift in channel parameters.

title: A new recurrent neural network based predictive model for Faecal Calprotectin analysis: A retrospective study
Abstract: Faecal Calprotectin (FC) is a reliable marker for intestinal inflammation associated with Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD), but not for cancer. This retrospective study, involving 804 patients, presents an enhanced benchmark predictive model for analyzing FC, based on a novel Echo State Network (ESN). ESN is an advanced dynamic recurrent neural network that employs a biologically plausible architecture and a supervised learning mechanism. The proposed machine learning-driven predictive model outperforms a conventional logistic regression model, demonstrating statistically significant improvements in performance.

title: Learning to predict where to look in interactive environments using deep recurrent q-learning
Abstract: Bottom-Up (BU) saliency models struggle in complex interactive environments where humans actively engage in tasks, such as sandwich making or video games. This paper proposes a Reinforcement Learning (RL) approach to highlight task-relevant locations in input frames. A soft attention mechanism, integrated with the Deep Q-Network (DQN) model, teaches an RL agent to play a game and identify important areas within its visual input. Evaluations on Atari 2600 games show that the soft attention-based model significantly outperforms bottom-up models like Itti-Kochs saliency and Graph-Based Visual Saliency (GBVS).

title: Machine Learning, Linear and Bayesian Models for Logistic Regression in Failure Detection Problems
Abstract: This research investigates the application of logistic regression for detecting manufacturing failures. Using data from the Kaggle Bosch Production Line Performance competition, the study explores machine learning, linear, and Bayesian models. For machine learning, XGBoost tree-based classifier was employed to achieve high-scoring classification. The generalized linear model framework of logistic regression facilitates analysis of the influence of factors under study. The Bayesian approach for logistic regression provides statistical distributions for the model's parameters, enabling probabilistic analysis, such as risk assessment.

title: Contrasting Prediction Methods for Early Warning Systems at Undergraduate Level
Abstract: This study explores prediction methods for an early warning system designed for a large STEM undergraduate course. Existing research suggests the benefit of early warning systems for identifying at-risk students, often utilizing data from student engagement with Learning Management Systems (LMSs). We investigate eight prediction methods, examining the optimal time for applying an early warning system within a course. Results from a statistics course with extensive LMS Blackboard resources and weekly assessments show that weeks 5-6 (mid-semester) offer the best timing, balancing student intervention opportunities with prediction accuracy. Employing detailed variables, clustering, and the BART (Bayesian Additive Regressive Trees) prediction method, we achieve a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 6.5 percentage points in predicting final grades by week 6. Our R code for implementing the prediction methods is available on a GitHub repository.

title: Towards Wide Learning: Experiments in Healthcare
Abstract: This paper proposes a Wide Learning architecture that aims to automate the feature engineering phase of the machine learning (ML) pipeline. Feature engineering is widely recognized as the most time-consuming and expert knowledge-demanding aspect of ML tasks. The proposed feature recommendation approach is tested on three healthcare datasets: PhysioNet Challenge 2016 phonocardiogram (PCG) signals, MIMIC II blood pressure classification using photoplethysmogram (PPG) signals, and an emotion classification dataset based on PPG signals. While surpassing state-of-the-art techniques for the second and third datasets, it achieves 94.38% of the accuracy of the winner of the PhysioNet Challenge 2016. In all cases, achieving satisfactory performance required significantly less effort (a few days) compared to manual feature engineering.

title: Exploiting sparsity to build efficient kernel based collaborative filtering for top-N item recommendation
Abstract: The increasing availability of implicit feedback datasets has spurred interest in developing effective collaborative filtering techniques that handle unambiguous positive feedback and ambiguous negative feedback asymmetrically. This paper proposes a principled kernel-based collaborative filtering method for top-N item recommendation using implicit feedback. An efficient implementation using the linear kernel is presented, and its generalization to kernels of the dot product family while preserving efficiency is shown. The factors influencing the sparsity of a standard cosine kernel are investigated. This analysis reveals that kernel sparsity is heavily dependent on dataset properties, particularly the long-tail distribution. Our method is compared to state-of-the-art algorithms, demonstrating good results in terms of both efficiency and effectiveness.
label: AI

title: Mutual information for fitting deep nonlinear models
Abstract: Deep nonlinear models present challenges in parameter fitting due to the unknown nature of the hidden layer and potentially non-affine relationships between the initial and observed layers. This work explores the use of information theoretic measures, such as mutual information and Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, as objective functions for fitting these models without knowledge of the hidden layer. One model serves as a proof of concept, with another applied to cognitive performance. The use of optimizers with these methods is also investigated. Mutual information proves largely successful as an objective, depending on the parameters. KL divergence exhibits similar success, given some knowledge of the hidden layer's statistics.

title: Reinforcement Learning Using Quantum Boltzmann Machines
Abstract: This research examines whether quantum annealers with specific chip layouts can outperform classical computers in reinforcement learning tasks. A transverse field Ising spin Hamiltonian is associated with a qubit layout resembling that of a deep Boltzmann machine (DBM). Simulated quantum annealing (SQA) is used to numerically simulate quantum sampling from this system. A reinforcement learning algorithm is designed where the visible nodes representing the states and actions of an optimal policy constitute the first and last layers of the deep network. In the absence of a transverse field, simulations demonstrate that DBMs are trained more effectively than restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) with the same number of nodes. A framework for training the network as a quantum Boltzmann machine (QBM) in the presence of a significant transverse field for reinforcement learning is then developed. This method also outperforms the RBM-based reinforcement learning approach.

title: A User Simulator for Task-Completion Dialogues
Abstract: Despite widespread interest in reinforcement learning for task-oriented dialogue systems, research and development progress faces several obstacles. Reinforcement learners require interaction with the environment, limiting the use of conventional dialogue corpora. Each task presents specific challenges, necessitating separate sets of task-specific annotated data. Additionally, collecting and annotating human-machine or human-human conversations for task-oriented dialogues demands extensive domain knowledge. Building appropriate datasets is both costly and time-consuming, leading to the use of user simulators based on example dialogues. Reinforcement learning agents are trained online as they interact with the simulator, providing an effective starting point. Once agents master the simulator, they can be deployed in real environments to interact with humans and continue training online. This paper introduces a publicly available simulation framework, designed for the movie-booking domain, leveraging both rules and collected data. The simulator supports two tasks: movie ticket booking and movie seeking. The paper demonstrates several agents and outlines the procedure for adding and testing custom agents within the framework.

title: Causal Learning via Manifold Regularization
Abstract: This paper presents a machine learning approach to causal structure estimation. The idea is to treat indicators of causal relationships between variables as 'labels' and utilize available data on the variables to provide features for the labeling task. Background scientific knowledge or interventional data provide labels for some causal relationships, while others remain unlabeled. To illustrate these concepts, a distance-based approach (based on bivariate histograms) within a manifold regularization framework is developed. Empirical results on three biological datasets, including cases where causal effects can be verified through experimental intervention, demonstrate the approach's effectiveness, general applicability, and user-friendliness.
label: AI

title: An Alternative Softmax Operator for Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: The softmax operator, applied to a set of values, behaves like both a maximization function and an average. In sequential decision making, softmax is often used to maximize utility while mitigating the risks associated with solely relying on a single maximum utility decision. The Boltzmann softmax operator is commonly used, but this paper shows that it is susceptible to misbehavior. A differentiable softmax operator is proposed, possessing properties including non-expansion, which ensures convergent behavior in learning and planning. A variant of the SARSA algorithm is introduced, utilizing this new operator to compute a Boltzmann policy with a state-dependent temperature parameter. The algorithm is shown to be convergent and demonstrates favorable practical performance.

title: An MM Algorithm for Split Feasibility Problems
Abstract: The classical multi-set split feasibility problem aims to find a point in the intersection of multiple closed convex domain constraints, whose image under a linear mapping also lies in the intersection of multiple closed convex range constraints. Split feasibility generalizes important inverse problems, including convex feasibility, linear complementarity, and constrained regression. When a feasible point does not exist, methods that minimize a proximity function can be used to obtain optimal approximate solutions. This paper extends the proximity function approach to generalize the linear split feasibility problem to non-linear mappings. The algorithm, based on majorization-minimization principles, is amenable to quasi-Newton acceleration and offers convergence guarantees under mild assumptions. Additionally, the Euclidean norm in the proximity function can be replaced with arbitrary Bregman divergences. The paper explores examples highlighting the advantages of non-linear formulations over the linear case, focusing on optimization for intensity-modulated radiation therapy.
label: AI

title: Asymptotic Optimality in Stochastic Optimization
Abstract: This research investigates local complexity measures for stochastic convex optimization problems, providing a local minimax theory analogous to H\\'{a}jek and Le Cam's theory for classical statistical problems. Complementary optimality results are presented, developing fully online methods that adaptively achieve optimal convergence guarantees. These results establish function-specific lower bounds and convergence results that connect statistical difficulty with the geometric concept of tilt-stability from optimization. The study demonstrates how variants of Nesterov's dual averaging, a stochastic gradient-based procedure, guarantee finite-time identification of constraints in optimization problems, while standard stochastic gradient procedures fail. Furthermore, it highlights a gap between problems with linear and nonlinear constraints: standard stochastic gradient-based procedures are suboptimal even for the simplest nonlinear constraints, requiring the development of asymptotically optimal Riemannian stochastic gradient methods.

title: SonoNet: Real-Time Detection and Localisation of Fetal Standard Scan Planes in Freehand Ultrasound
Abstract: Identifying and interpreting fetal standard scan planes during 2D ultrasound mid-pregnancy examinations are highly complex tasks requiring years of training. Beyond guiding the probe to the correct location, identifying relevant structures within the image can be challenging for non-experts. Automatic image processing can provide tools to assist experienced and inexperienced operators with these tasks. This paper proposes a novel convolutional neural network-based method for automatically detecting 13 fetal standard views in freehand 2D ultrasound data and localizing fetal structures using bounding boxes. A key contribution is the network's ability to localize target anatomy using weak supervision based solely on image-level labels. The network architecture is designed for real-time operation while optimizing output for the localization task. Results are presented for real-time annotation, retrospective frame retrieval from saved videos, and localization on a large and challenging dataset comprising images and video recordings of full clinical anomaly screenings. The proposed method achieved an average F1-score of 0.798 in a realistic classification experiment simulating real-time detection, 90.09% accuracy for retrospective frame retrieval, and 77.8% accuracy for the localization task.

title: Neuromorphic Deep Learning Machines
Abstract: A significant challenge in neuromorphic computing is the development of general and computationally efficient models of inference and learning compatible with the brain's spatial and temporal constraints. One promising approach is to draw inspiration from inference and learning algorithms employed in deep neural networks. However, the gradient descent Back Propagation (BP) rule, a cornerstone of deep learning, often relies on readily available network-wide information stored with high-precision memory and precise operations that are difficult to realize in neuromorphic hardware. Notably, recent work has shown that exact backpropagated weights are not crucial for learning deep representations. Random BP replaces feedback weights with random ones, encouraging the network to adjust its feedforward weights to learn pseudo-inverses of the random feedback weights. Building upon these findings, this paper demonstrates an event-driven random BP (eRBP) rule that utilizes error-modulated synaptic plasticity for learning deep representations in neuromorphic hardware. The rule requires only one addition and two comparisons for each synaptic weight using a two-compartment leaky Integrate & Fire (I&F) neuron, making it suitable for implementation in digital or mixed-signal neuromorphic hardware. Results show that eRBP enables rapid learning of deep representations, achieving classification accuracies comparable to artificial neural network simulations on GPUs while being robust to neural and synaptic state quantizations during learning.

title: Supervised Quantum Learning without Measurements
Abstract: This paper proposes a quantum machine learning algorithm for efficiently solving a class of problems encoded in quantum controlled unitary operations. The protocol's central physical mechanism involves iterating a quantum time-delayed equation that introduces feedback into the dynamics and eliminates the need for intermediate measurements. The quantum algorithm's performance is analyzed by comparing results from numerical simulations with those obtained from classical machine learning methods for the same problem. The use of time-delayed equations expands the toolbox of quantum machine learning, potentially enabling unprecedented applications in quantum technologies.
label: AI

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning with Successor Features for Navigation across Similar Environments
Abstract: This paper addresses the problem of robot navigation in simple maze-like environments where the robot relies solely on its onboard sensors. The focus is on solutions that do not require localization, mapping, or planning, and that can quickly adapt to changing navigation goals and environments. This problem is framed as a sequence of related reinforcement learning tasks. A successor feature-based deep reinforcement learning algorithm is proposed to transfer knowledge from previously mastered navigation tasks to new problem instances. This significantly reduces the required learning time after the first task instance is solved, enabling adaptability to changing environments. The method is validated in both simulated and real robot experiments using a Robotino and compared to baseline methods, including classical planning-based navigation.

title: Edge-exchangeable graphs and sparsity (NIPS 2016)
Abstract: Many popular network models rely on the assumption of vertex exchangeability, where the graph distribution is invariant to vertex relabelings. However, the Aldous-Hoover theorem dictates that these graphs are dense or empty with probability one, which contradicts the sparsity observed in many real-world graphs. This paper presents an alternative notion of exchangeability for random graphs called edge exchangeability, where the distribution of a graph sequence is invariant to the order of the edges. Unlike traditionally vertex-exchangeable models, edge-exchangeable models can exhibit sparsity. To demonstrate this, a general framework for graph generative models is outlined. Unlike the pioneering work of Caron and Fox (2015), models within this framework are stationary across steps of the graph sequence. Specifically, the model grows the graph by instantiating more latent atoms of a single random measure as the dataset size increases, rather than adding new atoms to the measure. |||

title: On-bird Sound Recordings: Automatic Acoustic Recognition of Activities and Contexts
Abstract: We propose a novel approach to studying animal behavior using microphone backpacks worn by free-flying birds. These devices can record not only vocalizations but also movement and environmental sounds, providing valuable insights into the context of behavior. To analyze these recordings, we investigate automatic annotation methods using two paradigms: scene classification with feature learning and event detection with probabilistic latent component analysis (PLCA). We tested these methods on recordings from Eurasian jackdaws in both captive and field settings. Our results demonstrate comparable performance to state-of-the-art sound scene analysis methods, suggesting that this approach can enable scalable automatic annotation of audio logger data. However, we also identified limitations related to individual differences in animals and backpacks, which require further investigation.

title: Unsupervised Pixel-Level Domain Adaptation with Generative Adversarial Networks
Abstract: Collecting large, well-annotated image datasets for training machine learning algorithms is expensive. Synthetic data generation is a promising alternative, but models trained solely on rendered images often fail to generalize to real images. We introduce a novel unsupervised domain adaptation approach that learns a pixel-space transformation between synthetic and real image domains. Our generative adversarial network (GAN)-based method adapts source-domain images to mimic the target domain. Our approach not only generates plausible samples but also significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on various unsupervised domain adaptation scenarios. Importantly, this adaptation process generalizes to object classes unseen during training.

title: Deep Residual Hashing
Abstract: Hashing aims to generate compact, similarity-preserving code words for efficient large-scale image retrieval. Most existing methods use a two-stage process: first encoding images as handcrafted feature vectors, followed by binarization to generate hash codes. This approach can lead to suboptimal encoding. We propose Deep Residual Hashing (DRH), a novel deep architecture for supervised hashing that combines representation learning and hash coding into an end-to-end framework. DRH consists of four key components: (1) a sub-network with stacked residual blocks, (2) a hashing layer for binarization, (3) a supervised retrieval loss function based on neighborhood component analysis for similarity preserving embedding, and (4) hashing-related losses and regularization to minimize quantization error and improve hash coding quality. Our extensive experiments on a large public chest x-ray database with co-morbidities demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods.

title: The VQA-Machine: Learning How to Use Existing Vision Algorithms to Answer New Questions
Abstract: The Visual Question Answering (VQA) challenge is characterized by the unpredictable nature of questions, demanding a wide range of image operations for answering them. Training a model to perform these diverse operations accurately from limited {image, question, answer} tuples is challenging. We propose a more general and scalable approach that leverages the fact that highly effective algorithms for these operations already exist. Our method learns to exploit these external, off-the-shelf algorithms to achieve its goal, similar to the concept of a Neural Turing Machine. The core of our approach is a novel co-attention model. Additionally, it generates human-readable reasons for its decisions and can be trained end-to-end without requiring ground truth reasons. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on two publicly available datasets, Visual Genome and VQA, achieving state-of-the-art results in both cases.

title: Neural networks based EEG-Speech Models
Abstract: We present a novel end-to-end neural network (NN) based EEG-speech (NES) modeling framework for mapping imagined EEG signals to phonemes. Our NES models incorporate three network structures: a language model based EEG feature extraction layer, an acoustic feature mapping layer, and a restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) based feature learning layer. These models jointly represent multichannel EEG signals and project acoustic speech signals. Two augmented NES models utilize spoken EEG signals as either bias or gate information to enhance feature learning and translation of imagined EEG signals. Our experimental results demonstrate that all three proposed NES models outperform the baseline support vector machine (SVM) method for EEG-speech classification. Moreover, our approach achieves comparable results to the deep belief network approach for binary classification.

title: Deep Learning and Its Applications to Machine Health Monitoring: A Survey
Abstract: Since 2006, deep learning (DL) has emerged as a transformative research direction, significantly advancing performance in various fields, including object recognition, image segmentation, speech recognition, and machine translation. In modern manufacturing systems, data-driven machine health monitoring is gaining traction due to the widespread deployment of low-cost sensors connected to the internet. Deep learning provides powerful tools for processing and analyzing this big machinery data. This paper reviews and summarizes the emerging research on deep learning for machine health monitoring. After a brief introduction to deep learning techniques, we review its applications in machine health monitoring systems, focusing on Auto-encoders (AE), Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBM), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN). Finally, we discuss emerging trends in DL-based machine health monitoring methods.

title: Learning Residual Images for Face Attribute Manipulation
Abstract: Face attributes provide a detailed description of human faces. Unlike prior research focusing on attribute prediction, we address the inverse and more challenging problem of face attribute manipulation, aiming to modify a face image according to a given attribute value. Instead of manipulating the entire image, we propose learning the corresponding residual image, defined as the difference between the original and manipulated images. This allows for efficient manipulation with minimal pixel modification. Our approach is based on the Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) framework, consisting of two image transformation networks and a discriminative network. The transformation networks handle attribute manipulation and its inverse operation, while the discriminative network distinguishes generated images from real ones. We also apply dual learning to enable the transformation networks to learn from each other. Experiments show that residual images can be effectively learned and utilized for attribute manipulation, preserving most of the details in attribute-irrelevant areas.

title: FusionNet: A deep fully residual convolutional neural network for image segmentation in connectomics
Abstract: Electron microscopic connectomics aims to create comprehensive brain connectivity maps using high-throughput, nano-scale microscopy. A major challenge in connectomics research is developing scalable image analysis algorithms that require minimal user intervention. Deep learning has recently gained significant attention in computer vision due to its exceptional performance in image classification tasks. Therefore, its application to connectomic analyses holds great promise. We introduce FusionNet, a novel deep neural network architecture for automatic segmentation of neuronal structures in connectomics data. FusionNet leverages recent advances in machine learning, such as semantic segmentation and residual neural networks, with the introduction of summation-based skip connections to enable a deeper network architecture for improved segmentation accuracy. We demonstrate the performance of our method by comparing it with state-of-the-art electron microscopy (EM) segmentation methods from the ISBI EM segmentation challenge. We also present segmentation results on two different tasks, including cell membrane and cell body segmentation, and provide a statistical analysis of cell morphology.

title: Projected Semi-Stochastic Gradient Descent Method with Mini-Batch Scheme under Weak Strong Convexity Assumption
Abstract: We propose a projected semi-stochastic gradient descent method with mini-batches to enhance both the theoretical complexity and practical performance of the general stochastic gradient descent method (SGD). We prove linear convergence under a weak strong convexity assumption. This method requires no strong convexity assumption for minimizing the sum of smooth convex functions subject to a compact polyhedral set, a common problem in machine learning. Our PS2GD method maintains low-cost per iteration and high optimization accuracy through a stochastic gradient variance-reduced technique. It also admits a simple parallel implementation with mini-batches. Furthermore, PS2GD is applicable to the dual problem of SVM with hinge loss.
label: AI

title: Machine Reading with Background Knowledge
Abstract: Intelligent systems capable of understanding natural language text are crucial for various artificial intelligence applications, including mobile phone voice assistants, computer vision, and robotics. Understanding language often involves integrating new information into a previously acquired world view. However, many machine reading systems rely solely on the text to infer its meaning. This paper explores a different approach: machine reading methods that utilize background knowledge to facilitate language understanding. We present two methods: The first addresses prepositional phrase attachment ambiguity, using background knowledge within a semi-supervised machine learning algorithm that learns from both labeled and unlabeled data. This approach achieves state-of-the-art results on two datasets, outperforming strong baselines. The second method extracts relationships from compound nouns. Our knowledge-aware method for compound noun analysis accurately extracts relationships and significantly outperforms a baseline that does not use background knowledge.

title: Towards a Deep Learning Framework for Unconstrained Face Detection
Abstract: Robust face detection is a critical pre-processing step for various facial analysis tasks, including facial expression analysis, facial landmarking, face recognition, pose estimation, and 3D facial model building. Despite decades of research, face detection remains challenging due to the wide variations in face images found in real-world scenarios. We propose Multiple Scale Faster Region-based Convolutional Neural Network (MS-FRCNN), a novel approach for robustly detecting human facial regions from images captured under challenging conditions, such as large occlusions, extremely low resolutions, facial expressions, and strong illumination variations. Our approach is benchmarked on two challenging face detection databases: the Wider Face database and the Face Detection Dataset and Benchmark (FDDB), and compared to recent methods like Two-stage CNN, Multi-scale Cascade CNN, Faceness, Aggregate Chanel Features, HeadHunter, Multi-view Face Detection, Cascade CNN, etc. The experimental results show that our proposed approach consistently achieves highly competitive results, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance compared to other recent face detection methods.

title: A Survey of Inductive Biases for Factorial Representation-Learning
Abstract: With the resurgence of interest in neural networks, representation learning has become a central focus in artificial intelligence. Representation learning aims to discover useful encodings of data that explicitly reveal domain-relevant information. Factorial representations identify underlying independent causal factors of variation in data. A factorial representation is compact and faithful, makes the causal factors explicit, and facilitates human interpretation of data. Factorial representations have various applications, including the generation of novel examples, indexing and search, novelty detection, and transfer learning. This article surveys various constraints that encourage learning algorithms to discover factorial representations. We categorize these constraints into unsupervised and supervised inductive biases. Unsupervised inductive biases exploit assumptions about the environment, such as the statistical distribution of factor coefficients, assumptions about perturbations a factor should be invariant to (e.g., a representation of an object can be invariant to rotation, translation, or scaling), and assumptions about how factors combine to synthesize an observation. Supervised inductive biases are constraints on representations based on additional information related to observations. Supervisory labels come in various types, differing in how strongly they constrain the representation, how many factors are labeled, how many observations are labeled, and whether or not we know the associations between the constraints and the factors they relate to. This survey brings together a wide variety of models that address the problem of learning factorial representations and provides a framework for comparing these models based on the strengths of their underlying supervised and unsupervised inductive biases.
label: AI

title: Automatic time-series phenotyping using massive feature extraction
Abstract: Across diverse scientific and industrial applications, a common key problem involves relating the structure of time-series data to a meaningful outcome, such as detecting anomalous events from sensor recordings or diagnosing patients based on physiological time-series measurements like heart rate or brain activity. Currently, researchers must manually devise or search for properties of their time series that are suitable for their specific analysis problem. To address this non-systematic and time-consuming procedure, we introduce hctsa, a new tool that automatically selects interpretable and useful properties of time series by comparing implementations of over 7700 time-series features drawn from diverse scientific literatures. Using two exemplar biological applications, we show how hctsa allows researchers to leverage decades of time-series research to quantify and understand informative structure in their time-series data.

title: Learning Optimal Control of Synchronization in Networks of Coupled Oscillators using Genetic Programming-based Symbolic Regression
Abstract: Networks of coupled dynamical systems provide a powerful way to model systems with complex dynamics, such as the human brain. Control of synchronization in these networked systems has far-reaching applications in various domains, including engineering and medicine. This paper formulates synchronization control in dynamical systems as an optimization problem and presents a multi-objective genetic programming-based approach to infer optimal control functions that drive the system from a synchronized to a non-synchronized state and vice-versa. The genetic programming-based controller allows for learning optimal control functions in an interpretable symbolic form. The effectiveness of our proposed approach is demonstrated by controlling synchronization in coupled oscillator systems linked in networks of increasing order complexity, ranging from a simple coupled oscillator system to a hierarchical network of coupled oscillators. The results show that our method can learn highly-effective and interpretable control functions for such systems.
label: AI

title: A Simple Approach to Multilingual Polarity Classification in Twitter
Abstract: Sentiment analysis has gained significant attention recently due to the interest in mining opinions from social media users. Sentiment analysis involves determining the polarity of a given text, i.e., its degree of positiveness or negativeness. Traditionally, Sentiment Analysis algorithms have been tailored to specific languages due to the complexity of lexical variations and errors introduced by content creators. This contribution aims to provide a simple-to-implement and user-friendly multilingual framework that can serve as a baseline for sentiment analysis contests and as a starting point for building new sentiment analysis systems. We compare our approach in eight different languages, three of which have important international contests: SemEval (English), TASS (Spanish), and SENTIPOLC (Italian). Within these competitions, our approach achieves medium to high rankings; while in the remaining languages, our approach outperforms reported results.
label: AI

title: Neural Networks for Joint Sentence Classification in Medical Paper Abstracts
Abstract: Existing artificial neural network (ANN)-based models for sentence classification often do not incorporate the context in which sentences appear and classify sentences individually. However, traditional sentence classification approaches have shown significant benefits from jointly classifying subsequent sentences, as demonstrated by conditional random fields. In this work, we present an ANN architecture that combines the effectiveness of typical ANN models for classifying sentences in isolation with the strengths of structured prediction. Our model achieves state-of-the-art results on two different datasets for sequential sentence classification in medical abstracts.
label: AI

title: Private Learning on Networks
Abstract: Continual data collection and widespread deployment of machine learning algorithms, particularly distributed variants, have introduced new privacy challenges. In a distributed machine learning scenario, the dataset is stored across multiple machines, which collaboratively solve a distributed optimization problem to learn the underlying model. We present a secure multi-party computation-inspired privacy-preserving distributed algorithm for optimizing a convex function consisting of multiple possibly non-convex functions. Each individual objective function is privately stored by an agent, while agents communicate model parameters with neighboring machines connected in a network. We demonstrate that our algorithm accurately optimizes the overall objective function and learns the underlying model. We further prove that under a vertex connectivity condition on the network topology, our algorithm preserves privacy of individual objective functions. We establish limits on what a coalition of adversaries can learn by observing messages and states shared over the network.

title: Visual Compiler: Synthesizing a Scene-Specific Pedestrian Detector and Pose Estimator
Abstract: We introduce the concept of a Visual Compiler that generates a scene-specific pedestrian detector and pose estimator without any pedestrian observations. Given a single image and auxiliary scene information, such as camera parameters and geometric layout, the Visual Compiler first infers geometrically and photometrically accurate images of humans in that scene using computer graphics rendering. Using these renders, we learn a scene-and-region-specific spatially-varying fully convolutional neural network for simultaneous detection, pose estimation, and segmentation of pedestrians. We demonstrate that when real human annotated data is scarce or non-existent, our data generation strategy provides an excellent solution for bootstrapping human detection and pose estimation. Experimental results show that our approach outperforms off-the-shelf state-of-the-art pedestrian detectors and pose estimators trained on real data.

title: Tunable Efficient Unitary Neural Networks (EUNN) and their application to RNNs
Abstract: Using unitary (instead of general) matrices in artificial neural networks (ANNs) is a promising approach for solving the gradient explosion/vanishing problem and enabling ANNs to learn long-term correlations in the data. This approach appears particularly promising for Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs). We present a new architecture for implementing an Efficient Unitary Neural Network (EUNN), offering several key advantages. Firstly, the representation capacity of the unitary space in an EUNN is fully tunable, ranging from a subspace of SU(N) to the entire unitary space. Secondly, the computational complexity for training an EUNN is merely $\\mathcal{O}(1)$ per parameter. Finally, we test the performance of EUNNs on the standard copying task, the pixel-permuted MNIST digit recognition benchmark, as well as the Speech Prediction Test (TIMIT). We find that our architecture significantly outperforms both other state-of-the-art unitary RNNs and the LSTM architecture, in terms of final performance and/or wall-clock training speed. EUNNs are thus promising alternatives to RNNs and LSTMs for a wide variety of applications.

title: Multivariate Submodular Optimization
Abstract: Submodular functions have found widespread applications in data science and machine learning models in recent years. This has been accompanied by many algorithmic advances in submodular optimization (SO): $\\min/\\max~f(S): S \\in \\mathcal{F}$, where $\\mathcal{F}$ is a family of feasible sets over a ground set $V$ and $f:2^V \\rightarrow \\mathbb{R}$ is submodular. In this work, we focus on a more general class of multivariate submodular optimization (MVSO) problems: $\\min/\\max~f (S_1,S_2,\\ldots,S_k):\nS_1 \\uplus S_2 \\uplus \\cdots \\uplus S_k \\in \\mathcal{F}$. Here, $\\uplus$ denotes disjoint union, making this model attractive for scenarios where resources are allocated across $k$ agents who share a joint multivariate nonnegative objective $f(S_1,S_2,\\ldots,S_k)$ exhibiting submodularity (diminishing returns). We provide explicit examples and potential applications for this new framework. For maximization, we show that practical algorithms like accelerated greedy variants and distributed algorithms achieve good approximation guarantees for very general families (such as matroids and $p$-systems). For arbitrary families, we demonstrate that monotone (resp. nonmonotone) MVSO admits an $\\alpha (1-1/e)$ (resp. $\\alpha \\cdot 0.385$) approximation whenever monotone (resp. nonmonotone) SO admits an $\\alpha$-approximation over the multilinear formulation. This significantly expands the family of tractable models for submodular maximization. For minimization, we show that if SO admits a $\\beta$-approximation over modular functions, then MVSO admits a $\\frac{\\beta \\cdot n}{1+(n-1)(1-c)}$-approximation where $c\\in [0,1]$ denotes the curvature of $f$, and this is essentially tight. Finally, we prove that MVSO has an $\\alpha k$-approximation whenever SO admits an $\\alpha$-approximation over the convex formulation. |||

title: Tomography and Generative Data Modeling via Quantum Boltzmann Training
Abstract: Quantum neural networks, which leverage quantum effects to model intricate datasets, hold great promise for advancing quantum machine learning and quantum computing. This paper presents novel methods for training quantum Boltzmann machines, a class of recurrent quantum neural networks. These methods expand upon existing techniques and introduce new approaches for training quantum neural networks, demonstrating superior performance compared to current methods. Moreover, it is shown that quantum Boltzmann machines enable a form of quantum state tomography that not only estimates a state but also provides a prescription for generating copies of the reconstructed state. This capability is not achievable with classical Boltzmann machines. Finally, a comparison between small non-stoquastic quantum Boltzmann machines and traditional Boltzmann machines for generative tasks reveals evidence that quantum models outperform their classical counterparts.

title: CSVideoNet: A Real-time End-to-end Learning Framework for High-frame-rate Video Compressive Sensing
Abstract: This paper tackles the real-time encoding-decoding problem for high-frame-rate video compressive sensing (CS). Instead of relying on iterative optimization-based reconstruction methods employed in previous works, this paper proposes a non-iterative model called "CSVideoNet." CSVideoNet directly learns the inverse mapping of CS and reconstructs the original input in a single forward propagation. To address the limitations of existing CS cameras, a multi-rate CNN and a synthesizing RNN are proposed to improve the trade-off between compression ratio (CR) and spatial-temporal resolution of the reconstructed videos. Experimental results demonstrate that CSVideoNet significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches. Notably, it achieves 25dB PSNR recovery quality at 100x CR with a frame rate of 125 fps on a Titan X GPU without pre/post-processing. Due to the feedforward and high-data-concurrency nature of CSVideoNet, it leverages GPU acceleration to achieve three orders of magnitude speed-up over conventional iterative-based methods. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/PSCLab-ASU/CSVideoNet.
