title: TF.Learn: TensorFlow's High-level Module for Distributed Machine Learning
Abstract: TF.Learn is a high-level Python module for distributed machine learning within TensorFlow. It provides a user-friendly Scikit-learn style interface to simplify the process of creating, configuring, training, evaluating, and experimenting with machine learning models. TF.Learn integrates a wide range of state-of-the-art machine learning algorithms built on top of TensorFlow's low-level APIs for small to large-scale supervised and unsupervised problems. This module focuses on bringing machine learning to non-specialists using a general-purpose high-level language, as well as researchers who want to implement, benchmark, and compare their new methods in a structured environment. Emphasis is placed on ease of use, performance, documentation, and API consistency.
label: AI

title: Response to Comment on 'Perceptual Learning Incepted by Decoded fMRI Neurofeedback Without Stimulus Presentation'; How can a decoded neurofeedback method (DecNef) lead to successful reinforcement and visual perceptual learning?
Abstract: Huang (arXiv:1612.03270) argues that the perceptual learning induced by the decoded neurofeedback method (DecNef) can be explained by Hebbian synaptic plasticity of connections between V1/V2 and V3/V4 rather than within V1/V2. Additionally, Huang contends that reinforcement learning at a cellular level is not possible, challenging the conclusions of the paper. In response, this paper first shows that Huang's model is incompatible with the data, which strongly suggests plasticity within V1/V2. Second, a new analysis reveals that spontaneous activity is not random but largely accounted for by low-dimensional components. These findings, along with other results, indicate that learning to induce a stimulus-associated template voxel pattern in V1/V2 within as few as 100 trials is likely achieved through hyper-resolution and sub-voxel level control by DecNef. |||
label: AI

title: Multi-Perspective Context Matching for Machine Comprehension
Abstract: The SQuAD dataset addresses the shortcomings of previous machine comprehension (MC) datasets by providing a more realistic and challenging benchmark for evaluating MC models. This paper proposes a novel Multi-Perspective Context Matching (MPCM) model, an end-to-end system designed for directly predicting the answer's beginning and ending positions within a passage. The MPCM model first adjusts each word embedding vector in the passage by multiplying it with a relevancy weight computed against the question. It then encodes the question and weighted passage using bidirectional LSTMs. For every point in the passage, the model compares its context against the encoded question from multiple perspectives, generating a matching vector. Finally, another bidirectional LSTM aggregates all the matching vectors to predict the answer's starting and ending points. Experimental results on the SQuAD test set show that the MPCM model achieves a competitive performance on the leaderboard.
label: AI

title: Models of retrieval in sentence comprehension: A computational evaluation using Bayesian hierarchical modeling
Abstract: Research on interference has provided evidence that the formation of dependencies between non-adjacent words relies on a cue-based retrieval mechanism. Two models, Lewis and Vasishth's activation-based model and McElree's direct access model, can account for one of the main predictions of interference: a slowdown at a retrieval site when multiple items share a feature associated with a retrieval cue. While these models have been used interchangeably, they differ in their assumptions and predictions regarding the relationship between reading times and response accuracy. The activation-based model, based on ACT-R, assumes a lognormal race between evidence accumulators with a single variance. In this model, accuracy is determined by the winner of the race, and retrieval time by its accumulation rate. Conversely, the direct access model assumes a memory model where only the probability of retrieval varies between items. In this model, latency differences arise from the possibility and repair of incorrect retrievals. This study implements both models within a Bayesian hierarchical framework to evaluate and compare their performance. The results show that the direct access model provides a better fit for certain data aspects than the activation-based model. However, this finding does not eliminate the possibility that retrieval may function as a race model with assumptions that deviate from the ACT-R framework. By introducing a modification to the activation model—assuming that the accumulation of evidence for incorrect items is not only slower but also noisier (i.e., different variances for correct and incorrect items)—the model can achieve a fit comparable to the direct access model.
label: AI

title: Information Extraction with Character-level Neural Networks and Free Noisy Supervision
Abstract: This paper presents an architecture for information extraction from text that enhances an existing parser with a character-level neural network. The network is trained using a measure of consistency between extracted data and existing databases, acting as a form of noisy supervision. This architecture combines the strengths of constraint-based information extraction systems—ease of incorporating domain knowledge and constraints—with the capabilities of deep neural networks—learning complex features from large amounts of data. This system significantly improves the existing parser's precision, outperforming a mature and highly tuned constraint-based production information extraction system employed at Bloomberg for financial language text.
label: AI

title: Upper Bound of Bayesian Generalization Error in Non-negative Matrix Factorization
Abstract: Non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) is a knowledge discovery method with applications in text mining, signal processing, bioinformatics, and consumer analysis. However, its fundamental properties as a learning machine remain unclear due to its non-statistical nature, hindering the establishment of theoretical optimization methods. This paper investigates the real log canonical threshold of NMF and provides an upper bound for the generalization error in Bayesian learning. The results demonstrate that the generalization error of matrix factorization can be lower than regular statistical models when Bayesian learning is applied.
label: AI

title: Parsimonious Online Learning with Kernels via Sparse Projections in Function Space
Abstract: Despite their appeal, nonparametric function approximation techniques are often perceived as unsuitable for streaming data due to their memory requirements. This paper addresses this challenge by proposing an online technique based on functional stochastic gradient descent coupled with supervised sparsification using greedy function subspace projections. This method, called parsimonious online learning with kernels (POLK), offers a controllable trade-off between solution accuracy and memory consumption. The paper derives conditions under which the generated function sequence converges almost surely to the optimal function while ensuring a finite memory requirement. POLK is evaluated for kernel multi-class logistic regression and kernel hinge-loss classification on three canonical datasets: a synthetic Gaussian mixture model, MNIST hand-written digits, and the Brodatz texture database. Across all tasks, POLK demonstrates a favorable trade-off between objective function evaluation, classification performance, and complexity of the extracted nonparametric regressor.
label: AI

title: Corporate Disruption in the Science of Machine Learning
Abstract: This MSc dissertation examines the impact of current corporate interest on researchers in the field of machine learning. Situated within the cyclical history of academic, public, and corporate interest, the dissertation investigates how current researchers perceive recent developments and navigate their research practices within an environment of increased commercial interest and funding. The original research involves in-depth interviews with 12 machine learning researchers working in both academia and industry. Drawing upon theory from science, technology, and society studies, the dissertation challenges traditional narratives of neoliberalization in academic research by allowing researchers to discuss how their career choices, working environments, and interactions with others in the field have been affected by the reinvigorated corporate interest of recent years.
label: AI

title: Learning to Hash-tag Videos with Tag2Vec
Abstract: User-generated tags or labels are valuable resources for semantic understanding of visual media like images and videos. Recently, hash-tags have gained popularity as a labeling mechanism on social media platforms. This paper addresses the problem of generating relevant and useful hash-tags for short video clips. Traditional data-driven approaches for tag enrichment and recommendation rely on direct visual similarity for label transfer and propagation. This research proposes a direct low-cost mapping from video to hash-tags using a two-step training process. Firstly, a skip-gram model with neural network training, a natural language processing (NLP) technique, is used to learn a low-dimensional vector representation of hash-tags (Tag2Vec) from a corpus of 10 million hash-tags. Subsequently, an embedding function is trained to map video features to the Tag2Vec space. This embedding is learned for 29 categories of short video clips with hash-tags. A query video without tag information can then be directly mapped to the Tag2Vec space using the learned embedding, and relevant tags can be identified through a simple nearest-neighbor retrieval. The relevance of the suggested tags is validated qualitatively and quantitatively through a user study.
label: AI

title: Joint Bayesian Gaussian discriminant analysis for speaker verification
Abstract: State-of-the-art speaker verification systems based on i-vectors rely on variants of Probabilistic Linear Discriminant Analysis (PLDA) for discriminant analysis. This paper is motivated by the recent work on the joint Bayesian (JB) method, originally proposed for face verification. The paper applies JB to speaker verification and presents three key contributions beyond the original JB. Firstly, unlike the original JB that employs EM iterations with approximated statistics, this work utilizes EM iterations with exact statistics, leading to improved performance. Secondly, the paper proposes simultaneous diagonalization (SD) of the within-class and between-class covariance matrices for efficient testing, expanding the applicability of the method beyond the SVD-based efficient testing in the original JB. Finally, the paper analyzes the similarities and differences between various Gaussian PLDAs and JB, complementing previous analyses that compared JB only with Prince-Elder PLDA. Extensive experiments conducted on NIST SRE10 core condition 5 validate the superiority of JB, demonstrating faster convergence rates and a 9-13% EER reduction compared to state-of-the-art PLDA.
label: AI

title: Theory and Tools for the Conversion of Analog to Spiking Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) hold great promise for various real-world machine learning applications, but performing inference in large CNNs in real-time remains challenging. Previous work has demonstrated that traditional CNNs can be converted into deep spiking neural networks (SNNs), achieving similar accuracy while reducing latency and computational load due to their event-based computing style. This paper presents a novel theory explaining the success of this conversion process and derives new tools for converting a broader class of deep networks into SNNs. The paper identifies the main sources of approximation errors in previous conversion methods and proposes simple mechanisms to address these issues. Furthermore, the paper develops spiking implementations of common CNN operations, including max-pooling, softmax, and batch-normalization, enabling almost loss-less conversion of arbitrary CNN architectures into the spiking domain. Empirical evaluation of different network architectures on the MNIST and CIFAR10 benchmarks results in the best SNN performance reported to date.
label: AI

title: DizzyRNN: Reparameterizing Recurrent Neural Networks for Norm-Preserving Backpropagation
Abstract: The vanishing and exploding gradient problems are well-known obstacles that hinder recurrent neural networks (RNNs) from learning long-term temporal dependencies. This paper proposes a reparameterization of standard RNNs to update linear transformations in a provably norm-preserving manner through Givens rotations. Additionally, the absolute value function is used as an element-wise nonlinearity to preserve the norm of backpropagated signals throughout the network. This reparameterization reduces the number of parameters and maintains the same algorithmic complexity as standard RNNs while outperforming standard RNNs with orthogonal initializations and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks on the copy problem.
label: AI

title: Distributed Multi-Task Relationship Learning
Abstract: Multi-task learning aims to improve generalization performance for each task by jointly learning multiple related tasks. Traditionally, multi-task learning requires centralizing data from all tasks on a single machine. However, many real-world applications involve geo-distributed data across different local machines. Due to communication overhead and data privacy concerns, transmitting data to a central machine for multi-task learning is infeasible. This paper proposes a distributed multi-task learning framework that simultaneously learns predictive models for each task and task relationships between tasks alternately within the parameter server paradigm. The framework first introduces a general dual form for a family of regularized multi-task relationship learning methods. Then, a communication-efficient primal-dual distributed optimization algorithm is proposed to solve the dual problem by carefully designing local subproblems to make the dual problem decomposable. The paper provides a theoretical convergence analysis specifically for distributed multi-task relationship learning. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets evaluate the effectiveness and convergence of the proposed framework.
label: AI

title: Generative Adversarial Parallelization
Abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have become a prominent framework for unsupervised learning due to their intuitive formulation. While GANs have demonstrated success in generating convincing examples in limited domains, such as low-resolution images, they remain challenging to train in practice and tend to ignore modes of the data generating distribution. Quantitatively capturing effects like mode coverage and overall model quality remains elusive. This paper proposes Generative Adversarial Parallelization (GAP), a framework in which multiple GANs or their variants are trained concurrently, exchanging their discriminators. This eliminates the tight coupling between generators and discriminators, leading to improved convergence and enhanced mode coverage. The paper also introduces an improved variant of the recently proposed Generative Adversarial Metric, demonstrating its ability to score individual GANs or their collections under the GAP model.
label: AI

title: An empirical analysis of the optimization of deep network loss surfaces
Abstract: The success of deep neural networks relies on the ability to accurately and efficiently optimize high-dimensional, non-convex functions. This paper empirically investigates the loss functions of state-of-the-art networks and how commonly used stochastic gradient descent variants optimize these functions. The study visualizes the loss function by projecting it onto low-dimensional spaces determined by the convergence points of different optimization algorithms. Observations suggest that optimization algorithms encounter and choose different descent directions at multiple saddle points, resulting in distinct final weights. Based on observed consistency across re-runs of the same stochastic optimization algorithm, the paper hypothesizes that each algorithm makes characteristic choices at these saddle points.
label: AI

title: A Video-Based Method for Objectively Rating Ataxia
Abstract: For numerous movement disorders, such as Parkinson's disease and ataxia, disease progression is visually assessed by clinicians using a numerical disease rating scale. These tests are subjective, time-consuming, and require professional administration, posing challenges in situations where specialists are unavailable or patients lack consistent evaluations. This paper presents an automated method for quantifying the severity of motion impairment in patients with ataxia using only video recordings. The method focuses on videos of the finger-to-nose test, a common movement task used in ataxia progression assessment during routine clinical checkups. The approach leverages neural network-based pose estimation and optical flow techniques to track hand motion in video recordings. Features describing motion qualities, such as speed and performance variation, are extracted. Using expert clinician-provided labels, a supervised learning model is trained to predict severity according to the Brief Ataxia Rating Scale (BARS). The system's performance is comparable to ataxia specialists in terms of mean error and correlation, and its predictions consistently fall within the range of inter-rater variability. This work demonstrates the feasibility of using computer vision and machine learning to generate consistent and clinically valuable measures of motor impairment.
label: AI

title: Avoiding communication in primal and dual block coordinate descent methods
Abstract: Primal and dual block coordinate descent methods are iterative algorithms for solving regularized and unregularized optimization problems. Distributed-memory parallel implementations of these methods have gained popularity in analyzing large machine learning datasets. However, existing implementations communicate at every iteration, often dominating the cost of floating-point computation on modern data center and supercomputing architectures. Recent advances in communication-avoiding Krylov subspace methods suggest that significant speedups are possible by restructuring iterative algorithms to minimize communication. This paper shows how applying similar algorithmic transformations can lead to primal and dual block coordinate descent methods that communicate only every *s* iterations (where *s* is a tuning parameter) instead of every iteration, specifically for the regularized least-squares problem. The paper demonstrates that these communication-avoiding variants reduce the number of synchronizations by a factor of *s* on distributed-memory parallel machines without affecting the convergence rate, achieving strong scaling speedups of up to 6.1x on a Cray XC30 supercomputer.
label: AI

title: Models, networks and algorithmic complexity
Abstract: This paper aims to demonstrate that models, classification or generating functions, invariances, and datasets are algorithmically equivalent concepts when properly defined. It provides concrete examples of these equivalences. The paper then shows that: a) neural networks (NNs) of different types can be viewed as implementing models, b) perturbations of inputs and nodes in NNs trained to optimally implement simple models propagate strongly, and c) a framework exists where recurrent, deep, and shallow networks can be categorized into a descriptive power hierarchy aligned with concepts from the theory of recursive functions. The motivation for these definitions and subsequent analysis stems from cognitive neuroscience, specifically Ruffini (2016), which extensively uses the concepts of model and algorithmic complexity.

title: Hybrid Repeat/Multi-point Sampling for Highly Volatile Objective Functions
Abstract: A major drawback of current artificial decision-makers is their poor adaptation to unexpected changes in situations. This paper tackles this challenge by focusing on an AI for aerial dogfighting with tunable parameters governing its behavior. The AI optimizes behavior with respect to an objective function that must be evaluated and learned through simulations. Once modeled, the objective function enables the agent to select desired behaviors in different scenarios. Bayesian optimization with a Gaussian Process surrogate is employed for investigating the objective function. A key benefit is that during optimization, the Gaussian Process learns a global estimate of the true objective function, providing predicted outcomes and confidence measures for unexplored areas. However, standard Bayesian optimization struggles with volatile objective functions. This paper addresses these issues by introducing Hybrid Repeat/Multi-point Sampling, a novel sampling technique that enhances the AI's ability to learn optimal behaviors in highly uncertain environments. More importantly, this technique not only improves optimization reliability but also generates a better model of the entire objective surface, equipping the agent with enhanced behavioral adaptation capabilities.

title: ConceptNet 5.5: An Open Multilingual Graph of General Knowledge
Abstract: Machine learning about language can be enhanced by providing it with specific knowledge and external information sources. This paper introduces a new version of the linked open data resource ConceptNet, specifically designed for use with modern NLP techniques like word embeddings. ConceptNet is a knowledge graph that connects words and phrases of natural language with labeled edges. Its knowledge is gathered from various sources, including expert-created resources, crowd-sourcing, and games with a purpose. ConceptNet aims to represent the general knowledge involved in understanding language, improving natural language applications by enabling them to better comprehend the meanings behind words. When combined with word embeddings obtained from distributional semantics (like word2vec), ConceptNet provides applications with understanding that surpasses what they could achieve from distributional semantics alone or narrower resources like WordNet or DBPedia. The paper demonstrates this through state-of-the-art results on intrinsic evaluations of word relatedness, translating into improvements in word vector applications, including solving SAT-style analogies.

title: Tracking the World State with Recurrent Entity Networks
Abstract: This paper introduces the Recurrent Entity Network (EntNet), a novel model equipped with a dynamic long-term memory that allows it to maintain and update a representation of the world's state as it receives new data. For language understanding tasks, EntNet can reason on-the-fly while reading text, unlike Memory Networks (Sukhbaatar et al., 2015) which only reason when required to answer a question or respond. Similar to Neural Turing Machines or Differentiable Neural Computers (Graves et al., 2014; 2016), EntNet maintains a fixed-size memory and learns to perform location and content-based read and write operations. However, it differs from these models by having a simple parallel architecture where multiple memory locations can be updated simultaneously. EntNet sets a new state-of-the-art on the bAbI tasks, becoming the first method to solve all tasks in the 10k training examples setting. The paper further demonstrates EntNet's ability to solve a reasoning task requiring a large number of supporting facts, a task that other methods fail to solve. It also shows EntNet's generalization capabilities beyond its training horizon. Moreover, EntNet can be practically applied to large-scale datasets like the Children's Book Test, achieving competitive performance by reading the story in a single pass.

title: Probabilistic Bisection Converges Almost as Quickly as Stochastic Approximation
Abstract: The probabilistic bisection algorithm (PBA) solves a class of stochastic root-finding problems in one dimension by iteratively updating a prior belief about the root's location based on noisy responses to queries at chosen points. Responses indicate the root's direction from the queried point and are subject to a fixed probability of error. This paper extends the PBA to handle situations where the fixed-probability assumption is relaxed. The extension involves using a power-one test at each queried point. The paper explores the convergence behavior of the extended PBA, showing that it converges at a rate arbitrarily close to, but slower than, the canonical "square root" rate of stochastic approximation. |||

title: Neural Networks with Manifold Learning for Diabetic Retinopathy Detection
Abstract: The widespread use of remote retinal imaging programs has effectively reduced the risk of diabetic retinopathy, a leading cause of blindness in the US. However, manual verification of image quality and disease grading by trained personnel remains a bottleneck.  This paper proposes a set of neural networks for automated diabetic retinopathy classification of fundus retinal images. Preprocessing and augmentation techniques were implemented to improve classification accuracy, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of neural networks for large-scale diabetic retinopathy detection.  The scalability of these models facilitates faster diagnosis and detection processes.

title: Monte Carlo Structured SVI for Two-Level Non-Conjugate Models
Abstract: Stochastic variational inference (SVI), a powerful technique combining variational inference, natural gradients, and stochastic updates, has proven effective for large-scale Bayesian model analysis. This research explores a family of Bayesian latent variable models with two levels of hidden variables but without requiring conjugacy. The study reveals that SVI, with improved structured variational approximations, can be applied under more general conditions than previously thought, requiring only that the approximating variational distribution belongs to the same family as the prior. This extended approach, Monte Carlo Structured SVI (MC-SSVI), significantly broadens SVI's scope, enabling large-scale learning in non-conjugate models. For models with latent Gaussian variables, a hybrid algorithm utilizing both standard and natural gradients is proposed, demonstrating improved stability and convergence.  Applications in mixed effects models, sparse Gaussian processes, probabilistic matrix factorization, and correlated topic models highlight the generality and advantages of the proposed algorithms.

title: Nonnegative Matrix Factorization for identification of unknown number of sources emitting delayed signals
Abstract: Factor analysis, a powerful unsupervised machine learning tool, is widely used for reconstructing hidden features from mixtures of signals. While many model-free Blind Source Separation (BSS) algorithms effectively decompose instantaneous mixtures, the case of delayed signal mixtures remains less explored.  This paper presents a novel Nonnegative Matrix Factorization (NMF) based method for identifying the unknown number of sources with delays, their propagation speeds, and locations. The method can be applied to decompose records of mixed signals with delays emitted from an unknown number of sources in nondispersive media.  Examples include asynchronous electromagnetic signals from multiple antennas, mixed acoustic or seismic signals recorded by geographically dispersed sensors, or signals experiencing Doppler shift. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated on synthetic datasets, accurately identifying the number of sources, waveforms, delays, and signal strengths. Bayesian analysis provides estimations of uncertainties and helps identify the likelihood region for source locations.

title: Identification of release sources in advection-diffusion system by machine learning combined with Green function inverse method
Abstract: Identifying sources of advection-diffusion transport typically involves solving complex ill-posed inverse models against available state-variable data records. However, the presence of multiple sources with varying locations and strengths results in mixed data records rather than individual source influences.  This research introduces a novel hybrid method, HNMF, to address this challenge.  HNMF combines unsupervised learning through Nonnegative Matrix Factorization (NMF) with the inverse-analysis Green functions method. HNMF synergistically decomposes the recorded mixtures, determines the number of unknown sources, and utilizes the Green function of the advection-diffusion equation to identify source characteristics. The method is demonstrated on synthetic datasets, successfully identifying the advection velocity, dispersivity of the medium, and the number, locations, and properties of various release sources with different space and time dependencies.  HNMF can be directly applied to problems governed by partial-differential parabolic equations where mixtures from an unknown number of sources are measured at multiple locations.

title: Understanding the Impact of Precision Quantization on the Accuracy and Energy of Neural Networks
Abstract: Deep neural networks are gaining popularity due to their ability to achieve state-of-the-art results in computer vision and machine learning.  However, the increasing depth and complexity of these networks require significant computational resources. This research addresses the need for low-power, low-memory solutions by studying the impact of different bit precisions and arithmetic on both network accuracy and hardware metrics.  The study considers precision scaling from floating-point to fixed-point, powers of two, and binary, analyzing the effects on network accuracy, memory footprint, power and energy consumption, and design area.  Training-time methodologies to compensate for accuracy loss due to limited bit precision are also investigated. The results show that precision scaling can significantly benefit design metrics while only slightly affecting network accuracy.  Moreover, the paper proposes utilizing a portion of these benefits to increase network size and consequently improve accuracy.  Experiments conducted on three well-recognized networks and datasets validate the generality of the approach, highlighting the trade-offs and benefits of using lower precisions in terms of energy efficiency and memory footprint.

title: Deep Active Learning for Dialogue Generation
Abstract: This research proposes a novel online, end-to-end, neural generative conversational model for open-domain dialogue. The model is trained using a unique combination of offline two-phase supervised learning and online human-in-the-loop active learning. Unlike existing approaches that rely on offline supervision or handcrafted reward functions for online reinforcement, this study introduces a novel interactive learning mechanism based on hamming-diverse beam search for response generation and one-character user-feedback at each step.  Experiments demonstrate that the model inherently promotes semantically relevant and interesting responses, enabling the training of agents with customized personas, moods, and conversational styles.
label: AI

title: Design of Data-Driven Mathematical Laws for Optimal Statistical Classification Systems
Abstract: This research aims to develop data-driven, mathematical laws that generate optimal statistical classification systems with minimal error rates for data distributions with unchanging statistics.  The study focuses on designing learning machines that minimize expected risk or the probability of misclassification.  The research devises a system of fundamental equations for binary classification in statistical equilibrium, formulating the problem of learning unknown, linear, and quadratic discriminant functions from data as a locus problem within a statistical framework.  Three classes of data-driven, locus equations are proposed to generate optimal statistical classification systems.  Each class of learning machines adheres to fundamental statistical laws for a classification system in statistical equilibrium, forming scalable modules for optimal statistical pattern recognition systems.  These modules are capable of performing a wide range of statistical pattern recognition tasks, achieving optimal generalization performance for M-class feature spaces.

title: Deep Supervised Hashing with Triplet Labels
Abstract: Hashing is a widely used and powerful technique for approximate nearest neighbor search in large-scale image retrieval. Traditional hashing methods often rely on off-the-shelf visual features, which may not be optimal for hash code learning, leading to sub-optimal results.  Deep hashing methods have emerged to address this limitation by simultaneously learning image features and hash codes using deep neural networks.  While most deep hashing methods require supervised information in the form of pairwise or triplet labels, the state-of-the-art DPSH method (based on pairwise labels) performs feature and hash code learning simultaneously by maximizing pairwise similarity likelihood. This paper proposes a triplet label-based deep hashing method that aims to maximize the likelihood of the given triplet labels.  Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses all baselines on CIFAR-10 and NUS-WIDE datasets, including the state-of-the-art DPSH method and other triplet label-based deep hashing methods.
label: AI

title: Inverse Compositional Spatial Transformer Networks
Abstract: This paper establishes a theoretical connection between the classical Lucas & Kanade (LK) algorithm and Spatial Transformer Networks (STNs), which are gaining interest in the vision and learning communities due to their ability to combine alignment and classification within a single framework.  Inspired by the Inverse Compositional (IC) variant of the LK algorithm, the research introduces Inverse Compositional Spatial Transformer Networks (IC-STNs).  Results demonstrate that IC-STNs achieve better performance than conventional STNs with less model capacity, particularly excelling in pure image alignment tasks and joint alignment/classification problems on real-world applications.
label: AI

title: Knowledge Completion for Generics using Guided Tensor Factorization
Abstract: This research investigates the problem of inferring additional facts about common nouns or generics (e.g., "all trees produce oxygen," "some animals live in forests") from a knowledge base (KB) containing noisy facts. These KBs capture general knowledge about the world and are crucial for applications like question answering.  Unlike commonly studied named entity KBs, generics KBs involve quantification, exhibit more complex underlying regularities, tend to be incomplete, and violate the locally closed world assumption (LCWA).  The study shows that existing KB completion methods struggle with this task and presents a novel approach that successfully addresses this challenge.  The research demonstrates the power of external information, such as relation schemas and entity taxonomies, in this setting.  A knowledge-guided tensor factorization approach achieves state-of-the-art results on two generics KBs, significantly increasing their size while maintaining high precision.  A novel taxonomy-guided, submodular, active learning method for collecting annotations about rare entities proves highly effective in inferring new facts about them.

title: Estimating individual employment status using mobile phone network data
Abstract: This study presents the first confirmation that individual employment status can be predicted from standard mobile phone network logs, validated using household survey data.  Employment status and professional occupations of household breadwinners are closely linked to individual welfare, household vulnerability to shocks, and societal economic indicators like unemployment.  The research derives a novel set of mobile phone network indicators reflecting users' financial, social, and mobility patterns and demonstrates the use of machine learning models to predict 18 professional categories in a South-Asian developing country.  The model achieves 70.4% accuracy in predicting individual unemployment status. The study further shows how aggregated individual unemployment data can be mapped geographically at cell tower resolution, providing a promising approach to map labor market economic indicators and the distribution of economic productivity and vulnerability between censuses, especially in heterogeneous urban areas.  The method also presents a promising approach for supporting data collection on vulnerable populations, who are often under-represented in official surveys.

title: Neutrino Signatures From Young Neutron Stars
Abstract: Following a successful core collapse supernova (CCSN) explosion, a hot, dense proto-neutron star (PNS) is left as a remnant.  Over a period of approximately twenty seconds, this PNS emits the majority of neutrinos from the CCSN, contracts, and loses most of its lepton number. This process is likely responsible for the formation of all neutron stars in our galaxy.  Neutrinos emitted from SN 1987A were detected, and future galactic CCSNe will provide much more abundant neutrino detections. These detections offer a direct window into the properties of dense matter inside neutron stars and can impact nucleosynthesis in the material ejected during the CCSN.  This chapter reviews the fundamental physics of PNS cooling, including the basic equations of PNS structure and neutrino diffusion in dense matter.  The research discusses how the nuclear equation of state, neutrino opacities in dense matter, and convection influence the temporal behavior of the neutrino signal.  The study also explores insights gained from the late-time SN 1987A neutrinos, the prospects for detecting these neutrinos from future galactic CCSNe, and the effects these neutrinos have on nucleosynthesis.

title: Smart Scheduling of Continuous Data-Intensive Workflows with Machine Learning Triggered Execution
Abstract: Organizations often resort to data processing workflows to extract value from ever-growing data volumes from various sources and drive decision-making. Workflows offer expressiveness, flexibility, and scalability. However, the typical workflow model enforces strict temporal synchronization across processing steps, neglecting the actual effect of intermediate computations on the final output.  This research identifies a class of applications for continuous data processing where workflow output changes slowly and insignificantly over short-to-medium time windows, leading to inefficient resource utilization and energy waste.  To overcome this inefficiency, the paper introduces a novel workflow model for continuous and data-intensive processing. This model relaxes triggering semantics based on the assessed impact of input data on workflow output changes.  Machine learning is employed to assess this impact, learn the correlation between input and output variation, and guarantee correctness within a tolerated error constant.  The functionality of this workflow model is implemented in SmartFlux, a middleware framework that seamlessly integrates with existing workflow managers. Experimental results demonstrate significant resource savings without exceeding a small error constant with high confidence.

title: Distributed and Proximity-Constrained C-Means for Discrete Coverage Control
Abstract: This paper presents a novel distributed coverage control framework for a network of mobile agents tasked with covering a finite set of points of interest (PoIs), such as people in danger, geographically dispersed equipment, or environmental landmarks. The proposed algorithm draws inspiration from C-Means, an unsupervised learning algorithm originally designed for non-exclusive clustering and identifying cluster centroids from a set of observations.  To accommodate the agents' limited sensing range and avoid infeasible coverage solutions, traditional C-Means is enhanced with proximity constraints, ensuring that each agent considers only neighboring PoIs.  The proposed coverage control framework provides valuable information regarding the ranking or importance of different PoIs to the agents, enabling further application-dependent data fusion processes, patrolling, or disaster relief applications.

title: Tensor Decompositions via Two-Mode Higher-Order SVD (HOSVD)
Abstract: Tensor decompositions find extensive applications in statistics and machine learning, making the development of efficient and accurate algorithms for this problem highly important.  This research presents a new method based on Kruskal's uniqueness theorem to decompose symmetric, nearly orthogonally decomposable tensors. Unlike the classical higher-order singular value decomposition, which unfolds a tensor along a single mode, this method considers unfoldings along two modes and utilizes rank-1 constraints to characterize the underlying components.  This tensor decomposition method demonstrably handles a higher level of noise compared to previous methods and achieves high estimation accuracy.  Numerical results showcase the algorithm's robustness to various noise distributions, particularly excelling as the order increases.

title: Generalizable Features From Unsupervised Learning
Abstract: Humans develop predictive models of the world and use them to reason about future events and the consequences of actions. Unlike most machine predictors, humans possess a remarkable ability to generalize to unseen scenarios and reason intelligently in these settings. One crucial aspect of this ability is physical intuition. This research explores the potential of unsupervised learning to discover features that promote better generalization to settings outside the supervised training distribution. The task involves predicting the stability of towers constructed from square blocks.  The study demonstrates that an unsupervised model, trained to predict future frames of video sequences depicting stable and unstable block configurations, can generate features that support extrapolating stability prediction to block configurations outside the training set distribution.

title: Self-Learning Determinantal Quantum Monte Carlo Method
Abstract: Self-learning Monte Carlo (SLMC) is a powerful general-purpose numerical method recently introduced for simulating many-body systems.  This research implements SLMC within the framework of determinantal quantum Monte Carlo simulation of interacting fermion systems.  Guided by a self-learned bosonic effective action, the method utilizes a cumulative update algorithm for fast and efficient sampling of auxiliary field configurations.  The results show that SLMC can reduce auto-correlation time significantly, leading to a significant speedup.  This enables the simulation of interacting fermion systems on a large lattice for the first time, allowing for the calculation of critical exponents with high accuracy.
label: AI

title: DeepMind Lab
Abstract: DeepMind Lab is a first-person 3D game platform designed for research and development of general artificial intelligence and machine learning systems.  DeepMind Lab enables the study of how autonomous agents learn complex tasks in large, partially observed, and visually diverse environments.  It provides a simple and flexible API for designing creative tasks and exploring novel AI designs, allowing for rapid iteration. The platform is powered by a fast and widely recognized game engine and tailored for effective use by the research community.

title: A Unit Selection Methodology for Music Generation Using Deep Neural Networks
Abstract: This research explores the use of unit selection and concatenation for generating music using a ranking-based procedure, considering a unit as a variable-length sequence of musical measures.  The study investigates whether a unit selection method, limited to a finite unit library, can encompass a wide spectrum of music by developing a deep autoencoder that encodes a musical input and reconstructs it using selections from the library.  A generative model combining a deep structured semantic model (DSSM) with an LSTM is then proposed to predict the next unit, with units consisting of four, two, and one musical measures.  The generative model is evaluated using objective metrics (mean rank and accuracy) and a subjective listening test involving expert musicians.  Comparisons are drawn with a note-level generative baseline consisting of a stacked LSTM trained to predict forward by one note.

title: Online Reinforcement Learning for Real-Time Exploration in Continuous State and Action Markov Decision Processes
Abstract: This paper presents a novel method for learning online policies in continuous state, continuous action, model-free Markov decision processes.  The method possesses two critical properties for practical applications: low computational cost for policy implementation and versatility.  The method builds upon the Fitted Q-iteration algorithm, which represents the Q-value as an average of multiple regression trees.  The proposed Fitted Policy Forest algorithm (FPF) computes a regression forest representing the Q-value and transforms it into a single tree representing the policy, while controlling policy size through resampling and leaf merging.  An adapted version of Multi-Resolution Exploration (MRE) is introduced, particularly suited to FPF.  FPF's performance is assessed on three classical reinforcement learning benchmarks: the "Inverted Pendulum," "Double Integrator," and "Car on the Hill."  The results show that FPF performs as well as or better than other algorithms, despite these algorithms relying on specific representations of the policies tailored to each problem.  Furthermore, the combination of FPF and MRE demonstrates the ability to find nearly optimal solutions in problems where epsilon-greedy approaches would fail. |||

title: PoseAgent: Budget-Constrained 6D Object Pose Estimation via Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: Computer vision algorithms often use discrete choices to optimize efficiency, but these decisions are non-differentiable, making end-to-end training difficult. We propose a reinforcement learning approach to train an efficient 6D object pose estimation system. Our system optimizes an existing state-of-the-art pose estimation system by using it as a stochastic policy parameterized by a CNN. We introduce an efficient training algorithm that significantly reduces computation time. Our learned pose estimation procedure outperforms state-of-the-art methods on a challenging dataset by effectively utilizing limited resources. This approach enables differentiable end-to-end training of complex algorithmic pipelines and optimizes the use of computational budget.
label: AI

title: Hybrid Learning of Optical Flow and Next Frame Prediction to Boost Optical Flow in the Wild
Abstract: CNN-based optical flow estimation, while achieving high frame rates on synthetic datasets, struggles with real-world videos due to the lack of ground truth optical flow for training. To address this, we leverage the self-supervised task of next-frame prediction to boost CNN-based optical flow estimation in real scenes. We train the network in a hybrid manner, combining synthetic and real videos. A sample-variant multi-tasking architecture allows the network to adapt to the availability of ground truth for different tasks. We explore predicting "next-flow" instead of current flow, which intuitively aligns with next-frame prediction and yields improved results. Our approach demonstrates significant improvement in optical flow estimation on the real-world KITTI benchmark. We further evaluate the indirect impact of optical flow on action classification. Notably, our work also achieves substantial improvements in next-frame prediction.

title: Neurogenesis Deep Learning
Abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs), while achieving remarkable success in various data processing tasks, lack the continuous learning capability of biological neural systems. This limits their ability to adapt to dynamic datasets. Inspired by adult neurogenesis in the hippocampus, we propose a method for adding new neurons to deep layers of DNNs to facilitate continuous learning while preserving previously learned representations. Our results on the MNIST and NIST SD 19 datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of neurogenesis in addressing the stability-plasticity dilemma, a long-standing challenge in adaptive machine learning.

title: Cerebral Synchrony Assessment Tutorial: A General Review on Cerebral Signals' Synchronization Estimation Concepts and Methods
Abstract: The human brain, responsible for all thoughts and actions, plays a crucial role in human-environment interaction. Understanding brain function is the goal of cerebral signal analysis, focusing on functional segregation and integration. Reentry, a brain feedback mechanism, necessitates synchronized firing rates among neurons. Consequently, phase synchronization has gained prominence for measuring connectivity in cerebral signals. This paper provides a comprehensive review of concepts and methods for assessing cerebral synchrony, focusing on phase synchronization as a tool for evaluating brain connectivity.

title: Generalized Coherent States, Reproducing Kernels, and Quantum Support Vector Machines
Abstract: Support vector machines (SVMs), a popular machine learning classification method, struggle with scalability due to the need to evaluate the kernel function for all pairs of input feature vectors, especially in high-dimensional spaces. We propose using canonical and generalized coherent states to efficiently calculate specific nonlinear kernel functions. Leveraging the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) property inherent in these states, we demonstrate fast evaluation of radial kernels through a positive operator valued measure (POVM) on a quantum optical system. This approach offers potential for speeding up calculations of other kernels not typically used in classical algorithms.

title: Empirical Evaluation of A New Approach to Simplifying Long Short-term Memory (LSTM)
Abstract: While the standard LSTM excels in modeling long-range dependencies, its complex structure can be simplified. This paper compares the standard LSTM to three new simplified variants obtained by eliminating input signal, bias, and hidden unit signal from individual gates. We evaluated these variants on two sequence datasets and found that they achieve comparable performance with reduced parameters.  However, adjusting the learning rate is crucial for achieving high accuracies.

title: Segmentation of large images based on super-pixels and community detection in graphs
Abstract: Image segmentation, a crucial task in machine learning and medical diagnosis, is addressed in this paper by proposing a framework based on super-pixels and community identification algorithms in graphs. Super-pixel pre-segmentation reduces the number of nodes in the graph, enabling efficient processing of large images. Community detection algorithms offer more accurate segmentation compared to traditional approaches like spectral graph partition.  We compare our method to two existing algorithms: Felzenszwalb and Huttenlocher's graph-based approach and Arbelaez's contour-based method. Our results show that our method provides more precise segmentation and is faster than both alternatives.

title: Poincaré inequalities on intervals -- application to sensitivity analysis
Abstract: Global sensitivity analysis of numerical model outputs has led to renewed interest in 1-dimensional Poincaré inequalities. These inequalities link sensitivity indices, providing upper bounds for interpretable indices using cheaper-to-compute indices. This facilitates screening of unessential variables. The efficiency of this screening depends on the accuracy of the upper bounds in the Poincaré inequalities. The novelty lies in the wide range of probability distributions involved, often truncated on intervals. This paper provides an overview of existing knowledge, introduces theory on Poincaré constants on intervals with improvements for symmetric intervals, and exploits the spectral interpretation to compute exact values of Poincaré constants for any admissible distribution. We present semi-analytical results for frequent distributions (truncated exponential, triangular, truncated normal) and offer a numerical method for general cases. Finally, an application to a hydrological problem demonstrates the benefits of the new Poincaré inequality results for sensitivity analysis.

title: Analysis and Optimization of Loss Functions for Multiclass, Top-k, and Multilabel Classification
Abstract: Top-k error is a widely used performance measure for large-scale image classification benchmarks like ImageNet and Places. This work provides deeper insights into this metric beyond the well-studied top-1 error. Firstly, we conduct an in-depth analysis of established and newly proposed single-label multiclass methods, including efficient optimization algorithms. Our findings reveal the surprising competitiveness of softmax loss and smooth multiclass SVM for top-k error across all k values. We explain this through our analysis of multiclass top-k calibration. Further improvements for specific k values are possible with proposed top-k loss functions. Secondly, we leverage top-k methods to explore the transition from multiclass to multilabel learning. We demonstrate effective multilabel classifiers on Pascal VOC using single-label per image training, while highlighting the significant gap between multiclass and multilabel methods on MS COCO. Additionally, we contribute efficient algorithms for training with top-k and multilabel loss functions, which are of independent interest.

title: Learning to Drive using Inverse Reinforcement Learning and Deep Q-Networks
Abstract: We present an inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) approach using Deep Q-Networks to extract reward functions in problems with large state spaces. We evaluate our approach in a simulated autonomous driving scenario. Our results demonstrate the intuitive relationship between the reward function and distance sensor readings. We also show that our simulated agent learns to generate collision-free motions and performs human-like lane change behavior after several learning rounds.

title: FastText.zip: Compressing text classification models
Abstract: This paper tackles the challenge of creating compact architectures for text classification to fit within limited memory constraints.  We propose a method built upon product quantization to store word embeddings, addressing the accuracy loss inherent in the original technique. Our experiments across various benchmarks show that our approach requires significantly less memory than fastText, achieving comparable accuracy. This results in a superior compromise between memory usage and accuracy compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.
label: AI

title: Connection Discovery using Shared Images by Gaussian Relational Topic Model
Abstract: Social graphs, representing online friendships, are crucial for applications like recommendation, virality prediction, and marketing in social media. However, privacy concerns often limit the availability of this data. Inferring user interests and discovering connections through shared multimedia content is gaining attention. This paper proposes a Gaussian relational topic model for connection discovery using user-shared images in social media. The model not only models user interests as latent variables but also considers connections as a result of shared images. This approach provides a hierarchical and systematic way to relate user-shared images to connections, offering an end-to-end solution. We develop efficient variational inference and learning algorithms for the latent variables and model parameters. Experiments with over 200k images from Flickr demonstrate that our proposed method significantly outperforms previous approaches.

title: Kernel-based Reconstruction of Space-time Functions on Dynamic Graphs
Abstract: Graph-based methods are widely employed in various disciplines, including sociology, biology, neuroscience, physics, chemistry, and engineering. A major challenge involves determining vertex attributes given those of a subset at different time instants. Utilizing spatiotemporal dynamics reduces the number of observed vertices and the cost of sampling. This paper expands the existing kernel-based graph function reconstruction framework to accommodate time-evolving functions over time-varying topologies. This approach maintains the versatility and generality of kernel-based methods, requiring no knowledge of distributions or second-order statistics. We provide guidelines for constructing two families of space-time kernels with complementary strengths: one for controlled regularization on a space-time frequency plane and another for time-varying topologies. We also propose batch and online estimators, along with a novel kernel Kalman filter, for obtaining estimates efficiently. Numerical tests with real datasets demonstrate the superiority of our proposed methods compared to alternatives.
label: AI

title: Search Personalization with Embeddings
Abstract: Recent research highlights the importance of rich user profiles, representing topical interests, for effective search personalization. This paper proposes a novel embedding approach to learn user profiles by embedding users on a topical interest space. We directly utilize these profiles for search personalization. Experiments on query logs from a major commercial web search engine demonstrate that our embedding approach enhances search engine performance and surpasses other strong baselines.
label: AI

title: Statistics of Visual Responses to Object Stimuli from Primate AIT Neurons to DNN Neurons
Abstract: Cadieu et al. (2014) reported that deep neural networks (DNNs) can match the representational capabilities of primate inferotemporal cortex for object recognition. Lehky et al. (2011, 2014) analyzed neural responses to object stimuli in primate AIT cortex, finding an intrinsic dimensionality of around 100. Given the outstanding performance of DNNs in object recognition, this paper investigates whether DNN neuron responses share similar response statistics with AIT neurons. Our analysis of DNN neuron response statistics and intrinsic dimensionality reveals fundamental differences in kurtosis and Pareto tail index compared to IT neurons, except for specific cases. Notably, increasing the number of neurons and stimuli significantly impacts these conclusions. Additionally, with the increasing importance of convolutional layers in DNNs, single-neuron selectivity and population sparseness increase, suggesting that the last convolutional layer learns features for object representations, while subsequent fully-connected layers learn categorization features. Our findings also highlight the need for sufficient stimuli and neurons to obtain stable dimensionality. This work, to our knowledge, is the first to analyze the response statistics of DNN neurons in comparison to AIT neurons, providing insights into the discrepancy between DNN and IT neurons in object representation. Our results also shed light on potential outcomes for IT neurons when the number of recorded neurons and stimuli exceeds the levels investigated in previous studies.

title: On the Pragmatic Design of Literature Studies in Software Engineering: An Experience-based Guideline
Abstract: Systematic literature studies have gained significant attention in empirical software engineering, becoming a powerful tool for systematically and reproducibly collecting and structuring reported knowledge. This paper distinguishes systematic literature reviews for in-depth analysis of reported evidence from systematic mapping studies for broader, often quantified, structuring of fields of interest. The rapidly expanding body of knowledge in software engineering presents researchers with a substantial volume of publications requiring screening, relevance rating, classification, and analysis. While existing guidelines for conducting literature studies exist, they lack support for addressing practical difficulties encountered in applying these guidelines.  This paper provides an experience-based guideline to aid researchers in designing systematic literature studies, particularly focusing on data collection and selection procedures. Our guideline aims to offer a practical and pragmatic blueprint for navigating the plethora of available practices and deliverables, highlighting dependencies among individual steps. The guideline emerges from various mapping studies and literature reviews conducted by the authors and provides recommendations for general study design, data collection, and study selection procedures. Finally, we share our experiences and lessons learned in applying the different practices within the proposed guideline.

title: An Artificial Neural Networks based Temperature Prediction Framework for Network-on-Chip based Multicore Platform
Abstract: The advancements in silicon process technologies have enabled the integration of hundreds of cores on a single chip. However, power and heat have become dominant constraints in designing these multicore chips, leading to reliability issues, timing variations, and reduced chip lifespan. Dynamic Thermal Management (DTM) is a solution to mitigate high temperatures on the die.  While typical DTM schemes address core-level thermal issues, the Network-on-Chip (NoC) paradigm, crucial for integrating hundreds to thousands of cores, contributes significantly to thermal challenges. Traditional DTM relies on reactive temperature measurements from on-chip sensors, leading to delays. Predictive DTM, on the other hand, estimates future temperatures proactively, avoiding temperature overshoot. Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs), known for their learning and adaptation capabilities, have been utilized for modeling and prediction in various domains. This thesis focuses on designing an ANN prediction engine to predict the thermal profiles of cores and NoC elements within the chip. This thermal profile is then used by the predictive DTM, which combines both core-level and network-level DTM techniques. On-chip wireless interconnect, envisioned to enable energy-efficient data exchange between cores, provides a broadcast-capable medium for efficient distribution of thermal control messages to manage DTM schemes.

title: Text-guided Attention Model for Image Captioning
Abstract: Visual attention plays a crucial role in image understanding and is effective in generating natural language descriptions. Recent studies show that language associated with an image can steer visual attention during our cognitive process. Inspired by this, we introduce a text-guided attention model for image captioning that learns to drive visual attention using associated captions. We propose an exemplar-based learning approach that retrieves relevant captions from training data for each image and utilizes them to learn attention on visual features. Our attention model effectively distinguishes small or confusable objects, enabling detailed scene descriptions. We validate our model on the MS-COCO Captioning benchmark, achieving state-of-the-art performance in standard metrics.

title: PIGMIL: Positive Instance Detection via Graph Updating for Multiple Instance Learning
Abstract: Positive instance detection, especially for true positive instances (TPIs) within positive bags, is crucial for multiple instance learning (MIL), a classification problem where only bag labels are provided. Existing MIL methods often overlook global similarity among positive instances and the non-i.i.d. nature of negative instances, resulting in imprecise TPI detection and sensitivity to outliers. We propose PIGMIL, a positive instance detection method for MIL using graph updating. PIGMIL selects instances from working sets of working bags as a positive candidate pool (PCP). It then constructs a consistent similarity and discrimination graph (CSDG) based on global positive instance similarity and robust discrimination of PCP instances from negative instances. This transforms TPI detection into PCP updating, efficiently approximated by updating CSDG with a random walk ranking algorithm and an instance updating strategy. Finally, bags are converted to feature representation vectors based on identified TPIs for classifier training. Extensive experiments demonstrate the high precision of PIGMIL in detecting TPIs and its superior performance compared to classical baseline MIL methods.

title: On kernel design for regularized LTI system identification
Abstract: Kernel-based regularization methods face two key challenges: designing a suitable kernel that embeds prior knowledge of the LTI system to be identified and tuning the kernel to achieve a good bias-variance tradeoff in the resulting regularized impulse response estimator. This paper focuses on kernel design. We propose two kernel design methods based on machine learning and system theory perspectives, depending on the type of prior knowledge. We provide analysis results for both methods, enhancing our understanding of existing kernels and guiding the design of new ones. |||

title: An Attention-Driven Approach of No-Reference Image Quality Assessment
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel method for no-reference image quality assessment (NR-IQA) that predicts the perceptual quality score of an image without using a reference image. The method leverages three key components: (1) a visual attention mechanism that focuses on fixation areas assumed to contain key information for IQA, (2) a robust averaging strategy to integrate multiple pieces of evidence for a final perceptual judgment, and (3) multi-task learning to shape representation learning and create a more generalized model. The NR-IQA is treated as a dynamic perception process where the model samples a sequence of "informative" areas and aggregates information to learn a representation for jointly predicting image quality and distortion type.  Reinforcement learning, implemented via a deep network with the policy gradient method, guides the learning of an optimal sampling policy for accurate and efficient prediction. Experimental results on the TID2008 dataset show the model outperforming state-of-the-art methods with high efficiency using a small number of fixations.

title: Self-calibrating Neural Networks for Dimensionality Reduction
Abstract: This paper introduces novel online algorithms for reducing the dimensionality of streaming data based on the similarity matching principle. These algorithms adaptively determine the number of output dimensions by thresholding the singular values of the input data matrix. To address the challenge of setting the threshold without knowing the desired singular values in advance, the proposed algorithms employ a self-calibrating threshold based on the singular values computed from existing observations.  These algorithms are derived from the similarity matching cost function using novel regularizers and can be implemented by Hebbian/anti-Hebbian neural networks with learning rules dependent on the chosen regularizer. Mathematical and simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of these online algorithms across various settings.

title: A General Approach for Predicting the Behavior of the Supreme Court of the United States
Abstract: Drawing on advancements in machine learning and prior work in the science of judicial prediction, this paper constructs a model to predict the behavior of the U.S. Supreme Court in a generalized, out-of-sample context. The model, a time-evolving random forest classifier, employs unique feature engineering to predict over 240,000 justice votes and 28,000 case outcomes spanning nearly two centuries (1816-2015). Utilizing data available prior to decision, the model outperforms null models at both the justice and case level under both parametric and non-parametric tests.  Achieving 70.2% accuracy at the case outcome level and 71.9% at the justice vote level over nearly two centuries, the model demonstrates improved performance, especially over the past century, where it surpasses an in-sample optimized null model by nearly 5%. This work represents a significant advancement in quantitative legal prediction, offering a range of potential applications beyond a single term of the Court.

title: Reinforcement Learning With Temporal Logic Rewards
Abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of specifying complex rules for robot behavior in reinforcement learning (RL) by utilizing the expressive power of temporal logic (TL).  The authors propose Truncated Linear Temporal Logic (TLTL) as a suitable specification language for robotics applications, incorporating domain knowledge into learning. The paper introduces a RL approach that learns tasks expressed as TLTL formulae using their associated robustness degree as reward functions. This method surpasses traditional approaches relying on handcrafted heuristics, leading to faster learning and policies with improved robustness. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated in simulated trials and in a toast-placing task learned by a Baxter robot.

title: Noisy subspace clustering via matching pursuits
Abstract: Sparsity-based subspace clustering algorithms have gained prominence due to their effectiveness in practical applications. The sparse subspace clustering (SSC) algorithm, relying on spectral clustering based on a sparsely represented adjacency matrix, faces computational limitations with large datasets or high-dimensional spaces.  SSC-OMP, employing orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP) in place of Lasso, offers significantly reduced computational complexity while maintaining performance. This paper provides an analytical performance characterization of SSC-OMP for noisy data and introduces SSC-MP, which utilizes matching pursuit (MP) instead of OMP.  Both algorithms are proven to succeed even with subspace intersections and severe noise. The paper analyzes the clustering conditions for both algorithms and provides numerical results, demonstrating that SSC-OMP and SSC-MP with a data-dependent stopping criterion can automatically detect subspace dimensions. Experimental results on synthetic and real data show that SSC-MP outperforms existing methods in terms of clustering performance and running time, highlighting its robustness and favorable performance compared to SSC-OMP.

title: Lock-Free Optimization for Non-Convex Problems
Abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and its variants have gained significant attention in machine learning due to their efficiency and effectiveness for optimization.  Researchers have proposed lock-free strategy based parallel SGD (LF-PSGD) methods to address large-scale problems on multi-core systems. While the convergence of LF-PSGD methods has been proven for convex problems, their convergence for non-convex problems remains unexplored. This paper provides theoretical proof about the convergence of two representative LF-PSGD methods, Hogwild! and AsySVRG, for non-convex problems. Empirical results on non-convex problems confirm the convergence of both methods, validating the theoretical findings.

title: Non-Redundant Spectral Dimensionality Reduction
Abstract: Spectral dimensionality reduction algorithms, widely used in recognition, segmentation, tracking, and visualization, suffer from the "repeated Eigen-directions" phenomenon, where embedding coordinates capture the same direction along the data manifold. This redundancy leads to inefficient representations that fail to reveal the true intrinsic dimensionality of the data. This paper introduces a general method for avoiding redundancy in spectral algorithms by replacing orthogonality constraints with unpredictability constraints. The authors prove that these constraints prevent redundancy and provide a simple technique for incorporating them into existing methods.  Illustrated on challenging high-dimensional scenarios, the proposed approach produces more informative and compact representations, improving visualization and classification tasks.

title: A New Spectral Method for Latent Variable Models
Abstract: This paper presents an algorithm for unsupervised learning of latent variable models from unlabeled datasets based on spectral decomposition. The technique demonstrates robustness both theoretically and practically.  The algorithm is applied to learn parameters for two well-known text mining models: single topic model and Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), providing an efficient approach to retrieve parameters for the algorithm. The results of the proposed algorithm are compared to existing algorithms on synthetic data, and real-world text corpora are analyzed for both single topic model and LDA, yielding meaningful results.

title: Automated Inference on Sociopsychological Impressions of Attractive Female Faces
Abstract: This article builds upon prior work, exploring the potential of supervised machine learning in face-induced social computing and cognition, leveraging successes in face processing, analysis, and recognition. The paper presents a case study of automated statistical inference on sociopsychological perceptions of female faces, controlling for race, attractiveness, age, and nationality. The empirical evidence suggests the possibility of training machine learning algorithms, using face images characterized by internet users, to predict perceptions of personality traits and demeanors.

title: Multiple Instance Learning: A Survey of Problem Characteristics and Applications
Abstract: Multiple instance learning (MIL), a form of weakly supervised learning where training instances are grouped into labeled sets called bags, is gaining interest for its suitability to various problems and its ability to leverage weakly labeled data.  While MIL has seen applications in computer vision and document classification, learning from bags poses unique challenges. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the characteristics that define and differentiate MIL problems. The authors group these characteristics into four categories: bag composition, data distribution, instance label ambiguity, and task type.  Methods addressing each category are reviewed, and their manifestation in key MIL application areas is described.  Experiments comparing 16 state-of-the-art MIL methods on selected problem characteristics provide insights into how these characteristics impact algorithm performance, offering recommendations for future benchmarking and research avenues.

title: Technical Report: A Generalized Matching Pursuit Approach for Graph-Structured Sparsity
Abstract: Sparsity-constrained optimization, a crucial and challenging problem with applications in data mining, machine learning, and statistics, is addressed in this paper. The focus is on optimizing general nonlinear functions with sparsity constraints defined by a graph-structured sparsity model.  While existing methods explore this problem for sparse estimation in linear models, this paper presents an efficient approximation algorithm, Graph-structured Matching Pursuit (Graph-Mp), for optimizing general nonlinear functions subject to graph-structured constraints. The algorithm enjoys strong guarantees, analogous to those for linear models, in terms of convergence rate and approximation accuracy. As a case study, Graph-Mp is applied to optimize well-known graph scan statistic models for connected subgraph detection, demonstrating superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods designed specifically for this task.

title: Non-negative Factorization of the Occurrence Tensor from Financial Contracts
Abstract: This paper proposes an algorithm for non-negative factorization of an occurrence tensor built from heterogeneous networks.  The l0 norm is utilized to model sparse errors over discrete values (occurrences), while decomposed factors model embedded groups of nodes. An efficient splitting method is developed to optimize the nonconvex and nonsmooth objective. Both synthetic problems and a new dataset, resMBS, built from financial documents, are analyzed.

title: An Empirical Study of ADMM for Nonconvex Problems
Abstract: The alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) is a common optimization tool for constrained and non-differentiable problems. This paper presents an empirical study of ADMM's practical performance on various nonconvex applications, including l0 regularized linear regression, l0 regularized image denoising, phase retrieval, and eigenvector computation. The experiments suggest ADMM's effectiveness on a broad class of non-convex problems.  Furthermore, adaptive ADMM methods, which automatically tune penalty parameters, are shown to improve algorithm efficiency and solution quality compared to ADMM with fixed parameters.

title: Knowledge Elicitation via Sequential Probabilistic Inference for High-Dimensional Prediction
Abstract: Predicting in small-sized samples with a large number of covariates, the "small n, large p" problem, is challenging and arises in various applications, such as precision medicine.  This paper addresses the challenge of effectively utilizing domain experts as a valuable source of information to improve prediction accuracy. Knowledge elicitation is formulated as a probabilistic inference process where expert knowledge is sequentially queried.  In the specific case of sparse linear regression, assuming expert knowledge about regression coefficients or feature relevance, the paper proposes an algorithm and computational approximation for efficient interaction. This approach sequentially identifies the most informative features for querying expert knowledge. Evaluations on simulated and real users demonstrate improved prediction accuracy with minimal expert effort.

title: Anytime Monte Carlo
Abstract: Monte Carlo algorithms simulate a prescribed number of samples, taking random real time to complete computations.  This paper explores the converse: imposing a real-time budget on computation, resulting in a random number of simulated samples. The real time for each simulation may depend on the sample, leading to a length bias with respect to compute time.  This is particularly problematic when using a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm and requiring the final state of the Markov chain, as in parallel tempering implementations.  This paper focuses on addressing the length bias in sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) algorithms using an anytime framework based on a continuous-time Markov jump process.  The authors demonstrate that length bias in the final state distribution can be eliminated using a multiple chain construction for any MCMC algorithm. This construction's utility is showcased on a large-scale SMC^2 implementation, utilizing four billion particles across 128 graphics processing units, demonstrating reduced idleness and improved control over the compute budget.
