title: N-gram Opcode Analysis for Android Malware Detection
Abstract: Android malware has seen a significant rise in recent years, fueled by the growing popularity of Android and the proliferation of third-party application markets. Emerging Android malware families are increasingly adopting sophisticated detection avoidance techniques, necessitating more effective detection approaches. This paper presents and evaluates an n-gram opcode features based approach that utilizes machine learning to identify and categorize Android malware. This approach enables automated feature discovery without relying on prior expert or domain knowledge. Additionally, employing a data segmentation technique for feature selection allows our analysis to scale up to 10-gram opcodes. Experiments on a dataset of 2520 samples show an f-measure of 98% using this n-gram opcode based approach. We provide empirical findings that highlight factors potentially impacting the overall n-gram opcodes performance trends.
label: AI

title: Proportional Rankings
Abstract: This paper extends the principle of proportional representation to rankings, focusing on scenarios where alternatives need to be ranked based on approval preferences. Proportional representation requires cohesive groups of voters to be proportionally represented in each initial segment of the ranking. Proportional rankings are desirable in situations where initial segments of varying lengths might be relevant, such as hiring decisions (where the number of positions is unclear), presenting competing proposals on a liquid democracy platform (where the number of proposals considered is unclear), or recommender systems (where rankings need to accommodate different user types). The paper analyzes the proportional representation provided by various ranking methods and proves theoretical guarantees. It also experimentally evaluates these methods, presenting preliminary evidence on the methods best suited for producing proportional rankings.
label: AI

title: A New Type-II Fuzzy Logic Based Controller for Non-linear Dynamical Systems with Application to a 3-PSP Parallel Robot
Abstract: Uncertainty pervades complex systems, including parallel robots, prominent examples of dynamic robotics systems. As the name suggests, uncertainty signifies missing information beyond human knowledge. Proper handling of uncertainty is crucial to minimize its adverse effects during the control process. Type-II fuzzy logic has proven superior to traditional fuzzy logic in addressing uncertainty. Type-II fuzzy logic controllers, relatively newer and promising approaches, have recently been applied across diverse fields due to their significant contributions, particularly in the presence of noise (a significant instance of uncertainty). When designing Type-I fuzzy logic systems, we often assume certainty regarding fuzzy membership functions, which is not always true in practice. T2FLS, a more realistic approach for practical applications, offers significant potential. Type-II fuzzy logic accounts for higher levels of uncertainty, where the membership grade for a Type-II fuzzy variable is not a crisp number but rather itself a Type-I linguistic term. This thesis examines the impact of uncertainty on the dynamic control of a parallel robot. Specifically, it aims to incorporate the Type-II Fuzzy Logic paradigm into a model-based controller, known as computed torque control, and apply the results to a 3 degrees of freedom parallel manipulator.  ...
label: AI

title: Message Passing Multi-Agent GANs
Abstract: Communication and intelligence sharing among agents are crucial for achieving Artificial General Intelligence. This paper introduces a novel framework for image generation: Message Passing Multi-Agent Generative Adversarial Networks (MPM GANs). While GANs have proven effective for image generation and other tasks, they are typically limited to single generator-discriminator networks. This study demonstrates that multi-agent GANs can achieve better image generation through message passing communication. Agents in this framework have dual objectives: a co-operation objective and a competing objective. The co-operation objective ensures that the message sharing mechanism guides other generators to generate better outputs than themselves. Conversely, the competing objective encourages each generator to outperform its counterpart. The paper analyzes and visualizes the messages shared among these GANs in various scenarios. Quantitative analysis shows that message sharing serves as a regularizer during adversarial training. Qualitative analysis demonstrates that different generators capture distinct traits of the underlying data distribution.
label: AI

title: On a Well-behaved Relational Generalisation of Rough Set Approximations
Abstract: This study examines non-dual relational extensions of rough set approximations and identifies an extension satisfying a surprising number of traditional rough set properties. This definition is then used to explain an observation made by Samanta and Chakraborty in their recent paper "Interface of rough set systems and modal logics: A survey."
label: AI

title: Cryptocurrency Portfolio Management with Deep Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: Portfolio management involves deciding how to allocate funds across different financial investment products. Cryptocurrencies, electronic and decentralized alternatives to government-issued money, like Bitcoin, are gaining prominence. This paper presents a model-less convolutional neural network that takes historical prices of a set of financial assets as input and outputs portfolio weights for the set. The network is trained using 0.7 years of price data from a cryptocurrency exchange. Training is conducted in a reinforcement manner, maximizing the cumulative return, which serves as the network's reward function. Backtest trading experiments with a 30-minute trading period are conducted in the same market, achieving 10-fold returns over 1.8 months. The paper also compares the network's performance to other recently published portfolio selection strategies using the same backtests. Notably, the network is not limited to cryptocurrencies and can be applied to any financial market.
label: AI

title: Real-time Collision Handling in Railway Network:An Agent-based Approach
Abstract: Advancements in intelligent transportation systems with complex operations necessitate autonomous planning and management to prevent collisions in daily traffic. As failures or inadequacies in traffic safety systems can have life-critical consequences, collisions must be detected and resolved efficiently to manage continuously rising traffic. This paper addresses different collision scenarios and explores techniques for their early detection and resolution within a complex railway system. A novel agent-based solution is proposed, leveraging the max-sum algorithm, where each agent (train agent, station agent, and junction agent) communicates and collaborates with others to generate a feasible solution that maintains a safe (collision-free) system state. The proposed mechanism is implemented in the Java Agent DEvelopment Framework (JADE). Extensive experiments evaluate the results, comparing them to existing collision handling methods, showcasing the efficiency of the proposed approach.
label: AI

title: Do What I Want, Not What I Did: Imitation of Skills by Planning Sequences of Actions
Abstract: This paper proposes a learning-from-demonstration approach for grounding actions from expert data and an algorithm for using these actions to perform a task in new environments. The approach is based on applying sampling-based motion planning to navigate the tree of discrete, high-level actions derived from a symbolic representation of a task. Recursive sampling-based planning is used to explore the space of potential continuous-space instantiations of these actions. The paper demonstrates the approach's utility using a magnetic structure assembly task, showing the robot's ability to intelligently select a sequence of actions in different parts of the workspace and in the presence of obstacles. This approach can effectively adapt to new environments by selecting the appropriate high-level actions for the specific environment while considering human preferences.
label: AI

title: Throughput of Infrastructure-based Cooperative Vehicular Networks
Abstract: This paper provides a detailed analysis of the achievable throughput of an infrastructure-based vehicular network with finite traffic density under a cooperative communication strategy. This strategy explores the combined use of vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I) communications, vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) communications, vehicle mobility, and cooperation among vehicles and infrastructure to facilitate data transmission. A closed-form expression for achievable throughput is obtained, revealing the relationship between throughput and key performance-impacting parameters like the distance between adjacent infrastructure points, radio ranges of infrastructure and vehicles, transmission rates of V2I and V2V communications, and vehicular density. Numerical and simulation results demonstrate that the proposed cooperative communication strategy significantly increases vehicular network throughput compared to its non-cooperative counterpart, even at low traffic densities. The findings shed light on optimal deployment of vehicular network infrastructure and optimal design of cooperative communication strategies to maximize throughput.
label: AI

title: Neural Symbolic Machines: Learning Semantic Parsers on Freebase with Weak Supervision (Short Version)
Abstract: Extending the success of deep neural networks to natural language understanding and symbolic reasoning requires complex operations and external memory. Recent neural program induction approaches have attempted to address this challenge but are typically limited to differentiable memory, hindering scalability beyond small synthetic tasks. This work introduces the Manager-Programmer-Computer framework, integrating neural networks with non-differentiable memory to support abstract, scalable, and precise operations through a user-friendly neural computer interface. Specifically, the paper presents a Neural Symbolic Machine (NSM), which consists of a sequence-to-sequence neural "programmer" and a non-differentiable "computer" that is a Lisp interpreter with code assistance. To successfully apply REINFORCE for training, the paper augments it with approximate gold programs found through an iterative maximum likelihood training process. NSM can learn a semantic parser from weak supervision over a large knowledge base. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on WebQuestionsSP, a challenging semantic parsing dataset, with weak supervision. Unlike previous approaches, NSM is end-to-end, eliminating the need for feature engineering or domain-specific knowledge.
label: AI

title: The Complexity of Bayesian Networks Specified by Propositional and Relational Languages
Abstract: This paper explores the complexity of inference in Bayesian networks defined by logical languages. The study considers representations ranging from fragments of propositional logic to function-free first-order logic with equality, encompassing various plate models and probabilistic relational models. The paper investigates the complexity of inferences under different input scenarios: network, query, and domain as input (inferential and combined complexity); fixed network with query and domain as input (query/data complexity); and fixed network and query with domain as input (domain complexity). The paper draws connections with probabilistic databases and liftability results, yielding complexity classes ranging from polynomial to exponential levels.
label: AI

title: Representing Independence Models with Elementary Triplets
Abstract: In an independence model, triplets representing conditional independences between singletons are termed elementary. It is known that elementary triplets unambiguously represent the independence model under certain conditions. This paper demonstrates how this representation facilitates various operations with independence models, such as finding dominant triplets or a minimal independence map of an independence model, computing the union or intersection of independence model pairs, or performing causal reasoning. For causal reasoning, the paper rephrases some of Pearl's results for computing causal effects in terms of conditional independences.
label: AI

title: Deep Learning of Robotic Tasks without a Simulator using Strong and Weak Human Supervision
Abstract: This paper proposes a scheme for training a computerized agent to perform complex human tasks, such as highway steering, by mirroring a natural learning process where a human instructor teaches a computerized trainee. The learning process involves five elements: (i) unsupervised feature learning; (ii) supervised imitation learning; (iii) supervised reward induction; (iv) supervised safety module construction; and (v) reinforcement learning. The last four elements of the scheme are implemented using deep convolutional networks and applied to successfully create a computerized agent capable of autonomous highway steering in the well-known racing game Assetto Corsa. The paper demonstrates that utilizing these four elements is essential for effectively executing the steering task using vision alone, without access to a driving simulator's internals, and operating in real-time. This is achieved through the introduction of a safety network, a novel method for preventing catastrophic mistakes during the reinforcement learning stage.
label: AI

title: Enhancing Use Case Points Estimation Method Using Soft Computing Techniques
Abstract: Software estimation, encompassing cost, effort, schedule, and size, is a crucial aspect of software engineering. Its importance becomes critical in the early stages of the software life cycle, when software details remain unclear. Various commercial and non-commercial tools exist to estimate software in these early stages. Many software effort estimation methods require software size as a key input metric, making software size estimation essential in the early stages. One approach used for over two decades in early size and effort estimation is use case points. The use case points method relies on the use case diagram to estimate the size and effort of software projects. Although widely used, this method has limitations that can negatively impact estimation accuracy. This paper presents techniques using fuzzy logic and neural networks to improve the accuracy of the use case points method. Results indicate that an improvement of up to 22% can be achieved using the proposed approach.
label: AI

title: Algorithmic Songwriting with ALYSIA
Abstract: This paper introduces ALYSIA: Automated LYrical SongwrIting Application. ALYSIA is built upon a machine learning model utilizing Random Forests, and the paper discusses its success in pitch and rhythm prediction. It further demonstrates how ALYSIA was used to create original pop songs that were subsequently recorded and produced. Finally, the paper outlines the vision for the future of Automated Songwriting, encompassing both co-creative and autonomous systems.
label: AI

title: Localization of networked robot systems subject to random delay and packet loss
Abstract: This paper addresses the localization problem of a mobile robot subject to communication delays and packet loss. Delays and losses can occur randomly in both control inputs and observation measurements. A unified state-space representation is constructed to describe these mixed uncertainties. Based on this representation, the optimal linear estimator is developed. The core idea involves deriving a relevance factor to incorporate delayed measurements into the current estimate. This estimator is then extended for nonlinear systems. The method's performance is evaluated through simulations in MATLAB and experiments on a real robot system. The robust localization results demonstrate the method's efficiency for localizing networked mobile robots.
label: AI

title: Short-term traffic flow forecasting with spatial-temporal correlation in a hybrid deep learning framework
Abstract: Deep learning approaches have gained prominence in the field of artificial intelligence, with their success largely attributed to Convolutional Networks (CNN) and Recurrent Networks. CNNs, by exploiting fundamental spatial properties of images and videos, consistently achieve dominant performance on visual tasks. Recurrent Networks (RNN), particularly long short-term memory methods (LSTM), effectively characterize temporal correlation, exhibiting superior capabilities for time series tasks. Traffic flow data exhibit rich characteristics in both time and space domains. However, applications of CNN and LSTM approaches to traffic flow are limited. This paper proposes a novel deep architecture combining CNN and LSTM for forecasting future traffic flow (CLTFP). A 1-dimension CNN is employed to capture spatial features of traffic flow, while two LSTMs are utilized to extract short-term variability and periodicities. Given these meaningful features, feature-level fusion is performed to achieve short-term forecasting. The proposed CLTFP is compared to other popular forecasting methods on an open dataset. Experimental results indicate that CLTFP exhibits significant advantages in traffic flow forecasting. Furthermore, the proposed CLTFP is analyzed from the perspective of Granger Causality, revealing and discussing several interesting properties.
label: AI

title: DeepBach: a Steerable Model for Bach Chorales Generation
Abstract: DeepBach, a graphical model designed for generating polyphonic music, particularly hymn-like pieces, is presented in this paper. Trained on Johann Sebastian Bach's chorale harmonizations, our model demonstrates the ability to produce highly convincing chorales in his style. The model's strength stems from its use of pseudo-Gibbs sampling combined with an adapted representation of musical data, distinguishing it from many sequential music composition techniques. Additionally, DeepBach allows for user control by enabling constraints on the generated score, such as specific notes, rhythms, or cadences. A plugin for the MuseScore music editor enhances user interaction with DeepBach, making it user-friendly.
label: AI

title: A microprocessor based on a two-dimensional semiconductor
Abstract: The widespread adoption of microcomputers in the 1970s has significantly transformed society. While silicon has been the primary material for microprocessors, the growing demand for increased integration density, speed, lower power consumption, and seamless integration with everyday objects has driven the search for alternative materials. Germanium, III-V compound semiconductors, thin-film plastic technology, and carbon nanotubes are promising contenders for future high-performance processor generations and chips capable of embedding electronic intelligence in everyday objects for the Internet of Things. This paper introduces a 1-bit microprocessor implemented using a two-dimensional semiconductor, molybdenum disulfide. The device can execute user-defined programs stored in external memory, perform logical operations, and communicate with its periphery. Importantly, our 1-bit design is scalable to multi-bit data. Comprising 115 transistors, this device represents the most complex circuitry yet to be fabricated from a two-dimensional material.
label: AI

title: RecSys Challenge 2016: job recommendations based on preselection of offers and gradient boosting
Abstract: This paper presents the Mim-Solution's approach to the RecSys Challenge 2016, which secured second place. The challenge aimed to develop job recommendations for users of the Xing.com website. Our two-phase algorithm, consisting of candidate selection followed by candidate ranking, predicts the probability of a user positively interacting with a job offer to rank candidates. Gradient Boosting Decision Trees serve as the regression tool for this approach.
label: AI

title: Using Discourse Signals for Robust Instructor Intervention Prediction
Abstract: We investigate the prediction of instructor intervention in student posts within discussion forums of Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs). Our findings demonstrate that incorporating automatically obtained discourse relations improves the prediction of instructor intervention compared to a state-of-the-art, feature-rich baseline. Our supervised classifier leverages an automatic discourse parser that outputs Penn Discourse Treebank (PDTB) tags representing in-post discourse features. We show that PDTB relation-based features enhance the classifier's robustness and complement baseline features by uncovering diverse instructor intervention patterns. Extensive experiments across 14 MOOC offerings from various disciplines reveal that PDTB discourse features consistently improve performance on average. The resulting models exhibit reduced dependency on domain-specific vocabulary, facilitating better generalization to new courses.
label: AI

title: A Matrix Splitting Perspective on Planning with Options
Abstract: This paper demonstrates that the Bellman operator underlying the options framework leads to a matrix splitting, a method commonly used to accelerate convergence of iterative solvers for large linear systems of equations. Based on standard comparison theorems for matrix splittings, we establish a relationship between the asymptotic rate of convergence and the inherent timescales of the options. This new perspective highlights a trade-off between asymptotic performance and the computational cost associated with constructing a suitable set of options.
label: AI

title: Commonly Uncommon: Semantic Sparsity in Situation Recognition
Abstract: Semantic sparsity poses a significant challenge in structured visual classification problems, particularly when the output space is complex. This results in a scenario where a vast majority of possible predictions rarely, if ever, appear in the training set. This paper examines semantic sparsity within the context of situation recognition, the task of generating structured summaries of image content, including activities, objects, and their roles within the activity. Our empirical findings reveal that most object-role combinations are rare, leading to significant underperformance of current state-of-the-art models in this sparse data regime. To mitigate these errors, we introduce two key innovations: (1) a novel tensor composition function that learns to share examples across role-noun combinations and (2) semantic augmentation of our training data using automatically gathered examples of rarely observed outputs from web data. Integration of these innovations within a complete CRF-based structured prediction model results in a significant performance improvement. The tensor-based approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art models by a relative improvement of 2.11% and 4.40% in top-5 verb and noun-role accuracy, respectively. Further incorporating 5 million images using our semantic augmentation techniques leads to additional relative improvements of 6.23% and 9.57% in top-5 verb and noun-role accuracy, respectively.
label: AI

title: Making the V in VQA Matter: Elevating the Role of Image Understanding in Visual Question Answering
Abstract: Problems at the intersection of vision and language present both challenging research questions and valuable opportunities for diverse applications. However, inherent structure in our world and bias in language tend to overshadow visual information during learning, leading to models that prioritize language over visual cues, resulting in an inflated sense of their capabilities. This paper proposes to counter these language priors for the Visual Question Answering (VQA) task and emphasize the importance of vision. To achieve this, we balance the popular VQA dataset by collecting complementary images, ensuring that every question is associated with a pair of similar images that yield different answers. Our balanced dataset, by design, surpasses the original VQA dataset in terms of balance and contains approximately twice the number of image-question pairs. The complete balanced dataset is publicly available at www.visualqa.org as part of the 2nd iteration of the Visual Question Answering Dataset and Challenge (VQA v2.0). We further benchmark several state-of-the-art VQA models on our balanced dataset. The results show that all models exhibit significantly worse performance on the balanced dataset, indicating their reliance on language priors. This finding provides the first concrete empirical evidence for what is commonly observed among practitioners. Additionally, our data collection protocol for identifying complementary images enables the development of a novel interpretable model. Beyond providing an answer to a given (image, question) pair, this model offers a counter-example based explanation. It identifies an image similar to the original image but with a different answer to the same question. This feature contributes to building trust in machine-based answers among users.
label: AI

title: Summary - TerpreT: A Probabilistic Programming Language for Program Induction
Abstract: This paper investigates machine learning formulations for inductive program synthesis, which involves synthesizing source code that maps inputs to corresponding outputs based on input-output examples. Our key contribution is TerpreT, a domain-specific language designed to express program synthesis problems. A TerpreT model comprises a specification of a program representation and an interpreter that defines how programs map inputs to outputs. The inference task entails observing input-output examples and inferring the underlying program. Using a TerpreT model, we automate inference through four different back-ends: gradient descent (where each TerpreT model can be seen as defining a differentiable interpreter), linear program (LP) relaxations for graphical models, discrete satisfiability solving, and the Sketch program synthesis system. TerpreT offers two key benefits: it facilitates rapid exploration across domains, program representations, and interpreter models, and it separates model specification from the inference algorithm, enabling meaningful comparisons between different inference approaches. We demonstrate the value of TerpreT by developing several interpreter models and conducting an extensive empirical comparison of alternative inference algorithms across various program models. Notably, this work is the first to compare gradient-based search over program space to traditional search-based alternatives. Our key empirical finding reveals that constraint solvers outperform gradient descent and LP-based formulations. This is a workshop summary of a longer report available at arXiv:1608.04428.
label: AI

title: Overcoming catastrophic forgetting in neural networks
Abstract: The ability to learn tasks sequentially is crucial for the advancement of artificial intelligence. Neural networks, in general, lack this capability, and catastrophic forgetting has been widely perceived as an inherent limitation of connectionist models. This paper demonstrates that it is possible to overcome this limitation and train networks capable of maintaining expertise on tasks they haven't encountered for extended periods. Our approach addresses this issue by selectively slowing down learning on weights crucial for previously learned tasks. We showcase the scalability and effectiveness of our approach by solving a set of classification tasks based on the MNIST handwritten digit dataset and by learning several Atari 2600 games sequentially.
label: AI

title: Decision Theory in an Algebraic Setting
Abstract: In decision theory, an act is defined as a function mapping a set of conditions to a set of real numbers. The set of conditions constitutes a partition within an algebra of events. The expected value of an act can be calculated when a probability measure is available. We adopt an algebraic perspective by replacing the algebra of events with a finite distributive lattice and the probability measure with a lattice valuation. We introduce a partial order on acts that generalizes the dominance relation and demonstrate that the set of acts forms a lattice with respect to this order. Finally, we analyze various forms of comparison between acts without assuming a common set of conditions for comparison.
label: AI

title: Asynchronous Stochastic Gradient MCMC with Elastic Coupling
Abstract: This paper explores parallel asynchronous Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling for problems where (stochastic) gradients can be leveraged to define continuous dynamics that explore the target distribution. We propose a solution strategy based on stochastic gradient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampling (SGHMC) modified to incorporate an elastic coupling term that connects multiple MCMC instances. This strategy transforms inherently sequential HMC algorithms into asynchronous parallel versions. Initial experiments empirically demonstrate that the resulting parallel sampler significantly accelerates exploration of the target distribution compared to standard SGHMC. It is also less susceptible to the detrimental effects of stale gradients compared to a naive parallelization approach.
label: AI

title: Cognitive Deep Machine Can Train Itself
Abstract: Machine learning is making significant strides in diverse applications, primarily due to advances in deep learning. However, deep learning can make errors, and its generalization abilities to new tasks are questionable. This paper investigates the potential for combining network outputs when (i) details of observations are evaluated by learned deep components and (ii) facts and confirmation rules are available in knowledge-based systems. We demonstrate that, in limited contexts, the required number of training samples can be reduced, and self-improvement of pre-trained networks in more general contexts is possible. We argue that combining sparse outlier detection with deep components that mutually support each other mitigates the fragility of deep methods, a crucial requirement for engineering applications. Under certain conditions, we propose that supervised learning of labels can be entirely eliminated. A component-based architecture coupled with a knowledge-based system can train itself and provide high-quality answers. These concepts are illustrated using the State Farm Distracted Driver Detection benchmark. Our findings suggest that the view expressed by the Study Panel (2016) regarding the need for "years of focused research" and "careful, unique construction" for "AI systems" may be overly conservative.
label: AI

title: Automated assessment of non-native learner essays: Investigating the role of linguistic features
Abstract: Automatic essay scoring (AES) refers to the process of evaluating free text responses to given prompts, using human grader scores as the gold standard. This practice is essential for many language and aptitude exams. AES has become an active and established field of research, with numerous proprietary systems currently used in real-world applications. However, there is limited knowledge regarding which specific linguistic features are useful for prediction and the consistency of these features across datasets. This article addresses this gap by exploring the role of various linguistic features in automatic essay scoring using two publicly available datasets of non-native English essays written in test-taking scenarios. The linguistic properties are modeled by incorporating lexical, syntactic, discourse, and error types of learner language into the feature set. Predictive models are then developed using these features on both datasets, and the most predictive features are compared. While the results demonstrate that the employed feature set yields good predictive models for both datasets, the question of "what are the most predictive features?" yields different answers for each dataset.
label: AI

title: Probabilistic Neural Programs
Abstract: This paper introduces probabilistic neural programs, a framework for program induction that allows flexible specification of both a computational model and inference algorithm while simultaneously enabling the use of deep neural networks. Probabilistic neural programs combine a computation graph for defining a neural network with an operator for weighted nondeterministic choice. Consequently, a program describes both a collection of decisions and the neural network architecture used to make each decision. We evaluate our approach on a challenging diagram question answering task, where probabilistic neural programs successfully execute nearly twice as many programs compared to a baseline model.
label: AI

title: Inferring Cognitive Models from Data using Approximate Bayesian Computation
Abstract: A critical challenge for HCI researchers is estimating the parameter values of a cognitive model from behavioral data. This is a complex task due to the significant complexity and variety in human behavioral strategies. This paper presents an investigation into a new approach using approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) to condition model parameters to data and prior knowledge. We examine menu interaction as a case study, where only click time data is available to infer a cognitive model that implements a search behavior with parameters such as fixation duration and recall probability. Our results demonstrate that ABC (i) improves estimates of model parameter values, (ii) enables meaningful comparisons between model variants, and (iii) supports fitting models to individual users. ABC offers significant opportunities for theoretical HCI research by facilitating principled inference of model parameter values and their uncertainty.
label: AI

title: Active Search for Sparse Signals with Region Sensing
Abstract: Autonomous systems can be employed to search for sparse signals in a vast space; for instance, aerial robots can be deployed to locate threats, detect gas leaks, or respond to distress calls. Intuitively, search algorithms can enhance efficiency by collecting aggregate measurements summarizing large contiguous regions. However, most existing search methods either disregard the possibility of such region observations (e.g., Bayesian optimization and multi-armed bandits) or rely on strong assumptions about the sensing mechanism, allowing each measurement to arbitrarily encode all signals in the entire environment (e.g., compressive sensing). We propose an algorithm that actively collects data to search for sparse signals using only noisy measurements of the average values on rectangular regions (including single points), based on greedy maximization of information gain. Our analysis in 1d shows that this algorithm requires $\\tilde{O}(\\frac{n}{\\mu^2}+k^2)$ measurements to recover all $k$ signal locations with a small Bayes error, where $\\mu$ and $n$ are the signal strength and the size of the search space, respectively. We also demonstrate that active designs can be fundamentally more efficient than passive designs with region sensing, contradicting the results of Arias-Castro, Candes, and Davenport (2013). Empirical performance of our algorithm is demonstrated on a search problem using satellite image data and in high dimensions.
label: AI

title: Self-critical Sequence Training for Image Captioning
Abstract: Recent research has shown that policy-gradient methods for reinforcement learning can be utilized to train deep end-to-end systems directly on non-differentiable metrics for the task at hand. This paper focuses on optimizing image captioning systems using reinforcement learning. We show that significant performance gains can be realized by carefully optimizing our systems using the test metrics of the MSCOCO task. Our systems are built using a new optimization approach called self-critical sequence training (SCST). SCST is a variation of the popular REINFORCE algorithm that, instead of estimating a "baseline" to normalize rewards and reduce variance, utilizes the output of its own test-time inference algorithm for reward normalization. This approach eliminates the need for estimating the reward signal (as required by actor-critic methods) and normalization (as typically done by REINFORCE algorithms), while simultaneously aligning the model with its test-time inference procedure. Empirically, we find that directly optimizing the CIDEr metric with SCST and greedy decoding at test-time is highly effective. Our results on the MSCOCO evaluation server establish a new state-of-the-art for the task, improving the best CIDEr score from 104.9 to 114.7.
label: AI

title: Transfer Learning Across Patient Variations with Hidden Parameter Markov Decision Processes
Abstract: Due to physiological variations, patients diagnosed with the same condition may exhibit divergent but related responses to the same treatments. Hidden Parameter Markov Decision Processes (HiP-MDPs) address this transfer-learning problem by embedding these tasks into a low-dimensional space. However, the original HiP-MDP formulation had a critical flaw: the embedding uncertainty was modeled independently of the agent's state uncertainty, requiring an unnatural training procedure where all tasks visit every part of the state space. This is possible for robots that can be moved to specific locations but impractical for human patients. This paper updates the HiP-MDP framework and extends it to more robustly develop personalized medicine strategies for HIV treatment.
label: AI

title: Generalizing Skills with Semi-Supervised Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) can acquire complex behaviors from low-level inputs, such as images. However, real-world applications of these methods necessitate generalization to the vast variability of the real world. Deep networks achieve remarkable generalization when provided with massive amounts of labeled data, but can we provide this breadth of experience to an RL agent, such as a robot? Robots could continuously learn while exploring the world around them, even during deployment. However, this learning requires access to a reward function, which is often challenging to measure in real-world domains, where the reward could depend on, for example, unknown object positions or the user's emotional state. Conversely, providing the agent with reward functions in a limited set of situations, such as with a human supervisor or in a controlled setting, is often practical. Can we leverage this limited supervision while still benefiting from the broad experience an agent might gather independently? This paper formalizes this problem as semi-supervised reinforcement learning, where the reward function can only be evaluated in a set of "labeled" MDPs, and the agent must generalize its behavior to the wide range of states it might encounter in a set of "unlabeled" MDPs using experience from both settings. Our proposed method infers the task objective in the unlabeled MDPs through an algorithm resembling inverse RL, using the agent's own prior experience in the labeled MDPs as a demonstration of optimal behavior. We evaluate our method on challenging tasks requiring control directly from images and show that our approach can improve the generalization of a learned deep neural network policy by leveraging experience for which no reward function is available. We also demonstrate that our method outperforms direct supervised learning of the reward.
label: AI

title: Playing Doom with SLAM-Augmented Deep Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: Several recent approaches to policy learning in 2D game domains have achieved success in directly mapping raw input images to actions. However, when applied to complex 3D environments, they often encounter challenges related to partial observability, combinatorial exploration spaces, path planning, and a scarcity of rewarding scenarios. Inspired by prior work in human cognition suggesting that humans utilize a variety of semantic concepts and abstractions (object categories, localization, etc.) to reason about the world, we develop an agent model that incorporates these abstractions into its policy-learning framework. We augment the raw image input to a Deep Q-Learning Network (DQN) by adding details of objects and structural elements encountered, along with the agent's localization. The different components are automatically extracted and composed into a topological representation using on-the-fly object detection and 3D-scene reconstruction. We evaluate the efficacy of our approach in Doom, a 3D first-person combat game that exhibits several of the discussed challenges, and show that our augmented framework consistently learns better, more effective policies. |||
label: AI

title: Piecewise Latent Variables for Neural Variational Text Processing
Abstract: Advances in neural variational inference have enabled the development of powerful directed graphical models with continuous latent variables, such as variational autoencoders. These models hold promise for learning complex, multi-modal latent factors in real-world data, such as natural language text. However, current models often rely on simplistic priors for latent variables, such as the unimodal Gaussian distribution, which are insufficient for effectively representing intricate latent factors. To address this limitation, we propose the piecewise constant distribution, a simple yet highly flexible alternative. This distribution can represent an exponential number of modes in a latent target distribution while maintaining mathematical tractability. Our findings demonstrate that incorporating this new latent distribution into various models significantly improves performance on natural language processing tasks such as document modeling and dialogue generation.

title: Spatial Decompositions for Large Scale SVMs
Abstract: Despite the theoretical understanding of support vector machines (SVMs), their underlying optimization problem becomes computationally expensive when dealing with, for example, hundreds of thousands of samples and a non-linear kernel. Various approaches have been proposed to address this issue. This work investigates a decomposition strategy that trains on small, spatially defined data chunks. Our contributions are twofold: theoretically, we establish an oracle inequality for the overall learning method using the hinge loss and show that the resulting rates match those known for SVMs solving the complete optimization problem with Gaussian kernels. Practically, we compare our approach to learning SVMs on small, randomly chosen chunks. Our results demonstrate that, for comparable training times, our approach significantly outperforms random chunking in terms of testing speed and reduces test error in most cases. Moreover, we show that our approach scales easily to 10 million training samples, with the entire training, including hyperparameter selection using cross-validation, completing in just a few hours on a single machine. Finally, we report an experiment on 32 million training samples. All experiments utilize liquidSVM (Steinwart and Thomann, 2017).
label: AI

title: Large-scale Validation of Counterfactual Learning Methods: A Test-Bed
Abstract: Effective off-policy learning has the potential to revolutionize the development of better interactive systems, such as search engines and recommendation systems for e-commerce, computational advertising, and news. Recent approaches for off-policy evaluation and learning in these domains show promising results. This paper provides real-world data and a standardized testbed for systematically investigating these algorithms using data from display advertising. Specifically, we address the problem of filling a banner ad with an aggregation of multiple products that the user may want to purchase. This paper presents our testbed, the sanity checks we conducted to ensure its validity, and shows results comparing state-of-the-art off-policy learning methods such as doubly robust optimization, POEM, and reductions to supervised learning using regression baselines. Our findings provide experimental evidence that recent off-policy learning methods can surpass state-of-the-art supervised learning techniques on a large-scale real-world dataset.
label: AI

title: Bootstrapping incremental dialogue systems: using linguistic knowledge to learn from minimal data
Abstract: We introduce a method for inducing new dialogue systems from very small amounts of unannotated dialogue data. By combining word-level exploration using Reinforcement Learning (RL) with an incremental and semantic grammar - Dynamic Syntax (DS) - our approach enables systems to discover, generate, and understand numerous new dialogue variants. This method avoids the need for costly and time-consuming dialogue act annotations and supports more natural (incremental) dialogues than turn-based systems. We treat language generation and dialogue management as a joint decision/optimization problem, and the MDP model for RL is constructed automatically. Using an implemented system, we demonstrate that our method allows for a wide range of dialogue variations to be captured automatically, even when trained on a single dialogue. These variants include question-answer pairs, over- and under-answering, self- and other-corrections, clarification interactions, split-utterances, and ellipsis. This generalization property stems from the structural knowledge and constraints embedded within the DS grammar and highlights limitations of recent systems solely based on machine learning techniques.
label: AI

title: A Compositional Object-Based Approach to Learning Physical Dynamics
Abstract: We present the Neural Physics Engine (NPE), a framework for learning simulators of intuitive physics that naturally generalize across varying object counts and different scene configurations. We propose a factorization of a physical scene into composable object-based representations and a neural network architecture whose compositional structure factorizes object dynamics into pairwise interactions. Like a symbolic physics engine, the NPE is endowed with generic notions of objects and their interactions; realized as a neural network, it can be trained via stochastic gradient descent to adapt to specific object properties and dynamics of different worlds. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach on simple rigid body dynamics in two-dimensional worlds. By comparing to less structured architectures, we show that the NPE's compositional representation of the structure in physical interactions improves its ability to predict movement, generalize across variable object count and different scene configurations, and infer latent properties of objects such as mass.

title: An Evaluation of Models for Runtime Approximation in Link Discovery
Abstract: Time-efficient link discovery is crucial for realizing the vision of the Semantic Web. Some of the fastest Link Discovery approaches rely internally on planning to execute link specifications. Recent works have employed linear models to estimate the runtime of the fastest planners. However, other categories of models have not been explored for this purpose. This paper investigates non-linear runtime estimation functions for runtime estimation. Specifically, we study exponential and mixed models for estimating the runtimes of planners. To this end, we evaluate three different models for runtime on six datasets using 400 link specifications. Our results show that exponential and mixed models achieve better fits when trained but are only preferable in certain cases. Our evaluation also demonstrates that utilizing better runtime approximation models positively impacts the overall execution of link specifications.
label: AI

title: On Coreferring Text-extracted Event Descriptions with the aid of Ontological Reasoning
Abstract: Systems for automatically extracting semantic information about events from large textual resources are now available. These tools can generate RDF datasets about text-extracted events, and this knowledge can be used for reasoning about the recognized events. Conversely, text-based tasks for event recognition, such as event coreference (i.e., recognizing whether two textual descriptions refer to the same event), do not incorporate ontological information of the extracted events in their process. This paper proposes a method for deriving event coreference on text-extracted event data using semantic-based rule reasoning. We demonstrate our method using a limited (but representative) set of event types. We introduce a formal analysis of their ontological properties and define a set of coreference criteria based on this analysis. We then implement these criteria as RDF-based reasoning rules to be applied to text-extracted event data. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach using a standard coreference benchmark dataset.
label: AI

title: Interaction Networks for Learning about Objects, Relations and Physics
Abstract: Reasoning about objects, relations, and physics is central to human intelligence and a key goal of artificial intelligence. We introduce the interaction network, a model capable of reasoning about how objects in complex systems interact, supporting dynamical predictions as well as inferences about the abstract properties of the system. Our model takes graphs as input, performs object- and relation-centric reasoning analogous to a simulation, and is implemented using deep neural networks. We evaluate its ability to reason about several challenging physical domains: n-body problems, rigid-body collision, and non-rigid dynamics. Our results demonstrate that it can be trained to accurately simulate the physical trajectories of dozens of objects over thousands of time steps, estimate abstract quantities such as energy, and generalize automatically to systems with different numbers and configurations of objects and relations. Our interaction network implementation is the first general-purpose, learnable physics engine and a powerful general framework for reasoning about objects and relations in a wide variety of complex real-world domains.

title: Analysis of the Human-Computer Interaction on the Example of Image-based CAPTCHA by Association Rule Mining
Abstract: This paper analyzes the interaction between humans and computers in terms of response time while solving image-based CAPTCHAs. The analysis focuses on the attitude of different Internet users in easily solving four distinct types of image-based CAPTCHAs featuring facial expressions: animated character, old woman, surprised face, worried face. To achieve this goal, an experiment was conducted involving 100 Internet users solving the four CAPTCHA types. Participants were categorized by age, Internet experience, and education level. Response times were collected for each user, and association rules were extracted from user data to evaluate the dependence of the response time in solving the CAPTCHA on age, education level, and Internet usage experience using statistical analysis. The results implicitly capture users' psychological states, indicating when users are more susceptible. This novel and insightful analysis contributes to the state-of-the-art in this field.

title: Structured Filtering
Abstract: A significant challenge facing existing sequential Monte-Carlo methods for parameter estimation in physics stems from the inability of current approaches to robustly handle experiments with different mechanisms yielding results with equivalent probability. We address this problem by proposing a form of particle filtering that clusters the particles comprising the sequential Monte-Carlo approximation to the posterior before applying a resampler. Through a new graphical approach to understanding such models, we devise an artificial intelligence-based strategy that automatically learns the shape and number of clusters in the support of the posterior. We demonstrate the power of our approach by applying it to randomized gap estimation and a form of low circuit-depth phase estimation, where existing methods from the physics literature either exhibit much worse performance or fail completely.
label: AI

title: CDVAE: Co-embedding Deep Variational Auto Encoder for Conditional Variational Generation
Abstract: Problems such as predicting a new shading field (Y) for an image (X) are ambiguous, with many distinct solutions being equally good. Representing this ambiguity requires building a conditional model P(Y|X) of the prediction, conditioned on the image. Training such a model is challenging because we typically lack training data containing multiple different shadings for the same image. Consequently, we need different training examples to share data to produce good models. This presents a danger we call "code space collapse" - the training procedure produces a model with a very good loss score but poorly represents the conditional distribution. We demonstrate an improved method for building conditional models by exploiting a metric constraint on training data that prevents code space collapse. We evaluate our model on two example tasks using real data: image saturation adjustment and image relighting. We describe quantitative metrics to evaluate ambiguous generation results. Our results demonstrate quantitative and qualitative improvements over various strong baselines.
label: AI

title: A Novel Artificial Fish Swarm Algorithm for Pattern Recognition with Convex Optimization
Abstract: Image pattern recognition is a critical area in digital image processing. An efficient pattern recognition algorithm should provide accurate recognition with reduced computational time. Among machine learning pattern recognition algorithms, the Artificial Fish Swarm Algorithm (AFSA) is a swarm intelligence optimization algorithm that operates based on population and stochastic search. To achieve acceptable results, several parameters need to be adjusted in AFSA. Among these parameters, visual and step are highly significant, as artificial fish primarily move based on these parameters. In standard AFSA, these two parameters remain constant until algorithm termination. Large values of these parameters enhance the algorithm's capability for global search, while small values improve its local search ability. This paper empirically studies the performance of AFSA and tests various approaches to balance between local and global exploration based on adaptive modification of visual and step during algorithm execution. The proposed approaches are evaluated using four well-known benchmark functions. Experimental results demonstrate a significant positive impact on AFSA performance. Convex optimization has been integrated into the proposed work to achieve ideal segmentation of the input image, which is a MR brain image.
label: AI

title: When to Reset Your Keys: Optimal Timing of Security Updates via Learning
Abstract: Cybersecurity is increasingly threatened by advanced and persistent attacks. As these attacks are often designed to disable a system (or a critical resource, e.g., a user account) repeatedly, it is crucial for the defender to continuously update security measures to strike a balance between the risk of compromise and the cost of security updates. Furthermore, these decisions often need to be made with limited and delayed feedback due to the stealthy nature of advanced attacks.  In addition to targeted attacks, an optimal timing policy under incomplete information has broad applications in cybersecurity. Examples include key rotation, password change, application of patches, and virtual machine refreshing. However, rigorous studies of optimal timing are rare. Moreover, existing solutions typically rely on a pre-defined attack model known to the defender, which is often unrealistic in practice. This work makes an initial effort toward achieving optimal timing of security updates in the face of unknown stealthy attacks. We consider a variant of the influential FlipIt game model with asymmetric feedback and unknown attack time distribution, providing a general model for consecutive security updates. The defender's problem is then modeled as a time associative bandit problem with dependent arms. We derive upper confidence bound based learning policies that achieve low regret compared with optimal periodic defense strategies, which can only be derived when attack time distributions are known.
label: AI

title: Robust Optimization for Tree-Structured Stochastic Network Design
Abstract: Stochastic network design is a general framework for optimizing network connectivity. It has several applications in computational sustainability, including spatial conservation planning, pre-disaster network preparation, and river network optimization. A common assumption in previous work is that network parameters (e.g., probability of species colonization) are precisely known, which is unrealistic in real-world settings. We address the robust river network design problem, where the goal is to optimize river connectivity for fish movement by removing barriers. We assume that fish passability probabilities are known only imprecisely but are within some interval bounds. We then develop a planning approach that computes policies with either high robust ratio or low regret. Empirically, our approach scales well to large river networks. We also provide insights into the solutions generated by our robust approach, which has significantly higher robust ratio than the baseline solution with mean parameter estimates.
label: AI

title: Optimizing Quantiles in Preference-based Markov Decision Processes
Abstract: In the Markov decision process model, policies are typically evaluated based on expected cumulative rewards. As this decision criterion is not always suitable, we propose an algorithm in this paper for computing a policy optimal for the quantile criterion. Both finite and infinite horizons are considered. Finally, we experimentally evaluate our approach on random MDPs and a data center control problem.
label: AI

title: Computer Assisted Composition with Recurrent Neural Networks
Abstract: Sequence modeling with neural networks has led to powerful models of symbolic music data. We address the problem of leveraging these models to achieve creative musical goals by combining them with human input. To this end, we generalize previous work that sampled Markovian sequence models under the constraint that the sequence belong to the language of a given finite state machine provided by the human. We consider more expressive non-Markov models, thus requiring approximate sampling, which we provide in the form of an efficient sequential Monte Carlo method. Additionally, we provide and compare with a beam search strategy for conditional probability maximization. Our algorithms demonstrate convincing re-harmonization of famous musical works. We provide visualizations, quantitative experiments, a human listening test, and audio examples to illustrate our findings. We find both the sampling and optimization procedures to be effective, though complementary in nature. For highly permissive constraint sets, sampling is preferable due to the overly regular nature of optimization-based results. The generality of our algorithms enables countless other creative applications.
label: AI

title: A Novel Propulsion Method of Flexible Underwater Robots
Abstract: This paper aims to improve the mobility of flexible underwater robots. For this purpose, a novel propulsion method using planar structural vibration patterns is proposed and tested on two prototype designs. Experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of movements in multiple directions: forward, backward, turn, rotation, drift, and combinations thereof. These movements are achieved using a single structure with two actuators. The results also indicate the possibility of driving using eigenmodes since movements were concentrated in the low driving frequency area. To investigate the relationship between movement and structural vibration patterns, a simulation model was established.
label: AI

title: Two-dimensional Phononic Crystals with Acoustic-Band Negative Refraction
Abstract: A two-dimensional phononic crystal (PC) can exhibit longitudinal-mode negative energy refraction on its lowest (acoustic) frequency passband. The effective elastodynamic properties of a typical PC are calculated, and it is observed that the components of the effective density tensor can attain negative values at certain low frequencies on the acoustic branches for the longitudinal-mode passband. This phenomenon can be accompanied by either positive or negative effective density. Furthermore, such a PC exhibits a high anisotropy ratio at certain low frequencies, offering potential applications in acoustic cloaking, where effective material anisotropy is essential.
label: AI

title: Joint Causal Inference from Multiple Contexts
Abstract: The gold standard for discovering causal relations is through experimentation. Over the past decades, alternative methods have been proposed to infer causal relations between variables from certain statistical patterns in purely observational data. We introduce Joint Causal Inference (JCI), a novel approach to causal discovery from multiple datasets from different contexts that elegantly unifies both approaches. JCI is a causal modeling framework rather than a specific algorithm, and it can be implemented using any causal discovery algorithm that can take into account certain background knowledge. JCI can handle different types of interventions (e.g., perfect, imperfect, stochastic, etc.) in a unified fashion, and does not require knowledge of intervention targets or types in case of interventional data. We explain how several well-known causal discovery algorithms can be viewed as addressing special cases of the JCI framework, and we also propose novel implementations that extend existing causal discovery methods for purely observational data to the JCI setting. We evaluate different JCI implementations on synthetic data and on flow cytometry protein expression data, concluding that JCI implementations can significantly outperform state-of-the-art causal discovery algorithms.

title: Comparing Apples and Oranges: Two Examples of the Limits of Statistical Inference, With an Application to Google Advertising Markets
Abstract: We show how the classic Cramer-Rao bound limits how accurately one can simultaneously estimate the values of a large number of Google Ad campaigns (or similarly limit the measurement rate of many confounding A/B tests). |||

title: The observer-assisted method for adjusting hyper-parameters in deep learning algorithms
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel method for adjusting hyperparameters in Deep Learning (DL) algorithms. The method involves an external agent-observer that monitors the performance of a selected DL algorithm. This observer learns to model the DL algorithm by conducting a series of random experiments. Subsequently, it can predict the algorithm's response based on a chosen quality metric and a set of hyperparameters. This enables the construction of an ensemble comprising a series of evaluators, forming an observer-assisted architecture. This architecture facilitates gradual iteration towards the optimal achievable quality score in tiny steps governed by a progress unit. The algorithm terminates when the maximum number of steps is reached or no further improvement is observed.

title: Bandit algorithms to emulate human decision making using probabilistic distortions
Abstract: Inspired by models of human decision-making that explain deviations from conventional expected value preferences, we formulate two stochastic multi-armed bandit problems with distorted probabilities on the reward distributions: the classic $K$-armed bandit and the linearly parameterized bandit settings. We analyze these problems in the regret minimization and best arm identification frameworks for multi-armed bandits. For regret minimization in both $K$-armed and linear bandit problems, we propose algorithms based on Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) principles, incorporating reward distortions, and achieving sublinear regret. For the $K$-armed bandit setting, we derive an upper bound on the expected regret for our proposed algorithm and prove a matching lower bound, establishing its order-optimality. In the linearly parameterized setting, our algorithm achieves a regret upper bound of the same order as the regular OFUL (Optimism in the Face of Uncertainty Linear) bandit algorithm, but unlike OFUL, it handles distortions and an arm-dependent noise model. For the best arm identification problem in the $K$-armed bandit setting, we propose algorithms, derive performance guarantees, and demonstrate their order optimality by proving matching fundamental limits. For best arm identification in linear bandits, we propose an algorithm and establish sample complexity guarantees. Finally, we present simulation experiments demonstrating the advantages of using distortion-aware learning algorithms in a vehicular traffic routing application.

title: Predicting Melting point and Viscosity of Ionic Liquids Using New Quantum Chemistry Descriptors
Abstract: Ionic liquids (ILs) are an emerging class of chemical compounds with promising properties, including negligible vapor pressure. These designer solvents have the potential to replace volatile organic compounds in industrial applications. A wide variety of ILs can be synthesized through the combination of different cations and anions. In this context, computer-aided methods for intelligently designing customized ILs would be highly beneficial. However, practical limitations necessitate the ability to accurately predict the melting point and viscosity of new ILs, as experimental data will not be readily available for designed structures. This paper presents two novel correlation equations for predicting the melting point and viscosity of ILs, based solely on quantum chemistry calculations, without relying on experimental data or simulation results. These correlations were developed using data related to the size, shape, and electrostatic properties of cations and anions that constitute ILs. New descriptors were employed, including the dielectric energy of cations and anions, as well as values predicted by an ad-hoc model for the radii of cations and anions (instead of their van der waals radii). A comprehensive range of correlation equations, encompassing all possible combinations of descriptors as model inputs, were tested. The average relative errors were measured to be 3.16% for the melting point (Tm) and 6.45% for ln(vis).

title: Unit Commitment using Nearest Neighbor as a Short-Term Proxy
Abstract: We introduce the Unit Commitment Nearest Neighbor (UCNN) algorithm as a proxy for quickly approximating outcomes of short-term decisions, enabling tractable hierarchical long-term assessment and planning for large power systems. Experimental results on updated versions of IEEE-RTS79 and IEEE-RTS96 demonstrate high accuracy in operational cost estimation, achieved with runtimes significantly lower (several orders of magnitude) than the traditional approach.
label: AI

title: Fusion of EEG and Musical Features in Continuous Music-emotion Recognition
Abstract: Emotion estimation in music listening faces challenges in capturing the emotional variations of listeners. Recent years have witnessed attempts to improve emotion recognition performance by leveraging multimodality, fusing information from musical content and physiological signals captured from listeners. This paper presents a study of signal fusion at the decision level, combining electroencephalogram (EEG), a tool for capturing brainwaves with high temporal resolution, and musical features, to recognize the time-varying binary classes of arousal and valence. Empirical results show that the fusion outperforms emotion recognition using only EEG modality, which suffers from inter-subject variability. This highlights the promise of multimodal fusion in improving the accuracy of music-emotion recognition.
label: AI

title: System-Generated Requests for Rewriting Proposals
Abstract: We present an online deliberation system that utilizes mutual evaluation to collaboratively develop solutions. Participants submit proposals and evaluate each other's proposals; some may then be invited by the system to rewrite "problematic" proposals. Two scenarios are discussed: a proposal supported by many, but not by a given person, who is then invited to rewrite it for broader acceptance; and a poorly presented but potentially interesting proposal. The first scenario has been successfully implemented. Proposals are evaluated along two axes: understandability (clarity or quality) and agreement. The agreement score is used to cluster proposals based on their ideas, while understandability is used to present the best proposals at the top of their clusters and to identify poorly written proposals for rewriting. These functionalities are essential components of a large-scale online deliberation system.
label: AI

title: Comparison of the COG Defuzzification Technique and Its Variations to the GPA Index
Abstract: The Center of Gravity (COG) method is a popular defuzzification technique in fuzzy mathematics. Previous research has successfully adapted the COG technique as an assessment model (RFAM) and developed several variations (GRFAM, TFAM, and TpFAM) for the same purpose. This paper compares the outcomes of these models with the corresponding outcomes of a traditional assessment method based on bi-valued logic, the Grade Point Average (GPA) Index. Examples are provided to illustrate the findings.
label: AI

title: Anticipating Moves to Prevent Botnet Generated DDoS Flooding Attacks
Abstract: Volumetric Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks have become a persistent issue on the Internet. These attacks overwhelm targeted servers or network links with a flood of fake network traffic. Despite numerous efforts to detect and mitigate them, attackers have consistently circumvented countermeasures. The increasing number of infected devices, particularly with the advent of the Internet of Things and flexible communication technologies, exacerbates the problem. Leveraging device-to-device short-range wireless communications and other methods, infected devices can coordinate sophisticated botnets, intensifying DDoS attacks. These new-generation botnets are even harder to detect due to their adaptive and dynamic behavior, facilitated by infected mobile portable devices. Additionally, the geographically distributed nature of these devices significantly amplifies DDoS traffic. To address this evolving threat and the increasing volume of DDoS traffic, novel and intelligent-driven approaches are required. Specifically, we advocate for proactively anticipating trends of DDoS attacks in their early stages. This work provides an overview of approaches that can be employed to anticipate trends of DDoS attacks generated by botnets in their early stages and offers an insightful discussion of the advantages and open issues associated with each approach.
label: AI

title: Machine Learning for Dental Image Analysis
Abstract: To explore the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in dental imaging, we applied AI technology to classify a set of panoramic radiographs using (a) a convolutional neural network (CNN), a type of artificial neural network (ANN), (b) representative image cognition algorithms implementing scale-invariant feature transform (SIFT), and (c) histogram of oriented gradients (HOG).

title: Low-dimensional Data Embedding via Robust Ranking
Abstract: We introduce a new method called t-ETE for finding low-dimensional embeddings of a set of objects in Euclidean space. We formulate the embedding problem as a joint ranking problem over a set of triplets, where each triplet captures the relative similarities between three objects. By leveraging recent advances in robust ranking, t-ETE produces high-quality embeddings even in the presence of significant noise and better preserves local scale than known methods like t-STE and t-SNE. Our method significantly outperforms t-SNE on benchmark datasets while also being faster to compute.
label: AI

title: Contextualizing Geometric Data Analysis and Related Data Analytics: A Virtual Microscope for Big Data Analytics
Abstract: The relevance and importance of contextualizing data analytics are discussed. Qualitative characteristics can form the context for quantitative analysis. Key topics include: contrast, baselining, secondary data sources, supplementary data sources, dynamic and heterogeneous data. Various case studies are both experimented with and reviewed within the framework of geometric data analysis, particularly using the Correspondence Analysis platform. Implicitly and explicitly, a significant point made is the major relevance of this work for burgeoning analytical needs and new analytical areas, including Big Data analytics. The aim is to present and describe, first, the analytical outcomes subject to analysis and then detail the quantitative outcomes that fully support the analytics conducted.
label: AI

title: Neural Combinatorial Optimization with Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: This paper presents a framework for tackling combinatorial optimization problems using neural networks and reinforcement learning. We focus on the traveling salesman problem (TSP) and train a recurrent network that, given a set of city coordinates, predicts a distribution over different city permutations. Using negative tour length as the reward signal, we optimize the recurrent network parameters using a policy gradient method. We compare learning network parameters on a set of training graphs versus learning them on individual test graphs. Despite the computational expense, without significant engineering or heuristic design, Neural Combinatorial Optimization achieves near-optimal results on 2D Euclidean graphs with up to 100 nodes. Applied to the KnapSack, another NP-hard problem, the same method obtains optimal solutions for instances with up to 200 items.
