title: Proportional Justified Representation
Abstract: The goal of multi-winner elections is to select a fixed-size committee based on voter preferences. A critical concern in this setting is representation: large groups of voters with cohesive preferences should be adequately represented by the elected committee. Recently, Aziz et al. (2015a; 2017) proposed two axioms to capture this concept: justified representation (JR) and its strengthening, extended justified representation (EJR). This paper expands upon the work of Aziz et al. in several directions. First, we answer an open question posed by Aziz et al. by showing that Reweighted Approval Voting satisfies JR for k = 3, 4, 5, but fails it for k ≥ 6. Second, we observe that EJR is incompatible with the Perfect Representation criterion, crucial for many multi-winner voting applications, and propose a relaxation of EJR called Proportional Justified Representation (PJR). PJR is more demanding than JR but, unlike EJR, is compatible with perfect representation. A committee satisfying PJR can be computed in polynomial time if the committee size divides the number of voters. Moreover, similar to EJR, PJR can be used to characterize the classic PAV rule within the class of weighted PAV rules. On the other hand, we demonstrate that EJR provides stronger guarantees regarding average voter satisfaction than PJR.
label: AI

title: Choquet integral in decision analysis - lessons from the axiomatization
Abstract: The Choquet integral is a powerful aggregation operator encompassing many well-known models as special cases. We examine these special cases and provide their axiomatic analysis. Where axiomatization has been previously presented in the literature, we connect those results to the framework developed here. We then address the question of learning, which is particularly crucial for practical applications of the model. To date, learning the Choquet integral has primarily focused on learning the capacity. This approach requires a strong assumption that all dimensions (e.g., criteria) are evaluated on the same scale, which is rarely justified in practice. Categorical data is often arbitrarily assigned numerical labels (e.g., AHP), and numerical data is assumed to be cardinally and ordinally commensurate, sometimes after simple normalization. These approaches lack scientific rigor yet are common in various applications. We discuss the pros and cons of making such an assumption and examine the implications for learning problems based on axiomatization uniqueness results. Finally, we review some applications of the Choquet integral in decision analysis. Beyond MCDA, the primary area of interest for our findings, we discuss how the model can be interpreted in the social choice context. We delve into state-dependent utility and show how comonotonicity, central to previous axiomatizations, implies state-independency in the Choquet integral model. We also discuss the conditions required for a meaningful state-dependent utility representation and highlight the novelty of our findings compared to previous state-dependent model building methods.
label: AI

title: Capacity and Trainability in Recurrent Neural Networks
Abstract: Two potential limitations on the expressiveness of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are their ability to store task information in their parameters and their ability to store input history information in their units. We demonstrate experimentally that all common RNN architectures, with careful training, achieve nearly the same per-task and per-unit capacity bounds across a variety of tasks and stacking depths. These networks can store an amount of task information that is linear in the number of parameters, approximately 5 bits per parameter. Additionally, they can store approximately one real number from their input history per hidden unit. Furthermore, we find that for several tasks, the per-task parameter capacity bound determines performance. These results suggest that many previous comparisons of RNN architectures are primarily driven by differences in training effectiveness rather than differences in capacity. Supporting this observation, we compare training difficulty for various architectures and show that vanilla RNNs are significantly harder to train but have slightly higher capacity. Finally, we propose two novel RNN architectures, one of which is easier to train than the LSTM or GRU for deeply stacked architectures.
label: AI

title: C-RNN-GAN: Continuous recurrent neural networks with adversarial training
Abstract: Generative adversarial networks have been proposed as a way of efficiently training deep generative neural networks. We introduce a generative adversarial model that operates on continuous sequential data and apply it by training it on a collection of classical music. We conclude that the generated music improves in quality as the model is trained, report statistics on the generated music, and allow the reader to judge its quality by downloading the generated songs.
label: AI

title: Exploration for Multi-task Reinforcement Learning with Deep Generative Models
Abstract: Exploration in multi-task reinforcement learning is crucial for training agents to deduce the underlying Markov Decision Process (MDP). Many existing exploration frameworks, such as $E^3$, $R_{max}$, and Thompson sampling, assume a single stationary MDP and are not suitable for system identification in the multi-task setting. We present a novel method to facilitate exploration in multi-task reinforcement learning using deep generative models. We supplement our method with a low-dimensional energy model to learn the underlying MDP distribution and provide a resilient and adaptive exploration signal to the agent. We evaluate our method on a new set of environments and provide an intuitive interpretation of our results.
label: AI

title: NewsQA: A Machine Comprehension Dataset
Abstract: We introduce NewsQA, a challenging machine comprehension dataset consisting of over 100,000 human-generated question-answer pairs. Crowdworkers provide questions and answers based on a set of over 10,000 news articles from CNN, with answers being spans of text from the corresponding articles. This dataset is collected through a four-stage process designed to elicit exploratory questions requiring reasoning. A thorough analysis confirms that NewsQA demands capabilities beyond simple word matching and recognizing textual entailment. We measure human performance on the dataset and compare it to several strong neural models. The performance gap between humans and machines (0.198 in F1) indicates significant potential for improvement on NewsQA through future research. The dataset is freely available at https://datasets.maluuba.com/NewsQA.
label: AI

title: Dialogue Learning With Human-In-The-Loop
Abstract: A critical aspect of developing conversational agents is equipping bots with the ability to improve through communication with humans and learn from their mistakes. Most research has focused on learning from fixed training sets of labeled data rather than interacting with a dialogue partner online. This paper explores this direction in a reinforcement learning setting, where the bot enhances its question-answering ability based on feedback provided by a teacher following its generated responses. We construct a simulator to test various aspects of this learning process in a synthetic environment and introduce models that operate in this regime. Finally, real experiments conducted using Mechanical Turk validate the approach.
label: AI

title: Measuring and modeling the perception of natural and unconstrained gaze in humans and machines
Abstract: Humans demonstrate remarkable skill in interpreting the gaze direction of others in their surroundings. This ability is fundamental to engaging in joint visual attention, essential for establishing social interactions. To what extent are humans accurate in determining the gaze direction of others in lifelike scenes, where individuals can freely move their heads and eyes? What are the sources of information for the underlying perceptual processes? These questions pose a challenge from both empirical and computational perspectives due to the complexity of visual input in real-life situations. This study empirically measures human accuracy in perceiving the gaze direction of others in lifelike scenes and computationally investigates the sources of information and representations underlying this cognitive capacity. We demonstrate that humans perform better in face-to-face conditions compared to recorded conditions, and this advantage is not attributable to the availability of input dynamics. We further show that humans maintain good performance even when only the eyes-region is visible, rather than the whole face. We develop a computational model that replicates the pattern of human performance, including the finding that the eyes-region alone contains the necessary information for estimating both head orientation and direction of gaze. Consistent with neurophysiological findings on task-specific face regions in the brain, the learned computational representations reproduce perceptual effects like the Wollaston illusion when trained to estimate direction of gaze but not when trained to recognize objects or faces. |||

title: Fractional Order Fuzzy Control of Hybrid Power System with Renewable Generation Using Chaotic PSO
Abstract: This paper investigates a novel fuzzy control scheme for optimizing a hybrid power system. The system utilizes various autonomous energy sources, including wind turbines, solar photovoltaic panels, diesel engines, fuel cells, and aqua electrolyzers, along with energy storage devices like batteries, flywheels, and ultra-capacitors. A fractional-order (FO) fuzzy control scheme is implemented and its parameters tuned using a particle swarm optimization (PSO) algorithm enhanced with chaotic maps to improve performance. This FO fuzzy controller surpasses the classical PID and integer-order fuzzy PID controllers in both linear and nonlinear operating modes. It also exhibits superior robustness to system parameter variations and rate constraint nonlinearities, making it well-suited for handling dynamic changes in the hybrid power system's components.

title: SeDMiD for Confusion Detection: Uncovering Mind State from Time Series Brain Wave Data
Abstract: Understanding brain function has been a long-standing challenge. Recent advancements in data collection and technology have fueled interest in decoding brain wave data into meaningful mental states. Many machine learning models and algorithms, particularly those designed for time-series data, have been revisited and developed. However, traditional time-series models like HMM and State Space Models often struggle with handling multiple sources of information simultaneously. This paper proposes an extension of the State Space Model capable of integrating diverse information sources, along with its learning and inference algorithms. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated by decoding the mental states of students during lectures using their brain waves, achieving significantly better results compared to conventional methods.
label: AI

title: Fractional Order AGC for Distributed Energy Resources Using Robust Optimization
Abstract: This paper investigates the application of fractional-order (FO) automatic generation control (AGC) for mitigating power system frequency oscillations in a system with distributed energy generation. The hybrid power system includes various autonomous generation sources, such as wind turbines, solar photovoltaic panels, diesel engines, fuel cells, and aqua electrolyzers, as well as energy storage devices like batteries and flywheels. The controller is situated remotely and communicates over an unreliable network with stochastic delays. Robust optimization techniques, including various Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) algorithms, are employed to tune the controller parameters and compare them with optimal solutions. An archival-based strategy is used to reduce the number of function evaluations during optimization. The robust optimization approach enables the controller to handle larger variations in gains and orders without significant performance degradation. This is beneficial for FO controller implementation, as it accommodates variations in system parameters arising from approximations of FO operators using different realization methods and accuracy orders. The paper also compares FO and integer-order (IO) controllers, highlighting the strengths and weaknesses of each approach.

title: Getting Closer to the Essence of Music: The Con Espressione Manifesto
Abstract: This text presents a personal and subjective perspective on the current state of Music Information Research (MIR). Motivated by the desire to create systems with a deeper understanding of music, the author outlines several challenges for the next decade of MIR research, grouped around six widely accepted but often ignored truths about music.

title: Semantic Parsing of Mathematics by Context-based Learning from Aligned Corpora and Theorem Proving
Abstract: This paper explores methods for automated parsing of informal mathematical expressions into formal ones, a crucial step towards enabling computers to deeply understand informal mathematical texts. The proposed approach combines efficient statistical learning of deep parse trees with semantic pruning using type checking and large-theory automated theorem proving. The results demonstrate significant improvement over previous methods in parsing theorems from the Flyspeck corpus.

title: Pareto Efficient Multi Objective Optimization for Local Tuning of Analogy Based Estimation
Abstract: Analogy-Based Effort Estimation (ABE) is a prominent method for software effort estimation. ABE mirrors the reasoning of expert estimators but employs an automated procedure where effort estimates are generated by reusing data from similar past projects. A key challenge in ABE is adapting the effort estimates of retrieved nearest neighbors. This adaptation process is crucial for generating accurate estimates by tuning the selected raw solutions using a suitable strategy. This study identifies three interconnected decision variables that significantly impact the success of the adaptation method: the number of nearest analogies (k), the optimal feature set required for adaptation, and the adaptation weights. Finding the optimal values for these variables requires exploring all possible combinations and evaluating them individually to select the one that improves all prediction evaluation measures. Existing evaluation measures often exhibit different and sometimes conflicting trends in evaluating prediction methods, meaning that changing one decision variable could improve one measure while degrading others. Therefore, this research proposes a multi-objective optimization approach to determine the best decision variables that optimize the adaptation strategy and overall evaluation measures without compromising performance. The Particle Swarm Optimization Algorithm (PSO) is employed to find optimal solutions for these decision variables by optimizing multiple evaluation measures simultaneously.
label: AI

title: Collective Motion of Predictive Swarms
Abstract: Theoretical models of populations and swarms typically assume that agent movement is driven by local stimuli. However, intelligent agents, with some understanding of their environment's laws, can anticipate the future and make predictions to gather resources more effectively. This paper studies a specific model where agents aim to maximize their consumption of a diffusing resource by predicting the future of the resource field and the actions of other agents. The findings indicate that as agents attempt to predict further into the future, their predictions become less accurate, leading to reduced resource consumption. The paper also examines the scenario where predictive agents compete with non-predictive agents, revealing that predictors only outperform non-predictors when their relative numbers are very small. The conclusion suggests that predictivity pays off only when predictors have limited foresight or when their population is small.

title: Generic and Efficient Solution Solves the Shortest Paths Problem in Square Runtime
Abstract: This paper introduces new methods for solving the shortest paths problem on a given fixed-weighted instance, an open problem with significant real-world applications. The proposed methods prioritize genericity, efficiency, and precision. The paper provides proof to guarantee the methods' functionality and focuses on the underlying theory of computation and logic. The extension of these methods has potential applications in decision-making, operations, economics, management, robotics, artificial intelligence, and other fields.
label: AI

title: A Large-scale Distributed Video Parsing and Evaluation Platform
Abstract: Visual surveillance systems have become a major source of Big Visual Data in the real world. However, existing video analysis systems struggle with scalability, expansibility, and error-proneness, despite advancements in visual recognition tasks and surveillance applications. This paper addresses these challenges by developing a scalable video parsing and evaluation platform that combines advanced Big Data processing techniques, including Spark Streaming, Kafka, and Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS). The platform also includes a Web User Interface to collect user satisfaction ratings on recognition tasks, enabling evaluation of the system's overall performance. The extensible platform, capable of handling long-term surveillance videos, facilitates the development of more intelligent incremental algorithms to improve the performance of various visual recognition tasks.
label: AI

title: Learning Concept Hierarchies through Probabilistic Topic Modeling
Abstract: With the rise of the Semantic Web, various tools and techniques have been introduced for representing and organizing knowledge. Concept hierarchies, which play a crucial role in creating domain ontologies, have gained significant attention for their usefulness in semantic web applications. Automated concept hierarchy learning algorithms aim to extract relevant concepts from unstructured text corpora and connect them using potential relations between them. This paper proposes a novel approach for identifying relevant concepts from plain text and learning their hierarchy by exploiting the subsumption relation between them. The method uses a probabilistic topic model to represent topics and then utilizes lightweight linguistic processing to extract semantically rich concepts. Concepts are then connected by identifying an "is-a" relationship between pairs of concepts. The proposed method is completely unsupervised and does not require a domain-specific training corpus for concept extraction and learning. Experiments conducted on large, real-world text corpora, such as the BBC News dataset and Reuters News corpus, demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing methods for concept extraction and enables efficient concept hierarchy learning when guided by a probabilistic topic modeling algorithm.
label: AI

title: Learning Filter Banks Using Deep Learning For Acoustic Signals
Abstract: Designing effective features for acoustic event recognition tasks remains an active area of research. Expressive features should enhance task performance and be easily interpretable. Currently, heuristically designed features based on domain knowledge require significant hand-crafting effort, while features extracted through deep networks are often difficult for humans to understand. This work explores experience-guided learning for designing acoustic features. This novel hybrid approach combines domain knowledge with data-driven feature design. Based on the procedure of log Mel-filter banks, the paper introduces a filter bank learning layer. This layer is concatenated with a convolutional neural network (CNN) model. After training the network, the weight of the filter bank learning layer is extracted to facilitate the design of acoustic features. The trained weight of the learning layer is then smoothed and re-initialized in the filter bank learning layer as an audio feature extractor. For the environmental sound recognition task based on the UrbanSound8K dataset, experience-guided learning achieves a 2% accuracy improvement compared to fixed feature extractors (log Mel-filter bank). The visualization and explanation of the shape of the new filter banks demonstrate the effectiveness of the feature design process.
label: AI

title: Maximizing Non-Monotone DR-Submodular Functions with Cardinality Constraints
Abstract: This paper addresses the problem of maximizing a non-monotone DR-submodular function subject to a cardinality constraint. Diminishing returns (DR) submodularity is a generalization of the diminishing returns property for functions defined over the integer lattice. This generalization can be applied to solve various machine learning and combinatorial optimization problems, including optimal budget allocation and revenue maximization. This work presents the first polynomial-time approximation algorithms for non-monotone constrained maximization. The algorithms are implemented for a real-world revenue maximization problem to assess their efficiency and performance.
label: AI

title: Input Switched Affine Networks: An RNN Architecture Designed for Interpretability
Abstract: Interpretability is crucial for the deployment of neural network models in many problem domains. This paper introduces a recurrent architecture composed of input-switched affine transformations—an RNN without explicit nonlinearities, but with input-dependent recurrent weights. This simple structure enables analysis using straightforward linear methods, allowing for exact characterization of each input's linear contribution to model predictions, disentanglement of input, output, and computational hidden unit subspaces, and full reverse-engineering of the architecture's solution to simple tasks. Despite its interpretability, the input-switched affine network achieves reasonable performance on text modeling tasks and offers greater computational efficiency than networks with standard nonlinearities.
label: AI

title: Emergence of foveal image sampling from learning to attend in visual scenes
Abstract: This paper describes a neural attention model with a learnable retinal sampling lattice. The model is trained on a visual search task that requires classifying an object embedded in a visual scene amidst background distractors using the fewest fixations. The paper investigates the tiling properties that emerge in the model's retinal sampling lattice after training. Specifically, the paper demonstrates that this lattice resembles the eccentricity-dependent sampling lattice of the primate retina, characterized by a high-resolution region in the fovea surrounded by a low-resolution periphery. Furthermore, the paper identifies conditions where these emergent properties are amplified or eliminated, providing insights into their function.
label: AI

title: Safety-Aware Robot Damage Recovery Using Constrained Bayesian Optimization and Simulated Priors
Abstract: The recently introduced Intelligent Trial-and-Error (IT&E) algorithm has demonstrated that robots can adapt to damage in a matter of a few trials. This algorithm's success relies on two components: prior knowledge acquired through simulation with an intact robot and Bayesian optimization (BO) operating online on the damaged robot. While IT&E enables rapid damage recovery, it lacks safety constraints to prevent the robot from attempting harmful behaviors. This paper addresses this limitation by replacing the BO component with a constrained BO procedure. The approach is evaluated on a simulated damaged humanoid robot that needs to crawl as fast as possible while minimizing unsafe trials. The new "safety-aware IT&E" algorithm is compared to IT&E and a multi-objective version of IT&E where safety constraints are treated as separate objectives. The results demonstrate that the new algorithm outperforms the other approaches in both crawling speed within safe regions and the number of unsafe trials.

title: Split-door criterion: Identification of causal effects through auxiliary outcomes
Abstract: This paper presents a method for estimating causal effects in time series data when fine-grained information about the outcome of interest is available. Specifically, the paper examines the "split-door" setting, where the outcome variable can be divided into two parts: one potentially affected by the cause being studied and another independent of it, both sharing the same (unobserved) confounders. The paper shows that under these conditions, the identification problem reduces to testing for independence among observed variables. A method is presented that uses this approach to automatically find subsets of the data that are causally identified. The method is demonstrated by estimating the causal impact of Amazon's recommender system on traffic to product pages, identifying thousands of examples in the dataset that satisfy the split-door criterion. Unlike previous studies based on natural experiments that were limited to a single product category, the method applies to a large and representative sample of products viewed on the site. Consistent with prior work, the paper finds that the widely used click-through rate (CTR) metric overestimates the causal impact of recommender systems; depending on the product category, the estimated impact ranges from 50-80% of the traffic attributed to recommender systems, with the remaining portion likely occurring even without any recommendations. The paper concludes with guidelines for using the split-door criterion and discusses other contexts where the method can be applied.
label: AI

title: Accelerated Gradient Temporal Difference Learning
Abstract: The family of temporal difference (TD) methods spans a spectrum from computationally frugal linear methods like TD(λ) to data-efficient least squares methods. Least squares methods make optimal use of available data by directly computing the TD solution, eliminating the need to tune a sensitive learning rate parameter, but require quadratic computation and storage. Recent algorithmic advancements have yielded several sub-quadratic methods that approximate the least squares TD solution but incur bias. This paper proposes a new family of accelerated gradient TD (ATD) methods that offer similar data efficiency benefits as least-squares methods but with significantly reduced computation and storage requirements. ATD methods also demonstrate significantly reduced parameter sensitivity compared to linear TD methods and are asymptotically unbiased. The paper supports these claims with a proof of convergence in expectation and experiments on several benchmark domains and a large-scale industrial energy allocation domain.
label: AI

title: Improving Policy Gradient by Exploring Under-appreciated Rewards
Abstract: This paper presents a novel form of policy gradient for model-free reinforcement learning (RL) with improved exploration properties. Current policy-based methods rely on entropy regularization to encourage undirected exploration of the reward landscape, which is ineffective in high-dimensional spaces with sparse rewards. The paper proposes a more directed exploration strategy that promotes exploration of under-appreciated reward regions. An action sequence is considered under-appreciated if its log-probability under the current policy underestimates its resulting reward. The proposed exploration strategy is easy to implement, requiring minor modifications to the REINFORCE algorithm. The approach is evaluated on a set of algorithmic tasks that have posed significant challenges for RL methods. The results demonstrate reduced hyperparameter sensitivity and significant improvements over baseline methods. The algorithm successfully solves a benchmark multi-digit addition task and generalizes to long sequences, marking the first time a pure RL method has solved addition using only reward feedback.
label: AI

title: DrivingStyles: A mobile platform for driving styles and fuel consumption characterization
Abstract: Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) rely on connected vehicle applications to address real-world problems in safety, mobility, and environmental domains. This paper presents the DrivingStyles architecture, which utilizes data mining techniques and neural networks to analyze and classify driving styles and fuel consumption based on driver characterization. The paper focuses on an algorithm capable of characterizing the degree of aggressiveness of each driver. It also outlines a methodology for calculating, in real-time, the consumption and environmental impact of spark ignition and diesel vehicles using variables obtained from the vehicle's Electronic Control Unit (ECU). The paper demonstrates the impact of driving style on fuel consumption and its correlation with greenhouse gas emissions generated by each vehicle. The platform assists drivers in correcting bad driving habits and provides tips for improving fuel economy and driving safety.

title: Analyzing Features for the Detection of Happy Endings in German Novels
Abstract: This paper examines the use of sentiment analysis for happy ending detection in German novels, focusing on the computational representation of literary plot. The paper investigates previously proposed sentiment features to gain insights into their relevance and performance implications. Various partitionings of novels are studied, considering the variability of the "ending" concept. The paper demonstrates that the approach, while still relatively simple, can potentially yield substantial findings relevant to literary studies. |||

title: Blocking and Other Enhancements for Bottom-Up Model Generation Methods
Abstract: Model generation, a problem closely related to theorem proving, plays a vital role in analyzing faults and debugging formal specifications of security protocols, programs, and terminological definitions. This paper explores various techniques for enhancing the paradigm of bottom-up model generation. The main contributions are new, generalized blocking techniques and a novel range-restriction transformation. The blocking techniques, based on simple transformations of the input set combined with standard equality reasoning and redundancy elimination techniques, offer general methods for identifying small, finite models. The range-restriction transformation refines existing transformations for range-restricted clauses by carefully limiting the creation of domain terms. Extensive experiments were conducted on the clausal problems of the TPTP Version 6.0.0 using an implementation based on the SPASS theorem prover with a hyperresolution-like refinement, evaluating all possible combinations of the introduced techniques and classical range-restriction. Unrestricted domain blocking consistently yielded the best results for satisfiable problems, highlighting its significance for bottom-up model generation methods. Both in combination with the new range-restricting transformation and the classical range-restricting transformation, promising results were obtained. Limiting the creation of terms during the inference process using the new range-restricting transformation proved beneficial, especially when coupled with a shifting transformation. Experimental results also demonstrate that classical range restriction with unrestricted blocking provides a valuable complementary approach. Overall, the findings indicate that bottom-up model generation methods are effective for disproving theorems and generating models for satisfiable problems, but less efficient than SPASS in auto mode for unsatisfiable problems.

title: DeepSetNet: Predicting Sets with Deep Neural Networks
Abstract: This paper tackles the challenge of set prediction using deep learning, a crucial task due to the inherent set-based nature of many computer vision tasks, such as image tagging and object detection. Unlike vectors, sets have variable sizes and are invariant to the ordering of their elements. The paper introduces a likelihood function for a set distribution and leverages a deep neural network to learn its parameters. It also derives a loss function for predicting a discrete distribution corresponding to set cardinality. The efficacy of set prediction is demonstrated on the problem of multi-class image classification. Furthermore, the proposed cardinality loss is shown to be readily applicable to object counting and pedestrian detection. The proposed approach consistently surpasses existing methods across all three tasks on standard datasets.
label: AI

title: Measuring Impact of Adaptive and Cooperative Adaptive Cruise Control on Throughput of Signalized Intersections
Abstract: To accurately assess the impact of (cooperative) adaptive cruise control (ACC/CACC), a comprehensive model of vehicle dynamics is essential. The car following model, which governs vehicle flow as vehicles accelerate from standstill or decelerate due to obstacles ahead, is a key component of this model. The maximal vehicle acceleration rate significantly influences intersection throughput. This paper analyzes three car following behaviors: the Gipps model, Improved Intelligent Driver Model (IIDM), and Helly model. The Gipps model exhibits aggressive acceleration behavior, potentially leading to overly optimistic estimates of intersection throughput. The Helly model, while convenient for analysis due to its linear nature, demonstrates unrealistically abrupt deceleration behavior in the presence of obstacles. The IIDM, showcasing the most realistic acceleration and deceleration behavior among the three, is deemed more suitable for ACC/CACC impact evaluation. The paper examines the influence of the maximal vehicle acceleration rate and the presence of different proportions of ACC/CACC vehicles on intersection throughput within the context of the three car following models. The analysis considers two scenarios: (1) a free road downstream of the intersection, and (2) a red light at a certain distance downstream of the intersection. Finally, the paper introduces the platoon model and evaluates ACC and CACC with platooning in terms of travel time and network throughput using SUMO simulations of a 4-mile stretch of Colorado Boulevard/Huntington Drive arterial with 13 signalized intersections in Arcadia, Southern California.
label: AI

title: Architectures of Soft Robotic Locomotion Enabled by Simple Mechanical Principles
Abstract: In nature, a diverse array of limbless locomotion patterns thrives, from the microscopic (Escherichia coli, amoeba) to the large and intelligent (slugs, starfishes, earthworms, octopuses, jellyfish, and snakes). Inspired by these biological systems, numerous bioinspired soft robots based on locomotion have been developed in recent decades. This work, based on the kinematics and dynamics of two prominent locomotion modes (worm-like crawling and snake-like slithering), proposes a broad set of innovative designs for soft mobile robots through simple mechanical principles. Inspired by and extending beyond existing biological systems, these designs encompass 1-D (dimensional), 2-D, and 3-D robotic locomotion patterns enabled by simple actuation of continuous beams. The paper reports over 20 locomotion modes, achieving diverse locomotion functions, including crawling, rising, running, creeping, squirming, slithering, swimming, jumping, turning, turning over, helix rolling, wheeling, etc. Some of these modes exhibit high speeds, high efficiency, and the ability to overcome obstacles. All these locomotion strategies and functions can be integrated into a simple beam model. The proposed simple and robust models are adaptable to severe and complex environments. These elegant designs for diverse robotic locomotion patterns are expected to pave the way for future deployments of soft robots and inspire a series of advanced designs.

title: Nonparametric General Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) problems are often formulated in terms of Markov decision processes (MDPs). This thesis delves beyond MDPs and examines RL in environments that exhibit non-Markovian, non-ergodic, and partially observable characteristics. The focus is not on practical algorithms but rather on the fundamental underlying problems: how to balance exploration and exploitation, how to explore optimally, and when an agent achieves optimality. The nonparametric realizable paradigm is adopted. Negative results are established on Bayesian RL agents, particularly AIXI. The study reveals that unfortunate or adversarial prior choices can lead to drastic agent misbehavior. Therefore, Legg-Hutter intelligence and balanced Pareto optimality, heavily reliant on prior selection, are entirely subjective. Moreover, within the class of all computable environments, every policy is Pareto optimal. This undermines all existing optimality properties for AIXI. However, there are Bayesian approaches to general RL that satisfy objective optimality guarantees: Thompson sampling is proven to be asymptotically optimal in stochastic environments, meaning its value converges to the value of the optimal policy. Asymptotic optimality is linked to regret under a recoverability assumption on the environment, allowing the agent to recover from mistakes. Consequently, Thompson sampling achieves sublinear regret in these environments. The results culminate in a formal solution to the grain of truth problem: A Bayesian agent operating in a multi-agent environment learns to predict other agents' policies if its prior assigns positive probability to them (the prior contains a grain of truth). A large but limit computable class containing a grain of truth is constructed, demonstrating that agents based on Thompson sampling over this class converge to play Nash equilibria in arbitrary unknown computable multi-agent environments.
label: AI

title: The BIN_COUNTS Constraint: Filtering and Applications
Abstract: This paper introduces the BIN_COUNTS constraint, addressing the problem of counting the number of decision variables in a set that are assigned values within given bins. The paper presents both a decomposition and a filtering algorithm that achieves generalized arc consistency. The filtering power of these two approaches is compared, and various applications are discussed. The paper demonstrates that BIN_COUNTS can be utilized to develop a decomposition for the $\chi^2$ test constraint, a novel statistical constraint introduced in this work. The paper also explores how this new constraint can be employed in the context of the Balanced Academic Curriculum Problem and the Balanced Nursing Workload Problem. Numerical studies involving these reformulations are conducted for both problems. Finally, the paper presents an additional application of the $\chi^2$ test constraint in the context of confidence interval analysis.

title: "Model and Run" Constraint Networks with a MILP Engine
Abstract: Constraint Programming (CP) users require significant expertise to model their problems effectively, particularly in selecting propagators and search strategies, hindering widespread adoption of CP. This paper introduces MICE, a comprehensive Java CP modeler that can leverage any Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) solver as a solution technique. The aim is to provide an alternative tool for democratizing "CP-style" modeling, thanks to its ease of use and reasonable solving capabilities. Key contributions include new decompositions of (reified) constraints and constraints on numerical variables.
label: AI

title: Long-Term Image Boundary Prediction
Abstract: Boundary estimation in images and videos has been an active area of research, with the organization of visual information into boundaries and segments considered a cornerstone of visual perception. While prior work has focused on estimating boundaries for observed frames, this work aims to predict boundaries in future unobserved frames. This requires the model to learn the fate of boundaries and corresponding motion patterns, including a notion of "intuitive physics". Experiments are conducted on natural video sequences alongside synthetic sequences with deterministic physics-based and agent-based motions. While not the primary goal, the paper also demonstrates that fusing RGB and boundary prediction leads to improved RGB predictions.
label: AI

title: Handwriting Profiling using Generative Adversarial Networks
Abstract: Handwriting, a skill acquired by humans from a very early age, involves the ability to develop unique handwriting and mimic another person's writing style, a task learned by the brain through practice. This paper addresses this very problem, where an intelligent system aims to learn the handwriting of an entity using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). The paper proposes a modified architecture of DCGAN (Radford, Metz, and Chintala 2015) to achieve this. It also discusses the application of reinforcement learning techniques to accelerate learning. The algorithm aims to provide new insights in this area, with potential applications including identification of forged documents, signature verification, computer-generated art, and document digitization. Early implementation of the algorithm demonstrates promising performance on MNIST datasets.
