title: Computationally Efficient Target Classification in Multispectral Image Data with Deep Neural Networks
Abstract: Detecting and classifying targets in video streams from surveillance cameras is a cumbersome, error-prone, and expensive task. The incurred costs are often prohibitive for real-time monitoring. This leads to data being stored locally or transmitted to a central storage site for post-incident examination. The required communication links and archiving of video data are still expensive, and this setup excludes preemptive actions to respond to imminent threats. An effective way to overcome these limitations is to build a smart camera that transmits alerts when relevant video sequences are detected. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have surpassed humans in visual classification tasks. The concept of DNNs and Convolutional Networks (ConvNets) can be easily extended to utilize higher-dimensional input data such as multispectral data. We explore this opportunity in terms of achievable accuracy and required computational effort. To analyze the precision of DNNs for scene labeling in an urban surveillance scenario, we created a dataset with 8 classes obtained in a field experiment. We combine an RGB camera with a 25-channel VIS-NIR snapshot sensor to assess the potential of multispectral image data for target classification. We evaluate several new DNNs, showing that spectral information fused with RGB frames can be used to improve system accuracy or achieve similar accuracy with a 3x smaller computational effort. We achieve a very high per-pixel accuracy of 99.1%. Even for scarcely occurring but particularly interesting classes, such as cars, 75% of the pixels are labeled correctly, with errors occurring only around the borders of the objects. This high accuracy was obtained with a training set of only 30 labeled images, paving the way for fast adaptation to various application scenarios.

title: Encoding monotonic multi-set preferences using CI-nets: preliminary report
Abstract: CP-nets and their variants constitute one of the primary AI approaches for specifying and reasoning about preferences. CI-nets, in particular, are a CP-inspired formalism for representing ordinal preferences over sets of goods, typically requiring monotonicity. Considering that goods often come in multi-sets rather than sets, a natural question arises: can CI-nets be used more or less directly to encode preferences over multi-sets? We provide some initial ideas on how to achieve this, demonstrating that at least a restricted form of reasoning in our framework, which we call "confined reasoning," can be efficiently reduced to reasoning on CI-nets. Our framework nonetheless allows for encoding preferences over multi-sets with unbounded multiplicities. We also show the extent to which it can be used to represent preferences where multiplicities of the goods are not explicitly stated ("purely qualitative preferences"), as well as a potential use of our generalization of CI-nets as a component of a recent system for evidence aggregation.

title: Sequence Tutor: Conservative Fine-Tuning of Sequence Generation Models with KL-control
Abstract: This paper proposes a general method for improving the structure and quality of sequences generated by a recurrent neural network (RNN), while preserving information originally learned from data and maintaining sample diversity. An RNN is first pre-trained on data using maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), and the probability distribution over the next token in the sequence learned by this model is treated as a prior policy. Another RNN is then trained using reinforcement learning (RL) to generate higher-quality outputs that account for domain-specific incentives while remaining close to the prior policy of the MLE RNN. To formalize this objective, we derive novel off-policy RL methods for RNNs from KL-control. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated on two applications: 1) generating novel musical melodies and 2) computational molecular generation. For both problems, we show that the proposed method improves the desired properties and structure of the generated sequences while maintaining information learned from data. |||

title: RL$^2$: Fast Reinforcement Learning via Slow Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (deep RL) has achieved success in automatically learning complex behaviors; however, the learning process demands a substantial number of trials. In contrast, animals can learn new tasks with only a few trials, leveraging their prior knowledge of the world. This research aims to bridge this gap. Rather than designing a "fast" reinforcement learning algorithm, we propose to represent it as a recurrent neural network (RNN) and learn it from data. In our proposed method, RL², the algorithm is encoded in the weights of the RNN, which are learned slowly through a general-purpose ("slow") RL algorithm. The RNN receives all information that a typical RL algorithm would receive, including observations, actions, rewards, and termination flags; and it maintains its state across episodes in a given Markov Decision Process (MDP). The activations of the RNN store the state of the "fast" RL algorithm on the current (previously unseen) MDP. We experimentally evaluate RL² on both small-scale and large-scale problems. On the small-scale side, we train it to solve randomly generated multi-arm bandit problems and finite MDPs. After RL² is trained, its performance on new MDPs is comparable to human-designed algorithms with optimality guarantees. On the large-scale side, we test RL² on a vision-based navigation task and demonstrate that it scales up to high-dimensional problems.

title: Recursive Decomposition for Nonconvex Optimization
Abstract: Continuous optimization is a significant problem in numerous areas of AI, including vision, robotics, probabilistic inference, and machine learning. However, most real-world optimization problems are nonconvex, leading standard convex techniques to find only local optima, even with extensions such as random restarts and simulated annealing. We observe that, in many cases, the local modes of the objective function exhibit combinatorial structure, suggesting the application of ideas from combinatorial optimization. Building on this observation, we propose a problem-decomposition approach to nonconvex optimization. Similar to DPLL-style SAT solvers and recursive conditioning in probabilistic inference, our algorithm, RDIS, recursively sets variables to simplify and decompose the objective function into approximately independent sub-functions, until the remaining functions are sufficiently simple to be optimized by standard techniques like gradient descent. The variables to set are selected through graph partitioning, ensuring decomposition whenever possible. We analytically demonstrate that RDIS can solve a broad class of nonconvex optimization problems exponentially faster than gradient descent with random restarts. Experimentally, RDIS outperforms standard techniques on problems such as structure from motion and protein folding.

title: Sentence Ordering and Coherence Modeling using Recurrent Neural Networks
Abstract: Modeling the structure of coherent texts is a fundamental NLP problem. The task of coherently organizing a given set of sentences has been commonly used to develop and evaluate models that understand this structure. We propose an end-to-end unsupervised deep learning approach based on the set-to-sequence framework to address this problem. Our model significantly outperforms previous methods in the order discrimination task and a novel task of ordering abstracts from scientific articles. Furthermore, our work demonstrates that useful text representations can be obtained by learning to order sentences. Visualizing the learned sentence representations reveals that the model captures high-level logical structure in paragraphs. Our representations perform comparably to state-of-the-art pre-training methods on sentence similarity and paraphrase detection tasks.

title: On interestingness measures of formal concepts
Abstract: Formal concepts and closed itemsets have proven to be highly important for knowledge discovery, both as a tool for concise representation of association rules and as a tool for clustering and constructing domain taxonomies and ontologies. Exponential explosion makes it challenging to consider the entire concept lattice arising from data, necessitating the selection of the most useful and interesting concepts. This paper examines interestingness measures of concepts and compares them with respect to various aspects, such as computational efficiency, applicability to noisy data, and ranking correlation performance.

title: Can the periodic spectral modulations of the 236 SETI candidate Sloan Survey stars be due to Dark Matter effects?
Abstract: The search for dark matter (DM) is one of the most active and challenging areas of current research. Possible DM candidates include ultralight fields such as axions and weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs). Axions accumulated in the center of stars are believed to generate matter/DM configurations with oscillating geometries at a very rapid frequency, which is a multiple of the axion mass $m_B$ [1,2]. Borra and Trottier recently discovered peculiar ultrafast periodic spectral modulations in $236$ main sequence stars in the sample of $2.5$ million spectra of galactic halo stars from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, which were interpreted as optical signals from extraterrestrial civilizations, potential candidates for the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI) program [3]. We argue, instead, that this could be the first indirect evidence of bosonic axion-like DM fields inside main sequence stars, with a stable radiative nucleus, where a stable DM core can be hosted. These oscillations were not observed in earlier stellar spectral classes likely due to the impossibility of establishing a stable oscillatory regime because of chaotic motions in their convective nuclei. The axion mass values, $(50 < m_B < 2.4 \\times 10^{3})~ \\mathrm{\\mu eV}$, obtained from the observed frequency range, $(0.6077< f <0.6070$) THz, are consistent with recent theoretical results from high-temperature lattice quantum chromodynamics [4,5].

title: The Neural Noisy Channel
Abstract: We frame sequence-to-sequence transduction as a noisy channel decoding problem and utilize recurrent neural networks to parameterize the source and channel models. Unlike direct models, which can suffer from explaining-away effects during training, noisy channel models must produce outputs that explain their inputs, and their component models can be trained not only with paired training samples but also with unpaired samples from the marginal output distribution. By using a latent variable to control how much of the conditioning sequence the channel model needs to read in order to generate a subsequent symbol, we obtain a tractable and effective beam search decoder. Experimental results on abstractive sentence summarization, morphological inflection, and machine translation demonstrate that noisy channel models outperform direct models, and that they significantly benefit from increased amounts of unpaired output data that direct models cannot easily utilize.

title: Cognitive Discriminative Mappings for Rapid Learning
Abstract: Humans can learn concepts or recognize items from just a few examples, while machines require significantly more samples to perform the same task. This paper develops a computational model to investigate the possibility of this kind of rapid learning. The proposed method aims to enhance the learning task of input from sensory memory by leveraging information retrieved from long-term memory. We present a simple and intuitive technique called cognitive discriminative mappings (CDM) to explore this cognitive problem. First, CDM separates and clusters the data instances retrieved from long-term memory into distinct classes using a discrimination method in working memory when a sensory input triggers the algorithm. CDM then maps each sensory data instance to be as close as possible to the median point of the data group with the same class. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the CDM approach for learning discriminative features of supervised classifications with few training sensory input instances.

title: The Data Complexity of Description Logic Ontologies
Abstract: We analyze the data complexity of ontology-mediated querying where the ontologies are formulated in a description logic (DL) of the ALC family and queries are conjunctive queries, positive existential queries, or acyclic conjunctive queries. Our approach is non-uniform in the sense that we aim to understand the complexity of each single ontology rather than for all ontologies formulated in a certain language. In doing so, we quantify over the queries and are interested in, for example, whether all queries can be evaluated in polynomial time with respect to a given ontology. Our findings include a PTime/coNP-dichotomy for ontologies of depth one in the description logic ALCFI, the same dichotomy for ALC- and ALCI-ontologies of unrestricted depth, and the non-existence of such a dichotomy for ALCF-ontologies. For the latter DL, we additionally show that it is undecidable whether a given ontology admits PTime query evaluation. We also consider the connection between PTime query evaluation and rewritability into (monadic) Datalog.

title: Combining observational and experimental data to find heterogeneous treatment effects
Abstract: Every design choice will have different effects on different units. However, traditional A/B tests are often underpowered to identify these heterogeneous effects. This is especially true when the set of unit-level attributes is high-dimensional and our prior knowledge about which specific covariates are important is weak. However, observational data sets, which are often orders of magnitude larger, are frequently available. We propose a method to combine these two data sources to estimate heterogeneous treatment effects. First, we use observational time series data to estimate a mapping from covariates to unit-level effects. These estimates are likely biased, but under certain conditions, the bias preserves unit-level relative rank orderings. If these conditions hold, we only need sufficient experimental data to identify a monotonic, one-dimensional transformation from observationally predicted treatment effects to real treatment effects. This significantly reduces power demands and makes the detection of heterogeneous effects much easier. As an application, we demonstrate how our method can be used to improve Facebook page recommendations.
label: AI

title: Learning from Untrusted Data
Abstract:
The vast majority of theoretical results in machine learning and statistics assume that the available training data is a reasonably reliable reflection of the phenomena to be learned or estimated. Similarly, most machine learning and statistical techniques used in practice are susceptible to the presence of large amounts of biased or malicious data. In this work, we consider two frameworks in which to study estimation, learning, and optimization in the presence of significant fractions of arbitrary data.
  The first framework, list-decodable learning, asks whether it is possible to return a list of answers, with the guarantee that at least one of them is accurate. For example, given a dataset of $n$ points for which an unknown subset of $\\alpha n$ points are drawn from a distribution of interest, and no assumptions are made about the remaining $(1-\\alpha)n$ points, is it possible to return a list of $\\operatorname{poly}(1/\\alpha)$ answers, one of which is correct? The second framework, which we term the semi-verified learning model, considers the extent to which a small dataset of trusted data (drawn from the distribution in question) can be leveraged to enable the accurate extraction of information from a much larger but untrusted dataset (of which only an $\\alpha$-fraction is drawn from the distribution).
  We demonstrate strong positive results in both settings and provide an algorithm for robust learning in a very general stochastic optimization setting. This general result has immediate implications for robust estimation in a number of settings, including for robustly estimating the mean of distributions with bounded second moments, robustly learning mixtures of such distributions, and robustly finding planted partitions in random graphs in which significant portions of the graph have been perturbed by an adversary.
label: AI

title: Normalizing Flows on Riemannian Manifolds
Abstract: We examine the problem of density estimation on Riemannian manifolds. Density estimation on manifolds has numerous applications in fluid mechanics, optics, and plasma physics, and it often arises when dealing with angular variables (such as those used in protein folding, robot limbs, gene expression) and, in general, directional statistics. Despite the multitude of algorithms available for density estimation in Euclidean spaces $\\mathbf{R}^n$ that scale to large n (e.g., normalizing flows, kernel methods, and variational approximations), most of these methods are not directly applicable for density estimation in more general Riemannian manifolds. We revisit techniques related to homeomorphisms from differential geometry for projecting densities to sub-manifolds and use this to generalize the idea of normalizing flows to more general Riemannian manifolds. The resulting algorithm is scalable, simple to implement, and suitable for use with automatic differentiation. We demonstrate concrete examples of this method on the n-sphere $\\mathbf{S}^n$.
label: AI

title: Optimal Binary Autoencoding with Pairwise Correlations
Abstract: We formulate the learning of a binary autoencoder as a biconvex optimization problem that learns from the pairwise correlations between encoded and decoded bits. Among all possible algorithms that use this information, ours finds the autoencoder that reconstructs its inputs with worst-case optimal loss. The optimal decoder is a single layer of artificial neurons, emerging entirely from the minimax loss minimization, and with weights learned by convex optimization. All of this is reflected in competitive experimental results, demonstrating that binary autoencoding can be done efficiently by conveying information in pairwise correlations in an optimal manner.
label: AI

title: Gaussian Attention Model and Its Application to Knowledge Base Embedding and Question Answering
Abstract: We propose the Gaussian attention model for content-based neural memory access. With the proposed attention model, a neural network has the additional degree of freedom to control the focus of its attention from a laser-sharp attention to a broad attention. It is applicable whenever we can assume that the distance in the latent space reflects some notion of semantics. We use the proposed attention model as a scoring function for the embedding of a knowledge base into a continuous vector space and then train a model that performs question answering about the entities in the knowledge base. The proposed attention model can handle both the propagation of uncertainty when following a series of relations and also the conjunction of conditions in a natural way. On a dataset of soccer players who participated in the FIFA World Cup 2014, we demonstrate that our model can handle both path queries and conjunctive queries well.
label: AI

title: Hierarchical compositional feature learning
Abstract: We introduce the hierarchical compositional network (HCN), a directed generative model capable of discovering and disentangling, without supervision, the building blocks of a set of binary images. The building blocks are binary features defined hierarchically as a composition of some of the features in the layer immediately below, arranged in a particular manner. At a high level, HCN is similar to a sigmoid belief network with pooling. Inference and learning in HCN are very challenging, and existing variational approximations do not work satisfactorily. A main contribution of this work is to show that both can be addressed using max-product message passing (MPMP) with a particular schedule (no EM required). Also, using MPMP as an inference engine for HCN makes new tasks simple: adding supervision information, classifying images, or performing inpainting all correspond to clamping some variables of the model to their known values and running MPMP on the rest. When used for classification, fast inference with HCN has exactly the same functional form as a convolutional neural network (CNN) with linear activations and binary weights. However, HCN's features are qualitatively very different.
label: AI

title: Minimax-optimal semi-supervised regression on unknown manifolds
Abstract: We consider semi-supervised regression when the predictor variables are drawn from an unknown manifold. A simple two-step approach to this problem is to: (i) estimate the manifold geodesic distance between any pair of points using both the labeled and unlabeled instances; and (ii) apply a k nearest neighbor regressor based on these distance estimates. We prove that given sufficiently many unlabeled points, this simple method of geodesic kNN regression achieves the optimal finite-sample minimax bound on the mean squared error, as if the manifold were known. Furthermore, we show how this approach can be efficiently implemented, requiring only O(k N log N) operations to estimate the regression function at all N labeled and unlabeled points. We illustrate this approach on two datasets with a manifold structure: indoor localization using WiFi fingerprints and facial pose estimation. In both cases, geodesic kNN is more accurate and much faster than the popular Laplacian eigenvector regressor.
label: AI

title: Playing SNES in the Retro Learning Environment
Abstract: Mastering a video game requires skill, tactics, and strategy. While these attributes may be acquired naturally by human players, teaching them to a computer program is a far more challenging task. In recent years, extensive research has been conducted in the field of reinforcement learning, and numerous algorithms have been introduced, aiming to learn how to perform human tasks such as playing video games. As a result, the Arcade Learning Environment (ALE) (Bellemare et al., 2013) has become a commonly used benchmark environment allowing algorithms to train on various Atari 2600 games. In many games, the state-of-the-art algorithms outperform humans. In this paper, we introduce a new learning environment, the Retro Learning Environment --- RLE, that can run games on the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES), Sega Genesis, and several other gaming consoles. The environment is expandable, allowing for more video games and consoles to be easily added to the environment, while maintaining the same interface as ALE. Moreover, RLE is compatible with Python and Torch. SNES games pose a significant challenge to current algorithms due to their higher level of complexity and versatility.
label: AI

title: Crowdsourcing in Computer Vision
Abstract: Computer vision systems require large amounts of manually annotated data to properly learn challenging visual concepts. Crowdsourcing platforms offer an inexpensive method to capture human knowledge and understanding for a vast number of visual perception tasks. In this survey, we describe the types of annotations computer vision researchers have collected using crowdsourcing, and how they have ensured that this data is of high quality while annotation effort is minimized. We begin by discussing data collection on both classic (e.g., object recognition) and recent (e.g., visual story-telling) vision tasks. We then summarize key design decisions for creating effective data collection interfaces and workflows, and present strategies for intelligently selecting the most important data instances to annotate. Finally, we conclude with some thoughts on the future of crowdsourcing in computer vision.
label: AI

title: EpistAid: Interactive Interface for Document Filtering in Evidence-based Health Care
Abstract: Evidence-based healthcare (EBHC) is a crucial practice in medicine that aims to provide systematic scientific evidence to answer clinical questions. In this context, Epistemonikos (www.epistemonikos.org) is one of the first and most important online systems in the field, providing an interface that supports users in searching and filtering scientific articles for practicing EBHC. The system currently requires a significant amount of expert human effort, with close to 500 physicians manually curating articles for use on the platform. To scale up the large and continuous amount of data needed to keep the system updated, we introduce EpistAid, an interactive intelligent interface that assists clinicians in the process of curating documents for Epistemonikos within lists of papers called evidence matrices. We present the characteristics, design, and algorithms of our solution, as well as a prototype implementation and a case study to demonstrate how our solution addresses the information overload problem in this area.
label: AI

title: Reinforcement-based Simultaneous Algorithm and its Hyperparameters Selection
Abstract: Many algorithms for data analysis exist, especially for classification problems. To solve a data analysis problem, a suitable algorithm should be chosen, and its hyperparameters should be selected. In this paper, we present a novel method for the simultaneous selection of an algorithm and its hyperparameters. To achieve this, we reduce this problem to the multi-armed bandit problem. We consider an algorithm as an arm, and algorithm hyperparameter search during a fixed time as the corresponding arm play. We also suggest a problem-specific reward function. We conducted experiments on 10 real datasets and compared the suggested method with the existing one implemented in Auto-WEKA. The results show that our method is significantly better in most cases and never worse than Auto-WEKA. |||
label: AI

title: Reinforcement Learning Approach for Parallelization in Filters Aggregation Based Feature Selection Algorithms
Abstract: MeLiF, an algorithm using ensembles of ranking filters, effectively addresses the challenge of feature selection in machine learning and data mining. This paper proposes two methods to enhance MeLiF's performance through parallelization, demonstrating significant improvements in both execution speed and feature selection quality.
label: AI

title: Averaged-DQN: Variance Reduction and Stabilization for Deep Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) algorithms often suffer from instability and variability, negatively impacting their performance. Averaged-DQN, a simple extension of DQN, mitigates these issues by averaging previous Q-value estimates. This results in a more stable training process and improved performance due to a reduction in approximation error variance in the target values. The paper analyzes the source of value function estimation errors and provides an analytical comparison within a simplified model. Experiments on the Arcade Learning Environment benchmark demonstrate the proposed extension's effectiveness in significantly enhancing stability and performance.
label: AI

title: An Information-Theoretic Framework for Fast and Robust Unsupervised Learning via Neural Population Infomax
Abstract: This paper presents a framework for unsupervised learning of representations based on the infomax principle, designed for large-scale neural populations. The framework leverages an asymptotic approximation of Shannon's mutual information to achieve a good initial approximation of the global information-theoretic optimum using a hierarchical infomax method. Building on this initial solution, an efficient gradient descent algorithm is proposed to learn representations from input datasets. The method effectively handles complete, overcomplete, and undercomplete bases. Numerical experiments validate the robustness and efficiency of this method in extracting salient features from input datasets. Compared to existing methods, the proposed algorithm demonstrates significant advantages in both training speed and robustness for unsupervised representation learning. Additionally, it can be easily extended to supervised or unsupervised models for training deep structure networks.
label: AI

title: Challenges of Feature Selection for Big Data Analytics
Abstract: Feature selection is a crucial technique for dimensionality reduction, addressing the curse of dimensionality in handling large-scale, high-dimensional data. This paper explores the challenges posed by big data characteristics like data velocity and variety to the feature selection problem. It provides an overview of feature selection and delves into the challenges specific to structured, heterogeneous, and streaming data, including scalability and stability issues. To facilitate and promote research in feature selection, the paper presents an open-source feature selection repository (scikit-feature), encompassing a wide range of popular feature selection algorithms.
label: AI

title: Neuro-Symbolic Program Synthesis
Abstract: Program Induction, the task of learning mappings from input-output examples to generalize to new inputs, has seen the development of various neural architectures. While these architectures achieve impressive results, they face significant limitations: high computational cost and training difficulty, separate model training for each task, and difficulty in interpreting or verifying the learned mapping. This paper introduces Neuro-Symbolic Program Synthesis, a novel technique addressing these limitations. It automatically constructs computer programs in a domain-specific language that are consistent with input-output examples provided at test time. The approach employs two novel neural modules: a cross-correlation I/O network for representing input-output examples and a Recursive-Reverse-Recursive Neural Network (R3NN) for program synthesis. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated in the complex domain of regular expression-based string transformations. Experiments show that R3NN can construct programs from new input-output examples and even generate new programs for tasks not encountered during training.
label: AI

title: Learning to Perform Physics Experiments via Deep Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: Humans exhibit the ability to infer physical properties like mass, friction, and deformability of novel objects through goal-driven interaction. This process of active interaction mirrors the experimental approach of scientists in discovering hidden facts. While AI has achieved superhuman performance in various domains, its ability to match the scientific intuition of even young children remains unclear. This paper introduces a set of tasks requiring agents to estimate object properties like mass and cohesion in a simulated environment where they can manipulate objects and observe the consequences. The results show that state-of-the-art deep reinforcement learning methods can learn to perform experiments necessary to discover these hidden properties. By systematically varying task difficulty and experiment costs, the study finds that agents learn different strategies balancing information gathering and error avoidance.
label: AI

title: A Semi-Automatic Approach for Detecting Dataset References in Social Science Texts
Abstract: Datasets in scientific articles are often stored separately from the full text. Dataset registries aim to bridge this gap by making datasets citable. However, inconsistencies in dataset abbreviations and heterogeneous metadata (e.g., title, publication year) hinder reproducibility, data access, and impact assessment. Manual detection of dataset references in scientific articles is time-consuming and requires domain expertise. This paper proposes and evaluates a semi-automatic approach for identifying dataset references in social science articles. The method involves extracting features from dataset titles in the da|ra registry, detecting references using these features, and finally matching the detected references to corresponding dataset titles. This approach avoids the cold start problem by not requiring a corpus of articles and achieves promising performance on a test corpus. An F-measure of 0.84 was achieved for reference detection in full texts, and an F-measure of 0.83 for matching detected references to the da|ra registry.
label: AI

title: Self-Wiring Question Answering Systems
Abstract: Question Answering (QA) has experienced a resurgence in recent years, leading to the development of numerous QA systems by companies and research institutions. While some components are reused across implementations, most systems fall short of fully leveraging component reuse potential. Consequently, QA system development remains a tedious and time-consuming process. This paper addresses the challenge of accelerating the creation of novel or tailored QA systems by proposing a concept for a self-wiring approach to QA system composition. This approach allows the reuse of existing, web-based QA systems or modules during the development of new platforms. It relies on describing QA modules using the Web Ontology Language, enabling automatic QA system composition based on a data-driven approach.
label: AI

title: Learning to Act by Predicting the Future
Abstract: This paper presents an approach to sensorimotor control in immersive environments that utilizes a high-dimensional sensory stream and a lower-dimensional measurement stream. The cotemporal structure of these streams provides a rich supervisory signal, enabling the training of a sensorimotor control model through interaction with the environment. The model is trained using supervised learning techniques without extraneous supervision. It learns to act based on raw sensory input from a complex three-dimensional environment. This formulation allows for learning without a fixed goal at training time and pursuing dynamically changing goals at test time. Extensive experiments conducted in three-dimensional simulations based on the first-person game Doom demonstrate the approach's superiority to prior formulations, especially on challenging tasks. The trained models successfully generalize across environments and goals, with one even winning the Full Deathmatch track of the Visual Doom AI Competition in previously unseen environments.
label: AI

title: A Compare-Aggregate Model for Matching Text Sequences
Abstract: Many NLP tasks like machine comprehension, answer selection, and text entailment require comparing sequences. Identifying important units between sequences is key to solving these problems. This paper proposes a general "compare-aggregate" framework using Convolutional Neural Networks for word-level matching followed by aggregation. The focus is on exploring different comparison functions for vector matching. Evaluations on four datasets reveal that simple comparison functions based on element-wise operations can outperform standard neural network and neural tensor network approaches.
label: AI

title: Analytical Derivation of Downlink Data Rate Distribution for 5G HetNets with Cell-Edge Located Small Cells
Abstract: Efficient resource allocation in Heterogeneous Networks (HetNets) is essential to minimize interference among users. This paper analytically derives probability distributions of per-user downlink data rate, spectral efficiency (SE), and energy efficiency (EE) for a HetNet model with cell-edge located small cells. The accuracy of the derived cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) is verified through simulations. These CDF expressions are then employed to optimize key performance indicators (KPIs), specifically the 10th percentile downlink user data rate (R10), SE (SE10), and EE (EE10). Beyond separate KPI optimization, the paper investigates the variation of KPIs relative to each other. Results indicate that resource allocation parameters maximizing R10 are close to those maximizing SE10. However, optimal values for SE10 and R10 differ from those for EE10, highlighting the trade-off between EE and SE in HetNets. A metric, θ, is proposed for jointly optimizing SE and EE. The results show that the resource sharing parameter optimizing θ is closer to the value maximizing SE, suggesting SE's prominence in the SE-EE trade-off.
label: AI

title: Causes for Query Answers from Databases: Datalog Abduction, View-Updates, and Integrity Constraints
Abstract: Causality has been introduced to databases to model, characterize, and potentially compute causes for query answers. Connections between QA-causality and consistency-based diagnosis and database repairs (regarding integrity constraint violations) have been established. This paper establishes precise connections between QA-causality and both abductive diagnosis and the view-update problem in databases. These connections lead to new algorithmic and complexity results for QA-causality. The paper further presents new results on the complexity of view-conditioned causality and explores the notion of QA-causality in the presence of integrity constraints, obtaining complexity results through a link with view-conditioned causality. The abduction connection under integrity constraints provides algorithmic tools for QA-causality.
label: AI

title: Detecting Dependencies in Sparse, Multivariate Databases Using Probabilistic Programming and Non-parametric Bayes
Abstract: Datasets with hundreds of variables and numerous missing values are common, posing statistical and computational challenges in detecting true predictive relationships between variables and suppressing false positives. This paper proposes an approach combining probabilistic programming, information theory, and non-parametric Bayes. It demonstrates the use of Bayesian non-parametric modeling for building an ensemble of joint probability models for all variables, efficiently detecting marginal independencies, and estimating conditional mutual information between arbitrary subsets of variables under various constraints. These capabilities are accessible through BayesDB, a probabilistic programming platform for probabilistic data analysis, using a simple SQL-like language. The method's effectiveness is shown through empirical demonstrations on challenging synthetic problems and its ability to improve sensitivity and specificity compared to baselines from statistics and machine learning on a real-world database of over 300 sparsely observed macroeconomic development and public health indicators.
label: AI

title: TopicRNN: A Recurrent Neural Network with Long-Range Semantic Dependency
Abstract: This paper introduces TopicRNN, a recurrent neural network (RNN)-based language model designed to directly capture the global semantic meaning of words in a document through latent topics. While RNNs are adept at capturing local structure in word sequences, they can struggle with remembering long-range dependencies, which are often semantically driven. In contrast, latent topic models capture the global semantic structure of a document but disregard word order. TopicRNN combines the strengths of both approaches: using an RNN to capture local dependencies and latent topics for global dependencies. Unlike previous contextual RNN language models, TopicRNN is learned end-to-end. Empirical results on word prediction demonstrate TopicRNN's superior performance compared to existing contextual RNN baselines. Additionally, TopicRNN can be used as an unsupervised feature extractor for documents, achieving a comparable error rate to the state-of-the-art semi-supervised approach for sentiment analysis on the IMDB movie review dataset. TopicRNN also produces meaningful topics, making it a valuable alternative to document models like latent Dirichlet allocation.
label: AI

title: A Differentiable Physics Engine for Deep Learning in Robotics
Abstract: Optimizing controllers is a crucial aspect of robotics. Existing approaches often treat robots as black boxes, leading to the prevalence of derivative-free optimization methods like evolutionary algorithms or reinforcement learning. Gradient-based methods, while faster, are limited by the need for small models or finite difference approximations for the Jacobian, becoming expensive with increasing parameters, as encountered in deep learning. This paper proposes the implementation of a modern physics engine capable of differentiating control parameters, available for both CPU and GPU. The paper demonstrates how this engine accelerates the optimization process, even for small problems. It also outlines the advantages of this approach over deep Q-learning for integrating deep learning into robotics. The paper argues that this engine represents a significant step forward for deep learning in robotics, opening new avenues for optimizing both hardware and software.
label: AI

title: Combining policy gradient and Q-learning
Abstract: Policy gradient is a powerful technique for policy improvement in reinforcement learning settings. However, traditional online variants are limited to on-policy learning, unable to leverage off-policy data. This paper introduces a novel technique combining policy gradient with off-policy Q-learning, drawing experience from a replay buffer. This approach is motivated by the connection between the fixed points of the regularized policy gradient algorithm and Q-values. This connection allows for estimating Q-values from the policy's action preferences, which are then updated using Q-learning. The new technique is termed "PGQL" (policy gradient and Q-learning). The paper establishes an equivalency between action-value fitting techniques and actor-critic algorithms, demonstrating that regularized policy gradient methods can be interpreted as advantage function learning algorithms. Numerical examples demonstrate PGQL's improved data efficiency and stability. Notably, testing on the full suite of Atari games shows that PGQL outperforms both asynchronous advantage actor-critic (A3C) and Q-learning.
label: AI

title: Dynamic Coattention Networks For Question Answering
Abstract: Several deep learning models have been proposed for question answering. However, their single-pass nature limits their ability to recover from local maxima leading to incorrect answers. This paper introduces the Dynamic Coattention Network (DCN) to address this problem. DCN first fuses co-dependent representations of the question and document, focusing on relevant parts of both. A dynamic pointing decoder then iterates over potential answer spans. This iterative procedure allows the model to recover from initial local maxima associated with incorrect answers. On the Stanford question answering dataset, a single DCN model surpasses the previous state of the art, achieving an F1 score of 75.9% compared to 71.0%. An ensemble of DCN models further improves performance, reaching an F1 score of 80.4%.
label: AI

title: A Joint Many-Task Model: Growing a Neural Network for Multiple NLP Tasks
Abstract: Transfer and multi-task learning have traditionally focused on single source-target pairs or a limited number of similar tasks. Ideally, linguistic levels like morphology, syntax, and semantics would benefit from training in a single model. This paper introduces a joint many-task model along with a strategy for progressively increasing its depth to solve increasingly complex tasks. Higher layers include shortcut connections to lower-level task predictions, reflecting linguistic hierarchies. A simple regularization term allows for optimizing all model weights to improve one task's loss without causing catastrophic interference in other tasks. This single end-to-end model achieves state-of-the-art or competitive results on five tasks spanning tagging, parsing, relatedness, and entailment.
label: AI

title: Neural Architecture Search with Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: Neural networks are powerful and flexible models, excelling in various challenging learning tasks in image, speech, and natural language understanding. However, designing neural networks remains a complex endeavor. This paper leverages a recurrent network to generate model descriptions of neural networks. This RNN is trained using reinforcement learning to maximize the expected accuracy of the generated architectures on a validation set. On the CIFAR-10 dataset, this method, starting from scratch, designs a novel network architecture that rivals the best human-designed architecture in terms of test set accuracy. The CIFAR-10 model achieves a test error rate of 3.65%, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art model using a similar architectural scheme by 0.09% and demonstrating a 1.05x speed improvement. On the Penn Treebank dataset, the model constructs a novel recurrent cell that outperforms the widely used LSTM cell and other state-of-the-art baselines. This cell achieves a test set perplexity of 62.4 on Penn Treebank, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art model by 3.6 perplexity points. The cell is also transferable to the character language modeling task on PTB, achieving a state-of-the-art perplexity of 1.214.
label: AI

title: Quasi-Recurrent Neural Networks
Abstract: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are powerful for modeling sequential data. However, their reliance on previous timestep outputs for each timestep's computation limits parallelism and makes them unwieldy for very long sequences. This paper introduces quasi-recurrent neural networks (QRNNs), a novel approach to neural sequence modeling that alternates convolutional layers (applied in parallel across timesteps) and a minimalist recurrent pooling function (applied in parallel across channels). Despite lacking trainable recurrent layers, stacked QRNNs demonstrate better predictive accuracy than stacked LSTMs of the same hidden size. Their increased parallelism also leads to significant speed enhancements during training and testing, up to 16 times faster. Experiments on language modeling, sentiment classification, and character-level neural machine translation showcase these advantages, highlighting the potential of QRNNs as a fundamental building block for various sequence tasks. |||
label: AI

title: QBF Solving by Counterexample-guided Expansion
Abstract: We propose a novel extension of Counterexample-Guided Inductive Synthesis (CEGIS) and demonstrate its effectiveness in developing a new, competitive algorithm for solving Quantified Boolean Formulas (QBF). Current QBF solvers based on counterexample-guided expansion employ a recursive approach that exhibits poor scalability with increasing quantifier alternations. Our generalization of CEGIS eliminates the need for this recursive approach, resulting in a simplified and efficient algorithm for QBF solving. Furthermore, our work is supported by a robust, yet straightforward, implementation of the algorithm, enabling the examination of the practical impact of our design decisions, alongside various optimizations.
label: AI

title: Estimating Causal Direction and Confounding of Two Discrete Variables
Abstract: We present a method to classify the causal relationship between two discrete variables solely based on their joint distribution, acknowledging an inherent baseline error in the process. We assume that the causal system is acyclic, but allow for hidden common causes. Our algorithm relies on the assumption that the probability distribution of a cause is independent from the probability distribution of the cause-effect mechanism. While our classifier is trained under a Bayesian assumption of flat hyperpriors, this assumption does not extend to our test data. This work connects to recent advancements in the identifiability of causal models over continuous variables under the assumption of "independent mechanisms". Thoroughly-commented Python notebooks, replicating all our experiments, are publicly available at http://vision.caltech.edu/~kchalupk/code.html.
label: AI

title: Understanding Deep Neural Networks with Rectified Linear Units
Abstract: This study investigates the family of functions representable by deep neural networks (DNNs) utilizing rectified linear units (ReLU). We present an algorithm for training a ReLU DNN with a single hidden layer to global optimality, with a runtime that is polynomial in the data size but exponential in the input dimension. Furthermore, we improve upon existing lower bounds on the size (from exponential to super-exponential) for approximating a ReLU deep net function using a shallower ReLU network. Our gap theorems hold for smoothly parametrized families of "hard" functions, contrasting with countable, discrete families found in existing literature. An example consequence of our gap theorems is the following: for any natural number k, there exists a function representable by a ReLU DNN with k^2 hidden layers and total size k^3, such that any ReLU DNN with at most k hidden layers will require at least 1/2 * k^(k+1) - 1 total nodes. Finally, for the family of R^n to R DNNs with ReLU activations, we demonstrate a new lower bound on the number of affine pieces, surpassing previous constructions in certain regimes of the network architecture. Notably, our lower bound is proven through an explicit construction of a smoothly parameterized family of functions attaining this scaling. Our construction leverages the theory of zonotopes from polyhedral theory.
label: AI

title: Ways of Conditioning Generative Adversarial Networks
Abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are generative models capable of producing random samples that realistically resemble natural images. While GANs can generate samples with specific attributes by incorporating a condition vector into the input, research in this area remains relatively unexplored. We propose novel methods for conditioning GANs that achieve state-of-the-art results on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets. We introduce two main models: an information retrieval model that extracts conditional information from the samples and a spatial bilinear pooling model that generates bilinear features derived from the spatial cross product of an image and a condition vector. These methods significantly improve the log-likelihood of test data under the conditional distributions compared to concatenation-based methods.
label: AI

title: Learning Continuous Semantic Representations of Symbolic Expressions
Abstract: Combining abstract, symbolic reasoning with continuous neural reasoning presents a significant challenge in representation learning. As a step towards addressing this challenge, we introduce a new architecture, termed neural equivalence networks, for the problem of learning continuous semantic representations of algebraic and logical expressions. These networks are trained to represent semantic equivalence, even for expressions that are syntactically dissimilar. The challenge lies in computing semantic representations in a syntax-directed manner, as semantics is compositional. However, small syntactic changes can lead to substantial semantic alterations, which can be challenging for continuous neural architectures. We conduct an exhaustive evaluation on the task of checking equivalence across a highly diverse range of symbolic algebraic and boolean expression types, demonstrating that our model significantly outperforms existing architectures.
label: AI

title: Platooning of Connected Vehicles with Undirected Topologies: Robustness Analysis and Distributed H-infinity Controller Synthesis
Abstract: This paper investigates the robustness analysis and distributed H-infinity controller synthesis for a platoon of connected vehicles with undirected topologies. We first develop a unified model to describe the collective behavior of homogeneous platoons with external disturbances using graph theory. By leveraging the spectral decomposition of a symmetric matrix, the collective dynamics of a platoon are equivalently decomposed into a set of subsystems of the same size as a single vehicle. Subsequently, we provide an explicit scaling trend of the robustness measure gamma-gain and introduce a scalable multi-step procedure to synthesize a distributed H-infinity controller for large-scale platoons. Our analysis reveals that communication topology, particularly the leader's information, exerts a significant influence on both robustness performance and controller synthesis. Furthermore, we formulate an intuitive optimization problem to optimize an undirected topology for a platoon system and explicitly analyze the upper and lower bounds of the objective. These bounds suggest that coordination of multiple mini-platoons represents a reasonable architecture for controlling large-scale platoons. Numerical simulations are conducted to illustrate our findings.
label: AI

title: Bayesian Non-parametric model to Target Gamification Notifications Using Big Data
Abstract: We propose an approach that assists online marketers in targeting their gamification elements to users by modifying the order of the task list sent to users. This approach is more realistic and flexible, allowing the model to learn more parameters as online marketers collect more data. The targeting approach is scalable and efficient, and it can be applied to streaming data.
label: AI

title: Probabilistic Modeling of Progressive Filtering
Abstract: Progressive filtering is a straightforward method for performing hierarchical classification, inspired by the way most humans categorize items according to an underlying taxonomy. Each node in the taxonomy corresponds to a different category, and the categorization process can be visualized as the item traversing downwards through all nodes that accept it as belonging to the corresponding category. This paper aims to model the progressive filtering technique from a probabilistic perspective, within a hierarchical text categorization setting. This probabilistic framework aims to facilitate the design, training, and testing of systems based on progressive filtering.
label: AI

title: LQG for portfolio optimization
Abstract: We introduce a generic solver for dynamic portfolio allocation problems when the market exhibits return predictability, price impact, and partial observability. We assume that the price modeling can be encoded into a linear state-space, demonstrating how the problem then fits into the LQG framework. We derive the optimal control policy and introduce analytical tools that preserve the intelligibility of the solution. Furthermore, we establish a link between the existence and uniqueness of the optimal controller and a dynamical non-arbitrage criterion. Finally, we illustrate our method using a synthetic portfolio allocation problem.

title: Maximizing Investment Value of Small-Scale PV in a Smart Grid Environment
Abstract: Determining the optimal size and orientation of small-scale residential-based PV arrays will become increasingly complex in the future smart grid environment with the introduction of smart meters and dynamic tariffs. However, consumers can leverage the availability of smart meter data to conduct a more detailed exploration of PV investment options tailored to their specific circumstances. This paper proposes an optimization method for PV orientation and sizing, where maximizing the PV investment value is set as the defining objective. Solar insolation and PV array models are described to form the foundation of the PV array optimization strategy. A constrained particle swarm optimization algorithm is chosen due to its strong performance in non-linear applications. The optimization algorithm is applied to real-world metered data to quantify the potential investment value of a PV installation under different energy retailers and tariff structures. The arrangement with the highest value is identified to enable prospective small-scale PV investors to select the most cost-effective system.

title: Extracting Actionability from Machine Learning Models by Sub-optimal Deterministic Planning
Abstract: A major focus of machine learning research has been improving the generalization accuracy and efficiency of prediction models. Numerous models, such as SVM, random forest, and deep neural networks, have been proposed and achieved significant success. However, many applications lack actionability, meaning the ability to translate prediction results into actions. For example, in applications such as customer relationship management, clinical prediction, and advertising, users require not only accurate predictions but also actionable instructions that can transform an input into a desired outcome (e.g., higher profit returns, lower morbidity rates, higher ad hit rates). Existing efforts in deriving such actionable knowledge are limited in scope and confined to simple action models that only allow for changes to a single attribute per action. The challenge arises from the fact that in many real-world applications, action models are often more complex and extracting an optimal solution becomes more difficult. This paper presents a novel approach that achieves actionability by combining learning with planning, two core areas of AI. Specifically, we propose a framework to extract actionable knowledge from random forest, one of the most widely used and effective off-the-shelf classifiers. We formulate the actionability problem as a sub-optimal action planning (SOAP) problem, which aims to find a plan to modify certain features of a given input to ensure the random forest produces a desirable output while minimizing the total cost of actions. Technically, the SOAP problem is formulated in the SAS+ planning formalism and solved using a Max-SAT based approach. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed approach on a personal credit dataset and other benchmarks. Our work represents a new application of automated planning in an emerging and challenging machine learning paradigm.

title: Quantile Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: In reinforcement learning, the standard criterion for evaluating policies in a state is the expected (discounted) sum of rewards. However, this criterion may not always be suitable. We consider an alternative criterion based on the notion of quantiles. In the case of episodic reinforcement learning problems, we propose an algorithm based on stochastic approximation with two timescales. We evaluate our proposition using a simple model of the TV show, Who wants to be a millionaire.

title: On convergence rates of game theoretic reinforcement learning algorithms
Abstract: This paper examines a class of multi-player discrete games where each player aims to maximize its own utility function. Each player lacks knowledge of the other players' action sets, their deployed actions, or the structures of their own or others' utility functions. Instead, each player only knows its own deployed actions and its received utility values in recent history. We propose a reinforcement learning algorithm that converges to the set of action profiles with maximal stochastic potential with probability one. Moreover, we quantify the convergence rate of the proposed algorithm. The algorithm's performance is validated using two case studies in the smart grid and cybersecurity domains.

title: When to Reset Your Keys: Optimal Timing of Security Updates via Learning
Abstract: Cybersecurity is increasingly threatened by sophisticated and persistent attacks. As these attacks are often designed to repeatedly disable a system (or a critical resource, e.g., a user account), it is crucial for the defender to continuously update its security measures to achieve a balance between the risk of compromise and the cost of security updates. Furthermore, these decisions often need to be made with limited and delayed feedback due to the stealthy nature of advanced attacks. In addition to targeted attacks, such an optimal timing policy under incomplete information has broad applications in cybersecurity. Examples include key rotation, password change, application of patches, and virtual machine refreshing. However, rigorous studies of optimal timing are scarce. Existing solutions typically rely on a predefined attack model known to the defender, which is often not the case in practice. This work makes an initial effort towards achieving optimal timing of security updates in the face of unknown stealthy attacks. We consider a variant of the influential FlipIt game model with asymmetric feedback and unknown attack time distribution, providing a general model for consecutive security updates. The defender's problem is then modeled as a time-associative bandit problem with dependent arms. We derive upper confidence bound-based learning policies that achieve low regret compared with optimal periodic defense strategies, which can only be derived when attack time distributions are known.

title: A Public Comment on NCCoE's White Paper on Privacy-Enhancing Identity Brokers
Abstract: The National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence (NCCoE) (in the United States) published a white paper on "privacy-enhanced identity brokers" on October 19, 2015. This paper presents a response to their request for public comments. We identify concerns that we consider paramount for the design of a privacy-enhancing identity brokering solution, for identification and authentication of citizens into numerous online services, and recommend incorporating them into a revised white paper. Our observations, focused on privacy, security, auditability, and forensics, are primarily based on a recently published research paper (PETS 2015) about two nation-scale brokered identification systems.

title: Artificial Intelligence Safety and Cybersecurity: a Timeline of AI Failures
Abstract: This work presents and analyzes reported failures of artificially intelligent systems and extrapolates our analysis to future AIs. We suggest that both the frequency and severity of future AI failures will steadily increase. AI Safety can be improved based on insights derived from cybersecurity experts. For narrow AIs, safety failures are at a similar, moderate, level of criticality as in cybersecurity; however, for general AI, failures have a fundamentally different impact. A single failure of a superintelligent system may cause a catastrophic event with no chance of recovery. The goal of cybersecurity is to reduce the number of successful attacks on the system; the goal of AI Safety is to ensure that zero attacks succeed in bypassing the safety mechanisms. Unfortunately, such a level of performance is unattainable. Every security system will eventually fail; there is no such thing as a 100% secure system.

title: The Third Offset and a Fifth Domain? Balancing Game-Changing Innovation and Cyber Risk Mitigation
Abstract: Cyber has transformed the scope of the national security mission and is placing new strains on our diplomatic, warfighting, legal, and economic/budgetary processes. Cybersecurity processes and techniques are becoming increasingly crucial to our warfighting missions, but they can also hinder the pace and potential for high-impact, game-changing innovation. Throughout its history, the Navy has demonstrated the ability of innovation (in policy, process, and technology) to change the game when our security is at stake. We believe the Navy is capable of significantly impacting not only U.S. capabilities in cyber conflict and information operations, but also in cyber defense and information assurance, as well as cybersecurity for our society. While cyber risk management is challenging, the transition from DoD Information Assurance Certification and Accreditation Process (DIACAP) to the Risk Management Framework (RMF) has the potential to harmonize our cybersecurity efforts with our need (and demonstrated ability) to provide game-changing strategies, tactics, and technologies. We offer a foundation for the foregoing assertions and recommendations on ways to encourage innovation in the context of effective cyber risk management.

title: Automated Big Text Security Classification
Abstract: In recent years, traditional cybersecurity safeguards have proven ineffective against insider threats. Notable cases of sensitive information leaks caused by insiders, including the WikiLeaks release of diplomatic cables and the Edward Snowden incident, have significantly harmed the U.S. government's relationships with other governments and its own citizens. Data Leak Prevention (DLP) is a solution for detecting and preventing information leaks from within an organization's network. However, state-of-the-art DLP detection models are only able to detect a limited range of sensitive information, and research in the field has been hampered by the lack of available sensitive texts. Many researchers have focused on document-based detection with artificially labeled "confidential documents" for which security labels are assigned to the entire document, when in reality only a portion of the document is sensitive. This type of whole-document-based security labeling increases the likelihood of preventing authorized users from accessing non-sensitive information within sensitive documents. This paper introduces Automated Classification Enabled by Security Similarity (ACESS), a new and innovative detection model that tackles the complexity of big text security classification/detection. To analyze the ACESS system, we constructed a novel dataset containing formerly classified paragraphs from diplomatic cables made public by the WikiLeaks organization. To our knowledge, this paper is the first to analyze a dataset that contains actual formerly sensitive information annotated at paragraph granularity.

title: The Future Internet of Things and Security of its Control Systems
Abstract: We consider the future cyber security of industrial control systems. As best as we can see, much of this future unfolds in the context of the Internet of Things (IoT). In fact, we envision that all industrial and infrastructure environments, and cyber-physical systems in general, will take on a form reminiscent of what is currently referred to as the IoT. IoT is envisioned as a multitude of heterogeneous devices densely interconnected and communicating with the objective of accomplishing a diverse range of objectives, often collaboratively. It is arguable that in the relatively near future, the IoT construct will encompass industrial plants, infrastructures, housing, and other systems that are currently controlled by ICS and SCADA systems. In IoT environments, cybersecurity will largely derive from system agility, moving-target defenses, cybermaneuvering, and other autonomous or semi-autonomous behaviors. Cyber security of IoT may also benefit from new design methods for mixed-trusted systems and from big data analytics, both predictive and autonomous.

title: Using Non-invertible Data Transformations to Build Adversarial-Robust Neural Networks
Abstract: Deep neural networks have proven to be highly effective in a wide range of machine learning tasks, from improving speech recognition systems to advancing the development of autonomous vehicles. However, despite their superior performance in many applications, these models have recently been shown to be susceptible to a specific type of attack possible through the generation of particular synthetic examples referred to as adversarial samples. These samples are constructed by manipulating real examples from the training data distribution to "fool" the original neural model, resulting in the misclassification (with high confidence) of previously correctly classified samples. Addressing this weakness is of paramount importance if deep neural architectures are to be applied to critical applications, such as those in the domain of cybersecurity. This paper presents an analysis of this fundamental flaw lurking in all neural architectures to uncover the limitations of previously proposed defense mechanisms. More importantly, we present a unifying framework for protecting deep neural models using a non-invertible data transformation, developing two adversary-resilient architectures utilizing both linear and nonlinear dimensionality reduction. Empirical results indicate that our framework provides enhanced robustness compared to state-of-the-art solutions while exhibiting negligible degradation in accuracy. |||

title: Adversary Resistant Deep Neural Networks with an Application to Malware Detection
Abstract: Deep learning, despite its success in areas like Go, has been applied to cybersecurity, particularly malware detection. However, deep neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial samples, which can easily bypass malware detection systems. Existing defenses have limited effectiveness and lack theoretical guarantees. This paper proposes a novel adversary-resistant technique that randomly nullifies features within samples, hindering attackers from constructing effective adversarial samples. The technique is validated theoretically and empirically on real-world datasets, demonstrating significant improvement in robustness against adversarial attacks while maintaining high classification accuracy. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets illustrate the method's general applicability.

title: A Dictionary-based Approach to Racism Detection in Dutch Social Media
Abstract: This research presents a dictionary-based approach to detect racism in Dutch social media comments. Three dictionaries were created: one based on possibly racist and neutral terms from the training data, another expanded using a word2vec model, and a third manually cleaned. Support Vector Machines were trained using the word distribution across categories in the dictionaries as features. The best-performing model, using the manually cleaned dictionary, achieved an F-score of 0.46 on a test set. Automated dictionary expansion only slightly boosted performance, suggesting that the added words, while present in the corpus, did not significantly impact the model's ability to detect racism. The dictionaries, code, and data access procedures are available at https://github.com/clips/hades.

title: Given Enough Eyeballs, All Bugs Are Shallow? Revisiting Eric Raymond with Bug Bounty Programs
Abstract: Bug bounty programs offer a platform for organizations to crowdsource software security and for researchers to be rewarded for vulnerabilities. However, these programs create tension between organizations and researchers. Researchers face a decreasing likelihood of finding new bugs, making it difficult to justify higher rewards. Program managers, meanwhile, incentivize competition by attracting a larger pool of researchers. This leads to researchers switching to newly launched programs with more readily discoverable vulnerabilities. This study investigates the technical and economic dynamics of bug bounty program contributions, providing insights that can inform the design of more effective programs.

title: Darknet and Deepnet Mining for Proactive Cybersecurity Threat Intelligence
Abstract: This paper presents an operational system for gathering cyber threat intelligence from social platforms, particularly darknet and deepnet sites. The system focuses on hacker forums and marketplaces offering malicious hacking products and services, collecting information on emerging cyber threats, including newly developed malware and exploits. The system gathers an average of 305 high-quality cyber threat warnings per week, providing valuable information to cyber defenders. Data mining and machine learning techniques enhance the system's performance, enabling it to recall 92% of products in marketplaces and 80% of forum discussions related to malicious hacking with high precision. The collected data is analyzed to demonstrate its application in threat analysis.

title: Unethical Research: How to Create a Malevolent Artificial Intelligence
Abstract: Cybersecurity research involves publishing information on both malicious exploits and defensive tools. While much research focuses on creating safe AI, little is known about designing malevolent AI. This paper provides guidelines for developing a Malevolent Artificial Intelligence (MAI), arguing that such information is valuable for those involved in AI safety, particularly in preventing the deliberate creation or spontaneous emergence of dangerous AI that could harm humanity.

title: Using Private and Public Assessments in Security Information Sharing Agreements
Abstract: Information sharing among organizations has emerged as a potential method for improving cybersecurity. However, disclosure costs act as deterrents to voluntary cooperation. This research uses a game-theoretic approach to understand firms' incentives in information-sharing agreements. It proposes the design of inter-temporal incentives, where future cooperation depends on past interactions. Specifically, the paper demonstrates that incentives for full cooperation can be achieved by allowing firms to share their assessments of other firms' disclosure decisions through a common platform. Similar incentives can be designed based on public rating systems.

title: Active Cyber Defense Dynamics Exhibiting Rich Phenomena
Abstract: Cybersecurity is a complex system under constant attack. This paper explores the phenomena exhibited when a defender employs active defense to combat cyberattacks. It demonstrates, for the first time, that active cyber defense dynamics can exhibit bifurcation and chaos phenomena. This has significant implications for cybersecurity measurement and prediction: it may be impossible to accurately measure and predict cybersecurity under certain conditions. Defenders must manipulate these dynamics to avoid unmanageable situations during real-life operations.

title: Spatiotemporal patterns and predictability of cyberattacks
Abstract: This research explores the existence of intrinsic patterns in cyberattacks, challenging the conventional wisdom that such patterns are absent due to cyberspace's complexity. Through a detailed analysis of attack frequencies across a wide range of consecutive IP addresses, the study identifies two distinct spatiotemporal patterns: deterministic and stochastic. Notably, a limited number of major attackers account for the majority of attacks, as their attack fingerprints and target selection strategies can be uniquely identified based on limited spatiotemporal characteristics. Quantitative measures, including the flux-fluctuation law, Markov state transition probabilities, and predictability measures, are employed to comprehensively characterize the attack patterns. The study reveals high degrees of predictability in these patterns, suggesting the potential for anticipating and mitigating large-scale cyberattacks using macroscopic approaches.

title: A Characterization of Cybersecurity Posture from Network Telescope Data
Abstract: This paper analyzes real data collected by CAIDA's network telescope to understand cybersecurity posture from a data-driven perspective. Cybersecurity posture is formalized based on three time series: the number of victims, attackers, and attacks observed by the telescope. The paper investigates the phenomena and statistical properties of these time series and explains their cybersecurity meanings. For example, the concept of sweep-time is introduced, demonstrating its stochastic nature. The study reveals that the number of attackers and attacks from a specific country dominates the total number observed by the telescope. It also highlights that smaller network telescopes may be less effective than larger ones.

title: Preventive and Reactive Cyber Defense Dynamics Is Globally Stable
Abstract: The cybersecurity dynamics approach aims to understand cybersecurity holistically by modeling the evolution of the global cybersecurity state. This paper investigates a specific type of cybersecurity dynamics caused by interactions between preventive and reactive defenses against push- and pull-based cyberattacks. Previous studies have shown the dynamics to be globally stable in a specific parameter regime, but the behavior outside this regime remained unclear. This research resolves this open problem by proving that the dynamics is globally stable across the entire parameter universe. The cybersecurity implications of this theoretical result are discussed. The paper also demonstrates that the dynamics converges exponentially to the equilibrium except for a specific parameter regime where convergence is polynomial. New bounds for the equilibrium are proposed, offering tighter estimates than those previously available.

title: Impact of integrity attacks on real-time pricing in smart grids
Abstract: Modern information and communication technologies used in smart grids are vulnerable to cybersecurity threats. This paper investigates the impact of integrity attacks on real-time pricing (RTP), a key feature of smart grids that utilizes these technologies to improve efficiency. The study highlights the closed-loop nature of RTP, where price signals and demand are mutually dependent. This closed loop can be exploited by adversaries seeking to destabilize the pricing system. Small malicious modifications to price signals can be amplified by the closed loop, leading to inefficiency and potential blackouts. Using a control-theoretic approach, the paper analyzes the stability of RTP under two types of integrity attacks: scaling and delay attacks. The results demonstrate that RTP is at risk of destabilization only if adversaries can manipulate price signals by reducing their values (scaling attack) or providing outdated prices (delay attack). This research provides valuable guidelines for system operators to analyze the impact of attack parameters on system stability and implement appropriate security measures.

title: Injective stabilization of additive functors. I. Preliminaries
Abstract: This paper is the first in a series exploring the concept of injective stabilization of the tensor product and its applications. It compiles known facts and establishes a basic operational calculus for use in subsequent parts. Several results of independent interest are presented, including connections to satellites, explicit construction of stabilization, exactness properties of injectively stable functors, and the construction of a doubly-infinite exact sequence from a functor and a short exact sequence. When specialized to the tensor product with a finitely presented module, the injective stabilization is isomorphic to the 1-torsion functor. The Auslander-Reiten formula is generalized, and characterizations of zeroth derived functors are derived. The subsequent papers will focus on applications of these techniques, including new notions of torsion and cotorsion modules and the concept of asymptotic stabilization of the tensor product.
