To manage this large volume of information and provide accurate measurements, service providers can adopt information fusion, which, given the decentralized nature of urban deployments, can be performed using consensus algorithms. These algorithms allow distributed agents to (iteratively) compute linear functions on the exchanged data and make decisions based on the outcome, without requiring support from a central entity. However, the use of consensus algorithms raises several security concerns, particularly when private or security-critical information is involved in the computation. This paper proposes ODIN, a novel algorithm that enables information fusion over encrypted data. ODIN is a privacy-preserving extension of the popular consensus gossip algorithm that prevents distributed agents from having direct access to the data while they iteratively reach consensus. Agents cannot access even the final consensus value but can only retrieve partial information, such as a binary decision. ODIN utilizes efficient additive obfuscation and proxy re-encryption during the update steps, and Garbled Circuits to make final decisions on the obfuscated consensus. We discuss the security of our proposal and demonstrate its practicability and efficiency on real-world resource-constrained devices, developing a prototype implementation for Raspberry Pi devices.

title: Continuum Kinetic and Multi-Fluid Simulations of Classical Sheaths
Abstract: Kinetic studies of plasma sheaths are critical for understanding heat deposition on walls, the effect of sputtering, and contamination of the plasma with detrimental impurities. The plasma sheath also provides a boundary condition and can often have a significant global impact on the bulk plasma. This paper performs kinetic studies of classical sheaths using the continuum code, Gkeyll, which directly solves the Vlasov-Poisson/Maxwell equations. The code employs a novel version of the finite-element discontinuous Galerkin (DG) scheme that conserves energy in the continuous-time limit. The electrostatic field is computed using the Poisson equation. Ionization and scattering collisions are included, but surface effects are neglected. The aim of this work is to introduce the continuum-kinetic method and compare its results to those obtained from an already established finite-volume multi-fluid model also implemented in Gkeyll. Novel boundary conditions on the fluids allow the sheath to form without specifying wall fluxes, so the fluids and fields adjust self-consistently at the wall. The work presented here demonstrates that the kinetic and fluid results are in agreement for the momentum flux, showing that in certain regimes, a multi-fluid model can be a useful approximation for simulating the plasma boundary. There are differences in the electrostatic potential between the fluid and kinetic results. Furthermore, the direct solutions of the distribution function presented here highlight the non-Maxwellian distribution of electrons in the sheath, emphasizing the need for a kinetic model.

title: Security Testbed for the Internet of Things

This paper proposes an innovative security testbed framework targeted at IoT devices. The security testbed supports both standard and context-based security testing, with a set of security tests conducted under the different environmental conditions in which IoT devices operate. The requirements and architectural design of the proposed testbed are discussed, and the testbed operation is demonstrated in several testing scenarios. |||

title: Asynchronous Distributed Execution Of Fixpoint-Based Computational Fields
Abstract: Coordination is crucial for dynamic distributed systems with interacting, autonomous components. Computational fields, which are spatially distributed and locally interacting, offer a promising solution for enabling seamless component entry and exit with minimal overhead. These fields are fundamental to aggregate programming, a software engineering methodology particularly relevant for the Internet of Things. Our approach uses a fixed graph-shaped field to represent the space topology, with attributes assigned to both nodes and arcs. The arcs represent interaction capabilities between nodes. We introduce the SMuC calculus, where modal formulas, resembling mu-calculus, define how values stored in neighboring nodes are combined to update the current node. Fixpoint operations can be interpreted globally as recursive definitions or locally as asynchronous converging propagation processes. We present a distributed implementation of this calculus, achieved through mapping SMuC programs into a normal form, purely iterative programs, and finally into distributed programs. Key results demonstrate the convergence of fixpoint computations under fair asynchrony and reinitialization of nodes. The first result allows for varying processing speeds among nodes, while the second ensures robustness against certain failures. We showcase our approach with a case study involving a disaster recovery scenario, implemented using a prototype simulator to evaluate the performance of the recovery strategy.

These methods are easy to implement and have broad applicability, making them valuable to the sports community. We demonstrate their use in analyzing both NBA and NHL metrics, highlighting the most reliable metrics and providing insights into their effective application. Furthermore, these meta-metrics offer guidance for constructing new metrics that provide independent and reliable information about athletes.

title: Conservation of Charge and Conservation of Current
Abstract: Conservation of current and conservation of charge are closely related concepts, with conservation of current derived from conservation of charge when sufficient knowledge of charge movement is available, as in ideal dielectrics. Conservation of current is implicitly enforced in ideal dielectrics by theories that conserve charge. However, charge movement in real materials, such as semiconductors or ionic solutions, deviates from ideal behavior. We present a seemingly universal derivation of conservation of current and advocate for its explicit inclusion as a distinct part of theories and calculations involving charge movement in complex fluids and environments. Classical models using ordinary differential equations, including those based on the law of mass action and Markov models, rarely satisfy conservation of current. These models require modifications to ensure current conservation. Strict enforcement of this principle is likely to enhance numerical analysis by preventing the artificial accumulation of charge.

title: SWoTSuite: A Development Framework for Prototyping Cross-domain Semantic Web of Things Applications

It minimizes the need for direct interaction with semantic web technologies, reducing the burden of designing SWoT applications that involve ontology design, sensor data annotation, and reasoning mechanisms for data enrichment. Inspired by sharing and reuse approaches, SWoTSuite leverages existing technologies and reuses data and vocabularies. title: Cognitive Random Access for Internet-of-Things Networks
Abstract: This paper focuses on cognitive radio (CR) Internet-of-Things (IoT) networks where spectrum sensors are deployed for IoT CR devices. These devices lack the hardware capability to identify unoccupied spectrum independently. In this sensor-enabled IoT CR network, CR devices and sensors are spatially separated, leading to potential discrepancies in spectrum occupancy measurements between their respective locations. To address this difference, we investigate a conditional interference distribution (CID) at the CR device for a given measured interference at the sensor. This CID reveals a spatial correlation in the aggregate interference distribution. Based on the CID, we develop a cognitive random access scheme that adaptively adjusts transmission probability based on the sensor's interference measurement. Our scheme demonstrates improved area spectral efficiency (ASE) compared to conventional ALOHA and an adaptive transmission scheme that sends data when the sensor measurement falls below a specific interference threshold.

title: Modeling generic aspects of ideal fibril formation
Abstract: Numerous proteins self-aggregate into insoluble fibrils that grow apically through the reversible addition of elementary building blocks. However, beyond this fundamental principle, the modalities of fibril formation exhibit considerable diversity, with various intermediate forms that can be rearranged by subtle changes in physico-chemical conditions or amino-acid sequences. To overcome this complexity, we simplify the multifaceted phenomenon of fibril formation to its most elementary principles, defined for a linear prototype of fibril. We model selected generic features, including nucleation, elongation, and conformational recruitment, using minimalist hypotheses and tools, separating equilibrium from kinetic aspects and in vitro from in vivo conditions. These reductionist approaches reveal both known and novel rudiments, including the kinetic and equilibrium effects of nucleation, the dual influence of elongation on nucleation, the kinetic limitations on nucleation and fibril numbers, and the accumulation of complexes in vivo due to rescue from degradation. We also highlight overlooked aspects of these processes: the exponential distribution of fibril lengths can be recovered using various models, as it is attributed solely to randomness. Additionally, we suggest that the term "critical concentration" is used inconsistently, referring to either nucleation or elongation.

title: Differentially-Private Counting of Users' Spatial Regions
Abstract: Spatial data mining is a crucial technology for mobile services, Internet-connected cars, and the Internet of Things. However, the very characteristics of spatial data that drive its utility can compromise user privacy. Previous research has focused on differentially-private release of points and trajectories. This work extends the tradition of privacy-preserving spatial analytics, focusing not on point or path data, but on planar spatial regions, representing a user's most frequent visitation areas, such as "around home and nearby shops." Specifically, we consider the differentially-private release of data structures that support range queries for counting users' spatial regions. Counting planar regions presents unique challenges not encountered in existing work. A user's spatial region spanning multiple data structure cells can lead to duplicate counting during query time. We avoid this pitfall by leveraging the Euler characteristic for the first time with differential privacy. To address the increased sensitivity of range queries to spatial region data, we calibrate privacy-preserving noise using bounded user region size and a constrained inference method that employs robust least absolute deviations. Our novel constrained inference reduces noise and promotes covertness by privately imposing consistency. We provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis of both differential privacy and high-probability utility for our approach using concentration bounds. A thorough experimental study on several real-world datasets establishes practical validity.

title: Testing MOG, Non-Local Gravity and MOND with rotation curves of dwarf galaxies
Abstract: Modified Gravity (MOG) and Non-Local Gravity (NLG) are alternative theories to General Relativity. They offer an explanation for the rotation curves of spiral galaxies and clusters of galaxies without invoking dark matter. In the weak-field approximation, these two theories exhibit similar forms, with an effective gravitational potential comprising two components: (i) Newtonian gravity with a gravitational constant enhanced by a factor $(1+\\alpha)$ and (ii) a Yukawa type potential that generates a repulsive force with length scale $1/\\mu$. This work compares the rotation curves of dwarf galaxies in the LITTLE THINGS catalog with predictions from MOG, NLG, and Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND). We find that the universal parameters of these theories can fit the rotation curves of dwarf galaxies with a higher stellar mass to light ratio compared to nearby stars in the Milky Way galaxy. Future direct observations of the mass function of stars in dwarf galaxies can be used to further examine different modified gravity models.

title: Axiomatization and complexity of modal logic with knowing-what operator on model class K
Abstract: Standard epistemic logic focuses on propositional knowledge; however, other knowledge types, such as "knowing whether," "knowing what," and "knowing how," are frequently and widely used in everyday life and academic fields. title: Idology and Its Applications in Public Security and Network Security

The model is used to characterize the capacity of cellular networks to accommodate IoT traffic and to evaluate and compare three different transmission strategies that incorporate transmission persistency, backoff, and power-ramping. title: A Multi-Service Oriented Multiple-Access Scheme For M2M Support in Future LTE
Abstract: A novel multiple-access technique, Multi-service Oriented Multiple Access (MOMA), is proposed to address the limitations of current Long-Term Evolution (LTE) proposals. MOMA offers a unified radio access system that seamlessly integrates traditional cellular services and Machine-to-Machine (M2M) connections arising from Internet-of-Things (IoT) applications. By establishing distinct user classes based on relevant criteria, implementing service-dependent hierarchical spreading of data signals, and employing a mix of multi-user and single-user detection schemes, MOMA efficiently handles densely connected devices with diverse quality-of-service (QoS) profiles. This approach optimizes the allocation of receiver computational resources to the most demanding connections, leading to scalable and efficient use of radio resources. Notably, MOMA integrates into LTE with minimal impact on protocol structure and signaling overhead, offering significant advantages for future communication scenarios.

title: cesium: Open-Source Platform for Time-Series Inference
Abstract: cesium is a comprehensive time series analysis framework designed to facilitate robust and reproducible inference workflows for researchers. This Python-based framework, with a user-friendly web front-end interface, empowers researchers to featurize raw data and apply modern machine learning techniques in a straightforward and extensible manner.  Users can leverage pre-built feature engineering workflows or customize their own analyses, with the flexibility to save and replay their work.  Furthermore, all front-end actions can be exported to Jupyter notebooks, enabling iterative model exploration and fine-tuning using the back-end library's extensive capabilities.  cesium leverages popular Python toolkits, including xarray, dask, Celery, Flask, and scikit-learn, providing a powerful and versatile platform for time series analysis.

title: Global bifurcation analysis of mean field equations and the Onsager microcanonical description of two-dimensional turbulence
Abstract: This research delves into the global behavior of the Entropy for the mean field Microcanonical Variational Principle (MVP) on strictly starshaped domains of the second kind, providing solutions to long-standing open problems related to the mean field equation.  The study extends existing results by establishing a full unbounded interval of strict convexity for the Entropy, confirming observations made in Caglioti et al. Comm.Math.Phys. (1995).  To achieve this, the research provides a detailed qualitative description of the global branch of solutions emanating from  $\\lm=0$ and crossing  $\\lm=8\\pi$, complementing findings from Suzuki A.I.H.P. (1992) and Chang et al. New Stud. Adv. Math. (2003) for  $\\lm\\leq 8\\pi$.  This analysis has independent mathematical significance as it provides a deeper understanding of global branches in semilinear elliptic equations, which are generally poorly understood.  The MVP suggests the energy as the appropriate variable for achieving a global parametrization of solutions, leading to a crucial spectral simplification by leveraging the fact that solutions maximize entropy at fixed energy and total vorticity.

title: Privacy of the Internet of Things: A Systematic Literature Review (Extended Discussion)
Abstract: This paper presents a systematic literature review examining privacy-preserving solutions proposed in research and media for addressing the Internet of Things' potential for privacy invasion. The analysis assesses the effectiveness of these solutions based on the techniques employed and their adherence to core privacy principles.  The review reveals that few solutions satisfy all core privacy principles.  It also identifies key knowledge gaps, particularly the assumption that end users are willing to invest effort in preserving their privacy.  The validity of this assumption requires further investigation, as it cannot be taken for granted that individuals will readily engage with privacy-preserving solutions.  The paper suggests this topic as a promising area for future research.

title: CONDENSE: A Reconfigurable Knowledge Acquisition Architecture for Future 5G IoT
Abstract: The paper introduces Condense, a novel architecture designed to address the data volume challenge posed by the Internet of Things (IoT) to existing communication infrastructures.  Condense integrates the IoT-communication infrastructure into data analysis by leveraging the concept of network function computation.  Instead of simply transferring data from IoT sources to the cloud, the communication infrastructure actively participates in the analysis through carefully designed en-route processing.  The paper defines the architecture, its layers, and the interactions between its modules.  From an implementation perspective, it outlines how Condense can be integrated into the 3GPP Machine Type Communications (MTC) architecture, exploring its feasibility through Network Function Virtualization (NFV) and Software Defined Networking (SDN).  Theoretically, the paper surveys relevant literature on computing "atomic" functions in both analog and digital domains, as well as on function decomposition over networks, highlighting challenges, insights, and future directions for exploiting these techniques within practical 3GPP MTC architecture.

title: Valorising the IoT Databox: Creating Value for Everyone

The paper examines the research challenges associated with building these Databoxes, considering aspects like data privacy, security, and interoperability.  The emergence of personal Databoxes is anticipated to play a significant role in the data-driven digital economy, offering opportunities for data monetization while respecting individual privacy.

title: Pointwise convergence of solution to Schrodinger equation on manifolds
Abstract: The paper investigates the regularity conditions necessary for pointwise convergence of solutions to the free Schrödinger equation on Riemannian manifolds without boundary.  Specifically, it examines the impact of initial data belonging to the Sobolev space $H^\\alpha(M)$ on the convergence behavior.  For Hyperbolic Space, standard Sphere, and the 2-dimensional Torus, the study shows that $\\alpha>\\frac{1}{2}$ is sufficient for pointwise convergence.  However, due to the lack of local smoothing effects on general compact manifolds, it proves challenging to improve upon the bound  $\\alpha>1$ obtained through interpolation.  The research manages to achieve a lower bound of  $\\alpha>1$ for dimensions  $\\leq 3$.  Furthermore, for 1-dimensional compact manifolds, it demonstrates that $\\alpha>\\frac{1}{3}$ is sufficient.  These findings provide valuable insights into the relationship between initial regularity and pointwise convergence of solutions to the free Schrödinger equation.

title: Joint Optimization of Energy Efficiency and Data Compression in TDMA-Based Medium Access Control for the IoT - Extended Version

This innovative approach optimizes resource utilization and enhances the energy efficiency of IoT deployments.

title: I(FIB)F: Iterated Bloom Filters for Routing in Named Data Networks
Abstract: This research explores the potential of Named Data Networks (NDN) for efficient content distribution in the context of the Internet of Things (IoT).  The paper acknowledges the limitations of constrained IoT devices, which often have limited resources, and addresses the need for optimization in NDN design to accommodate IoT scenarios.  It introduces I(FIB)F, a novel routing strategy that leverages Iterated Bloom Filters to construct a Forwarding Information Base (FIB).  This strategy, employing content names based on iterative hashes, reduces packet overhead, memory requirements, and computational complexity compared to existing solutions.  The paper compares I(FIB)F with hierarchical name-based solutions and Standard Bloom Filters, demonstrating its efficiency.  It further explores optimizations for I(FIB)F, exploiting the structure of hierarchical content names to minimize memory consumption or reduce the probability of false positives.

title: Large-Scale Multi-Antenna Multi-Sine Wireless Power Transfer
Abstract: This paper addresses the design of efficient multiuser algorithms for wireless power transfer (WPT), a technology poised to reshape the landscape of low-power applications like the Internet of Things and Radio Frequency identification (RFID) networks.  The research focuses on the challenge of large-scale WPT design, akin to massive MIMO in communications.  The paper derives multiuser algorithms based on a generalizable optimization framework that maximizes the weighted-sum/minimum rectenna output DC voltage by optimizing transmit sinewaves.  The analysis highlights the impact of nonlinearity introduced by the rectification process on waveform design in multiuser systems.  Interestingly, in the single-user case, the optimal spatial domain beamforming prior to frequency domain power allocation optimization turns out to be Maximum Ratio Transmission (MRT).  However, in the general weighted-sum criterion maximization problem, the spatial domain beamforming optimization and the frequency domain power allocation optimization are interconnected.  Assuming channel hardening, the paper proposes low-complexity algorithms based on asymptotic analysis to maximize the two criteria.  The structure of the asymptotically optimal spatial domain precoder can be identified before the optimization.  Numerical evaluations confirm the inefficiency of linear model-based designs for both single and multi-user scenarios, showcasing the benefits of the proposed nonlinear model-based algorithms in handling increasing numbers of sinewaves.

title: A Model for Partial Kantian Cooperation
Abstract: This paper introduces a game theoretic model aimed at capturing game situations where players' behavior is influenced by ethical considerations, particularly by Kant's "Categorical Imperative."  The model, designed for games with a continuum of players, assumes that participants perceive themselves as belonging to virtual groups where they optimize their actions as if bound by the same strategy.  The paper introduces the concept of an $r$-Kant-Nash equilibrium, representing a partially cooperative equilibrium.  The relationship between the $r$-Kant-Nash equilibrium and other solution concepts, including Nash, (Bentham-) Harsanyi, Rawls difference, and Roemer solutions, is explored.  For cases with a finite set of player types, the paper establishes sufficient conditions for the existence and uniqueness of the $r$-Kant-Nash equilibrium, characterizing it in terms of a variational inequality.  For continuous player types, the paper derives necessary conditions characterizing the partial Kantian equilibria using a reduction to a set of optimal control problems.  Finally, the paper provides illustrative numerical examples.

title: An IoT application development using IoTSuite

These applications have been tested across a range of IoT technologies, including Android, Raspberry PI, Arduino, and JavaSE-enabled devices, utilizing messaging protocols like MQTT, CoAP, WebSocket, server technologies such as Node.js, relational databases like MySQL, and Microsoft Azure Cloud services.

title: Boosting Wigner's nj-symbols
Abstract: This paper delves into the SL(2,C) Clebsch-Gordan coefficients that appear in the Lorentzian EPRL spin foam amplitudes within loop quantum gravity.  The paper demonstrates how these amplitudes decompose into SU(2) nj-symbols at the vertices and integrals over boosts at the edges.  These integrals define edge amplitudes that can be evaluated analytically by adapting existing results from the literature, leading to a pure state sum model formulation.  This procedure introduces virtual representations, analogous to virtual momenta in Feynman amplitudes, which are off-shell of the simplicity constraints in the theory but with integrands peaking at on-shell values.  The paper highlights key properties of the edge amplitudes that facilitate numerical and analytical evaluations of spin foam amplitudes.  It also proposes a simpler model useful for calculating certain low-order amplitudes.  As an application, the paper estimates the large spin scaling behavior of the simpler model on a closed foam with all 4-valent edges and Euler characteristic X, finding it to be  N^(X - 5E +\nV/2).  The paper includes a review and extension of results on SL(2,C) Clebsch-Gordan coefficients among unitary representations of the principal series, with applications extending beyond quantum gravity.

title: New Moduli for Banach Spaces
Abstract: This paper introduces novel moduli for Banach spaces, inspired by the moduli of supporting convexity and supporting smoothness.  These new moduli are defined as lengths of catheti in right-angled triangles constructed through a concept called quasi-orthogonality.  These triangles have two boundary points of the unit ball of a Banach space as endpoints of their hypotenuse, with the third vertex located on a supporting hyperplane of one of the other vertices.  The goal of this research is to quantify the local deviation of the unit sphere from its supporting hyperplanes using these triangles.  The paper proves corresponding Day-Nordlander type results involving generalizations of the modulus of convexity and the modulus of Bana\\'{s}.

title: Composable Models for Online Bayesian Analysis of Streaming Data
Abstract: The rapid growth in data volume and velocity, fueled in part by the Internet of Things (IoT), presents significant challenges for data storage and analysis.  This paper addresses the need for online data analysis to mitigate these challenges.  The paper focuses on modeling data streams generated by IoT devices with irregular sampling frequencies, interruptions, and event-based data generation.  Traditional state space modeling tools assume data on a fixed regular time grid, making them unsuitable for such scenarios.  The paper proposes modeling the system as a partially and irregularly observed Markov process evolving in continuous time, accommodating both non-linear process and observation models.  Particle filters are presented as the simplest approach to online analysis in this context.  The paper describes the development of a functional Scala library of composable continuous time Markov process models, designed to handle the diverse data captured by IoT devices.

title: On the nature of bright compact radio sources at z>4.5
Abstract: High-redshift radio-loud quasars serve as valuable tools for testing cosmological predictions, constraining black hole growth in the early universe, and understanding galaxy evolution.  This paper reports on observations of ten additional z>4.5 radio sources at 1.7 and 5 GHz using the European VLBI Network (EVN), significantly expanding the number of imaged sources at these redshifts.  Combining these new observations with existing data from the literature, the paper creates a substantial sample of 30 z>4.5 VLBI sources, enabling a detailed study of their nature.  Analyzing spectral indices, variability, and brightness temperatures, the paper concludes that of the 27 sources with sufficient information, one exhibits radio emission from star formation, 13 are flat-spectrum radio quasars, and 13 are steep-spectrum sources.  The paper argues that the steep-spectrum sources are off-axis (unbeamed) radio sources with rest-frame self-absorption peaks at or below GHz frequencies, classifying them as gigahertz peaked-spectrum (GPS) and megahertz peaked-spectrum (MPS) sources.  This research provides valuable insights into the characteristics and evolution of high-redshift radio-loud quasars.

title: The solar chromosphere as induction disk and the inverse Joule-Thomson effect
Abstract: The paper investigates the complex connection between nuclear fusion in the Sun's core and solar irradiance, highlighting the uncertainty surrounding coronal heating as a key factor.  Data analysis of solar wind density and velocity, sunspot number, and EUV flux suggests that electromagnetic energy from the Sun's convection zone is converted into thermal energy through induction in the chromosphere.  The helium and hydrogen mixture released by the Sun is then heated by the inverse Joule-Thomson effect as it expands through the corona into space.  The near-complete shutdown of the solar wind on 10-11 May 1999 demonstrates that solar wind velocity is a more reliable indicator of solar activity than sunspots, as it reflects short-term variations in coronal heating rather than cyclical fluctuations in the Sun's magnetism.  The paper suggests that reconstructing solar wind velocity from cosmic ray flux using isotopes spanning 800,000 years will benefit the analysis and long-term forecasting of Earth and space weather.

title: Simultaneous Information and Energy Flow for IoT Relay Systems with Crowd Harvesting

The paper examines time-switching and power-splitting operation modes, as well as associated optimization algorithms.  It explores the potential of crowd energy harvesting from transmission nodes belonging to multiple radio networks, highlighting how combining source and crowd energy harvesting can significantly reduce battery power reliance and enhance the reliability of relaying.  The paper provides insights into the fundamental limits of crowd energy harvesting reliability based on real city data analysis.  Furthermore, it examines the optimization of transmissions in crowd harvesting, particularly through node collaboration while ensuring Quality-of-Service (QoS).

title: Relationalism about mechanics based on a minimalist ontology of matter
Abstract:
This paper explores relationalism in space and time, arguing that it is best supported by a minimalist ontology of the physical world. This ontology posits that only matter points exist, and these are individuated by the distance relations between them, which change over time. The paper examines two strategies for reconciling this ontology with physics, using classical mechanics as an example: the Humean strategy and the alternative theory strategy. The Humean strategy accepts standard, non-relationalist physical theories, reinterpreting their formal apparatus as bookkeeping for changing distance relations rather than requiring additional ontological elements. The alternative theory strategy seeks a relationalist physical theory that reproduces the predictions of standard theories in empirically tested domains. The paper concludes that, at present, the alternative theory strategy cannot be realized without compromising a minimalist relationalist ontology. ||| 
The Internet of Things (IoT) is expected to involve billions of low-complexity devices connected wirelessly. This presents challenges for wireless information transfer (WIT) and energy transfer (WET) in IoT, due to high device density, ad-hoc communication, and the difficulty of replacing batteries in such a massive number of devices. This paper proposes a novel approach to address these challenges through full-duplex backscatter communication (BackCom) networks. BackCom networks leverage full-duplex WIT to reduce latency and improve spectrum utilization while also utilizing passive IoT devices with backscatter antennas to facilitate WET. To mitigate the intensified interference caused by increased simultaneous links, the paper proposes a time-hopping spread-spectrum (TH-SS) based multiple-access scheme that enables both one-way WET and two-way WIT in coexisting backscatter reader-tag links. Comprehensive performance analysis of BackCom networks is provided, including forward/backward bit-error rates, WET efficiency, and outage probabilities. The analysis accounts for energy harvesting at tags, non-coherent and coherent detection at tags and readers, and the effects of asynchronous transmissions. ||| 
Urban growth analysis typically involves two processes: describing the size and shape of cities and understanding the principles governing their growth. Shape indexes are commonly used to describe urban form, but their comparability is often affected by the resolution of remote sensing images or digital maps, as calculated values depend on spatial measurement scales. This paper investigates the scaling properties of classical shape indexes using mathematical methods. The analysis utilizes two regular fractals, Koch's island and Vicsek's figure, to illustrate the scale dependence of shape indexes. The paper derives formulas from the geometric measure relation to associate fractal dimension for boundary lines with shape indexes. Drawing on insights from fractals, the study addresses two key problems: normalizing and unifying different shape indexes by substituting Feret's diameter for the major axis of urban figures, and identifying three levels of scaling in shape indexes, classifying them into three groups. The study's significance lies in its contribution to understanding the underlying structure of urban form and clarifying the appropriate spheres of application for different types of shape indexes. ||| 
This paper examines the influence of stellar feedback on the density and velocity structure of neutral hydrogen (HI) in disc galaxies. Using N-body+adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) hydrodynamic simulations with ~4.6 pc resolution, the study models isolated galaxies resembling the Milky Way, Large Magellanic Cloud, and Small Magellanic Cloud. The density and velocity structure of the interstellar medium is quantified using power spectra, and the simulations are compared to observed HI data from the THINGS survey. The results show that models incorporating stellar feedback accurately reproduce the observed HI density power spectra in THINGS. The simulations reveal that kinetic energy power spectra in feedback-regulated galaxies, regardless of galaxy mass or size, exhibit scalings consistent with supersonic turbulence on scales below the HI layer thickness. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that feedback impacts the gas density field and drives turbulence up to large (kpc) scales, in contrast to density fields generated by large-scale gravity-driven turbulence. The paper concludes that the neutral gas content of galaxies bears the imprint of stellar feedback across all scales. ||| 
Quantum-statistical effects manifest during the propagation of electromagnetic (EM) waves through dielectric media or metamaterials, including nanophotonic and plasmonic waveguides with dissipation and noise. This paper rigorously derives the effective Hamiltonian operator that describes EM wave propagation, exploiting the formal analogy between the Schrödinger equation and the Maxwell equations for dielectric linear media. The derived Hamiltonian is generally non-Hermitian, becoming pseudo-Hermitian in specific cases. Employing the density operator approach for general non-Hermitian Hamiltonians, the paper derives a master equation describing the statistical ensembles of EM wave modes. This method further characterizes the quantum dissipative and decoherence processes occurring during wave propagation, revealing the conditions necessary to control energy and information loss in the aforementioned materials. ||| 
Internet of Things (IoT) endpoint devices require extremely low power consumption, typically in the milliwatt range, alongside flexible computing capabilities spanning from a few kOPS to GOPS. Near-threshold (NT) operation can achieve higher energy efficiency, while parallelism enables performance scalability. This paper presents the design of an open-source RISC-V processor core optimized for NT operation within tightly coupled multi-core clusters. The core incorporates instruction extensions and microarchitectural optimizations to enhance computational density and minimize pressure on the shared memory hierarchy. For data-intensive sensor processing workloads, the proposed core achieves on average 3.5x faster execution and 3.2x higher energy efficiency compared to conventional designs. These improvements are attributed to a smart L0 buffer that reduces cache access contentions and supports compressed instructions. SIMD extensions like dot-products and built-in L0 storage further reduce shared memory accesses, decreasing contention by 3.2x. A cluster of four NT-optimized cores operates from 0.6V to 1.2V, reaching a peak efficiency of 67 MOPS/mW in a low-cost 65nm bulk CMOS technology. In a low-power 28nm FDSOI process, a peak efficiency of 193 MOPS/mW (40MHz, 1mW) is achievable. ||| 
Persistent Identifiers (PIDs) serve as the foundation for referencing digital assets in scientific publications, books, and digital repositories. PIDs contain metadata and resolving targets in the form of URLs that point to datasets located on the network. However, unlike PIDs, target URLs are dynamic, requiring continuous maintenance efforts. This paper presents a new approach for embedding location-independent targets into PIDs, enabling the creation of maintenance-free PIDs utilizing content-centric network technology and overlay networks. To demonstrate the validity of this approach, the Handle PID System is integrated with Magnet Link access information encoding, decentralized data distribution using BitTorrent, and Named Data Networking (NDN) for location-independent data access. This approach eliminates the need for green-field PID implementations or major modifications of the Handle System, facilitating location-independent data dissemination with maintenance-free PIDs. ||| 
Smart living envisions a lifestyle characterized by reduced energy consumption, effective public services, and improved quality of life. The Internet of Things (IoT) provides a compelling platform for realizing smart living by connecting various sensors to the internet. Spintronic sensors, with their superior measuring ability and unique advantages, hold significant potential as a cornerstone for IoT. This review examines successful applications of spintronic sensors in areas such as electrical current sensing, transmission and distribution lines monitoring, vehicle detection, and biodetection. Traditional monitoring systems with limited sensors and wired communication often provide fragmented data. The paper proposes and illustrates wireless spintronic sensor networks (WSSNs) as a means of establishing pervasive monitoring systems for intelligent surveillance and management of buildings, power grids, transportation, and healthcare. The collected data can be invaluable for policy making in public services and city planning. This work sheds light on realizing smart living through the integration of IoT with spintronic sensor technology. ||| 
Determining provenance in the age of Big Data presents a significant research challenge. Granular evaluation of provenance for physical goods, such as tracking ingredients in pharmaceuticals or demonstrating authenticity in luxury goods, has often been elusive due to complex, inter-organizational supply chains that span international borders. The advent of Internet of Things (IoT) and Blockchain technologies offers promising solutions for enhancing supply chain provenance. This paper focuses on the potential of blockchain, a technology widely favored for provenance tracking applications, to contribute to enhanced supply chain provenance. It also explores the role of ontologies, as previous work has demonstrated their usefulness in knowledge provenance, traceability, and food provenance. The paper argues for the integration of ontologies into blockchain design, supported by an analysis of a traceability ontology and its translation into smart contracts that execute a provenance trace and enforce traceability constraints on the Ethereum blockchain platform. ||| 
The Internet of Things (IoT) has gained significant global attention, transforming everyday objects into proactive actors on the internet, generating and consuming information. A crucial aspect of large-scale self-coordinating IoT is ensuring reliability and collaboration among objects in the presence of environmental hazards. High failure rates can lead to substantial data loss, making data survivability a major challenge in IoT. This paper presents a compartmental e-Epidemic SIR (Susceptible-Infectious-Recovered) model to address data survivability in IoT networks. The model incorporates the dynamic topology of the network, considering natural death (crashing nodes) and birth. Theoretical methods and simulations are employed to solve and simulate the system of equations developed and to analyze the model's behavior. ||| 
The rapid growth of mobile IP, coupled with the emergence of the Internet of Things (IoT) and cloud-based applications, is driving a paradigm shift in wireless networking. Massive multiple-input-multiple-output (MIMO) technology, leveraging spatial degrees of freedom, promises significant gains in data rates and link reliability. This paper presents a time-division duplex (TDD)-based 128-antenna massive MIMO prototyping system designed to operate on a 20 MHz bandwidth. The system can serve up to twelve single-antenna users simultaneously. The paper provides a system model and conducts link-level simulations corresponding to the practical TDD-based massive MIMO prototyping system, validating the design and performance of the algorithms. Based on the demonstrated hardware design, both uplink real-time video and downlink data transmissions are realized. Experimental results show that a rate of 268.8 Mbps is achieved for eight single-antenna users using QPSK modulation. The designed system's maximum spectral efficiency is 80.64 bit/s/Hz with twelve single-antenna users utilizing 256-QAM modulation. ||| 
Energy transparency is a concept that makes a program's energy consumption visible across different system layers, from hardware to software. This transparency enables energy optimizations at each layer and between layers, facilitating energy-aware decisions by programmers and operating systems. This paper focuses on deeply embedded devices commonly used in Internet of Things (IoT) applications and demonstrates how to achieve energy transparency using existing Static Resource Analysis (SRA) techniques and a novel target-agnostic profiling technique, without relying on hardware energy measurements. The paper introduces a novel mapping technique for software energy consumption estimation at a level higher than the Instruction Set Architecture (ISA), namely the LLVM Intermediate Representation (IR) level. This introduces energy transparency directly to the LLVM optimizer. The paper applies the energy estimation techniques to a comprehensive set of benchmarks, including single- and multi-threaded embedded programs from two commonly used concurrency patterns: task farms and pipelines. Using SRA, the LLVM IR results demonstrate high accuracy with a deviation within 1% of the ISA SRA. The profiling technique captures actual energy consumption at the LLVM IR level with an average error of 3%. ||| 
Achieving accurate and precise measurements of CP asymmetries in the decays of beauty and charm hadrons requires meticulous attention to detail and a comprehensive understanding of various factors. This paper highlights key considerations: consistent parametrization of the CKM matrix, limitations in probing multi-body final states, the role of broken U-spin symmetry in spectroscopy and weak transitions, and the distinction between penguin operators and penguin diagrams. This paper utilizes the potential-density phase shift approach, developed by the authors in previous work, to estimate the magnitude of radial mass accretion/excretion rates across the disks of six nearby spiral galaxies with varying Hubble types. The goal is to examine these rates in the context of bulge building and secular morphological evolution along the Hubble sequence. Stellar surface density maps are derived from SINGS 3.6um and SDSS i-band images, while corresponding molecular and atomic gas surface densities are obtained from published CO(1-0) and HI interferometric observations. Mass flow rate calculations use a volume-type torque integral to determine the angular momentum exchange rate between the basic state disk matter and density wave modes. The potential-density phase shift approach yields angular momentum transport rates significantly higher than those estimated using the Lynden-Bell and Kalnajs (1972) approach. The current approach predicts substantial mass redistribution induced by quasi-steady density wave modes, sufficient for morphological evolution of disk types over their lifetime. The difference from earlier conclusions reflects the dominant role of collisionless shocks in secular evolution, enabling significant morphological transformation along the Hubble sequence within a Hubble time. The study demonstrates, using observational data, that stellar mass accretion/excretion is equally important, and often more significant, than corresponding processes in the gaseous component, contradicting previous secular evolution studies that primarily focused on the latter. ||| 
This paper addresses a question raised by Daws concerning the Arens regularity of B(X), the algebra of operators on a Banach space X. Among other findings, the paper proves that B(X) is Arens regular if and only if X is ultrareflexive. ||| 
Hash functions are cryptographic tools essential for integrity checking and password storage, playing a crucial role in enhancing security of internet exchanges. However, recent security flaws identified in current hashing standards necessitate the exploration of new approaches. This paper evaluates an original keyed hash function based on asynchronous iterations that have been proven chaotic. This function possesses various topological properties, including uniformity and sensitivity to initial conditions, which contribute to its strong security properties. Diffuse Focal Axonal Swellings (FAS) are a hallmark cellular feature in numerous neurodegenerative diseases and traumatic brain injuries. FAS significantly impact spike-train encodings propagating through affected neurons, leading to compromised signal processing on a neuronal network level. This paper, for the first time, integrates three fields of study: signal processing in excitatory-inhibitory (EI) neuronal networks via population codes, decision-making theory driven by evidence production, and compromised spike-train propagation through FAS. The study presents a mathematical framework for characterizing compromised decision-making based on cellular mechanisms. This computational model leads to novel predictions and diagnostics for understanding injury level and cognitive deficits, revealing that decision-making reaction times, rather than accuracy, are indicative of network-level damage. These findings hold translational implications, suggesting that the level of network damage can be characterized through simple cognitive and motor tests. ||| 
This paper highlights the remarkable distances achievable using millimeter wave communications and introduces a new rural macrocell (RMa) path loss model for millimeter wave frequencies, based on measurements at 73 GHz in rural Virginia. Path loss models are crucial for estimating signal coverage and interference in wireless network design, but little is known about rural propagation at millimeter waves. The paper identifies problems with the RMa model used by the 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) TR 38.900 Release 14 and proposes a close-in (CI) reference distance model that offers improved accuracy, fewer parameters, and better stability compared to the existing 3GPP RMa model. This paper investigates circular motion in the NUT (Newman-Unti-Tamburino) spacetime, focusing on the determination of circular time-like geodesic orbits, particularly the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO) and marginally bound circular orbit. title: Blockchain in internet of things: Challenges and Solutions

title: Behaviour of linear multifractional stable motion: membership of a critical Hölder space

title: What Information Really Matters in Supervisor Reduction?

This allows users or control designers to easily verify whether a designed controller meets its objectives and requirements. title: Chebyshev centers that are not farthest points

title: An assessment of orthographic similarity measures for several African languages

title: Turbulence and Star Formation in a Sample of Spiral Galaxies

Individual grid maps of kurtosis are created for each galaxy. To investigate the relationship between these moments and star formation, the maps are compared with far-ultraviolet images obtained by the Galaxy Evolution Explorer (GALEX) satellite. The study finds that the moments are largely uniform across the galaxies, with variations that do not appear to trace any star-forming regions. However, this may be due to the spatial resolution of the analysis, which could potentially limit the sensitivity to turbulent motions larger than ~700 pc. Comparing the moments themselves reveals that the gas motions in the sampled galaxies are largely supersonic. The analysis also suggests that Burkhart et al. (2010)'s methods can be applied not only to dwarf galaxies but also to normal spiral galaxies.

title: Maximum-Likelihood Detection for Energy-Efficient Timing Acquisition in NB-IoT

In contrast, a maximum likelihood cross-correlation detector achieves low latency at a higher complexity, as demonstrated in this paper. The paper presents a hardware implementation of the maximum likelihood cross-correlation detection. This detector achieves an average detection latency that is half that of an auto-correlation method and reduces the required energy per timing acquisition by up to 34%.

title: Decaying turbulence for the fractional subcritical Burgers equation

For solutions $u$ of this equation, the paper generalizes results obtained for the case $\\alpha=2$ (i.e., when $-\\Lambda^{\\alpha}$ is the Laplacian) in [10]. Sharp estimates are derived for the time-averaged Sobolev norms of $u$ as a function of $\\nu$. These results provide sharp estimates for natural analogues of quantities characterizing hydrodynamical turbulence, namely the averages of the increments and of the energy spectrum. In the inertial range, these quantities behave as a power of the norm of the relevant parameter, which is respectively the separation $\\ell$ in the physical space and the wavenumber $\\mathbf{k}$ in the Fourier space. title: Quantum Causal Graph Dynamics

title: Jamming in the Internet of Things: A Game-Theoretic Perspective

Furthermore, localized states along the barrier are observed in the presence of a single barrier. title: Serendipity and strategy in rapid innovation

title: A Survey about Prediction-Based Data Reduction in Wireless Sensor Networks
Abstract: A key characteristic of Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) is the limited energy resources of their sensor nodes. While energy harvesting and wireless charging techniques have addressed this issue, the increasing demand for spectrum resources due to the integration of WSNs into the Internet of Things presents a new challenge. To mitigate this challenge, data prediction techniques can be employed to reduce the amount of data transmission and alleviate congestion in the wireless medium. This paper analyzes and categorizes existing prediction-based data reduction mechanisms designed for WSNs. Our primary contribution is a systematic procedure for selecting a prediction scheme, considering the constraints of WSNs, characteristics of prediction methods, and the type of data being monitored. The paper concludes with a discussion of future challenges and open research directions in using prediction methods to support WSN growth.

title: Tractable Stochastic Geometry Model for IoT Access in LTE Networks
Abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) is inherently large-scale, characterized not only by the vast number of connected devices but also by the high volumes of traffic it generates. Cellular networks are a natural choice for handling the data tsunami expected from IoT, alongside existing human-type traffic. However, the random access process for scheduling requests poses a major bottleneck in supporting IoT via LTE cellular networks. This paper develops a mathematical framework to model and study the scalability of the random access channel (RACH) for accommodating IoT traffic. The model utilizes stochastic geometry and discrete time Markov chains (DTMC) to account for different access strategies and potential sources of inter-cell and intra-cell interference. We assess and compare three different access strategies incorporating transmission persistency, back-off, and power ramping. The analysis and results illustrate the vulnerability of the random access procedure as IoT intensity increases. Finally, we provide insights into effective scenarios for each transmission strategy in terms of IoT intensity and RACH detection thresholds.

title: Programming Internet of Things, Service, and People (IoTSP) Applications
Abstract: Application development for the Internet of Things, Service, and People (IoTSP) presents significant challenges due to the heterogeneity inherent in both the physical and internet worlds. Stakeholders involved in application development must address issues related to different life-cycles, encompassing design, implementation, and deployment. This paper addresses the critical challenge of enabling efficient and effective application development for IoTSP applications from various stakeholders. We build upon existing frameworks, developed in the fields of Wireless Sensor Networks (WSN) and Pervasive Computing, precursors to modern IoTSP. However, existing approaches fall short in addressing the full spectrum of challenges in the IoTSP context. Our proposed framework for developing IoTSP applications incorporates substantial additions and enhancements in high-level modeling languages and their integration. We present comparative evaluation results with existing approaches, providing a benchmark for the IoTSP community. The evaluation is conducted on real devices exhibiting heterogeneity, demonstrating a significant reduction in development effort for IoTSP applications compared to existing approaches.

title: Mobile Internet of Things: Can UAVs Provide an Energy-Efficient Mobile Architecture?
Abstract: This paper investigates the optimal trajectory and deployment of multiple unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) acting as aerial base stations to collect data from ground Internet of Things (IoT) devices. To ensure reliable uplink communications with minimal energy consumption, a new approach for optimizing UAV mobility is proposed. First, given a fixed ground IoT network, the total transmit power of the devices is minimized by clustering IoT devices based on proximity and assigning a UAV to each cluster. To maintain energy-efficient communications in dynamic mobile IoT networks, the optimal trajectories of the UAVs are determined using the framework of optimal transport theory. Simulation results indicate that the proposed approach reduces the total transmit power of IoT devices by 56% compared to the fixed Voronoi deployment method, enabling reliable uplink communications. Furthermore, the results yield optimal paths for UAVs to serve mobile IoT devices with minimum energy consumption.

title: Poisson stochastic process and basic Schauder and Sobolev estimates in the theory of parabolic equations

The method relies on the Poisson stochastic process and, to the best of our knowledge, there is no other available method at this time. Finding a purely analytic approach to proving such results remains a challenging problem.

title: A Jamming-Resilient MAC-layer Device Identification for Internet of Things
Abstract: In many practical scenarios, a wireless device needs to signal its presence to an access point, for example, to be assigned a transmission slot or update the network node count. While various protocols achieve this goal, this paper focuses on the simplest messaging model, the beeping model. We constrain our design to eliminate modulated information transmission and avoid the need for receiver demodulation/decoding. Our objective is to send a short "beep" signal, resilient to random interference, and capable of identifying devices sending the signal, rather than just detecting their presence. We achieve this by leveraging temporal correlations in a sequence of beeps emitted by a device, where the timing of beeps follows a predefined probability distribution, acting as the device's fingerprint. |||

title: A Knowledge-Based Resource Discovery for Internet of Things

Abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) is experiencing widespread adoption across various domains, from industrial to home applications. title: Analytics-as-a-Service in a Multi-Cloud Environment through Semantically enabled Hierarchical Data Processing

title: A Distributed Sensor Data Search Platform for Internet of Things Environments

title: Matroid Online Bipartite Matching and Vertex Cover
Abstract: The Adwords and Online Bipartite Matching problems have gained renewed attention due to their relevance to Internet advertising. The research community has contributed new models (notably stochastic) and extensions to address practical issues. This paper proposes a new generalization based on matroids, extending previous results to a broader setting. Matroids, with their rich structures and expressive power, hold potential for both theoretical and practical applications. The classical version of the problem involves an offline side of a bipartite graph known initially, while vertices from the online side arrive sequentially with their incident edges. The goal is to maintain an approximate matching from which no edge can be removed. The paper's generalization, called Matroid Online Bipartite Matching, adds the constraint that the set of matched offline vertices must be independent in a given matroid. The case of partition matroids corresponds to scenarios where each advertiser manages multiple ads with a fixed total budget. The algorithms achieve the same performance as in the classical version of the problems, often being provably optimal. The paper presents 1-1/e-competitive algorithms for Matroid Online Bipartite Matching under the small bid assumption, as well as a 1-1/e-competitive algorithm for the random arrival model. A key technical element is a primal-dual waterfilling procedure designed to accommodate matroid constraints, inspired by the extension of a recent charging scheme for Online Bipartite Vertex Cover.

title: Is the Bellman residual a bad proxy?
Abstract: This paper compares two standard optimization criteria in Reinforcement Learning: maximization of the mean value and minimization of the Bellman residual. The paper focuses on policy search algorithms, typically designed for mean value maximization, and derives a method to minimize the residual ||T_* v_\\pi - v_\\pi||_{1,\\nu} over policies. Theoretical analysis reveals the effectiveness of this proxy for policy optimization, demonstrating its superiority over its value-based counterpart. Experiments conducted on randomly generated generic Markov decision processes, specifically designed to assess the influence of the concentrability coefficient, show that the Bellman residual is generally a poor proxy for policy optimization. Direct maximization of the mean value proves significantly better, despite the lack of deep theoretical analysis. While this might seem intuitive, given the prevalence of (projected) Bellman residual minimization in value-based reinforcement learning, the paper emphasizes the importance of this consideration.

title: Benchmarking Distributed Stream Processing Platforms for IoT Applications

This paper develops a benchmark suite and performance metrics to evaluate DSPS for streaming IoT applications. The benchmark includes 13 common IoT tasks, categorized into functional micro-benchmarks, and two IoT applications for statistical summarization and predictive analytics, leveraging various dataflow compositional features of DSPS. These are coupled with stream workloads derived from real IoT observations from smart cities. The paper validates the IoT benchmark for the popular Apache Storm DSPS and presents empirical results.

title: Review on Physically Flexible Nonvolatile Memory for Internet of Everything Electronics
Abstract: Solid-state memory is a fundamental component of the digital age. Advancements in healthcare technology and the Internet of Things (IoT) have led to a growing demand for ultra-dense, ultra-low-power memory. This review provides a comprehensive overview of notable approaches to fabricating physically flexible memory devices. With the goal of replacing traditional mechanical hard disks with solid-state storage devices, a fully flexible electronic system requires two key components: transistors and nonvolatile memory. Transistors perform logic operations and gate memory arrays, while nonvolatile memory (NVM) devices are essential for storing information in main memory and cache storage. Due to the high density of transistors and storage structures in memories, this review focuses on flexible NVM. The paper discusses flexible NVM components in terms of functionality, performance metrics, and reliability aspects, crucial for mainstream consumer electronics, IoT, and advanced healthcare devices. Finally, flexible NVMs are benchmarked, and future prospects are explored.

title: Low Power Wide Area Networks: An Overview
Abstract: Low Power Wide Area (LPWA) networks are gaining significant attention due to their ability to provide affordable connectivity to low-power devices distributed over vast geographical areas. In realizing the vision of the Internet of Things (IoT), LPWA technologies complement and sometimes surpass conventional cellular and short-range wireless technologies in performance for emerging smart city and machine-to-machine (M2M) applications. This review paper examines the design goals and techniques employed by different LPWA technologies to achieve wide-area coverage for low-power devices at the expense of low data rates. The paper notes that LPWA technologies often share similar approaches, resulting in common limitations and challenges. It further explores these research challenges and identifies potential solutions. title: Incentivizing Evaluation via Limited Access to Ground Truth: Peer-Prediction Makes Things Worse
Abstract: In many settings, an effective approach to evaluating objects of interest involves collecting evaluations from dispersed individuals and aggregating these evaluations. Examples include categorizing online content and evaluating student assignments through peer grading. One challenge in this data science problem is motivating participants to conduct evaluations carefully and report honestly, particularly when doing so is costly. Existing approaches, notably peer-prediction mechanisms, can incentivize truth-telling in equilibrium. However, they also lead to equilibria where agents avoid the costs of accurate evaluation, failing to elicit useful information. This paper demonstrates that this problem is unavoidable when agents can coordinate using low-cost signals about the items being evaluated (e.g., text labels or pictures). The paper then explores ways to circumvent this problem by comparing agents' reports to ground truth, which is often available in practice when trusted evaluators (e.g., teaching assistants in peer grading) can perform a limited number of unbiased (but noisy) evaluations. While ground truth is available, a simpler approach is also possible: rewarding each agent based on agreement with ground truth with some probability, and unconditionally rewarding them otherwise. Surprisingly, the paper shows that this simpler mechanism achieves stronger incentive guarantees with less access to ground truth than a large set of peer-prediction mechanisms.

title: On Amalgamated Banach algebras
Abstract: Let A and B be Banach algebras,  theta: A->B be a continuous Banach algebra homomorphism, and I be a closed ideal in B. The direct sum of A and I with respect to theta, denoted A bowtie^theta I, equipped with a special product, forms a Banach algebra known as the amalgamated Banach algebra. This paper, among other findings, calculates the topological center of A bowtie^theta I in terms of the topological centers of A and I. This result is then used to characterize the Arens regularity of A bowtie^theta I. Additionally, the paper determines the character space of A bowtie^theta I in terms of the character spaces of A and I. Finally, the paper investigates the weak amenability of A bowtie^theta I.

title: A Delay Optimal MAC and Packet Scheduler for Heterogeneous M2M Uplink
Abstract: Uplink data arriving at the Machine-to-Machine (M2M) Application Server (AS) via M2M Aggregators (MAs) exhibits significant heterogeneity across dimensions such as maximum tolerable packet delay, payload size, and arrival rate. This necessitates the design of a Quality-of-Service (QoS) aware packet scheduler. This paper classifies M2M uplink data into multiple QoS classes and utilizes a sigmoidal function to map the delay requirements of each class onto utility functions. The paper proposes a proportionally fair delay-optimal multiclass packet scheduler at the AS that maximizes a system utility metric. The paper notes that the average class delay under any work-conserving scheduling policy can be achieved through appropriate time-sharing between all possible preemptive priority policies. Therefore, the optimal scheduler is determined iteratively to find the optimal time-sharing between all priority scheduling policies, maximizing system utility. The proposed scheduler can be implemented online with reduced complexity due to the iterative optimization process. The paper then extends this work to determine jointly optimal MA-AS channel allocation and packet scheduling schemes at the MAs and AS. A joint optimization problem is formulated and solved centrally at the AS. The paper then proposes a low-complexity distributed optimization problem solved independently at the MAs and AS. It demonstrates that the distributed optimization solution converges quickly to the centralized optimization result with minimal information exchange overhead. Using Monte-Carlo simulations, the paper verifies the optimality of the proposed scheduler and demonstrates its outperformance over other state-of-the-art packet schedulers like weighted round robin and max-weight scheduler. The proposed scheduler also offers low delay jitter for delay-sensitive traffic.

title: On lifting and modularity of reducible residual Galois representations over imaginary quadratic fields
Abstract: This paper investigates deformations of mod p Galois representations tau (over an imaginary quadratic field F) of dimension 2 whose semi-simplification is the direct sum of two characters tau_1 and tau_2. Unlike previous work, the paper does not impose restrictions on the dimension of the crystalline Selmer group H^1_{\\Sigma}(F, {\\rm Hom}(\\tau_2, \\tau_1)) \\subset {\\rm Ext}^1(\\tau_2, \\tau_1). The paper establishes the existence of a basis \\mathcal{B} of H^1_{\\Sigma}(F, {\\rm Hom}(\\tau_2, \\tau_1)) arising from automorphic representations over F (Theorem 8.1). Assuming, among other conditions, that the elements of \\mathcal{B} admit only finitely many crystalline characteristic 0 deformations, the paper proves a modularity lifting theorem stating that if tau itself is modular, then so are all of its crystalline characteristic zero deformations (Theorems 8.2 and 8.5).

title: Goldstone origin of black hole hair from supertranslations and criticality
Abstract: Degrees of freedom responsible for black hole entropy and hair can be described using the concept of the Goldstone phenomenon. They represent pseudo-Goldstone bosons of certain supertranslations, known as A-transformations, which are spontaneously broken by the black hole metric. This breaking gives rise to a tower of Goldstone bosons generated by the spontaneously broken generators, which can be labeled by spherical harmonics. Classically, the number of charges is infinite, they have vanishing vacuum expectation values (VEVs), and the corresponding Goldstone modes are gapless. Consequently, the resulting hair and entropy are infinite but unresolvable. In quantum theory, two significant changes occur. First, the number of legitimate Goldstone modes, restricted by the requirement of weak-coupling, becomes finite and scales as the black hole area in Planck units. Second, the Goldstones generate a tiny gap, controlled by their gravitational coupling. This gap turns out to be equal to the inverse of the black hole half-life, t_{BH}. Correspondingly, in quantum theory, the charges are neither conserved nor vanishing, but their non-conservation time is determined by t_{BH}. This picture aligns well with the idea of a black hole as a critical system composed of numerous soft gravitons. The A-Goldstones of the geometric picture represent the near-gapless Bogoliubov-Goldstone modes of the critical soft-graviton system.

title: Deformed Matter Bounce with Dark Energy Epoch
Abstract: This paper extends the Loop Quantum Cosmology matter bounce scenario to include a dark energy era, ending abruptly at a Rip singularity. The Rip singularity arises at the end of the dark energy era, but the system cannot reach this singularity due to the complex nature of the effective energy density and pressure. This suggests that the ordinary Loop Quantum Cosmology matter bounce evolution ceases, ending the infinite repetition of the scenario. Furthermore, the complex values of pressure and density indicate the need for a more fundamental theory of quantum gravity near the would-be Rip singularity. title: Approximate nonparametric maximum likelihood inference for mixture models via convex optimization
Abstract: Nonparametric maximum likelihood (NPML) for mixture models is a statistical technique for estimating mixing distributions. Recent advancements in approximate NPML methods have made them practical for various applications. This paper explores a class of flexible, scalable, and easy-to-implement approximate NPML methods for multivariate mixing distributions. It provides concrete guidance on implementing these methods, covering topics like identifying the support set of the mixing distribution and comparing algorithms across different metrics. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of these methods through three real-world data applications: baseball data analysis, high-dimensional microarray classification, and online blood-glucose density prediction. The empirical results highlight the advantages of using multivariate mixing distributions for NPML-based approaches.

title: iFogSim: A Toolkit for Modeling and Simulation of Resource Management Techniques in Internet of Things, Edge and Fog Computing Environments
Abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) aims to connect every object online, generating massive data volumes that can overwhelm storage systems and data analytics applications. To address this, the Fog computing paradigm extends cloud services to the edge of the network, reducing latency and congestion. This paper presents iFogSim, a simulator for modeling IoT and Fog environments to evaluate resource management techniques in terms of latency, network congestion, energy consumption, and cost. The paper demonstrates iFogSim's capabilities through two case studies, illustrating its use for comparing resource management policies and verifying the simulator's scalability.

title: Content-based Cognitive Interference Control for City Monitoring Applications in the Urban IoT
Abstract: In the Urban Internet of Things (IoT), interconnected devices and systems at the city scale deliver innovative services to citizens. However, the traffic generated by these systems can overload local access networks, leading to interference and resource competition among concurrent applications. This paper introduces the concept of content-oriented cognitive interference control in heterogeneous local access networks supporting urban IoT computing and data processing. The paper focuses on city monitoring applications, where video data streams are remotely processed for object detection. The cognitive network paradigm is extended to dynamically shape interference patterns generated by concurrent data streams, ensuring compatibility with video processing algorithms. Numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed cognitive transmission strategy in enhancing the throughput of interfering applications while maintaining target accuracy for the monitoring application.

title: Trustworthy and Secure Service-Oriented Architecture for the Internet of Things
Abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) connects heterogeneous devices, enabling data exchange and service provision. However, the high degree of heterogeneity presents a significant challenge in developing software applications that can operate across diverse devices and interact with a wider array of systems. This paper emphasizes the need for a common middleware infrastructure to address this challenge, allowing developers to focus on application logic rather than low-level implementation details.

title: Maturity of the Internet of Things Research Field: Or Why Choose Rigorous Keywords
Abstract: Researchers periodically conduct field examinations to assess maturity, identify prevalent theories and methods, and uncover areas of research emphasis. This paper proposes using metadata analysis to streamline this process, applying it to the Internet of Things (IoT) research field using data from three academic databases. The study reveals the immaturity of the IoT research field, with experimental methods dominating research outputs. However, challenges with keyword metadata, including synonyms, abbreviations, lack of accuracy, and omissions of methods and theories, are highlighted. The paper suggests a keyword schema to address these issues and facilitate future research.

title: From Mechatronic Components to Industrial Automation Things - An IoT model for cyber-physical manufacturing systems
Abstract:
The Internet of Things (IoT) is a pivotal enabling technology for Industry 4.0. This paper focuses on the mechatronic component, the lowest level in the system composition hierarchy, which integrates mechanics with electronics and software, transforming mechanical systems into intelligent (smart) objects that offer specific services to their environment. To integrate this mechatronic component into an IoT-based industrial automation environment, a software layer, called the IoTwrapper, is required. This layer converts the conventional interface of the mechatronic component into an IoT compliant one, creating an Industrial Automation Thing (IAT). The IAT is the key element of an IoT model developed specifically for the manufacturing domain. The model is compared to existing IoT models, highlighting its main differences. This paper presents a model-to-model transformer that automatically transforms legacy mechatronic components into IATs, ready for integration into the IoT-based industrial automation environment. The UML4IoT profile, utilized as a Domain Specific Modeling Language, automates this transformation. A prototype implementation of an Industrial Automation Thing, developed using C and the Contiki operating system, demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed approach. |||

Abstract: This paper provides a theoretical analysis of electrical conduction in molecular tunnel junctions, examining the validity of coherent and incoherent theoretical formulations for single-level tunneling. The analysis aims to explain experimental results obtained under various conditions, including measurements in individual molecules connecting the leads of electromigrated single-electron transistors and junctions of self-assembled monolayers (SAM) of molecules sandwiched between macroscopic contacts. The study demonstrates that the restriction of transport through a single level in solid-state junctions (no solvent) makes coherent and incoherent tunneling formalisms indistinguishable when only one level participates in transport. Similar to Marcus relaxation processes in wet electrochemistry, the thermal broadening of the Fermi distribution describing the electronic occupation energies in the electrodes accounts for the exponential dependence of the tunneling current on temperature. The paper further demonstrates that a single-level tunnel model satisfactorily explains experimental results obtained in three different molecular junctions, both single-molecule and SAM-based, formed by ferrocene-based molecules. The model is used to map the electrostatic potential profile in EGaIn-based SAM junctions, where the ferrocene unit is placed at different positions within the molecule. Abstract: Device-to-Device (D2D) communication emerges as a crucial communication paradigm for realizing the vision of the Internet of Things (IoT). It supports heterogeneous object interconnection in large-scale networks, encompassing various objects with embedded intelligence and communication capabilities, such as smartphones, cars, and home appliances. However, D2D communication poses a challenge due to interference with cellular communication. To mitigate this, proper power control and resource allocation must be coordinated within the D2D network to prevent excessive interference and drastic throughput reduction in the cellular system. This paper investigates the problem of cross-layer resource allocation in time-varying cellular wireless networks with D2D communication. It incorporates average interference to the cellular system as a quality-of-service constraint. Each D2D pair in the network injects packets into its queue at rates chosen to maximize a global utility function, subject to network stability and interference constraints. The interference constraint ensures arbitrarily low interference to the cellular system caused by D2D communication. The paper first derives the stability region for the multiuser system assuming that the nodes have full channel state information (CSI) of their neighbors. It then presents a joint flow control and scheduling scheme, proven to achieve a utility arbitrarily close to the maximum achievable utility.
