title: Acceleration of Deep Neural Network Training with Resistive Cross-Point Devices
Abstract:
Deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated significant business impact in large-scale analysis and classification tasks, including speech recognition, visual object detection, pattern extraction, and more. However, training large DNNs is widely considered time-consuming and computationally intensive, requiring data center-scale computational resources for extended periods. This paper proposes the concept of resistive processing unit (RPU) devices, which have the potential to accelerate DNN training by orders of magnitude while consuming significantly less power. 

The proposed RPU device can store and update weight values locally, minimizing data movement during training and enabling full exploitation of the locality and parallelism of the training algorithm. The paper identifies RPU device and system specifications for implementing an accelerator chip for DNN training in a realistic CMOS-compatible technology. For large DNNs with approximately 1 billion weights, this massively parallel RPU architecture can achieve acceleration factors of 30,000X compared to state-of-the-art microprocessors, while offering power efficiency of 84,000 GigaOps/s/W. Problems that currently require days of training on a data center-size cluster with thousands of machines can be addressed within hours on a single RPU accelerator. A system consisting of a cluster of RPU accelerators would be capable of tackling Big Data problems with trillions of parameters, which is currently impossible, including tasks such as natural speech recognition and translation between all world languages, real-time analytics on large streams of business and scientific data, and integration and analysis of multimodal sensory data flows from massive numbers of IoT (Internet of Things) sensors.

title: Energy-Efficient ConvNets Through Approximate Computing
Abstract:
ConvNets, or convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have emerged as state-of-the-art classification and detection algorithms, achieving near-human performance in visual detection. However, ConvNet algorithms are typically very computation and memory intensive. To enable the embedding of ConvNet-based classification into wearable platforms and embedded systems, such as smartphones or ubiquitous electronics for the internet-of-things, their energy consumption must be drastically reduced. This paper proposes methods based on approximate computing to reduce energy consumption in state-of-the-art ConvNet accelerators. 

By combining techniques at both the system and circuit levels, the paper achieves energy savings in the system's arithmetic: up to 30x without compromising classification accuracy and more than 100x at 99% classification accuracy compared to the commonly used 16-bit fixed-point number format. |||

title: On noise-induced synchronization and consensus of nonlinear network systems under input disturbances
Abstract: This paper investigates synchronization and consensus phenomena in complex networks of diffusively coupled nodes subject to external disturbances. Using stochastic Lyapunov functions, we derive conditions for synchronization and consensus in networks of nonlinear, diffusively coupled nodes where noise diffusion is state-dependent. The derived condition, which links network topology, coupling strength, and noise diffusion, offers two key interpretations. First, as expected, achieving synchronization/consensus requires sufficient connectivity among network nodes. Second, counterintuitively, properly designed noise diffusion can drive an unsynchronized network towards synchronization/consensus. Motivated by ongoing research in Smart Cities and Internet of Things, we demonstrate the applicability of our results by illustrating how they can be used to control collective decision-making processes.

title: Notes on "An Effective ECC based User Access Control Scheme with Attribute based Encryption for WSN"
Abstract: The rapid development of networking and communication technologies has led to the integration of the Internet of Things (IoT) and Wireless Sensor Networks (WSN) into WSNIT. WSNIT enables WSNs to connect dynamically to the internet and exchange data with the external world. However, the sensitive data stored in sensor nodes, related to patient health and the environment, is vulnerable to attacks through insecure internet access. To address this security concern, there is a growing need for data integrity and controlled data access using highly secure and lightweight authentication schemes. Santanu et al. proposed an attribute-based authentication framework for WSN, highlighting its security strengths. In this paper, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of Santanu et al.'s scheme and demonstrate its susceptibility to privileged insider attacks and node capture attacks. We also expose significant inconsistencies in the scheme that hinder its practical implementation.

title: Virtually Semisimple Modules and a Generalization of the Wedderburn-Artin Theorem
Abstract: Semisimple modules constitute one of the most important classes of modules, playing a pivotal role in module theory and its applications. The Wedderburn-Artin theorem is a fundamental result in this field. This paper establishes natural generalizations of semisimple modules and presents a generalization of the Wedderburn-Artin theorem. We introduce the concept of "virtually semisimple modules," where every submodule is isomorphic to a direct summand. A module $_RM$ is called "completely virtually semisimple" if each of its submodules is virtually semisimple. Consequently, a ring $R$ is termed "left (completely) virtually semisimple" if $_RR$ is a left (completely) virtually semisimple $R$-module. This paper provides various characterizations of left (completely) virtually semisimple rings. For instance, we demonstrate that a ring $R$ is left completely virtually semisimple if and only if $R \\cong \\prod _{i=1}^ k M_{n_i}(D_i)$, where $k, n_1, ...,n_k\\in\n\\Bbb{N}$ and each $D_i$ is a principal left ideal domain. Moreover, the integers $k,~ n_1, ...,n_k$ and the principal left ideal domains $D_1, ...,D_k$\nare uniquely determined (up to isomorphism) by $R$.

title: Two-variable Logic with a Between Predicate
Abstract: This paper explores an extension of FO^2[<], first-order logic interpreted in finite words, restricted to using only two variables. We augment this language with two-variable atomic formulas that express the property "the letter a appears between positions x and y." This property, in a sense, is the simplest that cannot be expressed using only two variables. We introduce several logics, both first-order and temporal, that possess the same expressive power. We establish matching lower and upper bounds for the complexity of satisfiability in each of these formulations. Additionally, we provide an effective necessary condition, based on the syntactic monoid of a regular language, for a property to be expressible in this logic. For words over a two-letter alphabet, this condition is also shown to be sufficient. Through this algebraic analysis, we demonstrate, among other findings, that our new logic has strictly less expressive power than full first-order logic FO[<].

title: Modulation-Specific Multiuser Transmit Precoding and User Selection for BPSK Signalling
Abstract: Motivated by challenges faced by existing multiuser transmission methods in low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) regimes, and the emergence of massive numbers of low data rate ehealth and internet of things (IoT) devices, this paper proposes a novel approach that leverages knowledge of modulation type in multiuser transmit precoder design. Specifically, we introduce a transmit precoding (beamforming) scheme tailored for BPSK modulation, which achieves maximum power efficiency and capacity in poor channel conditions. In a multiuser scenario, we formulate an objective function based on the weighted sum of error probabilities of BPSK-modulated users. Utilizing convex optimization, we transform and solve this ill-behaved non-convex minimum probability of error (MPE) precoding problem. Numerical results confirm significant performance improvements. We then develop a low-complexity user selection algorithm for MPE precoding. Building upon line packing principles in Grassmannian manifolds, the proposed approach can support more simultaneous users than the number of transmit antennas, exceeding the capabilities of existing multiuser transmit precoding methods.

title: Exceptional collections and the bicanonical map of Keum's fake projective planes
Abstract: This paper leverages recent findings by Galkin et al. [GKMS15] to investigate the geometric properties of Keum's fake projective planes. Among other results, we demonstrate that the bicanonical map of Keum's fake projective planes is always an embedding. Furthermore, we construct a nonstandard exceptional collection on the unique fake projective plane $X$ with $H_{1}(X;\n\\mathbb{Z})=(\\mathbb{Z}/2\\mathbb{Z})^{4}$.

title: Generic Points for Dynamical Systems with Average Shadowing
Abstract: This paper proves that every invariant measure of a compact dynamical system can be associated with a specific asymptotic pseudo orbit. Any point that asymptotically traces this pseudo orbit on average is generic for the measure. Consequently, the asymptotic average shadowing property implies that every invariant measure has a generic point. The proof relies on the properties of the Besicovitch pseudometric DB, which are of independent interest. We show that the set of generic points of ergodic measures forms a closed set with respect to DB. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the weak specification property implies the average asymptotic shadowing property, thus generalizing most known results on the existence of generic points for arbitrary invariant measures.

title: Powering the Internet of Things with RIOT: Why? How? What is RIOT?
Abstract: The significance of software platforms has been highlighted by recent events, both at the political level (e.g., renewed calls for digital data and operating system "sovereignty" following E. Snowden's revelations) and at the business level (e.g., Android's emergence as a new industry generating billions of euros annually). In the Internet of Things (IoT), projected to generate significant business but also pose greater threats to individual privacy, these aspects will be amplified. The need for an operating system like RIOT arises from this context, and this short article outlines RIOT's key non-technical aspects and its core technical characteristics.

title: Almost gentle algebras and their trivial extensions
Abstract: This paper introduces almost gentle algebras, which are monomial special multiserial algebras that generalize gentle algebras. We prove that the trivial extension of an almost gentle algebra by its minimal injective co-generator is a symmetric special multiserial algebra, and therefore a Brauer configuration algebra. Conversely, we establish that every almost gentle algebra is an admissible cut of a unique Brauer configuration algebra. As a consequence, we demonstrate that every Brauer configuration algebra with a multiplicity function identically one is the trivial extension of an almost gentle algebra. We associate a hypergraph to each almost gentle algebra A, showing that this hypergraph induces the Brauer configuration of the trivial extension of A. Notably, this provides a combinatorial criterion for determining when two almost gentle algebras have isomorphic trivial extensions.

title: Comparing Properties of Massively Multiplayer Online Worlds and the Internet of Things
Abstract: The emergence of the Internet of Things (IoT) necessitates the development of architectures capable of handling billions of devices and their interactions. A virtual world engine at the massively multiplayer scale is known as a massively multiplayer online world (MMOW). One key realization from MMOWs, as they scale to massive levels, is the cost associated with maintaining a potentially quadratic number of interactions among a large number of objects distributed spatially. Research into IoT was fueled by advancements in wireless sensor networks; however, this article departs from a device-centric perspective and focuses on how architectures address interacting entities at large scale. We analyze the MMOW domain for properties affected by scale. Subsequently, we evaluate the IoT domain to determine if these properties exist and how they are managed. By comparing the state-of-the-art in MMOWs and IoT regarding scalability, we elucidate the challenges of scaling IoT and integrating an MMOW with IoT into a pervasive platform. The article concludes with three case studies showcasing an MMOW interfacing with IoT.

title: Two-Party Privacy Games: How Users Perturb When Learners Preempt
Abstract: Internet tracking technologies and wearable electronics provide a wealth of data for machine learning algorithms. This data volume is projected to grow further with advancements in the internet of things and cyber-physical systems. While these technologies offer numerous benefits, they also raise the risk of sensitive information disclosure. To mitigate this risk, machine learning algorithms can introduce noise to outputs based on differential privacy formulations. Simultaneously, users can prioritize privacy by injecting noise into the data they submit. This paper conceptualizes the interplay between privacy and accuracy, as well as between user (input) perturbation and learner (output) perturbation in machine learning, utilizing frameworks of empirical risk minimization, differential privacy, and Stackelberg games. Specifically, we solve for the Stackelberg equilibrium in the case of an averaging query. Our findings indicate that in equilibrium, either users perturb their data before submission or the learner perturbs the machine learning output, but never both. The learner perturbs if and only if the number of users exceeds a threshold that increases with the misalignment of incentives. Motivated by these conclusions and observations from privacy ethics, we suggest future research directions. While other studies have investigated privacy markets and mechanism design for truthful reporting of user information, our approach distinctively considers both user and learner perturbation. We anticipate that this work will pave the way for further research in the area of differential privacy games.

title: Sumfree sets in groups: a survey
Abstract: This paper explores several questions concerning sum-free sets in groups, initially raised by Erdős in his 1965 survey "Extremal problems in number theory" (Proceedings of the Symp. Pure Math. VIII AMS). Among other findings, we present a characterization for large sets A in an abelian group G that do not contain a subset B of fixed size k where the sum of any two distinct elements of B does not belong to A (meaning B is sum-free with respect to A). In his survey, Erdős conjectured that if |A| is sufficiently large compared to k, then A contains two elements that sum to zero. This has been proven true for k ≤ 3. However, we provide counterexamples for all k ≥ 4. On the other hand, using the newly derived characterization result, we prove a positive result for the case when |G| is not divisible by small primes.

title: A Performance Evaluation of Container Technologies on Internet of Things Devices
Abstract: The use of virtualization technologies in various contexts, including Cloud Environments, Internet of Things (IoT), and Software Defined Networking (SDN), has witnessed rapid growth in recent years. Among these technologies, container-based solutions offer distinct advantages for deploying distributed and lightweight applications. This paper presents a performance evaluation of container technologies on constrained devices, specifically on Raspberry Pi. Our study demonstrates that the overhead introduced by containers is negligible overall.

title: Smart Context-aware Rejuvenation of Engagement on Urban Ambient Augmented Things
Abstract: The growing concern over global urbanization trends promotes smart-city as an enabling information and communication technology (ICT) for enhancing urban governance. However, the focus on better living spaces is further stimulated by the socioeconomic impact of an increasing senior population. Consequently, ambient assisted living (AAL) emerges as a solution for autonomously providing pervasive things or objects from relevant perturbations for advanced scientific instrumentation. Meanwhile, citizens are captivated by the lively stimuli of monotonous urban events through the advent of virtual reality or augmented things. Thus, with the involvement of situation-awareness or contextualization, engagement/participation information as a utility promises to improve urban experiences. However, grasping meaningful concepts is complex due to personalization obstacles, such as citizen psychology, information gaps, and service visualization. Moreover, recommended practices lack adaptation to monochromatic choices, disparate impairments, mobility, and annotation-richness in urban spaces. Therefore, rejuvenating engagement relies on monitoring and quantifying "service consumption and graceful degradation" of experience. Nonetheless, paramount challenges arise regarding unobservability, independence, and the composite relationship of contexts. Accordingly, a parametric Bayesian-based model is envisioned to address the observability and scalability of contexts and their interplay with engagement. Finally, a systematic framework is demonstrated that pinpoints key goals for context-aware engagement based on participant opinions, usages, and feedback.
label: AI

title: Still Wrong Use of Pairings in Cryptography
Abstract: Several pairing-based cryptographic protocols have been proposed recently, offering a wide range of novel applications, including those in emerging technologies like cloud computing, internet of things (IoT), e-health systems, and wearable technologies. However, these primitives have been misused in numerous instances. The paper by Galbraith, Paterson, and Smart (2006) highlighted most of the issues related to the incorrect use of pairing-based cryptography. However, we observed that some recently proposed applications still fail to utilize these primitives correctly. This has led to unrealizable, insecure, or inefficient designs of pairing-based protocols. One contributing factor is a lack of awareness regarding recent advancements in solving discrete logarithm problems in certain groups. We deliberately avoid technical details and emphasize the importance of correctly utilizing bilinear maps for designing secure cryptographic protocols. We list a collection of recent papers exhibiting incorrect security assumptions or realizability/efficiency issues. Finally, we present a concise and updated recipe for the proper application of pairings.

title: The red one!: On learning to refer to things based on their discriminative properties

title: Microprocessor Optimizations for the Internet of Things: A Survey
Abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) refers to a pervasive presence of interconnected and uniquely identifiable physical devices. These devices aim to gather data and drive actions to enhance productivity, ultimately reducing or eliminating human intervention in data acquisition, interpretation, and utilization. The proliferation of these connected low-power devices will result in a data explosion, significantly increasing data transmission costs in terms of energy consumption and latency. Edge computing mitigates these costs by performing computations at edge nodes prior to data transmission, facilitating data interpretation and utilization. While much research has focused on the IoT's connected nature and communication challenges, the challenges of IoT embedded computing with respect to device microprocessors have received less attention. This paper investigates the execution characteristics of IoT applications from a microarchitectural perspective, exploring the microarchitectural characteristics that enable efficient and effective edge computing. To represent a wide variety of next-generation IoT applications tractably, we introduce a broad IoT application classification methodology based on application functions, enabling quicker workload characterizations for IoT microprocessors. We then survey and discuss potential microarchitectural optimizations and computing paradigms that facilitate the design of appropriately provisioned microprocessors that are efficient, configurable, extensible, and scalable. This paper lays the foundation for analyzing and designing diverse sets of microprocessor architectures for next-generation IoT devices.

title: Linear sets in the projective line over the endomorphism ring of a finite field
Abstract: Let $\\mathrm{PG}(1,E)$ be the projective line over the endomorphism ring $E=End_q({\\mathbb F}_{q^t})$ of the $\\mathbb F_q$-vector space ${\\mathbb\nF}_{q^t}$. As is well known, there exists a bijection $\\Psi:\\mathrm{PG}(1,E)\\rightarrow{\\cal G}_{2t,t,q}$ with the Grassmannian of the $(t-1)$-subspaces in $\\mathrm{PG}(2t-1,q)$. This paper investigates a subset $L_T$ of $\\mathrm{PG}(1,E)$ associated with any $\\mathbb F_q$-linear set $L$ of rank $t$ in $\\mathrm{PG}(1,q^t)$, determined by a $(t-1)$-dimensional subspace $T^\\Psi$ of $\\mathrm{PG}(2t-1,q)$. We examine some properties of linear sets expressed in terms of the projective line over the ring $E$. Notably, we focus on the relationship between $L_T$ and the set $L'_T$, corresponding via $\\Psi$ to a collection of pairwise skew $(t-1)$-dimensional subspaces, with $T\\in L'_T$, each of which determines $L$. This analysis leads, among other findings, to a characterization of linear sets of pseudoregulus type. We demonstrate that a scattered linear set $L$ related to $T\\in\\mathrm{PG}(1,E)$ is of pseudoregulus type if and only if there exists a projectivity $\\varphi$ of $\\mathrm{PG}(1,E)$ such that $L_T^\\varphi=L'_T$.

title: Six Functor Formalisms and Fibered Multiderivators

Finally, we demonstrate that a fibered multiderivator (specifically, a closed monoidal derivator) can be interpreted as a six-functor-formalism on diagrams (small categories). This interpretation provides a considerable simplification of the axioms and proofs of basic properties, clarifying the relationship between the internal and external monoidal products in a (closed) monoidal derivator. The development of a theory of derivator versions of six-functor-formalisms serves as our primary motivation.

title: Normal subgroups of invertibles and of unitaries in a C*-algebra

Turning to non-closed subgroups, we demonstrate, among other results, that in a simple unital C*-algebra, the commutator subgroup of the group of invertibles in the connected component of the identity is a simple group modulo its center. title: Young star clusters in the outer disks of LITTLE THINGS dwarf irregular galaxies
Abstract: We analyzed far-ultraviolet (FUV) images of nearby dwarf irregular (dIrr) and Blue Compact Dwarf (BCD) galaxies to locate young star-forming regions in their outer disks. These regions, detected by the Galaxy Evolution Explorer satellite, are found at distances of 1 to 8 disk scale lengths from the galaxy centers, with ages less than 20 million years and masses ranging from 20 to 100,000 solar masses. The presence of young star clusters and OB associations in the outer disks demonstrates ongoing star formation despite the extreme environment. Most of these regions occur where the hydrogen surface density is approximately 1 solar mass per square parsec, while both hydrogen and older stars extend much further. This limiting density suggests a threshold for the formation of distinct OB associations and potentially even individual stars. Comparing star formation rates in the FUV regions to the average rates expected based on gas content, we find that the localized rates are typically 10% of the expected average rates for the outer disks. This discrepancy suggests that either star formation in dIrrs at surface densities below 1 solar mass per square parsec occurs without forming distinct associations, or the Kennicutt-Schmidt relation overestimates the rate beyond this point. In the latter scenario, stars in the far-outer parts of dIrrs would originate from scattering from the inner disk.

The performance of the proposed MIMO-NOMA scheme is demonstrated through analytical and numerical results.

title: A comparison of two methods for detecting abrupt changes in the variance of climatic time series
Abstract: Two methods for detecting abrupt changes in variance, Integrated Cumulative Sum of Squares (ICSS) and Sequential Regime Shift Detector (SRSD), were compared using both synthetic and real-world time series. Monte Carlo experiments revealed that SRSD consistently outperformed ICSS in various scenarios with different variance regimes, particularly when outliers were present. When applied to climate time series, both methods typically identified the same change points in longer series (252-787 monthly values), except for the Arctic Ocean SST series where ICSS detected an additional, likely spurious change point. However, in shorter series (66-136 yearly values), ICSS failed to detect any changes, even with variance doubling or tripling between regimes. For these shorter series, SRSD is recommended. Notably, all tested climate series, from Arctic to tropical regions, exhibited a common trend: the last shift detected in each series transitioned towards a high-variance regime. This aligns with other findings of increased climate variability in recent decades.

title: A Complex-Network Perspective on Alexander's Wholeness
Abstract: Wholeness, as defined and developed by Christopher Alexander, represents a concept present in space and matter that can be described mathematically. Despite its mathematical nature, wholeness remains elusive, making it difficult to grasp. This paper presents a complex network perspective on wholeness to better understand the nature of order and beauty for sustainable design. Combining complexity-science subjects such as complex networks, fractal geometry, and the scaling hierarchy derived from head/tail breaks, the paper aims to make Alexander's profound ideas accessible to design practitioners and complexity-science researchers. Through case studies, including some analyzed by Alexander, the complex-network perspective is shown to demystify wholeness and provide new insights into Alexander's concepts of wholeness and objective beauty. This perspective allows for a holistic understanding of how structural beauty emerges from local actions guided by Alexander's 15 fundamental properties, differentiation, and adaptation processes. The concept of wholeness extends beyond current complex network theory, encompassing the design and creation of living structures.

title: On the cylindrically symmetric wormholes WhCR^e: The motion of test particles
Abstract: This article partially implements the program outlined in a previous paper by the authors [A. V. Aminova and P. I. Chumarov, Phys. Rev. D 88, 044005 (2013)], inspired by a comment in [M. Cvetič and D. Youm, Nucl. Phys. B, 438, 182 (1995), Addendum-ibid. 449, 146 (1995)] regarding axially symmetric stationary configurations in Kaluza--Klein theory. We investigate the radial and non-radial motion of test particles in cylindrically symmetric wormholes of type WhCR^e, found in the authors' previous work, within a 6-dimensional reduced Kaluza--Klein theory with an Abelian gauge field and two dilaton fields. We focus on the traversability of these wormholes. For non-radial motion along a hypersurface with constant z, we demonstrate that, similar to Kerr and Schwarzschild geometries, orbits can be classified based on their impact parameter relative to a critical value D_c. This value corresponds to the unstable circular orbit of radius u_c (r_c). For impact parameters greater than D_c, two types of orbits exist: those arriving from infinity with pericenter distances larger than u_c and those with apocenter distances smaller than u_c, ending at the singularity at u = -∞ (r = 0). When the impact parameter equals D_c, both types of orbits merge and spiral infinitely towards the unstable circular orbit u = u_c. For impact parameters smaller than D_c, only one type of orbit exists, originating at infinity, crossing the wormhole throat, and terminating at the singularity.

title: Loongson IoT Gateway: A Technical Review

title: Enhancing Contention Resolution ALOHA using Combining Techniques
Abstract: Random access protocols have gained renewed interest in various fields, including satellite communications, Internet of Things, and machine-to-machine communications. Evolutionary ALOHA approaches use time diversity through proactive packet replication, but the receiver doesn't fully exploit this diversity. This paper presents the Enhanced Contention Resolution ALOHA (ECRA) scheme, which combines techniques such as selection combining and maximal-ratio combining to enhance time diversity exploitation. A tight approximation of the packet loss rate for asynchronous random access, including ECRA, particularly suited for low channel load regions, is derived. ECRA is evaluated in terms of spectral efficiency, throughput, and packet loss rate compared to recent protocols, demonstrating its ability to significantly outperform both slotted synchronous and asynchronous schemes.

title: A parsimonious theory of evidence-based choice

Axioms are defined to establish that this relation is a partial order, a minimally specific evidential state exists, and the relation is separative. Choice alternatives are another primitive entity. A plan assigns a choice alternative to each evidential state. In general, plans satisfying a version of the sure-thing principle cannot be rationalized by expected utility. However, such a rationalization is possible if the evidential structure resembles a tree.

title: Refining Wi-Fi Based Indoor Localization with Li-Fi Assisted Model Calibration in Smart Buildings

title: Effective Static and Adaptive Carrier Sensing for Dense Wireless CSMA Networks

title: Mobile Big Data Analytics Using Deep Learning and Apache Spark

title: Correlation Hashing Network for Efficient Cross-Modal Retrieval
Abstract: Hashing is widely employed for approximate nearest neighbor search in large-scale multimodal retrieval, offering storage and computation efficiency. Cross-modal hashing enhances hash coding quality by leveraging semantic correlations across different modalities. Existing methods typically involve transforming data into low-dimensional feature vectors, followed by a separate quantization step to generate binary codes. However, this approach can result in suboptimal hash codes due to the lack of explicit minimization of quantization error and joint optimization of feature representation and binary codes. This paper introduces a Correlation Hashing Network (CHN) approach to cross-modal hashing, jointly learning data representations tailored for hash coding and formally controlling the quantization error. CHN is a hybrid deep architecture incorporating a convolutional neural network for image representation learning, a multilayer perceptron for text representation learning, two hashing layers for generating compact binary codes, and a structured max-margin loss function. This integrated approach enables the learning of similarity-preserving, high-quality hash codes. Extensive empirical studies demonstrate CHN's state-of-the-art cross-modal retrieval performance on standard benchmarks.

title: IOTSim: a Cloud based Simulator for Analysing IoT Applications

title: On noise-induced synchronization and consensus

title: Geo-spatial Location Spoofing Detection for Internet of Things

title: Composable Industrial Internet Applications for Tiered Architectures

Due to potential communication unreliability between tiers, data is synchronized between storage replicas when communication is available. The platform services provide a common ecosystem for data exchange, uniting data storage, applications, and data processing components. title: Conservative Bandits

title: OneClock to Rule Them All: Using Time in Networked Applications
Abstract: OneClock introduces a generic approach for utilizing time in networked applications. It provides two basic time-triggered primitives: scheduling operations at remote devices and receiving feedback on event occurrence or operation execution times.  The paper presents a novel prediction-based scheduling approach that leverages runtime timing information to accurately schedule future operations.  An extension to the Network Configuration protocol (NETCONF) enables OneClock in real-world systems. This extension has been published as an IETF RFC, and a prototype of the NETCONF time extension is available as open source.  Experimental evaluation demonstrates the accuracy of the prediction-based approach across diverse environments with varying hardware capabilities and workloads.  OneClock is a versatile approach applicable to any managed device, including sensors, actuators, IoT devices, routers, and even toasters.

title: Parametric Bayesian Rejuvenation in Ambient Assisted Living through Software-based Thematic 5G Management
Abstract: Enhancing elderly engagement is crucial for promoting independent living. However, existing practices often overlook individual traits despite their socioeconomic importance. Key requirements include discovering relevant contexts and scaling engagement over time. Challenges include context unobservability, independence, and complex relationships.  A Topic-model based model is proposed to address context scalability and its relationship with engagement. A systematic framework is demonstrated, highlighting key goals of context-aware services as identified through user opinions, usage, and feedback.

title: Towards a General Software Engineering Methodology for the Internet of Things

By synthesizing current state-of-the-art research, this paper aims to identify key concepts and abstractions that underpin the design and development of IoT systems and applications, and proposes a software engineering methodology centered on these abstractions.

title: Entropy along expanding foliations
Abstract: The measure-theoretic entropy of a diffeomorphism along an expanding invariant foliation represents the rate of complexity generated by the diffeomorphism along the leaves of the foliation. This paper demonstrates that this entropy value varies upper semi-continuously with the diffeomorphism (C^1 topology), the invariant measure (weak* topology), and the foliation itself. This has several important consequences.  For instance, it implies that the set of Gibbs u-states of C^{1+} partially hyperbolic diffeomorphisms is an upper semi-continuous function of the map. Additionally, it shows that the sets of partially hyperbolic diffeomorphisms with mostly contracting or mostly expanding centers are C^1 open. New examples of partially hyperbolic diffeomorphisms with mostly expanding centers are provided, and the existence of physical measures for a C^1 residual subset of diffeomorphisms is discussed.  Furthermore, the paper introduces a new class of robustly transitive diffeomorphisms, proving that any C^2 volume-preserving, accessible partially hyperbolic diffeomorphism with a one-dimensional center and non-vanishing center exponent is C^1 robustly transitive.

title: Using quantum theory to reduce the complexity of input-output processes
Abstract: All natural systems process and transform information. They receive environmental information as input and transform it into appropriate output responses.  Much of science aims to create models of these systems, algorithmic abstractions of their input-output behavior that enable simulating future behavior based on past events. This paper demonstrates that classical models are inherently inefficient, storing unnecessary past information.  The authors construct quantum models that mitigate this waste whenever physically possible. This suggests that the complexity of general input-output processes fundamentally depends on the information theory used to describe them.

title: M2M Massive Access in LTE: RACH Performance Evaluation in a Smart City Scenario
Abstract: Several studies have raised concerns about the effectiveness of the Long Term Evolution (LTE) cellular standard's random access procedure when a massive number of simultaneous connection attempts occur, as might be expected in IoT or Smart City scenarios. However, detailed simulation studies in real deployment scenarios are lacking due to the limited implementation of the LTE random access procedure in many system-level simulators. This paper proposes a patch for the LTE module of ns-3, a prominent open-source network simulator, to enhance the accuracy of the random access channel (RACH) simulation. The patched version is compared with the default version, and a simulation campaign assesses the challenges posed by massive simultaneous access from mobile terminals in LTE. |||

title: Quantum optics and frontiers of physics: The third quantum revolution
Abstract: The International Year of Light in 2015 marked the 20th anniversary of the first observation of Bose-Einstein condensation in atomic vapors by Eric Cornell, Carl Wieman, and Wolfgang Ketterle. This discovery is considered a major achievement in quantum optics, sparking a surge of groundbreaking discoveries and advancements. This essay for the focus issue on "Quantum Optics in the International Year of Light" highlights recent revolutionary developments in quantum optics at the forefront of various fields: atomic physics, molecular physics, condensed matter physics, high-energy physics, and quantum information science.  Following the lines of our book "Ultracold atoms in optical lattices: Simulating quantum many-body systems" [1], published in 2012, this essay incorporates the latest developments.

title: Secure Information Sharing in an Industrial Internet of Things
Abstract: This paper delves into the secure sharing of information with external vendors in an Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) environment. It identifies crucial security requirements for secure information sharing, based on industry-identified security challenges. The paper proposes a roadmap for enhancing security in IIoT, exploring both short-term and long-term solutions for protecting IIoT devices. The short-term solution focuses on integrating existing best practices. The paper also outlines a long-term solution for protecting IIoT devices with fine-grained access control for data sharing between external entities, supporting cloud-based data storage.

title: Non-Parametric Bayesian Rejuvenation of Smart-City Participation through Context-aware Internet-of-Things (IoT) Management
Abstract: Optimizing citizen participation is vital for promoting Smart City services. However, conventional practices fall short in realizing personal traits, despite socioeconomic promise. The recent trend of IoT-enabled smart objects and personalized services pave the way for context-aware services. title: Big Data: Understanding Big Data
Abstract: Steve Jobs, a visionary leader, stated in 1996 that "a lot of times, people do not know what they want until you show it to them" [38]. This suggests that he advocated developing products based on human intuition rather than research. With advancements in mobile devices, social networks, and the Internet of Things, organizations capture vast amounts of complex data, both structured and unstructured, hoping to make better business decisions. Data has become essential for organizational success. This enormous volume of data, referred to as Big Data, provides a competitive edge when processed and analyzed effectively. However, Big Data Analytics faces challenges, including data lifecycle management, privacy and security, and data representation. This paper reviews the fundamental concept of Big Data, the data storage domain, the MapReduce programming paradigm used for processing large datasets, and examines two case studies demonstrating the effectiveness of Big Data Analytics. It presents how Big Data Analytics can be harnessed for greater good when managed appropriately.

title: A combinatorial approach to small ball inequalities for sums and differences
Abstract: Small ball inequalities have been extensively investigated in the context of Gaussian processes and related Banach or Hilbert spaces. This paper focuses on studying small ball probabilities for sums or differences of independent, identically distributed random elements taking values in very general sets. Depending on the setting—abelian or nonabelian groups, vector spaces, or Banach spaces—we provide a collection of inequalities relating different small ball probabilities, which are sharp in many cases of interest. These distribution-free probabilistic inequalities are proven by demonstrating underlying inequalities of an extremal combinatorial nature, related to classical packing problems like the kissing number problem. Applications are given to moment inequalities.

title: Big Data Analytics = Machine Learning + Cloud Computing
Abstract: Big Data can hold different meanings for different people. The scale and challenges of Big Data are often described using three attributes: Volume, Velocity, and Variety (3Vs). However, these only reflect some aspects of data. This chapter reviews the historical aspects of the term "Big Data" and its associated analytics. We augment 3Vs with additional attributes of Big Data to make it more comprehensive and relevant. We demonstrate that Big Data encompasses not just 3Vs, but 32 Vs, including 9 Vs that cover the fundamental motivation behind Big Data, which is to incorporate Business Intelligence (BI) based on different hypotheses or statistical models. This enables Big Data Analytics (BDA) to help decision-makers make useful predictions for crucial decisions or research results. The history of Big Data shows that the most cost-effective way to perform BDA is to employ Machine Learning (ML) on a Cloud Computing (CC) based infrastructure, or simply ML + CC -> BDA. This chapter aims to help decision-makers by defining BDA as a solution and opportunity to address their business needs.

title: Inferring Energy Bounds via Static Program Analysis and Evolutionary Modeling of Basic Blocks
Abstract: The ever-increasing number and complexity of energy-bound devices, such as those used in Internet of Things applications, smartphones, and mission-critical systems, present a significant challenge for optimizing energy consumption and verifying their performance within the available energy budget. This work addresses this challenge from a software perspective and proposes a novel parametric approach to estimating tight bounds on the energy consumed by program executions. This approach is practical for its application to energy verification and optimization.  The approach divides a program into basic (branchless) blocks and estimates the maximal and minimal energy consumption for each block using an evolutionary algorithm. It then combines the obtained values according to the program's control flow using static analysis to infer functions that provide both upper and lower bounds on the energy consumption of the entire program and its procedures, as functions of input data sizes. We have tested this approach on C-like embedded programs running on the XMOS hardware platform. However, our method is general enough to be applied to other microprocessor architectures and programming languages. Our experimental evaluation shows that the bounds obtained by our prototype implementation can be tight while remaining on the safe side of budgets in practice.

title: Fog Computing: Principles, Architectures, and Applications
Abstract: Internet of Everything (IoE) solutions are gradually bringing every object online. However, processing data in centralized clouds does not scale to the requirements of such an environment.  Applications like health monitoring and emergency response demand low latency, and the delay caused by transferring data to the cloud and back can significantly impact performance. Fog computing has emerged as a solution, extending cloud computing to the edge of the network to reduce latency and network congestion. Fog computing is a paradigm for managing a highly distributed and possibly virtualized environment that provides compute and network services between sensors and cloud data centers. This chapter provides background and motivations for the emergence of Fog computing, defining its key characteristics. Additionally, a reference architecture for Fog computing is presented, and recent related developments and applications are discussed.

title: Interpretation of 750 GeV Diphoton Excess at LHC in Singlet Extension of Color-octet Neutrino Mass Model
Abstract: We propose that the possible 750 GeV diphoton excess can be explained in the color-octet neutrino mass model extended with a scalar singlet $\\Phi$. The model generally contains $N_s$ species of color-octet, electroweak doublet scalars $S$ and $N_f$ species of color-octet, electroweak triplet $\\chi$ or singlet $\\rho$ fermions. While both scalars and fermions contribute to the production of $\\Phi$ through gluon fusion, only the charged members induce the diphoton decay of $\\Phi$. The diphoton rate can be significantly enhanced due to interference between the scalar and fermion loops. We show that the diphoton cross section can be from 3 to 10 fb for O(TeV) color-octet particles while evading all current LHC limits.

title: Sublinear scaling of country attractiveness observed from Flickr dataset
Abstract: The number of people sharing their photographs publicly is increasing daily, providing new, almost real-time insights into human behavior during travel. Instead of waiting for monthly or yearly statistics, urban planners and tourism workers can now make decisions almost simultaneously with the emergence of new events. These datasets can be used not only to compare the popularity of different tourist destinations but also to predict their future popularity based on their characteristics. This paper investigates how country attractiveness scales with population and size using the number of foreign users taking photographs (observed from the Flickr dataset) as a proxy for attractiveness. The results showed two things:  country attractiveness scales with population to a certain extent but not with size; and unlike Spanish cities, country attractiveness scales sublinearly with population, not superlinearly.

title: Towards Semantic Integration of Heterogeneous Sensor Data with Indigenous Knowledge for Drought Forecasting
Abstract: In the Internet of Things (IoT) domain, diverse heterogeneous ubiquitous devices will be able to seamlessly connect and communicate with each other, regardless of their domain. Semantic representation of data through detailed standardized annotation has been shown to improve the integration of interconnected heterogeneous devices. However, the semantic representation of these heterogeneous data sources for environmental monitoring systems is not yet well-supported. To fully leverage the benefits of IoT for drought forecasting, a dedicated semantic middleware solution is required. This research proposes a middleware that semantically represents and integrates heterogeneous data sources with indigenous knowledge based on a unified ontology for an accurate IoT-based drought early warning system (DEWS).

title: About the Suitability of Clouds in High-Performance Computing
Abstract: Cloud computing has become the ubiquitous computing and storage paradigm.  It is also attractive for scientists, as it eliminates the need to manage their own IT infrastructure, allowing them to outsource it to a Cloud Service Provider of their choice. However, for High-Performance Computing (HPC) in a cloud, as needed in simulations or for Big Data analysis, the situation becomes more complex. HPC codes must remain highly efficient, even when executed by many virtual cores (vCPUs). Older clouds or new standard clouds can only fulfill this requirement under specific precautions, which are outlined in this article. The results can be extrapolated to other cloud OSes than OpenStack and to other codes than OpenFOAM, which were used as examples.

title: A Microscopic approach to Souslin-tree constructions. Part I
Abstract: We propose a parameterized proxy principle from which $\\kappa$-Souslin trees with various additional features can be constructed, regardless of the identity of $\\kappa$. We then introduce the microscopic approach, a simple method for deriving trees from instances of the proxy principle. As a demonstration, we provide a construction of a coherent $\\kappa$-Souslin tree that applies also for $\\kappa$ inaccessible. We then carry out a systematic study of the consistency of instances of the proxy principle, distinguished by the vector of parameters serving as its input. Among other things, it will be shown that all known $\\diamondsuit$-based constructions of $\\kappa$-Souslin trees may be redirected through this new proxy principle.

title: Radial gas motions in The HI Nearby Galaxy Survey (THINGS)
Abstract: Studying 21cm line observations of atomic hydrogen provides detailed insights into the kinematics of spiral galaxies. We use sensitive high-resolution VLA data from The HI Nearby Galaxy Survey (THINGS) to search for radial gas flows primarily in the outer parts (up to $3\\times r_{25}$) of ten nearby spiral galaxies. Inflows are expected to replenish the gas reservoir and fuel star formation under the assumption that galaxies evolve approximately in steady state. We conduct a detailed investigation of existing tilted ring fitting schemes and uncover systematics that can hinder their ability to detect signatures of radial flows.  We develop a new Fourier decomposition scheme that fits for rotational and radial velocities and simultaneously determines position angle and inclination as a function of radius. Using synthetic velocity fields, we demonstrate that our novel fitting scheme is less prone to such systematic errors and is well-suited for detecting radial inflows in disks. We apply our fitting scheme to ten THINGS galaxies and find clear indications of, at least partly previously unidentified, radial gas flows, particularly for NGC 2403 and NGC 3198 and to a lesser degree for NGC 7331, NGC 2903, and NGC 6946. The mass flow rates are of the same order but usually larger than the star formation rates. At least for these galaxies, a scenario in which continuous mass accretion feeds star formation seems plausible. The other galaxies show a more complicated picture with either no clear inflow, outward motions, or complex kinematic signatures.

title: Toward Organic Computing Approach for Cybernetic Responsive Environment
Abstract: The development of the Internet of Things (IoT) concept revitalizes Responsive Environments (RE) technologies.  Today, the idea of a permanent connection between the physical and digital world is technologically feasible. The capillary Internet relates to the Internet's extension into everyday appliances, making them actors of the Internet like any human. The parallel development of Machine-to-Machine communications and Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques initiates a new area of cybernetics. This paper presents an approach for Cybernetic Organisms (Cyborgs) for RE based on Organic Computing (OC). In this approach, each appliance is a part of an autonomic system to control a physical environment. The underlying idea is that such systems must possess self-x properties to adapt their behavior to external disturbances with a high degree of autonomy.

title: Fog Networking: An Overview on Research Opportunities
Abstract: The past 15 years have witnessed the rise of the Cloud, accompanied by a rapid increase in Internet backbone traffic and more sophisticated cellular core networks. There are three types of Clouds: (1) data center, (2) backbone IP network, and (3) cellular core network, responsible for computation, storage, communication, and network management. Now, the functions of these three types of Clouds are descending to be among or near end-users, i.e., to the edge of networks, as Fog. This article presents an overview of research opportunities in Fog networking: an architecture that utilizes one or a collaborative multitude of end-user clients or near-user edge devices to carry out a substantial amount of storage, communication, and management. This architecture allocates functionalities, while engineering artifacts that may use a Fog architecture include 5G, home/personal networking, and the Internet of Things.

title: Quadratic polynomial maps with Jacobian rank two
Abstract: Let $K$ be any field and $x = (x_1,x_2,\\ldots,x_n)$. We classify all matrices $M \\in {\\rm Mat}_{m,n}(K[x])$ whose entries are polynomials of degree at most 1, for which ${\\rm rk} M \\le 2$. As a special case, we describe all such matrices $M$, which are the Jacobian matrix $J H$ (the matrix of partial derivatives) of a polynomial map $H$ from $K^n$ to $K^m$. Among other things, we show that up to composition with linear maps over $K$, $M = J H$ has only two nonzero columns or only three nonzero rows in this case. In addition, we show that ${\\rm trdeg}_K K(H) = {\\rm rk} J H$ for quadratic polynomial maps $H$ over $K$ such that $\\frac12 \\in K$ and ${\\rm rk} J H \\le 2$.  Furthermore, we prove that up to conjugation with linear maps over $K$, nilpotent Jacobian matrices $N$ of quadratic polynomial maps, for which ${\\rm rk} N \\le 2$, are triangular (with zeroes on the diagonal), regardless of the characteristic of $K$. This generalizes several results by others.  In addition, we prove the same result for Jacobian matrices $N$ of quadratic polynomial maps, for which $N^2 = 0$. This generalizes a result by others, namely the case where $\\frac12 \\in K$ and $N(0) = 0$.

title: Energy Efficient Location and Activity-aware On-Demand Mobile Distributed Sensing Platform for Sensing as a Service in IoT Clouds
Abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) envisions billions of sensors deployed around us and connected to the Internet, where mobile crowd sensing technologies are widely used to collect data in different contexts of the IoT paradigm. Due to the popularity of Big Data technologies, processing and storing large volumes of data has become easier than ever. However, large-scale data management tasks still require significant amounts of resources that can be expensive, whether purchased or rented (e.g., pay-as-you-go infrastructure). Furthermore, not everyone is interested in such large-scale data collection and analysis. More importantly, not everyone has the financial and computational resources to handle such large volumes of data.  Therefore, a timely need exists for a cloud-integrated mobile crowd sensing platform that can capture sensor data on demand, based on conditions enforced by the data consumers. In this paper, we propose a context-aware, specifically, location and activity-aware mobile sensing platform called C-MOSDEN (Context-aware Mobile Sensor Data ENgine) for the IoT domain. We evaluated the proposed platform using three real-world scenarios that highlight the importance of "selective sensing." The computational effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed platform are investigated, highlighting the advantages of context-aware selective sensing.

title: On twisting real spectral triples by algebra automorphisms
Abstract: We systematically investigate ways to twist a real spectral triple via an algebra automorphism and, in particular, naturally define a twisted partner for any real graded spectral triple. Among other things, we investigate the consequences of twisting on the fluctuations of the metric and possible applications to the spectral approach to the standard model of particle physics.

title: The co-surface graph and the geometry of hyperbolic free group extensions
Abstract: We introduce the co-surface graph $\\mathcal{CS}$ of a finitely generated free group $\\mathbb{F}$ and use it to study the geometry of hyperbolic group extensions of $\\mathbb{F}$.  Among other things, we show that the Gromov boundary of the co-surface graph is equivariantly homeomorphic to the space of free arational $\\mathbb{F}$-trees and use this to prove that a finitely generated subgroup of $\\mathrm{Out}(\\mathbb{F})$ quasi-isometrically embeds into the co-surface graph if and only if it is purely atoroidal and quasi-isometrically embeds into the free factor complex. This answers a question of I. Kapovich. Our earlier work [Hyperbolic extensions of free groups, arXiv:1406.2567] shows that every such group gives rise to a hyperbolic extension of $\\mathbb{F}$, and here we prove a converse to this result that characterizes the hyperbolic extensions of $\\mathbb{F}$ arising in this manner.  As an application of our techniques, we additionally obtain a Scott–Swarup-type theorem for this class of extensions. |||

title: Convergence of Siegel-Veech constants
Abstract: We demonstrate that for any sequence of ergodic $SL_2(\mathbb{R})$-invariant probability measures on a stratum of unit-area translation surfaces that converges weakly, the corresponding Siegel-Veech constants converge to the Siegel-Veech constant of the limiting measure. Combining this with a measure equidistribution result due to Eskin-Mirzakhani-Mohammadi, we establish the convergence of sequences of Siegel-Veech constants associated to Teichmüller curves in genus two, a previously conjectured result. The proof relies on a recurrence result closely related to techniques developed by Eskin-Masur. We also leverage this recurrence result to obtain an asymptotic quadratic upper bound, with a uniform constant depending only on the stratum, for the number of saddle connections of length at most $R$ on a unit-area translation surface.

title: Low Threshold Results and Limits from the DRIFT Directional Dark Matter Detector
Abstract: We present results from a 54.7 live-day shielded run of the DRIFT-IId detector, the world's most sensitive, directional, dark matter detector. Compared to our previous work, we have incorporated several improvements, including a lower detection threshold, a more robust analysis, and a tenfold enhancement in our gamma rejection factor. After analysis, no events remain in our fiducial region, leading to an exclusion curve for spin-dependent WIMP-proton interactions that reaches 0.28 pb at 100 GeV/c^2, a fourfold improvement over our previous work. We also present results from a 45.4 live-day unshielded run of the DRIFT-IId detector, during which 14 nuclear recoil-like events were observed. We demonstrate that the observed nuclear recoil rate of 0.31+/-0.08 events per day is consistent with the detection of ambient, fast neutrons emanating from the walls of the Boulby Underground Science Facility.

title: Abstracting Event-Driven Systems with Lifestate Rules
Abstract: We introduce lifestate rules, an approach for abstracting event-driven object protocols. Developing applications for event-driven software frameworks is notoriously challenging. One reason is that developers must understand the complex protocols that abstract the framework's internal behavior to create functioning applications. These protocols intertwine proper callback registration to receive control from the framework with appropriate API calls to delegate back to it. Lifestate rules unify lifecycle and typestate constraints within a single specification language. Our primary contribution is a model of event-driven systems from which lifestate rules can be derived. We then apply specification mining techniques to learn lifestate specifications for Android framework types. Our implementation successfully identifies several rules that characterize the actual behavior of the Android framework.

title: NIPS 2016 Tutorial: Generative Adversarial Networks

Finally, the tutorial includes three exercises for readers to complete, along with their solutions.

title: Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations in p and n-type topological insulator (Bi$_{x}$Sb$_{1-x}$)$_{2}$Te$_{3}$
Abstract: We observe Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations in topological insulator (Bi$_{x}$Sb$_{1-x}$)$_{2}$Te$_{3}$ films with both p-type (x = 0.29, 0.34) and n-type (x = 0.42) carrier types. By tuning the Fermi-level position with the concentration x, we significantly alter physical properties such as the Berry phase, mobility, and scattering time. The Landau-level fan diagram in the sample with x = 0.42 exhibits a $\pi$ Berry phase and a high mobility of 17,000 cm$^{2}$/V/s, while the others exhibit a 2$\pi$ Berry phase and significantly lower mobility. This suggests that the sample with x = 0.42 becomes bulk insulating because its bulk band does not cross the Fermi level, resulting in the topological surface state dominating transport. Therefore, we can transition sample properties from degenerate to bulk insulating by tuning the concentration x, consistent with angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy results.

title: Elastic Splines II: unicity of optimal s-curves and $G^2$ regularity of splines
Abstract: Given points $P_1,P_2,\ldots,P_m$ in the complex plane, we focus on the problem of finding an interpolating curve with minimal bending energy, known as an optimal interpolating curve. Previous work has shown that existence is guaranteed when requiring the interpolating curve segments to be s-curves. In this article, we further restrict these s-curves to have chord angles no greater than $\pi/2$ in magnitude. With this setup, we have identified a sufficient condition for the $G^2$ regularity of optimal interpolating curves. This condition relates to the stencil angles $\{\psi_j\}$, where $\psi_j$ is defined as the angular change in direction from segment $[P_{j-1},P_j]$ to segment $[P_j,P_{j+1}]$. We identify a distinguished angle $\Psi$ ($\approx 37^\circ$) and demonstrate that if the stencil angles satisfy $|\psi_j|<\Psi$, then optimal interpolating curves are globally $G^2$. As in our previous work, most of our efforts are dedicated to the geometric Hermite interpolation problem of finding an optimal s-curve connecting $P_1$ to $P_2$ with prescribed chord angles $(\alpha,\beta)$. While existence, and sometimes uniqueness, were previously shown, this article begins by establishing uniqueness when $|\alpha|, |\beta| \leq \pi/2$ and $|\alpha - \beta| < \pi$.

title: Parichayana: An Eclipse Plugin for Detecting Exception Handling Anti-Patterns and Code Smells in Java Programs
Abstract: Anti-patterns and code smells are indicators of deeper, larger problems within source code, though they are not defects themselves (they do not prevent program functionality or cause compilation errors). Exception handling is a programming construct designed to manage the occurrence of anomalous or exceptional conditions that disrupt the normal flow of program execution. This paper introduces Parichayana, an Eclipse plug-in for detecting exception handling anti-patterns and code smells in Java programs. Parichayana can automatically detect several common exception handling programming errors. We extend the Eclipse IDE by creating new menu entries and associated actions through the Parichayana plug-in, which is free and open-source, hosted on GitHub. We compare and contrast Parichayana with other code smell detection tools, demonstrating that our tool offers unique capabilities in relation to existing tools. We have created an update site, allowing developers to use the Eclipse update manager to install Parichayana. We have employed Parichyana on several large open-source Java-based projects and detected the presence of exception handling anti-patterns.

title: Loss of brain inter-frequency hubs in Alzheimer's disease
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) causes alterations in both brain network structure and function. The latter manifests as connectivity changes between oscillatory processes at different frequency channels. We propose a multi-layer network approach to analyze multiple-frequency brain networks inferred from magnetoencephalographic recordings during resting-states in AD subjects and age-matched controls. Our main results demonstrate that brain networks tend to facilitate information propagation across different frequencies, as measured by the multi-participation coefficient (MPC). However, regional connectivity in AD subjects shows an abnormal distribution across frequency bands compared to controls, leading to significant decreases in MPC. This effect is primarily localized in association areas and the cingulate cortex, which act as a true inter-frequency hub in the healthy group. MPC values significantly correlate with memory impairment in AD subjects, as measured by the total recall score. The most predictive regions belong to components of the default-mode network, typically affected by atrophy, metabolic disruption, and amyloid-beta deposition. We evaluated the diagnostic power of the MPC and found that it leads to increased classification accuracy (78.39%) and sensitivity (91.11%). These findings provide new insights into the brain functional alterations underlying AD and offer analytical tools for identifying multi-frequency neural mechanisms of brain diseases.

title: Shadows of Einstein-dilaton-Gauss-Bonnet black holes
Abstract: We investigate the shadows of fully non-linear, asymptotically flat Einstein-dilaton-Gauss-Bonnet (EdGB) black holes (BHs), considering both static and rotating solutions. We find that in all cases, these shadows are smaller than those of comparable Kerr BHs with the same total mass and angular momentum under similar observation conditions. To compare both cases, we provide quantitative shadow parameters, observing that the differences in the mean radii of the shadows never exceed the percent level. Therefore, EdGB BHs cannot be generically excluded based solely on (near-future) shadow observations. Theoretically, we find no clear signature of exotic features of EdGB BHs on their corresponding shadows, such as regions of negative (Komar, for example) energy density outside the horizon. We speculate that this is due to the Komar energy interior to the light rings (or more precisely, the surfaces of constant radial coordinate that intersect the light rings in the equatorial plane) always being smaller than the ADM mass, leading to smaller shadows than those of comparable Kerr BHs. Our analysis provides a clear example where the light ring impact parameter, rather than its "size", determines a BH shadow.

title: Auslander's Formula for contravariantly finite subcategories
Abstract: A relative version of Auslander's formula with respect to a contravariantly finite subcategory will be presented, along with its dual version. Several examples and applications will be provided. title: Collective Transport of Lennard-Jones Particles through One-Dimensional Periodic Potentials
Abstract: Transport environments are replete with various fields, such as particle potential and external potential. Under these conditions, how do elements behave, and how do position and momentum redistribute during diffusion? To enrich Fick's law, the complex process must be disintegrated using non-equilibrium statistics physics in ordinary settings. This study aims to discuss particle transport in a one-dimensional channel under external potential fields. Two types of potentials, potential well and barrier, are constructed during the diffusion process, without altering the overall potential. These one-dimensional periodic potentials exhibit distinct phenomena. We meticulously explore the reasons behind the impact of external potential fields on transport using the subsection and statistics method. Furthermore, we confirm one of the evidences of the Maxwell velocity distribution under the assumption of local equilibrium. We also investigate the influence of temperature and concentration on the collective diffusion coefficient under various external forces, integrating thermodynamic analysis into these opposing phenomena. The model's simplicity highlights its valuable contribution: the idea of relating flux to sectional statistics of position and momentum can be referenced in similar transport problems.

Previous work on thermally-driven disk winds relied on analytical approximations for these rates. Specifically, the thermal disk wind is much denser and slower, exhibiting a mass-loss rate twice as high and characteristic velocities three times lower. The sensitivity of these correlations to the equation of state, viscosity, and diffusion is illustrated by considering simple models without transverse expansion. title: Adoption of Innovations with Contrarians and Repentant Agents
Abstract: The dynamics of innovation adoption is a crucial topic in various fields, including technological development, industrial processes, social behavior, fashion, and marketing. The number of adopters of a new technology typically increases following a logistic function. However, empirical data suggests a more complex behavior, as various factors influence the decision to adopt an innovation. While some individuals are inclined to adopt an innovation if many others do the same, others act in the opposite direction, seeking differentiation from the "herd." Individuals who prefer to behave like others are termed mimetic, while those who resist adopting new products, the stronger the greater the number of adopters, are named contrarians. Furthermore, new adopters may experience second thoughts and change their decisions accordingly. Agents who regret and abandon their decisions are denominated repentant. This paper investigates a simple model for innovation adoption in a society composed of mimetic and contrarian individuals whose decisions are primarily based on three elements: the appeal of the novelty, inertia or resistance to adopt it, and social interactions with other agents. Within this process, agents can repent and revert to the old technology. Analytic calculations and numerical simulations are presented to determine the conditions for the establishment of the new technology. The inclusion of repentant agents alters the balance between the global incentive to adopt and the number of contrarians who prevent full adoption, generating a rich landscape of temporal evolution, including cycles of adoption.

This mechanism is supported by a predictive mathematical model and extensive experimental validation and can explain previously reported results for diverse cell types. In melanoma, this mechanism also accounts for the effects of genetic and environmental perturbations, including mutations linked to invasive cell spread. The resulting mechanistic understanding of cell polarity quantitatively captures the relationship between population variability and phenotypic plasticity, with the potential to account for a wide range of cell migration states in diverse pathological and physiological conditions.

First, compared to previous studies, it avoids the iteration procedure, retaining the inherent merits of the standard LB method and outperforming the iteration method in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. Second, a volumetric LB scheme, instead of the bounce-back scheme, is employed to realize the no-slip velocity condition in the interface and solid phase regions, aligning with the actual situation. Lastly, the MRT collision model is utilized, providing additional degrees of freedom and reducing numerical diffusion across the phase interface induced by solid-liquid phase change. Numerical tests demonstrate that the present method serves as an accurate and efficient numerical tool for studying metal foam-enhanced solid-liquid phase change heat transfer in latent heat storage. title: Signifying the Schrodinger cat in the context of testing macroscopic realism

This paper examines two such models: the first where the second premise is that the macroscopically distinguishable states are quantum states (MQS), and the second where they are localized hidden variable states (LMHVS). It is pointed out that in each case, to negate the model, it is necessary to assume that the predetermined states provide microscopic detail for predictions of measurements. Therefore, it is argued that many cat-signatures do not negate MR but could be explained by microscopic effects, such as photon-pair nonlocality. Finally, a third model, macroscopic local realism (MLR), is considered, where the second premise is that measurements at one location cannot cause an instantaneous macroscopic change to the system at another. By considering amplification of the quantum noise level via a measurement process, the paper discusses how negation of MLR may be possible.

This type of band structure is termed the "pudding mold type band." n ≥ 4 belongs to the pudding mold type band, but since the density of states diverges even for n = 2 in one-dimensional systems, it is also categorized as the pudding mold type. Due to the high density of states and rapid change in group velocity around the band edge, the spectral conductivity of the pudding mold type band structures becomes larger than that of the usual parabolic band structures. The pudding mold type band exhibits a coexistence of a large Seebeck coefficient and high electric conductivity, along with a small Lorenz number in the Wiedemann-Franz law, attributed to the specific band shape. The study also finds that low dimensionality of the band structure can contribute to high electronic conductivity and, consequently, a small Lorenz number. title: Genotypic complexity of Fisher's geometric model
Abstract: Fisher's geometric model, originally proposed to explain the evolution of complex adaptations in small steps due to pleiotropic constraints, can also be used to understand the emergence of genotypic epistasis. This model, when combined with the assumption that mutations have additive effects on phenotypic traits, leads to a nonlinear mapping between phenotypes and fitness, resulting in genotypic epistasis. Reciprocal sign epistasis, a crucial condition for the existence of multiple fitness peaks, is particularly interesting. This study investigates the probability of sign epistasis between randomly chosen mutations, finding that it decreases with increasing phenotypic dimensionality and exhibits non-monotonic behavior with distance from the phenotypic optimum. The analysis also derives expressions for the average number of fitness maxima in genotypic landscapes consisting of all possible combinations of L random mutations. This number grows exponentially with L, and its corresponding growth rate serves as a measure of landscape complexity. The study reveals a complex dependence of complexity on model parameters, identifying three distinct phases characterized by different landscape structures. Importantly, the findings demonstrate that phenotypic dimensionality, often considered a measure of phenotypic complexity, does not always correlate with the complexity of fitness landscapes. title: Photoexcitation Circular Dichroism in Chiral Molecules

This paper proposes and demonstrates a novel approach, photoexcitation circular dichroism, that achieves significantly higher sensitivity in detecting chirality in neutral molecules. Unlike traditional methods, photoexcitation circular dichroism does not rely on weak magnetic effects. Instead, it leverages the coherent helical motion of bound electrons excited by ultrashort circularly polarized light. This results in an ultrafast chiral response and the efficient excitation of a macroscopic chiral density in an initially isotropic ensemble of randomly oriented chiral molecules. The excitation is probed using linearly polarized laser pulses, eliminating the need for further chiral interactions. Short-range recurrence and lexical diversity stabilize after elementary school, while graph size and long-range recurrence stabilize only after high school. This gradual maturation is disrupted in individuals with psychosis, who retain a near-random structure in adulthood. In literature, remarkable monotonic asymptotic changes are observed over time. Lexical diversity, long-range recurrence, and graph size increase away from near-randomness, while short-range recurrence decreases, moving from above to below random levels. Bronze Age texts exhibit structural similarities to childish or psychotic discourse, but subsequent texts converge abruptly to the healthy adult pattern around the onset of the Axial Age (800-200 BC), a period of significant cultural change. Recent theoretical models indicate that this interplay can be understood using percolation models, where network connectivity is influenced by motor activity. title: Speculation and Power Law

This paper identifies a simple principle behind the power law: the inherent feedback associated with speculation. This feedback, characterized by buying when a price rise is anticipated (and selling when a price fall is expected), leads to price changes following a random coefficient autoregressive process, resulting in a power law distribution according to Kesten's theorem.

title: ASAP: Asynchronous Approximate Data-Parallel Computation
Abstract: Emerging workloads, such as graph processing and machine learning, often involve approximations due to the large scale of data and the stochastic nature of underlying algorithms. However, data-parallel processing primitives, such as repeated barrier and reduce operations, introduce significant synchronization overheads. Consequently, many existing data processing platforms utilize asynchrony and staleness to enhance performance. While these systems often convert synchronous communication to asynchronous communication between worker nodes in the cluster, this can lead to reduced accuracy in the final output due to inconsistencies in intermediate outputs arising from varying processing speeds. ASAP facilitates fine-grained worker synchronization using NOTIFY-ACK semantics, enabling independent workers to execute asynchronously. title: Active rotational and translational microrheology beyond the linear spring regime
Abstract: Active particle tracking microrheometers have the potential to perform accurate broad-band measurements of viscoelasticity within microscopic systems. Their maximum precision is generally limited by Brownian motion and low-frequency changes to the system. The signal-to-noise ratio is typically improved by increasing the size of the driven motion compared to Brownian motion and averaging over repeated measurements. New theory is presented that provides the complex shear modulus when the motion of a spherical particle is driven by non-linear forces. In certain scenarios, error can be further reduced by applying a variable transformation that linearizes the equation of motion. This allows normalization, eliminating low-frequency drift in the particle's equilibrium position. This method significantly increases signal strength, reducing measurement time for the same error. It is therefore more conducive to measuring viscoelasticity in slowly changing microscopic systems, such as living cells.
