title: 4D Crop Monitoring: Spatio-Temporal Reconstruction for Agriculture
Abstract: Autonomous crop monitoring at high spatial and temporal resolution is a critical challenge in precision agriculture. While Structure from Motion and Multi-View Stereo algorithms can accurately reconstruct the 3D structure of a field using low-cost image sensors, these algorithms fail to capture the dynamic nature of continuously growing crops. This paper proposes a 4D reconstruction approach for crop monitoring, which employs a spatio-temporal model of dynamic scenes suitable for precision agriculture applications. Additionally, we provide a robust data association algorithm to address the problem of large appearance changes due to scenes being viewed from different angles at different points in time, which is crucial for achieving 4D reconstruction. Finally, a high-quality dataset with ground truth statistics is collected to evaluate the performance of our method. We demonstrate that our 4D reconstruction approach provides models that are visually accurate and quantitatively accurate when measured against the ground truth geometric properties of the monitored crops.

title: The Role of Rating and Loan Characteristics in Online Microfunding Behaviors
Abstract: This paper provides an in-depth study of lending behaviors on Kiva using a combination of quantitative and large-scale data mining techniques. Kiva is a non-profit organization that facilitates online connections between lenders and borrowers. Their platform, kiva.org, allows individuals to microlend small amounts of money to entrepreneurs (borrowers) from different countries. Borrowers are always affiliated with a Field Partner (FP), which can be a microfinance institution (MFI) or another type of local organization that has partnered with Kiva. Field partners provide loans to selected businesses based on their local knowledge regarding the country, the business sector (including agriculture, health, or manufacturing), and the borrower. Our research aims to understand the relationship between lending activity and various features offered by the online platform. Specifically, we focus on two research questions: (i) the role of MFI ratings in driving lending activity and (ii) the role of various loan features in lending behavior. The first question analyzes whether there is a relationship between the MFI ratings (accessible to lenders online) and their lending volumes. The second research question investigates whether certain loan features available online at Kiva, such as the type of small business, the borrower's gender, or the loan's country information, affect lender behavior.

title: A big-data spatial, temporal and network analysis of bovine tuberculosis between wildlife (badgers) and cattle
Abstract: Bovine tuberculosis (TB) poses a significant threat to the agricultural industry in many countries. The disease involves potential interactions between wildlife and cattle and creates societal problems related to human-wildlife conflict. This study employs connectedness network analysis to investigate the spatial and temporal dynamics of TB between cattle in farms and the European badger (Meles meles), utilizing a large dataset generated by a calibrated agent-based model. The results show that infected network connectedness was lower in badgers than in cattle. The contribution of an infected individual to the mean distance of disease spread over time was considerably lower for badgers than cattle; badgers primarily spread the disease locally while cattle infected both locally and across longer distances. Most badger-induced infections occurred when individual badgers left their home sett, and this was positively correlated with badger population growth rates. Point pattern analysis indicated aggregation in the spatial pattern of TB prevalence in badger setts across all scales. The spatial distribution of farms that were not TB-free was aggregated at different scales than the spatial distribution of infected badgers and became random at larger scales. The spatial cross-correlation between infected badger setts and infected farms revealed that, in general, infected setts and farms do not coexist except at a few scales. Temporal autocorrelation detected a two-year infection cycle for badgers, while there was both within-the-year and longer cycles for infected cattle. Temporal cross-correlation indicated that infection cycles in badgers and cattle are negatively correlated. The implications of these results for understanding the dynamics of the disease are discussed.

title: Online Informative Path Planning for Active Classification Using UAVs
Abstract: This paper introduces an informative path planning (IPP) framework for active classification using unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). Our algorithm combines global viewpoint selection and evolutionary optimization to refine the planned trajectory in continuous 3D space while satisfying dynamic constraints. We model the presence of weeds on farmland using an occupancy grid and generate adaptive plans based on information-theoretic objectives, enabling the UAV to gather data efficiently. We validate our approach in simulation by comparing it to existing methods and analyze the effects of different planning strategies. Our results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm builds maps with over 50% lower entropy compared to traditional "lawnmower" coverage in the same amount of time. We showcase the planning scheme on a multirotor platform with different artificial farmland set-ups.

title: BioLeaf: a professional mobile application to measure foliar damage caused by insect herbivory
Abstract: Soybean is one of the ten most important crops globally, generating multi-billion dollar businesses annually. However, current methods for measuring foliar damage are expensive and dependent on laboratory facilities, sometimes requiring complex devices. To address these shortcomings, we introduce an image processing methodology for measuring foliar damage in soybean leaves. We developed a non-destructive imaging method based on two techniques, Otsu segmentation and Bezier curves, to estimate foliar loss in leaves with or without border damage. We implemented our methodology in a mobile application named BioLeaf, which is freely available for smartphone users. We tested our approach on real-world leaves collected from a soybean crop in Brazil. Our results demonstrated that BioLeaf achieves foliar damage quantification with precision comparable to that of human specialists. With these findings, our proposal could assist soybean producers by reducing the time required to measure foliar damage, lowering analytical costs, and providing a commodity application applicable not only to soy but also to various other crops such as cotton, beans, potatoes, coffee, and vegetables.

title: Young People's Burden: Requirement of Negative CO2 Emissions
Abstract: Global temperature is a fundamental climate metric highly correlated with sea level. Maintaining shorelines near their present location requires keeping global temperature within or close to its preindustrial Holocene range. However, global temperature, excluding short-term variability, now exceeds +1 degC relative to the 1880-1920 mean, and the annual 2016 global temperature was almost +1.3 degC. We show that global temperature has risen well outside the Holocene range and Earth is now as warm as during the prior interglacial, when sea level reached 6-9 meters higher than today. Furthermore, Earth is out of energy balance with the current atmospheric composition, implying further warming is inevitable. We demonstrate that the growth rate of greenhouse gas climate forcing has accelerated significantly in the past decade. The rapidity of ice sheet and sea level response to global temperature is difficult to predict but depends on the magnitude of warming. Targets for limiting global warming should aim to avoid leaving global temperature at Eemian or higher levels for centuries. Such targets require "negative emissions," the extraction of CO2 from the air. If the phase-down of fossil fuel emissions begins soon, improved agricultural and forestry practices may provide much of the extraction, and the magnitude and duration of global temperature excursion above the natural range of the current interglacial could be limited, minimizing irreversible impacts. Conversely, continued high emissions place a burden on future generations to undertake massive technological CO2 extraction to limit climate change and its consequences. Proposed methods of extraction have estimated costs of 89-535 trillion dollars this century, pose substantial risks, and have uncertain feasibility. Continued high emissions unarguably condemn future generations to a massive, implausible cleanup, growing deleterious climate impacts, or both.

title: Toward a Science of Autonomy for Physical Systems: Service

title: Evidence of natural hybridization and introgression between Medicago ciliaris and Medicago intertexta

title: Nonstationary Spatial Prediction of Soil Organic Carbon: Implications for Stock Assessment Decision Making
Abstract: The Rapid Carbon Assessment (RaCA) project, conducted by the US Department of Agriculture's National Resources Conservation Service between 2010 and 2012, aimed to provide contemporaneous measurements of soil organic carbon (SOC) across the United States. However, the spatial resolution of the RaCA data is insufficient for studying carbon storage in soil and its implications for climate science and agriculture. To address this limitation, this paper compares various statistical methods for predicting SOC at locations not included in the RaCA project. The study investigates the performance of both stationary and nonstationary methods, including a novel nonstationary approach based on partitioning spatially-varying covariate processes. This new method addresses open questions regarding domain partitioning, incorporating partially observed covariates, and accounting for uncertainty in the partitioning. While the different methods show minimal differences in out-of-sample criteria for this dataset, significant variations exist in the maps of uncertainty in SOC predictions. The authors argue that the spatially-varying measures of prediction uncertainty produced by the novel approach are valuable for decision-makers, as they can be used to benchmark mechanistic models, identify target areas for soil restoration projects, and inform carbon sequestration projects.

title: A Bayesian Network approach to County-Level Corn Yield Prediction using historical data and expert knowledge
Abstract: Crop yield forecasting is essential for various stakeholders, including commodity futures markets, agricultural policy formulation, and crop insurance rating. The model, based on Bayesian network analysis, constructs a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) between predictors and yield. Expert knowledge is used to refine the graph structure by pruning or strengthening edges, optimizing the connectivity and edge weights to maximize the likelihood of observing training data. title: Aristotle vs. Ringelmann: On Superlinear Production in Open Source Software
Abstract: Organizations provide production gains compared to market-based resource allocation. On the one hand, Sornette et al. uncovered a superlinear production mechanism, suggesting that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. Conversely, Scholtes et al. found opposite results, aligning with the Ringelmann effect, which posits decreasing individual productivity with increasing group size. This paper compares these two theories, highlighting their strengths and weaknesses and discussing empirical testing. The authors argue that these two perspectives might not be as contradictory as initially claimed, suggesting further investigation is needed.

The analysis reveals that one-off control strategies are sufficient for low to intermediate pest immigration rates, while periodic release strategies are preferable for high immigration rates. title: Modelling the impact of financialization on agricultural commodity markets
Abstract: This paper proposes a stylized model of production and exchange involving long-term investors and financial investors with differing time horizons and information advantages. The equilibrium solution reveals that long-term producers adjust their production decisions to anticipate the impact of short-term investor allocations on prices. Short-term investments yield a positive expected profit commensurate with their informational advantage. title: Big Data For Development: Applications and Techniques
Abstract: The widespread adoption of social media platforms and digital devices has led to the generation of vast amounts of public data on a daily basis. This massive dataset holds the potential for real-time insights into emerging trends and early warnings of potential emergencies, such as disease outbreaks. Moreover, thorough analysis of this data can reveal valuable indicators of socioeconomic and political events, aiding in the development of effective public policies. This study examines the application of big data analytics for human development. The emergence of big data techniques for development (BD4D) promises to revolutionize healthcare, education, and agriculture, contribute to poverty alleviation, and facilitate response to humanitarian crises and conflicts. Despite its potential benefits, the large-scale deployment of BD4D faces several challenges due to the sheer volume, rapid change, and diverse nature of big data. Key concerns include efficient data acquisition and sharing, establishing context (such as geolocation and time), ensuring data veracity, and safeguarding privacy. This study reviews existing BD4D work to analyze the impact of big data on societal development. It highlights key challenges and open issues, while examining significant contributions in the field.

title: A model-based approach to assess the effectiveness of pest biocontrol by natural enemies
Abstract: This paper explores a modeling approach for assessing the effectiveness of pest biocontrol by natural enemies in diverse agricultural landscapes that incorporate various pesticide-based management strategies. The approach integrates a stochastic landscape model with a spatially-explicit model of population dynamics, enabling analysis of the impact of landscape composition (including semi-natural habitats, untreated crops, slightly treated crops, and conventionally treated crops) on the effectiveness of pest biocontrol. Effectiveness is evaluated through environmental and agronomic descriptors, measuring the impact of pesticides on the environment and the average agronomic productivity of the landscape, respectively. The study reveals that pesticide effectiveness, treatment intensity, and pest intrinsic growth rate are key drivers of landscape productivity. Biocontrol can partially compensate for productivity losses caused by reduced pesticide use. However, the model indicates that maintaining constant productivity levels while reducing pesticide use is not possible, even with highly efficient natural enemies. Fragmentation of semi-natural habitats and increased crop rotation slightly enhance biocontrol effectiveness but have minimal impact compared to predation rates by natural enemies. This study was conducted within the framework of the ANR project PEERLESS "Predictive Ecological Engineering for Landscape Ecosystem Services and Sustainability" (ANR-12-AGRO-0006).

title: Footprint Characteristics Revised for Field-Scale Soil Moisture Monitoring with Cosmic-Ray Neutrons
Abstract: Cosmic-ray neutron probes are widely utilized to monitor environmental water content near the surface. This method averages over vast areas (tens of hectares) and provides unparalleled data for agricultural and hydrological models at the hectometer scale. However, recent experiments suggest a lack of complete understanding regarding the sensor's response to environmental heterogeneity. Knowledge of the support volume is essential for accurate interpretation and validation of hydrogeophysical data. Previous research simplified a neutron transport model to derive characteristics of the cosmic-ray probe's footprint. This study utilizes a refined source and energy spectrum for cosmic-ray neutrons to simulate their response to various environmental conditions. The results demonstrate that the method is particularly sensitive to soil moisture within the first tens of meters surrounding the probe, while radial weights change dynamically with ambient water levels. The footprint radius ranges from 130 to 240 meters, influenced by air humidity, soil moisture, and vegetation. The moisture-dependent penetration depth, varying from 15 to 83 centimeters, decreases exponentially with distance from the sensor. However, the footprint circle remains nearly isotropic in complex terrain with nearby rivers, roads, or hillsides. These findings underscore the importance of dynamically weighted averages of point measurements for accurate calibration and validation. This insight has significant implications for signal interpretation, sensor installation, data interpolation from mobile surveys, and selecting appropriate resolutions for data assimilation into hydrological models.

title: Astronomy and landscape at the prehistoric settlement Villaggio dei Faraglioni, Ustica, Sicily

From the village, it was possible to observe the rising and setting of the sun during the months near the winter solstice on two elevated peaks located on the opposite side of the island, exhibiting a symmetrical alignment. This alignment enabled inhabitants to determine the day of the winter solstice with an approximation of a few days, utilizing this partial calendar for agricultural and navigational purposes. The study also examines a potential astronomical orientation of the urban layout.

title: Modelling correlated ordinal data by random-effects logistic regression models: simulation and application

This article presents and compares random-effects logistic regression models for analyzing ordered categorical data. The proposed models are applied to an agricultural experimental dataset. A simulation study is conducted to assess the performance of random-effects and homogeneous models. The analysis, real-data application, and simulation results demonstrate that homogeneous models poorly estimate the probability of individual categories. title: Data-Driven Forecast of Dengue Outbreaks in Brazil: A Critical Assessment of Climate Conditions for Different Capitals

The analysis identifies two key variables and a specific period within the annual cycle that strongly predict epidemic outbreaks. These key variables are the frequency of precipitation and temperature during an approximately two-month window of the winter season preceding the outbreak. This suggests that simple climate signatures may influence Dengue outbreaks months before their occurrence. The results indicate that each Brazilian capital examined exhibits a unique frequency of precipitation and temperature signature during the winter preceding a Dengue outbreak. title: Deep neural heart rate variability analysis

title: Multi-Party Privacy-Preserving Record Linkage using Bloom Filters
Abstract: Privacy-preserving record linkage (PPRL), the challenge of identifying records corresponding to the same real-world entity across multiple data sources held by different parties without revealing sensitive information about these records, is increasingly essential in various real-world application areas. Examples range from public health surveillance to crime and fraud detection, and national security. While numerous techniques have been developed to address PPRL, most focus on linking data from only two sources. However, many real-world applications require linking data from more than two sources. This paper proposes a viable solution for multi-party PPRL using two efficient privacy techniques: Bloom filter encoding and distributed secure summation. The proposed protocol efficiently identifies matching sets of records held by all data sources exhibiting similarity above a specified minimum threshold. While efficient, the protocol is also secure under the semi-honest adversary model, ensuring that no party can learn sensitive information about any other party's data. All parties, however, learn which of their records share high similarity with records held by other parties. Evaluation of the protocol on a large real voter registration database demonstrates its scalability, linkage quality, and privacy.

title: Unsupervised Learning for Computational Phenotyping

For example, this approach might fail to recognize that a disease treated as a single condition might actually encompass several subtypes with distinct phenotypes, as observed with asthma and heart disease. Recent studies have highlighted successful applications of unsupervised learning, demonstrating its potential for uncovering patterns in Electronic Health Records that would otherwise remain hidden, leading to a deeper understanding of conditions and treatments. This work implements a method derived from Lasko et al., but leverages Apache Spark and Python and generalizes it to laboratory time-series data in MIMIC-III. title: Development of UMLS Based Health Care Web Services for Android Platform

title: "420 Friendly": Revealing Marijuana Use via Craigslist Rental Ads

title: The restricted Erlang-R Queue: Finite-size effects in service systems with returning customers
Abstract: Motivated by healthcare systems with repeated services facing both personnel (nurse and physician) and space (beds) constraints, this study investigates a restricted version of the Erlang-R model. title: A deep learning approach for predicting the quality of online health expert question-answering services
Abstract: Currently, a growing number of health consumers are seeking health-related information online, anytime and anywhere, effectively reducing healthcare costs. As the availability of HQA services increases, the ability to predict answer quality using machine learning becomes increasingly important and challenging. In HQA services, answers are typically short texts, which are significantly affected by data sparsity. Finally, a deep belief network (DBN)-based HQA answer quality prediction framework is proposed to predict answer quality by learning high-level hidden semantic representations from physicians' answers. title: Partially blind domain adaptation for age prediction from DNA methylation data

title: A Hidden Absorbing Semi-Markov Model for Informatively Censored Temporal Data: Learning and Inference
Abstract: Modeling continuous-time physiological processes that reflect a patient's evolving clinical states is crucial in addressing many healthcare challenges. This paper introduces the Hidden Absorbing Semi-Markov Model (HASMM), a versatile probabilistic model capable of analyzing modern electronic health record (EHR) data. Unlike existing models, HASMM accommodates irregularly sampled, temporally correlated, and informatively censored physiological data, and can effectively describe non-stationary clinical state transitions. HASMM learning from EHR data is achieved through a novel forward-filtering backward-sampling Monte-Carlo EM algorithm. This algorithm leverages knowledge of endpoint clinical outcomes (informative censoring) present in EHR data and implements the E-step by sequentially sampling patient clinical states in reverse-time, while conditioning on future states. Real-time inferences are derived via a forward-filtering algorithm operating on a virtually constructed discrete-time embedded Markov chain that mirrors the patient's continuous-time state trajectory. The paper demonstrates the diagnostic and prognostic utility of HASMM in a critical care prognosis setting using a real-world dataset from patients admitted to the Ronald Reagan UCLA Medical Center.

title: The Dem@Care Experiments and Datasets: a Technical Report

title: Bayesian Distributed Lag Interaction Models to Identify Perinatal Windows of Vulnerability in Children's Health
Abstract: Epidemiological research supports an association between maternal exposure to air pollution during pregnancy and adverse children's health outcomes. However, this approach may provide an incomplete picture, as it does not account for subgroups having the same vulnerability window but different within-window effects, or different windows but the same within-window effect. Since the timing of some developmental processes is common across infant subpopulations while differing in others, both scenarios are important to consider when evaluating health risks of prenatal exposures. This paper proposes a new approach that partitions the DLM into a constrained functional predictor, estimating vulnerability windows, and a scalar effect representing the within-window effect directly. The proposed method allows for heterogeneity in either the window, the within-window effect, or both. A simulation study demonstrates that a model assuming a shared component across groups results in lower bias and mean squared error for estimated windows and effects when that component is truly constant across groups. The proposed method is applied to estimate vulnerability windows in the association between prenatal exposures to fine particulate matter and both birth weight and asthma incidence, and assesses how these associations vary by sex and maternal obesity status in a Boston-area prospective pre-birth cohort study.

title: Deep Learning and Its Applications to Machine Health Monitoring: A Survey

title: Prerequisites for International Exchanges of Health Information: Comparison of Australian, Austrian, Finnish, Swiss, and US Privacy Policies

title: A Data-Driven Compressive Sensing Framework Tailored For Energy-Efficient Wearable Sensing

title: Quantification of free-living activity patterns using accelerometry in adults with mental illness
Abstract: Physical activity is disrupted in many psychiatric disorders. title: Spatio-temporal data mining in ecological and veterinary epidemiology
Abstract: Understanding the spread of any disease is a highly complex and interdisciplinary exercise, as biological, social, geographic, economic, and medical factors influence how a disease moves through a population and its eventual control or eradication. Disease spread poses a serious threat to animal and plant health, impacting ecosystem functioning and species extinctions, and has societal implications through food security and potential disease transmission to humans. Space-time epidemiology is based on the concept that various characteristics of pathogenic agents and the environment interact to alter the probability of disease occurrence and form temporal or spatial patterns. Epidemiology aims to identify these patterns and factors, assess relevant uncertainty sources, and describe disease within the population. Therefore, disease spread at the population level differs from the approach traditionally taken by veterinary practitioners, who are primarily concerned with individual health status. Patterns of disease occurrence provide insights into the factors influencing population health by investigating the individuals affected, their locations, and the timing of infection. The rapid development of smart sensors, social networks, digital maps, and remotely sensed imagery has made spatio-temporal data more ubiquitous and richer than ever. The availability of these large datasets (Big data) presents significant challenges in data analysis. Furthermore, increased computational power facilitates the use of computationally intensive methods for data analysis. Therefore, new methods and case studies are needed to understand veterinary and ecological epidemiology. This special issue aims to address this topic.

title: Consensus clustering approach to group brain connectivity matrices

Unlike previous implementations of consensus clustering, this approach utilizes the consensus strategy to combine information from the connectivity patterns of each node. The proposed approach can be viewed as either an exploratory technique or an unsupervised pre-training step to facilitate the subsequent construction of a supervised classifier. Applications on a toy model and two real datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methodology, which represents subject heterogeneity in terms of a weighted network, the consensus matrix.

title: Microparticle assembly pathways on lipid membranes

The study suggests that this membrane-mediated microparticle aggregation could contribute to the reported long retention times of polymer microparticles in organisms.

Abstract: Maps of infectious diseases, charting spatial variations in infection force, endemicity, and human health burden, provide an essential evidence base for planning towards global health targets. The most common approach is Gaussian process regression, a mathematical framework comprising two components: a mean function leveraging the predictive power of multiple independent variables, and a covariance function yielding spatio-temporal shrinkage against residual variation from the mean. While many techniques have been developed to enhance the flexibility and fitting of the covariance function, models for the mean function have been typically restricted to simple linear terms. For infectious diseases, known to be driven by complex interactions between environmental and socioeconomic factors, improved modeling of the mean function can significantly enhance predictive power. This paper presents an ensemble approach based on stacked generalization that allows for multiple, non-linear algorithmic mean functions to be jointly embedded within the Gaussian process framework. The method is applied to mapping Plasmodium falciparum prevalence data in Sub-Saharan Africa, demonstrating that the generalized ensemble approach significantly outperforms any individual method.

title: Measuring Adverse Drug Effects on Multimorbity using Tractable Bayesian Networks

title: Condensed Memory Networks for Clinical Diagnostic Inferencing

title: Optimization-based design and analysis of tailor-made ionic liquids
Abstract: Solvents constitute two-thirds of all industrial emissions. Traditional organic solvents readily reach the atmosphere due to their high vapor pressure, leading to various negative environmental effects, including climate change, urban air quality deterioration, and human illness. Room temperature ionic liquids (RTILs), on the other hand, exhibit low vapor pressure and are neither flammable nor explosive, resulting in reduced environmental burdens and health hazards. However, their life cycle environmental impacts and freshwater ecotoxicity implications remain poorly understood. RTILs are molten salts that exist as liquids at relatively low temperatures and possess unique properties. Ionic liquids consist of a large organic cation and a charge-delocalized inorganic or organic anion of smaller size and asymmetric shape. The organic cation can undergo unlimited structural variations through modification of the alkyl groups attached to the side chain of the base cation skeleton. Most of these structural variations are feasible from a chemical synthesis perspective due to the ease of preparation of their components. Functionally, ionic liquids can be fine-tuned to impart specific desired properties by switching anions/cations or by incorporating functionalities into the cations/anions. It is estimated that theoretically, more than a trillion ionic liquid structures can be formed. Their tunable nature makes these molten salts potential candidates for use as solvents in a wide range of applications.

title: Modeling trajectories of mental health: challenges and opportunities

Our findings indicate that while GP models come close in terms of accuracy in predicting future trajectories, LCMMs predict trajectories with comparable accuracy in a fraction of the time. title: Multi-stage Clustering of Breast Cancer for Precision Medicine

The first stage involves broad grouping based on phenotypes such as demographic information and clinical features. title: A Natural Language Query Interface for Searching Personal Information on Smartwatches

Based on this analysis, a lightweight natural language based query interface, including a text parser algorithm and user interface, is constructed to process user queries for searching quantified-self information. title: GRAM: Graph-based Attention Model for Healthcare Representation Learning

title: Item response models for the longitudinal analysis of health-related quality of life in cancer clinical trials

title: Approximate Negative-Binomial Confidence Intervals: Asbestos Fiber Counts

The accuracy of the approximation is verified through simulations and compared to traditional approximate confidence intervals in cases where the negative binomial distribution approaches the Poisson distribution. The resulting statistics connect directly to earlier research on the accuracy of asbestos sampling and analysis. Uncertainty in estimating mean asbestos fiber concentrations based on a single count is derived. title: The emergence and evolution of the research fronts in HIV/AIDS research

The largest and oldest front relates to clinical knowledge about the disease in patients. Nine fronts focus on specific molecular structures and mechanisms, including two related to drug development. The remaining fronts explore the disease at the cellular level. Notably, the emergence of these fronts occurred in successive "waves" over time, suggesting a transition in paradigmatic focus. An efficient unsupervised learning algorithm is presented that leverages informatively censored data in electronic health records (EHR) to learn the parameters of the SSLGM. The learned model can then be used to assess the risk of clinical deterioration in new inpatients in an online fashion, allowing for timely ICU admission. Experiments conducted on a heterogeneous cohort of 6,094 patients admitted to a large academic medical center demonstrate that the proposed model significantly outperforms currently deployed risk scores such as Rothman index, MEWS, SOFA, and APACHE.

title: Learning To Score Olympic Events

title: Causal Inference in Observational Data
Abstract: The aging population increasingly faces multiple chronic diseases simultaneously, necessitating comprehensive treatment. To address this issue, a novel framework based on the Rubin-Neyman causal model is proposed for extracting causal rules from observational data, correcting for common biases. Specifically, given a set of interventions and items defining subpopulations (e.g., diseases), the goal is to identify all subpopulations with effective intervention combinations and, within each subpopulation, find all intervention combinations where removing any intervention reduces treatment efficacy. A key concept in this framework is closed intervention sets, extending the quantification of a single intervention's effect to a set of concurrent interventions. The causal rule mining framework was evaluated on Electronic Health Records (EHR) data from a large cohort of patients at Mayo Clinic, demonstrating that the extracted patterns are rich enough to explain controversial findings in medical literature regarding the effect of cholesterol drugs on Type-II Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM).

title: Event Detection and Localization in Distribution Grids with Phasor Measurement Units

Using convex relaxation and a matrix partitioning technique, the proposed algorithm can identify topology changes and attribute them to specific event categories. The algorithm's performance is evaluated on a standard test distribution feeder with synthesized loads. The results show that a tripped line can be accurately and timely detected and localized, highlighting its potential for real-world applications.

title: Hypertemporal Imaging of NYC Grid Dynamics
Abstract: Hypertemporal visible imaging of an urban lightscape can reveal the phase of the electrical grid down to individual housing units. This method offers broad, persistent, real-time, and non-permissive coverage through a single camera placed at an urban vantage point, unlike in-situ monitoring or metering. Rapid changes in the phase of individual housing units indicate load changes (e.g., appliances turning on and off), while slower building or neighborhood-level changes can signal the health of distribution transformers. This concept is demonstrated by observing the 120 Hz flicker of lights across the New York City skyline. A liquid crystal shutter driven at 119.75 Hz down-converts the flicker to 0.25 Hz, which is imaged at a 4 Hz cadence by an inexpensive CCD camera. The grid phase of each source is determined by analyzing its sinusoidal light curve over an imaging "burst" of about 25 seconds. Analysis of bursts taken at approximately 15-minute intervals over several hours shows both the stability and variation of phases in halogen, incandescent, and some fluorescent lights. Correlating these results with ground-truth data will validate a method that can be applied to better monitor electricity consumption and distribution in both developed and developing cities.

title: Ranking medical jargon in electronic health record notes by adapted distant supervision

This paper presents a data-driven approach that mines EHRs to identify and rank medical jargon based on its importance to patients, supporting the development of EHR-centric lay language resources. An innovative adapted distant supervision (ADS) model based on support vector machines is developed to rank medical jargon from EHRs. For distant supervision, the open-access, collaborative consumer health vocabulary, a publicly available resource linking lay terms to medical jargon, is utilized. Knowledge-based features from the Unified Medical Language System and distributed word representations learned from unlabeled large corpora are explored. The ADS model is evaluated using physician-identified important medical terms. The ADS model significantly outperforms two state-of-the-art automatic term recognition methods, TF*IDF and C-Value, with an ROC-AUC of 0.810 compared to 0.710 and 0.667, respectively. title: Coupled, multi-strain epidemic models of mutating pathogens

The mathematical and biological properties of a general class of multi-strain epidemic models are investigated, where the infectious compartments of each strain are coupled together in a general manner. Explicit expressions for the basic reproduction number of each strain are derived, highlighting their importance in regulating system dynamics (e.g., the potential for an epidemic outbreak) and the existence of non-negative endemic solutions. Importantly, the basic reproduction number of each strain is found to be independent of the mutation rates between the strains, even under general assumptions regarding the form of the infectious compartment coupling. The coupling term is shown to promote strain coexistence (as an extension of the competitive exclusion principle), and it is demonstrated that the strain with the greatest reproductive capacity is not necessarily the most prevalent. Finally, the implications of these results for public health policy and planning are briefly discussed.

title: Prognostics of Surgical Site Infections using Dynamic Health Data
Abstract: Surgical Site Infection (SSI) is a national priority in healthcare research. Significant research effort has been dedicated to developing better SSI risk prediction models. Emerging mobile health (mHealth) tools can closely monitor patients and generate continuous measurements of various wound-related variables and other evolving clinical variables. Existing SSI prediction models have limited capacity to utilize evolving clinical data. To address this, a solution is developed to equip these mHealth tools with decision-making capabilities for SSI prediction. This solution seamlessly combines several machine learning models to address the analytical challenges arising from spatiotemporal data. The basic idea is to exploit the low-rank property of the spatiotemporal data through a bilinear formulation and further enhance it with automatic missing data imputation using the matrix completion technique. Efficient optimization algorithms are derived to implement these models, and the superior performance of the new predictive model is demonstrated on a real-world SSI dataset compared to various state-of-the-art methods.

title: Personalized Donor-Recipient Matching for Organ Transplantation
Abstract: Organ transplants can improve life expectancy and quality of life for recipients but carry the risk of serious post-operative complications, such as septic shock and organ rejection. The probability of a successful transplant depends subtly on compatibility between the donor and recipient, but current medical practice lacks domain knowledge regarding the complex nature of recipient-donor compatibility. A data-driven approach for learning compatibility has the potential for significant improvements in match quality. This paper proposes a novel system (ConfidentMatch) trained using data from electronic health records. ConfidentMatch predicts the success of an organ transplant (in terms of 3-year survival rates) based on clinical and demographic traits of the donor and recipient. ConfidentMatch captures the heterogeneity of donor and recipient traits by optimally dividing the feature space into clusters and constructing different optimal predictive models for each cluster. The system controls the complexity of the learned predictive model, allowing for more granular and confident predictions for a larger number of potential recipient-donor pairs. This ensures that predictions are "personalized" and tailored to individual characteristics with the finest possible granularity. Experiments conducted on the UNOS heart transplant dataset demonstrate the superior prognostic value of ConfidentMatch compared to other benchmarks. ConfidentMatch can provide predictions of success with 95% confidence for 5,489 patients out of a total population of 9,620 patients, which corresponds to 410 more patients than the most competitive benchmark algorithm (DeepBoost).

title: The 2016 Al-Mishraq sulphur plant fire: source and risk area estimation

An extensive plume of toxic sulfur dioxide and hydrogen sulfide resulted in widespread casualties. A long-range dispersion model was used to simulate atmospheric transport over the Middle East. The ground-level concentrations predicted by the simulation were compared with observations from the Turkey National Air Quality Monitoring Network. Finally, the simulation data, using a probit analysis, provided an estimate of the health risk area, which was compared to reported urgent medical treatments. title: Revisiting FPGA Acceleration of Molecular Dynamics Simulation with Dynamic Data Flow Behavior in High-Level Synthesis
Abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation is a crucial tool for biology scientists and researchers to explore human health and diseases. However, due to the computational complexity of the MD algorithm, simulating even simple biological entities can take weeks or months on conventional multicore processors. The critical path in MD simulations is the force calculation between particles within the simulated environment, which exhibits abundant parallelism. Among various acceleration platforms, FPGA is an attractive alternative due to its low power and high energy efficiency. However, the high programming cost using RTL has prevented mainstream MD software packages from adopting FPGA for acceleration. This paper revisits FPGA acceleration of MD using high-level synthesis (HLS) to provide affordable programming costs. Experience with MD acceleration demonstrates that HLS optimizations such as loop pipelining, module duplication, and memory partitioning are crucial for performance improvement, achieving a 9.5X speedup compared to a 12-core CPU. Notably, even the fully optimized HLS design can be 2X slower than the reference RTL architecture due to the common dynamic (conditional) data flow behavior that is not yet supported by current HLS tools. To address this, an array of processing elements together with a data-driven streaming network is customized through a common RTL template, automating the design flow. The final experimental results demonstrate a 19.4X performance speedup and 39X energy efficiency for the widely used ApoA1 MD benchmark on the Convey HC1ex FPGA compared to a 12-core Intel Xeon server.

However, existing methods for estimating optimal dynamic treatment regimes are designed for a limited number of fixed decision points on a coarse time-scale. The proposed method accommodates indefinite time horizons and minute-by-minute decision making, common in mobile health applications. Abstract: Cardiovascular diseases (CVD) are a major health concern in patients with schizophrenia (SCZ) and bipolar disorder (BD). However, BMI showed an inverse genetic correlation and polygenic link with SCZ. Conversely, polygenic associations with an overall favorable CM profile were observed in BD. MR analysis indicated that SCZ may be causally linked to elevated triglyceride and that lower fasting glucose may be linked to BD. Otherwise, MR did not reveal other significant causal relationships in general. Numerous SNPs and pathways shared between SCZ/BD and cardiometabolic traits were also identified, some of which are related to inflammation or the immune system. In conclusion, SCZ patients may be genetically associated with several CM abnormalities independent of medication side effects, and proper surveillance and management of CV risk factors may be required from the onset of the disease. title: Stitching Inter-Domain Paths over IXPs
Abstract: Modern Internet applications, ranging from high-definition video conferencing to health monitoring and remote control of power plants, necessitate stringent network requirements in terms of latency, bandwidth, and availability. These brokers centralize routing control for mission-critical traffic across domains, operating in parallel with the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP). This research proposes leveraging Internet exchange points (IXPs) as natural points for stitching inter-domain paths under the control of inter-domain routing brokers. To evaluate the potential of this approach, a global substrate of inter-IXP pathlets that IXP members could offer is mapped based on measurements from 229 IXPs worldwide. The study reveals two key benefits of using IXPs as stitching points: up to 91% of the total IPv4 address space can be served by inter-domain routing brokers working in conjunction with a limited number of large IXPs and their associated Internet service providers (ISPs), and path diversity on the inter-IXP graph increases up to 29 times compared to current BGP valley-free routing. To exploit this rich path diversity, algorithms are introduced that inter-domain routing brokers can employ to embed paths, subject to bandwidth and latency constraints. These algorithms demonstrate scalability to the size of measured graphs and can serve diverse simulated path request mixes. This work highlights a novel direction for Software-Defined Networking (SDN) innovation across domains, centered on logically centralized control and programmable IXP fabrics.

title: EpistAid: Interactive Interface for Document Filtering in Evidence-based Health Care
Abstract: Evidence-based healthcare (EBHC) is a crucial practice in medicine that seeks to provide systematic scientific evidence to address clinical questions. In this context, Epistemonikos (www.epistemonikos.org) stands as one of the pioneering and most influential online systems in the field, providing an interface to support users in searching and filtering scientific articles for practicing EBHC. However, the system currently necessitates significant expert human effort, with nearly 500 physicians manually curating articles for inclusion in the platform. To address the challenge of scaling up the large and continuous influx of data to maintain the system's currency, this paper introduces EpistAid, an interactive intelligent interface. EpistAid assists clinicians in the process of curating documents for Epistemonikos within lists of papers called evidence matrices. The paper details the characteristics, design, and algorithms of EpistAid, along with a prototype implementation and a case study to illustrate how the solution tackles the information overload problem in this domain.

title: Exploring the Pathways of Adaptation an Avatar 3D Animation Procedures and Virtual Reality Arenas in Research of Human Courtship Behaviour and Sexual Reactivity in Psychological Research
Abstract: Utilizing 3D animation and virtual reality in sexuality research offers numerous advantages. Beyond providing a means to (re)experience specific situations, these technologies offer four key benefits: (a) the ability to create and customize bespoke animated stimuli, which is particularly important for research on paraphilia and sexual preferences; (b) less expensive and easier stimulus production compared to real-world stimuli; (c) the capacity of virtual reality to capture physiological responses to stimuli that would otherwise be inaccessible without resorting to self-report measures, which are problematic in this research domain; and (d) less complex ethical, legal, and health and safety considerations as no physical or psychological harm is inflicted on animated characters, enabling the safe presentation of stimuli involving vulnerable targets. The animation sub-group has explored various production quality levels and animation procedures in available software. The aim is to develop both static and dynamic, interactive sexual stimuli for sexual diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. The chapter acknowledges and analyzes ethical considerations related to the use of virtual reality in this research.

title: Activity Recognition Based on Micro-Doppler Signature with In-Home Wi-Fi
Abstract: Device-free activity recognition and monitoring has emerged as a promising research area, driven by increasing public interest in pattern-of-life monitoring and chronic health condition management. This paper presents a novel framework for in-home Wi-Fi signal-based activity recognition in e-healthcare applications using passive micro-Doppler (m-D) signature classification. The framework encompasses signal modeling, Doppler extraction, and m-D classification. A data collection campaign was conducted to validate the framework, successfully detecting and classifying six m-D signatures corresponding to typical daily activities using a software-defined radio (SDR) demo system. Data analysis focused on potential discriminative characteristics, such as maximum Doppler frequency and time duration of activity. Finally, a sparsity-induced classifier is applied to adapt the method for healthcare application scenarios, and the results are compared with those obtained using the well-known Support Vector Machine (SVM) method.

title: Detecting Dependencies in Sparse, Multivariate Databases Using Probabilistic Programming and Non-parametric Bayes
Abstract: Datasets characterized by hundreds of variables and numerous missing values are prevalent in contemporary data analysis. Detecting true predictive relationships between variables while suppressing false positives poses significant statistical and computational challenges in this setting. This paper proposes a novel approach that integrates probabilistic programming, information theory, and non-parametric Bayes. The approach leverages Bayesian non-parametric modeling to: (i) construct an ensemble of joint probability models for all variables; (ii) efficiently detect marginal independencies; and (iii) estimate the conditional mutual information between arbitrary subsets of variables, subject to a broad class of constraints. These capabilities are accessible through BayesDB, a probabilistic programming platform for probabilistic data analysis, using a simple, SQL-like query language. Empirical demonstrations validate the method's capacity to: (i) detect context-specific dependencies and independencies on challenging synthetic problems; and (ii) yield improved sensitivity and specificity compared to baseline methods from statistics and machine learning on a real-world database containing over 300 sparsely observed indicators of macroeconomic development and public health.

title: Network model of human aging: frailty limits and information measures
Abstract: Aging is associated with the accumulation of damage throughout an individual's lifespan. The Frailty Index (FI) provides a quantitative measure of individual health by calculating the proportion of accumulated age-related deficits relative to the total, with a theoretical maximum of 1. Observational studies have consistently reported a more stringent bound, where the maximum value of the FI is less than 1. While the specific value of this maximum varies across studies, it is often reported to be approximately 0.7. A previously developed network model of individual aging failed to reproduce this observed maximum value while retaining other features such as the increasing FI and mortality rates with age. This research presents a computationally accelerated network model that allows for tuning the scale-free network exponent. The network exponent significantly influences the growth of mortality rates with age. However, the study finds that recovering the observed maximum value of the FI necessitates the introduction of a deficit sensitivity parameter, equivalent to a false-negative rate. The value of this parameter obtained in the study is comparable to reported sensitivities of age-related deficits in relation to mortality. Considering this non-zero false-negative rate, the study utilizes mutual information as a non-parametric measure of the FI's predictive value with respect to individual mortality. It finds that mutual information is modestly degraded by the false-negative rate, and this degradation is mitigated by increasing the number of deficits included in the FI. Additionally, the information spectrum, representing the mutual information of individual deficits versus connectivity, exhibits an approximately power-law dependence influenced by the network exponent. Therefore, mutual information serves as a valuable tool for characterizing the network topology of aging populations.

title: Social influence makes self-interested crowds smarter: an optimal control perspective
Abstract: It is common to observe crowds of individuals independently solving similar problems using shared information. This research argues that crowds can become "smarter," i.e., more efficient and robust, by partially adopting the average opinion. This observation challenges the widely held belief that the wisdom of crowds deteriorates with social influence. The key distinction lies in the self-interest of individuals, who tend to reject feedbacks that do not improve their performance. The paper proposes a control-theoretic methodology to compute the optimal degree of social influence, which quantifies the level to which individuals accept population feedback. An experiment with human subjects (N = 194) was conducted where participants initially solved an optimization problem independently, i.e., without social influence. The proposed methodology estimates an optimal degree of social influence of 30%, leading to a 29% improvement in crowd performance. The same cohort then solved a new problem with access to the average opinion. Remarkably, the observed average degree of social influence in the cohort was 32%, resulting in a 29% performance improvement. This suggests that the crowd self-organized into a near-optimal setting. The authors believe that this new paradigm for enhancing crowd intelligence holds significant potential for diverse fields, ranging from population health to government planning. A case study is included to illustrate how a crowd of states can collectively learn the optimal level of taxation and expenditure to maximize economic growth.

title: Efficient Monte Carlo Estimation of the Expected Value of Sample Information using Moment Matching
Abstract: The Expected Value of Sample Information (EVSI) is used to calculate the economic value of a new research strategy. While this value is crucial for both researchers and funders, its practical applications are limited due to computational challenges associated with calculating the EVSI in real-world health economic models using nested simulations. This paper presents an approximation method for the EVSI based on estimating the distribution of the posterior mean of the incremental net benefit across all possible future samples, known as the distribution of the preposterior mean. The paper proposes estimating this distribution using moment matching coupled with simulations readily available for probabilistic sensitivity analysis, which is often mandatory in health economic evaluations. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated using an example previously applied to other EVSI approximation methods. The paper concludes by discussing how this method fits within the broader literature on EVSI approximation methods.

title: Can Big Media Data Revolutionarize Gun Violence Prevention?
Abstract: The scientific method drives advancements in public health. However, a strategy of obstructionism has hindered scientists from gathering even basic information to address America's gun violence epidemic. This paper argues that despite a lack of federal investment, ample publicly available data offers scientists an opportunity to measure a range of firearm-related behaviors. The diversity of available data sources, including news coverage, social media, web forums, online advertisements, and internet searches, provides a rich landscape for studying trends in specific types of gun violence, gun-related behaviors (such as purchases and safety practices), and public understanding and sentiment towards gun violence reduction measures. The paper emphasizes the need for scientists to leverage this vast media data stream and contribute to resolving the gun violence crisis.

title: Inter-WBANs Interference Mitigation Using Orthogonal Walsh Hadamard Codes
Abstract: A Wireless Body Area Network (WBAN) provides essential health care services. However, interference can degrade the performance and utility of WBANs. This paper proposes a novel distributed orthogonal code allocation scheme, OCAIM, to mitigate co-channel interference among coexisting WBANs. The scheme involves each WBAN generating sensor interference lists (SILs), and then allocating orthogonal codes to all sensors belonging to these lists. The paper also introduces a distributed time reference correlation scheme, DTRC, which serves as a building block for OCAIM. DTRC enables each WBAN to generate a virtual time-based pattern to correlate different superframes. Consequently, DTRC provides each WBAN with knowledge about: (1) which superframes, and (2) which time-slots within those superframes interfere with its own superframe's time-slots. The paper further analyzes the success and collision probabilities of frame transmissions as the number of coexisting WBANs increases. Simulation results demonstrate that OCAIM outperforms competing schemes in terms of interference mitigation and power savings.

title: Sliding Dictionary Based Sparse Representation For Action Recognition
Abstract: Action recognition is a key research area with applications in gaming, surveillance, and healthcare. This paper proposes a simple yet effective approach for both offline and online action recognition using skeletal joints. The approach constructs a sliding dictionary containing training data along with their time stamps. This dictionary is used to compute sparse coefficients of the input action sequence, which is divided into overlapping windows. Each window yields a probability score for each action class. Additionally, a simple feature is calculated that calibrates each action sequence to the training sequences and models the deviation of the action from each training data point. Finally, a score-level fusion of these two heterogeneous but complementary features for each window is obtained. The scores for available windows are successively combined to provide confidence scores for each action class. This method of score combination makes the approach suitable for scenarios where only a portion of the sequence is available. Extensive experimental evaluation on three publicly available datasets demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed approach for both offline and online action recognition tasks.

title: A study on the evolution of a community population by cumulative and fractional calculus approaches
Abstract: In today's globalized world, local and intercountry population movements have intensified. This necessitates accurate population predictions for both native and immigrant populations in host countries. Knowledge of future population numbers is crucial for planning purposes in areas such as education, health, employment, housing, and safety. This research revisits historically known formulas for population dynamics of a community, incorporating compound growth and fractional calculus to obtain more realistic relationships. Within this framework, the population evolution of a society with two distinct components is calculated for a given time t. Corresponding relations are developed to compare the native population with the immigrant population, considering the influx of a colonial population at each time interval. The research examines the scenario where the native population becomes equal to the immigrant population at time t. Furthermore, the differential equation of a probability function for the equilibrium state of the accumulated population is derived. The study finds that the equilibrium solution can be expressed as a series in terms of Bernoulli numbers. In the calculation of population dynamics, the Mittag-Leffler (M-L) function replaces the exponential function.

title: Temporal Matrix Completion with Locally Linear Latent Factors for Medical Applications
Abstract: Regular medical records are valuable for medical practitioners to analyze and monitor patient health status, particularly for individuals with chronic diseases. However, these records are often incomplete due to patient unpunctuality and absence. To address the missing data problem over time, recent papers have proposed tensor-based models for missing data imputation, leveraging the low-rank tensor assumption for highly correlated data. However, when time intervals between records are long, data correlation along the temporal direction may not be high, rendering this assumption invalid. To address this limitation, this paper proposes decomposing a matrix with missing data into its latent factors. The paper then imposes locally linear constraints on these factors for matrix completion. Using a publicly available dataset and two medical datasets collected from hospitals, experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing methods.

title: Feature-Augmented Neural Networks for Patient Note De-identification
Abstract: Patient notes contain a wealth of valuable information for medical investigators. However, to protect patient privacy, Protected Health Information (PHI) must be removed before these notes can be legally released, a process known as patient note de-identification. The primary objective of a de-identification system is to achieve the highest possible recall. Recently, the first neural-network-based de-identification system was introduced, achieving state-of-the-art results. Unlike other systems, it does not rely on human-engineered features, enabling rapid deployment, but does not leverage knowledge from human experts or electronic health records (EHRs). This research explores a method to incorporate human-engineered features, as well as features derived from EHRs, into a neural-network-based de-identification system. The results show that the addition of features, particularly EHR-derived features, further enhances the state-of-the-art in patient note de-identification, particularly for sensitive PHI types such as patient names. Given that patient notes typically come with EHRs in real-life settings, the research recommends that developers of de-identification systems leverage the information contained within EHRs.

title: Predicting Urban Water Quality with Ubiquitous Data
Abstract: Urban water quality is paramount to our daily lives. Predicting urban water quality is essential for controlling water pollution and safeguarding human health. However, this prediction task is challenging as water quality varies non-linearly across urban spaces and depends on multiple factors, including meteorology, water usage patterns, and land uses. This paper proposes a data-driven approach to forecast water quality at a specific station over the next few hours. The approach leverages water quality and water hydraulic data from existing monitoring stations, along with various data sources observed in the city, such as meteorology, pipe networks, road network structure, and points of interest (POIs). The research first identifies influential factors affecting urban water quality through extensive experiments. Second, it introduces a multi-task multi-view learning method to fuse these diverse datasets from different domains into a unified learning model. Evaluation using real-world datasets demonstrates the advantages of the proposed method over existing baselines and validates its effectiveness in predicting urban water quality.

title: Leveraging contact network structure in the design of cluster randomized trials
Abstract: In settings where proof-of-principle trials have been successful but the effectiveness of different implementation forms remains uncertain, trials that not only generate information about intervention effects but also provide public health benefits are highly desirable. Cluster randomized trials (CRTs) capture both direct and indirect intervention effects; the latter is heavily influenced by contact networks within and across clusters. This paper proposes a novel class of connectivity-informed trial designs that leverage information about these networks to enhance public health impact while preserving the ability to detect intervention effects. The research considers CRTs where the order of enrollment is based on the total number of ties between individuals across clusters, either considering all inter-cluster connections or only connections to untreated clusters. The paper includes options analogous to both traditional Parallel and Stepped Wedge designs, allowing for control clusters to be held back from re-randomization for a specified period. The performance of these designs in terms of epidemic control and power to detect vaccine effects is investigated through simulations of vaccination trials during an SEIR-type epidemic using a network-structured agent-based model. The simulation results indicate that connectivity-informed designs exhibit lower peak infectiousness compared to traditional designs and reduce cumulative incidence by 20%. However, these designs show a minor impact on time to end of epidemic and reduced power to detect differences in incidence across clusters. Nevertheless, even a brief holdback period restores most of the power lost compared to traditional approaches. The research concludes that incorporating information about cluster connectivity in CRT designs can increase their public health impact, especially in acute outbreak settings, with a modest cost in power to detect an effective intervention. |||

title: Personalized Risk Scoring for Critical Care Prognosis using Mixtures of Gaussian Processes
Abstract: This research introduces a personalized real-time risk scoring algorithm for ward patients. It leverages temporal lab tests and vital signs to provide timely and granular assessments of clinical acuity. The algorithm aims to ensure prompt ICU admissions for patients experiencing clinical deterioration. The system identifies latent patient subtypes from electronic health record data and uses a mixture of Gaussian Process experts to model physiological data streams associated with each subtype. Transfer learning techniques establish a relationship between patient subtypes and static admission information. Evaluation on a diverse cohort of 6,321 patients from Ronald Reagan UCLA Medical Center demonstrates significant improvements in timeliness, true positive rate, and positive predictive value compared to existing risk scores like Rothman Index, MEWS, APACHE, and SOFA. These findings highlight the importance of personalized medicine in critical care settings, highlighting the potential for achieving substantial accuracy and timeliness gains by acknowledging patient heterogeneity. The methodology offers significant clinical and social benefits, particularly for the over 200,000 critically ill inpatients experiencing cardiac arrests annually in the US.

title: Stratification of patient trajectories using covariate latent variable models
Abstract: Traditional models categorize disease progression into discrete stages based on known clinical markers. However, this approach may conflict with the understanding of underlying biology, which in complex systems suggests a continuous evolution of disease from its onset to the terminal stage. To address this, the study proposes a novel approach for learning a continuous disease score by inferring a latent variable from dynamic "omics" data, specifically RNA-seq, which correlates with an outcome of interest, such as survival time. However, such analyses can be confounded by additional data, like clinical covariates captured in electronic health records (EHRs). To overcome this challenge, the research introduces covariate latent variable models, a novel type of latent variable model that learns a low-dimensional data representation in the presence of two distinct views of the same data source. Applying this model to TCGA colorectal cancer RNA-seq data demonstrates how incorporating microsatellite-instability (MSI) status as an external covariate enables the identification of genes that stratify patients based on an immune-response trajectory. The study further proposes an extension called Covariate Gaussian Process Latent Variable Models for learning nonparametric, nonlinear representations. An R package implementing variational inference for covariate latent variable models is available at http://github.com/kieranrcampbell/clvm.

title: Predicting seasonal influenza transmission using Regression Models with Temporal Dependence
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to predict influenza incidence in Galicia, Spain, using meteorological information. The approach extends generalized least squares (GLS) methods to functional regression models with dependent errors. Through a simulation study, the GLS estimators are shown to provide more accurate parameter estimations for the regression model and deliver superior predictive results compared to the classical linear approach. The paper introduces an iterative version of the GLS estimator (iGLS) to model complex dependence structures and utilizes the distance correlation measure to select relevant information for influenza rate prediction. Finally, the GLS procedure is applied to predict influenza rate using readily available functional variables. These models offer valuable tools for health managers in proactively allocating resources during epidemic outbreaks.

title: Kissing Cuisines: Exploring Worldwide Culinary Habits on the Web
Abstract: Food and nutrition have a growing online presence, with shared recipes offering valuable insights into global culinary cultures and attitudes. Ingredients, flavors, and nutritional information act as strong indicators of taste preferences for individuals and civilizations. However, these palate variations are not well understood. This paper presents a large-scale study of online recipes and their content to gain insights into cuisines and culinary habits worldwide. Analyzing over 157,000 recipes from over 200 cuisines, the study examines ingredients, flavors, and nutritional values that distinguish dishes from different regions and uses this knowledge to assess the predictability of recipes from diverse cuisines. The study then links these factors to health indicators of different nations, such as obesity, diabetes, migration, and health expenditure. The results confirm the strong influence of geographical and cultural similarities on recipes, health indicators, and culinary preferences across the globe.

title: An Improved Approach for Prediction of Parkinson's Disease using Machine Learning Techniques
Abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a significant public health concern globally, affecting approximately 5 million people worldwide, including over one million in the United States. Early prediction of PD is crucial for timely treatment planning. While motor symptoms are commonly associated with PD, research is increasingly focused on predicting PD based on non-motor symptoms that precede motor manifestations.  This paper extends previous work that used non-motor features such as Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (RBD) and olfactory loss. It incorporates important biomarkers to enhance prediction accuracy. The study develops automated diagnostic models using Multilayer Perceptron, BayesNet, Random Forest, and Boosted Logistic Regression. Results indicate that Boosted Logistic Regression achieves the best performance with an impressive accuracy of 97.159% and an area under the ROC curve of 98.9%. These findings suggest the potential of these models for early prediction of Parkinson's disease.

title: A Physician Advisory System for Chronic Heart Failure Management Based on Knowledge Patterns
Abstract: Managing chronic diseases like heart failure, diabetes, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) poses significant challenges in healthcare. Existing approaches often rely on complex guidelines developed by expert committees for physicians to follow. However, the complexity of these guidelines can lead to their neglect or non-compliance, potentially compromising medical practices. This paper presents a physician-advisory system for CHF management that encodes the entire set of clinical practice guidelines for CHF using answer set programming. The system utilizes reasoning templates, termed "knowledge patterns," to systematically code clinical guidelines as ASP rules. These patterns simplify the development process. Given a patient's medical information, the system generates treatment recommendations, mimicking a human physician's decision-making process based on the guidelines. The system functions even with incomplete information. This research contributes by demonstrating the successful coding of highly complex guidelines as ASP rules and by introducing a set of knowledge patterns that facilitate coding from natural language and have broader application potential. This paper is under consideration for acceptance in TPLP.

title: The Effect of Pokémon Go on The Pulse of the City: A Natural Experiment
Abstract: Poké­mon Go, a location-based augmented reality game, gained widespread media attention due to claims of increased public space access, heightened pedestrian activity, and overall improvements in health, social, and security indices. However, the game's actual impact on urban mobility patterns remained largely unknown. This paper examines the effect of Poké­mon Go on Santiago, Chile, by conducting a natural experiment using mobile phone network data. The study reveals significant effects of the game on the city's floating population compared to pre-release mobility patterns in August 2016. The week following the game's release saw an increase of up to 13.8% in the number of people spending time outside at certain times of the day, despite not necessarily deviating from their usual routes. These effects were identified through regression analysis using count models applied to cellphone network states. The models incorporated controls for land use, daily patterns, and points of interest within the city. The findings indicate that on weekdays, more people were on the street during commuting hours, suggesting that individuals adapted their routines to incorporate the game. However, on Saturday and Sunday nights, people actively went out to play, favoring locations close to their residences.  While the game's statistical effects may not reflect the massive change in mobility behavior portrayed by the media, particularly in terms of expanse, they do highlight the emergence of "the street" as a new leisure space. This shift holds implications for long-term infrastructure investment by city officials and the development of public policies aimed at promoting pedestrian traffic.

title: Improved liver T1rho measurement precision with a breathhold black blood single shot fast spin echo acquisition: a validation study in healthy volunteers
Abstract: This study explores the usability and normal T1rho value of liver parenchyma using a novel single breathhold black blood single shot fast spin echo acquisition-based liver imaging sequence.  A total of 19 healthy subjects (10 males, 9 females, mean age 37.4 years, range 23-54 years) participated. Scan-rescan repeatability was assessed in 11 subjects scanned twice in a single session, while scan-rescan reproducibility was evaluated in 12 subjects scanned twice over a 7-10 day interval. MRI was performed using a 3.0 T scanner with dual transmitter, acquiring four spin lock times (TSLs: 0 ms, 10 ms, 30 ms, 50 ms) within 10 seconds. The inherent black blood effect of fast spin echo and double inversion recovery enabled blood signal suppression. Results demonstrated good image quality and minimal artifacts. For liver parenchyma, the Bland-Altman plot showed a scan-rescan repeatability mean difference of 0.025 ms (95% limits of agreement: -1.163 to 1.213 ms), and an intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) of 0.977. Scan-rescan reproducibility yielded a mean difference of -0.075 ms (95% limits of agreement: -3.280 to 3.310 ms), and an ICC of 0.820, surpassing the ICC of 0.764 achieved by a previous bright blood multi-breath hold gradient echo acquisition technique. The liver T1rho value was 39.9 +/- 2.4 ms (range: 36.1 - 44.2 ms), lower than the 42.8 +/- 2.1 ms value obtained with the previous bright blood technique. This study validates the application of a single breathhold black blood single shot fast spin echo acquisition for human liver T1rho imaging. The lower liver parenchyma T1rho value and improved scan rescan reproducibility suggest enhanced sensitivity of this technique.
