title: Motion of a nano-ellipsoid in a cylindrical vessel flow: Brownian and hydrodynamic interactions
Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive numerical investigation of the motion of a buoyant or nearly neutrally buoyant nano-sized ellipsoidal particle in a fluid-filled cylindrical tube, both with and without an imposed pressure gradient (weak Poiseuille flow).  Two approaches, fluctuating hydrodynamics and deterministic methods, were employed, ensuring the satisfaction of the fluctuation-dissipation relation and the principle of thermal equipartition of energy. The study focuses on the impact of the confining boundary on particle motion. Results for the velocity and angular velocity autocorrelations (VACF and AVACF), diffusivities, drag and lift forces as functions of shape, aspect ratio, inclination angle, and proximity to the wall are presented.  For the parameters examined, the boundary modifies the VACF and AVACF, revealing three distinct regimes: an initial exponential decay, followed by an algebraic decay culminating in a second exponential decay. The first regime is attributed to thermal noise, the algebraic regime to a combination of thermal noise and hydrodynamic correlations, while the second exponential decay reflects momentum reflection from the confining wall. The study's predictions show excellent agreement with previously published results for the algebraic regime.  The study also discusses the role of off-diagonal elements of the mobility and diffusivity tensor, enabling the quantification of lift and margination of the nano-particle within the vessel. This investigation covers a range of parameters relevant to nanotechnology and targeted drug delivery in health sciences.

title: The demand for road transport in China: imposing theoretical regularity and flexible functional forms selection
Abstract: The road transport sector is identified as a significant contributor to air pollution and public health losses.  The demand elasticity of transportation is a crucial parameter for understanding the economic, environmental, and health impacts of transport demand shocks. While numerous studies have used flexible functional forms, many have neglected the theoretical regularity conditions implied by microeconomic theories. Additionally, even studies that have checked or imposed regularity conditions often equate curvature alone with regularity, overlooking the importance of other regularities.  This can lead to biased results.  To address these shortcomings, this paper examines the demand for road transport in China using three widely used flexible functional forms: the Rotterdam model, the Almost Ideal Demand System (AIDS), and the quadratic AIDS (QUAIDS).  The analysis utilizes annual expenditure data from 2002 to 2014, covering three expenditure categories in the transportation sector: private transportation, local transportation, and intercity transportation. Estimation results indicate that the AIDS model is the only model providing theoretically consistent estimates of residents' demand for road transport in China.  The study finds that private transportation is a luxury good among transportation goods and is relatively elastic to price changes. Empirical results suggest that private and local transportation, as well as local and intercity transportation, are gross complements. Private transportation acts as a substitute for intercity transportation, while intercity transportation is complementary to private transportation.

title: New Survey Questions and Estimators for Network Clustering with Respondent-Driven Sampling Data
Abstract: Respondent-driven sampling (RDS) is a commonly used method for sampling hard-to-survey populations, leveraging social network connections through peer recruitment. While primarily used for estimating the prevalence of infections and risk behaviors of interest to public health, like HIV/AIDS or condom use, RDS is rarely employed to draw inferences about the structural properties of social networks within these populations due to the absence of necessary data collection. Building on recent advances in computer science, this paper introduces a set of data collection instruments and RDS estimators for network clustering, a significant topological property linked to network diffusion potential for information, disease, and health behaviors. Simulations are conducted to evaluate the performance of these estimators, originally designed for random walk samples of computer networks, when applied to RDS samples with characteristics encountered in real-world field settings that deviate from random walks.  Specifically, the study examines the effects of multiple seeds, sampling with and without replacement, branching chains, imperfect response rates, preferential recruitment, and misreporting of ties. The findings suggest that clustering coefficient estimators maintain desirable properties in RDS samples. This study marks an important step towards calculating network characteristics using non-traditional sampling methods and expands the potential of RDS to provide researchers with more insights into hidden populations and the social factors driving disease prevalence.

title: Clinical Text Prediction with Numerically Grounded Conditional Language Models
Abstract: Assisted text input techniques can save time and effort while improving text quality. This paper investigates how grounded and conditional extensions to standard neural language models can enhance word prediction and completion tasks. These extensions incorporate a structured knowledge base and numerical values from the text into the context used for predicting the next word. Automated evaluation on a clinical dataset demonstrates that extended models significantly outperform standard models. The best system utilizes both conditioning and grounding, leveraging their orthogonal benefits. For word prediction with a list of 5 suggestions, it improves recall from 25.03% to 71.28%, and for word completion, it improves keystroke savings from 34.35% to 44.81% (with a theoretical bound of 58.78% for this dataset). A qualitative investigation reveals that models with lower perplexity sometimes perform better at the tasks, suggesting that numbers exert a greater influence on the document level than on individual word probabilities at test time.

title: Event count distributions from renewal processes: fast computation of probabilities
Abstract: Discrete distributions derived from renewal processes, specifically distributions of the number of events by time t, are gaining traction in econometrics and health sciences. This paper presents a fast new method for computing probabilities for these distributions.  The count probabilities are calculated by repeatedly convolving the discretized distribution and then corrected using Richardson extrapolation. A second algorithm, an adaptation of De Pril's method, is described for situations requiring only one probability. This algorithm's computational time is independent of the ordinality, enabling rapid computation of even high-order probabilities. Any survival distribution can be used to model inter-arrival times, leading to a diverse class of models with flexibility for handling both underdispersed and overdispersed data. This work paves the way for routine use of these distributions as an additional tool for modeling event count data.  An empirical example using fertility data illustrates the application of the method and was fully implemented using an R package Countr, developed by the authors and available from the Comprehensive R Archive Network.

title: Nonstationary POT modelling of air pollution concentrations: Statistical analysis of the traffic and meteorological impact
Abstract: Predicting the occurrence, level, and duration of high air pollution concentrations exceeding a given critical level allows researchers to study the health impact of road traffic on local air quality and inform public policy actions. Obtaining precise estimates of the probabilities of occurrence and level of extreme concentrations is challenging due to the complex interplay of physical and chemical processes involved. This highlights the need for sophisticated extreme value models, particularly those accommodating non-stationarity in environmental time series. This paper investigates extremes of nitrogen oxide (NO), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), and ozone (O3) concentrations using two models. Model I is based on an extended peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach developed by A.C. Davison and R.L. Smith, where the parameters of the underlying generalized Pareto distribution (GPD) are treated as functions of covariates (traffic and meteorological factors). Model II addresses the lack of threshold stability in the Davison-Smith model by constructing a specialized functional form for the GPD parameters. For each model, the effects of traffic and meteorological factors on the frequency and size of extreme values are estimated using Markov chain Monte Carlo methods.  Goodness-of-fit tests and model selection criteria confirm that Model II significantly outperforms Model I in estimation and forecasting of extremes.

title: Improving Covariance-Regularized Discriminant Analysis for EHR-based Predictive Analytics of Diseases
Abstract: Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) is a well-established technique for feature extraction and dimension reduction. However, the performance of classical LDA deteriorates significantly when dealing with High Dimension Low Sample Size (HDLSS) data, leading to an ill-posed inverse problem.  Existing approaches for HDLSS data classification typically assume Gaussian distribution and employ regularization techniques. However, these assumptions are often too restrictive for many real-life applications, such as personalized predictive analysis using Electronic Health Records (EHRs) data.  This paper addresses the challenge of predictive analysis of disease using personal EHR data and the LDA classifier.  The research begins by examining an analytical model that explains the accuracy of LDA for classifying data with arbitrary distributions. The model provides a theoretical upper bound for the LDA error rate, influenced by two factors: (1) the statistical convergence rate of (inverse) covariance matrix estimators, and (2) the divergence of training/testing datasets from fitted distributions.  To minimize the error rate and enhance classification performance, the study aims to balance these two factors.  A novel LDA classifier, De-Sparse, is proposed, leveraging De-sparsified Graphical Lasso to improve LDA estimation. De-Sparse outperforms existing LDA approaches designed for HDLSS data.  Both theoretical analysis and extensive experiments on EHR datasets further demonstrate these advancements and effectiveness.

title: The Health Status of a Population: Health State and Survival Curves, and HALE Estimates
Abstract: This paper focuses on finding a health measure analogous to the survival curve but independent of the standard deviation parameter.  This is achieved by estimating the health state curve and calculating the total area under the curve, offering a compelling comparison with survival curves. The resulting health status measure (HSM or HS) is expressed in terms of years of age, similar to life expectancy (LE). The HS is independent of the standard deviation.  When the survival curve exhibits perfect rectangularization, the LE equals the age at which the health state curve approaches zero.  The proposed HS form leads to an insightful classification of various countries. The results closely align with those obtained by the LE estimator, with an interesting reorganization of country rankings. The study provides illustrations of estimated Health Status along with comparative presentations of Healthy Life Expectancy and HALE measures in several countries. Theoretical aspects are discussed, and significant stochastic simulations are conducted, including the reproduction of death probability density forms.

title: On the combination of omics data for prediction of binary outcomes
Abstract: Enriching predictive models with new biomolecular markers is a critical task in high-dimensional omics applications.  Clinical studies increasingly incorporate multiple sets of omics markers for each patient, measuring different levels of biological variation.  A key challenge in predictive research is integrating different sources of omics biomarkers to predict health traits. This paper reviews several approaches for combining omics markers in the context of binary outcome prediction, all based on double cross-validation and regularized regression models. The performance of these approaches is evaluated in terms of calibration and discrimination, and their results are compared with single-omic source predictions.  The methods are illustrated using two real datasets.  The first dataset combines two fractions of proteomic mass spectrometry to calibrate a diagnostic rule for detecting early-stage breast cancer. The second dataset utilizes transcriptomics and metabolomics as predictors of obesity, drawing data from the Dietary, Lifestyle, and Genetic determinants of Obesity and Metabolic syndrome (DILGOM) study, a population-based cohort from Finland.

title: Beer-brewing powered by controlled hydrodynamic cavitation: Theory and real-scale experiments
Abstract: The traditional beer-brewing industry has remained largely unchanged for decades. While reliable and proven, these methods have resisted significant innovation.  However, hydrodynamic cavitation technology, which has emerged since the 1990s in various fields like liquid food processing, offers advantages like faster extraction, disinfection, and energy efficiency. The study compares the physical and chemical characteristics of the resulting beer with both published literature and data from traditional brewing methods.  The results reveal significant improvements: traditional processes like dry malt milling and wort boiling become unnecessary, the saccharification temperature is dramatically reduced, starch extraction efficiency is increased and accelerated, and substantial energy savings are achieved. All this while maintaining safety, reliability, scalability, and universal application to any brewing recipe, preserving beer quality.  These findings have broad implications, considering beer's position as the most widely consumed alcoholic beverage globally, impacting health, the environment, the economy, and even local identities.

title: The reproductive number of Zika in municipalities of Antioquia, Colombia: stratifying the potential transmission of an ongoing epidemic
Abstract: The Zika epidemic in the Americas was declared a public health emergency due to its rapid spread. Understanding the potential transmission patterns of the disease is crucial for developing effective surveillance and control measures. This study compares the basic reproductive number (R0) of Zika in different municipalities in Antioquia, Colombia, the second most affected country after Brazil, using an SIR model with implicit vector dynamics based on daily case reports. The study estimated R0 for 20 municipalities, all located below 2200 meters above sea level. Between January and April 2016, these municipalities reported 17 to 347 cases.  Fifteen municipalities showed high potential for transmission (R0>1), while five had lower potential (R0<1).  However, three of these municipalities had an upper confidence interval of R0 greater than one, indicating potential future transmission. The study concludes that Zika surveillance and control efforts should be primarily directed towards municipalities with R0>1.  Moreover, strengthening case detection and management strategies in other municipalities will benefit the entire Antioquia region.

title: CLOEE - Cross-Layer Optimization for Energy Efficiency of IEEE 802.15.6 IR-UWB WBANs

The proposed algorithm, Cross-Layer Optimization for Energy Efficiency (CLOEE), allows for cross-layer resource allocation, addressing the rate and reliability trade-off in the physical (PHY) layer and optimizing packet size and transmission efficiency in the medium access control (MAC) layer. title: Spatial Multiresolution Analysis of the Effect of PM2.5 on Birth Weights
Abstract: Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) at a specific location is a combination of locally generated pollution and long-distance atmospheric transport. Identifying spatial scales associated with health effects can help pinpoint the pollution sources responsible for these effects, informing targeted regulatory policies.  High-resolution spatial estimates of PM2.5 exposure, made possible by recent prediction methods, allow for evaluating scale-specific associations. This study introduces a two-dimensional wavelet decomposition that relaxes restrictive assumptions in standard wavelet decompositions.  The method decomposes daily PM2.5 surfaces to identify pollution scales most strongly associated with adverse health outcomes.  A key feature of this approach is its ability to eliminate the temporal component of PM2.5 variability, enabling effect estimates solely from spatial contrasts. This eliminates potential confounding by temporal factors, such as seasonality, in exposure-outcome associations. Applying this method to birth weight data in Massachusetts from 2003-2008, the study found that both local and urban sources of pollution are strongly negatively associated with birth weight.  Results suggest that previous analyses failing to address temporal confounding underestimated the overall effect size, which increased in magnitude when this variability was removed.

title: Phenotyping using Structured Collective Matrix Factorization of Multi--source EHR Data
Abstract: The increasing availability of electronic health records (EHRs) has fueled precision medicine initiatives utilizing data-driven approaches.  A crucial component of this effort is the ability to identify patients with specific medical conditions through simple EHR queries, or EHR-based phenotypes.  While existing rule-based phenotyping approaches are extremely labor-intensive, machine learning techniques like dimensionality reduction and latent factor estimation can be adapted for phenotype extraction with minimal or no human supervision. This paper proposes identifying an interpretable latent space shared across multiple EHR data sources (diagnosis, medications, lab reports) as potential phenotype candidates.  A generalized Collective Matrix Factorization (CMF) method is used to incorporate heterogeneous data types, generating rich phenotypes.  Further, achieving interpretability in phenotyping applications requires sparse representations of candidate phenotypes. For example, each phenotype derived from medication and diagnosis data should ideally be represented by a handful of diagnosis and medications (5-10 active components).  The study proposes a constrained formulation of CMF to estimate sparse phenotypes.  Empirical studies on EHR data from Vanderbilt University Medical Center demonstrate the model's efficacy.

title: Gaia Data Release 1, Pre-processing and source list creation
Abstract: The first data release from the Gaia mission provides accurate positions and magnitudes for over a billion sources, along with proper motions and parallaxes for the majority of the 2.5 million Hipparcos and Tycho-2 stars. This paper describes three essential elements of the initial data processing leading to this catalog: image analysis, source list construction, and near real-time monitoring of payload health.  It also discusses limitations in the attainable precision at the current stage of the mission.  Image parameters for point sources are derived from one-dimensional scans using a maximum likelihood method under the assumption of a constant line spread function and comprehensive modeling of bias and background.  However, these conditions are not fully met. The Gaia source list is built from a large ground-based catalog, but a significant number of new entries have been added, and a large number removed. The autonomous onboard star image detection identifies numerous spurious images, particularly around bright sources.  Another critical step in source list creation involves organizing the more than 10 billion individual detections into spatially isolated groups for individual analysis.  Complete software systems have been developed for Gaia's initial data treatment, managing approximately 50 million focal plane transits daily. This provides transit times and fluxes for 500 million individual CCD images to the astrometric and photometric processing chains.  The software also performs detailed daily monitoring of Gaia's health.

title: Role of Mobility and Health Disparities on the Transmission Dynamics of Tuberculosis

The modeling framework captures the daily dynamics of individuals within and between places of residence, work, or business, considering the proportion of time spent in residence and as visitors to TB-risk environments (patches).  The effective population size of each patch must account for both visitors and residents at a given time. The study investigates the impact of effective population size and the distribution of individual residence times in different patches on TB transmission and control using selected scenarios where risk is defined by estimated or perceived first-time infection and/or exogenous re-infection rates. title: A high-throughput analysis of ovarian cycle disruption by mixtures of aromatase inhibitors
Abstract: Combining computational toxicology with ExpoCast exposure estimates and ToxCast assay data allows for predicting human health risks from exposure to chemical mixtures. This study explores, through mathematical modeling and simulations, the potential effects of random mixtures of aromatase inhibitors on the dynamics of women's menstrual cycles.  The study simulated random exposures to millions of potential mixtures of 86 aromatase inhibitors. A pharmacokinetic model predicted the internal concentration of these chemicals over time (up to two years). A ToxCast aromatase assay provided concentration-inhibition relationships for each chemical.  The resulting total aromatase inhibition was then input into a mathematical model of the hormonal hypothalamus-pituitary-ovarian control of ovulation in women.  The results indicate that aromatase inhibitors, above 10% inhibition of estradiol synthesis, can lead to noticeable (eventually reversible) effects on ovulation.  Individual chemical exposures did not produce such effects.  The study estimates that around 10% of the combined exposures simulated had mild to catastrophic impacts on ovulation, with a lower bound of 0.3% under an optimistic exposure scenario.  The findings demonstrate the potential to predict large-scale mixture effects for endocrine disrupters using a predictive toxicology approach suitable for high-throughput ranking and risk assessment.  The predicted effects align with an increased risk of infertility in women due to everyday exposures to the chemical environment.

title: Integrated, reliable and cloud-based personal health record: A scoping review
Abstract: Personal Health Records (PHRs) are emerging as an alternative to integrate patient health information, providing a comprehensive view of their status. This paper presents a scoping review of PHR systems that meet three characteristics: integrated, reliable, and cloud-based.  The review analyzed 101 articles addressing these characteristics, identifying four main research topics: proposed/developed systems, PHR development recommendations, system integration and standards, and security and privacy. Integration is achieved through the HL7 CDA standard. Information reliability is based on ABE security-privacy mechanisms.  Cloud-based technology access is achieved through SOA (Service-Oriented Architecture).

title: Sensor-based Gait Parameter Extraction with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: Measuring stride-related, biomechanical parameters is a common approach for objectively scoring gait impairment. However, state-of-the-art double integration methods for extracting these parameters from inertial sensor data face limitations in their clinical applicability due to underlying assumptions. Two modeling approaches are compared: a combined network estimating all parameters and an ensemble approach that utilizes less complex networks for each parameter individually.  The ensemble approach outperforms the combined model in this application.  On a clinically relevant and publicly available benchmark dataset, the study estimates stride length, width, and medio-lateral change in foot angle with high accuracy. Stride, swing, and stance time, as well as heel and toe contact times, are also estimated with accuracy comparable to or exceeding state-of-the-art methods. title: Bio-Inspired Filter Banks for SSVEP-based Brain-Computer Interfaces
Abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have the potential to revolutionize future healthcare technologies by providing alternative communication and control mechanisms.  Steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP)-based BCIs offer advantages in accuracy and information transfer rate (ITR).  Understanding SSVEP characteristics and designing systems that account for its biological features are crucial for maximizing the capabilities of these devices.  This paper introduces bio-inspired filter banks (BIFB) for a novel SSVEP frequency detection method.  The SSVEP response to a flickering visual stimulus is frequency-selective and weakens as the stimulus frequency increases.  The proposed approach designs and tunes the gain and bandwidth of filters based on these characteristics, incorporating harmonic SSVEP responses. This method improves accuracy and increases the number of available commands by allowing the use of stimuli frequencies that elicit weak SSVEP responses. The BIFB method demonstrated reliable performance when tested on online datasets and compared to well-known SSVEP frequency detection methods like power spectral density analysis (PSDA) and canonical correlation analysis (CCA).  The results highlight the potential of bio-inspired design, which can be extended to include additional SSVEP characteristics (e.g., time-domain waveform) for future SSVEP-based BCIs.

title: The more you test, the more you find: Smallest P-values become increasingly enriched with real findings as more tests are conducted
Abstract: The increasing accessibility of data to researchers has made it possible to conduct massive amounts of statistical testing.  Rather than following a carefully crafted set of scientific hypotheses with statistical analysis, researchers can now test numerous potential relationships and rely on p-values or other statistical summaries to generate hypotheses.  The field of genetic epidemiology exemplifies this paradigm shift.  Driven by technological advancements, testing a handful of genetic variants in relation to a health outcome has been replaced by agnostic screening of the entire genome, followed by the selection of top hits based on the smallest association p-values.  While the field has faced criticism due to a near-total lack of replication of claimed associations, a flow of reports with robustly replicating findings has emerged.  Researchers may have adopted better statistical practices, but this study suggests that a significant increase in the amount of statistical testing itself plays a crucial role. Regardless of statistical significance, an increased number of tested hypotheses leads to an enrichment of the smallest p-values with genuine associations.  This study quantifies how the expected proportion of genuine signals (EPGS) among top hits changes with an increasing number of tests.  When the rate of occurrence of genuine signals does not decrease sharply as more tests are performed, the smallest p-values are increasingly likely to represent genuine associations in studies with a larger number of tests.

title: An Information Extraction Approach to Prescreen Heart Failure Patients for Clinical Trials
Abstract: To reduce the extensive time spent screening, identifying, and recruiting patients for clinical trials, we need prescreening systems that automate data extraction and decision-making tasks traditionally handled by clinical research study coordinators. The study demonstrates highly accurate results, achieving recall and precision values of 0.95 and 0.86, respectively.  The system significantly reduces prescreening time, from weeks to minutes.  The open-source information extraction modules are available for researchers and can be tested and validated in other cardiovascular trials.  This approach can reduce costs, expedite clinical trials, and enhance trial reproducibility across institutions and populations.

title: Using Natural Language Processing to Screen Patients with Active Heart Failure: An Exploration for Hospital-wide Surveillance
Abstract: This paper proposes two approaches, a rule-based approach and a machine-learning based approach, to automatically identify active heart failure cases by analyzing electronic health records (EHR). For the rule-based approach, cardiovascular data elements are extracted from clinical notes, and patients are categorized according to their heart failure condition using expert-provided rules. title: The Devil is in the Tails: Regression Discontinuity Design with Measurement Error in the Assignment Variable

This poses a challenge to treatment effect identification.  This paper provides sufficient conditions for identifying the RD treatment effect using the mismeasured assignment variable, treatment status, and outcome variable.  The paper proves identification separately for discrete and continuous assignment variables and examines the properties of various estimation procedures.  The proposed methods are illustrated in an empirical application estimating Medicaid take-up and its crowdout effect on private health insurance coverage. |||

title: The new world atlas of artificial night sky brightness

This study introduces the world atlas of artificial sky luminance, generated using light pollution propagation software, high-resolution satellite data, and precise sky brightness measurements. The atlas reveals that over 80% of the global population, including 99% of residents in the US and Europe, live under light-polluted skies. The Milky Way is obscured from more than one-third of humanity, impacting 60% of Europeans and nearly 80% of North Americans. Moreover, 23% of the Earth's land surface between 75°N and 60°S, 88% of Europe, and almost half of the US experience light-polluted nights.

title: Cuba: the strategic choice of advanced scientific development, 1959-2014

These accomplishments are a direct result of Cuba's 1959 decision to establish an advanced scientific system dedicated to addressing the nation's most pressing development challenges and overcoming its historical subalternity. This ambitious objective was tackled in a unique manner, leveraging extensive and multifaceted support and collaboration, encompassing both Soviet and Western scientists and institutions, alongside a distinctively Cuban ingenuity. Notably, immediately following the revolution, Cuba developed a sophisticated and integrated scientific system, achieving excellence in leading scientific fields, such as biotechnology, independent of the Soviet Union, which lagged behind in this field. Even the collapse of the Soviet Union in the early 1990s, which could have jeopardized the Revolution's achievements and reintroduced the threat of subalternity under an intensified American embargo, did not alter this trend. Cuba once again met this challenge by reaffirming its strategic commitment to supporting its most advanced and profitable scientific sectors, especially the capital-intensive and typically American field of health biotechnologies. title: Smart Computing and Sensing Technologies for Animal Welfare: A Systematic Review

title: Data Integration Model for Air Quality: A Hierarchical Approach to the Global Estimation of Exposures to Ambient Air Pollution
Abstract: Air pollution poses a significant global health risk, with both ambient and household air pollution contributing substantially to the overall global disease burden. Fine particulate matter ambient pollution (PM2.5) is a key driver of adverse health effects, estimated to be responsible for 3 million deaths annually. Ground monitoring networks have traditionally provided the primary source of information for estimating exposures, but despite increasing coverage, monitoring remains limited in some regions. Ground monitoring data, therefore, requires supplementation with information from other sources, such as satellite retrievals of aerosol optical depth and chemical transport models. This study proposes a hierarchical modeling approach for integrating data from multiple sources, allowing for spatially varying relationships between ground measurements and other factors that estimate air quality. Set within a Bayesian framework, the resulting Data Integration Model for Air Quality (DIMAQ) is used to estimate exposures, along with associated measures of uncertainty, on a high-resolution grid covering the entire world. Bayesian analysis on this scale can be computationally demanding, leading to the use of approximate Bayesian inference through Integrated Nested Laplace Approximations. Model selection and assessment were conducted through cross-validation, resulting in a final model that demonstrates substantial improvements in predictive accuracy, particularly in regions with sparse ground monitoring, compared to current approaches: root mean square error (RMSE) reduced from 17.1 to 10.7, and population weighted RMSE from 23.1 to 12.1 µgm-3. Based on summaries of the posterior distributions for each grid cell, it is estimated that 92% of the world's population resides in areas exceeding the World Health Organization's Air Quality Guidelines.

title: Statistical physics of vaccination
Abstract: Historically, infectious diseases have inflicted considerable damage on human societies, and their impact persists today. To mitigate their effects, mathematical models of disease transmission have been studied to understand disease dynamics and inform prevention strategies. Vaccination, a cornerstone of modern preventive measures, holds significant theoretical and empirical interest. In contrast to traditional approaches, recent research increasingly emphasizes the crucial implications of individual behavior and heterogeneous contact patterns within populations. This report reviews the development of theoretical epidemiology, focusing on vaccination, tracing its evolution from classical models assuming homogeneously mixing (mean-field) populations and disregarding human behavior to contemporary models that account for behavioral feedback and/or population spatial/social structure. Many of the methods employed originated in statistical physics, such as lattice and network models, and their associated analytical frameworks. Similarly, the feedback loop between vaccination behavior and disease propagation forms a coupled nonlinear system with parallels in physics. The review also explores the new paradigm of digital epidemiology, where sources of digital data, such as online social media, are mined for high-resolution information on epidemiologically relevant individual behavior. Leveraging the tools and concepts of statistical physics, further aided by new sources of digital data, models capturing nonlinear interactions between behavior and disease dynamics offer a novel approach to modeling real-world phenomena and can contribute to improved health outcomes. The review concludes by discussing open problems in the field and promising directions for future research.

title: Potential outcome approach to causal inference in assessing the short term impact of air pollution on mortality

This paper reformulates the problem of assessing the short-term impact of air pollution on health using the potential outcome approach to causal inference. The study focuses on the impact of high daily levels of PM10 on mortality within two days of exposure in the metropolitan area of Milan (Italy) during the period 2003-2006. After defining the number of attributable deaths in terms of the difference between potential outcomes, the study utilizes the estimated propensity score to match each high exposure-day with a day exhibiting similar background characteristics but a lower PM10 level. Subsequently, the impact is estimated by comparing mortality between matched days. The study found that during the study period, daily exposures exceeding 40 micrograms per cubic meter were responsible for 1079 deaths (116; 2042). The impact was more pronounced among the elderly compared to younger age groups. Propensity score matching emerged as a compelling method for assessing historical impacts in this field.

title: Motion-Compensated Handheld Quantum Key Distribution System
Abstract: Mobile devices have become an indispensable part of our daily lives, used to transmit an ever-increasing volume of sensitive health, financial, and personal information. This exposure leaves us vulnerable to the escalating scale and sophistication of cyberattacks. Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) offers unconditional and future-proof data security, but its implementation for handheld mobile devices presents unique challenges. To establish security, secret keys of sufficient length need to be transmitted during the time of a handheld transaction (~1s) despite device misalignment, ambient light, and inevitable user hand movements. Transmitters and receivers should ideally be compact and cost-effective while avoiding security loopholes. This study demonstrates the first QKD transmission from a handheld transmitter with a key rate sufficient to overcome finite key effects. Using dynamic beam-steering, reference-frame-independent encoding, and fast indistinguishable pulse generation, the study achieves a secret key rate exceeding 30kb/s over a distance of 0.5m under ambient light conditions.

title: Some Models for Epidemics of Vector-Transmitted Diseases
Abstract: Vector-transmitted diseases, such as dengue fever and chikungunya, have been spreading rapidly in various parts of the world. Zika has become a serious global health concern because, while most cases are asymptomatic or mild, babies born to Zika-infected mothers may develop microcephaly and other severe birth defects. This study formulates and analyzes two epidemic models for vector-transmitted diseases, one suitable for dengue and chikungunya fever outbreaks and another incorporating direct transmission appropriate for Zika virus outbreaks. This is particularly significant as Zika is the first known disease spread both indirectly through a vector and directly (through sexual contact). In both cases, expressions for the basic reproduction number are derived, demonstrating how to use the initial exponential growth rate to estimate this number. However, for the model incorporating direct transmission, additional data would be necessary to determine the proportion of cases transmitted directly. Data from the 2015 Zika virus outbreak in Barranquilla, Colombia, has been used to fit parameters to the model developed in this study and to estimate the basic reproduction number.

title: Multi-Sensor Prognostics using an Unsupervised Health Index based on LSTM Encoder-Decoder

LSTM-ED is trained to reconstruct the time-series corresponding to the healthy state of a system. The reconstruction error is then used to compute the HI, which is subsequently employed for RUL estimation. The study evaluates its approach on publicly available Turbofan Engine and Milling Machine datasets. title: RETAIN: An Interpretable Predictive Model for Healthcare using Reverse Time Attention Mechanism
Abstract: Accuracy and interpretability are two defining characteristics of successful predictive models. This tradeoff poses challenges in medicine, where both accuracy and interpretability are paramount. This study addresses this challenge by developing the REverse Time AttentIoN model (RETAIN) for application to Electronic Health Records (EHR) data. RETAIN achieves high accuracy while maintaining clinical interpretability and is based on a two-level neural attention model that identifies influential past visits and significant clinical variables within those visits (e.g., key diagnoses). RETAIN mimics physician practice by attending to EHR data in reverse time order, so recent clinical visits receive higher attention. RETAIN was tested on a large health system EHR dataset encompassing 14 million visits completed by 263K patients over an 8-year period, demonstrating predictive accuracy and computational scalability comparable to state-of-the-art methods like RNN, along with ease of interpretability comparable to traditional models.

title: The languages of actions, formal grammars and qualitive modeling of companies
Abstract: This paper explores methods for utilizing the language of actions, formal languages, and grammars for qualitative conceptual linguistic modeling of companies as technological and human institutions. The authors anticipate that the language structure of external and internal base flows determines the structure of companies. In the structural modeling of an abstract industrial company, an internal base flow of information is constructed as a specific flow of words composed on the theoretical parts-processes-actions language. The language of procedures is identified for an external base flow of information for an insurance company. The formal stochastic grammar for the language of procedures is derived using statistical methods and is applied to understanding trends in the healthcare industry. title: Efficient real-time monitoring of an emerging influenza epidemic: how feasible?
Abstract: An effective public health response to a new epidemic depends on the ability to monitor and predict its evolution in real-time as data accumulates. The SMC algorithm significantly reduces computation time compared to standard MCMC, ensuring timely delivery of real-time epidemic assessments. title: Generic Inference on Quantile and Quantile Effect Functions for Discrete Outcomes
Abstract: Quantile and quantile effect functions are essential tools for both descriptive and causal analyses due to their clear and intuitive interpretation. Existing methods for inferring these functions, however, are not applicable to discrete random variables. This paper proposes a straightforward and practical method for constructing simultaneous confidence bands for quantile and quantile effect functions of potentially discrete random variables. This method relies on a natural transformation of simultaneous confidence bands for distribution functions, which are readily available for various problems. The proposed construction is versatile and does not depend on the specific nature of the underlying problem. It can be employed in conjunction with parametric, semiparametric, and nonparametric modeling methods for observed and counterfactual distributions, regardless of the sampling scheme. This paper applies the proposed method to analyze the distributional impact of insurance coverage on healthcare utilization and to decompose the racial test score gap distributionally. The analysis reveals that universal insurance coverage increases the number of doctor visits across the entire distribution and that the racial test score gap is negligible at young ages but widens with age due to socioeconomic factors impacting child development, particularly at the top of the distribution. These are novel and insightful empirical findings that complement previous studies that only focused on mean effects. Both applications involve discrete outcomes of interest, rendering existing inference methods unsuitable for obtaining uniform confidence bands for observed and counterfactual quantile functions and their difference - the quantile effects functions.

title: Mediation Analysis for Censored Survival Data under an Accelerated Failure Time Model
Abstract: Recent advancements in causal mediation analysis have formalized conditions for estimating direct and indirect effects in various contexts. These approaches have been extended to models for survival outcomes, including accelerated failure time (AFT) models, which are widely used in numerous health applications due to their intuitive interpretation. In this setting, it has been suggested that under standard assumptions, the "difference" and "product" methods produce equivalent estimates of the indirect effect of exposure on the survival outcome. This paper formally demonstrates that these two methods may produce significantly different estimates in the presence of censoring or truncation due to model misspecification. Specifically, while the product method remains valid under standard assumptions with independent censoring, the difference method can be biased in the presence of such censoring whenever the error distribution of the AFT model fails to be collapsible upon marginalizing over the mediator. This will invariably be the case for most choices of mediator and outcome error distributions. A notable exception arises with normal mediator-normal outcome, where both difference and product estimators are shown to be consistent in the presence of independent censoring. These findings are confirmed through simulation studies and two data applications.

title: Ultra High-Dimensional Nonlinear Feature Selection for Big Biological Data

title: On the Dynamics of Local to Global Campaigns for Curbing Gender-based Violence
Abstract: Gender-based violence (GBV) is a human-generated crisis, existing in various forms, including offline, via physical and sexual violence, and now online via harassment and trolling. While studying social media campaigns for different domains such as public health, natural crises, etc., has received attention in the literature, such studies for GBV are still in their early stages. The dynamics of campaigns responding to curb this crisis could benefit from systematic investigation. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to examine such public campaigns involving social media by organizations operating at the local, national, and global levels, aiming to answer the following research questions: (1) How do members of one campaign community engage with other campaign communities? (2) How do demographic variables such as gender affect campaign engagement in light of given regional crime statistics? (3) Is there any coordination among organizational users for campaigns with similar underlying social causes?

title: Toward Development of a New Health Economic Evaluation Definition

Academic literature offers a vast and growing variety of economic evaluation definitions, highlighting that existing definitions do not meet the requirements of economists. This study aimed to examine existing definitions and reveal their common features.

title: Instrumental variables estimation of exposure effects on a time-to-event response using structural cumulative survival models
Abstract: The use of instrumental variables for estimating the effect of an exposure on an outcome is popular in econometrics and increasingly so in epidemiology. This increasing popularity can be attributed to the natural occurrence of instrumental variables in observational studies that incorporate elements of randomization, either by design or by nature (e.g., random inheritance of genes). Instrumental variables estimation of exposure effects is well-established for continuous outcomes and, to some extent, for binary outcomes. However, it is largely lacking for time-to-event outcomes due to complications arising from censoring and survivorship bias. This paper proposes a novel approach within a class of structural cumulative survival models that parameterize time-varying effects of a point exposure directly on the scale of the survival function; these models are essentially equivalent to a semi-parametric variant of the instrumental variables additive hazards model. The paper proposes a class of recursive instrumental variable estimators for these exposure effects and derives their large sample properties along with inferential tools. The performance of the proposed method is examined through simulation studies and illustrated in a Mendelian randomization study to evaluate the effect of diabetes on mortality using data from the Health and Retirement Study. The paper further utilizes the proposed method to investigate potential benefits from breast cancer screening on subsequent breast cancer mortality based on the HIP-study.

The proposed anchoring mechanism ensures a one-to-one identifiable and interpretable mapping between the latent factors and the target comorbidities. Qualitative assessment of the empirical results by clinical experts suggests that the proposed model learns clinically interpretable phenotypes while being predictive of 30-day mortality. The proposed method can be readily adapted to any non-negative EHR data across various healthcare institutions.

The neural networks are compared to a logistic regression with several hand-engineered, clinically relevant features. The findings indicate that the representation-based learning approaches significantly outperform this baseline. title: Learning Tree-Structured Detection Cascades for Heterogeneous Networks of Embedded Devices
Abstract: We present a novel approach to learning cascaded classifiers for use in resource-constrained computing environments involving networks of heterogeneous, low-power embedded compute and sensing nodes. Each node accesses different features and potentially different computational and energy resources. Our focus is on jointly learning the parameters for all classifiers in the cascade, given a fixed cascade architecture and known costs for computation at each node. To achieve joint learning, we propose a novel method for combining classifier outputs during training, better aligning with the hard cascade setting for deployment. title: Assessing Site Effects and Geographic Transferability when Interpolating Point Referenced Spatial Data: A Digital Soil Mapping Case Study
Abstract: When making inferences about the environment, ground-truthed data often comes as point-referenced (geostatistical) observations clustered into multiple sites rather than being uniformly distributed across the area of interest. In such cases, the similarity of the dominant processes influencing the observed data across sites and the accuracy of models fitted to data from one site in predicting data from another site provide valuable information for scientists seeking to draw inferences from these data. This information can motivate a more informed second round of data modeling and provides insight into the generalizability of the developed models, indicating their performance in predicting observations from other sites. We investigated the geographic transferability of site-specific models and compared the results of using different implementations of site-specific effects in models for data combined from two sites. Given access to data on a broad collection of environmental characteristics, each potentially aiding the interpolation of our geostatistical response observations, we investigated these issues within the framework of a computationally efficient method for variable selection when the number of explanatory variables exceeds the number of observations. We applied Least Absolute Shrinkage Selection Operator (LASSO) regularized Multiple Linear Regression (MLR) fitted by the computationally efficient Least Angle Regression algorithm. The response variable in our case study, soil carbon, is of interest as a potential location for atmospheric carbon dioxide sequestration and for its positive contributions to soil health and fertility.

title: gLOP: the global and Local Penalty for Capturing Predictive Heterogeneity
Abstract: When faced with a supervised learning problem, we hope to have enough data to build a model that accurately predicts future instances. However, in practice, problems can exhibit predictive heterogeneity: most instances might be relatively easy to predict, while others might be predictive outliers for which a model trained on the entire dataset performs poorly. Identifying these outliers can help focus future data collection. We introduce gLOP, the global and Local Penalty, a framework for capturing predictive heterogeneity and identifying predictive outliers. gLOP is based on penalized regression for multitask learning, which improves learning by leveraging training signal information from related tasks. We provide two optimization algorithms for gLOP, one space-efficient and another giving the full regularization path. We also characterize uniqueness in terms of the data and tuning parameters and present empirical results on synthetic data and two health research problems.

title: The competing risks Cox model with and without auxiliary case covariates under weaker or no missing-at-random cause of failure
Abstract: When analyzing time-to-event data with multiple causes using a competing risks Cox model, the cause of failure is often unknown for some cases. The probability of a missing cause is typically assumed to be independent of the cause, given the time of the event and covariates measured before the event occurred. However, in practice, the underlying missing-at-random assumption may not hold. Motivated by colorectal cancer subtype analysis, we develop semiparametric methods for valid analysis, first when additional auxiliary variables are available for cases only. We consider a weaker missing-at-random assumption, where the missing pattern depends on observed quantities, including the auxiliary covariates. Overlooking these covariates can lead to biased estimates. We use an informative likelihood approach that yields consistent estimates even when the underlying model for missing cause of failure is misspecified. We then consider a method for conducting valid statistical analysis when there are no auxiliary covariates in the not-missing-at-random scenario. The superiority of our methods in finite samples is demonstrated by simulation study results. We illustrate the use of our method in an analysis of colorectal cancer data from the Nurses' Health Study cohort, where the traditional missing-at-random assumption appears to fail for specific molecular subtypes.

title: Identifying Unvaccinated Individuals in Canada: A Predictive Model
Abstract: Recently, the media and public health officials have become increasingly aware of the rise in anti-vaccine sentiment. Vaccinations offer numerous health benefits for immunized individuals and the general public through herd immunity. Given the rise in immunization-preventable diseases due to people opting out of routine vaccinations, we determined that Canadian health data can identify individuals over the age of 60 who chose not to get vaccinated (80.1% negative predictive value) and individuals under the age of 60 who have recently been vaccinated (96.4% positive predictive value). Using the 2009-2014 Canadian Community Health Surveys (CCHS), a probit model identified the variables most commonly associated with flu vaccination outcomes. Of 1,381 variables, 47 with the most significant marginal effects were selected, including the presence of diseases (e.g., diabetes and cancer), behavioral characteristics (e.g., smoking and exercise), exposure to the medical system (e.g., whether the individual gets a regular check-up), and a person's living situation (e.g., having young children in the household). These variables were then used to generate a Random Forest classification model, trained on the 2009-2013 dataset and tested on the 2014 dataset. We achieved an overall accuracy of 87.8% between the two final models, each using 25 classification trees with a bounded depth of 20 nodes, randomly selecting from all 47 variables. With the two proposed policies, this model can be leveraged to efficiently allocate vaccination promotion efforts. Additionally, it can be applied to future surveys, requiring only 3.6% of the variables in the CCHS for successful prediction.

title: Mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake in skeletal muscle health and disease
Abstract: Muscle cells utilize Ca2+ as a messenger to control contraction and rely on ATP to maintain intracellular Ca2+ homeostasis. Mitochondria are the primary subcellular organelles for ATP production. With a negative inner membrane potential, mitochondria take up Ca2+ from their surroundings, a process known as mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake. Under physiological conditions, Ca2+ uptake into mitochondria promotes ATP production. Excessive uptake leads to mitochondrial Ca2+ overload, activating downstream adverse responses resulting in cell dysfunction. Additionally, mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake can shape the spatiotemporal patterns of intracellular Ca2+ signaling. Malfunction of mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake is implicated in muscle degeneration. Unlike non-excitable cells, mitochondria in muscle cells experience dramatic changes in intracellular Ca2+ levels. Besides the sudden elevation of Ca2+ levels induced by action potentials, Ca2+ transients in muscle cells can range from a few milliseconds during a single twitch to minutes during tetanic contraction. This raises the question of whether mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake is fast and substantial enough to shape intracellular Ca2+ signaling during excitation-contraction coupling, posing technical challenges for quantifying the dynamic changes of Ca2+ within mitochondria. This review focuses on characterizing mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake in skeletal muscle and its role in muscle physiology and diseases.

title: Confidence sets for phylogenetic trees
Abstract: Inferring evolutionary histories (phylogenetic trees) has significant applications in biology, criminology, and public health. While our mathematical, algorithmic, and probabilistic understanding of phylogenies in their metric space is mature, rigorous inferential infrastructure is still underdeveloped. This manuscript unifies recent computational and probabilistic advances to construct tree-valued confidence sets. The procedure accounts for both the center and multiple directions of tree-valued variability. We utilize block replicates to improve testing, identifying the best-supported most recent ancestor of the Zika virus and formally testing the hypothesis that a Floridian dentist with AIDS infected two of his patients with HIV. The method demonstrates connections between variability in Euclidean and tree space, opening phylogenetic tree analysis to techniques available in the multivariate Euclidean setting.

This can be addressed by assuming that genetic features linked on a biological network are more likely to work jointly towards explaining the phenotype of interest. We review three families of methods for feature selection that integrate prior knowledge in the form of networks.

title: A Non-Parametric Control Chart For High Frequency Multivariate Data
Abstract: Support Vector Data Description (SVDD) is a machine learning technique used for single-class classification and outlier detection. SVDD-based K-charts were first introduced by Sun and Tsung for monitoring multivariate processes when the underlying distribution of process parameters or quality characteristics deviates from Normality. The method first trains an SVDD model on data obtained from stable or in-control operations of the process to obtain a threshold $R^2$ and kernel center $a$. For each new observation, its Kernel distance from the Kernel center $a$ is calculated. The kernel distance is compared against the threshold $R^2$ to determine if the observation is within the control limits. The non-parametric K-chart offers an attractive alternative to traditional control charts such as Hotelling's $T^2$ charts when the distribution of the underlying multivariate data is either non-normal or unknown. However, there are challenges when deploying K-charts in practice. The K-chart requires calculating the kernel distance of each new observation, but there are no guidelines on how to interpret the kernel distance plot and infer about shifts in process mean or changes in process variation. This limits the application of K-charts in big-data applications such as equipment health monitoring, where observations are generated at a very high frequency. In this scenario, the analyst using the K-chart is inundated with kernel distance results at a very high frequency, generally without any recourse for detecting the presence of assignable causes of variation. We propose a new SVDD-based control chart, called the $K_T$ chart, which addresses challenges encountered when using K-charts for big-data applications. The $K_T$ charts can be used to simultaneously track process variation and central tendency. We illustrate the successful use of the $K_T$ chart using the Tennessee Eastman process data.

title: Permutation, Multiscale and Modified Multiscale Entropies a Natural Complexity for Low-High Infection Level Intracellular Viral Reaction Kinetics
Abstract: Viral infectious diseases, such as HIV virus growth, pose a significant health concern. Studying intracellular viral processes can help develop drugs and understand the drug dose required to decrease HIV virus growth. Kinetics Monte Carlo simulations have been conducted to solve the Master equation concerning the dynamics of intracellular viral reaction kinetics. A scaling relationship between equilibrium time and the initial population of the template has been found as a power law,  $t_e = aN^b$, where $N$ is the number of the initial population of template species, $t_e$ is the equilibrium time, $a = 163.1$, and $b = -0.1429$, respectively. Stochastic dynamics show that increasing the initial population of the template decreases the time to equilibrium. Entropy generation has been considered in low, intermediate, and high infection levels of intracellular viral kinetics reactions during the dynamical process. Permutation, multi-scaling, and modified multi-scaling entropies have been calculated for three kinds of species in intracellular reaction dynamics: genome, structural protein, and template. Our results show that the presence of noise in the dynamical process of intracellular reaction will change the order of permutation entropy for the mentioned three species. Additionally, multi-scaling entropy is computed for the mentioned model and follows this order: template > structural protein > genome. The dependency of the permutation entropy result on the permutation order becomes small at high infection levels in intracellular viral kinetics dynamics. At short time scales in intracellular reaction dynamics, convergence of permutation entropy occurs with a medium permutation order value. In the large time scale of intracellular dynamics, permutation entropy scales with the permutation order $n$ as a scaling relation.

title: Handling Missing Data in Within-Trial Cost-Effectiveness Analysis: a Review with Future Guidelines

We examine how missing cost and effect outcome data are handled in RCT-based CEAs, complementing a previous review (covering 2003-2009, 88 articles) with a new systematic review (2009-2015, 81 articles) focusing on two different perspectives. First, we review the description of the missing data, the statistical methods used to deal with them, and the quality of the judgment underpinning the choice of these methods. Second, we provide guidelines on how information about missingness and related methods should be presented to improve the reporting and handling of missing data. Our review shows that missing data in within-RCT CEAs are still often inadequately handled, and the overall level of information provided to support the chosen methods is rarely satisfactory.

Abstract: Intensive Care Unit (ICU) mortality scoring systems attempt to predict patient mortality using predictive models with various clinical predictors, such as APACHE, SAPS, and MPM. However, most scoring systems neglect interaction terms, despite physicians intuitively considering such interactions during diagnosis. Including interaction terms in high-dimensional datasets poses challenges for most variable selection methods. This study utilizes a genetic algorithm framework for variable selection with logistic regression models to search for two-way interaction terms in a clinical dataset of adult ICU patients, with separate models built for each diagnostic category upon admission to the ICU. The models demonstrate good discrimination across categories, with a weighted average AUC of 0.84 (exceeding 0.90 for several categories). The genetic algorithm identified significant interaction terms, potentially providing greater insight into mortality prediction for healthcare professionals. The GA-selected models outperform stepwise selection and random forest models, offering greater flexibility in variable selection by optimizing any modeler-defined performance metric rather than a specific variable importance metric.

title: Excitation and reception of pure shear horizontal waves by using face-shear d24 mode piezoelectric wafers
Abstract: The fundamental shear horizontal (SH0) wave in plate-like structures is crucial for non-destructive testing (NDT) and structural health monitoring (SHM) due to its non-dispersive nature. The study shows that the face-shear d24 PZT wafer can exclusively receive the SH0 wave, filtering out Lamb waves across a wide frequency range (120 kHz to 230 kHz).  The directionality of the excited SH0 wave was investigated using face-shear d24 PZT wafers as both actuators and sensors.  Results indicate that pure SH0 wave can be excited symmetrically along two orthogonal directions (0° and 90°), maintaining over 90% of maximum amplitude when the deviation angle is within 30°.  This work has significant implications for advancing the application of SH waves in NDT and SHM.

title: Using Extreme Value Theory for Determining the Probability of Carrington-Like Solar Flares
Abstract: Space weather events can have detrimental effects on satellites, the electricity grid, navigation systems, and human health. These events are characterized by phenomena such as X-ray flares, solar energetic particle fluxes, coronal mass ejections, and various geophysical indices (Dst, Kp, F10.7).  This paper employs extreme value theory (EVT) to investigate the probability of extreme solar flares.  While previous work assumed a power law distribution for solar flares, this can lead to inaccurate estimations of return times due to uncertainties in the tails of the probability distribution function.  Using EVT and GOES X-ray flux data, we found that the expected 150-year return level is approximately an X60 flare, while a Carrington-like flare is a one in a 100-year event.  These EVT results are consistent with flare data from the Kepler space telescope mission.

title: Towards personalized causal inference of medication response in mobile health: an instrumental variable approach for randomized trials with imperfect compliance
Abstract: Mobile health studies can leverage longitudinal sensor data from smartphones to guide personalized medical interventions. Our investigations yield encouraging results in terms of power and control of type I error rates. title: Spatio-temporal Modelling of Temperature Fields in the Pacific Northwest

title: When Fashion Meets Big Data: Discriminative Mining of Best Selling Clothing Features
Abstract: The rise of e-commerce websites and the ease of online shopping have led consumers to embrace a vast array of product choices. Shopping is an essential activity in society, and understanding consumer shopping behavior is crucial for industries as well as sociology and psychology. The clothing industry is one of the most popular e-commerce categories, necessitating the analysis of popular and attractive clothing features. These insights can further enhance emerging applications like clothing recommendation and advertising. This work proposes a novel system with three key components: 1) Exploring and organizing a large-scale clothing dataset from an online shopping website. 2) Pruning and extracting images of best-selling products from clothing item data and user transaction history. 3) Utilizing a machine learning-based approach to discover fine-grained clothing attributes as representative and discriminative characteristics of popular clothing style elements. Experiments conducted on a large-scale online clothing shopping dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed system, providing valuable insights into clothing consumption trends and profitable clothing features. |||

title: A Possible Role for Entropy in Creative Cognition
Abstract: This paper argues for applying the concepts and analytical tools of entropy from physical systems to human cognition, with a focus on creative thinking. It proposes that the human mind minimizes psychological entropy, which manifests as arousal-inducing uncertainty. This uncertainty can be experienced negatively as anxiety or positively as a source of creativity, or both. The paper suggests that intrinsic creativity begins with the detection of high psychological entropy material (e.g., questions or inconsistencies), which provokes uncertainty and arousal. The mind then recursively considers this material from new perspectives until the uncertainty is resolved and entropy reaches an acceptable level. This restructuring process involves neural synchronization and dynamic binding, and may be facilitated by shifting to a more associative mode of thinking. Creative outcomes can similarly induce restructuring in others, contributing to cultural evolution through the development of more nuanced understandings. The paper concludes by advocating for cross-disciplinary research into this potential new domain of entropy studies.

title: Me, Myself and My Killfie: Characterizing and Preventing Selfie Deaths
Abstract: In recent years, taking and posting selfies has become a popular trend. However, since March 2014, 127 people have died and many more have been injured while attempting to take selfies. Researchers have studied selfies to understand the psychology of the individuals who take them and the impact they have on social media platforms. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of selfie-related casualties to determine the reasons behind these deaths. Using inferences from these incidents and an understanding of selfie features, the researchers have developed a system to raise awareness about the dangers of taking selfies in certain situations. This system uses a combination of text-based, image-based, and location-based features to classify selfies as dangerous or not. The system was tested on a dataset of 3,155 annotated selfies collected from Twitter and achieved an accuracy of 73%. Image-based features were found to be the most informative for the prediction task, and the combination of image-based and location-based features resulted in the highest accuracy. The code and dataset are publicly available at http://labs.precog.iiitd.edu.in/killfie.

title: Exploring the Pathways of Adaptation an Avatar 3D Animation Procedures and Virtual Reality Arenas in Research of Human Courtship Behaviour and Sexual Reactivity in Psychological Research
Abstract: The use of 3D animation and virtual reality in sexuality research presents numerous advantages. Beyond simply providing a means to (re)experience certain situations, these technologies offer four primary benefits: a) bespoke animated stimuli can be created and customized, which is particularly important for researching paraphilia and sexual preferences; b) stimulus production is less expensive and easier compared to real-world stimuli; c) virtual reality allows for the capture of physiological responses to stimuli, which would be difficult or impossible without relying on self-reported measures, which are especially problematic in this research domain; d) ethical, legal, and health and safety issues are less complex, as neither physical nor psychological harm is inflicted on animated characters, enabling the safe presentation of stimuli involving vulnerable targets. The animation sub-group is currently exploring different levels of production quality and animation procedures in various available software. The aim is to develop static and dynamic, interactive sexual stimuli for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. This chapter acknowledges and analyzes the ethical considerations related to the use of virtual reality in the proposed research.

title: Bayesian Heuristics for Group Decisions
Abstract: This paper presents a model of inference and heuristic decision-making in groups that is rooted in Bayes' rule but avoids the complexities of rational inference in partially observed environments with incomplete information, which are characteristic of group interactions. The model is also consistent with a dual-process psychological theory of thinking, suggesting that group members initially behave rationally (slow and deliberative mode) but rely on heuristics that replicate their early experiences in subsequent decision epochs (fast automatic mode). The model is applied to a group decision scenario where individuals receive private observations initially and aim to make the best decision based on the aggregate observations of all group members. The paper examines the implications of the information structure and the properties of the probability distributions that determine the structure of the "Bayesian heuristics" that individuals follow in the model. The paper also analyzes group decision outcomes in two classes of linear action updates and log-linear belief updates, demonstrating that inefficiencies arise in group decisions due to repeated interactions between individuals, leading to overconfident beliefs and choice shifts towards extremes. However, balanced regular structures exhibit a degree of efficiency in aggregating initial information. These findings not only validate known insights about group decision-making but also provide mechanistic interpretations for the group decision process, as well as psychological and cognitive intuitions about the group interaction model.

title: Folding with a protein's native shortcut network
Abstract: This paper proposes a complex network approach to protein folding. The network object is the network of shortcut edges present in a native-state protein (SCN0). While SCN0s are found via an intuitive message passing algorithm, they are meaningful enough that their contact order (SCN0_lnCO) correlates significantly with protein kinetic rates, regardless of protein size. Additionally, the clustering coefficient of a SCN0 (CSCN0) can be used to iteratively combine protein segments within the Restricted Binary Collision model to form the whole native structure. This simple yet effective strategy identified reasonable folding pathways for 12 small single-domain two-state folders and three non-canonical proteins: ACBP (non-two-state), Top7 (non-cooperative), and DHFR (non-single-domain, >100 residues). For two-state folders, CSCN0 is relatable to folding rates, transition-state placement, and stability. The influence of CSCN0 on folding extends to non-native structures. Moreover, SCN analysis of non-native structures suggests three fold success factors for the fast folding Villin headpiece peptide. These results support the view of protein folding as a bottom-up hierarchical process guided by native-state topology and could facilitate constructive demonstrations of this hypothesis for larger proteins.

title: How well do Network Models predict Observations? On the Importance of Predictability in Network Models
Abstract: Network models are increasingly popular for abstracting complex psychological phenomena. While research on the structure of these models has yielded significant insights, the predictive power of network models has received little attention. This is despite the fact that predictability is crucial for judging the practical relevance of network edges; for instance, in clinical practice, the predictability of a symptom indicates whether an intervention targeting that symptom through the symptom network is promising. This paper addresses this methodological gap by introducing nodewise predictability, which quantifies how well a given node can be predicted by all other nodes connected to it in the network. The paper also provides fully reproducible code examples of how to compute and visualize nodewise predictability for both cross-sectional and time-series data.

title: The Effect of Pets on Happiness: A Data-Driven Approach via Large-Scale Social Media
Abstract: Psychologists have demonstrated the positive impact of pets on their owners' happiness. For example, lonely individuals are often advised to have a pet to alleviate social isolation. Traditional psychological research methods using surveys and self-reported questionnaires are time-consuming and lack scalability. Utilizing social media as an alternative and complementary resource has the potential to address both limitations and offer new perspectives on this psychological phenomenon. This paper proposes a novel approach that leverages social media to study the effect of pets on owners' happiness. The proposed framework consists of three key components: 1) collecting user-level data from Instagram, including approximately 300,000 images from 2905 users; 2) constructing a convolutional neural network (CNN) for pet classification and, combined with timeline information, identifying pet owners and a control group; 3) measuring the confidence score of happiness by detecting and analyzing selfie images. Additionally, various demographic factors are employed to analyze the nuanced effects of pets on happiness. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, suggesting its potential application in other related domains as a large-scale, high-confidence methodology for analyzing user activity through social media.

title: The Composition and Formation of Effective Teams. Computer Science meets Psychology
Abstract: The formation of effective teams is crucial for companies to maintain competitiveness and for a wide range of emerging applications that rely on multi-agent collaboration (e.g., crowdsourcing, human-agent collaborations). This article provides an integrative perspective on team composition, team formation, and their relationship with team performance. The authors review contributions from both the computer science and organizational psychology literature on these topics. The review has two objectives: first, to identify the strengths and weaknesses of contributions from these two diverse fields; and second, to identify opportunities for cross-fertilization that would benefit both disciplines. Given the volume of existing literature, the review is not exhaustive but focuses on the most significant contributions from both fields, along with recent groundbreaking contributions that can inspire innovative research.
