title: Agencies and Science-Experiment Risk
Abstract: There is a notable lack of legal constraints on U.S. government agencies undertaking potentially risky scientific research. Some of these activities could pose a risk of killing millions or even destroying the planet. Current law leaves it to agencies to decide for themselves whether their activities fall within acceptable risk boundaries. This article explores the extent to which and under what circumstances the law should allow private actions against non-regulatory agency endeavors. Engaging with this issue is not only interesting in its own right, but it also allows us to test fundamental concepts of agency competence and the role of the courts. Two case studies provide a foundation for discussion: NASA's use of plutonium power supplies on spacecraft, which critics argue could cause millions of cancers in the event of atmospheric disintegration, and a Department of Energy particle-collider experiment (the RHIC) that allegedly poses a small risk of collapsing the Earth (via a "killer strangelet"). These extreme examples serve as a test-bed for applying insights from neoclassical economics, behavioral economics, risk-management studies, and cognitive psychology. The resulting analysis suggests that in low-probability/high-harm scenarios, agencies are likely to do a poor job of judging the acceptability of risk to the public. Instead, generalist judges working within a common-law framework may have surprising advantages. This suggests that under certain circumstances, the government should be subject to legal action that provides non-deferential review of discretionary agency actions that are non-regulatory in nature.

title: Fair prediction with disparate impact: A study of bias in recidivism prediction instruments
Abstract: Recidivism prediction instruments provide decision-makers with an assessment of the likelihood that a criminal defendant will reoffend in the future. While such instruments are gaining popularity across the country, their use is attracting considerable controversy, much of which centers on potential discriminatory bias in the risk assessments produced. This paper discusses a fairness criterion originating from the field of educational and psychological testing that has recently been applied to assess the fairness of recidivism prediction instruments. The authors demonstrate how adherence to this criterion may lead to considerable disparate impact when recidivism prevalence differs across groups.

title: Virtual Embodiment: A Scalable Long-Term Strategy for Artificial Intelligence Research
Abstract: Meaning has been described as the "holy grail" of numerous scientific disciplines, ranging from linguistics and philosophy to psychology and neuroscience. Artificial intelligence (AI) is also very much part of this quest: developing sophisticated natural language semantics is crucial for achieving human-level intelligence. Embodiment theories in cognitive science suggest that human semantic representation depends on sensory-motor experience; the extensive evidence that human meaning representation is grounded in the perception of physical reality leads to the conclusion that meaning must rely on a fusion of multiple (perceptual) modalities. Despite this, AI research, particularly its subdisciplines such as computational linguistics and computer vision, has primarily focused on tasks involving a single modality. This paper proposes virtual embodiment as an alternative, long-term strategy for AI research that is multi-modal in nature and allows for the scalability required to develop the field coherently and incrementally in an ethically responsible manner.

title: Modeling Heterogeneous Peer Assortment Effects using Finite Mixture Exponential Random Graph Models
Abstract: This article develops a class of models called Sender/Receiver Finite Mixture Exponential Random Graph Models (SRFM-ERGMs) that enable inference on networks. This class of models extends the existing Exponential Random Graph Modeling framework to allow analysts to model unobserved heterogeneity in the effects of nodal covariates and network features. An empirical example regarding substance use among adolescents is presented, and simulations across a variety of conditions are used to evaluate the performance of this technique. The authors conclude that unobserved heterogeneity in the effects of nodal covariates can be a major cause of mis-fit in network models, and the SRFM-ERGM approach can alleviate this misfit. The implications for the analysis of social networks in psychological science are discussed.

title: Psycho-Demographic Analysis of the Facebook Rainbow Campaign
Abstract: Over the past decade, online social media has profoundly impacted how people engage in social activism. For example, approximately 26 million Facebook users expressed their support for marriage equality by overlaying their profile pictures with rainbow-colored filters. Similarly, hundreds of thousands of users changed their profile pictures to a black dot to condemn incidents of sexual violence in India. This act of demonstrating support for social causes by changing online profile pictures is referred to as pictivism. This paper analyzes the psycho-demographic profiles, social networking behavior, and personal interests of users who participated in the Facebook Rainbow campaign. The study is based on a sample of about 800,000 detailed Facebook user profiles, combining questionnaire-based psychological scores with Facebook profile data. The analysis provides detailed insights into the psycho-demographic profiles of campaign participants. The study found that personality traits such as openness and neuroticism are positively associated with the likelihood of supporting the campaign, while conscientiousness exhibits a negative correlation. Additionally, females, religious disbelievers, democrats, and adults in the age group of 20 to 30 years are more likely to participate in the campaign. The research further confirms findings from previous studies suggesting that a user is more likely to participate in an online campaign if a large fraction of their friends are already doing so. The paper also developed machine learning models for predicting campaign participation. Users' personal interests, approximated by Facebook user like activity, turned out to be the best indicator of campaign participation. The results demonstrate that a predictive model leveraging these features accurately identifies campaign participants (AUC=0.76).

title: Employing Game theory and Multilevel Analysis to Predict the Factors that affect Collaborative Learning Outcomes: An Empirical Study
Abstract: This study proposes a model that predicts the social and psychological factors influencing individuals' collaborative learning outcomes in group projects. The model is based on two theories: multilevel analysis and cooperative game theory (CGT). In CGT, a group of players form a coalition, and a set of payoffs is assigned to each member in the coalition. Shapley values are a key solution concept in CGT, representing a fair and efficient distribution of payoffs among coalition members. The proposed approach was applied to a sample of 78 freshman students in their first semester, studying a philosophical thinking course taught by the same professor. Data collection tools included self-assessments, peer assessments, quizzes, and observations. The research concluded that learning outcomes and contribution are best predicted by the extent of engagement with the content being taught. Personality traits and learning styles had the least impact on contribution. Additionally, results show that Shapley values can be used as effective predictors of individuals' learning outcomes. These findings indicate that CGT can serve as a valuable tool for analyzing interactions that occur in collaborative learning.

title: Mean Field Dynamics of Graphs II: Assessing the Risk for the Development of Phase Transitions in Empirical Data
Abstract: Psychological disorders like major depressive disorder can be viewed as complex dynamical systems. By analyzing symptom activation patterns, one can investigate the dynamic behavior of individuals to determine if they are at risk for sudden changes (phase transitions). This paper demonstrates how a mean field approximation can be used to reduce a dynamic multidimensional system to a one-dimensional system for analyzing dynamics. Using maximum likelihood estimation, the parameter of interest can be estimated, which, in combination with a bifurcation diagram, reflects the risk of experiencing a transition. After validating the proposed method with simulated data, the researchers applied it to three empirical examples, validating the method using data containing a transition and demonstrating its use in clinical and general samples. Results show an increased risk for a transition when the transition actually occurred, and that members of both the clinical and general samples were not susceptible to transitions from a healthy to a depressed mood, or vice versa. The authors conclude that the mean field approximation is valid for assessing the risk of a transition and could potentially aid clinical therapists in the treatment of depressed patients.

title: Is psychosis caused by defective dissociation? An Artificial Life model for schizophrenia
Abstract: Both neurobiological and environmental factors are known to play a role in the origin of schizophrenia, but no model has been proposed that accounts for both. This paper presents a functional model of schizophrenia that merges psychodynamic elements with ingredients borrowed from the theory of psychological trauma, evidencing the interplay of traumatic experiences and defective mental functions in the pathogenesis of the disorder. The model proposes that dissociation is a standard tool used by the mind to protect itself from emotional pain. In cases of repeated trauma, the mind learns to adopt selective forms of dissociation to avoid pain without losing touch with external reality. The authors conjecture that this process is defective in schizophrenia, where dissociation is either too weak, leading to positive symptoms, or too strong, causing negative symptoms.

title: Quantifying moral foundations from various topics on Twitter conversations
Abstract: Moral foundations theory explains variations in moral behavior using innate moral foundations: Care, Fairness, Ingroup, Authority, and Purity, along with experimental support. However, little is known about the roles of and relationships between these foundations in everyday moral situations. To address this gap, the researchers quantify moral foundations from a large amount of online conversations (tweets) about moral topics on the social media site Twitter. They measure moral loadings using latent semantic analysis of tweets related to topics on abortion, homosexuality, immigration, religion, and immorality in general, demonstrating how the five moral foundations function in spontaneous conversations about moral violating situations. The results indicate that although the five foundations are mutually related, Purity is the most distinctive foundation, and Care is the most dominant foundation in everyday conversations on immorality. This study highlights a new possibility of using natural language processing and social big data for moral psychology research.

title: Honing Theory: A Complex Systems Framework for Creativity
Abstract: This paper proposes a theory of creativity, referred to as honing theory, which posits that creativity fuels the process by which culture evolves through communal exchange amongst minds that are self-organizing, self-maintaining, and self-reproducing. According to honing theory, minds, like other self-organizing systems, modify their contents and adapt to their environments to minimize entropy. Creativity begins with the detection of high psychological entropy material, which provokes uncertainty and arousal. The creative process involves recursively considering this material from new contexts until it is sufficiently restructured that arousal dissipates. Restructuring involves neural synchrony and dynamic binding, and may be facilitated by temporarily shifting to a more associative mode of thought. A creative work may similarly induce restructuring in others, and thereby contribute to the cultural evolution of more nuanced worldviews. Since lines of cultural descent connecting creative outputs may exhibit little continuity, it is proposed that cultural evolution occurs at the level of self-organizing minds, outputs reflecting their evolutionary state. Honing theory addresses challenges not addressed by other theories of creativity, such as the factors that guide restructuring, and in what sense creative works evolve. Evidence comes from empirical studies, an agent-based computational model of cultural evolution, and a model of concept combination.

title: Clinical and Educational Applications of LIVEIA: An Immersive Visualization Environment
Abstract: The association between light and psychological states has a long history and permeates our language. LIVEIA (Light-based Immersive Visualization Environment for Imaginative Actualization) is a new immersive, interactive technology that uses physical light as a metaphor for visualizing people's inner lives and relationships. This paper outlines its educational value as a tool for understanding and explaining aspects of how people think and interact, and its potential therapeutic value as a form of art therapy in which the artwork has straightforwardly interpretable symbolic meanings.

title: A Music-generating System Inspired by the Science of Complex Adaptive Systems
Abstract: This paper presents NetWorks (NW), an interactive music generation system that uses a hierarchically clustered scale-free network to generate music ranging from orderly to chaotic. NW was inspired by the Honing Theory of creativity, which posits that human-like creativity relies on (1) the ability to self-organize and maintain dynamics at the "edge of chaos" using something akin to "psychological entropy," and (2) the capacity to shift between analytic and associative processing modes. At the "edge of chaos," NW generates patterns that exhibit emergent complexity through coherent development at low, mid, and high levels of musical organization, often suggesting goal-seeking behavior. The architecture consists of four 16-node modules: one each for pitch, velocity, duration, and entry delay. The Core allows users to define how nodes are connected and rules that determine when and how nodes respond to their inputs. The Mapping Layer allows users to map node output values to MIDI data that is routed to software instruments in a digital audio workstation. By shifting between bottom-up and top-down processing, NW transitions between analytic and associative processing modes.

title: Geometric-optical illusions and Riemannian geometry
Abstract: Geometric-optical illusions (GOIs) are a type of visual illusion characterized by the distortion of a simple geometric figure ("target") when superimposed with an array of non-intersecting curved elements ("context"). This research focuses on circular targets and proposes a model based on hyperbolic geometry to explain the perceived deformations. The study presents computational methods for predicting these distortions in different contexts and reports the results of a psychophysical pilot experiment. The findings suggest a common scheme for modeling GOIs associated with various target curves, expanding upon previous research.

title: Neural correlates of self-generated imagery and cognition throughout the sleep cycle
Abstract: Humans have long recognized the diverse nature of sleep and its accompanying mental content. The findings suggest intriguing correlations between sleep stage, brain activity, and subjective experiences, particularly in the relationship between brain network activation and dream mentation.

title: Comparative study of LSA vs Word2vec embeddings in small corpora: a case study in dreams database

LSA outperformed Skip-gram in smaller training sets, demonstrating its ability to capture word associations in dream reports, even with limited data or low-frequency words. The study proposes LSA as a valuable tool for exploring word relationships in dreams, offering new insights into this classic psychological research area.

title: Psychologically Motivated Text Mining

The method is applied to data in three languages, demonstrating the psychological validity of the identified patterns.

title: Atlantis, Carli and Bailly, and a short discussion about 'demonstration' in cultural astronomy
Abstract: Scholars in the late 18th century debated the myth of Atlantis, considering the evolution of Earth, the origins of civilization, and the development of astronomy. Atlantis was seen as the cradle of civilization, with J.S. Bailly proposing its location in the Arctic and G.R. Carli advocating for the classical Atlantic Ocean position. The arguments and counterarguments between Bailly and Carli highlight the challenges inherent in cultural astronomy and archaeoastronomy, particularly regarding the role of evidence and demonstration. This paper briefly discusses methodological problems in these fields and suggests a possible psychological limit to understanding these topics.

title: Inflow process of pedestrians to a confined space
Abstract: Understanding human crowd movement is essential for designing safe and comfortable urban spaces. However, the complex decision-making processes and various factors involved make it difficult to measure precise pedestrian interactions. This study investigates human reactions to other individuals in a confined area (e.g., an elevator), focusing on the "inflow process" where pedestrians successively enter and seek temporary positions. Unlike traditional bottleneck and corridor scenarios, the inflow process offers a wider range of motion options, highlighting the relevance of other factors. By analyzing pedestrian density profiles, the study reveals non-trivial patterns of space acquisition, suggesting the importance of psychological and anticipatory factors beyond those discussed in previous literature. Four major factors, namely flow avoidance, distance cost, angle cost, and boundary preference, are identified and confirmed through a simple mathematical model, providing insights for optimizing design and safety in crowded public spaces and transportation.

title: Perceptual uniform descriptor and Ranking on manifold: A bridge between image representation and ranking for image retrieval
Abstract: Image retrieval systems often face the challenge of incompatibility between image descriptors and ranking methods. Using manifold ranking and PUD, the study implements image retrieval, achieving significant accuracy improvements on various benchmark datasets. Experiments on Ukbench and Corel-1K demonstrate the effectiveness of PUD, achieving higher scores compared to other holistic and even some local image descriptors and state-of-the-art retrieval methods.

title: The face-space duality hypothesis: a computational model
Abstract: Valentine's face-space model proposes a multidimensional psychological representation of faces based on their perceived properties. The face-space duality hypothesis is introduced to capture both invariant and dynamic facial features, validated through a mathematical approach to dimensionality reduction.  Experiments using real facial images demonstrate the model's ability to support both identity and expression recognition and confirm the anticipated twofold structure.

title: From Facial Expression Recognition to Interpersonal Relation Prediction
Abstract: Interpersonal relationships are defined by the association between individuals, encompassing traits like warmth, friendliness, and dominance. The network demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on facial expression recognition benchmarks. To predict interpersonal relationships, the expression recognition network is integrated into a Siamese model. Extensive experiments showcase the model's capability in mining mutual context from facial images for accurate fine-grained interpersonal predictions.

title: NPCs Vote! Changing Voter Reactions Over Time Using the Extreme AI Personality Engine
Abstract: The question of whether non-player characters (NPCs) in video games can possess human-realistic personalities that evolve over time based on interactions is explored. title: NPCs as People, Too: The Extreme AI Personality Engine

title: Can the Many-Worlds-Interpretation be probed in Psychology?
Abstract: This paper explores the measurement problem and quantum-to-classical transition within a framework of a universally valid quantum formalism, governed by the Schrödinger equation. Decoherence, a mechanism for describing the measurement process, is highlighted as resulting in a "Many-Worlds" or "Many-Minds" scenario. However, the existence of incomplete information about the environment entangled with the object system during measurement is a crucial assumption for decoherence. The paper delves into the origin of this information, drawing upon recent models of consciousness in neuroscience. This investigation leads to a modern perspective on the von-Neumann-Wigner interpretation, suggesting that the information available to the observer's consciousness is critical for defining the environment. While challenging to probe physically, this interpretation implies that the quantum-to-classical transition may be testable in psychological studies.

title: Visual Stability Prediction and Its Application to Manipulation
Abstract: Humans and animals rely on understanding physical phenomena to navigate and interact with uncertain environments containing novel objects and configurations. Developmental psychology highlights the early acquisition of these skills in infants. The study explores the feasibility and quality of learning stability prediction in a data-driven manner, bypassing the need for explicit simulation during runtime.  A learning-based approach, trained on simulated data, is presented, predicting the stability of towers built from wooden blocks under varying conditions and quantities related to potential falls. The approach is evaluated on synthetic data and compared to human judgments, further extended to reason about future tower states, enabling successful stacking.

title: Conformity in virtual environments: a hybrid neurophysiological and psychosocial approach
Abstract: This study investigates the effects of a virtual environment on social conformity, focusing on the impact of different task types and psychological variables on social influence. Additionally, five psychological scales are administered to assess various personality traits. The results, obtained from 181 university students, reveal that conformity increases with task ambiguity, but normative influence is significantly weaker in virtual environments compared to face-to-face settings.  While psychological traits did not significantly influence conformity, they affected response times. ERP analysis detected N200 and P300 components distinguishing conformist and non-conformist subjects, along with other components, showcasing consistent differences between the two groups.

title: Formalizing Neurath's Ship: Approximate Algorithms for Online Causal Learning
Abstract: Higher-level cognition relies on the ability to learn models of the world, characterized computationally as a structure-learning problem aiming to identify causal relationships between elements. However, the computational cost of performing exact Bayesian inference over causal models increases rapidly with the number of elements.  This suggests that cognitive processes underlying causal learning must be approximate.  The study draws inspiration from Neurath's ship metaphor in philosophy of science, which views theory change as a gradual, stochastic process shaped by limitations in abandoning current theories and the pursuit of ground truth. Based on this metaphor and algorithms for approximating Bayesian inference in machine learning, the paper proposes an algorithmic model of causal structure learning where learners update a single global hypothesis locally as they gather evidence. The study presents a scheme for understanding how learners choose informative interventions to elucidate causal system workings under these limitations.  The findings support the approach through the analysis of four experiments.

title: The Gaussian Graphical Model in Cross-sectional and Time-series Data
Abstract: This paper discusses the Gaussian graphical model (GGM), an undirected network of partial correlation coefficients, and its utility as an exploratory data analysis tool. The GGM reveals which variables predict each other, enables sparse modeling of covariance structures, and can illuminate potential causal relationships between observed variables. The study explores GGM's applicability in three types of psychological datasets: cross-sectional data, temporally ordered datasets (time series), and a mixture of the two. In time-series analysis, GGM can model the residual structure of a vector-autoregression analysis (VAR), resulting in temporal and contemporaneous networks.  Analyzing data from multiple subjects allows for the creation of a GGM on the covariance structure of stationary means, known as the between-subjects network. The paper provides interpretations of these models and proposes estimation methods implemented in the R packages graphicalVAR and mlVAR.  Two empirical examples and simulation studies showcase the methods and their interpretation.

title: When categorization-based stranger avoidance explains the uncanny valley: A comment on MacDorman & Chattopadhyay (2016)
Abstract: The uncanny valley phenomenon describes the eerie feeling evoked by artificial objects resembling humans to a certain degree. This Discussions paper examines two cognitive psychology explanations: object categorization and realism inconsistency. While MacDorman and Chattopadhyay (2016) presented evidence supporting the latter, the study argues that their findings remain consistent with categorization-based stranger avoidance. The paper explores why categorization-based stranger avoidance remains a viable explanation, despite the evidence, and how it offers a more inclusive explanation for the eeriness experienced in the uncanny valley.

title: Identifying Dogmatism in Social Media: Signals and Models
Abstract: This study investigates linguistic and behavioral features of dogmatism in social media, developing statistical models to identify dogmatic comments.  The model is built upon a corpus of Reddit posts, collected across diverse topics and annotated through crowdsourcing.  The research operationalizes key aspects of dogmatism, described by existing psychology theories, finding predictive power in their presence.  The study identifies new signals of dogmatism, such as the tendency of dogmatic posts to avoid signaling cognitive processes.  When analyzing millions of Reddit posts using the predictive model, the study reveals that dogmatism appears as a deeper personality trait, consistent across domains.  Additionally, users engaging in dogmatic comments tend to exhibit increased dogmatism themselves.

title: Engagement Detection in Meetings
Abstract: Group meetings are frequent business events aimed at developing and conducting project work, such as Big Room design and construction meetings. The Engagement Framework integrates multimodal information from 2D and 3D imaging and sound, detecting and evaluating engagement at individual and group levels. The study utilizes empirical data from the Konica Minolta, Inc. lab to test initial applications of the framework, presenting examples of engagement classifiers based on research in psychology, communication, and human-computer interaction.  The paper illustrates the accuracy of these classifiers in dyadic interactions and discusses potential extensions to complex group collaboration settings and future feedback implementations.

title: Semantics derived automatically from language corpora contain human-like biases
Abstract: Artificial intelligence and machine learning are experiencing rapid growth, raising concerns about their potential to perpetuate existing prejudices and unfairness. This study demonstrates that human-like semantic biases arise from the application of standard machine learning to everyday language. The research replicates a spectrum of standard human biases, similar to those identified through the Implicit Association Test and other psychological studies, using a widely used statistical machine-learning model—GloVe word embedding—trained on a corpus of web text.  The findings indicate that language itself contains retrievable and accurate imprints of historical biases, including morally neutral biases, problematic biases related to race and gender, and veridical biases reflecting existing distributions. These regularities are captured by machine learning alongside semantic information.  Beyond empirical findings, the study contributes new methods for evaluating bias in text: the Word Embedding Association Test (WEAT) and the Word Embedding Factual Association Test (WEFAT). The implications of these findings extend beyond AI and machine learning, impacting psychology, sociology, and ethics, suggesting that mere exposure to everyday language could account for the observed biases. |||

title: Practical optimal experiment design with probabilistic programs
Abstract: Scientists often design experiments to differentiate between competing theories. This process demands patience, meticulousness, and ingenuity, as the space of potential experiments is vast. However, we can automate the search for effective experiments by representing theories as formal models and explicitly defining the experimental space. This automation aims to identify experiments with high expected information gain. We propose a comprehensive and principled approach to experiment design based on probabilistic programming languages (PPLs). PPLs provide a clean separation between problem declaration and solution, allowing scientists to automate experiment design simply by specifying their model and experiment spaces within the PPL, without needing to worry about the intricacies of information gain calculation. We demonstrate our system's effectiveness in two case studies drawn from cognitive psychology, where we use it to design optimal experiments in the domains of sequence prediction and categorization. Empirical validation strongly supports the optimality of our automatically designed experiments. We conclude by highlighting several intriguing questions for future research.

title: Aristotle vs. Ringelmann: On Superlinear Production in Open Source Software
Abstract: Organizations exist because they offer enhanced production gains compared to horizontal resource allocation mechanisms like markets. The open source movement is considered a novel form of peer-production organization, bridging the gap between hierarchically structured firms and markets. However, to establish itself as a unique organizational form, open source must demonstrate measurable production gains. The open source movement presents a fascinating subject for studying this aspect. We analyze and contrast two opposing perspectives recently reported in the literature. Sornette et al. discovered a superlinear production mechanism, quantifying Aristotle's adage: "the whole is more than the sum of its parts." Conversely, Scholtes et al. found opposing results, referencing the work of Maximilien Ringelmann, a French agricultural engineer (1861-1931), who observed that individual group members become less productive as group size increases. The topic of collective intelligence has intrigued numerous researchers in social sciences and social psychology, along with management practitioners seeking to improve team performance. While the Ringelmann effect is frequently observed in research and practice case studies, the superlinear effect discovered by Sornette et al. is novel and may challenge conventional wisdom. We compare these two theories, assess their strengths and weaknesses, and discuss how they have been tested using empirical data. Our analysis suggests that they may not be as contradictory as claimed by Scholtes et al.

title: Adapting Deep Network Features to Capture Psychological Representations
Abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated increasing success in solving classic perception problems such as object recognition, semantic segmentation, and scene understanding, often achieving or exceeding human-level accuracy. This success partly stems from DNNs' ability to learn useful representations of high-dimensional inputs, a challenge that humans must also overcome. We investigate the relationship between the representations learned by these networks and human psychological representations derived from similarity judgments. We find that deep features learned for object classification account for a significant portion of the variance in human similarity judgments for a set of animal images. However, these features do not capture certain qualitative distinctions that are crucial to human representations. To address this limitation, we develop a method for adapting deep features to align with human similarity judgments, resulting in image representations that have the potential to expand the scope of psychological experiments.

title: HyperLex: A Large-Scale Evaluation of Graded Lexical Entailment
Abstract: We introduce HyperLex, a dataset and evaluation resource that quantifies the extent of semantic category membership, also known as the type-of relation, hyponymy-hypernymy, or lexical entailment (LE) relation between 2,616 concept pairs. Cognitive psychology research has established that typicality and category/class membership are computed in human semantic memory as a gradual rather than binary relation. However, most NLP research and existing large-scale inventories of concept category membership (WordNet, DBPedia, etc.) treat category membership and LE as binary. To address this issue, we engaged hundreds of native English speakers to indicate typicality and strength of category membership between a diverse range of concept pairs on a crowdsourcing platform. Our results confirm that category membership and LE are indeed more gradual than binary. We then compare these human judgments with the predictions of automatic systems, revealing a significant gap between human performance and state-of-the-art LE, distributional, and representation learning models. We observe substantial differences between the models themselves. We propose a pathway for enhancing semantic models to bridge this discrepancy and highlight future application areas for improved graded LE systems.

title: Personalized Emphasis Framing for Persuasive Message Generation

We demonstrate how the analysis results can be utilized in automated personalized content selection for generating persuasive messages.

title: Cognitive Science in the era of Artificial Intelligence: A roadmap for reverse-engineering the infant language-learner
Abstract: During their first years of life, infants learn the languages of their environment at an astonishing speed despite substantial cross-cultural variations in the quantity and complexity of available language input. This fundamental fact remains elusive to current cognitive and linguistic theories. Recent advancements in engineering sciences, particularly machine learning and wearable technology, hold the promise of revolutionizing the study of cognitive development. Machine learning offers powerful learning algorithms capable of achieving human-like performance on numerous linguistic tasks. Wearable sensors capture vast amounts of data, enabling the reconstruction of infants' sensory experiences in their natural environment. The project of "reverse engineering" language development, i.e., constructing an effective system that emulates infants' achievements, appears within reach. We analyze the conditions under which such a project can contribute to our scientific understanding of early language development. We argue that computational models should address the full complexity of the learning situation and take as input the raw sensory signals available to infants, rather than focusing on sub-problems or simplifying the data. This implies the need for: (1) accessible but privacy-preserving repositories of home data that are widely shared, (2) models evaluated at different linguistic levels through a benchmark of psycholinguistic tests passable by both machines and humans alike, and (3) linguistically and psychologically plausible learning architectures scaled up to real data using probabilistic/optimization principles from machine learning. We discuss the feasibility of this approach and present preliminary results.

title: Psychologically inspired planning method for smart relocation task
Abstract: Behavior planning is recognized as a fundamental cognitive function essential for any cognitive architecture of a control system used in robotics. While many prevalent planning algorithms employed in these systems are developed using only Artificial Intelligence approaches and models, they fail to consider the extensive results of cognitive experiments. Consequently, there is a pressing need for novel behavior planning methods suitable for modern cognitive architectures designed for robot control. This work presents and examines one such method within a specific class of navigation tasks known as smart relocation tasks. The method relies on a hierarchical two-level model of abstraction and knowledge representation, encompassing symbolic and subsymbolic levels. At the symbolic level, a sign world model is used for knowledge representation, and the hierarchical planning algorithm, PMA, is utilized for planning. At the subsymbolic level, the task of path planning is addressed and resolved as a graph search problem. We analyze the interaction between both planners and describe inter-level interfaces and feedback loops. Preliminary experimental results are presented.

title: The Python user interface of the elsA cfd software: a coupling framework for external steering layers

This approach enhances the success of complex simulations. Alongside describing the technical aspects of the interface, we strive to highlight the salient points from a psychological perspective on user experience (UX). We emphasize the differences between user interfaces and pure data management systems like cgns.

title: Towards Personality-Aware Recommendation
Abstract: In recent years, the emergence of new online shopping methods has significantly simplified and accelerated the process of purchasing products and services. In this evolving context, personality plays a pivotal role in consumer decision-making during shopping. This influence is driven by two primary factors: (1) psychological factors such as impulsiveness impact buying choices, and (2) certain consumers are more susceptible to making impulse purchases than others. To our knowledge, the impact of personality factors on advertisements has been largely disregarded in the realm of recommender systems. This work proposes a highly innovative research approach that utilizes a personality perspective to determine the unique associations between consumer buying tendencies and advertisement recommendations. The lack of a publicly available benchmark for computational advertising hinders both the exploration of this intriguing research direction and the evaluation of state-of-the-art algorithms. We introduce the ADS Dataset, a publicly available benchmark for computational advertising enriched with Big-Five users' personality factors and 1,200 personal user pictures. The proposed benchmark facilitates two primary tasks: rating prediction for 300 real advertisements (including Rich Media Ads, Image Ads, and Text Ads) and click-through rate prediction. Furthermore, this work conducts experiments, reviews various evaluation criteria used in the literature, and provides a library for each within a unified toolbox.

title: Adaptive Artificial Intelligence in Games: Issues, Requirements, and a Solution through Behavlets-based General Player Modelling
Abstract: We present the final installment of a series of three academic essays exploring the question of how and why to build a generalized player model. We propose that a general player model requires parameters for subjective experience of play, encompassing player psychology, game structure, and actions of play. Based on this proposition, we formulate three interconnected research questions: RQ1: What is a necessary and sufficient foundation for a general player model? RQ2: Can such a foundation enhance the performance of a computational intelligence-based player model? RQ3: Can such a player model improve the efficacy of adaptive artificial intelligence in games?  We present the arguments behind these research questions in each of the three essays, published as preprints. The third essay, in this preprint, argues that adaptive game artificial intelligence will be enhanced by a generalized player model. This is because games are inherently human artifacts, requiring some encoding of the human perspective to effectively autonomously respond to individual players. The player model informs the necessary constraints on the adaptive artificial intelligence. A generalized player model is not only more efficient than a per-game solution but also allows for comparisons between games, making it a valuable tool for studying play in general. We define the concept and meaning of an adaptive game. Drawing on first principles from the games research literature, we propose requirements for functional adaptive AI. We propose solutions to these requirements based on a formal model approach to our existing "Behavlets" method for psychologically-derived player modeling: Cowley, B., & Charles, D. (2016). Behavlets: a Method for Practical Player Modelling using Psychology-Based Player Traits and Domain Specific Features. User Modeling and User-Adapted Interaction, 26(2), 257-306.

title: Neural scaling laws for an uncertain world
Abstract: Autonomous neural systems must efficiently process information across a diverse range of novel environments, which may exhibit significantly different statistical properties. We address the problem of optimally distributing receptors along a one-dimensional continuum, guided by the following design principles. First, neural representations of the world should adhere to a neural uncertainty principle, making as few assumptions as possible about the statistical structure of the world. Second, neural representations should convey, as much as possible, equivalent information about environments with different statistics. The results of these arguments resemble the structure of the visual system and provide a natural explanation for the behavioral Weber-Fechner law, a foundational concept in psychology. The generality of this derivation suggests that similar scaling relationships should be observed not only in sensory continua but also in neural representations of "cognitive" one-dimensional quantities like time or numerosity.

title: Re-presenting a Story by Emotional Factors using Sentimental Analysis Method
Abstract: Remembering an event is influenced by personal emotional status. We obtained summaries of a story, Chronicle of a Death Foretold (Gabriel García Márquez, 1981), from them. We implemented a sentiment analysis model based on a convolutional neural network (LeCun & Bengio, 1995) to evaluate each summary. Drawing on the principle of transfer learning (Pan & Yang, 2010), we collected 38,265 movie review data to train the model and then used it to score summaries for each student. The results of CES-D and PANAS demonstrate the relationship between emotion and memory retrieval: depressed individuals exhibited a tendency to represent the story more negatively and appeared less expressive. Individuals high in PANAS (full of emotion) retrieved their memories more expressively than others, utilizing more negative words. Our study contributes in two key ways: (1) elucidating the connection between emotion and its impact during memory storage and retrieval, and (2) proposing objective methods for evaluating the intensity of emotion in natural language format using a sentiment analysis model.

title: Pseudo-Centroid Clustering
Abstract: Pseudo-Centroid Clustering replaces the traditional concept of a centroid, expressed as a center of gravity, with the notion of a pseudo-centroid (or a coordinate-free centroid). This approach has the advantage of applying to clustering problems where points lack numerical coordinates (or categorical coordinates translated into numerical form). Such problems, for which classical centroids do not exist, are particularly relevant in social sciences, marketing, psychology, and economics, where distances are not computed from vector coordinates but rather expressed in terms of characteristics such as affinity relationships, psychological preferences, advertising responses, polling data, market interactions, and so forth. These distances, broadly conceived, measure the similarity (or dissimilarity) of characteristics, functions, or structures.  We formulate a K-PC algorithm analogous to a K-Means algorithm and identify two key types of pseudo-centroids: MinMax centroids and (weighted) MinSum centroids. We describe how they respectively give rise to a K-MinMax algorithm and a K-MinSum algorithm, analogous to a K-Means algorithm. The K-PC algorithms can leverage problem structure to identify special diversity-based and intensity-based starting methods for generating initial pseudo-centroids and associated clusters. Theorems for the intensity-based methods establish their ability to obtain optimal clusters of a selected size from the points available at each stage of construction. We also introduce a Regret-Threshold PC algorithm that modifies the K-PC algorithm along with an associated diversification method and a new criterion for evaluating the quality of a collection of clusters.

title: The usability canary in the security coal mine: A cognitive framework for evaluation and design of usable authentication solutions
Abstract: Over the past 15 years, researchers have identified an increasing number of security mechanisms that are so unusable that intended users either circumvent them or abandon a service rather than endure the inconvenience. In retrospect, the reasons are easily discernible: either the security task itself is excessively cumbersome and time-consuming, or it creates significant friction with users' primary task. The research presented here aims to equip designers who select and implement security mechanisms with a method for identifying the "best fit" security mechanism during the design stage. Since many usability problems have been identified with authentication, we focus on "best fit" authentication and present a framework that allows security designers not only to model the workload associated with a particular authentication method but more importantly to model it within the context of the user's primary task. We draw on results from cognitive psychology to create a method that enables designers to understand the impact of a specific authentication method on user productivity and satisfaction. In a validation study using a physical mockup of an airline check-in kiosk, we demonstrate that the model can accurately predict user performance and satisfaction. Additionally, design experts suggested personalized order recommendations similar to our model's predictions. Our model is the first to support the identification of a holistic fit between the task of user authentication and the context in which it is performed. When applied to new systems, we believe it will assist designers in understanding the usability impact of their security choices and thus develop solutions that maximize both security and user experience.

title: Bipartisanship breakdown, functional networks and forensic analysis in Spanish 2015 and 2016 national elections
Abstract: This paper presents a social network and forensic analysis of the vote counts from Spanish national elections held in December 2015 and their subsequent election in June 2016. Vote counts are extracted at the municipal level, resulting in an exceptionally high-resolution dataset with over 8,000 samples. We begin by examining the phenomenon of bipartisan breakdown by analyzing the spatial distributions of several bipartisan indices. Our findings indicate that this breakdown is more pronounced near cosmopolitan and densely populated areas and less significant in rural areas where bipartisanship remains prevalent. The evolution of bipartisanship mildly consolidates in the 2016 round, with some evidence of bipartisanship reinforcement, which we hypothesize is due to psychological mechanisms of risk aversion. In the third stage, we explore the extent to which vote data is reliable by applying forensic techniques to vote statistics. We first investigate the conformance of first digit distributions to Benford's law for each of the main political parties. The results and interpretations are mixed and vary across different levels of aggregation. We find a general good quantitative agreement at the national scale for both municipalities and precincts, but systematic nonconformance at the level of individual precincts. As a complementary metric, we further explore the co-occurring statistics of vote share and turnout, finding a mild tendency for clusters of the conservative party to smear out towards the area of high turnout and vote share. This pattern has been previously interpreted as a possible sign of incremental fraud. In all cases, results are qualitatively similar between the 2015 and 2016 elections.

title: Bayesian emulation for optimization in multi-step portfolio decisions
Abstract: We discuss the Bayesian emulation approach to computationally solving multi-step portfolio studies in financial time series. "Bayesian emulation for decisions" involves mapping the technical structure of a decision analysis problem to that of Bayesian inference in a purely synthetic "emulating" statistical model. This approach grants access to standard posterior analytic, simulation, and optimization methods that yield indirect solutions to the decision problem. We develop this in time series portfolio analysis using classes of economically and psychologically relevant multi-step ahead portfolio utility functions. Studies with multivariate currency, commodity, and stock index time series illustrate the approach and demonstrate some of the practical utility and benefits of the Bayesian emulation methodology.

title: The Effects of Cultural dimensions and Demographic Characteristics on E-learning Acceptance
Abstract: This study aims to develop and test an amalgamated conceptual framework based on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and other models from social psychology, such as the theory of reasoned action and TAM2. This framework captures the salient factors influencing user adoption and acceptance of web-based learning systems. It has been applied to the study of higher educational institutions in both developing and developed countries (e.g., Lebanon and the UK). Additionally, the framework investigates the moderating effect of Hofstede's four cultural dimensions at the individual level and a set of individual differences (age, gender, experience, and educational level) on the key determinants that influence behavioral intention to use e-learning. A total of 1,197 questionnaires were collected from students utilizing web-based learning systems at higher educational institutions in Lebanon and the UK, with opposite scores on cultural dimensions. Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) was employed to perform reliability and validity checks, and Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) in conjunction with a multi-group analysis method was used to test the hypothesized conceptual model. Our findings suggest that individual, social, cultural, and organizational factors are crucial considerations in explaining students' behavioral intentions and usage of e-learning environments. The research contributes to the literature by validating and supporting the applicability of our extended TAM in the Lebanese and British contexts, providing several prominent implications for theory and practice at individual, organizational, and societal levels.

title: A Tutorial on Regularized Partial Correlation Networks
Abstract: Recent years have witnessed the emergence of network modeling applied to moods, attitudes, and problems in the realm of psychology. We explain how regularization techniques can be effectively used to estimate a parsimonious and interpretable network structure in psychological data. Additionally, we discuss the effect of the hyperparameter that must be manually set by the researcher, how to handle non-normal data, how to determine the required sample size for a network analysis, and provide a checklist with potential solutions for problems that may arise when estimating regularized partial correlation networks.

title: EmoFit: Affect Monitoring System for Sedentary Jobs
Abstract: Emotional and physical well-being in the workplace is crucial for a positive work environment and enhanced productivity. Many employees experience a lack of motivation, ranging from mild to extreme depression, due to factors such as aversion to job responsibilities and incompatibility with coworkers or their boss. title: Risk and Ambiguity in Information Seeking: Eye Gaze Patterns Reveal Contextual Behaviour in Dealing with Uncertainty
Abstract: Information foraging connects optimal foraging theory in ecology with how humans search for information. The theory proposes that, following an information scent, the information seeker must optimize the trade-off between exploration (repeated steps in the search space) and exploitation (utilizing the encountered resources). We hypothesize that this trade-off characterizes how a user manages uncertainty and its two aspects, risk and ambiguity, in economic theory. Risk relates to the perceived quality of the currently visited information patch and can be reduced by exploiting and understanding the patch to a greater extent. Ambiguity, on the other hand, represents the opportunity cost of potentially higher quality patches elsewhere in the search space. This trade-off depends on numerous attributes, including user traits. At the two extreme ends of the spectrum, analytic and wholistic searchers employ entirely different strategies. Analytic searchers prioritize exploitation, interspersed with bursts of exploration, while wholistic searchers prefer to explore the search space first and consume later. Based on an eye-tracking study of experts' interactions with novel search interfaces in the biomedical domain, we demonstrate that perceived risk shifts the balance between exploration and exploitation in both types of users, tilting it against or in favor of ambiguity minimization. Since the pattern of behavior in information foraging is inherently sequential, risk and ambiguity minimization cannot occur simultaneously, leading to a fundamental limit on how effective this trade-off can be. This connection between information seeking and the emerging field of quantum decision theory further underscores the significance of this finding. |||

title: Bayesian Games with Intentions

title: Identifiability and testability in GRT with Individual Differences
Abstract: Silbert and Thomas (2013) demonstrated that failures of decisional separability are generally not identifiable in fully parameterized $2 \\times 2$ Gaussian GRT models. A recent extension of these models, GRTwIND, was developed to address this problem and a related issue of simultaneous identifiability of means and marginal variances. GRTwIND relies on the assumption of universal perception, where shared perceptual distributions are modified by attentional and global scaling parameters. While GRTwIND solves these issues if universal perception holds, this paper shows that GRTwIND with universal perception and subject-specific failures of decisional separability is mathematically equivalent to a model with decisional separability but lacking universal perception. We also formally prove the non-identifiability of means and marginal variances in $2 \\times 2$ GRT models, including GRTwIND. These findings precisely define the requirements for the assumption of universal perception. Based on these results and recent mathematical advancements in the GRT framework, we propose that, in addition to parameters determining location and scale, GRT models must also have parameters fixing the orthogonality of modeled perceptual dimensions, a fundamental concept in GRT. The paper concludes with a discussion of perceptual primacy and its relationship to universal perception.

title: Using instrumental variables to disentangle treatment and placebo effects in blinded and unblinded randomized clinical trials influenced by unmeasured confounders

title: Personality Traits and Echo Chambers on Facebook

title: BigEAR: Inferring the Ambient and Emotional Correlates from Smartphone-based Acoustic Big Data

BigEAR's overarching goal is to identify the wearer's mood based on activities like laughing, singing, crying, arguing, and sighing. These annotations are relevant for psychologists aiming to monitor and infer the social context of individuals coping with breast cancer. We conducted a case study on couples coping with breast cancer to understand the impact of conversations on emotional and social well-being. Current methods require psychologists to manually analyze audio recordings, which is time-consuming, costly, and demanding in terms of data coding. The BigEAR framework automates this analysis. We evaluated BigEAR's accuracy against ground truth obtained from a human rater, achieving an average accuracy of 88.76% on real-world data from couples coping with breast cancer.

title: Towards Anthropo-inspired Computational Systems: the $P^3$ Model
Abstract: This paper proposes a model aimed at providing a more cohesive framework for agent design. We identify three interconnected anthropo-centered domains operating at distinct functional levels: human physiology, psychology, and philosophy. By abstracting from these domains, we create the $P^3$ model, a multi-tier approach for addressing complex problems. The model comprises three layers: PhysioComputing, MindComputing, and MetaComputing. Finally, we present several instantiations of this model related to various IT areas, including artificial intelligence, distributed computing, software, and service engineering.

title: What is Learning Analytics about? A Survey of Different Methods Used in 2013-2015
Abstract: The field of Learning Analytics has significantly evolved since the first International Conference on Learning Analytics and Knowledge (LAK) in 2011. It combines disciplines like computer science, statistics, psychology, and pedagogy to achieve its objectives. These objectives include creating effective learning interventions, optimizing the learning environment, and improving the learning process for stakeholders. As the field matures and adapts to diverse educational settings, a comprehensive analysis of its research methods, objectives, and challenges is crucial. This paper examines publications from the LAK conference between 2013 and 2015, identifying significant research areas within Learning Analytics. We categorize research methods into seven categories with brief descriptions. Furthermore, we analyze the most cited method categories using Google Scholar. Finally, we discuss the ethical challenges and constraints affecting the field through a meta-analysis. This paper aims to assist researchers in identifying common methods employed in Learning Analytics and provide a roadmap for future research that considers privacy and ethical issues within this rapidly evolving field.

title: Robot-stated limitations but not intentions promote user assistance
Abstract: Human-Robot-Interaction (HRI) research typically focuses on robots assisting humans in achieving human-led goals or shared tasks. However, there are scenarios where robots may require human assistance for shared tasks or goal achievement. Using the ROBO-GUIDE model as a case study and drawing insights from social psychology, we examine how a robot's personality influences user cooperation. A study involving 364 participants suggests that individuals may prefer interacting with likable social robots over those designed to appear more capable. This outcome aligns with known social decision-making patterns in human interpersonal relationships. This work further emphasizes the value of social psychology in developing social robots and exploring HRI.

title: How Deep is the Feature Analysis underlying Rapid Visual Categorization?
Abstract: Rapid categorization paradigms, characterized by brief presentation times and fast behavioral responses, have a long history in experimental psychology. These tasks highlight the efficiency of our visual system in processing natural object categories. Previous studies have shown that feed-forward hierarchical models of the visual cortex accurately predict human visual decisions. Meanwhile, recent advancements in computer vision have achieved significant improvements in object recognition accuracy using increasingly deep hierarchical architectures. However, it remains unclear how well these models explain human visual decisions and what insights they offer about underlying brain processes. We conducted a large-scale psychophysics study to assess the correlation between computational models and human participants on a rapid animal vs. non-animal categorization task. We analyzed the output of different processing stages in three state-of-the-art deep networks, considering visual representations of varying complexity. Our findings show that recognition accuracy increases with higher visual processing stages, with higher-level stages even outperforming human participants on the task. However, human decisions best align with predictions from intermediate processing stages. These results suggest that humans may rely on visual features of intermediate complexity, and the complexity of representations in modern deep networks may exceed those used by humans during rapid categorization.

title: Death and Suicide in Universal Artificial Intelligence
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a widely applicable paradigm for studying intelligent behavior, with applications ranging from artificial intelligence to psychology and economics. AIXI, a universal solution to the RL problem, can learn any computable environment. A key aspect of AIXI is its definition using a mixture over semimeasures, which may not sum to 1, rather than proper probability measures. This work argues that the shortfall of a semimeasure can be interpreted as the agent's estimate of its probability of death. We formally define death for generally intelligent agents like AIXI and prove several related theorems about their behavior. Notably, we discover that agent behavior can drastically change under positive linear transformations of the reward signal, transitioning from suicidal to dogmatically self-preserving. We also show that the agent's posterior belief in its survival increases over time.

title: How to advance general game playing artificial intelligence by player modelling
Abstract: General game playing artificial intelligence has recently experienced significant advancements through techniques known as "deep learning." However, these advancements mask equally important limitations in their reliance on massive datasets, fortuitously constructed problems, and a lack of human-level complexity, including the absence of human opponents. While deep learning systems that outperform human champions, such as in Go, exist, their generalizability remains limited. The power of deep learning simultaneously exposes its weakness. Given that deep learning primarily involves clever reconfigurations of established methods, surpassing the state of the art requires forward-thinking solutions rather than simply more of the same. This paper argues that general game playing artificial intelligence will require a generalized player model. This is because games are inherently human creations, encompassing scenarios that necessitate a human-style problem-solving approach. This argument is linked to the performance of current state-of-the-art general game playing agents. The paper then outlines a concept for a formal category theoretic basis for a generalized player model. This formal model approach integrates the author's existing "Behavlets" method for psychologically-derived player modeling.

title: Predicting Human Intentions from Motion Only: A 2D+3D Fusion Approach
Abstract: This paper addresses the novel problem of predicting human intents. Neuro-psychological evidence suggests that human actions are anticipated by specific motor acts that distinguish the type of action to be performed subsequently. In other words, an actual intent can be forecasted by analyzing the kinematics of the preceding movement. To demonstrate this computationally and quantitatively, we devise a new experimental setup where, without using contextual information, we predict human intents originating from the same motor act. We frame this problem as a classification task and introduce a new multi-modal dataset consisting of motion capture marker 3D data and 2D video sequences. By analyzing similar movements in both training and test phases, we can predict the underlying intent, which is the future, never observed action. We present an extensive experimental evaluation as a baseline, customizing state-of-the-art techniques for both 3D and 2D data analysis. While video processing methods yield inferior performance, they provide complementary information to 3D data sequences. We developed a 2D+3D fusion analysis that achieves improved classification accuracies, demonstrating the superiority of the multi-modal approach for context-free prediction of human intents.

title: Psychologically based Virtual-Suspect for Interrogative Interview Training
Abstract: This paper presents the Virtual-Suspect system, a training tool for inexperienced law enforcement personnel in interrogation strategies. The system supports various scenario configurations based on historical data. The Virtual-Suspect's responses are selected based on its psychological state, which can be configured. Each interrogator statement influences the Virtual-Suspect's psychological state, potentially leading the interrogation in different directions. The model also considers the context in which statements are made. Experiments with 24 subjects demonstrate that the Virtual-Suspect's behavior is comparable to that of a human playing the role of the suspect.
label: AI

title: Aesthetical criterion in art and science
Abstract: This paper explores recent research regarding the originality of artworks in terms of self-organization within complex systems physics. The research demonstrates that the concept of originality leads to a criterion of substantial aesthetics applicable not only to fine arts but also to physics, biology, cosmology, and other fields within the framework of complex systems. This criterion is also linked to the traditional concept of personality, revealing an ontological context transcending the gnoseological dualism of subjective and objective reality characteristic of modern science and humanities. Thus, it is considered an aesthetic criterion substantiating art and science, as well as other developments of the postmodern era. The paper briefly outlines its impact on psychology, education, ecology, culture, and other humanities. |||

title: Structural balance and opinion separation in trust-mistrust social networks
Abstract: Structural balance theory, which explains how agents with mixed trust and mistrust relationships form polarized groups, has been extensively studied in sociology and psychology. Previous work has shown that structural balance is essential for polarization in networks with fixed, strongly connected relationships, where opinion dynamics are governed by DeGroot-type averaging rules. This paper extends this research by investigating two key aspects: fixed, non-strongly connected relationships and time-varying relationships. The study demonstrates that if a network contains a strongly connected subnetwork with mistrust, and this subnetwork influences the rest of the network, opinion clustering is impossible when the subnetwork is not structurally balanced. In such cases, all opinions become neutralized. However, if the subnetwork is structurally balanced, agents within it evolve into two polarized camps, and the opinions of other agents in the network align with these polarized positions. The study further shows that the opinion separation criteria hold for time-varying relationships if the conditions for fixed graphs are extended to joint graphs. These findings apply to both discrete-time and continuous-time models.

title: Engineering Deep Representations for Modeling Aesthetic Perception
Abstract: Aesthetic models in computer vision often struggle with two main shortcomings: 1) lack of descriptiveness and interpretability of handcrafted aesthetic criteria, which fail to capture region-level aesthetics, and 2) difficulty in adaptively and automatically engineering aesthetic features for diverse image sets. This paper introduces a deep architecture that learns aesthetically relevant visual attributes from Flickr1, localized by multiple textual attributes in a weakly-supervised setting. Using a bag-of-words (BoW) representation of frequent Flickr image tags, a sparsity-constrained subspace algorithm identifies a compact set of textual attributes for each image (e.g., landscape, sunset). A weakly-supervised learning algorithm then projects these image-level attributes to highly responsive image patches at pixel-level. These patches indicate where humans focus on appealing regions related to each textual attribute and are used to learn visual attributes. Inspired by psychological and anatomical studies demonstrating hierarchical human visual concept perception, the patches are normalized and fed into a five-layer convolutional neural network (CNN) to mimic this hierarchical process. The learned deep features are applied to image retargeting, aesthetics ranking, and retrieval. Both subjective and objective experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and competitiveness of this approach.

title: Functional neuroimaging of psychedelic experience: An overview of psychological and neural effects and their relevance to research on creativity, daydreaming, and dreaming
Abstract: Throughout history, humans have utilized a wide array of plant-derived substances to alter consciousness and perception. While numerous narcotics, analgesics, ordeal drugs, and other psychoactive substances have been discovered and used in ritualistic contexts by various cultures, psychedelic substances stand out due to their profound psychological effects and the highly charged political and legal atmosphere surrounding them since their widespread adoption around 50 years ago. This paper examines functional neuroimaging investigations of the neural correlates of psychedelic experiences, highlighting their connections to the psychological and neural underpinnings of creativity, daydreaming, and dreaming.

title: Textual Paralanguage and its Implications for Marketing Communications
Abstract: Both face-to-face communication and online communication convey information beyond the literal verbal message. In face-to-face conversations, paralanguage, encompassing nonverbal aspects of speech, provides contextual information that helps participants understand the intended meaning. This paper introduces the concept of textual paralanguage (TPL), defined as written manifestations of nonverbal audible, tactile, and visual elements that supplement or replace written language. TPL can be expressed through words, symbols, images, punctuation, demarcations, or combinations thereof. Using data from Twitter, Facebook, and Instagram, the paper develops a typology of textual paralanguage and presents a conceptual framework outlining the antecedents and consequences of brands' use of TPL. Implications for both theory and practice are discussed.

title: Recent reproducibility estimates indicate that negative evidence is observed over 30 times before publication
Abstract: A recent study by the Open Science Collaboration found that only 36% of published findings from psychological studies were reproducible by independent researchers. Utilizing this information along with Bayes theorem, this paper estimates the statistical power needed to produce these findings under various assumptions and calculates the expected distribution of positive and negative evidence for a range of prior probabilities of the tested hypotheses. By comparing this distribution to other findings suggesting that over 90% of publications in the psychological literature are statistically significant in support of the authors' hypothesis, the paper estimates the magnitude of publication bias. The results indicate that negative evidence was observed 30 to 200 times before one was published.

title: Understanding Social-Force Model in Psychological Principles of Collective Behavior
Abstract: Microscopic models, which simulate individual behavior and psychological status, have been developed to understand crowd behavior. The social-force model, a prominent example, has been widely used in crowd evacuation simulations. However, a disconnect exists between the model's testing results and psychological findings, leading to misunderstandings among psychologists. This paper bridges this gap by reinterpreting the social-force model from a psychological perspective, demonstrating its consistency with psychological theories on stress, including time-related and interpersonal stress. Based on this stress conception, the model is renewed at both micro and macro levels, incorporating multi-agent simulation for the microscopic view and fluid-based analysis for the macroscopic view. Individual agents' cognition and behavior are modeled as responses to environmental stimuli. Existing simulation results, such as the faster-is-slower effect, are reinterpreted through the Yerkes-Dodson law, and herding and grouping effects as well as oscillation phenomena are discussed for pedestrian crowds. In essence, the social-force model acts as a bridge between physics laws and psychological principles regarding crowd motion. This paper renews and reinterprets the model based on psychological studies.

title: A Proposal for Linguistic Similarity Datasets Based on Commonality Lists
Abstract: Similarity, a fundamental concept in psychology and linguistics, is often measured using datasets that differ in design. Psychological datasets focus on specific topics, while linguistic datasets contain words from various categories. This disparity can lead to ambiguous similarity scores, particularly for words with little in common or contrasting meanings. This paper addresses this issue by discussing the similarity collection procedure for a multi-category dataset that avoids score ambiguity. It suggests changes to the evaluation procedure to align with insights from psychological literature for word, phrase, and sentence similarity. Instead of numerical similarity scores, the paper proposes asking participants to provide lists of commonalities and differences. This approach leverages the structure of human judgments beyond pairwise similarity for model evaluation. The authors believe that this method will create datasets that more thoroughly test meaning representation models in relation to human understanding of similarity.

title: Proceedings of the 5th Workshop on Machine Learning and Interpretation in Neuroimaging (MLINI) at NIPS 2015
Abstract: This volume represents a collection of contributions from the 5th Workshop on Machine Learning and Interpretation in Neuroimaging (MLINI) at the Neural Information Processing Systems (NIPS 2015) conference. The rapid growth of machine learning has led to the increased application of modern multivariate statistical methods to various neuroimaging problems, including cognitive state detection, clinical diagnosis, and prognosis. Multivariate pattern analysis methods are designed to examine complex relationships between high-dimensional signals, such as brain images, and outcomes of interest, such as stimulus categories, mental states, or specific mental disorders. These techniques contrast with traditional mass-univariate approaches that dominated neuroimaging previously and treated each imaging measurement in isolation. The authors believe that machine learning is crucial in shaping how questions in neuroscience are framed, and that the machine-learning mindset is now impacting modern psychology and behavioral studies. They emphasize the importance of practical applications in these fields motivating research in the machine learning community. Furthermore, there is a growing interest in understanding brain function within rich naturalistic environments and scenes. Efforts are underway to move beyond highly specific paradigms focused on single functions and toward schemes for measuring interactions with natural and varied scenes. The workshop aims to identify key issues and challenges across neuroscience, neuroimaging, psychology, and machine learning, and to outline future directions and open questions in light of novel methodologies.

title: Building a Large Scale Dataset for Image Emotion Recognition: The Fine Print and The Benchmark
Abstract: Psychological research has confirmed that people experience different emotional responses to different visual stimuli. Numerous papers have been published on visual emotion analysis, particularly focusing on analyzing and predicting emotional reactions to images. Various hand-tuned features have been proposed for this purpose, demonstrating promise in analyzing carefully selected and labeled small image datasets. However, despite the success of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in other computer vision tasks, visual emotion analysis has not achieved comparable progress. This may be attributed to the lack of confidently labeled and relatively large image datasets for visual emotion analysis. This paper introduces a new dataset, starting with 3+ million weakly labeled images of different emotions and ultimately becoming 30 times larger than the current largest publicly available visual emotion dataset. The authors hope this dataset will encourage further research in visual emotion analysis. The paper also provides extensive benchmarking analyses on this large dataset using state-of-the-art methods, including CNNs.
