title: From conjecture generation by maintaining dragging to proof
Abstract: This paper proposes a hypothesis regarding the influence of different uses of maintaining dragging, either as a physical tool in a dynamic geometry environment or as a psychological tool for generating conjectures, on subsequent proof processes. Through two examples, the paper supports the hypothesis that using maintaining dragging as a physical tool may foster a cognitive rupture between the conjecturing phase and the proof, while using it as a psychological tool may foster cognitive unity between them.

title: Modeling of human society as a locally interacting product-potential networks of automaton
Abstract: Central problems in social sciences concern the social and psychological mechanisms and conditions required for the emergence and stability of human groups. This paper focuses on the stability of human groups. Using local interacting systems of automata with relations and reactions, and drawing on structural balance theory, the paper models human groups. Structural balance theory links the emergence of a human group to an actor's thoughts about another actor's treatment of them and their perception of other actors. While Cartwright and Harary's formalization of balance theory within a graph theoretical setting has yielded mathematical results related to an algebraic formulation, a deeper generalization of balance theory as smooth product-potential fields on domains allows for the development of a theory of "smooth product potential social fields." The paper reveals that all discrete product-potential systems are tightly connected to other processes, including process multiplication on randomly chosen matrices, and establishes connections between stationary measures and certain algebraic objects.

title: Exploratory graph analysis: a new approach for estimating the number of dimensions in psychological research
Abstract: The estimation of the correct number of dimensions is a long-standing problem in psychometrics. Various methods have been proposed, including parallel analysis (PA), Kaiser-Guttman's eigenvalue-greater-than-one rule, multiple average partial procedure (MAP), maximum-likelihood approaches using fit indexes like BIC and EBIC, and the less commonly used very simple structure (VSS). This paper introduces a new approach called exploratory graph analysis (EGA) to estimate the number of dimensions and compares it to traditional techniques through simulations. EGA is based on the graphical lasso with the regularization parameter specified using EBIC. The number of dimensions is verified using the walktrap algorithm, a random walk algorithm for community identification in networks. A total of 32,000 datasets were simulated to fit known factor structures, varying across factors (2 and 4), items (5 and 10), sample size (100, 500, 1000, and 5000), and correlation between factors (orthogonal, .20, .50, and .70), resulting in 64 different conditions. For each condition, 500 datasets were simulated using lavaan. Results show that EGA performs comparably to parallel analysis, EBIC, eBIC, and the Kaiser-Guttman rule in several situations, especially when the number of factors is two. Notably, EGA is the only technique that correctly estimates the number of dimensions in the four-factor structure when the correlation between factors is .7, achieving 100% accuracy for a sample size of 5,000 observations. Finally, EGA is used to estimate the number of factors in a real dataset, comparing its performance to the other six techniques tested in the simulation study.

title: WEPSAM: Weakly Pre-Learnt Saliency Model
Abstract: Visual saliency detection aims to mimic human vision psychology, which focuses on sparse, important areas within natural images. Traditionally, saliency prediction research has relied on low-level features like contrast and edges. However, recent advancements have shifted towards learning high-level semantics using ground truth eye fixation datasets. This paper introduces WEPSAM (Weakly Pre-Learnt Saliency Model), a pioneering effort in using domain-specific pre-learning on ImageNet for saliency prediction using a lightweight CNN architecture. The paper proposes a two-step hierarchical learning approach: 1) developing a framework for weakly pre-training on a large-scale dataset like ImageNet, which lacks human eye fixation maps, and 2) refining the pre-trained model on a limited set of ground truth fixations. Analysis of loss on iSUN and SALICON datasets reveals that the pre-trained network converges much faster compared to a randomly initialized network. WEPSAM also outperforms several recent state-of-the-art saliency prediction models on the challenging MIT300 dataset.

title: Estimating Psychological Networks and their Accuracy: A Tutorial Paper
Abstract: The use of psychological networks, which conceptualize psychological behavior as a complex interplay of psychological and other components, has gained popularity in various fields of psychology. While previous publications have addressed network estimation and interpretation, little work has been done to assess the accuracy and stability of network estimates. This tutorial paper aims to introduce the reader to this field and address the problem of accuracy under sampling variation. The paper first introduces the current state-of-the-art in network estimation. It then provides a rationale for investigating the accuracy of psychological networks. The paper describes how bootstrap routines can be used to assess the accuracy of estimated network connections, investigate the stability of centrality indices, and test whether network connections and centrality estimates for different variables differ. Two novel statistical methods are introduced: the correlation stability coefficient for stability assessment and the bootstrapped difference test for edge-weights and centrality indices for comparing different variables. Simulation studies are conducted to evaluate the performance of these methods. Finally, the paper presents the free R-package bootnet, which facilitates the estimation of psychological networks within a generalized framework, in addition to the proposed bootstrap methods. A tutorial, accompanied by R syntax, showcases bootnet in analyzing a dataset of 359 women with posttraumatic stress disorder available online.

title: Estimating psychopathological networks: be careful what you wish for
Abstract: Network models, which conceptualize psychopathological disorders as a complex interplay of psychological and biological components, have become increasingly popular in recent psychopathological literature. These network models often contain numerous unknown parameters, while sample sizes available in psychological research are limited. To reduce the number of free parameters, general assumptions about the true network are introduced. However, incorporating these assumptions means that the resulting network will reflect the specific structure assumed by the estimation method—a crucial and often overlooked aspect of psychopathological networks. For example, observing a sparse structure while simultaneously assuming a sparse structure does not guarantee that the true model is actually sparse. To illustrate this point, the paper discusses recent literature and shows the effect of the assumption of sparsity in three simulation studies.

title: Humans and deep networks largely agree on which kinds of variation make object recognition harder
Abstract: View-invariant object recognition, a challenging problem that has garnered significant attention in psychology, neuroscience, and computer vision, involves recognizing objects regardless of their orientation. Humans excel at this task, though certain variations may be more difficult to handle than others (e.g., 3D rotations). Humans are believed to solve this problem through hierarchical processing along the ventral stream, gradually extracting more invariant visual features. This feed-forward architecture has inspired a new generation of bio-inspired computer vision systems called deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs), which are currently the best algorithms for object recognition in natural images. This paper, for the first time, systematically compares human feed-forward vision and DCNNs in view-invariant object recognition using the same images and controlling for both the types of transformation and their magnitude. Four object categories were used, with images rendered from 3D computer models. A total of 89 human subjects participated in 10 experiments where they had to discriminate between two or four categories after rapid presentation with backward masking. Two recent DCNNs were also tested on the same tasks. The results show that humans and DCNNs largely agree on the relative difficulties of each type of variation: rotation in depth is the most challenging, followed by scale, rotation in plane, and finally position. This suggests that humans recognize objects primarily through 2D template matching rather than constructing 3D object models, and that DCNNs provide a reasonable model of human feed-forward vision. The study also reveals that variation levels in rotation in depth and scale significantly affect both human and DCNN recognition performance. The authors argue that these variations should be controlled in image datasets used in vision research.

title: The SP theory of intelligence and the representation and processing of knowledge in the brain
Abstract: The "SP theory of intelligence," with its realization in the "SP computer model," aims to simplify and integrate observations and concepts across AI-related fields, with information compression as a unifying theme. This paper describes how abstract structures and processes within the theory can be realized in terms of neurons, their interconnections, and the transmission of signals between neurons. This part of the SP theory, "SP-neural," is a tentative and partial model for the representation and processing of knowledge in the brain. In the SP theory (aside from SP-neural), all types of knowledge are represented using "patterns," where a pattern is an array of atomic symbols in one or two dimensions. In SP-neural, the concept of a "pattern" is realized as an array of neurons called a "pattern assembly," similar to Hebb's concept of a "cell assembly" but with significant differences. Central to information processing in the SP system is the powerful concept of "multiple alignment," borrowed and adapted from bioinformatics. Processes such as pattern recognition, reasoning, and problem solving are achieved through the construction of multiple alignments, while unsupervised learning, significantly different from "Hebbian" learning, is achieved by creating patterns from sensory information and from multiple alignments where there is a partial match between patterns. Short-lived neural structures equivalent to multiple alignments are created through an interplay of excitatory and inhibitory neural signals. The paper discusses several associated issues, with relevant empirical evidence.

title: Accurate and scalable social recommendation using mixed-membership stochastic block models
Abstract: With the ever-increasing amount of online information available, modeling and predicting individual preferences—for books or articles, for example—is becoming increasingly important. Accurate predictions enable improved advice for users and a better understanding of the socio-psychological processes that determine preferences. This paper presents a collaborative filtering model, with an associated scalable algorithm, that accurately predicts individuals' preferences. The approach is based on the explicit assumption that there are groups of individuals and items, and that an individual's preference for an item is determined solely by their group memberships. Notably, the paper allows each individual and each item to belong to mixtures of different groups and, unlike many popular approaches such as matrix factorization, does not assume implicitly or explicitly that individuals in each group prefer items in a single group. The resulting overlapping groups and predicted preferences can be inferred with an expectation-maximization algorithm whose running time scales linearly (per iteration). This approach enables accurate prediction of individual preferences in large datasets and outperforms current algorithms for such datasets.

title: Building Machines That Learn and Think Like People
Abstract: Recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) have renewed interest in building systems that learn and think like humans. Many breakthroughs have resulted from using deep neural networks trained end-to-end in tasks such as object recognition, video games, and board games, achieving performance that rivals or surpasses human capabilities in some areas. However, despite their biological inspiration and performance achievements, these systems differ from human intelligence in crucial ways. This paper reviews progress in cognitive science, suggesting that truly human-like learning and thinking machines will need to go beyond current engineering trends in both what they learn and how they learn it. Specifically, the authors argue that these machines should (a) build causal models of the world that support explanation and understanding, rather than merely solving pattern recognition problems; (b) ground learning in intuitive theories of physics and psychology to support and enrich the learned knowledge; and (c) harness compositionality and learning-to-learn to rapidly acquire and generalize knowledge to new tasks and situations. The paper proposes concrete challenges and promising pathways towards these goals that combine the strengths of recent neural network advances with more structured cognitive models.
label: AI

title: To Fall Or Not To Fall: A Visual Approach to Physical Stability Prediction
Abstract: Understanding physical phenomena is a key competence that enables humans and animals to act and interact under uncertain perception in previously unseen environments containing novel objects and their configurations. Developmental psychology has shown that infants acquire these skills from observations at a very early stage. This paper contrasts a traditional model-based approach, which uses explicit 3D representations and physical simulation, with an end-to-end approach that directly predicts stability and related quantities from appearance. The paper investigates whether and to what extent such a skill can be acquired directly in a data-driven way, bypassing the need for explicit simulation. The paper presents a learning-based approach based on simulated data that predicts the stability of towers composed of wooden blocks under different conditions and quantities related to the potential fall of the towers. Evaluation is conducted on synthetic data and compared to human judgments on the same stimuli.
label: AI

title: Utility of a Behavlets approach to a Decision theoretic predictive player model
Abstract: This academic essay proposes a framework for building a generalized player model, suggesting that such a model requires parameters for subjective play experience, including player psychology, game structure, and actions of play. It outlines three linked research questions: (1) what constitutes the necessary and sufficient foundation for a general player model, (2) can this foundation enhance the performance of a computational intelligence-based player model, and (3) can such a model improve the efficacy of adaptive artificial intelligence in games. This essay focuses on the 'Behavlets' method, demonstrating how it can enhance the performance and accuracy of a predictive player model in Pac-Man by providing a basic foundation for the proposed parameters. The essay outlines future work to address RQ2 by conclusively testing the Behavlets approach, building on the work presented in the first preprint to address RQ1 and providing support for work on RQ3.

title: Pointing the Unknown Words
Abstract: Dealing with rare and unknown words is a significant issue that affects the performance of many NLP systems, including both traditional count-based and deep learning models. This paper proposes a novel approach to address this problem for neural network models using attention. The proposed model incorporates two softmax layers to predict the next word in conditional language models: one predicts the word's location in the source sentence, while the other predicts a word from a shortlist vocabulary. An MLP, conditioned on the context, adaptively decides which softmax layer to use at each time-step. This approach is inspired by psychological evidence suggesting humans naturally point to objects in the context or environment when they don't know their names. The paper demonstrates improvements on two tasks: neural machine translation on the Europarl English to French parallel corpora and text summarization on the Gigaword dataset using the proposed model.
label: AI

title: Possibilities Determine the Combinatorial Structure of Probability Polytopes
Abstract: This study examines the set of no-signalling empirical models in a measurement scenario, demonstrating that the combinatorial structure of the no-signalling polytope is entirely determined by the possibilistic information provided by the support of the models. This finding is a specific instance of a general result applicable to all polytopes presented in standard form, defined by linear equations along with non-negativity constraints on the variables.

title: Fisher, Neyman-Pearson or NHST? A Tutorial for Teaching Data Testing
Abstract: Despite frequent calls for a complete overhaul of null hypothesis significance testing (NHST), this controversial procedure remains ubiquitous in behavioral, social, and biomedical teaching and research. This paper proposes a tutorial approach to teaching data testing procedures, often referred to as hypothesis testing theories, recognizing the difficulty of changing deeply ingrained practices. The tutorial presents three procedures: Fisher's approach to data testing (tests of significance), the approach followed by Neyman and Pearson (tests of acceptance), and the current approach (NHST) as an incongruent combination of the previous two theories. For those researchers who continue to use NHST, the tutorial concludes with two compromise solutions on how to improve the method.

title: Short Literature Review for a General Player Model Based on Behavlets
Abstract: This essay, the first in a series of three, proposes a framework for building a generalized player model. The framework suggests that such a model requires parameters for the subjective play experience, including player psychology, game structure, and actions of play. It outlines three linked research questions: (1) what constitutes the necessary and sufficient foundation for a general player model, (2) can this foundation enhance the performance of a computational intelligence-based player model, and (3) can such a model improve the efficacy of adaptive artificial intelligence in games. This essay focuses on reviewing the literature for the core foundations of a general player model, proposing a plan for future work to systematically extend this review and provide an empirical answer to RQ1. The extended review will directly support the proposed approach to address RQ2 and RQ3.

title: Functional neuroanatomy of meditation: A review and meta-analysis of 78 functional neuroimaging investigations
Abstract: This study systematically reviewed 78 functional neuroimaging (fMRI and PET) studies of meditation, meta-analyzing 257 peak foci from 31 experiments involving 527 participants to investigate the brain activity patterns associated with various meditation techniques. The study found reliably dissociable patterns of brain activation and deactivation for four common meditation styles (focused attention, mantra recitation, open monitoring, and compassion/loving-kindness) and suggestive differences for three others (visualization, sense-withdrawal, and non-dual awareness practices). The dissociable activation patterns are consistent with the psychological and behavioral aims of each practice. While some brain areas are consistently recruited across multiple techniques – including insula, pre/supplementary motor cortices, dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, and frontopolar cortex – convergence is the exception rather than the rule. title: Mining Valence, Arousal, and Dominance - Possibilities for Detecting Burnout and Productivity?

title: Identifiability of restricted latent class models with binary responses

title: How deep is knowledge tracing?
Abstract: In theoretical cognitive science, there is a tension between highly structured models with directly interpretable psychological parameters and highly complex, general-purpose models with less interpretable parameters and representations. While the former offer insights into cognition, the latter often perform better. This tension has recently surfaced in educational data mining, where deep learning approaches to predicting student performance during a series of exercises—termed deep knowledge tracing (DKT)—have demonstrated significant performance advantages over the mainstay of the field, Bayesian knowledge tracing (BKT). This article attempts to understand the basis of DKT's advantage by examining the sources of statistical regularity in the data that DKT can leverage but BKT cannot. The article hypothesizes four forms of regularity that BKT fails to exploit: recency effects, the contextualized trial sequence, inter-skill similarity, and individual variation in ability. By extending BKT to allow for greater flexibility in modeling statistical regularities using previously proposed extensions, the article demonstrates that BKT achieves performance indistinguishable from DKT. It argues that while DKT is a powerful and useful general-purpose framework for modeling student learning, its gains do not stem from the discovery of novel representations, the fundamental advantage of deep learning. The article concludes that knowledge tracing may not require "depth," and shallow models like BKT can perform just as well while offering greater interpretability and explanatory power.

title: Testing boundaries of applicability of quantum probabilistic formalism to modeling of cognition
Abstract:
The mathematical formalism of quantum mechanics, especially methods of quantum probability theory, has recently gained widespread use in applications outside of physics, including cognition and psychology as well as economy and finance. These models, often called "quantum-like," are distinguished from genuine quantum physical models. The increasing use of quantum-like models in diverse fields has generated a number of foundational questions. This paper discusses the emergence of a new science—foundations of quantum-like modeling—which initially focused on comparing classical and quantum models, particularly in the probabilistic setting. The study found that statistical data from cognitive psychology violates basic constraints imposed by classical probability theory (Kolmogorov, 1933), specifically those related to the formula of total probability and Bell's type inequalities. The paper highlights a new question that has recently attracted attention: while quantum probability models have shown real success in applications, there is no reason to believe that they can completely address all problems in, for example, cognition. The need to explore more general probability models has emerged. A similar problem led to extensive research in the foundations of quantum physics, culminating in experiments to test Sorkin's equality for the triple-slit experiment by Weihs' group. This paper presents a similar test in a cognitive experimental setting. The performance of this test would either confirm the adequacy of the quantum probability model to cognitive applications or reject the conventional quantum model, opening the door for a series of exciting experimental tests for the quantum-like model of cognition.

title: Variations on chaos in physics: from unpredictability to universal laws
Abstract: The widespread popularity of Chaos Theory shares similarities with the success of Relativity, both built on a misunderstanding. Ironically, the scientific meaning of these terms for mathematicians and physicists is diametrically opposed to the perception held by most people. The enduring allure of these concepts may stem from the ambiguity in their names, combined with superficial clichés and slogans like "the butterfly effect" or "everything is relative." Some individuals may secretly hope to find evidence that undermines the pillars of science, namely its predictive power and its ability to establish universal objectivity. By focusing on Chaos Theory, we aim to demonstrate, through several examples, how it strengthens the position it seemingly contradicts at first glance.  Just as Relativity does, Chaos Theory overcomes the limitations of predictability and leads to precise, stable, and even more universal predictions.

Individuals within a crowd possess social identities, shared with others in the crowd. The process of self-categorization establishes norms within the crowd and influences behavior in evacuation situations. We propose an algorithmic implementation of social identity in pedestrian simulation. Our goal is to investigate whether integrating this psychological model into computer models of pedestrian motion can achieve simulation results aligned with observations from crowd psychology. We aim to quantify and formalize empirical research and verbal descriptions of the effect of group identity on behavior. We discuss hypothesis testing using the Bayes factor and model selection using cross-validation. title: Generalizing Prototype Theory: A Formal Quantum Framework

title: Towards Resolving Unidentifiability in Inverse Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: We consider a setting for Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) where the learner is equipped with the ability to actively select multiple environments, observing an agent's behavior in each environment. We demonstrate that if the learner can experiment with any transition dynamics on a fixed set of states and actions, then an algorithm exists that reconstructs the agent's reward function to the maximum extent theoretically possible, requiring only a small (logarithmic) number of experiments. We contrast this result with the established understanding of IRL in single fixed environments, where the true reward function is fundamentally unidentifiable. We then extend this setting to a more realistic scenario where the learner may not select any transition dynamic but is restricted to a fixed set of environments that it can explore. We connect the problem of maximizing information derived from experiments to submodular function maximization and demonstrate that a greedy algorithm is near optimal (up to logarithmic factors). Finally, we empirically validate our algorithm in an environment inspired by behavioral psychology.

Existing studies provide evidence supporting the use of reminders to address prospective memory failures. However, people remain dissatisfied with existing reminders due to limitations in various aspects, including reliability, optimization, and adaptation. By analyzing the functions and features of existing reminder systems, this book draft summarizes their advantages and limitations. We are motivated to enhance the performance of reminder systems. These improvements necessitate the incorporation and application of relevant theories and mechanisms of prospective memory from psychology. Based on our literature review, a new reminder model is proposed, encompassing a novel reminder planner, a prospective memory-based agent, and a personalized user model. The reminder planner is responsible for determining the optimal reminder plan (including the optimal number of reminders, the optimal reminding schedule, and the optimal reminding method). The prospective memory agent executes the reminding processes, while the personalized user model learns from user behaviors and preferences based on human-system interactions and adapts the reminder plan to meet user preferences as closely as possible.

Abstract: Behavioral finance posits that stock market returns are influenced by emotional, social, and psychological factors. Controlling for factors that could bias the study using multivariate regression models is challenging due to the complexity of stock market data. False assumptions about model linearity or non-linearity and inaccuracies in model specification can lead to misleading conclusions. In this work, we introduce a novel framework for causal inference that does not rely on any assumptions about the statistical relationships among variables in the study and can effectively control for a large number of factors. title: Models of latent consensus
Abstract: The paper studies the problem of achieving consensus in multi-agent systems in the case where the dependency digraph $\Gamma$ has no spanning in-tree.  We consider the regularization protocol that amounts to the addition of a dummy agent (hub) uniformly connected to the agents.  The presence of such a hub guarantees the achievement of an asymptotic consensus.  For the "evaporation" of the dummy agent, the strength of its influences on the other agents vanishes, which leads to the concept of latent consensus.  We obtain a closed-form expression for the consensus when the connections of the hub are symmetric, in this case, the impact of the hub upon the consensus remains fixed.  On the other hand, if the hub is essentially influenced by the agents, whereas its influence on them tends to zero, then the consensus is expressed by the scalar product of the vector of column means of the Laplacian eigenprojection of $\Gamma$ and the initial state vector of the system. title: Quark Wars - a particle physics outreach game in the age of Star Wars

title: Investigation of a Structured Fisher's Equation with Applications in Biochemistry

To this end, we derive a structured Fisher's Equation with independent variables of time, space, and biochemical pathway activity level and prove the existence of a self-similar traveling wave solution to this equation. title: Coupling Adaptive Batch Sizes with Learning Rates
Abstract: Mini-batch stochastic gradient descent and variants thereof have become standard for large-scale empirical risk minimization like the training of neural networks.  These methods are usually used with a constant batch size chosen by simple empirical inspection.  The batch size significantly influences the behavior of the stochastic optimization algorithm, though, since it determines the variance of the gradient estimates.  This variance also changes over the optimization process; when using a constant batch size, stability and convergence is thus often enforced by means of a (manually tuned) decreasing learning rate schedule.  We propose a practical method for dynamic batch size adaptation.  It estimates the variance of the stochastic gradients and adapts the batch size to decrease the variance proportionally to the value of the objective function, removing the need for the aforementioned learning rate decrease.  In contrast to recent related work, our algorithm couples the batch size to the learning rate, directly reflecting the known relationship between the two.  On popular image classification benchmarks, our batch size adaptation yields faster optimization convergence, while simultaneously simplifying learning rate tuning. title: Space-time nature of causality
Abstract: In a causal world, the direction of the time arrow dictates how past causal events in a variable $X$ produce future effects in $Y$.  $X$ is said to cause an effect in $Y$ if the predictability (uncertainty) about the future states of $Y$ increases (decreases) as its own past and the past of $X$ are taken into consideration.  Causality is thus intrinsically dependent on the observation of the past events of both variables involved, to the prediction (or uncertainty reduction) of the future event of the other variable.  We will show that this *temporal* notion of causality leads to another natural spatio-temporal definition for it, and that can be exploited to detect the arrow of influence from $X$ to $Y$, either by considering shorter time-series of $X$ and longer time-series of $Y$ (an approach that explores the time nature of causality) or lower precision measured time-series in $X$ and higher precision measured time-series in $Y$ (an approach that explores the spatial nature of causality).  Causality has thus space and time signatures, causing a break of symmetry in the topology of the probabilistic space, or causing a break of symmetry in the length of the measured time-series, a consequence of the fact that information flows from $X$ to $Y$.

title: Large-scale environmental dependence of the abundance ratio of nitrogen to oxygen in blue, star-forming galaxies fainter than L*

We estimate the abundances of oxygen and nitrogen using these temperature and density estimates and the emission line fluxes [O II] 3727, [O III] 4959, 5007, and [N II] 6548, 6584 with the direct Te method. Our results indicate that the interfacial thermal conductance is not a monotonic function of either chemical parameter, but instead maximizes at an optimal set of mass and bonding strength. We also demonstrate the intrinsic relationship between the Diffusive Mismatch Model (DMM) and the properties from NEGF, and provide an approach to get DMM from first principles NEGF. We analyzed data from the ASAS-3 and SuperWASP archives, supplemented with additional photometry, to verify the sky survey data. We conducted period analyses and discussed each object in detail. Based on our findings, we propose that pulsational variability is the driving force behind the variability observed in HD 67983, HD 77013, and HD 81076, offering a unique opportunity to study the interplay between atomic diffusion and pulsation. HD 67983 and HD 77013 exhibit multiperiodic variability in the gamma Doradus frequency range, while HD 81076 is classified as a delta Scuti star. The CP2 star HD 98000 shows monoperiodic variability with a frequency of f~2.148 c/d (P~0.466 d), which we interpret as its rotational period. title: Virtual Breathalyzer
Abstract: Driving under the influence of alcohol is a pervasive issue in the US, recognized as a leading cause of fatal accidents. title: On the role of moisture in triggering out-of-plane displacement in paper: from the network level to the macroscopic scale

At this scale, moisture-induced instabilities and out-of-plane deformations can occur. This research focuses on several aspects of this issue. A macroscopic phenomenological hygro-mechanical model is proposed, aiming to predict moisture-induced out-of-plane deformations in paper sheets. The constitutive model relies on the relationship between these deformations and typical irreversible phenomena linked to paper manufacturing history, specifically the release of dried-in strains. The model is used to describe bending caused by moisture gradients across the sheet's thickness as well as buckling due to moisture variations in the presence of mechanical constraints. The model results demonstrate that the anisotropic sheet-level hygro-expansion significantly influences the instability phenomena. Moreover, a comparison with experimental data provides adequate semi-quantitative estimates. To this end, a meso-structural model is developed, consisting of a network of fibers randomly positioned in a planar region according to an orientation probability density function. Network simulations reveal that, upon moisture content variations, the expansion of inter-fiber bonding regions drives the overall deformation. Particularly in the case of anisotropic fiber orientation, this explains the origin of the macro-scale anisotropic hygro-expansion, which is crucial for the observed sheet-level instability phenomena.

title: A Comprehensive Model of Usability

Ideally, the posterior should be robust to reasonable variations in the prior choice, as this choice is often subjective. A simple approximate non-local robustness measure is proposed and its effectiveness is demonstrated on a simulated data set.

This study develops information-theoretical tools based on the Fisher metric to demonstrate that photoreceptor absorption properties account for approximately 87% of the variance in human color discrimination ability, as evidenced by prior behavioral experiments. According to this theory, the bottleneck in chromatic information processing is determined by photoreceptor absorption characteristics. Subsequent encoding stages have only minor modifications to the chromatic discriminability established at the photoreceptor level.

title: Cosmic Bell Test: Measurement Settings from Milky Way Stars
Abstract: Bell's theorem establishes that certain predictions of quantum mechanics cannot be replicated by a local-realist theory. This conflict is expressed by Bell's inequality, usually derived under the assumption of no statistical correlations between the choices of measurement settings and anything else that can causally affect the measurement outcomes. Previous experiments addressed this "freedom of choice" by ensuring space-like separation between the selection of measurement settings using conventional "quantum random number generators" and the creation of entangled particles. However, this left open the possibility of an unknown cause affecting both setting choices and measurement outcomes as recently as mere microseconds before each experimental trial. This paper reports on a new experimental test of Bell's inequality that, for the first time, utilizes distant astronomical sources as "cosmic setting generators." In tests with polarization-entangled photons, measurement settings were chosen using real-time observations of Milky Way stars while simultaneously ensuring locality. Assuming fair sampling for all detected photons and that each stellar photon's color was set at emission, statistically significant violations of Bell's inequality are observed, with estimated p-values of ≤1.8 × 10-13 and ≤4.0 × 10-33, respectively. These results push back by ~600 years the most recent time by which any local-realist influences could have engineered the observed Bell violation.

This study extends the method developed in [J. Chem. Phys. 142, 074702 (2015)], initially applied to a simple discrete lattice-gas model, to continuum density functional theory (DFT) to calculate the binding potential for a Lennard-Jones fluid and other simple liquids. The DFT employed is based on fundamental measure theory and incorporates the influence of layered packing of molecules at the surface and the corresponding oscillatory density profile. The binding potential is often used as input in mesoscale models to calculate liquid drop shapes and even dynamics. This study demonstrates that the equilibrium droplet profiles calculated using the mesoscale theory are in good agreement with the profiles calculated directly from the microscopic DFT. For liquids composed of particles where the range of attraction is much less than the particle diameter, it is found that at low temperatures g(h) decays in an oscillatory fashion with increasing h, leading to highly structured terraced liquid droplets.

The precision of these models is limited by our incomplete understanding of internal mixing processes that significantly impact the lifetime of these objects, such as core overshoot, chemical mixing, or internal differential rotation. Custom masks were employed to construct light curves from Kepler pixel data, and standard time-series analysis tools were used to construct a set of significant frequencies for each target. These sets were first filtered from combination frequencies and then screened for period spacing patterns. Gravity mode period series of modes with the same degree l and consecutive radial order n are detected in four new and one revisited SPB star. These predominantly prograde dipole series (covering ~10-40 radial orders) are influenced by rotation and carry signatures of chemical mixing processes. A set of equations of state for the system is derived based on the minimization principle for the Gibbs energy. These equations of state combine parameters describing the elastic properties (relative volume deformation) and magnetic properties (magnetization changes). The formalism is extensively illustrated through numerical calculations performed for a system of ferromagnetically coupled spins S=1/2 localized at the sites of a simple cubic lattice. Notably, the significant influence of the magnetic subsystem on the elastic properties is demonstrated. This manifests in significant modifications of quantities like relative volume deformation, thermal expansion coefficient, or isothermal compressibility, particularly in the vicinity of the magnetic phase transition. Conversely, the influence of the lattice subsystem on the magnetic one is also evident. Due to the inference process, networks estimated from experimentally obtained biological data represent a single instance of a larger number of realizations with similar underlying topology. Therefore, a modeling approach is needed to support statistical inference on the bottom-up local connectivity mechanisms influencing the formation of the estimated brain networks. We employed a statistical model based on exponential random graphs (ERGM) to reproduce brain networks, or connectomes, estimated by spectral coherence between high-density electroencephalographic (EEG) signals. This approach was validated in a dataset of 108 healthy subjects during eyes-open (EO) and eyes-closed (EC) resting-state conditions. Results indicated that the tendency to form triangles and stars, reflecting clustering and node centrality, better explained the global properties of the EEG connectomes compared to other combinations of graph metrics. The main governing parameters determining macroscopic friction, including a dimensionless oscillation amplitude, a dimensionless sliding velocity, and the relationship between three characteristic frequencies (that of externally excited oscillation and two natural oscillation frequencies associated with the contact stiffness and the system stiffness), are identified. In the limiting cases of a very soft system and a very stiff system, our results reproduce the findings of previous studies. Between these two limiting cases, there is also a resonant case, which is investigated for the first time in this paper. The resonant case is notable in that it lacks a critical sliding velocity above which oscillations no longer reduce friction. Both models were validated against experimental measurements in a 60cm body phantom. The influence of detector size was simulated using leaded sleeves of varying sizes wrapped around a 100mm pencil chamber. The model accurately describes the experimental data for the cases studied. Except for the smallest collimation of 5mm, linear regression analysis showed good correlation between data and model according to the R^2 values at all collimations. Further analysis of the model revealed the minimum detector size that will integrate 98% of the signal for a given collimation (d=4.95L) and the minimum collimation at which a given detector will collect 98% of the signal (L=5.49d). title: The environmental dependence of gas accretion onto galaxies: quenching satellites through starvation
Abstract: Galaxies that have fallen into massive haloes may experience a phenomenon known as "starvation" or "strangulation," where they are no longer able to accrete gas from their surroundings. This research investigates the environmental dependence of gas accretion onto galaxies using the EAGLE cosmological, hydrodynamical simulation. The study quantifies the dependence of gas accretion on stellar mass, redshift, and environment, using halo mass and galaxy overdensity as environmental indicators. The results show a significant suppression of gas accretion rates in dense environments, particularly for satellite galaxies. This suppression becomes stronger at lower redshifts. However, the scatter in accretion rates is substantial for satellites, partly due to the variation in halocentric radius, with gas accretion being more suppressed at smaller radii. Central galaxies are less influenced by their environment and exhibit less scatter in their gas accretion rates. Star formation rates of both central and satellite galaxies exhibit similar behavior to their gas accretion rates. The relatively small differences between gas accretion and star formation rates indicate that galaxies tend to exhaust their gas reservoirs faster at higher stellar masses, lower redshifts, and in denser environments. This environmental suppression of gas accretion could directly contribute to the quenching of star formation.

The study also provides the first direct estimate of Lagrangian nonlocal bias in N-body simulations, confirming the model prediction. The model's simplicity, with essentially a single free parameter, facilitates the development of efficient and accurate non-universal fitting functions for halo abundances and bias in precision cosmology.

title: Proxima's orbit around Alpha Centauri
Abstract: Proxima Centauri and Alpha Centauri AB have remarkably similar distances and proper motions with respect to the Sun. This study utilizes HARPS high-precision absolute radial velocity measurements and a recent revision of the Alpha Cen pair parameters to demonstrate with high confidence that Proxima and Alpha Cen are gravitationally bound. The orbital period of Proxima is approximately 550,000 years, with an eccentricity of 0.50. At periastron, Proxima comes within 4.3 kau of Alpha Cen. Its current orbital phase is close to apastron (13.0 kau). This inequality accounts for the complementarity between strangeness oscillations and lifetime information previously considered in the literature, showcasing how entanglement correlations affect this relationship. The study identifies two dimensionless parameters: (re-scaled) Planck's constant and the ratio of the lattice spacing to the scale of variation of the external potential. The special case where both parameters are equal (denoted as ε) is examined. In the limit ε→0, the study proves the existence of semiclassical wavepackets that are asymptotic up to "Ehrenfest time" (t~ln(1/ε)). The center of mass and average quasi-momentum of these solutions evolve along trajectories generated by the classical Hamiltonian, which is the sum of the Bloch band energy and the external potential. The study derives all corrections to the evolution of these observables proportional to ε. These corrections depend on the gauge-invariant Berry curvature of the Bloch band and a coupling to the evolution of the wave-packet envelope, which satisfies Schrödinger's equation with a time-dependent harmonic oscillator Hamiltonian. This infinite-dimensional coupled "particle-field" system can be derived from an "extended" ε-dependent Hamiltonian. The coupling of observables (discrete particle-like degrees of freedom) to the wave-envelope (continuum field-like degrees of freedom) can significantly impact the overall dynamics.

The well-resolved Raman signatures reveal a reduced crystal field splitting at the interface and an enhancement at the surface, highlighting its strong dependence on the local atomic environment.

The tripartite system is initially prepared in either a GHZ or W state, and the composite four-qubit system evolves with unitary dynamics. The environmental qubit is then traced out, and the impact of the DM interaction on the initial entanglement of the system is studied. The results show that the bipartite partitions of W states experience entanglement sudden death (ESD), while tripartite entanglement remains unaffected. In contrast, both bipartite partitions and tripartite entanglement in GHZ states remain unaffected by the DM interaction. This indicates that GHZ states are more robust than W states. The study considers generalized GHZ and W states and utilizes three π as an entanglement measure. These findings have implications for quantum information processing where unwanted DM interaction can occur.

The frequency Ωmax at which the detector signal is maximal yields the distance. The semiconductor FSF laser system operates without external injection seeding and relies on frequency counting, allowing flexible choice of accuracy or speed by adjusting the frequency measurement interval.

title: Effects of additive noise on the stability of glacial cycles
Abstract: The glacial-interglacial cycle sequence is known to be driven by astronomical forcing. However, the robustness of this sequence against natural fluctuations, such as those arising from chaotic motions of the atmosphere and oceans, is an important question. The study focuses on the influence of additive white Gaussian noise on the sequence of glacial cycles generated by stochastic versions of low-order dynamical system models proposed in the literature. In the original deterministic case, these models exhibit various attractors, including quasiperiodic, piecewise continuous, strange nonchaotic, and chaotic attractors. The study shows that the combination of quasiperiodic astronomical forcing and additive fluctuations induces a form of temporarily quantized instability. Climate trajectories corresponding to different noise realizations generally cluster around a small number of stable or transiently stable trajectories present in the deterministic system. These stochastic trajectories exhibit sensitive dependence on small perturbations at key times. The number of trajectories leaking from these clusters varies depending on the complexity of the attractor, ranging from nearly zero (quasiperiodic attractor) to a significant fraction (chaotic attractor), with strange nonchaotic attractors exhibiting intermediate behavior. The study discusses the implications of these findings for research programs based on numerical simulators. |||

title: Instabilities in granular gas-solid flows
Abstract: A linear stability analysis of the hydrodynamic equations is performed to investigate the stability conditions of a suspension of solid particles within a viscous gas. The dissipation in such systems originates from two sources: inelastic particle collisions and viscous friction dissipation due to the gas phase's influence on the solid particles. The analysis utilizes a suspension model based on the inelastic Enskog kinetic equation, where the gas phase's effect is represented by a viscous drag force. The study is conducted in two stages. Firstly, the transport coefficients of the system are determined by solving the Enskog equation using the Chapman-Enskog method up to first order in spatial gradients. With these transport properties established, the linearized hydrodynamic equations are solved to obtain the dispersion relations. In contrast to previous studies, the hydrodynamic modes are analytically derived as functions of the system's parameter space. As anticipated, linear stability reveals d-1 transversal (shear) modes (where d is the dimensionality of the system) and a longitudinal "heat" mode to be unstable for sufficiently long-wavelength excitations. The results also demonstrate that the gas phase primarily decreases the value of the critical length Lc (beyond which the system becomes unstable) compared to a dry granular fluid. Comparisons with direct numerical simulations for Lc show good agreement for practical conditions.

We illustrate potential applications, showing that the higher-order terms give rise to localized bright flat-top solitons, which can spontaneously form in polariton condensates.

title: On estimating the force-freeness based on observed magnetograms
Abstract: In the solar physics community, it is common practice to assess the force-freeness of measured photospheric or chromospheric vector magnetograms using the Maxwell stress. Previous studies suggest that magnetic fields of active regions in the solar chromosphere are close to being force-free, while there is no consensus on whether magnetic fields in the solar photosphere are force-free. This study utilizes three types of representative magnetic fields (analytical force-free solutions, modeled solar-like force-free fields, and observed non-force-free fields) to analyze how measurement issues like limited field of view, instrument sensitivity, and measurement error could affect the estimation of force-freeness based on observed magnetograms. Unlike previous studies focusing on the effect of limited field of view or instrument sensitivity, this analysis shows that measurement error alone can significantly influence the force-freeness estimate. This is due to the larger measurement errors in horizontal magnetic fields compared to vertical fields. This property, combined with the specific form of the force-freeness estimate formula, can lead to incorrect judgments of force-freeness: a truly force-free field might be mistakenly classified as non-force-free, and a true non-force-free field might be estimated as force-free. The findings emphasize the need for caution when interpreting force-freeness estimates based on measured magnetograms and suggest that the true photospheric magnetic field might be further away from being force-free than currently perceived.

title: Atmospheric Signatures of Giant Exoplanet Formation by Pebble Accretion
Abstract: Atmospheric chemical abundances of giant planets provide crucial constraints on planetary formation and migration. Studies have shown that giant planets migrating through the protoplanetary disk can accrete significant amounts of oxygen-rich planetesimals, leading to super-solar metallicities in their envelopes and solar or sub-solar C/O ratios. Pebble accretion has been demonstrated to play a vital role in core accretion and exhibits growth rates consistent with planetary migration. The high pebble accretion rates enable planetary cores to initiate their growth beyond 10 AU and subsequently migrate to cold (>~ 1 AU), warm (~0.1 AU- 1AU), or hot (<~ 0.1 AU) orbits. This work investigates how the formation of giant planets via pebble accretion influences their atmospheric chemical compositions. The findings indicate that under the standard pebble accretion scenario, where the core is isolated from the envelope, the resulting metallicities (O/H and C/H ratios) are sub-solar, while the C/O ratios are super-solar. Planets migrating through the disk to become hot Jupiters accrete substantial amounts of water vapor but still acquire slightly sub-solar O/H and super-solar C/O ratios of 0.7-0.8. The metallicity can be substantially sub-solar (~0.2-0.5x solar), and the C/O can even approach 1.0 if the planet accretes its envelope primarily beyond the CO2 ice line, resulting in cold Jupiters or hot Jupiters forming far out and migrating inward through scattering. title: Geophysical flows under location uncertainty, Part II: Quasi-geostrophy and efficient ensemble spreading
Abstract: Models under location uncertainty are derived assuming that a component of the velocity is uncorrelated in time. Based on numerical simulations, the benefits of the proposed stochastic formalism are demonstrated. A single realization of models under location uncertainty can restore small-scale structures. An ensemble of realizations further helps to assess model error prediction and outperforms perturbed deterministic models by one order of magnitude. This high uncertainty quantification skill is of primary interest for assimilation ensemble methods. MATLAB code examples are available online.

title: Understanding and reducing deleterious defects in metastable alloy GaAsBi

To mitigate the influence of these deleterious defects, the study suggests shifting growth away from As-rich conditions and/or using hydrogen passivation to reduce the minority-carrier traps. This work is expected to aid in the application of GaAsBi to novel electronic and optoelectronic devices and shed light on controlling deleterious defects in other metastable materials.

Each particle undergoes Newtonian motion under the influence of an external force, with no interactions between particles. If the external force is bounded, the trajectories of any two particles in phase space do not intersect, meaning that at any given time, two particles either have different coordinates or different velocities. The system is classified as regular if no particle collisions occur in the coordinate space. title: Bayes-Optimal Effort Allocation in Crowdsourcing: Bounds and Index Policies

Abstract: Most recent matrix completion methods assume that the matrix under consideration is low-rank or that the columns are in a union of low-rank subspaces. However, in real-world scenarios, the linear structure underlying these models is often distorted by a (typically unknown) nonlinear transformation. This paper addresses the challenge of matrix completion in the presence of such nonlinearities. Given a few observations of a matrix obtained by applying a Lipschitz, monotonic function to a low-rank matrix, our task is to estimate the remaining unobserved entries. We propose a novel matrix completion method that alternates between low-rank matrix estimation and monotonic function estimation to estimate the missing matrix elements. Mean squared error bounds provide insight into how well the matrix can be estimated based on its size, rank, and properties of the nonlinear transformation. Empirical results on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the competitiveness of the proposed approach.

title: Feed-Forward Networks with Attention Can Solve Some Long-Term Memory Problems
Abstract: We propose a simplified model of attention applicable to feed-forward neural networks and demonstrate that the resulting model can solve the synthetic "addition" and "multiplication" long-term memory problems for sequence lengths that are both longer and more widely varying than the best published results for these tasks.

title: A Stochastic Majorize-Minimize Subspace Algorithm for Online Penalized Least Squares Estimation
Abstract: Stochastic approximation techniques play a crucial role in solving many problems encountered in machine learning and adaptive signal processing. In these contexts, the statistics of the data are often unknown a priori or their direct computation is too intensive, requiring them to be estimated online from the observed signals. For batch optimization of an objective function, which is the sum of a data fidelity term and a penalization (e.g., a sparsity promoting function), Majorize-Minimize (MM) methods have recently gained significant attention due to their speed, flexibility, and effectiveness in ensuring convergence. This paper aims to demonstrate how these methods can be successfully extended to the case where the data fidelity term corresponds to a least squares criterion and the cost function is replaced by a sequence of stochastic approximations. In this context, we propose an online version of an MM subspace algorithm and analyze its convergence using suitable probabilistic tools. Simulation results illustrate the good practical performance of the proposed algorithm, associated with a memory gradient subspace, when applied to both non-adaptive and adaptive filter identification problems.

title: Error Bounds for Compressed Sensing Algorithms With Group Sparsity: A Unified Approach
Abstract: In compressed sensing, the most popular approach for recovering a sparse or nearly sparse vector from possibly noisy measurements is $\\ell_1$-norm minimization.  Upper bounds for the $\\ell_2$- norm of the error between the true and estimated vectors are provided in [1] and reviewed in [2], while bounds for the $\\ell_1$-norm are given in [3]. When the unknown vector is not conventionally sparse but is "group sparse" instead, various alternatives to the $\\ell_1$-norm have been proposed in the literature, including the group LASSO, sparse group LASSO, and group LASSO with tree structured overlapping groups. However, no error bounds are available for any of these modified objective functions.  This paper presents a unified approach for deriving upper bounds on the error between the true vector and its approximation, based on the notion of decomposable and $\\gamma$-decomposable norms. The bounds presented cover all of the norms mentioned above, and also provide a guideline for choosing norms in future to accommodate alternate forms of sparsity.

title: Robust Scene Text Recognition Using Sparse Coding based Features
Abstract: This paper introduces an effective scene text recognition method using sparse coding-based features, called Histograms of Sparse Codes (HSC) features.  For character detection, we use HSC features instead of Histograms of Oriented Gradients (HOG) features.  HSC features are extracted by computing sparse codes with dictionaries learned from data using K-SVD, and aggregating per-pixel sparse codes to form local histograms. For word recognition, we integrate multiple cues including character detection scores and geometric contexts in an objective function. The final recognition results are obtained by searching for the words corresponding to the maximum value of the objective function. The parameters in the objective function are learned using the Minimum Classification Error (MCE) training method. Experiments on several challenging datasets demonstrate that the proposed HSC-based scene text recognition method outperforms HOG-based methods significantly and surpasses most state-of-the-art methods.

title: Testing for Differences in Gaussian Graphical Models: Applications to Brain Connectivity
Abstract: Functional brain networks are well described and estimated from data with Gaussian Graphical Models (GGMs), e.g., using sparse inverse covariance estimators. Comparing functional connectivity of subjects in two populations requires comparing these estimated GGMs. Our aim is to identify differences in GGMs known to have similar structure. We characterize the uncertainty of differences with confidence intervals obtained using a parametric distribution on parameters of a sparse estimator. Sparse penalties enable statistical guarantees and interpretable models even in high-dimensional and low-sample settings. Characterizing the distributions of sparse models is inherently challenging as the penalties produce a biased estimator. Recent work leverages the sparsity assumptions to effectively remove the bias from a sparse estimator such as the lasso. These distributions can be used to give confidence intervals on edges in GGMs, and by extension their differences. However, in the case of comparing GGMs, these estimators do not utilize any assumed joint structure among the GGMs. Inspired by priors from brain functional connectivity, we derive the distribution of parameter differences under a joint penalty when parameters are known to be sparse in the difference. This leads us to introduce the debiased multi-task fused lasso, whose distribution can be characterized efficiently.  We then demonstrate how the debiased lasso and multi-task fused lasso can be used to obtain confidence intervals on edge differences in GGMs. We validate the proposed techniques on a set of synthetic examples as well as a neuro-imaging dataset created for the study of autism.

title: Democratizing Children's Computation: Learning Computational Science as Aesthetic Experience
Abstract: This paper argues that a democratic approach to children's computing education in a science class must focus on the aesthetics of children's experience. In Democracy and Education, Dewey links "democracy" with a distinctive understanding of "experience". For Dewey, the value of educational experiences lies in "the unity or integrity of experience" (DE, 248). In Art as Experience, Dewey presents aesthetic experience as the fundamental form of human experience that undergirds all other forms of experiences, and can also bring together multiple forms of experiences, locating this form of experience in the work of artists. Particularly relevant to our current concern (computational literacy), Dewey calls the process through which a person transforms a material into an expressive medium an aesthetic experience (AE, 68-69). We argue here that the kind of experience that is appropriate for a democratic education in the context of children's computational science is essentially aesthetic in nature. Given that aesthetics has received relatively little attention in STEM education research, our purpose here is to highlight the power of Deweyan aesthetic experience in making computational thinking available to and attractive to all children, including those who are disinterested in computing, and especially those who are likely to be discounted by virtue of location, gender, or race.

title: Tight Bounds for Approximate Carathéodory and Beyond
Abstract: We present a deterministic nearly-linear time algorithm for approximating any point inside a convex polytope with a sparse convex combination of the polytope's vertices. Our result provides a constructive proof for the Approximate Carathéodory Problem, which states that any point inside a polytope contained in the $\\ell_p$ ball of radius $D$ can be approximated to within $\\epsilon$ in $\\ell_p$ norm by a convex combination of only $O\\left(D^2\np/\\epsilon^2\\right)$ vertices of the polytope for $p \\geq 2$.  We also show that this bound is tight, using an argument based on anti-concentration for the binomial distribution.  In establishing the upper bound, we develop a technique for minimizing norms over convex sets with complicated geometry.  This is achieved by running Mirror Descent on a dual convex function obtained via Sion's Theorem. As simple extensions of our method, we then provide new algorithms for submodular function minimization and SVM training. For submodular function minimization, we obtain a simplification and (provable) speed-up over Wolfe's algorithm, the method commonly found to be the fastest in practice.  For SVM training, we obtain $O(1/\\epsilon^2)$ convergence for arbitrary kernels; each iteration only requires matrix-vector operations involving the kernel matrix, overcoming the obstacle of having to explicitly store the kernel or compute its Cholesky factorization.

title: Optimal Selective Attention in Reactive Agents
Abstract: In POMDPs, information about the hidden state, delivered through observations, is both valuable to the agent, allowing it to base its actions on better informed internal states, and a "curse", exploding the size and diversity of the internal state space. One attempt to deal with this is to focus on reactive policies, that only base their actions on the most recent observation.  However, even reactive policies can be demanding on resources, and agents need to pay selective attention to only some of the information available to them in observations. In this report, we present the minimum-information principle for selective attention in reactive agents. We further motivate this approach by reducing the general problem of optimal control in POMDPs, to reactive control with complex observations. Lastly, we explore a newly discovered phenomenon of this optimization process - period doubling bifurcations. This necessitates periodic policies and raises many more questions regarding stability, periodicity, and chaos in optimal control.

title: Structured Pruning of Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: Real-time application of deep learning algorithms is often hindered by high computational complexity and frequent memory accesses. Network pruning is a promising technique to address this problem. However, pruning typically results in irregular network connections that not only demand extra representation efforts but also do not fit well on parallel computation. We introduce structured sparsity at various scales for convolutional neural networks, including channel-wise, kernel-wise, and intra-kernel strided sparsity. This structured sparsity is advantageous for direct computational resource savings on embedded computers, parallel computing environments, and hardware-based systems.  To determine the importance of network connections and paths, the proposed method uses a particle filtering approach. The importance weight of each particle is assigned by computing the misclassification rate with the corresponding connectivity pattern. The pruned network is then re-trained to compensate for the losses due to pruning. While implementing convolutions as matrix products, we particularly show that intra-kernel strided sparsity with a simple constraint can significantly reduce the size of kernel and feature map matrices. The pruned network is finally fixed-point optimized with reduced word length precision. This results in a significant reduction in the total storage size, providing advantages for on-chip memory-based implementations of deep neural networks.
label: AI

title: Taming the Noise in Reinforcement Learning via Soft Updates
Abstract: Model-free reinforcement learning algorithms, such as Q-learning, perform poorly in the early stages of learning in noisy environments, as much effort is spent unlearning biased estimates of the state-action value function. This bias arises from selecting, among several noisy estimates, the apparent optimum, which may actually be suboptimal. We propose G-learning, a new off-policy learning algorithm that regularizes the value estimates by penalizing deterministic policies in the beginning of the learning process. We show that this method reduces the bias of the value-function estimation, leading to faster convergence to the optimal value and the optimal policy.  Moreover, G-learning enables the natural incorporation of prior domain knowledge when available. The stochastic nature of G-learning also allows it to avoid some exploration costs, a property usually attributed only to on-policy algorithms. We illustrate these ideas in several examples, where G-learning results in significant improvements of the convergence rate and the cost of the learning process.

title: When Coding Style Survives Compilation: De-anonymizing Programmers from Executable Binaries
Abstract: The ability to identify authors of computer programs based on their coding style poses a direct threat to the privacy and anonymity of programmers. While recent work found that source code can be attributed to authors with high accuracy, attribution of executable binaries appears to be much more difficult. Many distinguishing features present in source code, such as variable names, are removed in the compilation process, and compiler optimization may alter the structure of a program, further obscuring features known to be useful in determining authorship. We examine programmer de-anonymization from the standpoint of machine learning, using a novel set of features that include ones obtained by decompiling the executable binary to source code. We adapt a powerful set of techniques from the domain of source code authorship attribution along with stylistic representations embedded in assembly, resulting in successful de-anonymization of a large set of programmers.  We evaluate our approach on data from the Google Code Jam, obtaining attribution accuracy of up to 96% with 100 and 83% with 600 candidate programmers. We present an executable binary authorship attribution approach, for the first time, that is robust to basic obfuscations, a range of compiler optimization settings, and binaries that have been stripped of their symbol tables. We perform programmer de-anonymization using both obfuscated binaries and real-world code found "in the wild" in single-author GitHub repositories and the recently leaked Nulled.IO hacker forum. We show that programmers who would like to remain anonymous need to take extreme countermeasures to protect their privacy.

title: Mining Massive Hierarchical Data Using a Scalable Probabilistic Graphical Model
Abstract: Probabilistic Graphical Models (PGMs) are highly useful in the fields of machine learning and data mining. However, a crucial limitation of these models is their scalability. The Bayesian Network, one of the most common PGMs used in machine learning and data mining, demonstrates this limitation when the training data consists of random variables, each having a large set of possible values. In the big data era, one would expect new extensions to existing PGMs to handle the massive amounts of data produced by computers, sensors, and other electronic devices.  With hierarchical data – data arranged in a treelike structure with several levels – one would expect to see hundreds of thousands or millions of values distributed over even just a small number of levels. When modeling this kind of hierarchical data across large datasets, Bayesian Networks become infeasible for representing the probability distributions. In this paper, we introduce an extension to Bayesian Networks to handle massive sets of hierarchical data in a reasonable amount of time and space. The proposed model achieves perfect precision of 1.0 and high recall of 0.93 when it is used as a multi-label classifier for the annotation of mass spectrometry data. On another dataset of 1.5 billion search logs provided by CareerBuilder.com, the model was able to predict latent semantic relationships between search keywords with accuracy up to 0.80.

title: Visually Indicated Sounds
Abstract: Objects make distinctive sounds when they are hit or scratched. These sounds reveal aspects of an object's material properties, as well as the actions that produced them.  In this paper, we propose the task of predicting what sound an object makes when struck as a way of studying physical interactions within a visual scene. We present an algorithm that synthesizes sound from silent videos of people hitting and scratching objects with a drumstick. This algorithm uses a recurrent neural network to predict sound features from videos and then produces a waveform from these features with an example-based synthesis procedure.  We show that the sounds predicted by our model are realistic enough to fool participants in a "real or fake" psychophysical experiment, and that they convey significant information about material properties and physical interactions.
label: AI

title: A Simple Baseline for Travel Time Estimation using Large-Scale Trip Data
Abstract: The increased availability of large-scale trajectory data around the world provides rich information for the study of urban dynamics. For example, the New York City Taxi Limousine Commission regularly releases source-destination information about trips in the taxis they regulate. Taxi data provide information about traffic patterns and thus enable the study of urban flow – what will traffic between two locations look like at a certain date and time in the future? Existing big data methods try to outdo each other in terms of complexity and algorithmic sophistication. In the spirit of "big data beats algorithms", we present a very simple baseline that outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, including Bing Maps and Baidu Maps (whose APIs permit large-scale experimentation). Such a travel time estimation baseline has several important uses, such as navigation (fast travel time estimates can serve as approximate heuristics for A* search variants for path finding) and trip planning (which uses operating hours for popular destinations along with travel time estimates to create an itinerary).

title: Q-caching: an integrated reinforcement-learning approach for caching and routing in information-centric networks
Abstract: Content delivery, such as video streaming, is one of the most prevalent Internet applications. Although very popular, the continuous growth of such applications poses novel performance and scalability challenges. Information-centric networks put content at the center and propose novel solutions to such challenges but also pose new questions on the interface between caching and routing. In this paper, building on top of Q-routing, we propose a caching strategy, namely Q-caching, which leverages information already collected by the routing algorithm. Q-caching promotes content diversity in the network, reducing the load at custodians and average download times for clients.  In stylized topologies, we show that the gains of Q-caching against state-of-the-art algorithms are significant. We then consider the RNP topology and show that Q-caching performance is more flexible while competitive when compared against existing algorithms.

title: Approximate Hubel-Wiesel Modules and the Data Structures of Neural Computation
Abstract: This paper describes a framework for modeling the interface between perception and memory at the algorithmic level of analysis.  It is consistent with phenomena associated with many different brain regions, including view-dependence (and invariance) effects in visual psychophysics and inferotemporal cortex physiology, as well as episodic memory recall interference effects associated with the medial temporal lobe. The perspective developed here relies on a novel interpretation of Hubel and Wiesel's conjecture for how receptive fields tuned to complex objects, and invariant to details, could be achieved.  It complements existing accounts of two-speed learning systems in neocortex and hippocampus (e.g., McClelland et al. 1995) while significantly expanding their scope to encompass a unified view of the entire pathway from V1 to hippocampus.

title: Knowledge and Influence of MOOC Courses on Initial Teacher Training
Abstract: The impact of MOOC courses on distance learning processes has been extremely significant from the beginning. They offer an innovative model of massive teaching, which paradigmatically exploits the potential and relevance that ICTs currently have in modern society. This article aims to analyze the presence of these courses and their role in teacher training, as well as their knowledge and influence on future teachers currently being formed at the university level. A case study was conducted using descriptive, not experimental, methodology, from a quantitative base. The sample study was undertaken in Spain (n=200). The main result is the determination of the minimal impact that the MOOC phenomenon has had on the students polled.  Equally, a significant lack of knowledge was revealed in all its dimensions (professional, pedagogical, structural, etc.), with only a minority of those in the sample group indicating they have studied any of the courses or know to some extent the main platforms where they are offered worldwide.  A large number of those surveyed are therefore unaware of the existence of these courses. As a result, it has been established that regardless of the quality of the learning and the didactic and methodological characteristics that MOOC courses offer, their study and analysis are considered necessary for future educational professionals.  It is imperative that at the level of Higher Education, and especially in the faculties of teacher training, the most recent advances in the field of ICTs are introduced in the study plan and in the academic programs, for they constitute the base of modern society. |||
