title: Full-scale Cascade Dynamics Prediction with a Local-First Approach
Abstract: Information cascades are ubiquitous on social networking sites. Understanding how information spreads through these networks, the structure and evolution of cascades over time, and the factors that influence user adoption of specific messages are vital for applications like viral marketing, rumor prevention, and link prediction. Existing research primarily focuses on predicting final cascade size, relying on cascade graph-dependent methods that are limited to predicting large cascades. This paper addresses the challenge of full-scale cascade dynamics prediction – predicting user activation at any point in a cascade process. It proposes a unified framework, FScaleCP, which models local spreading behaviors as a classification problem. By learning patterns from historical cascades, FScaleCP predicts full-scale dynamics through an asynchronous propagation method that aggregates local behaviors. Extensive experiments demonstrate FScaleCP's superior performance compared to existing baselines.

title: GELATO and SAGE: An Integrated Framework for MS Annotation
Abstract: Several algorithms and tools have been developed to automate glycan identification by analyzing Mass Spectrometric data. However, these tools struggle to annotate large MSn data sets using uncurated public databases, especially for data where n > 2. We propose a novel software package designed to automate the annotation of tandem MS data. This package consists of two key components: 1) GELATO, a free, semi-automated MSn data interpreter that expands and automates existing open source projects like GlycoWorkbench (GWB) and GlycomeDB; and 2) SAGE, a machine learning model that learns the behavior of glycoanalysts to select annotations generated by GELATO, mirroring human interpretation of spectra.

title: Convexified Modularity Maximization for Degree-corrected Stochastic Block Models
Abstract: The Stochastic Block Model (SBM), a popular framework for community detection in networks, assumes that all nodes within a community are statistically equivalent with equal expected degrees. The Degree-Corrected Stochastic Block Model (DCSBM) addresses this limitation by allowing for degree heterogeneity within communities. This paper introduces a convexified modularity maximization approach for estimating hidden communities under DCSBM. Our approach employs a convex programming relaxation of the classical (generalized) modularity maximization formulation, followed by a novel doubly-weighted $ \\ell_1 $-norm $\nk $-median procedure. We provide non-asymptotic theoretical guarantees for both approximate and perfect clustering, with results insensitive to the minimum degree and applicable to sparse regimes with bounded average degrees. These theoretical results match the best known performance guarantees of computationally feasible algorithms for the special case of SBM. Our algorithm is implemented efficiently and tested on synthetic and real-world networks, demonstrating competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

title: Natural Language Inference by Tree-Based Convolution and Heuristic Matching
Abstract: This paper introduces the TBCNN-pair model for recognizing entailment and contradiction between two sentences. The model utilizes a tree-based convolutional neural network (TBCNN) to capture sentence-level semantics and then combines the information from individual sentences through heuristic matching layers like concatenation and element-wise product/difference. Experimental results show that our model significantly outperforms existing sentence encoding-based approaches.

title: Using Students as Experimental Subjects in Software Engineering Research -- A Review and Discussion of the Evidence
Abstract: The question of whether students should be used as experimental subjects in software engineering is a debated topic. While students are readily available and inexpensive, they may not represent the target population of "real" developers in terms of experience and proficiency, raising concerns about the external validity of student-based experiments. This paper challenges the notion that using students is inherently problematic, arguing that it can be justifiable in many cases. Based on a comprehensive review of literature comparing students and professionals, the paper highlights two main points: 1) Classifying subjects solely by their student status is a proxy for more meaningful classifications like skill level, and research should focus on defining and using these classifications. 2) Using students is reasonable in many situations, especially when basic programming skills are involved, tools or methodologies with low learning curves are being compared, or initial research stages of large industrial initiatives are being explored.

title: Inferring Volatility in the Heston Model and its Relatives -- an Information Theoretical Approach
Abstract: Stochastic volatility models describe asset prices $S_t$ as driven by an unobserved process representing the random dynamics of volatility $\\sigma_t$. This work quantifies the amount of information about $\\sigma_t$ that can be inferred from asset prices $S_t$ in terms of Shannon's mutual information $I(S_t :\n\\sigma_t)$. This motivates a detailed numerical and analytical study of the information theoretic properties of the Heston model. Additionally, a general class of discrete time models is studied from a machine learning perspective. In all cases, a significant uncertainty in volatility estimates is observed due to fundamental information theoretic reasons.

title: Comparing molecules and solids across structural and alchemical space
Abstract: Evaluating the (dis)similarity of crystalline, disordered, and molecular compounds is crucial for developing algorithms that automatically navigate the configuration space of complex materials. This paper proposes a new approach, Regularized Entropy Match (REMatch), for comparing atomic coordination environments using local descriptors like the Smooth Overlap of Atomic Positions (SOAP). REMatch combines these local descriptors to describe the similarity of both molecular and bulk periodic structures, providing powerful metrics for navigating alchemical and structural complexity within a unified framework. Furthermore, using this kernel and a ridge regression method, the paper demonstrates prediction of atomization energies for a database of small organic molecules with a mean absolute error below 1kcal/mol, representing a significant step in the application of machine learning techniques to molecular property evaluation.

title: Data Driven SMART Intercontinental Overlay Networks
Abstract: This paper explores the application of Big Data and machine learning based analytics to the real-time management of Internet scale Quality-of-Service Route Optimization using an overlay network. By analyzing massive amounts of data collected every 2 minutes over numerous source-destination pairs, the paper shows that intercontinental Internet Protocol (IP) paths are far from optimal in terms of Quality of Service (QoS) metrics like end-to-end round-trip delay.  A machine learning based scheme is developed that leverages data collected from communicating node pairs in a multi-hop overlay network to select paths with significantly better QoS than IP. Inspired by the Cognitive Packet Network protocol, this scheme uses Random Neural Networks with Reinforcement Learning to select optimal overlay hops, resulting in improved QoS compared to IP itself. This routing scheme is tested on a 20-node intercontinental overlay network, collecting close to $2\\times 10^6$ measurements per week and making scalable distributed routing decisions. Experimental results show significant and efficient QoS improvements in a scalable manner.

title: Feedforward Sequential Memory Networks: A New Structure to Learn Long-term Dependency
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel neural network architecture, the feedforward sequential memory network (FSMN), for modeling long-term dependency in time series without using recurrent feedback. The proposed FSMN is a standard fully-connected feedforward neural network incorporating learnable memory blocks in its hidden layers. These memory blocks utilize a tapped-delay line structure to encode long context information into a fixed-size representation, acting as a short-term memory mechanism. The effectiveness of FSMNs is evaluated in several standard benchmark tasks, including speech recognition and language modeling. Experimental results demonstrate that FSMNs significantly outperform conventional recurrent neural networks (RNNs), including LSTMs, in modeling sequential signals like speech or language. Moreover, FSMNs are learned more reliably and quickly than RNNs or LSTMs due to their non-recurrent model structure.

title: Post-Regularization Inference for Time-Varying Nonparanormal Graphical Models
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel class of time-varying nonparanormal graphical models for modeling high-dimensional heavy-tailed systems and the evolution of their latent network structures. Statistical tests for the presence of edges, both locally at a fixed index value and globally over a range of values, are developed within this model. These tests are designed for high-dimensional regimes, robust to model selection mistakes, and do not require commonly assumed minimum signal strength. The testing procedures rely on a high-dimensional, debiasing-free moment estimator using a novel kernel smoothed Kendall's tau correlation matrix as input. This estimator consistently estimates the latent inverse Pearson correlation matrix uniformly across both the index variable and kernel bandwidth, achieving minimax optimal convergence rate. The method is validated through thorough numerical simulations and an application to a neural imaging dataset.

title: Using Causal Discovery to Track Information Flow in Spatio-Temporal Data - A Testbed and Experimental Results Using Advection-Diffusion Simulations
Abstract: Causal discovery algorithms based on probabilistic graphical models have gained traction in geoscience for identifying and visualizing dynamical processes. These algorithms learn the structure of a graphical model from observed spatio-temporal data, revealing information flow and interaction pathways within the observed physical system. Studying these pathways helps geoscientists understand the underlying dynamical mechanisms governing our planet. Initial studies using this approach on real-world atmospheric data showed promising potential for scientific discovery, but lacked ground truth evaluation. This paper addresses this gap by developing a testbed simulating two dominant geoscience processes, advection and diffusion, on a 2D grid. Causal discovery based information tracking algorithms are applied to the simulation data to assess their performance across different scenarios and gain insights into the physical meaning of the graph results, particularly instantaneous connections. All datasets used in this study are made publicly available as a benchmark.

title: Statistical and Computational Guarantees for the Baum-Welch Algorithm
Abstract: The Hidden Markov Model (HMM) is a fundamental tool for statistical modeling of discrete time series, with applications spanning speech recognition, computational biology, computer vision, and econometrics. Estimating an HMM from its observation process is often addressed using the Baum-Welch algorithm, known for its susceptibility to local optima. This paper provides a comprehensive characterization of the basin of attraction associated with any global optimum of the population likelihood. Exploiting this characterization, non-asymptotic finite sample guarantees are provided for Baum-Welch updates, ensuring geometric convergence to a small ball around a global optimum with a radius on the order of the minimax rate. A concrete example demonstrating a linear rate of convergence for a hidden Markov mixture of two isotropic Gaussians with suitable mean separation and initialization is presented. These are the first rigorous local convergence guarantees to global optima for the Baum-Welch algorithm in a nonconvex likelihood setting. The theoretical results are complemented with thorough numerical simulations, studying the algorithm's convergence and validating the accuracy of the predictions.

title: Robust Semi-supervised Least Squares Classification by Implicit Constraints
Abstract: The Implicitly Constrained Least Squares (ICLS) classifier is a novel semi-supervised version of the least squares classifier. This classifier minimizes the squared loss on labeled data while considering the set of parameters implied by all possible labelings of unlabeled data. Unlike other discriminative semi-supervised methods, ICLS avoids introducing explicit assumptions into the objective function, leveraging implicit assumptions inherent to the choice of the supervised least squares classifier. This method can be formulated as a quadratic programming problem and solved using a simple gradient descent procedure. The paper proves that, in a limited 1-dimensional setting, ICLS never performs worse than the supervised classifier. Experimental results demonstrate that performance improvements can be expected in general multidimensional cases, both in terms of squared loss and expected classification error.

title: Improving Facial Analysis and Performance Driven Animation through Disentangling Identity and Expression
Abstract: This paper presents techniques for improving performance-driven facial animation, emotion recognition, and facial key-point or landmark prediction by leveraging learned identity invariant representations. Existing approaches to these problems often struggle when limited labeled examples are available for a specific identity or when factors of variation are not tightly controlled. This work addresses this challenge by explicitly modeling variations related to identity and expression. A weakly-supervised approach is employed, using identity labels to learn distinct factors of variation related to identity and expression. Probabilistic modeling of these sources of variation enables the learning of identity-invariant representations for expressions, which can then be used to identity-normalize various facial expression analysis and animation control procedures. The paper also shows how to extend the widely used active appearance models and constrained local models by replacing their point distribution models with identity-expression factorized representations. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent performance improvements in emotion recognition, markerless performance-driven facial animation, and facial key-point tracking.

title: New Perspectives on $k$-Support and Cluster Norms
Abstract: This paper introduces the box-norm, a regularizer defined as a parameterized infimum of quadratics. The paper shows that the k-support norm, proposed for sparse vector prediction problems, is a member of this family, and the box-norm can be generated as a perturbation of the k-support norm. An improved algorithm for computing the proximity operator of the squared box-norm is derived, along with a method for computing the norm. The norms are extended to matrices, introducing the spectral k-support norm and spectral box-norm. The paper notes that the spectral box-norm is essentially equivalent to the cluster norm, a multitask learning regularizer, and can be interpreted as a perturbation of the spectral k-support norm. Centering the norm is crucial for multitask learning, and a method for using centered versions of the norms as regularizers is provided. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the spectral k-support and box-norms, and their centered variants, achieve state-of-the-art performance in matrix completion and multitask learning problems, respectively.

title: Learning Document Embeddings by Predicting N-grams for Sentiment Classification of Long Movie Reviews
Abstract: Despite the loss of semantic information, bag-of-ngram based methods still achieve state-of-the-art results for tasks like sentiment classification of long movie reviews. While numerous document embedding methods have been proposed to capture semantics, they have yet to surpass the performance of bag-of-ngram based methods in this task. This paper modifies the architecture of the Paragraph Vector, allowing it to learn document vectors by predicting both words and n-gram features. This model effectively captures both semantics and word order in documents while retaining the expressive power of learned vectors. Experimental results on the IMDB movie review dataset show that the model outperforms previous deep learning models and bag-of-ngram based models, demonstrating its ability to capture semantics and word order. The model's performance is further enhanced when combined with other models. The source code is made publicly available alongside the paper.
label: AI

title: Electricity Demand Forecasting by Multi-Task Learning
Abstract: This paper explores the application of kernel-based multi-task learning techniques to forecast electricity demand in multiple nodes of a distribution network. The paper shows that recently developed output kernel learning techniques are particularly well-suited for this problem, enabling flexible modeling of the complex seasonal effects characterizing electricity demand data while learning and exploiting correlations between multiple demand profiles. The paper also demonstrates that kernels with a multiplicative structure outperform widely adopted (generalized) additive models in predictive performance. The study is based on residential and industrial smart meter data provided by the Irish Commission for Energy Regulation (CER).

title: Self-Excitation: An Enabler for Online Thermal Estimation and Model Predictive Control of Buildings
Abstract: This paper investigates a method for improving buildings' thermal predictive control performance through online identification and excitation (active learning process) with minimal disruption to normal operations. Previous studies demonstrated scalable methods for acquiring multi-zone thermal models of passive buildings using a gray-box approach leveraging building topology and measurement data. This paper extends the method to multi-zone actively controlled buildings and explores how to improve thermal model estimation by utilizing the controller to excite unknown portions of the building's dynamics. Comparing against a baseline thermostat controller, the paper demonstrates the utility of both initially acquired and improved thermal models within a Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework, which accounts for weather uncertainty and time-varying temperature set-points. A simulation study shows that self-excitation improves model estimation, leading to enhanced MPC energy savings and occupant comfort. By integrating building topology, estimation, and control routines into a single online framework, the paper highlights the potential for low-cost scalable methods to actively learn and control buildings for occupant comfort and energy minimization, leveraging existing HVAC sensors and hardware.

title: Online Model Estimation for Predictive Thermal Control of Buildings
Abstract: This study proposes a general, scalable method for learning control-oriented thermal models of buildings, enabling wide-scale deployment of cost-effective predictive controls. An Unscented Kalman Filter, augmented for parameter and disturbance estimation, is shown to accurately learn and predict a building's thermal response. Recent studies of heating, ventilating, and air conditioning (HVAC) systems have shown significant energy savings with advanced model predictive control (MPC). However, a scalable and cost-effective method for acquiring accurate, robust models of individual buildings' unique thermal envelopes has been elusive, hindering the widespread adoption of prediction-based control systems. This paper proposes a novel gray-box approach using an Unscented Kalman Filter based on a multi-zone thermal network and validates it using EnergyPlus simulation data. The filter quickly learns parameters of a thermal network during periods of known or constrained loads and then characterizes unknown loads to provide accurate 24+ hour energy predictions. This study extends earlier research by formalizing parameter and disturbance estimation routines and demonstrating results across a year-long study.

title: The Utility of Abstaining in Binary Classification
Abstract: This paper explores the problem of binary classification in machine learning, where the classifier is allowed to abstain from making predictions, professing ignorance about the true class label without committing to a prediction. This approach is directly motivated by applications like medical diagnosis and fraud risk assessment, where incorrect predictions can have severe consequences. The paper focuses on recent theoretical work in this area, characterizing how allowing abstentions can lead to fewer errors in very general settings. Two key areas are highlighted: the surprising possibility of zero-error learning and the fundamental tradeoff between predicting frequently and avoiding incorrect predictions. Efficient algorithms with provable guarantees are reviewed for each area. The paper also discusses connections to other scenarios, like active learning, suggesting promising avenues for future research in this emerging field.

title: Distributed Linearized Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers for Composite Convex Consensus Optimization
Abstract: We investigate the problem of consensus optimization in a network of agents, where each agent aims to minimize its private convex composite function while respecting privacy constraints. We propose a distributed proximal gradient method (DPGA) for consensus optimization over both unweighted and weighted static communication networks. DPGA iteratively computes the proximal map of each agent's private function and its gradient, followed by communication with neighboring agents. We also study its stochastic gradient variant (SDPGA), which handles noisy gradient estimates. Both methods achieve ergodic convergence in sub-optimality error and consensus violation, with rates of O(1/t) for DPGA and O(1/√t) for SDPGA. These results find applications in distributed sensing, machine learning, and statistical inference.

title: Regularized Orthogonal Tensor Decompositions for Multi-Relational Learning
Abstract: We present a scalable method for multi-relational learning, called Regularized Orthogonal Iteration Decomposition (ROID), which addresses the limitations of existing methods regarding computational cost and sensitivity to given ranks. ROID utilizes a core tensor trace norm regularization for full or incomplete tensor analytics and can be extended to a graph Laplacian regularized version or a sparse higher-order orthogonal iteration (SHOOI) version. By exploiting the equivalence between the Schatten p-norm of a low multi-linear rank tensor and its core tensor, we reduce the problem to a smaller matrix trace norm minimization problem. We solve this problem using two efficient augmented Lagrange multiplier algorithms with convergence guarantees. Experiments on real and synthetic datasets demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of our proposed methods.

title: Inverse Reinforcement Learning via Deep Gaussian Process
Abstract: We propose a new approach to inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) based on the deep Gaussian process (deep GP) model. Our model leverages multiple latent GP layers to learn abstract representations of the state feature space, which is linked to the demonstrations through the Maximum Entropy learning framework. To handle the intractability introduced by incorporating IRL into the nonlinear latent structure, we develop a non-standard variational approximation framework that extends previous inference schemes. This framework enables approximate Bayesian treatment of the feature space and prevents overfitting. Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks ("object world," "highway driving") and a new benchmark ("binary world") by simultaneously performing representation and inverse reinforcement learning.

title: Statistical Learning under Nonstationary Mixing Processes
Abstract: We study a special case of statistical learning without the i.i.d. assumption, considering a learning method presented with a sequence of data points where it must make predictions and observe the associated losses. We go beyond traditional analyses focused on stationary mixing processes or nonstationary product processes by allowing for nonstationary mixing processes, specifically β-mixing processes with sublinear growth in the sum of changes in marginal distributions. Under these conditions, we propose a learning method and prove that for bounded VC subgraph classes, the cumulative excess risk grows sublinearly in the number of predictions at a quantified rate.

title: On Temporal Regularity in Social Interactions: Predicting Mobile Phone Calls
Abstract: This paper investigates the predictability of mobile phone call activity using a machine learning approach. We leverage the temporal regularity observed in social interactions to predict future calls based on past calling patterns. Our analysis uses an anonymized mobile phone usage dataset containing data from 783 users and over 12,000 caller-callee pairs. Results demonstrate that historical calling patterns can predict future calls with reasonable accuracy, suggesting that caller-callee interactions are not purely random but exhibit temporal patterns.

title: Using Data Analytics to Detect Anomalous States in Vehicles
Abstract: As vehicles become increasingly connected, they face a larger attack surface, posing risks to passengers and those around them. Existing vulnerabilities stem from the use of the less secure CAN bus framework, which lacks basic authentication. To address this issue, we propose a data analytics solution using machine learning techniques for securing vehicles. We develop a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) to detect anomalous states from real-world vehicle data. This model enables the detection and alerting of anomalies during vehicle operation, potentially serving as a plug-n-play device for new and older cars.

title: Device and System Level Design Considerations for Analog-Non-Volatile-Memory Based Neuromorphic Architectures
Abstract: This paper provides an overview of recent advancements in brain-inspired computing, focusing on implementations using emerging memories as electronic synapses. Design challenges and considerations are discussed, encompassing requirements for multilevel states, device variability, programming energy, array-level connectivity, fan-in/fanout, wire energy, and IR drop. The paper emphasizes the increasing importance of wires in design decisions for large systems and highlights the significant impact of cycle-to-cycle variations on learning performance.

title: Discovering topic structures of a temporally evolving document corpus
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for discovering the topical content of a data corpus and tracking its structural changes over time. Unlike previous work, our model does not impose a prior on the document addition rate or rely on the Markovian assumption, allowing for more complex changes to be captured. Our framework consists of: (i) time discretization into epochs, (ii) epoch-wise topic discovery using a hierarchical Dirichlet process-based model, and (iii) a temporal similarity graph for modeling complex topic changes (emergence, disappearance, evolution, splitting, and merging). The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated on two medical literature corpora focused on Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and Metabolic Syndrome (MetS). We provide an extensive empirical analysis, examining the effects of free parameters and discussing the significance of findings in the context of practical applications and existing literature on temporal topic analysis. Qualitative case studies related to ASD and MetS showcase the algorithm's ability to capture actual developments in these fields.

title: Inducing Generalized Multi-Label Rules with Learning Classifier Systems
Abstract: Multi-label classification has gained significant attention due to real-world applications like text classification and medical diagnoses. This paper explores the suitability of Learning Classifier Systems (LCS) for multi-label classification problems, which often involve multiple highly specific niches. We introduce a generalized multi-label rule format that allows for flexible label-dependency modeling without requiring explicit knowledge of correlations. This format is integrated into the Michigan-style supervised LCS framework, resulting in a novel algorithm for multi-label classification. The algorithm's behavior is studied through artificial problems and thoroughly evaluated on multi-label datasets, demonstrating competitiveness with other state-of-the-art methods.

title: Bridging the Gap between Stochastic Gradient MCMC and Stochastic Optimization
Abstract: Stochastic gradient Markov chain Monte Carlo (SG-MCMC) methods are Bayesian analogs of popular stochastic optimization methods, but this connection is not well studied. We explore this relationship by applying simulated annealing to an SGMCMC algorithm. Furthermore, we extend recent SG-MCMC methods with adaptive preconditioners (similar to ADAgrad or RMSprop) and adaptive element-wise momentum weights. The zero-temperature limit yields a novel stochastic optimization method with adaptive element-wise momentum weights, unlike conventional methods that use a shared, static momentum weight. Theoretical analysis suggests that the proposed simulated annealing approach converges close to the global optima under certain assumptions. Experiments on deep neural network models demonstrate state-of-the-art performance compared to related stochastic optimization algorithms.

title: Histogram Meets Topic Model: Density Estimation by Mixture of Histograms
Abstract: The histogram method is a powerful non-parametric approach for estimating probability density functions of continuous variables. However, it requires a large number of observations compared to parametric approaches, making it unsuitable for analyzing sparse data sets. This paper presents a novel Bayesian approach to alleviate sparsity issues in histogram estimation using probabilistic topic models. Our method estimates a unit's density function as a mixture of basis histograms, where the number of bins and their heights are automatically determined. The estimation procedure utilizes fast and easy-to-implement collapsed Gibbs sampling. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness on synthetic data.

title: A Combined Deep-Learning and Deformable-Model Approach to Fully Automatic Segmentation of the Left Ventricle in Cardiac MRI
Abstract: Segmenting the left ventricle (LV) from cardiac magnetic resonance (MRI) datasets is crucial for calculating clinical indices like ventricular volume and ejection fraction. This paper proposes a fully automatic segmentation tool for the LV from short-axis cardiac MRI datasets, combining deep learning algorithms with deformable models. Deep learning algorithms learn the segmentation task from ground truth data, with convolutional networks used to automatically detect the LV chamber and stacked autoencoders to infer the LV shape. The inferred shape is then integrated into deformable models to improve segmentation accuracy and robustness. Validation on 45 cardiac MR datasets from the MICCAI 2009 LV segmentation challenge demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods, achieving excellent agreement with ground truth.

title: Toward a Research Agenda in Adversarial Reasoning: Computational Approaches to Anticipating the Opponent's Intent and Actions
Abstract: This paper defines adversarial reasoning as computational approaches for inferring and anticipating an enemy's perceptions, intents, and actions. It argues that adversarial reasoning goes beyond game theory and requires leveraging disciplines like cognitive modeling, control theory, AI planning, and others. The paper explores lessons learned from the CADET battle planning system, which focuses on brigade-level ground operations and involves adversarial reasoning. Building upon current capabilities, the paper describes RAID, a DARPA program aimed at developing adversarial reasoning capabilities, highlighting their potential applications in defense and other areas.

title: Multi-Level Cause-Effect Systems
Abstract: We present a domain-general account of causation applicable to settings where macro-level causal relations between two systems are of interest, but the relevant causal features are poorly understood and need to be aggregated from vast micro-measurements. Our approach generalizes the work of Chalupka et al. (2015) to cases where the macro-level effect is unspecified. We formalize the connection between micro- and macro-variables in such situations and provide a framework describing causal relations at multiple levels of analysis. We propose an algorithm for discovering macro-variable causes and effects from micro-level measurements obtained from an experiment. Additionally, we show how to design experiments to uncover macro-variables from observational micro-variable data. Finally, we demonstrate that under specific conditions, multiple levels of causal structure can be identified. Throughout the article, a simulated neuroscience multi-unit recording experiment illustrates the concepts and algorithms.

title: An Experimental Evaluation of Computational Techniques for Planning and Assessment of International Interventions
Abstract: This paper describes the experimental methodology employed in a series of experiments within the DARPA COMPOEX program. The program aimed to develop tools and methods for analyzing, planning, and predictively assessing plans for complex operations where integrated PMESII (political-military-economic-social-infrastructure-information) considerations are crucial. Our team conducted several broad-based experiments involving dozens of experts from multiple agencies. The methodology evolved across experiments based on lessons learned. We present the motivation, objectives, structure, methods explored, results, lessons learned, and recommendations for future interagency experiment series.

title: Learning Transferrable Knowledge for Semantic Segmentation with Deep Convolutional Neural Network
Abstract: We propose a novel weakly-supervised semantic segmentation algorithm based on Deep Convolutional Neural Network (DCNN). Unlike existing weakly-supervised approaches, our algorithm utilizes auxiliary segmentation annotations available for different categories to guide segmentations on images with only image-level class labels. To ensure knowledge transfer across categories, we design a decoupled encoder-decoder architecture with an attention model. This architecture generates spatial highlights of each category in an image using an attention model and subsequently generates foreground segmentation for each highlighted region using a decoder. By incorporating the attention model, we demonstrate that the decoder, trained with segmentation annotations from different categories, can improve the performance of weakly-supervised semantic segmentation. Our algorithm shows substantial performance improvements compared to state-of-the-art weakly-supervised techniques on the challenging PASCAL VOC 2012 dataset when trained with annotations from 60 exclusive categories in the Microsoft COCO dataset.

title: An unsupervised spatiotemporal graphical modeling approach to anomaly detection in distributed CPS
Abstract: Modern distributed cyber-physical systems (CPSs) encounter a wide range of physical faults and cyber anomalies, making them vulnerable to catastrophic fault propagation scenarios due to strong connectivity among subsystems. This paper presents a data-driven framework for system-wide anomaly detection to address these issues. The framework utilizes a spatiotemporal feature extraction scheme based on symbolic dynamics for discovering and representing causal interactions among CPS subsystems. The extracted features are then used to learn system-wide patterns via a Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM). Results show that: (1) the RBM free energy in off-nominal conditions differs from that in nominal conditions, enabling anomaly detection; (2) the framework can capture multiple nominal modes with a single graphical model; and (3) case studies with simulated data and an integrated building system validate the proposed approach.

title: Context-Based Prediction of App Usage
Abstract: With the increasing number of apps on smartphones (around 100 on average) and the limited screen space for app icons, a new paradigm is needed to improve app visibility for users. This paper proposes a novel online algorithm for dynamically predicting the apps a user is likely to use. The algorithm runs on the user's device and continuously learns the user's habits based on time, location, and device state. It aims to actively guide users to their desired apps and provide a personalized experience, maximizing the Area Under the Curve (AUC). Both theoretical and empirical analyses demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness in maximizing the AUC and achieving good results on a dataset of 1,000 devices.

title: Unveiling Contextual Similarity of Things via Mining Human-Thing Interactions in the Internet of Things
Abstract: Recent advancements in RFID, wireless sensor networks, and Web services have made physical things an integral part of the emerging ubiquitous Web. Discovering correlations among these ubiquitous things is crucial for various applications like things search, discovery, classification, recommendation, and composition. This article presents DisCor-T, a novel graph-based method for uncovering underlying connections between things by mining the rich content embodied in human-thing interactions, including user, temporal, and spatial information. We model this information using two graphs: a spatio-temporal graph and a social graph. Random walk with restart (RWR) is applied to determine proximities among things, and a relational graph of things (RGT) indicating implicit correlations is learned. This correlation analysis contributes to improved effectiveness in things management. To demonstrate utility, we develop a flexible feature-based classification framework on top of RGT and perform a systematic case study. Our evaluation highlights the strength and feasibility of the proposed approach.

title: Visualizations Relevant to The User By Multi-View Latent Variable Factorization
Abstract: A primary goal of data visualization is to identify, from all available mappings, those that are most relevant to the user's needs in 2D/3D displays. Assuming user interaction data or other auxiliary information about items or their relationships, the objective is to determine which aspects in the primary data support the user's input and, conversely, which aspects of the potentially noisy user input find support in the primary data. To address this challenge, we introduce a multi-view embedding where a latent factorization identifies aspects that are related across both the primary data and user data views, as well as aspects specific to each view. This factorization is a generative model where the display is parameterized as part of the factorization, and other factors account for aspects not expressible in a two-dimensional display. We demonstrate the model's functioning on several datasets. |||

title: The Lovász Hinge: A Novel Convex Surrogate for Submodular Losses
Abstract: Learning with non-modular losses is crucial when sets of predictions are made simultaneously. Margin and slack rescaling are common tools for constructing convex surrogate loss functions for set prediction. We demonstrate that these strategies lead to tight convex surrogates only if the underlying loss function is increasing with the number of incorrect predictions. However, gradient or cutting-plane computation for these functions is NP-hard for non-supermodular loss functions. We propose a novel surrogate loss function for submodular losses, the Lovász hinge, which offers O(p log p) complexity with O(p) oracle accesses to the loss function for gradient or cutting-plane computation. We prove that the Lovász hinge is convex and provides an extension. This work presents the first tractable convex surrogates in the literature for submodular losses. We demonstrate the utility of this novel convex surrogate through various set prediction tasks, including the PASCAL VOC and Microsoft COCO datasets.

title: Hardware Architecture for Large Parallel Array of Random Feature Extractors applied to Image Recognition
Abstract: We present a low-power, compact hardware implementation of a Random Feature Extractor (RFE) core. With complex tasks like Image Recognition demanding a large feature set, we show how weight reuse can virtually expand the random features available from the RFE core. We also demonstrate how to avoid computation cost wasted on propagating "incognizant" or redundant random features. To validate our approach, we used our RFE core as the first stage of an Extreme Learning Machine (ELM), a two-layer neural network, achieving over 97% accuracy on the MNIST database of handwritten digits. The RFE stage of the ELM is implemented on an analog ASIC occupying 5mm x 5mm area in 0.35µm CMOS and consuming 5.95µJ/classify while using approximately 5000 effective hidden neurons. The second stage of the ELM, consisting solely of adders, can be implemented as a digital circuit with an estimated power consumption of 20.9 nJ/classify. With a total energy consumption of only 5.97 µJ/classify, this low-power mixed-signal ASIC can act as a co-processor in portable electronic gadgets with cameras.

title: Real-Time Audio-to-Score Alignment of Music Performances Containing Errors and Arbitrary Repeats and Skips
Abstract: This paper presents a real-time alignment of music performance audio signals with the corresponding score, known as score following. This approach can handle tempo changes, errors, and arbitrary repeats or skips in performances, making it especially useful for automatic accompaniment during practice and rehearsals where errors and repeats are common. Simple extensions of previous algorithms are not suitable for scores of practical length due to high computational complexity. To address this, we introduce two hidden Markov models for monophonic performance with errors and arbitrary repeats/skips, deriving efficient score-following algorithms under the assumption that the prior probability distributions of score positions before and after repeats/skips are independent. We verified the real-time operation of these algorithms for practical length music scores (around 10,000 notes) on a modern laptop, demonstrating their ability to track input performance within 0.7 seconds on average after repeats/skips in clarinet performance data. Future improvements and extensions for polyphonic signals are also discussed.

title: RDF2Rules: Learning Rules from RDF Knowledge Bases by Mining Frequent Predicate Cycles
Abstract: The development of large-scale RDF knowledge bases has enabled their use in various knowledge-based applications. To further expand the number of facts in these knowledge bases, logic rules can be used to predict new facts based on existing ones. This makes the automatic learning of reliable rules from large-scale knowledge bases increasingly important. We introduce RDF2Rules, a novel rule learning approach specifically designed for RDF knowledge bases. RDF2Rules first mines frequent predicate cycles (FPCs), a type of interesting frequent patterns in knowledge bases, and then generates rules from these mined FPCs. As each FPC can produce multiple rules and effective pruning is applied during FPC mining, RDF2Rules is highly efficient. Another advantage of RDF2Rules lies in its use of entity type information when generating and evaluating rules, resulting in more accurate learned rules. Our experimental findings demonstrate that RDF2Rules outperforms existing approaches in both efficiency and accuracy.

title: Fast Parallel SVM using Data Augmentation
Abstract: Linear SVMs remain a popular classifier, but they still face challenges when dealing with very large-scale problems, despite the development of linear or sub-linear algorithms for single machines. Parallel computing methods have been developed for learning large-scale SVMs. However, existing methods rely on solving local sub-optimization problems. This paper presents a novel parallel algorithm for learning large-scale linear SVMs. Our approach is based on a data augmentation equivalent formulation, which recasts the problem of learning SVM as a Bayesian inference problem, allowing us to develop efficient parallel sampling methods. We present empirical results for this parallel sampling SVM and extend it to support SVR, non-linear kernels, and provide a parallel implementation of the Crammer and Singer model. This approach is highly promising and provides a useful technique for parallelizing a broader family of general maximum-margin models.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning in Large Discrete Action Spaces
Abstract: Reasoning in environments with a large number of discrete actions is crucial for extending reinforcement learning to a wider range of problems. Recommender systems, industrial plants, and language models are just a few examples of real-world tasks involving large numbers of discrete actions where current methods struggle or are often impossible to apply. The ability to generalize over the set of actions and achieve sub-linear complexity relative to the size of the set are both essential for handling such tasks. Existing approaches lack these capabilities, motivating the work presented in this paper. Our proposed approach leverages prior information about the actions to embed them in a continuous space where generalization is possible. Additionally, approximate nearest-neighbor methods enable logarithmic-time lookup complexity relative to the number of actions, which is necessary for computationally efficient training. This combined approach enables reinforcement learning methods to be applied to large-scale learning problems previously intractable with current methods. We demonstrate the capabilities of our algorithm on a series of tasks involving up to one million actions.

title: Composite Bayesian inference
Abstract: We revisit and generalize the concept of composite likelihood as a method for probabilistic inference through the aggregation of multiple Bayesian agents, defining a class of predictive models termed composite Bayesian. This perspective provides insights into choosing the weights associated with composite likelihood, either a priori or through learning. In the latter case, the weights can be tuned to minimize prediction cross-entropy, leading to an easy-to-solve convex problem. We argue that composite Bayesian inference offers a middle ground between generative and discriminative models, balancing interpretability and prediction performance, both of which are crucial for many artificial intelligence tasks.

title: Machine-z: Rapid Machine Learned Redshift Indicator for Swift Gamma-ray Bursts
Abstract: The study of high-redshift gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) provides valuable information about the early Universe, such as the rates of stellar collapsars and mergers, metallicity content, constraints on the re-ionization period, and probes of the Hubble expansion. Rapid selection of high-z candidates from real-time GRB samples reported by dedicated space missions like Swift is crucial for identifying the most distant bursts before the optical afterglow becomes too dim for spectral analysis. We introduce "machine-z", a redshift prediction algorithm and a "high-z" classifier for Swift GRBs based on machine learning. Our method relies exclusively on canonical data commonly available within the first few hours after the GRB trigger. Using a sample of 284 bursts with measured redshifts, we trained a randomized ensemble of decision trees (random forest) to perform both regression and classification. Cross-validated performance studies show a correlation coefficient of nearly 0.6 between machine-z predictions and true redshifts. Our high-z classifier achieves 80% recall of true high-redshift bursts while incurring a false positive rate of 20%. With a 40% false positive rate, the classifier achieves nearly 100% recall. The most reliable selection of high-redshift GRBs is obtained by combining predictions from both the high-z classifier and the machine-z regressor.

title: Reinforcement Learning: Stochastic Approximation Algorithms for Markov Decision Processes
Abstract: This article provides a concise overview of stochastic approximation algorithms in reinforcement learning of Markov decision processes. These algorithms can also be used as a suboptimal method for partially observed Markov decision processes.

title: Preconditioned Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics for Deep Neural Networks
Abstract: Training deep neural networks effectively faces two main challenges. Firstly, the parameter spaces of these models exhibit pathological curvature. Recent methods address this issue by using adaptive preconditioning for Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), improving convergence by adapting to the local geometry of parameter space. Secondly, overfitting is a common problem, typically addressed by early stopping. However, recent research has shown that Bayesian model averaging mitigates this issue. The posterior can be sampled using Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD). However, the rapidly changing curvature makes default SGLD methods inefficient. We propose combining adaptive preconditioners with SGLD, supported by theoretical properties on asymptotic convergence and predictive risk. We provide empirical results for Logistic Regression, Feedforward Neural Nets, and Convolutional Neural Nets, demonstrating that our preconditioned SGLD method achieves state-of-the-art performance on these models.

title: High-Order Stochastic Gradient Thermostats for Bayesian Learning of Deep Models
Abstract: Learning in deep models using Bayesian methods has gained significant attention recently, driven by the feasibility of modern Bayesian methods to achieve scalable learning and inference while maintaining a measure of uncertainty in the model parameters. Stochastic gradient MCMC algorithms (SG-MCMC) are a family of diffusion-based sampling methods for large-scale Bayesian learning. In SG-MCMC, multivariate stochastic gradient thermostats (mSGNHT) augment each parameter of interest with a momentum and a thermostat variable to maintain stationary distributions as target posterior distributions. As the number of variables in a continuous-time diffusion increases, numerical approximation error becomes a practical bottleneck, highlighting the need for improved numerical integrators. To address this, we propose using an efficient symmetric splitting integrator in mSGNHT instead of the traditional Euler integrator. We demonstrate that the proposed scheme is more accurate, robust, and converges faster. These desirable properties are particularly relevant for Bayesian deep learning. Extensive experiments on two canonical models and their deep extensions show that the proposed scheme improves general Bayesian posterior sampling, especially for deep models.

title: Homology Computation of Large Point Clouds using Quantum Annealing
Abstract: Homology, a tool in topological data analysis, measures the shape of data. In many cases, these measurements provide new insights not available through other means. Homology computation relies on mathematical constructions that scale exponentially with the size of the data. Consequently, for large point clouds, computation becomes infeasible using classical computers. This paper presents a quantum annealing pipeline for computing homology of large point clouds. The pipeline takes a graph approximating the given point cloud as input. It utilizes quantum annealing to compute a clique covering of the graph and then uses this cover to construct a Mayer-Vietoris complex. The pipeline concludes with simplified homology computation of the Mayer-Vietoris complex. We introduce three different clique coverings and their quantum annealing formulation. Our pipeline scales polynomially in the size of the data once the covering step is solved. To demonstrate the algorithm's correctness, we include tests using the D-Wave 2X quantum processor.

title: The Max $K$-Armed Bandit: PAC Lower Bounds and Efficient Algorithms
Abstract: We examine the Max K-Armed Bandit problem, where a learning agent interacts with multiple stochastic arms, each providing independent and identically distributed rewards with unknown distributions. At each time step, the agent selects an arm and observes the reward of the obtained sample. Each sample is considered a separate item with the reward signifying its value. The objective is to find the item with the highest possible value. Our fundamental assumption is a known lower bound on the tail function of the reward distributions. Within the PAC framework, we provide a lower bound on the sample complexity of any (ε, δ)-correct algorithm and propose an algorithm that achieves this bound up to logarithmic factors. We analyze the robustness of the proposed algorithm and compare its performance to a variant where arms are indistinguishable and randomly selected at each stage. Interestingly, when the maximal rewards of the arms are similar, the latter approach may provide better performance.

title: Satisficing in multi-armed bandit problems
Abstract: Satisficing, a relaxation of maximizing, enables less risky decision-making in the face of uncertainty. We propose two sets of satisficing objectives for the multi-armed bandit problem, aiming to achieve reward-based decision-making performance above a given threshold. We demonstrate that these new problems are equivalent to various standard multi-armed bandit problems with maximizing objectives, utilizing this equivalence to find performance bounds. The different objectives can lead to qualitatively distinct behaviors; for instance, agents explore their options continuously in one case and only a finite number of times in another. For Gaussian rewards, we establish an additional equivalence between the two sets of satisficing objectives, enabling algorithms developed for one set to be applied to the other. We then develop variants of the Upper Credible Limit (UCL) algorithm that solve the problems with satisficing objectives and demonstrate that these modified UCL algorithms achieve efficient satisficing performance.

title: Deep Value of Information Estimators for Collaborative Human-Machine Information Gathering
Abstract: Effective human-machine collaboration can significantly enhance learning and planning strategies for information gathering by fusing "hard" and "soft" data from machine and human sensors, respectively. However, acquiring the most informative data from human sensors without task overloading remains a critical challenge. Value of Information (VOI) is a crucial decision-theoretic metric for scheduling interaction with human sensors. We introduce a new Deep Learning-based VOI estimation framework for scheduling collaborative human-machine sensing, enabling computationally efficient online inference with minimal policy hand-tuning. Supervised learning is used to train deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to extract hierarchical features from "images" of belief spaces obtained via data fusion. These features can be associated with soft data query choices to reliably compute VOI for human interaction. We detail the CNN framework and provide a performance comparison to a feature-based POMDP scheduling policy. The practical feasibility of our method is demonstrated on a mobile robotic search problem with language-based semantic human sensor inputs.

title: A Latent-Variable Lattice Model
Abstract: Markov random field (MRF) learning is computationally expensive, with approximation algorithms being particularly costly. We focus on a specific subset of MRFs frequently used in computer vision. We characterize this subset using three concepts: Lattice, Homogeneity, and Inertia; and propose a non-Markov model as an alternative. Our goal is robust learning from small datasets. Our learning algorithm employs vector quantization and achieves a time complexity of O(U log U) for a dataset of U pixels, significantly faster than general-purpose MRF methods.

title: k-Means Clustering Is Matrix Factorization
Abstract: This paper demonstrates that the objective function of conventional k-means clustering can be expressed as the Frobenius norm of the difference between a data matrix and a low-rank approximation of that data matrix. In essence, we show that k-means clustering is a matrix factorization problem. These notes serve as a reference and provide a guided tour towards a result often mentioned but rarely made explicit in the literature.

title: A New PID Neural Network Controller Design for Nonlinear Processes
Abstract: This paper presents a novel adaptive tuning method for a PID neural network (PIDNN) controller for nonlinear processes. The method utilizes an improved gradient descent method to adjust PIDNN parameters, where margin stability is employed to achieve high tracking performance and robustness against external load disturbance and parameter variation. Simulation results showcase the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm compared to other well-known learning methods.

title: Recovering 6D Object Pose and Predicting Next-Best-View in the Crowd
Abstract: Object detection and 6D pose estimation in crowded scenes, characterized by multiple object instances, severe foreground occlusions, and background distractors, has become a critical problem in rapidly evolving technological fields like robotics and augmented reality. Single shot-based 6D pose estimators relying on manually designed features struggle to address these challenges, motivating research into unsupervised feature learning and next-best-view estimation. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for both single shot-based 6D object pose estimation and next-best-view prediction based on Hough Forests, the state-of-the-art object pose estimator that performs classification and regression jointly. Instead of manually designed features, we propose a) unsupervised feature learning from depth-invariant patches using a Sparse Autoencoder and b) a comprehensive evaluation of various state-of-the-art features. Furthermore, leveraging the clustering performed in the leaf nodes of Hough Forests, we learn to estimate the reduction of uncertainty in other views, formulating the problem of selecting the next-best-view. To further enhance pose estimation, we introduce an improved joint registration and hypotheses verification module as a final refinement step to reject false detections. We provide two additional challenging datasets inspired by realistic scenarios for comprehensive evaluation of the state-of-the-art and our framework. One dataset focuses on domestic environments, while the other depicts a bin-picking scenario prevalent in industrial settings. Our findings demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art on both public and our datasets.

title: Convolutional Architecture Exploration for Action Recognition and Image Classification
Abstract: Convolutional Architecture for Fast Feature Encoding (CAFFE) is a software package for training, classifying, and extracting features from images. The UCF Sports Action dataset, a widely used machine learning dataset, contains 200 videos in 720x480 resolution, showcasing nine different sporting activities: diving, golf, swinging, kicking, lifting, horseback riding, running, skateboarding, swinging (various gymnastics), and walking. This report presents a CAFFE feature extraction pipeline for images taken from the videos of the UCF Sports Action dataset. A similar test was performed on Overfeat, yielding inferior results compared to CAFFE. This study aims to explore the architecture and hyperparameters necessary for effective static analysis of action in videos and classification across various image datasets. |||

title: Evaluation-as-a-Service: Overview and Outlook
Abstract: Evaluation in empirical computer science is crucial for demonstrating progress and assessing the technologies developed. Traditionally, domains like information retrieval relied on the Cranfield paradigm, using shared test collections, defined search tasks, and ground truth for evaluation. However, new challenges have emerged in recent years, including massive datasets, confidential data, and rapidly changing data, which pose problems for this paradigm. Additionally, crowdsourcing has changed how industry tackles problems, with companies offering challenges and monetary rewards to incentivize participation, especially in machine learning. This white paper discusses the Evaluation-as-a-Service (EaaS) paradigm, which addresses these challenges by keeping data central and providing access via APIs, virtual machines, or other methods. The paper aims to summarize and compare current EaaS approaches, analyze their usage scenarios and advantages/disadvantages, and identify the next steps for sustainable EaaS research infrastructures. It also examines the motivations of various stakeholders, including funding agencies, challenge organizers, researchers, participants, and industry seeking real-world solutions.
label: AI

title: Adaptive Ensemble Learning with Confidence Bounds
Abstract: Extracting actionable intelligence from distributed, heterogeneous, correlated, and high-dimensional data sources necessitates real-time processing and learning both locally and globally. Meta-learning techniques have gained popularity in the past decade, where local learners make online predictions based on their data and feed these predictions to an ensemble learner for global predictions. However, most existing meta-learning approaches lack performance guarantees, or those guarantees are only asymptotic. Additionally, confidence estimates for predictions and learning rate guarantees for the ensemble learner are often missing. This paper introduces Hedged Bandits, a systematic ensemble learning method that provides both long-run (asymptotic) and short-run (learning rate) performance guarantees. Hedged Bandits offer performance guarantees relative to the optimal local prediction strategy and adapt its predictions in a data-driven manner. The effectiveness of Hedged Bandits is demonstrated in the context of medical informatics, where it outperforms various online and offline ensemble learning methods.
label: AI

title: A Learning Algorithm for Change Impact Prediction
Abstract: Change impact analysis aims to predict the impact of code modifications on software applications. This paper approaches change impact analysis from a learning perspective, focusing on predicting the impact of method code changes on test method failures. The proposed algorithm, LCIP, learns from past impacts to predict future impacts. The evaluation of LCIP is conducted on seven Java software applications totaling over 214,000 lines of code. Through code mutations simulating 17,574 changes and their actual impacts, the study shows that LCIP achieves a precision of 69%, a recall of 79%, and an F-score of 55% in predicting impact.
label: AI

title: Adaptive Algorithms for Online Convex Optimization with Long-term Constraints
Abstract: This paper proposes an adaptive online gradient descent algorithm for solving online convex optimization problems with long-term constraints. These constraints need to be satisfied over a finite number of rounds but can be violated during intermediate rounds. The algorithm achieves cumulative regret bounds of O(T^max{$\\beta$,1--$\\beta$}) for the loss and O(T^(1--$\\beta$/2)) for constraint violations, where $\\beta$ is a user-defined trade-off parameter between 0 and 1. This holds for convex losses and can handle arbitrary convex constraints without requiring prior knowledge of the number of rounds. The proposed algorithm improves upon the best known cumulative regret bounds by Mahdavi et al. (2012), which are respectively O(T^1/2) and O(T^3/4) for general convex domains and O(T^2/3) for polyhedral domains. Experimental results validate the practical performance of the algorithm.
label: AI

title: Multi-centrality Graph Spectral Decompositions and their Application to Cyber Intrusion Detection
Abstract: Modern datasets often have graph representations, making spectral decompositions like graph principal component analysis (PCA) valuable for analysis. Unlike previous graph decomposition methods that focused on a single topological feature, this paper proposes spectral decomposition approaches for graph PCA and graph dictionary learning that integrate multiple features, including graph walk statistics, centrality measures, and distances to reference nodes. Specifically, the paper introduces multi-centrality graph PCA (MC-GPCA) for single graph analysis and multi-centrality graph dictionary learning (MC-GDL) for ensembles of graphs. Both methods leverage spectral decomposition of multi-centrality matrices. In the context of cyber intrusion detection, MC-GPCA can serve as an indicator of anomalous connectivity patterns, while MC-GDL provides a discriminative basis for attack classification.
label: AI

title: Musical instrument sound classification with deep convolutional neural network using feature fusion approach
Abstract: This paper presents a new musical instrument classification method using convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Unlike traditional methods, this approach focuses on classifying instruments using learned features from CNNs. To extract these features, the method utilizes not only conventional spectrogram images but also introduces multiresolution recurrence plots (MRPs) that incorporate phase information from the raw input signal. This captures the characteristic timbre of instruments, which cannot be extracted using phase-blind representations like spectrograms. By combining MRPs and spectrogram images with a multi-column network, the proposed classifier system outperforms systems relying solely on spectrograms and traditional handcrafted features and classifiers.
label: AI

title: Incremental Method for Spectral Clustering of Increasing Orders
Abstract: Spectral clustering and community detection rely on the smallest eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors (eigenpairs) of a graph Laplacian matrix. However, the number of clusters or communities is often unknown beforehand. Existing methods either heuristically choose the number of clusters or repeat clustering with different choices, resulting in suboptimal or computationally expensive solutions. This paper proposes an incremental method for constructing the eigenspectrum of the graph Laplacian matrix. The method leverages the eigenstructure to efficiently obtain the K-th eigenpair given the K-1 smallest eigenpairs. The Laplacian matrix is adapted to transform the batch eigenvalue decomposition problem into a sequential leading eigenpair computation problem. As a practical application, the paper demonstrates user-guided spectral clustering, allowing users to utilize the incremental method for effective eigenpair computation and determining the desired number of clusters based on various metrics.
label: AI

title: A Deep Generative Deconvolutional Image Model
Abstract: This paper presents a deep generative model for image representation and analysis based on a hierarchical convolutional dictionary-learning framework. Stochastic unpooling links consecutive layers in the model, enabling top-down image generation. A Bayesian support vector machine is connected to the top-layer features, providing max-margin discrimination. During testing, deep deconvolutional inference infers latent features, and the top-layer features are connected to the max-margin classifier for discrimination tasks. The model is efficiently trained using a Monte Carlo expectation-maximization (MCEM) algorithm implemented on GPUs for large-scale learning and fast testing. The model achieves highly competitive results on several benchmark datasets, including ImageNet, demonstrating its effectiveness compared to similarly sized convolutional neural networks.
label: AI

title: Latent Variable Modeling with Diversity-Inducing Mutual Angular Regularization
Abstract: Latent Variable Models (LVMs) are a prominent family of machine learning models that effectively extract underlying patterns, structure, and knowledge from data. However, the increasing volume and complexity of data pose challenges for traditional LVMs, including capturing long-tail patterns, reducing model complexity, and improving interpretability. This paper proposes a novel regularization technique for LVMs that controls the geometry of the latent space during learning, encouraging diverse latent components that are mutually different. This approach addresses the challenges of long-tail coverage, low redundancy, and better interpretability. The paper introduces a mutual angular regularizer (MAR) to promote larger mutual angles between components. To address the non-convex and non-smooth nature of MAR, a smooth lower bound is derived and optimized. The paper demonstrates how MAR affects the generalization performance of neural networks and shows its effectiveness in capturing long-tail patterns, reducing model complexity without sacrificing expressivity, and improving interpretability in restricted Boltzmann machines and distance metric learning.
label: AI

title: Mid-level Representation for Visual Recognition
Abstract: Visual Recognition, a fundamental challenge in AI, aims to understand the semantics of visual data. Mid-level representations have shifted the paradigm in visual recognition by discovering and training a set of mid-level visual patterns (e.g., parts and attributes) for representing images and videos. This thesis focuses on utilizing mid-level representations for different high-level visual recognition tasks: image understanding and video understanding. For image understanding, the thesis investigates object detection/recognition by discovering and learning a set of mid-level patches for representing object category images. The approach employs discriminative patches in a subcategory-aware webly-supervised fashion. The thesis also examines the effects of using subcategory-based models for mitigating dataset bias.
label: AI

title: Efficient Thresholded Correlation using Truncated Singular Value Decomposition
Abstract: Efficiently computing a subset of a correlation matrix containing values above a specified threshold is crucial for various applications. Real-world problems in genomics, machine learning, finance, and other fields can produce correlation matrices that are too large to form and compute explicitly. Often, only highly correlated values are of interest, representing a small fraction of the entire matrix. This paper presents a method based on the singular value decomposition (SVD) and its relationship to the data covariance structure. The method efficiently computes thresholded subsets of very large correlation matrices.
label: AI

title: Feature Selection for Classification under Anonymity Constraint
Abstract: The proliferation of online platforms and their widespread adoption have significantly increased the privacy risks for users. Security research has shown that even anonymized microdata containing online activity information can be used to identify users by cross-referencing with other data sources. Existing privacy-preserving methods, such as k-anonymity, l-diversity, and differential privacy, modify data in isolation, potentially compromising its utility for knowledge discovery tasks. This paper addresses this challenge by focusing on labeled data used for classification and proposing two feature selection methods. The goal is to reduce the disclosure risk while preserving data utility for classification. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and practicality of the proposed methods.
label: AI

title: Refined Error Bounds for Several Learning Algorithms
Abstract: This article investigates the achievable guarantees on the error rates of learning algorithms, particularly focusing on refining logarithmic factors. The results are based on a general technique for obtaining bounds on error rates of sample-consistent classifiers with monotonic error regions in the realizable case. Bounds are derived in terms of either the VC dimension or sample compression size. This technique also enables new bounds for general sample-consistent learning algorithms and refined bounds on the label complexity of the CAL active learning algorithm. Additionally, the paper establishes a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of a distribution-free bound on the error rates of all sample-consistent learning rules, converging at a rate inversely proportional to the sample size. The paper also examines learning with classification noise, deriving a new excess error rate guarantee for general VC classes under Tsybakov's noise condition and establishing a condition for minimax excess risk under bounded noise to converge inversely proportionally to the sample size.
label: AI

title: Recent Advances in Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: Deep learning has achieved significant performance improvements in various domains, including visual recognition, speech recognition, and natural language processing. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been extensively studied, leveraging the growth of annotated data and advances in GPUs. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of recent advancements in CNNs. It details improvements in various aspects, including layer design, activation functions, loss functions, regularization, optimization, and fast computation. The paper also presents applications of CNNs in computer vision, speech, and natural language processing.
label: AI

title: Implementing a Bayes Filter in a Neural Circuit: The Case of Unknown Stimulus Dynamics
Abstract: Intelligent interaction with objects requires animals to translate neural population responses into estimates of the dynamic, unknown stimuli that caused them. The Bayesian solution, known as a Bayes filter, combines population responses with predictions from an internal model using Bayes' rule. This paper presents a method for learning to approximate a Bayes filter when stimulus dynamics are unknown. It utilizes the inferential properties of probabilistic population codes to compute Bayes' rule and trains a neural network to approximate predictions through maximum likelihood estimation. Stochastic gradient descent is performed on the negative log-likelihood using a novel gradient approximation. The method is demonstrated on finite-state, linear, and nonlinear filtering problems, showing how the hidden layer of the neural network develops tuning curves consistent with findings in experimental neuroscience.
label: AI

title: Cost-based Feature Transfer for Vehicle Occupant Classification
Abstract: Knowledge of human presence and interaction in vehicles is crucial for design and safety purposes. This paper presents a framework for occupant detection and classification using a single overhead camera for automatic child locks and airbag suppression. The framework operates on all passenger seats and employs a transfer learning technique to leverage training data from all seats while controlling bias, crucial for a system that penalizes certain misclassifications more than others. An evaluation on a challenging dataset with weighted and unweighted classifiers demonstrates the effectiveness of the transfer process.
label: AI

title: Move from Perturbed scheme to exponential weighting average
Abstract: In online decision problems, decisions are often made with a pool of decision sequences (experts) without knowledge of the future. Each decision incurs a cost based on the chosen action and observed outcome. A common goal is to perform as well as the best expert in the pool. The exponential weighting algorithm is a well-known method for achieving this goal, but recently, the follow-the-perturbed-leader algorithm has emerged as an alternative with similar performance. This paper first identifies shared properties between the two algorithms that explain their performance similarities. It then demonstrates that the two algorithms are identical for a specific perturbation. Finally, the paper shows how follow-the-leader algorithms naturally extend to a wider class of structured online problems where exponential algorithms are inefficient.
label: AI

title: Implementation of deep learning algorithm for automatic detection of brain tumors using intraoperative IR-thermal mapping data
Abstract: Deep machine learning has proven effective for automatic tumor area delineation in intraoperative neuronavigation using active IR-mapping with the cold test. The proposed approach utilizes a matrix IR-imager to remotely register the space-time distribution of surface temperature patterns, determined by local cerebral blood flow dynamics. This technique offers non-invasiveness, zero health risks, low implementation and operational costs, and ease of use. Traditional IR-diagnostic techniques rely on diagnosticians to determine tumor boundaries, leading to uncertainty and potential errors. This study demonstrates that incorporating deep learning algorithms eliminates this drawback.
label: AI

title: Deep Learning with S-shaped Rectified Linear Activation Units
Abstract: Rectified linear activation units are crucial components of state-of-the-art deep convolutional networks. This paper introduces a novel S-shaped rectified linear activation unit (SReLU) that learns both convex and non-convex functions, mimicking multiple function forms inspired by the Webner-Fechner law and Stevens law in psychophysics and neural sciences. SReLU consists of three piecewise linear functions defined by four learnable parameters. It is learned jointly with the deep network during training using back propagation. A "freezing" method is proposed to initialize SReLU in different layers by degenerating it into a predefined leaky rectified linear unit during initial training epochs, followed by adaptive learning of good initial values. SReLU can be universally applied to existing deep networks with minimal additional parameters and computational cost. Experiments using Network in Network and GoogLeNet architectures on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, MNIST, and ImageNet datasets show that SReLU achieves significant improvement compared to other activation functions.
