title: FAASTA: A fast solver for total-variation regularization of ill-conditioned problems with application to brain imaging
Abstract: The total variation (TV) penalty, like many analysis-sparsity problems, lacks separable factors or a closed-form proximal operator, unlike the soft thresholding operator for the $\\ell\\_1$ penalty. This results in challenging non-smooth optimization problems in variational formulations of inverse problems or statistical learning estimation, often addressed with elaborate single-step first-order methods. When the data-fit term originates from empirical measurements, such as in brain imaging, it is often ill-conditioned and lacks simple structure. This makes the gradient step computationally expensive in proximal splitting methods, highlighting the need to minimize the number of gradient steps. This paper presents fAASTA, a variant of FISTA, that uses an internal solver for the TV proximal operator and refines its tolerance to balance computational costs between gradient and proximal steps. Benchmarks and illustrations are provided for "brain decoding," recovering brain maps from noisy measurements to predict behavior. The algorithm and its convergence speed study are valuable for non-exact proximal operators, especially in analysis-sparsity problems. |||

title: On the Differential Privacy of Bayesian Inference
Abstract: This research explores methods for securely communicating Bayesian inference results to third parties while adhering to differential privacy principles. The paper introduces four distinct algorithms for private Bayesian inference on probabilistic graphical models. These include two mechanisms for adding noise to Bayesian updates, either directly to the posterior parameters or to their Fourier transform, preserving update consistency. Additionally, the paper investigates a recently introduced posterior sampling mechanism, proving bounds for the specific case of discrete Bayesian networks, and proposes a maximum-a-posteriori private mechanism. The analysis includes utility and privacy bounds, with a novel focus on the influence of graph structure on privacy. Worked examples and experiments with Bayesian naive Bayes and Bayesian linear regression illustrate the application of these mechanisms.
label: AI

title: Seeing through the Human Reporting Bias: Visual Classifiers from Noisy Human-Centric Labels
Abstract: This paper addresses the problem of learning image classifiers from noisy "human-centric" annotations, which reflect subjective human judgments about what to ignore and mention. These annotations, like image tags and keywords, are inconsistent and incomplete, but exhibit structural noise. The paper proposes an algorithm to decouple the human reporting bias from the visually correct labels. Results demonstrate the algorithm's efficacy in differentiating "what's in the image" from "what's worth saying," outperforming traditional algorithms for image classification and captioning, even doubling the performance of existing methods in some cases.
label: AI

title: Multi-Instance Visual-Semantic Embedding
Abstract: Multi-Instance visual-semantic embedding (MIE) is a novel model for embedding images with single or multiple labels into a continuous semantic label space. This approach addresses the challenges of handling multi-label images, which traditional single-label embedding models struggle with. MIE discovers and maps semantically meaningful image subregions to their corresponding labels, improving upon existing methods for multi-label image annotation and zero-shot learning.
label: AI

title: Facility Deployment Decisions through Warp Optimizaton of Regressed Gaussian Processes
Abstract: This research presents a fast algorithm for determining deployment schedules in fuel cycles that meet given demand. This algorithm leverages Gaussian process regression models to predict production curves as a function of time and facility deployment, measured against the demand curve using dynamic time warping distance. The deployment schedule minimizing this distance is then evaluated in a full fuel cycle simulation, refining the model for the next optimization iteration. The method typically converges within five to ten iterations to a distance less than one percent of total deployable production. A representative once-through fuel cycle demonstrates the methodology for reactor deployment.
label: AI

title: A C++ library for Multimodal Deep Learning
Abstract: MDL, Multimodal Deep Learning Library, is a deep learning framework designed to support multiple models. This document outlines its philosophy and functionality. MDL is compatible with Linux, Mac, and Unix platforms, relying on OpenCV.
label: AI

title: Transformed Residual Quantization for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
Abstract: Product Quantization (PQ) for fast nearest neighbor search relies on exponentially reduced storage and computational complexities with respect to the codebook size. This paper explores Residual Quantization (RQ), an alternative with similar properties as PQ, and proposes a novel approach to optimizing RQ and related hybrid PQ-RQ models. By observing the general randomness increase in residual space, the authors propose a strategy that jointly learns a local transformation per residual cluster, aiming to minimize quantization errors. This approach demonstrably achieves significantly higher accuracy in nearest neighbor search compared to both original and optimized PQ on large-scale benchmarks.
label: AI

title: What Happens to a Manifold Under a Bi-Lipschitz Map?
Abstract: This paper investigates the geometric and topological properties of the image of a smooth submanifold of $\\mathbb{R}^{n}$ under a bi-Lipschitz map to $\\mathbb{R}^{m}$. The focus is on characterizing the relationships between the original manifold's dimension, diameter, volume, and reach with those of the embedded manifold. The main result establishes a lower bound on the reach of the embedded manifold for linear bi-Lipschitz maps when $m \\le n$. The paper discusses implications of these findings for signal processing and machine learning, where bi-Lipschitz maps on low-dimensional manifolds have been constructed using randomized linear operators.
label: AI

title: Predicting the Co-Evolution of Event and Knowledge Graphs
Abstract: Embedding learning, also known as representation learning, has proven effective in modeling large-scale semantic knowledge graphs. This paper addresses the evolution of knowledge graphs, where triple states depend on time. Assuming changes arrive as events, the paper proposes an event prediction model utilizing both knowledge graph background information and recent event data. By predicting future events, the model predicts likely knowledge graph changes, enabling the modeling of knowledge graph evolution. Experiments demonstrate the approach's effectiveness in clinical applications, recommendation engines, and sensor networks.
label: AI

title: On Distributed Cooperative Decision-Making in Multiarmed Bandits
Abstract: This research explores the explore-exploit tradeoff in distributed cooperative decision-making using the multiarmed bandit (MAB) problem. For the distributed cooperative MAB problem, the paper presents the cooperative UCB algorithm, which comprises two interleaved distributed processes: consensus algorithms for reward estimation and upper-confidence-bound-based heuristics for arm selection. The paper rigorously analyzes the performance of the cooperative UCB algorithm and characterizes the influence of communication graph structure on the group's decision-making performance.
label: AI

title: Students' epistemologies about experimental physics: Validating the Colorado Learning Attitudes about Science Survey for Experimental Physics
Abstract: This study investigates students' epistemologies about experimental physics through the development of the Colorado Learning Attitudes about Science Survey for Experimental Physics (E-CLASS).  The paper presents the statistical validity and reliability of E-CLASS as a measure of student epistemologies, analyzing data from multiple institutions and a broad student population.  The study demonstrates that E-CLASS exhibits acceptable levels of validity and reliability, considering item and test discrimination, test-retest reliability, partial-sample reliability, internal consistency, concurrent validity, and convergent validity.  Principal Component Analysis reveals that E-CLASS does not exhibit strong factors, as expected.

title: Addressing Complex and Subjective Product-Related Queries with Customer Reviews
Abstract: This paper explores the fusion of online reviews and Q/A systems to provide relevant product information to users. The proposed system, Moqa, uses a mixture-of-experts framework to learn whether a product review is relevant to a given query. Each review is an "expert" that votes on the response, while the model learns a relevance function to identify relevant reviews. This learned function surfaces relevant reviews on-demand for new queries. Moqa is evaluated on a corpus of 1.4 million questions and answers and 13 million reviews, demonstrating its effectiveness in addressing binary and open-ended queries and surfacing reviews considered relevant by human evaluators.

title: Exploring the spectroscopic diversity of type Ia supernovae with DRACULA: a machine learning approach
Abstract: The existence of multiple subclasses of Type Ia supernovae (SNeIa) is a debated topic in astrophysics. This paper demonstrates how machine learning tools facilitate the identification of SNeIa subtypes through a hierarchical group structure in the continuous space of spectral diversity. Using Deep Learning, the authors achieve subtype identification in a 4-dimensional feature space (+1 for time evolution), surpassing the performance of Principal Component Analysis using 15 principal components. This suggests that the progenitor system and explosion mechanism are describable by a small number of initial physical parameters. The results align with a previously proposed classification scheme and confirm the velocity of lines as a primary factor in subtype determination, followed by 91bg-like events. Given the anticipated data surge in the coming years, this approach is crucial for quick and statistically coherent identification of SNeIa subtypes and outliers. The tools used are publicly available in the Python package DRACULA and COINtoolbox.

title: Information-Theoretic Bounded Rationality
Abstract: Bounded rationality, decision-making and planning under resource limitations, is a significant challenge in artificial intelligence, reinforcement learning, computational neuroscience, and economics. This paper presents a consolidated theory of bounded rationality based on information-theoretic ideas. The paper justifies using the free energy functional as the objective function for bounded-rational decisions, highlighting its key properties: control over the solution space, exact Monte Carlo planners that bypass exhaustive search, and capture of model uncertainty. The paper discusses the single-step decision-making case and extends it to sequential decisions using equivalence transformations, yielding a general class of decision problems encompassing classical decision rules as limit cases.
label: AI

title: Beyond Classification: Latent User Interests Profiling from Visual Contents Analysis
Abstract: User preference profiling is vital in modern online social networks (OSN), particularly for image-centric platforms like Pinterest. This research explores learning latent visual preferences directly from image content, proposing a distance metric learning method based on Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN). The method extracts similarity information from visual content, enabling the mining of fine-grained individual visual preferences. Experiments on 5,790 Pinterest users reveal distinct and identifiable visual preferences, consistent across users' history, highlighting the potential of fine-grained visual preference profiling in understanding user behavior.
label: AI

title: GraphConnect: A Regularization Framework for Neural Networks
Abstract: Deep neural networks excel in domains with large training datasets, but their performance suffers from overfitting when training data is limited. This paper introduces GraphConnect, a data-dependent method to combat overfitting, motivated by the observation that data lies near a manifold. GraphConnect encourages learned decision relationships to resemble a graph representing the manifold structure, focusing on learning attributes present in data samples rather than simply reducing fitting to noise. Empirical Rademacher complexity connects generalization error to the graph's spectral properties, demonstrating GraphConnect's superiority over weight decay. Experimental results on benchmark datasets validate the theoretical analysis, showing significant performance improvements over weight decay when training data is limited.
label: AI

title: Multilinear Subspace Clustering
Abstract: This paper presents a new model and algorithm for unsupervised clustering of 2-D data, particularly images. Assuming the data comes from a union of multilinear subspaces (UOMS) model, a structured case of the union of subspaces (UOS) model, the paper develops the Multilinear Subspace Clustering (MSC) algorithm. The paper evaluates MSC on the YaleB and Olivietti image datasets, demonstrating its competitiveness with UOS-based algorithms in terms of clustering performance while offering computational complexity improvements.
label: AI

title: Sparse Coding with Fast Image Alignment via Large Displacement Optical Flow
Abstract: Sparse representation-based classifiers excel in image classification tasks despite intense noise and occlusion, but their performance degrades when test images or dictionary atoms are misaligned, violating the sparse linear representation assumption. This paper addresses this challenge by introducing a sparse coding framework that adapts dictionary atoms to test images through large displacement optical flow. In the proposed algorithm, each dictionary atom is aligned with the input image, and the sparse code is recovered using the adapted dictionary atoms. A corresponding supervised dictionary learning algorithm is also developed. Experimental results on digit datasets demonstrate the efficacy and robustness of the algorithm.
label: AI

title: Deep Learning for Surface Material Classification Using Haptic And Visual Information
Abstract: This research explores the use of acceleration signals captured during surface scratching with a handheld tool for surface material classification. The paper proposes a novel deep learning method based on a Fully Convolutional Network (FCN) that takes both acceleration signals and corresponding surface texture images as input. This method, unlike previous approaches that rely on hand-crafted features, automatically extracts discriminative features using advanced deep learning methodologies. Experiments on the TUM surface material database demonstrate state-of-the-art classification accuracy, showcasing the method's robustness and efficiency.
label: AI

title: Statistics-Free Sports Prediction
Abstract: This research investigates the prediction of baseball, basketball, football, and hockey games using a simple machine learning model: logistically-weighted regularized linear least squares regression. Using only historical data on game dates, teams, and final scores, the model achieves better results in basketball due to its high-scoring nature and long seasons. The model performs better in football and hockey compared to baseball, while baseball predictions are closer to theoretical optimality. The study concludes that most basketball statistics are subsumed by game scores, while further exploration of game and player statistics is necessary for improved predictions in football. Baseball and hockey fall between these extremes.
label: AI

title: Backward and Forward Language Modeling for Constrained Sentence Generation
Abstract: This paper explores language generation using recurrent neural networks (RNNs), specifically addressing the challenge of generating text with hard constraints, requiring the presence of a specific word in the sentence. Existing language models struggle with this constraint. The paper proposes a novel backward and forward language model using RNNs to generate previous and future words, either simultaneously or asynchronously, around the given word. This approach allows for flexible word placement in the generated sentence. Experimental results demonstrate comparable text quality to sequential language models. |||
label: AI

title: SLiMFast: Guaranteed Results for Data Fusion and Source Reliability
Abstract: We propose SLiMFast, a novel data fusion framework that addresses the challenge of unifying conflicting data from multiple sources by estimating their accuracies. Our approach casts data fusion as a statistical learning problem, utilizing discriminative probabilistic models—often equivalent to logistic regression—to effectively integrate diverse data sources. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on complex generative models and restrictive distributional assumptions, SLiMFast offers theoretical guarantees and flexibility. Moreover, our framework facilitates the incorporation of domain knowledge, leading to substantial accuracy improvements—up to 50%—over existing state-of-the-art baselines. Building on our theoretical insights, we have developed an optimizer that eliminates the need for manual algorithm selection for learning SLiMFast's parameters. We validate our optimizer through rigorous testing on numerous real-world datasets, demonstrating its ability to accurately predict the optimal learning algorithm for achieving the best data fusion outcomes.
label: AI

title: ATD: Anomalous Topic Discovery in High Dimensional Discrete Data
Abstract: We propose an algorithm for detecting anomalous patterns in high-dimensional discrete data. Unlike most anomaly detection (AD) methods that identify individual anomalies, our algorithm detects groups of anomalies—clusters of points exhibiting abnormal patterns collectively. This approach enhances the understanding of atypical behavior and pinpoints anomaly sources. Our method particularly excels in scenarios where anomalous patterns manifest in a small subset of the high-dimensional feature space. Individual AD techniques and those relying on all features struggle with such anomalies, but our algorithm can detect these instances collectively, reveal the shared anomalous patterns, and identify the salient features. We apply our algorithm to the problem of detecting anomalous topics in text documents, employing topic models as the foundation. Our experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the algorithm's accuracy in detecting anomalous topics and their salient features (words). Notably, our method outperforms both standard group AD and individual AD techniques. The code for reproducing our experiments is available at https://github.com/hsoleimani/ATD.
label: AI

title: Behavioral Modeling for Churn Prediction: Early Indicators and Accurate Predictors of Custom Defection and Loyalty
Abstract: Churn prediction, identifying customers likely to discontinue service, is a significant concern for businesses across diverse industries. As firms amass large-scale, heterogeneous data on customer characteristics and behaviors, new churn prediction methods become possible. This paper presents a unified framework for detecting early warning signs of churn and assigning a "Churn Score" to each customer, indicating their likelihood of churning within a predetermined timeframe. Our framework employs a comprehensive feature engineering approach, followed by feature selection to refine the set of relevant attributes. The final feature set is then fed into a suite of supervised learning algorithms. Using terabytes of data from a major mobile phone network, our method identifies numerous intuitive and surprising early warning signs of churn. Our best model achieves an 89.4% accuracy in predicting whether a subscriber will churn.
label: AI

title: Latent variable model selection for Gaussian conditional random fields
Abstract: We address the problem of learning conditional Gaussian graphical models in the presence of latent variables. Drawing upon recent advancements, we introduce a method that decomposes the parameters of a conditional Markov random field into the sum of a sparse and a low-rank matrix. We derive convergence bounds for this estimator, demonstrating its robust behavior in high-dimensional settings and its ability to recover the graph structure (i.e., "sparsistency"). We further showcase how proximal gradient algorithms and semi-definite programming techniques can be employed to fit the model to datasets with thousands of variables. Through extensive simulations, we delineate the conditions for identifiability and demonstrate the model's superior performance in a broad range of scenarios compared to existing alternatives. Notably, our model effectively accommodates a greater number of latent variables. We apply the suggested method to two real-world datasets containing individual-level data on genetic variants and metabolite levels. Our results outperform alternative approaches and exhibit enriched biological signals.

title: Revisiting Differentially Private Regression: Lessons From Learning Theory and their Consequences
Abstract: Private regression has attracted attention from both database and security communities. Recent work by Fredrikson et al. (USENIX Security 2014) analyzed the functional mechanism (Zhang et al. VLDB 2012) for training linear regression models over medical data. Unfortunately, they found that model accuracy becomes unacceptably low with differential privacy when ε = 5. To address this issue, we present an explicit connection between differential privacy and stable learning theory, resulting in a substantially improved privacy/utility tradeoff. Notably, our theory reveals that the fundamental mechanism in differential privacy, output perturbation, can be leveraged to achieve better tradeoffs for all convex-Lipschitz-bounded learning tasks. The simplicity of output perturbation makes our approach potentially widely applicable. We apply it to the same medical data used by Fredrikson et al. Encouragingly, we achieve accurate models even for ε = 0.1. In the latter part of this paper, we examine the impact of our improved differentially private mechanisms on model inversion attacks, a privacy attack introduced by Fredrikson et al. Our analysis reveals that the enhanced tradeoff makes the resulting differentially private model more susceptible to inversion attacks.

title: Collaborative Filtering for Predicting User Preferences for Organizing Objects
Abstract: As service robots become more capable of performing useful tasks, the need to teach robots how to execute tasks according to our preferences grows. However, individual users often have distinct preferences regarding tasks, for example, when arranging objects on shelves. These preferences are influenced by personal taste, cultural background, and common sense, making it challenging to pre-program robots to accommodate all users. Constantly querying users for task instructions is impractical. In this work, we present an approach to learn patterns in user preferences for tidying up objects in containers like shelves or boxes. Our method leverages the collaborative filtering paradigm for personalized recommendations and utilizes data collected from diverse users through crowdsourcing. To address novel objects with no data, we propose a method that complements standard collaborative filtering by extracting information from the web. When performing a tidy-up task, we first predict pairwise object preferences of the user. Subsequently, we subdivide objects in containers by modeling a spectral clustering problem. Our solution is easily updatable, does not require complex modeling, and improves with the amount of user data. We evaluate our approach using crowdsourced data from over 1,200 users and demonstrate its effectiveness in two tidy-up scenarios. Additionally, we show that a real robot can reliably predict user preferences using our approach.

title: Kernel principal component analysis network for image classification
Abstract: To classify nonlinear features using a linear classifier and enhance classification accuracy, we propose a deep learning network called Kernel Principal Component Analysis Network (KPCANet). The process involves mapping data into a higher-dimensional space using kernel principal component analysis (KPCA) to make the data linearly separable. Subsequently, a two-layer KPCANet is constructed to obtain the principal components of the image. Finally, the principal components are classified using a linear classifier. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed KPCANet in face recognition, object recognition, and handwritten digit recognition. Importantly, KPCANet generally outperforms the traditional Principal Component Analysis Network (PCANet). Furthermore, KPCANet exhibits invariance to illumination and robustness to occlusion and slight deformation.

title: A Mathematical Theory of Deep Convolutional Neural Networks for Feature Extraction
Abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks have revolutionized numerous practical machine learning tasks, including image classification (ImageNet), control policy learning (Atari games and Go), and image captioning. Many of these applications first extract features and then feed these extracted features into a trainable classifier. Mallat (2012) initiated the mathematical analysis of deep convolutional neural networks for feature extraction. Specifically, he explored scattering networks based on a wavelet transform followed by the modulus non-linearity in each network layer, proving translation invariance (asymptotically in the wavelet scale parameter) and deformation stability of the corresponding feature extractor. This paper complements Mallat's findings by developing a theory that encompasses general convolutional transforms (or, technically, general semi-discrete frames), including Weyl-Heisenberg filters, curvelets, shearlets, ridgelets, wavelets, and learned filters. It also incorporates general Lipschitz-continuous non-linearities (e.g., rectified linear units, shifted logistic sigmoids, hyperbolic tangents, and modulus functions) and general Lipschitz-continuous pooling operators (e.g., sub-sampling and averaging). All these elements can vary across network layers. For the resulting feature extractor, we prove a translation invariance result of a vertical nature, signifying that features become progressively more translation-invariant with increasing network depth. We also establish deformation sensitivity bounds that apply to signal classes such as band-limited functions, cartoon functions, and Lipschitz functions.

title: The Limitations of Optimization from Samples
Abstract: This paper investigates the intriguing question: can we optimize objective functions from the training data used to learn them? We formalize this question within a novel framework we call Optimization from Samples (OPS). In OPS, we are provided with sampled values of a function drawn from a distribution, and the objective is to optimize the function under some constraint. While certain classes of functions can be optimized from samples, our primary finding is an impossibility result. We demonstrate that there are classes of functions that are both statistically learnable and optimizable, yet no reasonable approximation for optimization from samples is attainable. Specifically, our main result proves the absence of a constant factor approximation for maximizing coverage functions under a cardinality constraint using polynomially-many samples drawn from any distribution. We also present tight approximation guarantees for maximization under a cardinality constraint of several interesting function classes, including unit-demand, additive, and general monotone submodular functions. Moreover, we establish a constant factor approximation for monotone submodular functions with bounded curvature.

title: Using machine learning for medium frequency derivative portfolio trading
Abstract: We utilize machine learning to design a medium-frequency trading strategy for a portfolio of 5-year and 10-year US Treasury note futures. We formulate this task as a classification problem, predicting the weekly direction of movement of the portfolio using features extracted from a deep belief network trained on technical indicators of the portfolio constituents. Our experimentation demonstrates the effectiveness of this pipeline in generating profitable trades.

title: A new robust adaptive algorithm for underwater acoustic channel equalization
Abstract: We introduce a novel family of adaptive robust equalizers for highly challenging underwater acoustic (UWA) channel equalization. As the underwater environment is highly non-stationary and prone to impulsive noise, we employ adaptive filtering techniques based on a relative logarithmic cost function, inspired by competitive methods from online learning literature. To improve the convergence performance of conventional linear equalization methods while mitigating stability issues, we intrinsically combine different norms of the error in the cost function using logarithmic functions. This approach achieves convergence performance comparable to the Least Mean Fourth (LMF) equalizer, while significantly enhancing stability performance in such an adverse communication medium. We validate the performance of our algorithms through highly realistic experiments conducted on accurately simulated underwater acoustic channels.

title: Poseidon: A System Architecture for Efficient GPU-based Deep Learning on Multiple Machines
Abstract: Deep learning (DL) has achieved remarkable successes in numerous machine learning tasks. Several frameworks, including Caffe, Torch, and Theano, have been developed to accelerate the design and training of deep neural networks (DNNs). While these frameworks can harness multiple GPUs on a single machine, they currently lack the ability to utilize GPUs distributed across multiple machines. Given that even average-sized DNNs can take days to train on a single GPU with hundreds of GBs to TBs of data, distributed GPUs offer a prime opportunity for scaling up DL. However, the limited bandwidth of commodity Ethernet networks presents a bottleneck for distributed GPU training, hindering its straightforward realization. To explore how existing frameworks can be efficiently adapted to support distributed GPUs, we propose Poseidon, a scalable system architecture for distributed inter-machine communication within existing DL frameworks. We integrate Poseidon with Caffe and evaluate its performance in training DNNs for object recognition. Poseidon introduces three key contributions that accelerate DNN training on clusters: (1) a three-level hybrid architecture enabling support for both CPU-only and GPU-equipped clusters, (2) a distributed wait-free backpropagation (DWBP) algorithm to enhance GPU utilization and balance communication, and (3) a structure-aware communication protocol (SACP) to minimize communication overheads. We empirically demonstrate that Poseidon converges to the same objectives as a single machine and achieves state-of-the-art training speedup across multiple models and well-established datasets using a commodity GPU cluster of 8 nodes (e.g., 4.5x speedup on AlexNet, 4x on GoogLeNet, 4x on CIFAR-10). On the much larger ImageNet22K dataset, Poseidon with 8 nodes achieves better speedup and competitive accuracy compared to recent CPU-based distributed systems like Adam and Le et al., which utilize tens to thousands of nodes.

title: Discriminative Subnetworks with Regularized Spectral Learning for Global-state Network Data
Abstract: Data mining practitioners face challenges from data with network structure. This paper addresses a specific class of global-state networks, consisting of network instances sharing a similar structure but having different values at local nodes. Each instance is associated with a global state indicating the occurrence of an event. The objective is to uncover a small set of discriminative subnetworks that can optimally classify global network values. Unlike most existing studies that explore an exponential subnetwork space, we address this difficult problem by adopting a space transformation approach. Specifically, we present an algorithm that optimizes a constrained dual-objective function to learn a low-dimensional subspace capable of discriminating networks labeled by different global states while reconciling with shared common network topology across instances. Our algorithm draws inspiration from spectral graph learning, and we demonstrate that the globally optimal solution can be achieved via matrix eigen-decomposition.

title: Regularized Estimation of Piecewise Constant Gaussian Graphical Models: The Group-Fused Graphical Lasso
Abstract: The time-evolving precision matrix of a piecewise-constant Gaussian graphical model encodes the dynamic conditional dependency structure of a multivariate time-series. Traditionally, graphical models are estimated under the assumption that data is drawn identically from a generating distribution. By introducing sparsity and sparse-difference inducing priors, we relax these assumptions and propose a novel regularized M-estimator to jointly estimate both the graph and changepoint structure. The resulting estimator possesses the ability to favor sparse dependency structures or smoothly evolving graph structures, as required. Moreover, our approach extends current methods to allow estimation of changepoints that are grouped across multiple dependencies in a system. We present an efficient algorithm for structure estimation and study the empirical recovery properties in a synthetic setting. The qualitative effect of grouped changepoint estimation is then demonstrated by applying the method to two real-world datasets.

title: Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) and Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) Conceptual Design Report Volume 2: The Physics Program for DUNE at LBNF
Abstract: The Physics Program for the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) at the Fermilab Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) is described.

title: Morphological Inflection Generation Using Character Sequence to Sequence Learning
Abstract: Morphological inflection generation is the task of generating the inflected form of a given lemma corresponding to a specific linguistic transformation. We model the problem of inflection generation as a character sequence-to-sequence learning problem and present a variant of the neural encoder-decoder model for solving it. Our model is language-independent and can be trained in both supervised and semi-supervised settings. We evaluate our system on seven datasets of morphologically rich languages and achieve either better or comparable results to existing state-of-the-art models of inflection generation.

title: Expectation propagation for continuous time stochastic processes
Abstract: We consider the inverse problem of reconstructing the posterior measure over the trajectories of a diffusion process from discrete-time observations and continuous-time constraints. We frame the problem within a Bayesian framework and derive approximations to the posterior distributions of single-time marginals using variational approximate inference. We then demonstrate how this approximation can be extended to a wide class of discrete-state Markov jump processes by leveraging the chemical Langevin equation. Our empirical results showcase the computational efficiency of the proposed method and its ability to provide good approximations for these classes of inverse problems.

title: Bayesian anti-sparse coding
Abstract: Sparse representations have proven their efficacy in solving a wide range of inverse problems encountered in signal and image processing. Conversely, enforcing the information to be spread uniformly over representation coefficients exhibits relevant properties in various applications such as digital communications. Anti-sparse regularization can be naturally expressed through an ℓ∞-norm penalty. This paper derives a probabilistic formulation of such representations. We introduce a new probability distribution, termed the democratic prior, and derive its main properties along with three random variate generators. This probability distribution is then used as a prior to promote anti-sparsity in a Gaussian linear inverse problem, yielding a fully Bayesian formulation of anti-sparse coding. Two Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms are proposed to generate samples according to the posterior distribution. The first algorithm is a standard Gibbs sampler, while the second uses Metropolis-Hastings moves that exploit the proximity mapping of the log-posterior distribution. These samples are used to approximate maximum a posteriori and minimum mean square error estimators of both parameters and hyperparameters. Simulations on synthetic data illustrate the performance of the two proposed samplers for both complete and over-complete dictionaries. All results are compared to the recent deterministic variational FITRA algorithm.

title: Demonstration of quantum advantage in machine learning
Abstract: The main promise of quantum computing is to efficiently solve certain problems that are prohibitively expensive for a classical computer. Most problems with a proven quantum advantage involve the repeated use of a black box, or oracle, whose structure encodes the solution. One measure of algorithmic performance is the query complexity, i.e., the scaling of the number of oracle calls needed to find the solution with a given probability. Few-qubit demonstrations of quantum algorithms, such as Deutsch-Jozsa and Grover, have been implemented across diverse physical systems like nuclear magnetic resonance, trapped ions, optical systems, and superconducting circuits. However, at the small scale, these problems can already be solved classically with a few oracle queries, and the attainable quantum advantage is modest. Here, we solve an oracle-based problem, known as learning parity with noise, using a five-qubit superconducting processor. Running classical and quantum algorithms on the same oracle, we observe a significant gap in query count favoring quantum processing. This gap grows by orders of magnitude as a function of the error rates and the problem size. This result demonstrates that, while complex fault-tolerant architectures will be required for universal quantum computing, a quantum advantage already emerges in existing noisy systems.

title: Asymptotic Behavior of Mean Partitions in Consensus Clustering
Abstract: Although consistency is a minimum requirement for any estimator, little is known about the consistency of the mean partition approach in consensus clustering. This study investigates the asymptotic behavior of mean partitions. We demonstrate that under normal assumptions, the mean partition approach is consistent and asymptotically normal. To derive these results, we represent partitions as points in a geometric space called orbit space. We then leverage results from the theory of Fréchet means and stochastic programming. These asymptotic properties hold for continuous extensions of standard cluster criteria (indices). Our findings justify consensus clustering using finite but sufficiently large sample sizes. Furthermore, the orbit space framework provides a mathematical foundation for exploring further statistical, geometrical, and analytical properties of sets of partitions.

title: Face Hallucination using Linear Models of Coupled Sparse Support
Abstract: Face super-resolution methods often assume similar local geometry between low-resolution and high-resolution manifolds, using local models on the low-resolution manifold. This assumption is flawed due to the one-to-many relationship between low- and high-resolution patches, leading to distortions. This paper proposes a novel method that learns linear models based on the high-resolution manifold's local structure. It initially generates a globally optimal high-resolution patch estimate from the low-resolution patch, which is smooth but lacks texture details. Using sparse coding, the method identifies the support of the high-resolution manifold and learns a local projection model between the manifolds using Multivariate Ridge Regression. Experimental results show improved performance in both recognition and quality compared to existing methods, highlighting the importance of stitching techniques for preserving texture details and achieving higher recognition rates.

title: Can Pretrained Neural Networks Detect Anatomy?
Abstract: Convolutional neural networks excel in computer vision and speech recognition tasks with abundant labeled training data. However, medical imaging presents a challenge due to the scarcity of annotated data across various modalities and contrasts. This paper proposes two approaches to tackle this challenge. The first approach utilizes a network pre-trained on a different domain with abundant data as a feature extractor, followed by training a classifier on a small target dataset. The second approach employs a deep architecture trained with extensive augmentation and sophisticated regularization methods. The effectiveness of these approaches is evaluated on a corpus of X-ray images to design an anatomy detection system.

title: Energy Consumption Forecasting for Smart Meters
Abstract: Energy, particularly electricity, is crucial for human survival and plays a vital role in daily life, from lighting to heating and food preparation. The unique characteristics of the electricity industry, including real-time production and consumption, make it a prime candidate for machine learning and data science-driven innovations. This paper explores the application of Machine Learning algorithms, specifically Boosted Decision Tree Regression, to model and forecast energy consumption for smart meters. The study utilizes data from DECC and EMA Singapore, focusing on feature engineering for time series forecasting and developing personalized electricity plans based on usage history.

title: Complexity and Approximation of the Fuzzy K-Means Problem
Abstract: The fuzzy K-means problem extends the classical K-means problem to soft clusterings, where points belong to clusters with varying degrees. Despite its practical relevance, the fuzzy K-means problem has not been rigorously analyzed from a complexity theoretic or algorithmic perspective. This paper demonstrates that optimal solutions for fuzzy K-means are generally inexpressible by radicals over the input points, even for simple one-dimensional inputs. Consequently, exact computation of optimal solutions is infeasible. The paper introduces the first (1+ε)-approximation algorithms for the fuzzy K-means problem. A deterministic algorithm is presented with polynomial runtime in N and linear runtime in the input set dimension D, given a constant K. This is achieved by linking soft clusterings to hard clusterings with similar properties. Additionally, using coreset constructions for the K-means problem, another deterministic algorithm is developed with almost linear runtime in N but exponential runtime in D. The paper concludes with a randomized algorithm imposing natural restrictions on the input set, achieving efficiency comparable to existing K-means approximation algorithms.

title: Operator Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces
Abstract: Motivated by the need to process functional-valued or more general operator-valued data, this paper introduces the concept of the operator reproducing kernel Hilbert space (ORKHS). This space features a unique operator reproducing kernel that reproduces a family of continuous linear operators. The paper develops the theory of ORKHSs and their associated kernels, focusing on a class of ORKHSs known as perfect ORKHSs. These perfect ORKHSs reproduce both the standard point-evaluation operators and another family of continuous linear operators, characterized by their features, especially for those related to integral operators. The paper presents several specific examples of perfect ORKHSs and applies the ORKHS framework to sampling and regularized learning with operator-valued data. A general complete reconstruction formula from linear operator values is established, with specific applications to vector-valued function reconstruction. The paper explores regularized learning schemes in the ORKHS setting, deriving representer theorems that highlight the role of ORKHSs and operator reproducing kernels in machine learning from operator-valued data. The continuity of linear operators is shown to be crucial for the stability of the numerical reconstruction algorithm using the resulting data.

title: A novel Bayesian strategy for the identification of spatially-varying material properties and model validation: an application to static elastography
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel Bayesian computational strategy for model-based inverse problems in elastostatics. The aim is to provide probabilistic estimates of material properties and their spatial variability, accounting for uncertainty sources. Additionally, the paper addresses the question of model fidelity in relation to experimental reality, particularly concerning the adopted material constitutive law. This is particularly important in biomedical settings where inferred material properties are used for decision-making or diagnosis. The paper proposes an expanded parametrization that enables the quantification of model discrepancies along with constitutive parameters. Scalable computational strategies are introduced for inference and learning tasks, demonstrating their effectiveness through numerical examples with noiseless and noisy synthetic data.

title: Domain Adaptation and Transfer Learning in StochasticNets
Abstract: Transfer learning addresses the challenge of insufficient training data in a domain of interest, particularly relevant for traditional deep neural networks with high data requirements. StochasticNets, with their sparse connectivity, aim to reduce the number of parameters learned, potentially mitigating data size requirements. This paper investigates the efficacy of transfer learning on StochasticNet frameworks. Experimental results demonstrate a 7% improvement in StochasticNet performance when transfer learning is applied during the training step.

title: Deep Poisson Factorization Machines: factor analysis for mapping behaviors in journalist ecosystem
Abstract: The online news ecosystem is complex, with social media facilitating interactions between journalists and individuals. However, understanding the information feedback loop in the public sphere remains a challenge for journalists. This paper proposes the Poisson Factorization Machine (PFM), a Bayesian analogue to matrix factorization that assumes a Poisson distribution for the generative process. PFM generalizes recent studies on Poisson Matrix Factorization to account for temporal interaction with tensor-like structure and label information. Two inference procedures are developed, one based on batch variational EM and the other on a stochastic variational inference scheme. Importantly, the paper explores the possibility of stacking PFM layers to create a deep architecture. The potential applications of the model and the usefulness of latent factors for analyzing latent behaviors are discussed.

title: Learning the Preferences of Ignorant, Inconsistent Agents
Abstract: A significant application of machine learning is to infer what people value, such as in personalized recommendations or job matching. This inference is often approached as Bayesian inverse planning, assuming choices are approximately optimal according to a utility function. However, human behavior deviates from optimality due to factors like false beliefs, suboptimal planning, and temporal inconsistency. This paper demonstrates how to incorporate these deviations into preference inference algorithms by constructing generative models of planning for agents exhibiting false beliefs and time inconsistency. The inferences made by these models regarding preferences, beliefs, and biases are explored. A behavioral experiment is conducted to compare human subjects' preference inferences with the model's predictions, highlighting the potential for systematic deviations from optimal behavior in explaining choices and influencing preference inferences.

title: Relay Backpropagation for Effective Learning of Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks have gained popularity in recent years, but performance improvement is not always achieved by simply increasing the number of layers. This paper examines the issue from an information theoretical perspective and proposes a novel method called Relay Backpropagation, aimed at encouraging the propagation of effective information through the network during training. This method enabled the authors to achieve first place in the ILSVRC 2015 Scene Classification Challenge. Extensive experiments on large-scale datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of Relay Backpropagation, showcasing its applicability across datasets and network architectures.

title: Successive Ray Refinement and Its Application to Coordinate Descent for LASSO
Abstract: Coordinate descent is a widely used approach for solving Lasso and its extensions due to its simplicity and efficiency. This paper aims to improve the computational efficiency of coordinate descent by reducing the number of iterations. The novel technique proposed, Successive Ray Refinement (SRR), utilizes the ray continuation property observed in successive iterations. This property suggests that the value of a particular coordinate in the next iteration often lies on a ray originating from the previous iteration and passing through the current iteration. SRR performs coordinate descent on a refined search point that lies on such a ray and minimizes the objective function value. Two schemes for defining the search point are proposed, and empirical results on real and synthetic datasets demonstrate the significant reduction in coordinate descent iterations achieved by SRR, especially for small Lasso regularization parameters.

title: A hidden confining world on the 750 GeV diphoton excess
Abstract: The recent diphoton excesses observed by ATLAS and CMS around 750 GeV are explained by a singlet scalar Φ that couples to SM gluon and neutral gauge bosons through higher-dimensional operators. The paper proposes that Φ is a pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson (pNGB) receiving parity violation through anomalies due to a hidden strong dynamics. The singlet and other light pNGBs decay into two SM gauge bosons and could be meta-stable colored states, potentially detectable in future experiments. By measuring their relative decay and total production rate, the underlying strong dynamics parameters can be further understood. The lightest baryon in this confining theory is suggested as a viable dark matter candidate.

title: A Survey of Available Corpora for Building Data-Driven Dialogue Systems
Abstract: Data-driven models have yielded significant breakthroughs in various areas of speech and language understanding, but the same progress has been less evident in dialogue systems. Many practical systems rely on extensive engineering and expert knowledge. However, recent results suggest the feasibility and promise of data-driven approaches. To facilitate research in this area, this paper provides a comprehensive survey of publicly available datasets suitable for data-driven learning of dialogue systems. The paper discusses key characteristics of these datasets, their application in learning diverse dialogue strategies, and their potential uses. It also examines methods for transfer learning between datasets and the integration of external knowledge. Finally, the paper explores appropriate evaluation metrics for the learning objective.

title: Oracle inequalities for ranking and U-processes with Lasso penalty
Abstract: This paper investigates the properties of estimators obtained by minimizing U-processes with the Lasso penalty in high-dimensional settings, focusing on the ranking problem in machine learning. The ranking problem involves inferring the order between objects based on observed predictors. The paper establishes an oracle inequality for the excess risk of the considered estimator and bounds for the L1 distance between the estimator and the oracle.

title: TermPicker: Enabling the Reuse of Vocabulary Terms by Exploiting Data from the Linked Open Data Cloud - An Extended Technical Report
Abstract: Selecting appropriate vocabulary terms when modeling data as Linked Open Data (LOD) is a complex task. Using overly general terms or terms from infrequently used vocabularies can hinder data comprehension and hinder consumption by Linked data applications. This paper introduces TermPicker, a novel approach for vocabulary reuse that recommends RDF types and properties based on how other data providers on the LOD cloud use them. The paper introduces schema-level patterns (SLPs) that capture the relationships between sets of RDF types and properties within data collections. TermPicker utilizes SLPs to generate a ranked list of vocabulary terms for reuse, ordered by a ranking model based on the Learning To Rank (L2R) approach. Evaluation results demonstrate a significant improvement in recommendation quality using SLPs compared to baselines that recommend solely popular terms or terms from the same vocabulary. The combination of SLPs and the Random Forests algorithm yields the best overall results.

title: Probabilistic Programming with Gaussian Process Memoization
Abstract: Gaussian Processes (GPs) are widely used in various fields, but their application can be challenging due to the complexity of covariance functions and the lack of simple analytical posteriors. This paper presents a method to embed GPs in any higher-order probabilistic programming language using memoization, showcasing its utility through classic and state-of-the-art GP applications. The interface, called gpmem, takes any real-valued computational process as input and returns a statistical emulator that improves automatically as the process is invoked and input-output behavior is recorded. The flexibility of gpmem is illustrated through three applications: robust GP regression with hierarchical hyper-parameter learning, discovering symbolic expressions from time-series data through Bayesian structure learning over kernels, and a bandit formulation of Bayesian optimization with automatic inference and action selection. These applications demonstrate the simplicity and versatility of gpmem, requiring minimal code and leveraging a single Python library.

title: Spacetime-constrained oblivious transfer
Abstract: In 1-out-of-2 oblivious transfer (OT), Alice inputs numbers x0, x1, Bob inputs a bit b, and outputs xb. Secure OT ensures that Alice and Bob learn nothing about b and x¬b, respectively. The paper defines spacetime-constrained oblivious transfer (SCOT) as OT in Minkowski spacetime where Bob must output xb within a specific spacetime region. It is proven that unconditionally secure SCOT is impossible with classical protocols in Minkowski or Galilean spacetime, or with quantum protocols in Galilean spacetime. The paper presents a quantum SCOT protocol in Minkowski spacetime and demonstrates its unconditional security.

title: Deep-Spying: Spying using Smartwatch and Deep Learning
Abstract: Wearable technologies, such as smartwatches and fitness trackers, are becoming ubiquitous, but their pervasive nature raises concerns about user privacy. The paper highlights the potential risks associated with motion sensors in wearable devices and demonstrates how advanced neural network architectures can be misused. The research utilizes an LSTM-based implementation to perform touchlogging and keylogging on 12-key keypads with high accuracy, even with unprocessed raw data. This demonstrates that deep neural networks can facilitate keystroke inference attacks based on motion sensors, eliminating the need for complex pre-processing and feature extraction. The findings suggest the vulnerability of user ecosystems when wearable wristband devices are worn.

title: Classification of weak multi-view signals by sharing factors in a mixture of Bayesian group factor analyzers
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel classification model for weak signal data, building upon Group Factor Analysis (GFA), a model for Bayesian multi-view learning. Instead of assuming all data comes from a single GFA model, the proposed model allows for latent clusters, each with a different GFA model and generating a distinct class distribution. Sharing information across clusters by sharing factors significantly improves classification accuracy. These shared factors form a flexible noise model that explains away data irrelevant to classification. The motivation stems from single-trial functional brain imaging data, characterized by low signal-to-noise ratio and a multi-view setting with various sensors, measurement modalities, and auxiliary information. The model is demonstrated on a MEG dataset.

title: Bayesian Covariance Modelling of Large Tensor-Variate Data Sets $\&$ Inverse Non-parametric Learning of the Unknown Model Parameter Vector
Abstract: This paper presents a method for modeling the covariance structure of tensor-variate data, aiming to learn an unknown model parameter vector. The high-dimensional observable is expressed as a function of this parameter vector, and learning this function is achieved by modeling it as a realization from a tensor-variate Gaussian Process (GP). The likelihood of the unknowns given training data becomes tensor-normal. Vague priors are assigned to the unknown GP parameters, and the posterior probability density is calculated. Posterior sampling is performed using Random-Walk Metropolis-Hastings. The unknown model parameter vector is then learned through posterior sampling, generating 95% HPD credible regions on each unknown. The paper demonstrates the application of this method to learning the location of the Sun in the Milky Way disk.

title: An Empirical Comparison of Neural Architectures for Reinforcement Learning in Partially Observable Environments
Abstract: This paper investigates the effectiveness of fitted neural Q iteration for reinforcement learning in partially observable environments using three recurrent neural network architectures: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), and MUT1, an evolved recurrent neural architecture. A variant of fitted Q iteration based on Advantage values is also explored. The results show that GRU consistently outperforms LSTM and MUT1 in most scenarios, requiring less training episodes and computational time to learn a high-quality policy. Advantage learning also exhibits promising results.

title: Data-driven Inverse Optimization with Imperfect Information
Abstract: In data-driven inverse optimization, an observer aims to infer the preferences of an agent who solves a parametric optimization problem based on an exogenous signal. The observer seeks to identify the agent's objective function that best explains a historical sequence of signals and corresponding optimal actions. This research focuses on situations where the observer has imperfect information, meaning the agent's true objective function may not be included in the search space, the agent may exhibit bounded rationality or implementation errors, or the observed signal-response pairs are corrupted by noise. The inverse optimization problem is formalized as a distributionally robust program minimizing the worst-case risk that the predicted decision deviates from the agent's actual response to a random signal. This framework provides rigorous out-of-sample guarantees for various loss functions used to measure prediction errors and enables the reformulation of emerging inverse optimization problems as tractable convex programs using a new suboptimality loss function. Extensive numerical tests demonstrate that the proposed distributionally robust approach to inverse optimization often achieves better out-of-sample performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

title: Deep Active Object Recognition by Joint Label and Action Prediction
Abstract: An active object recognition system leverages the ability to interact with the environment to capture images that are more suitable for training and lead to better performance during testing. This paper presents a deep convolutional neural network for active object recognition that simultaneously predicts the object label and selects the next action to perform on the object, aiming to enhance recognition accuracy. Active object recognition is treated as a reinforcement learning problem, and the cost function for training the network to jointly predict the object label and action is derived. A generative model of object similarities based on the Dirichlet distribution is proposed and integrated into the network for encoding the system's state. Training is conducted by simultaneously minimizing the label and action prediction errors using gradient descent. Empirical results demonstrate the network's ability to predict both the object label and actions on the GERMS dataset for active object recognition. Comparing the test label prediction accuracy of the proposed model with Dirichlet and Naive Bayes state encoding, the experiments suggest that the proposed model with Dirichlet state encoding surpasses in performance and selects images that contribute to better training and higher accuracy of label prediction during testing.

title: Private Causal Inference
Abstract: Causal inference focuses on identifying which random variables influence or control other random variables. Recent advancements in causal inference based on statistical estimation and machine learning have resulted in practical algorithms. Causal inference holds immense potential in medical research, disease prevention and control, and identifying factors that impact economic changes, to name a few. However, these promising applications often involve sensitive or personal data of users requiring privacy protection, such as medical records and personal finances. Therefore, the development of causal inference methods that preserve data privacy is crucial. This paper explores the problem of inferring causality using the popular additive noise model (ANM) framework while simultaneously ensuring user privacy. The proposed framework provides differential privacy guarantees for various ANM variants. Extensive experiments demonstrate the practicality and ease of implementation of the proposed techniques.
label: AI

title: Unsupervised Feature Construction for Improving Data Representation and Semantics
Abstract: Feature-based format is the primary data representation format used by machine learning algorithms. When features fail to accurately describe the initial data, performance deteriorates. While some algorithms address this problem by internally changing the representation space, the newly constructed features are often incomprehensible. This research aims to construct new features in an unsupervised manner that are more appropriate for describing a given dataset while remaining comprehensible for human users. Two algorithms are proposed that construct these new features as conjunctions of the initial primitive features or their negations. The generated feature sets exhibit reduced correlations between features and successfully capture some of the hidden relationships between individuals in a dataset. For example, a feature like "$sky \\wedge \\neg building \\wedge panorama$" would be true for non-urban images and is more informative than simple features indicating the presence or absence of an object. Pareto optimality is used to evaluate feature sets and achieve a balance between total correlation and the complexity of the resulting feature set. Statistical hypothesis testing is employed to automatically determine the values of parameters used for constructing a data-dependent feature set. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approaches achieve the construction of informative feature sets for multiple datasets.
label: AI

title: Continuous online sequence learning with an unsupervised neural network model
Abstract: The ability to recognize and predict temporal sequences of sensory inputs is crucial for survival in natural environments. Building upon known properties of cortical neurons, hierarchical temporal memory (HTM) sequence memory is proposed as a theoretical framework for sequence learning in the cortex. This paper analyzes properties of HTM sequence memory and applies it to sequence learning and prediction problems with streaming data. The model demonstrates the ability to continuously learn a large number of variable-order temporal sequences using an unsupervised Hebbian-like learning rule. The sparse temporal codes formed by the model can robustly handle branching temporal sequences by maintaining multiple predictions until sufficient disambiguating evidence is available. Comparisons with other sequence learning algorithms, including statistical methods (ARIMA), feedforward neural networks (OSELM), and recurrent neural networks (LSTM and ESN), are conducted on sequence prediction problems involving both artificial and real-world data. The HTM model achieves comparable accuracy to other state-of-the-art algorithms. Additionally, the model exhibits properties crucial for sequence learning, including continuous online learning, the ability to handle multiple predictions and branching sequences with high-order statistics, robustness to sensor noise and fault tolerance, and good performance without task-specific hyperparameter tuning. Therefore, HTM sequence memory not only advances our understanding of how the brain solves the sequence learning problem but also finds applications in a wide range of real-world problems such as discrete and continuous sequence prediction, anomaly detection, and sequence classification.

title: Sign learning kink-based (SiLK) quantum Monte Carlo for molecular systems
Abstract: The Sign Learning Kink (SiLK) based Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) method is used to compute the ab initio ground state energies for various geometries of the H$_{2}$O, N$_2$, and F$_2$ molecules. The method is founded on Feynman's path integral formulation of quantum mechanics and comprises two stages. The first stage, known as the learning stage, mitigates the well-known QMC minus sign problem by optimizing linear combinations of Slater determinants, which are utilized in the second stage, a conventional QMC simulation. The method is evaluated using different vector spaces and compared against results obtained from other quantum chemical methods and exact diagonalization. The findings demonstrate that the SiLK method is accurate and significantly reduces or eliminates the minus sign problem.

title: Large Scale Business Discovery from Street Level Imagery
Abstract: Search with local intent is gaining popularity due to the widespread use of mobile devices. However, the creation and maintenance of accurate listings of local businesses worldwide is time-consuming and expensive. This paper proposes an approach to automatically discover businesses that are visible in street-level imagery. Precise business storefront detection enables accurate geo-location of businesses and provides input for business categorization, listing generation, and other applications. The wide variety of business categories across different countries makes this a challenging problem. Manual annotation is prohibitively expensive given the scale of the problem. The paper proposes a MultiBox-based approach that takes input image pixels and directly outputs storefront bounding boxes. This end-to-end learning approach eliminates the need for hand modeling in either the proposal generation or post-processing phases, leveraging large labeled training datasets. The proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art detection techniques significantly in terms of performance and runtime efficiency. Evaluation results demonstrate that this approach achieves human accuracy in low-recall settings. The paper also provides an end-to-end evaluation of business discovery in real-world scenarios.

title: Numerical Demultiplexing of Color Image Sensor Measurements via Non-linear Random Forest Modeling
Abstract: Simultaneously capturing imaging data at multiple wavelengths across the electromagnetic spectrum is a challenging task requiring complex and costly multispectral image sensors. This study introduces a comprehensive framework for performing simultaneous multispectral imaging using conventional image sensors with color filter arrays through numerical demultiplexing of color image sensor measurements. A numerical forward model characterizing the formation of sensor measurements from light spectra hitting the sensor is constructed based on a comprehensive spectral characterization of the sensor. A numerical demultiplexer is then learned via non-linear random forest modeling based on the forward model. Given the learned numerical demultiplexer, one can then demultiplex simultaneously acquired measurements made by the image sensor into reflectance intensities at discrete selectable wavelengths, resulting in a higher resolution reflectance spectrum. Simulation and real-world experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this method for simultaneous multispectral imaging.

title: Signal Recovery on Graphs: Fundamental Limits of Sampling Strategies
Abstract: This paper establishes theoretical foundations for the recovery of a newly proposed class of smooth graph signals, approximately bandlimited graph signals, under three sampling strategies: uniform sampling, experimentally designed sampling, and active sampling. Minimax lower bounds on the maximum risk for the approximately bandlimited class under these three sampling strategies are established, demonstrating that active sampling cannot fundamentally outperform experimentally designed sampling. A recovery strategy is proposed to compare uniform sampling with experimentally designed sampling. The proposed recovery strategy is amenable to statistical analysis, allowing the derivation of the exact mean square error for each sampling strategy. To study convergence rates, two types of graphs are introduced, revealing that (1) the proposed recovery strategy achieves optimal rates; and (2) experimentally designed sampling significantly outperforms uniform sampling for Type-2 class of graphs. Validation of the proposed recovery strategy is performed on five specific graphs: a ring graph with k nearest neighbors, an Erdős-Rényi graph, a random geometric graph, a small-world graph, and a power-law graph, showing that experimental results align well with the proposed theory. This work also provides a comprehensive explanation for the effectiveness of sampling for semi-supervised learning with graphs.

title: Multiregion Bilinear Convolutional Neural Networks for Person Re-Identification
Abstract: This work proposes a novel architecture for person re-identification. As the task of re-identification is inherently associated with embedding learning and non-rigid appearance description, the architecture is based on the deep bilinear convolutional network (Bilinear-CNN) recently proposed for fine-grained classification of highly non-rigid objects. While the original Bilinear-CNN architecture completely discards geometric information through orderless pooling in the final stages, the authors observe that a better embedding can be learned by performing bilinear pooling in a more localized manner, where each pooling operation is confined to a predefined region. The proposed architecture strikes a balance between traditional convolutional networks and bilinear CNNs, achieving a compromise between rigid matching and complete disregard for spatial information. Experimental validation of the new architecture is performed on three popular benchmark datasets (Market-1501, CUHK01, CUHK03), comparing it to baselines that include Bilinear-CNN and prior art. The new architecture surpasses the baseline on all three datasets, while performing better than state-of-the-art on two out of three. The code and pretrained models of the approach are available at https://github.com/madkn/MultiregionBilinearCNN-ReId.
