title: Feature Representation for ICU Mortality
Abstract: Accurate predictors of ICU mortality have the potential to identify high-risk patients early, optimize ICU resource allocation, and create more precise population-level risk models. Machine learning practitioners often make choices regarding feature representation in a particular model, but these choices are rarely evaluated quantitatively. This study compares the performance of different representations of clinical event data from MIMIC II in a logistic regression model to predict 36-hour ICU mortality. The most common representations, linear (normalized counts) and binary (yes/no), are compared alongside a novel representation termed "hill." Both L1 and L2 regularization are used for comparison. Results indicate that the introduced "hill" representation outperforms both the binary and linear representations, suggesting its potential to improve existing models of ICU mortality.
label: AI

title: A Theoretically Grounded Application of Dropout in Recurrent Neural Networks
Abstract: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are at the forefront of many recent advancements in deep learning. However, a major challenge with these models is their susceptibility to overfitting, and dropout, a common regularization technique, has proven ineffective when applied to recurrent layers. Recent research at the intersection of Bayesian modeling and deep learning provides a Bayesian interpretation of common deep learning techniques such as dropout. This grounding of dropout in approximate Bayesian inference suggests an extension of the theoretical results, offering insights into the use of dropout with RNN models. This paper applies this new variational inference-based dropout technique in LSTM and GRU models, evaluating it on language modeling and sentiment analysis tasks. The new approach surpasses existing techniques and, to the best of the authors' knowledge, improves upon the single model state-of-the-art in language modeling with the Penn Treebank (73.4 test perplexity). This expands the arsenal of variational tools available in deep learning.
label: AI

title: Blockout: Dynamic Model Selection for Hierarchical Deep Networks
Abstract: Most deep architectures for image classification, even those trained to classify a large number of diverse categories, learn shared image representations with a single model. Intuitively, however, categories that are more similar should share more information than those that are very different. While hierarchical deep networks address this problem by learning separate features for subsets of related categories, current implementations rely on simplified models with fixed architectures specified via heuristic clustering methods. This paper proposes Blockout, a method for regularization and model selection that simultaneously learns both the model architecture and parameters. A generalization of Dropout, Blockout offers a novel parametrization of hierarchical architectures that enables structure learning through back-propagation. Evaluation of Blockout on the CIFAR and ImageNet datasets demonstrates improved classification accuracy, better regularization performance, faster training, and the clear emergence of hierarchical network structures.
label: AI

title: Learning Games and Rademacher Observations Losses
Abstract: Recent research has shown that supervised learning with the popular logistic loss is equivalent to optimizing the exponential loss over sufficient statistics about the class: Rademacher observations (rados). This paper first demonstrates that this unexpected equivalence generalizes to other example/rado losses, outlining necessary and sufficient conditions for the equivalence, exemplified on four losses with popular names in various fields: exponential (boosting), mean-variance (finance), Linear Hinge (online learning), ReLU (deep learning), and unhinged (statistics). Second, the paper shows that this generalization reveals a surprising new connection to regularized learning, specifically a sufficient condition under which regularizing the loss over examples is equivalent to regularizing the rados (with Minkowski sums) in the equivalent rado loss. This leads to simple and powerful rado-based learning algorithms for sparsity-controlling regularization, exemplified on a boosting algorithm for the regularized exponential rado-loss, which formally boosts over four types of regularization, including the popular ridge and lasso, and the recently coined slope. This provides the first proven boosting algorithm for the slope regularization. Through the equivalence of rado and example-based losses, Omega-R.AdaBoost appears to be an efficient proxy for boosting the regularized logistic loss over examples using any of the four regularizers. Experiments demonstrate that regularization consistently improves the performance of rado-based learning and may challenge or surpass the state-of-the-art of example-based learning, even when learning over small sets of rados. Finally, the paper connects regularization to differential privacy and shows how tiny budgets can be afforded on large domains while surpassing protected example-based learning.
label: AI

title: Fine-grained Categorization and Dataset Bootstrapping using Deep Metric Learning with Humans in the Loop
Abstract: Existing fine-grained visual categorization methods often face three challenges: limited training data, a large number of fine-grained categories, and high intraclass vs. low inter-class variance. This paper proposes a generic iterative framework for fine-grained categorization and dataset bootstrapping that addresses these challenges. By employing deep metric learning with human involvement, a low-dimensional feature embedding is learned with anchor points on manifolds for each category. These anchor points capture intra-class variances while remaining discriminative between classes. In each round, images with high confidence scores from the model are presented to humans for labeling. By comparing with exemplar images, labelers classify each candidate image as either a "true positive" or a "false positive." True positives are added to the existing dataset, and false positives are treated as "hard negatives" for the metric learning model. The model is then retrained with the expanded dataset and hard negatives for the next round. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, a fine-grained flower dataset with 620 categories is bootstrapped from Instagram images. The deep metric learning scheme is evaluated on both this dataset and the CUB-200-2001 Birds dataset. Experimental evaluations show significant performance gains using dataset bootstrapping and demonstrate state-of-the-art results achieved by the proposed deep metric learning methods.

title: Learning a Hybrid Architecture for Sequence Regression and Annotation
Abstract: When learning a hidden Markov model (HMM), sequential observations can often be supplemented by real-valued summary response variables generated from the path of hidden states. Such settings arise in various domains, including numerous applications in biology, such as motif discovery and genome annotation. This paper presents a flexible framework for jointly modeling both latent sequence features and the functional mapping that relates the summary response variables to the hidden state sequence. The algorithm is compatible with a rich set of mapping functions. Results show that the availability of additional continuous response variables can simultaneously improve the annotation of sequential observations and yield good prediction performance in both synthetic data and real-world datasets.

title: DNA-Level Splice Junction Prediction using Deep Recurrent Neural Networks
Abstract: A eukaryotic gene comprises multiple exons (protein coding regions) and introns (non-coding regions), with a splice junction representing the boundary between an exon and an intron. Precise identification of splice junctions on a gene is crucial for deciphering its primary structure, function, and interactions. Experimental techniques for determining exon/intron boundaries include RNA-seq, which is often accompanied by computational approaches. While canonical splicing signals are known, computational junction prediction remains challenging due to a large number of false positives and other complications. This paper leverages deep recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to model DNA sequences and detect splice junctions therein. Various RNN units and architectures, including long short-term memory units, gated recurrent units, and the recently proposed iRNN, are tested for in-depth design space exploration. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms conventional machine learning-based methods, as well as a recent state-of-the-art deep belief network-based technique, in terms of prediction accuracy.

title: A Novel Minimum Divergence Approach to Robust Speaker Identification
Abstract: This work proposes a novel solution to the speaker identification problem by minimizing statistical divergences between the probability distribution of feature vectors from the test utterance and the probability distributions of feature vectors corresponding to speaker classes. This approach is made more robust to outliers through the use of suitably modified versions of standard divergence measures. The relevant solutions to the minimum distance methods are referred to as minimum rescaled modified distance estimators (MRMDEs). Three measures are considered: likelihood disparity, Hellinger distance, and Pearson's chi-square distance. The proposed approach is motivated by the observation that, in the case of likelihood disparity, when the empirical distribution function is used to estimate the probability distribution, it becomes equivalent to maximum likelihood classification with Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) for speaker classes, a highly effective approach used, for example, by Reynolds based on Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs) as features. Significant improvements in classification accuracy are observed under this approach on the benchmark speech corpus NTIMIT and a new bilingual speech corpus NISIS, with MFCC features, both in isolation and in combination with delta MFCC features. Moreover, the ubiquitous principal component transformation, both by itself and in conjunction with the principle of classifier combination, is found to further enhance performance.

title: Streaming Kernel Principal Component Analysis
Abstract: Kernel principal component analysis (KPCA) provides a concise set of basis vectors that capture non-linear structures within large datasets and is a central tool in data analysis and learning. To accommodate non-linear relationships, a full n x n kernel matrix is typically constructed over n data points, but this requires excessive space and time for large values of n. Techniques such as the Nyström method and random feature maps offer potential solutions, but they do not explicitly maintain the basis vectors in a stream and require more space than desired. This paper proposes a new approach for streaming KPCA that maintains a small set of basis elements in a stream, requiring space only logarithmic in n, and also improves the dependence on the error parameter. The proposed technique combines random feature maps with recent advancements in matrix sketching, providing guaranteed spectral norm error bounds with respect to the original kernel matrix and comparing favorably in practice to state-of-the-art approaches. |||

title: Morpho-syntactic Lexicon Generation Using Graph-based Semi-supervised Learning
Abstract: Morpho-syntactic lexicons provide information about the morphological and syntactic functions of words in a language. However, these lexicons are not readily available for all languages, and even when they are, their coverage can be limited. This research proposes a graph-based semi-supervised learning method that leverages the morphological, syntactic, and semantic relationships between words to automatically create extensive coverage lexicons from small seed sets. The method is language-independent, and it has demonstrated the ability to expand a 1000-word seed lexicon to over 100 times its size with high accuracy across 11 languages. Furthermore, the automatically generated lexicons provide features that improve performance in two downstream tasks: morphological tagging and dependency parsing.
label: AI

title: Multiple penalized principal curves: analysis and computation
Abstract: We investigate the problem of discovering one-dimensional structure within a given dataset. In other words, we explore methods to approximate a given measure (data) using curves. We introduce an objective functional whose minimizers are a regularization of principal curves and propose a new functional that allows for multiple curves. We prove the existence of minimizers and establish their fundamental properties. We develop an efficient algorithm for obtaining (near) minimizers of the functional. While both functionals are nonconvex, we argue that expanding the configuration space to accommodate multiple curves simplifies the energy landscape, leading to fewer undesirable (high-energy) local minima. Notably, the proposed approach can uncover one-dimensional structure even in data with significant noise.
label: AI

title: A Light Touch for Heavily Constrained SGD
Abstract: Minimizing empirical risk subject to a set of constraints can be a valuable strategy for learning restricted classes of functions, such as monotonic functions, submodular functions, or classifiers that guarantee a certain class label for a specific subset of examples. However, these restrictions can lead to a very large number of constraints. Projected stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is often the default choice for large-scale optimization in machine learning but requires a projection after each update. For heavily-constrained objectives, we propose an efficient extension of SGD that remains close to the feasible region while applying constraints probabilistically at each iteration. Theoretical analysis reveals a compelling trade-off between per-iteration work and the number of iterations required on problems with a large number of constraints.
label: AI

title: Relative Density and Exact Recovery in Heterogeneous Stochastic Block Models
Abstract: The Stochastic Block Model (SBM) is a widely used random graph model for networks with communities. Despite the recent surge in interest in recovering communities in the SBM from statistical and computational perspectives, gaps remain in understanding the fundamental information theoretic and computational limits of recovery. This paper considers the SBM in its full generality, without restrictions on the number and sizes of communities or how they grow with the number of nodes, as well as on the connection probabilities within or across communities. This generality enables us to move beyond the artifacts of homogeneous SBM and identify the appropriate parameters (such as the relative densities of communities) that define the various recovery thresholds. We outline the implications of our generalizations through a set of illustrative examples. For instance,  log n is considered the standard lower bound on the cluster size for exact recovery using convex methods in homogeneous SBM. We demonstrate that it is possible, under specific conditions (when sizes are spread and smaller clusters are denser), to recover very small clusters (up to sqrt(log n) size) if there are only a few of them (at most polylogarithmic in n).
label: AI

title: Deep Learning Stock Volatility with Google Domestic Trends
Abstract: We have employed a Long Short-Term Memory neural network to model S&P 500 volatility, incorporating Google domestic trends as indicators of public sentiment and macroeconomic factors. In a held-out test set, our Long Short-Term Memory model achieves a mean absolute percentage error of 24.2%, outperforming linear Ridge/Lasso and autoregressive GARCH benchmarks by at least 31%. This evaluation is based on an optimal observation and normalization scheme that maximizes the mutual information between domestic trends and daily volatility in the training set. Our preliminary investigation shows strong promise for better predicting stock behavior using deep learning and neural network models.
label: AI

title: Strategies for Training Large Vocabulary Neural Language Models
Abstract: Training neural network language models over large vocabularies remains computationally expensive compared to count-based models like Kneser-Ney. Simultaneously, neural language models are gaining popularity for various applications such as speech recognition and machine translation, whose success depends on scalability. This paper presents a systematic comparison of strategies to represent and train large vocabularies, including softmax, hierarchical softmax, target sampling, noise contrastive estimation, and self normalization. We extend self normalization to be a proper estimator of likelihood and introduce an efficient variant of softmax. We evaluate each method on three popular benchmarks, examining performance on rare words, the speed/accuracy trade-off, and complementarity to Kneser-Ney.

title: Increasing the Action Gap: New Operators for Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: This paper introduces novel optimality-preserving operators on Q-functions. We first describe an operator for tabular representations, the consistent Bellman operator, which incorporates a notion of local policy consistency. We demonstrate that this local consistency leads to an increase in the action gap at each state; we argue that increasing this gap mitigates the undesirable effects of approximation and estimation errors on the induced greedy policies. This operator can also be applied to discretized continuous space and time problems, and we provide empirical results demonstrating superior performance in this context. Extending the idea of a locally consistent operator, we then derive sufficient conditions for an operator to preserve optimality, leading to a family of operators that includes our consistent Bellman operator. As corollaries, we provide a proof of optimality for Baird's advantage learning algorithm and derive other gap-increasing operators with interesting properties. We conclude with an empirical study on 60 Atari 2600 games illustrating the strong potential of these new operators.

title: Energy-Efficient Classification for Anomaly Detection: The Wireless Channel as a Helper
Abstract: Anomaly detection has numerous applications, including condition monitoring and fault diagnosis. The objective is to sense the environment, learn the normal system state, and then periodically classify whether the instantaneous state deviates from the normal one. A flexible and cost-effective approach to monitoring a system state is to use a wireless sensor network. In the traditional approach, sensors encode their observations and transmit them to a fusion center using some interference-avoiding channel access method. The fusion center then decodes all the data and classifies the corresponding system state. As this approach can be highly inefficient in terms of energy consumption, this paper proposes a transmission scheme that exploits interference to carry out anomaly detection directly in the air. In other words, the wireless channel assists the fusion center in retrieving the sought classification outcome immediately from the channel output. To achieve this, the chosen learning model is linear support vector machines. After discussing the proposed scheme and proving its reliability, we present numerical examples demonstrating that the scheme reduces energy consumption for anomaly detection by up to 53% compared to a strategy using time division multiple-access.

title: Data Driven Resource Allocation for Distributed Learning
Abstract: In distributed machine learning, data is dispatched to multiple machines for processing. Motivated by the fact that similar data points often belong to the same or similar classes, and more generally, classification rules of high accuracy tend to be "locally simple but globally complex" (Vapnik & Bottou 1993), we propose data-dependent dispatching that takes advantage of this structure. We present an in-depth analysis of this model, providing new algorithms with provable worst-case guarantees, analysis proving existing scalable heuristics perform well in natural non-worst-case conditions, and techniques for extending a dispatching rule from a small sample to the entire distribution. We overcome novel technical challenges to satisfy important conditions for accurate distributed learning, including fault tolerance and balancedness. We empirically compare our approach with baselines based on random partitioning, balanced partition trees, and locality-sensitive hashing, demonstrating that we achieve significantly higher accuracy on both synthetic and real-world image and advertising datasets. We also show that our technique strongly scales with the available computing power.
label: AI

title: Feature-Level Domain Adaptation
Abstract: Domain adaptation is the supervised learning setting where training and test data are sampled from different distributions: training data is sampled from a source domain, while test data is sampled from a target domain. This paper proposes and studies an approach, called feature-level domain adaptation (FLDA), that models the dependence between the two domains using a feature-level transfer model trained to describe the transfer from source to target domain. Subsequently, we train a domain-adapted classifier by minimizing the expected loss under the resulting transfer model. For linear classifiers and a large family of loss functions and transfer models, this expected loss can be computed or approximated analytically, and minimized efficiently. Our empirical evaluation of FLDA focuses on problems involving binary and count data where the transfer can be naturally modeled using a dropout distribution, allowing the classifier to adapt to differences in the marginal probability of features in the source and target domain. Our experiments on several real-world problems show that FLDA performs on par with state-of-the-art domain-adaptation techniques.
label: AI

title: Causal and anti-causal learning in pattern recognition for neuroimaging
Abstract: Pattern recognition in neuroimaging distinguishes between two types of models: encoding and decoding models. This distinction is based on the insight that brain state features, found to be relevant in an experimental paradigm, carry a different meaning in encoding than in decoding models. This paper argues that this distinction is not sufficient: Relevant features in encoding and decoding models carry a different meaning depending on whether they represent causal or anti-causal relations. We provide a theoretical justification for this argument and conclude that causal inference is essential for interpretation in neuroimaging.
label: AI

title: From One Point to A Manifold: Knowledge Graph Embedding For Precise Link Prediction
Abstract: Knowledge graph embedding aims to provide a numerical knowledge representation paradigm by transforming entities and relations into a continuous vector space. However, existing methods have struggled to characterize the knowledge graph with enough detail to make precise predictions. This limitation stems from two reasons: being an ill-posed algebraic system and applying an overly strict geometric form. As precise prediction is crucial, we propose a manifold-based embedding principle (ManifoldE) that can be treated as a well-posed algebraic system that expands the position of golden triples from a single point in current models to a manifold in ours. Extensive experiments show that the proposed models achieve substantial improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, particularly for precise prediction tasks, while maintaining high efficiency.
label: AI

title: On Deep Representation Learning from Noisy Web Images
Abstract: The ever-growing content of Web images may be the next significant data source for scaling up deep neural networks, which recently achieved great success in the ImageNet classification challenge and related tasks. This prospect, however, has not been validated on convolutional networks (convnet), one of the best-performing deep models, due to their supervised regime. While unsupervised alternatives are not as effective as convnet in generalizing the learned model to new domains, we leverage convnet for semi-supervised representation learning. Our approach involves training convnets as general feature detectors using massive amounts of unlabeled and noisy Web images despite challenges arising from data such as a high level of mislabeled data, outliers, and data biases. Extensive experiments are conducted at several data scales, different network architectures, and data reranking techniques. The learned representations are evaluated on nine public datasets of various topics. The best results obtained by our convnets, trained on 3.14 million Web images, outperform AlexNet trained on 1.2 million clean images of ILSVRC 2012 and are closing the gap with VGG-16. These prominent results suggest a budget solution for using deep learning in practice and motivate further research in semi-supervised representation learning.
label: AI

title: Predicting links in ego-networks using temporal information
Abstract: Link prediction is a central problem in network science, as it seeks to uncover the mechanisms governing the micro-dynamics of the network. This work focuses on ego-networks, specifically the information about interactions between a node and its neighbors, in the context of social relationships. Due to the limited structural information, we rely on another source of information to predict links among egos' neighbors: the timing of interactions. We define several features to capture different types of temporal information and apply machine learning methods to combine these various features and enhance the quality of the prediction. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this temporal approach using a cellphone interaction dataset, highlighting features that perform well in this context, particularly the temporal profile of interactions and elapsed time between contacts.
label: AI

title: Learning optimal nonlinearities for iterative thresholding algorithms
Abstract: Iterative shrinkage/thresholding algorithm (ISTA) is a well-studied method for finding sparse solutions to ill-posed inverse problems. This letter presents a data-driven scheme for learning optimal thresholding functions for ISTA. The proposed scheme is obtained by relating iterations of ISTA to layers of a simple deep neural network (DNN) and developing a corresponding error backpropagation algorithm that allows fine-tuning the thresholding functions. Simulations on sparse statistical signals illustrate potential gains in estimation quality due to the proposed data-adaptive ISTA.
label: AI

title: Pileup Subtraction and Jet Energy Prediction Using Machine Learning
Abstract: In the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), multiple proton-proton collisions cause pileup in reconstructing energy information for a single primary collision (jet). This project aims to select the most important features and create a model to accurately estimate jet energy. Various machine learning methods were explored, including linear regression, support vector regression, and decision trees. The best result is obtained using linear regression with predictive features, and the performance is significantly improved from the baseline method.
label: AI

title: Hyper-Heuristic Algorithm for Finding Efficient Features in Diagnose of Lung Cancer Disease
Abstract: Lung cancer is a primary cancer with a survival rate of around 15%. Early detection is the leading factor in increasing survival rates. However, all symptoms (features) of lung cancer do not appear until the cancer spreads to other areas. Accurate early detection is crucial for improving survival rates, requiring the identification of efficient features and elimination of redundancy among all features. Feature selection is the process of choosing informative features from a set of available features. This study utilizes a lung cancer database consisting of 32 patient records with 57 features, collected by Hong and Young and indexed in the University of California Irvine repository. The data includes information extracted from clinical data and X-ray data. The data describes three types of pathological lung cancers, and all features take integer values from 0 to 3. We propose a new method based on Hyper-Heuristic for identifying efficient features of lung cancer. Our results show an accuracy of 80.63% using a reduced set of 11 features. The proposed method outperforms five other machine learning feature selection methods, which achieved accuracies of 60.94, 57.81, 68.75, 60.94, and 68.75, respectively. The proposed method demonstrates superior performance with the highest level of accuracy. Therefore, it is recommended for identifying efficient symptoms of lung cancer. These findings are crucial for health research, particularly in allocating medical resources to patients predicted as high-risk.
label: AI

title: Linear Models of Computation and Program Learning
Abstract: We consider two classes of computations that allow for taking linear combinations of execution runs: probabilistic sampling and generalized animation. We argue that the task of program learning should be more tractable for these architectures than for conventional deterministic programs. We examine recent advances in the "sampling the samplers" paradigm in higher-order probabilistic programming. We also discuss connections between partial inconsistency, non-monotonic inference, and vector semantics.
label: AI

title: Semantic-enriched Visual Vocabulary Construction in a Weakly Supervised Context
Abstract: Content-based image classification is a prevalent learning task involving images. However, it is challenging because low-level features used to digitally describe images often capture little information about the images' semantics. This paper addresses this challenge by enriching the semantic content of the image representation using external knowledge. Our work is based on the hypothesis that creating a more semantically rich representation for images would lead to improved machine learning performance without needing to modify the learning algorithms themselves. The external semantic information is presented in the form of non-positional image labels, positioning our work in a weakly supervised context. Two approaches are proposed: the first leverages labels into the visual vocabulary construction algorithm, resulting in dedicated visual vocabularies. The second approach adds a filtering phase as a pre-processing step for vocabulary construction. Known positive and known negative sets are constructed, and features unlikely to be associated with the objects denoted by the labels are filtered. We apply our proposition to the task of content-based image classification and demonstrate that semantically enriching the image representation yields higher classification performances than the baseline representation.

title: Relaxed Linearized Algorithms for Faster X-Ray CT Image Reconstruction
Abstract: Statistical image reconstruction (SIR) methods are extensively studied for X-ray computed tomography (CT) due to their potential to acquire CT scans with reduced X-ray dose while maintaining image quality. However, the longer reconstruction time of SIR methods hinders their practical use in X-ray CT. To accelerate statistical methods, many optimization techniques have been investigated. Over-relaxation is a common technique to speed up the convergence of iterative algorithms. For instance, using a relaxation parameter close to two in the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) has been shown to significantly accelerate convergence. This paper proposes a relaxed linearized augmented Lagrangian (AL) method that exhibits theoretically faster convergence rates with over-relaxation and applies the proposed relaxed linearized AL method to X-ray CT image reconstruction problems. Experimental results using both simulated and real CT scan data show that the proposed relaxed algorithm (with ordered-subsets [OS] acceleration) is about twice as fast as existing unrelaxed fast algorithms, with negligible computation and memory overhead. |||

title: About the tensorial nature of the Christoffel symbols, or lack thereof
Abstract: The Christoffel symbols, fundamental to General Relativity, are often mistakenly presented as tensors in textbooks. This paper explores the mathematical foundation behind this misconception, clarifying why some authors treat them as tensors. This discussion is aimed at those with prior knowledge of General Relativity, as it assumes familiarity with certain theoretical concepts.

title: On non-iterative training of a neural classifier
Abstract: A recently discovered algorithm separates points in n-dimensional space using planes in such a way that every pair of points is separated by at least one plane. This paper proposes two novel, non-iterative and deterministic classification methods for neural networks based on this algorithm. The effectiveness of these methods is demonstrated using the classic IRIS flower dataset. The non-iterative, deterministic nature, efficiency, and speed of these methods make them ideal for training neural networks in deep learning, potentially surpassing other iterative classification methods.

title: Dropout Training of Matrix Factorization and Autoencoder for Link Prediction in Sparse Graphs
Abstract: Matrix factorization (MF) and autoencoders (AE) are widely used in unsupervised learning. While MF has seen extensive application in graph modeling and link prediction, AE's role in this domain remains underdeveloped. This paper investigates both MF and AE in the context of link prediction for sparse graphs. It establishes a connection between AE and MF from the perspective of multiview learning and introduces MF+AE, a model that jointly trains MF and AE with shared parameters. By applying dropout to both MF and AE training, the paper demonstrates its ability to prevent overfitting through adaptive regularization. Experiments on six real-world sparse graph datasets show that MF+AE consistently outperforms other methods, particularly on datasets with strong non-cohesive structures.

title: Multimodal, high-dimensional, model-based, Bayesian inverse problems with applications in biomechanics
Abstract: This paper focuses on solving model-based Bayesian inverse problems numerically, particularly when likelihood evaluations are computationally expensive and the number of unknown variables is high. These characteristics are common in computational physics problems involving forward models with nonlinear PDEs and parameters representing spatially and temporally varying coefficients, resulting in high-dimensional unknowns. The inherent ill-posedness of inverse problems can lead to multiple solutions, which are encoded in the posterior density within a Bayesian framework. However, discovering these modes, especially multiple ones, is a challenging task. This paper addresses this by proposing approximate, adaptive inference strategies using mixture densities to capture multi-modal posteriors and extending previous work on dimensionality reduction techniques to identify low-dimensional subspaces where most posterior variance is concentrated. Importance Sampling validation confirms the small bias introduced by the model, which can be corrected if desired. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach in nonlinear elastography, where identifying mechanical properties of biological materials is crucial for non-invasive medical diagnosis. The ability to uncover multiple modes (solutions) in such problems is essential for achieving diagnostic goals.

title: Semisupervised Autoencoder for Sentiment Analysis
Abstract: This paper explores the use of autoencoders for modeling textual data. Traditional autoencoders face challenges with scalability due to high vocabulary dimensionality and dealing with task-irrelevant words. To address these issues, the paper introduces supervision through the autoencoder's loss function. By first training a linear classifier on labeled data and then defining a loss for the autoencoder based on the classifier's learned weights, the model utilizes supervision. To mitigate bias introduced by a single classifier, the paper defines a posterior probability distribution on classifier weights and derives a marginalized loss for the autoencoder using Laplace approximation. The rationale behind this loss function is explained from the perspective of Bregman Divergence, highlighting the model's soundness. The effectiveness of the model is evaluated on six sentiment analysis datasets, demonstrating significant performance improvement compared to other methods. The paper also shows that the model can leverage unlabeled data for further performance enhancement and learns highly discriminative feature maps, explaining its superior performance.

title: Teaching the Foundations of Data Science: An Interdisciplinary Approach
Abstract: The exponential growth of data necessitates the education of skilled data scientists capable of extracting meaningful insights from large, complex datasets. This paper presents an interdisciplinary approach and experiences in teaching a Data Science course, the first of its kind offered at Wright State University. Designed and co-taught by faculty from the Management Information Systems (MIS) and Computer Science (CS) departments, the course leverages their research and teaching experiences. Students from diverse backgrounds, primarily MIS and CS majors, were enrolled. The course delivered a comprehensive overview of data science, fostering collaboration among students from different majors through group lab assignments and a semester-long project. The interdisciplinary pedagogy promoted collaboration and student satisfaction.

title: Memory-based control with recurrent neural networks
Abstract: Partially observed control problems pose a significant challenge in reinforcement learning. This paper extends two model-free algorithms for continuous control – deterministic policy gradient and stochastic value gradient – to handle partially observed domains using recurrent neural networks trained with backpropagation through time. The paper demonstrates that this approach, coupled with long-short term memory, can solve various physical control problems exhibiting different memory requirements, including short-term integration of information from noisy sensors, identification of system parameters, and long-term memory problems. It also showcases success in solving a combined exploration and memory problem using a simplified version of the Morris water maze task. Additionally, the paper highlights the ability of the approach to handle high-dimensional observations by learning directly from pixels. The study finds that both recurrent deterministic and stochastic policies can effectively learn solutions for these tasks, including the water maze, where agents must develop efficient search strategies.

title: Near-Optimal Bounds for Binary Embeddings of Arbitrary Sets
Abstract: This paper examines embedding a subset K of the unit sphere into the Hamming cube {-1,+1}^m. It characterizes the tradeoff between distortion and sample complexity m in terms of the Gaussian width ω(K) of the set. For subspaces and several structured sets, the paper demonstrates that Gaussian maps provide the optimal tradeoff m~δ^-2ω^2(K). Specifically, for δ distortion, m≈δ^-2d is needed, where d is the subspace dimension. For general sets, the paper provides sharp characterizations, simplified to m≈δ^-4ω^2(K). The paper also presents improved results for local embedding of points in close proximity, which is related to locality-sensitive hashing. It further discusses faster binary embedding, leveraging an initial sketching procedure based on the Fast Johnson-Lindenstauss Transform. Finally, the paper presents several numerical observations and discusses open problems.

title: We Are Humor Beings: Understanding and Predicting Visual Humor
Abstract: Humor, despite its significant impact on human life, remains poorly understood. With increasing interactions between humans and AI systems, teaching these systems to understand subtle human expressions like humor becomes crucial. This work investigates the question of what content within a scene makes it funny. As a first step toward understanding visual humor, the paper analyzes humor in abstract scenes and designs computational models. Two datasets of abstract scenes are collected to facilitate humor study at both scene and object levels. Human studies are conducted to analyze funny scenes and explore different humor types depicted within them. The paper models two tasks that demonstrate an understanding of aspects of visual humor: predicting the funniness of a scene and altering its funniness. The models demonstrate quantitative performance and qualitative validation through human studies. The datasets are publicly available.

title: Automatic Incident Classification for Big Traffic Data by Adaptive Boosting SVM
Abstract: Modern cities experience frequent traffic congestion across space and time. Monitoring these situations is crucial for Traffic Control and Surveillance Systems (TCSS). Advanced TCSS benefit from automatic detection and classification of different traffic incidents, such as congestion severity, abnormal driving patterns, and abrupt or illegal stops. While most TCSS are equipped with basic incident detection algorithms, they lack the sophistication for accurate classification. This paper addresses the lack of research in Automated Incident Classification (AIC) by proposing a novel AIC method. The method extracts traffic signals from captured videos and converts them into spatial-temporal (ST) signals. Based on the characteristics of ST signals, realistic simulation data are generated to create an extended big traffic database encompassing a variety of traffic situations. A Mean-Shift filter is then introduced to suppress noise and extract significant features from ST signals. These features are linked to various types of traffic data, including one normal type (inliers) and multiple abnormal types (outliers). An adaptive boosting classifier is trained to automatically detect outliers in traffic data, and a Support Vector Machine (SVM) based method is employed to train the model for outlier category identification. This hybrid approach, termed Adaptive Boosting Support Vector Machines (AB-SVM), achieves a high classification accuracy of over 92% on average.

title: Data-driven Sequential Monte Carlo in Probabilistic Programming
Abstract: Most existing probabilistic programming systems utilize model priors as proposal distributions for Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) and sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) algorithms, which is suboptimal. This paper presents an approach to train a discriminative model, specifically a neural network, to approximate the optimal proposal using posterior estimates from previous inference runs. The paper demonstrates an example incorporating a data-driven proposal for use in a non-parametric model within the Anglican probabilistic programming system. The results show that data-driven proposals significantly improve inference performance, reducing the number of particles required for accurate posterior estimation.

title: Nuquantus: Machine learning software for the characterization and quantification of cell nuclei in complex immunofluorescent tissue images
Abstract: Determining fundamental disease mechanisms often relies on histopathology visualization and quantitative image analysis. Current analysis of multi-channel fluorescence tissue images primarily involves manual measurements of tissue cellular content and sub-cellular compartments. This manual methodology is tedious and subjective, highlighting the need for an automated analytical technique for processing large-scale image datasets. This paper introduces Nuquantus (Nuclei quantification utility software), a novel machine learning-based analytical method that identifies, quantifies, and classifies nuclei based on cells of interest in composite fluorescent tissue images where cell borders are not visible. Nuquantus is an adaptive framework that learns the morphological attributes of intact tissue, accounting for anatomical variability and pathological processes. The software enables robust quantitative image analysis of remodeling cardiac tissue after myocardial infarction, reliably classifying cardiomyocyte versus non-cardiomyocyte nuclei and detecting cell proliferation and death in different cell classes. Nuquantus provides an innovative computerized methodology for analyzing complex tissue images, significantly facilitating image analysis and minimizing human bias.

title: Origami: A 803 GOp/s/W Convolutional Network Accelerator
Abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks are increasingly employed in computer vision and image/video processing tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results in various domains, including object recognition and detection, semantic segmentation, action recognition, optical flow, and superresolution. Hardware acceleration of these algorithms is crucial for adopting these advancements in embedded and mobile computer vision systems. This paper presents a novel architecture, design, and implementation, along with the first reported silicon measurements, of a deep convolutional neural network accelerator that surpasses previous work in terms of power, area, and I/O efficiency. The manufactured device achieves up to 196 GOp/s on 3.09 mm^2 of silicon using UMC 65nm technology and achieves a power efficiency of 803 GOp/s/W. The significantly reduced bandwidth requirements make it the first architecture scalable to TOp/s performance.

title: Small-footprint Deep Neural Networks with Highway Connections for Speech Recognition
Abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have significantly improved speech recognition accuracy in benchmark datasets and application domains. However, compared to traditional Gaussian mixture models, DNN-based acoustic models typically have a much larger number of parameters, posing challenges for applications on resource-constrained platforms like mobile devices. This paper investigates the application of the recently proposed highway network for training smaller-footprint DNNs, which are thinner and deeper, with significantly fewer parameters compared to conventional DNNs. The approach was evaluated on the AMI meeting speech transcription corpus, containing approximately 70 hours of audio data. Highway neural networks consistently outperformed their plain DNN counterparts, enabling substantial reduction in model parameters without compromising recognition accuracy.

title: Decoding index finger position from EEG using random forests
Abstract: While invasively recorded brain activity provides detailed information about motor commands, the level of detail at which information about body part positions can be decoded from non-invasive signals remains an open question. This work demonstrates that index finger positions can be differentiated from non-invasive electroencephalographic (EEG) recordings in healthy human subjects. Using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, a random forest model successfully distinguished different index finger positions on a numerical keyboard with above-chance accuracy. Among the investigated spectral features, high β-power (20-30 Hz) over the contralateral sensorimotor cortex carried the most information about finger position. These findings indicate that finger position is, in principle, decodable from non-invasive features of brain activity that generalize across individuals.

title: Watch-Bot: Unsupervised Learning for Reminding Humans of Forgotten Actions
Abstract: This paper presents a robotic system that observes a human using a Kinect v2 RGB-D sensor, detects forgotten actions during an activity, and reminds the person using a laser pointer to point out the related object. This simple setup is easily deployable on any assistive robot. The approach is based on a learning algorithm trained in a purely unsupervised setting, eliminating the need for human annotations. This makes the approach scalable and applicable to various scenarios. The model learns action/object co-occurrence and action temporal relations within the activity, using these learned relationships to infer forgotten actions and related objects. The paper demonstrates that the approach not only improves unsupervised action segmentation and action cluster assignment performance but also effectively detects forgotten actions on a challenging human activity RGB-D video dataset. Robotic experiments showcase the robot's ability to successfully remind people of forgotten actions.

title: Preconditioned Stochastic Gradient Descent
Abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) remains the primary method for many practical problems. However, its slow convergence and difficulty in tuning present challenges. Preconditioning SGD can significantly accelerate its convergence. While various attempts have been made, they either focus on specialized problems or result in methods more complex than SGD. This paper proposes a new method to estimate a preconditioner, aligning the amplitudes of preconditioned stochastic gradient perturbations with those of the parameters being optimized, similar to the Newton method for deterministic optimization. Unlike preconditioners based on secant equation fitting, as used in deterministic quasi-Newton methods, which assume a positive definite Hessian and approximate its inverse, the new preconditioner works effectively for both convex and non-convex optimizations with exact or noisy gradients. When applied to stochastic gradient, it naturally dampens gradient noise, stabilizing SGD. Efficient preconditioner estimation methods are developed, and with reasonable simplifications, they can be applied to large-scale problems. Experimental results show that preconditioned SGD, equipped with the new preconditioner and requiring no tuning, efficiently solves challenging problems such as training deep neural networks or recurrent neural networks with long-term memories.

title: Understanding Human-Centric Images: From Geometry to Fashion
Abstract: Understanding humans from photographs has been a fundamental goal of computer vision. This thesis develops a hierarchy of tools covering various topics aimed at understanding humans from monocular RGB images, from low-level feature point descriptors to high-level fashion-aware conditional random fields models. Building these high-level models requires robust and reliable low and mid-level cues. Two low-level keypoint descriptors are proposed: one based on heat diffusion theory on images, and the other using a convolutional neural network to learn discriminative image patch representations. The thesis introduces distinct low-level generative models for representing human pose: a discrete model based on a directed acyclic graph and a continuous model clustering poses on a Riemannian manifold. Two 3D human pose estimation algorithms are proposed as mid-level cues: one estimating 3D pose from noisy 2D estimations, and another simultaneously estimating both 2D and 3D pose. Finally, higher-level models built upon low and mid-level cues are formulated for understanding humans from single images. The focus is on two fashion-related tasks: semantic segmentation of clothing and predicting fashionability from images with metadata to provide fashion advice. Extensive results and comparisons with state-of-the-art methods are presented for all approaches, demonstrating significant improvements across the various tasks addressed.

title: Fighting Bandits with a New Kind of Smoothness
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel family of algorithms for the adversarial multi-armed bandit problem and provides a simple analysis technique based on convex smoothing. Two main results are presented: First, regularization via the Tsallis entropy, which includes EXP3 as a special case, achieves the Θ(√TN) minimax regret. Second, a wide class of perturbation methods achieve near-optimal regret of O(√TN log N) if the perturbation distribution has a bounded hazard rate. Distributions like Gumbel, Weibull, Frechet, Pareto, and Gamma satisfy this key property.

title: Learning Deep Features for Discriminative Localization
Abstract: This work revisits the global average pooling layer proposed in [13], shedding light on its ability to enable convolutional neural networks to achieve remarkable localization ability despite training on image-level labels. While previously proposed as a regularization technique, the paper demonstrates that it builds a generic localizable deep representation applicable to various tasks. Despite the simplicity of global average pooling, the paper achieves a 37.1% top-5 error for object localization on ILSVRC 2014, close to the 34.2% top-5 error achieved by a fully supervised CNN approach. The paper demonstrates that the network can localize discriminative image regions across various tasks despite not being specifically trained for them.

title: Modeling Eating Behaviors: the Role of Environment and Positive Food Association Learning via a Ratatouille Effect
Abstract: Eating behaviors in school-aged children are complex and influenced by social and cultural factors. This research investigates how food association learning, inspired by a pilot study in Arizona, can be used to create population-level models of dietary habits. Mathematical analyses highlight the potential impact of nutrition education on community health. Model results suggest that traditional nutrition programs may have limited effectiveness in improving eating behaviors. This research proposes integrating food association learning into intervention strategies as a more sustainable approach to promoting healthy eating habits.  The "Ratatouille effect," where food association learners transition into food preference learners, could lead to long-term behavioral changes and shift the distribution of healthy eaters in a community. Ultimately, this work emphasizes the importance of developing nutrition programs that consider economic, social, cultural, and environmental factors to create healthy communities.

title: A machine learning approach to anomaly-based detection on Android platforms
Abstract: Mobile platforms with increased storage and computing capabilities have become increasingly vulnerable to malware attacks due to their use in sensitive applications like online banking and e-commerce. Traditional signature-based malware detection techniques are becoming ineffective against new and unknown threats. This research proposes a machine learning-based approach for detecting malware on Android platforms. The system monitors and extracts features from running applications and utilizes a trained K-Nearest Neighbour classifier for in-device malware detection. The results demonstrate high detection accuracy (93.75%), low error rate (6.25%), and a low false positive rate, effectively identifying real Android malware.

title: Policy Gradient Methods for Off-policy Control
Abstract: Off-policy learning aims to estimate the value of a specific policy while following a different policy. While gradient-based algorithms like GTD and TDC/GQ offer solutions, they are limited to fixed behavior policies. This paper introduces the first gradient-based learning algorithms that allow for adaptive behavior policies, gradually making them more greedy with respect to the learned value function. The algorithms rely on the framework of policy gradient and are supported by mathematical derivations, a convergence theorem, and empirical evidence demonstrating their effectiveness compared to existing approaches.

title: Deep Relative Attributes
Abstract: Visual attributes provide a common language for describing images and scenes, understood by both humans and computers. Relative attributes, which measure the strength of a property compared across images, have been used to establish correspondences and enable image comparisons. However, past methods relied on handcrafted features, limiting their applicability to real-world scenarios. This paper presents a deep neural network architecture for predicting relative attributes. A convolutional neural network (ConvNet) learns features, including a ranking layer that ranks images based on these features. An appropriate ranking loss is used to train the network end-to-end. The proposed method surpasses baseline and state-of-the-art methods in relative attribute prediction across various datasets. Qualitative results and visualizations of saliency maps demonstrate the network's ability to learn effective features for each specific attribute.

title: Stack Exchange Tagger
Abstract: This project aims to develop an accurate tagger for questions posted on Stack Exchange, tackling the broader challenge of classifying large-scale text datasets. The multilabel classification problem, where each item can belong to multiple classes, is addressed by predicting tags based on the question text and title. The research compares the performance of Support Vector Classification (SVC) with different kernel functions and loss functions. Results indicate that linear SVC with the Crammer Singer technique achieves the best performance.

title: True Online Temporal-Difference Learning
Abstract: The temporal-difference methods TD($\lambda$) and Sarsa($\lambda$) are fundamental in reinforcement learning. Their attractiveness stems from their efficiency, low computational cost, and simple interpretation based on the forward view. Recently, true online versions of these methods, called true online TD($\lambda$) and true online Sarsa($\lambda$), have been introduced, maintaining exact equivalence with the forward view at all times, unlike their traditional counterparts. This paper empirically compares the performance of true online methods with regular ones across various domains, including random MRPs, a myoelectric prosthetic arm, and a domain from the Arcade Learning Environment, using different feature representations. The results suggest that true online methods consistently outperform regular methods in terms of learning speed, providing a significant advantage with no need for choosing between traces. The paper also provides an in-depth theoretical analysis of true online temporal-difference learning, highlighting its potential for deriving new methods.

title: Deep Learning-Based Image Kernel for Inductive Transfer
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel method for classifying images from target classes with limited training data by leveraging transfer learning from non-target classes. A Siamese net is trained to estimate the probability of two images belonging to the same class without using any information beyond class labels from non-target classes. The Siamese net's output, after post-processing, forms a gram matrix of a Mercer kernel. This kernel, when combined with a support vector machine (SVM), achieves reasonable classification accuracy on target classes without fine-tuning. Furthermore, partial fine-tuning of the Siamese net using a small number of target class samples significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. The paper provides insights into the learning process and class separation capabilities of this kernel on MNIST, Dogs vs. Cats, and CIFAR-10 datasets.

title: Learning the Correction for Multi-Path Deviations in Time-of-Flight Cameras
Abstract: The Multipath effect in Time-of-Flight (ToF) cameras poses a significant challenge for accurate 3D data processing. This research explores the use of machine learning to correct this effect. Two new datasets of ToF images, rendered using LuxRender's ToF simulator, were created, featuring corners in various orientations and material properties. Corners were chosen because they exhibit the most pronounced multipath effects. A learning model based on Random Forests was constructed to predict real-valued corrections for ToF data. The results show that, in the smaller dataset, real-valued corrections can be effectively predicted, significantly improving the quality of depth images by removing multipath bias. The algorithm reduced relative per-pixel error from an average of 19% to 3%, while also lowering error variance by an order of magnitude.

title: Big Data Scaling through Metric Mapping: Exploiting the Remarkable Simplicity of Very High Dimensional Spaces using Correspondence Analysis
Abstract: This research presents new findings in data analysis within very high-dimensional spaces, exploring dimensions up to one million. Correspondence Analysis is highlighted for its suitability in orthonormally mapping or scaling power law distributed data, a common data distribution across many domains. Correspondence factor analysis provides a latent semantic or principal axes mapping. The experiments use data from digital chemistry, finance, and statistically generated data to demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach.

title: Online Visual Analytics of Text Streams
Abstract: This paper introduces an online visual analytics approach to assist users in understanding hierarchical topic evolution within high-volume text streams. The key concept is to identify representative topics in incoming documents and align them with their immediate predecessors (in time). Streaming tree cuts are learned from topic trees based on user-selected focus nodes, and a dynamic Bayesian network model is used to derive these cuts, balancing fitness and smoothness between adjacent cuts. Corresponding topics across different times are connected, providing an overview of evolving hierarchical topics. A sedimentation-based visualization allows interactive analysis of streaming text data, enabling exploration from global patterns to local details. The method is evaluated on real-world datasets, showcasing its effectiveness in analyzing large-scale text streams.

title: Distributed Optimization with Arbitrary Local Solvers
Abstract: Distributed optimization methods are essential for efficiently handling large datasets. This research presents a framework for distributed optimization that allows the use of arbitrary solvers locally on each machine while maintaining competitive performance against specialized distributed methods. Strong primal-dual convergence rate guarantees are provided for the framework, which holds for any local solver. The impact of local solver selection is demonstrated both theoretically and experimentally. The paper also includes implementation details and highlights practical performance optimization techniques.

title: Tracking Idea Flows between Social Groups
Abstract: Many applications involve the flow of ideas represented by sets of words between different user groups. A tensor-based technique clusters these linked words into ideas and tracks their flow. The tensor representation introduces two additional dimensions for time and lead-lag relationships. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show that the proposed method surpasses traditional clustering techniques, achieving higher accuracy. A case study demonstrates the method's effectiveness in understanding the flow of ideas on social media.

title: L1-Regularized Distributed Optimization: A Communication-Efficient Primal-Dual Framework
Abstract: Sparsity is crucial in many large-scale applications, but existing methods for distributed optimization of sparsity-inducing objectives are limited. By framing classical objectives within a general primal-dual setting, a new class of methods is developed that can be efficiently distributed and applied to common sparsity-inducing models, such as Lasso, sparse logistic regression, and elastic net-regularized problems. Theoretical convergence guarantees are provided for the framework, and its efficiency and flexibility are demonstrated through extensive experimental comparisons on Amazon EC2. The proposed framework achieves speedups of up to 50x compared to state-of-the-art methods for distributed L1-regularized optimization.

title: Quantum Privacy-Preserving Data Mining
Abstract: Data mining plays a vital role in big data analytics, extracting knowledge patterns from large datasets. Privacy concerns arise when mining sensitive data like medical records, commercial data, and national security information. This paper presents a quantum protocol for mining association rules on vertically partitioned databases. The proposed protocol enhances privacy levels compared to classical protocols while simultaneously reducing computational complexity and communication cost exponentially.

title: Cloud-based Electronic Health Records for Real-time, Region-specific Influenza Surveillance
Abstract: Accurate real-time monitoring systems for influenza outbreaks are crucial for informed decision-making and public health intervention. This research demonstrates the potential of using information extracted from cloud-based electronic health records databases, combined with machine learning techniques and historical epidemiological data, to provide near real-time regional predictions of flu outbreaks in the United States.

title: The Power of Depth for Feedforward Neural Networks
Abstract: This research proves that there exists a simple, approximately radial function in high-dimensional space, expressible by a small three-layer feedforward neural network, that cannot be effectively approximated by any two-layer network, unless the width of the latter is exponentially large in the dimension. This holds for various activation functions, including rectified linear units, sigmoids, and thresholds, demonstrating the exponential advantage of depth over width for standard feedforward neural networks. This result extends previous work on Boolean functions with fewer assumptions and utilizes different proof techniques and construction.

title: RNN Fisher Vectors for Action Recognition and Image Annotation
Abstract: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have achieved significant success in classifying and predicting sequences. The methodology leverages Fisher Vectors, with RNNs serving as generative probabilistic models, and partial derivatives are computed using backpropagation. The approach achieves state-of-the-art results in two distinct sequence-based tasks: video action recognition and image annotation. title: Active Distance-Based Clustering using K-medoids
Abstract: The k-medoids algorithm, a partitional, centroid-based clustering algorithm, uses pairwise distances between data points to decompose a dataset into disjoint clusters. However, calculating all pairwise distances can be computationally expensive. This paper introduces a method that requires only a small proportion of the distances, estimating an upper bound for unknown distances based on the known ones. This algorithm leverages the triangle inequality to estimate unknown distances and employs a recursive approach to cluster objects, actively selecting prominent points and querying their distances. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method, using only a subset of distances, effectively finds proper clustering on real-world and synthetic datasets.

title: Quantum assisted Gaussian process regression
Abstract: Gaussian processes (GP) are widely used for regression problems in supervised machine learning, typically requiring O(n^3) logic gates for implementation. This paper shows that the quantum linear systems algorithm can be applied to Gaussian process regression (GPR), leading to exponential computational time reduction in certain cases. Even in less ideal scenarios, the paper demonstrates a polynomial efficiency increase.

title: Sparse Generalized Principal Component Analysis for Large-scale Applications beyond Gaussianity
Abstract: Principal Component Analysis (PCA), a dimension reduction technique, produces inconsistent estimators when dealing with moderate to high dimensionality, a common problem in modern large-scale applications. Existing sparse PCA methods address inconsistency but are limited to Gaussian assumptions and fail to address scalability issues. A family of iterative sparse generalized PCA (SG-PCA) algorithms is proposed, guaranteeing loss function decrease in each iteration despite non-convexity and non-smoothness. The sparsity-inducing regularization is more intuitive and easier to tune than Lasso. Accelerated gradient is integrated for fast convergence, and a progressive screening technique efficiently eliminates nuisance dimensions, enhancing scalability. High-dimensional simulations and real data experiments demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of SG-PCA. |||

title: Active Sampler: Light-weight Accelerator for Complex Data Analytics at Scale
Abstract: Recent research has shown that "Big Models" trained on "Big Data" have produced remarkable results. Most common algorithms for model training are iterative, and due to the massive volume of data, only a small fraction of the training data can be processed in each iteration. This paper investigates the impact of data access patterns on model training. The authors propose an Active Sampler algorithm that prioritizes training data with higher "learning value" by sampling them more frequently. This approach aims to concentrate training efforts on valuable instances close to classification boundaries, rather than focusing on obvious cases, noisy data, or outliers. The theoretical correctness and optimality of Active Sampler are demonstrated, along with a lightweight vectorized implementation. The Active Sampler is compatible with most approaches optimizing large-scale data analytics and can be applied to various analytics models trained using the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm. Extensive experimental evaluations show that Active Sampler can significantly speed up the training process of SVM, feature selection, and deep learning while maintaining comparable training quality, achieving a 1.6-2.2x improvement.

title: Minimal Perceptrons for Memorizing Complex Patterns
Abstract: Feedforward neural networks have been extensively studied for their ability to understand learning and memory, and they have been successfully applied to various practical problems in pattern classification. It is generally understood that more complex tasks require larger networks. However, designing optimal network architectures for specific tasks remains a fundamental problem. This study focuses on three-layered neural networks for memorizing binary patterns. The authors introduce a novel complexity measure for binary patterns and estimate the minimal network size required to memorize them based on their complexity. They formulate the minimal network size for regular, random, and complex patterns. Notably, the minimal size for complex patterns, which are neither ordered nor disordered, is predicted by measuring their Hamming distances from known ordered patterns. The authors' predictions align with simulations based on the back-propagation algorithm.

title: Efficient Deep Feature Learning and Extraction via StochasticNets
Abstract: Deep neural networks are powerful tools for feature learning and extraction due to their ability to model high-level abstractions in complex data. Efficient neural connectivity formation for faster feature learning and extraction is an area worth exploring in this context. Inspired by findings on stochastic synaptic connectivity formation in the brain and its ability to efficiently represent information, the authors propose StochasticNets, a deep neural network architecture with sparse connections formed stochastically between neurons. To evaluate the feasibility of StochasticNets for feature learning and extraction, they train deep convolutional StochasticNets to learn abstract features using the CIFAR-10 dataset. The learned features are then extracted from images and used for classification on the SVHN and STL-10 datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that features learned using deep convolutional StochasticNets, with fewer connections than conventional deep convolutional neural networks, achieve better or comparable classification accuracy. Notably, StochasticNets achieve a relative test error decrease of approximately 4.5% for classification on the STL-10 dataset and 1% on the SVHN dataset. Furthermore, StochasticNets achieve comparable classification accuracy even when using only 10% of the training data for feature learning. Finally, significant gains in feature extraction speed are observed in embedded applications using StochasticNets. Overall, StochasticNets enable faster feature learning and extraction performance while maintaining or exceeding the accuracy of conventional deep neural networks.
