title: A Bayesian Generalized CAR Model for Correlated Signal Detection
Abstract: Large-scale multiple testing has become a cornerstone of modern data analysis in recent years. In many applications, data exhibit correlations, meaning that the observed test statistic used for detecting signals at each location in a dataset provides information about the likelihood of a true signal at other locations. This paper proposes a generalized conditional autoregressive (CAR) model for Bayesian multiple testing, extending previous work that accounted for dependencies between neighboring volume elements in neuroimaging. The proposed model allows for the inclusion of points with no neighbors, which is not possible under conventional CAR models. This generalization provides a unified framework for modeling both dependent and independent cases, leading to stronger Bayesian learning in the posterior and increased precision in signal estimates. The authors justify their chosen prior distribution and prove the properness of the resulting posterior distribution. They illustrate the effectiveness and applicability of their model by analyzing simulated and real microarray data where genes exhibit dependence based on physical adjacency on a chromosome or predefined gene pathways.
label: AI

title: Improving Human Activity Recognition Through Ranking and Re-ranking
Abstract: This paper proposes two ranking-based methods to enhance the performance of existing human activity recognition systems. First, the authors introduce Rank Normalization (RaN), a parameter-free ranking technique that normalizes each dimension of video features. RaN addresses the sparse and bursty distribution problems commonly encountered in Fisher Vectors and VLAD. Second, inspired by curriculum learning, the authors propose Multi-Class Iterative Re-Ranking (MIR), a training-free re-ranking technique. MIR captures relationships among action classes by separating easy and typical videos from difficult ones, re-ranking the prediction scores of classifiers accordingly. The authors demonstrate that their proposed methods significantly improve the performance of state-of-the-art motion features on six real-world datasets.
label: AI

title: Understanding Customers' Evaluations Through Mining Airline Reviews
Abstract: Data mining can be used strategically to identify customer profiles, understand customer expectations, and enhance customer satisfaction. By analyzing passenger reviews about their trip experiences, airline companies can improve their services. This study investigates customer review data for in-flight services of airline companies to create customer models based on these data. Two approaches are employed: feature-based and clustering-based modeling. Feature-based modeling groups customers into categories based on features like cabin type and airline company. Clustering-based modeling uses k-means clustering to group customers, followed by modeling. Multivariate regression analysis is applied to model customer groups in both cases. The study aims to understand how customers evaluate services and identify dominant characteristics of in-flight services from the customer perspective.
label: AI

title: Deep Feature Learning with Relative Distance Comparison for Person Re-identification
Abstract: Identifying the same individual across different scenes is a crucial yet challenging task in intelligent video surveillance. The main difficulty lies in preserving similarity for the same person despite large appearance and structure variations while discriminating different individuals. This paper presents a scalable distance-driven feature learning framework based on deep neural networks for person re-identification. The framework addresses these challenges effectively. Specifically, the authors train a convolutional neural network on training images with person IDs, generating triplet units consisting of three images: one person with a matched reference and a mismatched reference. The network generates layered representations, which are then compared using the L2 distance metric. Parameter optimization maximizes the relative distance between the matched and mismatched pairs for each triplet unit. To address the cubic increase in training triplets, the authors develop an efficient triplet generation scheme and optimized gradient descent algorithm. The computational load is primarily determined by the number of original images rather than the number of triplets. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of their approach on several challenging databases, outperforming other state-of-the-art methods.
label: AI

title: Macroeconomic Dynamics of Assets, Leverage and Trust
Abstract: This paper proposes a macroeconomic model based on assets, leverage (debt over assets), and trust (maximum sustainable leverage) to analyze the role of credit in economic growth dynamics and its association with economic performance and confidence. The model reveals a reward/penalty mechanism linked to patience, quantified by the return on assets. In regular economies where the EBITA/Assets ratio exceeds the cost of debt, starting with a trust level higher than leverage results in the highest long-term return on assets (a proxy for economic growth). The model also suggests a central bank's optimal response to external shocks affecting economic growth. Late policy intervention leads to the highest long-term return on assets and asset value, but at the cost of a prolonged crisis until intervention occurs. This phenomenon stems from the fact that delaying intervention allows trust to increase first, making intervention most effective when trust is high. These findings are derived from two fundamental model assumptions: trust increases when it surpasses leverage, and economic agents optimally adjust debt for a given level of trust and assets. The model is calibrated using a Markov Switching Model for the EBITA/Assets ratio, matching empirical data on the return on equity of the EURO STOXX 50 from 2000 to 2013. The model reveals highly non-monotonous leverage and trust dynamics with curved trajectories, resulting from the nonlinear coupling between the variables.
label: AI

title: Learning algorithms at the service of WISE survey
Abstract: This paper presents a dedicated program for automatic source classification in the WISE database merged with SuperCOSMOS scans. The program accurately identifies galaxies, quasars, and stars across most of the unconfused sky. The authors utilize a Support Vector Machines classifier, trained on SDSS spectroscopic data, for this purpose. The classification is applied to a photometric dataset based on all-sky WISE 3.4 and 4.6 micron information cross-matched with SuperCOSMOS B and R bands, yielding a reliable sample of approximately 170 million sources, including galaxies at a median redshift of 0.2, as well as quasars and stars. The classification method demonstrates high purity and completeness (over 96%) of the separated sources. The resulting catalogs are valuable for sophisticated analyses, such as generating all-sky photometric redshifts.
label: AI

title: Words are not Equal: Graded Weighting Model for building Composite Document Vectors
Abstract: Composing phrases from word vectors remains a challenge despite the success of distributional semantics. Various methods have been explored for benchmark tasks like sentiment classification, including word vector averaging, matrix-vector approaches based on parsing, and on-the-fly learning of paragraph vectors. Most models omit stop words from the composition. This paper proposes alternative graded schemes where words are weighted based on their discriminatory relevance to their use in the document (e.g., using inverse document frequency (idf)). Some of these methods, particularly tf-idf, significantly improve performance compared to previous state-of-the-art models. Combining these approaches into an ensemble based on alternate classifiers like the RNN model further enhances performance, resulting in a 1.6% improvement on the IMDB movie review dataset and a 7.01% improvement on Amazon product reviews. These language-free models can be obtained unsupervised, making them suitable for under-resourced languages like Hindi and many others. The authors demonstrate the language-free aspects by achieving a 12% gain for two review datasets over earlier results and release a new larger dataset for future testing.
label: AI

title: Distilling Knowledge from Deep Networks with Applications to Healthcare Domain
Abstract: The rapid growth of Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) presents new opportunities and urgent needs for discovering meaningful data-driven representations and patterns of diseases in Computational Phenotyping research. While Deep Learning models excel at robust prediction in computational phenotyping tasks, they suffer from a lack of interpretability, which is crucial for clinicians involved in decision-making. This paper introduces Interpretable Mimic Learning, a novel knowledge-distillation approach that learns interpretable phenotype features for robust prediction while mimicking the performance of deep learning models. The framework employs Gradient Boosting Trees to learn interpretable features from deep learning models such as Stacked Denoising Autoencoder and Long Short-Term Memory. Extensive experiments on a real-world clinical time-series dataset demonstrate that the proposed method achieves similar or better performance than deep learning models while providing interpretable phenotypes for clinical decision-making.
label: AI

title: Evolution of Privacy Loss in Wikipedia
Abstract: Collective online participation has a significant and potentially adverse impact on individual privacy. As online systems evolve, new digital traces of individual behavior can reveal previously hidden statistical links between an individual's past actions and their private traits. This paper quantifies the evolution of individual privacy loss by analyzing the edit history of Wikipedia over 13 years, encompassing over 117,523 users and 188,805,088 edits. The authors track each Wikipedia contributor using apparently harmless features like the number of edits performed on predefined broad categories within a given time period (e.g., Mathematics, Culture, or Nature). They demonstrate that even at this unspecific level of behavior description, off-the-shelf machine learning algorithms can uncover undisclosed personal traits like gender, religion, or education. Empirical evidence shows consistent improvement in prediction accuracy for almost all private traits over time. Surprisingly, prediction performance for users who stopped editing after a given time also continues to improve, suggesting that activities performed by new users contribute more to this effect than additional activities from existing users. This study provides valuable insights for users, system designers, and policymakers to understand and make informed long-term design choices in online content creation systems.
label: AI

title: A Unified Approach to Error Bounds for Structured Convex Optimization Problems
Abstract: Error bounds, inequalities that bound the distance of vectors in a test set to a given set using a residual function, have proven invaluable in analyzing the convergence rates of numerous iterative methods for solving optimization problems. This paper presents a new framework for establishing error bounds for a class of structured convex optimization problems where the objective function is the sum of a smooth convex function and a general closed proper convex function. This class encompasses a wide range of constrained minimization problems and regularized loss minimization formulations in machine learning, signal processing, and statistics. Using the proposed framework, the authors demonstrate that several existing error bound results can be recovered in a unified and transparent manner. The framework is then applied to a class of nuclear-norm regularized loss minimization problems, establishing a new error bound under a strict complementarity-type regularity condition. An example is provided to show that the error bound may not hold without the regularity condition. This work offers a comprehensive answer to a question raised by Tseng and suggests potential applications in the study of error bounds for structured convex optimization problems.
label: AI

title: Prediction of grain boundary structure and energy by machine learning
Abstract: Grain boundaries significantly influence the properties of polycrystalline materials due to variations in atomic configuration. Understanding the relationship between grain boundaries and materials properties necessitates systematic studies of grain boundary atomic structure. However, these studies are limited by the computationally intensive process of determining the structure of a single grain boundary. Efficient computational methods for predicting grain boundary structure could accelerate the understanding of grain boundary behavior. This paper proposes a machine-learning approach for predicting grain boundary structures and energies. Training data for non-linear regression were obtained from four symmetric-tilt grain boundaries of copper. The regression analysis results were then used to predict the structures of 12 other grain boundaries. The method accurately predicts both the structures and energies of grain boundaries. This general method has potential applications in understanding various complex interfaces.
label: AI

title: Mined Semantic Analysis: A New Concept Space Model for Semantic Representation of Textual Data
Abstract: Mined Semantic Analysis (MSA) is a novel concept space model that employs unsupervised learning to generate semantic representations of text. MSA represents textual structures (terms, phrases, documents) as a Bag of Concepts (BoC) where concepts are derived from concept-rich encyclopedic corpora. While traditional concept space models rely solely on target corpus content to construct the concept space, MSA uncovers implicit relations between concepts by mining their associations (e.g., analyzing Wikipedia's "See also" link graph). The authors evaluate MSA's performance on benchmark datasets for measuring semantic relatedness of words and sentences. Empirical results demonstrate MSA's competitive performance compared to prior state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, they introduce the first analytical study to examine the statistical significance of results reported by different semantic relatedness methods. The study reveals that the nuances of results across top-performing methods may be statistically insignificant. MSA emerges as one of the state-of-the-art methods for measuring semantic relatedness, offering interpretability and simplicity in the generated semantic representation.

title: Integral Concurrent Learning: Adaptive Control with Parameter Convergence without PE or State Derivatives
Abstract: Concurrent learning is a recently developed adaptive update scheme that guarantees parameter convergence without requiring persistent excitation. However, this technique requires knowledge of state derivatives, which are often not directly sensed and must be estimated. This paper introduces a novel integral concurrent learning method that eliminates the need to estimate state derivatives while preserving parameter convergence properties. A Monte Carlo simulation illustrates improved robustness to noise compared to the traditional derivative formulation.
label: AI

title: Cross-Validated Variable Selection in Tree-Based Methods Improves Predictive Performance
Abstract: Recursive partitioning approaches, producing tree-like models, are a long-standing staple of predictive modeling, commonly used as "sub-learners" within ensemble methods like Boosting and Random Forest. However, a fundamental flaw in the partitioning rule of commonly used tree building methods prevents them from treating different types of variables equally. This is particularly evident in their inability to properly utilize categorical variables with a large number of categories, which are prevalent in big data. These variables can be highly informative, but current tree methods force a choice between not using them or exposing models to overfitting. This paper proposes a conceptual framework for splitting using leave-one-out (LOO) cross-validation for selecting the splitting variable, followed by a regular split for the selected variable. The key advantage of this approach is that categorical variables with many categories can be safely used in tree building and are only chosen if they contribute to predictive power. Extensive simulations and real data analysis demonstrate that the novel splitting approach significantly improves the performance of both single tree models and ensemble methods utilizing trees. Importantly, an algorithm for LOO splitting variable selection is designed that, under reasonable assumptions, does not increase the overall computational complexity compared to CART for two-class classification. For regression tasks, the approach carries an increased computational burden, replacing the O(log(n)) factor in the CART splitting rule search with an O(n) term.
label: AI

title: Scalable Modeling of Conversational-role based Self-presentation Characteristics in Large Online Forums
Abstract: Online discussion forums are complex networks of overlapping subcommunities (macrolevel structure across threads) where users adopt different roles depending on the subcommunity they are participating in at a given time (microlevel structure within threads). This sub-network structure is implicit in massive collections of threads. To uncover this structure, this paper develops a scalable algorithm based on stochastic variational inference and leverages topic models (LDA) along with mixed membership stochastic block (MMSB) models. The model is evaluated on three large-scale datasets: Cancer-ThreadStarter, Cancer-NameMention, and StackOverFlow. Qualitative analysis demonstrates that the model provides useful explanations of microlevel and macrolevel user presentation characteristics in different communities using the topics discovered from posts. Quantitative analysis shows that the model outperforms MMSB and LDA in predicting user reply structure within threads. Synthetic data experiments further demonstrate the stability of the proposed active sub-network discovery model, accurately recovering the original parameters of the experimental setup with high probability.
label: AI

title: The p-filter: multi-layer FDR control for grouped hypotheses
Abstract: In many applications of multiple hypothesis testing using the False Discovery Rate (FDR), the hypotheses can be naturally partitioned into groups. The goal is to control not only the number of false discoveries (incorrectly rejected null hypotheses) but also the number of falsely discovered groups of hypotheses (a group is falsely discovered if at least one hypothesis within it is rejected, despite containing only nulls in reality). This paper introduces the p-filter, a procedure that unifies and generalizes the standard FDR procedure by Benjamini and Hochberg and the global null testing procedure by Simes. The authors prove that the proposed method can simultaneously control the overall FDR at the finest level (treating individual hypotheses separately) and the group FDR at coarser levels (when groups are user-specified). The p-filter procedure is further generalized to handle multiple partitions of hypotheses, which can be naturally occurring in many applications. For example, in neuroscience experiments, one might have a hypothesis for every location in the brain and every time point, exploring whether the stimulus correlates with activity at a given location and time. The procedure can handle multiple partitions that are nonhierarchical, allowing for separate partitions based on voxel and time point. The authors prove that the procedure controls FDR simultaneously across these multiple layers under standard assumptions in the literature, requiring a nonnegative dependence condition known as PRDS, but not necessarily independence of hypotheses.
label: AI

title: Boosted Sparse Non-linear Distance Metric Learning
Abstract: This paper proposes a boosting-based solution for addressing metric learning problems in high-dimensional data. Distance measures are commonly used as natural measures of similarity or dissimilarity and serve as the foundation of various learning methods. The effectiveness of distance-based learning methods depends heavily on the chosen distance metric. However, traditional metric learning methods face challenges in scalability and linearity limitations with increasing dimensionality and data complexity. The true signals often reside within a low-dimensional nonlinear subspace. To address these challenges, the authors propose a nonlinear sparse metric learning algorithm using boosting. They restructure a global optimization problem into a forward stage-wise learning of weak learners based on a rank-one decomposition of the weight matrix in the Mahalanobis distance metric. A gradient boosting algorithm is devised to obtain a sparse rank-one update of the weight matrix at each step. Nonlinear features are learned through a hierarchical expansion of interactions incorporated within the boosting algorithm. An early stopping rule controls the overall complexity of the learned metric. This approach ensures three desirable properties of the final metric: positive semi-definiteness, low rank, and element-wise sparsity. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the learning model performs favorably compared to state-of-the-art methods in metric learning. |||
label: AI

title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition
Abstract: Training very deep neural networks is challenging. This paper proposes a residual learning framework to simplify this process.  Instead of learning unreferenced functions, the layers are explicitly reformulated to learn residual functions with respect to the layer inputs. Extensive empirical evidence demonstrates that these residual networks are easier to optimize and can achieve higher accuracy due to their increased depth.  On the ImageNet dataset, residual networks with up to 152 layers were evaluated - eight times deeper than VGG networks but still maintaining lower complexity.  An ensemble of these residual networks achieved a 3.57% error rate on the ImageNet test set, winning first place in the ILSVRC 2015 classification task.  Analysis on CIFAR-10 with 100 and 1000 layers is also provided. The depth of representations is crucial for visual recognition tasks. The extremely deep representations yielded a 28% relative improvement on the COCO object detection dataset. Deep residual networks were the foundation of submissions to the ILSVRC & COCO 2015 competitions, winning first place in ImageNet detection, ImageNet localization, COCO detection, and COCO segmentation.
label: AI

title: VRFP: On-the-fly Video Retrieval using Web Images and Fast Fisher Vector Products
Abstract: VRFP is a real-time video retrieval framework based on short text input queries.  After the query is known, weakly labeled training images are retrieved from the web.  The retrieved web images representing the query and each database video are treated as unordered image collections, each represented using a single Fisher Vector built on CNN features. Experiments show that a Fisher Vector is robust to noise present in web images and compares favorably in terms of accuracy to other standard representations.  While a Fisher Vector can be constructed efficiently for a new query, matching against the test set is slow due to its high dimensionality.  To achieve real-time matching, a lossless algorithm is presented that accelerates the inner product computation between high dimensional Fisher Vectors.  It is proven that the expected number of multiplications required decreases quadratically with the sparsity of Fisher Vectors.  Not only is it possible to construct and apply query models in real-time, but with the help of a simple re-ranking scheme, VRFP outperforms state-of-the-art automatic retrieval methods by a significant margin on TRECVID MED13 (3.5%), MED14 (1.3%), and CCV datasets (5.2%). A direct comparison between two different paradigms for automatic video retrieval - zero-shot learning and on-the-fly retrieval - is also provided.
label: AI

title: Convolutional Monte Carlo Rollouts in Go
Abstract: This work presents a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based Go-playing program that utilizes convolutional networks throughout. The method performs MCTS in batches, explores the Monte Carlo search tree using Thompson sampling and a convolutional network, and evaluates convnet-based rollouts on the GPU.  The program achieves strong win rates against open source Go programs and attains competitive results against state-of-the-art convolutional net-based Go-playing programs.
label: AI

title: Adaptive Neural Control for Mobile Robots Autonomous Navigation
Abstract: This paper proposes a combined strategy for tracking a non-holonomic mobile robot under specific operating conditions for system parameters and disturbances. The strategy includes kinematic steering and velocity dynamics learning of the mobile robot system simultaneously. In the neural network-based learning controller, the velocity dynamics learning control participates in tracking the reference velocity trajectory by learning the inverse function of robot dynamics. Meanwhile, the reference velocity control input stabilizes the kinematic steering system to the desired reference model of the kinematic system, even without assuming perfect velocity tracking.
label: AI

title: Guaranteed inference in topic models
Abstract: One of the core problems in statistical models is estimating the posterior distribution.  For topic models, posterior inference for individual texts is particularly important, especially when dealing with data streams.  However, this problem is often intractable in the worst case.  As a result, existing methods for posterior inference are approximate and lack guarantees on quality or convergence rate. This paper introduces a provably fast algorithm, Online Maximum a Posteriori Estimation (OPE), for posterior inference in topic models. OPE offers several advantages over existing inference approaches, including theoretical guarantees on quality and a fast convergence rate to a local maximal/stationary point of the inference problem.  The discussion about OPE is general and can be easily applied in various contexts.  Finally, OPE is used to design three methods for learning Latent Dirichlet Allocation from text streams or large corpora. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior behavior of OPE and the new learning methods.
label: AI

title: Inference in topic models: sparsity and trade-off
Abstract: Topic models are commonly used for modeling discrete data (e.g., texts, images, videos, links) and provide an efficient way to discover hidden structures/semantics in massive data. One of the core problems in this field is the posterior inference for individual data instances.  This problem is particularly important in streaming environments but is often intractable.  This paper explores the use of the Frank-Wolfe algorithm (FW) for recovering sparse solutions to posterior inference.  From detailed elucidation of both theoretical and practical aspects, FW exhibits many interesting properties beneficial to topic modeling.  FW is then employed to design fast methods, including ML-FW, for learning Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) at large scales.  Extensive experiments show that to reach the same predictive level, ML-FW can perform tens to thousands of times faster than existing state-of-the-art methods for learning LDA from massive/streaming data.
label: AI

title: Norm-Free Radon-Nikodym Approach to Machine Learning
Abstract: For Machine Learning (ML) classification problems, where a vector of $\\mathbf{x}$--observations (values of attributes) is mapped to a single $y$ value (class label), a generalized Radon--Nikodym type of solution is proposed. Quantum--mechanics --like probability states $\\psi^2(\\mathbf{x})$ are considered and "Cluster Centers", corresponding to the extremums of $<y\\psi^2(\\mathbf{x})>/<\\psi^2(\\mathbf{x})>$, are found from generalized eigenvalues problem. The eigenvalues give possible $y^{[i]}$ outcomes and corresponding eigenvectors $\\psi^{[i]}(\\mathbf{x})$ define "Cluster Centers". The projection of a $\\psi$ state, localized at given $\\mathbf{x}$ to classify, on these eigenvectors defines the probability of $y^{[i]}$ outcome, thus avoiding using a norm ($L^2$ or other types), required for "quality criteria" in a typical Machine Learning technique. A coverage of each `Cluster Center" is calculated, what potentially allows to separate system properties (described by $y^{[i]}$ outcomes) and system testing conditions (described by $C^{[i]}$ coverage). As an example of such application $y$ distribution estimator is proposed in a form of pairs $(y^{[i]},C^{[i]})$, that can be considered as Gauss quadratures generalization. This estimator allows to perform $y$ probability distribution estimation in a strongly non--Gaussian case.
label: AI

title: Gated networks: an inventory
Abstract: Gated networks are networks that contain gating connections, in which the outputs of at least two neurons are multiplied.  Initially, gated networks were used to learn relationships between two input sources, such as pixels from two images.  More recently, they have been applied to learning activity recognition or multi-modal representations. This paper aims to: 1) explain the basic computations in gated networks to the non-expert while emphasizing their symmetric nature, 2) serve as a quick reference guide to the recent literature, by providing an inventory of applications of these networks, as well as recent extensions to the basic architecture, and 3) suggest future research directions and applications.
label: AI

title: Can small quantum systems learn?
Abstract: This paper examines the question of whether quantum mechanics places limitations on the ability of small quantum devices to learn.  Specifically, the question is examined in the context of Bayesian inference, where the prior and posterior distributions are encoded in the quantum state vector. Based on lower bounds from Grover's search, it is concluded that an efficient blackbox method for updating the distribution is impossible.  A new adaptive form of approximate quantum Bayesian inference is then proposed that is polynomially faster than its classical analogue and tractable if the quantum system is augmented with classical memory or if the low-order moments of the distribution are protected using a repetition code. This work suggests a possible connection between fault tolerance and the capacity of a quantum system to learn from its surroundings.
label: AI

title: Predicting proximity with ambient mobile sensors for non-invasive health diagnostics
Abstract: Modern smartphones are becoming increasingly helpful in the areas of Internet-of-Things (IoT) and ambient health intelligence.  By learning data from several mobile sensors, this paper presents a method for detecting the nearness of the human body to a mobile device in a three-dimensional space without physical contact with the device, enabling non-invasive health diagnostics.  The human body generates wave patterns that interact with other naturally occurring ambient signals (e.g., temperature, humidity, magnetic field, acceleration, gravity, and light) that can be measured by mobile sensors.  This interaction alters the patterns of the naturally occurring signals, exhibiting characteristics that can be learned to predict the nearness of the human body to a mobile device, providing diagnostic information for medical practitioners.  The proposed prediction technique achieved an accuracy of 88.75% and a specificity of 88.3%.
label: AI

title: Deep Learning Algorithms with Applications to Video Analytics for A Smart City: A Survey
Abstract: Deep learning has recently achieved promising results in various areas, including computer vision, speech recognition, and natural language processing.  It aims to learn hierarchical representations of data using deep architecture models.  In a smart city, a lot of data (e.g., videos captured from many distributed sensors) need to be automatically processed and analyzed.  This paper reviews the deep learning algorithms applied to video analytics in a smart city, considering different research topics: object detection, object tracking, face recognition, image classification, and scene labeling.
label: AI

title: RSG: Beating Subgradient Method without Smoothness and Strong Convexity
Abstract: This paper investigates the efficiency of a Restarted SubGradient (RSG) method that periodically restarts the standard subgradient method (SG).  It is shown that when applied to a broad class of convex optimization problems, the RSG method can find an $\\epsilon$-optimal solution with a lower complexity than the SG method.  In particular, it is first shown that RSG can reduce the dependence of SG's iteration complexity on the distance between the initial solution and the optimal set to that between the $\\epsilon$-level set and the optimal set {multiplied by a logarithmic factor}.  Moreover, the advantages of RSG over SG are demonstrated in solving three different families of convex optimization problems: (a) For problems whose epigraph is a polyhedron, RSG is shown to converge linearly. (b) For problems with local quadratic growth property in the $\\epsilon$-sublevel set, RSG has an $O(\\frac{1}{\\epsilon}\\log(\\frac{1}{\\epsilon}))$ iteration complexity. (c) For problems that admit a local Kurdyka-\\L ojasiewicz property with a power constant of $\\beta\\in[0,1)$, RSG has an $O(\\frac{1}{\\epsilon^{2\\beta}}\\log(\\frac{1}{\\epsilon}))$ iteration complexity.  The novelty of this analysis lies in exploiting the lower bound of the first-order optimality residual at the $\\epsilon$-level set. This novelty allows exploring the local properties of functions (e.g., local quadratic growth property, local Kurdyka-\\L ojasiewicz property, more generally local error bound conditions) to develop the improved convergence of RSG. { A practical variant of RSG is also developed that enjoys faster convergence than the SG method, which can be run without knowing the involved parameters in the local error bound condition.} The effectiveness of the proposed algorithms is demonstrated on several machine learning tasks, including regression, classification, and matrix completion.
label: AI

title: Gamma Belief Networks
Abstract: To infer multilayer deep representations of high-dimensional discrete and nonnegative real vectors, this paper proposes an augmentable gamma belief network (GBN) that factorizes each of its hidden layers into the product of a sparse connection weight matrix and the nonnegative real hidden units of the next layer. The GBN's hidden layers are jointly trained with an upward-downward Gibbs sampler that solves each layer with the same subroutine. The gamma-negative binomial process combined with a layer-wise training strategy allows inferring the width of each layer given a fixed budget on the width of the first layer. Example results illustrate interesting relationships between the width of the first layer and the inferred network structure and demonstrate that the GBN can add more layers to improve its performance in both unsupervisedly extracting features and predicting heldout data. For exploratory data analysis, trees and subnetworks are extracted from the learned deep network to visualize how the very specific factors discovered at the first hidden layer and the increasingly more general factors discovered at deeper hidden layers are related to each other.  Synthetic data is also generated by propagating random variables through the deep network from the top hidden layer back to the bottom data layer.
label: AI

title: Partial Reinitialisation for Optimisers
Abstract: Heuristic optimizers, which search for an optimal configuration of variables relative to an objective function, often get stuck in local optima where the algorithm is unable to find further improvement. The standard approach to circumvent this problem involves periodically restarting the algorithm from random initial configurations when no further improvement can be found. This paper proposes a method of partial reinitialization, whereby, in an attempt to find a better solution, only subsets of variables are reinitialized rather than the whole configuration. Much of the information gained from previous runs is retained, leading to significant improvements in the quality of the solution found in a given time for a variety of optimization problems in machine learning.
label: AI

title: Learning measures of semi-additive behaviour
Abstract: In business analytics, measure values (e.g., sales numbers or volumes of cargo transported) are often summed along values of one or more corresponding categories (e.g., time or shipping container). However, not every measure should be added by default (e.g., a mean is more typical for the heights of a set of people). Similarly, some measures should only be summed within certain constraints (e.g., population measures need not be summed over years). In systems such as Watson Analytics, the exact additive behavior of a measure is often determined by a human expert. This work proposes a small set of features for this issue. These features are used in a case-based reasoning approach, where the system suggests an aggregation behavior, achieving 86% accuracy in a collected dataset.
label: AI

title: Minimally Supervised Feature Selection for Classification (Master's Thesis, University Politehnica of Bucharest)
Abstract: In the context of the increasing number of features available today, this paper designs a robust and fast method for feature selection. The method aims to select the most representative features that are independent from each other but strong together.  An algorithm is proposed that requires very limited labeled data (as few as one labeled frame per class) and can accommodate as many unlabeled samples.  The supervised approach from which this method was developed is also presented.  The two formulations are compared with established methods like AdaBoost, SVM, Lasso, Elastic Net, and FoBa, demonstrating that this method is much faster and has constant training time.  Moreover, the unsupervised approach outperforms all the methods compared, and the difference can be quite prominent.  The supervised approach is better than other methods in most cases, especially when the number of training shots is very limited.  The algorithm only needs to choose from a pool of positively correlated features.  The methods are evaluated on the Youtube-Objects dataset of videos and on the MNIST digits dataset, while at training time, features obtained on the CIFAR10 dataset and others pre-trained on the ImageNet dataset were also used.  This demonstrates that transfer learning is beneficial even when the datasets differ significantly: from low-resolution centered images from 10 classes to high-resolution images with objects from 1000 classes occurring in different regions of the images or to very difficult videos with very high intraclass variance.

title: On Variants of k-means Clustering
Abstract: Clustering problems frequently arise in fields like data mining, machine learning, etc., to group a collection of objects into similar groups based on a similarity (or dissimilarity) measure. Among these clustering problems, *k*-means clustering has received significant attention from researchers. Despite the fact that *k*-means is a well-studied problem, its status in the plane is still open.  In particular, it is unknown whether it admits a PTAS in the plane. The best known approximation bound in polynomial time is $9+\\eps$.\n  This paper considers the following variant of *k*-means. Given a set $C$ of points in $\\mathcal{R}^d$ and a real $f > 0$, find a finite set $F$ of points in $\\mathcal{R}^d$ that minimizes the quantity $f*|F|+\\sum_{p\\in C}\n\\min_{q \\in F} {||p-q||}^2$. For any fixed dimension $d$, a local search PTAS is designed for this problem.  A "bi-criterion" local search algorithm for *k*-means is also provided that uses $(1+\\eps)k$ centers and yields a solution whose cost is at most $(1+\\eps)$ times the cost of an optimal *k*-means solution. The algorithm runs in polynomial time for any fixed dimension.  This paper contributes in two ways: first, handling the square of distances in an elegant manner yields a near-optimal approximation bound, leading to a better understanding of the *k*-means problem.  Second, the analysis of local search might also be useful for other geometric problems. This is important given the limited knowledge about the local search method for geometric approximation.

title: Get More With Less: Near Real-Time Image Clustering on Mobile Phones
Abstract: Machine learning algorithms, in conjunction with user data, hold the promise of revolutionizing how we interact with our phones.  Their widespread adoption in app design is a testament to this promise. However, currently, the computationally expensive segments of the learning pipeline (e.g., feature extraction and model training) are offloaded to the cloud, resulting in an over-reliance on the network and under-utilization of computing resources available on mobile platforms. This paper shows that by combining the computing power distributed over a number of phones, judicious optimization choices, and contextual information, it is possible to execute the end-to-end pipeline entirely on the phones at the edge of the network efficiently.  It also demonstrates that by harnessing the power of this combination, it is possible to execute a computationally expensive pipeline at near real-time.  To demonstrate the approach, an end-to-end image-processing pipeline (including feature extraction, vocabulary learning, vectorization, and image clustering) is implemented on a set of mobile phones. The results show a 75% improvement over the standard, full pipeline implementation running on the phones without modification - reducing the time to one minute under certain conditions. This result is a promising indication that fully distributed, infrastructure-less computing is possible on networks of mobile phones, enabling a new class of mobile applications that are less reliant on the cloud.
label: AI

title: Efficient Distributed SGD with Variance Reduction
Abstract: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) has become one of the most popular optimization methods for training machine learning models on massive datasets. However, SGD suffers from two main drawbacks: (i) the noisy gradient updates have high variance, which slows down convergence as the iterates approach the optimum, and (ii) SGD scales poorly in distributed settings, typically experiencing rapidly decreasing marginal benefits as the number of workers increases. This paper proposes a highly parallel method, CentralVR, that uses error corrections to reduce the variance of SGD gradient updates and scales linearly with the number of worker nodes. CentralVR enjoys low iteration complexity, provably linear convergence rates, and exhibits linear performance gains up to hundreds of cores for massive datasets. CentralVR is compared to state-of-the-art parallel stochastic optimization methods on a variety of models and datasets, demonstrating stronger scaling than other SGD variants.

title: Stochastic Interpretation of Quasi-periodic Event-based Systems
Abstract: Many networks used in machine learning and as models of biological neural networks utilize stochastic neurons or neuron-like units. This paper shows that stochastic artificial neurons can be realized on silicon chips by exploiting the quasi-periodic behavior of mismatched analog oscillators to approximate the neuron's stochastic activation function. Neurons are represented by finite state machines (FSMs) that communicate using digital events and whose transitions are event-triggered. The event generation times of each neuron are controlled by an analog oscillator internal to that neuron/FSM, and the frequencies of the oscillators in different FSMs are incommensurable.  It is shown that within this quasi-periodic system, the transition graph of a FSM can be interpreted as the transition graph of a Markov chain, and by using different FSMs, different stochastic activation functions can be approximated. The quality of the stochastic interpretation of such a deterministic system is investigated, and the system is used to realize and sample from a restricted Boltzmann machine. The quasi-periodic event-based system was implemented on a custom silicon chip, and the chip behavior can be used to closely approximate a stochastic sampling task. |||

title: Advances in quantum machine learning
Abstract: Quantum machine learning holds significant promise but faces considerable challenges. This review explores both current research and future directions, encompassing algorithms and experimental implementations. While the field's outlook is positive, substantial hurdles remain before it can become a primary application of quantum computation.

title: Where You Are Is Who You Are: User Identification by Matching Statistics
Abstract: This research investigates the identification of users based on their unique behavioral patterns. Specifically, it focuses on matching histograms of user data from two separate experiments, one anonymized and the other with known identities. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of this method across various datasets, including call data records, browsing histories, and GPS trajectories. The results show that a large portion of users can be easily identified using only histograms of their data, highlighting their potential as digital fingerprints. Furthermore, simultaneous identification of users outperforms one-by-one identification, and the optimal method surpasses heuristic approaches in practical scenarios. The research pinpoints key factors influencing identification accuracy, including data collection duration, the number of users in the anonymized dataset, and dataset resolution. The study also examines the effectiveness of k-anonymization in mitigating user identification attacks.

title: Embedding Label Structures for Fine-Grained Feature Representation
Abstract: Fine-grained image classification aims to distinguish subtle differences between subordinate classes. However, existing methods struggle to learn fine-grained and structured feature representations capable of locating similar images at different levels of relevance. This paper proposes a novel multi-task learning framework that effectively learns such representations by jointly optimizing classification and similarity constraints. By seamlessly embedding label structures like hierarchies or shared attributes using a generalized triplet loss, the framework captures multi-level relevance. Extensive experiments conducted on three fine-grained datasets demonstrate the competitive performance of this approach, achieving state-of-the-art classification accuracy and surpassing previous methods in image retrieval across different relevance levels.
label: AI

title: Multi-Player Bandits -- a Musical Chairs Approach
Abstract: This work addresses a variant of the stochastic multi-armed bandit problem where multiple players compete for rewards by simultaneously choosing from the same set of arms, with collisions resulting in no reward. Motivated by cognitive radio network challenges, this problem is particularly complex when communication between players is limited. The paper presents two communication-free algorithms: Musical Chairs, achieving constant regret with high probability, and Dynamic Musical Chairs, achieving sublinear regret for the more challenging scenario of dynamically entering and leaving players. Notably, both algorithms require no prior knowledge of the number of players. These are the first communication-free algorithms with such guarantees, rigorously compared to previous works and validated through experiments.
label: AI

title: Bigger Buffer k-d Trees on Multi-Many-Core Systems
Abstract: Buffer k-d trees, a variant of k-d trees for massively-parallel nearest neighbor search, offer significant speed-ups on modern many-core devices for large-scale data. However, their scalability is limited by the amount of data that can fit on a single device. This paper presents modifications to the original data structure and workflow, enabling it to handle massive datasets. Additionally, a simple yet efficient approach for utilizing multiple devices within a single workstation is provided. The applicability of this enhanced framework is demonstrated in the context of astronomy, a field dealing with immense datasets.
label: AI

title: Convergence of Entropic Schemes for Optimal Transport and Gradient Flows
Abstract: Entropy barriers are commonly used to approximate solutions to linear programs, particularly in the optimal transport problem, a technique tracing back to the early work of Schrödinger. This approach has proven successful in solving optimal transport related problems across various fields, including imaging sciences, machine learning, and social sciences. Its advantages lie in its high parallelizability and exploitation of computational grid geometry. This paper contributes two key findings. First, it proves the $\\Gamma$-convergence of the entropic regularized optimal transport problem to the Monge-Kantorovich problem for the squared Euclidean norm cost function, implying convergence of the optimal entropic regularized transport plan towards an optimal transport plan as entropy vanishes. Second, it demonstrates that implicit steps based on the entropic regularized distance converge towards the original gradient flow as both step size and entropic penalty vanish under controlled conditions.
label: AI

title: Affinity CNN: Learning Pixel-Centric Pairwise Relations for Figure/Ground Embedding
Abstract: Spectral embedding provides a framework for perceptual organization tasks like image segmentation and figure/ground organization. This method utilizes an affinity matrix representing pairwise relationships between pixels to cluster pixels into regions and order them according to layer using a complex-valued extension. This paper trains a convolutional neural network (CNN) to directly predict the pairwise relationships defining the affinity matrix. Spectral embedding then resolves these predictions into globally-consistent segmentation and figure/ground organization of the scene. Experiments highlight the significant benefits of this direct coupling compared to prior approaches using explicit intermediate stages like edge detection. The results suggest spectral embedding as a viable alternative to CRF-based globalization schemes typically paired with deep neural networks.
label: AI

title: A Novel Regularized Principal Graph Learning Framework on Explicit Graph Representation
Abstract: High-dimensional scientific datasets often require visual manipulation to preserve crucial data structures. Principal curves are widely used for this purpose, but many existing methods are limited to non-self-intersecting data structures, restricting their applicability in real-world scenarios. While some methods overcome this limitation, they either rely on complex human-made rules with limited convergence guarantees and adaptability or fail to extract explicit data structures. To address these issues, this paper proposes a new regularized principal graph learning framework that captures local information of the underlying graph structure using reversed graph embedding. The framework includes models for learning spanning trees and weighted undirected $\\ell_1$ graphs, along with a novel algorithm that simultaneously learns principal points and graph structure from data. The algorithm is simple and guarantees convergence. Furthermore, the framework is extended to handle large-scale data. Experimental results on various synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the method's superiority over baselines and its ability to accurately uncover underlying data structure.

title: Perfect Recovery Conditions For Non-Negative Sparse Modeling
Abstract: Sparse modeling has proven effective in various applications like computer vision, machine learning, and pattern recognition. Extensive research has explored theoretical limits and algorithm design for convex relaxations in sparse modeling, but theoretical analyses of non-negative versions remain limited, focusing primarily on noiseless settings or specific statistical noise models. This paper investigates the performance of non-negative sparse modeling in a more general scenario with unknown arbitrary distortion, specifically focusing on non-negativity constrained and L1-penalized least squares. It provides an exact bound for recovering correct signal elements. Two conditions are proposed for ensuring correct signal recovery: minimum coefficient condition (MCC) and nonlinearity vs. subset coherence condition (NSCC). MCC defines the minimum weight for each correct atom present in the signal, while NSCC determines the tolerable deviation from the linear model relative to positive subset coherence (PSC), a novel coherence metric. Rigorous performance guarantees based on these conditions are presented, experimentally verifying their predictive power in a hyperspectral data unmixing application.

title: Window-Object Relationship Guided Representation Learning for Generic Object Detections
Abstract: Current object detection representation learning approaches simplify the relationship between a candidate window and the ground truth bounding box of an object by thresholding their overlap, leading to information loss. This paper recognizes this simplification and proposes a representation learning pipeline that utilizes the relationship as supervision for improving object detection performance. This relationship extends beyond the target object category, encompassing surrounding objects of other categories. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of image regions with multiple contexts and rotations in capturing this relationship during representation learning, effectively handling semantic and visual variations caused by different window-object configurations. Experimental results show a significant improvement in object detection accuracy, achieving a 6.4% increase in mean average precision (mAP) on ILSVRC2014. The proposed single model achieves a 48.6% mAP on the challenging ILSVRC2014 test dataset, surpassing published results. On PASCAL VOC, it outperforms the state-of-the-art Fast RCNN by 3.3% in absolute mAP.

title: Distributed Training of Deep Neural Networks with Theoretical Analysis: Under SSP Setting
Abstract: This paper introduces a distributed approach for training deep neural networks (DNNs) that guarantees theoretical convergence and exhibits excellent empirical scalability, achieving a 6-fold speedup on ImageNet datasets when run with 6 machines. This scheme demonstrates near-optimal scalability in terms of machine count and convergence to the same optima as the undistributed setting. The convergence and scalability of the distributed setting are empirically validated across different datasets (TIMIT and ImageNet) and machine learning tasks (image classification and phoneme extraction). The convergence analysis provides novel insights into this complex learning scheme, including layerwise convergence and probabilistic convergence of weights.
label: AI

title: Reinforcement Control with Hierarchical Backpropagated Adaptive Critics
Abstract: Existing incremental learning methods struggle to achieve reliable credit assignment over a large number of time steps or events, a common scenario in dynamically controlled systems requiring frequent updates for stability and robustness while maintaining long-term action-consequence relationships. This paper explores the learning capabilities of a control architecture comprising two Backpropagated Adaptive Critics (BACs) arranged in a two-level hierarchy with continuous actions. The higher-level BAC updates less frequently than the lower-level one, controlling it to some extent. The response of the lower-level BAC to signals from the higher-level can be either predetermined or learned during the process. A general approach called Response Induction Learning is introduced to address the latter case.
label: AI

title: Speeding Up Distributed Machine Learning Using Codes
Abstract: Codes are widely used in engineering applications to enhance robustness against noise. Distributed machine learning algorithms face various types of noise, including straggler nodes, system failures, and communication bottlenecks. This paper explores how coded solutions can significantly outperform uncoded approaches in such distributed systems. The study focuses on two fundamental building blocks of distributed learning algorithms: matrix multiplication and data shuffling. For matrix multiplication, codes are used to mitigate the impact of stragglers, demonstrating that coded computation can accelerate distributed matrix multiplication by a factor of $\\log n$, where $n$ is the number of homogeneous workers assuming exponentially distributed subtask runtimes. For data shuffling, codes reduce communication bottlenecks by exploiting storage redundancy. The paper shows that coded shuffling reduces communication cost by a factor of $(\\alpha + \\frac{1}{n})\\gamma(n)$ compared to uncoded shuffling, where $\\alpha$ is the fraction of the data matrix cached at each worker, $n$ is the number of workers, and $\\gamma(n)$ is the ratio of unicasting $n$ messages to $n$ users to multicasting a common message to $n$ users. Experiment results corroborate the theoretical gains of the coded algorithms.
label: AI

title: Extremum Seeking-based Iterative Learning Model Predictive Control (ESILC-MPC)
Abstract: This paper addresses a tracking control problem for linear time-invariant systems with model parametric uncertainties, subject to input and state constraints. It applies the modular design concept introduced in Benosman et al. 2014 to solve this problem within the model predictive control (MPC) framework. The paper proposes an MPC with input-to-state stability (ISS) guarantee, complemented by an extremum seeking (ES) algorithm for iterative learning of model uncertainties. The resulting MPC algorithms can be classified as iterative learning control (ILC)-MPC.
label: AI

title: Deep Speech 2: End-to-End Speech Recognition in English and Mandarin
Abstract: This paper demonstrates the effectiveness of an end-to-end deep learning approach for recognizing both English and Mandarin Chinese speech, two vastly different languages. This approach replaces hand-engineered components with neural networks, enabling robust speech recognition across diverse speech types, including noisy environments, accents, and different languages. The paper highlights the crucial role of HPC techniques, resulting in a 7x speedup over previous systems, allowing for faster iteration and optimization of architectures and algorithms. In several cases, the system achieves performance comparable to human transcription when evaluated on standard datasets. Additionally, the paper showcases the system's ability to be deployed inexpensively in an online setting using Batch Dispatch with GPUs, offering low latency at scale.
label: AI

title: Selective Sequential Model Selection
Abstract: Many model selection algorithms produce a path of fits representing a sequence of increasingly complex models. This paper focuses on the problem of choosing the least complex model not falsified by the data, given a model path and the data used to generate it. Building upon the selected-model tests of Fithian et al. (2014), the paper constructs p-values for each step in the path, accounting for the adaptive selection of the model path using the data. In the case of linear regression, two specific tests are proposed: the max-t test for forward stepwise regression, generalizing a proposal by Buja and Brown (2014), and the next-entry test for the lasso. These tests improve upon the power of the saturated-model test of Tibshirani et al. (2014), sometimes significantly. The framework extends beyond linear regression to a broader class of parametric and nonparametric model selection problems. The single-step p-values can be used as inputs for sequential stopping rules to control the familywise error rate or false discovery rate (FDR). The FDR-controlling rules require independence of null p-values, a condition not met by the saturated-model p-values of Tibshirani et al. (2014). This paper derives intuitive and general sufficient conditions for independence and demonstrates that the proposed constructions yield independent p-values.
label: AI

title: Deep Learning for Single and Multi-Session i-Vector Speaker Recognition
Abstract: Deep Learning's (DL) promising performance in speech recognition has spurred its adoption in other speech technology applications, including speaker recognition. This paper presents a hybrid system utilizing Deep Belief Networks (DBN) and Deep Neural Networks (DNN) for discriminatively modeling each target speaker, taking i-vectors as inputs. The system incorporates an impostor selection algorithm and a universal model adaptation process. The paper explores the behavior of DL techniques in both single and multi-session speaker enrollment tasks through experiments conducted in both scenarios. Notably, global model parameters, referred to as universal DBN (UDBN), are normalized before adaptation, facilitating DNN training with multiple hidden layers. Experiments on the NIST SRE 2006 corpus demonstrate that the proposed impostor selection algorithm and UDBN adaptation process enhance the performance of conventional DNNs by 8-20% and 16-20% in terms of EER for single and multi-session tasks, respectively. The proposed architectures outperform baseline systems, achieving up to 17% reduction in EER.
label: AI

title: Gibbs-type Indian buffet processes
Abstract: This paper investigates a class of feature allocation models that generalize the Indian buffet process, parameterized by Gibbs-type random measures. Two existing classes are included as special cases: the original two-parameter Indian buffet process (corresponding to the Dirichlet process) and the stable (or three-parameter) Indian buffet process (corresponding to the Pitman--Yor process). Asymptotic behavior of Gibbs-type partitions, including power laws for the number of latent clusters, translates to similar characteristics for this class of Gibbs-type feature allocation models. Despite containing several distinct subclasses, the properties of Gibbs-type partitions enable the development of a black-box procedure for posterior inference within any subclass. Numerical experiments compare and contrast various subclasses, highlighting the utility of varying power-law behaviors in latent features.
label: AI

title: Breaking the log n barrier on rumor spreading
Abstract: $O(\\log n)$ rounds have long been recognized as an upper bound for rumor spreading using push&pull in the random phone call model (uniform gossip in the complete graph), with a matching lower bound of $\\Omega(\\log n)$. Under this model and with the natural addition of nodes being able to call a partner once they learn its address (e.g., IP address), this paper presents a new distributed, address-oblivious, and robust algorithm that utilizes push&pull with pointer jumping to spread a rumor to all nodes in just $O(\\sqrt{\\log n})$ rounds, with high probability. This algorithm can handle up to $F= O(n/2^{\\sqrt{\\log n}})$ node failures, ensuring that all but $O(F)$ nodes become informed within $O(\\sqrt{\\log n})$ rounds, with high probability.
label: AI

title: Deep Exemplar 2D-3D Detection by Adapting from Real to Rendered Views
Abstract: This paper introduces an end-to-end convolutional neural network (CNN) for 2D-3D exemplar detection. The paper highlights the importance of adapting features from natural images to better align with those of CAD rendered views. This adaptation is achieved by compositing rendered views of textured object models onto natural images, seamlessly integrated into the CNN detection pipeline. This approach leverages recent deep learning advancements to enhance accuracy and speed in 2D-3D exemplar detection. The method is applied to two tasks: instance detection, evaluated on the IKEA dataset, and object category detection, where it outperforms Aubry et al. for "chair" detection on a subset of the Pascal VOC dataset. |||

title: High-Dimensional Gaussian Copula Regression: Adaptive Estimation and Statistical Inference
Abstract: We propose novel adaptive estimation and inference methods for high-dimensional Gaussian copula regression. These methods achieve performance comparable to high-dimensional linear regression, even without knowledge of the marginal transformations. Utilizing a Kendall's tau-based covariance matrix estimator, we introduce an $l_1$ regularized estimator and develop a corresponding de-biased estimator for constructing confidence intervals and conducting hypothesis tests. We establish theoretical properties of these procedures and demonstrate their adaptability to unknown monotone marginal transformations. We also address the prediction of the response for a given set of covariates. Our methods are easy to implement and perform well numerically. We illustrate their application by analyzing the Communities and Crime Unnormalized Data from the UCI Machine Learning Repository.

title: Explaining NonLinear Classification Decisions with Deep Taylor Decomposition
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel methodology for interpreting generic multilayer neural networks by decomposing their classification decisions into contributions from input elements. Unlike traditional methods, which treat deep neural networks (DNNs) as black boxes, our method leverages deep Taylor decomposition to provide interpretability. While we focus on image classification, our approach is applicable to a broad range of input data, learning tasks, and network architectures. The method efficiently utilizes the network's structure by backpropagating explanations from the output to the input layer. We empirically evaluate the proposed method on the MNIST and ILSVRC datasets.
label: AI

title: Hankel Matrices for Weighted Visibly Pushdown Automata
Abstract: Hankel matrices, also known as connection matrices, of word functions and graph parameters find broad applications in automata theory, graph theory, and machine learning. We provide a characterization of real-valued functions on nested words recognized by weighted visibly pushdown automata in terms of Hankel matrices on nested words. This complements C. Mathissen's characterization using weighted monadic second order logic.

title: Learning Discrete Bayesian Networks from Continuous Data
Abstract: Learning Bayesian networks from raw data can provide valuable insights into relationships between variables. However, many Bayesian network structure learning algorithms assume all variables are discrete, requiring continuous variables to be discretized. The choice of discretization policy significantly impacts the accuracy, speed, and interpretability of the resulting models. This paper introduces a principled Bayesian discretization method for continuous variables in Bayesian networks with quadratic complexity. Compared to existing cubic-complexity techniques, our method demonstrates superior performance. We empirically show that it outperforms the established minimum description length algorithm. Additionally, we discuss how to integrate existing methods into the structure learning process to discretize all continuous variables and simultaneously learn Bayesian network structures.

title: Online Gradient Descent in Function Space
Abstract: Numerous problems in machine learning and operations research require optimizing functions with random variables or probability density functions as input, effectively solving optimization problems in infinite-dimensional spaces. Online learning offers advantages for handling streaming data and modeling dynamic environments. This paper extends the celebrated online gradient descent algorithm to Hilbert spaces (function spaces) and analyzes its convergence guarantee. We demonstrate the applicability of our algorithms to several crucial problems.

title: Online Crowdsourcing
Abstract: With the proliferation of internet-based platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk, collecting large datasets of hand-labeled samples from non-experts has become commonplace. The Dawid-Skene algorithm, based on Expectation-Maximization updates, is widely used to infer true labels from noisy crowdsourced labels. However, Dawid-Skene requires all data for each EM iteration, making it infeasible for streaming or large-scale data. This paper presents an online version of the Dawid-Skene algorithm that processes one data frame per iteration. We prove that under mild conditions, the online Dawid-Skene scheme with projection converges to a stationary point of the marginal log-likelihood of the observed data. Our experiments demonstrate that the online Dawid-Skene scheme achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to other methods based on the Dawid-Skene framework.

title: Fast spectral algorithms from sum-of-squares proofs: tensor decomposition and planted sparse vectors
Abstract: We address two machine learning problems: recovering a planted sparse vector in a random linear subspace and decomposing a random low-rank overcomplete 3-tensor. For both problems, the sum-of-squares method provides the best known guarantees. We develop new algorithms inspired by sum-of-squares analysis that achieve comparable or even better guarantees but with significantly faster running times. For the planted sparse vector problem, our algorithm, with nearly linear time complexity, recovers a planted sparse vector with up to constant relative sparsity in a random subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$ of dimension up to $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{n})$. These recovery guarantees match the best known results of Barak, Kelner, and Steurer (STOC 2014) up to logarithmic factors. For tensor decomposition, our algorithm, with time complexity close to linear in the input size (with exponent $\approx 1.086$), recovers a component of a random 3-tensor over $\mathbb{R}^n$ of rank up to $\tilde{\Omega}(n^{4/3})$. The best previous algorithm for this problem, due to Ge and Ma (RANDOM 2015), works up to rank $\tilde{\Omega}(n^{3/2})$ but requires quasipolynomial time.

title: Learning to Point and Count
Abstract: This paper introduces the point-and-count problem as a test case for overcoming the what-and-where deadlock in object detection. Unlike traditional detection tasks, the goal is to discover key salient points to simultaneously localize and count objects. We propose two alternative approaches: one that counts first and then points, and another that reverses the order. Fundamentally, they pivot around whether we address "what" or "where" first. We evaluate their performance on datasets containing multiple instances of the same class, highlighting their potential and synergy. Our experiences reveal key insights explaining the difficulty of this problem compared to classification, including strong data bias and the inability of state-of-the-art convolutional neural networks to robustly handle object scales.

title: Direct Intrinsics: Learning Albedo-Shading Decomposition by Convolutional Regression
Abstract: We introduce a novel approach to intrinsic image decomposition, the task of separating an image into albedo and shading components. Our method, termed direct intrinsics, trains a convolutional neural network (CNN) to directly predict output albedo and shading channels from an input RGB image patch. This departure from classical techniques, which rely on physically-motivated priors and graph-based inference algorithms, benefits from the large-scale synthetic ground-truth of the MPI Sintel dataset. We demonstrate results on both the synthetic images of Sintel and the real images of the classic MIT intrinsic image dataset. On Sintel, direct intrinsics, using only RGB input, outperforms all prior work, including methods using RGB+Depth input. Direct intrinsics also generalizes across modalities, producing reasonable decompositions on the real images of the MIT dataset. Our results suggest that the combination of CNNs and synthetic training data offers a powerful new technique for tackling classic problems in computer vision.

title: Nonparametric Reduced-Rank Regression for Multi-SNP, Multi-Trait Association Mapping
Abstract: Genome-wide association studies are crucial for understanding the genetic basis of disease. However, many complex traits, including personality traits, facial features, and disease subtyping, are inherently high-dimensional, hindering simple association mapping approaches. We developed a nonparametric Bayesian reduced rank regression model for multi-SNP, multi-trait association mapping that does not require specifying the rank of the linear subspace. Through simulations and real data analysis, we demonstrate that our model shares strength across SNPs and correlated traits, improving statistical power in identifying genetic associations. Our model provides an interpretable, SNP-supervised low-dimensional linear projection of the high-dimensional phenotype. Applied to the HapMap phase 3 gene expression QTL study data, we identify pleiotropic expression QTLs that classical univariate tests lack power to detect and that two-step approaches cannot recover. Our Python software, BERRRI, is publicly available at GitHub: https://github.com/ashlee1031/BERRRI.

title: Creating Electronic Books-Chapters for Computers and Tablets Using Easy Java/JavaScript Simulations, EjsS Modeling Tool
Abstract: This paper chronicles my journey in creating electronic book chapters (EPUB3 format) for computers and tablets using Easy Java/JavaScript Simulations (EjsS), a modeling tool. The theoretical foundation of this work lies in learning by doing through dynamic and interactive simulation models. These models offer greater comprehension compared to static printed materials. I began by combining related computer models with supporting texts and illustrations into cohesive chapters. This approach aims to provide teachers and students with tighter support. I developed prototype electronic chapters on Simple Harmonic Motion and Gravity tailored for the Singapore-Cambridge General Certificate of Education Advanced Level (A-level). My goal is to inspire more educators to create interactive and open educational resources for the benefit of all. Prototypes: http://iwant2study.org/ospsg/index.php/interactive-resources/physics/02-newtonian-mechanics/08-gravity/154-e-book-shm http://iwant2study.org/ospsg/index.php/interactive-resources/physics/02-newtonian-mechanics/09-oscillations/153-e-book-gravity and Apple iBook Store, Google Play Book, and Kindle Book.

title: Optimal strategies for the control of autonomous vehicles in data assimilation
Abstract: We propose a method for computing optimal control paths for autonomous vehicles deployed to infer a velocity field. These vehicles are not only advected by the flow but also capable of maintaining a fixed relative speed with controllable direction. The direction serves as the basis for the locally optimal control algorithm presented here, with the objective function derived from the variance trace of the expected posterior distribution. We present results for linear flows near hyperbolic fixed points.
