title: Pseudo-Bayesian Robust PCA: Algorithms and Analyses
Abstract: Robust PCA, commonly employed in computer vision and other applications, aims to reduce the sensitivity of classical PCA to outliers. The core idea is to learn a decomposition of a data matrix into low-rank and sparse components, with the latter representing unwanted outliers. While the resulting optimization problem is typically NP-hard, convex relaxations provide a computationally feasible alternative with theoretical support. However, in practical settings, performance guarantees break down, leading to the development of various non-convex alternatives, including Bayesian-inspired models, to enhance estimation quality. Unfortunately, without additional prior knowledge, none of these methods can significantly expand the critical operational range for achieving exact principal subspace recovery. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel pseudo-Bayesian algorithm that explicitly compensates for design weaknesses in existing non-convex approaches. Our algorithm achieves state-of-the-art performance with a sound analytical foundation and surprisingly outperforms convex matrix completion, even with perfect knowledge of uncorrupted entries.
label: AI

title: The Teaching Dimension of Linear Learners
Abstract: Teaching dimension is a learning theoretic concept that quantifies the minimum training set size required to teach a target model to a learner. Previous research on teaching dimension focused on version-space learners, which maintain all hypotheses consistent with the training data. This approach is not applicable to modern machine learners that select a specific hypothesis through optimization. This paper presents the first known teaching dimensions for ridge regression, support vector machines, and logistic regression. We also identify optimal training sets matching these teaching dimensions. Our approach generalizes to other linear learners.
label: AI

title: Learning Efficient Correlated Equilibria
Abstract: The majority of distributed learning literature focuses on convergence to Nash equilibria. In contrast, correlated equilibria often characterize more efficient collective behavior than even the best Nash equilibrium. However, there are no existing distributed learning algorithms that converge to specific correlated equilibria. This paper proposes such an algorithm, guaranteeing that the agents' collective joint strategy constitutes an efficient correlated equilibrium with high probability. The key to achieving efficient correlated behavior through distributed learning lies in incorporating a common random signal into the learning environment.
label: AI

title: A Large Dataset to Train Convolutional Networks for Disparity, Optical Flow, and Scene Flow Estimation
Abstract: Recent studies have shown that optical flow estimation can be formulated as a supervised learning task and successfully solved using convolutional networks. The training of FlowNet was enabled by a large synthetically generated dataset. This paper extends the concept of optical flow estimation via convolutional networks to disparity and scene flow estimation. To this end, we propose three synthetic stereo video datasets with sufficient realism, variation, and size to effectively train large networks. Our datasets are the first large-scale datasets suitable for training and evaluating scene flow methods. Additionally, we present a convolutional network for real-time disparity estimation that achieves state-of-the-art results. By jointly training a flow and disparity estimation network, we demonstrate the first scene flow estimation using a convolutional network.

title: Joint Time-Frequency Scattering for Audio Classification
Abstract: We introduce the joint time-frequency scattering transform, a time-shift invariant descriptor of time-frequency structure for audio classification. It is obtained by applying a two-dimensional wavelet transform in time and log-frequency to a time-frequency wavelet scalogram. We demonstrate that this descriptor effectively characterizes complex time-frequency phenomena, such as time-varying filters and frequency modulated excitations. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art results for signal reconstruction and phone segment classification on the TIMIT dataset.

title: Clustering by Deep Nearest Neighbor Descent (D-NND): A Density-based Parameter-Insensitive Clustering Method
Abstract: Most density-based clustering methods heavily rely on the accuracy of underlying density estimation. However, density estimation itself is a challenging problem, particularly in determining the kernel bandwidth. A large bandwidth leads to over-smoothed density estimation, resulting in fewer density peaks than true clusters. Conversely, a small bandwidth can lead to under-smoothed density estimation, generating spurious density peaks, or "ripple noise," in the estimated density. This paper proposes a density-based hierarchical clustering method, called Deep Nearest Neighbor Descent (D-NND), that learns the underlying density structure layer by layer and captures the cluster structure concurrently. D-NND effectively avoids over-smoothed density estimation and significantly mitigates the negative effects of under-estimated cases. Overall, D-NND demonstrates not only a strong capability for discovering the underlying cluster structure but also remarkable reliability due to its parameter insensitivity.

title: An Explicit Rate Bound for the Over-Relaxed ADMM
Abstract: The framework of Integral Quadratic Constraints (Lessard et al., 2014) reduces the computation of upper bounds on the convergence rate of various optimization algorithms to semi-definite programming (SDP). Follow-up work by Nishihara et al. (2015) applies this technique to the entire family of over-relaxed Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM). Unfortunately, they only provide an explicit error bound for sufficiently large values of certain problem parameters, leaving the computation for the general case as a numerical optimization problem. This paper provides an exact analytical solution to this SDP, deriving a general and explicit upper bound on the convergence rate of the entire family of over-relaxed ADMM. Furthermore, we demonstrate that it is impossible to extract from this SDP a general bound better than ours. We conclude with numerical illustrations of our result and a comparison between the convergence rate we obtain for the ADMM with known convergence rates for Gradient Descent.

title: Risk Minimization in Structured Prediction using Orbit Loss
Abstract: We introduce a new surrogate loss function called orbit loss within the structured prediction framework, offering significant theoretical and practical advantages. Although not convex, the orbit loss possesses a simple analytical gradient and a simple perceptron-like learning rule. We analyze the new loss theoretically and state a PAC-Bayesian generalization bound. We also prove that the new loss is consistent in the strong sense, meaning the risk achieved by the trained parameters approaches the infimum risk achievable by any linear decoder over the given features. Methods aiming for risk minimization, such as structured ramp loss, structured probit loss, and direct loss minimization, require at least two inference operations per training iteration. In this regard, the orbit loss is more efficient, requiring only one inference operation per iteration while achieving comparable performance. We conclude with an empirical comparison of the proposed loss function to the structured hinge loss, structured ramp loss, structured probit loss, and direct loss minimization method on several benchmark datasets and tasks. |||

title: Discriminative Nonparametric Latent Feature Relational Models with Data Augmentation
Abstract: We propose a discriminative nonparametric latent feature relational model (LFRM) for link prediction, which automatically infers the dimensionality of latent features. This model incorporates prediction loss with probabilistic inference within the RegBayes framework. We introduce distinct regularization parameters for different link types to address imbalance issues in real networks and unify the analysis of both the smooth logistic log-loss and the piecewise linear hinge loss. For nonconjugate posterior inference, we present a simple Gibbs sampler via data augmentation, avoiding restrictive assumptions commonly employed in variational methods. We also develop an approximate sampler using stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics to handle large networks with hundreds of thousands of entities and millions of links, surpassing the capabilities of existing LFRM models. Extensive evaluations on various real networks demonstrate promising performance.

title: Scalable domain adaptation of convolutional neural networks
Abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have become the standard approach for solving a wide range of computer vision problems. While their success is attributed to theoretical and practical advancements in their design, it also relies heavily on the availability of manually labeled visual resources, such as ImageNet. The creation of such datasets is laborious, prompting us to explore alternatives to manual labeling. We hypothesize that new resources are crucial in domains with limited or weak ImageNet coverage, such as tourism photographs. We begin by collecting noisy Flickr images related to tourist points of interest and apply automatic or weakly-supervised reranking techniques to reduce noise. Subsequently, we learn domain-adapted models using a standard CNN architecture and compare their performance to a generic model trained on ImageNet. Experimental validation is conducted on publicly available datasets including Oxford5k, INRIA Holidays, and Div150Cred. Results demonstrate that low-cost domain adaptation improves results compared to generic models and even surpasses strong non-CNN baselines, such as triangulation embedding.

title: How to Discount Deep Reinforcement Learning: Towards New Dynamic Strategies
Abstract: Deep neural networks as function approximators for reinforcement learning tasks have proven highly effective in solving problems of real-world complexity. Building on these results, we investigate the role of the discount factor in the learning process of a deep Q-network (DQN). We empirically show that progressively increasing the discount factor up to its final value can significantly reduce the number of learning steps. When combined with a varying learning rate, this approach empirically outperforms the original DQN in various experiments. We attribute this phenomenon to the instabilities of neural networks when used in an approximate Dynamic Programming setting. Additionally, we discuss the possibility of falling into a local optimum during the learning process, connecting our analysis with the exploration/exploitation dilemma.

title: Jointly Modeling Topics and Intents with Global Order Structure
Abstract: Modeling document structure is crucial for discourse analysis and related applications. This research aims to capture document intent structure by representing documents as a mixture of topic words and rhetorical words. While topics remain relatively consistent throughout a document, the rhetorical functions of sentences typically follow specific orders in discourse. We propose GMM-LDA, a topic modeling-based Bayesian unsupervised model, to analyze document intent structure while incorporating order information. Our model is flexible, enabling the combination of annotations and supervised learning. Moreover, entropic regularization can be introduced to model the significant divergence between topics and intents. We perform experiments in both unsupervised and supervised settings, demonstrating the superiority of our model over several state-of-the-art baselines.

title: A Novel Approach to Distributed Multi-Class SVM
Abstract: With data sizes constantly expanding and classical machine learning algorithms requiring increasingly more computational time and storage space, the need for distributed computation and memory management across multiple computers has become evident. While considerable effort has been dedicated to developing distributed binary SVM algorithms and multi-class SVM algorithms individually, the field of multi-class distributed SVMs remains largely unexplored. This research presents a novel algorithm that implements the Support Vector Machine on a multi-class dataset, achieving efficiency in a distributed environment, specifically Hadoop. The algorithm recursively divides the dataset in half, computing the optimal Support Vector Machine for each half during the training phase, similar to a divide and conquer approach. During testing, this structure effectively reduces prediction time. Our algorithm demonstrates improved computation time during the prediction phase compared to traditional sequential SVM methods (One vs. One, One vs. Rest) and outperforms them as the dataset size grows. This approach also achieves higher classification accuracy than traditional multi-class algorithms.

title: Learning population and subject-specific brain connectivity networks via Mixed Neighborhood Selection
Abstract: Gaussian graphical models are frequently used in neuroimaging data analysis to model statistical dependencies between spatially remote brain regions, known as functional connectivity. Data is typically collected across a cohort of subjects, with scientific objectives focusing on estimating population and subject-specific graphical models. A third objective, often overlooked, involves quantifying inter-subject variability to identify regions or sub-networks exhibiting heterogeneity across subjects. This information is crucial for a comprehensive understanding of the human connectome. We propose Mixed Neighborhood Selection to simultaneously address all three objectives. By reformulating covariance selection as a neighborhood selection problem, we efficiently learn the topology of each node. We introduce an additional mixed effect component to neighborhood selection, enabling the simultaneous estimation of a graphical model for the population of subjects and for each individual subject. The proposed method is empirically validated through simulations and applied to resting-state data for healthy subjects obtained from the ABIDE consortium.

title: Fast Optimization Algorithm on Riemannian Manifolds and Its Application in Low-Rank Representation
Abstract: This paper addresses the problem of optimizing a class of composite functions on Riemannian manifolds and proposes a new first-order optimization algorithm (FOA) with a fast convergence rate. Theoretical analysis proves that FOA exhibits quadratic convergence. Experiments on the matrix completion task demonstrate that FOA outperforms other first-order optimization methods on Riemannian manifolds. A fast subspace pursuit method based on FOA is proposed to solve the low-rank representation model based on the augmented Lagrange method on the low rank matrix variety. Experimental results on synthetic and real datasets highlight the superior performance of both FOA and SP-RPRG(ALM) in terms of faster convergence and higher accuracy.

title: Thinking Required
Abstract: The possibility of a single general-purpose learning algorithm that explains the principles of its operation exists. This theory assumes an initial rough architecture and a small library of simple innate circuits prewired at birth, proposing that all significant mental algorithms are learned. This paper reviews and lists the ingredients of such an algorithm from architectural and functional perspectives, based on current understanding and observations.

title: Rademacher Complexity of the Restricted Boltzmann Machine
Abstract: Boltzmann machines, as fundamental building blocks of deep belief networks and deep Boltzmann machines, are widely used in the deep learning community, achieving significant success. However, theoretical understanding of many aspects of Boltzmann machines remains unclear. This paper investigates the Rademacher complexity of both the asymptotic restricted Boltzmann machine and its practical implementation with the single-step contrastive divergence (CD-1) procedure. Our results reveal that the practical implementation training procedure indeed increases the Rademacher complexity of restricted Boltzmann machines. A promising research direction might involve investigating the VC dimension of the compositional function used in the CD-1 procedure.

title: Gauss quadrature for matrix inverse forms with applications
Abstract: We present a framework for accelerating a spectrum of machine learning algorithms requiring the computation of bilinear inverse forms $u^\\top A^{-1}u$, where $A$ is a positive definite matrix and $u$ is a given vector. Our framework, based on Gauss-type quadrature, readily scales to large, sparse matrices. Moreover, it allows for the retrospective computation of lower and upper bounds on $u^\\top A^{-1}u$, further accelerating various algorithms. We prove that these bounds iteratively tighten and converge at a linear (geometric) rate. To our knowledge, this is the first work to demonstrate these key properties of Gauss-type quadrature, a well-established and extensively studied topic. We illustrate the empirical implications of our results by using quadrature to accelerate machine learning tasks involving determinantal point processes and submodular optimization, observing significant speedups in multiple instances.

title: A Simple and Practical Linear Algebra Library Interface with Static Size Checking
Abstract: Linear algebra, a major field of numerical computation, finds wide applications. Most linear algebra libraries (across various programming languages) lack static guarantees for the consistency of vector and matrix dimensions, leading to runtime errors. While advanced type systems, particularly dependent types on natural numbers, can ensure consistency among the sizes of collections like lists and arrays, these systems typically require substantial modifications to existing languages and application programs or complex type-level programming. We have developed a linear algebra library interface that verifies the consistency (regarding dimensions) of matrix operations using generative phantom types, implemented through standard ML types and module systems. To assess its usability, we ported a practical machine learning library from a traditional linear algebra library. We discovered that most porting changes could be made mechanically, with human-required modifications being minor.

title: Improving Type Error Messages in OCaml
Abstract: Cryptic type error messages pose a major obstacle to learning OCaml or other ML-based languages. In many cases, interpreting error messages necessitates a precise model of the type inference algorithm. The problem of improving type error messages in ML has been extensively researched over the past two decades, with many different strategies explored. The challenge lies not only in producing error messages that are both concise and systematically useful to programmers but also in handling a complete programming language and efficiently managing large-sized programs. This work presents a modification to the traditional ML type inference algorithm implemented in OCaml, significantly reducing the left-to-right bias. This modification enables more helpful error messages for programmers. Our algorithm remains fully predictable and continues to produce concise error messages that guide programmers towards fixing the code. We implemented this approach as a patch to the OCaml compiler, requiring just a few hundred lines of code. We believe that this patch will benefit beginners and experienced programmers developing large-scale OCaml programs alike.

title: In the Age of Web: Typed Functional-First Programming Revisited
Abstract: Most programming languages were designed before the advent of the web. This is significant because the web challenges many assumptions taken for granted by typed functional language designers. For instance, programs do not operate in a closed world but must interact with changing and potentially unreliable services and data sources. Communication is often asynchronous or event-driven, and programs need to interoperate with untyped environments. This paper examines how the F# language and libraries address the challenges posed by the web. Technically, this involves using type providers for integration with external information sources and untyped environments, lightweight meta-programming for targeting JavaScript, and computation expressions for writing asynchronous code. The holistic perspective is more important than individual features. We use a practical case study as a starting point to explore how the F# language and libraries approach web-related challenges. While the specific lessons learned may be less interesting, our attempt to uncover hidden assumptions that no longer hold in the web era is significant.

title: Sparsifying Neural Network Connections for Face Recognition
Abstract: This paper proposes learning high-performance deep ConvNets with sparse neural connections, referred to as sparse ConvNets, for face recognition. Sparse ConvNets are learned iteratively, sparsifying one additional layer at a time and retraining the entire model using initial weights from previous iterations. One key finding is that directly training a sparse ConvNet from scratch fails to find good solutions for face recognition. Initializing a sparser model with a previously learned denser model is critical to continuing learning effective features for face recognition. This paper also introduces a new neural correlation-based weight selection criterion and empirically verifies its effectiveness in selecting informative connections from previously learned models during each iteration. With a moderately sparse structure (26%-76% of weights in the dense model), the proposed sparse ConvNet model significantly improves the face recognition performance of the previous state-of-the-art DeepID2+ models given the same training data while maintaining the performance of the baseline model with only 12% of the original parameters.

title: Using SVM to pre-classify government purchases
Abstract: The Brazilian government frequently misclassifies the goods it purchases, making it difficult to audit government expenditures. We cannot determine whether the price paid for a ballpoint pen (code #7510) is reasonable if the pen is misclassified as a technical drawing pen (code #6675) or any other good. This paper shows how machine learning can reduce misclassification. We trained a support vector machine (SVM) classifier that takes a product description as input and returns the most likely category codes as output. The classifier was trained using 20 million goods purchased by the Brazilian government between 1999-04-01 and 2015-04-02. In 83.3% of cases, the correct category code was among the three most likely codes identified by the classifier. We used the trained classifier to develop a web app that may help the government reduce misclassification. The code is open-sourced on GitHub, allowing anyone to use and modify it.

title: Recognition from Hand Cameras
Abstract: We revisit the study of a wrist-mounted camera system (referred to as HandCam) for recognizing hand activities. HandCam offers two unique advantages compared to egocentric systems (referred to as HeadCam): (1) it eliminates the need for hand detection, and (2) it consistently observes hand activities. Leveraging these properties, we propose a deep-learning-based method to recognize hand states (free vs. active hands, hand gestures, object categories) and discover object categories. Additionally, we introduce a novel two-stream deep network to further exploit both HandCam and HeadCam. We have collected a new synchronized HandCam and HeadCam dataset comprising 20 videos captured in three scenes for hand states recognition. Experiments demonstrate that our HandCam system consistently outperforms a deep-learning-based HeadCam method (with estimated manipulation regions) and a dense-trajectory-based HeadCam method in all tasks. We also show that HandCam videos captured by different users can be easily aligned to improve free vs. active recognition accuracy (3.3% improvement) in cross-scene use cases. Moreover, we observe that fine-tuning Convolutional Neural Networks consistently improves accuracy. Finally, our novel two-stream deep network combining HandCam and HeadCam features achieves the best performance in four out of five tasks. With more data, we believe a joint HandCam and HeadCam system can robustly log hand states in daily life.

title: Driverseat: Crowdstrapping Learning Tasks for Autonomous Driving
Abstract: While emerging deep-learning systems have surpassed knowledge-based approaches in many tasks, their application to detection tasks for autonomous technologies remains an open area for scientific research. Two major developmental bottlenecks exist: the unavailability of comprehensively labeled datasets and expressive evaluation strategies. Approaches for labeling datasets have relied on intensive hand-engineering, and strategies for evaluating learning systems have failed to identify failure-case scenarios. Human intelligence offers an untapped approach to overcome these bottlenecks. This paper introduces Driverseat, a technology for embedding crowds around learning systems for autonomous driving. Driverseat utilizes crowd contributions to (a) collect complex 3D labels and (b) tag diverse scenarios for ready evaluation of learning systems. We demonstrate how Driverseat can crowdstrap a convolutional neural network on the lane-detection task. More generally, crowdstrapping introduces a valuable paradigm for any technology that benefits from leveraging the powerful combination of human and computer intelligence.

title: Rank Pooling for Action Recognition
Abstract: We propose a function-based temporal pooling method that captures the latent structure of video sequence data, such as how frame-level features evolve over time in a video. We show how the parameters of a function fitted to the video data can serve as a robust new video representation. As a specific example, we learn a pooling function via ranking machines. By learning to rank the frame-level features of a video chronologically, we obtain a new representation that captures the video-wide temporal dynamics, suitable for action recognition. Beyond ranking functions, we explore different parametric models that can also explain temporal changes in videos. The proposed functional pooling methods, particularly rank pooling, are easy to interpret and implement, fast to compute, and effective in recognizing a wide variety of actions. We evaluate our method on various benchmarks for generic action, fine-grained action, and gesture recognition. Results show that rank pooling provides an absolute improvement of 7-10 over the average pooling baseline. Additionally, rank pooling is compatible with and complementary to various appearance and local motion-based methods and features, such as improved trajectories and deep learning features.

title: Explaining reviews and ratings with PACO: Poisson Additive Co-Clustering
Abstract: Understanding a user's motivations provides valuable information beyond simply recommending items. This often involves analyzing both ratings and review texts, as the latter explicitly expresses reasoning for specific preferences. Matrix factorization approaches to recommendation result in large, complex models that are difficult to interpret and provide recommendations that are hard to explain to users. This paper tackles this problem through succinct additive co-clustering. We develop a novel Bayesian technique for summing co-clusterings of Poisson distributions. Using this technique, we propose a new Bayesian model for joint collaborative filtering of ratings and text reviews through a sum of simple co-clusterings. The simple structure of our model yields easily interpretable recommendations. Despite its simplicity, our model outperforms competitors in terms of predicting ratings with reviews.
label: AI

title: Linear Readout of Object Manifolds
Abstract: Objects are represented in sensory systems by continuous manifolds due to the sensitivity of neuronal responses to changes in physical features like location, orientation, and intensity. What makes certain sensory representations better suited for invariant decoding of objects by downstream networks? We present a theory that characterizes the ability of a linear readout network, the perceptron, to classify objects from variable neural responses. We demonstrate how the readout perceptron capacity depends on the dimensionality, size, and shape of the object manifolds in its input neural representation.

title: SentiBench - a benchmark comparison of state-of-the-practice sentiment analysis methods
Abstract: Sentiment analysis is a hot topic, with numerous research papers, startups, and products emerging in recent years. Despite the widespread popularity of various methods, there is no clear consensus on which approach is best for identifying message polarity (positive or negative). This research addresses this gap by providing a comprehensive benchmark comparison of 24 widely used sentiment analysis methods. The evaluation is based on 18 labeled datasets, covering messages from various sources like social networks, reviews, and news articles. The results reveal significant variations in prediction performance across datasets, highlighting the importance of understanding the strengths and limitations of different methods. To facilitate further research, the methods' code and datasets are made publicly available through an open API for accessing and comparing sentence-level sentiment analysis techniques.

title: PatchBatch: a Batch Augmented Loss for Optical Flow
Abstract: We propose a novel pipeline for optical flow computation utilizing Deep Learning techniques. Our approach leverages a Siamese CNN to independently compute descriptors for both images in parallel. These descriptors are then efficiently compared using the L2 norm, eliminating the need for network processing of patch pairs. The method's success hinges on an innovative loss function that calculates higher moments of the loss distributions for each training batch. When combined with an Approximate Nearest Neighbor patch matching method and a flow interpolation technique, our pipeline achieves state-of-the-art performance on the most challenging and competitive optical flow benchmarks.

title: Large Scale Distributed Semi-Supervised Learning Using Streaming Approximation
Abstract: Traditional graph-based semi-supervised learning (SSL) methods, while widely used, struggle with massive datasets and large label scenarios due to their linear scaling with the number of edges and distinct labels. To address this issue, recent work has explored sketch-based methods to approximate the label distribution per node, achieving space reduction under certain conditions. This paper introduces a novel streaming graph-based SSL approximation that captures label distribution sparsity, ensuring accurate label propagation and further reducing space complexity per node to O(1). A distributed version of the algorithm is also presented, which scales well to large datasets. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed method compared to existing state-of-the-art algorithms, while significantly reducing memory footprint. Additionally, we explore different graph construction mechanisms for natural language applications and propose a robust graph augmentation strategy trained using unsupervised deep learning architectures, resulting in further significant quality gains.

title: Similarity Learning via Adaptive Regression and Its Application to Image Retrieval
Abstract: We investigate similarity learning and its application to image retrieval with large-scale data. Image pair similarity can be measured using the distances between their high-dimensional representations. Distance metric learning is often used to learn the appropriate similarity; however, it requires the learned metric to be a PSD matrix, which is computationally expensive and unnecessary for retrieval ranking. In contrast, the bilinear model offers greater flexibility for large-scale image retrieval tasks, leading us to adopt it for learning a matrix to estimate pairwise similarities within a regression framework. By adaptively updating the target matrix in regression, we can mimic the hinge loss, better suited for similarity learning. Although the regression problem has a closed-form solution, its computational cost can be substantial due to the large number of images and high-dimensional image features. We address the first challenge by compressing data using a randomized algorithm with theoretical guarantees. For the high-dimensional issue, we leverage a low-rank assumption and apply an alternating method to obtain a partial matrix with a global optimal solution. Empirical studies on real-world image datasets (Caltech and ImageNet) demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed method.

title: Vanishing point attracts gaze in free-viewing and visual search tasks
Abstract: To investigate the role of vanishing point (VP) in gaze guidance, we conducted two experiments. In the first experiment, we recorded fixations of 10 participants viewing 532 images, 319 of which contained a VP. We found significantly higher fixations at the VP location compared to random locations. To account for saliency, we trained a combined model of bottom-up saliency and VP, achieving significantly higher performance compared to the original saliency model and VP-only model. In the second experiment, we tasked 14 participants with searching for a target character on a 3x3 grid overlayed on an image. Participants were significantly faster and more accurate when the target was located within the VP cell. These findings support the hypothesis that vanishing point, similar to faces, text, and gaze direction, attracts attention in free-viewing and visual search.

title: Generating News Headlines with Recurrent Neural Networks
Abstract: This paper presents an encoder-decoder recurrent neural network with LSTM units and attention for generating headlines from news articles. Our model demonstrates effectiveness in concisely paraphrasing news articles. We further analyze how the network decides which input words to focus on, specifically identifying the function of neurons in a simplified attention mechanism. Interestingly, our simplified attention mechanism outperforms the more complex one on a held-out set of articles.

title: Variance Reduction for Distributed Stochastic Gradient Descent
Abstract: Variance reduction (VR) methods enhance the performance of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) by enabling larger, constant stepsizes and preserving linear convergence rates. However, current VR-SGD methods require either high memory usage or exact gradient computation at the end of each epoch, limiting their practicality in distributed settings. This paper introduces VR-lite, a variance reduction method that avoids full gradient computations or extra storage. We explore distributed synchronous and asynchronous variants that are scalable and stable with low communication frequency. Empirical comparisons demonstrate the favorable performance of our proposed algorithms compared to other stochastic optimization methods.

title: Stabilizing the unstable output of persistent homology computations
Abstract: We propose a general technique for extracting a larger set of stable information from persistent homology computations. Persistent homology is typically viewed as a procedure that generates a persistence diagram from a filtered complex. While this procedure is stable, other valuable information produced during the computation is unstable. This instability affects aspects like the correspondence between diagram points and simplices, and the diagram's sensitivity to thresholding procedures. We address these issues by representing the unstable information as real-valued functions that, while discontinuous, are measurable. Convolving these functions with a suitable function produces a Lipschitz function, which can be estimated by perturbing the input and averaging the output. This approach yields stable functions, demonstrated in examples including the stable localization of a persistent homology generator from brain imaging data.
label: AI

title: Deep Attention Recurrent Q-Network
Abstract: A deep learning approach to reinforcement learning, known as Deep Q-Network (DQN), enabled a general learner to train on visual input and play various arcade games at human and superhuman levels. We extend DQN by incorporating "soft" and "hard" attention mechanisms. Tests of the proposed Deep Attention Recurrent Q-Network (DARQN) algorithm on multiple Atari 2600 games show superior performance compared to DQN. The built-in attention mechanisms allow direct online monitoring of the training process by highlighting the regions of the game screen that the agent focuses on when making decisions.

title: Maximum Entropy Binary Encoding for Face Template Protection
Abstract: This paper presents a framework for secure identification using deep neural networks, specifically applied to template protection for face authentication. Deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are used to learn a mapping from face images to maximum entropy binary (MEB) codes. This mapping is robust enough to handle exact matching, ensuring the same code for new samples of a user as the code assigned during training. These codes are then hashed using a random oracle model (like SHA-512) to generate protected face templates, analogous to text-based password protection. The algorithm makes no unrealistic assumptions and offers high template security, cancelability, and state-of-the-art matching performance. The approach's effectiveness is demonstrated on CMU-PIE, Extended Yale B, and Multi-PIE face databases, achieving high (~95%) genuine accept rates (GAR) at zero false accept rate (FAR) with up to 1024 bits of template security.

title: A Shapley Value Solution to Game Theoretic-based Feature Reduction in False Alarm Detection
Abstract: False alarms in intensive care units are a major concern, leading to care disruption, sleep deprivation, and caregiver insensitivity. While methods exist to suppress false alarms by improving signal quality and sensor accuracy, intrinsic correlations among extracted features limit the performance of most data mining techniques. These techniques often discard predictors with low individual impact, potentially overlooking strong discriminatory power when combined with others. We propose a model based on coalition game theory to account for inter-feature dependencies in determining salient predictors for false alarm detection. This approach results in improved classification accuracy, as demonstrated by simulation results using PhysionNet's MIMIC II database.

title: Stochastic Collapsed Variational Inference for Sequential Data
Abstract: Stochastic variational inference for collapsed models has proven successful in large-scale topic modeling. This paper proposes a stochastic collapsed variational inference algorithm for the sequential data setting. Our algorithm is applicable to both finite hidden Markov models and hierarchical Dirichlet process hidden Markov models, as well as any datasets generated by emission distributions in the exponential family. Experiments on two discrete datasets demonstrate the efficiency and accuracy advantages of our inference compared to its uncollapsed version.

title: Stochastic Collapsed Variational Inference for Hidden Markov Models
Abstract: Stochastic variational inference for collapsed models has recently shown promise in large-scale topic modeling. This paper introduces a stochastic collapsed variational inference algorithm for hidden Markov models in a sequential data setting. We break down the long Markov chain of a collapsed hidden Markov Model into shorter subchains and propose a novel sum-product algorithm to update subchain posteriors, considering boundary transitions due to sequential dependencies. Our experiments on two discrete datasets demonstrate that our collapsed algorithm scales to very large datasets, is memory efficient, and significantly more accurate than existing uncollapsed algorithms.

title: Approximated and User Steerable tSNE for Progressive Visual Analytics
Abstract: Progressive Visual Analytics enhances interactivity in analytics techniques through visualization and interaction with intermediate results. Dimensionality reduction is a key method for data analysis, producing 2D embeddings for visualization and analysis. t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (tSNE) is suitable for visualizing high-dimensional data, but its slow initialization limits its application in Progressive Visual Analytics. We introduce a controllable tSNE approximation (A-tSNE) that balances speed and accuracy, enabling interactive data exploration. Real-time visualization techniques, including a density-based solution and a Magic Lens, provide feedback on the approximation level. This feedback allows users to refine local areas and control the approximation level during analysis. Our technique is demonstrated with various datasets, showcasing its effectiveness for interactive data analysis in research and real-time analysis of high-dimensional streams.

title: A Deep Structured Model with Radius-Margin Bound for 3D Human Activity Recognition
Abstract: Understanding human activity is challenging even with advanced 3D/depth sensors. This work proposes a novel deep structured model that adaptively decomposes activity instances into temporal parts using convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Our model advances traditional deep learning approaches by incorporating latent temporal structure, accounting for variations in human activities. We utilize latent variables to decompose the input activity into temporally segmented sub-activities, feeding them into the parts of the deep architecture. We further incorporate a radius-margin bound as a regularization term to enhance generalization performance for classification. We propose a principled learning algorithm that iteratively discovers optimal latent variables, updates classifiers based on generated features, and updates the parameters of multi-layer neural networks. Experiments on complex human activity recognition scenarios validate our approach, demonstrating superior performance compared to other state-of-the-art methods.

title: Unsupervised comparable corpora preparation and exploration for bi-lingual translation equivalents
Abstract: The multilingual nature of the world makes translation essential. While human-constructed parallel dictionaries are widely available, they are limited and insufficient for high-quality translation due to out-of-vocabulary words and neologisms. This motivates the use of statistical translation systems, but they are reliant on the quantity and quality of training data, which is scarce for many languages and text domains. This research presents improvements to existing comparable corpora mining methodologies by re-implementing comparison algorithms (using the Needleman-Wunch algorithm), introducing a tuning script, and enhancing computation time through GPU acceleration. Experiments are conducted on bilingual data extracted from Wikipedia across various domains. Additional cross-lingual comparison heuristics are introduced for Wikipedia itself. These modifications positively impact the quality and quantity of mined data, leading to improved translation quality.

title: PJAIT Systems for the IWSLT 2015 Evaluation Campaign Enhanced by Comparable Corpora
Abstract: This paper aims to enhance Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) systems for diverse language pairs: Czech-English, Vietnamese-English, French-English, and German-English. We achieved this by training translation models, adapting training settings for each language pair, and obtaining comparable corpora for our SMT systems. Innovative tools and data adaptation techniques were employed, utilizing the TED parallel text corpora for the IWSLT 2015 evaluation campaign for language model training, system development, tuning, and testing. We also prepared Wikipedia-based comparable corpora for our SMT system, compliant with the IWSLT 2015 evaluation guidelines. We explored domain adaptation techniques, symmetrized word alignment models, unsupervised transliteration models, and the KenLM language modeling tool. Experiments were conducted to evaluate the effects of different preparations on translation results using BLEU, NIST, and TER metrics. Our results demonstrate a positive impact on SMT quality.

title: Hierarchical Sparse Modeling: A Choice of Two Group Lasso Formulations
Abstract: Demanding sparsity in estimated models is common practice in statistics. Often, we need to ensure that the sparsity patterns obtained adhere to problem-specific constraints. Hierarchical sparse modeling (HSM) refers to situations where these constraints specify that one set of parameters must be set to zero whenever another is set to zero. Numerous papers have developed convex regularizers for this sparsity structure, which arises in various statistical fields like interaction modeling, time series analysis, and covariance estimation. This paper observes that these methods fall into two frameworks: group lasso (GL) and latent overlapping group lasso (LOG). We provide a comparative analysis of these frameworks for HSM, examining their statistical properties and computational efficiency. We highlight GL's more aggressive parameter shrinkage deep in the hierarchy, a property not shared by LOG. Computationally, we introduce a finite-step algorithm that exactly solves the proximal operator of LOG for a simple HSM structure. This algorithm is then exploited to develop a novel path-based block coordinate descent scheme for general HSM structures, significantly improving the computational performance of LOG. Finally, we compare the two methods in the context of covariance estimation, introducing a new sparsely-banded estimator using LOG, which achieves the statistical advantages of an existing GL-based method while being simpler and more efficient.

title: Risk-Constrained Reinforcement Learning with Percentile Risk Criteria
Abstract: Many sequential decision-making problems focus on minimizing expected cumulative cost while considering risk, particularly events with low probability and high consequences. This paper presents efficient reinforcement learning algorithms for risk-constrained Markov decision processes (MDPs), where risk is represented via a chance constraint or a constraint on the conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) of the cumulative cost. We refer to these problems as percentile risk-constrained MDPs. We derive a formula for computing the gradient of the Lagrangian function for percentile risk-constrained MDPs. Subsequently, we devise policy gradient and actor-critic algorithms that estimate this gradient, update the policy in the descent direction, and update the Lagrange multiplier in the ascent direction. Convergence to locally optimal policies is proven for these algorithms. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithms in an optimal stopping problem and an online marketing application.

title: Guarding against Spurious Discoveries in High Dimensions
Abstract: Numerous data mining and statistical machine learning algorithms have been developed to select a subset of covariates associated with a response variable. In high-dimensional data analysis, spurious discoveries can easily arise due to the vast number of possible selections. This paper defines a measure of goodness of spurious fit, which quantifies how well a response variable can be fitted by an optimally selected subset of covariates under the null model. We propose a simple and effective LAMM algorithm to compute this measure. This measure coincides with the maximum spurious correlation for linear models and can be viewed as a generalized maximum spurious correlation. We derive the asymptotic distribution of this goodness of spurious fit for generalized linear models and L1 regression. This distribution depends on sample size, ambient dimension, number of variables used in the fit, and covariance information. It can be consistently estimated using multiplier bootstrapping and serves as a benchmark to guard against spurious discoveries. It can also be applied to model selection, considering only candidate models with goodness of fit better than those achieved by spurious fits. The theory and method are illustrated through simulated examples and an application to binary outcomes from German Neuroblastoma Trials. |||

title: A Package for the Automated Classification of Periodic Variable Stars
Abstract: This paper introduces a machine learning tool designed for classifying periodic variable stars. The tool can analyze any single-band optical light curve with at least several tens of observations, spanning durations from weeks to years, and with varying time sampling. The model was trained on light curves of periodic variable stars from OGLE and EROS-2, using 16 features extracted from the light curves (e.g., period, skewness, Fourier amplitude ratio). The model categorizes light curves into one of seven superclasses (Delta Scuti, RR Lyrae, Cepheid, Type II Cepheid, eclipsing binary, long-period variable, non-variable) and further distinguishes subclasses within these (e.g., ab, c, d, and e types for RR Lyraes). When trained for superclass classification, the model achieved 0.98 recall and precision on an independent validation dataset. When trained for subclass classification, it achieved 0.81 recall and precision.  To evaluate the subclass model's performance, it was applied to MACHO, LINEAR, and ASAS periodic variables, yielding recall/precision scores of 0.92/0.98, 0.89/0.96, and 0.84/0.88, respectively. The subclass model was also tested on Hipparcos periodic variable stars of other variability types absent from the training set, revealing the impact of these types on the target class classification performance. The study investigated the influence of data point count and observation duration on performance. The results indicate that recall and precision remain largely consistent when the data point count exceeds 80 and the observation duration surpasses a few weeks. The classifier software for the subclass model is accessible through the GitHub repository (https://goo.gl/xmFO6Q).

title: Creation of a Deep Convolutional Auto-Encoder in Caffe
Abstract: This paper details the development of a deep (stacked) convolutional auto-encoder within the Caffe deep learning framework. It outlines the principles employed in its creation. This convolutional auto-encoder model currently lacks pooling/unpooling layers. The research findings demonstrate that the model achieves comparable accuracy in dimensionality reduction compared to a classic auto-encoder when applied to the MNIST dataset.

title: Extracting Biomolecular Interactions Using Semantic Parsing of Biomedical Text
Abstract: This paper presents a significant advancement in biomolecular interaction extraction, achieved through three key contributions: (i) The paper demonstrates that deep, Abstract Meaning Representations (AMR) significantly enhance the accuracy of a biomolecular interaction extraction system compared to a baseline that relies solely on surface- and syntax-based features; (ii) In contrast to previous sentence-by-sentence approaches, this framework extends to consistently predict across sets of sentences (documents); (iii) The study further modifies and expands a graph kernel learning framework to enable the concurrent utilization of automatically induced AMR (semantic) and dependency structure (syntactic) representations. Experiments indicate that this approach results in more robust interaction extraction systems, particularly in environments with significant mismatch between training and test conditions.
label: AI

title: State of the Art Control of Atari Games Using Shallow Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: The Deep Q-Networks (DQN) algorithm, a pioneering combination of deep neural networks and reinforcement learning, has gained significant attention for its success in the Arcade Learning Environment (ALE). This challenging framework, consisting of numerous Atari 2600 games, evaluates general competency in artificial intelligence. DQN achieved remarkable results, surpassing previous approaches, highlighting its robust and general capability in learning effective representations. This paper aims to unravel the principles underlying DQN's impressive performance and contextualize its success. It systematically evaluates the importance of key representational biases encoded by DQN's network through the introduction of simple linear representations incorporating these concepts. By incorporating these characteristics, the study obtains a computationally practical feature set that achieves performance comparable to DQN in the ALE. This not only provides insights into DQN's strengths and weaknesses, but also introduces a generic representation for the ALE, significantly reducing the burden of learning a representation for each game. Additionally, it provides a straightforward and reproducible benchmark for comparison with future work in the ALE.

title: Reuse of Neural Modules for General Video Game Playing
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to knowledge transfer, where an agent controlled by a neural network dynamically adapts its reuse of existing networks as it learns in a new domain. Networks trained for a new domain can improve their performance by selectively routing activation through previously learned neural structures, regardless of their origin or purpose. The paper introduces a neuroevolution implementation of this approach, showcasing its application in high-dimensional sequential decision-making domains. This approach surpasses previous methods for neural transfer in reinforcement learning due to its domain-agnostic nature and lack of prior assumptions about task relatedness or mappings. The method is analyzed in a stochastic version of the Arcade Learning Environment, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing performance in some of the more complex Atari 2600 games. The success of transfer is shown to be predictable based on a high-level characterization of game dynamics.
label: AI

title: Learning the Semantics of Manipulation Action
Abstract: This paper introduces a formal computational framework for modeling manipulation actions. This formalism provides semantic meaning to manipulation actions and finds applications in both observing and understanding human manipulation actions as well as executing them using robotic mechanisms (e.g., a humanoid robot). The framework is based on Combinatory Categorial Grammar. Its objective is to: (1) represent manipulation actions with both syntactic and semantic components, utilizing lambda-calculus for the semantic part; (2) enable a probabilistic semantic parsing schema to learn the lambda-calculus representation of manipulation actions from an annotated action corpus of videos; (3) utilize (1) and (2) to develop a system that visually observes manipulation actions, understands their meaning, and can reason beyond observations using propositional logic and axiom schemata. Experiments conducted on a publicly available large manipulation action dataset validate the theoretical framework and its implementation.

title: Neuron's Eye View: Inferring Features of Complex Stimuli from Neural Responses
Abstract: Traditional neural encoding experiments focus on a limited set of features in the world, such as contrast and luminance for vision or pitch and intensity for sound, using stimuli systematically varied along these dimensions. Analysis typically relies on regression models with experimenter-controlled features as predictors and spike counts or firing rates as responses. This approach requires prior knowledge of the features encoded by a given neuron population. However, in complex domains like social interaction or natural movement, the relevant feature space is poorly understood, leading to potential confirmation bias if arbitrary features are chosen. This paper presents a Bayesian model for exploratory data analysis capable of automatically identifying features in unstructured stimuli solely based on neuronal responses. The approach distinguishes itself within latent state space models of neural activity by assuming that neuron firing rates are sensitive to multiple discrete time-varying features tied to the stimulus, each exhibiting Markov (or semi-Markov) dynamics. This model analyzes neural activity as driven by multiple simultaneous stimulus features rather than intrinsic neural dynamics. The paper derives a fast variational Bayesian inference algorithm and demonstrates its ability to accurately recover hidden features in synthetic data and ground-truth stimulus features in a prototypical neural dataset. To illustrate its utility, the algorithm is applied to cluster neural responses, successfully recovering features corresponding to monkeys and faces in an image set.
label: AI

title: Max-Pooling Dropout for Regularization of Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: Dropout, increasingly used in deep learning, is known to be effective in fully-connected layers of deep convolutional neural networks. However, its impact on pooling layers remains unclear. This paper demonstrates that max-pooling dropout is equivalent to randomly selecting activation based on a multinomial distribution during training. Based on this insight, the paper advocates employing probabilistic weighted pooling instead of the commonly used max-pooling, acting as model averaging during testing. Empirical evidence supports the superiority of probabilistic weighted pooling. The paper also compares max-pooling dropout and stochastic pooling, both introducing stochasticity based on multinomial distributions at the pooling stage.
label: AI

title: Locally Adaptive Translation for Knowledge Graph Embedding
Abstract: Knowledge graph embedding aims to represent entities and relations within a large-scale knowledge graph as elements in a continuous vector space. Existing methods, such as TransE and TransH, learn embedding representations by defining a global margin-based loss function over the data. However, the optimal loss function is determined through experiments with parameters explored within a closed set of candidates. Moreover, embeddings across knowledge graphs with different entities and relations share the same set of candidate loss functions, neglecting the locality of both graphs. This limits the performance of embedding-related applications. This paper proposes a locally adaptive translation method for knowledge graph embedding, called TransA, which identifies the optimal loss function by adaptively determining its margin over different knowledge graphs. Experiments on two benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of this approach compared to state-of-the-art methods.
label: AI

title: Proposition of a Theoretical Model for Missing Data Imputation using Deep Learning and Evolutionary Algorithms
Abstract: Missing data imputation has witnessed significant advancements in recent decades. Techniques employed include Expectation Maximization, Neural Networks with Evolutionary Algorithms or optimization techniques, and K-Nearest Neighbor approaches. Missing data entries in databases pose challenges to decision-making and data analysis. Consequently, this area has attracted considerable research interest, aiming to develop accurate, time-efficient, and sensitive missing data imputation techniques, particularly for time-sensitive applications like power plants and winding processes. This article hypothesizes that deep neural networks built using autoencoders and denoising autoencoders, combined with genetic algorithms, swarm intelligence, and maximum likelihood estimator methods, can achieve superior imputed values compared to existing techniques, considering arbitrary and monotone missing data patterns. The study also considers missing at random, missing completely at random, and missing not at random missing data mechanisms. The paper proposes utilizing fuzzy logic in conjunction with deep neural networks for missing data imputation tasks, as well as exploring different building blocks for deep neural networks, such as Stacked Restricted Boltzmann Machines and Deep Belief Networks, to test the hypothesis. This article is motivated by the need for missing data imputation techniques that outperform existing methods with higher accuracies and lower errors.
label: AI

title: Staple: Complementary Learners for Real-Time Tracking
Abstract: Correlation Filter-based trackers have recently achieved impressive performance, exhibiting strong robustness to challenging situations involving motion blur and illumination changes. However, their strong dependence on the tracked object's spatial layout makes them highly sensitive to deformation. Models based on color statistics offer complementary traits: they handle shape variations effectively but struggle with inconsistent illumination throughout a sequence. Additionally, color distributions alone can be insufficiently discriminative. This paper demonstrates that a simple tracker combining complementary cues within a ridge regression framework operates faster than 80 FPS and outperforms not only all entries in the popular VOT14 competition but also recent and far more sophisticated trackers based on multiple benchmarks.
label: AI

title: Neural Generative Question Answering
Abstract: This paper presents an end-to-end neural network model, named Neural Generative Question Answering (GENQA), capable of generating answers to simple factoid questions based on facts within a knowledge base. Specifically, the model is built on the encoder-decoder framework for sequence-to-sequence learning, equipped with the ability to query the knowledge base. It is trained on a corpus of question-answer pairs, along with their associated triples in the knowledge base. Empirical studies show the model's effectiveness in handling variations in questions and answers, generating accurate and natural answers by referring to the facts in the knowledge base. Experiments on question answering demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms an embedding-based QA model and a neural dialogue model trained on the same data.

title: Q-Networks for Binary Vector Actions
Abstract: This paper investigates reinforcement learning with binary vector actions. It proposes an effective architecture for neural networks to approximate an action-value function with binary vector actions. This architecture approximates the action-value function by a linear function with respect to the action vector but remains non-linear with respect to the state input. The paper demonstrates that this approximation method enables efficient calculation of greedy action selection and softmax action selection. Using this architecture, the paper introduces an online algorithm based on Q-learning. Empirical results in the grid world and the blocker task suggest that this approximation architecture is effective for RL problems with large discrete action sets.

title: Toward a Taxonomy and Computational Models of Abnormalities in Images
Abstract: The human visual system excels at recognizing abnormal images and identifying the underlying reasons for their peculiarity. This capability has not received sufficient attention in computer vision. This paper delves into various types of atypicalities in images in a more comprehensive manner than previous studies. It proposes a new dataset of abnormal images showcasing a wide range of atypicalities. Human subject experiments were designed to develop a coarse taxonomy of abnormality reasons. These experiments revealed three major categories of abnormality: object-centric, scene-centric, and contextual. Based on this taxonomy, the paper introduces a comprehensive computational model capable of predicting all types of abnormality in images, outperforming previous methods in abnormality recognition.
label: AI

title: Fixed-Point Performance Analysis of Recurrent Neural Networks
Abstract: Recurrent neural networks have proven highly effective in numerous applications, but they necessitate increased complexity in hardware or software implementations. Hardware complexity can be significantly reduced by minimizing the word-length of weights and signals. This work analyzes the fixed-point performance of recurrent neural networks using a retrain-based quantization method. The quantization sensitivity of each layer in RNNs is examined, and the overall fixed-point optimization results, minimizing weight capacity while maintaining performance, are presented. Examples include a language model and a phoneme recognition task.

title: What can we learn about CNNs from a large scale controlled object dataset?
Abstract: Tolerance to image variations, such as translation, scale, pose, and illumination, is a crucial desired property for any object recognition system, whether human or machine. The trend in computer vision has been towards larger datasets, particularly with the rise of popular deep learning models. While beneficial for learning invariance to object inter- and intra-class shape variability, these large-scale wild datasets are less useful for learning invariance to other parameters, forcing researchers to rely on other training tricks. This paper introduces a large-scale synthetic dataset, freely and publicly available, to address fundamental questions regarding invariance and selectivity properties of convolutional neural networks. The dataset comprises two parts: (a) objects shot on a turntable (16 categories, 8 rotation angles, 11 cameras on a semicircular arch, 5 lighting conditions, 3 focus levels, diverse backgrounds (23.4 per instance) generating 1320 images per instance (over 20 million images in total), and (b) scenes where a robot arm captures images of objects in a 1:160 scale scene. The paper investigates: (1) invariance and selectivity of different CNN layers, (2) knowledge transfer between object categories, (3) systematic or random image sampling for building a training set, (4) domain adaptation from synthetic to natural scenes, and (5) the order of knowledge delivery to CNNs. The analysis explores how these findings can lead to the development of more efficient CNNs.

title: An Online Unsupervised Structural Plasticity Algorithm for Spiking Neural Networks
Abstract: This article proposes a novel Winner-Take-All (WTA) architecture employing neurons with nonlinear dendrites and an online unsupervised structural plasticity rule for training. For hardware implementation convenience, the network utilizes only binary synapses. The proposed learning rule is inspired by spike time-dependent plasticity (STDP) but varies for each dendrite based on its activation level. It trains the WTA network through the formation and elimination of connections between inputs and synapses. To demonstrate the performance of the proposed network and learning rule, the paper applies it to two, four, and six-class classification of random Poisson spike time inputs. The results indicate that by appropriately tuning the inhibitory time constant of the WTA, a trade-off between specificity and sensitivity can be achieved. The inhibitory time constant is used to set the number of subpatterns per pattern for detection. The paper shows that while successful trial percentages are 92%, 88%, and 82% for two, four, and six-class classification without pattern subdivisions, these increase to 100% when each pattern is subdivided into 5 or 10 subpatterns. However, the scenario without pattern subdivision exhibits greater resilience to jitter compared to the latter scenarios.

title: Predicting and visualizing psychological attributions with a deep neural network
Abstract: Judgments about personality based on facial appearance significantly influence social decision-making, impacting areas from presidential elections to jury decisions. Recent research has shown that it is possible to predict perceptions of memorability, trustworthiness, intelligence, and other attributes from human face images. The most successful approaches require face images meticulously annotated with key facial landmarks. This paper presents a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model capable of performing the same task without requiring landmark features, significantly enhancing efficiency. The model achieves high accuracy, surpassing human-level performance in some cases. Moreover, the paper employs a deconvolutional approach to visualize important features for perception of 22 attributes and introduces a novel method for separately visualizing positive and negative features.
label: AI

title: Adjusting for Chance Clustering Comparison Measures
Abstract: Adjusted for chance measures are widely used to compare partitions/clusterings of the same dataset. Notably, the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) based on pair-counting and the Adjusted Mutual Information (AMI) based on Shannon information theory are highly popular in the clustering community. However, determining the optimal application scenarios for each measure remains an open question. Literature guidelines for their usage are sparse, leading users to often employ both. Generalized Information Theoretic (IT) measures based on the Tsallis entropy have been shown to bridge pair-counting and Shannon IT measures. This paper aims to close the gap between adjusted measures based on pair-counting and those based on information theory. It solves the key technical challenge of analytically computing the expected value and variance of generalized IT measures. This enables the proposal of adjustments for generalized IT measures, reducing to well-known adjusted clustering comparison measures as special cases. Using the theory of generalized IT measures, the paper provides guidelines for using ARI and AMI as external validation indices: ARI should be preferred when the reference clustering has large, equal-sized clusters; AMI is more suitable when the reference clustering is unbalanced and contains small clusters.

title: Predicting the top and bottom ranks of billboard songs using Machine Learning
Abstract: The music industry is a $130 billion enterprise. Predicting whether a song will resonate with the audience significantly impacts the industry. This paper analyzes language within song lyrics using computational linguistic algorithms to predict whether a song will chart high or low on the Billboard rankings based on language features. An SVM classifier with a radial kernel function was trained and tested on these linguistic features. The results indicate that the model can classify whether a song belongs to the top or bottom of the Billboard charts with a precision of 0.76.

title: MXNet: A Flexible and Efficient Machine Learning Library for Heterogeneous Distributed Systems
Abstract: MXNet, a multi-language machine learning library, simplifies the development of ML algorithms, particularly for deep neural networks. It integrates declarative symbolic expressions with imperative tensor computation, providing automatic differentiation for gradient calculation. MXNet is computationally and memory efficient, running on various heterogeneous systems, from mobile devices to distributed GPU clusters. This paper details MXNet's API design and system implementation, explaining how it unifies symbolic expression and tensor operation embedding. Preliminary experiments demonstrate promising results in large-scale deep neural network applications using multiple GPU machines.
label: AI

title: CrossCat: A Fully Bayesian Nonparametric Method for Analyzing Heterogeneous, High Dimensional Data
Abstract: CrossCat, a domain-general data analysis method, addresses the need for statistical methods capable of analyzing high-dimensional datasets without imposing restrictive or opaque modeling assumptions. It infers multiple non-overlapping views of the data, each encompassing a subset of variables, using separate nonparametric mixtures for modeling. CrossCat employs approximate Bayesian inference in a hierarchical, nonparametric model for data tables. This model consists of a Dirichlet process mixture over the table's columns, where each mixture component is itself an independent Dirichlet process mixture over the rows. The inner mixture components are simple parametric models whose form depends on the data types within the table. CrossCat combines the strengths of mixture modeling and Bayesian network structure learning. Similar to mixture modeling, it can model a wide range of distributions by positing latent variables, producing representations that can be efficiently conditioned and sampled for prediction. Like Bayesian networks, CrossCat represents dependencies and independencies between variables, maintaining accuracy when multiple statistical signals are present. Inference is performed through a scalable Gibbs sampling scheme, shown to be effective in practice. Empirical results on heterogeneous tabular data, including hospital cost and quality measures, voting records, unemployment rates, gene expression measurements, and handwritten digit images, demonstrate CrossCat's ability to infer structures consistent with accepted findings and common-sense knowledge in multiple domains, yielding predictive accuracy competitive with generative, discriminative, and model-free alternatives.

title: MERLiN: Mixture Effect Recovery in Linear Networks
Abstract: Causal inference aims to identify cause-effect relationships between variables, such as establishing whether a stimulus affects activity in a specific brain region. However, observed variables often do not represent meaningful causal variables, necessitating the consideration of linear combinations. In electroencephalographic studies, for instance, the focus is on cause-effect relationships between cortical signals (causal variables) rather than electrode signals (observed variables), where cortical signals can be recovered as linear combinations of electrode signals. This paper introduces MERLiN (Mixture Effect Recovery in Linear Networks), a family of causal inference algorithms that employ a novel approach to construct causal variables from non-causal variables. The application of the basic MERLiN algorithm to EEG data demonstrates its extensibility to different (neuroimaging) data modalities. Given an observed linear mixture, the algorithms can recover a causal variable that is a linear effect of another given variable. MERLiN enables the recovery of a cortical signal affected by activity in a specific brain region, even when not a direct effect of the stimulus. The Python/Matlab implementation for all presented algorithms is available at https://github.com/sweichwald/MERLiN.

title: K2 Variable Catalogue II: Machine Learning Classification of Variable Stars and Eclipsing Binaries in K2 Fields 0-4
Abstract: As astronomical surveys generate unprecedented quantities of data, automated data analysis techniques are crucial to maximizing their potential. This paper presents a new methodology for variable star classification, combining Kohonen Self Organizing Maps (SOM, an unsupervised machine learning algorithm) with the more common Random Forest (RF) supervised machine learning technique. Applying this method to data from the K2 mission fields 0-4, the researchers identified 154 ab-type RR Lyraes (10 newly discovered), 377 Delta Scuti pulsators, 133 Gamma Doradus pulsators, 183 detached eclipsing binaries, 290 semi-detached or contact eclipsing binaries, and 9399 other periodic (mostly spot-modulated) sources, after taking into account class significance cuts. The paper presents lightcurve features for all K2 stellar targets, including their three strongest detected frequencies, which can be used to study stellar rotation periods where variability arises from spot modulation. The resulting catalog of variable stars, classes, and associated data features is made available online. The SOM code in Python is published as part of the open-source PyMVPA package, allowing users to easily recreate the method using available RF modules.

title: An attractor neural network architecture with an ultra high information capacity: numerical results
Abstract: Attractor neural networks provide a theoretical framework for modeling memory function in the hippocampus and cortex. In these models, memories are stored in the plastic recurrent connections of neural populations as "attractor states." Conventional abstract attractor networks with unconstrained connections have a maximal information capacity of 2 bits/synapse. However, an unconstrained synapse can theoretically store an infinite amount of bits in a noiseless scenario, a capacity that conventional attractor networks cannot achieve. This paper proposes a hierarchical attractor network capable of attaining ultra-high information capacity. The network consists of two layers: a visible layer with Nv neurons and a hidden layer with Nh neurons. The visible-to-hidden connections are randomly set and kept fixed during the training phase, where memory patterns are stored as fixed-points of the network dynamics. The hidden-to-visible connections, initially normally distributed, are learned via a local, online learning rule called the Three-Threshold Learning Rule, and there are no within-layer connections. Simulations suggest that the maximal information capacity grows exponentially with the expansion ratio Nh/Nv. To understand the mechanism behind this high capacity, a naive mean-field approximation (nMFA) was simulated. The nMFA captured the exponential increase, revealing that correlation between the hidden and visible units is a key underlying factor. Additionally, the degree of symmetry of the connectivity between the hidden and visible neurons was observed to increase with the expansion ratio at maximal capacity. These results highlight the role of hierarchical architecture in significantly enhancing the information storage performance of attractor networks.
