title: Prototypical Priors: From Improving Classification to Zero-Shot Learning
Abstract: Recent advancements in zero-shot learning utilize side information, such as visual attributes or natural language semantics, to define relationships between output visual classes. These relationships are then used to draw inferences on unseen classes during testing. This paper proposes a novel extension to this idea by incorporating visual prototypical concepts as side information. While establishing a unique prototype can be challenging for most real-world visual object categories, it is readily available for categories like traffic signs, brand logos, flags, and even natural language characters. This information can be leveraged for improved recognition performance. The paper proposes a deep learning framework that incorporates prototypical information. Using prototypes as prior information, the deepnet pipeline learns input image projections into the prototypical embedding space, minimizing the final classification loss. Experiments with two datasets of traffic signs and brand logos demonstrate that prototypical embeddings integrated into a conventional convolutional neural network enhance recognition performance. The recognition accuracy on the Belga logo dataset is particularly noteworthy, establishing a new state-of-the-art. In zero-shot learning scenarios, the same system can be directly deployed to draw inferences on unseen classes by simply adding the prototypical information for these new classes during testing. Unlike earlier approaches, the system handles testing on both seen and unseen classes using the same pipeline, enabling the tuning of a trade-off between seen and unseen class performance based on task requirements. Comparison with recent works in the zero-shot learning domain yields top results on the two datasets.

title: Building Memory with Concept Learning Capabilities from Large-scale Knowledge Base
Abstract: This paper presents a new perspective on neural knowledge base (KB) embeddings, building a framework capable of modeling symbolic knowledge in the KB along with its learning process. This framework effectively regularizes previous neural KB embedding models, leading to superior performance in reasoning tasks. It also possesses the ability to deal with unseen entities by learning their embeddings from natural language descriptions, mimicking human behavior in learning semantic concepts.

title: Kalman-based Stochastic Gradient Method with Stop Condition and Insensitivity to Conditioning
Abstract: Modern proximal and stochastic gradient descent (SGD) methods are considered efficient for minimizing large composite objective functions. However, they face two algorithmic challenges: (1) a lack of fast or justified stop conditions and (2) sensitivity to the objective function's conditioning. Current proximal and SGD methods guarantee convergence only after multiple epochs, making them infeasible when the number of component functions is very large or infinite. Second-order SGD methods, developed to address the conditioning issue, suffer from complex analysis. This work tackles these challenges for the linear regression problem by introducing and analyzing a second-order proximal/SGD method based on Kalman Filtering (kSGD). The analysis reveals kSGD's asymptotic optimality, leading to a fast algorithm for large, infinite, or streaming data sources with a justified stop condition. kSGD is proven to be insensitive to problem conditioning, and a unique approach for analyzing the complex second-order dynamics is developed. Numerical experiments on three regression problems (linear, nonparametric wavelet, and logistic) using three large publicly available datasets support the theoretical results. These findings lay a foundation for embedding kSGD in multiple-epoch algorithms, extending it to other problem classes, and developing parallel and low-memory kSGD implementations.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning with Attention for Slate Markov Decision Processes with High-Dimensional States and Actions
Abstract: Many real-world problems involve action spaces represented as feature vectors. While high-dimensional control remains largely unsolved, recent progress has been made for modest dimensionalities. This paper addresses problems with dimensionalities as high as 2000, focusing on a specific form. Motivated by applications like recommendation systems that do not fit standard reinforcement learning frameworks, the paper introduces Slate Markov Decision Processes (slate-MDPs). A slate-MDP is an MDP with a combinatorial action space consisting of slates (tuples) of primitive actions, where only one action from the slate is executed in an underlying MDP. The agent does not control the choice of the executed action, and it may not even be from the slate, as seen in recommendation systems where all recommendations can be ignored. The paper utilizes deep Q-learning with feature representations of both the state and action to learn the value of entire slates. Unlike existing methods, the proposed approach optimizes for both the combinatorial and sequential aspects of the tasks. The new agent's superiority over agents that ignore either combinatorial or sequential long-term value aspects is demonstrated across a range of environments with dynamics from a real-world recommendation system. The paper also employs deep deterministic policy gradients to learn a policy that guides attention towards the highest-value part of the action space for each slate position. This attention is used within a sequentially greedy procedure leveraging submodularity. Finally, the paper shows how introducing risk-seeking can dramatically improve the agent's performance and ability to discover more far-reaching strategies.
label: AI

title: Bayesian Matrix Completion via Adaptive Relaxed Spectral Regularization
Abstract: Bayesian matrix completion has been studied based on a low-rank matrix factorization formulation with promising results. However, there has been limited work on Bayesian matrix completion based on the more direct spectral regularization formulation. This paper presents a novel Bayesian matrix completion method based on spectral regularization. To circumvent the difficulties of dealing with the orthonormality constraints of singular vectors, a new equivalent form with relaxed constraints is derived. This derivation leads to the design of an adaptive version of spectral regularization suitable for Bayesian inference. The proposed Bayesian method requires no parameter tuning and can automatically infer the number of latent factors. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate encouraging results on rank recovery and collaborative filtering, particularly for very sparse matrices.
label: AI

title: Effective LSTMs for Target-Dependent Sentiment Classification
Abstract: Target-dependent sentiment classification poses a challenge in modeling the semantic relatedness of a target with its context words within a sentence. Different context words have varying influences on determining the sentiment polarity of a sentence towards the target. Therefore, integrating the connections between the target word and context words during system development is crucial. This paper develops two target-dependent long short-term memory (LSTM) models that automatically incorporate target information. Evaluation on a benchmark dataset from Twitter shows that sentence representation using standard LSTM performs poorly. Integrating target information into LSTM significantly improves classification accuracy. The target-dependent LSTM models achieve state-of-the-art performance without relying on syntactic parsers or external sentiment lexicons.

title: Correlated fluctuations in strongly-coupled binary networks beyond equilibrium
Abstract: Randomly coupled Ising spins constitute the classical model for collective phenomena in disordered systems, with applications spanning ferromagnetism, combinatorial optimization, protein folding, stock market dynamics, and social dynamics. The thermodynamic limit of the phase diagram for these systems is obtained by averaging over the quenched randomness of the couplings. However, many applications require the statistics of activity for a single realization of possibly asymmetric couplings in finite-sized networks. Examples include reconstruction of couplings from observed dynamics, learning in the central nervous system through correlation-sensitive synaptic plasticity, and representation of probability distributions for sampling-based inference. This paper presents a systematic cumulant expansion for kinetic binary (Ising) threshold units with strong, random, and asymmetric couplings. Going beyond mean-field theory, the expansion is applicable outside thermodynamic equilibrium. A system of approximate non-linear equations predicts average activities and pairwise covariances in quantitative agreement with full simulations down to hundreds of units. The linearized theory yields an expansion of the correlation- and response functions in collective eigenmodes, leading to an efficient algorithm for solving the inverse problem. It also demonstrates that correlations are invariant under scaling of interaction strengths.

title: Interactive audio-tactile maps for visually impaired people
Abstract: Visually impaired individuals face significant challenges related to orientation and mobility. In France, 56% of visually impaired individuals report problems with autonomous mobility, impacting their personal and professional lives and leading to social exclusion. Accessible geographic maps are helpful for understanding a city's or neighborhood's configuration and selecting routes to destinations. Traditionally, raised-line paper maps with braille text have been used. While effective for acquiring spatial knowledge, these maps have limitations. Due to the tactile sense's limitations, only a limited amount of information can be displayed on a single map, requiring multiple maps. Representing specific information like distances is also difficult. Braille labels are used for textual descriptions, but only a small percentage of the visually impaired population reads braille. Recent technological advancements have enabled the design of interactive maps to overcome these limitations. Interactive maps have the potential to provide a broad spectrum of the population with spatial knowledge, regardless of age, impairment, skill level, or other factors. They represent an efficient means for visually impaired individuals to access geospatial information. This paper provides an overview of research on making geographic maps accessible to visually impaired individuals.

title: Occlusion-Aware Human Pose Estimation with Mixtures of Sub-Trees
Abstract: This paper investigates the problem of learning a human pose estimation model as mixtures of compositional sub-trees in two layers of prediction. This involves estimating the pose of a sub-tree followed by identifying the relationships between sub-trees to handle occlusions between different parts. Mixtures of sub-trees are learned using both geometric and appearance distances. The Chow-Liu (CL) algorithm is recursively applied to determine inter-relations between nodes and build the structure of sub-trees. These structures are used to learn the latent parameters of sub-trees, and inference is performed using a standard belief propagation technique. The proposed method handles occlusions during inference by identifying overlapping regions between different sub-trees and introducing a penalty term for overlapping parts. Experiments on three datasets (Leeds Sports, Image Parse, and UIUC People) demonstrate the method's robustness to occlusions compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

title: Approaches for Sentiment Analysis on Twitter: A State-of-Art study
Abstract: Microblogging, particularly Twitter, has become an extremely prevalent broadcast medium where people share their opinions and sentiments on various subjects. Sentiment analysis plays a crucial role in prediction and opinion mining systems. Twitter's 140-character limit encourages users to express concise opinions, generating a vast ocean of sentiments to analyze. Twitter also provides a developer-friendly streaming API for data retrieval, enabling real-time tweet analysis from various users. This paper provides a survey of the state-of-the-art in sentiment analysis on Twitter, examining lexical, machine learning, and hybrid approaches.
label: AI

title: Simulations for Validation of Vision Systems
Abstract: As computer vision matures into a systems science and engineering discipline, there is a growing trend in leveraging computer graphics simulations for performance evaluation, learning, and inference. However, the utility of graphics simulations for vision remains an open question, with conflicting views in the literature. This paper places recent research findings in the context of performance characterization methodology outlined in the 1990s. It highlights that insights derived from simulations can be qualitative or quantitative, depending on the fidelity of models used in simulation and the nature of the question posed by the experimenter. The paper describes a simulation platform incorporating recent graphics advancements and uses it for systematic performance characterization and trade-off analysis in vision system design. The platform's utility is validated through a case study involving a generative model-inspired vision hypothesis, the Rank-Order consistency model, in the contexts of global and local illumination changes, bad weather, and high-frequency noise. This approach establishes a link between alternative viewpoints, involving models with physics-based semantics and signal and perturbation semantics, confirming insights in the literature on robust change detection.

title: Bag Reference Vector for Multi-instance Learning
Abstract: Multi-instance learning (MIL) has a wide range of applications due to its distinctive characteristics. Although many state-of-the-art algorithms have achieved decent performance, a plurality of existing methods solve the problem at the instance level rather than exploring relationships between bags. This paper proposes an efficient algorithm to describe each bag with a corresponding feature vector by comparing it with other bags. In other words, crucial information about a bag is extracted from the similarity between that bag and other reference bags. The paper also applies extensions of Hausdorff distance to represent similarity, partially overcoming the key challenge in MIL, the ambiguity of instance labels in positive bags. Experimental results on benchmarks and text categorization tasks demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art algorithms.

title: Fast Low-Rank Matrix Learning with Nonconvex Regularization
Abstract: Low-rank modeling has numerous important applications in machine learning, computer vision, and social network analysis. While matrix rank is often approximated by the convex nuclear norm, the use of nonconvex low-rank regularizers has shown improved recovery performance. However, the resulting optimization problem becomes much more challenging. A recent state-of-the-art approach relies on the proximal gradient algorithm, but it requires an expensive full SVD in each proximal step. This paper demonstrates that for commonly used nonconvex low-rank regularizers, a cutoff can be derived to automatically threshold singular values obtained from the proximal operator. This allows the use of the power method to efficiently approximate SVD. Additionally, the proximal operator can be reduced to that of a much smaller matrix projected onto this leading subspace. Convergence, with a rate of O(1/T) where T is the number of iterations, is guaranteed. Extensive experiments on matrix completion and robust principal component analysis show that the proposed method achieves significant speedup over the state-of-the-art. The matrix solution obtained is also more accurate and has a lower rank than that of the traditional nuclear norm regularizer.

title: Neural Enquirer: Learning to Query Tables with Natural Language
Abstract: Neural Enquirer is a neural network architecture designed to execute natural language (NL) queries on a knowledge-base (KB) for answers. It finds the distributed representation of a query and executes it on knowledge-base tables to retrieve the answer as one of the table values. Unlike similar efforts in end-to-end training of semantic parsers, Neural Enquirer is fully "neuralized": it provides distributional representations of the query and knowledge-base and realizes the execution of compositional queries as a series of differentiable operations, with intermediate results (consisting of table annotations at different levels) saved on multiple memory layers. Neural Enquirer can be trained with gradient descent, allowing for the learning of the controlling components, semantic parsing component, and embeddings of tables and query words from scratch. Training can be performed end-to-end but can benefit from stronger guidance, such as step-by-step supervision for complicated queries. Neural Enquirer represents a step towards building neural network systems that understand language by executing it in real-world scenarios. Experiments show that Neural Enquirer can learn to execute complex NL queries on tables with rich structures.

title: Modeling Human Understanding of Complex Intentional Action with a Bayesian Nonparametric Subgoal Model
Abstract: Most human behaviors involve multiple parts, steps, or subtasks. These structures guide action planning and execution. However, when observing others, the latent structure of their actions is often unobservable and must be inferred to learn new skills by demonstration or assist others in completing tasks. For example, an assistant who has learned the subgoal structure of a colleague's task can more quickly recognize and support their actions as they unfold. This paper models how humans infer subgoals from observations of complex action sequences using a nonparametric Bayesian model. This model assumes that observed actions are generated by approximately rational planning over unknown subgoal sequences. The model is tested through a behavioral experiment where humans observed different series of goal-directed actions and inferred the number and composition of subgoal sequences associated with each goal. The Bayesian model predicts human subgoal inferences with high accuracy, significantly better than several alternative models and straightforward heuristics. This result motivates the simulation of how learning and inference of subgoals can improve performance in an artificial user assistance task. The Bayesian model learns the correct subgoals from fewer observations and better assists users by more rapidly and accurately inferring the goal of their actions than alternative approaches. |||

title: Triplet Spike Time Dependent Plasticity: A floating-gate Implementation
Abstract: Synapse plays a crucial role in neural network learning. Spike Time Dependent Plasticity (STDP) is a learning rule that modifies synaptic strength based on the timing difference between pre- and post-synaptic spikes. Doublet STDP (DSTDP) is a commonly used rule based on the time difference between one pre- and one post-spike. However, DSTDP fails to reproduce the results of many biological experiments. Triplet STDP (T-STDP), which considers triplets of spikes as the fundamental unit, has been proposed to address this limitation. This paper presents a compact implementation of a synapse using a single floating-gate (FG) transistor that can store weights in a nonvolatile manner. It demonstrates the T-STDP learning rule by modifying drain voltages according to triplets of spikes. The paper outlines a mathematical procedure to obtain control voltages for the FG device for T-STDP and presents measurement results from an FG synapse fabricated in the TSMC 0.35um CMOS process to support the theory. Possible VLSI implementations of drain voltage waveform generator circuits are also presented with simulation results.

title: A New Statistical Framework for Genetic Pleiotropic Analysis of High Dimensional Phenotype Data
Abstract: Genetic pleiotropic analysis of multiple phenotypes is often designed for examining the relationship between common variants and a few phenotypes. These methods are not suitable for analyzing both high-dimensional phenotypes and high-dimensional genotype (next-generation sequencing) data. To address these limitations, we propose sparse structural equation models (SEMs) as a general framework for a new paradigm of genetic analysis of multiple phenotypes. We extend traditional multivariate SEMs to sparse functional SEMs to incorporate both common and rare variants into the analysis. To handle high-dimensional phenotype and genotype data, we employ functional data analysis and the alternative direction methods of multiplier (ADMM) techniques to reduce data dimension and improve computational efficiency. Using large-scale simulations, we demonstrate that the proposed methods have higher power to detect true causal genetic pleiotropic structures than other existing methods. Simulations also indicate that gene-based pleiotropic analysis has higher power than single variant-based pleiotropic analysis. The proposed method is applied to exome sequence data from the NHLBI Exome Sequencing Project (ESP) with 11 phenotypes, identifying a network with 137 genes connected to 11 phenotypes and 341 edges. Among them, 114 genes showed pleiotropic genetic effects, and 45 genes were reported to be associated with phenotypes in the analysis or other cardiovascular disease (CVD) related phenotypes in the literature.

title: Probabilistic Integration: A Role in Statistical Computation?
Abstract: A research frontier has emerged in scientific computation where numerical error is considered a source of epistemic uncertainty that can be modeled. This poses several statistical challenges, including the design of statistical methods that enable the coherent propagation of probabilities through a computational workflow. This paper investigates the case for probabilistic numerical methods in routine statistical computation. We focus on numerical integration, where a probabilistic integrator is equipped with a full distribution over its output, reflecting the presence of unknown numerical error. Our main technical contribution establishes rates of posterior contraction for these methods. These results show that probabilistic integrators can potentially enjoy the "best of both worlds," leveraging the sampling efficiency of Monte Carlo methods while providing a principled approach to assess the impact of numerical error on scientific conclusions. Several substantial applications are provided for illustration and critical evaluation, including examples from statistical modeling, computer graphics, and a computer model for an oil reservoir.

title: The Indian Spontaneous Expression Database for Emotion Recognition
Abstract: Automatic recognition of spontaneous facial expressions presents a major challenge in the field of affective computing. Attributes like head rotation, face pose, illumination variation, and occlusion increase the complexity of recognizing spontaneous expressions in practical applications. Effective recognition of expressions depends significantly on the quality of the database used. Most well-known facial expression databases consist of posed expressions. However, there is a growing demand for spontaneous expression databases for the practical implementation of facial expression recognition algorithms. This paper proposes and establishes a new facial expression database containing spontaneous expressions from both male and female participants of Indian origin. The database comprises 428 segmented video clips of spontaneous facial expressions from 50 participants. In our experiment, emotions were induced among participants using emotional videos, and their self-ratings were collected for each experienced emotion. Facial expression clips were carefully annotated by four trained decoders and further validated by the nature of the stimuli used and self-reported emotions. An extensive analysis was conducted on the database using several machine learning algorithms, and the results are provided for future reference. This spontaneous database will contribute to the development and validation of algorithms for recognizing spontaneous expressions.

title: Mean-Field Inference in Gaussian Restricted Boltzmann Machine
Abstract: A Gaussian restricted Boltzmann machine (GRBM) is a Boltzmann machine defined on a bipartite graph and an extension of traditional restricted Boltzmann machines. A GRBM consists of two different layers: a visible layer composed of continuous visible variables and a hidden layer composed of discrete hidden variables. This paper derives two different inference algorithms for GRBMs based on the naive mean-field approximation (NMFA). One is an inference algorithm for whole variables in a GRBM, and the other is an inference algorithm for partial variables in a GRBM. We compare the two methods analytically and numerically and demonstrate that the latter method performs better.

title: Innovation Pursuit: A New Approach to Subspace Clustering
Abstract: In subspace clustering, data points belonging to a union of subspaces are assigned membership to their respective subspaces. This paper presents a new approach called Innovation Pursuit (iPursuit) for subspace clustering, utilizing a novel geometric idea where subspaces are identified based on their relative novelties. Two frameworks are presented where innovation pursuit is used to distinguish the subspaces. The first framework is an iterative method that finds subspaces consecutively by solving a series of simple linear optimization problems, each searching for a direction of innovation in the span of the data potentially orthogonal to all subspaces except the one to be identified in one step of the algorithm. A detailed mathematical analysis is provided establishing sufficient conditions for iPursuit to correctly cluster the data. The proposed approach can provably yield exact clustering even when subspaces have significant intersections. The complexity of the iterative approach scales linearly in the number of data points and subspaces, and quadratically in the dimension of the subspaces. The second framework integrates iPursuit with spectral clustering to yield a new variant of spectral-clustering-based algorithms. Numerical simulations with both real and synthetic data demonstrate that iPursuit can often outperform state-of-the-art subspace clustering algorithms, particularly for subspaces with significant intersections, and significantly improves the state-of-the-art result for subspace-segmentation-based face clustering.

title: Compressive hyperspectral imaging via adaptive sampling and dictionary learning
Abstract: This paper proposes a new sampling strategy for hyperspectral signals based on dictionary learning and singular value decomposition (SVD). First, we learn a sparsifying dictionary from training spectral data using dictionary learning. Then, an SVD is performed on the dictionary, and the first few left singular vectors are used as the rows of the measurement matrix to obtain compressive measurements for reconstruction. The proposed method provides significant improvement over conventional compressive sensing approaches. Reconstruction performance is further enhanced by reconditioning the sensing matrix using matrix balancing. We demonstrate the robustness of combining dictionary learning and SVD by applying them to different datasets.

title: Estimating Learning Effects: A Short-Time Fourier Transform Regression Model for MEG Source Localization
Abstract: Magnetoencephalography (MEG) has a high temporal resolution, making it well-suited for studying perceptual learning. However, to identify where learning occurs in the brain, source localization techniques are needed to project MEG sensor data into brain space. Previous source localization methods, such as the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) method by Gramfort et al. (2013), produced intriguing results but were not designed to incorporate trial-by-trial learning effects. This paper modifies the approach in Gramfort et al. (2013) to create an STFT-based source localization method (STFT-R) that includes an additional regression of the STFT components on covariates such as the behavioral learning curve. We exploit a hierarchical L21 penalty to induce structured sparsity of STFT components and emphasize signals from regions of interest (ROIs) selected according to prior knowledge. In reconstructing ROI source signals from simulated data, STFT-R achieved smaller errors than a two-step method using the popular minimum-norm estimate (MNE). In a real-world human learning experiment, STFT-R yielded more interpretable results about which time-frequency components of the ROI signals were correlated with learning.

title: Zero-Shot Event Detection by Multimodal Distributional Semantic Embedding of Videos
Abstract: We propose a new zero-shot event detection method using multi-modal distributional semantic embedding of videos. Our model embeds object and action concepts, along with other available modalities from videos, into a distributional semantic space. To our knowledge, this is the first zero-shot event detection model built on top of distributional semantics and extends it in the following ways: (a) semantic embedding of multi-modal information in videos (with a focus on the visual modalities), (b) automatically determining the relevance of concepts/attributes to a free text query, which could be useful for other applications, and (c) retrieving videos by free text event query (e.g., "changing a vehicle tire") based on their content. We embed videos into a distributional semantic space and then measure the similarity between videos and the event query in a free text form. We validated our method on the large TRECVID MED (Multimedia Event Detection) challenge. Using only the event title as a query, our method outperformed the state-of-the-art that uses big descriptions, achieving 12.6% to 13.5% improvement with the MAP metric and 0.73 to 0.83 with the ROC-AUC metric. It is also an order of magnitude faster.

title: Optimal whitening and decorrelation
Abstract: Whitening, or sphering, is a common preprocessing step in statistical analysis to transform random variables to orthogonality. However, due to rotational freedom, there are infinitely many possible whitening procedures. Consequently, a diverse range of sphering methods exist, for example, based on principal component analysis (PCA), Cholesky matrix decomposition, and zero-phase component analysis (ZCA), among others. This paper provides an overview of the underlying theory and discusses five natural whitening procedures. Subsequently, we demonstrate that investigating the cross-covariance and cross-correlation matrix between sphered and original variables breaks the rotational invariance and identifies optimal whitening transformations. As a result, we recommend two particular approaches: ZCA-cor whitening to produce sphered variables that are maximally similar to the original variables, and PCA-cor whitening to obtain sphered variables that maximally compress the original variables.
label: AI

title: Actions ~ Transformations
Abstract: What defines an action like "kicking a ball"? We argue that the true meaning of an action lies in the change or transformation an action brings to the environment. This paper proposes a novel representation for actions by modeling an action as a transformation that changes the state of the environment before the action happens (precondition) to the state after the action (effect). Motivated by recent advancements in video representation using deep learning, we design a Siamese network that models the action as a transformation on a high-level feature space. We demonstrate that our model achieves improvements on standard action recognition datasets, including UCF101 and HMDB51. More importantly, our approach generalizes beyond learned action categories and shows significant performance improvement on cross-category generalization on our new ACT dataset.
label: AI

title: Microclustering: When the Cluster Sizes Grow Sublinearly with the Size of the Data Set
Abstract: Most generative models for clustering implicitly assume that the number of data points in each cluster grows linearly with the total number of data points. Finite mixture models, Dirichlet process mixture models, and Pitman--Yor process mixture models make this assumption, as do all other infinitely exchangeable clustering models. However, for some tasks, this assumption is undesirable. For example, when performing entity resolution, the size of each cluster is often unrelated to the size of the data set. Consequently, each cluster contains a negligible fraction of the total number of data points. Such tasks require models that yield clusters whose sizes grow sublinearly with the size of the data set. We address this requirement by defining the "microclustering property" and introducing a new model exhibiting this property. We compare this model to several commonly used clustering models by checking model fit using real and simulated data sets.

title: Learning Semantic Similarity for Very Short Texts
Abstract: Leveraging data on social media, such as Twitter and Facebook, requires information retrieval algorithms to relate very short text fragments to each other. Traditional text similarity methods like tf-idf cosine-similarity, based on word overlap, often fail to produce good results in this case because word overlap is minimal or nonexistent. Recently, distributed word representations, or word embeddings, have been shown to successfully allow words to match on the semantic level. To pair short text fragments as a concatenation of separate words, an adequate distributed sentence representation is needed, often obtained by naively combining individual word representations in existing literature. We investigated several text representations as a combination of word embeddings in the context of semantic pair matching. This paper investigates the effectiveness of these naive techniques, as well as traditional tf-idf similarity, for fragments of different lengths. Our main contribution is a first step towards a hybrid method that combines the strength of dense distributed representations (as opposed to sparse term matching) with the strength of tf-idf based methods to automatically reduce the impact of less informative terms. Our new approach outperforms existing techniques in a toy experimental setup, leading to the conclusion that combining word embeddings and tf-idf information might lead to a better model for semantic content within very short text fragments.

title: Active Learning for Delineation of Curvilinear Structures
Abstract: Many recent delineation techniques owe their increased effectiveness to path classification algorithms that distinguish promising paths from others. The downside of this development is the need for annotated training data, which is tedious to produce. This paper proposes an Active Learning approach that significantly speeds up the annotation process. Unlike standard ones, it leverages the specificities of the delineation problem. It operates on a graph and can reduce the training set size by up to 80% without compromising reconstruction quality. We demonstrate that our approach outperforms conventional ones on various biomedical and natural image datasets, showing its broad applicability.
label: AI

title: Recognizing Semantic Features in Faces using Deep Learning
Abstract: The human face constantly conveys information, both consciously and subconsciously. While humans visually interpret this information easily, it presents a significant challenge for machines. Conventional semantic facial feature recognition and analysis techniques are already in use and are based on physiological heuristics, but they suffer from lack of robustness and high computation time. This thesis aims to explore ways for machines to learn to interpret semantic information available in faces in an automated manner without requiring manual design of feature detectors, using the approach of Deep Learning. This thesis provides a study of the effects of various factors and hyper-parameters of deep neural networks in determining an optimal network configuration for the task of semantic facial feature recognition. It explores the effectiveness of the system to recognize various semantic features (like emotions, age, gender, ethnicity, etc.) present in faces. Furthermore, the relationship between the effect of high-level concepts on low-level features is explored through an analysis of similarities in low-level descriptors of different semantic features. This thesis also demonstrates a novel idea of using a deep network to generate 3-D Active Appearance Models of faces from real-world 2-D images. For a more detailed report on this work, please refer to [arXiv:1512.00743v1].

title: Duelist Algorithm: An Algorithm Inspired by How Duelist Improve Their Capabilities in a Duel
Abstract: This paper proposes an optimization algorithm based on how humans fight and learn from each duelist. Since this algorithm is population-based, it starts with an initial set of duelists. The duel determines the winner and loser. The loser learns from the winner, while the winner tries a new skill or technique that may improve their fighting capabilities. Duelists with the highest fighting capabilities are called champions. Champions train new duelists in their skills. The new duelist joins the tournament as a representative of each champion. All duelists are re-evaluated, and those with the worst fighting capabilities are eliminated to maintain the number of duelists. Two optimization problems are applied for the proposed algorithm, along with genetic algorithm, particle swarm optimization, and imperialist competitive algorithm. The results show that the proposed algorithm can find the better global optimum and achieve faster iteration.

title: Implicit Location Sharing Detection in Social Media from Short Turkish Text
Abstract: Social media has become a significant venue for information sharing of live updates. Users of social media produce and share large amounts of personal data as part of live updates. A significant percentage of this data contains location information that can be used by others for various purposes. Some social media users deliberately share their location information with other social network users. However, a large number of social media users blindly or implicitly share their location without noticing it or its possible consequences. Implicit location sharing is investigated in this paper. We perform a large-scale study on implicit location sharing for one of the most popular social media platforms, namely Twitter. After a careful study, we built a dataset of Turkish tweets and manually tagged them. Using machine learning techniques, we built classifiers that can classify whether a given tweet contains implicit location sharing or not. The classifiers are shown to be very accurate and efficient. Moreover, the best classifier is employed as a browser add-on tool that warns the user whenever implicit location sharing is predicted from the tweet to be released. The paper provides the methodology and technical analysis. Furthermore, it discusses how these techniques can be extended to different social network services and languages.

title: Hybrid Approach for Inductive Semi Supervised Learning using Label Propagation and Support Vector Machine
Abstract: Semi-supervised learning methods have gained importance in today's world due to the high cost and time involved in labeling unlabeled data by human experts. The proposed hybrid approach uses SVM and Label Propagation to label unlabeled data. In this process, SVM is trained at each step to minimize error, thus improving prediction quality. Experiments are conducted using SVM and logistic regression (Logreg). Results demonstrate that SVM performs significantly better than Logreg. The approach is tested using 12 datasets of different sizes ranging from the order of 1000s to 10000s. Results show that the proposed approach outperforms Label Propagation by a large margin with an F-measure almost twice as high on average. The parallel version of the proposed approach is also designed and implemented, and the analysis shows that the training time decreases significantly when the parallel version is used.

title: Centroid Based Binary Tree Structured SVM for Multi Classification
Abstract: Support Vector Machines (SVMs) were primarily designed for 2-class classification. However, they have been extended for N-class classification due to the requirement of multiclasses in practical applications. While N-class classification using SVM has received considerable research attention, obtaining the minimum number of classifiers during training and testing remains an ongoing research area. We propose a new algorithm, CBTS-SVM (Centroid-based Binary Tree Structured SVM), to address this issue. We build a binary tree of SVM models based on the similarity of class labels by finding their distance from the corresponding centroids at the root level. Experimental results demonstrate comparable accuracy for CBTS with OVO with reasonable gamma and cost values. On the other hand, when CBTS is compared with OVA, it achieves better accuracy with reduced training time and testing time. Furthermore, CBTS is also scalable as it can handle large datasets.

title: A machine learning-based selective sampling procedure for identifying the low energy region in a potential energy surface: a case study on proton conduction in oxides
Abstract: This paper proposes a selective sampling procedure to preferentially evaluate a potential energy surface (PES) in a part of the configuration space governing a physical property of interest. The proposed sampling procedure is based on a machine learning method called the Gaussian process (GP), which is used to construct a statistical model of the PES for identifying the region of interest in the configuration space. We demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed procedure for atomic diffusion and ionic conduction, specifically proton conduction in a well-studied proton-conducting oxide, barium zirconate BaZrO3. The results of the demonstration study indicate that our procedure can efficiently identify the low-energy region characterizing proton conduction in the host crystal lattice, and the descriptors used for the statistical PES model have a significant influence on performance. |||

title: Object-based World Modeling in Semi-Static Environments with Dependent Dirichlet-Process Mixtures
Abstract:
Robots operating in human environments need to understand the world in terms of objects and their properties. We refer to this attribute-based representation as a world model and explore how to acquire it from noisy sensory data and maintain it over time, as objects are added, changed, or removed.  Previous work has framed this as a multiple-target tracking problem, assuming objects are constantly in motion. However, this approach is computationally expensive. We argue that this level of generality is unnecessary in typical world modeling tasks, where objects only change state infrequently. More efficient approaches are possible by focusing on semi-static environments. 

We extend a previously proposed clustering-based world modeling approach, originally designed for static environments, to semi-static domains by incorporating a dependent Dirichlet-process (DDP) mixture model. We derive a novel MAP inference algorithm under this model, subject to data association constraints. We demonstrate that our approach significantly improves computational performance in semi-static environments.

title: Attribute2Image: Conditional Image Generation from Visual Attributes
Abstract: This paper explores the novel problem of generating images from visual attributes. We model the image as a combination of foreground and background elements and develop a layered generative model with disentangled latent variables that can be learned end-to-end using a variational auto-encoder. We experiment with natural images of faces and birds and demonstrate that our models can generate realistic and diverse samples with disentangled latent representations. We use a general energy minimization algorithm for posterior inference of latent variables given novel images. Consequently, the learned generative models achieve excellent quantitative and visual results in attribute-conditioned image reconstruction and completion tasks.
label: AI

title: Protein secondary structure prediction using deep convolutional neural fields
Abstract: Predicting protein secondary structure (SS) is crucial for understanding protein structure and function. Existing predictors using only sequence (profile) information achieve approximately 80% Q3 accuracy, a plateau reached over a decade ago. We introduce DeepCNF (Deep Convolutional Neural Fields) for protein SS prediction. DeepCNF is a Deep Learning extension of Conditional Neural Fields (CNF), integrating Conditional Random Fields (CRF) and shallow neural networks. DeepCNF not only models complex sequence-structure relationships through a deep hierarchical architecture but also captures the interdependency between adjacent SS labels, making it significantly more powerful than CNF. Experimental results show that DeepCNF achieves approximately 84% Q3 accuracy, 85% SOV score, and 72% Q8 accuracy on CASP and CAMEO test proteins, significantly outperforming current popular predictors. As a general framework, DeepCNF can be applied to predict other protein structure properties such as contact number, disorder regions, and solvent accessibility.
label: AI

title: Efficient learning algorithm for quantum perceptron unitary weights
Abstract: For the past two decades, researchers have sought to create a Quantum Neural Network (QNN) by combining the strengths of quantum computing and neural computing. To fully exploit the advantages of these fields, the QNN must effectively integrate the unitary dynamics of quantum computing with the dissipative dynamics of neural computing. The core building blocks of quantum computing and neural computing are the qubit and perceptron, respectively. Existing implementations of the quantum perceptron model have struggled to elegantly fuse these two concepts due to slow learning rules and disregard for the unitary requirement. This paper presents a quantum perceptron capable of computing functions beyond the reach of classical perceptrons while analytically solving for parameters and preserving both unitary and dissipative requirements.
label: AI

title: Labeling the Features Not the Samples: Efficient Video Classification with Minimal Supervision
Abstract: Feature selection is essential for effective visual recognition. We propose an efficient joint classifier learning and feature selection method that discovers sparse, compact representations of input features from a vast pool of candidates using an almost unsupervised formulation. Our method only requires knowledge of the *feature sign*—whether or not a particular feature has, on average, stronger values over positive samples than over negatives. We show how this can be estimated using as few as a single labeled training sample per class. Using these feature signs, we extend an initial supervised learning problem into an (almost) unsupervised clustering formulation that can incorporate new data without needing ground truth labels. Our method serves as both a feature selection mechanism and a fully competitive classifier. It boasts low computational cost and excellent accuracy, particularly in scenarios with limited training data. We conduct experiments on large-scale recognition in video and demonstrate superior speed and performance compared to established feature selection approaches like AdaBoost, Lasso, greedy forward-backward selection, and powerful classifiers like SVM.

title: Loss Functions for Top-k Error: Analysis and Insights
Abstract: To push the performance of realistic computer vision tasks, modern benchmark datasets have witnessed a significant increase in the number of classes in recent years. This increase in class count introduces greater ambiguity between class labels, prompting the question of whether top-1 error is the appropriate performance measure. This paper provides an extensive comparison and evaluation of established multiclass methods, comparing their top-k performance from both practical and theoretical perspectives. We also introduce novel top-k loss functions as modifications of the softmax and multiclass SVM losses, along with efficient optimization schemes. Our experiments, conducted on various datasets, compare all proposed and established methods for top-k error optimization. A key finding is that the softmax loss consistently yields competitive top-k performance for all k values. For specific top-k errors, our new top-k losses generally lead to further improvements while being faster to train than the softmax.

title: Fast k-Nearest Neighbour Search via Dynamic Continuous Indexing
Abstract: Existing methods for retrieving k-nearest neighbors suffer from the curse of dimensionality. We argue that this is partly due to inherent limitations of space partitioning, the underlying strategy employed by most current methods. We propose a new strategy that avoids partitioning the vector space and introduce a novel randomized algorithm that runs in time linear in the dimensionality of the space and sub-linear in the intrinsic dimensionality and the size of the dataset. The algorithm requires space constant in dimensionality and linear in the size of the dataset. This algorithm offers fine-grained control over accuracy and speed on a per-query basis, automatically adapts to variations in data density, supports dynamic updates to the dataset, and is easy to implement. We demonstrate appealing theoretical properties and empirically show that our algorithm outperforms locality-sensitivity hashing (LSH) in terms of approximation quality, speed, and space efficiency.

title: A New Approach for Scalable Analysis of Microbial Communities
Abstract: Microbial communities play vital roles in the function and maintenance of various biosystems, ranging from the human body to the environment. Current methods for analyzing microbial communities typically rely on taxonomic phylogenetic alignment using 16S rRNA metagenomic or Whole Genome Sequencing data. Characterizations often involve aligning billions of microbial sequences to a phylogenetic tree. We introduce a new approach for efficient analysis of microbial communities. Our reference-free analysis technique is based on n-gram sequence analysis of 16S rRNA data, dramatically reducing processing data size (by 105 fold) without requiring taxonomic alignment. This approach is applied to characterize phenotypic microbial community differences in various settings. Specifically, we demonstrate its use in classifying microbial communities across different body sites, characterizing oral microbiomes associated with healthy and diseased individuals, and classifying microbial communities longitudinally during infant development. We introduce various dimensionality reduction methods, offering a more scalable analysis framework while minimizing losses in classification accuracies. Among these methods, we propose a continuous vector representation for microbial communities, applicable to deep learning applications in microbial informatics.

title: Taxonomy grounded aggregation of classifiers with different label sets
Abstract: We address the problem of aggregating label predictions from diverse classifiers using a class taxonomy. Such a taxonomy might not have been available or referenced during the design and training of individual classifiers, yet mapping the output labels to the taxonomy is desirable to integrate the effort invested in training the constituent classifiers. A hierarchical taxonomy representing domain knowledge may differ from, but be partially mappable to, the label sets of the individual classifiers. We present a heuristic approach and a principled graphical model to aggregate label predictions by grounding them within the available taxonomy. Our model aggregates labels using the taxonomy structure as constraints to identify the most likely hierarchically consistent class. We experimentally validate our proposed method on image and text classification tasks.

title: Highly Scalable Tensor Factorization for Prediction of Drug-Protein Interaction Type
Abstract: Understanding the type of inhibitory interaction is crucial for drug design. Researchers are interested in determining whether a drug exhibits competitive or non-competitive interaction with specific protein targets. We propose a factorization method, Macau, to analyze interaction types. This method combines different measurement types into a single tensor along with proteins and compounds. Compounds are characterized by high-dimensional 2D ECFP fingerprints. The novelty of Macau lies in its ability to incorporate high-dimensional side information (millions of unique 2D ECFP compound features) using a specially designed noise injection MCMC sampler, even for large-scale datasets containing millions of compounds. Without side information, tensor factorization would be practically infeasible. Using public IC50 and Ki data from ChEMBL, we trained a model that identifies the latent subspace separating the two measurement types (IC50 and Ki). The results suggest that our method can detect competitive inhibitory activity between compounds and proteins.

title: Extracting Traceability Information from C# Projects
Abstract: The maintenance phase of the software lifecycle represents a significant drain on resources for most software companies. The transition from programmers to maintainers is high-risk, as maintainers typically need to learn the system from scratch before modifying it appropriately. This paper introduces a method for automatically extracting important traceability information from the source code of a C# software project. Utilizing this traceability information, both maintainers and programmers can better assess the impacts of their actions on the entire project.

title: Sequential visibility-graph motifs
Abstract: Visibility algorithms transform time series into graphs, encoding dynamic information in their topology. This opens the door for graph-theoretical time series analysis and bridges nonlinear dynamics with network science. We introduce and study the concept of sequential visibility graph motifs—smaller substructures of n consecutive nodes that appear with characteristic frequencies. We develop a theory for computing in an exact manner the motif profiles associated with general classes of deterministic and stochastic dynamics. We find that this simple property is highly informative and computationally efficient, capable of distinguishing different dynamics and robust against noise contamination. We demonstrate its practical applicability in unsupervised learning by extracting motif profiles from experimental heart-rate series and successfully distinguishing meditative states from other relaxation states. Applications of this general theory include the automatic classification and description of physical, biological, and financial time series.

title: Transfer Learning in Brain-Computer Interfaces
Abstract: Brain-computer interface (BCI) performance improves with the amount of available training data. However, the statistical distribution of this data varies across subjects and sessions within individual subjects, limiting the transferability of training data or trained models between them. This article reviews current transfer learning techniques in BCIs that exploit shared structure between training data of multiple subjects and/or sessions to enhance performance. We present a framework for transfer learning in the context of BCIs, applicable to any arbitrary feature space, and introduce a novel regression estimation method specifically designed for the structure of a system based on the electroencephalogram (EEG). We demonstrate the utility of our framework and method on subject-to-subject transfer in a motor-imagery paradigm and on session-to-session transfer in a patient diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Our approach outperforms other comparable methods on an identical dataset.

title: Towards Dropout Training for Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: Dropout has seen increasing use in deep learning recently. For deep convolutional neural networks, dropout is known to work well in fully-connected layers. However, its effect in convolutional and pooling layers remains unclear. This paper demonstrates that max-pooling dropout is equivalent to randomly picking activation based on a multinomial distribution during training. Based on this insight, we advocate for using our proposed probabilistic weighted pooling instead of commonly used max-pooling, which acts as model averaging at test time. Empirical evidence validates the superiority of probabilistic weighted pooling. We also empirically show that the effect of convolutional dropout is non-trivial despite the significantly reduced possibility of over-fitting due to the convolutional architecture. By carefully designing dropout training simultaneously in max-pooling and fully-connected layers, we achieve state-of-the-art performance on MNIST and very competitive results on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, compared to other approaches without data augmentation. Finally, we compare max-pooling dropout and stochastic pooling, both of which introduce stochasticity based on multinomial distributions at the pooling stage.

title: MOCICE-BCubed F$_1$: A New Evaluation Measure for Biclustering Algorithms
Abstract: Validating biclustering algorithms remains a challenging task despite numerous proposed measures for evaluating their quality. While no criterion is universally accepted as the overall best, several meta-evaluation conditions that biclustering algorithms should satisfy have been articulated. This work presents MOCICE-BCubed F$_1$, a new external measure for evaluating biclusterings in scenarios where gold-standard annotations are available for both the object clusters and the associated feature subspaces. Our proposal leverages the micro-objects transformation and fulfills the most comprehensive set of meta-evaluation conditions articulated for biclusterings. Additionally, the proposed measure effectively handles overlapping in both the object and feature spaces. Furthermore, when used to evaluate traditional clusterings, which are viewed as a particular case of biclustering, our measure also satisfies the most comprehensive set of meta-evaluation conditions for this task.

title: LSTM Neural Reordering Feature for Statistical Machine Translation
Abstract: Artificial neural networks are powerful models widely applied in various aspects of machine translation, such as language modeling and translation modeling. Despite significant improvements in these areas, the reordering problem remains a challenge in statistical machine translation. This paper presents a novel neural reordering model that directly models word pairs and alignment. By leveraging LSTM recurrent neural networks, much longer contexts can be learned for reordering prediction. Experimental results on NIST OpenMT12 Arabic-English and Chinese-English 1000-best rescoring tasks show that our LSTM neural reordering feature is robust and achieves significant improvements over various baseline systems.

title: Learning Using 1-Local Membership Queries
Abstract: Classic machine learning algorithms learn from labeled examples. For instance, to design a machine translation system, a typical training set consists of English sentences and their translations. A more powerful model allows the algorithm to also query for labels of new examples it creates. For example, in the translation task, the algorithm can create a new English sentence and request its translation from the user during training. This combination of examples and queries has been extensively studied. However, despite numerous theoretical results, query algorithms are rarely used in practice. One major reason for this is a report (Baum and Lang, 1992) highlighting the disappointing empirical performance of a query algorithm. These poor results were primarily attributed to the algorithm querying for labels of artificial examples that are impossible for humans to interpret. This work investigates a new model of local membership queries (Awasthi et al., 2012), attempting to address the issue of artificial queries. In this model, the algorithm can only query for labels of examples that are close to examples from the training set. For instance, in translation, the algorithm can modify individual words in a sentence it has already seen and then request its translation. In this model, the examples queried by the algorithm will be similar to natural examples, hopefully avoiding artificial or random appearance. We focus on 1-local queries (i.e., queries of distance 1 from an example in the training sample). We demonstrate that 1-local membership queries are already stronger than the standard learning model. We also present an experiment on a well-known NLP task of sentiment analysis. In this experiment, users were asked to provide more information than just indicating the label. Our results illustrate the practical benefits of this extra information.

title: Covariance-domain Dictionary Learning for Overcomplete EEG Source Identification
Abstract: We propose an algorithm targeting the identification of more sources than channels for electroencephalography (EEG). Our overcomplete source identification algorithm, Cov-DL, utilizes dictionary learning methods applied in the covariance domain. Assuming that EEG sources are uncorrelated within moving time-windows and the scalp mixing is linear, the forward problem can be transferred to the covariance domain, which has higher dimensionality than the original EEG channel domain. This allows for learning the overcomplete mixing matrix that generates the scalp EEG, even when there might be more sources than sensors active at any time segment, i.e., when there are non-sparse sources. This contrasts with straightforward dictionary learning methods that rely on the assumption of sparsity, which is not satisfied in the case of low-density EEG systems. We present two different learning strategies for Cov-DL, determined by the size of the target mixing matrix. We demonstrate that Cov-DL outperforms existing overcomplete ICA algorithms in various scenarios of EEG simulations and real EEG experiments.

title: Optimal Estimation and Completion of Matrices with Biclustering Structures
Abstract: Biclustering structures in data matrices were first formalized in a seminal paper by John Hartigan (1972), where the goal is to cluster cases and variables simultaneously. Such structures are also prevalent in block modeling of networks. This paper develops a unified theory for the estimation and completion of matrices with biclustering structures, where the data is a partially observed and noise-contaminated data matrix with a specific biclustering structure. Specifically, we show that a constrained least squares estimator achieves minimax rate-optimal performance in several of the most important scenarios. To this end, we derive unified high probability upper bounds for all sub-Gaussian data and also provide matching minimax lower bounds in both Gaussian and binary cases. Due to the close connection of graphon to stochastic block models, an immediate consequence of our general results is a minimax rate-optimal estimator for sparse graphons.

title: Inferring Interpersonal Relations in Narrative Summaries
Abstract: Characterizing relationships between people is fundamental for understanding narratives. This work addresses the problem of inferring the polarity of relationships between people in narrative summaries. We formulate the problem as a joint structured prediction for each narrative and present a model that combines evidence from linguistic and semantic features, as well as features based on the structure of the social community in the text. We also provide a clustering-based approach that can exploit regularities in narrative types, for example, learning an affinity for love-triangles in romantic stories. On a dataset of movie summaries from Wikipedia, our structured models provide more than a 30% error-reduction over a competitive baseline that considers pairs of characters in isolation. |||

title: Multilingual Language Processing From Bytes
Abstract: We propose a Byte-to-Span (BTS) model, an LSTM-based architecture that directly processes text as Unicode bytes, enabling multilingual analysis with a single model. BTS outputs span annotations in the form [start, length, label], where each component is represented as a distinct entry in a vocabulary.  This approach allows for compact models due to the small vocabulary size.  Despite its simplicity, BTS achieves performance on par with, or even exceeding, state-of-the-art methods for Part-of-Speech tagging and Named Entity Recognition, solely using the provided training data without external resources.  Significantly, BTS operates without any reliance on standard NLP pipeline elements, including tokenization, making it a standalone system for raw text processing.

title: Decoding Hidden Markov Models Faster Than Viterbi Via Online Matrix-Vector (max, +)-Multiplication
Abstract: We present an algorithm for maximum a posteriori decoding (MAPD) in time-homogeneous Hidden Markov Models (HMMs), offering a logarithmic improvement over the classical Viterbi algorithm's worst-case runtime. Our approach reinterprets the Viterbi algorithm as a series of matrix-vector (max, +)-multiplications. For time-homogeneous HMMs, this computation becomes online: a predefined matrix must be multiplied with multiple vectors sequentially revealed one at a time.  Our primary contribution is an algorithm achieving subquadratic time for this matrix-vector (max, +)-multiplication by pre-processing the matrix polynomially. This fast multiplication algorithm enables MAPD solving in O(mn²/log n) time for any time-homogeneous HMM of size n and observation sequence of length m, with an additional polynomial preprocessing cost negligible for m > n.  To the best of our knowledge, this is the first algorithm achieving subquadratic time per observation for the MAPD problem, solely requiring the assumption (commonly observed in practice) of a constant transition probability matrix.

title: "I got in trouble": A case study of faculty "doing school" during professional development
Abstract: Professional development workshops are widely used to promote research-based instructional strategies among physics and astronomy faculty.  While these workshops motivate faculty to adapt these strategies, research suggests that they may lack the preparation to effectively implement them in ways that maintain the positive student outcomes intended by the designers.  This paper analyzes the experiences of a focal group of faculty during a session of the Physics and Astronomy New Faculty Workshop, where they participated in a task as mock physics students.  We compare their experiences to student behaviors documented in other studies and find that their group coordination and sense-making poorly reflect the types of interactions our community encourages them to cultivate in their own students.  These preliminary findings highlight potential implications for professional development and inform our plans for future research.

title: HH 1158: The lowest luminosity externally irradiated Herbig-Haro jet
Abstract: We have identified a new externally irradiated Herbig-Haro (HH) jet, designated HH 1158, located within ~2 pc of the massive OB-type stars in the sigma Orionis cluster.  With an Lbol ~ 0.1 Lsun, HH 1158 represents the least luminous irradiated HH jet detected to date in any cluster.  Analysis of high-resolution optical spectra reveals asymmetries in brightness, morphology, electron density, velocity, and mass outflow rates between the blue and red-shifted lobes.  We estimate the position angle of the HH 1158 jet at 102+/-5 degrees.  Utilizing multiple diagnostics, the mass outflow rate and mean accretion rate for HH 1158 are estimated to be (5.2 +/- 2.6) x 10^(-10) Msun/yr and (3.0 +/- 1.0) x 10^(-10) Msun/yr, respectively.  The properties of HH 1158 exhibit remarkable similarities to the previously identified externally irradiated HH 444 -- HH 447 jets in sigma Orionis.  In particular, the weaker jet beam is tilted towards the massive stars, suggestive of a greater extent of photo-evaporation.  The high value of the Halpha/[SII] ratio aligns with ratios observed in other irradiated jets, including HH 444 -- HH 447.  The presence of an extended, bipolar, collimated jet and evidence of shocked emission knots make HH 1158 the first distinct instance of irradiated HH jets at the low-luminosity end, providing a unique opportunity to study the physical properties of extremely faint HH jet sources.

title: Optimization theory of Hebbian/anti-Hebbian networks for PCA and whitening
Abstract: Our brains process sensory information facing challenges akin to those addressed in statistical signal processing. This suggests that biologically plausible implementations of online signal processing algorithms may model neural computation. We explore this analogy by focusing on foundational signal processing techniques like Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and whitening, which optimize information transmission in noisy environments. We adopt the similarity matching framework, recently developed for principal subspace extraction, but enhance the objective functions by incorporating a decorrelating term. From these modified objective functions, we derive online PCA and whitening algorithms that are implementable by neural networks with local learning rules, i.e., synaptic weight updates dependent only on pre- and postsynaptic neuronal activity.  Our theory offers a principled model of neural computation and generates testable predictions, such as the silencing of underutilized neurons.

title: Universality laws for randomized dimension reduction, with applications
Abstract: Dimension reduction, the process of mapping high-dimensional data into a lower-dimensional space, is crucial for data analysis. In the Euclidean setting, applying a random linear map to the data is a fundamental dimension reduction technique. Its success hinges on preserving key geometric features of the dataset. This paper examines a natural family of randomized dimension reduction maps and a broad class of datasets.  We prove the existence of a phase transition in the success probability of the dimension reduction map as the embedding dimension increases.  Remarkably, the location of this phase transition is identical for all maps within this family given a particular dataset.  Furthermore, each map exhibits identical stability properties, quantified through the restricted minimum singular value. These findings can be interpreted as novel universality laws in high-dimensional stochastic geometry. These universality laws for randomized dimension reduction have wide-ranging applications in applied mathematics, signal processing, and statistics. They provide design principles for numerical linear algebra algorithms, compressed sensing measurement ensembles, and random linear codes.  Moreover, these results have implications for the performance of statistical estimation methods under a vast class of random experimental designs.

title: A Normative Theory of Adaptive Dimensionality Reduction in Neural Networks
Abstract: Our brains analyze high-dimensional datasets streamed by our sensory organs to make sense of the world.  Since dimensionality reduction is the initial step in this analysis, modeling early sensory processing necessitates biologically plausible online dimensionality reduction algorithms. We previously derived such an algorithm, termed similarity matching, from a Multidimensional Scaling (MDS) objective function. However, the existing algorithm has a fixed number of output dimensions determined by the number of output neurons, lacking adaptability.  As the number of informative dimensions in sensory inputs is variable, there is a need for adaptive dimensionality reduction. Here, we derive biologically plausible dimensionality reduction algorithms that dynamically adjust the number of output dimensions based on the eigenspectrum of the input covariance matrix.  We propose three objective functions that, in the offline setting, are optimized by projecting the input dataset onto its principal subspace scaled by the eigenvalues of the output covariance matrix.  The output eigenvalues are calculated as i) soft-thresholded, ii) hard-thresholded, iii) equalized thresholded eigenvalues of the input covariance matrix.  In the online setting, we derive the corresponding adaptive algorithms and map them to neuronal activity dynamics in networks with biologically plausible local learning rules.  Remarkably, in the last two networks, neurons are classified into two categories, which we identify with principal neurons and interneurons in biological circuits.

title: A General Framework for Constrained Bayesian Optimization using Information-based Search
Abstract: We present an information-theoretic framework for solving global black-box optimization problems with black-box constraints.  Our focus is on efficiently solving problems with decoupled constraints, where subsets of the objective and constraint functions can be evaluated independently. For example, evaluating the objective on a CPU while independently evaluating the constraints on a GPU. These problems require an acquisition function that can be decomposed into contributions from individual function evaluations.  We develop one such acquisition function called Predictive Entropy Search with Constraints (PESC). PESC approximates the expected information gain criterion and outperforms alternative approaches in terms of improvement across various synthetic and real-world problems.  Furthermore, we address problems with a mix of fast and slow-to-evaluate functions.  These problems require balancing the time spent on PESC's meta-computation and the actual evaluation of the target objective. We adopt a bounded rationality approach and develop partial updates for PESC, trading off accuracy for speed. We then propose a method for adaptively switching between partial and full PESC updates, enabling us to interpolate between versions efficient in terms of function evaluations and those efficient in terms of wall-clock time.  Overall, we demonstrate that PESC is a promising algorithm offering a unified solution for constrained Bayesian optimization.

title: Modeling Dynamic Relationships Between Characters in Literary Novels
Abstract: Understanding characters plays a crucial role in computationally representing and interpreting narratives. Unlike previous work focused on inferring character roles, we investigate the problem of modeling their relationships. Rather than assuming fixed relationships between character pairs, we hypothesize that relationships are dynamic and evolve over time as the narrative progresses.  We frame the problem of relationship modeling as a structured prediction problem. We propose a semi-supervised framework for learning relationship sequences from both fully and partially labeled data.  Our Markovian model, capable of accumulating historical beliefs about the relationship and status changes, is introduced. We utilize a rich set of linguistic and semantically motivated features incorporating world knowledge to analyze the narrative's textual content.  Empirically, we demonstrate that this framework outperforms competing baselines.

title: Cost-aware Pre-training for Multiclass Cost-sensitive Deep Learning
Abstract: Deep learning has emerged as one of the most prominent machine learning techniques, achieving state-of-the-art results in numerous applications requiring automatic feature extraction.  Many of these applications also involve varying costs for different misclassification errors. However, it remains unclear whether or how this cost information can be effectively integrated into deep learning to enhance performance.  This work proposes a novel cost-aware algorithm that incorporates cost information not only during the training stage but also during the pre-training stage of deep learning.  This approach empowers deep learning to perform automatic feature extraction while effectively considering cost information. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that our proposed approach surpasses other deep learning models that neglect cost information during pre-training.

title: Behavior Discovery and Alignment of Articulated Object Classes from Unstructured Video
Abstract: We introduce an automated system for organizing the content of a collection of unstructured videos featuring an articulated object class (e.g., tiger, horse). By leveraging recurring motion patterns across videos, our system: 1) identifies characteristic behaviors; and 2) recovers pixel-to-pixel alignments between different instances.  Our system can be valuable for organizing video collections for indexing and retrieval.  Furthermore, it can serve as a platform for learning the appearance or behaviors of object classes from Internet videos. Traditional supervised techniques are ill-suited for directly exploiting this vast amount of data, requiring substantial and time-consuming manual annotations.  The behavior discovery stage generates temporal video intervals, each automatically trimmed to a single instance of the discovered behavior, clustered by type. This stage relies on our novel motion representation for articulated motion based on the displacement of ordered pairs of trajectories (PoTs). The alignment stage aligns hundreds of instances of the class with high accuracy despite considerable appearance variations (e.g., an adult tiger and a cub).  This stage employs a flexible Thin Plate Spline deformation model that can vary over time.  We carefully evaluate each stage of our system on a new, fully annotated dataset. On behavior discovery, we surpass the state-of-the-art Improved DTF descriptor.  In terms of spatial alignment, we outperform the widely used SIFT Flow algorithm.
