We achieve this by learning style ranking for a given input using a large photo collection and selecting a diverse subset of matching styles for final style transfer. We also propose a novel technique that transfers the global color and tone of the chosen exemplars to the input photograph while avoiding the common visual artifacts produced by existing style transfer methods. Our style selection and transfer techniques produce compelling, artifact-free results on a wide range of input photographs. A user study demonstrates that our results are preferred over other techniques.
label: AI

title: Grounding of Textual Phrases in Images by Reconstruction
Abstract: Grounding (i.e., localizing) arbitrary, free-form textual phrases in visual content is a challenging problem with numerous applications for human-computer interaction and image-text reference resolution. Few datasets provide ground truth spatial localization of phrases, making it desirable to learn from data with minimal or no grounding supervision. We propose a novel approach that learns grounding by reconstructing a given phrase using an attention mechanism, which can be either latent or optimized directly. During training, our approach encodes the phrase using a recurrent network language model and then learns to attend to the relevant image region to reconstruct the input phrase. At test time, the correct attention, i.e., the grounding, is evaluated. If grounding supervision is available, it can be directly applied via a loss over the attention mechanism. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the Flickr 30k Entities and ReferItGame datasets with varying levels of supervision, from no supervision to full supervision. Our supervised variant significantly improves over the state-of-the-art on both datasets.
label: AI

title: Deep Multimodal Semantic Embeddings for Speech and Images
Abstract: This paper presents a model that takes as input a corpus of images with relevant spoken captions and finds a correspondence between the two modalities. We employ a pair of convolutional neural networks to model visual objects and speech signals at the word level, tying the networks together with an embedding and alignment model that learns a joint semantic space over both modalities. We evaluate our model using image search and annotation tasks on the Flickr8k dataset, which we augmented by collecting a corpus of 40,000 spoken captions using Amazon Mechanical Turk.
label: AI

title: Online Principal Component Analysis in High Dimension: Which Algorithm to Choose?
Abstract: In the current era of data explosion, online techniques that do not require storing all data in memory are essential for performing tasks like principal component analysis (PCA) routinely. Recursive algorithms that update the PCA with each new observation have been studied in various research fields and found wide applications in industrial monitoring, computer vision, astronomy, and latent semantic indexing, among others. This work provides guidance for selecting an online PCA algorithm in practice. We present the main approaches to online PCA, namely, perturbation techniques, incremental methods, and stochastic optimization, and compare their statistical accuracy, computation time, and memory requirements using artificial and real data. Extensions to missing data and functional data are discussed. All studied algorithms are available in the R package onlinePCA on CRAN. |||
label: AI

title: A Continuous Max-Flow Approach to Cyclic Field Reconstruction
Abstract: Image reconstruction from noisy data using Markov Random Field theory has been explored using graph-cuts and continuous max-flow methods, exemplified by the Potts and Ishikawa models. However, these models fail to account for the cyclic topology of specific intensity types, such as hue in natural color images or phase in complex-valued MRI. This paper introduces cyclic continuous max-flow image reconstruction, which models the reconstructed intensity as inherently cyclic. This model complements the Ishikawa model by incorporating the topology of the intensity space within the model and allowing for easy extension to arbitrary intensity resolution.
label: AI

title: Complete Dictionary Recovery over the Sphere I: Overview and the Geometric Picture
Abstract: Recovering a complete (square and invertible) matrix  $\mathbf{A}_0$ from $\mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$ with $\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{A}_0 \mathbf{X}_0$, given that $\mathbf{X}_0$ is sufficiently sparse, is a fundamental problem in dictionary learning. This problem aims to find a sparse representation for a collection of input signals and has applications in signal processing and machine learning. This paper presents the first efficient algorithm that provably recovers $\mathbf{A}_0$ when $\mathbf{X}_0$ has $O(n)$ nonzeros per column, under suitable probability models for $\mathbf{X}_0$. Previous algorithms could only guarantee recovery for $O(\sqrt{n})$ nonzeros per column or required multiple rounds of SDP relaxation for $O(n^{1-\delta})$ nonzeros per column. The proposed algorithm involves solving a nonconvex optimization problem with a spherical constraint. The paper provides a geometric characterization of the objective landscape, demonstrating that the problem is highly structured: (1) there are no spurious local minimizers with high probability, and (2) the objective has a negative directional curvature around all saddle points. This structure enables the use of efficient optimization algorithms. A companion paper (arXiv:1511.04777) presents a second-order trust-region algorithm over the sphere that provably converges to a local minimizer from arbitrary initializations, despite the presence of saddle points.
label: AI

title: Hierarchical Recurrent Neural Encoder for Video Representation with Application to Captioning
Abstract: Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (ConvNets) have achieved remarkable accuracy and speed in image classification. Incorporating temporal structure with deep ConvNets for video representation is crucial for video content analysis. This paper proposes a Hierarchical Recurrent Neural Encoder (HRNE) to exploit temporal information in videos. Compared to existing video representation inference approaches, HRNE offers three key contributions: (1) Efficient exploitation of video temporal structure over longer ranges by reducing input information flow length and compositing multiple consecutive inputs at higher levels. (2) Significant reduction in computation operations while achieving greater non-linearity. (3) Ability to uncover temporal transitions between frame chunks with different granularities, modeling both transitions between frames and between segments. The method is applied to video captioning, where temporal information is essential. Experiments demonstrate that HRNE outperforms state-of-the-art methods on video captioning benchmarks, even surpassing systems that combine multiple inputs (RGB ConvNet plus 3D ConvNet) by using a single network with only RGB stream as input.
label: AI

title: God(s) Know(s): Developmental and Cross-Cultural Patterns in Children Drawings
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to data analysis tailored for specialists in the psychology of religion. The study focuses on detecting developmental and cross-cultural patterns in children's drawings of God(s) and other supernatural agents. The paper develops methods for objectively evaluating empirical observations of these drawings based on: (1) the gravity center, (2) the average intensities of the colors green and yellow, (3) the use of different colors (palette), and (4) the visual complexity of the drawings. Statistically significant differences across ages and countries were found in the gravity centers and average color intensities. These findings support the hypotheses of experts and raise new questions for further investigation.
label: AI

title: A Directional Diffusion Algorithm for Inpainting
Abstract: Image inpainting aims to reconstruct missing areas of an image, with applications in restoring old damaged photographs or removing obfuscations. This paper introduces the directional diffusion algorithm for inpainting. While traditional diffusion algorithms struggle to accurately propagate edges from the image into the unknown masked regions, the directional diffusion algorithm improves upon regular diffusion by more precisely reconstructing edges. This approach outperforms regular diffusion in reconstructing images obfuscated by a text mask.
label: AI

title: Visual7W: Grounded Question Answering in Images
Abstract: Despite significant progress in basic perceptual tasks like object recognition and detection, AI models still fall short of human capabilities in high-level vision tasks due to their limited reasoning abilities. Visual question answering (QA) has emerged as a new task for evaluating deep image understanding. Previous works have established a loose, global association between QA sentences and images. However, many questions and answers relate to specific image regions. This paper introduces object-level grounding to establish a semantic link between textual descriptions and image regions. This enables a new type of QA with visual answers in addition to the textual answers used previously. The paper investigates visual QA tasks in a grounded setting using a large collection of 7W multiple-choice QA pairs. It also evaluates human performance and several baseline models on these tasks. Finally, the paper proposes a novel LSTM model with spatial attention to address the 7W QA tasks.
label: AI

title: A GMM-Based Stair Quality Model for Human Perceived JPEG Images
Abstract: Based on the notion of just noticeable differences (JND), a stair quality function (SQF) was recently proposed to model human perception of JPEG images. A k-means clustering algorithm was used to aggregate JND data from multiple subjects, generating a single SQF. This work presents a new method for deriving the SQF using the Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM). The derived SQF represents the mean viewer experience and has a lower information criterion (BIC) value than the previous SQF, indicating a better model. A specific example highlights the advantages of this new approach.
label: AI

title: Multimodal MRI Neuroimaging with Motion Compensation Based on Particle Filtering
Abstract: Head movement during fMRI scanning hinders activation detection. While image registration can be used to align images onto a reference volume and compensate for motion in slice-based Echo Planar Imaging (EPI), volume-to-volume registration fails to account for head motion between slices, leading to biased estimates. Slice-to-volume registration provides more accurate motion parameters for each slice but is limited by information content, with middle slices being more informative than edge slices prone to distortion. This paper proposes a Gaussian particle filter based head motion tracking algorithm to reduce image misregistration errors. The algorithm utilizes a dynamic state space model of head motion with an observation equation that models continuous slice acquisition. This model enables the particle filter to generate more accurate motion and voxel position estimates. The approach demonstrates significant performance improvement compared to registration-only methods for head motion estimation and brain activation detection.
label: AI

title: Computational Pathology: Challenges and Promises for Tissue Analysis
Abstract: The histological assessment of human tissue is a crucial challenge for cancer detection and treatment. Multiple data sources, including tissue microarray data, gene expression, proteomics, and metabolomics data, provide a comprehensive view of a patient's health status. Medical doctors rely on data-driven automatic analysis tools to assess these information sources. Methods for classification, grouping, and segmentation of heterogeneous data sources, along with regression of noisy dependencies and estimation of survival probabilities, are incorporated into the processing workflow of a pathology diagnosis system at various stages. This paper reviews the state-of-the-art in computational pathology workflows and discusses future research directions in this emerging field of medical informatics and diagnostic machine learning.
label: AI

title: Write a Classifier: Predicting Visual Classifiers from Unstructured Text
Abstract: Humans typically learn through exposure to visual concepts associated with linguistic descriptions. Teaching visual object categories to children often involves textual or spoken descriptions. In a machine learning context, this motivates the question of whether this learning process can be computationally modeled to learn visual classifiers. Specifically, this work explores how to utilize purely textual descriptions of visual classes, without any training images, to learn explicit visual classifiers. The paper proposes and investigates two baseline formulations, based on regression and domain transfer, that predict a linear classifier. It then introduces a new constrained optimization formulation that combines a regression function and a knowledge transfer function with additional constraints to predict the parameters of a linear classifier. The paper also proposes generic kernelized models where a kernel classifier is predicted using the representer theorem. These models allow for the use of any two RKHS (Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space) kernel functions in the visual space and text space, respectively. Finally, a kernel function between unstructured text descriptions based on distributional semantics is proposed, showing an advantage in this setting and potential for other applications. All models were applied to predict visual classifiers on two fine-grained and challenging categorization datasets (CU Birds and Flower Datasets), with the results indicating successful predictions by the proposed model over several baselines.
label: AI

title: Selecting Near-Optimal Learners via Incremental Data Allocation
Abstract: This paper investigates a novel machine learning (ML) problem setting where small subsets of training data are sequentially allocated amongst a large set of classifiers. The goal is to select a classifier that achieves near-optimal accuracy when trained on all data while minimizing the cost of misallocated samples. This is motivated by large modern datasets and ML toolkits with numerous combinations of learning algorithms and hyper-parameters. Inspired by the principle of "optimism under uncertainty," the paper proposes Data Allocation using Upper Bounds (DAUB), a strategy that effectively achieves these objectives across various real-world datasets. The paper develops substantial theoretical support for DAUB in an idealized setting where the expected accuracy of a classifier trained on n samples is known exactly. Under these conditions, a rigorous sub-linear bound on the regret of the approach (in terms of misallocated data) and a rigorous bound on the suboptimality of the selected classifier are established. The accuracy estimates using real-world datasets only entail mild violations of the theoretical scenario, suggesting that the practical behavior of DAUB likely approaches the idealized behavior.
label: AI

title: An (MI)LP-based Primal Heuristic for 3-Architecture Connected Facility Location in Urban Access Network Design
Abstract: This paper investigates the 3-architecture Connected Facility Location Problem, which arises in the design of urban telecommunication access networks. An original optimization model for the problem is proposed, incorporating additional variables and constraints to account for wireless signal coverage. As the problem can be challenging even for modern optimization solvers, the paper proposes a primal heuristic that combines a probabilistic fixing procedure guided by specific Linear Programming relaxations with an exact MIP heuristic based on a very large neighborhood search. Computational experiments on realistic instances demonstrate that the proposed heuristic achieves significantly lower optimality gaps compared to a state-of-the-art solver.
label: AI

title: Evolving Non-linear Stacking Ensembles for Prediction of Go Player Attributes
Abstract: The paper presents an application of non-linear stacking ensembles for predicting Go player attributes. An evolutionary algorithm is used to create a diverse ensemble of base learners, which are then aggregated by a stacking ensemble. This methodology enables efficient prediction of various attributes of Go players based on sets of their games. These attributes can be quite general, and the paper focuses on predicting player strength and style.
label: AI

title: Bayes-Optimal Effort Allocation in Crowdsourcing: Bounds and Index Policies
Abstract: This paper considers effort allocation in crowdsourcing, where labeling tasks are assigned to imperfect homogeneous crowd workers to maximize overall accuracy within a continuous-time Bayesian setting, subject to budget and time constraints. The Bayes-optimal policy for this problem is the solution to a partially observable Markov decision process, but computational complexity renders it infeasible. Based on Lagrangian Relaxation techniques, the paper provides a computationally tractable instance-specific upper bound on the value of the Bayes-optimal policy. This bound can then be used to estimate the optimality gap of any sub-optimal policy. Inspired by the Whittle index for restless multiarmed bandits, the paper presents an index policy for effort allocation in crowdsourcing and demonstrates numerically that it outperforms other state-of-the-art methods and performs close to the optimal solution.
label: AI

title: Benders Decomposition for the Design of a Hub and Shuttle Public Transit System
Abstract: The BusPlus project aims to improve off-peak hours public transit services in Canberra, Australia. To address the challenge of covering a large geographic area, BusPlus proposes a hub and shuttle model, combining high-frequency bus routes between key hubs with a large number of shuttles connecting passengers from their origins to the nearest hub and from their last bus stop to their destinations. This paper focuses on designing the bus network and proposes an efficient solution method for this multimodal network design problem based on the Benders decomposition method. Starting from a MIP formulation of the problem, the paper presents a Benders decomposition approach using dedicated solution techniques for independent sub-problems, Pareto optimal cuts, cut bundling, and core point update. Computational results using real-world data from Canberra's public transit system justify the design choices and demonstrate that the approach outperforms the MIP formulation by two orders of magnitude. Moreover, the results show that the hub and shuttle model can reduce transit time by a factor of 2 while remaining within the costs of the existing transit system.

title: A Notation for Markov Decision Processes

title: Nonparametric Bayesian Factor Analysis for Dynamic Count Matrices
Abstract: A gamma process dynamic Poisson factor analysis model is proposed to factorize a dynamic count matrix with sequentially observed count vectors. The model introduces a novel Markov chain that utilizes the latent gamma random variables at time (t-1) as shape parameters for those at time t, which are linked to observed or latent counts under the Poisson likelihood. The significant challenge of inferring the gamma shape parameters is addressed using unique data augmentation and marginalization techniques for the negative binomial distribution. The same nonparametric Bayesian model also applies to factorizing a dynamic binary matrix through a Bernoulli-Poisson link that connects a binary observation to a latent count, with closed-form conditional posteriors for the latent counts and efficient computation for sparse observations. The model is applied to text and music analysis, demonstrating state-of-the-art results.

title: Evaluating Go Game Records for Prediction of Player Attributes
Abstract: This paper proposes a method for extracting and aggregating per-move evaluations from sets of Go game records. The evaluations capture various aspects of the games, including played patterns and statistics of sente/gote sequences. These evaluations can be used to predict relevant target variables using machine learning algorithms. The paper applies this methodology to predict player strength and playing style (e.g., territoriality or aggressivity) with good accuracy. Potential applications include assisting Go study, seeding real-world ranks of internet players, and tuning Go-playing programs.

title: Simple, Robust and Optimal Ranking from Pairwise Comparisons
Abstract: This paper considers data in the form of pairwise comparisons of n items, with the goal of accurately identifying the top k items for some value of k < n, or alternatively, recovering a ranking of all items. The paper analyzes the Copeland counting algorithm, which ranks items based on the number of pairwise comparisons won, and shows that it has three key features: (a) its computational efficiency leads to significant speed-ups compared to previous work; (b) its robustness is ensured by theoretical guarantees that impose no conditions on the underlying matrix of pairwise-comparison probabilities, unlike some prior work that applies only to the BTL parametric model; and (c) it is an optimal method up to constant factors, achieving the information-theoretic limits for recovering the top k-subset. The paper extends these results to obtain sharp guarantees for approximate recovery under the Hamming distortion metric and more generally, to any arbitrary error requirement satisfying a simple and natural monotonicity condition.

title: Modeling Variations of First-Order Horn Abduction in Answer Set Programming
Abstract: This paper studies abduction in First Order Horn logic theories where all atoms can be abduced, aiming to find preferred solutions with respect to three objective functions: cardinality minimality, coherence, and weighted abduction. The paper represents this reasoning problem in Answer Set Programming (ASP) to create a flexible framework for experimenting with global constraints and objective functions, testing the boundaries of what is possible with ASP. Implementing this problem in ASP is challenging as it requires value invention and equivalence between certain constants, as the Unique Names Assumption does not hold universally. To enable reasoning in cyclic theories, the paper formally describes fine-grained variations of limiting Skolemization. Term equivalence is identified as a primary instantiation bottleneck, and the efficiency of the approach is improved using on-demand constraints to address this bottleneck, as seen in state-of-the-art solvers. The approach is evaluated experimentally on the ACCEL benchmark for plan recognition in Natural Language Understanding. The encodings are publicly available, modular, and the approach is more efficient than state-of-the-art solvers on the ACCEL benchmark. |||

title: Closing the Gap Between Short and Long XORs for Model Counting
Abstract: Many recent algorithms for approximate model counting rely on reducing the problem to combinatorial searches over random subsets of the space defined by parity or XOR constraints. While long parity constraints (involving many variables) offer strong theoretical guarantees, they are computationally challenging. Conversely, short parity constraints are easier to solve but have weaker statistical properties. The optimal length of these parity constraints remains unknown. This paper addresses this gap by providing matching necessary and sufficient conditions for the required asymptotic length of the parity constraints. Furthermore, we introduce a novel family of lower bounds and the first non-trivial upper bounds on the model count that are valid for arbitrarily short XORs. The effectiveness of these bounds is demonstrated empirically on model counting benchmarks and in a Satisfiability Modulo Theory (SMT) application motivated by the analysis of contingency tables in statistics.

title: Learning Natural Language Inference with LSTM
Abstract: Natural language inference (NLI) is a crucial task in natural language processing with numerous applications. The recent release of the Stanford Natural Language Inference (SNLI) corpus has enabled the development and evaluation of learning-centered methods, such as deep neural networks, for NLI. This paper proposes a specialized long short-term memory (LSTM) architecture for NLI, building upon a previously proposed neural attention model but employing a significantly different approach. Instead of generating sentence embeddings for the premise and hypothesis for classification, our solution utilizes a match-LSTM to perform word-by-word matching of the hypothesis with the premise. This LSTM effectively emphasizes important word-level matching results, particularly remembering significant mismatches that are critical for predicting contradiction or neutral relationship labels. Our model achieves an accuracy of 86.1% on the SNLI corpus, surpassing the state-of-the-art.

title: Internet of Things for Residential Areas: Toward Personalized Energy Management Using Big Data
Abstract: Intelligent management of machines, particularly in residential areas, has been a focus of research for many years. However, system design has historically been limited to simple local or remote control via the internet. This report proposes an innovative intelligent system that not only provides intelligent control capabilities for machines to users but also leverages big data and optimization techniques to offer personalized promotions for optimizing energy consumption. Due to the high traffic communication involved among machines and the optimization-big data core of the system, the communication core is designed based on the cloud, posing challenges such as spectrum assignment and resource management. To address these challenges, the communication network in the home area network (HAN) is designed based on the cognitive radio system, incorporating a novel spectrum assignment method based on the ant colony optimization (ACO) algorithm for allocating spectrum to machines in the HAN. Performance evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed spectrum assignment method in achieving fair spectrum allocation among machines.

title: Combining Fuzzy Cognitive Maps and Discrete Random Variables
Abstract: This paper proposes an extension to Fuzzy Cognitive Maps (FCMs) aimed at aggregating multiple reasoning tasks into a single parallel run. The approach replaces real-valued activation levels of concepts (and influence weights) with random variables. This extension, along with the implemented software tool, enables determining ranges reached by concept activation levels, sensitivity analysis, and statistical analysis of multiple reasoning results. The paper replaces multiplication and addition operators in the FCM state equation with appropriate convolutions applicable for discrete random variables. To ensure computational feasibility, the model is further augmented with aggregation operations for discrete random variables. Four implemented aggregators are discussed, and the results of preliminary tests are reported.

title: Interactive Discovery of Coordinated Relationship Chains with Maximum Entropy Models
Abstract: Modern visual analytic tools promote human-in-the-loop analysis but are limited in their ability to guide users towards interesting and promising directions of study. This limitation is particularly acute during exploratory analysis, such as the discovery of potentially coordinated relationships in massive text datasets. Such tasks are prevalent in domains like intelligence analysis and security forensics, where the goal is to uncover unexpected coalitions spanning multiple types of relations. We introduce novel maximum entropy models for discovering surprising chains of relationships leveraging count data about entity occurrences in documents. These models are embedded in a visual analytic system called MERCER that treats relationship bundles as first-class objects and directs users towards promising lines of inquiry. We demonstrate how user input can effectively guide analysis towards valid conclusions, while a purely algorithmic approach might be misled. Experimental results on both synthetic and real datasets from the intelligence community are presented.

title: On the Foundations of the Brussels Operational-Realistic Approach to Cognition
Abstract: The scientific community is increasingly interested in applying the mathematical formalism of quantum theory to model human decision-making. This paper provides the theoretical foundations of the quantum approach to cognition developed in Brussels. These foundations are based on two decades of research on axiomatic and operational-realistic approaches to the foundations of quantum physics. Deep analogies between the foundations of physics and cognition motivate the investigation of quantum theory's validity as a general and unified framework for cognitive processes. The empirical success of the Hilbert space models derived from this investigation provides strong theoretical confirmation of this validity. However, two situations in the cognitive realm, "question order effects" and "response replicability", suggest that even the Hilbert space framework may be insufficient to reproduce collected data. This does not invalidate the operational-realistic approach, but rather indicates that a larger class of measurements may be in effect in human cognition, necessitating an extended quantum formalism to encompass them. As explained, the recently derived "extended Bloch representation" of quantum theory (and the associated "general tension-reduction" model) precisely provides such an extended formalism, while remaining within the same unitary interpretative framework.

title: Taming the Noise in Reinforcement Learning via Soft Updates
Abstract: Model-free reinforcement learning algorithms, such as Q-learning, exhibit poor performance in the early stages of learning in noisy environments. This is attributed to the significant effort spent unlearning biased estimates of the state-action value function. The bias arises from selecting the apparent optimum, which may be suboptimal, among several noisy estimates. We propose G-learning, a novel off-policy learning algorithm that regularizes value estimates by penalizing deterministic policies at the beginning of the learning process. We demonstrate that this method reduces the bias of value-function estimation, leading to faster convergence to the optimal value and policy. Furthermore, G-learning enables the natural incorporation of prior domain knowledge, when available. The stochastic nature of G-learning also mitigates some exploration costs, a property usually attributed only to on-policy algorithms. These ideas are illustrated through several examples, where G-learning results in substantial improvements in convergence rate and the cost of the learning process.

title: Conditional probability generation methods for high reliability effects-based decision making
Abstract: Decision making often relies on Bayesian networks, whose building blocks are conditional probability tables (CPTs). These tables are obtained through parameter estimation methods or elicited from subject matter experts (SMEs). However, some of these knowledge representations are insufficient approximations. Knowledge fusion of cause and effect observations can lead to improved predictive decisions. We propose three novel methods for generating CPTs, even when only soft evidence is provided. The first two methods are novel ways of mapping conditional expectations to the probability space. The third is a column extraction method that obtains CPTs from nonlinear functions like multinomial logistic regression. Case studies on military effects and burnt forest desertification have demonstrated that these derived CPTs exhibit highly reliable predictive power, surpassing the CPTs obtained from SMEs. In this context, new quality measures for determining the goodness of a CPT and for comparing CPTs have been introduced. The predictive power and enhanced reliability of decision making based on the novel CPT generation methods presented in this paper have been confirmed and validated within the case study context.

title: Mining Massive Hierarchical Data Using a Scalable Probabilistic Graphical Model
Abstract: Probabilistic Graphical Models (PGM) are highly valuable in the fields of machine learning and data mining. However, a crucial limitation of these models is scalability. Bayesian Networks, one of the most common PGMs used in machine learning and data mining, exhibit this limitation when training data consists of random variables, each with a large set of possible values. In the big data era, new extensions to existing PGMs are needed to handle the massive amounts of data generated by computers, sensors, and other electronic devices. Hierarchical data, arranged in a tree-like structure with multiple levels, can have hundreds of thousands or millions of values distributed across even a small number of levels. When modeling this type of hierarchical data across large datasets, Bayesian Networks become impractical for representing probability distributions. This paper introduces an extension to Bayesian Networks for handling massive sets of hierarchical data in a reasonable amount of time and space. The proposed model achieves perfect precision of 1.0 and high recall of 0.93 when used as a multi-label classifier for annotating mass spectrometry data. On another dataset of 1.5 billion search logs from CareerBuilder.com, the model was able to predict latent semantic relationships between search keywords with an accuracy of up to 0.80.

title: GELATO and SAGE: An Integrated Framework for MS Annotation
Abstract: Several algorithms and tools have been developed to (semi) automate glycan identification by interpreting mass spectrometric data. However, each has limitations when annotating MSn data with thousands of MS spectra using uncurated public databases. Moreover, existing tools are not designed to manage MSn data where n > 2. We propose a novel software package to automate the annotation of tandem MS data. This software comprises two major components. The first is a free, semi-automated MSn data interpreter called the Glycomic Elucidation and Annotation Tool (GELATO). This tool extends and automates the functionality of existing open source projects, namely, GlycoWorkbench (GWB) and GlycomeDB. The second is a machine learning model called Smart Anotation Enhancement Graph (SAGE), which learns the behavior of glycoanalysts to select annotations generated by GELATO that emulate human interpretation of the spectra.

title: Regularized Orthogonal Tensor Decompositions for Multi-Relational Learning
Abstract: Multi-relational learning has garnered significant attention from researchers in various research communities. Most existing methods either suffer from superlinear per-iteration cost or are sensitive to the given ranks. To address both issues, we propose a scalable core tensor trace norm regularized Orthogonal Iteration Decomposition (ROID) method for full or incomplete tensor analytics. This method can be generalized as a graph Laplacian regularized version by using auxiliary information or a sparse higher-order orthogonal iteration (SHOOI) version. We first establish the equivalence relation of the Schatten p-norm (0 < p < ∞) of a low multi-linear rank tensor and its core tensor. Then, we achieve a significantly smaller matrix trace norm minimization problem. Finally, we develop two efficient augmented Lagrange multiplier algorithms to solve our problems with convergence guarantees. Extensive experiments using both real and synthetic datasets, even with limited observations, verify the efficiency and effectiveness of our methods.

title: Using Data Analytics to Detect Anomalous States in Vehicles
Abstract: Vehicles are becoming increasingly connected, expanding the attack surface and affecting not only passengers inside vehicles but also people around them. These vulnerabilities arise from the relatively less secure and outdated CAN bus framework, lacking even basic authentication. Since a new protocol can only benefit future vehicles, our approach tackles this issue as a data analytics problem, employing machine learning techniques to secure cars. We develop a Hidden Markov Model to detect anomalous states from real data collected from vehicles. This model enables the detection and alerting of anomalies while a vehicle is in operation. Our model can be integrated as a plug-and-play device in both new and older cars.

title: Device and System Level Design Considerations for Analog-Non-Volatile-Memory Based Neuromorphic Architectures
Abstract: This paper provides an overview of recent advancements in the brain-inspired computing field, focusing on implementation using emerging memories as electronic synapses. Design considerations and challenges are presented, including requirements and design targets for multilevel states, device variability, programming energy, array-level connectivity, fan-in/fan-out, wire energy, and IR drop. Wires are becoming increasingly important in design decisions, especially for large systems, and cycle-to-cycle variations have a significant impact on learning performance.

title: Toward a Research Agenda in Adversarial Reasoning: Computational Approaches to Anticipating the Opponent's Intent and Actions
Abstract: This paper defines adversarial reasoning as computational approaches for inferring and anticipating an enemy's perceptions, intentions, and actions. It argues that adversarial reasoning goes beyond the boundaries of game theory and must also leverage disciplines such as cognitive modeling, control theory, AI planning, and others. To illustrate the challenges of applying adversarial reasoning to real-world problems, the paper examines lessons learned from CADET, a battle planning system focusing on brigade-level ground operations that involves adversarial reasoning. Building upon this example of current capabilities, the paper describes RAID, a DARPA program aimed at developing capabilities in adversarial reasoning, and how these capabilities would address practical requirements in defense and other application areas.

title: Multi-Level Cause-Effect Systems
Abstract: We present a domain-general account of causation that applies to settings where macro-level causal relations between two systems are of interest, but the relevant causal features are poorly understood and must be aggregated from vast arrays of micro-measurements. Our approach generalizes that of Chalupka et al. (2015) to the setting where the macro-level effect is not specified. We formalize the connection between micro- and macro-variables in such situations and provide a coherent framework describing causal relations at multiple levels of analysis. We present an algorithm that discovers macro-variable causes and effects from micro-level measurements obtained from an experiment. We further show how to design experiments to discover macro-variables from observational micro-variable data. Finally, we show that under specific conditions, one can identify multiple levels of causal structure. Throughout the article, we use a simulated neuroscience multi-unit recording experiment to illustrate the ideas and the algorithms.

title: Probabilistic Model-Based Approach for Heart Beat Detection
Abstract: Hospitals are ubiquitous and integral to modern society. Patients navigate a complex system of paperwork, consultations, and potential inpatient admissions, which is not without flaws. One of the most significant flaws in the medical system is perhaps an unexpected one: the patient alarm system. A longitudinal study reported an 88.8% rate of false alarms, with other studies reporting similar numbers. These false alarm rates lead to various detrimental effects that significantly lower the standard of care across clinics. This paper discusses a model-based probabilistic inference approach for identifying variables at a detection level. We design a generative model that aligns with an overview of human physiology and perform approximate Bayesian inference. A primary goal of this paper is to justify a Bayesian modeling approach for increasing robustness in a physiological domain. We utilize three datasets provided by Physionet, a research resource for complex physiological signals, in the form of the Physionet 2014 Challenge set-p1 and set-p2, as well as the MGH/MF Waveform Database. On the extended dataset, our algorithm performs on par with the other top six submissions to the Physionet 2014 challenge.

title: RDF2Rules: Learning Rules from RDF Knowledge Bases by Mining Frequent Predicate Cycles
Abstract: Recently, several large-scale RDF knowledge bases have been built and applied in numerous knowledge-based applications. To further increase the number of facts in RDF knowledge bases, logic rules can be used to predict new facts based on existing ones. Therefore, automatically learning reliable rules from large-scale knowledge bases is becoming increasingly important. This paper proposes a novel rule learning approach named RDF2Rules for RDF knowledge bases. RDF2Rules first mines frequent predicate cycles (FPCs), a type of interesting frequent patterns in knowledge bases, and then generates rules from the mined FPCs. Because each FPC can produce multiple rules, and an effective pruning strategy is used during FPC mining, RDF2Rules operates very efficiently. Another advantage of RDF2Rules is its use of entity type information when generating and evaluating rules, which improves the accuracy of learned rules. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms the compared approach in terms of both efficiency and accuracy.

title: Measuring pattern retention in anonymized data -- where one measure is not enough
Abstract: This paper explores the impact of modifying data to preserve privacy on the quality of discoverable patterns within the data. For any analysis of modified data to be valuable, the data must be as close to the original as possible. This raises the question of how to ensure that modified data still retains the information it had before modification. This question is distinct from asking whether an accurate classifier can be built from the modified data. The literature often uses the prediction accuracy of a classifier built from modified (anonymized) data as evidence of data similarity to the original. We demonstrate that this is not always the case and propose a new methodology for measuring the retention of patterns that existed in the original data. We then use our methodology to design three measures that are easily implementable, each measuring aspects of the data that no pre-existing techniques can measure. These measures do not negate the usefulness of prediction accuracy or other measures; they complement them and support our argument that one measure is rarely sufficient.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning in Large Discrete Action Spaces
Abstract: The ability to reason in an environment with a large number of discrete actions is crucial for extending reinforcement learning to a broader range of problems. Recommender systems, industrial plants, and language models are just a few examples of real-world tasks involving large numbers of discrete actions for which current methods are difficult or even impossible to apply. The ability to generalize over the set of actions and sub-linear complexity relative to the size of the set are both necessary to handle such tasks. Existing approaches fail to provide both of these, motivating the work presented in this paper. Our proposed approach leverages prior information about the actions to embed them in a continuous space where generalization is possible. Additionally, approximate nearest-neighbor methods allow for logarithmic-time lookup complexity relative to the number of actions, which is necessary for time-wise tractable training. This combined approach enables reinforcement learning methods to be applied to large-scale learning problems previously intractable with current methods. We demonstrate our algorithm's capabilities on a series of tasks with up to one million actions.

title: Composite Bayesian inference
Abstract: We revisit and generalize the concept of composite likelihood as a method for probabilistic inference through the aggregation of multiple Bayesian agents, thereby defining a class of predictive models we call composite Bayesian. This perspective provides insights into choosing the weights associated with composite likelihood, either a priori or through learning. In the latter case, weights can be tuned to minimize prediction cross-entropy, resulting in an easy-to-solve convex problem. We argue that composite Bayesian inference offers a middle ground between generative and discriminative models, trading off interpretability and prediction performance, both of which are critical to many artificial intelligence tasks. |||

title: The Max $K$-Armed Bandit: PAC Lower Bounds and Efficient Algorithms
Abstract: The Max K-Armed Bandit problem involves an agent trying to find the most valuable item from a collection of stochastic arms with unknown reward distributions. We establish a lower bound on the sample complexity of any (epsilon, delta)-correct algorithm under the assumption of a known lower bound on the tail function of the reward distributions. We propose an algorithm that achieves this bound up to logarithmic factors and analyze its robustness. Additionally, we compare its performance to a variant where arms are indistinguishable and randomly chosen. Interestingly, when the maximal rewards are similar, the random approach might outperform the proposed algorithm.

title: Representation and Coding of Signal Geometry
Abstract: Traditional signal representation and coding theory aims to achieve the most concise representation of signals with minimal distortion. This paper explores a different approach where the objective is to preserve specific information about the signal rather than the signal itself. We investigate the problem of encoding signals to preserve pairwise distances and inner products using randomized embeddings. We analyze the performance of these embeddings and demonstrate the possibility of representing different ranges of distances with varying precision. Our findings provide a framework for designing and analyzing embeddings, generalizing existing techniques like random Fourier kernels and universal embeddings.

title: Randomized Social Choice Functions Under Metric Preferences
Abstract: This paper analyzes the quality of randomized social choice mechanisms in a setting where agents have metric preferences. We assume the mechanisms (and possibly the agents themselves) do not know these preferences, which prevents us from simply selecting the optimal alternative that minimizes the total cost. Instead, we rely on agents' ordinal preferences induced by the metric space. We explore randomized social choice functions that utilize this ordinal information and select an alternative that performs well in expectation with respect to the metric costs. We quantify the performance by bounding the distortion, which represents the ratio between the expected cost of the chosen alternative and the cost of the optimal one. Our work presents new distortion bounds for various randomized mechanisms, both for general metrics and specific cases, demonstrating significant improvement in distortion compared to deterministic mechanisms.

title: Selecting the top-quality item through crowd scoring
Abstract: This paper investigates crowdsourcing algorithms for identifying the top-quality item from a large collection of objects with unknown quality values. These algorithms rely on crowd workers providing noisy and biased evaluations of objects. We propose a probabilistic model for the system and develop a class of efficient adaptive algorithms that effectively assign objects to workers. Through simulations, we compare the performance of different algorithms with varying design parameters and metrics. Our findings show that certain algorithms achieve near-optimal performance for specific system parameter settings.

title: Adaptive Ensemble Learning with Confidence Bounds
Abstract: Extracting actionable intelligence from distributed, heterogeneous, correlated, and high-dimensional data sources requires real-time processing and learning at both local and global levels. We present a systematic ensemble learning method called Hedged Bandits, which provides performance guarantees for both long-term (asymptotic) and short-term (rate of learning) behavior. Our approach guarantees performance relative to the optimal local prediction strategy and adapts predictions based on data. We illustrate the effectiveness of Hedged Bandits in the context of medical informatics, demonstrating superior performance compared to other online and offline ensemble learning methods.

title: A Learning Algorithm for Change Impact Prediction
Abstract: Change impact analysis predicts the impact of code changes in software applications. We propose a learning-based approach to this problem, where methods of object-oriented software are considered artifacts, code changes are the subject of study, and the impact is measured by failed test methods due to the change. Our algorithm, called LCIP, learns from past impacts to predict future ones. We evaluate LCIP using 7 Java applications totaling 214,000+ lines of code, simulating 17574 changes and their actual impacts through code mutations. Our results show that LCIP achieves a precision of 69%, a recall of 79%, and an F-Score of 55% in predicting change impact.

title: The ERA of FOLE: Foundation
Abstract: This paper discusses the representation of ontologies within the first-order logical environment FOLE. Ontologies define the fundamental elements used to model knowledge resources for a specific community of discourse, including classes, relationships, and properties. Formal axioms constrain the interpretation of these elements, defining a logical theory. We continue the discussion of ontology representation and interpretation in FOLE, exploring both the classification and interpretation forms of first-order logic. Two papers, this one defining the concept of a structure and "The ERA of FOLE: Superstructure" defining sound logic, represent the classification form. Two other papers, "The FOLE Table" defining relational tables and "The FOLE Database" defining relational databases, represent the interpretation form. Finally, "FOLE Equivalence" demonstrates the equivalence between the classification and interpretation forms. The FOLE representation utilizes a conceptual structures approach compatible with theories of institutions, formal concept analysis, and information flow.

title: A Deep Generative Deconvolutional Image Model
Abstract: This paper presents a deep generative model for image representation and analysis based on a hierarchical convolutional dictionary-learning framework. Stochastic unpooling links consecutive layers in the model, enabling top-down image generation. A Bayesian support vector machine is connected to the top-layer features for max-margin discrimination. During testing, deep deconvolutional inference infers latent features, and the top-layer features are used for discrimination tasks. The model is efficiently trained using a Monte Carlo expectation-maximization (MCEM) algorithm implemented on GPUs, enabling large-scale learning and fast testing. The model achieves competitive results on benchmark datasets like ImageNet, demonstrating its effectiveness in image representation and analysis.

title: Heuristic algorithms for finding distribution reducts in probabilistic rough set model
Abstract: Attribute reduction is a key concept in rough set theory, with heuristic algorithms often used for this purpose. Fitness functions play a crucial role in developing these algorithms, and their monotonicity guarantees the validity of the algorithms. In probabilistic rough set models, distribution reducts ensure that decision rules derived from the reducts are consistent with those from the original decision table. However, developing heuristic attribute reduction algorithms for finding distribution reducts is challenging due to the lack of monotonic fitness functions. This paper proposes two monotonic fitness functions that yield equivalence definitions of distribution reducts. Additionally, two modified monotonic fitness functions are introduced to evaluate the significance of attributes more effectively. Based on these functions, we develop two heuristic attribute reduction algorithms using addition-deletion and deletion methods. The monotonicity of the fitness functions ensures the rationality of these algorithms. Experimental analysis quantifies the effectiveness of the proposed fitness functions and distribution reducts.

title: SR-Clustering: Semantic Regularized Clustering for Egocentric Photo Streams Segmentation
Abstract: Wearable cameras are gaining popularity, but finding relevant information within large, unstructured egocentric image collections remains a challenge. This paper addresses the problem of organizing egocentric photo streams into semantically meaningful segments. We extract contextual and semantic information for each image using a Convolutional Neural Network approach. By integrating language processing, a vocabulary of concepts is defined in a semantic space. Finally, exploiting temporal coherence in photo streams, images with similar contextual and semantic attributes are grouped together. This temporal segmentation facilitates further analysis, including activity and event recognition, semantic indexing, and summarization. Experiments on egocentric sets with nearly 17,000 images demonstrate the superiority of the proposed approach over state-of-the-art methods.

title: Implementing a Bayes Filter in a Neural Circuit: The Case of Unknown Stimulus Dynamics
Abstract: To interact intelligently with the world, animals must transform neural population responses into estimates of the dynamic stimuli that caused them. The Bayesian solution to this problem is a Bayes filter, which combines population responses with predictions from an internal model. This paper presents a method for learning to approximate a Bayes filter when stimulus dynamics are unknown. We leverage the inferential properties of probabilistic population codes to compute Bayes' rule and train a neural network to approximate predictions using maximum likelihood. Stochastic gradient descent is performed on the negative log-likelihood with a novel gradient approximation. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness on finite-state, linear, and nonlinear filtering problems, showing how the hidden layer of the neural network develops tuning curves consistent with experimental neuroscience findings.

title: Keeping it Short and Simple: Summarising Complex Event Sequences with Multivariate Patterns
Abstract: This paper explores how to obtain concise descriptions of discrete multivariate sequential data using rich multivariate sequential patterns. Our pattern language spans all sequence domains (alphabets), allows patterns to overlap temporally, and accommodates gaps in occurrences. We formalize our goal using the Minimum Description Length principle, aiming to discover the set of patterns that provides the most succinct data description. To achieve this, we introduce DITTO, a highly efficient algorithm that effectively approximates the ideal solution. Experiments demonstrate DITTO's ability to correctly discover patterns in synthetic data and its favorable scalability with data length, number of attributes, and alphabet sizes. On real datasets ranging from sensor networks to annotated text, DITTO discovers easily interpretable summaries that provide insights into both univariate and multivariate structures.

title: Beauty and Brains: Detecting Anomalous Pattern Co-Occurrences
Abstract: While our world has both beautiful and intelligent individuals, the combination of both traits is often rarer than expected. We focus on this class of anomaly: individuals who possess an unexpected combination of beauty and intelligence. This paper defines this anomaly class and proposes a method for identifying them quickly within transaction data. Our pattern set-based approach provides explanations for why a transaction is anomalous. The effectiveness of our method is rigorously validated through experiments on real-world and synthetic datasets.

title: News Across Languages - Cross-Lingual Document Similarity and Event Tracking
Abstract: News today is distributed globally, with significant events reported by various sources in multiple languages. This paper addresses the problem of tracking events within a large multilingual stream using Event Registry. We examine two aspects of this problem: comparing articles in different languages and linking collections of articles across languages that refer to the same event. We compare cross-lingual document similarity measures based on Wikipedia to compute the similarity of any two articles regardless of language. Building on previous work, we demonstrate scalable methods for computing meaningful similarity between articles from languages with limited or no direct overlap in training data. Using this capability, we propose an approach to link article clusters across languages that represent the same event. We provide an extensive evaluation of the overall system, including the quality and robustness of the similarity measure and the linking algorithm.

title: Evaluation of Time-Critical Communications for IEC 61850-Substation Network Architecture
Abstract: Present-day developments in electrical power transmission and distribution necessitate attention to reliability and environmental impact. This motivates the development of dependable systems, particularly intelligent (smart) grids. The International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) standard IEC 61850, a leading standard for substation automation systems (SAS) communications, promotes modern technological trends in this field. This standard emphasizes low end-to-end latency and time-critical status transmission. This experimental study focuses on the IEC 61850 SAS communication standard, specifically IEC 61850 GOOSE (Generic Object Oriented Substation Events), to implement an investigation method for determining protection communication delay. The method utilizes monitoring and analysis capabilities to observe GOOSE behavior. Network test equipment, such as SPAN (Switch Port Analyser) and TAP (Test Access Point) devices, are employed with readily available hardware and software solutions.
