title: On the Differential Privacy of Bayesian Inference
Abstract: We study how to communicate findings of Bayesian inference to third parties while preserving differential privacy guarantees. This paper presents four algorithms for private Bayesian inference on probabilistic graphical models. Two mechanisms are proposed for adding noise to Bayesian updates, either directly to the posterior parameters or to their Fourier transform to maintain update consistency. We also utilize a recently introduced posterior sampling mechanism and prove bounds for the specific case of discrete Bayesian networks. Finally, we introduce a maximum-a-posteriori private mechanism. Our analysis includes utility and privacy bounds, with a focus on the influence of graph structure on privacy. Worked examples and experiments with Bayesian naïve Bayes and Bayesian linear regression illustrate the application of our mechanisms.
label: AI

title: Restricted Predicates for Hypothetical Datalog
Abstract: Hypothetical Datalog, based on intuitionistic semantics rather than classical logic, allows embedded implications in rule bodies. While regular implications (in Horn clauses) are used for inferring facts, embedded implications assume their premise for deriving their consequence. This paper introduces a new concept, restricted predicates, that allows negative assumptions by pruning the usual semantics of a predicate. This extension enables negative assumptions in the premise of rules, building upon previous work that allowed positive assumptions for both facts and rules. This new setting has been implemented in the deductive system DES.
label: AI

title: An Evaluation of Yelp Dataset
Abstract: Yelp is a major online platform for searching and reviewing businesses. Analyzing real-world data from Yelp provides valuable insights into user interests, which can be used to improve the design of future systems. This paper analyzes the Yelp dataset provided in the Yelp Data Challenge and presents several interesting findings. For instance, the average path length in the Yelp social network is 4.5 hops, supporting the six degrees of separation theory. The Elite user mechanism is effective in maintaining network health. Users who write fewer than 100 reviews dominate the platform. These insights are expected to guide Yelp's future business decisions.
label: AI

title: Addressing Complex and Subjective Product-Related Queries with Customer Reviews
Abstract: Online reviews are a primary resource when making online purchases. However, finding relevant information in massive amounts of consumer reviews can be challenging. This paper explores how to automatically determine if a product review is relevant to a given query, fusing the paradigms of review browsing and Q/A systems. We formulate this as a machine learning problem using a mixture-of-experts framework, where each review acts as an expert voting on the response to a query. We simultaneously learn a relevance function that identifies "relevant" reviews as those that vote correctly. This relevance function enables us to surface relevant reviews on-demand for new queries. We evaluate our system, Moqa, on a novel corpus of 1.4 million questions and answers and 13 million reviews. Our findings show that Moqa effectively addresses both binary and open-ended queries and surfaces reviews considered relevant by human evaluators.
label: AI

title: Information-Theoretic Bounded Rationality
Abstract: Bounded rationality, or decision-making and planning under resource limitations, is a significant challenge in artificial intelligence, reinforcement learning, computational neuroscience, and economics. This paper presents a unified theory of bounded rationality based on information-theoretic ideas. We justify using the free energy functional as the objective function for characterizing bounded-rational decisions. This functional exhibits three crucial properties: it controls the solution space size; it enables exact Monte Carlo planners without exhaustive search; and it captures model uncertainty due to insufficient evidence or interactions with agents having unknown intentions. We discuss the single-step decision-making case and extend it to sequential decisions using equivalence transformations. This extension yields a general class of decision problems that encompass classical decision rules like EXPECTIMAX and MINIMAX as limiting cases, as well as trust- and risk-sensitive planning. |||
label: AI

title: Multivariate Time Series Classification Using Dynamic Time Warping Template Selection for Human Activity Recognition
Abstract: Accurate and computationally efficient methods for classifying human activities have been the subject of extensive research. Existing approaches often focus on extracting complex features to achieve high classification accuracy. This paper presents a novel template selection approach based on Dynamic Time Warping, which avoids the need for complex feature extraction and domain knowledge. The effectiveness of the proposed algorithm is demonstrated on both simulated and real smartphone data.
label: AI

title: Constrained Sampling and Counting: Universal Hashing Meets SAT Solving
Abstract: Constrained sampling and counting are fundamental problems in artificial intelligence with diverse applications, including probabilistic reasoning, planning, and constrained-random verification. While these problems were extensively studied in the 1980s, existing methods either failed to scale to industrial-size instances or sacrificed correctness guarantees for scalability. This paper presents a novel approach that combines universal hashing and SAT solving, achieving scalability to formulas with hundreds of thousands of variables without compromising correctness guarantees. Key ingredients of the approach are discussed along with challenges for handling larger real-world instances.
label: AI

title: Remote Health Coaching System and Human Motion Data Analysis for Physical Therapy with Microsoft Kinect
Abstract: This paper explores recent advancements in computer vision technologies for physical therapy using accessible and affordable devices. The authors introduce a remote health coaching system developed with Microsoft Kinect, addressing the issue of noisy motion data captured by the device. A data accuracy analysis of Kinect compared to a high-accuracy motion capture system is presented, along with an outlier data removal algorithm based on data distribution. To generate kinematic parameters from noisy Kinect data, a kinematic filtering algorithm based on Unscented Kalman Filter and the kinematic model of the human skeleton is proposed. This algorithm effectively reduces noise and produces smoother kinematic parameters compared to raw Kinect data.
label: AI

title: Serifos: Workload Consolidation and Load Balancing for SSD Based Cloud Storage Systems
Abstract: Achieving high performance in virtualized data centers requires both deploying high-throughput storage clusters based on Solid State Disks (SSDs) and optimally consolidating workloads across storage nodes. Current cloud storage providers often over-provision storage nodes to guarantee performance, as existing workload scheduling mechanisms lack the intelligence to allocate block storage volumes optimally based on SSD performance. This paper introduces Serifos, an autonomous performance modeling and load balancing system designed for SSD-based cloud storage. Serifos considers SSD storage unit characteristics and constructs hardware-dependent workload consolidation models, predicting latency caused by workload interference and average latency for concurrent workloads. Furthermore, Serifos utilizes an I/O load balancing algorithm to dynamically balance volumes across the cluster. Experimental results demonstrate that Serifos's consolidation model effectively maintains a mean prediction error of around 10% for heterogeneous hardware. The load balancing capabilities of Serifos significantly reduce latency variance and maximum average latency by 82% and 52%, respectively. The supported Service Level Objectives (SLOs) on the testbed show improvements of 43% in average latency, 32% in maximum read latency, and 63% in maximum write latency.
label: AI

title: Towards Integrated Glance To Restructuring in Combinatorial Optimization
Abstract: This paper introduces a new class of combinatorial problems focusing on restructuring solutions (sets/structures) in combinatorial optimization. The restructuring process is characterized by two main features: the cost of restructuring and the closeness to a goal solution. Three types of restructuring problems are investigated: one-stage structuring, multi-stage structuring, and structuring over changed element sets. Both one-criterion and multicriteria problem formulations are considered. These restructuring problems correspond to redesign, improvement, or upgrade of modular systems or solutions. The paper provides a detailed description and illustration (problem statements, solving schemes, examples) of the restructuring approach for various combinatorial optimization problems, including the knapsack problem, multiple choice problem, assignment problem, spanning tree problems, clustering problem, multicriteria ranking (sorting) problem, and morphological clique problem. Numerical examples illustrate the restructuring problems and solving schemes.
label: AI

title: A Mathematical Theory of Deep Convolutional Neural Networks for Feature Extraction
Abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks have achieved remarkable results in numerous machine learning tasks, including image classification, control-policy learning for games, and image captioning. Many of these applications first perform feature extraction followed by a trainable classifier. This paper extends the mathematical analysis of deep convolutional neural networks for feature extraction initiated by Mallat in 2012. The authors develop a theory encompassing general convolutional transforms (semi-discrete frames), general Lipschitz-continuous non-linearities, and general Lipschitz-continuous pooling operators. These elements can vary across different network layers. For the resulting feature extractor, the authors prove a translation invariance result, demonstrating progressively increasing translation invariance with network depth. Deformation sensitivity bounds are established for signal classes such as band-limited functions, cartoon functions, and Lipschitz functions.
label: AI

title: Test-Driven Development of ontologies (extended version)
Abstract: Emerging ontology authoring methods focus on ameliorating the validation bottleneck in knowledge addition to ontologies. However, verification of newly added axioms remains a trial-and-error process due to the absence of a systematic testbed for ontology authoring. This paper addresses this issue by introducing a test-driven development approach for ontology authoring. The authors define 36 generic tests as TBox queries and TBox axioms tested through individuals, providing a transparent structure covering OWL 2 DL language features. This approach is implemented as a Protege plugin, enabling TDD tests as black box tests. The authors evaluate the performance of two test approaches, demonstrating faster execution times for TBox queries, especially in larger ontologies. A general sequence of a TDD process for ontology engineering is presented as a foundation for a TDD methodology.
label: AI

title: Ontology-driven Information Extraction
Abstract: Homogeneous unstructured data (HUD) refers to collections of unstructured documents sharing common properties like similar layout, file format, or domain of values. To access main information through a semantic layer (ontology) called semantic view, this paper proposes an ontology-based approach for extracting semantically rich information from HUD. This approach integrates and extends recent technologies and results from information extraction, table recognition, ontologies, text annotation, and logic programming. The authors design and implement a system named KnowRex, successfully applied to curriculum vitae in the Europass style, offering a semantic view and enabling tasks like selecting candidates based on required skills.
label: AI

title: Can Pretrained Neural Networks Detect Anatomy?
Abstract: Convolutional neural networks have shown outstanding performance in computer vision and speech recognition tasks with abundant labeled training data. However, medical imaging presents a challenge due to a vast variety of imaging modalities and contrasts, where annotated data is scarce. This paper proposes two approaches to address this challenge: using a network pretrained in a different domain with abundant data as a feature extractor, followed by training a classifier on a small target dataset; and using a deep architecture trained with heavy augmentation and sophisticated regularization methods. These approaches are tested on a corpus of X-ray images to design an anatomy detection system.
label: AI

title: A Planning based Framework for Essay Generation
Abstract: Generating an article automatically with a computer program is a challenging task in artificial intelligence and natural language processing. This paper focuses on essay generation, which takes a topic word as input and generates an organized article under the theme of the topic. Following the idea of text planning, the authors develop an essay generation framework consisting of three components: topic understanding, sentence extraction, and sentence reordering. For each component, several statistical algorithms are explored and compared empirically in terms of qualitative and quantitative analysis. While experiments are conducted on a Chinese corpus, the method is language-independent and easily adaptable to other languages. The authors outline remaining challenges and suggest avenues for future research.
label: AI

title: Quadripolar Relational Model: a framework for the description of borderline and narcissistic personality disorders
Abstract: Borderline personality disorder and narcissistic personality disorder are important nosographic entities that have been intensively investigated. The prevailing psychodynamic theory for mental disorders focuses on the repertoire of defense mechanisms employed. Another line of research explores psychological traumas and dissociation as defensive responses. Both theories shed light on aspects of pathological mental functioning and share points of contact. This work integrates these two psychological theories and builds a model of mental function in a relational context called the Quadripolar Relational Model. Enriched with ideas from computer science, the model leads to a novel therapeutic proposal for psychological traumas and personality disorders.
label: AI

title: On Voting and Facility Location
Abstract: This paper investigates mechanisms for candidate selection that minimize social cost, where voters and candidates are represented as points in an underlying metric space. The social cost of a candidate is the sum of its distances to all voters. Some results focus on modeling points on a real line, while others are more general. The authors explore the connection between candidate selection and facility location problems, noting that candidate selection involves a fixed set of candidates while facility location considers every point in the metric space as a potential candidate. This leads to three types of mechanisms: voting, ranking, and location mechanisms, differing in their input space granularity. The paper analyzes the relationships between these mechanism classes. While Black's 1948 median algorithm appears optimal for candidate selection on the line, the authors demonstrate otherwise, providing matching upper and lower bounds for various settings. The universally truthful spike mechanism achieves a tight approximation of two when candidates and voters are on the line. The paper examines desirable properties of candidate selection mechanisms, including efficiency, truthfulness, and simplicity, quantifying the impact of truthfulness and simplicity on efficiency.
label: AI

title: Modeling Progress in AI
Abstract: Recent discussions on AI-related issues, including intelligence explosion and technological unemployment, have yielded diverse claims about the nature, pace, and drivers of AI progress. However, these theories lack sufficient detail for systematic evaluation of their assumptions or quantitative extrapolation of progress. This paper contributes to a research program on rigorous AI progress modeling by suggesting ways to account for the relationship between hardware speed increases and algorithmic improvements in AI, the role of human inputs in enabling AI capabilities, and the relationships between different sub-fields of AI. The authors outline how to tailor AI progress models to generate insights on technological unemployment and propose future research directions on AI progress.
label: AI

title: Learning the Preferences of Ignorant, Inconsistent Agents
Abstract: Machine learning plays a crucial role in understanding human values, informing decisions about content recommendation, job or activity selection, and other areas where past choices reveal preferences. Assuming that choices are approximately optimal according to a utility function, preference inference can be framed as Bayesian inverse planning. This involves inverting an optimal decision-making process to infer a posterior distribution on utility functions given a prior and observed choices. However, people often deviate from approximate optimality due to factors like false beliefs, suboptimal planning, and temporal inconsistencies. This paper demonstrates how to incorporate these deviations into preference inference algorithms by constructing generative models of planning for agents susceptible to false beliefs and time inconsistency. The authors explore inferences these models make about preferences, beliefs, and biases. A behavioral experiment is conducted, where human subjects perform preference inference based on the same choice observations as the model. Results show that humans, like the model, explain choices in terms of systematic deviations from optimal behavior and suggest that they consider such deviations when inferring preferences.
label: AI

title: A Survey of Available Corpora for Building Data-Driven Dialogue Systems
Abstract: The past decade has witnessed significant breakthroughs in speech and language understanding from data-driven models. However, progress in dialogue systems is less evident, with most practical systems relying on extensive engineering and expert knowledge. Recent research suggests that data-driven approaches are feasible and promising in this area. To facilitate research, this paper presents a comprehensive survey of publicly available datasets suitable for data-driven learning of dialogue systems. The authors discuss key dataset characteristics, their use in learning diverse dialogue strategies, and other potential applications. They also examine methods for transfer learning between datasets and the use of external knowledge. Finally, the authors discuss appropriate evaluation metrics for the learning objective.
label: AI

title: Probabilistic Programming with Gaussian Process Memoization
Abstract: Gaussian Processes (GPs) are widely used in statistics, machine learning, robotics, computer vision, and scientific computation. Despite their popularity, GPs can be challenging to apply, as complex covariance functions often require specification and inference over analytical posteriors. This paper demonstrates how to embed Gaussian processes in any higher-order probabilistic programming language using memoization. The authors illustrate the utility of this approach by implementing and extending classic and state-of-the-art GP applications. The interface to Gaussian processes, called gpmem, takes an arbitrary real-valued computational process as input and returns a statistical emulator that automatically improves as the original process is invoked and its input-output behavior is recorded. The paper highlights the flexibility of gpmem through three applications: robust GP regression with hierarchical hyper-parameter learning, discovering symbolic expressions from time-series data by Bayesian structure learning over kernels generated by a stochastic grammar, and a bandit formulation of Bayesian optimization with automatic inference and action selection. All applications share a single 50-line Python library and require minimal probabilistic code.
label: AI

title: A thermodynamical approach towards multi-criteria decision making (MCDM)
Abstract: Multi-criteria decision making (MCDM) problems involve assigning ratings to alternatives based on different criteria by a group of experts. This paper proposes a thermodynamically consistent model for MCDM, drawing analogies to thermodynamic indicators like energy, exergy, and entropy. The commonly used Technique for Order of Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS) method relies on an energy-based measure for ranking alternatives. The authors demonstrate that using exergy instead of energy provides a more meaningful ranking, as exergy incorporates a factor accounting for the quality of expert ratings. Entropy measures the unevenness in expert ratings. The paper explains the calculation procedure for thermodynamic indicators in both crisp and fuzzy environments and presents two case studies to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model.
label: AI

title: An Empirical Comparison of Neural Architectures for Reinforcement Learning in Partially Observable Environments
Abstract: This paper investigates the performance of fitted neural Q iteration for reinforcement learning in partially observable environments, employing three recurrent neural network architectures: Long Short-Term Memory, Gated Recurrent Unit, and MUT1 (an evolved recurrent neural architecture). A variant of fitted Q iteration based on Advantage values instead of Q values is also explored. Results show that GRU consistently outperforms LSTM and MUT1 for most problems, requiring fewer training episodes and less CPU time to learn effective policies. Advantage learning also tends to produce better results.
label: AI

title: Blind, Greedy, and Random: Ordinal Approximation Algorithms for Matching and Clustering
Abstract: This paper explores Matching and related problems in a partial information setting where agents' utilities for being matched are hidden, and the mechanism only has access to ordinal preference information. The model is motivated by real-world scenarios where agents can rank outcomes but cannot express numerical utility values. The ground truth is represented as a weighted graph, and the goal is to design algorithms that approximate the optimal matching using only preference orderings as input. Without restrictions on weights, the greedy algorithm achieves half-optimal matching. Surprisingly, the authors show that by imposing structure on weights (metric inequality), they can significantly improve upon the trivial algorithm. They propose a 1.6-approximation algorithm for instances obeying the metric inequality. Using these matching algorithms as a black box, the authors develop new approximation algorithms for related problems: a 3.2-approximation for clustering agents into equal-sized partitions, a 4-approximation for Densest k-subgraph, and a 2.14-approximation for Max TSP. These are the first non-trivial ordinal approximation algorithms for these problems, demonstrating the possibility of designing robust algorithms even with limited knowledge of agent utilities.
label: AI

title: Deep Active Object Recognition by Joint Label and Action Prediction
Abstract: An active object recognition system leverages environmental interaction to capture images suitable for training and improve performance at test time. This paper proposes a deep convolutional neural network for active object recognition that jointly predicts the object label and selects the next action to perform on the object. The system treats active object recognition as a reinforcement learning problem, deriving a cost function to train the network for joint prediction. A generative model of object similarities based on the Dirichlet distribution is proposed and integrated into the network to encode the system state. Training involves minimizing both label and action prediction errors using gradient descent. Empirical results on the GERMS dataset demonstrate the network's ability to predict both object labels and actions. Comparing test label prediction accuracy with Dirichlet and Naive Bayes state encoding, the authors conclude that the model with Dirichlet state encoding outperforms other methods and selects images leading to better training and higher label prediction accuracy at test time. |||
label: AI

title: Unsupervised Feature Construction for Improving Data Representation and Semantics
Abstract: Machine learning algorithms often rely on feature-based data representations. However, when these features don't adequately describe the original data, performance suffers. Some algorithms attempt to address this by internally altering the representation space, but the resulting features are rarely interpretable. This paper proposes two unsupervised algorithms for constructing new features that are both more suitable for a given dataset and comprehensible to human users. The proposed algorithms generate features as conjunctions of the initial primitive features or their negations. The generated feature sets exhibit reduced correlations between features, effectively capturing hidden relationships between data points. For instance, a feature like "$sky \\wedge \\neg building \\wedge panorama$" would be true for non-urban images, providing more information than simple features indicating the presence or absence of an object. The concept of Pareto optimality is employed to evaluate feature sets, balancing total correlation with the complexity of the resulting feature set. Statistical hypothesis testing is utilized to automatically determine the parameters for constructing a data-dependent feature set. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approaches in constructing informative feature sets for various datasets.
label: AI

title: Differential Evolution with Event-Triggered Impulsive Control
Abstract: Differential evolution (DE) is a robust evolutionary algorithm widely used across diverse domains. This paper introduces an event-triggered impulsive control scheme (ETI) to enhance DE's performance. Drawing inspiration from control theory, impulsive control aims to regulate network states by instantaneously adjusting the states of a subset of nodes at specific moments, determined by an event-triggered mechanism (ETM). By integrating impulsive control and ETM into DE, this work seeks to positively impact the search performance of the population by revising the positions of certain individuals at strategic moments. At the end of each generation, impulsive control is triggered when the population's update rate decreases or reaches zero. Inspired by impulsive control concepts, the paper presents two types of impulses within the DE framework: stabilizing impulses and destabilizing impulses. Stabilizing impulses enable individuals with lower rankings to instantaneously move to a desired state dictated by individuals with better fitness values. Destabilizing impulses randomly alter the positions of inferior individuals within the current population's range. By intelligently modifying the positions of a portion of individuals with these two impulses, both exploitation and exploration abilities of the entire population can be improved. Additionally, the proposed ETI is adaptable for integration into various state-of-the-art DE variants. Experimental results on CEC 2014 benchmark functions demonstrate the simplicity and effectiveness of the proposed scheme, significantly improving the performance of the considered DE algorithms.
label: AI

title: Signal Representations on Graphs: Tools and Applications
Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive framework for representing and modeling data on graphs. Within this framework, the study investigates three common classes of graph signals: smooth graph signals, piecewise-constant graph signals, and piecewise-smooth graph signals. For each class, the paper provides a clear definition of the graph signals and constructs a corresponding graph dictionary with desirable properties. The paper then explores the application of these graph dictionaries in two standard tasks: approximation and sampling followed by recovery, from both theoretical and algorithmic perspectives. Finally, for each class, the paper presents a case study of a real-world problem using the proposed methodology.
label: AI

title: Feature Representation for ICU Mortality
Abstract: Accurate prediction of ICU mortality holds significant potential for identifying high-risk patients early, optimizing ICU resource allocation, and creating more precise population-level risk models. Machine learning practitioners often make choices regarding feature representations in their models, but these choices are rarely evaluated quantitatively. This study examines the performance of different representations of clinical event data from MIMIC II in a logistic regression model for predicting 36-hour ICU mortality. The study compares the most common representations, linear (normalized counts) and binary (yes/no), with a novel representation termed "hill" using both L1 and L2 regularization. The results demonstrate that the introduced "hill" representation surpasses both binary and linear representations, suggesting its potential to enhance existing models of ICU mortality.
label: AI

title: Solving stable matching problems using answer set programming
Abstract: Since the introduction of the stable marriage problem (SMP) by Gale and Shapley in 1962, numerous variants and extensions have been explored. While this diversity expands the problem's applicability, each variant requires a new algorithm for finding stable matchings. To address this challenge, this paper proposes an encoding of the SMP using answer set programming (ASP), which can be easily adapted and extended to meet the needs of specific applications. The use of ASP also leverages highly efficient off-the-shelf solvers. To illustrate the flexibility of this approach, the paper demonstrates how the ASP encoding naturally allows for selecting optimal stable matchings, defined by user-specified criteria. To the best of the author's knowledge, this encoding offers the first exact implementation for finding sex-equal, minimum regret, egalitarian, or maximum cardinality stable matchings for SMP instances where individuals can designate unacceptable partners and ties between preferences are permitted. This paper is currently under consideration for publication in Theory and Practice of Logic Programming (TPLP).
label: AI

title: Symphony from Synapses: Neocortex as a Universal Dynamical Systems Modeller using Hierarchical Temporal Memory
Abstract: Reverse engineering the brain presents a formidable challenge, potentially even an impossible one. While many believe it's merely a matter of time and effort, this paper proposes an alternative approach that might provide a more fruitful path. The paper outlines a simple idea that explains the brain's power and structure by exploiting complex dynamics rather than abstracting them away. Just as a Turing Machine serves as a Universal Digital Computer operating in a world of symbols, the paper suggests that the brain is a Universal Dynamical Systems Modeller. It postulates that the brain evolved bottom-up, itself utilizing nested networks of interconnected, self-organized dynamical systems, to thrive in a world of dynamical systems. Recent advancements in Applied Mathematics have revealed striking evidence of the consequences of interactions between abstract Dynamical Systems. The paper highlights how latent information describing one system (A) can be extracted by another system (B) from very simple signals, and how signals can be used by one system to control and manipulate others. Leveraging these insights, the paper demonstrates how a region of the neocortex intrinsically "computes" about the external and internal world using its dynamics. Building on an existing "static" model of cortical computation (Hawkins' Hierarchical Temporal Memory - HTM), the paper describes how a region of neocortex can be viewed as a network of components collectively forming a Dynamical Systems modelling module. This module is connected via sensory and motor pathways to the external world and forms part of a larger dynamical network within the brain. Empirical modelling and simulations of Dynamical HTM are feasible with simple extensions and combinations of currently available open source software. The paper concludes by listing several relevant projects.
label: AI

title: Smart Data Pricing Models for Internet-of-Things (IoT): A Bundling Strategy Approach
Abstract: The Internet of things (IoT) has emerged as a transformative paradigm for the future Internet. In IoT, a vast number of devices are connected to the Internet, forming a massive data source for numerous applications. This paper focuses on addressing data management in IoT through the use of a smart data pricing (SDP) approach. SDP enables flexible and efficient data management through intelligent and adaptive incentive mechanisms. Furthermore, it serves as a major revenue source for providers and partners. The paper proposes a novel pricing scheme for IoT service providers to determine the buying price of sensing data for sensor owners and the subscription fee for IoT services for service users. Additionally, the paper adopts a bundling strategy, allowing multiple providers to form coalitions and bid their services as a bundle, attracting more users and generating higher revenue. Finally, the paper outlines key open research issues for SDP and IoT.
label: AI

title: BayesDB: A probabilistic programming system for querying the probable implications of data
Abstract: Is it possible to make statistical inference accessible to non-statisticians without compromising mathematical rigor or inference quality? This paper introduces BayesDB, a probabilistic programming platform aiming to empower users to query the probable implications of their data as directly as SQL databases enable them to query the data itself. The paper focuses on four key aspects of BayesDB: (i) BQL, an SQL-like query language for Bayesian data analysis that answers queries by averaging over an implicit space of probabilistic models; (ii) techniques for implementing BQL using a broad class of multivariate probabilistic models; (iii) a semi-parametric Bayesian model-builder that automatically constructs ensembles of factorial mixture models to serve as baselines; and (iv) MML, a "meta-modeling" language for imposing qualitative constraints on the model-builder and combining baseline models with custom algorithmic and statistical models that can be implemented in external software. BayesDB is illustrated using three applications: cleaning and exploring a public database of Earth satellites; assessing the evidence for temporal dependence between macroeconomic indicators; and analyzing a salary survey.
label: AI

title: Conditions for Normative Decision Making at the Fire Ground
Abstract: This paper discusses the evolution of decision-making attitudes at fire grounds, driven by recent technological advancements. Emerging new approaches in sensing and data processing, under the umbrella of Cyber-Physical Systems, are narrowing the gap in perception of the fire ground between humans and machines. Moreover, findings from descriptive decision theory question the rationality of human choices. This creates a need for exploring and testing novel approaches to decision-making during emergencies. The paper proposes a framework that addresses this need. The framework's primary characteristic is its ability to incorporate normative and prescriptive approaches to decision-making. It also allows for comparing the performance of decisions made by humans and machines.
label: AI

title: Increasing the Action Gap: New Operators for Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: This paper introduces novel optimality-preserving operators on Q-functions. It first describes an operator for tabular representations, the consistent Bellman operator, which incorporates a notion of local policy consistency. The paper demonstrates that this local consistency leads to an increased action gap at each state, arguing that increasing this gap mitigates the detrimental effects of approximation and estimation errors on the induced greedy policies. This operator can also be applied to discretized continuous space and time problems, and the paper provides empirical results showcasing superior performance in this context. Extending the concept of a locally consistent operator, the paper derives sufficient conditions for an operator to preserve optimality, leading to a family of operators that includes the consistent Bellman operator. As corollaries, the paper provides a proof of optimality for Baird's advantage learning algorithm and derives other gap-increasing operators with interesting properties. The paper concludes with an empirical study on 60 Atari 2600 games, illustrating the strong potential of these new operators.
label: AI

title: From One Point to A Manifold: Knowledge Graph Embedding For Precise Link Prediction
Abstract: Knowledge graph embedding aims to offer a numerical knowledge representation paradigm by transforming entities and relations into a continuous vector space. However, existing methods struggle to characterize the knowledge graph with sufficient granularity for precise prediction. This is attributed to two reasons: the ill-posed nature of the algebraic system and the application of an overly strict geometric form. Recognizing the importance of precise prediction, this paper proposes a manifold-based embedding principle (ManifoldE), which can be treated as a well-posed algebraic system that expands the representation of golden triples from a single point in current models to a manifold in the proposed model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed models achieve significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, particularly for the precise prediction task, while maintaining high efficiency.
label: AI

title: Hyper-Heuristic Algorithm for Finding Efficient Features in Diagnose of Lung Cancer Disease
Abstract: Lung cancer is a leading cause of death, with a survival rate of approximately 15%. Early detection is crucial for improving survival rates. However, all symptoms of lung cancer do not manifest until the cancer spreads to other areas. This necessitates accurate early detection methods. To enhance accuracy, efficient feature selection is crucial, identifying informative features and eliminating redundancies among all features. This paper proposes a novel method for identifying efficient features of lung cancer based on Hyper-Heuristic. The study utilizes a lung cancer database consisting of 32 patient records with 57 features, collected by Hong and Young and indexed in the University of California Irvine repository. The data encompasses clinical and X-ray information, representing three types of pathological lung cancers. All features are assigned integer values ranging from 0 to 3. The proposed method achieves an accuracy of 80.63% using a reduced feature set of 11 features. This outperforms the accuracy of five machine learning feature selection methods, which yielded accuracies of 60.94%, 57.81%, 68.75%, 60.94%, and 68.75%. The paper concludes that the proposed method exhibits superior performance with the highest level of accuracy. Therefore, it is recommended for identifying efficient symptoms of lung cancer, particularly for allocating medical resources effectively for patients identified as high-risk.
label: AI

title: Semantic-enriched Visual Vocabulary Construction in a Weakly Supervised Context
Abstract: Content-based image classification is a prevalent learning task involving images. This task is challenging due to the limited semantic information captured by the low-level features used to digitally describe images. This paper addresses this challenge by enriching the semantic content of the image representation using external knowledge. The underlying hypothesis is that a more semantically rich image representation would lead to higher machine learning performance without requiring modifications to the learning algorithms themselves. The external semantic information is presented as non-positional image labels, positioning this work in a weakly supervised context. The paper proposes two approaches: the first leverages labels into the visual vocabulary construction algorithm, resulting in dedicated visual vocabularies. The second approach introduces a filtering phase as a preprocessing step for vocabulary construction. Known positive and negative sets are constructed, and features unlikely to be associated with the objects denoted by the labels are filtered. The proposed methods are applied to the task of content-based image classification, demonstrating that semantically enriching the image representation leads to higher classification performance compared to the baseline representation.
label: AI

title: Sentence Entailment in Compositional Distributional Semantics
Abstract: Distributional semantic models represent words as vectors by gathering co-occurrence frequencies from textual corpora. Compositional distributional models extend this concept from words to phrases and sentences. In categorical compositional distributional semantics, phrase and sentence representations are functions of their grammatical structure and the representations of their constituent words. Grammatical structures are formalized as morphisms of a compact closed category, while word meanings are formalized as objects of the same category. These can be instantiated as vectors or density matrices. This paper explores the application of this model to phrase and sentence-level entailment. The paper argues that entropy-based distances of vectors and density matrices provide a suitable candidate for measuring word-level entailment, highlighting the advantage of density matrices over vectors for this purpose. The paper also proves that these distances extend compositionally from words to phrases and sentences. The theoretical constructions are illustrated with real data and a toy entailment dataset, providing preliminary experimental evidence.

title: Data-driven Sequential Monte Carlo in Probabilistic Programming
Abstract: Most Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) and sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) algorithms in existing probabilistic programming systems suboptimally utilize only model priors as proposal distributions. This paper presents an approach for training a discriminative model, namely a neural network, to approximate the optimal proposal by leveraging posterior estimates from previous inference runs. The paper demonstrates an example that incorporates a data-driven proposal for use in a non-parametric model within the Anglican probabilistic programming system. The results show that data-driven proposals can significantly enhance inference performance, reducing the number of particles required for accurate posterior estimation.

title: An Event Calculus Production Rule System for Reasoning in Dynamic and Uncertain Domains
Abstract: Action languages have emerged as a significant field in Knowledge Representation for reasoning about change and causality in dynamic domains. This paper introduces Cerbere, a production system designed for online causal, temporal, and epistemic reasoning based on the Event Calculus. The framework implements the declarative semantics of the underlying logic theories in a forward-chaining rule-based reasoning system, combining the expressiveness of its formalisms with the efficiency of rule-based systems. To illustrate its applicability, the paper presents both the modeling of benchmark problems in the field and its utilization in the challenging domain of smart spaces. A hybrid framework that combines logic-based with probabilistic reasoning has been developed to accommodate activity recognition and monitoring tasks in smart spaces. This paper is under consideration for publication in Theory and Practice of Logic Programming (TPLP).

title: Origami: A 803 GOp/s/W Convolutional Network Accelerator
Abstract: A growing number of computer vision and image/video processing challenges are being tackled using deep convolutional neural networks, achieving state-of-the-art results in areas such as object recognition and detection, semantic segmentation, action recognition, optical flow, and superresolution. Hardware acceleration of these algorithms is crucial for adopting these advancements in embedded and mobile computer vision systems. This paper presents a novel architecture, design, and implementation, along with the first reported silicon measurements, of a deep convolutional neural network accelerator. This accelerator outperforms previous work in terms of power, area, and I/O efficiency. The manufactured device delivers up to 196 GOp/s on 3.09 mm^2 of silicon using UMC 65nm technology and achieves a power efficiency of 803 GOp/s/W. The significantly reduced bandwidth requirements make it the first architecture scalable to TOp/s performance.

title: Evaluation of Pose Tracking Accuracy in the First and Second Generations of Microsoft Kinect
Abstract: Microsoft Kinect cameras and their skeletal tracking capabilities have been embraced by numerous researchers and commercial developers in various applications of real-time human movement analysis. This paper evaluates the accuracy of the human kinematic motion data in the first and second generations of the Kinect system, comparing the results with an optical motion capture system. The study collected motion data in 12 exercises for 10 subjects from three different viewpoints. The paper reports on the accuracy of joint localization and bone length estimation of Kinect skeletons compared to the motion capture data. It also analyzes the distribution of joint localization offsets by fitting a mixture of Gaussian and uniform distribution models to identify outliers in the Kinect motion data. The analysis reveals that Kinect 2 overall exhibits more robust and accurate tracking of human pose compared to Kinect 1.

title: Building and Measuring Privacy-Preserving Predictive Blacklists
Abstract: Collaborative security initiatives are increasingly advocated to improve the timeliness and effectiveness of threat mitigation. Collaborative predictive blacklisting (CPB) aims to forecast attack sources based on alerts contributed by multiple organizations that might be targeted similarly. However, existing CPB proposals have only focused on improving hit counts, neglecting the impact of collaboration on false positives and false negatives. Additionally, sharing threat intelligence often raises concerns regarding privacy, confidentiality, and liability. This paper first presents a comprehensive measurement analysis of two state-of-the-art CPB systems: one employing a trusted central party for alert collection and a peer-to-peer system relying on controlled data sharing. The study investigates the impact of collaboration on both correct and incorrect predictions. The paper then introduces a novel privacy-friendly approach that significantly improves upon previous work, achieving a better balance of true and false positive rates while minimizing information disclosure. Finally, the paper presents an extension that allows the system to scale to a large number of organizations.

title: Policy Gradient Methods for Off-policy Control
Abstract: Off-policy learning addresses the challenge of learning the value function of a policy while following a different policy. Gradient-based off-policy learning algorithms, such as GTD and TDC/GQ, converge even when using function approximation and incremental updates. However, they have been developed for fixed behavior policies. In control problems, it is desirable to adapt the behavior policy over time to become more greedy with respect to the existing value function. This paper introduces the first gradient-based learning algorithms for this problem, relying on the framework of policy gradient to modify the behavior policy. The paper presents derivations of the algorithms, a convergence theorem, and empirical evidence demonstrating their favorable comparison to existing approaches. |||

title: Using Linear Constraints for Logic Program Termination Analysis
Abstract: Function symbols are crucial in answer set programming because they simplify modeling, enhance expressive power, and enable dealing with infinite domains. However, their introduction can lead to program evaluation non-termination, which is an undecidable problem. To address this issue, various classes of logic programs have been proposed that restrict the use of function symbols while ensuring program evaluation termination. Despite extensive research in this area, current approaches lack support for many simple, practical programs that terminate. This paper introduces novel classes of rule-bounded and cycle-bounded programs, which overcome the limitations of existing approaches by performing a more global analysis of term propagation from rule bodies to heads. The paper provides results on the correctness, complexity, and expressivity of the proposed approach.

title: True Online Temporal-Difference Learning
Abstract: The temporal-difference methods TD($\lambda$) and Sarsa($\lambda$) are fundamental in modern reinforcement learning due to their good performance, low computational cost, and simple interpretation based on their forward view. Recently, true online versions of these methods, called true online TD($\lambda$) and true online Sarsa($\lambda$), were introduced (van Seijen & Sutton, 2014), maintaining exact equivalence with the forward view at all times, unlike the traditional versions that approximate it for small step-sizes. This article empirically tests the hypothesis that these true online methods not only possess better theoretical properties but also outperform the regular methods. The study compares the performance of true online TD($\lambda$)/Sarsa($\lambda$) with regular TD($\lambda$)/Sarsa($\lambda$) on random MRPs, a real-world myoelectric prosthetic arm, and a domain from the Arcade Learning Environment. Linear function approximation with tabular, binary, and non-binary features is utilized. The findings suggest that the true online methods consistently outperform the regular methods, exhibiting faster learning speeds across all domains/representations. Notably, the true online methods require no choice between traces. Alongside the empirical results, the paper provides an in-depth analysis of the theory behind true online temporal-difference learning and demonstrates the derivation of new true online methods through modifications to the online forward view.

title: The Rationale behind the Concept of Goal
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel perspective on the concept of goals, arguing that motivational attitudes like desire, goal, and intention are merely facets of the broader notion of (acceptable) outcomes. The authors propose representing an agent's preferences as sequences of "alternative acceptable outcomes." The paper then investigates how the agent's beliefs and norms can be used to filter mental attitudes from these sequences. Finally, these intuitions are formalized in a novel Modal Defeasible Logic, and the computational feasibility of the resulting formalization is proven.

title: Query Answering over Contextualized RDF/OWL Knowledge with Forall-Existential Bridge Rules: Decidable Finite Extension Classes (Post Print)
Abstract: The proliferation of contextualized knowledge in the Semantic Web (SW) has popularized knowledge formats such as quads in the SW community. A quad extends an RDF triple with contextual information. This paper examines the problem of query answering over quads augmented with forall-existential bridge rules, which facilitate interoperability of reasoning between triples in various contexts. A set of quads combined with such expressive bridge rules is termed a quad-system. Query answering over quad-systems is generally undecidable. This work derives decidable classes of quad-systems where query answering can be performed using forward chaining. Sound, complete, and terminating procedures, adaptations of the well-known chase algorithm, are provided for these classes to decide query entailment. The safe, msafe, and csafe classes of quad-systems restrict the structure of blank nodes generated during chase computation to directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) of bounded depth. The RR and restricted RR classes disallow the generation of blank nodes during chase computation. Both data and combined complexity of query entailment have been established for the derived classes. Additionally, the paper demonstrates that quad-systems are equivalent to forall-existential rules with ternary predicates, modulo polynomial time translations. It is further shown that the technique of safety strictly subsumes in expressivity some well-known and expressive techniques, such as joint acyclicity and model faithful acyclicity, used for decidability guarantees in the realm of forall-existential rules.

title: Deep Feature Learning with Relative Distance Comparison for Person Re-identification
Abstract: Identifying the same individual across different scenes is a crucial but challenging task in intelligent video surveillance. The difficulty arises from preserving similarity of the same person despite significant appearance and structural variations while discriminating different individuals. This paper proposes a scalable distance-driven feature learning framework based on deep neural networks for person re-identification, showcasing its effectiveness in addressing these challenges. The framework utilizes training images with person ID labels to generate a large number of triplet units, each containing three images: one person with a matched reference and a mismatched reference. These units serve as input for a convolutional neural network, generating layered representations followed by the L2 distance metric. Through parameter optimization, the framework aims to maximize the relative distance between the matched pair and the mismatched pair for each triplet unit. The paper addresses the issue of triplet organization cubically increasing the number of training triplets by developing an effective triplet generation scheme and an optimized gradient descent algorithm, making the computational load primarily dependent on the number of original images rather than the number of triplets. The approach achieves promising results on challenging databases, outperforming other state-of-the-art methods.

title: Hierarchical Quantification of Synergy in Channels
Abstract: Decomposing channel information into synergies of different orders is an active research area in the theory of complex systems. Most approaches utilize information theory, proposing decompositions of mutual information between inputs and outputs in various ways, none of which has gained general acceptance yet. This paper presents a new perspective on the topic, modeling a multi-input channel as a Markov kernel. The channel is projected onto a series of exponential families, forming a hierarchical structure. This is accomplished using tools from information geometry, analogous to the projections of probability distributions introduced by Amari. A Pythagorean relation naturally leads to a decomposition of the mutual information between inputs and outputs into terms representing single node information, pairwise interactions, and n-node interactions. The synergy measures introduced in this paper can be easily evaluated using an iterative scaling algorithm, a standard procedure in information geometry.

title: Subsumptive reflection in SNOMED CT: a large description logic-based terminology for diagnosis
Abstract: Description logic (DL)-based biomedical terminology, such as SNOMED CT, is routinely used in medical practice. However, the complexity of this terminology hinders diagnostic inference. This paper proposes a model simplifying these inferential components. Three concepts classifying clinical features are introduced and their effect on SNOMED CT inference is examined. The analysis utilizes the PAIRS (Physician Assistant Artificial Intelligence Reference System) database, containing 1964 findings for 485 disorders and 18,397 disease feature links. A 50-million medical word corpus is also used to estimate the vectors of disease-feature links. The major findings include: 10% of finding-disorder links are concomitant in both assertion and negation, while 90% are either concomitant in assertion or negation. Logical implications of PAIRS data on SNOMED CT reveal that 70% of the links do not share any common system, while 18% share an organ and 12% share both system and organ. The paper discusses applications of these principles for inference and provides suggestions for deriving a diagnostic process using SNOMED CT. Limitations of these processes and suggestions for improvements are also discussed.

title: Convolutional Monte Carlo Rollouts in Go
Abstract: This paper presents a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based Go-playing program that utilizes convolutional networks in all its components. The program performs MCTS in batches, explores the Monte Carlo search tree using Thompson sampling and a convolutional network, and evaluates convnet-based rollouts on the GPU. The program achieves strong win rates against open source Go programs and demonstrates competitive performance against state-of-the-art convolutional net-based Go-playing programs.

title: Mobile Robots Adaptive Control Using Neural Networks
Abstract: The paper proposes a feed-forward control strategy for mobile robot control that accounts for a non-linear model of the vehicle with interaction between inputs and outputs. The strategy allows for the inclusion of specific model uncertainties in the robot's dynamic model, enabling a comprehensive approach to the control problem. A neural network feed-forward controller is employed to handle the real non-linear mathematical model of the vehicle. The classical velocity control strategy is extended using artificial neural networks to compensate for modeling uncertainties, leading to an intelligent mobile robot control strategy.

title: Diversity and Intelligence in Multi-robot Teams
Abstract: This research explores behavioral diversity in multi-robot systems by introducing new investigation tools and presenting a significant body of results obtained through simulated and real mobile robot experiments. The experiments focus on defining behavior-based strategies for multi-robot tasks such as robot foraging, robot soccer, and robot formation, specifically within the context of motor schema-based multi-robot systems, which represent an important example of behavior-based control.

title: Predicting proximity with ambient mobile sensors for non-invasive health diagnostics
Abstract: Modern smartphones are becoming increasingly helpful in Internet-of-Things (IoT) and ambient health intelligence applications. By analyzing data from mobile sensors, this research demonstrates a method for detecting the nearness of the human body to a mobile device in a three-dimensional space without physical contact, enabling non-invasive health diagnostics. The research shows that the human body generates wave patterns that interact with naturally occurring ambient signals, such as temperature, humidity, magnetic field, acceleration, gravity, and light. This interaction alters the patterns of these ambient signals, creating characteristics that can be learned to predict the nearness of the human body to the device, thereby providing diagnostic information for medical practitioners. The prediction technique achieves 88.75% accuracy and 88.3% specificity.

title: Learning measures of semi-additive behaviour
Abstract: In business analytics, measure values, such as sales numbers or cargo volumes, are often summed along corresponding categories like time or shipping containers. However, not all measures should be added by default, and some measures should only be summed within specific constraints. This paper proposes a small set of features to address this issue. These features are incorporated into a case-based reasoning approach where the system suggests an aggregation behavior, achieving 86% accuracy on a collected dataset.

title: ShapeNet: An Information-Rich 3D Model Repository
Abstract: ShapeNet is introduced as a richly-annotated, large-scale repository of 3D shapes represented by 3D CAD models of objects. ShapeNet comprises models from various semantic categories organized under the WordNet taxonomy. It provides numerous semantic annotations for each 3D model, including consistent rigid alignments, parts, bilateral symmetry planes, physical sizes, keywords, and planned annotations. These annotations are accessible through a public web-based interface to enable data visualization of object attributes, promote data-driven geometric analysis, and provide a large-scale quantitative benchmark for research in computer graphics and vision. As of this report, ShapeNet has indexed over 3,000,000 models, with 220,000 models classified into 3,135 categories (WordNet synsets). This report describes the ShapeNet effort comprehensively, detailing available datasets and outlining future plans.

title: A Novel Regularized Principal Graph Learning Framework on Explicit Graph Representation
Abstract: Many scientific datasets are high-dimensional, requiring visual manipulation for analysis while retaining important data structures. Principal curves are widely used for this purpose but often only work for data with non-self-intersecting structures, limiting their applicability. Existing methods addressing this limitation either require complex human-made rules with no convergence guarantee or lack adaptation flexibility, or they fail to obtain explicit data structures. To address these issues, a new regularized principal graph learning framework is developed, capturing local information of the underlying graph structure using reversed graph embedding. Models for learning a spanning tree or a weighted undirected $\ell_1$ graph are proposed, and a new learning algorithm is developed to simultaneously learn principal points and a graph structure from data. This algorithm is simple and guarantees convergence. The framework is extended to handle large-scale data. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets show that the proposed method outperforms baselines and accurately uncovers underlying structures.

title: Setup of a photomultiplier tube test bench for use at LHAASO-KM2A
Abstract: To test the photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) of the electromagnetic detector at the Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO), a multi-functional PMT test bench with a two-dimensional scanning system has been developed. This 2D scanning system enables simultaneous testing of 16 PMTs for characteristics such as uniformity, cathode transit time difference, single photo-electron spectrum, gain vs. high voltage, linear behavior, and dark noise. The programmable hardware and intelligent software of the test bench ensure user-friendliness and reliable results. The paper describes the test methods in detail and presents primary results.

title: Architecture of the LHCb muon Frontend control system upgrade
Abstract: The LHCb experiment (Fig. 1), currently taking data at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC), aims to study CP violation in the B meson sector. Its key element is the Muon detector [1], which enables triggering and muon identification from inclusive b decays. The electronic system (Fig. 2) of the entire detector is complex, with the Muon detector Experiment Control System (ECS) allowing monitoring and control of over 7000 Front-End boards. The current system responsible for controlling Muon detector Front-End (FE) Electronics consists of 10 Crates of equipment, each containing a Pulse Distribution Module (PDM) and up to 20 Service Boards (SB) connected via a custom Backplane, totaling approximately 800 microcontrollers [2]. The LHCb upgrade planned for 2018/19 will enable the detector to exploit higher luminosity running, leading to increased luminosity accumulation and more precise measurements. The new architecture leverages CERN's fast communication protocol GBT [3] developed for radiation environments, maintaining the detector's extensive connectivity and modularity. The new GBTx and GBT-SCA [4] chipsets developed at CERN, along with more powerful computers, enable the design of a new system with fast links to the detector. In this new system, control units are moved from the apparatus to computers in the control room, replacing low-speed buses sending high-level commands to intelligent units in the detector.

title: Learning Discrete Bayesian Networks from Continuous Data
Abstract: Learning Bayesian networks from raw data can provide valuable insights into relationships between variables. While real data often contains a mixture of discrete and continuous-valued variables, many Bayesian network structure learning algorithms assume all variables are discrete. Therefore, continuous variables are typically discretized during Bayesian network learning. However, the choice of discretization policy significantly impacts the accuracy, speed, and interpretability of the resulting models. This paper introduces a principled Bayesian discretization method for continuous variables in Bayesian networks, offering quadratic complexity compared to the cubic complexity of standard techniques. Empirical demonstrations highlight the superiority of the proposed method over the established minimum description length algorithm. Additionally, the paper shows how to integrate existing methods into the structure learning process to discretize all continuous variables and simultaneously learn Bayesian network structures.

title: Optical SETI Observations of the Anomalous Star KIC 8462852
Abstract: To investigate the hypothesis that KIC 8462852's aperiodic dimming is caused by artificial megastructures in orbit (Wright et al. 2015), rather than natural causes like cometary fragments in a highly elliptical orbit (Marengo et al. 2015), researchers searched for electromagnetic signals from KIC 8462852 indicative of extraterrestrial intelligence. The primary observations were conducted in the visible optical regime using the Boquete Optical SETI Observatory in Panama. As a preparatory exercise for potential future candidate signal detection (Heidmann 1991), three out of six observing runs simultaneously searched radio frequencies at the Allen Telescope Array in California. No periodic optical signals exceeding 67 photons/m2 within a 25 ns timeframe were detected, corresponding to isotropic optical pulses of 8E22 joules. However, if inhabitants of KIC 8462852 were targeting our solar system (Shostak & Villard 2004), the required energy would be significantly reduced. Limits on narrowband radio signals were 180 - 300 Jy Hz at 1 and 8 GHz, respectively, corresponding to a transmitter with an effective isotropic radiated power of 4E15 W (and 7E15 W) at the distance of KIC 8462852. While these power requirements are high, even modest targeting, similar to optical signals, could substantially lower these numbers.

title: Sensitivity analysis, multilinearity and beyond
Abstract: Sensitivity methods for analyzing the outputs of discrete Bayesian networks have been extensively studied and implemented in various software packages. These methods typically focus on sensitivity functions and the impact of parameter changes on the Chan-Darwiche distance. Although not fully recognized, most of these results heavily rely on the multilinear structure of atomic probabilities in terms of the conditional probability parameters associated with this type of network. By defining a statistical model through the polynomial expression of its associated defining conditional probabilities, a unifying approach to sensitivity methods is developed, applicable to a wide range of models, including extensions of Bayesian networks like context-specific and dynamic ones, and chain event graphs. By focusing on models with a multilinear defining polynomial, this algebraic approach proves that the Chan-Darwiche distance is minimized for a certain class of multi-parameter contemporaneous variations when parameters are proportionally covaried.

title: Digital Genesis: Computers, Evolution and Artificial Life
Abstract: The application of evolution in the digital realm, with the goal of creating artificial intelligence and artificial life, has a history as long as the digital computer itself. This paper traces the intertwined history of these ideas, starting with the early theoretical work of John von Neumann and the pioneering experimental work of Nils Aall Barricelli. It argues that evolutionary thinking and artificial life will continue to play an integral role in the future development of the digital world.

title: From rules to runs: A dynamic epistemic take on imperfect information games
Abstract: The interpretation of information sets in extensive form games can lead to confusion and paradoxes due to the mixing of two different interpretations: game rules and game runs. This paper proposes a dynamic epistemic framework to separate and connect these two views, enabling the computation of game runs from the rules and player assumptions. A modal logic is developed to describe players' knowledge and its evolution during gameplay, and a complete axiomatization is provided. The paper demonstrates that, under certain conditions, the mixing of rules and runs has minimal impact due to their structural similarity.

title: How to Discount Deep Reinforcement Learning: Towards New Dynamic Strategies
Abstract: Deep neural networks have emerged as powerful function approximators for reinforcement learning tasks. This paper investigates the role of the discount factor in the learning process of deep Q-networks (DQNs). By gradually increasing the discount factor, the authors demonstrate a significant reduction in learning steps. When combined with a varying learning rate, this approach outperforms the original DQN on various experiments. The paper links this phenomenon to instabilities of neural networks in approximate dynamic programming settings and discusses the potential for local optima during learning, highlighting the exploration/exploitation dilemma.

title: A Novel Approach to Distributed Multi-Class SVM
Abstract: The ever-increasing size of datasets demands distributed computation and memory management in machine learning. While distributed binary and multi-class SVM algorithms exist, the field of multi-class distributed SVMs remains largely unexplored. This paper proposes a novel algorithm for multi-class SVMs that leverages Hadoop's distributed environment. The algorithm recursively divides the dataset, computing the optimal SVM for each half during training. This structure effectively reduces prediction time during testing. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms traditional sequential SVM methods (One vs. One, One vs. Rest) in terms of computational time and accuracy, especially with larger datasets.

title: Thinking Required
Abstract: This paper explores the theory of a single general-purpose learning algorithm that could explain the principles of human learning. It postulates that a small library of innate circuits, prewired at birth, serves as the initial architecture, and that all significant mental algorithms are learned. Based on current understanding and observations, the paper reviews and lists the essential components of such an algorithm from both architectural and functional perspectives.

title: Knowledge Sharing in Coalitions
Abstract: This paper investigates the connection between knowledge sharing among agents and their coalition ability in the context of imperfect information concurrent games. It assumes that agents share their knowledge before forming coalitions to achieve a goal. A new semantics for alternating-time temporal logic with imperfect information and perfect recall is proposed, which preserves the desirable properties of coalition ability in traditional coalitional logics. The paper analyzes how knowledge sharing contributes to coalitional ability through the interplay of epistemic and coalition modalities, providing insights into the type of group knowledge required for successful goal achievement in imperfect information scenarios.

title: Probabilistic Structural Controllability in Causal Bayesian Networks
Abstract: This paper addresses the problem of probabilistic controllability in Causal Bayesian Networks (CBNs), which involves identifying driver variables that can influence the probability of achieving desired or undesired states for target variables within an uncertain environment. The paper introduces and formalizes the concept of probabilistic structural controllability, identifying a sufficient set of driver variables for this purpose. The minimality properties of the identified set are also discussed, considering scenarios where only the structure of the CBN is known.

title: Driverseat: Crowdstrapping Learning Tasks for Autonomous Driving
Abstract: Despite their success in many tasks, emerging deep-learning systems face challenges in applying to detection tasks for autonomous technologies, namely the lack of comprehensively labeled datasets and expressive evaluation strategies. This paper introduces Driverseat, a technology that leverages crowds to overcome these limitations. Driverseat utilizes crowd contributions for 3D labeling and scenario tagging, enabling efficient evaluation of learning systems. The paper demonstrates how Driverseat can crowdstrap a convolutional neural network for lane detection. Crowdstrapping represents a valuable paradigm for technologies that benefit from human-computer intelligence collaboration.

title: Rank Pooling for Action Recognition
Abstract: This paper presents a novel function-based temporal pooling method that captures the latent structure of video sequences, such as the evolution of frame-level features over time. The parameters of a function fitted to the video data serve as a robust new representation.  Specifically, the paper utilizes ranking machines to learn a pooling function that ranks frame-level features chronologically, capturing video-wide temporal dynamics for action recognition.  The proposed functional pooling methods, including rank pooling, are easily interpretable, fast to compute, and effective for recognizing various actions.  Evaluation on action, fine-grained action, and gesture recognition benchmarks demonstrates significant performance improvements over average pooling baselines, highlighting the method's compatibility and complementarity with other appearance and local motion-based methods.

title: Fast Algorithms for Game-Theoretic Centrality Measures
Abstract: This dissertation examines the computational properties of game-theoretic centrality measures, which treat network nodes as players in a cooperative game. The value of node coalitions is determined by graph properties, and individual node centrality is calculated using game-theoretic solution concepts like the Shapley value.  While game-theoretic centrality measures provide a comprehensive ranking based on node contributions to various coalitions, they often pose computational challenges. The dissertation demonstrates that numerous game-theoretic solution concepts on networks can be computed in polynomial time, focusing on Shapley value-based centralities and its extensions.  It also proves the #P-hardness of computing the Shapley value in connectivity games and proposes an algorithm for its computation. The dissertation concludes by analyzing the computational properties of generalized cooperative games where player order matters, introducing generalized marginal contribution networks for polynomial computation of Shapley value extensions.

title: Large Scale Distributed Semi-Supervised Learning Using Streaming Approximation
Abstract: Traditional graph-based semi-supervised learning (SSL) approaches are ill-suited for massive data and large label scenarios due to their linear scaling with the number of edges and distinct labels. This paper presents a novel streaming graph-based SSL approximation that addresses this challenge. The proposed method captures the sparsity of the label distribution, ensuring accurate label propagation and reducing space complexity per node to O(1). It also provides a distributed version that scales well to large datasets. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the method's superior performance and memory efficiency compared to existing algorithms. The paper further investigates graph construction mechanisms for natural language applications and proposes a robust graph augmentation strategy, leveraging unsupervised deep learning architectures for significant quality gains.

title: A Restricted Visual Turing Test for Deep Scene and Event Understanding
Abstract: This paper introduces a restricted visual Turing test (VTT) for assessing story-line based deep understanding in long-term, multi-camera videos. Given videos of a scene and story-line queries, the task is to provide binary ("true/false") or natural language answers. Queries involve both view-based and scene-centered inferences. The paper distinguishes this VTT from visual question answering and video captioning by focusing on spatial, temporal, and causal understanding. A vision system is proposed that integrates vision modules, a knowledge base, and a query engine to perform joint video and query parsing. The system provides flexible interfaces for reconfiguring individual modules. The paper provides a benchmark dataset, a toolkit for ontology-guided story-line query generation, and a baseline implementation with result analysis.

title: Risk-Constrained Reinforcement Learning with Percentile Risk Criteria
Abstract: This paper presents efficient reinforcement learning algorithms for risk-constrained Markov decision processes (MDPs), where risk is quantified using chance constraints or conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) constraints on the cumulative cost. The algorithms aim to minimize expected cumulative cost while considering risk.  The paper derives a formula for computing the gradient of the Lagrangian function for these problems, and proposes policy gradient and actor-critic algorithms that estimate the gradient, update the policy, and adjust the Lagrange multiplier. Convergence to locally optimal policies is proven. The algorithms' effectiveness is demonstrated through applications in optimal stopping and online marketing.
