title: A Novel Paradigm for Calculating Ramsey Number via Artificial Bee Colony Algorithm
Abstract: This paper presents a novel methodology for constructing Ramsey graphs using Artificial Bee Colony (ABC) optimization to raise the lower bound of the Ramsey number R(3,10).  The paper defines an optimization problem where minimizing the number of complete graphs of order 3 and independent sets of order 10 in a graph corresponds to maximizing the lower bound of R(3,10).  Simulations using ABC optimization are conducted, resulting in the discovery of four r(3,9,39) graphs with the best approximation for inf R(3,10), supporting the current lower bound for R(3,10). The experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed paradigm for Ramsey number calculation, highlighting its high precision and robustness.

title: Extracting Biomolecular Interactions Using Semantic Parsing of Biomedical Text
Abstract: This paper advances the state-of-the-art in biomolecular interaction extraction through three key contributions: (i) Demonstrating the significant accuracy improvement achieved by incorporating deep Abstract Meaning Representations (AMRs) into a biomolecular interaction extraction system compared to a baseline relying solely on surface and syntax-based features; (ii) Expanding the framework to enable consistent predictions over sets of sentences (documents), in contrast to previous sentence-by-sentence approaches; (iii) Modifying and expanding a graph kernel learning framework to exploit both automatically induced AMRs (semantic) and dependency structures (syntactic) representations concurrently. Experiments show that the proposed approach yields more robust interaction extraction systems, particularly in environments with significant mismatches between training and testing conditions.

title: Reuse of Neural Modules for General Video Game Playing
Abstract: This paper introduces a general approach to knowledge transfer using neural networks, enabling an agent to adapt its reuse of existing networks as it learns in a new domain. Networks trained for a new domain can improve performance by selectively routing activation through previously learned neural structures, regardless of their origin or purpose. The paper presents a neuroevolution implementation of this approach and applies it to high-dimensional sequential decision-making domains. This method is more general than previous approaches to neural transfer for reinforcement learning, being domain-agnostic and requiring no prior assumptions about task relatedness. Analysis in a stochastic version of the Arcade Learning Environment demonstrates performance improvements in complex Atari 2600 games and highlights the predictability of transfer success based on game dynamics.

title: On the Min-cost Traveling Salesman Problem with Drone
Abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicles (drones), initially used in military domains, have emerged as part of a new commercial sector logistics method called "last-mile delivery." In this approach, small UAVs are deployed alongside trucks to improve service quality or reduce transportation costs. This paper introduces a new variant of the traveling salesman problem (TSP), called TSP with drone (TSP-D), with the objective of minimizing total transportation cost.  Two heuristics, "Drone First, Truck Second" (DFTS) and "Truck First, Drone Second" (TFDS), are proposed to solve this problem.  The paper presents a mixed integer programming (MIP) formulation with different profit functions to build drone routes and provides numerical results obtained on various instances, offering recommendations on promising algorithm choices.

title: What Makes it Difficult to Understand a Scientific Literature?
Abstract: This paper investigates the challenge of enabling computers to understand human language and provide assistance. The authors analyze the reading comprehension process of scientific literature using semantic link models. By conducting tests on two papers written in different styles, they identify the obstacles people face in understanding scientific texts. The analysis highlights the characteristics and problems encountered by individuals with varying knowledge levels in comprehending complex science and technology literature, which can be modeled using semantic link networks. The paper suggests that these insights can inform the design of new machine models for improved reading comprehension.

title: Locally Adaptive Translation for Knowledge Graph Embedding
Abstract: Knowledge graph embedding aims to represent entities and relations in large-scale knowledge graphs as elements in a continuous vector space. Existing methods, such as TransE and TransH, learn embedding representations by defining a global margin-based loss function. However, the optimal loss function is determined experimentally and is limited to a closed set of candidates. This paper proposes TransA, a locally adaptive translation method for knowledge graph embedding, which finds the optimal loss function by adaptively determining its margin for different knowledge graphs. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of TransA compared to state-of-the-art methods.

title: Proposition of a Theoretical Model for Missing Data Imputation using Deep Learning and Evolutionary Algorithms
Abstract: This paper explores recent advancements in the domain of missing data imputation, highlighting techniques like Expectation Maximization, neural networks with evolutionary algorithms, and K-Nearest Neighbor approaches. The presence of missing data poses challenges for decision-making and data analysis. The paper proposes a novel approach using deep neural networks built with autoencoders and denoising autoencoders in conjunction with genetic algorithms, swarm intelligence, and maximum likelihood estimation methods for missing data imputation. The authors hypothesize that this approach will lead to more accurate and efficient imputation compared to existing techniques, considering various missing data mechanisms.  The paper also explores the integration of fuzzy logic with deep neural networks for missing data imputation.

title: Toward a Taxonomy and Computational Models of Abnormalities in Images
Abstract: The human visual system can detect abnormal images and reason about their unusual features. This paper investigates various types of atypicalities in images, proposing a new dataset of abnormal images showcasing a wide range of abnormalities. Human subject experiments are conducted to establish a coarse taxonomy of abnormality reasons, revealing three categories: object-centric, scene-centric, and contextual. Based on this taxonomy, the paper proposes a comprehensive computational model that can predict all types of abnormality in images, outperforming prior arts in abnormality recognition. |||

title: Predicting and visualizing psychological attributions with a deep neural network
Abstract: Predicting personality traits from facial images is a significant factor in social decision-making, impacting areas like elections and jury decisions.  Current methods rely on manually annotated facial landmarks, which are time-consuming.  This research introduces a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model that predicts memorability, trustworthiness, intelligence, and other attributes without requiring landmark features, significantly improving efficiency.  The model achieves high accuracy, surpassing human performance in some cases.  Moreover, a deconvolutional technique is employed to visualize key features associated with the perception of 22 attributes, introducing a novel method for visualizing positive and negative features separately.

title: CrossCat: A Fully Bayesian Nonparametric Method for Analyzing Heterogeneous, High Dimensional Data
Abstract: Analyzing high-dimensional datasets without restrictive modeling assumptions is a crucial need. This paper introduces CrossCat, a domain-general data analysis method that identifies multiple non-overlapping data views.  Each view comprises a subset of variables and is modeled using a separate nonparametric mixture.  CrossCat's foundation lies in approximate Bayesian inference within a hierarchical, nonparametric model for data tables. This model utilizes a Dirichlet process mixture over the table's columns, where each component is itself an independent Dirichlet process mixture over the rows. The inner mixture components are simple parametric models whose form depends on the table's data types. CrossCat combines the strengths of mixture modeling and Bayesian network structure learning.  Like mixture modeling, CrossCat models a wide range of distributions by introducing latent variables and generates representations suitable for efficient conditioning and sampling for prediction.  Similar to Bayesian networks, CrossCat represents variable dependencies and independencies, ensuring accuracy even with multiple statistical signals. Inference is achieved through a scalable Gibbs sampling scheme, demonstrated to work well in practice.  The paper presents empirical results on diverse tabular data, including hospital data, voting records, and gene expression measurements, showing that CrossCat infers structure consistent with established findings and common knowledge. CrossCat delivers competitive predictive accuracy compared to generative, discriminative, and model-free alternatives.

title: A Smartphone-Based Acquisition System for Hips Rotation Fluency Assessment
Abstract: Motivated by recent studies on assessing body movement fluency during complex tasks, this paper focuses on estimating the Cartesian kinematic jerk (acceleration derivative) of hip orientation during 3D movement. The kinematic jerk index is derived from gyroscopic signals obtained through a smartphone. A free mobile application, HyperIMU, for Android, acquires the gyroscopic data and transmits it to a personal computer using UDP protocol.  The computer processes the data using a MATLAB script, either in real-time or offline, to calculate the kinematic jerk index associated with the motor task.

title: Building Memory with Concept Learning Capabilities from Large-scale Knowledge Base
Abstract: This work presents a novel framework for neural knowledge base (KB) embeddings, incorporating both symbolic knowledge and its learning process.  The framework effectively regularizes previous neural KB embedding models, enhancing their performance in reasoning tasks.  It also enables the handling of unseen entities by learning their embeddings from natural language descriptions, mirroring human semantic concept learning.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning with Attention for Slate Markov Decision Processes with High-Dimensional States and Actions
Abstract: Many real-world problems involve action spaces represented as feature vectors.  While high-dimensional control remains a challenge, recent progress has been made for moderate dimensionalities.  This paper tackles high-dimensional problems with up to 2000 dimensions, focusing on a specific form.  Motivated by applications like recommendation systems that do not fit standard reinforcement learning frameworks, the paper introduces Slate Markov Decision Processes (slate-MDPs). A slate-MDP is an MDP with a combinatorial action space composed of slates (tuples) of primitive actions, where only one action is executed in an underlying MDP. The agent does not control the selection of this executed action, and it may not even be from the slate, as in recommendation systems where all recommendations can be ignored.  Deep Q-learning is employed, using feature representations of both state and action, to learn the value of whole slates.  Unlike existing methods, optimization occurs for both the combinatorial and sequential aspects of the tasks. The superiority of the new agent over those ignoring either combinatorial or sequential value is demonstrated in environments with dynamics from a real-world recommendation system.  Deep deterministic policy gradients are used to learn a policy that guides attention towards the most valuable parts of the action space for each slate position.  This attention is leveraged within a sequentially greedy procedure based on submodularity.  Finally, the paper demonstrates how introducing risk-seeking significantly enhances agent performance and the ability to discover broader strategies.

title: Bayesian Matrix Completion via Adaptive Relaxed Spectral Regularization
Abstract: Bayesian matrix completion, based on low-rank matrix factorization, has yielded promising results.  However, little research has been conducted on Bayesian matrix completion using the more direct spectral regularization formulation. This paper bridges this gap by introducing a novel Bayesian matrix completion method based on spectral regularization.  To overcome the challenges of dealing with singular vector orthonormality constraints, a new equivalent form with relaxed constraints is derived, leading to an adaptive version of spectral regularization suitable for Bayesian inference. The Bayesian method requires no parameter tuning and automatically infers the number of latent factors.  Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate encouraging results in rank recovery and collaborative filtering, particularly for sparse matrices.

title: Querying with Łukasiewicz logic
Abstract: This paper presents a proof-of-concept, using an automotive dataset prototype, showcasing the potential of Łukasiewicz propositional logic formulas for fuzzy database queries.  The approach emphasizes purely linguistic query formulations, contrasting with numerical methods.  Queries are expressed in pure logical language, with integer numbers serving as syntactic formula shortenings and semantic linguistic hedges.  The case-study queries demonstrate that each numerical threshold fuzzy query can be simulated by a Łukasiewicz formula.  Furthermore, the expressive power of Łukasiewicz logic is highlighted, allowing for query updates with clauses and modifications through various linguistic hedges implemented using a uniform syntactic mechanism.  The paper suggests how, even at the propositional level, Łukasiewicz natural semantics exhibits a degree of reflection, enabling the formulation of syntactically simple queries that semantically act as meta-queries, weighting the contribution of simpler ones.

title: Discrete Equilibrium Sampling with Arbitrary Nonequilibrium Processes
Abstract: This research introduces a framework for statistical sampling, expectation estimation, and partition function approximation using arbitrary heuristic stochastic processes over discrete state spaces.  A highly parallel construction, termed the sequential constraining process, simultaneously generates states using the heuristic process and accurately estimates their probabilities, even for extremely small probabilities.  The paper demonstrates that both theoretically correct importance sampling and Markov chain Monte Carlo are feasible using the sequential constraining process.  This process is integrated into a methodology called state space sampling, extending state space search from computer science to the sampling context.  The methodology includes a dynamic data structure that constructs a robust Bayesian model of the statistics generated by the heuristic process, subject to an accuracy constraint, the posterior Kullback-Leibler divergence.  Sampling from the dynamic structure typically yields partial states, which are completed by recursively calling the heuristic to refine the structure and resume sampling.  Experiments on various Ising models indicate that state space sampling enables heuristic state generation with accurate probability estimates.  This is illustrated by the convergence of a simulated annealing process to the Boltzmann distribution with increasing run length.  Consequently, previously unprecedented direct importance sampling using the final (marginal) distribution of a generic stochastic process becomes possible, potentially expanding the range of algorithms available to Monte Carlo practitioners.

title: A Chessboard Model of Human Brain and One Application on Memory Capacity
Abstract: The widely accepted notion that humans only utilize 10% of their brain capacity has been challenged. Researchers now argue that the entire brain is likely used, contradicting the 10% claim.  Evidence from neuroscience studies related to memory supports this view, suggesting that neural pathways would degenerate if 90% of the brain remained unused.  This article explores memory and brain function, examining the potential limits of memory capacity.  It proposes a model based on human brain physiological and neurological characteristics, providing theoretical support and scientific explanation for various phenomena. This model holds theoretical significance in neuroscience and could have practical applications in bridging the gap between natural and artificial intelligence.
label: AI

title: A Study on Artificial Intelligence IQ and Standard Intelligent Model
Abstract: The potential threats posed by artificial intelligence (AI) to humanity have sparked significant societal debate.  At the heart of this issue lies the question of whether AI systems can be evaluated quantitatively.  This article analyzes the challenges facing AI development and proposes that evaluation methods for human intelligence tests and AI systems are not uniform.  The primary reason for this disparity is the lack of a unified model capable of describing both AI systems and human beings.  To address this, the study establishes a standard intelligent system model that uniformly describes both AI systems and human beings.  Based on this model, the article provides an abstract mathematical description and constructs a standard intelligent machine mathematical model.  It expands on the Von Neumann architecture by proposing the Liufeng-Shiyong architecture.  The article defines artificial intelligence IQ, establishes an artificial intelligence scale and evaluation method, and conducts testing on 50 search engines and three human subjects of different ages across the globe.  The results yield rankings of both absolute IQ and deviation IQ for artificial intelligence IQ in 2014.

title: Neural Enquirer: Learning to Query Tables with Natural Language
Abstract: Neural Enquirer is a novel neural network architecture designed to execute natural language (NL) queries on a knowledge-base (KB) for answers.  Neural Enquirer first identifies the distributed representation of a query and then executes it on KB tables to retrieve the answer as a table value.  Unlike similar efforts in end-to-end training of semantic parsers, Neural Enquirer is fully "neuralized": it provides distributional representations of both the query and KB, and it implements compositional query execution as a series of differentiable operations, storing intermediate results (consisting of table annotations at different levels) in multiple memory layers.  Neural Enquirer can be trained using gradient descent, allowing for learning of parameters for controlling components, semantic parsing components, and embeddings of tables and query words from scratch.  Training can be performed end-to-end, but it can also benefit from stronger guidance, such as step-by-step supervision for complex queries.  Neural Enquirer represents a step towards building neural network systems that understand language through execution on real-world data.  Experiments demonstrate Neural Enquirer's ability to execute fairly complex NL queries on tables with intricate structures.

title: Modeling Human Understanding of Complex Intentional Action with a Bayesian Nonparametric Subgoal Model
Abstract: Most human behaviors consist of multiple parts, steps, or subtasks.  These structures guide action planning and execution, but when observing others, the latent structure of their actions is typically unobservable and must be inferred to learn new skills through demonstration or to assist others in completing their tasks.  For instance, an assistant who understands the subgoal structure of a colleague's task can more quickly recognize and support their actions as they unfold.  This research models how humans infer subgoals from observing complex action sequences using a nonparametric Bayesian model. The model assumes that observed actions are generated through approximately rational planning based on unknown subgoal sequences.  The model is tested through a behavioral experiment where individuals observed different goal-directed action sequences and inferred the number and composition of associated subgoal sequences.  The Bayesian model predicts human subgoal inferences with high accuracy, outperforming alternative models and heuristics.  Based on this result, the paper simulates how subgoal learning and inference can enhance performance in an artificial user assistance task. The Bayesian model learns the correct subgoals from fewer observations and assists users by rapidly and accurately inferring the goal of their actions, outperforming alternative approaches.

title: The GTR-model: a universal framework for quantum-like measurements
Abstract: This paper presents the "general tension-reduction" (GTR) model, a very general geometrico-dynamical description of physical or abstract entities.  The GTR model represents not only states but also measurement-interactions and calculates associated outcome probabilities.  The model is based on the hypothesis that indeterminism arises from unavoidable fluctuations in the experimental context, aligning with the "hidden-measurements interpretation" of quantum mechanics. When the state space structure is Hilbertian and measurements are "universal" (averaged over all possible outcome selections), the GTR model produces the same predictions as the Born rule, thus providing a natural completed version of quantum mechanics. However, for non-Hilbertian state spaces or when not all possible outcome selections are available, the model's predictions generally differ from quantum ones, especially for sequential measurements.  The paper discusses paradigmatic examples from physics and human cognition, focusing on psychological effects like question order effects and response replicability, which are shown to generate non-Hilbertian statistics. The paper suggests a realistic interpretation of the GTR model when applied to human cognition and decision-making, proposing it as the generally adopted interpretative framework in quantum cognition research.

title: Recognizing Semantic Features in Faces using Deep Learning
Abstract: The human face constantly conveys information, both consciously and unconsciously. While humans naturally interpret this visual information, it presents a significant challenge for machines. Existing semantic facial feature recognition and analysis techniques, based on physiological heuristics, suffer from lack of robustness and high computation time. This thesis explores automated methods for machines to learn to interpret semantic information in faces without manual feature detector design, using the Deep Learning approach.  The thesis investigates the effects of various factors and hyper-parameters of deep neural networks to determine an optimal configuration for semantic facial feature recognition.  It examines the system's effectiveness in recognizing various semantic features (emotions, age, gender, ethnicity, etc.) present in faces.  Furthermore, the relationship between high-level concepts and low-level features is explored through an analysis of similarities in low-level descriptors for different semantic features.  The thesis also introduces a novel approach using a deep network to generate 3-D Active Appearance Models of faces from real-world 2-D images.  For a more detailed report, refer to [arXiv:1512.00743v1].

title: Assessing forensic evidence by computing belief functions
Abstract: The paper examines shortcomings in the classical probabilistic approach to forensic evidence assessment, specifically its inability to differentiate between lack of belief and disbelief and its limitations in modeling complete ignorance within a given population.  Shafer belief functions, a generalization of probability distributions, are presented as a solution addressing these issues.  The paper utilizes a belief function calculus that avoids the criticized Dempster rule of combination, focusing on Dempster-Shafer conditioning. This calculus is then applied to classical forensic problems like the island problems and parental identification.  Assuming only that the culprit or parent belongs to a specific population, the paper's answers differ from classical approaches using uniform or other priors. The classical answers can be retrieved by imposing the relevant priors, implying that the paper's setup is a generalization of the classical methodology, providing increased flexibility. The paper shows how the calculus can be used to develop an analogue of Bayes' rule using belief functions instead of probabilities.  It also discusses the implications of the theory for legal practice.

title: Quantifying knowledge with a new calculus for belief functions - a generalization of probability theory
Abstract: This paper highlights practical situations, such as forensic and gambling contexts, where the application of classical probability theory (based on Kolmogorov's axioms) is problematic.  Shafer belief functions are then introduced and discussed as a generalization of probability distributions. Philosophically, belief functions relate to individual or shared knowledge of facts rather than facts themselves, generalizing epistemic probability (probability theory interpreted epistemologically).  Belief functions offer greater flexibility and better address certain types of uncertainty than classical probability distributions.  The paper develops a new calculus for belief functions that avoids the criticized Dempster's rule of combination by generalizing the classical notions of conditioning and independence in a natural and uncontroversial manner.  This new calculus provides a detailed explanation for the rejection of Dempster's rule. The theory is applied to various examples, including gambling and forensic settings.  A law of large numbers for belief functions is proven, and a betting interpretation is offered, similar to the Dutch Book Theorem for probability distributions.

title: Object-based World Modeling in Semi-Static Environments with Dependent Dirichlet-Process Mixtures
Abstract: Robots navigating human-centric indoor environments require the ability to represent and understand the world in terms of objects and their attributes. This attribute-based representation is referred to as a world model, and the paper explores methods for acquiring it from noisy perception and maintaining it over time, as objects are added, changed, or removed.  Previous work has framed this as a multiple-target tracking problem where objects are potentially in motion constantly.  While this approach is general, it is computationally expensive. The paper argues that such generality is unnecessary in typical world modeling tasks, where objects change state only occasionally. More efficient approaches are possible by focusing on semi-static environments.  The paper examines a previously proposed clustering-based world modeling approach, designed for static environments, and extends it to semi-static domains using a dependent Dirichlet-process (DDP) mixture model.  A novel MAP inference algorithm is derived for this model, subject to data association constraints.  The paper demonstrates the approach's improved computational performance in semi-static environments.

title: Attribute2Image: Conditional Image Generation from Visual Attributes
Abstract: This paper explores a novel problem: generating images from visual attributes. The image is modeled as a composite of foreground and background, and a layered generative model with disentangled latent variables is developed.  This model can be trained end-to-end using a variational auto-encoder.  Experiments with natural images of faces and birds demonstrate the model's ability to generate realistic and diverse samples with disentangled latent representations.  A general energy minimization algorithm is used for posterior inference of latent variables given novel images. Consequently, the learned generative models show excellent quantitative and visual results in attribute-conditioned image reconstruction and completion tasks.
label: AI

title: Fast k-Nearest Neighbour Search via Dynamic Continuous Indexing
Abstract: Existing k-nearest neighbor retrieval methods suffer from the curse of dimensionality. The paper argues that this is partially due to inherent limitations in space partitioning, the underlying strategy used by most current methods.  A new strategy is proposed that avoids partitioning the vector space, along with a novel randomized algorithm that runs in time linear in dimensionality and sub-linear in intrinsic dimensionality and dataset size. The algorithm requires space constant in dimensionality and linear in dataset size.  The proposed algorithm offers fine-grained control over accuracy and speed on a per-query basis, automatically adapts to varying data density, supports dynamic dataset updates, and is easy to implement. The paper presents appealing theoretical properties and demonstrates empirically that the algorithm outperforms locality-sensitivity hashing (LSH) in terms of approximation quality, speed, and space efficiency.

title: A New Approach for Scalable Analysis of Microbial Communities
Abstract: Microbial communities play essential roles in the function and maintenance of various biosystems, from the human body to the environment. Current microbial community analysis methods rely on taxonomic phylogenetic alignment using 16S rRNA metagenomic or whole genome sequencing data.  Characterizations of microbial communities typically involve billions of sequences, aligning them to a phylogenetic tree. This paper introduces a new approach for efficient microbial community analysis. The novel reference-free technique is based on n-gram sequence analysis of 16S rRNA data, dramatically reducing processing data size (by 105 fold) without requiring taxonomic alignment.  The approach is applied to characterize phenotypic microbial community differences in various settings, including classification across body sites, characterization of oral microbiomes associated with health and disease, and longitudinal classification during infant development.  The paper introduces different dimensionality reduction methods to create a more scalable analysis framework while minimizing classification accuracy loss.  Among these techniques, a continuous vector representation for microbial communities is proposed, which can be widely applied in deep learning applications in microbial informatics. |||

title: Taxonomy grounded aggregation of classifiers with different label sets
Abstract: We address the problem of combining label predictions from diverse classifiers using a class taxonomy. Although the taxonomy might not have been considered during classifier design and training, integrating predictions into this structure is desirable. This allows us to leverage the effort invested in training the individual classifiers. We propose a heuristic approach and a principled graphical model to achieve this integration. Our model uses the taxonomy as constraints to identify the most likely hierarchically consistent class by aggregating labels. We validate our method on image and text classification tasks.

title: A Hybrid Intelligent Model for Software Cost Estimation
Abstract: Accurate estimation of software development effort is crucial for project success. Despite numerous techniques and algorithmic models, predicting this effort remains challenging, especially when dealing with uncertain, imprecise inputs and collinear characteristics. This paper proposes a hybrid intelligent model combining a neural network with a fuzzy model (neuro-fuzzy model) to improve estimation accuracy. We evaluate the model's performance using published project and industrial data. The results demonstrate a significant 18% improvement in estimation accuracy based on the Mean Magnitude of Relative Error (MMRE) criterion.
label: AI

title: Transfer Learning in Brain-Computer Interfaces
Abstract: The performance of brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) is directly influenced by the availability and distribution of training data. However, the statistical characteristics of this data vary across subjects and sessions within individuals, limiting the transferability of training data or trained models. This article reviews existing transfer learning techniques for BCIs that exploit shared structures between training data from multiple subjects or sessions to enhance performance. We introduce a framework for transfer learning in BCIs applicable to any feature space and a novel regression estimation method tailored to the structure of electroencephalogram (EEG)-based systems. The framework and method are validated in motor-imagery paradigms for subject-to-subject and session-to-session transfer. Results demonstrate superior performance compared to other methods on identical datasets, particularly in a patient with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).

title: Evaluating Morphological Computation in Muscle and DC-motor Driven Models of Human Hopping
Abstract: Morphological computation refers to processes conducted by the body (and environment) in embodied artificial intelligence, eliminating the need for the brain to perform these tasks. Leveraging environmental and morphological properties is a key feature of embodied systems, as it significantly reduces controller complexity. This work explores the behavior- and state-dependent nature of morphological computation. We evaluate two measures of morphological computation applicable to robotic systems and computer simulations of biological movement. These measures are demonstrated on muscle and DC-motor driven hopping models. A state-dependent analysis of hopping behaviors reveals insights not obtainable from averaged measures alone. This work provides algorithms and computer code for these measures.

title: LSTM Neural Reordering Feature for Statistical Machine Translation
Abstract: Artificial neural networks are powerful models widely applied in various aspects of machine translation, including language modeling and translation modeling. Despite significant advancements, the reordering problem remains a challenge in statistical machine translation. This paper introduces a novel neural reordering model directly modeling word pairs and alignment. Using LSTM recurrent neural networks, we can learn much longer context for reordering prediction. Experimental results on NIST OpenMT12 Arabic-English and Chinese-English 1000-best rescoring tasks demonstrate the robustness of our LSTM neural reordering feature, achieving significant improvements over various baseline systems.

title: Learning Using 1-Local Membership Queries
Abstract: Traditional machine learning algorithms learn from labeled examples. For instance, a machine translation system's training set typically consists of English sentences and their translations. A more robust model allows the algorithm to query for labels of new examples it creates. In the translation task, for example, the algorithm can create a new English sentence and request its translation during training. This combination of examples and queries has been extensively studied. However, despite theoretical advancements, query algorithms are rarely employed. A primary reason is a report (Baum and Lang, 1992) highlighting the poor empirical performance of a query algorithm. These unsatisfactory results were attributed to the algorithm querying for labels of artificial examples, difficult for humans to interpret. This work explores a new model of local membership queries (Awasthi et al., 2012) that aims to address the issue of artificial queries. In this model, the algorithm is only allowed to query labels of examples close to those from the training set. This ensures that queried examples remain close to natural examples, mitigating the perception of artificiality or randomness. We focus on 1-local queries (queries within distance 1 from a training example). Our findings demonstrate that 1-local membership queries are superior to the standard learning model. An experiment on the well-known sentiment analysis task in natural language processing (NLP) further illustrates this advantage. In this experiment, users provided more information than just the label. The results show that this additional information is beneficial in practice.

title: Inferring Interpersonal Relations in Narrative Summaries
Abstract: Understanding relationships between people is crucial for comprehending narratives. This work tackles the problem of inferring the polarity of relationships between individuals in narrative summaries. We frame the problem as a joint structured prediction for each narrative and propose a model that combines evidence from linguistic, semantic, and social community structure features. Additionally, we introduce a clustering-based approach that leverages regularities in narrative types. For instance, it can learn an affinity for love triangles in romantic stories. Our structured models achieve over 30% error reduction compared to a competitive baseline that considers character pairs in isolation, demonstrating their effectiveness on a dataset of Wikipedia movie summaries.

title: Imitation-Induced Criticality: Network Reciprocity and Psycho-logical Reward
Abstract: Nodes in a regular two-dimensional lattice participate in a game influenced by two distinct levels. In the initial step, a random prescription assigns half of the players the cooperation state and the other half the defection state. At the bottom level, strategy choice is based solely on imitation according to the homo imitans principle, generating collective intelligence that makes the system sensitive to the criteria governing the strategy choice at the top level. Units at the top level play the prisoner's dilemma game and can update their strategies by either adopting the strategy of the most successful nearest neighbor (success model) or based solely on maximizing financial benefit (selfishness model). The intelligence emerging from imitation-induced criticality leads to the extinction of defection in the former case and the extinction of cooperation in the latter. The former case represents network reciprocity enhanced by imitation-induced criticality, contributing to the evolution towards cooperation. We introduce morality pressure into the selfishness model through a psychological reward (Lambda) for cooperation to assess the sensitivity of collective intelligence to morality. Our findings reveal that when Lambda exceeds the temptation to cheat, the system transitions from the supercritical defection state to the critical regime. However, excessive morality and religion pressure may hinder the criticality-induced resilience of the system.

title: Ask, and shall you receive?: Understanding Desire Fulfillment in Natural Language Text
Abstract: The ability to comprehend wishes or desires and their fulfillment is critical for Natural Language Understanding. This paper introduces the task of identifying whether a desire expressed by a subject in a short piece of text was fulfilled. We propose various unstructured and structured models capturing fulfillment cues, including the subject's emotional state and actions. Experiments on two datasets demonstrate the importance of understanding narrative and discourse structure for addressing this task.

title: Modeling Dynamic Relationships Between Characters in Literary Novels
Abstract: Studying characters is fundamental to computationally representing and interpreting narratives. Unlike prior work focusing on character roles, this study investigates the problem of modeling their relationships. Rather than assuming fixed relationships between characters, we propose that relationships are dynamic and evolve temporally with the narrative's progression. We formulate the problem of relationship modeling as a structured prediction problem. We present a semi-supervised framework to learn relationship sequences from both fully and partially labeled data. A Markovian model capable of accumulating historical beliefs about relationship and status changes is introduced. We utilize a set of rich linguistic and semantically motivated features incorporating world knowledge to analyze the textual content of the narrative. Empirical results demonstrate that this framework outperforms competitive baselines.

title: Influence diagrams for the optimization of a vehicle speed profile
Abstract: Influence diagrams, decision-theoretic extensions of Bayesian networks, are applied to diverse decision problems. This paper explores their application in optimizing a vehicle speed profile. We present results from computational experiments where an influence diagram is used to optimize the speed profile of a Formula 1 race car at the Silverstone F1 circuit. The computed lap time and speed profiles closely match those achieved by test pilots. An extended version of our model incorporating a more complex optimization function and various traffic constraints is currently undergoing testing onboard a testing car by a major car manufacturer. This paper opens doors for new applications of influence diagrams.

title: On Learning to Think: Algorithmic Information Theory for Novel Combinations of Reinforcement Learning Controllers and Recurrent Neural World Models
Abstract: This paper addresses the general problem of reinforcement learning (RL) in partially observable environments. In 2013, our large RL recurrent neural networks (RNNs) learned from scratch to drive simulated cars from high-dimensional video input. However, real brains are more powerful in many ways. They learn a predictive model of their initially unknown environment and utilize it for abstract (e.g., hierarchical) planning and reasoning. Inspired by algorithmic information theory, we describe RNN-based AIs (RNNAIs) designed to emulate this capability. Such an RNNAI can be trained on never-ending sequences of tasks, some provided by the user and others invented by the RNNAI itself through curiosity and playfulness, to enhance its RNN-based world model. Unlike our previous model-building RNN-based RL machines from 1990, the RNNAI actively queries its model for abstract reasoning, planning, and decision-making, essentially "learning to think." The fundamental concepts outlined in this report can be applied to numerous scenarios involving one RNN-like system leveraging the algorithmic information content of another. These concepts stem from a grant proposal submitted in Fall 2014 and explain notions like "mirror neurons." Experimental results will be detailed in separate papers.

title: Scaling POMDPs For Selecting Sellers in E-markets-Extended Version
Abstract: In multiagent e-marketplaces, buying agents need to select good sellers by querying other buyers (called advisors). Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) have proven to be an effective framework for optimal seller selection through selective querying of advisors. However, current solution methods do not scale to hundreds or even tens of agents operating in the e-market. This paper proposes the Mixture of POMDP Experts (MOPE) technique, which leverages the inherent structure of trust-based domains, like the seller selection problem in e-markets, by aggregating solutions of smaller sub-POMDPs. We present several variants of the MOPE approach with theoretical and empirical analysis. Experiments demonstrate that MOPE can scale to a hundred agents, utilizing the presence of more advisors to significantly improve buyer satisfaction.
label: AI

title: Machine Learning Sentiment Prediction based on Hybrid Document Representation
Abstract: Automated sentiment analysis and opinion mining are complex processes involved in extracting useful subjective information from text. The explosion of user-generated content on the web, particularly the daily expression of opinions on products and services by millions of users across blogs, wikis, social networks, message boards, etc., necessitates reliable automated extraction of sentiments and opinions from unstructured text for various commercial applications. This paper presents a novel hybrid vectorization approach for textual resources combining a weighted variant of the popular Word2Vec representation (based on Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency) with a Bag-of-Words representation and a vector of lexicon-based sentiment values. The proposed text representation approach is assessed using several machine learning classification algorithms on a widely used sentiment detection dataset in literature. The classification accuracy achieved through the proposed hybrid vectorization approach surpasses the performance of its individual components and is comparable to state-of-the-art sentiment detection methodologies.

title: Exploiting Anonymity in Approximate Linear Programming: Scaling to Large Multiagent MDPs (Extended Version)
Abstract: Many exact and approximate solution methods for Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) attempt to exploit structure in the problem and are based on factorization of the value function. However, multiagent settings are known to experience an exponential increase in value component sizes as interactions become denser, limiting approximation architectures in the problem sizes and types they can handle. We propose an approach to mitigate this limitation for certain types of multiagent systems, exploiting a property termed "anonymous influence" in the factored MDP. Anonymous influence efficiently summarizes joint variable effects when the explicit representation of variable identity in the problem can be avoided. We demonstrate how representational benefits from anonymity translate into computational efficiencies, both for general variable elimination in a factor graph and specifically for the approximate linear programming solution to factored MDPs. This allows scaling linear programming to factored MDPs previously unsolvable. Our results are illustrated for the control of a stochastic disease process over a densely connected graph with 50 nodes and 25 agents.
label: AI

title: Sparse Coral Classification Using Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: Autonomous repair of deep-sea coral reefs is a recently proposed idea to support the oceans ecosystem, which is vital for commercial fishing, tourism, and other species. This concept involves employing numerous small autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) and swarm intelligence techniques to locate and replace broken coral chunks, enabling regrowth and habitat maintenance. This project aims to develop machine vision algorithms to enable an underwater robot to locate a coral reef and a coral chunk on the seabed, prompting the robot to pick it up. Although there is no existing literature on this specific problem, related work on fish counting may provide some insight. Technical challenges arise primarily from potential water clarity issues, platform stabilization, and spurious artifacts (rocks, fish, and crabs). We present an efficient sparse classification for coral species using a supervised deep learning method called Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). We compute Weber Local Descriptor (WLD), Phase Congruency (PC), and Zero Component Analysis (ZCA) Whitening to extract shape and texture feature descriptors, which serve as supplementary channels (feature-based maps) alongside basic spatial color channels (spatial-based maps) of the coral input image. We also experiment with state-of-the-art underwater preprocessing algorithms for image enhancement, color normalization, and color conversion adjustment. Our proposed coral classification method, developed on the MATLAB platform, is evaluated using two different coral datasets: the University of California San Diego's Moorea Labeled Corals and Heriot-Watt University's Atlantic Deep Sea.
label: AI

title: Solving Transition-Independent Multi-agent MDPs with Sparse Interactions (Extended version)
Abstract: In cooperative multi-agent sequential decision making under uncertainty, agents must coordinate to find an optimal joint policy that maximizes joint value. Traditional algorithms exploit additive structure in the value function, but in the fully-observable multi-agent MDP setting (MMDP), such structure is absent. We propose a new optimal solver for transition-independent MMDPs, where agents can only affect their own state, but their reward depends on joint transitions. We represent these dependencies compactly in conditional return graphs (CRGs). Using CRGs, the value of a joint policy and bounds on partially specified joint policies can be efficiently computed. We introduce CoRe, a novel branch-and-bound policy search algorithm based on CRGs. CoRe typically requires less runtime than available alternatives and finds solutions to problems previously unsolvable.
label: AI

title: Robotic Search & Rescue via Online Multi-task Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a widely known method for robots to learn an optimal control policy to solve specific tasks. We aim to develop a versatile robot capable of learning multiple tasks. However, applying RL to each task would be prohibitively expensive in terms of time and robot wear-and-tear. To address this issue, we utilize the Policy Gradient Efficient Lifelong Learning Algorithm (PG-ELLA), an online multi-task RL algorithm enabling the robot to efficiently learn consecutive tasks by sharing knowledge between them. This accelerates learning and improves performance. We implemented and evaluated three RL methods – Q-learning, policy gradient RL, and PG-ELLA – on a ground robot tasked with finding a target object in an environment under varying surface conditions. This paper discusses our implementations and presents an empirical analysis of their learning performance.
label: AI

title: Bootstrapping Ternary Relation Extractors
Abstract: Binary relation extraction methods have been extensively studied in recent years. However, few methods have been developed for higher n-ary relation extraction. One limiting factor is the effort required to generate training data. For binary relations, a few dozen pairs of entities per relation suffice as training data. For ternary relations (n=3), each training instance is a triplet of entities, increasing the cognitive load on individuals. For example, many people know that Google acquired YouTube but not the dollar amount or the date of the acquisition. Similarly, many people know that Hillary Clinton is married to Bill Clinton but not the location or date of their wedding. This makes generating higher n-ary training data a time-consuming exercise in web searching. We present a resource for training ternary relation extractors generated using a minimally supervised yet effective approach. We provide statistics on the size and quality of the dataset.
label: AI

title: Column-Oriented Datalog Materialization for Large Knowledge Graphs (Extended Technical Report)
Abstract: Evaluating Datalog rules over large Knowledge Graphs (KGs) is essential for many applications. This paper presents a novel method for materializing Datalog inferences, combining a column-based memory layout with optimization methods that avoid redundant inferences at runtime. Proactive caching of specific subqueries further enhances efficiency. Our empirical evaluation shows that this approach can often match or surpass the performance of state-of-the-art systems, particularly under resource constraints. |||
label: AI

title: Applying deep learning to classify pornographic images and videos
Abstract: Pornographic content is easily accessible, including to children. Social media platforms are working to isolate adult material. Intelligent image analysis can help detect and isolate these images. However, these methods require extensive expertise to design classifiers. This paper proposes using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for this purpose. CNNs automatically extract features and classify images, simplifying the process and achieving higher accuracy than existing methods.
label: AI

title: Semantic Folding Theory And its Application in Semantic Fingerprinting
Abstract: Human language is complex, and no computer system has matched human performance in language processing. While we learn more about the brain, its computational processes remain unclear. This lack of understanding hinders progress in natural language processing (NLP). To address this, statistical models are used, but the representation of language within the brain remains an unsolved problem. This paper presents a theory of language data representation called Semantic Folding, based on Jeff Hawkins' Hierarchical Temporal Memory (HTM) theory. Semantic Folding converts language from its symbolic form (text) into a semantically grounded representation suitable for processing by HTM networks. This change in representation improves performance in various NLP tasks, overcoming challenges such as high computational cost, the precision-recall trade-off, and complex tuning procedures.
label: AI

title: Multiagent Cooperation and Competition with Deep Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: Multiagent systems are common in social, economic, and political settings. This paper extends the Deep Q-Learning Network architecture to multiagent environments, investigating the interaction of two agents controlled by independent Deep Q-Networks in the game Pong. By manipulating the game's reward system, the authors demonstrate the emergence of competitive and collaborative behaviors. Competitive agents learn to play efficiently, while collaborative agents develop strategies to keep the ball in play for as long as possible. This work suggests that Deep Q-Networks can be used to study decentralized learning in multiagent systems.
label: AI

title: War of 2050: a Battle for Information, Communications, and Computer Security
Abstract: Future warfare will be significantly influenced by advancements in information technologies, with information becoming the decisive domain. This paper outlines four key developments: the proliferation of intelligent systems, augmented humans, the battle for information dominance, and networked command and control. These capabilities share a vulnerability: attacks on the information, communications, and computers that enable human-robot teams to operate effectively. The unseen battle for cybersecurity will determine the success of adversaries on the battlefield of 2050.
label: AI

title: On the convergence of cycle detection for navigational reinforcement learning
Abstract: This paper explores a reinforcement learning framework where agents navigate from start to goal states. The authors prove the convergence of a cycle-detection learning algorithm for a class of tasks called "reducible," which have acyclic solutions. They characterize the form of the final policy, enabling the detection of convergence during simulations. The findings demonstrate that even simple algorithms can effectively learn nontrivial tasks. This framework uses basic concepts to formally prove convergence.
label: AI

title: Word Existence Algorithm
Abstract: The speed of data access is crucial in modern computing. This paper introduces the "word existence algorithm," which checks if a given word is present in a database. The algorithm uses a uniformly distributed hash function to solve the lookup problem, addressing clustering and collision issues. It utilizes a direct hashed model where hash values link to another table if continuity holds. The algorithm focuses on forming a continuity series and validating word existence in the database. This approach can be used in applications requiring efficient word existence searches, such as artificial intelligence, neural networks, and dictionary lookups. The authors have observed faster search times with this algorithm.
label: AI

title: Shaping Proto-Value Functions via Rewards
Abstract: This paper combines task-dependent reward shaping and task-independent proto-value functions to create reward-dependent proto-value functions (RPVFs). RPVFs utilize immediate rewards during sampling, which are not used in the PVF construction. Experiments demonstrate that learning with RPVFs outperforms learning with just reward shaping or PVFs. RPVFs capture asymmetry better than PVFs in state spaces with symmetrical structures and asymmetrical rewards.
label: AI

title: A Stochastic Process Model of Classical Search
Abstract: A* is an efficient search algorithm, but in many situations optimal solutions are infeasible. This paper formalizes the process of classical search as a meta-level decision problem, the Abstract Search MDP. This framework establishes a notion of optimal behavior for search algorithms and provides a theoretical approach to algorithm design. The authors solve a version of the Abstract Search MDP for anytime algorithms, resulting in a new algorithm called SMIRI (Search by Maximizing the Incremental Rate of Improvement). SMIRI outperforms existing anytime search algorithms on a stochastic tree model for most parameter values.
label: AI

title: Some Epistemological Problems with the Knowledge Level in Cognitive Architectures
Abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of handling complex knowledge structures in cognitive systems, comparable in size and typology to the knowledge humans process daily. Handling and retrieving knowledge selectively based on situational needs is essential for human intelligence. Humans use heuristics due to bounded rationality. Cognitive systems should be designed to identify and retrieve relevant knowledge from their long-term memory (LTM) heuristically. Existing systems lack this capability. This paper argues that this is an epistemological as well as a technological problem and sketches a potential solution.
label: AI

title: Incremental Truncated LSTD
Abstract: Balancing computational efficiency and sample efficiency is crucial in reinforcement learning. Temporal difference (TD) algorithms are computationally efficient but sample-inefficient, while least-squares temporal difference (LSTD) algorithms are sample-efficient but computationally expensive. This paper presents an efficient incremental low-rank LSTD({\\lambda}) algorithm that strikes a balance between computation and sample efficiency. The algorithm reduces computational and storage complexity while effectively summarizing past samples, achieving the sample complexity of LSTD. The authors derive a simulation bound on the solution, illustrating a bias-variance trade-off depending on the chosen rank. The algorithm demonstrates effective balancing of computational complexity and sample efficiency in policy evaluation tasks.
label: AI

title: Bayesian Network Models for Adaptive Testing
Abstract: Computerized adaptive testing (CAT) is a promising approach to evaluating human abilities. This paper uses Bayesian networks to model students taking grammar school tests. The authors collected data from paper tests and propose several Bayesian networks that are tested and compared through cross-validation. The analysis provides insights into the model selection problem. Future research directions are outlined in the concluding section.
label: AI

title: An Introduction to Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) have revolutionized machine learning, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs). CNNs are used for image-driven pattern recognition tasks and offer a simplified approach to ANNs. This document provides a brief introduction to CNNs, discussing recent research and techniques in developing these image recognition models. This introduction assumes basic knowledge of ANNs and machine learning.
label: AI

title: A Symbolic SAT-based Algorithm for Almost-sure Reachability with Small Strategies in POMDPs
Abstract: Partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) are standard models for probabilistic planning problems. This paper studies the problem of almost-sure reachability, where the goal is to determine if a policy exists to reach a target set of states with probability 1. While the problem is generally EXPTIME-complete, practical scenarios often require policies with limited memory. The existing solution involves explicitly constructing an exponential reduction to a belief-support MDP. This paper investigates the existence of observation-stationary strategies (which is NP-complete) and small-memory strategies. The authors present a symbolic algorithm based on SAT encoding and a SAT solver to address this problem. Experimental results demonstrate the scalability of this approach.
label: AI

title: Who Can Win a Single-Elimination Tournament?
Abstract: Single-elimination (SE) tournaments are widely used in sports and elections. This paper investigates the tournament fixing problem (TFP): given match outcomes, can an organizer rig an SE tournament to ensure a specific player wins? The authors prove new sufficient conditions for the existence of a seeding where the favorite player wins. These results significantly generalize previous findings. The relationship between SE winners and other tournament solutions is also explored. The authors extend prior work on probabilistic models for generating tournaments, showing that every player in a Condorcet Random Model tournament will be an SE winner even with minimal noise. New results are established for more general generative models.
label: AI

title: Beyond OWL 2 QL in OBDA: Rewritings and Approximations (Extended Version)
Abstract: Ontology-based data access (OBDA) provides access to relational data by linking data sources to an ontology through declarative mappings. DL-Lite_R, the logic underlying OWL 2 QL and widely used in OBDA, has limited expressive power. This paper aims to extend OBDA to more expressive ontology languages while leveraging relational technology for query answering. The authors achieve this by combining conservative rewriting and approximation techniques, incorporating the mapping layer into the process. They develop techniques to rewrite OBDA specifications with a rich ontology to equivalent ones using DL-Lite_R, or approximate them otherwise. This approach leverages the mapping layer to capture domain semantics from rich ontology languages. The implemented system, OntoProx, demonstrates the feasibility and effectiveness of these techniques.
label: AI

title: A global Constraint for mining Sequential Patterns with GAP constraint
Abstract: Sequential pattern mining (SPM) under gap constraint is a challenging task. Existing methods lack genericity, and constraint programming approaches struggle due to large encodings. This paper proposes a global constraint called GAP-SEQ for SPM, which handles gap constraints efficiently. GAP-SEQ relies on right pattern extensions. Experiments show that this approach outperforms CP methods and the state-of-the-art cSpade method on large datasets.
label: AI

title: Welfare of Sequential Allocation Mechanisms for Indivisible Goods
Abstract: Sequential allocation is a simple and efficient method for allocating indivisible goods, but it may not maximize social welfare. This paper examines the relationship between welfare and efficiency in sequential allocation. The authors investigate the computational complexity of determining possible and necessary welfare levels based on different allocation policies. They also consider a novel control problem where a chair chooses a policy to improve social welfare.
label: AI

title: A Deep Architecture for Semantic Matching with Multiple Positional Sentence Representations
Abstract: Matching natural language sentences is crucial for tasks like information retrieval and question answering. Existing deep models rely on single or multi-granularity sentence representations, which cannot effectively capture contextualized local information during matching. This paper proposes a new deep architecture for sentence matching using multiple positional sentence representations. Each representation is generated by a bidirectional long short-term memory (Bi-LSTM), capturing the context of the whole sentence. Matching scores are aggregated through k-Max pooling and a multi-layer perceptron. This model leverages the rich context of the whole sentence and provides flexibility to aggregate different important contextualized information, improving performance on question answering and sentence completion tasks.
label: AI

title: Recurrent Instance Segmentation
Abstract: Instance segmentation involves detecting and delineating individual objects in an image. Current approaches consist of independently trained modules, limiting opportunities for joint learning. This paper introduces a new instance segmentation paradigm based on an end-to-end method that learns to segment instances sequentially. The model uses a recurrent neural network with a spatial memory to track explained pixels and handle occlusions. A principled loss function accurately represents the instance segmentation problem. Experiments demonstrate superior performance on person segmentation and leaf counting compared to recent approaches.
label: AI

title: Plan Explicability and Predictability for Robot Task Planning
Abstract: Intelligent robots and machines are becoming increasingly prevalent in human environments. A desirable capability is goal-oriented task planning, but this autonomy can lead to cognitive overload and safety risks if agents behave unexpectedly. This paper introduces the concepts of plan explicability and predictability to ensure human understanding. The authors propose that humans understand plans by associating abstract tasks with agent actions, which can be learned using conditional random fields (CRFs). These measures enable agents to proactively choose or synthesize plans that are more explicable and predictable to humans. Evaluations on a synthetic domain and with human subjects using physical robots demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. |||
label: AI

title: Reinstating Combinatorial Protections for Manipulation and Bribery in Single-Peaked and Nearly Single-Peaked Electorates
Abstract: Computational complexity plays a vital role in safeguarding elections from manipulation. However, recent research has shown that some previously considered NP-hardness shields become ineffective when voters have single-peaked or nearly single-peaked preferences. This paper explores the possibility of re-establishing these shields by allowing voters to submit partial preferences instead of complete ballots.  It demonstrates that in single-peaked and nearly single-peaked electorates, requiring voters to provide top-truncated ballots increases the complexity of manipulation and bribery for many voting rules, shifting them from P to NP-complete.
label: AI

title: Unifying Decision Trees Split Criteria Using Tsallis Entropy
Abstract: The construction of efficient and effective decision trees is a fundamental challenge in machine learning due to their simplicity and flexibility. While various heuristic algorithms have been proposed to create near-optimal decision trees, the split criteria employed by classical algorithms like ID3, C4.5, and CART—Shannon entropy, Gain Ratio, and Gini index respectively—can be unified within a Tsallis entropy framework. Tsallis entropy, a generalization of Shannon entropy, introduces an adjustable parameter 'q' that enhances decision tree performance. This paper presents the Tsallis Entropy Criterion (TEC) algorithm, which unifies the split criteria of decision trees by generalizing them using Tsallis entropy.  Importantly, it reveals the relationships between Tsallis entropy with different 'q' values and other split criteria.  Experimental results on UCI datasets demonstrate the TEC algorithm's statistically significant improvement over traditional algorithms.
label: AI

title: A Roadmap towards Machine Intelligence
Abstract: Building intelligent machines that effectively communicate and learn is a major challenge in computer science. This paper proposes fundamental properties these machines should possess, focusing on communication and learning.  It discusses a simple environment designed to incrementally teach a machine the basics of natural-language-based communication, a crucial step towards more complex human interaction.  The paper also presents conjectures on the algorithms the machine should support to learn effectively from the environment.
label: AI

title: Strategic Dialogue Management via Deep Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: Developing artificially intelligent agents capable of strategic negotiation during interactions with other agents (natural or artificial) remains an area of active research. This paper presents a successful application of Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) to train intelligent agents with strategic conversational skills in a situated dialogue setting. While previous studies have modeled strategic agent behavior using supervised learning and traditional reinforcement learning, this research applies DRL to a high-dimensional state space within the strategic board game Settlers of Catan. In this game, players can exchange resources and negotiate offers. Experimental results demonstrate that the DRL-based learned policies significantly outperform baselines including random, rule-based, and supervised-based approaches. The DRL-based policy achieves a 53% win rate against three automated players, compared to a supervised player's 27% win rate. This result highlights the promise of DRL for training dialogue systems and strategic agents with negotiation capabilities.
label: AI

title: Learning with Memory Embeddings
Abstract: Embedding learning, a type of representation learning, has proven effective in modeling large-scale semantic knowledge graphs. A key principle involves mapping the knowledge graph to a tensor representation where entries are predicted by models using latent representations of generalized entities. Latent variable models are well-suited to address the high dimensionality and sparsity characteristic of knowledge graphs. Recent work has extended these embedding models to incorporate temporal evolutions, time patterns, and subsymbolic representations. This paper maps embedding models, originally developed for technical problems in temporal knowledge graph modeling, to various cognitive memory functions, including semantic and concept memory, episodic memory, sensory memory, short-term memory, and working memory. It discusses learning, query answering, the pathway from sensory input to semantic decoding, and the relationship between episodic and semantic memory.  Several hypotheses about human memory are introduced, derived from the developed mathematical models.
label: AI

title: Breaking Symmetries in Graph Search with Canonizing Sets
Abstract: Many complex combinatorial problems involve searching for an undirected graph that meets specific constraints. These problems are often challenging due to the vast number of isomorphic representations of their solutions.  This paper introduces effective and compact, complete symmetry breaking constraints for small graph search. Enumerating with these symmetry breaks generates all and only non-isomorphic solutions. For small search problems with up to 10 vertices, instance-independent symmetry breaking constraints are computed. For larger problems, instance-dependent constraints are demonstrated to be complete.  The paper illustrates the application of complete symmetry breaking constraints to extend two known sequences from the OEIS related to graph enumeration. It also demonstrates the application of a generalization of this approach to fully-interchangeable matrix search problems.
label: AI

title: MOOCs Meet Measurement Theory: A Topic-Modelling Approach
Abstract: This paper adapts topic models to the psychometric testing of MOOC students based on their online forum postings. Measurement theory in education and psychology provides statistical models for quantifying a person's intangible attributes, such as attitudes, abilities, or intelligence.  These models infer latent skill levels by relating them to observed responses on a series of items, such as quiz questions.  A set of items can effectively measure a latent skill if individuals' responses conform to a Guttman scale.  Well-scaled items differentiate between individuals and inferred levels span the entire range from basic to advanced.  However, manually devising well-scaled items is costly and requires expertise, limiting the use of psychometric testing in everyday teaching. This research aims to develop usable measurement models for highly-instrumented MOOC platforms by utilizing participation in automatically-extracted online forum topics as items. The challenge lies in formalizing the Guttman scale educational constraint and incorporating it into topic models.  To favor topics that automatically conform to a Guttman scale, a novel regularization is introduced into non-negative matrix factorization-based topic modeling. The paper demonstrates the suitability of this approach through quantitative experiments on three Coursera MOOCs and a qualitative survey of topic interpretability on two MOOCs via domain expert interviews.
label: AI

title: A Python Engine for Teaching Artificial Intelligence in Games
Abstract: Computer games are a valuable tool in our society, motivating people to learn computer science. As artificial intelligence (AI) is central to most games, they can be used to teach AI principles.  This paper introduces the Game AI Game Engine (GAIGE), a Python game engine specifically designed to teach about AI in computer games. A progression of seven assignments leads to a complete, working Multi-User Battle Arena (MOBA) game.  The paper describes the engine, assignments, and experiences using it in a class on Game Artificial Intelligence.
label: AI

title: Searching for Objects using Structure in Indoor Scenes
Abstract: Passive computer vision systems generally process all regions of an image to identify objects of a particular class. However, scene structure can be leveraged to search for objects without processing the entire image. This paper proposes a search technique that sequentially processes image regions, prioritizing those more likely to correspond to the query class object.  The problem is framed as a Markov decision process, and an imitation learning algorithm is used to learn a search strategy. Since scene structure is essential for search, the focus is on indoor scene images, which contain both unary scene context information and object-object context. Experiments on the NYU-depth v2 dataset demonstrate that unary scene context features alone can achieve significantly high average precision while processing only 20-25% of the regions for classes like bed and sofa. Incorporating object-object context further improves performance for classes like counter, lamp, pillow, and sofa.
label: AI

title: Approximate Probabilistic Inference via Word-Level Counting
Abstract: Hashing-based model counting has emerged as a promising approach for large-scale probabilistic inference on graphical models.  A key aspect of these techniques is the use of xor-based 2-universal hash functions operating over Boolean domains.  Many counting problems in probabilistic inference, however, are naturally encoded over finite discrete domains. Techniques based on bit-level (or Boolean) hash functions require these problems to be propositionalized, hindering the utilization of advances in SMT (Satisfiability Modulo Theory) solvers that can reason directly over words (or bit-vectors). This work presents the first approximate model counter that uses word-level hashing functions, directly leveraging the power of sophisticated SMT solvers. Empirical evaluation on a comprehensive set of benchmarks demonstrates the promise of this approach.
label: AI

title: Exploiting Environmental Computation in a Multi-Agent Model of Slime Mould
Abstract: Simple organisms like the single-celled amoeboid slime mold Physarum polycephalum, despite lacking neural tissue, exhibit complex biological and computational behavior. This raises the question of whether environmental stimuli contribute to the complexity of slime mold behavior.  This paper uses a multi-agent collective model of slime mold to explore a two-way mechanism where collective behavior is influenced by simulated chemical concentration gradient fields and, in turn, this behavior alters the spatial pattern of the concentration gradients. This simple mechanism generates complex behavior amidst dynamically changing gradient profiles, suggesting that the seemingly intelligent response of the slime mold could be attributed to outsourcing computation to the environment.
label: AI

title: A Survey of Signed Network Mining in Social Media
Abstract: Many real-world relationships can be represented by signed networks with positive and negative links, leading to increasing interest in signed network analysis across various disciplines. With the growing prevalence of social media networks, signed network analysis has shifted from theoretical development and measurement towards mining tasks.  This article presents a review of mining signed networks in the context of social media, discussing promising research directions and new frontiers. It begins by introducing basic concepts, unique properties, and principles of signed networks. The article then classifies and reviews tasks of signed network mining with representative algorithms.  It also delineates tasks that have not been extensively studied, providing formal definitions and proposing research directions to expand the field of signed network mining.
label: AI

title: Planning in the Wild: Modeling Tools for PDDL
Abstract: While sophisticated AI planning algorithms exist, many integrated, large-scale projects do not utilize planning. One reason for this gap seems to be the lack of support from engineering tools, such as syntax highlighting and visualization. This paper proposes myPDDL, a modular toolbox for efficiently creating PDDL domains and problems. To evaluate myPDDL, it compares it to existing knowledge engineering tools for PDDL and experimentally assesses its usefulness for novice PDDL users.
label: AI

title: Learning Visual Predictive Models of Physics for Playing Billiards
Abstract: The ability to plan and execute goal-specific actions in varied, unexpected settings is crucial for intelligent agents. This paper explores how an agent can be equipped with an internal model of the dynamics of the external world and utilize this model to plan novel actions by running multiple internal simulations ("visual imagination").  The models directly process raw visual input and employ a novel object-centric prediction formulation based on visual glimpses centered on objects (fixations) to enforce translational invariance of the learned physical laws.  The agent gathers training data through random interaction with various environments, enabling the resulting model to plan goal-directed actions in unseen environments.
