The paper demonstrates the agent's ability to accurately plan actions for playing a simulated billiards game, requiring the agent to push a ball into a target position or into collision with another ball.
label: AI

title: MazeBase: A Sandbox for Learning from Games
Abstract: MazeBase is introduced: a sandbox environment for simple 2D games designed to facilitate the development of machine learning approaches to reasoning and planning.  Ten simple games are created within MazeBase, each embodying a range of algorithmic tasks (e.g., if-then statements or set negation). A variety of neural models (fully connected, convolutional network, memory network) are deployed via reinforcement learning on these games, with and without a procedurally generated curriculum. Despite the simplicity of the tasks, the performance of the models is far from optimal, suggesting directions for future development.  The versatility of MazeBase is further demonstrated by emulating small combat scenarios from StarCraft. Models trained on the MazeBase version can be directly applied to StarCraft, consistently outperforming the in-game AI.
label: AI

title: What is the plausibility of probability?(revised 2003, 2015)
Abstract: This paper presents and examines a result related to uncertainty reasoning, namely that a certain plausibility space of Cox's type can be uniquely embedded in a minimal ordered field. While this is a purely mathematical result, it implies that any rational method for reasoning with uncertainty must be based on sets of extended probability distributions, where extended probability is standard probability extended with infinitesimals. This claim is supported by non-mathematical argumentation, as pure mathematics does not provide insight into the world. The paper proposes one such argumentation and relates it to results from the literature on uncertainty and statistics.  A retrospective section discusses developments in the area regarding countable additivity, partially ordered domains, robustness, and philosophical stances on the Cox/Jaynes approach since 2003. The paper also shows that the most general partially ordered plausibility calculus embeddable in a ring can be represented as a set of extended probability distributions, or algebraically, as a subdirect sum of ordered fields. In other words, the robust Bayesian approach is universal. This result is exemplified by relating Dempster-Shafer's evidence theory to robust Bayesian analysis.
label: AI

title: Interpretable Two-level Boolean Rule Learning for Classification
Abstract: This paper proposes algorithms for learning two-level Boolean rules in Conjunctive Normal Form (CNF, i.e., AND-of-ORs) or Disjunctive Normal Form (DNF, i.e., OR-of-ANDs) as a type of human-interpretable classification model. The goal is to achieve a favorable trade-off between classification accuracy and the simplicity of the rule. Two formulations are proposed: the first is an integer program whose objective function combines the total number of errors and the total number of features used in the rule. This formulation generalizes a previously proposed linear programming (LP) relaxation from one-level to two-level rules.  The second formulation replaces the 0-1 classification error with the Hamming distance from the current two-level rule to the closest rule that correctly classifies a sample. Based on this second formulation, block coordinate descent and alternating minimization algorithms are developed. Experiments show that two-level rules can yield noticeably better performance than one-level rules due to their greater modeling capacity, and the two algorithms based on the Hamming distance formulation are generally superior to other two-level rule learning methods. An approach to binarize fractional values in the optimal solutions of LP relaxations is also shown to be effective.
label: AI

title: Learning Simple Algorithms from Examples
Abstract: This paper presents an approach for learning simple algorithms, such as copying, multi-digit addition, and single-digit multiplication directly from examples. The framework consists of a set of interfaces accessed by a controller. Typical interfaces include 1-D tapes or 2-D grids that hold the input and output data.  For the controller, a range of neural network-based models are explored, varying in their ability to abstract the underlying algorithm from training instances and generalize to test examples with many thousands of digits. The controller is trained using Q-learning with several enhancements, and it is shown that the bottleneck lies in the capabilities of the controller rather than the search incurred by Q-learning.
label: AI

title: Noisy Submodular Maximization via Adaptive Sampling with Applications to Crowdsourced Image Collection Summarization
Abstract: This paper addresses the problem of maximizing an unknown submodular function that can only be accessed through noisy evaluations. The work is motivated by the task of summarizing content, such as image collections, by leveraging user feedback in the form of clicks or ratings. For summarization tasks aiming to maximize coverage and diversity, submodular set functions are a natural choice. When the underlying submodular function is unknown, user feedback provides noisy evaluations of the function that we seek to maximize. The paper presents a generic algorithm, \submM{}, for maximizing an unknown submodular function under cardinality constraints. This algorithm incorporates a novel exploration module, \blbox{}, which proposes good elements based on adaptively sampling noisy function evaluations. \blbox{} can accommodate different observation models, such as value queries and pairwise comparisons. PAC-style guarantees are provided on the quality and sampling cost of the solution obtained by \submM{}. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated in an interactive, crowdsourced image collection summarization application.
label: AI

title: Multi-Agent Continuous Transportation with Online Balanced Partitioning
Abstract: The concept of continuous transportation tasks is introduced to the context of multi-agent systems. In a continuous transportation task, a multi-agent team visits fixed locations, picks up objects, and delivers them to a final destination. The objective is to maximize the transportation rate while objects are replenished over time. Examples of such problems include foraging, area sweeping, and the first/last mile problem. Previous approaches often neglect interference and rely heavily on communication among agents, sometimes incorporating an additional reconnaissance agent for information gathering. This paper presents a hybrid of centralized and distributed approaches that minimize interference and communication in the multi-agent team without the need for a reconnaissance agent. Two partitioning-transportation algorithms inspired by existing algorithms are contributed, along with a novel online partitioning-transportation algorithm incorporating information gathering within the multi-agent team. These algorithms have been implemented and extensively tested in simulation. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of these algorithms, outperforming existing methods even without communication between agents or a reconnaissance agent. |||
label: AI

title: SceneNet: Understanding Real World Indoor Scenes With Synthetic Data
Abstract: Scene understanding is crucial for automated intelligent machines operating in real-world environments. Supervised learning approaches have shown promise, but require vast amounts of labeled data, which is expensive and time-consuming to acquire. This paper explores the potential of computer graphics to generate virtually unlimited labeled data from synthetic 3D scenes for depth-based semantic per-pixel labeling. By incorporating appropriate noise models in the data synthesis process, the authors achieve performance comparable to state-of-the-art RGBD systems on the NYUv2 dataset, using only depth data as input. They also establish a benchmark for depth-based segmentation on the SUN RGB-D dataset. Additionally, the paper outlines a method for generating synthesized frame or video data and discusses factors influencing performance gains.
label: AI

title: Non-Sentential Utterances in Dialogue: Experiments in Classification and Interpretation
Abstract: Non-sentential utterances (NSUs), such as "OK", "where?", or "probably at his apartment," lack complete sentential form but convey meaning within a dialogue context. Interpreting NSUs is crucial in computational linguistics due to their frequent occurrence and context-dependency. This thesis addresses the problem of retrieving the full semantic content of NSUs from their form and the dialogue context. The first part focuses on NSU classification, building upon previous work with new features and semi-supervised learning techniques, achieving modest but significant improvement in classification performance. The second part tackles the inference of semantic representations for NSUs based on dialogue context, reimplementing existing resolution rules with a probabilistic account of the dialogue state. This probabilistic approach allows for encoding probabilistic knowledge, providing a principled account of ambiguities in the NSU resolution process.
label: AI

title: Evaluating Prerequisite Qualities for Learning End-to-End Dialog Systems
Abstract: Building intelligent conversational agents is a long-term goal in machine learning. Training end-to-end models on large amounts of real dialogue transcripts is a popular approach but lacks clarity in understanding the model's successes and limitations. Synthetic data tasks, such as the bAbI tasks, offer a contrasting approach by measuring reasoning capabilities over toy language. However, their small scale may encourage methods that don't generalize well. This paper proposes a suite of larger-scale tasks in the domain of movies, testing models' ability to answer factual questions, provide personalization, engage in short conversations, and perform on natural dialogues from Reddit. The dataset encompasses 75k movie entities and 3.5M training examples, providing a benchmark for evaluating various models.
label: AI

title: Countering Social Engineering through Social Media: An Enterprise Security Perspective
Abstract: Social engineering attacks targeting social media channels pose a growing threat to enterprise data security. This paper examines concerns related to social engineering on social media within organizations and explores countermeasures implemented to mitigate the risks. It also analyzes existing social media security policies and guidelines in both the public and private sectors.
label: AI

title: Near-Optimal Active Learning of Multi-Output Gaussian Processes
Abstract: This paper addresses the problem of active learning for a multi-output Gaussian process (MOGP) model representing correlated environmental phenomena. Unlike existing works, this approach focuses on selecting not only the most informative sampling locations but also the types of measurements at each location to minimize the predictive uncertainty of a target phenomenon given a limited sampling budget. The entropy criterion used for optimization scales poorly with the number of candidate locations and observations. To address this, the authors derive a novel active learning criterion based on sparse MOGP model structures and exploit a relaxed submodularity property to develop a polynomial-time approximation algorithm with performance guarantees. Empirical evaluation on real-world datasets demonstrates the superiority of the proposed approach compared to existing active learning algorithms for MOGP and single-output GP models.
label: AI

title: Gaussian Process Planning with Lipschitz Continuous Reward Functions: Towards Unifying Bayesian Optimization, Active Learning, and Beyond
Abstract: This paper presents a novel, nonmyopic adaptive Gaussian process planning (GPP) framework using a general class of Lipschitz continuous reward functions. This framework unifies various active learning/sensing and Bayesian optimization criteria, offering flexibility for defining new tasks and problems. It employs a principled Bayesian sequential decision problem framework to jointly optimize the exploration-exploitation trade-off. Due to the uncountable set of candidate observations, the induced GPP policy cannot be derived exactly. The authors leverage the Lipschitz continuity of reward functions to solve for a nonmyopic adaptive epsilon-optimal GPP policy and propose an asymptotically optimal, branch-and-bound anytime variant for real-time planning. Empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the epsilon-GPP policy and its anytime variant in Bayesian optimization and an energy harvesting task.
label: AI

title: Applying Social Media Intelligence for Predicting and Identifying On-line Radicalization and Civil Unrest Oriented Threats
Abstract: Social media platforms, such as Twitter, Tumblr, Facebook, YouTube, blogs, and discussion forums, have been exploited by extremist groups for spreading their ideologies, promoting radicalization, recruiting members, and creating online communities with shared agendas. Twitter, in particular, serves as a real-time platform for information sharing and communication during civil unrest events. Predicting and identifying online radicalization and civil unrest-related threats using social media intelligence has garnered significant research interest over the past decade. This paper reviews existing techniques and algorithms for countering cyber-extremism and predicting protest-related events, analyzing the state-of-the-art, trends, and research gaps. A one-class classification approach is employed to gather scholarly articles relevant to the research scope, followed by characterization, classification, and meta-analysis of approximately 100 conference and journal papers to gain a comprehensive understanding of the existing literature.
label: AI

title: A Model for Web-Intelligence Index to Evaluate the Web Intelligence Capacity of Government Web Sites of Sri Lanka
Abstract: Web intelligence, a subset of artificial intelligence, utilizes existing web data to generate new data, knowledge, and wisdom for decision-making and predictions for web users. While artificial intelligence is widely used in web-based business applications in developed countries, its application in Sri Lanka remains unexplored. This paper proposes a model for evaluating web intelligence capability based on weighting key functionalities in relation to web intelligence. Government websites were assessed using the proposed criteria to determine the potential of web intelligence technologies for providing website-based services. The results indicate that the use of web intelligence techniques for public service delivery through government websites is unsatisfactory. The paper highlights the limitations in leveraging web intelligence technologies in public service websites, hindering the benefits that citizens and the government could gain from such technological advancements.
label: AI

title: Hand Pose Estimation through Semi-Supervised and Weakly-Supervised Learning
Abstract: This paper proposes a method for hand pose estimation using a deep regressor trained on two different input types: raw depth data and an intermediate representation in the form of a hand segmentation into parts. The segmentation representation provides topological information and cues for reasoning about joint locations. The mapping from raw depth to segmentation is learned semi/weakly-supervised from two datasets: a synthetic dataset with dense ground truth segmentations and a real image dataset with ground truth joint positions but no dense segmentations. Loss for training on real images is generated from a patch-wise restoration process aligning tentative segmentation maps with a synthetic pose dictionary. This approach assumes that the domain shift between synthetic and real data is smaller in the intermediate representation compared to the raw input domain. Experiments on the NYU dataset show that this training method reduces joint error by 15.7% compared to direct joint regression from depth data.
label: AI

title: Contamination-Free Measures and Algebraic Operations
Abstract: This research paper explores a recent development in rough set theory: the concept of rough evolution and an axiomatic approach to granules. These concepts are applied in the formal framework of rough Y-systems (RYS) to develop granular correspondences for comparing rough algebraic semantics across different semantic domains. These correspondences preserve rough evolution and aim to minimize contamination. The paper proposes new methods and develops a semantics for handling potentially contaminated operations and structured bigness, addressing issues of relative consistency between knowledge collections.
label: AI

title: Stories in the Eye: Contextual Visual Interactions for Efficient Video to Language Translation
Abstract: Integrating higher-level visual and linguistic interpretations is a cornerstone of human intelligence. While automatic visual category recognition in images is approaching human performance, understanding dynamic spatiotemporal video content and translating it into natural language remains a challenge. This paper presents a vision-based approach for learning how to translate video content into language without relying on pre-learned linguistic models. The method discovers the story played by main actors using only visual cues to represent objects and their interactions. A hierarchical learning process generates higher-level representations for recognizing subjects, actions, objects, their contextual background, and their interactions over time. This three-stage approach analyzes individual entity features, object-action-background relationships, and spatiotemporal relations to generate linguistic descriptions of videos in the form of subject-verb-object triplets, based on the visual story learned directly from training data. The approach's efficiency is tested on a large-scale dataset of YouTube clips, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance, often surpassing current approaches that utilize complex, pre-learned linguistic knowledge.
label: AI

title: Tracklet Association by Online Target-Specific Metric Learning and Coherent Dynamics Estimation
Abstract: This paper presents a novel method for tracklet (track fragment) association in long-term multi-person tracking based on online target-specific metric learning and coherent dynamics estimation using network flow optimization. The framework aims to exploit appearance and motion cues to prevent identity switches during tracking and recover missed detections. Target-specific metrics (appearance cue) and motion dynamics (motion cue) are learned and estimated online during the tracking process. The approach remains effective even when these cues fail due to occlusions or object interactions. Learning the weights of these tracking cues addresses challenging situations, such as severe occlusions and object-to-object interactions. The method's effectiveness is validated on several public datasets, demonstrating superior performance compared to state-of-the-art tracking methods.
label: AI

title: A Model for Safety Case Confidence Assessment
Abstract: Building a safety case is a common approach for making expert judgment explicit about the safety of a system. However, confidence in such argumentation remains an open research area. This paper explores current approaches for quantifying confidence and proposes a new model based on Belief Theory for defining confidence and Bayesian Belief Networks for propagating it within safety case networks.
label: AI

title: Crowd Behavior Analysis: A Review where Physics meets Biology
Abstract: Crowd behavior often exhibits non-deliberative traits, but mass impulse can lead to crowd disasters. The increasing frequency of such disasters has driven advancements in computer vision for effective and proactive crowd surveillance. This survey reviews state-of-the-art methods in crowd behavior analysis from the perspectives of physics (complex systems) and biology (animal swarms). It highlights the surprisingly common insights and contradictions between these studies, inspired by biology and physics. The survey provides a comprehensive discussion for a better understanding of the potential for integrating physics and biology studies in computer vision.
label: AI

title: Joint Word Representation Learning using a Corpus and a Semantic Lexicon
Abstract: Learning word representations using large text corpora has gained significant attention due to their impressive performance in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks, including semantic similarity measurement and word analogy detection. While these data-driven methods are successful, they neglect the rich semantic relational structure between words in co-occurring contexts. Semantic lexicons, like WordNet, represent word meanings through defined relationships, requiring manual effort. This paper explores the potential for improving word representations by integrating knowledge from semantic lexicons. It proposes a joint word representation learning method that simultaneously predicts word co-occurrences in sentences while considering relational constraints from a semantic lexicon. Relationships between words in the lexicon are used to regularize word representations learned from the corpus. The proposed method significantly outperforms existing methods for incorporating semantic lexicons into word representations on various benchmark datasets for semantic similarity and word analogy.
label: AI

title: Better Computer Go Player with Neural Network and Long-term Prediction
Abstract: Competing with top human players in the ancient game of Go has been a long-standing goal in artificial intelligence. Go's high branching factor renders traditional search techniques ineffective, even with advanced hardware, and the evaluation function can change drastically with a single stone change. Recent work demonstrates that search may not be essential for machine Go players. Pure pattern-matching approaches, utilizing deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs), can perform as well as Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based Go engines with limited search budgets. This paper introduces "darkforest," a Go bot relying on a DCNN designed for long-term predictions. Darkforest significantly improves the win rate for pattern-matching approaches against MCTS-based approaches, even with looser search budgets. Against human players, the newest versions, darkfores2, achieve a stable 3d level on the KGS Go Server, surpassing the estimated 4k-5k ranks for DCNNs reported in previous studies. Adding MCTS to darkfores2 creates a stronger player, darkfmcts3, achieving a stable 5d level on the KGS server, comparable to state-of-the-art Go AIs except for AlphaGo.
label: AI

title: Unsupervised Learning of Visual Structure using Predictive Generative Networks
Abstract: Predicting future states of the environment is fundamental to intelligence. Effective prediction requires an internal model of the world and understanding its changing rules. This paper explores the internal models developed by deep neural networks trained to predict future frames in synthetic video sequences using a CNN-LSTM-deCNN framework. The architecture achieves excellent performance in visual sequence prediction tasks, including state-of-the-art performance on a standard "bouncing balls" dataset. Using a weighted mean-squared error and adversarial loss, the same architecture successfully extrapolates out-of-the-plane rotations of computer-generated faces. Notably, despite being trained to predict only pixel-level information, these predictive generative networks learn a representation of the latent structure of the underlying three-dimensional objects themselves. This representation is naturally tolerant to object transformations and generalizes well to new tasks, such as static image classification. Similar models trained solely with a reconstruction loss fail to generalize as effectively. The authors argue that prediction can serve as a powerful unsupervised loss for learning rich internal representations of high-level object features.
label: AI

title: Dynamic Adaptive Network Intelligence
Abstract: Accurate representational learning of both explicit and implicit relationships within data is crucial for machines to perform more complex and abstract reasoning tasks. This paper describes the efficient, weakly supervised learning of such inferences by the Dynamic Adaptive Network Intelligence (DANI) model. The authors report state-of-the-art results for DANI on question-answering tasks in the bAbI dataset, which have proven challenging for contemporary representation learning approaches.
label: AI

title: Actor-Mimic: Deep Multitask and Transfer Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: The ability to act in multiple environments and transfer previous knowledge to new situations is a crucial aspect of any intelligent agent. This paper defines a novel multitask and transfer learning method, termed "Actor-Mimic," which enables an autonomous agent to learn how to behave in multiple tasks simultaneously and generalize its knowledge to new domains. Actor-Mimic utilizes deep reinforcement learning and model compression techniques to train a single policy network that learns how to act in a set of distinct tasks with guidance from multiple expert teachers. The representations learned by the deep policy network are capable of generalizing to new tasks without prior expert guidance, accelerating learning in novel environments. Although applicable to a wide range of problems, the authors use Atari games as a testing environment to demonstrate the method's effectiveness.
label: AI

title: Communicating Semantics: Reference by Description
Abstract: Messages often refer to entities such as people, places, and events. Correctly identifying the intended reference is essential for communication. However, the lack of unique names can complicate entity reference. Shared knowledge can be used to construct uniquely identifying descriptive references for entities with ambiguous names. This paper introduces a mathematical model for "Reference by Description," deriving results on the conditions under which programs can construct unambiguous references to most entities in the domain of discourse with high probability. The paper provides empirical validation of these results. |||
label: AI

title: Preprint WebVRGIS Based Traffic Analysis and Visualization System
Abstract: This paper explores the use of Virtual Reality Geographic Information Systems (VR GIS) for analyzing and visualizing city traffic data.  The authors argue that city traffic data is a prime example of "Big Data" due to its large volume, diverse sources, and time-sensitive nature. They propose a VR GIS-based system with intelligent visual analysis and forecasting capabilities, including a detailed passenger flow forecasting algorithm.
label: AI

title: Abstract Attribute Exploration with Partial Object Descriptions
Abstract: The authors examine attribute exploration, a knowledge acquisition method, in a theoretical context. While the basic method is simple and transparent, its complexity increases when incorporating background knowledge and partially described counter-examples.  The paper focuses on providing a clear terminology to clarify the abstract strategy of the method, without delving into specific algorithmic implementation.
label: AI

title: Coreset-Based Adaptive Tracking
Abstract: This research proposes a novel method for learning from streaming visual data, using a compact, constant-size representation called a "coreset".  This coreset is constructed using a parallelized algorithm and approximates a set based on squared distances.  From this coreset, the authors develop an adaptive object appearance model for object tracking by detection. The method demonstrates excellent results on three standard datasets across over 100 videos. The coreset approach's efficiency makes it particularly well-suited for tracking in long videos with limited space and time resources.
label: AI

title: Detection of Slang Words in e-Data using semi-Supervised Learning
Abstract: The paper focuses on detecting abusive language, specifically slang words, in electronic communication.  The proposed approach uses supervised learning to identify abusive words, but acknowledges that slang often appears in abbreviated forms (e.g., sound-alikes, taboo morphemes).  To address this, the paper introduces a semi-supervised learning procedure to detect these abbreviated forms. The probability of a suspicious word being slang is evaluated using synset and concept analysis of the text.
label: AI

title: A Hybrid Approach to Word Sense Disambiguation Combining Supervised and Unsupervised Learning
Abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) that aims to overcome the limitations of traditional supervised methods.  Supervised WSD relies on manually tagged data, which can be insufficient and ineffective for learning.  The proposed method introduces a dynamic learning set that is enriched with new data through a trivial filtering method. It combines the Modified Lesk approach with a Bag-of-Words model, leveraging enriched bags created using the learning methods. Experimental results demonstrate that this mixed methodology outperforms both individual methods.
label: AI

title: Overcoming Language Variation in Sentiment Analysis with Social Attention
Abstract: This paper investigates how social network data can be used to improve the accuracy of sentiment analysis, especially in the context of social media, where language variation is common.  The authors leverage the concept of "linguistic homophily", the tendency of socially connected individuals to use similar language.  They propose a novel attention-based neural network architecture that assigns attention to different basis models based on the user's position in the social network. This approach smooths the classification function across the network, enabling personalized classifiers even for users without labeled data or demographic information. The model significantly improves sentiment analysis accuracy on Twitter and review data.
label: AI

title: BIRDNEST: Bayesian Inference for Ratings-Fraud Detection
Abstract: This paper addresses the problem of review fraud, where fraudulent sellers manipulate product reviews to deceive consumers. Traditional detection methods rely on identifying bursts of reviews and skewed rating distributions, but these patterns can also occur naturally.  The authors introduce a Bayesian Inference for Rating Data (BIRD) model that combines these two approaches in a principled manner. This model utilizes a likelihood-based suspiciousness metric called Normalized Expected Surprise Total (NEST).  The paper proposes a linear-time algorithm for Bayesian inference and NEST calculation. Experiments on real data demonstrate the model's success in identifying fraudulent reviews on a large online marketplace.
label: AI

title: Unitary-Group Invariant Kernels and Features from Transformed Unlabeled Data
Abstract: The paper explores learning representations that are invariant to common transformations of the data, a crucial aspect of machine learning. Traditional methods focus on local approximate invariance within expensive optimization frameworks, lacking explicit theoretical guarantees. This paper investigates kernels that are invariant to the unitary group, providing theoretical guarantees and addressing practical challenges.  The authors present a theoretically motivated approach to invariant kernel SVM, addressing the limitations of previous methods.  They also extend a recent technique for extracting linear unitary-group invariant features, providing guarantees regarding invariance and stability.  Experimental results on UCI ML datasets validate the proposed methods.
label: AI

title: Behavior Query Discovery in System-Generated Temporal Graphs
Abstract: This paper focuses on analyzing large amounts of system logs generated by computer system monitoring.  Extracting meaningful information from these logs is challenging due to their dynamic and heterogeneous nature. The authors view system monitoring data as heterogeneous temporal graphs, where nodes represent system entities and edges represent their interactions over time.  To address the complexity of manually querying these graphs, the paper introduces TGMiner, a tool for mining discriminative patterns from system logs. TGMiner leverages temporal information to prune patterns with similar growth trends, resulting in faster pattern discovery without compromising quality. Experimental results on real system data demonstrate the effectiveness of TGMiner.
label: AI

title: Censoring Representations with an Adversary
Abstract: This research addresses the challenge of incorporating explicit constraints into machine learning applications. These constraints can arise from legal requirements or the need to avoid sensitive information leakage in representations.  The authors propose an adversarial approach where a flexible representation is learned by minimizing the capability of an adversary to predict sensitive variables from the representation. This effectively ensures that the representation contains minimal information about sensitive variables. The method is demonstrated on two problems: discrimination-free decision-making and removing private information from images.  The adversarial model is formulated as a minimax problem and optimized using a stochastic gradient alternate min-max optimizer.  The paper shows the ability to create discrimination-free representations for standard test problems and compares the performance to previous state-of-the-art fairness methods, demonstrating significant improvement.  The paper also explores the novel application of removing annotations from images using unaligned training data.
label: AI

title: Alternative Markov and Causal Properties for Acyclic Directed Mixed Graphs
Abstract: This paper extends Andersson-Madigan-Perlman chain graphs by relaxing the semidirected acyclity constraint to allow undirected cycles and allowing up to two edges between any pair of nodes.  The authors introduce global, local, and pairwise Markov properties for these new models. They demonstrate the equivalence of these properties for strictly positive probability distributions.  The paper shows that, for continuous random variables, the new models can be interpreted as systems of structural equations with correlated errors. This allows for adapting Pearl's do-calculus to these models.  Finally, the authors describe an exact algorithm for learning the new models from observational and interventional data using answer set programming.
label: AI

title: Towards Lateral Inhibition and Collective Perception in Unorganised Non-Neural Systems
Abstract: This research investigates whether simple organisms, such as slime molds, can exhibit Lateral Inhibition (LI) without requiring neural tissue.  The authors propose a model where LI emerges through bulk transport effects without explicit inhibitory wiring.  They use a multi-agent slime mold model to reproduce LI's edge contrast amplification effects using attractant-based stimuli. The model also explores Lateral Activation, where stimulated regions are inhibited and lateral regions are excited, using simulated light irradiation.  The model exhibits restoration of baseline activity upon stimulus removal. In addition to edge contrast enhancement, the model captures the long-term change in population density distribution, representing a collective response to global brightness.  This demonstrates the potential for LI-like phenomena and global brightness perception in unorganized systems without fixed neural architectures.
label: AI

title: Solution Repair/Recovery in Uncertain Optimization Environment
Abstract: This paper examines the challenge of applying optimal solutions from operations management models to real-world organizational contexts.  While optimization models provide optimal solutions, the conditions under which these solutions are computed rarely match the real-world operating conditions.  As a result, the optimal solution may no longer be optimal or even feasible in the organization. The paper proposes "repair solutions", which are solutions that maintain good performance across different scenarios and uncertainties.  These repair solutions are achieved through local re-optimization guided by users or limited changes that minimize the impact of incorporating real-world scenarios.
label: AI

title: Using Abduction in Markov Logic Networks for Root Cause Analysis
Abstract: This paper focuses on improving risk management in IT infrastructure by automating root cause analysis for failures.  The authors propose a new approach using Abduction in Markov Logic Networks.  Abduction aims to find an explanation for an observation based on background knowledge. In failure diagnosis, the explanation corresponds to the root cause, the observation to the failure of a component, and the background knowledge to the dependency graph extended by potential risks.  The paper extends Markov Logic Networks for abductive reasoning and demonstrates its reusability and applicability even for users without specific infrastructure knowledge. The method is implemented in a tool and illustrated through a sample scenario.
label: AI

title: Discovering Underlying Plans Based on Distributed Representations of Actions
Abstract: This paper addresses the problem of plan recognition, where the goal is to discover the target plan (sequence of actions) behind observed actions using plan libraries or domain models.  Traditional approaches either rely on matching observed actions to plan libraries or inferring plans by executing domain models.  However, real-world applications often encounter situations where target plans are not in libraries or complete domain models are unavailable. The paper introduces a novel approach that treats plan libraries as corpora and learns vector representations of actions.  Target plans are then discovered based on these vector representations, enabling the discovery of plans not present in the libraries without requiring domain models. The approach is empirically evaluated on three planning domains, demonstrating its effectiveness compared to traditional plan recognition methods.
label: AI

title: A New Smooth Approximation to the Zero One Loss with a Probabilistic Interpretation
Abstract: This research examines a new smooth approximation to the zero-one loss function, using a reformulation of the logistic function. The authors introduce a generalized Beta-Bernoulli formulation that leads to a generalized logistic function approximating the zero-one loss while retaining a probabilistic formulation. This approach readily generalizes to kernel logistic regression and integrates well into structured prediction methods. The paper presents experimental results where models are learned using a combination of gradient descent and coordinate descent with localized grid search.  The experiments show improved optimization quality and performance relative to logistic and hinge loss methods across various tasks, including standard datasets, product review predictions, and visual information extraction. The approach exhibits robustness to outliers, outperforms logistic and max margin models on larger scale problems, yields sparser solutions with Gaussian-Laplacian mixture priors, and provides more accurate probabilities for improved inference and information extraction.
label: AI

title: Return of Frustratingly Easy Domain Adaptation
Abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of domain shifts in machine learning, where the training (source) and test (target) input distributions differ.  Such shifts can significantly degrade the performance of traditional methods. While supervised domain adaptation methods exist for labeled target data, practical scenarios often involve unlabeled target domains. The paper proposes CORrelation ALignment (CORAL), a simple and efficient unsupervised domain adaptation method. CORAL aligns the second-order statistics of source and target distributions, minimizing domain shift without requiring target labels.  Despite its simplicity (implementable in four lines of Matlab code), CORAL demonstrates remarkable performance on benchmark datasets.
label: AI

title: Neurocontrol methods review
Abstract: The paper explores the application of neural networks in controlling plants.  It discusses various methods and schemes for neural network-based plant control, highlighting their advantages and disadvantages.
label: AI

title: Gated Graph Sequence Neural Networks
Abstract: This paper investigates feature learning techniques for graph-structured data, which appears frequently in domains like chemistry, natural language semantics, and social networks.  Building upon previous work on Graph Neural Networks, the authors modify the architecture to utilize gated recurrent units and modern optimization techniques, extending it to output sequences.  The result is a flexible and broadly applicable class of neural network models with favorable inductive biases compared to purely sequence-based models (e.g., LSTMs) in graph-structured problems. The paper demonstrates the model's capabilities on AI (bAbI) and graph algorithm learning tasks. It then shows state-of-the-art performance on a program verification problem, where subgraphs need to be matched to abstract data structures.
label: AI

title: Active exploration of sensor networks from a robotics perspective
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to developing simple, adaptive, and reusable algorithms for mobile robots operating in wireless networks.  Focusing on the basic task of finding another node's position, the paper introduces an algorithm that can be readily adapted to solve other related tasks, such as finding the optimal position to bridge two static network nodes. The authors introduce a meta-algorithm inspired by autonomous robot learning strategies and the concept of internal models, resulting in a class of source-seeking algorithms for mobile nodes. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated in real-world experiments using a physical robot and a standard 802.11 wireless LAN in an office environment. The paper discusses the differences from conventional algorithms and provides a robotics perspective on this class of algorithms.  It then shows how more complex tasks, like bridging two network nodes, can be encoded within the same framework. The bridging scenario is implemented on a real robot and demonstrates the robot's ability to solve this complex task in a real-world experiment. |||
label: AI

title: Bayesian Optimization with Dimension Scheduling: Application to Biological Systems
Abstract: Bayesian Optimization (BO) is a data-efficient method for optimizing black-box functions that are expensive to evaluate.  BO typically assumes that the computational cost of optimization is negligible, but this is not always the case in practice.  In some scenarios, such as simulating complex models, the cost of BO can become comparable to the cost of running experiments. To address this challenge, we propose a new Dimension Scheduling Algorithm (DSA) that reduces the computational burden of BO. DSA works by optimizing the fitness function along only a subset of dimensions at each iteration. This strategy reduces the computation time, finds good solutions faster than traditional BO, and can be easily parallelized. We evaluate DSA on the problem of optimizing microalgae metabolism models and show that it converges faster than traditional BO.
label: AI

title: The Use of Machine Learning Algorithms in Recommender Systems: A Systematic Review
Abstract: Recommender systems use algorithms to suggest products or services to users.  While machine learning algorithms have become increasingly popular in this domain, choosing the right algorithm for a recommender system can be difficult. There is a lack of comprehensive information about current approaches to algorithm selection, and the development of recommender systems often presents challenges and open questions. This paper presents a systematic review of the literature on machine learning algorithms in recommender systems, identifying potential research opportunities in software engineering. The study concludes that Bayesian and decision tree algorithms are widely used due to their simplicity, and that the requirement and design phases of recommender system development offer opportunities for further research.
label: AI

title: Ask, Attend and Answer: Exploring Question-Guided Spatial Attention for Visual Question Answering
Abstract: Visual Question Answering (VQA) is a task that requires understanding both images and language to answer questions about a given image.  While deep captioning methods have been applied to VQA, they often fail to capture spatial relationships. To address this, we propose a model called the Spatial Memory Network that incorporates spatial inference. Memory networks are recurrent neural networks with an explicit attention mechanism that selects relevant information from memory. Our Spatial Memory Network stores neural activations from different spatial regions of the image in memory, and uses the question to select relevant regions for computing the answer, a process known as a "hop." We introduce a novel spatial attention architecture that aligns words with image patches in the first hop, and achieve improved results by adding a second attention hop that considers the whole question to choose visual evidence based on the first hop. To better understand the inference process, we design synthetic questions that require spatial inference and visualize the attention weights. We evaluate our model on two VQA datasets, DAQUAR and VQA, and obtain improved results compared to a strong baseline model (iBOWIMG).
label: AI

title: Convolutional Models for Joint Object Categorization and Pose Estimation
Abstract: Object recognition involves two distinct tasks: object categorization and pose estimation. While deep architectures have achieved great success in object categorization, pose estimation has received less attention. This paper demonstrates how deep architectures, specifically convolutional neural networks (CNNs), can be adapted to simultaneously categorize and estimate the pose of objects. We analyze the layers of various CNN models to understand how distributed representations capture pose information and how this interacts with object category representations. We conduct extensive experiments on two challenging multi-view datasets and achieve state-of-the-art performance on both.
label: AI

title: How (not) to Train your Generative Model: Scheduled Sampling, Likelihood, Adversary?
Abstract: Modern deep learning research has led to renewed interest in generative models for text and images. However, the best objective functions for training and evaluating these models remain unclear. This paper presents two contributions. Firstly, we critique scheduled sampling, a state-of-the-art training method that contributed to the winning entry in the MSCOCO image captioning benchmark in 2015. Despite its impressive empirical performance, we show that the objective function underlying scheduled sampling is improper and leads to an inconsistent learning algorithm. Secondly, we revisit the problems that scheduled sampling aimed to address and offer an alternative interpretation. We argue that maximum likelihood is an inappropriate training objective when the goal is to generate natural-looking samples. We derive an ideal objective function for this scenario and introduce a generalization of adversarial training that can interpolate between maximum likelihood training and our ideal objective. This analysis provides the first theoretical explanation for why adversarial training tends to produce higher-quality samples.
label: AI

title: Performing Highly Accurate Predictions Through Convolutional Networks for Actual Telecommunication Challenges
Abstract: We investigate the use of deep learning, specifically convolutional networks trained with GPUs, to build better predictive models in telecommunication business environments, focusing on the challenging problem of predicting customer churn. Our model, called WiseNet, employs a convolutional network and a novel encoding method that transforms customer activity data and Call Detail Records (CDRs) into images. Experimental evaluation with various machine learning classifiers demonstrates WiseNet's ability to learn features from structured input data. WiseNet outperforms machine learning models with hand-crafted features and eliminates the labor-intensive process of feature engineering. Notably, the same model achieved consistent results when applied to a different market without retraining, confirming WiseNet's generalization ability and its power to extract meaningful representations.
label: AI

title: Quality assessment of voice converted speech using articulatory features
Abstract: We propose a novel application of acoustic-to-articulatory inversion for assessing the quality of voice-converted speech.  Effortless speech production requires coordinated movements of articulators, muscles, etc., which contribute to naturalness, intelligibility, and speaker identity, qualities often lost in voice conversion. In this paper, we quantify this loss for male voice by showing an increase in RMSE error and a decrease in mutual information for voice-converted speech compared to natural speech. Similar results are obtained for female voice.  We demonstrate that articulatory features can be used as an objective measure of voice conversion quality, illustrating its effectiveness compared to MCD by examining their correlation with Mean Opinion Score.

title: Heterogeneous Knowledge Transfer in Video Emotion Recognition, Attribution and Summarization
Abstract: Emotion is a key element in user-generated videos, but understanding emotions conveyed in such videos is challenging due to the complexity and unstructured nature of the content and the sparsity of emotional video frames. This paper presents the first study on transferring knowledge from heterogeneous external sources, including image and textual data, to facilitate three related tasks in understanding video emotion: emotion recognition, emotion attribution, and emotion-oriented summarization. Specifically, our framework learns a video encoding from an auxiliary emotional image dataset to improve supervised video emotion recognition, and transfers knowledge from an auxiliary textual corpus for zero-shot recognition of emotion classes unseen during training. This knowledge transfer technique enables novel applications of emotion attribution and emotion-oriented summarization. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework.

title: Applying Semantic Web Technologies for Improving the Visibility of Tourism Data
Abstract: The tourism industry is highly information-intensive, complex, and dynamic.  Due to the heterogeneity of information sources and the high volume of online data, semantic Web technologies can be leveraged to improve the industry. Ontologies provide methods and standards that facilitate the management of semantically diverse annotated tourism data, enabling flexible and intelligent access to online information. This paper describes initial results from the Tourinflux project, which aims to apply semantic Web technologies to help tourism actors effectively find and publish information on the web.

title: Word Embedding based Correlation Model for Question/Answer Matching
Abstract: The development of community-based question answering (Q&A) services has led to the accumulation of vast Q&A archives, which serve as important information and knowledge resources on the web.  Question and answer matching is crucial for reusing knowledge stored in these systems, enhancing user experience with recurrent questions.  This paper aims to improve matching accuracy by addressing the lexical gap between question and answer pairs. We propose a Word Embedding based Correlation (WEC) model that combines the advantages of translation models and word embedding. Given a random pair of words, WEC can score their co-occurrence probability in Q&A pairs, leveraging the continuity and smoothness of continuous space word representation to handle new, rare word pairs. Experimental studies on Yahoo! Answers and Baidu Zhidao datasets demonstrate the promising potential of this new method.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning with a Natural Language Action Space
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel architecture for reinforcement learning with deep neural networks designed to handle state and action spaces characterized by natural language, as found in text-based games.  Called a deep reinforcement relevance network (DRRN), this architecture represents action and state spaces using separate embedding vectors, which are combined with an interaction function to approximate the Q-function in reinforcement learning. We evaluate the DRRN on two popular text games, showing superior performance compared to other deep Q-learning architectures. Experiments with paraphrased action descriptions demonstrate that the model extracts meaning rather than simply memorizing text strings.

title: Demand-Driven Incremental Object Queries
Abstract: Object queries are essential in information seeking and decision-making across various applications. However, queries can involve complex conditions on objects and sets, which can be arbitrarily nested and aliased. The objects, sets, and demand (the given parameter values of interest) can change arbitrarily.  This paper describes an automatic method for efficiently implementing object queries under all possible updates, providing complexity guarantees. The method allows powerful queries to be expressed declaratively by transforming demand and all objects and sets into relations. It defines invariants for not only the query results but also all auxiliary values about the objects and sets involved, including those for propagating demand, and incrementally maintains them. Implementation and experiments with problems from various application areas, including distributed algorithms and probabilistic queries, confirm the analyzed complexities, trade-offs, and significant improvements over prior work.

title: Dynamic Sum Product Networks for Tractable Inference on Sequence Data (Extended Version)
Abstract: Sum-Product Networks (SPNs) have recently emerged as a new class of tractable probabilistic graphical models. Unlike Bayesian networks and Markov networks, where inference can be exponential in network size, inference in SPNs is linear in network size.  Since SPNs represent distributions over fixed sets of variables, we propose dynamic sum-product networks (DSPNs) as a generalization of SPNs for sequence data of varying length. A DSPN consists of a template network that is repeated as many times as needed to model data sequences of any length. We present a local search technique for learning the structure of the template network. Unlike dynamic Bayesian networks, where inference is generally exponential in the number of variables per time slice, DSPNs inherit the linear inference complexity of SPNs. We demonstrate the advantages of DSPNs over DBNs and other models on several datasets of sequence data.

title: Symbol Grounding Association in Multimodal Sequences with Missing Elements
Abstract: This paper extends a symbolic association framework to handle missing elements in multimodal sequences. The general scope of the work is the symbolic associations of object-word mappings, as it happens in language development in infants. In other words, two different representations of the same abstract concept can associate in both directions. This scenario has been a long-standing interest in Artificial Intelligence, Psychology, and Neuroscience. This work extends a recent approach for multimodal sequences (visual and audio) to handle missing elements in one or both modalities. Our method uses two parallel Long Short-Term Memories (LSTMs) with a learning rule based on the EM algorithm, aligning both LSTM outputs via Dynamic Time Warping (DTW). We propose an extra step for combination with the max operation to exploit common elements between both sequences, acting as a condition selector for choosing the best representation from both LSTMs. We evaluate the proposed extension in scenarios with missing elements in one or both modalities, achieving better results than the original model and similar results to individual LSTMs trained in each modality.

title: HackAttack: Game-Theoretic Analysis of Realistic Cyber Conflicts
Abstract: Game theory is a suitable framework for studying cyber conflict because it allows for the modeling of intelligent, goal-driven adversaries.  Applications of game theory have led to insights about optimal attack and defense strategies. However, most applications explore overly simplistic games with full visibility of actions. These simplifications disregard the fundamental properties of real cyber conflicts, such as probabilistic alerting, hidden actions, and unknown opponent capabilities. This paper demonstrates the feasibility of analyzing a more realistic game, where different resources have varying weaknesses, players have unique exploits, and moves occur in secrecy but can be detected. While optimal strategies can be found for simpler games using calculus, case-by-case analysis, or Q-learning, our more complex game is best analyzed using methods used for other complex games, like checkers and chess. We define a simple evaluation function and employ multi-step searches to create strategies. We show that such scenarios can be analyzed and find that in cases of extreme uncertainty, it is often advantageous to ignore the opponent's potential moves. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a simple evaluation function in a complex game can lead to nuanced and interesting strategies.

title: Combining Monte-Carlo and Hyper-heuristic methods for the Multi-mode Resource-constrained Multi-project Scheduling Problem
Abstract: Multi-mode resource and precedence-constrained project scheduling is a challenging real-world optimization problem.  A critical variant requires scheduling activities for multiple projects, considering the availability of local and global resources while adhering to various constraints. The primary objective in the benchmarks discussed here is to minimize the sum of project completion times, with makespan minimization as a secondary objective. This leads to a distinct structure of good solutions, influencing algorithm design. This paper presents a carefully designed hybrid of Monte-Carlo tree search, novel neighborhood moves, memetic algorithms, and hyper-heuristic methods. The implementation is engineered to enhance speed and exploit multicore computing power. Empirical evaluation shows that the resulting information-sharing multi-component algorithm significantly outperforms other solvers on a set of "hidden" instances, which were not available during algorithm design.

title: Introduzione all'Intelligenza Artificiale
Abstract: This paper provides an accessible and informal but precise introduction to Artificial Intelligence (AI), focusing on the algorithmic aspects of the discipline. It presents the main techniques used in AI systems, categorized as symbolic and subsymbolic. The final part discusses the ongoing debate among experts and the public at large regarding the advantages, disadvantages, and potential dangers of AI. The author concludes the paper with their personal opinion on this topic.

title: Novel Feature Extraction, Selection and Fusion for Effective Malware Family Classification
Abstract: Modern malware is designed with mutation characteristics, namely polymorphism and metamorphism, which lead to a massive increase in the number of malware variants. Categorizing malware samples based on their behavior is essential for the computer security community, as they receive a large number of samples daily, and signature extraction relies on identifying malicious parts characteristic of malware families.  Microsoft released a malware classification challenge in 2015 with a dataset of almost 0.5 terabytes, containing over 20,000 malware samples. The analysis of this dataset inspired the development of a novel paradigm for effectively categorizing malware variants into their actual family groups. This paradigm is presented and discussed in this paper, emphasizing the phases related to the extraction and selection of a set of novel features for effectively representing malware samples. Features are grouped according to different malware behavior characteristics, and their fusion is performed according to a per-class weighting paradigm. The proposed method achieved very high accuracy (approximately 0.998) on the Microsoft Malware Challenge dataset.

title: Uncertainty relations in quantum optics. Is the photon intelligent?
Abstract: This paper presents the Robertson-Schrödinger, Heisenberg-Robertson, and Trifonov uncertainty relations for arbitrary functions f1 and f2 depending on the quantum phase and the number of photons, respectively.  Intelligent states and states that locally minimize the product of uncertainties (Δf1)²·(Δf2)² or the sum (Δf1)²+(Δf2)² are investigated for the cases f1=φ, exp(iφ), exp(-iφ), cosφ, sinφ and f2=n.

title: On Choosing Committees Based on Approval Votes in the Presence of Outliers
Abstract: We study the computational complexity of committee selection problems for several approval-based voting rules in the presence of outliers.  Our first result demonstrates that outlier consideration makes committee selection intractable for approval, net approval, and minisum approval voting rules. We then analyze the parameterized complexity of this problem with five natural parameters: the target score, the size of the committee (and its dual parameter, the number of candidates outside the committee), the number of outliers (and its dual parameter, the number of non-outliers).  For net approval and minisum approval voting rules, we provide a dichotomous result, resolving the parameterized complexity of this problem for all subsets of the five parameters considered (showing either FPT or W[1]-hardness).  For the approval voting rule, we resolve the parameterized complexity for all parameter subsets except one. We also study approximation algorithms for this problem. We show that no α(.) factor approximation algorithm exists for approval and net approval voting rules for any computable function α(.), unless P=NP.  For the minisum voting rule, we provide a pseudopolynomial (1+ε) factor approximation algorithm. |||

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning in Parameterized Action Space
Abstract: Deep neural networks have been successfully applied to reinforcement learning problems with continuous state and action spaces. However, their application to parameterized continuous action spaces remains unexplored. This paper addresses this gap by focusing on a simulated RoboCup soccer domain, which features discrete action types parameterized by continuous variables. The trained agent surpasses the 2012 RoboCup champion in goal-scoring reliability, demonstrating the successful extension of deep reinforcement learning to parameterized action space MDPs.

title: Seeing the Unseen Network: Inferring Hidden Social Ties from Respondent-Driven Sampling
Abstract: Understanding the social structures of hidden populations, such as drug users and sex workers, is crucial for public health research on risk behaviors and disease prevention. Respondent-driven sampling (RDS) is a widely used peer-referral method where participants recruit others from their social networks. This research proposes a novel method for reconstructing the underlying network structure of RDS, despite privacy concerns that prevent the disclosure of acquaintance identities. The dynamics of RDS are formulated as a continuous-time diffusion process over the network, and an efficient stochastic optimization algorithm called RENDER is developed to identify the network that best explains the observed recruitment data. Experiments on both synthetic and real data validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

title: ICON Challenge on Algorithm Selection
Abstract: This paper presents the outcomes of the ICON Challenge on Algorithm Selection.

title: Software Agents with Concerns of their Own
Abstract: This paper explores the possibility of artificial software agents developing first-person or intrinsic meanings for their actions and their environment. The paper defines first-person meaning as the relationship between an entity's actions, the environment's properties, and the system's goals and capabilities. The paper argues that for a system to develop first-person meanings, it must perceive itself as a goal-directed actor operating within constraints and opportunities. The paper presents preliminary proposals and achievements from actual software implementations that aim to develop software agents with intrinsic understanding of their actions and experiences. This approach focuses on allowing agents to acquire knowledge about their goals, capabilities, and environment through self-observation. By analyzing these acquired notions, the paper defines the cold first-person meanings of the agent's actions and its interactions with the environment. While not providing a complete solution to the problem of first-person meanings, this approach and its preliminary results offer confidence in addressing the remaining challenges, particularly the phenomenal aspect of first-person meanings.

title: IfcWoD, Semantically Adapting IFC Model Relations into OWL Properties
Abstract: Ontologies play a significant role in achieving information interoperability in the context of Building Information Modelling (BIM). Several IFC (Industry Foundation Classes) based ontologies have been developed, such as IfcOWL, for the construction and facility management domains. This paper proposes an adaptation of the IFC model into OWL that leverages all modeling constraints imposed by IFC's object-oriented structure. This adaptation goes beyond a syntactic transformation and includes semantic considerations, encompassing the meaning of entities, relationships, properties, and attributes defined by the IFC standard. The proposed approach offers advantages over previous initiatives, including optimized query execution time. These advantages are demonstrated through practical examples and benchmarks.
label: AI

title: Characterizing Concept Drift
Abstract: Traditional machine learning models are static, posing challenges in the dynamic real-world context of evolving data distributions, a phenomenon known as concept drift. While qualitative categorizations of drift have been proposed, rigorous formal definitions and quantitative descriptions for precise understanding of learner performance have been lacking. This paper presents the first comprehensive framework for quantitative analysis of concept drift. This framework facilitates the development of a comprehensive set of formal definitions for different types of concept drift, addressing ambiguities and gaps in previous definitions. The proposed framework establishes a taxonomy of concept drift types and provides a solid foundation for research on mechanisms to detect and address concept drift.

title: Complexity of the Description Logic ALCM
Abstract: This paper demonstrates that checking consistency of a knowledge base in the Description Logic ALCM is ExpTime-complete. ALCM refers to the Description Logic ALC with meta-modelling, as defined by Motz, Rohrer, and Severi. The ExpTime-completeness is established by defining an ExpTime Tableau algorithm, which extends an existing algorithm for checking consistency of a knowledge base in ALC by Nguyen and Szalas.

title: Doubly Robust Off-policy Value Evaluation for Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: Off-policy value evaluation in reinforcement learning (RL) aims to estimate the value of a new policy using data collected under a different policy. This is a crucial step in applying RL to real-world scenarios. While existing general methods suffer from uncontrolled bias or high variance, this paper extends the doubly robust estimator for bandits to sequential decision-making problems. This estimator combines the advantages of being unbiased and exhibiting lower variance compared to popular importance sampling estimators. The paper demonstrates the estimator's accuracy through benchmark problems and illustrates its application as a subroutine in safe policy improvement. Theoretical results on the problem's hardness are also presented, showing that the estimator can match the lower bound in specific scenarios.

title: Deep Multimodal Semantic Embeddings for Speech and Images
Abstract: This paper proposes a model that establishes a correspondence between images and their spoken captions. The model utilizes a pair of convolutional neural networks to represent visual objects and speech signals at the word level. These networks are linked through an embedding and alignment model that learns a shared semantic space for both modalities. The model is evaluated using image search and annotation tasks on the Flickr8k dataset, augmented with a corpus of 40,000 spoken captions collected using Amazon Mechanical Turk.

title: The capabilities and performance of the Automated Planet Finder Telescope with the implementation of a dynamic scheduler
Abstract: This paper presents initial performance results obtained from 600 hours of observations using the Automated Planet Finder (APF) telescope and Levy Spectrometer at UCO/Lick Observatory. The study analyzes multiple spectra of 80 G, K, and M-type stars, yielding 4,954 Doppler radial velocity (RV) measurements with a median internal uncertainty of 1.35 ms$^{-1}$. A strong correlation is observed between the number of photons accumulated in the iodine region of the spectrum and the resulting internal uncertainty estimates. Additionally, an offset is found between the populations of G/K stars and M stars when comparing these parameters. M-type stars, due to their increased spectral line densities, achieve the same level of internal uncertainty with twice fewer photons compared to G/K stars. The study demonstrates that the APF/Levy achieves comparable speed-on-sky performance to Keck/HIRES for precision RVs when observing M stars. To facilitate long-duration RV surveys, the paper discusses a dynamically scheduling algorithm that monitors ambient conditions and uses on-sky information to make intelligent real-time targeting decisions.

title: IBMMS Decision Support Tool For Management of Bank Telemarketing Campaigns
Abstract: Direct marketing, despite being a viable method for banks to compete in a challenging market, often exhibits poor performance and can reinforce negative customer perceptions of banks. To address these challenges, the paper proposes an Intelligent Bank Market Management System (IBMMS) designed for bank managers seeking to manage efficient marketing campaigns. IBMMS integrates data mining and expert system capabilities, providing intelligence features such as a knowledge base, inference engine, and advisor. This system allows managers to effectively target marketing campaigns, understand individual and group customer behavior, and make informed decisions to achieve desired customer responses.

title: Instantaneous Modelling and Reverse Engineering of DataConsistent Prime Models in Seconds!
Abstract: This paper introduces a theoretical framework for automated construction of dynamic prime models solely from experimental time series data. This framework enables the automatic generation of data-driven models for any time series data within seconds. This invention has led to the development of new reverse engineering and dynamic methods for automated systems modeling of complex systems, including biological, financial, control, and artificial neural network systems. The underlying theory of this invention is formalized as a new and robust system identification strategy complementary to process-based modeling. The proposed dynamic modeling and network inference solutions address complex parameter estimation challenges, inferring unknown network structures and constructing intelligent ODE models for complex systems. The paper presents a robust step-by-step mathematical and computational analysis of the prime model construction process, capable of determining a model from data in under a minute.

title: Discovery Radiomics via StochasticNet Sequencers for Cancer Detection
Abstract: Radiomics has emerged as a powerful prognostic tool for cancer detection, demonstrating success in lung, breast, prostate, and head-and-neck cancer studies. However, current radiomics methods rely on predefined, handcrafted feature sets, limiting their ability to capture unique cancer traits. This study introduces a novel discovery radiomics framework that directly discovers custom radiomic features from vast medical imaging data. This approach leverages StochasticNet radiomic sequencers to extract custom features tailored to characterizing unique cancer tissue phenotypes. Using StochasticNet sequencers trained on a large lung CT dataset, the study performs binary classification on 42,340 lung lesions from 93 patients in the LIDC-IDRI dataset. Preliminary results demonstrate significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the potential of discovery radiomics for enhancing cancer screening and diagnosis.

title: From Images to Sentences through Scene Description Graphs using Commonsense Reasoning and Knowledge
Abstract: This paper proposes the construction of linguistic descriptions of images by extracting scene description graphs (SDGs) from visual scenes using an automatically constructed knowledge base. SDGs are constructed using both vision and reasoning, integrating detections from perception methods with a commonsense knowledge base derived from image annotations and lexical ontological knowledge from resources like WordNet. Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) evaluations on Flickr8k, Flickr30k, and MS-COCO datasets show that sentences automatically generated from SDGs provide more relevant and comprehensive descriptions of images compared to recent state-of-the-art image captioning approaches. The paper's Image-Sentence Alignment Evaluation results are comparable to those of current state-of-the-art methods.

title: Taxonomy of Pathways to Dangerous AI
Abstract: Understanding the development of a dangerous Artificially Intelligent (AI) system is crucial for addressing potential risks. While popular culture often portrays AI as becoming self-aware and rebelling against humanity, this paper explores more plausible scenarios for the emergence of malevolent AI. The study surveys, classifies, and analyzes various circumstances that could lead to the development of malicious AI. This is the first systematic classification of pathways leading to malevolent AI. Previous work has focused on specific goals or undesirable behaviors exhibited by AI systems at different stages of development. This paper provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the potential risks associated with AI development, offering valuable insights for mitigating such threats.

title: Evolution of Collective Behaviors for a Real Swarm of Aquatic Surface Robots
Abstract: Swarm robotics is a promising approach for coordinating large numbers of robots. Previous research has demonstrated the application of evolutionary robotics techniques for achieving robust and efficient self-organized behaviors in simulated robot swarms. However, real-world applications have been limited to laboratory settings. This paper presents the first successful implementation of a swarm robotics system with evolved control operating in a real and uncontrolled environment. Neural network-based controllers are evolved in simulation for canonical swarm robotics tasks, including homing, dispersion, clustering, and monitoring. The performance of these controllers is then assessed on a real swarm of up to ten aquatic surface robots. The results demonstrate successful transfer of evolved controllers to real robots, achieving performance comparable to simulations. The evolved controllers exhibit key properties of swarm intelligence-based control, including scalability, flexibility, and robustness in the real swarm. The paper concludes with a proof-of-concept experiment showcasing the swarm's ability to perform a complete environmental monitoring task by combining multiple evolved controllers.

title: The cave of Shadows. Addressing the human factor with generalized additive mixed models
Abstract: Generalized additive mixed models are introduced as an extension of generalized linear mixed models, addressing the temporal autocorrelational structure often observed in experimental data. This autocorrelational structure likely arises from learning, fatigue, or attention fluctuations within the experiment, collectively known as the "human factor." Unlike inanimate subjects, participants in psycholinguistic experiments are intelligent beings constantly adapting to their environment, including the experimental context. The paper presents three data sets illustrating how the human factor interacts with both factorial and metric predictors. The paper also discusses the challenges of fitting overly complex models in the nonlinear world and advocates for alternative modeling strategies for both confirmatory and exploratory data analysis.

title: Big Data and Business Intelligence: Debunking the Myths
Abstract: Big data is a widely discussed but often misunderstood term in business today. While it is touted as offering unprecedented levels of business intelligence and heralding a business revolution, the complexities of big data, particularly regarding social media's "dark data," are often overlooked. This paper aims to debunk common myths surrounding big data, focusing on the role of data from social media. The paper highlights two common misconceptions: first, that the sheer size of a dataset negates traditional methodological concerns, and second, that big data is a complete and unbiased source of information for decision-making. The paper emphasizes the importance of addressing methodological issues and recognizing the limitations of big data in decision-making.

title: Information retrieval in folktales using natural language processing
Abstract: This paper focuses on extracting information about literary characters from unstructured texts using natural language processing and reasoning on domain ontologies. The first step involves identifying the main characters and the story segments where they are described or act. The system is demonstrated in a folktale scenario, relying on a folktale ontology developed based on Propp's model for folktale morphology.
