title: Cells in the Internet of Things
Abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) integrates diverse research areas, leading to fragmentation in research organized around pre-existing fields: distributed computing with services and objects, networks (combining 6lowpan with Zigbee for the last hop), artificial intelligence and the semantic web, and human-computer interaction. A unified model encompassing all perspectives—domain, device, service, agent, etc.—is still lacking. This paper introduces the concept of cells as units of structure and context in the IoT. This unified vocabulary enables the representation of single entities (ranging from simple motes to intelligent spimes and virtual services), intranets of things, and ultimately the complete IoT. The paper explores criteria for demarcating cell boundaries, suggesting potential answers. It also discusses the concept's integration with existing visions and protocols, proposing its use as a foundation for a formal model.
label: AI

title: Redesigning pattern mining algorithms for supercomputers
Abstract: Upcoming multi-core processors are expected to adopt a distributed memory architecture similar to existing supercomputers, but parallel pattern mining algorithms optimized for this architecture remain understudied. This paper presents a novel closed pattern mining algorithm incorporating a well-engineered communication protocol, which is generalized to discover statistically significant patterns from personal genome data. For even distribution of communication, it employs global load balancing with multiple stacks distributed across a set of cores organized as a hypercube with random edges. The algorithm achieves a remarkable 1175-fold speedup using 1200 cores to solve a problem involving 11,914 items and 697 transactions, while the naive approach of separating the search space fails completely.
label: AI

title: Empirical Study on Deep Learning Models for Question Answering
Abstract: This paper explores deep learning models with memory components or attention mechanisms for the question answering (QA) task. Three models, Neural Machine Translation, Neural Turing Machine, and Memory Networks, are combined and compared for a simulated QA dataset. This is the first work to utilize Neural Machine Translation and Neural Turing Machines for QA tasks. Results suggest that the combination of attention and memory holds promise for solving certain QA problems.
label: AI

title: Time-resolved emission from bright hot pixels of an active region observed in the EUV band with SDO/AIA and multi-stranded loop modeling
Abstract: Evidence of small amounts of extremely hot plasma has been detected in active regions, potentially indicating impulsive heating occurring at spatial scales smaller than the cross-section of a single loop. This study investigates the heating and substructure of coronal loops in the core of an active region by analyzing light curves from the smallest resolution elements of solar observations in two EUV channels (94 Å and 335 Å) obtained by the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly onboard the Solar Dynamics Observatory. The evolution of a bundle of strands heated by a storm of nanoflares is modeled using a hydrodynamic 0D loop model (EBTEL). Light curves generated from random combinations of single strand light curves are compared to observed light curves in single pixels or rows of pixels, simultaneously in both channels, using two independent methods: an artificial intelligent system (Probabilistic Neural Network, PNN) and a simple cross-correlation technique. Parameter space exploration is conducted to constrain the distribution of heat pulses, their duration, spatial size, and their signatures on the light curves. Both methods yield optimal agreement for a relatively large population of events (1000) with short duration (less than 1 minute) and a relatively shallow distribution (power law with index 1.5) within a limited energy range (1.5 decades). The data analysis indicates that bumps in the light curves, especially in the 94 Å channel, are signatures of excess heating occurring a few minutes prior.
label: AI

title: Vehicle Color Recognition using Convolutional Neural Network
Abstract: Vehicle color information is a critical element in Intelligent Traffic Systems (ITS). This paper proposes a vehicle color recognition method using a convolutional neural network (CNN). While CNNs are typically designed for shape-based classification, this study demonstrates their ability to learn color distribution-based classification. The method converts the input image to two different color spaces, HSV and CIE Lab, and processes them through a CNN architecture. Training follows the procedure introduced by Krizhevsky, where the learning rate decreases by a factor of 10 after specific iterations. The method is evaluated using a publicly available vehicle color recognition dataset provided by Chen. Results show that the model outperforms the original system provided by Chen, achieving a 2% higher overall accuracy.
label: AI

title: The Human Kernel
Abstract: Bayesian nonparametric models, such as Gaussian processes, offer a compelling framework for automated statistical modeling due to their high flexibility and automatic complexity calibration. However, automating human expertise remains elusive, as standard Gaussian processes with standard kernels struggle with function extrapolation problems that are trivial for humans. This paper constructs function extrapolation problems and acquires human responses, developing a kernel learning framework to reverse engineer the inductive biases of human learners across behavioral experiments. The learned kernels are utilized to gain psychological insights and enable human-like extrapolation beyond traditional stationary and polynomial kernels. Finally, the paper investigates Occam's razor in both human and Gaussian process-based function learning.
label: AI

title: Safe Control under Uncertainty
Abstract: Synthesizing controllers for hybrid systems that satisfy temporal specifications expressing various system properties is a challenging problem. However, assuming deterministic temporal properties deviates from reality, as many such properties are learned from sensor input data through machine learning techniques. This paper proposes a novel logic, Probabilistic Signal Temporal Logic (PrSTL), as an expressive language for defining stochastic properties and enforcing probabilistic guarantees. It demonstrates how to synthesize safe controllers using this logic for cyber-physical systems, assuming that the stochastic properties are based on a set of Gaussian random variables. A key distinguishing feature of PrSTL is its adaptability, allowing the encoded logic to evolve as the system encounters additional data and updates its beliefs about the latent random variables defining safety properties. The approach is illustrated through the synthesis of safe controllers under PrSTL specifications for various case studies, including the control of quadrotors and autonomous vehicles in dynamic environments.
label: AI

title: Impact of Dual Slope Path Loss on User Association in HetNets
Abstract: Intelligent load balancing is crucial for maximizing the benefits of dense heterogeneous networks (HetNets). Existing techniques have primarily focused on single slope path loss models, despite the fact that multi-slope models more accurately represent real-world deployments. This paper investigates the performance of biasing and uplink/downlink decoupling for user association in HetNets with dual slope path loss models. It demonstrates that dual slope path loss models alter the trade-offs inherent in biasing, reducing gains from both biasing and uplink/downlink decoupling. Results indicate that with dual slope path loss models, the bias maximizing median rate is not optimal for other users, particularly edge users. Additionally, optimal downlink biasing is shown to realize most of the gains from downlink-uplink decoupling. Furthermore, user association gains in dense networks are observed to be highly sensitive to the path loss exponent beyond the critical distance in a dual slope model. |||
label: AI

title: An Efficient Implementation for WalkSAT
Abstract: Stochastic local search (SLS) algorithms have proven remarkably effective in finding models for random instances of the Boolean satisfiability problem (SAT). WalkSAT, a renowned and widely used SLS algorithm, has played a pivotal role in the evolution of SLS for SAT and continues to deliver state-of-the-art performance on random instances. This work proposes a novel WalkSAT implementation that significantly reduces redundant calculations, resulting in a substantial speed-up, outperforming even the latest versions of WalkSAT, including its advanced variants.
label: AI

title: Intelligent Financial Fraud Detection Practices: An Investigation
Abstract: Financial fraud poses a serious threat with far-reaching consequences across the finance industry, government, corporate sectors, and ordinary consumers. The increasing reliance on new technologies like cloud and mobile computing has exacerbated the problem. Traditional detection methods rely heavily on manual audits, where trained individuals scrutinize reports and transactions for signs of fraudulent behavior. This approach is not only time-consuming, expensive, and inaccurate but also impractical in the era of big data. As a result, financial institutions have turned to automated processes using statistical and computational methods. This paper presents a comprehensive investigation of financial fraud detection practices using data mining techniques, with a particular focus on computational intelligence-based methods. It provides a classification of these practices based on key aspects such as the detection algorithm used, the fraud type investigated, and the success rate. The paper also identifies issues and challenges associated with current practices and explores potential future research directions.
label: AI

title: Evolutionary Landscape and Management of Population Diversity
Abstract: The effectiveness of an Evolutionary Algorithm (EA) in search is directly tied to the variation present among the individuals in its population. Maintaining optimal diversity within the EA population is crucial for ensuring that the EA search progresses without being hindered by premature convergence to suboptimal solutions. A deeper understanding of population diversity, particularly in relation to evolutionary search and premature convergence, is key to designing efficient EAs. This paper first provides a brief analysis of population diversity issues in EAs. It then explores a counter-niching EA technique that introduces and maintains constructive diversity within the population. The proposed approach utilizes informed genetic operations to reach promising, but unexplored or under-explored, areas of the search space while discouraging premature local convergence. Simulation runs on a suite of standard benchmark test functions using a Genetic Algorithm (GA) implementation demonstrate promising results.
label: AI

title: Path integral distance for data interpretation
Abstract: The process of data interpretation inherently involves the introduction of equivalence relations on the set of walks over the database. Each equivalence relation on the set of walks defines a Markov chain that describes the transitions of a discrete-time random walk. To geometrize and interpret data, we propose a novel distance between data units defined as a "Feynman path integral," which considers all possible paths between any two nodes in a graph model of the data. While some paths are more preferable than others, the path integral distance approach to database analysis has proven its efficiency and success, particularly on multivariate strongly correlated data where other methods fail to detect structural components. Examples include applications in urban planning, historical language phylogenies, music analysis, and street fashion trend analysis. We believe that this approach will become an invaluable tool for intelligent complexity reduction and big data interpretation.
label: AI

title: Fusing Loop and GPS Probe Measurements to Estimate Freeway Density
Abstract: In an era of widespread GPS-enabled mobile devices, the potential of real-time "probe" location information for estimating the state of transportation networks is gaining increasing attention. Extensive research has been conducted on using probe data to estimate current vehicle traffic speeds (or equivalently, trip travel times). While travel times are beneficial to individual drivers, the state variable for a large class of traffic models and control algorithms is vehicle density. Our goal is to utilize probe data to augment traditional, fixed-location loop detector data for density estimation. To this end, we propose a method based on Rao-Blackwellized particle filters, a sequential Monte Carlo scheme. We present a simulation that demonstrates a 30% reduction in density mean absolute percentage error when fusing loop and probe data compared to using only loop data. We also present results using real data from a 19-mile freeway section in Los Angeles, California, where we achieve a 31% reduction. Additionally, our method's estimate using only real-world probe data, without any loop data, outperformed the estimate obtained using only loop data (an 18% reduction). These results demonstrate the potential of probe data for accurate traffic density estimation.
label: AI

title: Soft-Defined Heterogeneous Vehicular Network: Architecture and Challenges
Abstract: Heterogeneous Vehicular NETworks (HetVNETs) can meet various quality-of-service (QoS) requirements for intelligent transport system (ITS) services by integrating different access networks seamlessly. However, the current network architecture for HetVNET is not equipped to efficiently handle the increasing demands of the rapidly evolving network landscape. The centralized and flexible nature of the cloud radio access network (Cloud-RAN) allows for the convenient application of soft-defined networking (SDN) to support the dynamic nature of future HetVNET functions and applications while reducing operating costs. In this paper, we propose a multi-layer Cloud RAN architecture for implementing this new network, where multi-domain resources can be dynamically allocated to vehicle users as needed. We then present a detailed high-level design of the soft-defined HetVNET. Finally, we discuss key challenges and solutions for this new network, demonstrating its feasibility in the emerging fifth-generation (5G) era.
label: AI

title: Coordinating Truck Platooning by Clustering Pairwise Fuel-Optimal Plans
Abstract: We consider the fuel-optimal coordination of trucks into platoons. Truck platooning, a promising technology, enables trucks to achieve significant fuel savings by driving close together, thereby reducing air drag. We investigate the computation of fuel-optimal speed profiles for platooning. Using a first-order fuel model, we derive pairwise optimal plans. We formulate an optimization problem that combines these pairwise plans into a comprehensive plan for a large number of trucks. The problem resembles a medoids clustering problem. We propose an approximation algorithm similar to the partitioning around medoids algorithm and discuss its convergence. The method is evaluated using Monte Carlo simulations. Our results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm can efficiently compute a plan for thousands of trucks and achieve substantial fuel savings.
label: AI

title: Optimization as Estimation with Gaussian Processes in Bandit Settings
Abstract: Recently, there has been growing interest in Bayesian optimization, a method for optimizing an unknown function by making assumptions usually expressed through a Gaussian Process (GP) prior. We explore an optimization strategy that directly utilizes an estimate of the function's argmax. This strategy offers both practical and theoretical benefits: it eliminates the need to select any trade-off parameter, and we establish close connections to the widely used GP-UCB and GP-PI strategies. Our approach can be viewed as automatically and adaptively balancing exploration and exploitation in GP-UCB and GP-PI. We illustrate the effects of this adaptive tuning through bounds on the regret as well as an extensive empirical evaluation on robotics and vision tasks, demonstrating the robustness of this strategy across various performance criteria.
label: AI

title: Time-Sensitive Bayesian Information Aggregation for Crowdsourcing Systems
Abstract: Crowdsourcing systems often face the challenge of aggregating multiple judgments from potentially unreliable workers. Moreover, designing efficient crowdsourcing processes, including defining worker bonuses, fair prices, and task time limits, requires knowledge of the likely duration of the task at hand. In this work, we introduce a new time-sensitive Bayesian aggregation method that simultaneously estimates a task's duration and obtains reliable aggregations of crowdsourced judgments. Our method, called BCCTime, leverages the key insight that the time a worker takes to perform a task is a significant indicator of the likely quality of the produced judgment. To capture this, BCCTime utilizes latent variables to represent the uncertainty about the workers' completion time, the tasks' duration, and the workers' accuracy. To connect the quality of a judgment to the time a worker spends on a task, our model assumes that each task is completed within a latent time window during which all workers with a genuine intention to attempt the labeling task (i.e., no spammers) are expected to submit their judgments. Conversely, workers with a lower propensity for valid labeling, such as spammers, bots, or lazy labelers, are assumed to complete tasks considerably faster or slower than the time required by normal workers. Specifically, we utilize efficient message-passing Bayesian inference to learn approximate posterior probabilities of (i) the confusion matrix of each worker, (ii) the propensity to valid labeling of each worker, (iii) the unbiased duration of each task, and (iv) the true label of each task. Using two real-world public datasets for entity linking tasks, we demonstrate that BCCTime achieves up to 11% more accurate classifications and up to 100% more informative estimates of a task's duration compared to state-of-the-art methods.
label: AI

title: Creating Scalable and Interactive Web Applications Using High Performance Latent Variable Models
Abstract: This project outlines a modularized, scalable system for comparing Amazon products in an interactive and informative way using efficient latent variable models and dynamic visualization. We showcase how our system leverages the structure and rich review information of Amazon products to provide a fast, multifaceted, and intuitive comparison experience. By presenting a concise per-topic comparison visualization to the user, we effectively display aggregated information from the entire set of reviews while providing an interface that is at least as compact as the "most helpful reviews" currently displayed by Amazon, yet far more informative.
label: AI

title: High Performance Latent Variable Models
Abstract: Latent variable models have garnered considerable attention from both industry and academia due to their versatility across a wide range of applications. Extensive efforts have been made to develop systems that can scale to handle large-scale data, enabling their use in industry-scale applications. This paper describes a system that operates at a scale orders of magnitude higher than previous works and is an order of magnitude faster than state-of-the-art systems at the same scale, while simultaneously exhibiting greater robustness and achieving more accurate results. Our system incorporates several advances in distributed inference: high-performance synchronization of sufficient statistics with a relaxed consistency model; fast sampling using the Metropolis-Hastings-Walker method to overcome dense generative models; statistical modeling beyond Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) to encompass Pitman-Yor distributions (PDP) and Hierarchical Dirichlet Process (HDP) models; and sophisticated parameter projection schemes to resolve parameter conflicts arising from the relaxed consistency model. This work significantly expands the applicability of the Parameter Server paradigm. We achieve results with up to hundreds of billions of tokens, thousands of topics, and a vocabulary of a few million token-types, utilizing up to 60,000 processor cores operating on a production cluster of a large internet company. This demonstrates the feasibility of scaling to problems orders of magnitude larger than any previously published work.
label: AI

title: Intellectual interchanges in the history of the massive online open-editing encyclopedia, Wikipedia
Abstract: Wikipedia, a free online encyclopedia, boasts an immense amount of content. It is written collaboratively by volunteers with diverse backgrounds; anyone can access and edit most of the articles. This open-editing nature might lead to the perception that Wikipedia is an unstable and unreliable source; however, numerous studies suggest that Wikipedia is even more accurate and self-consistent than traditional encyclopedias. Scholars have attempted to understand this extraordinary credibility, but typically used the number of edits as the unit of time, neglecting real-time considerations. In this work, we delve into the formation of this collective intelligence through a systematic analysis of the entire history of 34,534,110 English Wikipedia articles between 2001 and 2014. From this massive dataset, we observe the universality of both timewise and lengthwise editing scales, suggesting the importance of considering real-time dynamics. By factoring in real time, we discover distinct growth patterns that remain hidden when using the number of edits as the time unit. To account for these findings, we present a mechanistic model that captures the article editing dynamics based on both editor-editor and editor-article interactions. The model successfully replicates key properties of real Wikipedia articles, such as distinct types of articles characterized by the interrelationship between the number of edits and editors, and the article size. Additionally, the model indicates that infrequently referred articles tend to grow faster than frequently referred ones, and articles attracting high motivation for editing counterintuitively reduce the number of participants. We suggest that this decay of participants eventually leads to inequality among the editors, which will become more severe over time.
label: AI

title: Semantic, Cognitive, and Perceptual Computing: Advances toward Computing for Human Experience
Abstract: The World Wide Web continues to evolve, serving as the infrastructure for vast amounts of multimodal and multisensory observations. These observations capture diverse situations relevant to people's needs and interests, encompassing all their idiosyncrasies. To support human-centered computing that empowers people to make better and timely decisions, we look towards computation inspired by human perception and cognition. With this goal in mind, we discuss computing paradigms of semantic computing, cognitive computing, and an emerging aspect of computing, which we call perceptual computing. In our view, these paradigms offer a continuum to make the most of vast, growing, and diverse data pertinent to human needs and interests. We propose details of perceptual computing characterized by interpretation and exploration operations, mirroring the interleaving of bottom and top brain processing. This article comprises two parts. First, we describe semantic computing, cognitive computing, and perceptual computing, highlighting their distinctions while acknowledging their complementary capabilities. We then provide a conceptual overview of perceptual computing, the newest of these three paradigms. For further insights, we focus on an application scenario of asthma management, converting massive, heterogeneous, and multimodal (big) data into actionable information, or "smart data."
label: AI

title: Discriminative Predicate Path Mining for Fact Checking in Knowledge Graphs
Abstract: Traditional fact-checking by experts and analysts cannot keep pace with the rapidly growing volume of newly created information. It is therefore crucial to enhance our ability to computationally determine the truth or falsity of factual statements. We view this problem as a link-prediction task in a knowledge graph and present a discriminative path-based method for fact-checking in knowledge graphs that incorporates connectivity, type information, and predicate interactions. Given a statement S of the form (subject, predicate, object), for example, (Chicago, capitalOf, Illinois), our approach mines discriminative paths that define the generalized statement (U.S. city, predicate, U.S. state) and uses the mined rules to evaluate the veracity of statement S. We evaluate our approach by examining thousands of claims related to history, geography, biology, and politics using a public, million-node knowledge graph extracted from Wikipedia and PubMedDB. Not only does our approach significantly outperform related models, but we also find that the discriminative predicate path model is easily interpretable and provides sensible reasons for the final determination.
label: AI

title: PERCH: Perception via Search for Multi-Object Recognition and Localization
Abstract: In many robotic domains, such as flexible automated manufacturing or personal assistance, a fundamental perception task is identifying and localizing objects whose 3D models are known. Canonical approaches to this problem include discriminative methods that find correspondences between feature descriptors computed over the model and observed data. While these methods have been successfully employed, they can become unreliable when the feature descriptors fail to capture variations in observed data; a classic cause is occlusion. As a step towards deliberative reasoning, we present PERCH: PErception via SeaRCH, an algorithm that seeks to find the best explanation of the observed sensor data by hypothesizing possible scenes in a generative fashion. Our contributions are: i) formulating the multi-object recognition and localization task as an optimization problem over the space of hypothesized scenes, ii) exploiting structure in the optimization to cast it as a combinatorial search problem on what we call the Monotone Scene Generation Tree, and iii) leveraging parallelization and recent advances in multi-heuristic search to make combinatorial search tractable. We prove that our system can guaranteedly produce the best explanation of the scene under the chosen cost function and validate our claims on real-world RGB-D test data. Our experimental results demonstrate that we can identify and localize objects under heavy occlusion, scenarios where state-of-the-art methods struggle.
label: AI

title: On the Computability of AIXI
Abstract: How could we solve the machine learning and artificial intelligence problem if we had infinite computational resources? Solomonoff induction and the reinforcement learning agent AIXI are proposed answers to this question. Both are known to be incomputable. In this paper, we quantify this incomputability using the arithmetical hierarchy and prove upper and corresponding lower bounds. We show that AIXI is not limit computable, implying that it cannot be approximated using finite computation. Our main result is a limit-computable ε-optimal version of AIXI with an infinite horizon that maximizes expected rewards.
label: AI

title: A New Empirical Constraint on the Prevalence of Technological Species in the Universe
Abstract: This paper addresses the cosmic frequency of technological species. Recent advancements in exoplanet studies provide robust constraints on all astrophysical terms in the Drake Equation. Utilizing these constraints and modifying the form and intent of the Drake Equation, we demonstrate that we can establish a firm lower bound on the probability that one or more additional technological species have evolved anywhere and at any time in the history of the observable Universe. We find that as long as the probability that a habitable zone planet develops a technological species is greater than ~10^-24, then humanity is not the only instance of technological intelligence that has evolved. This constraint has significant scientific and philosophical implications.
label: AI

title: System Descriptions of the First International Competition on Computational Models of Argumentation (ICCMA'15)
Abstract: This volume presents the system descriptions of the 18 solvers submitted to the First International Competition on Computational Models of Argumentation (ICCMA'15), providing an overview of the current state-of-the-art in computational approaches to abstract argumentation problems. Further information on the competition results and the performance of individual solvers can be found at http://argumentationcompetition.org/2015/.
label: AI

title: Social Media Analysis for Product Safety using Text Mining and Sentiment Analysis
Abstract: The increasing prevalence of counterfeiting and its associated economic and health consequences necessitate the development of active surveillance systems capable of providing timely and reliable information to all stakeholders involved in the anti-counterfeiting fight. User-generated content from social media platforms can offer early clues about product allergies, adverse events, and product counterfeiting. This paper reports work in progress, including contributions such as: the development of a framework for gathering and analyzing user views and experiences of drug and cosmetic products using machine learning, text mining, and sentiment analysis; the application of the proposed framework to Facebook comments and Twitter data for brand analysis; and the description of how to develop a product safety lexicon and training data for modeling a machine learning classifier for drug and cosmetic product sentiment prediction. Initial brand and product comparison results highlight the usefulness of text mining and sentiment analysis on social media data, while the use of machine learning classifiers for predicting sentiment orientation provides a valuable tool for users, product manufacturers, regulatory and enforcement agencies to monitor brand or product sentiment trends and take appropriate action in response to sudden or significant increases in negative sentiment.
label: AI

title: Causal Falling Rule Lists
Abstract: A causal falling rule list (CFRL) is a sequence of if-then rules that specifies heterogeneous treatment effects, where (i) the order of rules determines the treatment effect subgroup a subject belongs to, and (ii) the treatment effect decreases monotonically down the list. A given CFRL parameterizes a hierarchical Bayesian regression model in which the treatment effects are incorporated as parameters and assumed constant within model-specific subgroups. We formulate the search for the CFRL best supported by the data as a Bayesian model selection problem, where we perform a search over the space of CFRL models and approximate the evidence for a given CFRL model using standard variational techniques. We apply CFRL to a census wage dataset to identify subgroups with differing wage inequalities between men and women.
label: AI

title: Symbolic Neutrosophic Theory
Abstract: Symbolic Neutrosophic Theory utilizes abstract symbols like T, I, F, or their indexed variations (Tj, Ik, Fl) in neutrosophic studies. We extend the traditional dialectical triad (thesis-antithesis-synthesis) to a neutrosophic tetrad (thesis-antithesis-neutrothesis-neutrosynthesis). We introduce the neutrosophic system, which is a quasi or (t,i,f) classical system dealing with quasi-terms (concepts, attributes, etc.). Then, we define Neutrosophic Axioms, Neutrosophic Deducibility, Degree of Contradiction (Dissimilarity) between Neutrosophic Axioms, and other concepts. We then introduce (t, i, f) Neutrosophic Structures, showcasing their applications in geometry and algebra. We also provide a brief history of neutrosophic sets, neutrosophic numerical and literal components, neutrosophic numbers, etc.  We construct examples of splitting the literal indeterminacy (I) into literal subindeterminacies (I1, I2,..., Ir) and define a multiplication law for these literal subindeterminacies to build refined I neutrosophic algebraic structures. We define three neutrosophic actions and their properties, introducing the prevalence order on T, I, F with respect to a given neutrosophic operator. We further refine neutrosophic entities A, neutA, and antiA. We extend classical logical operators to neutrosophic literal (symbolic) logical operators and to refined literal (symbolic) logical operators, defining the refinement neutrosophic literal (symbolic) space. We introduce neutrosophic quadruple numbers (a+bT+cI+dF) and refined neutrosophic quadruple numbers, along with an absorbance law based on a prevalence order, to multiply these numbers.

title: Comprehensive indicator comparisons intelligible to non-experts: The case of two SNIP versions
Abstract: This framework compares various bibliometric indicators by introducing the Indicator Comparison Report. It offers a comprehensive analysis of the similarities and differences between indicators. The comparison highlights both the strengths and limitations of each indicator, avoiding biased promotion of one over others. It focuses on foundational notions, assumptions, and application contexts, making it accessible to non-experts. As an example, a comparison report is presented for the original and modified SNIP (Source Normalized Impact per Paper) indicator for journal citation impact.
label: AI

title: Normalization of Relative and Incomplete Temporal Expressions in Clinical Narratives
Abstract: We analyze RI-TIMEXes (temporal expressions) in temporally annotated corpora and propose two hypotheses regarding their normalization in the clinical narrative domain: the anchor point hypothesis and the anchor relation hypothesis. We annotate RI-TIMEXes in three corpora to investigate their characteristics across different domains. This informed the design of our RI-TIMEX normalization system for the clinical domain, comprising an anchor point classifier, an anchor relation classifier, and a rule-based RI-TIMEX text span parser. We experiment with different feature sets and conduct error analysis for each system component. The annotation confirmed our hypotheses, suggesting that the RI-TIMEXes normalization task can be simplified using two multi-label classifiers. Our system achieves anchor point classification, anchor relation classification, and rule-based parsing accuracy of 74.68%, 87.71%, and 57.2% (82.09% with relaxed matching criteria) respectively on the held-out test set of the 2012 i2b2 temporal relation challenge. Experiments with feature sets reveal interesting findings, such as the verbal tense feature not being as informative for anchor relation classification in clinical narratives as the tokens near the RI-TIMEX. Error analysis indicates that underrepresented anchor point and anchor relation classes are difficult to detect. We frame the RI-TIMEX normalization problem as a pair of multi-label classification problems. Focusing solely on RI-TIMEX extraction and normalization, the system exhibits statistically significant improvement over the RI-TIMEX results of the best systems in the 2012 i2b2 challenge.

title: Holographic Embeddings of Knowledge Graphs
Abstract: Learning entity and relation embeddings is an efficient and versatile approach for performing machine learning on relational data like knowledge graphs. We propose holographic embeddings (HolE) to learn compositional vector space representations of entire knowledge graphs. This method is inspired by holographic models of associative memory, employing circular correlation to create compositional representations. Using correlation as the compositional operator, HolE captures rich interactions while remaining computationally efficient, easy to train, and scalable to large datasets. Extensive experiments demonstrate that holographic embeddings outperform state-of-the-art methods for link prediction in knowledge graphs and relational learning benchmark datasets.
label: AI

title: Bad Universal Priors and Notions of Optimality
Abstract: A fundamental open question in algorithmic information theory is the choice of the universal Turing machine (UTM). For Kolmogorov complexity and Solomonoff induction, invariance theorems exist, meaning the choice of the UTM affects bounds only by a constant. However, for the universally intelligent agent AIXI (Hutter, 2005), no such invariance theorem is known. Our findings are entirely negative: we explore scenarios where unfortunate or adversarial UTM choices lead to AIXI's severe misbehavior. We demonstrate that Legg-Hutter intelligence and balanced Pareto optimality are entirely subjective, and every policy is Pareto optimal within the class of all computable environments. This undermines AIXI's existing optimality properties. While it may still serve as a gold standard for AI, our results imply that AIXI is a relative theory, dependent on the chosen UTM.
label: AI

title: Hybridization of Interval CP and Evolutionary Algorithms for Optimizing Difficult Problems
Abstract: The only rigorous approaches for achieving numerical proof of optimality in global optimization are interval-based methods that combine search-space branching with pruning of subdomains that cannot contain an optimal solution. Cutting-edge solvers typically integrate local optimization algorithms to compute a good upper bound of the global minimum for each subspace. This paper proposes a cooperative framework where interval methods collaborate with evolutionary algorithms. Evolutionary algorithms are stochastic algorithms where a population of candidate solutions iteratively evolves in the search-space to achieve satisfactory solutions. Within our cooperative solver Charibde, the evolutionary algorithm and the interval-based algorithm run concurrently and exchange bounds, solutions, and search-space information via advanced message passing. Comparing Charibde with state-of-the-art interval-based solvers (GlobSol, IBBA, Ibex) and NLP solvers (Couenne, BARON) on a benchmark of challenging COCONUT problems, results show that Charibde is highly competitive against non-rigorous solvers and converges significantly faster than rigorous solvers.
label: AI

title: Change Detection in Multivariate Datastreams: Likelihood and Detectability Loss
Abstract: We address the problem of detecting changes in multivariate datastreams and investigate the challenges change-detection methods face as data dimensionality increases. We focus on a general approach where changes are detected by comparing the distribution of the log-likelihood of the datastream across different time windows. While this approach forms the basis of several change-detection methods, its effectiveness with scaling data dimensionality remains unexplored. We show that the change magnitude can be measured by the symmetric Kullback-Leibler divergence between the pre- and post-change distributions. We demonstrate that the detectability of a change with a given magnitude worsens as data dimensionality increases. This problem, which we call "detectability loss," arises due to the linear relationship between the variance of the log-likelihood and the data dimension. We analytically derive the detectability loss for Gaussian-distributed datastreams and empirically confirm this issue on real-world datasets, highlighting its negative impact even at low data dimensions (e.g., 10).

title: Evaluating the Competency of a First-Order Ontology
Abstract: We evaluate the competency of a first-order ontology for its use with automated theorem provers (ATPs). The evaluation follows the adaptation of the competency questions (CQs) methodology [Grüninger&Fox,1995] to the framework of first-order logic, as presented in [Álvez&Lucio&Rigau,2015], and is applied to Adimen-SUMO [Álvez&Lucio&Rigau,2015]. The set of CQs used for this evaluation was automatically generated from a small set of semantic patterns and the mapping of WordNet to SUMO. Analyzing the results, we conclude that it is feasible to utilize ATPs for working with Adimen-SUMO v2.4, enabling the resolution of goals through non-trivial inferences.
label: AI

title: Improving the Competency of First-Order Ontologies
Abstract: We introduce a new framework to evaluate and improve first-order (FO) ontologies using automated theorem provers (ATPs) based on competency questions (CQs). Our framework encompasses both the adaptation of an ontology evaluation methodology to the first-order logic framework and a new set of non-trivial CQs designed for evaluating FO versions of SUMO, significantly expanding the limited set of CQs proposed in the literature. Most of these new CQs were automatically generated from a small set of patterns and the mapping of WordNet to SUMO. Applying our framework, we demonstrate that Adimen-SUMO v2.2 surpasses TPTP-SUMO. Furthermore, utilizing the feedback provided by ATPs, we developed an improved version of Adimen-SUMO (v2.4). This new version outperforms its predecessors in terms of competency. For example, "Humans can reason" is automatically inferred from Adimen-SUMO v2.4, while it is not deducible from either TPTP-SUMO or Adimen-SUMO v2.2.

title: SRMR variants for improved blind room acoustics characterization
Abstract: Reverberation, particularly in large rooms, significantly degrades speech recognition performance and intelligibility. Since direct measurement of room characteristics is usually not feasible, blind estimation of reverberation-related metrics like reverberation time (RT) and direct-to-reverberant energy ratio (DRR) can be valuable information for speech recognition and enhancement algorithms operating in enclosed environments. This work evaluates the performance of five variants of blind RT and DRR estimators based on a modulation spectrum representation of reverberant speech using single- and multi-channel speech data. These models are all based on variations of the Speech-to-Reverberation Modulation Energy Ratio (SRMR). We demonstrate that these measures outperform a state-of-the-art baseline based on maximum-likelihood estimation of sound decay rates in terms of root-mean square error (RMSE) and Pearson correlation. Compared to the baseline, the best proposed measure, called NSRMR_k, achieves a 23% relative improvement in RMSE and allows for relative correlation improvements ranging from 13% to 47% for RT prediction.
label: AI

title: Layer-Specific Adaptive Learning Rates for Deep Networks
Abstract: The increasing complexity of deep learning architectures is leading to training times spanning weeks or even months. This slow training is partly due to vanishing gradients, where the gradients used by back-propagation are extremely large for weights connecting deep layers (near the output layer) and extremely small for shallow layers (near the input layer), resulting in slow learning in the shallow layers. Additionally, highly non-convex problems like deep neural networks suffer from a proliferation of high-error low curvature saddle points, further slowing down learning significantly. This paper aims to overcome these issues by proposing an optimization method for training deep neural networks that utilizes learning rates specific to each layer in the network and adaptive to the function's curvature, increasing the learning rate at low curvature points. This enables faster learning in the shallow layers of the network and quick escape from high-error low curvature saddle points. We test our method on standard image classification datasets like MNIST, CIFAR10, and ImageNet, demonstrating that our method improves accuracy while reducing training time compared to standard algorithms.
label: AI

title: Narrative Science Systems: A Review
Abstract: Automatic narration of events and entities is crucial, particularly for live reporting where timely updates are critical and the volume of information to be narrated is immense. This paper explores the challenges in this context, along with the algorithms used to build such systems. A systematic study reveals that most work in this area focuses on statistical data. Furthermore, subjective evaluation or expert input remains limited in the narration context.
label: AI

title: Scatter Component Analysis: A Unified Framework for Domain Adaptation and Domain Generalization
Abstract: This paper addresses classification tasks in a target domain where labeled training data is only available from source domains that are different from (but related to) the target. Two closely related frameworks, domain adaptation and domain generalization, tackle such tasks, differing only in the availability of unlabeled target data: domain adaptation leverages unlabeled target information, while domain generalization does not. We propose Scatter Component Analysis (SCA), a fast representation learning algorithm applicable to both domain adaptation and domain generalization. SCA utilizes a simple geometric measure, scatter, which operates in reproducing kernel Hilbert space. SCA finds a representation that balances maximizing class separability, minimizing domain mismatch, and maximizing data separability, each quantified by scatter. The optimization problem of SCA can be reduced to a generalized eigenvalue problem, resulting in a fast and exact solution. Comprehensive experiments on benchmark cross-domain object recognition datasets validate that SCA performs much faster than several state-of-the-art algorithms and achieves top-tier classification accuracy in both domain adaptation and domain generalization. We also demonstrate that scatter can be used to establish a theoretical generalization bound in the domain adaptation scenario.
label: AI

title: A synchronous rendering of hybrid systems for designing Plant-on-a-Chip (PoC)
Abstract: Hybrid systems are discrete controllers used to control a physical process (plant) exhibiting continuous dynamics. Hybrid automata (HA) are a well-established and widely used formal model for specifying such systems. While numerous methods exist for simulating hybrid automata, no known approaches for automatically generating semantically preserving code from HA are available. Enabling this would facilitate the design of a plant-on-a-chip (PoC) system that emulates the plant to validate discrete controllers. Such an approach requires mathematical soundness and should not rely on numerical solvers. We propose a novel method for PoC design for plant emulation, previously not possible. The approach restricts input/output (I/O) HA models using a set of criteria for well-formedness that are statically verified. After verification, we use an abstraction based on a synchronous approach to enable code generation. This is feasible through a sound transformation to synchronous HA. We compare our method (using the tool Piha) with the widely used Simulink R simulation framework, demonstrating that our method excels in both execution time and code size. Our approach to the PoC problem paves the way for the emulation of physical plants in diverse domains such as robotics, automation, medical devices, and intelligent transportation systems.
label: AI

title: Inheritance in Object-Oriented Knowledge Representation
Abstract: This paper examines the inheritance mechanism in knowledge representation models like object-oriented programming, frames, and object-oriented dynamic networks. Additionally, inheritance within the representation of vague and imprecise knowledge is discussed. The paper introduces new types of inheritance, provides a general classification of all known inheritance types, and presents an approach that avoids problems with exceptions, redundancy, and ambiguity within object-oriented dynamic networks and their fuzzy extension. The proposed approach is based on the concepts of homogeneous and inhomogeneous or heterogeneous classes of objects, enabling more flexible and efficient inheritance hierarchy construction.
label: AI

title: Exploiters-Based Knowledge Extraction in Object-Oriented Knowledge Representation
Abstract: This paper delves into knowledge extraction mechanisms within object-oriented knowledge representation models like frames, object-oriented programming, and object-oriented dynamic networks. The paper also explores the concept of universal exploiters within object-oriented dynamic networks. The key contribution of this work is the introduction of a new exploiters-based knowledge extraction approach that generates a finite set of new object classes based on a basic set of classes. The paper proposes methods for calculating the quantity of new classes obtainable using this approach and the number of types each class describes. It provides proof that the basic set of classes, extended according to this approach, along with the union exploiter, forms an upper semilattice. This approach guarantees the generation of a finitely defined set of new object classes for any object-oriented dynamic network. The number of these classes can be precisely calculated beforehand, allowing for the storage of only the basic set of classes in the knowledge base.
label: AI

title: Object-Oriented Dynamic Networks
Abstract: This paper describes the Object-Oriented Dynamic Network (OODN) model, which facilitates the representation of knowledge that evolves over time, allowing for the construction of new relationships between objects and classes of objects, and the representation of the results of their modifications. The model is based on representing objects via their properties and methods. This enables object classification and, in a sense, hierarchy construction of their types. Moreover, it allows representing the modification relationship between concepts, constructing new object classes from existing ones, and creating sets and multisets of concepts. OODN can be visualized as a connected and directed graph, where nodes represent concepts and edges represent relationships between them. Using this model of knowledge representation, modifications to knowledge and movement through the network graph can be viewed as a process of logical reasoning, finding optimal solutions, or even creativity. The proposed approach provides a framework for modeling some aspects of human knowledge systems and the primary mechanisms of human thought, particularly the acquisition of new experiences and knowledge.
label: AI

title: Universal and Determined Constructors of Multisets of Objects
Abstract: This paper examines the creation of sets and multisets as an approach for modeling specific aspects of human thinking. Set creation is considered within the constructive object-oriented version of set theory (COOST) from various perspectives, including classical set theory, object-oriented programming (OOP), and the development of intelligent information systems (IIS). The key feature of COOST, in contrast to other set theory versions, is the ability to describe object essences more precisely using their properties and methods that can be applied to them. This makes COOST object-oriented and closely aligned with OOP. Within COOST, the author proposes a universal constructor for multisets of objects, enabling the creation of arbitrary multisets of objects. Additionally, the paper introduces several determined constructors for multisets of objects, allowing for the creation of multisets using strictly defined schemas. These constructors are highly useful for multisets with large cardinalities, as they facilitate the calculation of the multiplicity of each object and the cardinality of the multiset before its creation. The proposed constructors of multisets of objects allow us to model, in a sense, corresponding processes of human thought, which, in turn, provides opportunities for developing IIS using these tools.
label: AI

title: Mathematical Foundations for Designing and Development of Intelligent Systems of Information Analysis
Abstract: This article attempts to combine different approaches for working with sets of objects and their classes to design and develop artificial intelligent systems (AIS) for information analysis using object-oriented programming (OOP). The paper examines basic OOP concepts and their relationship to set theory and artificial intelligence (AI). The process of sets and multisets creation is considered from various perspectives, including mathematical set theory, OOP, and AI. The paper defines objects and their properties, homogeneous and inhomogeneous classes of objects, sets of objects, multisets of objects, and proposes constructive methods for their creation and classification. Moreover, the paper highlights the need for extending existing OOP tools to practically implement AIS for information analysis using the proposed approach.
label: AI

title: Embarrassingly Parallel Variational Inference in Nonconjugate Models
Abstract: We develop a parallel variational inference (VI) procedure for use in data-distributed settings, where each machine only has access to a subset of data and runs VI independently without communication. This type of "embarrassingly parallel" procedure has recently been developed for MCMC inference algorithms. However, in many cases, directly extending this procedure to VI methods requires restrictive exponential family conditions on the model's form. Furthermore, most existing (nonparallel) VI methods are limited to conditionally conjugate models, restricting their applicability. To address these challenges, we leverage the recently proposed nonparametric VI to facilitate an embarrassingly parallel VI procedure applicable to a broader range of models, including nonconjugate ones. We derive our embarrassingly parallel VI algorithm, analyze it theoretically, and demonstrate its empirical performance on several nonconjugate models. |||
label: AI

title: On Arthur Eddington's Theory of Everything
Abstract: Arthur Eddington, a prominent physicist, dedicated a significant portion of his career (1929-1944) to developing a comprehensive theory of fundamental physics encompassing all physical phenomena, from the subatomic realm to the vast universe. His unfinished work combined abstract mathematics and spiritual philosophy, creating a unique approach that proved challenging for other scientists to comprehend. Eddington placed considerable emphasis on the constants of nature, aiming to deduce them purely through theoretical means. Despite its originality, Eddington's attempt to establish a new foundation for physics was ultimately unsuccessful, receiving rejection from the majority of physicists. This failure can be attributed to his unconventional perspective on quantum mechanics.
label: AI

title: Structured Memory for Neural Turing Machines
Abstract: Neural Turing Machines (NTMs), inspired by the brain's "working memory", employ a memory component to store and retrieve information, thereby simplifying the learning of algorithms. However, current NTMs are limited to linearly organized memory, leading to issues like non-convergence and overfitting in specific tasks. Recognizing the memory component's role in these shortcomings, this paper proposes various alternative memory structures for NTMs. Experimental results demonstrate that two of these structured-memory NTMs achieve improved convergence, both in speed and prediction accuracy, on tasks like copy and associative recall, as seen in previous work by Graves et al. (2014).
label: AI

title: UAVs using Bayesian Optimization to Locate WiFi Devices
Abstract: This research tackles the problem of localizing non-collaborative WiFi devices within a large area, particularly focusing on locating humans by tracking their WiFi devices during search-and-rescue operations following natural disasters. The proposed solution utilizes an active sensing approach, employing Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) to gather signal strength measurements at strategically selected locations. The challenge lies in the sporadic nature of these measurements, acquired only when the UAV is close to the device. Therefore, efficient decision-making with limited measurements is critical. To address this, the paper employs a Bayesian optimization approach based on Gaussian process (GP) regression. GPs provide reliable predictions even with minimal data points, while Bayesian optimization intelligently balances exploration and exploitation. Field experiments conducted over a 1000 x 1000 meter region demonstrate the approach's effectiveness, reducing the search area to less than 100 meters around the WiFi device within just 5 minutes. Overall, the method accurately localizes the device within 15 minutes, with an error margin of under 20 meters.
label: AI

title: A Multilevel Coordinate Search Algorithm for Well Placement, Control and Joint Optimization
Abstract: Optimizing well placement and control strategies is crucial in oil field development, posing computationally expensive and non-convex challenges with multiple optima. Effective and robust algorithms are essential for practical solutions. This paper leverages the multilevel coordinate search (MCS) algorithm for solving both well placement and control optimization problems. MCS, a derivative-free approach, combines global and local search techniques. The study examines both synthetic and real oil fields and compares MCS's performance against generalized pattern search (GPS), particle swarm optimization (PSO), and covariance matrix adaptive evolution strategy (CMA-ES). Results show that MCS is highly competitive, outperforming other algorithms, especially for the joint optimization problem with limited computational resources. The impact of parameter settings for MCS is also investigated, comparing the performance of simultaneous and sequential procedures for the joint optimization problem, highlighting the benefits of the latter.

title: Asymptotic Logical Uncertainty and The Benford Test
Abstract: This paper presents algorithm A, which assigns probabilities to logical sentences. For any simple infinite sequence of sentences whose truth values resemble a biased coin with a "true" probability of p, the probabilities assigned by algorithm A to these sentences converge to p.
label: AI

title: Evaluating Real-time Anomaly Detection Algorithms - the Numenta Anomaly Benchmark
Abstract: Anomaly detection in streaming data is crucial for extracting valuable insights from real-time data across various domains, such as finance, IT, security, healthcare, and energy. However, detecting anomalies in real-time presents significant challenges, requiring detectors to process data continuously, learn dynamically, and make predictions simultaneously. The absence of suitable benchmarks hinders the testing and evaluation of these real-time anomaly detectors. This paper introduces the Numenta Anomaly Benchmark (NAB), an open-source framework designed to provide a controlled and repeatable environment for testing and evaluating anomaly detection algorithms on streaming data. The perfect anomaly detector would identify all anomalies promptly, avoid false alarms, handle real-world time-series data from diverse domains, and adapt seamlessly to evolving data patterns. NAB incorporates these characteristics into its scoring algorithm, tailored for streaming data. It evaluates detectors on a benchmark dataset containing labeled real-world time-series data. The paper presents the components of NAB and provides results and analysis for several open-source and commercially used algorithms. NAB aims to establish a standardized open-source framework for comparing and evaluating different algorithms dedicated to detecting anomalies in streaming data.
label: AI

title: The Inductive Constraint Programming Loop
Abstract: Constraint programming is widely employed for addressing real-world optimization problems, such as planning, scheduling, and resource allocation. However, existing constraint programming software does not utilize the vast amounts of data collected about these problems to update schedules, resources, and plans. This paper introduces a novel framework called the Inductive Constraint Programming loop. This approach systematically gathers and analyzes data to dynamically revise and adapt constraints and optimization criteria. Inductive Constraint Programming bridges the gap between data mining and machine learning on one hand and constraint programming on the other.
label: AI

title: Data structuring for the ontological modelling of wind energy systems
Abstract: Small-scale wind energy projects face challenges in efficient deployment, partly due to the inefficient management of data and information. Ontologies can address this issue by providing a semantic middleware that bridges the gap between low-level data and general knowledge, thereby mitigating the drawbacks of partially available, noisy, inconsistent, and heterogeneous data sources. This paper proposes an ontology for the wind energy domain, utilizing description logic as the underlying technology. The aim is to integrate a corpus of heterogeneous knowledge, encompassing both digital and human data, to assist users in accelerating the initialization of small-scale wind projects. The paper demonstrates a use case scenario where the ontology automatically verifies the compliance of a planned wind project with active regulations.
label: AI

title: Context-Aware Bandits
Abstract: This paper introduces an efficient Context-Aware clustering of Bandits (CAB) algorithm, capable of capturing collaborative effects. CAB is readily deployable in real-world recommendation systems, where multi-armed bandits have proven effective, particularly for addressing the cold-start problem. CAB leverages context-aware clustering augmented by exploration-exploitation strategies. The algorithm dynamically clusters users based on the content universe being considered. The paper presents a theoretical analysis in the standard stochastic multi-armed bandits setting. The efficiency of CAB is demonstrated on both production and real-world datasets, showcasing its scalability and, importantly, significant improvements in prediction performance compared to several state-of-the-art methods.
label: AI

title: Fast detection of multiple objects in traffic scenes with a common detection framework
Abstract: Traffic scene perception (TSP) aims to extract accurate real-time information about the on-road environment, involving three key phases: detection of objects of interest, recognition of detected objects, and tracking of moving objects. As recognition and tracking rely heavily on the results of detection, accurate object detection is crucial for effective TSP. This paper focuses on three critical object classes: traffic signs, cars, and cyclists. It proposes a unified learning-based detection framework to detect all three objects simultaneously. The proposed framework consists of a dense feature extractor and individual detectors for each of the three object classes. Once the dense features are extracted, they are shared among all detectors. This shared framework accelerates detection speed by evaluating dense features only once during the testing phase. Unlike previous approaches, which used different features for each object, this paper utilizes a common framework. To enhance feature robustness against noise and image deformations, spatially pooled features are incorporated as part of the aggregated channel features. Further generalization performance is improved through an object subcategorization method that captures intra-class variation. The paper experimentally validates the proposed framework's effectiveness and efficiency in three detection applications: traffic sign detection, car detection, and cyclist detection. The framework achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods on various benchmark datasets.
label: AI

title: Influence of network topology on cooperative problem-solving systems
Abstract: The concept of collective intelligence driving the intricate natural structures created by organisms suggests that social network organization evolves to optimize group-level problem-solving capabilities. This research investigates the impact of social network topology on the performance of agents tasked with finding global maxima in NK fitness landscapes. Agents collaborate by broadcasting messages about their fitness, using this information to emulate the fittest agent within their influence networks. For scenarios where messages accurately reflect the proximity to the solution (e.g., smooth fitness landscapes), high connectivity and centralization enhance group performance. However, for rugged landscapes, these characteristics are advantageous only for small groups. In larger groups, slowing down information transmission through the network proves beneficial to avoid local maximum traps. Long-range links and modularity have minimal impact on group performance except for a limited range of model parameters.
label: AI

title: ParallelPC: an R package for efficient constraint based causal exploration
Abstract: Discovering causal relationships from data is a central goal in many research areas. Constraint-based causal exploration algorithms, such as PC, FCI, RFCI, PC-simple, IDA, and Joint-IDA, have made significant advancements and found numerous applications. However, a common challenge with these methods is their high computational complexity, hindering their use in real-world high-dimensional datasets, such as gene expression datasets. This paper introduces an R package, ParallelPC, which incorporates parallelized versions of these causal exploration algorithms. The parallelization accelerates the procedure for analyzing large datasets and reduces memory consumption during algorithm execution. The package is suitable not only for supercomputers or clusters but also for researchers using personal computers with multi-core CPUs. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the practicality of exploring causal relationships in high-dimensional datasets containing thousands of variables using a single multi-core computer. ParallelPC is accessible through the CRAN repository at https://cran.rproject.org/web/packages/ParallelPC/index.html.
label: AI

title: Mining Interesting Trivia for Entities from Wikipedia
Abstract: Trivia encompasses any factual information about an entity that is considered interesting due to its unusualness, uniqueness, unexpectedness, or weirdness. These captivating facts are often presented in "Did You Know?" sections. While trivia may seem trivial in terms of importance, this paper explores their use for enhancing user engagement. These fun facts pique curiosity and encourage users to interact more with the entity, promoting repeated engagement. The paper cites case studies that highlight the significant impact of trivia on increasing user engagement and promoting product/service publicity. This paper proposes a novel approach for extracting entity trivia from their Wikipedia pages. Given an entity, the system extracts relevant sentences from its Wikipedia page and generates a ranked list of sentences based on their interestingness as trivia. At the core of the system lies an interestingness ranker, which learns the notion of interestingness through a rich set of domain-independent linguistic and entity-based features. The ranking model is trained using existing user-generated trivia data available on the web, eliminating the need to create new labeled data specifically for the movie domain. For other domains like sports, celebrities, countries, etc., labeled data would need to be created, as described in the paper. The system was evaluated on the movie and celebrity domains, demonstrating significant performance improvements over defined baselines. Qualitative analysis of the results reveals that the engineered set of features effectively identifies interesting trivia among the top ranks.
label: AI

title: Pseudo-Marginal Slice Sampling
Abstract: Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods asymptotically sample from complex probability distributions. The pseudo-marginal MCMC framework only requires an unbiased estimator of the unnormalized probability distribution function to construct a Markov chain. However, the resulting chains are more challenging to tune to a target distribution compared to conventional MCMC, and the available update types are limited. This paper describes a general method for clamping and updating the random numbers used in the unbiased estimator of a pseudo-marginal method. This framework allows for the use of slice sampling and other adaptive methods, resulting in more robust Markov chains that often mix more rapidly.
label: AI

title: On oblivious branching programs with bounded repetition that cannot efficiently compute CNFs of bounded treewidth
Abstract: This paper investigates the complexity of an extension of ordered binary decision diagrams (OBDDs) called c-OBDDs on CNFs with bounded (primal graph) treewidth. The paper shows that for any k, there exists a class of CNFs with treewidth k ≥ 3 where the equivalent c-OBDDs have a size of Ω(n^(k/(8c-4))). Importantly, this lower bound holds even when considering non-deterministic and semantic c-OBDDs. The second result uses this lower bound to distinguish the model from sentential decision diagrams (SDDs). To achieve the lower bound, the paper employs a structural graph parameter called matching width. The third result establishes a linear relationship between matching width and pathwidth.
label: AI

title: Attend, Adapt and Transfer: Attentive Deep Architecture for Adaptive Transfer from multiple sources in the same domain
Abstract: Transferring knowledge from prior source tasks to solve a new target task can be beneficial in various learning applications. However, applying transfer presents two major challenges: avoiding negative transfer, where the transfer hampers or slows down learning, and selectively transferring knowledge from multiple source tasks for different parts of the target task's state space. This paper proposes A2T (Attend, Adapt and Transfer), an attentive deep architecture that adapts and transfers from these source tasks. The model is versatile enough to transfer policies or value functions. Empirical evaluations across different learning algorithms show that A2T is an effective architecture for transfer, effectively avoiding negative transfer while selectively transferring from multiple source tasks within the same domain.
label: AI

title: Artificial Intelligence and Asymmetric Information Theory
Abstract: When human agents collaborate to make decisions, information asymmetry often arises, where one agent possesses more information than the other. This asymmetry distorts the market. Agents may intentionally signal false or accurate information to manipulate decisions, or they may engage in screening to minimize the impact of asymmetric information on decisions. The advent of artificial intelligence has facilitated both signaling and screening. This paper explores the impact of artificial intelligence on the theory of asymmetric information. It suggests that artificial intelligent agents reduce information asymmetry, leading to increased market efficiency. The paper further postulates that as the number of artificial intelligent agents in a market increases, the volume of trades decreases. This is because a certain level of information asymmetry is necessary for trading to occur, creating opportunities for arbitrage.
label: AI

title: Gelisp: A Library to Represent Musical CSPs and Search Strategies
Abstract: This paper introduces Gelisp, a novel library for representing musical Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSPs) and search strategies in an intuitive manner. Gelisp offers two interfaces: a command-line interface for Common Lisp and a graphical interface for OpenMusic. Using Gelisp, the paper addresses a problem of automatic music generation proposed by composer Michael Jarrell and finds solutions for the All-interval series.

title: Learning optimal quantum models is NP-hard
Abstract: Physical modeling bridges the gap between perception (measurements) and abstraction (theoretical models). It is a central objective in physics and is generally considered a creative process. This paper explores the capabilities of computers in tackling this task, a question of both philosophical and practical interest, as a positive answer would enable artificial intelligence to comprehend the physical world. Quantum mechanics, the most fundamental physical theory, suggests that nature operates according to its rules. Therefore, the paper investigates whether computers can learn optimal quantum models from measured data. It demonstrates that in the absence of physical heuristics, inferring optimal quantum models cannot be computed efficiently unless P = NP. This result sheds light on the limitations of computers in furthering our understanding of nature.

title: Dreaming More Data: Class-dependent Distributions over Diffeomorphisms for Learned Data Augmentation
Abstract: Data augmentation is a crucial aspect of training high-dimensional models. This approach synthesizes new observations by applying predefined transformations to the original training data, for example, generating new images by rotating existing ones. Current augmentation methods rely on manually specifying these transformations, making data augmentation an implicit form of feature engineering. Aiming for true end-to-end learning, this paper proposes learning the applied transformations on a per-class basis. Specifically, it aligns image pairs within each class under the assumption that the spatial transformation between images belongs to a broad class of diffeomorphisms. The paper then learns a class-specific probabilistic generative model of these transformations within a Riemannian submanifold of the Lie group of diffeomorphisms. Significant performance improvements in training deep neural networks are demonstrated over manually specified augmentation schemes. The code and augmented datasets are available online. |||

title: Bifurcation-based adiabatic quantum computation with a nonlinear oscillator network: Toward quantum soft computing
Abstract: Bifurcations in nonlinear systems lead to qualitative changes in their dynamics based on their parameters. A quantum-mechanical nonlinear oscillator can undergo quantum adiabatic evolution through its bifurcation point, resulting in a superposition of two oscillation states, known as a Schrödinger cat state. This study proposes a quantum computer utilizing these oscillators, rather than quantum bits, to solve complex combinatorial optimization problems. The network of nonlinear oscillators finds optimal solutions through quantum adiabatic evolution, gradually increasing nonlinear terms. This contrasts with conventional adiabatic quantum computation and quantum annealing, where quantum fluctuation terms are slowly decreased. Numerical simulations show that quantum superposition and quantum fluctuation effectively contribute to finding optimal solutions. The proposed computer has similarities to neural computers, which are also networks of nonlinear components. This approach opens new possibilities in quantum computation, nonlinear science, and artificial intelligence.

title: A novel mutation operator based on the union of fitness and design spaces information for Differential Evolution
Abstract: Differential Evolution (DE) is a powerful evolutionary algorithm for global optimization. Its core mutation operator randomly selects parent solutions. Recent advancements aim to enhance the intelligence of this operator by strategically choosing parents for mutation. These strategies often focus on design space or fitness space criteria, but neglect half of the problem space's valuable information. This paper introduces Universal Differential Evolution (UDE), which utilizes both design and fitness space criteria for intelligent mutation vector selection. Experimental analysis using CEC2005 benchmarks demonstrates that UDE significantly outperforms methods relying on single criteria, improving DE's overall performance.

title: Data-Efficient Learning of Feedback Policies from Image Pixels using Deep Dynamical Models
Abstract: Data-efficient reinforcement learning (RL) in continuous state-action spaces with high-dimensional observations remains a key challenge in developing fully autonomous systems. The pixels-to-torques problem, where an RL agent learns a closed-loop control policy from pixel information, is a particularly important instance of this challenge. This paper presents a data-efficient, model-based reinforcement learning algorithm that learns such a closed-loop policy directly from pixel information. The algorithm utilizes a deep dynamical model to learn a low-dimensional feature embedding of images alongside a predictive model in this low-dimensional space. This joint learning is crucial for long-term predictions, which are essential for the adaptive nonlinear model predictive control strategy used for closed-loop control. Compared to state-of-the-art RL methods, this approach exhibits faster learning, scales to high-dimensional state spaces, is lightweight, and represents a significant step towards fully autonomous end-to-end learning from pixels to torques.

title: Asymptotically tight bounds for inefficiency in risk-averse selfish routing
Abstract: This paper examines a nonatomic selfish routing model with independent stochastic travel times, represented by mean and variance latency functions for each edge depending on their flows. To separate the impact of risk-averse player preferences from selfish behavior on system performance, Nikolova and Stier-Moses defined the price of risk aversion as the worst-case ratio of the cost of an equilibrium with risk-averse players to that of an equilibrium with risk-neutral users. For risk-averse users minimizing the mean plus variance of travel time, they proved an upper bound on the price of risk aversion independent of the latency functions, growing linearly with the graph size and players' risk aversion. This paper presents a matching lower bound for graphs with vertices equal to powers of two, using a graph family inductively generated from the Braess graph. It also introduces functional bounds that depend on the class of mean latency functions, providing characterizations independent of network topology. Additionally, a new asymptotically-tight lower bound supplements the upper bound. The third contribution is a tight bound on the price of risk aversion for graphs generalizing series-parallel graphs, applying to users minimizing the mean plus standard deviation of a path. This refines previous results characterizing the price of risk aversion for series-parallel graphs and the Braess graph.
