title: Budget Constraints in Prediction Markets
Abstract: This paper comprehensively analyzes optimal trades under budget constraints within a prediction market using a cost-function-based automated market maker. It investigates how budget constraints impact individual traders' ability to influence the market price. As a concrete example, it establishes sufficient conditions for budget additivity, where two traders with budgets B and B' and identical beliefs have a combined impact equivalent to a single trader with budget B+B'. This implies that even if a single trader cannot significantly move the market, a group of like-minded traders can achieve the same desired effect. The paper shows that a generalized logarithmic market scoring rule exhibits budget additivity, while the quadratic market scoring rule does not, when the set of payoff vectors associated with outcomes is affinely independent. This analysis provides both descriptive insights into market maker vulnerability to budget constraints and prescriptive guidance for market construction.

title: Towards a general framework for an observation and knowledge based model of occupant behaviour in office buildings

It represents human behavior through probabilistic cause-effect relationships, incorporating knowledge from previous studies and conditional probabilities derived from expert knowledge or observations. This approach has been successfully implemented in co-simulating building physics and human behavior to evaluate the CO2 concentration in an office.

title: Using Ontology-Based Context in the Portuguese-English Translation of Homographs in Textual Dialogues
Abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of message translation in dialogue systems, where submitted messages are often treated as isolated sentences, hindering disambiguation of homographs in ambiguous sentences due to missing contextual information. It introduces a novel approach that utilizes concepts from existing ontologies to overcome this disambiguation problem.

title: VBPR: Visual Bayesian Personalized Ranking from Implicit Feedback
Abstract: Modern recommender systems model people and items by uncovering underlying dimensions that encode item properties and user preferences. These dimensions are typically learned from user feedback, often implicitly (e.g., purchase histories, browsing logs). Some systems also incorporate side information like product attributes, temporal information, or review text. However, a crucial feature often ignored is the visual appearance of items. This paper presents a scalable factorization model that integrates visual signals into predictors of user opinions, applied to large, real-world datasets. It utilizes visual features extracted from product images using pre-trained deep networks, learning an additional layer to uncover visual dimensions explaining user feedback variations. This approach not only improves personalized ranking accuracy but also mitigates cold start issues and enables qualitative analysis of visual dimensions influencing user opinions.

title: DKP-AOM: results for OAEI 2015

This marked DKP-AOM's first successful participation in the Conference, OA4QA, and Anatomy tracks of OAEI. Two versions, DKP-AOM and DKP-AOM_lite, were evaluated. DKP-AOM performs coherence analysis. In the OA4QA track, DKP-AOM outperformed other systems, generating accurate alignments that answered all evaluation queries. It also achieved competitive results in the conference track evaluation. In the anatomy track, DKP-AOM produced alignments within the allocated time and generated coherent results. The paper concludes by discussing future development plans for DKP-AOM.

title: Disjunctive Answer Set Solvers via Templates
Abstract: Answer set programming is a declarative programming paradigm for solving challenging combinatorial search problems. A fundamental task is computing stable models, solutions of logic programs, which is performed by answer set solvers. Deciding whether a disjunctive program has a stable model is a $\\Sigma^P_2$-complete problem. The high complexity of reasoning within disjunctive logic programming limits the number of solvers capable of handling such programs, including DLV, GnT, Cmodels, CLASP, and WASP. This paper demonstrates that transition systems, used to model and analyze satisfiability solvers, can be adapted for disjunctive answer set solvers. Transition systems provide a unified perspective and clarify solver descriptions and comparisons. They can be used for analyzing, comparing, and proving the correctness of search algorithms, as well as inspiring new ideas for designing disjunctive answer set solvers. This paper introduces a general template capturing major techniques implemented in disjunctive solvers and illustrates how it captures solvers DLV, GnT, and Cmodels. It also shows how this framework facilitates designing new solving algorithms by combining techniques from different solvers.

title: Where to look first? Behaviour control for fetch-and-carry missions of service robots
Abstract: This paper presents the behavior control of a service robot for intelligent object search in domestic environments. A key challenge in service robotics is enabling fetch-and-carry missions that are efficient and human-oriented. The proposed behavior controller provides informed intelligent search using a semantic segmentation framework for indoor scenes, integrating it with object recognition and grasping. Instead of manual annotation of search positions, the framework automatically suggests likely locations for an object based on contextual information, such as proximity to tables and shelves. Preliminary experiments demonstrate the controller's efficiency compared to manually annotated locations. This approach aims to reduce programming labor associated with fetch-and-carry tasks and enhance human-orientation in service robots.

title: Local Rademacher Complexity Bounds based on Covering Numbers
Abstract: This paper presents a general result on controlling local Rademacher complexities, providing an elegant way to relate complexities with expected norm constraints to those with empirical norm constraints. This result is easily applied to real applications and can yield refined local Rademacher complexity bounds for function classes satisfying general entropy conditions. The effectiveness of these complexity bounds is demonstrated by applying them to derive effective generalization error bounds.

title: Within-Brain Classification for Brain Tumor Segmentation
Abstract: This paper explores a framework for interactive brain tumor segmentation, treating the problem as a machine learning task. This approach avoids the need for intensity bias correction and MRI-specific noise handling, common issues with typical machine learning methods for this task. The proposed semi-automatic method segments brain tumors by training and generalizing within the same brain, based on minimal user interaction. The paper investigates how adding spatial feature coordinates ($i$, $j$, $k$) to intensity features significantly improves the performance of various classification methods, including SVM, kNN, and random forests. This improvement is only achievable within an interactive framework. The paper also explores the use of more appropriate kernels and hyperparameter adaptation for each brain. Experiments on the MICCAI-BRATS 2013 dataset show that the proposed interactive method achieves the second-highest accuracy among published methods, while requiring significantly less memory and processing power.

title: A Common-Factor Approach for Multivariate Data Cleaning with an Application to Mars Phoenix Mission Data
Abstract: Data quality is crucial for reliable decision-making by stakeholders. In real-world applications, such as scientific exploration of extreme environments, perfect data collection is unrealistic. When cleaning up data, it is often infeasible to determine the exact causes and mechanisms of data errors. This paper proposes a data-driven learning method, the common-factor data cleaning approach, to address this challenge. This method identifies the intrinsic structure of the signal to find common factors in multivariate data. By analyzing all signal measurements simultaneously, it identifies hidden common factors that drive all measurements to vary together, but not as a result of the true data measurements. These common factors are then used to reduce data variations without altering the base mean level, preserving the physical meaning of the data. This approach offers a novel solution for multivariate data cleaning when complex external impacts interfere with multiple data measurements.

title: 5G Ultra-Reliable Vehicular Communication
Abstract: Cooperative Intelligent Transport Systems (C-ITS) applications represent a significant step towards a safer and more efficient (green) road transport system, supporting a sustainable future. Wireless communication between vehicles and road infrastructure is crucial for high-performance C-ITS applications. State-of-the-art communication systems for supporting low-latency C-ITS applications rely on IEEE 802.11 medium access control (MAC) and physical (PHY) layers. This paper argues that a well-designed 5G system can complement or even replace these systems. The paper reviews C-ITS application requirements and demonstrates their alignment with the foreseen generic 5G service of ultra-reliable machine-type communication (uMTC). Key technology components suitable for constructing the uMTC service are identified: reliable service composition (RSC) and device-to-device (D2D) links for all-to-all broadcast communication, operating at high mobility and with varying degrees of network assistance. Important problems for future studies, including radio-resource management, medium access control, and physical layer challenges, are discussed.

title: Boosting in the presence of outliers: adaptive classification with non-convex loss functions
Abstract: This paper examines the role and efficiency of non-convex loss functions for binary classification problems, particularly focusing on designing a robust boosting algorithm resilient to data outliers. The analysis of a particular non-convex loss for prediction accuracy depends on the diminishing tail properties of the loss gradient (adaptability to outliers), local convex properties of the loss, and the proportion of contaminated data. To leverage these properties effectively, a new family of non-convex losses called $\\gamma$-robust losses is proposed. This paper introduces a new boosting framework, Arch Boost, designed to enhance existing approaches by making the corresponding classification algorithm more adaptable to unknown data contamination. Combined with the Arch Boosting framework, the non-convex losses lead to a new class of boosting algorithms called adaptive, robust, boosting (ARB). The paper presents theoretical examples demonstrating the robustness properties of these algorithms, including a new breakdown point analysis and influence function analysis. New theoretical results based on local curvatures establish statistical and optimization properties of the proposed Arch boosting algorithms with highly non-convex loss functions. Extensive numerical calculations illustrate these theoretical properties and highlight advantages over existing boosting methods when data contains outliers.

title: Cross-convolutional-layer Pooling for Image Recognition
Abstract: Recent studies have shown that a Deep Convolutional Neural Network (DCNN) pretrained on a large image dataset can serve as a universal image descriptor, leading to impressive performance in various image classification tasks. Most studies utilize activations from a single DCNN layer, typically the fully-connected layer, as the image representation. This paper proposes a novel approach for extracting image representations from two consecutive convolutional layers: one for local feature extraction and the other for guiding feature pooling. Two schemes are developed to implement this idea. The first directly utilizes convolutional layers from a DCNN. The second applies the pretrained CNN to densely sampled image regions, treating the fully-connected activations of each region as convolutional feature activations. A new convolutional layer is then trained on top of this as the pooling-guidance layer. Applying this method to three popular visual classification tasks shows that the first scheme tends to perform better when strong discrimination on subtle object patterns within small regions is required, while the second excels in cases requiring discrimination on category-level patterns. Overall, the proposed method outperforms existing approaches for extracting image representations from a DCNN.

title: Client Profiling for an Anti-Money Laundering System
Abstract: This paper presents a data mining approach for profiling bank clients to support the detection of anti-money laundering operations. It first outlines the overall system architecture and then focuses on a specific component. The paper details experiments conducted on real-world data from a financial institution, which enabled the grouping of clients into clusters and the generation of classification rules. The relevance of these client profiles and classification rules is discussed. These rules will be integrated into the knowledge base of intelligent agents responsible for flagging suspicious transactions within the defined agent-based architecture.

title: Approximate Fisher Kernels of non-iid Image Models for Image Categorization
Abstract: The bag-of-words (BoW) model treats images as sets of local descriptors and represents them using visual word histograms. The Fisher vector (FV) representation extends BoW by considering the first and second-order statistics of local descriptors. Both representations assume identically and independently distributed (iid) local descriptors, which is often unrealistic. Experimentally, the performance of BoW and FV representations can be improved using discounting transformations like power normalization. This paper introduces non-iid models by treating model parameters as latent variables that are integrated out, making all local regions dependent. Using the Fisher kernel principle, an image is encoded by the gradient of the data log-likelihood with respect to model hyperparameters. These models naturally generate discounting effects in the representations, suggesting the success of discounting transformations due to their resemblance to non-iid model representations. To enable tractable computation, variational free-energy bounds are used to learn hyperparameters and compute approximate Fisher kernels. Experimental results validate that these models lead to performance improvements comparable to using power normalization, as seen in state-of-the-art feature aggregation methods.

title: Intelligent Search Optimization using Artificial Fuzzy Logics
Abstract: The web contains vast amounts of information, making it challenging for users to find relevant content. Search engines index and categorize web pages based on their content using crawlers and rank them accordingly. For a given user query, they retrieve millions of webpages and display them according to page rank. Each search engine utilizes its own algorithms based on specific parameters for ranking webpages. Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is a technique used by webmasters to improve their website's ranking by optimizing it according to search engine ranking parameters. This research aims to identify the most popular SEO techniques used by search engines for ranking webpages and establish their importance for indexing and categorizing web data. The research aims to demonstrate that using more SEO parameters in ranking algorithms improves search results and user satisfaction. This research proposes a web-based Meta search engine that aggregates search results from different search engines and ranks webpages based on a new page ranking algorithm. This algorithm assigns heuristic page rank to webpages based on SEO parameters such as title tag, Meta description, sitemap, etc. It also provides insights into techniques that webmasters can use to improve their website's ranking in Google and Bing. Initial results indicate that using certain SEO parameters in the current ranking algorithm improves search result relevance for user queries. These results generated from the Meta search engine outperform existing search engines in terms of improved search results and higher precision. |||

title: Bayesian modeling of networks in complex business intelligence problems
Abstract: This research investigates the use of complex network data in strategic marketing.  The study focuses on customer choices of specific products and co-subscription networks, which reflect multiple purchasing behaviors.  A Bayesian hierarchical model is developed to cluster agencies based on common customer choices and co-subscription networks.  Within each cluster, a mixture of latent eigenmodels is used to efficiently model customer behavior.  This approach provides insights into customer choices and purchasing behavior, informing targeted cross-sell strategies.  The researchers develop simple algorithms for tractable inference and evaluate performance through simulations and a real-world application.

title: Online Vision- and Action-Based Object Classification Using Both Symbolic and Subsymbolic Knowledge Representations
Abstract: A novel system is presented for object recognition in robotic environments where a comprehensive object database is not available. The system analyzes features of encountered objects and compares them to known objects, allowing for the derivation of appropriate actions based on similarity. The system also enables the robot to learn object categories by grouping similar objects or splitting existing categories.  A hybrid representation, combining symbolic and subsymbolic elements, is used to represent knowledge.

title: Contribution to the Formal Specification and Verification of a Multi-Agent Robotic System
Abstract: The paper addresses the challenge of formally specifying and verifying multi-agent robotic systems to ensure safety and liveness properties.  The approach leverages formal verification methods based on model-checking, which are flexible and have a concrete syntax.  The system is constructed incrementally from subcomponents, based on software architecture, enabling formal verification during the specification definition phase.  The paper presents a case study of a multi-agent robotic system for stock transportation, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed development approach.

title: Exposing the Probabilistic Causal Structure of Discrimination
Abstract: This paper presents a principled causal approach to discrimination detection in databases.  Building upon Suppes' probabilistic causation theory, the method extracts causal structures from historical decision records, resulting in a constrained Bayesian network called a Suppes-Bayes Causal Network (SBCN).  The researchers develop a toolkit of methods based on random walks on the SBCN to address different anti-discrimination legal concepts, including direct and indirect discrimination, group and individual discrimination, genuine requirement, and favoritism.  Experiments on real-world datasets confirm the inferential power of the approach in these diverse tasks.

title: Implementing Efficient All Solutions SAT Solvers
Abstract: The paper provides a comprehensive survey and discussion of major techniques used in AllSAT solvers, a variant of the propositional satisfiability problem.  The researchers faithfully implement these techniques and conduct extensive experiments using a large number of instances and various types of solvers, including one of the few publicly available AllSAT solvers.  The experiments reveal characteristics of different solvers, and the implemented solvers are made publicly available for use by other researchers.

title: Multimodal Hierarchical Dirichlet Process-based Active Perception
Abstract: An active perception method for recognizing object categories based on the multimodal hierarchical Dirichlet process (MHDP) is proposed.  The MHDP allows a robot to form object categories using multimodal information, such as visual, auditory, and haptic data obtained through interactions with objects.  To optimize action selection in real-time scenarios, the paper proposes an MHDP-based active perception method that utilizes the information gain (IG) maximization criterion and a lazy greedy algorithm.  The IG maximization criterion is shown to be optimal in minimizing the expected Kullback--Leibler divergence between final and interim recognition states.  An efficient Monte Carlo approximation method for IG is derived, leveraging the properties of the MHDP.  The submodular and non-decreasing properties of IG as a set function are also demonstrated, reducing the IG maximization problem to a submodular maximization problem.  This allows the use of effective greedy and lazy greedy algorithms.  The paper presents experimental results using a humanoid robot and synthetic data, demonstrating the method's ability to quickly and accurately recognize target objects.

title: Proceedings of the ACE Challenge Workshop - a satellite event of IEEE-WASPAA (2015)
Abstract: The paper reviews established parameters and metrics used to characterize room acoustics, including the Direct-To-Reverberant Ratio (DRR), Reverberation Time (T60), and reflection coefficient. The paper focuses on the emerging area of blind acoustic parameter estimation directly from speech and audio signals, as traditional methods relying on measured Acoustic Impulse Responses (AIRs) are often impractical.  The paper highlights a challenge to evaluate state-of-the-art algorithms for blind acoustic parameter estimation from speech and promote research in this field. title: A Generative Model of Words and Relationships from Multiple Sources
Abstract: The paper proposes a generative model for learning semantic vector representations of words in highly specialized domains where training data is limited. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated by outperforming recent models on a link prediction task and by its ability to learn from partially or fully unobserved data. title: Transfer Learning from Deep Features for Remote Sensing and Poverty Mapping
Abstract: This paper tackles the challenge of extracting large-scale socioeconomic indicators from high-resolution satellite imagery, a critical need in developing countries where reliable data is scarce. title: Clamping Improves TRW and Mean Field Approximations

title: Supporting interoperability of collaborative networks through engineering of a service-based Mediation Information System (MISE 2.0)

title: Knowledge-based system for collaborative process specification
Abstract: This paper proposes an ontology-based approach for designing a collaborative business process model (CBP) as a specification of needs for building a collaboration information system (CIS) for a network of organizations. title: A Sentence Meaning Based Alignment Method for Parallel Text Corpora Preparation

title: Real-Time Statistical Speech Translation

title: Moving Object Detection in Video Using Saliency Map and Subspace Learning
Abstract: Moving object detection is a crucial component of intelligent video analysis. title: Multi-objective Differential Evolution with Helper Functions for Constrained Optimization
Abstract: This paper introduces a new multi-objective method for solving constrained optimization problems using evolutionary algorithms. title: Asynchronous Gibbs Sampling
Abstract: Asynchronous Gibbs sampling, a parallel version of Gibbs sampling (a Markov Chain Monte Carlo method often used in Bayesian learning), is investigated. title: Symbol Emergence in Robotics: A Survey
Abstract: The paper introduces a field of research called symbol emergence in robotics (SER), which focuses on understanding how humans learn language through physical interaction and semiotic communication. title: Two Phase $Q-$learning for Bidding-based Vehicle Sharing

title: On the Min-cost Traveling Salesman Problem with Drone
Abstract: This paper explores a variant of the traveling salesman problem (TSP) called TSP with drone (TSP-D), which arises in the context of last-mile delivery using unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). title: Reasoning in Infinitely Valued G-IALCQ
Abstract: Fuzzy Description Logics (FDLs) are formal systems based on logic that are used to represent and reason with vague or imprecise knowledge. Recent research has shown that reasoning in most FDLs, using truth values from the interval [0,1], becomes undecidable in the presence of negation and general concept inclusion axioms. An exception to this finding is FDLs whose semantics are based on the infinitely valued Gödel t-norm (G). This paper extends previous decidability results for G-IALC to include qualified number restrictions. title: Variational Information Maximisation for Intrinsically Motivated Reinforcement Learning

Many learning algorithms that involve optimizing mutual information rely on the Blahut-Arimoto algorithm, an enumerative algorithm with exponential complexity that is unsuitable for modern machine learning applications. This paper presents a new approach for scalable optimization of mutual information by merging techniques from variational inference and deep learning. Focusing on the problem of intrinsically-motivated learning, where mutual information defines the well-known internal drive called empowerment, we develop our approach by combining a variational lower bound on mutual information with convolutional networks for handling visual input streams. This leads to a stochastic optimization algorithm that enables scalable information maximization and empowerment-based reasoning directly from pixels to actions.

title: Towards Unveiling the Ontology Key Features Altering Reasoner Performances

Empirically, the specific aspects of an ontology that degrade reasoner performance are not well understood. This paper investigates the state-of-the-art research that attempted to correlate reasoner empirical behavior with specific ontological features. We analyze these works and categorize them, then propose a set of ontology features that cover a wide range of structural and syntactic characteristics. We argue that these features are good indicators of ontology hardness levels when performing reasoning tasks.

title: Tuned and GPU-accelerated parallel data mining from comparable corpora

This data is often scarce, especially for certain languages and specific text domains. In this research, we present improvements to the Yalign mining methodology by reimplementing the comparison algorithm, introducing tuning scripts, and enhancing performance through GPU computing acceleration. title: Learning dynamic Boltzmann machines with spike-timing dependent plasticity
Abstract: We propose a specifically structured Boltzmann machine, referred to as a dynamic Boltzmann machine (DyBM), as a stochastic model for multi-dimensional time-series. We demonstrate that the learning rule for updating DyBM parameters to maximize the likelihood of given time-series can be interpreted as STDP with long-term potentiation and long-term depression. The learning rule guarantees convergence and can be implemented in a distributed manner (local in space) with limited memory (local in time).

title: Boolean Matrix Factorization and Noisy Completion via Message Passing

title: Ensemble UCT Needs High Exploitation

title: An Innovative Approach for online Meta Search Engine Optimization

title: Theoretical Analysis of the Optimal Free Responses of Graph-Based SFA for the Design of Training Graphs

title: Thermodynamics and efficiency of an autonomous on-chip Maxwell's demon

This letter explores the thermodynamics of information using an experimentally feasible Maxwell's demon setup based on a single electron transistor capacitively coupled to a single electron box, where both the system and the demon can be clearly identified. Such an engineered on-chip demon measures and performs feedback on the system, which can be observed as cooling whose efficiency can be adjusted. We present a detailed analysis of the system and the demon, including the second law of thermodynamics for bare and coarse-grained entropy production, the flow of information, and the efficiency of information production and utilization. Our results demonstrate how information thermodynamics can be used to improve the functionality of modern nanoscale devices.

title: An intelligent extension of Variable Neighbourhood Search for labelling graph problems

title: Approximation and Heuristic Algorithms for Probabilistic Physical Search on General Graphs
Abstract: We consider an agent seeking to acquire an item potentially available at different locations in a physical environment. Given this scenario, the problem is to find a plan that maximizes the probability of acquiring the good while minimizing both travel and purchase costs. Sample applications include agents in search-and-rescue or exploration missions, such as a rover on Mars seeking to mine a specific mineral. These probabilistic physical search problems have been previously studied, but this paper presents the first approximation and heuristic algorithms for solving such problems on general graphs. We establish an interesting connection between these problems and classical graph-search problems, which led us to provide the approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation results for our settings. We further suggest several heuristics for practical use and demonstrate their effectiveness with simulations on real graph structures and synthetic graphs.

title: Optimal Release Time Decision from Fuzzy Mathematical Programming Perspective

title: Discovery and Visualization of Nonstationary Causal Models

Second, we present a way to determine some causal directions by taking advantage of information carried by changing distributions. title: Training Deep Networks with Structured Layers by Matrix Backpropagation
Abstract: Deep neural network architectures have recently achieved excellent results in various areas of artificial intelligence and visual recognition, significantly surpassing traditional shallow architectures trained using hand-designed features. The power of deep networks stems from their ability to perform local computations followed by pointwise non-linearities over increasingly larger receptive fields, as well as the simplicity and scalability of the gradient-descent training procedure based on backpropagation. An open problem is the inclusion of layers that perform global, structured matrix computations like segmentation (e.g., normalized cuts) or higher-order pooling (e.g., log-tangent space metrics defined over the manifold of symmetric positive definite matrices) while preserving the validity and efficiency of an end-to-end deep training framework. This paper proposes a sound mathematical apparatus to formally integrate global structured computation into deep computation architectures. At the heart of our methodology is the development of the theory and practice of backpropagation that generalizes to the calculus of adjoint matrix variations. The proposed matrix backpropagation methodology broadly applies to various problems in machine learning or computational perception. Here, we illustrate it by performing visual segmentation experiments using the BSDS and MSCOCO benchmarks, showing that deep networks relying on second-order pooling and normalized cuts layers, trained end-to-end using matrix backpropagation, outperform counterparts that do not leverage such global layers.

title: Deep Multimodal Embedding: Manipulating Novel Objects with Point-clouds, Language and Trajectories

To learn semantically meaningful spaces throughout our network, we use a loss-based margin to bring embeddings of relevant pairs closer together while driving less-relevant cases from different modalities further apart. We use this both to pre-train its lower layers and fine-tune our final embedding space, resulting in a more robust representation. We test our algorithm on the task of manipulating novel objects and appliances based on prior experience with other objects. title: Computational Intelligence Challenges and Applications on Large-Scale Astronomical Time Series Databases

The LSST will stream data at rates of 2 Terabytes per hour, effectively capturing an unprecedented movie of the sky. The LSST is expected not only to enhance our understanding of time-varying astrophysical objects but also to reveal a plethora of yet unknown faint and fast-varying phenomena. To adapt to this data-driven paradigm shift in astronomy, the fields of astroinformatics and astrostatistics have emerged recently. These new data-oriented paradigms for astronomy combine statistics, data mining, knowledge discovery, machine learning, and computational intelligence to provide automated and robust methods for the rapid detection and classification of known astrophysical objects, as well as the unsupervised characterization of novel phenomena. This article presents an overview of machine learning and computational intelligence applications to TDA. Future big data challenges and new lines of research in TDA, focusing on the LSST, are identified and discussed from the viewpoint of computational intelligence/machine learning. title: Linear-time Learning on Distributions with Approximate Kernel Embeddings
Abstract: Many machine learning problems are best addressed by considering inputs that are distributions or sample sets drawn from distributions. While effective for small datasets, this method becomes computationally prohibitive for large datasets due to the need for computing an N×N Gram matrix. Recent scalable estimators for PDFs have been limited to kernels using Euclidean metrics, such as the L2 distance. However, other useful metrics exist, such as total variation, Hellinger distance, and Jensen-Shannon divergence. This work introduces the first random features for PDFs that approximate kernels using these non-Euclidean metrics. By utilizing these random features, estimators based on these metrics can be scaled to large datasets by operating in a primal space without computing large Gram matrices. We analyze the approximation error introduced by our proposed random features and empirically demonstrate their effectiveness in both Gram matrix estimation and solving learning tasks on real-world and synthetic data.

title: Speech Dereverberation in the STFT Domain

This method constructs enhanced frames as a linear sum of nearby frames using knowledge of the channel impulse response. title: CRDT: Correlation Ratio Based Decision Tree Model for Healthcare Data Mining
Abstract: The rapid growth of healthcare data motivates the development of robust and scalable models for data mining. However, IG-based decision trees may not perform well in all cases, as they favor attributes with a higher number of distinct values. Healthcare datasets often have many attributes with numerous distinct values. To address this, we propose a variant of the decision tree model that utilizes Correlation Ratio (CR) as the splitting criterion. Unlike IG-based approaches, CR-based approaches are unbiased towards attributes with a higher number of distinct values. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed technique by applying it to benchmark healthcare datasets.

title: Exploration and Exploitation of Victorian Science in Darwin's Reading Notebooks
Abstract: Navigating environments with uncertain resource distribution involves a trade-off between exploiting past discoveries and exploring new possibilities. This principle extends to information foraging, where knowledge seekers balance in-depth reading with exploring new domains. We investigate this decision-making process by analyzing the reading choices of Charles Darwin, one of the most celebrated scientists of the modern era. We utilize topic models generated from the full-text of books listed in his chronologically organized reading journals to quantify his local (text-to-text) and global (text-to-past) reading decisions using Kullback-Liebler Divergence, a cognitively validated, information-theoretic measure of relative surprise. Rather than simply minimizing surprise, corresponding to pure exploitation, Darwin's behavior shifts from early exploitation to later exploration, seeking unusually high levels of cognitive surprise relative to previous eras. These shifts, detected by an unsupervised Bayesian model, correlate with major intellectual epochs in his career, as identified both by qualitative scholarship and Darwin's self-commentary. Our methods allow us to compare his reading patterns with the order of book publication. We find Darwin's reading to be more exploratory than the cultural production, suggesting that individual exploration and discovery drive deeper changes than gradual societal shifts. Our quantitative methods advance the study of cognitive search by providing a framework for examining interactions between individual and collective behavior and short- and long-term consumption choices. This novel application of topic modeling to characterize individual reading complements existing research on collective scientific behavior.

title: Quantification of sand fraction from seismic attributes using Neuro-Fuzzy approach

While seismic data aids in extrapolating reservoir properties away from boreholes, delineating thin sand and shale reservoirs remains difficult due to its limited resolvability. Therefore, developing advanced intelligent methods for calibrating a nonlinear mapping between seismic data and target reservoir variables is crucial. Neural networks have demonstrated potential in modeling these nonlinear mappings; however, uncertainties associated with the model and datasets remain a concern. To address these uncertainties, we integrate Fuzzy Logic (FL) into the model. Specifically, NF methods, hybrid variants of Artificial Neural Network (ANN) and fuzzy logic, are capable of modeling reservoir characteristics by combining the explicit knowledge representation power of FL with the learning ability of neural networks. The results obtained in this study demonstrate acceptable agreement between target and predicted variables, encouraging the use of integrated machine learning approaches like Neuro-Fuzzy for reservoir characterization. title: Boolean Hedonic Games
Abstract: We investigate hedonic games with dichotomous preferences. Hedonic games are cooperative games where players aim to form coalitions based solely on the composition of the coalitions they are members of, indifferent to the composition of other coalitions. The assumption of dichotomous preferences further specifies that each player's preference relation partitions the set of coalitions they can join into two equivalence classes: satisfactory and unsatisfactory. Players are indifferent between satisfactory coalitions and between unsatisfactory coalitions, but strictly prefer any satisfactory coalition over any unsatisfactory one. We develop a succinct representation for such games using propositional formulas to represent each player's preference relation. We show how solution concepts for hedonic games with dichotomous preferences can be characterized using propositional formulas.

title: Interception in Distance-Vector Routing Networks
Abstract: Despite substantial efforts in cybersecurity research over the past decades, cyber intrusions and attacks continue to rise. title: Triggered star formation in giant HI supershells: ionized gas
Abstract: We investigated star formation triggered within kiloparsec-sized HI supershells in three dwarf galaxies: IC 1613, IC 2574, and Holmberg II. The morphology and kinematics of ionized and neutral gas were analyzed using data from the SAO RAS 6-meter telescope's scanning Fabry-Perot interferometer and 21 cm archival data from the THINGS and LITTLE THINGS surveys. Our qualitative analysis aimed to address two key questions: why star formation occurred in specific locations within the supershells, and how ongoing star formation at the rims of the HI supershells influences their evolution. Notably, we discovered a previously unobserved phenomenon in IC 2574 and Holmberg II – faint giant (kiloparsec-sized) ionized shells in H-alpha and [SII]6717,6731 lines within the supergiant HI shells.

title: Weakly compactly generated Banach lattices
Abstract: We explore different ways in which a weakly compact set can generate a Banach lattice. We demonstrate that in an order continuous Banach lattice X, the existence of a weakly compact set K within X, where X coincides with the band generated by K, implies that X is weakly compactly generated.

title: Thirty eight things to do with live slime mould

This paper provides a concise overview of computing and sensing operations implemented using live slime mold. Physarum devices range from morphological processors for computational geometry to experimental archeology tools, self-routing wires to memristors, shortest-path approximation devices to analog physical models of space exploration.

title: A characterization of A_5 by its Same-order type
Abstract: Let G be a group. Define an equivalence relation 's' as follows: for any two elements g and h in G, g is related to h if and only if the order of g equals the order of h. The set of sizes of equivalence classes under this relation is termed the same-order type of G. Shen et al. (Monatsh. Math. 160 (2010), 337-341) proved that A5 is the only group with same-order type {1, 15, 20, 24}. This paper demonstrates, among other findings, that a nonabelian simple group G has same-order type {r, m, n, k} if and only if G is isomorphic to A5.

title: Towards Approaches to Continuous Assessment of Cyber Risk in Security of Computer Networks
Abstract: This review delves into the current state and research challenges in cybersecurity, specifically focusing on continuous monitoring and risk scoring (CMRS). We highlight two key aspects of CMRS: continuous data collection through automated feeds and analysis of collected data for risk assessment. The continuous monitoring process involves gathering information like network traffic and host data from host-based agents. Risk scoring entails assessing vulnerabilities and exposures, as well as computing metrics that characterize the overall network risk level. Current risk metrics often rely on simple sums or counts of vulnerabilities and missing patches. CMRS research challenges fall into two main categories: integrating and fusing highly heterogeneous information and the lack of rigorous approaches to risk computation. Existing risk scoring algorithms often employ ad hoc heuristics, such as simple sums of vulnerability scores or counts of missing patches or open ports. The weaknesses and potentially misleading nature of such metrics are well recognized. For example, individual vulnerability scores are heavily dependent on subjective, human, qualitative input, which can be inaccurate and costly to obtain. Additionally, the total number of vulnerabilities may be less important than their distribution across hosts or over time. Similarly, network topology and the dynamics of inter-host interactions are often ignored by simple sums of vulnerabilities or missing patches.

title: Unveiling Contextual Similarity of Things via Mining Human-Thing Interactions in the Internet of Things
Abstract: Recent advancements in radio-frequency identification (RFID), wireless sensor networks, and Web services have led to the emergence of the ubiquitous Web, where physical things become integral components. Finding correlations among these ubiquitous things is crucial for various applications such as thing search, discovery, classification, recommendation, and composition. This article introduces DisCor-T, a novel graph-based method for discovering underlying connections between things by mining rich content embodied in human-thing interactions, considering user, temporal, and spatial information. Two graphs, namely spatio-temporal graph and social graph, are used to model this diverse information. Random walk with restart (RWR) is then applied to calculate proximities among things, enabling the learning of a relational graph of things (RGT) that indicates implicit correlations. This correlation analysis provides a robust foundation for improving effectiveness in things management. To demonstrate its utility, a flexible feature-based classification framework is developed on top of RGT, and a systematic case study is conducted. Evaluation results highlight the strength and feasibility of the proposed approach.

title: Blind Deconvolution Meets Blind Demixing: Algorithms and Performance Bounds
Abstract: Imagine a scenario where 'r' sensors aim to transmit functions (signals or images) to a common receiver. During transmission, each function is convolved with a specific function. The receiver records the sum of all these convolved signals. This paper investigates the recovery of individual signals and blurring functions from a single received signal. This challenging problem, combining blind deconvolution with blind demixing, arises in various applications like audio processing, image processing, neuroscience, spectroscopy, and astronomy. It is also expected to play a pivotal role in the future Internet of Things. We demonstrate that under reasonable and practical assumptions, this ill-posed problem can be solved efficiently and reliably, recovering the transmitted functions and impulse responses from a single received signal using a semidefinite program. Explicit bounds on the number of measurements required for successful recovery are derived, and the method's robustness to noise is proven. Interestingly, numerical experiments show that recovery is still possible even when the number of measurements is close to the number of degrees of freedom.

title: Heuristic algorithms for finding distribution reducts in probabilistic rough set model
Abstract: Attribute reduction is a cornerstone of rough set theory. Heuristic attribute reduction algorithms have been developed to address the attribute reduction problem, with fitness functions playing a crucial role in their design. The monotonicity of fitness functions ensures the validity of these algorithms. In probabilistic rough set models, distribution reducts guarantee that decision rules derived from the reducts are compatible with those obtained from the original decision table. However, limited research focuses on developing heuristic attribute reduction algorithms for finding distribution reducts. This is partly due to the lack of monotonic fitness functions suitable for designing such algorithms in the probabilistic rough set model. This paper aims to develop heuristic attribute reduction algorithms for finding distribution reducts in probabilistic rough set models. It introduces two monotonic fitness functions from which equivalence definitions of distribution reducts can be derived. Additionally, two modified monotonic fitness functions are proposed to evaluate attribute significance more effectively. Based on these, two heuristic attribute reduction algorithms are developed for finding distribution reducts, using addition-deletion and deletion methods. The monotonicity of fitness functions ensures the rationality of the proposed heuristic algorithms. Experimental analysis results quantify the effectiveness of the proposed fitness functions and distribution reducts.

title: Closed Systems of Invertible Maps
Abstract: This paper generalizes clones, which are sets of functions mapping from A^n to A, to sets of mappings from A^n to A^m. This generalization is formalized, and a specialized language is developed to discuss it. We then investigate bijective mappings, which are connected to reversible computation, a concept crucial for both physical (e.g., quantum computation) and engineering (e.g., heat dissipation) applications. This paper generalizes Toffoli's seminal work on reversible computation to arbitrary arity logics. Notably, it demonstrates that certain restrictions he found for reversible computation on alphabets of order 2 do not apply to odd order alphabets. For odd A, we can create all invertible mappings using the Toffoli 1- and 2-gates, showing that all reversible mappings can be realized from four generators. This work explores various forms of closure, corresponding to different systems of allowed manipulations. These correspond to discussions about ancilla bits in quantum computation, among other things.

title: Mobile Cloud Business Process Management System for the Internet of Things: A Survey

However, traditional BPMS have not adequately addressed challenges posed by managing large-scale interconnected heterogeneous IoT entities. Without a complete understanding of the behavior, capabilities, and state of IoT entities, BPMS may struggle to manage IoT-integrated information systems. This paper analyzes existing BPMS for IoT, identifies limitations and drawbacks from a Mobile Cloud Computing perspective, and discusses open challenges in BPMS for IoT.

title: Up in the Air: When Homes Meet the Web of Things

title: Sparsity of the Hawking flux
Abstract: It is widely known that the Hawking flux reaching spatial infinity is extremely sparse and thin, with Hawking quanta slowly escaping the black hole one by one. The typical time between quanta reaching infinity is much longer than the timescale set by the quanta's energy. This implies that the Hawking evaporation of a black hole should be viewed as a sequential cascade of 2-body decays.

title: Smart Data Pricing Models for Internet-of-Things (IoT): A Bundling Strategy Approach

Moreover, a bundling strategy is adopted, allowing multiple providers to form coalitions and bid their services as a bundle, attracting more users and generating higher revenue. title: Horn Linear Logic and Minsky Machines
Abstract: This paper provides a detailed proof for a crucial aspect of Minsky machine simulation: any linear logic derivation for a specific Horn sequent can be transformed into a Minsky computation, transitioning from an initial configuration to the halting configuration. The paper utilizes a 3-step program, distributing non-trivial aspects across independent parts, each justified using its own intrinsic methodology. The three steps are: 1) From LL to HLL – using purely proof-theoretic arguments. 2) From HLL to Horn programs – translating trees (HLL derivations) into trees (Horn programs) of the same shape, almost. 3) From Horn programs to Minsky computations – utilizing purely computational arguments.

title: An Elementary, First Principles Approach to the Indefinite Spin Groups
Abstract: This work presents an elementary derivation of the indefinite spin groups in low dimensions. The last point is particularly crucial, revealing a surprisingly ubiquitous role for an alternative to the standard representation of the symplectic form in dimension four. Our approach has the advantage of identifying these spin groups as explicit groups of matrices within the same collection of matrices that define Cl(p, q). In other words, we do not work in the algebra of matrices to which the collection of even vectors in Cl(p, q) is isomorphic. This is crucial in some applications and also offers the benefit of being didactically simple.

title: An Energy Consumption Model for IEEE 802.11ah WLANs

title: Ramsey-type theorems for lines in 3-space
Abstract: This study explores geometric Ramsey-type statements on collections of lines in 3-space, guaranteeing the existence of large cliques or independent sets within (hyper)graphs induced by incidence relations between lines, points, and reguli. Key findings include: (1) The intersection graph of n lines in R^3 contains a clique or independent set of size Omega(n^{1/3}). (2) Any set of n lines in R^3 possesses a subset of n^{1/2} lines all stabbed by a single line, or a subset of Omega((n/log n)^{1/5}) lines where no 6-subset is stabbed by a single line. (3) Every set of n lines in general position in R^3 has a subset of Omega(n^{2/3}) lines lying on a regulus, or a subset of Omega(n^{1/3}) lines with no 4-subset contained in a regulus. The proofs leverage geometric incidence bounds, such as the Guth-Katz bound, combined with Turán-type results on sparse graph and hypergraph independent sets. The obtained lower bounds surpass those achievable through existing algebraic frameworks. These proofs directly yield polynomial-time algorithms for finding the claimed sized subsets.

title: Predicting proximity with ambient mobile sensors for non-invasive health diagnostics

These interactions alter the patterns of ambient signals, creating distinctive characteristics that can be learned to predict body proximity. Our prediction technique achieves 88.75% accuracy and 88.3% specificity.

title: Measuring Neutron Star Radii via Pulse Profile Modeling with NICER
Abstract: The Neutron-star Interior Composition Explorer (NICER) mission, set to be deployed on the International Space Station, aims to precisely measure the pulse profiles emitted by rotation-powered pulsars. These profiles, generated by non-uniform thermal surface emission, can be analyzed to determine neutron star radii and constrain their equation of state. Accurate knowledge of source, sky, and instrument backgrounds is crucial for this endeavor. This paper employs simple analytical estimates to quantify the required background accuracy for meaningful constraints on neutron star properties. Even in a minimal information scenario, background knowledge at a few percent level with a background-to-source countrate ratio of 0.2 enables a measurement of the neutron star compactness to within 10% uncertainty across most of the parameter space. These constraints further improve when more realistic assumptions are made regarding neutron star emission and spin, and when additional source information, such as mass or distance, is incorporated.

title: Driven neutron star collapse: Type~I critical phenomena and the initial black hole mass distribution
Abstract: This study investigates the general relativistic collapse of neutron star (NS) models in spherical symmetry. Initially stable NS models are driven to collapse by introducing either an in-going velocity profile or a shell of minimally coupled, massless scalar field falling onto the star. These models utilize Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff (TOV) solutions with an initially isentropic, gamma-law equation of state. Extensive parameter space surveys encompassing the amplitude of the velocity profile and the star's central density reveal a rich spectrum of possible NS collapse end states. The survey delineates the boundary between Type I and Type II critical behavior in perfect fluids, coinciding on the subcritical side with the boundary between dispersed and bound end states. For the specific model employed, initial velocity amplitudes exceeding 0.3c are required to probe the regime where arbitrarily small black holes can form. Additionally, Type I behavior is examined by varying the initial amplitude of the imploding scalar field. The Type I critical solutions resemble TOV solutions on the 1-mode unstable branch of equilibrium solutions, with critical solution frequencies closely matching the fundamental mode frequencies of the unstable equilibria. The critical solution's scaling exponent is shown to be well approximated by a linear function of the initial star's central density.

title: Black Hole Singularity, Generalized (Holographic) $c$-Theorem and Entanglement Negativity
Abstract: This paper explores the interpretation of empty $AdS_{5}$ black brane geometry as an RG-flow. A holographic $c$-function is constructed using the causal horizon in the black brane geometry. The UV value of the $c$-function is $a_{UV}$, which then decreases monotonically to zero at the curvature singularity. This behavior can be understood intuitively by recognizing that the dual CFT is in a thermal state, effectively massive with a gap determined by the temperature. In field theory, logarithmic entanglement negativity is a suitable entanglement measure for mixed states. Notably, in two-dimensional CFTs on an infinite line at finite temperature, the renormalized entanglement negativity of an interval exhibits a UV (low-T) value of $c_{UV}$ and an IR (high-T) value of zero, making it a potential candidate for the $c$-function. While the same behavior is expected in four dimensions based on physical grounds, the causal horizon residing behind the black brane horizon renders the holographic $c$-function sensitive to the physics of the interior. Correspondingly, the field theory $c$-function should also encode information about the interior. These results suggest that the high-temperature (IR) expansion of negativity (or any candidate $c$-function) could serve as a method to probe aspects of the physics near the singularity. Negativity at finite temperature depends on the full operator content of the theory, potentially limiting its applicability to specific cases. The existence of this $c$-function in the bulk serves as an extreme example of the paradigm that spacetime is built from entanglement. The fact that the $c$-function vanishes at the curvature singularity establishes a correlation between the loss of quantum entanglement in the IR field theory and the termination of geometry in the bulk, which in this case is the formation of the curvature singularity.

title: Evaluation of Energy-Efficient Heuristics for ACO-based Routing in Mobile Wireless Sensor Networks
Abstract: Mobile ad-hoc networks necessitate routing algorithms capable of adapting to constantly changing network topologies. The rise of the Internet of Things (IoT) further introduces challenges for mobile networks, demanding algorithms that comply with low-power consumption, small size, and low-cost constraints. ADHOP (Ant-based Dynamic Hop Optimization Protocol), a routing algorithm based on ant-colony optimization, addresses these requirements by minimizing memory and processing power usage. This paper investigates the integration of energy-related heuristics into ADHOP to guide routing decisions, aiming to minimize network usage without compromising functionality. The original ADHOP heuristic based on network latency is replaced by two energy-aware heuristics based on battery charge and estimated node lifetime. Simulations comparing energy-aware ADHOP variants to the original version, AODV, and AOER demonstrate their ability to balance network load among nodes, leading to fewer battery depletion failures. Energy-aware ADHOP variants also exhibit improved packet delivery, outperforming the original ADHOP by delivering twice as many packets, and surpassing AOER and AODV by delivering five and nine times more packets, respectively.

title: Unification of Force and Substance
Abstract: Maxwell's mature presentation of his equations emphasized the unity of electromagnetism and mechanics, encompassing both within the framework of "dynamical systems". A significant aspect of Maxwell's work lies in its utilization of redundant potentials and the associated requirement of gauge symmetry. This paper delves into two key aspects: the physical significance of gauge invariance, in broad terms, and the tantalizing prospects for further unification built upon this concept, currently emerging on the horizon. Should these prospects materialize, Maxwell's vision of the unity of field and substance would reach a new level of realization.

title: The Impact of Molecular Gas on Mass Models of Nearby Galaxies
Abstract: This study presents CO velocity fields and rotation curves for a sample of nearby galaxies, utilizing data from the HERACLES survey. The data is combined with literature results from THINGS, SINGS, and KINGFISH to form a comprehensive sample of mass models for disk galaxies incorporating molecular gas. The kinematics of molecular (CO from HERACLES) and atomic (${\\rm H{\\scriptstyle\nI}}$ from THINGS) gas distributions are compared to assess the suitability of CO for probing galaxy dynamics in their inner regions. Generally, good agreement is observed between CO and ${\\rm H{\\scriptstyle I}}$ kinematics, with minor discrepancies in the inner regions of some galaxies. The contribution of molecular gas to the mass models is incorporated using two different conversion factors $\\mathrm{\\alpha_{CO}}$ to convert CO luminosity to molecular gas mass surface density: the constant Milky Way value and radially varying profiles determined in recent studies based on THINGS, HERACLES, and KINGFISH data. The relative impact of molecular gas on the halo rotation curves for Navarro-Frenk-White (NFW) and observationally motivated pseudo-isothermal halos is analyzed. The contribution of molecular gas varies significantly across the galaxy sample. Galaxies with substantial molecular gas content exhibit substantial differences in the relative contribution of molecular gas based on the choice of $\\mathrm{\\alpha_{CO}}$, leading to variations in the shape of the dark matter halo rotation curves in the central regions of these galaxies.

title: On the arithmetic of abelian varieties
Abstract: This paper presents novel findings on the arithmetic of abelian varieties over function fields of one variable over finitely generated (infinite) fields. It introduces new objects, "discrete Selmer groups" and "discrete Shafarevich-Tate groups", and proves that they are finitely generated $\\Bbb Z$-modules. Additionally, it is demonstrated that in the isotrivial case, the discrete Shafarevich-Tate group vanishes and the discrete Selmer group coincides with the Mordell-Weil group. A key component of these proofs is a new specialization theorem à la Néron for first Galois cohomology groups of the ($l$-adic) Tate module of abelian varieties. This theorem generalizes Néron's specialization theorem for rational points of abelian varieties.

title: Bayesian Social Influence in the Online Realm
Abstract: Our preferences and opinions are heavily influenced by the opinions of those around us. In today's world, we are often swayed by the opinions of online strangers expressed in comments and ratings on various platforms. This study conducts novel "academic A/B testing" experiments involving over 2,500 participants to quantify this influence. Participants watch and evaluate videos on mirror proxies of YouTube and Vimeo, with controlled comments and ratings displayed beneath each video. The study reveals that between 5% and 40% of subjects adopt the majority opinion of strangers expressed in the comments. Utilizing Bayes' theorem, a flexible and interpretable family of social influence models is derived, where each individual forms posterior opinions stochastically based on a logit model. The variants of the mixture model maximizing Akaike information criterion represent two sub-populations: non-influenceable and influenceable individuals. The prior opinions of non-influenceable individuals strongly correlate with external opinions and have low standard error, while influenceable individuals have high standard error in their prior opinions, which become correlated with external opinions due to social influence. These findings suggest that opinions are random variables updated through Bayes' rule, with standard deviation correlated with opinion influenceability. Based on these findings, strategies for hindering opinion manipulation and misinformation diffusion in the online realm are discussed.

title: The XMM Newton spectra of the 2012 outburst of the black-hole candidate 4U 1630-47 revisited
Abstract: Recent XMM-Newton observations of the black hole candidate 4U 1630-47 during its 2012 outburst revealed three relativistically Doppler-shifted emission lines, interpreted as originating from baryonic matter in the jet of this source. The proposed model allows for non-solar abundance of S and Fe in the interstellar material along the line of sight to the source. This significantly impacts the emission predicted by the model around 7.1 keV, where the edge of neutral Fe appears, rendering the lines unnecessary. Fits to all 2012 XMM-Newton observations of this source require a moderately broad emission line around 7 keV, along with several absorption lines and edges due to highly ionized Fe and Ni, indicating the presence of a highly ionized absorber near the source. The model also successfully fits the observations where the lines were detected when using the latest calibration files, unlike the model with the three Doppler-shifted emission lines.

title: On Constructing Secure and Hardware-Efficient Invertible Mappings
Abstract: Our society is becoming increasingly reliant on wireless communications. The rapid growth in the number and variety of wirelessly connected devices coupled with the decreasing cost of cyberattacks presents new challenges for securing services and applications provided by next-generation wireless communication networks. The situation is further complicated by the limited resources available on many end-point Internet of Things (IoT) devices for implementing security functionality. This paper tackles one aspect of this multifaceted problem - the design of hardware-efficient cryptographic primitives suitable for protecting resource-constrained IoT devices. The focus lies on cryptographic primitives based on invertible mappings of type $\\{0,1,\\ldots,2^n-1\\} \\rightarrow \\{0,1,\\ldots,2^n-1\\}$. Traditionally, verifying the invertibility of a given mapping requires an exponential number of steps in $n$. This paper derives a sufficient condition for invertibility that can be checked in $O(n^2 N)$ time, where $N$ is the size of the representation of the largest function in the mapping. These findings can be used to construct cryptographically secure invertible mappings efficiently implemented in hardware.

title: Relaxion Monodromy and the Weak Gravity Conjecture
Abstract: The recently proposed relaxion models require extremely large trans-Planckian axion excursions and a potential explicitly violating the axion shift symmetry. This latter property, however, conflicts with the axion periodicity, which corresponds to a gauged discrete shift symmetry. Monodromy, where both the axion and potential parameters transform under the discrete shift symmetry, offers a solution to this inconsistency. The structure is better described in terms of a 3-form field $C_{\\mu \\nu \\rho}$ coupling to the SM Higgs through its field strength $F_4$. The 4-form also couples linearly to the relaxion in the Kaloper-Sorbo fashion. The extremely small relaxion-Higgs coupling arises in a see-saw fashion as $g\\simeq F_4/f$, with $f$ being the axion decay constant. This paper discusses constraints on this type of construction arising from membrane nucleation and the Weak Gravity Conjecture. The latter necessitates the existence of membranes, whose excessively fast nucleation could potentially destabilize the theory unless the cut-off scale is lowered. This allows for the constraint of relaxion models on purely theoretical grounds. Possible avenues to embed this structure into string theory are also discussed.

title: Implementation of the Spherical Coordinate Representation of Protein 3D Structures and its Applications Using FORTRAN 77/90 Language
Abstract: This paper builds upon previous work describing the representation of protein 3D structures in spherical coordinates (rho, phi, theta) and its applications: separation of the outer layer (OL) from the inner core (IC) of proteins and assessment of protein surface protrusions and invaginations. The paper presents results demonstrating the performance of the FORTRAN 77 and 90 programs used to implement these applications, and provides instructions for implementing both applications. title: Herschel Spectroscopic Observations of LITTLE THINGS Dwarf Galaxies
Abstract: We present far-infrared spectral line observations of five galaxies from the LITTLE THINGS sample: DDO 69, DDO 70, DDO 75, DDO 155, and WLM. While most dwarf galaxy studies focus on bright systems or starbursts due to observational constraints, our data expand the observed parameter space into the regime of low surface brightness dwarf galaxies with low metallicities and moderate star formation rates. Our targets were observed with Herschel at the [CII] 158um, [OI] 63um, [OIII] 88um, and NII 122um emission lines using the PACS Spectrometer. These high-resolution maps allow us to study the far-infrared properties of these systems on the scales of larger star-forming complexes for the first time. The spatial resolution in our maps, combined with star formation tracers, allows us to identify separate photodissociation regions (PDRs) in some of the observed regions. Our systems exhibit widespread [CII] emission that is bright relative to continuum, averaging near 0.5% of the total infrared budget, higher than in solar-metallicity galaxies of other types. [NII] is weak, suggesting that the [CII] emission in our galaxies originates mostly from PDRs instead of the diffuse ionized interstellar medium (ISM). These systems exhibit efficient cooling at low dust temperatures, as shown by ([OI]+[CII])/TIR in relation to 60um/100um, and low [OI]/[CII] ratios indicating that [CII] is the dominant coolant of the ISM. We observe [OIII]/[CII] ratios in our galaxies that are lower than those published for other dwarfs, but similar to levels noted in spirals.

title: The Impact of Dual Prediction Schemes on the Reduction of the Number of Transmissions in Sensor Networks
Abstract: Future Internet of Things (IoT) applications will require billions of wireless devices to transmit data to the cloud frequently. However, wireless medium access is a bottleneck for next-generation wireless networks. The number of data transmissions in Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) can quickly become a bottleneck, hindering the exponential growth in interconnected devices, sensors, and data production. Therefore, minimizing data transmissions is crucial for incorporating new sensor nodes and measuring a diverse range of parameters in future generations of WSNs. Dual Prediction Schemes (DPSs), utilizing high-accuracy and low-complexity forecasting algorithms, are potential candidates for optimizing data transmissions in WSNs at the finest level. DPSs enable sensor nodes to avoid unnecessary transmissions without compromising measurement quality. This work presents a sensor network model employing statistical theorems to describe the expected impact of DPSs and data aggregation in WSNs. We aim to provide a foundation for future research by characterizing the theoretical gains of processing data in sensors and conditioning transmission based on prediction accuracy. Our simulation results demonstrate that the number of transmissions can be reduced by almost 98% in sensor nodes with the highest workload. We also detail the impact of predicting and aggregating transmissions based on parameters observed in common scenarios, such as sensor node transmission ranges, correlation between measurements from different sensors, and the period between consecutive measurements in a sensor.

title: Adaptive Broadcast Suppression for Trickle-Based Protocols
Abstract: Low-power wireless networks play a crucial role in the Internet of Things, typically consisting of a large number of lossy and low-capacity devices, posing challenges for protocol design. In this context, the Trickle algorithm is essential, serving as the basic message dissemination mechanism in protocols such as RPL and MPL. While Trickle's broadcast suppression mechanism has been proven efficient, recent work has shown its inherent unfairness in terms of load distribution and its strong dependence on network topology. This can lead to increased end-to-end delays (MPL) or the creation of sub-optimal routes (RPL). Moreover, there is no clear consensus within the research community about the proper parameter settings for the suppression mechanism. We propose an extension to the Trickle algorithm, called adaptive-k, which allows nodes to individually adapt their suppression mechanism to local node density. Supported by analysis and a case study with RPL, we demonstrate that this extension simplifies the configuration of Trickle, making it more robust to network topology.

title: Some properties of generalized and approximately dual frames in Hilbert spaces
Abstract: This paper investigates sufficient and necessary conditions for two frames, Phi=(varphi_n)_n and Psi=(psi_n)_n, to be approximately or generalized dual frames, based on the properties of their analysis and synthesis operators. We also provide a new characterization for approximately dual frames associated with a given frame and operator using bounded operators. Notably, we prove that if two frames Phi=(varphi_n)_n and Psi=(psi_n)_n are close to each other, we can find approximately dual frames Phi^{ad}=(varphi^{ad}_n)_n and Psi^{ad}=(psi^{ad}_n)_n that are also close to each other and satisfy T_Phi U_{Phi^{ad}}=T_Psi U_{Psi^{ad}}, where T_Phi and T_Psi (resp. U_{Phi^{ad}} and U_{Psi^{ad}}) are the analysis operators (resp. synthesis operators) of the frames Phi and Psi (resp. Phi^{ad} and Psi^{ad}). We then explore consequences for generalized dual frames. Finally, we apply these results to construct approximately dual frames for a given Gabor frame.

title: Measure preserving actions of affine semigroups and {x+y,xy} patterns
Abstract: Ergodic and combinatorial results obtained in [10] involved measure-preserving actions of the affine group {mathcal A}_K of a countable field K. This paper develops a new approach based on ultrafilter limits, refining and extending the results from [10] to a more general situation involving measure-preserving actions of non-amenable affine semigroups of a large class of integral domains. (The results in [10] heavily depend on the amenability of the affine group of a field). Notably, we obtain the following result as a corollary of an ultrafilter ergodic theorem: Let K be a number field and let {mathcal O}_K be the ring of integers of K. For any finite partition K=C_1cupcdotscup C_r, there exists iin{1,dots,r} and many xinK and yin{mathcal O}_K such that {x+y,xy}subset C_i.

title: Unsupervised Online Bayesian Autonomic Happy Internet-of-Things Management
Abstract: In Happy IoT, service provider revenue is synchronized with the unobservable and dynamic usage-contexts (e.g., emotion, environmental information) of Smart-device users. Estimating usage-context from unreliable Smart-device sensed data is justified as an unsupervised and non-linear optimization problem. Autonomic Happy IoT Management aims to attract initial user groups based on common interests (i.e., recruitment), then uncover their latent usage-contexts from unreliable sensed data (i.e., revenue-renewal) and synchronize with usage-context dynamics (i.e., stochastic monetization). In this context, we propose an unsupervised online Bayesian mechanism called Whiz (Greek word meaning "Smart"), where: (a) latent user groups are initialized (i.e., measurement model), (b) usage-context is iteratively estimated from unreliable sensed data (i.e., learning model), and (c) online filtering of Bayesian knowledge about usage-context is performed (i.e., filtering model). We propose an Expectation Maximization (EM)-based iterative algorithm, Whiz, which facilitates Happy IoT by solving (a) recruitment, (b) revenue-renewal, and (c) stochastic-monetization problems with (a) measurement, (b) learning, and (c) filtering models, respectively. |||

title: Examples of non-constructive proofs in quantum theory
Abstract: Unlike mathematics, where truth is abstract, physics emphasizes algorithmic procedures for obtaining verifiable numerical results.  Physical science is essentially a set of algorithmic procedures, grounded in mathematical formalism, for deriving verifiable conclusions from basic hypotheses.  A physical theory loses its concrete applicability and verifiability when it admits non-constructivist statements.  Therefore, constructivism is essential for any physical theory.  However, some physical theories, especially quantum mechanics, contain non-constructive statements.  This paper examines two examples of such statements, focusing on macroscopic quantum states and the applicability of the standard quantum formalism to macroscopic systems.  The proofs of existence for these macroscopic quantum states rely on logical principles that allow one to determine the truth of predicates over an infinite number of things.

title: The Missing Mass Problem as a Manifestation of GR Contextuality
Abstract: In Newtonian gravity, mass is an intrinsic property, but in general relativity (GR), mass is contextual.  This means that matter can have two different mass values when it's responsible for two different spacetime geometries.  This paper explores the possibility that the missing mass attributed to non-baryonic dark matter (DM) in astrophysics actually arises from our assumption of the Newtonian view of mass, rather than the GR view.  Since exact GR solutions for realistic astrophysical situations are infeasible, the paper explores GR-motivated ansatzes relating proper mass and dynamic mass for the same baryonic matter, as justified by GR contextuality.  Four GR alternatives are considered, and the results show that the GR ansatz motivated by metric perturbation theory accurately fits galactic rotation curves (THINGS data), the mass profiles of X-ray clusters (ROSAT and ASCA data), and the angular power spectrum of the cosmic microwave background (CMB, Planck 2015 data), without requiring DM.  Comparisons are made to modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND), Burkett halo DM, and Navarro-Frenk-White (NFW) halo DM for galactic rotation curves, metric skew-tensor gravity (MSTG) and core-modified NFW DM for X-ray cluster mass profiles, and scalar-tensor-vector gravity (STVG) and ΛCDM for CMB angular power spectrum.  The fits are comparable to those of MOND, MSTG, STVG, ΛCDM, Burkett, and NFW.  Correlations and trends are presented and discussed for the best-fit parameter values, which are mostly consistent with well-established results across all scales.

Second, it analyzes Diophantus' solutions to these problems through a modern lens, revealing how they correspond to parametrizations of these surfaces or parametrizations of rational curves lying on them.

title: A City Is a Complex Network
Abstract: A city is not a simple tree structure but a complex network, resembling a semi-lattice. This complex network perspective offers a unique topological view of cities, enhancing our understanding of their inherent challenges. This topological perspective distinguishes itself from Euclidean geometry and Gaussian statistics, which focus on regular shapes and similar elements. Many urban theories, such as Central Place Theory, Zipf's Law, the Image of the City, and the Theory of Centers, can be interpreted through the lens of complex networks. A livable city is characterized by a preponderance of small elements over large ones, with irregular and rough shapes. This chapter advocates for embracing the complex network perspective and moving away from the Euclidean and Gaussian frameworks, instead adopting fractal geometry, power-law statistics, and Alexander's living geometry for the development of sustainable cities.
