It delves into new prime power divisibility results, presents novel methods for deriving the period, establishes new identities, and explores derivations involving powers of matrices generated by these general recurrences.

title: Are Compton-Thick AGN the Missing Link Between Mergers and Black Hole Growth?
Abstract: This study investigates the host morphologies of heavily obscured active galactic nuclei (AGN) at z~1 to determine whether obscured supermassive black hole growth at this epoch is preferentially linked to galaxy mergers.  The sample consists of 154 obscured AGN with N<sub>H</sub>>10<sup>23.5</sup> cm<sup>-2</sup> and z<1.5.  Visual classifications are used to compare the morphologies of these AGN to control samples of moderately obscured (10<sup>22</sup> cm<sup>-2</sup><N<sub>H</sub><10<sup>23.5</sup> cm<sup>-2</sup>) and unobscured (N<sub>H</sub><10<sup>22</sup> cm<sup>-2</sup>) AGN, matched in redshift and intrinsic X-ray luminosity.  The results show that heavily obscured AGN at z~1 are twice as likely to be hosted by late-type galaxies compared to unobscured AGN (65.3<sup>+4.1</sup><sub>-4.6</sub>% vs 34.5<sup>+2.9</sup><sub>-2.7</sub>%) and three times as likely to exhibit merger or interaction signatures (21.5<sup>+4.2</sup><sub>-3.3</sub>% vs 7.8<sup>+1.9</sup><sub>-1.3</sub>%), with a significant increase in merger fraction at the 3.8σ level.  The incidence of point-like morphologies is inversely proportional to obscuration.  Even when excluding point sources and considering only extended hosts, a correlation between merger fraction and obscuration persists, albeit with reduced statistical significance (2.5σ).  The differing disk/spheroid fraction versus obscuration suggests that viewing angle alone cannot explain the differences between the three AGN samples, challenging the simple unification model.  The increased fraction of disturbed morphologies with obscuration supports an evolutionary scenario where Compton-thick AGN represent a distinct phase of obscured SMBH growth following a merger/interaction event.  These findings indicate that some of the merger-triggered SMBH growth predicted by recent AGN fueling models might be hidden within the heavily obscured, Compton-thick population.

title: ptp++: A Precision Time Protocol Simulation Model for OMNeT++ / INET
Abstract: Precise time synchronization is crucial for emerging distributed and real-time applications like the smart grid and Internet of Things (IoT).  The Precision Time Protocol (PTP) is considered a leading synchronization solution over packet-switched networks, supporting microsecond synchronization accuracy.  This paper introduces a PTP simulation model for OMNeT++ INET, enabling the investigation of synchronization accuracy under varying network configurations and conditions.  To illustrate the model's capabilities, the paper examines the impact of network load fluctuations on PTP performance by simulating a network with class-based quality-of-service (QoS) support.  Simulation results demonstrate that network load significantly affects network delay symmetry, leading to the proposal of a new technique called class probing to enhance PTP accuracy and mitigate the effects of load fluctuations.

This report outlines the motivation for integrating uIP into the NSC, the chosen approach, and potential use cases for simulating uIP in OMNeT++.

title: Federating OMNeT++ Simulations with Testbed Environments
Abstract: This paper presents the development of a system architecture for opportunistic and information-centric communications, called Keetchi, designed for the Internet of Things (IoT).  The architecture aims to empower applications to perform distributed and decentralized communications among smart devices.  A three-step evaluation approach is employed.  The first step involves creating a testbed with smart devices (primarily smartphones and tablets) equipped with this architecture and applications.  The second step evaluates the architecture in large-scale scenarios using the OMNeT++ simulation environment.  The third step utilizes traces of data collected from experiments on the testbed to feed the OMNeT++ simulation environment.  To implement these environments, the functionality of the architecture is developed as a common code base capable of operating within the OMNeT++ environment as well as on the testbed's smart devices (e.g., Android, iOS, Contiki).  This paper details the "Write once, compile anywhere" (WOCA) code base architecture of Keetchi.

title: On Capacity Formulation with Stationary Inputs and Application to a Bit-Patterned Media Recording Channel Model
Abstract: This correspondence highlights the use of the stationarity property of capacity-achieving inputs in capacity calculations.  Specifically, a bit-patterned media recording channel model is used as a case study to formulate new lower and upper bounds on its capacity, surpassing existing results.  Inspired by the tightness of the new bounds at low noise levels, the paper also characterizes the capacity of this model as a series expansion in the low-noise regime.  The key to these findings lies in the realization of stationarity in the supremizing input set within the capacity formula.  While this property is common in capacity formulations within the ergodic-theoretic literature, the paper demonstrates its applicability in the Shannon-theoretic framework where a channel is defined as a sequence of finite-dimensional conditional probabilities, by defining a new class of consistent stationary and ergodic channels.

title: A classical postselected weak amplification scheme via thermal light cross-Kerr effect
Abstract: Common sense suggests that postselected weak amplification is related to destructive interference in the meter system, and that a single photon has no impact on a thermal field via cross-phasemodulation (XPM) interaction.  This letter presents, for the first time, a thermal light cross-Kerr effect.  Through analysis, two unexpected results are revealed: 1) postselection and weak amplification can be explained classically without destructive interference, and 2) weak amplification and weak value are not synonymous.  Postselection leads to the generation of a new mixed light that exhibits nonclassical properties.  This scheme can be realized through electromagnetically-induced transparency.

title: Two-Dimensional Oxide Topological Insulator With Iron-Pnictide Superconductor LiFeAs Structure
Abstract: First-principles calculations suggest that ZrSiO can be considered a three-dimensional (3D) oxide weak topological insulator (TI) and its single layer represents a long-sought-after 2D oxide TI with a band gap of up to 30 meV.  The calculated phonon spectrum of the single layer ZrSiO indicates its dynamic stability.  The experimental achievements in growing oxides with atomic precision ensure its feasibility for synthesis.  This discovery has the potential to lead to novel "topotronic" devices based on TIs, operating at room temperature and stable in air.  This could usher in a new era of "topotronics."  Interestingly, this oxide 2D TI shares a similar crystal structure with the well-known iron-pnictide superconductor LiFeAs.  This offers exciting possibilities for combining superconductivity and TIs, paving the way for extraordinary quantum phenomena like topological superconductors and Majorana modes.  Furthermore, the paper identifies many other isostructural compounds exhibiting a similar electronic structure, forming a WHM-family where W represents Zr, Hf, or La, H represents a group IV or V element, and M represents a group VI element.

title: Decomposition of Brownian loop-soup clusters
Abstract: This paper investigates the structure of Brownian loop-soup clusters in two dimensions.  Among other findings, it provides a decomposition of clusters with critical intensity: When a loop-soup cluster is conditioned by its outer boundary γ (known to be an SLE(4)-type loop), the union of all excursions away from γ by all Brownian loops in the loop-soup touching γ is distributed exactly like the union of all excursions of a Poisson point process of Brownian excursions within the domain enclosed by γ.  A related result, utilized in this analysis, states that the couplings of the Gaussian Free Field (GFF) with CLE(4) via level-lines (by Miller-Sheffield), of the square of the GFF with loop-soups via occupation times (by Le Jan), and of the CLE(4) with loop-soups via loop-soup clusters (by Sheffield and Werner) can be made to coincide.  Lupu's description of CLE(4) as limits of discrete loop-soup clusters plays a crucial role in proving this fact.

title: Persistence of a Non-Equilibrium State: Observation of a Boltzmannian Special Case
Abstract: Long before the atomistic nature of matter was experimentally confirmed, Ludwig Boltzmann's bold attempt to explain the macroscopic world in terms of microscopic processes faced significant opposition. One point of contention was the problem of irreversibility: while the microscopic equations of motion are reversible, friction and viscosity cause things to slow down and heat up, never the reverse.  Worse, Boltzmann himself discovered that his transport equation predicts special cases where gases never reach thermal equilibrium, such as the monopole "breathe" mode of a gas confined in 3D to a perfectly isotropic harmonic potential, which would never damp.  This nondamping was not observed in nature.  Only recently has nondamping of a monopole mode in lower dimensional systems been observed using cold atoms.  Kinoshita et al. and Chevy et al. experimentally observed suppressed relaxation in highly elongated geometries.  However, the difficulty in creating sufficiently spherical harmonic confinement for ultracold atoms meant that Boltzmann's fully 3D, isotropic case remained unobserved.  With the development of a new magnetic trap capable of producing near-spherical harmonic confinement, this paper presents the first observation of this historically significant oddity.  A monopole mode was observed where the collisional contribution to damping vanishes, providing long-delayed vindication for Boltzmann's microscopic theory.

title: Backreaction for Einstein-Rosen waves coupled to a massless scalar field
Abstract: This paper presents a one-parameter family of exact solutions to Einstein equations, offering a valuable tool for studying the nature of the Green-Wald backreaction framework. The explicit example is a family of Einstein-Rosen waves coupled to a massless scalar field, which can also be interpreted as a generalized three-torus polarized Gowdy cosmology with scalar and gravitational waves. This solution serves to illustrate key properties of the Green-Wald approach. Notably, the paper shows that within this model, the Green-Wald framework uniquely determines backreaction for finite-size inhomogeneities on a predefined background. These results align with those calculated using the Charach-Malin approach. In the vacuum limit, the Green-Wald, Charach-Malin, and Isaacson methods yield identical backreaction, as expected.

title: Supernovae as cosmological probes
Abstract: The current cosmological standard model is widely accepted as containing significant unknowns, particularly the puzzling appearance of a Cosmological Constant or dark energy. Today, a much larger dataset of supernovae is available.  This paper performs a rigorous statistical analysis of this dataset, considering the calibration of supernovae as standard candles, which introduces some analytical subtleties.  Surprisingly, this new dataset, an order of magnitude larger than the original, reveals only mild evidence of an accelerated universe under standard assumptions.

title: Anomaly Detection for malware identification using Hardware Performance Counters
Abstract: Computers are ubiquitous today, but internet-based applications like e-commerce and e-banking attract criminals who use sophisticated techniques to introduce malware onto victim computers.  This risk extends beyond computer users to encompass smartphones, smartwatches, smart cities, Internet of Things devices, and more.  Various techniques have been tested against malware, with pattern matching being the default approach in antivirus software.  Machine learning has also proven effective.  Building on this trend, this article proposes an anomaly-based method that leverages hardware performance counters (HPC) found in most modern computer architectures.  Because anomaly detection is an unsupervised process, it can detect new malware and Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) even if they are unknown.

title: Graphulo: Linear Algebra Graph Kernels for NoSQL Databases
Abstract: The era of big data and the Internet of Things poses continuous challenges for computational systems.  To address this, technology solutions like NoSQL databases have emerged.  Analysts often rely on graph representations to generate meaningful insights from large datasets, offering an intuitive approach.  Graph vertices represent users and events, while edges represent relationships between them.  Graph algorithms extract valuable information from these massive graphs.  The Graphulo initiative at MIT aims to perform graph algorithms directly within NoSQL databases like Apache Accumulo or SciDB, which feature inherently sparse data storage schemes.  Sparse matrix operations have a history of efficient implementations, and the Graph Basic Linear Algebra Subprogram (GraphBLAS) community has developed key kernels for efficient linear algebra operations.  However, utilizing GraphBLAS kernels requires recasting common graph algorithms using linear algebra building blocks.  This article examines common classes of graph algorithms and reinterprets them as linear algebra operations using GraphBLAS building blocks.

title: Using Thought-Provoking Children's Questions to Drive Artificial Intelligence Research
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel method for driving artificial intelligence research and evaluating general-purpose AI systems: thought-provoking children's questions (TPCQs), specifically Highlights BrainPlay questions.  These questions are designed to stimulate thinking and learning in children and can be used to achieve the same in AI systems, demonstrating their reasoning capabilities.  The paper introduces the TPCQ task, which takes a TPCQ question as input and outputs 1) answers to the question and 2) learned generalizations.  The paper discusses how BrainPlay questions facilitate learning and analyzes 244 BrainPlay questions, providing statistics on question type, class, answer cardinality, class, required knowledge, and reasoning needed.  The results reveal that BrainPlay questions encompass a wide range of intelligence aspects.  Due to the often open-ended nature of answers and generalizations, human judges are recommended for evaluation. |||

title: Topologically protected acoustic helical edge states and interface states in strongly coupled metamaterial ring lattices
Abstract: Time-reversal (T) invariant topological insulators are a fundamental discovery in condensed matter physics, known for their spin-based topological protection, which effectively eliminates scattering of conduction electrons with specific spins on the material's surface.  This concept has extended the realm of topological insulators beyond electronics to encompass photonics, phononics, and mechanics, unveiling new physics and potential applications in robust wave transport. While there has been growing interest in realizing topologically protected acoustic wave transport, a T-invariant acoustic topological insulator has remained elusive.  This research reports the first experimental demonstration of an acoustic topological insulator: a strongly coupled metamaterial ring lattice that facilitates one-way propagation of helical edge states under T-symmetry, rendering backscattering immune to abrupt boundary variations. The unique characteristic lies in the formation of spin-filtered interface states due to lattice dislocations. The mechanism underlying the formation of topologically protected edge states and interface states is applicable to various other wave systems and higher dimensions.

title: Deconstructing Bataknese Gorga Computationally
Abstract: The intricate carved and painted decorations, known as "gorga," found in traditional Batak houses and buildings, are the source of their exotic charm. Each house boasts unique ornamentation patterns, closely linked to the ancient Batak's depiction of the dynamic "tree of life," a central element in their cosmology and mythology.  A survey of Batak house and building ornaments in Northern Sumatra, Indonesia, revealed a complex pattern.  The fractal dimensions of the geometric shapes in "gorga" were calculated, suggesting a range of 1.5-1.6, falling between the dimensions of a line and a plane. The drawing method employed in "gorga" is captured through a modified L-System model, a popular model for simulating the growth of plants.  The results suggest that Bataknese "gorga" represents a traditional heritage with the potential to enrich studies of generative art.

title: $L^p$-norms and Mahler's measure of polynomials on the $n$-dimensional torus
Abstract: This research proves Nikol'skii type inequalities for polynomials on the n-dimensional torus, $\\mathbb{T}^n$, which relate the $L^p$-norm to the $L^q$-norm (with respect to normalized Lebesgue measure and 0 < p < q < $\\infty$).  Notable findings include demonstrating that $C=\\sqrt{q/p}$ is the optimal constant for the inequality $\\|P\\|_{L^q}\\leq C^{\\text{deg}(P)} \\|P\\|_{L^p}$ for all homogeneous polynomials P on $\\mathbb{T}^n$.  Additionally, the research establishes an exact inequality between the $L^p$-norm of a polynomial P on $\\mathbb{T}^n$ and its Mahler measure M(P), which represents the geometric mean of |P| with respect to the normalized Lebesgue measure on $\\mathbb{T}^n$.  Extrapolation techniques are employed to transform this estimate into a Khintchine-Kahane type inequality, which, for polynomials on $\\mathbb{T}^n$, relates a specific exponential Orlicz norm to Mahler's measure. The research includes applications, including interpolation estimates.

Abstract: The advancement of information technology, particularly in computer networks, has facilitated faster and more complex information exchange, resulting in diverse data transmission. Data security in network communication is a critical concern. While Secure Socket Layer (SSL) offers a solution, further research on the security of SSL protocol transactions is essential to determine the extent to which SSL can secure data on the network. When computers transmit data over the network, it is divided into packets. Sniffing is a technique for monitoring each packet traversing the network. The security threat posed by sniffers lies in their ability to capture all incoming and outgoing packets, including sensitive information like passwords, usernames, and other confidential data. Packet sniffers capture data intended for other devices, storing it for later analysis.  Sniffing can also be utilized by system administrators to monitor the network and troubleshoot problems.

title: Snow Leopard Permutations and Their Even and Odd Threads
Abstract: Caffrey, Egge, Michel, Rubin, and Ver Steegh recently introduced snow leopard permutations, defined as anti-Baxter permutations compatible with doubly alternating Baxter permutations. They demonstrated, among other findings, that these permutations preserve parity, and the number of snow leopard permutations of length $2n-1$ corresponds to the Catalan number $C_n$. This research delves into the permutations induced by snow leopard permutations on their even and odd entries, referred to as even threads and odd threads, respectively.  Recursive bijections are established between these permutations and certain families of Catalan paths. The research characterizes the odd (resp. even) threads that form the other half of a snow leopard permutation whose even (resp. odd) thread is layered in terms of pattern avoidance.  A constructive bijection is provided between the set of permutations of length $n$ that are both even threads and odd threads and the set of peakless Motzkin paths of length $n+1$.

title: Fractal percolation, porosity, and dimension
Abstract: This research investigates the porosity properties of fractal percolation sets $E\\subset\\mathbb{R}^d$.  Among other findings, for all $0<\\varepsilon<\\tfrac12$, dimension bounds are obtained for the set of exceptional points where the upper porosity of E is less than $\\tfrac12-\\varepsilon$, or the lower porosity is larger than $\\varepsilon$.  The methodology extends to inhomogeneous fractal percolation and more general random sets whose offspring distribution aligns with a Galton-Watson process.

title: Thou shalt not take sides: Cognition, Logic and the need for changing how we believe
Abstract: We tend to support ideas and consider them valid while dismissing doubts, taking sides on ideas and theories as if it were the correct approach.  However, from a rational perspective, this type of support and belief lacks justification.  Given our current understanding, the best we can hope for when describing the real world is probabilistic knowledge, assigning probabilities to each statement.  Even achieving this reliably can be challenging.  Furthermore, when we defend ideas and believe in them as if they were true, cognitive psychology experiments reveal that our ability to analyze the question we believe in is compromised. This research compiles evidence regarding taking sides and presents the obvious but overlooked conclusion: these combined facts necessitate that we should never truly believe in anything about the real world, except in a probabilistic manner. We must never take sides because doing so hinders our ability to seek the most accurate description of the world. This implies a need to reformulate the way we debate ideas, from our teaching to our political discussions, if we truly desire to reach the best solutions based on available evidence. This research demonstrates that this approach has profound implications for numerous problems, ranging from the rise of extremism to the reliability of entire scientific fields. Inductive reasoning demands that we allow every idea to generate predictions so that we can rank them based on their effectiveness, a principle with significant consequences in scientific practice. The crisis surrounding p-values is also analyzed and better understood in light of the findings presented in this research. Finally, the paper explores potential solutions to mitigate the problem.

title: The SP theory of intelligence: distinctive features and advantages
Abstract: This research highlights the distinctive features of the "SP theory of intelligence" and its potential advantages compared to AI-related alternatives.  The distinctive features and advantages include simplification and integration of observations and concepts; simplification and integration of structures and processes in computing systems; the theory itself being a theory of computing; the potential to serve as a foundation for new computer architectures; information compression through pattern matching and unification, particularly via multiple alignment; transparency in the representation and processing of knowledge; the discovery of 'natural' structures through information compression (DONSVIC); interpretations of mathematics; interpretations in human perception and cognition; and the realization of abstract concepts in terms of neurons and their interconnections ("SP-neural"). These elements relate to AI-related alternatives such as minimum length encoding and related concepts; deep learning in neural networks; unified theories of cognition and related research; universal search; Bayesian networks and more; pattern recognition and vision; the analysis, production, and translation of natural language; unsupervised learning of natural language; exact and inexact forms of reasoning; representation and processing of diverse forms of knowledge; IBM's Watson; software engineering; solving problems associated with big data; and the development of intelligence in autonomous robots. In conclusion, the SP system offers a robust foundation for the long-term development of AI, with numerous potential benefits and applications. It may also yield valuable results on relatively short timescales. A highly parallel, open-source version of the SP machine, derived from the SP computer model, would provide researchers worldwide with a platform to explore the system's capabilities and develop new versions.

title: Autonomic Resilient Internet-of-Things(IoT)Management
Abstract: In Resilient IoT, the revenue of service providers is resilient to unpredictable usage contexts (e.g., emotion, environmental conditions) of smart device users.  Therefore, the Autonomic Resilient IoT Management problem is decomposed into two subproblems: m-connectivity and k-dominance.  The goal is to ensure that m-alternations in the revenue-generating process are resilient to common user interests, which can be represented through k-1 alternations of usage contexts.  In this context, a greedy approximation scheme called Bee is proposed, which addresses the aforementioned subproblems through five consecutive models: Maverick, Siren, Pigmy, Arkeo, and Augeas, respectively. Theoretical analysis confirms that the problem is NP-hard, a combinatorial optimization problem that lends itself to greedy approximation.  Furthermore, Bee establishes the theoretical foundation of Resilient Fact-finding, supported by theoretical and experimental (synthetic) evidence demonstrating how Bee-resilience resolves acute CDS measurement problems.  Experiments conducted on real social rumor datasets extract dominator and dominate elements, validating how Bee resilience enhances CDS measurement. Finally, a case study and prototype development are performed on Android and Web platforms in a Resilient IoT scenario, where service providers recommend personalized services to smart device users.

title: Nonparametric Distributed Learning Architecture for Big Data: Algorithm and Applications
Abstract: The escalating size and complexity of modern datasets have rendered traditional "centralized" statistical inference impractical.  Beyond the computational challenges associated with big data learning, the presence of numerous data types (e.g., discrete, continuous, categorical, etc.) makes automation and scalability difficult.  A pressing concern is how to design a data-intensive statistical inference architecture without compromising the fundamental statistical modeling principles developed for "small" data over the past century. To address this challenge, this research presents MetaLP, a flexible, distributed statistical modeling framework.
label: AI

title: Wireless Coverage Area Computation and Optimization
Abstract: Wireless network design necessitates the optimization of coverage areas for wireless transmitters, including mobile and base stations in cellular networks, wireless access points in WLANs, or nodes on a transmit schedule in a wireless ad-hoc network. Traditionally, coverage optimization for common channels is achieved through spatial multiplexing, keeping access networks physically separated. However, with increasing densities of wireless network deployments (including the Internet of Things), spectrum scarcity, and new developments like whitespace devices and self-organizing, cognitive networks, there is a need for algorithms that efficiently manage interference and optimize coverage by setting transmit powers appropriately to ensure that transmissions only consume the necessary power.  This research examines methods for computing and optimizing interference-limited coverage maps for a set of transmitters. The research progressively analyzes increasingly realistic network scenarios.  Initially, a disk model with a fixed set of transmitters is considered, presenting an optimal algorithm for computing the coverage map.  The model is then enhanced to incorporate network updates, such as adding or deleting a transmitter.  In this dynamic setting, an optimal algorithm is presented for maintaining updates to the coverage map.  The research then transitions to a more realistic interference model – the SINR model. For the SINR model, geometric bases for coverage maps are established.  The research then introduces a method for approximating the measure of the coverage area.  Finally, an algorithm is presented that utilizes this measure to optimize the coverage area while minimizing total transmit power.

title: Flats in spaces with convex geodesic bicombings
Abstract: In spaces with non-positive curvature, the existence of isometrically embedded flat (hyper)planes is often guaranteed by seemingly weaker conditions on large scales. This research demonstrates that some such results hold true for metric spaces with non-unique geodesic segments, under suitable convexity assumptions on the distance function along distinguished geodesics.  The discussion encompasses, among other aspects, the Flat Torus Theorem and Gromov's hyperbolicity criterion, which pertain to embedded planes.  This generalizes results established by Bowditch for Busemann spaces.

title: Type-Constrained Representation Learning in Knowledge Graphs
Abstract: Large knowledge graphs are increasingly valuable for various applications requiring machines to recognize and understand queries and their semantics, such as in search or question answering systems. Latent variable models have gained significant attention for statistical knowledge graph modeling, demonstrating promising results in tasks related to knowledge graph completion and cleaning. Besides storing facts about the world, schema-based knowledge graphs are supported by rich semantic descriptions of entities and relation types, enabling machines to understand the concept of things and their semantic relationships.  This research investigates how type constraints can enhance statistical modeling with latent variable models.  Specifically, the study integrates prior knowledge in the form of type constraints into various state-of-the-art latent variable approaches.  Experimental results demonstrate that prior knowledge on relation types significantly improves these models, achieving up to 77% improvement in link-prediction tasks.  The observed improvements are particularly prominent when a low model complexity is enforced, a critical requirement when applying these models to very large datasets.  Unfortunately, type constraints are not always available or complete; for instance, they can become ambiguous when entities lack proper typing.  The research shows that in such cases, applying a local closed-world assumption that approximates the semantics of relation types based on data observations can be beneficial.

title: Multi-Comm-Core Architecture for Terabit/s Wireless
Abstract: Wireless communications, alongside the Internet, have been the most transformative technologies of the past 50 years.  Anticipated wireless data growth driven by new mobile applications, the need to connect all of humanity (not just 1/3), and the integration of billions of things into the internet necessitate Terabit/s shared links for ground-based local area and wide area wireless access, wireless backhaul, as well as access via unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and satellites. This research presents a novel scalable radio architecture referred to as multi-comm-core (MCC) to enable low-cost ultra-high speed wireless communications utilizing both traditional and millimeter wave spectrum.
label: AI

title: Allocation of Heterogeneous Resources of an IoT Device to Flexible Services
Abstract: Internet of Things (IoT) devices can be equipped with multiple heterogeneous network interfaces.  A vast number of services may require some or all of these interfaces' available resources. This research presents a precise mathematical formulation for assigning services to interfaces with heterogeneous resources in one or more rounds. For reasonable instance sizes, the presented formulation produces optimal solutions for this computationally challenging problem.  The research proves the NP-Completeness of the problem and develops two algorithms to approximate the optimal solution for large instance sizes.  The first algorithm prioritizes allocating the most demanding service requirements first, considering the average cost of interface resources.  The second algorithm calculates the demanding resource shares and prioritizes allocating the most demanding of them first, selecting randomly among equally demanding shares.  Finally, simulation results provide insights into service splitting across different interfaces for both cases.
label: AI

title: Modeling mutual feedback between users and recommender systems
Abstract: Recommender systems exert a significant influence on our online decision-making processes daily. While considerable attention has been given to aspects like recommendation accuracy and user privacy, the long-term mutual feedback between a recommender system and the decisions of its users has largely been overlooked. This research proposes a model of network evolution that allows for the study of the complex dynamics induced by this feedback, including the hysteresis effect, a phenomenon typical of systems with non-linear dynamics.  Despite the common belief that recommendation helps users discover new things, the research finds that prolonged use of recommendation can contribute to the rise of extremely popular items, ultimately narrowing user choice. These findings are supported by measurements of the time evolution of item popularity inequality in real systems.  The research demonstrates that this adverse effect of recommendation can be mitigated by sacrificing some short-term recommendation accuracy.

title: Partial clones containing all Boolean monotone self-dual partial functions
Abstract: The study of partial clones on $\\mathbf{2}:=\\{0,1\\}$ was initiated by R. V. Freivald.  In his fundamental 1966 paper, Freivald showed, among other things, that the set of all monotone partial functions and the set of all self-dual partial functions are both maximal partial clones on $\\mathbf{2}$.  Several subsequent papers have explored intersections of maximal partial clones on $\\mathbf{2}$.  It is known that there are infinitely many partial clones that contain the set of all monotone self-dual partial functions on $\\mathbf{2}$, and the challenge of describing all of them was posed by some authors.  This research demonstrates that the set of partial clones containing all monotone self-dual partial functions has a cardinality of continuum on $\\mathbf{2}$.

title: On the characters of the Sylow p-subgroups of untwisted Chevalley groups Y_n(p^a)
Abstract: Let $UY_n(q)$ be a Sylow p-subgroup of an untwisted Chevalley group $Y_n(q)$ of rank n defined over $\\mathbb{F}_q$, where q is a power of a prime p.  This research partitions the set $Irr(UY_n(q))$ of irreducible characters of $UY_n(q)$ into families indexed by antichains of positive roots of the root system of type $Y_n$.  The focus is on the families of characters of $UY_n(q)$ indexed by antichains of length 1.  For each positive root $\\alpha$, a one-to-one correspondence is established between the minimal degree members of the family indexed by $\\alpha$ and the linear characters of a specific subquotient $\\overline{T}_\\alpha$ of $UY_n(q)$.  For $Y_n = A_n$, the single-root character construction recovers, among other things, the elementary supercharacters of these groups.  Most importantly, this research lays the groundwork for classifying the elements of $Irr(UE_i(q))$, $6 \\le i \\le 8$, and $Irr(UF_4(q))$.

title: A Visual Embedding for the Unsupervised Extraction of Abstract Semantics
Abstract: Vector-space word representations derived from neural network models have demonstrated the capability of enabling semantic operations based on vector arithmetic. This research investigates the existence of similar information in vector representations of images.  A methodology for obtaining large, sparse vector representations of image classes is defined, and vectors are generated using the state-of-the-art deep learning architecture GoogLeNet for 20K images obtained from ImageNet.  The research first evaluates the resultant vector-space semantics through its correlation with WordNet distances, finding a strong correlation between vector distances and linguistic semantics.  The research then explores the location of images within the vector space, observing that elements close in WordNet are clustered together, regardless of significant visual variations (e.g., 118 dog types).  More surprisingly, the space unsupervisedly separates complex classes without prior knowledge (e.g., living things). Subsequently, the research considers vector arithmetic.  While meaningful results are not obtained in this regard, the research discusses the encountered challenges and potential solutions.  Finally, the impact of the research on cognitive systems is discussed, emphasizing the role of the architecture being used.

title: A System Architecture for Software-Defined Industrial Internet of Things
Abstract: Wireless sensor networks have been a driving force behind the advancement of the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) in process control and manufacturing.  The emergence of IIoT opens up significant potential for ubiquitous field device connectivity and manageability through an integrated and standardized architecture, encompassing low-level device operations to high-level data-centric application interactions. This technological development necessitates software definability in key IIoT architectural elements, including wireless field devices, IIoT gateways, network infrastructure, and IIoT sensor cloud services. This research proposes a novel software-defined IIoT (SD-IIoT) to address critical challenges in a holistic IIoT system, such as reliability, security, timeliness scalability, and quality of service (QoS). A new IIoT system architecture is proposed based on the latest networking technologies, including WirelessHART, WebSocket, IETF constrained application protocol (CoAP), and software-defined networking (SDN). A new scheme based on CoAP and SDN is proposed to address QoS issues.  Computer experiments in a case study are implemented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed system architecture. |||

title: Zero and negative energy dissipation at information-theoretic erasure
Abstract: Information erasure based on Shannon's binary channel formula is introduced. This erasure is a natural, energy-dissipation-free way information is lost in double-potential-well memories, potentially explaining the brain's effortless forgetting. A novel charge-based memory scheme is presented where erasure can be associated with negative energy dissipation, implying cooling during information erasure and contradicting Landauer's principle. However, writing new information into the memory requires positive energy dissipation. Lastly, a simple system is demonstrated where even classical erasure processes yield negative energy dissipation of arbitrarily large energy.
label: AI

title: Towards a Decoupled Context-Oriented Programming Language for the Internet of Things
Abstract: Programmability poses a significant challenge for large-scale, reconfigurable deployments in the Internet of Things. These devices often require externalizing aspects of their behavior, such as sensing, data aggregation, or code offloading. Current context-oriented programming languages typically integrate the entire behavior within a single class or closely layered structures. We propose abstracting and separating context tracking from the decision process, connecting them using event-based handlers. This approach maintains a simple, declarative, and non-layered programming model. We illustrate our proposal by defining an extension to Golo, a JVM-based dynamic language.
label: AI

title: The likelihood principle does not entail a `sure thing', `evil demon' or `determinist' hypothesis
Abstract: The likelihood principle, which makes strong claims about the nature of statistical evidence, is controversial due to its implications regarding the deterministic hypothesis. This hypothesis posits that whatever occurred was inevitable, potentially dominating all other hypotheses with unity probability. While this issue is often considered a significant obstacle to the likelihood principle, we re-analyze Birnbaum's 1969 "counter-example" to demonstrate that standard analyses of such examples involve improper treatment of nuisance parameters. When these parameters are adequately considered, no conflict arises between the evidential consequences of the likelihood principle and intuitive evidential accounts. Furthermore, the conclusion that the likelihood principle allows the deterministic hypothesis to dominate with unity probability stems from a misconception about its scope or inappropriately specified statistical models. Ultimately, whatever happened did not have to happen.
label: AI

title: The resolution bias: low resolution feedback simulations are better at destroying galaxies
Abstract: Feedback from super-massive black holes (SMBHs) is believed to play a crucial role in regulating the growth of their host galaxies. Cosmological and galaxy formation simulations using smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH), typically employing a fixed mass for SPH particles, often utilize the same sub-grid active galactic nuclei (AGN) feedback prescription across varying resolutions. Therefore, it is important to understand how the impact of simulated AGN feedback on a galaxy changes solely due to numerical resolution adjustments. We present a series of simulations modeling the interaction of an AGN outflow with the turbulent and clumpy interstellar medium (ISM) within the inner region of the host galaxy at different mass resolutions. Our results reveal that, with other factors constant, degrading the resolution leads to more efficient feedback, clearing all gas in its path. Specifically, the mass of gas ejected by AGN feedback varies by over tenfold between our highest and lowest resolution simulations. This discrepancy arises because feedback-resistant high-density clumps are washed out at lower effective resolutions. Moreover, we observe undesirable artifacts in how AGN feedback affects the AGN's immediate environment due to changes in numerical resolution.

title: Spontaneous mass generation and the small dimensions of the Standard Model gauge groups U(1), SU(2) and SU(3)
Abstract: The gauge symmetry of the Standard Model, SU(3)_c x SU(2)_L x U(1)_Y, remains unexplained. One intriguing aspect to consider is the low dimensionality of all its subgroups. Why not larger groups like SU(7), or even SP(38) or E7? We observe that fermions charged under large groups acquire significantly larger dynamical masses compared to ordinary quarks, assuming equal conditions at a high GUT scale. If such multicharged fermions exist, their excessive mass would make them unobservable today, leading to their decay early on (if they couple to the rest of the Standard Model) or becoming reliquial dark matter (if they don't). This result stems from strong antiscreening of the running coupling for those larger groups (with a suitably small number of flavors) combined with scaling properties of the Dyson-Schwinger equation for the fermion mass.

title: HMIoT: A New Healthcare Model Based on Internet of Things
Abstract: The expanding use of internet-connected equipment and devices necessitates a comprehensive understanding of its applications across various scientific disciplines. The widespread adoption of intelligent and autonomous devices in our daily lives makes the internet a central component in their interaction. This paper explores the application and utilization of the Internet of Things from a multidisciplinary perspective, highlighting its potential impact on future human health.

title: Web Tracking: Mechanisms, Implications, and Defenses
Abstract: This article examines the existing literature on methods employed by web services to track users online, exploring their purposes, implications, and potential user defenses. While a significant portion of the reviewed articles and web resources date back to 2012-2014, the issue of privacy remains a critical concern in today's web environment. Web services consistently strive to gather as much information as possible about user activities, including searches, visited websites, contacts, and purchases. This tracking is typically driven by commercial interests. We present five primary groups of user tracking methods: session-based, client storage, client cache, fingerprinting, and other approaches. We focus specifically on mechanisms utilizing web caches, operational caches, and fingerprinting, known for their creative methodologies. Our analysis reveals how users can be identified online and linked to their real names, email addresses, phone numbers, or even street addresses. We discuss the motivations behind tracking and its potential implications for users, including price discrimination, financial credibility assessment, insurance coverage determination, government surveillance, and identity theft. For each tracking method, we provide possible defenses. Beyond describing methods and tools for safeguarding personal data, we also present several research tools aimed at discovering tracking methods, identifying the tracking entity, and visualizing this information in an accessible manner. Finally, we discuss emerging future approaches to user tracking and their potential privacy threats.

title: Entropy spectrum of the apparent horizon of Vaidya black holes via adiabatic invariance
Abstract: The spectroscopy of the apparent horizon of Vaidya black holes is investigated using adiabatic invariance. We obtain an equally spaced entropy spectrum, where its quantum is equal to the one given by Bekenstein. This demonstrates that entropy and area quantization is a generic property of horizons, not just for stationary black holes but also in dynamical ones. Our work also reveals that black hole quantization is closely related to Hawking temperature, which presents an intriguing observation.

title: Unification of Fusion Theories, Rules, Filters, Image Fusion and Target Tracking Methods (UFT)
Abstract: The author has dedicated previous work to unifying fusion theories, combining fusion rules, image fusion procedures, filter algorithms, and target tracking methods for more accurate real-world applications. This unification seeks to address the limitations of individual approaches, as neither fusion theory nor fusion rule fully satisfies all application requirements. The proposed unification scenario, still in its early stages, aims to periodically incorporate new discoveries from fusion and engineering research.

title: Precision Predictions for the Primordial Power Spectra of Scalar Potential Models of Inflation
Abstract: This paper presents a novel numerical technique for evaluating tree order contributions to the primordial scalar and tensor power spectra for scalar potential models of inflation. Using this formalism, we develop an analytical approximation that surpasses generalized slow roll expansions by addressing key shortcomings. Notably, it eliminates contamination from the physically irrelevant phase, possesses an exact 0th order term for constant first slow roll parameter, and provides a multiplicative rather than additive correction. These features allow our formalism to capture first-order effects that are higher order in other expansions. While this level of accuracy might not be essential for comparing current data with specific models, our method offers various applications due to its simplified representation of the relationship between power spectra and the expansion history of a general model.
label: AI

title: Decision Maker based on Atomic Switches
Abstract: We introduce a simple model for an atomic switch-based decision maker (ASDM) and demonstrate that, as long as its total volume of precipitated Ag atoms is conserved during coupled operations, an atomic switch system exhibits sophisticated "decision-making" capabilities. These capabilities are comparable to human intellectual abilities, particularly in the context of the multi-armed bandit problem (MAB). This problem involves finding the most profitable option from a set of options offering stochastic rewards, both accurately and swiftly. Decisions are made based on the volume of precipitated Ag atoms, which is moved in a manner resembling the fluctuations of a rigid body in a tug-of-war game. The "tug-of-war (TOW) dynamics" of the ASDM surpasses the efficiency of conventional MAB solvers. Analytical calculations validate the statistical reasons behind the ASDM's high performance, despite its simplicity. These results suggest that various physical systems, governed by conservation laws, can be used to implement efficient "decision-making objects." Efficient MAB solvers are valuable for numerous practical applications, as MAB abstractly represents various real-world decision-making scenarios requiring efficient trial-and-error processes. Our proposed scheme introduces a novel physics-based analog computing paradigm, encompassing elements like "intelligent nano devices" and "intelligent information networks" based on self-detection and self-judgment.

title: DTLS Performance in Duty-Cycled Networks
Abstract: The Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) protocol is the IETF standard for securing the Internet of Things. Protocols such as Constrained Application Protocol, ZigBee IP, and Lightweight Machine-to-Machine (LWM2M) mandate its use for securing application traffic. However, there has been extensive debate within both standardization and research communities regarding the applicability of DTLS to constrained environments. Primary concerns center around the communication overhead and latency of the DTLS handshake, as well as the memory footprint of DTLS implementations. This paper provides a comprehensive performance evaluation of DTLS in various duty-cycled networks through real-world experimentation, emulation, and analysis. Specifically, we measure the duration of the DTLS handshake when using three duty cycling link-layer protocols: preamble-sampling, the IEEE 802.15.4 beacon-enabled mode, and the IEEE 802.15.4e Time Slotted Channel Hopping mode. Our results demonstrate surprisingly poor performance of DTLS in radio duty-cycled networks. Due to the exchange of more than ten signaling packets between a DTLS client and server, the DTLS handshake takes between a few seconds and several tens of seconds, with similar results across different duty cycling protocols. Furthermore, typical constrained nodes, with their limited memory, can only maintain 3-5 simultaneous DTLS sessions, highlighting the need for using DTLS sparingly.

title: Secure management of logs in internet of things
Abstract: Data management has been crucial since the advent of computing. As network infrastructure expands, the volume of data requiring storage increases proportionally. The emergence of the Internet of Things (IoT) anticipates billions of devices connecting to the internet within the next decade. These devices will communicate regularly with minimal human intervention, generating vast amounts of real-time data and resulting in numerous log files. Alongside the storage complexity, ensuring confidentiality and integrity of these logs in IoT-enabled devices becomes essential. This paper provides a brief overview of efficient and secure log storage methods in IoT devices.
label: AI

title: Reputational Learning and Network Dynamics
Abstract: In many real-world networks, agents initially lack knowledge about each other's qualities and must learn through repeated interactions over time. This paper presents the first methodology for studying the dynamics of such networks, considering agent differences, incomplete initial information, and the need for learning from past experiences to form and break connections. The network dynamics in our model diverge significantly from those in models with complete information. With incomplete information and learning, agents providing high benefits develop high reputations and remain within the network, while those offering low benefits experience declining reputations and become ostracized. Among other findings, we demonstrate that the information accessible to agents and the speed at which they learn and act can significantly impact network dynamics. Our model allows us to compute ex ante social welfare given an arbitrary initial network, enabling us to characterize socially optimal network structures for different sets of agents. Notably, we show through examples that the optimal network structure is strongly influenced by both the initial beliefs of agents and their learning rate. Due to the potential negative consequences of ostracism, it may be necessary to place agents with lower initial reputations in less central positions within the network.

title: Matrix weighted norm inequalities for commutators and paraproducts with matrix symbols
Abstract: Let $B$ be a locally integrable matrix function, $W$ a matrix A${}_p$ weight with $1 < p < \\infty$, and $T$ be any of the Riesz transforms. We will characterize the boundedness of the commutator $[T, B]$ on $L^p(W)$ in terms of the membership of $B$ in a natural matrix weighted BMO space. To achieve this, we will characterize the boundedness of dyadic paraproducts on $L^p(W)$ via a new matrix weighted Carleson embedding theorem. Finally, we will utilize some of the ideas from these proofs to obtain quantitative weighted norm inequalities for these operators. We will also use them to prove sharp $L^2$ bounds for the Christ/Goldberg matrix weighted maximal function associated with matrix A${}_2$ weights.

title: Monitoring in IOT enabled devices
Abstract: As network size experiences exponential growth, the number of nodes in corresponding networks increases proportionally. With the advent of the Internet of Things (IoT), many more devices are expected to connect to the existing network infrastructure. Consequently, network monitoring becomes increasingly complex for administrators as networks become more heterogeneous. Furthermore, addressing IoT devices poses additional complexity due to the scale at which devices will be added. This paper examines the challenges of monitoring IoT networks and explores potential monitoring mechanisms and their effectiveness.

title: Magnetars: the physics behind observations
Abstract: Magnetars, the most powerful magnets in the observable universe, present unique laboratories for probing current physical theories under extreme conditions. Their combination of intense magnetic fields, gravity, and density allows us to study quantum electrodynamics and general relativity in the strong field limit. Magnetars are observed as peculiar, burst-active X-ray pulsars, classified as Anomalous X-ray Pulsars (AXPs) and Soft Gamma Repeaters (SGRs). The latter have emitted three "giant flares," incredibly powerful events reaching luminosities of up to 10^47 erg/s for about one second. Recent years have witnessed a surge in magnetar research, leading to the discovery of transient or "outbursting" and "low-field" magnetars. Significant progress has also been made on the theoretical front. Detailed models have been developed and validated against observations to explain the persistent X-ray emission, burst properties, and flux evolution in transient sources. Improved models of magnetar oscillations have yielded new insights into neutron star asteroseismology. The long-debated issue of magnetic field decay in neutron stars has been addressed, recognizing its importance in the evolution of magnetars and their connection to other isolated neutron star families. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of magnetar observations and their implications within the context of current theoretical models. This not only addresses the specific case of magnetar sources but also the broader issue of constraining physics in strong magnetic fields through observations of these unique objects.

title: Lines in positive genus: An introduction to flat surfaces
Abstract: This text is designed for undergraduate students, as well as anyone interested in exploring the interplay between shapes and numbers. Its goal is to encourage deep thinking about seemingly simple concepts. The primary objects of study are lines, squares, and the effects of basic geometric motions on them. The text and figures illustrate much of the beauty of this subject, while leaving some for the student to discover through exercises. We encourage readers to actively engage with examples, work through exercises, and uncover the elegance and richness of this area of mathematics.

title: A New Vision for Smart Objects and the Internet of Things: Mobile Robots and Long-Range UHF RFID Sensor Tags
Abstract: This paper presents a new vision for smart objects and the Internet of Things, where mobile robots interact with wirelessly-powered, long-range, ultra-high frequency radio frequency identification (UHF RFID) tags equipped with sensing capabilities. We explore the technological advancements driving this vision by examining recently commercialized sensor tags that can be attached to or embedded within objects or the environment, enabling true embodied intelligence. Utilizing a pair of autonomous mobile robots equipped with UHF RFID readers, we explore several potential applications where mobile robots interact with sensor tags to perform tasks such as soil moisture sensing, remote crop monitoring, infrastructure monitoring, water quality monitoring, and remote sensor deployment.

title: A reasonable thing that just might work
Abstract: In 1964, John Bell demonstrated the "unreasonableness" (using Einstein's term) of quantum mechanics by proving the existence of nonlocal bipartite quantum correlations. However, these correlations are not the most nonlocal bipartite correlations compatible with relativistic causality ("no superluminal signalling"). Maximally nonlocal "superquantum" (or "PR-box") correlations are also consistent with relativistic causality. I show that, unlike quantum correlations, these correlations lack a classical limit compatible with relativistic causality. Generalizing this result to all stronger-than-quantum nonlocal correlations leads to the derivation of Tsirelson's bound, a theorem of quantum mechanics, from three axioms: relativistic causality, nonlocality, and the existence of a classical limit. But is it reasonable to derive (a part of) quantum mechanics from the unreasonable axiom of nonlocality? I propose replacing the nonlocality axiom with an equivalent axiom that even Bell and Einstein might have found reasonable: an axiom of local retrocausality. |||
label: AI

title: Intelligent Data in the context of the internet-of-things
Abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) promises to optimize equipment and resource usage, leading to increased automation efficiency and new, cost-effective business models. However, the rapid growth of IoT presents significant challenges, including managing diverse devices across multiple networks, handling the exponential increase in sensor data, and extracting meaningful insights from this data influx. Open systems, architectures, and applications are crucial for addressing this diversity. Real-time analytics are essential for gaining intelligence and responding to events as they occur. Historical analysis can be used to identify trends, correlate sensor data, and provide insights based on usage patterns. This paper presents a framework that overcomes diversity by flexibly representing sensor data on the internet. The framework incorporates business goals-driven information processing, intelligence derived from information, and information control, enabling the development of innovative applications that enhance and leverage the value of IoT.
label: AI

title: Proof of a conjecture on the zero forcing number of a graph
Abstract: Amos et al. (Discrete Appl. Math. 181 (2015) 1-10) introduced the concept of the k-forcing number of a graph as a generalization of the zero forcing number. The k-forcing number, denoted by Fk(G), represents the minimum number of vertices that need to be initially colored to eventually color all vertices in a simple graph G, following a specific rule. This rule involves coloring uncolored neighbors of colored vertices if the colored vertex has at most k uncolored neighbors. Notably, F1(G) is closely related to the maximum nullity of a graph and is widely known as the zero forcing number, denoted by Z(G). Amos et al. proved that for a connected graph G of order n with maximum degree Δ ≥ 2, Z(G) ≤ (Δ-2)n+2/(Δ-1), and this inequality is sharp. They further conjectured that Z(G) = (Δ-2)n+2/(Δ-1) if and only if G is a cycle, a complete graph of order Δ+1, or a complete bipartite graph with equal parts. This note demonstrates the truth of this conjecture.
label: AI

title: Reaction-diffusion equation for quark-hadron transition in heavy-ion collisions
Abstract: Reaction-diffusion equations with appropriate boundary conditions exhibit propagating solutions that closely resemble the moving interfaces observed in first-order phase transitions. We show that the dynamics of the chiral order parameter in chiral symmetry breaking transitions in heavy-ion collisions, incorporating dissipative dynamics, is governed by the Newell-Whitehead equation. The geometry of the collision automatically satisfies the required boundary conditions. Consequently, the chiral transition proceeds through a propagating interface, mirroring a first-order transition, despite being a crossover for relativistic heavy-ion collisions. This phenomenon also occurs when considering the initial confinement-deconfinement transition with the Polyakov loop order parameter. The resulting equation, incorporating dissipative dynamics, can be identified with the Fitzhugh-Nagumo equation, used in population genetics, which also exhibits reaction-diffusion behavior. We discuss the implications of these findings for heavy-ion collisions and explore potential extensions to the early universe.
label: AI

title: City Data Fusion: Sensor Data Fusion in the Internet of Things
Abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) has gained significant attention recently and plays a crucial role in smart city application deployments. Many of these smart city applications rely on sensor data fusion capabilities in the cloud from diverse data sources. This paper introduces the concept of IoT and presents ten parameters that govern our sensor data fusion evaluation framework. We then evaluate the current state-of-the-art sensor data fusion approaches against this framework. Our primary objective is to examine and survey different sensor data fusion research efforts based on our evaluation framework. title: End-to-End Privacy for Open Big Data Markets
Abstract: The concept of an open data market envisions a data trading model that facilitates data exchange between different parties within the Internet of Things (IoT) domain. Data collected by IoT products and solutions is expected to be traded in these markets. Data owners collect data using IoT products and solutions, while interested data consumers negotiate with data owners to gain access. Data captured by IoT products provides data consumers with insights into the preferences and behaviors of data owners, enabling them to generate additional business value through various techniques ranging from waste reduction to personalized service offerings. In open data markets, data consumers can give back a portion of the generated value to data owners. However, privacy becomes a significant concern when data that can be used to derive highly personal information is traded. This paper explores the importance of privacy in the IoT domain, particularly within open data markets, and surveys existing privacy-preserving strategies and design techniques that can ensure end-to-end privacy for these markets. title: Full-Duplex vs. Half-Duplex Secret-Key Generation
Abstract: Full-duplex (FD) communication is considered a key technology for future 5G and Internet of Things (IoT) systems. Beyond achieving high data rates, the success of these systems hinges on ensuring confidentiality and security. Secret-key agreement based on reciprocal wireless channels provides a valuable complement to security at the physical layer. This work investigates the role of FD communication in conjunction with secret-key agreement. We introduce two complementary key generation models for FD and half-duplex (HD) settings, comparing their performance using the key-reconciliation function. Furthermore, we study the impact of the probing-reconciliation trade-off, the role of a strong eavesdropper, and analyze the system in the high SNR regime. Our findings reveal that under specific conditions, FD communication hinders the eavesdropper's capabilities and offers several advantages in terms of secret-key rate compared to conventional HD setups. Interestingly, our analysis shows that perfect self-interference cancellation is not essential for achieving performance gains over the HD mode.

title: Irreducible quantum group modules with finite dimensional weight spaces. II

In that paper, the classification is reduced to the classification of torsion-free simple modules. This paper utilizes procedures similar to those used by O. Mathieu to reduce the classification to the classification of infinite-dimensional admissible simple highest weight modules. We then classify these infinite-dimensional modules and demonstrate, among other findings, that they only exist for types A and C. Finally, we complete the classification of simple torsion-free modules for types A and C, concluding the classification of simple torsion-free modules.

title: Probabilistic Knowledge as Objective Knowledge in Quantum Mechanics: Potential Powers Instead of Actual Properties
Abstract: In classical physics, probabilistic or statistical knowledge has always been associated with ignorance or inaccurate subjective knowledge about the actual state of affairs. This idea has been extended to quantum mechanics through an incoherent interpretation of Fermi-Dirac and Bose-Einstein statistics in terms of "strange" quantum particles. This interpretation, naturalized through widespread "way of speaking" in the physics community, contradicts Born's physical account of Ψ as a "probability wave" that provides statistical information about outcomes which cannot be interpreted as ignorance about an actual state of affairs. This paper examines how the metaphysics of actuality has limited the possibilities of understanding things differently. We propose a metaphysical scheme based on powers with definite potentia, allowing us to re-evaluate quantum probability as providing objective knowledge about a potential state of affairs.

title: Cofinite Graphs and Groupoids and their Profinite Completions
Abstract: We define cofinite graphs and cofinite groupoids in a unified manner that extends the notion of cofinite groups introduced by Hartley. The common underlying structure of these objects is that they are directed graphs equipped with a specific type of uniform structure, which we call a cofinite uniformity. We begin by exploring the fundamental theory of cofinite directed graphs in full generality. The general theory turns out to be remarkably analogous to that of cofinite groups. For example, every cofinite directed graph has a unique completion that is a compact cofinite directed graph. Moreover, compact cofinite directed graphs are precisely the profinite directed graphs, i.e., projective limits of finite discrete topological directed graphs. We then apply the general theory to directed graphs with additional structure such as graphs (in the sense of Serre) and groupoids, leading to the notions of cofinite graphs and cofinite groupoids. Cofinite groupoids with finitely many identities behave similarly to cofinite groups, which are equivalent to cofinite groupoids with a single identity. However, the situation for cofinite groupoids with infinitely many identities is more complex.

title: Hamiltonian system for the elliptic form of Painlevé VI equation

Among other findings, we prove that the isomonodromic equation is a new Hamiltonian system, equivalent to the elliptic form of the Painlevé VI equation for generic parameters. For Painlevé VI equations with specific parameter values, the isomonodromy theory of the generalized Lamé equation significantly simplifies the computation of the monodromy group in ℂℙ¹. This is one of the advantages of the elliptic form.

title: On the stability of a generalized additive functional equation

title: Next Generation M2M Cellular Networks: Challenges and Practical Considerations

The heterogeneous network model provides an alternative approach to accommodating a larger number of users. title: Thermodynamics of Spherically Symmetric Spacetimes in Loop Quantum Gravity
Abstract: The choice of the area operator in loop quantum gravity is not unique. Using Krasnov's area operator, we investigate the thermodynamics of spherically symmetric spacetimes with horizons in loop quantum gravity. Our approach implies, in a straightforward manner, that every spacetime horizon emits thermal radiation and possesses entropy, which in natural units, is one-quarter of its area. When applied to de Sitter spacetime, loop quantum gravity provides an explanation for both the presence and the smallness of the cosmological constant.

title: The Peano software - parallel, automaton-based, dynamically adaptive grid traversals

The traversal can leverage regular grid subregions and shared memory as well as distributed memory systems with minimal modifications to serial application code. We formalize the software design using two interacting automata—one for multiscale grid traversal and one for application-specific algorithmic steps. This leads to a callback-based programming paradigm. We outline the supported application types and two realized data storage schemes before detailing high-performance computing aspects and lessons learned. Particular emphasis is placed on observations regarding programming idioms and algorithmic concepts, transforming this report from a "one way to implement things" code description into a generic discussion and summary of alternatives, rationale, and design decisions for any tree-based adaptive mesh refinement software.

title: CamFlow: Managed Data-sharing for Cloud Services

From the outset, strong isolation between cloud tenants was deemed crucial, initially provided by virtual machines (VMs) and later by containers, which share the operating system (OS) kernel. Increasingly, applications require facilities for isolation and protection of the data they manage. They also necessitate flexible data sharing with other applications, often across traditional cloud-isolation boundaries, such as when government agencies provide related services for citizens on a common platform. Similar considerations apply to application end-users. However, the integration of cloud services within Internet of Things (IoT) architectures is driving the need for both protection and cross-application data sharing. These concerns relate to data management. Traditional access control is application and principal/role specific, applied at policy enforcement points, but provides no subsequent control over data flow, a crucial issue once data leaves its owner's control through cloud-hosted applications and within cloud services. Information Flow Control (IFC), in addition, offers system-wide, end-to-end flow control based on data properties. We discuss the potential of cloud-deployed IFC for enforcing owners' dataflow policies regarding protection and sharing, as well as safeguarding against malicious or buggy software. Furthermore, the audit log associated with IFC provides transparency, enabling configurable system-wide visibility over data flows. [...]

title: Dialogues about geometry and light
Abstract: Throughout human history, people have relied on sight to understand the world, but the science of light has only been developed relatively recently. Egyptians and Mesopotamians created the first known lenses out of quartz, giving rise to what became known as optics. Geometry, on the other hand, is a branch of mathematics that emerged from practical studies concerning lengths, areas, and volumes in early cultures, although it wasn't formalized axiomatically until the 3rd century BC. This work explores the connection between these two timeless topics and reveals "new things in old things." While there have been several works in this direction, taking into account the didactic approach of the Enrico Fermi Summer School, we aim to address the subject and our audience in a new light.

title: The radial variation of HI velocity dispersions in dwarfs and spirals
Abstract: Gas velocity dispersions are essential diagnostics for understanding the forces counteracting gravity to prevent gas collapse. We utilize the 21 cm line of neutral atomic hydrogen (HI) to study HI velocity dispersion and HI phases as a function of galaxy morphology in 22 galaxies from The HI Nearby Galaxy Survey (THINGS). By stacking individual HI velocity profiles and decomposing them into broad and narrow Gaussian components, we investigate HI velocity dispersion and surface density as a function of radius. In spirals, the velocity dispersions of the narrow and broad components decrease with radius, and their radial profiles are well described by an exponential function. However, for dwarfs, the profiles are much flatter. The single Gaussian dispersion profiles are generally flatter than those of the narrow and broad components. In most cases, the dispersion profiles in the outer disks do not decrease as rapidly as the star formation profiles reported in the literature. This suggests the importance of other energy sources in driving HI velocity dispersion in the outer disks. The radial surface density profiles of spirals and dwarfs are similar. The surface density profiles of the narrow component decline more steeply than those of the broad component, but not as steeply as previously found for the molecular component. Consequently, the surface density ratio between the narrow and broad components, an estimate of the mass ratio between cold HI and warm HI, tends to decrease with radius. On average, this ratio is lower in dwarfs than in spirals. This lack of a narrow, cold HI component in dwarfs may explain their low star formation activity.

title: The Hawking cascade from a black hole is extremely sparse
Abstract: The Hawking flux from a black hole, at least as observed from asymptotic infinity, is extremely sparse and thin, with the average time between the emission of successive Hawking quanta being significantly longer than the natural timescale set by the energies of the emitted quanta. Although this result has been known for over 30 years, it has largely been forgotten. We focus on the early-stage low-temperature regime and confront numerical estimates with semi-analytic approximations based on a naive Planck spectrum. First, we identify several natural dimensionless figures of merit and thereby compare the mean time between the emission of successive Hawking quanta to several distinct but natural timescales associated with the emitted quanta, demonstrating that very large ratios are typical for the emission of massless quanta from a Schwarzschild black hole. Furthermore, these ratios are independent of the black hole's mass as it slowly evolves. We then show that the situation for the more general Reissner-Nordstrom and generic "dirty" black holes is even worse, at least as long as the surrounding matter satisfies suitable energy conditions. The situation for Kerr and Kerr-Newman black holes (or even for charged particle emission from a Reissner-Nordstrom black hole) is considerably more complex and depends on a careful accounting of the super-radiant modes. Overall, the Hawking quanta are seen to be slowly dribbling out of the black hole one at a time, in an extremely slow cascade of 2-body decays. This implies, among other things, that the Hawking flux is subject to "shot noise." Observationally, the Planck spectrum of the Hawking flux can only be determined by collecting and integrating data over a very long timescale. We conclude by connecting these points back to various kinematic aspects of the Hawking evaporation process.

title: Does telling white lies signal pro-social preferences?
Abstract: The opportunity to tell a white lie (i.e., a lie that benefits another person) creates a moral conflict between two opposing moral dictates: one urging truth-telling and the other encouraging helping others. This study investigates how individuals resolve this moral conflict. What does telling a white lie signal about a person's pro-social tendencies? To address this question, we conducted a two-stage 2x2 experiment. In the first stage, we used a Deception Game to measure aversion to telling a Pareto white lie (i.e., a lie that benefits both the liar and the listener) and aversion to telling an altruistic white lie (i.e., a lie that benefits the listener at the expense of the liar). In the second stage, we measured altruistic tendencies using a Dictator Game and cooperative tendencies using a Prisoner's Dilemma. Our findings revealed three main results: (i) both altruism and cooperation are positively correlated with aversion to telling a Pareto white lie; (ii) both altruism and cooperation are negatively correlated with aversion to telling an altruistic white lie; (iii) men are more likely than women to tell an altruistic white lie, but not a Pareto white lie. Our results shed light on the moral conflict between pro-sociality and truth-telling. Notably, the first finding suggests that a significant proportion of individuals hold non-distributional notions of what the right thing to do is: irrespective of their economic consequences, they tell the truth, cooperate, and share their money.

title: Application of Multi factor authentication in Internet of Things domain

Furthermore, the rise of the Internet of Things (IoT) with its exponential growth in devices makes it impractical for users to remember countless passwords. Therefore, it is essential to address this concern by devising methods that require multiple forms of authentication for accessing smart devices while maintaining high usability. This paper discusses a methodology for deploying authentication mechanisms within the IoT domain.

title: Discrete linear multiple recurrence with multi-periodic coefficients
Abstract: This paper focuses on formulating and solving problems related to linear multiple periodic recurrence equations. The Floquet approach simplifies the initial linear multiple recurrence system by reducing it to another linear multiple recurrence system with constant coefficients along specific directions.
