title: A Proof of the Thue-Siegel Theorem about the Approximation of Algebraic Numbers for Binomial Equations
Abstract: In 1908, Thue demonstrated that algebraic numbers of the form $\xi = \sqrt[n]{\frac{a}{b}}$ can only be closely approximated by a finite number of rational numbers $\frac{p}{q}$ for any positive $\epsilon$, subject to the inequality $|\xi - \frac{p}{q}| \leq q^{-(\frac{n}{2}+1+\epsilon)}$. The proof utilizes, albeit subtly, the continued fraction expansion of the binomial series $(1-z)^\omega$. Thue's subsequent work on approximating algebraic numbers employed a different method, Dirichlet's drawer principle, to establish the validity of the aforementioned statement for all algebraic numbers. Later, Siegel generalized Thue's methods, showing that for any algebraic number in the inequality, the exponent $\frac{n}{2}+1+\epsilon$ can be replaced with $\frac{n}{m}+m-1+\epsilon$, where $m$ is a natural number. This note presents a generalization of Thue's methods as outlined in (1). Similar to Thue, we focus on the roots $\xi = \sqrt[n]{\frac{a}{b}}$ of the binomial equations. The continued fraction expansion of the binomial series is extended, and algebraic approximation functions are introduced instead of rational approximation functions, mirroring the approach used in our work on the exponential function (8). By establishing integrals for these approximation functions, we simplify the estimations and demonstrate Thue's theorem with Siegel's exponents for the binomial algebraic equations without relying on the pigeonhole principle.

title: Automorphisms of $\mathscr{P}(λ)/\mathscr{I}_κ$

We prove, among other things, that every cardinality-preserving automorphism of $P(2^\kappa)/I_{\kappa^+}$ which is trivial on all sets of cardinality $\kappa^+$ is also trivial. Additionally, we show that $MA_{\aleph_1}$ implies that every automorphism of $P(\mathbb{R})/Fin$ is trivial on a cocountable set.

title: Another derivation of generalized Langevin equations
Abstract: The formal derivation of Langevin equations (and, equivalently, Fokker-Planck equations) using the projection operator techniques of Mori, Zwanzig, Kawasaki, and others has not been widely adopted in textbooks. While the derivation has been replicated numerous times with references to existing literature, it has not seen significant advancements. In this paper, we follow this tradition while striving to present a self-contained text. Additionally, we address questions that naturally arise during the derivation. We clarify the meaning of the divergence of Poisson brackets and elucidate the role of nonlinear damping coefficients. The derivation is grounded in classical mechanics and encompasses everything that can be constructed from point particles and potentials: solids, liquids, liquid crystals, conductors, polymers, systems with spin-like degrees of freedom, etc. Einstein relations and Onsager reciprocity relations are derived as natural consequences.

title: License Plate Recognition System Based on Color Coding Of License Plates
Abstract: License Plate Recognition Systems are employed to determine the license plate number of a vehicle. The current system predominantly utilizes Optical Character Recognition for this task. This paper proposes a novel system for recognizing license plate numbers by utilizing color coding of license plates. Easier localization of license plates can be achieved by searching for specific start or stop patterns. The proposed system incorporates an eight-segment display system alongside traditional numbering, with the first and last segments reserved for start or stop patterns. Practical applications of this system extend to various areas within the Internet of Things (IoT).

title: EMMA: A Resource Oriented Framework for Service Choreography over Wireless Sensor and Actor Networks
Abstract: Current Internet of Things (IoT) development necessitates service distribution over Wireless Sensor and Actor Networks (WSAN) to address the significant increase in network management complexity. Due to the specific constraints of WSAN, centralized approaches are severely limited. Multi-hop communication employed by WSAN introduces challenges such as transmission latency, packet errors, router congestion, and security issues. A decentralized service model, leveraging local services, avoids long-path communications between nodes and applications. However, the primary issue is ensuring the installation of these local services on the desired nodes. The Environment Monitoring and Management Agent (EMMA) system presents a suite of software for deploying and executing such services over WSAN through a middleware based on Resource-Oriented Architecture (ROA). The system's Internet integration and local management of data heterogeneity are facilitated through the use of current standard protocols like IPv6 Low Power Wireless Area Networks (6LoWPAN) and Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP). This contribution presents EMMA middleware, methodologies, and tools used to determine efficient service mapping and its deployment.

title: Autonomics: an autonomous and intelligent economic platform and next generation money tool
Abstract: We propose a high-level network architecture for an economic system that integrates money, governance, and reputation. We introduce a method for issuing and redeeming a digital coin using a mechanism to create a sustainable global economy and a free market. To maintain a currency's value over time, and therefore be considered true money, we argue that it must be issued by the buyer and backed for value by the seller, exchanging the products of labor in a free market. We further claim that a free market and sustainable economy cannot be sustained using arbitrary creation and allocation of money. Nakamoto, with Bitcoin, introduced a new technology called the cryptographic blockchain to operate a decentralized and distributed accounts ledger without the need for an untrusted third party. This blockchain technology creates and allocates new digital currency as a reward for "proof-of-work," to secure the network. However, no currency, digital or otherwise, has solved the challenge of creating and allocating money in a non-arbitrary economic manner or governing and fostering trust in a world-scale free enterprise money system. We propose an "Ontologically Networked Exchange" (ONE), with purpose as its highest-order domain. Each purpose is defined in a contract, and the entire economy of contracts is structured in a unified ontology. We aim to secure the ONE network using economically non-arbitrary methodologies and economically incentivized human behavior. Decisions influenced by reputation contribute to securing the network without an untrusted third party. The stack of contracts, organized in a unified ontology, functions as a super recursive algorithm, with individual users programming the algorithm, acting as the "oracle." The state of the algorithm becomes the "memory" of a scalable and trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI). This AI offers a new platform for what we call the "Autonomy-of-Things" (AoT).

title: Forgery-Resistant Touch-based Authentication on Mobile Devices
Abstract: Mobile devices store a diverse collection of private user data and have become central to controlling users' other personal Internet-of-Things devices. However, password authentication is cumbersome, as users need to enter a password each time they want to use the device. Moreover, existing biometrics such as face, fingerprint, and touch behaviors are susceptible to forgery attacks. We propose a novel touch-based biometric authentication system that is passive and secure against forgery attacks. In our touch-based authentication, a user's touch behaviors are a function of a random "secret." The user can subconsciously know the secret while touching the device's screen. However, an attacker cannot know the secret at the time of the attack, making it difficult to perform forgery attacks even if the attacker has already obtained the user's touch behaviors. We evaluate our touch-based authentication system by collecting data from 25 subjects. The results are promising: the random secrets do not impact user experience, and for targeted forgery attacks, our system achieves 0.18 smaller Equal Error Rates (EERs) than previous touch-based authentication methods.

title: Discrete multitime multiple recurrence

title: Dissipative dark matter and the rotation curves of dwarf galaxies

Dark matter halos surrounding disk galaxies may exhibit non-trivial dynamics if dark matter interacts strongly with itself and experiences dissipation. Multicomponent hidden sector dark matter featuring a massless "dark photon" (from an unbroken dark $U(1)$ gauge interaction) that kinetically mixes with the ordinary photon provides a concrete example of such dark matter. The kinetic mixing interaction enables halo heating by allowing ordinary supernovae to be a source of these "dark photons." Dark matter halos can expand and contract in response to heating and cooling processes. However, for a sufficiently isolated halo, it may have evolved to a steady state or "equilibrium" configuration where heating and cooling rates locally balance. This dynamic allows the dark matter density profile to be related to the distribution of ordinary supernovae in the disk of a given galaxy. In a previous paper, a simple and predictive formula was derived encoding this relationship. This work refines previous efforts by modeling the supernovae distribution using measured UV and $H\alpha$ fluxes. We compare the resulting dark matter halo profiles with the rotation curve data for each dwarf galaxy in the LITTLE THINGS sample. The concept of dissipative dark matter is further developed, and conclusions are drawn.

title: A mutation-selection model for evolution of random dispersal

Our results show that in the limit of a small mutation rate, the solution remains regular in spatial variables but concentrates in the trait variable, forming a Dirac mass supported at the lowest diffusion rate. Hastings (Theor. Pop. Biol. 24, 244-251, 1983) and Dockery et al. (J. Math. Biol. 37, 61-83, 1998) demonstrated that for two competing species in a spatially heterogeneous but temporally constant environment, the slower diffuser always prevails, assuming all other factors are equal. title: Learning with hidden variables

title: Privacy in the Internet of Things: Threats and Challenges

This paper analyzes the privacy issues in the Internet of Things in detail. We discuss the evolving features and trends in the Internet of Things to scrutinize their privacy implications. title: Networking technologies for robotic applications

title: Generalized communities in networks

title: Semi-autonomous, context-aware, agent using behaviour modelling and reputation systems to authorize data operation in the Internet of Things

title: A U.S. Research Roadmap for Human Computation
Abstract: The Web has made it possible to harness human cognition on a massive scale to achieve new capabilities. Some of these successes are well-known; for example, Wikipedia has become the go-to source for basic information on all topics; Duolingo engages millions of people in real-life text translation while simultaneously teaching them to speak foreign languages; and Foldit has enabled public-driven scientific discoveries by transforming complex biomedical challenges into popular online puzzle games. These early successes hint at the immense potential for future crowd-powered capabilities for the benefit of health, education, science, and society. In the process, a new field called Human Computation has emerged to better understand, replicate, and improve upon these successes through scientific research. Human Computation refers to the science underlying online crowd-powered systems and was the topic of a recent visioning activity where a representative cross-section of researchers, industry practitioners, visionaries, funding agency representatives, and policy makers came together to understand what makes crowd-powered systems successful. Teams of experts considered past, present, and future human computation systems to explore which types of crowd-powered systems have the greatest potential for societal impact and which research areas will best enable the efficient development of new crowd-powered systems to achieve this impact. This report summarizes the products and findings of these activities, as well as the unconventional process and activities employed by the workshop, which were informed by human computation research. |||

title: Improved estimates for nonoscillatory phase functions
Abstract: Recent research has demonstrated that solutions to a broad class of highly oscillatory second-order linear ordinary differential equations can be accurately approximated using nonoscillatory phase functions. Under certain conditions on the coefficients and wavenumber of the equation, the existence of a function with a rapidly decaying Fourier transform is established, capable of representing solutions with accuracy on the order of . This paper presents a refined existence theorem for nonoscillatory phase functions, showcasing that solutions can be represented with the same accuracy using functions belonging to the space of rapidly decaying Schwartz functions, whose Fourier transforms exhibit both exponential decay and compact support. This advancement has significant implications for the development of efficient numerical methods for solving such differential equations.

title: CCG Parsing and Multiword Expressions
Abstract: This thesis explores the integration of Multiword Expressions (MWEs) into parsing with Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG). Building upon previous work that demonstrated the benefits of incorporating MWE information into syntactic parsing, the authors implement a similar pipeline with CCG parsing. The study involves collapsing MWEs into single tokens within both training and test data in the CCGbank corpus, a corpus annotated with CCG derivations. The collapsing algorithm employed, however, is limited to MWEs forming constituents in the data. The research investigates the impact of this collapsing approach on parsing and training effects. The results indicate that collapsing data improves parsing performance, particularly evident in a significant outperformance of the baseline model on the gold standard. Additionally, the baseline model exhibits enhanced performance on the gold standard when data are collapsed before parsing, suggesting a parsing effect. While improvements in performance on the non-collapsed benchmark are observed, the significance is not conclusive.  The authors conclude that, despite limitations in the settings, incorporating MWEs into parsing yields noticeable improvements.  The thesis discusses ways to further enhance this integration and hypothesizes that such improvements will lead to more substantial results.  Finally, the study highlights the benefits of making MWE recognition an experimental component of the pipeline, as different recognizers yield varying results.

title: Optimal linear estimation under unknown nonlinear transform

The authors propose a novel spectral-based estimation procedure and demonstrate its effectiveness in recovering the model parameter in settings where previous algorithms fail. This algorithm imposes minimal restrictions on the unknown functional relationship between the response and the linear combination. Furthermore, the paper tackles the high-dimensional setting where the model parameter is sparse, introducing a two-stage nonconvex framework that addresses estimation challenges in scenarios where the number of features exceeds the number of observations. The work establishes minimax lower bounds for a broad class of link functions, demonstrating the optimality of the proposed estimators in both classical and high-dimensional settings.

title: Generic properties for random repeated quantum iterations
Abstract: The paper investigates the transformation induced by the interaction of a complex matrix Q with an external source represented by a density matrix β and a unitary operator U. The main focus is on understanding the behavior of repeated applications of Φ to an initial density operator Q0.  The authors demonstrate the existence of an open and dense set of unitary operators for which the associated transformation Φ possesses a unique fixed point.  The paper also provides a detailed analysis of the case when n=2, presenting explicit results.  The analysis considers the C0 topology on the coefficients of the unitary operator, explicitly defining the conditions on these coefficients that guarantee the existence of a unique fixed point. title: A critical regularity condition on the angular velocity of axially symmetric Navier-Stokes equations
Abstract: This paper examines the regularity of the velocity field of Leray-Hopf solutions to the axially symmetric three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations.  The authors demonstrate that the velocity field is regular if the angular velocity satisfies a specific integral condition, which is critical under the standard scaling.  This condition allows functions satisfying  , where r denotes the distance from a point to the axis, and C and ε are positive constants. This condition differs from the critical a priori bound  by a logarithmic factor at worst.  The authors' work is inspired by a recent paper establishing an almost critical regularity condition on the angular velocity.  The proof leverages a new observation that all vortex stretching terms in the 3D axially symmetric Navier-Stokes equations, when viewed from a different perspective, become critical rather than supercritical.

title: Physical Layer Security in Massive MIMO
Abstract: The paper analyzes the security of single-cell downlink massive MIMO communication in the presence of an adversary capable of both jamming and eavesdropping. It is shown that massive MIMO communication is inherently resilient to no training-phase jamming attacks, where the adversary only jams data communication and eavesdrops both data and training. Specifically, the secure degrees of freedom (DoF) achieved under such an attack are identical to the maximum DoF achievable without any attack.  The paper then explores the number of antennas required at the base station (BS) to establish information-theoretic security without Wyner encoding.  However, the situation changes significantly when the adversary begins jamming during the training phase.  The paper demonstrates that training-phase jamming attacks, where the adversary jams and eavesdrops both training and data communication, result in zero secure DoF and vanishing achievable user rates even in the asymptotic regime of increasing BS antennas. To counter this attack, the paper proposes a defense strategy employing a secret key to encrypt pilot sequence assignments, effectively concealing them from the adversary. This strategy enables the users to achieve secure DoF identical to the maximum achievable DoF under no attack.  The paper concludes by discussing computational cryptography as a viable candidate for hiding pilot signal assignments, acknowledging that while information-theoretic security is not attainable with cryptography, the computational power required by the adversary to achieve non-zero mutual information leakage rate becomes unbounded.

title: The DIR Net: A Distributed System for Detection, Isolation, and Recovery
Abstract: This document provides a detailed description of the DIR net, a distributed environment forming part of the EFTOS fault tolerance framework. The DIR net comprises two components: the DIR Manager and the DIR Backup Agent. One manager and a set of backups are deployed within the system to be guarded, with one component per node. The DIR net essentially serves two key functions: fault tolerance and information gathering. In the event of an error within the DIR net, the system executes built-in recovery actions, enabling it to continue processing despite hardware or software failures, potentially with a graceful degradation of its features.  When errors occur in the user application, the DIR net, through custom- and user-defined detection tools, is notified of these events and initiates recovery strategies, both built-in and user-defined using an ancillary compile-time tool known as the rl translator. This tool translates user-defined strategies into binary "R-code," interpreted by a dedicated component of the DIR net, the Recovery Interpreter (rint).  This document provides a description of the generic component of the DIR net, capable of functioning as either a manager or a backup.

title: The Shape of LITTLE THINGS Dwarf Galaxies DDO 46 and DDO 168: Understanding the stellar and gas kinematics
Abstract: This paper presents a kinematic analysis of the dwarf galaxies DDO 46 and DDO 168 based on data from the LITTLE THINGS survey. The authors determine the Vmax/sigma_z,0 values for each galaxy, which are indicative of their disk properties.  The study utilizes long-slit spectroscopy obtained using the KPNO 4-meter telescope with the Echelle spectrograph. Spectra were acquired along four position angles for DDO 168, while only one data point was obtained for DDO 46 due to unfavorable weather conditions. The central stellar velocity dispersion perpendicular to the disk, sigma_z,0, was determined to be 13.5 +/- 8 km/s for DDO 46 and <sigma_z,0> of 10.7 +/- 2.9 km/s for DDO 168.  The maximum rotation speed for both galaxies was derived using the LITTLE THINGS HI data.  Bulk motions were separated from non-circular motions through a double Gaussian decomposition technique, and a tilted-ring model was applied to the bulk velocity field.  The observed HI rotation speeds were corrected for asymmetric drift, yielding maximum velocities (Vmax) of 77.4 +/- 3.7 and 67.4 +/- 4.0 km/s for DDO 46 and DDO 168, respectively. The derived kinematic measure, Vmax/sigma_z,0, was found to be 5.7 +/- 0.6 for DDO 46 and 6.3 +/- 0.3 for DDO 168.  Comparing these values to those observed in spiral galaxies, the authors conclude that DDO 46 and DDO 168 exhibit Vmax/sigma_z,0 values characteristic of thin disks, contradicting the findings of minor-to-major axis ratio studies.

title: A Heart for Interaction: Shared Physiological Dynamics and Behavioral Coordination in a Collective, Creative Construction Task
Abstract: This paper investigates the role of shared physiological dynamics, particularly heart rate dynamics, in interpersonal rapport, empathy, and team performance during individual and collective creative LEGO construction tasks. Inspired by the model of interpersonal synergy, the authors explore the presence, temporal development, possible mechanisms, and impact of shared heart rate dynamics in these scenarios. Study 1 reveals that shared heart rate dynamics are influenced by a variety of factors, including task constraints and behavioral coordination. The study finds that shared heart rate dynamics are more prevalent in individual trials, where participants perform the same actions, compared to collective trials with alternating turns and complementary actions. However, collective trials demonstrate more stable shared heart rate dynamics when compared to virtual pairs, suggesting the importance of online social interaction.  Furthermore, shared heart rate dynamics are found to increase across collective trials, unlike individual trials. Study 2 examines the potential drivers of these effects, demonstrating that shared heart rate dynamics are statistically predicted by interpersonal speech and building coordination. Study 3 investigates the relationship between heart rate dynamics, behavioral coordination, and self-reported measures of rapport and group competence. While behavioral coordination is found to predict rapport and group competence, shared heart rate dynamics do not.  Despite the reliable observation of shared physiological dynamics in the study, the authors caution against considering heart rate dynamics as a general driving mechanism of social coordination.  Conversely, behavioral coordination appears to be a more informative predictor of both shared physiological dynamics and collective experience.

title: F-theory and All Things Rational: Surveying U(1) Symmetries with Rational Sections
Abstract: This paper delves into elliptic fibrations for F-theory compactifications, focusing on 4d and 6d supersymmetric gauge theories with abelian gauge factors. The authors provide a comprehensive characterization of all possible U(1) charges of matter fields by identifying the corresponding codimension two fibers with rational sections.  One key example explored is the analysis of U(1) symmetries for SU(5) gauge theories with  and 10 matter, relevant for modeling supersymmetric Grand Unified Theories.  The authors leverage constraints on the normal bundle of rational curves in Calabi-Yau three- and four-folds, alongside the splitting of rational curves in the fibers in codimension two, to determine possible configurations of smooth rational sections.  This analysis extends readily to multiple U(1)s.  The paper further examines flops of these fibers and investigates Yukawa couplings in codimension three.  It also conducts a comprehensive study of U(1)-charged GUT singlets, including their KK-charges, and characterizes all singlet fibers.  By assigning vacuum expectation values to these singlets, the authors propose a systematic approach for analyzing the Higgsing of U(1)s to discrete gauge symmetries within F-theory.

title: Gradual Classical Logic for Attributed Objects - Extended in Re-Presentation
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to formal logic, called gradual logic, designed to capture our intuitive understanding of concepts and their attributes.  The author argues that our understanding of the world is conceptual, with concepts being manipulated rather than objects themselves.  The paper acknowledges that considering infinitely extending notions like space, time, size, and color makes it difficult to affirm atomicity in the concept of an object.  However, traditional formal logics typically presume atomic entities as the foundation for other expressions.  The paper addresses this discrepancy by proposing gradual logic, which reflects the observation that we cannot definitively determine whether a seemingly atomic entity is truly atomic or simply sufficiently atomic to be considered non-atomic. This logic aims to capture phenomena related to concepts with attributes, such as presupposition and contraries. The paper presents the logical particulars of gradual logic and maps it onto formal semantics, considering two linguistically relevant semantics.  The paper concludes by demonstrating the decidability of gradual logic.

title: Is $\hat{q}$ a physical quantity or just a parameter? and other unanswered questions in High-$p_T$ Physics
Abstract: Various theoretical studies on energy loss of a quark or gluon traversing a medium share a common element: the transport coefficient of a gluon in the medium, denoted as $\\hat{q}$. This coefficient represents the mean 4-momentum transfer squared, $\\left<q^2\\right>$, by a gluon to the medium per gluon mean free path, $\\lambda_{\\rm mfp}$. In the original BDMPSZ formalism, the energy loss of an outgoing parton, $-dE/dx$, per unit length ($x$) of a medium with total length $L$, due to coherent gluon bremsstrahlung, is proportional to $\\left< q^2\\right>$ and takes the form: ${-dE/dx }\\simeq \\alpha_s\n\\left<{q^2(L)}\\right>=\\alpha_s\\, \\mu^2\\, L/\\lambda_{\\rm mfp} =\\alpha_s\\,\n\\hat{q}\\, L\\ $ , where $\\mu$, is the mean momentum transfer per collision. Consequently, the total energy loss in the medium scales as $L^2$. Additionally, the accumulated momentum squared, $\\left<{k_{\\perp}^2}\\right>$, transverse to a gluon traversing a length $L$ in the medium is well approximated by $\\left<{k_{\\perp}^2}\\right>\\approx\\left<{q^2(L)}\\right>=\\hat{q}\\, L$. A simple estimate suggests that $\\left<{k_{\\perp}^2}\\right>\\approx\\hat{q}\\,L$ should be observable at RHIC at $\\sqrt{s_{NN}}=200$ GeV through the broadening of di-hadron azimuthal correlations, resulting in an azimuthal width $\\sim\\sqrt{2}$ larger in Au$+$Au than in $p+p$ collisions. The paper discusses measurements related to this issue, as well as recent STAR jet results presented at QM2014. Other topics include the potential problems of using forward energy to define centrality in $p(d)+$A collisions for high $p_T$ measurements and the lack of using comparison $p+p$ data at the same $\\sqrt{s}$ in the same detector for $R_{AA}$ or $R_{pA}$ measurements.

title: From Animaculum to single-molecules: 300 years of the light microscope
Abstract: While not claiming to be the inventor of the light microscope, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek (1632-1723) was arguably the first to bring this technological wonder to the attention of natural scientists interested in studying living organisms. This Dutch draper, with no formal scientific training, used magnifying glasses to observe threads in cloth. He later developed over 500 simple single-lens microscopes, which he used to examine various biological samples. He communicated his findings to the Royal Society through a series of letters, including the one republished in this edition of Open Biology. This review examines van Leeuwenhoek's work and summarizes key developments over the past 300 years, highlighting how the light microscope has evolved from a simple single-lens device into an instrument capable of observing the dynamics of single biological molecules within living cells and tracking every cell nucleus during the development of entire embryos and plants.

title: Strategic Interaction Among Different Entities in Internet of Things
Abstract: The economic model of the Internet of Things (IoT) consists of end users, advertisers, and three different providers: IoT service provider (IoTSP), Wireless service provider (WSP), and cloud service provider (CSP). This paper investigates three interaction models among these providers: a push model where the IoTSP prices a bundled service to end-users, with the WSP and CSP paying the IoTSP; a pull model where end-users independently pay each provider; and a hybrid model combining the two. The paper characterizes and quantifies the impact of advertisement revenue on equilibrium pricing strategies, payoffs of providers, and corresponding demands of end users in each interaction model. The analysis reveals that demand and payoffs are non-decreasing functions of advertisement revenue. For sufficiently high advertisement revenue, the IoTSP offers its service free of cost in all models. However, payoffs and demand vary across different models. The paper demonstrates that demand and WSP payoffs are highest in the pull (push, resp.) model in the low (high, resp.) advertisement revenue regime. The IoTSP payoff is always higher in the pull model regardless of advertisement revenue. The CSP payoff is highest in the hybrid model in the low advertisement revenue regime. However, in the high advertisement revenue regime, the CSP payoff in the hybrid or push model can be higher, depending on the chosen equilibrium in the push model.

title: Cosmological ensemble and directional averages of observables
Abstract: This paper demonstrates that at second order, ensemble averages of observables and directional averages do not commute due to gravitational lensing. title: Algebraic quantum field theory in curved spacetimes
Abstract: This paper establishes the framework of algebraic quantum field theory in curved spacetimes based on the concept of local covariance. Within this framework, a quantum field theory is modeled as a functor from a category of spacetimes to a category of ($C^*$)-algebras, satisfying specific conditions. The paper explores various aspects of this framework, including: (a) a detailed description of the key idea of relative Cauchy evolution and its relation to the stress-energy tensor; (b) a systematic "rigidity argument" generalizing results from flat to curved spacetimes; (c) a detailed discussion of physical state selection, linking notions of stability at different scales; (d) the formalization of subtheories and global gauge transformations; and (e) a demonstration that the framework excludes the existence of a single preferred state in each spacetime if state selection is local and covariant. The paper illustrates these ideas using the free Klein-Gordon theory, presenting a new "universal definition" for it.

title: Optimality of the Laplace Mechanism in Differential Privacy
Abstract: The interconnected nature of the Internet of Things (IoT) raises significant privacy concerns regarding the exchange of sensitive information. The Laplace mechanism, which adds Laplace-distributed artificial noise to sensitive data, is a widely used method for providing privacy guarantees within the framework of differential privacy. This paper introduces Lipschitz privacy, a slightly tighter version of differential privacy. It proves that the Laplace mechanism is optimal in minimizing the mean-squared error for identity queries that provide privacy with respect to the $\\ell_{1}$-norm. The paper further investigates the $\\ell_{2}$-norm, which provides privacy for high-dimensional data, and demonstrates that a variation of the Laplace mechanism achieves optimal mean-squared error for identity queries in this context. Finally, it derives the optimal mechanism for scenarios where individuals submit their high-dimensional sensitive data.

title: MORE: Merged Opinions Reputation Model
Abstract: Reputation, generally defined as a group's opinion on a particular aspect of something, is the focus of this paper, which presents a reputation model based on probabilistic modeling of opinions. The model incorporates three key concepts: (1) opinion value decays over time, (2) the reputation of the opinion source impacts its reliability, and (3) opinion certainty influences its weight relative to other opinions. The model is flexible in its use of opinion sources, allowing for both explicit and implicit opinions extracted from agent behavior in domains with sparse explicit opinions. The paper illustrates this with an approach to extract opinions from behavioral information in the sports domain, specifically football. One application of a reputation model is behavior prediction. The paper tackles the challenge of predicting football team behavior in matches, arguing that this is a challenging but interesting approach for evaluating the model. |||

title: Nonlinear time-series analysis revisited
Abstract:
Nonlinear time-series analysis, pioneered in 1980 and 1981, uses dynamical systems theory to analyze univariate data. This approach, built on the concept of state-space reconstruction, allows us to calculate essential quantities like Lyapunov exponents and fractal dimensions. It also enables time-series prediction and, in some cases, reconstruction of the equations of motion. However, limitations arise from factors like signal quality, noise, and numerical algorithm imperfections. Nonetheless, nonlinear time-series analysis has been successfully applied to numerous real and synthetic datasets across diverse domains, from roulette wheels to lasers and human hearts. Even when data don't fully meet the mathematical and algorithmic requirements, this analysis offers valuable insights for understanding, characterizing, and predicting dynamical systems. ||| 
Optically induced motion in pristine single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWNTs) on the macro-scale and the subsequent separation of metallic and semiconducting-enriched SWNT aggregates are reported. Experiments demonstrate both positive and negative photophoresis of SWNTs in solution, meaning movement away from or towards light, respectively. This motion is found to be dependent on light frequency and intensity. Aggregates of pristine SWNTs, moving under UV and visible lamps, were separated and analyzed using absorption and Raman spectroscopy. The separated aggregates exhibit enrichment in metallic or semiconducting SWNTs depending on the lamp's spectral frequency. Photophoresis in selective SWNTs demonstrates a direct relationship between illumination frequency and the absorption of specific nanotubes. The observed phenomenon is further validated using pre-separated metallic and semiconducting SWNTs in solution. Metallic SWNTs show enhanced photophoresis under an UV lamp, while pre-separated semiconductor SWNTs exhibit motion under a mercury lamp with broadband visible frequencies. However, under an IR lamp, both metallic and semiconducting-enriched SWNTs display continuous motion, similar to unseparated pristine SWNTs, where no specificity is observed. ||| 
The integration of sensing and computing capabilities is enabling the embedding of increasing computational power into smaller devices. This allows sensing devices not only to passively capture data at high resolution but also to take sophisticated actions in response. Combined with advancements in communication, this gives rise to a highly interconnected ecosystem of devices known as the Internet of Things (IoT). Simultaneously, breakthroughs in machine learning facilitate the development of models utilizing ever-increasing amounts of data. Consequently, devices ranging from heavy assets like aircraft engines to wearables like health monitors are capable of generating massive datasets and leveraging aggregate analytics to improve their performance over time. Big data analytics has been identified as a key enabler for the IoT. This chapter examines various avenues within the IoT where big data analytics is already making a significant impact or is poised to do so. It also discusses social implications and areas of concern. ||| 
This polemical response to Travis Norsen's critique of Howard Wiseman's paper addresses the titular question. Norsen's response acknowledges the distinct nature of Bell's 1964 theorem from his 1976 theorem, conceding that the former lacks a rigorous presentation of the EPR argument. This aligns with the author's previous work emphasizing the different interpretations of "Bell's theorem" between "operationalists" and "realists."  While this agreement is encouraging, several points of contention remain, including the ambiguity of "locality" prior to 1964 and the assumptions made by Einstein in the paper cited by Bell in 1964. These issues, along with their relation to Bell's theorem, are further discussed. ||| 
Wireless communications, a remarkably successful technology, has witnessed exponential growth in traffic for over a century, a phenomenon known as Cooper's law. This trend is poised to continue driven by innovative applications like augmented reality and the Internet of Things. Massive MIMO (multiple-input multiple-output) has been identified as a crucial technology to handle the massive increase in data traffic. Despite its prominence within the communication community, Massive MIMO faces several common misconceptions. This article debunks ten widespread myths surrounding the technology, explaining why they are inaccurate. It also addresses a crucial question for practical adoption, emphasizing the need for future research to provide a definitive answer. Key technical papers supporting the claims are referenced, while a comprehensive list of related overview and technical papers can be found at the Massive MIMO Info Point: http://massivemimo.eu. ||| 
The derivation of the differential-valued field $\mathbb{T}_{\log}$ of logarithmic transseries induces a specific map $\psi$ on its value group $\Gamma_{\log}$. The structure $\Gamma = (\Gamma_{\log}, \psi)$ constitutes a divisible asymptotic couple. This paper builds upon the previous work in \cite{gehret}, which initiated a study of the first-order theory of $(\Gamma_{\log}, \psi)$.  It proves that the theory $T_{\log} = \operatorname{Th}(\Gamma_{\log}, \psi)$ has a universal axiomatization, is model complete, and admits elimination of quantifiers (QE) in a natural first-order language. The paper also addresses the question of whether $T_{\log}$ possesses the Non-Independence Property (NIP), answering affirmatively. The proof relies on a comprehensive analysis of the 1-types of $T_{\log}$, which, in the presence of QE, is equivalent to characterizing all simple extensions $\Gamma\langle\alpha\rangle$ of $\Gamma$. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that $T_{\log}$ lacks the Steinitz exchange property and examines the relationship between models of $T_{\log}$ and the precontraction groups discussed in \cite{kuhlmann1}. ||| 
The growing popularity of anime makes it susceptible to undesirable uses such as copyright violations and pornography. This necessitates the development of methods for detecting and recognizing animation characters. Skin detection is a crucial step in this process. While methods for detecting human skin color exist, they are ineffective for anime characters. Anime skin exhibits significant variations in color, texture, tone, and under different lighting conditions.  Furthermore, non-skin elements like leather, shirts, and hair can have colors similar to skin. This paper proposes three new methods that successfully identify anime character skin compared to existing methods like Kovac, Swift, Saleh, and Osman, which are primarily designed for human skin detection. The proposed methods are based on RGB values and their comparative relationships. ||| 
This paper focuses on the category Pos-$S$, consisting of $S$-posets and $S$-poset maps, where $S$ is a pomonoid. The paper characterizes pomonoids where all projectives in Pos-$S$ are generator or free.  It further investigates regular injectivity and weakly regularly $d$-injectivity, leading to homological classification results for pomonoids. The paper establishes relationships between regular injectivity in the slice category Pos-$S/B_S$ and generators or cyclic projectives in Pos-$S$. ||| 
This manuscript explores the properties of the pullback functor $\Pi_B: \mathcal{E} \rightarrow \mathcal{E}/B$ in relation to topology, where $j$ is a Lawvere-Tierney topology on an arbitrary topos $\mathcal{E}$, $B$ is an object of $\mathcal{E}$, and $j_B = j \times 1_B$ is the induced topology on the slice topos $\mathcal{E}/B$. For a left cancelable class $\mathcal{M}$ of all $j$-dense monomorphisms in $\mathcal{E}$, the paper derives necessary and sufficient conditions for $(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{M}^{\perp})$ to be a factorization system in $\mathcal{E}$, relating it to factorization systems in slice topoi $\mathcal{E}/B$, where $B$ ranges over the objects of $\mathcal{E}$.  The paper proves that an arrow $f : X \rightarrow B$ in $\mathcal{E}$ is a $j_B$-sheaf whenever the graph of $f$ is a section in $\mathcal{E}/B$, and the object of sections $S(f)$ of $f$ is a $j$-sheaf in $\mathcal{E}$. The paper introduces a class of monomorphisms in $\mathcal{E}$ called $j$-essential and explores their equivalent forms and properties. It also demonstrates that any presheaf in a presheaf topos has a maximal essential extension. Finally, the paper discusses similarities and differences between the obtained results and those achieved using a (productive) weak topology $j$ instead of a topology. ||| 
This paper investigates the transverse spatial profile of down-converted light produced by noncollinear, degenerate, Type-I spontaneous parametric down-conversion in two types of nonlinear crystals: beta barium borate (BBO) and bismuth triborate (BiBO). The study finds that BBO produces a circular down-conversion pattern, while BiBO generates an elliptical pattern. This difference is attributed to the angle-independent refractive index experienced by daughter photons in BBO, compared to the angle-dependent refractive index in BiBO. The transverse spatial profile of the generated light is imaged to determine the eccentricity produced by each crystal, and a model is developed to explain the observed behavior. This model predicts a specific wavelength for which the eccentricity from BiBO is nearly zero. The paper also examines the potential impact of the elliptical ring pattern produced in BiBO on polarization entanglement for experimental setups collecting biphotons around the entire down-conversion ring. It demonstrates that polarization entanglement quality, measured by the overlap integral of the spectra of the two rings, can remain high (>99.4%) around the entire ring, albeit with a reduced biphoton rate. ||| 
This paper provides a rigorous formulation of the intuitive notion that a differentiable map is equivalent to a locally, or infinitesimally, linear map.  Analogous to linear maps respecting addition and scalar multiplication in vector spaces or modules, a locally linear map respects two canonical operations defined "over" its domain. These operations are composition laws of a canonical groupoid and a scaled action category, forming a canonical double category.  Local linear algebra (of first order) explores these double categories and their morphisms, offering a purely algebraic and conceptual (i.e., categorical and chart-independent) approach to first-order differential calculus.  Subsequent work will investigate the higher-order theory using higher multiple categories. ||| 
This paper proposes a statistical approach to tornado modeling for predicting and simulating tornado occurrences and accumulated cost distributions over time intervals.  This is achieved by modeling the tornado intensity, measured using the Fujita scale, as a stochastic process.  Since the Fujita scale categorizes tornado intensity into six states, Markov and semi-Markov models can be employed. The paper demonstrates that the semi-Markov approach effectively reproduces the duration effect observed in tornado occurrences. The superiority of the semi-Markov model compared to the Markov chain model is further confirmed through a statistical hypothesis test. As an application, the paper calculates the expected value and variance of costs generated by tornadoes over a given time interval in a specific area. This research contributes to the literature by highlighting the effectiveness of semi-Markov models for both physical analysis of tornadoes and estimation of economic damages to human infrastructure. ||| 
Zdenek Svestka's research significantly impacted various fields of solar physics, particularly flare research. This article examines five key areas of interest for Svestka, comparing his insights with modern advancements. While his contributions were insightful, contemporary knowledge has surpassed his initial understanding in many areas. Svestka's own perspectives on his research journey were published recently in this journal, to which he contributed greatly. His memoir provides additional scientific and personal information, as documented in Svestka (2010). ||| 
The digital fabrication era faces challenges due to the limited affordability, accessibility, and usability of its media. While 3D fabrication media (DFM) like 3D printers have gained popularity, 3D scanners remain expensive and difficult to operate. This paper introduces the RhoScanner Project, an affordable and efficient Three-dimensional Projective Scanner for Smart-phones, highlighting the potential for expanding the capabilities of digital fabrication media in everyday use. ||| 
This paper provides a detailed description of the structure of $\aleph_0$-categorical trees and cycle-free partial orders. It examines the maximal branches of $\aleph_0$-categorical trees followed by the configuration of ramification orders. These elements are then combined to provide necessary and sufficient conditions for a tree to be $\aleph_0$-categorical. The classification of $\aleph_0$-categorical cycle-free partial orders is derived as a corollary. ||| 
This paper evaluates the performance of four methods used to measure mass segregation in star-forming regions: the radial variation of the mass function $\mathcal{M}_{\rm MF}$, the minimum spanning tree-based $\Lambda_{\rm MSR}$ method, the local surface density $\Sigma_{\rm LDR}$ method, and the $\Omega_{\rm GSR}$ technique. While all methods are proposed for quantifying mass segregation, they often produce conflicting results due to their distinct measurement objectives.  The paper applies each method to synthetic star-forming regions to identify their shortcomings. When a star-forming region is smooth and centrally concentrated, all four methods accurately identify mass segregation. However, in spatially substructured regions, the $\Omega_{\rm GSR}$ method fails due to its arbitrary grouping definitions and disregard of positional information for massive stars. The paper also shows that the $\Lambda_{\rm MSR}$ and $\Sigma_{\rm LDR}$ methods can sometimes yield apparently contradictory results due to their different definitions of mass segregation. The paper concludes that only $\Lambda_{\rm MSR}$ measures mass segregation in the classical sense, without requiring the definition of a region's center, although $\Sigma_{\rm LDR}$ provides insights into the extent of previous dynamical evolution within a star-forming region. ||| 
The Internet of Things (IoT), encompassing machine-to-machine and human-to-machine computing, has ushered in a modern-day smart industry where humanoids can seamlessly cooperate, coexist, and interact. This burgeoning field of smart communication is driving the development of smart things, with numerous projects underway. This paper presents GOptimaEmbed, a novel smart database management system (DBMS) designed for intelligent querying of databases in device-constrained embedded systems.  GOptimaEmbed leverages genetic algorithms as its primary search engine and simplifies the query process using a stored in-memory model based on a device-dependent Short-messaging-Structured Query Language (SMS SQL) schema translator. Querying is performed over the air using an integrated GSM module within the smart space. The system has been successfully applied to query a plant database. ||| 
Inspired by research surrounding Igusa's local zeta function, this paper introduces topological representation zeta functions of unipotent algebraic groups over number fields. These group-theoretic invariants encapsulate common features of established $p$-adic representation zeta functions associated with pro-$p$ groups derived from unipotent groups. The paper investigates fundamental properties of the topological zeta functions and develops a method for computing them under non-degeneracy assumptions.  As an application, the paper provides a complete classification of topological representation zeta functions of unipotent algebraic groups with dimensions up to six. ||| 
This study explores the use of natural language to give instructions that can be interpreted by Internet of Things (IoT) devices in a domestic "smart home" environment. The paper posits that reminders can be considered a form of end-user programming, where executed actions can be performed either by an automated agent or the reminder's author. An experiment was conducted where participants wrote sticky notes specifying future actions in their homes. These notes were addressed to themselves, others, or a computer agent under different conditions. The study analyzes the linguistic features and strategies employed to achieve these tasks, including the use of graphical resources as an informal visual language. The findings provide design guidance for end-user development within the Internet of Things. ||| 
Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) are essential components of the emerging Internet of Things (IoT) paradigm.  They are widely used across various application domains. While WSNs are typically deployed to support specific applications, the growing power of WSN nodes necessitates research into how multiple applications can share the same WSN infrastructure. Virtualization offers a potential solution for enabling this sharing. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of WSN virtualization, reviewing the state-of-the-art and discussing research issues in depth. It introduces the fundamentals of WSN virtualization and illustrates its relevance with carefully selected scenarios. Existing works are presented in detail and critically evaluated based on a set of requirements derived from these scenarios. Pertinent research projects are also reviewed, and several research issues are discussed along with suggestions for tackling them. |||

title: Node.DPWS: High performance and scalable Web Services for the IoT
Abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) promises to revolutionize our lives by connecting devices and enabling new services. However, challenges related to performance, scalability, usability, and interoperability arise. This paper presents Node.DPWS, a Node.js-based implementation of the Devices Profile for Web Services (DPWS) that addresses these challenges. Node.DPWS allows for the deployment of lightweight, efficient, and scalable Web Services across heterogeneous nodes, including resource-constrained devices. Its performance is evaluated on typical embedded devices, comparing it with alternative DPWS toolkits.

title: Realizations via Preorderings with Application to the Schur Class
Abstract: We extend Agler's function algebra concept to include products, similar to the practice in real algebraic geometry. This extension, called a preordering, is defined over abstract sets without requiring any additional properties, such as analyticity. Realization theorems provide equivalent characterizations of the unit ball (the Schur-Agler class) of these algebras. These include Agler decompositions, transfer function representations, and analogues of the von Neumann inequality. The key addition is the use of matrix-valued "auxiliary test functions" in constructing transfer functions. These realization theorems can be strengthened for applications to Pick-type interpolation problems, among others. The domain of principle examples is the polydisk $\\mathbb D^d$. The algebras then include $H^\\infty(\\mathbb D^d,\\mathcal{L(H)})$ (where the unit ball is traditionally known as the Schur class) and $A(\\mathbb D^d,\\mathcal{L(H)})$, the multivariable analogue of the disk algebra. As an application, it is shown that over the polydisk $\\mathbb D^d$, (weakly continuous) representations that are $2^{d-2}$ contractive are completely contractive (thus having a commuting unitary dilation), providing a fresh perspective on examples like Parrott's of contractive representations of $A(\\mathbb D^3)$ that are not completely contractive.

title: An Interoperable Realization of Smart Cities with Plug and Play based Device Management
Abstract: The lack of interoperability, particularly at the device level, poses a significant obstacle for Internet of Things (IoT) solutions in smart cities. While numerous platforms from various manufacturers exist, the ecosystem remains largely closed. This paper proposes SNaaS (Sensor/Network as a Service), a service layer designed to enable plug-and-play infrastructure across platforms from multiple vendors. This facilitates interoperability and enables the successful deployment of large-scale city-wide IoT systems. To properly position this new service layer, the paper presents a high-level reference IoT architecture for smart city implementations, followed by workflow details of SNaaS and preliminary microbenchmarks.

title: Heuristic Algorithm using Internet of Things and Mobility for solving demographic issues in Financial Inclusion projects
Abstract: Globally, the population in rural and semi-urban areas presents a significant challenge for policymakers as they require the most technological support to improve their living conditions. Financial inclusion projects aim to address this issue. However, the reach of financial institutions in these areas is significantly lower than in urban areas. New policies and strategies are being developed to make banking services more accessible to people in rural and semi-urban areas. Technology, particularly the Internet of Things (IoT) and mobility, can play a crucial role in this context as an enabler and multiplier. This paper explores an IoT and mobility-driven approach that financial institutions may consider when developing financial inclusion projects.

title: SciRecSys: A Recommendation System for Scientific Publication by Discovering Keyword Relationships
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach for discovering relationships between keywords in scientific publications based on a Markov Chain model. Keywords are fundamental elements for representing abstract entities like documents, user profiles, topics, and more. This model effectively combines four important factors in scientific publications: content, publicity, impact, and randomness. It also presents SciRecSys, a recommendation system designed to assist users in efficiently finding relevant articles.

title: Dissipative dark matter explains rotation curves
Abstract: This study investigates dissipative dark matter, where dark matter particles interact with a massless (or very light) boson. This type of dark matter can arise in simple hidden sector gauge models, including those featuring an unbroken $U(1)'$ gauge symmetry, leading to a dark photon. Previous research has shown that these models can explain large-scale structure (LSS) and cosmic microwave background (CMB) observations, potentially also addressing dark matter phenomena on smaller scales, like the inferred cored structure of dark matter halos. In this picture, dark matter halos of disk galaxies cool through dissipative interactions and are heated by ordinary supernovae (facilitated by an assumed photon-dark photon kinetic mixing interaction). This interaction between the dark matter halo and ordinary baryons, a unique feature of these models, plays a critical role in determining the physical properties of the dark matter halo. This paper further explores the implications of dissipative dark matter for disk galaxies. Building on previous work, a simple formalism is developed to describe the effects of dissipative dark matter in a fairly model-independent way. This formalism is then applied to generic disk galaxies and specific examples, including NGC 1560 and a sample of dwarf galaxies from the LITTLE THINGS survey. The findings indicate that dissipative dark matter effectively accounts for the rotation curves of the galaxies considered. It explains the linear rise of the rotational velocity of dwarf galaxies at small radii and can also explain the observed wiggles in rotation curves that are known to be correlated with corresponding features in the disk gas distribution.

title: Object-Oriented Networking
Abstract: This paper proposes the Object-Oriented Networking (OON) framework, aiming to meet the generalized interconnection, mobility, and technology integration requirements of the Internet. In OON, various objects accessed through the Internet (content, smart things, services, people, etc.) are treated as network layer resources rather than application layer resources, as in the IP communications model. Abstracting them as computing objects with attributes and methods, these objects are identified by expressive, discoverable names, while data is exchanged between them in the context of their methods based on suitably defined system-specific names. An OON-enabled Internet is not only a global data delivery medium but also a universal object discovery and service development platform. Service-level interactions can be achieved through native network means, eliminating the need for standardized protocols. OON can be implemented using existing software-defined networking or network functions virtualization technologies and can be deployed incrementally.

title: Note on a Family of Monotone Quantum Relative Entropies
Abstract: Lewin and Sabin studied the relative entropy defined by $\\mathcal{H}(A,B)=\\text{Tr} [ \\varphi(A) - \\varphi(B) - \\varphi\'(B)(A-B) ]$, where $\\varphi$ is a convex function and $A$ and $B$ are Hermitian matrices. They proved that this quantity is monotone if and only if $\\varphi\'$ is operator monotone. This monotonicity property enables the proper definition of $\\mathcal{H}(A,B)$ for self-adjoint bounded operators on an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space through a limiting procedure. Specifically, for an increasing sequence of finite-dimensional projections $\\lbrace P_n \\rbrace_{n=1}^{\\infty}$ with $P_n \\to 1$ strongly, the limit $\\lim_{n \\to \\infty} \\mathcal{H}(P_n A P_n, P_n B P_n)$ is shown to exist and be independent of the sequence of projections $\\lbrace P_n \\rbrace_{n=1}^{\\infty}$. The question of whether this sequence converges to its "obvious" limit, namely $\\text{Tr} [ \\varphi(A)- \\varphi(B) - \\varphi\'(B)(A-B) ]$, remained unanswered. This paper provides a positive answer in principle, demonstrating that $\\lim_{n \\to \\infty} \\mathcal{H}(P_n A P_n, P_n B P_n) = \\text{Tr}[ \\varphi(A) - \\varphi(B) - \\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d} \\alpha} \\varphi( \\alpha A + (1-\\alpha)B )|_{\\alpha = 0} ]$. If the operators $A$ and $B$ are sufficiently regular, meaning that $(A-B)$, $\\varphi(A)-\\varphi(B)$, and $\\varphi\'(B)(A-B)$ are trace-class, the identity $\\text{Tr}[ \\varphi(A) - \\varphi(B) - \\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d} \\alpha} \\varphi( \\alpha A + (1-\\alpha)B )|_{\\alpha = 0} ] = \\text{Tr} [ \\varphi(A)- \\varphi(B) - \\varphi\'(B)(A-B) ]$ holds.

title: Non-existence of isometry-invariant Hadamard states for a Kruskal black hole in a box and for massless fields on 1+1 Minkowski spacetime with a uniformly accelerating mirror
Abstract: We conjecture that, with a suitable adaptation of the notion of a Hadamard state, there is no isometry-invariant Hadamard state for the massive or massless covariant Klein-Gordon equation defined on the region of the Kruskal spacetime to the left of a surface of constant Schwarzschild radius in the right Schwarzschild wedge, when Dirichlet boundary conditions are imposed on that surface. We also prove that, with a suitable definition of 'boost-invariant Hadamard state' (which we call 'strongly boost-invariant globally-Hadamard'), accounting for both the existence of the timelike boundary and the special massless 1+1 infra-red pathology, there is no such state for the massless wave equation on the region of 1+1 Minkowski space to the left of an eternally uniformly accelerating mirror, with Dirichlet boundary conditions. This result is significant because such a state exists if there is also a symmetrically placed decelerating mirror in the left wedge (and the region to the left of this mirror is excluded). We expect a similar existence result to hold for Kruskal when there are symmetrically placed spherical boxes in both right and left Schwarzschild wedges. Our Kruskal no-go conjecture raises fundamental questions about black holes in boxes, as considered in black hole thermodynamics. If true, it would further support the conclusion of B.S. Kay 'Instability of enclosed horizons', Gen. Rel. Grav. 47, 1-27 (2015) (arXiv: 1310.7395) that the closest description of a black hole in equilibrium in a box, using a classical spacetime with quantum fields propagating on it, has, for the classical spacetime, the exterior Schwarzschild solution, with the classical spacetime picture breaking down near the horizon. An appendix points out the existence of, and partially fills, a gap in the proofs of the theorems in B.S. Kay and R.M. Wald Phys. Rep. 207, 49-136 (1991).

title: Comment on arXiv:1301.3829 and Reply to 'Comment on "Can disorder really enhance superconductivity?"' arXiv:1501.05148 by I.M. Suslov
Abstract: In arXiv:1301.3829 and arXiv:1501.05148, I.M. Suslov proposes a theoretical description of the interplay between disorder and superconductivity, which claims to predict situations where superconductivity is enhanced by disorder. This comment shows that Suslov's results do not provide any sound predictions regarding this problem. Suslov also suggests that the percolation approach, recently employed by the authors to compute the global critical temperature of inhomogeneous superconductors induced by weak multifractality, is inadequate. This opinion is refuted using simple ideas from the Bardeen-Cooper-Schiaffer (BCS) theory of superconductivity. Importantly, the authors' theory makes quantitative analytical predictions for observables like the global critical temperature and the spatial distribution of the order parameter. Their work can be easily confirmed or refuted through numerical or experimental studies.

title: Orthogonal bases of Brauer symmetry classes of tensors for groups having cyclic support on non-linear Brauer characters
Abstract: This paper investigates properties of Brauer symmetry classes of tensors. Using this formula, the necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of the o-basis of Dicyclic groups, Semi-dihedral groups, and Dihedral groups are investigated. Criteria for the non-vanishing elements in the Brauer symmetry classes of tensors associated with these groups are also included.

title: Twisted algebras and Rota-Baxter type operators
Abstract: The concept of a weak pseudotwistor for an algebra $(A, \\mu)$ in a monoidal category $\\mathcal{C}$ is introduced, defined as a morphism $T:A\\otimes A\\rightarrow A\\otimes A$ in $\\mathcal{C}$, satisfying axioms that ensure $(A, \\mu \\circ T)$ is also an algebra in $\\mathcal{C}$. This concept generalizes the previous notion of pseudotwistors and encompasses a wider range of twisted algebras, including examples provided by Rota-Baxter operators and related operators like Leroux's TD-operators and Reynolds operators. Using weak pseudotwistors, an equivalence relation called "twist equivalence" is introduced for algebras in a given monoidal category.

title: Block-Level Unitary Query: Incorporating Orthogonal-like Space-time Code with Query Diversity for MIMO Backscatter RFID
Abstract: The emerging field of the Internet of Things (IoT) necessitates more reliable and data-intensive backscatter RFID technology. Motivated by this need, orthogonal space-time block code (OSTBC), known for its low complexity and high performance in mobile communications, has been investigated for backscatter RFID. A recently proposed scheme called unitary query has demonstrated its ability to significantly improve the reliability of backscatter radio by utilizing query diversity. Combining classical OSTBC (at the tag end) with unitary query (at the query end) appears promising. However, this paper demonstrates that directly employing OSTBC with unitary query results in a linear decoding problem, leading to severe performance degradation. As a redesign of the recently proposed unitary query and classical OSTBC specifically for MIMO backscatter RFID, the paper introduces the BUTQ-mOSTBC design pair. This pair comprises a block-level unitary query (BUTQ) at the query end and the corresponding modified OSTBC (mOSTBC) at the tag end. The proposed BUTQ-mOSTBC resolves the linear decoding problem, maintains the simplicity and high performance characteristics of classical OSTBC, and achieves query diversity for the $M \\times L \\times N$ MIMO backscatter RFID channel.

title: Color Image Enhancement Using the lrgb Coordinates in the Context of Support Fuzzification
Abstract: Image enhancement is a crucial step in image processing. Histogram equalization is a well-known automated method that simultaneously modifies brightness and contrast for monochrome images and brightness, contrast, saturation, and hue for color images. Simple and efficient methods can be achieved using affine transforms within logarithmic models. The coordinate system used for color space representation is vital in determining the affine transform for color images. Using RGB coordinates leads to simultaneous modification of luminosity and saturation. This paper proposes using the lrgb perceptual coordinates to define affine transforms that enable separate modification of luminosity (l) and saturation (s), where saturation is calculated using the rgb component in the chromatic plane. Improved results can be obtained by defining partitions on the image support and processing pixels separately in each window within the defined partition. Classical partitions often lead to discontinuities at window boundaries. To avoid these issues, classical partitions can be replaced by fuzzy partitions. These partitions use fuzzy windows, with an affine transform defined in each window using parameters based on the fuzzy mean, fuzzy variance, and fuzzy saturation computed for the pixels within the analyzed window. The final image is obtained by weighted summation of the images from each fuzzy window.

title: "Bring it on": Explaining persistence in science at the intersection of identity and epistemology
Abstract: Research has documented a significant decline in students' interest and persistence in science, particularly among students from underrepresented populations, starting in middle school. title: Wholeness as a Hierarchical Graph to Capture the Nature of Space

This paper defines wholeness as a hierarchical graph, where individual centers are represented as nodes and their relationships as directed links. This hierarchical graph derives its name from the inherent scaling hierarchy revealed by the head/tail breaks, a classification scheme and visualization tool for data with a heavy-tailed distribution. Abstract: Despite its remarkable achievements, the Standard Model of Particle Physics cannot be considered a complete theory of fundamental interactions. Among other limitations, it fails to describe gravitational interaction and relies on 19 parameters. The Standard Model includes 12 fermions (matter elementary particles with spin $\\frac{1}{2}$), which are divided into three generations, groups with identical interactions but varying masses. Each generation can be classified into two leptons (with electric charges $Q=-1$, electron-like, and $Q=0$, neutrino) and two quarks (with electric charges $Q=-\\frac{1}{3}$, down-type, and $Q=\\frac{2}{3}$, up-type). However, the understanding of the relationship between generations and the ratio of masses of different generations remains unknown. This paper demonstrates a simple relationship between masses of different generations that depends solely on the electric charges for $Q=-1,\\,\n\\, Q=-\\frac{1}{3}$, and $Q=\\frac{2}{3}$. This relationship exhibits good agreement with experimental data. Assuming that the same relation holds for $Q=0$, we can calculate neutrino masses. Therefore, our findings could pave the way for further investigations beyond the Standard Model.

In addition to handling these issues, stakeholders must also address other lifecycle aspects, such as changes in application requirements and deployed devices. However, existing approaches only address limited subsets of these challenges when applied to the IoT. This paper proposes an integrated approach for addressing these challenges. The primary contributions of this paper are: (1) a development methodology that separates IoT application development into distinct concerns and provides a conceptual framework for application development, (2) a development framework that implements the development methodology to support the actions of stakeholders. The development framework offers a set of modeling languages to specify each development concern and abstracts the scale and heterogeneity-related complexity. It integrates code generation, task-mapping, and linking techniques to provide automation. Code generation supports the application development phase by producing a programming framework that enables stakeholders to focus on the application logic, while our mapping and linking techniques collectively support the deployment phase by generating device-specific code, resulting in a distributed system collaboratively hosted by individual devices. Our extension preserves the principal type system's key characteristic: type inference remains independent of the policy being enforced. title: Micro-location for Internet of Things equipped Smart Buildings
Abstract: Micro-location involves pinpointing the location of an entity with high accuracy (potentially in centimeters), while geofencing creates a virtual boundary around a Point of Interest (PoI). This paper delves into various micro-location enabling technologies and services, exploring how they can accelerate the integration of the Internet of Things (IoT) into smart buildings. We argue that micro-location-based location-aware solutions can significantly enhance the experience for tenants of an IoT-equipped smart building. These advanced technologies can facilitate minimal tenant actions for smart building control. We also highlight existing and envisioned services facilitated by micro-location enabling technologies. Additionally, we address the challenges posed by these technologies and propose potential solutions for their seamless integration with IoT-enabled smart buildings.

title: Research-based assessment affordances and constraints: Perceptions of physics faculty
Abstract: To empower faculty to effectively utilize research-based materials, we investigate their perceived needs and desires, leveraging this information to suggest ways for the Physics Education Research community to address these requirements. When research-based resources align well with faculty's perceived needs, adoption rates increase. Through phenomenographic interviews with ordinary physics faculty and department chairs, we identified four categories of issues that faculty face regarding research-based assessments (RBAs). Firstly, many faculty are interested in using RBAs but require practical guidance on how to do so: finding resources, identifying available options, and administering them. They seek support in addressing these practical needs. Secondly, many faculty perceive limitations in RBAs, believing they do not measure various factors they value or are not applicable in their specific courses. They desire assessments that measure skills, perceptions, and specific concepts. Thirdly, numerous faculty seek to engage with communities of other faculty and experts to interpret assessment results and explore alternative assessment approaches. They aim to normalize their assessment outcomes by comparing them with others and engaging with faculty from other institutions to learn about their assessment practices. Lastly, many faculty consider their courses within the broader context of accountability and their departmental structures. They seek support for assessment within these broader contexts. We also discuss how faculty roles within their departments and types of institutions influence their perceived wants and needs around assessment.

title: Optimal eigen expansions and uniform bounds
Abstract: Let $\{X_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} \in \mathbb{L}^2(\mathcal{T})$ be a stationary process with associated lag operators $\{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}_h\}$. We establish uniform asymptotic expansions of the corresponding empirical eigenvalues and eigenfunctions under near-optimal conditions on the lag operators, expressed in terms of the eigenvalues (spectral gap). Moreover, the underlying dependence assumptions are optimal, encompassing both short and long memory processes. This allows us to study the relative maximum deviation of the empirical eigenvalues under highly general conditions. Notably, we demonstrate convergence to an extreme value distribution, enabling the construction of simultaneous confidence sets. We further discuss how these asymptotic expansions transfer to the long-run covariance operator $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}$ within a general framework.

title: Concept-oriented programming: from classes to concepts and from inheritance to inclusion
Abstract: For decades, programmers have modeled real-world entities using hierarchies of classes and object-oriented programming (OOP) languages, represented as trees. This paper introduces a novel programming paradigm called concept-oriented programming (COP), which generalizes classes and inheritance by introducing concepts and inclusion, respectively.

title: Function of Forgetfulness for the Tedium of Oblivion on Liquidity of Ontology Matching
Abstract: The shallow and fragile knowledge prevalent on the web lacks in-depth examination of concepts, exhibiting a superficial approach. The web's environment fosters a fleeting attention span, making it difficult to concentrate for extended periods as we are trained to "surf" without delving deeper. While the web offers near-infinite knowledge availability, it leads to a decline in the ability to retain and evaluate that knowledge, resulting in increasing forgetfulness. This paper explores how the "function of forgetfulness" appears linked to tedium and the oblivion of knowledge through the fluidity of ontology matching.

title: Head/tail Breaks for Visualization of City Structure and Dynamics
Abstract: The world around us exhibits significant variation, leading to a greater abundance of smaller things compared to larger ones—for instance, there are far more small cities than large ones globally. This dramatic variation is often referred to as fractal or scaling. To better reveal this fractal or scaling structure, we introduce a new classification scheme called head/tail breaks. This scheme recursively derives different classes or hierarchical levels. Head/tail breaks work as follows: divide entities into a few large ones in the head (those above the average) and many small ones (those below the average) in the tail. Recursively continue this division process for the large ones (or the head) until the notion of far more small things than large things is violated. This paper argues that head/tail breaks can be a powerful visualization tool for illustrating the structure and dynamics of natural cities. Natural cities are naturally or objectively defined human settlements based on a meaningful cutoff averaged from a massive amount of units extracted from geographic information. To demonstrate the effectiveness of head/tail breaks in visualization, several case studies are presented using natural cities derived from points of interest, social media location data, and time series nighttime images. The paper further elaborates on head/tail breaks in relation to fractals, beauty, and big data. Keywords: Big data, social media, nighttime images, natural cities, fractals, head/tail breaks, ht-index
