title: The Structurally Dynamic Cellular Network and Quantum Graphity Approaches to Quantum Gravity and Quantum Geometry - A Review and Comparison
Abstract: Starting from the working hypothesis that both physics and its corresponding mathematics, particularly geometry, must be described using discrete concepts at the Planck scale, one of the many challenges in this endeavor is finding the discrete protoforms of the building blocks of our ordinary continuum physics and mathematics, residing on a smooth background. Perhaps more importantly, we need to discover how this continuum limit emerges from the aforementioned discrete structure. We model this underlying substratum as a structurally dynamic cellular network (essentially a generalization of a cellular automaton). We consider these continuum concepts, especially continuum spacetime, as emergent, coarse-grained, and derived relative to this underlying erratic and disordered microscopic substratum, which we refer to as quantum geometry. This substratum is expected to adhere to different rules, namely generalized cellular automaton rules. A central role in our analysis is played by a geometric renormalization group, which creates, among other things, a sparse translocal network of correlations between points in classical continuous spacetime. In our view, this network underlies mysterious phenomena like holography and the black hole entropy-area law. The same perspective holds for quantum theory, which we also regard as a low-energy, coarse-grained continuum theory, emerging from something more fundamental. This paper reviews our approach and compares it to the quantum graphity framework.

title: Event Specific Multimodal Pattern Mining with Image-Caption Pairs
Abstract: This paper presents a novel framework and algorithms for discovering image patch patterns from a large corpus of weakly supervised image-caption pairs generated from news events. While existing pattern mining techniques aim to find patterns that are representative and discriminative, we stipulate that our discovered patterns should be recognizable by humans and preferably accompanied by meaningful names. We propose a novel multimodal pattern mining approach that leverages the descriptive captions often accompanying news images to learn semantically meaningful image patch patterns. These multimodal patterns are then named using words extracted from the associated image captions for each pattern. A novel evaluation framework demonstrates that our patterns are 26.2% more semantically meaningful than those discovered by state-of-the-art vision-only pipelines. We also show that we can provide tags for the discovered image patches with 54.5% accuracy without direct supervision. Our methods uncover named patterns beyond those covered by existing image datasets like ImageNet. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first algorithm developed to automatically mine image patch patterns that possess strong semantic meaning specific to high-level news events and subsequently evaluate these patterns based on that criteria.

title: Exoplanet Exploration Program Analysis Group (ExoPAG) Report to Paul Hertz Regarding Large Mission Concepts to Study for the 2020 Decadal Survey
Abstract: This document summarizes the reports from the three Astrophysics Program Analysis Groups (PAGs) in response to the "Planning for the 2020 Decadal Survey" directive issued by the Astrophysics Division Director Paul Hertz. This joint executive summary presents points of consensus across all three PAGs. Additional findings specific to individual PAGs are detailed separately in their respective reports. The PAGs agree that all four large mission concepts identified in the white paper as candidates for maturation before the 2020 Decadal Survey should be studied in detail. These include the Far-IR Surveyor, the Habitable-Exoplanet Imaging Mission, the UV/Optical/IR Surveyor, and the X-ray Surveyor. This conclusion is based on assumptions outlined in the white paper and subsequent charge, namely that 1) major development of future large flagship missions under consideration will follow the implementation phases of JWST and WFIRST; 2) NASA will collaborate with the European Space Agency on its L3 Gravitational Wave Surveyor; and 3) the Inflation Probe will be classified as a probe-class mission to be developed according to the 2010 Decadal Survey report. If these key assumptions were to change, this PAG finding would require reassessment. The PAGs find strong community support for the second phase of this activity—maturation of the four proposed mission concepts through Science and Technology Definition Teams (STDTs). There is a strong consensus among the PAGs that all STDTs include broad and interdisciplinary representation of the science community. Finally, the PAGs find community support for a line of Probe-class missions within the Astrophysics mission portfolio (condensed). |||

title: How Resonance-Continuum Interference Changes 750 GeV Diphoton Excess: Signal Enhancement and Peak Shift
Abstract: The interference between the scalar resonance contribution and the continuum background in the $gg \rightarrow \gamma \gamma$ process significantly affects the diphoton signal at the LHC 13 TeV. The interference can either enhance or suppress the diphoton signal rate due to the imaginary part, and distort the resonance shape due to the real part. Using two benchmark models, two Higgs doublets with $\sim$50 GeV widths and a singlet scalar with 5 GeV width, both extended with vector-like fermions, we find that the resonance contribution to the 750 GeV excess can be enhanced by a factor of 2 (1.6) for 3 (6) fb signal rate. The 68% (95%) CL best-fit mass range can shift by 1-4 (any ${\cal O}$(1)) GeV. The significance of these interference effects increases if the best-fit excess rate decreases with future data. These interferences provide a consistency check of a resonance hypothesis, whether or not future precision shape measurements confirm a Breit-Wigner shape or reveal interesting deviations.

title: Polarization Engineering in Nano-Scale Waveguides Using Lossless Media
Abstract: A novel device that achieves controllable rotation of the state of polarization by rotating the orientation of the eigenmodes of a waveguide by 45 degrees is introduced and analyzed. This device, implementable using lossless materials at the nanoscale, circumvents the inherent polarization dependence of photonic devices on the silicon-on-insulator platform. Two polarization rotator-based schemes are proposed and evaluated for polarization engineering: (1) A multi-purpose device, with dimensions on the order of a few wavelengths, functioning as a polarization splitter or an arbitrary linear polarization state generator; and (2) An energy-efficient optical modulator that utilizes eigenmode rotation and epsilon near zero (ENZ) effects to achieve high extinction ratio, polarization-insensitive amplitude modulation without the need for geometry sweeping to match TE and TM mode attributes. Using indium tin oxide (ITO) as a tunable material, the proposed modulator provides polarization-insensitive operation and can be realized with a modulation bandwidth of 112 GHz, a length of 1800 nm, an energy per bit of 7.5 fJ, and an optical bandwidth of 210 nm.

title: De novo visual proteomics in single cells through pattern mining
Abstract: Cryo-electron tomography enables three-dimensional visualization of cells in a near-native state at molecular resolution. Cellular tomograms provide detailed information about all macromolecular complexes, including their structures, abundances, and specific spatial locations within the cell. However, extracting this information is challenging, and current methods typically rely on templates of known structures. This paper formulates a template-free visual proteomics analysis as a de novo pattern mining problem and proposes a new framework called "Multi Pattern Pursuit" for proteome-scale de novo discovery of macromolecular complexes in cellular tomograms without using templates of known structures. Tests on simulated and experimental tomograms demonstrate that the proposed method is a promising tool for template-free visual proteomics analysis.

title: Optimised multi-ion cavity coupling
Abstract: Recent advancements in cavity quantum electrodynamics (CQED) pave the way for utilizing multiple quantum emitters confined within a single optical cavity. Controlling the quantum mechanical coupling of individual emitters to the cavity mode is crucial in such systems. Combining ion trap technologies with CQED offers a promising approach due to the well-established motional control over trapped ions. This work experimentally demonstrates the coupling of up to five trapped ions in a string to a high-finesse optical cavity. By changing the axial position and spacing of the ions in a fully deterministic manner, the coupling to the cavity mode is systematically characterized through visibility measurements of the cavity emission. The results, in good agreement with the theoretical model, demonstrate that the geometrical configuration of multiple trapped ions can be manipulated to achieve optimal cavity coupling. This system presents a new platform for exploring CQED with multiple quantum emitters, enabled by the highly controllable collective light-matter interaction.

title: Unitary-Scaling Decomposition and Dissipative Behaviour in Finite-Dimensional Linblad Dynamics
Abstract: This paper investigates the decomposition of a unital Lindblad dynamical map of an open quantum system into two distinct types of mapping on the Hilbert-Schmidt space of quantum states. One component corresponds to reversible behaviors, while the other corresponds to irreversible characteristics. For a finite-dimensional system, real vectors or Bloch representations are employed, and the dynamical map on the state space is expressed as a real matrix acting on the representation. The real-polar decomposition reveals that rotation and scaling transformations on the real vector space form building blocks for the dynamical map. Consequently, the change in linear entropy or purity, indicative of dissipative behaviors, depends solely on the scaling part of the dynamical matrix. The rate of change of the entropy depends on the structure of the scaling part, such as eigensubspace partitioning, and its relationship with the initial state. Specifically, the linear entropy is expressed as a weighted sum of exponential-decay functions in each scaling component, where the weight is equal to $|\vec{x}_k(\rho)|^2$ of the initial state $\rho$ in the subspace. The dissipative behaviors and the partition of eigensubspaces in the decomposition are discussed and illustrated for qubit systems.

title: Magidor-Malitz Reflection
Abstract: This paper examines the consequences and consistency of the downward Löwenheim-Skolem theorem for extending first-order logic with the Magidor-Malitz quantifier. The paper derives combinatorial results and improves the known upper bound for the consistency of Chang's Conjecture at successor of singular cardinals.

title: A CP-conserving multi-Higgs model without real basis
Abstract: Models beyond the Standard Model (bSM) often involve elaborate Higgs sectors, which can be a source of CP violation. This raises the question of efficiently identifying whether a model exhibits CP violation. There is a common belief that explicit CP invariance is linked to the existence of a basis where all coefficients are real. A decade-old theorem claims that the scalar sector of any multi-Higgs doublet model is explicitly CP-conserving if and only if all its coefficients can be made real by a basis change. This belief is reinforced by the fact that all specific multi-Higgs models considered so far comply with this claim. This paper presents the first counterexample to this statement: a CP-conserving three-Higgs-doublet model for which no real basis exists. The paper outlines the phenomenological consequences of this model and notes that the extra neutral Higgs bosons are neither CP-even nor CP-odd but are "half-odd" under the generalized CP-symmetry of the model.

title: On a notion of toric special linear systems
Abstract: This note studies linear systems on complete toric varieties $X$ with an invariant point, whose orbit under the action of the automorphism group of $X$ contains the dense torus $T$ of $X$. The paper characterizes such varieties in terms of their defining fan and introduces a new definition of expected dimension of linear systems that considers the contribution given by certain toric subvarieties. Finally, the paper studies degenerations of linear systems on these toric varieties induced by toric degenerations.

title: Maximum entropy analysis of cosmic ray composition
Abstract: This paper focuses on the primary composition of cosmic rays with the highest energies that cause extensive air showers in the Earth's atmosphere. It presents a method for examining the two lowest order moments of the sample distribution of the depth of shower maximum. The aim is to demonstrate that useful information about the composition of the primary beam can be inferred with limited knowledge about the underlying processes. A superposition model is used to describe how the moments of the depth of shower maximum depend on the type of primary particles and their energies. By applying the principle of maximum entropy, the paper determines what trends in the primary composition are consistent with the input data, relying on a limited amount of information from shower physics. The capabilities and limitations of the proposed method are discussed. To achieve a realistic description of the primary mass composition, special attention is paid to the choice of parameters in the superposition model. The paper presents two examples that illustrate the consequences for energy-dependent changes in the primary composition.

title: A global $SU(3)/U(3)$ flavor symmetry analysis for $B\to PP$ with $η-η'$ Mixing
Abstract: A large amount of new experimental data on $B$ decay into two light pseudoscalar ($P$) mesons has been collected by the LHCb collaboration. This data confirms information on $B_{u,d} \rightarrow PP$ decays obtained earlier by B-factories at KEK and SLAC, and provides new information on $B_s \rightarrow PP$ as well as more decay modes with $P$ being $\eta$ or $\eta'$. Using this new data, the paper performs a global fit for $B \rightarrow PP$ to determine decay amplitudes within the framework of $SU(3)/U(3)$ flavor symmetry. The paper finds that $SU(3)$ flavor symmetry can explain the data well. The annihilation amplitudes are found to be small as expected. Several CP violating relations predicted by $SU(3)$ flavor symmetry are in good agreement with the data. Current available data can give constraints on the amplitudes which induce $P = \eta, \; \eta'$ decays in the framework of $U(3)$ flavor symmetry, and can also determine the $\eta-\eta'$ mixing angle $\theta$ with $\theta = (-18.4 \pm 1.2)^\circ$. Several $B \rightarrow PP$ decay modes which have not been measured are predicted with branching ratios accessible at the LHCb. These decays can provide further tests for the framework of $SU(3)/U(3)$ flavor symmetry for $B$ decays.

title: Corrections to the thermodynamics of Schwarzschild-Tangherlini black hole and the generalized uncertainty principle
Abstract: This paper investigates the thermodynamics of the Schwarzschild-Tangherlini black hole in the context of the generalized uncertainty principle (GUP). The corrections to the Hawking temperature, entropy, and heat capacity are obtained using the modified Hamilton-Jacobi equation. These modifications reveal that GUP alters the evolution of the Schwarzschild-Tangherlini black hole. Specifically, the GUP effect becomes significant when the radius or mass of the black hole approaches the Planck scale, leading to the black hole ceasing radiation and forming a remnant. The Planck scale remnant can be confirmed through analysis of the heat capacity. These phenomena imply that GUP may offer a solution to the information paradox. The paper also investigates the possibility of observing the black hole at the LHC and finds that it cannot be produced at the current LHC.

title: Galerkin Methods for Boltzmann-Poisson transport with reflection conditions on rough boundaries
Abstract: This paper focuses on the mathematical and numerical modeling of reflective boundary conditions (BC) associated with Boltzmann-Poisson systems, including diffusive reflection in addition to specularity, in the context of electron transport in semiconductor device modeling at nano scales, and their implementation in Discontinuous Galerkin (DG) schemes. The paper studies these BC on the physical boundaries of the device and develops a numerical approximation to model an insulating boundary condition, or equivalently, a pointwise zero flux mathematical condition for the electron transport equation. This condition balances the incident and reflective momentum flux at the microscopic level, pointwise at the boundary, in the case of a more general mixed reflection with momentum-dependent specularity probability $p(\vec{k})$. The paper compares the computational prediction of physical observables given by the numerical implementation of these different reflection conditions in the DG scheme for BP models and observes that the diffusive condition influences the kinetic moments over the entire domain in position space.

title: Surface brightness profiles of blue compact dwarf galaxies in the GOODS-N and GOODS-S field
Abstract: This paper investigates the structural properties of the underlying hosts of 34 blue compact dwarf (BCD) galaxies using deep near-infrared (NIR) photometry. The BCD sample is selected from the Cosmic Assembly Near-IR Deep Extragalactic Legacy Survey in the Great Observatories Origins Deep Survey North and South fields. The paper extracts the surface brightness profile (SBP) in the optical F 435W and NIR F 160W bands. The SBPs of BCDs in the H band reach 26 mag arcsec^-2 at the 3$\sigma$ level, representing the deepest NIR imaging of BCDs to date. The SBPs are then fitted with one- and two-component Sersic models. Approximately half of the BCDs favor the two-component model, which significantly improves the fit quality. The effective radii of the underlying hosts of BCDs in the B band are smaller than those of early-type dwarfs (dEs) and dwarf irregulars at a fixed luminosity. This discrepancy aligns with findings in previous studies. However, the difference in structural parameters between BCDs and other dwarf galaxies appears less significant in the H band. Moreover, a remarkable agreement is observed between the underlying hosts of BCDs and dEs. All dwarf galaxies seem to follow a similar luminosity-radius relationship, suggesting a unified structural evolution for dwarf galaxies. The paper concludes that a possible evolution track from BCDs to dEs cannot be ruled out, with no significant change of structure needed in the evolutionary scenario.

title: Light Stop Mass Limits from Higgs Rate Measurements in the MSSM: Is MSSM Electroweak Baryogenesis Still Alive After All?
Abstract: This paper investigates the implications of the Higgs rate measurements from Run 1 of the LHC for the mass of the light scalar top partner (stop) in the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM). The paper focuses on light stop masses and decouples the second, heavy stop and the gluino to the multi-TeV range to obtain a Higgs mass of around 125 GeV. The paper derives lower mass limits for the light stop within various scenarios, taking into account the effects of a possibly light scalar tau partner (stau) or chargino on the Higgs rates, of additional Higgs decays to undetectable new physics, as well as of non-decoupling of the heavy Higgs sector. Under conservative assumptions, the stop can be as light as 123 GeV. Relaxing certain theoretical and experimental constraints, such as vacuum stability and model-dependent bounds on sparticle masses from LEP, the paper finds that the light stop mass can be as light as 116 GeV. These indirect limits are complementary to direct limits on the light stop mass from collider searches and have important implications for electroweak baryogenesis in the MSSM as a possible explanation for the observed matter-antimatter asymmetry of the Universe.

title: Finite amplitude method applied to giant dipole resonance in heavy rare-earth nuclei
Abstract: The quasiparticle random phase approximation (QRPA), within the framework of the nuclear density functional theory (DFT), has been a standard tool for accessing the collective excitations of atomic nuclei. Recently, the finite amplitude method (FAM) has been developed to perform QRPA calculations efficiently without any truncation on the two-quasiparticle model space. This paper discusses the nuclear giant dipole resonance (GDR) in heavy rare-earth isotopes, for which the conventional matrix diagonalization of the QRPA is numerically demanding. The role of the Thomas-Reiche-Kuhn (TRK) sum rule enhancement factor, connected to the isovector effective mass, is also investigated. The electric dipole photoabsorption cross section was calculated within a parallelized FAM-QRPA scheme, employing the Skyrme energy density functional self-consistently in the DFT calculation for the ground states and FAM-QRPA calculation for the excitations. The mean GDR frequency and width are mostly reproduced with the FAM-QRPA, when compared to experimental data, although some deficiency is observed with isotopes heavier than erbium. The role of the TRK enhancement factor in actual GDR strength is clearly shown: its increment leads to a shift of the GDR strength to a higher-energy region, without a significant change in the transition amplitudes. The newly developed FAM-QRPA scheme demonstrates remarkable efficiency, enabling systematic analysis of GDR for heavy rare-earth nuclei. The theoretical deficiency of the photoabsorption cross section could not be improved by only adjusting the TRK enhancement factor, suggesting the necessity of a beyond-self-consistent QRPA approach or a more systematic optimization of the EDF parameters.

title: Dynamic Time-Dependent Route Planning in Road Networks with User Preferences
Abstract: Tremendous progress has been made in algorithmic methods for computing driving directions on road networks. Most of this work focuses on time-independent route planning, assuming a constant cost per query on each arc. However, in practice, current traffic situations significantly influence travel time on large parts of the road network, and these situations change throughout the day. Traffic congestion can be predicted using historical traffic data, but unpredictable events, such as accidents, can also contribute to congestion. This paper studies the dynamic and time-dependent route planning problem, which accounts for both prediction (based on historical data) and live traffic. The paper proposes a practical algorithm that, while robust to user preferences, can integrate global changes in the time-dependent metric (e.g., due to traffic updates or user restrictions) faster than previous approaches, allowing for subsequent queries that enable interactive applications.

title: Miura-type transformations for lattice equations and Lie group actions associated with Darboux-Lax representations
Abstract: Miura-type transformations (MTs) are essential tools in the theory of integrable nonlinear partial differential and difference equations. This paper presents a geometric method for constructing MTs for differential-difference (lattice) equations from Darboux-Lax representations (DLRs) of such equations. The method is applicable to parameter-dependent DLRs satisfying certain conditions. The paper constructs MTs and modified lattice equations from invariants of some Lie group actions on manifolds associated with such DLRs. Using this construction, from a given suitable DLR one can obtain many MTs of different orders. The main idea behind this method is closely related to the results of Drinfeld and Sokolov on MTs for the partial differential KdV equation. Examples considered include the Volterra, Narita-Itoh-Bogoyavlensky, Toda, and Adler-Postnikov lattices. Some of the constructed MTs and modified lattice equations appear to be new.

title: Unoccupied electronic structure and signatures of topological Fermi arcs in the Weyl semimetal candidate Mo$_x$W$_{1-x}$Te$_2$
Abstract: Weyl semimetals have sparked intense research interest, but experimental work has been limited to the TaAs family of compounds. Recent theoretical works predict that compounds in the Mo$_x$W$_{1-x}$Te$_2$ series are Weyl semimetals. These proposals are particularly exciting because Mo$_x$W$_{1-x}$Te$_2$ has a quasi two-dimensional crystal structure well-suited to many transport experiments, while WTe$_2$ and MoTe$_2$ have already been the subject of numerous proposals for device applications. However, available ARPES techniques make it challenging to demonstrate a Weyl semimetal in Mo$_x$W$_{1-x}$Te$_2$. According to predictions, the Weyl points are above the Fermi level, the system approaches two critical points as a function of doping, there are many irrelevant bulk bands, the Fermi arcs are nearly degenerate with bulk bands, and the bulk band gap is small. This paper studies Mo$_x$W$_{1-x}$Te$_2$ for $x = 0.07$ and 0.45 using pump-probe ARPES. The system exhibits a dramatic response to the pump laser, and the paper successfully accesses states $> 0.2$eV above the Fermi level. For the first time, the paper observes direct, experimental signatures of Fermi arcs in Mo$_x$W$_{1-x}$Te$_2$, which agree well with theoretical calculations of the surface states. However, the interpretation of these features depends sensitively on free parameters in the surface state calculation. The paper comments on the prospect of conclusively demonstrating a Weyl semimetal in Mo$_x$W$_{1-x}$Te$_2$.

title: Geometry from Information Geometry

title: Repositories with Direct Representation

title: Pairing Dynamics of Polar States in a Quenched p-wave Superfluid Fermi Gas
Abstract: We investigate the pairing dynamics of polar states in a single-species p-wave superfluid Fermi gas after a sudden change in interaction strength. The anisotropic pair interaction, combined with the centrifugal barrier, creates fundamentally different pairing dynamics compared to the s-wave case. Depending on the quench direction, quenches to the BCS regime result in either a significant oscillatory depletion of momentum occupation within the Fermi sea or a substantial filling of momentum occupation. Our research highlights the critical role of the resonant state, supported by the centrifugal barrier, in these pairing dynamics.

title: Cosmology and stellar equilibrium using Newtonian hydrodynamics with general relativistic pressure
Abstract: We re-examine the analysis conducted by Hwang and Noh (JCAP 1310 (2013)), which aimed to construct a Newtonian set of equations incorporating the pressure effects characteristic of General Relativity. We explicitly derive the Hwang-Noh equations, comparing them to similar calculations found in the literature. We then analyze: i) cosmological expansion, ii) linear cosmological perturbation theory, and iii) stellar equilibrium using the new set of equations. We compare these results to those obtained from standard Newtonian theory, Neo-Newtonian theory, and General Relativity. Our findings reveal that the predictions for the Universe's background evolution significantly differ from General Relativity: the acceleration of the Universe is achieved with positive pressure. However, the behavior of small cosmological perturbations closely resembles the relativistic context, albeit only at small scales. We argue that this last result could pave the way for new numerical simulations for structure formation in the Universe. Finally, while Hwang-Noh equations qualitatively reproduce neutron star properties, their upper mass limit is at least an order of magnitude higher than that determined by General Relativity.

title: Fast atom diffraction inside a molecular beam epitaxy chamber, a rich combination
Abstract: This paper reviews two key contributions of grazing incidence fast atom diffraction (GIFAD) to molecular beam epitaxy (MBE): its ability to provide in-situ, precise descriptions of atomic-scale surface topology and its capacity to monitor larger-scale changes in surface roughness during layer-by-layer growth. We summarize recent experimental and theoretical results obtained for the He atom beam incident along the highly corrugated $[ 1\bar{1}0 ]$ direction of the $\beta_{2}(2\times4)$ reconstructed GaAs(001) surface. These results are complemented by measurements and calculations for beam incidence along the weakly corrugated [010] direction, where a periodicity twice as small as expected is observed. The combination of experiment, quantum scattering matrix calculations, and semiclassical analysis allows us to reveal structural characteristics of the surface.  For in-situ GIFAD measurements during MBE of GaAs on GaAs surfaces, we analyze changes in elastic and inelastic contributions in the scattered beam, as well as variations in the diffraction pattern in polar angle scattering. This analysis highlights the robustness, simplicity, and richness of GIFAD as a technique for monitoring layer-by-layer epitaxial growth.

title: Z'-induced FCNC decays of top, beauty and strange quarks
Abstract: Anomalous b --> s transitions observed in LHCb data hint at the existence of a new massive gauge boson Z' that couples to the left-handed b --> s current. This implies a coupling to the t --> c current as well. This paper investigates flavor-changing neutral current (FCNC) decays of the top quark induced by a Z' boson, specifically t --> c Z', within the framework of a gauged L_mu - L_tau symmetry model (the difference between muon and tauon numbers) with vector-like quarks. This model was introduced to explain the anomalous LHCb data. We demonstrate that searching for t --> c Z' via Z' --> mu^+ mu^- using LHC Run 1 data can already probe a parameter region unexplored by B physics for Z' masses around O(10) GeV or more. We extend the model to very light Z' with masses below 400 MeV, motivated by the muon g-2 anomaly.  Considering rare B and K meson decay data, we derive upper limits on the t --> c Z' branching ratio for the light Z' case and discuss its observability at the LHC. title: Roberge-Weiss transition in $N_\text{f}=2$ QCD with Wilson fermions and $N_τ=6$

The RW endpoint is found to be a triple point connecting the deconfinement/chiral transitions in the heavy/light quark mass regions, transitioning into a second-order endpoint for intermediate masses. These regimes are separated by two tricritical values of the quark mass, determined through a finite size scaling analysis of the Binder cumulant of the imaginary part of the Polyakov loop. The study explains a previously observed finite size effect in the scaling of the Binder cumulant and reveals a shift in the tricritical masses towards smaller values compared to coarser lattices. title: Computing the $L_1$ Geodesic Diameter and Center of a Polygonal Domain

The algorithms leverage several interesting observations regarding L1 shortest paths in polygonal domains.

title: The unreasonable effectiveness of hydrodynamics in heavy ion collisions

Further analysis using the 2+1 Lagrangian hydrodynamic code v-USPhydro confirms this robustness, showing that anisotropic flow coefficients are only sensitive to long wavelength scales and are minimally impacted by variations in the initial local Knudsen number. The robustness of the results supports the effectiveness of the nearly perfect fluid paradigm in heavy ion collisions.

title: Frames of translates with prescribed fine structure in shift invariant spaces

The study then focuses on characterizing finite sequences where the norms of the vectors are fixed, leading to a determination of optimal SG Bessel sequences with minimal spectral spread. The spread is measured using a convex potential induced by the FSI subspace and an arbitrary convex function.

title: Generalization of the Brauer Theorem to Matrix Polynomials and Matrix Laurent Series

title: Mass measurements of neutron-rich Rb and Sr isotopes

title: Policy documents as sources for measuring societal impact: How often is climate change research mentioned in policy-related documents?

title: $E_6$ Inspired SUSY Benchmarks, Dark Matter Relic Density and a 125 GeV Higgs

title: The risk of divergence

title: A Stochastically Evolving Non-local Search and Solutions to Inverse Problems with Sparse Data

title: Observation of the Singly Cabibbo-Suppressed Decay $D^{+}\toωπ^{+}$ and Evidence for $D^{0}\toωπ^{0}$

title: Quantum walled Brauer algebra: commuting families, Baxterization, and representations

title: Structural topography-mediated high temperature wetting symmetry breaking
Abstract: Controlling the movement of liquid droplets is crucial in various industrial processes. The broken wetting symmetry at high temperatures causes the droplet to preferentially move towards the region with higher heat transfer. Experimental and analytical findings confirm that the droplet's trajectory is intricately linked to the interplay between the surface topography and its imposed thermal state. This fundamental understanding and ability to control droplet dynamics at high temperatures represent a significant advancement, enabling the rational design of surfaces for multifunctional applications, particularly in high-temperature thermal systems where energy efficiency, safety, and stability are paramount.

title: Vector Leptoquarks and the 750 GeV Diphoton Resonance at the LHC

The study finds that specific parameter space can explain the correct cross-section for a putative 750 GeV resonance decaying to photons, consistent with unitarity, Higgs boson properties, and direct resonance searches in other channels. Furthermore, it demonstrates that constraints can be imposed on any Beyond the Standard Model explanation of the 750 GeV resonance, where the only new particles are scalars, which are strong enough to entirely rule out certain model types.

title: Automatic Inference of Specifications in the K Framework
Abstract: Formal specifications, despite their numerous benefits, are not widely used in industrial software development. The analysis of KernelC programs explains the execution of a modifier function using observer routines within the program. This technique is implemented in the Kindspec 2.0 tool, which generates axioms describing the precise input/output behavior of C routines handling pointer-based structures, including result values and state changes. title: Query Stability in Monotonic Data-Aware Business Processes [Extended Version]

Different restrictions are considered, including negation in conditions, cyclic executions, read access to written data, the presence of pending process instances, and the ability to start new process instances. The study identifies facet combinations where stability of conjunctive queries is decidable and provides encodings into Datalog variants that are optimal regarding the problem's worst-case complexity.

title: Predicting the Co-Evolution of Event and Knowledge Graphs
Abstract: Embedding learning, also known as representation learning, has proven effective in modeling large-scale semantic knowledge graphs. A key concept is mapping the knowledge graph into a tensor representation, where entries are predicted by models using latent representations of generalized entities. Traditionally, knowledge graphs are treated as static, expanding with more links as new facts become available but considering the ground truth values associated with links as time-invariant. This paper addresses the challenge of knowledge graphs where triple states depend on time. It assumes that changes in the knowledge graph always arrive in the form of events, acting as the gateway to the knowledge graph. An event prediction model is trained, leveraging both knowledge graph background information and recent event data. By predicting future events, the model also predicts likely changes in the knowledge graph, providing a model for its evolution. Experiments demonstrate the approach's effectiveness in clinical, recommendation engine, and sensor network applications.

title: GENIE Production Release 2.10.0

title: A dynamic Bayesian Markov model for health economic evaluations of interventions in infectious disease
Abstract: Health economic evaluations of interventions against infectious diseases often rely on predictions from ordinary differential equation (ODE) systems or Markov models (MMs). While standard MMs are static, ODE systems are dynamic and account for herd immunity, crucial for preventing overestimation of infection prevalence. However, complex ODE systems with probabilistic model parameters are computationally demanding. Therefore, literature mainly presents ODE-based models with deterministic parameters, neglecting parameter uncertainty, hindering probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA), a crucial component of health economic evaluations. This research presents a dynamic MM within a Bayesian framework, extending a static MM by incorporating the force of infection into the state allocation algorithm. The output reflects dynamic changes in prevalence, thus accounting for herd immunity. Unlike deterministic ODE-based models, PSA can be conducted directly. A case study of a fictional sexually transmitted infection compares the dynamic Bayesian MM to deterministic and Bayesian ODE systems, calibrated to time series data. The case study shows that the methodology produces outcomes comparable to the "gold standard" Bayesian ODE system. Unlike ODE systems in the literature, the dynamic MM setting is probabilistic with manageable computational effort, including calibration. The Bayesian ODE system's runtime is 44 times longer.

title: Minimally packed phases in holography
Abstract: This research numerically constructs asymptotically AdS black brane solutions of D=4 Einstein-Maxwell theory coupled to a pseudoscalar. The study analyzes the three-dimensional moduli space of lattice solutions, which are generally oblique. For a specific magnetic field value, the free energy is minimized by the triangular lattice, associated with minimal packing of circles in the plane. The average stress tensor for the thermodynamically preferred phase is shown to be that of a perfect fluid, applicable more generally to spontaneously generated periodic phases. The triangular structure persists at low temperatures, indicating the existence of novel crystalline ground states.

title: Standard Model in multiscale theories and observational constraints
Abstract: This research explores the Standard Model of electroweak and strong interactions in multiscale spacetimes with (i) weighted derivatives and (ii) q-derivatives. Both theories can be formulated in two different frames, called fractional and integer pictures. By definition, the fractional picture is where physical predictions should be made. In the theory with weighted derivatives, gauge invariance and the requirement of constant masses in all reference frames make the Standard Model in the integer picture indistinguishable from the ordinary one. Experiments involving only weak and strong forces are insensitive to a change of spacetime dimensionality even in the fractional picture, and only the electromagnetic and gravitational sectors can break the degeneracy. For the simplest multiscale measures with only one characteristic time, length, and energy scale, the Lamb shift in the hydrogen atom is computed, and the multiscale correction to the ordinary result is constrained, resulting in an absolute upper bound. Stronger bounds are obtained from measuring the fine-structure constant. In the theory with q-derivatives, considering the muon decay rate and the Lamb shift in light atoms, independent absolute upper bounds are obtained. For a specific fractional exponent value, the Lamb shift alone yields specific bounds.

title: Thermoelectric transport signatures of Dirac composite fermions in the half-filled Landau level
Abstract: The half-filled Landau level is expected to exhibit approximate particle-hole symmetry, requiring an extension of the Halperin-Lee-Read (HLR) theory of the compressible state observed at this filling. Recent research suggests that when particle-hole symmetry is preserved, composite Fermions experience a quantized π-Berry phase upon winding around the composite Fermi-surface, analogous to Dirac fermions at the surface of a 3D topological insulator. Conversely, the effective low-energy theory of the composite fermion liquid initially proposed by HLR lacks particle-hole symmetry and has a vanishing Berry phase. This paper explains how thermoelectric transport measurements can be used to test the Dirac nature of the composite Fermions by quantitatively extracting this Berry phase. It highlights that longitudinal thermopower (Seebeck effect) is non-vanishing due to the unusual nature of particle-hole symmetry in this context and is insensitive to the Berry phase. In contrast, off-diagonal thermopower (Nernst effect) is directly related to the topological structure of the composite Fermi surface, vanishing for zero Berry phase and reaching its maximum value for π Berry phase. While purely electrical transport signatures show Berry phase contributions as small corrections to a large background signal, the Nernst effect offers a promising diagnostic tool for the Dirac nature of composite fermions.

title: Vector Dark Matter through a Radiative Higgs Portal

title: LHC diphotons from electroweakly pair-produced composite pseudoscalars

The model predicts significant numbers of 4-photon events from the decays of pseudoscalar pairs, as well as same-sign dilepton pairs at slightly lower invariant mass, or multijet signals, originating from decays of charge-2 pseudoscalars. These states and their decays are crucial for avoiding stable charged baryon-like relics in the new confining sector. A neutral baryon-like dark matter candidate with a mass roughly proportional to the number of colors multiplied by 375 GeV is a further prediction of the model for SU(Nc) confining gauge groups.

title: Forging the Link between Nuclear Reactions and Nuclear Structure
Abstract: This paper provides a review of recent applications of the dispersive optical model (DOM), focusing on the nonlocal implementation of the DOM, which accurately describes ground-state properties when data like the nuclear charge density is available. The DOM, developed by Claude Mahaux, provides a unified description of both elastic nucleon scattering and structural information related to single-particle properties below the Fermi energy. The paper introduces a nonlocal dispersive optical potential for both the real and imaginary parts. Nonlocal absorptive potentials yield equivalent elastic differential cross sections for 40Ca compared to local ones but change the l-dependent absorption profile, suggesting significant implications for analyzing nuclear reactions. Below the Fermi energy, nonlocality is crucial for accurately representing particle number and nuclear charge density. Spectral properties implied by (e,e'p) and (p,2p) reactions are correctly described, including the energy distribution of approximately 10% high-momentum protons obtained at Jefferson Lab. The nonlocal DOM allows a complete description of experimental data both above (up to 200 MeV) and below the Fermi energy in 40Ca. The research further demonstrates that elastic nucleon-nucleus scattering data constrain the spectral strength in the continuum of orbits nominally bound in the independent-particle model. Extending this analysis to 48Ca allows for the prediction of this nucleus's neutron skin, which is larger than most existing predictions.

title: Lattice QCD on Non-Orientable Manifolds
Abstract: A common issue in lattice QCD simulations on the torus is the extremely long autocorrelation time of the topological charge when approaching the continuum limit due to suppressed tunneling between topological sectors. This problem can be circumvented by replacing the torus with a different manifold, altering the connectivity of the configuration space. This can be achieved using open boundary conditions on the fields, as previously proposed. This approach has the side effect of significantly breaking translational invariance. This research proposes using a non-orientable manifold and shows how to define and simulate lattice QCD on it. Simulations demonstrate a drastic reduction in the autocorrelation time. A key feature of the new proposal is the preservation of translational invariance up to exponentially small corrections. A Dirac-fermion on a non-orientable manifold poses a numerical challenge: the fermion determinant becomes complex. The paper suggests two approaches to address this issue.

title: Mobile Cloud Business Process Management System for the Internet of Things: A Survey
Abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) represents a comprehensive environment comprising a vast number of smart devices connecting heterogeneous physical objects to the internet. However, past BPMS have not adequately considered the challenges they will face in managing large-scale connected heterogeneous IoT entities. Without fully understanding the behavior, capabilities, and state of IoT entities, BPMS may fail to manage the integrated IoT information systems. This paper analyzes existing BPMS for IoT, identifying their limitations and drawbacks from a Mobile Cloud Computing perspective. It then discusses open challenges in BPMS for IoT.

title: An index obstruction to positive scalar curvature on fiber bundles over aspherical manifolds

The proof relies on a new variant of the multi-partitioned manifold index theorem, potentially of independent interest. Additionally, an analogous statement is presented for codimension one submanifolds. The paper also discusses basic obstructions using the A-genus of certain submanifolds.

title: Realizing posets as prime spectra of Leavitt path algebras
Abstract: This research naturally associates a directed graph EP to any partially ordered set (P, ≤) (where the vertices of EP correspond to elements of P, and the edges of EP correspond to related pairs of elements of P) and then describes the prime spectrum of the resulting Leavitt path algebra LK(EP). This construction allows for the realization of a broad class of partially ordered sets as the prime spectra of rings. Specifically, any partially ordered set where every downward directed subset has a greatest lower bound, and these greatest lower bounds satisfy certain compatibility conditions, can be realized in this way. title: Dynamical interstellar medium with Gaia and ground-based massive spectroscopic stellar surveys
Abstract: The ongoing Gaia mission of ESA will provide precise spatial and kinematical information for a large fraction of stars in the Milky Way galaxy. Studies of interstellar extinction and line absorption towards numerous stars at varying distances and directions can create a 3-dimensional distribution map of interstellar absorbers, achieving similar spatial precision. Under certain morphologies, such as geometrically thin absorption curtains, a complete velocity vector can be inferred from its radial velocity component, yielding dynamical information comparable to stars. However, observations of many stars at different distances are needed to determine the location of absorption pockets. Therefore, techniques are required to measure interstellar absorptions towards cool stars, which are abundant. A complex mix of colliding absorption clouds is found in the Galactic plane. Therefore, starting with deep observations to detect the weak but simpler interstellar absorptions at high Galactic latitudes is recommended. Finally, interstellar atomic line absorption studies toward cool stars in the optical are largely limited to Sodium and Potassium doublets, not covered by many surveys, including Gaia. Diffuse interstellar bands can provide similar information to interstellar atomic absorption lines. Combining both approaches might highlight differences in the dynamics of various interstellar medium components. Notably, the Gaia DIB at 862 nm can be used to build absorption maps, as demonstrated by RAVE. Additionally, several ground-based surveys, such as APOGEE, Gaia-ESO, and Galah, are upgrading this approach. Utilizing this new information can significantly advance our understanding in various areas, including the determination of star membership in clusters, studies of a few Myr old supernova remnants, and investigations of Galactic fountains.

title: Supersymmetric $SO(10)$-inspired leptogenesis and a new $N_2$-dominated scenario
Abstract: This study investigates the supersymmetric extension of SO(10)-inspired thermal leptogenesis, exploring constraints on neutrino parameters and the reheating temperature (TRH) derived from the condition of successful leptogenesis from next-to-lightest right-handed (RH) neutrino (N2) decays and the more stringent constraints when independence of the initial conditions (strong thermal leptogenesis) is imposed. In the latter case, increasing the lightest right-handed neutrino (N1) decay parameters helps wash out a pre-existing asymmetry, relaxing constraints compared to the non-supersymmetric case. Significant changes occur, particularly for large tanβ values (≳ 15). Specifically, for normal ordering, the atmospheric mixing angle can now be maximal as well. The lightest (ordinary) neutrino mass is still constrained within a specific range, corresponding to a specific range for the sum of neutrino masses. Inverted ordering remains disfavored, but an allowed region satisfying strong thermal leptogenesis opens up at large tanβ values. The study also examines the lower bound on TRH, finding a specific value independently of the initial N2 abundance. Finally, it proposes a new N2-dominated scenario where the N1 mass is lower than the sphaleron freeze-out temperature. In this case, there is no N1 wash-out, and a specific lower bound on TRH is found. These findings suggest that SO(10)-inspired thermal leptogenesis can be made compatible with the upper bound from the gravitino problem, a crucial result given the role often played by supersymmetry in achieving a realistic model of fermion masses.

title: Off-resonant many-body quantum carpets in strongly tilted optical lattices

The study shows that dipole wavefunction evolution in the short-time limit is ballistic, and finite size effects induce dynamical self-interference patterns known as quantum carpets. It also presents the effects of the boundary right after the first reflection, demonstrating that the wavefunction diffuses normally, with the variance changing linearly over time. This work expands the rich physical phenomenology of tilted one-dimensional lattice systems into a scenario of many interacting quantum particles, known as the many-body Wannier-Stark system. |||

title: Scalar field as an intrinsic time measure in coupled dynamical matter-geometry systems. I. Neutral gravitational collapse
Abstract: The notion of time in classical gravity cannot be directly applied to quantum gravity. To address this issue, researchers are exploring methods for quantifying time in a way that is suitable for gravity quantization. One promising approach involves utilizing evolving matter as an intrinsic "clock" to study the dynamics of gravitational systems. This research investigates whether scalar fields can serve as time variables during the dynamical evolution of a coupled multi-component matter-geometry system. The focus is on a neutral system, meaning it lacks electric and magnetic charges. To explore this, the research analyzes the gravitational collapse of self-interacting complex and real scalar fields in the Brans-Dicke theory using the 2+2 spacetime foliation. The analysis emphasizes the high-curvature region near the emerging singularity, which is crucial for understanding quantum gravity. The study examines different formulations of the theory for various values of the Brans-Dicke coupling constant and the coupling between the Brans-Dicke field and the matter sector. The results suggest that evolving scalar fields can be treated as time variables in close proximity to the singularity for the following reasons: the constancy hypersurfaces of the Brans-Dicke field are spacelike near the singularity, except in the case where the field's equation of motion reduces to the wave equation due to specific free evolution parameters; the hypersurfaces of constant complex and real scalar fields are spacelike in the regions near the singularities formed during the investigated process; and the field function values change monotonically in areas where the constancy hypersurfaces are spacelike.

title: Coexistence of Nematic Order and Superconductivity in the Hubbard Model

As a consequence, the superconducting gap exhibits unusual features, including altered nodal directions. The findings also indicate that in the optimally doped regime, the superconducting phase is typically unstable towards developing nematicity (breaking of the C4 symmetry). This has implications for cuprate high-Tc superconductors, where intertwined orders have been observed in this regime. The coexisting phase can be viewed as a precursor to these more complex patterns of symmetry breaking.

title: Star formation laws in the Andromeda galaxy: gas, stars, metals and the surface density of star formation

The research explores and compares the well-known Kennicutt-Schmidt law, the extended Schmidt law, and the metallicity/star formation correlation. The power-law index also changes with distance from the galaxy's center. The study compares these results with those obtained using the ordinary least squares fitting method, highlighting differences in power-law indices due to variations in fitting methods. A correlation is observed between the surface density of SFR and the stellar mass surface density, suggesting the need to expand the Kennicutt-Schmidt law to incorporate other physical properties of galaxies. Finally, a weak correlation is found between metallicity, SFR, and the stellar mass surface density.

title: Interpreting the 750 GeV Di-photon Resonance using photon-jets in Hidden-Valley-like models
Abstract: Motivated by the di-photon resonance reported by the ATLAS and CMS collaborations at √s = 13 TeV, this study interprets the resonance as a scalar boson X (750) within hidden-valley-like models. The scalar boson X can mix with the standard model Higgs boson, enabling its production via gluon fusion. It then decays into a pair of very light hidden particles Y of sub-GeV mass, each decaying into a pair of collimated π0s. These π0s subsequently decay into photons, forming photon-jets. title: Structural evolution of epitaxial SrCoOx films near topotactic phase transition
Abstract: Controlling oxygen stoichiometry in complex oxides through topotactic phase transitions offers a promising approach to modifying their physical properties and enabling their use in various energy technologies, such as energy storage and catalysis. However, detailed structural evolution in the vicinity of the topotactic phase transition in multivalent oxides remains largely unexplored. This work utilizes strontium cobaltites (SrCoOx) epitaxially grown by pulsed laser epitaxy (PLE) as a model system to investigate the oxidation-driven evolution of structural, electronic, and magnetic properties. Coherently strained SrCoO2.5 thin films were grown and subsequently annealed at various temperatures for topotactic conversion into the perovskite phase (SrCoO3-{\\delta}). Significant changes in electronic transport, magnetism, and microstructure were observed near the critical temperature for the topotactic transformation from the brownmillerite to the perovskite phase. Notably, the overall crystallinity was well preserved with minimal structural degradation, highlighting the potential of topotactic phase control as a valuable tool for repeatedly controlling physical properties through redox reactions.

title: Closure operations that induce big Cohen-Macaulay modules and classification of singularities
Abstract: Geoffrey Dietz formulated a set of axioms defining a closure operation on a complete local domain R, demonstrating that the existence of such a closure operation is equivalent to the existence of a big Cohen-Macaulay module. These closure operations are known as Dietz closures. In complete rings of characteristic p > 0, tight closure and plus closure satisfy these axioms. To facilitate the study of these closures, the concept of module closures is introduced and their properties are examined. It is shown that for many of these properties, a smallest closure operation satisfying the property exists. The properties of big Cohen-Macaulay module closures are discussed, and it is proven that every Dietz closure is contained within a big Cohen-Macaulay module closure. Utilizing this result, it is established that under mild conditions, a ring R is regular if and only if all Dietz closures on R are trivial. Finally, it is demonstrated that solid closure in equal characteristic 0, integral closure, and regular closure are not Dietz closures, and that all Dietz closures are contained within liftable integral closure.

title: Planetary Candidates Observed by Kepler. VII. The First Fully Uniform Catalog Based on The Entire 48 Month Dataset (Q1-Q17 DR24)
Abstract: This paper presents the seventh Kepler planet candidate catalog, which is the first to be based on the entire, uniformly processed, 48 month Kepler dataset. It is the first fully automated catalog, employing robotic vetting procedures to uniformly evaluate every periodic signal detected by the Q1-Q17 Data Release 24 (DR24) Kepler pipeline. While prioritizing uniform vetting over the absolute correctness of individual objects, the robotic vetting is found to be comparable to, and in many cases superior to, the human vetting procedures used in past catalogs. This catalog is the first to utilize artificial transit injection to evaluate the performance of its vetting procedures and quantify potential biases, which are crucial for accurate computation of planetary occurrence rates. Compared to the cumulative Kepler Object of Interest (KOI) catalog, 1,478 new KOIs are designated, of which 402 are dispositioned as planet candidates (PCs). Additionally, 237 KOIs previously categorized as false positives (FPs) are reclassified as PCs, and 118 PCs are reclassified as FPs. These changes bring the total number of known KOIs to 8,826 and PCs to 4,696. Comparisons between the Q1-Q17 DR24 KOI catalog and previous KOI catalogs, as well as ancillary Kepler catalogs, reveal good agreement between them. The catalog highlights new PCs that are potentially rocky and potentially located within the habitable zone of their host stars, many of which orbit solar-type stars. This research represents significant progress in accurately determining the fraction of Earth-size planets in the habitable zone of Sun-like stars. The full catalog is publicly available at the NASA Exoplanet Archive.

title: Rigidity of transmembrane proteins determines their cluster shape
Abstract: Protein aggregation within cell membranes is crucial for numerous biological functions. Recent experimental findings suggest that transmembrane domains of proteins, such as $\\alpha$-helices and $\\beta$-sheets, exhibit distinct structural rigidities. Molecular dynamics simulations of a coarse-grained model of protein-embedded lipid membranes were conducted to investigate the mechanisms of protein clustering. Simulations under thermal equilibrium conditions across various protein concentrations revealed that the structural rigidity of transmembrane domains significantly impacts interactions and alters the shape of the cluster. Stable large aggregates were observed even in the absence of hydrophobic mismatch, which had previously been proposed as the mechanism of protein aggregation. The results show that semi-flexible proteins aggregate to form two-dimensional clusters, while rigid proteins, in contrast, form one-dimensional string-like structures. By assuming two probable scenarios for the formation of a two-dimensional triangular structure, the lipid density around protein clusters was calculated. The findings indicate that the difference in lipid distribution around rigid and semiflexible proteins determines the one- or two-dimensional nature of aggregates. It was observed that lipids move faster around semiflexible proteins compared to rigid ones. The aggregation mechanism proposed in this paper can be experimentally validated using current state-of-the-art facilities.

title: Modeling and Querying Data Cubes on the Semantic Web

With the emergence of initiatives like Open Data and Open Government, organizations are eager to share their multidimensional data cubes and make them accessible for online querying. The QB4OLAP vocabulary extends QB to address these limitations, enabling the implementation of typical OLAP operations, such as rollup, slice, dice, and drill-across, using standard SPARQL queries. This paper introduces a formal data model where the data cube is the primary object, and defines OLAP operations using this model, independent of the underlying representation of the cube. It then demonstrates that a cube expressed using this model can be represented using the QB4OLAP vocabulary and provides a SPARQL implementation of OLAP operations over data cubes in QB4OLAP.

title: The X-ray luminosity function of low mass X-ray binaries in early-type galaxies, their metal-rich, and metal-poor globular clusters
Abstract: This paper presents the X-ray luminosity function (XLF) of low mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) in the globular clusters (GCs) and fields of seven early-type galaxies. These galaxies were selected for having both deep Chandra observations, allowing the observation of their LMXB populations down to X-ray luminosities of $10^{37}-10^{38}$ erg/s, and HST optical mosaics, enabling the separation of X-ray sources into field LMXBs, GC LMXBs, and contaminating background and foreground sources. The results show that the number of field LMXBs per stellar mass is similar across these galaxies at all luminosities. This suggests that the field LMXB populations in these galaxies are not affected by the GC-specific frequency and that properties such as binary fraction and the stellar initial mass function are either similar across the sample or change in a way that does not impact the number of LMXBs. Comparing the XLF of the field LMXBs to that of the GC LMXBs reveals significant differences with a p-value of $3\\times10^{-6}$ (equivalent to 4.7$\\sigma$ for a normal distribution). The difference is characterized by a flatter XLF for GC LMXBs compared to field LMXBs, with GCs hosting relatively more bright sources and fewer faint sources. Comparing the XLF of metal-rich and metal-poor GCs hints that metal-poor GCs may have more bright LMXBs, but the difference is not statistically significant.

title: Modeling Colors of Single Attribute Variations with Application to Food Appearance

The inter-image color sub-spaces are observed to be robust unless drastic illumination changes are involved. The paper demonstrates the application of this analysis for discriminating between shading-change and reflectance-change for patches, and object detection, segmentation, and recognition based on a single exemplar. title: DES14X3taz: A Type I Superluminous Supernova Showing a Luminous, Rapidly Cooling Initial Pre-Peak Bump

Multi-color photometry reveals a double-peaked light curve: an initial blue and relatively bright peak that fades rapidly before the slower rise of the main light curve. This multi-color photometry allows, for the first time, the observation of the initial peak cooling from 22,000K to 8,000K over 15 rest-frame days, which is faster and brighter than any published core-collapse supernova, reaching 30% of the bolometric luminosity of the main peak. No physical Nickel powered model can adequately fit this initial peak. The paper proposes a shock-cooling model followed by a magnetar driving the second phase of the light curve as a potential explanation for the entire light curve of DES14X3taz. Models involving the shock-cooling of extended circumstellar material at a distance of ~400 solar radii are favored over the cooling of shock-heated surface layers of a stellar envelope. DES14X3taz is compared to a handful of double-peaked SLSN-I events documented in the literature. Although the rise-times and characteristics of these initial peaks differ, the paper suggests a tantalizing possibility that they can be explained by a single physical interpretation.

title: Numerical Simulations of a Shock-Filament Interaction
Abstract: This paper presents 3D hydrodynamic adiabatic simulations of a shock interacting with a dense, elongated cloud. The impact of the filament's length and orientation relative to the shock, along with the shock Mach number and the density contrast of the filament, on the nature of the interaction is investigated. Comparisons with 3D spherical-cloud calculations are made. Significant differences in the morphology of the interaction are observed when M=10 and chi=100: in many cases, 3 parallel rolls are formed, which spread further apart with time, and periodic vortex shedding can occur off the ends of oblique filaments. Sideways-on filaments experience faster acceleration and initially lose mass more quickly than spherical clouds due to their greater surface area to volume ratio. However, at later stages, they lose mass more slowly due to the reduced relative speed between the filament and the postshock flow. The acceleration and mixing timescales can vary by a factor of 2 as the filament orientation changes. Oblique filaments can achieve transverse velocities up to 10% of the shock speed. Some aspects of the simulations are compared against experimental and numerical work on rigid cylinders.

title: The Cohen-Macaulayness of the bounded complex of an affine oriented matroid
Abstract: An affine oriented matroid is a combinatorial abstraction of an affine hyperplane arrangement. Novik, Postnikov, and Sturmfels constructed a squarefree monomial ideal in a polynomial ring, known as an oriented matroid ideal, from this abstraction, resulting in significant findings. Building upon their theory, the following results are presented: (1) If an oriented matroid ideal is Cohen-Macaulay, then the bounded complex (a regular CW complex associated with it) of the corresponding affine oriented matroid is a contractible homology manifold with boundary. This is closely related to Dong's theorem, previously known as "Zaslavsky's conjecture." (2) The affine oriented matroid whose corresponding ideal is Cohen-Macaulay is characterized. (3) In the Cohen-Macaulay case, a description of the canonical module of the residue class ring by an oriented matroid ideal is provided.

title: Higgs singlet boson as a diphoton resonance in a vector-like quark model
Abstract: Recent results from ATLAS and CMS, obtained from the second run of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at $\\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV, indicate a resonant bump at a mass of around 750 GeV in the diphoton invariant mass spectrum, with a corresponding diphoton production cross section of around 3-10 fb. Motivated by this LHC diphoton excess, this paper proposes that the possible resonance candidate is a Higgs singlet. To produce the Higgs singlet through the gluon-gluon fusion process, the Higgs singlet is embedded within the framework of the vector-like triplet quark (VLTQ) model. Consequently, the Higgs singlet decays into a diphoton final state via VLTQ loops. By leveraging the enhanced number of new quarks and new Yukawa couplings of the VLTQs and Higgs singlet, the paper successfully explains the diphoton production cross section. The analysis reveals that the Higgs singlet width is below 1 GeV, its production cross section can be on the order of 1 pb at $\\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV, and its branching ratio for decaying into a diphoton is around $0.017$ and insensitive to the masses of VLTQs and new Yukawa couplings. A strong correlation between the Higgs Yukawa couplings to $s$-$b$ and $c$-$t$ is observed, with the resultant branching ratio for $t \\to c h$ being $1.1\\times 10^{-4}$ when the constraint from $B_s$ oscillation is applied. With the constrained parameter values, the signal strength for the SM Higgs decaying to diphoton is $\\mu_{\\gamma\\gamma}< 1.18$, which is consistent with current measurements at ATLAS and CMS.

title: Sign Stability via Root Locus Analysis
Abstract: The rise of network science has brought renewed attention to topics in ecology and economics, such as structural stability (also referred to as qualitative stability or sign stability). A system is considered structurally stable if it remains stable for all possible parameter variations as long as the parameters do not change sign. This type of stability analysis is particularly appealing when studying real systems as the underlying stability result only requires knowledge of the sign of the parameters in the model and not their specific values. However, the necessary and sufficient conditions for qualitative stability are not transparent. To clarify these conditions, root locus analysis is employed. This technique effectively illustrates the necessary conditions for qualitative stability.

title: Persistence-driven durotaxis: Generic, directed motility in rigidity gradients
Abstract: Cells exhibit different movement patterns on substrates with varying elasticities. Notably, their motion persistence time is higher on stiffer substrates. This paper demonstrates that this behavior results in a net transport of cells directed up a soft-to-stiff gradient. Using simple random walk models with controlled persistence and stochastic simulations, the propensity to move is characterized in terms of the durotactic index measured in experiments. A one-dimensional model captures the essential features of this motion and highlights the competition between diffusive spreading and linear, wavelike propagation. Since the directed motion is rooted in a non-directional change in the behavior of individual cells, the motility is classified as a kinesis rather than a taxis. Persistence-driven durokinesis is a generic phenomenon that may be useful in designing instructive environments for cells and other motile, mechanosensitive objects.

title: Network Cartography: Seeing the Forest and the Trees
Abstract: Real-world networks often exhibit complexity and large scale with millions of nodes, posing a significant challenge for analysts to quickly grasp the overall picture for subsequent analysis. This paper aims to facilitate the exploration of node-attributed networks by creating representations that are concise, expressive, interpretable, and provide multi-resolution views. A {\\it map} representation is developed, one of the first to explore principled network cartography for general networks. Similar to common maps, this map includes landmarks, which aggregate nodes homogeneous in their traits and interactions with nodes elsewhere, and roads, which represent the interactions between the landmarks. Node homogeneity is captured by the similar roles they play. To concretely model the landmarks, a probabilistic generative model of networks with roles as latent factors is proposed. Additionally, novel model-based constrained optimization is formulated to enable interactive zooming. Efficient linear-time algorithms are designed for these optimizations. Experiments using real-world and synthetic networks demonstrate that the proposed method produces more expressive maps than existing methods, with up to a 10-fold improvement in network reconstruction quality. It is also shown that the method extracts landmarks with more homogeneous nodes, exhibiting up to a 90\\% improvement in the average attribute/link entropy among the nodes over each landmark. Sense-making of a real-world network using a map computed by this method qualitatively verifies the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

title: Origin of X-shaped radio-sources: further insights from the properties of their host galaxies
Abstract: This paper analyzes the properties of a sample of X-shaped radio-sources (XRSs). These objects exhibit, in addition to the main lobes, a pair of wings producing their distinctive radio morphology. The sample was obtained by selecting from the initial list of Cheung (2007, AJ, 133, 2097) the 53 galaxies with the best-defined wings and available SDSS images. The host galaxies were identified, and their optical position angle was measured, resulting in a positive outcome in 22 cases. The orientation of the secondary radio structures shows a strong correlation with the optical axis, with all (but one) wings forming an angle larger than 40 degrees with the host major axis. The probability of this being compatible with a uniform distribution is P = 0.9 10E-4. Spectra from SDSS are available for 28 XRSs, which were modeled to extract information on their emission lines and stellar population properties. The sample is composed of approximately an equal number of high and low excitation galaxies (HEG and LEG); this classification is crucial for proper comparison with non-winged radio-galaxies. XRSs follow the same relations between radio and line luminosity defined by radio-galaxies in the 3C sample. While young stellar populations are often present in HEGs, this is not detected in the 13 LEGs, consistent with the properties of non-XRSs. The absence of young stars in LEGs supports the notion that they have not experienced a recent gas-rich merger. The connection between the optical axis and the wings orientation, along with the stellar population and emission lines properties, further supports a hydro-dynamic origin of the radio-wings (for example, associated with the expansion of the radio cocoon in an asymmetric external medium) rather than a change in orientation of the jet axis.

title: Chiral and Non-Chiral Edge States in Quantum Hall Systems with Charge Density Modulation
Abstract: This paper examines a system of weakly coupled wires exhibiting quantum Hall effect (QHE) and subject to a spatially periodic modulation of the chemical potential along the wire, equivalent to a charge density wave (CDW). It is shown that by adjusting the ratio between the amplitudes of the CDW modulation and the tunneling between wires, it is possible to switch between a non-topological CDW-dominated phase and a topological QHE-dominated phase. Both phases feature edge states of chiral and non-chiral nature, robust to on-site disorder. However, only in the topological phase are the edge states immune to disorder in the phase shifts of the CDWs. Analytical solutions are provided for filling factor $\\nu=1$, and the effects of disorder are studied numerically, along with numerical results for higher filling factors.

title: Technical Design Report for the AMoRE $0νββ$ Decay Search Experiment
Abstract: The AMoRE experiment, a collaboration of researchers from eight countries, aims to search for neutrinoless double-beta decay of molybdenum-100 using advanced cryogenic techniques. The experiment utilizes highly purified, molybdenum-100 enriched and calcium-48 depleted calcium molybdate crystals located deep underground in Korea. The choice of molybdenum-100 is based on its high Q-value and favorable nuclear matrix element. The crystals produce bright scintillation light at both room and cryogenic temperatures, with the calcium molybdate crystals exhibiting the highest scintillation yield among all molybdate crystals. These crystals are operated at milli-Kelvin temperatures and are read out by metallic-magnetic-calorimeter (MMC) temperature sensors, offering excellent energy resolution and fast response times. This combination provides effective signal-background discrimination and minimizes background from random coincidence events. The experiment utilizes both scintillating light and phonon signals for redundant rejection of alpha-ray-induced backgrounds. With a 200 kg array of calcium molybdate crystals operating for three years, the AMoRE experiment aims to achieve a sensitivity to the effective Majorana neutrino mass reaching the expected range of the inverted neutrino mass hierarchy, i.e., 20-50 meV.

This temperature increase is sufficient to raise the local temperature above the CO desorption temperature. The findings suggest that radial drift-induced disk density structures can create multiple CO snow-lines. Inner disk CO remains in the gas phase, freezing out near the classical snow-line at R ~ 20-40 AU. Moving outward, CO sublimates again beyond the truncation radius (80 AU in the models) and subsequently re-freezes out at larger stellar distances, beyond R ≥ 130-200 AU. The study finds that thermal desorption of CO in the outer disk becomes competitive with external UV photodesorption, and this additional transition from solid-state CO to the gas phase significantly impacts the C/O ratio in the outer disk.

In doing so, it incorporates effects of rearranging charge and other electronic properties due to changing site occupancies. title: The cell cycle related rhythms, cells' states correlation and the cancer

title: Private Causal Inference

title: Unsupervised Feature Construction for Improving Data Representation and Semantics

The research generalizes the shape of the dust law using an empirical model, A λ,δ=E(B-V) k λ (λ/λ V) δ, where k λ represents the dust law of Calzetti et al. (2000). The study demonstrates a correlation between the color excess E(B-V) and tilt δ, with δ=(0.62±0.05)log(E(B-V)) + (0.26±0.02). title: Deformations of Q-curvature I

title: Calibration and simulation of arbitrage effects in a non-equilibrium quantum Black-Scholes model by using semiclassical methods

The white noise amplitude f(t), termed an "arbitrage bubble," generates a time-dependent potential U(t) that alters the equilibrium dynamics of the traditional Black-Scholes model. This article addresses the inverse problem: can we extract the time-dependent potential U(t) and its associated bubble shape f(t) from empirical financial data? To answer this, the interacting Black-Scholes equation is interpreted as a quantum Schrödinger equation with Hamiltonian operator H=H0+U(t), where H0 represents the equilibrium Black-Scholes Hamiltonian and U(t) is the interaction term. If U(t) is sufficiently small, it can be considered a perturbation, allowing for an approximate solution of the interacting Black-Scholes equation using perturbation theory. In [2], applying semi-classical considerations, an approximate solution for the non-equilibrium Black-Scholes equation was developed for an arbitrary bubble shape f(t). Utilizing this semi-classical solution and knowledge about mispricing in financial data, one can derive an equation whose solutions yield the functional form of the potential term U(t) and its associated bubble f(t). In all cases studied, the non-equilibrium model provides a better estimation of real data compared to the standard equilibrium model. title: Operational meaning of quantum measures of recovery
