The relative entropy of recovery is a related measure where fidelity is replaced by relative entropy. This paper provides concrete operational interpretations of these recovery measures in terms of a computational decision problem and a hypothesis testing scenario. It is demonstrated that the fidelity of recovery equals the maximum probability with which a computationally unbounded quantum prover can convince a computationally bounded quantum verifier that a given quantum state is recoverable. The quantum interactive proof system for this operational meaning requires four messages exchanged between the prover and verifier. However, by forcing the prover to perform actions in superposition, a different proof system requiring only two messages is constructed. This implies that the associated decision problem lies in QIP(2) and is shown to be hard for QSZK (both classes contain problems believed to be difficult to solve for a quantum computer). Finally, it is proven that the regularized relative entropy of recovery equals the optimal Type II error exponent when trying to distinguish many copies of a tripartite state from a recovered version, while keeping the Type I error below a constant.

title: Live Exploration of Dynamic Rings
Abstract: The graph exploration problem involves a team of mobile computational entities, called agents, arbitrarily positioned at nodes of a graph, tasked with cooperating to ensure that every node is visited by at least one agent. Few studies have explored dynamic graphs, and most have been limited to the centralized case, assuming complete prior knowledge of changes and their timing. This paper investigates the decentralized exploration of dynamic graphs, specifically those with a ring topology, where agents are unaware of the location and timing of changes. The analysis first considers fully-synchronous systems, where all agents are active at each time step, as traditionally assumed in the literature. Subsequently, the concept of semi-synchronous systems is introduced, where only a subset of agents might be active at each time step, with the adversary deciding the subset. This model, common in the context of mobile agents in continuous spaces, is novel for agents moving in graphs. The study focuses on the impact of synchrony levels, anonymity, knowledge of the ring size, and chirality (common orientation) on the problem's solvability, particularly on the minimum number of agents required. An extensive map of feasibility and complexity, in terms of minimum agent movements, is presented. All sufficiency proofs are constructive, and most solution protocols are asymptotically optimal.

title: Pragmatic Information in Quantum Mechanics
Abstract: An objective definition of pragmatic information, coupled with recent findings on information processing in the human brain, can help overcome traditional difficulties in interpreting quantum mechanics. Instead of attempting to define information a priori, the concept of interaction between material bodies is introduced as a primary concept. Two distinct categories are identified: (1) Interactions reducible to a superposition of physical interactions (forces) between elementary constituents; (2) Interactions between complex bodies that cannot be reduced to a superposition of interactions between parts, where patterns and forms (in space and/or time) play a decisive role. Pragmatic information is then defined as the correspondence between a given pattern and the ensuing pattern-specific change. It is shown that pragmatic information is a biological concept that plays no active role in the purely physical domain; it only becomes relevant when a living organism intervenes. The consequences for the foundations of both classical and quantum physics are significant and are discussed in detail. Since, by its very definition, pragmatic information (the kind our brain uses to represent, think about, and react to the outside world) cannot operate in the quantum domain, it is advisable to avoid using it in our mental representation of what happens "inside" a quantum system. Although the theoretical framework developed for quantum mechanics handles mathematical entities specifically attributed to a quantum system, the only truly pragmatic information it can provide relates to macroscopic effects on the environment (natural or artificial, as in a measurement instrument) with which the system interacts.

title: A practical theorem on using interferometry to measure the global 21-cm signal
Abstract: The sky-averaged, or global, background of redshifted 21 cm radiation is expected to be a rich source of information on cosmological reheating and reionization. However, measuring this signal is technically challenging, as one must extract a small, frequency-dependent signal from under much brighter spectrally smooth foregrounds. Traditional approaches using single antennas require calibration of the frequency-dependent structure in the overall system gain (due to internal reflections, for example) and removal of noise bias from auto-correlating a single amplifier output. This has led to proposals for measuring the signal using cross-correlations in interferometric setups, where additional calibration techniques are available. This paper focuses on the general principles driving the sensitivity of interferometric setups to the global signal. It is proven that this sensitivity is directly related to two characteristics of the setup: cross-talk between readout channels (i.e., the signal picked up at one antenna when the other is driven) and correlated noise due to thermal fluctuations of lossy elements (e.g., absorbers or the ground) radiating into both channels. Therefore, in an interferometric setup, suppressing cross-talk and correlated thermal noise without simultaneously reducing sensitivity to the global signal by the same factor is impossible. Instead, the challenge lies in characterizing these effects and their frequency dependence. The general theorem is illustrated through explicit calculations within toy setups consisting of two short dipole antennas in free space and above a perfectly reflecting ground surface, as well as two well-separated identical lossless antennas arranged to achieve zero cross-talk.

The primary limitation of this scheme is the low damage threshold of the materials employed in nanostructure engineering. The behavior and efficiency of these systems in generating coherent harmonic emission are thoroughly discussed. This class of theories contains undetermined functions, but only three theories are unambiguously determined based on consistency requirements. For the first such theory, we derive the action of the vacuum theory, which arises as the limit of the full matter theory. We identify a symmetry transformation of this vacuum action in the Jordan frame, consisting of a conformal transformation of the metric along with a redefinition of the scalar field. As the general family of vacuum theories is parameterized by an arbitrary function of the scalar field, we also derive the action of this family. Concerning the full matter theory, we only determine the action of the system when the matter Lagrangian vanishes on-shell, as for pressureless dust. Due to the interaction, this matter Lagrangian is non-minimally coupled in both the Jordan and Einstein frames.

We clearly demonstrate the continuous transition from single-particle to collective character of these excitations and how screening modifies their dispersion relations. We prove that $\pi$ and $\pi+\sigma$ plasmons exist in graphene, although they occur only for a specific range of wavevectors and with a finite damping rate. We pay particular attention to comparing the theoretical results with available EELS measurements in the optical ($\mathrm{Q\approx 0}$) and other ($\mathrm{Q\neq 0}$) limits. The conclusions, based on microscopic numerical results, are confirmed in an approximate analytical approach.

title: Neighborhood approximations for non-linear voter models
Abstract: Non-linear voter models assume that an agent's opinion depends on the opinions of its neighbors in a non-linear fashion, allowing for voting rules beyond majority voting. While the linear voter model is known to reach consensus, non-linear voter models can result in the coexistence of opposing opinions. Our aim is to derive approximations that accurately predict the time-dependent dynamics or, at least, the asymptotic outcome of such local interactions. We emphasize a probabilistic approach to decompose the opinion distribution in a second-order neighborhood into lower-order probability distributions. This approach is compared with an analytic pair approximation for the expected value of the global fraction of opinions and a mean-field approximation. Our reference case is averaged stochastic simulations of a one-dimensional cellular automaton. We find that the probabilistic second-order approach captures the dynamics of the reference case very well for different non-linearities, including both majority and minority voting rules, which only partially holds for the first-order pair approximation and not at all for the mean-field approximation. We further discuss the interesting phenomenon of correlated coexistence, characterized by the formation of large domains of opinions that dominate for some time but slowly change.

title: On the dipole moment of quantized vortices generated by flows

It is shown that if the order parameter changes over macroscopic distances, the polarization charge $\rho_{pol}$ is proportional to $A\nabla^2 n$, and the polarization $\mathbf{P}$ is proportional to $A\nabla n$, where $n$ is the density of the system. For non-interacting atoms, the proportionality coefficient $A$ is independent of density, and in the presence of interaction, $A$ is proportional to $n$. The change in the Bose gas density is determined in the presence of a flow $\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{v}_n - \mathbf{v}_s$ passing through the vortex. It is found that a vortex in a superfluid film creates an electric potential above the film. This potential has the form of a dipole potential, allowing the assignment of a dipole moment to the vortex. The dipole moment is a sum of two terms, the first proportional to the relative flow velocity $\mathbf{w}$ and the second proportional to $[\mathbf{\kappa} \times \mathbf{w}]$, where $\mathbf{\kappa}$ is the vortex circulation. |||

title: The consequences of dependence between the formal area efficiency and the macroscopic electric field on linearity behavior in Fowler-Nordheim plots

The authors propose that the number of emitting spots, which determines the apparent formal area efficiency of CFE surfaces, depends on the macroscopic electric field. The non-uniformity is described by local enhancement factors ($\gamma_j$), which are randomly assigned to each emitter, and are drawn from a discrete probability distribution $\rho(\gamma_j)$. The local current density is then evaluated considering a standard Schottky-Nordheim barrier. The model successfully reproduces the two distinct slope regimes observed in FN plots when $F_M$ is within the range of 2-20 V/µm. This result is further analyzed by considering the apparent formal area efficiency, the distribution $\rho$, and the slopes in the corresponding FN plot. Additionally, the numerical solution of Laplace's equation for an array of conducting nano-emitters with uniform apex radii of 50 nm but different local heights supports the theoretical assumptions and can be used to experimentally test the predictions.

title: Non-equilibrium helium ionization in an MHD simulation of the solar atmosphere
Abstract: The ionization state of the gas in the dynamic solar chromosphere can deviate significantly from the instantaneous statistical equilibrium typically assumed in numerical models. This study improves upon previous simulations of the solar atmosphere, which only included non-equilibrium hydrogen ionization, by performing a 2D radiation-magneto-hydrodynamics simulation that includes non-equilibrium ionization of both hydrogen and helium. The simulation considers the impact of hydrogen Lyman-$\alpha$ and the EUV radiation from the corona on the ionization and heating of the atmosphere. The results reveal helium ion fractions that deviate significantly from their equilibrium values. Comparison with models using the local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) ionization assumption shows that non-equilibrium helium ionization leads to higher temperatures in wave fronts and lower temperatures in the gas between shocks. LTE ionization results in a thermostat-like behavior, with matter accumulating around temperatures where the LTE ionization fractions change rapidly. The comparison of differential emission measure (DEM) curves computed from the models demonstrates that non-equilibrium ionization leads to more radiating material in the temperature range of 11-18 kK compared to models using LTE helium ionization. Therefore, the study concludes that non-equilibrium helium ionization is crucial for the dynamics and thermal structure of the upper chromosphere and transition region. This finding may also contribute to resolving the discrepancy between the intensities of chromospheric lines computed from current models and those observed.

title: A MHD invariant and the confinement regimes in Tokamak

title: Excursions through KK modes

While the entire KK mass spectrum is independent of the gauge choice, the mode number depends on the gauge. The masses of the KK modes also depend on the field value of the zero-mode of the extra dimensional component of the gauge field. Notably, one of the KK modes in the KK tower of each massless 5D charged field becomes massless at specific values of the extra-dimensional component of the gauge field. When the extra-dimensional component of the gauge field is identified with the inflaton, this structure leads to recursive cosmological particle productions.

title: Testing a coupled hydro-thermo-chemo-geomechanical model for gas hydrate bearing sediments using triaxial compression lab experiments

These hydrates contribute to the strength and stiffness of hydrate-bearing sediments, but during gas production, the geomechanical stability of the sediment is compromised. Understanding the mechanical behavior of gas hydrate-bearing sediments is crucial due to potential geotechnical risks and process management issues. This study proposes a coupling concept that simplifies the mathematical description of complex interactions during gas production by isolating the effects of sediment deformation and hydrate phase changes. The concept assumes that soil grains form the load-bearing solid skeleton, while the gas hydrate enhances the mechanical properties of this skeleton. The authors test this coupling concept by numerically simulating a high-pressure isotropic compression experiment combined with methane hydrate formation and dissociation. A linear-elastic stress-strain relationship is considered due to its unique definition and ease of calibration. Although the geomechanical response of hydrate-bearing sediment is typically inelastic and characterized by significant shear-volumetric coupling, the experiment is carefully controlled to maintain small deformations within the assumptions of poro-elasticity. The closely coordinated experimental and numerical procedures validate the proposed simplified geomechanics-to-flow coupling, serving as a precursor for enhancing coupled hydro-geomechanical hydrate reservoir simulators with more suitable elasto-plastic constitutive models.

title: Lepton flavour violating B meson decays via scalar leptoquark

In the Standard Model, these transitions are extremely rare due to two-loop suppression or proceeding via box diagrams with tiny neutrino masses in the loop. However, in the leptoquark model, they can occur at tree level and are expected to have significantly larger branching ratios. The leptoquark parameter space is constrained using experimental limits on the branching ratios of $B_q \rightarrow l^+ l^-$ processes. Using this constrained parameter space, the study predicts the branching ratios of LFV semileptonic $B$ meson decays, such as $B^+ \to K^+ (\pi^+) l_i^+ l_j^-$, $B^+ \to (K^{* +}, \rho^+) l_i^+ l_j^-$, and $B_s \to \phi l_i^+ l_j^-$, which are found to be within the experimental reach of LHCb and the upcoming Belle II experiments. The study also investigates the rare leptonic $K_{L, S} \to \mu^+ \mu^- (e^+ e^-)$ and $K_L \to \mu^\mp e^\pm$ decays in the leptoquark model.

title: Size-Independent Quantification of Ligand Binding Site Depth in Receptor Proteins
Abstract: This study presents a web server that implements two complementary methods to quantify the depth of the ligand binding site (LBS) in protein-ligand complexes: the "secant plane" (SP) and "tangent sphere" (TS) methods. The protein molecular centroid (global centroid, GC) and the LBS centroid (local centroid, LC) are first determined. The SP is the plane passing through the LC and normal to the line connecting the LC and GC. The "exterior side" of the SP is the side opposite GC. The TS is the sphere centered at GC and tangent to the SP at LC. The percentage of protein atoms inside the TS (TS index) and on the exterior side of the SP (SP index) are complementary measures of LBS depth, with SPi directly proportional to LBS depth and TSi inversely proportional. The methods were tested using a test set of 67 well-characterized protein-ligand structures and an artificial protein in the form of a grid of points shaped like a sphere with LBS of variable depth. Both SP and TS methods show good agreement with reported data and confirm their suitability as measures of LBS depth. The web server operates in two modes: "ligand mode" requiring protein PDB coordinates and ligand coordinates, and "LBS mode" assuming ligand coordinates are unavailable, requiring user input for the coordinates of the LBS amino acid residues. In both cases, the server outputs the SP and TS indices. The ability to quantify LBS depth, which is usually directly related to the amount of conformational change a protein undergoes upon ligand binding, allows for meaningful comparisons of protein flexibility and dynamics. The URL of the web server will be announced publicly at a later time.

title: Wisent: Robust Downstream Communication and Storage for Computational RFIDs
Abstract: Computational RFID (CRFID) devices are emerging platforms that enable perpetual computation and sensing by eliminating the need for batteries. While much research has focused on improving upstream communication rates between CRFID and RFID readers, the opposite direction has been neglected due to the challenges of guaranteeing fast and error-free data transfer amidst frequent power interruptions of CRFID. As CRFID devices become increasingly embedded in various structures, addressing this communication gap is crucial. To this end, the authors propose Wisent, a robust downstream communication protocol for CRFID devices that operates on top of the legacy UHF RFID communication protocol, EPC C1G2. The novelty of Wisent lies in its ability to adaptively change the frame length sent by the reader based on a length throttling mechanism, minimizing transfer times under varying channel conditions. The study presents an implementation of Wisent for the WISP 5 and an off-the-shelf RFID reader. Experiments show that Wisent enables transfer up to 16 times faster than a non-adaptive baseline case (single word length) at sub-meter distances. title: On the stability of a class of non-monotonic systems of parallel queues

The study provides sufficient conditions for the existence of a stationary workload, which indicate a "splitting" of the system in heavy traffic into a loss system of $p$ servers and an FCFS system of $S-p$ servers. To prove this result, the authors establish an original sufficient condition for the existence and uniqueness of a stationary workload for a multiple-server loss system.

title: Critical assessment of the equilibrium melting-based, energy distribution theory of supercooled liquids and application to jammed systems

This study demonstrates that the same form can be derived from a different starting point and then critically examines its performance. The results show that the proposed functional form fits the viscosity data of a diverse group of 45 liquids exceptionally well over a wide temperature range. The study also reveals several interesting correlations of the single parameter with various thermodynamic quantities, ultimately allowing for the prediction of low-temperature viscosity from high-temperature data. Additionally, similar physical reasoning is used to derive a similar, single-parameter form for the viscosity of hard-sphere/jammed liquids, accurately reproducing the viscosity of hard spheres and suggesting an underlying universality in metastable dynamics.

title: Origin of the Metallicity Distribution in the Thick Disc
Abstract: This study uses a suite of cosmological chemodynamical disc galaxy simulations to assess how (a) radial metallicity gradients evolve with scaleheight, (b) the vertical metallicity gradients change through the thick disc, and (c) the vertical gradient of the stellar rotation velocity varies through the disc. The results are then compared to the Milky Way to search for analogous trends. The study analyzes five simulated spiral galaxies with masses comparable to the Milky Way. The simulations span a range of star formation and energy feedback strengths and prescriptions, particle- and grid-based hydrodynamical implementations, as well as initial conditions/assembly history. Consistently, the study finds that the steeper, negative, radial metallicity gradients seen in the mid-plane flatten with increasing height away from the plane. In simulations with stronger (and/or more spatially-extended) feedback, the negative radial gradients invert, becoming positive for heights exceeding 1 kpc. This behavior aligns with recent observational findings. Measurements of the vertical metallicity gradients show no clear correlation with galactocentric radius and are in good agreement with those observed in the Milky Way's thick disc (locally). The simulations employing stronger/more extended feedback prescriptions possess radial and vertical metallicity and kinematic gradients that are more in line with recent observations. The inverted, positive, radial metallicity gradients seen in the simulated thick stellar discs originate from a population of younger, more metal-rich, stars formed in-situ, superimposed upon a background population of older migrators from the inner disc. The contrast provided by the former increases radially due to the inside-out growth of the disc. A similar behavior may be responsible for the flattening of the radial gradients with scaleheight observed in the Milky Way.

title: On the reconstruction of Lifshitz spacetimes

title: Shepherding Tidal Debris with the Galactic Bar: The Ophiuchus Stream
Abstract: This study provides the first explanation for the dynamics of stellar streams in rotating barred potentials. Neighboring stream stars reach pericenter at slightly different times, experiencing different bar orientations during pericentric passage due to the rotating bar. This results in each star receiving a different torque from the bar, reshaping the angular momentum and energy distribution of stars in the stream, and ultimately affecting the growth rate of the stream. For a progenitor orbiting in the same direction as the bar's rotation and satisfying a resonance condition, the resulting stream can be significantly shorter or longer than expected, depending on whether the pericentric passages of the progenitor occur along the bar's minor or major axis, respectively. The study presents a comprehensive discussion of this phenomenon, focusing primarily on streams confined to the Galactic plane. In contrast to the evolution in static potentials, which produce streams that grow steadily over time, rotating barred potentials can generate dynamically old, short streams. This challenges the traditional view that the inner halo consists of well phase-mixed material, while tidally-disrupted structures in the outer halo are more spatially coherent. The study argues that this mechanism plays a significant role in explaining the mysteriously short Ophiuchus stream recently discovered near the bulge region of the Milky Way.

title: Cross-correlation of gravitational lensing from DES Science Verification data with SPT and Planck lensing
Abstract: This study measures the cross-correlation between weak lensing of galaxy images and of the cosmic microwave background (CMB). The effects of gravitational lensing on different sources will be correlated if the lensing is caused by the same mass fluctuations. The analysis uses galaxy shape measurements from 139 deg$^{2}$ of the Dark Energy Survey (DES) Science Verification data and overlapping CMB lensing from the South Pole Telescope (SPT) and Planck. The DES source galaxies have a median redshift of $z_{\rm med} \sim 0.7$, while the CMB lensing kernel is broad and peaks at $z \sim 2$. The resulting cross-correlation is maximally sensitive to mass fluctuations at $z \sim 0.44$. Assuming the Planck 2015 best-fit cosmology, the amplitude of the DES$\times$SPT cross-power is found to be $A = 0.88 \pm 0.30$ and that from DES$\times$Planck to be $A = 0.86 \pm 0.39$, where $A=1$ corresponds to the theoretical prediction. These results are consistent with the expected signal and correspond to significances of $2.9 \sigma$ and $2.2 \sigma$, respectively. The study demonstrates that the results are robust to several important systematic effects, including shear measurement method, estimator choice, photometric redshift uncertainty, and CMB lensing systematics. Significant intrinsic alignment of galaxy shapes would increase the cross-correlation signal inferred from the data. The study calculates a value of $A = 1.08 \pm 0.36$ for DES$\times$SPT when correcting the observations with a simple IA model. With three measurements of this cross-correlation now existing in the literature, there is not yet reliable evidence for any deviation from the expected LCDM level of cross-correlation, given the size of the statistical uncertainties and the significant impact of systematic errors, particularly IAs. The study provides forecasts for the expected signal-to-noise of the combination of the five-year DES survey and SPT-3G.

title: Towards Axion Monodromy Inflation with Warped KK-Modes

The axion obtains an exponentially small mass from the IR-region where the $S^2$ shrinks to zero size, both with respect to the Planck scale and the mass scale of local modes of the throat. title: On the replica symmetry phase of the independent set problem

title: Small noise and long time phase diffusion in stochastic limit cycle oscillators
Abstract: This study investigates the impact of additive Brownian noise on an ordinary differential equation (ODE) system with a stable hyperbolic limit cycle. Furthermore, the study reveals that on longer time scales, the dephasing dynamics is dominated by the drift term. The choice of coordinates that simplifies the dynamics near the cycle to a rotation plays a crucial role and connects the study to the applied science literature, where noisy limit cycle dynamics is often modeled as a diffusion process for the phase of the limit cycle.

title: Carl's inequality for quasi-Banach spaces
Abstract:
This research establishes that for any pair of quasi-Banach spaces X and Y and any positive real number α, there exists a constant γα such that the inequality 
sup_{1≤k≤n}kαek(T) ≤ γα sup_{1≤k≤n} kαck(T) holds for all linear and bounded operators T mapping X to Y. Here, ek(T) denotes the k-th entropy number of T, and ck(T) represents the k-th Gelfand number of T. While this inequality is well-known and widely used for Banach spaces X and Y, it constitutes a novel result for general quasi-Banach spaces.

title: Analysis of electrolyte transport through charged nanopores

The study analyzes the general case with overlapping electric double layers in the pore and a non-zero axial salt concentration gradient. The 3×3 matrix relating these quantities exhibits Onsager symmetry, and the paper reports a significant new simplification for the diagonal element connecting axial salt flux to the gradient in chemical potential. It proves that Onsager symmetry is preserved under changes of variables, illustrated by a transformation to a different flux-force matrix given by Gross and Osterle (1968). The capillary pore model is well-suited to describe the nonlinear response of charged membranes or nanofluidic devices for electrokinetic energy conversion and water desalination, as long as the transverse ion profiles remain in local quasi-equilibrium. As an example, the paper evaluates electrical power production from a salt concentration difference by reverse electrodialysis, using an efficiency vs. power diagram. title: Involutions on the affine Grassmannian and moduli spaces of principal bundles

As a result, the fixed-point set of the involution can be partitioned into strata indexed by conjugacy classes of homomorphisms from the normalizer of Gm in SL(2) to G. title: Task-related edge density (TED) - a new method for revealing large-scale network formation in fMRI data of the human brain

These networks consist of nodes (corresponding to voxels in fMRI data) and edges connecting them, with edge weights determined by task-related changes in dynamic synchronization between their respective time series. Based on these definitions, the paper presents a new data analysis algorithm that identifies edges in a brain network that differentially respond in unison to a task onset and occur in dense packs with similar characteristics. This approach, termed "Task-related Edge Density" (TED), proves to be a robust marker for dynamic network formation that readily lends itself to statistical analysis using large-scale statistical inference. A major advantage of TED compared to other methods is its independence from any specific hemodynamic response model and its ability to handle large networks consisting of tens of thousands of voxels without requiring presegmentation of the data for dimensionality reduction. The study applies TED to fMRI data from a fingertapping task provided by the Human Connectome Project, revealing network-based involvement of numerous brain areas that evade detection using traditional general linear model (GLM)-based analysis. title: Photoconduction and low-temperature Ohmic conduction of Peierls conductor o-TaS$_3$ under uniaxial strain

title: Hypergraph Two-Coloring in the Streaming Model
Abstract:
This paper explores space-efficient algorithms for two-coloring n-uniform hypergraphs H=(V,E) in the streaming model, where hyperedges arrive one at a time. It is known that any such hypergraph with at most 0.7√(n/ln n) 2^n hyperedges has a two-coloring (Radhakrishnan & Srinivasan, RSA, 2000), which can be found deterministically in polynomial time with full access to the input. 
 1. The minimum space required by a deterministic one-pass streaming algorithm, denoted as sD(v, q, n), that produces a proper two-coloring of H on v vertices and q hyperedges is investigated. It is shown that sD(n^2, q, n) = Ω(q/n) when q ≤ 0.7 √(n/ln n) 2^n and sD(n^2, q, n) = Ω(√(1/(n ln n)) 2^n) otherwise.
  2. The paper analyzes the minimum space required by a randomized one-pass streaming algorithm, denoted as sR(v, q,n), that with high probability produces a proper two-coloring of H (or declares failure). It is shown that sR(v, 1/10 √(n/ln n) 2^n, n) = O(v log v) by presenting an efficient randomized streaming algorithm.
  These findings are inspired by the study of the number q(n), the minimum possible number of hyperedges in an n-uniform hypergraph that is not two-colorable. It is known that q(n) = Ω(√(n/ln n)) (Radhakrishnan-Srinivasan) and q(n)= O(n^2 2^n) (Erdos, 1963). The first result shows that no space-efficient deterministic streaming algorithm can match the performance of the offline algorithm by Radhakrishnan and Srinivasan. The second result, however, demonstrates the existence of a space-efficient randomized streaming algorithm for this task.

title: Optimal occlusion uniformly partitions red blood cells fluxes within a microvascular network
Abstract: In animals, gas exchange between blood and tissues occurs within narrow vessels whose diameter is comparable to that of a red blood cell. Red blood cells must deform to squeeze through these vessels, transiently blocking or occluding them as they pass. While the dynamics of vessel occlusion have been extensively studied, the rationale behind the narrowness of microvessels remains an open question. This research investigates occlusive dynamics within a model microvascular network: the embryonic zebrafish trunk. The study shows that pressure feedbacks generated when red blood cells enter the finest vessels of the trunk act together to uniformly partition red blood cells throughout the microvasculature. Using mathematical models and direct observation, the paper demonstrates that these occlusive feedbacks are fine-tuned throughout the trunk network to prevent the vessels closest to the heart from short-circuiting the network. This finding connects occlusion to another open question in microvascular function: how are red blood cells delivered at the same rate to each micro-vessel? The analysis reveals that tuning of occlusive feedbacks increases the total dissipation within the network by a factor of 11, suggesting that the microvascular network prioritizes uniformity of flows over minimizing transport costs.

title: The Absence of Stokes Drift in Waves
Abstract: Stokes drift, a fundamental concept in wave theory, has historically been challenging to observe experimentally. Wave tanks and open body experiments struggle to detect Stokes drift without significant cancellation by "Eulerian flows." This paper demonstrates that the explanation for this challenge lies in subtle end-of-packet and wavetrain gradient effects, including microbreaking events and wave-flow decomposition subtleties required to conserve mass and momentum and avoid fictitious external forces. These losses occur at both ends of packets and can lead to significant nonviscous energy loss for translating and spreading surface wave packets and wavetrains. In contrast, monochromatic sound wave packets are shown to distort asymmetrically to conserve momentum. This provides an interesting analogy to how such internal forces arise for gradients of electromagnetic wavetrains in media. These examples highlight the system dependence and nonuniversality of wave interactions in media. The paper emphasizes the importance of carefully considering boundary effects for conservation laws, particularly when dealing with harmonic functions. The induced flows in establishing surface waves are shown to be time-changing and dependent on wave history, suggesting that some classical work based on mass flux and wave interactions may need to be revisited.

title: Combinatorial Representation of Parameter Space for Switching Systems

These networks have at least 5-10 nodes, involve multiple interactions, and require decades of parameters to describe their behavior. The database takes a regulatory network as input, which is represented as a directed graph with edges indicating up or down regulation. This network is then transformed into a computational model based on switching networks. The phase space dimension corresponds to the number of nodes, while the parameter space consists of decay rates for each node and three parameters for each edge. The nonlinearities of switching systems lead to a natural decomposition of phase space into cells, allowing for a combinatorial description of the dynamics in terms of a state transition graph. This in turn leads to a compact representation of the global dynamics known as an annotated Morse graph, which identifies recurrent and non-recurrent states. This paper focuses on constructing a natural computable finite decomposition of parameter space into domains where the annotated Morse graph description of dynamics remains constant. This decomposition is used to construct an SQL database that can be effectively searched for dynamic signatures such as bistability, stable or unstable oscillations, and stable equilibria. The paper provides two simple 3-node networks as explicit examples of the type of information stored in the DSGRN database. The study reveals that while these two-dimensional materials are not wetting transparent, the underlying substrate significantly influences their wetting properties due to dominant vdW forces. Contact angle measurements indicate that graphene and graphene-like layered transitional metal dichalcogenides inherently possess dispersive surfaces with a dominant London-vdW force-mediated wettability. Electric field-controlled wetting studies of MoS2/WS2/SiO2/Si heterostructures were performed, but no noticeable changes in the water contact angle were observed despite two orders of magnitude change in resistance. title: True Online Temporal-Difference Learning
Abstract: Temporal-difference methods TD($\\lambda$) and Sarsa($\\lambda$) are fundamental components of modern reinforcement learning, valued for their performance, low computational cost, and straightforward interpretation through their forward view. Recently, new versions of these methods, known as true online TD($\\lambda$) and true online Sarsa($\\lambda$), were introduced (van Seijen & Sutton, 2014). These true online versions maintain an exact equivalence with the forward view at all times, whereas the traditional versions only approximate it for small step-sizes. This paper hypothesizes that these true online methods not only possess better theoretical properties but also outperform regular methods empirically. To test this hypothesis, an extensive empirical comparison is conducted. The performance of true online TD($\\lambda$)/Sarsa($\\lambda$) is compared with regular TD($\\lambda$)/Sarsa($\\lambda$) on random MRPs, a real-world myoelectric prosthetic arm, and a domain from the Arcade Learning Environment. Linear function approximation with tabular, binary, and non-binary features is used. The results indicate that true online methods indeed dominate regular methods, exhibiting superior learning speeds in all domains and representations without the need to choose between traces. In addition to empirical results, the paper provides an in-depth analysis of the theory behind true online temporal-difference learning and demonstrates that new true online temporal-difference methods can be derived by modifying the online forward view and rewriting the update equations.

title: Horizon Quantum Mechanics: a hitchhiker's guide to quantum black holes
Abstract: Viewing space-time geometry as an emergent structure exhibiting classical features only at a specific observational level aligns with the quantum nature of the universe. This perspective suggests that the space-time manifold is a purely theoretical arena where quantum states are defined, with the freedom to change coordinates as a symmetry. Observables, including positions and distances, should be represented by operators acting on these quantum states. While the top-down (canonical) quantization of Einstein-Hilbert gravity theoretically fits this picture, it is notoriously complex. This complexity arises from treating all classical canonical variables appearing in the fundamental action as quantum observables acting on the "superspace" of all metrics, regardless of their relevance to specific physical systems. This review instead revisits the more simplified "minisuperspace" approach, choosing gravitational observables not solely based on symmetry but also motivated by their established relevance in the classical description of a given system. Specifically, this review focuses on compact, spherically symmetric, quantum mechanical sources to determine the probability of them being black holes rather than regular particles. The gravitational radius is elevated to the status of a quantum mechanical operator acting on the "horizon wave-function," which is determined by the quantum state of the source. This formalism is then applied to various sources with a mass near the fundamental scale, considered natural candidates for quantum black holes.

title: Fracture in Sheets Draped on Curved Surfaces

Unlike previous studies on cracked plates and shells, the experiments here involve constraining flat elastic sheets to adopt fixed curvature profiles. This constraint provides a geometric tool for controlling fracture behavior: curvature can either stimulate or suppress crack growth, and steer or arrest crack propagation. A simple analytical model captures crack behavior at the onset of propagation, while a two-dimensional phase-field model with an added curvature term successfully predicts the crack's path. As the curvature-induced stresses are independent of material parameters for isotropic, brittle media, these results are applicable across scales.

title: Shadow of the rotating black hole with quintessential energy in the presence of the plasma

As the plasma refraction index increases, the apparent radius of the shadow also increases. However, for large values of the quintessential field parameter, the change in the black hole shadow's shape due to the presence of plasma is negligible. Conversely, increasing the DM interaction causes the phase transition to occur for larger values of the anisotropy parameter. Furthermore, for small magnetic field values, the concurrence measure is a suitable indicator for quantum phase transition, but for large magnetic field values, the Berry phase exhibits sharp changes at the phase transition points. title: Quantum systems under frequency modulation
Abstract: This review examines the physical phenomena arising from the time modulation of quantum mechanical energy levels. The dynamics resulting from changes in the transition frequency have been studied since the early days of quantum mechanics and continue to attract experimental and theoretical interest. The simple two-state model serves as an inexhaustible source of novel concepts. When the transition frequency of a quantum system is modulated, several phenomena can be observed, such as Landau-Zener-St\\"uckelberg-Majorana interference, motional averaging and narrowing, and the formation of dressed states with sidebands in the spectrum. Adiabatic changes lead to the accumulation of geometric phases, which can be used to create topological states. In recent years, exquisite experimental control in the time domain has been achieved through the parameters entering the Hamiltonian, and high-fidelity readout schemes have enabled non-destructive monitoring of the system's state. These advancements have been made in the field of quantum devices, particularly superconducting qubits, as well as in atomic physics, especially ultracold gases. As a result of these breakthroughs, many fundamental effects arising from the modulation of transition frequencies in a quantum system have been demonstrated. This review aims to present some of these developments, ranging from two-state atoms and harmonic oscillators to multilevel and many-particle systems.

title: Spatial Scaling of Land Cover Networks
Abstract: Spatial networks of land cover exhibit power law rank-size distributions, a pattern observed across various types of land cover, including human settlements, agriculture, and forests. This scaling persists over multiple orders of magnitude. Segmentation of these continuous fields into networks reveals rank-size distributions with slopes near -1, irrespective of the segmentation threshold. This suggests a universal explanation for this scaling, independent of specific land cover types. The conditions underlying scale-free networks can lead to power law distributions of component sizes in bounded spatial networks on a plane or surface. Progressive segmentation naturally expands the network, and the growing perimeters of components favor attachment to larger components. Simulation of two random continuous fields demonstrates the emergence of power law rank-size distributions in networks approaching the point of explosive percolation. These findings suggest that the scaling properties and uniform area distribution associated with a unity power law rank-size distribution may be a general characteristic of bounded spatial networks generated through the segmentation of continuous fields. Therefore, distinct process-specific mechanisms may not be necessary to explain the observed rank-size distributions in diverse land cover types.

The model reveals critical thresholds for disease expansion and decrease, influenced by host lifespan, prion growth rate, and prion circulation between hosts. Abstract: Node localization algorithms that seamlessly integrate with deployed wireless sensor networks (WSNs) and proprietary lower-layer communication protocols running on off-the-shelf modules can alleviate the challenges, costs, and time involved in manual or satellite-based node localization techniques. The algorithm proposed here is tailored for applications like pest control and irrigation in large farms and orchards, where power efficiency and scalability are paramount, but location accuracy demands are less stringent. The algorithm leverages received signal strength indicator (RSSI) values to estimate the distribution of distances between nodes, subsequently updating the location probability mass function (pmf) of nodes in a distributed manner. At each time step, the most recently communicated path loss samples and location prior pmf received from neighboring nodes are sufficient for nodes with unknown locations to update their location pmf, rendering the algorithm recursive and computationally efficient. A particular realization of the method involves a single node broadcasting at each time step, while neighboring nodes update their location pmf based on all communicated samples from previous time steps. This approach aligns well with realistic WSN deployments, such as ZigBee, based on the ad hoc on-demand distance vector (AODV) protocol, where nodes flood route request (RREQ) and route reply (RREP) packets across the network.

The general estimation strategy is developed within the targeted minimum loss-based estimation (TMLE) framework. The paper includes simulations comparing the sensitivity of the first and second-order estimators to the convergence rate of initial estimators for the outcome regression and missingness score. The simulations show that the second-order TMLE improves the coverage probability of a confidence interval by up to 85%. Additionally, the paper proposes a first-order estimator inspired by a second-order expansion of the parameter functional. This estimator only requires one-dimensional smoothing, while the second-order TMLE generally requires kernel smoothing on the covariate space. The proposed first-order estimator is expected to have improved finite sample performance compared to existing first-order estimators. The direction of motion of a subject across a set of scenes (left-to-right, right-to-left, up-to-down, and down-to-up) is inferred using cross-correlation analysis. title: An open access repository of images on plant health to enable the development of mobile disease diagnostics

One potential application is the development of mobile disease diagnostics through machine learning and crowdsourcing. This paper announces the release of over 50,000 expertly curated images of healthy and infected crop plant leaves through the existing online platform PlantVillage. The paper describes both the data and the platform, which serve as the beginning of an ongoing crowdsourcing effort to enable computer vision approaches to address yield losses caused by infectious diseases in crop plants.

title: Importance of method validation: Implications of non-correlated observables in sweet taste receptor studies
Abstract: Validation of research methodology is essential for robust research design. Correlation between experimental observables must be established before conducting extensive experiments or proposing mechanisms. This article demonstrates that observables in the popular calcium flux strength assay, used to characterize sweetener-sweet taste receptor (STR) interactions, are uncorrelated. This assay measures calcium flux generated via G-protein coupling for wildtype and mutant receptors expressed on cell surfaces to identify and localize sweetener binding sites, aiding in sweetener development and impacting public health. The article reveals that flux strength is independent of EC50 and sweet potency, while the sweet potency-EC50 relationship is nonlinear and anticorrelated. Published research on single point mutants affecting receptor efficiency without significant EC50 shifts indicates that flux strength is independent of ligand binding. The study concludes that the G-protein coupling step is likely observed in the assay. As a result, years of research have yielded uncorrelated data, rendering results meaningless. Despite this, the majority of research in the field relies on changes in calcium flux strength to study the receptor. The paper urges researchers to move away from flux strength monitoring for sweetener development and re-establish sweetener binding localization established by the flux strength method. The article serves as a reminder for researchers to validate methodology before embarking on long-term projects. Neglecting validation testing has proven to be a costly mistake in the field. The concepts discussed are applicable whenever observables in biological systems are several steps removed from the event of interest. |||

title: Bayesian Identification of Fixations, Saccades, and Smooth Pursuits
Abstract: Smooth pursuit eye movements provide valuable insights into a subject's behavior and health, but they can interfere with the performance of standard fixation/saccade classification algorithms. I-BDT efficiently separates fixations, saccades, and smooth pursuits in real-time, even for low-resolution eye trackers. The algorithm's effectiveness was evaluated on four datasets containing diverse mixtures of eye movements, including fixations, saccades, and straight and circular smooth pursuits. Data was collected at 30 Hz from six subjects, resulting in 24 evaluation datasets. I-BDT exhibited high and consistent performance across all datasets and movements, surpassing manual annotation by a domain expert and significantly improving upon the state-of-the-art I-VDT algorithm. title: Dengue Fever in Perspective of Clustering Algorithms

title: Dynamical Networks for Smog Pattern Analysis

Furthermore, the study found that internal factors, such as industrial pollution and vehicle emissions, are more critical than external factors like pollution spreading from nearby regions. title: Conducting sparse feature selection on arbitrarily long phrases in text corpora with a focus on interpretability
Abstract: We propose a general framework for topic-specific summarization of large text corpora, which can be applied to various contexts. Our summarization framework, built on sparse classification methods, offers a balance between simple word frequency-based methods and more complex, model-intensive approaches like Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA). For a specific topic of interest, we regress document labeling onto the high-dimensional counts of all other words and phrases within those documents. This approach yields a small set of predictive phrases, which are then extracted as the summary. Using a branch-and-bound approach, this method can be extended to accommodate phrases of arbitrary length, enabling potentially rich summarization. We discuss how the intended purpose of the summaries can guide choices of regularization parameters and model constraints. We evaluate this tool by comparing its computational time and summary statistics with three existing methods. We also present a new R package, textreg. Overall, we argue that sparse methods hold significant potential for text analysis and warrant further exploration in this context.

title: WFIRST-AFTA Coronagraphic Operations: Lessons Learned from the Hubble Space Telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope
Abstract: The coronagraphic instrument currently being developed for the WFIRST-AFTA mission will be the first space-based coronagraph optimized for extremely high contrasts, essential for the direct imaging of exoplanets reflecting the light of their host stars. We identify five crucial operational aspects that will require attention: 1) detector health and evolution, 2) wavefront control, 3) observing strategies/post-processing, 4) astrometric precision/target acquisition, and 5) polarimetry. title: Part I - A case study in post-secondary mathematics: the importance of mental health awareness
Abstract: The shift from the Industrial Age to the Information Age has made mathematical literacy an essential skill in the twenty-first century. However, to fully engage in and contribute to the mathematical community, individuals must be in a state of good mental health. This includes developing healthy coping strategies, being in a positive learning environment, and having a social support system. Traditionally, universities have served as the venue for such higher learning. To remain thriving grounds for higher education and engines of research, post-secondary institutions must recognize these factors and actively contribute to the well-being of their students and faculty. Unfortunately, students often lack the support necessary to maintain their mental health. The surveys investigated the students' experiences at the university, particularly within the Mathematics Department. The scores for alternative-scheduled assignments are statistically analyzed and compared to those of traditional assignment schedules currently implemented at the University of Waterloo. title: Doctor AI: Predicting Clinical Events via Recurrent Neural Networks

Encounter records, including diagnosis codes, medication codes, and procedure codes, were input into RNN to predict all diagnosis and medication categories for a subsequent visit. Doctor AI analyzes the patient's history to make multi-label predictions, one label for each diagnosis or medication category. Based on separate blind test set evaluation, Doctor AI achieved a recall@30 of up to 79%, significantly surpassing several baselines in differential diagnosis. Moreover, we demonstrated the model's remarkable generalizability by adapting it from one institution to another without substantial loss of accuracy.

title: Automatic Region-wise Spatially Varying Coefficient Regression Model: an Application to National Cardiovascular Disease Mortality and Air Pollution Association Study
Abstract: Motivated by analyzing a national database of annual air pollution and cardiovascular disease mortality rates for 3,100 counties in the United States (areal data), we developed a novel statistical framework to automatically detect spatially varying region-wise associations between air pollution exposures and health outcomes. The automatic region-wise spatially varying coefficient model comprises three parts: first, we calculate the similarity matrix between the exposure-health outcome associations of all spatial units. Second, we segment the entire map into disjoint regions based on the adjacency matrix, with constraints that all spatial units within a region are contiguous and have similar associations. Lastly, we estimate the region-specific associations between exposure and health outcomes. We implement the framework using regression and spectral graph techniques. We develop goodness-of-fit criteria for model assessment and selection. Simulation studies confirm the satisfactory performance of our model. We further apply our method to investigate the association between airborne particulate matter smaller than 2.5 microns (PM 2.5) and cardiovascular disease mortality. The results successfully identify regions with distinct associations between the mortality rate and PM 2.5, providing insightful guidance for environmental health research.

title: Identification of homophily and preferential recruitment in respondent-driven sampling
Abstract: Respondent-driven sampling (RDS) is a link-tracing procedure for surveying hidden or hard-to-reach populations, where subjects recruit other subjects through their social networks. There is considerable research interest in detecting clustering or dependence of epidemiological traits in networks. However, researchers disagree on whether data from RDS studies can reveal such dependence. Two distinct mechanisms contribute to dependence in traits of recruiters and recruitees in an RDS study: homophily, the tendency for individuals to share social ties with others exhibiting similar characteristics, and preferential recruitment, where recruiters do not recruit uniformly at random from their available contacts. The different effects of network homophily and preferential recruitment in RDS studies have caused confusion in methodological research on RDS and empirical studies examining the social context of health risk in hidden populations. In this paper, we provide rigorous definitions of homophily and preferential recruitment and demonstrate that neither can be precisely measured in general RDS studies. We derive nonparametric identification regions for homophily and preferential recruitment and show that these parameters are not point-identified unless the network takes a degenerate form. Our findings suggest that claims of homophily or recruitment bias measured from empirical RDS studies may not be credible. We apply our identification results to a study involving both a network census and RDS on a population of injection drug users in Hartford, Connecticut.

title: Bayesian analysis of ambulatory blood pressure dynamics with application to irregularly spaced sparse data

To overcome the data analytic constraint that empirical measurements are typically collected at irregular and much larger time intervals than those evaluated in simulation studies of SDEs, we adopt a Bayesian approach with a regularized Brownian Bridge sampler (RBBS) and an efficient multiresolution (MR) algorithm to fit the proposed SDE. The MR algorithm can produce more efficient MCMC samples, crucial for valid parameter estimation and inference. Using this model and algorithm on data from the Duke Behavioral Investigation of Hypertension Study, results indicate that age, caffeine intake, gender, and race influence the distinct dynamic characteristics of participants' CV trajectories.

title: Deep Kalman Filters
Abstract: Kalman Filters are one of the most influential models for time-varying phenomena. They offer an intuitive probabilistic interpretation, have a simple functional form, and are widely adopted across various disciplines. Notably, temporal generative models have significant potential for counterfactual inference. We investigate the efficacy of such models for counterfactual inference and introduce the "Healing MNIST" dataset, where long-term structure, noise, and actions are applied to sequences of digits. title: Infrastructure and methods for real-time predictions of the 2014 dengue fever season in Thailand
Abstract: Outbreaks of communicable diseases pose a significant burden on public health infrastructure worldwide. Producing accurate and actionable forecasts of infectious disease incidence at short and long time scales can enhance public health responses to outbreaks. However, scientists and public health officials face numerous challenges in creating accurate and actionable real-time forecasts of infectious disease incidence. We established an operational and computational infrastructure that generates multi-step predictions of dengue incidence in Thai provinces every two weeks throughout 2014. title: On the linearization of identifying the stored energy function of a hyperelastic material from full knowledge of the displacement field
Abstract: We address the nonlinear, inverse problem of computing the stored energy function of a hyperelastic material from the complete knowledge of the displacement field. The displacement field is described as the solution of the nonlinear, dynamic, elastic wave equation, where the first Piola-Kirchhoff stress tensor is defined as the gradient of the stored energy function. We assume that we have a dictionary available such that the energy function is represented as a conic combination of the dictionary's elements. In this context, the mathematical model of the direct problem is the nonlinear operator that maps the vector of expansion coefficients to the solution of the hyperelastic wave equation. This article summarizes some continuity results for this operator and derives its Fréchet derivative, as well as the adjoint of this derivative. Since the stored energy function encodes the mechanical properties of the underlying hyperelastic material, the considered inverse problem is highly relevant for structural health monitoring systems where defects are detected from boundary measurements of the displacement field. For iteratively solving the inverse problem using the Landweber method or Newton-type methods, knowledge of the Fréchet derivative and its adjoint is crucial.

title: Seeing the Unseen Network: Inferring Hidden Social Ties from Respondent-Driven Sampling
Abstract: Understanding the social structure of hidden and hard-to-reach populations, such as drug users and sex workers, is a major goal of epidemiological and public health research on risk behaviors and disease prevention. Respondent-driven sampling (RDS) is a peer-referral process widely used by many health organizations, where research subjects recruit other subjects from their social networks. In such surveys, researchers observe who recruited whom, along with the time of recruitment and the total number of acquaintances (network degree) of respondents. However, due to privacy concerns, the identities of acquaintances are not disclosed. In this work, we demonstrate how to reconstruct the underlying network structure through which subjects are recruited. We formulate the dynamics of RDS as a continuous-time diffusion process over the underlying graph and derive the likelihood for the recruitment time series under an arbitrary recruitment time distribution. We develop an efficient stochastic optimization algorithm called RENDER (REspoNdent-Driven nEtwork Reconstruction) that identifies the network that best explains the collected data. We validate our analytical results through a comprehensive set of experiments on both synthetic and real data.

title: Whom Should We Sense in "Social Sensing" -- Analyzing Which Users Work Best for Social Media Now-Casting
Abstract: Given the ever-increasing amount of publicly available social media data, there is growing interest in using online data to study and quantify phenomena in the offline "real" world. As social media data can be obtained in near real-time and at low cost, it is often used for "now-casting" indices such as levels of flu activity or unemployment. The term "social sensing" is frequently used in this context, describing the idea that users act as "sensors," publicly reporting their health status or job losses. Sensor activity during a given time period is typically aggregated in a "one tweet, one vote" fashion by simply counting. However, researchers acknowledge that social media users are not a perfect representation of the actual population. Additionally, users vary in the amount of detail they reveal about their personal lives. Intuitively, it should be possible to improve now-casting by assigning different weights to different user groups.  In this paper, we ask "How does social sensing actually work?" or, more precisely, "Whom should we sense--and whom not--for optimal results?". We investigate how different sampling strategies affect the performance of now-casting for two common offline indices: flu activity and unemployment rate. We show that now-casting can be improved by 1) applying user filtering techniques and 2) selecting users with complete profiles. We also find that using the right type of user groups, now-casting performance does not degrade even when drastically reducing the dataset size. More fundamentally, we describe which type of users contribute most to accuracy by asking if "babblers are better." We conclude by providing guidance on how to select better user groups for more accurate now-casting.

title: Learning to Diagnose with LSTM Recurrent Neural Networks
Abstract: Clinical medical data, especially in the intensive care unit (ICU), consist of multivariate time series of observations. For each patient visit (or episode), sensor data and lab test results are recorded in the patient's Electronic Health Record (EHR). While potentially containing a wealth of insights, this data is difficult to mine effectively due to varying length, irregular sampling, and missing data. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), particularly those using Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) hidden units, are powerful and increasingly popular models for learning from sequence data. They effectively model sequences of varying length and capture long-range dependencies. We present the first study to empirically evaluate the ability of LSTMs to recognize patterns in multivariate time series of clinical measurements. Specifically, we consider multi-label classification of diagnoses, training a model to classify 128 diagnoses given 13 frequently but irregularly sampled clinical measurements. First, we establish the effectiveness of a simple LSTM network for modeling clinical data. Then, we demonstrate a straightforward and effective training strategy in which we replicate targets at each sequence step. Trained only on raw time series, our models outperform several strong baselines, including a multilayer perceptron trained on hand-engineered features.

title: Modeling And Control Battery Aging in Energy Harvesting Systems

title: Examination of the scientific review process: Ten best practice suggestions for an improved process

Ensuring that proposals submitted are treated fairly and transparently is essential for the health of any research program and a duty to the public who ultimately funds the research. The paper outlines the general requirements of a review process and, at each step, highlights potential issues and suggests potential improvements and fundamental requirements for any scientific review. We also include a series of tips for the scientific community. Our objectives are 1) to demystify the process for everyone, including policymakers who are sometimes perplexed by the results of scientific reviews, 2) to stimulate discussions about reviews and review processes within the scientific community, 3) to inform scientists whose careers are directly impacted by review results about their own role in this process, and 4) to suggest a path towards a more efficient, fairer, and overall more transparent process. title: Quantile regression for mixed models with an application to examine blood pressure trends in China
Abstract: Cardiometabolic diseases have significantly increased in China over the past two decades, with blood pressure emerging as a key modifiable risk factor. Given the importance of extremely high blood pressure values, the researchers model the conditional quantile functions of systolic and diastolic blood pressure. This approach allows the covariate effects in the middle of the distribution to differ from those in the upper tail, which is the primary focus of the analysis. The distributions of systolic and diastolic blood pressure are then combined using a copula, enabling the sharing of information regarding the relationships between covariates and the two responses and facilitating probabilistic statements about both types of blood pressure jointly. This copula maintains the marginal distributions of the group quantile effects while accounting for within-subject dependence, allowing for inference at both the population and individual levels. The population-level regression effects exhibit variation across quantile level, year, and blood pressure type, offering a rich environment for inference. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this is the first quantile function model explicitly incorporating within-subject autocorrelation and the first quantile function approach to simultaneously model multivariate conditional responses. The study finds that the association between high blood pressure and urban living has shifted from positive to negative, with the most pronounced changes occurring in the upper tail. The rise in urbanization over the past twenty years, coupled with the transition from a positive association between urbanization and blood pressure in earlier years to a more uniform association, suggests an overall increase in blood pressure across China over time, even in less urbanized regions. title: Linear-time Detection of Non-linear Changes in Massively High Dimensional Time Series
Abstract: Change detection in multivariate time series finds applications in various domains, including healthcare and network monitoring. A common approach to detect changes involves comparing the divergence between the distributions of a reference window and a test window. However, when the number of dimensions is extremely large, this naive approach presents challenges in terms of both quality and efficiency. To ensure robustness, the window size needs to be large, which not only leads to missed alarms but also increases runtime. To address this, the authors propose LIGHT, a linear-time algorithm for robustly detecting non-linear changes in massively high-dimensional time series. Importantly, LIGHT offers high flexibility in choosing the window size, allowing domain experts to tailor the level of detail required. This is achieved by 1) performing scalable Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to reduce dimensionality, 2) performing scalable factorization of the joint distribution, and 3) scalably computing divergences between these lower-dimensional distributions. Extensive empirical evaluations on both synthetic and real-world data demonstrate that LIGHT outperforms state-of-the-art methods with up to a 100% improvement in both quality and efficiency.

title: Beyond prediction: A framework for inference with variational approximations in mixture models
Abstract: Variational inference is a widely used method for estimating model parameters and conditional distributions in hierarchical and mixed models, which arise frequently in various fields such as health, social, and biological sciences. In a frequentist context, variational inference approximates intractable conditional distributions with a tractable family and optimizes the resulting lower bound on the log-likelihood. The variational objective function is typically less computationally intensive to optimize than the true likelihood, enabling scientists to fit complex models even with extremely large datasets. Despite its widespread use, there is limited knowledge regarding the general theoretical properties of estimators derived from variational approximations to the log-likelihood, hindering their application in inferential statistics. This paper establishes a connection between such estimators and profile M-estimation, which allows the authors to provide regularity conditions for consistency and asymptotic normality of variational estimators. The theory also motivates three methodological improvements to variational inference: estimation of the asymptotic model-robust covariance matrix, a one-step correction to enhance estimator efficiency, and an empirical assessment of consistency. The proposed results are evaluated using simulation studies and data on marijuana use from the National Longitudinal Study of Youth.

This process is mediated by a conformational change in the protein structure, transitioning from a dimer to a trimer state. Previous research has identified an existing cavity on the dimer structure of the envelope protein. The results showed that the PYRRP ligand could support the stability of the DENV envelope protein dimer structure at 310 K and 312 K. title: The Complexity of Molecular Interactions and Bindings between Cyclic Peptide and Inhibit Polymerase A and B1 (PAC-PB1N) H1N1
Abstract: The influenza/H1N1 virus has posed a significant public health threat in numerous countries. Existing influenza drugs have proven ineffective against H1N1 infection due to the virus's high mutation rate. To address this, a new approach to block the virus has been developed. The polymerase PAC-PB1N enzyme is responsible for the replication of the H1N1 virus. Consequently, novel inhibitors have been developed to counteract the enzyme's functionality. This research focuses on cyclic peptides as inhibitors of PAC-PB1N due to their proven stability in reaching the drug target. A computational method has been developed using the LigX tools from MOE 2008.10 software to elucidate the molecular interactions between cyclic peptides and PAC-PB1N. The tools can identify the bindings involved in the interactions, allowing visualization of the interactions between individual amino acids in the inhibitor and the enzyme. Based on this analysis, the peptide sequences of CKTTC and CKKTC were chosen as lead compounds. The 2D and 3D modeling of the molecular interactions demonstrate the potential of cyclic peptides to serve as drug candidates for H1N1.

title: Verifying the HALE measures of the Global Burden of Disease Study: Quantitative Methods Proposed
Abstract: To validate the Global Burden of Disease Study and the healthy life expectancy (HALE) estimates provided by the World Health Organization (WHO), this study proposes a straightforward model based on the mortality (μx) of a population, as presented in a classical life table and a mortality diagram. The study utilizes abridged life tables provided by WHO. The model's estimates are compared with the HALE estimates for World territories and WHO countries. Additionally, a simple Excel program has been developed to readily provide estimates for life expectancy, loss of healthy life years, and healthy life expectancy. The health state function theory is also applied to generate additional estimates and comparisons. The findings suggest improved WHO estimates in recent years for the majority of cases. Keywords: Health state function, Healthy life expectancy, Mortality Diagram, Loss of healthy years, LHLY, HALE, DALE, World Health Organization, WHO, Global burden of Disease, Health status.

title: Non-separable Dynamic Nearest-Neighbor Gaussian Process Models for Large spatio-temporal Data With an Application to Particulate Matter Analysis
Abstract: Particulate matter (PM) is a class of harmful environmental pollutants known to be detrimental to human health. Regulatory efforts to curb PM levels in various countries often require high-resolution space-time maps that can pinpoint regions exceeding statutory concentration limits. Continuous spatio-temporal Gaussian Process (GP) models offer maps depicting predicted PM levels and quantifying predictive uncertainty. However, GP-based approaches frequently encounter computational challenges posed by large datasets. To address this, the authors construct a novel class of scalable Dynamic Nearest Neighbor Gaussian Process (DNNGP) models that provide a sparse approximation to any spatio-temporal GP, including those with non-separable covariance structures. The DNNGP developed in this study can serve as a sparsity-inducing prior for spatio-temporal random effects in any Bayesian hierarchical model, delivering full posterior inference. Storage and memory requirements for a DNNGP model are linear in the size of the dataset, enabling massive scalability without sacrificing inferential richness. Extensive numerical studies reveal that the DNNGP provides significantly superior approximations to the underlying process compared to low-rank approximations. Finally, the authors apply the DNNGP to analyze a massive air quality dataset to significantly improve predictions of PM levels across Europe in conjunction with the LOTOS-EUROS chemistry transport models (CTMs).

title: Hierarchy of knowledge translation: from health problems to ad-hoc drug design
Abstract: This paper explores an innovative approach to analyzing the complexity of translating novel molecular entities and nanomaterials into pharmaceutical alternatives, a process known as knowledge translation (KT). The discussion begins by reviewing key concepts related to the organization and translation of biomedical knowledge, including paradigms, homophily, power law distributions, hierarchy, modularity, and research fronts.  The authors then propose a model for knowledge translation (KT) in Drug Discovery that considers the complexity of interdisciplinary communication. Specifically, the model addresses two highly relevant aspects: 1) Successful KT requires the emergence of organized bodies of inter-and transdisciplinary research, and 2) The hierarchical and modular topological organization of these bodies of knowledge. The paper focuses on a set of previously published studies on KT that rely on a combination of network analysis and computer-assisted analysis of scientific literature and patents. These selected studies provide two complementary perspectives: the demand for knowledge (cervical cancer and Ebola hemorrhagic fever) and the supply of knowledge (liposomes and nanoparticles for treating cancer and the paradigmatic Doxil, the first nanodrug to be approved).

title: A latent shared-component generative model for real-time disease surveillance using Twitter data
Abstract: Exploiting the vast amount of available data to address significant social problems has emerged as a key challenge in data mining. These efforts, often termed "data science for social good," have attracted the attention of numerous researchers and institutions. This paper contributes to this objective by addressing a challenging public health issue: the timely monitoring of dengue epidemics in small geographic areas. The authors develop a generative, simple yet effective model to connect the fluctuations of disease cases and disease-related Twitter posts. The model assumes a hidden Markov process driving both the fluctuations in reported dengue cases and the tweets issued in each region. A stable but random source of tweets is incorporated to represent posts when no disease cases are recorded. The model is learned through a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm that produces the posterior distribution of the relevant parameters. Using data from a significant number of large Brazilian towns, the study empirically demonstrates that the model can accurately predict the next few weeks of disease counts using both tweets and disease cases jointly.
