title: Social Media Analysis for Product Safety using Text Mining and Sentiment Analysis
Abstract: The increasing prevalence of counterfeiting and its associated economic and health consequences necessitate the development of active surveillance systems capable of delivering timely and reliable information to all stakeholders involved in the anti-counterfeiting fight. User-generated content from social media platforms can provide early clues about product allergies, adverse events, and product counterfeiting. This paper presents a work in progress, highlighting contributions including: the development of a framework for gathering and analyzing user views and experiences of drug and cosmetic products using machine learning, text mining, and sentiment analysis, the application of the proposed framework on Facebook comments and data from Twitter for brand analysis, and the description of how to develop a product safety lexicon and training data for modeling a machine learning classifier for drug and cosmetic product sentiment prediction. Initial brand and product comparison results indicate the usefulness of text mining and sentiment analysis on social media data, while the use of a machine learning classifier for predicting sentiment orientation provides a valuable tool for users, product manufacturers, regulatory agencies, and enforcement agencies to monitor brand or product sentiment trends and act in response to sudden or significant rises in negative sentiment.

title: Insights from Machine-Learned Diet Success Prediction
Abstract: To support individuals striving to lose weight and maintain a healthy lifestyle, an increasing number of fitness apps have emerged, incorporating features to track both calorie intake and expenditure. Users of such apps are part of a broader "quantified self" movement, with many opting to publicly share their logged data. This paper utilizes public food diaries from over 4,000 long-term active MyFitnessPal users to study the characteristics of successful and unsuccessful diets. The study trains a machine learning model to predict repeated instances of exceeding or falling short of self-set daily calorie goals and then analyzes which features contribute to the model's predictions. The findings include both expected results, such as the token "mcdonalds" or the category "dessert" being indicative of exceeding the calorie goal, as well as less obvious ones, like the difference between pork and poultry concerning dieting success, or the use of the "quick added calories" functionality being indicative of exceeding calorie goals. The study also suggests the feasibility of using such data for more in-depth data mining, for example, examining the interaction between consumed foods, such as the combination of protein- and carbohydrate-rich foods. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this is the first systematic study of public food diaries.

title: A Method for Modeling Co-Occurrence Propensity of Clinical Codes with Application to ICD-10-PCS Auto-Coding
Abstract: Natural language processing methods for medical auto-coding, or the automatic generation of medical billing codes from electronic health records, typically assign each code independently of the others. This can lead to the assignment of codes for closely related procedures or diagnoses to the same document, even when they do not tend to occur together in practice, simply because inferring the correct choice from the clinical narrative can be challenging. This paper proposes a method that incorporates awareness of code co-occurrence propensities into the auto-coding process. Initially, a model is trained to estimate the conditional probability that one code is assigned by a human coder, given that another code is known to have been assigned to the same document. Then, at runtime, an iterative algorithm applies this model to the output of an existing statistical auto-coder to modify the confidence scores of the codes. The method was tested in combination with a primary auto-coder for ICD-10 procedure codes, achieving a 12% relative improvement in F-score compared to the primary auto-coder baseline. The proposed method, with appropriate features, can be used in combination with any auto-coder that generates codes with different confidence levels. The promising results obtained for ICD-10 procedure codes suggest that the method may have broader applications in auto-coding.

title: Automatic Stress Detection in Working Environments from Smartphones' Accelerometer Data: A First Step
Abstract: The increasing workload across many organizations and the consequent rise in occupational stress are negatively affecting the health of the workforce. Measuring stress and other human psychological dynamics is challenging due to the subjective nature of self-reporting and variability between and within individuals. With the advent of smartphones, it is now possible to monitor various aspects of human behavior, including objectively measured behavior related to psychological state and consequently stress. This study uses data from smartphone-built-in accelerometers to detect behavior that correlates with subjects' stress levels. Accelerometer sensors were chosen because they raise fewer privacy concerns (compared to location, video, or audio recording) and their low power consumption makes them suitable for embedding in smaller wearable devices, such as fitness trackers. Thirty subjects from two different organizations were provided with smartphones. The study lasted for eight weeks and was conducted in real working environments without any restrictions on smartphone usage. Subjects reported their perceived stress levels three times during their working hours. By employing a combination of statistical models to classify self-reported stress levels, the study achieved a maximum overall accuracy of 71% for user-specific models and an accuracy of 60% for the use of similar-users models, relying solely on data from a single accelerometer.

title: Persistent Sharing of Fitness App Status on Twitter

The study investigates how specific features such as user profile, fitness activity, and fitness network in social media can potentially impact the long-term engagement of fitness app users. The paper also discusses the implications of these findings for achieving better retention of users and promoting more sharing of their status updates.

title: A study on the effect of age, gender and paralysis on sEMG signals

Signals were obtained from several volunteers across different age groups, genders, and individuals with paralysis. The sEMG data acquisition was performed using a computer's soundcard, minimizing the need for additional hardware. Finally, the data is analyzed to investigate the relationship between electromyography and factors such as age, gender, and health condition, including paralysis.

title: Low-cost Sensor Glove with Force Feedback for Learning from Demonstrations using Probabilistic Trajectory Representations

title: IoT enabled Insurance Ecosystem - Possibilities Challenges and Risks
Abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) is poised to transform the business processes of many industries, including the insurance sector. Existing lines of business such as Property and Casualty, Health, and Life Insurance can benefit immensely from the contextual and relevant data generated by billions of connected devices, including smartphones, wearable gadgets, and other electronic smart sensors. For P&C insurers, the biggest challenges are not the rapidly changing environment but tackling these challenges with strategies anchored in the past. This paper presents the key opportunities, challenges, potential applications, and risks of IoT in the insurance domain. It focuses on the efficient use of data analytics from data generated in the IoT ecosystem and highlights the business model changes that insurance industries may face in the near future.

title: Inferring disease correlation from healthcare data
Abstract: Electronic Health Records (EHRs) maintained in healthcare settings represent a potential source of substantial clinical knowledge. The massive volume of data, unstructured nature of records, and the obligatory requirement of domain expertise pose challenges in extracting knowledge from EHRs. This study aims to overcome these challenges through methodical analysis, abstraction, and summarization of EHR data. The study attempts to explain clinical observations through biomedical and genomic data. Discharge summaries of obesity patients were processed to extract coherent patterns. This process was supported by machine learning and natural language processing-based technologies, a concept mapping tool, and biomedical, clinical, and genomic knowledge bases. Semantic relations between diseases were extracted and filtered using a chi-square test to remove spurious relations. The remaining relations were validated against biomedical literature and gene interaction networks. A collection of binary relations of diseases was derived from the data. One set implied co-morbidity, while the other set contained diseases that are risk factors for others. Validation against biomedical literature increased the likelihood of correlation between diseases. The gene interaction network revealed that the diseases are related and their corresponding genes are in close proximity. The study focuses on deducing meaningful relations between diseases from discharge summaries. For analytical purposes, the scope was limited to a few common, well-researched diseases. The study can be extended to incorporate relatively unknown, complex diseases and discover new traits to assist in clinical assessments. |||

title: Characterization of behavioral patterns exploiting description of geographical areas
Abstract: The abundance of readily available mobile phone data offers unprecedented insights into human behavior. Early identification and prediction of behavioral patterns are crucial for various societal applications, including urban planning, transportation optimization, and healthcare.  Understanding the connection between human behaviors and their surrounding environment is a growing area of interest for analyzing human-environmental dynamics. The widespread availability of Web 2.0, characterized by user-generated content and social platforms, presents an opportunity to study these environmental contexts. This research examines the relationships between human behavior and location context by analyzing mobile phone data records. A novel approach is introduced to categorize urban areas based on the presence and distribution of human activity categories (e.g., eating, working, shopping). This classification is evaluated by comparing it to patterns of temporal variation in mobile phone activity and employing machine learning techniques to predict communication activity timelines in specific locations, leveraging the relationship between activity category and land-use type. The proposed classification demonstrates greater consistency with temporal variations in human communication activity, proving to be a more effective predictor compared to traditional land-use classifications.

title: Heart beat classification from single-lead ECG using the Synchrosqueezing Transform
Abstract: Processing electrocardiogram (ECG) signals provides valuable information about cardiac function and overall cardiovascular health. While multi-lead ECG recordings are often required for accurate assessment of cardiac rhythms, they are not always readily available or practical, particularly in fetal ECG applications. The increasing availability of small, non-invasive single-lead ECG ambulatory monitoring devices enables the derivation of heart rate variability (HRV) and other health-related metrics.  Reliable HRV assessment relies on accurate beat detection and classification of abnormal rhythms, which can be challenging in single-lead ECG monitoring.  This manuscript models the heart rate signal as an adaptive non-harmonic model and utilizes the newly developed synchrosqueezing transform (SST) to characterize ECG patterns. The study demonstrates the model's effectiveness in enhancing heart beat detection and classification between normal and abnormal rhythms. Using the Massachusetts Institute of Technology-Beth Israel Hospital (MIT-BIH) arrhythmia database and the Association for the Advancement of Medical Instrumentation (AAMI) beat classes, a support vector machine (SVM) classifier was trained and validated on a subset of the annotated beat database using SST-derived features. The results demonstrate sensitivities and positive predictive values comparable to other published algorithms that utilize multiple leads and a larger number of features.

title: FairTest: Discovering Unwarranted Associations in Data-Driven Applications
Abstract: In a world where traditional notions of privacy are increasingly challenged by data collection and analysis practices, it is essential that decision-making entities are held accountable for unfair treatments arising from irresponsible data usage. The lack of appropriate methodologies and tools poses a significant challenge to identifying unfair or discriminatory effects in practice. This paper introduces the unwarranted associations (UA) framework, a principled methodology for detecting unfair, discriminatory, or offensive user treatment in data-driven applications. The UA framework integrates and rationalizes previous attempts at formalizing algorithmic fairness.  It uniquely combines multiple investigative primitives and fairness metrics with broad applicability, granular exploration of unfair treatment in user subgroups, and incorporation of natural notions of utility that account for observed disparities. The UA framework is implemented in FairTest, the first comprehensive tool that assists developers in checking data-driven applications for unfair user treatment. FairTest enables scalable and statistically rigorous investigation of associations between application outcomes (e.g., prices or premiums) and sensitive user attributes (e.g., race or gender). Additionally, FairTest provides debugging capabilities that help programmers rule out potential confounders for observed unfair effects. The study reports on the use of FairTest to investigate and, in some cases, address disparate impact, offensive labeling, and uneven rates of algorithmic error in four data-driven applications.  The results reveal subtle biases against older populations in the distribution of error in a predictive health application and offensive racial labeling in an image tagger.

title: Computational Modelling of Atherosclerosis
Abstract: Atherosclerosis is a primary pathology associated with cardiovascular disease, with blood cholesterol being a significant risk factor. The World Health Organisation estimates that approximately 2.5 million deaths occur annually due to elevated cholesterol levels, with 39% of adults worldwide at future risk. Atherosclerosis arises from a complex interplay of various dynamic factors, including haemodynamics, endothelial damage, innate immunity, and sterol biochemistry. Despite its significance to public health, the dynamics that drive atherosclerosis remain poorly understood. As a disease that depends on multiple factors operating across different length scales, the natural framework for studying atherosclerosis is mathematical and computational modeling. A computational model offers an integrated description of the disease and serves as an in silico experimental system for gaining insights and developing therapeutic hypotheses. While research in this area has been limited, there is growing interest and the establishment of a nascent field. This paper discusses the current state of modeling in this area, compiling recent results for the first time. It reviews the work that has been done, explores its scope, and highlights gaps in our understanding that could lead to future opportunities.

title: High Precision Fault Injections on the Instruction Cache of ARMv7-M Architectures
Abstract: The hardware and software components of secure embedded systems are susceptible to physical attacks. Fault injection attacks exploit vulnerabilities in the data and control flow, enabling attackers to compromise cryptographic or secure algorithm implementations. While numerous research studies have focused on successful attacks on the data flow, only a few have targeted the instruction flow. This paper concentrates on electromagnetic fault injection (EMFI) on the control flow, specifically targeting the instruction cache. The study focuses on the widely used ARMv7-M architecture, commonly found in smartphones, tablets, settop boxes, health-industry monitors, and sensors. A practical EMFI platform is described, along with a methodology that provides high control level and reproducibility over fault injections. The research observes a precise fault model occurring in up to 96% of cases, characterizing and exhibiting this practical fault model on the cache. The effects of this fault model are comprehensively described, demonstrating its potential to reproduce well-known fault attacks. The study concludes by explaining how this fault model can be exploited by attackers to launch powerful new attacks or simplify existing ones.

title: Monitoring Potential Drug Interactions and Reactions via Network Analysis of Instagram User Timelines
Abstract: Recent research endeavors to identify evidence of Drug-Drug Interactions (DDI) and Adverse Drug Reactions (ADR) from the biomedical scientific literature.  Beyond the "Bibliome," the vast universe of social media presents a promising source of large-scale data for identifying DDI and ADR in ways previously unattainable. The analysis of social media data can be useful for identifying under-reported, population-level pathology associated with DDI, contributing to improvements in population health. This approach also allows for the inference of drug interactions with natural products, including cannabis, which have been poorly explored by biomedical research thus far. This research aims to determine the potential of Instagram for public health monitoring and surveillance of DDI, ADR, and behavioral pathology. Using drug, symptom, and natural product dictionaries for identifying various types of DDI and ADR evidence, approximately 7000 timelines have been collected. The paper reports on (1) the development of a monitoring tool for observing user-level timelines associated with drug and symptom terms of interest, and (2) population-level behavior analysis through the analysis of co-occurrence networks computed from user timelines at three different scales: monthly, weekly, and daily occurrences. Analysis of these networks reveals (3) direct and indirect associations between drugs and symptoms with greater support in user timelines, as well as (4) clusters of symptoms and drugs identified by the collective behavior of the observed population. The findings demonstrate that Instagram contains significant drug- and pathology-specific data for public health monitoring of DDI and ADR, and that complex network analysis provides a valuable toolkit for extracting health-related associations and their support from large-scale social media data.

title: Supporting interoperability of collaborative networks through engineering of a service-based Mediation Information System (MISE 2.0)
Abstract: The Mediation Information System Engineering project is concluding its second iteration (MISE 2.0). The MISE 2.0 platform implements a model-driven engineering approach for designing a service-oriented MIS to support collaborative situations. This approach is structured in three layers, each offering key innovative aspects: (i) gathering individual and collaborative knowledge to provide appropriate collaborative business behavior (key point: knowledge management, including semantics, exploitation, and capitalization), (ii) deployment of a mediation information system capable of computerizing the previously deduced collaborative processes (key point: automatic generation of collaborative workflows, including connection with existing devices or services), and (iii) management of the agility of the obtained collaborative network of organizations (key point: supervision of collaborative situations and relevant exploitation of gathered data). The derivation of the method and its advantages over traditional techniques are presented, along with simulation studies demonstrating its viability. The method is applied to a model of intestinal microbial communities, highlighting the insights that can be gained. title: Online Social Activity Reflects Economic Status

title: Dependable Structural Helath Monitoring Using Wireless Sensor Networks
Abstract: As an alternative to current wired-based networks, wireless sensor networks (WSNs) are becoming increasingly attractive for engineering structural health monitoring (SHM) due to their relatively low cost, ease of installation, and other advantages. However, an unaddressed challenge remains: application-specific dependability in terms of sensor fault detection and tolerance. Dependability is also affected by reduced monitoring quality when mitigating WSN constraints (e.g., limited energy, narrow bandwidth). To address these challenges, a dependable distributed WSN framework for SHM, called DependSHM, is designed and evaluated for its ability to handle sensor faults and constraints. The study finds evidence that faulty sensors can corrupt results related to health events (e.g., damage) in a structural system without being detected.  Specifically, it highlights an undiscovered fact: real measured signals introduced by faulty sensors can lead to an undamaged location being identified as damaged (false positive) or a damaged location being identified as undamaged (false negative). These errors can be caused by faults in sensor bonding, precision degradation, amplification gain, bias, drift, noise, and other factors. DependSHM introduces a distributed automated algorithm for detecting these types of faults and offers an online signal reconstruction algorithm to recover from incorrect diagnoses. The effectiveness of DependSHM is evaluated through comprehensive simulations and a WSN prototype system implementation.

title: Examining socioeconomic health disparities using a rank-dependent Rényi index
Abstract: The Rényi index (RI) is a one-parameter class of indices that summarizes health disparities among population groups by measuring divergence between the distributions of disease burden and population shares. This paper introduces the rank-dependent RI, a two-parameter class of health disparity indices that also accounts for the association between socioeconomic rank and health. This index can be derived from a rank-dependent social welfare function. Two competing classes are discussed, and the rank-dependent RI is shown to be more robust to changes in the distribution of either socioeconomic rank or health. The standard error and sampling distribution of the rank-dependent RI are evaluated using linearization and resampling techniques. The methodology is illustrated using health survey data from the U.S. National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey and registry data from the U.S. Surveillance, Epidemiology and End Results Program. Such data underpin many population-based objectives within the U.S. Healthy People 2020 initiative. The rank-dependent RI provides a unified mathematical framework for eliciting various societal positions regarding policies tied to wide-reaching public health initiatives.  For example, if population groups with lower socioeconomic positions were found to be more likely to utilize costly public programs, the parameters of the RI could be selected to reflect prioritizing those groups for intervention or treatment.

title: Jump detection in generalized error-in-variables regression with an application to Australian health tax policies
Abstract: In the absence of measurement errors in predictors, the discontinuity of a nonparametric regression function at unknown locations can be estimated using existing approaches.  However, this becomes a challenging problem when predictors contain measurement errors. This paper proposes an error-in-variables jump point estimator for a nonparametric generalized error-in-variables regression model. A key feature of this method is that it does not impose any parametric distribution on the measurement error. Its performance is evaluated through both numerical studies and theoretical justifications. The method is applied to studying the impact of the Medicare Levy Surcharge on the private health insurance take-up rate in Australia.

title: Adaptive Geostatistical Design and Analysis for Sequential Prevalence Surveys
Abstract: Non-adaptive geostatistical designs (NAGD) provide standard methods for collecting and analyzing geostatistical data where sampling locations are fixed beforehand.  In contrast, adaptive geostatistical designs (AGD) allow the collection of exposure and outcome data over time to depend on information obtained from previous data to optimize data collection towards the analysis objective. AGDs are becoming increasingly important in spatial mapping, particularly in resource-constrained settings where uniformly precise mapping may be prohibitively costly and the priority is often to identify critical areas for intervention. Two AGD constructions are: singleton and batch adaptive sampling. In singleton sampling, locations are chosen sequentially, with each location depending on data collected at previous locations.  In batch sampling, locations are chosen in batches of size greater than one, allowing each new batch to depend on data collected at previous locations. Batch sampling is more realistic than singleton sampling in most settings. This paper proposes specific batch AGDs and assesses their efficiency relative to singleton adaptive and non-adaptive counterparts using simulations.  The findings are applied to inform an AGD of a rolling Malaria Indicator Survey, part of a large-scale, five-year malaria transmission reduction project in Malawi.

title: The Propensity to Cycle Tool: An open source online system for sustainable transport planning
Abstract: Increasingly, getting people cycling is a common objective for transportation planning institutions worldwide.  A growing body of evidence indicates that high-quality infrastructure can boost local cycling rates. However, for infrastructure and other cycling measures to be effective, it is crucial to intervene in the right places, such as along "desire lines" of high latent demand. This necessitates tools and methods to answer the question: "Where to build?". This paper, following a brief review of policy and research related to this question, describes the design, features, and potential applications of such a tool. The Propensity to Cycle Tool (PCT) is an online, interactive planning support system initially developed to explore and map cycling potential across England. Based on origin-destination data, it models and visualizes cycling levels at area, desire line, route, and route network levels for current levels of cycling and for scenario-based "cycling futures." Four scenarios are presented, including "Go Dutch" and "Ebikes," exploring what would happen if English people cycled as much as Dutch people and the potential impact of electric cycles on cycling uptake. The cost-effectiveness of investment depends not only on the number of additional trips cycled but also on wider impacts such as health and carbon benefits. The PCT reports these impacts at area, desire line, and route level for each scenario. The PCT is open-source, facilitating the creation of additional scenarios and its deployment in new contexts. The paper concludes that the PCT illustrates the potential of online tools to inform transportation decisions and raises the broader issue of how models should be used in transportation planning.

title: Semiparametric time to event models in the presence of error-prone, self-reported outcomes - With application to the women's health initiative
Abstract: The onset of several silent, chronic diseases, such as diabetes, can only be detected through diagnostic tests. Using a semiparametric likelihood-based approach, this paper presents time-to-event models to estimate the association of one or more covariates with an error-prone, self-reported outcome.  Simulation studies are conducted to assess the effect of error in self-reported outcomes on bias in the estimation of the regression parameter of interest. The current analysis is based on follow-up through 2010, with a median duration of follow-up of 12.1 years. title: Mesoscale Elucidation of Biofilm Shear Behavior
Abstract: The formation of bacterial colonies as biofilm on the surface or interface of various objects has the potential to impact not only human health and disease but also energy and environmental considerations. Biofilms can be considered soft materials, and understanding their shear response to external forces is crucial for fundamental comprehension. This article presents a mesoscale model based on the digitization of a biofilm microstructure. Its response under externally applied shear load is analyzed.  Strain stiffening behavior is readily observed under high strain loads due to the unfolding of chains within the soft polymeric substrate. Sustained shear loading of the biofilm network results in strain localization along the diagonal direction. title: Anti-Fall: A Non-intrusive and Real-time Fall Detector Leveraging CSI from Commodity WiFi Devices

title: Correlated Random Measures
Abstract: This research introduces correlated random measures, a new type of random measure where atom weights can exhibit flexible dependencies. Correlated random measures address this limitation by modeling correlation within the measure using a Gaussian process in conjunction with a Poisson process.  The researchers illustrate the potential of correlated random measures by developing several examples, including a latent feature model where properties of latent features and their dependency patterns can be inferred.  The paper also investigates a correlated random measure model for pairwise count data, deriving an efficient variational inference algorithm and demonstrating improved predictive performance on large datasets of documents, web clicks, and electronic health records.

title: Effects of adaptive protective behavior on the dynamics of sexually transmitted infections
Abstract: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) continue to pose a significant challenge to public health programs due to their complex nature and associated costs.  The preferences and social dynamics of a population can significantly influence the course of an outbreak and the effectiveness of interventions aimed at changing individual behavior.  Individuals may also alter their sexual behavior in response to the presence of STIs, creating a feedback loop between transmission and behavior.  This research investigates the consequences of modeling the interaction between STI transmission and prophylactic use by linking a Susceptible-Infectious-Susceptible (SIS) system with evolutionary game dynamics that determine the effective contact rate. This combined model framework allows for the consideration of protective behavior by both infected and susceptible individuals.  Feedback between behavioral adaptation and prevalence leads to a wide range of dynamic behaviors in the model, including damped and sustained oscillations as well as bistability, depending on behavioral parameters and disease growth rate. The findings demonstrate that disease extinction is possible even in regions with R0 > 1 due to behavior adaptation driving the epidemic downward. Conversely, endemic prevalence for arbitrarily low R0 is also possible if contact rates are sufficiently high.  The study further examines the impact of model misspecification on disease forecasting and parameter estimation.  The researchers found that alternative models neglecting the behavioral feedback or only considering behavior adaptation by susceptible individuals can potentially yield misleading parameter estimates or omit significant features of the disease trajectory.

title: Joint modelling of longitudinal and multi-state processes: application to clinical progressions in prostate cancer
Abstract: Joint modeling of longitudinal and survival data is increasingly employed in clinical trials involving cancer.  In prostate cancer, for instance, these models allow researchers to account for the link between longitudinal measures of prostate-specific antigen (PSA) and the time of clinical recurrence when studying the risk of relapse.  In practice, multiple types of relapse may occur successively.  Distinguishing these transitions between health states would allow evaluation of how PSA trajectory and classical covariates impact the risk of dying after a distant recurrence post-radiotherapy or predicting the risk of specific types of clinical recurrence post-radiotherapy based on PSA history. This paper introduces a joint model for a longitudinal process and a multi-state process, divided into two sub-models: a linear mixed sub-model for longitudinal data and a multi-state sub-model with proportional hazards for transition times, both linked by shared random effects.  The parameters of this joint multi-state model are estimated within the maximum likelihood framework using an EM algorithm coupled with a quasi-Newton algorithm for slow convergence.  The model is implemented in R, combining and extending the mstate and JM packages.  The estimation program is validated through simulations and applied to pooled data from two cohorts of men with localized prostate cancer treated with radiotherapy.  By leveraging baseline covariates and repeated PSA measurements during follow-up, the researchers are able to assess the biomarker's trajectory, define the risks of transitions between health states, and quantify the impact of PSA dynamics on each transition intensity.

title: Infrared Spectroscopy with Visible Light
Abstract: Infrared (IR) spectral measurements offer unique fingerprints of materials, proving valuable for material analysis, environmental sensing, and health diagnostics.  Current IR spectroscopy techniques rely on optical equipment specifically designed for operation in the IR range, facing challenges of inferior performance and high cost.  This research introduces a novel spectroscopy technique that enables IR spectral measurements using visible spectral range components.  The technique utilizes nonlinear interference of infrared and visible photons generated through Spontaneous Parametric Down Conversion (SPDC).  The intensity interference pattern for a visible photon depends on the phase of an IR photon traversing the media.  This relationship allows for the determination of media properties in the IR range from visible photon measurements. The technique has the potential to replace or complement conventional IR spectroscopy techniques as it leverages well-developed visible range optical components.

title: Strategic Classification
Abstract: Machine learning typically relies on the assumption that unseen test instances follow the same distribution as observed training data.  However, this assumption can break down when machine learning is used to make decisions affecting the welfare of strategic individuals (e.g., employment, education, health).  Individuals, aware of the classifier's workings, may manipulate their attributes to obtain a favorable classification outcome.  This behavior, known as "gaming," can significantly deteriorate classifier performance.  Gaming is a recognized obstacle in practical machine learning applications, known as Goodhart's law in financial policy-making.  This paper formalizes the problem and explores algorithms for learning classifiers robust to gaming.  The researchers model classification as a sequential game between two players: "Jury" and "Contestant."  Jury designs a classifier, while Contestant receives an input to the classifier, which they can modify at a cost.  Jury aims for high classification accuracy based on Contestant's original input and an underlying target classification function, while Contestant seeks a favorable classification outcome while considering the cost of achieving it.  The paper derives computationally efficient learning algorithms that are near-optimal for a natural class of cost functions, even on concept classes computationally hard to learn.  For general cost functions, designing an approximately optimal strategy-proof classifier for inverse-polynomial approximation is NP-hard.

title: Modelling air pollution abatement in deep street canyons by means of air scrubbers
Abstract: Deep street canyons are characterized by weak ventilation and recirculation of air, leading to increased exposure to particulate matter and other air pollutants, impacting safety and health.  While the international community focuses on emission reduction, this theoretical study explores a novel solution: removing air pollutants close to their sources using a network of Air Pollution Abatement (APA) devices.  APA technology utilizes a portable and low-consuming scrubbing system to remove gaseous and particulate air pollutants, mimicking wet and dry deposition processes.  The researchers used Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) methods to estimate the potential pollutant abatement efficacy of a single absorber.  The presence of the scrubber effectively creates an additional sink at the bottom of the canyon, accelerating the cleaning process by up to 70% when simulating an almost perfect scrubber (90% efficiency).  The absorber's efficacy is not proportional to its internal abatement efficiency but increases rapidly at low efficiencies, reaching a saturation point.  In the specific canyon configuration analyzed (aspect ratio of 3), the upwind corner proves most favorable for absorber application.  The maximum pollutant abatement in the downwind corner is -24%, while in the upwind corner, it reaches -51%.  The absorber's efficacy increases significantly faster at low efficiencies:  at 25% efficiency, the abatement is roughly half that achieved with 90% efficiency.  These initial results suggest strategies for real-world application of an absorber network and motivate further theoretical study to better understand the details of air flow inside and around the absorber.

The non-stigmatizing design, ease of maintenance, simplistic interaction, and seamless intervention make wHealth potentially conducive to widespread adoption of telehealth services for managing elderly healthcare. title: Anxiety, Alcohol, and Academics: A Textual Analysis of Student Facebook Confessions Pages
Abstract: This study examines what college students reveal to their peers on social media under complete anonymity and how their campus environments relate to their disclosures. While event-related confessions often mentioned timely school-related events, many referenced global and domestic events outside the local campus sphere.  Results suggest that undergraduates from different campuses disclose differently about topics like race, socioeconomics, and politics but post in similar patterns over time. title: A Real-Time Soft Robotic Patient Positioning System for Maskless Head-and-Neck Cancer Radiotherapy: An Initial Investigation

title: Impact of the spatial context on human communication activity
Abstract: Technology development generates vast amounts of data from human activity in space and time.  This "big data" is crucial for providing decision-makers with new insights. This paper investigates relevant geographical areas based on their categories of human activities (e.g., working and shopping), identified from geographic information (e.g., Openstreetmap).  The researchers use spectral clustering followed by a k-means clustering algorithm based on TF/IDF cosine similarity metric.  The quality of observed clusters is evaluated using silhouette coefficients, estimated based on the similarities of mobile communication activity temporal patterns.  The area clusters are then used to explain typical or exceptional communication activities.  The study demonstrates the approach using a real dataset containing 1 million Call Detailed Records.  This type of analysis and its applications are crucial for understanding the dependency of human behaviors on external factors and for uncovering hidden relationships, unknown correlations, and other valuable information to support decision-making.

title: The non-linear health consequences of living in larger cities
Abstract: Urbanization promotes economic growth, mobility, access to resources, and resource availability but also contributes to higher levels of pollution, violence, crime, and mental distress.  The health consequences of densely populated urban areas are not fully understood, particularly how variations in population size across cities impact population health.  This paper analyzes the deviations from linearity of the scaling of various health-related quantities, including incidence and mortality of diseases, external causes of death, well-being, and healthcare availability, in relation to the population size of cities in Brazil, Sweden, and the USA.  The findings reveal that deaths from non-communicable diseases tend to be less common in larger cities, while the per capita incidence of infectious diseases is relatively higher with increasing population size.  Healthier lifestyles and access to medical support are disproportionately higher in larger cities.  These results are linked to the optimization of human and physical resources and the non-linear effects of social networks in larger populations.  An urban advantage in terms of health is not evident, and using rates as indicators to compare cities with different population sizes may be insufficient.

title: What do they know about me? Contents and Concerns of Online Behavioral Profiles

title: Multi-View Factorization Machines
Abstract: For a learning task, data can typically be collected from multiple sources or represented from various perspectives. MVMs can be used in conjunction with various loss functions for diverse machine learning tasks.  A stochastic gradient descent method is presented to learn the MVM model. title: Mixed model and estimating equation approaches for zero inflation in clustered binary response data with application to a dating violence study
Abstract:
The NEXT Generation Health study uses a survey to investigate dating violence among adolescents. The study aims to identify instances of violence in dating relationships. However, the study may be biased due to non-relationship students participating, leading to an excess of zero responses. This paper proposes likelihood-based and estimating equation approaches to analyze the zero-inflated clustered binary data. A mixed model method is adopted to account for the cluster effect. Model parameters are estimated using a maximum-likelihood (ML) approach, implemented using Gaussian-Hermite quadrature (GHQ) approximation. To address potential bias from incorrect random effects distribution assumptions, generalized estimating equations (GEE) are constructed, eliminating the need for precise within-cluster correlation specification. Simulation studies assess the performance of ML and GEE methods in terms of bias, efficiency, and robustness. The paper emphasizes the importance of addressing zero inflation by reanalyzing the NEXT data, where this issue has previously been ignored. |||

Hybrid quantum mechanical-molecular mechanical (QM/MM) simulations are widely used in studies of enzymatic catalysis. This slow approach to the asymptotic limit is attributed to charge transfer from protein residues to the reacting substrates. Large QM/MM calculations identify charge separation in transition state fragments as a key contributor to enzymatic methyl transfer rate enhancement. The study introduces charge shift analysis, revealing the minimum number of protein residues (around 11-16 residues or 200-300 atoms for COMT) needed for quantitative agreement with large-QM simulations. The identified residues are not those typically selected based on chemical intuition or proximity. The resting brain exhibits self-organized dynamics, forming a finite number of correlated patterns known as resting state networks (RSNs). Techniques like independent component analysis can separate brain activity at rest to reveal these RSNs, but the specific patterns of interaction between RSNs remain unclear. Subsequently, IF (estimated using Transfer Entropy) is calculated between different RSNs by systematically increasing k (the number of principal components used). Oxygen is transported throughout the body by hemoglobin in red blood cells. While the oxygen affinity of blood is well understood and routinely assessed in patients using pulse oximetry, variability at the single-cell level has not been measured previously. Conversely, single-cell measurements of red blood cell volume and hemoglobin concentration are taken millions of times daily by clinical hematology analyzers and are crucial factors in determining hematologic health. The results show that single-cell saturation variability peaks at an oxygen partial pressure of 2.5%, corresponding to the maximum slope of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve. Furthermore, single-cell oxygen affinity is positively correlated with hemoglobin concentration but independent of osmolarity, suggesting variation in the hemoglobin to 2-3 DPG ratio at the cellular level. By quantifying the functional behavior of a cellular population, this system adds a new dimension to blood cell analysis and other single-cell variability measurements. |||

The system addresses challenges such as noise elimination, interfering humans, sudden user movements, and detecting abnormal breathing situations. Additionally, UbiBreathe can detect apnea with over 96% accuracy in both device-on-chest and hands-free scenarios, highlighting its suitability for a new class of anywhere respiratory monitoring. |||

Historically, Plasmodium vivax was believed to have limited morbidity and minimal mortality; however, evidence from various settings now suggests that P. vivax infections can be severe and fatal. This realization highlights a critical research gap: the vast majority of research has focused on P. falciparum, neglecting epidemiological and clinical studies of P. vivax. A substantial body of historical data exists on human experimental infections with P. vivax, providing valuable information based on expert opinion. This thesis re-examines portions of this evidence base using modern epidemiological analyses with two objectives: critically examining the accumulated knowledge base and informing current research agendas towards global malaria elimination for all Plasmodium species. Chapter 2 examines geographic variation in P. vivax epidemiology, focusing on the timing of incubation periods and relapses by parasite origin. Chapter 3 re-assesses the impact of sporozoite dosage on incubation and pre-patent periods. Chapter 4 provides well-defined mathematical distributions for incubation and relapse periods in experimental infections and explores their epidemiological impacts using simple transmission models. Chapter 5 examines the epidemiology of mixed-strain P. vivax infections and compares these findings with studies in murine models and general ecological theory. title: Sensor Fault Detection, Isolation and Identification Using Multiple Model-based Hybrid Kalman Filter for Gas Turbine Engines
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel sensor fault detection, isolation, and identification (FDII) strategy based on the multiple model (MM) approach. Furthermore, the FDI scheme is extended to identify the magnitude of sensor faults using a modified generalized likelihood ratio (GLR) method. This method relies on the system's healthy operational mode. To illustrate the effectiveness of this FDII methodology, extensive simulations were conducted on a nonlinear gas turbine engine. The simulations considered various single and concurrent sensor fault scenarios, demonstrating the effectiveness of the online hierarchical multiple HKF-based FDII scheme under diverse flight modes. Comparative studies comparing the HKF-based FDI approach with other filtering methods, including linear, extended, unscented, and cubature Kalman filters, were conducted using both interacting and non-interacting multiple model (MM) based schemes. The results confirm the superiority of the HKF method in terms of prompt fault detection, reduced false alarm rates, and robustness with respect to engine health parameter degradations.

title: Spatio-temporal Dynamics of Foot-and-Mouth Disease Virus in South America

The spread of serotype A was best explained by geographic distances, while trade in live cattle was the most significant predictor for the spread of serotype O. The findings highlight that the two serotypes exhibit different evolutionary and spatial dynamics, posing distinct threats to control programs.

title: Analysis of food pairing in regional cuisines of India

Food pairing was assessed at the cuisine, recipe, and ingredient pair levels by quantifying flavor sharing between ingredient pairs. The results revealed a negative food pairing pattern in each regional cuisine, indicating that the greater the flavor sharing between two ingredients, the less likely they are to be used together in that cuisine. Ingredient usage frequency plays a crucial role in shaping the characteristic food pairing patterns of each cuisine. Spice and dairy emerged as the most significant ingredient classes influencing the food pairing patterns. Interestingly, while individual spices contribute to negative food pairing, dairy products tend to deviate food pairing towards a more positive side. This data-analytical study reveals the culinary fingerprints of regional cuisines, potentially enabling the development of algorithms for generating novel recipes and recipe recommendation systems. title: Hidden population size estimation from respondent-driven sampling: a network approach
Abstract: Estimating the size of stigmatized, hidden, or hard-to-reach populations is a significant challenge in epidemiology, demography, and public health research. While capture-recapture and multiplier methods are standard tools for inferring hidden population sizes, they require independent random sampling, which is often impractical. Respondent-driven sampling (RDS) is a survey method for hidden populations that utilizes social link tracing. The RDS recruitment process aims to spread through the social network connecting members of the target population. This paper proposes a method to estimate hidden population size using network data revealed by RDS. The key insight is that the recruitment chain, timing of recruitments, and network degrees of recruited subjects provide information about the individuals within the target population who are not yet in the sample. A computationally efficient Bayesian method is employed to integrate over missing edges in the subgraph of recruited individuals. The method was validated using simulated data and applied to estimate the number of people who inject drugs in St. Petersburg, Russia.

title: Thermodynamics of firms' growth
Abstract: The distribution of firm growth and sizes has been a subject of intense research. This paper demonstrates that a thermodynamic model based on the Maximum Entropy Principle, with dynamical prior information, can effectively describe the dynamics and distribution of firm growth. The theoretical framework is validated against a comprehensive database of Spanish firms, encompassing a vast majority of Spain's economic activity with over 1,155,142 firms tracked over a decade. The study explains the empirical exponent of Pareto's law, often observed in the rank distribution of large-size firms, based on the economic system's capacity for firm creation and destruction. The exponent can serve as a measure of the health of a capitalist-based economy. The model predicts that a larger exponent than 1 favors firm creation, while a smaller exponent than 1 favors firm destruction. An exponent of 1, matching Zipf's law, signifies a full macroeconomic equilibrium with balanced firm creation and destruction. For medium and smaller firm sizes, the dynamical regime shifts; the entire distribution can no longer be fitted to a single simple analytic form and numerical prediction becomes necessary. The model serves as the foundation for a predictive framework for the economic evolution of a firm ensemble, with potential applications in simulations and testing hypothetical scenarios, such as economic crises or responses to policy measures.

Abstract: The Expected Value of Perfect Partial Information (EVPPI) is a decision-theoretic measure of the "cost" of parametric uncertainty in decision-making, primarily used in health economic decision-making. This approach improves upon previous work by eliminating an approximation and incorporating a constraint on stiffness increases. title: Reversals of Least-Squares Estimates and Model-Independent Estimation for Directions of Unique Effects

Geometrically, the reversal region is represented as an elliptical cone for single covariate additions, with the axis of symmetry indicating optimal reversal conditions. For multiple covariate additions, model-independent estimation can be implemented using subject matter knowledge. title: Web Similarity in Sets of Search Terms using Database Queries

Notably, NWD reveals new correlations between health hazards. It extends the earlier normalized google distance (NGD) by providing a more comprehensive similarity measure for sets. title: Correcting for non-ignorable missingness in smoking trends

title: Spices form the basis of food pairing in Indian cuisine
Abstract: Culinary practices are shaped by factors such as climate, culture, history, and geography. The molecular composition of recipes within a cuisine reveals patterns in food preferences. Its culinary system boasts a long history of health-centric dietary practices focused on disease prevention and health promotion. This study examines food pairing in Indian cuisine recipes, revealing a unique pattern of negative food pairing. Contrary to the positive food pairing observed in some Western cuisines, Indian cuisine exhibits an inverse relationship between flavor sharing and co-occurrence of ingredients; the greater the flavor overlap between two ingredients, the less likely they are to appear together in a recipe. This characteristic is independent of recipe size and not solely explained by ingredient category-based recipe composition. Ingredient frequency emerges as the primary factor defining the cuisine's characteristic flavor sharing pattern. Spices, both individually and as a category, form the foundation of ingredient composition in Indian cuisine. The study also presents a culinary evolution model that successfully replicates both ingredient usage distribution and negative food pairing within the cuisine. The findings offer a foundation for designing novel signature recipes, healthy recipe alterations, and recipe recommendation systems.

title: Conditional Spectral Analysis of Replicated Multiple Time Series with Application to Nocturnal Physiology
Abstract: This article tackles the analysis of associations between power spectra of multiple time series and cross-sectional outcomes when data is collected from numerous subjects. The motivation arises from sleep medicine, where researchers can non-invasively record physiological time series signals during sleep. The frequency patterns of these signals, quantifiable through power spectra, offer valuable insights into biological processes. A critical challenge in sleep research is establishing connections between power spectra of time series signals and clinical characteristics, which are essential for understanding how sleep affects health and identifying potential treatment approaches. Analyzing these complex associations is challenging due to the intricate structure of power spectra from multiple time series, which are represented as complex positive-definite matrix-valued functions. This article proposes a novel approach based on a tensor-product spline model of Cholesky components of outcome-dependent power spectra. The approach flexibly models power spectra as nonparametric functions of frequency and outcome while adhering to geometric constraints. Formulated within a fully Bayesian framework, a Whittle likelihood-based Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm is developed for automated model fitting and inference on associations between outcomes and spectral measures. The method is applied to analyze data from a sleep study involving older adults, revealing new insights into the link between stress and arousal and the amount of time spent in bed.

title: Air quality and acute deaths in California, 2000-2012
Abstract: Numerous studies have investigated the potential association between air quality and acute deaths, with many suggesting a plausible causal link between current air quality levels and increased mortality. However, several factors complicate the determination of causality and even association. Observational datasets are often large and complex, increasing the risk of false positive findings due to multiple testing and model selection. Publication bias, confirmation bias, and other biases also pose potential problems. Furthermore, the lack of public availability for most datasets used in air quality and public health studies hinders the reproducibility of findings. This study addresses these limitations by constructing and making publicly available a dataset containing daily air quality levels (PM2.5 and ozone), daily temperature levels (minimum and maximum), and daily relative humidity levels for the eight most populous California air basins. The dataset is analyzed using a moving median analysis, a standard time series analysis, and a prediction analysis following a systematic approach. The study examines each of the eight air basins separately to assess the replicability of findings across locations. Leave-one-year-out cross-validation is employed to evaluate predictions. Both the moving medians analysis and the standard time series analysis revealed limited evidence for an association between air quality and acute deaths. The prediction analysis, conducted as a large factorial design using different models and holding out one year at a time, indicated that most of the daily death variability is explained by time of year or weather variables. In summary, the empirical evidence suggests that current levels of air quality, specifically ozone and PM2.5, are not causally related to acute deaths in California. Furthermore, a logical argument can be made that air quality is not causally related to acute deaths in the rest of the United States.

title: Asymmetric Independence Model for Detecting Interactions between Variables
Abstract: Identifying complex interactions among risk factors in case-control studies is a fundamental task in clinical and population research. While logistic regression (LR) offers a convenient solution for hypothesis testing, it suffers from limitations, particularly in scenarios involving missing or unmeasured risk factors, imperfectly correlated "surrogates," and multiple disease subtypes. These limitations stem from the way the null hypothesis is defined within the LR framework. This paper introduces the Asymmetric Independence Model (AIM) as a biologically-inspired alternative to LR. AIM is based on the key observation that the mechanisms associated with acquiring a "disease" and maintaining "health" are inherently asymmetric. The study mathematically proves that unlike LR, AIM is a robust model under the aforementioned confounding scenarios. Furthermore, the paper provides a mathematical definition of "synergistic" interaction and demonstrates that AIM theoretically offers greater power than LR in detecting such interactions. Experimental analysis using simulations and four real datasets showcases AIM's superior performance compared to LR. While the primary application focuses on genetic or environmental variables in the life sciences, the methodology is readily adaptable to other types of measurements and inferences, such as in the social sciences.

title: Musical practice and cognitive aging: two cross-sectional studies point to phonemic fluency as a potential candidate for a use-dependent adaptation

Study 1 revealed that musicians outperformed controls in processing speed and auditory-verbal short-term memory, but both groups exhibited similar age-related differences. Musicians also scored higher than controls on verbal fluencies, displaying distinct age effects. Study 2 examined the impact of lifetime period at training onset (childhood vs. adulthood) on fluency performance. The results indicated that training onset in childhood was associated with better phonemic, but not semantic, fluency performances (musicians who began practicing in adulthood did not outperform non-musicians on phonemic fluency). Current training frequency did not explain the observed differences in scores for musicians on either fluency measure. The study discusses these findings in light of the hypothesis of a transformative effect of musical practice versus a non-causal explanation.

title: Big Data: Opportunities and Privacy Challenges
Abstract: Recent advancements in data collection, computational statistics, increased computer processing power, and decreasing storage costs are making technologies for analyzing large, heterogeneous datasets ubiquitous. This paper examines the benefits of big data for individuals and society, focusing on seven key use cases: (1) business optimization and customer analytics, (2) scientific research, (3) healthcare, (4) finance, (5) emerging energy distribution systems, (6) government transparency and efficiency, and (7) big data security. Alongside the benefits and opportunities, the paper discusses the security, privacy, and ethical issues at stake.

title: Stochastic Unrelatedness, Couplings, and Contextuality
Abstract: R. Duncan Luce once remarked that he did not consider Kolmogorov's probability theory well-constructed because it treats stochastic independence as a "numerical accident" when it should be considered a fundamental relation, more basic than numerical probabilities. This paper argues that stochastic independence is indeed a "numerical accident," a special form of stochastic dependence between random variables (broadly defined). The idea that stochastic independence is fundamental may stem from the confusion of stochastic independence with stochastic unrelatedness, where two or more random variables have no joint distribution and are independent. Kolmogorov's probability theory cannot be consistently constructed without allowing for stochastic unrelatedness, making it a default situation. Any two random variables recorded under mutually incompatible conditions are stochastically unrelated. However, stochastically unrelated random variables can be probabilistically coupled, meaning a joint distribution can be imposed upon them, and this can be done in an infinity of ways, independent coupling being just one. The notions of stochastic unrelatedness and all possible couplings play a central role in the foundation of probability theory and, particularly, in the theory of probabilistic contextuality.

Perhaps the most distinctive characteristic of this fundamental concept is absolute time, constituting the flow of consciousness according to Husserl, the reflection of pure (human) nature without the distinction between exo and endo. title: Should we really use post-hoc tests based on mean-ranks?
Abstract: Comparing multiple algorithms across multiple datasets is fundamental in machine learning, typically accomplished using the Friedman test. When the Friedman test rejects the null hypothesis, multiple comparisons are conducted to identify significant differences between algorithms. These multiple comparisons often rely on the mean-ranks test. This technical note discusses the inconsistencies of the mean-ranks post-hoc test and discourages its use in machine learning, medicine, psychology, and other fields. It demonstrates that the mean-ranks test's outcome is influenced by the pool of algorithms initially included in the experiment. Consequently, the comparison between algorithms A and B might reveal a significant difference when algorithms C, D, and E are included, but not when algorithms F, G, and H are considered. This leads to paradoxical situations. To address these issues, the authors suggest performing multiple comparisons using tests whose outcomes solely depend on the two algorithms being compared, such as the sign-test or the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

title: The amplification of risk in experimental diffusion chains

Conversely, risk perception is propagated with higher fidelity due to participants manipulating messages to align with their preconceptions, thereby influencing the judgments of subsequent participants. Computer simulations implementing this simple influence mechanism demonstrate that small judgment biases tend to become more extreme, even when the injected message contradicts preconceived risk judgments. These findings provide quantitative insights into the social amplification of risk perception, offering valuable information for policymakers to better anticipate and manage public responses to emerging threats.

In visualizations allowing shifting between and/or combining Cartesian and polar coordinate representations, such as Biplots, the location of this origin is crucial. Origin-centric visualizations enhance graphical perception psychology by generating scatters that can be interpreted as Dyson swarms. The key factor is typically the analyst's choice of origin through an initial "centering" translation; this choice determines whether the recovered scatter will have either no points depicted as being near the origin or one (or more) points exactly coincident with this origin.

title: Evaluation Evaluation a Monte Carlo study

Although rationality is essential for poker success, the format of the challenges plays a significant role in these dynamics, influencing the underlying nature of the game. title: Differentiation with stratification: a principle of theoretical physics in the tradition of the memory art
Abstract: The Art of Memory originated with Aristotle's inquiries about memory. Throughout its lengthy evolution, it received significant contributions from alchemists, underwent transformation through Ramon Llull, and seemingly concluded with Giordano Bruno, considered the most renowned representative of this art. This tradition did not disappear, but lives on in the formulations of modern scientific theories. From its initial form as a method for retaining information through associations, it evolved into a principle for classifying and structuring knowledge. This principle, termed "differentiation with stratification," serves as the structural foundation for classical mechanics. Integrating two distinct scientific traditions into a single framework, this physical theory became the modern paradigm of science. This paper demonstrates that this principle can also be formulated as a set of questions. This is achieved through an analysis of theories based on the epistemology of observational realism. This epistemology combines Rudolph Carnap's concept of theory as a system of observational and theoretical languages with a criterion for separating observational languages, drawing on analytical psychology. The "nuclear" role of observational laws and the differentiations emanating from this nucleus, reproducing the general cases of phenomena, reveal the legacy of the Art of Memory in scientific theories. This paper argues that this design is also present in special relativity and quantum mechanics.

title: Quantum Structure of Negation and Conjunction in Human Thought

The findings refine existing analyses on conceptual combinations, revealing systematic and remarkable deviations from classical (fuzzy set) logic and probability theory. Moreover, the results provide substantial evidence supporting the validity of a quantum-theoretic framework for combining two concepts. The representation of conceptual negation arises naturally from the general assumptions of the two-sector Fock space model, aligning accurately with the collected data. Additionally, the study identifies a significant deviation from classicality that was not expected a priori. This deviation can be precisely explained by assuming that human reasoning is a superposition of "emergent reasoning" and "logical reasoning," and that these two processes can be successfully represented in a Fock space algebraic structure.

title: Quantum Information Biology: from information interpretation of quantum mechanics to applications in molecular biology and cognitive psychology
Abstract: This paper discusses foundational issues of quantum information biology (QIB), one of the most successful applications of the quantum formalism outside of physics. QIB provides a multi-scale model of information processing in biological systems, ranging from proteins and cells to cognitive and social systems. This theory must be sharply distinguished from "traditional quantum biophysics," which focuses on quantum biophysical processes, such as those occurring in cells or brains. QIB models the dynamics of information states in biological systems. It is based on the quantum-like paradigm: complex biological systems process information according to the laws of quantum information and probability. This paradigm is supported by a wealth of statistical bio-data collected at all scales, from molecular biology and genetics/epigenetics to cognitive psychology and behavioral economics. The authors argue that the information interpretation of quantum mechanics (its various forms elaborated by Zeilinger and Brukner, Fuchs and Mermin, and D'Ariano) is the most natural interpretation of QIB. They also suggest that QBIsm (Quantum Bayesianism) can be used to find a proper interpretation of bio-quantum probabilities. Biologically, QIB is based on two principles: a) adaptivity; b) openness (biological systems are fundamentally open). These principles are mathematically represented in the framework of a novel formalism, quantum adaptive dynamics, which, in particular, encompasses the standard theory of open quantum systems as a special case of adaptivity (to the environment).

title: On a possibility to combine the order effect with sequential reproducibility for quantum measurements
Abstract: This paper examines the possibility of using quantum observables to describe a potential combination of the order effect and sequential reproducibility in quantum measurements. The order effect refers to the dependence of probability distributions (of measurement results) on the order of measurements.  Two types of sequential reproducibility are considered: adjacent reproducibility (A-A) and separated reproducibility (A-B-A). Adjacent reproducibility signifies reproducibility with probability 1 of a result obtained by measuring an observable A twice consecutively. Separated reproducibility (A-B-A) refers to reproducibility with probability 1 of an A measurement result when another quantum observable B is measured between the two A measurements.  Intuitively, separated reproducibility appears complementary to the order effect. Surprisingly, the paper shows that for a significant class of quantum observables defined by positive operator valued measures (POVMs), this might not be the case. The order effect can coexist with both separated and adjacent reproducibility for observables A and B. However, the additional constraint of separated reproducibility of the B-A-B type eliminates this coexistence.  Mathematically, the paper focuses on the operator algebra for effects composing POVMs. This research was motivated by attempts to apply the quantum formalism outside of physics, particularly in cognitive psychology and psychophysics. However, it also holds significance for the foundations of quantum physics as part of the problem concerning the structure of sequential quantum measurements.

title: Are Effective Leaders Creative?
Abstract: This paper explains, in layperson's terms, how an agent-based model was used to investigate the widely held belief that creativity is an important component of effective leadership. The study found that creative leadership increased the mean fitness of cultural outputs across an artificial society. However, the more creative the followers were, the more the beneficial effect of creative leadership was diminished.  Early in the simulation, when the fitness of ideas was low, a leadership style characterized by the highest possible degree of creativity was most beneficial for the mean fitness of outputs across the society.  As the mean fitness of outputs increased, an inevitable transition occurred, after which a less creative leadership style proved more effective. The paper discusses the implications of these findings.

title: Heart rate and its variability as an indicator of mental health in male prisoners
Abstract: Heart rate (HR) and its variability (HRV) have been proposed as markers for depressive symptoms and other aspects of mental health. However, the actual correlation between them remains uncertain, as previous studies have typically been based on small samples. This study analyzed correlations between five HR/HRV measures and five psychological measures of mental health aspects (depression, state and trait anxiety, and social relationships) in a sample of 113 adult male prisoners.  Nadaraya-Watson non-parametric regression was used in both directions, and age-stratified Spearman correlation was employed to detect potential relationships. Despite strong correlations among HR/HRV measures and psychological measures, correlations between HR/HRV and psychological measures were low and non-significant for the overall sample. However, the study discovered an age dependency, suggesting some correlations in younger individuals (HR with STAI-State, r = 0.39; with HADS-Anxiety, r = 0.52; both p < 0.005).  Overall, the general utility of HR/HRV as a marker for mental health across populations remains unclear. Future research should consistently address age and other potential confounders.

title: What do we learn about development from baby robots?
Abstract: Understanding infant development is one of the most significant scientific challenges of our time. A major obstacle stems from the fact that the development of skills in infants results from the interaction of multiple mechanisms across various spatio-temporal scales. Concepts like "innate" or "acquired" are inadequate tools for explanations, necessitating a shift from reductionist to systemic approaches.  Addressing this challenge requires building and experimenting with robots that model the developing infant brain and body. Systemic explanations of pattern formation in sensorimotor, cognitive, and social development, viewed as a complex dynamical system, demand formal models based on mathematics, algorithms, and robots.  Formulating hypotheses about development using such models and exploring them through experiments allows for a detailed examination of the interaction between multiple mechanisms and parameters. This complements traditional experimental methods in psychology and neuroscience, where only a few variables can be studied simultaneously. The use of robots is particularly crucial. The laws of physics generate spontaneous patterns in the inorganic world and strongly influence the living world.  They constrain and guide infant development through the properties of the (changing) body interacting with the physical environment.  The ability to consider the body as an experimental variable, systematically altered to study its impact on skill formation, has long been a dream for developmental scientists. Developmental robotics is making this dream a reality. |||

title: How Creative Ideas Take Shape

Independent judges found that the responses strongly supported the honing theory predictions over structure mapping.

title: Bayesian mixture of Plackett-Luce models for partially ranked data
Abstract: Ranking data is commonly collected in psychological and behavioral experiments to understand preference and choice. The Plackett-Luce model, a popular parametric distribution for analyzing rankings, is extended in this study using a Bayesian finite mixture approach. This method effectively accounts for unobserved sample heterogeneity in partially ranked data. The paper describes an efficient algorithm for incorporating latent group structure within the data augmentation framework, and derives existing maximum likelihood procedures as special cases. Inference is conducted using a combination of the Expectation-Maximization algorithm for maximum a posteriori estimation and Gibbs sampling. The paper also explores various Bayesian criteria for selecting the optimal mixture configuration and outlines diagnostic tools for assessing the fitness of ranking distributions, both conditionally and unconditionally, based on the number of ranked items. The utility of the proposed Bayesian Plackett-Luce mixture is demonstrated through applications to simulated and real preference-ranked data. Comparisons are made with frequentist approaches and a Bayesian nonparametric mixture model, both employing the Plackett-Luce model as a mixture component. Analysis of real datasets highlights the importance of accurate diagnostic checks for comprehending the heterogeneous nature of partial ranking data.

title: Sorting and Selection with Imprecise Comparisons
Abstract: This study investigates a model of imprecise comparisons where two elements are compared, and the outcome is accurate if their perceived values differ by at least a threshold "delta." The model is inspired by imprecision in human judgment and adversarial errors in sporting tournaments. The model is related to concepts in psychophysics like the "just noticeable difference unit" (JND) or "difference threshold." The method of paired comparisons, requiring all possible comparisons, is traditionally used to mitigate imprecise human judgments in preference ranking. This work demonstrates that in the proposed model, the method of paired comparisons achieves optimal accuracy but is wasteful. It then presents an alternative method that achieves the same accuracy using fewer comparisons (4n^(3/2)) and proves its optimality. The study explores the trade-off between error guarantees and the number of comparisons for sorting, max-finding, and selection problems, providing strong lower bounds and near-optimal solutions.

title: SPRITE: A Response Model For Multiple Choice Testing
Abstract: Item response theory (IRT) models are widely used in educational data analysis, computerized adaptive testing, and psychological surveys, but often rely on the assumption of strictly ordered categories with a priori knowledge.
