Existing unordered categorical IRT models often have restrictive assumptions and poor data fitting performance. This work introduces SPRITE (Stochastic Polytomous Response Item Model), a novel methodology for unordered categorical IRT that: (i) analyzes both ordered and unordered categories, (ii) offers interpretable outputs, and (iii) provides improved data fitting compared to existing models. SPRITE is compared to existing IRT models and evaluated on both synthetic and real-world educational datasets.

title: Noncontextuality with Marginal Selectivity in Reconstructing Mental Architectures
Abstract: This paper introduces a general theory for understanding series-parallel mental architectures with selectively influenced, stochastically non-independent components. The focus is on analyzing the time it takes to perform a task under varying parameters. The theory proposes that the network contains processes selectively influenced by different experimental factors, and investigates their arrangement within the network. The paper leverages the concept of selective influences in psychology as a special application of the interdisciplinary theory of (non)contextuality, which originates in quantum theory. The lack of contextuality is shown to be equivalent to the existence of a hidden random entity influencing all random variables. Consequently, for a specific value of this hidden entity, processing times and their compositions become deterministic. These deterministic quantities can be treated as random variables with Heaviside distribution functions, allowing for simple computation of various linear combinations, including interaction contrasts. This mathematical framework leads to a novel and general method for investigating and characterizing interaction contrasts in different types of series-parallel architectures.

title: Depletion-Induced Forces and Crowding in Polymer-Nanoparticle Mixtures: Role of Polymer Shape Fluctuations and Penetrability

Monte Carlo simulations are used to compute the depletion-induced potential of mean force between hard nanospheres and crowding-induced shape distributions of polymers in the protein limit. Comparing results from ellipsoidal and spherical polymer models with predictions from polymer field theory and free-volume theory reveals that depletion-induced interactions and crowding are highly sensitive to polymer shapes and penetrability. These findings have significant implications for bulk thermodynamic phase behavior.

title: Dark influences III. Structural characterization of minor mergers of dwarf galaxies with dark satellites
Abstract: In the current concordance cosmology, small dark halos are expected to significantly perturb low-mass galaxies during minor mergers. The most sensitive indicators include asymmetries in gaseous and stellar distributions, enhanced central surface brightness and starbursts, and velocity offsets and misalignments between cold gas and stellar components. Merging systems exhibit a wide range of values for these indicators, while isolated objects have more confined values. Notably, the simulations reveal that off-centered star formation bursts can pinpoint the location of the dark satellite, making such observational systems promising for uncovering the presence of these missing satellites.

title: Fine-tuning the etch depth profile via dynamic shielding of ion beam

title: Galerkin Methods for Boltzmann-Poisson transport with reflection conditions on rough boundaries

Numerical approximations are developed to model an insulating boundary condition, equivalent to a zero flux condition for the electron transport equation. This condition balances incident and reflective momentum flux at the boundary, considering a mixed reflection with momentum-dependent specularity probability. The computational predictions of physical observables are compared for different reflection conditions implemented in the DG scheme for BP models. The results indicate that the diffusive condition influences kinetic moments across the entire domain.

title: Average-atom treatment of relaxation time in X-ray Thomson scattering from warm-dense matter
Abstract: The influence of finite relaxation times on Thomson scattering from warm-dense plasmas is investigated within the average-atom approximation. While most calculations rely on the collision-free Lindhard dielectric function, this work employs the Mermin dielectric function, explicitly incorporating relaxation time. This relaxation time is evaluated by treating the average atom as an impurity within a uniform electron gas and is highly dependent on the transport cross section. The calculated relaxation rates show good agreement with values inferred from the Ziman formula for static conductivity and with rates derived from a fit to the frequency-dependent conductivity. Transport cross sections determined through phase-shift analysis in the average-atom potential are compared with those evaluated using the Born approximation. While the Born approximation converges to the exact cross sections at high energies, differences at low energies lead to discrepancies in relaxation rates. The significance of including relaxation time in modeling X-ray Thomson scattering spectra is examined by comparing calculations of the free-electron dynamic structure function using Lindhard and Mermin dielectric functions. Applications are presented for warm-dense Be plasmas, covering a range of temperatures (2-32 eV) and densities (2-64 g/cc).

title: Dynamic Time-Dependent Route Planning in Road Networks with User Preferences

This work focuses on the dynamic and time-dependent route planning problem, incorporating both predicted and live traffic information. A practical algorithm is proposed that integrates global changes in the time-dependent metric, while remaining robust to user preferences. This algorithm enables interactive applications by allowing subsequent queries for faster updates than previous approaches.

title: Actor-Action Semantic Segmentation with Grouping Process Models

Supervoxels provide cues for grouping nodes at different scales within the CRFs, facilitating adaptive, high-order groups for more effective labeling. This model is dynamic, with continuous information exchange during inference: local CRFs influence active supervoxels, which in turn influence CRF connectivity, leading to a grouping process model. Experimental results on a large-scale video dataset demonstrate a significant improvement over state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the effectiveness of the dynamic, bidirectional flow between labeling and grouping.

title: Cross-Cultural Differences in Students' Intention to Use RSS Feeds between Lebanon and the United Kingdom: A Multi-Group Invariance Analysis Based on the Technology Acceptance Model

The Technology Adoption Model (TAM) was used as a framework, and 437 students responded to a questionnaire assessing intention to use (INT), attitude towards benefit (ATT), perceived usefulness (PU), and perceived ease of use (PEOU). Principle components analysis (PCA) and structural equation modeling (SEM) were employed to analyze the psychometric properties of the scale. Results showed significantly higher, but still modest, adoption in the British context (36%). Configural and metric invariance were fully supported, while scalar and factorial invariance were partially supported. Analysis revealed significant cultural differences between PU and PEOU across the two contexts, suggesting a possible cultural influence. It is recommended that faculty actively demonstrate the effective use of RSS to students to enhance awareness and emphasize its usefulness.

title: Asteroid flux towards circumprimary habitable zones in binary star systems: II. Dynamics
Abstract: Secular and mean motion resonances (MMRs) play a significant role in shaping planetary systems, particularly in binary star systems, during both early and late formation stages. This study investigates the correlation between orbital resonances and the rate of icy asteroids crossing the habitable zone (HZ) from a circumprimary disk of planetesimals in binary star systems. A model of a planetesimal belt is developed, encompassing both inner and outer regions around a primary G-type star, with a gas giant planet. The planetesimals are distributed around the primary star and influenced by the gravity of both stars and the gas giant. The system is numerically integrated for 50 Myr, varying parameters such as the secondary star's type (M- to F-type), semimajor axis (50 au or 100 au), and eccentricity (0.1 or 0.3). The gas giant's orbital and physical parameters are also varied for comparison. Simulations demonstrate that the planetesimal disk undergoes perturbations due to a perturbed gas giant, mean motion, and secular resonances. A secular resonance, with location and width dependent on the secondary star's characteristics, is identified in the icy asteroid belt region, overlapping with MMRs, influencing the disk's dynamical lifetime. The study highlights the importance of the 2:1 MMR, 5:3 MMR, and secular resonance in driving icy asteroids towards the HZ and transporting water therein.

title: Triggered star formation in giant HI supershells: ionized gas

title: Unveiling the influence of the radiation pressure in nature of orbits in the photogravitational restricted three-body problem

Interpreting collisional motion as leaking in the phase space, we connect our results to chaotic scattering and the theory of leaking Hamiltonian systems. We successfully identified the escape and collision basins and correlated them with corresponding escape and collision times. Our contribution provides valuable insights into the escape and collision properties of motion in this intriguing version of the restricted three-body problem.

title: Photon Emission Dynamics of a Two-Level Atom in a Cavity
Abstract: The collapse and revival of quantum states is a phenomenon observed in diverse areas of physics. In quantum optics, the Jaynes-Cummings model (JCM) predicts and experimentally verifies the occurrence of this phenomenon in the evolution of an atomic state interacting with a light field initially in a coherent state. This paper revisits the JCM using the Monte-Carlo wave function approach to investigate the time evolution of the photon emission rate of an atom within a cavity. Analytical and numerical quantum trajectory calculations demonstrate that the cavity and the initial field statistics significantly influence the photon emission dynamics. While a coherent field indeed leads to collapse and revival behavior mirroring atomic state evolution, differences exist. The emission rate for a field in a Fock number state exhibits sinusoidal oscillations, and a quiescent period emerges for a thermal field, contrasting with free space behavior. Our study also reveals that fluctuations in photon emission are significantly less than those of the atomic population.

title: The influence of interchain coupling on intramolecular oscillation mobility in coupled macromolecular chains: the case of coplanar parallel chains
Abstract: Extending our previous investigation of the hopping mechanism for oscillation excitation transport in a 1D model of a biological macromolecular chain, we now consider a system composed of two parallel 1D chains, incorporating the properties of intramolecular oscillation excitations. We assume that exciton interaction with thermal oscillations (generated by mechanical phonon subsystem) of structural elements (consisting of peptide groups) in the chains leads to self-trapping and the formation of polaron states. Our model generalizes the modified Holstein polaron model to the case of two macromolecular chains. We find that interchain coupling splits the exciton energy band into two subbands. The exciton migration hopping process along the macromolecular chains is analyzed in dependence of system parameters and temperature. Focusing on the temperature range relevant for living cells (near T=300 K), we identify a critical point where the exciton migration nature transitions abruptly from practically free (light) exciton motion to an immobile (heavy, dressed by a phonon cloud) quasiparticle. We discuss the application of our findings to exciton transport within deoxyribonucleic acid molecules and in 2D polymer films organized from such macromolecular chains.

title: Proliferating Lévy Walkers and Front Propagation

title: Lithium in Open Cluster Red Giants Hosting Substellar Companions

However, numerous factors affect A(Li) during the red giant phase, and when comparing our sample's abundances to those of red giants in other open clusters from the literature, we find that they fall within a much broader distribution of A(Li) and 12C/13C. title: Imaging an Event Horizon: Mitigation of Source Variability of Sagittarius A*
Abstract: The black hole at the center of our Galaxy, associated with the compact source Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*), is predicted to cast a shadow on the emission from the surrounding plasma flow, showcasing general relativity's influence in the strong-field regime. This changing source structure during observations violates a fundamental assumption of radio interferometry imaging. By simulating realistic EHT observations of a model movie of Sgr A*, we demonstrate that an image of the average quiescent emission, featuring the characteristic black hole shadow and photon ring predicted by general relativity, can still be obtained by observing over multiple days and subsequently processing the visibilities (scaling, averaging, and smoothing) before imaging. Furthermore, we show that this procedure can be combined with an existing method to mitigate the effects of interstellar scattering. These techniques, together, enable the recovery of the black hole shadow in the Galactic center on the reconstructed image.

title: Knowledge and Influence of MOOC Courses on Initial Teacher Training

title: Work/Precision Tradeoffs in Continuum Models of Biomolecular Electrostatics
Abstract: The structure and function of biological molecules are profoundly influenced by the surrounding water and dissolved ions. This aqueous solution (solvent) exerts significant electrostatic forces in response to the biomolecule's ubiquitous atomic charges and polar chemical groups. This work investigates a simple approach to numerically calculating this model using boundary-integral equation (BIE) methods and boundary-element methods (BEM). Traditional BEM discretizes the protein-solvent boundary into boundary elements (panels), and the approximate solution is defined as a weighted combination of basis functions with compact support. This results in a BEM matrix requiring integration of singular or near-singular functions, which can be computationally slow and challenging. We investigate the accuracy and convergence of a simpler representation by modeling the unknown surface charge distribution as a set of discrete point charges on the surface. Our findings indicate that at low resolution, point-based BEM is more accurate than panel-based methods, due to direct protein surface sampling. This simpler approach can be valuable for numerous calculations requiring moderate accuracy, such as the preliminary stages of rational drug design and protein engineering.

title: The Proficiency-Congruency Dilemma: Virtual Team Design and Performance in Multiplayer Online Games

We analyze publicly available data from 3.36 million users to assess the influence of these constructs on team performance. We also conduct focus groups with novice and elite players to understand how team design practices vary with expertise. Our findings reveal that player proficiency enhances team performance more significantly than team congruency. These results have implications for players, designers, and theorists in recommending team designs that prioritize both individual expertise and team compatibility.

title: Phase statistics of light wave reflected from one-dimensional optical disordered media and its effects on light transport properties

We numerically solve the full Fokker-Planck (FP) equation for the joint probability distribution in the RR* - phase(theta) space for different sample lengths and disorder strengths. We calculate the statistical optical transport properties of 1D optical disordered media using the full FP equation numerically. This constitutes a complete solution for the reflection phase statistics and its effects on light transport properties in a 1D Gaussian white-noise disordered optical potential. Our results reveal the regime of validation for the random phase approximations (RPA) or uniform phase distribution, within the Born approximation, as well as the contribution of phase statistics to different reflection averages for strong disorder regimes. title: Large Deviations on a Cayley Tree I: Rate Functions
Abstract: We investigate the spherical model of a ferromagnet on a Cayley tree, demonstrating that under empty boundary conditions, the ferromagnetic phase transition occurs at the critical temperature T<sub>c</sub> = (6√2)/5J, where J is the interaction strength. For any temperature, the equilibrium magnetization, m<sub>n</sub>, tends to zero in the thermodynamic limit, and the true order parameter is the renormalized magnetization r<sub>n</sub> = n<sup>3/2</sup>m<sub>n</sub>, where n is the number of generations in the Cayley tree. Below T<sub>c</sub>, the equilibrium values of the order parameter are given by ρ<sup>*</sup> = ± (2π)/((√2 - 1)<sup>2</sup>)√(1 - T/T<sub>c</sub>). The model exhibits another notable temperature, T<sub>p</sub>, below which the influence of a homogeneous boundary field penetrates throughout the tree. We refer to T<sub>p</sub> as the penetration temperature, defined by T<sub>p</sub> = J/(W<sub>Cayley</sub>(3/2))(1 - (1/√2)(h/2J)<sup>2</sup>). title: An Empirical Relation Between The Large-Scale Magnetic Field And The Dynamical Mass In Galaxies
Abstract: The origin and evolution of cosmic magnetic fields, along with their influence on galaxy evolution, remain unknown. While not without challenges, dynamo theory can explain the large-scale coherent magnetic fields governing galaxies, but observational evidence is scarce. By analyzing available data on non-interacting, non-cluster galaxies with known large-scale magnetic fields, we discover a strong correlation between the integrated polarized flux density, S(PI), and the rotation speed, v(rot), of galaxies. This leads to an almost linear correlation between the large-scale magnetic field B and v(rot), assuming that the number of cosmic ray electrons is proportional to the star formation rate. Assuming equipartition between magnetic fields and cosmic rays, a super-linear correlation is observed. This correlation cannot be attributed to an active linear alpha-Omega dynamo, as no correlation exists with global shear or angular speed. Instead, it suggests a coupling between the large-scale magnetic field and the dynamical mass of the galaxies, B ~ M^(0.25-0.4). Consequently, faster rotating and/or more massive galaxies exhibit stronger large-scale magnetic fields. title: When is a bottleneck a bottleneck?

It is shown that in most cases the non-linearity in the μ(p) relation is mainly due to process (e) (frictional heating), which softens the rubber, increases the area of contact, and (in most cases) reduces the viscoelastic contribution to the friction. In fact, since the temperature distribution in the rubber at time t depends on the sliding history (i.e., on the earlier time t0 < t), the friction coefficient at time t will also depend on the sliding history, i.e., it is, strictly speaking, a time integral operator. The energy dissipation in the contact regions between solids in sliding contact can result in high local temperatures which may strongly affect the area of real contact and the friction force (and the wear-rate). This is the case for rubber sliding on road surfaces at speeds above 1 mm/s. Equations describing the frictional heating for solids with arbitrary thermal properties were derived in Ref. [14]. To accomplish this, the study considers the 2D Random Field Ising Model at T = 0 driven by an external field (H) with athermal dynamics implemented with periodic and forced boundary conditions. A convenient scaling variable (z) is chosen to account for the deformation of the distance to the critical point caused by the aspect ratio. Moreover, assuming that the dependence of the finite-size scaling functions on the aspect ratio can be accounted for by an additional multiplicative factor, the study successfully collapses data for different system sizes, aspect ratios, and boundary condition types into a single scaling function (Q).

title: The contribution of young core-collapse supernova remnants to the X-ray emission near quiescent supermassive black holes
Abstract: Significant star formation, and consequently, numerous massive stars, are commonly found near supermassive black holes (SMBHs). This implies that core-collapse supernovae in these regions should also occur. This paper investigates the observational consequences of predicting the fate of supernova remnants (SNRs) within the sphere of influence of quiescent SMBHs. The results are presented within the context of the 'autarkic' nuclei model, which describes quiescent nuclei as steady-state, self-sufficient environments where the SMBH accretes stellar winds with minimal inflow of material from beyond the sphere of influence. These regions exhibit properties, such as gas density, that scale with the SMBH mass. Using predictions of the X-ray lifetimes of SNRs originating within the sphere of influence, the study estimates the number of core-collapse SNRs present at any given time. By considering the lifetimes of SNRs and their association with young stars, the study predicts a number of core-collapse SNRs that increases from approximately 1 around Milky Way-like (4.3 x 10^6 Msun) SMBHs to around 100 around the most massive (10^10 Msun) SMBHs. The presence of young SNRs amplifies X-ray emission near quiescent SMBHs, and the paper shows that the total core-collapse SNR emission can potentially influence soft X-ray searches for very low-luminosity SMBHs. The SNR lifetime estimates also enable predictions of star formation rates in these regions. Assuming a steady-state replenishment of massive stars, the study estimates a star formation rate density of 2 x 10^-4 Msun/yr/pc^2 around the Milky Way SMBH, with a similar value around other SMBHs due to weak dependence on SMBH mass. This value aligns with currently available observations.

title: Progenitor-dependent Explosion Dynamics in Self-consistent, Axisymmetric Simulations of Neutrino-driven Core-collapse Supernovae
Abstract: This research presents self-consistent, axisymmetric core-collapse supernova simulations conducted using the Prometheus-Vertex code for 18 pre-supernova models ranging from 11 to 28 solar masses, encompassing progenitors recently investigated by other groups. All models produce explosions but can be categorized into two classes based on their progenitor structure. Models with a steep density decline at the Si/Si-O interface experience a sudden drop in mass-accretion rate upon the arrival of this interface at the shock front, triggering a rapid approach to explosion. Conversely, models with a more gradual decrease in accretion rate require a longer time for neutrino heating to overcome the accretion ram pressure, resulting in delayed explosions. Early explosions are facilitated by high mass-accretion rates after bounce and correspondingly high neutrino luminosities, combined with a pronounced drop in accretion rate and ram pressure at the Si/Si-O interface. Due to rapidly shrinking neutron star radii and receding shock fronts after their peak values, the models exhibit short advection time scales, favoring efficient growth of the standing accretion-shock instability. This instability plays a supportive role, at least for initiating the re-expansion of the stalled shock before runaway. Incorporating the effects of turbulent pressure in the gain layer, the study derives a generalized condition for the critical neutrino luminosity that accurately captures the explosion behavior of all models. The study validates the robustness of its findings by testing the influence of stochasticity, numerical resolution, and approximations in aspects of the microphysics.

title: Modeling of the substrate influence on multielement THz detector operation

The study investigates how substrate thickness (h) and relative permittivity (epsilon) influence antenna patterns and antenna-detector matching for each element. It shows that the antenna pattern is more sensitive to the detector position than antenna-detector impedance matching. The gain of array elements, antenna-detector matching, and homogeneity of detector sensitivity can be simultaneously optimized by carefully selecting substrate thickness (h) and relative permittivity (epsilon). The study reveals that multielement systems with large substrate thickness and high relative permittivity are not suitable for imaging system implementation. To achieve uniform multielement system sensitivity, substrates with low permittivity (epsilon < 5) or low thickness (h < 60 mkm for a Si substrate) should be used. title: Modeling of electron energy spectra and mobilities in semi-metallic Hg1-xCdxTe quantum wells

Results show that increasing electron concentration within the well enhances screening of the 2D electron gas, reduces hole concentration, and ultimately leads to higher electron mobility at liquid nitrogen temperatures. This increased electron concentration can be achieved in situ through delta-doping of barriers or applying top-gate potential. The modeling reveals that for low molar composition x, the concentration of holes in the well remains high over a wide range of electron concentrations. In such cases, sample purity does not significantly influence electron mobility. These findings are crucial for establishing optimal parameters for fabricating high-mobility Hg1-xCdxTe quantum wells capable of operating at liquid nitrogen temperature, making them suitable for applications in terahertz detectors.

title: Attenuation of vacuum ultraviolet light in liquid argon
Abstract: This study experimentally measures the wavelength-resolved transmission of liquid argon for a wavelength range of 118 to 250 nm. The wavelength-dependent attenuation length is presented for pure argon. The study shows that a universal wavelength-independent attenuation length cannot be assigned to liquid argon for its own fluorescence light due to the interplay between wavelength-dependent emission and absorption. A decrease in transmission is observed below 130 nm in both chemically cleaned and distilled liquid argon, attributed to absorption by the analogue of the first argon excimer continuum. For not perfectly cleaned argon, a strong influence of impurities on transmission is observed. Two strong absorption bands at 126.5 and 141.0 nm, with approximately 2 and 4 nm width, respectively, are assigned to traces of xenon in argon. A broad absorption region below 180 nm is found for unpurified argon and tentatively attributed to the presence of water in the argon sample.

title: Mean field models for interacting ellipsoidal particles

A mean-field equation and corresponding equations for the marginals of the distribution function are derived. Numerical comparisons are presented between the different levels of the model hierarchy, clearly justifying the suitability of the proposed approximations for the example cases under consideration.

title: The formation of Cataclysmic Variables: the influence of nova eruptions
Abstract: While pre-cataclysmic variables (pre-CVs) are theoretically and observationally dominated by systems with low-mass white dwarfs (WDs), the WDs in cataclysmic variables (CVs) typically exhibit higher masses. Additionally, the space density of CVs is significantly lower than predicted by theoretical models. This study explores the influence of nova outbursts on the formation and initial evolution of CVs. Specifically, the study calculates the stability of mass transfer under the assumption that all material accreted onto the WD is lost in classical novae, with part of the energy for ejecting this material originating from a common-envelope-like interaction with the companion. The study also investigates the effect of asymmetric mass ejection, which could lead to small eccentricities in the orbit. The findings reveal that a common-envelope-like ejection significantly reduces the stability of mass transfer, particularly for low-mass WDs. Similarly, the influence of asymmetric mass loss can be significant for short-period systems and even more so for low-mass WDs, but likely diminishes long before the next nova outburst due to orbital circularization. Both scenarios lead to increased mass-transfer rates, which could have observable (and potentially already observed) consequences for systems that survive to become CVs. However, a more detailed investigation of the interaction between nova ejecta and the companion, as well as the evolution of slightly eccentric CVs, is required for definitive conclusions. |||

This peak is primarily driven by a quadrupolar relaxation mechanism. The data are analyzed using a two-phonon Raman process, based on a theory involving localized anharmonic oscillators. The model provides excellent agreement with experimental data, suggesting a uniform array of localized oscillators with significant anharmonicity.

title: Gaussian quantum steering and its asymmetry in curved spacetime
Abstract: This study explores Gaussian quantum steering and its asymmetry in the context of a Schwarzschild black hole. Using a Gaussian channel description, the evolution of quantum states under the influence of Hawking radiation is investigated. The analysis reveals that thermal noise introduced by Hawking radiation destroys steerability between an inertial observer (Alice) and an accelerated observer (Bob) outside the event horizon, while concurrently generating steerability between Bob and a hypothetical observer (anti-Bob) inside the horizon. Unlike entanglement behavior in curved spacetime, steering from Alice to Bob exhibits a "sudden death" with increasing Hawking temperature, while steering from anti-Bob to Bob experiences a "sudden birth". Furthermore, Gaussian steering is always asymmetric, with the maximum asymmetry bounded by ln 2. The study identifies the parameter settings that maximize steering asymmetry and demonstrates the transition between one-way and two-way steerability for the two-mode Gaussian state under Hawking radiation.

title: Two-Dimensional Phononic Crystals: Disorder Matters

The findings demonstrate that increasing surface roughness and introducing short-range disorder modify the phonon dispersion and coherence in the hypersonic (GHz) range without impacting room-temperature thermal conductivity. title: Extrinsic Rayleigh coefficient and domain mobility in critical MPB compositions of high-performance piezoceramics: A revisit
Abstract: Enhanced domain mobility is a key feature of morphotropic phase boundary (MPB) ferroelectrics, contributing to their exceptional piezoelectric response. While the high extrinsic Rayleigh coefficient at the MPB is generally attributed to enhanced domain mobility, this study challenges that notion. Comparing three high-performance piezoelectrics, we find that the MPB compositions of lead-based systems do not exhibit the highest domain mobility, despite displaying maximum piezoelectric response and extrinsic Rayleigh coefficient. Conversely, the lead-free system shows the highest domain mobility at its critical MPB composition.  Our findings suggest that the large Rayleigh coefficient at the MPB does not necessarily indicate enhanced domain mobility. Instead, the large piezoresponse in MPB systems arises from a complex interplay of field-induced motion of interphase boundaries and domain walls. In lead-based systems, interphase boundary motion hinders domain wall mobility, leading to a large Rayleigh coefficient and piezoresponse driven by interphase boundary motion rather than enhanced domain mobility.

title: Background subtraction - separating the modeling and the inference

Specifically, it is crucial to have a background likelihood, a foreground likelihood, and a prior at each pixel. A simple application of Bayes' rule then yields a posterior probability for the label. The only remaining question is the quality of the component models: the background likelihood, the foreground likelihood, and the prior. This paper describes a model for the likelihoods built using not only past observations at a given pixel location but also including observations in a spatial neighborhood around the location. This enables modeling the influence between neighboring pixels, improving upon earlier pixelwise models that did not account for such influence. While similar in spirit to the joint domain-range model, this model overcomes certain deficiencies in that model. A spatially dependent prior is used for the background and foreground. This inherent computational expense makes it challenging to investigate the role of polarizability or electronic structure effects in influencing interfacial fluctuations. Thermodynamic integration is employed to estimate the free energy differences between biased ensembles, circumventing the umbrella sampling requirement of overlap between adjacent biased distributions. Utilizing this phenomenological anchoring potential, the study elucidates how the nature of anchoring in the presence of dual easy axes (inducing bi-stability or an average orientation between the two easy axes) can be related to the microscopic nature of the interface. However, this also pertains to fundamental problems such as wetting phenomena and all phenomena related to the orientation of soft matter bulk induced by the presence of an interface. In LCs at interfaces, easy axes correspond to the favored orientations of the LC director near the interface. When only one easy axis is defined for a given interface, the bulk director aligns with or near this axis [1].  It is well-established that in anchoring phenomena, two major effects compete to determine the anchoring directions of a liquid crystal: interactions between molecules and the interface and substrate roughness, the latter having been analyzed by Berreman [2]. The influence of adsorbed molecular functional groups at the interface is often dominant, with, for example, in carbon substrates, a primary influence of unsaturated carbon bond orientation at the interface [3].  While typical LC displays feature a unique easy axis, surface modifications have led to the discovery of promising new anchoring-related properties.  For instance, the first anchoring bi-stability was established on rough surfaces associated with electric ordo-polarization [4], and the competition between a stabilizing short-range term and a destabilizing long-range term induced by an external field can induce a continuous variation of anchoring orientation [5].  More recently, surfaces with multiple easy axes have been extensively studied.  It has been shown that the control of a continuous variation of director pretilt, achieved in various systems [6, 7], is linked to the presence of two distinct easy axes, one perpendicular to the substrate (homeotropic) and the other planar [7, 8].  Similar models can explain the continuous evolution of anchoring between two planar orientations observed on some crystalline substrates [9].  However, concurrently, two easy axes can also lead to anchoring bi-stability [10, 11] or discontinuous anchoring transitions [9], incompatible with the model established to interpret observed pretilt control. The role of the environment's geometry (obstacles, compartmentalization) and distributed reactivity (competitive reactants, traps) is key in modulating the rate constants of DI reactions and is therefore a prime design parameter. title: Interdependent Security Games on Networks under Behavioral Probability Weighting
Abstract: We consider a class of interdependent security games on networks where each node chooses a personal level of security investment. The attack probability experienced by a node is a function of her own investment and the investment by her neighbors in the network. In contrast, studies in behavioral decision theory have shown that individuals often deviate from risk-neutral behavior while making decisions under uncertainty. In particular, the true probabilities associated with uncertain outcomes are often transformed into perceived probabilities in a highly nonlinear fashion by the users, which then influence their decisions. In this paper, we investigate the effects of such behavioral probability weightings by the nodes on their optimal investment strategies and the resulting security risk profiles that arise at the Nash equilibria of interdependent network security games. This unparsing process results in documents where the input data neither influences the structure of the document nor changes their intended semantics. Individual human actions impact the environment both locally (e.g., air/water quality, noise) and globally (e.g., climate change, resource use). Urban environments are crucial examples, with growing recognition that citizen involvement in monitoring campaigns (a bottom-up approach) is the most effective way to drive change. This is possible by developing novel technologies and IT infrastructures that enable large-scale citizen participation. This paper, within the broader framework of one of the first such projects, presents results from an international competition involving citizens in mobile air pollution monitoring using low-cost sensing devices. This is combined with a web-based game to monitor perceived pollution levels. The study provides measures of shifts in perceptions throughout the campaign, along with insights into participatory patterns. Interesting effects related to inertia and direct involvement in measurement activities, compared to indirect information exposure, are highlighted. Direct involvement appears to enhance learning and environmental awareness, potentially leading to better policy adoption for pollution reduction in the future.

title: Multiple populations in globular clusters: the distinct kinematic imprints of different formation scenarios
Abstract: Several scenarios have been proposed to explain the presence of multiple stellar populations in globular clusters. Many invoke multiple generations of stars to account for observed chemical abundance anomalies, while others suggest self-enrichment through accretion of ejecta from massive stars onto the circumstellar disk of low-mass pre-main sequence stars. These scenarios imply different initial conditions for the kinematics of the various stellar populations. Assuming some net angular momentum initially, models where a second generation forms from gas collected in a cooling flow into the cluster's core predict a larger initial rotational amplitude for the polluted stars compared to the pristine stars. This contrasts with the accretion model, where polluted stars cross the core and are preferentially on radial (low-angular momentum) orbits, resulting in lower rotational amplitude. This study presents the results of a suite of N-body simulations with initial conditions designed to capture the distinct kinematic properties of these pollution scenarios. The simulations demonstrate that initial differences in the kinematics of polluted and pristine stars can persist to the present epoch in the outer regions of a large fraction of Galactic globular clusters. The differential rotation of pristine and polluted stars is identified as a unique kinematic signature that could distinguish between these scenarios, while other kinematic imprints are generally very similar across scenarios.

title: Long-distance weak annihilation contribution to the $B^{\pm}\to (π^{\pm},K^{\pm}) \ell^+\ell^-$ decays
Abstract: This paper proposes an alternative evaluation of the long-distance weak annihilation (WA, also referred to as one-photon exchange) contribution to the rare semileptonic B±→(π±,K±)ℓ+ℓ− (ℓ=e,μ) decays. This hadronic description at low energies is matched at intermediate energies to its short-distance counterpart in terms of quark and gluon degrees of freedom. While the WA contribution does not resolve the possible breaking of lepton-universality observed by LHCb in the B±→K±(μ+μ−/e+e−) ratio, nor significantly contaminate their decay rates, its contribution to the branching ratios (and direct CP asymmetry) of the B±→π±ℓ+ℓ− transitions is significant. This hadronic pollution should be considered when searching for new physics effects in decays into pions, suggesting restricting these searches to squared lepton-pair invariant mass in the (1,8) GeV2 range. The interference of the one-photon exchange contribution with the dominant short-distance one-loop amplitude induces a sizable CP asymmetry in these rare decays, calling for dedicated measurements.

title: Lithium abundances in globular cluster giants: NGC 1904, NGC 2808, and NGC 362
Abstract: The presence of multiple populations in globular clusters is well-established thanks to high-resolution spectroscopy. It is widely accepted that distinct populations result from different stellar generations, requiring intra-cluster pollution episodes to produce the peculiar chemistry observed in almost all clusters. However, the responsible progenitors have left an ambiguous signature, and their nature remains unresolved. To constrain candidate polluters, this study measured lithium and aluminum abundances in over 180 giants across three systems: NGC 1904, NGC 2808, and NGC 362. This investigation, alongside previous analyses of M12 and M5, provides the largest database of simultaneous Li and Al abundance determinations. The results indicate that Li production has occurred in each of the three clusters. In NGC 362, an M12-like behavior was detected, with first and second-generation stars sharing very similar Li abundances, favoring an AGB star progenitor capable of producing Li. Multiple progenitor types are possible in NGC 1904 and NGC 2808, as they possess both an intermediate population comparable in lithium to the first-generation stars and an extreme population enriched in Al but depleted in Li. A simple dilution model fails to reproduce this complex pattern. Finally, the internal Li variation suggests that the production efficiency of this element is a function of the cluster's mass and metallicity, with low-mass or relatively metal-rich clusters being more adept at producing Li.

title: Stable Multiscale Petrov-Galerkin Finite Element Method for High Frequency Acoustic Scattering
Abstract: This paper presents and analyzes a pollution-free Petrov-Galerkin multiscale finite element method for the Helmholtz problem with large wave number κ as a variant of [Peterseim, ArXiv:1411.1944, 2014]. Standard continuous Q1 finite elements at a coarse discretization scale H are used as trial functions, while the test functions are computed as solutions of local problems at a finer scale h. The diameter of the support of the test functions behaves like mH for some oversampling parameter m. Provided m is of the order of log(κ) and h is sufficiently small, the resulting method is stable and quasi-optimal in the regime where H is proportional to κ−1. In homogeneous (or more generally periodic) media, the fine-scale test functions depend only on local mesh configurations. Therefore, the seemingly high cost of computing the test functions can be significantly reduced on structured meshes. The paper presents numerical experiments in two and three spatial dimensions.

title: A Fourier penalty method for solving the time-dependent Maxwell's equations in domains with curved boundaries
Abstract: This paper presents a high-order, Fourier penalty method for Maxwell's equations in the vicinity of perfect electric conductor boundary conditions. The approach involves extending the smooth non-periodic domain of the equations to a periodic domain by removing the exact boundary conditions and introducing an analytic forcing term in the extended domain. The forcing, or penalty term, is chosen to systematically enforce the boundary conditions to high order in the penalty parameter, enabling higher-order numerical methods. The paper presents an efficient numerical method for constructing the penalty term and discretizes the resulting equations using a Fourier spectral method. Convergence orders of up to 3.5 are demonstrated for the one-dimensional Maxwell's equations, showing that the numerical method does not suffer from dispersion (or pollution) errors. The approach is also illustrated in two dimensions, demonstrating convergence orders of 2.5 for transverse magnetic modes and 1.5 for the transverse electric modes. The paper concludes with various test cases in dimensions two and three, including waves traveling in an irregular waveguide and scattering off a windmill-like geometry.

title: The incidence of magnetic fields in cool DZ white dwarfs
Abstract: Little is known about the incidence of magnetic fields among the coolest white dwarfs. Their spectra typically lack absorption lines due to vanishingly small bound-bound opacities of hydrogen and helium, making probing for magnetic fields extremely challenging. However, external pollution of a cool white dwarf by, for example, planetary debris, leads to the appearance of metal lines in its spectral energy distribution. These lines provide a unique tool for identifying and measuring magnetism in the coolest and oldest white dwarfs in the Galaxy. This paper reports the identification of 7 strongly metal-polluted, cool (T_eff < 8000 K) white dwarfs with magnetic field strengths ranging from 1.9 to 9.6 MG. An analysis of a larger magnitude-limited sample of cool DZ white dwarfs reveals a lower limit on the magnetic incidence of 13+/-4%, significantly higher than among hot DA white dwarfs.

title: SETI at Planck Energy: When Particle Physicists Become Cosmic Engineers
Abstract: The Fermi Paradox raises the question of whether we are alone in the universe, or if interstellar travel is simply rare. This paper explores the possibility that the search for answers to this paradox and the unification of general relativity with quantum mechanics might intersect. It is known that an accelerator capable of energizing particles to the Planck scale requires cosmic proportions, with the energy required for a Planck accelerator being of order 100 M_sun c^2 for a hadron collider due to the tiny natural cross section for Planck physics. If extraterrestrial civilizations are interested in fundamental physics, they might resort to cosmic engineering for their experiments. These colliders would be detectable through the vast amount of "pollution" they produce, motivating a YeV SETI program. This paper investigates the types of radiation such colliders would emit in a fireball scenario and the feasibility of detecting YeV radiation at Earth, particularly YeV neutrinos. While current limits on YeV neutrinos are weak, Kardashev 3 YeV neutrino sources appear to be at least 30-100 Mpc apart on average, assuming they are long-lived and emit isotropically. The paper considers the feasibility of much larger YeV neutrino detectors, including an acoustic detection experiment spanning all of Earth's oceans and instrumenting the entire Kuiper Belt. Detecting YeV neutrinos would imply an extraordinary phenomenon, whether artificial or natural. Searches for YeV neutrinos from any source are naturally commensal, giving a YeV neutrino SETI program value beyond SETI itself, particularly in limiting topological defects. The universe is remarkably faint in all kinds of nonthermal radiation, indicating that cosmic engineering is extremely rare.

title: Functional Time Series
Abstract: The continuous advancements in data collection and storage techniques allow us to observe and record real-life processes in great detail. Examples include financial transaction data, fMRI images, satellite photos, and temporal distribution of Earth's pollution. Due to the high dimensionality of such data, classical statistical tools become inadequate and inefficient. The need for new methods emerges, and functional data analysis (FDA) is one of the most prominent techniques in this context. This article focuses on presenting techniques for analyzing temporal dependence in FDA. Such dependence occurs, for example, when data consist of a continuous time process that has been segmented, such as daily data. This leads to the context of functional time series.

title: Exploiting the Symmetries of P and S wave for B --> K^* mu^+ mu^-
Abstract: This paper summarizes the current theoretical status of the four-body decay B --> K^*(--> K pi) mu^+ mu^-, and applies the formalism of spin-symmetries to the full angular distribution, including the S-wave part involving a broad scalar resonance K0^*. While the known relationship between the angular observables Pi(') is recovered in the P-wave sector, two new relations connecting the coefficients of the S-wave angular distribution are found in the S-wave sector. These relations reduce the number of independent S-wave observables from six to four. Inclusion in experimental data analysis can help reduce background from S-wave pollution. The paper also highlights the discriminative power of the maximum of the angular observable P2 as a charm-loop insensitive probe of right-handed currents. Furthermore, it shows that in the absence of right-handed currents, the angular observables P4' and P5' fulfill the relation P4' = beta P5' at the position where P2 reaches its maximum.

title: Reduced-rank spatio-temporal modeling of air pollution concentrations in the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis and Air Pollution
Abstract: The epidemiologic literature provides growing evidence of the relationship between air pollution and adverse health outcomes. Predicting individual air pollution exposure in the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)-funded Multi-Ethnic Study of Atheroscelerosis and Air Pollution (MESA Air) study relies on a flexible spatio-temporal prediction model that integrates land-use regression with kriging to account for spatial dependence in pollutant concentrations. Temporal variability is captured using temporal trends estimated via modified singular value decomposition and temporally varying spatial residuals. This model utilizes monitoring data from existing regulatory networks and supplementary MESA Air monitoring data to predict concentrations for individual cohort members. However, spatio-temporal models are generally limited in their efficacy for large datasets due to computational intractability. This paper develops reduced-rank versions of the MESA Air spatio-temporal model. Low-rank kriging is applied to account for spatial variation in the mean process, and the limitations of this approach are discussed. As an alternative, spatial variation is represented using thin plate regression splines. The performance of these models is compared using EPA and MESA Air monitoring data for predicting concentrations of oxides of nitrogen (NOx) - a pollutant of primary interest in MESA Air - in the Los Angeles metropolitan area via cross-validated R². The findings suggest that using reduced-rank models can improve computational efficiency in certain cases. Low-rank kriging and thin plate regression splines were competitive across the formulations considered, although TPRS appeared more robust in some settings.

title: Sensor Deployment for Air Pollution Monitoring Using Public Transportation System
Abstract: Air pollution monitoring is a popular research topic, leading to the development of numerous monitoring systems. This paper formulates the Bus Sensor Deployment Problem (BSDP) to select the bus routes on which sensors are deployed. Chemical Reaction Optimization (CRO), a recently proposed metaheuristic designed to solve a wide range of optimization problems, is used to solve BSDP. Using real-world data from Hong Kong Island bus route data, a series of simulations are conducted. The results show that CRO can efficiently solve this optimization problem.

title: Death by Dynamics: Planetoid-Induced Explosions on White Dwarfs
Abstract: At intervals as short as ten thousand years, each white dwarf (WD) passes within a solar radius of a planetoid, such as a comet, asteroid, or planet. Gravitational tidal forces tear the planetoid apart, and its metal-rich debris falls onto the WD, enriching its atmosphere. One-third of WDs exhibit atmospheric "pollution." For roughly every hundred planetoid disruptions, a planetoid collides with a WD. This paper simulates a small number of collisions, where "death-by-dynamics" refers to the fate of the planetoid. The energies and likely durations of a broad sample of collision events are computed, and detection strategies at optical and X-ray wavelengths are identified. Collisions with the most massive planetoids can be detected in external galaxies. Some collisions may trigger nuclear burning. If one in ~10^7-10^8 WD-planetoid collisions creates the conditions needed for a Type Ia supernova (SN Ia), "death-by-dynamics" would also refer to the fate of the WD and could provide a novel channel for the production of SN Ia. The circumstances under which the rate of SNe Ia can be increased by interactions with planetoids are considered.

title: Another shock for the Bullet cluster, and the source of seed electrons for radio relics
Abstract: Observations with the Australia Telescope Compact Array reveal a highly elongated Mpc-scale diffuse radio source on the eastern periphery of the Bullet cluster 1E0657-55.8. This source is argued to have the positional, spectral, and polarimetric characteristics of a radio relic. This powerful relic (2.3+/-0.1 x 10^25 W Hz^-1) consists of a bright northern bulb and a faint linear tail. The bulb emits 94% of the observed radio flux and has the highest surface brightness of any known relic. Coincident with the linear tail, a sharp X-ray surface brightness edge is found in the deep Chandra image of the cluster, indicating a shock front in the hot intracluster medium (ICM) located on the opposite side of the cluster from the famous bow shock. This new example of an X-ray shock coincident with a relic further supports the hypothesis that shocks in the outer regions of clusters can form relics via diffusive shock (re-)acceleration. Intriguingly, the new relic suggests that seed electrons for reacceleration are coming from a local remnant of a radio galaxy, which was fortunate to be observed before its complete disruption. If this scenario, where a relic forms when a shock crosses a well-defined region of the ICM polluted with aged relativistic plasma, as opposed to the usual assumption that seeds are uniformly mixed in the ICM, applies to other relics, it might explain several peculiar properties of peripheral relics. |||

title: Weather forecasting using Convex hull & K-Means Techniques An Approach
Abstract: Data mining using clustering is a powerful tool for analyzing and predicting data. This paper applies data mining techniques to forecast the daily average temperature, humidity, and overall weather conditions of Kolkata city. It utilizes air pollution data from the West Bengal Pollution Control Board to build a dataset for prediction. The paper introduces a new approach using convex hull to extract structural data from non-structural time series data, followed by incremental K-means clustering to define appropriate clusters. The database is then split into four separate databases based on different weather conditions. The final prediction is determined using a priority-based protocol defined by mathematical deductions.

title: Locating the source of diffusion in complex networks by time-reversal backward spreading
Abstract: Locating the source of a dynamic process in complex networks is a crucial but challenging task, with applications ranging from epidemic spreading to cancer metastasis. This paper addresses the limitations of accessing complete information from large-scale networks and presents a time-reversal backward spreading algorithm to efficiently locate the source of diffusion-like processes. The algorithm is tested using epidemic spreading and consensus dynamics, demonstrating its effectiveness in precisely locating sources in arbitrary networks under certain conditions. The study highlights the potential of this algorithm for controlling various dynamic processes in complex networks, including controlling epidemics, rumor spreading, pollution, and environmental protection.

title: A speed and departure time optimization algorithm for the Pollution-Routing Problem
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel speed and departure time optimization algorithm for the Pollution-Routing Problem (PRP), which provides a certified optimal schedule in quadratic time. The algorithm is integrated into an iterated local search-based metaheuristic for combined speed, scheduling, and routing optimization. By making the start of the working day a decision variable for individual routes, the algorithm enables better allocation of human resources and identifies potentially profitable routes that may not be viable at the beginning of the day. This expanded search space offers further opportunities for distance optimization through service consolidation. Computational experiments conducted on PRP benchmark instances demonstrate the algorithm's efficiency, leading to an 8.36% reduction in operational costs for the tested instances.

title: An unconditionally stable discontinuous Galerkin method for the elastic Helmholtz equations with large frequency
Abstract: This paper proposes and analyzes an interior penalty discontinuous Galerkin (IP-DG) method for solving elastic Helmholtz equations with a first-order absorbing boundary condition. The method utilizes piecewise linear polynomials and is proven to be unconditionally stable in both frequency and mesh size regimes. The paper derives sub-optimal error estimates in the broken $H^1$-norm and $L^2$-norm for all mesh regimes, which improve to optimal order when the mesh size is restricted to the pre-asymptotic regime. The IP-DG method innovates by penalizing not only the jumps in function values but also the jumps in normal derivatives, with complex penalty parameters. The main challenge in achieving unconditional stability is addressed by exploiting a simple property of linear functions. The error estimate is derived using a nonstandard technique, and numerical experiments validate the theoretical results and examine the pollution effect in the error bounds.

title: Exploring Anticorrelations and Light Element Variations in Northern Globular Clusters Observed by the APOGEE Survey
Abstract: This study analyzes the light-element behavior of red giant stars in Northern globular clusters (GCs) using data from the SDSS-III Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment (APOGEE). The study derives abundances of nine elements (Fe, C, N, O, Mg, Al, Si, Ca, and Ti) for 428 red giant stars in 10 GCs. The intrinsic abundance range relative to measurement errors is examined, and the C-N and Mg-Al anticorrelations are explored using an extreme-deconvolution code. The findings reveal that Mg and Al primarily drive population membership in most clusters, except for the most metal-rich clusters, M107 and M71, where N plays a more significant role. The study also observes diverse abundance distributions, with some clusters exhibiting clear bimodalities while others show extended distributions. The spread of Al abundances increases with decreasing cluster average metallicity, supporting the idea that low metallicity, intermediate mass AGB polluters were more common in metal-poor clusters. The correlation between [Al/Fe] and [Si/Fe] in M15 suggests that $^{28}$Si leakage has occurred in this cluster. The study also presents C, N, and O abundances for cooler stars and examines the behavior of A(C+N+O) as a function of temperature and [Al/Fe]. The scatter of A(C+N+O) is close to its estimated uncertainty in all clusters and independent of stellar temperature. While small correlations and anticorrelations between A(C+N+O) and [Al/Fe] are observed in some clusters, further research is needed to confirm these relations due to the size of abundance uncertainties. Variations in $\\alpha$-element abundances are comparable to estimated errors in all clusters.

title: Mechanics-based solution verification for porous media models
Abstract: This paper presents a new approach for verifying the accuracy of computational simulations using mathematical theorems that serve as a posteriori error estimation techniques. The methodology is demonstrated on problems involving flow through porous media and can be extended to other models. The paper constructs mathematical properties satisfied by the solutions to Darcy and Darcy-Brinkman equations, including the total minimum mechanical power, minimum dissipation theorem, reciprocal relation, and maximum principle for vorticity. These theorems have firm mechanical bases and are independent of numerical methods, making them suitable for solution verification across various numerical methods. The paper shows that, for a given set of boundary conditions, Darcy velocity exhibits the minimum total mechanical power among all kinematically admissible vector fields. A similar result is also shown for Darcy-Brinkman velocity. Additionally, the paper demonstrates that, for a conservative body force, Darcy and Darcy-Brinkman velocities have the minimum total dissipation among their respective kinematically admissible vector fields. Numerical examples illustrate how the minimum dissipation and total mechanical power theorems can be used to identify pollution errors in numerical solutions. The solutions to Darcy and Darcy-Brinkman equations are shown to satisfy a reciprocal relation, potentially helpful in identifying errors in the numerical implementation of boundary conditions.

title: Time Reversal-based Transmissions with Distributed Power Allocation for Two-Tier Networks
Abstract: The paper addresses radio pollution and power consumption problems in heterogeneous networks (HetNet) by exploring the use of time reversal (TR) technique as a linear precoder for femtocells. The TR technique, validated for both wide-band and narrow-band transmissions, offers superior energy harvesting capabilities. The paper proposes a HetNet model with a TR-employed femtocell for power savings, while the macrocell utilizes a beam-forming algorithm based on the zero-forcing principle over frequency selective channels. Considering limited signaling information exchange through backhaul connections, a distributed power loading strategy is implemented, prioritizing macrocell users over femtocell users. Monte-Carlo simulations demonstrate the superiority of TR over zero-forcing in femtocell environments due to its significantly higher energy-saving gain. The validity of the power loading strategy is verified over multipath channels.

title: Stringy Instanton Counting and Topological Strings
Abstract: The paper studies the stringy instanton partition function of four-dimensional ${\\cal N}=2$ $U(N)$ supersymmetric gauge theory, previously derived by Bonelli et al in 2013. In type IIB string theory, the stringy $U(N)$ instantons are represented by D1-branes wrapping around $\\mathbb{P}^1$ and bound to D5-branes. The study finds a relationship between the stringy instanton partition function with removed quantum stringy corrections and the K-theoretic instanton partition function. This relationship is also linked to the refined topological A-model partition function on a local toric Calabi-Yau threefold. The study further investigates quantum stringy corrections in the stringy instanton partition function that are not captured by the refined topological strings.

title: Four-winged flapping flyer in forward flight
Abstract: This paper investigates the performance of a four-winged flapping flyer with chord-wise flexible wings in a self-propelled setup. The study explores the kinematic parameter space defined by flapping frequency and forewing-hindwing phase lag, measuring cruising speed and consumed electric power for each point in the parameter space. The analysis focuses on understanding the relationship between performance, efficiency, and phase lag in four-winged flapping flight. The study finds that different phase lags are required to optimize for fastest flight or lowest energy consumption. A conjecture regarding the underlying mechanism is proposed, suggesting a coupled dynamics between the forewing-hindwing phase lag and the deformation kinematics of the flexible wings.

title: Aluminium as catalyst for ZnO nanostructures growth
Abstract: This paper reports the growth of Al-catalyzed ZnO nanowires (NWs) using a thermal evaporation technique. The substrates were pre-coated with Al nano-islands that act as seeds for NW growth. The study finds that the density of NWs increases with increasing seed density, confirming the catalytic properties of Al. The critical growth parameters investigated include substrate temperature, oxygen partial pressure, and initial Al layer thickness. The results show that oxygen pressure strongly influences structural characteristics. NWs grown at low oxygen flow exhibit preferential orientation in the (00l)-planes, while high oxygen flow leads to polycrystalline NWs. The paper proposes a vapor-solid-solid (VSS) process as the dominant growth mechanism.

title: Effects of Data Resolution and Human Behavior on Large Scale Evacuation Simulations
Abstract: Traffic Analysis Zones (TAZ)-based macroscopic simulation studies are widely used in evacuation planning. However, the large size of TAZs and aggregated information can underestimate actual evacuation performance. This paper leverages high-resolution demographic data from LandScan USA and agent-based microscopic traffic simulation models to address these limitations. The study investigates the use of LandScan USA Population Cells (LPC) data for evacuation assignments with various network configurations, travel demand models, and traveler compliance behaviors. It introduces a new Multiple Source Nearest Destination Shortest Path (MSNDSP) problem for generating Origin Destination matrix in evacuation assignments when using LandScan data. Additionally, the paper proposes a new agent-based traffic assignment framework integrating LandScan and TRANSIMS modules for evacuation planning and operation studies. The impact analysis covers various aspects, including traffic analysis area resolutions (TAZ vs. LPC), evacuation start times (daytime vs. nighttime), and departure time choice models (normal S shape model vs. location-based model). Furthermore, the study implements multi-scale network configurations and routing schemes for evacuation performance comparison. Finally, the paper analyzes traveler compliance behavior under evacuation operations, considering different compliance levels.

title: Revisiting Correlations Between Broad-Line and Jet Emission Variations for AGNs: 3C 120 and 3C 273
Abstract: This paper investigates the cross-correlations between broad-line and jet emission variations in active galactic nuclei (AGNs) to determine the position of radio and gamma-ray emitting regions in the jet. By considering the radial profiles of the radius and number density of clouds in a spherical broad-line region (BLR), the study derives new formulae connecting the jet emitting position $R_{\\rm{jet}}$ to the time lag $\\tau_{\\rm{ob}}$ between broad-line and jet emission variations, and the BLR radius. Similar formulae are derived for a disk-like BLR and a spherical shell BLR. The model-independent FR/RSS method is used to estimate $\\tau_{\\rm{ob}}$. For 3C 120, positive lags of about 0.3 yr are found between the 15 GHz emission and the H$\\beta$, H$\\gamma$, and He II $\\lambda 4686$ lines, suggesting the line variations lead the 15 GHz ones. Each broad-line light curve corresponds to a radio outburst. $R_{\\rm{jet}}=$1.1--1.5 parsec (pc) are obtained for 3C 120. For 3C 273, a common feature of negative time lags is found in the cross-correlation functions between light curves of radio emission and the Balmer lines, as well as Ly$\\alpha \\/\\ \\lambda 1216$ and C~{\\sc iv} $\\lambda 1549$ lines. $R_{\\rm{jet}}=$ 1.0--2.6 pc are obtained for 3C 273. The estimated $R_{\\rm{jet}}$ values are comparable for 3C 120 and 3C 273, indicating that the gamma-ray emitting positions are likely within $\\sim$ 1--3 pc from the central engines. The study finds that the cloud number density and radius radial distributions, as well as the BLR structures, have negligible effects on $R_{\\rm{jet}}$.

title: Enhanced thermoelectric coupling near electronic phase transition: the role of fluctuation Cooper pairs
Abstract: Thermoelectric energy conversion is a direct but inefficient process, hindering its widespread adoption. These coefficients lead to the definition of the thermodynamic figure of merit, which diverges at finite temperature, indicating optimal use of the thermoelectric working fluid. This occurs only in the fluctuation regime due to increased compressibility near the phase transition. The results highlight the potential of focusing research efforts on systems with possible electronic phase transitions to enhance thermoelectric efficiency.

title: Understanding and Designing Complex Systems: Response to "A framework for optimal high-level descriptions in science and engineering---preliminary report"
Abstract: This commentary recounts the history behind building compact models of nonlinear, complex processes and identifying their relevant macroscopic patterns or "macrostates". Computational mechanics offers a method for extracting the optimal minimal predictive model for a given process, while rate-distortion theory provides methods for systematically approximating such models. The commentary ends by discussing future prospects for developing a general framework that automatically discovers optimal compact models. title: Photon-mediated interactions: a scalable tool to create and sustain entangled states of N atoms
Abstract: This paper proposes and studies the use of photon-mediated interactions for generating long-range steady-state entanglement between N atoms. The achievable steady-state fidelities for entanglement and its scaling with the number of qubits are analyzed for existing superconducting quantum circuits. While primarily discussed for a superconducting circuit architecture, the protocol can be realized in any Cavity QED platform that allows controllable delivery of coherent electromagnetic radiation to specific locations.

title: Accounting for Earnings Announcements in the Pricing of Equity Options
Abstract: This paper analyzes an option pricing framework that accounts for the price impact of an earnings announcement (EA) and examines the behavior of the implied volatility surface prior to the event. The study also derives analytic bounds and asymptotics for the pre-EA implied volatility under different models. Calibration results demonstrate a good fit for the entire implied volatility surface before an announcement. The risk-neutral distribution of the EA jump is compared to its historical distribution. title: Upscaling nonlinear adsorption in periodic porous media - Homogenization approach
Abstract: This paper investigates the homogenization of a model of reactive flows through periodic porous media, involving a single solute that can be absorbed and desorbed on pore boundaries. Under the assumption of equal drift velocities in the bulk and on the pore boundaries, the study obtains a nonlinear monotone diffusion equation as the homogenized model. The method of two-scale convergence with drift is the main technical tool used. Numerical test cases in two space dimensions support the theoretical analysis. |||

title: Outage Analysis of Cooperative Transmission with Energy Harvesting Relay: Time Switching vs Power Splitting
Abstract: Energy harvesting (EH) is a promising approach for realizing green communications. This paper investigates a multiuser transmission network with an EH cooperative relay, where a source transmits independent information to multiple destinations with the help of an energy-constrained relay. The relay harvests energy from the radio frequency (RF) signals transmitted by the source and assists multiuser transmission using the harvested energy. By employing time switching and power-splitting relay receiver architectures, two protocols are proposed: the time-switching cooperative multiuser transmission (TSCMT) protocol and the power-splitting cooperative multiuser transmission (PSCMT) protocol. These protocols enable simultaneous information processing and EH at the relay. The system outage probability is analyzed for both protocols, and explicit expressions are derived for each. The effects of system configuration parameters, such as source power and relay location, on system performance are also discussed. Numerical results demonstrate the accuracy of the analytical results and highlight the advantages of the proposed protocols over traditional non-cooperative schemes, providing green solutions for reliable communication and lower system outage probability without consuming additional energy. Notably, for the same transmit power at the source, the PSCMT protocol outperforms the TSCMT protocol in achieving a lower system outage probability.

Traditionally, these bonds are assumed to be one-to-one and non-crossing for secondary structures. This paper focuses on pattern matching and local alignment between two RNA structures. For pattern matching, two algorithms are presented: one for obtaining an exact match and the other for approximate match. An algorithm for RNA local structural alignment is also presented.

Abstract: High-density VLSI networks require fast communication. This paper proposes a closed-form delay model for current mode signaling in VLSI interconnects with resistive load termination. Current mode dissipates 0.015pJ energy, while VM consumes 0.045pJ for a single bit transmission across the interconnect over CNT material. Abstract: Inferring proteins from complex peptide samples in shotgun proteomic workflows poses significant challenges for computational resources. This paper presents a model-based inference approach developed and validated to address this problem. title: Well-balanced and flexible morphological modeling of swash hydrodynamics and sediment transport
Abstract: Existing numerical models of the swash zone are relatively inflexible in dealing with sediment transport due to a high dependence on empirical sediment transport relations. The nonlinear shallow water equations and the Exner equation are discretized using the shock-capturing finite volume method, where the numerical flux and the bed slope source term are estimated using a well-balanced version of the SLIC (Slope LImited Centered) scheme. This scheme does not rely on empirical sediment transport relations. The model's well-balanced property is demonstrated through simulations of quiescent coastal flow. Its quantitative accuracy in reproducing key parameters, including notional shoreline position, swash depth, flow velocity, overtopping flow volume, beach change depth, and sediment transport rate, is validated through comparisons with analytical solutions, experimental data, and previous numerical solutions. This work facilitates an improved modeling framework for swash hydrodynamics and sediment transport.

title: LHAPDF6: parton density access in the LHC precision era
Abstract: The LHAPDF library, a long-standing tool in particle physics, provides standardized access to parton density functions (PDFs) for both experimental and theoretical purposes. This new design, currently restricted to interpolated PDFs, utilizes centralized numerical routines and a robust cascading metadata system to decouple software releases from the provision of new PDF data and enable complete flexibility in parton content. Over 200 PDF sets have been migrated from LHAPDF 5 to the new universal data format, undergoing rigorous quality control. LHAPDF 6 is supported by numerous Monte Carlo generators and other physics programs, including full compatibility routines in some cases. Additionally, modulation lane structures are detected, appearing continuous across LHC and RHC emissions, suggesting that both polarizations may originate from the same hemisphere of Jupiter. The paper examines rare S-bursts detected during an Io-D event, demonstrating drift rates consistent with those from other Io-related sources. title: Einstein and Besso: from Zürich to Milano
Abstract: The period between 1896 and 1901 in Milan is crucial for understanding Albert Einstein's formative years. While attending the Swiss Federal Polytechnic (ETH Zurich) from 1896 to 1900, he regularly traveled back to Milan to stay with his family, who were involved in the development of the electricity industry in northern Italy. Between 1899 and 1901, he met his close friend and collaborator, Michele Besso, in Milan on a frequent basis. This period foreshadows the later Bern period (1904) due to their strong relationship. To understand the circumstances behind their encounters, the paper explores the interconnected social networks of their respective families, particularly through the electricity sector and the polytechnic engineering universities of Zurich and Milan. The Cantoni family branch, on Michele's mother's side, previously overlooked, played a significant role, especially Vittorio Cantoni, a renowned electrical engineer, and Giuseppe Jung, a professor at the Milan Polytechnic. The paper also reveals that while in Milan, Einstein, residing in a prominent palace in the city's heart, worked in the nearby rich library of the Istituto Lombardo, Accademia di Scienze e Lettere in Brera.
