title: Polarities & Focussing: a journey from Realisability to Automated Reasoning
Abstract: This dissertation explores the roles of polarities and focussing in various aspects of computational logic. These concepts play a pivotal role in interpreting proofs as programs, also known as the Curry-Howard correspondence, within the context of classical logic. Originating from linear logic, they enable the construction of meaningful semantics for cut-elimination in classical logic, some of which relate to the Call-by-Name and Call-by-Value disciplines of functional programming. The first part of this dissertation provides an introduction to these interpretations, highlighting the significance of polarities and focussing. For instance, proofs of positive formulae provide structured data, while proofs of negative formulae consume such data. Focussing allows for the description of the interaction between these two types of proofs as pure pattern-matching. This idea is further developed in the second part of the dissertation and connected to realisability semantics, where structured data is interpreted algebraically, and its consumption is modeled using an orthogonality relation. Most of this part has been formally verified in the Coq proof assistant. Polarities and focussing were also introduced with applications to logic programming in mind, where computation is proof-search. In the third part of the dissertation, the authors extend this idea by exploring the roles of these concepts in other applications of proof-search, such as theorem proving, particularly automated reasoning. They utilize these concepts to describe the main algorithm of SAT-solvers and SMT-solvers: DPLL. Subsequently, they describe the implementation of a proof-search engine called Psyche. Its architecture, based on the concept of focussing, provides a platform where intelligent techniques from automated reasoning (or a user interface) can be safely and reliably implemented through an API.

title: Performance comparison between Java and JNI for optimal implementation of computational micro-kernels
Abstract: General-purpose CPUs used in high-performance computing (HPC) employ vector instruction sets and out-of-order execution engines to enhance instruction-level parallelism. Consequently, optimizing code for these features is crucial to improve the performance of computationally intensive applications. The HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), a Java runtime environment, presents an attractive alternative for HPC due to its programming flexibility and productivity, where performance is guaranteed by the Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler. However, the JIT compiler suffers from two key limitations: its black-box nature hinders developer control over generated code and optimization feedback, and its time constraints restrict optimization levels compared to static compilers like GCC or LLVM. Therefore, statically compiled code offers advantages due to its ability to achieve further optimization and reduce performance bottlenecks. Java allows calling native code from dynamic libraries via the Java Native Interface (JNI). However, JNI methods lack inlining and incur an overhead during invocation compared to native Java methods. To reap the benefits of better static optimization through JNI, the computational workload at each JNI invocation must outweigh the call overhead. This paper addresses this problem by analyzing a set of micro-kernels to select the most efficient implementation based on the computational requirements of the calling context. The paper also explores the performance impact of various optimization strategies including vectorization, out-of-order optimization, data alignment, method inlining, and the use of native memory for JNI methods.

Specifically, it considers a molecule with three nuclear spins (qubits) – the system, reservoir, and ancilla – to measure the heat dissipated during a global system-reservoir unitary interaction that alters the system's information content. An interferometric technique is employed to reconstruct the heat distribution associated with the unitary interaction. Quantum state tomography is then used to measure the relative change in the system's entropy. This approach verifies that an operation changing the information content of a system inevitably generates heat in the reservoir, as predicted by Landauer's principle. title: Point Process-based Monte Carlo estimation

title: Data-Driven Allocation of Vaccines for Controlling Epidemic Outbreaks
Abstract: This paper proposes a mathematical framework, based on conic geometric programming, for controlling a susceptible-infected-susceptible viral spreading process in a directed contact network with unknown contact rates.  The framework assumes access to time series data describing the evolution of the spreading process observed by a collection of sensor nodes over a finite time interval. It presents a data-driven robust convex optimization framework to determine the optimal allocation of protection resources (e.g., vaccines and/or antidotes) to eradicate the viral spread at the fastest possible rate. Unlike current network identification heuristics, which identify a single network to explain the observed data, this framework uses available data to define an uncertainty set containing all networks consistent with empirical observations. The characterization of this uncertainty set of networks is tractable within the context of conic geometric programming, allowing for efficient identification of the optimal resource allocation to control the worst-case spread within the uncertainty set of networks. title: Improved guaranteed computable bounds on homogenized properties of periodic media by Fourier-Galerkin method with exact integration

The GaNi scheme, fully equivalent to the original Moulinec-Suquet algorithm, was used to evaluate guaranteed upper-lower bounds on homogenized coefficients incorporating a closed-form double grid quadrature. This paper extends these concepts, based on the primal and dual formulations, to the Ga scheme. For the same computational effort, Ga outperforms GaNi with more accurate guaranteed bounds and more predictable numerical behavior. The quadrature technique leading to block-sparse linear systems is extended to materials defined via high-resolution images, enabling effective treatment using FFT. Memory demands are reduced by reformulating the double to the original grid scheme using FFT shifts. Minimizing the bounds during conjugate gradient iterations is effective, particularly when incorporating a solution from a coarser grid. The methodology presented for the scalar linear elliptic problem could be extended to more complex frameworks.

title: Fragmentation trees reloaded

The study demonstrates the superiority of this new scoring method for two tasks: de novo identification of molecular formulas for unknown compounds and searching a database for structurally similar compounds. The new method significantly outperforms the previous scoring method and other comparable techniques. title: Validation of equilibrium tools on the COMPASS tokamak

title: Tuning the Band Gap in Silicene by Oxidation

This work demonstrates the feasibility of tuning the band gap of silicene using oxygen adatoms, expanding the range of available two-dimensional electronic materials for devices with properties difficult to achieve with graphene oxide.

title: Functional Time Series Models for Ultrafine Particle Distributions

title: Reading Text in the Wild with Convolutional Neural Networks

title: Protein residue networks from a local search perspective
Abstract: This paper examines protein residue networks (PRNs) from a local search perspective to understand the high clustering observed in these networks despite the importance of short paths for protein functionality. The study discovers that adopting a local search perspective resolves this conflict between form and function, as increased clustering actually helps reduce path length in PRNs.  Furthermore, the paths identified using the EDS local search algorithm are more congruent with the characteristics of intra-protein communication. EDS identifies a subset of PRN edges called short-cuts, which are distinct, have high usage, impact EDS path length, diversity, and stretch, and are dominated by short-range contacts. These short-cuts form a network (SCN) that increases in size and transitivity as a protein folds. The structure of an SCN supports its function and formation, and the function of an SCN influences its formation. The study reveals significant differences in terms of SCN structure, function, and formation between successful and unsuccessful MD trajectories. By connecting the static and dynamic aspects of PRNs, the protein folding process becomes a problem of graph formation with the purpose of creating suitable pathways within proteins.

title: Convolutional Neural Networks at Constrained Time Cost

The study presents an architecture that achieves highly competitive accuracy on the ImageNet dataset (11.8% top-5 error, 10-view test), yet is 20% faster than "AlexNet" (16.0% top-5 error, 10-view test).

title: Core-Shell Structured Dielectric-Metal Circular Nanodisk Antenna: Gap Plasmon Assisted Magnetic Toroid-like Cavity Modes

title: Scalable, High-Quality Object Detection

title: Multi-objective Robust Optimization using a Post-optimality Sensitivity Analysis Technique: Application to a Wind Turbine Design
Abstract: In the pursuit of robust multi-objective optimization problems, variations in design variables and design environment parameters can be classified into small variations and large variations.  Small variations have a limited impact on performance functions and/or constraints, while large variations exert a substantial influence.  This paper focuses on the robustness of performance functions. A post-optimality sensitivity analysis technique is presented for multi-objective robust optimization problems, introducing two robustness indices.  The first index addresses the robustness of performance functions to small variations in design variables and design environment parameters.  The second robustness index characterizes the robustness of performance functions to large variations in design environment parameters. It evaluates the ability of a solution to maintain a good Pareto ranking under different design environment parameters subject to large variations.  Robustness of solutions is represented as vectors within the robustness function space, defined by the two proposed robustness indices.  This enables the designer to compare the robustness of all Pareto optimal solutions and make informed decisions.  Two illustrative examples are provided to highlight the contributions of the paper. The first example involves a numerical problem, while the second problem addresses the multi-objective robust optimization design of a floating wind turbine.

title: Clock-Driven Quantum Thermal Engines

Furthermore, the paper shows that when the engine incorporates a quantum work storage device, it is possible to approximately perform completely general unitaries on the remaining parts of the engine.  This framework has implications for quantum thermodynamics, enabling arbitrary transformations of a system with high accuracy and near-optimal extracted work while adhering to the first and second laws of thermodynamics. The research concludes that autonomous thermal machines do not inherently incur any thermodynamic cost compared to externally controlled ones.

title: Degradation-based residual life prediction under different environments

Many models assume that these historical signals are acquired under consistent environmental conditions and can be observed throughout the component's lifespan. The paper also considers applications where historical signals are not necessarily observed continuously, that is, historical signals are sparse or fragmented.  Two scenarios are analyzed: one where historical degradation signals are collected under known environmental states and another where the environmental conditions are unknown during data acquisition. For the former, a classification algorithm is used to identify the environmental state of units operating in the field. In the latter case, a clustering step is required to group historical degradation signals. The proposed model can provide accurate predictions of the lifetime or residual life distributions of engineering components still in operation. title: Brownian Carnot engine
Abstract: The Carnot cycle sets a fundamental upper limit on the efficiency of macroscopic motors operating between two thermal baths.  However, this bound requires reinterpretation at microscopic scales, where molecular bio-motors and certain artificial micro-engines operate. As described by stochastic thermodynamics, energy transfers in microscopic systems are random, and thermal fluctuations cause transient entropy decreases, potentially allowing for violations of the Carnot limit.  Despite its potential relevance for developing a thermodynamics of small systems, experimental studies of microscopic Carnot engines are still lacking. This paper presents an experimental realization of a Carnot engine utilizing a single optically trapped Brownian particle as the working substance. The study provides a comprehensive investigation of the engine's energetics and analyzes the fluctuations of the finite-time efficiency, demonstrating that the Carnot bound can be surpassed for a small number of non-equilibrium cycles.  Similar to its macroscopic counterpart, the energetics of the Carnot device exhibit fundamental properties expected in any microscopic energy transducer operating with baths at different temperatures.  The results identify the sources of irreversibility in the engine and the statistical properties of efficiency, offering insights that could inspire innovative strategies in the design of efficient nano-motors.

title: ASTRO-H White Paper - AGN Reflection
Abstract: X-ray observations provide a powerful tool for probing the central engines of active galactic nuclei (AGN). A hard X-ray continuum originates from deep within the accretion flow onto the supermassive black hole, and all optically thick structures in the AGN, including the dusty torus of AGN unification schemes, broad emission line clouds, and the black hole accretion disk, "light up" in response to irradiation by this continuum. This White Paper outlines the prospects for investigating AGN physics through observations of these X-ray reflection signatures. High-resolution SXS spectroscopy of the resulting fluorescent iron line in type-2 AGN will provide an unprecedented view of the obscuring torus, allowing for assessment of its dynamics (through line broadening) and geometry (through the line profile and observations of the "Compton shoulder"). ASTRO-H will also facilitate robust study of the relativistically broadened reflection spectrum from the inner accretion disk, even in complex systems with features like warm absorption and composite soft excesses. title: Horn Clauses for Communicating Timed Systems

The resulting analysis method is fully symbolic and applicable to systems with large or infinite discrete state spaces. title: Verification of Programs by Combining Iterated Specialization with Interpolation
Abstract: The paper presents a verification technique for program safety that integrates Iterated Specialization and Interpolating Horn Clause Solving. This novel method modularly combines these two techniques by exploiting the common Horn Clause representation of the verification problem. The Iterated Specialization verifier transforms an initial set of verification conditions using unfold/fold equivalence-preserving transformation rules.  During transformation, program invariants are discovered through the application of widening operators.  Subsequently, the output set of specialized verification conditions is analyzed by an Interpolating Horn Clause solver, incorporating the effect of interpolation alongside widening. The specialization and interpolation phases can be iterated and combined with other transformations that alter the direction of constraint propagation (forward from program preconditions or backward from error conditions).  The verification technique is implemented by integrating the VeriMAP verifier with the FTCLP Horn Clause solver, which are based on Iterated Specialization and Interpolation, respectively. title: DeepEdge: A Multi-Scale Bifurcated Deep Network for Top-Down Contour Detection

title: The information-complete quantum theory
Abstract: Quantum mechanics is a cornerstone of our current understanding of nature and remarkably successful in describing physics across a vast range of scales.  However, its interpretation has been the subject of controversy since the early days of quantum mechanics.  What is the true meaning of a quantum state? Is there a way to address the so-called quantum measurement problem? It is assumed that a quantum system's state provides an information-complete description of the system within the trinary picture. The paper presents a consistent formalism of quantum theory that explicitly incorporates information-completeness and argues that conventional quantum mechanics is an approximation of the ICQT.  The study then demonstrates how ICQT offers a coherent picture and new perspectives on existing problems in physics. title: Gamma-ray burst engines may have no memory

This distribution contrasts with the exponential case expected for a memoryless process. This research investigates whether the simple hypothesis of a temporally uncorrelated sequence of pulses can be rejected, as a lognormal distribution necessarily implies. A number of multi-peaked CGRO/BATSE GRBs were selected and analyzed, along with simulated time profiles. The crucial difference in the simulated profiles was the assumption of exponentially distributed interpulse times, as expected for a memoryless stationary Poisson process. Peaks in both data sets were identified using a novel peak search algorithm, which is more efficient than those previously employed. The observed interpulse time distribution was independently confirmed to be approximately lognormal. However, similar results were obtained on the simulated profiles, despite their intrinsic exponential distribution. While intrinsic lognormality cannot be ruled out, this finding suggests that the intrinsic interpulse time distribution in real data could still be exponential. The observed lognormal distribution might be attributable to the low efficiency of peak search algorithms at short values coupled with the limitations of bin-integrated profiles. This result suggests that GRB engines may emit pulses in a manner similar to nuclear radioactive decay, as a memoryless process.

title: Bounded Quadrant System: Error-bounded Trajectory Compression on the Go
Abstract: Long-term location tracking, where trajectory compression is commonly used, has garnered significant interest in various applications like transportation, ecology, and wearable computing. However, state-of-the-art compression methods face challenges with high space-time complexity or unsatisfactory compression rates, leading to rapid exhaustion of memory, computation, storage, and energy resources. This research proposes a novel online algorithm for error-bounded trajectory compression called the Bounded Quadrant System (BQS). BQS compresses trajectories with minimal space and time costs using convex hulls. The algorithm builds a virtual coordinate system centered at the starting point and establishes a rectangular bounding box, along with two bounding lines in each quadrant. Points within each quadrant are bounded by the convex hull formed by the box and lines. Various compression error bounds are derived to make quick compression decisions without requiring expensive error computations. Additionally, a lightweight version of the BQS algorithm is proposed, achieving O(1) complexity in both time and space for processing each point, making it suitable for highly constrained computational environments. The algorithm's natural extension to the 3-D case is also briefly discussed. Using empirical GPS traces from flying foxes, cars, and simulations, the study demonstrates the effectiveness of the algorithm in significantly reducing the time and space complexity of trajectory compression while greatly improving the compression rates compared to existing algorithms (up to 47%). title: Stochastic thermodynamics of rapidly driven systems

The first and second laws of thermodynamics are identified at the trajectory level. We identify mechanical work through initial and final projections on energy eigenstates of the system. We demonstrate that this two-step measurement becomes unnecessary in the long time limit. A steady-state fluctuation theorem for the currents and rate of mechanical work is also established. This relation does not require the introduction of a time-reversed external driving, which is usually needed when considering systems subjected to time-asymmetric external fields. This is understood as a consequence of the secular approximation applied in consistency with the large time scale separation between the fast driving oscillations and the slower relaxation dynamics induced by the environment. title: Exciton-polariton condensates
Abstract: Recently, a new type of system exhibiting spontaneous coherence has emerged – the exciton-polariton condensate. Exciton-polaritons (or polaritons for short) are bosonic quasiparticles that exist inside semiconductor microcavities, consisting of a superposition of an exciton and a cavity photon. Above a threshold density, the polaritons macroscopically occupy the same quantum state, forming a condensate. The lifetime of the polaritons is typically comparable to or shorter than thermalization times, making them inherently non-equilibrium in nature. Nevertheless, they display many features expected of equilibrium Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs). The non-equilibrium nature of the system raises fundamental questions about the meaning of a BEC and introduces new physics beyond that seen in other macroscopically coherent systems. This review focuses on several physical phenomena exhibited by exciton-polariton condensates, examining topics such as the difference between a polariton BEC, a polariton laser, and a photon laser, as well as physical phenomena such as superfluidity, vortex formation, BKT (Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless), and BCS (Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer) physics. We also discuss the physics and applications of engineered polariton structures. |||

Comparing the broadband properties of X-ray flares with the standard late internal shock model suggests that these flares might be generated by a late-time relativistic outflow at radii of 10^13-10^14 cm. This conclusion depends on the variability timescale being significantly shorter than the observed flare duration. The findings imply that X-ray flares can directly probe the activity of the GRB central engine.

title: Power enhancement of heat engines via correlated thermalization in multilevel systems

The study demonstrates that a degenerate V-type three-level heat engine produces the same maximal power output as two independent two-level systems. For N levels, this maximum enhancement is (N-1)-fold, highlighting level degeneracy as a thermodynamic resource for power output enhancement. The efficiency, however, remains unaffected. The results indicate that coherence is not crucial for multilevel-based heat machines. The presence of multiple thermalization pathways sharing a common ground state is sufficient for power enhancement.

title: Tunable dichroism and optical absorption of graphene by strain engineering
Abstract: This theoretical study explores the transmittance of linearly polarized light passing through two media separated by a strained graphene monolayer. The authors analytically characterize the degree of dichroism and transparency of graphene as a function of uniform strain and incident polarization. They propose that measurements of dichroism and transparency for different polarization directions can be used to determine the strain's magnitude and direction. The findings provide valuable tools for tuning graphene absorption through mechanical strain and designing nano-devices to detect crack propagation in materials.

title: Tuning of the electronic and optical properties of single layer black phosphorus by strain
Abstract: First principles calculations reveal a strong dependence of the electronic and optical properties of single-layer black phosphorus (BP) on applied strain. Due to BP's anisotropic atomic structure, its electronic conductivity and optical response are sensitive to the magnitude and orientation of applied strain. The study emphasizes the importance of incorporating many-body effects for accurately describing monolayer BP's electronic properties. The inclusion of many-body effects leads to a significant increase in the electronic gap from 0.90 eV to 2.31 eV. The applied tensile strain enhances electron transport along the zigzag direction of BP. Moreover, biaxial strain effectively tunes the optical band gap of monolayer BP from 0.38 eV to 2.07 eV. The exciton binding energy is also sensitive to the magnitude of applied strain, ranging from 0.40 eV to 0.83 eV. These calculations demonstrate that strain engineering can significantly tune the optical response of BP, offering potential for designing novel photovoltaic devices capturing a broad range of the solar spectrum.

title: Entanglement-enhanced time-continuous quantum control in optomechanics
Abstract: The cavity-optomechanical radiation pressure interaction enables entanglement creation between a mechanical oscillator and an electromagnetic field interacting with it. This paper investigates how this entanglement can be harnessed within the framework of time-continuous quantum control to engineer the quantum state of the mechanical system. Specifically, it analyzes the preparation of low-entropy mechanical states using feedback cooling in the blue detuned regime, the creation of bipartite mechanical entanglement via time-continuous entanglement swapping, and the preparation of a squeezed mechanical state through time-continuous teleportation. These protocols are feasible in optomechanical systems exhibiting a cooperativity larger than 1.

title: An Open Distributed Architecture for Flexible Hybrid Assembly Systems: A Model Driven Engineering Approach
Abstract: Assembly systems are critical in today's industry. This paper proposes an open distributed architecture for engineering evolvable flexible hybrid assembly systems. The proposed architecture relies on model-driven development, where models represent structure and behavior, and a domain-specific engineering tool facilitates the assembly system engineer during the process. Specific meta-models capturing domain knowledge guide the engineer in constructing the models required for assembly system development. This work extends a previous framework for embedded industrial automation systems by adapting it to the assembly system domain. The proposed architecture can be used to develop a framework for evolvable, flexible, and reconfigurable assembly systems leveraging the benefits of the Cyber Physical paradigm using web technologies, the Internet of Things, cloud computing, and big data.

title: Far-infrared line spectra of Seyfert galaxies from the Herschel-PACS Spectrometer
Abstract: Spectroscopic observations of far-infrared fine-structure lines in 26 Seyfert galaxies using Herschel-PACS spectrometer, complemented by Spitzer-IRS and Herschel-SPIRE spectroscopy, are presented. The ratios of OIII, NII, SIII, and NeV lines determine electron densities in the ionized gas regions. CI lines, observed with SPIRE, measure the densities in the neutral gas, while OI lines provide a measure of gas temperature at densities below 10000 cm-3. An anti-correlation of temperature with gas density is found using OI145/63um and SIII33/18um line ratios. The study reveals that density stratification is common in these active galaxies, with electron densities increasing with the ionization potential of the ions producing NII, SIII, and NeV emission. The infrared emission lines originate from different regions: the Narrow Line Region (NLR) photoionized by the AGN central engine, HII regions photoionized by hot stars, and neutral gas in photo-dissociated regions (PDRs). The contributions from these regions are separated by comparing emission line ratios to empirical and theoretical values. The combination of Spitzer and Herschel lines, particularly the mixed mid-IR/far-IR line ratio of OIII88um/OIV26um, reliably discriminates between AGN and star formation emission regimes, while the far-IR line ratio of CII157um/OI63um provides a milder separation. Comparing the observed CII157um/NII205um ratio with photoionization models reveals that most CII emission in these galaxies arises from PDRs.

title: Multiscale Universal Interface: A Concurrent Framework for Coupling Heterogeneous Solvers
Abstract: Concurrently coupled numerical simulations using heterogeneous solvers are powerful tools for modeling multiscale phenomena. However, enabling such simulations often requires significant modifications to existing codes. This paper introduces a C++ library, the Multiscale Universal Interface (MUI), designed to facilitate the coupling effort for a wide range of multiscale simulations. The library adopts a header-only form with minimal external dependency, making it easily integrable into existing codes. A data sampler concept is introduced, combined with a hybrid dynamic/static typing mechanism, to create a customizable framework for solver-independent data interpretation. The library integrates MPI MPMD support and an asynchronous communication protocol to handle inter-solver information exchange regardless of the solvers' own MPI awareness. Template metaprogramming significantly enhances both runtime performance and code flexibility. The library's validation through three different multiscale problems demonstrates its flexibility in handling heterogeneous models and solvers. These examples include simulating Couette flow with two coupled SPH simulations of different spatial resolutions, coupling SPH with DPD to study the effect of surface grafting, and coupling eDPD with FEM for conjugate heat transfer between solid and fluid domains.

title: Breakout character of islet amyloid polypeptide hydrophobic mutations at the onset of type-2 diabetes
Abstract: Toxic fibrillar aggregates of Islet Amyloid PolyPeptide (IAPP) are the physical manifestation of a peptidic phase transition signaling the onset of type-2 diabetes mellitus in various mammalian species. Experimentally verified mutations in the amyloidogenic segment 20-29 in humans, cats, and rats are strongly correlated with molecular aggregation propensities. This study uses a microcanonical analysis of IAPP_{20-29} isoforms to demonstrate that a minimalist one-bead hydrophobic-polar continuum model for protein interactions accurately quantifies these propensities based on free-energy barriers. The results highlight the critical role of sequence-dependent hydrophobic mutations on hotspots for stabilization and, consequently, the engineering of such biological peptides.

title: Room temperature magnetic order on zigzag edges of narrow graphene nanoribbons
Abstract: Magnetic order emerging in non-magnetic materials like carbon is a novel type of s-p electron magnetism predicted to exhibit exceptional high-temperature stability. While atomic-scale structural defects in graphene can host unpaired spins, the conditions for long-range magnetic order from these defect-bound magnetic moments remain unclear. This study proposes that atomic-scale engineering of graphene edges with specific crystallographic orientations, comprising edge atoms solely from one sub-lattice of the bipartite graphene lattice, can lead to robust magnetic order. Employing a nanofabrication technique based on scanning tunneling microscopy, the researchers define graphene nanoribbons with nanometer precision and well-defined crystallographic edge orientations. While armchair ribbons display quantum confinement gaps, zigzag ribbons narrower than 7 nm reveal a bandgap of approximately 0.2-0.3 eV, indicating interaction-induced spin ordering along their edges. A semiconductor to metal transition is observed upon increasing the ribbon width, suggesting a switch in magnetic coupling between opposite ribbon edges from antiferromagnetic to ferromagnetic configuration. The magnetic order on graphene edges with controlled zigzag orientation remains stable even at room temperature, raising hope for graphene-based spintronic devices operating under ambient conditions.

title: A Survey on Software Testing Techniques using Genetic Algorithm
Abstract: The software industry aims to deliver high-quality software to end users. Testing is essential for ensuring this quality, ensuring that software meets user specifications and requirements. However, software testing faces challenges such as effective test case generation and prioritization. These challenges demand significant effort, time, and cost. To address these issues, various techniques and methodologies have been proposed, including the use of evolutionary algorithms for automatic test generation. Genetic Algorithm (GA) is one such evolutionary algorithm. This research paper presents a survey of GA approaches for addressing the challenges encountered during software testing.

title: Enhancing software module reusability using port plug-ins: an experiment with the iCub robot
Abstract: Developing high-quality reusable software components is a challenging task requiring careful design to balance potential reuse, functionalities, and ease of implementation. Extendibility is a crucial property for software, as it reduces development costs and enhances reusability. This work introduces an approach to enhance component reusability by extending their functionalities using plug-ins at the connection point (port) level. Application-dependent functionalities, such as data monitoring and arbitration, can be implemented using conventional scripting languages and plugged into component ports. The approach avoids introducing application-dependent modifications to existing components, minimizing development time and promoting the creation of simpler and more reusable components. Additionally, it reduces communication and deployment overheads as extra functionalities can be added without introducing additional modules.

title: Do Convnets Learn Correspondence?
Abstract: Convolutional neural nets (convnets) trained on massive labeled datasets have significantly improved the state-of-the-art in image classification and object detection. However, visual understanding requires establishing correspondence at a finer level than object category. Given their large pooling regions and whole-image label training, it is unclear whether convnets derive their success from an accurate correspondence model suitable for precise localization. This paper investigates the effectiveness of convnet activation features for tasks requiring correspondence. It presents evidence that convnet features localize at a much finer scale than their receptive field sizes, can be used for intraclass alignment as well as conventional hand-engineered features, and outperform conventional features in keypoint prediction on objects from PASCAL VOC 2011.

title: A Machine Learning Method to Infer Fundamental Stellar Parameters from Photometric Light Curves
Abstract: A fundamental challenge in wide-field imaging surveys is obtaining follow-up spectroscopic observations, as there are billions of photometrically cataloged sources, while modern spectroscopic surveys are limited to a few million targets. As we approach the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope (LSST) era, new algorithmic solutions are needed to manage the data deluge. This paper reports the development of a machine-learning framework for inferring fundamental stellar parameters (Teff, log g, and [Fe/H]) using photometric brightness variations and color alone. A training set is constructed from a systematic spectroscopic survey of variables with Hectospec/MMT, including approximately 9000 spectra with stellar parameters measured using the SEGUE Stellar Parameters Pipeline (SSPP). The random forest algorithm performs non-parametric regression to predict Teff, log g, and [Fe/H] from photometric time-domain observations. The optimized model produces a cross-validated root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 165 K, 0.39 dex, and 0.33 dex for Teff, log g, and [Fe/H], respectively. Examining the subset of sources with reliable SSPP measurements reduces the RMSE to 125 K, 0.37 dex, and 0.27 dex, comparable to low-resolution spectroscopy. For variable stars, this represents a 12-20% improvement in RMSE compared to models trained with single-epoch photometric colors. The method is applied to estimate stellar parameters for approximately 54,000 known variables. This approach can convert photometric time-domain surveys into pseudo-spectrographic engines, enabling the construction of detailed maps of the Milky Way, its structure, and history.

title: Continuous Generation and Stabilization of Mesoscopic Field Superposition States in a Quantum Circuit
Abstract: While dissipation is generally considered detrimental to quantum coherence, it can, when carefully engineered, lead to the stabilization of non-trivial pure quantum states. This paper proposes a scheme for continuous generation and stabilization of Schrödinger cat states in a cavity using dissipation engineering. Non-classical photon states with definite parity are first generated through a two-photon drive and dissipation, followed by stabilizing these transient states against single-photon decay. This single-photon stabilization is autonomous and implemented through a second engineered bath, exploiting the photon number-dependent frequency-splitting due to Kerr interactions in the strongly dispersive regime of circuit QED. Starting with the Hamiltonian of the baths plus cavity, an effective model of only the cavity photon states is derived, along with analytic expressions for relevant physical quantities, such as the stabilization rate. The deterministic generation of such cat states is crucial for performing universal quantum computation.

title: Probabilistic verification of partially observable dynamical systems
Abstract: The construction and formal verification of dynamical models are essential in engineering, biology, and other disciplines. This study focuses on non-linear models with parameters governing their dynamics, where the parameter values are often unknown and unobservable through noisy measurements. Treating parameters as random variables, their distribution can be constrained by conditioning on observations, thereby constructing a posterior probability distribution. The aim is to perform model verification with respect to this posterior. The primary challenge is obtaining independent samples from the posterior, especially for non-linear dynamical models. Standard statistical model checking methods, requiring independent system realizations, are not applicable in this context. This paper proposes a Markov chain Monte Carlo-based statistical model checking framework, generating a sequence of dependent random realizations of the model dynamics over the parameter posterior. Statistical hypothesis tests are used on this sequence to verify whether the model satisfies a bounded temporal logic property with a specific probability. Sample size bounds tailored to dependent samples are employed for fixed sample size and sequential tests. The method is applied to a case study from systems biology, modeling the JAK-STAT biochemical pathway as a system of non-linear ODEs with unknown parameters. Noisy, indirect observations of the system state are available from an experiment. The results demonstrate that the proposed method enables probabilistic verification with respect to the parameter posterior with specified error bounds.

title: Bayesian two-step estimation in differential equation models
Abstract: Ordinary differential equations (ODEs) are used to model dynamic systems appearing in engineering, physics, biomedical sciences, and other fields. These equations contain unknown parameters, denoted by $\bm{\theta}$, with physical significance that needs to be estimated from noisy data. Often, there is no closed-form analytic solution for the equations, preventing the use of standard non-linear least squares techniques for parameter estimation. A two-step approach is employed, where the first step involves nonparametric data fitting. In the second step, the parameter is estimated by minimizing the distance between the nonparametrically estimated derivative and the derivative suggested by the system of ODEs. The statistical aspects of this approach have been studied under the frequentist framework. This paper considers this two-step estimation under the Bayesian framework. The response variable is allowed to be multidimensional, and its true mean function is not assumed to be in the model. A prior is induced on the regression function using a random series based on B-spline basis functions. The Bernstein-von Mises theorem is established for the posterior distribution of the parameter of interest. Interestingly, even though the posterior distribution of the regression function based on splines converges at a rate slower than $n^{-1/2}$, the parameter vector $\bm{\theta}$ is estimated at a rate of $n^{-1/2}$.

title: Verifying Chemical Reaction Network Implementations: A Pathway Decomposition Approach
Abstract: Verifying the correctness of molecular implementations of abstract chemical reaction networks presents a significant challenge. These systems operate stochastically, asynchronously, concurrently, and often involve multiple intermediate steps, parallel pathways, and side reactions. This problem is related to the verification of Petri nets, but existing approaches are insufficient for providing a single guarantee covering an infinite set of possible initial states (molecule counts) and an infinite state space potentially explored by the system. This paper addresses these issues by formulating a new theory of pathway decomposition, providing a formal basis for comparing chemical reaction network implementations. An algorithm is presented to compute this basis. The theory naturally handles situations like "delayed choice" that are not easily accommodated by other approaches. Pathway decomposition is combined with weak bisimulation to handle a wider class that includes most known enzyme-free DNA implementation techniques. The notion of logical equivalence between chemical reaction network implementations is expected to be valuable for other molecular implementations, such as biochemical enzyme systems, and perhaps more broadly in concurrency theory.

title: A Nanomembrane-Based Bandgap-Tunable Germanium Microdisk Using Lithographically-Customizable Biaxial Strain for Silicon-Compatible Optoelectronics
Abstract: Strain engineering has proven crucial for germanium-based photonics, particularly light emission. However, applying a large permanent biaxial strain to germanium has been challenging. This paper presents a simple, CMOS-compatible technique for conveniently inducing a large, spatially homogenous strain in microdisks patterned within ultrathin germanium nanomembranes. The technique concentrates and amplifies a pre-existing small strain into the microdisk region. Biaxial strains as large as 1.11% are observed using Raman spectroscopy and confirmed by photoluminescence measurements, which show enhanced and redshifted light emission from the strained microdisks. This technique allows for customizable biaxial strain through lithography, enabling independent bandgap tuning of different microdisks in a single mask process. Theoretical calculations demonstrate that this platform can deliver substantial performance improvements, including a >200x reduction in the lasing threshold, to biaxially strained germanium lasers for silicon-compatible optical interconnects.

title: Time-Periodic Solutions of Driven-Damped Trimer Granular Crystals
Abstract: This work investigates time-periodic structures of trimer granular crystals consisting of alternating chrome steel and tungsten carbide spherical particles with a spatial periodicity of three. The configuration at the left boundary is driven by a harmonic in-time actuation with a specific amplitude and frequency, while the right boundary is a fixed wall. Similar to the case of a dimer chain, the combination of dissipation, boundary driving, and intrinsic nonlinearity leads to complex dynamics. For fixed driving frequencies in each of the spectral gaps, the study finds that nonlinear surface modes and the states dictated by the linear drive collide in a saddle-node bifurcation as the driving amplitude increases. Beyond this bifurcation, the system's dynamics become chaotic. While the bifurcation structure is similar for solutions within the first and second gaps, those in the first gap appear less robust. A continuation in driving frequency reveals a complex bifurcation diagram involving an intricate set of loops of branches, especially within the spectral gap. The theoretical findings are qualitatively corroborated by experimental full-field visualization of the time-periodic structures. |||

title: Synthesis from Formal Partial Abstractions
Abstract:
Developing complex software systems is often expensive, time-consuming, and prone to errors. Model-driven development (MDD) promises to improve software productivity, timeliness, quality, and cost by transforming abstract application models into code-level implementations. However, building the modeling languages and translators required for software synthesis remains challenging. This challenge limits the applicability of MDD and hinders the reliability of MDD tools. This dissertation research aims to reduce the cost, expand the applicability, and improve the quality of model-driven development systems by embedding modeling languages within established formal languages and utilizing the analyzers associated with these languages for synthesis purposes. This approach reduces the need for hand-coding translators. Specifically, this dissertation explores the proposed approach using relational logic as expressed in Alloy as the general specification language and the Alloy Analyzer as the general-purpose analyzer. Consequently, synthesis is driven by finite-domain constraint satisfaction. A significant aspect of this work focuses on partial specifications of specific system aspects, such as application architectures and target platforms, and the synthesis of partial code bases from these specifications. This work contributes novel insights, methods, and tools for: (1) synthesizing architectural models from abstract application models; (2) synthesizing partial, platform-specific application frameworks from application architectures; and (3) synthesizing object-relational mapping tradeoff spaces and database schemas for database-backed object-oriented applications. ||| 
Phenotypes are the observable characteristics of an organism resulting from its interaction with the environment. Phenotypes associated with engineered and natural genetic variation are extensively documented using phenotype ontologies in model organisms, as are signs and symptoms of human Mendelian diseases in databases such as OMIM and Orphanet. Leveraging these resources, several computational methods have been developed for integrating and analyzing phenotype data to identify the genetic etiology of diseases or suggest potential interventions. A similar resource would be highly beneficial not only for rare and Mendelian diseases but also for common, complex, and infectious diseases. We employ a semantic text-mining approach to identify the phenotypes (signs and symptoms) associated with over 8,000 diseases. Our method demonstrates the generation of phenotypes that accurately identify known disease-associated genes in mice and humans with high precision. Utilizing a phenotypic similarity measure, we generate a human disease network where diseases sharing signs and symptoms cluster together. This network is then used to identify phenotypic disease modules. ||| 
The availability of geocoded health data and the inherent temporal structure of communicable diseases have sparked increased interest in statistical models and software for spatio-temporal data with epidemic characteristics. The open-source R package "surveillance" can handle various levels of aggregation at which infective events have been recorded: individual-level time-stamped geo-referenced data (case reports) in either continuous or discrete space, as well as counts aggregated by period and region. For each of these data types, the "surveillance" package implements tools for visualization, likelihood inference, and simulation from recently developed statistical regression frameworks capturing endemic and epidemic dynamics. This paper serves as a guide to the spatio-temporal modeling of epidemic phenomena, exemplified by analyses of public health surveillance data on measles and invasive meningococcal disease. ||| 
Engineers frequently encounter the challenge of assessing the lifetime of industrial components based on observed industrial feedback data. Typically, lifetime is modeled as a continuous random variable, such as exponentially or Weibull distributed. However, in certain cases, the characteristics of the equipment under investigation suggest the use of discrete probabilistic models. This is particularly relevant for equipment that operates only on cycles or on demand. In these instances, lifetime is measured in the number of cycles or demands before failure, theoretically making discrete models more appropriate. This article explores the practical interest for reliability engineers in using two popular discrete models: the Inverse Polya distribution (IPD), based on a Polya urn scheme, and the Weibull-1 (W1) model. The study demonstrates that, for various reasons, the practical application of both models should be restricted to specific industrial situations. Particularly, when there is no prior knowledge about the nature of aging, or data are heavily right-censored, these models may have limited utility compared to more flexible continuous lifetime models, such as the conventional Weibull distribution. Nevertheless, the intuitive meaning attributed to the IPD distribution favors its use by engineers in low (decelerated) aging scenarios. ||| 
While impurity is widely known to affect phase transitions, the atomistic mechanisms remain largely underexplored. We directly demonstrate at the atomic scale how impurity atoms induce the condensation of a representative electronic phase, charge density wave (CDW), using scanning tunneling microscopy. Oxygen impurity atoms on the self-assembled metallic atomic wire array on a silicon crystal condense CDW locally even above the transition temperature. More intriguingly, the CDW along the wires is induced not by a single atomic impurity but by the cooperative action of multiple impurities. First-principles calculations reveal the mechanism of this cooperation as the coherent superposition of the local lattice strain induced by impurities, highlighting the coupled electronic and lattice degrees of freedom for CDW. This newly discovered mechanism can be broadly applied to various important electronic orders coupled to the lattice, opening up the possibility of atomic-scale strain engineering. ||| 
We investigate the influence of ripple waves originating from electromechanical effects on spin relaxation caused by electromagnetic fields in armchair and zigzag graphene nanoribbons (GNRs). Utilizing analytical expressions supported by numerical simulations, we demonstrate the possibility of tuning the spin flip behaviors ON and OFF due to ripple waves in GNRs, potentially enabling applications in straintronic devices. This finding aligns with recent observations on the design of spintronic devices in III-V semiconductor quantum dots, where the sign change in the effective Landé g-factor can be engineered through the application of gate-controlled electric fields. Notably, we show that the tuning of spin extends to larger widths for armchair GNRs compared to zigzag GNRs. Additionally, we report that the relaxation rate diminishes as L^5. ||| 
Recently, x-ray illumination using synchrotron radiation has been employed to manipulate defects, stimulate self-organization, and probe their structure. This study explores a method of defect-engineering low-dimensional systems using focused laboratory-scale X-ray sources. We demonstrate an irreversible change in the conducting properties of the 2-dimensional electron gas at the interface between the complex oxide materials LaAlO3 and SrTiO3 by X-ray irradiation. The electrical resistance is monitored during exposure as the irradiated regions are driven into a high resistance state. Our findings suggest the need for caution regarding electronic structure modification in X-ray spectroscopic studies and highlight large-area defect manipulation and direct device patterning as potential new applications for focused laboratory X-ray sources. |||

Reverberation measurements have been widely used to estimate the size of the broad-line region (BLR) and the mass of the central black hole. However, reverberation mapping studies have primarily focused on radio-quiet sources where the contribution of the jet can be disregarded. In radio-loud AGN, jets and outflows may significantly influence the observed relationship between the ionizing continuum and the line emission. To investigate this relationship, we conducted a series of multiwavelength studies of radio-loud AGN, combining optical spectral line monitoring with regular Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) observations. Our results suggest that at least a portion of the broad-line emitting material may reside in a sub-relativistic outflow ionized by non-thermal continuum emission generated within the jet at significant distances (> 1pc) from the central engine of AGN. This finding could have substantial implications for black hole mass estimates based on measured widths of the broad emission lines and for the gamma-ray emission mechanisms. ||| 
This paper aims to provide preliminary insights for discussing the implications of the Hierarchy Theory of Evolution for the design and evolution of artificial systems and socio-technical organizations. To achieve this goal, we draw analogies between Leibniz's System, the socio-technical architecture known as Fractal Social Organization, resilience and related disciplines, and Hierarchy Theory. Through this process, we hope to offer elements for reflection and potentially enrich the discussion on these topics by incorporating considerations from related fields and disciplines, including computer science, management science, cybernetics, social systems, and general systems theory. ||| 
Data is poised to become one of the most valuable assets we possess. According to a study by McKinsey Global Institute, 43 trillion gigabytes of data will be generated by 2020. It is estimated that 2.3 trillion gigabytes of data are created daily, and most US companies store 100,000 gigabytes of data. Data is recorded, stored, and analyzed to enable the technologies and services upon which the world relies every day. This technology is becoming increasingly sophisticated, and we are on the verge of inhabiting a world of smart services or what is known as smart cities. This article provides an overview of this topic, highlighting its current state and forecasting its critical future roles. We will define big data analytics and smart cities and explore their potential contributions to transforming our way of life. Finally, we will discuss the potential downsides of these emerging technologies and how they could deceive us, violate our privacy, and potentially turn us into puppets or technology slaves. ||| 
Recent studies from social, biological, and engineering network systems have drawn attention to the dynamics of signed networks, where each link is associated with a positive or negative sign indicating trustful/mistrustful, activator/inhibitor, or secure/malicious interactions. This research examines asymptotic dynamical patterns that emerge among a set of nodes interacting in a dynamically evolving signed random network. Node interactions occur randomly on a sequence of deterministic signed graphs. Each node receives positive or negative recommendations from its neighbors based on the sign of the interaction arcs and updates its state accordingly. Recommendations along a positive arc follow the standard consensus update. Similar to the work of Altafini, negative recommendations utilize an update where the sign of the neighbor state is flipped. Nodes may assign different weights to positive and negative recommendations, and random processes are introduced to model the time-varying attention nodes pay to these recommendations. Conditions for almost sure convergence and divergence of the node states are established. We demonstrate that under this so-called state-flipping model, all links contribute to a consensus of the absolute values of the nodes, even under switching sign patterns and a dynamically changing environment. A no-survivor property is established, indicating that every node state diverges almost surely if the maximum network state diverges. ||| 
Traditional image processing is a field of science and technology developed to facilitate human-centered image management. However, today, with the overwhelming volume of visual data inundating our surroundings—driven by the explosive growth of image-capturing devices, the proliferation of Internet communication means, and video sharing services over the World Wide Web—human-centered handling of Big Data flows is no longer feasible. Therefore, it must be replaced with a machine (computer) supported counterpart. Naturally, such an artificial counterpart must be equipped with cognitive abilities typically characteristic of a human being. Indeed, in the past decade, a new computer design trend—Cognitive Computer development—has become increasingly visible. Cognitive image processing will undoubtedly be one of its primary functions. It is worth noting that this trend is a specific case of a more general movement—the transition from a "computational data-processing paradigm" to a "cognitive information-processing paradigm"—which is impacting many fields of science, technology, and engineering today. This transition is a welcome innovation, but its success is hindered by the lack of a clear distinction between the concepts of data and information. By elaborating on the case of cognitive image processing, this paper aims to clarify these critical research issues. ||| 
The first stage of the ATLAS Fast TracKer (FTK) is an ATCA-based input interface system, where hits from the entire silicon tracker are clustered and organized into overlapping eta-phi trigger towers before being transmitted to the tracking engines. Initially, FTK Input Mezzanine cards receive hit data and perform clustering to reduce data volume. Subsequently, the ATCA-based Data Formatter system organizes the trigger tower data, sharing data among boards over full mesh backplanes and optic fibers. This paper presents the board and system-level design concepts and implementation details, as well as operational experiences from the FTK full-chain testing. ||| 
We discuss methods for analyzing a quantum Gibbs family in the ultra-cold regime where the norm closure of the Gibbs family fails due to discontinuities in the maximum-entropy inference. The current discussion of maximum-entropy inference and irreducible correlation in the realm of quantum phase transitions serves as a primary motivation for this research. We extend a representation of the irreducible correlation from finite temperatures to absolute zero. ||| 
Many scientific-software projects test their codes inadequately, or not at all. Despite its well-known benefits, adopting routine testing is often challenging. Development teams may harbor doubts about establishing effective test procedures, writing test software, or managing the ever-growing complexity of test cases. They may need to run (and test) on restrictive High-Performance Computing (HPC) platforms. They almost certainly face time and budget pressures that can push testing to the bottom of their priorities. This paper introduces DDTS, a framework for building test suite applications designed to meet the requirements of scientific-software projects. DDTS aims to simplify the introduction of rigorous testing and alleviate the growing pains as needs mature. It decomposes the testing problem into practical, intuitive phases; makes configuration and extension easy; is portable and suitable for HPC platforms; and exploits parallelism. DDTS is currently utilized for automated regression and developer pre-commit testing for several scientific-software projects with diverse testing requirements. ||| 
Quantum fluctuations of the vacuum are both a surprising and fundamental phenomenon of nature. While understood as virtual photons fleeting into and out of existence, they still exert a very real impact, as exemplified in the Casimir effects and the lifetimes of atoms. Engineering vacuum fluctuations is therefore becoming increasingly crucial for emerging technologies. In this study, we shape vacuum fluctuations using a "mirror," creating regions in space where they are suppressed. As we effectively move an artificial atom in and out of these regions, measuring the atomic lifetime reveals the strength of the fluctuations. The weakest fluctuation strength we observe is 0.02 quanta, a factor of 50 lower than what would be expected without the mirror, demonstrating that we can effectively shield the atom from the vacuum. ||| 
An integrated coherent matter wave circuit is a single device, analogous to an integrated optical circuit, where coherent de Broglie waves are created and then launched into waveguides. These waveguides allow for switching, division, recombination, and detection of the waves as they propagate. Applications of such circuits include guided atom interferometers, atomtronic circuits, and precisely controlled delivery of atoms. This research presents experimental demonstrations of integrated circuits for guided coherent matter waves. The circuit elements are created using the painted potential technique, a form of time-averaged optical dipole potential where a rapidly-moving, tightly-focused laser beam exerts forces on atoms through their electric polarizability. The source of coherent matter waves is a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC). We launch BECs into painted waveguides that guide them around bends and form switches, phase-coherent beamsplitters, and closed circuits. These elements serve as the foundational building blocks for engineering arbitrarily complex matter wave circuitry. ||| 
We study a Wiener disorder problem involving the detection of the minimum of N change-points in N observation channels coupled by correlated noises. It is assumed that observations in each dimension may have different strengths and that the change-points might vary across channels. The goal is the quickest detection of the minimum of the N change-points. We adopt a min-max approach and consider an extended Lorden's criterion, which is minimized subject to a constraint on the mean time to the first false alarm. It is observed that under partial information about the post-change drifts and a general nonsingular stochastic correlation structure in the noises, the minimum of N cumulative sums (CUSUM) stopping rules is asymptotically optimal as the mean time to the first false alarm increases without bound. We further discuss applications of this result, emphasizing its implications for the efficiency of decentralized versus centralized systems of observations that arise in engineering. |||

title: Finite element model based on refined plate theories for laminated glass units

Nodal Lagrange multipliers ensure compatibility between layers. The model is discretized using bi-linear functions and solved by Newton's method with consistent linearization. Validation examples demonstrate the model's reliability and accuracy in reproducing laminated glass behavior. This represents an initial step toward a comprehensive, mechanics-based model for laminated glass systems, suitable for integration into common engineering finite element solvers.

title: Photonic chip based optical frequency comb using soliton induced Cherenkov radiation

This enables applications in coherent communications, broadband dual comb spectroscopy, and Raman spectral imaging, while significantly relaxing dispersion requirements for broadband microresonator frequency combs and paving the way for their generation in the visible and UV. title: Prognosis of Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Reconstruction: A Data Driven Approach

title: Cycling in stochastic general equilibrium

Empirical data from the United States (1960-2013) significantly exhibit similar cycles. The resemblance between cycles in general equilibrium and mixed strategy Nash equilibrium suggests the presence of dynamic fine structures accompanying equilibrium. Abstract: The Weaire-Thorpe (WT) model, a standard tool for analyzing three-dimensional (3D) silicon, has been applied to silicene, a 2D material with a buckled structure, to understand its electronic properties. In this work, we re-formulate the WT model using the overlapping molecular-orbital (MO) method, enabling the description of flat bands away from the electron-hole symmetric point. This approach reveals a significant difference between the 3D and 2D cases: while in 3D, dispersive bands with cones are sandwiched by doubly-degenerate flat bands, in 2D, they are sandwiched by triply-degenerate and non-degenerate (nearly) flat bands. Unlike existing shotgun proteomics search engines that calculate independent scores between an observed spectrum and each potential candidate peptide from the database, word lattices represent the set of candidate peptides in a single data structure, enabling shared computations among different candidates. This operation relies on the interference of the mode to be manipulated with an auxiliary single-photon state at a beam splitter, resulting in the entanglement of the two output modes. A conditional projective measurement onto a single photon at one output mode heralds the success of the process. This operation, which implements a measurement-induced nonlinearity, is capable of suppressing specific photon-number probability amplitudes of an arbitrary quantum state. To identify the key sources of experimental imperfection, we develop a model of the process and identify three primary contributions that significantly hinder its efficacy. The reconstructed tensor is compared with a model of the process, taking into account sources of experimental imperfection, with fidelity exceeding 0.95. The proposed system was tested on FERET, HP, and Bosphorus face databases and compared to conventional and state-of-the-art techniques. The recognition rates achieved using the proposed FVF approach for the FERET database were 99.78% compared to 79.60% and 68.80% for conventional gray-scale LBP and Principle Component Analysis (PCA) based face recognition techniques, respectively. ||| 
This study presents a method for gesture detection and localization based on multi-scale and multi-modal deep learning. Each visual modality captures spatial information at a particular spatial scale (e.g., motion of the upper body or hand), and the system operates at three temporal scales. The key to this technique is a training strategy that leverages: i) careful initialization of individual modalities; and ii) gradual fusion involving random dropping of separate channels (dubbed ModDrop) for learning cross-modality correlations while preserving the uniqueness of each modality-specific representation. Experiments were conducted on the ChaLearn 2014 Looking at People Challenge gesture recognition track, where the proposed system achieved first place out of 17 teams. Fusing multiple modalities across several spatial and temporal scales significantly increases recognition rates, allowing the model to compensate for errors in individual classifiers and noise in separate channels. The ModDrop training technique ensures robustness of the classifier to missing signals in one or more channels, enabling meaningful predictions from any number of available modalities. Additionally, the paper demonstrates the applicability of the proposed fusion scheme to modalities of arbitrary nature through experiments on the same dataset augmented with audio. ||| 
This paper proposes a deep learning method for single image super-resolution (SR) that directly learns an end-to-end mapping between low/high-resolution images. The mapping is represented as a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) that takes the low-resolution image as input and outputs the high-resolution counterpart. The study highlights the potential of traditional sparse-coding-based SR methods as deep convolutional networks. However, unlike traditional methods that handle each component separately, the proposed method jointly optimizes all layers. The deep CNN has a lightweight structure while delivering state-of-the-art restoration quality and fast processing speeds for practical online usage. The paper explores different network structures and parameter settings to achieve trade-offs between performance and speed. Furthermore, the network is extended to handle three color channels simultaneously, resulting in improved overall reconstruction quality. ||| 
Dictionary learning algorithms or supervised deep convolution networks have significantly enhanced the efficiency of predefined feature representations, such as SIFT. This study introduces a deep scattering convolution network, utilizing predefined wavelet filters across spatial and angular variables. This representation significantly improves upon results previously obtained with predefined features on object image databases such as Caltech and CIFAR. The resulting accuracy is comparable to results achieved with unsupervised deep learning and dictionary-based representations. This finding suggests that refining image representations using geometric priors is a promising avenue for improving image classification and understanding. ||| 
The main contribution of this paper is an iterative procedure for tubular structure segmentation of 2D images, combining tight frame Curvelet transforms with a SURE technique thresholding based on the principle of minimizing Stein Unbiased Risk Estimate for denoising. This algorithm builds upon the TFA proposal presented in [1, 9], incorporating eigenvectors of the image Hessian matrix to enhance the iterative process for segmenting unclear and narrow vessels and bridging gaps between detected vessel fragments. Experimental results showcase the effectiveness of the proposed model. ||| 
The input numerical aperture (NA) of multimode fiber (MMF) can be effectively increased by placing turbid media at the input end of the MMF, potentially enabling high-resolution imaging through MMF. While the input NA is increased, the number of propagation modes in the MMF, and thus the output NA, remains the same. This makes the image reconstruction process underdetermined, potentially limiting image reconstruction quality. This paper focuses on improving the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of image reconstruction in imaging through MMF. The study observes that turbid media placed at the input of the MMF transforms incoming waves into a more suitable format for information transmission and extraction, termed holistic random (HR) encoding. By exploiting HR encoding, the SNR of image reconstruction is significantly enhanced. For efficient utilization of HR encoding, sparse representation (SR), a relatively new signal reconstruction framework, is employed when provided with a HR encoded signal. This study demonstrates, for the first time to our knowledge, the benefits of utilizing HR encoding of turbid media for recovery in optically underdetermined systems where the output NA is smaller than the input NA in imaging through MMF. ||| 
This study introduces a simple modification of local image descriptors, such as SIFT, based on pooling gradient orientations across different domain sizes, in addition to spatial locations. This resulting descriptor, dubbed DSP-SIFT, outperforms other methods in wide-baseline matching benchmarks, including those based on convolutional neural networks, despite having the same dimension as SIFT and requiring no training. ||| 
Artificial neural networks are powerful pattern classifiers; however, they have been surpassed in accuracy by methods such as support vector machines and random forests, which are also easier to use and faster to train. Backpropagation, used to train artificial neural networks, suffers from the herd effect problem, leading to long training times and limited classification accuracy. This study utilizes disjunctive normal form and approximates boolean conjunction operations with products to construct a novel network architecture. The proposed model can be trained by minimizing an error function and allows for effective and intuitive initialization, addressing the herd-effect problem associated with backpropagation. This leads to state-of-the-art classification accuracy and fast training times. Additionally, the model can be jointly optimized with convolutional features in a unified structure, achieving state-of-the-art results on computer vision problems with rapid convergence rates. A GPU implementation of LDNN with optional convolutional features is also available. ||| 
Accurate information about a camera's location and orientation in mobile devices is crucial for utilizing location-based services (LBS). Most mobile devices rely on GPS data, which is prone to inaccuracies due to imperfections in the quality of satellite signals. This shortcoming has spurred research into improving localization accuracy. Since mobile devices have cameras, a significant focus of this research has been to acquire local scenes and apply image retrieval techniques by querying a GPS-tagged image database for the best match to the captured scene. However, these techniques are computationally demanding and unsuitable for real-time applications, such as assistive technology for navigation by the blind and visually impaired. To address this challenge, this study investigates the use of inertial sensors to aid in image-retrieval-based approaches. Using information from sources other than images, such as data from the GPS module and orientation sensors (accelerometer and gyro), the study aims to limit the size of the image set for searching the best match. Specifically, data from orientation sensors along with Dilution of Precision (DOP) from GPS are used to determine the angle of view and estimate position. The study presents an analysis of the reduction in the image set size for the search and simulations to demonstrate the effectiveness of a fast implementation, achieving 98% Estimated Position Error. ||| 
Generating a novel textual description of an image is an interesting problem that connects computer vision and natural language processing. This paper presents a simple model capable of generating descriptive sentences from a given image. The model strongly emphasizes the syntax of the descriptions. It trains a purely bilinear model that learns a metric between an image representation (generated from a previously trained Convolutional Neural Network) and phrases used to describe them. The system can then infer phrases from a given image sample. Based on caption syntax statistics, a simple language model is proposed that can generate relevant descriptions for a given test image using the inferred phrases. This approach, considerably simpler than state-of-the-art models, achieves comparable results on the recently released Microsoft COCO dataset. ||| 
Data vectors are obtained from multiple domains, including feature vectors of images or vector representations of words. Domains may have varying numbers of data vectors with different dimensions. These data vectors from multiple domains are projected to a common space using linear transformations to search for closely related vectors across domains. The goal is to find projection matrices that minimize distances between closely related data vectors. This formulation of cross-domain matching is considered an extension of spectral graph embedding to a multi-domain setting and includes several multivariate analysis methods of statistics, such as multiset canonical correlation analysis, correspondence analysis, and principal component analysis. Similar approaches are highly popular in pattern recognition and vision. Instead of proposing a novel method, this paper introduces a straightforward idea of coding data vectors to explain the aforementioned approaches. A data vector is concatenated with zero vectors from all other domains to create an augmented vector. Cross-domain matching is achieved by applying the single-domain version of spectral graph embedding to these augmented vectors from all domains. An interesting connection to the classical associative memory model of neural networks is also discussed by noticing a coding for association. A cross-validation method for selecting the dimension of the common space and a regularization parameter will be discussed in an illustrative numerical example. ||| 
The need for accurate and autonomous spectral classification methods in astrophysics is significant. This thesis focuses on training a convolutional neural network (ConvNet) to recognize an object class (quasar, star, or galaxy) from one-dimensional spectra. The author developed several scripts and C programs for dataset preparation, preprocessing, and postprocessing of the data. The EBLearn library (developed by Pierre Sermanet and Yann LeCun) was used to create ConvNets. Application to a dataset of over 60,000 spectra yielded a success rate of nearly 95%. This thesis conclusively proves the immense potential of convolutional neural networks and deep learning methods in astrophysics. |||
