title: Statistical models and regularization strategies in statistical image reconstruction of low-dose X-ray CT: a survey
Abstract: Statistical image reconstruction (SIR) methods have shown promise in significantly improving the image quality of low-dose X-ray computed tomography (CT) compared to the conventional filtered back-projection (FBP) method for various clinical applications. According to maximum a posterior (MAP) estimation, SIR methods are typically formulated using an objective function composed of two terms: (1) a data-fidelity (or equivalently, data-fitting or data-mismatch) term modeling the statistics of projection measurements, and (2) a regularization (or equivalently, prior or penalty) term reflecting prior knowledge or expectations about the characteristics of the image to be reconstructed. Existing SIR methods for low-dose CT can be categorized into two groups: (1) methods utilizing calibrated transmitted photon counts (before log-transform) with a penalized maximum likelihood (pML) criterion, and (2) methods employing calibrated line-integrals (after log-transform) with a penalized weighted least-squares (PWLS) criterion. Accurate statistical modeling of projection measurements is essential for SIR, while the regularization term in the objective function plays a pivotal role in successful image reconstruction. This paper provides a comprehensive review of various statistical models for CT projection measurements and different regularization strategies incorporating prior knowledge or anticipated properties of the image to be reconstructed. These elements collectively form the objective function of SIR methods for low-dose X-ray CT.

title: Convolutional Neural Networks at Constrained Time Cost
Abstract: While recent advancements in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have significantly improved image recognition accuracy, the models are becoming increasingly complex and time-consuming.  Real-world applications in industrial and commercial settings often necessitate adherence to constrained time budgets. This paper investigates the accuracy of CNNs under such time constraints.  Under these constraints, the design of network architectures must exhibit trade-offs among factors such as depth, number of filters, filter sizes, and so on.  Through a series of controlled comparisons, we progressively modify a baseline model while preserving its time complexity. This approach is also helpful in understanding the relative importance of different factors in network design.  We present an architecture that achieves highly competitive accuracy on the ImageNet dataset (11.8% top-5 error, 10-view test) while being 20% faster than "AlexNet" (16.0% top-5 error, 10-view test).

title: Fisher Kernel for Deep Neural Activations
Abstract: Compared to image representations based on low-level local descriptors, deep neural activations from Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) offer richer mid-level representations but exhibit poorer geometric invariance properties. This paper presents a straightforward framework for improving image representation by combining these two approaches. To leverage the strengths of both representations, we propose an efficient method for extracting a significant amount of multi-scale dense local activations from a pre-trained CNN. We then aggregate these activations using the Fisher kernel framework, which has been modified with a simple scale-wise normalization essential for adaptation to CNN activations. Replacing the direct use of a single activation vector with our representation yields substantial performance improvements: +17.76 (Accuracy) on MIT Indoor 67 and +7.18 (mAP) on PASCAL VOC 2007. The results suggest that our proposal can serve as a primary image representation for enhanced performance in visual recognition tasks.

title: On using the Microsoft Kinect$^{\rm TM}$ sensors in the analysis of human motion
Abstract: This paper aims to provide the theoretical foundation necessary for investigating the use of Microsoft Kinect$^{\\rm TM}$ (`Kinect', for brevity) sensors (original and upgraded) in the analysis of human motion. Our methodology is designed to be readily adaptable for comparative studies of other systems used in capturing human motion data. Our future plans include applying this methodology to two scenarios: first, in a comparative study of the performance of the two Kinect sensors; second, in validating them through comparisons with a marker-based system (MBS). A key feature of our approach is the transformation of MBS output into Kinect-output format, enabling the analysis of measurements from different systems using the same software application, specifically the one we use to analyze Kinect-captured data. An example of such a transformation, for a popular marker-placement scheme (`Plug-in Gait'), is detailed. We propose assessing the similarity of the output from different systems by comparing a series of waveforms, representing variations in gait cycle quantities commonly used in human motion modeling. Data acquisition may involve commercially-available treadmills with various velocity settings: for instance, walking motion data may be collected at $5$ km/h, running motion data at $8$ and $11$ km/h. We recommend focusing on systematic effects associated with the subject's knee and lower leg, as well as the ability of Kinect sensors to reliably capture details in the asymmetry of motion for the left and right parts of the human body. Previous versions of this study have been withdrawn due to the use of a non-representative database.

title: Metric Learning Driven Multi-Task Structured Output Optimization for Robust Keypoint Tracking
Abstract: As a significant and challenging problem in computer vision and graphics, keypoint-based object tracking is typically formulated within a spatio-temporal statistical learning framework. However, most existing keypoint trackers struggle to effectively model and balance the following three aspects simultaneously: temporal model coherence across frames, spatial model consistency within frames, and discriminative feature construction. To address this issue, we propose a robust keypoint tracker based on spatio-temporal multi-task structured output optimization driven by discriminative metric learning. This approach achieves temporal model coherence through multi-task structured keypoint model learning across multiple adjacent frames, while spatial model consistency is modeled by solving a geometric verification-based structured learning problem. Discriminative feature construction is enabled by metric learning to ensure intra-class compactness and inter-class separability. Finally, these three modules are jointly optimized in a unified learning scheme. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our tracker.

title: Parsing Occluded People by Flexible Compositions
Abstract: This paper presents an approach to parsing humans even in the presence of significant occlusion. We model humans using a graphical model with a tree structure, building on recent work [32, 6], and exploit the connectivity prior that, even with occlusion, the visible nodes form a connected subtree of the graphical model. We refer to each connected subtree as a flexible composition of object parts. This involves a novel method for learning occlusion cues. During inference, we need to search over a mixture of different flexible models. By leveraging part sharing, we demonstrate that this inference can be performed extremely efficiently, requiring only twice the computations needed to search for the entire object (i.e., without modeling occlusion). We evaluate our model on the standard "We Are Family" Stickmen dataset and achieve significant performance improvements over the best alternative algorithms.

title: The myth of the Digital Earth between fragmentation and wholeness
Abstract: Daring predictions about the proximate future can establish shared discursive frameworks, mobilize capital, and steer complex processes. Among the prophetic visions that encouraged and accompanied the development of new communication technologies was the "Digital Earth," described in a 1998 speech by Al Gore as a high-resolution representation of the planet to share and analyze detailed information about its state. This article traces a genealogy of the Digital Earth as a techno-scientific myth, placing it within a constellation of media futures, arguing that a common subtext of these visions consists of a dream of wholeness, a yearning to overcome perceived fragmentation among humans and between humans and the Earth.

title: Textural Approach for Mass Abnormality Segmentation in Mammographic Images
Abstract: Mass abnormality segmentation is a crucial step in the medical diagnostic process and is attracting increasing interest from numerous research groups. Currently, most works in this area have utilized the Gray Level Co-occurrence Matrix (GLCM) as texture features within a region-based approach. These features are either used in a preceding phase for the segmentation stage or as inputs for the classification stage. The work discussed in this paper aims to experiment with the GLCM method within a contour-based approach. Additionally, we apply the proposed approach to various tissue densities to obtain more significant results. To this end, we explore challenging breast images from the BIRADS medical database. Our initial experiments have yielded promising results in terms of mass segmentation methods based on edges. This paper first discusses the main achievements in this field. Sections 2 and 3 present materials and our methodology. The key results are presented and evaluated before concluding our paper.

title: Event Retrieval Using Motion Barcodes
Abstract: We introduce a simple yet effective method for retrieving videos showcasing a specific event, even when the videos were captured from significantly different viewpoints. Appearance-based methods fail in such scenarios as appearances change dramatically with large viewpoint variations. Our method relies on a pixel-based feature, "motion barcode," which records the presence or absence of motion as a function of time. While appearance, motion magnitude, and motion direction can vary considerably between disparate viewpoints, the existence of motion remains viewpoint invariant. Based on the motion barcode, a similarity measure for videos capturing the same event from drastically different viewpoints is developed. This measure proves robust to occlusions common under diverse viewpoints and can be computed efficiently. Event retrieval is demonstrated using challenging videos captured by stationary and handheld cameras.

title: Memory Bounded Deep Convolutional Networks
Abstract: This work investigates the use of sparsity-inducing regularizers during the training of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). These regularizers encourage fewer connections in convolution and fully connected layers to take on non-zero values, effectively resulting in sparse connectivity between hidden units in the deep network. This reduction in connectivity, in turn, minimizes memory and runtime costs associated with deploying the learned CNNs. We demonstrate that training with such regularization can still be performed using stochastic gradient descent, indicating its easy integration into existing codebases.  Experimental evaluation of our approach on MNIST, CIFAR, and ImageNet datasets reveals that our regularizers can lead to dramatic reductions in memory requirements. For example, when applied to AlexNet, our method can reduce memory consumption by a factor of four with minimal loss in accuracy.

title: Scalable, High-Quality Object Detection
Abstract: Current high-quality object detection approaches utilize a scheme of salience-based object proposal methods followed by post-classification using deep convolutional features. This has spurred recent research on improving object proposal methods. However, domain-agnostic proposal generation has the principal drawback of producing unranked or weakly ranked proposals, making it challenging to trade off quality for running time. This raises the fundamental question of whether high-quality proposal generation necessitates careful engineering or can be derived solely from data. We demonstrate that learning-based proposal methods can effectively match the performance of hand-engineered methods while enabling highly efficient runtime-quality trade-offs. Using the multi-scale convolutional MultiBox (MSC-MultiBox) approach, we significantly advance the state-of-the-art on the ILSVRC 2014 detection challenge dataset, achieving $0.5$ mAP for a single model and $0.52$ mAP for an ensemble of two models. MSC-Multibox notably improves proposal quality over its predecessor MultiBox method: AP increases from $0.42$ to $0.53$ for the ILSVRC detection challenge. Finally, we demonstrate improved bounding-box recall compared to Multiscale Combinatorial Grouping with fewer proposals on the Microsoft-COCO dataset.

title: Convolutional Feature Masking for Joint Object and Stuff Segmentation
Abstract: The field of semantic segmentation has witnessed significant progress thanks to the powerful features learned by convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Current leading approaches for semantic segmentation leverage shape information by extracting CNN features from masked image regions. This strategy introduces artificial boundaries on the images, potentially impacting the quality of the extracted features. Moreover, operations in the raw image domain require the computation of thousands of networks on a single image, making it time-consuming. This paper proposes exploiting shape information by masking convolutional features. Segmentation proposals (e.g., super-pixels) are treated as masks applied to the convolutional feature maps. CNN features of segments are directly masked out from these maps and used to train classifiers for recognition. We further introduce a joint method to handle objects and "stuff" (e.g., grass, sky, water) within the same framework. State-of-the-art results are demonstrated on benchmarks of PASCAL VOC and new PASCAL-CONTEXT, showcasing compelling computational speed.

title: Deeply learned face representations are sparse, selective, and robust
Abstract: This paper introduces a high-performance deep convolutional network (DeepID2+) for face recognition. It is trained with the identification-verification supervisory signal. By increasing the dimensionality of hidden representations and adding supervision to early convolutional layers, DeepID2+ achieves new state-of-the-art performance on the LFW and YouTube Faces benchmarks. Through empirical studies, we have identified three key properties of its deep neural activations that are crucial for achieving high performance: sparsity, selectiveness, and robustness. (1) We observe that neural activations are moderately sparse. Moderate sparsity maximizes the discriminative power of the deep net and the distance between images. Surprisingly, DeepID2+ maintains high recognition accuracy even after binarizing neural responses. (2) Neurons in higher layers exhibit high selectivity for identities and identity-related attributes. We can identify distinct subsets of neurons that are either constantly excited or inhibited when different identities or attributes are present. Although DeepID2+ is not explicitly trained to distinguish attributes, it implicitly learns such high-level concepts. (3) DeepID2+ demonstrates significantly improved robustness to occlusions, despite occlusion patterns not being included in the training set.

title: Colorisation et texturation temps réel d'environnements urbains par système mobile avec scanner laser et caméra fish-eye
Abstract: This paper presents a real-time mobile mapping system mounted on a vehicle. The terrestrial acquisition system is based on a geolocation system and two sensors: a laser scanner and a camera equipped with a fish-eye lens. We produce 3D colored point clouds and textured models of the environment. Once the system is calibrated, data acquisition and processing occur "on the way." This article primarily focuses on our methods for point cloud colorization, triangulation, and texture mapping.

title: Simple Two-Dimensional Object Tracking based on a Graph Algorithm
Abstract: The visual observation and tracking of cells and other micrometer-sized objects have numerous biomedical applications. Automating these tasks using computer methods aids in evaluating such measurements. This work presents a general-purpose algorithm that excels at evaluating deterministic behavior of micrometer-sized objects. Our specific application is the tracking of fast-moving objects over large distances along deterministic trajectories in microscopic videos. This allows us to determine characteristic properties of these objects. For this purpose, we employ a set of basic algorithms, including blob recognition, feature-based shape recognition, and a graph algorithm, and combine them in a novel way. An evaluation of the algorithm's performance shows high accuracy in both object recognition and complete trajectory recognition. Furthermore, a direct comparison with a similar algorithm reveals superior recognition rates.

title: Gradient Boundary Histograms for Action Recognition
Abstract: This paper introduces a highly efficient local spatiotemporal descriptor called gradient boundary histograms (GBH). The proposed GBH descriptor is built upon simple spatiotemporal gradients, which are computationally fast. We demonstrate that it can better represent local structure and motion compared to other gradient-based descriptors and significantly outperforms them on large realistic datasets. A comprehensive evaluation shows that recognition accuracy is preserved while spatial resolution is significantly reduced, resulting in both high efficiency and low memory usage.
label: AI

title: Detector Discovery in the Wild: Joint Multiple Instance and Representation Learning
Abstract: We propose a novel method for detector learning that leverages joint training on both weak and strong labels, and transfers learned perceptual representations from strongly-labeled auxiliary tasks. Existing methods for weak-label learning often train detector models independently using latent variable optimization, but fail to share deep representation knowledge across classes and usually require strong initialization. Other methods transfer deep representations from domains with strong labels to those with only weak labels, but they do not optimize over individual latent boxes and thus may miss specific salient structures for a particular category. Our model combines the strengths of these approaches by simultaneously training a representation and detectors for categories with either weak or strong labels present. We introduce a novel formulation of a joint multiple instance learning method that incorporates examples from classification-style data when available, and also performs domain transfer learning to improve the underlying detector representation. Our model surpasses existing methods on ImageNet-200 detection with weak labels.

title: DeepEdge: A Multi-Scale Bifurcated Deep Network for Top-Down Contour Detection
Abstract: Contour detection is a fundamental component in many image segmentation and object detection systems. Most existing methods rely on low-level features such as texture or saliency to detect contours and then use them as cues for a higher-level task such as object detection. However, we argue that recognizing objects and predicting contours are two mutually related tasks. Contrary to traditional approaches, we demonstrate that we can invert the commonly established pipeline: instead of detecting contours with low-level cues for a higher-level recognition task, we exploit object-related features as high-level cues for contour detection. We achieve this goal through a multi-scale deep network consisting of five convolutional layers and a bifurcated fully-connected sub-network. The section from the input layer to the fifth convolutional layer is fixed and directly lifted from a pre-trained network optimized over a large-scale object classification task. This section of the network is applied to four different scales of the image input. These four parallel and identical streams are then connected to a bifurcated sub-network comprising two independently-trained branches. One branch learns to predict the contour likelihood (with a classification objective), while the other branch is trained to learn the fraction of human labelers agreeing about the contour presence at a given point (with a regression criterion). Our multi-scale deep learning approach achieves state-of-the-art results in contour detection without any feature engineering.

title: Covariance estimation using conjugate gradient for 3D classification in Cryo-EM
Abstract: Classifying structural variability in noisy projections of biological macromolecules is a crucial challenge in Cryo-EM. In this work, we build upon a previous method for estimating the covariance matrix of the three-dimensional structure present in the molecules being imaged. Our proposed method allows for the incorporation of contrast transfer function and non-uniform distribution of viewing angles, making it more suitable for real-world data. We evaluate its performance on both a synthetic dataset and an experimental dataset obtained by imaging a 70S ribosome complex.

title: Semantic HMC for Big Data Analysis
Abstract: Analyzing Big Data can help corporations improve their efficiency. In this work, we present a new vision to derive value from Big Data using a Semantic Hierarchical Multi-label Classification called Semantic HMC based on a non-supervised Ontology learning process. We also propose a Semantic HMC process using scalable Machine-Learning techniques and Rule-based reasoning.

title: Hashing on Nonlinear Manifolds
Abstract: Learning-based hashing methods have attracted considerable attention due to their ability to greatly increase the scale at which existing algorithms can operate. Most of these methods are designed to generate binary codes preserving the Euclidean similarity in the original space. Manifold learning techniques, in contrast, are better able to model the intrinsic structure embedded in the original high-dimensional data. However, the complexities of these models and the problems with out-of-sample data have previously rendered them unsuitable for application to large-scale embedding. This work addresses how to learn compact binary embeddings on their intrinsic manifolds. To address the above-mentioned difficulties, we propose an efficient, inductive solution to the out-of-sample data problem, and a process by which non-parametric manifold learning can be used as the basis of a hashing method. Our approach enables the development of a range of new hashing techniques that exploit the flexibility of the wide variety of manifold learning approaches available. We demonstrate that hashing based on t-SNE outperforms state-of-the-art hashing methods on large-scale benchmark datasets and is very effective for image classification with very short code lengths. Our proposed hashing framework can be easily improved, for example, by minimizing the quantization error with learned orthogonal rotations. Additionally, we develop a supervised inductive manifold hashing framework by incorporating label information, which significantly enhances the semantic retrieval performance.

title: Analytical Comparison of Noise Reduction Filters for Image Restoration Using SNR Estimation
Abstract: Noise removal from images is a crucial aspect of image restoration, where we aim to reconstruct or recover an image that has been degraded by using prior knowledge of the degradation phenomenon. Noises present in images can be of various types with their characteristic Probability Distribution Functions (PDF). Noise removal techniques depend on the type of noise present in the image rather than on the image itself. This paper explores the effects of applying noise reduction filters having similar properties on noisy images with an emphasis on Signal-to-Noise-Ratio (SNR) value estimation for comparing the results.
label: AI

title: Fast Steerable Principal Component Analysis
Abstract: Cryo-electron microscopy often requires the analysis of hundreds of thousands of 2D images, each as large as a few hundred pixels in each direction. We introduce an algorithm that efficiently and accurately performs principal component analysis (PCA) for a large set of two-dimensional images, including their uniform rotations in the plane and reflections. For a dataset consisting of $n$ images of size $L \\times L$ pixels, the computational complexity of our algorithm is $O(nL^3 + L^4)$, whereas existing algorithms take $O(nL^4)$. The new algorithm efficiently computes the expansion coefficients of the images in a Fourier-Bessel basis using the non-uniform fast Fourier transform. We compare the accuracy and efficiency of the new algorithm with traditional PCA and existing algorithms for steerable PCA.

title: Feedforward semantic segmentation with zoom-out features
Abstract: We present a purely feed-forward architecture for semantic segmentation. We map small image elements (superpixels) to rich feature representations extracted from a sequence of nested regions of increasing extent. These regions are obtained by "zooming out" from the superpixel all the way to scene-level resolution. This approach leverages statistical structure in both the image and label space without setting up explicit structured prediction mechanisms, thus avoiding complex and expensive inference. Instead, superpixels are classified by a feedforward multilayer network. Our architecture achieves new state-of-the-art performance in semantic segmentation, obtaining 64.4% average accuracy on the PASCAL VOC 2012 test set.

title: Learning Spatiotemporal Features with 3D Convolutional Networks
Abstract: We propose a simple yet effective approach for spatiotemporal feature learning using deep 3-dimensional convolutional networks (3D ConvNets) trained on a large-scale supervised video dataset. Our findings are three-fold: 1) 3D ConvNets are more suitable for spatiotemporal feature learning compared to 2D ConvNets; 2) A homogeneous architecture with small 3x3x3 convolution kernels in all layers is among the best performing architectures for 3D ConvNets; and 3) Our learned features, namely C3D (Convolutional 3D), with a simple linear classifier outperform state-of-the-art methods on 4 different benchmarks and are comparable with current best methods on the other 2 benchmarks. Additionally, the features are compact: achieving 52.8% accuracy on the UCF101 dataset with only 10 dimensions, and also very efficient to compute due to the fast inference of ConvNets. Finally, they are conceptually very simple and easy to train and use.

title: Fast Sublinear Sparse Representation using Shallow Tree Matching Pursuit
Abstract: Sparse approximations using highly over-complete dictionaries are a state-of-the-art tool for many imaging applications, including denoising, super-resolution, compressive sensing, light-field analysis, and object recognition. Unfortunately, the applicability of such methods is severely hampered by the computational burden of sparse approximation: these algorithms are linear or super-linear in both the data dimensionality and size of the dictionary. We propose a framework for learning the hierarchical structure of over-complete dictionaries that enables fast computation of sparse representations. Our method builds on tree-based strategies for nearest neighbor matching and presents domain-specific enhancements that are highly efficient for the analysis of image patches. Contrary to most popular methods for building spatial data structures, our methods rely on shallow, balanced trees with relatively few layers. We show an extensive array of experiments on several applications such as image denoising/superresolution, compressive video/light-field sensing, where we practically achieve 100-1000x speedup (with a less than 1dB loss in accuracy).

title: Material Recognition in the Wild with the Materials in Context Database
Abstract: Recognizing materials in real-world images is a challenging task. Real-world materials have rich surface texture, geometry, lighting conditions, and clutter, which combine to make the problem particularly difficult. In this paper, we introduce a new, large-scale, open dataset of materials in the wild, the Materials in Context Database (MINC), and combine this dataset with deep learning to achieve material recognition and segmentation of images in the wild. MINC is an order of magnitude larger than previous material databases, while being more diverse and well-sampled across its 23 categories. Using MINC, we train convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for two tasks: classifying materials from patches and simultaneous material recognition and segmentation in full images. For patch-based classification on MINC, we found that the best performing CNN architectures can achieve 85.2% mean class accuracy. We convert these trained CNN classifiers into an efficient fully convolutional framework combined with a fully connected conditional random field (CRF) to predict the material at every pixel in an image, achieving 73.1% mean class accuracy. Our experiments demonstrate that having a large, well-sampled dataset such as MINC is crucial for real-world material recognition and segmentation.

title: Classification and Reconstruction of High-Dimensional Signals from Low-Dimensional Features in the Presence of Side Information
Abstract: This paper characterizes fundamental limits on the classification and reconstruction of high-dimensional signals from low-dimensional features, in the presence of side information. We consider a scenario where a decoder has access to both linear features of the signal of interest and linear features of the side information signal; while the side information may be in a compressed form, the objective is recovery or classification of the primary signal, not the side information. The signal of interest and the side information are each assumed to have (distinct) latent discrete labels; conditioned on these two labels, the signal of interest and side information are drawn from a multivariate Gaussian distribution. With joint probabilities on the latent labels, the overall signal-(side information) representation is defined by a Gaussian mixture model. We then provide sharp sufficient and/or necessary conditions for these quantities to approach zero when the covariance matrices of the Gaussians are nearly low-rank. These conditions, reminiscent of the well-known Slepian-Wolf and Wyner-Ziv conditions, are a function of the number of linear features extracted from the signal of interest, the number of linear features extracted from the side information signal, and the geometry of these signals and their interplay. Moreover, assuming that the signal of interest and the side information obey such an approximately low-rank model, we derive expansions of the reconstruction error as a function of the deviation from an exactly low-rank model; such expansions also allow identification of operational regimes where the impact of side information on signal reconstruction is most relevant. Our framework, which offers a principled mechanism to integrate side information in high-dimensional data problems, is also tested in the context of imaging applications.

title: Orthogonal Matrix Retrieval in Cryo-Electron Microscopy
Abstract: In single particle reconstruction (SPR) from cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), the 3D structure of a molecule needs to be determined from its 2D projection images taken at unknown viewing directions. Zvi Kam showed already in 1980 that the autocorrelation function of the 3D molecule over the rotation group SO(3) can be estimated from 2D projection images whose viewing directions are uniformly distributed over the sphere. The autocorrelation function determines the expansion coefficients of the 3D molecule in spherical harmonics up to an orthogonal matrix of size $(2l+1)\\times (2l+1)$ for each $l=0,1,2,...$. In this paper, we show how techniques for solving the phase retrieval problem in X-ray crystallography can be modified for the cryo-EM setup for retrieving the missing orthogonal matrices. Specifically, we present two new approaches that we term Orthogonal Extension and Orthogonal Replacement, in which the main algorithmic components are the singular value decomposition and semidefinite programming. We demonstrate the utility of these approaches through numerical experiments on simulated data.

title: Recovering Spatiotemporal Correspondence between Deformable Objects by Exploiting Consistent Foreground Motion in Video
Abstract: Given unstructured videos of deformable objects, we automatically recover spatiotemporal correspondences to map one object to another (such as animals in the wild). While traditional methods based on appearance fail in such challenging conditions, we exploit consistency in object motion between instances. Our approach discovers pairs of short video intervals where the object moves in a consistent manner and uses these candidates as seeds for spatial alignment. We model the spatial correspondence between the point trajectories on the object in one interval to those in the other using a time-varying Thin Plate Spline deformation model. On a large dataset of tiger and horse videos, our method automatically aligns thousands of pairs of frames to a high accuracy and outperforms the popular SIFT Flow algorithm.
label: AI

title: Fuzzy human motion analysis: A review
Abstract: Human Motion Analysis (HMA) is currently one of the most popularly active research domains, driven by a number of real-world applications such as video surveillance, sports analysis, healthcare monitoring, and so on. However, most of these real-world applications face high levels of uncertainties that can affect their operations. Hence, fuzzy set theory has been applied and showed great success in the recent past. In this paper, we aim to review the fuzzy set-oriented approaches for HMA, individuating how the fuzzy set may improve the HMA, envisaging and delineating the future perspectives. To the best of our knowledge, there is not found a single survey in the current literature that has discussed and reviewed fuzzy approaches towards the HMA. For ease of understanding, we conceptually classify human motion into three broad levels: Low-Level (LoL), Mid-Level (MiL), and High-Level (HiL) HMA.

title: Approximate MAP Estimation for Pairwise Potentials via Baker's Technique
Abstract: The theoretical models providing mathematical abstractions for several significant optimization problems in machine learning, combinatorial optimization, computer vision, and statistical physics have intrinsic similarities. We propose a unified framework to model these computation tasks where the structures of these optimization problems are encoded by functions attached on the vertices and edges of a graph. We show that computing MAX 2-CSP admits polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) on planar graphs, graphs with bounded local treewidth, $H$-minor-free graphs, geometric graphs with bounded density, and graphs embeddable with bounded number of crossings per edge. This implies computing MAX-CUT, MAX-DICUT, and MAX $k$-CUT admits PTASs on all these classes of graphs. Our method also gives the first PTAS for computing the ground state of the ferromagnetic Edwards-Anderson model without external magnetic field on $d$-dimensional lattice graphs. These results are widely applicable in vision, graphics, and machine learning.

title: Untangling Local and Global Deformations in Deep Convolutional Networks for Image Classification and Sliding Window Detection
Abstract: Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) commonly use generic `max-pooling' (MP) layers to extract deformation-invariant features, but we argue in favor of a more refined treatment. First, we introduce epitomic convolution as a building block alternative to the common convolution-MP cascade of DCNNs; while having identical complexity to MP, Epitomic Convolution allows for parameter sharing across different filters, resulting in faster convergence and better generalization. Second, we introduce a Multiple Instance Learning approach to explicitly accommodate global translation and scaling when training a DCNN exclusively with class labels. For this, we rely on a `patchwork' data structure that efficiently lays out all image scales and positions as candidates to a DCNN. Factoring global and local deformations allows a DCNN to `focus its resources' on the treatment of non-rigid deformations and yields a substantial classification accuracy improvement. Third, further pursuing this idea, we develop an efficient DCNN sliding window object detector that employs explicit search over position, scale, and aspect ratio. We provide competitive image classification and localization results on the ImageNet dataset and object detection results on the Pascal VOC 2007 benchmark.

title: Kernel Methods on Riemannian Manifolds with Gaussian RBF Kernels
Abstract: This paper develops an approach to exploiting kernel methods with manifold-valued data. In many computer vision problems, the data can be naturally represented as points on a Riemannian manifold. Due to the non-Euclidean geometry of Riemannian manifolds, usual Euclidean computer vision and machine learning algorithms yield inferior results on such data. We define Gaussian radial basis function (RBF)-based positive definite kernels on manifolds that permit us to embed a given manifold with a corresponding metric in a high-dimensional reproducing kernel Hilbert space. These kernels make it possible to utilize algorithms developed for linear spaces on nonlinear manifold-valued data. Since the Gaussian RBF defined with any given metric is not always positive definite, we present a unified framework for analyzing the positive definiteness of the Gaussian RBF on a generic metric space. We then use the proposed framework to identify positive definite kernels on two specific manifolds commonly encountered in computer vision: the Riemannian manifold of symmetric positive definite matrices and the Grassmann manifold, i.e., the Riemannian manifold of linear subspaces of a Euclidean space. We show that many popular algorithms designed for Euclidean spaces, such as support vector machines, discriminant analysis, and principal component analysis, can be generalized to Riemannian manifolds with the help of such positive definite Gaussian kernels.

title: A Clearer Picture of Blind Deconvolution
Abstract: Blind deconvolution is the problem of recovering a sharp image and a blur kernel from a noisy blurry image. Recently, there has been a significant effort to understand the basic mechanisms to solve blind deconvolution. While this effort resulted in the deployment of effective algorithms, the theoretical findings generated contrasting views on why these approaches worked. On the one hand, one could observe experimentally that alternating energy minimization algorithms converge to the desired solution. On the other hand, it has been shown that such alternating minimization algorithms should fail to converge and one should instead use a so-called Variational Bayes approach. To clarify this conundrum, recent work showed that a good image and blur prior is instead what makes a blind deconvolution algorithm work. Unfortunately, this analysis did not apply to algorithms based on total variation regularization. In this manuscript, we provide both analysis and experiments to get a clearer picture of blind deconvolution. Our analysis reveals the very reason why an algorithm based on total variation works. We also introduce an implementation of this algorithm and show that, in spite of its extreme simplicity, it is very robust and achieves a performance comparable to the state of the art.

title: Simple pairs of points in digital spaces. Topology-preserving transformations of digital spaces by contracting simple pairs of points
Abstract: Transformations of digital spaces preserving local and global topology play an important role in thinning, skeletonization, and simplification of digital images. In this paper, we introduce and study contractions of simple pairs of points based on the notions of a digital contractible space and contractible transformations of digital spaces. We show that the contraction of a simple pair of points preserves the local and global topology of a digital space. Relying on the obtained results, we study properties of digital manifolds. In particular, we show that a digital n-manifold can be transformed to its compressed form with the minimal number of points by sequential contractions of simple pairs. Key Words: Graph, digital space, contraction, splitting, simple pair, homotopy, thinning. |||

title: Robust Camera Location Estimation by Convex Programming
Abstract: 3D structure reconstruction from a set of 2D images requires estimating the camera positions and orientations, known as camera motion. Existing methods for estimating camera locations, which can be formulated as the inverse problem of estimating n locations in 3D space from noisy measurements of pairwise directions, are susceptible to outliers in direction measurements. This paper provides a complete characterization of well-posed instances of the location estimation problem by relating it to the existing theory of parallel rigidity. To robustly estimate camera locations, a two-step approach is introduced, comprising a pairwise direction estimation method robust to outliers in point correspondences between image pairs and a convex program to maintain robustness to outlier directions. In the presence of partially corrupted measurements, our convex formulation can even recover the locations accurately. Finally, experiments on Internet photo collections demonstrate the utility of these formulations.

title: Color image quality assessment measure using multivariate generalized Gaussian distribution
Abstract: This paper focuses on color image quality assessment within the reduced-reference framework using natural scene statistics. We propose modeling the statistics of the steerable pyramid coefficients with a Multivariate Generalized Gaussian distribution (MGGD), which allows us to account for the high correlation between the components of the RGB color space. For each selected scale and orientation, we extract a parameter matrix from the three color component subbands. To quantify visual degradation, we utilize the closed-form Kullback-Leibler Divergence (KLD) between two MGGDs. Compared to the most influential methods in the FRTV1 VQEG framework, the proposed measure demonstrates effectiveness for a wide range of distortion types. Importantly, this measure requires only minimal information about the original image.

title: Multiple Instance Reinforcement Learning for Efficient Weakly-Supervised Detection in Images
Abstract: State-of-the-art visual recognition and detection systems rely heavily on large amounts of training data and complex classifiers, leading to increasing costs in both manual dataset annotation and maintaining acceptable running times for practical applications. This paper proposes two solutions to address these issues. Firstly, we introduce a weakly supervised, segmentation-based approach to learn accurate detectors and image classifiers from weak supervisory signals that provide only approximate constraints on target localization. We demonstrate this system on the problem of action detection in static images (Pascal VOC Actions 2012), using human visual search patterns as our training signal. Secondly, inspired by the saccade-and-fixate operating principle of the human visual system, we utilize reinforcement learning techniques to train efficient search models for detection. Our sequential method is weakly supervised and general (it does not require eye movements), finds optimal search strategies for any given detection confidence function, and achieves performance comparable to exhaustive sliding window search at a fraction of its computational cost.

title: Pedestrian Detection aided by Deep Learning Semantic Tasks
Abstract: Deep learning methods have achieved significant success in pedestrian detection due to their ability to learn features from raw pixels. However, they primarily capture middle-level representations, such as pedestrian pose, but often confuse positive with hard negative samples, which have high ambiguity (e.g., the shape and appearance of "tree trunk" or "wire pole" are similar to pedestrians from certain viewpoints). High-level representations can distinguish this ambiguity. To address this, we jointly optimize pedestrian detection with semantic tasks, including pedestrian attributes (e.g., "carrying backpack") and scene attributes (e.g., "road," "tree," and "horizontal"). Instead of expensively annotating scene attributes, we transfer attribute information from existing scene segmentation datasets to the pedestrian dataset by proposing a novel deep model to learn high-level features from multiple tasks and data sources. Since distinct tasks have different convergence rates and data from different datasets have different distributions, a multi-task objective function is carefully designed to coordinate tasks and reduce discrepancies among datasets. The importance coefficients of tasks and network parameters in this objective function can be iteratively estimated. Extensive evaluations show that the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the challenging Caltech and ETH datasets, reducing the miss rates of previous deep models by 17 and 5.5 percent, respectively.

title: 3D Hand Pose Detection in Egocentric RGB-D Images
Abstract: This paper focuses on the task of estimating everyday hand poses from egocentric viewpoints. We demonstrate that depth sensors are particularly informative for extracting near-field interactions of the camera wearer with their environment. Despite recent advancements in full-body pose estimation using Kinect-like sensors, reliable monocular hand pose estimation in RGB-D images remains an unsolved problem. This challenge is further exacerbated when analyzing hands performing daily activities from a first-person viewpoint due to severe occlusions arising from object manipulations and a limited field-of-view. Our system addresses these difficulties by leveraging strong priors over viewpoint and pose within a discriminative tracking-by-detection framework. These priors are operationalized through a photorealistic synthetic model of egocentric scenes, used to generate training data for learning depth-based pose classifiers. We evaluate our approach on an annotated dataset of real egocentric object manipulation scenes and compare it to both commercial and academic approaches. Our method provides state-of-the-art performance for both hand detection and pose estimation in egocentric RGB-D images.

title: A Bayesian Framework for Sparse Representation-Based 3D Human Pose Estimation
Abstract: This paper introduces a Bayesian framework for 3D human pose estimation from monocular images based on sparse representation (SR). Our probabilistic approach aims to simultaneously learn two overcomplete dictionaries (one for the visual input space and the other for the pose space) with a shared sparse representation. Existing SR-based pose estimation approaches only provide a point estimation of the dictionary and the sparse codes, which can be unreliable with limited training examples. Our Bayesian framework estimates a posterior distribution for the sparse codes and the dictionaries from labeled training data, making it robust to overfitting on small training datasets. Experimental results on various human activities demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method over state-of-the-art pose estimation algorithms.

title: Egocentric Pose Recognition in Four Lines of Code
Abstract: We address the problem of estimating the 3D pose of an individual's upper limbs (arms + hands) from a chest-mounted depth camera, particularly during everyday interactions with objects. Previous work highlights the importance of strong pose + viewpoint priors and depth-based features for robust performance. In egocentric views, hands and arms are observable within a well-defined volume in front of the camera, referred to as the egocentric workspace. Notably, hand appearance correlates with workspace location. To exploit this correlation, we classify arm + hand configurations in a global egocentric coordinate frame instead of a local scanning window, simplifying the architecture and improving performance. We propose an efficient pipeline that: 1) generates synthetic workspace exemplars for training using a virtual chest-mounted camera with intrinsic parameters matching our physical camera, 2) computes perspective-aware depth features on this entire volume, and 3) recognizes discrete arm + hand pose classes through a sparse multi-class SVM. Our method achieves state-of-the-art hand pose recognition performance from egocentric RGB-D images in real-time.

title: Effective Face Frontalization in Unconstrained Images
Abstract: "Frontalization" is the process of synthesizing frontal-facing views of faces appearing in single, unconstrained photos. Recent reports suggest that this process can significantly enhance the performance of face recognition systems by transforming the challenging problem of recognizing faces from unconstrained viewpoints to the easier problem of recognizing faces in constrained, forward-facing poses. Previous frontalization methods attempted to approximate 3D facial shapes for each query image. We observe that 3D face shape estimation from unconstrained photos may be a more difficult problem than frontalization and can potentially introduce facial misalignments. Instead, we explore the simpler approach of using a single, unmodified, 3D surface as an approximation to the shape of all input faces. This leads to a straightforward, efficient, and easy-to-implement method for frontalization. Notably, it produces aesthetically pleasing frontal views and proves surprisingly effective when used for face recognition and gender estimation.
label: AI

title: Learning Face Representation from Scratch
Abstract: Driven by big data and deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs), the performance of face recognition is becoming comparable to human capabilities. Several groups, using private large-scale training datasets, have achieved very high performance on LFW, reaching 97% to 99%. While there are numerous open-source implementations of CNNs, no large-scale face dataset is publicly available. Currently, in the field of face recognition, data is more important than algorithms. To address this issue, this paper proposes a semi-automated method for collecting face images from the Internet and building a large-scale dataset, called CASIAWebFace, containing approximately 10,000 subjects and 500,000 images. Utilizing this database, we employ an 11-layer CNN to learn discriminative representations and achieve state-of-the-art accuracy on LFW and YTF. The publication of CASIAWebFace is expected to attract more research groups to this field and accelerate the development of face recognition in the wild.

title: On Rendering Synthetic Images for Training an Object Detector
Abstract: We propose a novel approach for synthesizing images that are effective for training object detectors. Starting from a small set of real images, our algorithm estimates the rendering parameters required to synthesize similar images given a coarse 3D model of the target object. These parameters can then be reused to generate an unlimited number of training images of the object of interest in arbitrary 3D poses, which can be used to improve classification performance. A key insight of our approach is that the synthetically generated images should be similar to real images not in terms of image quality, but rather in terms of features used during the detector training. We demonstrate in the context of drone, plane, and car detection that using such synthetically generated images yields significantly better performance than simply perturbing real images or even synthesizing images in a way that makes them look very realistic, as is often done when only limited amounts of training data are available.

title: Articulated motion discovery using pairs of trajectories
Abstract: This paper proposes an unsupervised approach for discovering characteristic motion patterns in videos of highly articulated objects performing natural, unscripted behaviors, such as tigers in the wild. Consistent patterns are discovered in a bottom-up manner by analyzing the relative displacements of large numbers of ordered trajectory pairs through time, where each trajectory is attached to a different moving part on the object. The pair of trajectories descriptor relies solely on motion and is more discriminative than state-of-the-art features that employ single trajectories. Our method generates temporal video intervals, each automatically trimmed to one instance of the discovered behavior, and clusters them by type (e.g., running, turning head, drinking water). Experiments on two datasets – dogs from YouTube-Objects and a new dataset of National Geographic tiger videos – confirm that our proposed descriptor outperforms existing appearance- and trajectory-based descriptors (e.g., HOG and DTFs) on both datasets and enables us to segment unconstrained animal video into intervals containing single behaviors.

title: V-variable image compression
Abstract: V-variable fractals, where V is a positive integer, are intuitively fractals with at most V different "forms" or "shapes" at all levels of magnification. This paper describes how V-variable fractals can be used for image compression.
label: AI

title: Cross-Modal Learning via Pairwise Constraints
Abstract: In multimedia applications, the text and image components in a web document form a pairwise constraint that potentially indicates the same semantic concept. This paper studies cross-modal learning via this pairwise constraint, aiming to find the common structure hidden in different modalities. We propose a compound regularization framework to handle the pairwise constraint, which can be used as a general platform for developing cross-modal algorithms. For unsupervised learning, we propose a cross-modal subspace clustering method to learn a common structure for different modalities. For supervised learning, to reduce the semantic gap and outliers in pairwise constraints, we propose a cross-modal matching method based on compound L21 regularization along with an iteratively reweighted algorithm to find the global optimum. Extensive experiments demonstrate the benefits of joint text and image modeling with semantically induced pairwise constraints, showing that the proposed cross-modal methods can further reduce the semantic gap between different modalities and improve clustering/retrieval accuracy.

title: Deep Learning Face Attributes in the Wild
Abstract: Predicting face attributes in the wild is challenging due to complex face variations. We propose a novel deep learning framework for attribute prediction in the wild. This framework cascades two CNNs, LNet and ANet, which are fine-tuned jointly with attribute tags but pre-trained differently. LNet is pre-trained using massive general object categories for face localization, while ANet is pre-trained using massive face identities for attribute prediction. This framework not only outperforms the state-of-the-art with a large margin but also reveals valuable insights into learning face representation. (1) It shows how the performances of face localization (LNet) and attribute prediction (ANet) can be improved by different pre-training strategies. (2) It reveals that although the filters of LNet are fine-tuned only with image-level attribute tags, their response maps over entire images strongly indicate face locations. This enables training LNet for face localization using only image-level annotations, without requiring face bounding boxes or landmarks, which are essential for all existing attribute recognition works. (3) It also demonstrates that the high-level hidden neurons of ANet automatically discover semantic concepts after pre-training with massive face identities, and these concepts are significantly enriched after fine-tuning with attribute tags. Each attribute can be well explained using a sparse linear combination of these concepts.

title: Flying Objects Detection from a Single Moving Camera
Abstract: This paper proposes an approach to detect flying objects, such as UAVs and aircraft, when they occupy a small portion of the field of view, possibly moving against complex backgrounds, and are filmed by a moving camera. Solving this challenging problem requires combining both appearance and motion cues. To this end, we propose a regression-based approach to motion stabilization of local image patches, enabling effective classification on spatio-temporal image cubes and outperforming state-of-the-art techniques. As the problem is relatively new, we collected two challenging datasets for UAVs and aircraft, which can serve as benchmarks for flying objects detection and vision-guided collision avoidance.

title: Features in Concert: Discriminative Feature Selection meets Unsupervised Clustering
Abstract: Feature selection is a fundamental problem in computer vision, crucial for category learning and recognition. With the rapid development of a wide range of visual features and classifiers, there is an increasing need for efficient feature selection and combination methods to construct powerful classifiers for more complex, higher-level recognition tasks. We propose an algorithm that efficiently discovers sparse, compact representations of input features or classifiers from a vast pool of candidates, possessing important optimality properties, low computational cost, and excellent accuracy in practice. Unlike boosting, we begin with a discriminant linear classification formulation that encourages sparse solutions. We then obtain an equivalent unsupervised clustering problem that jointly discovers ensembles of diverse features. These features are independently valuable but even more powerful when combined in a cluster of classifiers. We evaluate our method on the task of large-scale recognition in video and demonstrate that it significantly outperforms classical selection approaches, such as AdaBoost and greedy forward-backward selection, and powerful classifiers such as SVMs, in terms of training speed and performance, especially in the case of limited training data.

title: On color image quality assessment using natural image statistics
Abstract: Color distortion can significantly degrade visual quality perception, but most existing reduced-reference quality measures are designed for grayscale images. This paper explores a basic extension of well-known image-statistics based quality assessment measures to color images. To evaluate the impact of color information on measure efficiency, we investigate two color spaces: RGB and CIELAB. Results from an extensive evaluation using the TID 2013 benchmark demonstrate that significant improvement can be achieved for a wide range of distortion types when the CIELAB color representation is used.
label: AI

title: Visual Representations: Defining Properties and Deep Approximations
Abstract: Visual representations are defined in terms of minimal sufficient statistics of visual data for a class of tasks, which are also invariant to nuisance variability. Minimal sufficiency guarantees that we can store a representation in lieu of raw data with minimal complexity and no performance loss on the task at hand. Invariance guarantees that the statistic is constant with respect to uninformative transformations of the data. We derive analytical expressions for such representations and show that they are related to feature descriptors commonly used in computer vision, as well as to convolutional neural networks. This link highlights the assumptions and approximations tacitly assumed by these methods and explains empirical practices such as clamping, pooling, and joint normalization.
