title: A Novel Approach to Develop a New Hybrid Technique for Trademark Image Retrieval
Abstract: Trademark image retrieval plays a crucial role in content-based image retrieval (CBIR) systems, as trademarks hold significant status value for companies. This paper presents a hybrid retrieval system for detecting fake or copied trademarks, combining two feature vectors for improved accuracy. The system extracts corner features from edge pixel images, followed by invariant moment feature extraction for further refinement. Experimental results demonstrate an 85% efficiency rate, highlighting the system's effectiveness in trademark image retrieval.
label: AI

title: Conditional Generative Adversarial Nets
Abstract: Generative Adversarial Nets (GANs) have emerged as a novel approach for training generative models. This paper introduces the conditional version of GANs, where conditioning data is fed to both the generator and discriminator. The model can generate MNIST digits conditioned on class labels, demonstrating its potential for learning multi-modal models. The paper illustrates an application to image tagging, showcasing the ability to generate descriptive tags not included in training labels.
label: AI

title: Submodular meets Structured: Finding Diverse Subsets in Exponentially-Large Structured Item Sets
Abstract: In domains such as Computer Vision and Natural Language Processing, robust prediction methods often seek a diverse set of high-quality candidate solutions. This poses a challenge in structured prediction problems, where the solution space is exponentially large. This paper explores greedy algorithms for finding diverse subsets of solutions in structured-output spaces by drawing connections between submodular functions and High-Order Potentials (HOPs). The paper shows that structured representations of marginal gains from submodular diversity functions enable efficient approximation by reducing the greedy augmentation step to inference in a factor graph with constructed HOPs. The paper discusses benefits, tradeoffs, and demonstrates the construction's effectiveness in generating significantly better proposals. |||
label: AI

title: Large-Margin Determinantal Point Processes
Abstract: Determinantal point processes (DPPs) are a powerful tool for modeling diversity in applications where the goal is to select a diverse subset. This paper investigates the problem of learning the parameters (the kernel matrix) of a DPP from labeled training data.  Two key contributions are presented: first, a reparameterization of the DPP's kernel matrix using multiple kernel functions is proposed, which enhances modeling flexibility.  Second, a novel parameter estimation technique based on the principle of large margin separation is introduced.  This technique explicitly models errors in target subset selection, offering greater customization in balancing different types of errors (precision vs. recall).  The effectiveness of these contributions is validated through extensive empirical studies, including challenging document and video summarization tasks where flexible kernel matrix modeling and error balancing are essential.
label: AI

title: Convolutional Neural Network-based Place Recognition
Abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance in various classification tasks. This paper proposes a novel place recognition technique based on CNN models, combining the powerful features learned by CNNs with a spatial and sequential filter.  The technique is evaluated on a 70 km benchmark place recognition dataset, achieving a 75% increase in recall at 100% precision, significantly outperforming prior methods.  A comprehensive performance comparison of features extracted from all 21 CNN layers is conducted, both for the benchmark dataset and a second dataset with more significant viewpoint changes.
label: AI

title: Electrocardiography Separation of Mother and Baby
Abstract: Extracting Electrocardiography (ECG or EKG) signals from mother and baby poses a challenge due to the reception of a mixed signal from a single device. This paper aims to design a filter capable of separating the individual signals.
label: AI

title: Optical Character Recognition, Using K-Nearest Neighbors
Abstract: Optical character recognition (OCR) is a well-studied problem in computer science, aiming to recognize text from handwritten input.  While various approaches exist, it remains an open challenge.  This paper proposes a K-nearest neighbors based approach achieving over 90% accuracy with short training and runtime.
label: AI

title: Online SLAM with Any-time Self-calibration and Automatic Change Detection
Abstract: A framework for online simultaneous localization, mapping, and self-calibration is presented that can detect and handle significant changes in calibration parameters. Estimates are computed efficiently by factoring the problem and focusing on the most informative trajectory segments for calibration.  A novel technique detects the probability of significant calibration parameter changes, enabling the system to recalibrate.  Maximum likelihood trajectory and map estimates are computed using asynchronous and adaptive optimization. The system requires no prior information and can initialize without special motions or routines, even when observability over calibration parameters is delayed.  The system is experimentally validated by calibrating camera intrinsic parameters for a nonlinear camera model on a monocular dataset featuring a zoom event.  High accuracy is achieved despite unknown initial calibration parameters, with self-calibration and recalibration parameters closely matching estimates derived using a calibration target.  SLAM results demonstrate sub-1% distance-travel error even with significant recalibration events.
label: AI

title: Edge Detection based on Kernel Density Estimation
Abstract: Image edges are crucial information, extractable using edge detectors employing diverse methodologies.  Edge detection is vital in computer vision tasks for pattern recognition and visual interpretation.  This paper proposes a novel edge detection method based on kernel estimation of the probability density function.  In this algorithm, pixels with minimal density function values are labeled as edges.  The boundary between homogeneous regions is defined in both the spatial/lattice and range/color domains. Extensive experimental evaluations demonstrate the competitiveness of this edge detection method.
label: AI

title: Tensor object classification via multilinear discriminant analysis network
Abstract: This paper introduces a Multilinear Discriminant Analysis Network (MLDANet) for recognizing multidimensional objects, known as tensor objects.  MLDANet is a variation of Linear Discriminant Analysis Network (LDANet) and Principal Component Analysis Network (PCANet), both of which are recent deep learning algorithms.  MLDANet consists of three parts: 1) an encoder learned by MLDA from tensor data, 2) feature maps obtained from a decoder, and 3) binary hashing and histogram for feature pooling.  A learning algorithm for MLDANet is described, and evaluations on the UCF11 database demonstrate superior performance compared to PCANet, LDANet, MPCA + LDA, and MLDA in terms of tensor object classification.
label: AI

title: Multilinear Principal Component Analysis Network for Tensor Object Classification
Abstract: The recently proposed Principal Component Analysis Network (PCANet) has shown high performance in visual content classification. This letter develops a tensorial extension of PCANet, namely, Multilinear Principal Component Analysis Network (MPCANet), for tensor object classification. Compared to PCANet, MPCANet leverages the spatial structure and inter-dimensional relationships of tensor objects more effectively.  Experiments conducted on UCF sports action video sequences and the UCF11 database show that MPCANet achieves higher classification accuracy than PCANet for tensor object classification.
label: AI

title: Do Convnets Learn Correspondence?
Abstract: Convolutional neural networks (convnets) trained on massive labeled datasets have significantly improved the state-of-the-art in image classification and object detection.  However, visual understanding requires establishing correspondence at a finer level than object category.  Given their large pooling regions and training from whole-image labels, it is unclear whether convnets derive their success from an accurate correspondence model suitable for precise localization.  This paper investigates the effectiveness of convnet activation features for tasks requiring correspondence. Evidence is presented that convnet features localize at a much finer scale than their receptive field sizes, can be used for intraclass alignment like conventional hand-engineered features, and outperform conventional features in keypoint prediction on objects from the PASCAL VOC 2011 dataset.
label: AI

title: Deep Gaze I: Boosting Saliency Prediction with Feature Maps Trained on ImageNet
Abstract: Recent results suggest that state-of-the-art saliency models fall short in predicting fixations, attributed to their inability to model the influence of high-level image features such as objects.  Advancements in deep neural networks for tasks like object recognition suggest their capacity to capture this structure.  However, the extensive training data required makes them difficult to apply directly to saliency prediction.  This paper presents a novel method for reusing existing neural networks pretrained on object recognition for fixation prediction.  Utilizing the well-known network of Krizhevsky et al. (2012), a new saliency model is proposed that significantly outperforms existing models on the MIT Saliency Benchmark.  The structure of this network provides new insights into the psychophysics of fixation selection and potential neural implementation.  To train the network, recent work on modeling saliency as point processes is leveraged.
label: AI

title: A random algorithm for low-rank decomposition of large-scale matrices with missing entries
Abstract: A Random SubMatrix method (RSM) is proposed for calculating the low-rank decomposition of large-scale matrices with known entry percentage ρ.  RSM is highly efficient in terms of floating-point operations (flops) compared to state-of-the-art algorithms and is memory-saving.  With homogeneously distributed known entries in the matrix, sub-matrices formed by these entries are randomly selected.  A theorem is proven stating that the subspace associated with smaller singular values is less perturbed by noise, enabling the calculation of null vectors (right singular vectors) corresponding to minor singular values for each sub-matrix.  These vectors represent the null vectors of the corresponding sub-matrix in the ground truth of the large-scale matrix.  By randomly choosing enough sub-matrices, the low-rank decomposition can be estimated.  Experimental results on synthetic matrices (e.g., 131072X1024) and real datasets demonstrate the speed, memory efficiency, and high precision of RSM, achieving or approximating the best results.
label: AI

title: Simultaneous Localization, Mapping, and Manipulation for Unsupervised Object Discovery
Abstract: This paper presents an unsupervised framework for simultaneous appearance-based object discovery, detection, tracking, and reconstruction using RGBD cameras and a robot manipulator.  The system performs dense 3D simultaneous localization and mapping concurrently with unsupervised object discovery.  Putative objects that are spatially and visually coherent are manipulated by the robot to obtain additional motion cues.  The robot utilizes appearance, followed by structure and motion cues, to jointly discover, verify, learn, and improve object models.  Induced motion segmentation reinforces learned models, which are represented implicitly as 2D and 3D level sets to capture both shape and appearance.  Three different approaches for appearance-based object discovery are compared, with a novel form of spatio-temporal super-pixels yielding the highest quality candidate object models in terms of precision and recall.  Live experiments with a Baxter robot demonstrate a holistic pipeline capable of automatic discovery, verification, detection, tracking, and reconstruction of unknown objects.
label: AI

title: A Robust Point Sets Matching Method
Abstract: Point sets matching is a crucial method in computer vision, feature extraction, fingerprint matching, motion estimation, and other applications.  This paper proposes a robust point sets matching method, presenting an iterative algorithm robust to noise.  The algorithm first calculates all transformations between two points and then computes a similarity matrix to measure the probability of both transformations being true.  The matching score matrix is iteratively updated using the similarity matrix.  Applying a matching algorithm on a graph yields the final matching result.  Experimental results demonstrate the robustness of this approach to outliers and jitter.
label: AI

title: A Weighted Common Subgraph Matching Algorithm
Abstract: A weighted common subgraph (WCS) matching algorithm is proposed to find the most similar subgraphs in two labeled weighted graphs.  WCS matching, a natural generalization of equal-sized graph matching or subgraph matching, finds broad applications in computer vision and machine learning.  This paper formulates WCS matching as a combinatorial optimization problem over the set of partial permutation matrices and approximately solves it using the Graduated NonConvexity and Concavity Procedure (GNCCP).  Experimental comparisons on both synthetic graphs and real-world images validate the algorithm's robustness against noise level, problem size, outlier number, and edge density.
label: AI

title: State-of-the-Art in Retinal Optical Coherence Tomography Image Analysis
Abstract: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is a rapidly developing imaging modality widely used in biomedical imaging. Since its emergence in the 1990s, significant hardware and software advancements have been made.  Applications span ophthalmology, dermatology, coronary imaging, and more.  This paper focuses on OCT applications in ophthalmology and retinal imaging.  OCT non-invasively produces cross-sectional volume images of tissues, enabling analysis of tissue structure and properties.  Due to underlying physics, OCT images often suffer from speckle noise, hindering interpretation and requiring specialized noise reduction techniques.  Furthermore, the microscopic scale of OCT images (μm-level) necessitates further analysis to distinguish different structures, highlighting the importance of segmentation techniques.  Tissue movement during imaging or disease progression can impact image quality and interpretation, emphasizing the utility of image registration techniques.  This paper provides an overview of these image analysis techniques.
label: AI

title: Affective Facial Expression Processing via Simulation: A Probabilistic Model
Abstract: Understanding the mental state of others is crucial for intelligent agents and robots operating in social environments.  The mental processes involved in "mind-reading" are complex.  One explanation, Simulation Theory, is supported by extensive neuropsychological research.  However, determining the optimal computational model or theory for simulation-style emotion detection remains unclear.  This paper leverages Simulation Theory and neuroscience findings on Mirror-Neuron Systems to develop a novel computational model for handling affective facial expressions.  The model is based on a probabilistic mapping of observations from multiple identities onto a single fixed identity ("internal transcoding of external stimuli"), followed by a mapping onto a latent space ("phenomenological response").  Preliminary results using this architecture are promising.
label: AI

title: Non Binary Local Gradient Contours for Face Recognition
Abstract: Traditional Local Binary Patterns (LBP) and Local Directional Patterns (LDP) features are often ineffective for face recognition.  This paper proposes a novel approach based on Information sets, eliminating information loss during binarization.  Information sets extend the scope of fuzzy sets by associating attributes with corresponding membership function values as products.  Since faces exhibit smooth texture in limited areas, extracted features must be highly discernible.  To limit the number of features, only non-overlapping windows are considered.  Applying information set theory reduces the number of features in an image.  The derived features demonstrate effectiveness compared to eigenface, fisherface, and LBP methods.
label: AI

title: Sparsity Constrained Graph Regularized NMF for Spectral Unmixing of Hyperspectral Data
Abstract: Hyperspectral images contain mixed pixels due to the low spatial resolution of hyperspectral sensors.  Mixed pixels consist of multiple distinct materials called endmembers.  The abundance fractions represent the percentages of endmembers present in mixed pixels.  Spectral unmixing decomposes these pixels into a set of endmembers and abundance fractions.  Due to the nonnegativity constraint on abundance fractions, nonnegative matrix factorization methods (NMF) have been widely used for spectral unmixing.  This paper utilizes a graph regularized NMF (GNMF) method combined with a sparseness constraint to decompose mixed pixels in hyperspectral imagery.  This method preserves the geometrical structure of data while representing it in low-dimensional space.  An adaptive regularization parameter based on the temperature schedule in the simulated annealing method is also employed for the sparseness term.  The proposed algorithm is applied to synthetic and real datasets.  Synthetic data is generated using endmembers from the USGS spectral library, while the AVIRIS Cuprite dataset serves as the real dataset for evaluation.  Results are quantified using spectral angle distance (SAD) and abundance angle distance (AAD) measures.  Comparisons with other methods show the proposed method's effectiveness in unmixing data, particularly for the Cuprite dataset where performance is approximately 10% better than VCA and Sparse NMF in terms of root mean square of SAD.
label: AI

title: High Dynamic Range Imaging by Perceptual Logarithmic Exposure Merging
Abstract: This paper highlights a similarity between the Logarithmic-Type Image Processing (LTIP) model and the Naka-Rushton model of the Human Visual System (HVS).  LTIP is a derivation of Logarithmic Image Processing (LIP), replacing the logarithmic function with a ratio of polynomial functions.  Based on this similarity, a unifying framework for the High Dynamic Range (HDR) imaging problem is presented, demonstrating that exposure merging under the LTIP model is equivalent to standard irradiance map fusion.  The resulting HDR algorithm exhibits high quality in both subjective and objective evaluations.
label: AI

title: Geodesic Exponential Kernels: When Curvature and Linearity Conflict
Abstract: This paper explores kernel methods on general geodesic metric spaces, presenting both negative and positive results.  It is shown that the common Gaussian kernel can only be generalized to a positive definite kernel on a geodesic metric space if the space is flat.  Consequently, for data on a Riemannian manifold, the geodesic Gaussian kernel is only positive definite if the manifold is Euclidean.  This implies that attempting to design geodesic Gaussian kernels on curved Riemannian manifolds is futile.  However, it is demonstrated that for spaces with conditionally negative definite distances, the geodesic Laplacian kernel can be generalized while preserving positive definiteness.  This allows geodesic Laplacian kernels to be generalized to some curved spaces, including spheres and hyperbolic spaces.  Empirical verification of the theoretical results is provided. |||
label: AI

title: Entropy of Overcomplete Kernel Dictionaries
Abstract: In signal analysis and synthesis, linear approximation theory uses a linear decomposition of a signal into a set of atoms, which are organized into a dictionary. Sparse representations are achieved by relaxing the orthogonality condition of the atoms, resulting in overcomplete dictionaries with an extended number of atoms. Going beyond linear decomposition, overcomplete kernel dictionaries offer a nonlinear extension by defining atoms through a mapping kernel function (e.g., the Gaussian kernel). Such kernel dictionaries are employed in models like neural networks, Gaussian processes, and online learning with kernels. The quality of an overcomplete dictionary is assessed using measures such as diversity, distance, approximation, coherence, and Babel. This paper introduces a framework to examine overcomplete kernel dictionaries using entropy from information theory. A higher entropy value indicates a more uniform distribution of the atoms across the space. We derive lower bounds on the entropy for each of the aforementioned diversity measures and investigate several definitions of entropy, providing an extensive analysis in both the input space and the mapped feature space.
label: AI

title: A Two-phase Decision Support Framework for the Automatic Screening of Digital Fundus Images
Abstract: This paper reviews existing automated detection systems for diabetic retinopathy screening. It further proposes an enhanced detection procedure consisting of two steps. Initially, a pre-screening algorithm classifies input fundus images based on the severity of abnormalities. Images identified as severely abnormal are excluded from further analysis using robust lesion detector algorithms. To improve this process, a novel feature extraction approach based on clinical observations is introduced. The second step focuses on detecting regions of interest with potential lesions on the images that successfully pass the pre-screening stage. These regions are then analyzed in detail using specific lesion detectors. This procedure enhances the computational performance of the screening system. Experimental results demonstrate the efficiency of both steps in excluding a significant amount of data from further processing, ultimately reducing the computational load of the automatic screening system.
label: AI

title: Detection of texts in natural images
Abstract: This paper introduces a framework utilizing connected components and supervised support vector machines for text recognition. The image undergoes preprocessing, and an edge graph is calculated using a probabilistic framework to mitigate photometric noise. Connected components are identified in the resulting image, bounded, and pruned using geometric constraints. Finally, a Gabor feature-based SVM classifies the presence of text in the candidates. The proposed method was evaluated using the ICDAR 10 dataset and additional images from the internet. It achieved a recall and precision score of 0.72 and 0.88, outperforming the benchmark Eiphstein's algorithm. In natural images, the method recorded 0.70 and 0.74, significantly surpassing current methods. Moreover, the proposed method scales nearly linearly for high-resolution, cluttered images.
label: AI

title: Provable Submodular Minimization using Wolfe's Algorithm
Abstract: Fast submodular function minimization (SFM) has gained prominence due to its applications in large-scale learning and vision problems. Theoretically, unconstrained SFM can be solved in polynomial time. However, these algorithms are often impractical. Wolfe proposed an algorithm in 1976 to find the minimum Euclidean norm point in a polytope, and in 1980, Fujishige demonstrated how Wolfe's algorithm can be applied to SFM. For general submodular functions, the Fujishige-Wolfe minimum norm algorithm seems to have the best empirical performance. Despite its practical success, little is known about Wolfe's minimum norm algorithm theoretically. The only existing result is an exponential time analysis by Wolfe himself. This paper presents the first convergence analysis of Wolfe's algorithm. It is proven that in t iterations, Wolfe's algorithm returns an O(1/t)-approximate solution for the min-norm point on any polytope. Furthermore, a robust version of Fujishige's theorem is established, showing that an O(1/n^2)-approximate solution for the min-norm point on the base polytope implies exact submodular minimization. As a result, this paper provides the first pseudo-polynomial time guarantee for the Fujishige-Wolfe minimum norm algorithm for unconstrained submodular function minimization.
label: AI

title: Complex Events Recognition under Uncertainty in a Sensor Network
Abstract: Automated extraction of semantic information from sensor networks for cognitive analysis and human-like reasoning is a desirable capability in future ground surveillance systems. This paper addresses the challenge of complex decision-making under uncertainty in a network information environment. The lack of effective visual processing tools and incomplete domain knowledge often lead to uncertainty in visual primitives, resulting in suboptimal decisions. While existing vision techniques excel in detecting visual entities (humans, vehicles, and scene elements), a crucial missing element is the ability to merge this information to reveal meaningful insights for high-level inference. This work proposes a probabilistic first-order predicate logic (FOPL)-based reasoning system for recognizing complex events in synchronized video streams acquired from sensors with non-overlapping fields of view. Markov Logic Networks (MLN) are employed to model uncertainty in observations and fuse information from heterogeneous data in a probabilistically consistent manner. MLN mitigates strong dependence on purely empirical learning by incorporating domain knowledge through user-defined rules and associated confidences. This research demonstrates that the MLN-based decision control system can be scaled to model statistical relations between various entities and over extended video sequences. Experiments using real-world data under diverse settings showcase the mathematical soundness and wide-ranging applicability of this approach.
label: AI

title: Generalized Adaptive Dictionary Learning via Domain Shift Minimization
Abstract: Visual data-driven dictionaries have been successfully used in object recognition and classification tasks. However, the challenge intensifies when training and test data originate from contrasting domains. This paper proposes a novel and generalized approach to learning an adaptive and common dictionary for multiple domains. Specifically, data from different domains are projected onto a low-dimensional space while preserving the intrinsic structure of data from each domain. Additionally, domain shift is minimized among the data from each pair of domains. Simultaneously, a common adaptive dictionary is learned. The algorithm can be modified to learn class-specific dictionaries for classification purposes. Furthermore, a discriminative manifold regularization is proposed, which imposes the intrinsic structure of class-specific features onto the sparse coefficients. Image classification experiments demonstrate that this approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.
label: AI

title: Supermassive Black Hole Tests of General Relativity with eLISA
Abstract: Motivated by the parameterized post-Einsteinian (ppE) scheme by Yunes and Pretorius, which introduces corrections to the post-Newtonian coefficients of the frequency domain gravitational waveform to emulate alternative theories of gravity, this paper computes analytical time domain waveforms that, after a numerical Fourier transform, aim to represent (phase corrected only) ppE waveforms. In this formalism, alternative theories manifest through corrections to the phase and frequency predicted by General Relativity (GR) at different post-Newtonian (PN) orders. For a generic test of alternative theories of gravity, the coupling constant of each alternative theory is assumed to be manifestly positive, allowing corrections to GR waveforms to be either positive or negative. By exploring the capabilities of massive black hole binary GR waveforms in detecting and estimating parameters of corrected time domain ppE signals, using the current eLISA configuration, this paper demonstrates that for corrections arising at higher than 1PN order in phase and frequency, GR waveforms suffice for both detecting and estimating parameters of alternative theory signals. However, for theories introducing corrections at the 0 and 0.5 PN order, GR waveforms are insufficient to cover the entire parameter space, requiring the use of non-GR waveforms for detection and parameter estimation.
label: AI

title: Addressing the non-functional requirements of computer vision systems: A case study
Abstract: Computer vision plays a crucial role in the robotics industry, where vision data is frequently used for navigation and high-level decision-making. Although substantial research exists on algorithms and functional requirements, there is a relative lack of focus on effectively mapping these abstract concepts onto an appropriate software architecture. This study differentiates between the functional and non-functional requirements of a computer vision system. Using a RoboCup humanoid robot system as a case study, it proposes and develops a software architecture that fulfills the non-functional criteria. The modifiability of the proposed architecture is demonstrated by detailing several feature detection algorithms and highlighting the aspects of the underlying framework modified to support their integration. To demonstrate portability, the vision system (designed for an application-specific DARwIn-OP humanoid robot) is ported to a general-purpose Raspberry Pi computer. Performance evaluation on both platforms is conducted and compared to a vision system optimized solely for functional requirements. The architecture and implementation presented in this study provide a highly generalizable framework for computer vision system design, particularly beneficial in research and development, competition, and other environments where rapid system evolution is necessary.
label: AI

title: Symmetric low-rank representation for subspace clustering
Abstract: This paper proposes a symmetric low-rank representation (SLRR) method for subspace clustering, assuming that a dataset is approximately drawn from the union of multiple subspaces. The technique unveils the membership of multiple subspaces through the self-expressiveness property of the data. The SLRR method combines collaborative representation with low-rank matrix recovery techniques to learn a symmetric low-rank representation, preserving the subspace structures of high-dimensional data. Unlike iterative singular value decomposition in existing low-rank representation-based algorithms, the symmetric low-rank representation in SLRR can be calculated as a closed-form solution by solving the symmetric low-rank optimization problem. An affinity graph matrix is constructed for spectral clustering using the angular information of the principal directions of the symmetric low-rank representation. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that this approach outperforms state-of-the-art subspace clustering algorithms.
label: AI

title: DeepSentiBank: Visual Sentiment Concept Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: This paper introduces a visual sentiment concept classification method based on deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Visual sentiment concepts, defined as adjective-noun pairs (ANPs), are automatically discovered from the tags of web photos and serve as effective statistical cues for detecting emotions depicted in images. Nearly one million Flickr images tagged with these ANPs are downloaded to train the concept classifiers. The popular deep convolutional neural network model, known for its performance improvement in classifying large-scale web-based image datasets like ImageNet, is adopted. The deep CNN model is trained using Caffe, a deep learning framework. To address the bias in training data, which only contains images with strong sentiment, and prevent overfitting, the model is initialized with weights trained from ImageNet. Performance evaluation shows that the newly trained deep CNN model SentiBank 2.0 (or DeepSentiBank) exhibits significant improvements in annotation accuracy and retrieval performance compared to its predecessors, which primarily relied on binary SVM classification models.
label: AI

title: An Ensemble-based System for Microaneurysm Detection and Diabetic Retinopathy Grading
Abstract: Reliable microaneurysm detection in digital fundus images remains an open issue in medical image processing. This paper proposes an ensemble-based framework to enhance microaneurysm detection. Unlike the common approach of combining outputs of multiple classifiers, this framework combines internal components of microaneurysm detectors, namely preprocessing methods and candidate extractors. The approach has been evaluated in an online competition, where it currently ranks first, and on two additional databases. As microaneurysm detection is crucial for diabetic retinopathy grading, the proposed method was tested for this task on the publicly available Messidor database, achieving a promising AUC of 0.90 with 0.01 uncertainty in a 'DR/non-DR'-type classification based on the presence or absence of microaneurysms.
label: AI

title: An ensemble-based system for automatic screening of diabetic retinopathy
Abstract: This paper proposes an ensemble-based method for diabetic retinopathy (DR) screening. This approach utilizes features extracted from the output of several retinal image processing algorithms, including image-level (quality assessment, pre-screening, AM/FM), lesion-specific (microaneurysms, exudates), and anatomical (macula, optic disc) components. The final decision regarding the presence of the disease is made by an ensemble of machine learning classifiers. The approach was tested on the publicly available Messidor database, achieving 90% sensitivity, 91% specificity, 90% accuracy, and 0.989 AUC in a disease/no-disease setting. These highly competitive results in this field suggest that retinal image processing is a viable approach for automatic DR screening.
label: AI

title: A Solution for Multi-Alignment by Transformation Synchronisation
Abstract: Aligning a set of objects using transformations is a fundamental problem in computer vision. While the case of two objects can be solved globally, iterative methods are typically used when dealing with multiple objects. These iterative methods perform well when the relative transformations between any pair of objects are noise-free. However, if only noisy relative transformations are available (e.g., due to missing data or incorrect correspondences), iterative methods may fail. Recognizing that the underlying noise-free transformations can be retrieved from the null space of a matrix directly obtained from pairwise alignments, this paper presents a novel method for synchronizing pairwise transformations to ensure transitive consistency. Simulations demonstrate that for noisy transformations, a significant proportion of missing data, and even for incorrect correspondence assignments, the method delivers encouraging results.
label: AI

title: Power-Law Graph Cuts
Abstract: Algorithms based on spectral graph cut objectives, such as normalized cuts, ratio cuts, and ratio association, have gained popularity in recent years due to their wide applicability and ease of implementation using standard eigenvector computations. Despite their strong performance in various clustering tasks, spectral graph cut algorithms face several limitations. First, they require the number of clusters to be known a priori, which is often unavailable. Second, they tend to produce clusters with uniform sizes. In some cases, the true clusters exhibit a known size distribution; for instance, human-segmented images in image segmentation tend to yield segment sizes following a power-law distribution. This paper proposes a general framework of power-law graph cut algorithms that produce clusters with power-law distributed sizes and do not fix the number of clusters upfront. The Pitman-Yor exchangeable partition probability function (EPPF) is treated as a regularizer to graph cut objectives. Since the resulting objectives cannot be solved by relaxing via eigenvectors, a simple iterative algorithm is derived to locally optimize the objectives. Moreover, the proposed algorithm can be viewed as performing MAP inference on a specific Pitman-Yor mixture model. Experiments on various datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of these algorithms.
label: AI

title: A comparison of dense region detectors for image search and fine-grained classification
Abstract: This paper examines a pipeline for image classification or search based on coding approaches like Bag of Words or Fisher vectors. In this context, the most common approach is to extract image patches regularly in a dense manner on multiple scales. This paper proposes and evaluates alternative choices for extracting patches densely. Beyond simple strategies derived from regular interest region detectors, approaches based on super-pixels, edges, and a bank of Zernike filters used as detectors are proposed. The different approaches are evaluated on recent image retrieval and fine-grain classification benchmarks. Results show that the regular dense detector is outperformed by other methods in most situations, leading to improved state-of-the-art results in comparable setups on standard retrieval and fine-grain benchmarks. As a byproduct of this study, it is demonstrated that existing methods for blob and super-pixel extraction achieve high accuracy if the patches are extracted along the edges and not around the detected regions.
label: AI

title: Towards a Visual Turing Challenge
Abstract: As language and visual understanding by machines progress rapidly, there is increasing interest in holistic architectures that tightly interlink both modalities in a joint learning and inference process. This trend has enabled the community to tackle more challenging and open tasks, rekindling the hope of achieving the long-standing AI dream of building machines that could pass a Turing test in open domains. To make steady progress toward this goal, quantifying performance becomes increasingly difficult. This paper explores how to precisely define such challenges and how to evaluate different algorithms on open tasks. It summarizes and discusses these challenges, offering answers where appropriate options are available in the literature. Some solutions are exemplified on a recently presented dataset of question-answering tasks based on real-world indoor images, which establishes a visual Turing challenge. Finally, despite the success of unique ground-truth annotation, the paper argues that we need to move away from carefully curated datasets and instead rely on "social consensus" as the main driving force for creating suitable benchmarks. Providing coverage in this inherently ambiguous output space is an emerging challenge we face to make quantifiable progress in this area.
label: AI

title: Extended Dynamic Programming and Fast Multidimensional Search Algorithm for Energy Minization in Stereo and Motion
Abstract: This paper presents a novel extended dynamic programming approach for energy minimization (EDP) to solve the correspondence problem in stereo and motion. A significant speedup is achieved using a recursive minimum search strategy (RMS). The speedup is particularly important for 2D and 3D disparity spaces. The proposed RMS can also be applied to the well-known dynamic programming (DP) approach for stereo and motion. In this case, the general 2D problem of global discrete energy minimization is reduced to several mutually independent sub-problems of one-dimensional minimization. The EDP method is used when approximating the general 2D discrete energy minimization problem. The RMS algorithm is an essential part of the EDP method. The EDP algorithm yields a lower energy bound than the graph cuts (GC) expansion technique on stereo and motion problems. The proposed calculation scheme exhibits natural parallelism, can be implemented on graphics processing unit (GPU) platforms, and can potentially be further restricted by the number of scanlines in the image plane. Furthermore, the RMS and EDP methods can be used in any optimization problem where the objective function meets specific conditions in the smoothness term.

title: Collaborative Multi-sensor Classification via Sparsity-based Representation
Abstract: This paper proposes a general collaborative sparse representation framework for multi-sensor classification, which considers both correlations and complementary information between heterogeneous sensors simultaneously while incorporating joint sparsity within each sensor's observations. The models are robust to sparse noise and low-rank interference signals. The paper demonstrates that incorporating the noise or interference signal as a low-rank component in the models is crucial in a multi-sensor classification problem where multiple co-located sources/sensors simultaneously record the same physical event. The frameworks are extended to kernelized models, which rely on sparsely representing a test sample in terms of all training samples in a feature space induced by a kernel function. A fast and efficient algorithm based on the alternating direction method is proposed, with guaranteed convergence to an optimal solution. Extensive experiments on various real multi-sensor datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods compared to conventional classifiers.

title: A hierarchical framework for object recognition
Abstract: Object recognition in the presence of background clutter and distractors is a central problem in both neuroscience and machine learning. However, models inspired by cortical mechanisms, including deep networks like convolutional neural networks and deep belief networks, show a significant decline in performance when exposed to noise and background objects. This paper develops a computational framework that is hierarchical, heavily relying on key properties of the visual cortex, including mid-level feature selectivity in visual area V4 and Inferotemporal cortex (IT), high degrees of selectivity and invariance in IT, and the prior knowledge built into cortical circuits (such as the emergence of edge detector neurons in primary visual cortex before the onset of visual experience). This approach specifically addresses large deformations, allows flexible communication between different layers of representation, and learns highly selective filters from a small number of training examples.

title: New similarity index based on entropy and group theory
Abstract: This work proposes a new similarity index for images, incorporating the entropy function and group theory. The index considers an algebraic group of images, defined by an inner law that introduces a novel approach for image subtraction. Through an equivalence relationship in the field of images, the existence of the quotient group is proven, on which the new similarity index is defined. The main properties of the new index are presented, along with its immediate application as a stopping criterion for the "Mean Shift Iterative Algorithm." |||

title: A Short Image Series Based Scheme for Time Series Digital Image Correlation
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to digital image correlation, dubbed Short Time Series DIC (STS-DIC). Instead of processing individual deformed speckle images, STS-DIC aggregates several consecutive images from a short time series. The averaged image, incorporating temporal deformation continuity, is then processed. The deformation of these adjacent images is assumed to be linear over time, leading to a new spatial-temporal displacement representation method with eight unknowns based on the subset-based representation method. Subsequently, the STS-DIC model is constructed, and a solving scheme based on the Newton-Raphson iteration is developed. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through numerical and experimental cases, showing significant accuracy improvements over traditional DIC under both simple and complex deformation scenarios while maintaining acceptable computational cost.

title: Robust Piecewise-Constant Smoothing: M-Smoother Revisited
Abstract: This paper revisits the M-smoother, a robust estimator for piecewise-constant smoothing. Starting from its generalized formulation, a numerical framework is proposed for solving it through a series of weighted-average filtering techniques like box, Gaussian, bilateral, and guided filtering. Recognizing the equivalence between M-smoother and local-histogram-based filters, such as the median and mode filters, the proposed framework enables fast approximation of histogram filters using multiple box or Gaussian filtering operations. Furthermore, high-quality piecewise-constant smoothing is achieved by integrating multiple bilateral or guided filtering steps within the framework. Experiments on depth map denoising demonstrate the efficacy of this framework.

title: Abrupt Motion Tracking via Nearest Neighbor Field Driven Stochastic Sampling
Abstract: Stochastic sampling-based trackers have gained popularity in recent years for their effectiveness in tracking abrupt motions. However, traditional methods employ a two-stage sampling paradigm, involving an inefficient preliminary sampling phase to uniformly explore the search space. This paper proposes a novel sampling-based approach within the Bayesian filtering framework to address this issue. Utilizing nearest neighbor field estimation, the importance proposal probabilities are calculated, guiding the Markov chain search towards promising regions and enhancing sampling efficiency. Leveraging motion priors, a smoothing stochastic sampling Monte Carlo algorithm is introduced to approximate the posterior distribution using a smoothing weight-updating scheme. Additionally, an abrupt-motion detection scheme is developed to identify the presence of abrupt motions during online tracking, enabling the simultaneous tracking of both smooth and abrupt motions. Extensive experiments on challenging image sequences showcase the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed algorithm in handling abrupt motions.

title: Deep Structured learning for mass segmentation from Mammograms
Abstract: This paper presents a novel method for segmenting breast masses from mammograms, leveraging the power of structured and deep learning. Specifically, a model is formulated using structured support vector machines (SSVM) that combines different types of potential functions, including one that classifies image regions using deep learning. The main goal of this work is to demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency improvements these relatively new techniques can offer for breast mass segmentation in mammograms. The paper also proposes an easily reproducible quantitative analysis to assess the performance of breast mass segmentation methodologies based on widely accepted accuracy and running time measurements on public datasets, facilitating further comparisons for this segmentation problem. Two publicly available datasets, DDSM-BCRP and INbreast, are utilized, and the computation of running time and the Dice index are proposed to measure the segmentation accuracy and running time, respectively. Results from both databases show that the proposed methodology delivers competitive results in terms of accuracy and running time.

title: Consensus Message Passing for Layered Graphical Models
Abstract: Generative models provide a powerful framework for probabilistic reasoning; however, their practical use is often hindered by inference difficulties, especially in computer vision, where models of the imaging process are typically large, loopy, and layered. This has led to the dominance of bottom-up conditional models in such domains. This paper finds that widely-used, general-purpose message passing inference algorithms like Expectation Propagation (EP) and Variational Message Passing (VMP) struggle even on the simplest vision models. Addressing this issue, a modification to message passing is introduced, learning to exploit the layered structure of these models by passing "consensus" messages that guide inference towards good solutions. Experiments on various problems demonstrate that the proposed technique leads to significantly more accurate inference results compared to standard EP and VMP, and even outperforms competitive bottom-up conditional models.

title: Higher-order MRFs based image super resolution: why not MAP?
Abstract: A trainable filter-based higher-order Markov Random Fields (MRFs) model, known as Fields of Experts (FoE), has proven to be a highly effective image prior model for numerous classic image restoration problems. Generally, two options exist for incorporating the learned FoE prior into the inference procedure: (1) sampling-based minimum mean square error (MMSE) estimate, and (2) energy minimization-based maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate. This paper focuses on the FoE prior-based single image super resolution (SR) problem and suggests using the MAP estimate for inference based on two key observations: (I) MAP inference offers a notable advantage in computational efficiency compared to the time-consuming sampling-based MMSE estimate. (II) Practical SR experiment results demonstrate that the MAP estimate performs equally well as the MMSE estimate with the same FoE prior model, and even leads to further improvements when incorporated with a discriminatively trained FoE prior model. In conclusion, for higher-order natural image prior-based SR problems, it is recommended to employ the MAP estimate for inference.

title: Visual Chunking: A List Prediction Framework for Region-Based Object Detection
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach for object detection in images, termed visual chunking, which involves iteratively selecting from a set of arbitrarily shaped candidate regions. This approach reasons about the locations of multiple object instances in an image while providing expressive descriptions of object boundaries. An optimization criterion is designed to measure the performance of a list of such detections, extending a common per-instance metric. An efficient algorithm with provable performance is presented for constructing a high-quality list of detections from any candidate set of region-based proposals. Additionally, a simple class-specific algorithm is developed for generating a candidate region instance in near-linear time with respect to the number of low-level superpixels, outperforming other region generating methods. To enable predictions on novel images at test time without ground truth access, learning approaches are developed to emulate the algorithm's behaviors. The new approach demonstrates superior performance compared to sophisticated baselines on benchmark datasets.

title: Exact Expression For Information Distance
Abstract: Information distance can be defined not only between two strings but also within a finite multiset of strings with cardinality greater than two. This paper provides an elementary proof for expressing information distance in terms of plain Kolmogorov complexity. This expression is exact since, for each cardinality of the multiset, the lower bound for some multiset equals the upper bound for all multisets up to a constant additive term.

title: An Unsupervised Ensemble-based Markov Random Field Approach to Microscope Cell Image Segmentation
Abstract: This paper proposes an approach to unsupervised image segmentation using Markov Random Field (MRF), based on the idea of Bit Plane Slicing. The planes are used as initial labelings for an ensemble of segmentations, enabling robust segmentation through pixelwise voting. The approach is demonstrated on microscope cell images and tested on a publicly available database, showcasing its competitive performance against other methods and manual segmentation.

title: Iris Biometric System using a hybrid approach
Abstract: Iris Recognition Systems are ocular-based biometric devices primarily used for security purposes. The complexity and randomness of the iris, along with other factors, ensure the reliability and accuracy of this biometric identification system. The algorithm handles automatic localization and segmentation of boundaries using circular Hough Transform, noise reduction, image enhancement, and feature extraction across numerous images in the database. This paper delves into the various techniques required to approximate the pupillary and limbic boundaries of the enrolled iris image, captured using a suitable image acquisition device. Feature extraction is then performed on the normalized iris image using Haar Wavelets to encode the input data into a binary string format. These techniques were validated using images from the CASIA database, and various other procedures were tested.

title: Phase transitions during fruiting body formation in Myxococcus xanthus
Abstract: The formation of collectively moving groups offers various advantages to individuals within a population, including enhanced sensitivity to perturbation, collective feeding modes, and protection from environmental stress. While some collective groups rely on a single organizing principle, others dynamically adjust their group behavior by modifying individual-level interaction rules. The surface-dwelling bacterium Myxococcus xanthus forms dynamic collective groups both for prey consumption and aggregation during starvation. The latter behavior, known as fruiting-body formation, involves a complex, coordinated series of density changes that ultimately lead to three-dimensional aggregates comprising hundreds of thousands of cells and spores. This multi-step developmental process likely involves various single-celled behaviors as the population condenses from a loose, two-dimensional sheet to a three-dimensional mound. This study utilizes high-resolution microscopy and computer vision software to spatiotemporally track the motion of thousands of individuals during the initial stages of fruiting body formation. The findings reveal a combination of cell-contact-mediated alignment and internal timing mechanisms driving a phase transition from exploratory flocking, where cell groups move rapidly and coherently over long distances, to reversal-mediated localization into streams, which act as slow-spreading, quasi-one-dimensional nematic fluids. These observations lead to an active liquid crystal description of the myxobacterial development cycle.

title: A method for context-based adaptive QRS clustering in real-time
Abstract: Continuous follow-up of heart conditions through long-term electrocardiogram (ECG) monitoring is invaluable for diagnosing certain cardiac arrhythmias. In this context, providing tools for rapid detection of alterations in normal conduction patterns is crucial and remains an open issue. This paper presents a real-time method for adaptive clustering of QRS complexes from multilead ECG signals, providing the set of QRS morphologies present during an ECG recording. The method processes QRS complexes sequentially, grouping them into a dynamic set of clusters based on the information content of the temporal context. These clusters are represented by templates that evolve over time and adapt to QRS morphology changes. Rules for creating, merging, and removing clusters are defined, alongside techniques for noise detection to prevent their proliferation. To address beat misalignment, Derivative Dynamic Time Warping is employed. The proposed method was validated against the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database and the AHA ECG Database, achieving a global purity of 98.56% and 99.56%, respectively. Results show that the proposed method not only outperforms previous offline solutions but also meets real-time requirements.

title: Directional Bilateral Filters
Abstract: This paper proposes a bilateral filter with a locally controlled domain kernel for directional edge-preserving smoothing. Traditional bilateral filters utilize a range kernel for edge preservation and a fixed domain kernel for smoothing. The intuition behind this approach is that the orientation and anisotropy of image structures should be incorporated into the domain kernel during smoothing. To achieve this, an oriented Gaussian domain kernel, locally controlled by a structure tensor, is employed. The combination of this oriented domain kernel and a range kernel forms the directional bilateral filter. The two kernels assist each other in effectively suppressing the influence of outliers while smoothing. To find the optimal parameters for the directional bilateral filter, Stein's unbiased risk estimate (SURE) is utilized. The capabilities of the kernels are tested separately and together, first on synthetic images and then on real endoscopic images. The directional bilateral filter exhibits better denoising performance than the Gaussian bilateral filter at various noise levels in terms of peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR).

title: Estimating the intrinsic dimension in fMRI space via dataset fractal analysis - Counting the `cpu cores' of the human brain
Abstract: Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) is a powerful non-invasive tool for localizing and analyzing brain activity. This study focuses on a crucial aspect of the functional properties of the human brain, specifically the estimation of the level of parallelism during complex cognitive tasks. Using fMRI as the primary modality, human brain activity is investigated through a purely data-driven signal processing and dimensionality analysis approach. The fMRI signal is treated as a multi-dimensional data space, and its intrinsic "complexity" is studied via dataset fractal analysis and blind-source separation (BSS) methods. One simulated and two real fMRI datasets are used in combination with Independent Component Analysis (ICA) and fractal analysis to estimate the intrinsic (true) dimensionality, providing data-driven experimental evidence on the number of independent brain processes running in parallel when visual or visuo-motor tasks are performed. Although this number cannot be defined as a strict threshold but rather as a continuous range, when a specific activation level is defined, a corresponding number of parallel processes, or the casual equivalent of "CPU cores," can be detected in normal human brain activity.

title: On Chord and Sagitta in ${\mathbb Z}^2$: An Analysis towards Fast and Robust Circular Arc Detection
Abstract: While chord and sagitta, when considered together, can reflect many underlying geometric properties of circles on the Euclidean plane, their implications on the digital plane are not yet fully understood. This paper explores some of their fundamental properties on the digital plane, which have a strong impact on the unsupervised detection of circles and circular arcs in a digital image. It is shown that, although the chord-and-sagitta properties of a real circle do not readily translate to the digital plane, they can be utilized for analysis in the discrete domain based on certain bounds on their deviations, derived from the real domain. Specifically, an upper bound on the circumferential angular deviation of a point in the context of the chord property and an upper bound on the relative error in radius estimation with regard to the sagitta property are derived. Using these two bounds, a novel algorithm is designed for detecting and parameterizing circles and circular arcs without requiring any heuristic initialization or manual tuning. The chord property is employed for detecting circular arcs, while the sagitta property is used to estimate their centers and radii. To further enhance estimation accuracy, the notion of restricted Hough transform is utilized. Experimental results demonstrate the superior efficiency and robustness of the proposed methodology compared to existing techniques.

title: Improved depth imaging by constrained full-waveform inversion
Abstract: This paper proposes a formulation of full-wavefield inversion (FWI) as a constrained optimization problem and describes a computationally efficient technique for solving constrained full-wavefield inversion (CFWI). This technique leverages a total-variation regularization method, with the regularization weighted to prioritize constraining deeper subsurface model sections. This approach promotes "edge-preserving" blocky model inversion, where fitting the seismic data alone fails to adequately constrain the model. The method is demonstrated on synthetic datasets with added noise and is shown to enhance the sharpness of the inverted model and correctly reposition mispositioned reflectors by better constraining the velocity model at depth.

title: Data Assimilation of Satellite Fire Detection in Coupled Atmosphere-Fire Simulation by WRF-SFIRE
Abstract: Currently available satellite active fire detection products from the VIIRS and MODIS instruments on polar-orbiting satellites produce detection squares in arbitrary locations. There is no global fire/no fire map, no detection under cloud cover, false negatives are common, and the detection squares are much coarser than the resolution of a fire behavior model. As a result, current active fire satellite detection products should be used to improve fire modeling statistically only, rather than as a direct input. This paper describes a new data assimilation method for active fire detection, based on a modification of the fire arrival time to simultaneously minimize the difference from the forecast fire arrival time and maximize the likelihood of the fire detection data. This method is inspired by contour detection methods used in computer vision and can be cast as a Bayesian inverse problem technique, or a generalized Tikhonov regularization. After the new fire arrival time on the whole simulation domain is found, the model can be re-run from a time in the past using the new fire arrival time to generate the heat fluxes and to spin up the atmospheric model until the satellite overpass time, when the coupled simulation continues from the modified state.

title: A Framework for On-Line Devanagari Handwritten Character Recognition
Abstract: The primary challenge in online handwritten character recognition in Indian languages is the large size of the character set, the significant similarity between different characters in the script, and the substantial variation in writing style. This paper proposes a framework for online handwritten script recognition drawing inspiration from speech signal processing literature. The framework focuses on identifying strokes, which in turn lead to the recognition of handwritten online characters, rather than the traditional character identification. While the framework is described for the Devanagari script, it is general and can be applied to any language. The proposed platform consists of pre-processing, feature extraction, recognition, and post-processing, similar to conventional character recognition, but applied to strokes. Online Devanagari character recognition is reduced to recognizing one of 69 primitives, and character recognition is performed by recognizing a sequence of these primitives. The paper further highlights the impact of noise removal on online raw data, which is often noisy. The use of Fuzzy Directional Features to improve the accuracy of stroke recognition is also described. The recognition results are compared with commonly used directional features in the literature using several classifiers.

title: Detecting Figures and Part Labels in Patents: Competition-Based Development of Image Processing Algorithms
Abstract: This paper reports the findings of a month-long online competition where participants developed algorithms for augmenting the digital version of patent documents published by the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO). The goal was to detect figures and part labels in U.S. patent drawing pages. The challenge attracted 232 teams of two, with 70 teams (30%) submitting solutions. Collectively, teams submitted 1,797 solutions that were compiled on the competition servers. Participants reported an average of 63 hours spent developing their solutions, totaling 5,591 hours of development time. A manually labeled dataset of 306 patents was used for training, online system tests, and evaluation. The design and performance of the top-5 systems are presented, along with a system developed after the competition, demonstrating that winning teams produced near state-of-the-art results under strict time and computation constraints. For the 1st place system, the harmonic mean of recall and precision (f-measure) was 88.57% for figure region detection, 78.81% for figure regions with correctly recognized figure titles, and 70.98% for part label detection and character recognition. Data and software from the competition are available through the online UCI Machine Learning repository to inspire further work by the image processing community.

title: On The Effect of Hyperedge Weights On Hypergraph Learning
Abstract: Hypergraphs provide a powerful representation in various computer vision, machine learning, and pattern recognition problems. Over the past decade, many researchers have focused on developing different hypergraph models. However, less attention has been paid to the design of hyperedge weights. Numerous studies on pairwise graphs show that the choice of edge weight can significantly influence the performance of graph algorithms. This paper argues that this principle also applies to hypergraphs. The paper empirically discusses the influence of hyperedge weight on hypergraph learning by proposing three novel hyperedge weights from the perspectives of geometry, multivariate statistical analysis, and linear regression. Extensive experiments on ORL, COIL20, JAFFE, Sheffield, Scene15, and Caltech256 databases verify this hypothesis. Similar to graph learning, several representative hyperedge weighting schemes can be concluded from these experimental studies. Moreover, the experiments demonstrate that combining these weighting schemes with conventional hypergraph models can achieve very promising classification and clustering performances compared to some recent state-of-the-art algorithms. |||

title: A Novel Visual Word Co-occurrence Model for Person Re-identification
Abstract: Person re-identification aims to maintain the identity of an individual across different camera views. This task is challenging due to appearance variations caused by factors like pose, illumination, and camera configuration. To address these difficulties, we introduce a novel visual word co-occurrence model. We first map each image pixel to a visual word using a codebook learned in an unsupervised manner. The appearance transformation between camera views is then encoded by a co-occurrence matrix of visual word joint distributions in probe and gallery images. Our appearance model inherently considers spatial similarities and variations induced by pose, illumination, and camera configuration changes. Finally, linear SVMs are trained as classifiers using these co-occurrence descriptors. On the VIPeR and CUHK Campus benchmark datasets, our method achieves 83.86% and 85.49% at rank-15 on the Cumulative Match Characteristic (CMC) curves, surpassing the state-of-the-art results by 10.44% and 22.27%, respectively.

title: Foreground-Background Segmentation Based on Codebook and Edge Detector
Abstract: Background modeling techniques are widely employed for moving object detection in video sequences. While numerous algorithms exist in this domain, we propose an enhancement to moving object detection based on codebook segmentation. We integrate the original codebook algorithm with an edge detection algorithm. Our aim is to demonstrate the effectiveness of combining an edge detection algorithm with a background modeling algorithm. Our study compares the quality of moving object detection when the codebook segmentation algorithm is paired with several standard edge detectors. We employ frame-based metrics to evaluate the detection performance. The results are presented and analyzed.

title: Density-Based Region Search with Arbitrary Shape for Object Localization
Abstract: Region search is a commonly used technique for object localization. Typically, region search methods project the score of a classifier onto an image plane and then search for the region with the highest score. Recent advancements, such as efficient subwindow search and efficient region search, localize objects from the score distribution on an image and are significantly more efficient than sliding window search. However, for certain classifiers and tasks, the projected scores are predominantly positive, leading to nearly the entire image being localized as the object, rendering the result meaningless. This paper observes that high scores tend to be concentrated on or around objects. Based on this observation, we propose a method called level set maximum-weight connected subgraph (LS-MWCS) that localizes objects with arbitrary shapes by searching regions with the densest score rather than the highest score. The region density can be flexibly controlled by a parameter. We prove an important property of LS-MWCS, guaranteeing the searchability of the region with the densest score. Moreover, LS-MWCS can be efficiently optimized using belief propagation. The method is evaluated on the problem of weakly-supervised object localization, and quantitative results showcase the superior performance of our LS-MWCS compared to other state-of-the-art methods.

title: A Regularization Approach to Blind Deblurring and Denoising of QR Barcodes
Abstract: QR bar codes are prototypical images where part of the image is a priori known (required patterns). Open source bar code readers, such as ZBar, are readily available. We exploit both these facts to propose and evaluate purely regularization-based methods for blind deblurring of QR bar codes in the presence of noise.

title: Canonical Polyadic Decomposition with Auxiliary Information for Brain Computer Interface
Abstract: Physiological signals often exhibit multi-dimensional organization (e.g., channel, time, task, and 3D voxel). Preserving this original structure during processing is crucial. Unlike vector-based methods that destroy data structure, Canonical Polyadic Decomposition (CPD) aims to process physiological signals as multi-way arrays, considering relationships between dimensions and preserving structural information. CPD is currently utilized as an unsupervised method for feature extraction in classification problems. Subsequently, a classifier, such as a support vector machine, is required to classify these features. This approach results in two isolated steps for the classification task. We propose supervised Canonical Polyadic Decomposition by directly incorporating auxiliary label information during decomposition, allowing for classification without an additional classifier training step. The proposed method merges decomposition and classifier learning, simplifying the classification process compared to separate decomposition and classification steps. To evaluate the performance of the proposed method, three different types of signals are used: synthetic signal, EEG signal, and MEG signal. Evaluations based on synthetic and real signals demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed method.

title: Capturing spatial interdependence in image features: the counting grid, an epitomic representation for bags of features
Abstract: Recent scene recognition research often represents images or large image regions as disorganized "bags" of features, which are then analyzed using models originally developed for capturing co-variation of word counts in text. However, image feature counts are likely to be constrained in different ways than word counts in text. For example, as a camera pans upwards from a building entrance over its first few floors and then further up into the sky (Fig. 1), some feature counts in the image decrease while others increase, only to decrease again giving way to features found more frequently at higher elevations. The space of all possible feature count combinations is constrained by both the properties of the larger scene and the size and location of the window into it. To capture such variation, this paper proposes the use of the counting grid model. This generative model is based on a grid of feature counts, significantly larger than any of the modeled images and significantly smaller than the real estate required to tightly tile the images next to each other. Each modeled image is assumed to have a representative window in the grid where the feature counts mimic the feature distribution in the image. We provide a learning procedure that jointly maps all images in the training set to the counting grid and estimates the appropriate local counts within it. Experimentally, we demonstrate that the resulting representation captures the space of feature count combinations more accurately than traditional models, not only when the input images come from a panning camera, but even when modeling images of different scenes from the same category.

title: Motion Estimation via Robust Decomposition with Constrained Rank
Abstract: This work addresses the problem of outlier detection for robust motion estimation by leveraging modern sparse-low-rank decompositions, i.e., Robust PCA-like methods, to impose global rank constraints. Robust decompositions have proven effective in splitting a corrupted matrix into an uncorrupted low-rank matrix and a sparse matrix containing outliers. However, this process only works when matrices have relatively low rank with respect to their ambient space, a property not met in motion estimation problems. As a solution, we propose exploiting the partial information present in the decomposition to identify outlier matches. We provide evidence showing that even when it is not possible to recover an uncorrupted low-rank matrix, the resulting information can be utilized for outlier detection. To this end, we introduce Robust Decomposition with Constrained Rank (RD-CR), a proximal gradient-based method that enforces the rank constraints inherent to motion estimation. We also present a general framework for robust estimation for stereo Visual Odometry, based on RD-CR and a simple yet effective compressed optimization method that achieves high performance. Our evaluation on synthetic data and the KITTI dataset demonstrates the applicability of our approach in complex scenarios and yields state-of-the-art performance.

title: Is it Possible to Accurately Identify a Shooter's Face as Illuminated by the Muzzle Flash of a 22 LR Pistol?
Abstract: The science of firearms muzzle flash has been dominated by three perspectives: 1) Does the muzzle flash reveal friendly positions to naked eye observers, potentially drawing enemy fire? 2) Can flash signatures be recognized by electronic surveillance with sufficient accuracy to identify the source firearms? 3) Is the muzzle flash sufficiently bright to diminish the night vision of friendly forces during a firefight? This paper addresses a fourth question: Does the muzzle flash of a specific cartridge provide sufficient duration and intensity of visible light illumination to allow observers to positively identify a shooter's face? The experiment involved two shooters firing a total of 20 shots from a 22 LR semi-automatic pistol. Shooters fired in randomized order, while eight observers (male US military veterans) attempted to identify the shooter for each trial shot. The firing range was mostly darkened, with only enough ambient light to safely conduct firing tests under the supervision of a range safety officer. There was insufficient ambient light to identify the shooter's face. Observers correctly identified the shooter 54% of the time and failed to do so 46% of the time. Observers unanimously confirmed that there was no visible illumination on the shooter's face provided by the muzzle flash. In cases where the shooter was correctly identified, observers reported using visual cues such as the silhouette of the shooters' hair and slight differences in arm positions when firing the pistol. Other individuals in the room (including the author) unanimously agreed that there was no illumination of the shooters' faces from the discharge of a 22 LR pistol.

title: Salient Object Detection: A Discriminative Regional Feature Integration Approach
Abstract: Salient object detection has garnered considerable attention, leading to the development of various heuristic computational models. This paper formulates saliency map computation as a regression problem. Our method, based on multi-level image segmentation, utilizes a supervised learning approach to map the regional feature vector to a saliency score. Saliency scores across multiple levels are ultimately fused to generate the saliency map. The contributions are twofold. First, we propose a discriminative regional feature integration approach for salient object detection. Compared to existing heuristic models, our proposed method can automatically integrate high-dimensional regional saliency features and select discriminative ones. Second, by investigating standard generic region properties along with two widely studied concepts for salient object detection – regional contrast and backgroundness – our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on six benchmark datasets. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method runs as fast as most existing algorithms.

title: Vehicle Detection and Tracking Techniques: A Concise Review
Abstract: Vehicle detection and tracking applications play a crucial role in both civilian and military domains, finding applications in highway traffic surveillance control, management, and urban traffic planning. Vehicle detection processes on roads are used for various purposes, including vehicle tracking, counting, determining the average speed of individual vehicles, traffic analysis, and vehicle categorization, and can be implemented under varying environmental conditions. This review presents a concise overview of image processing methods and analysis tools utilized in building these applications, focusing on developing traffic surveillance systems. In contrast to other reviews, we classify the processing methods into three categories for greater clarity in explaining traffic systems.
