title: A web-based tool to Analyze Semantic Similarity Networks
Abstract: In computational biology, biological entities like genes and proteins are annotated with terms from Gene Ontology (GO). Semantic Similarity Measures (SSM) are used to evaluate the functional similarity between GO terms. The increasing use of SSMs has led to the development of Semantic Similarity Networks (SSNs), edge-weighted graphs where nodes represent concepts (e.g., proteins) and edge weights represent semantic similarity between related pairs of nodes. Analyzing SSNs can reveal biologically meaningful knowledge. This paper presents SSN-Analyzer, a web-based tool for constructing and preprocessing SSNs. Using community detection algorithms on filtered (thresholded) networks is shown to improve the biological relevance of the results compared to using raw, unfiltered networks.
label: AI

title: SENNS: Sparse Extraction Neural NetworkS for Feature Extraction
Abstract: Drawing inspiration from optimization theory, artificial neural networks (ANNs), graph embeddings, and sparse representations, this paper introduces a novel technique called SENNS (Sparse Extraction Neural NetworkS) for addressing the feature extraction problem. SENNS uses deep ANNs to project input attribute vectors into an output space where distances between vectors from different classes are maximized, while distances between vectors from the same class are minimized, simultaneously enforcing sparsity on the ANN outputs. These projected vectors can then be used as features in any desired classifier. Mathematically, SENNS is formulated as the minimization of an objective function that, in the ANN output space, represents a negative factor of the sum of squared distances between output vectors from different classes, plus a positive factor of the sum of squared distances between output vectors from the same classes, along with sparsity and weight decay terms. To derive an algorithm for minimizing this objective function via gradient descent, the multivariate chain rule is employed to obtain partial derivatives with respect to ANN weights and biases. Each of the required partial derivatives is expressed as a sum of six terms, four of which can be computed using standard backpropagation, the fifth using a slight modification of backpropagation, and the sixth via simple arithmetic. The paper proposes experiments on various datasets, including the ARABASE Arabic corpora of digits and letters, the CMU PIE database of faces, the MNIST digits database, and other standard machine learning databases.
label: AI

title: Quantifying Natural and Artificial Intelligence in Robots and Natural Systems with an Algorithmic Behavioural Test
Abstract: A crucial goal in robotics, artificial intelligence, and artificial life is the creation of systems and machines as versatile and reliable as living organisms in performing complex human-like tasks. However, evaluating artificial systems poses a challenge due to the lack of clear methods for measuring these capabilities in living systems, let alone defining life or intelligence. This paper explores a concrete metric for measuring abstract properties of both natural and artificial systems, such as the ability to respond to the environment and control one's own behavior.
label: AI

title: Qualitative shape representation based on the qualitative relative direction and distance calculus eOPRAm
Abstract: This technical report details the representation and reconstruction of simplified polygons using qualitative spatial descriptions, as defined by the eOPRAm qualitative spatial calculus.
label: AI

title: In Search of the Real Inductive Bias: On the Role of Implicit Regularization in Deep Learning
Abstract: This paper presents experimental evidence suggesting that capacity control mechanisms, distinct from network size, play a significant role in the learning process of multilayer feed-forward networks. By analogy to matrix factorization, the paper argues that this capacity control acts as an inductive bias, providing insights into deep learning.
label: AI

title: KF metamodel formalization
Abstract: The KF metamodel is a comprehensive unifying metamodel encompassing the static structural entities and constraints of UML Class Diagrams (v2.4.1), ER, EER, ORM, and ORM2, aiming to enhance interoperability among common conceptual data modeling languages. Initially designed in UML with textual constraints, this report presents its formalizations in FOL and OWL, complementing the accompanying paper that provides detailed descriptions, discussions, and analyses of the KF metamodel. These new formalizations contribute to defining the metamodel precisely, understanding its complexity properties, and laying the foundation for future implementations.
label: AI

title: Estimating a Common Period for a Set of Irregularly Sampled Functions with Applications to Periodic Variable Star Data
Abstract: This paper addresses the estimation of a common period for a set of functions sampled at irregular intervals, a problem encountered in astronomy where the functions represent a star's brightness observed over time through different photometric filters. While existing methods can accurately estimate periods when the brightness is well-sampled in at least one filter, they lack the capability to provide accurate estimates when no brightness function is well-sampled. Two new methods are introduced for period estimation when brightnesses are poorly-sampled across all filters. The first, multiband generalized Lomb-Scargle (MGLS), extends the widely used Lomb-Scargle method by naively combining information across filters. The second, penalized generalized Lomb-Scargle (PGLS), builds upon MGLS by intelligently borrowing strength across filters. PGLS incorporates constraints on the phases and amplitudes across different functions using a non-convex penalized likelihood function. A fast algorithm is developed to optimize the penalized likelihood by combining block coordinate descent with the majorization-minimization (MM) principle. The effectiveness of these methods is demonstrated using synthetic and real astronomy data, showing that while both advance the state-of-the-art in period estimation, PGLS significantly outperforms MGLS when all functions are extremely poorly-sampled.
label: AI

title: Simplified firefly algorithm for 2D image key-points search
Abstract: Human eyes identify objects by first searching for points or areas with particular properties. These properties are then used to recognize the image or object. This process can serve as a model for developing computer algorithms for image identification. This paper proposes the application of a simplified firefly algorithm for searching key-areas in 2D images. The proposed version of the firefly algorithm is evaluated on a set of input test images, with the results showcasing the efficiency of this evolutionary computation method.
label: AI

title: Grounding Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning Models for Knowledge Transfer
Abstract: Deep machine learning methods effectively reuse low-level representations to generate more abstract high-level representations. Traditionally, deep learning has been applied passively (e.g., for classification). Recently, it has been extended to estimate the value of actions for autonomous agents within the framework of reinforcement learning (RL). Explicit models of the environment can be learned to augment this value function. While "flat" connectionist methods have been used for model-based RL, deep learning has only been applied to model-free variants of RL. This paper proposes a variant of deep model-based RL that allows an agent to learn arbitrarily abstract hierarchical representations of its environment. The research focuses on how these hierarchical representations can be grounded in sensorimotor interactions between an agent and its environment.
label: AI

title: From dependency to causality: a machine learning approach
Abstract: The relationship between statistical dependency and causality is central to all statistical approaches to causal inference. Recent findings in the ChaLearn cause-effect pair challenge have demonstrated that causal directionality can be inferred with high accuracy, even in Markov indistinguishable configurations, using data-driven approaches. This paper proposes a supervised machine learning approach to infer the existence of a directed causal link between two variables in multivariate settings with n>2 variables. The approach relies on the asymmetry of certain conditional (in)dependence relations between the members of the Markov blankets of two causally connected variables. Results indicate that supervised learning methods can be successfully used to extract causal information based on asymmetric statistical descriptors, even for n>2 variate distributions.
label: AI

title: Example Selection For Dictionary Learning
Abstract: Unsupervised learning typically employs an unbiased uniform sampling strategy to ensure learned features accurately reflect the statistical structure of the training data. This paper explores whether active example selection strategies, which select examples based on the current feature estimate, can accelerate learning. Specifically, it investigates the effects of heuristic and saliency-inspired selection algorithms on the dictionary learning task with sparse activations. The results show that certain selection algorithms improve the speed of learning, prompting speculation on the underlying mechanisms for their effectiveness.
label: AI

title: Stochastic Local Search for Pattern Set Mining
Abstract: Local search methods offer a rapid approach to finding high-quality solutions in situations where systematic search methods may be time-consuming. In the context of pattern set mining, exhaustive search methods are not feasible due to the vast search space. This paper proposes the application of stochastic local search to solve pattern set mining, particularly in the task of concept learning. The paper applies various local search algorithms to standard benchmark instances for pattern set mining, revealing promising results for further exploration.
label: AI

title: GraATP: A Graph Theoretic Approach for Automated Theorem Proving in Plane Geometry
Abstract: Automated Theorem Proving (ATP) is an established field in Artificial Intelligence. ATP aims to design systems capable of automatically determining an algorithm to prove or disprove a mathematical claim based on given premises, fundamental postulates, and logical inference. This paper introduces GraATP, a generalized framework for automated theorem proving in plane geometry. GraATP translates geometric entities into graph nodes and their relationships into graph edges. The automated system searches for different paths to reach the conclusion of a claim via graph traversal, thereby verifying the validity of the geometric theorem.
label: AI

title: Decision making based on optical excitation transfer via near-field interactions between quantum dots
Abstract: Optical near-field interactions between nanostructured matter, such as quantum dots, lead to unidirectional optical excitation transfer when energy dissipation is induced. This results in versatile spatiotemporal dynamics of the optical excitation, which can be controlled by manipulating dissipation processes. This control can be exploited to realize intelligent capabilities like solution searching and decision making. This paper demonstrates the experimental ability to solve a decision-making problem based on optical excitation transfer via near-field interactions using colloidal quantum dots of different sizes, deposited on a geometry-controlled substrate. The energy transfer behavior is characterized under multiple control light patterns, experimentally demonstrating the ability to solve the multi-armed bandit problem. This work represents a significant step towards the practical design of nanophotonic systems capable of efficient decision making, one of the most important intellectual attributes of the human brain.
label: AI

title: Revisiting Non-Progressive Influence Models: Scalable Influence Maximization
Abstract: While influence maximization in social networks has been extensively studied in the computer science community for a decade, the focus has been on progressive influence models, such as independent cascade (IC) and Linear threshold (LT) models, which cannot capture the reversibility of choices. This paper introduces the Heat Conduction (HC) model, a non-progressive influence model with real-world interpretations. HC unifies, generalizes, and extends existing nonprogressive models, such as the Voter model and non-progressive LT. It is proven that selecting the optimal seed set of influential nodes is NP-hard for HC; however, by establishing the submodularity of influence spread, the influence maximization problem can be addressed with a scalable and provably near-optimal greedy algorithm. This paper presents the first scalable solution for influence maximization under the nonprogressive LT model, as a special case of the HC model. Unlike other greedy influence maximization methods, the C2GREEDY algorithm benefits from two analytically computable steps: closed-form computation for finding the influence spread and the greedy seed selection. Extensive experiments on large real and synthetic networks demonstrate that C2GREEDY outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of influence spread and scalability.

title: Towards a constructive multilayer perceptron for regression task using non-parametric clustering. A case study of Photo-Z redshift reconstruction
Abstract: Choosing the architecture of an artificial neuron network (ANN) remains a challenging task for users, significantly impacting the accuracy of the built network. There is no single optimal method applicable to all implementations. This paper proposes an ANN construction method based on clustering that addresses the limitations of random and ad hoc approaches for multilayer ANN architecture. This method can be applied to regression problems. Experimental results obtained with different datasets reveal the efficiency of the proposed method.
label: AI

title: H-Index Manipulation by Merging Articles: Models, Theory, and Experiments
Abstract: An author's profile on Google Scholar comprises indexed articles and associated data, such as citation count and H-index. Authors are permitted to merge articles, which can affect their H-index. This paper analyzes the computational complexity of maximizing the H-index using article merges. To model realistic manipulation scenarios, a compatibility graph is defined where edges represent plausible merges. Additionally, different measures are considered for computing the citation count of a merged article. For the measure used by Google Scholar, an algorithm is provided that maximizes the H-index in linear time if the compatibility graph has constant-size connected components. In contrast, if arbitrary article merges are allowed (compatibility graphs that are cliques), then even increasing the H-index by one becomes NP-hard. Experiments on Google Scholar profiles of AI researchers reveal that significant H-index manipulation is only possible when merging articles with highly dissimilar titles. |||

title: Extremal states for photon number and quadratures as gauges for nonclassicality
Abstract: Rotated quadratures carry phase-dependent information about the electromagnetic field, making them essentially conjugate to the photon number. We analyze this noncanonical pair, deriving an exact uncertainty relation along with weaker inequalities obtained by relaxing certain problem constraints. We also identify intelligent states that saturate this relation and fully characterize them by considering additional constraints on the second-order moments of the involved variables. Utilizing these moments, we construct performance measures specifically designed to diagnose photon-added and Schrödinger catlike states, among others.
label: AI

title: Multi-criteria neutrosophic decision making method based on score and accuracy functions under neutrosophic environment
Abstract: A neutrosophic set is a versatile framework that effectively represents uncertainty, imprecision, incompleteness, and inconsistency. This paper introduces novel score and accuracy functions for single-valued neutrosophic sets, enabling their differentiation. The concept is then extended to interval neutrosophic sets. A multi-criteria decision-making method, based on these score-accuracy functions, is developed where criterion values for alternatives are represented by single-valued and interval neutrosophic sets. During the decision-making process, neutrosophic weighted aggregation operators (arithmetic and geometric averages) are employed to aggregate the neutrosophic information associated with each alternative. This allows for ranking all alternatives and selecting the optimal choice(s) using the score-accuracy functions. Finally, illustrative examples are presented to demonstrate the practicality and effectiveness of the proposed approach.
label: AI

title: Deep Learning for Multi-label Classification
Abstract: Multi-label classification focuses on developing methods to learn and leverage the underlying dependencies between labels. While efforts have predominantly aimed at improving feature-space representations to reduce complexity, e.g., by eliminating unhelpful features, this paper explores a different approach. We demonstrate that a carefully designed feature space can significantly reduce label interdependence, simplifying model training and prediction during inference. We utilize a deep learning approach with restricted Boltzmann machines to achieve this. Our deep network, in an empirical evaluation, outperforms several competitive methods from the literature.
label: AI

title: Learning unbiased features
Abstract: A key aspect of transfer learning is representation learning, where the goal is to develop representations that capture the relevant factors underlying the data, facilitating the learning of new tasks and domains based on mappings of these factors. This paper emphasizes the importance of unbiased representations in this process. Different types of representation learning can be derived by considering various definitions of unwanted bias, such as bias towards specific tasks, domains, or irrelevant data dimensions. Maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), a measure of distance between probability distributions, provides a valuable approach to estimating the amount of bias in a representation. While not the first to suggest MMD's utility in developing cross-domain or cross-task representations, we present novel applications of this criterion based on the principle of creating unbiased representations. These applications include a standard domain adaptation framework, a method for learning invariant representations, a noise-insensitive autoencoder approach, and a novel form of generative model.
label: AI

title: Application of Topic Models to Judgments from Public Procurement Domain
Abstract: This work focuses on automatically analyzing themes present in a large corpus of judgments from the public procurement domain. The employed technique is unsupervised Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA). Additionally, we propose combining LDA with a recently developed unsupervised keyword extraction method. This approach enhances the interpretability of the automatically obtained topics and improves computational performance. The described analysis demonstrates the method's potential in detecting recurring themes and discovering temporal trends in lodged contract appeals. These results may be applied in the future to enhance information retrieval from legal text repositories or serve as auxiliary material for legal analysis conducted by human experts.
label: AI

title: Are We Ready for Driver-less Vehicles? Security vs. Privacy- A Social Perspective
Abstract: Autonomous vehicles currently represent a leading technology in the Robotics Research Community. Despite significant advancements in recent years, a fully autonomous car remains a distant reality. This article explores existing systems and examines the potential for Computer Vision-enabled driving to surpass LiDar-based systems. A detailed analysis of privacy violations that may arise from autonomous driving is discussed, encompassing both technical and legal perspectives. Evidence and arguments demonstrate that achieving efficient and accurate estimation and solving the constraint satisfaction problem in autonomous vehicles negatively correlates with user privacy preservation. This presents a challenging trade-off as both safety and privacy are crucial aspects that must be considered. Given the non-negotiable nature of vehicle safety, addressing the potential for serious privacy concerns with adverse social and political implications is unavoidable.
label: AI

title: A Multi-criteria neutrosophic group decision making metod based TOPSIS for supplier selection
Abstract: Multiple criteria decision making (MCDM) involves selecting the best choice from a set of potential alternatives. Supplier selection, where decision-makers often possess vague and imprecise knowledge, exemplifies a typical multi-criteria group decision-making problem. Conventional crisp techniques prove ineffective for solving MCDM problems due to the imprecise and fuzzy nature of linguistic assessments. Obtaining exact values for MCDM problems in real-world scenarios is both difficult and often impossible. Therefore, representing alternative values according to criteria as single-valued neutrosophic sets (SVNS) is more reasonable. This paper explores the Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS) approach and extends it to handle MCDM problems with single-valued neutrosophic information. The value of each alternative and the weight of each criterion are characterized by single-valued neutrosophic numbers. Here, the importance of criteria and alternatives is determined by aggregating individual opinions of decision-makers (DMs) using the single-valued neutrosophic weighted averaging (IFWA) operator. The proposed method is user-friendly, precise, and practical for solving MCDM problems with single-valued neutrosophic data. Finally, a numerical experiment for supplier choice is provided as an application of the single-valued neutrosophic TOPSIS method at the end of this paper.

title: Belief as Willingness to Bet
Abstract: We investigate modal logics of high probability incorporating two unary modal operators: $K$, representing probabilistic certainty, and $B$, expressing probability exceeding a fixed rational threshold $c\geq\frac 12$. Identifying knowledge with $K$ and belief with $B$, we can interpret $c$ as the agent's betting threshold, leading to the motto "belief is willingness to bet." The logic $\\mathsf{KB.5}$ for $c=\frac 12$ features an $\\mathsf{S5}$ $K$ modality alongside a sub-normal $B$ modality extending the minimal modal logic $\\mathsf{EMND45}$ through four schemes relating $K$ and $B$, one of which is a complex scheme derived from a theorem by Scott. Lenzen was the first to employ Scott's theorem to demonstrate the soundness and completeness of a version of this logic for the probability interpretation. We reformulate and present Lenzen's results in a modern and accessible format. Additionally, we introduce a new epistemic neighborhood semantics, more familiar to modern modal logicians. Using Scott's theorem, we provide the Lenzen-derivative properties that must be imposed on finite epistemic neighborhood models to guarantee the existence of a probability measure respecting the neighborhood function appropriately for threshold $c=\frac 12$. This establishes a link between probabilistic and modal neighborhood semantics, which we hope will contribute to future research on modal logics of qualitative probability. The question of which properties must be imposed on finite epistemic neighborhood models to guarantee the existence of an appropriate probability measure for thresholds $c\neq\frac 12$ remains open.

title: Max-Product Belief Propagation for Linear Programming: Applications to Combinatorial Optimization
Abstract: The max-product belief propagation (BP) is a popular message-passing heuristic for approximating the maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) assignment in a joint distribution represented by a graphical model (GM). In recent years, it has been demonstrated that BP can solve specific classes of linear programming (LP) formulations for combinatorial optimization problems, including maximum weight matching, shortest path, and network flow, effectively serving as a message-passing solver for certain combinatorial optimization problems. However, these LPs and corresponding BP analysis are highly sensitive to the underlying problem setup, leaving the extent of their generalizability unclear. This paper establishes generic criteria for BP convergence to the optimal solution of a given LP, proving its satisfaction in LP formulations associated with numerous classical combinatorial optimization problems, including maximum weight perfect matching, shortest path, traveling salesman, cycle packing, vertex/edge cover, and network flow.
label: AI

title: Searching for Extraterrestrial Intelligence with the Square Kilometre Array
Abstract: The vast collecting area of the Square Kilometre Array (SKA), coupled with sensitive receivers, flexible digital electronics, and increased computational capacity, could enable the most sensitive and comprehensive search for technologically-produced radio emissions from advanced extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI) ever undertaken. For instance, SKA1-MID will be capable of detecting a source roughly analogous to terrestrial high-power radars (e.g., air route surveillance or ballistic missile warning radars, EIRP (EIRP = equivalent isotropic radiated power, ~10^17 erg sec^-1) at 10 pc in less than 15 minutes. Additionally, a modest four-beam SETI observing system could search every star in the primary beam out to ~100 pc for radio emission comparable to that emitted by the Arecibo Planetary Radar (EIRP ~2 x 10^20 erg sec^-1) in a single minute. The flexibility of the signal detection systems used for SETI searches with the SKA will allow the implementation of new algorithms, providing sensitivity to a broader range of signal types than previously explored. This paper discusses the astrobiological and astrophysical motivations for radio SETI and explains how the SKA's technical capabilities will explore the radio SETI parameter space. We detail several conceivable SETI experimental programs for all components of SKA1, including commensal, primary-user, targeted, and survey programs, and project the enhancements they could achieve with SKA2. We also discuss target selection criteria for these programs and, in the case of commensal observing, how the diverse use cases of other primary observers can be leveraged for SETI.
label: AI

title: On the Inductive Bias of Dropout
Abstract: Dropout is a simple yet effective technique for learning in neural networks and other settings. A solid theoretical understanding of dropout is crucial to determine its optimal application and use. This paper continues the exploration of dropout as a regularizer initiated by Wager et al. We focus on linear classification where a convex proxy to the misclassification loss (i.e., the logistic loss used in logistic regression) is minimized. Our findings demonstrate: (a) conditions for a unique minimizer of the dropout-regularized criterion, (b) conditions for the dropout-regularization penalty to approach infinity with the weights and when it remains bounded, (c) the non-monotonic nature of dropout regularization as individual weights increase from 0, and (d) the potential non-convexity of the dropout regularization penalty. This last point is particularly surprising given that the combination of dropout regularization with any convex loss proxy always results in a convex function. To contrast dropout regularization with $L_2$ regularization, we formalize the concept of compatibility between different sources and regularizers. We then identify distributions that are demonstrably more compatible with dropout regularization than $L_2$ regularization, and vice versa. These findings provide further insights into the differences in the inductive biases of dropout and $L_2$ regularization. Similar results are also presented for $L_1$ regularization.
label: AI

title: Translating Videos to Natural Language Using Deep Recurrent Neural Networks
Abstract: Solving the visual symbol grounding problem has been a long-standing goal in artificial intelligence. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning for natural language grounding in static images have brought the field closer to this objective. This paper proposes a unified deep neural network, with both convolutional and recurrent structures, to directly translate videos into sentences. Due to the scarcity of described video datasets and the limited vocabulary of most existing methods, our approach leverages knowledge transfer from over 1.2 million images with category labels and 100,000+ images with captions. This enables the creation of sentence descriptions for open-domain videos using large vocabularies. We compare our method with recent work using language generation metrics, subject, verb, and object prediction accuracy, and a human evaluation.

title: Worst-case Optimal Query Answering for Greedy Sets of Existential Rules and Their Subclasses
Abstract: The need for an ontological layer atop data, coupled with advanced reasoning mechanisms capable of exploiting the semantics encoded in ontologies, has been recognized by both database and knowledge representation communities. This paper focuses on the ontological query answering problem, which involves querying data while considering ontological knowledge. Specifically, we analyze the complexity of the conjunctive query entailment problem for classes of existential rules (also known as tuple-generating dependencies, Datalog+/- rules, or forall-exists-rules). Our contribution is twofold. First, we introduce the class of greedy bounded-treewidth sets (gbts) of rules, encompassing guarded rules and their most well-known generalizations. We provide a generic algorithm for query entailment under gbts, which is worst-case optimal for combined complexity with or without bounded predicate arity, as well as for data complexity and query complexity. Second, we classify several gbts classes, whose complexity was previously unknown, with respect to combined complexity (with both unbounded and bounded predicate arity) and data complexity. This provides a comprehensive understanding of the complexity of existential rule fragments based on various guardedness notions. Upper bounds are established by demonstrating the proposed algorithm's optimality for all of them.

title: CITlab ARGUS for historical data tables
Abstract: We present CITlab's recognition system for the ANWRESH-2014 competition, held in conjunction with the 14th International Conference on Frontiers in Handwriting Recognition (ICFHR 2014). The task involves word recognition from segmented historical documents. Our system's core components are based on multi-dimensional recurrent neural networks (MDRNN) and connectionist temporal classification (CTC). The underlying software modules and essential utility technologies are powered by PLANET's ARGUS framework for intelligent text recognition and image processing.

title: Generating Graphical Chain by Mutual Matching of Bayesian Network and Extracted Rules of Bayesian Network Using Genetic Algorithm
Abstract: With technological advancements, the need for analyzing and extracting valuable information is increasing. Bayesian networks encapsulate knowledge derived from data and experts, proving useful for decision-making processes. However, their lack of comprehensibility has led to the use of rule extraction methods, which, in turn, suffer from high computational costs. To address this challenge, we propose extracting rules from Bayesian networks using genetic algorithms. We then generate a graphical chain by mutually matching the extracted rules and the Bayesian network. This graphical chain illustrates the sequence of events leading to the target, facilitating informed decision-making. Experimental results on small networks demonstrate that the proposed method achieves comparable results to the brute force method, while significantly reducing computational costs.
label: AI

title: The Computational Theory of Intelligence: Applications to Genetic Programming and Turing Machines
Abstract: This paper extends the concepts of the Computational Theory of Intelligence (CTI) to encompass computational processes in terms of Genetic Algorithms (GAs) and Turing Machines (TMs). Active, passive, and hybrid computational intelligence processes are introduced and discussed. We examine the implications of CTI assumptions regarding the qualities of reproduction and virility. Applications in Biology, Computer Science, and Cyber Security are also explored.

title: Multi-Context Models for Reasoning under Partial Knowledge: Generative Process and Inference Grammar
Abstract: Obtaining complete probabilistic knowledge of a domain, i.e., learning how all variables interact, is a challenging task. Real-world scenarios often arise where individuals possess only partial knowledge of the domain and are expected to provide adequate answers to various queries. Although precise answers to certain queries may be unattainable, a range of plausible answers can be determined for each query based on the available partial knowledge. This paper introduces the Multi-Context Model (MCM), a novel graphical model for representing the state of partial knowledge regarding a domain. MCM serves as a middle ground between Probabilistic Logic, Bayesian Logic, and Probabilistic Graphical Models. We discuss: (i) the dynamics of constructing a contradiction-free MCM, i.e., forming partial beliefs about a domain in a gradual and probabilistically consistent manner, and (ii) how to perform inference, i.e., evaluate the probability of interest involving specific variables within the domain.
label: AI

title: Combinatorial Structure of the Deterministic Seriation Method with Multiple Subset Solutions
Abstract: Seriation methods order a set of descriptions based on a specific criterion (e.g., unimodality or minimum distance between similarity scores). Seriation inherently involves finding the optimal solution from a set of object permutations. This technical note reviews the combinatorial structure of the classical seriation problem, which seeks a single solution from a set of objects. We then extend these results to the iterative frequency seriation approach introduced by Lipo (1997). This approach finds optimal subsets of objects that each satisfy the unimodality criterion within their respective subsets. The number of possible solutions across multiple solution subsets exceeds $n!$, highlighting the need for novel algorithms and heuristics to aid in the deterministic frequency seriation problem.
label: AI

title: A Robust Transformation-Based Learning Approach Using Ripple Down Rules for Part-of-Speech Tagging
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach for constructing a system of transformation rules for the Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging task. Our approach utilizes an incremental knowledge acquisition method where rules are stored in an exception structure. New rules are added only to correct errors made by existing rules, enabling systematic control of rule interactions. Experimental results on 13 languages demonstrate the approach's fast training time and tagging speed. Moreover, our approach achieves highly competitive accuracy compared to state-of-the-art POS and morphological taggers.
label: AI

title: CITlab ARGUS for historical handwritten documents
Abstract: We describe CITlab's recognition system for the HTRtS competition, held in conjunction with the 14th International Conference on Frontiers in Handwriting Recognition (ICFHR 2014). The task entails the recognition of historical handwritten documents. Our system's core algorithms are based on multi-dimensional recurrent neural networks (MDRNN) and connectionist temporal classification (CTC). The underlying software modules and essential utility technologies are powered by PLANET's ARGUS framework for intelligent text recognition and image processing. |||

title: Belief revision in the propositional closure of a qualitative algebra
Abstract: Belief revision aims to modify existing beliefs to align with new information. This process has been studied in qualitative algebras (QAs), where the result often involves a disjunction of belief bases, which may not be representable in a QA. This motivates exploring belief revision within formalisms extending QAs, specifically their propositional closures. These closures ensure that the outcome of belief revision remains within the formalism. Additionally, the Harper identity allows for the definition of a contraction operator. This paper investigates belief revision within the propositional closure of QAs, presents an algorithm for a family of revision operators, and offers an open-source implementation freely available online.

title: Distinguishing cause from effect using observational data: methods and benchmarks
Abstract: Identifying causal relationships from observational data is a fundamental scientific problem. A simplified version involves determining whether variable X causes variable Y or vice versa, given only joint observations. Despite assumptions of no confounding, feedback loops, or selection bias, bivariate causal discovery remains challenging. This paper reviews two prominent approaches: Additive Noise Methods (ANM) and Information Geometric Causal Inference (IGCI). The CauseEffectPairs benchmark dataset is introduced, comprising data from various domains for 100 cause-effect pairs. The paper provides justification for the "ground truth" causal directions. It evaluates the performance of different bivariate causal discovery methods on both real-world and simulated data. The results indicate that some methods can distinguish cause from effect using solely observational data, though further research is needed for conclusive statistical significance. Notably, the additive-noise method achieves a 63+-10% accuracy and a 0.74+-0.05 AUC on the real-world benchmark, demonstrating its effectiveness. The paper also formally proves the consistency of this method.

title: Feature Weight Tuning for Recursive Neural Networks
Abstract: This paper addresses how recursive neural network models can automatically filter out irrelevant information and prioritize important evidence, effectively performing "weight tuning" for acquiring higher-level representations. Two models are proposed: Weighted Neural Network (WNN) and Binary-Expectation Neural Network (BENN), which dynamically regulate the contribution of individual units to the higher-level representation. This approach can be interpreted as incorporating a more powerful compositional function for embedding acquisition in recursive neural networks. Experimental results demonstrate significant improvements compared to standard neural models.
label: AI

title: Exploiting n-gram location for intrusion detection
Abstract: Signature-based and protocol-based intrusion detection systems (IDS) are employed to detect content-based network attacks. While effective against known attacks and exploits, these systems struggle to identify new attack types or carefully crafted variations. This paper presents an anomaly-based IDS technique designed to detect content-based attacks carried out over application-level protocols like HTTP and FTP. To identify anomalous packets, the payload is segmented into equal-length chunks, and the n-gram technique is used to learn common byte sequences within each chunk. The developed technique builds a distinct model for each <protocol of interest, packet length> pair, using them to classify incoming traffic. Model creation utilizes a semi-supervised approach. Experimental results demonstrate excellent accuracy with a very low false positive rate.
label: AI

title: Quantum computing for pattern classification
Abstract: Quantum computing has demonstrated superiority over classical computing for specific tasks. This paper explores the application of quantum information theory to enhance or expand classical machine learning algorithms. It provides a brief introduction to quantum machine learning using the example of pattern classification. A quantum pattern classification algorithm is presented, based on Trugenberger's proposal for measuring the Hamming distance on a quantum computer (CA Trugenberger, Phys Rev Let 87, 2001), and its advantages are discussed using handwritten digit recognition from the MNIST database.
label: AI

title: Handover Management in Highly Dense Femtocellular Networks
Abstract: Dense femtocells present challenges in integrated femtocell/macrocell network architecture, including the need for a minimal yet effective neighbor cell list, efficient call admission control (CAC), and handover procedures with appropriate signaling. A suitable traffic model for this integrated network is also lacking. This paper addresses mobility management in this context. A novel algorithm is proposed for creating a minimal neighbor cell list for handover, along with detailed handover procedures and a novel traffic model for the integrated network. The proposed CAC effectively handles various calls. Numerical and simulation results highlight the importance of the integrated femtocell/macrocell network and the performance enhancements of the proposed schemes. These schemes offer practical solutions for researchers and industry professionals seeking to implement dense femtocell networks.
label: AI

title: Logic of temporal attribute implications
Abstract: This paper investigates logic for reasoning with if-then formulas that describe dependencies between attributes of objects observed at consecutive time points. Semantic entailment of these formulas is introduced, along with its fixed-point characterization. Model class closure properties are analyzed, an axiomatization is presented and proved complete, and alternative axiomatizations and normalized proofs are explored. Decidability and complexity issues are investigated, proving the NP-hardness and EXPSPACE membership of the entailment problem. By restricting the analysis to predictive formulas, the entailment problem becomes decidable in pseudo-linear time.
label: AI

title: Turing Test for the Internet of Things
Abstract: The advent of the Internet of Things (IoT) and the integration of AI into devices raise the question of how to evaluate the progress of this "smartening" process. While the Turing Test is a standard evaluation tool for AI, it was designed for computers. Applying this test to diverse IoT devices presents several challenges that require adaptation. This paper discusses these challenges and potential solutions.
label: AI

title: fVSS: A New Secure and Cost-Efficient Scheme for Cloud Data Warehouses
Abstract: Cloud business intelligence is gaining popularity as a method for delivering decision support capabilities through elastic, pay-per-use resources. However, data security remains a major concern, particularly when dealing with sensitive information. This paper proposes a novel approach for securing cloud data warehouses using flexible verifiable secret sharing (fVSS). Secret sharing encrypts and distributes data across multiple cloud service providers, ensuring data privacy and availability. fVSS addresses four key limitations of existing secret sharing-based methods. First, it enables data warehouse refresh even when some service providers fail. Second, it supports on-line analysis processing. Third, it enforces data integrity using both inner and outer signatures. Fourth, it allows users to manage cloud warehousing costs by balancing the workload across service providers based on their pricing policies.  The paper provides a comprehensive comparison of fVSS with existing approaches, highlighting its advantages in terms of security features, querying power, and data storage and computing costs.
label: AI

title: Appropriate Causal Models and the Stability of Causation
Abstract: Causal models defined using structural equations offer a powerful representation of causal knowledge. However, several authors have presented examples suggesting that the Halpern-Pearl (HP) definition of causality yields counterintuitive results. This paper demonstrates that for each of these examples, two stories can be constructed that are consistent with the provided description but yield contrasting intuitions regarding causality. By introducing additional variables, the stories can be disambiguated. In the resulting causal models, the HP definition of causality provides the intuitively correct answer. The paper also shows that adding extra variables may render a modification to the original HP definition, introduced to address an example by Hopkins and Pearl, unnecessary. While adding extra variables can be beneficial, there is a potential concern that causality may be unstable. The paper addresses this concern by showing that adding extra variables in a "conservative" manner, preserving all relations between the original variables, can lead to an infinite alternation between "yes" and "no" answers to the question "Is X=x a cause of Y=y?". However, if normality is considered, this alternation is impossible. Under suitable normality assumptions, adding an extra variable can change the answer from "yes" to "no", but cannot reverse this change back to "yes".
label: AI

title: Quantum Deep Learning
Abstract: Deep learning has significantly impacted machine learning and artificial intelligence in recent years. Simultaneously, quantum computer algorithms have shown the ability to efficiently solve problems intractable for classical computers. This paper demonstrates that quantum computing not only accelerates the training of deep restricted Boltzmann machines but also provides a more comprehensive framework for deep learning than classical computing, leading to substantial improvements in the optimization of the underlying objective function. Quantum methods also allow for the efficient training of full Boltzmann machines and multi-layer, fully connected models, lacking analogous classical counterparts.
label: AI

title: Teaching Deep Convolutional Neural Networks to Play Go
Abstract: Mastering the game of Go has long posed a challenge for the field of AI. Modern computer Go systems rely on analyzing millions of potential future positions to play effectively, but intuitively, a stronger and more "humanlike" approach would involve pattern recognition rather than brute force computation. This paper explores training deep convolutional neural networks to play Go by learning to predict the moves of expert Go players.  Novel techniques are introduced, including a method for tying weights within the network to "hard code" expected symmetries in the target function. Ablation studies demonstrate the significant performance enhancements achieved by these techniques. The resulting networks achieve move prediction accuracies of 41.1% and 44.4% on two different Go datasets, exceeding previous state-of-the-art results by considerable margins. Importantly, unlike previous move prediction programs, the trained networks exhibit high levels of skill. These convolutional neural networks consistently defeat the well-known Go program GNU Go, showcasing state-of-the-art performance among programs that do not utilize Monte Carlo Tree Search. Additionally, they can even win games against the state-of-the-art Go program Fuego while utilizing significantly less play time. This success in playing Go demonstrates the acquisition of high-level game principles by the networks.
label: AI

title: The category of networks of ontologies
Abstract: The semantic web has led to the deployment of ontologies on the web interconnected through various relationships, particularly alignments of their vocabularies.  Different semantics exist for these alignments, posing challenges for interoperability across different interpretations of ontology networks. This paper proposes an abstraction of these semantics that allows for defining the concepts of closure and consistency for networks of ontologies independently of the specific semantics. Additionally, it is shown that networks of ontologies with particular morphisms define categories of ontology networks.
label: AI

title: Bach in 2014: Music Composition with Recurrent Neural Network
Abstract: This paper proposes a framework for computer music composition using resilient propagation (RProp) and long short term memory (LSTM) recurrent neural networks. The paper demonstrates that LSTM networks can effectively learn the structure and characteristics of music pieces by showcasing their ability to recreate music. It also demonstrates that predicting existing music using RProp outperforms Back propagation through time (BPTT).
label: AI

title: Computoser - rule-based, probability-driven algorithmic music composition
Abstract: This paper introduces the Computoser hybrid probability/rule-based algorithm for music composition (http://computoser.com) and provides a reference implementation. It addresses the issues of unpleasantness and lack of variation commonly found in existing approaches by combining the two methods, basing rule parameters on data obtained from preliminary analysis.  A sample of over 500 musical pieces was analyzed to derive probabilities for musical characteristics and events (e.g., scale, tempo, intervals). The algorithm was designed to generate music using these derived probabilities combined with a comprehensive set of composition rules, obtained and structured based on established composition practices. Generated pieces were published on the Computoser website, where evaluation was conducted by listeners. The feedback was positive (58.4% approval), validating the merits of this hybrid approach. The paper compares this approach to other algorithmic composition methods and presents a survey of the pleasantness of the resulting music.
label: AI

title: Hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts Model for Large-Scale Gaussian Process Regression
Abstract: This paper presents a practical and scalable Gaussian process model for large-scale nonlinear probabilistic regression. This mixture-of-experts model is conceptually simple and hierarchically recombines computations to approximate a full Gaussian process. Closed-form and distributed computations enable efficient and massive parallelization while keeping memory consumption low. With sufficient computing resources, the model can handle arbitrarily large datasets without explicit sparse approximations. Strong experimental evidence shows its applicability to datasets exceeding millions of entries. Consequently, this model has the potential to lay the foundation for general large-scale Gaussian process research.

title: The Computational Complexity of Structure-Based Causality
Abstract: Halpern and Pearl introduced a definition of actual causality. Eiter and Lukasiewicz demonstrated the NP-completeness of computing whether X=x is a cause of Y=y in binary models (where variables have two values) and the Σ_2^P-completeness in general models. Halpern and Pearl slightly modified the definition of actual cause in the final version of their paper to address problems pointed out by Hopkins and Pearl. As shown in this paper, this modification has a significant impact on the complexity of computing actual cause. To characterize this complexity, a new family D_k^P, k= 1, 2, 3, ..., of complexity classes is introduced, generalizing the class DP (DP is simply D_1^P). The paper demonstrates that the complexity of computing causality under the updated definition is D_2^P-complete. Chockler and Halpern extended the definition of causality by introducing notions of responsibility and blame. The complexity of determining the degree of responsibility and blame using the original definition of causality was fully characterized. Again, this paper shows that changing the definition of causality affects the complexity, and provides a complete characterization using the updated definition.

title: Nested Sparse Approximation: Structured Estimation of V2V Channels Using Geometry-Based Stochastic Channel Model
Abstract: Future intelligent transportation systems promise increased safety and energy efficiency. Realizing these systems will require vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) communication technology. High-fidelity V2V communication, in turn, relies on accurate V2V channel estimation. V2V channels possess distinct characteristics compared to traditional cellular communication channels. This paper employs geometry-based stochastic modeling to develop a characterization of V2V channels. The resulting model exhibits significant structure, with the V2V channel characterized by three distinct regions within the delay-Doppler plane. Each region features a unique combination of specular reflections and diffuse components, leading to specific element-wise and group-wise sparsity. This joint sparsity structure is exploited to develop a novel channel estimation algorithm. A general framework is provided to solve the jointly element/group sparse channel (signal) estimation problem using proximity operators of a broad class of regularizers. The alternating direction method of multipliers using the proximity operator is adapted to optimize the mixed objective function. The paper proves key properties of the proposed objective functions that ensure the optimal solution is found by the new algorithm. The effects of pulse shape leakage are explicitly characterized and compensated, resulting in measurable performance improvements. Numerical simulations and real V2V channel measurement data are used to evaluate the performance of the proposed method. Results demonstrate significant gains over previously proposed methods.

title: Cause, Responsibility, and Blame: oA Structural-Model Approach
Abstract: This paper revisits a definition of causality introduced by Halpern and Pearl, utilizing structural equations. A more refined definition is then considered, incorporating notions of normality and typicality, factors known to influence causal ascriptions. Causality is typically an all-or-nothing concept; either A is a cause of B, or it is not. An extension of the definition of causality to capture degrees of responsibility and blame, developed by Chockler and Halpern, is reviewed. For example, if someone wins an election with a large margin, each person who votes for them is less responsible for the victory than if the margin was narrow. Degree of blame takes into account an agent's epistemic state.  Roughly speaking, the degree of blame of A for B is the expected degree of responsibility of A for B, averaged over the agent's epistemic state. Finally, the structural-equations definition of causality is compared to Wright's NESS test.

title: Plan or not: Remote Human-robot Teaming with Incomplete Task Information
Abstract: Human-robot interaction can be categorized based on the physical distance between the human and robot: remote and proximal. In proximal interaction, humans and robots engage in close coordination, whereas in remote interaction, communication constraints lead to looser coupling. As a result, automation becomes more crucial in remote interaction. Human factor studies on automation in remote human-robot interaction have mainly focused on various forms of supervision, essentially utilizing the robot as a smart mobile manipulation platform with sensing capabilities. This paper investigates incorporating general planning capability into the robot to facilitate peer-to-peer human-robot teaming, where the human and robot are considered teammates physically separated. They share a common goal and collaborate to achieve it. It's important to note that humans might feel uncomfortable with such robot autonomy, potentially affecting teaming performance. A key distinction between peer-to-peer teaming and supervised teaming is that an autonomous robot in peer-to-peer teaming can achieve the goal independently when task information is complete. However, incompleteness often exists, leading to information asymmetry. While information asymmetry can be advantageous, it can also lead to the robot making inappropriate decisions that negatively impact teaming performance. This paper aims to investigate the various trade-offs, such as mental workload and situation awareness, between these two types of remote human-robot teaming. |||

title: Unsupervised Induction of Semantic Roles within a Reconstruction-Error Minimization Framework
Abstract: We propose a novel approach for unsupervised estimation of feature-rich semantic role labeling models. Our model integrates two components: an encoding component, which predicts roles based on syntactic and lexical features, and a reconstruction component, a tensor factorization model that uses roles to predict argument fillers. Jointly minimizing errors in argument reconstruction encourages the learned roles to align with those defined in annotated resources. Our method achieves comparable performance to the most accurate role induction methods on English and German, despite not relying on prior linguistic knowledge about the languages.

title: A New Approach of Learning Hierarchy Construction Based on Fuzzy Logic
Abstract: Adaptive learning systems increasingly rely on learning hierarchies to personalize their educational logic. Existing approaches often neglect the fuzzy nature of prerequisite relationships between skills. This paper introduces a new approach that applies fuzzy logic techniques to the construction of learning hierarchies. We utilize a learning hierarchy predefined by experts, acknowledging that prerequisite relationships are not absolute but fuzzy. We quantify the relevance degree of relationships within the hierarchy, aiming to determine if the predefined prerequisites are correctly established.

title: A tool for implementation of a domain model based on fuzzy relationships
Abstract: Domain models play a crucial role in adaptive learning systems, enabling them to automatically generate customized courses for learners. This paper presents a new tool for implementing domain models based on fuzzy relationships among concepts. This tool empowers experts and teachers to identify optimal parameters for adapting to individual learner differences.

title: When Computer Vision Gazes at Cognition
Abstract: Joint attention, a fundamental form of social interaction, relies on our ability to discern the objects other people are looking at. While we are adept at determining if someone is looking directly at us, our ability to discriminate gaze directed at distant objects, especially in unconstrained situations, remains unclear. This paper investigates this question by combining human psychophysics with a cognitively motivated computer vision model that detects gaze direction from 2D face images. Our results show that human accuracy in discriminating targets 8-10 degrees of visual angle apart is around 40% in a free-looking gaze task, and that individual differences in interpreting gaze exist, which are captured by the computational model. While humans outperform the current model, these findings demonstrate the impressive acuity of human joint attention, highlighting the computational challenges of natural looking tasks.  Further research is needed to understand the underlying mechanisms employed by humans for this complex task.

title: Cells in Multidimensional Recurrent Neural Networks
Abstract: Handwritten text transcription on images is a common machine learning task, often addressed using multi-dimensional recurrent neural networks (MDRNNs) with connectionist temporal classification (CTC). MDRNNs can incorporate long short-term memory (LSTM) cells, capable of learning long-term dependencies. However, their stability diminishes when the dimension exceeds one. This paper defines crucial properties for the one-dimensional LSTM cell and extends them to the multi-dimensional case, introducing new cells with improved stability. We present a method for designing these cells using the theory of linear shift-invariant systems. Comparing the new cells to LSTM cells on the IFN/ENIT and Rimes databases shows improved recognition rates, suggesting their potential for enhancing applications where LSTM cells are used in MDRNNs.

title: Computational Protein Design Using AND/OR Branch-and-Bound Search
Abstract: Determining the global minimum energy conformation (GMEC) is a significant and challenging problem in structure-based computational protein design. This paper proposes a new protein design algorithm based on the AND/OR branch-and-bound (AOBB) search, a variation of the traditional branch-and-bound algorithm, to tackle this combinatorial optimization problem. By integrating a powerful heuristic function, AOBB efficiently exploits the graph structure of the residue interaction network within a backbone template, significantly accelerating the design process. Testing on real protein data demonstrates the ability of our new algorithm to solve problems previously intractable for traditional exact search algorithms. Moreover, for problems solvable by conventional methods, our algorithm offers significant speedup while guaranteeing the identification of the GMEC solution.

title: Phishing Detection in IMs using Domain Ontology and CBA - An innovative Rule Generation Approach
Abstract: User ignorance regarding communication services like instant messengers, emails, websites, and social networks is exploited by phishers. Addressing this issue requires raising user awareness through educational initiatives and developing phishing detection applications. These applications should provide timely alerts, preventing users from inadvertently ignoring phishing messages. The lack of basic security features to detect and prevent phishing has profoundly impacted IM clients, eroding trust in e-banking and e-commerce transactions, potentially causing significant damage to corporate, banking, and internet-reliant sectors. Research on phishing detection in instant messengers is limited. This paper proposes a context-based, dynamic, and intelligent phishing detection methodology for IMs, utilizing domain ontology (OBIE) to analyze and detect phishing in instant messages. It employs Classification based on Association (CBA) to generate phishing rules and alert victims. A PDS Monitoring system algorithm identifies phishing activity during message exchanges, achieving high precision and recall rates. Results demonstrate improved precision and recall compared to existing methods.

title: Learning Word Representations from Relational Graphs
Abstract: Attributes of words and relationships between words are central to numerous tasks in Artificial Intelligence, including knowledge representation, similarity measurement, and analogy detection. Shared attributes often indicate semantic relationships between words, while numerous semantic relations between words imply the inheritance of attributes. Motivated by this close connection, we propose a method for learning latent representations of individual words within a relational graph where words are interconnected through semantic relations. Our approach considers not only word co-occurrence but also the semantic relations in which they co-occur. We evaluate the accuracy of learned word representations by applying them to solve semantic word analogy problems. Our experiments demonstrate the potential for learning more effective word representations by incorporating semantic relations between words.

title: On the Behavioural Formalization of the Cognitive Middleware AWDRAT
Abstract: This paper presents ongoing work and initial results towards the (behavioral) correctness analysis of the cognitive middleware AWDRAT. Provable behavioral correctness is fundamental for a software system's security. Therefore, we aim to formally define the behavioral semantics of the middleware as a prerequisite for proving its behavioral correctness. This paper focuses on the core and critical component of the middleware, the Execution Monitor, which is part of the "Architectural Differencer" module of AWDRAT. The Execution Monitor identifies inconsistencies between runtime observations of the target system and predictions from the specification System Architectural Model. We formalize the denotational semantics of observations (runtime events) and predictions (executable specifications) and use these formal semantics to formalize the behavior of the "Execution Monitor."

title: Visual Causal Feature Learning
Abstract: We provide a rigorous definition of the visual cause of a behavior, applicable to visually driven behavior in humans, animals, neurons, robots, and other perceiving systems. Our framework generalizes standard accounts of causal learning to settings where causal variables need to be constructed from micro-variables. We prove the Causal Coarsening Theorem, which enables us to gain causal knowledge from observational data with minimal experimental effort. The theorem connects to standard inference techniques in machine learning that identify image features correlated with, but not necessarily causing, the target behavior. We propose an active learning scheme to learn a manipulator function that optimizes image manipulations for automatically identifying the visual cause of a target behavior. Experiments using both synthetic and real data illustrate our inference and learning algorithms.

title: Possible and Necessary Allocations via Sequential Mechanisms
Abstract: Sequential allocation, where agents take turns selecting items, is a simple mechanism for allocating indivisible resources. This paper focuses on possible and necessary allocation problems, investigating whether allocations of a specific form occur in some or all mechanisms within various commonly used classes of sequential allocation mechanisms. We specifically consider whether a given agent receives a given item, a set of items, or a subset of items for five natural classes of sequential allocation mechanisms: balanced, recursively balanced, balanced alternating, strictly alternating, and all policies. We identify characterizations of allocations produced by balanced, recursively balanced, balanced alternating policies, and strictly alternating policies, extending the well-known characterization by Brams and King [2005] for unrestricted policies. Additionally, we analyze the computational complexity of possible and necessary allocation problems for these classes.

title: Declarative Statistical Modeling with Datalog
Abstract: Formalisms for specifying statistical models, such as probabilistic programming languages, typically involve two components: a specification of a stochastic process (the prior) and a specification of observations that restrict the probability space to a conditional subspace (the posterior). These formalisms have applications in machine learning and artificial intelligence. We propose and investigate a declarative framework for specifying statistical models on top of a database through an appropriate extension of Datalog. Our framework leverages the inherent integration with the database provided by Datalog and possesses a robust declarative semantics. Our Datalog extension facilitates the inclusion of numerical probability functions, allowing rule conclusions to contain values drawn from such functions. The semantics of a program is a probability distribution over the possible outcomes of the input database with respect to the program; these outcomes are minimal solutions with respect to a related program with existentially quantified variables in conclusions. Observations are naturally integrated using integrity constraints over the extensional and intensional relations. We focus on programs using discrete numerical distributions, although even then the space of possible outcomes may be uncountable. We define a probability measure over possible outcomes by applying the concept of cylinder sets to a probabilistic chase procedure. We demonstrate the robustness of the resulting semantics under different chases and identify conditions guaranteeing the finiteness of all possible outcomes (resulting in a discrete probability space). We argue that our proposed framework retains the purely declarative nature of Datalog while enabling natural specifications of statistical models.

title: Using Artificial Neural Network Techniques for Prediction of Electric Energy Consumption
Abstract: Due to imprecision and uncertainties in real-world problems, artificial neural network (ANN) techniques have become increasingly valuable for modeling and optimization. This paper presents an ANN approach for forecasting electric energy consumption. Effective planning and operation of power systems require optimal forecasting tools to maximize profit and enhance consumer satisfaction. Monthly data for electric energy consumption in the Gaza Strip from 1994 to 2013 was collected and used to train and validate the proposed model using 2-Fold and K-Fold cross-validation techniques. The model was tested with actual energy consumption data and achieved satisfactory performance.

title: Rule reasoning for legal norm validation of FSTP facts
Abstract: Non-obviousness or inventive step is a fundamental requirement for patentability in most patent law systems. An invention must demonstrate a sufficient distance beyond its prior art to be eligible for patent protection. This brief paper provides an overview of a proposed methodology for validating FSTP facts (facts relating to non-obviousness) using a rule reasoning approach.

title: A Portfolio Approach to Algorithm Selection for Discrete Time-Cost Trade-off Problem
Abstract: The performance of optimization algorithms for NP-Hard problems varies considerably across different instances. This observation applies to multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs) when applied to six benchmark instances of the discrete time-cost trade-off problem (DTCTP) in construction projects. Instead of relying on a single algorithm, this paper proposes a portfolio approach that utilizes multiple algorithms. We introduce a portfolio comprising four MOEAs: Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II), Strength Pareto Evolutionary Algorithm II (SPEA-II), Pareto archive evolutionary strategy (PAES), and Niched Pareto Genetic Algorithm II (NPGA-II) to solve DTCTP. Results demonstrate that the portfolio approach is computationally efficient and qualitatively superior to its constituent algorithms for all benchmark instances. Moreover, the portfolio approach provides insights into selecting the best algorithm for each DTCTP benchmark instance.

title: Deep Neural Networks are Easily Fooled: High Confidence Predictions for Unrecognizable Images
Abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have recently achieved state-of-the-art performance on various pattern recognition tasks, particularly in visual classification problems. Given the near-human-level performance of DNNs in object classification, questions arise about the remaining differences between computer and human vision. A recent study revealed that imperceptible image modifications (e.g., of a lion) can cause a DNN to misclassify the image (e.g., labeling a lion as a library). This paper presents a related finding: it is easily possible to create images that are completely unrecognizable to humans but that state-of-the-art DNNs confidently label as recognizable objects with 99.99% certainty (e.g., labeling white noise as a lion). We demonstrate this by employing convolutional neural networks trained on ImageNet or MNIST datasets and using evolutionary algorithms or gradient ascent to find images that DNNs confidently classify as belonging to each dataset class. These "fooling images" (or fooling examples) are completely unrecognizable to humans but are confidently classified as familiar objects by DNNs. Our findings highlight intriguing differences between human vision and current DNNs, raising questions about the generality of DNN computer vision.

title: Knowledge, Justification, and Adequate Reasons
Abstract: Is knowledge definable as justified true belief ("JTB")? We argue that a positive or negative answer is legitimate, depending on whether one's true belief is justified by what we term adequate reasons. To facilitate our argument, we introduce a simple propositional logic of reason-based belief and provide an axiomatic characterization of the notion of adequacy for reasons. We show that this logic is flexible enough to accommodate various useful features, including quantification over reasons. Our framework allows us to contrast two notions of JTB: one internalist, the other externalist. We contend that Gettier cases challenge the internalist notion but not the externalist one. Our approach commits us to a form of infallibilism about knowledge but also presents a puzzle: does knowledge involve only adequate reasons, or does it allow for inadequate reasons? We favor the latter position, which reflects a milder and more realistic version of infallibilism.

title: Symmetric Weighted First-Order Model Counting
Abstract: The FO Model Counting problem (FOMC) involves determining the number of models of a first-order logic sentence $\Phi$ over a domain of size $n$. The Weighted variant (WFOMC) generalizes this problem by associating a weight to each tuple and defining the weight of a model as the product of weights of its tuples. This paper investigates the complexity of the symmetric WFOMC, where all tuples within a given relation share the same weight. This problem has important applications in inference within knowledge bases with soft constraints, like Markov Logic Networks, and is also of theoretical interest. We examine both data complexity and combined complexity for FOMC and WFOMC. For data complexity, we prove the existence of an FO$^3$ formula for which FOMC is #P$_1$-complete and the existence of a Conjunctive Query for which WFOMC is #P$_1$-complete. We also demonstrate that all $\gamma$-acyclic queries have polynomial time data complexity. Regarding combined complexity, we prove that for every fragment FO$^k$, $k\geq 2$, the combined complexity of FOMC (or WFOMC) is #P-complete.

title: On the abundance of extraterrestrial life after the Kepler mission
Abstract: Data accumulated by the Kepler mission has revealed the prevalence of small planets and suggests that a significant fraction of all stars may host an Earth-like planet within their Habitable Zone. These findings are combined with a Drake-equation formalism to derive the space density of biotic planets, considering uncertainty in astronomical data and the unknown probability of biotic life evolution, $F_b$. We propose that $F_b$ can be estimated through future spectral observations of exoplanet biomarkers. If $F_b$ falls within the range of 0.001 to 1, a biotic planet could be expected within 10 to 100 light years from Earth. Extrapolating these biotic results to advanced life, we derive expressions for the distance to putative civilizations using two additional Drake parameters: the probability of civilization evolution, $F_c$, and its average longevity. Assuming optimistic probability values ($F_b F_c$ = 1) and a broadcasting longevity of a few thousand years, the likely distance to the nearest detectable civilizations would be of the order of a few thousand light years. We calculate the probability of detecting intelligent signals with current and future radio telescopes as a function of the Drake parameters. Finally, we discuss how detecting intelligent signals would constrain the Drake parameters. |||

title: Highly comparative fetal heart rate analysis
Abstract: A database containing fetal heart rate (FHR) time series from 7221 patients during labor was analyzed to identify features associated with low cord pH. Over 9000 time-series analysis features were extracted from each FHR recording, including measures of autocorrelation, entropy, distribution, and various model fits. This extensive feature set, derived from prior work, is publicly available. The study identified five features that most accurately classified a balanced training set of 59 'low pH' and 59 'normal pH' FHR recordings. Additionally, five features were identified with the strongest linear correlation to cord pH across the full dataset. These identified features can serve as part of a system for guiding interventions during labor in the future. This research successfully demonstrates the value of comparative analysis across a broad, interdisciplinary literature on time-series analysis to automatically generate new scientific findings for specific biomedical signal processing challenges.

title: Approximate Lifted Inference with Probabilistic Databases
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach for approximate evaluation of #P-hard queries in probabilistic databases. The proposed method evaluates every query entirely within the database engine by evaluating a fixed number of query plans, each providing an upper bound on the true probability, and then taking their minimum. An algorithm is presented that considers essential schema information to enumerate only the minimal necessary plans among all possible plans. This algorithm is a strict generalization of all known results for PTIME self-join-free conjunctive queries, meaning that a query is safe if and only if the algorithm returns a single plan. Three relational query optimization techniques are applied to evaluate all minimal safe plans efficiently. The paper provides a detailed experimental evaluation of this approach, highlighting the value of probabilistic methods over non-probabilistic methods for ranking query answers.

title: Semantic HMC for Big Data Analysis
Abstract: Analyzing Big Data can enhance corporate efficiency. This paper presents a novel vision for extracting value from Big Data using Semantic Hierarchical Multi-label Classification (Semantic HMC), based on an unsupervised Ontology learning process. The paper proposes a Semantic HMC process that leverages scalable Machine-Learning techniques and Rule-based reasoning.

title: Expressiveness of Logic Programs under General Stable Model Semantics
Abstract: The stable model semantics has been generalized to non-Herbrand structures, providing a unified framework and solid logical foundation for answer set programming. This paper investigates the expressiveness of normal and disjunctive programs under the general stable model semantics. A translation from disjunctive programs to normal programs is proposed for infinite structures. Over finite structures, it is proven that some disjunctive programs are intranslatable to normal programs if the arities of auxiliary predicates and functions are bounded in a specific way. The equivalence of the expressiveness of normal programs and disjunctive programs over arbitrary structures is shown to coincide with that over finite structures and with whether NP is closed under complement. Moreover, to capture the exact expressiveness, intertranslatability results between logic program classes and fragments of second-order logic are obtained.
