title: Optimal Tourist Problem and Anytime Planning of Trip Itineraries
Abstract: We introduce and study the problem in which a mobile sensing robot (our tourist) is tasked with traveling among and gathering intelligence at a set of spatially distributed points of interest (POIs). The quality of the information collected at each POI is characterized by some non-decreasing reward function over the time spent at the POI. With a limited time budget, the robot must balance between spending time traveling to POIs and spending time at POIs for information collection (sensing) to maximize the total reward. Alternatively, the robot may be required to acquire a minimum amount of reward and aims to do so with the least amount of time. We propose a mixed integer programming (MIP)-based anytime algorithm for solving these two NP-hard optimization problems to arbitrary precision. The effectiveness of our algorithm is demonstrated using an extensive set of computational experiments, including planning a realistic itinerary for a first-time tourist in Istanbul.

title: Non-myopic learning in repeated stochastic games
Abstract: In repeated stochastic games (RSGs), an agent must quickly adapt to the behavior of previously unknown associates, who may themselves be learning. This machine-learning problem is particularly challenging due, in part, to the presence of multiple (even infinite) equilibria and inherently large strategy spaces. This paper introduces a method to reduce the strategy space of two-player general-sum RSGs to a handful of expert strategies. This process, called Mega, effectively reduces an RSG to a bandit problem. We demonstrate that the resulting strategy space preserves several important properties of the original RSG, enabling a learner to produce robust strategies within a reasonably small number of interactions. To better establish the strengths and weaknesses of this approach, we empirically evaluate the resulting learning system against other algorithms in three different RSGs.
label: AI

title: An agent-driven semantical identifier using radial basis neural networks and reinforcement learning
Abstract: Due to the vast availability of documents in digital form and the increased potential for deception related to the essence of digital documents and their dissemination, the authorship attribution problem has become increasingly relevant. Today, authorship attribution, for both information retrieval and analysis, has gained significant importance in the context of security, trust, and copyright preservation. This work proposes an innovative multi-agent driven machine learning technique developed for authorship attribution. Through preprocessing for word-grouping and time-period-related analysis of the common lexicon, we determine a bias reference level for the recurrence frequency of words within analyzed texts. We then train a Radial Basis Neural Networks (RBPNN)-based classifier to identify the correct author. The primary advantage of the proposed approach lies in the generality of the semantic analysis, which can be applied to different contexts and lexical domains without requiring any modification. Moreover, the proposed system is able to incorporate external input to tune the classifier and then self-adjust through continuous learning reinforcement.

title: Interference Effects in Quantum Belief Networks
Abstract: Probabilistic graphical models, such as Bayesian Networks, are among the most powerful structures known to the Computer Science community for deriving probabilistic inferences. However, modern cognitive psychology has revealed that human decisions may not follow the rules of classical probability theory, as humans cannot process large amounts of data to make judgments. Consequently, the inferences performed are based on limited data coupled with several heuristics, leading to violations of the law of total probability. This implies that probabilistic graphical models based on classical probability theory are too limited to fully simulate and explain various aspects of human decision-making. Quantum probability theory was developed to accommodate the paradoxical findings that classical theory could not explain. Recent findings in cognitive psychology have revealed that quantum probability can fully describe human decisions within an elegant framework. Their findings suggest that, before making a decision, human thoughts are seen as superimposed waves that can interfere with each other, influencing the final decision. This work proposes a new Bayesian Network based on the psychological findings of cognitive scientists. We conducted experiments using two well-known Bayesian Networks from the literature. The results obtained indicated that the quantum-like Bayesian Network can drastically affect probabilistic inferences, especially when the levels of uncertainty in the network are very high (no pieces of evidence observed). When the levels of uncertainty are very low, the proposed quantum-like network collapses to its classical counterpart. |||

title: Computational Beauty: Aesthetic Judgment at the Intersection of Art and Science
Abstract: Immanuel Kant argued that aesthetic judgment is not cognitive but rather based on subjective experience. While the nature of aesthetic discernment has been extensively debated, the role of those who make such judgments has often been assumed rather than questioned. Art historians, critics, connoisseurs, and curators have long held the position of aesthetic judges, relying on their training, intuition, and experience. The rise of artificial intelligence (AI), specifically computer vision analysis, presents a new challenge to the perceived ineffability of human aesthetic judgment. This paper examines the implications of computer vision technology in the field of art history, focusing on its application to canonical Western art movements and the reactions of art historians to its use. By investigating the ethical consequences of this technology, the paper challenges the unquestioned authority of art experts and reignites the philosophical debate surrounding the subjective nature of aesthetic judgment.

title: Medical diagnosis as pattern recognition in a framework of information compression by multiple alignment, unification and search
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to medical diagnosis based on the SP theory of computing and cognition. The approach offers several advantages: a simple and intuitive representation of diseases, the ability to handle errors and uncertainties in diagnostic information, the ease of storing statistical information as frequencies of disease occurrence, a method for evaluating alternative diagnostic hypotheses that generates true probabilities, and a framework that facilitates unsupervised learning of medical knowledge and integration with other AI applications.

title: Autonomous robots and the SP theory of intelligence
Abstract: This article explores the potential of the "SP theory of intelligence" and its embodiment in the "SP machine" to address challenges in designing autonomous robots. The SP system aims to create robots that are independent of external intelligence or power sources, exhibit mobility, and possess human-like intelligence. The article focuses on three key areas: enhancing computational and energy efficiency in computers, achieving human-like versatility in intelligence, and enabling human-like adaptability in intelligence. The SP system offers potential for significant gains in computational and energy efficiency and reductions in the bulkiness of computers through data reduction, exploitation of statistical information, and a revised version of Hebb's concept of a "cell assembly". In terms of human-like versatility, the SP system excels in unsupervised learning, natural language processing, pattern recognition, information retrieval, various forms of reasoning, planning, problem solving, and more, seamlessly integrating structures and functions. The system's strengths in unsupervised learning and other aspects of intelligence facilitate human-like adaptability by enabling the learning of natural language, visual perception, 3D modeling of objects and surroundings, detection of regularities in robot operation and environment, exploration and play, acquisition of major skills, and secondary forms of learning. The article also discusses parallel information processing, knowledge generalization, correction of over-generalization, learning from noisy data, cost reduction in learning, and the roles of reinforcement, motivation, goals, and demonstration.

title: The Utility of Text: The Case of Amicus Briefs and the Supreme Court
Abstract: This paper explores the concept of text authorship as an act of maximizing expected utility. The authors focus on the decisions of the United States Supreme Court as a case study of societally significant decision-making. Drawing on existing quantitative political science research, the paper develops a framework for empirically modeling the decisions of justices and their relationship to text. The model incorporates texts authored by amici curiae ("friends of the court") who provide perspectives on the decision, explicitly modeling their goals within a random utility framework. The paper demonstrates the advantages of this approach, highlighting its ability to improve vote prediction and conduct counterfactual analysis.

title: Lazier Than Lazy Greedy
Abstract: This paper investigates whether it is possible to maximize a monotone submodular function faster than the widely used lazy greedy algorithm, both theoretically and practically. The authors introduce STOCHASTIC-GREEDY, a novel linear-time algorithm for maximizing a general monotone submodular function subject to a cardinality constraint. The randomized algorithm is shown to achieve a (1-1/e-ε) approximation guarantee in expectation, operating in time linear to the data size and independent of the cardinality constraint. Empirical evaluations demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness on submodular functions arising in data summarization, including training large-scale kernel methods, exemplar-based clustering, and sensor placement. The results show that STOCHASTIC-GREEDY practically achieves the same utility value as lazy greedy but with significantly faster execution. Surprisingly, the algorithm often evaluates less than the entire fraction of data points even once while still delivering indistinguishable results compared to lazy greedy.
label: AI

title: When Darwin meets Lorenz: Evolving new chaotic attractors through genetic programming
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel methodology for automatically finding new chaotic attractors using multi-gene genetic programming (MGGP), a computational intelligence technique. The method is applied to the Lorenz attractor, evolving several new chaotic attractors based on its structure. MGGP automatically generates new nonlinear expressions for the state variables, starting from the original Lorenz system. Lyapunov exponents for each attractor are calculated numerically using time delay embedding techniques based on the time series of the state variables. The MGGP algorithm searches the functional space of attractors by maximizing the largest Lyapunov exponent (LLE) of the evolved attractors. The paper presents over one hundred newly discovered chaotic attractor structures with their parameters, evolved solely from the Lorenz system.
label: AI

title: How good is the Shapley value-based approach to the influence maximization problem?
Abstract: The Shapley value has recently gained attention as a method for selecting seed nodes in information diffusion processes. The Shapley value measures the average marginal contribution of a player in a coalitional game, and in the network context, it can be used to assess the marginal contribution of a node in information diffusion given various groups of "infected" nodes. While this research direction appears promising, a comprehensive assessment of its performance is lacking. This paper aims to provide such an assessment of existing Shapley value-based approaches to information diffusion.
label: AI

title: Audio Surveillance: a Systematic Review
Abstract: Despite the increasing prevalence of surveillance systems in our living environment, automated surveillance, currently based on video sensing and machine intelligence, often lacks the robustness and reliability required for real-world applications. To address this issue, audio sensory devices have been incorporated, both independently and in combination with video, leading to a surge of research in the past decade. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of audio-based automated surveillance methods, organizing them into a taxonomy inspired by the more established video surveillance field. The taxonomy systematically describes methods covering background subtraction, event classification, object tracking, and situation analysis. For each task, the paper reviews significant works, detailing their advantages and disadvantages and the contexts in which they have been proposed. A dedicated section examines audio features, discussing their expressiveness and their use in the aforementioned tasks. Unlike other surveys focusing on audio processing and analysis, this one specifically targets automated surveillance, highlighting the target applications of each method and providing tables and schemes to guide readers in selecting the most suitable algorithms for specific needs.

title: Using Answer Set Programming for pattern mining
Abstract: Serial pattern mining involves extracting frequent sequential patterns from a single sequence of itemsets. This paper explores the feasibility of using a declarative language, Answer Set Programming (ASP), to solve this problem efficiently. The authors propose several ASP implementations of frequent sequential pattern mining, including non-incremental and incremental resolutions. While the incremental resolution proves more efficient than its non-incremental counterpart, both ASP programs exhibit less efficiency compared to dedicated algorithms. Nevertheless, this approach serves as a preliminary step towards a generic framework for sequential pattern mining with constraints.

title: Entanglement-Based Machine Learning on a Quantum Computer
Abstract: Machine learning, a branch of artificial intelligence, optimizes performance through experience, finding applications in various fields such as computer science, financial analysis, robotics, and bioinformatics. However, the rapid growth of "big data" poses a challenge to traditional machine learning techniques, making them potentially intractable for classical computers. Recent advancements have led to the development of quantum machine learning algorithms, potentially offering exponential speedups over classical algorithms. This paper reports the first experimental entanglement-based classification of 2-, 4-, and 8-dimensional vectors into different clusters using a small-scale photonic quantum computer. The experiment implements supervised and unsupervised machine learning, demonstrating the working principle of using quantum computers to manipulate and classify high-dimensional vectors, a core mathematical routine in machine learning. The method, in principle, can be scaled to a larger number of qubits, potentially offering a novel path to accelerate machine learning.

title: Multiple Object Tracking: A Literature Review
Abstract: Multiple Object Tracking (MOT) has gained considerable attention due to its academic and commercial potential. While various approaches have been proposed to address this problem, it remains challenging due to factors such as abrupt appearance changes and severe object occlusions. This paper provides the first comprehensive and up-to-date review on this topic, examining recent advancements in various aspects and proposing promising directions for future research. To the best of the authors' knowledge, no extensive review on MOT has been previously conducted within the community. The paper aims to offer a thorough overview of the problem's development over recent decades. The key contributions of the review are fourfold: 1) discussion of key aspects in an MOT system, including formulation, categorization, key principles, and evaluation; 2) examination of existing approaches based on various aspects, grouping methods and providing detailed discussions of principles, advancements, and limitations; 3) analysis of experiments from existing publications and summarization of results on popular datasets to provide quantitative and comprehensive comparisons, highlighting key agreements within the field; and 4) exploration of issues in MOT research and identification of promising directions for future research efforts.

title: Gradient-based Taxis Algorithms for Network Robotics
Abstract: Finding the physical location of a specific network node is a crucial task for navigation within a wireless network. This paper delves into the implications of wireless communication as a measurement input for gradient-based taxis algorithms. The paper discusses how gradients can be measured and examines the errors associated with this estimation. It then introduces a gradient-based taxis algorithm as an example of a family of convergent gradient-based algorithms, analyzing its convergence in the context of network robotics. The paper further presents an exemplary experiment demonstrating how to overcome specific challenges related to network robotics. Finally, it explores how to adapt this framework to more complex objectives.

title: Revisiting Algebra and Complexity of Inference in Graphical Models
Abstract: This paper investigates the form and complexity of inference in graphical models using the abstraction offered by algebraic structures. The authors broadly formalize inference problems in graphical models by viewing them as sequences of operations based on commutative semigroups. They then analyze the computational complexity of inference by categorizing various problems within an "inference hierarchy". When the underlying structure of an inference problem is a commutative semiring, a combination of two commutative semigroups with the distributive law, a message passing procedure called belief propagation can leverage this distributive law to perform polynomial-time inference for certain problems. After establishing the NP-hardness of inference in any commutative semiring, the paper examines the relationship between algebraic properties and further demonstrates that polynomial-time inference using the distributive law does not trivially extend to inference problems involving more than two commutative semigroups. The paper extends the algebraic treatment of message passing procedures to survey propagation, providing a novel perspective using a combination of two commutative semirings. This formulation generalizes the application of survey propagation to new settings.

title: Optimal high-level descriptions of dynamical systems
Abstract: Many fields in science and engineering rely on high-level descriptions, often referred to as "macrostates," "coarse-grainings," or "effective theories" to analyze high-dimensional systems. These descriptions encompass examples such as the thermodynamic properties of a large collection of point particles undergoing reversible dynamics, the variables in a macroeconomic model describing individuals participating in an economy, and the summary state of a cell composed of numerous biochemical networks. While these high-level descriptions are often constructed without explicitly considering the underlying reason for their necessity, this paper formalizes and quantifies one such purpose: the need to predict observables of interest concerning the high-dimensional system with maximum accuracy while minimizing computational cost. The resulting State Space Compression (SSC) framework provides a guide for determining the optimal high-level description of a given dynamical system, rather than relying solely on human intuition. The paper introduces SSC and illustrates it with several information-theoretic quantifications of "accuracy," each with distinct implications for optimal compression. It also explores other potential applications of SSC beyond accurate prediction, including its use as a measure of dynamical system complexity and as a means to quantify information flow between scales within a system.

title: Optimizing Hybrid Spreading in Metapopulations
Abstract: Epidemic spreading phenomena are ubiquitous in nature and society, manifesting in the spread of diseases, information, and computer viruses. Epidemics can spread through local mechanisms, where infected nodes only infect a limited set of direct targets, or global mechanisms, where an infected node can infect any other node. In reality, many epidemics spread through a hybrid mix of both types. This study develops a theoretical framework for investigating hybrid epidemics, examining the optimal balance between spreading mechanisms in terms of achieving the maximum outbreak size. The study demonstrates the existence of critically hybrid epidemics where neither spreading mechanism alone can cause significant spread, but a combination of both mechanisms results in a massive outbreak. The findings offer new strategies for maximizing beneficial epidemics and estimating the worst-case outcome of damaging hybrid epidemics.

title: Causal Graph Justifications of Logic Programs
Abstract: This paper introduces a multi-valued extension of logic programs under the stable models semantics, where each true atom in a model is associated with a set of justifications. These justifications are expressed in terms of causal graphs composed of rule labels and edges representing their application ordering. For positive programs, the causal justifications obtained for a given atom correspond directly to relevant syntactic proofs of that atom using the program rules involved in the graphs. The most significant contribution lies in the semantic derivation of this causal information through algebraic operations (product, sum, and application) on a lattice of causal values, where the ordering relation indicates the relative strength of justifications. For programs with negation, the concept of a causal stable model is defined by introducing an analogous transformation to Gelfond and Lifschitz's program reduct. As a result, default negation behaves as "absence of proof," and no justifications are derived from negative literals.

title: A Semidefinite Programming Based Search Strategy for Feature Selection with Mutual Information Measure
Abstract: Feature subset selection, a special case of the general subset selection problem, has garnered considerable attention due to the growing importance of data mining applications. The problem involves two primary challenges: (i) finding an appropriate measure function that can be computed quickly and robustly for high-dimensional data, and (ii) developing a search strategy to optimize the measure over the subset space within a reasonable time. This article utilizes mutual information between features and class labels as the measure function. The authors propose two series expansions for mutual information and demonstrate that most heuristic criteria suggested in the literature are truncated approximations of these expansions. Recognizing that searching the entire subset space is an NP-hard problem, the authors propose a parallel search strategy based on semidefinite programming (SDP) as an alternative to conventional sequential search algorithms. This SDP-based approach enables polynomial-time search through the subset space. By exploiting similarities between the proposed algorithm and an instance of the maximum-cut problem in graph theory, the approximation ratio of the algorithm is derived and compared with the approximation ratio of the backward elimination method. Experiments demonstrate that judging the quality of a measure solely based on classification accuracy can be misleading without considering the impact of non-optimal search strategies.

title: Feature-based tuning of simulated annealing applied to the curriculum-based course timetabling problem
Abstract: This paper addresses the university course timetabling problem, a well-studied problem in educational timetabling. The authors focus on the curriculum-based course timetabling problem, a formulation that has been extensively investigated and for which numerous benchmarks exist. The paper's contributions are twofold. First, it proposes an effective and robust single-stage simulated annealing method for solving the problem. Second, it presents a comprehensive and statistically-principled methodology for parameter tuning. This analysis establishes a framework for modeling the relationship between search method parameters and instance features, allowing parameter settings for unseen instances based on a simple inspection of the instance itself. Despite its apparent simplicity, this methodology enables the algorithm to achieve high-quality results on a set of popular benchmarks. The paper also introduces a novel set of real-world instances that can serve as a benchmark for future comparisons.

title: Impact of credit default swaps on financial contagion
Abstract: Traditional financial practice has suggested that transferring the risk of loan defaults reduces the risk of a bank going bankrupt. However, the failure of American International Group in 2008 revealed a more complex aspect of financial contagion. This study extends the asset network systemic risk model (ANWSER) to investigate whether credit default swaps mitigate or intensify the severity of financial contagion. In a credit default swap, a protection buyer bank transfers the risk of every possible debtor bank default to protection seller banks. The extended model is used to obtain the empirical distribution of the number of bank bankruptcies, from which the systemic capital buffer ratio is calculated. This ratio quantifies the effective loss absorbency capability of the entire financial system to counter financial contagion. The key finding is that the leverage ratio serves as a good estimate of the systemic capital buffer ratio, acting as a backstop for the financial system. The risk transfer from smaller and medium banks to larger banks within an interbank network does not mitigate the severity of financial contagion.

title: Efficiency Evaluation Metrics for Wireless Intelligent Sensors Applications
Abstract: The metrology field has advanced with the emergence of wireless intelligent sensor systems, offering capabilities such as signal processing, remote multi-sensing fusion, etc. These devices are rapidly being adopted in medical and industrial monitoring, collision avoidance, traffic control, automotive, and other applications. However, numerous design challenges for wireless intelligent sensor systems arise due to physical limitations in data traffic, including system noise, real-time communication, signal attenuation, response dynamics, power consumption, and effective conversion rates, particularly for applications demanding specific performance levels. This paper analyzes the performance metrics of these sensing devices, emphasizing superior measurement, accuracy, and reliability. The study findings provide researchers, developers/engineers, and users with insights for realizing an optimal sensing motes design strategy, offering operational advantages and cost-effective solutions for various applications.

title: The entropic basis of collective behaviour
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel perspective on the collective behavior of intelligent agents. The authors develop a general model encompassing possible future outcomes influenced by agent decisions. Within this framework, they demonstrate that the causal entropic principle, where agents maximize entropy across future paths, accurately predicts many observed features of social interactions in both human and animal groups. The study suggests that group cohesion maximizes future path entropy, leading to collectively intelligent outcomes significantly impacted by the distribution of possible future paths. The authors derive social interaction rules consistent with maximum-entropy group behavior for both discrete and continuous decision spaces. Furthermore, their analysis predicts that social interactions are fundamentally rooted in Weber's law, aligning with numerous neurological studies and providing a novel foundation for the common assumption of linear additive 'social forces' in collective behavior simulations.

title: Comparative Performance Analysis of Wireless Communication Protocols for Intelligent Sensors and Their Applications
Abstract: The paper discusses the increasing use of intelligent sensor systems and the challenges associated with selecting the most suitable wireless communication technology. Various wireless technologies, including Wi-Fi, Wi-Max, UWB, Bluetooth, ZigBee, ZigBeeIP, and GSM/GPRS, are compared based on their performance and limitations in specific application areas. The paper highlights the importance of choosing a technology that optimizes communication quality, minimizes energy consumption, reduces implementation costs, and avoids time constraints.

title: The Application of Differential Privacy for Rank Aggregation: Privacy and Accuracy
Abstract: The paper addresses the issue of privacy preservation in social platforms, where users may hesitate to share their true opinions due to the risk of privacy leakage. The authors propose a framework based on differential privacy to protect user privacy when the query returns a histogram of rankings. The error probability of the aggregated ranking resulting from noise added to achieve differential privacy is analyzed. Upper bounds on the error rates for any positional ranking rule are derived under the assumption of uniformly distributed profiles. Simulations are provided to validate the probabilistic analysis.

title: HSR: L1/2 Regularized Sparse Representation for Fast Face Recognition using Hierarchical Feature Selection
Abstract: This paper presents a novel method for fast face recognition called L1/2 Regularized Sparse Representation using Hierarchical Feature Selection (HSR). HSR compresses the scale and dimension of the global dictionary, significantly reducing the computational cost of sparse representation. The approach uses Gabor wavelets and Extreme Learning Machine Auto-Encoder (ELM-AE) hierarchically. Gabor wavelets extract local features at multiple scales and orientations, improving recognition rates. Additionally, the scale of the Gabor-feature-based global dictionary can be compressed in the presence of occluded face images due to redundancies. ELM-AE compresses the dimension of the Gabor-feature-based global dictionary by representing high-dimensional face images with low-dimensional features. By introducing L1/2 regularization, HSR produces sparser and more robust representation compared to regularized Sparse Representation based Classification (SRC), further reducing computational cost. Experimental results on various face databases demonstrate the significant computational advantages of HSR compared to related approaches like SRC and Gabor-feature-based SRC (GSRC). Additionally, HSR achieves comparable or even better recognition rates.

title: Neighborhood Selection and Rules Identification for Cellular Automata: A Rough Sets Approach
Abstract: This paper proposes a method for selecting neighborhoods and determining update rules for cellular automata (CA) using data mining techniques based on rough sets theory. The approach identifies neighborhoods through reducts calculations and employs a rule-learning algorithm to induce a set of decision rules defining CA evolution. Experiments conducted with both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in identifying both deterministic and probabilistic CA-based models of real-world phenomena.

title: On tensor rank of conditional probability tables in Bayesian networks
Abstract: The paper addresses the challenge of eliciting numerical parameters for Bayesian networks, particularly in the context of large conditional probability tables (CPTs) with extensive parent sets. The authors demonstrate that most CPTs from real-world applications can be effectively approximated by tables requiring significantly fewer parameters. This finding has practical implications for both model elicitation and efficient probabilistic reasoning with these networks.

title: Touch attention Bayesian models for robotic active haptic exploration of heterogeneous surfaces
Abstract: This work explores the development of active haptic exploration strategies for surfaces using robotic hands in environments with unknown structures. The proposed approach relies on two main Bayesian models: pi_per and pi_tar.  Pi_per perceives and discriminates different materials (haptic stimulus) by integrating compliance and texture features extracted from haptic sensory data. Pi_tar actively infers the next region of the workspace to be explored by the robot, considering task information, updated saliency and uncertainty maps from the perceived haptic stimulus map, and inhibition-of-return mechanisms. Experimental results demonstrate that pi_per can distinguish between 10 material classes with an average recognition rate exceeding 90%. The generalization capabilities of the proposed models were experimentally confirmed. The ATLAS robot, in simulations, successfully followed discontinuities between two regions made of different materials with a divergence smaller than 1cm (30 trials) across three different configurations of the discontinuity. The Bayesian models demonstrate the ability to manage uncertainty about surface structures and sensory noise, enabling accurate motor decisions based on haptic perceptions.

title: Software & Systems Engineering Process and Tools for the Development of Autonomous Driving Intelligence
Abstract: The paper discusses the importance of a well-defined engineering process when a project involves a large number of individuals with diverse knowledge and skills, particularly in the context of developing an autonomous driving car for the 2007 DARPA Urban Challenge. It outlines the essential elements of a software and system engineering process incorporating agile concepts like test-first approach, continuous integration, and robust release and configuration management. The paper emphasizes the critical role of a flexible and modular simulator for urban situations in efficiently testing the behavior of the developed system.

title: Automated Testing of Graphical Models in Heterogeneous Test Environments
Abstract: The paper highlights the importance of automated and repeatable tests in product lines to maintain software quality and developer efficiency. It presents methods for fully automated testing of SIMULINK models using the slUnit framework and techniques for integrating slUnit tests into a general test framework, enabling integrated and automated test reports.
label: AI

title: Engineering Autonomous Driving Software
Abstract: The paper emphasizes the need for a flexible and skill-specific engineering process when a project involves a large number of individuals with diverse knowledge and skills, especially when developing highly innovative technologies like autonomous driving vehicles. It presents key elements of a software and systems engineering process for developing artificial intelligence capable of navigating complex urban environments. The process incorporates agile concepts like test-first approach, continuous integration, and robust release and configuration management. The paper highlights the importance of a flexible and modular system simulation for urban situations, allowing for both interactive and unattended testing, which the authors refer to as the "simulate first approach."

title: Oblivious Bounds on the Probability of Boolean Functions
Abstract: This paper proposes a method for deriving upper and lower bounds for the probability of Boolean functions by treating multiple occurrences of variables as independent and assigning them new individual probabilities. This approach, referred to as dissociation, provides an exact characterization of optimal oblivious bounds, where new probabilities are chosen independently of other variables. The motivation stems from the #P-hard weighted model counting problem (or computing the probability of a Boolean function). Multiple dissociations transform a Boolean formula with complex probability into one with simpler probability while guaranteeing upper or lower bounds on the original formula's probability. The derived bounds clarify the relationship between previous relaxation-based and model-based approximations and unify them as concrete choices within a larger design space. Additionally, the study shows how relational database management systems (DBMS) can use this theory to upper and lower bound hard probabilistic queries in guaranteed polynomial time.

title: Domain Adaptive Neural Networks for Object Recognition
Abstract: The paper proposes a simple neural network model for addressing the domain adaptation problem in object recognition. The model incorporates the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) measure as a regularization in supervised learning to minimize distribution mismatch between source and target domains in the latent space. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of MMD regularization in achieving good domain adaptation models using both SURF features and raw image pixels. The proposed model, preceded by denoising auto-encoder pretraining, outperforms recent benchmark models on the same datasets. This work is the first to explore the application of MMD measure in the context of neural networks.
label: AI

title: Reconfigurable Wireless Networks
Abstract: The paper provides a comprehensive overview of reconfigurable wireless networks and analyzes reconfiguration at all layers of the protocol stack. It highlights the increasing complexity and dynamics of wireless networks driven by sophisticated applications and growing information needs. Reconfigurable networks, capable of adapting hardware and software components and architectures, are crucial for delivering diverse services and maintaining robust operation under dynamic conditions. The paper offers a unifying framework for research in this area, providing a holistic view of concepts, methods, and strategies. It focuses on reconfigurable systems in emerging areas like cognitive radio networks, cross-layer reconfiguration, and software-defined networks. Recognizing the need for intelligent and self-organizing networks, the paper also discusses network intelligence as a means to enable reconfiguration in highly complex and dynamic environments. Finally, the paper includes examples and case studies illustrating the significant impact of reconfiguration on wireless networks.
label: AI

title: IP Tracing and Active Network Response
Abstract: Active security focuses on implementing security functions when a host in a communication network is under attack. These functions involve taking appropriate actions against attackers. To effectively manage active security responses, a set of software subsystems must be integrated to automatically detect and address vulnerabilities in the underlying network. This work proposes an integrated model for active security response, introducing the Active Response Mechanism (ARM) for tracing anonymous attacks back to their source. Motivated by the growing frequency and sophistication of denial-of-service attacks and the difficulty in tracing packets with spoofed source addresses, the paper presents two tracing approaches within the proposed model: Sleepy Watermark Tracing (SWT) for unauthorized access attacks and Probabilistic Packet Marking (PPM) in the network for Denial of Service (DoS) and Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks. Based on the proposed model, cooperative network security tools like firewalls and intrusion detection systems with IP tracing mechanisms are designed for rapid active responses against real attacker IPs. The proposed model is capable of detecting network vulnerabilities, tracing attack source IPs, and reconfiguring the attacked subnetworks.

title: Effects of Coupling in Human-Virtual Agent Body Interaction
Abstract: This paper examines the dynamic coupling between a user and a virtual character during body interaction. Coupling is directly linked to dimensions like co-presence, engagement, and believability. It was measured in an experiment where participants described their subjective feelings about these dimensions. The experiment involved a theatrical game with slow upper-body movements, where participants and the virtual agent imitated each other's movements and proposed new ones. The agent's autonomy varied, ranging from solely imitating user movements to initiating new movements or combining both behaviors. After the game, participants completed a questionnaire assessing their engagement, perception of the agent's co-presence, etc. The paper tests several hypotheses against the experimental results based on four main dimensions of interest.
label: AI

title: On the Impact of Multiobjective Scalarizing Functions
Abstract: Recent advancements in evolutionary multiobjective optimization have led to renewed interest in decomposition-based approaches. However, the impact of the choice of underlying scalarizing function(s) remains unclear. This paper investigates the behavior of different scalarizing functions and their parameters. The study abstracts from specific algorithms and focuses on the difficulty of single scalarized problems in terms of a (1+lambda)-EA's search ability on biobjective NK-landscapes. Combining outcomes of independent single-objective runs allows for more general statements on set-based performance measures. Finally, the paper explores the correlation between the opening angle of the scalarizing function's underlying contour lines and the position of the final solution in the objective space. This analysis provides fundamental insights into the key characteristics of multiobjective scalarizing functions.
label: AI

title: Local Optimal Sets and Bounded Archiving on Multi-objective NK-Landscapes with Correlated Objectives
Abstract: The paper examines the properties of local optimal solutions in multi-objective combinatorial optimization problems, which are crucial for the effectiveness of local search algorithms, particularly those based on Pareto dominance. These algorithms typically return a set of mutually nondominated Pareto local optimal (PLO) solutions. The study investigates two aspects of PLO-sets through experiments with Pareto local search (PLS). First, it examines the impact of problem characteristics on the properties of PLO-sets for multi-objective NK-landscapes with correlated objectives. The results indicate that increasing the number of objectives or decreasing the correlation between objectives leads to an exponential increase in the size of PLO-sets, while variable correlation has a minimal effect. Second, the paper analyzes the running time and quality achieved when using bounding archiving methods to limit the size of the archive handled by PLS, thus limiting the maximum size of the found PLO-set. The findings suggest a clear relationship between the running time of PLS and the difficulty of a problem instance.
label: AI

title: Efficient Feature Group Sequencing for Anytime Linear Prediction
Abstract: This paper focuses on anytime linear prediction in machine learning settings where features are grouped with associated costs. Anytime (or interruptible) predictions are achieved by sequencing the computation of feature groups and reporting results based on computed features at interruption. The paper extends Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP) and Forward Regression (FR) to greedily learn the sequencing in this group setting with costs. Theoretical guarantees ensure that the algorithms achieve near-optimal linear predictions at each budget when a feature group is selected. Through a novel analysis of OMP, its theoretical bound is improved to match that of FR. Additionally, a new algorithm is developed that approximates the optimal performance of any cost B with cost 4B. The paper proves that such an approximation is impossible with cost less than 4B. These are the first anytime bounds for all budgets. The algorithms are tested on two real-world datasets and evaluated for anytime linear prediction performance against cost-weighted Group Lasso and other greedy algorithms.
label: AI

title: Belief revision by examples
Abstract: In belief revision, it is often assumed that the reliability of information sources is either given, derived from temporal information, or equal for all sources. This article does not propose a new semantics for integration but focuses on obtaining the reliability of sources based on the results of previous merging. For example, the relative reliability of two sensors can be assessed based on certain observations, allowing for subsequent merging of data from these sensors.
label: AI

title: Virtual Electrode Recording Tool for EXtracellular potentials (VERTEX): Comparing multi-electrode recordings from simulated and biological mammalian cortical tissue
Abstract: Local field potentials (LFPs), measured using extracellular electrodes, are frequently used as indicators of population neuronal activity. However, linking these measurements to underlying neuronal behavior and connectivity poses a significant challenge. To facilitate this research, the authors developed the Virtual Electrode Recording Tool for EXtracellular potentials (VERTEX).  First, they identified a reduced neuron model that retained the spatial and frequency filtering characteristics of extracellular potentials from neocortical neurons. Then, they developed VERTEX as a user-friendly Matlab tool for simulating LFPs from large populations (>100,000 neurons).  VERTEX simulations successfully reproduced features of LFPs observed in in vitro multi-electrode array recordings of macaque neocortical tissue. The model, with virtual electrodes placed anywhere in 3D, allows for direct comparison with the in vitro recording setup. The authors anticipate that VERTEX will inspire experimentalists, clinicians, and computational neuroscientists to use models to understand the mechanisms underlying measured brain dynamics in health and disease. |||

title: A Bayesian model for recognizing handwritten mathematical expressions
Abstract: Recognizing handwritten mathematical expressions presents a challenging classification problem. This is because it requires simultaneous identification of individual symbols within an input, as well as understanding the complex two-dimensional relationships between symbols and subexpressions. Given the inherent ambiguity in handwritten input, achieving consistently perfect recognition accuracy is often unrealistic. This paper proposes a system that captures all recognizable interpretations of an input and organizes them into a parse forest. Individual parse trees can then be extracted and presented to the user. If the top-ranked interpretation is incorrect, the user can request alternate interpretations and choose the desired result. The tree extraction process utilizes a novel probabilistic tree scoring strategy. This strategy constructs a Bayesian network based on the structure of the input, where each joint variable assignment corresponds to a unique parse tree. Parse trees are subsequently ranked based on their probability scores, with the highest probability tree presented first.  Two accuracy evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed recognition system. The system outperforms previous versions that relied on non-probabilistic methods and other academic math recognizers.

title: Why Local Search Excels in Expression Simplification
Abstract: Simplifying expressions is crucial for making numerical integration of large expressions from High Energy Physics tractable. Horner's method can be effectively employed for this purpose. Finding optimal Horner schemes is generally considered difficult due to the lack of local heuristics. Recent studies have shown that Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) can find near-optimal schemes, but require manual fine-tuning of several parameters. This paper explores the state space properties of Horner schemes and discovers that the domain is relatively flat with only a few local minima. This characteristic makes the Horner space well-suited for Stochastic Local Search (SLS), which has only two parameters: the number of iterations (computation time) and the neighborhood structure.  The paper identifies a suitable neighborhood structure, leaving only the computation time as a parameter. Through extensive experiments, the authors demonstrate that SLS achieves similar or better results compared to MCTS, but significantly faster, at least 10 times faster. By using SLS, numerical integration of many real-world large expressions can be accelerated by a factor of 24, effectively reducing weeks-long integrations to hours.
label: AI

title: Convolutional Neural Networks over Tree Structures for Programming Language Processing
Abstract: Programming language processing, analogous to natural language processing, has emerged as a prominent research area in software engineering and has gained significant interest within the artificial intelligence community. Unlike natural language sentences, programs possess rich, explicit, and complex structural information, rendering traditional NLP models inadequate for program analysis. This paper proposes a novel tree-based convolutional neural network (TBCNN) for programming language processing. TBCNN utilizes a convolution kernel designed to operate on programs' abstract syntax trees, effectively capturing structural information. This generic architecture is effective in two different program analysis tasks: classifying programs based on functionality, and detecting code snippets with specific patterns. TBCNN outperforms baseline methods, including several neural models for NLP.

title: Solving Graph Coloring Problems with Abstraction and Symmetry
Abstract: This paper introduces a general methodology, based on abstraction and symmetry, for solving challenging graph edge-coloring problems. The methodology is demonstrated through its application to the Ramsey number R(4,3,3), often considered the most likely unknown Ramsey number to be determined. The precise value of R(4,3,3) has remained unknown for over 50 years. The paper illustrates the approach by showing that: (1) there are exactly 78,892 (3,3,3;13) Ramsey colorings; and (2) if a (4,3,3;30) Ramsey coloring exists, it must be (13,8,8) regular.  This means that each node has 13 edges in the first color, 8 in the second, and 8 in the third.  The authors conjecture that these results will contribute to proving the non-existence of a (4,3,3;30) Ramsey coloring, implying that R(4,3,3)=30.

title: A Tabu Search Algorithm for the Multi-period Inspector Scheduling Problem
Abstract: This paper introduces the multi-period inspector scheduling problem (MPISP), a new variant of the multi-trip vehicle routing problem with time windows (VRPTW). In MPISP, each inspector is scheduled to perform a route over a multi-period planning horizon. At the end of each period, inspectors are not required to return to the depot but must stay at one of the vertices for recuperation.  If an inspector lacks sufficient time within the current period to travel from vertex A to vertex B, they can choose to either wait at vertex A until the next period begins or travel to a closer vertex C. Consequently, the shortest transit time between any vertex pair depends on the period length and departure time. The paper presents an approach for computing the shortest transit time between any vertex pair with an arbitrary departure time. To solve the MPISP, the paper proposes several local search operators adapted from classical VRPTW operators and integrates them into a tabu search framework. Additionally, a constrained knapsack model is presented to provide an upper bound for the problem. Extensive experiments are conducted using a set of test instances to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm. The computational results demonstrate that the approach produces high-quality solutions.
label: AI

title: Ensembles of Random Sphere Cover Classifiers
Abstract: This paper proposes and evaluates alternative ensemble schemes for a new instance-based learning classifier: the Randomised Sphere Cover (RSC) classifier. RSC fuses instances into spheres, and classification is based on distance to spheres rather than individual instances.  The randomized nature of RSC makes it suitable for ensemble methods. The paper proposes two ensemble methods tailored to the RSC classifier: αβRSE, an ensemble based on instance resampling, and αRSSE, a subspace ensemble. Comparing αβRSE and αRSSE to tree-based ensembles on a set of UCI datasets shows that RSC ensembles consistently outperform some tree-based ensembles and perform comparably to others. A case study on six gene expression datasets demonstrates that αRSSE outperforms other subspace ensemble methods on high-dimensional data when used in conjunction with an attribute filter.  Bias/Variance decomposition experiments are conducted to analyze the source of improvement observed in comparison to a base classifier.

title: ICE: Enabling Non-Experts to Build Models Interactively for Large-Scale Lopsided Problems
Abstract: Quick interaction between a human teacher and a learning machine presents numerous benefits and challenges when working with web-scale data. The human teacher guides the machine towards accomplishing a specific task, while the learning machine leverages big data to find examples that maximize the training value of its interaction with the teacher. When the teacher is restricted to labeling examples selected by the machine, this problem falls under the domain of active learning.  However, if the teacher can provide additional information to the machine (e.g., suggestions on examples or predictive features to use) during the learning process, the problem becomes one of interactive learning.  To facilitate the two-way communication channel required for efficient interactive learning, the teacher and the machine need a shared environment with a supporting interaction language. The machine can access, process, and summarize more examples than the teacher could ever see in a lifetime.  Based on the machine's output, the teacher can refine the task definition or make it more precise.  Both the teacher and the machine continuously learn and benefit from the interaction. The authors have developed a platform designed to (1) produce valuable and deployable models and (2) support research on both the machine learning and user interface challenges of interactive learning. This platform relies on a dedicated, low-latency, distributed, in-memory architecture that enables the construction of web-scale learning machines with fast interaction speeds. This paper describes the architecture and demonstrates its support for research efforts. Preliminary results are presented to illustrate the architecture's capabilities, but are not the primary focus.

title: Performance analysis of a 240 thread tournament level MCTS Go program on the Intel Xeon Phi
Abstract: In 2013, Intel introduced the Xeon Phi, a novel parallel co-processor board. The Xeon Phi is a cache-coherent many-core shared memory architecture, claiming to offer CPU-like versatility, programmability, high performance, and power efficiency.  Early micro-benchmark studies suggest that many of Intel's claims hold true. This paper presents the first study on the Xeon Phi for a complex artificial intelligence application: an open-source Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) application designed to play tournament-quality Go. The paper reports speedup figures for up to 240 parallel threads on a real machine, enabling a direct comparison to previous simulation studies. After extensive research, the authors observed performance scaling well up to 32 threads, largely confirming previous simulation results for the Go program. However, surprisingly, performance deteriorates between 32 and 240 threads. The paper also highlights unexpected performance discrepancies between the Xeon Phi and Xeon CPU for smaller problem sizes and thread counts. Furthermore, the performance is found to be sensitive to scheduling choices. Achieving optimal performance on the Xeon Phi for complex programs is not straightforward and requires a deep understanding of search patterns, scheduling, and the architecture's many cores and caches.  In practice, programming the Xeon Phi proves to be more challenging than originally envisioned by Intel.
label: AI

title: Dispute Resolution Using Argumentation-Based Mediation
Abstract: Mediation is a process where both parties agree to resolve their dispute through negotiations, guided by a mediator who proposes alternative solutions.  Mediation introduces additional information, knowledge, and resources to the negotiation table. This paper presents an automated mediation machinery that replicates this process. It introduces an argumentation-based mediation approach that extends the logic-based approach to argumentation-based negotiation involving BDI agents. The paper describes the mediation algorithm and illustrates its functionality through a case study, previously used in an earlier work. The study demonstrates how the computational mediator can handle realistic scenarios where negotiating agents might fail due to insufficient knowledge or resources.

title: Crowdsourcing Pareto-Optimal Object Finding by Pairwise Comparisons
Abstract: This paper presents the first study on crowdsourcing Pareto-optimal object finding, applicable in areas such as public opinion collection, group decision making, and information exploration.  Unlike previous studies on crowdsourcing skyline and ranking queries, this work addresses the case where objects lack explicit attributes, and preference relations on objects are strict partial orders. These partial orders are derived by aggregating responses from crowdsourcers to pairwise comparison questions. The goal is to identify all Pareto-optimal objects using the fewest possible questions.  The paper proposes an iterative question-selection framework guided by the principle of eagerly identifying non-Pareto optimal objects.  The framework only selects candidate questions meeting three specific conditions. This design ensures both sufficiency and efficiency, as it is proven to find a short terminal question sequence.  The framework is further guided by two ideas: macro-ordering and micro-ordering. Utilizing various micro-ordering heuristics, the framework is instantiated into several algorithms with varying power in pruning questions. Experimental results using both real crowdsourcing marketplaces and simulations demonstrate not only orders of magnitude reductions in questions compared to a brute-force approach, but also near-optimal performance from the most efficient instantiation.

title: Hardness of parameter estimation in graphical models
Abstract: This paper investigates the problem of learning the canonical parameters specifying an undirected graphical model (Markov random field) from the mean parameters.  For graphical models representing a minimal exponential family, the canonical parameters are uniquely determined by the mean parameters, making the problem theoretically solvable. The paper focuses on exploring the computational feasibility of this statistical task. The main result demonstrates that parameter estimation is generally intractable. No algorithm can learn the canonical parameters of a generic pair-wise binary graphical model from the mean parameters in polynomial time (unless RP = NP).  This result, although previously believed to be true, had no known proof. The proof presented in this paper provides a polynomial-time reduction from approximating the partition function of the hard-core model, known to be computationally difficult, to learning approximate parameters. This reduction involves demonstrating that the marginal polytope boundary possesses an inherent repulsive property. This property validates an optimization procedure over the polytope, which does not require any prior knowledge of its structure (as needed by the ellipsoid method and other similar approaches).

title: The Missing Piece in Complex Analytics: Low Latency, Scalable Model Management and Serving with Velox
Abstract: Supporting complex data-intensive applications, such as personalized recommendations, targeted advertising, and intelligent services, has led the data management community to prioritize the design of systems for training complex models on large datasets.  However, these system designs often overlook a critical component of the overall analytics process: the deployment and serving of models at scale.  This paper presents Velox, a new component of the Berkeley Data Analytics Stack, designed to address this gap.  Velox is a data management system that facilitates the next steps in real-world, large-scale analytics pipelines: online model management, maintenance, and serving. Velox provides end-user applications and services with a low-latency, intuitive interface to models, transforming raw statistical models trained using existing offline large-scale compute frameworks into full-fledged, end-to-end data products capable of recommending products, targeting advertisements, and personalizing web content.  To ensure up-to-date results for these complex models, Velox also facilitates lightweight online model maintenance and selection (i.e., dynamic weighting).  This paper delves into the challenges and architectural considerations required to achieve this functionality, including the ability to bridge online and offline systems, adaptively adjust model materialization strategies, and exploit inherent statistical properties like model error tolerance, all while operating at "Big Data" scale.
label: AI

title: Probabilistic Selection in AgentSpeak(L)
Abstract: Agent programming is primarily a symbolic discipline, with limited benefits derived from probabilistic areas like machine learning and graphical models. However, the ultimate goal of agent research is to achieve autonomy in dynamic and complex environments, which necessitates embracing uncertainty and its associated representations, algorithms, and techniques. This paper proposes an innovative and conflict-free two-layer approach to agent programming that leverages established methods and tools from both symbolic and probabilistic artificial intelligence. The framework is illustrated using a widely used agent programming example: GoldMiners.

title: On Minimax Optimal Offline Policy Evaluation
Abstract: This paper explores the off-policy evaluation problem, where the goal is to estimate the value of a target policy based on a sample of observations collected under a different policy. The paper first examines the multi-armed bandit case, establishing a minimax risk lower bound and analyzing the risk of two common estimators.  It demonstrates, and verifies through simulations, that one estimator is minimax optimal up to a constant, while the other can exhibit arbitrarily worse performance despite its empirical success and popularity. These findings are then applied to related problems in contextual bandits and fixed-horizon Markov decision processes, and are also connected to semi-supervised learning.

title: A Formal Methods Approach to Pattern Synthesis in Reaction Diffusion Systems
Abstract: This paper presents a technique for detecting and generating patterns in a network of locally interacting dynamical systems. The core of this approach is a novel spatial superposition logic, whose semantics is defined over the quad-tree of a partitioned image. The paper demonstrates that formulas in this logic can be efficiently learned from positive and negative examples of various pattern types. It further shows that pattern detection, implemented as a model checking algorithm, performs very well on test datasets different from the learning sets.  The paper defines a quantitative semantics for the logic and integrates the model checking algorithm with particle swarm optimization in a computational framework for synthesizing parameters that lead to desired patterns in reaction-diffusion systems.

title: Building Program Vector Representations for Deep Learning
Abstract: Deep learning has achieved significant breakthroughs in various fields of artificial intelligence. Its advantages include the ability to capture highly complex features and minimal human engineering involvement. However, applying deep learning to program analysis remains virtually impossible because deep architectures cannot be effectively trained using pure backpropagation. This groundbreaking paper proposes the "coding criterion" to construct program vector representations, paving the way for deep learning in program analysis.  The proposed representation learning approach directly enables deep learning in this new domain.  The learned vector representations are evaluated qualitatively and quantitatively. Experimental results demonstrate the success of the coding criterion in building program representations.  To assess the benefits of deep learning for program analysis, the learned representations are fed into deep neural networks.  The results achieve higher accuracy in program classification tasks compared to "shallow" methods like logistic regression and support vector machines, confirming the feasibility of deep learning for program analysis.  This study provides initial evidence of its success in this new domain, suggesting that deep learning will become a prominent technique for program analysis in the future.

title: Intelligent Indoor Mobile Robot Navigation Using Stereo Vision
Abstract: The majority of existing robot navigation systems, which rely on laser range finders, sonar sensors, or artificial landmarks, can locate themselves in unknown environments and subsequently build a map of the surroundings.  While stereo vision is rapidly evolving in the field of autonomous mobile robots, its high implementation cost currently limits its widespread adoption.  This paper describes an experimental approach for building a cost-effective stereo vision system that enables robots to avoid obstacles and navigate through indoor environments. The paper explores the fusion of stereo vision and ultrasound sensors, facilitating successful navigation through diverse and complex environments. The sensor data allows the robot to create a two-dimensional topological map of unknown environments, while the stereo vision system models the three-dimensional representation of the same environment.
label: AI

title: Design and Implementation of Intelligent Community System Based on Thin Client and Cloud Computing
Abstract: With continuous advancements in science and technology, the intelligent development of community systems has become a prevailing trend.  Smart mobile devices and cloud computing technology are increasingly used in intelligent information systems. However, smart mobile devices, such as smartphones and smart pads, are limited by their capacity (CPU, memory, or battery) and network resources, often failing to meet user expectations for mobile service usage.  Mobile cloud computing, where resource-rich virtual machines for smart mobile devices are provided as a service, can address this limitation. However, resource utilization rates remain low, and information sharing is often hindered.  This paper proposes an information system for intelligent communities, composed of thin clients, a wideband network, and cloud computing servers.  Thin clients, characterized by energy efficiency, high robustness, and high computing capacity, efficiently address the limitations of PC architecture and mobile devices.  The cloud computing servers in the proposed system overcome resource sharing barriers.  The performance of the system is evaluated through real-world deployment in a community with over 2000 residents, demonstrating its robustness and efficiency.

title: A Study of Association Measures and their Combination for Arabic MWT Extraction
Abstract: Automatic Multi-Word Term (MWT) extraction is crucial for numerous applications, including information retrieval, question answering, and text categorization. While several methods have been employed for MWT extraction in English and other European languages, Arabic research in this area remains limited. This paper proposes a novel hybrid method for Arabic MWT extraction, combining linguistic and statistical approaches. The key contribution of this method lies in considering contextual information, termhood, and unithood for association measures during the statistical filtering step.  Additionally, the technique addresses the problem of MWT variation in the linguistic filtering step. The performance of the proposed statistical measure (NLC-value) is evaluated using an Arabic environment corpus by comparing it to existing competitors. Experimental results demonstrate that the NLC-value measure outperforms its competitors in terms of precision for both bi-grams and tri-grams.

title: Co-adaptation in a Handwriting Recognition System
Abstract: Handwriting is a natural and versatile method for human-computer interaction, particularly on small mobile devices like smartphones.  However, handwriting exhibits significant variation among individuals, making it challenging to design handwriting recognizers that perform well for all users.  A natural solution is to employ machine learning to adapt the recognizer to individual users.  One complicating factor is that as the computer adapts to the user, the user also adapts to the computer, potentially changing their handwriting.  This paper investigates the dynamics of co-adaptation, a process where both the computer and the user modify their behaviors to enhance the speed and accuracy of communication through handwriting.  The paper develops an information-theoretic framework for quantifying the efficiency of a handwriting system, encompassing both the user and the computer.  Using this framework, the paper analyzes data collected from an adaptive handwriting recognition system to characterize the impact of machine adaptation and human adaptation.  The study reveals that both machine adaptation and human adaptation have a significant impact on the input rate and must be considered together to improve the overall system efficiency. |||

title: Ambiguity-Driven Fuzzy C-Means Clustering: How to Detect Uncertain Clustered Records
Abstract: Fuzzy C-Means (FCM) is a popular clustering algorithm that allows data points to belong to multiple clusters, providing more flexibility than non-fuzzy methods. However, FCM can be susceptible to inaccurate results due to noisy data, poor feature selection, and inherent uncertainty. This paper proposes a method for identifying ambiguous data points in FCM by introducing a certainty factor. By identifying ambiguous data points, the proposed approach allows for a deeper analysis of these records using another discrimination method, leading to improved accuracy and reduced error rates. The method efficiently processes the majority of data points with minimal errors, avoiding performance losses compared to similar hybrid methods. Experiments on various datasets demonstrate significant reductions in error rates and improved algorithm sensitivity.

title: Combining the analytical hierarchy process and the genetic algorithm to solve the timetable problem
Abstract: School timetable creation presents challenges related to time allocation, curriculum, and classroom availability. Additionally, individual institutions may face unique constraints. This paper focuses on addressing the problem of satisfying teachers' preferred schedules while acknowledging their relative importance to the institution. The proposed approach utilizes the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) to assign scores to teachers based on various criteria. These scores then inform a Genetic Algorithm (GA)-based timetable solution, aiming to accommodate as many teachers' preferences as possible.

title: Prioritized Planning Algorithms for Trajectory Coordination of Multiple Mobile Robots
Abstract: Autonomous multi-robot systems require mechanisms to prevent collisions between robots. One approach is to plan conflict-free trajectories in advance and have each robot follow its pre-determined path. Prioritized planning, a widely used method for multi-robot trajectory planning, has proven effective but is generally incomplete. This paper introduces a revised version of prioritized planning, characterizing the class of problems that can be provably solved by the algorithm. Additionally, an asynchronous decentralized variant of prioritized planning is proposed, which retains the benefits of the centralized version while utilizing the distributed computational power of individual robots for faster trajectory generation. Experiments on real-world indoor maps demonstrate the effectiveness of the revised prioritized planning in handling scenarios where traditional methods fail, and the asynchronous decentralized algorithm outperforms its synchronized counterpart in terms of solution speed.

title: Rapid Integration and Calibration of New Sensors Using the Berkeley Aachen Robotics Toolkit (BART)
Abstract: Following the DARPA Grand Challenge competitions, significant research has been conducted towards developing autonomous vehicles capable of completing missions in various environments, but complete success in uncontrolled settings has remained elusive. This paper argues that while sensor technology and AI algorithms are crucial, the community should also focus on the systems engineering aspects of the problem. This includes addressing the limitations of the vehicle itself, such as space, power, and heat dissipation, and optimizing the software development cycle. The paper explores these issues and shares insights gained from overcoming them.

title: State-Based Modeling of Buildings and Facilities
Abstract: Research on building energy efficiency often focuses on monitoring a building's operational behavior. However, without a formalized description of the collected data, including their correlations and expected values, the full potential of the data cannot be realized. This paper presents a methodology for addressing this issue by integrating a formalized specification of a building's management system into an intelligent monitoring system. The proposed concept of state-based modeling, based on DIN EN ISO 16484, provides a structured way to model buildings and facilities while enabling sophisticated data analysis during monitoring.

title: Variational Inference for Uncertainty on the Inputs of Gaussian Process Models
Abstract: The Gaussian Process Latent Variable Model (GP-LVM) offers a flexible approach for non-linear dimensionality reduction. While current training methods rely on maximum likelihood estimation, this paper introduces a Bayesian approach that leverages variational inference to approximate the integration of latent variables. This allows for the training of GP-LVMs by maximizing an analytical lower bound on the marginal likelihood. The proposed method is applicable to both independent and identically distributed (iid) observations and temporally correlated data, as found in non-linear dynamical systems. It demonstrates robustness to overfitting and automatic dimensionality selection. This flexible framework can be extended to various applications, including Gaussian process regression with uncertain inputs and semi-supervised Gaussian processes. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated on synthetic and real-world datasets, including high-resolution video data.

title: Secure pseudo-random linear binary sequences generators based on arithmetic polynoms
Abstract: This paper proposes a new method for constructing pseudo-random binary sequences (PRS) generators that are resistant to attacks stemming from hardware errors and faults. The method leverages linear polynomial arithmetic to realize boolean characteristic functions of PRS generators. By applying residue system techniques to the process of PRS generation, the system achieves multisequencing and control of computing errors, ensuring high security of both the generator's operation and the cryptographic data protection tools based on those PRSs.

title: Contexts, Systems and Modalities: a new ontology for quantum mechanics
Abstract: This paper explores the potential for reconciling quantum mechanics with physical realism, defined as the existence of physical entities independent of observers and governed by universal laws. Instead of modifying the quantum formalism, the proposed approach alters the quantum ontology by attributing physical properties jointly to the system and its context. This non-classical definition of physical reality, combined with a quantization principle, offers insights into counter-intuitive aspects of quantum mechanics, such as the origin of probabilities, non-locality, and the quantum-classical boundary.

title: Simulating Non Stationary Operators in Search Algorithms
Abstract: This paper presents a model for simulating search operators whose behavior changes continuously during optimization searches. This behavior, often observed in exploitation and exploration operators, leads to decreasing performance with repeated applications. The proposed simulation model facilitates the comparison of operator selection policies and their ability to adapt to such dynamic operator behavior. Experimental results highlight the distinct performance characteristics of different selection policies when faced with non-stationary search scenarios.

title: Building-in-Briefcase (BiB)
Abstract: Building environments significantly impact occupant comfort and health. Continuous monitoring of building occupancy and environmental conditions is crucial for fault detection, intelligent control, and building commissioning. While wireless sensor networks offer solutions for environmental monitoring, they can be challenging for households and building owners to implement. This paper introduces Building-in-Briefcase (BiB), a portable sensor network platform that is easily deployable in any building environment. BiB's design utilizes TCP/IP protocol, WiFi technology, and a 3G radio for data collection, communication, and secure data transmission. The user-friendly web portal provides real-time access to aggregated data and visualized trends. To ensure long-term operation, BiB employs efficient communication protocols and data compression techniques, achieving a multi-year battery lifespan. BiB sensors are capable of collecting a diverse set of environmental parameters, including occupancy estimations and activity recognition, with potential for further expansion. This paper describes BiB's power characteristics and its occupancy estimation and activity recognition functionality, highlighting its potential for large-scale deployment and research opportunities.
