title: Accurate, fully-automated NMR spectral profiling for metabolomics
Abstract: Many diseases significantly alter the concentrations of small molecules (metabolites) in biofluids, making it possible to detect these diseases from a person's metabolic profile. This information can be extracted from biofluid NMR spectra. Traditional manual analysis by trained experts is slow, expensive, and prone to errors. This paper presents Bayesil, a tool that automatically produces detailed metabolic profiles from 1D1H NMR spectra. Bayesil employs novel algorithms for spectral processing and matches the resulting spectra against a reference compound library. The matching process utilizes a probabilistic graphical model to infer the most probable metabolic profile. Extensive testing on diverse complex mixtures demonstrates Bayesil's ability to accurately determine the concentrations of all NMR-detectable metabolites (90% correct identification, 10% quantification error) in less than 5 minutes on a single CPU. Bayesil represents the first fully automatic, publicly accessible system for quantitative NMR spectral profiling, exceeding the accuracy of trained experts. This tool is expected to accelerate metabolomics research and facilitate new clinical applications of NMR.

title: Unsynthesizable Cores - Minimal Explanations for Unsynthesizable High-Level Robot Behaviors
Abstract: The increasing prevalence of multi-purpose robots necessitates user-friendly control mechanisms for non-experts to execute complex tasks. Formal methods are being employed to automatically synthesize controllers from user-defined specifications, ensuring correctness by construction. Recent work has also addressed the challenge of providing understandable feedback to users when specifications fail to yield a suitable controller. While existing techniques offer feedback on the problematic parts of the specification, they lack granularity. This work proposes methods for refining this feedback by extracting minimal explanations of why a controller cannot be synthesized.

title: Atomic-resolution TEM Studies of Pillar-Matrix Structures in Epitaxially Grown Ultrathin ZrO2-La2/3Sr1/3MnO3 Films
Abstract: This study investigates ZrO2-La2/3Sr1/3MnO3 pillar matrix thin films, revealing anomalous magnetic and electron transport properties influenced by the amount of ZrO2. Utilizing an aberration-corrected transmission electron microscope, the atomic-resolution structure and chemical information of the system, particularly at the pillar-matrix interface, were elucidated. Minor amounts of Zr were found to occupy Mn positions within the matrix, with a solubility limit of less than 6 mol%. The Zr concentration exhibited a minimum at the interface, accompanied by oxygen deficiency. La and Mn diffusion into the pillar was observed, alongside a change in Mn valence state. Atomic-resolution imaging revealed La and Mn positions within the ZrO2 pillars. These findings provide detailed insights for future studies of the macroscopic properties of these materials.

title: Hybrid Systems Knowledge Representation Using Modelling Environment System Techniques Artificial Intelligence
Abstract: Knowledge-based or Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques are increasingly employed as alternatives to traditional approaches for modeling environmental systems. This paper explores various AI techniques, leveraging examples of human perception, learning, and reasoning to solve complex problems. Recognizing the increasing complexity of environmental systems, the paper discusses the use of hybrid mechanisms, combining multiple AI techniques to create more advanced and intelligent systems capable of supporting human decision-making in managing environmental change.

title: Augmented Neural Networks for Modelling Consumer Indebtness
Abstract: Consumer debt has become a significant problem in modern societies, prompting extensive research into the nature of consumer indebtedness. While previous modeling efforts have relied on statistical models, this paper argues that Computational Intelligence offers a more holistic approach. The study demonstrates that Neural Networks outperform linear regression models in capturing the complex relationships within indebtedness datasets. The results highlight the effectiveness of incorporating data mining insights into Neural Networks, leveraging their flexibility in designing network topology. This novel framework for modeling consumer indebtedness can be extended to various real-world applications.

title: Comparison of Distance Metrics for Hierarchical Data in Medical Databases
Abstract: Distance metrics are widely utilized in various research areas, including bioinformatics and data mining. While metrics like pq-gram and Edit Distance are specifically designed for hierarchical data, other metrics like geometric and Hamming distances are used for non-hierarchical data. This paper investigates the applicability of these metrics to the Health Improvement Network (THIN) database, which contains both hierarchical and non-hierarchical data. The study converts THIN data into a tree-like structure for hierarchical metrics and frequency tables for non-hierarchical metrics. By comparing the performance of different metrics in identifying patient similarities and clustering patient populations, the study concludes that the two groups of metrics exhibit distinct characteristics. Despite their differences, all metrics demonstrate the ability to represent similar patient data and effectively discriminate among patients using k-means clustering.

title: Tuning a Multiple Classifier System for Side Effect Discovery using Genetic Algorithms
Abstract: Previous research introduced a supervised framework employing a binary classifier for side effect discovery, achieving excellent results. Interestingly, the use of different binary classifiers within the framework identified unique side effects, prompting the investigation of multiple classifier systems. This paper explores the use of genetic algorithms to optimize a side effect multiple classifying system. Results indicate that the proposed framework, implementing a multiple classifier system trained with genetic algorithms, achieves a higher partial area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) than single classifier systems. Additionally, the framework demonstrates efficient side effect detection and a low false positive rate.

title: Provide High-QoS of the High-Speed Railway Mobile Communications in Cyber-Physical Systems
Abstract: Advances in networks, embedded computing, and wireless communications are driving the development of complex intelligent systems known as Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS). CPS promises to transform our interaction with the physical world. The paper examines the Chinese Train Control System Level 3 (CTCS-3), a critical system for ensuring national economic and public safety. CTCS-3 relies on GSM-R (GSM for Railway) for continuous, two-way communication between ground stations and trains. To meet the growing demand for safety, speed, and service diversity, achieving high quality of service (QoS) is paramount. The paper analyzes the characteristics of GSM-R and the requirements for all-layer QoS indicators. It summarizes key technologies for enhancing QoS indicators across all layers. A comprehensive scheme is proposed to improve delay and packet loss indicators, with a real-time implementation example provided. The paper concludes that GSM-R, leveraging CPS characteristics, can deliver reliable and real-time communication for message transmission.

title: Analysing Fuzzy Sets Through Combining Measures of Similarity and Distance
Abstract: Reasoning with fuzzy sets often relies on measures like similarity and distance. However, these measures can produce misleading results when considered independently, potentially assigning the same value to different pairs of fuzzy sets. This is particularly problematic when dealing with numerous fuzzy sets derived from real data. While multiple measures can be used for automatic comparison, interpreting conflicting results becomes challenging. This paper introduces a method for combining results from multiple measures into a single measure for analyzing and comparing fuzzy sets. The combined measure mitigates ambiguous results and aids in automatic fuzzy set comparison. The paper outlines the properties of the combined measure and demonstrates its advantages over using individual measures.

title: A Fuzzy Directional Distance Measure
Abstract: Measuring the distance between two fuzzy sets is fundamental to fuzzy set theory. However, existing distance measures utilize crisp values to represent fuzzy set distances. This paper proposes a fuzzy distance measure that better reflects the inherent uncertainty within fuzzy sets. It also introduces a fuzzy directional distance measure that accounts for the direction of change between fuzzy sets. A multiplicative version is explored, but due to the computational complexity of full maximal assignment, an intermediate solution is offered.

title: Visual Speech Recognition
Abstract: Lip reading, a technique mastered by people with hearing difficulties, allows understanding speech without auditory input. Automating this challenging task, known as visual speech recognition (VSR), holds promise for numerous applications, including human-computer interaction, audio-visual speech recognition, speaker recognition, and video surveillance. VSR focuses on recognizing spoken words using only the visual signals produced during speech, employing image processing, artificial intelligence, and pattern recognition techniques.

title: Bypassing Captcha By Machine A Proof For Passing The Turing Test
Abstract: For a decade, CAPTCHAs have been used by websites to prevent automated data manipulation. By exploiting the reverse Turing test, CAPTCHAs rely on the assumption that humans are more intelligent than machines. While traditionally effective, recent advancements in optical character recognition (OCR) are challenging the security of CAPTCHAs. This study investigates the vulnerability of CAPTCHAs to OCR-based attacks, demonstrating that simple and even more complex CAPTCHAs can be easily broken using OCR machines. The paper suggests enhancing CAPTCHAs with natural language and multiple objects to potentially thwart machine-based attacks, highlighting the need for advancements in AI to truly overcome the Turing test.

title: Action Recognition in the Frequency Domain
Abstract: This paper proposes a method for mitigating variability in temporal data series by focusing on long-term, frequency domain features. Applied to human action recognition, the method leverages the robustness of frequency domain features against motion variations, viewpoint changes, dynamic backgrounds, occlusion, and other sources of variability. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of these frequency-based features in combination with a simple forest classifier for accurate and robust action recognition on the KTH Actions dataset.

title: Semiparametric Inference of the Complier Average Causal Effect with Nonignorable Missing Outcomes
Abstract: Noncompliance and missing data are common challenges in randomized trials, complicating causal inference. Existing methods address these challenges for binary and continuous outcomes under the latent ignorable missing data mechanism. However, this mechanism may not hold true in practice, as missing data can depend on the missing outcome itself. This paper investigates the identifiability and estimation of the complier average causal effect in trials with both noncompliance and outcome-dependent nonignorable missing data for continuous outcomes. A two-step maximum likelihood estimator is proposed to address the issue of infinite-dimensional nuisance parameters, eliminating the need for parametric assumptions about the missing data mechanism. The paper validates the method through simulations and sensitivity analysis, illustrating its application to a psychiatric clinical trial.

title: Deontic modality based on preference

title: Friendly Artificial Intelligence: the Physics Challenge
Abstract: The rapid advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) raise concerns about machines replacing humans in the workforce and potentially beyond. The concept of "Friendly AI," designed to safeguard humanity, has been proposed as a solution. However, from a physics perspective, this may be a challenging endeavor. This paper argues that understanding the meaning of life within the context of particle arrangements is crucial to achieve a future where humans are preserved. It emphasizes the need for a rigorous definition of "meaning," "life," and the ultimate ethical imperative to guide the arrangement of particles in the universe and shape its future. Without such a definition, the future may not include humans.

title: Feature Selection in Conditional Random Fields for Map Matching of GPS Trajectories
Abstract: Map matching of GPS trajectories is a fundamental technique used in Location Based Services to recover the original route on a road network from noisy GPS data. This paper addresses the challenge of map matching at low sampling rates on urban road networks by leveraging the capabilities of Conditional Random Fields (CRFs).  The paper explores the use of contextual features and feature selection in CRFs to improve map matching accuracy. Experiments on a taxi trajectory dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in achieving competitive results while reducing model complexity, making it suitable for computationally limited applications.

title: Ensemble Learning of Colorectal Cancer Survival Rates
Abstract: This paper presents a dataset related to cellular and physical conditions of colorectal cancer patients undergoing tumor removal. This unique data provides insights into immunological status at the time of surgery, tumor classification, and post-operative survival. The paper explores an ensemble approach for identifying patients with clearer prognostic parameters by leveraging existing research on clustering and machine learning applied to this dataset. The paper showcases the performance of different survival prediction models and highlights the improvement in accuracy achieved when agreement is reached between models.

title: Data classification using the Dempster-Shafer method
Abstract: This paper explores the use of the Dempster-Shafer method as a theoretical framework for building data classification systems. The method is tested on three benchmark datasets with varying numbers of classes. The study involves training the system on a subset of the data to establish thresholds and likelihoods of class membership for each attribute. These values are then used to create mass functions that represent the probability of class membership for each attribute of the test data. Dempster's Rule of Combination is employed to classify each data item based on the combined probabilities. The results demonstrate high classification accuracy, comparable to other popular methods. While the D-S method offers promising performance, the complexity increases with the addition of new attributes due to the overhead of generating accurate mass functions. Overall, the paper suggests that the D-S approach provides a suitable framework for classification systems, with automated mass function design and calculation potentially enhancing its viability for complex problems.

title: An Approach for Assessing Clustering of Households by Electricity Usage
Abstract: This paper investigates the variability of household electricity usage patterns to enable effective targeting of behaviour modification initiatives for improving electricity network efficiency. The paper proposes a method for representing household behaviour variability and clustering households into meaningful groupings based on these variability measures. The effectiveness of the measures is evaluated using various cluster validity indexes, examining their sensitivity to the number of clusters, attributes, and attribute quality. The Cluster Dispersion Indicator (CDI) and Davies-Boulden Indicator (DBI) are identified as promising metrics for future work on developing indicators of household behaviour variability. The approach is tested using data from 180 UK households monitored for over a year at 5-minute intervals, focusing on the evening peak usage period from 4 pm to 8 pm.

title: Detect Adverse Drug Reactions for Drug Aspirin
Abstract: Adverse drug reactions (ADRs) pose a significant public health concern. This study proposes a novel approach for detecting ADRs using a feature matrix and feature selection. title: Team Behavior in Interactive Dynamic Influence Diagrams with Applications to Ad Hoc Teams
Abstract: Planning for ad hoc teamwork poses challenges due to the lack of prior coordination or communication between collaborating agents. This paper focuses on principled methods for a single agent to cooperate with others, investigating the ad hoc teamwork problem within the framework of individual decision-making. However, individual decision-making in multiagent settings requires reasoning about other agents' actions, leading to an infinite nesting problem. To address this, the paper proposes a solution based on level 0 models, which provide an approximation by bounding the nesting from below. The paper demonstrates that this finite nesting approach may not yield optimal team solutions in cooperative settings. To overcome this limitation, the paper incorporates learning into the level 0 models. The integration of learning into planning using interactive dynamic influence diagrams facilitates optimal team behavior, making it applicable to ad hoc teamwork.

title: Show Me the Money: Dynamic Recommendations for Revenue Maximization
Abstract: Recommender Systems (RS) play a crucial role in applications like e-commerce and content streaming. While existing RS research primarily focuses on predicting user preferences and maximizing user utilities, this paper investigates the connection between RS and business profitability. Recognizing recommendations as a communication channel between businesses and customers, the paper explores strategic dynamic recommendations for revenue maximization. A novel model is proposed that considers factors such as prices, valuations, saturation effects, and competition among products. The paper addresses the problem of finding revenue-maximizing recommendation strategies over a finite time horizon, proving its NP-hardness and establishing an elegant connection to matroid theory for achieving approximation guarantees. Due to the high complexity of the approximation algorithm, intelligent heuristics are developed for the original problem. Extensive experiments on real and synthetic datasets demonstrate the efficiency, scalability, and effectiveness of the proposed algorithms, significantly outperforming intuitive baselines.

title: Personalization of Itineraries search using Ontology and Rules to Avoid Congestion in Urban Areas
Abstract: Research on urban freight movements remains limited, with most urban mobility studies focusing on passenger vehicles rather than commercial vehicles transporting freight. However, urban freight transport significantly contributes to congestion, air pollution, noise, accidents, and increased fuel consumption, impacting logistical costs and product prices. This paper proposes a novel solution for mitigating congestion and optimizing the distribution process of goods in urban areas. The paper introduces a personalization technique for itinerary search based on city logistics ontology and rules, addressing the need to capture and satisfy the preferences of different stakeholders. The proposed approach is implemented for a freight transportation itinerary search problem, demonstrating its ability to provide intelligent decision support by retrieving optimal itineraries that meet the preferences of various stakeholders.

title: On computable abstractions (a conceptual introduction)

The paper defines abstractional machines, which are capable of building and using their own understanding based on computable abstractions through a mechanical process. The paper illustrates the application of abstractional machines to natural language processing through an example.

title: Cooperation with Disagreement Correction in the Presence of Communication Failures
Abstract: Vehicle-to-vehicle communication is essential for cooperative vehicular systems to achieve high performance and safety standards. Vehicles periodically exchange critical information with nearby vehicles to determine their maneuvers based on information quality and established strategies. However, wireless communication vulnerabilities can lead to information omissions, resulting in conflicting and potentially unsafe trajectories. This paper presents a deterministic solution that enables vehicles to utilize a default strategy in case of incomplete information reception. The solution relies on a timed distributed protocol that adapts its output to handle message omission failures, ensuring a short disagreement period. The paper formally proves the correctness of the solution and demonstrates its efficiency through experiments. The application of this solution to vehicular platooning is discussed, showcasing its potential for achieving high performance while maintaining safety standards despite communication failures.

title: An Information Retrieval Approach to Short Text Conversation
Abstract: Human-computer conversation remains one of the most challenging problems in artificial intelligence. This paper addresses a key sub-problem, short text conversation, focusing on generating reasonable responses to human messages. Leveraging the vast amount of short conversation data available on social media, the paper proposes formalizing short text conversation as a search problem and employing state-of-the-art information retrieval (IR) techniques. The paper explores the benefits and limitations of the IR approach, demonstrating its effectiveness in enabling "intelligent" system behavior when combined with a large repository of social media conversation data.

title: AI Evaluation: past, present and future
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) development requires regular performance evaluation to certify progress and foster advancements. This paper critically assesses different AI system evaluation methods, starting with the traditional task-oriented approach. The paper highlights the increasing prevalence of black-box (behavioural) evaluation as AI systems become more complex and unpredictable. Three types of evaluation are identified: human discrimination, problem benchmarks, and peer confrontation. The paper discusses the limitations of evaluation settings and competitions in these categories and proposes ideas for more systematic and robust evaluation. The paper then explores a less conventional ability-oriented evaluation approach, where systems are characterized by their cognitive abilities rather than specific tasks. The paper discusses the adaptation of cognitive tests used for humans and animals, the development of tests based on algorithmic information theory, and more general approaches within the framework of universal psychometrics.

title: Mathematical Knowledge Representation: Semantic Models and Formalisms
Abstract: This paper presents a survey of semantic methods for solving fundamental tasks in mathematical knowledge management. The paper explores ontological models and formalisms, proposing an ontology of mathematical knowledge that encompasses a wide range of mathematical fields. title: Scalability and Resilience of Software-Defined Networking: An Overview
Abstract: Software-Defined Networking (SDN) offers centralized control over network resources for optimized and flexible traffic management. However, scalability becomes a concern as network size and traffic volume increase, and centralized control points can create single points of failure, jeopardizing network resilience. This article examines SDN focusing on scalability challenges due to increased control overhead and resiliency in terms of protecting against controller failure, network topology failure, and malicious attacks.

title: Memcomputing and Swarm Intelligence
Abstract: Memcomputing, a paradigm employing memory for computation, is explored in relation to swarm intelligence algorithms. The study demonstrates that memristive networks can solve short-path optimization problems, analogous to those tackled by ant-colony algorithms. Notably, memristive networks achieve solutions in a single deterministic step, unlike the multi-step stochastic process of ant colony optimization. This finding opens avenues for nanoscale hardware implementations of diverse swarm intelligence algorithms, potentially encompassing scheduling problems and robotics.

title: Equilibrium States in Numerical Argumentation Networks
Abstract: Given an argumentation network with pre-assigned argument values, the paper seeks algorithms capable of generating extensions consistent with these initial values. The proposed approach involves an iterative formula that incorporates initial values and attack relationships, generating a sequence of intermediate values that converge to an extension. The paper comprehensively investigates the properties of this iterative formula and its connections with other numerical and non-numerical techniques.

title: Knowledge Engineering for Planning-Based Hypothesis Generation
Abstract: This paper addresses the knowledge engineering challenges in hypothesis generation, driven by applications requiring rapid hypothesis exploration under unreliable observations. Two applications are examined: malware detection and intensive care delivery. In intensive care, the goal is to formulate plausible hypotheses about patient conditions based on clinical observations and refine these hypotheses to develop recovery plans. Similarly, preventing malware propagation within a network involves generating hypotheses from network traffic data and implementing preventive measures. Building upon the established use of AI planning for similar problems, the paper proposes planning for hypothesis generation. However, to address uncertainty, incomplete model descriptions, and unreliable observations, the paper utilizes a planner capable of generating multiple high-quality plans. A language called LTS++ is introduced to capture model descriptions, along with a web-based tool for specifying LTS++ models and observations. A 9-step process is proposed to guide domain experts in specifying the LTS++ model. Hypotheses are generated by applying a planner to the translated LTS++ model and the provided trace. The generated hypotheses can be visualized, presented to analysts, or further investigated automatically.

title: Definition and properties to assess multi-agent environments as social intelligence tests
Abstract: Social intelligence in natural and artificial systems is typically assessed by evaluating traits or tasks associated with social behavior. These traits are then combined to form an intuitive understanding of social intelligence. In this paper, a parameterized definition of social intelligence is proposed, defined as the expected performance in a set of environments with multiple agents. Tests are derived from this definition, highlighting several explicit dependencies: (1) the definition depends on the choice and weighting of environments and agents, (2) the definition can incorporate both competitive and cooperative behaviors based on agent and reward team arrangements, (3) the definition heavily relies on the abilities of other agents, and (4) the distinction between social intelligence and general intelligence is influenced by these choices. The paper aims to transform this definition into a more precise one by incorporating fundamental properties ensuring social behavior, such as action and reward dependency and anticipation of competitive/cooperative behaviors, as well as more instrumental properties like secernment, boundedness, symmetry, validity, reliability, and efficiency. These properties facilitate converting the definition into a practical test. The paper then examines various multi-agent environments, tests, and games to assess their adherence to these properties.

title: Consensus and Consistency Level Optimization of Fuzzy Preference Relation: A Soft Computing Approach
Abstract: In group decision-making (GDM) problems, fuzzy preference relations (FPRs) are widely used to represent decision-makers' opinions on a set of alternatives. To avoid misleading solutions, consistency and consensus analysis have become crucial. This article presents a simulated annealing (SA)-based soft computing approach to optimize the consistency/consensus level (CCL) of a complete fuzzy preference relation to solve GDM problems. Consistency level indicates the quality of an expert's preferences, while consensus level measures the agreement among experts' opinions. The study also suggests a method to identify experts requiring modifications to their preference structures without moderator intervention.

title: A Complete framework for ambush avoidance in realistic environments
Abstract: Operating vehicles in adversarial environments between recurring origin-destination pairs necessitates novel planning techniques. A two-player zero-sum game is introduced, where the first player aims to minimize expected convoy casualties, while the second player seeks to maximize this damage. The game's outcome is determined through a linear program solving the corresponding minmax optimization problem. Various environment models are defined to compute routing strategies over unstructured environments. To compare these methods for increasingly accurate environment representations, a grid-based model is employed, highlighting the requirement for a sufficiently large network. A comprehensive framework for generating realistic routing strategies between any two points is described. This framework relies on accurately assessing potential casualties at each location, identifying crucial parameters. The framework is then tested in real-world environments.

title: Meta-Metrics for Simulations in Software Engineering on the Example of Integral Safety Systems
Abstract: Vehicles, passengers, and other traffic participants are increasingly protected by integrated safety systems. These systems continuously monitor the vehicle's environment to prevent dangerous situations through features like emergency braking systems. Research and development efforts are focused on enhancing vehicle intelligence to further reduce accident risks. However, validation methods should extend beyond proving grounds and real-world test runs, incorporating virtual testing approaches to model potentially dangerous situations or re-run specific traffic scenarios easily. This article highlights meta-metrics as a key challenge in the software engineering of these cyber-physical systems, providing guidance during development. For instance, unstable simulation test results over vehicle function revision history are identified as an indicator for focusing on real or further virtual testing. Similarly, varying acting time points for the same virtual traffic situation signal potential reliability issues in interpreting the specific situation. The article discusses several such meta-metrics and assigns them to different phases during series development and various levels of detail in virtual testing approaches.

title: Supervised Hashing Using Graph Cuts and Boosted Decision Trees
Abstract: Embedding image features into a binary Hamming space can enhance both speed and accuracy in large-scale query-by-example image retrieval systems. Supervised hashing aims to map original features to compact binary codes while preserving label-based similarities of the original data. Most existing approaches utilize a single hash function type and an optimization process tightly coupled to that specific form. This tight coupling restricts flexibility and can lead to complex optimization problems. This work proposes a flexible and straightforward framework capable of accommodating different loss functions and hash functions. The proposed framework provides a context for existing hashing approaches and simplifies the development of problem-specific methods. The framework decomposes the process into two steps: binary code (hash bits) learning and hash function learning. Binary code learning is typically formulated as a binary quadratic problem, while hash function learning is achieved by training standard binary classifiers. For large-scale binary code inference, the paper demonstrates how to ensure submodularity in the binary quadratic problems, enabling efficient graph cut approaches. To achieve efficiency and effectiveness with high-dimensional data, the paper proposes using boosted decision trees as hash functions, which are nonlinear, highly descriptive, and fast to train and evaluate. Experiments demonstrate the proposed method's superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods, particularly with high-dimensional data.

title: Three-Dimensional Triplet Tracking for LHC and Future High Rate Experiments
Abstract: The hit combinatorial problem is a significant challenge in track reconstruction and triggering at high-rate experiments. At hadron colliders, low-momentum tracks contribute significantly to hits, where multiple scattering (MS) effects dominate hit resolution. MS is also the primary source of hit confusion and track uncertainties in low-energy precision experiments. In environments where MS dominates, track reconstruction and fitting can be simplified by utilizing three-dimensional (3D) hit-triplets provided by pixel detectors. This simplification is possible due to track uncertainties being solely determined by MS when high-precision spatial information is available. Fitting hit-triplets is particularly straightforward for tracking detectors in solenoidal magnetic fields. The over-constrained 3D-triplet method provides a complete set of track parameters and is robust against false hit combinations. This method is ideal for pixel detectors where hits can be treated as 3D points. The availability of cost-effective and industrially produced CMOS sensors enables the construction of highly granular full-scale pixel tracking detectors, even for experiments at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) or future high-energy (hadron) colliders. This paper presents tracking performance studies for full-scale pixel detectors, including their optimization for 3D-triplet tracking. Results obtained for different tracker geometries and reconstruction methods are compared. The potential for reducing the number of tracking layers and material budget using this new tracking concept is discussed. The paper also highlights the possibility of using 3D-triplet tracking for triggering and fast online reconstruction.

title: Soft Neutrosophic Algebraic Structures and Their Generalization

This book explores soft neutrosophic algebraic structures, combining soft sets with neutrosophic algebraic structures. The book investigates soft neutrosophic groups, soft neutrosophic semigroups, soft neutrosophic loops, soft neutrosophic LA-semigroups, and their generalizations.

title: Automatic and efficient driving strategies while approaching a traffic light
Abstract: Vehicle-infrastructure communication offers new possibilities for improving traffic flow efficiency at signalized intersections. This study assumes that equipped vehicles can access information about relevant traffic light switching times in advance. This information is leveraged to improve traffic flow through strategies like "early braking," "anticipative start," and "flying start." These strategies can be implemented in driver-information mode or automatically through an Adaptive Cruise Controller (ACC). Quality criteria include cycle-averaged capacity, driving comfort, fuel consumption, travel time, and the number of stops. The study uses simulation to investigate the isolated strategies and complex interactions between strategies and between equipped and non-equipped vehicles. Relative performance indexes are proposed as a universal approach to assessing equipment level effects. At a maximum speed of 50 km/h, the study observed improvements of approximately 15% for the number of stops and around 4% for other criteria. These figures double when increasing the maximum speed to 70 km/h.

title: Towards Decision Support Technology Platform for Modular Systems
Abstract: This methodological survey paper explores a general decision support platform technology for modular systems (modular/composite alternatives/solutions) across various applied domains. The platform comprises seven fundamental combinatorial engineering frameworks: system synthesis, system modeling, evaluation, bottleneck detection, improvement/extension, multistage design, combinatorial evolution, and forecasting. The platform relies on decision support procedures (e.g., multicriteria selection/sorting, clustering), combinatorial optimization problems (e.g., knapsack, multiple choice problem, clique, assignment/allocation, covering, spanning trees), and their combinations. The paper describes (1) the general scheme of the decision support platform technology, (2) brief descriptions of modular (composite) systems, (3) trends in transitioning from alternative selection to composite alternative processing, (4) resource requirements (human and information-computer), and (5) basic combinatorial engineering frameworks and their applications across various domains.

title: New Ideas for Brain Modelling 2
Abstract: This paper presents a relatively simple method for enabling a brain model to self-organize its concept patterns through nested structures. For simulation purposes, time reduction is beneficial, allowing visualization of pattern formation and sequential firing during search or thought processes. A simple equation is used to demonstrate how inhibitors, specifically, can deactivate certain areas, enabling other areas to become prominent and define the current brain state. This provides a degree of control over what appears to be a chaotic structure within the brain. The method is attractive due to its largely mechanical nature, allowing for automatic processing or modeling. The paper also explains how the nested pattern structure can function as a basic counting mechanism. Another mathematical conclusion provides a foundation for maintaining memory or concept patterns. Self-organization can space itself through automatic processes, potentially facilitating the even distribution of new neurons and preserving concept integrity. This process could also aid in finding memory structures later. This extended version integrates further with the existing cognitive model and presents new conclusions.

title: Applications and Analysis of Bio-Inspired Eagle Strategy for Engineering Optimization
Abstract: Swarm intelligence-based optimization algorithms utilize stochastic components to enhance solution diversity during the search process. This randomization is often represented as random walks. This work analyzes these randomization methods within the context of nature-inspired algorithms. The study employs eagle strategy to provide basic observations and relate step sizes and search efficiency using Markov theory. These analyses and observations are then applied to solve four design benchmarks: a pressure vessel, a speed reducer, a PID controller, and a heat exchanger. The results indicate that eagle strategy with Lévy flights can significantly reduce overall computational effort.

title: Designing labeled graph classifiers by exploiting the Rényi entropy of the dissimilarity representation
Abstract: Representing patterns as labeled graphs is becoming increasingly common in the field of computational intelligence. Accordingly, a wide range of pattern recognition tools, including classifiers and knowledge discovery procedures, are available and tested for datasets of labeled graphs. However, designing effective learning procedures in the space of labeled graphs remains challenging, particularly from a computational complexity perspective. This paper presents a significant improvement to a general-purpose classifier for graphs, which is based on an interplay between dissimilarity representation, clustering, information-theoretic techniques, and evolutionary optimization algorithms. The improvement focuses on a key subroutine designed to compress the input data. The paper proves theorems fundamental to parameter setting for this compression operation. The effectiveness of the resulting classifier is demonstrated by benchmarking its variants on well-known datasets of labeled graphs, considering classification accuracy, computing time, and parsimony in terms of structural complexity of the synthesized classification models. The results showcase state-of-the-art performance in terms of test set accuracy and a substantial speed-up in computing time.

title: A Bayesian Ensemble Regression Framework on the Angry Birds Game
Abstract: An ensemble inference mechanism is proposed for the Angry Birds game domain. This mechanism utilizes an efficient tree structure for encoding and representing game screenshots, leveraging its enhanced modeling capabilities. This approach enables the creation of an informative feature space, transforming the task of game playing into a regression analysis problem. Assuming that each object material and bird pair has its own Bayesian linear regression model, a multi-model regression framework is designed. This framework simultaneously calculates the conditional expectations of several objects and makes a target decision through an ensemble of regression models. The learning procedure is implemented using an online estimation strategy for model parameters. Comparative experimental results across several game levels demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed methodology.

title: Improving the Interpretability of Support Vector Machines-based Fuzzy Rules
Abstract: Support vector machines (SVMs) and fuzzy rule systems are functionally equivalent under certain conditions. Consequently, learning algorithms developed for SVMs can be used to adapt the parameters of fuzzy systems. Extracting fuzzy models from SVMs offers the advantage of not requiring the determination of the number of rules in advance. However, post-SVM learning typically results in high complexity and reduced interpretability. This paper proposes a comprehensive framework for extracting interpretable SVM-based fuzzy modeling, addressing optimization issues within the models. Simulation examples illustrate the paper's concept. |||

title: A two-stage architecture for stock price forecasting by combining SOM and fuzzy-SVM
Abstract: This paper proposes a stock price prediction model that combines Self-Organizing Maps (SOM) and fuzzy-Support Vector Machines (f-SVM). The approach extracts fuzzy rules from raw data using a statistical machine learning model. SOM clusters the input space into distinct regions, and f-SVM extracts fuzzy rules for each region. These rules are then used to predict the test data using fuzzy inference algorithms. The performance of the proposed model is compared against other models using four datasets.

title: OpenHEC: A Framework for Application Programmers to Design FPGA-based Systems
Abstract: Today, there is a growing trend towards embedding intelligence, such as vision capabilities, into various devices, demanding high performance from computing systems. For embedded systems, low power consumption is also crucial alongside high computing power. Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs), known for their ability to support different types of fine-grained parallelism, offer significant power and performance advantages. However, traditional FPGA-based system design is complex and requires expertise beyond the scope of software programmers. This paper introduces the OpenHEC (Open Framework for High-Efficiency Computing) framework, a design framework that empowers application-level programmers to leverage FPGA-based platforms. OpenHEC simplifies the design process by abstracting away hardware and architectural details, allowing programmers to focus on algorithms and applications. It is integrated with the commercial Xilinx ISE/Vivado for immediate use. The effectiveness of OpenHEC is demonstrated by implementing a widely-used feature detection algorithm from a software programmer's perspective, highlighting its suitability for application programmers with limited hardware knowledge.

title: A Study of Proxies for Shapley Allocations of Transport Costs
Abstract: This paper explores solutions for calculating the cost of serving each location in a single-vehicle transport setting. This cost-to-serve analysis has strategic and operational implications in transportation. The problem is formally defined as the Traveling Salesperson Game (TSG), a cooperative total utility game where agents represent locations in a Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP). The cost to serve a location is a portion of the optimal tour cost. The Shapley value, a fundamental normative division scheme in cooperative games, provides a principled and fair allocation for both the TSG and general scenarios. The paper examines direct and sampling-based procedures for calculating the Shapley value and presents the first proof that approximating the Shapley value of the TSG within a constant factor is NP-hard. Using the Shapley value as an ideal baseline allocation, six computationally tractable proxies are developed. An experimental evaluation using synthetic Euclidean games and games derived from real-world tours calculated for fast-moving consumer goods scenarios is performed. The results indicate that several computationally efficient allocation techniques provide good proxies for the Shapley value.

title: Swarm Intelligence Based Multi-phase OPF For Peak Power Loss Reduction In A Smart Grid
Abstract: Computational intelligence is gaining traction in improving the efficiency of smart grids. A key challenge is designing optimal power flow (OPF) tools for solving important planning problems, including optimizing distributed generation (DG) capacities. While several OPF tools exist for balanced networks, research on unbalanced multi-phase distribution networks is limited. This paper presents a new OPF technique for DG capacity planning in a smart grid. The proposed algorithm considers a multi-phase power distribution system with unbalanced loadings, voltage control, and reactive power compensation devices. The algorithm employs a co-simulation framework that optimizes the objective function by adapting a constriction factor particle swarm optimization. The multi-phase OPF technique is validated using the IEEE 8500-node benchmark distribution system.

title: Incremental Cardinality Constraints for MaxSAT
Abstract: Maximum Satisfiability (MaxSAT) is an optimization variant of the Boolean Satisfiability (SAT) problem. MaxSAT algorithms typically involve a series of SAT solver calls to find an optimal solution, relying heavily on cardinality constraints. Many of these algorithms are non-incremental, meaning that the formula is rebuilt in each iteration, and no knowledge is retained from previous iterations. This paper introduces novel schemes for utilizing cardinality constraints incrementally, leveraging knowledge acquired across iterations. These schemes are integrated with several MaxSAT algorithms. Experimental results demonstrate a significant performance improvement for these algorithms compared to their non-incremental counterparts. These findings suggest that incremental cardinality constraints can be beneficial for other constraint solving domains.

title: Offline Signature-Based Fuzzy Vault (OSFV: Review and New Results
Abstract: An offline signature-based fuzzy vault (OSFV) is a bio-cryptographic implementation that uses handwritten signature images as biometrics instead of traditional passwords to secure private cryptographic keys. A reliable OSFV implementation is crucial for automating financial and legal authentication processes, enhancing the security of confidential documents through embedded handwritten signatures. This paper reviews a recently proposed OSFV implementation that employs a machine learning approach based on the dissimilarity representation concept to select reliable feature representations for the fuzzy vault scheme. Several variants of this system are proposed for improved accuracy and security. Notably, a new method for adapting the user key size is introduced. Performance comparisons using the Brazilian PUCPR and GPDS signature databases show that the key-size adaptation method effectively balances security and accuracy. While average system entropy is increased from 45 bits to about 51 bits, the average error rate (AER) is reduced by approximately 21%.

title: Learning Deep Representation for Face Alignment with Auxiliary Attributes
Abstract: This study challenges the conventional view of landmark detection or face alignment as a singular and independent problem. It demonstrates that the robustness of this task can be significantly enhanced by incorporating auxiliary information. The study proposes a joint optimization of landmark detection and recognition of heterogeneous but subtly correlated facial attributes, such as gender, expression, and appearance attributes. This approach is non-trivial due to varying learning difficulties and convergence rates among different attribute inference tasks. To address this, a novel tasks-constrained deep model is formulated. The model not only learns inter-task correlation but also employs dynamic task coefficients to facilitate optimization convergence when learning multiple complex tasks. Extensive evaluations show that the proposed task-constrained learning outperforms existing face alignment methods, particularly in dealing with faces with severe occlusion and pose variation. Additionally, it drastically reduces model complexity compared to state-of-the-art methods based on cascaded deep models.

title: On Detecting Messaging Abuse in Short Text Messages using Linguistic and Behavioral patterns
Abstract: Short text messages have become a popular communication channel in social media and instant messaging in recent years. This increased popularity has led to a rise in messaging threats, including spam, phishing, and malware. The presence of lexical variants, SMS-like contractions, and advanced obfuscations poses additional challenges for traditional filtering solutions. This paper explores the effectiveness of machine learning filters based on linguistic and behavioral patterns for detecting short text spam and abusive users in a network using a real-world SMS dataset from a large US telecommunications operator and a social media corpus. The paper examines different approaches to address challenges such as tokenization and entity detection by employing text normalization and substring clustering techniques. The obtained results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed solution by enhancing baseline approaches.

title: Classifying sequences by the optimized dissimilarity space embedding approach: a case study on the solubility analysis of the E. coli proteome
Abstract: This paper evaluates a version of the Optimized Dissimilarity Space Embedding (ODSE) classification system that operates in the input space of sequences of generic objects. ODSE was originally presented as a classification system for patterns represented as labeled graphs. However, as ODSE is based on the dissimilarity space representation of input data, it can be readily adapted to any domain where a meaningful dissimilarity measure can be defined. This paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the ODSE classifier for sequences by applying it to the recognition of the solubility degree of the Escherichia coli proteome. Solubility, or aggregation propensity, is a key property of protein molecules closely related to folding mechanisms. Each protein in the dataset is associated with a solubility degree and represented as a sequence of symbols denoting the 20 amino acid residues. The computational results, obtained without context-dependent tuning of the ODSE system, confirm the validity and generality of the ODSE-based approach for structured data classification.

title: Unsupervised learning segmentation for dynamic speckle activity images
Abstract: This paper proposes the design of decision models using computational intelligence techniques applied to dynamic laser speckle image sequences. These models aim to identify image regions of biological specimens illuminated by a coherent laser beam. The field image is pseudo-colored using a Self Organizing Map projection. This process utilizes a set of descriptors applied to intensity variations over time in each pixel of an image sequence. The models employ descriptors specifically selected to improve effectiveness based on the application. The paper presents two examples of applying these techniques to assess biological tissues. The obtained results are encouraging and significantly improve those achieved using a single descriptor.

title: Information Transfer Fidelity in Spin Networks and Ring-based Quantum Routers
Abstract: Spin networks possess an Information Transfer Fidelity (ITF), which defines an absolute upper bound on the probability of excitation transmission between spins. While ITF is easily calculable, reaching this bound asymptotically requires specific conditions. The paper establishes general conditions for achieving this bound and presents a dynamical model, the translation on the torus, for achieving maximum transfer probability. The time to reach maximum probability is estimated using simultaneous Diophantine approximation, implemented through a variant of the Lenstra-Lenstra-Lovasz (LLL) algorithm. For a ring with uniform couplings, the network can be treated as a metric space by defining a distance that quantifies the lack of transmission fidelity between nodes. The paper demonstrates that transfer fidelities and transfer times can be significantly improved through simple controls using non-dynamic, spatially localized bias fields. This opens possibilities for intelligent design of spin networks and dynamic information routing, offering greater flexibility compared to engineering fixed couplings or demanding fast dynamic control schemes.

title: Distributed Estimation with Information-Seeking Control in Agent Network
Abstract: This paper introduces a distributed, cooperative framework and method for Bayesian estimation and control in decentralized agent networks. The framework combines joint estimation of time-varying global and local states with information-seeking control that optimizes agent behavior. It is suitable for nonlinear and non-Gaussian problems, particularly in location-aware networks. For cooperative estimation, belief propagation message passing and consensus are combined. For cooperative control, the negative posterior joint entropy of all states is maximized through gradient ascent. The estimation layer provides the control layer with probabilistic information in the form of sample representations of probability distributions. Simulation results demonstrate intelligent agent behavior and excellent estimation performance for a simultaneous self-localization and target tracking problem. In a cooperative localization scenario with only one anchor, mobile agents can localize themselves with an accuracy exceeding that of distance measurements after a short time.

title: On the genetic architecture of intelligence and other quantitative traits
Abstract: This paper explores the impact of genes on cognitive ability and other quantitative human traits like height and disease risk. It provides a brief overview of psychometric measurements of intelligence, introducing the concept of a "general factor" or g score. The paper focuses on the stability, validity, and heritability of adult g. The largest component of genetic variance for both height and intelligence is additive (linear), simplifying predictive modeling and statistical estimation. Due to decreasing genotyping costs, researchers may soon identify loci responsible for a significant portion of total g variation. Analogous efforts are underway for height. The paper describes unpublished results concerning the genetic architecture of height and cognitive ability, suggesting that approximately 10,000 moderately rare causal variants, mostly with negative effects, contribute to normal population variation. Using results from Compressed Sensing (L1-penalized regression), the paper estimates the statistical power needed to characterize linear and nonlinear models for quantitative traits. The key unknown parameter, sparsity (s), represents the number of loci responsible for the majority of genetic variation. The required sample size is estimated to be in the hundreds for most traits, or roughly a million in the case of cognitive ability.

title: The New Approach on Fuzzy Decision Trees
Abstract: Decision trees are widely used in machine learning, but real-world data collection often involves fuzziness and uncertainty. This paper presents a method for constructing fuzzy decision trees, proposing a fuzzy decision tree induction method based on the iris flower dataset. The method calculates entropy from the distance between an average value and a particular value. An experimental result demonstrates the accuracy of the proposed method compared to the traditional ID3 algorithm.

title: Linear Contour Learning: A Method for Supervised Dimension Reduction
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to sufficient dimension reduction in regression, based on estimating contour directions of negligible variation for the response surface. These directions span the orthogonal complement of the minimal space relevant for regression and can be extracted according to a measure of variation in the response, leading to General Contour Regression (GCR). Compared to existing techniques, this contour-based methodology guarantees exhaustive estimation of the central space under ellipticity of the predictor distribution and minimal additional assumptions while maintaining consistency and computational ease. Furthermore, it demonstrates robustness to departures from ellipticity. The paper also establishes useful population properties for GCR. Simulations comparing performance with standard techniques such as ordinary least squares, sliced inverse regression, principal Hessian directions, and sliced average variance estimation confirm the advantages predicted by theoretical analyses. The paper illustrates the use of contour-based methods on a dataset concerning grades of students from Massachusetts colleges.

title: Matrix Completion under Interval Uncertainty
Abstract: Matrix completion under interval uncertainty can be formulated as matrix completion with element-wise box constraints. This paper presents an efficient alternating-direction parallel coordinate-descent method for solving this problem. The method demonstrates superior performance compared to other known methods on a benchmark for image in-painting in terms of signal-to-noise ratio. It also provides high-quality solutions for a collaborative filtering instance with 100,198,805 recommendations within 5 minutes.

title: Video Face Editing Using Temporal-Spatial-Smooth Warping
Abstract: Editing faces in videos is a popular but challenging task in computer vision and graphics, with applications in facial attractiveness enhancement, makeup transfer, face replacement, and expression manipulation. Applying image-based warping algorithms to video-based face editing often leads to temporal incoherence in synthesized videos because consistently localizing facial features across different faces or consecutive frames is difficult. This usually necessitates significant manual manipulation. This paper proposes a novel temporal-spatial-smooth warping (TSSW) algorithm to effectively exploit temporal information in consecutive frames and spatial smoothness within each frame. TSSW accurately estimates two control lattices in the horizontal and vertical directions from the corresponding lattices in the previous frame, by minimizing a novel energy function that integrates a data-driven term, a smoothness term, and feature point constraints. Corresponding warping surfaces then precisely map source frames to target frames. Experimental testing on facial attractiveness enhancement, makeup transfer, face replacement, and expression manipulation demonstrates that TSSW effectively preserves spatial smoothness and temporal coherence in editing facial geometry, skin detail, identity, and expression, outperforming existing face editing methods. Notably, TSSW is robust to subtle inaccuracies in feature point localization and represents a significant improvement over image-based warping methods.

title: In principle determination of generic priors
Abstract: Probability theory as extended logic is completed by considering propositional logic (instead of predicate logic) as syntactically sufficient and imposing a symmetry from propositional logic. This approach demonstrates how the notions of "possibility" and "property" can be adequately represented in propositional logic, resulting in: 1) the principle of indifference becoming essentially combinatorial in nature, and 2) the ability to represent assumptions where a space of possibilities is assumed without specifying its size.

title: Modeling Creativity: Case Studies in Python
Abstract: Modeling Creativity (doctoral dissertation, 2013) explores how creativity can be represented using computational approaches. The aim is to construct computer models that exhibit creativity in an artistic context, capable of generating or evaluating artwork, new ideas, or subjective opinions. The research, conducted from 2008 to 2012, focused on artistic creativity and explored various perspectives, from its origins in nature to humans and machines, covering both the generation of creative ideas and the evaluation and learning of their novelty and usefulness. Case studies and examples using the Python programming language were used to illustrate the concepts.

title: Exponentiated Gradient Exploration for Active Learning
Abstract: Active learning strategies address the cost of labelling in supervised classification by selecting the most informative unlabelled examples for training a predictive model. Many conventional active learning algorithms focus on refining the decision boundary rather than exploring new regions that could be more informative. This paper proposes a sequential algorithm named EG-Active that enhances any active learning algorithm with optimal random exploration. Experimental results show a statistically significant and substantial improvement in the performance of this new approach compared to existing active feedback methods.

title: Probabilistic inverse reinforcement learning in unknown environments
Abstract: We propose a method for learning from agents acting in unknown stochastic Markov environments or games. Our goal is to estimate agent preferences to construct improved policies for the same task the agents are trying to solve. We extend previous probabilistic approaches for inverse reinforcement learning in known MDPs to the case of unknown dynamics or opponents. We derive two simplified probabilistic models of the demonstrator's policy and utility. For tractability, we use maximum a posteriori estimation instead of full Bayesian inference. Under a flat prior, this results in a convex optimization problem. We find that the resulting algorithms are highly competitive against a variety of other methods for inverse reinforcement learning that have knowledge of the dynamics.

title: Scalable Matrix-valued Kernel Learning for High-dimensional Nonlinear Multivariate Regression and Granger Causality
Abstract: We propose a general matrix-valued multiple kernel learning framework for high-dimensional nonlinear multivariate regression problems. This framework allows a broad class of mixed norm regularizers, including those that induce sparsity, to be imposed on a dictionary of vector-valued Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces. We develop a highly scalable and eigendecomposition-free algorithm that orchestrates two inexact solvers for simultaneously learning both the input and output components of separable matrix-valued kernels. As a key application enabled by our framework, we show how high-dimensional causal inference tasks can be naturally cast as sparse function estimation problems, leading to novel nonlinear extensions of a class of Graphical Granger Causality techniques. Our algorithmic developments and extensive empirical studies are complemented by theoretical analyses in terms of Rademacher generalization bounds.

title: Normalized Online Learning
Abstract: We introduce online learning algorithms that are independent of feature scales, proving regret bounds dependent on the ratio of scales existent in the data rather than the absolute scale. This has several useful effects: there is no need to pre-normalize data, the test-time and test-space complexity are reduced, and the algorithms are more robust.

title: One-Class Support Measure Machines for Group Anomaly Detection
Abstract: We propose one-class support measure machines (OCSMMs) for group anomaly detection which aims at recognizing anomalous aggregate behaviors of data points. The OCSMMs generalize well-known one-class support vector machines (OCSVMs) to a space of probability measures. By formulating the problem as quantile estimation on distributions, we can establish an interesting connection to the OCSVMs and variable kernel density estimators (VKDEs) over the input space on which the distributions are defined, bridging the gap between large-margin methods and kernel density estimators. In particular, we show that various types of VKDEs can be considered as solutions to a class of regularization problems studied in this paper. Experiments on Sloan Digital Sky Survey dataset and High Energy Particle Physics dataset demonstrate the benefits of the proposed framework in real-world applications.

title: From Ordinary Differential Equations to Structural Causal Models: the deterministic case
Abstract: We show how, and under which conditions, the equilibrium states of a first-order Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) system can be described with a deterministic Structural Causal Model (SCM). Our exposition sheds more light on the concept of causality as expressed within the framework of Structural Causal Models, especially for cyclic models.

title: The Lovasz-Bregman Divergence and connections to rank aggregation, clustering, and web ranking
Abstract: We extend the recently introduced theory of Lovasz-Bregman (LB) divergences (Iyer & Bilmes 2012) in several ways. We show that they represent a distortion between a "score" and an "ordering," thus providing a new view of rank aggregation and order based clustering with interesting connections to web ranking. We show how the LB divergences have a number of properties akin to many permutation-based metrics, and in fact have as special cases forms very similar to the Kendall-tau metric. We also show how the LB divergences subsume a number of commonly used ranking measures in information retrieval, like NDCG and AUC. Unlike the traditional permutation based metrics, however, the LB divergence naturally captures a notion of "confidence" in the orderings, thus providing a new representation to applications involving aggregating scores as opposed to just orderings. We show how a number of recently used web ranking models are forms of Lovasz-Bregman rank aggregation and also observe that a natural form of Mallow's model using the LB divergence has been used as conditional ranking models for the "Learning to Rank" problem.

title: Warped Mixtures for Nonparametric Cluster Shapes
Abstract: A mixture of Gaussians fit to a single curved or heavy-tailed cluster will report that the data contains many clusters. To produce more appropriate clusterings, we introduce a model which warps a latent mixture of Gaussians to produce nonparametric cluster shapes. The possibly low-dimensional latent mixture model allows us to summarize the properties of the high-dimensional clusters (or density manifolds) describing the data. The number of manifolds, as well as the shape and dimension of each manifold is automatically inferred. We derive a simple inference scheme for this model which analytically integrates out both the mixture parameters and the warping function. We show that our model is effective for density estimation, performs better than infinite Gaussian mixture models at recovering the true number of clusters, and produces interpretable summaries of high-dimensional datasets.

title: Parallel Gaussian Process Regression with Low-Rank Covariance Matrix Approximations
Abstract: Gaussian processes (GP) are Bayesian non-parametric models that are widely used for probabilistic regression. Unfortunately, it cannot scale well with large data nor perform real-time predictions due to its cubic time cost in the data size. This paper presents two parallel GP regression methods that exploit low-rank covariance matrix approximations for distributing the computational load among parallel machines to achieve time efficiency and scalability. We theoretically guarantee the predictive performances of our proposed parallel GPs to be equivalent to that of some centralized approximate GP regression methods: The computation of their centralized counterparts can be distributed among parallel machines, hence achieving greater time efficiency and scalability. We analytically compare the properties of our parallel GPs such as time, space, and communication complexity. Empirical evaluation on two real-world datasets in a cluster of 20 computing nodes shows that our parallel GPs are significantly more time-efficient and scalable than their centralized counterparts and exact/full GP while achieving predictive performances comparable to full GP.

title: POMDPs under Probabilistic Semantics
Abstract: We consider partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) with limit-average payoff, where a reward value in the interval [0,1] is associated to every transition, and the payoff of an infinite path is the long-run average of the rewards. We consider two types of path constraints: (i) quantitative constraint defines the set of paths where the payoff is at least a given threshold lambda_1 in (0,1]; and (ii) qualitative constraint which is a special case of quantitative constraint with lambda_1=1. We consider the computation of the almost-sure winning set, where the controller needs to ensure that the path constraint is satisfied with probability 1. Our main results for qualitative path constraint are as follows: (i) the problem of deciding the existence of a finite-memory controller is EXPTIME-complete; and (ii) the problem of deciding the existence of an infinite-memory controller is undecidable. For quantitative path constraint we show that the problem of deciding the existence of a finite-memory controller is undecidable.

title: Scoring and Searching over Bayesian Networks with Causal and Associative Priors
Abstract: A significant theoretical advantage of search-and-score methods for learning Bayesian Networks is that they can accept informative prior beliefs for each possible network, thus complementing the data. In this paper, a method is presented for assigning priors based on beliefs on the presence or absence of certain paths in the true network. Such beliefs correspond to knowledge about the possible causal and associative relations between pairs of variables. This type of knowledge naturally arises from prior experimental and observational data, among others. In addition, a novel search-operator is proposed to take advantage of such prior knowledge. Experiments show that, using path beliefs improves the learning of the skeleton, as well as the edge directions in the network.

title: Active Sensing as Bayes-Optimal Sequential Decision Making
Abstract: Sensory inference under conditions of uncertainty is a major problem in both machine learning and computational neuroscience. An important but poorly understood aspect of sensory processing is the role of active sensing. Here, we present a Bayes-optimal inference and control framework for active sensing, C-DAC (Context-Dependent Active Controller). Unlike previously proposed algorithms that optimize abstract statistical objectives such as information maximization (Infomax) [Butko & Movellan, 2010] or one-step look-ahead accuracy [Najemnik & Geisler, 2005], our active sensing model directly minimizes a combination of behavioral costs, such as temporal delay, response error, and effort. We simulate these algorithms on a simple visual search task to illustrate scenarios in which context-sensitivity is particularly beneficial and optimization with respect to generic statistical objectives particularly inadequate. Motivated by the geometric properties of the C-DAC policy, we present both parametric and non-parametric approximations, which retain context-sensitivity while significantly reducing computational complexity. These approximations enable us to investigate the more complex problem involving peripheral vision, and we notice that the difference between C-DAC and statistical policies becomes even more evident in this scenario.

title: Guess Who Rated This Movie: Identifying Users Through Subspace Clustering
Abstract: It is often the case that, within an online recommender system, multiple users share a common account. Can such shared accounts be identified solely on the basis of the user-provided ratings? Once a shared account is identified, can the different users sharing it be identified as well? Whenever such user identification is feasible, it opens the way to possible improvements in personalized recommendations, but also raises privacy concerns. We develop a model for composite accounts based on unions of linear subspaces, and use subspace clustering for carrying out the identification task. We show that a significant fraction of such accounts is identifiable in a reliable manner, and illustrate potential uses for personalized recommendation.

title: Non-Convex Rank Minimization via an Empirical Bayesian Approach
Abstract: In many applications that require matrix solutions of minimal rank, the underlying cost function is non-convex leading to an intractable, NP-hard optimization problem. Consequently, the convex nuclear norm is frequently used as a surrogate penalty term for matrix rank. The problem is that in many practical scenarios there is no longer any guarantee that we can correctly estimate generative low-rank matrices of interest, theoretical special cases notwithstanding. Consequently, this paper proposes an alternative empirical Bayesian procedure build upon a variational approximation that, unlike the nuclear norm, retains the same globally minimizing point estimate as the rank function under many useful constraints. However, locally minimizing solutions are largely smoothed away via marginalization, allowing the algorithm to succeed when standard convex relaxations completely fail. While the proposed methodology is generally applicable to a wide range of low-rank applications, we focus our attention on the robust principal component analysis problem (RPCA), which involves estimating an unknown low-rank matrix with unknown sparse corruptions. Theoretical and empirical evidence are presented to show that our method is potentially superior to related MAP-based approaches, for which the convex principle component pursuit (PCP) algorithm (Candes et al., 2011) can be viewed as a special case.

title: Predicting the behavior of interacting humans by fusing data from multiple sources
Abstract: Multi-fidelity methods combine inexpensive low-fidelity simulations with costly but high-fidelity simulations to produce an accurate model of a system of interest at minimal cost. They have proven useful in modeling physical systems and have been applied to engineering problems such as wing-design optimization. During human-in-the-loop experimentation, it has become increasingly common to use online platforms, like Mechanical Turk, to run low-fidelity experiments to gather human performance data in an efficient manner. One concern with these experiments is that the results obtained from the online environment generalize poorly to the actual domain of interest. To address this limitation, we extend traditional multi-fidelity approaches to allow us to combine fewer data points from high-fidelity human-in-the-loop experiments with plentiful but less accurate data from low-fidelity experiments to produce accurate models of how humans interact. We present both model-based and model-free methods, and summarize the predictive performance of each method under different conditions.

title: Markov Chains on Orbits of Permutation Groups
Abstract: We present a novel approach to detecting and utilizing symmetries in probabilistic graphical models with two main contributions. First, we present a scalable approach to computing generating sets of permutation groups representing the symmetries of graphical models. Second, we introduce orbital Markov chains, a novel family of Markov chains leveraging model symmetries to reduce mixing times. We establish an insightful connection between model symmetries and rapid mixing of orbital Markov chains. Thus, we present the first lifted MCMC algorithm for probabilistic graphical models. Both analytical and empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the approach.

title: Algorithms for Approximate Minimization of the Difference Between Submodular Functions, with Applications
Abstract: We extend the work of Narasimhan and Bilmes [30] for minimizing set functions representable as a difference between submodular functions. Similar to [30], our new algorithms are guaranteed to monotonically reduce the objective function at every step. We empirically and theoretically show that the per-iteration cost of our algorithms is much less than [30], and our algorithms can be used to efficiently minimize a difference between submodular functions under various combinatorial constraints, a problem not previously addressed. We provide computational bounds and a hardness result on the multiplicative inapproximability of minimizing the difference between submodular functions. We show, however, that it is possible to give worst-case additive bounds by providing a polynomial time computable lower-bound on the minima. Finally we show how a number of machine learning problems can be modeled as minimizing the difference between submodular functions. We experimentally show the validity of our algorithms by testing them on the problem of feature selection with submodular cost features.
