title: Optimally-Weighted Herding is Bayesian Quadrature
Abstract: Herding and kernel herding are deterministic methods of choosing samples which summarise a probability distribution. A related task is choosing samples for estimating integrals using Bayesian quadrature. We show that the criterion minimised when selecting samples in kernel herding is equivalent to the posterior variance in Bayesian quadrature. We then show that sequential Bayesian quadrature can be viewed as a weighted version of kernel herding which achieves performance superior to any other weighted herding method. We demonstrate empirically a rate of convergence faster than O(1/N). Our results also imply an upper bound on the empirical error of the Bayesian quadrature estimate.

title: Selecting Computations: Theory and Applications
Abstract: Sequential decision problems are often approximately solvable by simulating possible future action sequences. Metalevel decision procedures have been developed for selecting which action sequences to simulate, based on estimating the expected improvement in decision quality that would result from any particular simulation; an example is the recent work on using bandit algorithms to control Monte Carlo tree search in the game of Go. In this paper we develop a theoretical basis for metalevel decisions in the statistical framework of Bayesian selection problems, arguing (as others have done) that this is more appropriate than the bandit framework. We derive a number of basic results applicable to Monte Carlo selection problems, including the first finite sampling bounds for optimal policies in certain cases; we also provide a simple counterexample to the intuitive conjecture that an optimal policy will necessarily reach a decision in all cases. We then derive heuristic approximations in both Bayesian and distribution-free settings and demonstrate their superiority to bandit-based heuristics in one-shot decision problems and in Go.

title: Bayesian Structure Learning for Markov Random Fields with a Spike and Slab Prior
Abstract: In recent years a number of methods have been developed for automatically learning the (sparse) connectivity structure of Markov Random Fields. These methods are mostly based on L1-regularized optimization which has a number of disadvantages such as the inability to assess model uncertainty and expensive crossvalidation to find the optimal regularization parameter. Moreover, the model's predictive performance may degrade dramatically with a suboptimal value of the regularization parameter (which is sometimes desirable to induce sparseness). We propose a fully Bayesian approach based on a "spike and slab" prior (similar to L0 regularization) that does not suffer from these shortcomings. We develop an approximate MCMC method combining Langevin dynamics and reversible jump MCMC to conduct inference in this model. Experiments show that the proposed model learns a good combination of the structure and parameter values without the need for separate hyper-parameter tuning. Moreover, the model's predictive performance is much more robust than L1-based methods with hyper-parameter settings that induce highly sparse model structures.

title: Decentralized Data Fusion and Active Sensing with Mobile Sensors for Modeling and Predicting Spatiotemporal Traffic Phenomena
Abstract: The problem of modeling and predicting spatiotemporal traffic phenomena over an urban road network is important to many traffic applications such as detecting and forecasting congestion hotspots. This paper presents a decentralized data fusion and active sensing (D2FAS) algorithm for mobile sensors to actively explore the road network to gather and assimilate the most informative data for predicting the traffic phenomenon. We analyze the time and communication complexity of D2FAS and demonstrate that it can scale well with a large number of observations and sensors. We provide a theoretical guarantee on its predictive performance to be equivalent to that of a sophisticated centralized sparse approximation for the Gaussian process (GP) model: The computation of such a sparse approximate GP model can thus be parallelized and distributed among the mobile sensors (in a Google-like MapReduce paradigm), thereby achieving efficient and scalable prediction. We also theoretically guarantee its active sensing performance that improves under various practical environmental conditions. Empirical evaluation on real-world urban road network data shows that our D2FAS algorithm is significantly more time-efficient and scalable than state-of-the-art centralized algorithms while achieving comparable predictive performance. |||

title: Video In Sentences Out

title: Efficient Clustering with Limited Distance Information
Abstract: Given a set of points S with an unknown metric d, this paper explores efficiently partitioning S into k clusters using only a limited number of distance queries. The model assumes access to "one versus all" queries, where a point s in S returns distances to all other points. Under a natural assumption about the instance structure, the paper demonstrates finding an accurate clustering using just O(k) distance queries. The algorithm is applied to cluster proteins based on sequence similarity, leveraging a fast sequence database search program for efficient querying. Empirical analysis shows that despite querying a small fraction of distances, the generated clusterings closely resemble those obtained through manual classification.

title: Matrix Coherence and the Nystrom Method
Abstract: The Nystrom method, a technique for speeding up large-scale learning applications by generating low-rank approximations, relies on the assumption that a matrix can be well approximated by focusing solely on a subset of its columns. This paper establishes a connection between this assumption and matrix coherence, linking coherence to the Nystrom method's performance. Leveraging existing work in compressed sensing and matrix completion, novel coherence-based bounds for the Nystrom method are derived in the low-rank setting. Empirical results confirm these theoretical bounds. Furthermore, the paper presents broader empirical findings for the full-rank setting, convincingly demonstrating the ability of matrix coherence to gauge the extent to which information can be extracted from a subset of columns.

title: Gaussian Process Structural Equation Models with Latent Variables

This sparse parameterization receives a full Bayesian treatment without compromising Markov chain Monte Carlo efficiency. The authors compare the sampling procedure's stability and model's predictive ability against current practices.

title: GraphLab: A New Framework For Parallel Machine Learning

The paper demonstrates GraphLab's expressiveness through parallel implementations of belief propagation, Gibbs sampling, Co-EM, Lasso, and Compressed Sensing. The results show that GraphLab achieves excellent parallel performance on large-scale real-world problems.

title: Prediction with Advice of Unknown Number of Experts

title: Incorporating Side Information in Probabilistic Matrix Factorization with Gaussian Processes

Replacing scalar latent features with functions varying over the covariate space, the GP priors enforce smooth variation and information sharing. title: On the Formal Semantics of the Cognitive Middleware AWDRAT

The monitor identifies inconsistencies between runtime observations of the target system and predictions generated by the System Architectural Model. title: Percolation of localized attack on complex networks

Specifically, it investigates this robustness in Erdős-Rényi networks, random-regular networks, and scale-free networks. The findings provide insights into protecting networks, enhancing cybersecurity, and designing more resilient infrastructures.

title: Insights from Nature for Cybersecurity

These bio-inspired solutions are discussed in the context of cybersecurity, highlighting the adoption of some principles. title: Combining Technical and Financial Impacts for Countermeasure Selection

The method incorporates industrial evaluation and simulations to assess the impact of each security measure, enabling the calculation of return on response investment for various candidates. title: The Multiple Facets of Software Diversity: Recent Developments in Year 2000 and Beyond

The survey encompasses classical work on design and data diversity for fault tolerance, alongside cybersecurity literature exploring randomization at various system levels. It further expands this scope to include the study and exploitation of natural diversity and the management of diverse software products. The survey covers the most recent works, particularly from 2000 to present, targeting researchers and practitioners in diverse fields seeking a comprehensive understanding of software diversity. title: A Graphical Adversarial Risk Analysis Model for Oil and Gas Drilling Cybersecurity

title: Ontological Approach toward Cybersecurity in Cloud Computing

title: Stochastic Relational Presheaves and Dynamic Logic for Contextuality

title: Big Data Privacy in the Internet of Things Era

title: Solving the Shortest Vector Problem in $2^n$ Time via Discrete Gaussian Sampling
Abstract: This paper presents a randomized algorithm for solving the Shortest Vector Problem (SVP) on n-dimensional Euclidean lattices, achieving a runtime and space complexity of 2^{n+o(n)}. This surpasses the previous fastest deterministic algorithm, achieving a runtime of  \\widetilde{O}(4^n) and space complexity of \\widetilde{O}(2^n) (Micciancio and Voulgaris, STOC 2010, SIAM J. Comp. 2013). The paper introduces a conceptually simple algorithm for solving the (arguably more interesting) problem of discrete Gaussian sampling (DGS). Specifically, it shows how to sample 2^{n/2} vectors from the discrete Gaussian distribution at any parameter in 2^{n+o(n)} time and space.  This SVP result is derived from a natural reduction from SVP to DGS. The paper also demonstrates that the DGS algorithm implies a 2^{n + o(n)}-time algorithm for approximating the Closest Vector Problem within a factor of 1.97. Additionally, the paper presents a refined DGS algorithm above the smoothing parameter of the lattice, capable of generating 2^{n/2} discrete Gaussian samples in just 2^{n/2+o(n)} time and space. title: Higher Spin Entanglement and W_N Conformal Blocks
Abstract: Two-dimensional conformal field theories (CFTs) with extended \\cal{W}-symmetry algebras possess dual descriptions in terms of weakly coupled higher spin gravity in AdS$_3$, particularly at large central charge.  Observables like Rényi and entanglement entropies, and correlation functions of local operators, can be computed and compared within these two descriptions.  This paper develops techniques for computing these observables in a manner that sheds light on when and why agreement between these quantities is expected. The computation of excited state Rényi entropies in the bulk is formulated using Chern-Simons connections, demonstrating its direct parallel to the CFT computation of correlation functions.  More generally, the vacuum conformal block for operators with \\Delta \\sim c is considered. When two operators satisfy ${\\Delta \\over c} \\ll 1, the paper shows, through explicit computation, that the vacuum conformal block is computed by a bulk Wilson line probing an asymptotically AdS$_3$ background with excited higher spin fields. These higher spin fields emerge as the effective bulk description of the excited state created by the heavy operators. This work provides stronger justification for a previous proposal for computing higher spin entanglement entropy via Wilson lines, clarifying its relationship to CFT.  The paper also investigates the corresponding computation in Toda theory, finding that this provides an independent means to arrive at the same result.

title: Micro-Navigation for Urban Bus Passengers: Using the Internet of Things to Improve the Public Transport Experience

title: Sequential Equilibrium in Computational Games
Abstract: This paper examines sequential equilibrium in the context of computational games, where agents incur costs for computation. In such games, agents can rationally choose to forget, leading to issues of imperfect recall. The paper considers two notions of sequential equilibrium within this setting. The first is an ex ante notion, where a player selects a strategy before the game begins and is committed to it, ensuring its optimality even off the equilibrium path. The second is an interim notion, allowing players to reconsider at each information set whether their current strategy is optimal and adjust it if necessary. While these notions coincide in games of perfect recall, they diverge in games with imperfect recall.  Although the interim notion appears more appealing, Halpern and Pass (2011) argue that it presents conceptual problems in standard games with imperfect recall. The paper demonstrates that these conceptual problems largely disappear in the computational setting. Furthermore, under natural assumptions, the two notions coincide within this setting. |||

title: Nonnegative measures belonging to $H^{-1}(\mathbb{R}^2)$

Using these results, the authors deduce implications for measures on $\mathbb{R}^2$ with arbitrary support and demonstrate, among other findings, that measures belonging to $H^{-1}(\mathbb{R}^2)$ can be supported on a set of Hausdorff dimension 0. title: The role of currents distribution in general relativistic equilibria of magnetized neutron stars

Notably, the research demonstrates how localized currents can modify the field strength at the stellar surface and explores general trends in energetic properties and magnetic field configurations. The findings indicate, among other things, that for a wide range of current distributions, the resulting magnetic configurations are consistently dominated by the poloidal component of the current.

title: Quantum Correlations in Dimers
Abstract: Quantum discord has been shown to be a more general tool for capturing non-classical correlations than quantum entanglement, as it can detect non-zero discord in mixed states where entanglement is absent. However, due to the optimization involved in its formulation, finding quantum discord for certain quantum states is computationally challenging. Geometric quantum discord, defined as the distance between a bipartite state and the closest zero-discord state, has been proposed as an alternative. This paper aims to provide a deeper understanding of geometric quantum discord by comparing it with quantum discord and measurement-induced non-locality, which is, in some sense, dual to geometric quantum discord. As the experimental study of quantum correlations is crucial in quantum information processing, the paper illustrates the differences between geometric quantum discord, quantum discord, and measurement-induced non-locality using a dimer (two spin-1/2 particles) system in multiple quantum nuclear magnetic resonance.

title: On non-commuting sets and centralizers in infinite group
Abstract: A subset $X$ of a group $G$ is considered a set of pairwise non-commuting elements if $ab \neq ba$ for any two distinct elements $a$ and $b$ in $X$. If $|X| \geq |Y|$ for any other set of pairwise non-commuting elements $Y$ in $G$, then $X$ is referred to as a maximal subset of pairwise non-commuting elements, and its cardinality is denoted by $\!(G)$. This paper demonstrates, among other findings, that for any positive integer $n$, there are only finitely many groups $G$, up to isoclinic, with $\!(G) = n$ (with exactly $n$ centralizers).

title: Equilibrium in risk-sharing games
Abstract: The majority of risk-sharing transactions involve a limited number of agents, each of whom can significantly influence the structure and pricing of securities. This paper proposes a game where agents' strategic sets encompass all possible sharing securities and pricing kernels consistent with Arrow-Debreu sharing rules. The paper establishes that agents' best response problems have unique solutions. The risk-sharing Nash equilibrium is shown to have a finite-dimensional characterization and is proven to exist for any number of agents, being unique in the two-agent game. In equilibrium, agents declare beliefs about future random outcomes that differ from their actual probability assessments. The risk-sharing securities are endogenously bounded, implying, among other things, a loss of efficiency. The analysis also indicates that extremely risk-tolerant agents benefit more from the Nash risk-sharing equilibrium compared to the Arrow-Debreu equilibrium.

title: An Experimental Evaluation of Machine-to-Machine Coordination Middleware: Extended Version

The report shows that the latter offers adequate performance for the targeted applications while providing increased flexibility.

title: Some Comments on Multiple Discovery in Mathematics

title: Stationary axisymmetric spacetimes with a conformally coupled scalar field

title: User-driven Privacy Enforcement for Cloud-based Services in the Internet of Things

title: Bridge numbers for virtual and welded knots
Abstract: Using Gauss diagrams, one can define the virtual bridge number ${\\rm vb}(K)$ and the welded bridge number ${\\rm wb}(K),$ invariants of virtual and welded knots with ${\\rm wb}(K) \\leq {\\rm vb}(K).$ For classical knots, Chernov and Manturov proved that ${\\rm vb}(K) = {\\rm br}(K)$, the bridge number as a classical knot. This paper explores whether the same holds true for welded knots. The paper demonstrates how to use other virtual and welded invariants to further investigate bridge numbers, including Manturov's parity and the reduced virtual knot group $\\overline{G}_K$. These methods are then applied to address Questions 6.1, 6.2, 6.3, and 6.5 raised by Hirasawa, Kamada, and Kamada in their paper "Bridge presentation of virtual knots," J. title: SenseMyCity: Crowdsourcing an Urban Sensor

title: Statistical Physics of Adaptation
Abstract: All living organisms exhibit adaptations that enable them to survive and reproduce in their natural environment. title: Applying Conceptual Blending to Model Coordinated Use of Multiple Ontological Metaphors

title: Local Langlands correspondence for $GL_n$ and the exterior and symmetric square $\varepsilon$--factors

The local Langlands correspondence associates to each continuous $n$-dimensional $\Phi$-semisimple representation $\rho$ of $W'_F$, the Weil–Deligne group for $\bar F/F$, an irreducible admissible representation $\pi(\rho)$ of $GL_n(F)$. This correspondence preserves, among other things, the local $L$- and $\varepsilon$-factors of pairs. This correspondence should be robust and preserve various parallel operations on the arithmetic and analytic sides, such as taking the exterior square or symmetric square. This paper shows that this is the case for the local arithmetic and analytic symmetric square and exterior square $\varepsilon$-factors, i.e., that $\varepsilon(s,\Lambda^2\rho,\psi)=\varepsilon(s,\pi(\rho),\Lambda^2,\psi)$ and $\varepsilon(s,Sym^2\rho,\psi)=\varepsilon(s,\pi(\rho),Sym^2,\psi)$. The agreement of the $L$-functions also follows by our methods, but this was already known by Henniart. The proof is a robust deformation argument, combined with local/global techniques, which reduces the problem to the stability of the analytic $\gamma$-factor $\gamma(s,\pi,\Lambda^2,\psi)$ under highly ramified twists when $\pi$ is supercuspidal. This last step is achieved by relating the $\gamma$-factor to a Mellin transform of a partial Bessel function attached to the representation and then analyzing the asymptotics of the partial Bessel function, inspired in part by the theory of Shalika germs for Bessel integrals. The stability for every irreducible admissible representation $\pi$ then follows from those of the corresponding arithmetic $\gamma$-factors as a corollary.

Additionally, the proposed strategy, which requires joint encoding over multiple sub-channels, is compared to another strategy that encodes over each sub-channel separately. title: Improvised Apriori Algorithm using frequent pattern tree for real time applications in data mining
Abstract: The Apriori algorithm is a fundamental algorithm used to extract frequent itemsets from large databases and derive association rules for knowledge discovery. It relies on two key parameters: minimum support and minimum confidence.  The algorithm first identifies frequent itemsets by checking if their support exceeds the minimum threshold. Then, association rules are formed based on the minimum confidence constraint. This paper identifies the limitations of the original Apriori algorithm, specifically its inefficiency in scanning the entire database for frequent itemsets. It proposes an improved version of the Apriori algorithm to address this shortcoming.

title: On selfadjoint extensions of semigroups of partial isometries
Abstract: This paper investigates the generation of selfadjoint semigroups  T  from semigroups  S  of partial isometries acting on a complex, infinite-dimensional, separable Hilbert space. The primary goal is to determine conditions that guarantee the elements of  T  are also partial isometries. The paper demonstrates that this is the case when the set of final projections of elements in  S  generates an abelian von Neumann algebra of uniform finite multiplicity.

title: What Teachers Should Know about the Bootstrap: Resampling in the Undergraduate Statistics Curriculum
Abstract: This article explores the potential of bootstrapping and permutation tests in enhancing students' understanding of fundamental statistical concepts, including sampling distributions, standard errors, bias, confidence intervals, null distributions, and p-values. The author delves into the underlying mechanisms of these methods, their limitations, and best practices for teaching. Through comparisons with common t-tests and intervals, the article highlights the inaccuracies of the latter and emphasizes the importance of resampling methods for more accurate and robust statistical analysis.

title: Study of Gesture Recognition methods and augmented reality
Abstract: With advancements in technology, there is a growing demand for intuitive and natural human-computer interaction.  Gestures offer a promising means of communication with machines. This paper presents a system for controlling a media player using gesture recognition. By leveraging image processing techniques, specifically augmentation, the proposed system can recognize gestures even in noisy environments.  The augmentation approach eliminates the need for restrictive conditions like gloves or color pointers, making it more versatile and user-friendly.

title: Central charges from the $\mathcal{N} = 1$ superconformal index
Abstract: This paper provides prescriptions for determining the central charges, a and c, of a four-dimensional superconformal quantum field theory from the superconformal index. In the large-N limit, for holographic theories dual to Sasaki-Einstein 5-manifolds, the prescriptions yield the leading-order terms of the central charges. This enables the precise AdS/CFT matching of a and c for arbitrary toric quiver conformal field theories without adjoint matter that are dual to smooth Sasaki-Einstein 5-manifolds. Moreover, the paper presents evidence from non-holographic theories suggesting the applicability of these results beyond the holographic setting and the large-N limit.

title: Strongly minimal pseudofinite structures
Abstract: This paper investigates the nonstandard finite cardinality of definable sets in strongly minimal pseudofinite structures. The paper demonstrates that the nonstandard finite cardinality of a definable set in a strongly minimal pseudofinite structure D is a polynomial over the integers in the nonstandard finite cardinality of D. This result implies that D is unimodular and, consequently, locally modular. Additionally, the paper establishes a regularity lemma for graphs definable in strongly minimal pseudofinite structures. The paper emphasizes the surprising nature of these results, given their previous absence in the literature, and includes comments on their connection to the work of Macpherson and Steinhorn, as well as the limitations of the examples.

title: Goedel's other legacy and the imperative of a self-reflective science
Abstract: The Goedelian approach, characterized by self-releasing objectification, is discussed as a paradigm for a science focused on the origins of things.  Unlike mere self-referential objectification, which is confined to its own byproducts, self-releasing objectification informs the formation of objects and their interconnections.  Drawing inspiration from Gödel's work, a self-reflective science can open paths that traditional approaches perceive as blocked.  The paper highlights a quote from Leibniz, who recognized the significance of analyzing the process of analysis itself as a fundamental aspect of human science.

title: Sixty Years of Fractal Projections
Abstract: This paper celebrates the legacy of John Marstrand's seminal work on the relationship between the Hausdorff dimension of a plane set and the dimensions of its orthogonal projections onto lines.  While initially overlooked, Marstrand's projection theorems have become foundational in fractal geometry, inspiring numerous variations and applications. These theorems continue to drive cutting-edge research in the field.

title: Dust continuum emission as a tracer of gas mass in galaxies
Abstract: This study investigates empirical relations between Herschel infrared (IR) luminosities and the total mass of interstellar gas (H2+HI) using a sample of 36 galaxies from the KINGFISH, HERACLES, and THINGS surveys. This approach offers a simple empirical relationship without relying on uncertain dust model fitting.  The analysis reveals tight correlations between Herschel luminosities and the total gas mass integrated across entire galaxies, with the strongest, almost linear, correlation observed for the longest wavelength data (SPIRE500). However, the study emphasizes the importance of accounting for gas-phase metallicity, which affects the dust-to-gas ratio, particularly for low-mass galaxies.  The molecular (H2) gas mass is found to be better correlated with the peak of the IR emission (e.g., PACS160), driven primarily by the correlation between stellar mass and mean dust temperature.  When examining these relations as a function of galactocentric radius, the same correlations persist, albeit with greater scatter, up to a radius of 0.7 r_25, encompassing most of the galaxy's baryonic mass.  Beyond this radius, the correlations break down, with the gas mass (predominantly HI) increasing relative to the infrared emission.  The tight relations observed for the bulk of the galaxy's baryonic content suggest that the total gas masses of disk-like (non-merging) galaxies can be inferred from far-infrared continuum measurements, particularly in scenarios where only such measurements are available, as in ALMA continuum observations of high-redshift galaxies.

title: The non-thermal superbubble in IC 10: the generation of cosmic ray electrons caught in the act
Abstract: Superbubbles are essential for stellar feedback, with presumed high thermalization rates (around 10%). This paper examines the non-thermal superbubble (NSB) in IC 10, a starburst dwarf irregular galaxy in the Local Group, combining multiband radio continuum observations from the Very Large Array (VLA) with Effelsberg data. Thermal emission was removed using Balmer Hα and VLA 32 GHz continuum maps. The bubble's non-thermal spectrum between 1.5 and 8.8 GHz exhibits curvature and aligns well with a standard model for an aging cosmic ray electron population.  Based on a derived equipartition magnetic field strength of 44±8 μG and the radiation energy density from Spitzer MIPS maps (5±1×10−11 erg cm−3), the spectral curvature indicates a spectral age of the bubble of 1.0±0.3 Myr. Analysis of the LITTLE THINGS HI data cube reveals an expanding HI hole with a 100 pc diameter and a dynamical age of 3.8±0.3 Myr, centered within 16 pc of IC 10 X-1, a massive stellar mass black hole (M > 23 M⊙). These findings align with the anticipated evolution of a superbubble with multiple massive stars, where a highly energetic event like a Type Ic supernova/hypernova occurred approximately 1 Myr ago. The paper discusses alternative interpretations of the results.

title: Dynamic properties of bacterial pili measured by optical tweezers
Abstract: The ability of uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) to cause urinary tract infections depends on its ability to colonize the uroepithelium. Infecting bacteria ascend the urethra to the bladder and kidneys by adhering to uroepithelial cells through differential expression of adhesins. P pili, associated with pyelonephritis (a severe kidney infection), are of particular interest for understanding and treating this condition. This paper examines the mechanical properties of individual P pili using optical tweezers. P pili, primarily composed of the PapA rod (a helical arrangement of ~1000 PapA subunits), mediate adhesion to host cells.  Previous research has characterized three distinct elongation regions in P pili, including one involving the unfolding of the PapA rod's quaternary structure at a force of 27 pN.  This paper focuses on the dynamic properties of the PapA rod, demonstrating that the unfolding force increases and the folding force decreases with the speed of unfolding and folding, respectively. Additionally, the PapA rod can undergo multiple cycles of folding and unfolding without losing its characteristics, a phenomenon crucial for the bacterium's persistent attachment to host tissue and colonization.

title: Quantum Mechanics in a New Light
Abstract: This paper offers a novel interpretation of quantum mechanics, viewing its formal apparatus as a calculus of correlations rather than solely an operationalist framework.  It establishes the consistency of these correlations with the existence of their correlata (measurement outcomes).  The paper distinguishes between a domain of outcome-indicating events and a domain whose properties exist only when indicated by such events.  The difference between these domains is conceptualized as the difference between the manifested world and its manifestation.  A single, intrinsically undifferentiated Being manifests the macroscopic world through reflexive spatial relations.  This atemporal process suggests a new form of causality and sheds light on the perplexing nonlocality of quantum mechanics.  Departing from evolving-states formulations, the interpretation draws upon Feynman's formulation of the theory and introduces a novel interpretive principle, replacing the collapse postulate and the eigenvalue-eigenstate link.  Applied to spatial distinctions, this principle suggests that the spatiotemporal differentiation of the physical world is incomplete.  Applied to distinctions between things, it asserts that all fundamental particles are intrinsically identical in the strong sense of numerical identity.  These particles represent the undifferentiated Being, manifesting the macroscopic world through reflexive spatial relations.

title: Why the wave function, of all things?
Abstract: This paper questions the notion that understanding the wave function beyond its role as a probability algorithm will contribute to a deeper understanding of quantum mechanics.  It demonstrates the consistency of quantum-mechanical correlation laws with the existence of their correlata, drawing upon the indeterminacy principle and the non-partitioning of physical space "all the way down." The paper proposes a new interpretive principle, replacing the eigenvalue-eigenstate link, and explores its implications.

title: Assigning UPDRS Scores in the Leg Agility Task of Parkinsonians: Can It Be Done through BSN-based Kinematic Variables?
Abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between kinematic variables associated with Leg Agility (LA), a task used to assess the severity of Parkinson's Disease (PD), and Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS) scores. The LA task is characterized using angular amplitude and speed of thigh motion, measured through body-worn wireless inertial nodes.  This represents an initial step towards developing a portable system, compatible with Internet of Things (IoT) scenarios, for automatic detection of PD severity based on UPDRS scores.  The experimental study involves 24 PD patients.

title: A Quick Empirical Reproof of the Asymptotic Normality of the Hirsch Citation Index (First proved by Canfield, Corteel, and Savage)
Abstract: The concept of "size of the Durfee square," once confined to the specialized realm of a handful of mathematicians, has gained widespread recognition as the h-index, a metric used to measure scientific productivity.  This paper explores the asymptotic normality of the random variable "size of the Durfee square" defined on integer partitions of n (as n approaches infinity).  While rigorous proofs of this property are complex, the paper presents an "empirical" approach that offers a faster path to proving the same result (modulo routine number and symbol manipulation).  This empirical methodology holds promise for tackling other instances where rigorous proofs are either excessively challenging or not deemed worthwhile.

title: Light on the Infinite Group Relaxation
Abstract: This survey explores the infinite group problem, an infinite-dimensional relaxation of integer linear optimization problems introduced by Ralph Gomory and Ellis Johnson.  The survey presents the infinite group problem within the modern context of cut generating functions, focusing on recent advancements, such as algorithms for testing extremality and breakthroughs in the k-row problem for general k >= 1.  These advancements extend previous work on single-row and two-row problems.  The survey also incorporates unpublished results, including the identification of piecewise linear extreme functions with more than four different slopes.  An interactive companion program, developed using the open-source computer algebra package Sage, provides a comprehensive compendium of known extreme functions.

title: Stochastic Komatu-Loewner evolutions and BMD domain constant
Abstract: This paper investigates conformal maps associated with standard slit domains, which are the upper half-plane excluding a finite number of mutually disjoint horizontal line segments.  Given a Jordan arc within the domain, the paper analyzes the conformal map from the domain excluding the arc to a standard slit domain, satisfying specific normalization conditions.  The conformal map satisfies a Komatu-Loewner equation in terms of the complex Poisson kernel of the Brownian motion with darning (BMD).  The paper introduces a randomized Jordan arc, governed by a system of probability measures, and demonstrates that the resulting process satisfies a Markov-type stochastic differential equation. Conversely, the paper shows that given specific functions with local Lipschitz continuity, the corresponding stochastic differential equation has a unique solution.  This solution generates random conformal maps through the Komatu-Loewner equation, leading to a family of random growing hulls.  The paper establishes scaling and domain Markov properties for these hulls and explores a locality property for a specific case.

title: Characterization of the stability of chains associated with $g$-measures
Abstract: This paper introduces a notion of asymptotic stability for a probability kernel, termed "dynamic uniqueness."  A kernel exhibits dynamic uniqueness if all stochastic chains initiated from a fixed past converge to the same future tail σ-algebra.  The paper proves that dynamic uniqueness is a stronger condition than the conventional notion of uniqueness for g-measures.  The main result establishes the equivalence of dynamic uniqueness with the weak-ℓ2 summability condition on the kernel.  This generalizes and strengthens the Johansson-Öberg ℓ2 criterion for uniqueness of g-measures.  The paper further demonstrates that the weak-ℓ2 criterion implies β-mixing of the unique g-measure compatible with a regular kernel, strengthening existing results in the literature. |||

title: Forty-Seven Milky Way-Sized, Extremely Diffuse Galaxies in the Coma Cluster
Abstract: We discovered 47 low surface brightness objects in deep images of a 3 x 3 degree field centered on the Coma cluster, using the Dragonfly Telephoto Array. These objects have central surface brightness ranging from 24 to 26 mag/arcsec^2 and effective radii of 3 to 10 arcseconds.  Based on their spatial distribution, we believe most, if not all, of these objects are galaxies within the Coma cluster.  Their large distance from us suggests they are very large:  with effective radii of 1.5 to 4.6 kpc, their sizes are comparable to L* galaxies even though their median stellar mass is only about 6 x 10^7 Solar masses.  These galaxies are relatively red and round, with a mean g-i color of 0.8 and a mean axis ratio of 0.74.  One of the 47 galaxies was fortuitously observed by the Hubble Space Telescope. The Hubble image shows a large spheroidal object with a central surface brightness of 25.8 mag/arcsec^2, a Sersic index of 0.6, and an effective radius of 7 arcseconds, corresponding to 3.4 kpc at the distance of Coma.  The galaxy is not resolved into stars, consistent with expectations for a Coma cluster object. We speculate that Ultra-Diffuse Galaxies may have lost their gas supply at early times, possibly resulting in very high dark matter fractions.

title: Code Injection Attacks on HTML5-based Mobile Apps
Abstract: HTML5-based mobile apps are becoming increasingly popular due to their ease of portability across different mobile platforms compared to native apps.  These apps are implemented using standard web technologies such as HTML5, JavaScript, and CSS, and rely on middlewares like PhoneGap to interact with the underlying operating system. Given that JavaScript is susceptible to code injection attacks, we conducted a systematic study of HTML5-based mobile apps to assess the security risks associated with using web technologies for mobile app development. Our findings were surprising:  if HTML5-based mobile apps continue to gain popularity, many everyday actions could become dangerous, including reading 2D barcodes, scanning Wi-Fi access points, playing MP4 videos, pairing with Bluetooth devices, and more. This paper describes how HTML5-based apps can become vulnerable, how attackers can exploit these vulnerabilities through various channels, and the potential damage they can inflict.  We have demonstrated these attacks with example apps, studied 186 PhoneGap plugins used by apps to achieve various functionalities, and found that 11 of them are vulnerable.  We also discovered two real HTML5-based apps that are vulnerable to the attacks.

title: Partner selection supports reputation-based cooperation in a Public Goods Game
Abstract: In dyadic models of indirect reciprocity, the history of giving by the receiver significantly influences the donor's decision. When more than two agents are involved, the situation becomes more complex, and cooperation in large groups is difficult to achieve.  In this work, we use a Public Goods Game to investigate whether publicly available reputation scores can support the evolution of cooperation, and whether this is affected by the network structure.  Our results indicate that if agents interact on a bipartite graph with partner selection, cooperation can flourish in large groups within a short period of time.

title: Searching for stochastic gravitational waves using data from the two co-located LIGO Hanford detectors
Abstract: Searches for a stochastic gravitational-wave background (SGWB) using terrestrial detectors typically involve cross-correlating data from pairs of detectors. The sensitivity of these cross-correlation analyses is influenced by the separation between the two detectors: smaller separation leads to higher sensitivity.  Therefore, a co-located detector pair is more sensitive to a gravitational-wave background than a non-co-located pair. However, co-located detectors are also susceptible to correlated noise from instrumental and environmental effects, which could contaminate the measurement of the background.  Effective methods for identifying and mitigating these correlated noise effects are crucial for realizing the potential sensitivity gains of co-located detectors. We report on the first SGWB analysis using the two LIGO Hanford detectors and address the complications arising from correlated environmental noise.  We applied correlated noise identification and mitigation techniques to data collected by the two LIGO Hanford detectors, H1 and H2, during LIGO's fifth science run.  At low frequencies (40 - 460 Hz), we were unable to sufficiently mitigate the correlated noise to confidently measure or bound the stochastic gravitational-wave signal.  However, at high frequencies (460-1000 Hz), these techniques were sufficient to set a 95% confidence level upper limit on the gravitational-wave energy density of Omega(f)<7.7 x 10^{-4} (f/ 900 Hz)^3, improving on the previous upper limit by a factor of ~180.  Our results demonstrate techniques that will be valuable for future searches using advanced detectors, where correlated noise (e.g., from global magnetic fields) may affect even widely separated detectors.

title: The physics of volume rendering
Abstract: Radiation transfer is a fundamental concept in various fields of physics, particularly astrophysics.  Computer scientists employ radiation transfer for tasks like visualizing complex datasets using direct volume rendering.  This note explores the connection between physical radiation transfer and volume rendering and describes an implementation of direct volume rendering within the astrophysical radiation transfer code RADMC-3D.  Examples are provided showcasing the use of this module on analytical models and simulation data.

title: On Random Matrix Averages Involving Half-Integer Powers of GOE Characteristic Polynomials
Abstract: Correlation functions involving products and ratios of half-integer powers of characteristic polynomials of random matrices from the Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE) frequently appear in applications of Random Matrix Theory (RMT) to physics of quantum chaotic systems, and beyond. We provide an explicit evaluation of the large-N limits of several non-trivial objects of this kind using a variant of the supersymmetry formalism, as well as a related but different method. One application of this work is the derivation of the distribution of an off-diagonal entry K_{ab} of the resolvent (or Wigner K-matrix) of GOE matrices, which is relevant for experiments on chaotic wave scattering in electromagnetic resonators.

title: Semantic Gateway as a Service architecture for IoT Interoperability
Abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) is poised to become a substantial component of the future Internet. The IoT connects sensors and devices that record physical observations to applications and services on the Internet. As a successor to technologies like RFID and Wireless Sensor Networks (WSN), the IoT has encountered vertical silos of proprietary systems, offering limited or no interoperability with similar systems.  To address the interoperability challenge in the IoT, which represents the future state of the Internet, an intelligent and scalable architecture is needed to connect these silos, enabling discovery of physical sensors and interpretation of messages between things. This paper proposes a gateway and Semantic Web enabled IoT architecture to provide interoperability between systems using established communication and data standards. The Semantic Gateway as Service (SGS) allows translation between messaging protocols such as XMPP, CoAP, and MQTT through a multi-protocol proxy architecture. The utilization of widely accepted specifications such as W3C's Semantic Sensor Network (SSN) ontology for semantic annotations of sensor data ensures semantic interoperability between messages and supports semantic reasoning to obtain higher-level actionable knowledge from low-level sensor data.

title: Rearrangement Problems with Duplicated Genomic Markers
Abstract: Understanding the dynamics of genome rearrangements is a major challenge in phylogenetics, the study of species evolution.  A key goal of phylogenetics is to establish evolutionary relationships within groups of species, inferring the topology of an evolutionary tree formed by this group and their common ancestors.  In this context, having methods to evaluate relative evolutionary distances between species, or to infer common ancestor genomes for a group of species, would be invaluable. This work, building on previous studies, aims to develop such methods specifically for the case of genomes with multiple occurrences of genes, which adds complexity. Several hypotheses regarding the presence of duplications were considered.  Distance formulae and scenario computing algorithms were developed, along with their complexity proofs.

title: Security - a perpetual war: lessons from nature
Abstract: Throughout history, people have sought inspiration from nature.  Biomimicry has driven inventions like Velcro tape and "cat's eyes" retroreflective road markings. Concurrently, scientists have been developing biologically inspired techniques such as genetic algorithms, neural and sensor networks. Although at first glance there is no direct inspiration between offensive and defensive techniques in the Internet and patterns in nature, closer inspection reveals many analogies between these two worlds.  Botnets, DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) attacks, IDS/IPSs (Intrusion Detection/Prevention Systems), and others, all employ strategies that closely resemble actions taken by certain species in the kingdoms of living things.  Our analysis suggests that the security community should look to nature for new offensive and defensive techniques to enhance virtual world security.

title: Weak Factorization System for Actions of Po-monoids on Posets
Abstract: Let S be a pomonoid. This paper examines {\\bf Pos}-$S$, the category of $S$-posets and $S$-poset maps.  One of the primary objectives of this paper is to highlight the concept of weak factorization systems in {\\bf Pos}-$S.$ We demonstrate that if the identity element of $S$ is the bottom element, then $(\\mathcal{C_D}, \\mathcal{E_S})$ forms a weak factorization system in {\\bf Pos}-$S,$ where $\\mathcal{C_D}$ and $\\mathcal{E_S}$ represent the class of down-closed embedding $S$-poset maps and the class of all split $S$-poset epimorphisms, respectively.  Furthermore, we utilize a fibrewise notion of complete posets in the category {\\bf Pos}-$S/B$ under a specific case where $B$ has a trivial action.  We obtain a necessary condition for regular injective objects in {\\bf Pos}-$S/B$.  Finally, we characterize these objects under a particular case where $S$ is a pogroup, concluding that $(Emb, Top)$ constitutes a weak factorization system in {\\bf Pos}-$S$.

title: Approximating Laplace transforms of meeting times for some symmetric Markov chains
Abstract: We investigate the distributions of meeting times for finite symmetric Markov chains.  For Markov kernels defined on large state spaces that satisfy certain weak inhomogeneity in return probabilities of points up to large numbers of steps, we obtain approximations, with explicit error bounds, of the Laplace transforms of some meeting times (without scaling) by ratios of Green functions closely related to hitting times of points.  In studying this approximation, we identify some key matrix power series in Markov kernels weighted with solutions to a discrete transport-like equation with explicit coefficients, which stems from the perspective that meeting time distributions are equivalent to correlations of some linear particle system. Our result applies, in particular, to random walks on large random regular graphs.  This provides a justification for the corresponding practice in Allen, Traulsen, Tarnita, and Nowak (2012) on approximating certain critical values for the emergence of cooperation when mutation is present.

title: Consistent estimation of the proportion of false nulls and FDR for adaptive multiple testing Normal means under weak dependence
Abstract: We examine multiple testing methods for many dependent Normal random variables that may not necessarily follow a joint Normal distribution.  Under weak dependence, we demonstrate the uniform consistency of proportion estimators constructed as solutions to Lebesgue-Stieltjes equations for the settings of a point, bounded, and one-sided null, respectively.  We characterize via the index of weak dependence the sparsest proportion that these estimators can consistently estimate.  On the other hand, under a principal correlation structure and employing a suitable definition of p-value for composite null hypotheses, we show that three key empirical processes induced by a single-step multiple testing procedure (MTP) satisfy the strong law of large numbers for testing each of the three types of nulls.  Furthermore, under this structure and for testing a point null and a one-sided null respectively, we construct an adaptive single-step MTP that utilizes a proportion estimator mentioned earlier, and show that the false discovery proportion of this procedure satisfies the weak law of large numbers, consistently estimating the false discovery rate of the procedure.  Additionally, we present some findings regarding the estimators of Jin and of Meinshausen and Rice for the proportion of false nulls in the critically and very sparse regimes under weak dependence and model misspecifications, respectively.

title: The physics of angular momentum radio
Abstract: Wireless communications, radio astronomy, and other radio science applications are primarily implemented with techniques built on the electromagnetic linear momentum (Poynting vector) physical layer.  As a supplement and/or alternative to this conventional approach, techniques rooted in the electromagnetic angular momentum physical layer have been proposed, and promising results from proof-of-concept radio communication experiments using angular momentum have been published recently. This sparingly exploited physical observable describes the rotational (spinning and orbiting) physical properties of the electromagnetic fields and the rotational dynamics of the pertinent charge and current densities.  To facilitate the exploitation of angular momentum techniques in real-world implementations, we present a systematic, comprehensive theoretical review of the fundamental physical properties of the electromagnetic angular momentum observable.  Starting with an overview that places it in its physical context among the other Poincaré invariants of the electromagnetic field, we describe the multi-mode quantized character and other physical properties that distinguish electromagnetic angular momentum from electromagnetic linear momentum.  These properties allow for, among other things, more flexible and efficient utilization of the radio frequency spectrum.  Implementation aspects are discussed and illustrated with examples based on analytical and numerical solutions.

title: The quark gluon plasma equation of state and the expansion of the early Universe
Abstract: Our understanding of the equation of state of the quark-gluon plasma has been continuously expanding due to experimental results from heavy ion collisions, recent astrophysical measurements, and advances in lattice QCD calculations.  These new findings about this state may have implications for the time evolution of the early Universe, which can be estimated by solving the Friedmann equations.  The solutions to these equations provide the time evolution of the energy density and temperature in the early Universe. In this work, we compute the time evolution of the QGP in the early Universe, comparing several equations of state, some based on the MIT bag model (and its variants) and some based on lattice QCD calculations.  Among other things, we investigate the effects of a finite baryon chemical potential on the evolution of the early Universe.

title: A Holistic, Non-algorithmic View of Cultural Evolution: Commentary on Review Article by Prof. Liane Gabora
Abstract: The notion that culture evolves holds some truth, but the Darwinian view of culture is trivial. Gabora accomplishes two things in this paper. First, she presents a well-reasoned and devastating critique of the adequacy of a Darwinian theory of cultural evolution, demonstrating that cultural evolution violates virtually all prerequisites to be encompassed by Darwin's standard theory. Second, she advances the central concept that it is whole world views that evolve. A world view emerges when the capacity of memories to evoke one another surpasses a phase transition, resulting in a richly interconnected conceptual web. She proposes that culture evolves not through a Darwinian process such as meme theory, but through communal exchange of facets of world views. Each section of her argument is entirely convincing.

title: Ergodic theorems in fully symmetric spaces of $τ-$measurable operators
Abstract: In [11], using the technique of noncommutative interpolation, a maximal ergodic theorem in noncommutative Lp-spaces, 1 < p < infinity, was established, and corresponding maximal ergodic inequalities and individual ergodic theorems were derived.  In this article, we derive maximal ergodic inequalities in noncommutative Lp-spaces directly from [25] and apply them to prove corresponding individual and Besicovitch weighted ergodic theorems.  We then extend these results to noncommutative fully symmetric Banach spaces with the Fatou property and non-trivial Boyd indices, in particular, to noncommutative Lorentz spaces Lpq.  Norm convergence of ergodic averages in noncommutative fully symmetric Banach spaces is also studied.

title: PlanetPack software tool for exoplanets detection: coming new features
Abstract: We provide a brief overview of the new features of PlanetPack2, the forthcoming update of PlanetPack, a software tool for exoplanet detection and characterization from Doppler radial velocity data.  This major update includes parallelized computing, new advanced models of the Doppler noise, handling of the so-called Keplerian periodogram, and routines for transit fitting and transit timing variation analysis.

title: Uplink Scheduling for LTE Video Surveillance Systems
Abstract: The proliferation of Internet of Things applications is leading to the deployment of an increasing number of machine-to-machine (M2M) devices.  One of the widely discussed M2M applications is video surveillance.  Long Term Evolution (LTE), which offers high data transmission rates and wide coverage, is a promising standard for use in M2M video surveillance systems.  This paper investigates a performance maximization problem in an LTE video surveillance system.  Given a set of objects and a set of cameras, each camera has its own performance grade and coverage area.  The goal is to maximize system performance by allocating limited resources to cameras while ensuring all objects are monitored by the selected cameras.  We propose a heuristic method to select cameras and allocate resources to them to solve this problem.  Furthermore, to reduce the load on the LTE system, we propose a dynamic adjustment method.

title: The equality case in a Poincaré-Wirtinger type inequality
Abstract: Generalizing existing results to the non-smooth case, we prove that for any convex planar set $\\Omega$, the first non-trivial Neumann eigenvalue $\\mu_1(\\Omega)$ of the Hermite operator is greater than or equal to 1.  Furthermore, and this is our main result, under some additional assumptions on $\\Omega$, we show that $\\mu_1(\\Omega)=1$ if and only if $\\Omega$ is any strip. The study of the equality case requires, among other things, an asymptotic analysis of the eigenvalues of the Hermite operator in thin domains.

title: Museum Automation with RFID
Abstract: With the growth of culture and knowledge, demand for museum visits has increased, making the management of these places more complex. Valuable objects in museums and ancient sites must be carefully preserved, and visitor management is crucial. To protect these objects from theft, as well as environmental factors like temperature, humidity, pH, chemical agents, and mechanical events, monitoring is necessary.  If these conditions become damaging, appropriate alerts or reports should be sent to managers and experts.  Visitors should also be monitored, guided, and provided with information about the environment.  By leveraging RFID technology and short-distance network tools, technical solutions can be implemented to achieve more efficient management and effective preservation in museums. |||

title: Strain-enhanced tunneling magnetoresistance in MgO magnetic tunnel junctions
Abstract: Strain in thin films can have both detrimental and beneficial effects. While it can lead to mechanical deformation and failure, it can also be used for applications like data storage, transistors, and solar cells. This study demonstrates that mechanical strain can significantly enhance the tunneling magnetoresistance (TMR) ratio in magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJs).  The researchers achieved a ~2-fold increase in TMR by introducing controllable mechanical strain and found this enhancement is associated with coherent spin tunneling through the MgO barrier.  These findings were further supported by quantum transport calculations, providing a deeper understanding of the TMR mechanism at the atomic level. This research paves the way for new methods to enhance and tune the quantum properties of nanoscale materials and devices.

title: Parabolic induction and restriction via C*-algebras and Hilbert C*-modules
Abstract: This paper delves into the reduced group C*-algebras of real reductive groups and the Hilbert C*-modules associated with them. It presents three key findings. Firstly, it analyzes the structure of the reduced C*-algebra using theorems from tempered representation theory. Secondly, it utilizes this structure to determine the structure of the Hilbert C*-bimodule representing parabolic induction. Lastly, the paper demonstrates that the parabolic induction bimodule possesses a secondary inner product, which allows for the definition of a parabolic restriction functor in tempered representation theory. The subsequent paper will further prove that parabolic restriction acts as an adjoint to parabolic induction on both the left and right sides.

title: Distributed Reception with Spatial Multiplexing: MIMO Systems for the Internet of Things
Abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) holds immense potential for distributed MIMO communication. This study explores a scenario where multiple data streams are transmitted from a multi-antenna transmitter to numerous geographically dispersed single-antenna receivers. The receivers then quantize their signals and forward the quantized data to a fusion center. The fusion center uses this quantized information and global channel knowledge to decode the transmitted symbols.  Assuming PSK constellation points for the transmitted data, the paper develops an optimal maximum likelihood (ML) receiver and a low-complexity zero-forcing (ZF)-type receiver for the fusion center. While the ZF-type receiver is simpler and performs comparably to the ML receiver at low SNR, it experiences an error rate floor at high SNR. This floor can be mitigated by increasing the number of receiver nodes, making the ZF-type receiver a practical solution for distributed reception with spatial multiplexing in IoT applications.

title: On the filtering and processing of dust by planetesimals 1. Derivation of collision probabilities for non-drifting planetesimals
Abstract: Circumstellar disks, the birthplaces of stars and planetary systems, contain substantial amounts of dust particles ranging in size from microns to centimeters. These particles serve as building blocks for planetesimals, the precursors of planets. This research examines the efficiency of dust collection by a swarm of non-drifting planetesimals of various sizes. The study analyzes different collision regimes based on the size of planetesimals, dust particles, and orbital distance, including geometric, Safronov, settling, and three-body regimes. Additionally, a hydrodynamical regime is considered for the movement of small dust grains carried by gas flows around planetesimals. The results show that dust filtering efficiency is generally low in the presence of standard turbulence. However, under weak turbulence conditions, efficient filtering can occur in two specific scenarios: (1) when planetesimals are smaller than 10 km, leading to collisions primarily in the geometric regime, and (2) when planetary embryos larger than 1000 km dominate, having a smaller scale height than the gas, and millimeter-sized or larger dust particles are present, resulting in collisions in the settling regime. These two regimes have distinct properties: the local filtering efficiency in the geometric regime scales inversely with the orbital distance to the power of 7/4, suggesting filtering of smaller planetesimals closer to the central star. Conversely, the filtering by embryos in the settling regime is more gradual and depends on the extent of the embryo disk. Dust particles significantly smaller than millimeter size are primarily captured by the smallest planetesimals as they move along gas streamlines and experience collisions in the hydrodynamical regime. These findings suggest an inside-out formation of planetesimals in the early solar system, where smaller planetesimals play a crucial role in filtering dust closer to the star. However, even a fully formed belt of planetesimals like the minimum-mass solar nebula (MMSN) only marginally captures inward-drifting dust, implying that smaller planetesimals or other mechanisms like orderly growth or capture into vortexes may have been responsible for dust collection in the protosolar disk. The research highlights the need for further refinement, including a quantitative description of the transition region between hydro and settling regimes, an assessment of the role of disk turbulence in collisions, and the coupling of the model to a planetesimal formation model.

title: Spatially independent martingales, intersections, and applications
Abstract: This paper introduces a new class of random measures called spatially independent martingales, generalizing the canonical random discrete set and encompassing various fractal percolation and Poissonian cut-out models. By pairing these random measures with parametrized measures, the study shows that under specific conditions, the total measure of their intersections is H\\"older continuous with respect to the parameter. This continuity property proves fundamental for understanding the geometry of these measures, unifying and extending a wide range of existing results on random Cantor sets and measures, and yielding numerous new findings.  Specifically, for various random fractals, the paper establishes: (a) strong versions of the Marstrand-Mattila projection and slicing results, along with dimension conservation, (b) slicing results for algebraic curves and self-similar sets, (c) smoothness of measure convolutions, including self-convolutions, and nonempty interior for sumsets, and (d) rapid Fourier decay. One application of these findings is the resolution of a question posed by I. {\\L}aba concerning the restriction problem for fractal measures.

title: The Making of Cloud Applications An Empirical Study on Software Development for the Cloud
Abstract: Cloud computing is rapidly gaining popularity as a deployment and provisioning model for software. While extensive research exists on cloud system optimization, little is known about how software engineers utilize clouds and how the cloud impacts development practices.  This paper presents the first systematic study on software development in the cloud, using a mixed-method approach combining interviews with 25 professional developers and a survey with 294 responses. The findings reveal that cloud adoption significantly affects the entire software development process, influencing how developers use tools and data. Notably, the study identified two key areas where developers require improvement: (1) better tools for anticipating runtime problems and rigorously defining metrics for improved fault localization, and (2) effective utilization of the abundance of operational data available in the cloud instead of relying solely on experience and intuition. Based on these findings, the paper extracts guidelines for cloud development and identifies challenges for researchers and tool vendors.

title: When Money Learns to Fly: Towards Sensing as a Service Applications Using Bitcoin
Abstract: Sensing-as-a-Service (S2aaS) is an emerging business model for the Internet of Things (IoT).  However, widespread adoption of S2aaS requires overcoming significant systemic challenges, particularly related to payment and sensor identification. This paper proposes Bitcoin as a protocol for S2aaS networks. By examining the core characteristics of Bitcoin, the paper lays the groundwork for a discussion about the disruptive potential of this technology for S2aaS and IoT in general. It presents a conceptual example and outlines the basic process of exchanging data for cash using Bitcoin.

title: Angles in hyperbolic lattices : The pair correlation density
Abstract: The angles in a lattice acting on hyperbolic n-space are known to become equidistributed. This paper derives a formula for the pair correlation density of these angles. Using this formula, the study determines the asymptotic behavior of the density function in both the small and large variable limits. This extends previous results by Boca, Pasol, Popa, and Zaharescu, and Kelmer and Kontorovich in dimension 2 to general dimension n. The proofs rely on the decay of matrix coefficients and careful estimates, leading to effective results with explicit rates.

title: The HI Chronicles of LITTLE THINGS BCDs II: The Origin of IC 10's HI Structure
Abstract: This paper analyzes Very Large Array (VLA) and Green Bank Telescope (GBT) atomic hydrogen (HI) data for the dwarf galaxy IC 10. The high-resolution VLA data provide insights into the detailed kinematics and morphology of IC 10's HI, while the high-sensitivity GBT data allow for a search of the surrounding region for faint HI. The HI distribution in IC 10 appears highly disturbed in both datasets, with a kinematically distinct northern extension, a southern plume, and several spurs in the VLA data that deviate from the general kinematics of the main disk. The paper explores three possible explanations for IC 10's HI structure and kinematics: a current interaction with a nearby companion, an advanced merger, and accretion of intergalactic medium. Based on the evidence, the researchers conclude that IC 10 is most likely an advanced merger or a galaxy undergoing accretion.

title: IAS15: A fast, adaptive, high-order integrator for gravitational dynamics, accurate to machine precision over a billion orbits
Abstract: This paper introduces IAS15, a 15th-order integrator for simulating gravitational dynamics. The integrator is built on a Gau\\ss-Radau quadrature and can handle both conservative and non-conservative forces. A step-size control mechanism ensures automatic selection of an optimal timestep. The algorithm is capable of handling close encounters and high-eccentricity orbits while maintaining systematic errors below machine precision. Long-term orbit integrations over 10^9 orbits demonstrate that IAS15 is optimal as it follows Brouwer's law, indicating that the energy error behaves like a random walk. Tests show that IAS15 outperforms mixed-variable symplectic integrators (MVS) and other commonly used integrators, including high-order ones, in both speed and accuracy. Moreover, IAS15 preserves the symplecticity of Hamiltonian systems more effectively than the commonly used nominally symplectic integrators. The paper provides an open-source implementation of IAS15 with numerous examples of applications, including resonant planetary systems, Kozai-Lidov cycles, close encounters, radiation pressure, quadrupole moment, and generic damping functions. The package can be readily extended to simulate various physical phenomena, such as planet-disk interactions.

title: Rieffel proper actions
Abstract: This paper provides a simple characterization of Rieffel proper actions of locally compact groups on C*-algebras, a concept crucial for constructing generalized fixed-point algebras. This characterization is used to generate several examples and counterexamples for the theory.  The study presents examples of Rieffel proper actions where properness is not induced by a nondegenerate equivariant *-homomorphism for any proper G-space.  Other examples, based on earlier work by Meyer, demonstrate that a single action can exhibit different Rieffel properness structures, leading to different generalized fixed-point algebras.

title: Object-Oriented Programming, Functional Programming and R
Abstract: This paper reviews programming techniques in R that have proven particularly useful for large-scale projects, focusing on object-oriented programming (OOP) as implemented in numerous R packages. The review clarifies the origins and ideas behind different OOP versions, each with value in specific contexts. R has also been influenced by functional programming and the desire to integrate functional and object-oriented approaches. To explain this unique blend, the paper first reviews the fundamental principles of both OOP and functional programming before tracing the evolution of R in relation to these concepts. Functional programming promotes well-defined, reproducible software, while OOP excels at managing complexity while maintaining user simplicity. These paradigms have been instrumental in developing major software for model fitting, statistical analysis, and other applications. The paper emphasizes the distinct adaptation of these paradigms in R: functional programming is a strong influence but not enforced, and OOP from a functional perspective differs from traditional OOP in non-functional languages. The review concludes by outlining the historical development of R, highlighting the influence of the S language and earlier program libraries, which helps explain the current, somewhat unusual, combination of ideas in R.

title: Why QBism is not the Copenhagen interpretation and what John Bell might have thought of it
Abstract: Christopher Fuchs and R\\"udiger Schack have proposed a new framework for understanding science, called QBism, which aims to address longstanding conceptual puzzles in quantum mechanics. This paper speculates on how John Bell might have reacted to QBism and highlights the key differences between QBism and the orthodox interpretations of quantum mechanics associated with the term "Copenhagen interpretation."

title: Weighted Hardy spaces on the unit disk
Abstract: This paper explores three key points regarding the space $H^p_u(\\mathbb{D})$.  Firstly, it demonstrates that there is no canonical norm on this space.  Secondly, it improves the weak-$*$\\ convergence of the measures $\\mu_{u,r}$.  Finally, the paper establishes that the dilations $f_t$ of the function $f\\in H^p_u(\\mathbb{D})$ converge to $f$ in $H^p_u$-norm, implying that polynomials are dense in $H^p_u(\\mathbb{D})$.

title: A New IEEE 802.15.4 Simulation Model for OMNeT++ / INET
Abstract: This paper introduces a new IEEE 802.15.4 simulation model for OMNeT++ / INET, a crucial standard for wireless sensor networks and Internet of Things (IoT) scenarios. The model is designed to be compatible with OMNeT++ 4.x and INET 2.x and can be extended to support future revisions of the 802.15.4 standard. The source code is available online at https://github.com/michaelkirsche/IEEE802154INET-Standalone.

title: Variability of Behaviour in Electricity Load Profile Clustering; Who Does Things at the Same Time Each Day?
Abstract: The changing UK electricity market presents opportunities to influence household electricity usage patterns for the benefit of the overall electricity network. Previous work on clustering similar households has focused on daily load profiles, neglecting the variability in regular household behaviors. This paper investigates whether incorporating variability in regular activities can lead to more consistent groupings of households compared to daily load profile clustering.  The study analyzes 204 UK households to identify repeating patterns (motifs) and uses the variability in motif timing as the basis for clustering households. Different clustering algorithms are assessed for the consistency of their results. The findings demonstrate that incorporating variability in behavior, using motifs, produces more consistent groupings across different clustering algorithms, enabling more efficient targeting of interventions aimed at changing behavior.

title: Attack of the Ants: Studying Ant Routing Algorithms in Simulation and Wireless Testbeds
Abstract: Wireless networks are becoming increasingly vital for our communications infrastructure, spanning from cellular networks to ad hoc and sensor networks used in wildlife monitoring and environmental applications.  With the rise of the Internet of Things (IoT), millions of physical and virtual objects will communicate wirelessly, enhancing daily life. Adaptability and scalability of wireless networks in the IoT pose significant challenges.  This paper presents a simulation framework based on OMNeT++ to implement ant routing algorithms, enabling the study and comparison of these algorithms at the algorithmic level and facilitating comprehensive large-scale simulation studies.

title: Bypassing Captcha By Machine A Proof For Passing The Turing Test
Abstract: CAPTCHAs have been widely used by websites for over a decade to prevent automated data updates by machines. Relying on the reverse Turing test, CAPTCHAs exploit the supposed superiority of human intelligence over machines. While CAPTCHAs have generally outwitted machines, advances in technology are rapidly changing the landscape.  This paper investigates the vulnerability of CAPTCHAs, which were built on the assumption of machine failure in the Turing test. The study demonstrates that simple OCR machines can break certain CAPTCHAs.  By reviewing other techniques, the paper shows that even more challenging CAPTCHAs can be broken using advanced OCR machines.  Current progress in OCR suggests that machines may soon be able to pass the Turing test in image recognition, directly challenging the effectiveness of CAPTCHAs.  The paper proposes enhancing traditional CAPTCHAs by incorporating not only characters but also natural language and multiple objects within the same CAPTCHA, potentially delaying machine-based attacks until a machine capable of passing the Turing test completely emerges.

title: Modelling Electrical Car Diffusion Based on Agents
Abstract: Replacing traditional fossil fuel vehicles with zero-emission vehicles in cities is a key strategy for achieving the UK government's 2020 target of reducing emissions.  This paper presents an agent-based simulation model developed to study the potential impact of various governmental interventions on the adoption of zero-emission vehicles.  The model can analyze a range of "what-if" scenarios, including car parking charges, electric car prices, energy awareness campaigns, and word-of-mouth effects.  The paper presents a case study focused on the introduction of a new car parking charging scheme at the University of Nottingham. An agent-based model simulates the impact of different car parking rates and other incentives on electric car adoption. This case study demonstrates the utility of agent-based modeling and simulation for such investigations.

title: Infrared Dynamics of a Large N QCD Model, the Massless String Sector and Mesonic Spectra
Abstract: A crucial consistency check for any UV complete model for large N QCD is the existence of well-defined vector and scalar mesonic spectra. This paper utilizes a UV complete model in type IIB string theory to study the IR dynamics and predict the mesonic spectra in the dual type IIA side. This approach has two key benefits: it validates the consistency of the supergravity approach and provides a means to compare the IR spectra and model with earlier proposals by Sakai and Sugimoto.  Interestingly, the spectra from the massless stringy sector are independent of the UV physics, although the massive string sector may present challenges regarding UV contributions and mappings to actual QCD. Additionally, the study reveals a role for the string landscape: there are points in the landscape where the spectra can be significantly improved compared to existing results in the literature.  These landscape points also determine specific background supergravity components and address various pathologies, ultimately leading to a consistent low-energy description of the theory.  |||

title: On computable abstractions (a conceptual introduction)
Abstract: This paper explores the concept of "computable abstractions," which are abstractions that are meaningful and can be built and used by computers according to their own criteria. It argues that abstractions serve as the building blocks for understanding and are essential for intellectual tasks. The paper defines "abstractional machines" that can build and use their own understanding of things based on computable abstractions through a mechanical process. The application of abstractional machines to natural language processing is illustrated through an example.

title: GPGPU Computing
Abstract: Since the advent of using GPUs for general purpose computing, various approaches to GPU programming have emerged. NVIDIA's CUDA (Compute Unified Device Architecture) and AMD's Stream are APIs designed for specific hardware. OpenCL (Open Computing Language) aims to unify different GPU general computing API implementations and provides a framework for programs executed across heterogeneous platforms, including CPUs and GPUs. OpenCL uses task-based and data-based parallelism for parallel computing. This paper focuses on the CUDA parallel computing architecture and programming model introduced by NVIDIA, presenting its benefits and comparing it to AMD APP (STREAM) and the unifying framework, OpenCL.

title: Polynomial approximation with doubling weights
Abstract: This paper establishes a relationship between the rate of convergence of best polynomial approximation in a weighted $L^p$ space and the smoothness of the function being approximated, measured by the $L^p$ modulus of smoothness. Specifically, for doubling weight functions $w$, it is shown that the best approximation error in the $L^p$ space with weight $w_n$ (a scaled version of $w$) is of order $O(n^{-\alpha})$ if and only if the $L^p$ modulus of smoothness with weight $w_n$ is also of order $O(n^{-\alpha})$. This result extends previous work on best approximation and moduli of smoothness for doubling weights, particularly by filling a gap in a previous paper by G. Mastroianni and V. Totik.
