title: Polynomials whose reducibility is related to the Goldbach conjecture
Abstract: This paper introduces a set of polynomials $F_N$, associated with each positive integer $N$, whose divisibility properties provide a new way to look at the Goldbach conjecture. While this reformulation does not solve the conjecture, it suggests two natural generalizations that are explored numerically. The paper further examines the fundamental properties of the polynomials $F_N$, including asymptotic estimates of the growth of their coefficients.

title: Temperature-dependent thermal conductivities of one-dimensional nonlinear Klein-Gordon lattices with soft on-site potential
Abstract: This paper investigates the thermal conductivities of one-dimensional nonlinear Klein-Gordon lattices with soft on-site potentials. The study confirms the existence of renormalized phonons in these lattices, similar to previously studied hard-KG lattices. The temperature dependence of renormalized phonon frequency predicted by classical field theory is verified through numerical simulations. However, the thermal conductivities of soft-KG lattices exhibit an opposite trend in temperature dependence compared to hard-KG lattices. Interestingly, both the temperature-dependent thermal conductivities of soft and hard-KG lattices can be interpreted within the framework of effective phonon theory, where the exponents of the power-law dependence of the thermal conductivities as a function of temperature are determined solely by the exponents of the soft or hard on-site potentials. These theoretical predictions are supported by extensive numerical simulations.

title: Convergence rates of adaptive methods, Besov spaces, and multilevel approximation
Abstract: This paper explores characterizations of approximation classes associated with adaptive finite element methods using isotropic h-refinements. The paper discusses the relationship between these classes and Besov spaces, highlighting the limitations of inverse embedding results for Besov spaces. It introduces multilevel approximation spaces, which are situated between adaptive approximation classes and Besov spaces, providing a more natural framework for relating them. The paper proves embeddings of multilevel approximation spaces into adaptive approximation classes, complementing existing inverse embedding theorems. Additionally, it introduces a theoretical framework for analyzing adaptive approximation classes defined using a modified notion of error, known as the "total error." This framework is applied to second order elliptic problems discretized by Lagrange finite elements, resulting in characterizations of modified approximation classes in terms of membership of the problem solution and data into certain approximation spaces, which are related to Besov spaces.

title: Random Walks in the Quarter-Plane: Advances in Explicit Criterions for the Finiteness of the Associated Group in the Genus 1 Case
Abstract: This paper investigates the invariant measure of random walks in the quarter plane with small jumps, focusing on the role of the "group" of the walk in determining the nature of solutions. It builds upon previous work that provided necessary and sufficient conditions for rational or algebraic solutions when the order of the group is finite. This paper proposes a concrete criterion for ensuring the finiteness of the group when the underlying algebraic curve is of genus 1. This criterion involves the cancellation of a determinant of a matrix of order 3 or 4, which depends polynomially on the coefficients of the walk.

title: Subcomplexes and fixed point sets of isometries of spherical buildings
Abstract: This paper studies convex subcomplexes of spherical buildings, paying particular attention to fixed point sets of type-preserving isometries. These sets are also convex subcomplexes of the building's natural polyhedral structure. The paper shows that if a fixed point set is top-dimensional, it is either a subbuilding or has a circumradius less than or equal to $\pi/2$. For buildings of type $A_n$ or $D_n$, the same conclusion holds for arbitrary (top-dimensional in the $D_n$ case) convex subcomplexes. This proves a conjecture of Kleiner-Leeb in these specific cases.

title: On the last question of Stefan Banach
Abstract: This paper examines Banach's last question, posed in 1944, regarding the extension of a ternary map to a superposition of a binary map. It explores the context of Polish mathematics at the time and touches upon subsequent developments in fields such as multivalued logics, binary and ternary semigroups, theory of clones, and Hilbert's 13th problem. By drawing a connection to a 1949 idea of Jacobson about envelopes of Lie triple systems, the paper shows how variants of Banach's question can be addressed.

title: A Study of Network Based Mobility Management Schemes, 6LoWPAN Mobility, Open Issues and Proposed Solutions
Abstract: Wireless Sensor Nodes (SNs), key components of the Internet of Things (IoT), are widely deployed for information gathering and transmission. The introduction of IPv6 over Low Power Wireless Personal Area Network (6LoWPAN) enables these constrained devices to connect to IPv6 networks and transmit IPv6 packets. With the increasing deployment of sensor nodes on mobile objects, such as mobile gadgets and physical objects, efficient mobility management schemes are crucial for data transmission. Host-based mobility protocols, like MIPv6 and its extensions, are not suitable for resource-constrained devices. This paper focuses on PMIPv6-based mobility management and explores various scenarios involving sensor devices. It addresses the challenges associated with existing mobility management schemes, particularly in terms of signaling cost and packet loss, especially in time-critical areas. The paper provides a comprehensive survey of network-based mobility management schemes, 6LoWPAN mobility, and potential solutions to overcome these challenges.

title: Weak value amplification: a view from quantum estimation theory that highlights what it is and what isn't
Abstract: Weak value amplification (WVA) is a technique often used to measure tiny changes in variables of interest. Despite its widespread application, there is ongoing debate about its true nature and whether it is essential for achieving high sensitivity. This paper aims to clarify the use of WVA using concepts from quantum estimation theory. While WVA cannot surpass fundamental sensitivity limits imposed by the quantum nature of states, it can enhance the sensitivity of real detection schemes that are affected by factors beyond quantum limitations, such as technical noise. Importantly, WVA offers a straightforward and accessible way to improve sensitivity.
label: AI

title: Tête-à-tête graphs and twists
Abstract: This PhD thesis delves into the realm of low-dimensional topology, specifically examining "tête-à-tête twists." These twists, defined by A'Campo, provide a simple combinatorial description of certain mapping classes on surfaces with boundaries. Unlike Dehn twists, which involve twists around a simple closed curve, tête-à-tête twists are twists around a graph. The thesis demonstrates that tête-à-tête twists encompass all (freely) periodic mapping classes, leading to a stronger version of Wiman's 4g+2 theorem for surfaces with boundaries. On closed surfaces, some tête-à-tête twists can generate the mapping class group. Additionally, the thesis presents a straightforward criterion for determining whether a Seifert surface of a link is a fiber surface, providing a concise topological proof of the equivalence between a Murasugi being fibred and its two summands being fibred.

title: Context-awareness of the IoT through the on-the-fly preference modeling
Abstract: This paper proposes a formal framework for representing user/inhabitant behaviors in multi-agent systems within the context of IoT networks. It suggests using graph transformations and temporal logic to represent knowledge about user behavior in IoT networks, which are considered as graph structures. Dynamic preference models are introduced, representing priorities in selection. These models, based on formal logic, are built on-the-fly by software agents. The agents gather knowledge about user preferences expressed logically and predict future behavior using logical inference. The predictive process aims to provide responses to new and important events within the IoT system. Due to the increasing prevalence of cyber systems interacting with physical environments, there is a growing need for context-aware technologies in IoT systems. The formal approach enhances the trustworthiness of the system. A simple example illustrates these concepts.

title: Generalized Qualitative Probability: Savage Revisited
Abstract: This paper analyzes preferences among acts in a manner similar to L. Savage, but with the preferences being partially ordered. The rationality postulates considered are weaker than Savage's in three key aspects. The paper derives the Sure Thing Principle in this setting and shows that the postulates lead to a characterization of generalized qualitative probability, which combines aspects of traditional qualitative probability and ranked structures used in logical approaches.

title: Brane Tilings as On-shell Diagrams
Abstract: A recent development in the computation of scattering amplitudes in a certain important quantum field theory (N=4 SYM) involves the use of an algebraic structure known as the positive Grassmannian. This mathematical structure is connected to bipartite graphs, which also appear in the formulation of a certain class of conformal field theories currently being generalized into Bipartite Field Theories (BFT). The commonality of these structures suggests a deeper connection between these two realms of physics that remains to be fully understood. This paper explores this potential connection by examining the graphs of a certain class of BFTs, known as brane tilings, through the lens of the mathematics developed for amplitude computations. This approach generates data that could be valuable in further developing the understanding of the connection between these fields.

title: Transverse Weitzenböck formulas and curvature dimension inequalities on Riemannian foliations with totally geodesic leaves
Abstract: This paper presents a family of new Weitzenböck formulas on a Riemannian foliation with totally geodesic leaves. These formulas are parametrized by the canonical variation of the metric. As a consequence, under natural geometric conditions, the horizontal Laplacian satisfies a generalized curvature dimension inequality. This inequality has significant implications, including Li-Yau estimates for positive solutions of the horizontal heat equation and a sub-Riemannian Bonnet-Myers compactness theorem that relies solely on the intrinsic geometry of the horizontal distribution.

title: 3D and Some Other Things Missing from the Theory of Massive Star Evolution
Abstract: This paper outlines a 321D approximation for stellar convection that incorporates nonlocality and thus includes nonzero fluxes of kinetic energy. Boundary conditions are discussed within a fluid dynamics context, analyzing predictions for overshoot, semiconvection, and entrainment. The plan is to integrate this approximation into the MESA stellar evolution code. The inclusion of kinetic energy fluxes appears to help resolve the solar abundance problem, while smaller cores could potentially alleviate problems related to core-collapse supernova simulations.

title: On the Degrees of Freedom of SISO X-Channel with Alternating CSIT
Abstract: This paper examines the degrees of freedom (DoF) of the two-user single input single output (SISO) X-channel with alternating channel state information at the transmitters (CSIT). Three cases are considered: perfect CSIT, delayed CSIT, and no CSIT, each associated with a fraction of time denoted by $\lambda_P$, $\lambda_D$, and $\lambda_N$, respectively. The paper provides new results for the DoF of the X-channel with alternating CSIT under a certain distribution $\Lambda(\lambda_P, \lambda_D, \lambda_N)$. Specifically, it shows that the X-channel with alternating CSIT for $\Lambda(1/8, 3/8, 1/2)$ can achieve 5/4 DoF. This result represents a compromise between the channel knowledge needed to steer interference and the achievable degrees of freedom. Furthermore, 5/4 is greater than 6/5, the upper bound for the X-channel with fixed delayed CSIT.

title: The trivial solution of the gravitational energy-momentum tensor problem
Abstract: The idea that there is no energy-momentum tensor for the gravitational field and that total energy-momentum conservation can only be defined using a gravitational energy-momentum pseudo-tensor is widely held. However, by relaxing the assumption that the gravitational energy-momentum tensor should only depend on first derivatives of the metric, the Einstein equation leads to the conclusion that the gravitational energy-momentum tensor is essentially the Einstein tensor. This paper explores the implications of this definition, discussing its various peculiarities and arguing that these peculiarities have sensible physical interpretations.

title: Distinguishing between evidence and its explanations in the steering of atomic clocks
Abstract: Quantum theory inherently separates evidence from explanations. This separation leads to a known proof that: (1) no wave function can be uniquely determined by evidence, and (2) any chosen wave function requires a guess that goes beyond logic to unforeseeable elements. Chosen wave functions are crucial for computer-mediated feedback in atomic clocks, including those used in computer operations and space vehicles. The propagation of logical symbols between computers requires a shared rhythm. This paper demonstrates how hypothesized metric tensors, based on guesswork, play a role in logical synchronization by influencing the rate and position of clocks toward target points that meet phase constraints. This links the physics of signal propagation with the sharing of logical symbols among computers. The dependence of symbol arrival phasing on guesses about signal propagation extends logical synchronization beyond digital communications, making it an essential aspect of physics. This paper explores questions that are invisible under any concept of time that fails to acknowledge unforeseeable events. It shows how variations in spacetime curvature limit the bit rate of logical communication. |||

title: Graph- versus Vector-Based Analysis of a Consensus Protocol
Abstract: The Paxos distributed consensus algorithm presents a significant challenge for conventional, vector-based model checking techniques. Asynchronous communication can lead to an explosion in the state space, even for small model instances. This paper explores graph transformation as an alternative modeling approach. We represent Paxos using a declarative transformation language that includes nested quantifiers, among other features.  This model is validated with GROOVE, a graph-based model checker that leverages isomorphism to reduce the state space through symmetry. We compare our results to those obtained by the standard model checker Spin using a vector-based encoding of the algorithm.

title: The Operationalization of "Fields" as WoS Subject Categories (WCs) in Evaluative Bibliometrics: The cases of "Library and Information Science" and "Science & Technology Studies"
Abstract: Normalization of citation scores using Web of Science Subject Categories (WCs) is a widely accepted practice in evaluative bibliometrics.  For instance, the Times Higher Education World University Rankings rely on this approach. However, WCs were developed decades ago for information retrieval purposes and have evolved incrementally with the database. The classification is machine-based with manual corrections.  Analyzing the WC "information science & library science" and those attributed to journals in "science and technology studies," we demonstrate that WCs lack analytical clarity for bibliometric normalization due to "indexer effects."  Can we replace adherence to "best practices" with the pursuit of "best possible practices"? This opens the door for new research questions.

title: On zeta elements for $\mathbb{G}_{m}$
Abstract: This paper introduces a unified approach to the general theory of abelian Stark conjectures. We define natural concepts of "zeta element," "Weil-'etale cohomology complexes," and "integral Selmer groups" for the multiplicative group $\\mathbb{G}_m$ over finite abelian extensions of number fields. We then propose a precise relationship between zeta elements and Weil-'etale cohomology complexes.  We show that this conjecture is equivalent to a special case of the equivariant Tamagawa number conjecture.  We also provide an unconditional proof of the analogous statement for global function fields.  Furthermore, we demonstrate that the conjecture implies detailed information about the arithmetic properties of generalized Stark elements, including a new family of integral congruence relations between Rubin-Stark elements (refining recent conjectures by Mazur and Rubin and the third author) and explicit formulas for the higher Fitting ideals of the integral Selmer groups of $\\mathbb{G}_m$, based on these elements. This provides a clear and comprehensive approach to the theory of abelian Stark conjectures.  As initial applications of this approach, we derive, among other things, a proof of (a refinement of) a conjecture by Darmon regarding cyclotomic units, a proof of (a refinement of) Gross's 'Conjecture for Tori' in the case of a base field of $\\mathbb{Q}$, a proof of new instances of the equivariant Tamagawa number conjecture in situations where the relevant $p$-adic $L$-functions have trivial zeroes, explicit conjectural formulas for both annihilating elements and, in certain cases, the higher Fitting ideals (and therefore explicit structures) of ideal class groups, a reinterpretation of the $p$-adic Gross-Stark Conjecture in terms of the properties of zeta elements, and a strong refinement of numerous previous results (by various authors) concerning abelian Stark conjectures.

title: Subspace Learning From Bits
Abstract: Networked sensing, where the goal is to perform complex inference using a vast number of inexpensive and decentralized sensors, has emerged as an increasingly attractive research topic due to its applications in wireless sensor networks and the Internet of Things. To reduce communication, sensing, and storage complexity, this paper proposes a simple sensing and estimation framework to faithfully recover the principal subspace of high-dimensional data streams using a collection of binary measurements from distributed sensors without transmitting the entire data. The binary measurements are designed to indicate comparison outcomes of aggregated energy projections of the data samples over pairs of randomly selected directions. When the covariance matrix is low-rank, we propose a spectral estimator that recovers the principal subspace of the covariance matrix as the subspace spanned by the top eigenvectors of a properly designed surrogate matrix, which is provably accurate as long as the number of binary measurements is sufficiently large. An adaptive rank selection strategy based on soft thresholding is also presented.  Furthermore, we propose a tailored spectral estimator when the covariance matrix is additionally Toeplitz, and demonstrate that reliable estimation can be obtained from a significantly smaller number of binary measurements. Our results remain valid even when a constant fraction of the binary measurements is randomly flipped. Finally, we develop a low-complexity online algorithm to track the principal subspace when new measurements arrive sequentially. Numerical examples are provided to validate the proposed approach.

title: A natural generalization of Balanced Tableaux
Abstract: We introduce the concept of "type" for a tableau, enabling the definition of new families of tableaux that encompass both balanced and standard Young tableaux.  We use these new objects to describe the set of reduced decompositions of any permutation.  Building on the work of Fomin *et al.*, we present a new proof of the equivalence in cardinality between balanced and standard tableaux, and we exhibit many new families of tableaux with combinatorial properties similar to those of balanced tableaux.

title: Social and Business Intelligence Analysis Using PSO
Abstract: This paper investigates the application of swarm intelligence for business intelligence decision making and the improvement of business rules management.  Swarm optimization, inspired by the collective behavior of living organisms, operates in groups. Spatial data, represented by 2D or 3D images, is currently only supported by SQL Server in 2D.  Location is a critical aspect of organizational data, including business data, as companies maintain customer address lists, own property, ship goods, manage transportation flows, and perform many other activities.  Enterprises, organizations, and other entities utilize and process spatial data to enhance visibility and self-description.  Our experiments indicate that Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) can facilitate intelligence in social and business behavior.

title: Characteristic Formulas 50 Years Later (An Algebraic Account)
Abstract: Jankov (characteristic) formulas were introduced by V. Jankov in 1963.  Today, Jankov (or frame) formulas are employed in virtually every branch of propositional logic, including intermediate, modal, fuzzy, relevant, many-valued, etc.  A common thread among these logics is the presence of the deduction theorem in some form. From an algebraic logic standpoint, this implies that their corresponding varieties possess a ternary deductive (TD) term.  It is natural to extend the notion of characteristic formulas to such varieties, thereby applying this concept to a broader class of logics, specifically those whose algebraic semantics is a variety with a TD term.

title: Super-radiance and flux conservation
Abstract: The theoretical foundations of the phenomenon known as super-radiance continue to be a subject of considerable interest.  Despite numerous attempts at providing pedagogically clear explanations, the effect still generates significant confusion.  Part of the confusion stems from the fact that super-radiance in a quantum field theory (QFT) context differs from super-radiance (super-fluorescence) in condensed matter contexts.  Additional confusion arises from traditional but sometimes awkward normalization conventions, and from the unnecessary blurring between fluxes and probabilities.  We argue that flux conservation (and, in the presence of dissipation, controlled flux non-conservation) is the key principle underlying this effect.  Attempting to express things in terms of reflection and transmission probabilities only works in the absence of super-radiance. To clarify the situation, we present a simple, exactly solvable toy model exhibiting both super-radiance and damping.

title: Long fully commutative elements in affine Coxeter groups
Abstract: An element of a Coxeter group $W$ is deemed fully commutative if any two of its reduced decompositions can be connected by a series of transpositions of adjacent commuting generators.  In the preprint "Fully commutative elements in finite and affine Coxeter groups" (arXiv:1402.2166), R. Biagioli and the authors proved, among other things, that for each irreducible affine Coxeter group, the sequence counting fully commutative elements with respect to length is ultimately periodic. In this work, we study this sequence in its periodic part for each of these groups, specifically determining the minimal period. We also observe that in type $A$ affine, we encounter an instance of the cyclic sieving phenomenon.

title: Geometry of the Ground State of Higgs Fields in Next-to-MSSM
Abstract: By decomposing the Higgs potential $\\mathcal{V}_{higgs}$ of the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (n-MSSM) as the sum of three contributions, namely $\\mathcal{V}_{ch}+\\mathcal{V}_{kah}+\\mathcal{V}_{expl}$, and assuming the following two conditions: $\\left( a\\right) $ $\\mathcal{V}_{higgs}$ is dominated by $\\mathcal{V}_{ch}$ from the chiral sector of supersymmetry: $\\mathcal{V}_{ch}=\\left \\vert \\mathrm{\\nu }\\right \\vert ^{2}\\mathcal{U}$ with $\\left \\vert \\mathrm{\\nu }\\right \\vert $ large and $\\frac{\\mathrm{r}}{\\left \\vert \\mathrm{\\nu }\\right \\vert }<<1$; and $\\left( b\\right) $ replacing the chiral down Higgs superfield doublet $\\left( \\boldsymbol{H}_{d}\\right) ^{i}$ of n-MSSM by a chiral anti-doublet $\\left( \\boldsymbol{\\Phi}_{d}\\right) _{i}$, we derive the explicit geometry of the Higgs fields in the ground state $\\left \\vert \\Sigma _{higgs}\\right \\rangle $.  This geometry is found to be defined by two intersecting conifolds.  We also demonstrate that the property $\\tan \\beta _{susy}=1$ residing at the singularity $r=0$ is a supersymmetric signal.  Furthermore, deviations from this property can be expressed in terms of the Kahler parameter $r$ and the $\\vartheta_{_{W}}$-Weinberg angle as $\\tan \\beta \\simeq1+\\frac{\\mathrm{r}}{2\\left \\vert \\mathrm{\\nu }\\right \\vert }\\sin^{2}\\vartheta _{_{W}}$. Other related topics are also explored.

title: Beurling moving averages and approximate homomorphisms
Abstract: The theory of regular variation, in its Karamata and Bojani\\'c-Karamata/de Haan forms, is well-established and makes essential use of homomorphisms. Both forms are encompassed by the recent theory of Beurling regular variation, further developed here, particularly certain moving averages that appear in the theory.  Extensive use of group structures leads to an algebraicization previously unseen in this context, and to the approximate homomorphisms of the title. Dichotomy results are obtained: things are either very well-behaved or very poorly behaved.  Quantifier weakening is extended, and the degradation resulting from working with limsup and liminf, rather than assuming limits exist, is studied.

title: Corrigendum to "Generators of the Hecke algebra of (S_{2n},B_n)"
Abstract: In [AC12], among other things, we observed that the structure constants of the Hecke algebra of the Gel'fand pair $(S_{2n},B_n)$ are polynomials in $n$.  Omar Tout has pointed out a missing argument in the proof. We provide the missing details by further analyzing various actions of the hyperoctahedral group.

title: Quantum Dynamics, Minkowski-Hilbert space, and A Quantum Stochastic Duhamel Principle
Abstract: This paper revisits the well-known Schrödinger and Lindblad dynamics of quantum mechanics.  However, these equations can be viewed as consequences of a more general, underlying dynamical process.  In both cases, we observe that the evolution of a quantum state $P_\\psi=\\varrho(0)$ takes a less familiar pseudo-quadratic form: $\\partial_t\\varrho(t)=\\mathbf{V}^\\star\\varrho(t)\\mathbf{V}$, where $\\mathbf{V}$ is a vector operator in a complex Minkowski space, and the pseudo-adjoint $\\mathbf{V}^\\star$ is induced by the Minkowski metric $\\boldsymbol{\\eta}$. The interesting aspect of this formalism is that its derivation has deep roots in a new understanding of the differential calculus of time.  This Minkowski-Hilbert representation of quantum dynamics is known as the *Belavkin Formalism*, a beautiful but not well-understood theory of mathematical physics that recognizes that both deterministic and stochastic dynamics can be "unraveled" in a second-quantized Minkowski space. Working in such a space enabled the author to construct a QS (quantum stochastic) Duhamel principle, and known applications to a Schrödinger dynamics perturbed by a continual measurement process are considered.  What is not known, but presented here, is the role of the Lorentz transform in quantum measurement. The emergence of Riemannian geometry in quantum measurement is also discussed.

title: Rigorous uniform approximation of D-finite functions using Chebyshev expansions
Abstract: A wide array of numerical methods exists for computing polynomial approximations of solutions to ordinary differential equations based on Chebyshev series expansions or Chebyshev interpolation polynomials. We explore the application of these methods in the context of rigorous computing (where we need guarantees on the accuracy of the result), and from the complexity perspective.  It is well-known that the order-$n$ truncation of the Chebyshev expansion of a function over a given interval is a near-best uniform polynomial approximation of the function on that interval.  In the case of solutions to linear differential equations with polynomial coefficients, the coefficients of the expansions obey linear recurrence relations with polynomial coefficients.  Unfortunately, these recurrences are not suitable for direct recursive computation of the coefficients, due to the lack of initial conditions, among other reasons.  We demonstrate how these recurrences can nonetheless be used, as part of a validated process, to compute good uniform approximations of D-finite functions, along with rigorous error bounds. We also study the complexity of the resulting algorithms. Our approach is based on a new perspective on a classical numerical method dating back to Clenshaw, combined with a functional enclosure method.

title: When Things Matter: A Data-Centric View of the Internet of Things
Abstract: Recent advancements in radio-frequency identification (RFID), low-cost wireless sensor devices, and Web technologies have propelled the Internet of Things (IoT) approach towards connecting everyday objects to the internet and facilitating machine-to-human and machine-to-machine communication with the physical world. While IoT offers the capability to connect and integrate both digital and physical entities, enabling a whole new class of applications and services, several significant challenges must be addressed before these applications and services can be fully realized. A fundamental challenge revolves around managing IoT data, which is typically generated in dynamic and volatile environments. This data is not only extremely large in scale and volume, but also noisy and continuous. This article surveys the main techniques and state-of-the-art research efforts in IoT from data-centric perspectives, including data stream processing, data storage models, complex event processing, and searching in IoT. Open research issues for IoT data management are also discussed.

title: A Cyber-Physical System-based Approach for Industrial Automation Systems
Abstract: Industrial automation systems (IASs) are commonly developed using languages defined by the IEC 61131 standard and are executed on PLCs. This paper adopts a system-based approach for the development of IASs. A framework is described to refine the UML model of the software part, which is extracted from the SysML system model, and obtain the implementation code.  Two implementation alternatives are considered to leverage PLCs, as well as the recent surge in embedded boards on the market.  For PLC targets, the new version of IEC 61131 supporting Object-Orientation is adopted, while Java is used for embedded boards. The case study was developed as a lab exercise to teach various technologies that address challenges in the domain of cyber-physical systems, where the Internet of Things (IoT) serves as the glue regarding their cyber interfaces.

title: The supergiant shell with triggered star formation in Irr galaxy IC 2574: neutral and ionized gas kinematics
Abstract: We analyze the ionized gas kinematics in the star formation regions of the supergiant shell (SGS) of the IC 2574 galaxy using observations obtained with the Fabry-Perot interferometer at the 6-m telescope of SAO RAS. Data from the THINGS survey is used to analyze the neutral gas kinematics in the area. We perform 'derotation' of the H-alpha and HI data cubes and demonstrate its effectiveness in kinematics analysis. We confirm the SGS expansion velocity of 25 km/s determined by Walter & Brinks (1999) and conclude that the SGS is located on the far side of the galactic disc plane. We determine the expansion velocities, kinematic ages, and the required mechanical energy input rates for four star formation complexes in the walls of the SGS.  For the remaining complexes, we provide limiting values for these parameters.  A comparison with the age and energy input of the complexes' stellar population shows that sufficient energy is supplied to all HII regions except one.  We discuss in detail the possible nature of this region and another region that was believed to be a supernova remnant (SNR) based on radio observations.  We measured the expansion velocity of the latter and confirm its identification as an old SNR.  Our observations have led to the identification of faint diffuse H-alpha emission inside the SGS, which has never been observed before.

title: Recommending Learning Algorithms and Their Associated Hyperparameters
Abstract: The success of machine learning on a given task depends, among other factors, on the selection of a suitable learning algorithm and its associated hyperparameters. Choosing an appropriate learning algorithm and setting its hyperparameters for a specific dataset can be a challenging task, especially for users without expertise in machine learning.  Previous work has explored the use of meta-features to predict the optimal learning algorithm and hyperparameters.  However, selecting a set of meta-features that are predictive of algorithm performance is difficult.  We propose the application of collaborative filtering techniques to learning algorithm and hyperparameter selection.  Our results show that this approach avoids the need to determine which meta-features to use and outperforms traditional meta-learning approaches in many cases.

title: Lectures on Isomorphism Theorems
Abstract: These notes originated from a series of lectures I delivered in Marseille in May 2013. I was invited to provide an introduction to the isomorphism theorems, originating with Dynkin, which connect Markov local times and Gaussian processes. This is an area I had worked on previously and even wrote a book about, but I have since moved on to other topics. However, isomorphism theorems have regained interest due to new applications in the study of cover times of graphs and Gaussian fields, as well as new isomorphism theorems for non-symmetric Markov processes and their connection with loop soups and Poisson processes.  Therefore, I felt it was an opportune time for a new introduction to this subject. In these notes, I have attempted to preserve the informal atmosphere of the lectures and often simply refer the reader to my book and other sources for details.

title: Categories of contexts
Abstract: Morphisms between (formal) contexts are specific pairs of mappings, one between objects and one between attributes of the contexts in question. We study several classes of such morphisms and their interrelationships.  Among other things, we show that the category CLc of complete lattices with complete homomorphisms is (up to a natural isomorphism) a full reflective subcategory of the category of contexts with so-called conceptual morphisms; the reflector associates with each context its concept lattice.  On the other hand, we obtain a dual adjunction between CLc and the category of contexts with so-called concept continuous morphisms.  Suitable restrictions of the adjoint functors yield a categorical equivalence and a duality between purified contexts and doubly based lattices, and in particular, between reduced contexts and irreducibly bigenerated complete lattices. Continuous maps between closure spaces and adjoint maps between complete lattices play a central role in this analysis. |||

title: AsterixDB: A Scalable, Open Source BDMS
Abstract:
AsterixDB is a comprehensive Big Data Management System (BDMS) offering unique features within the open source Big Data ecosystem. Its capabilities make it suitable for applications like web data warehousing, social data storage and analysis, and other Big Data use cases. AsterixDB employs a flexible NoSQL data model, supports a broad range of queries through its query language, and provides a scalable runtime. Its data storage and indexing mechanisms are based on a partitioned LSM architecture, including B+-tree, R-tree, and text indexes. The system allows both external and native data storage and offers a rich set of built-in types, including support for fuzzy, spatial, and temporal data types and queries. AsterixDB also incorporates a built-in notion of data feeds for data ingestion and provides transaction support akin to NoSQL stores.  The development of AsterixDB commenced in 2009 and resulted in an initial open source release in mid-2013. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the AsterixDB open source system, including its data model, query language, and software architecture. The paper also summarizes the current status of the project and offers an initial comparison of AsterixDB's performance against alternative technologies such as a parallel relational DBMS, a popular NoSQL store, and a popular Hadoop-based SQL data analytics platform.  The paper concludes with a brief description of initial trials conducted with the system, outlining the lessons learned and plans based on these early "customer" engagements. ||| 
An effective Internet of Things (IoT) architecture, particularly for an emerging nation like India with limited technology penetration, should be based on current technology advancements, practical application scenarios of social and entrepreneurial value, and ubiquitous capabilities that make the realization of IoT affordable and sustainable. Humans, data, communication, and devices play pivotal roles in the perceived IoT ecosystem. In a push towards this sustainable and practical IoT architecture for India, we synthesize ten design paradigms to consider. ||| 
This paper explores the class of positive operator-valued measures (POVMs) for qubit systems that arise from coupling the signal qubit with a probe qubit and then performing a projective measurement on the probe system. These POVMs, representing the simplest class of qubit POVMs, depend on 8 free parameters: 3 for the initial preparation of the probe qubit, 3 for the Cartan representative of the unitary coupling, and 2 for the projective measurement at the output. We delve into the properties of the POVM matrix elements and investigate their values for different ranges of the free parameters. The paper also analyzes in detail the tradeoff between information and disturbance for varying ranges of the free parameters. Among other findings, the analysis shows that (i) typical values of the tradeoff are close to optimal and (ii) even using a maximally mixed probe, one can achieve optimal tradeoff. ||| 
For a group $G$ definable in a structure $M$, we continue the study of the "definable topological dynamics" of $G$. The special case where all subsets of $G$ are definable in the structure $M$ corresponds to the usual topological dynamics of the discrete group $G$; in this case, the terms "externally definable" and "definable" can be omitted in the results presented below. This paper examines the interplay between three notions: a model-theoretic invariant $G^{*}/(G^{*})^{000}_{M}$ of $G$, which appears novel in the classical discrete case and is directly described in this paper; the [externally definable] generalized Bohr compactification of $G$; and [externally definable] strong amenability.  The paper essentially proves the following: (i) The "new" invariant $G^{*}/(G^{*})^{000}_{M}$ lies between the externally definable generalized Bohr compactification and the definable Bohr compactification, and these all coincide when $G$ is definably strongly amenable and all types in $S_G(M)$ are definable, (ii) the kernel of the surjective homomorphism from $G^*/(G^*)^{000}_M$ to the definable Bohr compactification naturally exhibits the structure of the quotient of a compact (Hausdorff) group by a dense normal subgroup, and (iii) when $Th(M)$ is NIP, then $G$ is [externally] definably amenable if and only if it is externally definably strongly amenable. In the situation where all types in $S_G(M)$ are definable, one can simply work with the definable (instead of externally definable) objects in the aforementioned results. ||| 
It has been said that "mathematics is biology's next microscope, only better; biology is mathematics' next physics, only better." This paper aims for something even better, seeking to combine mathematical physics and biology into a "picoscope" of life.  For this, the paper merges techniques introduced and developed in modern mathematical physics, particularly by Ludvig Faddeev, to describe objects like solitons and Higgs and to explain phenomena such as anomalies in gauge fields. This synthesis is proposed to help resolve the protein folding problem, a fundamental challenge in science. The paper applies the concept of gauge invariance to scrutinize the extrinsic geometry of strings in three-dimensional space. It leverages general principles of symmetry combined with Wilsonian universality to derive an essentially unique Landau-Ginzburg energy that describes the dynamics of a generic string-like configuration in the far infrared. The paper observes that this energy supports topological solitons, which relate to an anomaly in the way a string is framed around its inflection points. These solitons are explained as modular building blocks composing folded proteins. Crystallographic protein structures are described by multi-solitons with experimental precision, and the non-equilibrium dynamics of proteins under varying temperatures are investigated. The folding process of a protein is simulated at in vivo speed and with near pico-scale accuracy using a standard laptop computer.  With pico-biology as mathematics' next pursuit, the paper concludes that things can only get better. ||| 
One of the central themes of random matrix theory is the universality of many asymptotic properties of traditionally studied distributions of random matrices. This paper probes the edges of universality by investigating the spectral properties of random regular graphs. Specifically, the paper proves limit theorems for the fluctuations of linear spectral statistics of random regular graphs, revealing both universal and non-universal behavior.  The paper's most important tool is Stein's method for Poisson approximation, which is developed for use on random regular graphs. This paper is based on the author's Ph.D. thesis, stemming from joint work with Ioana Dumitriu, Elliot Paquette, and Soumik Pal. It largely combines elements from arXiv:1109.4094, arXiv:1112.0704, and arXiv:1203.1113, while incorporating some improvements and new material. Notably, Chapter 4 delves into more detail on certain proofs than arXiv:1203.1113 and includes a new section. Section 1.3 provides further discussion on the novel contributions and the individuals involved in each part of the work. ||| 
Line simplification is a crucial practice in map generalization, aimed at reducing the number of points in a cartographic curve without compromising its essential shape or salient character. This paper explores how fractal geometry can guide line simplification by leveraging the recurring scaling pattern of far more small things than large ones.  The line simplification process involves removing smaller elements while retaining larger ones based on head/tail breaks. ||| 
Disasters inflict devastating structural damage not only on buildings and transportation infrastructure but also on critical infrastructure like the power grid and communication backbones. Following such an event, the availability of minimal communication services is essential for efficient and coordinated disaster response, timely public information dissemination, and providing individuals in need with a means to post emergency messages.  The Internet of Things (IoT) involves the widespread deployment of heterogeneous devices, many of which are battery-powered and interconnected through wireless network interfaces. Typical IoT communication architectures enable these devices to connect to the communication backbone (i.e., the Internet) using an infrastructure-based wireless network paradigm and to communicate autonomously with each other without infrastructure reliance, using a spontaneous wireless network paradigm. This paper argues that the extensive deployment of IoT-enabled devices could enhance data network resilience in the face of disaster.  Leveraging their spontaneous wireless networking capabilities, IoT devices could facilitate minimal communication services (e.g., emergency micro-message delivery) while the conventional communication infrastructure is down. The paper identifies the main challenges that must be addressed to realize this potential, including physical connectivity requirements, network protocol stack enhancements, data traffic prioritization schemes, and social and political considerations. ||| 
This paper examines the feasibility, advantages, and challenges of using an Information-Centric Networking (ICN)-based approach in the Internet of Things (IoT). The paper presents the first Named Data Networking (NDN) experiments in a large-scale IoT deployment spanning tens of rooms across several floors of a building.  Drawing on insights from these experiments, the paper analyzes the shortcomings of Content-Centric Networking (CCN) applied to IoT. Several interoperable CCN enhancements are then proposed and evaluated, significantly reducing control traffic (i.e., interest messages) and leveraging data path and caching to meet IoT requirements in terms of energy and bandwidth constraints. These optimizations enhance content availability in scenarios where IoT nodes have intermittent activity. The paper also provides the first experimental comparison of CCN with the common IoT standards 6LoWPAN/RPL/UDP. ||| 
This paper provides a classification of countable homogeneous colored multipartite graphs with any finite number of parts.  According to Fraïssé's Theorem, this classification amounts to classifying families F of pairwise non-embeddable finite colored multipartite graphs for which the class Forb(F) of multipartite graphs that forbid these is an amalgamation class. The paper demonstrates that understanding such families F in the quadripartite case is sufficient, as things do not become more complex for a larger number of parts. ||| 
With the decline of the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics and recent experiments suggesting that quantum mechanics does indeed embody "objective reality", the question arises whether a "mechanical" conceptual model for quantum mechanics could be found. This paper proposes such a model.  Vacuum energy fluctuations imply mass fluctuations and, through general relativity, curvature fluctuations. These fluctuations are indicated by fluctuations of the metric tensor. The metric tensor fluctuations can potentially "explain" the uncertainty relations and non-commuting properties of conjugate variables. The paper argues that the probability density is proportional to the square root of minus the determinant of the metric tensor (the differential volume element). It further suggests that the metric elements are not stochastic but oscillate at a high enough frequency that their measured values appear stochastic (i.e., crypto-stochastic). These oscillations at the position of particles are described as torsional vibrations.  A crypto-stochastic (or chaotic) oscillating metric yields, among other things, models of superposition, photon polarization, and entanglement, all within the confines of a 4-dimensional space-time. ||| 
The Internet of Things (IoT) is a novel concept that envisions a global network of uniquely addressable interconnected smart objects. It aims to establish a new paradigm in computing, blurring the lines between the virtual and physical worlds. As the network becomes increasingly laden with previously unknown applications, security threats also become rampant. Current security solutions prove inadequate as new threats emerge, jeopardizing the reliability of information.  The network must transition to an IPv6-enabled network to accommodate the vast number of smart objects, leading to new addressing schemes and associated attacks. Real-time analysis of information from heterogeneous smart objects requires the use of cloud services, which can be susceptible to cloud-specific security threats.  This paper highlights the urgent need for a review of security threats in this rapidly evolving and high-demand area. It presents a brief study of security issues within the IoT domain. ||| 
A fractal can be simply understood as a set or pattern with far more small elements than large ones, such as more small geographic features than large ones on Earth's surface or more large-scale maps than small-scale maps for a geographic region. This paper argues for and provides evidence of the fractal nature of maps and mapping.  It is the underlying fractal structure of geographic features, both natural and human-made, that makes reality mappable, large-scale maps generalizable, and cities imageable. The fractal nature also underlies the beauty of maps. After introducing key fractal concepts like recursion, self-similarity, scaling ratio, and scaling exponent, the paper demonstrates that fractal thinking is rooted in long-standing map-making practices such as series map subdivision, visual hierarchy, and Töpfer's radical law. Drawing on previous studies on head/tail breaks, mapping can be considered a head/tail breaks process; that is, to divide elements around an average, based on their geometric, topological, or semantic properties, into the head (those above the average) and the tail (those below the average). The dividing process is recursively continued for the head for map generalization, statistical mapping, and cognitive mapping.  Given the fractal nature of maps and mapping, cartography should be viewed as a perfect combination of science and art, and scaling must be formulated as a law of cartography or geography in general. ||| 
This paper reviews growing theoretical evidence and motivation suggesting that the number of dimensions actually reduces at high energies. This reduction can occur near the Planck scale or earlier. The dimensions that are reduced can be effective, spectral, topological, or the usual dimensions, but many indicators point to the fact that high-energy theories seem to propagate in a lower-dimensional space rather than a higher-dimensional one.  The paper focuses on a particular scenario of "vanishing" or "evolving dimensions" where dimensions open up as the probed length scale increases but also mentions related models that point in the same direction, such as causal dynamical triangulation, asymptotic safety, as well as evidence from non-commutative quantum theories, the Wheeler-DeWitt equation, and the phenomenon of "asymptotic silence". Intriguingly, experimental evidence for high-energy dimensional reduction may already exist. A statistically significant planar alignment of events with energies higher than TeV has been observed in high-altitude cosmic ray experiments. Convincing evidence for dimensional reduction may be found in future collider experiments and gravity waves observatories. ||| 
Linear Support Vector Machines (SVMs) trained on Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG) features have become a de facto standard for numerous visual perception tasks. Their widespread adoption can largely be attributed to their performance breakthrough in pedestrian detection and subsequent successes in deformable parts models.  This paper explores the interactions that make the HOG-SVM symbiosis so effective. By connecting the feature extraction and learning processes instead of treating them as separate components, the paper shows that HOG features can be viewed as performing two functions: (i) inducing capacity in and (ii) adding prior to a linear SVM trained on pixels. From this perspective, preserving second-order statistics and locality of interactions are key to achieving good performance. The paper demonstrates surprising accuracy on expression recognition and pedestrian detection tasks, by assuming only the importance of preserving such local second-order interactions. ||| 
Let $A$ and $B$ be commutative rings with unity, $f:A\to B$ a ring homomorphism, and $J$ an ideal of $B$. Then the subring $A\bowtie^fJ:=\{(a,f(a)+j)|a\in A$ and $j\in J\}$ of $A\times B$ is called the amalgamation of $A$ with $B$ along with $J$ with respect to $f$. This paper investigates, among other things, the Cohen-Macaulay and (quasi-)Gorenstein properties on the ring $A\bowtie^fJ$. ||| 
This paper discusses how basic Clifford algebra, and indeed all of matrix algebra and matrix representations of finite groups, arise from iterants: very elementary processes such as an alternation of plus and minus one ...+-+-+- .... The square root of minus one can be viewed as a temporal iterant, a product of an A and a B where A represents the ...+-+-+-... sequence and B is a time shift operator. We have AA = BB =1 and AB + BA = 0, leading to (AB)(AB) = -1.  Clifford algebra forms the foundation of the (mathematical) world, and fermions are composed of these elements. The paper discusses the diagrammatics and topology of Majorana fermions, as well as the structure of the Dirac equation and how nilpotent and Majorana operators naturally arise in this context. It concludes by providing an expression in split quaternions (in iterant form) for the Majorana Dirac equation in one dimension of time and three dimensions of space. ||| 
McMillan and Mayer (MM) proved two significant theorems in their paper on the equilibrium statistical mechanics of liquid solutions. Firstly, they demonstrated that the grand canonical partition function for a solution can be reduced to a solute-only form by integrating out the solvent degrees of freedom. The total effective solute potential in the effective solute grand partition function can be decomposed into potentials of mean force for isolated groups of one, two, three, etc., solute molecules.  Secondly, building on the first result and assuming low solute concentration, MM derived an expansion for the osmotic pressure in powers of the solute concentration, analogous to the virial expansion of gas pressure in powers of the density at low density. The molecular expressions obtained for the osmotic virial coefficients have the same form as the corresponding gas virial coefficients, with potentials of mean force replacing vacuum potentials.  This paper focuses on binary liquid solutions with solute species $A$ and solvent species $B$ and undertakes three key tasks: (a) by working with a semi-grand canonical ensemble (grand with respect to solvent only) instead of the grand canonical ensemble used by MM and avoiding graphical methods, the derivation of the first MM result is greatly simplified, (b) using a simple non-graphical method developed by van Kampen for gases, the derivation of the second MM result (the osmotic pressure virial expansion) is also greatly simplified. As a byproduct, the paper demonstrates the precise relation between MM theory and Widom potential distribution theory, and (c) MM theory is extended by deriving virial expansions for other solution properties such as the enthalpy of mixing. This latter expansion, with modified independent variables corresponding to current experiments, is proving useful. ||| 
This paper presents a model that can produce boundary confining conditions on Dirac fields interacting with Abelian or non-Abelian gauge fields. The constraint is generated by a scalar field. This type of model can serve as a foundation for bag models that can produce confinement. The present work represents a generalization to the non-Abelian case of a previous result where the Abelian case was studied.  In the $U(1)$ case, the coupling to the gauge field contains a term of the form $g(\phi)j_\mu (A^{\mu} + \partial^{\mu}B)$ where $B$ is an auxiliary field and $j_\mu$ is the Dirac current. The scalar field $\phi$ determines the local value of the coupling of the gauge field to the Dirac particle. The consistency of the equations determines the condition $\partial^{\mu}\phi j_\mu = 0$, implying that the Dirac current cannot have a component in the direction of the gradient of the scalar field. title: Cartesian closed categories are distributive
Abstract: A folklore result in category theory states that a (weakly) Cartesian closed category with finite co-products is distributive. Typically, the proof of this result relies on the fact that the exponential functor is right adjoint to the product functor. Since functors with right adjoints preserve co-limits, the result follows directly. However, when attempting to explicitly construct the arrows, the process becomes more complex. In specific cases, it is beneficial to have the precise arrows that establish this isomorphism. This note aims to develop the explicit proof, constructing all involved arrows explicitly.

title: Categories in Control
Abstract: Control theory utilizes "signal-flow diagrams" to represent processes involving addition, scalar multiplication, differentiation, integration, duplication, and deletion of real-valued functions of time. These diagrams can be interpreted as string diagrams for the symmetric monoidal category FinVect_k of finite-dimensional vector spaces over the field of rational functions k = R(s), where the variable s acts as differentiation and the monoidal structure is direct sum rather than the conventional tensor product of vector spaces. We present a representation of FinVect_k in terms of the generators used in signal flow diagrams for any field k. A broader class of signal-flow diagrams also incorporates "caps" and "cups" to model feedback. We demonstrate that these diagrams can be viewed as string diagrams for the symmetric monoidal category FinRel_k, where objects remain finite-dimensional vector spaces but morphisms are linear relations. We also provide a presentation for FinRel_k. The relations imply, among other things, that the 1-dimensional vector space k possesses two special commutative dagger-Frobenius structures, such that the multiplication and unit of one and the comultiplication and counit of the other combine to form a bimonoid. This type of structure, but with tensor product replacing direct sum, is familiar from the "ZX-calculus" obeyed by a finite-dimensional Hilbert space with two mutually unbiased bases.

title: Kevoree Modeling Framework (KMF): Efficient modeling techniques for runtime use
Abstract: The development of Domain Specific Languages (DSLs) is a central goal in the field of Model-Driven Software Engineering (MDSE). These DSLs primarily aim to simplify the manipulation of domain-specific concepts by providing developers with specialized tools tailored to their area of expertise. A natural approach to DSL creation involves reusing existing modeling standards and tools. In this domain, the Eclipse Modeling Framework (EMF) has become the de facto standard in MDSE for constructing DSLs and tools based on generative techniques. However, using EMF-generated tools in domains like the Internet of Things (IoT), Cloud Computing, or Models@Runtime presents certain limitations. This paper identifies several properties that generated tools must satisfy to be applicable in domains beyond desktop-based software systems. We then evaluate EMF's compliance with these properties and outline our approach to overcoming its limitations. Our approach, implemented in the Kevoree Modeling Framework (KMF), is subsequently evaluated based on the identified properties and compared to EMF.

title: Lectures on piecewise distance preserving maps
Abstract: These lectures formed part of the geometry course offered during the Fall 2011 Mathematics Advanced Study Semesters (MASS) Program at Penn State (\\url{http://www.math.psu.edu/mass/}). The lectures are designed to be accessible to advanced undergraduate and early graduate students in mathematics. We have prioritized clarity and exposition, and included numerous exercises. Hints and solutions for most of the exercises are provided at the end. The lectures explore piecewise distance-preserving maps from a 2-dimensional polyhedral space into the plane. Broadly speaking, a polyhedral space is a space constructed by gluing together triangles, such as the surface of a polyhedron. If one envisions such a polyhedral space as a paper model, then a piecewise distance-preserving map into the plane essentially corresponds to folding the model so that it lies flat on a table. We restrict our focus to the 2-dimensional case for ease of visualization. However, most of the results can be generalized to higher dimensions. These generalizations are discussed in the Final Remarks, where appropriate credit and references are provided.

title: Cyclic codes over the ring $ \Z_p[u, v]/\langle u^2, v^2, uv-vu\rangle$
Abstract: Let $p$ be a prime number. This paper investigates cyclic codes over the ring $ \\Z_p[u, v]/\\langle u^2, v^2, uv-vu\\rangle$. We identify a unique set of generators for these codes. We also examine the rank and Hamming distance of these codes. All but one ternary optimal code of length 12 is obtained as the Gray image of the cyclic codes over the ring $ \\Z_p[u, v]/\\langle u^2, v^2,\nuv-vu\\rangle$. We also characterize the $p$-ary image of these cyclic codes under the Gray map.

title: A functional model of interactions in quantum theory
Abstract: This paper proposes a functional model of interactions in quantum theory (QT). A functional model describes the dynamic evolution of a physical system in terms of process steps and intermediate states. In essence, it explains how things function. The proposed functional model of QT interactions was developed in the context of the author's work towards a computer model of QT, with the goal of supporting the broadest possible range of QT concepts. In QT, the results of interactions are calculated using quantum field theory (QFT). Therefore, the proposed functional model of interactions is based on QFT. Several important QT concepts, such as measurement, entanglement, and decoherence, are related to interactions. The functional model of interactions also addresses these phenomena.

title: Algorithmic identification of probabilities is hard
Abstract: Consider an infinite binary sequence that is random for a Bernoulli measure with parameter $p$. According to the law of large numbers, the frequency of zeros in the sequence converges to~$p$, allowing us to obtain increasingly accurate approximations of $p$ as we read the sequence. This paper explores a similar question, but from the perspective of inductive inference. We assume that $p$ is a computable real number, but seek a stronger condition: as we read more and more bits of our random sequence, we must eventually guess the exact parameter $p$ (represented by a Turing code). Can this be achieved uniformly for all sequences that are random for computable Bernoulli measures, or even for a "large enough" fraction of them? This paper presents a negative answer to this question. In fact, we prove a very general negative result that extends beyond the class of Bernoulli measures.

title: Another Look at Confidence Intervals: Proposal for a More Relevant and Transparent Approach
Abstract: This paper explores the behavior of various confidence/credible interval constructions, particularly in the region of low statistics where methods diverge most significantly. We highlight several challenges, such as the treatment of nuisance parameters, and address common misconceptions associated with such constructions. An informal survey of the literature suggests that confidence intervals are not always defined in relevant ways and are too often misinterpreted or misapplied. This can lead to seemingly paradoxical behaviors and flawed comparisons regarding the relevance of experimental results. We conclude that a more pragmatic strategy is needed, acknowledging that while objectively conveying the information content of the data is crucial, there is also a strong desire to derive bounds on models and a natural inclination to interpret results in this manner. Accordingly, we attempt to set aside philosophical biases in favor of a practical approach, proposing a more transparent and self-consistent method that better addresses these issues.

title: Acoustic phonons and strain in core/shell nanowires
Abstract: This study theoretically investigates low-energy phonons and static strain in cylindrical core/shell nanowires (NWs). Assuming pseudomorphic growth, isotropic media, and a force-free wire surface, we derive algebraic expressions for the dispersion relations, displacement fields, and stress and strain components from linear elasticity theory. Our findings apply to NWs with arbitrary radii and arbitrary elastic constants for both core and shell. The expressions for the static strain are consistent with experimental results, simulations, and previous analytical investigations. The phonon expressions are consistent with known results for homogeneous NWs. Among other findings, we demonstrate that the dispersion relations of the torsional, longitudinal, and flexural modes vary differently with relative shell thickness. We also identify new terms in the corresponding strain tensors that are absent for uncapped NWs. We illustrate our results using the example of Ge/Si core/shell NWs, demonstrating that shell-induced strain has significant effects on the hole spectrum of these systems.

title: Bohm's approach and Individuality
Abstract: Ladyman and Ross (LR) argue that quantum objects are not individuals (or are at most weakly discernible individuals) and use this idea to support their metaphysical view, ontic structural realism, according to which relational structures are fundamental to things. LR acknowledge that a version of quantum theory, namely the Bohm theory (BT), postulates definite trajectories for particles at all times. However, LR interpret research by Brown {\\em et al.} as implying that "raw stuff" or {\\em haecceities} are necessary for the individuality of particles in BT, and dismiss this as idle metaphysics. This paper notes that Brown {\\em et al.}\'s research does not imply the need for {\\em haecceities}. Therefore, BT remains a viable option for those seeking to understand quantum particles as individuals. However, we proceed to discuss some problems with BT that led Bohm and Hiley to modify it. This modified version highlights that, due to features such as context-dependence and non-locality, Bohmian particles exhibit limited autonomy in situations where quantum effects are significant. While BT restores the possibility of quantum individuals, it also underscores the primacy of the whole over the autonomy of its parts. Later sections of the paper examine the Bohm theory in the general mathematical context of symplectic geometry. This provides another perspective on the subtle, holistic, and dynamic nature of Bohmian individuals. Finally, we briefly consider Bohm\'s other primary line of research, the "implicate order," which in some ways resembles LR\'s structural realism.

title: The Neumann eigenvalue problem for the $\infty$-Laplacian
Abstract: The first nontrivial eigenfunction of the Neumann eigenvalue problem for the $p$-Laplacian, appropriately normalized, converges as $p$ approaches $\\infty$ to a viscosity solution of an eigenvalue problem for the $\\infty$-Laplacian. We demonstrate, among other things, that the limit of the eigenvalue, at least for convex sets, is indeed the first nonzero eigenvalue of the limiting problem. We then derive a number of consequences, which are nonlinear analogues of well-known inequalities for the linear (2-)Laplacian.

title: Categories from scratch
Abstract: The concept of category from mathematics proves useful to computer programmers in numerous ways. Unfortunately, all "good" explanations of categories to date have been crafted by mathematicians, or at least theoreticians with a strong mathematical background, making categories particularly opaque to external audiences. More specifically, the typical explanatory approach to categories is: "here is a formal specification of what a category is; then consider these known objects from mathematics and theoretical computer science, and admire how they can be described using the notions of category theory." This approach is only successful if the audience can fully grasp a conceptual object solely based on its formal specification. In practice, many individuals adopt conceptual objects by abstracting from two or more contexts where the concepts are applicable. This is the path taken below: we reconstruct the abstractions from category theory using fragments of understanding from various fields of computer engineering.

title: A Novel Method for Developing Robotics via Artificial Intelligence and Internet of Things
Abstract: This paper presents a new methodology for advancing the field of robotics through artificial intelligence and the internet of things. Nowadays, artificial intelligence has revolutionized robotics. Robots are employed across various industries for numerous tasks, including the use of cooperative robots to perform diverse tasks. However, creating robots capable of handling multiple tasks has posed a challenge. Therefore, a new methodology for developing multi-tasking robots is needed. This can only be achieved through the integration of artificial intelligence and the internet of things.

title: On Nekovář's heights, exceptional zeros and a conjecture of Mazur-Tate-Teitelbaum
Abstract: Let $E/\\mathbb{Q}$ be an elliptic curve exhibiting split multiplicative reduction at a prime $p$ and whose analytic rank $r_{an}(E)$ equals one. The primary objective of this article is to establish a connection between the second-order derivative of the Mazur-Tate-Teitelbaum $p$-adic $L$-function $L_p(E,s)$ of $E$ and Nekov\\'{a}\\v{r}'s height pairing evaluated on natural elements arising from the Beilinson-Kato elements. In the process, we extend a Rubin-style formula by Nekov\\'a\\v{r} (or, in alternative terms, correct another Rubin-style formula of his) to encompass the presence of exceptional zeros. Our height formula allows us, among other things, to compare the order of vanishing of $L_p(E,s)$ at $s=1$ with its (complex) analytic rank $r_{an}(E)$ assuming the non-triviality of the height pairing. This has implications for a conjecture by Mazur, Tate, and Teitelbaum.

title: An Efficient Local Search for Partial Latin Square Extension Problem
Abstract: A partial Latin square (PLS) is a partial assignment of $n$ symbols to an $n \times n$ grid such that each symbol appears at most once in each row and each column. The partial Latin square extension problem is an NP-hard problem that seeks the largest extension of a given PLS. This paper proposes an efficient local search algorithm for this problem. We focus on local search where the neighborhood is defined by $(p,q)$-swap, i.e., removing exactly $p$ symbols and then assigning symbols to at most $q$ empty cells. For $p$ in {1,2,3}, our neighborhood search algorithm finds an improved solution or concludes that no such solution exists in $O(n^{p+1})$ time. We also introduce a novel swap operation, Trellis-swap, which generalizes $(1,q)$-swap and $(2,q)$-swap. Our Trellis-neighborhood search algorithm takes $O(n^{3.5})$ time to achieve the same result. Using these neighborhood search algorithms, we design a prototype iterated local search algorithm and demonstrate its effectiveness compared to state-of-the-art optimization solvers such as IBM ILOG CPLEX and LocalSolver.

title: A Simple Model for Global HI Profiles of Galaxies
Abstract: Context. Current and future blind surveys for HI generate extensive catalogs of spectral lines for which automated characterization would be convenient. Aims. A 6-parameter mathematical model for HI galactic spectral lines is described. The aim of this paper is to demonstrate the utility of this model for characterizing such lines. Methods. The model is fitted to spectral lines extracted from the 34 spiral galaxies of the recent high-definition THINGS survey. Three scenarios with differing instrumental characteristics are compared. Quantities derived from the model fits, most notably line width and total flux, are compared with analogous quantities measured using more standard, non-parametric methods. Results. The model is shown to provide a good fit to nearly all the THINGS profiles. When additional noise is introduced to the test spectra, the fits remain consistent. The model-fitting approach is also shown to yield superior estimates of linewidth and flux under such conditions.

title: A scenario based approach for dealing with challenges in a pervasive computing environment

An example Pattern Recognition scenario is presented, along with mathematical techniques that can be used to model uncertainty. These techniques are then applied to develop a system capable of sensing, computing, and communicating in a way that can enhance human life through the assistance of smart objects in their surroundings.

title: The Cellular Automaton Interpretation of Quantum Mechanics
Abstract: When investigating theories at the smallest conceivable scales in nature, nearly all researchers today rely on the quantum language, accepting the Copenhagen doctrine's verdict that the only way to describe what is happening will always involve states in Hilbert space, governed by operator equations. Returning to classical, i.e., non-quantum mechanical, descriptions is deemed forever impossible unless one accepts extremely contrived theoretical constructions that may or may not replicate the quantum mechanical phenomena observed in experiments. Dissatisfied, this author explored alternative perspectives. This book offers an overview of older material but also includes numerous new observations and calculations. Quantum mechanics is viewed as a tool rather than a theory. Examples are provided of models that are essentially classical but can be analyzed using quantum techniques. We argue that even the Standard Model, along with gravitational interactions, might be viewed as a quantum mechanical approach to analyzing a system that could be fundamentally classical. We explain how such thoughts can be reconciled with Bell's theorem and how the usual objections raised against the notion of "superdeterminism" can be overcome, at least in principle. Our proposal would eliminate the collapse problem and the measurement problem. Even the existence of an "arrow of time" might be explained more elegantly than usual. Discussions added in v3: the role of the gravitational force, a mathematical physics definition of free will, and an unconventional view on the arrow of time, among others.

title: Spectra of faint sources in crowded fields with FRODOSpec on the Liverpool Robotic Telescope
Abstract: We assess the performance of the FRODOSpec integral-field spectrograph for observations of faint sources in crowded fields. While the standard processing pipeline L2 produces excessively noisy fiber spectra, we present a new processing software (L2LENS) that generates accurate spectra for the two images of the gravitationally lensed quasar Q0957+561. Among other features, this L2LENS reduction tool accounts for the presence of cosmic-ray events, scattered-light backgrounds, blended sources, and chromatic source displacements due to differential atmospheric refraction. Our non-standard reduction of Q0957+561 data demonstrates FRODOSpec's ability to provide useful information on a wide variety of targets, highlighting the significant potential of integral-field spectrographs on current and future robotic telescopes.

title: Percolation on sparse networks
Abstract: We investigate percolation on networks, a model for the resilience of networked systems such as the internet to attacks or failures, as well as a simplified model for disease spread over human contact networks. We reformulate percolation as a message-passing process and demonstrate how the resulting equations can be used to calculate, among other things, the size of the percolating cluster and the average cluster size. The calculations are exact for sparse networks with a low number of short loops, but even on networks with many short loops, we find them to be highly accurate when compared to direct numerical simulations. By considering the fixed points of the message-passing process, we also show that the percolation threshold on a network with few loops is given by the inverse of the leading eigenvalue of the so-called non-backtracking matrix.

title: The Planck mission
Abstract: The Planck mission, aimed at precisely measuring the temperature variations in the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB), yielded significant findings announced on March 21st, 2013. This lecture discusses key steps involved in obtaining these results, including data processing techniques used to generate full-sky maps at 9 different frequencies. The lecture also explains how the CMB temperature anisotropy map and angular power spectrum were extracted. It concludes by highlighting major cosmological implications derived from the statistical characteristics of the CMB.  This lecture offers a concise overview of the Planck 2013 results, encouraging students to explore original research for a more comprehensive understanding.

title: OSCAR: Object Security Architecture for the Internet of Things
Abstract: Billions of interconnected smart devices, operating within constraints of the global network, require novel network design paradigms. New protocol standards, tailored for these devices, have been developed to address specific requirements like asynchronous application traffic, caching, and group communication. However, the existing connection-oriented security architecture falls short in terms of supported features, scalability, and latency on constrained devices. This paper proposes an architecture that leverages security concepts from both content-centric and traditional connection-oriented approaches. It relies on secure channels established through (D)TLS for key exchange, eliminating the need for a 'state' among communicating entities. The proposed approach utilizes CoAP for replay attack prevention. This object-based security architecture (OSCAR) inherently supports caching and multicast, without affecting the radio duty-cycling operation of constrained objects. The paper evaluates OSCAR in two scenarios: 802.15.4 Low Power and Lossy Networks (LLN) and Machine-to-Machine (M2M) communication. Evaluations were performed on two different hardware platforms and MAC layers using a real testbed and the Cooja emulator. Results demonstrate significant energy savings at constrained servers and reasonable delays. The paper also discusses the applicability of OSCAR to Smart City deployments.
