title: A Tale of Two Paradigms: the Mutual Incommensurability of LCDM and MOND
Abstract: The Lambda-CDM model (LCDM), a widely accepted model in cosmology, provides a satisfactory explanation for the universe's evolution and large-scale structure growth. However, it struggles to accurately describe small-scale structure and the dynamics of bound objects, such as individual galaxies. In contrast, Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND) offers a unique and successful description of galaxy dynamics, but lacks a cosmological framework. This paper examines these conflicting worldviews, highlighting the vast body of interlocking evidence supporting LCDM while emphasizing its inability to adequately explain the observed MOND phenomenology in galaxy dynamics. The paper also explores the baryon budget in galaxy groups and clusters, where neither model provides a completely satisfactory explanation. While MOND lacks a comprehensive theory of structure formation, the paper discusses the existing research. The paper notes that MOND correctly predicted the amplitude ratio of the first two peaks in the CMB power spectrum, but the third peak is more naturally explained by LCDM. The paper further highlights that MOND predicts faster structure formation than LCDM, leading to earlier reionization than initially expected in LCDM, which has been subsequently observed. This also provides a natural explanation for the existence of massive, early galaxy clusters and large empty voids. However, it remains unclear if MOND can adequately explain the mass spectrum of galaxy clusters and the power spectrum of galaxies, two areas where LCDM performs well. The paper concludes by emphasizing the critical outstanding issues in both models, namely the development of a relativistic parent theory for MOND and the nature of non-baryonic dark matter in LCDM. The paper questions the existence of suitable dark matter particles and explores the possibility of them being a modern version of the luminiferous aether.

title: The moduli space of vacua of N=2 class S theories
Abstract: This paper presents a systematic method to describe the moduli space of vacua of four-dimensional $\\mathcal{N}=2$ class ${\\cal S}$ theories, encompassing Coulomb branch, Higgs branch, and mixed branches. The paper determines Higgs and mixed branch roots, along with the dimensions of Coulomb and Higgs components of mixed branches. The methodology utilizes generalized Hitchin's equations, derived from twisted compactification of 5d maximal Super-Yang-Mills with local degrees of freedom at punctures represented by (nilpotent) orbits. The key aspects of the method include the holomorphic factorization of the Seiberg-Witten curve and singularity reduction at punctures. The paper illustrates the method with numerous examples, including ${\\mathcal N}=2$ SQCD, $T_N$ theory, and Argyres-Douglas theories.

title: Dark Matter In Disk Galaxies II: Density Profiles as Constraints on Feedback Scenarios
Abstract: The discrepancy between the density profiles of galactic dark matter haloes predicted by dark matter-only cosmological simulations and those inferred from rotation curve decomposition, known as the cusp-core problem, suggests that baryonic physics influences dark matter density in the central regions of galaxies. Feedback from black holes, supernovae, and massive stars might play a role by removing matter from the galaxy's center on shorter timescales than the dynamical time of the dark matter halo. This paper aims to determine constraints on these feedback scenarios based on the observed properties of nearby galaxies. Using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) analysis of galactic rotation curves, the paper constrains density profiles and estimates a minimum radius for baryon influence, $r_1$. This information is then combined with a feedback model to estimate the fraction of matter within that radius that must be expelled to produce the observed halo profile. The analysis demonstrates that in the case of the gas-rich dwarf irregular galaxy DDO 154, an outflow from a central source (e.g., a black hole or star-forming region) could effectively influence the halo without removing the disk gas. The paper further examines the rotation curves of 8 galaxies from the THINGS dataset and determines constraints on the radial density profiles of their dark matter haloes. For some galaxies, both cored haloes and cosmological $\\rho \\propto r^{-1}$ cusps are excluded. These intermediate central slopes necessitate finely tuned baryonic feedback. The analysis also reveals that galaxies exhibiting extended cores in their haloes (e.g., NGC 925) benefit from using a split power-law halo profile, resulting in models devoid of unphysical sharp features present in models based on the Einasto profile.

title: The hammock localization preserves homotopies
Abstract: The hammock localization provides a model for a homotopy function complex within any Quillen model category. It explores applications of this finding to the study of homotopy algebras over monads and homotopy idempotent functors. The paper demonstrates that, under Vop\\v{e}nka's principle, every homotopy idempotent functor in a cofibrantly generated model category is determined by simplicial orthogonality with respect to a set of morphisms. The paper also presents a novel proof of the fact that left Bousfield localizations with respect to a class of morphisms always exist in any left proper combinatorial model category under Vop\\v{e}nka's principle.

title: Quantum mechanics and the manifestation of the world
Abstract: Quantum theory's foundational empirical element is a probability calculus. While it assumes the events to which it assigns probabilities, it must be consistent with those events. This necessitates identifying a system of observables possessing measurement-independent values. The paper argues that this is achievable due to the incomplete spatiotemporal differentiation of the physical world. This concept is illustrated by applying a novel interpretive principle to interfering alternatives involving distinctions between regions of space. Applying the same principle to alternatives involving distinctions between things, the paper asserts that the macroworld arises through a progressive differentiation of a single, inherently undifferentiated entity. By entering into reflexive spatial relations, this entity gives rise to (i) what appears as a multiplicity of relata if the reflexive nature of relations is not considered and (ii) what appears as a substantial expanse if the spatial quality of the relations is reified. The paper proposes that the necessary distinction between two domains (classical and quantum, or macro and micro) and their interdependence is best understood as a distinction between the manifested world and its manifestation.

title: Manifesting the Quantum World
Abstract: Quantum mechanics, in its resistance to explaining the unity of a whole based on interacting parts, calls for an explanatory concept that operates in the reverse direction: from unity to multiplicity. The paper focuses on the process by which Sellars' Manifest Image of the world comes into being. This process involves the progressive differentiation of an inherently undifferentiated entity. By entering into reflexive spatial relations, this entity gives rise to (i) what appears as a multiplicity of relata if the reflexive nature of relations is not considered and (ii) what appears as a substantial expanse if the spatial quality of the relations is reified. The paper argues that if a distinctly quantum domain exists, it is a non-spatial and non-temporal dimension across which the transition from the unity of this entity to the multiplicity of the world takes place. Subatomic particles, atoms, and molecules, instead of being constituents of the physical world, play a role in its manifestation. The paper's conclusions are based on the following interpretive principle: whenever calculating probabilities necessitates adding amplitudes, the distinctions we make between alternatives lack objective reality. This principle, applied to alternatives involving distinctions between regions of space, implies that the spatiotemporal differentiation of the physical world is incomplete, rendering the existence of a real-valued spatiotemporal background an unrealistic idealization. This guarantees the existence of observables whose values are real *per se*, as opposed to "real by virtue of being indicated by the values of observables that are real *per se*." When applied to alternatives involving distinctions between things, the principle implies that all fundamental particles are inherently numerically identical and thus identifiable with the aforementioned undifferentiated entity.

title: Classification of "Quaternionic" Bloch-bundles: Topological Quantum Systems of type AII
Abstract: This paper provides a classification of type AII topological quantum systems in dimensions d=1,2,3,4. The analysis is based on the construction of a topological invariant, the FKMM-invariant, which completely classifies "Quaternionic" vector bundles (also known as "symplectic" vector bundles) in dimension d<4. This invariant takes values in a proper equivariant cohomology theory and reproduces the familiar Fu-Kane-Mele index in cases of physical interest. For d=4, the classification requires a combined use of the FKMM-invariant and the second Chern class. The paper proves that the FKMM-invariant is a bona fide characteristic class for the category of "Quaternionic" vector bundles, meaning it can be realized as the pullback of a universal topological invariant.

title: Using Scripting Languages to Teach Programming

Additionally, GUI programming with these languages is easy and rewarding due to the immediate visualization of results. The paper concludes that scripting languages combined with GUI toolkits are poised to become the next big advancement in computer education.

title: Nonhomogeneous Place-Dependent Markov Chains, Unsynchronised AIMD, and Network Utility Maximization
Abstract: This paper presents a solution to a class of network utility maximization (NUM) problems using minimal communication. The problem constraints are inspired not by TCP-like congestion control but by problems in the Internet of Things and related areas, where the need arises to optimize the behavior of a large group of agents. The proposed approach relies on intermittent feedback, no inter-agent communication, and no common clock. The algorithm combines the classical AIMD algorithm with a simple probabilistic rule for agents to respond to a capacity signal. This results in a nonhomogeneous Markov chain, and the paper demonstrates the almost sure convergence of this chain to the social optimum.

title: Beyond Bell's Theorem II: Scenarios with arbitrary causal structure
Abstract: Recent research has revealed that Bell scenarios represent a limited subclass of setups for investigating the non-classical features of quantum theory within spacetime. The paper's main contribution is its unifying nature: while notions like source, choice of setting, and measurement appear to play distinct roles in a Bell scenario, this formalism shows they are all instances of the same concept of "event". The paper also contributes to the field of causal inference with latent variables by introducing hidden Bayesian networks as a generalization of hidden Markov models.

title: Interactions, Specifications, DLR probabilities and the Ruelle Operator in the One-Dimensional Lattice
Abstract: This paper explores different interpretations of the Gibbs measure on the lattice $\\mathbb{N}$ within the context of finite alphabets (or state space). It analyzes distinct notions of DLR-Gibbs measures, Thermodynamic Limit, and eigenprobabilities for the dual of the Ruelle operator (also called conformal measures). The paper extends the classical notion of a Gibbsian specification on $\\mathbb{N}$ in a way that highlights the similarities between Statistical Mechanics and Dynamical Systems. One of the paper's main results is that the construction of conformal Measures in Dynamical Systems for Walters potentials using the Ruelle operator can be formulated in terms of Specification. The paper also describes the Ising model with $1/r^{2+\\varepsilon}$ interaction energy within the Thermodynamic Formalism setting and proves that its associated potential resides in Walters space. title: Peri-abelian categories and the universal central extension condition

It is demonstrated that if a category is peri-abelian, then condition (UCE), introduced and studied by Casas and the second author, holds for that category. Furthermore, using a result by Cigoli, the paper shows that all categories of interest in the sense of Orzech are peri-abelian and thus satisfy condition (UCE).

title: Some topological problems on the configuration spaces of Artin and Coxeter groups

The paper also partially computes the cohomology of the braid group with non-abelian coefficients derived from geometric representations. It introduces a new class of "sheaves over posets" called "weighted sheaves over posets" and uses them for explicit computations.

title: Proposal of a multiagent-based smart environment for the IoT

These models are created on-the-fly by software agents observing user/inhabitant behavior and gathering knowledge about preferences expressed as logical specifications. A three-level structure of agents has been introduced to support IoT inference. These agents cooperate based on a graph representation of system knowledge. The paper presents an example of such a system.

title: The RR Lyrae Variable Population in the Phoenix Dwarf Galaxy
Abstract: This paper presents the first detailed study of the RR Lyrae variable population in the Local Group dSph/dIrr transition galaxy, Phoenix, utilizing previously obtained HST/WFPC2 observations. Template light curve fitting routines were used to obtain best-fit light curves for RR Lyrae variables in Phoenix. This technique identified 78 highly probable RR Lyrae stars (54 ab-type; 24 c-type) with approximately 40 additional candidates. The paper finds mean periods for the two populations: $\\langle P_{ab}\\rangle = 0.60 \\pm 0.03$ days and $\\langle\nP_{c}\\rangle = 0.353 \\pm 0.002$ days. The paper uses the properties of these light curves to extract, among other things, a metallicity distribution function for ab-type RR Lyrae. The analysis reveals a mean metallicity of $\\langle\n[Fe/H]\\rangle = -1.68 \\pm 0.06$ dex for the RRab stars. Based on the mean period and metallicity calculated from the ab-type RR Lyrae, the paper concludes that Phoenix is more likely of intermediate Oosterhoff type; however, the morphology of the Bailey diagram for Phoenix RR Lyraes resembles that of an Oosterhoff type I system. The paper also studies the chemical enrichment law for Phoenix using the RRab stars. The analysis reveals that the metallicity distribution is reasonably well-fitted by a closed-box model. The parameters of this model align with findings from Hidalgo et al. (2009), further supporting the idea that Phoenix likely underwent chemical enrichment as a closed-box-like system during its early formation and evolution.

title: D-P2P-Sim+:A Novel Distributed Framework for P2P Protocols Performance Testing
Abstract: The rapid growth of data in Internet of Things (IoT) and Web 2.0 technologies presents a significant challenge in data storage and processing. It introduces a distributed framework that supports customized deployment of various indexing engines over million-node overlays. The proposed framework provides a comprehensive set of tools enabling applications processing large amounts of data to evaluate and test the performance of different application protocols for very large-scale deployments (multi-million nodes - billions of keys). The primary aim is to provide an environment facilitating informed decisions regarding protocol selection in storage P2P systems for diverse big data applications. Utilizing lightweight and efficient collection mechanisms, the system enables real-time registration of multiple measures, integrating support for real-life parameters such as node failure models and recovery strategies. Experiments conducted on the PlanetLab network and a typical research laboratory verify scalability and demonstrate the maximum reusability of the setup. title: A Percolation based M2M Networking Architecture for Data Transmission and Routing
Abstract: This paper proposes a percolation-based Machine-to-Machine (M2M) networking architecture and its data transmission method. The proposed architecture eliminates the need for servers and routers, enabling efficient routing based on percolation principles derived from six degrees of separation theory in small-world network modeling. Data transmission occurs in two phases: routing and data transmission. During the routing phase, probe packets are transmitted and forwarded within the network, selecting multiple paths based on maximum hop number constraints. In the second phase, information is encoded using fountain codes and transmitted along the paths generated in the first phase. This approach facilitates the construction of a low-cost, flexible, and ubiquitous network. The proposed networking architecture and data transmission method can be applied to various M2M communications, including the stub network of the Internet of Things, deep space networking, and more.

title: Weak Multiplier Hopf Algebras II. The source and target algebras
Abstract: This paper continues the study of weak multiplier Hopf algebras. It recalls the concepts of source and target maps $\\varepsilon_s$ and $\\varepsilon_t$, as well as source and target algebras. The paper further investigates these objects, demonstrating that the canonical idempotent E (which is eventually $\\Delta(1)$) belongs to the multiplier algebra $M(B\\otimes C)$ where $B=\\varepsilon_s(A)$ and $C=\\varepsilon_t(A)$, and that it is a separability idempotent. The paper explores special cases and examples, showing how for any weak multiplier Hopf algebra, it is possible to construct $C\\otimes B$ (with B and C as defined above) into a new weak multiplier Hopf algebra. This process effectively discards the 'Hopf algebra part' of the original weak multiplier Hopf algebra while retaining the source and target algebras. This concept is generalized to any pair of non-degenerate algebras B and C with a separability idempotent $E\\in M(B\\otimes C)$. The paper also presents an example derived from this theory associated with any discrete quantum group (a multiplier Hopf algebra of discrete type with a normalized cointegral). Finally, the paper considers the well-known 'quantization' of the groupoid arising from the action of a group on a set. All these constructions provide interesting new examples of weak multiplier Hopf algebras (that are not weak Hopf algebras). |||

title: Some supercongruences occurring in truncated hypergeometric series
Abstract: This paper investigates supercongruences, which are congruences between terminating hypergeometric series and quotients of p-adic Gamma functions that are stronger than those provable using commutative formal group laws. We establish several such supercongruences by utilizing classical hypergeometric transformation formulae. These formulae allow us to express terminating series as ratios of products of Gamma values, transforming sums into quotients. By rewriting these Gamma quotients as p-adic Gamma quotients, we create a framework suitable for proving p-adic congruences. Exploiting the p-adic approximation of these Gamma functions via their Taylor series expansions, we achieve stronger congruences through the cancellation of lower-order terms. This technique allows us to prove, among other results, a conjecture by Kibelbek and a strengthened version of a conjecture by van Hamme.

title: Invariant measures for frequently hypercyclic operators
Abstract: We analyze frequently hypercyclic and chaotic linear operators from a measure-theoretic perspective. Our findings demonstrate that any frequently hypercyclic operator T acting on a reflexive Banach space possesses an invariant probability measure with full support, which can be restricted to vanish on the set of all periodic vectors for T. Furthermore, we show the existence of frequently hypercyclic operators on the sequence space c_0 that lack ergodic measures with full support. Additionally, we establish that if an operator admits an ergodic measure with full support, it exhibits a comeager set of distributionally irregular vectors. We also provide necessary and sufficient conditions, satisfied by all known chaotic operators, for an operator T to possess an invariant measure supported on its hypercyclic vectors and belonging to the closed convex hull of its periodic measures. Finally, using a Baire category argument, we prove that any operator with a perfectly spanning set of unimodular eigenvectors admits an ergodic measure with full support.

title: Algorithms Visualization Tool for Students and Lectures in Computer Science

We believe this tool can be valuable for all those interested in algorithms, especially computer science students seeking to deepen their understanding and university lecturers seeking to enrich their data structures and algorithms courses. The key innovation of this tool lies in enabling users to animate their own algorithms.

title: Remote Home Management: An alternative for working at home while away

This paper details a system for managing and controlling home appliances using mobile phones, allowing users to remotely manipulate devices from afar before arriving home. For example, users can activate their room cooler or heater to ensure a comfortable temperature upon arrival. Similarly, appliances like washing machines and cookers can be started and, if the duration of their tasks is known, programmed to automatically switch off after completion. Controlling an appliance involves sending an SMS command from the user's mobile phone to a connected computer. Upon receiving the message, the computer relays the command to a microcontroller, enabling appropriate appliance control.

title: Teichmüller harmonic map flow into nonpositively curved targets
Abstract: The Teichmüller harmonic map flow concurrently deforms a map from an oriented closed surface M into an arbitrary closed Riemannian manifold and a constant curvature metric on M, aiming to minimize the energy of the map as rapidly as possible. Under suitable conditions, the flow strives to converge to a branched minimal immersion. The sole obstacle to convergence is the potential for finite-time degeneration of the metric on M, where one or more collars are pinched. In this paper, we demonstrate that finite-time degeneration cannot occur when the target manifold exhibits nonpositive sectional curvature, and more generally, when the target does not support bubbles. Notably, in conjunction with previous results, this finding establishes that the flow decomposes any such map into a collection of branched minimal immersions.

title: Cognitive Internet of Things: A New Paradigm beyond Connection
Abstract: Current research on the Internet of Things (IoT) primarily focuses on empowering general objects to perceive the physical world through senses like sight, hearing, and smell, enabling them to connect and share their observations. This paper argues that mere connectivity is insufficient, and instead advocates for general objects to possess the capacity for learning, thinking, and understanding both the physical and social worlds autonomously. This practical need motivates the development of a new paradigm, dubbed the Cognitive Internet of Things (CIoT), which aims to equip the current IoT with a "brain" for high-level intelligence. This paper provides a comprehensive definition of CIoT, drawing inspiration from the effectiveness of human cognition. We propose an operational framework for CIoT, outlining the interactions among five fundamental cognitive tasks: perception-action cycle, massive data analytics, semantic derivation and knowledge discovery, intelligent decision-making, and on-demand service provisioning. Furthermore, we present a systematic tutorial on key enabling techniques employed in these cognitive tasks and discuss the design of appropriate performance metrics for evaluating these techniques. Finally, we highlight research challenges and open issues. Building upon this work and potentially fruitful future studies, CIoT holds the promise of bridging the physical world (comprising objects, resources, etc.) with the social world (encompassing human demands, social behavior, etc.), thereby enhancing smart resource allocation, automatic network operation, and intelligent service provisioning.

title: Nonuniversal Gaugino Masses and Muon g-2
Abstract: This paper examines two classes of supersymmetric models featuring non-universal gaugino masses at M_GUT, aiming to resolve the apparent muon g-2 anomaly observed in the Standard Model. Two distinct scenarios are explored: one where all gaugino masses share the same sign at M_GUT and a second case with opposite sign gaugino masses. In both scenarios, sfermion masses are assumed to be universal at M_GUT. Leveraging the non-universality of gaugino masses, we achieve significant mass splitting between colored and non-colored sfermions. This allows sleptons to possess masses in the few hundred GeV range, while colored sparticles are an order of magnitude heavier. Both models successfully resolve the muon g-2 anomaly while maintaining consistency with a 125-126 GeV Higgs boson mass and the WMAP dark matter bounds.

title: Equiangular lines in Euclidean spaces
Abstract: This work contributes to the theory of real equiangular line systems by presenting several novel results. We provide a complete description of the two-graphs on 12 vertices and investigate Seidel matrices with exactly three distinct eigenvalues. These findings lead to improvements on two long-standing upper bounds regarding the maximum number of equiangular lines in dimensions d=14 and d=16. Furthermore, we prove the nonexistence of certain regular graphs with four eigenvalues and rectify some discrepancies in existing tables.

title: Application of Asynchronous Weak Commitment Search in Autonomous Quality of Service Provision in Cognitive Radio Networks
Abstract: This article presents a distributed solution for autonomous quality of service (QoS) provision in cognitive radio networks, focusing on cognitive STDMA and CDMA communication networks. Leveraging asynchronous weak commitment search, the task of QoS provision is distributed among various network nodes. Simulation results confirm that this scheme converges rapidly to an optimal solution, making it suitable for practical real-time systems. This application of artificial intelligence in wireless and mobile communications has potential applications in home automation and networking, and vehicular technology. Generalizations and extensions of this approach can be utilized in Long Term Evolution Self Organizing Networks (LTE-SONs). Moreover, it lays the groundwork for decentralized and autonomous QoS provision in capillary networks that reach end nodes in the Internet of Things, where centralized management is either unavailable or inefficient.

title: We Tweet Like We Talk and Other Interesting Observations: An Analysis of English Communication Modalities
Abstract: As technology advances, human communication modalities are rapidly expanding. Individuals seamlessly transition between these diverse forms of communication, prompting the question: How similar are these communication modalities? To understand technology's impact on English communication, we analyzed and compared four corpora: writing from books (Google Books 1-grams database), Twitter, IRC Chat, and transcribed Talking. Multi-word confusion matrices revealed that Talking exhibited the highest similarity to other communication modes, while 1-grams proved to be the least similar. Based on analyses of word usage, frequency distributions, and word class usage, Talking also demonstrated the greatest similarity to Twitter and IRC Chat. This suggests that Twitter and IRC Chat communication evolved from Talking rather than Writing. Even when writing online, we do not tweet or chat like we write books; we tweet and chat like we speak. Our analysis clearly distinguished nonfiction and fiction writing from Twitter and Chat, with the latter two being more similar to fiction than nonfiction. These hypotheses were subsequently tested using the writing, Twitter usage, and speech of author and journalist Cory Doctorow. Mr. Doctorow's writing, Twitter usage, and Talking demonstrated very similar vocabulary usage patterns to the amalgamated populations, as long as the writing was fiction. However, Mr. Doctorow's nonfiction writing differed significantly from 1-grams and other collected nonfiction writings. This data could potentially be utilized to create more engaging nonfiction works.

title: The Role of Feedback in Shaping the Structure of the Interstellar Medium
Abstract: This paper investigates the role of feedback in shaping the neutral hydrogen (HI) content of simulated disc galaxies. We analyze two realizations of two distinct Milky Way-like (L*) discs: one employing a conservative feedback scheme (MUGS) and the other featuring significantly more energetic feedback (MaGICC). To quantify the impact of these schemes, we generate zeroth moment (surface density) maps of the inferred HI distribution, construct power spectra associated with the underlying structure of the simulated cold ISM, and examine their radial surface density and velocity dispersion profiles. Our findings are compared with a parallel self-consistent analysis of empirical data from THINGS (The HI Nearby Galaxy Survey). Single power-law fits (P~k^gamma) to the power spectra of the stronger-feedback (MaGICC) runs (over spatial scales corresponding to 0.5 kpc to 20 kpc) yield slopes consistent with those observed in the THINGS sample (gamma = -2.5). The weaker-feedback (MUGS) runs exhibit shallower power law slopes (gamma = -1.2). While the power spectra of the MaGICC simulations are more consistent with a two-component fit, featuring a flatter distribution of power on larger scales (i.e., gamma = -1.4 for scales exceeding 2 kpc) and a steeper slope on scales below 1 kpc (gamma = -5), they align qualitatively with empirical claims and our previous work on dwarf discs. The radial HI surface density profiles of the MaGICC discs display a clear exponential behavior, while those of the MUGS suite are essentially flat. Both behaviors are observed in nature, although the THINGS sample aligns more closely with our stronger (MaGICC) feedback runs.

title: The Wiselib TupleStore: A Modular RDF Database for the Internet of Things
Abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) movement promotes self-configuring and universally interoperable devices. While these devices often have specific applications in mind, they frequently prove useful in other contexts. We posit that by universally describing device knowledge, IoT devices can become first-class citizens of the Internet. This allows them to exchange data across heterogeneous hardware, diverse applications, and extensive data sources on the Web. Our key innovation, contrasting with existing approaches, lies in not imposing any restrictions on the domain of knowledge expressible on the device while simultaneously ensuring that this knowledge is machine-understandable and linkable across different locations. We propose an architecture enabling the connection of embedded devices to the Semantic Web by expressing their knowledge in the Resource Description Framework (RDF). We introduce the Wiselib TupleStore, a modular embedded database tailored specifically for RDF storage. The Wiselib TupleStore is portable to various platforms, including Contiki and TinyOS, and offers trade-offs enabling scalability across a wide range of hardware scenarios. We discuss the applicability of RDF to heterogeneous resource-constrained devices and compare our system to existing embedded tuple stores, Antelope and TeenyLIME.

title: SPARQL for Networks of Embedded Systems
Abstract: The Semantic Web (or Web of Data) embodies the successful efforts towards linking and sharing data over the Web. The cornerstones of the Web of Data are RDF as the data format and SPARQL as the de facto standard query language. Recent trends indicate the evolution of the Web of Data towards the Web of Things, integrating embedded devices and smart objects. However, data originating from these devices lacks a common format, hindering integration and querying. To overcome this obstacle, we introduce our approach to elevate embedded systems to first-class citizens of the Web of Things. Our framework transcends individual deployments by representing them as unified data sources aligned with the principles of the Semantic Web. This includes the execution of arbitrary SPARQL queries over data from a pool of embedded devices and/or external data sources. Managing verbose RDF data and executing SPARQL queries within an embedded network presents significant challenges in minimizing processing and communication costs. To address this, we present an in-network query processor aimed at pushing processing steps onto devices. We demonstrate the practical application and potential benefits of our framework through a comprehensive evaluation using a real-world deployment and a range of SPARQL queries stemming from a common use case of the Web of Things.

title: Inflationary schism after Planck2013
Abstract: Classic inflation, as described in textbooks, rests on the premise that, starting from typical initial conditions and assuming a simple inflaton potential with minimal fine-tuning, inflation can generate exponentially vast volumes of space that are generically homogeneous, isotropic, and flat, with nearly scale-invariant spectra of density and gravitational wave fluctuations exhibiting adiabatic, Gaussian, and predictable properties. In a recent paper, we demonstrated that, in addition to conceptual problems recognized for decades, classic inflation is now contradicted by data, particularly the latest data from WMAP, ACT, and Planck2013. While Guth, Kaiser and Nomura, and Linde have published critiques of our paper, there is a shared consensus on the problematic state of classic inflation. Instead, they propose an alternative inflationary paradigm that revises the assumptions and goals of inflation, potentially extending to scientific methodology in general.

title: Zero-separating invariants for linear algebraic groups
Abstract: Let G be a linear algebraic group over a field k, and let V be a G-module. The nullcone of (G,V) is defined as the set of points v in V for which f(v)=0 holds for all positive degree homogeneous invariants f in k[V]^G. We introduce two numbers, δ(G,V) and σ(G,V), associated with a given representation: δ(G,V) denotes the smallest number d such that, for any point v in V^G outside the nullcone, there exists an invariant f of degree at most d for which f(v) is nonzero. σ(G,V) is defined similarly, replacing V^G with V. If k has positive characteristic, we show that δ(G,V) is infinite for all subgroups of GL_2(k) containing a unipotent subgroup, and that σ(G,V) is finite if and only if G is finite. In the case of characteristic zero for k, we demonstrate that δ(G,V)=1 for all linear algebraic groups, and that if σ(G,V) is finite, then the connected component of G is unipotent.

title: Split Sfermion Families, Yukawa Unification and Muon g-2
Abstract: We investigate two distinct classes of Yukawa unified supersymmetric SO(10) models with non-universal and universal soft supersymmetry breaking (SSB) gaugino masses at M_{\\rm GUT}. In both cases, we assume that the third family SSB sfermion masses at M_{\\rm GUT} are distinct from the corresponding sfermion masses of the first two families (which are equal). For the SO(10) model with essentially arbitrary (non-universal) gaugino masses at M_{\\rm GUT}, we demonstrate that t-b-τ Yukawa coupling unification is compatible with the 125 GeV Higgs boson mass, the WMAP relic dark matter density, and the resolution of the apparent muon g-2 anomaly. Notably, the colored particles in this scenario are quite heavy, exceeding 5 TeV, while the sleptons (smuon and stau) can be considerably lighter, around 200 GeV. In the SO(10) model with universal gaugino masses and NUHM2 boundary conditions, the muon g-2 anomaly cannot be resolved. However, the gluino in this class of models remains relatively light, \\lesssim 3 TeV, potentially observable at the LHC.

title: Empirical symptoms of catastrophic bifurcation transitions on financial markets: A phenomenological approach
Abstract: This work aims to empirically demonstrate the presence of catastrophic bifurcation breakdowns or transitions, preceded by flickering phenomena, in notoriously significant and unpredictable financial markets. We develop various metrics associated with catastrophic bifurcation transitions, particularly catastrophic slowing down (analogous to critical slowing down). These metrics are applied to a well-defined example of financial markets encompassing small, medium, and large capitalization. The catastrophic bifurcation transition appears to be connected to the question of whether early-warning signals exist in financial markets. This question continues to intrigue both the research community and the general public. Notably, early-warning signals have been recently identified and attributed to catastrophic bifurcation transition phenomena observed in multiple physical systems, such as ecosystems, climate dynamics, and medicine (epileptic seizures and asthma attacks). This work provides an analogical, positive identification of such phenomena by examining various indicators in the context of a well-defined daily bubble, induced by the recent global financial crisis in typical financial markets of small, medium, and large capitalization.

title: A Framework for the Implementation of Industrial Automation Systems Based on PLCs
Abstract: Industrial automation systems (IASs) are conventionally developed using a sequential approach where automation software, commonly based on the IEC 61131 languages, is developed after the design and often the implementation of mechanical parts. title: Block patterns in Stirling permutations

This result yields numerous applications, including Wilf equivalence of block patterns and a new interpretation of Bessel polynomials. We also demonstrate how our results can be applied to a specific class of labeled trees, which are in bijection with Stirling permutations. |||

title: Einstein's cosmological considerations

title: The nested simple conformal loop ensembles in the Riemann sphere

title: Affective and cognitive prefrontal cortex projections to the lateral habenula in humans
Abstract: The anterior insula (AI) and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC) are involved in processing information related to pain, loss, adversity, and negative choices or consequences that threaten survival or well-being. Pain and loss also activate the pregenual ACC (pgACC), associated with sadness, hurt, and regret. The lateral habenula (LHb) is stimulated by predicted and received pain, discomfort, and aversive outcomes. Chronic LHb stimulation leads to negative feelings and suppresses motivation for suboptimal choices, achieved through direct and indirect (via RMTg) inhibition of the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN) and ventral tegmental area/substantia nigra (VTA/SNc). The response selectivity of LHb neurons suggests cortical input from affective and cognitive regions that evaluate and anticipate negative outcomes. Based on these findings, I predicted direct corticohabenular projections from the dACC, pgACC, and AI, forming an adversity processing circuit that learns to avoid negative outcomes by suppressing dopamine and serotonin signals. Using diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), I identified projections from the dACC, pgACC, AI, adjacent caudolateral and lateral orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) to the LHb. I predicted no corticohabenular projections from reward processing regions, medial OFC (mOFC) and ventral ACC (vACC), as they are primarily activated by positive stimuli and outcomes, leading to serotonin and dopamine release, respectively. This lack of LHb projections was confirmed for vACC and likely for mOFC. Surprisingly, corticohabenular projections were observed from cognitive prefrontal cortex regions known for flexible reasoning, planning, and integrating relevant information for goal achievement. I propose that prefrontohabenular projections serve as a teaching signal for value-based decision-making, guiding the learning process to deselect, avoid, or inhibit potentially harmful, low-valued, or incorrect choices, goals, strategies, predictions, models, and actions to prevent negative consequences.

title: A Study Of Cyber Security Challenges And Its Emerging Trends On Latest Technologies

Governments and companies are implementing various measures to combat these cyber threats. Despite these efforts, cybersecurity remains a major concern for many. This paper focuses on the challenges faced by cybersecurity in the context of the latest technologies. It also examines emerging cybersecurity techniques, ethical considerations, and trends that are transforming the landscape of cybersecurity.

title: The Mitchell Spectrograph: Studying Nearby Galaxies with the VIRUS Prototype
Abstract: The Mitchell Spectrograph, also known as VIRUS-P, on the 2.7-meter Harlan J. Smith telescope at McDonald Observatory is currently the largest field-of-view (FOV) integral field unit (IFU) spectrograph globally, with a FOV of 1.7' x 1.7'. It was designed as a prototype for the highly replicable VIRUS spectrograph, which comprises a mosaic of IFUs spread over a 16' diameter FOV feeding 150 spectrographs similar to the Mitchell. VIRUS will be deployed on the 9.2-meter Hobby-Eberly Telescope (HET) and will be used for the HET Dark Energy Experiment (HETDEX). Since its first light in 2007, the Mitchell Spectrograph has been extensively used, among other applications, to study nearby galaxies in the local universe, allowing for detailed investigation of their internal structure and the spatial distribution of various physical parameters. These observations have provided valuable insights into numerous aspects of the physics behind galaxy formation and evolution, significantly enhancing the scientific impact of the 2.7-meter telescope. This review examines the contributions of the Mitchell Spectrograph to the study of nearby galaxies, encompassing investigations into the spatial distribution of dark matter, the properties of supermassive black holes, the process of star formation, and the chemical composition of stars and gas in the interstellar medium (ISM), providing critical information regarding the formation and evolution of these systems. The review highlights the effectiveness of wide-field integral field spectrographs on smaller and medium-sized telescopes as powerful and cost-effective tools for studying galaxy astrophysics. Finally, it briefly discusses the potential of HETDEX for conducting research on nearby galaxies, emphasizing its complementary and competitive nature with ongoing and future surveys such as SAMI and MANGA.

title: The Radio Continuum-Star Formation Rate Relation in WSRT SINGS Galaxies
Abstract: This study investigates the spatially resolved radio continuum-star formation rate (RC-SFR) relation using advanced star formation (SF) tracers in a sample of 17 THINGS galaxies. We utilize hybrid Σ_SFR maps (GALEX FUV plus Spitzer 24 µm), RC maps at 22/18 cm from the WSRT SINGS survey, and H-alpha maps to correct for thermal RC emission. We compare azimuthally averaged radial profiles of RC and FUV/MIR-based Σ_SFR maps and analyze pixel-by-pixel correlations at fixed linear scales of 1.2 and 0.7 kpc. The ratio of integrated SFRs from the RC emission to that of the FUV/MIR-based SF tracers is R_int = 0.78 ± 0.38, consistent with Condon's relation. We observe a strong correlation between the radial profiles of radio and FUV/MIR-based Σ_SFR across the entire disk extent. The ratio R of azimuthally averaged radio to FUV/MIR-based Σ_SFR aligns with the integrated ratio, exhibiting only small quasi-random fluctuations as a function of radius. Pixel-by-pixel plots reveal a tight correlation in log-log diagrams of radio to FUV/MIR-based Σ_SFR, with a typical standard deviation of a factor of two. Averaging across our sample, we find (Σ_SFR)_RC ~ (Σ_SFR)_hyb^(0.63±0.25), indicating that data points with high Σ_SFR are relatively radio-dim, while the opposite holds true for low Σ_SFR. This trend can be interpreted as a result of spectral aging of cosmic ray electrons (CRe), supported by the radio spectral index: data points dominated by young CRe are relatively radio-dim, while those dominated by old CRe are relatively radio-bright. From this perspective, B plays the role of the curve and F that of the disc-shaped cross-section of a conventional quantum waveguide. Our approach allows for waveguides with cross-sections F that deform along B and also the study of the Laplacian on the boundaries of such waveguides. title: Some Negative Remarks on Operational Approaches to Quantum Theory
Abstract: Over the past decade, a surge of "operational reconstructions" of quantum theory has emerged. This is highly significant as it sheds light on the numerous ways in which the quantum formalism can be broken down into primitives and, through meticulous effort, reassembled into a cohesive whole. The process resembles a brain-teaser puzzle with interlocking pieces. While undoubtedly valuable, particularly for understanding the intricate connections between various quantum information protocols, this approach seems to miss the mark for a comprehensive understanding of quantum theory. It leaves a lingering sense of incompleteness. The fundamental question of what intrinsic property of matter compels this formalism upon our information accounting remains unanswered. To paraphrase Einstein's words to Max Born, "The quantum reconstructions are certainly imposing. But an inner voice tells me that they are not yet the real thing. The reconstructions say a lot, but do not really bring us any closer to the secret of the `old one'." This talk aims to expand on these points and convey the fascination with the problem of symmetric informationally complete positive operator-valued measures (POVMs) over axiomatic reconstructions.

Consequently, a warm Jupiter observed alone in its system might have previously cleared away any interior planets. Even if an inner planet is terrestrial-sized, it can dampen the warm Jupiter's eccentricity before its eventual demise. Therefore, any inferences about the initial orbit of an observed warm Jupiter must consider the possibility of a greater initial eccentricity than estimated by assuming it has always been alone. Tidal evolution involving multiple planets also enhances the internal heating of the planets, readily exceeding stellar radiation for the inner planet and potentially influencing the internal structure of warm Jupiters. Secular theory provides valuable insights into tidal processes, offering a way to constrain eccentricities of transiting planets based on estimates of the tidal parameter Q.

title: Chasing diagrams in cryptography
Abstract: Cryptography is a theory of secret functions, while category theory is a general theory of functions. Cryptography has reached a stage where its structures often require several pages to define, and its formulas can span multiple pages. Category theory also involves complex definitions, but excels at taming intricate structures. Cryptography appears to require high-level methods, while category theory consistently seeks concrete applications. Why is there no categorical cryptography? One reason might be that modern cryptography's foundations are built upon probabilistic polynomial-time Turing machines, which category theory struggles to handle effectively. However, these foundational challenges might be the very reason why cryptographic constructions often resemble low-level machine programming. This paper presents preliminary explorations towards categorical cryptography, revealing that some fundamental security concepts can be readily characterized through the categorical technique of diagram chasing, first utilized in Lambek's influential "Lecture Notes on Rings and Modules".

title: Geospatial Analysis Requires a Different Way of Thinking: The Problem of Spatial Heterogeneity
Abstract: Geospatial analysis is largely dominated by Gaussian thinking, which assumes that entities in the world can be characterized by a well-defined mean, implying that things are relatively similar in size. However, this assumption is not always valid. Many phenomena in the world lack a well-defined mean, resulting in a greater abundance of smaller entities than larger ones. This paper argues that geospatial analysis requires a different approach—a Paretian way of thinking that underpins skewed distributions such as power laws, Pareto, and lognormal distributions. We review two properties of spatial dependence and spatial heterogeneity, highlighting that the current notion of spatial heterogeneity in spatial statistics is solely used to characterize local variance of spatial dependence. We advocate for a broader perspective on spatial heterogeneity, proposing it be formulated as a scaling law. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of Paretian thinking and the scaling law for better understanding geographic forms and processes, especially when dealing with vast amounts of social media data. In the spirit of Paretian thinking, geospatial analysis should aim to simulate geographic events and phenomena from the bottom up rather than relying on correlations as guided by Gaussian thinking.

title: Regularization by sup-inf convolutions on Riemannian manifolds: an extension of Lasry-Lions theorem to manifolds of bounded curvature
Abstract: This paper demonstrates how Lasry-Lions's result on regularizing functions defined on ℝⁿ or Hilbert spaces using sup-inf convolutions with squares of distances can be extended to (finite or infinite dimensional) Riemannian manifolds M with bounded sectional curvature. Specifically, we show that if the sectional curvature K of M satisfies -K₀ ≤ K ≤ K₀ on M for some K₀ > 0, and if the injectivity and convexity radii of M are strictly positive, then every bounded, uniformly continuous function f: M→ℝ can be uniformly approximated by globally C^(1,1) functions defined by (f_λ)^μ = sup_(z∈M) inf_(y∈M) {f(y) + (1/(2λ)) d(z,y)² - (1/(2μ))d(x,z)²} as λ, μ→0⁺, where 0 < μ < λ/2. Our definition of (global) C^(1,1) smoothness is intrinsic and natural, reducing to the usual definition in flat spaces. However, it's important to note that in the noncompact case, this definition differs from other notions of (rather local) C^(1,1) smoothness recently used, for instance, by A. Fathi and P. Bernard (based on charts). The significance of this regularization method lies not only in the degree of smoothness obtained but also in the fact that the correspondence f ↦ (f_λ)^μ is explicit and preserves many important geometrical properties of the given functions f, such as invariance under a set of isometries, infima, sets of minimizers, ordering, local or global Lipschitzness, and (only when additionally assuming that K ≤ 0) local or global convexity. title: Non-stationary Resource Allocation Policies for Delay-constrained Video Streaming: Application to Video over Internet-of-Things-enabled Networks
Abstract: Multi-user wireless video transmission applications face significant bandwidth requirements and stringent delay constraints. We propose a novel solution that addresses this problem without assuming detailed packet-level knowledge, which is unavailable during resource allocation. We translate the transmission delay deadlines of each sender's video packets into a monotonically decreasing weight distribution within the considered time horizon. Higher weights are assigned to slots with a higher probability of deadline-abiding delivery. Given the sets of weights for the senders' video streams, we introduce the low-complexity Delay-Aware Resource Allocation (DARA) approach to calculate the optimal slot allocation policy that maximizes deadline-abiding delivery for all senders. DARA's unique characteristic is its non-stationary slot allocation policy, which depends on previous slot allocations. We prove DARA's optimality for weight distributions that exhibit exponential decay over time. We further implement our framework for real-time video streaming in wireless personal area networks, which are gaining significant traction within the new Internet-of-Things (IoT) paradigm. For multiple surveillance videos encoded with H.264/AVC and streamed via the 6tisch framework (simulating the IoT-oriented IEEE 802.15.4e TSCH medium access control), our solution demonstrably ensures all video bitstreams are delivered with acceptable quality in a deadline-abiding manner.

Abstract: As a cornerstone of perturbative QCD theory, establishing a systematic and reliable method for setting the renormalization scale in high-energy processes is crucial. The conventional approach, which utilizes a typical momentum as the renormalization scale, introduces arbitrary ranges and systematic errors in pQCD predictions, leading to well-known renormalization scheme and scale ambiguities. The "Principle of Minimum Sensitivity" (PMS) has been proposed as a practical solution to this scale setting problem. PMS suggests determining an optimal scale for the pQCD approximant of an observable by requiring its slope with respect to scheme and scale changes to vanish. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive analysis of PMS properties using three quantities, $R_{e^+e^-}$, $R_\\tau$, and $\\Gamma(H\\rightarrow b\\bar{b})$, up to four-loop QCD corrections. We discuss the impact of PMS on the accuracy, convergence, and predictive power of pQCD predictions. Moreover, we compare PMS with the Principle of Maximum Conformality (PMC), another fundamental scale setting approach. Our findings demonstrate that PMS offers a practical means to set the effective scale for high-energy processes. Predictions based on PMS agree with PMC predictions when sufficient high-order QCD corrections are included, surpassing the accuracy of conventional scale setting predictions. However, PMS pQCD convergence is an accidental phenomenon, often failing to accurately predict unknown high-order contributions with only next-to-leading order QCD correction. Consequently, PMS predictions tend to deviate from "true" values obtained by incorporating higher-order contributions.

Initial Ru substitution (up to x ≈ 0.1) led to a significant increase in both the Curie temperature (T<sub>C</sub>) and spontaneous magnetization (M<sub>S</sub>), reaching maximum values of T<sub>C</sub> = 8.6 K and M<sub>S</sub> = 0.1 μ<sub>B</sub> per formula unit, respectively. However, superconductivity disappeared at x ≈ 0.03. Increasing the Ru content beyond x ≈ 0.1 resulted in a sharp decrease in both T<sub>C</sub> and M<sub>S</sub>, approaching a ferromagnetic quantum critical point (QCP) at x<sub>cr</sub> = 0.31. This resulted in a well-defined ferromagnetic dome in the T-x magnetic phase diagram. We analyzed the evolution of ferromagnetism with x based on band structure changes due to varying 5f-ligand hybridization, a scenario supported by electronic structure calculations and a simplified periodic Anderson model. Analyzing the temperature dependence of electrical resistivity and heat capacity at low temperatures near the QCP revealed non-Fermi liquid behavior, suggesting that the ferromagnetic quantum phase transition is likely continuous and of the Hertz-Millis type.

title: Structural properties and spin-phonon coupling in orthorhombic Y-substituted GdMnO$_{3}$
Abstract: A systematic study of the structure, lattice dynamics at room temperature, and phonon behavior at low temperatures in orthorhombic Gd<sub>1-x</sub>Y<sub>x</sub>MnO<sub>3</sub> manganites (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.4) was conducted using powder x-ray diffraction and Raman scattering. This research aimed to understand the correlation between structural and Raman mode parameters. Room temperature data revealed structural distortions arising from Jahn-Teller distortion and octahedra tilting. While the Jahn-Teller distortion appeared independent of x, an increase of approximately 0.5° was observed in the Mn-O1-Mn bond angle when x varied from 0 to 0.4. The Raman results evidenced spin-phonon coupling. Analyzing the temperature dependence of the B1g in-plane O2 stretching mode of the MnO6 octahedron revealed either a positive or negative shift relative to the pure anharmonic temperature dependence of the phonon frequency, strongly dependent on the Y concentration. This frequency renormalization was attributed to a competition between ferro and antiferromagnetic interactions. The ratio between the spin-phonon coupling constant and the effective magnetic exchange integral per spin was determined from the renormalized wave number of the in-plane O2 stretching mode, associated with the spin-spin correlation function.

title: Thermoelectric conductivities, shear viscosity, and stability in an anisotropic linear axion model
Abstract: This study investigates thermoelectric conductivities and shear viscosities in a holographically anisotropic model, which is dual to a spatially anisotropic  mathcal{N} = 4 super-Yang-Mills theory at finite chemical potential. Momentum relaxation is achieved by perturbing the linear axion field. The AC conductivity exhibits a coherent/incoherent metal transition. Deviations from the Wiedemann-Franz law are also observed in this model. The longitudinal shear viscosity for prolate anisotropy violates the bound conjectured by Kovtun-Son-Starinets. The study also finds that thermodynamic and dynamical instabilities are not always equivalent by examining the Gubser-Mitra conjecture.

title: The local-global principle for symmetric determinantal representations of smooth plane curves in characteristic two
Abstract: This paper applies Mumford's theory of canonical theta characteristics to a Diophantine problem in characteristic two. It proves that a smooth plane curve over a global field of characteristic two can be defined by the determinant of a symmetric matrix with entries in linear forms in three variables if and only if such a symmetric determinantal representation exists locally. This result is unique to characteristic two as analogous results do not hold in other characteristics.

title: Toolbox for reconstructing quantum theory from rules on information acquisition
Abstract: This paper presents an operational approach for reconstructing the quantum theory of qubit systems from elementary rules governing information acquisition. The focus is on an observer (O) interrogating a system (S) with binary questions. The system's state is considered as the observer's "catalogue of knowledge" about the system. The framework utilizes simple mathematical tools and attempts to clarify underlying assumptions. Four rules are imposed: (1) a limit on the information available to the observer; (2) the existence of complementary information; (3) preservation of the observer's total information between interrogations; and (4) continuous change of the observer's "catalogue of knowledge" in time between interrogations with all consistent evolutions being possible. This approach allows for a constructive derivation of quantum theory, explaining how the resulting independence, complementarity, and compatibility structure of the observer's questions matches that of projective measurements in quantum theory. It also explains how entanglement, monogamy of entanglement, non-locality, and the correlation structure of arbitrarily many qubits and rebits arise. The rules yield a reversible time evolution and a quadratic measure quantifying the observer's information about the system. Finally, it is shown that the four rules admit two solutions for the simplest case of a single elementary system: the Bloch ball and disc as state spaces for a qubit and rebit, respectively, along with their symmetries as time evolution groups. The reconstruction for arbitrarily many qubits is completed in a companion paper (arXiv:1511.01130) where an additional rule eliminates the rebit case. This approach is inspired by (but does not rely on) the relational interpretation and provides a novel formulation of quantum theory in terms of questions.

title: Drastic pressure effect on the extremely large magnetoresistance in WTe2: quantum oscillation study
Abstract: Quantum oscillations of the magnetoresistance in WTe<sub>2</sub> single crystals under ambient and high pressure were studied. Extremely large magnetoresistance was recently discovered in this material. Analysis of the Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations identified four Fermi surfaces, with two persisting to high pressure. The sizes of these two pockets were comparable but showed increasing difference with pressure. At 0.3 K and 14.5 T, the magnetoresistance decreased drastically from 1.25 × 10<sup>5</sup>% under ambient pressure to 7.47 × 10<sup>3</sup>% under 23.6 kbar, likely due to the relative change of Fermi surfaces. These findings support the hypothesis that the perfect balance between electron and hole populations is responsible for the extremely large magnetoresistance in WTe<sub>2</sub>.

title: Exciton binding energies and luminescence of phosphorene under pressure
Abstract: The optical response of phosphorene can be gradually modified by applying moderate uniaxial compression, as the material undergoes a transition into an indirect gap semiconductor and eventually into a semimetal. Strain not only tunes the gap between the valence band and conduction band local extrema, but also the effective masses, influencing the exciton anisotropy and binding strength. This theoretical study investigates the evolution of exciton stability and resulting luminescence energy under uniaxial strain. It finds that the exciton binding energy can be as high as 0.87 eV in vacuum for 5% transverse strain, ranking among the highest for 2D materials. The significant shift of the luminescence peak and its linear dependence on strain suggest its potential for directly probing the strain state of single layers.

title: Autonomous Hamiltonian flows, Hofer's geometry and persistence modules

This robustness is understood in terms of Hofer's metric. The approach utilizes the theory of persistence modules applied in the context of filtered Floer homology. Applications to geometry and dynamics of Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms are presented.

title: Suzaku Observation of Be/X-ray Binary Pulsar EXO 2030+375
Abstract: This paper investigates the timing and spectral properties of Be/X-ray binary pulsar EXO 2030+375 using a Suzaku observation on 2012 May 23 during a less intense Type I outburst. Pulsations were clearly detected in the X-ray light curves at a barycentric period of 41.2852 s, suggesting the pulsar is spinning up. The pulse profiles exhibited peculiar characteristics, differing from those observed in an earlier Suzaku observation on 2007 May 14. A single-peaked narrow profile in soft X-rays (0.5-10 keV range) transitioned to a double-peaked broad profile in the 12-55 keV energy range, reverting back to a smooth single-peaked profile in hard X-rays (55-70 keV range). The 1.0-100.0 keV broad-band spectrum of the pulsar was well described by three continuum models: (i) a partial covering high energy cut-off power-law model, (ii) a partially absorbed power-law with a high-energy exponential rolloff, and (iii) a partial covering Negative and Positive power law with EXponential (NPEX) continuum model. Unlike the earlier Suzaku observation where several low energy emission lines were detected, only a weak and narrow Iron K<sub>α</sub> emission line at 6.4 keV was present in the pulsar spectrum during the 2012 May outburst. The absence of any absorption-like feature in the 1-100 keV energy range supports the previous Suzaku observation's claim of no cyclotron resonance scattering feature in EXO 2030+375. Pulse-phase resolved spectroscopy revealed the presence of additional dense matter, explaining the absence of the second peak from the soft X-ray pulse profiles. This paper provides a detailed analysis of these results.

title: Pachner moves in a 4d Riemannian holomorphic Spin Foam model
Abstract: This work explores a Spin Foam model for 4d Riemannian gravity and proposes a new approach to imposing simplicity constraints using the recently developed holomorphic representation. By leveraging the power of holomorphic integration techniques and introducing two new tools: the homogeneity map and the loop identity, the paper provides the first analytic expressions for the behavior of Spin Foam amplitudes under 4-dimensional Pachner moves. This behavior is governed by the insertion of nonlocal mixing operators. In the case of the 5-1 move, the expression governing the change of the amplitude can be interpreted as a vertex renormalisation equation. The paper identifies a natural truncation scheme that achieves invariance up to an overall factor for the 4-2 and 5-1 moves but not for the 3-3 move. The study of divergences shows that a range of parameter space exists where the 4-2 move is finite while the 5-1 move diverges. This opens the possibility of recovering diffeomorphism invariance in the continuum limit of Spin Foam models for 4D Quantum Gravity.

title: Pattern Matching and Local Alignment for RNA Structures
Abstract: The primary structure of a ribonucleic acid (RNA) molecule can be represented as a sequence of nucleotides (bases) over the alphabet {A, C, G, U}. The secondary or tertiary structure of an RNA is a set of base pairs forming bonds between A-U and G-C. Traditionally, these bonds have been assumed to be one-to-one and non-crossing for secondary structures. This paper considers pattern matching and local alignment between two RNA structures. For pattern matching, it presents two algorithms: one for obtaining an exact match and the other for approximate match. Subsequently, an algorithm for RNA local structural alignment is presented.

title: The structure of solar radio noise storms
Abstract: The Nançay Radioheliograph (NRH) routinely produces snapshot images of the full Sun at frequencies between 150 and 450 MHz, with a typical resolution of 3 arcmin and a time cadence of 0.2 s. Combining visibilities from the NRH and the Giant Meterwave Radio Telescope (GMRT) allows the production of Sun images at 236 or 327 MHz, achieving a large field of view, high resolution, and time cadence. This study investigates the structure of noise storms, the most common non-thermal solar radio emission, focusing on the relation between position and altitude of noise storms and the observing frequency, as well as the lower limit of their sizes. Results for noise storms on four days are presented, revealing an extended halo and one or several compact cores with relative intensity changing over a few seconds. Core sizes can be almost stable over one hour, with a minimum in the range 31-35 arcsec (less than previously reported), and can remain stable over one hour. The heliocentric distances of noise storms are  ∼ 1.20 and 1.35 R<sub>☉</sub> at 432 and 150 MHz, respectively. This indicates that the regions where storms originate are much denser than the ambient corona and their vertical extent is smaller than expected from hydrostatic equilibrium. The smallest observed sizes impose upper limits on broadening effects due to scattering on density inhomogeneities in the low and medium corona and constrain the level of density turbulence in the solar corona. It is possible that scatter broadening has been overestimated in the past and that the observed sizes cannot solely be attributed to scattering. The vertical structure of the noise storms is difficult to reconcile with the classical columnar model.

title: An inequality for tensor product of positive operators and its applications
Abstract: This paper presents an inequality for the tensor product of positive operators on Hilbert spaces by considering the tensor product of operators as words on certain alphabets (i.e., a set of letters). Applications of the operator inequality and a multilinear approach are used to demonstrate some matrix inequalities concerning induced operators and generalized matrix functions, including determinants and permanents as special cases.

title: How to select the largest k elements from evolving data?
Abstract: This paper investigates the top-k-selection problem, which involves determining the largest, second largest, ..., and k-th largest elements in a dynamic data model. This model allows the order of elements to evolve dynamically over time. The algorithm can only probe data changes by comparing pairs of elements in each time step. Previous studies focused on two special cases: finding the largest element and the median; and sorting all elements. This paper systematically addresses k ∈ [n] and solves the problem almost completely. It identifies a critical point k* such that the top-k-selection problem can be solved error-free with probability 1-o(1) if and only if k = o(k*). A lower bound on the error for k = Ω(k*) is also determined, which is tight under certain conditions. Furthermore, the study shows that the top-k-set problem, which involves finding the largest k elements without sorting them, can be solved error-free for all k ∈ [n]. The paper extends the dynamic data model and demonstrates that most of these results remain valid.

title: The spatial, spectral and polarization properties of solar flare X-ray sources
Abstract: X-rays serve as a valuable diagnostic tool for studying high energy accelerated electrons. Bremsstrahlung X-rays, produced by and directly related to high energy electrons accelerated during a flare, provide a powerful diagnostic tool for determining both the properties of the accelerated electron distribution and the flaring coronal and chromospheric plasmas. This thesis focuses on the study of spatial, spectral, and polarization properties of solar flare X-ray sources through both modeling and X-ray observations using the Ramaty High Energy Solar Spectroscopic Imager (RHESSI). Firstly, a new model is presented, accounting for finite temperature, pitch angle scattering, and initial pitch angle injection. This model is developed to accurately infer the properties of the acceleration region from observations of dense coronal X-ray sources. Examining how the spatial properties of dense coronal X-ray sources change over time reveals interesting trends in length, width, position, number density, and thermal pressure. The potential causes for these changes are discussed. Further analysis of data combined with modeling X-ray transport in the photosphere allows changes in X-ray source positions and sizes due to the X-ray albedo effect to be deduced. Finally, this study demonstrates, for the first time, how the presence of a photospheric X-ray albedo component produces a spatially resolvable polarization pattern across a hard X-ray (HXR) source. It showcases how changes in the degree and direction of polarization across a single HXR source can be used to determine the anisotropy of the radiating electron distribution.

title: Characters of equivariant D-modules on Veronese cones
Abstract: For d > 1, consider the Veronese map of degree d on a complex vector space W, Ver<sub>d</sub>: W → Sym<sup>d</sup> W, w → w<sup>d</sup>, and denote its image by Z. This paper describes the characters of the simple GL(W)-equivariant holonomic D-modules supported on Z. In the case where d is 2, it presents a counterexample to a conjecture of Levasseur by exhibiting a GL(W)-equivariant D-module on the Capelli type representation Sym<sup>2</sup> W containing no SL(W)-invariant sections. The paper also studies the local cohomology modules H<sub>Z</sub><sup>j</sup>(S), where S is the ring of polynomial functions on the vector space Sym<sup>d</sup> W. It recovers a result of Ogus showing that only one local cohomology module is non-zero (namely in degree j = codim(Z)), and proves that this module is a simple D-module and determines its character.

title: Adapting Graph Application Performance via Alternate Data Structure Representation
Abstract: Graph processing is widely used in areas ranging from social networking mining to web indexing. This paper demonstrates that the performance and dependability of these applications critically depend on the graph data structure used. A fixed, compile-time choice of data structure can lead to poor performance or applications unable to complete. To address this problem, the paper introduces an approach that enables programmers to transform regular, off-the-shelf graph applications into adaptive, more dependable applications where adaptations are performed via runtime selection from alternate data structure representations. Using this approach, applications dynamically adapt to the input graph's characteristics and changes in available memory, allowing them to continue running under adverse conditions, such as low memory. Experiments with graph algorithms on real-world (e.g., Wikipedia metadata, Gnutella topology) and synthetic graph datasets show that adaptive applications complete with lower execution time and/or memory utilization compared to their non-adaptive versions.

title: Efficient simulation for light scattering from plasmonic core-shell nanospheres on a substrate for biosensing
Abstract: This paper presents an efficient numerical method for investigating light scattering from plasmonic nanospheres on a substrate covered by a shell, based on the half-space Green's function approach. This method is applied to study optical scattering from DNA molecules attached to metallic nanoparticles on a substrate and compared with experimental results. The study achieves fairly good agreement between theoretical predictions and measured ellipsometric spectra. Metallic nanoparticles were used to detect DNA molecule binding in a microfluidic setup via spectroscopic ellipsometry (SE), and a detectable change in ellipsometric spectra was observed upon DNA molecule capture on the Au nanoparticle surface. Theoretical simulations indicate that the coverage of Au nanospheres by a submonolayer of DNA molecules, modeled as a thin layer of dielectric material, can indeed lead to a small but detectable change in ellipsometric spectra. This study highlights the ultra-sensitive capability of SE for sensing submonolayer coverage of DNA molecules on Au nanospheres.

title: Hercules X-1 - another 'first': long-term decay of the cyclotron line energy
Abstract: Her X-1 is one of the most remarkable binary X-ray pulsars. It exhibits numerous observable features and has consistently been at the forefront of fundamental discoveries. It was the first to showcase a super-orbital modulation, the first to reveal a cyclotron line in its spectrum, and the first to demonstrate systematic variations of the cyclotron line energy, specifically variations with pulse phase (by ~25%) and a positive correlation with X-ray luminosity (~5% increase for a factor of two increase in luminosity). Now, a new "first" has been discovered: a long-term decrease of the pulse phase-averaged cyclotron line energy E<sub>cyc</sub> by ~5 keV over 20 years. The cyclotron line energy was initially measured at ~35 keV in 1976, reconfirmed around a similar energy by various instruments until 1990. Between 1990 and 1994, a jump upwards beyond 41 keV occurred, and the energy is now back at ~37 keV. Regarding the physical cause of this observed effect, the authors suggest it is connected to a geometric displacement of the cyclotron resonant scattering region in the polar magnetic field or a true physical change in the field configuration at the accretion mound or column due to continued accretion. The variation with time might be attributed to an imperfect equilibrium between the rate of material accretion and the rate of material loss at the base of the accretion mound, leading to variations in the configuration of the accretion mound (height, total mass, field distribution). The authors believe that they are observing the signature of a local change in the field configuration, rather than a decay of the global magnetic field, as the observed timescale of a few decades is very short.

title: Observation of a crossover in kinetic aggregation of Palladium colloids
Abstract: The growth of palladium colloids over the surface of thin films of WO<sub>3</sub>/glass was investigated using field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM). The films were prepared by pulsed laser deposition (PLD) at various temperatures. A PdCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) droplet was injected onto the surface, and in the presence of steam hydrogen, the droplet was dried through a reduction reaction process. Two distinct aggregation regimes of palladium colloids were observed over the substrates. The authors argue that the change in aggregation dynamics emerges when the measured water drop contact angle (CA) for the WO<sub>3</sub>/glass thin films exceeds a certain threshold value, namely CA = 46 degrees, where a crossover in kinetic aggregation of palladium colloids occurs. This suggests that the mass fractal dimension of palladium aggregates follows a power-law behavior. The fractal dimension (Df) in the fast aggregation regime, where the measured CA values range from 27 to 46 degrees, depending on the substrate deposition temperature, is Df = 1.75 (0.02). This Df value is consistent with kinetic aggregation observed in other colloidal systems in the fast aggregation regime. However, in the slow aggregation regime, with CA = 58 degrees, the fractal dimension changes abruptly to Df = 1.92 (0.03). A modified Box-Counting method was also used to calculate the fractal dimension of gray-level images, confirming the crossover at around CA = 46 degrees. |||

title: Spatial Variation of the Correlated Color Temperature of Lightning Channel
Abstract: We propose a novel approach to analyzing lightning based on color analysis. This method utilizes digital still images containing cloud-to-ground (CG) and intracloud (IC) lightning flashes. Applying digital image processing techniques, we extract lightning channels. Subsequently, we map the digital pixels of these channels to the CIE 1931 xy-chromaticity diagram to obtain their correlated color temperature (CCT). Our findings indicate that the CCT of lightning channels varies spatially. Additionally, our analysis suggests that the energy of lightning channels changes spatially.
