title: Perfect linkage of Cohen--Macaulay modules over Cohen--Macaulay rings
Abstract: This paper introduces and explores the concept of perfect linkage for Cohen-Macaulay modules over Cohen-Macaulay local rings. Perfect linkage is a special type of linkage defined by perfect modules. We investigate its connections to syzygies, maximal Cohen-Macaulay approximations, and Yoshino-Isogawa linkage. We recover a theorem of Yoshino and Isogawa and analyze the structure of double perfect linkage. Furthermore, we establish a criterion for determining when two Cohen-Macaulay modules of codimension one are perfectly linked and apply it to classical linkage theory for ideals. We also construct various examples of linkage for both modules and ideals.

title: Linking $U(2)\times U(2)$ to $O(4)$ model via decoupling
Abstract: The chiral phase transition of massless two-flavor Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) is influenced by the fate of the flavor singlet axial symmetry $U_A(1)$ at the critical temperature ($T_c$). Assuming a finite $U_A(1)$ breaking persists at $T_c$, we propose a three-dimensional effective theory comprising four massless and four massive scalar fields. We investigate the renormalization group flow of this effective theory in the $\epsilon$-expansion using a mass-dependent renormalization scheme and identify the region of the attractive basin that flows into the $O(4)$ fixed point. We focus on the dependence of this basin on the size of the $U_A(1)$ breaking. Our results are discussed from the perspective of massive field decoupling. Although the effective theory eventually reaches the $O(4)$ fixed point within the attractive basin, the approaching rate, a universal exponent, differs from the standard $O(4)$ model. We explain this peculiarity and propose a novel possibility for chiral phase transition in two-flavor QCD.

title: Fermiology of 122 family of Fe-based superconductors: An ab initio study
Abstract: First principles simulations are used to investigate the fermiology of various 122 systems. Electron doping results in the expansion of electron Fermi pockets and the shrinkage of hole Fermi pockets. Isovalent Ru substitution (up to 35%) does not significantly affect the electron and hole Fermi surfaces (FSs), providing no insight into the nature of charge carrier doping. However, in the case of 32% P doping, there are substantial changes in the hole FSs. Our calculations suggest that the two-dimensionality of FSs may favor electron pair scattering between quasi-nested FSs, which could be relevant to various ordering phenomena (magnetic, orbital, superconducting) observed in Fe-based superconductors.

title: An Effective Approach for Mobile ad hoc Network via I-Watchdog Protocol
Abstract: Mobile Ad Hoc Networks (MANETs) have gained popularity due to their fixed infrastructure-less nature and dynamic characteristics. These networks consist of a large number of nodes that communicate wirelessly with each other. MANETs are a wireless technology with high node mobility and are independent of centralized authority for administration. Nodes in a MANET communicate via radio waves and have limited resources and computational power. The network topology changes frequently due to its distributed nature and self-configurability. Due to the wireless nature and lack of centralized authority, MANETs are vulnerable to security and performance issues. Security significantly impacts network performance, and some prominent security issues include black hole attacks, flooding, and wormhole attacks. This paper investigates performance issues related to the Watchdog protocol used in MANETs and proposes an improved mechanism called I-Watchdog that addresses the limitations of the Watchdog protocol. I-Watchdog enhances network performance in terms of throughput and delay.

title: Reformulations of the Yang-Mills theory toward quark confinement and mass gap
Abstract: We propose reformulations of the $SU(N)$ Yang-Mills theory that aim to address quark confinement and the mass gap. We introduce a new framework using new field variables to reformulate the $SU(N)$ Yang-Mills theory. This framework encompasses previous work by Cho, Faddeev, and Niemi as a special case referred to as the maximal option in our reformulations. Our reformulations offer the advantage of transforming the original non-Abelian gauge field variables into new field variables. Notably, one of these new variables, called the restricted field, dominates quark confinement in a gauge-independent manner. We can combine our reformulations with the $SU(N)$ extension of the Diakonov-Petrov version of the non-Abelian Stokes theorem for the Wilson loop operator to provide a gauge-invariant definition for the magnetic monopole in the $SU(N)$ Yang-Mills theory without the need for a scalar field. In the minimal option, the restricted field is non-Abelian and involves a non-Abelian magnetic monopole with the stability group $U(N-1)$. This suggests a non-Abelian dual superconductivity picture for quark confinement. This should be compared with the maximal option: the restricted field is Abelian and involves only Abelian magnetic monopoles with the stability group $U(1)^{N-1}$, similar to Abelian projection. We provide applications of this reformulation, including stability for the homogeneous chromomagnetic condensation of the Savvidy type, the large N treatment for deriving dimensional transmutation and understanding the mass gap, and numerical simulations on a lattice discussed by Dr. Shibata in a subsequent talk.

title: First detections of FS Canis Majoris stars in clusters. Evolutionary state as constrained by coeval massive stars
Abstract: FS CMa stars are low-luminosity objects exhibiting the B[e] phenomenon, with their evolutionary state remaining enigmatic. These stars are surrounded by compact disks of warm dust of unknown origin. Membership of FS CMa stars in coeval populations has not been confirmed until now. The discovery of low-luminosity line emitters in the young massive clusters Mercer 20 and Mercer 70 motivates us to investigate the nature of these objects. Our aim is to confirm their membership in coeval populations to characterize these emission-line stars through cluster properties. Using ISAAC/VLT medium-resolution spectroscopy and NICMOS/HST photometry of massive cluster members, we perform new characterizations of Mercer 20 and Mercer 70. We investigate the coevality of each cluster and the membership of the newly discovered B[e] objects using our observations and literature data of the surroundings. We also study the infrared excess and narrow-band photometric properties of the B[e] stars. We confirm and classify 22 new cluster members, including Wolf-Rayet stars and blue hypergiants. The spectral types (O9-B1.5 V) and radial velocities of B[e] objects are consistent with the remaining cluster members. Emission features of Mg II, Fe II], and [Fe II] are identified in their spectra. These stars have ages of 4.5 and 6 Myr and show mild infrared excesses. We confirm the presence of FS CMa stars in the coeval populations of Mercer 20 and Mercer 70. We discuss the nature and evolutionary state of FS CMa stars, discarding a post-AGB nature and proposing a new hypothesis involving mergers. We also propose and test a new search method for FS CMa candidates in young massive clusters based on narrow-band Paschen-alpha photometry. This method yielded three new candidates in photometric data from other clusters.

title: Context-Aware Analytics in MOM Applications
Abstract: Manufacturing Operations Management (MOM) systems are complex as they integrate data from heterogeneous systems within the automation pyramid. The need for context-aware analytics arises from the dynamic nature of these systems, which influences data generation and hampers the comparability of analytics, especially predictive models (e.g., predictive maintenance). Concept drift affects the future application of these models. Recent research has focused on data integration using semantic context models. Manual construction of these models is an elaborate and error-prone task. Therefore, we address the challenge of applying combinations of knowledge extraction techniques in the domain of analytics in MOM, which encompasses data integration within Product Life-cycle Management (PLM), Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP), and Manufacturing Execution Systems (MES). We discuss the motivations, technological challenges, and benefits of context-aware analytics, which leverage and consider the interconnectedness of semantic context data. Our example scenario demonstrates the need for distribution and effective change tracking of context information.

title: Adding Context to Knowledge and Action Bases
Abstract: Knowledge and Action Bases (KABs) have been proposed as a formal framework for capturing the dynamics of systems that manipulate Description Logic (DL) Knowledge Bases (KBs) through action execution. In this work, we enhance the KAB setting by incorporating contextual information through different context dimensions. On one hand, context is determined by the environment using context-changing actions that utilize the current state of the KB and the current context. On the other hand, context influences the set of TBox assertions relevant at each time point and must be considered when processing queries posed over the KAB. We extend the results on verifying rich temporal properties expressed in mu-calculus, which were established for standard KABs, to our enriched setting. Specifically, we demonstrate that verification remains decidable under a run-boundedness condition.

title: Reasoning for Improved Sensor Data Interpretation in a Smart Home
Abstract: This paper proposes an ontological representation and reasoning paradigm for interpreting time-series signals from sensors observing a smart environment. The interpretation process is primarily carried out by an incremental ASP solver. This solver receives as input a logic program generated from the contents of the ontology. The contextual information and high-level domain knowledge provided in the ontology are utilized to infer explanations (answer sets) for changes in the ambient air detected by the gas sensors.

title: Potts models with magnetic field: arithmetic, geometry, and computation
Abstract: We provide a sheaf-theoretic interpretation of Potts models with external magnetic fields using constructible sheaves and their Euler characteristics. We demonstrate that the polynomial countability question for hypersurfaces defined by the vanishing of the partition function is affected by changes in the magnetic field. Elementary examples show non-polynomially countable cases that become polynomially countable after perturbing the magnetic field. The same recursive formula for the Grothendieck classes under edge-doubling operations holds as in the case without a magnetic field, but the closed formulae for specific examples like banana graphs differ in the presence of a magnetic field. We provide examples of computing the Euler characteristic with compact support for the set of real zeros and find a similar exponential growth with the size of the graph. This can be interpreted as a measure of topological and algorithmic complexity. We also consider the computational complexity question for evaluating the polynomial and demonstrate both tractable and NP-hard examples using dynamic programming.

title: Interfacial Fermi Loops from Interfacial Symmetries

We numerically demonstrate this using the Fu-Kane-Mele tight-binding model. We show that the Fermi loop originates from a sign change in the Pfaffian of a product between the Hamiltonian and a constant matrix.

title: Complex and Quaternionic hyperbolic Kleinian groups with real trace fields

title: Scaling of the dynamics of a homogeneous one-dimensional anisotropic classical Heisenberg model with long-range interactions

For the latter, different values for $\delta$ were reported for a few models. Recently, Rocha Filho and collaborators [Phys. Rev. E {\bf 90}, 032133 (2014)] showed that $\delta=2$ for the Hamiltonian mean-field model, provided that $N$ is sufficiently large, while small $N$ effects lead to $\delta\approx1.7$. More recently, Gupta and Mukamel [J. Stat. Mech. P03015 (2011)] introduced a classical spin model with an anisotropic interaction with a scaling in the dynamics proportional to $N^{1.7}$ for a homogeneous state. We demonstrate that this model reduces to a one-dimensional Hamiltonian system and that the scaling of the dynamics approaches $N^2$ with increasing $N$. title: Removal and Stability for Erdős-Ko-Rado
Abstract: A $k$-uniform family of subsets of $[n]$ is intersecting if it does not contain a disjoint pair of sets. The study of intersecting families is central to extremal set theory, dating back to the seminal Erdős-Ko-Rado theorem of 1961 that bounds the size of the largest such families. A recent trend has been to investigate the structure of set families with few disjoint pairs. Friedgut and Regev proved a general removal lemma, showing that when $\gamma n \le k \le (\tfrac12 - \gamma)n$, a set family with few disjoint pairs can be made intersecting by removing few sets. We provide a simple proof of a removal lemma for large families, showing that families of size close to $\ell \binom{n-1}{k-1}$ with relatively few disjoint pairs must be close to a union of $\ell$ stars. Our lemma holds for a wide range of uniformities; in particular, when $\ell = 1$, the result holds for all $2 \le k < \frac{n}{2}$ and provides sharp quantitative estimates. We use this removal lemma to settle a question of Bollobás, Narayanan, and Raigorodskii regarding the independence number of random subgraphs of the Kneser graph $K(n,k)$. The Erdős-Ko-Rado theorem shows $\alpha(K(n,k)) = \binom{n-1}{k-1}$. For some constant $c > 0$ and $k \le cn$, we determine the sharp threshold for when this equality holds for random subgraphs of $K(n,k)$ and provide strong bounds on the critical probability for $k \le \tfrac12 (n-3)$.

title: Weak convergence of the Wojcik model

title: Valley-polarized quantum anomalous Hall phase and disorder induced valley-filtered chiral edge channels

However, we discover that within an extended range of moderate scattering strength, transport through the system remains quantized and fully valley-polarized. This indicates that the system effectively behaves like a quantum anomalous Hall system with valley-filtered chiral edge channels. title: Timelines for mitigating methane emissions from energy technologies

title: Experimental Proof of Nonlocal Wavefunction Collapse for a Single Particle Using Homodyne Measurement
Abstract: A single quantum particle is described by a wavefunction that can extend over arbitrarily large distances, yet it is never detected in two (or more) locations simultaneously. We experimentally demonstrate this single-particle spooky action, for the first time without an efficiency loophole, by splitting a single photon between two laboratories and testing whether the measurement choice in one lab truly causes a change in the local quantum state in the other lab. To this end, we employ homodyne measurements with six different measurement settings and quantitatively verify Einstein's spooky action by violating an Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen-steering inequality by $0.042 \\pm 0.006$. Our experiment also confirms the entanglement of the split single photon even when one side is untrusted.

title: Optimal census by quorum sensing
Abstract: Quorum sensing is the regulation of gene expression in response to changes in cell density. These monitor proteins typically regulate both their own production and the production of autoinducers, establishing internal and external feedback loops. Employing variational methods, we demonstrate that feedback mechanisms can increase information transmission, enabling bacteria to resolve up to two additional ranges of cell density compared to bistable quorum-sensing systems. title: Constraints on changes in the proton-electron mass ratio using methanol lines

title: Advantages and challenges in coupling an ideal gas to atomistic models in adaptive resolution simulations

As particles transition between regions, their resolution changes dynamically. One of the primary advantages of such approaches is the computational efficiency gained in the coarse-grained region. Ideally, the ideal gas would be the most suitable coarse-grained system for the low-resolution region, eliminating the need for intermolecular force calculations in this subdomain. However, achieving smooth coupling in this case poses a challenge due to the significant energetic imbalance between typical liquids and a system of non-interacting particles. In this work, we investigate this approach using water, the most biologically relevant fluid, as a test case. We demonstrate that successful coupling of water to the ideal gas can be achieved using current adaptive resolution methods, and discuss the remaining challenges that need to be addressed.

title: Striving for Simplicity: The All Convolutional Net
Abstract: Most contemporary convolutional neural networks (CNNs) used for object recognition share a common design principle: alternating convolution and max-pooling layers followed by a small number of fully connected layers. This paper re-evaluates the state of the art for object recognition from small images using CNNs, questioning the necessity of different components in the pipeline. We find that max-pooling can be effectively replaced by a convolutional layer with increased stride without compromising accuracy on several image recognition benchmarks. Building upon this finding and drawing inspiration from recent research on simple network structures, we propose a novel architecture that solely consists of convolutional layers and delivers competitive or state-of-the-art performance on various object recognition datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet). To analyze the network, we introduce a new variant of the "deconvolution approach" for visualizing features learned by CNNs, which can be applied to a broader range of network structures than existing approaches.

title: KMS weights on graph C*-algebras II Factor types and ground states
Abstract: We characterize the types of extremal KMS weights for generalized gauge actions on graph algebras and identify the ground states for the action restricted to a vertex-defined corner. Our analysis covers cases with varying graph and action assumptions, including the gauge action on strongly connected graphs with countably many exits, which were previously investigated.

title: Risk measuring under liquidity risk
Abstract: This research introduces a general framework for quantifying liquidity risk. Our framework defines a class of risk measures that incorporate liquidity risk into traditional risk measures. We focus on a one-period risk measurement model, where liquidity risk is defined as the difficulty of selling or buying a security or portfolio without significant price fluctuations. We propose new risk measures that differ from conventional ones, particularly in their increasing monotonicity, convexity, and cash sub-additivity for long positions. Conversely, for short positions, these properties may not hold in certain situations. We provide dual representations for these new measures in the case of long positions, and in some specific cases, for short positions as well. We apply our framework to scenarios where financial institutions split large trades into smaller ones, and obtain dual representation results. The research provides practical examples of risk measures, deriving corresponding capital requirements, and analyzes the Value at Risk (VaR) measure as a specific example.

title: A Relativistic Dynamical Collapse Model
Abstract: This study proposes a model where all operators are constructed from a quantum scalar field with a continuous energy spectrum encompassing all real values. The Schrödinger picture wave function depends on space and time coordinates for each particle, as well as an increasing evolution parameter 's' indexing a foliation of space-like hypersurfaces. The model is explicitly Lorentz invariant in the interaction picture. We explore free particle states and interactions within this framework. We then apply the Continuous Spontaneous Localization (CSL) theory of dynamical collapse, using the particle number space-time density as the collapse-generating operator. Unlike previous relativistic models, the vacuum state remains unexcited. The collapse dynamics depends on two parameters: 'Lambda', representing the collapse rate per unit volume, and 'ell', a scaling factor. We analyze a common example of collapse dynamics involving a superposition of two locations for a clump of matter. The collapse rate is shown to be identical to that of non-relativistic CSL when 'ell' is set to the GRW-CSL value of 10^-5 cm, along with 'Lambda' equal to 'lambda' divided by 'a' cubed (GRW-CSL choice of 'lambda' is 10^-16 s^-1). However, this choice leads to an unacceptably large change in nucleon mass over the age of the universe. We then consider the scenario where 'ell' equals the size of the universe. The collapse behavior proves satisfactory, and the change in nucleon mass over the universe's lifespan is acceptably small when 'Lambda' is set to 'lambda' divided by 'ell' times 'a' squared.

title: A brief introduction to giant magnetoresistance
Abstract: Giant magnetoresistance (GMR) is a quantum mechanical effect observed in thin film structures comprising alternating ferromagnetic and nonmagnetic layers. It manifests as a significant decrease in electrical resistance (typically 10-80%) in the presence of a magnetic field. This effect finds commercial applications in hard disk drives. The discovery of GMR earned Albert Fert and Peter Grünberg the 2007 Nobel Prize in Physics.

title: Symmetry reduction of turbulent pipe flows
Abstract: This paper proposes and applies a Fourier-based symmetry reduction scheme to eliminate or quotient the streamwise translation symmetry of Laser-Induced-Fluorescence measurements of turbulent pipe flows, which are viewed as dynamical systems in a high-dimensional state space. The relation between Taylor's hypothesis and the comoving frame velocity U_d of the turbulent orbit in state space is also explained. Specifically, in physical space, we observe flow structures that deform as they advect downstream at a speed that differs significantly from U_d. The symmetry reduction analysis of planar dye concentration fields at a Reynolds number of 3200 reveals that the speed 'u' at which high concentration peaks advect is approximately 1.43 times U_d. In a physically meaningful symmetry-reduced frame, the excess speed 'u' minus U_d (approximately 0.43 U_d) can be explained in terms of the geometric phase velocity U_g associated with the orbit in state space. This 'self-propulsion velocity' U_g is induced by the shape-changing dynamics of passive scalar structures observed in the symmetry-reduced frame, analogous to the movement of a swimmer at low Reynolds numbers.

title: Electronic states of zigzag graphene nanoribbons with edges reconstructed with topological defects
Abstract: We investigate the energy spectrum and electronic density of states (DOS) of zigzag graphene nanoribbons with edges reconstructed using topological defects, employing the tight-binding method. In the case of the Stone-Wales zz (57) edge, the low-energy spectrum shows significant changes compared to pristine zz edges. We find that the electronic DOS at the Fermi level is non-zero for all graphene nanoribbon widths. Conversely, for ribbons with heptagons only on one side and pentagons on the other, the energy gap at the Fermi level remains open, and the DOS is zero. This behavior arises from the influence of uncompensated topological charges on the localized edge states, which are topological in nature. This effect resembles that observed with structured external electric potentials along the edges.

title: SVEN: Informative Visual Representation of Complex Dynamic Structure
Abstract: Graphs often change over time, and visual techniques like small multiples or animation are typically used to represent this dynamism. However, these classical methods have significant drawbacks. Therefore, we propose a new approach called Storyline Visualization of Events on a Network (SVEN). SVEN builds upon storyline techniques, visualizing nodes as continuous lines over time. Time is encoded naturally along the horizontal axis, and the vertical placement of storylines is optimized to minimize clutter (line crossings, straightness, and bends) in the drawing. This paper demonstrates SVEN using real-world dynamic data and outlines future research directions.

title: Suppressing Alignment: Joint PAPR and Out-of-Band Power Leakage Reduction for OFDM-Based Systems
Abstract: Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) inherently suffers from two major drawbacks: high out-of-band (OOB) power leakage and high peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR). This paper presents a novel approach called suppressing alignment for jointly reducing OOB power leakage and PAPR. Our approach leverages the temporal degrees of freedom provided by the cyclic prefix (CP), a necessary redundancy in OFDM systems, to generate a suppressing signal. When added to the OFDM symbol, this signal significantly reduces both OOB power leakage and PAPR. To prevent interference with the information data carried by the OFDM symbol, our approach utilizes the wireless channel to perfectly align the suppressing signal with the CP duration at the OFDM receiver. This essentially maintains a bit error rate (BER) performance similar to legacy OFDM without requiring any changes in the receiver structure.

title: Model selection for the segmentation of multiparameter exponential family distributions
Abstract: We examine the segmentation problem for univariate distributions belonging to the exponential family with multiple parameters. In segmentation, determining the optimal number of segments remains a challenging task due to the discrete nature of change-points. We propose a penalized log-likelihood estimator within this general exponential family distribution framework, where the penalty is inspired by the work of Birgé and Massart. The resulting estimator is proven to satisfy an oracle inequality. We then focus on the specific case of categorical variables by comparing the values of key constants derived from our general approach with those obtained by directly working with the distribution's characteristics. A simulation study evaluates the performance of our criterion for the exponential distribution, and an application on real data modelled by the categorical distribution is provided.

title: Background to Higgs-boson searches from internal conversions of off-shell photons associated with $Z/γ^*$-boson production at the LHC
Abstract: This paper investigates the background contribution to the H -> 4l searches arising from off-shell (virtual) photon emissions and their conversions into lepton pairs accompanying the production of Z/gamma*-bosons at the LHC. This study extends the analysis of irreducible background presented in the ATLAS and CMS Higgs papers by incorporating off-shell photon emissions from parton showers. Including these effects does not significantly change the Higgs-searches background level when the transverse momentum of each final-state lepton is restricted to the range of p_T, l > 7 GeV. However, in the kinematic region extending towards lower lepton transverse momenta, the parton-shower contribution becomes significant. We propose a measurement method to precisely determine the parton-shower effects.

title: On isometry and isometric embeddability between ultrametric Polish spaces
Abstract: We analyze the complexity, with respect to Borel reducibility, of the relations of isometry and isometric embeddability between ultrametric Polish spaces where a set 'D' of possible distances is fixed beforehand. These relations constitute an analytic equivalence relation and an analytic quasi-order, respectively. We demonstrate that their complexity depends solely on the order type of 'D'. When 'D' contains a decreasing sequence, isometry is Borel bireducible with countable graph isomorphism, and isometric embeddability exhibits maximal complexity among analytic quasi-orders. The situation is more complex if 'D' is well-ordered: for isometry, we observe an increasing sequence of Borel equivalence relations of length omega_1, which are cofinal among Borel equivalence relations classifiable by countable structures. For isometric embeddability, we have an increasing sequence of analytic quasi-orders of length at least omega + 3. These results are applied to resolve open problems in the literature. For instance, we answer a long-standing question posed by Gao and Kechris by proving that the relation of isometry on locally compact ultrametric Polish spaces is Borel bireducible with countable graph isomorphism.

title: Self-Fourier transform and self-Fourier beams due to parabolic potential
Abstract: We investigate the propagation of light beams, including Hermite-Gauss, Bessel-Gauss, and finite energy Airy beams, in a linear medium with a parabolic potential. As expected, the beams oscillate during propagation. However, surprisingly, they also undergo automatic Fourier transform—periodic change from the beam to its Fourier transform and back. The oscillating period for parity-asymmetric beams is twice that of parity-symmetric beams. In addition to oscillation, finite-energy Airy beams exhibit periodic inversion during propagation. Based on propagation in parabolic potential, we introduce a class of optically-interesting beams that are self-Fourier beams—beams whose Fourier transforms are identical to the beams themselves.

title: Coherent view of crystal chemistry and ab initio analyses of Pb(II) and Bi(III) Lone Pair in square planar coordination
Abstract: The stereochemistry of the 6s^2 (E) lone pair of divalent Pb and trivalent Bi (PbII and BiIII, denoted by M*) in structurally related PbO, PbFX (X= Cl, Br, I), BiOX (X= F, Cl, Br, I), and Bi2NbO5F is rationalized. The presence of the lone pair LP is determined by its sphere of influence 'E', which is equal to that of oxygen or fluorine anions. The center of 'E' then defines the M*-E directions and distances. A detailed description of the structural features of both elements in the title compounds, characterized by [PbEO]n and [BiEO]n layers, reveals the evolution of M*-E distance with changes in the square pyramidal SP coordination polyhedra. All these polyhedra are distinct: in red PbO, we find {PbEO4E4} square antiprism, a {[Bi.E]O4X4Xapical} monocapped square antiprism in PbFX and BiOX, and {BiEO4F4} square antiprism in Bi2NbO5F. To analyze the crystal chemistry results, the electronic structures of these compounds are calculated using density functional theory (DFT). Real-space analyses of electron localization illustrate a full volume development of the lone pair on PbII within {PbEO4E4} in PbOE, {PbEF4X4} in PbFXE, and Bi(III) within {BiEO4X4} square antiprisms, in contrast to Bi(III) within {[Bi.E]O4F4Fapical} monocapped square antiprism. Larger hardness (larger bulk modulus B0) and band gap characterize BiOF compared to PbO due to the presence of F, which introduces antibonding Bi-F interactions, in contrast to mainly bonding Bi-O. In the PbFX and BiOX series, there is a systematic decrease in B0 with increasing volume, following the nature and size of X, which is decreasingly electronegative and increasingly large. The electronic densities of states reflect these effects through the relative energy positions and electronegativities of F/X and O/X, leading to a decrease in the band gap.

title: Automatic Discovery and Optimization of Parts for Image Classification
Abstract: Part-based representations have proven highly beneficial for image classification. Learning part-based models is often approached as a two-stage problem. First, a collection of informative parts is discovered using heuristics that promote part distinctiveness and diversity. Then, classifiers are trained on the vector of part responses. This paper unifies these two stages, learning image classifiers and a shared set of parts jointly. An initial pool of parts is generated by randomly sampling part candidates and selecting a good subset using L1/L2 regularization. All steps are driven directly by the same objective: the classification loss on a training set. This eliminates the need for engineered heuristics. We introduce the concept of "negative parts," defined as parts negatively correlated with one or more classes. Negative parts complement the parts discovered by other methods, which focus only on positive correlations.

title: On Enriching the Levin-Wen model with Symmetry
Abstract: Symmetry-protected and symmetry-enriched topological phases of matter are of significant interest in condensed matter physics due to the emergence of new materials like topological insulators. The Levin-Wen model for spin/boson systems is a crucial rigorously solvable model for studying 2D topological phases. The input data for the Levin-Wen model is a unitary fusion category, but the same model also applies to unitary multi-fusion categories. This paper provides details for this extension of the Levin-Wen model and demonstrates that the extended model serves as a natural platform for theoretically studying symmetry-protected and symmetry-enriched topological phases of matter.

title: Low temperature Glauber dynamics under weak competing interactions
Abstract: We examine the low but non-zero temperature regimes of the Glauber dynamics in a chain of Ising spins with first and second neighbor interactions J1 and J2. For 0 < -J2 / |J1| < 1, it is known that at T = 0 the dynamics exhibits both metastability and non-coarsening, while always being ergodic and coarsening in the limit of T -> 0+. Based on finite-size scaling analyses of relaxation times, we argue that in the latter situation, the asymptotic kinetics of small or weakly frustrated -J2/|J1| ratios is characterized by an almost ballistic dynamic exponent z ≈ 1.03(2) and arbitrarily slow growth velocities. In contrast, for non-competing interactions, the coarsening length scales are estimated to be almost diffusive.

title: Cosmological perturbations in the (1+3+6)-dimensional space-times
Abstract: Cosmological perturbations in (1+3+6)-dimensional space-times including photon gas without viscous processes are investigated using Abbott et al.'s formalism. Space-times consist of an outer space (the 3-dimensional expanding section) and an inner space (the 6-dimensional section). The inner space initially expands and later contracts. Abbott et al. derived only power-type solutions in the small wave-number limit, which appear at the final stage of the space-times. This paper derives not only small wave-number solutions but also large wave-number solutions. These solutions are found to depend on the two wave-numbers k_r and k_R (defined in the outer and inner spaces, respectively). The k_r-dependent and k_R-dependent parts dominate the total perturbations when (k_r/r(t))/(k_R/R(t)) >> 1 or << 1, respectively, where r(t) and R(t) are the scale factors in the outer and inner spaces. By comparing the behavior of these perturbations, changes in the spectrum of perturbations in the outer space with time are discussed.

title: Recent Results of the Hadron Resonance Gas Model and the Chemical Freeze-out of Strange Hadrons
Abstract: This paper presents a detailed discussion of recent results obtained within the hadron resonance gas model, featuring multi-component hard core repulsion. These results include the adiabatic chemical freeze-out criterion, the concept of separate chemical freeze-out of strange particles, and the effects of enhancement and sharpening of wide resonances and quark gluon bags occurring in a thermal medium. These findings are discussed to strengthen the planned heavy-ion collision experimental programs at low collision energies. We argue that, due to these effects, at the center of mass collision energy of 4-8 GeV, quark gluon bags may appear directly or through decays as new heavy resonances with a narrow width of about 50-150 MeV and a mass exceeding 2.5 GeV.

title: On the robustness of learning in games with stochastically perturbed payoff observations
Abstract: Motivated by the scarcity of accurate payoff feedback in practical game theory applications, we examine a class of learning dynamics where players adjust their choices based on past payoff observations subject to noise and random disturbances. First, in the single-player case (corresponding to an agent adapting to an arbitrarily changing environment), we show that the stochastic dynamics under study lead to no regret almost surely, irrespective of the noise level in the player's observations. In the multi-player case, we find that dominated strategies become extinct, and we demonstrate that strict Nash equilibria are stochastically stable and attracting. Conversely, if a state is stable or attracting with positive probability, then it is a Nash equilibrium. Finally, we provide an averaging principle for 2-player games and show that in zero-sum games with an interior equilibrium, time averages converge to Nash equilibrium for any noise level.

title: On distinguishability criteria for estimating generative models
Abstract:
Two recently introduced criteria for estimating generative models are both based on a reduction to binary classification. Noise-contrastive estimation (NCE) is an estimation procedure where a generative model is trained to distinguish data samples from noise samples. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) consist of pairs of generator and discriminator networks, where the generator network learns to generate samples by attempting to fool the discriminator network into believing its samples are real data. Both estimation procedures utilize the same function to drive learning, naturally raising questions about their relationship to each other and whether this function is related to maximum likelihood estimation (MLE). NCE corresponds to training an internal data model belonging to the discriminator network but using a fixed generator network. We demonstrate that a variant of NCE with a dynamic generator network is equivalent to maximum likelihood estimation. Since pairing a learned discriminator with an appropriate dynamically selected generator recovers MLE, one might expect the reverse to hold for pairing a learned generator with a certain discriminator. However, we show that recovering MLE for a learned generator requires departing from the distinguishability game. Specifically: 
- The expected gradient of the NCE discriminator can be made to match the expected gradient of MLE if one is allowed to use a non-stationary noise distribution for NCE.
- No choice of discriminator network can make the expected gradient for the GAN generator match that of MLE.
- Existing theory does not guarantee that GANs will converge in the non-convex case.
This suggests that a crucial next step in GAN research is to determine whether GANs converge and, if not, to modify their training algorithm to force convergence. |||

title: Pooled Motion Features for First-Person Videos
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel feature representation for first-person videos that effectively captures both global scene dynamics (egomotion) and significant local motion. The representation leverages time series pooling to abstract short-term and long-term changes in feature descriptors. It can handle various per-frame descriptors, including conventional motion descriptors (like histogram of optical flows) and appearance descriptors from convolutional neural networks. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach surpasses previous representations, including bag-of-visual-words and improved Fisher vectors, when using identical underlying feature descriptors. Additionally, it outperforms state-of-the-art features like local spatio-temporal features and improved trajectory features in handling first-person videos. These findings are validated through comprehensive testing on multiple first-person activity datasets under diverse conditions.

title: Confirmation of a Star Formation Bias in Type Ia Supernova Distances and its Effect on Measurement of the Hubble Constant
Abstract: Supernovae Ia (SNe Ia) originating in locally star-forming environments are dimmer than those in passive environments. This study, using the Constitution sample and GALEX host galaxy data, independently confirms this previously observed effect. The difference in brightness is seen using both the SALT2 and MLCS2k2 lightcurve fitting and standardization methods, with values of 0.094 ± 0.037 mag for SALT2 and 0.155 ± 0.041 mag for MLCS2k2. Combining this measurement with previous data yields 0.094 ± 0.025 mag for SALT2. This difference in SNe Ia environments can introduce bias in cosmological measurements, as demonstrated by examining the direct measurement of H0. GALEX observations indicate that SNe Ia calibrated through Cepheid period-luminosity relation using HST originate primarily in star-forming environments, while only about 50% of the Hubble-flow comparison sample exhibit similar environments. Consequently, the current H0 measurement using SNe Ia is overestimated. Accounting for this bias, we obtain a corrected value of H0corr = 70.6 ± 2.6 km s−1 Mpc−1 using the LMC distance, Milky Way parallaxes, and NGC 4258 megamaser as the Cepheid zeropoint, and 68.8 ± 3.3 km s−1 Mpc−1 when only using NGC 4258. This correction brings the direct H0 measurement within 1σ of recent indirect measurements based on the CMB power spectrum.

title: Numerical Simulations of Mach Stem Formation via Intersecting Bow Shocks
Abstract: Hubble Space Telescope observations reveal bright Hα emission knots within outflowing young stellar jets. Velocity variations in the flow create secondary bow shocks, which can intersect and lead to enhanced emission. When these shocks intersect at or above a certain critical angle, a planar shock called a Mach stem forms. These shocks could produce brighter Hα emission due to the parallel incoming flow to the Mach stem's normal. This paper presents initial results of a study using 2-D numerical simulations to explore Mach stem formation at the intersection of bow shocks generated by hypersonic "bullets" or "clumps." The simulations demonstrate how the bow shock shapes and intersection angles vary with changes in the adiabatic index γ. The formation or absence of a Mach stem in these simulations aligns with the steady-state Mach stem formation theory. The ultimate objective of this ongoing research effort is to characterize the physical and observational implications of bow shock intersections, including the formation of Mach stems.

title: Experimental demonstration of information to energy conversion in a quantum system at the Landauer Limit
Abstract: Landauer's principle establishes fundamental thermodynamic constraints for both classical and quantum information processing, impacting various fields including physics, computer science, and engineering. While this principle has only recently been experimentally investigated for classical systems, this study utilizes a nuclear magnetic resonance setup to experimentally explore information-to-energy conversion in a quantum system. The experiment focuses on a three-spin (qubits) molecule, encompassing the system, reservoir, and ancilla, to measure the heat dissipated during the implementation of a global system-reservoir unitary interaction that alters the system's information content. Employing an interferometric technique, the researchers reconstructed the heat distribution associated with the unitary interaction. Subsequently, quantum state tomography was used to measure the relative change in the system's entropy. These measurements confirm that an operation modifying the system's information content necessarily generates heat in the reservoir, precisely as predicted by Landauer's principle. The presented scheme enables detailed analysis of irreversible entropy production in quantum information processors.

title: Serving Content with Unknown Demand:the High-Dimensional Regime
Abstract: This study explores content placement in the high-dimensional regime, where there are n servers and O(n) distinct types of content. Each server can store and serve O(1) types at any given time. Demands for content types arrive and need to be served online, totaling O(n) over time. The algorithmic task is to determine content placement (which types are on which server) when demand statistics (content popularity) are unknown a priori and must be inferred from the demands themselves. This high-dimensional regime, where everything scales with n, prevents consistent estimation of demand statistics and models many modern settings with large numbers of users, servers, and content. The paper characterizes the performance of schemes separating learning and placement, showing they are suboptimal. It then examines a simple adaptive scheme that myopically stores recently requested content on idle servers, demonstrating its superior performance to those separating learning and placement. These results generalize to scenarios where demand statistics change over time. Overall, the findings indicate that separating demand estimation and its subsequent application is suboptimal.

title: Bifurcations of Central Configurations in the Four-Body Problem with some equal masses

Then, using the Krawczyk method and equivariant bifurcation theory, the existence of these bifurcations is rigorously proven and classified.

title: Work and heat for two-level systems in dissipative environments: Strong driving and non-Markovian dynamics

Furthermore, the study addresses the role of system-bath correlations in the initial thermal state and their impact on heat flux. title: The Effect of Varying Co layer thickness on the Time-Temperature Characteristics of Co/Sb Semimetal Embedded Magnetic Nanoparticles
Abstract: This study investigates the effect of varying cobalt thickness on the temperature-dependent time decay of electrical resistance in Co/Sb multilayer samples. During deposition, cobalt forms single-domain magnetic nanoparticles on the Sb substrate, following either a Volmer-Weber or Stranski-Krastanov growth mode. This metastable state is then encased in 2.5 nm of Sb, creating an embedded nanoparticle system. Scanning tunneling microscopy measurements before and after aging (annealing at a given temperature for sufficient time to complete the resistance decay) reveal that these nanoparticles undergo morphological transformations during aging. These transformations lead to well-defined time-dependent decays in both magnetization and electrical resistance, making this material a promising candidate for an electronic time-temperature sensor.

title: Resonant inelastic x-ray scattering study of electronic excitations in insulating K$_{0.83}$Fe$_{1.53}$Se$_2$
Abstract: This study employs resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) at the Fe K-edge to investigate K0.83Fe1.53Se2, an insulator unlike many parent compounds of iron-based superconductors. The agreement between the experimental spectra and calculations with moderate Ueff suggests that electron correlations in both insulating and metallic iron-based superconductors are comparable.

title: Atmospheric Lepton Fluxes

title: Ellipticity Weakens Chameleon Screening
Abstract: The chameleon mechanism allows a long-range fifth force to be screened in dense environments by its mass increasing with local density due to self-interactions. This study focuses on ellipsoidal departures from spherical symmetry, computing the full form of the chameleon force and comparing its shape dependence to that of gravity. An enhancement of the chameleon force by up to 40% is possible when deforming a sphere to an ellipsoid of the same mass with an ellipticity ≈ 0.99.

title: Sequential Equilibrium in Computational Games
Abstract: This paper examines sequential equilibrium in the context of computational games where agents are charged for computation. In these games, agents can rationally choose to forget, leading to issues of imperfect recall. Two notions of sequential equilibrium are considered: ex ante, where a player chooses a strategy before the game starts and is committed to it but ensures it remains optimal even off the equilibrium path, and interim, where a player can reconsider at each information set whether their strategy is optimal and change it if necessary. While these notions coincide in games of perfect recall, they diverge in games of imperfect recall. Despite the interim notion's appeal, it faces conceptual problems in standard games of imperfect recall, as argued by Halpern and Pass. This study demonstrates that these problems largely disappear in the computational setting. Moreover, under natural assumptions, the two notions coincide in this setting.

title: Organization and clasification of trajectories in the time-delayed Mackey-Glass system

In wide parameter regions, different periodic or aperiodic solutions coexist, exhibiting similar waveforms with alternating peaks of different amplitudes. A symbolic algorithm is proposed to classify these solutions. The system's phase space is explored by varying the parameter values of two families of initial functions.

title: Achievement of Preassigned Spectra in the Synthesis of Band-Pass Constant-Envelope Signals by Rapidly Hopping through Discrete Frequencies

title: Existence and qualitative properties of travelling waves for an epidemiological model with mutations

title: Local inhibitory plasticity tunes global brain dynamics and allows the emergence of functional brain networks
Abstract: The brain exhibits rich, spontaneous activity across various temporal and spatial scales, thought to be crucial for efficient neural functioning. Experimental evidence suggests that these neural dynamics are preserved across different cognitive states, environmental alterations, and brain configuration changes (e.g., individuals, development, neurological disorders). This implies the brain has evolved mechanisms to stabilize dynamics and maintain them across various situations. This study employs a local homeostatic inhibitory plasticity mechanism, balancing inhibitory and excitatory activity in a model of macroscopic brain activity based on white-matter structural connectivity. The addition of homeostatic plasticity regulates network activity and enables the emergence of rich, spontaneous dynamics across a range of brain configurations. Moreover, the presence of homeostatic plasticity maximizes the overlap between empirical and simulated patterns of functional connectivity. This work presents a simple, local, biologically plausible inhibitory mechanism that facilitates stable dynamics and functional connectivity network formation in the brain.

title: Timelike pion form factor in lattice QCD
Abstract: This study performs a non-perturbative lattice calculation of the complex phase and modulus of the pion form factor in the timelike momentum region using the finite-volume technique. Two ensembles of 2+1-flavor overlap fermions at pion masses m_pi = 380 and 290 MeV are used. By calculating the I = 1 correlators in the center-of-mass and three moving frames, the form factor is obtained at ten different values of the timelike momentum transfer around the vector resonance. The results are compared with the phenomenological model of Gounaris-Sakurai and its variant.

title: Separable wave equations for gravitoelectromagnetic perturbations of rotating charged black strings
Abstract: Rotating charged black strings are solutions of four-dimensional Einstein-Maxwell equations with a negative cosmological constant and non-trivial topology. According to the AdS/CFT correspondence, these black strings are dual to rotating thermal states of a strongly interacting field theory with nonzero chemical potential that lives in a cylinder. The dynamics of fluctuations in the field theory can be studied from the perturbation equations for classical fields in a black-string spacetime. Motivated by this, this work develops a completely gauge and tetrad invariant perturbation approach to address the gravitoelectromagnetic fluctuations of rotating charged black strings in the presence of sources. As with any charged black hole, a perturbation in the background electromagnetic field induces a metric perturbation and vice versa. Despite this coupling and the non-vanishing angular momentum, linearization of the Newman-Penrose formalism leads to four separated second-order complex equations for suitable combinations of the spin coefficients, the Weyl and the Maxwell scalars. The Chandrasekhar transformation theory is generalized by the inclusion of sources and applied to reduce the perturbation problem to four decoupled inhomogeneous wave equations, one pair for each perturbation sector. The radial part of these wave equations can be transformed into Schrodinger-like forms after Fourier transforming them with respect to time. The resulting effective potentials form two pairs of supersymmetric partner potentials, leading to a relationship between the fundamental variables of one perturbation sector and those of the other. The relevance of this symmetry in connection to the AdS/CFT correspondence is discussed, and future applications of the developed perturbation theory are outlined.

title: Route to Topological Superconductivity via Magnetic Field Rotation
Abstract: Experimental verification of topological superconductivity remains a significant challenge. While some spin-triplet superconductors with p-wave pairing symmetry are candidates, another possibility is a conventional, two-dimensional (2D) s-wave superconductor in a magnetic field with strong Rashba spin-orbit coupling. However, the magnetic field required to achieve a topologically non-trivial state typically exceeds the upper critical field Hc2, preventing its realization. This study proposes that this problem can be overcome by rotating the magnetic field into the superconducting plane. The superconducting state's character is explored by varying the magnetic field's strength and orientation, demonstrating that a topological state established with a sufficiently strong out-of-plane field extends to an in-plane field orientation. title: Reentrant superconductivity in URhGe
Abstract: This work presents a phenomenological description of the phase diagram for the ferromagnet superconductor URhGe. Using Landau's phenomenological theory, it is found that the phase transition between anisotropic ferromagnetic and paramagnetic states under a strong enough magnetic field perpendicular to the easy magnetization direction changes from second-order to first-order. The analysis shows that magnetic susceptibility related to longitudinal magnetic fluctuations significantly increases near the first-order transition, promoting the reentrance of the superconducting state. This reentrant superconductivity is observed near the first-order transition line at temperatures approximately twice lower than the tricritical point temperature, existing in both ferromagnet and paramagnet states. The critical temperature for the transition to the superconducting state decreases at the intersection with the ferromagnet-paramagnet phase transition line.

title: Contact-induced charge contributions to non-local spin transport measurements in Co/MgO/graphene devices
Abstract: Recent studies have shown that oxide barriers in graphene-based non-local spin-valve structures can impede spin transport. These barriers may cause spin dephasing during or immediately after electrical spin injection, limiting spin transport parameters such as the spin lifetime of the device. This paper examines the impact of spatially inhomogeneous oxide barriers, particularly conducting pinholes within the barrier, on the background signal in non-local measurements of graphene/MgO/Co spin-valve devices. Through simulations and reference measurements on devices with non-ferromagnetic electrodes, the study demonstrates that the background signal can arise from inhomogeneous current flow through the oxide barriers. A significant finding is the presence of charge accumulation alongside the actual spin accumulation signal in non-local voltage measurements, which can be attributed to the redistribution of charge carriers by a perpendicular magnetic field, similar to the classical Hall effect. Additionally, the paper presents systematic investigations into the phase of the low-frequency non-local ac voltage signal measured in non-local spin measurements using ac lock-in techniques. This phase, often neglected in the analysis of non-local spin transport, is shown to be another indicator of the homogeneity of the MgO spin injection and detection barriers. The study links backgate-dependent changes in the phase to the interplay between the capacitance of the oxide barrier and the quantum capacitance of graphene.

title: Light mediators in dark matter direct detections
Abstract: This study investigates the effects of light mediators on dark matter (DM)-nucleus scattering event spectra within an extended effective operator framework. The presence of light mediators alters the interpretation of current experimental data, particularly in determining the DM particle mass. Through analytical and numerical illustrations, the analysis demonstrates that, for all operators relevant to spin-independent scatterings, the DM particle mass allowed by the data increases significantly as the mediator particle becomes lighter. For the data from CDMS-II-Si, the allowed DM particle mass can reach approximately 50 GeV, depending on the type of operator. The increase in DM particle mass saturates when the mediator mass falls below the order of 10 MeV. Upper limits from other experiments, such as SuperCDMS, CDMSlite, CDEX, XENON10/100, LUX, and PandaX, tend to be weaker in high DM mass regions. A combined analysis shows that the presence of light mediators can partially alleviate the tension in the current results from CDMS-II-Si, SuperCDMS, and LUX.

title: Photon Cascade Decay of the Warped Graviton at LHC14 and a 100 TeV Hadron Collider
Abstract: In warped 5D models of hierarchy and flavor, the first Kaluza-Klein (KK) state of the graviton (G1) is sufficiently heavy to decay into a photon and its first KK mode (γ1) on-shell: G1 → γ1 γ. While the volume suppression of the rate for this process (relative to 2-body decay into heavy Standard Model (SM) final states (W/Z/t/H)) may be partially compensated by the simplicity of the photon final state, the focus of this work lies on γ1 → W+W−, with a typical branching fraction of O(1), and specifically the semi-leptonic final state W(→ jj) W(→ ℓ, ν) with ℓ = e, μ. The SM background originates from 2→3 parton processes and is relatively suppressed compared to those for 2-body decays of G1. Additionally, to further reduce the background, an invariant mass window cut for γ1 (in addition to that for G1) can be implemented in this new channel. This "photon cascade" decay probes a different combination of (bulk and brane) interactions of the KK states compared to decays into two heavy SM states. Therefore, in combination with other channels, the cascade decay could be used to extract individual underlying geometric parameters. The 3σ reach for G1 in this channel extends up to 1.5 TeV at the high-luminosity (14 TeV) LHC and can be further expanded to about 4 TeV at 5σ at a future 100 TeV hadron collider. This analysis highlights the novel feature that the invariant mass distribution of KK graviton decay products deviates from the Breit-Wigner form due to the KK graviton coupling increasing with energy.

The study argues that this change is due to a transition from one pairing state to another, with different symmetries on either side of Pc. The work explores a potential link between scattering and pairing, suggesting a scenario where a d-wave state favored by high-Q scattering at low pressure transitions to a state with s+- symmetry favored by low-Q scattering at high pressure.

title: Mechanisms for the decomposition and dehydrogenation of Li amide/imide
Abstract: The reversible reaction involving Li amide (LiNH2) and Li imide (Li2NH) is a promising mechanism for hydrogen storage. Recent synchrotron x-ray diffraction experiments suggest that the transformation between LiNH2 and Li2NH is a bulk reaction occurring through non-stoichiometric processes and involving the migration of Li+ and H+ ions. To understand the atomistic mechanisms behind these processes, this study performs comprehensive first-principles investigations of native point defects and defect complexes in the two compounds. The analysis finds that both LiNH2 and Li2NH are susceptible to Frenkel disorder on the Li sublattice. Lithium interstitials and vacancies have low formation energies and exhibit high mobility, indicating their crucial role in mass transport and ionic conduction. Conversely, hydrogen interstitials and vacancies are responsible for forming and breaking N-H bonds, which is essential for the Li amide/imide reaction. Based on the structure, energetics, and migration of hydrogen-, lithium-, and nitrogen-related defects, the study proposes that LiNH2 decomposes into Li2NH and NH3 through two competing mechanisms with different activation energies. One mechanism involves the formation of native defects in the material's interior, while the other occurs at the surface. Consequently, the prevailing mechanism and hence the effective activation energy for decomposition depend on the surface-to-volume ratio or the specific surface area, which changes with particle size during ball milling. These mechanisms also explain the dehydrogenation of LiNH2+LiH mixtures.

title: Active patterning and asymmetric transport in a model actomyosin network

These processes are achieved through nonequilibrium self-organization, generating functional patterns and driving intracellular transport. This study constructs a minimal physical model that incorporates the coupling between nonlinear elastic responses of individual filaments and force-dependent motor action. Stochastic simulations reveal that the interplay of motor processes, described as driving anti-correlated motion of the network vertices, and network connectivity, which determines the percolation character of the structure, can capture the dynamical and structural cooperativity observed experimentally. The buckling instability of individual filaments is found to play a crucial role in localizing collapse events due to local force imbalance. Motor-driven buckling-induced node aggregation provides a dynamic mechanism that stabilizes two-dimensional patterns below the apparent static percolation limit. Coordinated motor action is also shown to suppress random thermal noise on large time scales, preserving the initial planar configuration of the system during structural development. Similar simulations on a three-dimensional anchored network suggest that myosin-driven isotropic contraction of a well-connected actin network, combined with mechanical anchoring that confers directionality to the collective motion, represents a novel mechanism of intracellular transport, as evidenced by chromosome translocation in the starfish oocyte.

title: Field topologies in ideal and near ideal magnetohydrodynamics and vortex dynamics
Abstract: This review examines magnetic field topology frozen in ideal magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) and its breakage in near-ideal MHD. The first part provides a comprehensive physical description of the frozen-in field topology, considering magnetic flux conservation as fundamental. It discusses four topics: Eulerian and Lagrangian descriptions of MHD, Chandrasekhar-Kendall and Euler-potential field representations, magnetic helicity, and inviscid vortex dynamics in comparison to ideal MHD. A corollary clarifies the challenges associated with achieving a high degree of the frozen-in condition in numerical MHD. The second part focuses on field topology breakage, centered on Parker's Magnetostatic Theorem concerning the incompatibility of a continuous magnetic field with the simultaneous requirement of force-free equilibrium and an arbitrarily prescribed, 3D field topology. Preserving field topology as a global constraint readily leads to the formation of tangential magnetic discontinuities, i.e., electric current sheets of zero thickness. A similar incompatibility exists in the steady, force, and thermal balance of a heated radiating fluid subject to an anisotropic thermal flux conducted strictly along the frozen-in magnetic field in the low beta limit. In a weakly resistive fluid, the thinning of current sheets by these incompatibilities inevitably results in sheet dissipation, resistive heating, and topological changes in the field despite the small resistivity. Faraday induction drives but also macroscopically limits this mode of energy dissipation, storing free energy in self-organized, ideal MHD structures. The review examines this property of MHD turbulence captured by the Taylor hypothesis in relation to the Sun's corona, highlighting the need for a basic quantitative description of the breakdown of flux conservation in the low resistivity limit. A cylindrical, initial boundary value problem provides specificity in the review.

title: Polyspectra searches for sharp oscillatory features in cosmic microwave sky data
Abstract: This study conducts a comprehensive search for signatures of sharp oscillatory features in the WMAP9 power spectrum and bispectrum, as well as the Planck power spectrum. For the first time, searches are performed simultaneously in both the power spectrum and bispectrum, employing well-defined look-elsewhere statistics to assess significances rigorously. By developing efficient methods to scan power spectrum likelihoods for oscillatory features, the analysis presents results for phenomenological bare sine and cosine modulations, allowing validation against existing Planck Likelihood surveys, as well as templates incorporating the correct sharp feature scaling. The study specifically investigates degeneracies between feature and cosmological parameters. For frequencies beyond the scale set by the acoustic peaks, dependencies are realized through uninteresting adjustments of the comoving distance to last scattering. Therefore, it is sufficient to keep cosmological parameters fixed and employ fast Gaussian approximations to the likelihood as a function of the feature model amplitude. In cases where results can be compared to the literature, the method shows excellent agreement. The analysis supplements results from the Planck Likelihood with an analysis based on the Planck SMICA component separation map, which, assuming the reliability of the component separation algorithm, allows for the inclusion of a larger sky fraction. This allows for the most stringent constraints to date on the amplitudes of feature models in the temperature power spectrum. Using the WMAP bispectrum, the study performs a combined power spectrum and bispectrum survey. It utilizes and slightly generalizes statistics developed in previous work to reliably judge the significance of large feature model amplitude estimates. The study concludes that its findings are entirely consistent with a featureless realization of a Gaussian CMB.

title: Intrinsic Spin Torque Without Spin-Orbit Coupling
Abstract: This work derives an intrinsic contribution to the non-adiabatic spin torque for non-uniform magnetic textures. This contribution differs from previously considered contributions in several ways and can be the dominant contribution in some models. Unlike previously reported non-adiabatic spin torques, it does not depend on the change in occupation of the electron states due to current flow but rather arises from the perturbation of the electronic states when an electric field is applied. Therefore, it should be viewed as electric-field-induced rather than current-induced. It does not originate from extrinsic relaxation mechanisms or spin-orbit coupling. This intrinsic non-adiabatic spin torque is related by a chiral connection to the intrinsic spin-orbit torque calculated from the Berry phase for Rashba systems.

title: Constraints on Radial Migration in Spiral Galaxies I. Analytic Criterion for Capture at Corotation
Abstract: Near the corotation resonance of a transient spiral arm, stellar orbital angular momenta can be altered without inducing significant kinematic heating, resulting in what is known as radial migration. When radial migration is highly efficient, a significant fraction of disk stars experience substantial, permanent changes to their individual orbital angular momenta over the lifetime of the disk, having significant implications for the evolution of disk galaxies. The first step for a star in a spiral disk to migrate radially is to be captured in a "trapped" orbit associated with the corotation resonance of the spiral pattern. An analytical criterion for determining whether or not a star is in a trapped orbit has previously been derived only for stars with zero random orbital energy in the presence of a spiral with fixed properties. This paper, the first in a series, derives an analytical criterion suitable for a star on an orbit with finite random orbital energy. The new criterion demonstrates that whether or not a star is in a "trapped" orbit primarily depends on the star's orbital angular momentum. This criterion could serve as a powerful tool in interpreting the results of N-body simulations. Future papers in this series will apply the criterion to explore the physical parameters crucial for determining the efficiency of radial migration and its potential importance to disk evolution.

title: Spinor Bose gas in an elongated trap

title: Quantum correlations of light and matter through environmental transitions
Abstract: One distinguishing aspect of solid-state photonic devices compared to their atomic counterparts is the unavoidable interaction between system excitations and lattice vibrations of the host material. The analysis shows that in solid-state cavity quantum electrodynamics, interactions with the host vibrational environment can generate quantum cavity-emitter correlations in regimes that are semiclassical for atomic systems. This behavior, which can be probed experimentally through the cavity emission properties, signifies a failure of the semiclassical approach in the solid state and challenges the notion that coupling to a thermal bath supports a more classical description of the system. Moreover, it does not rely on the spectral details of the host environment under consideration and is robust to temperature changes. Therefore, it is relevant to a wide range of photonic devices.

title: Forensics of Subhalo-Stream Encounters: The Three Phases of Gap Growth
Abstract: There is hope to detect dark matter subhalos, predicted by the current theory of structure formation, by observing the gaps they produce in tidal streams. This technique offers the most promising way to detect and characterize dark substructure, as these gaps grow with time, amplifying small perturbations into clear signatures observable by current and future galaxy surveys. To facilitate future inferences, we have developed a comprehensive framework for studying the growth of stream density perturbations. Starting with simple assumptions and focusing on streams on circular orbits, we derive analytical formulas that describe the evolution of all gap properties (size, density contrast, etc.) at all times. We uncover complex, previously unnoticed behavior, with the stream initially forming a density enhancement near the subhalo impact point. Shortly after, a gap forms due to the relative change in period induced by the subhalo's passage. There is an intermediate regime where the gap grows linearly in time. At late times, the particles in the stream overtake each other, forming caustics, and the gap grows like √t. In addition to the secular growth, we find that the gap oscillates as it grows due to epicyclic motion. Comparing this analytical model to N-body simulations, we find an impressive level of agreement. However, when analyzing the observation of a single gap, we find a large degeneracy between the subhalo mass, the impact geometry and kinematics, the host potential, and the time since flyby.

title: Fast and accurate approximate inference of transcript expression from RNA-seq data
Abstract: Accurately assigning RNA-seq reads to their transcript of origin is a fundamental task in transcript expression estimation. When ambiguities in assignments exist due to transcripts sharing sequence, for example, alternative isoforms or alleles, the problem can be solved through probabilistic inference. Bayesian methods have been shown to provide accurate transcript abundance estimates compared to competing methods. However, exact Bayesian inference is intractable, and approximate methods such as Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) and Variational Bayes (VB) are typically used. While providing a high degree of accuracy and modeling flexibility, standard implementations can be prohibitively slow for large datasets and complex transcriptome annotations. We propose a novel approximate inference scheme based on VB and apply it to an existing model of transcript expression inference from RNA-seq data. Recent advances in VB algorithmics are used to improve the convergence of the algorithm beyond the standard Variational Bayes Expectation Maximisation (VBEM) algorithm. We apply our algorithm to simulated and biological datasets, demonstrating a significant increase in speed with only very small loss in accuracy of expression level estimation. We carry out a comparative study against seven popular alternative methods and demonstrate that our new algorithm provides excellent accuracy and inter-replicate consistency while remaining competitive in computation time. The methods were implemented in R and C++ and are available as part of the BitSeq project at https://github.com/BitSeq. The method is also available through the BitSeq Bioconductor package. The source code to reproduce all simulation results can be accessed via https://github.com/BitSeq/BitSeqVB_benchmarking.

title: The StEllar Counterparts of COmpact high velocity clouds (SECCO) survey. I. Photos of ghosts
Abstract: We present an imaging survey aimed at searching for the stellar counterparts of recently discovered ultra-compact high-velocity HI clouds (UCHVC). Adams et al. (2013) proposed these clouds to be candidate mini-haloes in the Local Group and/or its surroundings, within a distance range of 0.25-2.0 Mpc. Using the Large Binocular Telescope, we obtain wide-field (~ 23' X 23') g- and r-band images of the twenty-five most promising and most compact clouds among the fifty-nine identified by Adams et al. Careful visual inspection of all the images does not reveal any stellar counterpart even slightly resembling LeoP, the only local dwarf galaxy that was found as a counterpart to a previously detected high-velocity cloud. Only a possible distant (D>3.0 Mpc) counterpart to HVC274.68+74.70-123 has been identified on our images. The point source photometry in the central 17.3' X 7.7' chips reaches r<= 26.5, and is expected to contain most of the stellar counterparts to the UCHVCs. However, no obvious stellar over-density is detected in any of our fields, in marked contrast to our comparison LeoP field in which the dwarf galaxy is detected at a >30 sigma significance level. Only HVC352.45+59.06+263 may be associated with a weak over-density, whose nature cannot be ascertained with our data. Sensitivity tests show that our survey would have detected any dwarf galaxy dominated by an old stellar population, with an integrated absolute magnitude M_V<= -8.0, a half-light radius r_h<= 300 pc, and lying within 1.5 Mpc from us, thereby confirming that it is unlikely that the observed UCHVCs are associated with stellar counterparts typical of known Local Group dwarf galaxies.

title: The unusual glitch recoveries of the high magnetic field pulsar J1119$-$6127
Abstract: Providing a link between magnetars and radio pulsars, high magnetic field neutron stars are ideal targets to investigate how bursting/magnetospheric activity and braking torque variations are connected to rotational glitches. The last spin-up glitch of the highly magnetized pulsar J1119−6127 back in 2007 was the first glitch in a rotationally powered radio pulsar to be accompanied by radiative changes. Moreover, it was followed by an uncommon glitch relaxation that resulted in a smaller spin-down rate relative to the prediction of the pre-glitch timing model. Here, we present four years of new radio timing observations and analyze the total of sixteen years of timing data for this source. The new data uncover an ongoing evolution of the spin-down rate, thereby allowing us to exclude permanent changes in the external or internal torque as a stand-alone cause of the peculiar features of the glitch recovery. Furthermore, no additional variations of the radio pulse profile are detected, strengthening the association of the previously observed transient emission features with the glitching activity. A self-consistent measurement of the braking index yields a value n≈2.7, indicating a trajectory in the P−Ṗ plane inclined towards the magnetars. Such a potential evolutionary link might be strengthened by a, possibly permanent, reduction of ~15% in n at the epoch of the 2007 glitch.

title: Magnetically-driven crustquakes in neutron stars
Abstract: Crustquake events may be connected with both rapid spin-up "glitches" within the regular slowdown of neutron stars and high-energy magnetar flares. We argue that magnetic field decay builds up stresses in a neutron star's crust, as the elastic shear force resists the Lorentz force's desire to rearrange the global magnetic-field equilibrium. We derive a criterion for crust-breaking induced by a changing magnetic-field configuration, and use this to investigate strain patterns in a neutron star's crust for a variety of different magnetic-field models. Universally, we find that the crust is most liable to break if the magnetic field has a strong toroidal component, in which case the epicenter of the crustquake is around the equator. We calculate the energy released in a crustquake as a function of the fracture depth, finding that it is independent of field strength. Crust-breaking is, however, associated with a characteristic local field strength of 2.4×1014 G for a breaking strain of 0.001, or 2.4×1015 G at a breaking strain of 0.1. We find that even the most luminous magnetar giant flare could have been powered by crustal energy release alone.
