title: FDR-Control in Multiscale Change-point Segmentation
Abstract: Fast multiple change-point segmentation methods, which additionally provide faithful statistical statements on the number, locations, and sizes of the segments, have recently received great attention. In this paper, we propose a multiscale segmentation method, FDRSeg, which controls the false discovery rate (FDR) in the sense that the number of false jumps is bounded linearly by the number of true jumps. In this way, it adapts the detection power to the number of true jumps. We prove a non-asymptotic upper bound for its FDR in a Gaussian setting, which allows the only parameter of FDRSeg to be calibrated properly. Change-point locations, as well as the signal, are shown to be estimated in a uniform sense at optimal minimax convergence rates up to a log-factor. The latter is w.r.t. Lp-risk, p ≥ 1, over classes of step functions with bounded jump sizes and either bounded, or possibly increasing, number of change-points. FDRSeg can be efficiently computed by an accelerated dynamic program; its computational complexity is shown to be linear in the number of observations when there are many change-points. The performance of the proposed method is examined by comparisons with some state-of-the-art methods on both simulated and real datasets. An R-package is available online.

title: On coarse geometric aspects of the Hilbert geometry
Abstract: We begin a coarse geometric study of Hilbert geometry. We give a necessary and sufficient condition for the natural boundary of a Hilbert geometry to be a corona, which is a nice boundary in coarse geometry. In addition, we show that any Hilbert geometry is uniformly contractible and with coarse bounded geometry. As a consequence, we see that the coarse Novikov conjecture holds for a Hilbert geometry with a mild condition. We also show that the asymptotic dimension of any two-dimensional Hilbert geometry is just two. This implies that the coarse Baum-Connes conjecture holds for any two-dimensional Hilbert geometry via Yu's theorem.

title: Quasi-periodic solutions for fully nonlinear forced reversible Schroedinger equations
Abstract: In this paper, we consider a class of fully nonlinear forced and reversible Schrödinger equations and prove the existence and stability of quasi-periodic solutions. We use a Nash-Moser algorithm together with a reducibility theorem on the linearized operator in a neighborhood of zero. Due to the presence of the highest order derivatives in the nonlinearity, the classic KAM-reducibility argument fails, and one needs to use a wider class of changes of variables such as diffeomorphisms of the torus and pseudo-differential operators. This procedure automatically produces a change of variables, well defined on the phase space of the equation, which diagonalizes the operator linearized at the solution. This gives the linear stability.

title: Dual regimes of ion migration in high repetition rate femtosecond laser inscribed waveguides
Abstract: Ion migration in high repetition rate femtosecond laser inscribed waveguides is currently being reported in different optical glasses. For the first time, we discuss and experimentally demonstrate the presence of two regimes of ion migration found in laser-written waveguides. Regime-I corresponds to the initial waveguide formation mainly via light element migration (in our case atomic weight < 31u), whereas regime-II majorly corresponds to the movement of heavy elements. This behavior brings attention to a problem that has never been analyzed before and that affects laser-written active waveguides in which active ions migrate, changing their local spectroscopic properties. The migration of active ions may in fact detune the pre-designed optimal values of active photonic devices. This paper experimentally evidences this problem and provides solutions to avert it.

title: Element- and charge-state-resolved ion energies in the cathodic arc plasma from composite AlCr cathodes in argon, nitrogen and oxygen atmospheres
Abstract: The energy distribution functions of ions in the cathodic arc plasma using composite AlCr cathodes were measured as a function of the background gas pressure in the range 0.5 to 3.5 Pa for different cathode compositions and gas atmospheres. The most abundant aluminum ions were Al+ regardless of the background gas species, whereas Cr2+ ions were dominating in Ar and N2 and Cr+ in O2 atmospheres. The energy distributions of the aluminum and chromium ions typically consisted of a high-energy fraction due to acceleration in the expanding plasma plume from the cathode spot and thermalized ions that were subjected to collisions in the plasma cloud. The fraction of the latter increased with increasing background gas pressure. Atomic nitrogen and oxygen ions showed similar energy distributions as the aluminum and chromium ions, whereas the argon and molecular nitrogen and oxygen ions were formed at a greater distance from the cathode spot and thus less subject to accelerating gradients. In addition to the positively charged metal and gas ions, negatively charged oxygen and oxygen-containing ions were observed in an O2 atmosphere. The obtained results are intended to provide a comprehensive overview of the ion energies and charge states in the arc plasma of AlCr composite cathodes in different gas atmospheres, as such plasmas are frequently used to deposit thin films and coatings.

title: Breaking Points in Quartic Maps
Abstract: Dynamical systems, whether continuous or discrete, are used by physicists to study non-linear phenomena. In the case of discrete dynamical systems, one of the most used is the quadratic map depending on a parameter. However, some phenomena can depend alternatively on two values of the same parameter. We use the quadratic map xn+1 = 1 - axn2 when the parameter alternates between two values during the iteration process. In this case, the orbit of the alternate system is the sum of the orbits of two quartic maps. The bifurcation diagrams of these maps present breaking points where abruptly change their evolution.

title: Classical and quantum conditional measures from a categorical viewpoint

We extend the Riesz-Markov-Kakutani representation theorem and the Gelfand duality theorem to an equivalence of categories between them. title: The first stars: CEMP--no stars and signatures of spinstars
Abstract: Carbon-enhanced metal-poor (CEMP) stars are a unique type of star that exhibit an overabundance of carbon but a deficiency in heavy elements. These stars are further divided into CEMP-no stars, which exhibit no evidence of s-process or r-process elements, and CEMP-low stars, which exhibit some s-process elements. The origin and nucleosynthetic sites of the peculiar CNO, Ne-Na, and Mg-Al abundances observed in CEMP-no stars are investigated in this study.

title: Watersheds in disordered media
Abstract: Determining the optimal method for dividing a rugged landscape is a complex problem with far-reaching implications. Historically, watersheds, which delineate the boundaries between adjacent water systems, have served as a practical means of dividing land. However, the subtle geometric characteristics of these lines can lead to intense border disputes between countries, as slight changes in the landscape can significantly alter watershed boundaries. Despite its origins in geomorphology, the watershed concept finds applications in diverse fields like image processing and medicine. This review explores the origins and definitions of watershed lines within a geomorphological framework, examining their geometrical and physical properties. Additionally, the review investigates the statistical properties of watersheds using artificial landscapes with long-range correlations, revealing a connection between watershed and statistical physics of disordered systems.

title: Dynamic Structure Embedded Online Multiple-Output Regression for Stream Data
Abstract: Online multiple-output regression is a crucial machine learning technique for modeling, predicting, and compressing multi-dimensional correlated data streams. This paper presents MORES, a novel online multiple-output regression method specifically designed for stream data. MORES dynamically adapts the structure of the coefficients at each update step, allowing for continuous model refinement. Recognizing that limited expressive power of regression models, particularly in the initial stages of online updates, can lead to dependencies among residual error variables, MORES dynamically learns and leverages the structure of residual errors to enhance prediction accuracy. To efficiently handle data streams, MORES defines three statistical variables that precisely represent all observed samples for incrementally calculating prediction loss in each online update round. This approach eliminates the need to load all training data into memory, preventing model fluctuations in the presence of noise. Additionally, MORES incorporates a forgetting factor to assign different weights to samples, enabling quick adaptation to the evolving characteristics of data streams. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of MORES, demonstrating a significant improvement in prediction accuracy and a processing speed exceeding 2000 samples per second.

title: Hyperon Puzzle of Neutron Stars with Skyrme Force Models
Abstract: The hyperon puzzle in neutron stars (NSs) poses a challenge for understanding the composition and properties of these dense celestial objects. This study investigates the impact of hyperons on the equation of state (EoS) and mass-radius relations of NSs. Using Skyrme force models to describe nucleon-nucleon, nucleon-Lambda hyperon (NΛ), and Lambda-Lambda (ΛΛ) interactions, the authors explore the effects of these interactions on the NS EoS and determine the maximum mass attainable by NSs.  The presence of hyperons generally softens the EoS, which has been difficult to reconcile with recent observations of large-mass NSs (M ≈ 2 M⊙). However, some Skyrme force models predict a maximum mass consistent with observations while simultaneously satisfying observationally constrained mass-radius relations, highlighting the importance of considering hyperon interactions.

title: Historical overview on Vacuum suitable Welding and fatigue resistance in Research Devices
Abstract: Advancements in orbital welding, laser welding, and robot welding have significantly improved the fabrication of large vacuum vessels. Despite these advancements, achieving perfect vacuum-suitable welds that can withstand dynamic stress remains a challenge. A historical review reveals systematic welding mistakes and their solutions, while the example of ASDEX-Upgrade demonstrates how attempts to conduct vacuum-suitable welding can compromise fatigue strength. The study warns that ITER, a future fusion reactor, could repeat the mistakes of ASDEX-Upgrade, particularly with unwanted welding.

title: The redemption of singularity confinement
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel method for applying the singularity confinement property as a criterion for determining discrete integrability. The approach involves treating free parameters in a mapping as functions of the independent variable and introducing additional terms to the mapping that do not alter the singularity structure. This "full deautonomisation" approach enables the exact computation of algebraic entropy for various mappings, including the Hietarinta-Viallet mapping. The study demonstrates that this method effectively distinguishes between integrable and non-integrable cases, even when both exhibit confined singularities.

title: Neutrino Constrains to the Diffuse Gamma-Ray Emission from Accretion Shocks
Abstract: Cosmic rays are thought to be accelerated by shocks generated during the formation of large-scale structures in the universe. These shocks contribute to the extragalactic gamma-ray background observed by Fermi-LAT, but their specific contribution remains difficult to constrain.  Recent detection of high-energy isotropic neutrino flux by IceCube provides a potential link to cosmic ray acceleration in accretion shocks. Assuming that these neutrinos originate from cosmic rays accelerated in accretion shocks during structure formation, the authors obtain the strongest constraint on the gamma-ray emission from these shocks. The results suggest that these shocks contribute at most 20% to the extragalactic gamma-ray background, corresponding to a neutrino flux with a spectral index of 2. This information can be used to investigate the gamma-ray emission of galaxy clusters and constrain the efficiency of cosmic ray acceleration, providing insights into the process of large-scale structure formation.

title: DeepID-Net: Deformable Deep Convolutional Neural Networks for Object Detection

A novel pre-training strategy enhances feature representations for object detection, improving generalization capability. By altering network structures, training strategies, and key components in the detection pipeline, the authors obtain diverse models that significantly enhance the effectiveness of model averaging. This approach achieves a mean averaged precision of 50.3% on the ILSVRC2014 detection test set, surpassing the state-of-the-art RCNN (31%) and the winner of ILSVRC2014, GoogLeNet (44.2%).

title: Nonlinear Factor Models for Network and Panel Data
Abstract: Factor structures provide a convenient method for incorporating latent variables into panel data models. This study examines fixed effect estimation of nonlinear panel single-index models with factor structures in the unobservables, including logit, probit, ordered probit, and Poisson specifications. The study establishes that fixed effect estimators of model parameters and average partial effects have normal distributions when the two dimensions of the panel grow large but may suffer from incidental parameter bias. Additionally, the study shows how factor structures can capture important features of network data, such as reciprocity, degree heterogeneity, homophily in latent variables, and clustering. The study provides an empirical example using a Poisson model with multiple factors to estimate a gravity equation of international trade between countries.

title: Probe-assisted spin manipulation in one-dimensional quantum dots
Abstract: This study investigates a spin structure in a one-dimensional quantum dot with zero total spin subjected to a charged scanning probe microscope tip in a weak magnetic field. The evolution of the spin structure with changing probe position reveals the potential for manipulating the spin using a movable probe. Spin structures form in specific regions along the dot due to the Coulomb interaction of electrons redistributed between sections separated by the potential barrier created by the probe. The study identifies two main states: spin-polarized and non-polarized. The transition between these states involves spin precession governed by the Rashba spin-orbit interaction induced by the probe's electric field. The spin density changes significantly in the transition region while the charge distribution remains relatively unchanged.

title: Learning from Data with Heterogeneous Noise using SGD
Abstract: Learning from data of varying quality obtained from diverse sources poses a significant challenge. This paper focuses on a specific model where data is observed through heterogeneous noise, reflecting the quality of the data source. The study investigates how stochastic gradient algorithms can be employed for learning in this model. Two concrete examples motivate the study: learning with local differential privacy based on data from sources with differing privacy requirements and learning from data with labels of varying quality.  The main contribution of the paper is to identify how heterogeneous noise impacts performance. The authors demonstrate that the order in which to use datasets with heterogeneous noise in standard SGD depends on the learning rate. They propose a method for dynamically adjusting the learning rate as a function of heterogeneity and provide new regret bounds for this method in two cases of interest. Experiments on real data show that the proposed method outperforms using a single learning rate or only using the less noisy dataset when the noise level is low to moderate.

title: Untangling features in the primordial spectra
Abstract: This paper explores the possibility of features in the primordial power spectrum and bispectrum generated during a single field cosmic inflation. The former are typically produced by heavy fields, while the latter are associated with features in the inflaton potential. The study derives a relation between the shapes of features in the bispectrum and power spectrum, revealing distinct footprints that can be observationally tested. This analysis suggests that features in the primordial power spectrum and bispectrum provide valuable information about the dynamics of the early universe.

title: Local constants of motion imply information propagation
Abstract: Interacting quantum many-body systems generally exhibit thermalization, meaning that local expectation values eventually reach a stationary value similar to a thermal ensemble. This intuition is challenged by the phenomenon of many-body localization, which is characterized by the persistent growth of entanglement over time.  This study establishes a connection between quantum information theory and condensed matter concepts to understand many-body localization in the Heisenberg picture. The authors demonstrate that the existence of local constants of motion, a defining characteristic of many-body localization, together with a generic spectrum, is sufficient to rigorously prove information propagation in these systems.  This implies that information can be transmitted over arbitrary distances, as the impact of a local perturbation can be detected far away. The study performs a detailed perturbation analysis of quasi-local constants of motion and shows their application in constructing efficient spectral tensor networks. These findings offer a comprehensive and model-independent picture of information propagation in many-body localized systems.

title: Matrix product operators for symmetry-protected topological phases: Gauging and edge theories
Abstract: Projected entangled pair states (PEPS) offer a natural ansatz for describing the ground states of gapped, local Hamiltonians. This paper develops a framework to describe on-site symmetries, such as those observed in systems exhibiting symmetry-protected topological (SPT) quantum order, in terms of virtual symmetries of the local tensors. These symmetries are expressed as a set of matrix product operators (MPOs) labeled by distinct group elements. These MPOs describe the possibly anomalous symmetry of the edge theory, whose local degrees of freedom are explicitly identified in a PEPS. The study classifies SPT phases by analyzing the obstructions to continuously deforming one set of MPOs into another, confirming results obtained for fixed-point models.  The proposed formalism accommodates perturbations away from fixed-point models, enabling the study of phase transitions between different SPT phases.  The authors demonstrate that applying the quantum state gauging procedure to a SPT PEPS yields a PEPS with topological order determined by the initial symmetry MPOs. This MPO framework unifies various approaches to classifying SPT phases, including fixed-point models, boundary anomalies, and gauging symmetry, into a single problem of classifying inequivalent sets of matrix product operator symmetries.

title: Five steps in the evolution from protoplanetary to debris disk
Abstract: The evolution of protoplanetary disks around Herbig Ae stars eventually leads to the formation of debris disks composed of planetesimals, dust, gas, and potentially planets. This study utilizes the properties of 10-20 Myr A star debris disks to investigate the transition from protoplanetary disks to debris disks. The authors argue that the key distinction between these two classes lies in the presence of primordial gas in protoplanetary disks, which dominates the motion of small dust grains. Based on this argument, they propose an observational classification based on the dust spectrum, requiring fractional excesses less than 3 at 12 µm and less than 2000 at 70 µm for A star debris disks. The study also hypothesizes that the main sequence planet/planetesimal structures are already in place, albeit obscured, during the protoplanetary disk phase. The authors discuss five steps in the transition: (i) carving an inner hole to form a transition disk, (ii) depletion of mm-sized dust in the outer disk, (iii) final clearing of inner regions, (iv) disappearance of gas, and (v) formation of ring-like planetesimal structures.

title: Floquet systems coupled to particle reservoirs
Abstract: Open quantum systems driven by a periodic field can relax to effective statistical ensembles resembling their equilibrium counterparts. This study investigates a class of problems where a periodically driven quantum system exchanges both energy and particles with a thermal reservoir. The authors demonstrate that, even for non-interacting systems, effective equilibration to the grand canonical ensemble requires fine-tuning of the system-bath coupling and a simple driving protocol.  Analytical determination of the long-time steady state of the system reveals that effective thermalization occurs with fine tuning but not for general system-bath couplings. When the driven system does not thermalize, it supports a tunable persistent current in the steady state without external bias. The study computes this current analytically for two examples: a driven double quantum dot, where the current is interpreted as a DC electrical current, and driven Dirac fermions in graphene, where it is interpreted as a valley current.

title: Our Supermassive Black Hole Rivaled the Sun in the Ancient X-ray Sky
Abstract: Sagittarius A* (SgrA*), located at the Galactic Center 8 kpc from Earth, hosts the closest known supermassive black hole. While currently inactive, evidence suggests that SgrA* experienced a powerful outburst approximately six million years ago, reaching near-Eddington luminosity.  Motivated by the strong X-ray emission observed from supermassive black holes in other galaxies with similar masses and near-Eddington luminosities, this study calculates the X-ray luminosity of SgrA* during its outburst. Assuming that the outburst was triggered by gas accretion or the tidal disruption of a star, the authors show that these scenarios could have produced a hard X-ray flux (hν > 2 keV) on Earth comparable to that from the current quiescent sun.  The flux in the harder energy band (20 keV < hν < 100 keV) would have surpassed that of an X-class solar flare.  The study investigates the potential impact of this radiation on the solar system, highlighting the significant effects on gas giant atmospheres and the potential role in the evolution of primitive atmospheres on Earth.

title: The interplay of disk wind and dynamical ejecta in the aftermath of neutron star - black hole mergers

The authors employ a two-step approach using two- and three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations to examine the combined evolution of these components.  Starting from the output of a merger simulation, the authors identify each component based on its phase-space distribution and evolve the accretion disk in axisymmetry. The wind generated by the disk is then injected into a three-dimensional computational domain where the dynamical ejecta is evolved. The results indicate that the wind can suppress fallback accretion on timescales longer than 100 ms, although late-time disk accretion approaches a power-law time dependence (∝ t-2.2). This can power some late-time GRB engine activity, although the available energy is significantly reduced compared to traditional fallback models. Inclusion of radioactive heating due to the r-process does not significantly alter fallback accretion or the disk wind properties.

title: Bayesian detection of abnormal segments in multiple time series

title: High Frequency Content based Stimulus for Perceptual Sharpness Assessment in Natural Images
Abstract: We propose a blind approach to evaluate the perceptual sharpness present in a natural image. While the literature demonstrates various visual cues for detecting or assessing the presence or absence of sharpness, we focus on the significance of high-frequency content and local standard deviation as strong features for computing perceived sharpness in any natural image. We argue that these features offer a viable alternative to existing cues. Unsharp areas in a natural image tend to exhibit uniform intensity or lack sharp changes between regions. Sharp region transitions are caused by the presence of spatial high-frequency content. Therefore, in our proposed approach, we hypothesize that utilizing high-frequency content as the primary stimulus, perceived sharpness can be quantified in an image. When an image is convolved with a high-pass filter, higher values at any pixel location indicate the presence of high-frequency content at those locations. Considering these values as the stimulus, the exponent of the stimulus is weighted by the local standard deviation to account for the contribution of local contrast in forming the sharpness map. The sharpness map highlights relatively sharper regions in the image and is used to calculate the perceived sharpness score of the image. The proposed method offers the advantages of simplicity, relying on basic visual cues like high-frequency content and local contrast to arrive at the perceptual score, and requiring no training with images. The promise of the proposed method is demonstrated by its ability to compute perceived sharpness for within-image and across-image sharpness changes and for blind evaluation of perceptual degradation caused by blur. Experiments conducted on several databases demonstrate improved performance of the proposed method over existing state-of-the-art techniques.

The measurement was conducted in a ~1 µT vertical magnetic holding field, using the apparatus designed to search for a permanent electric dipole moment of the neutron at the Paul Scherrer Institute. By seeking tiny changes in the precession frequencies of neutron and mercury spins, the measurement investigates a potential coupling between freely precessing polarized neutron spins and unpolarized nucleons of the wall material. Such a frequency change could indicate a short-range spin-dependent interaction potentially mediated by axions or axion-like particles. The interaction strength is proportional to the CP-violating product of scalar and pseudoscalar coupling constants $g_Sg_P$. Our findings confirm limits from complementary experiments with spin-polarized nuclei in a model-independent way. Limits from other neutron experiments are improved by up to two orders of magnitude in the interaction range of $10^{-6} < \lambda < 10^{-4}$ m.

Yukawa couplings are expressed as sums over worldsheet instantons. Our results extend known expressions to a non-factorisable torus. As a side note, we also provide some details for the factorisable torus and non-coprime intersection numbers.

title: Localization-delocalization transition of dipolar bosons in a four-well potential

We analyze the ground state of dipolar bosons by varying the strength of the interaction between particles in next-nearest-neighbor wells. This analysis is performed both numerically and analytically by reformulating the dipolar-boson model within the continuous variable picture used in [Phys. Rev. A {\\bf 84}, 061601(R) (2011)]. Utilizing this approach, we obtain an effective description of the transition mechanism and demonstrate that when the next-nearest-neighbor interaction surpasses a specific value of the on-site interaction, the ground state undergoes a change from the uniform state (delocalization regime) to a macroscopic two-pulse state, with strongly localized bosons (localization regime). These predictions are corroborated by the results obtained by numerically diagonalizing the four-site BH Hamiltonian.

title: Transition-Metal Substitutions in Iron Chalcogenides

The Hall coefficient $R_H$, positive for $y$ = 0, remains positive at high temperatures for all $y$. However, it changes sign to negative at low $T$ for $y > 0.135$ (Co) and $y > 0.06$ (Ni). Analysis based on a two-band model suggests that at high $T$, residual hole pockets persist despite doping, but holes become localized upon lowering $T$, making the effect of electron doping on transport evident. The suppression of $T_c$ by Co impurity is linked to electron doping, while in the case of Ni impurity, strong electron localization likely contributes to the rapid decrease in $T_c$.

As the quadratic running of the Higgs mass parameter leads to an additive renormalization (distinct from the logarithmic running with multiplicative renormalization), the symmetry breaking occurs when the sliding energy scale $\mu$ moves from $M_c$ down to a transition scale $\mu = \Lambda_{EW}$, where the additive renormalized Higgs mass parameter $m^2_H(M_c/\mu)$ changes sign. title: The Hele-Shaw model for the phase field method and the vortex sheet approach
Abstract: Various thermodynamic phenomena arise with changes in pressure, temperature, and volume. While we can manipulate these parameters, the underlying constraints remain fixed, necessitating the study of thermodynamics alongside physical properties in diverse contexts. Hele-Shaw flow, a classic problem in chemical engineering, exemplifies this interplay.  The Stokes flow, a simplified version of the Navier-Stokes equations, is often described using Darcy's law. This law originates from the Stokes equations, highlighting the fundamental interconnectedness of these concepts. Our research aims to elucidate the connection between the phase field method and the vortex sheet approach in the context of the Hele-Shaw model.

title: Appropriate Causal Models and the Stability of Causation
Abstract: Causal models, defined using structural equations, provide a powerful means for representing knowledge regarding causality. However, several authors have presented examples suggesting that the Halpern-Pearl (HP) definition of causality yields intuitively unreasonable answers. This study demonstrates that for each of these examples, two stories consistent with the description can be constructed, leading to differing intuitions about causality. By introducing additional variables, these stories can be disambiguated. Furthermore, in the resulting causal models, the HP definition of causality produces the intuitively correct answer. It is also shown that a modification to the original HP definition, proposed to address an example by Hopkins and Pearl, may not be necessary when additional variables are considered.  Given the significant impact of adding extra variables, there is a concern that the concept of causality might be unstable. Can adding extra variables in a "conservative" way (maintaining all relationships between variables in the original model) cause the answer to the question "Is X=x a cause of Y=y" to fluctuate between "yes" and "no"? This study shows that such alternation can occur infinitely often, but it cannot occur if normality is taken into account. Under suitable normality assumptions, adding an extra variable can change the answer from "yes" to "no", but it cannot be changed back to "yes" after that.

title: An integrated assessment of the impact of precipitation and groundwater on vegetation growth in arid and semiarid areas

The framework combines remote sensing technology, vadose zone water flow modeling, and field data analysis. Vegetation growth is quantified using remote sensing data through the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and simulated plant water uptake rates. Pearson correlation equations are used to analyze the relationships between precipitation, groundwater depth, and NDVI. The findings provide insights into the interplay between precipitation and groundwater and their contributions to vegetation growth. Strong correlations between groundwater depth, plant water uptake, and NDVI are observed in parts of the study area during a ten-year drought period. Numerical modeling results indicate an increased correlation between groundwater depth and vegetation growth, demonstrating that groundwater plays a significant role in maintaining effective soil moisture for vegetation growth during extended drought periods. Therefore, a decline in the groundwater table could pose a serious threat to vegetation survival during prolonged droughts.

title: Deconstruction, Holography and Emergent Supersymmetry

Moreover, dumbbell structures are observed not only on single-layer, monatomic honeycomb structures but also on their compounds like SiC and SiGe. title: Spiral arms in scattered light images of protoplanetary discs: Are they the signposts of planets?

H-band scattered light images are then calculated using a 3D continuum radiative transfer code to study the effect of surface density and pressure scale height perturbation on the detectability of the spirals.  The findings indicate that a relative change of about 3.5 in the surface density is required for the spirals to be detected with current telescopes in the near-infrared for sources at the distance of typical star-forming regions (140pc). This value is eight times higher than what is observed in hydrodynamic simulations. The study also finds that a relative change of only 0.2 in the pressure scale height is sufficient to create detectable signatures under the same conditions. Therefore, this study suggests that the spiral arms observed to date in protoplanetary discs are likely the result of changes in the vertical structure of the disc (e.g., pressure scale height perturbation) rather than surface density perturbations.

The calculations also confirm that the half-filled Mn $t_{2g}$ orbitals give rise to the antiferromagnetic Mott phase. This magnetic ordering leads to changes in ionic polar displacement and, consequently, to electronic polarization.  Furthermore, for a fixed ionic displacement, a reduction in the electronic contribution due to partial magnetic polarization of the Mn e$_g$ orbitals is observed. The reduction of polarization due to ionic displacement dominates over the additional electronic part, resulting in a negative net magneto-electric coupling.

title: Detecting the Escherichia coli metabolic backbone
Abstract: The heterogeneity of reaction fluxes present within a metabolic network in a single flux state can be exploited to construct the so-called backbone, a reduced version of metabolism. This makes it a valuable tool for extracting primary metabolic routes. This study unveils the metabolic backbone of Escherichia coli using computationally predicted fluxes that maximize the growth rate in glucose minimal medium and compares it to the backbone of Mycoplasma pneumoniae, a simpler organism.  The central core in both backbones is primarily composed of reactions in ancient pathways that still play a key role in energy metabolism.  In E. coli, the analysis of the backbone reveals that the synthesis of nucleotides and the metabolism of lipids form smaller cores that critically rely on energy metabolism, but not vice versa.  Analyzing the backbone's dependence on media composition leads to the identification of pathways sensitive to environmental changes. Therefore, the metabolic backbone of an organism serves as a useful tool for simultaneously tracing its evolutionary and adaptive fingerprints.

title: Expected geoneutrino signal at JUNO

As relative helicity approaches unity, the spectral slope tends towards -3/2. The paper demonstrates that this energy buildup is caused by an inverse cascade of magnetic energy related to magnetic helicity. This negative energy flux is solely attributed to magnetic-to-magnetic energy transfer, which disappears in the non-helical limit. In the context of astrophysical dynamos, these findings suggest that a large-scale dynamo can be influenced by magnetic helicity generated at small scales. Importantly, kinetic helicity does not participate in this process. A notable discovery is that an inverse cascade of magnetic energy can be driven by a small-scale source of magnetic helicity fluctuations without a mean injection of magnetic helicity.

Abstract: The Neyman-Fisher controversy, examined here, originated with Jerzy Neyman's 1935 presentation of "Statistical Problems in Agricultural Experimentation" to the Royal Statistical Society. title: Bayesian nonparametric models for spatially indexed data of mixed type
Abstract: This research develops Bayesian nonparametric models for spatially indexed data of mixed types. The work is motivated by challenges encountered in environmental epidemiology, where the presence of numerous confounding variables exhibiting complex interactions and high correlations complicates the estimation and understanding of risk factor effects on health outcomes. The adopted modeling approach assumes that responses and confounding variables are manifestations of continuous latent variables and uses multivariate Gaussians to jointly model them. Responses and confounding variables are not treated equally, as relevant parameters of the distributions of the responses only are modeled in terms of explanatory variables or risk factors. Spatial dependence is introduced by allowing the weights of the nonparametric process priors to be location-specific, obtained as probit transformations of Gaussian Markov random fields. Confounding variables and spatial configuration play similar roles in the model, influencing only the allocation probabilities of the areas into the mixture components. This allows for flexible adjustment of the effects of observed confounders while accounting for the possibility of residual spatial structure, potentially due to unmeasured or undiscovered spatially varying factors. The model's aspects are illustrated through simulation studies and an application to a real dataset.

Abstract: The effects of inbreeding on human health are heavily influenced by the number and severity of recessive, deleterious mutations carried by individuals. Comparing these findings to existing estimates of the deleterious effects of all recessive alleles suggests that a significant proportion of the burden of autosomal, recessive variants is due to single mutations causing death between birth and reproductive age. Furthermore, comparison to estimates from other eukaryotes reveals a surprising consistency in the average number of recessive lethal mutations across organisms with diverse genome sizes.

Displacements serve as a strong indicator of tie-strength and dominance. To quantify the directionality of interactions during these events, histograms of the dot products of motion orientation and relative position are constructed. title: Physiological Control of Human Heart Rate and Oxygen Consumption during Rhythmic Exercises
Abstract: Physical exercise offers significant benefits for improving human health and quality of life by enhancing cardiovascular and respiratory system function. However, controlling workload, such as the frequency of body movements, within an individual's capabilities is crucial for maximizing exercise efficiency. Workload is typically represented by heart rate (HR) and oxygen consumption (VO2). This research focuses on controlling HR and VO2 through manipulation of exercise rate (ER), the workload associated with a specific body movement. The first part of the paper addresses the modeling and control of HR during rhythmic exercise. A novel feature of the developed system is the control of HR through ER manipulation. The relationship between ER and HR is modeled using a simple autoregressive model with unknown parameters. These parameters are estimated using a Kalman filter, and an indirect adaptive H1 controller is designed. The system's performance is validated on six subjects during rowing and cycling exercise. The results demonstrate the ability of the designed control system to regulate HR to a predefined profile.  The second part of the paper focuses on estimating VO2 during rhythmic exercise, where direct measurement is not feasible. Non-invasive sensors are used to measure HR, RespR, and ER to estimate VO2. The developed approach for cycling and rowing exercise predicts the percentage change in maximum VO2 from resting to exercising phases using a Hammerstein model. Results indicate improved quality of fit as the exercise intensity increases.

title: Evaluation of Image Segmentation and Filtering With ANN in the Papaya Leaf
Abstract: Precision agriculture currently lacks affordable technologies.  The refinement of production systems offers significant advantages to producers, and image-based monitoring presents a cost-effective methodology. Macronutrient monitoring is crucial for determining plant health and vulnerability at specific growth stages.  This paper analyzes a computational intelligence-based method for image segmentation in identifying symptoms of plant nutrient deficiency. Artificial neural networks are evaluated for image segmentation and filtering, with various parameter variations and impulsive noise levels considered. The study achieves satisfactory results using artificial neural networks for segmentation, even with high noise levels.

title: Predictive Overlapping Co-Clustering
Abstract: Co-clustering has gained prominence as a data mining tool for analyzing data in two dimensions. It offers advantages over traditional one-dimensional clustering, such as identifying highly correlated subgroups of rows and columns. One underappreciated benefit of co-clustering is its ability to extract meaningful knowledge for various knowledge extraction purposes. For instance, building accurate predictive models with high-dimensional data and heterogeneous populations is challenging. Co-clusters extracted from such data, exhibiting similar patterns in both dimensions, can be used to construct more precise predictive models. Applications such as identifying patient-disease cohorts in healthcare analysis, user-genre groups in recommendation systems, and community detection problems can benefit from co-clustering techniques that leverage the data's predictive power to generate co-clusters for enhanced data analysis. This paper introduces the concept of Predictive Overlapping Co-Clustering (POCC) as an optimization problem to achieve more effective and improved predictive analysis. The POCC algorithm generates optimal co-clusters by maximizing their predictive power while adhering to constraints on the number of row and column clusters. Precision, recall, and F-measure are employed as evaluation metrics for the resulting co-clusters. The performance of POCC is compared to two established techniques, K-means and Spectral co-clustering, using four real datasets: Leukemia, Internet-Ads, Ovarian cancer, and MovieLens. The findings demonstrate the effectiveness and practical utility of the POCC algorithm.

title: Predicting patient risk of readmission with frailty models in the Department of Veteran Affairs
Abstract: Reducing preventable readmissions has been identified as a critical factor in lowering Medicare costs and enhancing the quality of care provided by hospitals. Previous research conducted by medical professionals suggests that preventable readmissions are caused by factors such as flawed patient discharge processes, insufficient post-discharge follow-ups, and patient non-compliance with discharge and follow-up instructions. Additionally, the risk of preventable readmission may be associated with certain patient characteristics, such as age, health condition, diagnosis, and even treatment specialty. This study develops a risk prediction model based on a hierarchical nonlinear mixed-effect framework to extract significant prognostic factors associated with patient risk of 30-day readmission, using both general demographic information and individual past readmission records. The model's effectiveness is validated using a real dataset from four VA facilities in Michigan. By simultaneously explaining both patient and population-based variations in the readmission process, this accurate model can be used to identify patients with a high likelihood of discharge non-compliance, enabling targeted post-care actions to be implemented to reduce further rehospitalization.

title: A multivariate hierarchical Bayesian framework for healthcare predictions with application to medical home study in the Department of Veteran Affairs
Abstract: The patient-centered medical home (PCMH) model has emerged as a popular approach to deliver improved care to patients. Current research suggests that the key to the model's success lies in achieving a balance between healthcare supply and demand. Without such a balance, issues such as excessive under and over-utilization of physicians, long waiting times for treatment, and non-continuity of care will negate many advantages of the medical home strategy. To address this, understanding both supply and demand within the healthcare system is essential. While healthcare supply can be readily calculated based on headcounts and available professional hours, healthcare demand is more complex and influenced by various healthcare, diagnostic, and demographic factors. This paper extends the hierarchical generalized linear model to incorporate multivariate responses, developing a clinical workload prediction model for care portfolio demands within a Bayesian framework. Analyses of recent data from the Veteran Health Administration demonstrate that the prediction model performs well with clinical data.

title: Epidemiological consequences of an ineffective Bordetella pertussis vaccine
Abstract: The recent rise in Bordetella pertussis incidence (whooping cough) poses a challenge to global health. Recent studies have questioned the effectiveness of acellular B. pertussis vaccination in reducing transmission. This study examines the epidemiological consequences of an ineffective B. pertussis vaccine. Using a dynamic transmission model, the study found that: 1) an ineffective vaccine can explain the observed increase in B. pertussis incidence, 2) asymptomatic infections can bias surveillance and hinder situational awareness of B. pertussis, and 3) vaccinating individuals in close contact with infants too young to receive vaccine ("cocooning" unvaccinated children) may be ineffective. These findings have significant implications for B. pertussis vaccination policy, suggesting a complex picture for achieving herd immunity and potential B. pertussis eradication.

title: An analytics approach to designing patient centered medical homes
Abstract: The patient-centered medical home (PCMH) model has become a popular team-based approach aimed at providing streamlined care to patients. This paper extends the hierarchical generalized linear model to include multivariate responses, developing a clinical workload prediction model for care portfolio demands within a Bayesian framework. The model accommodates heterogeneous variances and unstructured covariance matrices for nested random effects arising from complex hierarchical care systems. The paper demonstrates that using a multivariate approach significantly enhances the precision of workload predictions at both primary and non-primary care levels. It also shows that care demands are influenced not only by patient demographics but also by utilization factors such as length of stay. Analyses of recent data from the Veteran Health Administration further indicate that risk adjustment for patient health conditions can substantially improve the model's predictive power.

title: Mobile GIS and Open Source Platform Based on Android: Technology for System Pregnant Women
Abstract: According to World Health Organization statistics, approximately 287,000 women die annually, primarily during and following pregnancy and childbirth, primarily in Africa and South Asia. This paper proposes a system for serving pregnant women using open-source Android technology. The proposed system leverages mobile GIS to identify the nearest care center or hospital maternity on Google Maps for a pregnant woman who has completed online registration by sending an SMS via the GPRS network (or internet). The SMS includes her name, phone number, region (longitude and latitude), and other required information. The server saves this data in its database, locates the nearest care center, and calls the pregnant woman for an initial review. The system allows pregnant women to send help requests in emergency situations from their location (home, market, etc.) via an SMS button. The request includes the woman's ID and coordinates (longitude and latitude) transmitted via the GPRS network. The server locates the woman on Google Maps, retrieves her information from the database, and sends assistance to her location while simultaneously notifying the nearest hospital. The server also sends an SMS via IP to inform her husband and the hospital doctors. The proposed system for pregnant women has proven to be more cost-effective than other systems due to its reliance on economic modes (SMS) and its flexible (open-source platform) and rapid (mobile GIS based on Android) features. It offers local registration, emergency assistance, review date modifications, and various types of pregnancy-related advice.

title: A predictive analytics approach to reducing avoidable hospital readmission
Abstract: Hospital readmission has become a crucial metric of quality and cost in healthcare. Medicare estimates that nearly $17 billion is spent on the 20% of patients who are readmitted within 30 days of discharge. While interventions like transition care management and discharge reengineering have been implemented in recent years, their effectiveness and sustainability hinge on their ability to accurately identify and target high-risk patients. Existing risk prediction models often fail to achieve acceptable accuracy, neglect patient readmission history and the impact of attribute changes over time, and do not discriminate between planned and unnecessary readmissions. To address these shortcomings, this paper develops a new readmission metric based on administrative data to distinguish potentially avoidable readmissions from other types. A tree-based classification method is proposed to estimate the predicted probability of readmission, incorporating patient readmission history and risk factor changes over time. The methods are validated using 2011-12 Veterans Health Administration data from inpatients hospitalized for heart failure, acute myocardial infarction, pneumonia, or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in Michigan. Results demonstrate improved discrimination power compared to existing models (c-statistics > 80%) and good calibration.

title: Data Management Challenges in Paediatric Information Systems
Abstract: The integration and exploitation of heterogeneous biomedical information is crucial for enhancing clinical practice, medical research, and personalized healthcare across the European Union. The integration of paediatric information is particularly challenging, as patient physiology changes with growth, and different health aspects are regularly monitored over extended periods. Paediatricians require access to heterogeneous datasets, often collected in various locations using different apparatus and over extended timeframes. Using a Grid platform originally developed for physics at CERN and a novel integrated semantic data model, the Health-e-Child project has developed an integrated healthcare platform for European paediatrics, enabling seamless integration of traditional and emerging biomedical data sources. The project's long-term goal was to provide unrestricted access to universal biomedical knowledge repositories for personalized and preventive healthcare, large-scale information-based biomedical research and training, and informed policy making. The project established a Grid-enabled European network of leading clinical centers capable of sharing and annotating paediatric data, validating systems clinically, and disseminating clinical excellence across Europe by implementing new technologies, clinical workflows, and standards. The Health-e-Child project highlights the data management challenges facing the future of European paediatric healthcare and is the subject of this chapter.

title: Developing classification indices for Chinese pulse diagnosis
Abstract: This study aimed to develop classification criteria for Chinese pulse diagnosis and objectify this ancient diagnostic technique. Chinese pulse curves were treated as wave signals, and multidimensional variable analysis was performed to identify the best curve fit between recorded pulse waveforms and collective Gamma density functions. The study found that Chinese pulses can be quantitatively recognized using four newly developed classification indices: wavelength, relative phase difference, rate parameter, and peak ratio. This new quantitative classification not only reduces the dependence of pulse diagnosis on Chinese physician experience but also enables more precise interpretation of pathological wrist-pulse waveforms. Traditionally, Chinese physicians use fingertips to feel patients' wrist pulses to assess their health conditions. The qualitative theory of Chinese pulse diagnosis is based on the experience of Chinese physicians over thousands of years. However, no quantitative theories exist to relate these diverse wrist-pulse waveforms to patients' health conditions. This paper introduces new quantified classification indices to objectively interpret Chinese pulse waveform patterns.

title: Growth rates of modern science: A bibliometric analysis based on the number of publications and cited references
Abstract: Many studies in information science have explored the growth of science. This study re-examines the question of scientific growth by using current data up to publication year 2012 and analyzing it across all disciplines, as well as separately for the natural sciences and the medical and health sciences. The data was analyzed using segmented regression analysis, a sophisticated statistical technique capable of identifying specific segments with similar growth rates throughout scientific history. The study is based on two sets of bibliometric data: (1) the number of publications held as source items in the Web of Science (WoS, Thomson Reuters) per publication year and (2) the number of cited references in the publications of the source items per cited reference year. The study examined the rate at which science has grown since the mid-1600s. The analysis of cited references identified three growth phases in the development of science, each leading to a tripling of growth rates compared to the previous phase: from less than 1% up to the middle of the 18th century, to 2 to 3% up to the period between the two world wars, and 8 to 9% to 2012.

title: A Comparative Study of Machine Learning Methods for Verbal Autopsy Text Classification
Abstract: A Verbal Autopsy is a record of an interview about the circumstances of an uncertified death. The aim is to identify suitable approaches for classifying Verbal Autopsy text. The study demonstrates that normalized term frequency and standard TF-IDF achieve comparable performance across a range of classifiers. Results also show that Support Vector Machine outperforms other classification algorithms used in this research. Finally, the study demonstrates the effectiveness of employing a "locally-semi-supervised" feature reduction strategy to improve performance accuracy.

title: Construction d'une plate-forme intégrée pour la cartographie de l'exposition des populations aux substances chimiques de l'environnement
Abstract: Analyzing the link between the environment and health has become a major public health concern, as evidenced by the development of two national environmental health plans. To effectively address this concern, policymakers require tools to identify geographic areas where overexposure to toxic agents might occur. The SIGFRIED 1 project aims to create a spatial modeling platform to evaluate the exposure of the French population to chemical substances and identify the factors driving this exposure. Probabilistic multimedia modeling is used to assess exposure. The epistemological challenges associated with the absence of data are mitigated through the implementation of tools utilizing spatial analysis techniques. An example is provided for the Nord-Pas-de-Calais and Picardie regions, focusing on exposure to cadmium, nickel, and lead. Exposure calculations are conducted over a period of 70 years based on data collected around 2004 for a grid of 1 km squares. For example, in the Nord-Pas-de-Calais region, indicators define two areas for cadmium and three for lead. These areas are linked to the region's industrial history, including the mining basin, metallurgy activities, and the Lille metropolitan area. The contribution of different exposure pathways varies significantly from one pollutant to another. The resulting exposure maps identify the geographic areas where environmental field studies should be prioritized. The constructed GIS platform serves as a foundation for integrating source emission data, environmental exposure measurements, and ultimately health and socioeconomic data.

title: Graph-based Multivariate Conditional Autoregressive Models
Abstract: The conditional autoregressive model is a commonly used statistical model for areal data arising from fields such as epidemiology, socioeconomics, or ecology. Various multivariate conditional autoregressive models have been extensively studied, with evidence suggesting that extending from the univariate to the multivariate case is not trivial. This complexity stems from various aspects, including model validity, interpretability, flexibility, and computational feasibility. This paper approaches multivariate modeling from an element-based perspective instead of the traditional vector-based perspective. It focuses on the joint adjacency structure of elements and discusses graphical structures for both spatial and non-spatial domains. The paper assumes that the graph for the spatial domain is generally known and fixed, while the graph for the non-spatial domain may be unknown and random. It proposes a general specification for multivariate conditional modeling and then explores three special cases linked to well-known models in the literature. Bayesian inference for parameter and graph learning is provided for these cases, concluding with an illustration using public health data.

title: Three-step estimation of latent Markov models with covariates
Abstract: This paper proposes a modified version of the three-step estimation method for the latent class model with covariates, which can be used to estimate latent Markov models for longitudinal data. The proposed three-step estimation approach involves a preliminary clustering of sample units based solely on time-specific responses. This method provides a useful estimation tool when a large number of response variables are observed at each time point. In such contexts, full maximum likelihood estimation, typically based on the Expectation-Maximization algorithm, can have drawbacks, primarily due to the presence of numerous local maxima of the model likelihood. Moreover, the EM algorithm may be slow to converge and unstable with complex LM models. This paper proves the consistency of the proposed three-step estimator as the number of response variables tends to infinity. It also presents the results of a simulation study evaluating the performance of the proposed alternative approach compared to the full likelihood method. Finally, the paper illustrates an application using a real dataset on the health status of elderly people residing in Italian nursing homes.

title: Uniqueness and stability result for Cauchy's equation of motion for a certain class of hyperelastic materials
Abstract: This paper examines Cauchy's equation of motion for hyperelastic materials. The solution to this nonlinear initial-boundary value problem is the vector field that describes the displacement experienced by a particle of this material when subjected to stress and external forces. This equation is of paramount importance when investigating the behavior of elastic, anisotropic composites and for detecting defects in such materials using boundary measurements. As a result, understanding unique solvability and continuous dependence on initial values holds significant interest in materials research and structural health monitoring. This article presents such a result, assuming reasonable smoothness conditions for the displacement field and the boundary of the domain, for a specific class of hyperelastic materials where the first Piola-Kirchhoff tensor is expressed as a conic combination of finitely many given tensors.

title: Identifying Keystone Species in the Human Gut Microbiome from Metagenomic Timeseries using Sparse Linear Regression
Abstract: Human-associated microbial communities exert a significant influence on human health and disease. Modern metagenomic sequencing methods allow researchers to track the relative abundance of microbes within a community over time. These microbial communities exhibit complex ecological dynamics, and a central goal of microbial ecology is to infer species interactions from sequencing data. Any algorithm designed to infer species interactions must overcome three challenges: 1) correlation between the abundances of two species does not imply that those species are interacting, 2) the sum constraint on relative abundances obtained from metagenomic studies makes it difficult to infer parameters in timeseries models, and 3) errors due to experimental uncertainty, mis-assignment of sequencing reads into operational taxonomic units, or biases in inferences of species interactions. This paper introduces LIMITS (Learning Interactions from MIcrobial Time Series), an approach that addresses these challenges. LIMITS employs sparse linear regression with bootstrap aggregation to infer a discrete-time Lotka-Volterra model for microbial dynamics. Testing LIMITS on synthetic data demonstrated its ability to reliably infer the topology of inter-species ecological interactions. The study then used LIMITS to characterize species interactions in the gut microbiomes of two individuals, finding that interaction networks varied significantly between individuals. Furthermore, it found that the interaction networks of these two individuals were dominated by distinct "keystone species" - Bacteroides fragilis and Bacteroides stercosis - which have a disproportionate influence on the structure of the gut microbiome despite being present only in moderate abundance. Based on these results, the study hypothesizes that the abundances of certain keystone species may be responsible for individuality in the human gut microbiome. |||

title: Cytoplasmic nanojunctions between lysosomes and sarcoplasmic reticulum are required for specific calcium signaling
Abstract: This study demonstrates how nanojunctions between lysosomes and sarcoplasmic reticulum (L-SR junctions) facilitate coupling lysosomal activation to regenerative calcium (Ca2+) waves. The study utilizes transmission electron microscopy to provide detailed ultrastructural characterization of L-SR junctions, revealing their prominent features and estimating their dimensions. A quantitative model of the L-SR junction is developed using these measurements and kinetic data. Simulations demonstrate that NAADP-dependent junctional Ca2+ transients can reach the threshold for CICR via RyR3. Correlation analysis suggests that trigger zones containing 60-100 junctions are needed for a significant signal. Increasing the junctional width above 50 nm reduces the magnitude of junctional [Ca2+], hindering CICR. Therefore, L-SR junctions are essential for efficient Ca2+ signal coupling and potentially contribute to cellular function in health and disease.

title: Instrumental Variables Estimation with Some Invalid Instruments and its Application to Mendelian Randomization
Abstract: Instrumental variables are widely used for estimating causal effects between exposure and outcome. Conventional methods require complete knowledge of all instruments' validity, meaning they must not have a direct effect on the outcome or be related to unmeasured confounders. This paper proposes a method for estimating causal effects when complete knowledge of instrument validity is absent. The method identifies and estimates causal effects as long as less than 50% of instruments are invalid, regardless of which ones. It introduces conditions for identification even when this threshold is violated. A penalized L1 estimation method, sisVIVE, is developed to estimate the causal effect without knowing which instruments are valid, with theoretical performance guarantees. The method is demonstrated using simulated data and a real Mendelian randomization study on the effect of body mass index on health-related quality of life. An R package, sisVIVE, is available online.

The paper examines factors influencing the power of visual inference, including observer demographics, visual skills, experience, and the position of the data plot in the lineup.  Results from multiple visual inference studies suggest that individual skills play a significant role, while demographics have minimal impact. title: Complexity Measures and Concept Learning
Abstract: The nature of concept learning is a fundamental question in cognitive science. Theories must account for the varying difficulty encountered by supervised learners when acquiring different concepts. For a standard set of six category types, two distinct orderings of classification difficulty have been observed. One ordering, referred to as paradigm-specific, arises when adult human learners classify objects based on easily distinguishable characteristics, such as size, shape, and shading. The general order occurs in all other known cases: when adult humans classify objects using less readily distinguished characteristics (e.g., brightness, saturation, hue); for children and monkeys; and when categorization difficulty is extrapolated from identification learning errors. The paradigm-specific order was found to be mathematically predictable by measuring the logical complexity of tasks, i.e., the conciseness with which the solution can be represented by logical rules. However, logical complexity explains only the paradigm-specific order, not the general order. This work proposes a new difficulty measurement, information complexity, which calculates the amount of uncertainty remaining when a subset of the dimensions are specified. This measurement is based on Shannon entropy. It is shown that when the metric extracts minimal uncertainties, this new measurement predicts the paradigm-specific order for the canonical six category types, and when the metric extracts average uncertainties, it predicts the general order. Furthermore, for learning category types beyond the canonical six, the minimal-uncertainty formulation accurately predicts the paradigm-specific order as well as or better than existing metrics (Boolean complexity and GIST) in most cases.

title: Stopping the SuperSpreader Epidemic, Part III: Prediction
Abstract: Previous papers introduced SuperSpreader (SS) epidemic models, explored theoretical prevention issues, and fit models to data from the MERS epidemic (concluding that a pandemic is likely). This paper focuses on prediction: whether a rigorous decision point – declaring an imminent pandemic – can be defined in a superspreader-driven outbreak. The analysis shows that all prediction biases contribute to generating false negatives (i.e., dismissing the risk of a pandemic when it is impending or has already begun). However, these statistical challenges can be addressed by improved data collection and known techniques that reduce bias. A unique aspect of SS epidemics is that prediction can sometimes be made long before the actual pandemic onset, providing lead time to alert medical professionals and the public. Modeling is valuable for overcoming a false sense of security arising from the extended "kindling times" characteristic of SS epidemics, certain political/psychological factors, and enhancing the public health response.

title: Conjunction and Negation of Natural Concepts: A Quantum-theoretic Modeling
Abstract: Two experiments were conducted to investigate the impact of negation on the combination of natural concepts. In the first experiment, membership weights were tested for a list of exemplars with respect to two concepts, e.g., {\\it Fruits} and {\\it Vegetables}, and their conjunction {\\it Fruits And Vegetables}. The second experiment repeated the testing process for the same exemplars and concepts, but with the second concept negated, e.g., {\\it Fruits} and {\\it Not Vegetables}, and their conjunction {\\it Fruits And Not Vegetables}. The collected data support existing findings on conceptual combination, demonstrating significant deviations from predictions based on classical (fuzzy set) logic and probability theory. Specifically, the data exhibit conceptual vagueness, graded membership, overextension, and double overextension of membership weights with respect to the given conjunctions. The quantum probability model in Fock space, previously developed to model Hampton's data on concept conjunction (Hampton, 1988a) and disjunction (Hampton, 1988b), accurately aligns with the collected data. This quantum-theoretic modeling allows for the description of these non-classical effects in terms of genuine quantum effects, namely 'contextuality', 'superposition', 'interference', and 'emergence'. The obtained results confirm and strengthen the analysis in Aerts (2009a) and Sozzo (2014) regarding the identification of quantum aspects in experiments on conceptual vagueness. These findings contribute to the general research on identifying quantum structures in cognitive and decision processes.

title: Individual gain and engagement with mathematical understanding
Abstract: This study examines a measure of individual student gain by preservice elementary teachers, drawing inspiration from Richard Hake's use of mean gain in analyzing reform classes in undergraduate physics. The gain statistic assesses the extent to which individual students improve their test scores from the initial to the final test, expressed as a proportion of the potential increase for each student. The written work in mathematics classes of preservice elementary teachers with very high gain and those with very low gain was analyzed, revealing distinct psychological attitudes and dispositions towards learning mathematics in these two groups. The study found a statistically significant, albeit small, increase in average gain when course goals focused on patterns, connections, and meaning-making in mathematics. Contrary to a common belief that students with low initial test scores will experience higher gains and students with high initial test scores will experience lower gains, this study demonstrates that this is not the case for a cohort of preservice elementary teachers.

title: 'A Vehicle of Symbols and Nothing More.' George Romanes, Theory of Mind, Information, and Samuel Butler
Abstract: Today's "theory of mind" (ToM) concept originates from nineteenth-century philosopher William Clifford's distinction between "objects" that are directly perceived and "ejects," such as the mind of another person, which are inferred from one's subjective knowledge of their own mind. A founder, with Charles Darwin, of comparative psychology, George Romanes, considered the minds of animals as ejects, an idea that could be generalized to "society as eject" and, ultimately, "the world as an eject" – mind in the universe. However, Romanes and Clifford only vaguely linked mind to the abstraction we call "information," which requires "a vehicle of symbols" – a material transporting medium. Samuel Butler, however, addressed both organic evolution and mind in the universe in informational terms, devoid of theological baggage. This perspective harmonizes with insights from modern DNA research, the relative immortality of "selfish" genes, and recent advancements in brain research.

The advantages and disadvantages of each method in relation to applications in psychology are discussed.

title: Big Data, Socio-Psychological Theory, Algorithmic Text Analysis and Predicting the Michigan Consumer Sentiment Index
Abstract: This article describes an exercise using Big Data to predict the Michigan Consumer Sentiment Index, a widely used indicator of consumer confidence in the US economy. The exercise is conducted from a purely ex ante perspective. Algorithmic text analysis of an archive of brokers' reports from June 2010 to June 2013 is employed, guided by the social-psychological theory of agent behavior, namely conviction narrative theory. One-month ahead forecasts generated using this method are compared over a 15-month period with consensus predictions from Wall Street economists. The forecasts derived from text analysis provide significantly more accurate predictions, correctly identifying the direction of change on 12 out of 15 occasions, compared to only 7 for consensus predictions. Notably, this approach maintains significant predictive power even over a four-month ahead horizon.

title: Objective Bayesian Comparison of Constrained Analysis of Variance Models
Abstract: In the social sciences, we often seek to compare models defined by parametric equality or inequality constraints. For example, when examining three group means $\\{ \\mu_1, \\mu_2, \\mu_3\\}$ through an analysis of variance (ANOVA), one model might specify that $\\mu_1<\\mu_2<\\mu_3$, while another might state that $\\{ \\mu_1=\\mu_3\\} <\\mu_2$, and a third model might suggest unrestricted means. This presents a challenging problem, involving both non-nested models and nested models of the same dimension. This paper adopts an objective Bayesian approach, deriving the posterior probability of each model under consideration. The method is based on the intrinsic prior methodology, with modifications to accommodate equality and inequality constraints. Focusing on normal ANOVA models, a comparative assessment through simulation studies demonstrates that correct model identification is achievable, even in scenarios where frequentist power is low. An application to real data from a psychological experiment is also presented.

title: Contextual Abductive Reasoning with Side-Effects
Abstract: The belief bias effect is a phenomenon where individuals mistakenly believe they are judging an argument based on reasoning while being influenced by their beliefs and prior knowledge. Evans, Barston, and Pollard conducted a psychological syllogistic reasoning task to demonstrate this effect. Participants were asked to accept or reject given syllogisms. This paper analyzes one specific case commonly perceived as believable but logically invalid. By incorporating abnormalities, abduction, and background knowledge, this case is adequately modeled under the weak completion semantics. The formalization highlights new questions regarding potential extensions in abductive reasoning. For example, observations and their explanations might include relevant prior abductive contextual information concerning side effects or leading to contestable or refutable side effects. A weaker notion indicates the support of relevant consequences by a prior abductive context. Another definition describes jointly supported relevant consequences, capturing the idea of two observations containing mutually supportive side effects. Motivated by and exemplified through the ongoing psychology application, various new general abductive context definitions are introduced and provided with declarative semantics for the first time, offering a broader scope of application. Inspection points, a concept introduced by Pereira and Pinto, allow for the syntactic expression of these definitions and their integration into an operational semantics.

title: Exchanging Conflict Resolution in an Adaptable Implementation of ACT-R
Abstract: In computational cognitive science, the cognitive architecture ACT-R is widely popular. It provides a model of cognition amenable to computer implementation, paving the way for computational psychology. While its underlying psychological theory has been investigated in numerous psychological experiments, ACT-R lacks a formal mathematical-computational definition of its core concepts. Despite the modularization of the canonical ACT-R implementation, its production rule system remains difficult to adapt and extend in key components, such as the conflict resolution mechanism (which determines which applicable rule to apply next). This work presents a concise ACT-R implementation based on Constraint Handling Rules, derived from a formalization in previous work. To demonstrate its adaptability, various conflict resolution mechanisms discussed in the ACT-R literature are implemented. This work presents the first implementation of one such mechanism. For the other mechanisms, an empirical evaluation is conducted to determine if the implementation matches the results of reference ACT-R implementations.

title: How to Ask for a Favor: A Case Study on the Success of Altruistic Requests
Abstract: Requests are central to many social media systems, including question-and-answer sites and online philanthropy communities. While the success of these requests is crucial for community success, the factors influencing community members to fulfill a request are largely unknown. The success of a request depends on factors such as the requester, their communication style, the timing of the request, and most importantly, the nature of the request, ranging from minor favors to substantial monetary donations. This study presents a case study of altruistic requests in an online community where all requests seek the same contribution without offering tangible rewards, enabling the disentanglement of the request itself from textual and social factors. Drawing on social psychology literature, high-level social features are extracted from text to operationalize social relationships between recipient and donor. These extracted relationships are shown to be predictive of success. Specifically, clear communication of need through narrative is essential, and linguistic indications of gratitude, evidentiality, generalized reciprocity, and the requester's high status further increase the likelihood of success. Building on this understanding, a model is developed to predict the success of unseen requests, significantly outperforming several baseline models. These findings are linked to research in psychology on helping behavior, providing a foundation for further analysis of success in social media systems.
